units.la: {N}ON est mihi propositum tempora vestra longo praeloquio morari. Neque opus est, ut de operis hujus argumento & meo scopo prolixe apud vos sermocinor, qui isthoc labore in praefatione ad lectorem defunctus sum. Inspiciendum, non legendum vobis offero hunc meum Anti-barbarum, vobis, inquam, qui ante annos LVII. Academiam eum in finem fundastis, ut foedum illud monstrum, Barbariem, quae immundo contactu & sacra & Profana foedaverat, propulsaretis. Ex eo sacrum illud bellum, propitio numine coeptum, feliciter gessistis, viros excellentissimos ex omnib. Europae angulis, ductando huic exercitui, luculentis stipendiis vocastis, & Christiano orbi fecistis testatum, tutandæ purioris religionis & conservandarum bonarum literarum studium inter principes vestras curas fuisse.
units.tr: It is not my intention to detain your time with a long preface. Nor is there any need for me to speak at length before you about the subject of this work and my aim in writing it, since I have already dealt with that task in the preface to the reader. I offer you this Anti-barbarus of mine to be looked at, not read. You are the ones who, fifty-seven years ago, founded the Academy for this purpose: to drive back that foul monster, Barbarism, which had defiled both sacred and profane things with its unclean touch. From that time you have successfully carried on that holy war, which was begun under the favour of heaven. You have summoned from every corner of Europe men of outstanding distinction to lead this army, with generous pay, and you have shown the Christian world that the defence of a purer religion and the cultivation of good letters have been among the chief concerns of your government.

units.la: Qui scholas illustres & Academias pacatis & florentibus rebus aperuêre, plurimi sunt. At, inter belli tubas, in maxima rerum vertigine, rebus propemodum defperatis, nondum formata Republica, Academias fundare, propria Batavorum & Frisiorum laus est. Ex eo unitæ provinciæ in florentissimam Remp. assurrexere, & ab una Academia majus sumsere incrementum, quam à legionibus aliquot robustissimis expectari potuisset. Hoc prævidebant, qui inter adversarios nostros [πρόσω ἢ ὀπίσω] videbant. Erant inter eos, queis ad præclari istius instituti famam
units.tr: Many have opened illustrious schools and academies in times of peace and prosperity. But to found academies amid the blasts of war, in the greatest upheaval of affairs, with things almost despaired of and the commonwealth not yet established, is the peculiar glory of the Batavians and the Frisians. From that time the united provinces have risen to a most flourishing commonwealth, and they have gained from a single Academy a greater increase than could have been expected from several strong legions. Those who saw "forwards or backwards" [πρόσω ἢ ὀπίσω] among our adversaries foresaw this. Among them were those for whom the fame of this distinguished institution

units.la: Neque n. poterant ignorare, ex istis seminariis bene ordinatis nunquam vel Ecclesiæ pios & eruditos Pastores, Reipublicæ cordatos & intelligentes gubernatores defore. Adhæc, ex historiis didicerant, nulla certiora indicia crescentis vel inclinantis reipublicæ esse, quam pietatis literarumque curam vel incuriam. Quo magis omnibus Scholarum illustrium & Academiarum Ephoris cavendum censeo, ne Academiæ, laxatis dissolutæ juventuti frænis, ruptisque licentiæ & ebrietatis aggeribus, in gymnasia & officinas nequitiæ vertantur. Illud enim audebo dicere & scio mihi subscripturos omnes pios & intelligentes, horrendas illas calamitates, quæ Germaniam nunc urgent, ab inordinatis Academiis magnam partem ortas esse. Sed non penetrabo altius in hoc pelagus. Causam unam dixi, cur hunc libellum VV.AA. inspiciendum offeram. Altera me privatim spectat. Quoties ego vel audio vel lego nomen vestri Lugduni, quod ego ἥλιον ἢ ὀφθαλμὸν καὶ ψυχὴν Belgii vocitare soleo, toties recordor jucundissimæ istius vitæ, quam inibi ante annos xiv. agitavi: simulque animum subit recordatio honestissimæ vocationis, qua ante biennium à VV. AA. ad Ebraeæ linguæ professionem, quam magnus ille Erpenius immaturo suo excessu vacivam fecerat, vocabar. Equidem, quinam potissimum me VV. AA. commendaverint, non ignoro. Attamen illud bona ipsorum pace dicere me cogit conscientia, illos plusculum amori & affectui dedisse. Ego enim praeter voluntatem bene de φιλεβεγίων juvenum, & quidem tironum, studiis merendi, nihil vobis repraesentassem. Fateor tamen, me, illorum judiciis corruptum, nec non loci amoenitate & splendore, Bibliothecae publicae & bibliopoliorum commoditate, amicorum denique, quos illic habeo plurimos, candore illectum, eo audentiae processisse, ut reverendo viro, & de Ecclesiis Belgicis, vestraque adeo Academia optime merito, D. Festo Hommio, SS. Th. Doctori &c. quem VV. AA. huc ablegaverant, operam meam addixerim, hac conditione, ab Illustribus Frisiae Ordinibus & nobilissimis Academiae patriae Curatoribus mei dimissionem posset impetrare. Quam ut obtineret, nihil ille intentatum reliquit. Quid Illustres Frisiae Ordines obtenderint, neque attinet hic dicere, neque vos, Illustrissimi & Nobilissimi Domini, ignoratis. Exinde vere nobilem, pium & reverendum virum, D. Constantinum l'Eml'Empereur de Oppyk, SS Th. Doctorem, meum à multis retro annis consecraneum & amicum conjunctissimum, virum orientalium literarum peritissimum, diligentissimum, & quod supra omnia ista pono, discip-linæ amantissimum, prudentissimo delectu vocastis. Quem ego virum juventuti vestræ ex animo gratulor. Deumque O.M. veneror, ut eum juxta cum reliquis Academiæ vestræ Professoribus, viris celeberrimis, in multos annos sospitet. Dixi alteram causam, cur hoc opusculum VV. AA. inscripserim. Volui enim hoc extare tanquam pignus & testimonium gratitudinis & observantiæ, quam VV. AA. pro tam honesto de me & studiis meis judicio debeo. Accipite ergo, Viri Illustres, hoc quicquid est opellæ. Utinam dicere possem, operi! Nam hoc VV. AA. debetur. Accipite hanc confessoriam, non liberatoriam tabellam. Tangite & tollite expositam hanc prolem, partum infirmum & informem, partem, inquam, primam mei Anti-barbari, quam veluti in gustum damus & emittimus, tanquam ad incerta itinerum exploranda. units.tr: Nor could they fail to know that from such well-ordered seminaries there would never be lacking pious and learned ministers for the Church, or wise and understanding governors for the commonwealth. Moreover, they had learned from history that there are no surer signs of a rising or declining commonwealth than the care or neglect of piety and letters. For this reason I think all the overseers of illustrious schools and academies should take care lest, when the reins are loosened for young people and the barriers of licence and drunkenness are broken, the academies turn into schools and workshops of wickedness. For I will venture to say, and I know that all the pious and understanding will agree with me, that those dreadful calamities which now press upon Germany have arisen in large part from disorderly academies. But I will not go deeper into this sea. I have given one reason why I offer this little book to your Lordships for examination. The other concerns me personally. Whenever I hear or read the name of your Leiden, which I am accustomed to call the sun, eye and soul [ἥλιον ἢ ὀφθαλμὸν καὶ ψυχὴν] of Belgium, I recall that most pleasant life which I lived there some fourteen years ago, and at the same time there comes to mind the memory of the most honourable call by which, two years ago, I was summoned by your Lordships to the professorship of the Hebrew language, which the great Erpenius had left vacant by his untimely death. Indeed, I do not ignore who it was that most of all recommended me to your Lordships. Yet with all due respect to them, my conscience compels me to say that they gave rather too much to affection and personal feeling. For apart from my willingness to serve the studies of the eager [φιλεβεγίων] young men, and of beginners in particular, I would have offered you nothing. I confess, however, that I was swayed by their judgments, and also drawn on by the pleasantness and splendour of the place, the convenience of the public library and the bookshops, and finally by the kindness of the many friends I have there. So far did I go in boldness that I pledged my service, on this condition, that I might obtain my release from the Illustrious Frisian Estates and the most noble curators of my native Academy, to the reverend man Dr. Festus Hommius, Doctor of Sacred Theology, who deserves very well of the Dutch churches and of your Academy, and whom your Lordships had sent here. To obtain this, he left nothing untried. What the Illustrious Frisian Estates put forward in reply, it is not necessary for me to say here, and you, Most Illustrious and Most Noble Lords, are not ignorant of it. Then you chose, by a most prudent selection, the truly noble, pious and reverend man Dr. Constantine l'Empereur de Oppyck, Doctor of Sacred Theology, my colleague and very close friend for many years, a man most skilled and diligent in oriental letters, and, above all else, a great lover of discipline. I heartily congratulate your young people on this man. And I pray to God Almighty that He may keep him safe for many years, together with the other most distinguished professors of your Academy. I have said the second reason why I have inscribed this little work to your Lordships. For I wished it to stand as a pledge and token of the gratitude and respect which I owe your Lordships for so honourable a judgment about me and my studies. Accept, then, Most Illustrious Sirs, whatever this little work is. Would that I could call it a work! For it is owed to your Lordships. Accept it as a tablet of confession, not of deliverance. Touch and take up this offspring put out before you, a weak and unformed child, I mean the first part of my Anti-barbarus, which I give and send out, as it were, as a taste, to explore the uncertain paths of the journey. If there are few enemies, I will confidently bring forward a second part into the field. But if there are many snares and ambushes, my mind is firmly set on not stepping out of the safe camp of silence. I will end with the prayer that God Almighty, by whose power and not by human help or protection your Commonwealth has stood until now, may deign to guide and rightly prosper all your counsels and deeds. I wrote this on the 20th of June, in the year of our Saviour 1628, at Franeker in Friesland.

units.tr: ON THE ANTI-BARBARUS of the most distinguished and eminent man, SIXTINUS AMAMA.

units.la: Mproba ma jorumqua nata est tempore primum., Babaries, nostro tempore pulsa fuit. Gracia nata fuit: -Latiæ crevere Camœnæ: Quisque sua Musas fovit & auxit ope. Nec summi procerum, nec Regum prona voluntas Defuit, ex illis pars quoque nostra fuit. Orta dies fuerat: sed qua, vix orta, repente Occidit, & noctem sentit adesse suam. Has tenebras inter dubiaque crepuscula lucis, Altera fax oritur, nec prius orta dies. Sol oritur, Sixtine, tuus, quo vindice rursus Barbaries cedit, qua reditura fuit. Nec tibi Phœbeam satis est decerpere laurum, Quam Latium, vel quam Gracia docta colit: Pectus Idumæo caluisti accensus amore, Nobilior nulli lecta corona tua est. Laurum alii sibi quisque gerant, tibi palma parata est. Hanc Oriens soli servat, amice, tibi.
units.tr: Shameless barbarism, which first arose in the time of our forefathers, was driven out in our own time. Greece was born again, and the Latin Muses grew; each man nourished and advanced the Muses with his own resources. Nor was the ready goodwill of the great nobles and of kings lacking, and our own country had its share of them. A day had dawned, but it had barely risen before it suddenly set, and it feels that its night is upon it. Amid these shadows and the doubtful twilight of light, another torch rises, and a day not earlier risen. Your sun rises, Sixtinus, under whose champion Barbarism again gives way, as it was destined to give way. Nor is it enough for you to pluck the Phoebean laurel, which Latium or learned Greece cultivates. You have grown warm, kindled by Idumaean love, and no crown chosen for anyone is more noble than yours. Let each man bear the laurel for himself; a palm has been prepared for you. The East keeps this palm for you alone, my friend.

units.la: DAmus tibi, benevole Lector, Anti-barbari Biblici libros tres, totius operis partem primam, quorum primo, septem errores generales, ceu totidem omnis, quae superioribus se-culis sacras literas foedavit, barbariei fontes, ostenduntur; reliquis duobus crassissimi aliquot errores & inepta interpretationes particularium Scripturae locorum, quae ex istis fontibus emanarunt, repraesentantur. Quae occasione multis sacra pagina locis facem allucemus. Secuti autem hic sumus ordinem librorum Biblicorum. Secundus enim liber circa Pentateuchum; Tertius circa libros histo-ricos, Iobum, Psalmos, Proverbia, Koheleth, Canticum, & Ecclesiasticum (licet apochryphum) versatur. Atque ita substitimus ad Prophetarum vaticinia. Quod si Deus O. M. otium & valetudinem clementer porro indulserit & hunc laborem nostrum piis & eruditis viris probaverimus, dabimus brevi tres reliquos, quibus per Prophetarum & novi foederis libros ibimus. Et quidem syllabum & lemmata eo-rum, quae secundo tertioque libro continentur, indicis vicem, ad calcem tertii libri exhibuimus. Primum quod at-tinet, VII. errores generales, quorum jam jam meminimus, isti sunt.
units.tr: We give you, kind reader, the first part of the whole work: three books of the Biblical Anti-Barbarus. In the first book, seven general errors are shown, which are so many sources of the barbarism that has defiled the sacred letters in earlier ages. In the other two books, some very gross errors and silly interpretations of particular passages of Scripture, which have flowed from these sources, are set forth. On the occasion of these we shed some light on many places of the sacred page. We have followed the order of the biblical books. The second book deals with the Pentateuch; the third deals with the historical books, Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Koheleth, the Song, and Ecclesiasticus (although it is apocryphal). Thus we have come to a halt at the prophetic oracles. If God Almighty graciously grants us further leisure and health, and if we find that pious and learned men approve of this labour of ours, we shall soon give the remaining three books, by which we shall proceed through the Prophets and the books of the New Covenant. Indeed, we have set out a synopsis and the headings of the contents of the second and third books at the end of the third book, in place of an index. As for the first book, the seven general errors, which we have just mentioned, are these.

units.tr: That shameful barbarism, which first arose in the time of our ancestors, has in our own time been driven out. Greece was reborn, and the Latin Muses flourished. Each people nourished the Muses and enlarged them with its own resources. Neither the highest nobles nor the favourable will of kings was lacking, and our own land had its share of them. A day had dawned, but it had scarcely risen before it suddenly set, and it felt that its own night was at hand. Amid these shadows and the doubtful twilight of light, another torch rises, and a day that had not risen before. The sun rises, Sixtinus, your sun, by whose champion barbarism again gives way, as it was bound to do. It is not enough for you to pluck the Phoebean laurel that Latium or learned Greece cultivates. Your heart has glowed, kindled by love of the Idumaean land, and no garland has been gathered more distinguished than yours. Let others each wear the laurel for themselves; for you a palm has been prepared. The East reserves this, friend, for you alone.

Namque tribus prioribus exhibuimus generalem defensionem Ebraica & Graca veritatu, reliquis xi. detectum ivimus BONAM FIDEM, INFALLIBILITATEM & CONCORDIAM Romanorum Pontificum circa vulgatam Editionem. Singulis capitibus, quia prolixiora erant, sua præmisimus argumenta, quæ legisse non pœnitebit. Ad calcem vero plenioris istius tractatus, pag. vid. 92. communicavimus tibi Lector, superbam & famosam illam Sixti V. Bullam, quasua Editionis authoritatem constabilire molitus est. Quam hodie in Bibliorum Editionibus frustra quaiverus. Et subjecimus modestius illud Breve, quod Clemens VIII. biennio post, sua editioni præmisit, & nunc quoque à multis Editionibus abest. Adjecimus denique pag.116. Præfationem in Clementis Biblia, quæ cum Sixti Bullam gravissimis difficultatibus urgeret, Pontifex Pontifici cornua obvertere videtur, nec Clementis nec ullius Cardinalis Doctorisve nomen ostendit. Unde de ejus authoritate anxie inter Pontificios disputari cap. xi. ostendimus. Quis tamen persuaderi sibi sinat, eam præfationem, improbante pontifice, operi Biblico præmissam esse & in hunc usque diem tolerari? Tandem etiam transivimus ad consilium nostrum de continuatione censura ad vulgatam versionem, & quæ huic operi cum isthoc affinitas & conjunctio sit ostendimus.
units.tr: We have dealt with these two inverted-order errors in fourteen chapters. For in the first three we set out a general defence of the Hebrew and Greek truth, and in the remaining eleven we have gone on to expose the GOOD FAITH, INFALLIBILITY and AGREEMENT of the Roman Pontiffs concerning the Vulgate edition. Since each chapter was rather lengthy, we prefixed to each its own arguments, which it will not be a waste of time to read. At the end of this fuller treatise, pp. 92, we have shared with you, reader, the arrogant and notorious bull of Sixtus V, by which he laboured to establish the authority of his edition, and which you will look for in vain in today's editions of the Bible. We have also appended the more modest brief that Clement VIII issued two years later, to preface his edition, and which is now also missing from many editions. Finally, we have added at p. 116 the preface to the Clementine Bible, which seems to set the Pontiff against the Pontiff, since it was pressed by the most serious difficulties arising from the bull of Sixtus, and it names neither Clement nor any Cardinal or Doctor. Hence we have shown in chapter xi that its authority is anxiously disputed among the Papists. Yet who would allow himself to be persuaded that this preface was prefixed to the Biblical work with the Pontiff's disapproval, and has been tolerated down to the present day? Lastly, we have also turned to our plan for continuing the criticism of the Vulgate version, and have shown what affinity and connection this work has with that one.

units.la: IV. Linguarum istarum, quibus sacræ literæ originaliter conscriptæ sunt, vid. Ebrææ & Græcanicæ, totiusque adeo politioris literaturæ, studia hodie esse supervacanea. p. 118. Hac
units.tr: IV. That the study of the languages in which the sacred letters were originally written, namely Hebrew and Greek, and indeed of all more refined literature, is today superfluous. p. 118. Here

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: Hac occasione exhibemus tertiam, eamque prioribus auctiorem, editionem Paraenesis nostrae, qua omnes Evangelicarum Ecclesiarum Synodos, Episcopos & superintendentes ad excitanda SS. linguarum studia hortamur. Quem conatum meum quam praeclare Ecclesia Belgica promoverint, apographa aliquot decretorum synodicorum, quae subjeci, loquuntur.
units.tr: On this occasion we present the third edition of our Paraenesis, which is larger than the earlier ones, in which we urge all the synods, bishops and superintendents of the Evangelical Churches to stir up the study of the holy languages. How splendidly the Belgic Church has furthered this effort of mine is shown by the copies of several synodal decrees that I have appended.

units.la: V. Versiones Latinas ex gr. Pagnini, Junii, Erasmi, Bezae, nec non Germanicam, B. Lutheri, & quae ex ea expressa est, Belgicam, mentem Spirit. S. ubique ita expressisse, nullius ut correctionis amplius indigae sint. p. 152.
units.tr: V. The Latin versions, for example those of Pagninus, Junius, Erasmus and Beza, and also the German version of Luther and the Dutch version derived from it, have everywhere expressed the mind of the Holy Spirit so faithfully that they no longer need any correction. p. 152.

units.la: VI. Bibliorum lectionem Theologiae studioso non esse admodum necessariam, vel, posse aliquem Theologiae studere & Theologum esse, etiamsi non legat S. Literas. p. ibidem.
units.tr: VI. Reading the Bible is not very necessary for a student of theology; or, one can study theology and be a theologian even if one does not read Holy Scripture. p. ibidem.

units.la: VII. Omni Scripturae textui, singulisque locis, aut saltem plerisque, duplicem inesse sensum, Literalem & mysticum. Circa illum (literalem) versari Theologiam crassam: circa hunc (mysticum) occupari Theologiam secretiorem & spiritualem. Quin & uno loco plures posse subesse sensus literales. p. 158.
units.tr: VII. Every text of Scripture, and each passage, or at least most of them, has a twofold sense, literal and mystical. Crude theology concerns itself with the literal sense; a more secret and spiritual theology is occupied with the mystical sense. Indeed, in a single passage there may even be several literal senses. p. 158.

units.la: Hic vero intolerandum illum Allegorizandi pruritum in ipso limine gravissimi Serarii, Sixti Senensis & Riberae censuris notavimus. Ostendimus testimoniis Augustini & Hieronymi, a literalis sensus difficultate & cleri socordia hunc pruritum robur & incrementa acquisivisse. Egimus de duplici Scripturae sensu, literali & mystico. Variis nomenclaturis eos insigniri, & saepe terminos confundi, dum jam laxius jam strictius usurpantur. Non omnem allegoricum sensum in exilium mitti. Vitandos 3. istos errores I. Unius ejusdemque loci varios posse esse sensus literales. p. 165.
units.tr: Here, however, we have noted that intolerable itch for allegorizing at the very threshold of the censures of the most grave Serarius, Sixtus of Siena and Ribera. We have shown, by the testimonies of Augustine and Jerome, that this itch gained its strength and growth from the difficulty of the literal sense and the laziness of the clergy. We have discussed the twofold sense of Scripture, literal and mystical. These are labelled by various names, and the terms are often confused, since they are now used more loosely, now more strictly. Not every allegorical sense is to be banished into exile. We must avoid these three errors: I. That a single and same passage can have various literal senses. p. 165.

units.la: II. Quorundam locorum nullum esse sensum literalem.
units.tr: II. That some passages have no literal sense at all.

units.la: 3. In omnibus & singulis locis Scripturae duos esse sensus, literalem unum, mysticum alterum. Ea occasione agimus de de loco 1. Cor.x.6. omnia in figuris contingebant illis. Admonemus etiam eos, qui ex quolibet propemodum homine vel rebus in Vet. Teft. memorata, typum Christi aut Ecclesiae, aut rerum ad N. Teft. pertinentium, fabricant. Non, sufficere, ut aliquid alterius typus sit, similitudinem aliquam, sed ex sacra pagina ostendendum esse, illud à Spiritu S. huc suisse distinatum & ordinatum. Tales autem typos oppido paucos esse (pag.168.) In multis, de quorum evidentia multi non dubitant, tantum allusionem quandam esse. Illos quoque monemus, qui circa nominum propriorum originationem nimis curiosi pro concione sunt, iisque doctrinas, quin & integras saepe conciones, superstruunt. Concludimus denique dissertationem illam gravissimis admonitionibus Bonfrerii, Iesuita Galli, Leonardi Marii, Theologi Colonien sis, Adami Safboutii & Martini Buceri. Lege lector & non poenitebit.
units.tr: 3. That in all and each passage of Scripture there are two senses, one literal and the other mystical. On this occasion we treat the passage 1 Cor. 10:6, "all these things happened to them in figures." We also admonish those who fabricate, from almost any man or thing mentioned in the Old Testament, a type of Christ, or of the Church, or of things pertaining to the New Testament. It is not enough that something should be a type of something else by some resemblance; it must be shown from the sacred page that it was destined and ordained by the Holy Spirit for this purpose. Such types are very few indeed (p. 168). In many cases, about whose clearness many have no doubt, there is only a certain allusion. We also warn those who are too curious in preaching about the derivation of proper names, and build doctrines, and often whole sermons, upon them. Finally, we conclude this dissertation with the most serious admonitions of Bonfrère, a French Jesuit, Leonardus Marius, theologian of Cologne, Adam Safbout and Martin Bucer. Read, reader, and you will not regret it.

units.la: Habes brevem διατύπωσιν primi libri. Reliquorum, ut jam monui, ad calcem operis invenies. Nolumus tamen hoc loco te celare, Lector, nos duobus istis libris prolixiores quosdam excursus, quorum nonnullos jam pridem scripseramus, inseruisse. Inter eos & isti sunt.
units.tr: You have a brief outline [διατύπωσιν] of the first book. You will find the rest, as I have already said, at the end of the work. Yet, reader, I do not wish to hide from you here that in these two books I have inserted some rather lengthy digressions, some of which I had written long ago. Among them are these.

units.la: I. Responsio ad excursus eruditissimi viri D. MARINI MARSENNI, Theologi Parisiensis, qua defendo censuram meam vulgatae versionis ad vi. priora capita Geneseos ab ipso oppugnata. Inscripta Reverendis & Clarissimis Theologis, FRANCISCO GOMARO & D. ANDREÆ RIVETO. p. 294.
units.tr: I. A reply to the very learned excursus of Mr. Marin Mersenne, theologian of Paris, in which I defend my criticism of the Vulgate version of the first six chapters of Genesis, which he attacked. Dedicated to the Reverend and Distinguished Theologians Francis Gomarus and Mr. Andreas Rivetus. p. 294.

units.la: II. Commentatio de nomine Tetragrammato, cum modesta responsione ad argumenta Cl. Viri, D. NICOLAI FULLERI, quibus pro vulgatae lectionis JEHOVAH certitudine disputavit. Ad Reverendum & Clarissimum virum, D. FESTUM HOMMIUM SS. Th. Doctorem, &c. p. 292.
units.tr: II. A treatise on the Tetragrammaton, with a modest reply to the arguments of the distinguished man Mr. Nicolas Fuller, with which he argued for the certainty of the Vulgate reading JEHOVAH. Addressed to the Reverend and Distinguished Mr. Festus Hommius, Doctor of Sacred Theology, etc. p. 292.

units.la: III. Dissertatio de fundamentis allegoricae interpretatiotationis, qua omnia ista quæ Jobi XL. de Behemoth & Leviathan dicuntur, ad Diabolum vulgo transferunt, ad eximium & magnæ spei juvenem, D. THEODORUM SAEKMA, &c. p.434. IV. Dissertatio de Keri & Chetib, ad Reverendum & Clarissimum virum, D. Ludovicum de Dieu, &c. p.462. V. Dissertatio de crassioribus quibusdam interpretum erroribus, in quos vel per librariorum sphalmata, vel vocum ambiguitatem, dum ad originalem textum non recurrerunt, delati sunt, Ad Nobiliss. & magnæ spei adolescentem, D. EPEUM ab AYLVA. p.544. VI. Commentatio ad celebrem illum locum Proverb. viii. 22. Κύριος ἔκτισέ με; in qua explicatur & a calumnia vindicatur sententia celeberrimi Viri, D. JOH. DRUSI p. m. præceptoris & decessoris mei, de me præclarissime merito, ad Clarissimum Virum, D. JOHANNEM HACHTINGIUM; &c. p. 570.
units.tr: III. A dissertation on the foundations of allegorical interpretation, by which all those things said in Job 40 about Behemoth and Leviathan are commonly transferred to the Devil, addressed to the outstanding young man of great promise, Mr. Theodorus Saekma, etc. p. 434. IV. A dissertation on the Kethiv and Qere, addressed to the Reverend and Distinguished Mr. Louis de Dieu, etc. p. 462. V. A dissertation on certain cruder errors of the interpreters, into which they were led either by scribal blunders or by the ambiguity of words, since they did not have recourse to the original text. Addressed to the most noble young man of great promise, Mr. Epeus ab Aylva. p. 544. VI. A commentary on the famous passage Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me" [Κύριος ἔκτισέ με], in which the opinion of the most celebrated man, Mr. Johannes Drusius, of blessed memory, my teacher and predecessor, who deserved most splendidly of me, is explained and vindicated from calumny; addressed to the most distinguished Mr. Johannes Hachtingius, etc. p. 570.

units.la: Illud restat, ut tituli, quem huic libro feci, reddatur ratio. Is est, ANTI-BARBARUS BIBLICUS. Cum illis potissimum mihi negotium est, qui linguarum originalium studia, tanquam si nulli usui essent, proscribunt. Eos vel barbaros esse vel barbarici patrocinium præstare, nullas, opinor, infitebitur. Istorum furoribus hunc librum opposui, Merito ergo Anti-barbarum dixi. Addidi Biblicum. Nihil enim cum ista barbarie hic mihi negotii est, quae τὰς ἐξωθεν disciplinas superioribus seculis defloravit. Nec etiam eos tango, qui ad rerum Theologicarum tractationem barbarum, aut saltem minus Latinum, stylum attulere. Ipse mihi mea tenuitatis conscius sum. Atque hoc quoque debeo Patriæ meæ infelicitati, in cujus scholis & Academia styli exercitia, me juvene, omnino jacuere. Quamvis ne nunc quidem ea admodum floreant, juventute nostra ad ea potius studia properante, qua πρὸς τὰ ἀλφιτα sunt. Primarius mihi scopus fuit, ostendere, quantas frustrationes linguarum originalium ignorantia beatissimus patribus & acutissimus Scholasticis in scripturarum interpretatione attulerit. Non ego beatos Patres, non omnes Scholasticos, quorum interpretationes convello, inter barbaros pono. Illos hac nomenclatura noto, qui ad ista oculos claudunt & cum possent linguas discere, quod istis seculi infelicitas negabat, nec discunt ipsi, nec alios discere patiuntur, instar canum, qui cum fæno non vescantur, prohibent tamen accedere boves. Illis etiam, quibus in veteris illis Ægypti ollis animus est, qui Scholasticorum scriptis & Pontificiorum postillis semper inversantur, illis, inquam, hoc quoque scripto prodesse volui. Neque enim in Evangelicis Ecclesiis nulli sunt, qui malunt cum barbaris istis vesci glandibus, quam cum eruditissimis viris fruges edere. Queis volupe magis est cum Origene, Augustino, alisque ἀλληγορεῖν, quam cum praclaris istis Dei organis, Luthero, Calvino, Bucero, &c. scripturam solide interpretari. Hi sunt, qui quicquid in Patrum vel Homiliastarum scriptis legunt, pro oraculo accipiunt, pro concione proponunt. Hi sunt qui omne id quod ipsi non didicerunt, ut hereticum suspectant, qui sub qualibet Ebraea aut Graeca voce heterodoxiam latere mussitant. Hi sunt, qui cum sententiam aliquam vel loci alicujus explicationem ab ea, qua apud nos recepta est diversam in Patrum scriptis legunt, mox perculluntur. Hi denique sunt quibus miseri Grammatici semper vapulant, illam Johannis Dullardi sententiam, qua Ludovicum Vivem discipulum suum sufflaminare solebat, Quanto eris melior Grammaticus, tanto pejor Philosophus & Theologus, sape inculcantes. Illi si hac nostra legere dignabuntur, tanquam in speculo videbunt, praclaris istis viris (Patres intelligo & florem Scholasticorum) nil nisi linguarum notitiam defuisse, se quoque dum authores quosdam sine delectu & judicio legunt, & sequuntur, in scripturarum interpretatione &
units.tr: It remains that I give an account of the title I have given to this book. It is ANTI-BARBARUS BIBLICUS. I have chiefly to do with those who reject the study of the original languages as if they were of no use. That they are barbarians, or lend support to barbarism, I think no one will deny. Against their frenzies I have set this book, and so I rightly called it Anti-barbarus. I added Biblicus. For I have no quarrel here with that barbarism which in earlier centuries stripped bare the so-called external disciplines [τὰς ἐξωθεν]. Nor do I touch those who brought a barbarous, or at least not very Latin, style to the treatment of theological matters. I am myself conscious of my own slightness. And I owe this also to the misfortune of my country, in whose schools and Academy the exercises of style lay utterly neglected in my youth. Even now they do not flourish greatly, since our young people hasten rather to those studies which are toward barley-meal [πρὸς τὰ ἀλφιτα], that is, which bring in a living. My chief aim has been to show how great the frustrations were that ignorance of the original languages brought upon the most blessed Fathers and the most acute Scholastics in the interpretation of Scripture. I do not place the blessed Fathers, nor all the Scholastics whose interpretations I overturn, among the barbarians. I mark with this name those who close their eyes to these things, and who, when they could have learned the languages, which the unhappiness of their age denied to those men, neither learn themselves nor allow others to learn, like dogs that do not eat hay yet forbid the oxen to approach. To those too who have a mind for those old pots of Egypt, who are always busy with the writings of the Scholastics and the postils of the Papists, I wished to be of use also by this writing. For there are not lacking in the Evangelical Churches those who prefer to feed on those barbarous acorns rather than to eat the fruits with the most learned men. They take more pleasure in allegorizing [ἀλληγορεῖν] with Origen, Augustine and others than in interpreting Scripture soundly with those famous instruments of God, Luther, Calvin, Bucer, etc. These are the men who accept as an oracle whatever they read in the writings of the Fathers or of the homilists, and put it forward in the sermon. These are the men who suspect as heretical everything they have not learned themselves, and who mutter that heterodoxy lies hidden under any Hebrew or Greek word. These are the men who, when they read in the writings of the Fathers an opinion or an explanation of some passage different from that which is received among us, are at once thrown into a panic. Finally, these are the men by whom the poor grammarians are always beaten, constantly repeating that saying of John Dullaert, with which he used to check his pupil Ludovicus Vives: "The better grammarian you become, the worse philosopher and theologian you will be." If they deign to read these pages of ours, they will see as in a mirror that those famous men (I mean the Fathers and the flower of the Scholastics) lacked nothing but knowledge of the languages, and that they themselves, while they read and follow certain authors without selection and judgment, in the interpretation of Scripture

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: citatione saepe impingere. Illud autem hic semel moneo, me non cujuslibet scriptoris de qualibet re ineptias (quis enim modus, quae utilitas talium nugarum esset?) huc convectasse, sed lapsus & errores magnorum virorum, quorum lucubrationes multorum manibus teruntur, qui jam pridem in Ecclesia & Scholis dictaturam quandam gerunt. Inter quos sunt Augustinus, Ambrosius, Athanasius, Chrysostomus, Basilius, Epiphanius, Tertullianus, Lactantius, Gregorius Magnus, Thomas, Lombardus & alii. Quia vero non defuturos exstimo, qui me instar Chami patrum pudenda retegere clamabunt, rogandi mihi isti homines sunt, ut ad Sixti Senensis Bibliothecam S. oculos paulisper reflectant, qui Patrum in exponenda Scriptura errores, quos nec sine Catholicae pietatis offensione, nec sine magna legentium perturbatione dissimulari potuisse ait, studiose collegit, isque duos integros libros vid. quintum & sextum explevit. Ego illud insuper semel hic protestor, me non isthoc animo magnorum istorum virorum errores recensuisse, quasi levato sipario omnib. conspiciendos exhibuisse, ut illis convitium facerem, aut publice traducerem, nedam ut eorum scripta de juventutis manibus excuterem. Scio enim illos praclaris dotibus navos istos pensasse. Scio Patres absque praeviis ductoribus antea iter non calcatum ingressos, glaciem, quod ajunt, fregisse. Non solent prima quaeque disciplinarum tentamenta semper omnis culpae expertia esse. Nihil simul inventum & perfectum est. Quod si in hac saecula magni isti Heroes incidissent, aut ego valde fallor, aut omnib. qui post renatas literas in scripturar. interpretationem cum laude incubuere, otia fecissent. Quid ergo? Iam bis dixi. Ut juventus nostra tanquam in speculo videret, solam linguarum notitiam praestantissimis istius ingeniis saeculorum infelicitatem negasse, ne juventus nostra omnia, quae in authoribus istis occurrunt, tanquam oracula arripiat, populoque, ubi jam ad docendum admissa erit proponat. Juventutem nomine. Illud enim interest mea te sci-
units.tr: often stumble upon a citation. I note this once here: I have not gathered together the trifles of any writer on any subject (for what limit would there be, and what use would such nonsense be?), but the slips and errors of great men, whose works are worn by the hands of many and who have for some time exercised a kind of dictatorship in the Church and the schools. Among them are Augustine, Ambrose, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Basil, Epiphanius, Tertullian, Lactantius, Gregory the Great, Thomas, Lombard and others. Since I think there will be no lack of those who, like Ham, will cry out that I am uncovering the nakedness of the Fathers, these men must be asked to turn their eyes for a little while to the Bibliotheca Sancta of Sixtus of Siena, who carefully collected the errors of the Fathers in expounding Scripture, which he said could be passed over neither without offence to Catholic piety nor without great disturbance to readers, and who filled two whole books, the fifth and sixth. I here also protest once more that I have not listed the errors of these great men with the intention of setting them out for everyone to see as if the curtain had been lifted, in order to rail at them or expose them publicly, much less to snatch their writings out of the hands of young people. For I know that those men weighed these faults against their outstanding gifts. I know that the Fathers, entering a road not trodden before and without guides going ahead, broke the ice, as they say. The first attempts in any discipline are not always free from every fault. Nothing is invented and perfected at once. But if those great heroes had fallen into these times, either I am greatly mistaken or all who after the revival of letters have laboured with credit over the interpretation of Scripture would have been left idle. What then? I have said it twice already. So that our young people might see, as in a mirror, that knowledge of languages alone was denied to these most excellent minds of earlier ages, lest our young people seize upon everything that occurs in these authors as oracles, and put it before the people once they have been admitted to teach. I name no names, young people. For it matters to me that you should know...

units.la: PRÆFATIO
units.tr: PREFACE

units.la: re, Lector, me hanc operam juventuti & tironibus gratificatum esse. Eruditis & veteranis hic labor meus non defuit. Hinc tironem in meo scripto ubique alloquor. Hinc dum studui σαφέστερον loqui, sciens & volens sæpe ἀμαθέστερον dixi. Hinc minutiora, quod ea veteranos quoque Theologiæ studiosos crebro ignorare deprehendam, sæpe prolixiori sermone persecutus sum. Quamvis & illud confidam, studiosos adolescentes prolixitatem nostram non incusaturos, nisi forte aut indoctiores sint, quam ut intelligant; aut doctiores, quam ut egeant; aut negligentiores, quam ut curent; aut morosiores, quam ut perferant. Quibus hominum generibus hac non elaboravimus. Sed redeat eò unde digressus est sermo. Volui evidentib. exemplis ostendere, Omnia ad originarii textus regulam examinanda esse, præsertim, cum dogmata probanda vel confutanda sunt. Quid hic pecco? Recognoscant Pontificii in jure Canonico Distinct. ix. aura illa Augustini verba, ut veterum librorum fides de Hebræis voluminibus examinanda est, ita novorum veritas Græci sermonis normam desiderat. Nec non illa ejusdem, Negare non possum nec debeo, sicut in ipsis majoribus, ita multa esse in tam multis opusculis meis, quæ possunt justo judicio & nulla temeritate culpari. Et rursus ista, Alios ita lego, inquit August. ut quantalibet sanctitate aut doctrina polleant, ideo non verum putem, quod ipsi ita senserunt, sed quod mihi per alios autores vel canonicas scripturas vel probabiles rationes persuadere potuerunt. Et in prolog. lib. 3. de Trinitate, noli meis literis tanquam Canonicis deservire. Quæ omnia in distinctionem ix. Gratianus accongessit: Ejus enim hæc summa est, Patrum scripta ad Scripturas Canonicas examinanda, nec cum credendi necessitate, sed cum judicandi libertate legenda esse. Neque hic audio barbarum Glossatorem, qui hæc in ea tempora rejicit, quibus scripta Augustini & Hieron. nondum erant authentica. Hodie vero, inquit, jubentur omnia teneri
units.tr: I want you to know, reader, that I have undertaken this work as a gift to young people and beginners. It has not been without value for scholars and seasoned men either. For this reason I address the beginner throughout my writing. For this reason, while I aimed to speak more clearly [σαφέστερον], I knowingly and deliberately often spoke more simply [ἀμαθέστερον]. For this reason I have often gone at length over smaller points, since I notice that even experienced students of theology often overlook them. Yet I also trust that our young students will not blame our lengthiness, unless perhaps they are too untaught to understand it, too learned to need it, too careless to care, or too fussy to put up with it. I have not worked for those kinds of people. But let me return to where my discussion left off. I wished to show by plain examples that everything must be tested by the rule of the original text, especially when doctrines are to be proved or refuted. What wrong am I doing here? Let the Papists recognise, in the Canon Law, Distinction 9, those words of Augustine: just as the faith of the old books must be tested against the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the new books requires the standard of the Greek language. Likewise that other saying of his: I cannot and must not deny that, just as in the greatest writers, so too in my own many little works there are many things that may rightly and without rashness be found fault with. And again these words: "I read others in such a way," says Augustine, "that however much holiness or learning they excel in, I do not therefore hold as true what they themselves thought, but only what they have been able to persuade me of by other authors, or by the canonical Scriptures, or by probable reasons." And in the prologue to Book 3 of On the Trinity: "Do not serve my writings as if they were canonical." Gratian gathered all these things together in Distinction 9. For the sum of it is this: the writings of the Fathers are to be tested against the canonical Scriptures, and are to be read not with a necessity of believing but with a freedom of judging. Nor do I listen here to the barbarous Glossator, who puts these things back into those times when the writings of Augustine and Jerome were not yet authentic. "Today," he says, "everything is commanded to be held..."

units.la: a Epist. 8. ad Hieronymum.
units.tr: a Letter 8, to Jerome.

units.la: b Ad Vincent. lib. 2.
units.tr: b On Vincent, Book 2.

units.la: c Epist. 8. ad Hieron. usque ad ultimum Jota. Apage ineptias istas, Barbare. Aures potius substringo illustrissimo Baronio, qui ad annum 34. §. 213. Non omnes, inquit, qui loco Apostolorum successerunt, Episcopi, assecuti sunt sensum & intelligentiam scripturarum, vel eos ipsa semper excelluisse gratia, est necessarium. Nam Sanctissimos Patres, quos Doctores Ecclesiæ ob eorum sublimem eruditionem merito nominamus, quantumlibet eos Spiritus S. gratia præ cæteris imbutos esse liqueat, in interpretatione Scripturarum, non semper, nec in omnibus sequitur Catholica Ecclesia. Nec non Bellarmino, qui de Conc. lib. 2. cap. 12. diserte pronuntiat, sacra Patrum scripta non esse regulas, nec habere authoritatem obligandi. Quam etiam de facile Salmero Patrum consentientium authoritatem rejecterit, infra pag. 438. adducto luculento testimonio, ostendimus. Et quis tam in Bellarmino hospes, qui ignoret, Augustinum in expendendis quibusdam Scripturæ locis oscitantia ab illo argui? Quis non vidit Censuras Fevardentii in Irenæum? Billii in Iustinum? Hervetii in Clementem Alexandrinum? Pamelii in Tertullianum? &c.
units.tr: c Letter 8, to Jerome, to the very last iota. Away with those silly notions, you barbarian! I would rather stop my ears to the most illustrious Baronius, who at the year 34, §213, says: "Not all those who succeeded to the place of the Apostles as bishops attained the sense and understanding of the Scriptures, nor is it necessary that they always excelled in that grace. For the most holy Fathers, whom we rightly call Doctors of the Church on account of their sublime learning, however much it is clear that they were endowed with the grace of the Holy Spirit above others, the Catholic Church does not always, nor in all things, follow in the interpretation of the Scriptures." Nor to Bellarmine, who plainly declares in On the Councils, Book 2, chapter 12, that the holy writings of the Fathers are not rules and have no authority to bind. How readily Salmeron also rejected the authority of the agreeing Fathers, we have shown below on page 438 with a clear testimony. And who is so much a stranger to Bellarmine as not to know that Augustine is charged by him with carelessness in weighing certain passages of Scripture? Who has not seen the Censures of Fevardentius on Irenaeus? Of Billius on Justin? Of Hervetius on Clement of Alexandria? Of Pamelius on Tertullian? And so on.

units.la: Intellexisti, pie & erudite Lector, quem huius mei laboris scopum habeam. Eum si tibi probavero, misologorum & malignorum securus sinam praeterfluere iudicia. Modum tractandi & argumentum quod attinet, si quid displiceat, sicubi à veritatis aut modestia tramite divertisse videbor, mone libere. Non tam paratus quisquam esse potest ad monendum, quam ego ad corrigendum. Nemo est, qui non aliqua humani erroris culpa teneatur. Sed ea, in quibus ἡυσόχηΣα, veniam à tua æquitate illis impetrabunt, in quibus ἡσόχηΣα. Vale & plenioris anteloquii loco accipe hanc de barbarie orationem, quam ante biennium coram Nobilissimis & Amplissimis Academiæ Curatoribus & Academicis recitabam.
units.tr: You have understood, pious and learned reader, what aim I have in this my labour. If I have shown it to be acceptable to you, I shall be untroubled and let the judgements of the quarrelsome and the malicious flow past me. As for the manner of treatment and the subject matter, if anything displeases you, or if I seem anywhere to have strayed from the path of truth or modesty, advise me freely. No one can be more ready to be advised than I am to be corrected. No one is free of some fault of human error. But those in which I have been hasty [ἡυσόχηΣα] will obtain pardon from your fairness, and those in which I have been careful [ἡσόχηΣα] ... Farewell, and take this speech on barbarism, which I delivered two years ago before the most noble and distinguished Curators and Academics of the University, as a more extended preface.

units.la: DE BARBARIE ORATIO.
units.tr: ON BARBARISM: AN ORATION.

units.la: Habita in templo Academico 22. Sept. MDCXXVI.
units.tr: Delivered in the Academic temple, 22 September 1626.

units.la: IN Romana olim Republica seculares ludos à P. Valerio Publicola primitus institutos, ac centesimo quoque anno pompatice instauratos fuisse, Historiae docent. Tunc inclamabat Praeco, Venite ad ludos, quos nemo vestrum spectavit; nemo etiam postea spectaturus est. Caedebantur hostiae nigrae. Trinoctio indicebantur lecti-sternia, pervigilia & supplicationes. Pueri & puellae hymnos Apollini & Dianae canebant. In hunc modum coeciilli mortales suam erga superos inferosq;, quos sibi elegerant; Deos, gratitudinem declarare studuerunt. Ante annos VIII. jubilaeum quoque suum Evangelicae, qua late Reformatus orbis patet, Ecclesiae celebrarunt. Gratiae actae Deo, quod ante annos centum excitasset incomparabiles Heroas, Lutherum, Melanthonem, Erasinum; Reuchlinum &c. qui tot in Christianismo seculis grassatae barbariei intrepido animo bellum denunciavere, & felicissime gessere. Cujus inaestimabilis beneficii memoriam nos quoque, illorum exemplis provocati, in Auditorio nostro tunc temporis recentavimus. Ostendebamus, monstrum illud horrendum, informe, ingens universo Christianismo crassissimam rerum sacrarum ignorantiam & plusquam Cimmerias tenebras superinduxisse; ipsam Jurisprudentiam, qua nihil olim splendidius fuerat excultum, foedasse: Medicinam contaminasse, eum denique in modum deturpasse divinam illam Philosophiam, ut non amplius ingeniorum cos & lima, sed crudelis potius ingeniorum carnificina fuerit. At ubi oriens linguarum & humaniorum literarum Sol tenebras istas discussit, puriorem in templa cultum, quasi postliminio, rediisse, restiturum SS. Literis suum nitorem, caput suum exeruisse Jurisprudentiam, lacertos suos movisse Medicinam, ac longe nitidiori, quam olim unquam, vultu sespectandam praebuisse Philosophiam.
units.tr: Histories tell us that in the Roman republic the secular games were first instituted by Publius Valerius Publicola and were renewed with solemn pomp every hundredth year. Then the herald would cry out: "Come to the games, which none of you has seen and none of you will see again." Black victims were slaughtered. For three nights couches were spread, there were vigils and processions, and boys and girls sang hymns to Apollo and Diana. In this manner those blind mortals strove to express their gratitude to the gods above and below whom they had chosen for themselves. Eight years ago the evangelical Church, which the Reformed world now covers far and wide, also celebrated its jubilee. Thanks were given to God because a hundred years before he had raised up incomparable heroes, Luther, Melanchthon, Erasmus, Reuchlin, and others, who with fearless spirit declared war on the barbarism that had spread through so many centuries of Christianity, and waged it most successfully. Moved by their example, we too at our own lecture hall at that time renewed the memory of this inestimable benefit. We showed that that horrible, shapeless, huge monster had overspread the whole of Christendom with the thickest ignorance of sacred things and with darkness worse than Cimmerian; that it had disfigured jurisprudence itself, which once had been cultivated more splendidly than anything else; that it had contaminated medicine; and, finally, that it had so disfigured that divine philosophy that it was no longer a polishing file for minds but rather a cruel butchery of minds. But when the rising sun of languages and the humane letters dispelled those shadows, purer worship returned to the churches, as if by right of return; Scripture regained its lustre, jurisprudence raised its head, medicine moved its limbs, and philosophy presented a face far more radiant than ever before.

units.la: Hujusmodi orationibus tunc personabant Academiæ. Nundinarum Francofurtensium Catalogi nil nisi hujus argumenti seculares orationes & Academiarum Jubilæos loquebantur. Credo ego, splendida quoque alibi instituta fuisse convivia & plusquam Græcanicas compotationes. Credo multos, etiam quorum profession em id minime decuit, pluisculum mero incaluisse & magnis invicem culullis ad Ebrietatem provocasse. Credo auditas sæpe inter Academicos istas voces,
units.tr: Such were the speeches that rang out then in the universities. The catalogues of the Frankfurt fairs spoke of nothing but secular orations of this kind and jubilees of academies. I believe that splendid banquets and drinking bouts worthy of the Greeks were held elsewhere too. I believe that many men, even those whose profession ought least to allow it, grew rather warm with wine and challenged one another to drink deeply from great cups. I believe that among those academics the words were often heard:

units.la: Nunc bibendum, nunc pede libero pulsanda tellus.
units.tr: Now we must drink; now the earth must be struck with a free foot.

units.la: Interim nesciebant boni illi viri, nesciebamus & nos, quam magnis passibus alibi ad barbariem tenderent, quam paucis ab eadem alibi abessent Ecclesiæ. Ob barbariem propulsatam Deo agebantur gratiæ, sed ne denuo irreperet vel irrueret, profunde securi erant. Atque hic sigendus mihi pes est. Animus enim mihi est ostendere, Ejusdem Solis occasum superinduxisse orbi Christiano tenebras, cujus ortus eas discussit. Intelligo autem Solem linguarum. Sic dico. Quam occasus linguarum Sol superindixit, caliginem, eundem Solem orientem superiori sæculo dissipasse. Qui si denuo nobis occidat, novis, imo spissioribus Ecclesiam mersum iri tenebris, & longe fœdiorem in Christianismo grassaturam barbariem. Ut autem & illud clarius cernamus, & intelligamus eadem opera, quam vicinus sit iste Sol occasui, primo contemplabimur paucis, νῆ ὡς ἐν παρίδῳ[?], veterem barbariem, quæ SS. literas, & cui mea ancillatur professio, Christianam religionem oppressit. Contemplabimur autem irrepentem, progredientem, grassantem & propulsatam. Secundo, præsentem Evangelicarum Academiarum & Ecclesiarum statum considerabimus. Vos, Auditores, ex veteri formula linguis favete.
units.tr: Meanwhile those good men did not know, and we did not know either, how far elsewhere they were advancing towards barbarism, and how few churches elsewhere were distant from it. Thanks were given to God for barbarism driven back, but they were quite secure that it would not creep back in or rush in again. And here I must plant my foot firmly. For it is my intention to show that the same Sun whose rising dispelled the darkness has, by its setting, brought darkness over the Christian world. I mean the sun of languages. My claim is this: the sun that has set over languages has brought back the mist that the same sun had dispersed when it rose in the previous century. If it sets again for us, the Church will be plunged into new and even thicker darkness, and a far fouler barbarism will rage through Christendom. So that we may see this more clearly, and at the same time understand how near this sun is to its setting, I shall first briefly survey, as in a sketch [ὡς ἐν παραδείγματι], the old barbarism that oppressed the Holy Scriptures and the Christian religion, and to which my profession is a servant. I shall look at it as it crept in, advanced, raged and was driven back. Second, I shall consider the present state of the evangelical academies and churches. You, listeners, favour the tongues with the old formula.

units.la: Post Apostolorum tempora, linguæ Ebraæ peritiam paulatim obliviam & quasi fugitivam factam esse, Patrum monumenta evidenter demonstrant. In tanta Episcoporum & presbyterorum multitudine, (unum & alterum excipio,) nullum reperias, qui fontes Ebræos consulere fuerit quitus. Hinc Græcos Patres Græca veteris paginæ interpretatione contentos esse oportuit. In novo quidem fœdere fontes adire potuerunt, unde & in ejus interpretatione minus exorbitarunt, sed cum ejus phraseologia pura puta Ebraica sit; quam juxta cum ignarissimis ignorabant, non est mirum, si & hic plurimis in locis miserabiliter, ut cum D. + Beza, loquar, cœcutiverint. Quid de Patribus Latinis dicam? Illos, Græcarum quoque literarum Sole paulatim ad occasum vergente, sese tandem omnino subducente, Latinâ utriusque testamenti translatione contentos esse iussit necessitas. Cum vero utriusque linguæ translationes & invicem & ab originaria scriptura immane quantum sæpe discrepárent, fieri non potuit, quin crassissimi errores Ecclesiam Dei obnubilarent; quos eo facilius, quotquot Editione Lxx. Interpretum vel Græca, vel Latine versa utebantur, admisere, eoque altiores egere radices, quo majorem de ea opinionem conceperant. Credebant enim viri alias eruditissimi, dictos Interpretes prophetas fuisse, eodemque spiritu incaluisse, qui ipsos primigenios scriptores egerat. Atque hinc prima mali labes. Hujus autem erroris fontem linguæ Ebrææ imperitiam esse pronuntio. Quod si enim versionem Græcam cum Ebraeo textu conferre valuissent, nunquam tam crassum errorem errassent, nunquam vulgatissimæ isti & quæ Editionis istius authoritatem nimiopere auxit, de Lxx. cellulis fabulæ aures substrinxissent.
units.tr: That, after the time of the apostles, the skill in the Hebrew language gradually fell into oblivion and became almost a fugitive is clearly shown by the records of the Fathers. Among so great a multitude of bishops and elders (I except one or two) you will find none who thought it worth while to consult Hebrew sources. Hence the Greek Fathers had to be content with the Greek translation of the Old Testament. Indeed, they could have gone to the sources for the New Testament, and so they strayed less far in its interpretation; but since its phraseology is purely Hebrew, and they were ignorant of it, just as the most unskilled men are, it is no wonder that here too in very many places they went miserably astray, as Beza puts it. What shall I say of the Latin Fathers? When the sun of Greek letters too was sinking towards the west and at last withdrew altogether, necessity compelled them to be content with the Latin translation of both Testaments. But since the translations of both languages often differed hugely from one another and from the original scripture, it could not happen but that the grossest errors would cloud the Church of God. Those who used the edition of the Septuagint, whether in Greek or in Latin version, admitted these errors all the more readily, and they took deeper root the greater the esteem in which they held that edition. For learned men otherwise, believed that the said interpreters were prophets, and had been fired with the same Spirit that had moved the original writers. And from this came the first downfall. I declare that the source of this error is ignorance of the Hebrew language. For if they had been able to compare the Greek version with the Hebrew text, they would never have made so gross a mistake, and they would never have lent their ears to the fable of the seventy cells of the Seventy, a fable that greatly increased the authority of that most widely known edition.

units.la: Sed opponces mihi Origenem & Hieronymum, quorum uterque licet Ebraice fuerit peritissimus, in Scripturarum tamen interpretatione non semel à veritatis tramite ad gravissimos errores divertit. Ego vero impudentem eum dixerim, qui illud in se volet recipere, solam linguarum peritiam adversus omnes errores sufficiens esse antidotum. Præterquam enim quod aliis quoque opus sit adminiculis augusta nimis res est, & nulli mortalium concessa, nusquam errare. Quamvis illud quoque omnes mihi eruditi haud gravate concessuri sint, inter omnes Patres, qui veteris Test. paginam interpretati sunt, nullos extare, qui eam doctius, ubi literalem sensum persequuntur, illustraverint. Neque frustra addo, ubi literalem sensum persequuntur. Ubi enim ab ejus, uti vocabant, paupertate ad Allegoriarum divitias transvolarunt, non minus se ridiculos, quam aliorum quispiam, se præbuere.
units.tr: But you will object to me Origen and Jerome, both of whom, though highly skilled in Hebrew, nevertheless more than once turned from the path of truth into the gravest errors in interpreting the Scriptures. I, however, would call shameless the man who wished to maintain that skill in languages alone is a sufficient antidote against all errors. For apart from the fact that other aids are also needed, it is too lofty a claim, and granted to no mortal, to be never mistaken. Yet this too I think all learned men will readily grant: among all the Fathers who interpreted the Old Testament, none is found who has illuminated it more learnedly where they pursue the literal sense. Nor do I add this idly, "where they pursue the literal sense." For where they flew from its so-called poverty to the riches of allegories, they showed themselves no less ridiculous than any others.

units.la: Habetis ergo hic secundam mali labem, secundum ad barbariem gradum, pruritum vid. (sit venia huic verbo) Allegorizandi. Ubicunque in textu vel minima occurrebat difficultas, confestim Allegoria ad manum erat. Quod Judæorum Magistris fabulæ, ipsis Allegoriæ præstabant. Hic epidemius istorum temporum morbus, ceu pestilens aliquod fidus illam quoque patrum bigam præ aliis sic afflaverat, ut propemodum de Hieronymo dubitem, utrum plus boni peritia linguarum, qua excelluit, an mali suis Allegoriis, in quibus dominatus fuit, Ecclesiæ Dei attulerit.
units.tr: You have here, then, the second downfall, the second step towards barbarism: an itch (pardon the word) for allegorising. Wherever even the slightest difficulty appeared in the text, allegory was immediately at hand. What fables were to the masters of the Jews, allegories were to these men. This epidemic disease of those times breathed upon that pair of Fathers, as if it were some pestilential wind, more than upon others, so that I am almost in doubt whether Jerome's skill in languages, in which he excelled, or his allegories, in which he held sway, brought more good or more harm to the Church of God.

units.la: Insequentibus seculis ea incubit Latinis Ecclesiis barbaries, ut codices Latinos, ne cum Græcis quidem conferre potuerint. Unde secutus est is codicis Biblici neglectus dicam, an contempus, ut ne Latinos quidem codices inter se conferre voluerint: ut in Scholis Theologicis Moses, Prophetæ, Christus & Apostoli consuluerint.
units.tr: In the centuries that followed, barbarism lay so heavily on the Latin churches that they could not even compare the Latin codices with the Greek ones. Hence followed a neglect, or I might say a contempt, of the biblical codex, so that they did not even wish to compare the Latin codices with one another. Thus in the theological schools, Moses, the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles were consulted only at second hand.

units.la: Operæ pretium autem hic fuerit observare, quibus porro gradibus & per quæ temporum spiramenta ad ipsam ἀκμὴν promoverit barbaries, & quibus technis sacrum illum codicem Ecclesiæ manibus Satanas excusserit.
units.tr: It will be worth our while to observe here by what steps and through what breathing spaces of time barbarism advanced to its very height, and by what devices Satan shook that sacred book out of the hands of the Church.

units.la: Consueverant prisci Ecclesiæ Doctores integros Scripturæ libros cætibus suis prælegere & interpretari. Testes sunt Chrysostomi, Augustini & aliorum Homiliæ & Sermones. Adhæc, in majoribus Ecclesiis semel quotannis universa Biblia à capite ad calcem prælegebantur. Duravitque laudabilis illa consuetudo ad annum usque Christi DCCCVIII. Tunc enim Paulus Warnenfridus Caroli M. jussu textus Dominicales ex epistolis & Evangeliis excerpsit judicio adeo nullo, ut eorum quidam nec caput nec caudam habeant. Namque instar imperiti lanionis, securi sua anatomica non in ipsas articulorum junctūras, sed in ipsa ossa, prout imperita manus ferebatur, impacta, divulsit ea, quæ separari neutiquam permittebat textus. Hac ergo occasione factum est, ut ista tantum Scripturæ fragmenta populo prælecta & expósita sint. Quasi universa divina scriptura non fuisset divinitus inspirata, utilisque ad doctrinam, redargutionem, correctionem & institutionem. Ipsis ministris mollem pigritiæ lectum hoc compendio adornavit Satanas, multosque è populo in eam traxit sententiam, istis fragmentis universam scripturam contineri. Observatum autem est à viris cordatis, in eundem annum quatuor Eclipses incidisse, tres Lunæ, unam Solis, ac inde non inepte conjectatum, Deum istis luminarium obscurationibus de tenebris Ecclesiæ imminentibus voluisse concionari. Atque hic tertium ad barbariem gradum constituo. Quid vero Scholis factum est? In has introducta fuerunt nova quædam Biblia, nova quædam Theologia, quam Scholasticam vocant. Cujus primus fabricator P. Lombardus fuit, qui circa annum Domini MCXL. spinosam sui ævi Theologiam, illam non ex limpidis Israëlis fontibus, sed turbidis patrum & conciliorum lacunis haustam, quatuor libris complexus est. Quod magistri sententiarum systema, totius Scholasticæ Theologiæ basis & fundamentum est.
units.tr: The early teachers of the Church were accustomed to read aloud and expound whole books of Scripture to their congregations. The homilies and sermons of Chrysostom, Augustine and others bear witness to this. Moreover, in the larger churches the whole Bible used to be read through from beginning to end once a year. That praiseworthy custom lasted until the year of Christ 808. Then Paul the Deacon (Warnefrid), by order of Charlemagne, excerpted the Sunday texts from the Epistles and Gospels with such lack of judgement that some of them have neither head nor tail. For like an unskilled butcher, with his anatomical axe he struck not at the joints themselves but at the bones themselves, wherever his unskilled hand carried it, and tore apart what the text by no means allowed to be separated. Thus it came about on this occasion that only these fragments of Scripture were read and expounded to the people, as if the whole divine Scripture had not been divinely inspired and useful for teaching, reproof, correction and instruction. By this shortcut Satan prepared a soft bed of laziness for the ministers themselves, and drew many of the people into the opinion that the whole of Scripture was contained in these fragments. Moreover, wise men observed that in that same year four eclipses occurred, three of the Moon and one of the Sun, and from this they not unreasonably conjectured that God had wished to preach through these obscurations of the luminaries about the darkness hanging over the Church. And here I set down a third step towards barbarism. But what happened in the schools? Into them were introduced certain new Bibles and a new theology, which they call Scholastic. Its first builder was Peter Lombard, who around the year of the Lord 1140 comprised in four books the thorny theology of his age, drawn not from the clear springs of Israel but from the muddy pools of the Fathers and the councils. This book of the Master of the Sentences is the base and foundation of the whole Scholastic theology.

units.la: Post seculi unius intercapedinem Albertus Magnus caput humo sustulit, qui sacras literas non cum patrum scriptis tantum, ut Lombardus fecerat, sed cum ethnico, eoque barbare verso Aristotele miscuit. Hic principatum philosophiæ tradidit primus, & subnissis pagano Aristoteli fascibus imperium detulit. Hujus vestigia Auditor ejus Thomas secutus, ex Aristotele, Patribus, Conciliis & barbara Bibliorum versione, magnum illud Systema compilavit, cui titulum Summæ fecit. Ita duo isti Centones, Liber vid. Sententiarum & Summa Thomæ, tanquam duo testamenta, in pulpito introducti sunt. Hi in Scholis Theologicis utramque faciebant paginam. Hi prælegebantur. In hos vastissimi scribebantur Commentarii. Circa hos omnis discentium & docentium versabatur labor.
units.tr: After an interval of one century, Albertus Magnus raised his head out of the ground. He mixed sacred letters not only with the writings of the Fathers, as Lombard had done, but also with Aristotle, a pagan author in a barbarous translation. He was the first to hand philosophy the leadership, and he gave the rods of office to the pagan Aristotle to rule. His pupil Thomas followed in his footsteps and, out of Aristotle, the Fathers, the Councils and the barbarous Latin version of the Bible, compiled that great system to which he gave the title Summa. Thus these two patchwork works, the Book of Sentences and the Summa of Thomas, were introduced into the pulpit like two testaments. They filled both pages in the theological schools. They were lectured on. Vast commentaries were written on them. All the labour of students and teachers was spent on these.

units.la: Habetis, Auditores natales famosi istius monstri, quod, obstetricante. P. Lombardo primitus natum, Albertus Magnus, Halensis, Thomas & alii postmodum educarunt, & recentiores Scholastici tot jam annis in suo contubernio faginarunt. In cujus ego ἀχμῆ ipsius Barbariei ἀχμὴν posuerim.
units.tr: You have, listeners, the origin of this notorious monster, which was born with Peter Lombard as midwife, was then reared by Albertus Magnus, Halensis, Thomas and others, and has been fattened in its company by the more recent Scholastics for so many years now. I would call the peak of barbarism itself the peak [acme] of this monster [acme].

units.la: Illud interim summam mereri admirationem arbitror, ipsam Sorbonam veterem indigne tulisse, novam illam Theologiam adeo superbo gressu in meditullio Christianismi inambulasse. Ausa enim ea fuit Thomæ scripta publica censura notare, quod paganismum Aristotelis cum SS. literis miscuisset, vel ut ipsorum verbis utar, quod principia Philosophiæ ad conclusiones Theologicas nimis applicuisset. Non enim loqui taliter debent Theologi, inquiunt, qualiter loquuntur Philosophi. Oculatior quoque omnibus coætaneis suis Dominicus fuit, ille celeberrimi Prædicatorii ordinis Pater, qui circa annum MCC. vixit. Is enim cum videret scripturarum cognitionem in concionatore plane esse necessariam, author erat fratribus, ut indesinenter studerent in veteri & novo Testamento & ad prædicandum missi sola Biblia secum ferrent. Figmenta enim Philosophorum parvi faciebat, inquit author vitæ ejus. Quod si eadem mens omnibus, qui isto seculo vixerunt, fuisset, nunquam tam latam grassandi viam sibi hoc monstrum fecisset. Sed quia urgebant Ecclesiam Dei judicia, gravissima illa Sorbonæ censura & Dominici istius & si qui præterea istius animi fuere, commonefactiones insuper habitæ sunt. Perrexerunt enim quæstionarii simplicitatem fidei in curiositatem disputandi convertere, & si quid adhuc superfuit creperæ lucis, illud densiori nocte sepeliverunt; excogitantes quotidie quæstiones novas, inutiles, profanas, Prophetis & Apostolis adeo ignoratas, ut si illis lucis usuram denuo indulsisset Deus, nihil minus suturi fuissent quam Theologi. Illæ vero à Magistris nostris in utramque partem disputabantur verbis & terminis tam obscuris & barba-ris, ut Erasmus testatur, se magni nominis Theologum novisse, qui negitaret, ix. annos iis duntaxat intelligendis sufficere quæ Subtilis Doctor in Præfationem magistri commentatus est.
units.tr: Meanwhile I think it deserves great astonishment that the old Sorbonne took it so badly that this new theology strutted with such a proud step into the very middle of Christendom. For it dared to publicly censure Thomas's writings, because he had mixed the pagan philosophy of Aristotle with the Holy Scriptures; or, to use their own words, because he had applied the principles of philosophy too closely to theological conclusions. Theologians ought not to speak as philosophers speak, they say. Dominic, that most celebrated father of the Preaching Order, who lived around the year 1200, was also more far-sighted than all his contemporaries. For when he saw that knowledge of the Scriptures was absolutely necessary for a preacher, he urged his brothers to study the Old and New Testaments without ceasing, and when sent out to preach to carry only the Bible with them. For he held the fictions of the philosophers in little regard, as the author of his life says. If all who lived in that century had had the same mind, this monster would never have made for itself such a broad road to spread. But because the judgments of God's Church pressed upon them, that most grave censure of the Sorbonne, and the warnings of Dominic and of any others of his spirit, were moreover disregarded. For the questioners went on turning the simplicity of faith into a curiosity for disputing, and whatever little light of truth was left they buried in a thicker night, devising every day new, useless, profane questions, so unknown to the Prophets and Apostles that, had God granted them the use of light again, they would have become nothing less than theologians. These questions were argued by our masters on both sides in words and terms so obscure and barbarous that Erasmus bears witness that he knew a theologian of great name who denied that nine years were enough merely to understand what the Subtle Doctor commented on in the Preface of the Master.

units.la: Tantæ molis erat in sacra illa hujus Diuæ penetrare, atque illa discere, quæ nec scire jubebantur, nec expediebat. Nihil, ni-hil Ecclesiam sic perdidit, ac hoc portentum, nihil Evangelii do-ctrinam tam profunde demersit, ac hic vespillo.
units.tr: Such was the great effort in penetrating that sacred divinity, and in learning those things which they were neither ordered to know nor was it useful to know. Nothing, nothing destroyed the Church so much as this portent; nothing sank the doctrine of the Gospel so deeply as this gravedigger.

units.la: I nunc Serari & magno Erasmo magni Momi stigma inure, quod Scholasticæ Theologiæ proceribus ubique inequitet. Nihil ille ipsorum acumini, nihil ingenio & rerum philosophicarum peritiæ detractum voluit. Quam parum ab istis adminiculis, quæ in sacrarum literarum interprete requiruntur, instructi isti proceres fuerint, quam confidenter tamen in earum interpretatione versati fuerint, quam sæpe, quam turpiter à veritatis regione aberraverint, id vero fuit, quod Erasmus passim voluit ostendere. At inquam ego nimis lenem, nimis Placentinum hic fuisse Erasmum. De Servilio Consule refert Livius, eum medium se gerendo nec plebis odia, nec apud Patres gratiam iniisse. In eundem modum Erasmus medium se inter Evangelicos & Pontificios gerendo, nec apud Episcopos & Monachos gratiam inivit. Nullus Evangelicorum circa Ecclesiæ Rom. errores & abusus ipso oculatior fuit, quo minus tamen libere sententiam suam sæpe edissertaret, multa obstitere. Pusillanimitas & ἀνθρωποφοβία in præclaro hoc Dei organo præpotuere. Quanto generosius fuisset, Placentiam prætervectum, recta Veronam cursum direxisse? Certe pruriginosa istorum hominum, quibus cum illi res fuit, scabies asperiori strigile fricanda fuerat. Et tu, Melchior Cane, eos vel ad sidera usque sublima, ego Ludovico Vivi subscribam, qui Theologiam scholasticam non artes solummodo bonas, sed & ipsam Theologiam peremisse asserit; nec non magno Scaligero, qui non injuria Scholasticos appellat protervos, audaces, factiosos, garrulos, qui lucem tenebris, nigra verterunt candidis & spinarum tristitate omnia condivere. Calculum meum appono magno Calvino, qui Scholasticam Theologiam definit, diabolicam artem litigandi, nihil aliud continentem quam otiosas & ad nihil utiles speculationes, in quibus quo quis fuit doctior, eo fuit miserior. Et punctum quoque meum ferct nobilissimus Ant. Sadeel, qui candem cum caverna Caci & equo Trojano comparavit.
units.tr: Go now and brand Serarius and great Erasmus with the stigma of "great Momus," which rides roughshod over the leaders of Scholastic theology everywhere. Erasmus wanted nothing taken from their acuteness, their talent and their knowledge of philosophy. How poorly these leaders were equipped with the aids required in an interpreter of sacred letters, how confidently they nonetheless meddled in their interpretation, how often and how shamefully they strayed from the region of truth, this is what Erasmus wanted to show everywhere. But I say that Erasmus here was far too mild, far too much of a Placentian. Livy reports of Servilius the consul that by steering a middle course he won neither the hatred of the plebs nor the favour of the Fathers. In the same way Erasmus, by steering a middle course between the Evangelicals and the Papists, won favour neither with the bishops nor with the monks. No one among the Evangelicals saw the errors and abuses of the Roman Church more clearly than he did, yet many things stood in the way of his often setting out his opinion freely. Timidity and man-fear [ἀνθρωποφοβία] prevailed in this distinguished instrument of God. How much more nobly would he have done, sailing past Piacenza, to have turned his course straight for Verona? Surely the itching scab of those men with whom he had to deal should have been scraped with a rougher strigil. And you, Melchior Cano, may raise them even to the stars; I will add my voice to Ludovicus Vives, who asserts that Scholastic theology has destroyed not only the good arts but theology itself; and also to the great Scaliger, who not unjustly calls the Scholastics headstrong, bold, factious, garrulous men, who have turned light into darkness, white into black, and seasoned everything with the bitterness of thorns. I add my vote to great Calvin's, who defines Scholastic theology as the devilish art of wrangling, containing nothing but idle speculations useless for anything, in which the more learned a man is, the more wretched he is. My point too will be supported by that most noble Antoine de Sadeel, who compared it to the cave of Cacus and the Trojan horse.

units.la: In hoc luto aliquot seculis Christianus orbis haesit. In hoc coeno demersa erat Europa, cum ei superiori seculo Lutherus, Erasmus, Reuchlinus, Melanthon, Calvinus, Zuinglius, Oecolampadius, Bucerus & caetera illa luminaria exorirentur. Andreas Carolostadius jam octo annorum Doctor erat, cum ad scripturarum lectionem accederet; tamen, cum circa annum MDX, in Acad. Witeberg. pro licentia disputasset, Actis Academiae insertum fuit hoc elogium, quod fuerit sufficientissimus. Quidam doctor Theologus rogatus de Decalogo, negitabat se ejusmodi librum in Bibliotheca sua habuisse unquam. Fatebantur veterani aliquot Theologi se toto vitae curriculo in Magistro, Thoma, Scoto adeo suisse occupatos, ut Bibliorum lectioni vacare nunquam potuerint. Agnoscebant multi Sorbonici, imo per Diem jurabant, se plus quam quinquaginta annos habuisse, quod nescichant, quid esset novum Testam. quae ipsorum formalia refert Rob. Sthephanus. Jacobus Latomus in Dialogo, quem methodo Erasmi de studio Theologico opposuit, cum mira clementia sublevet Theologiae distinatum, ut nec Grammaticae nec linguis, oratoribus cum velit discruciari, imo ne quidem lectione divinorum voluminum, veterumve interpretum, ne eorum quidem quos sacrosanctos habet Ecclesia *simul ac ventum est ad Neotericos, inquit Erasmus, inclementissime obruit miserum juvenem, exigens, ut nihil hujus generis non evolvat, Lombardum, Alexandrum, Scotum, Thomam, Bonavent. Armachunum, Altisiodor. Holcot, Bricot, Petrum de Aliaco, Occam. Durandum, Aymonem, Carrensem, Aegid. Tartaretum, &c. nullius omnino libri gratiam facit. In his vult consenescere theologum, priusquam utriusque testamenti libris studeat. Ne Patres quidem vult legi, nisi hoc labore exantlato, veritus proculdubio periculum, ne si prius, non dicam SS. literas, sed Patres legat, proceres istos theologiae scholasticaque quos jam recensuit Erasmus, non sine nausea possit legere. Hoc illis erat Theologiae studere. Istis suis Pantheologiis, summinis & sententiis immorabantur & ὡς ὄνι π' ἀπλῶς immoriebantur. Qui his laboribus superstitabant, secem senectutis sacrarum literarum lectioni impendebant. Sed veluti iis, quorum linguam absynthium infecit, omnis cibus potuisse absynthium sapit, ita his quoque qui meliorem vitae partem his tricis transfiniserant, sacrae literae non sapie-
units.tr: For some centuries the Christian world stuck fast in this mire. Europe had sunk into this mud when in the previous century Luther, Erasmus, Reuchlin, Melanchthon, Calvin, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer and those other lights arose.
