Andreas Carlstadt was already a doctor of eight years' standing when he came to the reading of the Scriptures; yet when, around the year 1510, he disputed in the Academy of Wittenberg for his licence, this commendation was inserted in the Academy's records: that he was most sufficiently qualified. A certain doctor of theology, asked about the Decalogue, said that he had never had such a book in his library. Several veteran theologians confessed that they had been so occupied throughout their whole lives with the Master, Thomas and Scotus, that they had never been able to find time for the reading of the Bible. Many Sorbonists acknowledged, indeed swore by God, that they had had more than fifty years of it and did not know what the New Testament was, which Robert Estienne reports in their own words. Jacobus Latomus, in the dialogue he set against Erasmus's method of theological study, so kindly relieves the student of theology of the burden that he need not be tormented with grammar, languages or rhetoric, nor even with the reading of the divine volumes or of the ancient interpreters, not even of those whom the Church holds as sacrosanct. As soon as one comes to the modern writers, says Erasmus, he mercilessly overwhelms the poor young man, demanding that he unroll nothing of this kind: Lombard, Alexander, Scotus, Thomas, Bonaventure, Armachanus, Altisiodorensis, Holcot, Bricot, Pierre d'Ailly, Occam, Durandus, Aymon, Carrensis, Gilles Tartaret, etc. He grants no favour to any book at all. In these he wants the theologian to grow old before he studies the books of either Testament. He does not even want the Fathers read, unless this labour has first been endured, doubtless fearing the danger that if he read first, I will not say the Holy Scriptures, but the Fathers, he could not read those leaders of theology and Scholastic theology whom Erasmus has already reviewed without nausea. This was what studying theology meant to them. They lingered over their Pantheologies, summae and sentences, and as if on an ass, simply [ὡς ὄνι π' ἀπλῶς] they kept lingering over them. Those who survived these labours devoted the dregs of old age to the reading of the sacred letters. But just as, for those whose tongue wormwood has tainted, every food tastes of wormwood, so for those too who had spent the better part of their life on these trifles, the sacred letters did not taste

units.la: *In Apolog. adversus Latomum, p. 85, tomi 3. sapiebant, id quod sunt, sed quod illi secum afferebant. In Ecclesia quicquid pro concione dicebatur, vel Legenda vel Allegoria erat. Quidlibet ex quolibet exprimebatur. Atque ut sutores sordidas pelles suis dentibus extendunt, ita illi SS. literas quocunque volebant detorquebant. Atque hoc erat secretiorem theologiam tractare. Literalis sensus explicatio ad Grammaticos & crassos theologos relegabatur. Quin in nonnullis quoque locis eo deventum fuit, ut textus ex Ethica Aristotelis pro concione propositi interpretati sint; id quod dominus Melanthon suis se auribus audivisse testatur.
units.tr: *In the Apology against Latomus, p. 85, vol. 3. of what they are, but of what those men brought with them to them. In the Church whatever was said in a sermon was either a legend or an allegory. Anything was drawn out of anything. And just as cobblers stretch dirty hides with their teeth, so they twisted the sacred letters whichever way they wished. And this was what it meant to treat the more secret theology. The explanation of the literal sense was relegated to the grammarians and to the crude theologians. Indeed in some places things went so far that texts proposed for a sermon were interpreted from the Ethics of Aristotle; a thing which Lord Melanchthon testifies he heard with his own ears.

units.la: Possem equidem multa huc convectare, quae vel maxime <bl>ἀγελαστ</bl>ζῷον homini risum concitent, si prolubium mihi esset in re seria ludere. Nisi quoque Erasmus in Apologiis suis & alibi hunc laborem mihi compendi fecisset. Adite ad eas, evolvite ejus ad N. Test. annotationes & crassam istius seculi barbariem, ceu in terrissimo speculo, repraesentari vobis censebitis. Ex cujus Ecclesiaste unum insuper hic adjicere non pigrabor. David Burgundus, Philippi Boni filius, princeps, pro isthoc seculo, eruditissimus, cum ad Episcopatum Ultrajectensem sublimatus audivisset, ex illis qui sacris initiabantur, paucissimos esse, qui literas scirent, bonum factum putavit, si ipse rem proprius cognosceret. Jussit ergo sibi in aula cathedram poni. Proponit Candidatis quaestiones, singulis pro gradus, quem affectabant ratione faciles vel difficiles. Quid sit? Trecenti erant. Repulsavit omnes, exceptis tribus. Obstupescebant illi, qui examinibus istis praeesse solebant & multis exorabulis id contendebant apud Praesulem, ut sententiam suam moderaretur, reputans, hoc seculum non gignere Paulos & Hieronymos, contentus esset illis quos praesens terret aetas. Addebant, cum magno Ecclesiae dedecore conjunctum fore, si ex trecentis tres tantum admitterentur. Quid Episcopus? Ille, ut erat servido ingenio, respondebat se Paulos & Hieronymos non requirere, non commissurum tamen, ut pro hominibus asini admitterentur. Id enim si fieret, cum Ecclesiae publico dedecore fore conjunctum. Hac cum non succederet, alia aggressi sunt Praesulem via. Alius aries admotus. Si tu hos non admiseris, in quiebant, oportet ut nostra nobis augeas salaria, alioqui sine his asinis non est unde vivamus. Hoc ariete, qui tamen multis modis retundi potuisset, dejectus est erectus Praesulis animus. Quis fuerit Ecclesiarum Belgicarum isthoc seculo status, hinc judicare est.
units.tr: I could heap up many things here that would make even the man who never laughs [ἀγέλαστον ζῷον] laugh, if I felt any inclination to joke about a serious matter. Erasmus, in his Apologies and elsewhere, has also spared me much of this labour. Go to them, read through his annotations on the New Testament, and you will think you see the crude barbarism of that age reflected as in a very clear mirror. I will not hesitate to add one more instance from his account. David of Burgundy, son of Philip the Good, a prince most learned for his age, when he had been raised to the bishopric of Utrecht, heard that among those who were being ordained very few knew their letters. He thought it a good thing to find out the matter for himself. So he had a chair set up for him in the hall and put questions to the candidates, each according to the grade they were seeking, some easy, some hard. There were three hundred of them. He rejected all except three. Those who usually presided over these examinations were astonished, and with many entreaties they begged the bishop to moderate his judgement, reminding him that this age does not produce Pauls and Jeromes, and that he should be content with the men whom the present age can supply. They added that it would be a great disgrace to the Church if only three were admitted out of three hundred. What did the bishop say? He, being of a fiery temper, replied that he was not asking for Pauls and Jeromes, but he would not allow asses to be admitted in the place of men, for if that happened it would bring public disgrace on the Church. When this did not succeed, they tried another way with the bishop. Another battering ram was brought up: "If you do not admit these men," they said, "you ought to increase our salaries, since without these asses we have no means of living." By this ram, which could have been beaten back in many ways, the bishop's resolute spirit was brought down. From this one may judge what the state of the Belgian churches was in that age.

units.la: Expectatis Auditores, ut narrem vobis prælia, quæ primi litera-rum restauratores cum clero, cum Stunicis, Beddis & Latomis depugnanda habuerunt? Non illud mihi eloquentiæ flumen est, ut ea vobis repræsentare possim. Illud possum vobis asserere, tunc cum barbariei jugulum petitum fuit, sacrum ordinem quasi œstro percitum fuisse, infestisque furiis agitatum magnos illos Heroas sic impetivisse, ut extricare se sine vitæ & famæ dispendio vix potuerint.
units.tr: You expect, listeners, that I will recount for you the battles which the first restorers of letters had to fight with the clergy, with Stunica, Bedda and Latomus. I do not have such a flood of eloquence that I could set them before you. This much I can assert: when an attack was made on the throat of barbarism, the sacred order was stung as if by a gadfly, and driven on by hostile furies it assailed those great heroes so fiercely that they could scarcely extricate themselves without loss of life and reputation.

units.la: Cur vero ita furebat Satanas? Liceat mihi cum B. Luthero respondere, Er roch das brate wol. Satis sagaciter odorabatur hoc assum, & regno suo ab hoc Sole eam augurabatur tempestatem, quam multis seculis componere non valeret. Videbat linguarum ope redditas orbi authenticas verbi divini tabulas, eas publice prælegi, densam errorum noctem discuti, Allegorizandi pruritum imminui. Videbant Sophistæ, auditoria sua imminui & Majestatem suam evilescere. Quid facerent? An ipsi discerent elementa; At hoc infra dignitatem suam positum judicabant, & ut hoc gratificarentur hæreticis, neutiquam inducere animos suos poterant. An hortarentur alios, ut discerent? At crassi illi homines in hoc uno subtiles erant, quod fauam suam per hæc studia periclitaturam viderent. Unde canes imitabantur, qui cum ipsi fœno non vescantur, boves tamen accedere prohibent. Hinc linguarum peritos hæreticorum patriarchas appellabant. Atque ut ουκ‑ dicam, nihil fecerunt reliquum, quo a linguarum & Scripturarum studiis juventutem abstterrerent.
units.tr: Why, then, did Satan rage so? Let me answer with Blessed Luther: He smelled the roast well. Satan sniffed out this roast very keenly, and he foresaw from this sun such a storm for his kingdom as he could not calm for many centuries. He saw the authentic tablets of the divine Word restored to the world by the help of languages, read aloud in public, the thick night of error being dispelled, and the itch of allegorising being checked. The Sophists saw their lecture halls shrinking and their majesty dwindling. What were they to do? Should they learn the rudiments themselves? They judged that beneath their dignity, and they could never bring their minds to gratify the heretics in this way. Should they urge others to learn? But those dull men were clever in one respect only: they saw that their own favour would be endangered by these studies. So they imitated dogs, which, though they do not eat hay themselves, still keep oxen from approaching it. Hence they called the experts in languages the patriarchs of the heretics. And to avoid saying nothing, they left nothing undone by which they might frighten young people away from the study of languages and the Scriptures.

units.la: Sed quemadmodum Religio Christiana sub imperatoribus, tot gladios, secures, rogos & vivi-comburia, tot persecutionum æstus superavit, ita hæc quoque studia, non sine numine, ex omnibus adversarum tempestatum plusquam decumanis fluctibus tandem eluctata sunt. Cessit tandem totingeniorum pertinaci studio & indefesso labori defatigata barbaries. Ex eo commodis Sophistarum decessit, quicquid proventui melioris literaturæ accrevit. Ex eo Theologiam puriorem ex solo verbo Dei Ecclesiis & Scholis redditam, ex eo principes Chr. Religionis articulos mascule assertos & a priscæ caliginis vepretis feliciter eruderatos, & Sacras literas clariori face illustratas vidimus. Hic tamen principes illi Repurgatores posterorum diligentiæ multa reliquerunt. Nec enim illis, per assiduas illas cum adversariis disputationes, ita exhaurire omnia, ut posteritati otia facere potuerint.
units.tr: But just as the Christian religion, under the emperors, overcame so many swords, axes, pyres and burnings alive, so many heats of persecution, so these studies too, not without the divine will, have at last struggled free from all the storms of adversity, more than tenfold waves. Barbarism, worn out by the stubborn zeal and tireless labour of all good minds, has at last given way. From that time whatever has been added to the advantage of better learning has taken away from the profit of the Sophists. From that time we have seen a purer theology, drawn from the Word of God alone, restored to the Churches and the schools; from that time we have seen the principal articles of the Christian religion manfully asserted, happily dug out from the thickets of ancient darkness, and the Sacred Letters illuminated by a clearer torch. Yet those great men who purged the Church left much for the diligence of posterity. For they could not, through those constant disputes with their adversaries, exhaust everything so completely that they could leave leisure to posterity.

units.la: Refert Nehem cap. 4. juvenum alios laborasse, alios lanceis, gladiis & arcubus armatos excubias egisse, alios altera manu ædificasse, altera vero arma tenuisse, in utrumque paratos. Eadem Heroum istorum in spirituali isthoc Reformationis opere conditio fuit.
units.tr: Nehemiah, chapter 4, tells how some of the young men laboured while others stood guard armed with spears, swords and bows, and others built with one hand while holding weapons in the other, ready for either task. The condition of those heroes in this spiritual work of the Reformation was the same.

units.la: Hanc suam industriam ut posteri imitarentur; ut scopulos, quos ipsi notarunt, posteri vitarent; ut viae, quam ipsi præiverunt, posteri insisterent, præcipuum ipsorum votum fuit. Cui an successorum studia satis responderint, id demum est quod jam secundo loco videbimus.
units.tr: It was the chief wish of those men that posterity should imitate their diligence, avoid the rocks which they themselves had marked, and keep to the road which they had gone before. Whether the efforts of their successors have answered this well is what we shall now see in the second place.

units.la: Primum autem Heroum istorum votum fuit, ut linguarum studia in Ecclesia conservarentur, & magis magisque excolerentur. Hanc illi viam nobis præivere. Huic ut insisteremus, ἀκαίρως ἀκαίρως [?] hortati sunt. Novi ego, inquit alibi Lutherus quantopere mihi contra hostes meos profuerit Ebræ linguæ notitia. Ecce viam quam ipse præivit. Reverendus vir Mart. Lutherus, verba Melanthonis, quam graviter nos &c. [vide cetera pag.122.ne opus sit, eadem iterare] Audiamus iterum Lutherum, vel id solum socordiam nostram excitare debebat, quod Diabolus per Academias & Monasteria his studiis semper reluctatus sit. An nescis, inquit, quo furore Monachi &c. [cætera vide infra pag.144.]
units.tr: The first wish of those heroes was that the study of languages be preserved in the Church and cultivated more and more. They went before us on this path. To urge us to keep to it, they exhorted us in season and out of season [ἀκαίρως ἀκαίρως]. "I know," says Luther elsewhere, "how greatly my knowledge of the Hebrew tongue has helped me against my enemies." Behold the way which he himself went before. The reverend man Martin Luther, the words of Melanchthon, how gravely we … [see the rest on p. 122, so there is no need to repeat the same]. Let us hear Luther again. This alone should have stirred up our sloth: that the Devil has always struggled against these studies through the universities and monasteries. "Do you not know," he says, "with what fury the monks …" [see the rest below, p. 144.]

units.la: Alterum eorum votum fuit, ut sacrorum Bibliorum lectioni semper invigilaretur, ut posteri iis logicè & distincte percipiendis studerent, ex iis sensus ad discretionem boni & mali exercitos sibi acquirerent, ut studerent in iis non pauculis tantum dogmatibus & controversiis, sed omni informationi & institutioni, in omnis virtutis ac pietatis methodo & experientia; Sacras literas quasi in succum & sanguinem suum converterent, ex quibus & stamen & trama Theologiæ constat, omnesque conciones debent vivere & spirare. Cum juvenis essem, inquit Lutherus assuescebam Bibliis ut bonus Textualis essem. Postea alios authores legebam. Sed, eos tandem abjicere coactus fui neque enim poterant conscientiæ meæ satisfacere, atque ita solis Bibliis me denuo applicui. Quo exemplo docemur & hoc 3. eorum monitum fuit, non esse commentariis & postillis nimium fidendum; neque ita adhærescendum scriptis humanis, ut divinis æquentur; neque ita indormiendum versionibus, ut nefas existimetur, eas ad fontes examinare.
units.tr: Their second wish was that the reading of the holy Bible should always be attended to: that posterity should study to perceive it logically and distinctly, should gain from it senses trained to discern good from evil, and should study in it not only a few doctrines and controversies, but all instruction and training, in every method and experience of virtue and piety; that they should turn the Sacred Letters into their own juice and blood, from which both the warp and the woof of theology are made, and from which all sermons ought to live and breathe. "When I was young," says Luther, "I used to accustom myself to the Bible so that I would be a good textual scholar. Later I read other authors. But I was forced in the end to cast them aside, for they could not satisfy my conscience, and so I applied myself again to the Bible alone." From this example we are taught also. This was their third admonition: not to trust too much in commentaries and postils; not to cling to human writings so closely that they are made equal to divine ones; and not to sleep so soundly over translations that it is thought wrong to examine them against the sources.

units.la: Quartum eorum votum fuit, ne Scholastica Theologia, tanto labore & sudore ab ipsis propulsata, unquam denuo in Ecclesias admitteretur. Cujus voti omnia Lutheri, Melanth. Calvini, Wigandi & aliorum scripta plena sunt. Quomodo vero his satisfactum à posteris sit jam videbitis.
units.tr: Their fourth wish was that Scholastic theology, which they had driven out with so much labour and sweat, should never again be admitted into the Churches. The writings of Luther, Melanchthon, Calvin, Wigand and others are full of this wish. How posterity has satisfied it you shall now see.

units.la: Sub ipsa Reformationis initia, quamdiu eo tramite incessum est, habuerunt Ecclesiæ Theologos in Scripturis potentes, & qui cum ἐχνίᾳ docerent. Aspice mihi hæc Ecclesiæ reformatæ initia. Quot lumina uno eodemque tempore in sacro isto candelabro fulserunt! Lutherus, Zwinglius, Melanthon, Calvinus, Bucerus, Bullenց. Martyr, Farel, Gryn. Leo Judæ, Capito, Oecolamp. Pellic. &c. Tunc sacer ille codex versabatur, tunc ex limpidis Israëlis fontibus potabant Ecclesiæ. Sed postquam eadem in poenam ingratitudinis nostræ derepente extinxit Deus, ambitiosorum quidem & furiosorum Matæologorum fuit copia, at vix tot pietate & Scripturarum cognitione excellentes Theologos συγχρόνως videre unquam potuerunt Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ, quot sunt Thebarum portæ, vel divitiæ ostia Nili. Quis vero sibi à lacrymis temperet, cum præsentem, piorum & Scripturariorum Theologorum raritatem intuetur?
units.tr: At the very beginning of the Reformation, as long as the course was kept on that path, the Churches had theologians who were powerful in the Scriptures and who taught skilfully [ἐχνίᾳ]. Look at the beginnings of the reformed Church for me. How many lights shone at one and the same time in that sacred candelabrum! Luther, Zwingli, Melanchthon, Calvin, Bucer, Bullinger, Martyr, Farel, Gryneus, Leo Jud, Capito, Oecolampadius, Pellican, and others. Then that sacred codex was in use; then the Churches drank from the clear springs of Israel. But after God, in punishment for our ingratitude, suddenly extinguished those lights, there was indeed a plenty of ambitious and furious wranglers, yet the Evangelical Church could scarcely ever see at one time [συγχρόνως] theologians as excellent in piety and knowledge of the Scriptures as there are "the gates of Thebes, or the riches of the Nile's mouths." Who can hold back tears when he looks at the present rarity of pious and scriptural theologians?

units.la: Ποῖοι μὲν ταρῳ̈ηχοφόρῳ ταῦτα ... ἢ π Βάχχοι.
units.tr: Which ... these things ... or the Bacchants. [Ποῖοι μὲν ταρῳ̈ηχοφόρῳ ταῦτα ... ἢ π Βάχχοι]

units.la: Unde vero squallidus ille Ecclesiarum status? Non aliunde quam ex eo, quod votis priorum repurgatorum non satisfactum sit, quod viam, quam illi nobis præiverunt, non triverint. Quod scopulos ab illis monstratos non vitarint. Postquam enim obdormissent primi illi Heroës, qui omne opus Domini quod fecerat Israëli, fuerant experti, surrexit ætas altera, generatio hominum, quorum animus fuit in patinis & ollis veteris Ægypti, qui novas & noxias contentiones excitarunt, nihil aliud moliente Satanâ, quam ut Ecclesiarum præfectos à Biblicis studiis & simplici illa Theologia abstraheret. Ecce enim linguarum studia paulo post collapsa sunt & cum iis rursus negligi cœpit sacer codex. Luxuriabant theologi evangelici, ex theologis crucis jam derepente facti theologi gloriæ. Detumuerat persecutio, consilescebant tempestates. Non dormitavit hic semper vigil ille Synagogæ suæ Episcopus Excitavit quæstiones, quæ in cœlo, tecto, in terra, fundamento destituebantur, inutiles, curiosas, Scholasticorum disputationibus non absimiles. Quinam vero ex hoc fonte dimanaverint fructus, cui adeo cornea fibra est, ut ad solam de iis cogitationem eon eat in lacrymas? Tot jam annis funestorum super cœna Domini dissidiorum serra reciprocata est. Quisque absumsit carnem brachii fui. Manasses stetit contra Ephraim, Ephraim contra Manassem.
units.tr: Whence, then, that squalid condition of the Churches? From nothing other than this: that the wishes of the earlier reformers were not satisfied, and that their successors did not beat the path which those men had marked out for us. They did not avoid the rocks which had been pointed out to them by those men. For when those first heroes, who had experienced every work the Lord had done for Israel, had fallen asleep, there arose another age, a generation of men whose minds were set on the pots and kettles of old Egypt. They stirred up new and harmful disputes, Satan doing nothing else than trying to draw the leaders of the Churches away from biblical studies and from that simple theology. See, soon afterwards the study of languages collapsed, and with it the sacred text began again to be neglected. The evangelical theologians grew wanton, and at once changed from theologians of the cross into theologians of glory. The persecution subsided, the storms grew calm. That ever-watchful bishop of his synagogue did not sleep. He stirred up questions which have no foundation in heaven, on the roof, or on earth, useless and curious, not unlike the disputations of the Scholastics. And what fruits have come from this source, a source so hard-hearted that the mere thought of it brings a man to tears? For so many years the saw of ruinous disputes over the Lord's Supper has been worked back and forth. Each has consumed the flesh of his own arm. Manasseh stood against Ephraim, and Ephraim against Manasseh.

units.la: * Eoque securitatis àprotervis quibusdam ingeniis in publico Ecclesia luslin processum est, ut non solum illa Iosephi confractione commoti non fuerint, sed sub eadem facetaetiam dicacitati in scriptis & concionibus otiose indulserint, Qua in re malorum nostrorum apicem agnosco. Quin & nonnulli inconsulto zelo, ad versus viros bonos, qui hanc animorum impotentiam detestantur, eum in modum efferantur, ut eos omnibus haereticis pejores esse proclament, ut qui Christum & Belial conciliare velint, qui in media contignatione habitent, atque ideo digni qui inferiorum foetorem hauriant & superiorum lotio perfundantur. 8 Et quia urgebant Europam Dei judicia ne nullus reconciliationi locus relinqueretur, excogitata sunt odiosissima nomina, per qua nihil aliud effectum fuit, quam ut partes magis magisque exacerbata fuerint. h Totus spiritus Theologicus & quicquid fere Dei providentia donorum huic saeculo contulit, in contentionibus insumtum fuit, atque hoc solum fere crepuerunt cathedrae. Summa, per has declamationes ingeniis juvenilibus & ambitiosis res & fama quaesita fuit. Et licet istorum locorum magna ex parte ea sit ratio, ut in terra fundamento, in calo, tecto destituantur & sic in abyssum imperscrutabilis omnipotentia & sapientia Dei excurrant, in iis tamen illi mortales adeo secure versantur, ac si calculos lusorios in alea tractarent. Et miramur istos contentionum vorticcs tot praeclara ingenia abripuisse ut in illas solummodo intenta, reliqua Theologiae capita, universam Theologiam practicam & SS. linguarum studia insuper-habuerint? Miramur, i oves, dum pastores inter se de pascuis altercantur, relictis illis, in avia dispersas & lupis praedam factas? Miramur per funestam illa dissidia tantum respirandi intervallum, hinc Pontificis, illinc Photinianis, aliisque sectis esse concessum? Quae tamen haec vesania est adeo arctum in minimis etiam controversis articulis urgere consensum atque interim ad flagitia; quae sine controversia detestatur Scriptura, & in Ecclesia tamen grassantur, connivere? Quis furor, in nuda Theoria & paucis controversiis, ac si ab illis mors aut vita aeterna penderent, aetatem terere, ad illa subsistere, sicut Israelitae olim ad cadaver Hazaelis, & nullis interim Dei flagellis aut fustibus impelli posse, ut ulterius progrediamur, praxin cum theoria conjugamus, non ex eristicis, & quae affectuum sordibus nimis inquinata sunt, scriptis, sed ex ipsis fontibus pietatem hauriamus collapsam disciplinam restituamus? Abusus in Scholis & Ecclesiis tollamus abominationes coram oculis Domini removeamus, in spirituali illa Babylone, communi hoste, expugnanda ejusque fundamentis ab jma stirpe convellendis dextras jungamus? Atque hic non possum mihi moderari, quin cum Lucano exclamem. Quis furor, fratres, qua tanta licentia ferri, Gentibus invisis Latium praebere cruorem? Cumque superba foret BABYLON spolianda trophæis, Bella geri placuit nullos habitura triumphos. Heu quantum potuit terra pelagique parari, Hoc quem civiles hauserunt sanguine dextra!
units.tr: And from such carelessness, with some shameless wits, it has come about that in public the Church has been mocked so openly that they were not moved by that breaking of Joseph, but under the same cover they have idly indulged in wit and jesting in writings and sermons. In this matter I recognise the summit of our evils. Indeed, some, with ill-considered zeal, rage against good men who detest this lack of self-control, to such a degree that they declare these men worse than all heretics, as men who wish to reconcile Christ and Belial, who dwell in the middle of the beams, and who therefore deserve to drink the stench of those below and to be drenched with the slops of those above. And since the judgments of God were pressing upon Europe, lest any room for reconciliation be left, the most hateful names were invented, by which nothing else was achieved than that the parties were more and more inflamed. 8 The whole theological spirit, and nearly whatever gifts of God's providence this age has bestowed, has been spent on contentions, and almost nothing but these chairs have resounded. In short, through these declamations, reputation and advancement have been sought by youthful and ambitious minds. And although the reason of those places is for the most part that they are left without foundation on earth, in heaven, or on the roof, and so run out into the abyss of God's unsearchable omnipotence and wisdom, yet these mortals move about in them so carelessly, as if they were handling counters in a game of dice. And are we surprised that such whirlpools of contention have swept away so many distinguished minds, so that they have been wholly intent on these alone and have scorned the remaining heads of theology, the whole practical theology, and the study of the sacred languages? Are we surprised, sheep, while the shepherds quarrel among themselves over the pastures, that you, left behind, are scattered into strange places and made prey for the wolves? Are we surprised that through those deadly dissensions only a breathing space has been granted, on one side to the Papists, on the other to the Photinians and other sects? Yet what madness is this, to press so tight a consensus even in the smallest disputed articles, and meanwhile to connive at the crimes which Scripture unquestionably condemns but which nonetheless rage in the Church? What frenzy is this, to waste one's life over bare theory and a few controversies, as if eternal life or death hung on them, to cling to them as the Israelites once clung to the corpse of Hazael, and, though no scourges or whips of God can drive us, not to advance further: to join practice with theory, and to draw our piety not from contentious writings, which are too soiled with the filth of the passions, but from the very fountains, and to restore our fallen discipline? Shall we not remove the abuses in the schools and churches, take away the abominations from before the eyes of the Lord, and join right hands to storm that spiritual Babylon, our common enemy, and to tear up its foundations from the root? And here I cannot restrain myself from crying out with Lucan: "What madness, brothers, what such great license of steel, to offer the blood of Latium to hateful nations? And when proud Babylon was to be stripped of its trophies, it pleased us to wage a war that would bring no triumphs. Alas, how much of land and sea might have been gained with the blood which our civil hands have poured out!"

units.la: Quot enim, quaeso vos Auditores, animæ, quot provinciæ, quot regna Ecclesiis nostris addi potuissent istis chartis, isto labore, isto zelo, isto ingenio, istis vigiliis, quæ omnia non tantum hausere, sed & fere exhausere detestanda hæc dissidia?
units.tr: For how many souls, I ask you, hearers, how many provinces, how many kingdoms could have been added to our Churches by these pages, by this labour, this zeal, this talent, these vigils, all of which these detestable dissensions have not only drained but almost wholly exhausted!

units.la: Sed pergamus ad alia. Versionem B. Lutheri qui non magni æstimet, næ is indignißimus est, qui in ullo æstimio sit. Noluit tamen ipse plus ei deferri, quam Hieronymus suæ. Interpres, non vates haberi voluit. Et uno ore doctores Evangelici semper professi sunt, nullam omnino versionem, Ecclesiæ, ceu authenticam, obtrudendam esse, nullam recipiendam, nisi QUATERNUS cum originali textu convenit. Posuerunt tamen nonnulli Diotrephes, queis propositum fuit τῶν κλήρων ἐχυεσίων, pedes suos in ipsissima pontificiorum vestigia, tributumque ivere versioni Lutheri eam fere authoritatem, quam Pontificii suæ Latinæ transcribunt. Adeo quidem, ut ejus reprehensionem vel correctionem certissimum Calviniani criterium judicaverint. D. JOH. PISCATOR, cujus in Bibliorum versione fidem Graserus se agnoscere & suspicere profitetur, quid non passus est à doctoribus quibusdam Evangelicis, qui grande nefas existimabant, à recepta Lutheri vel latium unguem discedere? Vix credo sic exagitatum à Monachis fuisse Erasmum, cum novam novi fœderis interpretationem publico daret. Hinc videas, vix ulli Augustanæ confessionis theologo eam hodie esse fiduciam, ut vel in scriptis vel lectionibus vel concionibus, Lutheri versionem redarguat, nisi cum longa adulatoriæ & Germano pectore indignæ protestationis ambage. Hæc tyrannis multa præclara ingenia premit & opprimit. Adeo semper Diabolus antiquum obtinet, & si per anticam ejicias, per posticam denuo solet irrepere.
units.tr: But let us pass on to other matters. Whoever does not esteem the version of Luther highly, indeed, is most unworthy of any esteem at all. Yet he himself did not wish more to be granted to it than Jerome wished for his own version: he wished to be held an interpreter, not a prophet. And with one voice the evangelical teachers have always professed that no version whatever is to be pressed upon the Church as authentic, and none is to be received, except insofar as it agrees with the original text. Nevertheless some Diotrephes, who aimed to lord it over the clergy [τῶν κλήρων ἐξουσιῶν], have set their feet in the very footsteps of the Papists and have granted to Luther's version almost the same authority which the Papists ascribe to their Latin. So much so that they have judged any criticism or correction of it to be the most certain Calvinist criterion. Dr. Johann Piscator, in whose Bible translation Graserus professes that he recognises and admires his faithfulness, what did he not suffer from certain evangelical teachers, who thought it a great sin to depart even a hair's breadth from the received Luther? I hardly believe Erasmus was so harried by the monks when he published his new interpretation of the New Testament. From this you may see that scarcely any theologian of the Augsburg Confession today has such confidence that he may correct Luther's version, whether in writings, lectures, or sermons, except after a long circumlocution of flattering protestation unworthy of a German heart. This tyranny oppresses and crushes many distinguished minds. So always the Devil keeps his old ground, and if you drive him out by the front door, he is wont to creep back in again by the back.

units.la: Alibi Scholastica theologia, quam tanto sudore primi isti fæcum Exverræ propulsaverant, & cum ea Scholasticorum termini denuo introintroducti sunt, phrasi Scripturæ, tanquam si ea abjecta nimis & plebeja esset, derelictui habita. At graviter monuerat magnus ille artium restaurator, * P. RAMUS, Spiritum S. verissimum esse Doctorem sapientiæ, clarissimum rhetorem, verbisque uti ad id, quod a nobis intelligi necesse sit, perspicuis, significantibus idoneis. Loquamur ergo, inquit incomparabilis vir, verba scripturæ, utamur sermone Sp. Sancti, denique divinam sapientiam & linguam nostram infantia & sophistica necorrigamus. Alibi scripta humana ex pulpitis prælecta sunt, at Prophetam aut Apostolum qui interpretaretur, nullus fuit. Cum tamen ipse Carolus V. indignum hoc Christiana Acad. ratus, anno 1556. in Acad. Lovan. sententiarum Interpreti, SS. Literarum Professorem adjunxerit. Alibi linguarum professiones pro derelicto habitæ sunt, multisque annis sine ullius linguæ professione Academiæ quædam steterunt. Quarum præfecti de parietib. & tecto nimis anxie mihi solliciti fuisse, quale vero fundamentum jaciendum esset, parum imo nihil pensi habuisse videntur. Alia Illustrissimis Frisiæ Ordinibus, cum hanc Acad. fundarent, mens erat, quæis detrium linguarum professionib. princeps cura fuit. Alibi linguarum Professiones tanquam appendiculæ & lacinia quædam facultatum purpuræ aslutæ sunt, quasi nihil interesset inter horariam linguæ alicujus prælectionem, quam disciplinæ aut facultatis alicujus Professor facile præstabit, & propagationem, quæ integrum, eumque laboriosum hominem desiderat. Ubique vero in linguarum Auditoriis solitudo fuit. Omnes adhortationes, omnia incentiva frustra fuere. Postquam omnes machinas expugnandæ juvenum socordiæ dicam an pervicaciæ, admovisses, audiebatur illud, hac nihil ad farinam conferre. Hoc uno axiomate defungebantur. Hoc omnium βαρβαρίζοντων intercalare carmen erat. Quicquid a linguarum peritis, quos illi criticos & Grammaticos appellabant, vel observabatur vel docebatur, suspectum illis erat. Cordate alicubi Jul. Cæsar Bulengerus, Non debemus nobis invidere, inquit, quæ a partiariis nostris bene observata sunt. At nostri hi βαρβαρίζοντες, ab omni novitate se abhorrentes, veteres illos, quos Grammaticorum detexit industria, errores de pulmonibus suis revelli nequaquam passi sunt. Adeo verum ab omni ævo fuit illud Aristotelis, πάντων χαλεπώτατον τὸ μεταδιδάσκειν εἶναι. Ita factum est, Auditores, ut fœdo illi monstro, Barbariem dico, defensores & Patroni nunquam defuerint imo ne nunc quidem desint. Quid jam miramur, Ecclesias Evangelicas multis in locis, sub indoctisdoctissimorum hominum, quibus gravabantur, pondere, gemuisse? Quid miramur, multas fuisse provincias, distrinctus & classes, in quibus nullus fuerit Ebraice, pauci Graece periti? Quid exagitamus Bellarminum lib. 2. de verbo Dei cap. 10. hoc ingenuè de multis conciliis confitentem? At tunc barbaries erat. Tunc Linguarum Professiones Academiae ignorabant. Verbo, universo Christianismo nox atra incubabat.
units.tr: Elsewhere Scholastic theology, which those first men of the dregs of Ezra had driven out with such sweat, has been brought in again along with the Scholastic terms, and the phrasing of Scripture has been left aside, as if it were too abject and plebeian. But that great restorer of the arts, P. Ramus, had gravely warned: that the Holy Spirit is the truest teacher of wisdom and the most brilliant orator, and uses words that are clear and suited to signify what we must understand. Let us therefore speak, says that incomparable man, the words of Scripture; let us use the speech of the Holy Spirit; in short, let us correct divine wisdom and our own tongue from infancy and from sophistry. Elsewhere human writings have been read out from the pulpits, but there was no one to interpret a Prophet or an Apostle. Yet Charles V himself, thinking this unworthy of a Christian academy, in the year 1556 added to the Academy of Louvain a professor of Holy Scripture alongside the interpreter of the Sentences. Elsewhere professorships of languages have been treated as neglected, and for many years some academies have stood without any professor of language. Their leaders seem to have been too anxious about walls and roof, but to have had little or no concern as to what foundation ought to be laid. The most illustrious orders of Friesland, when they founded this academy, had the intention that the chief care should be given to the professorships of the languages. Elsewhere the professorships of languages have been tacked on as appendages and fringes of the purple of the faculties, as if it made no difference between the hourly lecture on some language, which any professor of a discipline or faculty will easily deliver, and the teaching which demands a whole, and laborious, man. Everywhere, however, there has been solitude in the lecture halls of the languages. All exhortations, all incentives were in vain. After you had applied all the machines to storm the sloth, or rather the obstinacy, of the young, it was heard: "These things contribute nothing to the bread." They dispatched the matter with this one axiom. This was the refrain of all these barbarizers [βαρβαρίζοντων]. Whatever was observed or taught by experts in languages, whom they called critics and grammarians, was suspect to them. Julius Caesar Bulenger, a man of sound judgment, said somewhere: "We should not begrudge ourselves what our predecessors have well observed." But these barbarizers of ours, shrinking from every novelty, have by no means allowed those errors which the industry of the grammarians had uncovered to be plucked out of their lungs. So true from every age is that saying of Aristotle, that it is the hardest of all things to teach others anew [πάντων χαλεπώτατον τὸ μεταδιδάσκειν εἶναι]. And so it has come about, hearers, that that foul monster, I mean barbarism, has never lacked defenders and patrons, and indeed does not lack them even now. Why then do we wonder that the Evangelical Churches in many places groaned under the weight of the most unlearned men by whom they were burdened? Why do we wonder that there were many provinces, districts, and classes in which there was no one skilled in Hebrew and few skilled in Greek? Why do we berate Bellarmine, Book 2 on the Word of God, chapter 10, who frankly confesses this of many councils? But then it was barbarism. Then the academies did not know professorships of languages. In a word, black night brooded over the whole of Christendom.

units.la: Interim juventus intelligens, quam facilis ad ministerium esset aditus, libidini, crapulae & socordiae fibulam laxavit. Omnis in postillis spes posita est. Ad quas in hac literarum luce tanta facta est novarum undequaque accessio, ut quod de Jurisprudentia argute pronunciavit Lipsius, ego de Postillis merito usurpari posse censeam, eas multorum camelorum onus esse. Has pigrorum pulvinaria non injuria pii Theologi vocitant. Et quidem haec sententia eo mihi probatur magis, quod videam sola Evangelia à plurimis retenta. Quod si enim epistolis quoque dominicalibus locum fecissent, alternisque septimanis populo expositissent, jam non singulis annis, sed biennis, labor ille in orbem rediisset.
units.tr: Meanwhile the young, understanding how easy the way into the ministry had become, loosened the bridle on their lust, gluttony and sloth. All their hope was placed in the postils. In this light of learning, new ones have been added from every quarter, so that what Lipsius shrewdly said of jurisprudence, I think can rightly be said of the postils: they are a burden for many camels. Good theologians not unjustly call them the pillows of the lazy. My opinion is confirmed the more because I see that only the Gospels have been kept by most. For if they had also given a place to the Sunday epistles and expounded them to the people every other week, that labour would not have come round again every year but every two years.

units.la: Utinam vero Dordracenae Synodi theologi de abrogandis istis Dominicalibus ferium decretum perrogassent! Namque ejus executione nihil fuisset facilius, modo recta & seriain Ecclesiis praecessisset institutio. Hac ratione Postillas istas manibus eorum, qui istis tantum adhaerescunt, multosque adeo ministros, qui hanc anniversarias postillas recitandi consuetudinem ad extremam vitae calcem perpetuant, ad totius Scripturae assiduam Lectionem volentes nolentes compulissent.
units.tr: Would that the theologians of the Synod of Dort had proposed a decree at their holidays for abolishing those Sunday postils! Its execution would have been easy, provided that a sound and orderly teaching had first gone before in the congregations. In this way they would have forced those postils out of the hands of those who cling only to them, and forced the many ministers who keep up this habit of reading annual postils to the end of their lives, willy-nilly, to the constant reading of the whole of Scripture.

units.la: Haec fuit, Auditores, studii theologici in Plerisque Academiis hactenus ratio. Ad quam tot annis à majori theologorum parte connictum fuit, donec tandem postremis his annis, queis Deus O. M. multarum Scholarum luxum in luctum commutavit, derepente ex omnibus angulis ἐξ ἀσεβῶν exorti sunt, qui Ecclesiis Evangelicis liquido ostendere, quantum à prima illa simplicitate recesserint. Extat in hanc rem aurea & cedro dignissima praefatio Conradi Graseri, Theol. olim Thorunensis sanctissimi, quam praefixit commentario suo in 1 x. caput Daniel. Legeris illic non sine fructu & lacrymis, ult. verba pii Theol. non ad famam propriam, non ad ullum hominem, sed ad solum Dei tribunal in fatali lectulo respicientis. Quorum ego verborum unam periodum pluris fecero, quam centum furiosorum & ebriosorum theologastrorum, aulicarum tubaExtat & opus Wolfgangi Francii, Theologi Witebergensis non minus pii, quam eruditi, de recta interpretatione Scripturæ. Inibi dequeritur venerandus Senex, quam in SS. Literis hospites & peregrini plerique Theologiæ studiosi fuerint, qui tamen in recitandis Poëtarum versibus erant expeditissimi. Quiritatur, multos impetrato Magisterii titulo & tot annis philosophico studio tantum insumptis, Academiam relinquere & Ministerio applicari, coemptis Postillis quibusdam. Viva voce, inquit, interpretantem S. paginam audiverunt neminem. Sed in theologicis evadunt αὐτόχθονες & αὐτοδίδακτοι. Mihi non est dubium, inquit pius Senex, quin tales sint fepenumero publicarum calamitatum precipua causa. Postea in exemplum omnibus SS. Theologiæ studiosis proponit magni Drusii filium, cujus studiorum cursum & methodum ex præfatione Patris in præterita seu Annot. in N. T. integram exhibet. id quod & alibi à D. Haffenreuffero factum vidi. Postquam vero illa descripsisset Franzius, sic inquit, Hactenus verba Drusii patris. Qui & ipse ad istud summum Ebræa eruditionis fastigium nunquam pervenisset, nisi mature in adolescentia, Hebræa tractare & Hebræos scriptores evolvere coepisset. Scatent autem eruditione multiplici, Hebræa, Theologica & Theologis utilia bona- que sunt omnia istius viri scripta, imprimis propter hanc causam, quod ex Hebraeis scriptoribus multa nobis proponit talia, quæ nos tanta lingua istius scientia & libris Hebræorum destituti nunquam legere ac percipere valeremus.
units.tr: This, hearers, has hitherto been the method of theological study in most academies. For many years the greater part of theologians have struggled to keep to it, until at last, in these latter years, in which God, the greatest and best, has turned the luxury of many schools into mourning, there suddenly arose from every corner men [ἐξ ἀσεβῶν], "from the ungodly," who clearly showed the Evangelical churches how far they have departed from that first simplicity. There exists on this matter a golden preface, worthy of being preserved with cedar oil, by Conrad Graser, once a most holy theologian of Thorn, which he placed before his commentary on the tenth chapter of Daniel. You will read there, not without profit and tears, the last words of this pious theologian, looking not to his own fame, not to any man, but to the tribunal of God alone, on his deathbed. I value one sentence of those words more than a hundred of those raving and drunken little theologasters, trumpets of the courtiers. There is also a work by Wolfgang Franz, a theologian of Wittenberg no less pious than learned, on the right interpretation of Scripture. In it the venerable old man complains how many of the students of theology, guests and strangers in the Holy Letters, were nevertheless most ready in reciting the verses of the poets. He laments that many, having obtained the title of Master and spent so many years on philosophical study, leave the academy and apply themselves to the ministry, after buying some postils. "They have heard no one," he says, "expounding the Holy Page aloud." But in theological matters they turn out to be [αὐτόχθονες] "sprung from the earth" and [αὐτοδίδακτοι] "self-taught." I have no doubt, says the pious old man, that such men are very often the chief cause of public calamities. Afterwards, as an example to all students of Holy Theology, he sets before them the son of the great Drusius, whose course and method of study he sets out in full from the father's preface to his Annotations on the New Testament. I have seen this also done elsewhere by Dr Haffenreuffer. But after Franz had described these things, he says: "So far the words of the father Drusius." He himself would never have reached that highest summit of Hebrew learning unless he had begun, early in youth, to handle Hebrew and to unroll the Hebrew writers. Indeed all the writings of this man abound in manifold learning, Hebrew and theological, and are useful to theologians, above all for this reason: that from the Hebrew writers he sets before us many things of such kind that we, lacking such knowledge of that language and the books of the Hebrews, could never read and understand.

units.la: Idem alibi optat, multos Theologos Cl. Drusii diligentiam in explicandis SS. Literis æmulari. Sed redeamus ad propositum nostrum. Idem ergo Francius pag. 18. conqueritur, integras sæpe audiri disputationes Academicas, in queis ne unius quidem dicti Scripturæ mentio ab opponentibus fiat, ad eum modum, inquit, quo olim disputarunt & docuerunt sub Papatu Scholastici. Certe de talibus disputationibus videor mihi jure adscribere hic posse cordatum Ludovici Vivis judicium, cujus hæc verba sunt, Omnis item jactantia, arrogantia, ostentationis occasio tollatur. Idcirco rara sint disputationes, in quibus non eruitur veritas. Nam nemo verum dicenti assentitur. Quaritur modo laus ingenii, vel peritiæ, in qua contentione laudis crescunt rixæ & convitia & simultates, quodque scelceratius est, ingenium contra veritatem sumit arma, & ad eam subvertendam cuniculos omnes agit & machinas, quascunque potest admovet, ut velit veritatem ab se superari & prosterni, non se veritati submittere. Quæ pugna adeo nefaria & impia bonos viros non decet, minus Christianos, quorum affectus purissimos esse convenit. & obsequentes veritati, qui est Christus ipse. Postremo ex illis disputatio-tionibus cavillosiores ac pervicaciores discedunt multi, doctior utique ac me-lior nemo. Hactenus Vives. Nunc ad Francium ex hoc diverticulo redeat oratio. Conqueritur postea, proscriptam rursus ejectamque ex multis scholis illam ex verbo Dei theologizandi rationem, a Luthero tantopere commendatam & magne cum fructu usurpatam. Adducit gravissimas * Joh. Wigandi & † Drusii in Scholasticam Theologiam invectivas. Asserit denique, reductae eidem in scholas Evangelicas Theologiae imputandos esse prosperos istos successus, quos multis in regnis Ponificia idolomania obtinuit. .
units.tr: Elsewhere he wishes that many theologians would emulate the diligence of the renowned Drusius in explaining the Holy Letters. But let us return to our purpose. Franz, then, on page 18 complains that entire academic disputations are often heard in which not even a single saying of Scripture is mentioned by the opponents, in the manner, he says, in which the Scholastics once disputed and taught under the Papacy. Certainly about such disputations I seem to be entitled to cite here the sensible judgment of Ludovicus Vives, whose words are these: "Every boasting, arrogance and occasion for display should be removed. Therefore disputations in which truth is not drawn out are rare. For no one assents to one who speaks the truth." Now the praise of talent or skill is sought, in whose contest of praise quarrels, insults and enmities grow; and, what is more wicked, talent takes up arms against truth, and brings up all the mines and engines it can to overthrow it, wishing to be overcome and cast down by truth rather than submitting itself to truth. Such a fight, so wicked and impure, does not befit good men, still less Christians, whose affections ought to be most pure, [and obedient to the truth, which is Christ himself]. "Finally, from those disputations many come away more cavilling and more obstinate, and none more learned or better." Thus far Vives. Now let my speech return from this digression to Franz. He complains afterwards that "that method of theologizing from the Word of God, so greatly commended by Luther and used with great fruit, has been banished and cast out again from many schools." He adduces the most serious invectives of [Joh. Wigandus and Drusius] against Scholastic Theology. Finally he asserts that the prosperous successes which Papist idolatry has obtained in many kingdoms must be imputed to the theology of the Evangelical schools, which has been brought back into them.

units.la: Paulo Tarnovio, primario Pietatis apud Roftochienses Profeff. justus quoque dolor gravissimam super praepostero studiorum Theologiae ordine querelam expressit. Namque inter causas proserpentis Socinani veneni secundo loco ponit errorem & imperitiam juventutis, quadam ministerio verbi se parat, neglecta linguarum & artium discendarum ratione legitima, (quae lucrose docentibus, sed damnose discentibus in leviculo illarum gustu & praepostero harum per disputationes cognoscendarum modo ponitur) id unice agit, quamdiu in scholis superioribus haeret, ut controversias quasque intricatas & difficillimas degustet, de iis cum aequalibus conferat, ne dicam altercetur, omissa interim, vel certe posthabita, SS. literarum lectione assidua & sedula. Idem alibi conqueritur, plerisque ordinis Theologici hominibus nihil curae esse praeter controversiarum subtilissimarum quovis aevo agitatarum in orbem reductionem, ventilationemque; aut concionum omni arte exornandarum & ad plebem cum applausu habendarum studium.
units.tr: Paulo Tarnovius, the chief professor of piety among the Rostock men, also expressed a just and grave complaint about the perverse order of theological studies. For among the causes of the creeping Socinian poison he places in second place "the error and inexperience of the young, who prepare themselves for the ministry of the Word while neglecting the proper method of learning languages and arts (which is set down as profitable to the teachers, but harmful to the learners, in a slight tasting of those things and in the perverse manner of learning them through disputations). They aim only at this, for as long as they remain in the higher schools, to taste all the intricate and most difficult controversies, to confer about them with their fellows, not to say to quarrel, meanwhile neglecting, or at least placing second, the constant and diligent reading of the Holy Letters." The same man complains elsewhere that most men of the theological order care for nothing except the endless rehashing and airing of the most subtle controversies that have been debated in every age, or the study of sermons adorned with every art and delivered to the common people with applause.

units.la: Quae vero sit vera Theologia & religio Christiana, paucos hodie scire, multo pauciores, quibus curae sit, ut id sciant. Omne studium pietatis ruere, Theologiam rursus in Sophisticam, seu potius curiosarum disputationum furores degenerare, atque ita non tam sublatam, quam mutatam superioris aevi Sophisticam.
units.tr: As to what the true theology and Christian religion is, few today know, and far fewer are concerned to know it. Every zeal for piety is collapsing, and theology is again degenerating into sophistry, or rather into the frenzies of curious disputations, so that the Scholasticism of an earlier age has not so much been abolished as changed.

units.la: Eodem spiritu incaluit hujus ex fratre nepos, JOH. TARNOVIUS felix ille SS. Literarum interpres, Academiae ejusdem Sol oriens, & ocellus, cujus viri pretium Academia Roftoch. & Ecclesiae Evangelicae ignorare mihi videntur. Hoc elogium praeclaris ejus laboribus debetur, licet in nos quos Calvinianos passim appellat, ex omni occasione incurrat. Is, inquam, Tarnovius Sentio, inquit, gravius haec a me dici, quam forte an pro hac mea aetate. Verum cum (prob dolor!) nimis verum sit quod queror & notius quam ut negari queat, quam turpiter hodie a plerisque Theologia studiosis, itemque aliis aliis nonnullis, qui eidem dant operam. Fontes ipsi, imo tota negligantur Biblia, justus in re tam ardua zelus hac mihi facile potuit exprimere. B. Meisnerus apud eundem illud in multis desiderat, quod fontes raro aspiciant, & delectum in dictis scripturae allegandis nullum habeant, certo argumento, eos ne versiones quidem legere, sed ad exemplum veterum Monachorum loca Scripturae ex concordantiis corradere, quod utinam in Ecclesiis, quas Lutheranas vocant, solis fieret! Ecce enim ne illae sua vulnera detegi, nostra tegi quiritentur, audiamus cygneam cantionem praestantissimi olim Heidelbergensium Theologi & Concionatoris, D. Abrah. Sculteti, Ἐν τῷ ἐν ἀγίοις.
units.tr: With the same spirit was kindled the nephew of this man from his brother, JOHANNES TARNOVIUS, that happy interpreter of the Holy Letters, the rising sun and little eye of the same academy, whose worth the Academy of Rostock and the Evangelical Church seem to me not to know. This praise is owed to his distinguished labours, although he everywhere attacks us, whom he calls Calvinists, on every occasion. This Tarnovius, I say, writes: "I feel that these things are said by me more severely than perhaps befits my age. But since (alas, what grief!) my complaint is too true and too well known to be denied, how shamefully today many students of theology, and likewise others who devote themselves to the same, neglect the sources themselves, indeed the whole Bible, a just zeal in so arduous a matter could easily have drawn this from me. B. Meisner also regrets in many places among the same men that they rarely look at the sources and have no selection in the sayings of Scripture they cite, a sure sign that they do not even read the versions, but, after the example of the old monks, gather the passages of Scripture from concordances. Would that this were done only in the churches which they call Lutheran! For let us hear, so that they may not complain that their own wounds are uncovered while ours are covered, the swan song of that most distinguished former theologian and preacher of Heidelberg, Dr Abraham Scultetus, in his swan song [Ἐν τῷ ἐν ἀγίοις]."

units.la: Qui in Scholis publicis sacra discunt hodie, eorum plerique in errore versantur longe maximo. Hoc enim sibi firmiter habent persuasum: praeclare se studiis suis consulere, si saepe multumque de doctrina Christiana Disputent. Itaque simulac pedem in Academiam intulerunt, de publica vel privata disputationis palaestra sunt solliciti: minime id facturi, si, quantum a vera discendi Theologiam ratione aberrant, intelligerent. Quod enim multorum aliorum errorum caput est, disputationes ipsam Theologiae animam esse putant: & cum e sacris literis verum Dei cultum proximique amorem addiscere debeant, illi contra ex Sophisticis disputationibus artem rixandi, altercandi, bene dicta pervertendi, familiarem sibi reddunt, omnis fere cura exercitiorum pietatis, fidei, invocationis abjecta. Res magna est, de Religionis capitibus disceptare cum aliis. Aetas ad eam matura; judicium confirmatum: linguarum cognitio proba requiritur. Quae omnia cum adolescentes in se nondum agnoscant: ordinem naturae invertunt, qui prius de Religione disputare, quam penitius illam nosse, volunt. Ac quam turpiter se dent hujusmodi disputatores, & ut prolata difficiliore aliqua Hebraica aut Graeca obmutescant, cotidiana Scholasticorum exempla docent. Praeceptum Servatoris est: scrutamini Scripturas, At nostra juventus magnam partem non Scripturas divinas, sed humanas scrutatur, & eristicos Magistrorum suorum libellos.
units.tr: Those who today learn sacred subjects in the public schools are, for the most part, caught in a very great error. They are firmly persuaded that they serve their studies well if they often and at length dispute about Christian doctrine. So as soon as they set foot in the Academy, they are anxious about the arena of disputation, public or private. They would certainly not do this if they understood how far they stray from the true method of learning Theology. For this is the source of many other errors: they think disputations are the very soul of Theology. Yet they ought to learn from the sacred letters the true worship of God and love of neighbour, whereas they make for themselves, out of sophistical disputations, a familiar skill in wrangling, quarrelling and twisting fine words, and almost all concern for the exercises of piety, faith and prayer is cast aside. It is a great matter to dispute with others about the heads of religion. It requires a mature age, a settled judgement and a sound knowledge of languages. Since young men do not yet recognise all these in themselves, they invert the order of nature when they want to dispute about religion before they know it more thoroughly. How shamefully such disputants behave, and how they fall silent as soon as some rather difficult Hebrew or Greek word is brought up, the daily examples of the Scholastics show. The command of the Saviour is: "Search the Scriptures." But our young people search for the most part not the divine Scriptures but human ones, and the contentious little books of their masters.

units.la: Nocturna versatque manu, versatque diurna:
units.tr: Night and day they turn it over in their hands

units.la: Quae de causa motiores ei sunt definitiones & distinctiones hominum, quam Dei, nec, ut Apollo, potens est in Scripturis Dei, sed in Scripturis hominum, magno suo, maximo Ecclesiae damno. Hanc enim cum adultiores factis studiosi nostri etudire debeant: exercitia autem concionandi neglexerint, disputandi urserint, de linguarum item studio & investigando gemino Scripturae sensu nunquam serio cogitarint: fit ut plurimum, ut in concionem productí constitutum sibi adversarium sustinere nullo modo possint. Nam qui μωρῶς ζητήσεις sectati sunt semper, qui scirent, quomodo germanus propositi Textus sensus eruendus? Quomodo ad auditorum usum exponendus? Quomodo ad consolationis, ad doctrinæ, ad exhortationis fructum, applicandus? Quin deridendos se eruditis proponunt dum vel coram indocto populo scholasticorum more disputant: vel pro verbo Dei venditant id quod in verbo Dei non continetur. Et paucis interjectis:
units.tr: For this reason definitions and distinctions of men are more familiar to them than those of God; and, unlike Apollos, they are not mighty in the Scriptures of God but in the writings of men, to the great and very serious harm of the Church. For although our students, once they are more mature, ought to study this, they have neglected the practice of preaching and pressed hard on disputation; nor have they ever seriously thought about the study of languages and the investigation of the twofold sense of Scripture. So it happens for the most part that when they are brought forward to preach, they can in no way hold their own against an adversary set in front of them. For those who have always pursued "foolish questions" [μωρῶς ζητήσεις], how would they know how the true sense of the proposed text is to be drawn out? How is it to be expounded for the use of the hearers? How is it to be applied to the fruit of comfort, of teaching and of exhortation? Indeed, they make themselves objects of ridicule to the learned, when they dispute in the manner of the Scholastics even before an untrained people, or when they peddle as the word of God what is not contained in the word of God. And after a few words intervened:

units.la: Vt ergò meo loco juventuti Academicæ consulerem, qui mecum de recta studium Theologicum excolendi ratione sententiam rogarunt, iis semper post doctrinam Catecheticam, commendavi accuratam considerationem Textus Biblici: in quo si potentes essent, tum verò illos & erudite cum quolibet disputaturos, & solide pro concione dicturos, affirmavi. Idem Theologus, quamdiu Embdæ vixit, sæpe illud ingeminabat, & audivi ipse ex ipsius ore sæpius, nunc plusquam tempus esse, das men der Bibel studirte, Es were genuch gehadert und geZanket: sat rixis eridique datum. Ipsum verò non alios solum ad hoc ipsum hortatum fuisse, sed & suo exemplo præivisse, postremæ ejus lucubrationes evidentes testes sunt. Quis non experitur inquit Clariss. Leidensium Theologus, D. Walæus, quæstiones plerasque, quibus tantum temporis in multis Academiis insumitur, aut nullum, aut omnino exiguum extra Scholas usum habere? Et ibidem, Quantum damni decreta Aristotelis cum divinis dogmatibus conjuncta dederint Ecclesiis, Scholastica Theologia abunde docet, à qua primi illi Reformatores eas cum magna laude repurgârunt. Videndum itaque etiam atque etiam, ne in idem vitium denuò relabamur. Quod si periculum illud procul abesse intellexissent, certe de eo vir prudentissimus non monuissent. Reverendus Theologus meusque in hac Academia collega, D. Gul. Amesius, nostri studiosi, inquit, eas tantum scripturæ particulas inspicere curant, quas ad locum aliquem communem vel controversiam definiendam ab aliis vident citari. Et paulo post, Satis est multis ad ministerium, imperfectum aliquod compendium leviter percurrisse, quamvis librum Dei signatum plane habeant, neque aperiri sibi curent. Et tamen indoctissimus quisque & pessimus audet & potest animum suum effœtum ad SS. Ministerium applicare.
units.tr: Therefore, so that in my own place I might look after the young Academics who asked my opinion about the right way to cultivate the study of Theology, I always commended to them, after the catechetical teaching, a careful consideration of the biblical text. I affirmed that if they were capable of this, then they would dispute learnedly with anyone and speak solidly in the pulpit. The same Theologian, as long as he lived at Emden, often repeated this, and I myself heard it from his own mouth more than once: that it was now more than time that one studied the Bible; "enough quarrelling and wrangling has been done" [es were genuch gehadert und gezanket]. That he not only urged others to this very thing but also went before them by his own example, his last writings are clear witnesses. "Who does not find," says the most illustrious Leiden Theologian, Dr. Walaeus, "that most of the questions on which so much time is spent in many Academies have either no use outside the schools or only a very slight one?" And in the same place: "Scholastic Theology abundantly teaches how much harm the decrees of Aristotle, joined with divine dogmas, have done to the Churches, and from it those first Reformers purged them with great praise. Therefore we must look again and again, lest we fall back into the same vice." If they had understood that this danger was far away, the most prudent man would certainly not have warned about it. The Reverend Theologian and my colleague in this Academy, Dr. Gulielmus Amesius, says: "Our students take care to inspect only those particles of Scripture which they see cited by others to define some common place or controversy." And a little later: "For many it is enough to have run lightly through some imperfect compendium for the ministry, although they have the book of God plainly sealed up and do not care to have it opened for them." And yet the most unlearned and the worst man dares and is able to apply his exhausted mind to the most holy ministry.

units.la: Celebris ille Acad. nostræ, dum vixit, Theologus, D. Sibr. Lubbertus b. m. publica oratione, qua aliquot ante beatum suum ex hac vita excessum mensibus Rectoratum auspicabatur, in studiosorum mores & circa SS. Literas socordiam gravissime detonabat, classibusque insuper nimiam in admittendis quibuslibet canditatis facilitatem objectabat. Nemo, inquiebat, tam probrose in Academia vixit, quin admittatur ad examen, nemo tam turpiter in
units.tr: That celebrated Theologian of our Academy, while he lived, the late Dr. Sibrandus Lubbertus, in a public oration with which he began his Rectorship a few months before his blessed departure from this life, most severely thundered against the laziness of the students in their morals and in their attitude towards the Holy Scriptures. He further complained of the excessive ease in admitting any candidates whatever to the classes. "No one," he said, "has lived so shamefully in the Academy that he is not admitted to the examination; no one has answered so disgracefully in the examination that he does not reach the ministry."

units.la: Orat. de studio Theol. instituendo.
units.tr: Oration on Establishing the Study of Theology.

units.la: Vide quæso supra p. 157. examine respondet, quin ad ministerium perveniat. Hinc Anabaptistæ dicunt, Quales sunt Reformatorum studentes, tales prædicantes. Quid vero belli isti homines jam ad cathedras sublimati agant, malo verbis aliorum, quam meis dicere. Gul. Telingius, vir magni zeli & eruditionis, ait ab hoc hominum genere cathedras disputationibus & controversiis subtilissimis impleri, idque inter homines in catechesi & religionis Christianæ fundamentis rudes, fructu adeo nullo, ut sæpe auditores existiment, sententiam illam, quam bellus Pastor confutavit, ipsius Pastoris & Reformatæ Ecclesiæ esse. Et tamen hunc docendi modum perpetuant, quia tunc in suo versantur elemento, quia hoc unum didicerunt, quia hoc sine labore præstare possunt, utpote qui nec spiritualis vitæ experientiam ullam habuerunt ipsi, nec ullam practicæ Theologiæ impenderunt operam. Hæc * Telingius. Qui paulo post ejusdem argumenti locum ex Bernardo producit, quem ex Belgico versum, quia Bernardus mihi ad manum non est, non pigrabor adscribere. Semper fere tractant controversias, quia ibi nihil necesse est malos hominum, quibus concionantur, mores redarguere. Oderunt enim plerunque homines conciones ejusmodi, quibus dissoluta ipsorum vita & peccata castigantur. Oderunt disciplinam. Et tamen qui in hunc modum populo norunt gratificari, concionatores discreti appellantur. At quam fervide religionis sint, cujus conscientia, & quo zelo accensi sunt erga correctionem hominum, Deo & piis Dei viris judicium defero. Quæ nec à rev. D. Telingio producta, nec à me ex eo descripta sunt, adversus eos, qui pro ratione textuum, locorum & temporum adversus hæreses & falsa dogmata solide & pie disputant, sed illos petimus, qui hoc SOLUM agunt, adhortationes ad pietatem Anabaptistis relinquentes, vel quia in hac palæstra non sunt exercitati, vel quia linguam conscientia ligat. Hi accipiant à me & æquis auribus audiant gravissimam Bernardi censuram, quæ extat in sermone ad fratres in Synodo congregatos.
units.tr: Please see above, p. 157. [...] Hence the Anabaptists say: "Such as the students of the Reformed are, such are their preachers." But what havoc these men now wreak, raised to their chairs, I prefer to say in the words of others rather than my own. Gulielmus Telingius, a man of great zeal and learning, says that chairs are filled by this kind of men with disputations and most subtle controversies, and that among people who are rude in catechizing and in the foundations of the Christian religion, with such little fruit that the hearers often think that opinion, which the good minister refuted, is the view of the minister himself and of the Reformed Church. And yet they perpetuate this method of teaching, because then they are in their own element, because this is the only thing they have learned, because they can perform this without labour, since they have had no experience of the spiritual life themselves and have spent no effort on practical Theology. So far Telingius. Shortly afterwards he brings forward a passage on the same subject from Bernard, which I will not hesitate to copy here, since I translate it from the Dutch version, as Bernard is not at hand for me. They almost always handle controversies, because there it is not necessary to rebuke the bad morals of the men to whom they preach. For men for the most part hate such sermons, in which their dissolute life and sins are chastised. They hate discipline. And yet those preachers who know how to please the people in this way are called discreet preachers. But how fervent in religion they are, whose conscience, and with what zeal they are inflamed for the correction of men, I leave to the judgement of God and of the godly men of God. These words were neither produced by the Reverend Dr. Telingius, nor copied by me from him, against those who, according to the nature of the texts, places and times, dispute solidly and piously against heresies and false dogmas; but we aim at those who do ONLY this, leaving exhortations to piety to the Anabaptists, either because they are not trained in this arena or because conscience binds their tongue. Let these men receive from me, and listen with fair ears to, the most grave censure of Bernard, which stands in his sermon to the brethren gathered in Synod.

units.la: Ad opera vos invito, vos maxime, qui pastores estis animorum, qui alios non debetis destruere, sed instruere. Vos inquam maxime, quia soli non possestis perire, qui praire debetis docendo & operando. Multi sunt Catholici prædicando, qui hæretici sunt operando. Quod hæretici faciebant per pravadogmata, hoc faciunt hodie plures per mala exempla. Seducunt sc. populum & inducunt in errorem, & tanto graviores sunt hæreticis, quanto prævalent opera verbis.
units.tr: I invite you to the work, you most of all who are shepherds of souls, who ought not to destroy but to instruct others. You, I say, most of all, because you alone cannot perish, you who ought to go before by teaching and by working. There are many who are Catholic in preaching but heretics in their works. What heretics did through perverse dogmas, many now do through bad examples. They lead the people astray and induce them into error, and they are all the more grievous than heretics as their works outweigh their words.

units.la: Sed quid his recensendis & me & vos delasso, Auditores? AnAnnon videmus hisce oculis nostris, vacua esse eorum, qui Scripturas interpretantur, auditoria? Annon ignotus in Evangelicis Academiis hospes est practicæ Theologiæ Professor? Annon ipsum nomen C a s u u m conscientiæ ludibrio apud plerosque etiam professione Theologos, est? Annon qui istos tractant aut subinde ore usurpant, per contemptum à profanis C a s u a l e s vocantur? Annon obstupit & ad rei novitatem attonita fuit nostra juventus, cum ante quadriennium Rev. D. Amesius, in præsens Academiæ Rector, professionem Theologiæ practicæ ab eruditissimis de conscientia thesibus auspicaretur? Annon contemptui apud multos sunt, qui suarum concionum tramam & stamen ex sola Scriptura depromunt & pietatem potissimum urgent? Annon male tractantur & petulan- tissimæ eujusque linguæ verbere flagellantur, qui ab inanium subtilitatum vorticibus ad Biblica & practica studia juventutem revocare satagunt? Loquantur etiam Francii & J. Tarnovii præloquia. Quorum ille insuper in ipso operis de interpr. Scripturæ titulo testatum facit, dictum opus singulari Electoris gratia, post varias censuras aulicas & Academicas, in dias luminis oras prodiisse. Vtendum tibi erit, inquit idem epistola quadam ad D. Joh. Tarnovium, eadem patientia, qua mihi cum primis opus fuit, annis proxime elapsis sex & am- plius. Dic bona fide, venerande Senex, quot passibus exstimas barbariem à tua Academia & Saxonia tunc temporis abfuisse?
units.tr: But why should I, and you, the audience, be wearied by listing these things? Do we not see with these very eyes of ours that the lecture halls of those who expound the Scriptures are empty? Is not the professor of practical Theology a stranger in the evangelical Academies? Is not the very name of cases of conscience a laughing-stock to many, even to those who profess Theology? Are not those who treat them, or from time to time take them on their lips, called Casuists by the profane, with contempt? Was not our youth astonished and stunned at the novelty of the matter, when some four years ago the Reverend Dr. Amesius, now Rector of this Academy, began his professorship of practical Theology with his most learned theses on conscience? Are there not many who hold in contempt those who draw the whole warp and woof of their sermons from Scripture alone and press piety above all? Are not those who strive to recall the youth from the whirlpools of empty subtleties to biblical and practical studies treated badly and whipped with the lash of every impudent tongue? Let the prefaces of Francius and J. Tarnovius also speak. Of these, Francius further declares in the very title of his work on the interpretation of Scripture that the said work, after various censures at court and in the Academy, came forth into the light of day by the singular grace of the Elector. "You will have to use," says the same man in a certain letter to Dr. Johann Tarnovius, "the same patience which I first of all had to use in the years just past, six years and more." Tell me in good faith, venerable old man, how many paces you think barbarism was from your Academy and from Saxony at that time?

units.la: Sed jam opinor, currentis sermonis rotæ fusflaminandæ sunt. Audivistis vota & lamenta virorum pietate & eruditione eminentium. Monstravi vobis viam, quam illi triverunt. Monstravi scopulos, quos ipsi vitarunt. Vos ex his capite, quod vobis ex usu sit. Disputationes omnes, arrige aures calumnia, non damnant. Sobrias, & quæ super utilibus thematibus, probant, si ab istis instituantur, quorum vita sanctæ professioni respondet, qui fundamenta religionis, inquit Tarn, ex S. codice & catechetica doctrina jam edocti sunt. Studium controversiarum non proscribunt, Illud monent, ne Tyro putet, aliquot controversiarum cancel- lis universam Theol. circumscribi, atque errorem volunt animis vestris evulsum, Posse aliquem Theologiæ studere, etiamsi non legat S. Literas. Illud insuper urgent, ut quæstiones à fructu æstimentur. Illa enim quæ nihil ædificant, inquit Calv. Com. in 1. ad Timoth. repudiandæ sunt, etiamsi nihil aliud vitii habeant. Quæcunque verò ad contentiones solum excitandas valent, duplici nomine damnantur. Talesporro sunt, inquit, omnes argutiæ, quibus ingenium suum suum ambitiosi homines exercent. Quemadmodum enim crassa in calore nubes non sine tonitru discutiuntur, ita necesse est, ut spinosa ista quaestiones in certamina ebulliant. Meminerimus ergo, ad hanc regulam exigendas omnes quaestiones, ut ea demum probentur, quae aedificant, quae vero disceptationum materiam praebent absque fructu, tanquam Ecclesiâ Dei indignae, respuantur. Hoc examen si fuisset aliquot supra saeculis observatum, etsi multis erroribus contaminata fuisset religio; saltem non adeo invaluisset Diabolica ista ars litigandi, quae Theologiae Scholasticae nomen obtinuit. Haec Calv.
units.tr: But I think the wheels of my discourse must now be drawn back. You have heard the wishes and laments of men eminent in piety and learning. I have shown you the path they have trodden and the rocks they have avoided. Take from this what is useful for you. Prick up your ears, critics: they do not condemn all disputations. They approve sober ones, and those that deal with useful topics, provided they are conducted by men whose lives match their holy profession, men already taught the foundations of religion, as Tarnovius puts it, from the sacred code and catechetical doctrine. They do not proscribe the study of controversies. What they warn against is that a beginner should think the whole of theology is marked out by the bounds of a few controversies, and they want the error uprooted from your minds: one can study theology even without reading the Holy Scriptures. They press this further, that questions should be judged by their fruit. For those questions which build up nothing, says Calvin in his commentary on 1 Timothy, must be rejected, even if they have no other fault. Whatever is good only for stirring up contention is condemned on two counts. Such, he says, are all the subtleties in which ambitious men exercise their wit. For just as a thick cloud in the heat is not dispersed without thunder, so these thorny questions must boil over into strife. Let us remember, therefore, that all questions are to be measured by this rule: those that build up are to be approved, while those that offer material for dispute without fruit are to be rejected as unworthy of the Church of God. If this test had been observed some centuries ago, religion, though contaminated by many errors, would at least not have grown so strong this devilish art of wrangling which has taken on the name of scholastic theology. So Calvin.

units.la: Ad quae illud liceat mihi addere, nisi idem quoque examen in posterum in Scholis & Ecclesiis nostris observetur, majores nobis imminere turbas, quam quae hactenus nos exercuere dum subinde in Theologorum scholis videmus proponi quaestiones, non solum curiosas, inutiles, & quae nihil aedificent, sed & prout proponuntur, plenas scandali & pietatis jugulum petentes. Controversiarum scientiam, inquit Cl. D. Amesius, necessariam fecerunt Haeretici. Quod si aliquando in eas provincias deportaremini, ubi nullae haereses, cuius usui vobis esset vestra Theologia, si illam polemicam tantum didicissetis? At contra studium pietatis absolutè necessarium Deus mandavit. Si ergo sic infaniamus circa quaestionum pugnas, ut doctrinam pietatis negligamus, nescio sane, an multae haereses non aeque fere noceant impugnantibus, quos ab utilioribus avocant, ac ipsis haereticis nocent, quos tamen in magna mala abstrahunt.
