Quid ergo? Controversiae in Theologicis, neque fugiendae, neque etiam quaerendae sunt. Sed ubi necessariae exstiterint, admitti & ex certis principiis breviter explicari debent. Solida autem Theologiae ratio, quam positivam vocant, in primis ex Script. hauriendā est & recta methodo imbibenda.
units.tr: To this I may add: unless this same test is observed in future in our schools and churches, greater troubles will hang over us than those which have troubled us so far, since from time to time we see in the schools of the theologians questions proposed that are not only curious, useless and edifying nothing, but, as they are put, full of scandal and aimed at the throat of piety. It is heretics who have made the knowledge of controversies necessary, says the distinguished Dr. Amesius. But if you were ever carried off to those regions where there are no heresies, what use would your theology be to you if you had learned only the polemical part? On the contrary, God has commanded the study of piety as absolutely necessary. If, then, we so rave over the battles of questions that we neglect the doctrine of piety, I really do not know whether many heresies do not harm those who are diverted by them from more useful things almost as much as they harm the heretics themselves, whom they drag into great evils. What then? Controversies in theology are neither to be shunned nor sought out. But where they have become necessary, they must be admitted and briefly explained from certain principles. The solid reasoning of theology, which they call positive, must above all be drawn from Scripture and absorbed by the right method.

units.la: Rursus, ne ita vobis linguarum studia commendari putetis, quasi ea solae utramque in Θεολογικὰ Theologica paginam faciant. Sobrie etiam philosophandum est, & utiliores philosophiae partes discendae sunt. Imprimis vero, Logicae, divinae isti judicii Limae & ingeniorum coti, litandum est. Nullam esse inter haec studia ἀντιπαθείας, nullas inimicitias, praeclara aliquot ingenia in hac etiam Academia suo exemplo docent, quorum exemplum si caeteri imitarentur, res Ecclesiarum aequabilius & constantius se haberent, quae nunc, dum indoctissimi & pessimi quique ad S. Ministerium aspirare audent, non parum foedantur.
units.tr: Again, do not think that the study of languages is recommended to you as though it alone makes both pages of theology [Θεολογικὰ]. Philosophy too must be pursued soberly, and the more useful parts of it must be learned. Above all, one must offer sacrifice to logic, that file of judgement and whetstone of minds. That there is no antipathy [ἀντιπαθείας], no enmity, between these studies, some outstanding minds in this very Academy teach by their example; if the rest imitated them, the affairs of the Churches would stand on a more even and steady footing, which now, while the most untaught and worst men dare to aspire to the holy ministry, are not a little disfigured.

units.la: Vestram autem hic tandem imploro opem, Magn. DD. Curatores, utrum jam inter nos grassetur morum & literarum Barbaries, an ad portas sit, vestri judicii facio. Si jam grassari putetis, cam masculis decretis expellite. Si imminere, arcete. Indoctorum Ministrorum, impudentium & barbarorum rabularum, imperitorum Medicastrorum satis est. Theologis & Ministris eruditis, Jurisconsultis literatis, Medicis politis, philosophis tersis, Rectoribus & præceptoribus doctis, bonarum literarum & linguarum propagatoribus & restauratoribus, omnibus autem illis piis, tempus eget, & egebit posteritas. Reformate scholarum & Academiæ studia, & brevi aliam Reip. & Ecclesiæ faciem videbitis. Scio equidem vos hoc ex animo velle. Et vero vos hoc etiam posse, omnes boni sperant. Magna est, fateor, in Rep. nostra omnium rerum vertigo, sed eam ex scholis dissolutis & Academiis male constitutis, magnam partem fluere, hinc esse primam malorum labem, iidem censent. Equidem, si adversus vestrum quoque zelum, vestramque authoritatem invaluit hoc monstrum, nobis propemodum desperandum censeo. Sed causam de VV. AA. desperandi nullam habemus. Adeo præclara masculæ virtutis vestræ documenta dedistis. Magnis animis & pectore firmo nunc opus est. Olim animi in literas propensi tantum, nunc constantiæ periculum subitur. Eo enim jam deventum, utor verbis magni Heinsii, ut vel eruditio ac virtus, tanquam clypeus, abjicienda, aut pro iis fortiter pugnandum sit. Porro ut in acie afflicta ac à ceteris deserta, qui postremus omnium tuetur locum, robur partis, causa ac momentum victoriæ habetur, quia animos ab hoste, à calamitate sumit vires: ita hac ætate plus meretur qui non cessat, quam superioribus, qui aliquid cum multis laude dignum præstiterunt. Quod ad clarissimos Academiæ hujus Professores, collegas meos honorandos, attinet, quisque spartam suam exornabit, vestrisque AA. in propulsando hoc monstro auxiliares præbebit manus. Quod ad me, novi quam exigua in me sit juvandi facultas, attamen interseos, quibus promta voluntas est, profiteor me velle.
units.tr: Here at last I beg your help, distinguished Curators: whether the barbarism of morals and letters is already raging among us or is only at the gates, I leave to your judgement. If you think it already rages, drive it out with manly decrees; if it is threatening, keep it off. Ignorant ministers, shameless and barbarous ranters, and untrained quacks are enough. What is needed, and what posterity will need, are learned theologians and ministers, literate jurists, polished physicians, refined philosophers, teachers and tutors who are learned, and propagators and restorers of good letters and languages, and all those pious people. Reform the studies of the schools and the Academy, and soon you will see another face of the Commonwealth and the Church. I know well that you wish this from your hearts. And that you are able to do it, all good men hope. Great, I admit, is the upheaval of everything in our Commonwealth, but the men who hold that it comes in large part from dissolute schools and badly organized Academies also hold that this is the first source of the evils. Indeed, if this monster has grown strong even against your zeal and your authority, I think we must almost despair. But we have no reason to despair of your Honours. You have given such brilliant proofs of manly virtue. What is needed now are great spirits and a firm heart. In former times minds were inclined only to letters; now the peril of constancy is undergone. For matters have reached the point, to use the words of the great Heinsius, that either learning and virtue must be cast aside like a shield, or one must fight bravely for them. Moreover, as in a battle-line that is broken and deserted by the rest, the one who holds the last place is regarded as the strength, cause and turning-point of victory, because he takes spirit from the enemy and strength from the calamity; so in this age he deserves more who does not give up than those earlier men who achieved something worthy of praise along with many others. As for the most distinguished professors of this Academy, my colleagues, each will adorn his own post and will offer helping hands to your Honours in repelling this monster. As for me, I know how small my ability to help is, yet I declare among those who have a ready will that I am willing.

units.la: Ἀιὲι ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων.
units.tr: [Ἀιὲι ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων.] Always to excel and to be superior to others.

units.la: D. I. X. I.
units.tr: D. I. X. I.

units.la: SPECVLVM SS. Ministerii Candidatorum qui minus digne Evangelio vivunt.
units.tr: A mirror for the holy candidates for the ministry who live less worthily than the Gospel requires.

units.la: COmmunicavit mihi aliquando pius & celebris quidam Theologus epistolam, quam ab amico quodam acceperat. Is aliquandiu Ecclesiae cuidam, quae celebri loco sub cruce est, inserviverat: Et quidem cum laude & fructu. Lubet autem ex ea decerpere, quae ad rem mihi pertinere visa sunt. Nomen authoris, ut & locorum, cur subticuerim, causas habui. Sciat tamen Lector, inculpatae vitae & insignis eruditionis hominem esse.
units.tr: A pious and well-known theologian once sent me a letter that he had received from a friend. This friend had for some time served a certain congregation in a famous place beneath the cross, and he had done so with praise and fruit. I have chosen to extract from it the parts that seemed relevant to my purpose. I had reasons for keeping silent about the author's name and about the places. Still, let the reader know that he is a man of blameless life and remarkable learning.

units.la: ......Forsan à Domino .... permanavit ad tuas aures de mea perturbatione rumor aliquis; si non, nunc lubet illam sibi aperire, tum ut precibus me tuis peculiariter commendatum habeas, tum ut pio (si fieri potest per occupationes tuas) consilio, & documentis instructior evadam. Res ita se habet.
units.tr: ......Perhaps some rumour of my distress has reached your ears from the Lord ....; if not, I now wish to disclose it to you, both so that you may hold me especially commended in your prayers, and so that I may become better instructed by your pious counsel (if it can be given amid your occupations) and by your teaching. The matter stands thus.

units.la: .... Synodus ante biennium misit me ............ ut ministerium obirem, testis est mihi Deus, me illuc alacri & generoso animo. Ibi aliquandiu non sine fructu per Dei gratiam versatus sum; sed tandem, cum mea simul & Ecclesiae cui eram propositus, sese mihi proderent peccata, & viderem me revera νόφυλον esse; & imparem tanto oneri, & ad tantos, quibus scatebat ille coetus, abusus reformandos ineptum; abjeci hastam, & gravissimo pressus maerore languebam, non solum ad reliquam curam Ecclesiasticam: sed ad concionandum quoque inutilis, ergo ab Ecclesiae illius Senioribus rursum ad ...... ablegatus sum, ut iis proponerem ea qua solicitarent tantopere animum meum; illi malum meum meram Melancholiam esse rati, consilium dederunt, ut in Patriam iter susciperem, & parentes consanguineosque inviserem: huic pa-rui rui consilio; sed calum non animum mutant qui trans mare currunt; hoc itinere potius aucta quam imminuta est afflictio; quippe contagiosa carnalium hominum societas reduplicavit mihi mentis aegritudinem: igitur ab amicis & consanguineis libentius aufugi quam accesseram; & hic ...... delitesco apud honestissimum virum cujus filium instruo in bonus literis: hic majori quidem quam olim quietę animi fruor; sed tamen multis adhuc inquietor dubitationibus, quae à ministerio abs terrerent animum meum. 1. Internam vocationem non percipio id est, quamvis cupiam potius in ministerio quam mechanico aut alio vitae genere aetatem transigere, tamen certitudo illa deest, qua spem quilibet recte vocatus fovere debet, Deum suis affuturum laboribus. 2. Præcipua pars veri ministerii hactenus mihi est incognita, neque de ea à quoquam praeceptorum meorum fui admonitus; sc. quid sit vigilare pro animabus gregis tanquam rationem redditurus? ut ait Apostolus ad Hebr. 13.17: qualis & quam particularis illa vigilia esse debeat, tum respectu personarum; tum respectu actionum. 3. Denique cum hac cura adhiberi nequeat sine judicatione, quomodo judicium illud (de quo Apostolus. 1. Cor. 5. 12. & alibi) & qua norma praestandum sit? Praeter hac, de quibus (ut mihi videtur) verus pastor neutiquam ambigere debet, alia sunt varia quae perplexum me reddunt, quaque privatam personam meam attingunt; sic enim ratiocinari cogor; si ille qui suam domum regere nequit, ad Ecclesiae regimen vocari non debet; quanto minus illi licebit ad tantum munus accedere qui seipsum in vita sua & meditationibus nec dum moderari addidicit: atqui tantum mihi hac in re defuit, non mihi solum, sed & aliis constare potest. Hic solent mortales exclamare non esse quaerendam aut somniandam in hac vita perfectionem plenam, & intemeratam sanctitatem; at mihi hic ego & iis regero; utinam vel summas saltem sordes & omnimodam imperfectionem devitare possemus, dum horrescimus ad vocem perfectionis, quam tamen scriptura tanquam metam nobis proponit Hebr. 6. studium purificationis
units.tr: .... The Synod sent me ............ to discharge the ministry. God is my witness that I went there with a willing and generous spirit. I spent some time there, not without fruit, by God's grace. But at last, when my own sins and those of the church to which I had been set over came to light, and I saw that I was really a novice [νεόφυτον], unequal to so great a burden and unfit to reform the many abuses that swarmed in that assembly, I threw down my spear. Weighed down by the heaviest sorrow, I languished, and I was useless not only for the rest of the pastoral care but also for preaching. Therefore I was sent back by the elders of that church to ......, so that I could lay before them the things that troubled my mind so greatly. They judged my ailment to be pure melancholy and advised me to take a journey to my homeland and visit my parents and kinsmen. I obeyed this advice, but those who run across the sea change their sky, not their mind. This journey increased my affliction rather than lessening it, for the contagious company of carnal men redoubled the sickness of my mind. So I fled from friends and kinsmen more willingly than I had come to them. And here ...... I am hiding at the house of a most honourable man, whose son I instruct in good letters. Here I enjoy a greater quietness of mind than I once had, but I am still troubled by many doubts, which frighten my mind away from the ministry. (1) I do not perceive an internal calling. That is, although I would rather spend my life in the ministry than in a mechanical or other kind of occupation, that certainty is lacking which everyone rightly called ought to cherish, the hope that God will be present with his labours. (2) The principal part of the true ministry has so far been unknown to me, and no one of my teachers has reminded me of it: namely, what it means to watch over the souls of the flock as one who must give account, as the Apostle says in Heb. 13.17; and what kind of particular watchfulness this ought to be, both with respect to persons and with respect to actions. (3) Finally, since this care cannot be exercised without judgement, how is that judgement to be exercised (of which the Apostle speaks in 1 Cor. 5.12 and elsewhere), and by what rule? Besides these matters, about which (as it seems to me) a true minister ought by no means to be in doubt, there are various other things that perplex me and touch my private person. For I am forced to reason thus: if one who cannot rule his own house ought not to be called to the governance of the Church, how much less may one approach so great an office who has not yet learned to govern himself in his life and meditations? But in this matter I have been so lacking that it can be evident not only to me but to others as well. Here mortals are wont to cry out that full perfection and unblemished holiness are not to be sought or dreamt of in this life. But to them and to myself I reply: would that we could at least avoid the greatest filth and every sort of imperfection, while we shudder at the word "perfection," which nonetheless Scripture sets before us as the goal (Heb. 6). The zeal for purification

units.la: feria omittimus; & tanquam sues amici lutô in volutabro cœ-ni haremus, alia parte cum externam meam vocationem intueor; & internam illam animi alacritatem, qua munus mihi tum incognitum subibam consídero; cum sciam vocationem externam fuisse legitimam, cum manuum acceperim impositionem, cum sciam me in Spiritu & veritate commotum suisse quamvis in negotio non satis perspecto; cum sentiam adhuc, & senserim continuo, etiam in gravissimis angoribus, in quibus vel mortem mihi optavi; desiderium inquam solum sine voluntate & cum horrore subeundi; cum inquam haec omnia contemplor & cogito, cogor ab alia parte memet ipsum condemnare quod à suscepto munere resilierim & admotam aratro manum retraxerim, sic undique mihi ipsi infestus, meque reum peragens in angustiis summis dego; tu mei miseretus, noli in precibus me praeterire; ita te tuamque uxorem & familiam omnem, Deus Pater noster, in Domino Iesu Christo, omnibus donis gratia & prosperitate cumulet & augeat. Amen.
units.tr: we neglect day by day; and like pigs that love the mire, we cling in the filth of the wallow. On the other hand, when I look at my external calling, and consider that inner eagerness of spirit with which I took up the office, then unknown to me, since I know that the external calling was lawful, since I received the laying on of hands, since I know that I was stirred in the Spirit and in truth, although in a matter not sufficiently examined; since I still feel, and have continually felt, even in the most grievous anguish, in which I even wished for death; I say, only a desire without will, and an undertaking with horror; when I contemplate and consider all these things, I am forced on the other hand to condemn myself, because I withdrew from the office I had taken up and drew back my hand from the plough to which it was set. Thus hostile to myself on every side, and making myself guilty, I live in the greatest distress. You, having pity on me, do not pass me by in your prayers. So may God our Father, in the Lord Jesus Christ, fill and increase you, your wife and your whole household with every gift, grace and prosperity. Amen.

units.la: SIXTINI AMAMA ORATIO ACADEMICA De barbarie morum, ubi & de praesenti Academiae Franekaranae statu disseritur.
units.tr: Oration of Sixtinus Amama on the Barbarity of Morals, in which the present state of the Franeker Academy is also discussed.

units.la: Reverendis & Clarissimis Viris, D. GULIELMO AMESIO, D. MEINARDO SCHOTANO, SS. Theolog. & Pietatis Professoribus, collegis conjunctissimis, felicitatem temporalem & aeternam precatur
units.tr: To the Reverend and Most Distinguished Men, Mr GUILIELMUS AMESIUS and Mr MEINARDUS SCHOTANUS, Professors of Sacred Theology and of Piety, my closest colleagues: he wishes temporal and eternal happiness.

units.la: S. A.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: EX quo tu celeberrime D. AMESI, juxta cum Cl. Viro D. JOH. HACHTINGIO Logices Professore diligentissimo, in hanc Academiam intulisti pedem (inferebatis autem simul) aliam Academiae faciem vidimus. Eodem enim anno in Senatum Academicum, cujus Cl. Vir, D. ARNOLDUS VERHEL tunc Praeses erat, liquidis auspiciis allecti, ad primam occasionem, una cum praedicto Academiae Rectore, intrepidis & commascula-tis animis horrendas illas & feroces belluas Ebrietatem & Licentiam, quae hic stabulabantur, ex Academia ejecistis, ac Christianam disciplinam, jam desperatam, Deo, supra quam a quoquam sperari potuisset, benedicente, Academiae redonastis. Cujus praeclari & aeterna gratitudine dignissimi facinoris sicuti invidiam apud dissolutam & barbaram juventutem sustinuistis, & quasi praepilatis hastis objecti fuistis soli, ita & aequissimum censeo, ut vobis quoque prae aliis tam egregii operis gloria transcribatur. Neque hic possum silentio praeterire maximos & de Rep. nostra meritissimos viros, D. GELLIUM HILLAMA & D. AUSONIUM AYSMA τὰς νῦν ἐν ᾰγίοις, nec non amplissimos viros D. JOHANNEM NYS & ABRAHAMUM ROORDA, tunc in Senatu Illúst. Frisiæ Ordinum consiliarios vigilantissimos, qui auxiliares manus quas promiserant, promptissime præbuere. Hæc princeps causa est, Cl. D. Amesi, cur tibi hanc orationem, ad cujus calcem super Academiæ nostræ statu differo, inscripserim. Te verò, reverende D. Schotane, collegæ tuo adjunxi, quia vos conjungunt pietas fraterna, & qualis inter ejusdem cathedræ Professores esse debet, caritas concordia, & Christianæ disciplinæ tutandæ zelus. Tu quidem, quæ fati tui felicitas fuit, post discussam atram illam noctem, in hanc Acad vocatus es: attamen ex eo ejusmodi dedisti masculi animi tui documenta, ut quid de te in simili tempestate, quam Deus clementer ab hac Acad. avertat, Illustres Ordines sperandum habeant, liquido omnibus constet. Adhæc, masculis illis & nisi pietatem spirantibus concionibus, quas cum ἐξσεία ad Academicos habes, potens in Scripturis, vitâ, eorum quoque qui extra Ecclesiam sunt, testimonio inculpatus, utilissimam Christo & Ecclesiæ navas operam. Vos denique conjunxi, ceu intemeratos Sacerdotes & Professores puriloris illius Theologiæ, cui omnis mea ancillatur industria. Valete reverendi Viri, atque hanc oratiunculam, incomptam illam quidem & inficetam, attamen à multis, qui eam audivére, petitam, æstimate ab animo offerentis, qui vos merito colit & veneratur. XII. Junii 1628.
units.tr: Since you, most celebrated Mr Amesius, together with the most diligent Mr Johannes Hachtingius, Professor of Logic, set foot in this Academy (and at the same time you were bringing in another), we have seen a different face of the Academy. For in that same year, invited under clear auspices into the Academic Senate, of which the distinguished Mr Arnoldus Verhel was then President, you, at the first opportunity and together with the aforementioned Rector of the Academy, with fearless and manly spirits drove out of the Academy those dreadful and savage beasts, Drunkenness and Licentiousness, which had been stabled here, and, with God blessing beyond what anyone could have hoped, you restored Christian discipline to the Academy, which had been given up for lost. For this distinguished deed, most worthy of eternal gratitude, you bore the hatred of the dissolute and barbarous youth and were, as it were, exposed alone to the pointed spears; so I judge it entirely fair that the glory of so outstanding a work should also be credited to you before others. Nor can I pass over in silence the greatest men, most deserving of our Commonwealth, Mr Gellius Hillama and Mr Ausonius Aysma [τὰς νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις], and the most distinguished men Mr Johannes Nys and Mr Abraham Roorda, then vigilant councillors in the Senate of the Illustrious Orders of Friesland, who most readily offered the auxiliary forces they had promised. This is the principal reason, Mr Amesius, why I have inscribed to you this oration, at the end of which I defer my account of the present state of our Academy. And you, Reverend Mr Schotanus, I have joined to your colleague, because brotherly piety unites you, and the love and harmony that ought to exist between professors of the same chair, and zeal for defending Christian discipline. You, indeed, by the good fortune of your destiny, were called to this Academy after that dark night had been dispelled; yet from then on you have given such proofs of your manly spirit that the Illustrious Orders may hope for what they can expect from you in a similar storm (which God graciously turn away from this Academy), and this is clear to all. Moreover, with those manly sermons breathing piety, which you deliver to the students along with the exercises, powerful in the Scriptures, and blameless in life, even by the testimony of those outside the Church, you render most useful service to Christ and the Church. Finally, I have joined you together as untainted ministers and professors of that purer theology, to which all my industry serves as handmaid. Farewell, reverend gentlemen, and judge this little oration, indeed unpolished and unrefined, but sought by many who heard it, by the spirit of the one offering it, who rightly honours and reveres you. 12 June 1628.

units.la: In nomine DOMINI ac Salvatoris nostri IESV CHRISTI. AMEN.
units.tr: In the name of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: ANni jam aliquot ivere, Reverendi, Clarissimi, Consultissimi, Nobilissimi & Lectissimi DD. Auditores, cum gravissimus ille JCtus, D. Timæus Faber p. m. Academiæ sceptra hoc ipso loco mihi traderet. Laborum & curarum, quæ isthoc anno, velut agmine facto in me incurrebant, etiamnum sum meminentissimus. Non sic ex squallido gurgustio liberationem captivus, ut ego tunc diem illum expectabam, quo ex molestissimis istis RectURÆ cotibus & plusquam decumanis fluctibus enavigare liceret. Tandem, post multas atras noctes & fœdas tempestates illuc effebat mihi ille Sol, qui me mihi, Musisque meis redonabat.
units.tr: Several years have now passed, Reverend, Distinguished, Most Learned, Most Noble and Most Chosen gentlemen, listeners, since that most serious man, the late Mr. Timaeus Faber, handed me the reins of the university in this very place. I still remember vividly the labours and cares that then rushed upon me as if in a column. I was no more eager for release from a foul prison, as a captive, than I then longed for the day when I could sail away from those most troublesome rowings of the rectorship and waves more than tenfold. At last, after many dark nights and foul storms, that sun rose for me, the one that gave me back to myself and to my Muses.

units.la: Credite, Auditores, me lætiori animo & fronte magis erugat a hæc sceptra successori meo tradidisse, quam ea vel antea suscepe-ram, vel jam rursus capesso.
units.tr: Believe me, listeners, I unburden myself of these reins to my successor with a happier spirit and a brighter brow than I had when I first took them up or now take them up again.

units.la: Cur tamen grave illud onus denuo mihi imponi passus sim, sub finem orationis suo loco edisseram.
units.tr: Why I have allowed that heavy burden to be laid on me again, I will explain in its proper place near the end of this address.

units.la: Julius Cæsar ad Rubiconem fluvium, Italiam à Gallia disterminat, paulisper hæsitans, animoque reputans, quam arduam rem molirctur, posteaquam ostento animus esset additus, in hæc verba erupisse traditur, ἐῤῥίφθω κύβος, jacta esto alea. Mihi quoque, si licet parva componere magnis, in arduo hoc negotio non parum primitus hæsitanti, Collegarum benevolentia, quæ mihi supra omnia Ethnicorum ostenta est, animum addidit, persuasitque pedem inhanc cymbam inferre. Ex qua cum honeste, nisi major quædam ingruat tempestas, aut infelicioribus ostentis terreat, egredi non possim, jactam aleam video. Deus O. M. qui corda & renes scrutatur, novit, quo animo hanc provinciam suscéperim.
units.tr: Julius Caesar, at the River Rubicon, which separates Italy from Gaul, is said to have hesitated for a while, reflecting in his mind how difficult an enterprise he was undertaking. When his courage had been strengthened by omens, he burst out in these words: let the die be cast [ἐῤῥίφθω κύβος]. In my own case, if small things may be compared with great, I too had hesitated not a little at the outset over this difficult business, and the goodwill of my colleagues, which has shown me more favour than any omens of the pagans, gave me courage and persuaded me to set foot in this boat. Since I cannot honourably leave it, unless some greater storm comes upon me or frightens me with more unlucky omens, I see that the die is cast. God, the Greatest and Best, who searches hearts and minds, knows with what spirit I have undertaken this charge.

units.la: Illo igitur Deo, conscientia mea, & collegarum favore subnixus, solvo hanc à litore cymbam, & dico cum Davide, Auxilium meum à DOMINO, qui fecit cœlum & terram.
units.tr: Relying therefore on that God, on my own conscience, and on the favour of my colleagues, I cast off this boat from the shore and say with David: My help is from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

units.la: Cum vero mihi hoc tempore necessitas partes dicendi imposuerit, vellem tam in manu mihi esset, quam in voto, talia afferre, quæ omnibus jucunda, nulli molesta, singulis utilia sint. Πολυ-πλέ· [?]ἐκλέξασθαι ἀνάλωμα ὁ χρόνος. Ideo religio mihi erit, inani rhetoricatione aures vestras fatigare. Omnia circumspectanti argumenta tale præ cæteris placuit, quod me mei, vos vestri officii posset commonefacere. Nullum autem mihi visum fuit efficacius, quam consideratio præsentis Ecclesiæ status, qui profecto adeo mihi videtur afflictus, ut corneam illi fibram esse oporteat, qui ad solam ejus cogitationem non illacrymet. Ejus dum speculum aliquod in V. Testamenti pagina quæro, oportunè occurrit notabilis ille locus Esther. 3. verf. ult. Ad eum, cum bono Deo, paucula dicturus sum. Eum ad meum propositum accommodabo. Auditorum benevolentiam adulationibus captare non didici. Et video illud fere magis ex consuetudine & formulis, quam ex utilitate fieri. Quicquid enim dixeris, accipiuntur fere verba, ut sunt animi audientium. In bonum interpres benignus omne mutat, etiam quod malum est. In malum interpres malignus omne mutat, etiam quod bonum est.
units.tr: Since necessity has now laid on me the part of speaking, I would wish to be able to bring forth, as readily as I wish it, things that are pleasant to all, troublesome to none, and useful to each. [Time is the most costly expense.] Therefore I shall think it wrong to weary your ears with empty rhetoric. Of all the considerations I turned over, this one pleased me above the rest: that it could remind me of my duty and you of yours. Nothing seemed to me more effective than a consideration of the present state of the Church, which indeed seems to me so afflicted that anyone who does not weep at the mere thought of it must have a heart of horn. While I was seeking some mirror of it in the pages of the Old Testament, the notable passage of Esther 3, last verse, came opportunely to hand. With God's good favour I shall say a few words about it and apply it to my purpose. I have not learned to win the goodwill of listeners by flattery, and I see that such praise is made more from custom and formula than from any real benefit. Whatever you say, words are received pretty much as the minds of the hearers are disposed. A kindly interpreter turns everything into good, even what is evil. A malicious interpreter turns everything into evil, even what is good.

units.la: Locus autem iste ita habet.
units.tr: The passage reads as follows.

units.la: Rex vero & Haman sedebant ad bibendum, cum civitas Susan esset perplexa.
units.tr: And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Shushan was perplexed.

units.la: Verba sunt perspicui, nec egent face Scholiorum. Retexamus breviter historiam. Erexerat Assuerus ad summa honorum fastigia superbum Amalekitam, adeo quidem ut poneret solium ejus supra solium omnium principum regni sui. Omnibus servis suis mandaverat, ut honorem supra humanum, qualis ipsi deferebatur, huic propudio haberent. At generosus ille Mardochæus à se impetrare non potuit, ut ejusmodi honore Amalekitam afficeret. Sed Mardochæus, inquit textus, non flectebat genua, nec incurvabat se coram Haman. Nec mirum, cum etiam Conon Atheniensis, homo ethnicus hanc ἀνεγκλησίαν indignam ratus, eo nomine à congressu justinus Regis abstinuerit, cum autem hanc Judæi pertinaciam aliquandiu vidisset Haman.
units.tr: The words are clear and need no torch of commentary. Let us briefly retrace the history. Ahasuerus had raised the proud Amalekite to the highest pinnacle of honour, so much so that he set his throne above the thrones of all the princes of his kingdom. He had ordered all his servants to pay to this man a reverence beyond the human, such as was paid to him, as a mark of honour. But that noble Mordecai could not bring himself to grant the Amalekite honour of this kind. But Mordecai, says the text, did not bow his knee, nor did he bend himself before Haman. This is no wonder, since Conon of Athens, a pagan, judged that [ἀνεγκλησίαν] blamelessness unworthy and on that account abstained from meeting the king, as was just. But when Haman had for some time seen this obstinacy of the Jew,

units.la: — Irarum magnos voluit sub pectore fluctus.
units.tr: He wished great waves of anger to lie within his breast.

units.la: Quid agit? Revocat hunc contemptum ad animum, ita tamen, ut dolorem suum non in lacrymas, sed in ultionis solatia intendat. At facinus illud unius recutiti capite expiari non posse ratus, universæ Judæorum gentis excidium molitur. Et certe, nisi Θεὸς [?]μην χαρὶς succurrisset, unus dies Judæis omnibus, quëis imperitabat Assuerus, feralis fuisset. Eo usque impium & sanguinarium illud suum consilium ambitiosus ille aulicus provexerat. Ecce enim postquam superstitiosa sors diem monstrasset, gentem Judaicam apud Regem criminatur, tanquam regi inimicam & Regno exitialem. Rex annulum tradit Hamani in symbolum traditæ authoritatis, eique potestatem facit literas ad singularum provinciarum satrapas mittendi, ad interficiendum & perdendum omnes Judæos, tam pueros quam senes, viros, fœminas, uno die, xiii. mensis, xii. Hanc ille oportunitatem non omittendam ratus, celeriter exequitur omnia, cursores exeunt equis celeribus vecti, statimque in Susan affixum est edictum.
units.tr: What does he do? He brings this contempt back to his mind, yet in such a way that he directs his grief not into tears but into the consolations of revenge. Thinking that such a crime could not be expiated by the beheading of one man alone, he plans the destruction of the whole Jewish nation. And indeed, had the grace of God [θεοῦ χάρις] not come to their aid, that one day would have been fatal to all the Jews who were under the rule of Ahasuerus. So far had that ambitious courtier advanced his impious and bloodthirsty plan. For behold, after a superstitious lot had pointed out the day, he accused the Jewish people before the king as hostile to the king and deadly to the realm. The king gave Haman his signet ring as a symbol of the authority handed over to him, and granted him power to send letters to the satraps of each province, for the killing and destruction of all the Jews, boys and old men, men and women alike, on one day, the thirteenth of the month. Thinking this opportunity not to be let slip, he carried out everything swiftly. Couriers went out mounted on swift horses, and at once the edict was posted up in Shushan.

units.la: Reputate cum animis vestris, Aud. quid animi Judæis fuerit, quæ lamenta, quæ ejulationes mulierum & parvulorum cœlo iverint. Ipsi Mardochæo, viro, & quidem prudenti & cordato viro, præ animi pavore Refugit sanguen atque exalbescit metu.
units.tr: Consider in your minds, listeners, what the feelings of the Jews must have been, and what laments and wailings of women and little children rose to heaven. Mordecai himself, a man, and indeed a prudent and wise man, from sheer fear of soul, shrinks from blood and grows pale with dread.

units.la: Ita enim afficitur hoc edicto, ut lacera veste, indutusque cilicio in civitate oberraverit, clamans clamore magno & amaro. In omnibus quoque provinciis erat;
units.tr: He was so affected by this edict that, with his garment torn and clothed in sackcloth, he wandered through the city, crying out with a loud and bitter cry. And in all the provinces there was

units.la: Luctus, ubique pavor & plurima mortis imago...
units.tr: Mourning everywhere, terror, and on every side the image of death...

units.la: Neque solum Judæi lugebant, sed & qui Susis erant, melioris notæ cives, Judæorum vices dolebant. Civitas Susan, Regia illa Regis Assueri perplexa; cives ejus plane consternati & attoniti erant. Quod unum poterant, civium suorum vices dolebant, utpote quos non utilitate publica, sed in ambitionem & sævitiam unius exitio devotos noverant.
units.tr: Not only the Jews mourned, but also the citizens of Susa, men of better standing, grieved for the Jews' plight. The city of Susa, that royal seat of King Ahasuerus, was thrown into utter dismay and bewilderment. The only thing they could do was grieve for their fellow citizens, whom they knew had been doomed to destruction not for the public good but for the ambition and cruelty of one man.

units.la: In hac totius urbis consternatione, in hoc communi integræ gentis luctu, Rex tamen & Assuerus, calamitatis illius authores, genio iudulgebant, Rex & Haman sedebant ad bib. cum S. esset perplexa. Lxx. Βασιλεὺς ἡ Αμαν ἐνωθωνίζοντο id est largiori potu & magnis poculis se provocabant. Largiorem enim potationem Graeci κωθωνισμὸν vocant. Haman jam defæcato erat animo. Vindicaverat jam injuriam, illudque à se præstitum putabat, ut hoc crudeli exemplo alii deterriti, caverent & horrerent opponere se illi, καὶ ἐμαιωθήμεναι ἀντίων.
units.tr: Amid this general dismay of the whole city, amid this common mourning of an entire nation, King Ahasuerus, the author of that calamity, nevertheless indulged his appetite: the king and Haman sat down to drink while the city was in confusion. The Seventy: Βασιλεὺς ἡ Αμαν ἐνωθωνίζοντο [the king and Haman were drinking], that is, they urged each other on with heavier draughts and large cups. The Greeks call such heavy drinking κωθωνισμόν [revelry]. Haman's mind was now calm. He believed he had already avenged the insult, and he thought that by this cruel example others would be frightened off and would take care not to oppose him [καὶ ἐμαιωθήμεναι ἀντίων].

units.la: Non de nihilo est, quod hanc compotationem Sp. S. memoraverit. Insignem & admirandam horum hominum crudelitatem ad omnem posteritatem voluit transmittere. Quæ enim hæc erat inhumahumanitas, dum tota urbs perplexa est, dum ejulatibus & lamentis omnia perstrepunt, dum lanienam expectant tot insontes animæ, non solum nullo affici dolore, sed & quasi in publica lætitia, convivari, epulari, comessari & κωμάζειν;
units.tr: It is no accident that the Holy Spirit recorded this drinking bout. He wished to hand down to all posterity the notable and amazing cruelty of these men. What inhumanity was this, that while the whole city was in dismay, while everything rang with wailing and lamentation, while so many innocent souls awaited slaughter, they not only felt no grief but feasted, dined, caroused and κωμάζειν [went revelling], as if in public rejoicing!

units.la: Multæ hic se offerunt observationes, quas si omnes laxatis sermonis rudentibus persequi sederet, nimis evagaretur oratio. Mihi, dum temporis, quod satis angustum est, & vestræ patientiæ habenda est ratio, vela astringenda sunt. Itaque tres tantum delibabo. quartæ plusculum immorabor.
units.tr: Many observations present themselves here. If I were to pursue them all, letting out the reins of speech, my discourse would wander too far. Since I must take account of the time, which is rather short, and of your patience, I must furl my sails. So I will touch on only three, and linger a little longer on the fourth.

units.la: Observamus ergo I. Eam fuisse ab omni ævo piorum & Ecclesiæ sortem, pati & affligi. Ipse Deus hæc fata in ipso Paradiso Ecclesiæ prædixit. Retexantur sacri Annales ab Habel usque ad Christum. Et rursus evolvantur acta Apostolorum & historiæ Ecclesiasticæ, & rem ita se habere omnes deprehendemus.
units.tr: We observe, then, first: that it has been the lot of the godly and of the Church in every age to suffer and be afflicted. God himself foretold this fate for the Church in Paradise itself. Let the sacred annals be unrolled from Abel to Christ; let the Acts of the Apostles and the ecclesiastical histories be read again, and we shall find that matters stand exactly so.

units.la: Causas hujus rei utriusque fœderis pagina passim inculcat. Inter alios Propheta David, Antequam humiliarer, errabam Domine, at nunc custodio verba tua. Bonum mihi est, quod me afflixeris, ut discerem statuta tua. Crux luxuriantibus Ecclesiis oculos aperit, quos res secundæ clauserant, ut videant, quantum à divini verbi tramite diverterint. Crux in memoriam ipsis vocat, unde exciderint. Crux est pædagogus ad pœnitentiam. Crux demetit cristas superbiæ nostræ,
units.tr: The page of both covenants everywhere impresses the causes of this. Among others the prophet David says: Before I was humbled I went astray, O Lord, but now I keep your word. It is good for me that you have afflicted me, that I might learn your statutes. The cross opens the eyes of Churches grown luxuriant, eyes that prosperity had closed, so that they may see how far they have strayed from the path of the divine word. The cross calls to their memory the place from which they have fallen. The cross is a tutor leading to repentance. The cross cuts down the crests of our pride.

units.la: Submittet ergo se homo, qui pulvis & cinis est, divinæ castigationi & sine murmure, quò magnus ille Imperator ducit aut vocat, sequetur. Illud vero imprimis cavendum est, ne in cruce & affl. induremus corda nostra. Nisi meliores evadamus ex cruce, infelix crux est. Est quoddam hominum genus, qui sub divina virga devoti & religiosi videntur. At simul ac Deus removit virgam suam & inducias dat, redeunt ad ingenium: redeunt ad vomitum, tanquam canes. Redeunt ad volutabrum cœni tanquam sues. Hos optime assimilaveris ferro, quod ab igne candens mollius est & cudi se patitur. Aut ubi illud igne excemeris, redit ad priorum duriticm. Hi utuntur specie aliqua pœnitentiæ, tanquam lacera veste, quam pluvio cœlo induimus, sereno abjicimus.
units.tr: Man, who is dust and ashes, must therefore submit himself to divine chastisement, and without murmuring follow wherever that great Commander leads or calls. Above all we must take care that we do not harden our hearts under the cross and affliction. Unless we come out of the cross better, the cross is unhappy. There is a kind of men who seem devout and religious under the divine rod. But as soon as God removes his rod and grants a truce, they return to their old nature: they return to their vomit like dogs, and to their wallowing in mud like swine. These men are best compared to iron, which, glowing from the fire, is softer and allows itself to be beaten; but once it has cooled, it returns to its former hardness. They put on some appearance of repentance, like a torn garment, which we wear in rainy weather and cast off when the sky is clear.

units.la: Observ. II. Inhumanum & illaudabile esse, aliis, præsertim si injuste patiantur, non συμπάσχειν, hoc est, mutuo molestiarum sensu non affici. Ecce enim notantur hic Rex & Haman, quod miserorum afflictione non fuerint commoti. Contra, tacite laudantur Susani, quod eorum vices doluerint. Urbs erat perplexa. Tota urbs. Atqui in ea minima pars Judæi erant. Ipsi illi barbari, idolorum cultores.
units.tr: Observation II: it is inhuman and blameworthy not to feel with others (συμπάσχειν), that is, not to be moved by a shared sense of their troubles, especially when they suffer unjustly. For here the king and Haman are censured because they were not moved by the affliction of the wretched. On the other hand, the people of Susa are tacitly praised because they grieved for their fellow citizens' plight. The city was in confusion. The whole city. Yet the Jews were only a very small part of it, and they were barbarians, worshippers of idols.

units.la: Non questus tenuere suos, magnusque peromnes / Errabat sine voce dolor.
units.tr: Complaints did not restrain their own; and great grief, without voice, wandered among them all.

units.la: Similia exempla in filia Pharaonis obstetricibus Exod. i. Melitensibus, Act. 28. & Samaritano Lucæ 10. habemus. Neroni durante isto quinquennio, quo plurima bonæ indolis documenta dabat, cum pro more damnati cujusdam hominis titulo subscrip-turus erat, ista verba expressit commiseratio, Quam vellem nescire literas! Neque audiendus hic est Lipsius, qui non ex Bibliis, sed ex Stoa illud paradoxum depromptit, miserationem à sapiente & constante viro spernendam esse; quod tractat lib. i. de const. cap. xii. Quo ergo loco Christum habuit Lipsius, qui bis flevit, sæpius σπλαγχνίζεσθαι legitur id est intima commiseratione commotus ex intuitu & commiseratione alienæ miseriæ, etiam eorum, qui juste patiebantur aut passuri erant. Lucæ cap. xix. Et ut appropinquavit visa urbe, flevit super eam, dicens, Si noisses tu &c. Ioh. xi. Jesus ergo ut vidit eam flentem & Judæos qui una venerant, flentes, infremuit spiritu & turbavit seipsum, & dixit, ubi posuistis eum? Et dicunt ei, Domine, veni & vide. Et lacrymatus est Jesus. Vt in Christo quoque valeat illud Græcorum.
units.tr: We have similar examples in Pharaoh's daughter and the midwives (Exod. 1.), in the Maltese (Acts 28.) and in the Samaritan (Luke 10.). When Nero, during those five years in which he gave many signs of a good disposition, was about to sign the sentence of a condemned man, as was his custom, pity forced from him these words: How I wish I did not know letters! Nor should we listen to Lipsius here, who draws from the Stoa, not from the Bible, the paradox that pity must be scorned by a wise and steadfast man; he treats this in book 1 of De constantia, chapter 12. Where then was the Christ whom Lipsius had? He wept twice; and we read more often that he was σπλαγχνίζεσθαι [moved with compassion], that is, stirred by deep pity at the sight of another's misery, even of those who suffered justly or were about to suffer. Luke 19: And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying, If you had known... John 11: Jesus therefore, when he saw her weeping and the Jews weeping who had come with her, groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said, Where have you laid him? They said to him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept. So that in Christ too that Greek saying holds true:

units.la: ἀγαθοὶ δ' ἀριδάκρυτοι ἀνδρες.
units.tr: ἀγαθοὶ δ' ἀριδάκρυτοι ἀνδρες [good men are quick to tears].

units.la: Non solum ergo fas, sed & officii nostri est, miserorum vices dolere, præsertim si injuste patiantur. Exigit hoc commune illud vinculum, quo Deus & natura nos constrinxere. Ab uno Deo creati, ex uno Adamo geniti, ex una Heva nati sumus. Omnes imaginem Dei & communis parentis circumferimus. Vna eademque nos excipit tellus. Ex uno aëre respiramus. Sub eodem cœli fornice, in eadem terræ pila vivimus.
units.tr: It is therefore not only right but also our duty to grieve for the plight of the wretched, especially when they suffer unjustly. This common bond, by which God and nature have bound us together, demands it. We were created by one God, born from one Adam, and born from one Eve. We all bear the image of God and of our common parent. One and the same earth receives us. We breathe one and the same air. We live under the same vault of heaven, on the same ball of earth.

units.la: Quod si peccati nos reos constituimus, non dolendo, quanto scelere nos obligabimus, si aliorum miseria nos oblectemus? Hæc est illa ἀπηχαρεκακία, vitium Diabolo proprium: Præsertim si ipsi miseriæ istius fabri simus. Fratres Iosephi cum fratrem in cisternam dimisissent, ut illic inedia periret miser, componebant se ad edendum & bibendum. Platina in descriptione vitæ Pauli ii. Pontificis edisserens carceres & tormenta, quibus jussu Pauli 2. præter omne suum meritum subjectus fuit, inter alia commemorat, Vianensium quendam, quem ei Pontifex commissarium dederat, tanquam alterum Minoa stratis tapetibus tanquam in nuptiis sedisse. Neque hoc contentus, inquit, dum penderem miser in ipsis ctncrucia tibus, monilia Sanga Clugiensis attrectans, hominem rogabat, & qua puella donum amoris habuisset. De amoribus locutus, ad me conversus est &c. Aspice mihi execrabile illud propudium, sceleratorum ultimam lineam, non solum Romanorum Caesarum, sed & omnium bipedum facile nequissimum, Neronem. Dicente quodam in sermone communi,
units.tr: If we make ourselves guilty of sin by not grieving, how great a crime shall we incur if we take delight in another's misery? This is that ἀπηχαρεκακία [malicious joy at another's misfortune], a vice proper to the Devil, especially if we ourselves are the makers of that misery. When Joseph's brothers had let the young man down into the cistern so that he would perish there of hunger, they sat down to eat and drink. Platina, describing the life of Pope Paul II, recounts at length the prisons and torments to which, by Paul's command, he was subjected beyond all his deserts. Among other things he mentions a certain Vianensis, whom the Pope had given him as commissioner, who sat on carpets like a second Minos, as if at a wedding feast. Not content with this, he says, while I, wretched, hung in the torments, fingering the necklaces of Sanga of Chiusi, he asked me by what girl each gift of love had been given. Having spoken of loves, he turned to me, etc. Look at that detestable shamelessness, the last line of wickedness, Nero, the most worthless of all two-legged creatures, not only of the Roman Caesars but of all men. When someone said in common conversation:

units.la: Ἐμὸς Ἰανόντος γαῖα μίχθητω πυρί.
units.tr: Ἐμὸς Ἰανόντος γαῖα μίχθητω πυρί [let the earth mingle with fire after my death].

units.la: Imo inquit, ἐμὸς ζῶντος. Planeque ita fecit. Nam quasi offensus deformitate veteris urbis & angustiis flexurisque vicorum, urbem incendit. Cladem illam valde exaggerat Tacitus Annal. xv. Per sex dies septemque noctes, inquit Suet. ea clade saevitum est, ad monumentorum bustorumque diversoria plebe compulsa. Misera erat urbis facies, omnia lamentis perstrepebant. Nemo restinguere incendium audebat, minis prohibentium, qui se auctorem habere clamabant, terrebantur omnes. Quid Nero? Ipso tempore flagrantis urbis, inquit Tac. inivit domesticam scenam & cecinit Trojanum excidium; praesentia mala veteris cladibus assimilans. Sueton. Hoc incendium ex turri Maecenatiana prospectans, laetusque flamma pulcritudine, uti ajebat ipse, incendium Troja in illo suo scenico habitu decantavit. Quae ibidem porro in hanc rem sequuntur, apud ipsos illos scriptores legere est. Sed facessamus ab hoc monstro, & gradum faciamus ad
units.tr: "Nay," he said, ἐμὸς ζῶντος [while I am alive]. And he did exactly that. For, as if offended by the ugliness of the old city and the narrowness and winding of its streets, he set the city on fire. Tacitus greatly magnifies that disaster in the Annals 15. Suetonius says: "For six days and seven nights the destruction raged, the common people being driven into monuments, tombs and shelters." The city's appearance was wretched, everything rang with lamentation. No one dared to put out the fire; threats from men who cried out that they had authority over it terrified everyone. And Nero? At the very time the city was burning, Tacitus says, he went up on the stage of his house and sang the fall of Troy, comparing the present evils with the ancient disasters. Suetonius: Viewing this fire from the tower of Maecenas, and delighted by the flames' beauty, as he himself said, he sang of the burning of Troy in his stage costume. What follows there on this matter may be read in those very writers. But let us turn away from this monster and take a step towards

units.la: OBSERV. III. Necessarium officium Christiani esse, com- moveri miseriis & persecutionibus eorum, qui pertinent ad idem corpus mysticum.
units.tr: OBSERVATION III. It is the necessary duty of a Christian to be moved by the miseries and persecutions of those who belong to the same mystical body.

units.la: Si hoc Regis & Hamanis, qui Judaei non erant, factum, ceu inhumanum & turpe a Sp. S. traducitur, quanta σχληροκαρδία, quantum scelus erit; Christianos Christianorum miseriis invicem non commoveri; Si cives Susani Judaeorum vices doluere, cum quorum sacris nihil commune habuere, quanto aequius erit, Christianos Christianis συμπάσχειν; Sicut in uno corpore multa habemus membra, inquit Apost. Rom. 12. eademque membra, non eandem functionem habent. Ita nos multi unum corpus sumus in Christo singulatim alii aliorum membra. Ita Danielem & Nehemiam, licet in exilio bene haberentur, miseratio erga popula res graviter exercuit. Legantur ipsorum libri. Nehemias a Rege suo clementissimo jussus causam sui moeroris dicere, Quomodo non esset afflictus vultus meus, inquit, cum civitas ipsa, locus sepulcrorum majorum meorum, vastata, & porta ejus maneant consumpta igne? Hoc ergo requirit quirit commune illud vinculum spiritus, spiritualis illa cognatio, Christiana charitas.
units.tr: If the king and Haman, who were not Jews, did this, and it is set down by the Holy Spirit as inhuman and shameful, what hardness of heart [σκληροκαρδία], what a crime it will be for Christians not to be moved by one another's miseries! If the citizens of Susa grieved over the fortunes of the Jews, with whose rites they had nothing in common, how much more fitting will it be for Christians to suffer with Christians [συμπάσχειν]? As in one body we have many members, says the Apostle in Romans 12, and these members do not all have the same function. So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. Thus Daniel and Nehemiah, although they were well treated in exile, were greatly afflicted by compassion for their people. Let their books be read. When Nehemiah was commanded by his most gracious king to say what caused his grief, he said: How should my face not be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies waste, and its gates are consumed by fire? This, then, is what that common bond of the Spirit, that spiritual kinship, that Christian love, requires.

units.la: OBSERV. IV. Et ultima, in qua pedem figam, illa esto. Horribile peccatum & desperati status indicium, est, in communi Ecclesiæ miseria secure genio indulgere. Si non συμπάσχειν est peccatum, quantum scelus, genio indulgere; Si hoc Hamanis & Assueri factum dignum censura censuit Spiritus Sanctus, qua censura Judæos notasset, si qui inter eos, sive primores, sive plebeii, in hac ἀγωνίᾳ bacchanalia vixissent; Audiamus ipsius Dei increpationes Amos vi. Væ accumbentibus in lectis eb. comedentibus agnos è grege & vitulos è medio faginarii, modulantibus ad præscriptum nablii, bibentibus ex crateribus vini, neque afficiuntur agritudine propter confractionem Joseph. Jesa. xxii. 12. Cum vocaret Dominus exercituum ad fletum, ad planctum, ad calvitium & cilicium: Ecce lætitiam & gaudium, occidendo boves, comedendo carnes & bibendo vinum, dicentium, Edamus, bibamus, cras moriemur.
units.tr: OBSERVATION IV. The last point, on which I will take my stand, is this. It is a horrible sin and a sign of a desperate state to indulge one's appetite securely in the common misery of the Church. If to suffer with [συμπάσχειν] is not a sin, what a crime it is to indulge one's appetite! If the Holy Spirit thought the conduct of Haman and Ahasuerus worthy of censure, what censure would He have passed on the Jews, had any of them, whether leaders or commoners, lived in revelry during this agony [ἀγωνία]? Let us hear the reproofs of God Himself in Amos 6: Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and eat the lambs from the flock and the calves from the midst of the stall, who sing to the sound of the harp and drink wine from bowls, and are not grieved over the breaking of Joseph. Isaiah 22:12: When the Lord of hosts called to weeping, to mourning, to baldness and sackcloth, behold joy and gladness, killing oxen, eating flesh and drinking wine, saying, Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.

units.la: Arguunt hi mores defectum caritatis erga proximum, erga Deum, arguunt mortem spiritualem. Membra illa, quæ nec dolorem sentiunt ipsa, nec ullam cum aliorum dolore συμπάθειαν habent, mortua, & ense resecanda sunt.
units.tr: These customs show a lack of love for the neighbour and for God; they show spiritual death. Those members which feel no pain themselves and have no sympathy [συμπάθειαν] with the pain of others are dead, and must be cut off with the sword.

units.la: Et jam opinor tempus erit ut cum hac Judæorum calamitate præsentis Ecclesiæ miserias, cum hac Regis & Hamanis profana impietate, nostros mores componamus. Conspiravit à tot jam retro annis in Evangelicorum excidium Romana Synagoga. Anno 1619. classicum S. belli cecinit Gasper Schioppius, domus Austriacæ consiliarius. Ille enim Cæsarem de ipsius erga Lutheranos officio, libello, quem ex professo super hoc argumento scripsit, edocturus. mollibus & lentulis consiliariis in maximam malam crucem irejussis, cap. i. in hunc modum Imperatorem alloquitur: Si una urbium fuerit inobediens & jugum Episcoporum abjecerit, ut novam religionem sectetur, non acquiescens iis, quæ docent sacerdotes, statim percuties habitatores ejus urbis ore gladii, & delebis eam; etiam parvulum & lactentem, qui hoc modo servantur, ne adultiores facti patrum scelere implicentur & æternum pereant. Quomodo verò principes Evangelicos tractaturus sit, eodem capite docet exemplo Moisis, cum principes populi, inquit, familiariter cum Moabitis comedissent & adorassent Deos eorum, suoque exemplo populum ad eadem facienda induxissent, iratus Dominus ait ad Mosem, Tolle cunctos principes populi & suspende eos contra solem in patibulis, ut avertatur furor meus ab Israel. Et postquam eodem cap. Lutheranos principes Diabolum loco Dei adorare, & subditis adorandum proponere, ipsumque adeo Lutherum ab ipso Imperatore pro incarnato Dæmone haberi, asseruissét, cap. 2. sic intonat. Sic igitur habes, imperator, decretum judicis, ex quo interficere debes omnem summo sacerdoti non obedientem. Idque statim, sic ut non audias eum, quibus argumentis suam sententiam probet neque parcat oculus tuus. Imitare Davidem, qui de se Psal. 102. gloriatur, in matutino interficiebam omnes peccatores terrae. Et paulo post, VVitebergam in tumulum disipabis & igne succendes, Lutheranismum in transmigrationem duces, ex Germania exterminabis praedicantes ejus & principes ejus simul. Et postquam omnes ingenii nervos intendisset & omnes machinas admovisset, quibus superstitiosas mentes facile concutias, postquam imperii translationem & insuper aeternas poenas ipsi denuntiasset, nisi suo huic consilio aures substringeret, proponit ei hoc exemplum: Cum Benhadad Rex Syriae, praelio ab Israelitis victus, fugeret in civitatem, dixerunt ei servi, Ecce audivimus Reges Israel clementes esse (quasi dicant, inquit, Austriaci pro ingenita sua clementia non facile hostes & rebelles suos debitis supplicis afficiunt) Ponamus itaque inquiunt servi Benhadad, saccos in lumbis nostris & egrediamur ad regem Israel, forsitan salvabit animas nostras. Quod cum fecissent, Achab praeclarum & generosum ratus, victo regi parcere, non modo vitam ei non ademit, sed & insuper fraternam ultro benevolentiam detulit, ac foederatum a se dimisit. Porro lucrum quod ex hac clementia facturus erat, his verbis continetur, dicit Dominus, quia dimisisti virum dignum morte de manu tua, erit anima tua pro anima ejus & populus tuus pro populo ejus. Piget taedetque plura huc convectare. Utinam, utinam, Auditores, Deus O. M. in cujus manu sunt corda mortalium, Imperatori & Germaniae Principibus, sanguinariis istis consiliis adversam mentem inspiraret! Quid enim hisce jam aliquot retro annis non passi sunt Evangelici, etiam a suo milite, Quis omnes miserias, aerumnas & tormenta recenseat, queis Evangelici a dissoluto milite excarnificati sunt; Quot chiliades hominum pallida fame, & quae eam insecuta est, pestilentia, extinctae sunt; Quot chiliades liberorum ante ora parentum obtruncatae sunt; Quot matronas & virgines, inspectantibus maritis & parentibus, libidinosus miles temeravit; Quot myriadas hominum recusata Romana religio in exilium misit, relictis possessionibus; Quot ministrorum chiliades sine ulla commiseratione ejectae, aut tristi mendicitate adhuc vitam trahunt, aut in summa egestate expiravere; Scil. quibus mundus iste & Germania mania digna non erat. Et quidem hæc licet corpus tantummodo tangant, maxima mala sunt, de quib. vere usurpaveris illud Euripidis, ἔργῳ δ᾽ ἐσὶ μείζονα, ἢ λόγῳ. At longe tristiora illa sunt, quæ alijmas spectant. Quot hominum chiliades aut imperatoris edicta coëgerunt, aut Jesuitarum institutiones permoverunt Romanam religionem amplecti, orthodoxam ejerare? Quis omnia templa, scholas & Acad. recenseat, olim purioris sacraria & seminaria, in quibus nunc stat abominatio illa de solationis, in quibus nunc potionatur juventus vino venenato scortationis magnæ illius meretricis? Quot jam urbes & vici sunt, ubi petunt panem illum verbi divini, & nemo est qui frangat illis; Quot si Deus O. M. ἀπὸ μηχανῆς [?] afflictis Ecclesiæ rebus non succurrerit, credite me vobis folium recitare Sibillæ, habebit brevi Germania equuleos, & vivicomburia, & quicquid Inquisitorum sævitia excogitavit. Hoc talo stant res Evangelicorum. Ut merito renovare possimus querelam Jeremiæ, Quomodo viæ Sionis lugent, quòd nulli veniant ad solennitatem, omnes portæ ejus sunt desolata. Sacerdotes ejus gemunt, virgines mæsta sunt. Quomodo densa nube ira sua obtegit Dominus filiam Sion, quomodo absorbet Dominus sine clementia omnia habitacula Jacob? Quomodo est Dominus similis inimico, absorbet Israelem, absorbet omnia palatia ejus, plurimum affert filiæ Judæ mœroris & mastitia?
units.tr: And I think the time has now come for us to set our own conduct in order, in view of the calamity of the Jews, and of the present miseries of the Church, and of the profane impiety of the king and Haman. For many years now the Roman synagogue has conspired for the destruction of the Evangelicals. In 1619 Gaspar Schioppius, councillor to the House of Austria, sounded the trumpet of holy war. He wrote a little book, expressly on this subject, to instruct the Emperor on his duty towards the Lutherans, and, having had the soft and feeble councillors sent to a great evil cross, he addresses the Emperor in this manner in chapter 1: If one of the cities is disobedient and throws off the yoke of the bishops, following a new religion and not submitting to what the priests teach, you shall at once strike the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword, and destroy it; even the little child and the suckling, who are spared in this way, lest, when they grow older, they become entangled in their fathers' sin and perish for ever. How he would deal with the Evangelical princes he teaches in the same chapter, by the example of Moses: When the princes of the people, he says, had eaten with the Moabites and worshipped their gods, and by their example had led the people to do the same, the Lord was angry and said to Moses, Take all the princes of the people and hang them up in the sun on gibbets, that my wrath may turn away from Israel. And after asserting in the same chapter that the Lutheran princes worship the Devil in place of God and propose that their subjects should worship him too, and that Luther himself was held by the Emperor to be an incarnate demon, in chapter 2 he thunders thus: So you have, Emperor, the judge's decree, by which you must kill everyone who does not obey the high priest. And do so at once, so that you do not listen to him, nor let your eye spare him, whatever arguments he uses to prove his opinion. Imitate David, who boasts of himself in Psalm 101: in the morning I destroyed all the sinners of the land. And a little later: You shall scatter Wittenberg into a heap and burn it with fire, you shall lead Lutheranism into exile, and drive out its preachers and its princes together from Germany. And after he had strained every nerve of his wit and brought to bear every contrivance by which superstitious minds can easily be shaken, after he had threatened the Emperor with the transfer of the empire and, besides, with eternal punishments, unless he lent his ears to this counsel, he sets before him this example: When Ben-hadad, king of Syria, defeated in battle by the Israelites, fled into the city, his servants said to him, Behold, we have heard that the kings of Israel are merciful (as if to say, the Austrians, by their native clemency, do not easily inflict due punishment on their enemies and rebels). Let us therefore, said the servants of Ben-hadad, put sackcloth on our loins and go out to the king of Israel; perhaps he will spare our lives. When they had done so, Ahab, thinking it a splendid and noble thing to spare a conquered king, not only did not take his life, but besides, of his own accord, offered him brotherly goodwill, and sent him away as an ally. Moreover, the reward that was to come from this clemency is stated in these words: The Lord says, because you have let go out of your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people. I am sorry and weary to bring forward more. Would that, would that, hearers, God Almighty, in whose hand are the hearts of mortals, would inspire the Emperor and the princes of Germany with a mind opposed to these bloody counsels! For what have the Evangelicals not suffered in these last few years, even at the hands of their own soldiers? Who could recount all the miseries, hardships and tortures by which the Evangelicals have been butchered by a licentious soldiery? How many thousands of people have perished from pallid famine and the pestilence that followed it? How many thousands of children have been slaughtered before their parents' eyes? How many matrons and virgins has the lustful soldier defiled while their husbands and parents looked on? How many myriads of men, refusing the Roman religion, has it sent into exile, leaving their possessions behind? How many thousands of ministers have been cast out without any pity, and either drag out their life in sad beggary or have expired in utter want? Namely those for whom this world and Germany were not worthy. And indeed, although these evils touch only the body, they are very great, and of them you may rightly use that saying of Euripides: greater in deed than in word [ἔργῳ δ᾽ ἐστὶ μείζονα ἢ λόγῳ]. But those evils are far sadder which concern souls. How many thousands of people have been either forced by the emperor's edicts, or moved by the teaching of the Jesuits, to embrace the Roman religion and abandon the orthodox faith? Who could enumerate all the churches, schools and academies, once sanctuaries and seminaries of purer doctrine, in which that abomination of desolation now stands, and in which the youth is now made drunk with the poisoned wine of the great harlot's fornication? How many towns and villages there are now where people seek the bread of the divine word, and there is no one to break it for them! How many (if Almighty God does not come to the afflicted affairs of the Church as if from the machine [ἀπὸ μηχανῆς]), believe me, I recite to you the leaves of the Sibyl, Germany will soon have racks and burnings alive, and whatever the cruelty of the Inquisitors has devised. Such is the state of the Evangelicals at present. So that we may rightly renew the lament of Jeremiah: How the ways of Zion mourn, because none come to the solemn feast; all her gates are desolate. Her priests groan, her virgins are sorrowful. How the Lord has covered the daughter of Zion with a dense cloud of his anger! How the Lord without mercy has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob! How the Lord has become like an enemy: he has swallowed up Israel, swallowed up all her palaces, and brought great mourning and sorrow upon the daughter of Judah.

units.la: Miseranda Ecclesiarum Rhæticarum fata jam non tango. Gallicanas Ecclesias aspice, illas,
units.tr: I will not touch on the wretched fates of the Rhaetian Churches any longer. Look at the Gallican Churches, those which,

units.la: — qua nostra doluerunt sæpe dolore.
units.tr: have often grieved with our grief.

units.la: Quis tam ferreus, ut vel sola afflictissimi earum status consideratio omnem exhilaritatem non expectoraret? Certe si unquam, nunc illic est dies caliginis & tenebrarum, dies angustiæ & obscuritatis. Est dies, quo venerunt filii ad os matricis & non est vis ad pariendum. Sed solabitur forsan aliquem latior nostrarum facies. Equidem, Auditores, bipedum essemus ingratissimi, nisi grato animo agnoscentes admirandam illam Dei nostri benignitatem, cum Jeremia diceremus, Summa DOMINI benignitas est, quod non simus consumpti: quod non finiantur miserationes ejus. Nova sunt singulis matutinis. Miraculum certe est, quod in hunc usque diem subsistimus. Miraculum inquam est, sive ad hostis nostri potentiam, sive ad civiles discordias & confusiones Reip. nostræ respiciamus. Communis hostis metum, concordiæ vinculum esse, politicorum canon est. Nobis Hannibal ad portas est, & tamen ambitio & avaritia civiles discordias alunt. Principes tui contumaces sunt & socii surum, ajebat olim Jesaias. Nos quoque in Rep. nostra fures habuisse, jam, opinor, fas erit dicere, postquam publico judicio rapaces quidam Veteres repetundarum postulati & condemnati sunt. Stamus tamen adhuc. Saltem nondum cecidimus. Dicam forsan verius, vacillamus & titubamus instar hominis ebrii, aut vertiginosi. Quis enim vere dixerit nos stare, ex quo nostris collegiis magnus ille consilio & amplus actione Deus non, ut olim, praesedit. Ex quo exercitus nostros non, ut olim, ductavit. Ex quo coeperunt omnia terra marique
units.tr: Who is so hard-hearted that the mere consideration of their most afflicted condition would not wring out all cheerfulness? Surely, if ever, now there is a day of darkness and gloom there, a day of distress and obscurity. It is a day when the children have come to the mouth of the womb, and there is no strength to bring forth. Yet perhaps our more favourable situation will console someone. Indeed, listeners, we would be the most ungrateful of bipeds if, acknowledging with a grateful heart that admirable kindness of our God, we did not say with Jeremiah, It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning. Certainly it is a miracle that we have survived to this day. It is a miracle, I say, whether we look to the power of our enemy or to the civil discords and confusions of our commonwealth. It is a maxim of the politicians that a common enemy is the bond of concord. For us Hannibal is at the gates, and yet ambition and greed nourish civil discords. Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves, Isaiah once said. I think it will now be right to say that we too have had thieves in our commonwealth, since certain greedy former officials have been accused and condemned in public trial for extortion. Yet we still stand. At least we have not yet fallen. I might say more truly that we totter and stagger like a drunken or dizzy man. For who could truly say that we stand, since that great God no longer presides over our councils with great counsel and ample action, as once he did? Since he no longer leads our armies, as once he did? Since all things by land and sea have begun

units.la: In pejus r- uere & retro sublapsa referri.
units.tr: To rush headlong into worse and be carried back, having slipped backwards.

units.la: Ex quo Deus coepit truncare hoc Reip. corpus, & lentis ictibus per spiramenta temporum sic flagellare, ut sentiamus nos mori. Ex quo tributa & onera crevere, negotiationes contra, primarius Reip. nostrae nervus, decrevere. Adhaec foederatos nostros difficillimis bellis implicitos, & in se invicem saevum convertere ferrum videmus. Aemulationes inter Regna & Resp. magnae sunt. Hostis imperium maris non amplius nobiscum divisum, sed, quae nostra vel socordia vel stupor est, fere solus habet. Summa summarum huc redit, ut cum pio Josaphato dicamus, non est in nobis vis obsistendi magnae isti multitudini invadenti nos, & addamus insuper ista, magnae sunt in Rep. nostra confusiones, nutant columnae hujus domus, nos nescimus quid facturi simus, sed in te defixi sunt oculi nostri.
units.tr: Since God has begun to cut off this body of the commonwealth, and with slow blows to scourge it through the pores of time, so that we feel ourselves dying. Since taxes and burdens have grown, while trade, the chief sinew of our commonwealth, has declined. Besides, we see our allies entangled in the most difficult wars and turning the cruel sword against one another. There are great rivalries between kingdoms and republics. The enemy holds the rule of the sea, no longer shared with us, but, by our negligence or stupidity, almost alone. The sum of the matter comes to this: that we should say with pious Jehoshaphat, we have no power to stand before this great multitude that cometh against us, and add moreover that there are great confusions in our commonwealth, the pillars of this house totter, we know not what to do, but our eyes are upon thee.

units.la: Consideravimus paucis praesentium temporum calamitates. Quam vellem, Auditores mihi hic liceret esse disertiori & prolixiori! Experior enim dum hac oberro chorda, esse aliquod calamitatum delinimentum, dedisse lacrymas malis & pectus laxasse suspiriis. Sed alio properat oratio. Componendi nunc cum afflictissimo hoc Ecclesiae statu, praesentis aevi & Ecclesiae mores sunt. Cum Susan erat perplexa, Rex & Haman sedisse ad bibendum traduntur. Quid dixisset <bl>Ἰσιδωρος</bl> scriptor, si Judaeorum primores, ipsique Judaei genio securi indulsissent? Hoc profecto monstri instar fuisset. Sed quid inter nos fit? Ego profecto quoties lego, Imperatorem, Episcopos, Principes & Duces Pontificios signa laetitiae dedisse, splendidis conviviis, spectaculis & venationibus animos laxasse, non possum admodum indignari. Illis enim ex voto fluunt omnia. Crebrescunt ipsis optatae auræ. Ipsequae adeo Imperator putat, opinor, se Ecclesiae R. pomoeria extendendo rem Deo gratam præstare. Hunc rerum suarum successum, zeli & pietatis suæ præmium interpretantur Pontificii. Quid igitur mirum esset, sidulci fortuna ebrii, quotidie Bachanalia viverent? At ipsos Evangelicos seu Protestantes in communi hac calamitate sedere ad bibendum, hoc est, genio indulgere, quam profanum, quam ab omni ratione alienum est?
units.tr: We have considered briefly the calamities of the present times. How I wish, listeners, that I might be more eloquent and more lengthy here! For while I wander on this string, I find that there is some solace in calamities, to have shed tears over evils and relieved the heart with sighs. But my speech hastens elsewhere. Now the customs of the present age and of the Church are to be compared with this most afflicted state of the Church. When Susa was in perplexity, the king and Haman are said to have sat down to drink. What would the writer Isidorus [Ἰσίδωρος] have said, if the chief men of the Jews and the Jews themselves had indulged in careless pleasure? That would surely have been like a monstrosity. But what is happening among us? I, for my part, whenever I read that the Emperor, the Bishops, the Princes and the Papist Dukes have shown signs of joy, relaxed their spirits with splendid banquets, spectacles and hunts, I cannot be greatly indignant. For all things flow to them according to their wish. The desired breezes blow strongly for them. And indeed the Emperor himself thinks, I suppose, that he does a thing pleasing to God by extending the boundaries of the Roman Church. The Papists interpret this success of their affairs as the reward of their zeal and piety. What wonder then would it be if they, drunk with such sweet fortune, lived every day in Bacchanalian revelry? But that the Evangelicals, or Protestants, should sit down to drink in this common calamity, that is, indulge their nature, how profane it is, how alien to all reason!

units.la: Politici de causis occasuum Rerump. & regnorum multa commentantur. Nos ex verbo Dei certissimum habemus Canonem, certissimam & unicam causam esse peccata. Hujus rei evidens documentum in civitate Jerusalem habemus, urbe illa, cujus olim portas dilexit Deus supra quam ulla tabernacula Jacobi. Habemus exempla in Epheso, Smyrna, Pergamo, Sardis, Philadelphia, Philippis, Colossis, quarum fata nostis omnes. Quod si hoc tempore Deo O. M. placeret excitare Prophetas & eorum calamo consignare annales regnorum & provinciarum quæ superioribus annis vastatæ sunt, proculdubio hæc aut similia legeremus, cum mitteret Deus ad ipsos nuntios suos inde à diluculo continenter, subsannabant nuntios Dei. Ideo ideo accensus est furor Domini contra eos, ut non esset curatio. Ideo superinduxit in Deus tales exercitus, qui avulserunt tabernaculum ex loco suo, qui interfecerunt juvenes eorum gladio, filias & uxores eorum constupraverunt, neque clementia usi sunt erga senem & grandævum. Qualia fere cap. ult. 2.Chron. Spiritus S. consignavit. Et annon justissimum est, ut illi, quos benignitas & patientia Dei ad frugem revocare non potuere, experiantur, quam amarum & malum sit Deum relinquere? Certe hoc casu, etiamsi Moses & Samuel, Job & Elias starent coram Domino, iram Dei deprecaturi, audirent duram illam vocem, Ne orate pro populo isto in bonum, nam non exaudirem vos, Tantumque abest, ut pereuntium lamenta Deum moveant ad commiserationem, ut Deus profiteatur se ex iis voluptatem & consolationem capere. Prov. 1. ridebo in calam. vestra, & subsannabo, cum advenerit, id, quod expavescitis. Eritque, inquit Moses Deut.28.63. ut quemadmodum latabatur Dominus de vobis, benefaciendo vobis, sic latetur de vobis; exscindendo & extirpando vos.
units.tr: Politicians make many speculations about the causes of the downfall of commonwealths and kingdoms. We have from the Word of God the most certain rule, that the one most certain and sole cause is sins. We have clear proof of this in the city of Jerusalem, that city whose gates God once loved above all the tents of Jacob. We have examples in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Sardis, Philadelphia, Philippi and Colossae, whose fates you all know. But if at this time it pleased the Lord God Almighty to raise up prophets and, by their pen, to record the annals of the kingdoms and provinces that have been laid waste in recent years, we would undoubtedly read words like these: when God sent his messengers to them early and continually, they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words. Therefore the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy. Therefore God brought upon them such armies as tore the tabernacle from its place, slew their young men with the sword, defiled their daughters and wives, and showed no mercy to the old man or the grey-haired. Such things as the Holy Spirit recorded in nearly the last chapter of 2 Chronicles. And is it not most just that those whom the kindness and patience of God could not recall to a better way should experience how bitter and evil it is to forsake God? Certainly in this case, even if Moses and Samuel, Job and Elijah stood before the Lord to plead against his wrath, they would hear that harsh voice, Pray not for this people for their good, for I will not hear you. So far is it from the case that the laments of those who are perishing move God to compassion, that God declares he takes pleasure and comfort from them. Prov. 1. I will laugh at your calamity, and mock when your fear comes. And, as Moses says, Deut. 28.63, it shall come to pass that, as the LORD rejoiced over you to do you good, so the LORD will rejoice over you to destroy you and bring you to nothing.

units.la: Illud extra omnem controversiæ aleam pono, ex quo Sol Evangelii Germaniæ illuxit, nunquam tam aspera eam ursille fata, quam jam urgent. Quid ergo? An Deus injustus est qui infert pœnam? Absit, inquit Apost. Rom. 3 5. Alioqui quomodo judex erit mundi? Deus non solet terram implere plagis, antequam terra peccatis repleta est. Cum Sodomorum iniquitas completa esset & coelo irent co-rum abominationes, tum demum extra ordinem eos punivit Deus. Ab extraordinariis plagis, quae integris Regnis & urbibus superinducuntur, ad extra-ordinaria peccata, optima in sacra Logica est consequentia. Frustra clamamus cum Judaeis, Templum Domini hic est, frustra cum Judaeis rectas facimus vias nostras, peccata nostra testanturin faciem nostram, nos esse filios degeneres gentem peccatricem, populum gravissimum inquitate, semen maleficum. Res ipsa loquitur, ipsam Dei Ecclesiam, quae in ejusmodi casibus Dei placatrix esse debeat, nihil aliud quam exacerbatricem esse. Et si pauculos pios excipias, Christianorum coe-tus multis in locis nihil aliud esse quam sententiam vitiorum.
units.tr: I lay this down beyond all dispute of controversy: since the Sun of the Gospel shone on Germany, she has never endured such harsh fates as now press upon her. What then?
