Is God unrighteous who inflicteth wrath? God forbid, says the Apostle, Rom. 3.5. For otherwise how shall God judge the world? God is not wont to fill the earth with plagues before the earth is filled with sins. When the iniquity of the Sodomites was complete and their abominations came up before heaven, only then did God punish them out of the ordinary course. From extraordinary plagues, which are brought upon entire kingdoms and cities, to extraordinary sins is, in sacred logic, a good consequence. We vainly cry out with the Jews, The temple of the LORD is here; in vain do we make our ways straight, as the Jews did; our sins testify to our face that we are degenerate children, a sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed. The thing itself speaks: the Church of God itself, which in such cases ought to appease God, is nothing other than an exacerbator. And, excepting a few pious people, the assemblies of Christians in many places are nothing else than a sentence of vices.

units.la: Sed dices, an is fuit Germaniae, an is in praesens est Belgii status, ut tale stigma mereatur? Nolo mihi credi. Producam contra Germaniam hominem Germanum, non patriae indecorem, sed gravem, antiqua fide & virtute Germanum, non furiosum, sed moderatum Theologum, Abrah. Schultetum, qui in notis ad v. cap. Jesa. haec habet, Status politia Judaica, qualis ea quidem tempore Jesaiae fuit, typus est cujuslibet ad interitum vergentis Reip. At non est Resp. sub Sole, quae exactius profligatos illos Judaeorum mores exprimat, quam haec nostra Germanica; unde conjectant prudentiores, aut interitum uni-versalem aut cladem certe insignem ei imminere. Haec. Schult. ante tot annos. Sed ne Germani quiritentur, nos minus aequos judices esse, addimus lubentes, nostram quoque Belgicam refertam esse a-bominationibus, ab una extremitate ad alteram. Addo, eo gravius esse nostrum peccatum, quo majori patientia nos tolerat Deus. In nos quadrare gravissimam illam Dei sentententiam apud Jerem.
units.tr: But you will say: is this the state of Germany, or is this the present state of Belgium, that it deserves such a stigma? I do not wish to be believed on my word. I will bring forward against Germany a German man, not one disgraceful to his fatherland but a grave theologian, German in ancient faith and virtue, not a frenzied but a moderate one: Abraham Scultetus, who in his notes on Isaiah chapter 5 has this: The state of the Jewish polity, such as it was in the time of Isaiah, is a type of any commonwealth tending to ruin. But there is no commonwealth under the sun that more exactly expresses those dissolute morals of the Jews than this our German one; whence the more prudent conjecture that either universal ruin or at least a notable disaster hangs over it. So Scultetus, many years ago. But lest the Germans complain that we are less fair judges, we gladly add that our own Belgic commonwealth too is crammed with abominations, from one extremity to the other. I add that our sin is the more grave, the greater the patience with which God bears with us. That most grievous sentence of God in Jeremiah applies to us:

units.la: Dedi Israeli libellum repudii, nec tamen timuit perfida Juda soror ejus sed abiens ipsa quoque scortata est. Fuitque praefamosa scortatione sua, ut contaminaret terram. Quapropter dixit Dominus mihi, justificat se-ipsam aversa Israel magis quam perfida Juda:
units.tr: I had given Israel a bill of divorce, yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but went and played the harlot too. Through her notorious harlotry she defiled the land. Therefore the Lord said to me: Backsliding Israel has justified herself more than treacherous Judah.

units.la: Non est mihi prolubium in aulas, curias, consistoria vel Germaniae vel Belgii penetrare. Non ego rusprando ventilabo principum adulteria & rapinas, profanum nominis divini abusum, horribiles imprecationes, diras, & plusquam belluinam ebrietatem. Non ego arguam ebriosos consiliarios, viros tantum strenuos ad bibendum & vires roboris ad exhauriendos magnos culullos. Neque lubet hic φιλοδειγματιζειν furiosos & ψιχολογυς illos Theologos, non tam pacis quam belli praecones, non ego jam illud tangam, quomodo singuli brachium carnis suae consumserint, quo-modo Manasses contra Ephraim steterit & Ephraim contra Manassem. Non conquerar de sublata omni disciplina Ecclesiastica & illata omnimoda licentia, qua uno eodemque die ad sacram mensam accumbere & ad vomitum se ingurgitare impune fuit. Academias visamus & in iis figamus pedem. Et quidem hoc eo iubentius faciam, quia sermo mihi est ad Academicos, quia ab Academiis prima mali labes. Academias Reip & Ecclesiae seminaria esse in confesso est. Quales ergo Academiae, talis Respublica, talis Ecclesia. Jam vero, qui in Academiis plerisque Germaniae vixerunt, & vel micam pietatis habent, uno ore fatentur omnes illas, magis Bacchi & Martis, quam Musarum sacraria fuisse; Ibi calamos in pugiones, atramentaria in thecas pulveris bom-bardici abiisse. Ibi irrisui fuisse sobrietatem, pietatem dedecori. Inno-xios adelescentes, quos studiorum gratia eo parentes ablegaverant, initiatos in ipso introitu Baccho fuisse, auspicia vitae Acad. facta a b infami & plena impietatis depositione. De cujus prima institutione nolim temere judicare. Illud ex ἀξιομίσων relatu habeo, eamplerisque in locis plane fuisse execrabilem: adactos illis fuisse innocentes juvenes ad juramentum, & quidem per ligneum Stephanum, se primo anno studiis non incubituros: nihil pecuniae ad parentes relaturos. Quod quidem juramentum & respectu materiae & formae abominabile, cautius servatum opinor, quam illud sanctum & verbo Dei & legibus conforme, quod Academiae Rectori praes-titum fuit. Accedit & illud, venerabile & tremendum illud Dei nomen multoties, atque adeo salutare Baptismi sacramentum plusquam diabolico imitamento profanatum fuisse. Quis in tali actione extremum Dei judicium, vel horam mortis expectare fuisset ausus; Duella creba, quae non solum gladiis sed & sclopetis peragebantur. Belluinae compotationes assiduae, nocturnae grassationes sine intermissione. Vexationes juniorum, qui plerunque seniorib-us meliores & innocentiores, intolerabiles, addo & injustissimae. Quis enim ferat, modestos & rerum suarum satagentes, à nebulonibus & decoctoribus & vere bacchantibus, Pennales, Bacchantes per contemptum appellari? Ausim pignus in omnes fortunas meas dare, vix centesimum ferocium istorum Bacchantium veram notionem & originem istius criminationis intelligere Βαχεῖντης, sequiori aevo ex Latino Vacans factum est, Suidas, Βαχαύντης, σχολαστὴς id est; otiosus, & Βαχάντες, σχολαστὴς, μὴ ἀμελημένος τὸ ἐσχημαν αὐτὸ, id est, otiosus non absolutus in suo negotio. Hoc ergo convitium in feroculos istos quadrat, qui in Acad. vagantur, nihil minus quam studia curantes, qui infra dignitatem suam existimant lectiones audire, collegiis misceri: carcinomiata ordinis scholastici, Deo & hominibus infesti, duplici nomine infames, per quos fit, ut divina & humana studia male audiant. Hæc dum in Germanorum Academiis odimus, ipsam nationem odisse per insignem calumniam dicimur. Atqui per Dei gratiam sunt adhuc Germani, qui hos mores detestantur. Sunt adhuc in Germania qui mores istos perosi, eo nomine liberos suos huc misere & mittunt. Serenissimus quoque Suecorum Rex hoc nomine nonnullas Germaniæ Academias in Academiæ Upsaliensis statutis censura notavit. Cum ergo is fuerit Academiarum status, cum ex talibus seminariis prodierint superintendentes, & Ministri & Principum consiliarii quis miretur, paucorum aliquot piorum conciones & commonefactiones frustra fuisse? Quis sævitiæ incuset Deum, quod tandem manum exseruerit?
units.tr: I have no wish to force my way into the courts, councils or consistories of Germany or the Netherlands. I will not rake up the adulteries and robberies of princes, their profane misuse of the divine name, their dreadful curses and their more than beastly drunkenness. I will not accuse drunken councillors, men strong only in drinking and in emptying great cups. Nor do I wish to play the moralist here against the frenzied and "psychological" theologians, heralds not of peace but of war. I will not touch on how individuals have consumed their own flesh, how Manasseh stood against Ephraim and Ephraim against Manasseh. I will not complain of the abolition of all ecclesiastical discipline and the unrestrained licence by which, on one and the same day, a man may sit down at the holy table and gorge himself to vomiting with impunity. Let us visit the universities and set foot in them. I shall do this all the more willingly because I am speaking to academics, since the first source of the evil lies in the universities. It is agreed that the universities are the seminaries of the commonwealth and the Church. Such universities, such commonwealth; such universities, such Church. Now, those who have lived in most of the German universities, and who have some grain of piety, all agree with one voice that these were shrines of Bacchus and Mars rather than of the Muses: there quills turned into daggers, inkpots into powder flasks. There sobriety was mocked and piety was a disgrace. Innocent young men, whom their parents had sent there for study, were initiated into Bacchus at the very entrance, and the beginning of their academic life was marked by an infamous and impious renunciation. I would not rashly judge its original institution. I have this from trustworthy report [ἀξιομίσων]: in most places it was utterly abominable. Innocent young men were bound by an oath, and indeed one sworn on a wooden Stephanus, that in their first year they would not devote themselves to study and would bring no money back to their parents. I think this oath, abominable both in its matter and its form, was kept more carefully than that holy oath, agreeable to the Word of God and the laws, which was given to the rector of the university. To this must be added that the venerable and awe-inspiring name of God was profaned many times, and the saving sacrament of baptism profaned by a more than diabolical imitation. Who in such a business would have dared to look for the last judgment of God, or the hour of death? There were frequent duels, fought not only with swords but also with pistols. Constant beastly drinking bouts, and night-time rampages without end. The harassment of juniors, who were often better and more innocent than their seniors, was intolerable, and I add, most unjust. For who could bear that modest men, intent on their own affairs, should be called by the scoundrels, the bankrupts and the truly rowdy, "Pennales" and "Bacchantes", as a term of contempt? I would stake all my fortune that scarcely one in a hundred of these fierce Bacchanals understands the true meaning and origin of this accusation. Βαχεῖντης, in a later age, was made from the Latin Vacans, as Suidas has it: Βαχαύντης, σχολαστὴς, that is, idle; and Βάχαντες, σχολαστὴς, μὴ ἀμελημένος τὸ ἐσχημαν αὐτὸ, that is, idle, not absorbed in his own business. This reproach therefore fits those little savages who wander about the universities, caring for nothing less than their studies, who think it beneath their dignity to attend lectures or to mix with classes: the cancers of the scholastic order, hostile to God and man, infamous on both counts, through whom it comes about that divine and human learning are ill spoken of. While we hate these things in the German universities, we are said, by a notable slander, to hate the nation itself. Yet, by the grace of God, there are still Germans who detest these customs. There are still in Germany those who abhor such customs and on that account have sent, and still send, their children here. The most serene King of the Swedes too, in the statutes of the University of Uppsala, has censured some German universities on this very ground. Since, then, such is the state of the universities, and since from such seminaries have come superintendents, ministers and councillors of princes, who can be surprised that the sermons and admonitions of a few pious men have been in vain? Who could blame God for cruelty, that at last He has stretched out His hand?

units.la: Sed dices, tempora illa jam transiisse. Nunc, ex quò flagellare Evangelicos cœpit Deus, alium vitæ cursum instituisse. Respondeo, etiamnum de Evangelicis tam in Belgio quam ipsa Germ. dici illud posse quod jam tractamus; eos vid. sedere ab bibendum, dum Sufan est perplexa. De Germania rem iterum testatam faciam verbis Germani. Is est Paulus Tarnovius Theol. primarius in Acad. Rostoch. Professor, vir pius & eruditus. Is ante quadriennium in Acad. sua orationem habuit de novo Evangelio. In ea solicite inquirit pia anima; in primam & præcipuam causam tantarum calamitatum, quibus Evangelicæ Ecclesiæ inundant, & omnes Academiæ periturœ videntur. Illam assignat opinionem quandam & persuasionem exitialem, quæ primum mundum & Jud. Remp. perdidit. Quæ Novi quoque Testamenti cœtus vastat & scholas destruit, Respublicas evertit. Eam vocat novum Evangelium, non quod hodie aut nuper illud natum sit, sed quod post antiquum in Paradiso promulgatum statim invaserit Ecclesiam. Illud definit dogma de misericordia Dei Patris, remissione peccatorum, salute æterna per externum Dei cultum consequenda. Vel aliter, inanem persuasionem de gratia & misericordia Dei, non ex verbo Dei notam, sed ex arcano consilio Diaboli natam, credulitate hominum carnali securitate laborantium conservata, in qua ipse promittit immunitatem pœnarum, vitam æternam, omnibus externum cultum præstantibus & verum Christianismum ore tantum profitentibus. Hinc illæ lacrymæ, inquit, quod Deum non esse tam acrem vindicem aut severum judicem peccatorum somnient, modo orthodoxæ doctrinæ hæreant, conciones audiant, hymnos canant, cœnam Dominicam percipiant. Sint duo pluresve eorundem parentum filii, unus bonæ indolis, alter pravæ, faciat uterque officium ex æquo, dum ætas, metus, magister, prohibent. Post, ubi liberior datur videndi potestas, alterum in officio contineat amor filialis, alterum metus exhæredationis. Utrique si tanquam custos adhibeatur servus, idemque magister improbus, is ægrotum illum animum ad deteriora facile flectet, nec difficulter sanum illum de integritate mentis deturbabit. Ridebit hæc forte non nemo, inquit, qui me tam puerilia in tam grave theatrum producere mirabitur. Cui non inconvenienter cum poëta Venusino respondero, Quid rides? mutato nomine de te Fabula narratur. Non enim in privatis ædibus tantum, aut scholis inter pueros, sed & in Academiis inter juvenes, in Ecclesia inter viros & senes, tales magistri improbi sunt, illic quoque huic scenæ extruendæ amplissimus conceditur locus. Nam simul ac è scholarum trivialium claustris emissa juventus in Academias infert pedem, non modo palam fit, quo quisque, sit ingenio, sed qui malo, indies fit pejor; qui bono, raro evadit melior. Hoc debetur novi Evangelii præconibus & professoribus. Et hæc, inquit, publica disciplina foventur, quæ ita in omni statu tam Eccl. quam Polit. collapsa est, ut pio intelligenti, hanc morum & temporum corruptelam intuenti, in mentem venire necesse sit illud Prophetæ, populemi, qui te ducunt, seducunt. Vide enim quid agatur. Postquam per omne genus flagitiorum libere decursum est, si unam doloris sui indicem valde fallacem ediderint & veniam delictorum flagitaverint, tum se in cœlo esse sibi persuasum habent, ejusque suæ opinionis pignus cœnam Dom. postulant & quamtumvis canes & sues sunt, impetrant. Quis vero honestus princeps in suam aulam, ad suam mensam admitteret omnibus flagitiis ex mera petulantia insignes, nec ad meliorem frugem reversos? Quis bonus paterf. in ædibus suis & convictu tam sui dissimile toleret famulitium? Et nos erimus adeo mentis inopes, ut sola stulta credulitate nobis persuadeamus, quod terrenis Dominis & patribus intolerabile novimus, id cœlestem illum patrem, Dominum illum dominum approbaturum? Hæc fere Tarnovius. Quod de Germanicis Ecclesiis verbis D. Tarnovii dixi, de Belgicis nostratis Theologi verbis edisseram. Is est Rev. vir, D. Gul. Telingius, qui in omnibus s propemodum scriptis suis hoc agit, ut offendat, quam patēn-fores Diabolus in his prouinciis huic novo Evangelio aperue-. Alibi conqueritur, doctrinam de justificatione solius fideisque operibus hoc tempore eodem modo tradi & urgeri, quo inireformationis tradebatur. Tunc exigebat necessitas, ut sola es urgeretur, extirpando pestilenti de merito bonorum operum ori. Nihil in solius fidei inculcatione erat periculi, quamdiu s, quia à Papatu descíverant, serio propositum erat, sancte & c doctrinæ convenienter vivere. At postquam contra iverunt nia, postquam salutaris hæc doctrina in licentiæ parrocinium ocari cœpit, postquam operi operato, hoc est, externo culplusculum tributum est, non quidem ista doctrina silere debuis-, sed insuper imagis vehementer, δικαίωσις & δικαιῶσις docendi lent Evangelici, de natura & criteriis verę justificantis fidei. vid. major eorum, qui Christianismum profitentur, pars ingeret, quanto adhuc intervallo à fide justificante abesset præptio. Siquidem in ea incidimus tempora, inquit idem, queis ieismus securitas & præsumptio adeo invaluere, ut negotium tis ita fere ab omnibus tractetur, quasi nihil facilius esset, quam portam illam angustam ingredi. Hoc est novum illud Evanum, Auditores, quod ceu, pestilens aliquod sidus tot in Eciis Evangelicis homines afflavit, ut qui de hoc negotio ex verDei & communi vita judicare velit, intrepide pronuntiaturus inter eos qui Christiani, Evangelici, Reformati & membra lesiæ dicuntur, longe plures esse qui pereant, quam qui salven-
units.tr: But you will say that those times have passed, and that since God began to scourge the evangelical churches, a different course of life has been adopted. I reply that what we are now discussing can still be said of the evangelicals, both in the Netherlands and in Germany itself: that they sit down to drink while Zion is in distress. I shall once more bear witness to the situation from Germany, in the words of a German. He is Paulus Tarnovius, the chief professor of theology in the University of Rostock, a pious and learned man. Four years ago he gave an address at his university on the "new gospel". In it, the pious soul anxiously inquires into the first and chief cause of the great calamities by which the evangelical churches are overwhelmed, and by which all the universities seem doomed to perish. He assigns it to a certain deadly opinion and persuasion, which first destroyed the world and the Jewish commonwealth. It also lays waste the assembly of the New Testament, destroys schools and overthrows commonwealths. He calls it the new gospel, not because it was born today or recently, but because, once the old gospel was proclaimed in Paradise, it at once invaded the Church. He defines it as the doctrine that the mercy of God the Father, the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation are to be obtained through outward worship of God. Or, put otherwise, an empty persuasion about the grace and mercy of God, not known from the Word of God but born from the secret counsel of the Devil, kept alive by the credulity of men suffering from carnal security, in which he promises immunity from punishments and eternal life to all who render outward worship and who profess true Christianity only with their lips. Hence, he says, those tears: men dream that God is not so fierce an avenger or so severe a judge of sins, provided they cling to orthodox doctrine, hear sermons, sing hymns and receive the Lord's Supper. Let there be two or more sons of the same parents, one of good disposition and the other of bad: each performs his duty equally while age, fear and a tutor restrain them. Afterwards, when a freer opportunity of seeing is given, love of the son keeps the one in his duty, and fear of disinheritance the other. If a slave is set over both as guardian, and the same wicked tutor is there, he will easily bend that sick mind towards worse things, and not with difficulty turn the sound mind away from its integrity. Perhaps someone will laugh, he says, who will wonder that I bring such childish things onto so serious a stage. To him I shall answer, not inappropriately, with the Venusian poet: Why do you laugh? Change the name, and the story is about you. For not only in private houses or among boys in schools, but also in the universities among young men, and in the Church among men and old people, there are such wicked tutors, and there too the widest room is given for setting up this stage. For as soon as youth, released from the cloisters of the grammar schools, sets foot in the universities, it is not only plain what each is like by nature, but the one who is bad daily becomes worse, and the one who is good seldom turns out better. This is owed to the heralds and professors of the new gospel. And, he says, this public discipline is nurtured by them, and it has so collapsed in every state, both Church and civil, that a pious and discerning person, observing this corruption of morals and times, must necessarily recall the words of the Prophet: "O my people, those who lead you cause you to err." For see what is going on. After they have run freely through every kind of wickedness, if they produce some very deceptive token of their sorrow and ask for pardon for their misdeeds, then they persuade themselves that they are in heaven, and they demand the Lord's Supper as the pledge of this opinion of theirs, and, however much like dogs and swine they are, they obtain it. But what honourable prince would admit to his court and his table men notable for every kind of vice out of sheer wantonness, and who had not turned back to better conduct? What good father would tolerate in his house and his company a servant so unlike himself? And shall we be so poor in mind that we persuade ourselves, by mere foolish credulity, that the heavenly Father and the Lord who is Lord will approve what we know to be intolerable to earthly lords and fathers? So far Tarnovius. What I have said of the German churches in Tarnovius' words, I shall now set out in the words of a theologian of our own land. He is the reverend man Gulielmus Telingius, who in almost all his writings aims to show how widely the Devil has opened the gates in these provinces to this new gospel. Elsewhere he complains that the doctrine of justification by faith alone, and of faith and works, is taught and urged at this time in the same way as it was taught at the beginning of the Reformation. Then necessity demanded that faith alone be urged, in order to root out the pestilent mouth that spoke of the merit of good works. There was no danger in the inculcation of faith alone, so long as, because they had broken away from the Papacy, it was seriously intended that they should live holily and in accordance with sound doctrine. But after they turned against it, after this wholesome doctrine began to be used as a shelter for licence, after a little was attributed to the ex opere operato, that is, to outward ceremony, this doctrine ought not to have been silenced, but rather should have been pressed even more vigorously: justification and justifying must be taught by evangelicals, concerning the nature and marks of true justifying faith. See how great a distance, he says, separates from justifying faith the greater part of those who profess Christianity. For we have fallen into those times, says the same author, when security and presumption about Christianity have so prevailed that the matter is generally treated as if nothing were easier than to enter that narrow gate. This is that new gospel, hearers, which, like some pestilent star, has breathed upon so many people in the evangelical churches that anyone who wishes to judge this matter from the Word of God and from common life will be ready to declare boldly that among those who are called Christians, evangelicals, reformed and members of the Church, far more are perishing than are being saved.

units.la: In sano de rebus divinis sensu & nudo assensu, in formulis & emoniis fere acquiescimus, de abnegatione nostri, de crucione carnis & cupiditatum nostrarum parum aut nihil cogitamus, non secundum carnem sed secundum Sp. mundo mortui, Deo vius, nealiis præbeamus offendicula, ut inculpati & simplices mus, in medio generationis pravæ & perversæ splendeamus vam faces in mundo, parum pensi habemus. Et tamen si hæc e nostra absunt, non potest esse fides justificans. Hanc; quam , præsumptionem evidenter in uno Ebrietatis peccato olten-. Quotus quisque, etiam eorum, qui hoc loco in hac urbe, meinbra Ecclesiæ censentur, Ebrietatem, uti par erat, detur? Multos videas quotidie sedere & ex professo componere potandum, mane surgere ad potandum, protrahere potatioique in noctem. Videas eos dies sacros & negotiosos juxta æstumare. Quin & parascevas istius diei Dominici, ipsumque illum diem, quo ad sacram mensam accumbimus, potando consumi. Veniunt ad conciones, canunt cum Ecclesia hymnos & externum illum cultum præstant. At post conciones redeunt ad ingenium. Non prolectati, sed sponte sua, & insuper alios prolectantes. Isti aut statuunt, Ebrietatem non esse tam grave peccatum, ut eo nomine ex regno Dei excludendi sunt: aut suæ, quam jactant fidei, ista peccata condonatum iri sperant. Si prius, pestilentem, & qui fundamentum salutis evertit, errorem errant. Si posterius, jam in hanc præsumptionem delati sunt & insuper in doctrina de fide justificante talem errant errorem, qui rursus fundamentum salutis ab ipsa stirpe convellit. Et hi tamen tam pestilentes errores, hi mores publica disciplina multis in locis foventur.
units.tr: In a sound understanding of divine things and bare assent, we are content for the most part with formulas and ceremonies. We think little or nothing of self-denial, of mortifying the flesh and our lusts, of not living according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, dead to the world and living to God, of not giving offence to others, and of shining as blameless and simple children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, like lights in the world. And yet if these things are absent from our lives, faith cannot be justifying. This presumption is shown clearly in the one sin of drunkenness. How few, even among those in this city who are counted members of the Church, drink as they ought? You may see many every day sitting down and deliberately planning to drink, rising in the morning to drink, and prolonging their drinking into the night. You may see them judge the holy days and the busy days by the same measure. Indeed, the eves of this Lord's Day, and the day itself, on which we sit down at the holy table, are spent in drinking. They come to the sermons, sing hymns with the Church, and perform that outward worship. But after the sermons they return to their old nature, not enticed but of their own accord, and they entice others besides. Such people either hold that drunkenness is not so grave a sin that they must be excluded from the kingdom of God on that account, or they hope that these sins will be pardoned on the strength of the faith they boast of. If the former, they hold a pestilent error that overturns the foundation of salvation. If the latter, they have already fallen into this presumption and, besides, hold in the doctrine of justifying faith an error that again tears up the foundation of salvation from its very root. And yet these pestilent errors and these manners are fostered in many places by public discipline.

units.la: Audias alibi simplicem idiotam aut mulierculam excommunicari, quod ad Pontificios vel Anabaptisticam sectam desciverit. Non culpo; sed illud doleo, adversus talia carcinomata Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ aciem hebescere. Nam nisi talia propudia reformatæ Ecclesiæ tolerarent, non tot simplices animæ ab Ecclesiarum nostrarum septis arcerentur, aut admissæ deficerent. Imo mirantur cordati viri, non plures ab Ecclesiis nostris ob unam hanc causam facere divortium. Sed videamus aliud. Is, quem supra nominavi Telingius, alibi conqueritur, multos in Ecclesiis Belgicis non tantum discentes, sed & docentes, totos in eo fuisse, sibi & populo ut persuaderent, ex plagis istis extraordinariis non posse semper evidenter concludi tantam morum corruptelam & tantam DOMINI erga Remp. vel Ecclesias indignationem, qualem nonnulli prædicabant, quos per contemptum, Casuales, Præcisianos, Puritanos, Pharisæos, & nasutulos appellatos fuisse dequeritur. Ita vita illa & anima veræ religionis, Sanctitas, sine qua nemo videbit Deum, sine qua fides exanime cadaver est, sub mantello hypocriseos, pharisaismi & melancholiæ traducta est. Sed mirum non est, imperitos & profanos quosdam juvenes, qui tabernas & lupanaria adhuc olentes, ne speciem quidem habentes pietatis, ad cathedras admissi sunt, hic cœcutire, aliisque qui acutius hic vident, & in Schola Sp. S. majora fecerunt spatia, insultare. Inimica quippe semper virtutibus vitia sunt, & optimi quique a malis tanquam exprobrantes aspiciuntur. Videtis rursus, Auditores, magnam hujus mali partem ex Academiis pullulare.
units.tr: Elsewhere you may hear a simple layman or a poor woman excommunicated because they have gone over to the Papists or the Anabaptist sect. I do not blame this; but I grieve that the edge of Church discipline grows dull against such cancers. For unless the reformed Church tolerated such disgraces, so many simple souls would not be kept out of the fold of our churches, or, once admitted, fall away. Indeed, thoughtful men marvel that more do not separate from our churches for this one reason alone. But let us look at another matter. Telingius, whom I named above, complains elsewhere that many in the Belgic churches, not only learners but teachers too, were wholly given to persuading themselves and the people that from these extraordinary plagues one could not always clearly conclude such a corruption of morals and such a wrath of the Lord against the commonwealth or the churches as some were preaching. These, he complains, were called by way of contempt Casuists, Precisians, Puritans, Pharisees and snobs. So that life and soul of true religion, holiness, without which no one will see God, without which faith is a lifeless corpse, has been dragged under the cloak of hypocrisy, Pharisaism and melancholy. But it is no wonder that some untrained and profane young men, who still stink of taverns and brothels and do not even have the appearance of piety, have been admitted to the chairs, and here grope in the dark, while others who see more keenly here, and have made greater progress in the School of the Holy Spirit, they insult. For vices are always hostile to virtues, and the best men are looked at by the bad as reproaches. You see again, hearers, that a great part of this evil springs up from the Academies.

units.la: Sed tempus est, ut ex hoc quoque orationis diverticulo in viam redeam am & finem orationi imponam. In pleri sque Germaniae locis cademiis etiamnum veteri more vivi, dum Evangelici ubique sslictionum pondere gemunt, volui ostendere. Qui ex suitibus Academiis hoc anno ad nos descenderunt, idem uno osirmant. Inter ipsos quoque Academiarum Professores, etiam essione Theologos, non deesse, qui præsentium temporum a vino quotidie pellant, non sine horrore narrantes audivimus. um symbolum & quasi intercalare est illud, non Christi, sed si Anacreontis carmen, ὅταν πίω τὸν οἶνον, Εὐδαιμονία αἱ μεμψιμαι. ego hominum generi vel Demetrii saltem mentem ex animo or, qui, cum in Seleuci potestatem, teste Plutarcho, deve- , primo quidem poculis & alea se dedit, iisque tempus trant, quo præsentis miseriæ cogitationes, quibus inquietabatur us devitaret, & ægram crapula velaret mentem, at tandem nimitatem & patientiam meliora curarum animi remedia esse it. Sed descendamus rursus in Belgium. Non curo quid in cis Belgii collegiis & provinciarum comitiis agatur. Non quæutrum illic fortassis quoque non sint, qui frequentiores & tiores sedeant ad bibendum, quam ad consultandum, ne quid nenti vel Resp. vel viduarum & orphanorum causæ capiant. anquiro, utrum illos mores in Academiis forsan non imbibe-
units.tr: But it is time for me to return from this digression in my speech to the path, and to bring my address to an end. I wished to show that in most places in Germany the Academies still live in the old way, while the Evangelicals everywhere groan under the weight of afflictions. Those who have come down to us this year from the other Academies confirm the same thing. We have also heard, not without horror, reports that among the professors of the Academies themselves, even among the theologians, there are not lacking those who drive the present times away with wine every day. The common refrain and, as it were, the chorus of this song is not Christ's but that of Anacreon: whenever I drink wine [ὅταν πίω τὸν οἶνον], happiness! away with complaints! [Εὐδαιμονία αἱ μεμψιμοιρίαι]. I would that the minds of such men were at least like that of Demetrius, who, when he was in the power of Seleucus, as Plutarch attests, at first gave himself up to cups and dice, and spent his time in them so that he might avoid the thoughts of present misery which disturbed him, and cover his sick mind with drunkenness; but at last he learned that moderation and patience are better remedies for the cares of the soul. But let us come down again to Belgium. I do not care what is done in the colleges of the Belgic provinces and in the assemblies of the provinces. I do not ask whether there are perhaps some there too who sit more often and longer at drinking than at deliberating, lest they take any care for the commonwealth or the cause of widows and orphans. I ask whether they perhaps have not imbibed those customs in the Academies.

units.la: In Academiis nostris quam multi sunt, etiam inter eos qui ro ministerio distinatos profitentur, qui magis in tabernis, Museis & auditoriis habitant? Quos nulla calamitatum, quiunc ubique Evangelici opprimuntur cura tangit? qui ad illas, s undequaque cingimur, indagines, oculos claudunt? Ecerte membra mystici istius corporis, seu Ecclesiæ, in qua erii sortem jam sibi desponderunt! O propudia, ὦ κακ' ἐλέ-
units.tr: In our Academies, how many are there, even among those who profess themselves destined for the ministry, who live more in taverns, in the Muses' halls and in lecture-rooms? Whom does no care for the calamities by which the Evangelicals are everywhere oppressed touch? Who close their eyes to those snares by which we are surrounded on every side? Surely these are members of that mystical body, or Church, in whose lot they have already pledged themselves! O disgraces, O wretched [ὦ κακ' ἐλέ-]

units.la: Annon hoc est sedere ad bibendum, dum Susan perplexa nnon hoc est omnes miserationes cum impiis Edomæis exuespice mihi rursus feroces illos Cyclopes, Canes illos venacrumeni-mulgas, in novellos & innoxios instar prædonum tes, intoleranda tyrannide prementes, qui sic vitam instiquasi se totos. Diabolo mancupio tradidissent, de quibus usurpavero illud Virgilianum,
units.tr: Is this not sitting down to drink, while Zion is in perplexity? Is this not casting off all compassion along with the impious Edomites? Let me call up again those fierce Cyclopes, those hunting dogs that milk the flocks, who, like pirates against the young and harmless, oppress them with intolerable tyranny, who live as though they had wholly handed themselves over to the Devil in bondage. Of them I shall use that verse of Virgil,

units.la: DI talem nostris terris avertite pestem.
units.tr: Ye gods, turn such a plague away from our lands.

units.la: , inquam, quia illud ex vero asseram, nos jampridem hanc niæ nostræ navem ista saburra exonerasse. Neque enim & nostro Athenæo tam licuit esse felici, ut affirmare liceat, ejusmodi Harpyas immundo suo contactu nostra quoque sacra non fœdasse. Vidimus aliquando, Auditores, vidimus ejusmodi belluas, queis Tristius haud unquam monstrum, nec savior nulla Pestis, & ira Deum Stygiis sese extulit undis. Vidimus, & subita multis formidine sanguis Diriguit, cecidere animi.
units.tr: I say this, I affirm it because it is true, that our Academy's ship has long been weighed down by this ballast. For our Athenaeum has not been so fortunate that we may say such Harpies have not defiled our sacred things with their foul touch. We have seen such monsters at some time, hearers, we have seen them: no more dreadful monster, no fiercer plague, ever rose from the Stygian waves, sent by the anger of the gods. We saw them, and the blood in many froze with sudden terror, their spirits fell.

units.la: Erant, qui non amplius disciplinæ acie,
units.tr: There were some who, no longer by the line of discipline,

units.la: Sed votis precibusque jubebant poscere pacem.
units.tr: But with vows and prayers bade us seek peace.

units.la: In ejusmodi tempora superior meus Rectoratus incidit. Capessebam eum, ut clarius loquar, hoc animo, ut eum more antecessorum administrarem, qui hoc satagebant, ne Academiam pejori statu successori traderent, quam acceperant. Et certe rem magnam præstabat, qui hoc vere præstabat. Hæc ergo summa votorum erat. In eo conquiescendum etiam illi suadebant, qui in ordine nostro cæteris ætate & authoritate antistabant. De meliori Academiæ statu nil nisi desperationis voces audiebantur. Quis tristitiam illorum temporum fando explicet? Si ea de re verba facere sederet, nec invenire principium, nec evoluere exitum possem. Singulas noctes insigne aliquod flagitium nobilitabat, nullum carebat exemplo nefas. Ipsi Reip. nostræ proceres, quibus recta liberorum suorum institutio cordi erat, de mittendis ad hanc Acad. liberis sermones vix sustinebant. Sed ex trivialibus scholis vindicta manumissos mox extra Proviciam ad alias Academias, magnis impendiis, quamvis sæpe non meliori successu, mittebant. Fuit aliquando tempus, Auditores, cum hic non liceret ulli esse pio, modesto, & legum observanti. Exeundum erat ex Academia & Oeconomia, qui sacramenti istius, quod Academiæ dixerat, memor vitam agitabat. Qui à nobis dissiti, & de Academiæ statu ex tot popularium naufragiis edoƈti erant, Academiam hanc pro derelicto habeant. Quin & publicis scriptis huic Academiæ, quam Christo & Ecclesiæ majorum pietas sacraverat infame illud inustum suit stigma, BACCHI SACRARIUM. Hæc cum aliquando legerem & audirem, memini me non leviter irasci & in eos destomachari, qui ejusmodi sermonibus Academiam nostram deturparent, aut aures substringerent. At ex quo ipse Rectoræ admotus us & soluta à litora navi, in altum provectus fui, cogno vi rues istos intra verum stetisse. Multa isto anno naufragia tristis emebundus spectavi. Multos generosæ indolis & magnæ spei lescentes, quos parentes & præceptores integros vitæ à se dierant & indulgens hæc mater acceperat, intra paucos dies per ales istas potationes, quibus in ipso introitu Baccho id est, Diao initiabantur, corruptos vidimus, & postea misere periisse ivimus. Præcipua autem horum malorum labes ab ejusmodi pyis fuit, quæ isthoc anno solito frequentiores Academiæ noincubabant. Namque, ut clarius mentem meam edisseram, etera Academiæ mala & inveteratos morbos magna miseriæ aco facta est ab insignibus aliquot & projectissimæ nequitiæ nebubus, qui magis incarnatos Diabolos, quam homines moribus imebant. Hæc tunc erat fati nostri infelicitas. Passi sumus; itores, passi sumus ab istis Harpyis.
units.tr: My own Rectorate fell in such times. I took it up, to speak more plainly, with this intention, that I might administer it after the manner of my predecessors, who took care that they should not hand the Academy over to a successor in a worse state than they had received it. And indeed he who truly did this accomplished a great thing. This, then, was the sum of our prayers. Those who stood above the rest of our order in age and authority urged us also to rest content with this. Nothing but voices of despair were heard about a better state for the Academy. Who could explain in words the sadness of those times? If I were to speak on that matter, I could neither find a beginning nor unroll an end. Every night some notable crime made itself famous, and no wickedness lacked an example. The very nobles of our commonwealth, to whom the proper upbringing of their children was dear, could scarcely bear to speak of sending their children to this Academy. But from the trivial schools they sent their freed sons away outside the province, at great expense, to other Academies, though often with no better success. There was once a time, hearers, when it was not allowed for anyone here to be pious, modest and observant of the laws. Whoever lived according to the sacred oath which he had sworn to the Academy, and remembered it, had to leave the Academy and the household. Those who had been driven from us, and had learned of the state of the Academy from so many wrecks of their fellow citizens, regard this Academy as abandoned. Nay, in public writings that infamous brand was stamped upon this Academy, which the piety of our forebears had consecrated to Christ and the Church: THE SHRINE OF BACCHUS. When I once read and heard these things, I remember that I was not a little angry and became indignant at those who disgraced our Academy with such talk, or who stopped their ears. But since I myself was brought to the helm and the ship was loosed from the shore and carried out into the deep, I have come to know that those men's words stood within the truth. In this year I watched many shipwrecks with sorrow. We saw many youths of generous disposition and great hope, whom their parents and teachers had handed over to us whole in character, and whom this indulgent mother had received, corrupted within a few days by those wretched drinking bouts into which they were initiated at the very entrance, into Bacchus, that is, into Diabolus; and afterwards we went and saw them wretchedly perish. The chief stain of these evils, however, came from such men as, this year, were more numerous than usual and swarmed over the Academy. For, to set out my mind more clearly, the other evils of the Academy and its long-standing diseases were made into a great misery by a few notable men of most abandoned wickedness, who looked more like incarnate devils than men in their morals. This was then the unhappiness of our fate. We suffered, hearers, we suffered from those Harpies.

units.la: — qua nec Sarmentus, iniquas Cæsaris ad mensas, vel vilis Galba tulisset.
units.tr: Which not even Sarmentus at Caesar's unjust tables, nor vile Galba, would have endured.

units.la: imen ex hoc numero nonnulli, ex quo fœdissimis vestigiis res-s hinc vel excessere, vel ejecti sunt, nullo edito resipitiæ specime, nullo Academiæ aut Ecclesiæ, aut ullius honesti testimonio instructi ad sacrum ministerium evecti sunt, ut non ie compellari hic possint Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ versibus istis ianis,
units.tr: From this number some, from whom the most foul traces of their conduct had either departed from here or they had been ejected, with no published evidence of repentance and no testimony from the Academy, the Church or any honourable person, were nonetheless raised to the sacred ministry. So the Evangelical Church cannot here be addressed with those verses,

units.la: Quo vobis mentes, recta qua stare solebant, Antehac, dementi sese flexere ruina?
units.tr: What has come over your minds, which used to stand upright, that you have bent down in mad ruin?

units.la: ἱ τὰ μὴ ἀποπνύχθαι ἐάσαμεν & Deo potius gratias agamus, l eam mentem patriæ proceribus & Academiæ Professoribus em infspiraverit, ut de rerum collapsarum restauratione cogirint, eam mascule in exemplum aliarum Acad. introduxerint, ıtenus laudabiliter conservaverint. Ex eo melior rediit Acadiæ facies & bonæ spei fidus affulsit omnibus, qui Academiæ bant. Ex eo proceres nostri magnis & extra-ordinarii stipenexteros Professores, viros celebres, quod antea vel sperare um fuisset, invitarunt, & Academiam, de qua solvendam sain suffragia iverant, ad omnem occasionem exornarunt. Peıvit melior ea fama in Arctonum usque orbem, unde modestiss & prioribus istis longe absimiles adolescentes, his postremis annis, habuimus, amavimus, etiamnum habemus & amamus. Ex eo is fuit Academiæ nostræ status, ut qui vel corrupti vel indocti ex ea excessere, nil nisi fatuitatem & socordiam suam accusare possint. Hujus elogii testes citare possem multos ex ipsa Germania. Quotquot enim ferocioribus istis moribus in Academiis Germanicis innutriti fuere, iisdemque hærere, illi hanc Academiam ceu ergastulum quoddam fugere. Qui contra animo studendi & pie vivendi peregre ivere, vel à parentibus ablegati sunt, hanc præ aliis elegere. Id quod multis epistolarum documentis, si opus esset, demonstrare possem. Fuerunt & complures, qui cum in aliis Academiis, per crebras sociorum interpellationes & assiduas compotationes Musis litare & in pace vivere non possent, hanc Academiam ceu secessum quendam petiere, inibique sic vixere, ut nec illos hic vixisse, nec nos tales cives habuisse pœnituerit.
units.tr: Let us pass over what ought not to be spoken of [ἀποπνύχθαι], and rather give thanks to God that he inspired the nobles of our fatherland and the professors of the Academy to think about restoring what had fallen, that they bravely introduced this as an example to other academies, and have preserved it commendably to this day. From then on the face of the Academy improved, and a fair hope of better things shone upon all who were devoted to it. From then on our nobles, at great and extraordinary expense, invited foreign professors, famous men, which before could hardly have been hoped for, and they adorned the Academy on every occasion, for which they had sought the votes of those who were to be dismissed. That better reputation has spread even to the Northern world, whence we have had, in these last years, very modest young men, quite unlike those earlier ones, whom we have loved, still have and love. From then on the condition of our Academy has been such that those who have left it corrupted or uneducated can accuse nothing but their own foolishness and sloth. I could cite many witnesses to this praise from Germany itself. For all who were brought up in those more savage customs at the German academies, and clung to them, fled this Academy as a kind of workhouse. Those who, on the contrary, went abroad with a mind to study and to live piously, or were sent away by their parents, chose it above others. I could demonstrate this by many letters, if need be. There were also several who, since in other academies they could not sacrifice to the Muses and live in peace because of frequent interruptions by companions and constant drinking bouts, sought this Academy as a kind of retreat, and lived here in such a way that neither did they regret having lived here, nor did we regret having such citizens.

units.la: Absque hoc esset, nunquam huic servitutis jugo humeros meos denuo suppositiurem. Ego certe de me id possum profiteri, malle me. Summam pauperiem & duros perferre labores, Stramineaque inopem ruri habitare casa.
units.tr: Were it not so, I would never again put my shoulders under this yoke of servitude. Certainly I can profess this of myself: I would rather bear the utmost poverty and hard labours, and dwell poor in the country in a straw hut.

units.la: Quam talis Academiæ qualis aliquando erat, vel Professorem vel Rectorem magere. Ita enim opinatus semper fui, beatius esse tristi mendicitate precarium spiritum trahere, quam ejusmodi peccatis non dico communicare, sed audiendis & videndis animam quotidie excruciare. Aucupentur alii à frequentia inutilium terræ ponderum & multitudine nominum, Academiæ famam. Differant alii ad palatum juventutis, de laxandis Academicæ disciplinæ frænis. Disputent, quam possunt subtilissime, de scholæ trivialis, Gymnasii & Academiæ discrimine. Ominentur Christianis Academiis vastitiem & solitudinem. Nos, nos, inquam (loquor enim & meo & DD. Collegarum nomine) veteris ἀπαξίας & molestiarum, quas perpessi sumus, æternum memores, melioris istius disciplinæ clavum, quoad possumus, manibus nostris tenebimus, neque extorqueri nobis, nisi à majori quadam vi, patiemur. Quod si talis quædam rebus nostris intervenerit, aut si quosdam disciplinæ masculos vindices aut mors aut vocationes nobis abstulerint, aut si hanc administrationem, (in qua tamen nos neutiquam conscientiis nostris & juramento, quod Illustrium Frisiæ Ordinum pietas Rectoribus & Assessoribus præscripsit, satis facere, cum dolore profitemur) iis, qui cum imperio sunt, invisam esse cognoverimus s, ibimus libenter, namerumque explebimus. Interim de, nec non cæteris collegis meis, viris reverendis & clarissimis, is affirmare possum, malle nos paucos vere generosos, vere iles, modestos & studiosos cives, quam multos feroces Ba- ‹, idest, otiosos ventres, qui eo tantum fine in Academiis antur, ut Senatui & vere studiosis negotium facessant, quieque publicam turbent. Qui profiteri non erubescunt, se stuium gratia in Acad. hac non morari. Qui infra dignitatem suonunt, lectiones audire, respondendi & opponendi & peromunia obire privatisque etiam exercitiis cæteris miscerí. Hi rentibus suis stipites & caudices faciunt, dum nobis persuadeagunt, se tantis parentum impendiis in hac Acad. ali, ut moominum videant. Quærant illi Romam, adeant Parisios, Lon- n, Venetias, ut multorum hominum mores & mundi com- a videant. Hic humiles casæ, hic obscura tecta sunt, quæ s Heroas capere non valent.
units.tr: Whatever sort of academy this was at some time, I have never thought it better to be a professor or rector of it. For I have always judged it better to draw a precarious breath in sad beggary than, I will not say to share in such sins, but to be daily tormented in soul by hearing and seeing them. Let others court the good opinion of the Academy by the number of useless fees and the multitude of names on its rolls. Let others argue, to please the palate of the young, for loosening the reins of academic discipline. Let them dispute, as subtly as they can, about the difference between the trivial school, the gymnasium and the academy. Let them foretell desolation and emptiness for Christian academies. We, I say (for I speak both in my own name and in that of my reverend colleagues), mindful for ever of the former [ἀπαξία] and of the troubles we have suffered, will hold the helm of this better discipline in our hands as far as we can, and we will not allow it to be wrested from us except by some greater force. If some such thing should befall our affairs, or if death or calls to other posts should take from us some of the men who are manly defenders of discipline, or if we should find that this administration (in which we sadly confess that we cannot in any way satisfy our consciences or the oath which the piety of the Illustrious Orders of Friesland prescribed for the rectors and assessors) is hateful to those who hold power, we will gladly go, and fulfil our time. Meanwhile I can affirm of myself and of my other colleagues, reverend and most distinguished men, that we would rather have a few truly noble, truly learned, modest and studious citizens than many fierce Bacchanals, that is, idle bellies, who are in the academies only for the purpose of causing trouble for the Senate and for those who are truly studious, and of disturbing the public. Men who are not ashamed to declare that they do not stay in this Academy for the sake of study. Men who think it beneath their dignity to attend lectures, to take part in disputations, to respond and to object, and to fulfil the other duties, and who mix themselves even in the private exercises. These men make stumps and blockheads of their parents, while they persuade us that they are being supported at such great expense by their parents in this Academy, so that they may see the manners of men. Let them seek Rome, let them visit Paris, London or Venice, so that they may see the customs of many men and the commerce of the world. Here there are humble cottages and modest roofs, which cannot hold heroes.

units.la: erim nos, Auditores, tam docentes quam discentes, illudimur sedulo, ut perpetuo memores sinus istarum calamitaquæ majorem reformati orbis partem jam inundarunt, noo impendent. Vitemus adhuc, dum benigna illa Dei paad resipiscentiam nos invitat, istos scopulos, ad quos & vifratres nostri naves suas allisere. Caveamus, ne crapula etate graventur corda nostra, ne operum DOMINI & noicii obliviscamur. Exulent porro nefandæ grassationes & nes, cessent hoc tempore, quo tota Ecclesia saccum & cilnduit, beluinæistæ compotationes, quæ ante hac Acadeanc fœtidam reddidere. Eas si nos forte pro nostra lenituerare vellemus, at Leges & decreta, & superiores, queis nto diximus, non tolerabunt. Et ne quispiam nos solos melancholicos homines & scholasticas vulpes, ita enim quiloqui libet, & pædagogos esse censeat, qui tolerare noliod in aliis Academiis toleratur, lubet prælegere cordatum n, quo Rector & Senatus Academiæ Renteliensis, quam in superioribus annis Illustriss. Princeps Scaumburgicus apedem furoribus occurrendum censuit.
units.tr: For we, hearers, both teachers and learners, are diligently being mocked, so that we may remain ever mindful of the calamities which have already flooded the greater part of the reformed world, and which hang over us too. Let us avoid, while that kindly patience of God still invites us to repentance, those reefs on which our brothers have dashed their ships. Let us take care that our hearts are not weighed down by drunkenness and surfeit, and that we do not forget the works of the Lord and the duties of our calling. Let wicked assaults and quarrels be banished, and at this time, when the whole Church has put on sackcloth and ashes, let those brutish drinking bouts cease, which before now have made this Academy foul. If we should perhaps wish to be lenient toward them for the sake of our own ease, the laws and decrees and the superiors whom I have just mentioned will not tolerate it. And so that anyone may not think that we alone are melancholy men and scholastic foxes (for so one may call us), and pedagogues who refuse to tolerate what is tolerated in other academies, it pleases me to read out the wise decree of the Rector and Senate of the Academy of Rinteln, which the most illustrious Prince of Schaumburg judged should be opposed to the furies of earlier years.

units.la: RECTOR ET SENATUS ACADEMIÆ HOL- SATO-SCHAUMBURGICÆ RINTHELENSIS.
units.tr: THE RECTOR AND SENATE OF THE UNIVERSITY OF HOLSTEIN-SCHAUMBURG AT RINTELN.

units.la: QUod Poëtarum Homerus olim de armatæ militiæ militibus reliquit: Nulla fides, pietasque Viris, qui castra sequuntur: Id imprimis hisce ultimis temporibus epilepticis, in quibus homines moriuntur pejores, quàm nascuntur, longè est verissimum. Cum pietate enim ac virtutibus aut nihil, aut parum illis est commercii. Et quid aliud fere possunt, magisque in votis habent, quam
units.tr: What Homer of old left concerning the soldiers of an armed host, "No faith or piety in men who follow the camp," is most true of these last, epileptic times, in which men die worse than they were born. For they have little or no dealings with piety and virtue. And what else can they do, or wish for more, than

units.la: Nocturno certare mero, potare diurno, Atque diem nocti, noctemque aquare dici?
units.tr: to vie in drinking wine by night, to drink by day, and to make day equal to night?

units.la: Adeo ut' ipsimet imprudenter confiteantur, nec Christum & Martem simul coli, nec quem bonum Christianum, & bonum militem simul esse posse. In LL. passim Justinianeis milites togati, & qui Musarum castra sequuntur, illis comparantur, ita ut Juris etiam Interp. non malè dicant, argumentum inde sumptum probabile esse, frequens ac utile. Nequaquam tamen in attactâ impietate ac malitiâ, malitiæ utrique dediti ab Imp. atque JCtis æquiparantur, sed quoties de privilegiis, beneficiis, eorumque acquisitione aliquid constituitur. Bene audiunt, quo ad LL. Imperiales, togati milites, bene etiam audiunt armati: unde non raro in jure devotissimi appellantur. Utinam hodie in Germaniæ Universitatibus, & imprimis in hac ERNESTINA tam bene omnes audirent Cives Academici! Sed id à nemine, nisi si qui qui palpum alicui obtrudere velit, affirmari po-st. Invasit, proh dolor, Academiam nostram ovam nova quædam contagiosa, & eod. modo in aliis actenus inaudita lues. Irrepserunt in eam pauci quilam Helluones, Lurcones, Comedones, ἀλληλοφάγοι ac Canes Venatici, qui à militibus istis armatis, inte depiĉtis, parum differentes, bona (ut cum Juvenale loquantur) summa putant alienâ vivere quadrâ. Qui non solum quibusdam Commilitonibus suis status quæstionem contra aperta jura, movere non dubitant, iisdem quoque, ut & juvenibus novellis sine ullo ferè personarum discrimine, tanquam vultures opimo cadaveri inhiant, eo ac quibuscunque possunt modis ac mediis sæpe in hac annonæ caritate universali plus extorquent pecuniæ, quam studiorum gratiâ secum attulere. Cum autem istiusmodi processum ἀναθαφλον illud τοπῦμα, & Prin-ceps vitiorum omnium Diabolus introduxerit: Membra ejus continuare, & ad successores posterosque propagare conentur: nec ulla major insania, futilitas, levitas, nulla pestis perniciosior ad inficiendam, prorsusque devastandam hanc Academiam fœliciter inceptam, ad iram Dei, ae Principis Illustriss. Mecœnatis ac ευεργέτης nostri munificentissimi disgratiam concitandam excogitari possit: Vos Crumenimulgas atque Lurcones (hos enim tantùm compellamus; pios, insontes, ac morigeros expresse excipimus; exceptosque esse volumus) ejusmodi facinorum non pigeat solum, sed & pudeat. Hæccine vita est Academica; Civesque decet, docet ac ostendit Academicos; Certè non Hierosolymis fuisse, sed Hierosolymis benè vixisse laudandum est. Sic nec per annos multos, multis in Academiis fuisse, sed benè vixisse commendandum. Ita, prout vos coepistis, milites horridi vivere solent, omnesque Epicuri de grege porci. Ita violatur Naturæ hæc νομὴ ἔννοια: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris. Ita vos, qui pietate, hone- honestate, virtute & vita bona exemplari aliis prælucere debeatis, non tantum floris juvenilis, modestiæ, sed & omnis vestræ salutis tam æternæ, quam temporalis naufragium facitis. Neque etiam nobis Professoribus ac Præceptoribus vestris (quos parentum instar honorare à lege divinâ jubemini) atque studiosis ingenuis. eo ipso parcitis, licet innocentissimi sint, propter vos tamen, etiam in locis remotioribus, malè nonnunquam audiunt, pessimeque traducentur. Nos igitur nolumus neque officii nostri ratione possumus, talibus tantisque facinoribus scurrilibus, factisque sordidissimis amplius connivere, sed nequid detrimenti nostra capiat Respublica, decrevimus hoc aconitum in ipsa, quod dicitur, herba suffocare, & istiusmodi Exactoribus ac carcinomatis Universitatis nostræ virulentis, competentibus remediis obviare: Et volumus nullos impositerum ex iis, qui vel compotationibus hujusmodi illicitis, turpibus ac omni jure prohibitis, sub quocunque etiam titulo & prætextu intersunt, ullo beneficio, bonis saltem atque tractabilibus studiosis ex liberalitate nunquam hactenus satis laudatâ laudatissimi Principis nostri &c. dando, dignos esse, sive realiter aliquo fruantur beneficio, sive spes duntaxat eos de suturo foveat. Illi beneficiis antè perceptis confestim cadere, & iis, quæ habent, privari debent. Hos, non attentâ aliquâ promissione fortè factâ, omni prorsus spe percipiendorum stipendiorum frustramur, tam contra hos, quam illos, ut & istos, qui commessationes sive heluationes sub quacunque convivii specie instituunt, pœnam quoque Carceris, vel pecuniariam reservantes. Ipsi vero Coryphæi, Gulones, Phagones, iniqui Exactores, & authores primi, non solum beneficii, quo gaudent, amissionem, verùm etiam aliam pœnam gravissimam, nec non severitatem competentem δωσοσωπολήπλως pro quantitate excessuum subibunt. Hæc, ne ulla posset allegari ignorantia, publicè significanda duximus, τῶν Φι-λοξένων ιν ἢ Φιλαρέτων patroni accuratissimi, sed ψευδοφίλων ἢ ἐλευφέγων vindices severissimi futuri. P. P. RINELII ad Visurgim 18. Novemb. Anno 1621.
units.tr: So much so that they themselves carelessly confess that Christ and Mars cannot be worshipped together, and that one cannot be at once a good Christian and a good soldier. Throughout the Justinianic law books, soldiers in gowns, those who follow the camp of the Muses, are compared with the others, so that the jurists also say not badly that an argument drawn from this is probable, frequent and useful. Yet in matters of impiety and wickedness they are by no means equated by the emperors and jurists with those devoted to wickedness, but whenever something is laid down about privileges, benefits and their acquisition. Under the imperial laws, soldiers in gowns are well regarded, and armed soldiers too are well regarded; hence in law they are often called most devoted. Would that today in the universities of Germany, and above all in this ERNESTINE university, all academic citizens were so well regarded! But this could be affirmed by no one except someone who wished to flatter. Alas, a certain new and hitherto unheard-of contagious plague, of the same kind as in other places, has invaded our university. A few gluttons, guzzlers, feasters, [ἀλληλοφάγοι] mutually devouring and hunting dogs have crept into it, differing little from those armed soldiers depicted above. They think, to use Juvenal's words, that the highest good is to live on another's purse. They not only do not hesitate to raise a question of status against some of their fellow soldiers in contravention of clear law, but they also gape at these same men, and at young novices, like vultures at a rich carcass, almost without any distinction of persons. By every means and method they can, in this general dearth of provisions, they often extort more money than they brought with them for the sake of their studies. Since that accursed [ἀνάθεμα] plague of this kind has been introduced, and the Devil, prince of all vices, has introduced it, they strive to continue its members and to propagate them to successors and descendants. No greater madness, frivolity or levity can be devised, no more pernicious pest can be devised, for infecting and utterly laying waste this university, happily begun, and for stirring up the anger of God and the disfavour of our most illustrious Prince, our patron and benefactor, most generous. You crowd-milkers and gluttons (for we address only these; we expressly except the pious, the blameless and the obedient, and we wish them to be excepted), not only should you be ashamed of such crimes but you should feel shame. Is this academic life? Does it befit, teach and show academic citizens? Surely it is not to be praised to have been in Jerusalem, but to have lived well in Jerusalem. So too it is not to be commended to have been in many universities for many years, but to have lived well. Thus, as you have begun, horrid soldiers are wont to live, and all the pigs of Epicurus' herd. Thus this law of nature is violated: "What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another." Thus you, who ought to shine as an example to others in piety, honesty, virtue and a good life, make a shipwreck not only of your youthful bloom and modesty, but of all your welfare, eternal as well as temporal. Nor do you spare us, your professors and teachers (whom divine law bids you honour as parents), or the honourable students, merely because they are most innocent; on your account they are sometimes ill spoken of, even in remote places, and most wickedly slandered. Therefore we do not wish, and by reason of our office we cannot, to connive any longer at such great scurrilous crimes and most sordid deeds. But so that the commonwealth may suffer no harm, we have decided to choke this aconite in the very herb, as they say, and to meet these extortioners and the virulent cancer of our university with fitting remedies. And we will that none of those who attend drinking bouts of this kind, illicit, shameful and forbidden by all law, under whatever title or pretext, shall be worthy of any benefit, at least of the good and tractable students, which is given from the liberality of our most excellent Prince, never sufficiently praised, whether they actually enjoy some benefit or whether hope alone fosters them for the future. Those who have already received benefits shall forthwith forfeit them and be deprived of what they have. As for those, we frustrate them of all hope of receiving stipends, not on account of some promise perhaps made, and against these as well as those, and likewise against those who hold carousings or revels under any appearance of a banquet, we reserve also the penalty of imprisonment or a fine. But the very leaders, gluttons, eaters, unjust extortioners and first authors shall undergo not only the loss of the benefit they enjoy, but also another most grave penalty, and the severity fitting in proportion to the amount of their excesses. We have thought fit to make this public, so that no ignorance can be pleaded: we shall be the most careful patrons of the lovers of strangers or of virtue [Φιλοξένων ἢ Φιλαρέτων], but severe avengers of the false friends or the free-spenders [ψευδοφίλων ἢ ἐλευθέρων]. Given at Rinteln on the Weser, 18 November, in the year 1621.

units.la: abetis cordatum Academiae Germanicae de istis togatae militiae iis judicium, & severam comminationem. Inquo, si nobilium illustrium Frisiae Ordinum & Nob. DD. Curatorum decreta suo ipso negotio novo programmate renovanda essent, ne joidem aut apicem mutaremus. Nos confidimus, nullam nopositum iri necessitatem ad duriora remedia descendendi.
units.tr: You have here the judgment and the severe warning of the German university on this sort of gown-wearing soldiery. In which, if the decrees of the illustrious Frisian orders and the noble curators were to be renewed by a new programme of their own accord, we would not alter so much as a jot or a tittle. We trust that there will be no necessity placed upon us to resort to harsher remedies.

units.la: Oderunt peccare boni virtutis amore.
units.tr: The good hate to sin out of love of virtue.

units.la: os, Nobilis. & Ornatissimi adolescentes officium vestrum e, ego, cum bono Deo, in hac functione ita versabor, ut nemonus de me jure conqueri possit. Ut autem quid officii nostri estri sit, intelligatur, Academiae Secretarius Leges & statuta eget.
units.tr: Noble and most distinguished young men, your duty is this. I, with God's good blessing, shall conduct myself in this office so that no one can justly complain of me. But so that it may be understood what our duty is, the Academic Secretary needs laws and statutes.

units.la: Splendis vacivis istis paginis, & firmandis istis, quae superiori oratione liberius dixi, exhibebo tibi insigniora quaedam loca ex duabus orationibus celeberrimi Theologi & Philosophi, D. IOH. ALSTEDII, quae extant in ejus Enchiridio Enp. col. 2764. & seq.
units.tr: To illustrate and confirm the things I have said more freely in the above oration, I shall set before you certain more striking passages from two orations of the celebrated theologian and philosopher, Dr Johann Heinrich Alsted, which are found in his Enchiridion, column 2764 and following.

units.la: olumna 2770. Orat. de Providentia Dei circa Scholas. Sed mihi videre, quid sibi velint, qui scholis talia improperant. Defixi oculos in vitia, quae in scholas irrepunt, iisdemque exitium minantur machinantur. Sed quid hac ad nostram Andromachen? Non enim acta est meretrix, sed ii, quibus hoc negotii a Deo datum, ut integritatem hujus divae castitatem propugnarent; hi, inquam, sui muneris, Dei vindicis iram provocarunt, utque ille phialas excandescentis (de quibus in Apocalypsi) super scholas quoque effunderet, effecerunt.
units.tr: Column 2770. Oration on the Providence of God concerning schools. But I see what they intend who cast such reproaches on the schools. They have fixed their eyes on the vices that creep into the schools and threaten and plot ruin for them. But what has this to do with our Andromache? For it is not the harlot who has been put on trial, but those to whom this task was given by God, to defend the integrity and chastity of this goddess; these men, I say, have provoked the anger of God the avenger of their office, and have brought it about that he should pour out the vials of his wrath (of which we read in the Apocalypse) upon the schools as well.

units.la: olumna 2775. Magna haec sunt, auditores, studiorum impedimenta; illud est maximum, quod juventus literaria diffluit luxu, quod vivit dissolutam, quod helluationibus, quod grassationibus se dedit & tantum tum non mancipat. Vix enim dederis mihi scholam, ubi clamoribus, graf-sationibus, debacchationibus, ululatu, boatu & rugitu viri boni non molestentur. Nihil hic peccavero, si ad scholam optavero novi mundi descriptionem, quam Mercurius Gallo-Britannicus evulgavit sub titulo, Mundus alter & idem; Est hic Crapulia divisa in Pamphagoniam seu terram Gulonum; est hic Terra ebriosa, divisa in OEnotriam & Lupulantam, cujus cives sunt equites aurei dolii; est hic terra Rixatia, Ploravia, Risia major & minor. Et quis omnes hujus novi orbis patres recenseat? Quam vellem nobis semper ob oculos versaretur catastrophe florentissima Academia Erfordiensis? Cum studiosi illic loci se petulantius gererent adversus cives, cum tumultib. nocturnis urbem lacesserent, cum lapidibus tecta domosque obruerent, cum fenestras & fores hospitum frangerent, populus magno agmine excitus collegiorum domos admotis bellicis tormentis obsedit, expugnavit, ac ut quemque studiosorum juvenum obvium habuit, velut hostem, arripuit, vulneravit, trucidavit; neque prius quievit, quam vitulantium adolescentium multitudo manibus urbis esset profligata. Facet ex illo die etiamnum, olim florentissima Academia, quam Lutherus, qui primam ibi lauream consecutus est, paradisum Germania id atatis fuisse testatur: in qua Eobanus Hessus mille & quingentos auditores habuit: qua denique id fuit in Germania, quod Bononia in Italia, mater scilicet studiorum.
units.tr: Column 2775. These, listeners, are great impediments to studies: the greatest is that the literary youth dissolves in luxury, that it lives dissolutely, that it has given itself over, and almost hands itself over, to carousing and to brawling. For you could hardly give me a school where good men are not troubled by shouting, brawling, raving, howling, bellowing and roaring. I should not be wrong here if I were to wish for a school the description of the new world which the Gallo-British Mercury published under the title The Other World and the Same. Here there is Drunkenness divided into Pamphagonia, or the land of gluttons; here is a drunken land, divided into Oenotria and Lupulanta, whose citizens are the knights of the golden barrel; here is the land of Brawling, of Weeping, Greater and Lesser Laughter. And who could enumerate all the fathers of this new world? Would that the most flourishing catastrophe of the Erfurt Academy were always before our eyes! When the students there behaved more insolently towards the citizens, when they harassed the city with nocturnal tumults, when they battered roofs and houses with stones, when they broke the windows and doors of hosts, the people, roused in a great throng, besieged the houses of the colleges, brought up siege engines, stormed them, and whatever student young men they met, they seized, wounded and slaughtered them as if they were enemies; nor did they rest until the multitude of frolicking youths had been crushed by the hands of the city. From that day the once most flourishing academy has been a ruin, which Luther, who there obtained his first laurel, testified was the paradise of Germany in its time: where Eobanus Hessus had fifteen hundred listeners; in short, it was in Germany what Bologna was in Italy, the mother of studies.

units.la: Orat. de causis corruptarum scholarum, columna 2779. Quid vero, si tristes quosdam & maligna natura, quas Saturnus infausto aspexit sidere, vociferentur, nullum virum bonum has sibi partes unquam sumisse, ut diceret de morbis scholarum, & causis istorum morborum? Hi homines produnt maximam suam inscitiam: cum plurima Theologorum, oratorum & historicorum extent scripta de scholis corruptis, de morbis scholarum, de fatalibus dissipationibus & ruinis Academiarum, & denique de scholis curandis & in integrum restituendis. Quod igitur facio, magnorum virorum citraque controversiam bonorum exemplo facio. Et vero quid est, quod nonnulli adeo stomachantur & tumultuantur, cum audiunt scapham vocari scapham & ficum ficum, nisi quod agre ferunt sua vita sibi ob oculos poni in publica quasi tabula. Non ita animati sunt viri boni, qui dolent adeo conclamatum esse nunc temporis, merito exclamare possimus: O schola, Hannibal ante portas vestras, vobisque ruinam & excidium minatur, nisi breviredicritis in viam regiam, quajam excidistis! Hi dico viri boni dolent famam rei literariae, & ex animo optant, ut morbi epidemici graphice depingantur: ut hac ratione iram Dei adversus scholas male administratas agnoscamus, illam averruncemus, quantum in nobis est, vitando scilicet peccata magna, peccata multa, quadam ex iis clamantia, ut vocant, & vinndictam divinam postulantia. Hi enim sunt morbi, qui petunt cor- rum & jugulum.
units.tr: Oration on the causes of corrupted schools, column 2779. But what if certain gloomy men of malignant nature, whom Saturn regarded with an unlucky star, cry out that no good man has ever taken upon himself the task of speaking about the diseases of schools and the causes of those diseases? Such men betray their own great ignorance, since there exist very many writings by theologians, orators and historians on corrupt schools, on the diseases of schools, on the fatal dispersions and ruins of academies, and finally on curing schools and restoring them to health. What I am doing, therefore, I do following the example of great men, good men beyond any controversy. And indeed, why do some men fume and rage so much when they hear a boat called a boat and a fig a fig, unless it is that they take it badly that their own lives are placed before their eyes as if on a public tablet? Good men are not so disposed. Those who grieve that the state of letters is now so widely cried down may rightly exclaim: O school, Hannibal is at your gates and threatens your ruin and destruction unless you quickly return to the royal road you have left! I say these good men grieve over the reputation of literary studies, and sincerely wish that the epidemic diseases be depicted vividly, so that by this means we may recognise God's anger against badly managed schools and turn it away, as far as lies in us, namely by avoiding great sins, many sins, some of which cry out, as they say, and call for divine vengeance. For these are the diseases that aim at the heart and the throat.

units.la: olumna 2790. Vltimo praeceptores infestat indulgentia, qua fra- laxatur juventuti ferocienti, adeo quidem, ut licentiosissima sit studiosorum omnibus scholis, vita, si modo vita dici potest, qua viam expeditissimam sternit ad mortem. Trepido hic, quando intueor deploratam scholam faciem. Tametsi enim illae optimis communitas sunt legibus: Perimen est ac si nulla sint leges. Lex enim sine executione nihil est aliud quam larva, & campana sine pistillo. Evigilent itaque, evigilent tan- quam antistites scholarum, neque diutius grassari patiantur licentiam: quae reddimur deteriores, ut ille in comico socco loquitur. Diligenter tendant illud Allexandri Severi Imperatoris, qui milites suos ita alloquitur. Disciplina majorum rempub. tenet, quae si dilatatur, & nen Romanum & imperium amissimus.
units.tr: Column 2790. Lastly, indulgence plagues the teachers, by which discipline is relaxed for the unruly young, so that the life of students in all schools is so licentious, if indeed it can be called life, that it lays out the quickest road to death. I tremble here when I look upon the deplorable face of the school. For although those schools are equipped with the best laws, it comes to the same thing as if there were no laws at all. For a law without enforcement is nothing but a mask, and a bell without a clapper. Let them therefore be vigilant, let them be vigilant as the overseers of the schools, and let them not allow licence to rage any longer, by which we are made worse, as the character in the comic buskin puts it. Let them diligently heed that saying of the Emperor Alexander Severus, who addressed his soldiers thus: "Discipline of our ancestors holds the commonwealth together; if it slips, we lose both the Roman name and the empire."

units.la: Et quemadmodum e disciplina militaris sinu (ut cum Valerio Maximo loquar) omnes triumphi manant: ita e disciplina scholastica tanquam corde spiritus vitalis in totum scholorum corpus derivatur & diffunditur. Non est, quod pluribus hic commemorem, quid possit disciplina in omni vita statu. Lachryma hic requirantur, quas deploremus cacoethes ingeniorum juvenilium, quae studiis dedita putantur.
units.tr: And just as all triumphs flow from the bosom of military discipline (to speak with Valerius Maximus), so from scholastic discipline, as the vital spirit from the heart, it is drawn off and diffused through the whole body of the schools. There is no need for me to recount here at length what discipline can accomplish in every condition of life. Here tears should be sought, which we may lament, the youthful wantonness of those minds that are thought to be devoted to study.

units.la: Plane mihi persuadeo eandem fore catastrophen scholarum, quam nuper exitus scholae florentissimae Berytiensis. Erat illa legum nutrix, ut Iustiniano vocatur. Erat totius Phoenicia Phoenix & lampas clarissima, ut Museum Romani orbis. Erat uno verbo tribunal justitiae. Sed non erat. Maximus enim fiebat maximorum privilegiorum, immunitatum & indultorum ab Imperatoribus concessorum abusus. Qua virtutis justitiae erat officina, in omne vitium & injustitiam, in inaequitatem, in violantiam, in lasciviam degenerabat. Omnis disciplina jacebat: Leges silebant: Professores irridebantur: Praeceptores spernebantur; Monitis injuriis & contumelia afficiebantur.
units.tr: I am fully persuaded that the schools will meet the same catastrophe as the recent end of the most flourishing school of Berytus. That was the nurse of laws, as Justinian calls it. It was the Phoenix and most brilliant lamp of all Phoenicia, like the Museum of the Roman world. In one word, it was a tribunal of justice. But it was not so. For the abuse of the greatest privileges, immunities and indulgences granted by the emperors grew to be enormous. The workshop of virtue and justice degenerated into every vice and injustice, into iniquity, violence and lewdness. All discipline lay prostrate: the laws were silent: the professors were mocked: the teachers were despised, and were subjected to insults, injuries and abuse.

units.la: Quarum rerum atrocitate optimus studiosorum amantissimus Imperator Justinianus adeo commovebatur, ut Salaminum, virum disertissimum, ita scripserit: Illud vero satis essarium constitutum, cum summa interminatione edicimus, nemo audeat, neque in hac splendidissima civitate neque in Beiensium pulcherrimo oppido, ex his qui legitima peragunt studia, indignos & pessimos, imo magis servilcs, & quorum esse injuria est, ludos exercere, & alia crimina, vel in ipsos praefores, vel in socios, & maxime in eos qui rudes ad recitationem usque pervenerint, perpetrare.
