units.tr: By the atrocity of these things the best emperor, Justinian, most loving of students, was so moved that he wrote to Salaminus, a most learned man, as follows: "We have thought it altogether necessary to decree, under the severest threat, that no one, neither in this most splendid city nor in the most beautiful town of Berytus, among those who pursue the legitimate studies, dare to carry on games and other crimes, shameful and worthless, indeed more fit for slaves, and such as it is an outrage to commit, either against the professors themselves or against their fellow students, and especially against those who have advanced only as far as recitation."

units.la: Quis enim ludos appellet, ex quibus crimina oriuntur? Hoc fieri nullo modo patimur, sed optioptimo ordini in nostris temporibus, & hanc partem tradimus, & toti nostro postero transinittimus seculo, cum oporteat prius animas, & postea linguas fieri eruditas. Egregio & verè regia Imperatoris optimi sententia, Quam utinam perpenderent doctores, imprimis scholarum! In hos enim culpa conferenda est laxa disciplina: quippe qui desunt muneri suo. Sane si currus in precipitia agatur, non currui, sed vectori hoc acceptum ferendum est. Sed valde vereor, ne surdo fabulam. Vt tamen in utramque aurem stertentes excitem, vellam ipsis aurem commemoratione miseri exitus, ut paulo ante recepi, qui mansit scholam Berytiensium florentissimam. Cum neque Imperatoris severissima prohibitiones gravissimaque comminationes, neque professorum ac praeceptorum fidelissima admonitiones, quidquam loci invenirent, Deus, vindex omnis iniquitatis certissimus, qui tarditatem poenarum supplicii gravitate compensare solet, subito intempestâ nocte, cum gurgustia helluationibus fumarent, ganea & lustra libidinibus ferverent, cyclopicis vel potius diabolicisclamoribus omnes angiportus civitatis arderent, terramotu terribili immisso, fundamenta urbis evertit, moenia prostravit, tecta diruit, domos disiecit, tanta hominum strage edita, ut testante Agathia, qui Justiniani res gestas scripsit, tria amplius mille studentium, vulgi numero praeterito, una illa miserrima nocte interierint. Quid quaso, Illustrissime & Clementissime Dn. Princeps, ex omnibus annalibus funestius, quid miserabilius, quid horribilius, literis & literarum cultoribus occurrere potest? Ejusmodi prosecto est hoc exemplum ut non tantum omnibus scholis juridicis, omnibus tribunalibus consistoriis, ut Viglius JCtus ad Carolum V. Imperatorem scripsisse legitur, sed etiam omnibus Academiis & gymnasiis sit appingendum, hoc Virgilii versu subscripto:
units.tr: For who would call them games, when crimes arise from them? We do not allow this to happen in any way, but we hand down this part to the best order in our times, and we transmit it to our whole posterity, since it is fitting that souls be made learned first, and tongues afterwards." This is the excellent and truly royal opinion of the best emperor. Would that the teachers of the schools, above all, would weigh it! For the fault of lax discipline must be laid upon them, since they fail in their duty. Indeed, if a chariot is driven headlong over a precipice, the blame is to be laid not on the chariot but on the driver. But I greatly fear that I am telling a tale to a deaf man. Yet, to rouse those who snore with both ears, I would like to pluck their ears by recalling the wretched end, which I mentioned a little while ago, of the school of Berytus, once so flourishing. When neither the most severe prohibitions and gravest threats of the Emperor, nor the most faithful admonitions of professors and teachers, found any place, God, the most certain avenger of all iniquity, who is accustomed to balance the delay of punishment with the severity of the penalty, suddenly, on an unseasonable night, while the hovels smoked with drinking bouts, the taverns and brothels seethed with lusts, and every alley of the city resounded with Cyclopean, or rather diabolical, shouts, sent a terrible earthquake, overthrew the foundations of the city, levelled its walls, tore down its roofs and scattered its houses, and such a slaughter of men was caused that, as Agathias, who wrote the deeds of Justinian, bears witness, more than three thousand students, not to mention the common people, perished in that one most wretched night. What, I ask you, Most Illustrious and Most Clement Lord Prince, can present itself from all the annals as more deadly, more miserable, more horrible, to letters and to the cultivators of letters? Indeed this example is of such a kind that it should be painted not only on all law schools and all consistorial courts, as Viglius the jurist is read to have written to the Emperor Charles V, but also on all academies and gymnasiums, with this verse of Virgil written beneath it:

units.la: Discite justitiam moniti, & non temnere divos:
units.tr: Learn justice, be warned, and do not scorn the gods.

units.la: Addita insuper (ut hoc addamus) voce illâ Servatoris nostri dulciss. quâ responḋit illis, quiruinam Siloæ turris, stragemq; referebant: Nisi ad frugem reversi poenitentiam egeritis, eodem fato cunêti peribitis. Eo autem diligentius hoc exemplum est frequentandum, quo res scholarum nunc sunt periculosiore loco. Praeceptores enim Berytî faciebant suum officium monendo & minando, quod pauci faciunt hodierno aevo professores & praeceptores. Etenim vel silendo, vel byssinis verbis adulando, vel comessationibus studiosorum se miscendo, ipsi pereunt & alios perdunt. Quanquam Berytienses illi praeceptores non fecerunt omne, quod debeant facere, officium. Non enim ad Ure, Seca progressi sunt. Quod omnino fieri debet in morbis desperatis, qui vires acquirunt eundo.
units.tr: Let us add, moreover, the sweet words of our Saviour, with which he answered those who reported the fall of the tower of Siloam and its slaughter: "Unless you return to a better way and repent, you will all likewise perish." This example ought all the more diligently to be kept in mind, since the affairs of the schools are now in a more perilous state. For the teachers at Berytus did their duty by admonishing and threatening, which few professors and teachers do in this present age. For either by silence, or by flattering with fine-spun words, or by mixing themselves in the revels of students, they themselves perish and destroy others. Yet those Berytian teachers did not do everything they ought to do. For they did not proceed to the cautery and the knife. This must indeed be done in desperate diseases, which gather strength as they advance.

units.la: Columna 2794. Ad extremum hic se offert egregia vitiorum coronis; vita scilicet dissoluta, quam plerique studiosi vivunt. Si quis hoc neget, paulisper commoretur in urbe, ubi schola est fundata, utcunque celebris. Audiet ibi clamantes, grassantes, debacchantes, boantes, rugientes, giganteo ausu mira meditantes studiosos, quos ita vocant, licet injuriâ. Quidvis enim potius illi sunt, quam bonarum literarum studiosi. Biberit sunt, capitones sunt, Rabirii sunt, sunt sponsi Penelopes, sunt ardeliones.
units.tr: Column 2794. Finally, here presents itself the outstanding crown of vices: the dissolute life which most students lead. If anyone denies this, let him linger for a while in the city where the school has been founded, however famous it may be. There he will hear students, so called although wrongly, shouting, raging, running wild, bellowing, roaring, and devising wonders with giant audacity. They are anything rather than students of good letters. They are drinkers, guzzlers, Rabirii, suitors of Penelope, busybodies.

units.la: Columna 2795. Hic verò cum omnia sunt misera, tum illud existit miserrimum, quod studiosi isti certatim conantur esse bibones, vespertiliones, & prope dixerim cacodaemones. Quam in sententiam facit historia tristis anridicula, quam paucis accipite. In Academia quadam Saxoniae, quae ex dissipata Pragensis schola ruderibus erat exitata, quasi colonia nova tum temporis deducta (Pragâ enim Germani supra duo millia propter exortas Husitarum contentiones, uno die discedentes, triumque dierum itinere illinc profecti hic consederunt, in hac dico Academia vixit eques quidam nobilis, hoc nomine celebris, quod omnibus compotoribus palmam prariperet. Cum enim Leonhardus Filsechius, eques nobilis, in paulo ante excitatam Academiam appulisset, deque sobrini sui studiis ac moribus perquisivisset, hoc responsum tulit: Optimè illius tui propinqui res se habent. Inter mille enim ac quingentos, qui in hac urbe studiorum causa commorantur, adolescentes, ille unus potandi gloriam ac palmam possidet. Egregiam verò palmam! Quis vero nostrum eosdem triumphos in Academiis hodiernis, & quidem multo superbiores non perspicit! quis non dolet hac fieri insuper & laudari! O utinam tandem aliquando Deus excitaret Herculem Academicum, qui more Herculis illius Thebani debellaret monstra illa scholastica. Thebanus ille, ut est apud Plautum.
units.tr: Column 2795. Here, while all things are wretched, this most wretched thing also appears: that these students strive eagerly to be tipplers, bats of the night, and, I might almost say, evil spirits. To this effect is a sad and yet laughable story, which hear in brief. In a certain academy of Saxony, which had been raised from the ruins of the dispersed school of Prague, and was then founded as a kind of new colony (for more than two thousand Germans, departing from Prague in a single day because of the disputes that had arisen with the Hussites, had gone from there in a three days' journey and settled here), in this academy, I say, there lived a certain noble knight, famous for this reason, that he snatched the palm from all his fellow drinkers. For when Leonhard Filsech, a noble knight, had come to the academy newly founded a little before, and had enquired about the studies and conduct of his nephew, he received this answer: "Your kinsman's affairs are going very well indeed. Among the fifteen hundred youths who stay in this town for the sake of study, he alone possesses the glory and palm of drinking." An excellent palm indeed! Who among us does not see the same triumphs in today's academies, and indeed far more boastful ones! Who does not grieve that such things are not only done but even praised! Oh, would that God would at last raise up an academic Hercules, who, in the manner of that Theban Hercules, would subdue those scholastic monsters. That Theban, as he is in Plautus.

units.la: Cum leone, & cum excetrâ, cum cervo, cum apro Ætolico, Cum avibus Stymphalicis, & cum Antaeo deluctatus est.
units.tr: With the lion, the hydra, the hind, the Aetolian boar, the Stymphalian birds, and he wrestled with Antaeus.

units.la: Haec monstra omnia, imo plura, & magis fera, in scholis nostris grassantur.
units.tr: All these monsters, indeed more and fiercer ones, roam about in our schools.

units.la: Columna 2777. Mesi quis interroget, quot sint columna status Ecclesiastici, & politici, respondebo tres. Primam dixero scholas: secundam, Scholas: tertiam itidem scholas. Tanta enim est scholarum necessitas, & utilitas tanta, ut absque illis fisit, homines transformentur in belluas, in truncos et lapides, in monstra denique immania; cujusmodi metamorphosin Ovidius acutè admodum descripsisse putatur. Quid enim? Annon homines natura sunt veluti tabula rasa, cui nihil inscriptum est, quidlibet autem inscribi potest; Annon sunt velut alba linea, quae colorem quemlibet recipere potest? Annon sunt instar lapidis, è quo qualibet statua fieri potest? In scholis autem tabulis hisce inscribuntur litera Pietatis & Humanitatis. In scholis alba ista linea tinguntur vivis Honestatis & Vtilitatis coloribus. In schոlis statuarii peritissimi, qui refingunt hominem ad imaginem Dei Opt. Maximi. Unde schola non immerito vocantur emporia & mercaturæ bonarum literarum: seminaria Ecclesiæ: armamentaria reipub. vivaria œconomiæ: officina pietatis: magistræ humanitatis: fontes honestatis: scaturigines utilitatis: nervi morum & disciplinæ: horti Gratiarum: & uno verbo, cornucopia omnimodæ felicitatis. In his enim gigantea audacia diffringitur, Cyclopica immanitas compescitur, vita Epicurea corrigitur. Absque his si sit, juventus, thesaurus ille utriusque politiæ, corrumpitur, & hoc thesauro corrupto ipsa respub. labascit, & hac labascente labat quoque Ecclesia, cujus hospitium est respub. Nam ex institutione mala pravi pueri, pejores adolescentes, pessimi viri evadunt, è contrario ex bona institutione boni pueri, meliores adolescentes, optimi viri existunt: ut non immerito majorum gentium politici scribant, è scholis tanquam fontibus felicitatem publicam & privatam, non secus ac ab Apollinis capillis destillare. O igitur beatas respub. in quibus hæc emporia sunt aperta! ô felices Ecclesias, quibus hæc pietatis domicilia sunt adjuncta! ô beatitatem hujus sæculi maximam, quod plurimis abundat scholis! Verum enimvero quod in omnibus fermè rebus naturâ sua præstantissimis & optimis usuvenire solet, ut technis, fallaciis & fraudibus antiqui istius veteratoris Diaboli mirum in modum depravantur, & tantum non in purum putum venenum commutentur: id etiam proh dolor scholis accidisse, & indies magis magisq; accidere videmus, & magno cum dolore videmus, si modo aliquid videmus. Tantum enim est hujus sæculi (quod nonnulli heroicum vocare solent; quam rectè ipsi viderint) tantum dicoest hujus exulcerati sæculi cacoëthes, ut in maxima scholarum copia sit maxima virorum publicè utilium, qui tum reipub. tum Ecclesiæ functionibus satis idonei sint, inopia: adeo quidem ut scholas in ipsis scholis desideres, & Tantalum in mediis aquis sitire, ac salamandram in mediis ignibus algere non inepte dicere possis &c.
units.tr: Column 2777. If anyone should ask me how many pillars support the ecclesiastical and political state, I would answer three. The first I would name schools, the second schools, and the third again schools. For the need for schools is so great, and their usefulness so great, that without them men are changed into beasts, into logs and stones, and finally into huge monsters, a metamorphosis which Ovid is thought to have described very sharply. For what? Are not men by nature like a blank tablet, on which nothing is written, yet anything can be written? Are they not like a white line, which can take on any colour? Are they not like a stone, from which any statue can be made? In schools, however, the letters of piety and humanity are inscribed on these tablets. In schools that white line is dyed with the living colours of honesty and usefulness. In the schools the most skilled sculptors remake man in the image of God, the best and greatest. Hence schools are not undeservedly called the marketplaces and trading-houses of good letters, the seedbeds of the Church, the arsenals of the commonwealth, the fishponds of household management, the workshops of piety, the teachers of humanity, the fountains of honesty, the springs of usefulness, the sinews of morals and discipline, the gardens of the Graces, and, in a word, the horn of plenty of every kind of happiness. For in them gigantic audacity is broken, Cyclopean savagery is restrained, and the Epicurean life is corrected. If without these the youth, that treasure of both polities, is corrupted, and with that treasure corrupted the commonwealth itself totters, and with the commonwealth tottering the Church too falls, since the commonwealth is her host. For from bad training boys turn out wicked, youths worse, and men of the worst sort; on the contrary, from good training boys become good, youths better, and men the best. So it is not undeservedly that the political writers of the greater nations write that public and private happiness flows from schools as from fountains, as if dripping from the locks of Apollo. O, therefore, happy the commonwealths in which these marketplaces are open! O happy the Churches to which these homes of piety are joined! O the greatest blessedness of this age, that it abounds in so many schools! But, truly, what usually happens in almost all things that are by nature most excellent and best, namely that they are wonderfully corrupted by the crafts, deceits and frauds of that old crafty deceiver the Devil, and are changed almost into pure poison, this, alas, we see has happened to the schools too, and we see it happening more and more every day, and we see it with great grief, if indeed we see anything at all. For so great is the itch of this age (which some are wont to call heroic, and how rightly they themselves may judge) of this ulcerated age, that in the greatest abundance of schools there is the greatest lack of men useful to the public, who are fit enough for the offices of both commonwealth and Church; so that you might not unfittingly say you look for schools in the very schools, and that Tantalus thirsts in the midst of waters, and the salamander freezes in the midst of fires, etc.

units.la: Author anonymus Latinissimi cujusdam scripti, cui titulus, L. Ex.
units.tr: Anonymous author of a very elegantly written work, entitled L. Ex.

units.la: Libertatem æstimare multi licentia scelerum solent, non bonis legibus, & perdito cuique mitius hoc imperium, cui IMPVNITAS pro amuleto est. Graßabantur palam injuriæ, convitia, pugnæ, furta, temulentia, quibus præcavendis duriore Senatus-consulto opus erat. Sistenda enim minora mala ex præscripto medicorum sunt, ut majora evitentur, quod tractu temporum exacerbata respuant medicinam.
units.tr: Many people are wont to treat liberty as licence for crimes, which is not what good laws intend; and for every reckless person this rule is milder, since impunity serves him as a charm. Injuries, insults, brawls, thefts and drunkenness were openly rampant, and a harsher decree of the Senate was needed to guard against them. For minor evils must be checked, as physicians prescribe, so that greater ones may be avoided, since over time diseases that have grown worse reject the remedy.

units.la: UT amicis quibusdam Angelis gratificarer & me describendi tædio levarem, placuit Commentariolum hunc de decimis inBodlæanâ aliquando à me concinnatum & jam à me recognitum edere. Nomina verò Amplissimarum DD. VV. præscripsi, non quod dignum eum putem qui vel uni DD. VV. offeratur, sed tantum ut tester animum beneficiorum mihi à tot jam retrò annis præstitorum meminentissimum, & simul ut obsesfit apud DD. VV. majoris operis, cujus editione, cum bono Deo, brevi viris aliquot non ex plebe ibo gratificatum. Valete diu interea Patriæ ornamenta, studiorum meorum Patroni, à quibus nunquam nisi ad diligentiam & virtutem dicessi inflammatior. Franek. 25. Febr. 1618.
units.tr: That I might oblige certain friends, the Angeli, and relieve myself of the tedium of copying it out, I have decided to publish this little commentary on tithes in the Bodleian, which I once put together and have now revised. I have inscribed the names of Your Honours at the head, not because I think it worthy of being offered to even one of you, but only so that I may bear witness to my mindfulness of the kindnesses you have shown me for so many years past, and also so that I may show my respect to Your Honours by a greater work, which, God willing, I shall soon present, in its edition, to some men not of the common people. Meanwhile, farewell for long, ornaments of the Fatherland, patrons of my studies, from whom I have never departed more inflamed than to diligence and virtue. Franeker, 25 February 1618.

units.la: VV. AA. devotissimus
units.tr: Your Honours' most devoted

units.la: SIXTINUS AMAMA Ebr. L. Prof.
units.tr: SIXTINUS AMAMA, Professor of the Hebrew Language.

units.la: S. AMAMA DE DECIMIS MOSAICIS COMMENTARIOLUS.
units.tr: S. AMAMA ON THE MOSAIC TITHES: A SHORT COMMENTARY.

units.la: Ecimabantur in V. T. vel pecudes vel proventus.
units.tr: Tithes in the Old Testament were paid either on livestock or on produce.

units.la: Decimationis annuæ pecudum hæc observata fuit ratio, ut quidem Ebræi ex Levit, 27. 32. colligunt. Colligebat pecuarius agnos vel vitulos in stabulum unum, quod habebat ostium parvum, ut ne duo simul egrederentur. Constituebantur matres illorum foras, ut, cum agni vitulive eas mugientes balantesve audirent, ordine alter post alterum egrederetur. Tum incipiebat numerare virgâ, primum, secundum, 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. & quod decimo loco egrediebatur sive masculum sive fœminam, sive integrum sive maculatum, signabat rubeo colore quo tincta erat virga, & dicebat, Hoc erit pro decima.
units.tr: The Hebrews, as they gather from Leviticus 27:32, observed this method for the annual tithe of livestock. The herdsman gathered the lambs or calves into a pen that had one small door, so that no two could go out together. Their mothers were stationed outside, so that when the young heard them lowing or bleating, they would come out one after another in order. He then began to count with a rod: first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth. Whichever animal came out in the tenth place, whether male or female, whole or blemished, he marked with the red colour in which the rod was dipped, and said, "This shall be the tenth."

units.la: Sed hac decimatione missa proventuum decima breviter persequi animis nobis est.
units.tr: But, having set aside this tithe of livestock, we must briefly pursue the tithe of produce.

units.la: De his illud Ebræorum axioma apud Dd. Thalmudicos extat.
units.tr: On this there is a maxim of the Hebrews in the Talmudic doctors:

units.la: כל אוכל הכשמר שגדולו מהארץ חייב בראשית בתרומה והמעשרות
units.tr: [כל אוכל הכשמר שגדולו מהארץ חייב בראשית בתרומה והמעשרות] Whatever edible thing grows from the earth is liable to first fruits, to the offering and to the tithes.

units.la: 1. Quicquid eduliorum ex terra incrementum capit, obnoxium est primitiis, oblationi & decimis.
units.tr: 1. Whatever food gains increase from the earth is bound to the first fruits, the offering and the tithes.

units.la: Sub quo etiam hortensia & vilissima quæque, modo esui hominibus sint, comprehenduntur, ut anethum, polegium, mentha, ruta, cuminum &c.
units.tr: Under this rule are included also garden herbs and all the humblest plants, provided they are used for human food, such as dill, pennyroyal, mint, rue, cumin and so on.

units.la: Sed an horum hortensium seu olerum decima in Lege divina exactæ sint, quæstio inter eruditos est. Hoc extra controversiam est, exactas in eâ decimas התבואה proventus & proventus seminis. Sed sub istis olera comprehendi negarunt Rabbinorum pars maxima, & inter eos author libri præceptorum sol. 145. col. 4. & Gerundensis in Mosen sol. 308. pag. 2. Quos secuti sunt viri magni, Beza, Piscator, Drusius in Matth. 23. & Casaub. exercitat. id est, cap. 9. quo inclinat & Jansen. comm. in Harm. Evangel. cap. 84.
units.tr: But whether the tithes of these garden herbs or vegetables were exacted under the divine Law is a question among the learned. It is beyond dispute that tithes of התבואה [the grain] and produce of seed were exacted. But most of the rabbis have denied that vegetables fall under these, and among them the author of the book of precepts, fol. 145, col. 4, and Gerundensis on Moses, fol. 308, p. 2. Great men have followed them: Beza, Piscator, Drusius on Matthew 23, and Casaubon in his exercitation (that is, chapter 9), to which Jansen also inclines, in his commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 84.

units.la: Pro his facere videtur, quod passim in Lege, quoties de decimis mis agitur & nomen תבואה proventus adhibetur, ei subjiciantur tantummodo hæ tres species, frumentum, oleum & mustum. Item quod Ebræi aliquot doctores vii. tantummodo species rerum ex præscripto Legis decimatarum enumerarint, sub- dividentes nempe frumentum in V. speciem, Triticum, speltam, hordeum, avenam & panicum quod spicam vulpis vocant.
units.tr: What seems to favour them is that, wherever the Law speaks of tithes and the word תבואה [produce] is used, only these three kinds are subjoined: grain, oil and must. Likewise, some Hebrew doctors have listed only seven kinds of things tithed under the prescription of the Law, subdividing grain into a fifth kind: wheat, spelt, barley, oats and millet, which they call the fox's tail.

units.la: Hinc est quod reliquorum fructuum & olerum decimationis originem non arcessant altius quam ab isto seculo quo suo superstitioni & operibus super erogatoriis indulgeri cæptum est, quo ut de colere cœperunt, dummodo de suo aliquid adderent.
units.tr: Hence it is that they do not trace the origin of the tithing of other fruits and vegetables further back than that age in which, with superstition and works of supererogation being indulged, it began to be the custom to tithe even the herbs, provided they added something of their own.

units.la: Hinc & illud est quod ad prædictam Traditionem non τὰ ῥητὸν Legis referant illud quod in Pharisæis sui seculi reprehendit Salvator Matth. 23. & Luc. 11. dum Væ denuntiat iis qui decimabant Rutam, anethum &c. olera, posthabitis interim misericordiâ, fide & judicio, quò & respexisse existimant Pharisæum istum Luc. 18. qui inter alia & hoc dese refert, δὶς τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἀποδεκατῶ πάντα, decimo omnia quæ possideo.
units.tr: Hence, too, they do not refer to the aforesaid tradition the τὰ ῥητὸν [written word] of the Law, in the words with which the Saviour rebuked the Pharisees of his own age, Matthew 23 and Luke 11, when he pronounced woe on those who tithed rue, dill and other herbs, while neglecting mercy, faith and judgement. They also think that the Pharisee in Luke 18 had this in mind, who among other boasts said, δὶς τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἀποδεκατῶ πάντα [I tithe all that I possess twice a week].

units.la: Sic illi. Sed non de sunt qui contra opinatur, urgentes maxime illud δεῖ oportebat Matth. 23. Hæc oportuit facere & illa sc. decimationem r. a. cum. non omittere, sc. oportuit.
units.tr: So they say. But there are some who hold the opposite, urging above all that word δεῖ [it behoved] in Matthew 23: These things it behoved you to do, and the others, namely the tithing of herbs, not to leave undone, that is, it behoved them to do.

units.la: Addi posset & locus Levit. 27. 30. qui infringit ternarium istum, vel ut alii subdividunt, septenarium numerum, Locus vero sic habet, omnis decima ex semine terra & pomis arborum Domini esto. Licet autem in Ebræo sit, & fructus ligni vel arboris (γῆ enim utrumque significat) & R. Sal. nulla hic difficultas sit; utpote qui semen terræ frumentum, fructum ligni vero mustum & oleum exponit, tamen mihi non persuasit ex quo locum istum 2. Chron. 31. 5. perpendi, qui sic sonat, & multiplicarunt filii Israel primitias (id est, Therumoth) frumenti, musti, olei & דבש & omnis proventus agri &c. Ut enim linquam illud posterius quod ἐξυμνικὸν forte dices, quò referes illud דבש? sive vocem eam mel sive dastylos palmarum cum Junio vartas. Certè si non olerum decimationem probat, saltem ternarium istum numerum discutit. Nec est quod quis vocem ראשית nobis opponat, cum eam Therumoth hic denotare probaturi simus & istis locis unde isti numerum illum extruxerunt, etiam adhibeatur, ut Deut. 18.4. Quin &, si non omnium forte quæ decimas debebant, offerebantur Therumæ, tamen omnium quorum Therumæ hoc sensu acceptæ offerebantur, debebantur decimæ.
units.tr: One might also add Leviticus 27:30, which breaks that threefold, or as others subdivide it, sevenfold number. The text runs: Every tithe of the seed of the land and of the fruit of the trees is the Lord's. In the Hebrew it reads and the fruit of the wood or of the tree (for γῆ [earth] signifies both), and Rashi sees no difficulty here, since he explains the seed of the land as grain and the fruit of the wood as must and oil. Yet I was not persuaded by this, from what we weigh in 2 Chronicles 31:5, which reads: And the children of Israel multiplied the first fruits (that is, terumoth) of grain, must, oil and דבש [honey] and of all the produce of the field, etc. For, to leave aside the last item, which you may perhaps call a supplement, to what will you refer דבש? Whether one takes the word as honey or as date syrup, as Junius translates it? Certainly, if this passage does not prove the tithing of herbs, it at least shakes that threefold number. Nor should anyone object to us the word ראשית [first fruits], since we shall prove that it here denotes terumoth, and it is also used in those passages from which they built up that number, as in Deuteronomy 18:4. Indeed, even if the terumoth were not offered for all the things that owed tithes, yet tithes were owed for all those things for which terumoth were offered in this sense.

units.la: * Deut. 14. 22. & 18. 4. & alibi. R. Salomo ad Deut. 26.
units.tr: * Deuteronomy 14:22 and 18:4, and elsewhere. Rashi on Deuteronomy 26.

units.la: De Repub. Ebr. lib. 2. cap. 17.
units.tr: On the Hebrew Commonwealth, book 2, chapter 17.

units.la: Nec hic authoritates Rabbinorum desunt, ut Ebræos Ebræis opponamus. Ecce enim Hiscuni ad Levit. 27, 30. de semine terræ: Complectitur etiam alium & שחלים (id est, Leonticen vel Leontium vel Leoninum semen Leontopetalium) & גרגיר Phesiétha, comprehendit semen alii והשחלים והגרגר Jam vero גרגר genus oleris esse colligitur ex libr. præc. majore, nam in eo diserté: Schachalim & Gargir ירקות ושאר & cætera olera. Rursus ad, ex fructu arborum: Phesiétha, comprehendit omnes fructus arborum. Rursus ad aliud, de semine terræ: non de semine omni, quia excipit legumina quæ non eduntur, ut semen næpæ & Raphani &c.
units.tr: Nor are there lacking here authorities of the rabbis, by which we may set Hebrews against Hebrews. For behold, Hiskuni on Leviticus 27:30, of the seed of the land: it includes also שחלים (that is, Leontice or Leontium, or the leonine seed of the lion's-foot plant) and גרגיר Phesietha [Peah], it includes the seed of others, והשחלים והגרגר [the schachalim and the gargir]. Now that גרגר is a kind of herb is gathered from the greater book of precepts, for there it says plainly: Schachalim and Gargir are vegetables, ירקות, and the other herbs. Again, on of the fruit of the trees: Phesietha includes all fruits of trees. Again, on the other phrase, of the seed of the land: not of every seed, because it excludes pulses which are not eaten, such as the seed of turnip and radish, etc.

units.la: Atque hoc modo probabiliter olerum decimationem, evidenter autem plurium quam trium vel 7. istarum specierum ostensam à me ex V. T. existimo. Unde de loco isto Matth. 23. & Luc. 11. & universo hoc negotio sic sentio, cum Lege tamen resiliendi si quis meliora; Ad minimorum istorum præstationem ex Lege ipsos fuisse obligatos, eam tamen progressu temporis Judaicæ genti incubuisse cœcitatem atque affectatæ pietatis studium, ut, cum minime fuerit, ipsi tamen Pharisæi Christi ævo pro supererogatoria eam habuerit.
units.tr: In this way I think that the tithing of herbs is made probable, and that the tithing of more than three or seven of these kinds is shown evidently from the Old Testament. Hence concerning that passage in Matthew 23 and Luke 11, and this whole matter, I think as follows: the Pharisees were indeed bound by the Law to render these very small tithes, though, with the Law still in force, one may depart from it if someone has something better. Yet with the passage of time such blindness and such an affectation of piety fell upon the Jewish people that, although the tithe was not required, the Pharisees of Christ's age nevertheless regarded it as supererogatory.

units.la: Sed ut hæc semel mittamus & cætera persequamur quæ potissimum hic se offerunt consideranda, hæc tria ordine observanda sunt* 1. Primitiæ. 2. Oblatio Theruma dicta. 3. Decimæ. Hic autem ordo inverti aut immutari non poterat. R. Sal. Exod. 22. non invertendus est ordo separationum istarum, ut theruma primitiæ, aut decima Therumam antevertant.
units.tr: But, to set these aside once and for all and pursue the rest, which chiefly present themselves here for consideration: these three things must be observed in order: * 1. The first fruits. 2. The offering called terumah. 3. The tithes. This order could not be inverted or changed. Rashi on Exodus 22: the order of these separations is not to be inverted, so that the terumah or the first fruits or the tithe should come before the terumah.

units.la: Primitiæ erant frugum maturescentium, quarum Omer, id est, manipulum sacerdoti, altero festi paschalis die, nimirum XV. vel ut alii numerant XVI. Martii sive Nisan (qui a) inde nomen Abib obtinuit) offerebant. b) Hæc oblatio messem præcedebat, unde primitiæ Messis (è vestigio scil. subsecutura) passim appellantur ut Ex. grat. Levit. 23. 10.
units.tr: The first fruits were the firstlings of the ripening crops, which they offered to the priest as an omer, that is, a sheaf, on the second day of the Passover festival, namely the fifteenth, or as others count, the sixteenth of March, or Nisan (which a) took the name Abib from this). b) This offering preceded the harvest, which is why the first fruits are everywhere called the first fruits of the harvest (which was to follow immediately), as for instance in Leviticus 23:10.

units.la: Theruma verò non nisi de fructibus jam elaboratis id est, ut Scaliger loquitur, frumento vannato, oleo & musta offerebatur. Ubi & hoc observavit magnus ille & incomparabilis Heros, Ejusmodi fructus Ebræis demum vocari פירות הנגמרות ut contra, nondum elaboratos שכל.
units.tr: The terumah, however, was offered only from fruits already processed, that is, as Scaliger puts it, from winnowed grain, oil and must. Here too that great and incomparable hero observed that such fruits are called by the Hebrews פירות הנגמרות [finished fruits], whereas those not yet processed are called שכל [unprocessed].

units.la: Hæc offerebatur in festo Pentecostes, ut sancitum passim in
units.tr: This was offered at the feast of Pentecost, as is enacted everywhere in

units.la: Lege est r. Eratque prima oblatio quæ de elaboratis separabatur & solis sacerdotibus d) cedebat. Eam Græci ἀφαίρεμα μίγα vel ἀφορίσμὸν μίγαν dixerunt, Oncelos vero אפרשותא id est, separationem.
units.tr: the Law. The first offering, which was separated from the processed produce, belonged solely to the priests. The Greeks called it ἀφαίρεμα μίγα or ἀφορίσμὸν μίγαν [a great separation], and Onkelos called it אפרשותא [afrashuta], that is, a separation.

units.la: Hanc oblationem præcedaneam Moses nusquam definivit, verum Νομοδιδασκάλοις placuit ut ne esset minor parte quadragesima aut quinquagesima aut sexagesima ad minimum. Quadragesimam dixere oblationem oculi boni. Quinquagesimam oculi mediani. Sexagesimam oculi mali id est, parci & illiberalis. Sic R. Salom. ad Deut. 18. 4. Ubi & isti παραδόσεως traditioni fundamentum substernit ex Ezech. 45.13. Ubi Deum voluisse Sacerdotum avaritiæ modum ponere multis etiam ex nostris placuit. Verba prophetæ hæc sunt; Ista est oblatio quam offeretis, sextam partem Ephæ &c. Et, sextabitis Ephām de Homer bordeorum. Verba R. Salomonis quibus locum istum illustrat hæc sunt, Sexta pars Ephæ est dimidium satum. Quando tu ponis dimidium satum de Coro (vel Homer) Ecce habes unum de sexaginta. Corus enim seu Homer continet triginta sata. Sed & elegantem de hoc loco ex Hieron. discursum videbis apud Cl. Druf. Præcept. nostrum ad loca difficiliora V. libr. Mosis pag. 591.
units.tr: Moses nowhere fixed this preliminary offering, but it pleased the Νομοδιδασκάλοις [teachers of the Law] that it should be not less than a fortieth, or a fiftieth, or at the least a sixtieth part. They called the fortieth the offering of the good eye, the fiftieth that of the middling eye, and the sixtieth that of the evil eye, that is, of the stingy and illiberal. So Rashi on Deuteronomy 18:4. There too they lay as a foundation for the παραδόσεως [tradition] a passage from Ezekiel 45:13, where many of our own writers also think God wished to set a limit to the greed of the priests. The words of the prophet are these: This is the offering which you shall offer: the sixth part of an ephah, etc. And: you shall give the sixth part of an ephah from a homer of barley. The words of Rashi with which he illustrates the passage are these: The sixth part of an ephah is half a seah. When you take half a seah from a kor (or homer), behold, you have one part in sixty, for a kor or homer contains thirty seahs. But you will also see an elegant discussion of this passage from Jerome in our teacher, the learned Drusius, on the more difficult passages of the five books of Moses, page 591.

units.la: Sed & hic sanctimoniæ laudem affectarunt Pharisæi dum in utroque termino communes Leges excessere. Liberalitatis; dum trigesimam partem frugum darent, aliis quadragesimam conferentibus. Parsimoniæ: quod ultra quinquagesimam numquam descenderint, Quibus verbis Polyhistor ille Casaub. explicat verba illa B. Epiphanii, τριακοντάδας καὶ πεντηκοντάδας· ἐδίδων.
units.tr: The Pharisees also sought a reputation for holiness here, going beyond the common laws at both ends. In generosity, they gave a thirtieth part of the produce while others gave a fortieth. In thrift, they never went below a fiftieth. With these words the learned Casaubon explains the words of blessed Epiphanius: they gave the thirtieths and fiftieths [τριακοντάδας καὶ πεντηκοντάδας· ἐδίδων].

units.la: Sed missas faciam Therumas ubi illud prius monuero Tyronem quod me non raro de his meditantem tardavit, hanc oblationem nempe nomine ראשית & בכורים / quod utrumque primitias Interp. Latini, ἀπαρχὰς Græci transtulerunt, frequenter in Lege occurrere, ut E. g. Deut. 18. 4. & 26. 2. & 2. Chron. 31. 5.
units.tr: But leaving aside the Therumas for now, I will first note one point that, as a beginner, often delayed me when I meditated on these matters. This offering, called by the name ראשית [reshit] and בכורים [bikkurim], which the Latin translators rendered as primitiae and the Greeks as ἀπαρχάς, occurs frequently in the Law, for example at Deut. 18.4, Deut. 26.2 and 2 Chron. 31.5.

units.la: Hinc & Pentecostæ Num. 28. 26. vocatur dies & festum primitiarum. Et contra ipsam vocem חרומה 2. Chron. 31. & alibi Lxx. ἀπαρχὰς, Vulg. & Pagn. primitias transtulerunt.
units.tr: Hence Pentecost (Num. 28.26) is also called the day and feast of the firstfruits. On the other hand, the very word תרומה [terumah] at 2 Chron. 31 and elsewhere was translated ἀπαρχὰς by the Seventy, and primitias by the Vulgate and Pagninus.

units.la: Fuit enim hæc oblatio revera primitiæ, non quidem messis & adhuc stantium frugum, ut istæ priores, sed jam elaboratarum.
units.tr: For this offering was truly firstfruits. It was not, like the earlier ones, of the harvest and of crops still standing, but of produce already processed.

units.la: Obserua itaque hanc Reg. Quoties vox Reseith primitiæ, jungitur cum frumento, oleo, musto &c. fructibus elaboratis, tunc Therumam hanc, de qua jam loquimur significat. Quam si observassent nonnulli Interpretes & Lexicographi non confudissent tam crebrò primitias cum Therumoth, nec quæ de his prodiderunt Ebræorum Dd. illis applicuissent. Atque hæc de primitiis & oblationibus impræsentiarum sufficerint.
units.tr: Observe, then, this rule: whenever the word Reseith [ראשית], firstfruits, is joined with grain, oil, must, and other processed fruits, it signifies this terumah of which we are now speaking. If some interpreters and lexicographers had observed this, they would not so often have confused primitiae with Therumoth, nor applied to these things what the Hebrew doctors have handed down about the others. Let this be enough on firstfruits and offerings for the present.

units.la: Hac delibatione fructuum universitate facta & sacerdotibus tradita, tunc de reliquo acervo a decima dabatur Levitis. Ebræis dicta מעשר ראשון decima prima, Græcis b δεκάτη πρώτη.
units.tr: When this first portion of the whole produce had been taken and handed to the priests, a tithe was then given to the Levites from the remaining heap. The Hebrews call it מעשר ראשון [maaser rishon], the first tithe; the Greeks call it δεκάτη πρώτη.

units.la: De hac decima prima Levitæ pendebant decimam c sacerdotibus, quam Textus ibi vocat decimam de decima & Therumain Domini; Rabbini verò & inter eos R. Sal. ad locum istum, תרומת מעשר oblationem decimæ. Quæ omnia diligenter annotare volui, saltem ad Ἀφαίρεμα alterius Therumæ quam magnam vocant, de qua supra actum est. Vocatur & decima sanctitatum 2. Chron. 31. 6.
units.tr: From this first tithe the Levites paid a tithe to the priests. The text there calls it the tithe of the tithe and the terumah of the LORD. The rabbis, however, and among them R. Sal. on that passage, call it תרומת מעשר, the offering of the tithe. I wanted to note all of this carefully, at least in relation to the ἀφαίρεμα of the other terumah, which they call the great one, of which we treated above. It is also called the tithe of holy things (2 Chron. 31.6).

units.la: Hæc decima decimæ Levitis d accepta ferebatur, non vero colonis à quibus ipsi acceperant. Hâc delibata reliqua Levitis erant quasi profana & ubivis e locorum extra Jerusalem consumi poterant, etiam in cœmeterio, inquit R. Sal; At Abenezra, in omni loco mundo. Eoque pervenerant ut חולין גמורין teste R. Sal. dicerentur, id est, profana consummata.
units.tr: This tithe of the tithe, once received by the Levites, was carried away, not from the farmers from whom they had received it. Once this was set aside, the remainder was for the Levites as if profane, and it could be consumed anywhere outside Jerusalem, even in the cemetery, says R. Sal.; but Abenezra says in every clean place. So far had matters gone that, according to R. Sal., they were called חולין גמורין [chullin gemurin], that is, wholly profane things.

units.la: Jam vero quod reliquum erat de Therumā magna & decima prima, dicebatur חולין ut Scaliger observavit id est, profana. Est enim חולין, inquit ille, universitas fructuum de detracta Therumā & decima prima.
units.tr: Now what remained of the great terumah and the first tithe was called חולין [chullin], as Scaliger observed, that is, profane. For חולין, he says, is the whole produce with the terumah and the first tithe taken away.

units.la: De illis pendenda Colono adhuc erat altera decima quam Ebræi מעשר שני decimam secundam, Græci vero f δεκάτην δευτέραν vocant.
units.tr: From the remainder the farmer still had to pay another tithe, which the Hebrews call מעשר שני [maaser sheni], the second tithe, and the Greeks δεκάτην δευτέραν.

units.la: Ea expresse sancitur in Lege; scil. in g Levit, & in h Deut. Et clarè à prima distinguitur, ut mirum sit i quosdam eas confudisse. Patet enim vel hinc discrimen, quod decima prima detracta decimâ decimæ profana fieret & extra urbem S. absumi poterat: hæc vero sacra erat, nec ea nisi k intra septa Templi coram Deo vesci licebat.
units.tr: This is expressly laid down in the Law, namely in Leviticus and in Deuteronomy, and it is clearly distinguished from the first. It is surprising that some have confused them. The difference is evident even from this: once the tithe of the tithe was removed, the first tithe became profane and could be consumed outside the city, whereas the second was holy, and it was not lawful to eat it before God except within the enclosure of the Temple.

units.la: Amplius, decimæ primæ necessariò aut à colono ipso aut ejus vicario Hierosolymas deportandæ erant: decimæ verò secundæ aut Hierosolymam deferendæ erant aut si impediretur erat via longiorve, adærari poterant à colono, & ex pecunia inde redacta vinum, oleum, mustum, victimasque Hierosolymis denuo coemebat, ut ex illis epulum instrueret (quod Ebræis יורי χαεισίεων dictum annotavit Scaliger) & ad illud Levitas & Sacerdotes in atrio Templi invitaret Deut. 14.24.
units.tr: Moreover, the first tithe had to be brought to Jerusalem, either by the farmer himself or by his agent. The second tithe either had to be brought to Jerusalem, or, if the way was too long or the journey hindered, the farmer could convert it into money. With that money he bought again in Jerusalem wine, oil, must and victims, to prepare a feast from them (which Scaliger notes the Hebrews called "feasts of rejoicing"), and to invite the Levites and priests to it in the court of the Temple (Deut. 14.24).

units.la: Sed quando secunda illa decima divendebatur, quintam partem decimæ adhuc addi solitam ex Lege Levit. 27. 31. collegerunt Ebræi, ut, inquit Scaliger, quæ in speciebus erant decem de centum, in adæratione fuerint XII.
units.tr: But when that second tithe was sold for money, the Hebrews gathered from Lev. 27.31 that a fifth part was still customarily added. So, as Scaliger says, what was ten in the hundred in kind came to be twelve in the money value.

units.la: Ita quod restabat fructuum, חולין מחוקבים id est, profana ἀτιμασμένα dicebantur & præparata, pollucta id est usibus profanis exposita.
units.tr: Thus the rest of the produce was called חולין מחוקבים [chullin mehukkavim], profane things that had been made cheap (ἀτιμασμένα), and prepared, that is, made available for profane uses.

units.la: Addam locum ex Josepho contra eos qui has decimas confuderunt. Is autem libro Ant. 4. 8. sic introducit Mosem mortijam vicinum: Sit autem & decima separatio vobis frugum, praeter eam quae Sacerdotibus & Levitis debetur, χωρὶς τῆς διελάξατε τοῖς ἱερεῦσι καὶ Λευίταις δίδοσθαι. Pergit Jos. ἡ ἀπέχειν μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν πατρίδων, εἰς δὲ τὰς ἀπωχίας ὑπηρετείτω καὶ τὰς ἱερὰς πόλεις, id est, quae diverdatur quidem in patriis, sed insumatur pecunia inde redacta in convivia & sacrificia in sancta urbe.
units.tr: I will add a passage from Josephus against those who confused these tithes. In book 4, chapter 8 of the Antiquities, he introduces Moses, already near death, speaking thus: But let there also be for you a tenth separation of the fruits, besides what is due to the priests and Levites [χωρὶς τῆς διελάξατε τοῖς ἱερεῦσι καὶ Λευίταις δίδοσθαι]. Josephus goes on: which is to be spent away from home, and used in the holy city for feasts and sacrifices [ἡ ἀπέχειν μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν πατρίδων, εἰς δὲ τὰς ἀπωχίας ὑπηρετείτω καὶ τὰς ἱερὰς πόλεις], that is, the money raised from it is to be spent on banquets and sacrifices in the holy city.

units.la: Clarus etiam est Tobiae locus 1.8. καὶ τῷ δευτέρῳ δεκάτῳ ἀπεπεξακπζόμενον, ἢ ἐπιδόσμεν ἐ ἐδαπάνων αὐτὰ ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις. id est, secundam decimam vendebam & ibam & expendebam ea in Jerusalem.
units.tr: The passage of Tobit 1.8 is also clear: and I sold the second tithe, and went and spent those things in Jerusalem [καὶ τῷ δευτέρῳ δεκάτῳ ... ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις].

units.la: Restat tertium decimarum genus quod tertio quoque anno recurrebat unde Trietericum vocant Tob. 1. 7. τῷ τρίτῳ δεκάτῳ. quod his verbis in Deut. sancitur, A fine trium annorum depromito omnes decimas frumenti tui provenientis isto anno & relinques intra portas tuas. Quem venientes Levita, peregrini, pupilli & viduae, quae sunt intra portas tuas, comedant & saturentur &c. Ubi nota quod pro à fine in Ebr. sit מקצה (in) extremo vel extremitate id est, in principio tertii cujusque anni, utraque enim rei extremitas קץ & מקצה dicitur. Sic Deut. 15. 1. alibi.
units.tr: There remains a third kind of tithe, which recurred every third year, and so they call it the triennial tithe (Tob. 1.7, τῷ τρίτῳ δεκάτῳ). It is laid down in Deuteronomy in these words: At the end of three years you shall bring out all the tithes of your produce of that year, and leave them within your gates. The Levites, strangers, orphans and widows who are within your gates shall come and eat and be satisfied, and so on. Note that where the Latin has à fine ("at the end"), the Hebrew has מקצה [miqtsheh], "at the extremity" (with "in"), that is, at the beginning of the third year of each cycle; for each extremity of a thing is called קץ [qets] and מקצה. So at Deut. 15.1 and elsewhere.

units.la: Et quia pauperibus hæ etiam cedebant, πωχοδεκάτας dictæ Hieronymo sunt & Rabb. מעשר עני.
units.tr: Because these also went to the poor, Jerome calls them πτωχοδεκάτας [ptochodekatas], and the rabbis call them מעשר עני [maaser ani], the tithe of the poor.

units.la: Sed quæri hic video an hæc decimatio, tertio quoque ab anno Remissionis anno, utrumque primo & secundo anno usitatam peremerit, an verò nullam, aut an unam tantum, & si unam, utram? an primam an secundam. Sunt qui eam loco secundæ fuisse aut quod idem est eo anno secundam omissam asserunt. Sunt qui neutram.
units.tr: But I see a question here: whether this tithing, every third year before the year of release, took the place of the tithe used in both the first and second years, or of neither, or of only one, and if of one, which: the first or the second. Some say it took the place of the second, or, what is the same, that in that year the second tithe was omitted. Others say neither.

units.la: Quid illos induxerit fateor me non videre. At hoc decepit quod Tob. 1.7. vocatur δεκάτη τρίτη, cum tamen ea nihil aliud sit quam decima tertii anni.
units.tr: I confess I do not see what led them to this. What misled them is that Tob. 1.7 calls it the third tithe (δεκάτη τρίτη), although it is nothing other than the tithe of the third year.

units.la: Magnus autem ille Scaliger vult nihil aliud eas fuisse quam decimas primas, quæ primo & secundo item quarto & quinto anno Hierosolymam à colono deportabantur in manus Ephemeriæ Levitarum tum Ministerium obeuntis, tertio autem & sexto anno hebdomadis annalis in horrea, cellas & apothecas condebantur, Levitis, viduis, orphanis & peregrinis in ostio coloni erogandæ.
units.tr: That great Scaliger holds that these were nothing else than first tithes. In the first, second, fourth and fifth years they were carried from the farmer to Jerusalem, into the hands of the Levitical course then performing its ministry. In the third and sixth years of the seven-year cycle, however, they were stored in barns, storerooms and cellars, to be distributed at the farmer's gate to Levites, widows, orphans and strangers.

units.la: Licet verò rationes suæ hujus sententiæ non afferat, non tamen sine ratione hoc statuisse putandus.
units.tr: Although he does not give reasons for this view, it must not be supposed that he held it without reason.

units.la: Hoc tantum vide. Aut fuit prima aut secunda, vel, aut fuit loco primæ aut secundæ, vel, aut peremit primam aut secundam. Utramque enim si peremisset, miserè cum Sacerdotibus actum fuisset.
units.tr: Consider only this. It was either the first or the second tithe; or it took the place of the first or of the second; or it destroyed the first or the second. For if it had destroyed both, things would have gone badly for the priests.

units.la: Non secundam, quæ in atrio præsente colono absumebatur, quia sic toto anno multum esurivissent sacerdotes, utpotè cum nihil expectandum fuisset præter decimas decimarum Levitarum & Therumas, quarum pars quotidiano victu insumenda, pars anno sexto in annum remissionis seu Sabbathicum (quo ut nulla messis ita nullæ decimæ, nulla Therumæ) reponenda. Quantillæ etiam istæ decimæ decimarum fuerint ad tantum numerum Sacerdotum per integrum annum nedum duos alendum, præter Therumam & ea quibus ex sacrificiis & pecoribus fruebantur, judicabit quicunque apud Josephum legerit quamque classem sacerdotum (quæ XXIV. erant) suo ævo ultra V. millia sacerdotum habuisse.
units.tr: Not the second, which was eaten in the court in the presence of the farmer, for then the priests would have gone very hungry all year, since nothing would have been expected except the tithes of the Levites' tithes and the terumahs. Part of these was to be used for daily food, and part was to be stored from the sixth year for the year of release, the Sabbath year, in which there is no harvest and so no tithes and no terumah. Anyone who reads Josephus will judge how small these tithes of tithes would have been for feeding so great a number of priests for a whole year, let alone two, apart from the terumah and what they enjoyed from sacrifices and flocks; Josephus says that each of the twenty-four priestly courses in his time had more than five thousand priests.

units.la: Ergo primam. Ut hoc pacto sacerdotibus tantum decimæ decimarum, Levitis tantum illud quod in Orphanos, viduas & pauperes conferebatur, decesserit. Atque ita exiguo utriusque ordinis dispendio à sapientiss. Legislatore communi egestati consultum est. Quæ omnia secus essent, si, ut quidam opinantur, hæ tricteriæ decimæ secundas peremisset.
units.tr: So, first: in this way the priests lost only the tithe of the tithes, and the Levites lost only what was contributed for orphans, widows and the poor. Thus, at a small cost to each order, the most wise Lawgiver provided for common need. All of this would be otherwise if, as some suppose, these threefold tithes had destroyed the second tithe.

units.la: Hæc omnia sic melius patebunt: Habet colonus in reditu hujus anni frumenti modium 6000.
units.tr: All of this will be clearer as follows: the farmer has 6000 modii of wheat from this year's yield.

units.la: 6000. | Proventus anni. 100. | Theruma sacerdotibus tradenda à colono parco minusque liberali. 5900. | Residuum de Therumâ bis decimandum. 590. | Decima prima quæ dabatur Levitis. 59. | Decima decimæ quam Lev. dabant sacerdotibus. 5310. | Residuum de Ther. & decima prima adhuc semel decimandum. 531. | Decima secunda quæ absumebatur in Templo. 4779. | Residuum deducta Ther. & utraque decima de 6000. 1121. | Utraque decima conjuncta quæ est ad 5900. ut 19. ad 100.
units.tr: 6000. | Yield of the year. 100. | Theruma to be handed over to the priests by a farmer who is sparing and less generous. 5900. | Remainder, from which the theruma is to be tithed twice. 590. | First tithe, which was given to the Levites. 59. | Tithe of the tithe, which the Levites gave to the priests. 5310. | Remainder, from the theruma and the first tithe, still to be tithed once. 531. | Second tithe, which was consumed in the Temple. 4779. | Remainder after deducting the theruma and both tithes from 6000. 1121. | Both tithes together, which are to 5900 as 19 is to 100.

units.la: Græcam Interpretationem Vet. Test. quæ LXXII. Interpretibus vulgò adscribitur, esse Θεόπνευστον.
units.tr: That the Greek translation of the Old Testament, commonly ascribed to the Seventy Interpreters, is inspired by God [θεόπνευστον].

units.la: HUNC errorem primaria primitivæ Ecclesiæ columina errarunt, ex quo innumeri alii propullularunt. Tali enim uno absurdo posito, quî fieri potuit aliter? Minus hîc culpandi fuêre Græci Patres, qui & Ebraicè & Latinè imperiti, unum & alterum excipio, aliis Editionibus non fuerunt usi. Eò fidentius suæ Editionis αὐθεντίαν assertum ivêre. Accessit recepta & credita vulgo fabula de LXXII. cellulis, queis boni illi viri, singuli seorsim inclusi, versionem hanc eo consensu elaboraverint, uti ne in minima quidem particulâ dissenserint. Fabulam voco cum viris magnis, qui & hoc & alia quæ vulgo de hac translatione circumferuntur, diligentissimè pensitarunt. Ædicularum nec Aristeas, μεγίστη τ̀ ἰσχὺς ταύτης σάλπιγξ, & qui universi hujus negotii director fuit, nec Philo, nec nobilissimus scriptor, suæque gentis studiosissimus Iosephus meminêre. Inter antiquissimos hujus opinionis assertores Iustinus Martyr est, cujus facilitate nimium abusi sunt fallaces Judæi. Is parænetico ad Græcos ait, Ptolomæum non in urbe suâ, sed in Pharo insulâ interpretibus assignasse locum, illic extrui jussisse ἰσαρίθμως τ̀ ἑρμηνευόντων οἰκίσκους μίκρας, i. ediculas pari cum interpretibus numero, ut sigillatim interpretationem adornarent, injunxisse vero iis qui inservirent, ut à congressu mutuo illos prohiberent. Subjungit autem, se ipsum in insulâ Pharo τὰ ἴχνη τ̀ οἰκίσκων vidisse, & rem ita se habere, ab incolis qui id à majoribus acceperant, audivisse. Ex eo hauserunt Cyrillus, Augustinus, Hilar. Tertull. tull. Philastrius, Isidorus, &c. Et ex recentioribus Serarius, Baronius, Leo Castrius, Salmeron & alii. Quod vero Iustino à Iudaeis impositum dixi, non mirabitur, qui ipsi quoque Hieronymo à propudiis istis saepe os sublitum fuisse, & Iudaeis hoc solenne esse novit. Vt autem scias apud Iudaeos hanc eandem extare fabulam, describam verba ipsius Thalmud quae extant in Massechet Sopherim, cap.1. Halacha 8.
units.tr: The first pillars of the early Church fell into this error, and countless others sprang up from it. Once such an absurdity was accepted, how could things have gone otherwise? The Greek Fathers are less to blame here, since they were unskilled in Hebrew and Latin, and with one or two exceptions they did not use other editions. This made them all the more confident in asserting the authority [αὐθεντία] of their own edition. To this was added the story, received and generally believed, of the seventy-two little cells, in which those good men, each shut up alone, are said to have produced this translation with such agreement that they did not differ even in the smallest particle. I call it a story, with great scholars who have carefully weighed both this and the other things commonly circulated about this translation. Neither Aristeas, who calls it "the greatest trumpet of this matter" [μεγίστη τῆς ἰσχύος ταύτης σάλπιγξ], and who was director of the whole undertaking, nor Philo, nor the most noble writer Josephus, who was most devoted to his own nation, mention these cells. Among the earliest advocates of this opinion is Justin Martyr, whose credulity the deceitful Jews greatly exploited. In his Exhortation to the Greeks he says that Ptolemy did not assign the translators a place in his own city but on the island of Pharos, and ordered little cells to be built there in the same number as the translators [ἰσαρίθμως τῶν ἑρμηνευόντων οἰκίσκους μικράς], so that each could prepare the translation separately, and that he commanded their attendants to keep them from meeting one another. He adds that he himself saw the traces [τὰ ἴχνη] of the cells on the island of Pharos, and that the matter stands thus, as he heard from the inhabitants, who had received it from their ancestors. From him drew Cyril, Augustine, Hilary, Tertullian, Philastrius, Isidore, and so on. Among more recent writers, Serarius, Baronius, Leo Castrius, Salmeron and others. As for my saying that Justin was imposed upon by the Jews, no one will be surprised who knows that Jerome too had often had his face smeared with such filth, and that this is a customary trick with the Jews. But so that you may know that this same story is found among the Jews, I will set out the words of the Talmud itself, which occur in Massechet Sopherim, chap. 1, Halacha 8.

units.la: שוב מעשרה בתלמי הלסך שכנס שבעים ושנים זקנים והושיבם בשבעים ושנים בתים ולא גלה להם על מה כנסם: נכנס לכל אחד ואחד מהם. אמר להם כתבו לי תורת משה רבכם נתן המקום עצה בלב כל אהד ואחד מהסו הסכימו רעתן לרעת אחרת וכתבו לי תורה בפני עצמה ושלשה עשר דבר שינו ברה וכולי
units.tr: Again, a story about King Ptolemy, who gathered seventy-two elders and seated them in seventy-two houses, without telling them why he had assembled them. He went in to each one and said: "Write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher." God put counsel into the heart of each of them, so they agreed in their opinion and wrote for him a Torah of their own, and they changed thirteen things, and so on. [שוב מעשרה בתלמי הלסך שכנס שבעים ושנים זקנים והושיבם בשבעים ושנים בתים ולא גלה להם על מה כנסם: נכנס לכל אחד ואחד מהם. אמר להם כתבו לי תורת משה רבכם נתן המקום עצה בלב כל אהד ואחד מהסו הסכימו רעתן לרעת אחרת וכתבו לי תורה בפני עצמה ושלשה עשר דבר שינו ברה וכולי]

units.la: Hoc est, Rursus exemplum in Ptolemaeo Rege, qui convocavit LXXII. senes, collocavitque eos totidem adiculis, cumque nondum aperuisset iis, quâ de re convocati essent, ingressus ad singulos, ait, Scribite mihi Legem Mosis magistri vestri. Porro Deus ita omnium mentem dirigebat, ut cum scriberent singuli, eandem unam undequaque legem omnes scriberent, unoque concentu in tredecim locis ab Ebraeo discederent. Haec illi. Mirantur ergo merito viri docti, unde * Epiphanius eumque secutus Iustinianus, Novella 146, de 36. cellulis, ut bini cellulis inclusi fuerint, fominaverint. Sed audiamus magni Hieronymi de hac re judicium, Nescio, inquit, praefat. in Pentateuchum, quis primus author septuaginta cellulas suo MENDACIO extruxerit, quibus divisi eadem scriptitarint, cum Aristaas ejusdem Ptolemai ὑπομνήματος & multa post tempora Iosephus nihil tale retulerint; sed in una basilica congregatos contulisse scribant. Et Prologo in Paralip. LXX. cellula, quae vulgo sine auctore feruntur. Haec & alia moverunt eruditissimos viros, Masium praefat. in Iosuam, Titelmannum prologo Apolog. pro Edit. vulg. Bellarminum lib.2. de V. D. cap.6. & alios, ut hanc de cellulis fabulam exploserint.
units.tr: That is, again, the example of King Ptolemy, who summoned seventy-two elders and seated them in seventy-two cells. When he had not yet told them why they had been summoned, he went in to each one and said, "Write for me the Law of Moses, your teacher." Moreover, God so directed the mind of all of them that, although each wrote separately, all wrote the same single law from every side, and in one harmony departed from the Hebrew in thirteen places. So he writes. Learned men therefore rightly wonder how Epiphanius, and Justinian after him (Novella 146, on the thirty-six cells, so that two were shut into each cell), came to report this. But let us hear the judgment of the great Jerome on this matter. "I do not know," he says in the preface to the Pentateuch, "who was the first author to build the seventy cells by his LIE, in which the translators, separated, are said to have written the same things, since Aristeas, in the memoir [ὑπομνήματος] of this same Ptolemy, and Josephus many years later, related nothing of the kind, but write that they were gathered and compared their work in one basilica. And in the prologue to Paralipomenon, on the Seventy: "the cells, which are commonly carried about without an author." These and other points have moved very learned men, Masius in the preface to Joshua, Titelmann in the prologue to his Apology for the Vulgate edition, Bellarmine in book 2 of On the Word of God, chapter 6, and others, to explode this fable of the cells.

units.la: Adhaesit tamen plerisque illorum eadem de mirabili consensu Interpretum in una basilica congregatorum opinio, unde non minorem ei authoritatem, quam cellularum defensores, conciliare studuerunt. Namque & hi LXX. Interpretationem, ὡς Φιλων, eosque non tam vertisse, quam prophetasse, dixere. Vide Philonem de vita Mosis, Clem. Alexand. Strom. lib. 1. August. de Civit. Dei 1. 18. cap. 42. 43. 44. & de doctrinâ Cristi. 2. 15. Ipse quoque Hieronymus qui praefat. in Pentat. eos non vates sed interpretes fuisse dixerat, Prefat. in Paralip. Spiritus sancti afflatum illis tribuit. Bel-larmi-
units.tr: Still, most of them retained the same opinion about the wonderful agreement of the translators gathered in one basilica, and they tried to give it no less authority than the defenders of the cells did. For these too said that the Seventy translated not merely but prophesied, as Philo says. See Philo on the Life of Moses, Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 1, Augustine, On the City of God, book 18, chapters 42, 43, 44, and On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 15. Jerome himself, who said in the preface to the Pentateuch that they were not prophets but interpreters, in the preface to Paralipomenon attributes to them the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Bellarmine

units.la: • in libro de mensuris & ponderibus. larminus peculiarem Spiritus S. assistentiam, ne quâ in re errarent, illis adscribit, ut non tam Interpretes quàm vates fuisse videantur. Et Gretzerus Spiritum propheticum illis impartitur, ejusque vim constituit 1. in eo, quod tam fuerint concordes, 2. quod tam brevi temporis spacio, vid.72.diebus, opus suum absolverint.
units.tr: • in the book On Weights and Measures. Bellarmine ascribes to them a special help of the Holy Spirit, so that they would make no error in any matter, so that they seem to have been not so much interpreters as prophets. And Gretser grants them a prophetic Spirit, and he rests its force on two things: first, that they agreed so closely, and second, that they finished their work in such a short space of time, namely seventy-two days.

units.la: Habuerunt ergo juxta illos Spiritus S. peculiarem assistentiam, ut nulla in re erraverint. Hoc Græcos Patres sensisse minus mirandû esse supra dicebam. Illorum enim vix ullus Fontes adire potuit, aut ex vulgatâ Latinâ meliorem multorum locorum versionem discere. Quod enim ad Aquilam, Theod. Symmachum & alios Græcos Interpretes attinet, cum vel Judæi vel hæretici illi fuerint, non mirum si ipsorum fidem suspectaverint. At Hieronymum subinde, & Augustinum ubique, ut de cæteris Latinæ Ecclesiæ Patribus nihil dicam, tam præclaram de ipsis fovisse opinionem, quis non miretur? Agnoscit August. in Ebræo legi Ion. 3. adhuc XL. dies & Ninive peribit. Noverat eundem locum in LXX. sic legi, Adhuc tres dies, &c. Hic sudat bonus pater, & celerem mentem nunc hùc nunc dirigit illùc, nec tamen se extricare valet, ut suo loco videbimus; Mordicus enim tenet id quod semel apprehenderat, * Spiritum qui in Prophetis erat cum illa dixerunt, eundem ipsum fuisse etiam in LXX. cum ista transferrent. Sed quid Augustinum memoro? Salmero & Gretzerus, qui plurima à LXX. addita, detracta & mutata vel ex sola vulgata deprehenderant, tantum abest, ut ex eo de versionis istius authoritate dubitare cæperint, ut totum hoc singulari Spiritus S. impulsu transcribant. Sed videant hi quid responsuri sint Andradio, cujus insignem hac de re locum infra ad errorem generalem de puritate fontium, cap. 3. producemus. Ille dictos interpretes labi potuisse asserit, & Bellarm. dictæ versionis sphalmata & ab Ebræo textu discrepantiam librariis imputat. Namque eorum versionem nunc adeo corruptam & vitiatam agnoscit, ut omnino alia esse videatur. nec dicendum, inquit idem, textum Ebr. esse corruptum ubi à Græco discrepat, ne fateri cogamur (Nota hoc Lector, ἀφ' ἐν Φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι) vulgatam Editionem, quam Concilium Trid. authenticam esse judicavit, totam quoque esse corruptam. nam excepto Psalterio, Latina Editio magis convenit cum Ebræo, quàm cum Græco. Ad obtentum vero impulsus Spiritus S. ab Augustino aliisque adhibitum, à Gretzero verò & Salmerone aliisq; probatum, candidè respondet idem Bellarm. Patres istos pie quaesivisse rationes excusan-
units.tr: According to them, then, the Holy Spirit gave them a special help, so that they made no error in any matter. I said above that it is less surprising that the Greek Fathers thought this. For hardly any of them could consult the sources, or learn from the Vulgate Latin a better version of many passages. As for Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus, and the other Greek translators, since they were either Jews or heretics, it is no wonder that the Fathers distrusted them. But who would not be surprised that Jerome at times, and Augustine everywhere (I say nothing of the other Fathers of the Latin Church), held such a high opinion of them? Augustine acknowledges that in the Hebrew of Jonah 3 it is read Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. He knew that the same passage is read in the Seventy as Yet three days, etc. Here the good father sweats, and turns his quick mind now this way, now that, yet cannot free himself, as we shall see in its place. For he holds firmly to what he had once grasped: the Spirit who was in the Prophets, when they said those things, was the same Spirit also in the Seventy, when they translated these. But why do I mention Augustine? Salmeron and Gretser, who had noted many additions, omissions, and changes in the Seventy, even from the Vulgate alone, are so far from beginning to doubt the authority of that version because of this, that they copy out the whole matter as the work of a singular impulse of the Holy Spirit. But let them see what they will answer to Andradius, whose striking passage on this subject we will quote below, in the section on the general error about the purity of the sources, chapter 3. He asserts that those translators could have slipped, and Bellarmine ascribes the errors of that version, and its disagreement with the Hebrew text, to copyists. For Bellarmine admits that their version is now so corrupted and vitiated that it seems to be altogether another thing. Nor, says the same man, should we say that the Hebrew text is corrupt where it differs from the Greek, lest we be forced to admit it (Note this, reader: [ἀφ' ἐν φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι] lay it to heart). The Vulgate edition, which the Council of Trent judged authentic, is also wholly corrupt, for except for the Psalter, the Latin edition agrees more with the Hebrew than with the Greek. As for the appeal to the impulse of the Holy Spirit, which Augustine used, Gretser and Salmeron and others approved, Bellarmine candidly answers that those Fathers piously sought reasons for excusing and defending that version which the Church then used.

units.la: * De Civit. D. 18. 41. vide & 15.23. & 18 44. cusandi & defendendi eam versionem, quā tunc Ecclesia utebatur.
units.tr: * On the City of God 18.41; see also 15.23 and 18.44. Excusing and defending that version which the Church then used.

units.la: Sed satis ostensum arbitror, in quod præcipuè intendebam, Patres non solùm Græcos, sed & Latinos plerosque, qui Latinâ Editione ex Græcâ τῶν LXX. tradućta utebantur, summum sceleus duxisse, verba * Andradii, à LXX. Interpretum versione quovis modo diffidere, eosque non aliter pro 70. Interpp. quàm pro ipsis divinis oraculis pugnasse & divino afflatu fuisse in interpretando actos, existimasse. Hoc negari non potest, hoc liquet, inquit Andradius, ut mirum non sit, * Hieronymum propter suam ex Ebraeo versionem non minorem invidiam sustinuisse, quàm novi nunc Interpretes apud quamplurimos sustinent.
units.tr: But I think I have shown enough of what I was chiefly aiming at: that the Fathers, not only the Greeks but also most of the Latins who used the Latin edition translated from the Greek of the Seventy, regarded it as the greatest sin, in the words of Andradius, to distrust the version of the Seventy in any way, and that they fought for it no differently than for the divine oracles themselves, and thought that the translators had been moved by divine inspiration in their work. In the words of Andradius, this cannot be denied; this is clear, so that it is no wonder that * Jerome, because of his translation from the Hebrew, bore no less hatred than the new translators now bear from very many people.

units.la: In hujus erroneæ sententiæ confutatione non ero prolixus. Præcipuum ejus fulcrum fuit illa de cellulis opinio. Eo sublato, ruit illa alto à culmine. Iam diximus, à quibus & quibus de causis ea fabula explosa sit. Adde, omnia fere quæ de universâ illa Interpretatione traduntur, adeò diversis authorum opionibus involvi, ut vix quippiam certi sit. Controversum est, utrùm sub Ptolomæo Lago, an Philadelpho ea elaborata sit; an solius Pentateuchi, an verò totius Vet. Testamenti versionem dederint; an omnes conjunctiinter sese contulerint, atque ita à capite ad calcem perrexerint, an vero in LXXII. vel pauciores particulas Scripturâ distributâ, vel singuli vel bini suum pensum absolverint: Controversum est an ex singulis tribubus seni delecti, an Demetrius Phalareus ullas sustinuerit partes in hâc fabulâ. Duo enim hæc posteriora negat Scaliger, animadversionibus ad Eusebium & Vvowerius in Syntagmate de Græcâ versione c.3. Ostendunt enim, neminem hoc tradidisse præter Aristæam; ex eo verò hoc hausisse Ecclesiasticos scriptores. Ostendunt eum Regi Philadelpho fuisse invisum, produnt odii causam, docent à Philadelpho sub initium regni sui in exilium ire jussum, atque in eo periisse: Bibliothecæ Alexandrinæ non fuisse præfectum, nullum antiquorum Scriptorum, qui vitam ejus descripsêre, hujus rei ullam mentionem scriptis suis inseruisse. Ad summam, tota Aristææ narratio in dubium vocatur à viris magnis. Epistolæ quæ ad Iudæos scriptæ finguntur, apud diversos authores diversæ. Ajunt esse scriptum ab Alexandrinis Iudæis confictum, Aristææ suppositum, more istis sæculis tralatitio, & Iudæis proprio, utpote qui ab omni ævo sine ulla religione, neglectâ omni specie veri, mentiri austi sunt, quasi tota posteritas Midæ aures fabulis eorum recipiendis assumsisset.
units.tr: I shall not be long in refuting this mistaken view. Its chief support was that opinion about the little cells. With that removed, the whole structure falls from its high summit. We have already said by whom, and for what reasons, that fable was exploded. Add that nearly everything handed down about that whole Interpretation is so tangled in the differing opinions of authors that scarcely anything is certain. It is disputed whether it was produced under Ptolemy Lagus or under Philadelphus; whether they gave a version of the Pentateuch only or of the whole Old Testament; whether they all came together, compared their work, and went through the text from beginning to end, or whether the Scripture was divided into seventy-two portions which each one or two men completed alone. It is disputed whether six were chosen from each tribe, and whether Demetrius Phalereus had any part in this fable. For Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius, and Vossius, in his Syntagma on the Greek version, chapter 3, deny these last two points. They show that no one handed this down except Aristeas, and that the ecclesiastical writers drew it from him. They show that he was hated by King Philadelphus, they give the cause of the hatred, they teach that at the beginning of his reign Philadelphus ordered him into exile, and that he died there; that he was not prefect of the Alexandrian library; and that no ancient writer who described his life made any mention of this matter in his writings. In short, the whole narrative of Aristeas is called into doubt by great men. The letters said to have been written to the Jews differ among various authors. They say it was a document forged by Alexandrian Jews and falsely attributed to Aristeas, in the manner traditional in those centuries and proper to the Jews, who from all time have been accustomed to lie without any religion, neglecting every semblance of truth, as if the whole posterity of Midas had given its ears to receiving their fables.

units.la: Sed demus haec omnia vera esse, LXXII. Senes, ex singulis tribubus senos, ab Eleazare Pontifice ad petitionem Ptolomei Philadelphi, à Demetrio Phalareo Bibliothecario suo moniti, Alexandriâ missos, ibique totum vetus Test. in basilicâ unâ congregatos, summo consensu 72. dierum spacio, cum peculiari assistentia Sp. S., sine errore, vertisse, quomodo haec definivit Bellarminus, illa tamen restabit difficultas, utrùm illa, quae in Graeco textu ab Ebraeo manifeste discrepant, quae ad eum addita, vel mutata sunt, cum Augustino, Salmerone, Gretzero, &c. Spiritui S. an verò librariorum incuriae adscribenda sint, sicuti volunt Andrad. Bellarm. Masius & alii. Si prius dixeris, oportet ut vel textum Ebraeum ibi corruptum dicas, ubi à Graeca discrepat, & sic vulgatam quoque Latinam incusari, Andradius & Belarm. suprà monuerunt, vel ut cum Augustino utramque Spiritui S. adscribas lectionem, spiritumq; illum veritatis non solum à semet ipso diversum, sed & tibi ipsi subinde contrarium facias, id quod sine insigni Spiritus S. injuria fieri non potest. Si posterius eligas, ut vid. librariis imputetur ea Graeci textus ab Ebraeo discrepantia, etiam illud largiendum erit, vetustissimam istam esse universi ferè textus curruptionem, cum antiquissimi etiam Patres loca ferè omnia eo modo, quo etiamnum leguntur, corrupta, citaverint, atque iis ipsis suos errores superaedificârint. Id quod ad illud quod nos intendimus, satis est. Sive enim ab ipsis Interpretibus, sive à librariis commissi sint errores isti, qui celebratissimam istam interpretationem deturpârunt, illud videbunt semper Lectores, eos, dum per linguae Sanctae ignorantiam, nec in erratis librariorum, nec haereticorum depravationibus, nec in varietate lectionis nec in ambiguitate vocis vel sententiae, vel similibus casibus, ne dum in locis male versis ad fontes recurrere, atque ex iis se extricare potuerunt, eâ ipsa ceu sacrosanctâ & θεοπνευστῳ fuisse usos. Sed & nos suo loco evidentissimis exemplis ostendemus, ipsos illos Interpretes multos quoque admisisse errores, homines enim fuere, non Dii; Interpretes non Vates. Et manifesta passim indicabimus vestigia, quibus illi insistentes, ab Ebraicae veritatis linea non semel aberrarunt. Certè * Augustinus. Steuchus Eugubinus, Episcopus Xisamensis, non erubuit pronunciare, LXX. Interpretes non adeo exquisitè Grammaticam Ebraeam tenuisse, atque ex hoc fonte quamplurimos errores ebullivisse. Sed jam dixi meae intentioni sufficere ingenuam Bellarmini & aliorum confessionem, adeo multis eam versionem erroribus librariorum & descriptorum esse depravatam, ut omnino alia esse videatur. Iam suo saeculo quiritabatur Hieronymus, post confusas Origenis notas (vid. obeliscos, quibus ex aliis editionibus adjecta confoderat; asteriscos, quibus detracta aut si quae Theodotionis irrepserant, notaverat; lemniscos, quibus discrepantes lectiones variorum librorum consensu firmatas, & Hypolemniscos, quibus paucorum librorum testimonio probatas indicaverat) versionem eam adeo fuisse vitiatam, ut vix unicum potuerit reperiri exemplar, in quo pura & integra τῶν LXX. interpretatio extaret. Origenem exceperunt Lucianus presbyter Antiochenus, & Hesychius, qui huic versioni emaculandae & pristino nitori restituendae manum admoverunt. Unde postmodum tres quasi Editiones matres extitere, de quibus Hieronym. Praefat. in Paralipom. Alexandria & AEgyptus, inquit, in LXX. suis Hesychium laudat authorem. Constantinopolis usque in Antiochiam Luciani Martyris exemplaria probat. Media inter has provincia Palaestinos codices legunt, quos ab Origene elaboratos Eusebius vulgaverat, totusque orbis in hac triplici varietate compugnat. Ecce tres primarias editiones versionis ꝟ LXX. singulas à correctore & recognitore suo denominatas.
units.tr: But grant that all this is true: that the seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, were sent from Alexandria at the request of Ptolemy Philadelphus by the high priest Eleazar, instructed by Demetrius Phalereus his librarian, gathered together in one basilica, and translated the whole Old Testament in complete agreement, within seventy-two days, without error, with the special assistance of the Holy Spirit, as Bellarmine defined. Still there will remain the difficulty of whether those places which clearly differ in the Greek text from the Hebrew, and which were added to or changed in it, are to be ascribed to the Holy Spirit, as Augustine, Salmeron, Gretser, etc., hold, or to the carelessness of copyists, as Andradius, Bellarmine, Masius and others wish. If you choose the former, you must either say that the Hebrew text was corrupt where it differs from the Greek, and thus also find fault with the Vulgate Latin, as Andradius and Bellarmine noted above; or else, with Augustine, you must ascribe both readings to the Holy Spirit and make that Spirit of truth not only different from himself but at times contrary to himself, which cannot be done without a serious injury to the Holy Spirit. If you choose the latter, so that the divergence of the Greek from the Hebrew is imputed to copyists, then it must also be conceded that this corruption of almost the whole text is very ancient, since the most ancient Fathers cited nearly all the passages in the form in which they are still read, corrupt, and built their own errors upon those very readings. This is enough for our purpose.
