For whether these errors which have disfigured that most celebrated translation came from the Interpreters themselves or from copyists, readers will always see this: through ignorance of the holy tongue they could not have recourse to the sources, nor extricate themselves from the errors of copyists, the corruptions of heretics, the variety of readings, the ambiguity of a word or sense, and similar cases, much less in passages badly rendered; and so they used that version as if it were sacrosanct and divinely inspired. But we too, in its place, shall show by the most evident examples that those very Interpreters admitted many errors, for they were men, not gods; interpreters, not prophets. And we shall point out clear traces everywhere, following which they more than once strayed from the line of Hebrew truth. Certainly Augustine, and Steuchus Eugubinus, bishop of Chisamos, did not blush to declare that the Seventy Interpreters did not hold Hebrew grammar so exactly, and that from this source very many errors welled up. But I have already said that the candid confession of Bellarmine and others is enough for my purpose: that this version has been so depraved by the errors of copyists and scribes that it seems altogether a different thing. Already in his own century Jerome complained, after the confused marks of Origen (see the obelisks, with which he had pierced additions taken from other editions; the asterisks, with which he marked omissions, or whatever Theodotion's work had crept in; the lemniscs, with which he marked readings confirmed by the agreement of various books; and the hypolemniscs, with which he indicated readings approved by the testimony of a few books), that the version had been so vitiated that scarcely a single copy could be found in which the pure and entire interpretation of the Seventy survived. Origen was followed by Lucian, presbyter of Antioch, and Hesychius, who laid hands on emending this version and restoring its former brilliance. Whence three so-called mother editions afterwards emerged, of which Jerome, in the preface to Paralipomenon, says: "Alexandria and Egypt, he says, praise Hesychius as the author of their Seventy. Constantinople as far as Antioch approves the copies of Lucian the martyr. The province between these uses the Palestinian codices, which Eusebius published, worked over by Origen, and the whole world struggles in this threefold variety." Behold the three primary editions of the version of the Seventy, each named after its corrector and reviser.

units.la: Quid vero de Latina versione, ex LXX. traducta, quae usque ad Hieronymi tempora usa est Ecclesia Latina, quam tanti faciebat Augustinus, ut de Hieron. laboribus non admodum bene senserit, dicemus? Si adeo corrupta fuit Graeca, quid de ejus rivo, Latina, miramur? Ex hac, inquit Augustinus de Civit. Dei 17. 43. LXX. interpretatione etiam in Latinam linguam traductum est, quod Ecclesiae Latinae tenent. Hujus Editionis tot fuisse exemplaria quot codices, & unumquemque pro suo arbitrio vel addidisse vel subtraxisse, quod ei visum fuit, queritur Hierony. Praefat. in Iosuam. Res ipsa etiam loquitur, ejus Interpretem Latinum multos librariorum errores transtulisse, ut E.G. Pf.132. χήρας viduam, ubi in Ebr. אלמנה / quod χήρα redditum erat ab ipsis LXX. & in vocibus ambiguis eam saepe elegisse notionem, quae minime quadrabat, ut Psal. 110. ἀρχὴν quod ille principium reddit, cum principatum reddere debuerit. Et quidem de his talibus porro praebebitur differendi oportunitas.
units.tr: What shall we say of the Latin version, translated from the Seventy, which the Latin Church used up to the time of Jerome, and which Augustine held in such esteem that, as regards the labours of Jerome, he was not very well disposed? If the Greek was so corrupt, why do we wonder at its offspring, the Latin? From this interpretation of the Seventy, says Augustine in City of God 17.43, it was also translated into the Latin tongue, which the Latin Church holds. Jerome complains, in his preface to Joshua, that there were as many copies of this edition as there were manuscripts, and that each man had added or subtracted whatever seemed good to him. The thing itself also speaks: its Latin translator carried over many errors of copyists, as for example in Pf.132, where χήρας [chēras] is rendered "widow" although the Hebrew has אלמנה [almanah], which the Seventy themselves had rendered by χήρα; and among ambiguous words he often chose the meaning that least suited, as in Ps. 110, where he renders ἀρχὴν [archēn] as "principium", though he ought to have rendered it "principatum". And indeed an opportunity to discuss such things further will be given.

units.la: vide Epiphan. de mensuris & ponderibus, lib. 2. contra haereses, haer. 64.
units.tr: See Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures; book 2 of Against Heresies, heresy 64.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS II.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR II.

units.la: Vulgatam translationem Latinam utriusque Testamenti, quae vulgò B. Hieronymo tribuitur, mentem Spiritus S. ubique examussim expressisse; eam esse authenticam, nulloque pratextu à Christianis rejici posse aut debere.
units.tr: That the Latin translation of both Testaments, which is commonly attributed to St. Jerome, has everywhere expressed exactly the mind of the Holy Spirit; that it is authentic, and may or ought to be rejected by Christians on no pretext.

units.la: Distinctè hic propono duo membra; primum Veteris Ecclesiae Theologis & Scholasticis, qui usque ad Concilii Tridentini vel potius Reformationis tempora eâ usi sunt, oppono. Ex illis multi fuere, qui quâ linguâ Scriptores sacri originaliter scripserint, nescivisse videntur, nedum, ut vel fontes, vel translationem Graecam, vel alterius idiomatis textum consuluerint. Secundum Concilii Tridentini Patribus & qui eos secuti sunt, Romanae Ecclesiae defensoribus oppotum volui, quorum error eò est detestabilior, quò majore linguarum luce Christianum orbem Deus O. M. illustravit.
units.tr: Here I set out two parts distinctly. The first I oppose to the theologians and schoolmen of the early Church, who used it right up to the time of the Council of Trent, or rather of the Reformation. Among them there were many who seem to have been ignorant of the language in which the sacred writers wrote originally, let alone to have consulted the sources, the Greek translation, or the text in another language. The second I have wished to oppose to the Fathers of the Council of Trent and those who followed them, the defenders of the Roman Church. Their error is all the more detestable because God, the Best and Greatest, has illuminated the Christian world with a greater light of languages.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS III.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR III.

units.la: Fontes seu originalem Scripturam haereticorum & Judaeorum malitiâ ita esse corruptam, ut non amplius norma Christian. dogmatum esse possit.
units.tr: That the original Scripture, or its sources, has been so corrupted by the malice of heretics and Jews that it can no longer be a rule of Christian doctrines.

units.la: Hic error natales suos superiori debet. Non potuit enim iste constabiliri, nisi hoc suffultus tibicine. De utroque ergo simul agendum erit. Disseram autem de his <bl>ὑτερον πρoτερον</bl>, sequentibus capitibus exhibiturus primò
units.tr: This error owes its origin to the previous one. For it could not have been established unless it were propped up by that support. Both must therefore be treated together. I shall discuss them, however, in reverse order [ὕστερον πρότερον], as I intend to set out in the following chapters, first

units.la: GENERALEM DEFENSIONEM EBRAICAE VERITATIS:
units.tr: A GENERAL DEFENSE OF THE HEBREW TRUTH:

units.la: Deinde vero luculentum tractatum, quo detectum ibo
units.tr: Then, moreover, a clear treatise, in which I shall expose

units.la: BONAM FIDEM, INFALLIBILITATEM & CONCORDIAM
units.tr: THE GOOD FAITH, INFALLIBILITY AND CONSISTENCY

units.la: Romanorum Pontificum & Romanae Ecclesiae circa vulgatam versionem.
units.tr: of the Roman Pontiffs and the Roman Church with regard to the Vulgate version.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: ARGUMENTUM. Quibus linguis originaliter scriptus sit sacer codex. Prærogativa fontium. Cur veritatis titulo eos insigniverint Patres. Gratiani judicium de iisdem. Quando ii corruptelæ incusaveri cœperint. Et cur, & à quibus. A quibus rursus defensi, vid. Bellarm. Andradio, Ariâ, &c. Discordia Ecclesiæ Romanæ. Verus status controversiæ proponitur & explicatur. Agnoscuntur in textu Ebr. variæ lectiones, ex mendosâ codicum descriptione orta, ubi de Keri & Chetib. Cur hoc nihil patrocinetur vulgatæ. Ostenditur Dei quoque providentia circa has varietates, utpote per quas nec Fidei nec bonis moribus ullum infertur detrimentum. Masorethæ, &c.
units.tr: ARGUMENT. In what languages the sacred codex was originally written. The pre-eminence of the sources. Why the Fathers honoured them with the title of truth. Gratian's judgement on the same. When and why, and by whom, the charge of corruption against them began. Who in turn defended them, see Bellarmine, Andradius, Arias, etc. The discord of the Roman Church. The true state of the controversy is set out and explained. Variant readings are acknowledged in the Hebrew text, arising from faulty copying of the manuscripts, where [we speak] of Keri and Chetib. Why this lends no support to the Vulgate. It is shown that God's providence is at work in these variations too, since through them no harm comes either to faith or to good morals. The Masoretes, etc.

units.la: VEtus Fœdus à sanctis Dei hominibus, Spiritus S. instinctu, ea lingua, quam Iudæi omnes intelligebant, vid, Ebraica, exaratum est, exceptis pauculis in Daniele & Ezra capitibus, quæ Chaldaicè scripta sunt. Novum verò, postquam jam paries ille intergerinus, quo Gentes à Iudæis secludebantur, esset ruptus, eâ lingua consignatum est, quæ tunc temporis in orbe terrarum maximè erat communis, vid. Græcâ: quam tamen ob Ebraïsmorum mixturam eruditi Hellenisticam, quod ea Iudæi Hellenistæ uterentur, vocare amant: Ego Ebraeo-Græcam vocitare soleo. Hisce linguis Sacram Scripturam authenticam esse & sana ratio suadet, & Ecclesia primitiva semper credidit. Hic enim * &res & verba à Spiritu S. dictata sunt, adeo ut originalis textus scriptores ne in minimis quidem errare potuerint. Hinc fontes ipsos præclaro VERITATIS titulo beati Patres insignivēre,& pulcerrimâ contesleratione iisdem eas tribuerunt prærogativas, quas omnes Protestantium Thelogi iis tribuendas hactenus contendère. Videantur hâc de re Eusebius præpat. Euang.8.2. Historiæ Ecclef.3.10. Origenes apud Hieron. in Iesa.6. Hilar. Psal.119. ad literam Lamed. Ambrof. de Spiritu S. 2.6. Augustt. de doct. Christianâ 2.11. Latinæ linguæ homines Ebraeæ & Græcæ lingua cognitione opus habent,ut ad exemplaria præcedentia recurrant, si quam dubitationem intulerit Latinorum Interpretum varietas. Hieron. Epistolâ ad Vitalem, profitetur, se ad Ebraicam veritatem tanquam ad arcem confugere, Et Epistolâ ad Suniam & Fretellam, Sicut in Novo Test. inquit, si quando apud Latinos quæstio exoritur, recurrimus ad fontem Græci sermonis, quo novum instrumentum scriptum est: ita in Veteri Testamento, si quando inter Gracos Latinosque diversitas est, ad
units.tr: The Old Covenant was written by the holy men of God, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, in that language which all the Jews understood, namely Hebrew, with the exception of a few passages in the chapters of Daniel and Ezra, which were written in Chaldee. The New Covenant, however, after that dividing wall by which the Gentiles were shut off from the Jews had been broken down, was set down in that language which at the time was most widely used throughout the world, namely Greek. Because of its admixture of Hebraisms, learned men like to call this Hellenistic, since the Hellenist Jews used it; I am accustomed to call it Hebrew-Greek. Both sound reason and the primitive Church have always held that Sacred Scripture is authentic in these languages. For here both the things and the words were dictated by the Holy Spirit, so that the writers of the original text could not have erred even in the smallest matters. Hence the blessed Fathers honoured these sources with the splendid title of TRUTH, and with a most beautiful commendation assigned to them those prerogatives which all Protestant theologians have hitherto contended should be assigned to them. See on this matter Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 8.2 and Ecclesiastical History 3.10; Origen, quoted by Jerome on Isaiah 6; Hilary on Psalm 119, at the letter Lamed; Ambrose, On the Holy Spirit 2.6; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine 2.11. People of the Latin tongue need knowledge of Hebrew and Greek, so that they may return to the earlier copies if the variety of Latin translators raises some doubt. Jerome, in his letter to Vitalis, declares that he takes refuge in the Hebrew truth as in a citadel. And in his letter to Sunia and Fretela: As in the New Testament, he says, if ever a question arises among the Latins, we return to the source of the Greek language in which the New Instrument was written; so in the Old Testament, if ever there is a difference between Greeks and Latins, we turn

units.la: * Gretzerus def. Bellarm. p. 510. addit que hoc in translatione non contingere. est, ad Ebraicam recurrimus VERITATEM. Et in caput 8. Zachariæ, Cogimur, inquit, ad Hebraeos recurrere & scientia veritatem de fonte magis quàm de rivulis quaerere. Eadem habet Præfat. in Pentateuchum, & contra Helvid. & alibi. Rursus August. de Civit. Dei 15.13. Cùm diversum aliquid in utrisque codicibus inventur, quandoquidem ad fidem rerum gestarum utrumque non potest esse verum, ei lingua potius credatur, unde est in aliam per interpretes facta translatio. Ad quae verba Lud. Vives, Hoc ipsum Hieron. clamat: Hoc ipsa docet ratio, & nullus est saniore judicio, qui repugnet. Idem æstimium fontibus mansit, saeculis aliquot subsecutis. Gratianus sententiam illam Hieronymi, quam ex eo ad 8. Zachariæ supra produximus, inter decreta retulit, distinct. 76. capite, Iejunium. Et distinct. 9. cap. ut Veterum, non veretur hæc effari, ut Veterum librorum fides de Ebrais voluminibus examinanda est, ita novorum veritas Graci sermonis normam desiderat. Ad quem locum Glossa, quantumcunque, inquit, authenticum sit aliquid, si tamen de ipso in dubium aliquid revocetur, semper exhibendum est illud à quo originem ducit. His rationibus suffulta praestantissima ingenia, quae supra vulgus sapere, libere à vulgatà versione, sicubi eam à fontibus recedere arbitrarentur, recessere, quod vel ex solis Lyra Burgensis lucubrationibus potest constare. At postquam, exoriente Linguarum Originalium, & cum iis purioris religionis, Sole, Theologi Euangelici ad ipsos quoque fontes provocassent, ut errores Papilini detegerent & refellerent, suamque Confessionem stabilirent, Pontificii vero a vulgata ad eos abstrahi nollent, ut cum aliquâ specie id recusare viderentur, dicam fontibus scripsère, Judaeosque nefandi sacrilegii, corruptorum vid. ex Christianismi odio fontium, postulârunt. Inter hos eminent Iacobus de Valentia Episc. Christopolitanus, Præfat. in Psalt. Lindanus de opt. genere interpretandi. cap. 11. Melchior Canus. 2.13. Leo Castrius in Apologetico, Salmeron proleg. 4. in Euang. Gordonus Huntlaeus, Epitome Theol. contraverf. tomo 1. controv. 1. cap. 8. & seqq. Serarius proleg. Bibl. p. 74. & 75. & alii, quos hic recensere omnes & longum & supervacaneum esset. At his, inter se non per omnia tamen consentientibus, cornua obverterunt doctiores & cordatiores Pontificii, Iohan. Isaac, Professor olim Ebraeae linguae apud Colonienses, qui peculiari libello Lindani impudentem assertionem retudit. Driedo de Dogmatibus Ecclesiasticis, lib. 2. Arius Montanus. Præfat. in Biblia Interlin. & Varias lect. textus Ebr. Bannes in Thomam partem 1. p. 56. Andradius Defens. Concilii Trid. lib. 4. Bellarm. de Verbo Dei lib. 2. cap. 2. Marinus Præfat. in arcam Noæ, Ludovicus de Tena lib. 1. de Script. Dissic. 3. Sect. 4. Seuensis, Acosta, Lorinus, Sanderus, ut Cajetanum, Pagninum, Hieronym. ab Oviedo & alios jam præteream.
units.tr: Gretser, in his defence of Bellarmine (p. 510), adds that this does not happen in translation. The sentence continues: we return to the Hebrew TRUTH. And on Zechariah chapter 8 he says: We are compelled to return to the Hebrews and to seek the truth from the source rather than from the streams. He has the same in the Preface to the Pentateuch, and against Helvidius, and elsewhere. Again, Augustine, City of God 15.13: When something different is found in the two codices, since both cannot be true for the faith of the events recorded, that language should rather be believed from which the translation into the other was made by interpreters. On these words Ludovicus Vives remarks: Jerome himself cries out this very thing: reason itself teaches it, and no one of sounder judgement would oppose it. The same esteem for the sources remained for several centuries afterwards. Gratian included that saying of Jerome, which we quoted above from his commentary on Zechariah 8, among the decrees, Distinction 76, chapter Jejunium. And in Distinction 9, chapter ut Veterum, he does not hesitate to say: As the trustworthiness of the old books must be tested by the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the new books requires the standard of the Greek language. On this passage the Gloss says: however authentic something may be, if any doubt is raised about it, it must always be referred back to that from which it derives its origin. Supported by these reasons, the most outstanding minds, who were wiser than the common run, felt free to depart from the Vulgate wherever they thought it departed from the sources; this can be established from the works of Lyra Burgensis alone. But after the Sun of the original languages arose, and with it of a purer religion, the Evangelical theologians appealed to the sources themselves, in order to expose and refute the errors of the Papists and to establish their own Confession. The Papists, who did not want to be drawn away from the Vulgate to those sources, wrote, so that they might seem to refuse this with some show of reason, that the sources were corrupted, and out of hatred of Christianity they charged the Jews with a wicked sacrilege. Among these stand out Iacobus de Valentia, bishop of Christopolis, in the Preface to the Psalter; Lindanus, On the Best Kind of Translation, ch. 11; Melchior Canus, 2.13; Leo Castrius in his Apologetic; Salmeron, Prolegomenon 4 on the Gospels; Gordonus Huntlaeus, Epitome of the Theological Controversies, vol. 1, controversy 1, ch. 8 and following; Serarius, Prolegomena to the Bible, pp. 74 and 75; and others, whom to list all here would be both long and superfluous. But against these, who are not in every respect in agreement among themselves, the more learned and judicious Papists turned their horns: Iohan. Isaac, once Professor of the Hebrew language at Cologne, who in a separate little book refuted the shameless assertion of Lindanus; Driedo, On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, book 2; Arius Montanus, Preface to the Interlinear Bible and the Variant Readings of the Hebrew text; Bannes, on the first part of Thomas, p. 56; Andradius, Defence of the Council of Trent, book 4; Bellarm., On the Word of God, book 2, ch. 2; Marinus, Preface to Noah's Ark; Ludovicus de Tena, book 1, On Scripture, dispute 3, section 4; Seuensis, Acosta, Lorinus, Sanderus; not to mention Cajetanum, Pagninum, Hieronym. ab Oviedo and others already passed over.

units.la: Quod ad priores illos attinet, qui textum Ebræum de industriâ à Iudæis corruptum esse clamarunt, eos nihil aliud sibi propositum habuisse, quàm ut vulgatæ Editioni major accederet authoritas & hæreticis contradicerent, verbis Andradii & Bellarmini docebo. Sic enim ille Defens. Concilii Trid. lib. 4. folio mihi 348. Principio demonstrabo, valde inconsideratè à quibusdam fuisse existimatum, Latinæ Editioni ideo plus fidei quam Ebraïs voluminibus tribuendum, quod hæc Iudæorum fuerint perfidia corrupta & adulterata. Et sol. 364. Amplissimè mihi videntur Ecclesiam spoliare ornamento, qui, ut vulgatam Editionem ab inanissimis vindicent calumniis, Hebræos Codices Iudæorum perfidiâ corruptos fuisse contendunt. Et ibid. Satis ergo demonstravimus, quam longè à proposito sibi fine aberrent, qui ut vulgata Editionis dignitatem tueantur, Hebræa gravissimis vexant contumeliis. Bellarm. verò lib. 2. c. 2. postquam de Thikkun Sopherim disputasset, & accusationem Galatini audacter rejecisset, disputationem illam obsignaturus, sic infit, Ex quo apparet, imprudenter quosdam, dum se Ebraos oppugnare credunt, Ecclesiam ipsam oppugnare. Et paulò post, Alii etiam occurrendum, qui Zelo quidem bono, at non secundum scientiam, omnino contendunt, Iudaos in odium Christianæ fidei studiosè depravasse & corrupisse multa Scripturarum loca. Atque hæc eò quoque à me producta sunt, ut æquus Lector judicium ferat, annon nostræ Ecclesiæ meliori jure Pontificios accusent, quod nimio amore & studio retinendi vulgatam præ authentica Scripturâ, ipsis fontibus detrahant, quàm ipsi nobis objicunt, nos odio vulgatæ nimium tribuere fontibus. Hæretici hujus temporis, inquit * Bellarminus odio vulgatæ Editionis nimium fontibus tribuunt. Quâ enim fronte hoc nobis objicit cardinalis, cum non ignoret, nos fontes constituere regulam & normam non hujus solum vulgatæ, sed omnium versionum, quales quales ex sint; cum insuper experientia hoc doceat & Ecclesiarum nostrarum praxis. Falsa ergo hæc criminatio Bellarm. & Pontificiorum est. Nostra contrà ab illis ipsiscomprobatur & confirmatur. Faciunt hoc ex zelo bono, inquit Bellarm. at quorsum spectat ille zelus? Hoc satis explicat Andradius, ut dignitatem vulgata versionis tueantur. At quæ hæc perversitas est? Textus Ebraici (verba Cl. * Amesii) puritatem defendi antea dicebat ex odio malo: Eandem autem temerè impugnari vult ex zelo bono. Sed quid miramur, adeò nullo in pretio esse sontes apud eos, qui eos à Judæis studio depravatos esse sentiunt, cum Gretserus non erubuerit (pag. 447.) affirmare, sibi persuaderi non posse, omnia ad Ebr. textum jam post tot secula corrigenda & exigenda esse, etiam si fons ille nunquam lutulentus, sed semper & ubique limpidus fluëret. Quæ verba obstinati & pervicacissimi propositi vulgatæ versioni mordicus & æternùm adhærescendi, fontibusque ἀκαταδον πόλεμιν indicendi, certum argumentum suppeditant.
units.tr: As for those former ones, who loudly claimed that the Hebrew text had been deliberately corrupted by the Jews, I shall show from the words of Andradii & Bellarmini that they had no other aim than that the Vulgate edition might gain greater authority and that they might contradict the heretics. For thus Andradius, in the Defence of the Council of Trent, book 4, page 348 in my copy: First I will show that it has been judged very thoughtlessly by some that the Latin edition is to be given more trust than the Hebrew volumes, because these have been corrupted and adulterated by the treachery of the Jews. And on page 364: They seem to me to strip the Church of its finest ornament, who, in order to defend the Vulgate edition from the emptiest slanders, contend that the Hebrew codices were corrupted by the treachery of the Jews. And in the same place: So we have shown well enough how far from their proper aim those wander who, in order to uphold the dignity of the Vulgate edition, vex the Hebrew with the gravest insults. But Bellarmine, book 2, ch. 2, after disputing about the Thikkun Sopherim and boldly rejecting the accusation of Galatinus, and about to seal that disputation, begins thus: From this it appears that some, imprudently, while they believe they are attacking the Hebrews, are attacking the Church itself. And a little later: Others too must be met, who with good zeal, but not according to knowledge, altogether maintain that the Jews deliberately depraved and corrupted many passages of Scripture out of hatred of the Christian faith. These things too I have brought forward so that the fair reader may judge whether our Church is not more justly accused by the Papists of this: that out of excessive love and zeal for retaining the Vulgate above authentic Scripture they detract from the sources themselves, than they throw at us that we ascribe too much to the sources out of hatred of the Vulgate. Heretics of this time, says Bellarminus, ascribe too much to the sources out of hatred of the Vulgate edition. For with what face does the cardinal throw this at us, when he is not unaware that we make the sources the rule and standard not only of this Vulgate but of all versions, whatever they may be? Moreover experience teaches this, and the practice of our Churches. This accusation of Bellarmine and of the Papists is therefore false; ours, on the contrary, is approved and confirmed by them. They do this from good zeal, says Bellarmine. But to what does that zeal tend? Andradius explains it well enough: so that they may defend the dignity of the Vulgate version. But what perversity is this? The illustrious Amesius (in his words) said that the purity of the Hebrew text was previously defended out of evil hatred; but now he wants the same rashly attacked out of good zeal. But why should we wonder that the sources are held in such little esteem by those who feel that they were deliberately depraved by the Jews, since Gretser was not ashamed to assert (p. 447) that he cannot be persuaded that everything must be corrected and checked against the Hebrew text, even after so many centuries, even if that fountain had never been muddy but had always and everywhere flowed clear. These words supply a sure sign of an obstinate and most stubborn purpose: to cling to the Vulgate version tooth and nail for ever, and to declare an implacable war [ἀκαταδον πόλεμιν] upon the sources.

units.la: Cæterùm qui præter Pontificios, pro ἀφθαρσία & incorrupta veritate fontium, Judæorumque in conservandis Ebraeis codicibus religione, disputarunt, multi sunt, VVitakerus, Lubbertus, Junius, Amesius, Rivetus, & alii. At qui in particularibus locis, quæ à Pontificiis quibusdam vel suspectantur vel palam incusantur, vindicandis plus præstiterit, non vidi quempiam præter Salomonem Glassium, virum eruditissimum, qui in Philologia sua Sacra 72. loca veteris, 20. verò novi Fœderis vindicavit. In quem si vel Huntlao vel Marsenno vel ejusdem gregis alteri cuipiam prolubium fuerit incurrere, abunde invenient quod agant. Nobis igitur ad particularia loca in hoc argumento descendere non est propositum. Fiet hoc & factum est in Censura. Mihi illud sedet, ex ipsis Pontificiis objectiones Pontificiorum diluere, ad quæ si accesserint ea, quæ à Theologis suprà nominatis super hac eadem quæstione disputata sunt, nescio quid harum controversiarum studiosus ultrà possit desiderare.
units.tr: Apart from the Papists, many have argued for the incorruption [ἀφθαρσία] and unadulterated truth of the sources, and for the Jews' scrupulous care in preserving the Hebrew manuscripts. They include Whitaker, Lubbertus, Junius, Amesius, Rivetus, and others. But of those who have done more to defend particular passages that some Papists either suspect or openly accuse, I know of no one except Salomon Glassius, a most learned man, who in his Philologia Sacra vindicated 72 passages of the Old Testament and 20 of the New. If Huntlao, Marsenus, or any other of that flock should be inclined to attack him, they will find plenty to do. So it is not my purpose to go down to particular passages on this subject. That will be done, and has been done, in the Censura. My concern is to answer the Papists' objections out of the Papists' own mouths. If to these we add what the theologians named above have argued on this same question, I do not see what more a student of these controversies could want.

units.la: Monendus autem hic initio lector est, Quæstionem de textu Originali veteris Instrum. (nam de Græco Novi postea dicetur) hanc esse, an textus Ebraeus à Judæis studiose (ut Bellarminus loquitur) i. studio & de industria, odio Christianæ religionis corruptus sit. Dixi, studiose & odio Christianismi. Haud enim * negare ausim, & injuriatemporum & descriptorum incuria, errata quædam & sphalmata in textum Ebraeum irrepsisse. Hoc autem dum admittimus, authoritati textus Ebraici nihil detrahimus. Manet n. nihilominus textus authenticus & omnium versionum norma. Hanc prærogativam ipsi relinquunt illibatam omnes versiones, excepta unica vulgata. Huic principatum quærit Rom. Ecclesia, cum ignominiosa fontium dimissione. At hic nihil obtinebit vulgata. Et cavent prudentiores Pontificii hac machina authentiam fontium oppugnare. Paucula enim illa sphalmata sunt, pro tanta librorum istorum antiquitate, pro tam variis & asperis Iudaeorum calamitatibus, dispersionibus & exiliis. Sed & insuper non tanti ea sunt momenti, verba * Ballarmini, ut in iis quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, scriptura sacra integritas desideretur. Plerunque enim tota discrepantia variarum lectionum in dictionibus quibusdam posita est, quae sensum aut parum aut nihil mutant, &c. Sic est profecto: Ex omnibus illis variantibus lectionibus nulla producetur una, unde vel orthodoxae fidei, vel pietati ullum detrimentum inferri possit, Certe his talibus nullam intervenisse Judaeorum malitiam, non tantum hinc apparet, quod nullum ex istis Judaicae perfidiae patrocinium exculpi possit, sed & ex eo, quod fontes variantium Lectionum assignari possint, inter quos primarii sunt, affinitas soni, e.g. לא &c. /vel affinitas figurae consonarum, ut הוא & היא / כארי & כארי vel indifferentia sensus. Multa n. occurrunt loca, in quibus adeo pulchre utraque quadrat lectio, ut nulla Logica vel Grammatica definire possit, utra lectio genuina sit, sicuti prolixius in dissertatione nostra de Keri & Chetib, quam Coronidi nostrae ad Grammaticam Martinio-Buxtorfianam praemisimus, ostensum est. Atque hic illud quoque non possum dissimulare, me haud gravatim adduci ut credam, fieri etiam potuisse, verba * Bellarmini, ut ex pravo affectu & odio in Christum (addo, vel in Christianos) ea lectio interdum ipsis magis probata sit, quae minus Christianis favebat. Neque enim haec adversari iis puto, quae paulo ante de summa Judaeorum in Bibliorum integritate conservanda, fide, dixerat Bellarminus, id quod unico exemplo facile ostensum dabo. Ps. 22. pro כארי foderunt, irrepsit in plerosque codices ex affinitate duarum literarum, כארי hanc esse variam lectionem ipse R. Iacob Ben Chaijim in Masora magna testatur, qui & illud addit se libros emendatissimos vidisse, in quibus Textus habuerit כארו / margo vero כארי / Originem si spectes, nulla hic malitia, ipso Bell. judice. At si quaeras, cur hodie adeo praefracte illud כארי tueantur, ut ne in margine quidem alteram lectionem tolerent, non putarem a vero aberraturum eum, qui hoc eorum pervicaciae, pravoque in Christianos affectui, quis nihil gratificari volunt; adscripserit, uti in Coronide nostra ad Ps. 22. ostendimus. Sed dices, dum admittuntur tot variae Lectiones in veteris Foederis codice, deflorari laudem illam religiosae BiblioBibliorum conservationis, quam & patres, ipfiqueadeo moderatiores Pontificii ipsis tribuunt Respondeo, manere ipsis solidam laudem, quod textum sacrum studio non corruperint. Caeteara temporis longitudo, exiliorum & calamitatum asperitas, errandi in scriptura Ebraica proclivitas apud aequos & quos studium illud ἀντιλογίας non afflavit, facile excusaverint. Potuisset quidem Deus ab his quoque erratulis divinas literas praefervare & supernaturali quadam gratia & ope omnibus, qui exemplaria Ebraica excripsêre, adeste, sicuti primorum exemplarium Θεοπνεύστως fcriptoribus adstitit, at quia id non fecit, an ideo cum eo expoftulabimus? Magnum fatis illud beneficium, & cui dignas fatis grates rependere non valemus, quod pro coelesti hoc Chirographo suo ita zelaverit Deus, ut adversus malitiosam depravationem illud farcum textum conservaverit. Quin & illud consideratione dignum, in his humanae infirmitatis erratis & παραγραφαι, non dormitaffe vigilem istum divinae providentiae oculum, dum cavit diligentissime, ne vel minimum ullaorthodoxae fidei particula, vel pietas, ex eorum ullo (sicuti supra quoque dicebamus) detrimentum caperet. Vis exemplum? Vnum illud ex multis mihi considera. Plurimis in locis pronomen Masc. הוא in foeminininum היא / & contrà hoc in illud demigravit, non alia de causa, quàm literarum Iod & Vau affinitate. At facilè in singulis locis ex antecedentibus vel consequentibus advertitur error. Ab hoc tamen mendo praeservavit Deus locum illustrem Gen.3.15. ubi primum Euangelium extat; Illic enim in omnibus ad unum usque codicibus, atque adeo ipso Interlineari anno 1572. edito, quod sacrilega manus temeravit, constanter lectum fuit & etiamnum legitur הוא / de quo, ubi ad locum istum pervenerimus, plenius dicendi dabitur occasio.
units.tr: Here at the outset the reader must be warned that the question concerning the original text of the Old Testament (for the Greek of the New will be discussed later) is this: whether the Hebrew text has been corrupted by the Jews deliberately (as Bellarmine puts it, that is, on purpose and by design) and out of hatred of the Christian religion. I said deliberately and out of hatred of Christianity. For I would not dare to deny that, through the injury of time and the carelessness of copyists, certain errors and slips have crept into the Hebrew text. Yet in admitting this we take nothing away from the authority of the Hebrew text. The authentic text remains, and remains the standard of all versions. All the versions leave this prerogative to it unimpaired, except the single Vulgate. The Roman Church seeks primacy for the Vulgate, and does so by dismissing the sources with contempt. But the Vulgate will gain nothing by this. The wiser Papists take care not to attack the authority of the sources with this engine. For those slips are few, considering the great antiquity of these books and the many harsh calamities, dispersions and exiles of the Jews. Moreover, they are not of such importance, as Bellarmine's words have it, that the integrity of Holy Scripture is lacking in those things which pertain to faith and morals. For for the most part the whole discrepancy of the variant readings consists in certain words which change the sense either little or not at all, etc. Truly it is so. Among all those variant readings not one can be produced from which any harm could come to orthodox faith or to piety. That no Jewish malice was involved in such matters is clear not only because none of these can be pressed into the service of Jewish perfidy, but also because the sources of the variant readings can be identified. Chief among them are affinity of sound, for example לא (lo) etc.; or affinity of the shape of the consonants, as הוא and היא, or כארי and כארו; or indifference of sense. For many passages occur in which either reading fits so beautifully that no logic or grammar can determine which reading is genuine, as has been shown at greater length in our dissertation on the Keri and Chetib, which we placed before our Coronis to the Martino-Buxtorfian Grammar. Here too I cannot conceal that I am not reluctant to be persuaded that it could also have happened, as Bellarmine's words have it, that out of a perverse disposition and hatred of Christ (I add, or of Christians) that reading was sometimes preferred by them which was less favourable to Christians. For I do not think this is inconsistent with what Bellarmine said a little earlier about the great fidelity of the Jews in preserving the integrity of the Bible, which I shall readily show by a single example. In Psalm 22, for כארי (ka'ari, "like a lion"), they pierced, the reading כארו (ka'aru) crept into most codices through the affinity of two letters. That כארו is a variant reading is attested by R. Jacob ben Chayyim himself in the Masora Magna, who also adds that he saw most accurate books in which the text had כארו while the margin had כארי. If you look at the origin, there is no malice here, by Bellarmine's own judgment. But if you ask why they now defend כארי so stubbornly that they will not tolerate even the other reading in the margin, I think I would not be far from the truth in ascribing it to their obstinacy and to their perverse disposition towards Christians, which they wish to gratify in nothing; as we have shown in our Coronis on Psalm 22. But you will say that, if so many variant readings are admitted into the codex of the Old Testament, the famous praise of religious preservation of the Bible, which the Fathers and even the more moderate Papists themselves attribute to the Jews, is undermined. I reply that they keep their solid praise, because they did not corrupt the sacred text deliberately. The length of time, the harshness of exiles and calamities, and the proneness to error in Hebrew writing will easily excuse these things in fair-minded men, and in those whom the spirit of contradiction has not inspired. God could indeed have guarded the divine letters from these small errors, and could have stood by all who copied the Hebrew manuscripts with some supernatural grace and help, as he stood by the writers of the first copies, who were inspired by God. But since he did not do so, shall we complain to him about it? It is a great benefit, and one for which we cannot render thanks worthy enough, that God so zealously guarded this heavenly handwriting of his that he preserved the sacred text against malicious corruption. Nor is it to be overlooked that in these errors and slips of human weakness, that vigilant eye of divine providence did not sleep; it took the greatest care that no least particle of orthodox faith, or piety, should suffer any harm from any of them (as we said above as well). Do you want an example? Consider just this one out of many. In very many places the masculine pronoun הוא (hu) has passed over into the feminine היא (hi), and conversely, for no other reason than the affinity of the letters yod and vav. Yet the error is easily noticed in individual places from what precedes or follows. God, however, preserved the famous passage Genesis 3:15, where the first Gospel stands, from this blemish. For there, in all the codices down to the last one, and indeed in the Interlinear edition of 1572 which a sacrilegious hand has tampered with, it has been read constantly and is still read as הוא. I shall have occasion to speak of this more fully when we come to that place.

units.la: Agnofcoitaque cum Bellarm. Bannes. Senensi & aliis, errata quaedam & errores qui irrepserunt negligentiâ & ignorantia librariorum & temporis injuriâ. Sed quid inde lucratur vulgata Editio? An illa hic immunis est? nnuquid in illam, aetate cum fontibus Ebraicis haudquaquam comparandam, longè plura librariorum (de erroribus enim ipsius Interpretis jam non loquar) errata irrepserĭe? Quantam variantium lectionum farraginem comportarunt Lovanienses? Elto librariorum incuria corruptus locus unus & item alter in originali textu. An propter unum naevum auferetur palma pulcherpulcherrimæ virgini, dabiturque alteri toto corpore deformi? jam & illud mihi consídera, ea quæ in textu Ebraico librariorum incuria & temporum injuriâ corrupta fuerant, loca, Masoretharum indefessam diligentiam restituisse. Dum verò Masorethas nomine, non tantùm illos intelligo, quos Tiberiade, tempore confecti Thalmud, convenisse Elias Levita in Masoreth Hammasoreth tradidit; Originem & initium celeberrimi Masoretharum collegii & sanctissimi hujus, circa Sacri textus emendationem, laboris, ab ipso Ezrâ, ceu Præside Synagogæ magnæ, cum magno illo Buxtorfio arcesso. Habuit iste Ezras collegas, Haggæum, Zachariam, Malachiam, Nehemiam, Zorobabelem, Iosuam & alios. Et quidem huic Ezræ ipse Bellarminus tribuit lib. 2. cap. 1. quod Scripturas ordinaverit in unum corpus, & etiam emendaverit, si quæ depravata erant negligentiâ scribarum. Cui astipulatur Genebrardus Chronol. lib. 2. referente D. Buxtorfio. Quæ verò post horum tempora in eosdem & ipsorum quoque Ezræ, Malachiæ, Haggai, &c. libros irrepserunt sphalmata, (id quod præcaveri non potuit, quamdiu integram Masoram non habuêre) eorum, qui ipsis, continuis aliquot sæculis, successerunt, diligentia restituit. Illud enim sciendum est, Masoram, quam hodie habemus, seu illud notarum Masorethicarum corpus, quod hodie in Venetis & Basileënsibus extat, non esse ab uno aut altero homine aut collegio, paucorum quorundam annorum spatio, compositum, sed esse farraginem & sylvam variarum observationum, quæ à plurimis hominibus, multis sæculis, ab Ezræ & virorum synagogæ magnæ sæculo, usque ad Tiberiensium seu post-Thalmudicorum Masoretharum tempora factæ sunt, sicuti egregiè docet Buxtorfius nosterin Tiberiade, Comment. Masoreth. c. 11. Ubi & illud notandum est, non hoc solum Masorethas allaborasse, ut textus sacer ab omnibus librariorum sphalmatis emaculawhile, sed & illud intendisse, ut sacer textus, jam emaculatus, in perpetuum purus conservaretur, ut nec sublati semel errores denuò redirent, nec alii de novo irreperent. Quod an assecuti sint, si forte quæsieris audi Iesuitæ Serarii judicium, Diligentiâ incredibili, inquit, hoc perfecerunt Masoritæ, ut in Canonicis, quos numerant ipsi, libris, malignè nihil addi, adimi, mutarive deinceps posset. Et certè non male judicasse Iesuitam, pronunciabit quisquis eam penitius inspexerit, aut Tiberiadem magni Buxtorfii, librum auro contra non carum, evolverit, aut a Arix
units.tr: I acknowledge, therefore, with Bellarmine, Bañez, Siena, and others, that certain errors and mistakes have crept in through the carelessness and ignorance of copyists and the injury of time. But what does the Vulgate edition gain from this? Is it immune here? Have far more errors of copyists crept into it (I shall not now speak of the translator's own errors), though it is by no means to be compared with the Hebrew sources in age? What a heap of variant readings the Louvain men have brought together! Suppose that one or another passage in the original text was corrupted by the carelessness of copyists. Shall the palm be taken away from the most beautiful virgin because of one blemish and given to another whose whole body is deformed? Consider also this: the Masoretes, by their tireless diligence, restored those passages in the Hebrew text which had been corrupted by the carelessness of copyists and the injury of time. By Masoretes I mean not only those whom Elias Levita, in his Masoreth Hammasoreth, reports as having met at Tiberias at the time when the Talmud was completed. I mean the origin and beginning of that most famous college of the Masoretes, and of their most sacred labour on the emendation of the sacred text, which goes back to Ezra himself, as president of the Great Synagogue; to this I summon the great Buxtorf as witness. This Ezra had colleagues: Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Nehemiah, Zerubbabel, Joshua, and others. Indeed Bellarmine himself attributes to this Ezra, in book 2, chapter 1, that he arranged the Scriptures into one body and also emended them, where they had been corrupted through the carelessness of the scribes. Genebrard agrees with him in his Chronology, book 2, citing Dr. Buxtorf. As for the errors that crept into these books, and into the books of Ezra himself, Malachi, Haggai, etc., after their time (which could not be guarded against as long as they did not have the complete Masora), the diligence of those who succeeded them over several continuous centuries restored them. For it must be understood that the Masora we have today, that is, the body of Masoretic notes which now exists in the Venice and Basel editions, was not composed by one or two men or by a single college in the space of a few years. It is a heap and forest of various observations, made by very many men over many centuries, from the age of Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue down to the times of the Tiberian, or post-Talmudic, Masoretes, as our Buxtorf teaches admirably in his Tiberias, Commentary on the Masora, chapter 11. Here it should also be noted that the Masoretes laboured not only so that the sacred text might be cleansed of all the slips of copyists, but also to ensure that the sacred text, once cleansed, would be preserved pure forever, so that errors once removed would not return again, nor others creep in anew. If you ask whether they achieved this, hear the judgment of the Jesuit Serarius: With incredible diligence, he says, the Masorites brought it about that in the canonical books, which they enumerate, nothing could thereafter be maliciously added, taken away, or changed. And certainly the Jesuit did not judge badly, as anyone will declare who has examined the matter more closely, either by reading the Tiberias of the great Buxtorf, a book not to be valued at any price of gold, or by reading the judgments of Arias Montanus, Marinus, and others on it. I have said these things here, first, so that I might also meet those who do not acknowledge the Keri and Chetib as variant readings arising from the carelessness or ignorance of copyists.

units.la: ◂Ariæ Montani, b Marini, & aliorum de eâ judicia legerit. Atque hæc eò à me dicta sunt, Primò, ut & illis occurrerem, qui Kerin & Chetibin pro variis lectionibus, ex descriptorum incuriâ vel ignorantiâ ortis, non agnoscunt. Tot jam annis, inquiunt, à Masoretharum temporibus in exilio vixerunt Iudæi, & tamen Biblia incorrupta conservant. Quod si ergo variæ lectiones ex mendosa descriptione ortum habent, oportuit numerum earum ab eo tempore fuisse auctum. His jam responsum est. Inter alias causas utilissimus ille Masoræ thesaurus est, quam non immeritò סייג לתורה sepem legu vocant. 2. ut ostenderem errores librariorum, de quibus hactenus actum est, Masoretharum industriâ jam esse sublatos. Quod si præter eos putant adhuc restare alios, ut Ps. 19. קְנָם pro קוֹלֹם Iel. 9. 6. יָקְרָא pro יְקָרָא & similia, quæ Bellarm. & alii quoque vel incuriæ librariorum, vel ignorantiæ Rabbinorum transcribunt, non persuadebunt, nisi evidentiores rationes & clariora indicia produxerint. Suspiciones vanæ cordatos non movent. Quàm autem pleræque vanæ sint, post omnes diligentissimè & ex professo ostendit Glassius.
units.tr: ...of Arias Montanus, b Marinus, and others on it. I have said these things here, first, to meet those who do not recognise the Kerin & Chetibin as variant readings arising from the carelessness or ignorance of copyists. They say: for so many years since the time of the Masoretes the Jews have lived in exile, and yet they preserve the Bible uncorrupted. If, then, the variant readings arose from faulty copying, the number of them ought to have grown since that time. This has now been answered. Among other causes, the most useful is that treasury of the Masorah, which is not without reason called fence of the law [סייג לתורה]. Second, I wished to show that the errors of copyists, of which we have spoken so far, have now been removed by the diligence of the Masoretes. If the Papists think that others still remain besides these, as at Ps. 19, kenam [קְנָם] for kolam [קוֹלֹם], and Joel 9.6, yiqra [יָקְרָא] for yeqara [יְקָרָא], and similar cases, which Bellarmine and others also attribute either to the carelessness of copyists or to the ignorance of the rabbis, they will not persuade anyone unless they produce more evident reasons and clearer indications. Empty suspicions do not move sensible people. How largely most of them are empty has been shown most thoroughly and expressly by Glassius.

units.la: Vt ergo huic capiti finem imponam, dico,
units.tr: So, to bring this chapter to an end, I say:

units.la: 1. Manifestos errores librariorum à Masoretis esse sublatos, & proinde non ingenuè adversus Ebræum textum objici.
units.tr: 1. The manifest errors of copyists have been removed by the Masoretes, and therefore the Hebrew text cannot fairly be objected to on this ground.

units.la: 2. Necdum probatum esse à Pontificiis, præter eos insuper restare alios universales errores, qui vid. omnes codices invaserint, qui correctione egeant.
units.tr: 2. It has not yet been proved by the Papists that, apart from these, there remain other universal errors, which have infected all the manuscripts and need correction.

units.la: 3. Dato, ejusmodi etiamnum superesse, eos tamen, testibus Bell. Bannes, Senensi, Andradio, Aria Montano, aliisque, non tanti momenti esse, ut in iis quæ ad fidem & mores pertinent, sacræ scripturæ integritatem lædant.
units.tr: 3. Granting that such errors still remain, they are, as Bellarmine, Bannes, Senensis, Andradius, Arias Montanus and others bear witness, not of such importance as to impair the integrity of Holy Scripture in those matters which pertain to faith and morals.

units.la: 4. Nihil hinc derogari authoritati textus Ebraïci, vulgatæ Editionis (à cæteris enim nulla lis movetur fontibus) respectu: id quod cap. 4. prolixius demonstrabitur.
units.tr: 4. Nothing is thereby taken from the authority of the Hebrew text, or with respect to the Vulgate edition (for no dispute is raised against the other sources); a point which will be demonstrated more fully in chapter 4.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Bellarminus minus candidus aut ex professo obscurus. Producuntur ex Patribus Bellar. Andrad. & aliis Pontificiis solidissima argumenta, fontes à Iudæis studio & malignè non esse depravatos. Examinantur loca duo Ps. 2. & Ief. 53.
units.tr: Bellarmine is less than candid, or deliberately obscure. The most solid arguments of Bellarmine, Andradius and other Papists are set out from the Fathers, to show that the sources were not corrupted by the Jews through malice and design. Two passages, Ps. 2 and Isa. 53, are examined.

units.la: SVperiori capite statum controversiæ & quæ ei illustrando necessaria nobis videbantur, propositimus. Nunc ad cætera accingamur. Dicimus, Fontes Ebraicos malitiâ Iudæorum non esse corruptos, seu, quod idem est, negamus fontes à Judæis odio Christianæ fidei studiosè. i. de industriâ depravatos. Hæc est sententia doctissimorum Pontificiorum, Bellarm. Senensis, Andradii, Arias Montani, Bannes, Drtedonis, Marci Marini, Acoslæ, Lorini, Sanderi, Pagnini & aliorum, quorum verbis sententiam hanc Euangelicorum confirmatum & argumenta impudentiorum quorundam Papistarum refutatum ibimus.
units.tr: In the previous chapter I set out the state of the controversy and what seemed to me necessary for clarifying it. Now let us turn to the rest. We say that the Hebrew sources were not corrupted by the malice of the Jews, or, which is the same thing, we deny that the sources were deliberately and studiously falsified by the Jews out of hatred of the Christian faith. This is the view of the most learned Papists: Bellarmine, Sanctius of Siena, Andradius, Arias Montanus, Bannes, Driedo, Marcus Marinus, Acosta, Lorinus, Sander, Pagninus and others. In their words I shall show that this view is confirmed by Evangelicals, and refute the arguments of some rather shameless Papists.

units.la: Antequam vero hoc agam, monendus est Lector, Bellarminum, dum hanc sententiam proponit, non candidè satis & ingenuè agere. Scriptura Ebraica, inquit, non sunt in universum depravata, opera vel malitia Iudæorum, nec etiam omnino integra & pura, sed habent suos quosdam errores, qui partim irrepserunt negligentiâ vel ignorantiâ librariorum, &c. Quorsum enim illud, in universum? Opponit Bellarminus duas sententias, quarum unam hæreticis adscribit, quos dicit odio vulgatæ Editionis nimium tribuere fontibus, eosque ab omni labe immunes pronunciare, & purissimos fontes appellare: Alteram tribuit quibusdam Catholicis, aitque eos, zelo quidem bono, at non secundum scientiam (.i. nimio amore vulgatæ Editionis & odio fontium) contendere, Judæos corrupisse MULTA Scripturæ loca. Hic Bellarminus se interponit Palæmonem & mediam tenet sententiam, utrinque parti contradicendo. Hæreticis enim contradicit his verbis, Scripturæ non sunt omnino puræ & integræ, habent enim quosdam errores, &c. Catholicis vero, illis zelotis, hæc opponit, Scriptura non sunt in universum depravata malitiâ Iudæorum. At hujus contrarium nusquam asseruerunt illi, adversus quos postea nervose disputat. Hoc n. tantum contendebant, Scripturam in MULTIS Locis à Iudæis corruptam. Aliud est, * in universum aliquid esse corruptum, aliud in multis locis. Vt jam taceam, quàm pulcrè hæc propositio conveniat cum sequentibus, quibus nervosè disputat, nihil à Iudæis malitiosè & studiosè in sacris literis corruptum, imò ne corrumpi quidem potuisse. Sed tempus jam est ut argumenta nostræ Theseos verbis Pontificiorum proponamus.
units.tr: Before I do this, the reader should be warned that Bellarmine, in putting forward this view, does not act quite candidly and frankly. The Hebrew Scriptures, he says, are not corrupted throughout, by the work or malice of the Jews, nor are they wholly entire and pure, but they have certain errors of their own, which have crept in partly through the carelessness or ignorance of the copyists, etc. Why does he add throughout? Bellarmine sets against each other two opinions. One he assigns to heretics, whom he says give too much to the sources out of hatred for the Vulgate edition, and declare them free from every blemish, calling them the purest sources. The other he assigns to certain Catholics, who, he says, with good zeal but not according to knowledge (that is, from excessive love of the Vulgate and hatred of the sources), maintain that the Jews corrupted MANY passages of Scripture. Here Bellarmine sets himself up as Palaemon and takes a middle course, contradicting both parties. He contradicts the heretics with the words: the Scriptures are not wholly pure and entire, for they have certain errors, etc. To those Catholics, the zealots, he opposes this: the Scriptures were not corrupted throughout by the malice of the Jews. Yet those against whom he then argues vigorously never asserted the contrary of this. They contended only that Scripture was corrupted by the Jews in MANY places. Being corrupted throughout is one thing; being corrupted in many places is another. Not to mention how poorly this proposition fits with what follows, where he argues vigorously that nothing in the sacred writings was maliciously and deliberately corrupted by the Jews, and indeed could not even have been corrupted. But it is now time to set out the arguments for our thesis in the words of the Papists.

units.la: Argum. I. A ratione temporis. Si Scripturas Ebrai corrupêre, vel id fecerunt ante Christi adventum, ejusque & Apostolorum ministerium
units.tr: Argument I, from the time. If the Jews corrupted the Hebrew Scriptures, they did so either before the coming of Christ and the ministry of him and his Apostles

units.la: * nisi hoc velit Bellar. in universum i. generaliter in omnibus exemplaribus, confer. §. Dicet aliquid. Item §. Quintum & ultimum. rium vel postea. Sed nec ante, nec post, Ergo, &c. Ita ex Origene & Hieron. ad Iesa. cap. 6. disputat Bellarminus. NON ANTE; hoc sic ostendit Serarius p. 73. I. Quia nulla iis tum proprios turbandi fontes causa erat. 2. Quia istiusmodi sceleris nunquam illos Christus vel Apostoli arguerunt, quin ad Scripturas ipsos ablegat Ioh. 5. 39. Dominus, eas apud ipsos explicat, Luc. 4. Ex iis disserit Matth. 22 neque textus depravationem illis unquam objicit. &c. 3. Ita docent Orig. lib. 8. in Iesa. Hieron. ad cap. 8. Iesaiae, Bellarm. 2. 2. Salmero, qui & superiori utuntur argumento. Haec Serarius. Addo, ne ipsos quidem Apostolos unquam hoc crimen Iudaeis objecisse, quod tamen Apostolus non dissimulasset Rom. 3. 2. si fuissent infideles custodes oraculorum, quae a Deo ipsis fuisse concredita isthic loci asserit. NON POST, quia testimonia quae a Christo & Apostolis ex vet. Test. citantur, eo fere modo adhuc in Mose & prophetis inveniuntur. Nunquid forte, rogat Bell. sic ea protulerunt, ut per Spiritum cognoscebant depravanda postmodum a Iudaeis fuisse? Adhaec assignari non potest tempus, quo scripturas corruperint. Quod si tempus, inquit Andradius, illi zelotae notare, authores atrocissimi sceleris describere, locum designare, caeteraque definire potuissent, qua Iudaeos tam capitalis flagitii convincerent, magna nos profecto cura & sollicitudine liberassent. Verum si tota causa ex nuda suspicione & ex Iudaeorum singulari dementia, perfidia, contumacia & in Christi sanctissimum nomen inveterato odio pendet, leviora sane illa sunt, quam ut sacris Hebraeorum voluminib. antiquitate illustrissimis, majorum commendatione egregiis & omnium saeculorum testimoniis, amplissimis, insignem turpitudinis notam ad ignominiam sempiternam inurere debeamus. Haec Andradius.
units.tr: (* Unless Bellarmine means this: throughout, that is, generally, in all the copies; compare the section beginning "Dicet aliquid", and again the section "Quintum & ultimum".) or afterwards. But neither before nor after. So Bellarmine argues, following Origen and Jerome on Isaiah ch. 6. NOT BEFORE: Serarius shows this on p. 73 as follows. 1. Because at that time they had no proper reason to disturb the sources. 2. Because Christ or the Apostles never accused them of this crime, but sent them to the Scriptures (John 5:39); the Lord explains them to them (Luke 4); he argues from them (Matt. 22), and never objects to them that the text was corrupted. Etc. 3. Thus teach Origen, book 8 on Isaiah; Jerome on Isaiah ch. 8; Bellarmine, book 2, against Salmeron, who also uses the first argument. So Serarius. I add that the Apostles themselves never brought this charge against the Jews, though the Apostle would not have passed over it in Rom. 3:2 if they had been unfaithful guardians of the oracles which he there says were entrusted to them by God. NOT AFTER, because the testimonies which Christ and the Apostles cite from the Old Testament are found in almost the same form still in Moses and the prophets. Bellarmine asks: did they perhaps cite them in such a way that, by the Spirit, they knew these would afterwards be corrupted by the Jews? Moreover, no time can be assigned at which they corrupted the Scriptures. But if, says Andradius, those zealots could have marked a time, named the authors of so atrocious a crime, pointed to a place, and defined the rest, so as to convict the Jews of so capital a wickedness, they would surely have freed us from great care and anxiety. But if the whole cause depends on bare suspicion, on the singular madness, perfidy and obstinacy of the Jews, and their long-standing hatred of the most holy name of Christ, then these reasons are surely too slight for us to inflict on the sacred volumes of the Hebrews, most illustrious for their antiquity, distinguished by the commendation of their forefathers, and recommended by the testimony of all ages, so grave a mark of foulness, to their everlasting disgrace. So Andradius.

units.la: Pergo. Si post Christi & Apostolorum tempora corruptus est Ebr. textus, tunc aut ante Hieronymi tempora, aut post id factum fuisse oportet. NON POST, qui, ut Serarius inquit p. 74. * mox eum insecuti sunt Masorethae. qui, ut vetus R. Aquibae dictum, Masoreth sejag lethorah. i. traditionem esse sepem legis, sibi vindicarent, diligentia incredibili perfecerunt, ut in Canonicis, quos ipsi numerant libris, nihil addi, adimi, mutarive deinceps possit. Nam singulorum librorum versus omnes, singulorum versuum vocabula omnia, singulorum vocabulorum literas omnes dinumerarunt, annotarunt, omnique posteritati transmiserunt. Vt in Masoreth utraque parva & magna videre est, &c. NON ANTE, sic probat Serarius, qui omnia quoque Bellarmini
units.tr: I go on. If the Hebrew text was corrupted after the times of Christ and the Apostles, then it must have been either before the times of Jerome or after that. NOT AFTER: as Serarius says on p. 74, the Masoretes followed soon after them. They, as the old saying of R. Akiba has it, masoret seyag lethorah (that is, the tradition is a fence round the Law), claimed for themselves the task of making sure, with incredible diligence, that nothing could afterwards be added to, taken from, or changed in the canonical books which they reckon up. For they counted all the verses of each book, all the words of each verse, and all the letters of each word, noted them, and handed them down to all posterity. As may be seen in the Masorah, both small and great, etc. NOT BEFORE: Serarius proves this as well, and he gathers up all the arguments of Bellarmine too.

units.la: C argumenta complexus est, In primis, inquit, DOMINI annis quingentis nihil à Iudæis malitiosè in Ebr. textu mutatum, ante Hieron. tempora. 1. Quia si quis alius, hoc vidisset & reprehendisset Hieron. At mutatum negat is ipse quicquam. 2. Addit etiam is rationem, Si quid à Iudæis maligne ob Christi odium mutatum esset, illa maximè mutata suissent testimonia; qua pro se & de se antea attulisset Dominus, & qua de ipso & pro ipso Apostoli. Sed ejusmodi nihil ab ipsis factum, Ergo Patris verba sunt hac, in 6.cap. Ief. Si dixerint aliqui, post adventum Domini Salvatoris & prædicationem Apostolorum libros Ebræos fuisse falsatos, cachinnum tenere non potero, ut Salvator & Apostoli ita testimonia protulerint, ut Judæi postea falsaturi erant. Adde & falsaturos maximè fuisse ea, qua iis hodie negotii plus facessunt in Ebrao, quàm in Græco aut Latino textu, V. C. Pf. 2. Osculamini Filium. 3. Qui iisdem vixit temporibus idem existimat, S. Augustinus lib. 15. de Civit. Dei, cap. 13. qui & duas subindicat rationes, quarum prior hic tertia fit, Si Christiana fidei odio vetus T. corrupissent Iudai, sibi ipsis nocuissent plurimum, quia suos ipsimet libros & scripturas, in quibus se vitam habere æternam putabant, ut ait Dominus, Joh. 5. 39. corrupissent, sibique suam, quam colunt veritatem, abstulissent. Posterior ratio hic quarta, Ingentes plurimas dispersi tunc fuere, ut etiam si vellent, non possent omnia ubique corrumpere exemplaria. Neque enim Synodus ab iis eam in rem coacta, neque pactio ulla usquam legitur. Absit inquit S. Pater, ut prudens aliquis Judæos cujuslibet perversitatis atque malitiæ tantum potuisse credat in codicibus tam multis, & tam late dispersis. 5. Addi & illa ex eodem S. Augustino citato antea cap. 4. qu. 10. potest ratio, ideo varias in partes orbis infelices sparsos Iudaeos, ut veteres apud nos scripturas testarentur esse veras, quia in iis, quas nimirum habent, nostra consentirent, &c. Hæc Serarius. Quibus verbis continetur.
units.tr: In the first place, he says, for five hundred years nothing was maliciously changed in the Hebrew text by the Jews before the time of Jerome. 1. Because if anyone else had seen this, Jerome would have rebuked it. Yet he himself denies that anything was changed. 2. He also gives this reason: if anything had been changed by the Jews out of malice towards Christ, then the testimonies which the Lord had earlier brought forward for himself and about himself, and which the Apostles brought about him and for him, would above all have been changed. But nothing of this kind was done by them. Therefore these are the Father's words, in the sixth chapter of Isaiah. If some should say that after the coming of the Lord Saviour and the preaching of the Apostles the Hebrew books were falsified, I could not keep from laughing, as if the Saviour and the Apostles had cited the testimonies in such a way as the Jews were going to falsify afterwards. Add that they would especially have falsified those passages which now cause them more trouble in the Hebrew than in the Greek or Latin text, e.g. Ps. 2, Kiss the Son. 3. He who lived in the same times thinks so too, Saint Augustine, book 15 of the City of God, chapter 13, who also hints at two reasons, of which the former is here the third: If the Jews had corrupted the Old Testament out of hatred of the Christian faith, they would have harmed themselves most of all, because they would have corrupted their own books and Scriptures, in which they thought they had eternal life, as the Lord says (John 5:39), and would have taken away from themselves the truth which they worship. The latter reason is here the fourth: The Jews were then so widely scattered that, even if they wished, they could not corrupt all the copies everywhere. For no synod was called by them for that purpose, and no agreement is read of anywhere. Far be it, says the holy Father, that any sensible person should believe that the Jews had such power of perversity and malice over so many codices, so widely dispersed. 5. To this may be added the reason from the same Saint Augustine, cited earlier in chapter 4, question 10: the Jews were scattered unhappily into various parts of the world so that they might bear witness that our ancient Scriptures were true, because in those they possessed, our books agreed with theirs, etc. So Serarius. In these words is contained

units.la: II. Argum. quod ab aliis seorsim huic probandæ thesi adducitur, vid.
units.tr: II. The argument which others also bring forward separately to prove this thesis; see

units.la: Si Iudai nec voluerunt nec potuerunt Biblia corrumpere, sequitur ea non esse studio ab ipsis corrupta. Quia vero utrumque assumptionis (Sed Iudai nec voluerunt, nec potuerunt, &c.) membrum prolixius ab aliis quoque Pontificiis illustratum est, paulo diutius iis inversabimur.
units.tr: If the Jews neither wished nor were able to corrupt the Bibles, it follows that they did not corrupt them deliberately. Since each part of the minor premise (But the Jews neither wished nor were able, etc.) has been illustrated at greater length by other Papists as well, we shall dwell on them a little longer.

units.la: NON VOLUERUNT. Audi Bellarm. Adversus illos, qui scripturas ajunt malitiosè à Judæis depravatas, pugnant gravissima argumenta ex Origene, August. Hieron. & Eusebio allata, quibus facile demonstratur, Iudeos, nec per diligentiam Christianorum ipsis adversantem POTVISSE: nec per Religionem suam VOLVISSE textum corrumpere: nam non defuere Christiani, qui eum integrum servassent, & tanta religione textum Ebraeum hodie venerantur, ut si forte contingat. Biblia in terram cadere, publicum jejunium indicant & centies mori sepatiantur, potius quam legem in aliquo immutari. ( Eadem habet Joh. Isaac) Adhac, si Iudaei falsare voluissent divinas scripturas in odium Christianorum, sine dubio praecipua vaticinia sustulissent; id autem minime fecerunt, imo saepe codices Ebraei plus vexant Iudaeos, quam Graeci aut Latini. Producit autem Bell. duo loca, 1. ex Ps. 2 ubi textus Ebr. habet, osculamini Filium, unde invictum adversus Iudaeos depromi posse argumentum asserit. Alterum ex Jes. 53. nos reputavimus eum quasi leprosum וּמֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים & percussum Deum, cum illic Vul. habeat, apprehendite disciplinam; hic vero, percussum a Deo. Quod autem ad haec duo loca attinet, non eadem utriusque ratio est. Nam de loco Ps. 2. verissime pronunciavit Bellarm. Sensus n. hic est, interprete * Andradio, Huic, quem omnipotens Pater filium esse suum palam profitetur, fasces ultro submittite, illius vos totos imperio & ditioni sponte subjicite, cujus indignationem fugere nequaquam potestis. Osculo enim manuum, Palaestini, sicut & nos subjectionem notabant. Ita Andradius. Cujus ego argumentum, quod ex hoc loco cum Bell. format, valde firmari existimo ex sequentibus, Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo, quae Psalmi 2. clausula est. Beati qui confidunt in eo. In quo; In Filio. Hoc non inficiabitur Judaeus. Jube eum jam cum hoc loco conferre illum Jer. 17. 5. Maledictus vir qui confidit in homine, & rediges eum ad summas angustias, cogeturque vel invitus pronunciare, Filium illum Psal. 2. non esse ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον. Quod vero nihil tale ex vulgata Edit. extrui possit, ingenue agnoscunt Bell. & Andrad. Quo concesso, an vulgata etiam in locis ad fidem pertinentibus integra sit, suo loco videbimus. Quod ad locum alterum attinet, non satis solidum est, quod volunt * Bell. & Andrad. Percussum Deum, id esset Ebraice, אֱלֹהִים מֻכֵּה / Notabene מֻכֵּה cum Sægol & post substantivum. Ebraei enim solent adjectiva praemittere, nisi praedicatum axiomatis constituant, & tunc est ellipsis verbi substantivi, ut טוֹבָה חָכְמָה bona [est] sapientia. Nunc vero, omnibus codicibus conspirantibus est מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים / Et quidem מֻכֵּה cum Tzeri, quae punctatio ostendit vocem illam esse in regimine, ut ad verbum sonet Percussum Dei, id est percussum a Deo, Genitivo in talibus causam efficientem denotante
units.tr: THEY DID NOT WISH. Hear Bellarmine: Against those who claim that the Scriptures were maliciously corrupted by the Jews, there stand the very weighty arguments brought forward by Origen, Augustine, Jerome and Eusebius, by which it is easily shown that the Jews could not do it, because of the diligence of the Christians opposing them, and nor did they wish to corrupt the text through their own religion. For there were never lacking Christians who kept it whole, and the Hebrew text is today venerated with such reverence that, if a Bible should chance to fall to the ground, they declare a public fast and would sooner suffer a hundred deaths than have the law changed in any point. (Joh. Isaac has the same.) Furthermore, if the Jews had wished to falsify the divine Scriptures out of hatred of the Christians, they would without doubt have removed the chief prophecies; but they did nothing of the kind, indeed the Hebrew codices often vex the Jews more than the Greek or Latin ones do. Bellarmine brings forward two passages. 1. From Psalm 2, where the Hebrew text has kiss the Son, from which he claims an unconquerable argument against the Jews can be drawn. 2. From Isaiah 53, we esteemed him as a leper and stricken of God [מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים] and smitten by God, whereas there the Vulgate has take up instruction, and here smitten by God. Yet the reasoning is not the same for these two passages. For concerning the passage in Psalm 2, Bellarmine spoke most truly. The sense here, according to the interpretation of * Andradius, is: To this one, whom the Almighty Father openly professes to be his Son, submit your rods of office of your own accord; subject yourselves wholly and willingly to his rule and authority, whose anger you can by no means escape. For by kissing the hands, the Palestinians, as we also do, marked submission. So Andradius. I think the argument which Bellarmine forms from this passage is greatly strengthened by what follows, Blessed are all who put their trust in him, which is the closing clause of Psalm 2: Blessed are those who trust in him. In whom? In the Son. The Jew will not deny this. Let him now compare with this passage that one in Jeremiah 17:5, Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and he will be forced, even against his will, to pronounce that this Son in Psalm 2 is not a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον]. That nothing of this kind can be constructed from the common edition, Bellarmine and Andradius frankly admit. Granted this, we shall see in its place whether the Vulgate is also intact in passages that pertain to faith. As for the second passage, what Bellarmine and Andradius want is not solid enough. Stricken God, in Hebrew, would be God stricken [אֱלֹהִים מֻכֵּה]. Note well that מֻכֵּה has a segol and follows the noun. For the Hebrews usually place adjectives before the noun, unless they make up the predicate of a statement, and then there is an ellipsis of the verb to be, as in טוֹבָה חָכְמָה [wisdom is] good. Now, however, with all the codices agreeing, the reading is מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים. And indeed the form is מֻכֵּה with a tsere, which pointing shows that the word stands in the construct state, so that word for word it means stricken of God, that is, stricken by God, the genitive in such cases denoting the efficient cause.

units.la: * sol. mihi 352. p. 2.
units.tr: * I have solved this myself; see p. 352, part 2.

units.la: * Ita quoque Hannibal Rosselus comm. in Poemandri Trismegisti lib 4. comm. 9. qu. 2. c. 3. notante, ut Job.14.1. natus mulieris, & in N. Test. Luc.7.28. & alibi διδαχθοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, & Math. 25.34. benedicti patris mei, quod & in affixis, quæ Participiis passivis adduntur, locum habere in Gramat. nostrâ ostendimus: e.g. בְּרוּכֵי benedicti ejus, &c.
units.tr: * Hannibal Rosselus also notes this in his commentary on the Poimandres of Trismegistus, book 4, comment 9, question 2, chapter 3, as in Job 14:1, born of a woman, and in the New Testament, Luke 7:28, and elsewhere, taught by God [διδαχθοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ], and Matthew 25:34, blessed of my Father. We have shown in our grammar that this also holds for suffixes attached to passive participles, e.g. his blessed ones [בְּרוּכֵי], etc.

units.la: Sed redeamus ex hoc diverticulo in viam. Docuimus verbis Bellar. & Serarii Judæos non corrupisse Scripturam, odio Christianæ fidei, quia si id fecissent, in præcipuas prophetias, eaque quæ ipsorum perfidiæ maximè adversantur, involassent, id quod factum non est. Lubet hic quoque audire suffragium Andradii, * Me vero illam fateor rationem vehementer induxisse, ut minimè crederem, tanto se Iudaeos scelere devinxisse, quod, cum in illud non nisi summâ in Christi nomen invidiâ impelli potuissent, ad ea quidem loca corrumpenda se potissimum conferre debuissent, quæ ad Christi majestatem illustrandam, gloriam & dignitatem prædicandam sunt amplissima: quæ non modò integra sunt & illibata, sed si Iudæorum quis voluerit petulantiam coercere, perfidiam Coarguere, dementiam reprimere, multò quidem apertiora atque illustriora ex Ebraïs quàm ex Latinis Græcisve voluminibus deducet argumenta. Quæ verò major potuisset excogitari dementia, quam * corvi fugam summo studio occultare, Christi verò, quem execrantur, numen atque amplitudinem minimè obscurare? Cum item capitalia quævis & atrocissima flagitia, si cum scripturarum corruptione conferantur levissima illi semper atque inanissima duxerint, quæ furia miseros homines exagitare potuerunt, ut inveteratum in Christum odium adulterandis & invertendis, quæ illius dignitatem minimè commendant, declararent? Nam maxima eorum pars, quæ adversarii à Iudæis corrupta esse clamant, ejusmodi sunt ut Christum nequaquam intueantur, aut ipsi non nisi allegoricè possint accommodari. Et paulo post, Si verò legis & prophetarum sententias, quæ Christianæ religionis mysteria continent, diligenter expendamus, facilè quidem videbimus, non solum in Ebraïs voluminibus non desiderari, sed multò aptius plerunque Ebraea quam Latina ea ipsa exprimere. Et rursus pauculis interjectis, Quin etiam qui Hebræa pie & religiosè tractant, multò in illis ampliora (propter linguæ fœcunditatem) de Christo testimonia, quàm in Latinis Græcisque offendunt, ut Psal.2.pro apprehendite disciplinam, Hebræi habent, osculamini Filium, &c. Et post paucula sic concludit, cum igitur nullam ex Ebraïs voluminibus invidiam conflare Christo Iudæi queant, illustrioraque ex illis quàm ex Latinis propter linguæ præstantiam argumenta ad eorundem coercendam impietatem petantur, non video sanè, quâ ratione corrumpi ab illis potuissent. Qua de causa, inquit Hieron, se, pudere contentionis nostrorum, qui Ebraicam arguunt veritatem, cum Iudai contra se legant, & quid pro se sit (N.B. N.B.) nesciant viri Ecclesiastici. Haec Andrad. Quae firmat Cl. Glasius ex collatione Chald. Paraphrasium. Cum enim & ab illis, quae tam illustria de persona & officio Christi continent testimonia, quibus in disputationibus supra modum & saepe magis quam ex ipsis fontibus, urgentur, manus abstinuerint, quis patietur sibi persuaderi, eos in ipsos fontes sacrilego ausu involasse; Exemplum unum esto pro omnibus locus Gen.49. non auferetur sceptrum de Iuda, &c. Quis adeo in Iudaicis controversiis hospes est, qui ignoret, quam strenue & pertinaciter plerique Iudaei negent, per Silo illic Messiam intelligi? At trina Paraphrasis isthic loci vocem שילה diserte addidit & Iudaeis, quibus earum authoritatem haud fas est rejicere, ora obstruit, adeo quidem ut nihil magis horreant, quam cum eiusmodi Christiano confligere, qui Chaldaeas Paraphrases & Rabbinorum interpretamenta legit & intelligit. Insignem etiam & in excessu peccantem circa sacras literas religionem in eo ostenderunt, quod ne manifesta quidem menda in ipso textu corrigere fuerint ausi, veriti scil. ne hoc ipso legem divinam, quâ mortales in divinis literis quippiam mutare, de eâ detrahere, vel ad eam addere prohibentur, temerarent. Unde satis ipsis fuit, vocis correctionem in margine exhibere, vocisque restitutae vocales consonis vocis mendosae in ipso textu subjicere. Cujusmodi praeposteram erga sacros codices reverentiam Canus quoque veteribus adscribit lib.2. cap.15. Atque haec de voluntate.
units.tr: But let us return from this digression to our path. We have shown, in the words of Bellarmine and Serarius, that the Jews did not corrupt Scripture out of hatred of the Christian faith, since if they had done so they would have attacked the chief prophecies, and especially those that are most opposed to their own unbelief, which has not happened. It is worth hearing here also the support of Andradius. I confess that I was greatly moved by this reasoning, that I could not believe the Jews had bound themselves to such a crime; for if they could be driven to it only by the utmost hatred of the name of Christ, they ought above all to have turned to corrupting those passages which are most ample for illustrating the majesty of Christ and proclaiming his glory and dignity. These are not only whole and unimpaired, but if anyone among the Jews should wish to restrain his wantonness, to confute his perfidy and to curb his madness, he would draw far clearer and more illustrious arguments from the Hebrew volumes than from the Latin or Greek ones. What greater folly could be imagined than to hide with the utmost care the flight of the raven, but not to obscure in the least the divine majesty and greatness of Christ, whom they curse? Likewise, whatever capital and most atrocious crimes they have committed, they have always considered those utterly slight and empty when compared with the corruption of Scripture. What fury could have driven these wretched men to such lengths, so that they might display their long-standing hatred of Christ by falsifying and perverting those passages that do not commend his dignity at all? For the greater part of what our opponents loudly claim the Jews have corrupted is of such a kind that it does not look to Christ at all, or can be applied to him only allegorically. And a little later: If, however, we carefully weigh the sayings of the Law and the Prophets which contain the mysteries of the Christian religion, we shall easily see that they are not only not lacking in the Hebrew volumes, but that the Hebrew often expresses these very things far more aptly than the Latin. And again, after a few intervening words: Indeed, those who handle the Hebrew piously and reverently find in it, because of the richness of the language, far fuller testimonies concerning Christ than in the Latin and Greek texts; for example, in Psalm 2, where the Hebrew has kiss the Son in place of the take up instruction of the Vulgate, and so on. And after a few more words he concludes thus: Since, therefore, the Jews can raise no hatred against Christ from the Hebrew volumes, and since clearer arguments for restraining their impiety are sought from them than from the Latin, because of the excellence of the language, I do not really see by what reasoning they could have corrupted them. For this reason, says Jerome, I am ashamed of the quarrelling of our people, who argue for the truth of the Hebrew, since the Jews read it against themselves, and our churchmen do not know what is for their side (N.B. N.B.). So Andradius. Glasius confirms this from a comparison with the Chaldee paraphrases.
