For since they have kept their hands off those passages that contain such illustrious testimonies about the person and office of Christ, which are pressed in disputations beyond measure and often more than the sources themselves warrant, who will allow himself to be persuaded that they dared with sacrilegious boldness to attack the sources themselves? Let Genesis 49 serve as one example for all: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, etc. Who is so much a stranger to Jewish controversies that he does not know how vigorously and stubbornly most Jews deny that Shiloh there means the Messiah? Yet the threefold Paraphrase at that place expressly adds the word Messiah [שילה] and stops the mouths of the Jews, to whose authority it is not right for them to object; so much so that they dread nothing more than to contend with a Christian of this sort, who reads and understands the Chaldee paraphrases and the interpretations of the rabbis. They have also shown an excessive and remarkable scruple concerning the sacred letters in this, that they did not dare to correct even the manifest errors in the text itself, fearing, namely, that by doing so they would violate the divine law by which mortals are forbidden to change anything in the divine writings, to take anything away from them, or to add to them. Hence it was enough for them to set out the correction of a word in the margin, and to place beneath the faulty word in the text the vowels of the restored word. Canus also ascribes this perverse reverence towards the sacred codices to the ancients, book 2, chapter 15. And so much for their will.

units.la: NON POTUERUNT.
units.tr: THEY COULD NOT.

units.la: Id vero Serarii nec non Bellarmini verbis, quae supra laudavimus, satis superque probatum confirmatumque est. Lubet autem hic adjicere insignem Iustini Martyris locum, qui in sermone ejus ad gentes extat, Quod si quis, inquit, obstinatus negget, bos Iudaorum libros ad se pertinere, qui usque hodie in Synagogis eorum asservantur, dicatque nos frustra inde pietatem discere, audiat ipsam Scripturam, quod haec doctrina non illorum sed nostra sit; Servari a etiam nunc apud Iudaeos nostram religionem, Dei erga nos est providentia, qui, ne maledicendi occasionem praebeamus iis, proferendo illos ex Ecclesia nostra, malumus illos ex eorum Synagoga proferri, ut ex lectione manifesto appareat, nostram esse doctrinam, &c. Cum quo egregiam contestationem tenet Augustinus, qui in Ps.41. Iudaeos capsarios nostros vocat, qui nobis studentibus Codices portent. Et quid aliud hodie est gens Judæorum, inquit idem August. lib. 12. contra Faust. cap. 23. quàm scriniaria bajulans legem & Prophetas. &c. Vnde non illepide impostor illie Muhammedes librorum venditoribus eos comparavit, qui libros quidem hùc illùc vehunt & gestant, ex iis tamen neque doctiores neque meliores fiunt. Atque eodem respexit Bellarm. non verisimile est, inquiens, Deum id passurum fuisse, ut verba tot illustrium Prophetarum generaliter falsarentur, cum ad hunc finem Iudaos per totum terrarum orbem disperserit & circumferre eos voluerit libros Legis & prophetarum, ut inimici nostri Christiana veritati testimonium praberent.
units.tr: Indeed, this has been shown and confirmed more than enough by the words of Serarius and Bellarmine, which we quoted above. It is worth adding here the notable passage of Justin Martyr in his address to the Gentiles: "But if anyone, being obstinate, denies that the books of the Jews, which are kept to this day in their synagogues, belong to us, and says that we learn piety from them in vain, let him hear Scripture itself, that this teaching is not theirs but ours. That our religion is still preserved among the Jews even now is by the providence of God, who, so that we should not give them occasion to speak ill of us by producing them from our Church, has preferred that they be produced from their synagogue, so that it may clearly appear from the reading that the teaching is ours, etc." With him agrees the excellent testimony of Augustine, who in Ps. 41 calls the Jews our bookcarriers, who carry the codices for us while we study. And what else, says the same Augustine in Contra Faustum 12, chap. 23, is the Jewish people today than a chest-bearer, carrying the Law and the Prophets, etc.? Hence that impostor Muhammad, not without wit, compared them to booksellers, who carry and bear books hither and thither, yet do not become either more learned or better through them. Bellarmine too had the same in mind when he said: "It is not likely that God would have allowed the words of so many illustrious prophets to be generally falsified, since to this end he scattered the Jews throughout the whole world and wished them to carry about the books of the Law and the Prophets, so that our enemies might furnish testimony to Christian truth."

units.la: CAP III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Proponuntur aliorum Pontificiorum Exceptiones adversus superiora Argumenta. Eorum dissensus super hac quaestione, quando Biblia sint corrupta. Diluuntur Pontificiorum Huntlai, Salmeronis, Cani & aliorum argumenta verbis aliorum Pontif. Serarii, Bellarm. Andradii, &c.
units.tr: The objections of other Papists against the foregoing arguments are set out. Their disagreement on the question of when the Bibles were corrupted. The arguments of the Papists Huntlaus, Salmeron, Cano and others are refuted in the words of other Papists: Serarius, Bellarmine, Andradius, etc.

units.la: THefin nostram, Textum Ebr. ex odio Christiana fidei à Iudaïs non esse depravatum, verbis & suffragiis doctissimorum Pontificiorum & Patrum confirmavimus. Restat ut videamus quibus argumentis hanc impugnent alii, & quibus responsionibus ea diluant ejusdem gregis Doctores.
units.tr: We have confirmed our thesis, that the Hebrew text was not corrupted by the Jews out of hatred of the Christian faith, by the words and the support of the most learned Papists and Fathers. It remains to see with what arguments others attack it, and with what replies the teachers of the same flock refute them.

units.la: Quoniam Hebraici Codices, inquit Greg. de Valentia, Analys. lib. 8. cap. 5. Rabbinorum fraude sape potuerunt depravari, satius est ut aliquando ex nitido fontis rivulo, quam ex turbido fonte aquam adbibendum hauriamus. Ita ille. Sed quod reponamus ad hoc POTUERUNT, Andradius suppeditat, * In re tam gravi, inquit, non ex nuda suspicione pronunciandum, aut ex frigidu calumniis accusationes ejusmodi petenda sunt.
units.tr: Since the Hebrew manuscripts, says Gregory of Valencia (Analysis, book 8, chapter 5), could often have been corrupted by the deceit of the rabbis, it is better that we sometimes draw water from the clear stream of the source than from its muddy waters. So he says. But what we may answer to this COULD, Andradius supplies: In a matter of such weight, he says, one must not pronounce on bare suspicion, nor must accusations of this kind be drawn from cold calumnies.

units.la: Rursus Pintus in cap. 7. Dan. Sane Iudaï Biblia Ebraa corruperunt. Et Sacrobosco Defens. decreti Trid. part. 1. cap. 3. neque omnino dubito, quin Rabbini Iudaï ex mala fide, odio ac invidia sensum prophetarum in rebus gravissimis mutaverint. Resp. Lorinus ad cap. 7. Act. Hoc dicitur, sed non probatur. Dicitur, sed ab iis, inquit Bannes, qui rem non intelligunt. Quis autem ferat cœcos de coloribus judicium pronunciare; Et quidem ego ipse, inquit Bannes, postquam postquam abhinc annos 8. Hebraica lingua operam dedi, quantum satis est, ut Rabbinorum sectatores non me fallant, aut quasi ignorantem spernant, quamvis olim opinatus fuerim, Hebraa exemplaria non minus quàm Graeca esse corrupta, jam tamen experientiâ ipsâ convictus ea incorrupta esse, nisi in locis quibusdam paucis, negligentia potius quam Iudaorum malitiâ, judico. Hinc non injuria urget Andradius loco jam producto, ut tempus, locum & personas nominent.
units.tr: Again, Pintus, on Daniel chapter 7: Certainly the Jews corrupted the Hebrew Bibles. And Sacrobosco, in the Defence of the Decree of Trent, part 1, chapter 3: nor do I at all doubt that the Jewish rabbis, from bad faith, hatred and envy, have altered the sense of the prophets in matters of the greatest importance. Lorinus replies on Acts chapter 7: This is said, but it is not proved. It is said, says Bannes, but by those who do not understand the matter. Who would tolerate blind men pronouncing judgment on colours? And indeed I myself, says Bannes, since I devoted myself to the Hebrew language eight years ago, as much as is enough so that the followers of the rabbis do not deceive me or look down on me as one who is ignorant, although I once supposed that the Hebrew copies were corrupted no less than the Greek, yet now, convinced by experience itself, I judge them to be uncorrupted, except in a few places, through negligence rather than the malice of the Jews. Hence Andradius, with good reason, presses in the passage already cited that they name the time, the place and the persons.

units.la: Sed alii sunt, qui licet non ante Christi adventum, attamen ante Hieronymi tempora hanc depravationem factam esse tuentur. Sed & hos & illos eadem premunt incommoda. Et hi Ecclesiam ipsam oppugnant, Ribera ad Hos. cap.9. Num.20. Si Ebraei Codices, tempore Hieronymi depravati erant, cùm ex Ebraeâ editio nostra deprompta erat, tum hæc quoque Ecclesiæ nostræ Editio depravata est, quo quid turpius dictu est? quid insanius? Mariana tractatu de Vulg. Edit. Epist. ad Sanderum, Placet mihi, inquit, argumenti tui acumen, quo ex vulgatæ Editionis fide Hebraicos Codices incorruptos esse defendis, cum convincas Ebraicos codices repudiari, incolumi vulgatâ Editione authoritate non posse.
units.tr: But there are others who maintain that this corruption was made, though not before the coming of Christ, yet before the times of Jerome. But both these and those are troubled by the same difficulties. And these attack the Church itself. Ribera, on Hosea chapter 9, Numbers 20: If the Hebrew manuscripts had been corrupted in Jerome's time, when our edition was drawn from the Hebrew, then this edition of our Church too was corrupted. What is more shameful to say? What more insane? Mariana, in his treatise on the Vulgate edition, in the letter to Sander: I am pleased, he says, with the sharpness of your argument, by which you defend the incorruption of the Hebrew manuscripts from the faithfulness of the Vulgate edition, since you prove that the Hebrew manuscripts cannot be rejected while the authority of the Vulgate edition remains intact.

units.la: Sed cum ad has angustias impudentiores & obstinatiores animi se viderent redactos, unicam rimulam repeierunt, per quam se elabi posse arbitrati sunt. Ecce enim Gordonus Huntlaus, & Serarius sic statuunt, 1. Ante Christi adventum nihil malitiosè à Iudais in sacrum textum admissum esse. 2. Nihil etiam hisce Domini annis mille & centum. 3. Nec primis quingentis Domini annis, ante tempora Hieronymi. Scilicet hæc ipsis extorsit non tam vis veritatis quàm vulgatam ab omni corruptionis suspicione vindicandi studium. 4. Post S. Hieronymi tempora usque ad Domini annum quingentesimum malitiosè ab ipsis, ubi aliqua fuit occasio, mutatum in Ebr. textu est aliquid. Ita Serar. At in explicatione dicit hoc esse verisimile: & proposit. 7. moraliter tamen non omnino, sed secundum quid textum Ebraeum corruptum esse dicit, secundum scilicet exemplaria non omnia, sed quædam; Hoc enim vult, malitiosas illas corruptelas, non universales, sed particulares esse, eòque tandem devenit, ut asserat, posse, si parum attendatur & res modestè agatur, in concordiam venire positas opiniones, ita ut neque à Christianis Iudai: nec Catholicis haretici, neque Catholici ab aliis hâc in punctione dissideant. * Marsennus, diligenter advertendum est, inquit, veritatem Ebraicam, quam D. Hieronymus lectionem Ebraeam vocat, esse veram, sanctam & legitimam: gitimam: veritatem verò Ebraicam, quam nostri temporis Haretici & alii nominant falsam, perfidam & Iudaicam lectionem esse, mille dolis refertam & ad perversam Rabbinorum interpretationem, contra Christum Dominum, & contra Apostolos ejus & Euangelistas & contra omnes Doctores & sacros Ecclesiasticos esse. Ita ille p.233. At p.238. ut videas problematicum ingenium, cum sectariis prælium deposcit non tantùm ex his fundamentis, sed etiam ex Ebræo textu, asserens, facillimum esse ostendere, textum Ebr. nusquam à vulgata discrepare. Quid Huntlaus? non eo candore hanc controversiam tractat, quo Serarius. Quamvis enim videret quàm frigida esset ea accusatio, non erubescit tamen asserere, divina providentia factum esse, ut statim post factam vulgatam Editionem depravaretur textus Ebraicus: ne vid. rejectâ vulgatâ Editione, confugeret quispiam ad textum Ebraicum, ut jam faciunt adversarii. Ecce impudens effatum. Textus Ebraici depravationem divinæ providentiæ audet adscribere cujus conservationem Bellarminus eidem deberi statuit. In eo tamen à Serario dissidet, quod cum Marsenno maximam tunc factam fuisse Exemplarium Ebr. & universalem corruptionem asserit. Quod item audacter assignet locum, Tiberiadem, Personas, Ma-foreth as Tiberienses. Quid jam requiris ultrà Andradi? Tu * tempus locum, personas designari tibi postulabas: Iam tandem prodiit Huntlaus & tuo desiderio satisfecit. Sed bene habet, respondit ad hoc quoque Bellar. Postquam enim Augustini testimonium pro sua sententia adduxisset, dicit aliquis, inquit, generalem istam depravationem Ebraicorum codicum post Augustin. & Hieron: tempora accidisse. Respondet autem, At Augustini rationes omni tempore locum habent. Deinde, si post illorum Patrum tempora depravatio illa contigisset, quæ causa reddi posset, cur Psalmorum Interpretatio Hieronymiana itacum textu Ebr. qui nunc extat, in omnibus conveniat, & tamen de Psalmorum depravatione præcipua querimonia est, num ita Hieron. vertit ut Iudæi falsaturi erant? Quod ad personas attinet, egregiam certè gratiam illis referunt pro incredibili illa diligentiâ, quæ perfecerunt, verba Serarii, ut in Canonicis libris maligne nihil addi, adimi, mutarive deinceps possit, p. 74. quâ effecerunt ne corrumpi deinceps amplius possint, p. 75. Quæ autem verisimilitudo est, ejusmodi viros quippiam depravasse confulto? Hâc suâ diligentiâ fraudi & imposturæ suæ in depravandis quibusdam locis, velum obtenderunt maximum, inquit Serarius, Quis enim opera data corrupisse quicquam illos putaret, qui tam studiose minuteque notassent etiam minima? Fraus, inquit apud Livium Q. Fabius, in parvis fidem sibi praestruit, ut cum operae pretium est majori mercede fallant. Haec Serarius. Egregia certe merces, pauculorum quorundam locorum in quibusdam tantum exemplaribus (hoc enim supra audivimus confitentem adversarium) depravatio, quae tamen, teste eodem prout depravata sunt, ad verum Christianumque sensum explicari possunt, pag.75. Quod autem de כאר rursus inculcat, frustra est, cum ipse Bellar. & alii hoc erratum non malitiae, sed vel ignorantiae, vel librariorum incuriae adscribant, id quod vel ex eo liquet, quod ipsi Masorethae & R. Iacob Ben Chaijim variam lectionem hic agnoscant, illudque ingenue confiteantur illud אלהיכם hic non significare, sicut Leo, quod certe minime fecissent, si malitiose hunc locum depravassent. Accedat jam illud, Masorethas vix interjectis 30. annis, Genebrardo teste, post Hieronymum, Masoreth. suam conscripsisse, & quidem ipso Gordono fatente, ad incommodo isti, vid. maximae depravationi & diversitati exemplarium, occurrendum. An vero illud verisimile, 30. annorum spacio tantam depravationem codicum potuisse accidere? An & illa simul subsistere possunt, depravare & depravationi serio occurrere?
units.tr: But when they saw themselves driven into these narrows by more shameless and obstinate minds, they grasped at a single small crack through which they thought they could slip away. For behold, Gordon Huntlaus and Serarius lay it down thus: 1. Before the coming of Christ nothing was maliciously admitted by the Jews into the sacred text. 2. Nor anything in the years of the Lord up to a thousand and one hundred. 3. Nor in the first five hundred years of the Lord, before the times of Jerome. Plainly this was extorted from them not so much by the force of truth as by the eagerness to clear the Vulgate of every suspicion of corruption. 4. From the times of St Jerome until the five hundredth year of the Lord, something was maliciously changed by them in the Hebrew text, wherever there was some occasion. So Serarius. But in his explanation he says this is probable; and in proposition 7 he says that the Hebrew text has been corrupted morally, yet not wholly, but in a certain respect, namely in some copies and not in all. For he means that those malicious corruptions were not universal but particular, and so at last he comes to assert that, if little attention is paid and the matter is handled modestly, the opposed opinions can come into agreement, so that the Jews do not differ from the Christians, nor the heretics from the Catholics, nor the Catholics from others on this point. Marsennus: it must be carefully noted, he says, that the Hebrew truth, which St Jerome calls the Hebrew reading, is true, holy and lawful; but the Hebrew truth which the heretics and others of our time call false, perfidious and Jewish reading, is full of a thousand tricks, and is opposed to Christ the Lord, to his Apostles and Evangelists, and to all the teachers and sacred ecclesiastical writers, by its perverse rabbinical interpretation. So he, p. 233. But at p. 238, so that you may see his contentious nature, he challenges the sectaries to battle not only on these foundations but also on the Hebrew text, asserting that it is very easy to show that the Hebrew text nowhere differs from the Vulgate. What of Huntlaus? He does not treat this controversy with the candour that Serarius does. For although he saw how cold that accusation was, he does not blush to assert that it came about by divine providence that the Hebrew text was corrupted straight after the Vulgate edition was made, lest, the Vulgate having been rejected, someone should have recourse to the Hebrew text, as our opponents now do. Behold the shameless saying. He dares to ascribe to divine providence the corruption of the Hebrew text, whose preservation Bellarmine holds is owed to that same providence. In this he differs from Serarius, in that, with Marsennus, he asserts that at that time there was a very great change of the copies and a universal corruption. He likewise boldly names the place, Tiberias, and the persons, the Masoretes, as the Tiberians. What more do you ask beyond Andradius? You were demanding that the time, the place and the persons be named: now at last Huntlaus has come forward and satisfied your wish. But all is well: Bellarmine answered this too. For after he had brought forward the testimony of Augustine for his own opinion, someone says, he goes on, that this general corruption of the Hebrew manuscripts happened after the times of Augustine and Jerome. He replies, But Augustine's reasons hold good at all times. Then: If that corruption had happened after the times of those Fathers, what cause could be given why Jerome's translation of the Psalms agrees in all things with the Hebrew text which now exists? Yet the chief complaint about the corruption concerns the Psalms. Did Jerome translate in such a way that the Jews were going to falsify it? As for the persons, they render them an outstanding favour for that incredible diligence which they showed, in the words of Serarius, so that nothing could henceforth be maliciously added, taken away or changed in the canonical books, p. 74, by which they made it so that they could no longer be corrupted, p. 75. But what probability is there that such men deliberately corrupted anything? By this their diligence they put up a very great veil for their deceit and fraud in corrupting certain places, says Serarius. For who would think that those who had taken such pains to note even the smallest things so carefully had corrupted anything? Fraud, says Quintus Fabius in Livy, secures trust for itself in small matters, so that when it is worth the effort they may deceive with a greater reward. So Serarius. An outstanding reward indeed: a corruption of a few places in certain copies only (for we heard above that our opponent confesses this), which yet, by the same author's testimony, can be explained in a true and Christian sense as they stand corrupted, p. 75. As for what he again insists on concerning the word [כאר], it is useless, since Bellarmine himself and others ascribe this error not to malice but either to ignorance or to the carelessness of the copyists; this is clear from the fact that the Masoretes themselves and R. Jacob ben Chayyim acknowledge a variant reading here, and frankly confess that the word [אלהיכם] here does not mean what Leo says, which certainly they would not have done if they had maliciously corrupted this place. Let it be added that the Masoretes, as Genebrard testifies, wrote their Masorah scarcely thirty years after Jerome, and indeed, as Gordon himself admits, this was done to meet that difficulty, namely the greatest corruption and diversity of copies. But is it probable that in a space of thirty years so great a corruption of the manuscripts could have happened? Or can these two things also stand together: to corrupt, and to resist the corruption seriously?

units.la: Sed jam tempus est, opinor, ut ipsa adversariorum argumenta in aciem producam; Spectabis hic Lector, Pontificiorum coryphaeos adversis frontibus concurrere, atque in se invicem ferrum convertere ferrum.
units.tr: But now, I think, it is time to bring forward the opponents' own arguments into the battle line. Here the reader will see the leaders of the Papists charging with opposed foreheads, turning iron against iron.

units.la: 1. Argum. Salmeronis, prout à Serario producitur pag. 72. Si Ebraeus textus corruptus non esset, & quidem saepe, versiones Graeca & Latina forent saepenumero falsae, quia ab illo discrepant.
units.tr: 1. The argument of Salmeron, as it is set out by Serarius, p. 72: If the Hebrew text were not corrupt, and often so, the Greek and Latin versions would frequently be false, because they disagree with it.

units.la: Respondet Serarius p. 76. Negatur connexum. Nec quippiam ultra addit. Operae autem pretium erit hoc argumentum paulo pleniùs excutere. Et quidem.
units.tr: Serarius replies on p. 76: The connection is denied. He adds nothing further. But it will be worth the effort to examine this argument a little more fully. And indeed:

units.la: 1. Quod conjungit Graecam & Latinam versionem, temerè facit. Audi Andradium, Hoc ipsum argumentum, inquit sol. mihi 354. p.2. quo Hebr. veritatem (ut Hieron. verbo utar) de gradu dejectam atque eversam nonnulli putant, non vulgatae tantummodò Latinae, sed LXX, etiam Interpretum editionis authoritatem firmat & stabilit: quam cum 400. prope annis Christi Ecclesia, florentissimis ipsius temporibus, usurpaverit, tantum veteres illi detulerunt, ut non minorem tunc Hieronymus propter suam ex Ebraeo versionem sustinuerit invidiam, quàm novi nunc Interpretes apud quamplurimos sustinent. Vt taceam de cellulis, negare certe non possumus, summum veteribus scelus fuisse ab illa quovis modo disidere. Augustinus eos sæpe prophetas vocat. Epiphanium, Irenæum, Euseb. caterosque antiquos Patres taceo, quos non aliter, pro 70. Interpretibus quàm pro ipsis divinis oraculis pugnasse liquet, atque divino afflatu fuisse in interpretando actos, existimasse. Quibus constitutis, libenter ab his Hebraorum voluminum adversariis discerem, an veterem Ecclesiam hac nostrâ fuisse aut eruditionis splendore, aut dignitatis præstantiâ, aut authoritatis excellentiâ inferiorem existiment? Quod si parem in illa ac hac dignitatem agnoscant, cum una & eadem Ecclesia sit, idemque ipse utramque veritatis spiritus instituerit & gubernaverit, rursus quaeram, perspiciantne, quantum inter hanc 70. & vulgatam Latinam sit discriminis, & quantum inter se non verbis modò, sed integris etiam sententiis dissideant. Demùm quaeram, an existiment corrupta fuisse Hebræa in locis, in quibus à 70. Interpretum Editione, dissentiunt? Quod si corrupta fuisse, ex veteris Ecclesiæ in 70. Interpretes observantiâ, evincunt, corruptam etiam adulteratamque nostram esse Editionem oportet, quæ 70. Interpretum versione posthabitâ, Hebraeam nobis orationem & sententias aptissimè reddidit; Esset enim infinitum omnia loca recensere, quibus vulgata cum Hebraïs mirum in modum, cum 70. verò Interpretib. nulla ratione consentit. Quod si hæc in Hebraïs voluminibus loca integra olim & incorrupta fuisse propter Editionis Latinæ authoritatem fatebuntur, cum veteris sanè Ecclesia authoritate illam 70. Interpretum labem nequaquam pugnasse, dicant necesse est, atque adeo posse sine ulla Ecclesiæ contumeliâ Hebræa exemplaria & esse incorrupta, & ab illis quibus nunc Ecclesia utitur, versionibus dissidere, neque oportere omnia ea à Iudæis perfidiosè depravata fuisse, qua cum nostra Editione minimè consentiunt. Atque hæc Andrad.
units.tr: 1. Whoever links the Greek and the Latin version does so rashly. Hear Andradius: Some think that the Hebrew truth (to use Jerome's words) has been cast down from its place and overthrown by this very argument, and yet it confirms and establishes the authority not only of the Vulgate Latin but also of the edition of the Seventy Interpreters. The Church of Christ used that edition for nearly 400 years, in its most flourishing times, and the ancients gave it such weight that Jerome, on account of his translation from the Hebrew, bore no less odium than the new translators bear among very many people today. To say nothing of the little cells, we certainly cannot deny that it was a great crime for the ancients to dissent from that edition in any way. Augustine often calls them prophets. I say nothing of Epiphanius, Irenaeus, Eusebius and the other ancient Fathers, who are plainly seen to have fought for the Seventy no differently than for the divine oracles themselves, and to have judged that they were moved by divine inspiration in their translating. Given these points, I would gladly learn from these adversaries of the Hebrew books whether they judge the ancient Church to have been inferior to ours in splendour of learning, in dignity, or in excellence of authority. If they recognise that it was equal in dignity, since it is one and the same Church, and since the same Spirit of truth founded and governed both, I will ask in turn whether they perceive how great the difference is between this Seventy version and the Latin Vulgate, and how far the two differ from each other not only in words but in whole sentences. Finally I will ask whether they think the Hebrew was corrupt in those places where it differs from the edition of the Seventy Interpreters. If they prove by the ancient Church's regard for the Seventy Interpreters that it was corrupt, then it must follow that our edition is also corrupt and adulterated, since it has set aside the version of the Seventy and rendered the Hebrew language and meaning most aptly for us. For it would be endless to list all the passages where the Vulgate agrees wonderfully with the Hebrew and in no way agrees with the Seventy Interpreters. But if they admit that these passages in the Hebrew books were once whole and uncorrupted on account of the authority of the Latin edition, then they must say that the ancient Church's authority did not in any way uphold that defect of the Seventy Interpreters. And so the Hebrew manuscripts can be both uncorrupted and differ from the versions the Church now uses, without any insult to the Church; and it is not necessary that everything which does not agree with our edition was treacherously corrupted by the Jews. Thus far Andradius.

units.la: 2. Magnam oportet eam esse necessitatem quæ ad has angustias Pontificios redegit, ut defendere cogantur, Hebræa volumina, rursus verba Andradii, * omnibus in locis vitiata esse, quibus à vulgatâ dissentiunt, sol.362. p.2. At Hieronymus, inquit idem, atque Origenes illorum opinionem, qui ut summis se difficultatib. explicarent, Hebræa volumina condemnabant, meram calumniam esse confirmant: cum quibus & D. Thomas in cap. 9. ad Rom. consentire videtur. Siillud urgerent Pontificii, Hebræa volumina iis in locis vitiata censenda esse, in quibus & Græci & Chaldæus & Latina ab iis pariter dissident, longè plausibilius & verisimilius dicerent. E. G. Psal. 22. Ebræa legunt, אֵרִי sicut leo, LXX. Aquila, Latina, Chald. foderunt
units.tr: 2. The necessity must be great that has driven the Papists into such a narrow place that they are forced to defend the Hebrew volumes as corrupted in all places where they differ from the Vulgate (in Andradius's words, sol. 362, p. 2). But Jerome, says the same author, and Origen confirm that the opinion of those who condemned the Hebrew volumes in order to escape great difficulties is pure calumny; and Thomas Aquinas also seems to agree with them on chapter 9 of Romans. If the Papists were to press the point that the Hebrew volumes should be judged corrupt in those places where the Greek, the Chaldee and the Latin all alike differ from them, they would be saying something far more plausible and probable. For example, Psalm 22: the Hebrew reads as a lion [אֵרִי]; the Seventy, Aquila, the Latin and the Chaldee read they pierced.

units.la: {*} Ex hoc fundamento disputat Leo Castrius, textum Ebr. esse corruptum, ubicunque à vulgato discrepat. derunt, quamvis hic alteram quoque expresserit lectionem. Hic, vel Judæis tacentibus, suspectus merito de mendo textus Ebræus. At Gen. 3.15. Hebr. Chald. Græci, Hieron. & bonæ notæ Codices vulgatæ Editionis legerunt הוא ipse, jungiturque idem pronomen in textu cum verbo Mascul. Editio tamen Clementina legit Ipsa; Quæ perversitas erit, in solius vulgatæ (cujus ipsius quoque exemplaria hic variant) gratiam, adversus Hebræos, Chald. Græcosque Codices pronunciare? Et tamen alterutrum hic faciendum, aut rejicienda Ebræorum tanquam corrupta (& quidem in loco ad fidem pertinente) aut Latinorum lectio. Alterutrum enim tantum scripsit Moses. Ps. 132. Vulgatus legit Viduam, At Hebræus Chaldæusque legunt, victum. Manifeste apparet, unde natus sit error. Secutus enim est Græcam versionem, in quam pro ϑιεσαν, unius literæ depravatione irrepsit χιεσαν, ut ingenuè præter alios agnoscit Genebr. Et tamen hic quoque jubemur credere, textum Ebræum esse vitiatum, siquidem ab eo Latina dissidet. Moderatius certè Sanderus statuit, qui apud Marianam tractatu supra citato p. 57. ita à Tridentinis Latinam probari asserit, ut nec Græca nec Ebræa repudientur: in vero locis, quibus Ebræa à Latinis dissidper, ubi post multa remedia nulla via se ostendit utrofq; Codices conciliandi, Ecclesia sententiam expectari jubet, quâ renuncietur, utri codices contaminati sint, &c.
units.tr: {*} On this foundation Leo Castrius argues that the Hebrew text is corrupt wherever it differs from the Vulgate. They pierced, although here he also sets out the other reading. Here, even if the Jews kept silent, the Hebrew text is rightly suspected of error. But at Genesis 3:15 the Hebrew, the Chaldee, the Greeks, Jerome and the good manuscripts of the Vulgate edition read [הוא] he, and the same pronoun is joined in the text to a masculine verb. The Clementine edition, however, reads she. Would it not be a perversity to pronounce the Hebrew, Chaldee and Greek manuscripts against themselves, for the sake of the Vulgate alone (whose own copies also vary here)? And yet one of the two must be done here: either the Hebrew is rejected as corrupt (and that in a passage bearing on the faith), or the Latin reading is. For Moses wrote only one of the two. At Psalm 132 the Vulgate reads widow (viduam), but the Hebrew and the Chaldee read provision (victum). It is plain where the error arose: the translator followed the Greek version, in which, through the corruption of a single letter, χιεσαν crept in for [ϑιεσαν], as Genebrardus frankly acknowledges, among others. And yet here too we are ordered to believe that the Hebrew text is corrupt, since the Latin differs from it. Far more moderately, Sanderus decides, who, as cited in Mariana's tract on p. 57 above, asserts that the Latin is approved by the Tridentines in such a way that neither the Greek nor the Hebrew is rejected. Where the Hebrew differs from the Latin, and no way appears, after many remedies, of reconciling the two manuscripts, he orders that the judgment of the Church be awaited, by which it will be declared which manuscripts are contaminated, and so on.

units.la: II. Argum. Salmeronis ibidem. Videtur id prædixisse Ierem. 8. verè mendacium operatus est stylus mendax Scribarum.
units.tr: II. Argument of Salmeron, in the same place. It seems he predicted this in Jeremiah 8: "Truly the lying pen of the scribes has wrought falsehood."

units.la: Resp. Serarius, Mendax est stylus Scribarum non in textus scripturæ depravatione, sed sensus explanatione.
units.tr: Answer: Serarius: The lying pen of the scribes is not in the corruption of the text of Scripture, but in the explanation of its sense.

units.la: III. Argum. Salmeronis, ab Inductione locorum undecim.
units.tr: III. Argument of Salmeron, from the induction of eleven places.

units.la: Serarius respondet, Iam dixi, scripturas istas in loca propria differendas, cum sæpe non ex Ebræo textu, sed aliunde harum vera explicatio petenda sit. Respondit etiam ad illas Glassius. Plane autem hic paratragœdiat Leo Castrius Hispanus, qui in Apologetico contendit, plus quam quadringentis locis de industria à Judæis corruptum esse textum. Cujus hominis impudentiam cum ferre non posset Pineda & ipse Hispanus Jesuita, merito cum notat hac censura, Sed is est author, dum in hujusmodi Ebraizationes incidit, vix sui compos, & bono licet zelo, tamen vel ignoratione rerum quarundam, vel vehementiori aliqua affectione, extra fines veritatis & modestia rapitur. Et si ex hujusmodi tantum unguibus Leonem illum æstimaremus, non etiam ex aliis præclaris cenatibus, aut murem aut vulpem censeremus, aut canem, aut quidvis quidvis aliud ignobilius.
units.tr: Serarius replies: I have already said that those Scriptures are to be deferred to their proper places, since often their true explanation must be sought not from the Hebrew text but from elsewhere. Glassius also replied to those arguments. But the Spaniard Leo Castrius plainly plays the tragedian here. In his Apologeticus he contends that the Jews deliberately corrupted the text in more than four hundred places. Since Pineda, himself a Spanish Jesuit, could not endure this man's impudence, he rightly remarks in this censure: But he is an author who, whenever he falls into such Hebraizings, is hardly master of himself, and, though with a good zeal, yet through ignorance of certain things or some more vehement feeling, is carried beyond the bounds of truth and moderation. And if we were to judge that lion only by such claws, and not by his other splendid efforts, we would judge him a mouse or a fox, or a dog, or something still more ignoble.

units.la: IV. Argumentum Salmeron. ab authoritate Patrum.
units.tr: IV. Argument of Salmeron, from the authority of the Fathers.

units.la: Resp. Serar. Loquuntur Patres de Graecis, aut translatoribus qui Judaizant, aut Translationibus etiam ipsorum LXX. p. 76. & p. 74. col. 1. Quod vero S. Hieron. inter S. Augustini Epistolas undecima cap. 6. ait se Biblia vertisse ut ea testimonia quae a Judaeis praetermissa sunt, vel corrupta in medium proferret, Judaeos appellat Graecos Interpretes, Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem, ut ex praefat. priore in Job & illa ipsa Epistola cap. 5. perspicuum est. Ita quoque Bellar. & Ludovicus de Tena, locis jam saepius indicatis. Et quod ad locum illum Psal. 95. Regnavit Deus a ligno, attinet, ex quo Judaeos illud, a ligno, sustulisse Justinus contra Tryphonem asserit, quod Justini testimonium bis hic adducitur, audi Andradium, Hoc si verum est, inquit, quomodo nostra quaeso & 70. Interpretum Editionis, ubi illa etiam desiderantur, dignitatem tueri possumus? aut qua major esse levitas poterit, quam ad latina extollenda, Hebraea vero deprimenda, illa adhibere, quae aut incerta sunt, aut parem utrique labem aspergunt. & sol. 364. ad locum Chrysost. sic inquit, cum Chrys. dicit, Judaeos Jesaiae locum corrupisse, qui pro virgine puellam legunt, non Ebr. codices, sed Aquilam & Symmachum notat, &c.
units.tr: Answer, Serarius: The Fathers speak of the Greeks, either of the translators who Judaize, or of the translations of the Seventy themselves, p. 76 and p. 74, col. 1. As for St. Jerome's statement in the eleventh of Augustine's Letters, chapter 6, that he translated the Bible so that he might bring forward those testimonies which the Jews had omitted or corrupted, he calls the Jews "Greek interpreters", namely Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, as is plain from the earlier preface on Job and from that same letter, chapter 5. Thus also Bellarmine and Ludovicus de Tena, in the places already cited many times. As for that passage of Psalm 95, The Lord reigned from the tree, from which Justin, in his dialogue with Trypho, asserts the Jews removed the words from the tree, since Justin's testimony is here adduced twice, hear Andradius: If this is true, he says, how, I ask, can we maintain the dignity of our own edition and that of the Seventy, where those words are also lacking? Or what greater frivolity could there be than to use, to exalt the Latin and depress the Hebrew, those things which are either uncertain or stain both alike? And at p. 364, on the passage of Chrysostom, he says: When Chrysostom says that the Jews corrupted the passage of Isaiah which reads "girl" instead of "virgin", he does not point to the Hebrew manuscripts but to Aquila and Symmachus, and so on.

units.la: V. Argum. Salmeronis, Christum eraserunt de cordibus suis Judaei. Ergo & de Bibliis. Haeretici corrumpunt scripturas, ergo & Judaei, &c. Resp. Serarius, In omnibus pene rationibus negatur connexum. Et dum proponit hanc V. objeet. dicit has rationes esse faciles nec magnopere urgere. Andradius vero gravius intonat, Satis opinor demonstravimus, inquit sol. 364. quam longe a propositio sibi fine aberrent, qui, ut vulgata dignitatem tueantur, Hebraea gravissime vexant contumeliis, cum praesertim aliunde illa quam ex frigidis calumniis petenda sint, ne dum rem tantam infirmis volumus fundamentis constituere, illius praeclarissimam authoritatem minuamus. Nam licet solenne fuerit Haereticis, sacras literas corrumpere, eodem se tamen sacrilegio Judaeos etiam devinxisse, nullis video firmis argumentis a quopiam demonstrari.
units.tr: V. Argument of Salmeron: the Jews have erased Christ from their hearts. Therefore also from the Bibles. Heretics corrupt the Scriptures, therefore so do the Jews, and so on. Answer, Serarius: The connection is denied in almost all the arguments. And while he sets out this fifth objection, he says these arguments are easy and not very forceful. Andradius thunders more gravely: I think I have sufficiently shown, he says on p. 364, how far wide of their own purpose those men go who, in order to uphold the Vulgate, savagely abuse the Hebrew with insults, especially when such charges must be sought from elsewhere than from frigid calumnies. For while we wish to build so great a matter on weak foundations, we diminish the most excellent authority of the Vulgate itself. For although it has been customary for heretics to corrupt the sacred letters, I see that no one has demonstrated by firm arguments that the Jews also bound themselves to the same sacrilege.

units.la: VI. Arg. Salmeron. Iudaei fatentur se quasdam mutationes in Bibliis habere, e.g. [saepe legitur] pro &c.
units.tr: VI. Argument of Salmeron: The Jews admit that they have certain changes in their Bibles, for example [it is often read] instead of, etc.

units.la: Resp. Serar Significantur variae lectiones de quibus supra. Eae vero non negantur. Sed hic de malitiosa & quae consulto facta sit, depravatione agimus.
units.tr: Answer, Serarius: What is meant are the variant readings mentioned above. These are not denied. But here we are dealing with a depravation that is malicious and made on purpose.

units.la: Atque haec fere argumenta Salmeronis fuere, prout ea recensuit & & refutauit Serarius. Restant paucula aliorum.
units.tr: These are nearly the arguments of Salmeron, as he listed them, and Serarius refuted them. A few of others remain.

units.la: VII. Iudæi sunt Christianorum hostes. Ergo potuerunt Scripturas corrumpere, inquit Greg. de Valentia, loco quem supra produximus: Vel etiam corruperunt, Canus 2. 13. Item, Ebræorum Doctores, nostri vid. inimici, multo studio contenderunt textum Ebr. corrumpere, ut V. Test. nostris exemplaribus facerent contrarium.
units.tr: VII. The Jews are enemies of the Christians. Therefore they could have corrupted the Scriptures, says Gregory of Valencia, in the passage I quoted above. Or even that they did corrupt them, says Canus, book 2, chapter 13. Likewise, the teachers of the Hebrews, our enemies as they are, have with great zeal striven to corrupt the Hebrew text, so that they might make it contrary to our copies of the Old Testament.

units.la: Respondeo, longe aliud ex hostili Iudæorum erga Christianos animo B. Augustinum intulisse, ad Ps. 56. Propterea, inquit, Iudai adhuc sunt, ut libros nostros portent in confusionem suam. Quando enim volumus ostendere, Christum esse prophetatum, proferimus Ethnicis istas literas. Et ne forte duri illi ad fidem dicant, nos Christianos composuisse libros istos, & unà cum Euangelio confinxisse, hinc illos convincimus, quod omnes illa literæ, quibus Christus prophetatus est, apud Iudæos sunt. Proferimus ergo codices ab inimicis Iudæis, ut confundamus inimicos infideles. Codicem portat Iudæus, unde credat Christianus.
units.tr: I reply that Saint Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 56, drew a very different conclusion from the hostile spirit of the Jews toward the Christians: For this reason, he says, the Jews still exist, so that they may carry our books to their own confusion. For when we want to show that Christ was prophesied, we produce those writings to the heathen. And lest those hard men say that we Christians composed those books and invented them along with the Gospel, we convince them by this: all those writings in which Christ was prophesied are among the Jews. We therefore produce the codices through the Jews, our enemies, so that we may confound the unbelieving enemies. The Jew carries the codex, so that the Christian may believe.

units.la: VIII. Arg. Iidem Iudæi, hostes nostri addiderunt puncta: Ergo credibile est, eos sua punctatione multa loca de industria corrupisse. Resp. Moderatius agit Bellarm. qui eos subinde in punctatione aberrasse dicit. Ego hanc disputationem de punctis jam non ingrediar. Respondebit Gordono Bellarminus, Errores qui ex punctorum additione addita sunt, nihil officiunt veritati. Puncta enim extrinsecus addita sunt, nec textum mutant. Addo facilius esse, accusare Iudæos falsæ punctationis, quam convincere. Fiat periculum [Sed operæ pretium erit hic audire Cl. Rivetum, qui postquam pag. 102. Isagoges dixisset, plerosque Pontificiorum in istam sententiam, puncta vid. consonantibus non esse coæva, concessisse, quod ea ipsis commoda visa esset ad detrahendam textui Ebraico authoritatem & certitudinem, pag. 105. sic infit, Sed posita hypothesi illorum, qui volunt pleraque in bibliis esse incerta, si punctis destituantur, corruit certitudo versionis vulgatæ. nisi probent, eum, qui Primus fuit versionis istius author, sive Hieronymus, sive alius fuerit, sive unus, sive plures, à Spiritu S. immediatè recepisse necessariarum vocalium revelationem: quam aliquin à Iudæorum traditione accepisse certum erit, quæ si incerta fuerit, nutabit per eos omnis authoritas sacri textus. Et tamen neminem existimo tam impudentis oris, qui talem revelationem in lectione textus Ebraici Hieron. tribuere ausit. Hæc Cl. Rivetus.]
units.tr: VIII. Argument: The same Jews, our enemies, added the vowel points. Therefore it is credible that they deliberately corrupted many passages by their pointing. Answer: Bellarmine takes a more moderate line, saying that they sometimes went astray in the pointing. I will not now enter into this dispute about the points. Bellarmine will be answered by Gordon: The errors which have been introduced by the addition of the points do no harm to the truth. For the points were added from outside and do not change the text. I add that it is easier to accuse the Jews of false pointing than to prove it. Let us make the attempt. [But it will be worth hearing here the distinguished Rivet, who, after saying on p. 102 of his Isagoge that most of the Papists had conceded to that opinion, that the points, namely the vowels, are not contemporary with the consonants, because it seemed to them convenient for detracting from the authority and certainty of the Hebrew text, goes on at p. 105 thus: But given the hypothesis of those who want most things in the Bible to be uncertain if they are deprived of points, the certainty of the Vulgate version collapses, unless they prove that the first author of that version, whether Jerome or someone else, whether one or several, received directly from the Holy Spirit the revelation of the necessary vowels. Otherwise it will certainly have been received from Jewish tradition, and if that tradition is uncertain, all authority of the sacred text will waver through them. And yet I do not think anyone has so impudent a mouth as to dare to attribute such a revelation to Jerome in his reading of the Hebrew text. So far the distinguished Rivet.]

units.la: IX. Arg. à Judæorum confessione. E.gr. tradunt quidam Ebræi 18. loca à Scribis olim mutata seu potius depravata, quam mutationem Tikkun Sopherim vocant, de quâ multa Galatinus in fine lib. 1. Ad hoc prolixè respondit Glassius, & quidem adeò nervosè, ut quæ ego olim Oxoniæ de istis meditatus sum, lubens premam. Ego Responsionem Bellarmini hic exhibebo, qui ostendit vulgatam versionem (addo & Chald. Paraphrasin) in plerisque itahabere, ut Scriba isti correxisse vel potius depravasse dicuntur. Ex quo apparet, inquit, imprudenter quosdam dum se Judæos oppugnare putant, ipsam Ecclesiam oppugnare. Si enim illa correctiones scribarum sint Hebr. textus corruptiones, sequitur aperte, vulgatam quoque Editionem esse corruptissimam, quam tamen Ecclesia nobis pro authentica tradidit. [Ergo 18. errores, quales isti, fatente Bell. authentiam vulgatæ Editionis possent evertere] Dicit a. postea, aut non esse verum, ullam talem emendationem factam fuisse à Scribis, cum origo ejus sententiæ sit * Thalmud, liber fabulosissimus: Aut si Tikkun Sopherim non est fabula, non esse corruptionem, sed veram Emendationem, non factam à quibuscunque Scribis, sed ab Ezra & sociis, &c. Quam sententiam multis rationibus probabilem reddidit Glassius. Bellar. hic quoque astipulantur Ludovicus de Tena, & Jacobus Bonfrerius Theol. Duacenus in præloquiis ad S. Scr. c.12. utriusque verba videbis apud Rivetum, p.110. Isag. Sed libet hic audire judicium clarissimi Buxtorfii, quod Glassius ex authoris Epistola ad calcem Philologiæ sacræ adjecit: Ita autem habet, In neutro Thalmud ulla plane istius Tikkun mentio fit, cum alias עיטור סופרים / longe minoris negotii, in Talmud commemoretur. Si aliter ista loca fuissent aliquando scripta. Oncelos & Jonathan id vel semel expressissent. Nec Josephus reticuisset, qui contrarium Ebræis adscribit, nullam sc. unquam literam mutatam fuisse in lege ab Ebræis popularibus suis, l.1. contra Appionem. Thalmudistæ in Lev.27.v. ult. diversis locis notant, nec prophetæ ulli licitum fuisse, vel minimum in Lege mutare vel innovare. Quomodo ergo Scribæ quidam vulgares hanc audiaciam sibi arrogassent? textum sacrum in literis & sensu corrigere? In silentio ergo omnium tibi dico, Sopherim istos fuisse ipsos auctores sacros, Mosen & Prohetas, qui nunquam aliter scripserunt, quàm hodie scriptum legitur. At Sapientes Ebræorum nasutiores animadvertentes inconvenientiam quandam in istis locis, scripserunt, aliter authores istos loqui debuisse. buisse, &, secundum cohærentiam propositi textus, sic vel sic scribere, sed pro eo maluisse sic scribere, & id sic efferre, ut illud hodie in textu est. E.g. Gen.18. 22. lectum scriptum, Et Abraham adhuc stabat coram Domino. Itane? ubi legitur inquiunt Sapientes, quod Abraham venerit ad Dominum & steterit coram eo? Contrarium dicitur in præcedentibus, Deus sc. venit ad Abrahamum, &c. Ideoque Moses scribere debuit, Et Dominus stabat adhuc coram Abrahamo. At ita serviliter de Deo loqui non debuit Moses, unde תיקון correxit & mutavit stylum sermonis, honores majoris causa, & dixit Et Abraham adhuc stabat coram Domino. Hinc R. Salomo adjicit, היה לו לכתוב / scribendum ipsi (Mosi) erat, scribere debebat, Et Dominus stabat adhuc coram Abrahamo. Non quod aliter sic scripserit antea, & postea id ab aliis Scribis correctum sit aut corruptum. Hinc Aben-Ezra ad aliquot loca ridet nasutos, inquiens; nullo Tikkun opus fuisse, .i. nihil esse quod nasuti isti sapientes putarint, authorem debuisse aliter loqui vel scribere. Vide & eum Iob. 32.3. Hactenus Cl. Buxtorfius.
units.tr: IX. Argument from the confession of the Jews. For example, some Hebrews report eighteen passages which the scribes once changed, or rather corrupted, which change they call Tikkun Sopherim [תיקון סופרים], about which Galatinus writes much at the end of book 1. Glassius has replied to this at length, and so forcefully that I gladly set aside what I once thought about these matters at Oxford. I shall set out here Bellarmine's reply, which shows that the Vulgate version (I add the Chaldee paraphrase also) in many places has what the scribes are said to have corrected, or rather corrupted. From this it appears, he says, that some men, while they think they are attacking the Jews, in fact attack the Church itself. For if those corrections were corruptions of the Hebrew text by the scribes, it clearly follows that the Vulgate edition is also most corrupt, which nevertheless the Church has handed down to us as authentic. [Therefore those eighteen errors of this kind, as Bellarmine admits, could overturn the authenticity of the Vulgate edition.] He then says either that no such emendation was ever made by the scribes, since the origin of this opinion is the Talmud, a most fabulous book; or, if the Tikkun Sopherim is not a fable, it is not a corruption but a true emendation, made not by any scribes at all but by Ezra and his companions, and so on. Glassius made this opinion probable by many arguments. Bellarmine's view is also supported by Ludovicus de Tena and by Jacobus Bonfrerius, the Theologian of Douai, in his prolegomena to Holy Scripture, chapter 12. You will see their words in Rivet, p. 110 of the Isagoge. But it pleases me here to hear the judgment of the most distinguished Buxtorf, which Glassius added from the author's letter at the end of his Philologia sacra. It reads thus: In neither Talmud is there any clear mention of that Tikkun, while elsewhere the ornament of the scribes [עיטור סופרים] is mentioned in the Talmud as a matter of much less importance. If those passages had ever been written differently, Onkelos and Jonathan would have expressed it at least once. Nor would Josephus have kept silent, who ascribes the contrary to the Hebrews, namely that no letter of the law was ever changed by his fellow Hebrews, book 1 against Apion. The Talmudists note at Leviticus 27, the last verse, in various places, that no prophet was permitted to change or alter the smallest thing in the Law. How, then, could certain common scribes have arrogated to themselves this audacity, to correct the sacred text in letter and sense? I say to you, then, in the silence of all, that those scribes (Sopherim) were the sacred authors themselves, Moses and the Prophets, who never wrote otherwise than as is now read in writing. But the Hebrew sages, sharper-eyed, noticed some incongruity in these passages, and wrote that those authors ought to have spoken differently, and should, according to the coherence of the text proposed, have written this or that. But they preferred to write it so, and to pronounce it as it now stands in the text. For example, Genesis 18:22 is read as written: And Abraham was still standing before the Lord. Really? the Sages say: where is it read that Abraham came to the Lord and stood before him? The opposite is said in what precedes: God came to Abraham, and so on. Therefore Moses ought to have written: And the Lord was still standing before Abraham. But Moses ought not to have spoken so servilely of God, and so the tikkun corrected and changed the style of speech, for the sake of honour, and said: And Abraham was still standing before the Lord. Hence Rabbi Solomon adds: it was for him (Moses) to write [היה לו לכתוב], he ought to have written: And the Lord was still standing before Abraham. Not that he wrote it so earlier and that it was afterwards corrected or corrupted by other scribes. Hence Aben Ezra mocks the subtle men at several places, saying that there was no need of any Tikkun, that is, that there is nothing which those subtle sages thought the author ought to have said or written otherwise. See also him on Job 32:3. So far the distinguished Buxtorf.

units.la: Atque hæc ferè sunt argumenta, quibus fontium impuritatem à Judæis studio introductam criminantur multi asserentes cum Cano, & Huntlæo, Hebraa potius ex Latinis, quam Latina ex Hebrais corrigenda, absurdumque esse à nostratibus ad alienos .i. Hebraos & Græcos appellare, & impium, ad Judæorum & Schismaticorum Senatum referre Catholica Fidei consultationem. Cui criminationi non possum quin opponam nervosum Andradii responsum, Ad Ecclesia, inquit, dignitatem non minus sane pertinent sacra litera, qua Græcis, Hebraisque sunt familiares, quàm qua Latinè sunt conscripta, neque minus ex illis quàm ex his decoris atque ornamenti eam sibi comparare liquet. Quare qui Græcos Latinosq; codices de Ebraïs supplendos emendandosve esse contendunt, non quidem ab Ecclesia ad externos (ut quidam putant) sed ad ipsammet Iesu Christi Ecclesiam provocant, & ab eàdem illi ipsi præsidia comparant. Nam cum Hebraea etiam volumina, non tanquam aliena, sed tanquam propria & peculiaria Ecclesia habeat & veluti sacra suspiciat, ex emendatis Ebraïs aut Græcis vitiata Latina corrigi permittit. Et paulo post, Quare amplissimo mihi videntur Christi Ecclesiam ornamento spoliare, qui in vulgatam Edit. ab inanissimis vendicent calumniis, Hebraea Iudæorum perfidia corrupta fuisse contendunt: Illud namque si semel persuadeant, nullum ab illis non suspectum, nullum non dubium, nullum non calumniæ obnoxium testimonium peti poterit. Facile enim quis omnia poterit poterit in dubium revocare — atque ita amplissimum hostium testimonium, divina providentia ad Christiani nominis splendorem inter tot procellas & naufragia, conservatum, Christi Ecclesia, nostra contentione, amittet. Haec Andrad. cui non refragatur Bannes, pag. 56. col. 2. in 1. Partem Thomae, asserens, ejusmodi homines non multum piam operam Ecclesiae praestituros, ad conversionem judaorum. Aštipulatur & Mariana, qui p. 62. docet etiam textum Ebraicum esse possessionem Ecclesiae.
units.tr: These are almost the only arguments by which many writers charge that the corruption of the sources was introduced by the Jews on purpose. They assert, with Cano and Huntlaeus, that Hebrew texts should be corrected by the Latin rather than the Latin by the Hebrew, that it is absurd to appeal from our own people to foreigners, that is, Hebrews and Greeks, and that it is impious to refer the consultation of the Catholic faith to the senate of the Jews and the schismatics. I cannot refrain from setting against this accusation the vigorous answer of Andradius: Holy Scripture, he says, pertains no less to the dignity of the Church when it is familiar in Greek and Hebrew than when it is written in Latin, and it is clear that the Church gains as much beauty and ornament from the one as from the other. Therefore those who contend that the Greek and Latin codices must be supplemented and emended from the Hebrew do not appeal from the Church to outsiders, as some think, but to the very Church of Jesus Christ itself, and they obtain their support from it. For since the Church holds the Hebrew volumes not as foreign but as its own and peculiar possession, and regards them as, so to speak, sacred, it permits the faulty Latin to be corrected from the emended Hebrew or Greek. And a little later: Those who, on the most empty pretexts, lay claim against the Vulgate edition and maintain that the Hebrew text was corrupted by the perfidy of the Jews seem to me to strip the Church of Christ of a most splendid ornament. For if they once persuade people of that, no witness taken from them will be free from suspicion, none free from doubt, none free from the danger of calumny. Anyone could easily call everything into question, and so the very ample testimony of enemies, which by divine providence has been preserved through so many storms and shipwrecks for the splendour of the Christian name, the Church of Christ will lose through our contention. Andradius is not contradicted by Bannes, p. 56, col. 2, on the first part of Thomas, who asserts that such men will render the Church little pious service toward the conversion of the Jews. Mariana also agrees, who teaches at p. 62 that even the Hebrew text is a possession of the Church.

units.la: Et postea, Angustè eos de rebus ac propositè sentire dicit, qui Ecclesiam longo indormiisse tempore, in eâ viros doctos fuisse arbitrantur, penes quos divini libri tum Graecè tum Ebraicè conservati ab omni temporis injuriâ & adversariorum insidiis tuti essent. Sit ergo fixum, inquit, non minus ad Ecclesiae curam Hebraicos & Graecos codices quàm Latinos pertinere. Unde primum efficitur, neque eos codices potuisse in universum in re majoris momenti corrumpi, continuo enim accurrisset Ecclesia, quae divino instinctu & inflatu regitur, & viri docti, quorum numerus semper fuit aliquis, periculum indicassent, &c. Iuvat hic etiam adscribere Arias Montani verba ex commentatione ejus, Bibliis Interlinearibus secundae editionis praemissâ, quibus non obscurè invehi mihi videtur in Guidonem Fabricium Boderianum, qui teste Hartio, privata authoritate in primâ Edit. Gen. 3. 15. Masc. נשים in foem. נשים mutaverit. Is itaque postquam dixisset se in isto opere exemplar Complutense, ut pote cui omnia alia, inquit, quae punctis vocalibus instructa sunt exemplaria astipulantur, secutum fuisse, sic addit, nec enim aliter citra Rom. Ecclesiae judicium & doctorum omnium sententiam fieri poterat, sine sacrilegio & nefario scelere. Sed Ecclesiam ipsam minimè permissuram esse, ut aliquid de consueta & constanti omnium Ebraicorum exemplarium lectione mutaretur, hoc profecto cum primis intellexeramus, vel ex eo, quod tot jam saeculis retrò elapsis, ex quo sermo ille ortus est, quo quaerebatur, an aliqua lectioni Ebraica mutatio Judaeorum vel incuriâ vel inscitiâ, vel fraude accideret, nec ne, tamen nihil Rom. Ecclesia de ea re, adversus eas, quae nunc constant, Lectiones decernendum duxerit, nihil decreverit. Quamobrem hujusmodi audaciam, ut plane nobis id religiosum vel cogitare fuerat, ita à mente omnino nostra alienum fuisse declaramus. Et columna sequenti recensens rationes, cur sententiam illam de non corruptis fontibus amplexetur, etiam has ponit, 1. quod prudentissima & piissima Ecclesia Romana, quanquam argumentum hoc identidem ad singulares disputationes abreptum fuerit, nec apicem nec jota unum de communi Ebraica lectione mutari hactenus passa est. 2. quod maxima sit.
units.tr: And later: He says that those think narrowly and not to the point about these matters who suppose that the Church slept for a long time, and that learned men were in it, in whose keeping the divine books, both Greek and Hebrew, were preserved and safe from every injury of time and the plots of adversaries. Let it therefore be settled, he says, that the Hebrew and Greek codices pertain no less to the care of the Church than the Latin ones. From this it follows first that those codices could not in general have been corrupted in a matter of such importance, for the Church, which is governed by divine inspiration and breath, would have hurried to the spot at once, and learned men, whose number has always been some, would have pointed out the danger, etc. It is also helpful here to quote the words of Arias Montanus from his preface to the commentary of the second edition of the Interlinear Bibles, in which he seems to me to attack, not obscurely, Guido Fabricius of Boderie, who, according to Hartius, on his own private authority changed in the first edition, Gen. 3.15, the masculine [נשים] into the feminine [נשים]. After saying that in this work he followed the Complutensian edition, since it agrees with all the other copies furnished with vowel points, he adds: for otherwise this could not be done without the judgment of the Roman Church and the opinion of all learned men, without sacrilege and a wicked crime. But that the Church itself would never permit anything to be changed in the customary and constant reading of all the Hebrew copies, this we have certainly understood above all, if only from the fact that in so many centuries past, since that discussion arose in which it was asked whether any change in the Hebrew reading occurred through the carelessness, ignorance or fraud of the Jews or not, the Roman Church has nevertheless thought nothing should be decided about that matter against the readings that now stand, and has decided nothing. Therefore we declare that such audacity, which we would have thought it impious even to contemplate, was entirely foreign to our mind. And in the next column, reviewing the reasons why he embraces the opinion that the sources are not corrupted, he also gives these: (1) that the most prudent and most pious Roman Church, although this question has often been dragged into separate disputations, has never allowed so much as an apex or a jot to be changed in the common Hebrew reading; (2) that it is very great.

units.la: Protestatio Ar. Montani. N B. sit constantia exemplarium Ebraicorum per universum terrarum orbem. 3. quod hoc pacto pernitiosissimum Mahometicæ doctrinæ fundamentum evertatur, quo seductor ille sua somnia pro divinis oraculis venditabat: asserens sc. Veteris Test. libros à Judæis; novi vero à Christianis fuisse depravatos. Sibi vero certa divinitus esse data responsa, quibus utraque corrigetur lectio.
units.tr: Protest of Arias Montanus. N.B. Let there be the constancy of the Hebrew copies throughout the whole world. (3) that in this way the most pernicious foundation of Mahometan doctrine is overthrown, by which that seducer peddled his dreams as divine oracles, asserting that the books of the Old Testament were corrupted by the Jews and those of the New Testament by the Christians, and that he himself had received certain divine responses by which either reading would be corrected.

units.la: Concludimus ergo, Textum Ebraeum, Masorethicis notis instructum & correctum, ab omni malitiosa depravatione omnino esse immunem, à libariorum vero & fortuitis erratis ita esse purum, ut non solum iis casibus, quos a Bellarminus & b Canus recensent, ad eum sit recurrendum, sed etiam in cujusvis loci, genuino sensu eruendo, in omni fidei & morum disputatione; atque ad eum examinandas esse omnes, qua veteres, quà recentes, nulla exceptâ, versiones, id quod Bellarm. quoque suo exemplo, nominatim in loco Dan. 2. l. 1. de Invocat. Sanct. c. 13. comprobavit. Verbo, eum etiamnum esse normam, regulam & Canonem omnium versionum. Seu, ut verbis Acosta Iesuitæ utamur, Hanc Ebraicam Editionem esse authenticam, dubitare non possumus. libro 2. de Christo revelato, cap. 16. Qui idem Jesuita cap. 10. primævam Bibliorum linguam incorruptum judicem nominaverat.
units.tr: We conclude therefore: The Hebrew text, furnished and corrected with the Masoretic notes, is wholly immune from every malicious corruption, and is so pure from the errors of scribes and chance mistakes that one must have recourse to it not only in those cases which Bellarmine and Cano list, but also in drawing out the genuine sense of any passage, in every dispute about faith and morals; and that all versions, ancient and recent, without exception, must be examined by it, as Bellarmine too confirmed by his own example, especially at Dan. 2, book 1, On the Invocation of the Saints, chapter 13. In a word, it is still the norm, rule and canon of all versions. Or, to use the words of the Jesuit Acosta: We cannot doubt that this Hebrew edition is authentic, book 2, On Christ Revealed, chapter 16. The same Jesuit in chapter 10 had called the primeval language of the Bible an incorrupt judge.

units.la: Verbum addam de fontibus Novi Test. quos à variantibus Lectionibus minime immunes esse agnoscimus. Eas librariorum incuriæ & insciitiæ merito transcribimus. Agnoscimus, in N. Testamentum, si librorum molem, numerum & Antiquitatem cum veteri conferamus, paucis annis longe plures irrepsisse lectionum varietates, quam in vetus aliquot sæculis. Cujus rei causa non postrema est defectus Masoræ, qua si Ecclesiarum Antistites novi Test. libros munivissent, constantiorem haberemus N. T. lectionem. Sed benedictus sit Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cujus providentiæ & hoc debemus, quod nec fides nec pietas ullum detrimentum ex carum ulla passa sit. Hæc autem ingenua nostrorum confessio nihil patrocinatur Pontificiis. Si enim variantes aliquot lectiones ἀνθενλίας alicujus textus possunt evertere, tum certe de vulgata actum erit, cujus variantes lectiones immane quantum exsuperant. Sed dicunt, Græcos fontes ab hæreticis studio esse depravatos. Hæc certe gravior accusatio est. Sed quam & Senensis libro 7. Biblioth. hæresi 1. & Bellarminus lib. 2. de V. D. cap. 7. & alii exploserunt. Verba Bellarm. Etsi hæretici multa depravare conati sint, nunquam tamen defuerunt Catholici, qui eorum corruptelas detexe-
units.tr: I will add a word about the sources of the New Testament, which we acknowledge are not free from variant readings. We rightly put these down to the carelessness and ignorance of scribes. We acknowledge that if we compare the bulk, number and antiquity of the books of the New Testament with the Old, far more variations of reading have crept in within a few years than in several centuries of the other. The cause of this is not the least the lack of a Masorah, and if the bishops of the Churches had fortified the books of the New Testament with one, we would have a more constant reading of the New Testament. But blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whose providence we also owe it that neither faith nor piety has suffered any harm from any of them. This frank confession of ours, however, offers no support to the Papists. For if a few variant readings could overthrow the contradiction [ἀντιλογίας] of any text, then certainly the case of the Vulgate would be decided, whose variant readings exceed the others by an immense amount. But they say that the Greek sources were corrupted on purpose by heretics. This is certainly a graver accusation, but both Siena in book 7 of his Bibliotheca, heresy 1, and Bellarmine, book 2, On the Word of God, chapter 7, and others have rejected it. The words of Bellarmine: Although heretics have tried to corrupt many things, there have never been lacking Catholics who detected their corruptions

units.la: E detexerunt, & non permiserunt libros sacros corrumpi. Et certe non benè de Matre Ecclesia merentur, qui fontes ab hæreticis depravatos clamitant. Quid enim; Annon pudendum stigma ei inurunt; Cujus quæso erat providere, ne quid detrimenti caperent sacræ tabulæ, si non Matris Ecclesiæ? Annon illa se unicam depositariam hujus codicis jactitat? Et quid si illa forsitan post tot noctium inconnivas vigilias dormitante, zizania sua in hoc agro sevissent hæretici, annon illius & opis & muneris erat, illis extirpatis radicitusque evulsis, codicem illum suo nitori restituere? Scriptura utiq;, teste Bannes, præcipuè est in corde Ecclesiæ, secundario vero in libris. Sed quot tandem sunt loca, quæ sacrilega Hæreticorum manus depravavit; Tentaverint corruptionem multorum locorum. Perfecerint eam in quibusdam codicibus. Quid hoc ad nostros codices? In illis corruptelæ istæ monstrandæ erant. Et si fortassis in quibusdam earum extarent vestigia, quid hoc ad rem; Nec enim puritatem omnium codicum præstare quisquam nostrum præsumsit. Frustra ergo hac oberratur chordâ. Quod si prolubium esset descendere ad particularia loca, queis librariorum incuria grave vulnus inflixerit, & hic liqueret, quam sterilem paratragædiandi materiam habeant Pontificii. Bellarminus ultra vi. vel vii. loca cruere non evaluit, quorum tamen nullus stringit. Cum interim singulis capitibus vulgatæ versionis, Interpretis manifesta sphalmata, præter variarum lectionum farraginem, ostendi possint. Sed fingamus, inquit Cl. Rivetus, Pauca in textum Græcum N. T. irrepsisse vitia, annon manifestissimum est indicium, purissima & sincerissima esse exemplaria, quæ ad infestissimorum animorum calculos revocata, adeo in paucis in dubium vocantur? Sed quia omnia fere illa, quæ huc spectant ex superioribus, quæ de textu Ebraeo disseruimus, peti possunt, hic abrumpam orationis telam, & concludam verbis Glassii, Textum Græcum N. Testamenti, improbatis codicibus, (licet diversitate lectionum aliquantum discrepantibus) asservatum à corruptelis, sive ea ab Hæreticis per malitiam, sive à librariis per incuriam illata esse dicantur, ita esse immunem, ut exacta norma & certa regula esse possit, ad quam omnes omnino versiones, & præsertim versio vulgata (ut ad fontem rivuli) exigi, examinari, & si-cubi opus, corrigi possint & debeant.
units.tr: and exposed them, and did not allow the sacred books to be corrupted. And indeed they do not serve the Mother Church well who cry out that the sources were corrupted by heretics. For what? Do they not brand her with a shameful mark? Was it her duty, I ask, to see to it that the sacred tablets suffered no loss, if not the Mother Church's? Does she not boast that she is the sole depositary of this codex? And if perhaps, while she slept after so many nights of unsleeping vigil, heretics had sown their tares in this field, was it not her duty and her task, once they were uprooted and torn out by the roots, to restore that codex to its brightness? Scripture, indeed, says Bannes, is chiefly in the heart of the Church, and only secondarily in books. But how many places, pray, has the sacrilegious hand of heretics corrupted? They have attempted the corruption of many places; they have accomplished it in some codices. What is that to our codices? In those the corruptions were to be shown. And even if traces of them were to be found in some of them, what has that to do with the matter? For none of us has presumed to guarantee the purity of all codices. Therefore they strike the string in vain. But if it were a pleasure to descend to particular places where the carelessness of scribes has inflicted a serious wound, it would also become clear how barren a material for tragic exaggeration the Papists have. Bellarmine has not managed to dig out more than six or seven places, and none of these is really troubling. Meanwhile, under each chapter of the Vulgate version, manifest blunders of the translator can be shown, apart from the mass of variant readings. But let us suppose, says the distinguished Rivet, that a few faults have crept into the Greek text of the New Testament; is it not a most manifest sign that the most pure and sincere copies, which are called in doubt in so few places when they are brought before the judgment of the most hostile minds, are indeed pure? But since nearly all the things that bear on this can be drawn from what we have discussed above concerning the Hebrew text, I will break off the thread of my discourse here and conclude with the words of Glassius: The Greek text of the New Testament, preserved from corruptions, with the codices rejected (although differing somewhat in variety of readings), whether those corruptions are said to have been brought in by heretics through malice or by scribes through carelessness, is so free from them that there can be an exact norm and a certain rule to which all versions whatever, and especially the Vulgate version (as to the source of a stream), can and ought to be referred, examined, and, where need be, corrected.

units.la: In part 1. Thomæ qu. 1. art. 8.
units.tr: In Part 1 of Thomas, question 1, article 8.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: Transitur ad vulgatam Editionem. Quanta sit versionum authoritas, Patrum & Euangelicorum judicium concors. Collatio Fontium & vulgata, quo ad errores librariorum. Andradii ingenua confessio; Monstrosum Tridentinorum de vulgata Edit. decretum. Proponuntur quinque in sequentibus ordine tractanda.
units.tr: The discussion turns to the Vulgate edition. The authority of the versions, and the agreed judgement of the Fathers and the Evangelicals. A comparison of the sources and the Vulgate with respect to the errors of copyists. Andradius's candid confession. The monstrous decree of the Tridentines on the Vulgate edition. Five points are proposed to be treated in the following order.

units.la: HAbemus ergo jam regulam & normam, ad quam omnes V. & N. Test. versiones examinari opportet. Ea demum habenda est interpretatio bona inquit Jesuita Acosta, qua concordat Originali lingua. Authoritas divina tota penes illam, in qua sacer scriptor edidit primum. Veterum librorum fidem de Ebraïs voluminibus examinandam esse docet Gratianus, quod decretum Gregorius XIII. in nuperâ Editione Juris Canonici suâ authoritate editi, retinuit.
units.tr: We therefore now have the rule and standard by which all versions of the Old and New Testament must be examined. That is the good translation, says the Jesuit Acosta, which agrees with the original language. Divine authority rests wholly in that text in which the sacred writer first published it. Gratian teaches that the trustworthiness of the ancient books is to be examined against the Hebrew volumes, and Gregory XIII retained this decree in the recent edition of the Canon Law issued under his authority.

units.la: Unde jam & illud liquet, quid de versionum authoritate judicandum sit. Pulcram hic contestationem cum Patribus, meliorisque notæ Scholasticis & inter se Euangelicæ Ecclesiæ tenent, dum docent, nullam versionem recipiendam esse pro verbo Dei, nisi quatenus cum authentico exemplari convenit; solum originalem textum, utpote qui tam quoad verba, quam quoad res à Spiritu sancto sanctis Dei hominibus inspiratus est, esse infallibilis veritatis. Omnes contrà versiones esse rivos, d verba Cl. Junii, ex purissimis ipsis fontibus ductos humanâ operâ, ac proinde sordibus ex infirmitate hominis inquinatos, authoritate cum authentica formâ non comparandos: adeo ut nulla dari possit versio, quæ in omnibus cum authenticis tabulis conveniat, divinosque illos Majestatis, gravitatis & energiæ, quos Spiritus S. authentico textui impressit, characteres valeat exprimere: ut proinde nulla versio, qualiscunque ea sit, textui Ebraico æquari, nedum præferri possit.
units.tr: From this it is also clear what must be judged about the authority of the versions. The Evangelical Church holds a fine agreement here with the Fathers and with the better sort of Scholastics, and with one another, in teaching that no version is to be received as the Word of God except insofar as it agrees with the authentic copy; that the original text alone, since it was inspired by the Holy Spirit in both its words and its matter into the holy men of God, is of infallible truth. On the contrary, all versions are streams, to use the words of the illustrious Junius, drawn by human labour from the purest fountains themselves, and therefore polluted with the filth of human frailty, and not to be compared in authority with the authentic form. So much so that no version can be given which agrees in every respect with the authentic tables, or can express those divine marks of majesty, gravity and energy which the Holy Spirit impressed on the authentic text; so that no version, of whatever kind it may be, can be equal, much less preferred, to the Hebrew text.

units.la: Ita Protestantes de omnibus versionibus veteribus & recentibus ad unum sentiant omnes. Præter Patres aliosque supra indicatos, idem quoque nobiscum statuunt Pontificii quamplurimi, Cajetanus, Oleaster & alii. Quin in ipsa vulgata, eorum quamplurimi, qui post Concilium Tridentinum scripserunt, errores, ipsius Interpretis incuriâ vel ignorantiâ admissos, agnoscunt, & multa insuper alia in eâ desiderat Jesuita Serarius, uti infrà videbimus. Et quid quæso te, cordate lector, æquius esse potest? Irrepserint in quosdam codices sphalmata, incuria librariorum & injuria temporum. Paucula ea sunt, fatente Bannes, exigui momenti sunt, inquit Bellar. Sed & illa in Ebræo textu à Masorethis indicata & restituta sunt. Et ut restituta non essent, vel paucula forsan adhuc restituenda superessent, tamen ejusmodi ea esse agnoscit Bellar. ut in iis quæ ad fidem & mores pertinent, scriptura integritas desiderari non possit. Irrepserint ergo in fontes paucula aliquot menda; in vulgatam, ætate cum Ebraicis codicibus neutiquam comparandam, millena aliquot irrepsere. Id quod ingenuè agnoscit Andradius pag. mihi 367. Qui errores librariorum si Ebraorum voluminum authoritatem extinguere & opprimere valent, quid in Gracis Latinisque ponderis inerit? Tot enim illa atque tantis erroribus, sunt conserta, ut doctorum hominum vigilantiâ exhauriri vix possint Dices in vulgatâ quoque Clementis VIII. industriâ & jussu, quamplurimos sublatos esse errores. Agnosco, sed & illud agnosces vicissim, quamplurima loca quæ emendari potuisse, medicamque manum postulare ipsi * Bellar. Bandinus, Brugensis, Serarius aliique agnoscunt, etiamnum in mendo cubare. Adhæc, in textum Ebr. universale erratum amplius irrepere non posse, idque Masoræ beneficio, Serarius agnoscit, id quod de vulgatâ asseri sperarive nequit. Illud ergo, omnium, queis sanum sinciput est, judicio stabit, nisi sphalmatum textus originalis numerus longe excedat numerum sphalmatum, quæ textum vulgatæ Latinæ deformârunt, manere textus originalis debitam prærogativam. Sed dato (id quod tamen longè à veritatis regione aberrat) hâc in parte eandem esse textus originalis & vulgatæ Latinæ rationem, paribusque passibus ambulare, annon alia insuper erunt, quæ vulgatæ versioni Textum Ebraicum præferent? Plenitudo & integritas Ebrai textus habet prærogativam istam, inquit * Gretzerus, quod non modo ressignificata, sed & ipsa verba immediatè sint à Deo, quod in translatione non contingit, cum verba suppeditet interpres & quidem humano studio, non illo peculiari ductu & instinctu, quo scriptor Canonicus ducitur ac regitur. Nihil jam dicam de aliis defectibus, quos in vulgata multi Pontificiorum agnoscunt, fontibus verò non nisi impudentissimi audent adscribere.
units.tr: Thus all Protestants, concerning all old and recent versions, are of one mind. Besides the Fathers and the others indicated above, very many Papists also hold the same view with us, Cajetan, Oleaster and others. Indeed, among those who wrote after the Council of Trent, many acknowledge errors in the Vulgate itself, admitted through the carelessness or ignorance of its translator, and the Jesuit Serarius laments that many other faults are found in it, as we shall see below.
