And what, I ask you, thoughtful reader, can be more fair? Some slips crept into certain codices through the carelessness of copyists and the injury of the times. They are few, as Bannes concedes, and of small importance, says Bellarmine. But even these have been pointed out and restored in the Hebrew text by the Masoretes. And even if they had not been restored, and perhaps a few still remained to be restored, Bellarmine nevertheless acknowledges that they are of such a kind that in those matters which pertain to faith and morals, the integrity of Scripture cannot be wanting. So a few errors have crept into the sources; into the Vulgate, which is by no means comparable with the Hebrew manuscripts, some thousands have crept. This Andradius candidly acknowledges, on page 367 of my edition: If the errors of copyists are able to extinguish and overwhelm the authority of the Hebrew volumes, what weight will remain in the Greek and Latin ones? For they are so crowded with so many and such great errors that they can scarcely be exhausted by the vigilance of learned men. You will say that in the Vulgate too, by the diligence and command of Clement VIII, very many errors were removed. I grant it; but you in turn will also grant that very many passages, which could have been emended and which call for a healing hand, are still lying in error, as Bellarmine, Bandinus, Bruegel, Serarius and others acknowledge. Besides, Serarius acknowledges that no universal error can creep further into the Hebrew text, and that this is owing to the Masora; something which cannot be asserted or hoped for in the Vulgate. Therefore this will stand by the judgement of all who have a sound head: unless the number of errors in the original text far exceeds the number of errors which have deformed the text of the Latin Vulgate, the original text retains its due pre-eminence. But granting (although this strays far from the region of truth) that the relation of the original text and the Latin Vulgate is the same in this respect, and that they walk with equal steps, will there not be other points in which the Hebrew text is preferred to the Vulgate version? The fullness and integrity of the Hebrew text has this pre-eminence, says Gretser, that not only the meanings but the very words are from God, which does not happen in a translation, since the words are supplied by the translator, and that by human effort, not by that special guidance and inspiration by which the canonical writer is led and governed. I will say nothing now of the other defects which many Papists acknowledge in the Vulgate, but which only the most shameless dare to ascribe to its sources.

units.la: Cum autem hæc ita sese habeant, non immeritò quæsierit aliquis, quæ causæ Concilium Tridentinum impulerint, ut vulgatam
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, someone may not unreasonably ask what causes moved the Council of Trent to thrust the Vulgate upon the Church of God as authentic tables, casting the original text down from its throne.

units.la: * pag. 520. gatam versionem, deturbato de solio textu originali, Ecclesiæ Dei tanquam authenticas tabulas obtruserint. Sic enim Sessione 4. Decreto 1. intonant.
units.tr: * p. 520. ...the Vulgate version, the original text having been cast down from its throne, they imposed on the Church of God as authentic tables. For thus they thunder in Session 4, Decree 1.

units.la: Si quis libros ipsos integros, cum OMNIBVS suis PARTIBVS, prout in Ecclesia Catholica legi consueverunt, & in VETERI VVLGATA LATINA EDITIONE habentur, pro sacris & Canonicis non susceperit, ANATHEMA SIT.
units.tr: If anyone does not receive as sacred and canonical the books themselves, entire with ALL their PARTS, as they have been customarily read in the Catholic Church, and are contained in the OLD VULGATE LATIN EDITION, let him be ANATHEMA.

units.la: Et Decreto 2.
units.tr: And in Decree 2:

units.la: Insuper eadem SS. Synodus considerans, non parum utilitatis accedere posse Ecclesiæ Dei, si ex omnibus Latinis Editionibus, quæ circumferuntur, sacrorum librorum, quænam pro authentica habendâ sit, innotescat, statuit & declarat, ut hæc ipsa vetus & vulgata Editio, qualongo tot seculorum usu, in ipsa Ecclesia probata est, in publicis Lectionibus, disputationibus, prædicationibus & expositionibus pro authentica habeatur, & ut nemo eam rejicere quovis prætextu audeat vel præsumat.
units.tr: Moreover, this same holy Synod, considering that not a little advantage could accrue to the Church of God if it were known, from among all the Latin editions of the sacred books that are in circulation, which one is to be held authentic, decrees and declares that this same old and common edition, which has been approved in the Church by the long use of so many centuries, is to be held authentic in public lectures, disputations, preachings and expositions, and that no one may dare or presume to reject it on any pretext whatever.

units.la: Prodigiosum certè decretum, & cujus cordatiores Pontificios, & tunc cum illud cuderetur, puduit & etiamnum dispudet. Nobis propositum est, hoc decretum brevi aliquo Commentario illustrare. Gratificabimur hanc operam juventuti, & ordine hæc V. expendemus. 1. Quis sit hujus versionis author. 2. Quæ & quanta huic versioni collata sit à Synodo authoritas, seu quis sit decreti sensus. 3. Quæ causæ impulerint Synodum ut hoc decretum scisceret. 4. Quibus difficultatibus hoc decretum ab ipsis Catholicis prematur. 5. Et ab ipsis quoque Pontificibus, Sixto V. & Clemente VIII.
units.tr: Certainly a prodigious decree, one which the more thoughtful Papists were ashamed of when it was drawn up, and are still ashamed of now. It is our purpose to illustrate this decree with a short commentary. We shall gratify young students in this labour, and we shall weigh these points in order: 1. Who is the author of this version. 2. What and how great authority the Synod conferred on this version, or what is the sense of the decree. 3. What causes moved the Synod to enact this decree. 4. By what difficulties this decree is pressed even by Catholics themselves. 5. And also by the Pontiffs themselves, Sixtus V and Clement VIII.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quis sit vulgata Editionis author, & an spiritu propheticô inter vertendum illustratus fuerit, discors Pontificiorum sententia. Serarius haesitat & quaestionem indecisam relinquit.
units.tr: Who is the author of the Vulgate edition, and whether he was enlightened by the prophetic Spirit in translating: the opinions of the Papists disagree. Serarius hesitates and leaves the question undecided.

units.la: DE authore Versionis non una inter ipsos Pontificios sententia est. Alii, ut Pagninus & Driedo eam Hieronymo simpliciter abjudicarunt. Quidam, & inter hos Augustt. Steuchus Eugubinus, eam universam B. Hieronymo adscripsêre. At audaculam hanc assertionem a Bellarminus, b Azorius, c Maldonatus, d Sacroboscus, e Lindanus & alii flagellarunt. Communis sententia haec est, f novum Testamentum non esse ab Hieron. ex Graeco versum, sed solummodo recognitum: vetus vero esse ex Hieronymi versione, quam ex Ebraeo confecit, exceptis Psalterio, Sapientia, Ecclesiastico & libris Machabaeorum: His Salmeron addit Baruch & Epist. Jeremiae. Hieronymum enim bis vetus Test. Latine vertisse, semel ex Graeca LXX. Interpretum, semelque rursus ex Ebraeo: atque ex duabus illis Editionibus, vulgatam in quibusdam libris, e.g. Regum & Proverbiis, esse mixtam: Psalterium autem esse ex versione B. Martyris Luciani, &c. D. Vitakerus & Junius volunt eam mixtam esse ex Veteri Latina, tempore Hieronymi vulgatâ & receptâ, quam Italam vocat Augustinus, (de qua supra p. 10.) & Hieronymi Emendatione. Licet autem hic valde tumultuetur more suo Gretzerus, & nil nisi mendacia piis & eruditissimis illis Heroibus objiciat, tamen ex ipsis Pontificiis nonnulli eandem sententiam amplexi sunt, vid. g Duacenses Theologi, & Fortunatus Fanensis, publicis scriptis, non ita pridem evulgatis, asserentes, versionem praditam, licet aliquando Hieronymi credita fuerit, tamen ut majoribus nostris, inquit Fanensis, quasi per manum traditum est, partim ex antiquissimâ & vetustissimâ Editione Latina, quam Hieronymus communem & vulgatam, Augustinus Italam, & Gregorius veterem appellant, retentam esse, partim, &c. Sed & omni exceptione major Praefatio quae Bibliis Clementinis praefixa est, pronunciat, eam partim ex Hieronymi translatione vel emendatione, partim ex Itala mixtam esse, in quam sententiam quoque descendit Mariana, Epistola ad Sanderum p. 57. Egregie ergo Sixtus V. Bell. Coccius, Gretzerus & caeteri, dum hanc Editionem ab authore, vid. eruditissimo Hieronymo, passim commendant, eique ab eximii istius Patris authoritate authentiam conciliare satagunt. Sed ad rem. Posteriorem hanc Witakeri, Junii, Fanensis, &c. sententiam probant etiam Baronius tom. 2. & Sixtus Senensis lib. 8. ad obj. octavam, & alii, quos hic recensere omnes nihil attinet. Sed & illud adde, Serarium in prolegomenis Biblicis p. 102. diserte asserere, praeter pauculos V. Test. libros, e.g. Job, Psalterium & libros Salomonis, nihil ab Hiero. ex Graeco translatum. Me quod attinet, non reciprocaverim super hac re contentionis seriram cum quopiam. Esto majore ex parte Hieronymi, seu Interpretis seu recognitoris, & videamus quantum ponderis ex eo ad versionem, de qua in praesens nobis sermo est, queat accedere. Hieronymum, ut & 70. Interpretes, Spiritu prophetico versiones suas confecisse, multorum opinio est. Audiamus Melchiorem Canum, qui non veretur asserere, aut veterem Interpretem, Spiritus S. peculiari dono, sacras literas convertisse, aut Ecclesiam Latinam multis retro saeculis non habuisse Dei Euangelium, sed hominis. Non fuerit Propheta, habuit tamen ut Titelmannus asseverat, & recte, Spiritum quendam prophetico vicinum & Proximum. Prodeat k & Gretzerus, qui statuit, Deum Interpretis manum & calamum ita direxisse, ne VSPIAM a Spiritus Sancti mente in translatione aberraret, Et pag. 541. Deum mentem Interpretis singulari opere ita rexisse & direxisse, ut NVSQVAM a Spiritus S. mente deflecteret, quae rursus inculcat pag. 542. 545. & alibi. Quin etiam de Theodotione homine a Christiana religione alienissimo non erubuit asserere, 1 Si quid est in vulgata pertinens ad dogmata fidei & morum, desumptum ex Theodotione, in iis Theodotionem non errasse, idque singulari protectione Dei, interpretem illum, quamvis perditum & impium, iis in locis, quae Ecclesia aliquando tanquam authentica approbatura erat, ab errore custodientis.
units.tr: Among the Papists themselves there is no single opinion about the author of the version. Some, such as Pagninus and Driedo, simply denied it to Jerome. Others, among them Augustinus Steuchus Eugubinus, ascribed the whole of it to St Jerome. But Bellarminus, Azorius, Maldonatus, Sacroboscus, Lindanus and others have lashed this rash assertion. The common view is this: the New Testament was not translated from the Greek by Jerome but only revised by him; the Old Testament, however, is from Jerome's version, which he made from the Hebrew, except for the Psalter, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus and the books of the Maccabees. Salmeron adds to these Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah. For they hold that Jerome translated the Old Testament into Latin twice, once from the Greek of the Seventy interpreters and once again from the Hebrew, and that the Vulgate is a mixture of those two editions in some books, for example Kings and Proverbs; the Psalter, however, is from the version of the blessed martyr Lucian, and so on. Whitaker and Junius hold that it is a mixture of the Old Latin version, which was current and accepted in Jerome's time and which Augustine calls the Itala (of which see above, p. 10), with Jerome's correction. Although Gretzer, as is his way, rages loudly here and throws nothing but lies at those pious and most learned heroes, nevertheless some of the Papists themselves have embraced the same view, namely the Theologians of Douai and Fortunatus of Fano, in published writings issued not long ago, asserting that the version, though at one time believed to be Jerome's, has nevertheless come down to us, as Fano puts it, as it were by hand from our forefathers, partly retained from the most ancient and venerable Latin edition, which Jerome calls the common and vulgate, Augustine the Itala, and Gregory the old, and partly, and so on. But also the Preface prefixed to the Clementine Bible, which is beyond all objection, declares that it is a mixture, partly of Jerome's translation or correction and partly of the Itala; Mariana too goes down this road, in his letter to Sander, p. 57. Accordingly Sixtus V, Bellarmine, Coccius, Gretzer and the rest, while they commend this edition everywhere as the work of its author, the most learned Jerome, and strive to win it authority from the reputation of that eminent Father, are doing so admirably. But to the point. This later view of Whitaker, Junius, Fano and others is also approved by Baronius, tom. 2, and Sixtus of Siena, book 8, on the eighth objection, and by others whom it would be pointless to list here. But add this as well: Serarius, in his Biblical Prolegomena, p. 102, plainly asserts that, apart from a few books of the Old Testament, for example Job, the Psalter and the books of Solomon, nothing was translated from the Greek by Jerome. As for me, I would not willingly engage in a long dispute over this matter with anyone. Let it be granted that the version is for the most part Jerome's, whether as translator or as reviser, and let us see how much weight can be added from that to the version with which we are now concerned. It is the opinion of many that Jerome, like the Seventy interpreters, made his versions under the prophetic Spirit. Let us hear Melchior Cano, who does not hesitate to assert that "either the ancient interpreter translated the sacred letters by a special gift of the Holy Spirit, or the Latin Church for many centuries past did not have the Gospel of God but that of man. He was not a prophet, yet he had, as Titelmann rightly asserts, a certain spirit close and akin to the prophetic." Let Gretzer also come forward, who holds that "God so directed the hand and pen of the interpreter that NOWHERE did he stray from the mind of the Holy Spirit in the translation"; and on page 541, "God so ruled and directed the mind of the interpreter by a singular work that he NEVER deviated from the mind of the Holy Spirit," which he presses again on pages 542 and 545, and elsewhere. Indeed he was not ashamed to assert even of Theodotion, a man most alien to the Christian religion, that "1 if anything in the Vulgate pertaining to the dogmas of faith and morals was taken from Theodotion, Theodotion did not err in those matters, and this by a singular protection of God, who kept that interpreter, however lost and impious, from error in those places which the Church at some time was going to approve as authentic."

units.la: Alia opinio censet, S. Hieronymum, verba m Serarii, ordinaria, qua homines, qui bene aliquid aiunt, prosequi solet Deus, ope, ac generali tantummodo concursu fuisse adjutum in Bibliis vertendis aut emendandis. Qua etiam opinio idcirco eum in isthoc opere velut hominem errare potuisse, ac fortasis etiam interdum errasse fatetur. In ea opinione e Catholicis videntur esse Joh. Driedo lib. 2. propos. 3. & 4. ac in solutione argumenti 1. 3. 4. & in 3. conclus. sol. 42. Andradius lib. 4. dum sol. 255 ilia. 255. & 256. copiosè satis hoc affirmat & ad Driedonem relegat, dumque postea sol. 292. (mihi 411.) ait se nolle interpretem nostrum extra omnis reprehensionis aleam positum, & se labes, quibus omnium mortalium lucubrationes respergi solent, in eo agnoscere, &c. Et Vega lib. 15. cap. 9. apertissimè. Bellarm. lib. 2. 11. ad Arg. 2. Admittimus, inquit Interpretem non esse prophetam & errare potuisse, Quamvis verò subjungat, tamen dicimus eum non errasse in ea versione, quam Ecclesia approbavit, non ideò asserit, peculiari SPIRITVS S. lumine illustratum fuisse. 1. Quia potest aliquis in aliqua versione non errare, qui solâ humanâ peritiâ & diligentiâ utitur. 2. Quia non simpliciter dicit, Interpretem non erras-se, sed cum restrictione quadam, non errasse in eâ versione quam Ecclesia approbavit, quasi concederet, eum alicubi quidem errasse, seu in aliquâ loci aut verbi alicujus versione. hanc tamen ab Ecclesia non approbatam, &c.
units.tr: Another opinion holds, in the words of Serarius, that St Jerome was aided in translating or correcting the Bibles only by the ordinary help and general concurrence which God usually gives to men who do something well; and this opinion accordingly admits that he, as a man in this work, could have erred, and perhaps even did sometimes err. Among Catholics, John Driedo, book 2, propositions 3 and 4, and in the answer to argument 1, 3 and 4, and in the 3rd conclusion, answer 42, appear to hold this view. Andradius, book 4, answer 255 and 256, affirms this quite fully and refers the reader to Driedo; and then, in answer 292 (for me 411), he says that he does not want our interpreter placed beyond the reach of all criticism, and that he recognises in him the blemishes with which the labours of all mortals are usually stained, and so on. And Vega, book 15, chapter 9, most plainly. Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 11, on the second argument: "We admit," he says, "that the interpreter was not a prophet and could have erred. Yet although he adds, 'nevertheless we say that he did not err in that version which the Church approved,' he does not thereby assert that he was enlightened by a peculiar light of the Holy Spirit. 1. Because someone who uses only human skill and diligence can fail to err in some version. 2. Because he does not simply say that the interpreter did not err, but adds a qualification, that he did not err in that version which the Church approved, as though he conceded that he had erred somewhere, in some version of a passage or word, which, however, the Church had not approved, and so on."

units.la: Quid tandem Serarius concludat, expectas audire Lector? Ille recusans se hic interponere Palæmonem, utra opinionum istarum probabilior sit, mihi quidem nondum satis liquet, inquit. Ratio, quia videntur opinionis utriusque argumenta posse non improbabiliter solvi. Sed quia hac de re in sequentibus plura dicenda erunt, tollam manum de hac tabulâ.
units.tr: What, finally, does Serarius conclude? You want to hear it, reader. He, declining to put himself forward here as Palaemon, says: "Which of these opinions is the more probable is not yet quite clear to me. The reason is that the arguments of each opinion seem to be capable of being answered not improbably." But since more will be said on this matter in what follows, I will take my hand off this tablet for now.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Circa interpretationem Decreti dissidium Rom. Ecclesiæ. Quæ turbæ hinc in Hispania exortæ. Mariana & Bannesii testimonia. Genuinum decreti interpretamentum, vulgatam ipsis quoque fontibus prælatam, ex Pinedâ, congregatione Cardinalium, Inquisitoribus Hisp. Valentiâ, Harto, Sacrobosco, Azorio, Ribera, &c. ostenditur. Quid sit authenticum in jure. Alia.
units.tr: The dispute among Roman Catholics over the interpretation of the Decree. The disturbances this caused in Spain. The testimonies of Mariana and Bannes. The genuine interpretation of the decree, which places the Vulgate above even the original sources, is shown from Pineda, the congregation of Cardinals, the Spanish Inquisitors, Valentia, Harto, Sacrobosco, Azorius, Ribera, and others. What is authentic in law. Other matters.

units.la: CIrca hujus decreti sensum discors est Pontificiorum Schola, verèque hoc decretum appellaveris pomum Eridos; adeo magnas inter ipsos, præsertim in Hispania, excitavit contentiones. Testis omni exceptione major mihi, Joh. Marianus erit, Jesuita Hispanus, qui in tractatu de vulgata versione cap. 1. sic infit, Opus molestum suscipimus, periculosam aleam, ac quâ nescio an ulla disputatio bis annis inter Theologos, in Hispania præsertim, odio partium magis implacabili agitata sit, usque adeo ut a probris & contumeliis, quibus se mutuò mutuò fœdabant, ad tribunalia ventum sit. Atque quæ pars magis sibi fidebat adversarios de religione postulatos gravissime exercuit, quasi impios, qui divinorum librorum authoritatem atque eam versionem, quæ vulgata Editio vocatur, audacter elevarent, novis interpretationibus pralatis, invectisque contra Concilii Trid. decreta. Tenuit ea causa multorum animos suspensos expectatione, quem tandem exitum habitura esset, cum viri eruditi è vinculis cogerentur causam dicere, haud levi salutis existimationisque discrimine. Miseranda virtutis conditio, quando pro laboribus, quos susceperat maximos, compellebatur, eorum, à quibus defendi par fuisset, odia, accusationes & contumelias perferre, quo exemplo multorum praeclaros impetus retardari, viresque debilitari & concidere necesse erat. Omnino fregit ea res multorum animos, alieno periculo considerantium, quantum procella immineret liberè affirmantibus quæ sentirent. Itaque aut in aliorum castra transibant frequentes, aut tempori cedendum judicabant. Hæc Mariana. Prodeat in hanc quoque scenam magni nominis Dominicanus, Fr. Dominicus Bannes, & ipse Hispanus, qui suam in proferenda animi sententia (quam tamen satis innuit) pusillanimitatem manifestè prodit his verbis queis disputationem hanc obsignat, Sed jam tandem, inquit, circa gravissimam difficultatem dicendi finem faciamus. Si ergo quæris, quænam istarum opinio mihi probabilior videatur, sit sexta conclusio, In re tam gravi expectanda est Ecclesiæ Catholicæ censura. Unde neque audeo neque debeo Ecclesiæ judicium meâ sententiâ prævenire. Scio quidem, si ab Ecclesiâ interrogarer, quid vivâ voce responderem; interim tamen pio justoque silentio me contineo. Hoc unum duntaxat dixerim, vehementer me desiderare, ut contentio hæc, inter pios Theologos exorta, summi Pontificis authoritate decideretur ac componeretur. Alioquin si Ecclesiâ prudente & sciente hæc inter Theologos varietas permittitur, perinde est ac si Ecclesia diceret, unusquisque in suo sensu abundet, dummodo fidei veritas, Ecclesiaque Catholica authoritas defendatur. Hæc Bannes. Ecce gravissimam hanc vocat difficultatem: atque ut Judæi suarum difficultatum decisionem ab Elia, ita isti hujus & id genus aliarum à Pontifice expectant. Sed unde hæc tanta difficultas? Si fontes maliosè carrupti sunt, si vulgatæ author errare in sua versione non potuit, quid restat? Quid nodum in scirpo quæritis? Quid tantos fluctus excitatis in simpulo? Credite concilio, cujus est imperare, vobis obsequii gloria relicta est. Nullam hic vident difficultatem delegati Cardinales; neque hic aqua hæret Villalpando, Ludovico de Tena Cano, Rhemensibus, Pinedæ, Zuaresio, Valentiæ & aliis, qui licet inter se in multis particularibus dissentiant, conspirant tamen in eo, prædictam versionem ita esse declaratam authenticam, ut ne prætextu quidem textus Ebraici, ab eâ liceat provocare. Sic enim Pineda Jesuita in tractatu de rebus Salomonis lib. 4. cap. 7. sect. 2. Ita de vulgati Interpretis lectione Latinâ honorificentissimè & gravissimè sentiendum, loquendumque, ut commissam illam nobis diligentissimè tuendam esse intelligamus, non solum in universum, sed etiam in singulis membris atque particulis, uti præcepit Tridentina Synodus, sess. 4. Libros ipsos integros cum omnibus suis partibus, prout in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ legi consueverunt, & in veteri vulgatâ habentur, pro sacris & Canonicis suscipiendos. Quod decretum Illustrissimorum & Reverendiss. DD. Cardinalium congregatio, Concilii Tridentini Interpretum enucleatè declaravit, 17. Januarii anni 1576. censens, nihil posse asseverari, quod repugnet vulgatæ Latinæ Editioni, etiam quod esset sola periodus, sola clausula, vel membrum, sive vox, vel dictio sola, aut syllaba jotave unum, Et acriter reprehendit Vegam, qui libro 15. de Justific. cap. 9. tam audacter locutus est, quoad oppositionem textus Graci aut Ebraici cum Latina vulgata Editione. Hæc Pineda. Nota hoc judicium delegati Cardinalium Senatus, cordate Lector. Id quod Serarium ita patefecit, ut in Proleg. Bibl. cap. 19. qu. 11. nesciat, quid responsurus sit. Nam primo, inquit, respondeo, istiusmodi declarationum, sive judicum sententia, sive Doctorum opiniones, sive sapientum responsa, sive hujusmodi aliud quippiam sint, authoritatem, uti par est, reverendo, dubitari posse, an sine depravatione ac mendo edita sint. 2. Typotheta operaque alia, ac istarum heruς haretici fuerunt, &c. Sed frustra est Serarius, nam præter Pinedam etiam Turrianus in Thomam & Ludovicus de Tena Isag. lib. 1. Diff. 6. sect. 1. ita citant hanc decisionem, ut ne vel minimam suspicionem vel de depravatione, vel ἀνταθολὴ ingerant. Ne quid tamen dissimulem, posteriora illa, quibus Vega reprehenditur, in Exemplari meo declarationum, Coloniæ 1609. edito, non comparent, sed hæc substituta sunt, Quoad oppositionem autem textus Graci aut Ebraici cum Latina vulgata editione, congregatio remisit ad tertiam regulam Indicis sub Pio IV. editam. Idem Pineda libro eodem pag. 229. Nos qui omnino tenemur tueri Latinam vulgatam Lectionem cum omnibus suis particulis, piaculum existimamus asserere, non solum in rē pertinente ad fidem, sed etiam ad rem Geographicam aut aliam cujuscunque generis, Latinum Interpretem, si non omnia semper assecutus est, neque prorsus sensum omnem verborum exhausit, aliquando aberrasse deceptumque fuisse. Unde & in Indice litera V. haec comparent, vulgata Lectionis authoritas & vel solus apex retinendus. Et, Latinus Interpres nunquam aberrans. Vbi illud non injuria quaeri posset, quomodo illa Pinedae verba, si non omnia semper assecutus est, &c. & eodem tendentia Grezeri, quadam reperiri in vulgata vocabula non satis apte conversa pag. 560. cum spiritu prophetico, quo Hieron. seu quemcunque alium vulgatae authorem illustratum asserunt, possint subsistere. Item an is qui putat se omnia apte reddidisse, & tamen id assecutus non est, nunquam aberrasse dici possit.
units.tr: The Papist school is divided over the meaning of this decree, and you could rightly call it an apple of discord, so great are the contentions it has stirred up among them, especially in Spain. The witness I accept above all exception will be John Mariana, a Spanish Jesuit, who in his treatise on the Vulgate version, chapter 1, begins thus: "We undertake a troublesome task, a dangerous venture, and I do not know whether any dispute has been pursued among theologians for these two years, especially in Spain, with a more implacable partisan hatred, to the point that from reproaches and insults, with which they defiled one another, they came to the law courts. And the party that trusted more in itself harassed its opponents most severely before the religious tribunals, as if they were impious men who boldly disparaged the authority of the divine books and of that version which is called the Vulgate edition, by bringing forward new interpretations and attacking the decrees of the Council of Trent. This case kept the minds of many in suspense, waiting to see what outcome it would have, when learned men were dragged from their chains to plead their cause, at no slight risk to their safety and reputation. Wretched is the condition of virtue, when, for labours it had undertaken at great cost, it was forced to bear the hatreds, accusations and insults of those by whom it should rather have been defended. By such an example the splendid efforts of many had to be held back, and their strength weakened and broken. That affair certainly broke the spirits of many who, seeing from another's danger how great a storm threatened those who spoke freely what they thought, either went over in numbers to the camps of others or judged that they must yield to the times." So Mariana. Let the great Dominican, Fr. Dominic Bannes, also a Spaniard, step onto this stage too. In setting out his opinion (which he nonetheless makes fairly clear) he plainly displays his timidity in the words with which he closes this disputation: "But now at last, let us make an end of this most weighty difficulty. If therefore you ask which of these opinions seems more probable to me, let the sixth conclusion be: in a matter so grave the judgment of the Catholic Church is to be awaited. Hence I neither dare nor ought to anticipate the Church's judgment with my own opinion. I know indeed what I would answer by word of mouth if the Church questioned me; yet meanwhile I keep a pious and just silence. This one thing only I will say: I earnestly desire that this contention, arisen among pious theologians, be decided and settled by the authority of the supreme Pontiff. Otherwise, if such variety among theologians is permitted by the prudence and knowledge of the Church, it is just as if the Church said: let each abound in his own sense, provided only the truth of the faith and the authority of the Catholic Church are defended." So Bannes. See, he calls this a most grave difficulty, and just as the Jews looked to Elijah to settle their difficulties, so these men expect the decision of this and similar questions from the Pope. But whence this great difficulty? If the sources have been corrupted by malice, if the author of the Vulgate could not err in his version, what is left? Why do you seek a knot in a bulrush? Why do you stir up such waves in a teacup? Trust the Council, whose task it is to command; the glory of obedience is left to you. The appointed Cardinals see no difficulty here; nor does Villalpando stick at it, nor Ludovicus de Tena the canon, nor the Rhemists, nor Pineda, Suárez, Valentia, and others, who, although they disagree among themselves on many particulars, nevertheless agree on this: that the said version has been so declared authentic that, not even on the pretext of the Hebrew text, is it lawful to appeal from it. For thus Pineda the Jesuit, in his treatise on the affairs of Solomon, book 4, chapter 7, section 2: "So we must think and speak of the Latin reading of the Vulgate interpreter with such honour and gravity that we understand it has been committed to us to be guarded most diligently, not only as a whole but also in its individual members and particles, as the Council of Trent ordained in session 4, that the books themselves, entire with all their parts, as they have been customarily read in the Catholic Church and are held in the old Vulgate, are to be received as sacred and canonical. This decree the congregation of the most illustrious and most reverend Cardinals, interpreters of the Council of Trent, clearly declared on 17 January 1576, judging that nothing may be asserted which contradicts the Latin Vulgate edition, even if it were a single period, a single clause, or a member, or a single word, or a single syllable or jot." And he sharply rebukes Vega, who in book 15 on justification, chapter 9, spoke so boldly about the opposition of the Greek or Hebrew text to the Latin Vulgate edition. So Pineda. Note, kind reader, this judgment of the Cardinals' senate. It so exposed Serarius that in the Prolegomena to the Bible, chapter 19, question 11, he does not know what he will answer. "First," he says, "I answer that the authority of such declarations, whether the judgment of judges, the opinions of teachers, the responses of wise men, or anything of this kind, is to be respected as it deserves, yet it may be doubted whether they were published without corruption and error. Second, printers and other workers, as well as heretics..." But Serarius labours in vain. For besides Pineda, Turrianus on Thomas, and Ludovicus de Tena in his Isagoge, book 1, Diff. 6, section 1, cite this decision in such a way as to suggest not even the slightest suspicion either of corruption or of contradiction. Yet, not to conceal anything, those later words by which Vega is rebuked do not appear in my copy of the declarations, printed at Cologne in 1609; instead these words have been substituted: "As for the opposition of the Greek or Hebrew text to the Latin Vulgate edition, the congregation referred the matter to the third rule of the Index issued under Pius IV." The same Pineda, in the same book, page 229: "We, who are wholly bound to defend the Latin Vulgate reading with all its particulars, count it a sin to assert, not only in matters pertaining to the faith but also in geography or any other kind of matter, that the Latin interpreter, if he did not always attain everything and did not exhaust the full sense of the words, sometimes went astray and was deceived." Hence also in the Index, under the letter V, these appear: "the authority of the Vulgate reading, and even a single stroke of a letter, is to be retained," and "the Latin interpreter never errs." Here one might not unreasonably ask how those words of Pineda, "if he did not always attain everything," and so on, and the similar words of Grezer, "certain words are found in the Vulgate not rendered aptly enough," page 560, can stand together with the prophetic spirit by which they assert that Jerome, or whoever else was the author of the Vulgate, was illuminated. Likewise, can someone who thinks he has rendered everything aptly, yet has not attained it, be said never to have erred?

units.la: [Ludovici de Tena, Isagog. ad Scripturam l.1. Diff.6. sect.1. haec est decisio, Latinam Editionem vulgatam, in omnibus suis locis & partibus, ita esse authenticam, ut non solum nullum contra fidem errorem contineat, sed etiam infallibilem veritatem & Spiritus S. mentem in omnibus suis partibus, quantumvis minimis, non minus quam originalis Scriptura, unde fuit transumpta. Neque ut fidem faciat, indigere recursu ad illam vel aliam. Sed adhuc quando ab Ebraea nunc existente differunt, esse veram regulam fidei, &c. Et Sect. 3. Non solum in iis quae gravia sunt & ad fidem morésque pertinent, sed etiam in omnibus aliis, quantumvis levibus, vulgatam nullum habere errorem. Quia cum concilium jubeat eam habere pro authentica regula sine ulla limitatione, absque ea debet admitti, cum lex generaliter loquens, pariter sit intelligenda, & ubi ea non distinguit, pariter distinguere non debeant. Praeterea, quia concilium non solum ad errorem gravem aut perniciosum, sed ad nullum prorsus inducere potest: Juduceret autem, si in vulgata aliquis error, etiam levis existeret, &c. Et ibidem, Licet essent nunc incorrupti codices Graci & Ebrai, tamen cum eorum voces habeant tam varias significationes, nec Ecclesia hactenus definierit, quae earum sint retinenda, bene tamen in vulgata; Hinc est, istam esse priori loco venerandam, ad eamque ut lapidem Lydium seu ut clarius loquar, tanquam ad authenticam regulam fidei, semper esse recurrendum, etiam in levibus. * Posse vinus eam insignit hoc elogio, Columna veritatis & portus, ad quem ex tot dissentientium versionum fluctibus debeamus appellere. Nihil etiam dissimulant qui Indicem expurgatorium in Hispania compilarunt, Licet ea, inquiunt, quae Augustinus & Hieron. docuerunt (nempe de authoritate fontium) vera sint, tamen post Concilii Tridentini
units.tr: [Ludovicus de Tena, Isagoge ad Scripturam, book 1, Diff. 6, section 1, gives this decision: the Latin edition, the Vulgate, in all its places and parts is so authentic that it not only contains no error against the faith, but also infallible truth and the mind of the Holy Spirit in all its parts, however minute, no less than the original Scripture from which it was taken. Nor, to make it trustworthy, does it need recourse to that or any other text. "But even where it differs from the Hebrew now in existence, it is the true rule of faith," and so on. And in section 3: "Not only in those matters which are weighty and pertain to faith and morals, but also in all others, however slight, the Vulgate has no error. For since the Council commands that it be held as the authentic rule without any limitation, it must be admitted without exception, since a law speaking generally must be understood in the same way, and where it makes no distinction, we ought not to make one. Moreover, because the Council can lead to no error at all, not only a grave or pernicious one but any whatever, it would lead to error if there were any error in the Vulgate, even a slight one, etc." And in the same place: "Although the Greek and Hebrew codices were now uncorrupted, yet since their words have such various meanings, and the Church has not so far defined which of them are to be retained, the Vulgate is nevertheless rightly venerated; hence it is to be preferred to them, and always to be appealed to as the touchstone, or, to speak more clearly, as the authentic rule of faith, even in slight matters."] * Possevinus marked it with this praise: "the pillar of truth and the harbour to which we ought to make landfall amid the waves of so many dissenting versions." Nor do those who compiled the expurgatory Index in Spain conceal anything: "Although," they say, "what Augustine and Jerome taught (namely about the authority of the sources) is true, nevertheless, since the decree of the Council of Trent, it is not lawful to reject the testimonies of the Vulgate version on any pretext." Hence the same men, from the words of Fr. George Venetus, Problem 107, which indicate the words of the true text, struck out the little word "true," and rightly so, in the judgment of Mersenne in his examination of that problem.

units.la: {*} Biblioth. sel lib.1.c.8. dentini decretum non licet, vulgata versionis testimonia quovis pratextu rejicere. Unde iidem quoque ex verbis Fr. Georgii Veneti Problem. 107. quod indicant verba veri textus, voculam veri expunxerunt, idque recte, judice Marsenno in examine dicti problematis, nec enim textum aut versionem ullam recipimus, inquit, prater vulgatam Latinam. Audiamus etiam Gregorium de Valentia qui privata Epistola ad Serarium, 16. Octobris 1590. data, sic inquit, Summa, mi Pater, hac est, existimare me, authoritate & definitione Concilii Tridentini vulgatam Editionem Latinam omnibus Editionibus, cujuscunque sit idiomatis, fuisse pralatam. Uti apud Serarium videre est in proleg. Biblicis p. 119. Eadem mens erat Harto, qui in colloquio cum Rainoldo cap. 6. urget verbailla quovis pratextu, Si nemo illam, inquit, quovis pratextu rejicere poterit, non pratextu igitur Ebraici scripti. Egregie certe & nervose. Nullum enim pratextum admittit, qui quemvis excladit, inquit Mortonus. Hoc volunt, hoc sentiunt omnes illi Theologi, quos Mariana notat his verbis nostra ætate Theologi quidem statuunt tempora jam esse mutata, post promulgationem Concilii Trid. probatâque vulgatâ versione, Græca & Ebraa uno impetu concidisse. p. 99. Et quid sibi aliud volunt illi, qui interpretem Prophetam faciunt, ut inter alios etiam Petrus Sutor de translat. Bibliorum & Titelmannus de Edit. vulg. nec non isti, qui in eádem tantùm errores librariorum agnoscunt, ut Gregorius de Valentia Analys. Fid. 8.5. Christoph. Sacrobosc us defens. Conc. Trid. pro vulg. vers. 2.9. & alii, Alias eam ab omni errore emendatissimam, & nefas esse ei vel in minimis contradicere, statuentes. Quid Azorius Instit. Moral. 8.3. Et si per Hypothefin concedamus, Interpretem in versione errare potuisse, tamen non potuit Ecclesia in approbanda versione vulgatâ errare aut decipi. Et paulo post, mihi autem videtur verior eorum sententia, qui existimant Latinam, non modo in rebus fidei & morum, sed & in cæteris OMNIBVS errore carere. Nec defugiet, scio, authoritatem Ribera, si & ipsi hanc mentem adscripsero, Sic enim ille ad Habacuc cap.
units.tr: {*} Biblioth. sel lib.1.c.8. Since the decree of Trent does not allow the testimonies of the Vulgate version to be rejected on any pretext. Hence also the same men, from the words of Fr. Georgius Venetus, Problem. 107: Because the words indicate the true text, they have removed the little word "true", and rightly so, in the judgement of Marsennus in his examination of the said problem, for we accept neither the text nor any version, he says, except the Latin Vulgate. Let us also hear Gregorius de Valentia, who in a private letter to Serarius, dated 16 October 1590, speaks thus: The sum, my Father, is this: I think that by the authority and definition of the Council of Trent the Latin Vulgate edition has been preferred to all editions, of whatever language. As can be seen in Serarius, Prolegomena Biblica, p. 119. Harto held the same mind. In his conversation with Rainolds, chapter 6, he presses the words on any pretext: If no one can reject it on any pretext, then not on the pretext of the Hebrew text. Certainly an excellent and forceful argument. For he who excludes anything admits no pretext, says Morton. This is what all those theologians want and think, whom Mariana notes in these words: Theologians in our age indeed hold that the times have now changed, and that after the promulgation of the Council of Trent and the approval of the Vulgate version, the Greek and Hebrew have fallen in one assault. p. 99. And what else do those mean who make the translator a prophet, such as, among others, Petrus Sutor, On the Translation of the Bible, and Titelmannus, On the Vulgate Edition, and also those who recognise in it only scribal errors, such as Gregorius de Valentia, Analysis of the Faith 8.5, Christophorus Sacrobosco, Defence of the Council of Trent for the Vulgate Version 2.9, and others, holding it to be otherwise most free from every error, and that it is wrong to contradict it even in the smallest points. What does Azorius say, Institutiones Morales 8.3? And even if we concede by hypothesis that the translator could have erred in the version, nevertheless the Church could not err or be deceived in approving the Vulgate version. And a little later: But their opinion seems truer to me, who think that the Latin is free from error not only in matters of faith and morals, but also in ALL other things. Nor, I know, will he escape the authority of Ribera, if I also ascribe this mind to him. For thus he writes on Habakkuk, chapter

units.la: 1. Num. 13. mihi & omnibus, quibus vulgata Editionis sancta & inviolabilis est authoritas longè alia mens est. Neque enim fas esse duco credere, Ecclesiam aliquid pati in ista Editione, quod non sit dictatum à Spiritu Sancto. Et ut finem tandem faciam, quid sibi vult Regula 3. Pii IV. qua piis & doctis viris conceduntur, Episcoporum Judicio, aliorum versiones, modo hujusmodi versionibus tanquam elucidationibus (non fontium, sed) vulgata versione utantur? Cur in hanc solam edunt commentaria? Cur hanc in vernaculas linguas solam transfundi curant? Habes ergo, mi Lector genuinam decreti Tridentini interpretationem, non ab haereticis, sed germanis Ecclesiæ Romanæ filiis editam. Et quid authoritatibus allegandis me delassavi? nunquid contextus verborum id disertè indicat? Authentica pronunciatur vulgata Editio. Quid est authenticum? Juris Civilis Doctoribus authenticum idem est quod originale. Unde authentica tabula, authenticum instrumentum. Sed hanc notionem non admittent, (pero Pontificiii in præsenti decreto. Dicent vocari authenticam, quod ex originali sine errore translata sit. Gregorius de Valentia Analys. Fidei lib. 8. cap. 5. Esse versionem aliquam authenticam, inquit, nihil aliud est hoc loco, quàm esse eam OMNINO in sententiâ conformem scripturæ originali. Scilicet ex hac sententiâ Tridentini Patres fuerunt quasi Notarii publici, utor verbis Cl. Amesii, à Deo constituti, ut post institutam diligentem collationem hujus exempli sive copiæ, ut vocant, cum originali instrumento, & accuratam examinationem, certam ei fidem facerent. Illud ergo manet, decreto huic non posse suas constare rationes, nisi cum piis Theologis, qui pio utilique animo, verba Bannes, affecti sunt, decretum sic intelligamus, vulgatam nullo prorsus in loco interpretis ignorantiâ aut vitio esse depravatam, sed omnino per omnia, etiam minima, rectè fuisse interpretatam. Id quod prolixè in sequentibus sub Doctorum istorum nomine explicat & confirmat.
units.tr: 1. Num. 13. To me and to all those for whom the Vulgate edition has a holy and inviolable authority, the mind is quite different. For I do not think it right to believe that the Church suffers anything in that edition which has not been dictated by the Holy Spirit. And, to make an end at last, what does Rule 3 of Pius IV mean, by which pious and learned men are permitted, by the judgement of the bishops, to use the versions of others, provided they use such versions as elucidations (not of the sources, but) the Vulgate version? Why do they publish commentaries on that one alone? Why do they take care that only this one is translated into the vernacular languages? You have, then, my reader, the genuine interpretation of the decree of Trent, published not by heretics but by the true sons of the Roman Church. And why have I wearied myself with gathering authorities? Does not the wording of the text state this plainly? The Vulgate edition is pronounced authentic. What is authentic? For the doctors of civil law, authentic means the same as original. Hence an authentic record, an authentic instrument. But the Papists in the present decree will not admit this meaning. They will say that what is translated from the original without error is called authentic. Gregorius de Valentia, Analysis of the Faith, book 8, chapter 5: To be some authentic version, he says, is nothing else in this place than to be wholly in agreement in sense with the original Scripture. Clearly, on this view the Fathers of Trent were, as I use the words of the illustrious Amesius, like public notaries, appointed by God, so that after a diligent comparison of this copy, or as they call it, copy, with the original instrument, and a careful examination, they might give it certain credibility. It therefore remains that this decree cannot agree with its own reasons unless with the pious theologians, who, moved by a pious and useful spirit, as Bannes puts it, we understand the decree thus: that the Vulgate has in no place been corrupted by the translator's ignorance or fault, but has been rightly translated in every respect, even in the smallest points. This these doctors, under whose name he does so, explain and confirm at length in what follows.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Qua causa impulerint Romanam Eccl. ut rogarent hoc decretum. Recensentur tres. Barbaries, pervicacia & diffidentia. De Barbarie confessio Espensæi. Querela Cani & Cochlæi de Hæreticorum superbia. Quo loco fuerint Biblia ante Lutherum. In quas angustias redacti fuerint Pontificii tempore Lutheri. Pagnini laus. Cur ejus versio non Canonizata. Cur vulgata ei prælata.
units.tr: The causes that moved the Roman Church to request this decree. Three are listed: barbarism, obstinacy and distrust. On the barbarism, the confession of Espencaeus. The complaint of Cano and Cochlaeus about the arrogance of the heretics. In what condition the Bible was before Luther. The straits to which the Papists were reduced in Luther's time. The praise of Pagninus. Why his version was not canonized. Why the Vulgate was preferred to it.

units.la: VIdimus mentem rectumque Interpretamentum decreti. Postulat ordo, ut causas videamus, quæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ hoc decretum extorsère. Video eas reduci posse ad tria hæc capita. Barbariem istius ævi, Pervicaciam & causæ diffidentiam. De barbarie vel solus Claudius Espensaeus, Episcopus, omni exceptione major testis erat. Conqueritur ille commentariis in 1. ad Timoth. cap. 3. circa Reformationis initia eam inter ipsos quoque Clericos graflatam fuisse linguarum originalium ignorantiam & barbariem, ut in Latinis authoribus Graece nosse suspectum fuerit, Ebraice prope hareticum. Etsi vero bonus ille Episcopus non evaserit Expurgatorum censuram, honoratur tamen à Catholicissimo Genebrardo libro 4. Chronol. hoc elogio, quod ab haereticorum furiis fuerit alienissimus. Lutherani contrà, inquit Cochlæus, de peritia linguarum superbiebant. Quod si quis novitatibus eorum contradiceret, pratendebant statim lectionem Gracam vel Ebraicam, & continuò in Graecarum & Hebraicarum literarum ignaros plenis convitiorum plaustris invehebantur. Praterea inquit Canus, Authores Scholastici CCC. integris annis solam Editionem Latinam retinuerant, quippe linguae Graecae & Ebraicae non habuerunt peritiam. Et tamen in dogmatibus Theologicis confirmandis aut etiam in haeresibus refellendis multum confecere. Ideoque nec haereticae pravitatis inquisitores his magis nasutos esse decet. Multò minus cogi poterant, aut etiamnum possunt, ut in refutandis haereticis & puniendis, ad Graecam & Ebraeam VERITATEM, QVAM MINIME NOVERVNT, recurrant, indignumque est, ut à RE PRORSVS INCOGNITA gravissimi Tribunalis pendeat judicium. Absurdum insuper est, à nostratibus ad alienos, id est, Ebraeos & Graecos appellare: Impium denique est ad Judaeorum & Schismaticorum Senatum Catholicae fidei consultationem rejicere. Atque haec omnia eò tendunt, ut doceat Latinam Editionem inconcussè tenendam esse.
units.tr: We have seen the intention and the correct interpretation of the decree. The order of the argument now requires us to look at the causes that extorted this decree from the Roman Church. I think they can be reduced to these three heads: the barbarism of that age, obstinacy, and distrust of the sources. As to barbarism, Claudius Espencaeus, the bishop, is a witness beyond all objection. In his commentary on 1 Timothy 3 he complains that around the beginning of the Reformation a great ignorance and barbarism of the original languages had spread even among the clergy themselves, so that to know Greek was thought suspect among Latin authors, and Hebrew almost heretical. Although that good bishop did not escape the censure of the Expurgatory Index, the most Catholic Genebrardus honours him in book 4 of his Chronology with this praise: that he was most remote from the frenzy of the heretics. The Lutherans, on the other hand, says Cochlaeus, took pride in their skill in languages. If anyone contradicted their novelties, they at once put forward the reading of Greek or Hebrew, and they immediately attacked those ignorant of Greek and Hebrew letters with cartloads of insults. Furthermore, says Canus, the Scholastic authors kept to the Latin edition alone for three hundred full years, since they had no skill in Greek and Hebrew. And yet they achieved much in confirming theological doctrines, or even in refuting heresies. Therefore it is not fitting that the inquisitors of heretical depravity should be more inquisitive than these men. Much less could they be compelled, or can they still be compelled, to have recourse to the Greek and Hebrew TRUTH, WHICH THEY HAVE VERY LITTLE KNOWLEDGE OF, in refuting and punishing heretics, and it is unworthy that the judgment of the most serious tribunal should depend on a THING ENTIRELY UNKNOWN. It is absurd, moreover, to appeal from our own people to foreigners, that is, to the Hebrews and the Greeks. Lastly, it is impious to refer the consultation of the Catholic faith to the senate of the Jews and the schismatics. And all of this tends to teach that the Latin edition must be held without wavering.

units.la: Sed & notatu digna sunt consequa ejus verba, Enimverò, inquit, qui hanc nostram Editionem infirmare cupiunt, videntur mihi nihil aliud moliri, nisi occultum quoddam haereticorum patrocinium. Nempe Inquisitores despicient, qui scripturam Latinam tanquam certam regulam tenent, sum veritatis Graecae & Ebraicae ignorantia teneantur; Scholasticos authores despicient, qui vulgari Latino Interpreti suam fidem alligarunt, &c. Dispicient sanctos etiam priscos, qui Ebraicae etiam linguae peritiâ caruere. Haec Canus. Sed haec ipsa quoque Latina Editio ante B. Lutheri tempora à paucis versabatur. Annos suos consumebant in Decretis & Decretalibus, Thoma, Scoto, Magistro Sententiarum & Aristotele. Hos authores publicè praelegebant, in hos scribebant glossas & commentaria. Moses, Prophetae, Christus & Apostoli consilescebant. Si quis ad Scripturae lectionem accede-ret. ret is jam provectæ ætatis erat. Ante paucos annos, inquit * Ste-phanus, quidam ex Sorbonâ sic loquebatur, miror quid isti juvenes nobis semper allegent novum Testamentum, Perdiem, ego plus habebam quam quinquaginta annos, quod nesciebam quid esset novum Testamentum. Addit, eos, siquando rogarentur, quo loco novi Testamenti aliquid scriptum esset, respondere solitos, se illud quidem apud Hieronymum aut in decretis legisse, quid vero novum Testamentum esset, ignorare. Carolostadius, teste * Luthero, Biblia non nisi octavo post impetratum supremum in Theologiâ gradum, anno, legere coepit. Albertus Archi-Episcopus Maguntinus, cum anno 1530. in Comitiis Augustinis Codicem Biblicum, quem in mensa collocatum reperiebat, obiter aperuisset, foliaque ejus aliquot perlustrasset, hæc tandem dixisse fertur, Equidem nescio quid hoc libri sit. Illud video, omnia quæ eo continentur, nobis adversa esse. Cardinalem Hosium in confessione Petrocoviensi eò impietatis prolapsum fuisse scribunt, ut dicere haud erubuerit, longe meliori talo res Ecclesiæ (Romanæ videlicet) staturas fuisse, si nullum Euangelium scriptum fuisset. Quid miramur ergo, eos omnes ingenii vires in hoc unum intendisse, ut hunc librum perpetuis tenebris sepelirent. Accedit & illud, quod multi inter Pontificios, iique non infimi subsellii, Scripturæ Latinæ Interpretes, nesciverint, quo idiomate Paulus Epistolas suas scripserit, sicuti de Remigio ostendit Lud. Vives, comment. in August. de Civit. Dei 2. 21. Plerique autem omnes, qui in tantâ otiosorum hominum multitudine Scripturam versabant, eam ita exponebant, & ad qualiacunque dogmata sic trahebant, ac si cereus aliquis nasus fuisset. Cardinalis Cusanus docebat, scripturas alio atque alio modo pro temporis ratione accipi & exponi posse, id quod Duræus in Anti-Witakerianis, sol. 45. utroque pollice approbavit. Hi fuerunt natales, atque hæc educatio monstri istius informis, quod Theologiam Scholasticam vocamus. Fontes autem sic oderant, ut plusquam probabile hæreseos argumentum fuerit, si quis eos versaret, iis adhærescceret, atque ad eos provocaret, id quod Reuchlinus, Erasmus, & istius ordinis quamplurimi alii, cætera Pontificii, abunde experti sunt.
units.tr: But the words that follow are also worth noting. Indeed, says he, those who want to weaken our edition seem to me to be undertaking nothing other than a hidden patronage of the heretics. Namely, they will despise the inquisitors, who hold the Latin Scripture as a certain rule, while they are held by ignorance of the Greek and Hebrew truth; they will despise the Scholastic authors, who tied their faith to the common Latin translator, etc. They will despise even the holy men of old, who lacked skill in the Hebrew language too. So Canus. But even before the time of the blessed Luther, this same Latin edition was known to few. They spent their years on the Decretum and the Decretals, on Thomas, Scotus, the Master of the Sentences and Aristotle. These authors they lectured on publicly; on these they wrote glosses and commentaries. Moses, the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles were kept in the background. If anyone approached the reading of Scripture, he was already advanced in years. A few years ago, says Stephanus, a certain man from the Sorbonne used to speak thus: "I wonder why these young men always cite the New Testament to us." For I, who was more than fifty years old, did not know what the New Testament was. He adds that when such men were asked, if they were ever asked, in what place of the New Testament something was written, they used to reply that they had indeed read it in Jerome or in the decrees, but what the New Testament was they did not know. Carlstadt, according to Luther, only began to read the Bible in the eighth year after he had gained his highest degree in theology. Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, when in 1530 at the Diet of Augsburg he happened to open a Bible which he found lying on a table, and leafed through some of its pages, is said finally to have said: "Truly, I do not know what sort of book this is. This I see, that everything contained in it is against us." They write that Cardinal Hosius in his Confession of Petrikau fell so far into impiety that he did not blush to say that the affairs of the Church (of Rome, that is) would have stood on a much better footing if no Gospel had ever been written. Why then are we surprised that all of them bent the strength of their intellects to this one end, that they should bury this book in perpetual darkness? To this must be added that many among the Papists, and not those of the lowest bench, who were translators of the Latin Scripture, did not know in what language Paul wrote his Epistles, as Ludovicus Vives shows about Remigius in his commentary on Augustine's City of God, 2.21. Moreover, almost all of those who, in so great a multitude of idle men, handled Scripture, expounded it in such a way and dragged it to whatever doctrines they pleased, as if it were a nose of wax. Cardinal Cusanus taught that the Scriptures can be understood and expounded in one way or another according to the circumstances of the time, a view which Duraeus, in his Anti-Whitakerians, page 45, approved with both thumbs. These were the origins and this the upbringing of that shapeless monster which we call Scholastic Theology. They hated the sources so much that it was more than a probable proof of heresy if anyone read them, adhered to them, or appealed to them. Reuchlin, Erasmus, and very many others of that order, the Papists have amply experienced this in other cases as well.

units.la: Sed de babarie res ita nota est, ut frustra futurus sim, si vel verbum amplius addam. De pertinacia & diffidentiâ causæ videamus amplius. Primi Reformatores nolebant Aduersarios suos hac ripâ sequi. Nihil apud ipsos ponderis habebant Scholasticorum placita, vel Traditionum μορμολυκεῖα; Provocabant ad Scripturam. Hic laborabant Monachi, hic sudabant, hic timidis refugiebat sanguen, atque exalbescebant metu. Magis versati erant in scriptis humanis quam divinis. Sed non hoc termino stetit cordolium. Non contenti iidem vulgatæ Latinæ textu, ad ipsos fontes provocabant. Cogita Lector, quid animi bonis istis viris fuerit. Quid enim? an hoc gratificarentur hæreticis, ut linguas Originales discerent, ut fontes, Christianorum dogmatum principia agnoscerent? An æquum erat, ipsos inquisitoribus & Scholasticis, qui harum linguarum ignari fuêre, esse nasutiores? Ipsi feliciter satis adversus hæreticos depugnaverant: Cur non hi facerent idem? Iam hæresèos maculam inusserant iis, qui linguis istis navabant operam, legentes hâc in re vestigia Pauli II. qui teste Platina, humanitatis studia ita oderat, ut ejus studiosos ad unum omnes haereticorum nomine verberare consueverit. Et quid, quæso te, fuisset stultius, quam admittere eum textum, quem legere non poterant? In conciliis generalibus aut paucissimos aut interdum nullos fuisse linguæ Ebraeæ peritos, ingenua Bellarmini confessio est, de V.D. lib. 2. 10. non meliora de sui ævi Episcopis & Abbatibus promittere sibi audebat Paulus III, quando Concilium Tridenti indicebat. Ipsi Patres suæ sibi hac in parte tenuitatis optime conscii erant. Quàm inconsideratè itaque & temerè, addo & pueriliter fecisset, si istas Editiones, quas illi ne legere quidem poterant, quas semper crepabant hæretici, quas plerisque erroribus suis adversari, vel ex nova Pagnini versione colligere poterant, declarassent authenticas? Videbant tamen se honeste Scripturam rejicere non posse. Videbant aliquem textum signandum esse, qui pro authenticis Scripturæ tabulis reciperetur. Providendum ergo censuerunt Ecclesiæ de ejusmodi textu, quem non omnes Laici, (ἰκὰς ἰκὰς ἐςτ βίβλοι) sed omnes saltem Episcopi & Clerici intelligerent. LATINAM ergo delegerunt, quam ab omnibus Episcopis intelligi, hoc ipso nobis voluere persuasum, licet * Alphonsus de Castro de plerisque Pontificibus, Episcoporum Episcopis, diserte afferat, eos adeo fuisse illiteratos, ut Grammaticam (Latinam intelligit) penitus ignorarint. Sed nec Latinam sine delectu. Variæ Editiones Latinæ circumferebantur. Pagninus ex ordine Prædicatorum Monachus cum animadvertisset (verba Sixti Senen-
units.tr: But the matter of barbarism is so well known that I would labour in vain if I added even a word more. Let us look further at the causes of obstinacy and distrust. The first Reformers were unwilling to follow their adversaries on this bank. The opinions of the Scholastics and the bugbears of tradition [μορμολυκεῖα] carried no weight with them; they appealed to Scripture. Here the monks laboured, here they sweated, here timid blood fled away and they turned pale with fear. They were more practised in human writings than in divine ones. But their zeal did not stop at this boundary. Not content with the text of the Latin Vulgate, they appealed to the sources themselves. Consider, reader, what the minds of those good men must have been. For what? Should they have gratified the heretics by learning the original languages, so as to recognize the sources, the principles of Christian doctrines? Was it fair that they should be keener than the inquisitors and Scholastics, who were ignorant of these languages? They had fought against the heretics quite successfully enough: why should these men not do the same? Already they had branded with the stain of heresy those who devoted their labour to those languages, following in this matter the footsteps of Paul II, who, according to Platina, so hated the study of humanity that he was accustomed to beat all its students, one and all, under the name of heretics. And what, I ask you, would have been more foolish than to admit a text which they could not read? In the general councils either very few or sometimes none have been skilled in the Hebrew language, is the frank confession of Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 2, chapter 10. Paul III did not dare to promise himself anything better from the bishops and abbots of his own time when he summoned the Council of Trent. The Fathers themselves were well aware of their own slightness in this respect. How inconsiderately and rashly, I would add how childishly, would they have acted if they had declared authentic those editions which they could not even read, which the heretics always decried, which they could gather from the new version of Pagninus to be opposed to many of their errors? Yet they saw that they could not honourably reject Scripture. They saw that some text had to be designated which would be accepted as the authentic records of Scripture. They therefore decided that provision should be made for the Church with a text of this kind, one that not all laymen [ἰκὰς ἰκὰς ἐςτ βίβλοι] but at least all bishops and clergy would understand. They therefore chose the Latin, which, by the very fact that all bishops understood it, they wished us to be persuaded of, although Alphonsus de Castro plainly asserts of most of the Pontiffs, the bishops of bishops, that they were so unlettered that they were utterly ignorant of grammar (of Latin, I mean). But not even the Latin without selection. Various Latin editions were in circulation. Pagninus, a monk of the Order of Preachers, when he had observed (the words of Sixtus of Siena) that the Vulgate had been corrupted for the most part either by the injury of time or by the carelessness of men, with Leo X encouraging him, after consulting the best Hebrew manuscripts, translated the whole of the Old Testament from Hebrew truth into Latin with all the faith and diligence he could muster.

units.la: * adversus Haereses I.1. cap. 4. Senensis) Vulgatam vel temporum injuria, vel hominum incuria maximâ ex parte fuisse corruptam, Leone X * HORTANTE, consultis optimis Ebraeorum exemplaribus, quantâ valebat fide & industriâ, omne V. Test. Ex Ebraicâ veritate Latinitate donaverat. Hanc multi probabant; Αλλ' ἐκ Ἀπρὼν Ἀχαμίμων ἠδαντ' ἡμῶ.
units.tr: *Against Heresies I.1, ch. 4, Sixtus of Siena: The Vulgate, either through the injury of time or the carelessness of men, had been corrupted for the most part; and Leo X, encouraging the work, having consulted the best Hebrew manuscripts, translated the whole Old Testament from Hebrew truth into Latin, with all the faith and diligence he could muster. Many approved this. [Αλλ' ἐκ Ἀπρὼν Ἀχαμίμων ἠδαντ' ἡμῶ.] (The Greek is a corrupt line; the sense is: "But this has come from the Achaeans, and we have it.")

units.la: Non conveniebat ea Patrum institutio. Quin & si forte convenisset, atque hoc modo considerata cum vulgatâ æquis passibus inambulassent, tamen honorem istum Pagnino & Dominicanorum ordini invidisset livor. Itum ergo ad Latinam veterem est, quam plerisque Ecclesiæ Romanæ erroribus haud leviter patrocinari, longo annorum usu didicerant. Irrepserat in codices ejus vox IPSA. Gen. 3.15. Inde idololatricas B. Virginis laudes stabilitum ivêre. Ex locis Gen. 6.5. & Luc. 2.14. pravè conversis viribus liberi Arbitrii quæsitum fuit velamentum. a Missam, b purgatorium, c limbum, d meritum congrui & condigni, e adorationem Sanctorum, f imaginum, g rerum sacrarum, h infallibilitatem conciliorum, i incertitudinem gratiæ, aliosque insuper errores loca ejus aliquot vel manifestè vel in speciem stat-uminabant, quibus ex textu originali aliisve versionibus nihil sperabant patrocinii.
units.tr: That teaching of the Fathers did not agree with it. Indeed, even if it had agreed, and had been weighed on equal terms against the Vulgate, envy would still have begrudged that honour to Pagninus and to the Dominican order. So they returned to the old Latin, which, through long years of use, they had learned to defend rather freely for most of the errors of the Roman Church. The word IPSA had crept into its manuscripts (Gen. 3.15), and from there they went on to establish idolatrous praises of the Blessed Virgin. From the passages Gen. 6.5 and Luke 2.14, wrongly rendered, a cover was sought for free will. They propped up with several of its passages, either openly or in appearance, a the Mass, b purgatory, c limbo, d merit of congruity and of condignity, e the worship of the saints, f of images, g of sacred relics, h the infallibility of councils, i the uncertainty of grace, and other errors besides; from the original text or other versions they hoped for no support for these.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Sectio I. Quibus difficultatibus in ipso concilio pressum sit hoc decretum. Aloïsii Catinæi libera vox. Cajetani judicium. Proponuntur difficultates IV. post concilium à Catholicis notæ. 1. difficultas eorum, qui statuunt in vulgatâ esse errores Interpretis. Quomodo illi sudent in conciliandâ sua sententia cum verbis decreti. Quos patronos sua limitationis advocent. Qui rursus adversentur & quibus argumentis. Iterum de voce Authentica. Ipse Hieron. fateatur se errasse. Quid ad hoc respondeatur. Sectione II. proponitur secunda difficultas, eorum, qui textum Ebr. pro incorrupto habent, & fontibus nihil derogatum statuunt. Quomodo hi explicent decretum. Gretzeri Sophistica & contradictiones. Sectione III. hæc proponuntur. III. diff. eorum qui dicunt ex decreto, ut vulgo exponitur, sequi, Græcos non habuisse Editionem authenticam. IV. Diff. Ante Concilium Trid. Ecclesiam non habuisse Scripturam authent. hent. Imo ne quidem ante annum 1590, quo emendata prodiit. Examinatur articulus ille decreti de emendatissimâ Editione. Ostenditur, eum Typographos concernere & praeter mentem concilii ad correctionem Papalem extendi. Quâ occasione id factum sit. Ex hypothesi proponuntur 4. consectaria in seqq. prolixius declaranda.
units.tr: Section I. The difficulties this decree met with at the council itself. The free voice of Aloysius Catinaeus. The judgment of Cajetan. Four difficulties raised by Catholics after the council. (1) The difficulty of those who hold that the Vulgate contains errors of the translator. How they sweat to reconcile their view with the words of the decree. Which patrons they call on for their limitation. Who in turn oppose it, and with what arguments. Again on the word "authentic". Jerome himself confesses that he erred. What is answered to this. Section II. The second difficulty is put forward, of those who regard the Hebrew text as uncorrupted and hold that nothing has been taken from the sources. How these men explain the decree. Gretser's sophistries and contradictions. Section III. These points are put forward. The third difficulty, of those who say that, as the decree is commonly explained, it follows that the Greeks had no authentic edition. The fourth difficulty: that before the Council of Trent the Church had no authentic Scripture. Indeed, not even before the year 1590, when the corrected edition appeared. That article of the decree about the most correct edition is examined. It is shown that it concerns the printers and was extended, contrary to the council's intention, to papal correction. The occasion on which this happened. On this hypothesis four corollaries are put forward, to be declared at greater length in what follows.

units.la: VIdimus sensum mentemque decreti. Vidimus causas. Restat ut proponamus difficultates, quibus ipsi Catholici hoc ipsum pressere, atque etiamnum exagitant. In ipso concilio non decerant, qui illud iniquum esse asserebant. Fr. Aloisus Catanaeus diserte pronunciabat, nullam omnino versionem eo modo recipi posse, salvo decreto, ut veterum, quod in jure Canonico extat. Citabant Cardinalem Cajetanum, asserens, eum, postquam 1523. in Germaniâ Legationem Pontificis nomine obiisset, dicere fuisse solitum, unicum haereticos refellendi & convertendi medium ex genuino intellectu sensus literalis in Originali linguâ petendum esse, ipsumque huic studio xi. reliquos vitae suae annos impendisse. Addebat, Cajetanum dicere solitum, eum qui Latinum solummodo textum intelligeret, dici non posse infallibile Dei verbum intelligere. Talis enim, inquiebat solummodo intelligit vocem interpretis, qui errare potest. Saepe denique optasse, eum SS. Literas interpretandi modum à superioris aevi doctoribus observatum & excultum fuisse, plenéque fuisse persuasum, Lutheranas haereses non fuisse exorituras. Post peractam Concilii fabulam, variae, uti supra attigimus, opiniones circa hoc decretum proponi & defendi coeperunt. Alii asserebant, authorem vulgatae Latinae Prohetam fuisse ac errare non potuisse, aut saltem, ut ut Interpres errare potuerit, Ecclesiam in approbanda eâ versione errare non potuisse. Vulgatam praedictam non solum in iis quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, sed & in caeteris OMNIBUS omni errore carere, ac proinde nullo praetextu, ne textus quidem originalis, eam esse rejiciendam: quorum verba cap.6. produximus. Alii contrà docebant, hoc decreto Concilium nihil voluisse Fontibus derogatum, Interpretem hominem fuisse ac proinde non solum errare potuisse, sed & erasse. Testor Jesuitam Azorium, cujus haec sunt verba, Instit moral. lib.8. cap. 3. Multi, inquit, qui post Concilium Tridentinum scripsêre, ut Vega, Sixtus Senensis, Andradius, Lindanus, Canus, fatentur aliquES quos esse in vulgatâ Latinâ errores, non solum vitiò scriptorum, sed etiam ipsius Interpretis incuriâ vel ignorantiâ. Lyrae, Burgensi, Isidoro Clario, Steucho, Driedoni, Hieron. ab Oleastro, Cajetano, Joh. Benedicto, aliisque vetustioribus eadem mens fuit. An ergo in his quoque ubi Interpres lapsus est, locis & partibus vulgata pro authentica habenda est? An in istis non licet a vulgatâ ad fontes provocare? non certè, si verba decreti, prout sonant, & vulgò a Pontificiis intelliguntur, accipiamus. E. gratiâ, Disputo cum Pontificio de Invocatione Sanctorum. Objicit mihi cum Eccio, Canisio & Monachis Burdigalensibus locum * Gen. 48. 16. Provoco ad textum Ebraeum, qui, testibus quamplurimis Pontificiis, exempli gratiâ, Ribera Cajetano, Hectore Pinto, Oleastrio, longè aliud sonat. Quaeritur, an consistere possit istiusmodi provocatio cum Decreto? Non putem. Iam enim hanc particulam vulgatae Latinae rejicio, & praetextu textus Ebraici eam non admitto. An ergo omnes isti, qui Interpreti errores aliquot ascribunt, decretum insuper habent? Hoc nunquam dabunt, nunquam fatebuntur. Quid ergo? Inventum est effugium. Decreti mens est, inquit Bellarminus, in iis praesertim quae ad fidem & mores spectant, nulla esse in hac versione Interpretum errata. Subdole adjecit vocalem praesertim. Ostensum satis superque jam est, Pontificiorum alios hanc versionem in OMNIBUS extra omnis omnino erroris suspicionem ponere: alios contrà eam non ubique, sed in locis ad fidem & mores pertinentibus ab errore immunem pronunciare. Satis ostendit Bellarminus, quarum sit partium, inquit Cl. Amesius, sed tamen ne secus sentientibus adversari videretur, de effugio sibi prospexit in vocula praesertim; Sic enim verba sua posset interpretari. Interpretes vulgatae immunes ab errore fuisse in omnibus partibus & particulis suae versionis, sed extra periculum erroris magis adhuc positos fuisse in iis, quae ad fidem & mores spectant. Quaeramus ergo, qui clarius animi sui sententiam expresserè. Canus ergo lib. 2. c. 13. concl. 1. Editionem hanc retinendam concludit in his omnibus, quae ad fidem & mores spectant, & concl. 2. omnes de fide & moribus quaestiones per eam esse definiendas. Et 4. In his, quae sunt fidei & morum, non esse Latina exemplaria ex Ebraicis & Graecis corrigenda. Gretzerus quoque, qui aliquando sic loquitur ut eam ubique extra omnem errorem ponat, non semel eadem restrictione utitur. Pag. enim
units.tr: We have seen the sense and intention of the decree. We have seen its causes. It remains to set out the difficulties by which the Catholics themselves have been pressed by this very decree, and which they still wrestle with. At the council itself there were not lacking those who declared it unjust. Friar Aloysius Catinaeus stated plainly that no version at all could be accepted in the manner of the decree, saving the decree, as the ancient version that is found in canon law. They cited Cardinal Cajetan, who, after he had discharged a papal legation in Germany in 1523, was said to have often declared that the only means of refuting and converting heretics was to be sought in the genuine sense of the literal text in the original language, and that he had devoted the remaining eleven years of his life to this study. He added that Cajetan used to say that one who understood only the Latin text could not be said to understand the infallible word of God; for such a person, he said, understands only the voice of the translator, who can err. Finally, he often wished that the method of interpreting Holy Scripture observed and cultivated by the teachers of the earlier age had been kept, and he was fully persuaded that the Lutheran heresies would not have arisen. After the play of the council was over, various opinions about this decree, as we touched on above, began to be put forward and defended. Some asserted that the author of the Latin Vulgate was a prophet and could not err, or at least that, however much the translator might have erred, the Church could not have erred in approving that version. They held that the aforesaid Vulgate is free from all error not only in matters pertaining to faith and morals but in ALL other matters as well, and that therefore, on no pretext, not even that of the original text, is it to be rejected: whose words we quoted in chapter 6. Others, on the contrary, taught that the council by this decree had intended no detraction from the sources, that the translator was a man, and that therefore he could not only err but also had erred. I call as witness the Jesuit Azor, whose words are these, in his Institutiones morales, book 8, chapter 3: "Many who wrote after the Council of Trent, such as Vega, Sixtus of Siena, Andradius, Lindanus and Canus, admit that there are some errors in the Latin Vulgate, due not only to the fault of the copyists but also to the carelessness or ignorance of the translator himself." Lyra, Burgensis, Isidore Clarius, Steuchus, Driedo, Jerome of Oleaster, Cajetan, John Benedict and other older writers had the same mind. Is then the Vulgate to be held authentic even in those places and parts where the translator has slipped? Or is it not permitted in those places to appeal from the Vulgate to the sources? Certainly not, if we take the words of the decree as they sound and as they are commonly understood by the Papists. For example: I am disputing with a Papist about the invocation of the saints. He objects to me, with Eck, Canisius and the Bordeaux monks, the passage Gen. 48:16. I appeal to the Hebrew text, which, as many Papists testify, for example Ribera, Cajetan, Hector Pinto and Oleaster, sounds quite different. The question is whether such an appeal can stand together with the decree. I do not think so. For I now reject this phrase of the Latin Vulgate, and on the pretext of the Hebrew text I do not admit it. Do all those, then, who ascribe some errors to the translator thereby hold the decree in contempt? They will never admit this, never confess it. What then? A way out has been found. The intention of the decree, says Bellarmine, is that in those matters especially which pertain to faith and morals there are no errors of the translators in this version. He slyly added the word especially. It has been shown well enough, and more than enough, that some Papists place this version in ALL things beyond every suspicion of error, while others, on the contrary, pronounce it free from error not everywhere but in the places pertaining to faith and morals. Bellarmine has sufficiently shown on which side he stands, says the distinguished Amesius; yet, lest he seem to oppose those who think otherwise, he provided himself with an escape in the little word especially. For his words could be interpreted thus: the translators of the Vulgate were free from error in all the parts and particulars of their version, but were placed more beyond the danger of error in those things which pertain to faith and morals. Let us therefore seek those who have expressed their opinion more clearly. Canus, then, in book 2, chapter 13, conclusion 1, concludes that this edition is to be retained in all those things which pertain to faith and morals, and in conclusion 2 that all questions of faith and morals are to be decided by it. And in the fourth: In those matters which belong to faith and morals, the Latin copies are not to be corrected by the Hebrew and Greek. Gretser also, who at times speaks in such a way as to place it everywhere beyond all error, more than once uses the same restriction. For, on page

units.la: 537. Editionis hujus authoritatem ita exponit, ut Spiritus Sancti sententiam ubique assequatur, quod ad doctrinam & mores attinet. Vide etiam pag.542. Et pag. 560. non ita probavit Ecclesia Editionem vulgatam, quasi nullum in ea reperiatur vocabulum non satis aptè ex Ebraeo versum, sed in iis quae ad fidem & m. pertinent, hanc editionem declaravit authenticam. Joh. Sacrobosco apud eundem Gretzerum pag. 541. Cum dicimus, inquit, nos habere Scripturam Latinè sermone authenticam, aliud nihil volumus, quam nostram translationem esse verum Dei verbum integrum, incorruptum, ex quo grex Christi doceri, & quaestiones de fide & moribus intrepidè definiri queant. Vega lib. 15. cap. 9. Versionem hanc ita esse authenticam statuit, ut certò sciant fideles, nullum inde haberi posse periculosum errorem, & tutò illam & citra periculum legi posse. Et postea. Eatenus voluit Synodus eam haberi authenticam, ut certum omnibus esset, nullo eam deformatam errore, ex quo perniciosum aliquod dogma in fide & moribus colligi posset. Eadem est Driedonis sententia lib. 2. cap. 1. Quos duos citat & sequitur Andradius, Defens. Conc. Trid. lib. 4. Ita quoque statuunt Senensis in fine lib. 8. Biblioth. & Serarius Proleg.
