Bibl. cap.19. qu.11. Summa huc redit, In rebus fidei & morum vulgatam à Tridentinis authenticam esse declaratam. In caeteris non item. Lapsus enim subinde est Interpres. Quid ad haec Patres Tridentini dicerent si viverent? Quid illi Decreti Interpretes, Cardinales & Theologi quos * supra produximus? Illi ajebant vulgatam omni in OMNIBUS errore carere, retinendamque ad minimum jota & apicem; Interpretem prophetam fuisse, ac errare non potuisse: Et ut ut errare potuerit Interpres, Ecclesiam tamen in approbanda ista versione non potuisse errare. Contrà Driedo, Hieronymus traducens sacram Scripturam, inquit, egit quidem negotium totius Ecclesiae quae non fallitur, sed non inde consequens est, editionem ejus usquam aberrare ab Ebraica veritate. Aliud enim est jussu Ecclesiae novum Test. castigare, aliud est id quod castigatum est, jussu Ecclesiae, in singulis libris sic approbare, ut non liceat unquam haesitare aut dubitare, ne forte interpres non recte verterit. Neque enim tenemur, inquit, credere, cujusquam Editionem sic esse in omnib. consonam, nisi vel eam ad suum fontem conferentes, talem esse videamus, vel Ecclesia universalis aut Spiritu S. aut experientia edocta, authoritate suâ definiat, eam penitus sic consonam esse, nihil autem horum factum esse credit Driedo. Quid ad haec alii? Quin, inquiet ad-verversarius, nunquid vides vocem Authentica in decreto? Quid est authenticum annon vel orginale, vel exemplum ex originali sine errore transumptum? Respondet pro Driedone Andradius, sol. mihi 361. An Authentici vocabulum, quo Synodus utitur, tantam hanc cum Ebraeis fontibus convenientiam pra se gerat, non desunt Viri eruditi qui dubitent. Juris enim consulti, sumpto ex Graecis vocabulo, Authentica ea scripta appellant, qua fidem in judiciis faciunt, & certam ac publicam authoritatem habent. Quare uir eruditissimus, Fr. Andreas Vega, qui Concilio Tridentino sub Paulo tertio maximâ cum laude interfuit, multis confirmat, Tridentinos Patres, cum vulgatam authenticam pronunciârunt, nihil aliud significare voluisse, quàm nullo eam deformatam errore existere, ex quo perniciosum aliquod dogma in fide & moribus, colligi posset. Ne vero hanc Concilii mentem fuisse dubitare quis posset, testem ea de re citat gravissimum Cardinalem S. Crucis, Concilii tunc Legatum, omni virtutum genere clarissimum, postea verò Pontificem Optim. Maxim. & Marcellum II. appellatum, a quo illud se inquit pridie quàm hoc decretum rogaretur, accepisse, & postea id ipsum confirmantem & obtestantem non semel audivisse. Eadem habet Mariana in tractatu de Vulgatâ Versione cap. 20. & 23. nec non Serarius, qui & illud insuper addit, Hoc scripsit Vega, cum Cardinalis ille adhuc superstes esset, possetque de totâ re interrogari. Huic testi alium addit Mariana, vid. Jacobum Laines, Iesuitarum generalem, qui & ipse concilio interfuerit, quorum testimoniis eam fidem habet Serarius, ut audacter concludat, Eam, quae à Conc. Trid. Vulgatae versioni tribuitur, authoritatem non esse infinitè accipiendam, sed definitè, certis cum modificationibus. Tanta eos sollicitat cura, ut lectoribus suis persuadere possint, suam sententiam decreto nequaquam adversari. Sed frustrà, Quod enim ad Vegam attinet, Collegium delegatorum Cardinalium nullas agit ei gratias, quin potius acri cum notat censurâ, quod tam audacter hac de re locutus sit. Nec etiam Cardinalis S. Crucis licet postea Pontificis, & Jacobi Laines testimonia efficere potuerunt, quominus Theologi aliquot, in Hispania, in vincula & carceres hoc solo nomine compacti fuerint. Et ut ut Vega exverbis ipsis decreti, aliisque consuetis concilii approbationibus, eam, quam ipse Decreto affingit mentem, probare satagat, tamen nulli cordato persuadebit. Etenim si haec vel Concilio, aut majori saltem ejus parti, aut summo, sine cujus approbatione nulla concilia ullius sunt authoritatis, Pontifici mens fuit, cur non hanc vel similem aliquam limitationem adhibuêre? Cur non delegati Cardinales ita interpretati sunt? Et cum gravissimæ hac de re contentiones inter Catholicos ortæ sint, quarum hodieque magnâ animorum impotentia reciprocatur ferra, cum tot devoti Romanæ Sedis Filii, Pontificis decisionem ardentissimis precibus expetant, cur nihil definit Pontifex? Cur nullis exorabulis se exorari sinit; Et si verum dicendum est, valde frigidum hoc effugium est, eam authenticam solummodo pronunciatam in rebus fidei & morum, atque ita declaratam esse authenticam, ut certò sciant fideles, nullum inde haberi posse periculosum errorem & tutò illam posse legi, &c. Quid enim tunc prærogativæ hoc decreto ad vulgatam Editionem accessit, quod non versioni quoque Paganinianæ (ut de hæreticorum Editionibus taceam) tribui possit.
units.tr: 537. He explains the authority of this edition as following the sense of the Holy Spirit throughout, so far as doctrine and morals are concerned. See also p. 542, and p. 560: the Church did not so approve the Vulgate edition as if no word in it were found that had not been rendered aptly from the Hebrew, but it declared this edition authentic in those matters which pertain to faith and morals. John Sacrobosco, quoted by the same Gretser, p. 541: When we say, he says, that we have Scripture authentic in the Latin language, we want nothing else than that our translation be the true, entire, uncorrupted Word of God, from which the flock of Christ may be taught and questions of faith and morals may be fearlessly settled. Vega, book 15, chapter 9, holds that this version is authentic so that the faithful may know for certain that no dangerous error can be derived from it, and that it may be read safely and without peril. And afterwards: So far the Synod wished it to be held authentic, that it should be certain to everyone that it has not been deformed by any error from which some pernicious dogma in faith and morals could be inferred. Driedo's opinion is the same, book 2, chapter 1. Andradius, in his Defence of the Council of Trent, book 4, cites and follows these two; so too Sixtus of Siena at the end of book 8 of the Bibliotheca, and Serarius, Prolegomena to the Bible, chapter 19, question 11, hold the same. The sum comes to this: the Tridentine Fathers declared the Vulgate authentic in matters of faith and morals; in other respects not so, since the translator sometimes slips. What would the Tridentine Fathers say to this if they were alive? What would those interpreters of the decree, the cardinals and theologians whom I cited above, say? They said that the Vulgate is free from error in ALL things, and that not so much as a jot or a tittle should be given up; that the translator was a prophet and could not err; and that even if the translator could err, the Church could not err in approving that version. Against this, Driedo: Jerome, in translating Holy Scripture, indeed carried out a task for the whole Church, which does not err; but it does not follow from this that his edition anywhere strays from Hebrew truth. For it is one thing to correct the New Testament by the command of the Church; it is another to approve, in each book, what has been so corrected by the command of the Church, in such a way that it is never allowed to hesitate or doubt lest perhaps the translator did not translate correctly. For we are not bound, he says, to believe that anyone's edition is so consonant in every respect, unless either we see it, comparing it with its source, to be such, or the universal Church, taught by the Holy Spirit or by experience, defines by its own authority that it is wholly consonant; but Driedo believes that none of this has been done. What do others say to this? "But," the opponent will say, "do you not see the word Authentic in the decree? What is authentic, if not either the original or a copy taken from the original without error?" Andradius answers on behalf of Driedo, solution to my objection 361: Whether the word Authentic, which the Synod uses, carries such agreement with the Hebrew sources, learned men are not lacking who doubt. For jurists, taking the word from the Greek, call authentic those writings which carry credit in judicial proceedings and have a certain and public authority. Hence the most learned man, Fr. Andreas Vega, who took part in the Council of Trent under Paul III with the greatest distinction, confirms with many arguments that the Tridentine Fathers, when they pronounced the Vulgate authentic, meant nothing other than that it exists undeformed by any error from which some pernicious dogma in faith and morals could be inferred. Lest anyone doubt that this was the mind of the Council, he cites as witness the most weighty Cardinal of Santa Croce, then the Council's legate, most distinguished in every kind of virtue, afterwards called the most excellent and greatest Pontiff and Marcellus II, from whom he says he received this the day before this decree was requested, and afterwards heard him confirming and affirming the same thing more than once. The same is found in Mariana, On the Vulgate Version, chapters 20 and 23, and also in Serarius, who adds this moreover: Vega wrote this while that Cardinal was still alive and could be questioned about the whole matter. To this witness Mariana adds another, James Laynez, general of the Jesuits, who was himself also present at the council; trusting their testimonies, Serarius holds the view, and boldly concludes that the authority which the Council of Trent assigns to the Vulgate version is not to be taken as unlimited but as definite, with certain modifications. So great is the care that troubles them, that they may persuade their readers that their opinion by no means conflicts with the decree. But in vain. For as far as Vega is concerned, the college of delegated cardinals gives him no thanks; rather, it sharply censures him for speaking so boldly on this matter. Nor could the testimony of the Cardinal of Santa Croce, though afterwards Pope, nor that of James Laynez, prevent several theologians in Spain from being bound in chains and prisons on this ground alone. And although Vega, from the very words of the decree and other customary approvals of the council, strives to prove the intention which he himself attaches to the decree, he will persuade no sensible person. For if this was the mind of the Council, or at least of its greater part, or of the Pope, without whose approval no council has any authority, why did they not add this or some similar limitation? Why did the delegated cardinals not interpret it so? And since most grave contentions over this matter have arisen among Catholics, which even today are kept up with great fury of spirits, while so many devoted sons of the Roman See beg for the Pontiff's decision with most ardent prayers, why does the Pontiff define nothing? Why does he allow himself to be moved by no entreaties? And, if the truth must be told, this is a very cold escape: that it was pronounced authentic only in matters of faith and morals, and declared authentic in such a way that the faithful may know for certain that no dangerous error can be derived from it, and may read it safely, and so on. For what prerogative has then been added to the Vulgate edition by this decree, which could not equally be attributed to the Pagnine version (not to mention the editions of the heretics)?

units.la: Eam enim Tholo gi Lovanienses, & Arias Montanus, non sine Pontificis, Hispaniarumque Monarchæ approbatione, omnium TVTISSIMAM judicarunt, quæ in Regiis Bibliis Ebraeo textui adnecteretur. Et quod ad illam glossam, quam ad ravim usque moderatiores isti ingeminant, in rebus Fidei & morum, attinet, ubi hoc dicit decretum? non est distinguendum ubi lex non distinguit, cum verbo unico distinguere atque hoc pacto sententiam jam tum à multis defensam constabilire potuisset. Si major concilii pars aut Pontifex illud gratificandum hæreticis censuisset, in vulgata esse errores aliquot Interpretis, licet in levioribus, nunquam certe eam & simpliciter indefinitè authenticam & nullo prætextu rejiciendam pronunciasset: nunquam eam cum omnibus suis partibus, sub poena anathematis, recipiendam decrevisset. Sancta Synodus absolute loquitur, inquit Bannes, ex Azorii, Pinedæ, Valentiæ & duriorum sententiâ, cum tamen hujusmodi limitationem facile potuisset adjicere. Deinde, pergit Bannes, in publicis disputationibus non solum de rebus ad fidem & mores pertinentibus, inter doctores controversatur, ergo etiam ubi non fuerit disputatio de fide & moribus, editio vulgata pro authentica habenda est. Præterea quænam res sit ad fidem & m. pertinens in sacris literis, non erit cujusvis judicare: At verò si semel hac janua aperiatur, facile quis audax dicere poterit, plurima esse errata ab Interprete, quia plurima non judicabit pertinere ad fidem, atque adeo historiarum narrationem & illarum circumstantias, quæ in Scripturis habentur, commutabit ad libitum, hujusmodi prætextu, quod quod non pertinent ad fidem moresque. Amplius, nihil videtur esse in Scriptu-ra, quod ad fidem non pertineat. Pergit, Quod si nos Catholici semel aliquos in eâ errores esse fateamur facile imperitum vulgus haereticorum dogmati consentiet, quos in linguarum peritia peritissimos esse judicat, ac proinde sacrarum literarum illibatam veritatem in illorum translationibus quaeret.
units.tr: For the Louvain theologians and Arias Montanus, not without the approval of the Pope and of the Monarch of Spain, judged it the most SAFE of all, which is attached to the Hebrew text in the Royal Bible. And as for that gloss, which these more moderate men repeat until they are hoarse, in matters of faith and morals, where does the decree say this? One must not distinguish where the law does not distinguish, especially since with a single word they could have made the distinction and thus established an opinion already defended by many. If the greater part of the Council or the Pope had judged that it should be granted to the heretics that the Vulgate contains some errors of the translator, though in minor matters, they would certainly never have pronounced it simply and indefinitely authentic, and to be rejected on no pretext; they would never have decreed that it be received with all its parts under penalty of anathema. The Holy Synod speaks absolutely, says Báñez, following the opinion of Azor, Pineda, Valencia and the harsher party, although it could easily have added such a limitation. Then, Báñez goes on, in public disputations the controversy is carried on among teachers not only about matters pertaining to faith and morals; therefore, even where there is no dispute about faith and morals, the Vulgate edition is to be held authentic. Moreover, what matter pertains to faith and morals in the sacred letters is not for just anyone to judge; but if once this door is opened, some bold person may easily say that very many errors have been made by the translator, since he will judge that very many things do not pertain to faith, and so will change at will the narrative of histories and their circumstances which are found in the Scriptures, under this pretext, that they do not pertain to faith and morals. Furthermore, there seems to be nothing in Scripture which does not pertain to faith. He goes on: But if we Catholics once confess that there are errors in it, the untrained crowd will easily agree with the doctrine of the heretics, whom he judges to be most skilled in the knowledge of languages, and so will seek the unimpaired truth of the sacred letters in their translations.

units.la: At postremae huic duriùs sententium rationi idem Bannes moderatiorum nomine sic occurrit, Qui aliquot interpretis errata in vulgatâ agnoscunt, inquit, non se haereticis favere, sed potius vere & fortiter contradicere arbitrantur. Idque prudentius & efficacius se efficere putant, quam prioris sententiae sectatores. Ratio est, quoniam cum fiant argumenta ad solvendum difficillima & quae more humano videntur convincere, quaedam esse errata in vulgatâ Editione, quae non sunt magni ponderis, si hac ipsa negaverimus, fortasis haretici nos ignorantia aut protervia redarguent, atque apud suos infamabunt, & reliqua magni ponderis & quae ad fidem moresve pertinent, quae ipsi in vulgata Editione errata esse contendunt, putabunt nos simili protervia clausis oculis defendere. Et haec eorum ratio, inquit idem Bannes, à simili confirmari potest. Quoniam inter Theologos communior & probabilior sententia est, quod summus Pontifex, ut particularis persona, errare possit in fide. Tametsi quidam, ut est Pigius lib. 4. Eccles. Hierarch. cap. 6. & 8. pietate quadam (nescio an secundum scientiam) susceperit hanc causam defendendam, nullum summum Pontificem hactenus errasse vel errare posse. Ratio autem cur prior sententia probabilior & tutior existimatur; haec est, Quoniam Apostolica sedis infallibilitatem nolumus dependere ab alicujus personae particularis fide, praesertim cum experientia testata fuerit, unum aut alterum summum pontificem, ut personam particularem, circa fidem defecisse. Id quod tam magnis argumentis probatur, ut oppositum sine aliqua temeritate defendi non possit. Ad hunc ergo modum editionis vulgatae auctoritatem magis pie & tutò se defendere arbitrantur, qui leviculos quosdam errores in eâ deprehensos ingenuè fatentur, corrigibiles tamen Apostolicae sedis authoritate. Et quemadmodum ejusdem Apostolicae sedis infallibilis authoritas non pendet ex fide particularis hominis, quem contingit esse Pontificem, sed pendet ab assistentia Sp. Sancti, qui illum in rebus fidei Pontificis officio fungentem errare nunquam permittet, sic etiam S. Scripturae infallibilis per omnia authoritas & integerrima in omnibus veritas non pendet ex omnimoda incorruptibilitate alicujus Editionis, sed ejus incorruptibilitas omnimoda in corde Ecclesiae ita conservatur, ut cum opus fuerit, oportune provideat, ipsosque codices corrigat & emendet. Haec Bannes. nes. Et quid verbis opus est? Ipse Hieronymus, inquiunt, agnoscit & profitetur, se aliquoties in translatione sua errasse, e. g. Isai. 19. caudam incurvantem & refrenantem, Qua ergo fronte negari potest, ullum ab Interprete commissum errorem? Interpretes potuerunt errare. Hieronymus agnoscit suos errores. Et tamen non erravit. Haec certe valde paradoxa sunt, quae obtusa Belgarum pectora non capiunt. Quod enim Bellarm. ait, Ecclesiam (cujus judicium majus est judicio Hieron.) multa judicasse non esse mutanda, quae Hieron. mutavit aut mutanda censuit in commentariis, frivolum est. Ostendere enim debuerat, quaenam Ecclesia & quod concilium contra Hieronymum pronunciaverit. Certe nimis jejunum est quod addit, certe non videtur casu factum sed judicio posteritatis vel potius ipsius Ecclesiae. Ubi enim extat tale judicium? Et quae fuit, in magna illa barbarie, illa posteritas, quae de Hieronymi laboribus potuit judicare? Certe non concilia potuere. In iis enim, Bellarmino teste, aut nulli aut quam paucissimi fuere Ebraeae linguae periti. Quod ad Tridentinos attinet, licet illic nonnulli fuerint linguarum periti, tamen nuspiam legimus, nuspiam narratur, versionem vulgatam cum fontibus, & Hieronymi commentariis, in iis quae ipse castigavit, conferendi, & singula expendendi provinciam ulli fuisse demandatam. Et quam grande hoc paradoxum, Hieronymum inter vertendum majore & plenore luce dum verteret, quam dum commentaretur, fuisse illustratum, sicuti Ribera docet in Abd. num. 114. & Salmeron Proleg. 3. observat. 5. atque hoc Tridentinis post tot annos innotuisse, quamvis Hieronymo id fuerit ignotum. Plura huc possent accongeri; sed illud jam clare satis ostensum arbitor, non parvam esse illam difficultatem, qua Concilii Trid. decretum illi premunt, quoquot vulgatae Editionis authoribus errores aliquot adscribunt, & proinde decretum illud cum certis limitationibus accipiendum esse tradunt. Neque est quod Serarius hic metuat, haereticos, aegre laturos, aut, culpaturos Romanam Ecclesiam, si in hoc negotio bonas adhibeant modificationes. Est magis cur metuat, ne Pontifex & duri-cervices isti Thelogi ipsum culpent, quod modificationibus istis decretum eludere satagat. certe si in Hispania esset, & rerum potirentur illi, de quibus Mariana conqueritur, non ferret impune. Illud autem quorsum spectat, quod dicit haereticos quoque suarum versionum authoritatem variè modificare & restringere? Quid enim? An unquam Reformatæ Ecclesiæ versiones suas declararunt authenticas? An unquam ullo decreto in ullo Euangelicorum cœtu cautum est, ne, quis versionem ullam quovis prætextu rejiciat? Plane ergo alienè hoc adduci etiam illi judicaverint, qui nondum ære lavantur.
units.tr: But against this harsher position, Bannes, speaking on behalf of the more moderate party, answers thus: Those who acknowledge some errors of the translator in the Vulgate, he says, do not thereby favour the heretics, but rather think they are contradicting them truly and bravely. They believe they do this more prudently and effectively than the adherents of the former opinion. The reason is this: since the most difficult arguments are put forward for solving problems, and these seem by human reasoning to be convincing, if we deny that there are certain errors in the Vulgate edition which are not of great weight, the heretics will perhaps refute us through ignorance or obstinacy and will defame us among their own people; and they will think that we defend with the same obstinacy, eyes closed, the rest of the errors of great weight, touching faith and morals, which they contend are errors in the Vulgate edition. And this reasoning of theirs, says Bannes, can be confirmed by analogy: since it is the more common and probable opinion among theologians that the supreme Pontiff, as a particular person, can err in faith. Although Pighius, in book 4 of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapters 6 and 8, out of a certain piety (I do not know whether according to knowledge), has undertaken to defend the cause that no supreme Pontiff has erred until now or can err, the reason why the former opinion is considered more probable and safer is this: since we do not wish to make the infallibility of the Apostolic See depend on the faith of any particular person, especially since experience has shown that one or another supreme Pontiff, as a particular person, has failed in matters of faith. This is proved by arguments so weighty that the opposite cannot be defended without some rashness. In this way, then, those who frankly confess that some slight errors have been detected in it, errors that can nevertheless be corrected by the authority of the Apostolic See, believe that they defend the authority of the Vulgate edition more devoutly and safely. And just as the infallible authority of that same Apostolic See does not depend on the faith of the particular man who happens to be Pope, but depends on the assistance of the Holy Spirit, who will never allow him, while discharging the office of Pontiff in matters of faith, to err, so too the infallible authority of Holy Scripture in all things, and its most perfect truth in all things, does not depend on the complete incorruptibility of any one edition, but its complete incorruptibility is so preserved in the heart of the Church that, when there is need, she provides in due time and corrects and emends the very manuscripts themselves. Thus Bannes. And what need is there of many words? Jerome himself, they say, acknowledges and professes that he erred several times in his translation, for example at Isaiah 19, bending and restraining tail. How then can it be denied that the translator committed any error? Translators could err; Jerome acknowledged his errors; and yet he did not err. These are indeed very paradoxical claims, which the dull minds of the Dutch cannot grasp. For what Bellarmine says, that the Church (whose judgment is greater than the judgment of Jerome) judged that many things which Jerome changed, or thought should be changed, in his commentaries ought not to be changed, is frivolous. For he ought to have shown what Church, and what council, has pronounced against Jerome. Certainly what he adds is far too thin: certainly it does not seem to have happened by chance but by the judgment of posterity, or rather of the Church itself. For where does such a judgment exist? And what posterity was there, in that great barbarism, which could judge of Jerome's labours? Certainly the councils could not, for, according to Bellarmine's own testimony, either none or very few of them had any skill in the Hebrew language. As for the Tridentines, although some of them were skilled in languages, nowhere do we read, nowhere is it reported, that the task of comparing the Vulgate version with the sources and with Jerome's commentaries, in those matters which he corrected, and of weighing each point, was entrusted to anyone. And how great a paradox this is: that Jerome, while translating, was illuminated by a fuller and greater light than while commenting, as Ribera teaches on Abdias, number 114, and Salmeron, Prolegomena 3, observation 5, and that this became known to the Tridentines after so many years, although it had been unknown to Jerome. Much more could be gathered here; but I consider it now clearly enough shown that the difficulty which presses upon the decree of the Council of Trent is not small, for all those who ascribe some errors to the authors of the Vulgate edition, and therefore they teach that the decree must be received with certain limitations. Nor is there any reason for Serarius to fear here that the heretics will take it badly, or will blame the Roman Church, if in this matter they apply good modifications. There is more reason for him to fear that the Pontiff and those stiff-necked theologians will blame him for striving to evade the decree by these modifications. Certainly, if he were in Spain, and those were in power of whom Mariana complains, he would not get off unpunished. But what does it matter that he says the heretics too variously modify and restrict the authority of their own versions? For what then? Did the Reformed Churches ever declare their versions authentic? Was it ever provided by any decree in any assembly of the Evangelicals that no one may reject any version on any pretext whatever? Clearly, then, even those who have not yet paid for their bath will judge that this has been brought in irrelevantly.

units.la: Sed alia aliunde exurgit tempestas. Namque plusquam decumanos fluctus illi excitant (& non infimi subsellii eos esse supra vidimus) qui textum Ebræum Judæorum malitia ullibi corruptum esse intrepidè & maximis rationibus negant. Sint in eo errores pauculi librariorum. Vulgata longè plures habet. Sed sint hac in parte pares. Illud tamen magnum fontium privilegium est, quod omnes uno ore Pontificii iplis tribuunt, Sanctos illos homines, quorum opera in consignandis sacris literis Deus O.M. usus est, nusquam errasse, cum non solùm res, sed & verba ipsis dictarit. Unde æquum esse colligunt, fontibus debitum manere æstimium, addentes, concilio nihil minus fuisse propositum, quam vulgatam Editionem fontibus anteferre. Ita Bellarm. videtur sentire cap.10. lib.2. ubi mendacium impingit Calvino, aitque, decretum nulla fontium mentione facta, vulgatam omnibus Latinis versionibus, quæ nunc circumferuntur, ante posuisse. Et Serarius cap.19. quæst.12. concl.1. Non antetulit Ebrais Græcisve fontibus Versionem Latinam Trid. Synodus. Ita & Salmeron Proleg.3. in secundâ disp. de Latinâ verf. Ita Mariana, Vega, Andrad. & alii. Sed quomodo hæc cum istis decreti verbis, quovis prætextu, conciliari possint, non vident illi, quos ceu fideliores decreti Interpretes suprà produximus. Et certè candidius illi agunt, laudandusque eorum candor est, qui sine verborum involucris dicunt quod sentiunt. Quid enim? Poteruntne in Ecclesia tolerari duo authentici textus, adeo inter se infinitis locis discrepantes? At eò adacti sunt moderatiores nostri Catholici. Fontibus emendatis emendativam nostram Latinam, quoad sententia consensum, æquiparat rite Trid. Synodus: inquit Serarius concl.2. Et Gretzerus, Sufficit nobis exæquatio, non postulatur prælatio, pag.537. Et pag.563. non puris fontibus prælata est sed summum æquata, quoad infallibilitatem fidei & morum doctrinam. Sed quam sincerè Bellarm. & Gretzerus hic agant, judicet Lector ex iis quæ jam proferam. Bellarminus, dum Calvinum mendacii arguit, videtur fontibus nihil derogare. Dum etiam cap.2. profitetur, pauculos istos librariorum errores, qui in textum Ebraum irrepsfere, non tanti esse, ut in iis quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, Scriptura integritas desideretur, videtur fontibus sic satis deferre. At cap. 11. postquam hanc posuit objectionem, magis credendum esse quod verbum Dei illud sit, quod habetur in fontibus, quam quod habetur in rivulis versionum, ita respondet, negari non potest quin fontes sint anteponendi rivulis, quando constat fontes non esse turbatos. Nunc autem fontes multis in locis turbidi fluunt. Multis in locis, inquit Bellarm. id est quinque locis non enim plures ex fontibus Ebraeis adduxit; Locis quinque, quae tamen ipsomet confitentes, Scripturae integritatem non vulnerant. Sustinet Bellarminus, verba Sacrobosci & Gretzeri p. 576. & fontes & versionem nostram in iis quae ad fidem & mores pertinent esse incorrupta, ac proinde authentica. Cur ergo negat fontes esse anteponendos? Cum extra controversiam sit, sacros scriptores in scribendo nunquam errasse, ut de aliis fontium praerogativis taceam. Gretzerum quod attinet, quoties purorum fontium meminit, iisque vulgatam statuit coauthenticam, ludere videtur. Non enim definit, utrum in iis quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, puri sint nec ne, nec aperte Bellarmini sententiam probat vel improbat. At pag.541. respondet Witakero, qui ait Pontificios nolle, ut Latina Editio ad fontes examinetur, sic ait, Quod vero subjungit, nos nolle nostram versionem ad fontes examinari, per fontes intelligens eos codices Graecos & Ebraos qui modo habentur, jure id facimus. Non enim constat eos cum suis fontibus, id est, primis exemplaribus convenire, quibus tamen conformem esse nostram versionem nos certos facit Ecclesia. Itaque sicubi exemplaria Ebraea aut Graeca discrepant a Latina, quod attinet ad fidei & morum dogmata, ea potius ad Latinam, quam ipsam ad illa comparandam & conferendam esse dicimus. Et pag. 1061. Sicubi sit dissensus inter Fontes & vulgatam, dicam potius corruptum esse textum Ebr. quam versioni inesse vitium. Et hoc dicam innixus Ecclesiae columna & firm. veritatis, quae hanc versionem ut authenticam repudiari nullo pretextu finit. Quid censes Lector, Estne hoc Latinam fontibus aequare an praeferre? Quicquid enim ad aliud ceu normam & regulam corrigitur, id non authenticum sed normae authenticae obnoxium, non norma, sed (sit venia verbo) normatum est. Et quid hoc, quaefo te, est, non constat Pontificiis, fontes, prout hodie extant, cum omnimis exemplaribus convenire. Quare? Quia non habemus, Gretzerus p. 537. ejusmodi decretum de fontibus, prout hodie extant. At unde constat illis, Latinam Editionem iis esse conformem? Ex judicio Ecclesiæ. Quia habemus judicium Ecclesiæ, inquit idem p. 537. & decretum, eam nunquam à mente Sp. sancti deviare, &c. Itaque si, quod ad dogmata fidei vel morum, fontes à vulgatâ discrepent, intrepidè eam hujusmodi fontibus præferimus. Sed iterum hic rogandus est Jesuita, unde constet Ecclesiæ de tali conformitate Latinæ Editionis cum primis fontium Exemplaribus, an ea unquam inspexit Trid. Synodus? Hæc enim est Ecclesia. Non putem. Libri enim Canonici, teste Bannes in 1. partem Thomæ quæst. 1. art. 8. quos sacri scriptores suis manibus exarârunt, non habentur in Ecclesiâ Christi. Nec est necessarium ut hujusmodi libri materiales in Ecclesia Christi depositò permanerent. Quod si dixeris cum eodem Bannes, Sacram scripturam primariò esse in corde Ecclesiæ, atque ita Ecclesiam Tridenti congregatam potuisse de hac conformitate Latinæ cum primis exemplaribus judicare, quærendum esset amplius annon eadem operâ de conformitate fontium, prout hodie extant, cum iisdem primis exemplaribus potuerit judicare, & si potuit, cur non fecerit? Sed expediam me, ubi unum insuper locum ex Gretzero addidero ex Append. 2. ad lib. 2. Bell. pag. 1055. Certum esse debet, inquit, ob infallibilem Ecclesiæ authoritatem, si quando vera & realis incidit dissonantia, quod ad dogmata fidei & morum attinet, Latinæ versionis & Hebr. sive Græci textus, Ebraum textum corruptum, Latinum verò sincerum & intaminatum censeri oportere.
units.tr: But another storm rises from another quarter. Those who boldly and on very strong grounds deny that the Hebrew text was ever corrupted anywhere by the malice of the Jews stir up waves more than tenfold (and, as we saw above, they are no humble men). Let there be a few scribal errors in it. The Vulgate has far more. But let them be equal in this respect. Yet this is a great privilege of the sources, which all the Papists with one voice grant them: that those holy men through whom God Almighty worked in recording the sacred letters never erred, since he dictated to them not only the matter but also the words. Hence they infer that it is fair for due esteem to remain with the sources, adding that the Council had no intention whatever of putting the Vulgate edition before the sources. So Bellarmine seems to think, book 2, chapter 10, where he charges Calvin with a lie and says that the decree, with no mention of the sources, placed the Vulgate before all the Latin versions now in circulation. And Serarius, chapter 19, question 12, conclusion 1: The Council of Trent did not put the Latin version before the Hebrew or Greek sources. So too Salmeron, Prolegomena 3, in the second disputation on the Latin version. So Mariana, Vega, Andrade and others. But how these things can be reconciled with those words of the decree, on any pretext, those men do not see, whom we brought forward above as the more faithful interpreters of the decree. Certainly they act more candidly, and their candour deserves praise, who say without verbal wrappings what they think. For what? Can two authentic texts, differing from each other in so many places, be tolerated in the Church? Yet our more moderate Catholics have been driven to this. The Council of Trent rightly makes our emended Latin equal to the emended sources, as far as agreement in sense goes, says Serarius, conclusion 2. And Gretzer: Equality is enough for us; preeminence is not demanded, p. 537. And p. 563: it is not preferred to the pure sources but is made equal to the highest, as regards infallibility in the doctrine of faith and morals. But let the reader judge from what I now set out how sincerely Bellarmine and Gretzer act here. Bellarmine, while accusing Calvin of lying, seems to detract nothing from the sources. Also, in chapter 2 he professes that those few scribal errors that crept into the Hebrew text are not so great that the integrity of Scripture is lacking in matters pertaining to faith and morals; he seems thereby to show the sources enough deference. But in chapter 11, after raising this objection, that what is found in the sources should rather be believed to be the word of God than what is found in the streams of the versions, he replies: It cannot be denied that the sources are to be put before the streams, when it is established that the sources are not muddied. But now the sources flow muddy in many places. In many places, says Bellarmine, that is, in five places; for he cited no more from the Hebrew sources. Five places which, however, by his own admission do not wound the integrity of Scripture. Bellarmine maintains, in the words of Sacrobosco and Gretzer, p. 576, that both the sources and our version are uncorrupted in matters pertaining to faith and morals, and therefore authentic. Why then does he deny that the sources are to be preferred? Since it is beyond controversy that the sacred writers never erred in writing, not to mention the other privileges of the sources. As for Gretzer, whenever he mentions the pure sources and makes the Vulgate co-authentic with them, he seems to be playing games. For he does not determine whether they are pure or not in matters of faith and morals, nor does he openly approve or disapprove Bellarmine's view. But at p. 541 he replies to Wittaker, who says that the Papists are unwilling for the Latin edition to be examined against the sources. He says: As for his addition that we are unwilling for our version to be examined against the sources, by "sources" meaning the Greek and Hebrew codices now extant, we do so rightly. For it is not established that they agree with their sources, that is, the original copies, to which the Church assures us our version is conformed. So wherever the Hebrew or Greek copies differ from the Latin as regards the doctrines of faith and morals, we say that they are rather to be compared with and corrected by the Latin, and not the Latin by them. And p. 1061: Wherever there is disagreement between the Sources and the Vulgate, I shall say that the Hebrew text is corrupt rather than that the version has a fault. And I say this leaning on the pillar and bulwark of truth, the Church, which allows this version, as authentic, to be rejected on no pretext. What do you think, reader? Is this to make the Latin equal to the sources, or to prefer it? For whatever is corrected by reference to something else as its norm and rule is not authentic but subject to an authentic norm; it is not a norm but, pardon the word, something normed. And what is this, I ask you: it is not established for the Papists that the sources, as they now exist, agree with the originals. Why? Because we do not have, says Gretzer p. 537, such a decree about the sources as they now exist. But how do they know that the Latin edition conforms to them? From the judgment of the Church. Because we have the judgment of the Church, says the same at p. 537, and the decree, that it never departs from the mind of the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore, if the sources differ from the Vulgate as regards doctrines of faith or morals, we boldly prefer it to such sources. But again the Jesuit must be asked here: how is it established for the Church that the Latin edition so conforms to the first original copies of the sources? Did the Council of Trent ever inspect them? For this is the Church. I do not think so. For the canonical books, which the sacred writers wrote with their own hands, are not held in the Church of Christ, as Bañez testifies on Thomas, part 1, question 1, article 8. Nor is it necessary that such material books should remain permanently in the Church of Christ. But if you say, with the same Bañez, that Sacred Scripture is primarily in the heart of the Church, and so the Church gathered at Trent could judge of this conformity of the Latin with the first copies, it would still have to be asked whether by the same labour it could have judged the conformity of the sources, as they now exist, with those same first copies; and if it could, why did it not do so? But I will free myself once I have added one more passage from Gretzer, from Appendix 2 to book 2 of Bellarmine, p. 1055. It must be certain, he says, that because of the infallible authority of the Church, if ever a true and real discrepancy arises, as far as doctrines of faith and morals are concerned, between the Latin version and the Hebrew or Greek text, the Hebrew text must be deemed corrupt and the Latin pure and unspotted.

units.la: [A quo non diversus abit Lud. de Tena, qui in eos arietans, qui asserunt per Decretum Trid. fas esse subinde ad fontes recurrere, sic inquit, Quasi vera essent, sequeretur vulgatam nihil majoris certitudinis quoad nos, aut approbationis à concilio accepisse ac antea habebat, sed esse cuique liberum ab ea discedere, sub prætextu discordandi ab Ebræo vel Græco textu, & ita non esset satis consultum liti, quæ in hoc agebatur: cum non solum esset de discordia Latinarum Editionum inter se, sicut falso supponit Serarius in Proleg. c. 11. qu. 12. sed etiam de dissensu à Græco aut Ebræo: imo hanc litem quæ frequentior erat, voluit Trid. Concilium sedare & quieti communi consulere.] Sed ut redeamus ad Gretz.
units.tr: [Not unlike him is Ludovicus de Tena, who, butting against those who assert that by the decree of Trent it is lawful from time to time to recur to the sources, says: As if it were true, it would follow that the Vulgate had received from the Council no greater certainty or approval as far as we are concerned than it had before, but that each person would be free to depart from it under the pretext of disagreeing with the Hebrew or Greek text; and so the dispute then at issue would not have been adequately settled, since the question was not only about the discord of the Latin editions among themselves, as Serarius falsely supposes in Prolegomena chapter 11, question 12, but also about disagreement with the Greek or Hebrew. Indeed the Council of Trent wished to settle this quarrel, which was the more frequent, and to consult common peace.] But to return to Gretzer.

units.la: Iterum tuum appello judicium Lector, utrùm hoc sit Latinam fontibus æquare, an verò potius præferre. Et iterum, utrùm sincerè agat Gretzerus, dum ejusmodi conditionem semper crepat, sine ulla assumptione, quâ eandem vel tollit vel ponit. Ego hæc solummodo afferre volui, ut ostenderem, quantarum difficultatum materiam famosum illud decretum Doctorum cathedris suppeditaverit. Sic enim statuendum arbitror, Aut Latinum interpretem, accommodabo huc verba Andradii, sensus a Sp. Sancto in Sacris literis consignatos, apte fideliterque reddidisse, aut ita se gessisse, ut minime in ejus sit nobis interpretatione, sed in Ebraicis voluminibus acquiescendum. Quod si fidelis interpretis munus pro dignitate obivit (id quod necessario statuendum, si decreto Trid. sua constabit ratio & authoritas) vitiatos profecto & corruptos Ebraeos codices esse plurimis in locis necesse est, cum diversam plerunque a Latinis sententiam contineant, sin integri illi sunt & incorrupti, in summa quidem maximarum rerum ignoratione Christi Ecclesiam versari, crassissimisque tenebris involutam esse confitearmur oportet, cum integris incorruptisque exemplaribus huc usque caruerit, &c. Hæc ex Andradio.
units.tr: I appeal again, dear reader, to your judgment: whether this is to equal the Latin with the sources, or rather to prefer it to them. And again, whether Gretzer acts sincerely when he keeps crying up this condition without any assumption by which he either removes it or lays it down. I wished only to set these things forth, so as to show how many difficulties the famous decree of the Council of Trent has supplied to the chairs of the teachers. For I think it must be held thus, in the words of Andradius: Either the Latin translator has aptly and faithfully rendered the senses which the Holy Spirit has recorded in the sacred letters, or he has so conducted himself that we must rest not in his translation but in the Hebrew volumes. But if he has discharged the duty of a faithful interpreter as befits its dignity (which must necessarily be held if the reasoning and authority of the decree of Trent are to stand), then the Hebrew codices must necessarily be vitiated and corrupt in very many places, since they generally contain a sense different from the Latin; but if those codices are whole and uncorrupted, we must confess that the Church of Christ has been living in the great ignorance of the highest matters and wrapped in the thickest darkness, since until now it has lacked whole and uncorrupted copies, etc. These things are from Andradius.

units.la: SECTIO III.
units.tr: SECTION III.

units.la: Restant duæ insuper aliæ difficultates, quas movet Bannes, pag. 48. col. 2. Prior, Ecclesiam Graecorum non habere scripturam sacram in Editione authentica, ex cujus testimonio certo & infallibiliter argumentamur. Quoniam Tridentina Synodus Latinam Editionem duntaxat tanquam authenticam pronunciavit. Hanc auget Andradius f. mihi 363. Christi Ecclesia, inquit, quæ a Rom. Pontifice Romanæ nomen accepit, non exiguis occidentis finibus, quibus Latina Editio familiaris est, continetur, sed per omnes hujus universitatis oras dispersa, omnes gentes & nationes, quæ Christo Jesu nomen dederunt, continet. Neque enim ad illam magis Itali, Galli, Germani & Hispani, quam Scytha, Indi, Graeci, Brachmanesque pertinent, dummodo Christum vera fide prosequantur: & tamen Latinam linguam cum non intelligant, in vulgata Editione sunt prorsus surdi. Unde sane fit, ut si sacram script. veram incorruptam in sola esse vulgata Editione putemus, maximam atque amplissimam Ecclesiæ partem illius splendore spoliemus. Quare qui Græcos Latinosque codices de Hebræis supplendos emendandosve esse contendunt, non quidem ab Ecclesia ad externos (ut quidam putant, Canum perstringit) sed ad ipsammet Christi Jesu Ecclesiam provocant, & ab eadem illi ipsi præsidia comparant. Posterior, apud eundem Bannes loco eodem, his verbis proponitur Ante prædictam Concilii Trident. definitionem non fuisse Theologis certum argumentum ab authoritate sacra scriptura, si quidem non habebant authenticam Editionem, unde sacra verba desume-
units.tr: There remain two further difficulties, which Bannes raises at p. 48, col. 2. The first: The Greek Church does not have Scripture in an authentic edition, from whose testimony we argue with certainty and infallibility, since the Council of Trent pronounced only the Latin edition to be authentic. Andradius enlarges on this at f. 363 of my copy: The Church of Christ, he says, which has taken its name from the Roman Pontiff, is not confined to the narrow bounds of the West, where the Latin edition is familiar, but is spread throughout every shore of this world, and contains all peoples and nations which have given their name to Jesus Christ. For Italians, Gauls, Germans and Spaniards belong to it no more than Scythians, Indians, Greeks and Brahmins, provided they follow Christ in true faith; yet since they do not understand Latin, they are completely deaf to the Vulgate edition. Hence it certainly follows that if we think the true and uncorrupted Holy Scripture is found only in the Vulgate edition, we strip of its splendour the greatest and most extensive part of the Church. Therefore those who contend that the Greek and Latin codices must be supplemented or corrected from the Hebrew do not appeal from the Church to outsiders (as some think, he gibes at the dogs), but to the Church of Christ Jesus itself, and obtain from it their support. The second, in the same Bannes at the same place, is put forward in these words: Before the aforesaid definition of the Council of Trent, theologians did not have a certain argument from the authority of Holy Scripture, since they did not have an authentic edition from which to take the sacred words-

units.la: Difficultas 1. & 4. vent. Hoc negabit Gretzerus, qui passim docet, vulgatam semper in se fuisse authenticam, eamque authoritatem acquisivisse à Deo, interpretis manum & calamum ita dirigente, ne Us-piam à spiritus sancti mente aberraret; Concilium verò nihil fecisse aliud, quàm quod eam authenticam declaraverit & promulgaverit, pag. 537. At regerit Bannes, ex sua sententia, Vulgatam majoris authoritatis esse propterea, quod ab Ecclesia ut authentica approbata est, quam proterea quod Interpres spiritum quasi propheticum habuerit, p. 56. col. 2. At ego παχύς τις ὢν, non capio, quomodo concilium potuerit hanc versionem declarare authenticam, nisi statuamus, Latinum Interpretem, qui certè homo fuit, extraordinariè à lapsu præservatum fuisse, Deo mentem ejus illuminante & calamum dirigente. Difficultatem hanc auget Serarius, & cum eo alii, dum vulgatam Editionem simpliciter declaratam authenticam & fontibus æquatam negat, ea quæ vulgata Editioni à Trid. Synodo tribuitur authoritas, non est infinitè accipienda, sed definitè, certis cum modificationibus pag. 117. col. 1. Inter eas modificationes prima est, ut versio hæc sit emendata velpotius emendatissima, col. 2. Et Pagina 115. col. 1. rectissimè huic vulgatæ nostræ versioni, sed emendata tributam ab eodem concilio auctoritatem. Dixi, sed emendata, pergit Serarius, quia de tali loquitur concilium, ut ex eâdem perspicuum sess. 4. dum decernit, ut hac deinceps quam emendatissimè imprimatur. Addit, idem monuisse Andradium, Vegam, Salmeronem, Gregorium de Valentia, &c. Verba Andradii, quibus Kemnitium arguit, hæc sunt, neque enim potuit non illam decreti partem perlegere, quâ S. Synodus statuit, ut posthac sacra Scriptura, potissimum hæc ipsa vetus & vulgata Editio, quam emendatissima imprimatur, ut demonstraret illam à se vulgatam Editionem solum approbari, quæ ab omnibus sit erratis summâ diligentiâ expurgata. Equidem illa quoque juxtà tecum verba lego, Andradi, sed nec in eodem, nec hunc immediatè sequente, sed in alio decreti articulo, qui ad solos impressores primario spectat. Sic enim habent verba;
units.tr: Difficulty 1 & 4. -rent. Gretzerus will deny this, for he teaches everywhere that the Vulgate was always authentic in itself, and that it obtained this authority from God, who directed the hand and pen of the translator so that nowhere did he stray from the mind of the Holy Spirit; the Council, on the other hand, did nothing more than declare and promulgate it as authentic, p. 537. But Bannes replies, in his own view, that the Vulgate has greater authority because the Church approved it as authentic, rather than because the translator had something like a prophetic spirit, p. 56, col. 2. But I, being a dull fellow [παχύς τις ὢν], do not grasp how the Council could have declared this version authentic unless we hold that the Latin translator, who certainly was a man, was preserved from error in an extraordinary way, God illuminating his mind and directing his pen. Serarius increases this difficulty, and with him others, by denying that the Vulgate was simply declared authentic and equated with the sources: the authority which the Council of Trent gives to the Vulgate edition is not to be taken without limit, but definitely, with certain modifications, p. 117, col. 1. The first of these modifications is that this version be emended, or rather most emended, col. 2. And on p. 115, col. 1: the authority given by the same council to our Vulgate version, which is most rightly ascribed to it, but emended. I said "but emended", Serarius goes on, because the council speaks of such a version, as is clear from the same session 4, where it decrees that henceforth it be printed as most emended. He adds that the same had been pointed out by Andradius, Vega, Salmeron, Gregory of Valentia, and others. The words of Andradius, with which he argues against Kemnitz, are these: For he could not have failed to read through that part of the decree by which the holy Synod ordained that henceforth Holy Scripture, especially this same old and Vulgate edition, be printed as most emended, so as to show that only that Vulgate edition was approved by it which had been purged of all errors with the greatest diligence. Indeed I also read those words of Andradius as you do, but not in the same place nor in the article immediately following, but in another article of the decree, which chiefly concerns printers alone. For they read thus:

units.la: Sed & impressoribus modum hac in parte, ut par est, imponere volens, jam sine modo, hoc est, putantes sibi licere quicquid libet, sine licentiâ superiorum Ecclesiasticorum, ipsos S. Scriptura libros & super illis annotationes & expositiones tiones quorumlibet indifferenter, sape tacito, sape etiam ementito pralo, & quod gravius est, sine nomine authoris imprimunt, alibi etiam impressos hujusmodi libros temerè venales habent, decernit & statuit, ut post hac sacra scriptura potissimùm verò hac ipsa vetus & vulgata Editio quàm emendatissimè imprimatur, nullique liceat imprimere vel imprimi facere quosvis libros de rebus sacris, sine nomine authoris, neque illos vendere, &c.
units.tr: But also wishing to impose a due restraint on printers in this matter, since they now print without measure, that is, thinking it lawful for them to do whatever pleases them, without the licence of ecclesiastical superiors, print Holy Scripture itself and annotations and expositions upon it by whomsoever, indifferently, often with a silent press, often even with a false imprint, and, what is worse, without the name of the author, and also carelessly keep such books on sale elsewhere, it decrees and ordains that henceforth Holy Scripture, and especially this same old and Vulgate edition, be printed as most emended, and that it be permitted to no one to print, or cause to be printed, any books on sacred matters without the name of the author, nor to sell them, etc.

units.la: Equidem falli possum, nec pertinax ero, si quis errorem mihi monstrârit: Puto tamen Pontificios nunquam cogitaturos fuisse de arripiendis his voculis,quàm emendatissime imprimatur,nisi Reformati Theologi hoc decretum tot difficultatibus & absurdis ursisfent. 1. enim hic articulus ad impressores spectat. Docet hoc exordium. 2. Exigit ut in excudenda vulgatâ Editione Typographi singularem curam gerant, ut quàm emendatissimè sine vitiis Typographicis excudatur. 3. Hoc ipsum exigit ab iisdem in excudendis etiam aliis Editionibus S. Script. puta, Bibliis Ebraeis, Græcis, Versione Pagnini, sic enim dicit, ut posthac sacra scriptura, potissimum verò hac ipsa vulgata Editio, quàm emendatissimè imprimatur. Exigit itaque, ut etiam aliæ Editiones quàm emendatissimè excudantur. 4. Agit insuper hic articulus etiam de aliis libris, commentariis, &c. 5. Nihil promittit hic articulus de emendatione, recognitione, aut revisione vulgatæ aut alicujus alterius Editionis, authoritate Sedis Apostolicæ, instituendâ. 6. Illud à Typographis exigit hic articulus, quod in ipsorum potestate est, quod ipsorum officii est. At vulgatæ Editionis correctio ad sedis Apostolicæ curam pertinet, inquit Præfatio in Editionem Clementinam. 7. Non interdicit hic articulus Typographis Editione vulgatæ versionis, usque dum emendatissimam eam daret Sedes Apostolica, id quod videtur decernendum fuisse, si hæc verba, quàm emendatissimè imprimatur, ad solos Typographos correctores & Typographiarum Inspectores non spectant. 8. Delecti Cardinales in Decreti hujus expositione nihil tale meminerunt, quod tamen præterm itti non potuisset, si eodem modo articulum istum interpretandum censuissent. 9. Bellarminus de Sacr. Euchar. lib. 4. cap. 24. ad locum 1. Cor. 10. disputans, sic inquit, Concilium Trid. non statuit recipiendam quamlibet lectionem vulgata Edit. sed eam quam constat esse lectionem vulgata Edit. Alioqui non jussisset idem concilium vulgatam Edit. quàm emendatissimè imprimi. Non dicit, Apostolicâ authoritate corrigi, sed simpliciter imprimi. Iste rationes me movent, ut putem, decreti hujus authores, tunc cum illud rogabant, non ita haec verba accepisse, nec etiam sic accipi posse, ut Serarius aliique, difficultatibus tantis pressi, ea accipiunt. Sed gratificemur hic Serario & caeteris Pontificiis, demusque haec verba istum, quem illi volunt, habere sensum, annon inde sequentur haec consectaria? 1. Versionem authenticam in concilio nominatam seu declaratam esse, antequam extitit, ineptamque proinde esse ac planè ridiculam illam delectorum Cardinalium decisionem, de quâ supra. 2. Quamdiu versio illa in mendis suis cubuit & non fuit emendatissima, Romanam Ecclesiam caruisse authenticis verbi divini tabulis. 3. Ecclesiam eandem ne nunc quidem authenticam habere Sacrarum literarum Editionem, cum necdum sit emendatissima. 4. Nimis probabiliter, nimisque verisimiliter astrui, plurimùm quoque errare potuisse, atque errasse à vero eandem, cum, quam sequeretur certò constanterque in veri investigatione ac dijudicatione, Cynosuram ac normam non haberet, ac indubitato authenticoque textu careret. Et quidem haec ex sequentibus clariora ac liquidiora evadent. Adeo verum est vetus illud,
units.tr: I may be mistaken, and I shall not be obstinate if anyone shows me an error. Yet I think the Papists would never have seized upon these little words as most emended be printed unless the Reformed theologians had burdened this decree with so many difficulties and absurdities. (1) For this article concerns printers; the preamble shows this. (2) It requires that in printing the Vulgate edition the printers take special care that it be printed as most emended, without printing errors. (3) It requires the same of them in printing other editions of Holy Scripture, for example the Hebrew and Greek Bibles and the version of Pagninus; for it says that henceforth Holy Scripture, and especially this same Vulgate edition, be printed as most emended. It therefore requires that other editions too be printed as most emended. (4) This article further deals also with other books, commentaries, etc. (5) This article promises nothing about emendation, recognition or revision of the Vulgate or of any other edition, to be undertaken by authority of the Apostolic See. (6) This article requires of printers what is within their power and belongs to their office; but correction of the Vulgate edition belongs to the care of the Apostolic See, says the preface to the Clementine edition. (7) This article does not forbid printers to print the Vulgate version until the Apostolic See gives it as most emended, which seems to have needed decreeing, if the words as most emended be printed do not refer only to printers, correctors and overseers of printing houses. (8) The chosen cardinals, in their exposition of this decree, mention nothing of the kind, which yet could not have been overlooked if they had judged this article to be interpreted in this way. (9) Bellarmine, On the Sacrament of the Eucharist, bk. 4, ch. 24, discussing 1 Cor. 10, says: The Council of Trent did not decree that any reading of the Vulgate edition be accepted, but that which is agreed to be the reading of the Vulgate edition. Otherwise the same council would not have ordered the Vulgate edition to be printed as most emended. He does not say to be corrected by apostolic authority, but simply printed. These reasons move me to think that the authors of this decree, when they were asked about it, did not understand these words thus, nor can they be so understood, as Serarius and others, pressed by such great difficulties, take them. But let us here indulge Serarius and the other Papists, and grant that these words have the sense they want: do not the following consequences follow? (1) That the authentic version was named or declared in the council before it existed, and that therefore the decision of the chosen cardinals, mentioned above, is inept and quite ridiculous. (2) As long as that version lay in its errors and was not most emended, the Roman Church lacked authentic tablets of the divine word. (3) The same Church does not even now have an authentic edition of the Sacred Letters, since it is not yet most emended. (4) It is far too readily and too plausibly asserted that it could have erred very much, and did in fact stray from the truth, since it would have had no cynosure or norm by which it could certainly and constantly investigate and judge the truth, and it would lack an indubitable and authentic text. And indeed these things will become clearer and plainer from what follows. So true is that old saying,

units.la: Incidit in Scyllam qui vult vitare Charybdin.
units.tr: He who wishes to avoid Charybdis falls into Scylla.

units.la: CAP. IX
units.tr: CHAPTER IX

units.la: SECTIO I. Primi consectarii probatio. Vulgatam Editionem pronunciatam esse authenticam XLVI. annis antequam extitit. Tot enim anni intercesserunt, antequam prodiit emendatissima. Historia partitudinis istius. Lucas Brugensis. Sixtus V. quà Papa, anno 1590. dedit Editionem emendatissimam. Ejus Bulla & insueta in corrigendo diligentia. SECTIO. II. Clemens VIII. biennio post aliam Editionem dedit, infinitis locis à Sixtinâ discrepantem, eaque emendatiorem. Ejus fraudes & impostura, ne in Sixto periclitaretur Pontificis infallibilitas. Th. Jamesii Bellum Papale. Ostenditur, nulla veritatis specie dici posse, ea quae in Sixtinâ emendavit Clemens, vitio prava in Sixtinam irrepsisse. Hoc erit evidenter ostenditur. Item de Sixti curiosâ diligentiâ. Excutitur Bulla Sixti. Inscriptio in Vaticana Sixto V. posita. Variorum Pontificiorum varia de hac gemina Editione judicia. Lepida Catharini adversus Cajetanum disputatio. Alponsi de Castrojudicium liberum de infallibilitate Papæ. Atque ita hoc capite & seqq. ostenditur, quantis difficultatibus ipsi Pontifices, Sixtus & Clemens hoc decretum involuerint, id quod quintum fuit in fine cap. 4. propositum.
units.tr: SECTION I. Proof of the first corollary. The Vulgate edition was declared authentic 46 years before the most correct edition appeared. For so many years passed before the most correct edition was published. The history of this partisanship. Lucas of Bruges. Sixtus V, as Pope, in 1590 gave the most correct edition. His Bull and his unusual diligence in correcting. SECTION II. Clement VIII, two years later, gave another edition, differing from the Sixtine in countless places, and he called it more correct. His frauds and imposture, so that the infallibility of the Pontiff would not be endangered in the case of Sixtus. Thomas James's Papal War. It is shown that nothing in the semblance of truth can be said: that the things Clement corrected in the Sixtine edition had crept into the Sixtine through a depraved error. This will be shown clearly. Likewise on Sixtus's careful diligence. The Bull of Sixtus is examined. The inscription placed on Sixtus V in the Vatican. The varied judgments of various Papists on this twofold edition. The witty disputation of Catharinus against Cajetan. The free judgment of Alphonsus de Castro on the infallibility of the Pope. And so in this chapter and those following it is shown with what difficulties the Pontiffs themselves, Sixtus and Clement, entangled this decree, which was the fifth point proposed at the end of chapter 4.

units.la: SECTIO I
units.tr: SECTION I

units.la: Primi consectarii veritas liquido apparebit, si observetur, hanc emendatissimam Editionem xlvi. post factum hoc decretum anno, demum prodiisse. Quadraginta enim sex integris annis Ecclesiam Romanam hanc Editionem parturivisse liquet ex Præfatione ad Editionem Clementinam. Decretum hoc rogatum est anno 1546. Ex eo Pius IV. & post Pius V. verba Præfationis, in hac emendatione laborârunt, negotio dato lectissimis aliquot Rom. Ecclesiæ Cardinalibus. Verùm conventum istum ob gravissimas Romanæ Sedis occupationes (potestne ergo major esse hâc occupatio?) jamdudum intermissum, Sixtus V. ad Pontificatum evectus revocavit & opus tandem confectum publicavit, anno Domini 1590. Habes intervalum xliv. annorum. Monstri simile est, utor verbis Rev. Mortoni, versionem aliquam pronunciari & decerni authenticam, priusquam sit & extet emendatissima, illudque perinde esse ac si quis infantem in utero matris baptizare præsumeret, quod tamen legibus Pontificiorum prohibetur. Nec video ego, cur non etiam ex his fluat consectarium illud secundum, Tot annis Ecclesiam Rom. sine authenticis Scripturæ tabulis fuisse, aut habuisse tabulas corruptissimas pro authenticis. Si prolubium est scire, quantam corruptelarum copiam suo judicio sustulerit Sixtus V. non suaserim, ut ejus Editionem cum pejoribus conferas, molestum enim nimis hoc esset: Compendifecit tibi laborem istum Lucas Brugensis Theol. & Decanus Pontificius, in libello cui titulum fecit, Romanæ correctionis loca aliquot insigniora. Magna fuit hujus correctionis expectatio. * Cum ab Apostolicâ sede, inquit Andradius, veterem vulgatam Editionem quàm emendatissimam acceperimus, omni erimus cura & dubitatione liberi. Compotem ergo hujus voti Ecclesiam Rom. tandem Sixtus V. fecit. Et ne ullus Catholicorum animis relinqueretur scrupulus,
units.tr: The truth of the first corollary will be plainly apparent if it is observed that this most correct edition appeared at last in the forty-sixth year after this decree was made. For it is clear from the Preface to the Clementine Edition that the Roman Church labored over this edition for forty-six full years. The decree was requested in the year 1546. From then on, Pius IV and afterwards Pius V, as the words of the Preface say, labored on this emendation, having assigned the task to some of the most select Cardinals of the Roman Church. But this meeting, because of the very grave occupations of the Roman See (can there be a greater occupation than this?), having been interrupted long ago, Sixtus V, raised to the Pontificate, revived, and at last published the work when it was finished, in the year of the Lord 1590. You have an interval of 44 years. It is a monstrous thing, to use the words of the Reverend Morton, to pronounce and decree a version authentic before the most correct one exists and has appeared; it is just as if someone presumed to baptize an infant in its mother's womb, which nevertheless is forbidden by the laws of the Papists. Nor do I see why the second corollary, that for so many years the Roman Church was without authentic tablets of Scripture, or had very corrupt tablets accepted as authentic, should not also follow from these things. If you are curious to know how great a number of corruptions Sixtus V removed in his own judgment, I would not advise you to compare his edition with the worse ones, for that would be far too tedious. Lucas of Bruges, theologian and Papist dean, has spared you this labor, in a little book which he entitled Several more notable passages of the Roman correction. Great was the expectation of this correction. * Since we have received from the Apostolic See, says Andradius, the old Vulgate edition as most correct, we shall be free of all care and doubt. Sixtus V therefore at last made the Roman Church a partaker of this wish. And so that no scruple might be left in the minds of any Catholics,

units.la: Pol. 361. loca aliquot insigniora. in Præfatione seu Bullâ suæ isti Editioni præfixa primo asserit Sixtus, Ad se pertinere negotium emendationis. Ad nos, inquit, in ejusdem Petri Cathedrâ in quâ ejus vivit potestas excellit authoritas, Deo sic disponente, constitutos, totum hoc judicium proprie ac specialiter pertinet. Cui concinit is, qui in Editionem Clementinam biennio post editam præfatus est, Is enim expresse dicit, executionem generalium conciliorum, ipsamque scripturarum integritatem & puritatem ad curam Apostolicæ sedis potissimum pertinere. Et Gretzerus p.1059. Sacrarum literarum, inquit, ultima & authentica emaculatio & recognitio primario pertinent ad sedem Apostolicam Secundò asserit Sixtus, se nihil intermisisse aut neglexisse, quod faceret ad hujus emendationis promotionem, Adeo ut, pergit in præfatione Sixtus, in hoc laboriosissima emendationis curriculo, in quo operam quotidianam, eamque pluribus horis collocandam duximus, aliorum quidem labor fuerit in consulendo, nostro autem in eo, quod ex pluribus esset optimum deligendo. Addit, se aliquot Romanæ Ecclesiæ Cardinales & insigne collegium doctissimorum virorum, fere ex omnibus Christiani orbis nationibus & celeberrimis studiorum generalium Universitatibus, amplis opulentisque reditibus dotatum in societatem hujus laboris & curæ coöptasse, & ad rem illam felicius perficiendam, quamplurimos codices Latinos, tam impressos quam manuscriptos, ex Bibliothecis variis conquirendos curasse.
units.tr: Pol. 361. Several more notable passages. In the Preface, or Bull, prefixed to his edition, Sixtus first asserts that the matter of emendation belongs to him. To us, he says, placed by God's disposition in the Chair of that same Peter, in which his power lives and his authority excels, the whole of this judgment pertains properly and specially. Agreeing with this is the one who wrote a preface to the Clementine Edition two years after it was issued. For he expressly says that the execution of general councils, and the integrity and purity of Scripture itself, pertain chiefly to the care of the Apostolic See. And Gretser, p. 1059: The final and authentic correction and revision of the sacred letters, he says, pertains primarily to the Apostolic See. Secondly, Sixtus asserts that he had neglected or omitted nothing that would advance this emendation, so that, Sixtus goes on in the preface, in this most laborious course of emendation, in which we have thought fit to spend daily effort, and that over many hours, the labor of others was in consulting, but ours in choosing from many readings what was best. He adds that he had admitted into the partnership of this labor and care some Cardinals of the Roman Church and a distinguished college of most learned men, drawn from almost all the nations of the Christian world and from the most famous universities of general study, endowed with ample and rich revenues; and that, to bring that task to a happier completion, he had caused very many Latin codices, both printed and manuscript, to be sought out from various libraries.

units.la: Tertiò, ne quis putaret eum solummodo directorem & ἐργοδιώκτην hic fuisse, ait se quoque manus huic operi admovisse & quidem summâ diligentiâ. Angelus Roccha Bibliothecæ Vaticanæ præfectus, p.227. Bibliothecæ Vaticanæ, ei hoc perhibet testimonium: Quarta quæ sequitur Inscriptio, inquit, ingentem indicat curam & verè Pontificiam, quam Sixtus V. toto suscepit conatu pro Bibliis vulgata Editionis emendandis & imprimendis, juxta Concilii Trid. præscriptum. Quâ in re præstandâ tot ac tantos diè noctuque perpessus est labores, quantos nemo unquam verbis exprimere posset, ut mihi persuadeo. qui hujus generis labores re ipsa videns non semel tanquam oculatus testis obstupui. Universa enim Biblia, antequam prælo committerentur, ad verbum perlegit, etiamsi quotidie in omnes totius Christiani orbis curas, & gravissimas quidem, totus incumberet. Si igitur paginam perlegit universam & emendavit: atque ita ut omnes sacri codices juxta ejusdem concilii decretum cum omnibus suis partibus legantur, prout in Ecclesiâ Catholicâ legi consueverunt, & in veteri vulgatâ Latinâ Editione habentur. Nec eo contentus, universa item Biblia sic emendata & recenter impressa de integro perlegit, ut omnia fideliter recognita in lucem prodiret. Hæc Roccha, oculatus testis. Ipse Sixtus V. in Bulla sua, Eaque res, inquit, quò magis incorrupte perficeretur, nostra nos ipsi manu correximus si qua pralo vitia obrepserant. Quartò, ne quis desideraret infallibile Pontificis judicium, Ad laudem, inquit, & gloriam omnipotentis Dei, hac nostra perpetuò valitura constitutione de venerabilium Fratrum nostrorum Cardinalium deputatorum consensu & consilio, de certa nostra scientia, & Apostolica potestatis plenitudine statuimus & declaramus, eam vulgatam sacra, tam veteris quam novi Testamenti, pagina Latinam Editionem, quæ pro authentica à Concilio Tridentino recepta est, sine ulla dubitatione aut controversia censendam esse hanc ipsam, quam nunc, prout optime fieri potuit, emendatam, & in Vaticana Typographia impressam, in universa Christiana Rep. atque in omnibus Christiani orbis Ecclesiis legendam evulgamus, decernentes eam, primùm quidem universali sancta Ecclesia ac SS. Patrum consensione, deinde verò Generalis Concilii Tridentini decreto, nunc etiam Apostolica nobis à Domino tradita auctoritate comprobatam, pro vera, legitima, authentica & indubitata, omnibus publicis privatisque disputationibus, lectionibus prædicationibus & explanationibus recipiendam & tenendam esse Adeò quidem ut expressè sanciat, Bibliorum codices juxta hoc suum exemplar in posterum exprimendos esse, ne minima quidem particula mutata, addita vel detracta: cætera verò exemplaria tam manuscripta quam impressa ejusdem vulgata Editionis, quæ vel ob characterum vetustatem, seu ob aliquod insigne codicis ornamentum, sive ob impressionis præstantiam, vel ob marginales notas asservantur ad hoc emendentur: Alias ea in iis quæ huic Editioni non consenserint, nullam in posterum fidem, nullam authoritatem habitura esse. Quin insuper majoris excommunicationis sententiam, à qua nisi mortis articulo constitutus ab alio quam pro tempore existente Romano Pontifice, absolvi non posit, ei denunciat, qui ad hanc suam Editionem Biblia sua non correxit. SECTIO II. Atque ita vidimus quam strenuè Sixtus gesserit, Pontifex errare nescius, infallibilis judex in negotio ad Apostolicam sedem primariò & proprie pertinente. Certè credidissent omnes Catholici, versionem suam jam ab omnibus erroribus esse emendatissimam, nisi Clemens VIII. ipsorum conscientias turbulentasset. Is enim biennio post, Anno * 1592. cum jam Sixtus mortalitatem explesset. plesset & in fata quoque concessissent Vrbanus VII. Gregorius XII. & Innocentius IX. aliam Editionem Bibliorum procuravit, jussu suo recognitam, quamplurimis locis auctiorem, in plurimis mutilatam, in multis contrariam adeoque diversam, ut diversæ versiones non immerito censeri possint. Ostendit hoc ad oculum Rev. Theologus Thomas Iamesius, amicus noster benemeritus, Bodlæanæ Bibliothecæ Proto-Bibliothecarius in Acad. Oxoniensi, qui utramque Editionem, Sixtinam & Clementinam, diligentissimè inter se contulit, variantibusque utriusque lectionibus volumen sic satis crassum explevit, cui titulum fecit, Bellum Papale. Quo in libro præter innumeras varietates ad bis mille lectiones produxit, quæ à Sixto authoritate Apostolicâ adversus Ebræam & Græcam veritatem confirmatas, Clemens eâdem authoritate resinxit & ad fontes reformavit. Cum autem animadverterent Romani Patres, hinc accepturos Hæreticos oppugnandæ Pontificiæ vel infallibilitatis vel sanctitatis argumenta, de velamento, quo hoc Ecclesiæ Rom. pudendum tegeretur, cogitarunt. Conversus ergo ad dolos & fraudes Papa Clemens, Bullæ Sixti V. in perpetuum exilium actæ (in nullis enim Editionibus ea amplius comparet) suam ipsius Sanctionem substituit, & tamen hæc nova Clementis VIII. recognitio & Editio in Sixti V. nomen data est. Idem manšit titulus Biblia S. vulgata Edit. Sixti V. Pontificu M. jussu recognita & edita Et quomodo Sixti ? Annon ille 1590. suam Editionem a Clementinâ immensum discrepantem publicaverat? Audi figmentum. Sixtus V. inquit Præfatio in Clementinam, hoc opus tandem confectum typis mandari jussit. Quod cum jam esset excusum, & ut in lucem emitteretur, idem Pontifex operam daret, animadvertens non pauca in S. Biblia prali vitio irrepsisse, quæ iterata diligentia indigere viderentur, totum opus sub incudem revocandum censuit & decrevit. Id verò cum morte praeventus præstare non potuisset, Gregorius XIII. qui Vrbano VII. successerat, perficere aggressus est, amplissimis aliquot Cardinalibus, aliisque viris doctis ad hoc iterum deputatis. Sed eo quoque & qui illi successit, Innocentio IX. brevissimo tempore de hac luce subtractis, tandem sub initium Pontificatus Clementis VIII. opus in quod Sixtus V. intenderat, Deo bene juvante, perfectum est. Et Gretzerus p. 1058. appendicis ad librum 2. Bellarm. de V. D. Biblia priora, inquit, quæ Sixtus ediderat, ipsemet Sixtus sub incudem revocare & accuratus recognoscere decreverat, offensus mendarum, quæ irrepserant, multitudine. Quam tamen cogitationem suam praproperâ morte abreptus, reipsa perficere non potuit. Quod ergo Sixti consilium imperfectum mansit, tandem Clemens perfecit, & mentem voluntatemque Sixti ad rem contulit, recognitis illis Sixtinis Bibliis, Qua causa cur & Sixtinomen praescriptum gerant, &c. Videris praetextum Clementinae correctionis. Vitia illa, si illis credimus, quae Clemens sustulit, fuerunt Typographica & praeli vitio in Sixtinam Editionem irrepserant, ac proinde ea suppressa fuit. Licet enim hoc expressè non dicat Praefatio, tamen non obscurè innuit, dum inquit, Quod opus cum jam esset excusum, & ut in lucem emitteretur, idem Pontifex operam daret. Non dicit, cum jam esset excusum & in lucem emissum & Bullâ praemunitum. Videtis, inquam praetextum, sed nimium quantum pellucidum. Quis enim credat, chiliadas sphalmatum praeli vitio in eam Editionem irrepsisse, quam adeò inusitatâ diligentiâ Sixtus procuraverat, quam Sixtus, antequam prælo mandaretur, à capite ad calcem perlegerat, quam emendatam & recenter impressam de integro perlegerat, ut omnia fideliter recognita in lucem prodirent, quae & de se Sixtus in Bulla, & de eo Roccha testatus est. Quis credat tot sententias & voces praeli vitio in Sixtinam irrepsisse, quas Clemens sustulit, E. gr. 1. Sam. 24. 8. & 25. 6. & 2. Sam. 6. 12. & 8. 8. & 19. 10. Prov. 24. verf. ult. Hab. 1. 3. Math. 24. 41. Act. 14. 6. Et contrà tot ex Sixtinâ ejectas, quas Clemens restituit, ut Num. 30. 11. Lev. 20. 9. Jud. 17. 2. 3. Prov. 25. 24. Math. 27. 35. 2. Chr. 2. 10. Quis sibi persuadeat, tot contrarietates praeli vitio admissas, ut Deut. 17. 8. Josh. 2. 18. & 11. 19. tot denique & tantas diversitates in numeris. Certè nisi hæc loca multis retrò sæculis variè fuissent lecta, persuaderi hic prætextus imperitioribus paulo facilius potuisset. At dum nulli fere loco manum admovit Sixtus, nisi ubi librariorum incuria atque ex eam nata Lectionum diversitas Lectorem tenebant suspensum, & de veriori lectione dubium, ubi necessitas postulabat, ut una aliqua authoritate Apostolicâ signaretur, dum passim Editionem Lovaniensem sequitur, quis credet in tam multis locis Typographica negligentia Editionem Sixtinam discrepare ab ipsius Sixti mente, quam Clemens sua se Editione dicit expressisse ? Quin &, unde constabit nobis de hac Sixti mente & intentione ? An reliquit ullas hac de re lucubrationes? Vndesciam, Sixtum, si superyixisset, Biblia sic corrce-tucturum fuisse, ut Clemens correxit ? Unde liquet hoc votum & desiderium Sixti, quod solum Bello Papali Jamesii opponit Gretzerus? nimis elumbis est haec responsio in re tam seria. Aliis defensoribus haec causa eget. Dicam aliquid amplius. Editio Sixtina ex Pontificis istius unde denominatur, mente adeo prodiit emendata, ut in exemplaribus ejus, 26. locis, errata praeter Sixti intentionem inter excudendum a Typographis commissa, partim calamo, si erratum fuit leviusculum, partim recusis novis vocabulis iisque voci mendose excusae superimpositis, & agglutinatis ubi videlicet difficilior fuisset correctio per calamum, sublata sint. Eorum catalogum in Praefatione Belli Papalis recensuit Th. Jamesius. E. g. Judith. 1. 2. excusum erat in Sixtinis, in latitudinem. Hoc vel per errorem Typographi factum fuit, vel ipse Sixtus post excusum hoc folium mutavit sententiam. Iussit ergo iisdem characteribus in minutis chartulis excudi, altitudinem, easque in exemplaribus, antequam distraherentur, voci alteri iussit imponi, id quod per ejusmodi pultem, qua librorum compactores utuntur, adeo artificiose erat factum, vix ut animadverti potuerit correctio. Quis ergo dicet illud in altitudinem praeli vitio in Sixtinam irrepsisse? Et tamen Clemens in suam Editionem revocavit vocem latitudinem, quam Sixtus superimposita voce altitudinem, tegi & expungi jusserat. Quod si praeter haec 26. errata, tantus insuper numerus occurrisset Sixto, proculdubio universam Editionem suppressisset. Cur ad hoc nihil respondet Gretzerus? Cur hic piscé mutior? Prodiit in lucem haec Editio, praefixa Bulla, jussi sunt omnes Typographi hanc editionem in posterum sequi, ne minimâ quidem particula mutata, addita vel detractâ, jussi sunt omnes docti juxta eandem suos codices corrigere, dispersa sunt exemplaria in omnes Christiani orbis provincias, & credemus Clementi & Gretzero, chiliadas sphalmatum praeli vitio irrepsisse? Aut enim observavit ipse Sixtus haec sphalmata, ante Bullam editam, vel post. Si ante, tunc certe oportet hominem eum fuisse valde temerarium & profanum. Quis enim prudens decernet Editionem aliquam esse emendatissimam, jubebitque eam ad minimas usque particulas recipi, quam scit in millenis aliquot mendis cubare, quarum nullam annotat?
