Si post; tunc certe larva detracta est omnibus Pontificum bullis, tunc mendacem & vanum hominem si quis Sixtum vocaret, non longe à veritatis regione aberraret. Quid enim, quæso te, esset fallere, si hoc non esset, de certa scientia & Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine statuere & declarare, vulgatam Editionem quam Tridentini pro authentica recepe-runt, sine ulla dubitatione aut controversia censendam HANC IPSAM veram, legitimam, authenticam & indubitatam, &c Item profiteri, se sua manu correxisse, si quæ præli vitio obrepserant? Et quid magis stultum & ridiculum, quàm anathema denunciare omnibus, quicunque huic mendosissimæ Editioni sacramento dicere detrectabunt. Valeant ergo hæc κρηπφύγελα.
units.tr: Thirdly, so that no one should think he was only the director and overseer of the work, he says that he also put his own hand to it, and with the greatest diligence. Angelus Roccha, prefect of the Vatican Library, p. 227 of the Bibliotheca Vaticana, bears him this witness: The fourth inscription that follows, he says, indicates an immense and truly Papal care, which Sixtus V undertook with his whole effort to emend and print the Bibles of the Vulgate edition, in accordance with the decree of the Council of Trent. In carrying this out he endured so many and such great labours, day and night, as no one could ever express in words, as I am persuaded. I, who saw these labours with my own eyes, was more than once astonished, as an eyewitness. For he read through the whole Bible word for word before it was committed to the press, although the whole Christian world, and very serious concerns at that, weighed on him every day. So he read through and corrected every page, so that all the sacred books, with all their parts, may be read according to the same council's decree, as they have customarily been read in the Catholic Church, and as they are found in the old Vulgate Latin edition. Nor, content with this, did he read through again from the beginning all the Bibles, so emended and newly printed, so that everything might come out into the light faithfully revised. So Roccha, the eyewitness. Sixtus V himself, in his bull: And so that this matter might be carried out the more without corruption, we ourselves corrected with our own hand whatever faults had crept in at the press. Fourthly, so that no one might miss the infallible judgement of the Pontiff: To the praise and glory of almighty God, by this our constitution, which shall remain valid forever, with the consent and counsel of our venerable brethren the Cardinals appointed for the purpose, of our own certain knowledge and with the fullness of apostolic power, we decree and declare that the Latin edition of the sacred pages of the Old and New Testament, the Vulgate, which the Council of Trent received as authentic, is to be judged without any doubt or controversy to be this very edition which we now publish, emended as well as it could be done and printed in the Vatican press, to be read throughout the Christian commonwealth and in all the churches of the Christian world; decreeing that it be approved, first by the universal holy Church and the consensus of the holy Fathers, then by the decree of the general Council of Trent, and now also by the apostolic authority handed down to us by the Lord, as true, lawful, authentic and indubitable, and that it be received and held in all public and private disputations, readings, preachings and explanations. So much so that he expressly sanctions: The codices of the Bible are in future to be printed according to this his exemplar, not the smallest particle being changed, added or removed; and the other copies, both manuscript and printed, of the same Vulgate edition, whether kept for the antiquity of their type, or for some notable ornament of the codex, or for the excellence of the printing, or for their marginal notes, are to be emended to agree with it. Otherwise, in those points which do not agree with this edition, they will in future have no credit and no authority. Moreover, he pronounces the sentence of the greater excommunication, from which no one except one at the point of death can be absolved by any Roman Pontiff other than the one in office, against anyone who has not corrected his own Bibles to this edition of his. SECTION II. Thus we have seen how vigorously Sixtus acted, a Pontiff ignorant of error, an infallible judge in a matter which pertains primarily and properly to the Apostolic See. Certainly all Catholics would have believed that his version was by now most thoroughly purged of all errors, had not Clement VIII disturbed their consciences. For two years later, in the year * 1592, when Sixtus had already completed his mortal course, and Urban VII, Gregory XIV and Innocent IX had also passed away, he procured another edition of the Bibles, revised by his own command, enlarged in very many places, mutilated in many, and in many contrary and so different that the different versions might not unfairly be considered different. This is shown plainly by the Reverend theologian Thomas James, our well-deserving friend, first librarian of the Bodleian Library in the University of Oxford, who most carefully compared the two editions, Sixtine and Clementine, with each other, and by listing their differing readings filled a fairly thick volume, which he titled The Papal War. In that book, besides innumerable variations, he brought together about two thousand readings which Clement, by the same apostolic authority, cut away and reformed to the sources, where Sixtus had confirmed them by apostolic authority against the Hebrew and Greek truth. But when the Roman Fathers noticed that heretics would take from this arguments against the Papal infallibility or holiness, they thought about a veil by which this shame of the Roman Church might be covered. Therefore Pope Clement, turning to tricks and frauds, substituted his own sanction for the bull of Sixtus V, which was sent into perpetual exile (indeed it no longer appears in any edition), and yet this new revision and edition of Clement VIII was given the name of Sixtus V. The same title remained: The Holy Vulgate Bible, edition of Sixtus V, revised and published by command of the Supreme Pontiff. And how is it Sixtus'? Did he not in 1590 publish his own edition, which differed immensely from the Clementine? Hear the fiction. Sixtus V, says the preface to the Clementine, ordered this work, now at last completed, to be committed to print. When it had already been printed, and the same Pontiff was labouring that it might be brought out into the light, he noticed that not a few faults had crept into the holy Bibles through the press's error, which seemed to need a repeated diligence; and he judged and decreed that the whole work be put back under the hammer. But when he was prevented by death from being able to accomplish this, Gregory XIV, who had succeeded Urban VII, set about completing it, with some very distinguished Cardinals and other learned men again appointed for this purpose. But when both he and Innocent IX, who succeeded him, were taken from this light in a very short time, at last, at the beginning of the pontificate of Clement VIII, with God's good help, the work which Sixtus V had intended was completed. And Gretser, p. 1058 of the appendix to the second book of Bellarmine On the Word of God: The earlier Bibles, he says, which Sixtus had published, Sixtus himself had decided to put back under the hammer and carefully revise, being offended by the multitude of errors that had crept in. But being carried off by a premature death, he could not actually accomplish this thought of his. What Sixtus's plan therefore left unfinished, Clement at last completed, and applied the mind and will of Sixtus to the matter, the Sixtine Bibles having been revised, for which reason they bear the name of Sixtus, etc. You see the pretext for the Clementine correction. Those faults which Clement removed, if we believe them, were typographical, and had crept into the Sixtine edition through the error of the press, and therefore that edition was suppressed. For although the preface does not say this expressly, it nonetheless hints at it obscurely, when it says: Since this work had already been printed, and the same Pontiff was labouring that it might be brought out into the light. It does not say: since it had already been printed and sent out into the light and fortified by a bull. You see the pretext, I say, but it is far too transparent. For who would believe that thousands of blunders crept into that edition through the error of the press, the edition which Sixtus had procured with such unusual diligence, which Sixtus, before it was committed to the press, had read through from head to foot, which he had read through again from the beginning when emended and newly printed, so that everything might come out into the light faithfully revised; as Sixtus himself testified of himself in the bull, and Roccha of him? Who would believe that so many sentences and words crept into the Sixtine through the error of the press, which Clement removed, e.g. 1 Sam. 24. 8 and 25. 6, and 2 Sam. 6. 12 and 8. 8 and 19. 10, Prov. 24 last verse, Hab. 1. 3, Matth. 24. 41, Acts 14. 6? And, on the contrary, so many which were cast out of the Sixtine and which Clement restored, such as Num. 30. 11, Lev. 20. 9, Judg. 17. 2, 3, Prov. 25. 24, Matth. 27. 35, 2 Chr. 2. 10? Who could persuade himself that so many contrarieties were admitted through the error of the press, such as Deut. 17. 8, Josh. 2. 18 and 11. 19, and finally so many and such great differences in numbers? Certainly, unless these passages had been read in various ways for many centuries past, this pretext could have been persuaded somewhat more easily to the less learned. But since Sixtus laid his hand to almost no passage except where the carelessness of the copyists and the variety of readings arising from it kept the reader in suspense and doubtful about the truer reading, and where necessity demanded that one reading be marked out by some apostolic authority, while he everywhere follows the Louvain edition, who would believe that in so many places the Sixtine edition, through typographical negligence, departs from the mind of Sixtus himself, which Clement says in his own edition he had expressed? Indeed, from where will it be established for us what this mind and intention of Sixtus was? Did he leave any writings on this matter? Whence am I to know that Sixtus, had he survived, would have corrected the Bibles just as Clement corrected them? Whence is this wish and desire of Sixtus clear, which Gretser alone opposes to James's Papal War? This answer is too feeble in a matter so serious. Other defenders this cause requires. I will say something more. The Sixtine edition, which takes its name from that Pontiff, came out so emended in his mind that in its copies, in 26 places, errors committed by the printers during printing, contrary to Sixtus's intention, were removed, partly with the pen, if the error was rather slight, partly by reprinting new words and pasting them over the faulty word, where correction with the pen would have been more difficult. Thomas James recorded a catalogue of these in the preface to The Papal War. E.g., Judith 1. 2 in the Sixtine edition was printed in latitudinem (in breadth). This happened either through a printer's error, or Sixtus himself changed his opinion after this page was printed. He therefore ordered that in altitudinem (in height) be printed with the same type on small slips of paper, and ordered these to be pasted over the other word in the copies before they were sold, which was done so skilfully, with that kind of paste which bookbinders use, that the correction could scarcely be noticed. Who, then, will say that that in altitudinem crept into the Sixtine through the error of the press? And yet Clement restored into his own edition the word latitudinem, which Sixtus had ordered to be covered and erased by the superimposed word altitudinem. But if, besides these 26 errors, so great a number had occurred to Sixtus, he would undoubtedly have suppressed the whole edition. Why does Gretser make no answer to this? Why this dumb fish? This edition came out with the bull prefixed; all printers were ordered to follow this edition in future, not the smallest particle being changed, added or removed; all learned men were ordered to correct their codices according to it; copies were dispersed into all the provinces of the Christian world; and shall we believe Clement and Gretser that thousands of blunders crept in through the error of the press? For either Sixtus himself noticed these blunders, before the bull was issued, or after. If before, then surely that man must have been very rash and profane: for what prudent man would decree that some edition is most thoroughly emended, and order it to be received down to the smallest particles, when he knows it lies hidden in some thousands of errors, none of which he notes? If after, then surely the mask has been torn from all the Pontiffs' bulls, and if anyone should call Sixtus a lying and vain man, he would not be far from the region of truth. For what, I ask you, would it be to deceive, if it were not this: to decree and declare, of certain knowledge and with the fullness of apostolic power, that the Vulgate edition which the Tridentine Fathers received as authentic is to be judged without any doubt or controversy to be THIS VERY edition, true, lawful, authentic and indubitable, etc.? Likewise to profess that he had corrected with his own hand whatever faults had crept in through the press? And what is more foolish and ridiculous than to pronounce an anathema on all who refuse to swear to this most faulty edition? Let these bugbears [κρηπφύγελα] therefore go hang.

units.la: Non obtusa adeo gestamus pectora Belgæ. Fefellit Catholicos Clemens, & pia fraude hic usus est. Adeo ut hic periclitetur in Sixto Pontificum infallibilitas, & in Clemente eorundem sanctitas. Quod enim ad Sixtum attinet, certa res est eum turpiter errasse, non quâ privatus doctor est, sed quâ Pontifex, vid. in negotio ad Apostolicæ Sedis curam, ipsis Papistis testibus, primariò & proprie pertinente. Videbat hoc Pontificius ille Doctor, quem citat Jamesius in Apologiâ Belli papalis? Is enim ingenuè confitebatur, Biblia illa Sixtina plane & omnino ad mentem Sixti fuisse edita; fuisse eum hominem præcipitis judicii, indulgentem affectibus, iracundum, tenacem propositi, ac proinde obnoxium erroribus: eum hoc habuisse propositum, ut hæc sua Editio esset authentica, à qua provocare nefas esset, etiam usque ad minimum jota & accentum. Quod decretum, inquiebat idem Doctor. si processisset, Periclitata fuisset, Papæ, supremi controversiarum judicis, infallibilitas, & jam triumphassent hæretici, Papam in rebus ad fidem pertinentibus in judicando errare posse. quo semel concesso, actum de Papatu fuisset. Dicebat itaque, Deum misertum Ecclesiæ suæ, præservando visibile ejus caput ab omni erroris periculo, bonum illum Sixtum, antequam animi sui consilium explere potuerit, rebus humanis exemisse. Sed & hic prætextus pellucet. Superavit enim Sixtus Editioni suæ. Biblia edita à capite ad calcem relegit, &, quæ vitio præli irrepserant, menda, ipse sua manu correxit, atque ad ejus correctionem, omnia exemplaria, partim calamo, partim eo, quem suprà diximus. modo, correcta sunt, antequam foràs prodirent, quorum 4. vel 5. sic correcta Jamesius se in Anglia vidisse affirmat. Ipse insuper bullam præfixit suam, atque in eâ statuit, vulgatam Editionem censendam hanc ipsam, inquit, quam jam EVVL-G4; GAMVS. Ecce dicit se evulgare, evulgat bullam, approbant omnia delegati Cardinales, distrahuntur exemplaria, eidem in Vaticano aureis literis positum hoc Elogium, Sacram paginam ex Concilii Trid. praescripto quàm emendatissimam divulgari mandavit, &c. & interim jubemur credere, illum non evulgasse sua Biblia. Puduit hujus effugii ipsum Gretzerum, dum inquit, Clementem priorem Editionem, quæ sub Sixti nomine PRODIERAT, ABOLEVISSE, p. 1059. Caditque adeo illud quoque quorundam commentum Biblia quidem illa fuisse edita, Bullam paratam, at non fuisse publicatam, intercedente nimirum Cardinalium collegio. Ita sibi à quodam Pontificio Doctore, cui nomen Bagshaw, responsum narrat D. Jamesius, qui & plateam & domum nominat, ubi hac de re collatio fuit instituta. Sed & illud friget. Distracta n. fuit illa Editio, nullo intercedente, nullo revocante aut recolligente exemplaria. Nec etiam Gregorius XIV. nec Vrbanus VII. nec Innocentius IX. quicquam tale tentarunt. Doctor Bishop, ipse Pontificius, agnoscebat decretum, sed ajebat hoc fuisse decretum Sixti non quà Pontificis; sed quà privati Doctoris. Ex quo & illud scire velim, annon & hoc magno cum Ecclesiæ Rom. periculo asseratur, Pontificem ita posse errare, ut putet adeoque in Bulla declaret, se, quà Pontificem, aliquid decernere & definire, cum interim privati tantùm Doctoris munus explet. Nec enim dicet quispiam, privati Doctoris esse Bullas edere, ex Apostolicæ authoritatis plenitudine decernere, declarare, denunciare anathema, &c. Hac enim ex Doctorum sententia, inquit * Marsennus, signa sunt, Papam ex Cathedrâ ut Papam loqui, Si contrarium sentientes anathemate feriat, vel cum rem, quam definit, toti Ecclesiæ proponit acceptandam, vel cum ait se ex consilio fratrum definire, tunc illa definitio à sede Apostolicâ oriri dicitur. Sed & hujus distinctionis subtilitatem (quà Papa, & quà privatus doctor) si ego me non satis capere dixero, habebo meæ hebetudinis socium, non incelebrem illum Cajetani adversarium, Catharinum, Episcopum Compsensem. Ille enim castigaturus Cajetanum, qui ad Math. 14. asserebat, Herodem contristatum fuisse quà Rex erat, non quà Herodes, Ego verò, inquit, picturam hanc non perspicio. Si enim verè contristatus est rex, & Rex est Herodes, cogor fateri juxta meam Logicam, etiam tristatum fuisse Herodem. Et, Herodes vult occidere Johannem, Rex vult occidere. Et si Rex fingit nolle se occidere Iohannem, etiam Herodes fingit. Vt Herodes rex, sic Sixtus est Papa. Si Sixtus erravit, etiam Papa, qui tunc erat, erravit. Si Papa, qui tunc erat, erravit, etiam Sixtus erravit. In societatem hanc etiam coit animosus ille Haereticorum malleus Alphonsus de Castro, qui l. 1. cap. 3. Omnem hominem etiam in fide errare posse, dicit, ETIAM SI PAPA SIT. Nam de Liberio Papa constat fuisse Arrianum & Anastasium suisse Nestorianis, qui historias legerit non dubitat. Quod autem alii dicunt, eum tunc non esse Papam, ac per hoc affirmant Papam non posse esse haereticum, est in re seria verbis velle jocari. Ad hunc enim modum posset quis citra impudentiam afferere, nullum fidelem posse in fide errare. Nam cum haereticus fuerit, jam desinet esse fidelis. Non enim dubitamus, an haereticum & Papam esse, coire in unum possint, sed id quaerimus, an hominem, qui alias in fide errare potuisset, dignitas pontificalis efficiat a fide inviabilem. Non enim credo aliquem esse adeo impudentem Papae assentatorem, ut ei tribuere hoc velit, ut nec errare, aut in interpretatione sacrarum literarum hallucinari possit. Nam cum constet, plurimos eorum adeo illiteratos esse, ut Gramaticam penitus ignorent, qui fit ut sacras literas interpretari possent? Sed nos haec missa faciamus, & veniamus ad Clementem VIII. Is alieno periculo edoctus cautius se gessit. Quin optimam ille operam vulgatae Editioni navarit, ne ipsa quidem invidia negaverit. Infinitis enim locis, pejore lectione, non obstante tot annorum praescriptione & Sixti judicio, in exilium ire jussa, meliorem & fontibus congruam postliminio restituit. Id quod aliquot locorum (quae ex magna sylva in libro Anglicano exhibuit Jamesius) inductione Lectori ad oculum demonstrabo. Eo autem libentius hanc operam Lectori gratificabor, quia ex his una opera duo illa colligit Lector, 1. Vix aliis locis medicam manum admovisse Pontifices, quam istis, quae jam antea varie legebantur, de iis vero quae manifesto errore ab ipso Interprete male conversa erant, plane securos fuisse. 2. Praetextum illum de praeli vitiis, quae Sixtinam deformarint & Clementem ad novam Editionem impulerint, immane quantum esse pellucidum. Videbit enim quisquis praejudicio occaecatus non est, Sixtinam in iis locis, ubi a Clementina variat, ex Lovaniensi maximam partem expressam esse.
units.tr: We Belgians do not carry such dull hearts. Clement deceived the Catholics, and here he used a pious fraud. So the infallibility of the Popes is put in danger in the case of Sixtus, and the holiness of the same men in the case of Clement. As for Sixtus, it is a settled matter that he erred disgracefully, not as a private teacher but as Pope, in a matter that pertains chiefly and properly to the care of the Apostolic See, as the Papists themselves bear witness. Did that Papist teacher whom Jamesius cites in his Apology for the Papal War see this? For he openly confessed that those Sixtine Bibles were published entirely and completely according to Sixtus's own mind; that he was a man of hasty judgment, given to his passions, angry, stubborn in his purpose, and therefore liable to errors; and that he had the purpose that this edition of his should be authentic, so that it would be wrong to appeal from it even as far as the smallest iota or accent. This decree, the same teacher said, if it had gone forward, would have endangered the infallibility of the Pope, the supreme judge of controversies, and the heretics would already have triumphed, holding that the Pope can err in judging matters pertaining to faith; once that was conceded, the Papacy would have been done for. He therefore said that God, having pity on his Church and preserving its visible head from every danger of error, took that good Sixtus out of human affairs before he could carry out his plan. But this pretext too is transparent. For Sixtus did finish his edition. He reread the Bibles from beginning to end and corrected with his own hand the faults that had crept in through printers' errors; and by his correction all the copies, partly with a pen and partly by the method we mentioned above, were corrected before they went out. Jamesius affirms that he himself saw four or five copies in England corrected in this way. Moreover, Sixtus prefixed his own bull to it, and in it he decreed that the Vulgate edition should be deemed this very one, he says, which now we have published. Behold, he says he publishes it, he publishes the bull; the delegated Cardinals approve everything; the copies are sold; at the Vatican this eulogy is placed in golden letters: He ordered the Sacred Page to be published as most accurately emended according to the decree of the Council of Trent, etc. And yet we are told to believe that he did not publish his own Bibles. Gretser himself was ashamed of this escape when he said that Clement abolished the earlier edition, which had appeared under the name of Sixtus, p. 1059. So that story of some men also falls: that the Bibles were indeed printed and the bull was prepared, but it was not made public, forsooth through the intervention of the college of Cardinals. Jamesius reports that this was the answer given him by a Papist teacher named Bagshaw, and he also names the square and the house where the discussion on this matter was held. But that too is feeble. For that edition was sold, with no one intervening, no one recalling or gathering up the copies. Nor did Gregory XIV, Urban VII, or Innocent IX attempt anything of the kind. The teacher Bishop, himself a Papist, acknowledged the decree, but said that this decree was Sixtus's not as Pope but as a private teacher. From this I would like to know also whether it is not asserted, with great danger to the Roman Church, that a Pope can err in such a way that he thinks, and so declares in a bull, that he is decreeing and defining something as Pope, while in fact he is performing only the office of a private teacher. For no one will say that it belongs to a private teacher to issue bulls, to decree, declare, and proclaim anathema by the fullness of Apostolic authority, and so on. For according to the opinion of the teachers, says Marsennus, these are the signs that the Pope speaks from the Chair as Pope: if he strikes with anathema those who think otherwise, or when he proposes the matter he defines to the whole Church to be accepted, or when he says that he defines it with the counsel of his brothers; then that definition is said to arise from the Apostolic See. But if I say that I do not grasp the subtlety of this distinction (that he is Pope in one respect and private teacher in another), I shall have as a companion in my dullness no less famous opponent of Cajetan, Catharinus, Bishop of Compsa. For he, rebuking Cajetan, who at Matthew 14 asserted that Herod was grieved as king and not as Herod, said: But I do not see this picture. For if the king was truly grieved, and Herod is the king, I am compelled, by my logic, to admit that Herod too was grieved. And Herod wants to kill John; the king wants to kill. And if the king pretends not to wish to kill John, Herod too pretends. As Herod is king, so Sixtus is Pope. If Sixtus erred, the Pope who then was also erred. If the Pope who then was erred, Sixtus too erred. Into this fellowship also comes that bold hammer of heretics, Alphonsus de Castro, who in book 1, chapter 3 says that every man, even if he is the Pope, can err in faith. For that Liberius the Pope was an Arian is established, and that Anastasius was a Nestorian no one who has read histories doubts. But that others say he was then not Pope, and therefore affirm that a Pope cannot be a heretic, is to want to joke in a serious matter. In this way anyone could, without shamelessness, assert that no believer can err in faith; for once he has become a heretic he will cease to be a believer. For we do not doubt whether a heretic and a Pope can come together in one person, but we ask whether the pontifical dignity makes a man who could otherwise err in faith unable to err. For I do not think anyone is so shameless a flatterer of the Pope as to want to grant him this: that he cannot err, or go astray in the interpretation of the sacred letters. For since it is established that many of them are so unlettered that they are utterly ignorant of grammar, how could they be able to interpret the sacred letters? But let us set these things aside and come to Clement VIII. Taught by the danger of another, he conducted himself more cautiously. Indeed he rendered the Vulgate edition an excellent service, which not even envy could deny. For in countless places, despite the long prescription of so many years and the judgment of Sixtus, he restored to their rightful place, after exile, readings that had been ordered into exile, which were worse, and which were in harmony with the sources. I shall demonstrate this to the reader by setting out some of these places (which Jamesius presented from a great forest in the English book). I shall gladly do this service for the reader, because from these examples the reader gathers two things at one stroke: (1) that the Popes had hardly applied the healing hand to any places other than those which had previously been read in various ways; but concerning those things which the translator himself had badly rendered through a manifest error, they were entirely unconcerned; (2) that the pretext of printers' faults, which had disfigured the Sixtine edition and driven Clement to a new edition, is immensely transparent. For whoever is not blinded by prejudice will see that the Sixtine edition, in those places where it differs from the Clementine, was for the most part copied from the Louvain edition.

units.la: CAP.
units.tr: CHAPTER.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAP. X.

units.la: Specimen diligentia à Clemente adhibita. Eum magis spectasse fontes, quàm Sixtus fecerat. Ostenditur illud quoque his exemplis, quam sit inanis ille pratextus de prali vitiis.
units.tr: A specimen of the diligence Clement applied. That he looked more to the sources than Sixtus had done. This also shows from these examples how empty that pretext about the printers' errors is.

units.la: SECTIO I Initium fiat à sententiis vocibusque, quas à Sixto male omissas, Clemens bene restituit.
units.tr: SECTION I. Let us begin with the sentences and words which Sixtus wrongly omitted and Clement rightly restored.

units.la: Num. 30.11. Vxor in domo viri, usque ad finem versus, qui desinit in haec verba, Et Dominus ei propitius erit. Haec leguntur etiam in Chald. Ebraeo & Graeco. Lucas Brugensis, in locis insignioribus Romanae correctionis, nullam hujus correctionis facit mentionem,
units.tr: Num. 30.11. The wife in her husband's house, to the end of the verse, which ends with these words: And the Lord will be merciful to her. These are also read in the Chaldee, the Hebrew and the Greek. Lucas of Bruges, in the more notable places of the Roman correction, makes no mention of this correction.

units.la: Prov. 25. 24. Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, quàm cum mulie-re litigiosa & in domo communi. Et hic versus restitutus est ex Ebr. Ch. Graeco. Lucas Brug. hanc varietatem non notavit.
units.tr: Prov. 25.24. It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop than with a contentious woman and in a common house. This verse too has been restored from the Hebrew, Chaldee and Greek. Lucas of Bruges did not note this variation.

units.la: Math. 27. 35. Vt impleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam dicentem, diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, & super vestem meam miserunt sortem. Haec ex Gr. Syriaco, & vetustis codicibus restituta sunt. Lucas Brug. tacet.
units.tr: Matt. 27.35. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots. This has been restored from the Greek, the Syriac and old codices. Lucas of Bruges is silent.

units.la: Levit. 10. 9. Patri matrique maledixit. Ex Ebr. Ch. Gr. & Lovanien-sibus Bibliis restituit haec Clemens nihil annotante Lucâ.
units.tr: Lev. 10.9. He cursed his father and his mother. Clement restored this from the Hebrew, Chaldee and Greek and from the Louvain Bibles, with Lucas noting nothing.

units.la: Jud. 17. verf. 2. 3. Reddidit ergo eos matri sua; qua dixerat ei, consecravi & vovi hoc argentum. Ex Ebr. Chald. Gr. & Lovan. Lucas tacet.
units.tr: Judg. 17.2–3. So he gave them back to his mother; and she said to him, I had dedicated and vowed this silver. From the Hebrew, Chaldee, Greek and the Louvain Bible. Lucas is silent.

units.la: 1. Sam. 4. 21. Quia capta est arca Dei. Ex Ebr. Chald. & Lovan. At Sixtus ea omisit, quòd in Gr. non extarent.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 4.21. Because the ark of God was taken. From the Hebrew, Chaldee and the Louvain Bible. But Sixtus omitted it, because it was not found in the Greek.

units.la: 1. Reg. 12. 10. Sic loqueris ad eos. Ex Ebr. Ch.Gr.
units.tr: 1 Kings 12.10. Thus shall you speak to them. From the Hebrew, Chaldee and Greek.

units.la: 2. Chron. 2. 10. Et vini viginti millia metretas. Hîc Lucas Burg. Mirum est, inquit, omitti à plerisque libris illud, Et vini viginti millia metretas, contra Ebraici fontis & Graeca Interpretationis fidem. Idem observaverunt Lovan. in margine. Et tamen & ille & Sixtus haec verba scientes volentes omisere. Clemens restituit.
units.tr: 2 Chron. 2.10. And twenty thousand measures of wine. Here Lucas of Bruges says: "It is strange, he says, that the clause, And twenty thousand measures of wine, is omitted by most books, contrary to the testimony of the Hebrew source and of the Greek translation." The Louvain editors likewise observed this in the margin. And yet both he and Sixtus, knowing these words, deliberately omitted them. Clement restored them.

units.la: SECTIO II.
units.tr: SECTION II.

units.la: Sententiæ & voces, quas à Sixto male interpolatas, Clemens bene expunxit.
units.tr: Sentences and words which Sixtus wrongly interpolated and Clement rightly struck out.

units.la: 1. Sam. 24. 8. Vivit Dominus, quia nisi Dominus percusserit eum, aut dies ejus venerit ut moriatur, aut descendens in prælium perierit, propitius mihi sit Dominus, ut non mittam manum meam in Christum Domini. Hæc expunxit Clemens, quia nec in Ebr. nec Chald. nec Gr. nec codicibus aliquot Latinis apparent.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 24. 8. As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strike him, or his day come that he die, or he go down into battle and perish, the Lord be merciful to me, that I should not lay my hand on the Christ of the Lord. Clement struck this out because it appears neither in the Hebrew, the Chaldee, nor the Greek, nor in some Latin manuscripts.

units.la: 1. Sam. 25. 6. Ex multis annis salvos faciens tuos & omnia tua. Hæc non comparent in Ebr. Chald Gr. ipsis quoque Lovanien-sibus testibus. Sixtus tamen, qui ea in Lov. reperiebat, non sustulit. Lucas ait ea redundare, & merito (à Clemente) sublata esse.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 25. 6. Saving your people and all your possessions from many troubles. These words do not appear in the Hebrew, the Chaldee, or the Greek, as the Louvain witnesses themselves admit. Sixtus, however, who found them in the Louvain edition, did not remove them. Lucas says they are superfluous and were rightly removed by Clement.

units.la: 2. Sam. 6. 12. Dixitque David, Ibo & reducam arcam. Nec in Ebr. nec Ch. nec Gr. nec multis vetustis cod. extant. Merito censuerunt Romani Patres, inquit Lucas, hæc omittenda. Intelligit correctores à Clemente delegatos. Sixtus enim ejusque delegati Patres (quorum Lucas nunquam distincte meminit) hæc approbaverant & civitate donaverant.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 6. 12. And David said, I will go and bring back the ark. These words are found neither in the Hebrew, the Chaldee, nor the Greek, nor in many ancient manuscripts. "The Roman Fathers rightly judged these words should be omitted," says Lucas. He means the correctors appointed by Clement. For Sixtus and the Fathers he appointed (of whom Lucas never clearly speaks) had approved these words and given them a place in the text.

units.la: 2. Sam. 8. 8. De quo fecit Salomo omnia vasa area, in templo & mare æneum & columnas & altare. Hæc verba non esse hujus loci, sed 1. Chron. 18. 8. annotavit Lucas. Nec Ebr. nec Chald. nec Græci codices ea legunt. Erant tamen in quibusdam codicibus Lat. & Lovan. Et à Sixto approbata.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 8. 8. Of which Solomon made all the vessels of the ark, in the temple, and the brazen sea, and the pillars and the altar. Lucas noted that these words do not belong to this place but to 1 Chron. 18. 8. Neither the Hebrew, the Chaldee, nor the Greek manuscripts read them. Yet they were in some Latin manuscripts and in the Louvain edition, and Sixtus approved them.

units.la: 2. Sam. 19. 10. Et consilium totius Israel venit ad Regem. Hæc ab Ebr. & Ch. absunt, etiam ex vetustis MS. exulant, confitentibus Lovan. Lovanienses tamen & Sixtus ex LXX. ea huc transtulerant.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 19. 10. And the counsel of all Israel came to the king. These words are absent from the Hebrew and the Chaldee, and they are missing even from ancient manuscripts, as the Louvain divines confess. Nevertheless, the Louvain divines and Sixtus had carried them over here from the Septuagint.

units.la: Prov. 24. verf. vlt. Vsque quo piger dormies usque quo de somno consurges? Ita Lov. & Sixtus. At in Ebr. Chald. Græcis & vetustis MS. non extant. Ideo Clemens expunxit. Lucas silet.
units.tr: Prov. 24, last verse. How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? So the Louvain edition and Sixtus. But these words are not found in the Hebrew, the Chaldee, the Greek, or ancient manuscripts. Therefore Clement struck them out. Lucas says nothing.

units.la: Sap. 1. verf. pen. Injustitia autem mortis est acquisitio. Lovanienses, cum nec in originali nec in vetustiss. & optimis MS. hæc invenirent, ejecerunt ea ex textu in marginem. Sixtus V. ut pontifex & legitimus hujusmodi controversiarum judex, restituit ea in integrum; Clemens & ipse Pontifex, Sixto authoritate nequaquam quam inferior, ea rursus ejecit, & ex textu & ex margine.
units.tr: Wis. 1, last but one verse. Injustice, moreover, is the acquisition of death. The Louvain divines, since they found these words neither in the original nor in the most ancient and best manuscripts, moved them from the text into the margin. Sixtus V, as pope and lawful judge of such controversies, restored them in full. Clement, himself also pope, but in no way of lesser authority than Sixtus, threw them out again, both from the text and from the margin.

units.la: Habac. 1. 3. Quare respicis contemptores & taces, concultante impio justiorem se? Et facies homines quasi pisces maris & quasi reptilia non habentia ducem. Hæc verba non esse hujus loci, sed verf. 13. & 14. ex Ebr. Ch. & Gr. judicavit Clemens. Ideo ea expunxit. Lovaniensem Edit. secutus fuit Sixtus.
units.tr: Hab. 1. 3. Why do you look on the scorners and hold your peace, while the wicked man oppresses the one more righteous than himself? And you will make men like the fishes of the sea, and like creeping things that have no leader. Clement judged that these words do not belong to this place but to verses 13 and 14, on the evidence of the Hebrew, the Chaldee, and the Greek. Therefore he struck them out. Sixtus followed the Louvain edition.

units.la: Math. 24. 41. Duo in lecto, unus assumetur & unus relinquetur. Circa has voces variæ opiniones sunt. Codices tam Græci quam Latini, Patres Orientalis & Occid. Ecclesiæ Pontificesque ipsi hic dissident. Hentenius secutus eorum sententiam, qui eas ex Lucâ hùc translatas judicârunt, eas ejecit. Sixtus eas restituit. Supervenit tandem Clemens & secundum Hentenium adversus Sixtum pronunciavit.
units.tr: Matt. 24. 41. Two in a bed; one shall be taken and one shall be left. Opinions about these words vary. Greek and Latin manuscripts alike, the Fathers of the Eastern and Western Church, and the popes themselves disagree here. Hentenius, following the opinion of those who judged that these words were transferred here from Luke, struck them out. Sixtus restored them. At last Clement came and gave judgment against Sixtus, in agreement with Hentenius.

units.la: Act. 14. 6. Et commota est omnis multitudo in doctrina eorum: Paulus autem & Barnabas morabantur Lystris. Hæc leguntur in quibusdam Gr. codicibus. At in melioribus & Syr. desunt. Sixtus ea retinuit: Clemens ejecit. Lucas quasi dubius non facilè ea addenda esse ait.
units.tr: Acts 14. 6. And all the multitude was stirred by their teaching; but Paul and Barnabas stayed at Lystra. These words are read in some Greek manuscripts, but they are absent from the better ones and from the Syriac. Sixtus retained them; Clement removed them. Lucas, as if in doubt, says they should not readily be added.

units.la: Act. 24. verf. 18. Et appehendèrunt me clamantes & dicentes, tolle inimicum nostrum. Hæc verba nec in Gr. nec Syr. nec MS. reperiri notârunt Lovan. Sixtus tamen retinuit. Clemens ejecit.
units.tr: Acts 24, verse 18. And they laid hold on me, crying and saying, Away with our enemy. The Louvain divines noted that these words are not found in the Greek, the Syriac, or the manuscripts. Sixtus nevertheless retained them. Clement removed them.

units.la: 2. Joh. 2. 11. Ecce prædixi vobis, ut in die Domini non confundamini Hæc Sixtus contra judicium Lovan. & fidem Græcorum codicum & plerorumque MS. recipit. Clemens ejecit.
units.tr: 2 John 2. 11. Behold, I have told you beforehand, that in the day of the Lord you may not be confounded. Sixtus received this against the judgment of the Louvain divines, the testimony of the Greek manuscripts, and most manuscripts generally. Clement removed it.

units.la: Sixt. Lov. Qui autem superbierit, obedire nolens sacerdotis imperio: ex decreto judicis moriatur homo ille. Ita hunc locum citat & Coccius tom. 1. p. 850. & Bellarm. tribus locis. Vid. Tom.1.p. 175.176. & 959. multumque praesidii in hoc loco ponunt & illi & alii, ut probent Papae supereminentem potestatem, eumque solum esse judicem in controversiis religionis. At si Bellar. aut alius quilibet Papista existimat sibi hunc locum ulli posse esse usui, fallitur. Nam Clemens locum sic restituit, & decreto judicis. Adi jam ad locum hunc lib.2. Antibarb. Jos. 3. 17. Sixt. Lovan. contra Jordanem. Cl. Ebr. Ch. Gr. contra Jericho. 1.Sam. 3. verf. 2. 3. Sixt. Lov. nec poterat videre lucernam Dei, antiquam expectaretur. Clemens, nec poterat videre : Lucerna Dei antequam extingueretur, &c. 1.Sam. 2. 28. Sixt. Lov. ad Salomonem. Cl. Ebr. Ch. Gr. ad Joab.
units.tr: Sixt. Lov.: But whoever is proud and refuses to obey the priest's command: let that man die by the decree of the judge. Coccius cites this passage in this way, vol. 1, p. 850, and Bellarmine in three places. See vol. 1, pp. 175–176 and 959. Both they and others place great reliance on this passage, to prove the supreme power of the Pope and that he alone is judge in controversies of religion. But if Bellarmine or any other Papist thinks this passage can be of any use to them, he is mistaken. For Clement restores the passage thus: and by the decree of the judge. Now turn to this passage in book 2 of the Antibarbarus. Josh. 3.17 Sixt. Lovan.: against the Jordan; Cl. Eb. Ch. Gr.: against Jericho. 1 Sam. 3, vv. 2–3, Sixt. Lov.: nor could he see the lamp of God before it was expected to be extinguished; Clement: nor could he see: the lamp of God before it was extinguished, etc. 1 Sam. 2.28 Sixt. Lov.: to Solomon; Cl. Eb. Ch. Gr.: to Joab.

units.la: Vtra lectio melior esset (dissentientibus codicibus) quæsitum à multis. Clemens ex fontibus controversiam illam diremit. 2.Reg. 15. 29. Sixt Lov. in Thersam. Cl. Ebr. Ch. Gr. in terram. Judith 1. 2. Sixt. Lov. in altitudinem 70. cub. Clem. Gr. in latitudinem 70. cub.
units.tr: Which reading was the better one, since the manuscripts disagree, has been asked by many. Clement settled that controversy from the sources. 2 Kings 15.29 Sixt. Lov.: into Thersa; Cl. Eb. Ch. Gr.: into the land. Judith 1.2 Sixt. Lov.: to a height of 70 cubits; Clem. Gr.: to a breadth of 70 cubits.

units.la: Hæc verba in altitudinem excusa sunt in Sixtinâ iisdem characteribus, queis tota Biblia, in exiguo chartæ segmento, & valde artificiosè glutino impositá his vocibus, in latitudinem. Sic enim antea fuerat excusum. Quod ipsum manifestum indicium est magnæ istius industriæ, quam Sixtus adhibuit in Latinâ Editione quàm emendatissimè ex sua sententia & mente edendâ. Et adhuc reperiuntur, qui nobis persuadere satagunt, Editionem illam, valde negligenter impressam & editam, ipsumque Sixtum decrevisse totum opus sub incudem revocare? Quis negare audet, hanc correctionem ex certo animi proposito & judicio factam? Apage ergo calvam istam excusationem, præli vitio, ea quæ Clemens correxit, irrepsisse. Corrector fuit Sixtus, nostra nos ipsi manu correximus, si qua præli vitia obrepserant, inquit ipse Sixtus, atque hujusmodi correctio fuit deliberatus actus. Ibidem, Sixt. Lovan. in latitudinem 30. cub. Clem. Gr. in altitudinem 30. cub. Job. 31. 7. Sixt. Greg. & Lov. Si secutus est oculus meus cor meum. Clem. Ebr. Ch. Gr. Si secutum est oculos meos cor meum. Ps 41. 3. Sixt. Lov. ad Deum fontem vivum. Cl Eb. Gr. & 14. MS. ad Deum fortem vivum.
units.tr: These words in altitudinem were printed in the Sixtine edition in the same type as the whole Bible, on a small strip of paper, and very skilfully glued over the words in latitudinem. For that is how it had been printed before. This itself is a clear sign of the great care Sixtus took in the Latin edition, which was to be published as correctly as possible according to his own judgment and intention. And are there still people who try to persuade us that that edition was printed and published very carelessly, and that Sixtus himself had decided to put the whole work back on the anvil? Who dares deny that this correction was made from a definite purpose and considered judgment? Away, then, with that bald excuse, that what Clement corrected crept in through a printing error. Sixtus himself was the corrector: we ourselves corrected with our own hand whatever printing errors had crept in, says Sixtus himself, and such a correction was a deliberate act. Ibid. Sixt. Lovan.: in breadth 30 cubits; Clem. Gr.: in height 30 cubits. Job 31.7 Sixt. Greg. and Lov.: If my eye has followed my heart. Clem. Eb. Ch. Gr.: If my heart has followed my eyes. Ps. 41.3 Sixt. Lov.: to God, the living fountain; Cl. Eb. Gr. and 14 MSS.: to God, the strong living one.

units.la: Lucas Br. Constanter retinenda est vox, fortem, &c. Editio tamen Fortunati Fanensis, quæ prodiit Venetiis, 1609. retinuit
units.tr: Lucas Br.: The word fortem is to be consistently retained, etc. The edition of Fortunatus of Fano, however, which came out at Venice in 1609, retained

units.la: vitiosam lectionem, fontem. Vnde apparet, quo loco editio Clementis sit apud Pontificios. Et tamen gravissimam majoris excommuniciationis poenam Clemens iis denunciat, qui hanc suam editionem non ad minimam usque voculam in posterum expresserint. Haec Jamesius. Ad quae illud adjiciam, editionem quoque Parisiensem 1618. privilegio Regis editam legere fontem, insuper habita correctione Clementis. Et tamen Theologi Parisienses, Garnier & Bazot testantur, se illam Editionem diligenter cum exemplari, Romae, Sixti V. Pontificis (id est Clementis VIII. ut supra dictum est) jussu excusa, contulisse & illam huic in omnibus conformem reperisse, praeter aliqua quae inter errata rejecta sunt. At in erratis altum de hoc loco silentium, cum tamen ex hoc eodem Psalmo vitium Typographicum ibi annotatum sit. [Sed fortassis in eodem luto haesunt cum Acosta Jesuita, qui de Christo revelato, 3.20. postquam professus fuisset, se non dubitare de veritate hujus correctionis, haec subjungit: Et Ecclesia pergit legere, fontem vivum, delectata contemplatione illius, apud quem est fons vitae. Recipiendus est iste quoque sensus, tanquam divinitus provisus atque intentus. Peccavit ergo, hoc judice, Clemens, quod sensum illum a Deo intentum loco moverit, aut saltem ei in margine locum non reliquerit. Caeterum, errorem istum levem & nequaquam perniciosum fuisse, lubentes concedimus, sed eum a Spiritu S. intentum & provisum fuisse, non sine perniciose errore dici potest. Vide Cl. Rivetum pag. Isag.221.]
units.tr: the faulty reading fontem. From this it appears in what place Clement's edition stands among the Papists. And yet Clement pronounces the gravest penalty of greater excommunication on those who in future do not reproduce his edition exactly, not even to the smallest word. So far James. To this I will add that the Paris edition of 1618, published by royal privilege, also reads fontem, disregarding Clement's correction. And yet the Parisian theologians Garnier and Bazot testify that they collated that edition carefully with the copy printed at Rome by order of Pope Sixtus V (that is, Clement VIII, as said above), and found it conformed to it in all things, except some things which were rejected among the errata. But in the errata there is a deep silence about this passage, although from this same Psalm a typographical error is noted there. [But perhaps they stick in the same mud as the Jesuit Acosta, who, in On Revealed Christ 3.20, after professing that he did not doubt the truth of this correction, adds: And the Church goes on reading "fontem vivum," delighted in contemplation of him with whom is the fountain of life. That sense too must be received as divinely provided and intended.] Clement therefore, by this judgment, sinned in moving that sense, intended by God, out of its place, or at least in not leaving it room in the margin. Moreover, we gladly concede that this error was slight and by no means harmful; but to say that it was intended and provided by the Holy Spirit cannot be said without a pernicious error. See Cl. Rivetus, Isagoge, p. 221.

units.tr: Prov. 20.25 Sixt. Lov. Gr.: to devour the saints; Cl. Eb. and 18 MSS.: to devour the saints.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: Chapter XI.

units.la: Clemens longe modestior quam Sixtus. Disputatur de authoritate Praefationis, quae Clementina praefixa est, contra Serarium. In eâ asseritur, Biblia non esse à Clemente accuratissimè castigata, sed multa adhuc esse relicta sine emendatione. Cur hoc factum sit. Inferetur ergo, ne nunc quidem Ecclesia Rom. de authentica Edit. prospectum esse. Nondum enim est emendatissima.
units.tr: Clement was far more moderate than Sixtus. This chapter discusses the authority of the Preface prefixed to the Clementine edition, against Serarius. In it the claim is made that the Bibles were not most carefully corrected by Clement, but that many things were still left uncorrected. The reason why this happened is given. It will therefore be inferred that the Church of Rome has not yet been provided with an authentic edition, since it is not yet most correct.

units.la: Ides itaque, benevole lector, Sixtum V. fere Lovaniensem editionem secutum esse. Vbi ergo praetextus sphalmatum Typographicorum? vides & illud, correctionem Clementis propius accedere ad textum originalem, id quod primario ostendere satagebam. Nihilominus Clemens, veritus fortassis, ne successorum aliquem alius incesseret genius, atque ita nova procella concuteretur arx Pontificiæ infallibilitatis intra terminos modestiæ se continuit, tam in præfatione, quam in Bullâ. Quod ad Præfationem attinet, ea licet. Clementis nomen non præterat, tamen non nisi eo volente & jubente & approbante, tam primæ editioni, quam omnibus ex eâ expressis præfixa est, ut frustrà fit Serarius, qui admodum anxiè de hujus Præfationis authoritate disputat, cap. 19. quæst. 16. Satis est, eam ex mente & sententiâ Clementis conceptam esse & editioni præfixam; Satis est, nullum ex eo Pontificem eam revocasse. In hunc usque diem omnibus Latinæ correctæ versionis editionibus præmittitur. At nullius Pontificis præscriptum est nomen, inquit Serarius, nullius Synodi. Quid tum postea? Prudenti consilio hoc factum esse innuis, quæst. 18. An persuadebis cuipiam, Serari, Pontificem, ad cujus curam & munus decretorum Synodicorum executio, imprimis vero sacræ scripturæ puritas & integritas pertinet, in editione à se procurata tolerarurum fuisse hanc præfationem, si vel minimam particulam ipsius menti adversantem habuisset? Sed quid tandem habet illa Præfatio? Accipe itaque Christiane Lector, eodem Clemente Summo Pont. annuente, vulgatam S. Scripturæ Editionem, quantâ fieri potuit diligentia castigatam: quam quidem sicut omnibus numeris absolutam pro humana imbecillitate affirmare difficile est, ita cæteris omnibus quæ huc usque prodierunt, emendatiorem & puriorem esse, minimè dubitandum. Horum, ut & subsequentium verborum, quem dabo fideliorem Interpretem ipso Serario? Is ergo in his verbis primò observat voculam ANNUENTE, non verò JUBENTE prudenter adhibitam.' Prodiit, inquit, hac emendatio Pontifice ANNUENTE, non autem JUBENTE, non omnia & singula quæ in illa sunt, sive magna sive parva censente ac mandante. Constat verò, pergit Jesuita, in re aliquâ, quæ fit, differre multum hac, annuere vel permittere rem illam fieri, & approbare vel jubere illam fieri. Et paulo post dicit Præfationem non dicere, Editionem hanc correctam à Papâ, omnino & quoad singula approbari & imperari, sed tantummodo annui. Secundò hic observat Serarius ista verba, quantâ fieri potuit diligentiâ. Intelligitur, inquit, non absolutè & Metaphysicè, quanta omnino posibilis fuit, sed moraliter, quanta illo tempore, loco, per illos, cum illis adjumentis. Si vero alio loco & tempore plus quiddam aliunde oportunitatis & adjumenti accedat, non negatur major adhuc aliquâ in re castigatio. III. observat illa verba, Eam omnibus numeris absolutam esse pro humanâ imbecillitate affirmare difficile est. Potest igitur adhuc, inqvit Serarius, in aliquo numerus deesse aliquis. Et vel Cardinalibus vel doctis hominibus, qui in castigatione ista laborárunt, omnis humana videtur negari imbecillitas, si omnia eos mendâ vidisse, omnia correxisse, nihil usquam correctione adhuc aliquâ dignum reliquisse dicantur. IV. notat illa verba, ceteris omnibus, qua usque prodierunt, emendationem, &c. nota, inquit, hoc praeteriti temporis verbum prodierunt. Quia si adhuc in isto opere tam feliciter coepto, ac, quantum fieri potuit, perfecto pergat Apostolica Sedis vigilantia, non negatur, quin possint deinceps aliquae praeterea Editiones prodire correctiores ac perfectiores. Sequuntur in eadem Praefatione alia, quae huc quoque adducit Serarius. Ergo ut compendium faciam, proponam ea ipsis verbis Serarii, quibus ea interpretatur. V. Diserte dicitur, (in eadem vid. Praefatione) in vulgato Vetere Bibliorum Interprete quaedam visa fuisse mutanda, quae consulto immutata relicta sunt. Illorum igitur ipsorum, qui correctioni huic praefuerunt, judicio, possent adhuc mutari nonnulla. VI. causam addunt isti, cur quae mutanda judicarent, mutare tamen nolucrint, triplicem. 1. est quorundam offensio. 2. suspicio de posteriorum saeculorum * libris, quod fortasse minus puri & integri evaserint. 3. Institutum ipsorum, quod non novam facere voluerint Bibliorum versionem, vel antiquum Interpretem ulla ex parte corrigere vel emendare, sed ipsam veterem ac vulgatam Latinam à mendis veterum librariorum nec non pravarum Emendationum erroribus repurgatam suae pristinae puritati, quoad ejus fieri potuit, restituere. Unde argumentor, si aliquâ in re cessset illa offensio, admitatur etiam illa suspicio, poterit aliqua adhuc in istis Bibliis correctio fieri. VII. notandum etiam in illa suspicione illud fortasse. Significat enim hac in re certi nihil esse, estque Particula, quae Christianae fidei objectis omnique negotio removenda. Et sicut fortasse fuerunt libri posteriores minus puri, sic fortasse in istis locis, quae mutanda videbantur & mutata non sunt, puri fuerunt & integri. Tam enim hoc fortasse certum ac illud. Haec Serarius ex Praefatione. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, opinor, veritas tertii consectarii in fine cap.8. propositi, vid. ne nunc quidem post geminam Sixti V. & Clementis VIII. correctionem, Eccle-
units.tr: You see therefore, kind reader, that Sixtus V followed the Louvain edition almost throughout. Where, then, is the pretext of typographical errors? You also see that Clement's correction comes closer to the original text, which is what I was chiefly labouring to show. Nevertheless Clement, perhaps fearing that some other spirit might attack one of his successors, and that the citadel of papal infallibility might thus be shaken by a new storm, kept himself within the bounds of moderation, both in the preface and in the bull. As for the Preface, although Clement's name does not appear on it, it was prefixed to the first edition and to all the editions printed from it only with his will, command and approval. So Serarius labours in vain when he disputes very anxiously about the authority of this Preface, chapter 19, question 16. It is enough that it was composed according to Clement's mind and meaning and prefixed to the edition; it is enough that no pope has ever revoked it. To this day it is placed at the head of all the editions of the corrected Latin version. "But no pope's name is attached to it," says Serarius, "nor that of any synod." What follows from that? You hint, question 18, that this was done by prudent design. But will you persuade anyone, Serarius, that the pope, to whose care and duty the execution of synodal decrees, and above all the purity and integrity of Holy Scripture, belongs, would have tolerated this preface in an edition he had himself procured, if it had contained even the smallest part opposed to his mind? But what does that Preface actually say? "Receive therefore, Christian reader, with the consent of the same Clement, Supreme Pontiff, the Vulgate edition of Holy Scripture, corrected with all the diligence that could be applied; which, though it is hard to affirm that it is perfect in every respect, given human weakness, yet there is no doubt that it is more correct and purer than all the others that have appeared up to now." Of these words, and of those that follow, what more faithful interpreter could I give than Serarius himself? He first observes in these words the word ANNUENTE, "with consent," used prudently and not JUBENTE, "by command." "It was published," he says, "with the Pontiff ANNUENTE, that is with his consent, not JUBENTE, by his command, the Pontiff not judging or ordering each and every thing in it, whether great or small. But it is clear," the Jesuit goes on, "that in any matter that is done, to consent or permit that thing to be done differs greatly from approving or commanding it to be done." And shortly after he says that the Preface does not say that this corrected edition was approved and ordered by the Pope in every respect and in each detail, but only that he consented. Secondly, Serarius notes these words, "with all the diligence that could be applied." It is understood, he says, not absolutely and metaphysically, as great as it could possibly have been, but morally, as great as was possible at that time, in that place, through those men, with those aids. But if at another place and time some more opportunity and assistance come from elsewhere, a still greater correction in some matter is not denied. Thirdly, he observes those words, "that it is hard to affirm that it is perfect in every respect, given human weakness." "Therefore," says Serarius, "some number may still be lacking in some respect. And human weakness would seem to be denied to the Cardinals or learned men who laboured in that correction, if they are said to have seen every error, to have corrected everything, and to have left nothing anywhere still worthy of further correction." Fourthly, he notes those words, "than all the others that have appeared up to now, the correction," and so on. "Note," he says, "this verb of past tense, have appeared. For if the vigilance of the Apostolic See continues in this work, so happily begun and, as far as possible, completed, it is not denied that other, more correct and more perfect editions may appear afterwards." Other things follow in the same Preface, which Serarius also cites here. So, to make a summary, I will set them out in Serarius's own words, in which he explains them. Fifthly, "It is plainly said (in the same Preface) that in the Vulgate Old Latin version some things seemed to need changing, which were deliberately left unchanged. Therefore, by the judgment of those very men who presided over this correction, some things could still be changed." Sixthly, "those men give a threefold reason why, though they judged some things should be changed, they nevertheless were unwilling to change them. 1. the offence of some people. 2. the suspicion about the books of later centuries, that perhaps they turned out less pure and less sound. 3. their intention, which was not to make a new version of the Bible, nor to correct or emend the ancient translator in any part, but to restore the old and Vulgate Latin, cleansed of the errors of ancient copyists and of the mistakes of faulty emendations, to its former purity, as far as that could be done. Hence I argue that if the offence in some matter ceases, then that suspicion too should be admitted, and some further correction could still be made in these Bibles." Seventhly, "it should also be noted in that suspicion the word perhaps. For it signifies that nothing is certain in this matter, and it is a particle which must be removed from the objects of the Christian faith and from all business of this kind. And just as the later books perhaps were less pure, so in those places which seemed to need changing and were not changed, perhaps they were pure and sound. For this perhaps is as certain as that." These are Serarius's words from the Preface. From all of these it appears, I think, the truth of the third corollary proposed at the end of chapter 8: that even now, after the double correction of Sixtus V and Clement VIII, the Church of Rome does not have an authentic Scripture.

units.la: * Ebraeos & Graecos intelligit. siam Rom. habere authenticam Scripturam. Necdum enim est emendatissima. At huic soli, concilium Trid. authenticam authoritatem detulit.
units.tr: * He means the Hebrews and the Greeks. For it is not yet most correct. Yet the Council of Trent conferred authentic authority on this alone.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: In Clementina Præfat. & Serarii deductionibus committuntur inter se Pontifices, Ostenditur hic laborare bonam fidem, & infallibilitatem Pontificum. Confessio Bellarm. Bandini, &c. quod Biblia neccdum sint accuratissimè emendata. Luca Brug. catalogus locorum adhuc corrigendorum. Catholicorum spes misere elusa. Requisita textus authentici. Quaeritur, an Pontifex non voluerit, an potius non potuerit Biblia accuratissimè castigare. Examinantur causæ cur non omnia castigata sint.
units.tr: In the Clementine Preface and in Serarius's inferences the Pontiffs contradict one another. It is shown here that they are not acting in good faith, and that the infallibility of the Pontiffs is in doubt. The confession of Bellarmine, Bandini, etc., that the Bibles are not yet most accurately emended. Lucas of Bruges's catalogue of places still to be corrected. The hopes of the Catholics wretchedly disappointed. The requirements of an authentic text. The question is asked whether the Pontiff did not wish, or rather could not, most accurately correct the Bibles. The reasons are examined why not everything has been corrected.

units.la: SUperioribus capitibus ostendimus veritatem tertii consectarii, nec nunc quidem Ecclesia Rom. de emendatissima, ac proinde authentica Scriptura prospectum esse. Antequam pergamus ad alia, illustranda & examinanda sunt ea, quæ ex Præfatione Clementinâ deduxit Serarius. Primam ejus observationem circa voculam annuente quod attinet, Si non aberrat in ejus interpretatione, ut vid. annuere hic opponatur τῷ approbare & mandare, tum certè non obtuso aculeo hic Sixtus pungitur, qui vocibus declaramus, statuimus, decernimus, &c. in sua bullâ usus, certam scientiam & Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudinem obtenderat. Nec capio etiam quomodo hæc unâ subsistant, Clementem tantùm annuere, & nihilominus in Sanctione declarare, hanc Edit. quàm accuratissimè mendis expurgatam esse, simulque mandare, ut correctus iste textus in posterum ita edatur, ut ne minima quidem particula mutetur, addatur, vel detrahatur, id quod se sua quoque Editione in Apostolicis illis literis sanxit Clemens. Et tamen post Serarium ea quoque fuit fiducia Leonardo Mario, Theologo Colon. ut asseruerit, Correctiones à sede Romana, non esse evulgatas, quasi pracife nos obligent, aut quasi præter eas nulla adhuc suggeri aut disquiri possint, sed ut probabilissimas correctiones, quas pia erga sacras literas reverentia & observantia explicare, imò & augere possumus. Proleg. in S. Script. sect. 6. Probationem autem primam ex eadem vocula annuente, depromit, quæ diversa sit ab istis, præcipiente, præscribente. Concilient hæc cum Bullis qui possunt. Mihi hic aquam hærere lubens agnosco. 2. Observ. fuit circa illa, quantâ fieri potuit diligentiâ. Hic multa dicit Serarius de loco, tempore, adjunctis, & ipsis correctoribus. At cur nihil de ipso Papâ? Illi enim adscribitur omnis correctio. Et sicuti nulla concilia ullius authoritatis sunt, nisi ab ipso approbata, ita & hæ correctiones, à delegatis Cardinalibus & Doctoribus elaboratæ, nullam authoritatem acquirunt, nisi ab eo probatæ, ad quem solum ultima & authentica sacrarum literarum emaculatio & recognitio primario pertinet, ut loquitur Gretzerus pag. 1059. undeidem Gretz. pag. 1062. de ipso Pontifice sic ait, qui (Clemens VIII.) veterem ac vulgatam Editionem, quantâ fieri potuit diligentiâ, castigatam dedit. Sed an satis commodè de Pontifice sic loquantur, viderint Pontificii. Pontifex enim quâ Pontifex, sive in judicando diligentiam adhibeat, sive indiligens sit, infallibiliter semper definit, ut ait Valentia, Analyt. Fid. 8.3. Et licet in mediis & argumentis hallucinari possit, in concludendo tamen nunquam impingit, Staplet. de principiis, 8.14. Idque propter prærogativam istius sedis & perpetuam Sp. sancti assistentiam.
units.tr: In the preceding chapters we have shown the truth of the third corollary: that even now the Roman Church has not provided a most correct and therefore authentic Scripture. Before we go on to other matters, those points must be illustrated and examined which Serarius drew from the Clementine Preface. As to his first observation, on the little word annuente: if he is not mistaken in its interpretation, and annuere is here set against to approve and command [τῷ], then Sixtus is certainly pricked with no blunt point, since he used in his bull the words we declare, we establish, we decree, etc., and claimed certain knowledge and the fullness of apostolic power. Nor do I see how these things can stand together: that Clement merely gave assent, and yet in his sanction declared that this edition has been cleansed of errors as accurately as possible, and at the same time commanded that this corrected text be published in future without the least particle being changed, added, or removed, which Clement also decreed in those apostolic letters, in his own edition. And yet after Serarius, Leonardo Marius, a theologian of Cologne, was so confident as to assert that the corrections issued from the Roman See are not so published as to bind us precisely, or as though no others could be suggested or sought beyond them, but as most probable corrections, which a pious reverence and observance toward the sacred letters can explain and even increase. Prolegomena to Holy Scripture, sect. 6. He draws his first proof from the same little word annuente, which is said to differ from those words commanding, prescribing. Let those who can reconcile these things with the Bulls do so. I freely admit that here I am stuck fast. The second observation concerned those words, with as much diligence as could be applied. Serarius says much here about the place, the time, the circumstances, and the correctors themselves. But why nothing about the Pope himself? For every correction is credited to him. And just as no councils have any authority unless approved by him, so these corrections, laboured over by the Cardinals and Doctors appointed for the task, acquire no authority unless approved by him, to whom alone the final and authentic emendation and revision of the sacred letters primarily belongs, as Gretzer says at page 1059. And the same Gretzer, at page 1062, says of the Pontiff himself: he (Clement VIII) gave the old and common edition, corrected with as much diligence as could be applied. But whether the Papists are right to speak of the Pontiff in this way, let them see to it. For the Pontiff, as Pontiff, whether he applies diligence in judging or is careless, always defines infallibly, as Valentia says, Analyt. Fid. 8.3. And although he may go astray in the middle steps and arguments, he never stumbles in the conclusion, Stapleton, de principiis, 8.14. And this is on account of the prerogative of that See and the perpetual assistance of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: III. Observatio fuit circa illa, Eam omnibus numeris absolutam esse, pro humanâ imbecillitate difficile est affirmare. Hic rursus de correctoribus agit Serarius, de Pontifice altum rursus silentium. Iterum hic pungitur Sixtus, qui de certa scientiâ & Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine magis magnificè de sua Editione senserat & sanxerat. Quod si hic quæsierit aliquis, quomodo hæc cohærerant, dubitare an Editio aliqua sit omnibus numeris absoluta, & postea affirmare, multa in eâ consultò relicta esse quæ mutanda videbantur, quæ distinctio satisfaciet? Observ. IV. circa illa, eam omnibus Editionibus, quæ prodierunt, emendatiorem esse. Non ergo dicit eam emendatissimam, infert Serarius, & rectè. Accedit testimonium Bellarmini, qui in Epistola quâdam datâ Capuæ 6. Dec. 1603. adFr. Lucam Brugensem sic inquit, De libello ad me missò gratias ago, sed scias velim, Biblia vulgata non esse à nobis accuratissimè castigata, multa enim de industriâ justis de causis praterivimus, quæ correctione indigere videbantur. Quibus verbis id quoque innuit Cardinalis, se ex numero correctorum fuisse. Eadem mens fuit Joh. Baptistæ Bandino, Typographiæ Vaticanæ Præfecto, qui in literis jussu Baronii ad Moretum, Romæ 1604. prid. Kal. Au-
units.tr: The third observation concerned those words: that it is absolute in all respects; it is hard to affirm this, given human weakness. Here again Serarius deals with the correctors, and about the Pontiff there is again deep silence. Here again Sixtus is pricked, who had spoken and decreed more magnificently about his own edition, with certain knowledge and the fullness of apostolic power. If anyone should ask here how these things cohere, that one doubts whether any edition is absolute in all respects, and afterwards affirms that many things were deliberately left in it which seemed to need changing, what distinction will satisfy him? The fourth observation concerned the claim that it is more correct than all the editions that have appeared. Therefore it is not said to be most correct, Serarius infers, and rightly. To this is added the testimony of Bellarmine, who in a letter written at Capua on 6 December 1603 to Fr. Lucas of Bruges says: I thank you for the little book sent to me, but I would have you know that the common Bibles have not been most accurately corrected by us, for we have deliberately passed over many things for just reasons, which seemed to need correction. By these words the Cardinal also hints that he himself was among the correctors. The same mind was held by Giovanni Battista Bandini, Prefect of the Vatican Printing House, who in a letter written at Rome, on the day before the Kalends of Aug-, 1604, by order of Baronius to Moretus,

units.la: Citatur in Præfat. Lucæ ad Blasium Epist. Audomaropol. quam præmisit alteri libello, quo colleg. Lucæ, quæ adhuc emendari possunt. Augusti datis, sic inquit, * fateor, in Bibliis nonnulla adhuc superesse quae in multis mutari possent; quaedam etiam nescio quo pacto sic impressa reperiuntur, ut e.g. 1. Sam. 2. 17. retrahebant homines a sacrificio, cum libri omnes & impressi & MS. habeant, detrahebant homines sacrificio. Unde Luc. Brug. ausus fuit alium conscribere catalogum, quo repraesentavit loca, quorum correctione post Sixti & Clem. curas, perfectior reddi posset feliciter coepta correctio, si accederet Pontificis auctoritas, quem catalogum Genev. quoque Typographi ad calcem Bibliorum Interlin. nuper adjecere, ex quo nos quoque ea, quae ad Pentateuchum pertinent, excepta in censura nostra exhibuimus. Biblia ergo de industria non sunt accuratissime castigata. Iterum ergo perstringitur Sixti temeritas. Et quomodo haec concessio stare potest cum ipsius quoque Clementis, ut de Sixto jam taceam, sanctione; qua textus accuratissime mendis expurgatus dicitur? Quomodo etiam satisfactum est Pii IV. qui has curas auspicatus est, desiderio, ut Biblia ACCURATISSIME, ut loquitur Praefatio, castigarentur? Quomodo etiam satis fit Decreto Tridentino, quo huic versioni EMENDATISSIMAE ex communi Pontificiorum interpretatione, authentica tribuitur authoritas. Quomodo stare potest illa inscriptio, quâ Sixtus V. in Vaticana honoratus est, quod vulgatam Editionem quam emendatissimam divulgari mandaverit. Quomodo defendet Gretzerus illud, quod p. 1059. tam audacter asserit, Quicquid cum hac Clementis Editione congruit, ratum gratumque accidet, quidquid disconvenit, irritum ingratumque quid eveniet, sive sit ex Hentenii, sive ex Lovaniensium, sive ex cujuslibet alterius officina depromptum. Quid enim? An valebit hoc quoque in locis illis mendosis, ubi de industria nulla facta fuit correctio? Et quid denique diceret Andradius, si ad nos rediret? Is enim ut supra vidimus, adeo accuratam expectavit correctionem, qua Catholicos ab omni cura & dubitatione liberos redderet. Pontifices ergo & concilium mandarunt, ut Biblia quam accuratissime emendarentur & quam emendatissima prodirent. Pontifices Sixtus & Clemens in Bullis suis declararunt illud jam esse praestitum, & quidem ille de certa scientia. Et tamen Bellarminus, qui correctorum pars magna fuit, affirmare audet, Biblia non esse accuratissime castigata. Et ipse & Bandinus & Serarius & saepius jam citata Praefatio, & qui integrum catalogum relictorum errorum edere ausus fuit, Lucas Brug. agnoscunt, multa adhuc superesse, quæ emendari possent. Ego, quomodo hæc cohæreant, libenter edoceri velim. Sic enim statuo & statuam, donec meliora edoctus fuero, æquissimum & necessarium requisitum esse, ut illud, quod sub Anathematis pœna ab omnibus, secundum omnes sui partes, pro authentico haberi debet, à quo nulli datur appellatio quocunque prætextu, à quo nec in minima quidem particula Typographis recedere fas est, quod denique ad minimum lota à Catholicis tenendum est, omnis omnino erroris, si præstari id ullo modo queat, expers sit. Nunc illud quærere mihi liceat, an Pontificis, infallibilis istius judicis, in cujus pectore omnes Sapientiæ thesauri clausi sunt, vires excedat, vulgatam versionem ab omnibus librariorum & pravarum emendationum mendis accuratissimè castigare? Potestne hoc præstare Pontifex? Si dixeris, non posse, cur ergo hanc provinciam ei demandavit concilium? Cur ergo tam præfidenter locutus est Sixtus? Ubi ergo ejus infallibilitas, ubi assistentia Sp. sancti in iis quæ ad munus ejus Pontificale, inter quæ hæc Bibliorum emaculatio censetur, pertinent? Si dixeris posse, quid ergo sibi volunt illa verba, quantâ fieri potuit diligentia, Et, omnibus numeris absolutam esse pro humanâ imbecillitate difficile est affirmare. Quid potuisset dici minus, si vel ab umbratico quodam Theologo processisset hæc Bibliorum recognitio? Sed dices, potuisse hoc Ponficem si voluisset. Certè noluisse Pontificem omnia emendare, videntur innuere illa Præfationis verba, circa quæ versabatur V. observatio Serarii, multa quæ videbantur mutanda, immutata relicta sunt, &c. Itemque illa Bellarmini; Biblia non sunt à nobis accuratissime castigata, multa enim de industriâ justis de causis praeterivimus, &c. Quid? an ergo Ecclesiæ suæ invidit correctissimam Editionem summus ille Pastor? An forte aliæ cautæ subsunt? Ita certè persuadere nobis satagit Præfator, qui tres enumerat. circa quas fuit VI observatio Serarii, 1. ad offensionem populorum vitandam.
