Dico 1. me non videre quomodo hæc conveniant cum illo obtentu humanæ imbecillitatis, quem paulò ante adhibuit Præfatio. Qui enim ad offen-
units.tr: It is cited in the Preface of Lucas to Blasius, the Audomaropolitan letter, which he prefixed to another little book, in which he gathers the places of Lucas that can still be emended, dated August, which says: * I admit that in the Bibles some things still remain which could be changed in many places; some also are, I know not how, printed in such a way that, for example, in 1 Samuel 2:17 they read "they drew men away from the sacrifice", whereas all the books, both printed and manuscript, have "they drew men from the sacrifice". Hence Lucas of Bruges ventured to write another catalogue, in which he set out the places whose correction, after the labours of Sixtus and Clement, could be made more perfect, if the authority of the Pontiff were added, which catalogue the printers of Geneva also recently appended to the end of the Interlinear Bibles, from which we too have set out here, in our censure, those things which pertain to the Pentateuch. The Bibles, therefore, have not been most accurately corrected on purpose. Again, then, the rashness of Sixtus is taken to task. And how can this concession stand together with the sanction of Clement himself, not to mention Sixtus, in which the text is said to be most accurately cleansed of errors? How also has the wish of Pius IV, who began these labours, been satisfied, that the Bibles should be most accurately, as the Preface says, corrected? How is the Tridentine Decree satisfied, by which this version is granted authentic authority, by the common interpretation of the Papists, as MOST CORRECT? How can that inscription stand, by which Sixtus V was honoured in the Vatican, because he commanded the common edition to be published as most correct? How will Gretzer defend what he asserts so boldly at page 1059: Whatever agrees with this edition of Clement will be ratified and welcomed; whatever disagrees will come to nothing and be unwelcome, whether it be taken from the workshop of Hentenius, or of the Louvain men, or of any other. For what? Will this also hold good in those faulty places where no correction was made on purpose? And what would Andradius say, if he came back to us? For he, as we saw above, looked for so accurate a correction as would render Catholics free from all care and doubt. The Pontiffs and the Council therefore commanded that the Bibles be emended as accurately as possible and be published as most correct. The Pontiffs Sixtus and Clement declared in their Bulls that this had now been accomplished, and indeed Sixtus did so with certain knowledge. And yet Bellarmine, who was a great part of the correctors, dares to affirm that the Bibles have not been most accurately corrected. Both he, and Bandini, and Serarius, and the Preface cited so often already, and Lucas of Bruges, who ventured to publish a complete catalogue of the errors that remain, acknowledge that many things still remain which could be emended. I should like to be taught how these things cohere. For so I judge, and shall judge, until I am taught better, that it is most just and necessary to require that what must be held as authentic under penalty of anathema by all, in every part, from which no appeal is allowed on any pretext, from which not even the least particle may be departed from by printers, and which in short must be held entirely by Catholics, should be free of every error, if this can be achieved in any way. Now let me ask this: whether the power of the Pontiff, that infallible judge in whose breast all the treasures of wisdom are shut up, goes beyond the ability to correct the common version most accurately from all the faults of copyists and of perverse emendations. Can the Pontiff accomplish this? If you say he cannot, why then did the Council entrust this task to him? Why then did Sixtus speak so confidently? Where then is his infallibility, where is the assistance of the Holy Spirit in those matters which pertain to his Pontifical office, among which this emendation of the Bibles is counted? If you say he can, what then do those words mean, with as much diligence as could be applied, and it is hard to affirm that it is absolute in all respects, given human weakness? What could have been said less, if this revision of the Bibles had come from some shadowy theologian? But you will say the Pontiff could have done it, had he wished. That the Pontiff certainly did not wish to emend everything seems to be suggested by those words of the Preface, on which Serarius's fifth observation turned, many things which seemed to need changing were left unchanged, etc. So too those of Bellarmine: The Bibles have not been most accurately corrected by us, for we have deliberately passed over many things for just reasons, etc. What then? Did that supreme Shepherd grudge his Church the most correct edition? Or do some other cautions lie beneath? The Preface certainly labours to persuade us so, and it lists three, on which Serarius's sixth observation turned: (1) to avoid offence to the peoples. For in this way the Pontiffs arrange all their actions and direct everything, so that they avoid offending their sheep and remove scandals. Of course. But as far as the present matter is concerned, Bellarmine also gives the same reason why those verses of Psalm 13 and certain other typographical faults were tolerated in the same edition, in De Verbo Dei, book 2, chapter 2, section "Dices". I say, first, that I cannot see how these things agree with that plea of human weakness which the Preface used a little earlier. For whoever leaves some fault in order to avoid offence

Genef. 3.15. Alii codices legebant Ipse, alii Ipsa. Viderunt in fonte legi Ipse, sed quia suspicio fuit, ibi olim fuisse pronomen fœm-non non ausi fuerunt illud Ipsa corrigere. Ita nudâ rursus suspicione fontes ως [illegible, ~12 letters]. Sed hanc suspicionem egregiè exagitavit Serarius & sustulit Andradius, uti supra visum est. 111. Causa, Institutum correctorum. Non fuit ipsis propositum, Interpretem ulla ex parte corrigere vel emendare, sed ipsam Interpretationem à mendis librariorum & pravarum emendationum erroribus repurgare. Anergo per illa verba [quæ mutanda videbantur, Et, antiquum Interpretem ulla ex parte corrigere,] innuunt errata ab ipso interprete commissa? Genef. 3.15. notárunt Lovân. Ebr. Ch. & 2. MS. legere Ipse. Correctores tamen mordicus retinuerunt Ipsa. Gen. 8.7. & fontes & codices 6. MS. magnæ authoritatis, inquit Sacrobofcus, non legunt negationem. units.tr: Whoever leaves an error in place to avoid giving offence certainly does so knowingly and deliberately. I say, second, why did this fear of offence carry more weight with the errors that were left than with those that were removed? I say, third, that Oleaster holds a different view. In the preface to his commentary on the Pentateuch he does not hesitate to assert that no scandal need be feared, and there would be no inconvenience, if Paul IV (under whom he lived) were to entrust the task of correcting the Vulgate version against the sources to men skilled in languages, as Damasus had done. Lucas of Bruges held the same view. In the preface to the last part of his catalogue of passages still needing correction, he also cites the testimony of a certain famous professor of sacred theology, in these words: And indeed, as for what has been raised about avoiding offence to those who are accustomed otherwise, and this on the example of Saint Jerome: it is not to be altogether neglected, but it loses its force more and more every day. For through the notes on various readings, hitherto published by Catholic and learned men, the way has already been prepared for correction, so that, the novelty having already been largely worn away, it hardly causes any offence. Then follows the emendation made by the legitimate authority of the Bibles, which produces reverence and gratitude rather than offence. As for Jerome, Lucas boldly asserts that the Preface-writer has wrongly cited his example. For, as Lucas himself, in another place, reminded me, Jerome was engaged in correcting the errors of the translators whose versions had already been received; but here the labour is not on correcting the translator, but on emending the translator's version from the copies of the same version, that is, on removing the errors of the copyists, by which nobody can easily be offended. As for what Lucas adds afterwards, Whether such passages, which perhaps could have been changed for the better, were omitted deliberately or by chance, etc., I marvel at the servile temper of this very learned man. For why does he hesitate on the page where he produces the very words of Bellarmine, whom he himself says was among the correctors, a confession from which it is clear that such a correction was omitted deliberately? And why that word perhaps? Since he later says that in this little book he sets out passages which, in his own judgement and that of others, could still be corrected? II. The cause was suspicion about the less pure books of later centuries. That is, they indeed saw in many places a variety of readings, of which this or that reading agreed more closely with the sources, but they did not dare always to prefer it, because a suspicion of corrupted sources always stuck in their minds. E.g. Genesis 3:15: other codices read ipse, others ipsa. They saw that ipse was read in the source, but because there was a suspicion that a feminine pronoun had once stood there, they did not dare to correct it to ipsa. Thus, once again, by bare suspicion, the sources [illegible]. But this suspicion Serarius has excellently chased away, and Andradius has removed, as has been shown above. III. The cause: the purpose of the correctors. It was not their intention to correct or emend the translator in any part, but to purge the translation itself of the errors of the copyists and of the mistakes of faulty emendations. But if this was their intention, why did they not carry it out? Why did they not correct many things that needed correcting? Why did they deliberately pass over many things? Truly, I cannot grasp these words. From Serarius's analysis, these words give the third reason why they did not change many things that seemed to need changing, namely: because their only and fuller purpose was to purge the version of the errors of the copyists and of the mistakes of faulty emendations, and indeed this was accomplished by them most accurately, as Clement himself testifies. Does he then mean by those words [which seemed to need changing, and, to correct the ancient translator in any part] that the errors were committed by the translator himself? Certainly this will fit very well, not only with this third reason but also with the two earlier ones. For one could ask why the correctors removed none of the translator's errors. They reply that they did not wish to do this, and that it was not enjoined or proposed to them. Indeed, in my stupidity, I do not see what third option there is between the errors of the translator and those of the copyists. But how again will this explanation agree with the decision of the most faithful translators, namely that in the Vulgate there are absolutely no errors of the translator, either because he was a prophet and so could not err, or because the Church, as Azorius and Bellarmine teach, could not err in approving this version? And how again will this agree with Bellarmine's declaration, which I quoted above, which deals with the copyists' errors left alone, and also with experience itself, which teaches that countless errors of copyists were left in place? E.g. Genesis 3:15: the Louvain editors, the Hebrew, the Chaldee, and two manuscripts noted that ipse should be read. Nevertheless the correctors stubbornly kept ipsa. Genesis 8:7: the sources and six manuscripts of great authority, says Sacrobosco, do not read the negation. And yet, in spite of these, the Roman correctors did not judge, says Lucas of Bruges of the more notable passages, that the mark of negation should be omitted. Exodus 20:23: in Hebrew it reads, you shall not make with me gods of silver. So also the manuscripts, and one has before me. Yet the Roman correctors did not judge that "with me" should be added, although it is read in Hebrew. These, again, are Lucas's words. Isaiah 40:2: in Hebrew it reads, that her warfare is accomplished [צבאה], her military service, in which sense we read in Job 7: Is not man's life upon earth a warfare (that is, a fixed time)? But that word has been corrupted into multitudo. What did the Roman correctors do here? They did not judge it to be corrected, says Lucas, into "warfare." John 21:22: the Greek has if I will that he tarry. So the manuscripts read, as do Chrysostom and Cyril. That i has been corrupted into sic. Jansenius, Benedictus, Erasmus and others too have pointed out the error. Yet the Roman correctors judged here too that nothing should be changed.
