units.la: Summa summarum hùc redit, versionem vulgatam, ipsius Præfatoris, & Bellarmini & Serarii & Bandini & Lucæ Brugensis & aliorum confessione, necdum esse emendatissimam, quod Præfatio imbecillitati humanæ adscribit,. Bellarminus vero & alii consultò & de industria factum esse asserunt, & proindè quod 3. Consectarium erat, Ecclesiæ Romanæ necdum de authenticis Scripturæ tabulis prospectum, Conciliique Tridentini decreto prout vulgò exponitur, de versione ea emendatissimè & accuratissimè castigandâ, necdum esse satisfactum.
units.tr: To sum up the whole matter: by the admission of the Preface-writer himself, of Bellarmine, Serarius, Bandinus and Lucas of Bruges and others, the Vulgate is not yet the most correct version, which the Preface attributes to human weakness. Bellarmine and others, however, assert that this was done deliberately and on purpose; and so, as a third consequence, the Roman Church has not yet provided for the authentic copies of the Scriptures, and the decree of the Council of Trent, as it is commonly explained, which demands that this version be most thoroughly and accurately corrected, has not yet been carried out.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: {*}Ex superioribus deducitur consect. IV. supra in fine cap 8. propositum. Pontificiorum quorundam limitatio. Nihil leve est in S. Scriptura. Difficile est definire quis locus ad fidem pertineat vel non. Pontificiorum quorundam pertinacia. Serarii discursus, quo probat posse adhuc fieri versionem aliquam vulgata meliorem. Responsio ejus ad argumenta in contrarium a Gretzero & aliis producta.
units.tr: From the above follows the fourth corollary, proposed at the end of chapter 8. Limitation by certain Papists. Nothing in Holy Scripture is trivial. It is difficult to determine which passages pertain to faith and which do not. The obstinacy of certain Papists. Serarius' discourse, by which he proves that some version better than the Vulgate can still be made. His reply to the arguments to the contrary put forward by Gretser and others.

units.la: SI in multis mendis librariorum adhuc cubat vulgata Editio, ut supra ostensum, Si in eâ multi sunt errores Interpretis, quod supra quoque doctissimi Pontificiorum confessi sunt, & innuere videtur Præfatio, quibus corrigendis nunquam admoverunt manum, non malè, opinor, inde extruetur 4. consectarium, plurimùm quoque errare potuisse, atque errasse à vero eandem, cum, quam sequeretur certò constanterque, in veri investigatione ac dijudicatione, Cynosuram ac normam non haberet, ac indubitato authenticoque textu careret. Hic Pontificii obvertunt suum illud Medusæ caput, quo in saxa convertunt intuentes, Eccle-fia fia non potest errare. Fuerint tot in vulgata Editione tolerata Librariorum menda. Cubet adhuc in mendis. Sint etiam in eā aliquot errores ipsius Interpretis. Quid tum postea? Ea fidem & mores non spectant, nullum inde Fidei vel moribus periculum. Nullus est error, inquit Serarius, qui veritati, fidei, bonis moribus ac tutissimæ Lectorum obedientiæ sit adversus, p. 120. Levicula illa sunt, & parvi momenti. Manet nihilominus vulgata Editio, textus authenticus & certa norma. Respondeo 1. quam verè dicantur suis locis incensura nostrâ ad Pentateuchum ostendimus, & porro, Deo volente, ad cæteros libros ostendemus. 2. Eodem modo à Bellarmino aliisque excusari fontes. Qua fronte ergo vulgata præfertur Fontibus, qui utut hic pari paslu cum vulgatâ inciderent, id tamen habent prærogativæ, quod nulli istis insint errores ab authoribus commissi. 3. Oppono Basilium, qui Epistolâ ad Amphilochium gravissimè, nihil esse in scriptura, inquit, quod non sit magni momenti, etiamsi nobis nihil aut parum esse videatur. Nec non Possevinum, qui in Bibl. selecta inquit, in Ebr. Scriptura tot esse Sacramenta, quot litera; tot mysteria, quot puncta: tot arcana, quot apices. Ipsum denique Bannes Dominicanum, qui Tomo 1. ad Thom. p. 46. Omnia quæ in Scr. continentur, utilia esse dicit, etsi minima videantur. Quia Deus author Scripturæ nihil sine causâ dixit. Omnia enim refert ad gloriam suam & utilitatem hominum, Jes. 48. Rom. 15. 2. Tim. 3. Dico 4. cum eodem Bannes, difficile esse dicere, quis locus pertineat ad fidem, quis non. Dico 5. Quò leviores sunt isti errores, quò minoris momenti, eò minori opera & labore potuisse corrigi. Cur ergo hoc factum non est, aut etiamnum sit? Hic occines mihi rursum causam secundam ex Præfatione, vid. suspicionem de libris posteriorum sæculorum minus puris. Et Bellarm. in Epistola ad Lucam Brug. cujus fragmentum extat in præfat. Lucæ ad Libellum, idem mihi innuere videtur, Si videro, inquit, textum ipsum certò in melius mutari posse, significabo id summo Pontifici & Cardinalibus Deputatis. Sed tu ipse facile vides, non facile hujusmodi mutationes in sacro textu esse faciendas, &c. Q. d. Tu quidem, Luca, valde urges, ut plura emendentur, sed non temere ejusmodi mutatio facienda est. Certò constare debet de mendo. Codicum alii sic, alii aliter legunt. Quis erit judex? Pontifex? Ille quidem errare in his talibus non potest, & hæc causa ad illum pertinet. At non vacat ei ad has minutias semper descendere? Fontes? At illi turbidi sunt & minus puri, quàm ut ad eos versiones (& imprimis hæc vulgata) possint examinari & corrigi. Est quidem ita, olim aliter sensi, cum in controversia de verbo Dei inter casus quos ad fontes liceat recurrere, etiam hos posui, Quando in codicibus est error aliquis librariorum: aut varians lectio, (lib. 2. cap. 11.) nunc aliter statuo, &c. Quin propugnator Gretzerus, Sicubi inter fontes & vulgatam, inquit, sit aliquis dissensus, dicam potius corruptum esse textum Ebraeum, quàm versioni inesse vitium. Et hoc dicam innixus (En iterum caput Medusæ) Ecclesiæ, columna & firmamento veritatis, &c. pag. 1061. Si ergo ad eo corrupti sint fontes, quæ nam affulget spes melioris & emendatioris alicujus versionis? Omnem spem præcidunt illi, qui adeò abjectè de fontibus sentiunt, vulgatam contrà tantopere sublimant. Unde enim fieret melior, id est, fontibus magis consentanea, nisi ex fontibus? Sed pro fontibus quantum satis est, disputavimus cap. 1. 2. 3. Mihi satis erit hoc loco zelotis istis opponere discursum Jesuitæ Serarii, p. 123. col. 2. &3. Si autem quaerat quis, inquit, Primò, An possit fieri versio aliqua vulgatâ melior? Videtur negare Bellarmini * propugnator lib. 2. cap. 10. dum in 2. Bell. argumento contra Hunnium disserit p. 540. Negandi tamen necessitas nulla, vel causa idonea. Nam 1. quae bona sunt, possint fieri meliora, dum ex eo rerum genere sunt, quae bonitatis ac perfectionis intensionem ac remissionem admittunt. Hujusmodi autem est Bibliorum è fontibus Ebraeis vel Græcis versio. 2. Interpretationis sermonum charisma potest majus & minus à Deo dari. Potest enim majore similiter aliquem ornare sapientiâ, intellectu, consilio, efficientiâ miraculorum. Cur non & majore sacras literas transferendi facultate? non est ejus restricta vel abbreviata manus Isa. 59.1. 3. Posset D. Hieronymo aliquis existere doctior, linguarum callentior diligentior & sanctior; Deo ipsi devotior & gratior. Quid huic ergo, quò minus meliorem nobis ederet versionem, deesset? 4. Si vel Pontifex vel Oecumenica Synodus, unum vel plures doctissimos, linguarumque scientissimos, qui & virtute & fide & timore Dei excellerent, uni ejusdemodi conficiendæ versioni admoveret, deinde confectam ab iis versionem totam vel uno aliquo tempore simul, vel paulatim & per partes diligenter examinaret & expenderet, nonne fieri aliquid posset perfectius? Si in Calendario, si in Bibliorum nostrorum & Breviariorum & Missalium correctione id potuit, cur non & in aliâ posset Bibliorum translatione? 5. Accipiantur omnia ea versionis nostræ loca, quæ fatentur Catholici Theologi versa obscurius, & ad fontes, ubi de eorum canone aliquo suspicandi causam non habent, minus etiam accommodate; Si omnia haec ab Ecclesia verterentur clarius & ad eosdem fontes accommodatius, in terminque retinerentur nostra versionis alia omnia, nonne talis foret Editio melior? Sumatur exemplum ex uno duntaxat Psal.67. alias 68.13. & 14. Rex virtutum dilecti, &c. Si dormiatis inter medios cleros, &c. 6. Et vero fieri hoc posse significat non obscure Praefatio, quae in Latinis Bibliis correctis ad lectorem est, dum ait in ea correctione propositum non fuisse, novam aliquam editionem cudere, quasi diceret, quod fieri quidem posset: necessarium tamen & utile jam non fuit, ideoque nec tentatum. 7. * Nec omnino id infirmat ulla, quae objici posset, ratio. Verbi causa. 1. Nostra est nunc quoad declarationem authentica & semper in se talis fuit. 2. Haec Spiritus S. prae aliis omnibus conservavit, &c. 3. Si melior aliqua fieri posset, posset itidem nostra haec aliquo pretextu rejici, cum posteriores jam partes tenerent. 4. Damnat Recognitorum nostrorum Bibliorum praefatio eorum judicium, qui quam S. Hieronymus meliora aut certe paria praestare se posse confidunt. Respondeo ad primum: posse duas esse versiones authenticas, quae adventitia tantum perfectione ac bonitate differant. Utraque enim bona esset, altera vero tantum melior. Ad secundum, Posset eandem porro adhuc conservare Deus, vel si nostram tolli vellet, suffecisset ejus in locum aliam perfectiorem. Ad tertium, Etiamsi nostra haec meliori alicui posponeretur, non ideo tamen velut prava & vitiosa rejiceretur, ut supra quaest. 12. expositum. Ad quartum, confidendi, quo praefatio illa utitur, verbum, temeritatem, arrogantiam & audaciam importat. * Si quis autem vel ut S. Hieronymus, a Damaso aliquo, vel Concilio Sancto monitus id suscipere operis, non confidentia aliqua, sed obedientia, charitate, Spirituque S. quod alias dissideret, faceret. Si quaerat quis secundo, An talis aliquando futura sit perfectior Editio? Respondeo 1. cum Amos 7. vers. 14. Nec sum propheta, nec prophetae filius 2. Si ex praeteritis capienda est conjectura, ea in utramque partem capi posset aliqua, &c.
units.tr: If the Vulgate edition still lies buried in many scribal errors, as shown above, and if there are many errors of the translator in it, as the most learned of the Papists have also confessed above, and as the Preface seems to hint, then I think it is not unreasonable to draw a fourth corollary: the same version could well have erred greatly, and indeed have strayed from the truth, since it would have no certain and consistent Cynosure or norm for investigating and judging the truth, and would lack an undoubted and authentic text. Here the Papists brandish their familiar Medusa's head, by which they turn onlookers to stone: the Church cannot err. Let so many scribal errors have been tolerated in the Vulgate edition. Let it still lie buried in errors. Let there also be some errors of the translator himself in it. What then? Those errors do not concern faith or morals, and so there is no danger to faith or morals from them. There is no error, says Serarius, that is contrary to the truth, to faith, to good morals, or to the most sure obedience of readers, p. 120. Those errors are trifling and of little moment. Nevertheless the Vulgate edition remains the authentic text and the certain norm. I reply, 1. how truly these things are said, we have shown in our commentary on the Pentateuch in its places, and further, God willing, we will show it for the other books. 2. In the same way the sources are excused by Bellarmine and others. With what face, then, is the Vulgate preferred to the sources, which, though they fall into the same kind of errors as the Vulgate, nevertheless have this advantage, that none of them contains errors committed by its authors? 3. I set against this Basil, who most weightily wrote in his letter to Amphilochius: there is nothing in Scripture, he says, that is not of great importance, even if to us it seems to be nothing or of little account. Likewise Possevinus, who says in his Bibliotheca selecta: in the Hebrew Scripture there are as many sacraments as letters, as many mysteries as points, as many secrets as strokes. Finally Bannes the Dominican, who says in volume 1 on Thomas, p. 46: all things that are contained in Scripture are useful, even if they seem very small, because God, the author of Scripture, said nothing without cause. For he refers all things to his own glory and the benefit of men, Isa. 48, Rom. 15, 2 Tim. 3. 4. I say, with the same Bannes, that it is difficult to say which passage pertains to faith and which does not. 5. The lighter these errors are, and the less their importance, the less effort and labour should have been needed to correct them. Why then has this not been done, or why is it still not done? Here you will once again sing me the second cause from the Preface, namely the suspicion that the books of the later centuries are less pure. Bellarmine too, in his letter to Lucas of Bruges, a fragment of which is extant in Lucas' preface to his little book, seems to me to hint at the same thing: If I see, he says, that the text itself can certainly be changed for the better, I will signify this to the supreme Pontiff and to the Cardinals appointed to the task. But you yourself easily see that such changes are not to be made lightly in the sacred text, etc. That is to say: you, Lucas, press hard that many things be emended, but such a change is not to be made rashly. It must be certain that there is an error. The copies read this way and that. Who will be the judge? The Pontiff? He indeed cannot err in such matters, and this question belongs to him. But does he not have leisure to descend always to such trifles? The sources? But they are muddy and less pure than that versions (and above all this Vulgate) can be examined and corrected by them. It is indeed so; I once thought otherwise, when in the controversy about the word of God, among the cases in which it is lawful to have recourse to the sources, I also listed this: when there is some error of the scribes in the manuscripts, or a variant reading (book 2, chapter 11). Now I judge otherwise, etc. Indeed, the champion Gretser says: if there is any disagreement between the sources and the Vulgate, he says, I would rather say that the Hebrew text is corrupt than that there is a fault in the version. And I shall say this relying (behold again the Medusa's head) on the Church, the pillar and firmament of truth, etc., p. 1061. If then the sources are so corrupt, what hope of some better and more correct version can shine forth? Those who think so meanly of the sources, while exalting the Vulgate so greatly, cut off all hope. For from what would a better version, that is, one more in agreement with the sources, be made, if not from the sources? But as for the sources, we have discussed enough in chapters 1, 2 and 3. For this place it will be enough for me to set against these zealots the discourse of the Jesuit Serarius, p. 123, col. 2 and 3: If anyone asks, he says, first, whether some version better than the Vulgate can be made: the champion of Bellarmine seems to deny it, lib. 2, cap. 10, while in the second argument of Bellarmine against Hunnius he discusses it on p. 540. Yet there is no necessity or good reason to deny it. For, 1. things that are good can become better, insofar as they belong to the kind of thing that admits of an increase and decrease of goodness and perfection. Of this sort is a version of the Bible from the Hebrew or Greek sources. 2. The gift of interpreting words can be given by God in greater or lesser measure. For he can similarly adorn someone with greater wisdom, understanding, counsel, and power to work miracles. Why not also with greater ability to translate the sacred letters? His hand is not restricted or shortened, Isa. 59.1. 3. Someone more learned than Jerome might have arisen, more skilled in languages, more diligent and holier, and more devoted and pleasing to God himself. What then would have been lacking to him, so that he could not have given us a better version? 4. If either the Pontiff or an ecumenical Synod were to set one or several most learned men, most skilled in languages, who excelled in virtue, faith and the fear of God, to the single task of making such a version, and then were to examine and weigh diligently the version so made, either all at once in one period of time or gradually and part by part, would not something more perfect be possible? If this could be done in the correction of the Calendar, and of our Bibles, Breviaries and Missals, why could it not be done in another translation of the Bible? 5. Let all those passages of our version be taken which Catholic theologians admit are translated obscurely, and less suitably to the sources, where they have no cause to suspect any of their canon. If all these were translated by the Church more clearly and more suitably to the same sources, and all the rest of our version were retained unchanged, would not such an edition be better? Let an example be taken from one psalm alone, Psalm 67, otherwise 68, verses 13 and 14: "The king of hosts of the beloved," etc.; "If you lie among the sheepfolds," etc. 6. And indeed that this can be done is not obscurely signified by the Preface addressed to the reader in the corrected Latin Bibles, where it says that in that correction it was not intended to fashion some new edition, as if to say that this could indeed be done, but was not then necessary or useful, and so was not attempted. 7. Nor is any argument that could be raised against this in any way weakened. For example: 1. Our version is now authentic as regards its declaration and always has been such. 2. The Holy Spirit has preserved this one above all others, etc. 3. If some better version could be made, this present one could likewise be rejected on some pretext, since the later versions would then hold the first place. 4. The Preface of our revised Bibles condemns the judgement of those who trust that they can do better than St. Jerome, or at least as well. I reply to the first: two authentic versions can exist that differ only in accidental perfection and goodness. For both would be good, but one would be only better. To the second: God could still preserve the same version, or, if he wished ours to be taken away, another more perfect one would suffice in its place. To the third: even if this version of ours were set after some better one, it would not therefore be rejected as bad and faulty, as was explained above in question 12. To the fourth: the word "trust" which that Preface uses implies rashness, presumption and audacity. But if anyone undertakes this work, as St. Jerome did when urged by some Damasus or a holy Council, he does so not from self-confidence but from obedience, charity and the Holy Spirit, which otherwise would disagree. If anyone asks secondly whether such a more perfect edition will ever be made in future, I reply, 1. with Amos 7, verse 14: "I am no prophet, nor a son of a prophet." 2. If a conjecture is to be drawn from past events, it could be drawn in either direction, etc.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Transitur ad occasionem & scopum nostra Censura. Consilium nostrum de ejus continuatione, Aria Montani Vaticinium de Iesuitis. Marino Marsenno cur respondendum censuerimus.
units.tr: We come now to the occasion and purpose of our criticism: our decision to continue the work, and the prophecy of Arias Montanus about the Jesuits. Why we thought we should answer Marin Mersenne.

units.la: VIdimus hactenus genuinum decreti interpretamentum: Vidimus difficultates, quibus doctissimi Pontificii, ipsique adeò Pontifices Sixtus V. & Clemens VIII. idipsum presserè, atque etiamnum premunt. Audivimus vota devotorum Ecclesiæ Rom. Filiorum, ut vel semel tandem gravissima illa circa decretum hoc exorta controversia à Romano Pontifice decidatur. At cum surdam iis aurem obvertat Pontifex, cum non revocet declaramentum illud, quod delecti Cardinales anno 1576. Januarii die 17. dedêre; cum in Hispaniâ, ubi Sanctæ Inquisitionis primaria Sedes est, moderatiores illi decreti interpretes malè multati sint, in eam plane descendi sententiam, eos ex mente Pontificis Rom. (in eum enim ultimò semper resolvitur Ecclesiæ speciosum nomen) atque ex dignitate celeberrimi concilii, decretum illud esse interpretatos, qui statuerunt, versionem vulgatam non modò in rebus Fidei & morum, sed & in aliis omnibus omni omnino errore carere, & proinde ne prætextu quidem fontium qui jam turbidi fluunt & malitiâ Judæorum corrupti sunt, rejiciendam. Hinc existimavi semper, optimè de Ecclesiis Euangelicis fuisse meritos qui huic decreto masculè intercessêre, qui non tantum hoc sibi agendum putârunt, ut incorruptam textus Ebr. veritatem astruerent, sed etiam ostenderent.
units.tr: So far we have seen the genuine interpretation of the decree. We have seen the difficulties which the most learned Papists, and the popes Sixtus V and Clement VIII themselves, pressed and are still pressing. We have heard the wishes of the devoted sons of the Roman Church, that this most serious controversy which has arisen over this decree should at last be settled once and for all by the Roman Pontiff. But the Pontiff turns a deaf ear to them. He does not revoke that declaration which the chosen Cardinals gave on 17 January 1576. In Spain, where the chief seat of the Holy Inquisition is, those more moderate interpreters of the decree were severely punished, and the view has been fully adopted that the decree, according to the mind of the Roman Pontiff (for to him the fair name of the Church always finally returns), and in keeping with the dignity of that famous council, was to be interpreted as follows: the Vulgate version is free of all error not only in matters of faith and morals but in all other matters whatever, and therefore must not be rejected, not even on the pretext of the sources, which now flow muddied and have been corrupted by the malice of the Jews. Hence I have always thought that those who strenuously opposed this decree have deserved very well of the Evangelical Churches. They believed it was their task not only to establish the uncorrupted truth of the Hebrew text, but also to show...

units.la: Eam versionem, quæ tot locis corrupta est, vitiosa, ambigua, & ob id sæpe periculosa, quæ multis locis vana, superflua, mutila, quæ Sp. Sancti mentem, etiam ubi exprimi potuisset, non exprimit, majestatem verò nusquam assequitur, quæ denique sat lucis in se non habet ad Scr. phrasin & sententiam illustrandam, nullo modo velsolam vel unà cum fontibus posse esse authenticam.
units.tr: That version, which is corrupt in so many places, faulty, ambiguous, and for that reason often dangerous, which in many places is empty, superfluous and mutilated, which does not express the mind of the Holy Spirit even where it could have been expressed, which nowhere attains to the majesty of the original, and which finally does not have enough light in itself to illuminate the phrase and sense of Scripture, cannot in any way be authentic, either alone or together with the sources.

units.la: Verum enimverò cum Syllogismi, cujus illa major est, minor em, vulgatam vid. talem esse, nullus, quod ego quidem sciam, ex professo suscepit probandam, seriò aliquoties cogitavi, nunquid cum fructu in singulos vulgatæ libros Censura institui posset, atque in unum volumen redigi, tum quicquid in eam à Theologis tam Euangelicis quàm Pontificiis sparsim & per occasionem noveram animadversum, tum quicquid ab iis posterorum industriæ striæ videbatur relictum. Hic postquam Theologi quidam ex Anglia nos consiliis & hortamentis suis animassent, succurit etiam judicium Cl. Theol. Witakeri, qui in accuratissimis suis de Scriptura disputationibus contr. 1. qu. 2. cap. 10. circa finem, postquam aliquot errores vulgati ex Genesi obiter indicassçt, sic tandem desinit, Et verò cum multi SS. literas ex fontibus in varias linguas transtulerint, hujusque vulgata Editionis errores in suis versionibus correxerint, ii sane mihi laborem perutilem præstare viderentur, qui librum de hujus versionis erroribus separatim diligenter & accurate conscriberent. Ex hoc enim labore omnes id commodi perciperent, ut quantum inter Ebræa veritatis purissimos fontes & hujus cænosos rivulos interesset, videre possent. Quod magni viri judicium cum ad aliorum consilia accessisset, accinxi lumbos meos, & cum priorem operis partem quæ circa Mosen versatur, elaborassem, adhibitis in consilium Theologis Belgicis, eam evulgavi. Quo in opere sic versatus sum ut crassiora tantum sphalmata detexerim, ne in immensum iret & labor & scriptum. Produxi passim advocatos ipsos Pontificios, quorum multi & commentariis & alibi extra disputationis calorem liberè satis vulgatam castigárunt. Eminent autem hic duo Romanæ Ecclesiæ lumina, Cajetanus, & Augustus Steuchus Eugubinus. Feci hoc edoctus à Jesuita Serario, qui his potissimum casibus hæreticos nominandos & citandos esse docet, Minervalis lib. 1. cap. 6. Primo cum committendi sunt inter se Ægypti. 2. cum sententia alicui, ut firmior apud alios Novatores sit, quadam veluti ἐξείσματα & anterides astruenda, ut eorum, ne illas duntaxat oppugnent acrius, linguarias cohibeant machinas. Multa quæ ipsi Papistæ carpsêre, transmisimus, non quod putaremus, ea injustè censoria virgula ab iis fuisse notata, sed 1. quia ipsi aliquod velamentum prævidebamus, quo ea aliquatenus tegi & obvolvi possent. 2. Ne videremur nimiâ carpendi prurigine & ἀμετρίᾳ τ' ἀνάλωσις laborare. 3. Quia prævidebamus vel sola inexcusabilia sphalmata satis fore sic satis crasso volumini implendo. Paucula tamen quædam periculo verbisque ipsorum Papistarum, e.g. Cajetani, Steuchi, Lyræ, Joh. Benedicti, &c. taxavimus, cujus rei rationes nobis non defuere. Sciens volensque nunquam prævaricatus sum, nullumque adeo locum meis verbis castigavi, de cujus excusatione post seriam meditationem non desperavi, nisi forte novum Lexicon & novam Grammaticam, Rom. Pontifex. sex procuderet. Dixi & professus tunc sum, me istis quæ ullo modo excusabilia mihi videbantur, præteritis, ea solummodo persecutum esse, quæ manifeste vitiosa, corrupta, superflua, mutila & periculose ambigua, quæ denique eam lucem ad Spiritus S. mentem exprimendam non habent, quam habere possent. Ne vero regererent Pontificii, vulgatam versionem, iis, quæ nos annotavimus, locis, ab Ebræo quidem textu, ut nunc extat, id est, ut Gretzerus loquitur, impuro & corrupto, dissentire, at non ab eo qui fuit olim, limpido vid. & puro, produxi passim LXX II. interpretes, queis vulgò communis, quæ jam extat, Græca versio adscribitur, & Chaldæum Paraphrasten, nec non Fragmenta Aquilæ, Theodotionis, Symmachi, &c. qui omnes Hieronymo, quem vulgatæ patrem faciunt, antiquiores. Certè quâ fronte asseret adversarius, ea loca textus Ebraici post Hieronymi ætatem corrupta, quæ ante eum eo quo etiamnum leguntur modo lecta fuere. Quod ideo notandum duxi, ne quis eas ideo à nobis productas arbitraretur, quod vitiosum putemus, quicquid ab iis diversum abit. Ariam Montanum & Pagninum in prima parte rarissime citavimus, eò quod præclaros istos viros eodem fere cum hæreticis ordine ab impudentioribus Papistis habitos atque etiamnum haberi non ignoraremus. Ariam certè ob præclaram illam operam, in Bibliorum Regiorum Editionem insumptam, variarum hæresium apud Romanum Pontificem postulatum ex Apologia ejus constat, quam Hispanicè conscriptam & in expugnatione Caletana ante annos aliquot inventam Anglii in patriam suam detulerunt, atque in Oxoniensi Bibliotheca etiamnum asservant. Utinam vero tandem Cl. Theologus, Thomas Jamesius, quod sæpe promisit, ejusve in curâ Bibliothecæ successor, scriptum illud Latine versum universo orbi communicaret! Sed quid verbis opus est & ad ἀνεχδοτα confugio; Vel sola Ariæ in Biblia Interlinearia præfatio docet, quam laborum gratiam ipsi retulerint Jesuitæ. Eos enim ab illo perstringi plane indubium est. Erostratus inquit, cum Pagninum vivum habere non potuit, nostrum pro aliis omnibus nomen proscindeundum suscepit, nactus fortasse opportunitatem in quorundam animis & consiliis, qui cum soli sapere, soli bene vivere, JESVMQVE propius insequi & COMITARI sibi videantur, me, qui minimum atque adeo inutilem Jesu Christi DISCIPVLVM ago, odio habuerunt gratis. Atque hi aliorum, quos ad eam
units.tr: Indeed, since the syllogism whose major premise is that, and whose minor premise is that the Vulgate is evidently such, has, so far as I know, never been undertaken as a proof in its own right, I have often seriously considered whether it might be worth while to institute a criticism of each book of the Vulgate and to gather it into one volume, including whatever I had noted here and there, from Theologians both Evangelical and Papist, as faults in it, and whatever seemed to have been left by the industry of later writers. When certain Theologians from England had encouraged me with their advice and exhortations, the judgment of the learned Theologian Witaker also came to mind. In his most careful disputations on Scripture, controversy 1, question 2, chapter 10, near the end, after briefly pointing out some errors of the Vulgate in Genesis, he concludes thus: And indeed, since many holy men have translated the Scriptures from the sources into various languages, and have corrected the errors of this Vulgate edition in their versions, those would seem to me to render a very useful labour who would write separately and carefully a book on the errors of this version. For from this labour everyone would gain the advantage of being able to see how great the difference is between the purest sources of Hebrew truth and these muddy little streams. When this great man's judgment had been added to the counsel of others, I girded up my loins, and after I had worked out the first part of the work, which concerns Moses, I published it, with Belgic Theologians consulted as advisers. In this work I proceeded in such a way that I brought to light only the grosser blunders, lest both the labour and the writing should run to immense length. Everywhere I brought forward the Papist advocates themselves, many of whom, both in their commentaries and elsewhere outside the heat of dispute, have quite freely censured the Vulgate. Two lights of the Roman Church stand out here: Cajetan, and Augustinus Steuchus of Gubbio. I did this, taught by the Jesuit Serarius, who teaches that heretics should be named and cited especially in these cases, Minerval, book 1, chapter 6: First, when the Egyptians are to be set against one another. Second, when some opinion is to be supported, by way of certain props and buttresses [ἐξείσματα], so that it may be firmer among other innovators, that they may restrain their tongues and machines of attack, lest they assail those very points more fiercely. Many things which the Papists themselves have criticised we have passed over, not because we thought they had been marked unjustly by that censorious rod, but first, because we foresaw that they had some veil by which they could be partly covered and wrapped up; second, lest we should seem to labour under an excessive itch for finding fault and under immoderation [ἀμετρίᾳ] and waste of time [ἀνάλωσις]; third, because we foresaw that the inexcusable blunders alone would be enough to fill a volume of sufficient bulk. Nevertheless we have censured a few points, with the danger and words of the Papists themselves, for example of Cajetan, Steuchus, Lyra, John Benedict, and so on, and for this we did not lack reasons. Knowingly and deliberately I have never acted deceitfully, and I have censured no passage in my words for which I did not, after serious reflection, hope for an excuse, unless perhaps the Roman Pontiff were to publish a new Lexicon and a new Grammar. I said then, and professed, that I had pursued only those points which I judged in no way excusable, passing over the rest: those which are manifestly faulty, corrupt, superfluous, mutilated and dangerously ambiguous, and which in short do not have the light for expressing the mind of the Holy Spirit that they could have. Lest the Papists should reply that the Vulgate, in those passages which we have noted, differs not from the Hebrew text as it now stands, that is, as Gretser puts it, impure and corrupt, but from the text which once existed, clear and pure, I have everywhere brought forward the Seventy translators, to whom the Greek version now extant is commonly ascribed, and the Chaldee paraphrast, as well as the fragments of Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus, and so on, all of whom are older than Jerome, whom they make the father of the Vulgate. Certainly, with what face will the adversary assert that those passages of the Hebrew text were corrupted after Jerome's time, which before him were read in the very form in which they are still read? I thought this should be noted, so that no one would suppose that I brought these forward because I think whatever differs from them is faulty. I have cited Arias Montanus and Pagninus very rarely in the first part, because we knew that these outstanding men were, by the more shameless Papists, placed in almost the same rank as heretics, and are still so regarded. That Arias was, on account of that splendid labour expended on the Royal Edition of the Bible, accused of various heresies before the Roman Pontiff, is clear from his Apology, which was written in Spanish and was brought to his homeland by Englishmen, who found it some years ago when Cadiz was taken, and they still keep it in the Oxford Library. Would that the learned Theologian Thomas James, or his successor in the care of that library, would at last publish that work, which he often promised, translated into Latin, for the whole world to share! But why do I need words, and take refuge in unpublished stories [ἀνέκδοτα]? The preface to Arias's Interlinear Bible alone shows what thanks the Jesuits gave him for his labours. For it is quite certain that he attacked them. "Since Erostratus," he says, "could not have Pagninus alive, he took on himself the task of tearing apart our name in preference to all others, perhaps having found an opportunity in the minds and counsels of certain men who seem to themselves alone to be wise, alone to live well, to follow Jesus more closely and to accompany him, and who have hated me, who am the least and indeed a useless disciple of Jesus Christ, for no reason." And these men, of others whom to this...

units.la: Digitized by Google iam rem occulte inducere possunt & ingenis & nominibus abutuntur. Horum autem nos nec artes fallunt, nec gregem prodere aut cognomen indicare juvat. Vtuntur illi quidem magno & ad res suas agendas inaccessibili mysterio, sed quod facile pelluceat, quodque non nisi post multos annos tandem aperiendum est, virtute illius qui illuminat abscondita cordis & occultas tenebrarum, Hæc Arias. Secuti sumus denique textum vulgatum, quem Clemens VIII. recognovit, minus ingenuum rati, ea exagitare, quæ ille suffulerat. Passim quoque annotavimus, quinam errores ex prava versione vel ortum & incrementum sumpserint. Prætereo alia quæ in Proleg. meis tunc edisserui.
units.tr: Digitized by Google Now they can bring the matter in secretly, and they abuse both talents and names. We are not deceived by their tricks, nor does it help to reveal their flock or name their leader. They do use a great mystery, inaccessible to those who would manage their affairs, but one that is easily seen through, and that cannot be disclosed until many years have passed, by the power of him who brings to light the hidden things of the heart and the secret places of darkness. So Arias. Finally, we have followed the common text, which Clement VIII revised, thinking it less honourable to attack what he had upheld. We have also noted throughout which errors arose or grew from a faulty translation. I pass over other matters that I set out in my Prolegomena.

units.la: Cum verò Ecclesiis Euangelicis placere cum laborem intellexissem, perrexi ad libros Historicos, in quibus paulò liberius nos diffudimus, difficiliora loca etiam à vulgata non male translata, ex fontibus præstantiorumque Interpretum versionibus illustravimus. Cum & illos absoluissem, animus mihi Ἀγῳδιχα μεχμήεξε, utrùm illam quoque partem seorsim ederem, an vero eam eo usque premerem, donec cæteros quoque V. T. libros percurrissem. Interim oblata mihi fuit occasio translationem nostram Belgicam, quæ ex Germanicâ B. Lutheri traducta est, cum fontibus & accuratioribus versionibus conferendi, cujus molesti operis, ut & Grammaticalium meorum opusculorum editio haud paucos mihi menses eripuit. At dum laboribus istis exantlatis ad vulgatam redeo, moneor à Rev. & Clarissimo Theologo, Andreâ Riveto, Theologum quendam Parisiensem in Censuram meam strinxisse calamum. Communicat mihi ejus scriptum, opus grande in folio, promittens quæstiones celeberrimas in Genesin cum accurata textus explicatione & vulgatæ Editionis ab hæreticorum calumniis vindicatione. Dum vero illud evolvo, video non ultra octavum Geneseos caput opus illud ab authore productum. Profitetur se monachum ordinis minimorum S. Francisci de Paula, vocat se omnium hominum minimum. At dum pergo, video eum, instar Aristarchi cujusdam & censoris, præstantissimis Heroibus non solùm Euangelicis, sed & Pontificiis insultare. Ibi miscellus ille Grammatica iter Amama.
units.tr: When I realised that the Evangelical Churches wanted this work, I went on to the historical books, in which I spoke somewhat more freely and cleared up the more difficult passages, which the Vulgate had not translated badly, from the sources and from the versions of the better interpreters. When I had finished these, I was divided [Ἀγῳδιχα μεχμήεξε] as to whether I should publish that part separately, or hold it back until I had gone through the other books of the Old Testament as well. Meanwhile I had the opportunity to compare with the sources and more accurate versions our Dutch translation, which was made from Luther's German. This troublesome work, along with the edition of my small grammatical works, took me several months. But while I was returning to the Vulgate after these labours, I was warned by the reverend and most distinguished theologian Andreas Rivetus that a certain Parisian theologian had turned his pen against my Censure. He sent me his writing, a large folio work, promising celebrated questions on Genesis with a careful explanation of the text and a defence of the common edition against the slanders of heretics. But as I turned it over, I saw that the author had not carried the work beyond the eighth chapter of Genesis. He professes to be a monk of the order of the Minims of S. Francis of Paula, and calls himself the least of all men. But as I went on, I saw that, like some Aristarchus and critic, he was attacking not only the most distinguished Evangelical heroes but also the Papists. There that medley of a grammarian turned up: Amama.

units.la: Se quoque principibus permixtum agnovit Achivis.
units.tr: He too recognised himself mixed among the chiefs of the Achaeans.

units.la: Quid facerem? Planè stabat sententia, insuperhabito hoc Theologo, in pertexendâ meâ censura, eâque in omnes V. T. libros edenedenda diligenter pergere, atque in Præfatione prædictum Marsennum amicè invitare, ut vulgatam, quo ad ejus fieri posset in locis à me notatis, defenderet; Putabam enim me tunc majori operæ pretio Apologiam meæ Censuræ editurum. At cum in libris Propheticis multa mihi adhuc deesse subsidia viderem in hoc præsertim Belgii angulo, ubi & libris & Bibliothecis non ex voto instructi sumus, opus illud non duxi esse præcipitandum. Interim hoc mihi opus Misologi nostri extorserunt, in quod illos quoque vulgati Interpretis lapsus conjeci, ex quibus alii errores vel nati vel constabiliti sunt, reliquos censuræ ex professo institutæ reservaturus. Interim ne Marsennus à longiori silentio meo cornua sumeret, placuit hic quoque in ipso limine libri 2. censuras nostras, suis quasque locis, adversus ejus convitia & dicteria defensare.
units.tr: What was I to do? I was quite determined, while disregarding this theologian, to continue diligently with my Censure, and to publish it on all the books of the Old Testament, and in the Preface to invite the aforementioned Marsennus in a friendly way to defend the Vulgate, so far as it could be done in the places I had noted. For I then thought I would publish an Apology for my Censure, a more worthwhile task. But since I saw that in the Prophetic books many aids were still lacking to me, especially in this corner of Belgium, where we are not equipped with books and libraries as we would wish, I did not think that work should be rushed. Meanwhile our Misologus has forced this work from me, in which I have also included those lapses of the common interpreter from which other errors have either arisen or been confirmed, reserving the rest for the Censure undertaken for its own sake. Meanwhile, so that Marsennus should not take up horns from my longer silence, I thought it right to defend my criticisms here too, at the very threshold of the second book, each in its proper place, against his insults and abuse.

units.la: Quia Bulla Sixti V. cujus sæpius in superioribus facta est mentio, in nullis amplius Bibliorum Editionibus, quæ tamen ab ipso Sixtina denominantur, comparet, neque in posterum comparebit, non existimavi pio Lectori fore nolenti, si eam hic repræsentarem.
units.tr: Because the Bull of Sixtus V, which has been mentioned often above, no longer appears in any editions of the Bible, although they are still called Sixtine, and will not appear in future, I did not think it would be unwelcome to the devout reader if I presented it here.

units.la: SIXTVS EPISCOPVS,
units.tr: SIXTUS, BISHOP,

units.la: Servus Servorum Dei,
units.tr: Servant of the servants of God,

units.la: Ad perpetuam rei memoriam.
units.tr: For perpetual remembrance of the matter.

units.la: ÆTERNUS ille, cælestium, terrestriumque rerum omnium conditor ac moderator Deus, Ecclesiam sanctam veluti deliciarum Paradisum, suâ ipsemet dextrâ, tanquam providus Agricola, varias plantas, stirpibusque mirificè consevit, simulque uberrimo sacrarum eandem dem scripturarum fonte, pluribus quasi fluviis, in universum terrarum orbem diffusis, sic irrigavit, ut sancta mysteria, oraculaque divina, quae sacris continentur libris, sicut in cunctarum gentium salutem parabantur, ita à tribus illis potissimum enunciaretur linguis, quae in omnium auribus nationum maximè percrebuerunt, nec non sanctissima crucis titulo consecrata, Salvatoris nostri Regnum, Hebrais, Graecus ac Latinis literis praedicarunt. At callidissimus humani generis hostis, cujus invidia mortis aculeus, cujus superbia peccandi magisterium fuit, nullum non movit lapidem, ut caelestem divini verbi sementem, quantum in ipso erat, aut nascentem opprimeret, aut extirparet enatam, aut adultam vitiaret, id verò praecipuè omni conatu, ac machinatione tentavit, ut sacrorum quaedam corruptissima Bibliorum editiones prodirent, atque ita impietas sub pietatis figura delitesceret, ac populis scoria pro argento, fel draconum pro vino, pro lacte sanies obtruderetur. Cumque non in Haereticis tantum, sed in Catholicis etiam quibusdam, tametsi consilio dissimili, subortum sit nimium quoddam nec plane laudabile studium, & quasi libido scripturas Latinè interpretandi: idem malorum omnium artifex Satanas per illos, licet tale nihil cogitantes, ex hac ipsa tam incerta ac multiplici versionum diversitate & varietate sumpta occasione, sic miscere omnia atque in dubium revocare, &, si fieri posset, rem eò perducere contendit, ut dum scripturarum verbis diversi interpretes aliam atque aliam formam, ac speciem induunt, nihil in iis certi, nihil rati ac firmi, nulla denique inviolabilis auctoritas sine magna difficultate reperiri posse videretur, ita ut hoc saeculo valdè timendum fuerit, ne in prisc cum illud editionum Chaos rediremus, de quo B. Hieronymus inquit: Apud Latinos tot sunt exemplaria quot codices: & unusquisque pro arbitrio suo addidit vel subtraxit, quod ei visum est; & utique non potest verum esse, quod dissonat. Itidemque sanctus Augustinus dixit, Latinos scripturarum interpretes nullo modo numerari posse. Vt enim (ait) cuique primis fidei temporibus in manus venit codex Graecus & aliquantulum facultatis sibimet utriusque linguae habere videbatur, interpretari ausus est. Quare huic morbo sacrosancta Tridentina Synodus mederi cupiens, statuit ut ex omnibus, quae circumferuntur sacrorum librorum Latinis editionibus, ipsa vetus, ac vulgata, quae longo tot saeculorum usu in Ecclesia probata est editio, in publicis lectionibus, disputationibus, praedicationibus, & expositionibus pro authentica habeatur, & nemo illam rejicere quovis pratextu audeat, vel praesumat. Hac autem vulgata editio cum una esset, varis lectionibus in plures quodammodo distracta videbatur. Quarum licet nonnullas, aut veterum codicum, aut sanctorum patrum invexisset auctoritas plurima nihilominus vel ex injuria temporum, vel ex librariorum incuria, vel ex impressorum imperitia, vel ex temere emendantium licentia, vel ex recentiorum interpretum audacia qui, Ecclesiae filii dum sint, minus tamen Ecclesiae doctoribus, quam judaeorum Rabbinis morem sibi gerendum putarunt: vel demum ex haereticorum scholiis ad marginem, captiosisque fallaciis obrepserant. Et, quamvis in hac tanta lectionum varietate nihil hucusque repertum sit, quod fidei & morum causis tenebras offundere potuerit, verendum tamen fuit, ne crescente magis ac magis in dies addendi, detrahendi temeritate, haec probatissima scripturarum Editio, quam vinculum pacis, fidei unitatem, charitatis nexum, dissentientium consensionem, certissimam in rebus dubiis normam esse oportebat, plerisque contra, schismatis, & haeresis inductio, dubitationum fluctus, involutio quaestionum, discordiarum leges, & piarum mentium implicatio multiplex evaderet. Quod in 70. interpretum Graeca editione beatus Hieronymus, in Latina vero sanctus Augustinus olim accidisse commemorant. In Praefat. in Esdram & Nehemiam. Idem in prioti praefat. in Paralipom. tom. 3. Epist. 10 ad Hieronymum tom. 2. rant. Tanta autem labes ne adhuc ulterius serperet, sensimque in vulgatam editionem nostram manaret, sapienter eadem Oecumenica Synodus Tridentina decrevit, ut hac ipsa vetus, & vulgata editio post hac quàm emendatissimè imprimeretur. Verum quia nihil profuisset hujus editionis auctoritatem gravissimo sanxisse decreto, si illius quae germana esset lectio nesciretur, sacerque textus ita disputantium pateret arbitrio, ut is qui adversus perfidum hostem, tanquam validissimus mucro districtus fuerat, idem & Clypeus fieri posset, quo debilitati jam, casique hostis latera tegerentur: Id igitur nos indignè ferentes, eòque indignius, quòd per hosce * viginti duos annos, qui a dicti Tridentini Concilii decreto, ad nostri usque Pontificatus exordium interfluxerant, licet hujusmodi opus aliquando captum fuerit, tamen ob alias fortasse occupationes intermissum, nullumque huic imminenti malo remedium adhibitum fuerat: ac propterea tanto impensiore cura ac studio id prosequendum censentes, quanto magis & ab omnibus Dei Ecclesiis expetitur, & a synagogu Satana reformidatur; Cum primum ad Apostolicam beati Petri sedem divina nos miseratio, meritis licet imparibus evocavit; nihil tandem antiquius habuimus, quàm ut primo quoque tempore, optatissimam istam vulgata editionis emendationem aggrederemur. Itaque viros complures doctos, qui sanctarum scripturarum, sacra Theologia, multarumque linguarum scientia, ac diuturno variarum rerum usu, acrique, cum aliquid discernendum est, judicio, ac solertia, praestarent, delegimus, ac simul congregavimus, ut in germana sinceraque sacri textus editione perquirenda, strenuè laborarent, nobisque adjumento forent. Nos enim rei magnitudinem perpendentes, ac proinde considerantes, ex praecipuo ac singulari Dei privilegio, & ex vera ac legitima successione Apostolorum Principis B. Petri, proque Dominus ac redemptor noster, ab aeterno Patre pro sua reverentia proculdubio
units.tr: ETERNAL God, Creator and Governor of all things in heaven and on earth, has planted the holy Church, as a paradise of delights, with his own right hand, like a provident farmer, setting various plants in it in a wonderful way; and he has watered it with the most abundant fountain of the sacred Scriptures, which flows out over the whole world like many rivers, so that the holy mysteries and divine oracles contained in the sacred books were prepared for the salvation of all nations, and were to be proclaimed especially in those three languages which have spread most widely in the ears of all nations, and proclaimed the Kingdom of our Saviour in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters, the title of the holy cross being consecrated as well. But the most crafty enemy of the human race, whose envy was the sting of death and whose pride was the teacher of sinning, left no stone unturned, so that, as far as he could, he might crush the heavenly seed of the divine word as it sprouted, or root it out once it had sprouted, or corrupt it once it had grown. Above all, he tried with every effort and device to bring about the publication of certain most corrupt editions of the Bible, so that impiety might lie hidden under the appearance of piety, and dross be foisted on the peoples instead of silver, dragons' gall instead of wine, and festering matter instead of milk. And since an excessive and not wholly praiseworthy zeal, and as it were a passion, for translating the Scriptures into Latin has arisen not only among heretics but also among certain Catholics, though with a different purpose, the same Satan, the author of all evils, has seized the occasion, through those who think no such thing, from this very uncertain and manifold diversity and variety of versions. He strives to throw everything into confusion and call it in doubt, and, if it were possible, to bring matters to such a point that, while the various interpreters put on one form and appearance after another of the words of Scripture, nothing certain, nothing sound and firm, and finally no inviolable authority, could be found without great difficulty. So in this age we had great reason to fear lest we should return to that former chaos of editions, of which St Jerome says: Among the Latins there are as many copies as there are codices, and each man has added or subtracted whatever seemed good to him; and certainly what disagrees cannot be true. Likewise St Augustine said that the Latin interpreters of the Scriptures cannot in any way be numbered. For, as he says, in the first times of the faith, whenever someone got hold of a Greek codex and seemed to have some ability in both languages, he dared to interpret. Wherefore to cure this disease the holy Council of Trent, desiring to remedy this evil, decreed that of all the Latin editions of the sacred books in circulation, that old and common edition itself, which has been approved in the Church by long use over so many centuries, should be held authentic in public lectures, disputations, preachings and expositions, and that no one should dare or presume to reject it on any pretext. Yet although this common edition was one, it seemed to be split up in some way into many variant readings. Some of these had crept in through the authority of old codices or of the holy Fathers; but many more had crept in through the injury of time, the carelessness of copyists, the ignorance of printers, the rash license of those who emended it, or the boldness of more recent interpreters, who, though they are sons of the Church, thought they ought to humour the teachers of the Church less than the rabbis of the Jews; or finally through the marginal glosses of heretics and captious sophistries. And although in this great variety of readings nothing has so far been found that could cast darkness on matters of faith and morals, nevertheless it had to be feared lest, with rashness in adding and subtracting increasing more and more from day to day, this most approved edition of the Scriptures, which ought to be the bond of peace, the unity of faith, the tie of charity, the agreement of those who disagree, and the surest rule in doubtful matters, should on the contrary become for most people an occasion of schism and heresy, a surge of doubts, an entanglement of questions, a source of discords, and a manifold entanglement of pious minds. The blessed Jerome records that this happened in the Greek edition of the Seventy interpreters, and St Augustine that it happened long ago in the Latin edition. In the Preface to Ezra and Nehemiah. The same in the preface to the first book of Paralipomenon, vol. 3; Letter 10 to Jerome, vol. 2. rant. Yet lest so great a corruption should creep further and gradually flow into our common edition, the same Ecumenical Council of Trent wisely decreed that this same old and common edition should henceforth be printed as correctly as possible. But since it would have availed nothing to have enacted the authority of this edition by a most weighty decree, if the genuine reading of it were not known, and the sacred text were thus left open to the judgment of disputants, so that the same weapon which had been drawn as a most powerful sword against the treacherous enemy could also become a shield, by which the flanks of the already weakened and fallen enemy would be protected: We, therefore, bearing this with indignation, and all the more with indignation because, during those twenty-two years which had passed from the decree of the said Council of Trent until the beginning of our present pontificate, although such a work was at one time undertaken, it was nevertheless interrupted, perhaps because of other occupations, and no remedy had been applied to this threatening evil: therefore, judging that it should be pursued with all the more earnest care and zeal, in proportion as it is sought by all the churches of God and dreaded by the synagogue of Satan; as soon as the divine compassion called us, though unequal to the merit, to the Apostolic See of the blessed Peter, we held nothing more important than to undertake, at the earliest opportunity, this most desired emendation of the common edition. Accordingly, we chose and at the same time gathered together several learned men, who excelled in the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, sacred theology and many languages, in long experience of various matters, and in sharp judgment and skill when something has to be discerned, so that they might labour vigorously in seeking a genuine and pure edition of the sacred text, and be of help to us. For we, weighing the greatness of the matter, and therefore considering that by the special and singular privilege of God, and by the true and lawful succession of the Prince of the Apostles, the blessed Peter, and because our Lord and Redeemer, heard by the eternal Father for his reverence, without doubt

units.la: * N B. terminum à quo ipsi esse annum 1536. quo finitum erit concilium. Nobis vero supra p. 64. annum 1546. quo rogatum fuit hoc decretum.
units.tr: * N.B. The starting point for them is the year 1536, the year in which the council was to end. For us, see above p. 64, the year 1546, in which this decree was requested.

units.la: Hebr. 2. exauditus, non semel tantum, sed semper rogavit, ut ejus fides non humana carne & sanguine, sed eodem Patre inspirante ei revelata, nunquam deficeret. Cui etiam Dominus injunxit, ut cateros Apostolos in eadem fide confirmaret: qui denique sicuti confidimus, divinam pro nobis opem usque ad consummationem saeculi, Ecclesia Catholica promissam, implorare non cessat, ad nos in ejusdem Petri cathedrâ, in qua ejus vivit potestas, & excellit auctoritas, Deo sic disponente constitutos, totum hoc judicium proprie ac specialiter pertinere, Dei omnipotentis auxilio suppliciter invocato, & ipsius Apostolorum Principis auctoritate confisi, ob publicam sanctam Dei Ecclesiae utilitatem haudquaquam gravati sumus, inter alias Pontificiae solicitudinis occupationes, hunc quoque non mediocrem accuratae lucubrationis laborem suscipere, atque ea omnia perlegere, quae alii collegerant, aut senserant, diversarum lectionum rationes perpendere, sanctorum doctorum sententias recognoscere: quae, quibus anteferenda essent, dijudicare, adeo, ut in hoc laboriosissimae emendationis curriculo, in quo operam quotidianam, eamque pluribus horis collocandam duximus, aliorum quidem labor fuerit in consulendo, noster autem in eo, quod ex pluribus esset optimum, deligendo: ita tamen, ut veterem multis in Ecclesia ab hinc saeculis receptam lectionem omnino retinuerimus. Novam interea Typographiam in Apostolico Vaticano Palatio nostro ad id potissimum magnificè extruximus, atque ad ejus curam, congregationem aliquot sanctae, Rom. Ecclesiae Cardinalium, & insigne collegium doctissimorum virorum ferè ex omnibus Christiani orbis nationibus, & celeberrimis studiorum generalium universitatibus, amplis opulentisque reditibus dotatum deputavimus, ut in ea emendatum jam Bibliorum volumen excuderetur: eaque res quo magis incorruptè perficeretur, nostra nos ipsi manu correximus, si qua pralo vitia obrepserant, & quae confusa, aut facile confundi posse videbantur. bantur, ea intervallo scripturæ, ac majoribus notis, & interpunctione distinximus. Caterum nostri ne hujus consilii, institutiqve rationes ignorentur, sed potius universa Ecclesia Catholica, ipsique posteritati notissima, ac testatissima relinquantur, cunctiqve facile intelligant, quisnam ordo in hoc opere conficiendo, qua lex aut methodus inita, qua indagandi veri norma à nobis servata sit: Illud sanè omnibus certum atque exploratum esse volumus, nostros hos labores, ac vigilias, nunquam eò spectasse, ut nova editio in lucem exeat, sed ut vulgata vetus ex Tridentina Synodi præscripto, emendatissima, pristinaque sua puritati, qualis primùm ab ipsius interpretis manu stiloque prodierat, quoad ejus fieri potest, restituta imprimatur. In hac autem germani textus pervestigatione, satis perspicui inter omnes constat, nullum argumentum esse certius ac firmius, quam antiquorum, probatorumque codicum Latinorum fidem, quos tam impressos, quàm manuscriptos, ex Bibliothecis variis conquirendos curavimus. In quacunque igitur le-ctione plures vetustiores, atque emendatiores libri consentire reperti sunt, ea jure optimo tanquam primigenii textus verba, aut his maximè finitima, retinenda decrevimus. Id verò ad germanam editionem constabiliendam, præsidium sic ubi desideratum est, tunc sanctorum patrum, veterumque expositorum enarrationes, quibus diversa scripturarum loca, & libros illustrarunt, subsidio fuere: è quibus quicquid è re nostra observatum fuit, id in hujus operis partem adscitum est. In iis tandem qua neque codicum neque doctorum magna consensione satis munita videbantur, ad Hebræorum, Græcorumque exemplaria duximus consugiendum, non eo tamen, ut inde Latini Interpretis errata corrigerentur, sed ut in eorum verborum locum, qua, cum apud Latinos ambigua sint, potuissent, quo non oporteret, inflecti, certum aliquid, atque indubitatum suffice-reretur sive ut, quod apud nos variantibus codicibus inconstans, diversum, ac multiplex erat, id uniforme, consonum, uniusque modi, ipsorum fontium veritate perspecta, sanciretur. Sapienter enim B. Hieronymus in explanandis sacris scripturis doctor maximus admonebat, ut quemadmodum in Novo Testamento, si quando apud Latinos quaestio exoritur & est inter exemplaria varietas, ad fontem Graeci sermonis, quo novum Testamentum est scriptum, recurri solet: Ita si quando inter Graecos Latinosque diversitas est in Testamento, tunc ad Hebraam recurramus veritatem, ut, quicquid de fonte proficiscitur, hoc queramus in rivulis: Quod etiam B. Augustinus iis qui scripturam tractant, inter alias regulas tradidit. Laudabilem itaque sanctorum Patrum consuetudinem religiose secuti sumus, dum in iis, quae apud Latinos nimis ambigue dicta, seu variata habentur, Hebraea Graecaque lingua fidem & codices inspeximus, sed ne id licentius fieret quam aequum erat, solers cautio adhibita fuit. Neque enim ignoramus multos esse, quiplerasque Latina huius editionis voces ac locutiones proprie, aut eleganter, aut perspicue, aut breviter, aut copiose magis, aut tanquam verbus ad verbum demensis, a Latino interprete verti potuisse existiment; verum de his minuta nimium & angusta concertatio videtur: neque enim tanti sunt, ut non iis & antiquioris Ecclesiae religio, & sanctissimorum Patrum jure anteponatur auctoritas; prorsusque indignum est, B. Gregorio teste, ut sub Donati regulis verba talestis oraculi restringantur: ac tanta perse est vulgata editionis auctoritas, tamque excellens praestantia, ut majorem desiderare, penitus inane videatur. Qui namque in ea libri continentur (ut a majoribus nostris quasi per manus traditum nobis est) retenti sunt partim ex communi, & antiquissima quadam editione Latina, quam sanctus Hieronymus vulgatam editionem, B. Augustinus ita:
units.tr: Heb. 2. He was heard, not once only but always, so that his faith, revealed to him not by flesh and blood but by the inspiration of the same Father, would never fail. The Lord also enjoined on him that he should strengthen the other Apostles in the same faith. Finally, as we trust, the Church Catholic, which was promised divine help for us until the end of the age, never ceases to implore it. Since God has so arranged it that we are set in the chair of the same Peter, in which his power lives and his authority excels, this whole judgment belongs to us properly and especially. Having humbly invoked the help of Almighty God and relying on the authority of the Prince of the Apostles himself, we were by no means reluctant, for the public and holy benefit of God's Church, to take up among the other occupations of the papal office this not small labour of careful study. We have read through everything that others had gathered or thought, weighed the reasons for the different readings, and examined the opinions of the holy teachers, judging which should be preferred. So in this course of most laborious correction, in which we resolved to spend daily effort and many hours, the labour of others was in consulting, but ours was in choosing the best from among many. Yet we have wholly retained the old reading, received in the Church for many centuries. Meanwhile we have magnificently built a new printing house in our Apostolic Vatican Palace for this very purpose, and for its care we have appointed a certain holy congregation of Cardinals of the Roman Church and a distinguished college of most learned men, drawn from almost all nations of the Christian world and from the most famous universities of general study, endowed with ample and rich revenues. Our purpose was that the corrected volume of the Bibles should be printed there. So that this might be carried out more faithfully, we ourselves corrected with our own hand whatever faults had crept into the proofs, and whatever seemed confused or easily liable to confusion. We have distinguished these by spacing, larger letters and punctuation. But so that the plans and method of our undertaking may not be unknown to ours, and may rather be left most well known and attested to the whole Catholic Church and to posterity itself, and so that all may readily understand what order was followed in making this work, what rule or method was adopted, and what standard of searching for the truth we kept, we wish this to be certain and clear to all: these our labours and vigils were never aimed at bringing a new edition into the light, but at having the old Vulgate, most emended and, as far as possible, restored to its original purity, as it first came from the hand and pen of its translator, printed in accordance with the prescription of the Council of Trent. In this search for the genuine text it is plainly agreed among all that there is no surer or firmer argument than the faith of ancient and approved Latin manuscripts. We took care to seek these out from various libraries, both printed and handwritten. Therefore, in whatever reading several older and more correct books were found to agree, we have decided, by the best right, to retain those words, or those closest to them, as the words of the original text. To establish this genuine edition, the commentaries of the holy Fathers and of the ancient expositors, by which they illustrated various passages and books of Scripture, were of help where support was needed. Whatever from these was found to suit our purpose has been admitted into this part of the work. Finally, in those places which seemed not sufficiently supported by a great agreement of manuscripts and teachers, we resolved to take refuge in the Hebrew and Greek copies. Not, however, so that the errors of the Latin translator should be corrected by them, but so that, where the Latin words are ambiguous and could have been bent to a sense where they ought not to go, something certain and undoubted should be supplied, or so that what was unsteady, divergent and manifold among our variant manuscripts might be made uniform, consonant and of one kind, the truth of the sources themselves having been clearly seen and confirmed. For the great teacher of the Scriptures, St. Jerome, wisely advised that just as in the New Testament, when a question arises among the Latins and there is variation among copies, we are wont to have recourse to the source of the Greek language in which the New Testament was written, so too, when there is a difference between Greeks and Latins in the Testament, we should recur to the Hebrew truth, so that whatever comes from the source we may seek in the streams. St. Augustine also handed down this same thing, among other rules, to those who handle Scripture. Accordingly we have religiously followed the praiseworthy custom of the holy Fathers, when in those passages which are held to be too ambiguously stated or varied among the Latins, we have consulted the faith of the Hebrew and Greek tongue and manuscripts. But lest this be done more freely than was fair, a careful caution was applied. For we are not unaware that there are many who think that many of the Latin words and phrases of this edition could have been rendered by the Latin translator more properly, or more elegantly, or more clearly, or more briefly, or more fully, or as if word for word. But about these things the dispute seems far too petty and narrow. For they are not so important that the reverence of the older Church and the authority of the most holy Fathers should not be preferred to them. And it is wholly unworthy, as St. Gregory testifies, that the words of such an oracle should be restricted by the rules of Donatus. Moreover, the authority of the Vulgate edition is so great, and its excellence so outstanding, that to desire a greater one seems utterly empty. For the books contained in it (as has been handed down to us by our forefathers, as if by hand) have been retained partly from a common and very ancient Latin edition, which St. Jerome called the Vulgate edition, and St. Augustine called the Italic.

Italam, sanctus Gregorius veterem translationem appellant, quam sanctus itidem Augustinus cæteris, quæ tunc plurimæ in usu erant etiam præferendam censuit, quod esset verborum tenacior cum perspicuitate sententiæ; partim ex sancti Hieron. translatione adsciti fuere, quibus idcirco quantus honor deferendus sit, ut facile intelligit, qui eorum interpretis dignitatem agnoscit. Fuit enim sanctus Hieron. (ut inter cæteros idem B. Augustinus testatur) Græco, Latino & Hebræo eruditus eloquio, & ex occidentali ad orientalem transiens Ecclesiam, in locus sanctis, literisque sacris, ad decrepitam usque vixit ætatem: atque omnes, qui ante illum ex utraque orbis parte doctrina Ecclesiastica scripserant, pene vidit aut legit: eumque non modo Augustinus, Chromatius, Paulinus, cæterique sanctissimi Episcopi, sed etiam Damasus Pontifex Rom. de scripturarum locis consulebant. Nec immerito tantam apud omnes nominis celebritatem, in sanctarum præsertim scripturarum scientia adeptus fuerat. Cum ad eam consequendam, nullis vigiliis, nullis peregrinationibus pepercerit, & doctissimos quosque in Gallia audiverit: Constantinopoli Gregor. Nazianzenum, Alexandriæ Didymum, & alios alibi conquiserit, usus denique clarissimis Hebraeæ linguæ magistris: Non enim uno aliquo doctore contentus fuit, sed plurimos eosque eruditissimos adhibebat: non rerum modo, verum etiam nominum sedulus indagator Quinimò & loca ipsa, quæ in scripturis sæpè commemorantur, inspexit, idque ad intelligentiarum scripturam summopere sibi profuisse testatur. Quicunque igitur tanti Interpretis sanctitatem, ingenium, eruditionem, solertiam, Magistros, labores, illud, in quo vixit, seculum, cum linguarum omnium, ac præsertim Hebraea studia florerent, diligenter spectaverint, facile judicium damnabunt eorum, qui aut tam eximii Doctoris lucubrationibus non acquiescunt, aut etiam meliora seu parem præstare se posse confidunt. St. Gregory calls it the old translation, the Italic, which St. Augustine likewise judged to be preferred over the other translations that were then most in use, because it was more tenacious of the words together with clarity of meaning. Partly, it was adopted from the translation of St. Jerome, and the honour due to them is easily understood by anyone who recognises the dignity of their translator. For St. Jerome (as St. Augustine himself testifies among others) was learned in Greek, Latin and Hebrew, and passing from the Western to the Eastern Church, he lived in holy places and sacred letters up to a decrepit age. He saw or read almost all who before him had written church teaching from either part of the world. Not only Augustine, Chromatius, Paulinus and the other most holy bishops, but also Damasus, the Roman Pontiff, consulted him on passages of Scripture. And not without reason had he obtained such fame in the eyes of all, especially in the knowledge of the holy Scriptures. For to attain it he spared no vigils and no journeys, and he heard all the most learned men in Gaul. At Constantinople he sought out Gregory Nazianzen, at Alexandria Didymus, and elsewhere others. Finally he made use of the most distinguished masters of the Hebrew language. For he was not content with any one teacher, but employed many, and those most learned. He was a diligent investigator not only of things but also of names. Indeed he also examined the places themselves that are often mentioned in the Scriptures, and he testifies that this greatly helped him to understand the Scriptures. Therefore whoever carefully considers the holiness, talent, learning, skill and teachers of so great an interpreter, and the age in which he lived, when the studies of all languages, and especially Hebrew, were flourishing, will readily condemn the judgment of those who either do not rest content with the labours of so distinguished a teacher, or trust that they themselves can produce something better or equal. Bernardus, Haymo, Richardus, & Hugo Victorinus, Petrus Cluniacensis, Rupertus Abbas aliique complures egregij doctores, qui per mille ab hinc annos in Ecclesia claruerunt, qui Hieron. versione ita in omnibus disputationibus, enarrationibus, declamationibus usi sunt, ut catera, quae pene innumerabiles erant, quasi lapsa de Catholicorum Patrum manibus obsoleverint. Ideoque legimus apud sanctum Isidorum, quoniam de Hebraeo in Latinum eloquium sanctus tantummodo Hieron. sacras scripturas convertit, ejus Editione generaliter omnes Ecclesias usquequaque uti, eo quod veracior est in sententiis & clarior in verbis. Et ante Isidorum B. Gregorius Magnus fere idem senserat. Nec Latini modo Patres, sed Hebraei quoq; Graecique cum Latinos alios Interpretes negligant, aut ignorent, Hieronymum tamen amplissimo suo testimonio & honore dignum esse censuerunt. Nam de Hebraeis idem Augustinus: de Graecis autem ipsemet sanctus Hieronymus scribit, à Sophronio viro optimè erudito Psalterium, & Prophetas, quos Hieronymus ex Hebraeo in Latinum verterat, in Graecum eleganti sermone translatos fuisse. Quemadmodum ergo laudabile est, ubicunque nostri codices ipsi per se aut conciliari, aut intelligi non possunt, linguarum externarum praesidia quaerere; ita, cum id necessarium non est, levissimis de causis majorum nostrorum sanctitatem, sapientiam, consensum, vetustissimamque Ecclesia consuetudinem non vereri, temeritas planè, pertinaciaque censenda est. Atque idcirco B. Hieronymus qui Hebraeos, Graecosque interrogandos esse dubiis in rebus admonet, idem etiam sentit, eo non nisi parcè, & quanto rarius fieri potest (ne, quae longo recepta sunt usu, fluctuent) recurrendum. Qua de causa ad Novi Testamenti translationem, quamvis hortante Damaso Pontifice, tardior fuit, piumi appellans laborem,

More rightly, St Isidore, the venerable Bede the presbyter, St Remigius, Alcuin, Fortunatus, Rabanus Maurus, St Anselm, St Bernard, Haymo, Richard and Hugh of St Victor, Peter of Cluny, Rupert the Abbot, and many other distinguished teachers, who flourished in the Church for a thousand years past, used Jerome's version in all their disputations, expositions and declamations, so that the others, which were almost countless, have fallen from the hands of the Catholic Fathers and fallen out of use. Hence we read in St Isidore that, since St Jerome alone translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin, all the Churches everywhere generally use his edition, because it is more faithful in its meaning and clearer in its words. Before Isidore, St Gregory the Great had held almost the same view. Not only the Latin Fathers but also the Hebrews and the Greeks, though they neglect or ignore the other Latin translators, have judged that Jerome deserves the fullest testimony and honour. Augustine says the same of the Hebrews, and St Jerome himself writes of the Greeks that Sophronius, a most learned man, had the Psalter and the Prophets, which Jerome had translated from Hebrew into Latin, rendered into Greek in an elegant style. Therefore, just as it is laudable to seek help from foreign languages wherever our own codices cannot themselves be reconciled or understood, so, when this is not necessary, to disregard the holiness, wisdom, agreement and very ancient custom of the Church of our elders for trivial reasons is to be judged plain rashness and obstinacy. And so St Jerome, who admonishes that doubtful matters should be put to the Hebrews and Greeks, also thinks that one should have recourse to them only sparingly and as rarely as possible, lest what has been received through long use be unsettled. units.la: In præfat. quatuor Evangeliorum tom 3. rem , sed periculosam præsumptionem judicare de cæteris, ipsum ab omnibus judicandum, senis mutare linguam & canescentem jam mundum ad initia retrahere parvulorum. Quis enim doctus pariter, vel indoctus, cum in manus volumen sumpserit, & à nativa, quam semel imbibit, viderit discrepare quod lectitat, non statim erumpat in vocem, falsarium illum clamitans, & sacrilegum, qui audeat in veteribus literis addere, mutare, corrigere? Notissimumque est illud de Iona cucurbita, quæ in veteri editione legebatur; pro quo cum Hieronymus hederam posuisset, quodam in Africa Episcopo interpretationem Hieronymi in Ecclesia lectitante, factus est tantus tumultus in plebe propter unius vocis dissonantiam, ut coactus sit Episcopus, ne sacerdotio dejiceretur, damnare quod legerat. Quare merito sacra Tridentina Synodus veteris vulgatæ editionis libros non aliter, quam prout in Ecclesia legi consueverit, pro Canonicis suscipiendos decrevit. Nos autem ut hæc vetus editio, quæ nunc prodit, nostro excusa prælo, ejusdem Synodi præscripto modis omnibus responderet, non solum veteres, & ab Ecclesia receptos loquendi modos conservavimus, sed etiam apocrypha rejecimus, authentica retinuimus. Nam tertium & quartum Esdræ libros inscriptos, & tertium Machabæorum, quos Synodus inter Canonicos non annumerat, assentientibus etiam in hoc prædictis Cardinalibus congregationis super Typographia Vaticana deputata, ab hac editione prorsus explosimus. Orationem etiam Manassæ, quæ neque in Hebræo, neque in Græco textu est, neque in antiquioribus manuscriptis Latinis exemplaribus reperitur; sed in impressis tantum post librum secundum Paralipomenon affixa est, tanquam insutam, adjectam, & in textu sacrorum librorum locum non habentem, repudiavimus. Non nullas etiam aliquando sententias, quæ aliunde accersita, vulgatæ editioni interpositæ erant neque in antiquis exemplaribus, neque in sanctorum commentariis inveniebantur, delevimus. Hanc denique editionem à variis, qui vitio multorum irrepserant, erroribus accuratè emendavimus, & purgavimus, atque in pristinam veritatem summa diligentia restituimus. Neque verò est quod quispiam miretur, si aliqua sacra loca aliter in sanctis quibusdam doctoribus legerit, quàm in hac editione conscripta sunt. Nam Ambrosius, Augustinus & alii plurimi septuaginta interpretum editionem plerunque secuti fuerunt. Ad laudem igitur & gloriam omnipotentis Dei, Catholica fidei conservationem & incrementum, ac sacrosanctæ universalis Ecclesiæ utilitatem, hac nostra perpetuò valitura constitutione de eorumdem venerabilium fratrum nostrorum S. R. E. Cardinalium super Typographia vaticana deputatorum consilio & assensu, quorum opera & industria in hac ipsa vulgata editionis emendatione, in rebus præsertim gravioribus usi sumus, & ex certa nostra scientia, deque Apostolica potestatis plenitudine statuimus, ac declaramus, eam vulgatam sacra, tam veteris, quàm novi Testamenti paginæ Latinam editionem, quæ pro authentica à Concilio Tridentino recepta est, sine ulla dubitatione, aut controversia censendam esse hanc ipsam, quam nunc, prout optimè fieri potuit, emendatam, & in vaticana Typographia impressam in universa Christiana Repub. atque in omnibus Christiani orbis Ecclesiis legendam evulgamus, decernentes, eam prius quidem universali sanctæ Ecclesiæ, ac sanctorum patrum consensione, deinde verò generalis Concilii Tridentini decreto, nunc demum etiam Apostolica nobis à Domino tradita auctoritate comprobatam, pro vera, legitima, authentica, & indubitata in omnibus publicis privatisque disputationibus, lectionibus, prædicationibus, & explanationibus recipiendam & tenendam esse.
