For who, whether learned or unlearned, when he takes a volume into his hands and sees that what he is reading differs from the native text he first drank in, does not at once burst out, calling him a forger and a sacrilegious man who dares to add to, change or correct the old writings? Very well known is the story of Jonah's gourd, which was read in the old edition; when Jerome had put "ivy" in its place, and a certain bishop in Africa read Jerome's translation in the Church, such an uproar arose among the people over the difference of a single word that the bishop was forced, lest he be deposed from his office, to condemn what he had read. Wherefore the sacred Council of Trent rightly decreed that the books of the old Vulgate edition should be received as canonical only in the form in which they have been customarily read in the Church. But we, so that this old edition, which is now published, printed at our press, should in every way correspond to the prescription of that same Council, have not only preserved the older ways of speaking which the Church has received, but also rejected the apocryphal books and retained the authentic ones. For the third and fourth books of Esdras, so called, and the third book of Maccabees, which the Council does not count among the canonical books, have been utterly excluded from this edition, with the agreement also of the aforesaid Cardinals of the congregation appointed over the Vatican Press. We have also rejected the Prayer of Manasseh, which is neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek text, nor is it found in the older Latin manuscript copies, but is only appended in printed editions after the second book of Chronicles, as though inserted, added, and having no place in the text of the sacred books. We have also removed some sentences which, brought in from elsewhere and inserted into the Vulgate edition, were found neither in the old copies nor in the commentaries of the saints. Finally, we have carefully emended and purged this edition of various errors which had crept in through the fault of many, and with the greatest diligence restored it to its former truth. Nor is there any reason for anyone to wonder if he reads some sacred passages in certain holy teachers differently from how they are written in this edition. For Ambrose, Augustine and many others generally followed the edition of the Seventy translators. Therefore, to the praise and glory of almighty God, for the preservation and increase of the Catholic faith, and for the benefit of the holy universal Church, by this our constitution, which shall remain valid for ever, with the counsel and assent of our venerable brothers the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church appointed over the Vatican Press, whose work and diligence we have used in this very emendation of the Vulgate edition, especially in more serious matters, and from our certain knowledge and the fullness of apostolic power, we decree and declare that this Latin edition of the Vulgate, of the sacred pages of both the Old and New Testament, which has been received as authentic by the Council of Trent, is to be considered without any doubt or controversy the same as this one which we now publish, emended as well as could be done and printed in the Vatican Press, to be read in the whole Christian commonwealth and in all the churches of the Christian world; decreeing that it is to be received and held as true, legitimate, authentic and indubitable in all public and private disputations, lectures, preachings and expositions, first approved by the universal consensus of the holy Church and of the holy Fathers, then by the decree of the general Council of Trent, and now at last also by the apostolic authority given to us by the Lord. units.la: N B. nova vulgatæ editionis posthac Bibliorum sine expressa Apostolicæ sedis licentia textus imprimatur: neve quisquam privato aut peculiari suo sensu aliam editionem sibi confingere, neve hanc ipsam veterem vulgatam à nobis, ut præfertur, restitutam editionem, intra decem annos à datu præsentium numerandos, tam citra, quam ultra montes, alibi quam in nostra Typographia vaticana, imprimere audeat, vel præsumat. Elapso autem præfato decennio, eam cautionem adhiberi præcipimus, ut nemo sanctas scripturas typis mandare præsumat, nisi habito prius exemplari in Typographia vaticana excuso, eodemque Inquisitoris hæretica pravitatis ejus provinciæ, vel si Inquisitor in ea provincia non sit deputatus, Episcopi ejusdem loci manu propria subscripto, juxta illud, ne minima quidem particula mutata, addita vel detracta. Postquam verò libri sacri sic fideliter excusi fuerint, ne tunc quidem vendantur, aut evulgentur, nisi prius delato rursus ad inquisitorem, vel deficiente inquisitore, ad Episcopum exemplari, abeis antea subscripto, iidem libri juxta illud impressi, cum eo diligenter ac accurate collati, & Inquisitoris, vel eventum prædictum, Episcopi signo, aut Chirographo quod inter se prorsus concordent fidem facientes, & attestante, approbati exstiterint. Verum, quoniam ex variis, quæ hactenus ad marginem adscribi consueverat, lectionibus illud sequitur incommodi, ac molestiæ, quod, cum primum hujusmodi varietas oculis objicitur, lectoris animum abeo, quod tunc instat agendum, avocat, illumque alieno planè tempore ad ea, quæ codicibus dissonant, inter se conserenda traducit, nec facile est in tanta lectionum multiplicitate scripturas inoffenso pede percurrere, & ea quasi silva diversitatis oblata, quæ quibus præponenda sint, internoscere: Nos optimum factu, piisque omnibus gratum fore arbitrati, ut Ecclesiæ filii ab his perplexitatibus ejusdem Ecclesiæ iudicio, liberentur, utique eos quibus unum baptisma, una fides, una spes vocationis, est, dissentiens non dividat lectio scripturarum, quarum potissimum indifferens consensio eos debuit in unitatem spiritus copulare; Auctoritate & tenore praemissis mandamus, ut vulgata editionis Biblia posthac nonnisi uniformia imprimantur, nec aliquid à textu diversum in margine scribatur. Quæ vero antehac quibuscunque in locis impressa sunt, juxta hunc nostrum textum ad verbum & ad literam corrigantur idque tam in impressis, quam in imprimendis Missalibus, Breviariis, Officiis Beatæ Mariæ virginis, Psalteriis, Ritualibus, Pontificalibus, Ceremonialibus & aliis Ecclesiasticis libris, quoad eas tantum scriptura lectiones & verba, quæ ex vulgata editione sumpta, atque in ejusdem libris inserta fuisse constat; ubique servetur. Si quis autem Typographus in quibuscunque regnis, Civitatibus, Provinciis & locis tam nostra, & S. R. E. ditioni in temporalibus subjectis, quàm non subjectis, Biblia sacramque scripturam intra decennium prædictum quoquomodo; lapso autem decennio aliter quam juxta hujusmodi exemplar ab Inquisitore, seu in ejus defectum, ab Episcopo sibi tradendum, etiam minima aliqua particula mutata, addita vel detracta, aut ad marginem, vel in textu adscripta etiam per modum scholiorum, annotationum, vel glossa, typis mandare, aut sic quidem codices impressos, & emendatos, sine tamen dicto signo, & attestatione, quod cum priori exemplari, sibi, ut prætertur, tradito concordent, vendere, venales habere, aut alias edere, vel evulgare; aut siquis Bibliopola à se vel ab aliis quibusvis, etiam ad hanc usque diem, vel in futurum ante vel post Dat: præsentium literarum impressos libros, seu imprimendos, à præfata per nos restituta, & correcta editione in aliquo discrepantes, vel juxta eam ad unguem non emendatos, ac similia Inquisitores, seu Episcopi, subscriptione
units.tr: N.B. the text of the new edition of the Vulgate Bible be printed hereafter without the express licence of the Apostolic See; nor let anyone dare or presume to devise another edition by his own private or peculiar sense, or to print this old Vulgate, restored by us as stated, within ten years counting from the date of these presents, on either side of the mountains, anywhere other than in our Vatican Press. After the said ten years have elapsed, we order this caution to be observed: that no one presume to commit the holy Scriptures to print unless he has first obtained a copy printed in the Vatican Press, subscribed with the hand of the Inquisitor of heretical depravity for that province, or, if no Inquisitor has been appointed in that province, of the bishop of the same place, according to that rule, with not even the smallest particle changed, added or removed. Moreover, once the sacred books have been so faithfully printed, they shall not be sold or published even then, unless the copy previously subscribed has first been carried back to the Inquisitor, or, if there is no Inquisitor, to the bishop, and the books printed according to it have been diligently and accurately collated with it and approved, with the sign or handwriting of the Inquisitor or the aforesaid bishop attesting and making it certain that they agree entirely with one another. But since from the various readings which have hitherto been customarily written in the margin there follows this inconvenience and annoyance: that as soon as such variety is set before the eyes it draws the reader's mind away from what he is then doing and leads him at a wholly unsuitable time to compare with one another the things that disagree with the codices, and it is not easy amid so great a multiplicity of readings to run through the Scriptures with an unhindered foot, and, with so many diversities offered like a forest, to discern which should be preferred: we, judging it best and welcome to all the pious, have decided that the sons of the Church should be freed from these perplexities by the judgement of the same Church, since a reading of the Scriptures that differs does not divide those to whom there is one baptism, one faith, one hope of calling, and whose agreement in these matters ought above all to bind them together in the unity of the Spirit. By the authority and tenor of the foregoing we command that the Bibles of the Vulgate edition be hereafter printed only in uniform form, and that nothing different from the text be written in the margin. Whatever has hitherto been printed in any places is to be corrected word for word and letter for letter according to this our text; and this is to be observed in printed and forthcoming Missals, Breviaries, Offices of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Psalters, Rituals, Pontificals, Ceremonials and other ecclesiastical books, in respect only of those readings and words of Scripture which are known to have been taken from the Vulgate edition and inserted into those books. If any printer, in whatever kingdoms, cities, provinces and places, whether subject or not subject to our temporal authority and that of the Holy Roman Church, prints the Bibles or sacred Scripture in any way within the aforesaid ten years, or after the ten years have lapsed prints them otherwise than according to such a copy to be handed to him by the Inquisitor, or in his default by the bishop, even with the smallest particle changed, added or removed, or with additions in the text or margin, even by way of scholia, annotations or glosses; or sells, keeps for sale, or otherwise issues or publishes codices printed and emended in such a way without the said sign and attestation that they agree with the earlier copy handed to him as stated; or if any bookseller, whether himself or through others, even up to this day or in future before or after the date of these letters, sells, offers for sale or publishes books printed or to be printed which differ in any respect from the edition restored and corrected by us, or which are not exactly emended according to it, or which are similar, not approved by the subscription of the Inquisitors or bishops, or printed with additions or various readings written in the margin: whoever presumes to do so in any of the aforesaid cases, or any of them, and does not obey this our constitution, shall, besides the loss of all the books and other temporal

units.la: I ptione non approbatos, seu additionibus, aut variis lectionibus ad marginem conscriptis excusos, pariter vendere, venales proponere, vel evulgare præsumpserit, is, qui in supradictis casibus, sive eorum quolibet nostra huic constitutioni non paruerit, ultra amissionem omnium librorum & alias temporales arbitrio infligendas pœnas, etiam majoris excommunicationis sententiam eo ipso incurret, à qua, nisi in mortis articulo constitutus, ab alio, quam pro tempore existente Rom. Pontifice absolvi non possit. Quod si Inquisitor aut Episcopus aliud exemplar ab eo, quod in vaticana typographia impressum est quoquo modo discordans Typographo ad imprimendum tradiderit, vel impresso suo signo, aut subscriptione approbaverit; quod revera ab eo discordet, in eum, si Antistes fuerit, etiamsi Archiepiscopali Primatiali, Patriarchali, vel alia majori præfulgeat dignitate, interdicti ingressus Ecclesiæ, si autem inferior, excommunicationis sententiam ab ipso facto incurrendam ex nunc per præsentes ferimus, ita ut ab alio, quam Rom. Pontifice absolutionis aut relaxationis beneficium consequi nequeat.
units.tr: ...not approved by subscription, or printed with additions or variant readings written in the margin, presumes to sell them likewise, offer them for sale, or publish them, he who in the above cases, or any of them, does not obey this our constitution incurs, besides the loss of all the books and other temporal penalties to be imposed at the discretion of the court, the sentence of major excommunication by that very fact. He cannot be absolved from this, unless he is at the point of death, by anyone other than the Roman Pontiff in office. But if an Inquisitor or Bishop hands over to a printer for printing another copy that in any way differs from the one printed in the Vatican press, or approves it by his own mark or subscription, when it truly differs from it, then, if he is a prelate, even if he excels in the dignity of Archbishop, Primate, Patriarch or any other higher rank, we decree by these presents that he incurs the interdict from entering the Church. If he is of lower rank, we pronounce by these presents, from now on, the sentence of excommunication, to be incurred by the very fact, so that he cannot obtain the benefit of absolution or relaxation from anyone other than the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Et nihilominus tam Inquisitor, seu Episcopus ipse, qui hujusmodi libros à prafata impressione vaticana differentes approbaverit, quam etiam Typographus, seu Bibliopola, qui nostris superius expressis præceptis, ac prohibitionibus in aliquo non obtemperaverit, in congregatione Cardinalium sanctæ Romanæ & universalis Inquisitionis adversus hereticam pravitatem pro tempore deputatorum, seu coram judice vel judicibus ab eadem congregatione delegatis, de hujusmodi facto in districto judicio rationem reddere teneatur, ac pro modo culpæ, severus pœnas ejusdem congregationis, seu judicis, vel judicum, ab ea deputatorum arbitrio puniatur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Inquisitor or Bishop himself who has approved such books differing from the aforesaid Vatican printing, as well as the printer or bookseller who has in any way failed to obey our precepts and prohibitions set out above, is bound to give an account of such action in strict judgment before the Congregation of the Cardinals of the holy Roman and universal Inquisition against heretical depravity, appointed for the time being, or before the judge or judges delegated by that Congregation. According to the degree of his fault, he is to be punished severely at the discretion of that Congregation, or of the judge or judges appointed by it.

units.la: Caterum si manuscripta, vel impressa Biblia hujus etiam vulgatæ Editionis, ob Characterum vetustatem, seu ob aliquod insigne codicis ornamentum, sive impressionis prapræstantiam, vel notationes ad marginem scriptas asser-vantur, & juxta nostrum hoc exemplar emendata non fuerint, ea in iis, quæ huic nostræ editioni non consenserint, nullam in posterum fidem, nullamque auctoritatem habitura esse decernimus ac declaramus: Mandantes universis & singulis Patriarchis, Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, caterisque Ecclesiarum, & locorum etiam Regularium prælatis, per universum orbem constitutis, ut præsentem constitutionem in suis quisque Ecclesiis, Provinciis, Civitatibus, Diœcesibus, & jurisdictionibus curent perpetuò, firmiter & inviolatè ab omnibus observari, contradictores & inobedien-tes per censuras Ecclesiasticas, aliaque opportuna juris, & facti remedia, appellatione postposita, compescendo, invocato etiam ad hoc, si opus fuerit, auxilio brachii sæcularis, non obstantibus constitutionibus, & ordinationibus Apo-stolicis, atque in generalibus, Provincialibus vel Synodalibus Conciliis editis, nec non quarumcunque Ecclesiarum, Ordinum, congregationum, collegiorum atque universi-tatum, etiam studiorum Generalium, juramento, confir-matione Apostolica, vel quavis firmitate alia roboratis, statutis, & consuetudinibus, etiam ab immemorabili tempore pacifice observatis, Privilegiis quoque, Indultis & literis Apostolicis illis, eorumque vel earum prælatis, Superioribus, & personis per quoscunque Romanos Pontifices, Prædecessores nostros, ac nos, & sedem prædictam motu proprio, & certa scientia, deque Apostolica potestatis plenitudine, & alias sub quibuscunque tenoribus, & formis, & cum quibusvis etiam derogatoriarum derogatoriis, aliisque efficacioribus, & insolitis clausulis, irritantibusque & aliis decretis in genere vel in specie quomodolibet concessis, & sæpius approbatis & innovatis. Quibus omnibus & singulis etiam si in eis caveatur expresse, quod illis nullatenus, aut non nisi de consensu certarum personarum, vel nisi nili sub certis modo & forma inibi expressis, derogari possit, & aliàs facta derogationes nulla sint eo ipso, ac pro illorum sufficienti derogatione, de illis eorumque totis tenoribus, specialis, specifica, & expresse mentio habenda, seu quavis alia exquisita forma ad hoc servanda foret; tenores hujusmodi pro expressis habentes ad effectum praesentium duntaxat, derogamus, ac nolumus illa cuiquam adversus praevisa in aliquo suffragari, aut, si aliquibus communiter, vel divisim ab Apostolica sit sede indultum quod interdici, suspendi, vel excommunicari non possint per literas Apostolicas, non facientes plenam, & expressam, ac de verbo ad verbum de indulto hujusmodi mentionem. Volumus autem praesentes literas in valvis Basilica Lateranensis, ac Principis Apostolorum de urbe ac Cancellaria Apostolica de more publicari, & intra quatuor menses, eos, qui citra montes sunt; qui vero ultra montes, intra octo menses a die publicationis hujusmodi numerandos, perinde arctare, & afficere, ac si eorum cuilibet personaliter intimata fuissent: Decernentes ut earum transumptis, etiam impressis, Notarii publici manu subscriptis, ac sigillo Pralati Ecclesiastici obsignatis, eadem ubique habeatur fides, quae ipsis originalibus exhibitis vel ostensis haberetur. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat hanc paginam nostri statuti, declarationis, derogationis infringere vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Siquis autem hoc attentare praesumpserit, indignationem omnipotentis Dei, ac Beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum ejus se noverit incursurum. Dat. Romae apud sanctam Mariam Majorem, Anno incarnationis Dominicae 1589. Kalendis Martii
units.tr: But if manuscript or printed Bibles of this edition of the Vulgate are kept, on account of the antiquity of the characters, or some notable decoration of the codex, or the excellence of the impression, or notes written in the margin, and they have not been corrected according to this our exemplar, we decree and declare that those copies, in the parts that do not agree with this our edition, shall have no credit or authority in future. We command all and each of the Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, and other prelates of churches and places, including regular prelates, established throughout the whole world, that they each take care in their own churches, provinces, cities, dioceses and jurisdictions that this constitution is perpetually, firmly and inviolably observed by all. Contradictors and the disobedient are to be restrained, without appeal, by ecclesiastical censures and other remedies allowed by law and fact, calling in, if need be, the aid of the secular arm. This applies notwithstanding apostolic constitutions and ordinances, and those issued in general, provincial or synodal councils, and notwithstanding the statutes and customs of any churches, orders, congregations, colleges and universities, even of general studies, confirmed by oath, apostolic confirmation or any other firm sanction, and customs peacefully observed from time immemorial. It also applies notwithstanding privileges, indults and apostolic letters granted to those churches, and to their prelates, superiors and persons, by any Roman Pontiffs, our predecessors, or by us and the said See, of our own motu proprio, of certain knowledge, and from the fullness of apostolic power, and otherwise under whatever tenors and forms, and with whatever even derogatory derogations, and other more effective and unusual clauses, irritating clauses and other decrees, in general or particular, however granted and often approved and renewed. To all of these and each of them, even if it is expressly provided that they cannot be derogated from in any way, or only with the consent of certain persons, or only in certain modes and forms expressed therein, and that otherwise derogations made are null by that very fact, we nevertheless, for the sufficient derogation of these, and so that a special, specific and express mention of them and of their whole tenors must be made, or any other exquisite form observed for this purpose, derogate, holding their tenors as expressed for the effect of these presents only. We do not wish those provisions to be of any help to anyone against what is foreseen here, in any respect. If an indult has been granted by the Apostolic See to any persons, in common or individually, that they may not be interdicted, suspended or excommunicated by apostolic letters, these letters do not count unless they make full and express mention of such an indult, word for word. We wish these present letters to be published, as is customary, on the doors of the Basilica of the Lateran and of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, and in the Apostolic Chancery. They shall bind and affect those on this side of the mountains within four months, and those beyond the mountains within eight months, counted from the day of such publication, just as if they had been personally notified to each of them. We decree that copies of them, even printed ones, signed by the hand of a public notary and sealed with the seal of an ecclesiastical prelate, shall have the same faith everywhere that would be given to the originals if they were produced or shown. Therefore it shall be lawful for no one at all to infringe this page of our statute, declaration and derogation, or to act against it with rash daring. If anyone presumes to attempt this, he is to know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at St Mary Major, in the year of the incarnation of the Lord 1589, on the Kalends of March.

units.la: Pontificatus nostri anno Quinto.
units.tr: In the fifth year of our pontificate.

units.la: Lubet huic subjicere Breve illud Apostolicum, quod Clemens VIII. ceu propylaeum quoddam suae Editioni praestruxit, quod itidem in quibusdam Editionibus Bibliorum jam desideratur. Illud vero excipiet Praefatio Editioni Clementis VIII. praefixa.
units.tr: It pleases me to append to this that apostolic brief which Clement VIII set before his edition as a kind of propylaeum, and which is likewise already missing from some editions of the Bible. The preface prefixed to Clement VIII's edition will follow it.

units.la: CLEMENS P. OCTAVVS,
units.tr: Clement VIII, Pope,

units.la: Ad perpetuam rei memoriam.
units.tr: For the everlasting memory of the matter.

units.la: CUM sacrorum Bibliorum vulgatæ Editionis Textus summis laboribus ac vigiliis restitutus, ac quam accuratissimè mendis expurgatus, benedicente Domino, ex nostrâ Typographiâ Vaticanâ in lucem prodeat, nos ut in posterum idem textus incorruptus, ut decet, conservetur, opportunè providere volentes, authoritate Apostolica tenore præsentium districtius inhibemus, ne intra X. annos à datâ præsentium, numerandos, tam citra quam ultra montes, alibi quam in nostrâ Vaticanâ Typographia à quoquam imprimatur. Elapso autem præfato decennio, eam cautionem adhiberi præcipimus, ut nemo hanc SS. Scripturarum editionem typis mandare præsumat, nisi habito prius exemplari in Typographiâ Vaticana excuso, cujus exemplaris forma, ne minima quidem particula de textu mutata, addita vel ab eo detracta, nisi aliquid occurrat, quod Typographicæ incuriæ manifestò adscribendum sit, inviolabiliter observetur. Si quis verò Typographus in quibuscunque regnis, Civitatibus, provinciis & locis tam nostræ & S.R.E. ditioni in temporalibus subjectis, quàm non subjectis, hanc eandem S. Scripturarum editionem intra decennium prædictum quoque modo; elapso autem decennio, aliter quàm juxta hujusmodi exemplar, ut præfertur, imprimere, vendere, venales habere aut alias evulgare vel edere, aut si quis Bibliopola à se vel ab aliis quibusvis post datam præsentium hujus Editionis impressos libros, seu imprimendos à præfato restituto & correcto textu in aliquo discrepantes, seu ab alio quam à Typographo Vaticano, intra decennium excusis, pariter vendere, venales proponere, vel evulgare præsumpserit, ultra amissionem omnium librorum & alias arbitrio nostro infligendas pœnas temporales, etiam majoris excommunicationis sententiam eo ipso incurrat à qua nisi à Rom. Pontifice, præterquam in mortis articulo constitutus, absolvi non possit. Mandamus itaque & universis & singulis, Patriarchis, Archi-Episcopis, Episcopis, cæterisque Ecclesiarum & locorum, etiam regularium Prælatis, ut præsentes literas in suis quisque Ecclesiis & jurisdictionibus ab omnibus inviolatè perpetuò observari curent & faciant. Contradictores per censuras Ecclesiasticas, aliaque opportuna juris & facti remedia, appellatione postposita, compescendo, invocato etiam ad hoc, si opus fuerit, auxilio brachii secularis: non obstantibus constitutionibus & ordinationibus Apostolicis, ac in Generalibus, Provincialibus, vel Synodalibus Conciliis editis, generalibus vel specialibus, ac quarumcunque Ecclesiarum, Ordinum, congregationum, collegiorum & universitatum, etiam Studiorum generalium, juramento, confirmatione Apostolica, vel quamvis firmitate alia roboratis, statutis & consuetudinibus, ac privilegiis, indultis, ac literis Apostolicis in contrarium, quomodocunque emanatis & emanandis: quibus omnibus ad hunc effectum latissime derogamus & derogatum esse decernimus. volumus autem ut præsentium transumptis etiam in ipsis voluminibus impressis, eadem in judicio & extra, fides ubique adhibeatur, quæ ipsi præsentibus adhiberetur, si forent exhibita vel ostensa.
units.tr: Since the text of the Vulgate edition of the holy Bible, restored with the greatest labour and vigilance and purged of errors as accurately as possible, is about to be published, by the Lord's blessing, from our Vatican Press, we, wishing to provide wisely that this same text be preserved uncorrupted in future, as is fitting, by apostolic authority and by the tenor of these present letters, strictly forbid anyone to print it anywhere other than in our Vatican Press, on either side of the mountains, for ten years to be counted from the date of these letters. After that ten-year period has passed, we order that such care be taken that no one presume to commit this edition of the Holy Scriptures to print unless a copy printed at the Vatican Press has first been obtained, and that the form of that copy be observed inviolably, without the smallest particle of the text being changed, added or removed, unless something occurs that is clearly to be attributed to a printer's carelessness. If any printer, in any kingdoms, cities, provinces and places, whether subject or not subject to our authority and to that of the Holy Roman Church in temporal matters, should print this same edition of the Holy Scriptures within the aforesaid decade in any way, or, after the decade has passed, should print it otherwise than according to such a copy as has been mentioned, or should sell, keep for sale or otherwise publish or put out such printed books; or if any bookseller should presume likewise to sell, offer for sale or publish books printed by himself or by any others after the date of these letters, or books to be printed from the restored and corrected text, which differ from it in any respect, or books printed within the decade by anyone other than the Vatican printer, then, besides the loss of all the books and other temporal penalties to be inflicted at our discretion, he shall incur by that very fact the sentence of major excommunication, from which he cannot be absolved except by the Roman Pontiff, unless he is at the point of death. We therefore command all and each of the patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and the other prelates of churches and places, including the regular prelates, that they see to it and cause these letters to be inviolably observed forever by all in their own churches and jurisdictions. Opponents are to be restrained by ecclesiastical censures and other fitting remedies of law and fact, without right of appeal, calling in also, if need be, the aid of the secular arm; notwithstanding apostolic constitutions and ordinances, and the statutes and customs of any churches, orders, congregations, colleges and universities, even of general studies, whether enacted in general, provincial or synodal councils, whether general or special, whether confirmed by oath, apostolic confirmation or any other firm sanction, and notwithstanding privileges, indults and apostolic letters issued or to be issued to the contrary in any manner. All of these we derogate most widely for this purpose and decree that they are derogated. We wish, moreover, that copies of these present letters, even when printed in the volumes themselves, be given the same faith everywhere, in court and out of it, as would be given to these present letters if they were exhibited or shown.

units.la: Datum Romæ apud S. Petrum sub annulo Piscatoris die 9. Nov. 1592. Pontif. nostri anno 1.
units.tr: Given at Rome, at St Peter's, under the Fisherman's ring, on 9 November 1592, in the first year of our pontificate.

units.la: Prefatio ad Lectorem, Præmissa Editioni Clementis VIII.
units.tr: Preface to the Reader, Prefixed to the Edition of Clement VIII.

units.la: Quæ in locum Sixtinæ Bullæ successit.
units.tr: Which took the place of the Sixtine Bull.

units.la: IN multis magnisque beneficiis, quæ per sacram Tridentinam Synodum Ecclesiæ suæ Deus contulit, idem primis numerandum videtur, quòd inter tot latinas editiones divinarum Scripturarum, solam veterem ac vulgatam, quæ longo tot sæculorum usu in Ecclesia probata fuerat; gravissimo Decreto authenticam declaravit. Nam ut illud omittamus quod ex recentibus editionibus, non paucæ ad hæreses huius temporis confirmandas licenter detortæ videbantur: ipsa certè tanta versionum varietas atque diversitas, magnam in Ecclesia Dei confusionem parere potuisset. Iam enim hac nostra ætate illud fere evenisse constat, quod sanctus Hieronymus tempore suo accidisse testatus est, tot scilicet fuisse exemplaria, quot codices: cum unusquisque pro arbitrio suo adderet vel detraheret. Hujus autem Veteris & Vulgatæ Editionis tanta semper fuit auctoritas tamque excellens præstantia, ut eam ceteris omnibus editionibus longè anteferendam esse, apud æquos judices in dubium revocari non posset. Qui namque in ea libri continentur (ut à majoribus nostris quasi per manus traditum nobis est) partim ex sancti Hieronymi translatione vel emendatione, suscepti sunt, partim retenti ex antiquissima quadam editione Latina, quam sanctus Hieronymus communem & vulgatam, sanctus Augustinus Italam, sanctus Gregorius veterem translationem appellat. Ac de veteris quidem hujus sive Italæ editionis sinceritate atque præstantia, præclarum sancti Augustini testimonium extat in secundo libro de Doctrina Christiana, ubi Latinis omnibus editionibus, quæ tunc primò circumferebantur, Italam præferendam censuit, quod esset, ut ipse loquitur, verborum tenacior cum perspicuitate sententiæ. De sancto verò Hieronymo multa exstant egregia veterum patrum testimonia, eum enim sanctus Augustinus hominem doctissimum ac trium linguarum peritissimum vocat; atque ejus translationem ipsorum quoque Hebræorum testimonio verācem esse confirmat. Eundem sanctus Gregorius ita prædicat ut ejus translationem, quam novam appellat, ex Hebræo eloquio cuncta verius transfudisse dicat: atque idcircò dignissimam esse, cui fides in omnibus habeatur. Sanctus autem Isidorus non uno in loco Hieronymianam versionem ceteris omnibus anteponit, eamque ab Ecclesiis Christianis communiter recipi ac probari affirmat, quod sit in verbis clarior, & veracior in sententiis. Sophronius quoque, vir eruditissimus, sancti Hieronymi translationem non Latinis modò, sed etiam Græcis valdè probars animadvertens, tanti camfecit ut Psalterium & Prophetas ex Hieronymi versione in Græcum elegantì sermone transfulerit. Porrò qui secuti sunt, viri doctissimi, Remigius, Beda, Rabanus, Haymo, Anselmus, Petrus Damiani, Richardus, Hugo, Bernardus, Rupertus, Petrus Lombardus, Alexander, Albertus, Thomas, Bonaventura ceterique omnes, qui his nongentis annis in Ecclesia floruerant sancti Hieronymi versione ita sunt usi, ut cetera, quæ penè innumerabiles erant, quasi lapsæ de manibus Theologorum penitus obsoleverint. Quare non immeritò Catholica Ecclesia, sanctum Hieronymum Doctorem maximum, atque que ad scripturas sacras interpretandas divinitus excitatum, ita celebrat, ut jam difficile non sit illorum omnium damnare judicium, qui vel tam eximij Doctoris lucubrationibus non acquiescunt, vel etiam meliora, aut certè paria, præstare e posse confidunt. Ceterum ne tam fidelis translatio, tamque in omnes partes Ecclesiæ utilis, vel injuria temporum, vel impessorum incuria vel temere emendantium audacia, ulla ex parte corrumperetur, eadem sacrosancta Synodus Tridentina illud Decreto suo sapienter adjecit, ut hæc ipsa vetus & vulgata Editio emendatissimè, quoad ejus fieri posset, imprimeretur: neque ulli liceret illam sine facultate & approbatione Superiorum excudere. Quo decreto simul typographorum temeritati ac licentiæ modum imposuit, & Pastorum Ecclesiæ, in tanto bono quàm diligentissimè retinendo & conservando vigilantiam atque industriam excitavit. Et quamvis insignium Academiarum Theologi in Editione vulgata pristino suo nitori restituenda magna cum laude laboraverint: quia tamen in tanta re nulla potest esse nimia diligentia; & codices manuscripti complures & vetustiores Summi Pontificis jussu conquisiti atque in Urbem advecti erant; & demum, quoniam executio generalium conciliorum & ipsa Scripturarum integritas ac puritas, ad curam Apostolicæ sedis potissimum pertinere cognoscitur: Ideò Pius IV. & Pontifex Maximus, pro sua in omnes Ecclesiæ partes incredibili vigilantia, lectissimis aliquot sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, Cardinalibus, aliisque tum sacrarum Literarum, tum variarum linguarum peritissimis viris eam provinciam demandavit, ut vulgatam editionem Latinam adhibitis antiquissimis Codicibus manuscriptis, inspectis quoque Hebraicis Græcisque Bibliorum fontibus; consultis denique veterum Patrum Commentariis accuratissimè castigaverunt. Quod itidem institutum Pius V. prosecutus est. Verum Conventum illum, ob varias gravissimasque Sedes Apostolicæ occupationes jamdudum interruptum, Sixtus V. divina providentia ad summum Sacerdotium evocatus, ardentissimo studio revocavit, & opus tandem confectum typis mandari jussit. Quod eum jam esset excusum, & ut in lucem emitteretur, idem Pontifex operam daret, animadvertens non pauca in sacra Biblia præli vitio irrepsisse, quæ iterata diligentia indigere viderentur; totum opus sub incudem revocandum censuit atque decrevit. Id vero, cum morte prævenitus præstare non potuisset, Gregorius XIII. qui post Urbani VII. duodecim dierum Pontificeatum Sixto successerat, ejus animi intentionem executus, perficere aggressus est, amplissimis aliquot Cardinalibus, aliisque doctissimis viris ad hoc iterum deputatis. Sed eo quoque & qui illi successit Innocentio IX. brevissimo tempore de hac luce subtractis; tandem sub initium Pontificatus Clementis VIII. qui nunc Ecclesiæ universæ gubernacula tenet, opus in quod Sixtus V. intenderat, Deo bene juvante perfectum est. Accipe igitur Christiane Lector, eodem Clemente Summo Pontifice annuente, ex vaticana Typographia Veterem ac Vulgatam Sacræ Scripturæ editionem, quanta fieri potuit diligentia castigatam: quam quidem sicuti omnibus numeris absolutam, pro humana imbecillitate affirmare difficile est, ita ceteris omnibus, quæ ad hanc usque diem prodierunt, emendationem, purioremque esse, minimè dubitandum. Et verò quamvis in hac Bibliorum recognitione, in codicibus manuscriptis, Hebraeis Græcisque fontibus, & ipsis Veterum Patrum Commentariis conferendis, non mediocre studium adhibitum fuerit: In hac tamen pervulgata Lectione, sicut nonnulla consultò mutata, ita etiam alia, quæ mutanda videbantur, consultò immutata relicta sunt: tum quod ita faciendum esse ad offen-
units.tr: Among the many great benefits that God bestowed on his Church through the sacred Council of Trent, the following deserves to be counted among the first: from among so many Latin editions of the divine Scriptures, it solemnly declared by a most weighty decree that the old and common Vulgate alone is authentic. It had been approved in the Church by long use over many centuries. To pass over the fact that some of the more recent editions were readily twisted to support the heresies of this time, the very great variety and diversity of versions could well have caused great confusion in the Church of God. Indeed, in our own age it is clear that what St. Jerome said had happened in his time has nearly come about again: there were as many copies as there were manuscripts, since each person added or removed what he pleased. The authority and outstanding excellence of this old Vulgate edition have always been so great that, among fair judges, no one could call into doubt that it must be preferred far above all other editions. The books it contains were received, as has been handed down to us by our forebears as it were from hand to hand, partly from the translation or revision of St. Jerome, and partly retained from a very ancient Latin edition, which St. Jerome calls the common and vulgate edition, St. Augustine the Italic, and St. Gregory the old translation. Concerning the sincerity and excellence of this old or Italic edition, there is a notable testimony of St. Augustine in the second book of On Christian Doctrine, where he judged that the Italic was to be preferred to all the Latin editions then first in circulation, because, as he himself puts it, it was more faithful to the words along with clarity of sense. Concerning St. Jerome there are many outstanding testimonies of the ancient Fathers. St. Augustine calls him a most learned man and most skilled in three languages, and affirms that his translation is true even by the testimony of the Hebrews themselves. St. Gregory extols him in such a way that he says his translation, which he calls the new one, has rendered everything from the Hebrew more truly, and that for this reason it is most worthy of being trusted in all things. St. Isidore, in more than one place, places Jerome's version above all others and affirms that it is commonly received and approved by Christian Churches, because it is clearer in its words and more accurate in its sense. Sophronius also, a most learned man, noticing that St. Jerome's translation was highly approved not only by the Latins but also by the Greeks, valued it so much that he rendered the Psalter and the Prophets from Jerome's version into elegant Greek. Moreover, those who followed, most learned men, Remigius, Bede, Rabanus, Haymo, Anselm, Peter Damian, Richard, Hugh, Bernard, Rupert, Peter Lombard, Alexander, Albert, Thomas, Bonaventure, and all the others who flourished in the Church during these nine hundred years, used St. Jerome's version in such a way that the other versions, which were almost innumerable, slipped, as it were, from the hands of the theologians and fell completely out of use. Therefore it is not without good reason that the Catholic Church honours St. Jerome as the greatest Doctor, divinely raised up to interpret the sacred Scriptures, so much so that it is now hard not to condemn the judgment of all those who either do not acquiesce in the labours of so excellent a Doctor, or who trust they can produce something better, or at least equal. Moreover, lest so faithful a translation, so useful to every part of the Church, be corrupted in any respect, either by the injury of the times, by the carelessness of printers, or by the rashness of those who correct it carelessly, the same sacred Synod of Trent wisely added to its decree that this old and common edition should be printed as correctly as possible, and that no one should be permitted to print it without the permission and approval of the superiors. By this decree it both set a limit to the recklessness and licence of the printers and stirred up the vigilance and diligence of the ministers of the Church in retaining and preserving so great a good as carefully as possible. And although the theologians of the famous universities laboured with great praise to restore the Vulgate edition to its former purity, nevertheless, since in so great a matter there can be no excessive diligence, and since several older manuscript codices were sought out by the Supreme Pontiff's command and brought to the City, and finally, since the carrying out of the general councils and the very integrity and purity of the Scriptures are known to pertain above all to the care of the Apostolic See, Pius IV, the Supreme Pontiff, with his incredible vigilance over every part of the Church, entrusted that task to some of the most distinguished cardinals of the holy Roman Church and to other men most skilled both in sacred letters and in various languages. They were to correct the Latin Vulgate edition most carefully, using the most ancient manuscript codices, also consulting the Hebrew and Greek sources of the Bible, and finally the commentaries of the ancient Fathers. Pius V followed the same plan. But that assembly, long interrupted by the various and very grave occupations of the Apostolic See, Sixtus V, called by divine providence to the supreme priesthood, revived with the most ardent zeal, and at last ordered the finished work to be sent to the press. When it had already been printed, and the same Pontiff was taking steps to have it brought out, he noticed that not a few errors from the printing had crept into the sacred Bibles, which seemed to need a second careful check. He decided and ordered that the whole work be called back to the anvil. But since he was prevented by death from doing this, Gregory XIII, who had succeeded Sixtus after the twelve-day pontificate of Urban VII, carried out the intention of his predecessor and undertook to complete it, with some most distinguished cardinals and other most learned men again appointed for this purpose. But since both he and Innocent IX, who succeeded him, were taken from this light in a very short time, at last at the beginning of the pontificate of Clement VIII, who now holds the reins of the whole Church, the work that Sixtus V had intended was completed, with God's good help. Accept therefore, Christian reader, with the approval of the same Clement, the Supreme Pontiff, the old and common edition of Sacred Scripture, corrected from the Vatican press with all the diligence that could be applied. It is hard to affirm that it is perfect in every respect, given human weakness, but there is no doubt at all that it is more emended and purer than all the others that have appeared down to this day. And indeed, although no small effort was applied in this revision of the Bible, comparing the manuscript codices, the Hebrew and Greek sources, and the very commentaries of the ancient Fathers, nevertheless in this most widely used reading some things were changed deliberately, while other things that seemed to need changing were deliberately left unchanged, both because the Fathers, especially St. Jerome, more than once warned that this must be done in order to avoid offending the peoples, and because it may reasonably be believed that our forebears, who made the Latin from the Hebrew and Greek, had a greater abundance of corrected copies than those who came to us after their time, and who, perhaps, having copied the text over such a long time, became less pure and less whole. Finally, because it was not the purpose of the sacred congregation of the most distinguished cardinals, and of the other most learned men appointed to this work by the Apostolic See, to cast some new edition or to correct or emend the ancient translator in any respect, but to restore the old and common Latin edition, cleansed of the errors of ancient scribes and of the mistakes of faulty emendations, to its former integrity and purity as far as this could be done, and once restored, to labour as best they could that it be printed as correctly as possible, in accordance with the decree of the Ecumenical Council. Moreover, in this edition nothing non-canonical, nothing added, nothing foreign was thought fit to be set forth. For this reason the Third and Fourth Books of Esdras, which the sacred Synod of Trent did not count among the canonical books, were omitted, as was the Prayer of King Manasseh, which exists neither in Hebrew nor in Greek, is not found in the older manuscripts, and is not part of any canonical book, but placed outside the series of canonical Scripture. And no marginal concordances (which are not forbidden to be placed there hereafter), no notes, no variant readings, and finally no prefaces or summaries at the beginnings of the books are to be seen. But just as the Apostolic See does not condemn the industry of those who have inserted concordances of passages, variant readings, the prefaces of St. Jerome, and other such things in other editions, so it also does not forbid that such aids, for the convenience and advantage of students, be added in future to this very Vatican edition, in another kind of type; provided, however, that the variant readings are not noted in the margin of the text itself.

units.la: offensionem populorum vitandam, sanctus Hieronymus non semel admonuit: tunc quod facile fieri posse credendum est, ut majores nostri, qui ex Hebraeis & Graecis Latina fecerunt, copiam codicum emendationum habuerint, quam ij, qui post illorum aetatem ad nos pervenerunt; qui fortasse, tam longo tempore identidem describendo minus puri atque integri evaserunt: tum denique quia sacrae congregationi Amplissimorum Cardinalium, aliisque eruditissimis viris ad hoc opus a Sede Apostolica delectis, propositum non fuit, novam aliquam editionem cudere, antiquum Interpretem ulla ex parte corrigere vel emendare; sed ipsam veterem ac vulgatam editionem Latinam, a mendis veterum librariorum, nec non pravarum emendationum erroribus repurgatam, suae pristinae integritati ac puritati, quoad ejus fieri potuit, restituere, eaque restituta, ut quam emendatissime imprimeretur juxta Concilij Oecumenici Decretum, pro viribus operam dare. Porro in hac editione nihil non Canonicum, nihil adscititium, nihil extraneum opponere visum est: atque ea causa fuit, cur Liber tertius & quartus Esdrae inscripti, quos inter Canonicos libros sacra Tridentina Synodus non annumeravit, ipsa etiam Manassae regis Oratio, quae neque Hebraice, neque Graece quidem exstat, neque in manuscriptis antiquioribus invenitur, neque pars est ullius Canonici Libri, extra canonicae scripturae seriem positafine: & nullae ad marginem concordantiae (quae posthac inibi apponi non prohibentur) nullae notae, nullae variae lectiones, nullae denique praefationes, nulla argumenta ad Librorum initia conspiciantur. Sed sicut Apostolica Sedes industriam eorum non damnat, qui concordantias locorum, varias lectiones, praefationes sancti Hieronymi, & alia id genus in aliis editionibus inseruerunt: ita quoque non prohibet, quin alio genere Characteris in hac ipsa vaticana editione ejusmodi adjumenta, pro studiosorum commoditate atque utilitate, in posterum adjiciantur; ita tamen, ut lectiones variae ad marginem ipsius Textus minime annotentur.
units.tr: To avoid offending the peoples, as St. Jerome warned more than once; then, because it may easily be believed that our forebears, who made the Latin from the Hebrew and Greek, had a greater supply of corrected copies than those who came to us after their time, and who perhaps, having copied the text again and again over so long a time, became less pure and less whole; and finally because it was not the purpose of the sacred congregation of the most distinguished cardinals and of the other most learned men appointed to this work by the Apostolic See to cast any new edition, or to correct or emend the ancient translator in any respect, but to restore the old and common Latin edition, cleansed of the errors of ancient scribes and of the mistakes of faulty emendations, to its former integrity and purity as far as could be done, and once restored, to labour as best they could that it be printed as correctly as possible, in accordance with the decree of the Ecumenical Council. Moreover, in this edition nothing non-canonical, nothing added, nothing foreign was thought fit to be set forth. For this reason the Third and Fourth Books of Esdras, which the sacred Synod of Trent did not count among the canonical books, were omitted, as was the Prayer of King Manasseh, which exists neither in Hebrew nor in Greek, is not found in the older manuscripts, and is not part of any canonical book, but placed outside the series of canonical Scripture; and no marginal concordances (which are not forbidden to be placed there hereafter), no notes, no variant readings, and finally no prefaces or summaries at the beginnings of the books are to be seen. But just as the Apostolic See does not condemn the industry of those who have inserted concordances of passages, variant readings, the prefaces of St. Jerome, and other such things in other editions, so it also does not forbid that such aids, for the convenience and advantage of students, be added in future to this very Vatican edition, in another kind of type; provided, however, that the variant readings are not noted in the margin of the text itself.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS IV. Linguarum istarum, quibus sacra litera originaliter exarata sunt, vid. Ebraea & Graeca, totiusque adeo politioris literaturae, quam Philologiae seu humanitatis nomine complectuntur, studia, hodie esse superva-canea.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR IV. That the languages in which the holy Scriptures were originally written, namely Hebrew and Greek, and indeed all the more refined literature that they embrace under the name of philology or humanity, are today superfluous.

units.la: Hic error dici vix potest, quam latam sibi in Ecclesiis Euangelicis grassandi viam fecerit.
units.tr: This error can hardly be described, in how wide a path it has made its way to rage through the Evangelical Churches.

units.tr: unless it is torn out of the lungs of the students, and of those to whom the care of the schools and examinations has been entrusted. Three years ago we made an attempt, with no unhappy success among some. May God, the best and greatest, bless those pious minds who have advanced this holy work.

units.la: Vt autem intelligat posteritas, quibus rationibus subnixæ Belgi-carum provinciarum Synodi pestilenti huic errori iverint obviam, ipsiusque Barbariei jugulum petierint, subjiciam primò meam super hoc negotio parænesin, quibus hunc errorem abunde consu-tatum, omnes, opinor, pii agnoscent. Postea ipsa Synodorum quarundam decreta Lectori communicabo. Duo autem hic observet Lector, I. ea quæ uncinulis inclusa videbit, ad primam editionem accessisse. II. Philologiæ secularis seu profanæ (liceat mihi eam sic vocare διαχείρισεως) patrocinium Rev. D. Scultetum ex professo suscepisse, oratione, qua professionem Theol. in Acad. Heidelbur. auspicatus est. Extat ea in Deliciis ejus Pragensibus & curriculo vitæ, hoc titulo, oratio de Philologia cum Theologia conjuncta, seu de quæstione, utrùm Theologo Scripturam interpretanti, externas etiam disciplinas & scriptores profanos in subsidium advocare liceat? Lege Lector & non pœnitebit
units.tr: So that posterity may understand on what grounds the Synods of the Belgic provinces opposed this pestilent error and aimed at the very throat of barbarism, I shall first set out my own exhortation on this matter, in which all the godly, I think, will recognise this error thoroughly refuted. Afterwards I shall communicate to the reader the decrees of certain Synods themselves. Yet the reader should observe two things here: I. that those passages which he sees enclosed in little hooks were added to the first edition. II. that the Reverend Dr. Scultetus expressly undertook the defence of secular or profane philology (let me so call it, διαχείρισεως), in the oration with which he began his professorship of theology at the Academy of Heidelberg. It is found in his Pragensian Delights and in the course of his life, under this title: Oration on philology joined with theology, or on the question whether a theologian interpreting Scripture may also call in external disciplines and profane writers as aids? Read it, reader, and you will not regret it.
