units.la: NON ingnoratis Reverendi Patres & Fratres, primarium Sacri Codicis è superiorum seculorum tenebris eruti, Tenebrarum Papisini discussarum, Religionisque repurgatæ instrumentum fuisse Solem Ebrææ & Græcæ linguæ, qui multis retrò sæculis Christianismo non illuxerat. Cum enim Gregorius Tifernas, decreto Concilii Viennensis subnixus, circa annum DOMINI 1470. Academiæ Parisiensis Rectori indicasset, sibi propositum esse literas Græcas profiteri, postulato etiam stipendio, demirabantur omnes hominis peregrini, nec ab Academiâ accersiti, audaciam. Cum autem ille urgeret decretum, quod Scholæ etiam Parisiensis mentionem faciebat, Rectorque ad Senatum retulisset, introducta in Scholam illam fuit ea professio, quæ tot seculis jacuerat. In eadem fere tempora incidit linguæ Ebrææ πανυχνεια. Joh. Reuchlinus, alias Capnio dictus, postquam fundamenta linguæ S. à Judæo quodam Abdia (cui pro singulis horis singulos aureos pendebat) Romæ in legatione didicisset, princeps Ebræas literas in Academ. Germanicis docuit, editis etiam Grammatica & Dictionario. Sed nec illud vos latet, quanto cum furore efferatus ille humani generis hostis per Colonienses, Lovanienses & Sorbonicos Theologos, atque adeò universam Monachorum confluxem, his initiis intercessierint. Quid enim intentatum reliquerunt? Quid non passi Reuchlinus, Erasmus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus & alii, cætera Pontificii, non aliam ob causam, quàm quod in propagationem linguarum incumberent. Adeo enim tristis erat facies istorum temporum, * utin authoribus Latinis Græce nosse suspectum fuerit: Ebraicè autem, prope hereticum. Sed magis notæ sunt istæ Tragœdiæ, quam ut opus sit iis recensendis immorari. Videamus progressum. Quò magis æstuabant Monachi in extinguenda hac luce, eò magis beata & divinitus excitata ista ingenia in eâ fovendâ & propaganda laborabant. Et sicuti palma quò magis premitur, eò insurgit vehementius, & nostri animos sumebant ab impotentibus Monachorum declamationibus, ipso quoque Leone X. (ubi digitum Dei agnoscitis) & Cardinali Grimano, studia humaniora promoventibus. Ex eo, Vulgata illa res suas sibi habere jussa, Textus Ebræus in V. Græcusque in N. T. authenticus haberi cœpit. Ex eo aditus apertus ad limpidissimos Israëlis fontes, quos Romanorum Pastorum invidia tot seculis obthuraverat. Ex eo
units.tr: YOU are not unaware, Reverend Fathers and Brethren, that the chief instrument for bringing the sacred Code out of the darkness of earlier centuries, for dispelling the shadows of the Papists and for purging religion, has been the Sun of the Hebrew and Greek languages, which for many centuries had not shone upon Christianity. For when Gregorius Tifernas, relying on the decree of the Council of Vienne, announced around the year of the Lord 1470 to the Rector of the University of Paris that he intended to profess Greek literature, and asked for a salary too, all were astonished at the boldness of this foreigner, whom the University had not summoned. When, however, he pressed the decree, which also mentioned the school of Paris, and the Rector had referred the matter to the Senate, that professorship, which had lain dormant for so many centuries, was introduced into that school. At about the same time the flourishing of the Hebrew language occurred. Johannes Reuchlin, otherwise called Capnio, after he had learned the foundations of the holy tongue in Rome during an embassy from a certain Jew, Abdias (to whom he paid a gold coin for every hour), was the first to teach Hebrew letters in the German academies, and he also published a grammar and a dictionary. But nor is it hidden from you with what fury that enemy of the human race was roused, through the theologians of Cologne, Louvain and the Sorbonne, and indeed through the whole crowd of monks, in their opposition to these beginnings. For what did they leave untried? What did Reuchlin, Erasmus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus and others not suffer, and the rest of the Papists, for no other reason than that they were devoted to the spread of the languages? So gloomy was the face of those times that * to know Greek in Latin authors was regarded as suspect, and to know Hebrew was almost heretical. But these tragedies are too well known for it to be necessary to dwell on them. Let us look at the progress. The more the monks raged to extinguish this light, the more those blessed and divinely stirred minds laboured to foster and spread it. And just as a palm, the more it is pressed down, the more vigorously it springs up, so our people took courage from the impotent declamations of the monks, and from Leo X himself (where you recognise the finger of God), and from Cardinal Grimani, who promoted the more humane studies. From that time on, the Vulgate was ordered to keep to its own affairs, and the Hebrew text of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New began to be held authentic. From that time on there was open access to the most limpid fountains of Israel, which the envy of the Roman pastors had blocked for so many centuries. From that time on

units.la: * utin authoribus Latinis Græce nosse suspectum fuerit: Ebraicè autem, prope hereticum. ad 2. Tim. 3. Biblia, liber tot seculis plebi incognitus, in omnium manus devenere. Ex eo Versiones S. Codicis, non ex lacunis Vulgatæ, sed ipsis fontibus derivatas, omnes fere nationes consecutæ sunt. Hac ratione Sol Euangelii vestris Ecclesiis illuxit. Adeo non fefellit Diabolum ejusque instrumenta triste augurium; nec frustrà Paulus 2. jam tum omnem movebat lapidem, ut omnia humanitatis studia extingueret. Quippe adeo oderat ea, * ut ejus studiosos ad unum omnes hæreticorum nomine verberare consueverit. Unde & Romanos sapius admonuit, ut filios suos diutius in literis occupari paterentur. Satis esse, si legere & scribere duntaxat didicissent. Novi, inquit alicubi B. Lutherus. quantopere mihi contra hostes meos profuerit lingua Ebr. notitia. Certè, inquit, quamvis exigua illa sit, cum omnibus tamen totius mundi Gazis eam non commutarem. Eadem magno ) Melanthoni sententia. Experti sunt id ipsum Monachi & Inquisitores, quâ de re lamentabilem Cochlæi & ) Melch. Cani querelam ) alibi produximus.
units.tr: * to know Greek in Latin authors was regarded as suspect, and to know Hebrew was almost heretical. ad 2 Tim. 3. The Bible, a book unknown to the common people for so many centuries, came into everyone's hands. From that time on, versions of the holy Code, derived not from the scraps of the Vulgate but from the very fountains, reached almost all nations. In this way the Sun of the Gospel shone upon your Churches. So little did the Devil and his instruments escape that sad augury; nor in vain did Paul already, at that time, move every stone to extinguish all the studies of humanity. Indeed he hated them so much that he was accustomed to beat all their students, every one, under the name of heretics. Whence also he often admonished the Romans to let their sons be occupied in letters for longer, saying that it was enough if they had learned merely to read and write. I know, said B. Luther somewhere, how greatly the knowledge of the Hebrew language has helped me against my enemies. Certainly, he said, though it is small, I would not exchange it for all the treasures of the whole world. Melanchthon's opinion was the same. The monks and Inquisitors likewise experienced this, about which matter we have quoted elsewhere the lamentable complaint of Cochlaeus and Melchior Canus.

units.la: Sed inæstimabile, hoc Dei donum quomodo excultum fuerit, breviter videamus. Reverendus Vir Lutherus, inquit) Melanth. quam graviter nos ad linguarum studia sæpe hortatus est. & negligentiam studiosorum castigavit? Videbat eum inquit Melanth. non aliam Veterem Barbariem reducendum, magis compendiariam esse viam, si studia ling. interirent. ) Musculus quoque Bucerus & alii piè docti Theologi supinam illam juventutis ignaviam κερτομίοις ἐπίτοτι insectati sunt.
units.tr: But let us briefly see how this priceless gift of God was cultivated. The Reverend Luther, said Melanchthon, how seriously he often urged us to the study of languages, and castigated the negligence of students! He saw, said Melanchthon, that the old barbarism could not be brought back by any shorter road than if the study of languages perished. Musculus too, Bucer and other piously learned theologians attacked that supine idleness of youth with bitter taunts.

units.la: Sed qui tunc temporis in Academiis studebant, respondere poterant, sibi rem esse cum ejusmodi adversariis, qui & ipsi literas istas ignorarent, ac proinde non valdè necessarium sibi viderilinguarum studium. Nostri verò adolescentes quid prætendent? Pontificii, inquit* J. Tarnovius, vigilant, tandem vigilant Photiniani, dum omnes Biblia sacra in fontibus perlustrant, &c. Nos verò maximam partem dormimus securi, nec fontes multum curamus, versionibus solis delectati. Atque utinam vel posterius illud de versionibus verum esset. Optimus Juris-Consultus, inquit B. Lutherus, qui in textu versatus. At jam inquit, mox ad Commentarios proruunt. Nostri studiosi, inquit Cl. Amesius, eas tantùm scripturæ particulas inspicere curant, quas ad locum aliquem communem vel controversiam definiendam ab aliis vident citari. Linguis perdiscendis nullam impendunt operam, Logicam supervacaneam esse autumant:
units.tr: But those who at that time studied in the Academies could answer that they had to do with adversaries of this sort, who were themselves ignorant of these letters, and therefore did not think the study of languages very necessary for them. But what do our young men allege? The Papists, said J. Tarnovius, keep watch; at last the Photinians keep watch too, while they all search the holy Bibles at their sources, etc. But we, for the most part, sleep securely, nor do we care much for the sources, delighted with versions alone. And would that the latter point about versions were at least true! The best jurist, said B. Luther, is the one who is versed in the text. But now, he says, they rush straight to the commentaries. Our students, said Cl. Amesius, take care to look only at those particles of Scripture which they see cited by others to define some common place or controversy. They spend no effort on learning languages, and think logic superfluous:

units.la: a Tom. 4. Orat pag. 471. b De locis lib. 2 cap. 13. c supra in tractatu de vulgata verf. pag. 76. d Orat. tomo 4. pag. 465. e In locis communibus titulo de linguis Scripturæ. Postillis, commentariis & sæpè etiam commentis hominum fidunt. Præceptum Servatoris est, inquit beatæ memoriæ * Sculletus, scrutaminí Scripturas. At nostra juventus, inquit, magnam partem non scripturas divinas, sed humanas scrutatur, eristicos Magistrorum suorum libellos, quâ de causâ notiores ei sunt definitiones & distinctiones hominum, quàm Dei, nec, ut Apollo, potens est in Scripturis Dei magno suo maximo Ecclesia damno. Ita ex Sophisticis disputationibus, artem rixandi, altercandi bene dicta pervertendi sibi familiarem reddunt, &c. De linguarum interim studio & investigando genuino Scripturæ sensu nunquam serio cogitantes. Veras esse has Euangelicorum querelas omnes qui Academiis vivunt oculati testes sunt. Magna hæc est ingratitudo viri P. & Fr. magna securitas. Ingratitudo: dum * oblata donorum Dei facultas adeo contemnitur, & quidem, quod peccatum auget, in ejusmodi locis, ubi dona gratia Dei expósita sunt, & sic in promptu, ut etiam fastidientibus obtrudantur. Securitas, dum videmus hostes Ecclesiæ sese nostris armis armare, & tamen in utramque aurem securi dormimus. Magna hæc rerum vicissitudo est, & agnosco hic profundum Satanæ stratagema. Initio Reformationis, cum apud illos plus quam Cimmeriæ tenebræ in Ecclesiis nostris florebant linguæ & S. Scripturæ studia. Magnos & incomparabiles, eosque quamplurimos Scripturæ interpretes & qui cum ἐξσσίᾳ potentes in Scripturis, docebant, habuerunt illo sæculo Protestantes. At postquam illos Sudor ad hæc quoque studia coegit, eadem apud nos frigere cæperunt. Celebris ille Dominicanus Bannes alicubi ait se in extremâ senectute Ebræam linguam didicisse ne amplius ab hæreticis rideretur Campanella querebatur, Hæreticos Belgas, totumque adeò Arctorum orbem adversus Papatum Grammaticulæ bellum gerere, ideoque quæstiones Grammaticas cum Hæreticis abrumpendas, eosque à studiis istis abducendos suadebat. Hoc consilium quò felicius illis successit, eò diligentius in linguarum studia incubuere. Testes sunt Jesuitarum Scholæ & Scripta. Testes illorum Grammaticæ, Orationes & Ellogia ex quibus unicum protulisse sufficit, eò magis mirandum, quia est & Hispani & Monachi. ] * Dico, inquit, non posse verò dici Theologum, qui in Ebraicis literis non mediocriter fuerit institutus. Quod elogium Jesuita Scrarius a) suo quoque calculo approbavit, & testimonio b) Villa-Vincentii firmavit. [ Hic autem non possum non intexere particu
units.tr: a Tom. 4. Orat. p. 471. b On the Places, book 2, chapter 13. c above, in the treatise on the Vulgate version, p. 76. d Orat., vol. 4, p. 465. e In the common places, under the title on the languages of Scripture. They trust in postils, commentaries and often even in the fictions of men. The precept of the Saviour is, said Scultetus of blessed memory, search the Scriptures. But our youth, he said, searches for the most part not the divine Scriptures but human ones, the disputatious little books of their masters; and for this reason the definitions and distinctions of men are better known to them than those of God, nor is it, like Apollos, mighty in the Scriptures of God, to the very great and greatest loss of the Church. Thus from sophistical disputations they make the art of wrangling and quarrelling, of twisting well-said words, familiar to themselves, etc. Meanwhile they never seriously think about the study of languages or about searching out the genuine sense of Scripture. All who live in the Academies are eyewitnesses that these Evangelical complaints are true. This is great ingratitude of you, Reverend Fathers and Brethren, great complacency. Ingratitude, while * the offered opportunity of God's gifts is so despised, and indeed, which increases the sin, in such places where the gifts of God's grace are set out and so ready to hand that they are thrust even upon those who are disgusted with them. Complacency, while we see the enemies of the Church arming themselves with our weapons, and yet sleep securely with both ears. This is a great reversal of affairs, and I recognise here the profound stratagem of Satan. At the beginning of the Reformation, when among them, in more than Cimmerian darkness, the study of languages and of Holy Scripture flourished in our Churches, the Protestants had great and incomparable interpreters of Scripture, and very many of them, who, powerful in Scripture with authority, taught. But after toil had driven them to these studies too, the same studies began to grow cold among us. The famous Dominican Bannes says somewhere that in extreme old age he learned the Hebrew language so that he would no longer be laughed at by heretics. Campanella complained that the Belgian heretics, and indeed the whole Arctic world, were waging a war of little grammars against the Papacy, and therefore he urged that grammatical questions be broken off with the heretics and that they be drawn away from those studies. The more successfully this counsel turned out for them, the more diligently they applied themselves to the study of languages. The schools and writings of the Jesuits are witnesses. Their grammars, orations and eulogies are witnesses, from which it is enough to produce a single one, all the more to be admired because it comes from a Spaniard and a monk. * I say, he says, that one cannot truly be called a theologian who has not been moderately well instructed in the Hebrew letters. The Jesuit Scarius, a) added his own approval to this eulogy, and b) Villavicencio confirmed it with his testimony. [Here, however, I cannot help but interweave a particle

units.la: * Præfat. in Exercit. Euangel. quæ cygnea beatæ animæ cautio fuit.
units.tr: Preface to the Exercises on the Gospel, which was the swan-song caution of a blessed soul.

units.la: * Verba Musculi, loco supra indicato.
units.tr: The words of Musculus, in the place indicated above.

units.la: * Alphonsus Mendoza Augustinianus, Præf. in Acad. Salamant. in Quæst. politivis; quæst. 10. & Marsennus, Theologus Parisiensis in observ. ad probl. G. Venetip. 366. Operaprecium esset, inquit, ut Christiani diligentius Ebraicam linguam addiscerent, quæ meum berent.
units.tr: Alphonsus Mendoza, Augustinian, Preface to the Academy of Salamanca, on the Quaestiones politivae, question 10; and Marsenne, Parisian theologian, in his observations on the problems of G. Venetip. 366. It would be worthwhile, he says, for Christians to learn the Hebrew language more diligently, since it clings closely to my ...

units.la: a Proleg. Bibl. p. 107. b Lib. I. de rat. studii Theolog. cap. 19. lam dissertationis, quam Andreas Valerius Desselius, Jurisconsultus & Linguæ Ebraeæ Professor publicus in Academiâ Lovaniensi, ante pauculos annos habuit. Quæstionem proponit, an non hæretici commodissimè convinci possint, si proprio quis eos jugulet gladio, quoties ad scripturam & linguas provocant. Circumstitione opus non est, inquit, De linguis, quia ea professionis mea sunt, id nunc dicam, ad solum sacrarum scripturarum linguarumque, quibus ea condita sunt, scopum collimandum esse. In manu palma erit, sape etiam ante conflictum. Et paulò post, Miramur, inquit, in haereticis linguarum & literarum studium, ridentibus illis in plerisque nostrum contemtum earundem. Notam istam eluamus, & cum principe illa scientiarum jungamus linguarum scientiam. Videbit mox quilibet, praeter literas & linguas nihil fere in illis esse reliqui. In his pueros torquent adhuc rudimentarios, & ad altiores istas disciplinas aditum patere volunt, nulli, qui in trivialibus scholis Graecas & Ebr. literas non didicerit: adeoque quarundam id apud eos statutum est, ut non prius dignos scientiarum dent titulos & honores, quam facti in linguis fructus profectusque specimen quis dederit. Hoc nimirum est quod nuper sanctissimus Paulus V. Pont. Max. brevi, ut vocant, Apostolico constituit, ut in promotione ad gradus doctoratus & ad alios sui ordinis honores, illi, caeteris paribus, praeferantur, qui in cognitione trium linguarum ita profecerint, ut ad docendas illas apti sint, Hortatur excitatque ad linguas summus Pontifex. Sequamur hortantem & excitantem volentes, lubentes, Hæc Andreas.
units.tr: a Prolegomena to the Bible, p. 107. b Book I, On the Rational Study of Theology, chapter 19. Consider the dissertation which Andreas Valerius Desselius, jurist and public professor of the Hebrew language at the University of Louvain, delivered a few years ago. He poses the question whether heretics can be most conveniently convicted if one slays them with their own sword, whenever they appeal to Scripture and the languages. There is no need, he says, for a long preamble. I shall not speak about languages, since those belong to my profession; I will say now only that the aim must be directed solely at the sacred Scriptures and the languages in which they were composed. The palm will be in hand, often even before the battle. And a little later: We wonder, he says, at the heretics' zeal for letters and languages, while in many cases they laugh at our contempt for them. Let us wash off that stain and join the knowledge of languages to that queen of the sciences. Anyone will soon see that there is hardly anything left in those studies apart from letters and languages. With these they still torment boys at the elementary stage, and they want access to those higher disciplines to lie open to no one who has not learned the Greek and Hebrew letters in the ordinary schools. So among some people it is established that they do not award the titles and honours of learning until someone has given a specimen of the fruit and progress he has made in languages. This is indeed what the most holy Pope Paul V recently decreed by a brief, as they call it, Apostolic: that in promotion to the degrees of doctorate and to other honours of their order, those who have advanced in knowledge of the three languages so far as to be fit to teach them are preferred, other things being equal. The highest Pontiff exhorts and urges us to the languages. Let us follow him as he exhorts and urges, willingly and gladly. Thus Andreas.

units.la: Cum autem hæc ita se habent, ut negari haud queant, duo ponam. 1. Omnibus Theologiæ studiosis annitendum esse, ut ad mediocrem peritiam Logices & Latinæ linguæ (quæ, licet unicum quidem originalis Dei verbi apicem possideat, tot tamen annos imo florem juventutis sibi vindicat) adjungant mediocrem Ebraeæ & Graecæ notitiam. 2. Ut autem S. Ministerii Candidati hac in parte officium suum in Academiis faciant, in VV. RR. potestate esse ostendam.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, and cannot be denied, I will set out two points. 1. All students of theology must strive to add to a moderate skill in logic and Latin (which, though it holds the one original of God's Word only, nevertheless claims for itself so many years, indeed the flower of youth) a moderate knowledge of Hebrew and Greek. 2. That candidates for the holy ministry may perform their duty in this respect in the academies, I will show to be within the power of the reverend gentlemen in authority.

units.la: Quod ad 1. attinet, illud vel ex eo satis superque probatum videri possit, quod praedictae linguae à c) Patribus d) jure Canonico, omnibus Theologis Evangelicis ipsisque adeo Socinianis & eruditissimis Iesuitis, hujusque aevi Monachis numerentur inter necessaria Theologiæ instrumenta. Sed ut distinctius & pressius id again quod intendo, sic progrediar.
units.tr: As to the first point, this may seem sufficiently and more than sufficiently proved by the fact that these languages are counted by the Fathers, by canon law, by all evangelical theologians, and even by the Socinians and the most learned Jesuits and the monks of this age, among the necessary instruments of theology. But to proceed more distinctly and precisely to what I intend, I shall go on thus.

units.la: 1. Tex-
units.tr: 1. Tex-

units.la: c Hieron. Epist ad Sun & Fret. & in Zach. 8. August. de Doctr. Christian. 2. 11. d Distinct. 9. cap. ut Veterum.
units.tr: c Jerome, Letter to Sunnia and Fretela, and on Zechariah 8; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine 2.11. d Distinction 9, chapter "ut Veterum".

units.la: 1. Textum Ebr. in Vet. Græcum in N. T. esse authenticas fidei Christianæ tabulas, apud nostros in confesso est. Quin & illud necessariò dabunt{a}) ex Pontificiis illi, qui in Vulgatâ Latinâ multos errores Interpretis. in textu autem Ebraeo paucula tantum librariorum errata agnoscunt. Hoc fuit Reformationis fundamentum. Pro hâc thesi primi Protestantium Theologi tantis animis decertârunt. Eritne ergo jam istarum linguarum studium adiaphorum?
units.tr: 1. That the Hebrew text of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New are the authentic records of the Christian faith is admitted among us. Indeed, those Papists too will necessarily grant this, who recognise many errors of the translator in the Latin Vulgate but only a few slips of copyists in the Hebrew text. This was the foundation of the Reformation, and for this thesis the first Protestant theologians contended with such zeal. Will the study of these languages then be an indifferent matter?

units.la: 2. Et illud constat, utrique tantùm isti textui, Græco & Ebraeo, competere magnificum & augustum illum authentici & infallibilis Verbi divini seu authentici instrumenti fœderis, titulum. Nulli enim versioni ista competunt, nisi cum hac restrictione, QUATENUS cum authenticis tabulis convenit.
units.tr: 2. It is also clear that the magnificent and august title of the authentic and infallible Word of God, or authentic instrument of the covenant, belongs to those two texts alone, the Greek and the Hebrew. For no version can claim it, except with this restriction: INSOFAR AS it agrees with the authentic records.

units.la: 3. Nec illud Euangelicorum quisquam, cui sanum suscipiut est, negaverit, versionem nullam dari posse, cui in omnibus cum authenticis tabulis conveniat. Ut omnes linguæ, ita Ebraea suas habet proprietates aliis imperceptibiles. Spiritus S. qui non solum materiam sed & verba suis amanuensibus inspiravit, ejusmodi characteres Majestatis, gravitatis & ἐναργείας huic authentico textui impressit, quos nulla interpretatio valeat exprimere. Unde praclarè judicabant omnes Veteres, verba Junii, singulas translationes vivos esse, ductos ex purissimis fontibus humanâ operâ, ac proindè sordibus ex infirmitate hominis inquinatos, authoritate cum authentica formâ non comparandos.
units.tr: 3. Nor will any of the evangelicals who has sound judgement deny that no version can be given which agrees with the authentic records in all things. Like all languages, Hebrew has its own properties, imperceptible to others. The Holy Spirit, who inspired not only the matter but also the words in his amanuenses, impressed on this authentic text such marks of majesty, gravity and vividness [ἐναργεία] that no interpretation can express them. Whence all the ancients rightly judged, in the words of Junius, that single translations are living things, drawn from the purest sources by human labour, and therefore stained with the dirt of human frailty, not to be compared in authority with the authentic form.

units.la: 4. Cavebunt Euangelici (certè caverunt hactenus) ne suis versionibus plus tribuant, quàm Pontificii Vulgatæ Latinæ, quod ad authoritatem attinet. Jam verò Vega, Senensis, Canus, Andradius, Lindanus, Eugubinus, Olcalter, Cajetanus, &c. agnoscunt in sua versione multos errores Interpretis. Serarius Jesuita) adversus Grezerum defendit, meliorem & perfectiorem versionem dari posse, cujus argumenta) alibi produximus. Frater Aloysius Catanæus, sententiam suam Tridenti dicturus de authenticatione, ut sic dicam, Vulgatæ Versionis, ajebat inter alia, Card. Cajetanum dicere solitum, eum qui Latinum solummodo textum intelligeret, dici non posse infallibile Dei verbum intelligere, Talis enim, inquiebat, solummodo intelligit vocem Interpretis, qui erroribus obnoxius est, &c. Cui ignoti sunt 4. isti Casus quels, judice * Bellarm. ad Fontes recurrendum est, quod enim hoc voluerit, exempla quæ adducit, satis ostendunt. 1. inquit cum in Lat. Codicibus est error librariorum. 2. Aut diversa lectio. 3. Aut aliquid anceps in Verbis aut sententiâ. 4. Aut cum in Versione energia aut proprietas vocabulorum intelligi non potest * Canus inter alios hos quoque addit, quædam loca intelligamus, quæ clarius verti potuissent, & quæ sine linguarum notitiâ explicari non possunt. 5. Ad intelligenda Ebraea vocabula, quæ ob rationes in Versionibus remanserunt. Judicate viri P. & Fr. annon totidem defectus in Vulgatâ agnoscant. Qui eosdem illos in versionibus nostris non agnoscunt, næ illi originalis Scripturæ pretium, & quid versioni præstet, omnino nesciunt. Hoc ergo rogare mihi liceat, utrùm is idoneus verbi D. Interpres haberi possit, qui per puram putam inertiam, & voluntariam insciitiam, ex prædictis istis casibus, puta variis lectionibus, erroribus librariorum & ambiguitatibus, ad fontes recurrendo, se extricare non potest? Qui proprietatem & emphasin verbi Dubi haberi ea potest, intelligere non vult, atque adeo multa loca, quæ sine originalis linguæ cognitione ex ipsorum Pontificiorum judicio intelligi non possunt, explicare non potest? Accedant huc duo alii casus, 1. Cum locus male versus est. 2. Cum alicujus varia & discrepantes interpretationes sunt, quomodo, quæsovos, is se expediet, qui hunc judicem adire & consulere non potest?
units.tr: 4. Evangelicals will beware (and so far they have been careful) of attributing more to their versions, as far as authority goes, than the Papists attribute to the Latin Vulgate. Yet Vega, Senensis, Canus, Andradius, Lindanus, Eugubinus, Olcalter, Cajetan, and others acknowledge many errors of the translator in that version. Serarius the Jesuit, against Grezer, maintains that a better and more perfect version can be given, and we have set out his arguments elsewhere. Brother Aloysius Catanaeus, about to give his opinion at Trent on the authentication, so to speak, of the Vulgate version, said among other things that Cardinal Cajetan used to say that one who understood only the Latin text could not be said to understand the infallible Word of God: such a person, he said, understands only the voice of the translator, who is liable to error, and so on. For those who do not know the four cases which, in the judgement of Bellarmine, require recourse to the sources, the examples he adduces show well enough what he meant. 1. he says, "when there is an error of copyists in the Latin manuscripts." 2. "Or a different reading." 3. "Or something ambiguous in the words or the sense." 4. "Or when the force or the proper meaning of the words cannot be understood in the version." Canus, among others, adds these too: "some passages which could have been translated more clearly, and which cannot be explained without knowledge of the languages"; and "Hebrew words which, for various reasons, have remained untranslated in the versions." Judge, gentlemen, whether they do not acknowledge just as many defects in the Vulgate. Those who do not recognise the same in our versions utterly fail to know the worth of the original Scripture and what a version can contribute. So let me ask this: can he be deemed a fit interpreter of the word of the Lord who, through sheer idleness and wilful ignorance, cannot extricate himself from the cases just mentioned, namely various readings, errors of copyists and ambiguities, by recourse to the sources? Can he explain the many passages which, by the Papists' own judgement, cannot be understood without knowledge of the original languages, if he does not wish to understand the propriety and emphasis of the word of God? Add two further cases: 1. "when a passage is badly translated"; 2. "when there are various and discordant interpretations of it." How, I ask, will he extricate himself who cannot consult this judge?

units.la: V. Illi, quos solis versionibus contentos esse cogit Orig. linguarum inscitia, aliorum oculis vident, aliorum manibus credulâ simplicitate ita committunt clavum seu gubernaculum mentis suæ, ut si incerti essent incerto mari. Hi cum Deo per interpretem loquuntur. Hi aliorum oculis vident. b) Hi cum plebe in atriis stantes è longinquo sacra contuentur. At qui Scripturam Originalem legit, & intelligit, suis oculis videt, c) & cum sacerdotibus in ipsa penetralia admissus, omnium quæ intus aguntur, ipse arbiter & testis est.
units.tr: V. Those whom the ignorance of the original languages compels to rest content with versions only see with the eyes of others; with credulous simplicity they entrust the helm of their mind to the hands of others, so that they are like men at sea who are uncertain of an uncertain sea. These speak with God through an interpreter; these see with others' eyes. They stand in the courtyards with the common people and gaze at the holy things from afar. But he who reads and understands the original Scripture sees with his own eyes, and, admitted with the priests into the innermost sanctuary, is himself the judge and witness of all that is done within.

units.la: Nunquid res insueta & insolens est, Legatum cum suo, cujus capessit jussa, principe, per interpretem agere? Atque adeo omnia, quæ per Interpretes instituuntur colloquia, non admodum incerta sunt? Themistoclem hoc docuerat experientia. d) Is apud Persas exul & colloquium Regis expetens, animi sui conceptus in Regis sinum per interpretem evaporare detrectavit, Sed ut fideliter mutua darentur & redderentur voces, integri anni spacium lingua Persicæ dif-
units.tr: Is it not an unusual and strange thing for an envoy to transact business with his own prince through an interpreter? And are not all the conversations carried on through interpreters rather uncertain? Experience had taught Themistocles this. d) When he was an exile among the Persians and wished for an audience with the King, he refused to let the thoughts of his mind be poured into the King's ear through an interpreter. But so that words could be exchanged and returned faithfully, he asked to learn the Persian language, which took a full year.

units.la: Exemplum hinc sumant Candidati nostri & Naziræi Domini, qui huc destinantur, ut non semel, sed quotidie & toto vita curriculo cum Rege Regum & Domino dominantium de rebus gravissimis, utpote salutem suam & aliorum concernentibus, loquantur, ejusque mandata deserant.
units.tr: Let our candidates and Nazirites of the Lord take this as an example. They are destined not once but every day, and over the whole course of their lives, to speak with the King of kings and Lord of lords about the most serious matters, which concern their own salvation and that of others, and to receive his commands. (hoc)

units.la: Mercatores mihi videre. Ut certius res suas agant, Gallicam, Hispan. Ital. Turcicam & quas non linguas magnâ cum molestiâ discunt.e) Et postquam naves nostra etiam alium orbem petierint cum Indis loquuntur barbarè. Tam ingeniosi & curiosi cum illi sint in sua generatione, nostri Naziræi solas illas linguas contemnunt, quas unicas didicisse esset operæ pretium. Sed ut redeat eo, unde delapsus est, sermo, Patrum & Scholasticorum commentaria docent quid sit Sacras literas & Dei oracula ex ore Interpretis accepta, sine Orig. linguarum notitia explicare. Aperuerunt illi, inquit Melanthon, feras securibus, & ligna clavo fiderunt. Magnus ille Lutherus, * nunquid hoc te movet, inquit, quod sanctissimi Patres in explicandis scripturis adeo frequenter impegerunt? Et licet subinde recte aliquid dixerint, incerti tamen fuerunt, an videlicet in Originali ita esset ut illi interpretabantur. E. G. Recte docuerunt, Christum esse filium Dei. Sed quam ridiculos se adversariis nostris præbent dum id probare satagunt ex Ps. 110. Tecum principium in die virtutis tuæ, cum isthic loci deitatis Christi nulla fiat mentio. Certe Adversarii hac ratione in erroribus suis magis magisque confirmantur. Rogas ergò causam cur Religio nostra sic derideatur? Non alia ea est quam linguarum ignorantia. - Atque hic nullum, nisi à notitia linguarum, expectes subsidium. Et paulo post, Nun sind aller alter Vater auslegung / die ohn sprachen die Schrift haben gehandelt/ (ob sie wol nichts unrechts lehren) doch der gestalt / das sie oft un gewisse / unbene / und unzeitige sprüche führen / und tappen wie ein blinder an der wand / das sie gar oft des rechten Texts fehlen/ und machen ihm eine nasen nach ihren andacht. Ad summam, dici non potest quantas frustrationes dictarum linguarum ignorantia Patribus & Scholasticis, quorum multi cæterae fuere excellentissimi, attulerit, &f) quam miserè plerisque in locis cæcutierint. Etdubitamus adhuc, quin verè dixerint Viri magni, g) Ebraismorum ignorantiam horrendos errores in Ecclesiam invexisse?
units.tr: I see that merchants, so that they may conduct their affairs more surely, learn French, Spanish, Italian, Turkish and other languages with great effort. And once our ships have sailed even to the other world, they speak with the Indians in a barbarous way. Though they are so clever and inquisitive in their own generation, our Nazirites despise those languages alone which it would be worth the effort to have learned. But to return to where my discourse fell away: the commentaries of the Fathers and the Schoolmen show what it is to explain the Holy Scriptures and the oracles of God received from the mouth of an interpreter, without knowledge of the original languages. They have opened up the wild beasts with axes, and trusted the timber to a nail, says Melanchthon. That great Luther says: "Does it not move you that the most holy Fathers so often stumbled in explaining the Scriptures? And although they sometimes said something correctly, they were nevertheless unsure whether the original really was as they translated it." For example: They rightly taught that Christ is the Son of God. But how ridiculous they make themselves to our adversaries when they strive to prove it from Ps. 110, "With you is the beginning in the day of your power," since in that place there is no mention at all of the deity of Christ. Certainly the adversaries are confirmed more and more in their errors by such reasoning. Do you ask, then, why our religion is so derided? It is none other than ignorance of languages. And here you should expect no help except from knowledge of the languages. And a little later: Now all the interpretations of the old Fathers, who handled Scripture without languages (although they teach nothing wrong), are of such a kind that they often make uncertain, weak and untimely assertions, and grope like a blind man along a wall, so that they very often miss the true text and make it into a nose according to their own devotion. In short, it cannot be said how many frustrations the ignorance of these languages has brought upon the Fathers and the Schoolmen, of whom many were otherwise most excellent, and how miserably in many places they have groped in the dark. And do we still doubt that great men have truly said that ignorance of Hebraisms has brought horrible errors into the Church?

units.la: 6. At omnia hæc incommoda mitigari aliquo modo possent, si
units.tr: 6. But all these inconveniences could be mitigated in some way, if

units.la: e) Epist. de Scholis erig. aut cum nullis, aut ejusmodi adversariis nobis res esset, qui aut linguas ipsi ignorarent, aut in recipiendâ unâ & certâ versione nobiscum consentirent. At res longè se habet aliter. Ajo itaque nullum Ministrum qui linguarum rudis sit, in arenam posse descendere cum docto Papistâ, Sociniano, &c. ne dum b) posse obthurare adversario, quod tamen Apost. in Ministro desiderat. Nulla Versio utrinque recepta est. Ultimum principium est originalis Textus.
units.tr: e) Letter on the founding of schools. ...if we had to deal with no adversaries, or with such as either did not know the languages themselves or agreed with us in accepting one certain version. But the matter stands far otherwise. I say, therefore, that no minister who is unskilled in the languages can enter the arena against a learned Papist, a Socinian, and so on, let alone be able to stop the mouth of his adversary, which nevertheless the Apostle requires of a minister. No version is accepted on both sides. The final principle is the original text.

units.la: 7. Quotquot ex Polonia, Transsylvaniâ vicinisque locis ad nos transeunt, uno ore testantur, Socinianos, tàm laicos quàm Ministros, etiam ætate exitâ, nulla sumptuum habita ratione, in hæc studia incumbere, dummodò vel minimam nancisci possint discendi occasionem. Quid putatis miseros istos mortales intermissuros, si ea offerretur iis opportunitas, qua juventus Belgica fruitur?
units.tr: 7. All who cross over to us from Poland, Transylvania and the neighbouring regions testify with one voice that the Socinians, both laymen and ministers, even when past their youth, devote themselves to these studies without counting the cost, provided they can obtain even the slightest opportunity of learning. What do you think these wretched mortals would give up, if they were offered the opportunity that Belgian youth enjoys?

units.la: 8. Dicam quid amplius, inter Anabaptistas, omnis olim eruditionis ostores accerrimos, hodiè non desunt, qui utramque linguam callent, Alii iis discendis adhuc fatigantur: sunt etiam qui filios suos linguarum notitiâ imbui curant. Judicent RR. VV. nunquid nostrorum negligentia eos ad hæc studia impulerit, & quid nostris Ecclesiis, nisi alia ineatur via. hinc expectandum sit.
units.tr: 8. I will say more: among the Anabaptists, once the most eager displayers of all learning, there are today not wanting those who have a good command of both languages, others are still labouring at learning them, and there are also those who take care to have their sons imbued with knowledge of the languages. Let your Reverences judge whether the negligence of our people has driven them to these studies, and what our Churches may expect, unless another way is entered upon.

units.la: 9. [ Cum præter alios Pontificios Marinus Marsennus promittat, se vulgatam versionem ex ipso Ebraeo, prout jam est, defensurum neque usurum isto aliorum præsidio, Textum Ebraeum seu fontes esse corruptos, ubicunque à vulgata discrepant, observat ad Problem. Georgii Veneti pag. 238. ] Cum ex Bellarm. aliisque Pontisiciis constet, eos huc subinde descendere, ut à vulgata ad fontes provocent, quæro annon res pudenda sit, inter Euangelicos tot reperiri, qui, tali casu, Pontificio ex fontibus satis facere non possent. Ipsorum doctissimi hodiè textum Ebraeum à Judæis corruptum esse negant. & utiliter ad fontes recurri posse, quin subinde necessariò ad eos recurrendum esse, asserunt. i) Bellar. & Andradius etiam invecta sæpè ex illis adversus Judæos argumenta peti posse agnoscunt, ubi vulgata nihil suppeditat. Nostri verò, quasi fontes corrupti, quasi pleni viperis & serpentibus essent (ut Monachus quidam olim concionabatur) ab iis abstinent. [ Non sine indignatione ante annos aliquot legi in Rosweido
units.tr: 9. [Although, among other Papists, Marinus Marsennus promises that he will defend the Vulgate version from the Hebrew itself, just as it is, and will not use that other support, that the Hebrew text or sources are corrupt wherever they differ from the Vulgate; he remarks on the Problem of George the Venetian, p. 238.] Since it is established from Bellarmine and other Papists that they sometimes descend to this point, so as to appeal from the Vulgate to the sources, I ask whether it is not a shameful thing that among the Evangelicals there are so many who, in such a case, could not satisfy a Papist from the sources. Their most learned men today deny that the Hebrew text has been corrupted by the Jews, and assert that one can usefully have recourse to the sources, though it is not necessary to have recourse to them constantly. (i) Bellarmine and Andradius also acknowledge that arguments drawn from them against the Jews can be brought forward where the Vulgate supplies nothing. But our people, as if the sources were corrupt, as if they were full of vipers and serpents (as a certain monk once preached), abstain from them. [Not without indignation I read a few years ago in Rosweyde,

units.la: i) Bellar. lib. 2. cap. 2. weido, Jesuitâ nequaquam barbaro, colloquium, quod se instituisse dicit cum Professore quodam Leidensi. Disputatio erat de textu authentico Bibliorum. Ille pro vulgatâ, hic pro fontibus stabat, asserens, se Græcum textum (in novo, opinor, Test.) pro authentico habere. Regessit Jesuita, quid ergo tot femini-verbu vestri agent, qui Græca ignorant? Andreas Valerius Professor Ebr. in Acad. Lovaniensi narrat Gubernatorem civitatis cujusdam ad epulas suas invitasse aliquando Ministrum verbi divini & Pastorem, ut ille vocat, Catholicum. Incidit controversia de loco Gen. 3. 15. utrùm Ipse, an ipsa legendum esset, Minister provocat ad fontes, Hebraica, inquit, veritas à nobis stat. Quid pastor? Habebat ad manum codicem Ebr. & Ministro nihil tale expectanti exhibet. Is videns rem sibi cum Ebraicæ linguæ perito esse, obstupuit. Et quia legere non poterat eum, ad quem ipse provocaverat, textum, eò confugiebat, se apud Batavos ita fuisse edoctum.]
units.tr: i) Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 2. Rosweyde, a Jesuit by no means barbarous, a colloquy which he says he held with a certain professor of Leiden. The dispute was about the authentic text of the Bible. The one stood for the Vulgate, the other for the sources, asserting that he held the Greek text (in the New Testament, I think) to be authentic. The Jesuit replied: "What, then, will so many of your little women do, who do not know Greek?" Andreas Valerius, professor of Hebrew at the Academy of Louvain, relates that the governor of a certain city once invited to his feasts a minister of the divine Word and a pastor, as he calls him, a Catholic. A controversy arose about the passage in Gen. 3:15, whether ipse or ipsa should be read. The minister appealed to the sources: "The Hebrew truth stands with us," he said. What did the pastor do? He had a Hebrew codex at hand and produced it when the minister expected nothing of the kind. Seeing that he was dealing with one skilled in the Hebrew language, he was astonished. And because he could not read the text to which he himself had appealed, he took refuge in saying that he had been taught thus among the Dutch.]

units.la: 10. Nullus eruditi Theologi commentarius, uti nec pleraque doctorum Polemica, cum fructu legi potest sine linguarum notitia. Quis intelliget nedum urgebit argumentum, quod à phrasi, voculâ, quin uno sæpè apiculo & accentu depromitur? Et quod ad Comm. attinet, periculum faciant in Hieron. item Calvino ad veteris & Bezâ ad N. fœderis libros.
units.tr: 10. No learned theologian's commentary, nor most of the controversial writings of the learned, can be read with profit without knowledge of the languages. Who will understand, let alone press, an argument that is drawn from a phrase, a little word, or often from a single small stroke or accent? And as for the commentaries, let them try this on Jerome and likewise on Calvin for the books of the Old Testament, and on Beza for the books of the New Testament.

units.la: 11. Digna consideratione est ingenua Bellarmini, quam nostri egregiè exagitant, confessio, k) multa, vid. celebrata fuisse Concilia, in quibus aut nulli aut quàm paucissimi fuerint Ebraæ linguæ periti. l) Patres Concilii Ariminensis ab Arrianorum fautoribus rogati, utrùm in Christum an ὁμοούσιον crederent, ὁμοιούσιον abnegantes, se in Christum credere professi sunt. Atque ita vox ea, pro qua tot prælia depugnata erant, in spongiam incubuit. Sed pro istis responderi posset, nullam de Vulgatâ ipsis litem fuisse motam, nullamque omninò tunc fuisse occasionem literas istas discendi. At si nosstis Ecclesiis idem aliquando eveniret quæ maria eluere possent tam pudendam ignominiam!
units.tr: 11. Worthy of consideration is Bellarmine's candid admission, which our people vigorously assail: (k) that many councils have been celebrated in which none or very few were skilled in the Hebrew language. (l) When the fathers of the Council of Ariminum were asked by the supporters of the Arians whether they believed in Christ as homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], they refused homoiousion [ὁμοιούσιον] and professed that they believed in Christ. And so that word, for which so many battles had been fought, fell into the sponge. But it could be replied to them that no dispute about the Vulgate had been raised among them, and that there was then no occasion at all for learning these letters. But if the same thing should ever happen to our Churches, what seas could wash away so shameful a disgrace!

units.la: 12. Sed & illud ab omni ævo docuit experientia, studium sacrarum linguarum & Scripturæ indivisos esse comites. Et unde peti possent illæ, nisi ex hac? Vbi exerceri nisi in hac? Contrâ neglectum & contemptum linguarum semper traxisse secum contemptum Scripturæ. Grassante superioris ævi barbarie, jacebat Codex sacer. Thomas, Lombardus, Aristoteles, utramque paginam faciebant in Scholis Theologicis. Christus, Prophetæ, Apostoli ᾗδεν ἐν ἀριθμῷ erant, ᾗδὲ τέλνοι, ᾗδὲ πνεῦμι. Quod si non ineatur ratio, ut studia linguarum magis floreant, certò certius est brevi futurum, verba Musculi, ut doctis aliquot viris e medio sublatis, pristina errorum tenebra, imò crassiores etiam, in Ecclesiis obtineant: Sic puniente Deo praesentium temporum ingratitudinem ac donorum suorum contemptum. Est enim aequissimum, ut qui benedictionem scientiæ Dei aversantur, hàc ablongatâ, maledictione errorum & ignorantiæ ad summum usque obruantur.
units.tr: 12. But experience has shown in every age that the study of the sacred languages and the study of Scripture are inseparable companions. Where could the languages be drawn from, if not from Scripture? Where could they be practised, if not there? On the other hand, neglect and contempt of the languages has always brought contempt of Scripture in its train. While the barbarity of the earlier age raged, the sacred Codex lay prostrate. Thomas, Lombard and Aristotle filled both pages in the theological schools. Christ, the Prophets and the Apostles were ᾗδεν ἐν ἀριθμῷ, ᾗδὲ τέλνοι, ᾗδὲ πνεῦμι. If no plan is adopted to make the study of languages flourish more, it is more certain than certain that it will shortly come about, in the words of Musculus, that with some learned men removed from the midst, the former darkness of error, and even cruder errors, will prevail in the Churches: thus God punishes the ingratitude of the present times and the contempt of his gifts. For it is most just that those who spurn the blessing of the knowledge of God should, with that blessing withdrawn, be overwhelmed to the uttermost by the curse of error and ignorance.

units.la: 13. In primitivâ Ecclesiâ, quando summa cum difficultate lingua Ebr. discebatur, non defuere in utroque sexu, qui animos suos ad ea studia appellerent. Hieron. quanto labore his ipsis Musis litavit? ) Origenes jam grandævus contra naturam ætatis & gentis suæ Ebraicè didicit. Augustinus jam progressâ ætate Græcè discebat, & passim dolet, sibi non licuisse Ebræ notitiam addere. Cum tamen intelligeret, quantas sibi frustrationes afferret ejus ignorantia, hortatur omnes Scripturæ studiosos, nullam ejus discendæ occasionem negligant. ) Paula & Eustochium Hieronymo ἐμαθητευ-σαν. ) Quin Blæsilla Paulæ Filia paucis diebus difficultates linguæ S. superavit, adeò ut in discendis canendisque Ebraicis Psalmis cum matre contenderet. Hoc Matronæ & Virgines isto difficili ævo præstitërunt. Et quem nostri Nazirei, qui doctissimo hoc ævo vivunt suæ inertiæ obtentum quærent? [Audiant gravissima * Wolfgangi Franzii Theologi Witebergensis verba. Ego iis, inquit, nullum pato partocininm, quin jam modo graviter in eam sententiam, de diligentiâ in Ebraïs collocandâ dixi, & eum qui secus fecerit, occasionibusque adolescentiæ & Academicæ vitæ abusus fuerit, nec fundamenta intima fontium comparare sategerit, divinam vindictam experturum pronuncio.]
units.tr: 13. In the primitive Church, when Hebrew was learned with the greatest difficulty, there were not lacking, of both sexes, those who applied their minds to these studies. With how much labour did Jerome sacrifice to these very Muses? Origen, though already old, learned Hebrew contrary to the nature of his age and people. Augustine, well advanced in years, was learning Greek, and everywhere laments that it had not been granted to him to add knowledge of Hebrew. Yet, understanding how much frustration his ignorance brought him, he urges all students of Scripture not to neglect any opportunity of learning it. Paula and Eustochium became disciples of Jerome [ἐμαθήτευσαν]. Indeed Blaesilla, daughter of Paula, in a few days overcame the difficulties of the sacred tongue, so that in learning and singing the Hebrew Psalms she vied with her mother. Matrons and virgins did this in that difficult age. And what excuse will our Nazirites, who live in this most learned age, seek for their sloth? [Let them hear the most serious words of Wolfgang Franz, theologian of Wittenberg. I, he says, allow them no excuse; I have already spoken gravely on this very point, on devoting diligence to Hebrew, and I declare that whoever does otherwise, and has abused the opportunities of youth and academic life, and has not striven to acquire the inner foundations of the sources, will experience divine vengeance.]

units.la: 14. Et superiore & hoc nostro seculo non defuêre Jurisconsulti, Philosophi, Politici, quorum alii, * etiam ad extremam ætatis regulam progressi, his studiis se applicuere, alii eadem magno studio insuper promoverunt, ut Masius, Vitmastadius, Veltuykius, Picus Mirandula, Bartolus, Rod. Agricola, Erasmus, &c. [Non defuerunt his proximis annis, inquit idem Franzius pag. 56. omnium ordinum venerandi Senes, qui hoc pietatis exercitium suæ senectu-ti divinam voluptatem constituerunt.] Habet & Belgium in utroque sexu, qui in linguarum Origin. studia sedulo incumbunt. Et postquam jam Grammaticam Ebræo-Belgicam & Dictionarium, quæ adjumenta jampridem Belgis promiseram, nacti sunt, bonæ spei sidus affulget, fore ut propediem plures Ebraïsmi cultores habeat.
units.tr: 14. Both in the previous century and in this one, there have not been lacking jurists, philosophers and politicians, some of whom, advanced even to the extreme limit of life, applied themselves to these studies, while others promoted the same with great zeal, such as Masius, Vitmastadius, Veltuykius, Pico della Mirandola, Bartolus, Rudolf Agricola, Erasmus, etc. [There were not lacking in these recent years, says the same Franz on p. 56, venerable old men of every rank, who made this exercise of piety the divine delight of their old age.] Belgium too has people of both sexes who apply themselves diligently to the study of the original languages. And now that they have obtained a Dutch-Hebrew grammar and dictionary, aids which I long ago promised to the Belgians, a star of good hope shines forth that there will soon be more cultivators of Hebrew.

units.la: 14. Provoco tandem ad conscientias omnium piorum Ministrorum, qui aut præceptorum defectu, aut negligentia, aut denique mala studiorum directione has linguas in Academiis non didicerunt, annon jam in sanctissimi muneris functione & SS. literarum assiduâ meditatione agnoscant, quantas sibi frustrationes illarum ignorantia afferat. Annon reapse nunc experiantur, quæstiones plerasque, quibus tantum temporis in multis Academiis insumitur, aut nullum aut omninò exiguum in Ministerio usum habere? [Certè Picus Mirandula, teste *Erasmo, & summi Theologi deplorarunt, se tot annos scholasticæ Theologiæ impendisse. Et quid sibi vult ingenua illa Joh. Ludovici Vivis, confessio, Quæ in juventute elato superciliō credebam esse thesauros in Philosophia, jam conversus & Senex video vix stercora esse & tantum remoras vitæ piæ & studiorum necessariorum fuisse. Dicant ingenuè ] Annon graviter doleant, q) quod in Trivialibus scholis tot annos profanis authoribus discendis impenderint? Annon vera sit r) magni viri querela, quam turpiter non solum fontes, sed tota Biblia à plerisque Theologiæ studiosis, aliisque, qui eidem dant operam, negligantur? Item alterius s) Theologi Veterani, in multis Ministris id non immerito desiderari, quod fontes raro inspiciant, & alectum in dictis allegandis nullum habeant, cum tamen magnâ hic opus sit discretione & prudentiâ, ut dicta primaria à secundaris, indirecta à directis, dubia à certis distinguantur. Eloquantur candidè, annon res ita se habeat. Ego plane confido, omnes pios affirmativam ituros, ac proinde cum Virgiliano illo exclamaturos singulos, O mihi præteritos referat si Iupiter annos!
units.tr: 14. Finally, I appeal to the consciences of all pious ministers who, for lack of teachers, through negligence, or finally through poor direction of their studies, did not learn these languages in the academies: do they not now recognise, in the discharge of their most holy office and in constant meditation on the Holy Scriptures, how much frustration their ignorance of them brings? Do they not now in fact find that most of the questions on which so much time is spent in many academies have either no use or only very slight use in the ministry? [Certainly Pico della Mirandola, as Erasmus reports, and great theologians lamented that he had spent so many years on scholastic theology. And what does the candid confession of Juan Luis Vives mean? "What in my youth I believed, with lofty pride, to be treasures in philosophy, I now, converted and old, see to be scarcely dung, and only hindrances to a pious life and to necessary studies." Let them say candidly.] Do they not grieve deeply that in the grammar schools they spent so many years learning profane authors? Is not the complaint of a great man true, that shamefully not only the sources but the whole Bible is neglected by most students of theology and others who devote themselves to it? Likewise the remark of another veteran theologian, that in many ministers there is rightly missed the fact that they seldom inspect the sources and take no care in the citing of passages, although great discretion and prudence are needed here, to distinguish primary passages from secondary, indirect from direct, doubtful from certain. Let them state candidly whether the matter is not so. I am quite confident that all pious people will answer yes, and so each will exclaim with Virgil's words: "O that Jupiter would restore to me the years that have gone by!"

units.la: Rogantur itaque per viscera misericordiæ D. nostri Jesu Christi, ut conjunctis operis id agant strenuè, ut sanctissima hæc studia, temporum injuria propemodum collapsa, in Ecclesia Dei reflorescant. [Imitentur nautas, qui cum ipsi, navi ad scopulum illis, nudi vix enatarint, nihilo secius aliis solventibus recte solent consulere, commostratus periculis. Sicujus ætas, inquit Erasmus, jam ad hoc praeteriit, is suam fortem boni consulat, modo ne bonæ spei juvenibus obstrepat. Quamquam ego profecto ne senibus quidem author su erim desperandi. Huc pertinent ea quæ supra numero 14. dicta sunt. Quibus hæc adjiciam ex Erasmo, Quatuor nominare possum, viros mihi notos & celebres, quorum unus 48. atatis anno, non nemo major XL. prima Græca linguæ elementa est aggressus. Quò verò profecerint, eorum monumenta ostendunt. Sed & ipse jam 53. annorum ad Ebraica studia recurro, &c. Et * alibi, Novi, inquit, senes canos & magni nominis Theologos, qui Tyrones Theologiæ hortabantur ut linguas discerent & bonas literas amplecterentur, deplorantes infelicitatem sui seculi, quod ipsis non contigissent eadem, non invidentes junioribus studiorum accessionem. ]
units.tr: Therefore they are asked, by the bowels of mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, to work together vigorously, so that these most holy studies, almost collapsed through the injuries of the times, may flourish again in the Church of God. [Let them imitate sailors who, when their ship has been wrecked on rocks and they have barely swum out naked, nonetheless, while others set out, are accustomed to give sound advice, having been made wise by dangers. Erasmus says: "Whoever's age has already passed to this point, let him be content with his lot, provided he does not clamour against young men of good hope. Yet I would certainly not be the author of despair even for old men." To this pertain the things said above in number 14. To these I add what Erasmus says: "I can name four men, known to me and celebrated, of whom one began the first elements of Greek in his forty-eighth year, and another, older than forty, did likewise. What they achieved their writings show. And I myself, now in my fifty-third year, return to Hebrew studies, etc." And elsewhere: "I know, he says, grey-haired old men of great name, theologians, who urged young students of theology to learn languages and embrace good letters, lamenting the unhappiness of their own age, that these things had not fallen to them, and not grudging the younger men the addition to their studies."]

units.la: 1. Cæteris, quæ hùc accongeri possent, missis, ad alteram partem transeo, ajoque & RR. VV. muneris & potestatis esse, prospicere, ne vetus illa Ecclesiis & Scholis denuò superinducatur barbaries.
units.tr: 1. Setting aside the other things that could be brought together here, I pass to the other part, and I say that it is also the duty and power of your Reverences to take care that that old barbarity is not again brought over the Churches and Schools.

units.la: 2. Quod ad munus vestrum attinet, non ignoratis illud Apostoli, r) Ne cui citò manus imposito, neque communicato peccatis alienis Audite Erasm. u) Si usquam vobis permittitis cessare, alibi cessate potius; si delinquere, ubi vis delinquite potius quam in hoc negotio omnium periculosissimo. Audite Chrysostomum, Qui ordinant indignos, isdem subjacent pœnis, quibus illi qui indigni sunt ordinati. Nostis illud Hieron. Qui indoctum (qualis is est qui adversario os obturare non potest) Pastorem ordinat, cæcum animal Deo offert. Noverat hoc in mediis Papismi tenebris Episcopus Vltrajectensis DAVID Burgundus, Philippi Boni Filius. Is cum intellexisset inter tam multos, qui sacris initiabantur, paucissimos esse qui literas scirent, voluit ipse rem propius cognoscere. Jussit sibi in aulâ cathedram poni. Propositi quaestiones. Quid sit? Ex trecentis tres tantùm admisit. Cumque rogaretur, ut moderaretur sententiam suam, reputans, hoc saeculum non gignere Paulos aut Hieronymos, perstitit Episcopus, negans se requirere Paulos aut Hieronymos, sed tamen asinos pro hominibus non admissurum. Quæ non ita accipi velim, quasi omnes Ebraicè & Græcè ignaros, pro asinis habeam (quæ enim hæc esset vesania?) sed illud volo, indignum esse, hoc & eruditissimo & hæresium feracissimo sæculo, præ quo illud Davidis Burgundi densissima nox fuit, ubi nullo labore aut sumptu linguæ istæ discipossunt, ad Ministerium admittij juvenes, qui, qua lingua Apostoli & Prophetæ scripserint, cujusque idiomatis aut significationis
units.tr: 2. As to your office, you are not ignorant of the Apostle's saying: "Lay hands on no one hastily, nor share in other men's sins." Hear Erasmus: "If you allow yourselves to be idle anywhere, be idle elsewhere rather; if you must err, err wherever you like rather than in this business, the most dangerous of all." Hear Chrysostom: "Those who ordain the unworthy are subject to the same punishments as those who are ordained unworthily." You know that saying of Jerome: "He who ordains an unlearned minister (such a one as cannot stop the mouth of an adversary) offers a blind animal to God." This was known, in the midst of Papist darkness, to David of Burgundy, Bishop of Utrecht, son of Philip the Good. When he understood that among so many who were being initiated into the sacred ministry very few knew letters, he wished to look into the matter more closely. He ordered a chair to be set for him in the hall and proposed questions: What is it? Of three hundred he admitted only three. And when he was asked to moderate his judgment, reflecting that this age did not produce Pauls or Jeromes, the bishop persisted, denying that he sought Pauls or Jeromes, but saying that he would not admit asses in place of men. I do not wish these words to be taken as if I regarded all who are ignorant of Greek and Hebrew as asses (for what madness would that be?), but this is my meaning: it is unworthy that in this most learned and most heresy-fertile age, compared with which that of David of Burgundy was a very dense night, young men should be admitted to the ministry, when these languages can be learned without labour or expense, who do not know in what language the Apostles and Prophets wrote, nor the idiom or meaning of

units.la: nis
Erasm. in Eccles. lib. 1. nis sint istæ, quæ nobis quotidie in ore sunt, voces sacræ, juxta cum ignarissimis plane ignorant.
units.tr: Erasm. in Eccles. lib. 1. What these sacred words are, which we have on our lips every day, they are entirely ignorant of, just as the most ignorant people are.

units.la: Potestatem etiam vestram hac in parte non ignoratis. Imitamini exemplum Davidis Burgundi & brevi aliam Ecclesiæ faciem videbimus. Sequimini laudabilem Gallicarum Ecclesiarum consuetudinem, ubi Theologiæ Candidato, in utriusque Testamenti originalitextu illud, quod Præsidi Codicem aperienti se primò exhibet, caput egendum & interpretandum proponitur. An minor in Angliâ, Germaniâ, Daniâ, Belgio, Helvetiâ caeterisque Provinciis, linguas illas discendi commoditas? An minor necessitas, hostiumve multitudo aut robur minus quam in Galliâ? An minor vestra vestris in regnis provinciisve authoritas, quam Synodorum Reformatarum in isthoc regno? Quod siid impetrari non possit, illud saltem in examinib. cognoscatur, utrum eos progressus in Scholis fecerint, ut in Ministerio, relictis jam Scholis, proprio Marte possint progredi illudque sanctè promittant, se qualemcunque illam notitiam porrò auctuaros nec ullo modo commissuros, ut sive negligentiâ sive inertia effluat. Fundamenta linguæ Græcæ in trivialibus docentur, quarum novi aliquot sic constitutas, ut quotquot ex iis prodeunt, Nov. Testamentum Græcum Grammaticè possint resolvere, Novi scholas, ubi fundamenta linguæ Ebraeæ, magno Ecclesiæ & juventutis bono jaciuntur. Quotquot enim ex illis vel minimam Ebrææarum literarum notitiam in Academias inferunt, felicissimè & inoffenso pede videas progredi, dum cæteros ad Elementa illa Alphabetica pudet descendere. Vtinam ex Cl. *Franzii voto, ad istarum Scholarum exemplum cæterae quoque constituerentur, & Naziræi nostri à teneris, dum florida est memoriæ vis, sacris Bibliis assuefierent! Vtinam vel semel tandem authores sacri profanis substituerentur, aut siid obtineri non possit, saltem conjungerentur! * Ipsa ratio suadet, inquit, capacissimis puerorum & recentis integritatis loculis memorialibus primo loco imponenda & ad custodiendum tradenda esse sacra illa κειμήλια, quorum usus & in hac & in altera vita est summopere & unice necessarius. Sæpenumero inquisivi, inquit, ex piis alioquin studiosis ordine, quinam essent primi versus, E. G. in Eclogis Virgilii, quis esset primus in 1.2.3.4. Georgic. Æneidos, &c. Hos versus isti mihi expeditissimè recensuerunt memoriter. Cumque studiosos Theol. esse scirem, è vestigio interrogavi, qua essent prima verba Geneseos, Exodi, &c. Ibi cogitabundi steterunt & ignorantiam suam cum dolore agnoverunt. Causa non alia, quam quod à praeceptoribus pueritia ad maturam Bibliorum lectionem non fuissent assuefacti, & quod à puericitia nil nisi profanos versus edisserere jussi fuissent. Judaica nec mala admonitio est, Filius quinque annorum ad Biblia accedat. At apud nos barbatus juvenis 25. annorum vix tandem ad Biblia legenda accedit, * ubi arcula memoriarum iis profanis expleta & completa fuerunt. Ita in solis profanis authoribus, proh dolor! florem ingenii & aetatis deterimus. At dices hanc querelam respectu eorum, qui Theologiae destinantur, forsan habere locum: at Jurif-Consultos, Medicos, Philosophos & Politicos non specare. Quasi non illi quoque Christiani esse, & Religionis principia imbibere debeant, Quasi non annitendum omnibus esset, ut sermo Christi inter nos copiosè habitet, atque ita notitia Domini universa terra, juxta Vaticinium Jesaiae 11.9. repleatur.
units.tr: You are not unaware of your authority in this matter. Follow the example of David Burgundus, and before long we shall see another face of the Church. Follow the praiseworthy custom of the French Churches, where a candidate for theology is set to explain and interpret, in the original text of both Testaments, whatever chapter first presents itself when the president opens the codex. Is there less opportunity for learning those languages in England, Germany, Denmark, the Low Countries, Switzerland and the other provinces than in France? Is there less need, or fewer enemies, or less strength? Is your authority in your kingdoms and provinces less than that of the Reformed Synods in this kingdom? But if this cannot be obtained, let it at least be ascertained in the examinations whether they have made such progress in the schools that, having left the schools, they can advance on their own strength in the ministry, and solemnly promise that they will increase whatever knowledge they have and will in no way let it slip away through negligence or indolence. The foundations of the Greek language are taught in the trivial schools, and some new ones have been so arranged that all who come out of them can grammatically resolve the Greek New Testament; there are new schools where the foundations of the Hebrew language are laid, to the great good of the Church and of youth. For whoever brings into the academies even the slightest knowledge of the Hebrew letters you will see progressing most happily and with unhindered step, while the others are ashamed to descend to those alphabetic elements. Would that, at the wish of the distinguished Franzius, other schools were set up after the model of these, and that our Nazirites were accustomed to the holy Bible from their youth, while the power of memory is in flower! Would that the sacred authors were at last, once and for all, substituted for the profane ones, or, if this cannot be obtained, at least joined with them! Reason itself suggests, he says, that those sacred treasures should be placed first in the most capacious memory-chests of children and of fresh integrity, and handed over to be kept, since their use is supremely and uniquely necessary both in this life and the next. Often, he says, I have asked pious and otherwise studious people, in order, which were the first verses, for example in Virgil's Eclogues, which was the first in the first four books of the Georgics, of the Aeneid, and so on. They recited those verses to me very readily from memory. And since I knew they were students of theology, I immediately asked them what the first words of Genesis, Exodus, and so on were. They stood pondering and with sorrow acknowledged their ignorance. The cause is nothing else than that their teachers had not accustomed them from childhood to the mature reading of the Bible, and that from boyhood they had been ordered to recite nothing but profane verses. The Jewish admonition is not a bad one: let a son of five years come to the Bible. But among us a bearded young man of twenty-five scarcely at last comes to reading the Bible, when the little chest of memories has already been filled and stuffed with those profane things. Thus, alas! we waste the flower of talent and of age on profane authors alone. But you will say that this complaint perhaps applies to those destined for theology, and does not concern jurists, physicians, philosophers and politicians. As if they too were not Christians, and ought not to imbibe the principles of religion! As if everyone should not strive that the word of Christ dwell richly among us, and so the knowledge of the Lord fill the whole earth, according to the prophecy of Isaiah 11:9.

units.la: a) Scriptura non potest intelligi Theologicè, nisi prius intelligatur Grammaticè, ajebat magnus Melanthon. Quomodo autem intelligetur Grammaticè, nisi calceas ejus linguae, qua edita ea est, Grammaticam? b) Qui enim nosse cupit verbum Dei, ut ab auctore Deo sint promulgatum, citra omnem literarum, vocabulorum, phrasium & sententiarum detorsionem, inflexionem, immutationem, additionem, detractionemque purum putum, is illud non leget aut intelliget, nisi in eadem lingua, quâ à Deo primitus est promulgatum. Itaque c) Ebraea & Graeca lingua studium deserere non potest Theologus & Theologiae studiosus, quamdiu huic facultati in his terris operam aliquam navabit.
units.tr: a) Scripture cannot be understood theologically unless it is first understood grammatically, said the great Melanthon. But how will it be understood grammatically unless one knows the grammar of the language in which it was published? b) For whoever wishes to know the word of God, as it was promulgated by God its author, without any distortion, inflection, alteration, addition or subtraction of letters, words, phrases and sentences, pure and simple, will not read or understand it unless in the same language in which it was first promulgated by God. Therefore c) a theologian and a student of theology cannot abandon the study of the Hebrew and Greek language, as long as he labours at this science on this earth.

units.la: Æquissimum ergo est, d) ut non solum admoneantur, sed etiam vehementer S. Scripturae Candidati, ut sacrarum linguarum Ebraeae & Graecae cognitionem studiis suis, non dico quasi παρεργον adjiciant, sed instar fundamenti in ipsum fundum mentium suarum submittant.
units.tr: It is therefore most fair that candidates for Holy Scripture be not only admonished but strongly urged to add knowledge of the sacred languages, Hebrew and Greek, to their studies. I do not say as a sideline [παρεργον], but to sink it like a foundation into the very bottom of their minds.

units.la: Excusationes &, effugia nulla hic admittenda. Olim ea operariorum erat inopia & messis magnitudo, & Academiarum status, ut multos minus bene instructos admiserit necessitas. At nunc ea est linguarum discendarum commoditas & Ministrorum abundantia, ut alios quam idoneos admittere nulla necessitas urgeat. Multos etiam, postquam ad Ministerium admissi, annos aliquot in vocationis expectatione videas consumere. At dicunt aliqui, se mediis destitui, ac proinde sibi festinandum esse. Πρόφασις haec tantum est. An magnas opes requirit Grammaticæ, Dictionarii & libelli Ebraici comparatio? Quis adeò à Patronis derelictus est? Rursus, quis horum recusantium adeò religiosus dispensator temporis est, ut non alterum tantum otio, ludo, atque utinam non etiam aleâ, compotationibus & scortationibus, consumat? Quod enim ad Græca attinet, illud extra controversiæ aleam pono, eam in trivialibus comparandam Græcismi notitiam, ut Novum Testamentum Grammaticè possit interpretari, Linguæ Ebraeæ mediocriter discendæ bimestris, vel ad summum trimestris industria sufficerit. Tentet aliquis & juxta consilium meum de instituendo hoc studio, quod Coronidi meæ præmisi, studia sua componat, & videbit, me nihil præter verum dicere. Possem ego nominare adolescentes, qui suo exemplo hujus rei veritatem comprobârunt. Mirantur hoc multi & ne expertis quidem fidem habent, vel ipsum credo Picum Mirandulam mendacii postulaturi, qui Epistolâ ad Marsil. Ficinum pag. operum 367. ait, se unius mensis spacio ita didicisse literas Ebraicas, ut citra culpam epistolam dictare potuerit. Sed quid hæreo? Monstretur unum individuum, quod adeò religiosè tempus suum dispenset, ut sanctissima hæc studia, iis in locis ubi ea florent, sine culpa intermisisse dici possit. Certè talis rara avis erit in Scholis, nigroque simillima Cygno. Et si verum dicendum est, Reverendi P. & Fr. Eritne rei angustæ obtentus sufficiens excusatio, quominus aliquis ad Sanctum Ministerium accedat iis dotibus destitutus, quas & Scriptura & Canones Ecclesiastici exigunt? An Rex ad institutionem Filii admitteret inidoneum, eò quod res angusta obstiterit, quominus ea sibi comparare potuerit præsidia, quæ in Principis formatore requiruntur? Non putem. Cur ergò Deo & Ecclesiis se orbtrudere patiamur, qui donis necessariis instructi non sunt? Si hos ex commiseratione promoves, crudelitatem exerchowever quam illud Nazianzeni, artem artium & scientiam scientiarum esse animas pascere, ac proinde olim viros doctissimos & sanctissimos ad Episcopatus, nonnisi invitos, sublimatos fuisse. * Lucullum ea ingenii felicitate & magnitudine valuisse ferunt, ut Roma ad Mithridaticum bellum profectus rei militaris omnino rudis, in Asiam venerit perfectus Imperator. Aut eadem ingenii felicitate nostri illi intempestivi Candidati valere debent, aut docent postea, quod nesciunt & quod nunquam didicerunt, ne hoc quidem scientes, quod nesciant illa quae docere debebant. Sed ut dicam quod res est, mera haec effugia sunt. & inanes πεφάσεις. Solam & unicam causam in pigritia esse, vel id solum argumento est, quod ejusmodi fucos, ne tum quidem, cum jam ad Ministerium admissi, vocationes expectant & in Academiis otiosi vivunt, horum studiorum ulla cura tangat.
units.tr: No excuses and evasions are to be admitted here. In former times there was such a shortage of workers, such a great harvest, and such a state of the academies, that necessity admitted many who were less well instructed. But now there is such convenience for learning languages and such an abundance of ministers that no necessity urges us to admit anyone but the fit. You may also see many, after being admitted to the ministry, spending some years waiting for a call. But some say they are deprived of means, and so must hurry. This is mere pretext [προφάσεις]. Does acquiring a grammar, a dictionary and a little Hebrew book require great wealth? Who is so abandoned by patrons? Again, which of these objectors is so scrupulous a steward of time that he does not spend just as much on idleness, play (and I wish not also on dice), drinking parties and whoring? As for Greek, I put beyond all dispute that the knowledge of Greek needed to interpret the New Testament grammatically can be acquired in the trivial schools, and that for learning Hebrew moderately, two months of diligence, or at most three, will suffice. Let someone try, arranging his studies according to my advice on pursuing this subject, which I prefaced to my Coronis, and he will see that I say nothing but the truth. I could name young men who by their own example have proved the truth of this. Many marvel at it and do not even believe the experts; I think even Pico della Mirandola would have to be called to account for a lie, he who writes in his letter to Marsilio Ficino, on page 367 of his works, that in the space of a single month he learned the Hebrew letters so well that he could dictate a letter without fault. But why do I hesitate? Let one individual be shown who dispenses his time so scrupulously that he can be said to have interrupted these most holy studies, in places where they flourish, without fault. Certainly such a rare bird would be found in the schools, most like a black swan. And if the truth must be told, Reverend Fathers and Brethren: will the plea of straitened circumstances be a sufficient excuse for someone to come to the holy ministry lacking the gifts which both Scripture and the ecclesiastical canons require? Would a king admit an unfit person to the education of his son because straitened circumstances prevented him from acquiring the resources required in the formation of a prince? I think not. Why then should we allow ourselves to be thrust upon God and the Churches by men who are not equipped with the necessary gifts? If you promote these men out of pity, you are exercising cruelty rather than kindness, as Nazianzen's saying shows: that the art of arts and the science of sciences is to feed souls, and that for this reason in former times the most learned and holy men were raised to bishoprics only against their will. They say Lucullus was so strong in felicity and greatness of talent that when he set out from Rome for the Mithridatic war, utterly unversed in military affairs, he came to Asia a finished general. Either our untimely candidates must have the same felicity of talent, or they teach afterwards what they do not know and never learned, not even knowing this very thing, that they do not know what they ought to teach. But to say how things really are: these are mere evasions and empty pretexts, [προφάσεις]. That the sole and only cause is laziness is shown by the fact that such drones, not even when they have already been admitted to the ministry and are waiting for calls, and live idly in the academies, are touched by any care for these studies.

units.la: Sed nec alii desunt, qui, ut ingeniosa hic est inertia, doctorum dissensiones obtendunt. Junius, inquiunt, aliter vertit haec & illa, quàm Lutherus. Piscator rursus à Junio, Beza ab Erasmo, A Beza rursus Piscator, Scultetus & alii dissident. Quorsum ergo linguarum studia? Resp. 1. An ergo doctissimorum istorum Virorum diligentia patrocinium inertiae praestabit?
units.tr: But there are also others who, just as this idleness is ingenious, put forward the disagreements of the learned. Junius, they say, translates this and that differently from Luther.
