Piscator again differs from Junius, Beza from Erasmus, Beza again from Piscator, and Scultetus and others disagree. What then is the point of studying languages? Reply 1: Will the diligence of those most learned men furnish a defence for idleness?

units.la: 2. An omnis ejusmodi dissensus & versionum varietas Ecclesiae noxia est? Longè aliter hac de re antiquitas judicavit. Namque praeter Augustinum, Hiero. Theodoretum, aliosque Patres etiam Origenes credidit, non aliud esse magis idoneum genuinae loci alicujus sententiae eruendae medium, quam diversarum Versionum inter se & cum fontibus collatio. Hoc fine Hexapla & Octapla sua Origenes publicavit. 3. Dicant mihi boni illi viri, cur ergo Grammaticam Latinam, cur Logicam didicerint, cur locis communibus & controversiis operam navarint? An in illis & praecipuè controversiis Theologicis nullae controversiae? An in illis nullae, inter ejusdem etiam confessionis & cathedrae Doctores opiniones dissidentes? 4. Agnosco libens, etiam Ebraicè & Graecè doctis magnas adhuc multis in locis esse tenebras. At quid hoc ignavis patrocinatur? Vel hoc solum calcar esse debebat ad diligentiam. Si enim in multa adhuc caligine versantur & per nebulam vident linguarum periti, quantis in tenebris & quam densa in nocte earum rudes versari putandum est?
units.tr: 2. Is every such disagreement and variety of versions harmful to the Church? Antiquity judged quite otherwise on this matter. For besides Augustine, Jerome, Theodoret and other Fathers, Origen too believed that there is no more suitable means of drawing out the genuine sense of any passage than comparing different versions with one another and with the sources. It was for this purpose that Origen published his Hexapla and Octapla. 3. Let those good men tell me why they learned Latin grammar, why they learned logic, why they took pains over commonplaces and controversies. Are there no controversies in those fields, and especially in theological controversies? Are there no differing opinions among teachers of the same confession and the same chair? 4. I gladly acknowledge that even for those learned in Hebrew and Greek there is still great darkness in many places. But what does this lend to the lazy? This very thing ought to be a spur to diligence. For if those skilled in languages still live in much obscurity and see through a mist, in how great darkness and in how thick a night must the unskilled be thought to dwell?

units.la: Sed porrò instant, versionibus & commentariis satis instructi sumus, & quae insignis eorum modestia est, nos doctissimorum virorum Junii, Bezæ, &c. versiones non corrigemus, inquiunt. Cur ergò linguas discemus? Quasi dicerent, nos possumus ab aliis duci, cui bono ergò oculi linguarum? Egregiè, inquit Martinius, Erue itaque tibi & oculos corporis. Quidni & iis carere potes Nec enim deerit qui ducat te.
units.tr: But they press further: we are sufficiently equipped with versions and commentaries, and, with remarkable modesty, they say, we will not correct the versions of the most learned men, Junius, Beza, etc. Why then should we learn languages? It is as if they said: we can be led by others, so what good are the eyes of the languages? "Splendidly," says Martinius, "then pluck out your bodily eyes too. Why not, since you can do without them? For there will be no lack of someone to lead you."

units.la: Sed serìò agendum mihi video in ludicrâ objectione. Resp. itaque 1. Piorum & Doctorum Theologorum Versionibus & Commentariis apud pios & bonos debitum manere æstimium. Et quod ad me attinet, Deo O. M. quotidie ago gratias quam maximas, quod ejusmodi organa superiori ævo excitarit & ornârit, quorum laboribus mihi quoque cum magno meo fructu utifrui datum est. Repeto tamen quod supra dixi, eruditum Commentarium legi non posse, nedum intelligi, sine Græcismi & Ebraismi mediocri notitia. Annon in Hieron. Calv. Bezæ, Drusii, Sculteti, Merceri, Paræi, Pisc. &c. commentariis ad singulas Ebræas voces dicendum tibi erit, Ebræum est, non legitur? 2. Versionem nullam eâ, quà à Ministro fieri par est, accuratione & fructu sine earundem notitia legi posse supra Num. 4. demonstratum est. Quæ omnia si quis præsractè negaverit, næ is ostendet, se ea, qua par est, attentione & diligentiâ sacras literas nunquam fuisse scrutatum cum tamen Apostoli mandatum sit, Intentus esto lectioni, hæc meditare, in his esto. Resp.3. Alios dari notitiæ linguarum fines, quam ut novæ versiones dentur, vel receptæ corrigantur. Nunquid præclari satis fines isti, aut utilitates satis magnæ videntur illæ, quas supra produximus? An nullum ergò operæ pretium erit versiones cum fontibus contulisse, atque in ipsis fontibus sese oblectare? An nihil ergò facit ad certitudinem fidei, Deum ipsum sine Interprete suis aurib. audire loquentem? Audite Melanth. communem Præceptorem, * Scia inquit modestissima anima, me vix primis labris degustasse Ebr. Gr. & Latinas literas. Sed tamen hoc ipsum quod didici quantulumcunque est, propter judicium de religione, omnibus mundi regnis, omniumque opibus longe antepono. Quod eò dico, inquit, ut cum mihi & aliis, qui parum didicimus, videatis ad veritatis agnitionem, hanc exiguam doctrinam plurimum prodesse, & ipsi speretis magnum vos opera pretium facturos si linguas mediocriter didiceritis. * Si fundus aut alia quævis hereditas tibi peregrinanti paterno testamento obtigisset, annon tabulas originales domum redux posceres? atque ex ipsis potius tuis ipsius oculis cognoscere, quam ex aliorum relatione accipere malles, quid & quantum tibi relictum esset? Qua ergo supinitas erit, originale aterni patris de caelesti & aeternum permansura hereditate testamentum despicere? At enim inquis, non est necesse. Verum est, nihil est necesse te ipsum oculos habere, & videre, quae sint opus. Potes enim & alienis oculis credere: potes, si quo eundum sit, manu a puero tuo duci. Erue igitur tibi oculos, quia carere iis potes. Etenim in sacris libris lumen & oculus, quo divina perspicimus, est Ebraea lingua, cujus scientia & fructu cum te tua sponte privers, tum tibi oculos eruis, quibus illa cernuntur & cognoscuntur. Et nota, quod ait, in sacris libris. Nam & N.T. libri hoc sole illustrantur. * Illi enim ita sunt Graeci, utverba quidem singula Graeca sint, conjunctio autem & phrasis, ut ab Ebraeis hominibus, Ebraea plurimum agnoscatur. Hinc N. Testamenti Idioma EbraeoGraecum vocitare solco. * Licet enim phrasis N.T. originaliter Graeca dici possit, non tamen pure fluit, sed liquore Ebraei & Syri sermonis permista est. Quare licet lector N.T. in Graecis literis sit dexterrime institutus, linguarum tamen Ebraea & Syra ignarus, in Graeca illius lectione infelicissime versabitur. Quibus suffragantur Illyricus, clavis parte 2. pag.664. Calvin. Beza, Pisc. Sculr. Druf. Fullerus, Scalig. Buxtorf. Paraeus, & alii tam Pontificii, quam Euangelici DD. passim. Quin & causas ejus rei reddit Beza, ad Act. x. in digressione de dono linguarum. [Et tamen adhuc ejusmodi praefractos homines reperias, qui, ut juventutem a sanctissimae linguae, tanquam rei nihili & circa quam generosa & subtilia, si Dis placet, ingenia versari indignum sit, studio abstrahant, Ebraeismos novo Testamento abjudicant. Quos ego homines vel ad linguae Ebraeae rudimenta, vel ad magni Heinsii Aristarchum sacrum, vel si ne hujus quidem liquidae demonstrationes eorum pertinaciam valebunt edomare, Anticyras relegandos censeo. Sed missis istis, praeteritisque illis quae ex superioribus inferri possent, ] contentus ero ad fontium dignitatem astruendam adjicere insigne Ellogium * Hispani Theologi, Qui Hebraea, inquit, pie & religiose tractant, multo in illis ampliora de Christo testimonia, quam in Graecis Latinisque offendent. Nec non illud * Jesuitae non infimi subsellii, In Ebraica scriptura tot esse sacramenta, quot litera; tot mysteria, quot puncta: tot arcana, quot apices. Necomittendum illud B. Lutheri, * Ebraeos Prophetas velle cogere, ut Germanice (addo ego quavis alia lingua) loquantur, perinde esset
units.tr: But I see that I must treat this playful objection seriously. Reply 1: The versions and commentaries of pious and learned theologians ought to remain in due esteem among the pious and good. As far as I am concerned, I daily give the most hearty thanks to God Most Good and Great that he raised up and adorned such instruments in the previous age, and that it has been granted to me to make use of their labours to my great profit. Yet I repeat what I said above: a learned commentary cannot be read, much less understood, without at least a moderate knowledge of Greek and Hebrew idioms. Will you not have to say of individual Hebrew words in the commentaries of Jerome, Calvin, Beza, Drusius, Scultetus, Mercer, Pareus, Piscator, etc.: "It is Hebrew, it is not to be read"? 2. That no version can be read with the accuracy and profit that a minister ought to have, without knowledge of the languages, has been shown above at No. 4. If anyone flatly denies all this, he will show that he has never scrutinised the sacred letters with the attention and diligence that are due, although the Apostle's command is: "Be diligent in reading, meditate on these things, be in these." Reply 3: The aims of knowledge of languages are other than merely producing new versions or correcting received ones. Do those aims seem sufficiently excellent, or the benefits we have set out above sufficiently great? Is there then no profit at all in comparing versions with the sources, and in delighting in the sources themselves? Does it then contribute nothing to certainty of faith to hear God himself speaking with our own ears, without an interpreter? Hear Melanchthon, our common teacher: "Know, most modest soul, that I have scarcely tasted the Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters even at the lips. Yet this very little that I have learned, however small it is, I prefer far above all the kingdoms of the world and all their riches, on account of judgement concerning religion. I say this," he says, "so that you may see that this small learning greatly benefits me and others who have learned little, for the knowledge of the truth, and that you yourselves may hope you will do a great service if you have learned languages moderately well." *If an estate or some other inheritance had fallen to you by your father's will while you were travelling abroad, would you not on returning home demand the original documents, and would you not rather know from your own eyes than accept from others' report what, and how much, had been left to you? What then would be the sloth of despising the original testament of the eternal Father concerning the heavenly and eternally lasting inheritance? But you will say: it is not necessary. True, it is not necessary for you to have eyes of your own and see what is needed. You may trust the eyes of others; you may, if you must go somewhere, be led by the hand by your boy. Pluck out your eyes, then, since you can do without them. For in the sacred books the light and the eye by which we perceive divine things is the Hebrew language; when you deprive yourself of its knowledge and profit, you pluck out for yourself the eyes by which those things are discerned and known. And note that he says "in the sacred books". For the books of the New Testament too are illuminated by this same sun. * For they are so Greek that, although the individual words are Greek, the connection and phrasing are recognised as very largely Hebrew, as written by Hebrew men. Hence I am accustomed to call the New Testament idiom Hebrew-Greek. * For although the phrasing of the New Testament can be called originally Greek, it does not flow purely, but is mingled with the liquor of the Hebrew and Syriac speech. Therefore, although a reader of the New Testament may be most skilfully trained in Greek letters, if he is ignorant of Hebrew and Syriac he will be most unhappily engaged in reading it in Greek. To this agree Illyricus (Clavis, part 2, p. 664), Calvin, Beza, Piscator, Scultetus, Drusius, Fuller, Scaliger, Buxtorf, Pareus, and other doctors, both Papist and Evangelical, everywhere. Indeed Beza gives the causes of this matter at Acts 10, in his digression on the gift of tongues. [And yet you may still find such obstinate men who, to draw young people away from study of the most holy language, as if it were a thing of no account and unworthy of generous and subtle minds, if God please, deny the Hebraisms of the New Testament. These men I think should be relegated, if not to the rudiments of the Hebrew language, or to the sacred Aristarchus of the great Heinsius, then, if even his clear demonstrations cannot tame their obstinacy, to Anticyra.] But setting these things aside, and passing over those which could be inferred from what has gone before, I shall be content, to establish the dignity of the sources, to add the notable eulogy of a Spanish theologian, who says: "Those who handle the Hebrew devoutly and religiously will find in it much fuller testimonies about Christ than in the Greek and Latin." Nor should we omit the saying of a Jesuit of no low rank: "In Hebrew Scripture there are as many sacraments as letters, as many mysteries as points, as many secrets as strokes." Nor must we omit that of blessed Luther: "To force the Hebrew prophets to speak German (I add, or any other language) would be"

units.la: Ibidem. ac si Philomelam quis cogeret, dulcissimâ suâ melodiâ relictâ, utrisonam cuculi vocem imitari.
units.tr: Ibid. just as if someone should force the nightingale, having abandoned her sweetest melody, to imitate the harsh voice of the cuckoo.

units.la: Et ut ad versiones revertar, quæso te, annon & iste præclarus satis finis, ut possis Versionem B. Lutheri, Bezæ, Junii, &c. contra adversarium defendere? An verò eò impudentiæ delaberis, ut versionibus istis tanquam authenticis, adhærescendum tibi putes? [ut, sicuti Sutor & Latomus clamabant, nobis satis est versio Hieronymi, ita & tu clames, nobis satis est versio Lutheri, Junii, &c.? ] At Socinianus & Jesuita tibi non dabunt tam magnum αἴνιγμα, nec difficile ipsis erit te ex hoc imperitiæ azylo extrahere.
units.tr: And to return to the versions: I ask you, is this not also a sufficiently excellent aim, that you could defend the version of Luther, Beza, Junius, etc. against an adversary? Or will you sink so far into impudence that you think you must cling to those versions as authentic? [So that, just as Sutor and Latomus cried, "the translation of Jerome is enough for us," so you too should cry, "the translation of Luther, Junius, etc. is enough for us"?] But the Socinian and the Jesuit will not give you so great a riddle [αἴνιγμα], nor will it be difficult for them to drag you out of this refuge of ignorance.

units.la: Resp. 4. Si hæc perversa modestia primorum reformatorum animos incessisset, ne nunc quidem ex tenebris Papatus fuissemus electuati. Lutherus Germanicam Versionem, quæ ex vulgatâ traducta erat, correxit, Lutheranam alii aliquot in locis polivêre. Eandem Vulgatam in V. Test. Junius, in Novo Erasmus correxêre. Junianam & Erasmicam Beza, Piscator, Scultetus, Fullerus, Drusius, Graserus, Rainoldus & alii magis magisque perfecêre. An putabimus priores à posterioribus contumelia affectos? aut hac ratione damnum SS. Literis & religioni illatum? Et quæ Logica hanc consequentiam probabit, Hic aliquid correxit in istius versione, ergo doctior fuit illo, aut saltem videri voluit? Nihil simul inventum & perfectum fuit. Qui prior aliquid præclari invenit & glaciem frangit, plus laudis meretur, quam qui inventis aliquid addit. Illud non nisi magnis ingeniis datum est: hoc etiam mediocribus concessum est. Præclare sanè Lutherus, Junius, Tremellius, Erasmus, Beza, de sacris literis meriti sunt, non eo tamen posterorum diligentiæ omnia præripuerunt. Deus liberè & variè sua dona dispensat. Dies diem docet. Multa olim obscurissima, eorum industria illuminavit. Longè plura in quibus ipsis fuerunt tenebræ posterorum diligentia partim illustravit, partim porrò illustratura est. Et ut hoc non esset, quid miramur bonum Homerum aliquando dormitare, præsertim in laboriosò versionis opere? Nimis augusta res est, nuspiam errare. Atque hæc non eo fine dicuntur, ut beatis illis viris vel tantillum detraham, sed ut ostendam verissimè dixisse Rev. D. * Scultetum, nec unius, nec plurium, quam libet doctissimorum virorum, versionem Ecclesiæ pro authentica obtrudendam. Habent bent enim omnes, ut suas virtutes, ita & vitia. Liceat mihi ergo de illis usurpare, quod de B. Hieronymo, Hieronymus ab Olez-stro Inquisitor, * Hieronymo, inquit, non plus tribuendum in sua Edit. si tamen illius est, quam sibi velit ipse tribui. Ipse vero, utpote vir Sanctus, se aliquando hallucinatum ingenuè fatetur, suamque versionem in multis emendasse. Qua non in eum finem produximus, inquit, ut virum sanctum traducamus, sed ut doceamus, eum non Prophetam, sed hominem fuisse. Et cur adolescentes nostri non ipsis magnis illis viris Junio & Trimellio aurem substringunt? Illi enim non placere sibi eos profitentur, qui rivis humana opera ductis ita acquiescunt, ut vix uno aut altero anno fontes ipsos investigent. Et cur quaeso? Quum enim praclare, inquiunt, secun agi existiment, si de rivulo humanitus ducto sorbeant, ubi fons pra foribus est, nihil mirum, si miseri justo Dei judicio tandem eo adducantur, ut palustri ulva implicentur & sordibus inquinentur: quas etsi suo ipsi torpore contrahunt, tamen ut ab aliis arreptas mordicus deinceps retinendas putant. At quanto melius veteres ex doctrina Johannis ad libros S. Scriptura fidem adhibendam, ad sua scripta judicium afferri postulárunt, &c.
units.tr: Reply 4. If this perverse modesty had taken hold of the minds of the first reformers, we would not even now have been led out of the darkness of Papacy. Luther corrected the German version, which had been translated from the Vulgate, and others have polished Luther's version in several places. Junius corrected the same Vulgate in the Old Testament, and Erasmus in the New. Beza, Piscator, Scultetus, Fuller, Drusius, Graser, Rainolds and others have brought the Junian and Erasmian versions ever closer to perfection. Shall we think that the earlier men were wronged by the later ones, or that the Scriptures and religion were harmed in this way? What logic would accept this inference: He corrected something in that man's version, therefore he was more learned than him, or at least wanted to appear so? Nothing has been found and perfected all at once. Whoever first discovers something excellent and breaks the ice deserves more praise than whoever adds something to what has been discovered. The former has been granted only to great minds; the latter is granted even to ordinary ones. Certainly Luther, Junius, Tremellius, Erasmus and Beza have deserved well of the sacred letters, yet they did not snatch away everything from the diligence of posterity. God distributes his gifts freely and variously. Day teaches day. Many things once very obscure have been illuminated by their industry, and far more things in which they were in darkness have been partly illuminated, and will be further illuminated, by the diligence of those who come after. And even if this were not so, why do we wonder that the good Homer sometimes nods, especially in the laborious work of translation? The matter is too weighty to err anywhere. I say this not to detract the least bit from those blessed men, but to show that Reverend Dr. Scultetus spoke very truly when he said that the version of no one, nor of several, however learned, should be forced upon the Church as authentic. They all have their vices as well as their virtues. So I may borrow about them what Inquisitor Hieronymus ab Oleastro said of St. Jerome: Jerome, he says, is not to be credited in his edition, if indeed it is his, more than he himself would wish to be credited. Jerome himself, being a holy man, frankly confesses that he sometimes erred and corrected his version in many places: We have not brought these things forward, he says, to make a holy man out of him, but to teach that he was a man and not a prophet. And why do our young men not lend an ear to those great men Junius and Tremellius? For they profess that they are not pleased with those who are so content with streams drawn from human effort that in a year or two they scarcely seek out the springs themselves. And why, I ask? For since they think it a fine thing to drink from a stream drawn by human hands when the spring is at the door, it is no wonder if the wretched are at last brought, by the just judgement of God, to be entangled in marsh reeds and defiled with filth; which, though they gather them by their own sluggishness, they then think should be held fast with teeth as if seized from others. But how much better did the ancients, following the teaching of John, demand that faith be given to the books of Holy Scripture and that judgement be brought to their own writings, etc.

units.la: Resp. 5. B. Lutherum, Junium, Bezam, Pisc. &c. suas versiones saepe sub incudem revocasse, multosque errores emendasse, prout vel ipsi, ut dies diem docet, suos errores animadverterunt: vel ab aliis, ut oculi plus vident quam oculus, fuere admoniti. Et credemus, illorum versionem ultima recognitione ad eum perfectionis gradum pertigisse, ut omnibus posterioribus otia fecerint? Addo, Lutheri & Junii versiones saepe διʼ διὰ πάσων, dissentire. Vbi ergo illi sunt, qui Lutheri in N. Test. pro authenticis habent, atque in iis securi acquiescunt, nunquam in causas varietatis inquirentes. Dubitas? Confer eas Psal. 68. 20. Jerem. 23. 23. Jezech. 5. 7. Hos. 6. 4. Jon. 2. 5. Mal. 2. 16. Quid ad haec dicent duricervices isti adolescentes? An duo textus adeo diversi, authentici simul erunt? Non opinor. Verum tamen sequeris? Certe nisi aliquid in linguis didiceris, talpa hic eris coecior, evenietque tibi illud, quod Hieron. de linguarum imperitis asserit, * ut, dum putabis te optimam sequi sententiam, pessimam eligas, & uniuscujusque interpretis errorem se-quaris.
units.tr: Reply 5. That Luther, Junius, Beza, Piscator and others often called their versions back to the anvil, and corrected many errors, as they themselves noticed their errors day by day, or were warned by others, since the eyes see more than the eye. And will we believe that by their final revision their version reached such a degree of perfection that they left nothing for any later workers? I add that the versions of Luther and Junius often differ widely [διὰ πάσων]. Where, then, are those who hold Luther's New Testament to be authentic and rest securely in it, never inquiring into the causes of the variation? Do you doubt it? Compare them at Psalm 68:20, Jeremiah 23:23, Ezekiel 5:7, Hosea 6:4, Jonah 2:5, Malachi 2:16. What will these stubborn young men say to this? Can two texts so different both be authentic at the same time? I do not think so. Yet will you still follow one of them? Surely unless you learn something of the languages, you will be blinder here than a mole, and it will happen to you what Jerome says of those ignorant of languages: that while you think you are following the best opinion, you choose the worst, and follow the error of each interpreter.

units.la: Et ut ad commentarios redeat Oratio, in tanta saepe Commentatorum varietate quàm misere haerebis, quam perpe-tuò tuò fluctuabis, si nihil judicii ipse ad eorum lectionem attuleris? Cur enim hunc magis quam illum sequeris, veré dictum à Poëtâ, quisquis fuit,
units.tr: And to return to the commentaries, amid such frequent variety among the commentators, how wretchedly you will hesitate, how constantly you will waver, if you bring no judgement of your own to reading them! For why will you follow this one rather than that one? It is the line rightly spoken by a poet, whoever he was:

units.la: redit actus in orbem
units.tr: the action comes round again in a circle

units.la: Ludus in hac mundi scenâ pene unus & idem.
units.tr: the play on this stage of the world is nearly one and the same.

units.la: Superiori sæculo Latomus, Sutor & id genus belluæ, cum quibus Erasmo pugnandum fuit, ad suos quoque commentarios provocabant. Hanc viam compendiosam: alteram, dispendiosam vocabant. Erasm. in Apolog. p. 625. Sed quam compendiaria ea via fuerit, duobus exemplis ad oculum demonstravit Erasmus p. 635. quorum alterum ex Ps. 45 alterum ex Thren. 3. desumsit, & nos illa, suo quoque loco, exhibemus. Ego verò in Lutherum, Calvinum, Bucerum & id genus interpretes injurius esset, si accuratissimos eorum commentarios, cum ineptis barbarorum istorum commentis conferrem. Manet tamen illud quod dixi, Fluctuabis semper, ubi illi dissentiunt. Et hic locum illud habet quod vulgò dicitur, compendia sæpe dispendia. Neque enim faber, qui parandis instrumentis horas aliquod impendit, serius absolvet opus, quàm qui, non satis apparatis illis, mox ad opus accingitur. Ego ita semper credidi, Linguæ Originalis notitiam multorum Commentariorum instar esse. [ Ac proinde hanc viam maximè esse compendiariam.] Hoc omnes pie docti agnoscunt. Tempore persecutionis verbi divini Minister Commentatorum suorum & Homiliastarum Bibliothecam ad manum habere non potest. O miserum ergò ejusmodi Concionatorem, si exsolis Bibliis suarum Concionum stamen & tramam conficere non possit! Atque hic iterum protestor, me doctissimorum virorum ut versiones, ita & Commentarios non contemnere, dum Scripturæ originalis studio primas defero. Advocatum do magnum illum Rostochiensium Theologum * Scio, inquit, plurimorum ex nostris laboribus in controversiis enodandis exantlatos, illudque studium sa-crum merito suspicio: scio item extare erudita multorum in libros Biblicos scripta commentaria, quae uti debeo, veneror, sed in iis TANTUM vel PRÆCIPUE occupari juventutem, neglectis Bibliis, id demum est quod sæpe multumque conqueror. Desunctum me putabam: Ecce restant aliæ, quæ adversus linguarum studia adhibentur, machinæ. Si Originalis linguæ notitia tantam facem sacris literis allucet, cur ergò tantæ apud Judæos tenebræ? Cur illi ergò tam ininfelices SS. literarum interpretes ? Hujus machinae impetum jam olim ) Melanthon & b) Flacius retuderunt. Ecce enim, dum cognitionem linguae Ebraeae Theologi Evangelici urgent, non urgent solùm eam, quae in verborum flexionibus, aut nominum cum affixis compositione, &c. consistit. Vlterius progrediendum est, vid. ut vocum propriae significationes ex diligenti locorum collatione investigentur, ut probè intelligatur dictio & phrasis, qua usi sunt sacri Scriptores. c) Judaei vero magnam partem, tantùm abest, ut phrasin & modum dicendi perspiciant, ut & primam Grammatica partem fere ignorent. Eruditiores vero, quorum magna apud eos raritas est. Canonem Biblicum Grammaticè quidem, attamen ita explicarunt, d) ut omninò contemni non debeat illorum labor. Quod autem in doctrina de Messia & quae inde dependent, adeò praevaricantur, e) non tam peccant infidelitate, quam voluntatis perversitate, ut olim Cajaphas & similes. Sed sit sanè infscitia. Ea ex hac potissimum causa oritur. Vt in arcâ fœderis, Cherubim se mutuo contuebantur, alasque jungebant, ita V. & N. Test. monumenta congruunt. Vetus est fons novi: Novum est lumen Veteris, & collatio utriusque ad utrumque intelligendum necessaria est. Cum autem aspernentur Judaei Christi & Apostolorum interpretationem, & sua somnia de Mundi imperio nolint abjicere, retinent corruptelas ab impostoribus excogitatas. Atque itaque occalluerunt mentes eorum, inquit f) Apostolus. Cujus verba consequa huc quoque pertinent. Nam usque ad diem hodiernum, inquit, in lectione Veteris Testamenti manet non retectum velamen illud, quod cordi eorum impositum est: ubi verò converterint se ad Dominum, tunc tolletur velamen illud.
units.tr: In the last century Latomus, Sutor and that kind of beast, with whom Erasmus had to fight, also appealed to their own commentaries. They called this the short way and the other the costly way. Erasmus, in his Apology, p. 625. But how short that way was, Erasmus demonstrated to the eye with two examples, p. 635, one taken from Psalm 45 and the other from Lamentations 3, and we shall set them out in their own place too. As for me, it would be unjust to Luther, Calvin, Bucer and that kind of interpreter if I compared their most careful commentaries with the silly inventions of those barbarians. Still, what I have said holds: you will always waver where they disagree. And here the common saying applies: shortcuts are often losses. For a craftsman who spends some hours preparing his tools will finish his work no later than one who, without having prepared them enough, sets straight to work. I have always believed this: a knowledge of the original language is equal to many commentaries. [ And therefore this way is by far the shorter.] All the piously learned acknowledge this. In a time of persecution of the divine Word, a minister cannot have a library of his commentators and homilists at hand. O wretched is such a preacher, if he cannot weave the warp and woof of his sermons from the Bible alone! And here again I protest that I do not despise the versions and commentaries of very learned men, while I give first place to the study of the original Scripture. I call as my great advocate that great Rostock theologian: I know, he says, that much has been undertaken by our men in unravelling controversies, and I rightly esteem that sacred zeal; I know too that learned commentaries on the biblical books of many men exist, which I ought to use and revere; but that youth should be occupied ONLY or CHIEFLY with these, while the Bibles are neglected, is the very thing I often and loudly complain of. I had thought the matter settled. Behold, there remain other engines brought up against the study of languages. If knowledge of the original language sheds so great a torch upon the sacred letters, why then such great darkness among the Jews? Why then are they such unhappy interpreters of the Holy Scriptures? The assault of this engine was long ago repulsed by a) Melanchthon and b) Flacius. For while evangelical theologians press the knowledge of the Hebrew tongue, they do not press only that which consists in the inflection of words, or in the composition of nouns with affixes, etc. One must go further, namely that the proper meanings of words are investigated from a careful comparison of passages, so that the diction and phrasing used by the sacred writers is rightly understood. c) The Jews, however, for the most part are so far from perceiving the phrasing and manner of speaking that they are almost ignorant even of the first part of grammar. The more learned among them, of whom there is great rarity, have explained the biblical canon grammatically indeed, yet in such a way that d) their labour ought by no means to be despised. But as to the doctrine of the Messiah and what depends upon it, they go so far astray that e) they sin not so much through unbelief as through perversity of will, like Caiaphas long ago and men like him. But let it certainly be ignorance. It arises chiefly from this cause. As in the ark of the covenant the cherubim looked at each other and joined their wings, so the monuments of the Old and New Testaments agree. The Old is the source of the New; the New is the light of the Old, and the comparison of each is necessary for understanding each. But since the Jews despise the interpretation of Christ and the Apostles, and are unwilling to cast off their dreams about the empire of the world, they keep the corruptions devised by impostors. And so their minds have been dulled, says the f) Apostle, whose words that follow pertain here as well: For to this day, he says, in the reading of the Old Testament that veil which lies upon their heart remains unlifted; but when they turn to the Lord, that veil will be taken away.

units.la: Illud etiam à nonnullis afferri memini, Florem ætatis inquiunt, in sola lingua Latina discenda detrivimus, sat vocum studio datum est. Rebus danda tandem est opera. Vita brevis, ars longa. Via longa & viatici parum. His jam supra abunde satisfactum arbitror. Quod verò de lingua Latina afferunt, non de nihilo est. Absit ut ejus studium atro Lapillo notem. Noctua essem, si non ferrem ILLUM Solem. Illud tamen dolor jubet dicere, pudendum esse eam ex solis profanis authoribus disci, tot annos ei impendi, Linguarum sacrarum fundamenta in Trivialibus non unà tradi, Linguae Latinae denique eum tribui honorem, ut ejus sola qualiscunque cognitio Ministrum doctum à Laïco seu Idiota discernere censeatur. g) Scire, inquit Aristoteles, est τὸ ὡφώτε χρῆσθαι scire, prima elementa & principia percipere. Iam vero prima Theologia Elementa non Latina reperies, sed Ebraica partim, partim Græca. Ne minima quidem Scripturæ particula Originaliter Latinè scripta est. Cur ergò Theologis futuris sola Latina adeò anxiè inculcatur? Quicquid responderint, illud tandem etiam inviti prodent, pluris apud se esse scripta hominum, quam authenticum Dei O. M. instrumentum. Et quod ad scholasticam institutionem attinet, quia eòrursus delapsus est sermo, non possum quin hùc transcribam seriam Caroli Sigonii,hominis nec Theologi, nec Euangelici, querelam, quam ut omnes Euangelici, quorum in ordinandis Trivialibus Scholis aliquæ partes sunt, ad animum revocent, propter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, ad cujus gloriam omnia referri æquum est, supplex rogo & obsecro. Vehementer erramus, inquit, ab iis ferme lustrandis monumentis exordientes, qua falsorum deorum traditiones, & commentitias fictorum heroum actiones a Græcis, acutissimis hominibus, sed veritatis plane ignaris proditas complectuntur: quibus neque ad aliquem prudentiæ usum, neque ad ullum pietatis fructum excolimur: cum si quid in nobis sensus, ne dicam sanitatis inesset, ab iis potius, quæ sacris continentur Ebraorum literis, initium ducere deberemus. Nam si prima rerum principia quærimus, non altius repetere, quàm ab ipso mundi hominumque, quod ibi tractatur, opificio possumus: si vera, nihil tam verum existit, quàm quod Dei ipsius viventis ore prolatum est: si gravia, quid magnificentius iis inveniri monumentis potest, in quibus sancta Dei mandata, salutaria promissa, certa oracula, cateraque his adnexa salutis nostra adminicula concluduntur? Porrò autem unde aut virtutum exempla præstantiora ad persequendum, aut vitiorum detestationes acriores ad declinandum, aut actiones insigniores ad memorandum, quàm ab ipsis Ebraorum peti commentariis possunt? in quibus solis aperte docetur, quantum humanum genus aut religione colendâ summo præsentis Dei auxilio sublevetur, aut eâ negligenda, acri ejusdem iracundiâ contera:ur.
units.tr: I remember that some people also raise this objection: "We have spent the flower of our age on learning the Latin language alone; enough effort has been given to words. Things must at last be given our attention. Life is short, art is long. The road is long and the provisions few." I think I have already answered this above fully enough. As for what they say about the Latin language, it is not without reason. Far be it from me to mark its study with a black pebble. I would be an owl if I could not bear that sun. Yet grief compels me to say this: it is shameful that the Latin language should be learned only from profane authors, that so many years should be spent on it, that the foundations of the sacred languages should not be taught alongside it in the schools, and that such honour should be given to Latin that a merely superficial knowledge of it is thought to distinguish a learned minister from a layman or an idiot. Knowing, says Aristotle, is [τὸ ὠφελίμως χρῆσθαι] to make profitable use of it, that is, to grasp the first elements and principles. Yet you will find that the first elements of theology are not in Latin but partly in Hebrew and partly in Greek. Not the smallest particle of Scripture was originally written in Latin. Why, then, is Latin alone so anxiously pressed upon future theologians? Whatever answer they give, they will at last reveal even against their will that they set the writings of men above the authentic instrument of God Almighty. As for scholastic instruction, since the discussion has again slipped that way, I cannot refrain from transcribing here the earnest complaint of Carlo Sigonio, a man who was neither a theologian nor an evangelical. I beg and beseech all evangelicals, who have some part in ordering the grammar schools, to take it to heart, for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whose glory all things rightly refer. We go badly wrong, he says, when we begin our reading with those monuments which contain the traditions of false gods and the invented deeds of fabled heroes, handed down by the Greeks, the sharpest of men but utterly ignorant of truth. By these we are not trained for any use of prudence or any fruit of piety, when we ought, if there were any sense or, let me say, sanity in us, to start rather from those writings of the Hebrews contained in the sacred literature. For if we seek the first principles of things, we can trace them back no further than to the very making of the world and of men, which is treated there. If we seek what is true, nothing is so true as what was uttered by the very mouth of the living God. If we seek what is weighty, what more magnificent can be found than those monuments in which the holy commands of God, the saving promises, the certain oracles, and the other aids to our salvation attached to these are contained? Moreover, where can more outstanding examples of virtue to follow, or sharper condemnations of vice to avoid, or more notable deeds to remember be sought than in the very commentaries of the Hebrews? In these alone it is plainly taught how much the human race is raised up, by the highest help of the present God, through the worship of religion, or how it is crushed by his fierce anger if that religion is neglected.

units.la: [ Huic admonitioni si aures nostras substringeremus, minus virium haberet ea objectio, quà literas Græcas & Latinas spectat. Sed adversus Ebræam & Græcam sacram, quam Hellenisticam vocant Scaliger, Drusius, & Heinsius, ficulneum plane telum est. An Medicus Galenum vel Hippocratem Græcè legens, aut Philosophus Platonem vel Aristotelem in primigeniâ scriscriptura evoluens, nihil præter sermonem discet? Eodem modo, qui Prophetas Ebraicè, Apostolos & Euangelistas Græce legit, nunquid simul cum sermone discet res sacris literis comprehensas?
units.tr: If we were to close our ears to this warning, the objection concerning Greek and Latin letters would have less force. But against the Hebrew and Greek sacred writings, which Scaliger, Drusius and Heinsius call Hellenistic, it is a plainly fig-wood weapon, a feeble one. Does a physician reading Galen or Hippocrates in Greek, or a philosopher unrolling Plato or Aristotle in the original, learn nothing but the language? In the same way, does one who reads the Prophets in Hebrew and the Apostles and Evangelists in Greek learn nothing together with the language about the things contained in the sacred letters?

units.la: Sed tempus tandem erit, opinor, ut vela contraham. Fiet autem illud, ubi duo ex B. Lutheri operibus loca produxero, quæ apud omnes bonos multum ponderis habitura mihi persuadeo. Prior extat Admonit. ejus ad Magistratus civitatum Germaniæ, tomo 7. Latino Witeb. sol. 441. pag. 2. & tomo 2. Jenensi, German. pag. 458. Sed & hic video, inquit, quid possis objicere, ut maximè, inquis, habenda sint schola, quid nobis proderunt lingua Ebr. Gr. Lat. &c. Annon possumus Biblia in vernaculam nostram transfusa legere? Respondeo, Iam pridem noveram nos Germanos non nisi bestias mansuros. Ja ich weiß/ leider / wol / das wir deutschen müssen immer bestien und tholle thier sein und bleiben / Verum hoc miror potius, cur non pari semel dicant operâ, Quò nobis sericum, byssus, purpura, vina exotica, pulveres aromatici, quicquid praterea peregrinarum est mercium, cum nobismet ipsis vini, frumenti, lana & lini, Regiones nostrates non solum copiam ad vivendum producant, sed etiam delectum ad ornandum relinquant. Artes liberales, linguarumque cognitionem, quæ præterquam quod damnosa non sint, etiam ornatum uberiorem, decus, utilitatem, tum ad intelligendas sacras literas, tum ad Reip. munia obeunda sunt allatura, posthabemus: verum merces peregrinas, quibus carere magno nostro poteramus compendio, ut pote funditus nos exhaurientibus, ultro cupimus. a ) Annon hoc est crassissimo stupore Germanam bestiam esse? Præterea si linguarum peritia alius non esset fructus, vel solum socordiam nostram excitare debebat, quod omnipotentis Dei adeo nobile donum sit, quo Germaniam nostram hac tempestate cumulatâ liberalitate, præcateris penè omnibus gentibus donavit. Videmus nimirum, Diabolum per Academias & Monasteria studiis semper fuisse reluctatum. An nescis quo furore Monachi contra emergentes linguas cem haresin manifestariam acti fuerint & adhuc sine intermissione furant? b ) Siquidem prospiciebat veterator ille malum, quod regno suo linguarum cognitio esset illatura ubi in lucem emersissent, cui multis seculis mederi non posset. Proinde cum prodeuntibus linguis obstare non potuit, cogitat eas ad a) Heissen das nicht billig deutsche Narren und Bestien? (marginal gloss) b) Den der Teufel rech des bösen, so wo die Sprachen herkommen, und sich darauf... (marginal gloss, partly illegible) Fach gewirr nen das er nicht licht kunt wider zuslopffen. Weil ernit nicht hatt mugen weren / das er herfür kemen/denckt er doch sie also schmal zu halten das sie von ihnen selbs wider sollen vergehen und fallen. Es ist ihm nicht ein lieber gast damit ins haus kommen / darum will er ihn auch also spersen/ dazer wil lange solle bleiben / etc. eas ad paucissimos quoque relegandas esse ut per se tandem, sterili paucitate cogente, denuò arescant & concidant. Ac sanè parùm gratus hospes diabolo linguarum peritia fuit, propterea eundem frugali culina tractare decrevit, ne diutinâ mansione premat hospitem: quam veteratoris nequissimi vafriciem pauci nostrum vident. Et paulo post, cum primùm emergerent linguæ, omnes ignorabant, quo consilio divina Sapientia linguas in lucem prodire sineret, donec re compertâ videmus, hoc Euangelii restaurandi causa factum esse, quod tum adhuc revelandum erat, ut per hoc papistica abominationis regnum everteret. Quamobrem credimus & Græciam Turcarum ditioni subjugatam, ut per Græcos sparsos & fugatos illorum lingua disseminaretur. Et rursus pauculis interjectis, c) Hac eo dicta sunt, ut intelligamus, nos Euangelium commodè nunquam retenturos esse, nisi fiat linguarum auxilio. Lingua enim sunt vagina, quibus gladius ille Spiritus, vid. verbum Dei, est insertus. Sunt arca, seu theca repositoria, quæ hoc nobile θησαυρὸν asservant. Pocula, quibus salubrem hanc potionem exceptam circumferimus. Cella promptuaria, ex quibus promus concionator, hac Euangelica cibaria depromit, Cophini in quibus panes una cum piscibus adeoque reliquiarum fragmenta custodiuntur, ne pereant. Quod si nobis supinè stertentibus, quod Deus avertat, per incuriam elabantur linguæ, timendum est non Euangelium solum amittamus, verùm eò rursùm miseriarum venturum nobiscum, ut nec linguam Lat. aut sermonem patrium recte sonare aut scribere possimus.
units.tr: But the time has come, I think, to shorten my sails. That will happen once I have produced two passages from the works of Luther, which I am persuaded will carry much weight with all good men. The first is found in his Admonition to the magistrates of the cities of Germany, in volume 7 of the Wittenberg Latin edition, page 441, column 2, and in volume 2 of the Jena German edition, page 458. But here too, he says, I see what you may object, namely, that the schools should be most held in esteem, and what good will the Hebrew, Greek and Latin languages do us? Can we not read the Bible translated into our own vernacular? I reply: I have long known that we Germans will remain nothing but beasts. Yes, I know, alas, well enough that we Germans must always be and remain beasts and stupid animals. But I rather wonder why they do not once and for all spend the same effort on this: why we need silk, fine linen, purple, exotic wines, aromatic spices, and whatever other foreign merchandise there is, when our own regions produce not only enough of wine, grain, wool and flax for living, but also leave a choice for adorning life. We set aside the liberal arts and the knowledge of languages, which are not only harmless but will also bring a richer adornment, honour and usefulness, both for understanding the sacred letters and for discharging the duties of the commonwealth. Yet we eagerly desire foreign wares, which we could have done without to our great advantage, since they drain us utterly dry. (a) Does this not mean, in the grossest stupidity, that Germans are beasts? Moreover, if knowledge of languages had no other fruit, it ought at least to rouse our sluggishness, since it is such a noble gift of Almighty God, with which He has, in this time, generously endowed our Germany above almost all other nations. We see, of course, that the Devil has always struggled against studies through the Academies and Monasteries. Do you not know with what fury the monks have been driven against the languages as they emerged, calling them a manifest heresy, and still rage without pause? For that old deceiver foresaw the evil that the knowledge of languages would bring to his kingdom once they had come into the light, an evil he could not cure for many centuries. Therefore, since he could not stand in the way of the languages as they came forth, he plans to confine them to very few people, so that at last, through their barren scarcity, they may dry up and collapse of themselves. Indeed, the knowledge of languages was a hardly welcome guest to the Devil, and so he has resolved to treat it on a meagre diet, so that it will not weigh down its host by a long stay. Few of us see this cunning of the most wicked deceiver. (b) And a little later: When the languages first emerged, all were ignorant of the purpose for which divine Wisdom allowed the languages to come into the light, until, the matter having been learned, we see that this was done for the restoration of the Gospel, which was then yet to be revealed, so that through it the papal kingdom of abomination might be overthrown. Therefore we believe that Greece too was subjected to the rule of the Turks so that the Greek language might be spread abroad through the Greeks who were scattered and driven out. And again, after a few more words: I say these things so that we may understand that we will never retain the Gospel conveniently unless it is done with the help of the languages. For languages are the scabbards in which that sword of the Spirit, namely the Word of God, is inserted. They are the chest or storehouse that keeps this noble treasure. They are the cups from which we pass round this healthful drink once it has been received. They are the pantry from which the preacher brings forth these Gospel victuals. They are the baskets in which the loaves together with the fishes, and indeed the fragments of the leftovers, are kept so that they do not perish. But if, while we lie snoring, which God forbid, the languages slip away through carelessness, we must fear that we will lose not only the Gospel but that misery will come back upon us, so that we can neither pronounce nor write the Latin language or our native tongue correctly.

units.la: Alterextat in ejus comment. ad Psalm. 45. Sæpe monui vos, inquit, ut Ebræam linguam. Etsi enim linguæ nullus alius esset usus, tamen pro gratiarum actione discenda erat: quod pars quædam religionis & cultus Dei sit, eam linguam docere vel discere, quæ sola, quicquid unquam divini est, docet. Auditur enim in ea Deus loqui, audiuntur sancti invocantes & maximas res gerentes, ut studium, quod in hanc linguam discendam impenditur, Missa quædam seu cultus Dei merito vocari possit. Quare serio vos hortor, ne eam negligatis: periculum enim est, ne Deus, hac ingratudine offensus, privet nos, non solùm cognitione hujus sanctæ linguæ, sed & Græcæ & Latinæ & totius religionis. Quàm facile enim ei est excitare barbarum aliquem populum, ut hæ linguæ unà intereant? Sed præterquam quod pars cultus divini est hoc studium, continet etiam maximam utilitatem. Si enim aliqui futuri sunt Theologi, sicut necesse est, neque que enim omnes Jura aut Medicinam discemus, oportet eos esse munitos contra Papam & aliud odiosum hominum vulgus, qui cum unam Ebræam vocem sonare didicerunt, statim putant se magistros hujus sanctæ linguæ esse. Ibi nisi eam nos teneremus, tanquam asinis illudent & insultabunt. Si autem nos quoque muniti fuerimus cognitione hujus linguæ, poterimus eis os imprudens obstruere. Sic enim Diabolo & ejus ministris resistendum est. Arbitror enim nos habituros religionis nostræ hostes, Hispanos, Gallos, Italos, &c. Ibi autem cognitione Ebraeæ linguæ opus erit. Scio enim quantum mihi profuerit contra hostes meos. Quare hac quantulacunque cognitione infinitis auriorum millibus carere nolim. Et vos quoque dabitis operam, qui aliquando docebitis religionem, ut hanc quoque linguam discatis, si non pecora campi & indoctum vulgus haberi vultis, quod editis Germanicis libellis adjutum, utcunque Dominicalia & Catechismum docet, &c. hactenus B. LUTHERUS.
units.tr: Also, in his commentary on Psalm 45, he writes: I have often urged you, he says, to learn the Hebrew language. Even if the language had no other use, it would still have to be learned for the sake of giving thanks, since teaching or learning that language is a part of religion and of the worship of God, for it alone teaches whatever is divine. In it we hear God speaking, and we hear the saints calling upon him and doing the greatest works, so that the study devoted to learning this language may rightly be called a kind of Mass or act of worship. I therefore earnestly exhort you not to neglect it. There is a danger that God, offended by this ingratitude, will deprive us not only of knowledge of this holy language but also of Greek and Latin and of all religion. For how easily could he stir up some barbarous people to destroy these languages together? Apart from the fact that this study is a part of divine worship, it also brings the greatest usefulness. For if there are to be theologians, as there must be (since we shall not all learn law or medicine), they must be armed against the Papists and other hateful common folk, who, once they have learned to pronounce a single Hebrew word, at once think they are masters of this holy language. Unless we ourselves have mastered it, they will mock us and insult us as if we were asses. But if we too are equipped with knowledge of this language, we shall be able to stop their foolish mouths. For this is how one must resist the Devil and his ministers. I expect that we will have the enemies of our religion among the Spaniards, the French, the Italians, and so on, and there we shall need knowledge of the Hebrew language. For I know how much it has helped me against my enemies. Therefore I would not want to be without this slight knowledge, which is worth thousands of ears. And you too will take pains, you who will one day teach religion, to learn this language as well, unless you want to be regarded as cattle of the field and an unlearned common people. This is aided by German booklets, which in some measure teach the Lord's Prayer and the Catechism, and so on. Thus far B. LUTHER.

units.la: Audivistis Rev. PP. & FF. judicia, vota & gemitus piorum. Vos ipsi hæc sacræ militiæ flagitia nostis optimè & doletis. Medicinam parate huic malo. Principiis obstate. Omne malum nascens facilè opprimitur, inveteratum fit plerunque robustius. Si vos hic silebitis, manusque remittetis, Pontificum edictis non erit opus. Sacra studia sponte in exilium ibunt. Cervicibus nostris denuò imminet Barbaries, vos depellite. Magno passu properamus ad veteres tenebras. Vos retrahite. Non votis aut supplicis muliebribus, sed vigilando, in medium consulendo, salutaria decernendo & exequendo restituenda res est. Hoc à vobis expectat Ecclesia, damnate eam hujus voti. Sic à vorticibus inutilium quæstionum, quæ tot jam annos, magno Papisini & Photinianæ hæreseos incremento, Ecclesias Germanicas, ad placida sacri Codicis & salutaria Theologiæ practicæ studia revocabitur juventus, & ad disputationes sobrias super utilibus thematibus, * non nisi jam fundamenta Religionis ex S. Codice & doctrinâ Catechetica edocta accedet. * Οὐ πάντὸς, οὐ πάντὸς ἐςι τὸ περὶ Θεοῦ φιλοσοφεῖν, περιφέρω δὲ· οὐδὲ πάντων, οὐδὲ πάσαν, οὐδὲ πάντα· Αλλ ἐσυόπη καὶ οἷς καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἑαυ. Sic, postquam gemina illa communis matris Ecclesiæ ubera Vet. & N. Testamentum suxerint, & in Christo adoleverint Nazirai nostri, adversus omnes Hæreticorum ictus animosius insurgent. * Hoc enim est unicum illud scutum scutum quod ipsis obvertendum est, sic dicit Dominus, quomodo legis, erratis nescientes scripturas. Uno verbo, latior erit Ecclesiæ & Scholarum facies. Theologus ego non sum, nec Theologi filius. Minimum me in domo Dei ministrum agnosco. Non ideo tamen rejicietis hoc, quod aliorum verbis vobis suggessi, consilium. In militia, equitum præcipua opera est, non spernuntur ideo pedites. In domo extruenda præcipuus architecti usus. Ideo non rejiciuntur operæ & administri. Ego quod hactenus feci, id porrò cum bono Deo agam, ut hæc studia augustæ illi Dominæ, Theologiæ, fideliter ancillentur, spartamque meam sic exornabo, ut juventutem nostram nulla necessitas coactura sit, ad aliquot miliaria cum * Grafero ob unam aut alteram vocem Ebraicam ad Judæos excurrendi. Ego pro meo modulo plantabo & rigabo, à magno illo messis Domino, & RR. VV. salutaribus decretis incrementum expectaturus, &, prout se dant initia, ringente etiam Satanâ, conscecuturus. Cum enim hanc Paraenesin, licet belgicè scriptam & contractiorem, anno superiori, aliquot provinciarum Synodis,
units.tr: You have heard, Reverend Fathers and Brothers, the judgments, wishes and groans of the pious. You yourselves know well the disgraceful failings of this sacred warfare, and you grieve over them. Prepare the remedy for this evil. Resist at the beginning; every evil, while it is still young, is easily overcome, but once it has grown old it usually becomes stronger. If you remain silent here and relax your hands, there will be no need for the edicts of the Pontiffs; sacred studies will go into exile of their own accord. Barbarism again threatens our necks; you must drive it away. We are hastening with great strides back into the old darkness; you must pull us back. The matter is to be restored not by prayers or womanish entreaties, but by vigilance, by consulting in common, and by decreeing and carrying out salutary measures. This is what the Church expects from you; do not disappoint her in this wish. Thus the youth will be called back from the whirlpools of useless questions, which for so many years, to the great increase of Papism and of the Photinian heresy, have drawn the German Churches away, to the calm study of the sacred Code and of the practical theology that brings salvation, and they will come to sober disputations on useful theses, only once the foundations of religion have been taught from the Holy Scripture and catechetical doctrine. * "It is not for everyone, not in every way, to philosophize about God, but ..." (Gregory Nazianzen) [Οὐ πάντὸς, οὐ πάντως ἐστὶ τὸ περὶ Θεοῦ φιλοσοφεῖν]. Thus, after that twin breast of our common mother, the Church, the Old and New Testaments, have been sucked and our Nazarite has grown up in Christ, they will rise up more boldly against all the blows of the heretics. * For this is the one shield that must be turned against them: thus says the Lord, you err, not knowing the Scriptures, as you read. In a word, the face of the Church and of the schools will be brighter. I am not a theologian, nor the son of a theologian. I acknowledge myself to be the least of ministers in the house of God. Nevertheless, you will not reject this advice, which I have offered you in the words of others. In an army the chief work belongs to the cavalry, yet the foot soldiers are not therefore despised. In building a house the architect has the principal use, yet the workmen and assistants are not therefore rejected. I shall continue what I have done so far, with God's blessing, so that these studies may faithfully serve that noble lady, Theology, and I shall so adorn my own portion that no necessity will ever force our youth to run for miles to the Jews for the sake of one or two Hebrew words, with Grafero. I shall plant and water according to my small measure, expecting the increase from the great Lord of the harvest and from your salutary decrees, and I shall follow up as the beginnings allow, even while Satan rages. For when I offered this exhortation last year to the synods of several provinces, though written in Dutch and more concise,

units.la: Αἱ μὲν Φιέπεραί τινὰ νοῦζος τι ζεῖναί τι, obtulissem, omnibus studium meum abundè probavi. Sicuti ex iis, quæ jam subjiciam, actis, liquebit.
units.tr: The Greek, as printed in the scan, is garbled and I cannot reliably restore it; it appears to be a proverb or sentence of an ancient writer. I had offered it, I have amply proved my zeal to all. As will become clear from the acts I am about to add.

units.tr: Acts of the Provincial Synod of Friesland, held at Harlingen in the year 1624.

units.tr: SESSION V.

units.la: xxvi. Maij, ante meridem, post habitas preces
units.tr: 26 May, before noon, after the prayers had been offered.

units.la: NOmine D. Professoris AMAMA exhibita sunt Synodo per Scribam xxvi. exemplaria Paraenesfeosejis: quibus distributis, lectis & examinatis, judicavit Synodus ejus petitionem esse laudabilem, edificatiram, valde utilem & perquam necessariam. ac proinde ei hoc nomine ververbis Synodi, per D. Christoph. Hardenbergium, electum Synodi Scribam gratias esse agendas. Decretumque est, ut in posterum Theologiae Candidati, quotquot ad examen Ministerii Eccles. admitti desiderabunt, praeter testimonia Senatus Academ. & Theologiae Professorum, exhibeant etiam testimonia Professorum Ebraeae & Graecae linguae, quibus doceant, se in praedictis linguis eos saltem progressus fecisse, ut originalem Veteris Novique Test. textum mediocriter possint intelligere; utque in Classe ista, cujus examini se offerunt, ejus quoque rei specimen edere teneantur.
units.tr: In the name of Professor Amama, twenty-six copies of his Paraenesis were presented to the Synod by the clerk. When they had been distributed, read and examined, the Synod judged his petition to be commendable, edifying, very useful and most necessary. Accordingly, the Synod resolved that thanks should be given to him on its behalf, through Dr Christoph Hardenberg, the clerk elected by the Synod. It was also decreed that in future, all theology candidates who wish to be admitted to the examination for the ministry of the Church must present, besides the testimonies of the university senate and the theology professors, testimonies from the professors of Hebrew and Greek showing that they have made at least such progress in those languages that they can reasonably understand the original text of the Old and New Testaments; and that they must also give a specimen of this in the classis before which they offer themselves for examination.

units.la: Quod vero ad Idiotas attinet, caterosque, qui non recenter ex Academiis veniunt, cum iis in omni discretione agetur, pro ratione rerum, personarumque juxta Ecclesiasticas Sanctiones. Porro, Deputati Synodi, hujus decreti causas Amplissimis Academia Franek. Curatoribus quamprimum indicabunt, ab iisque petent, ut hujus Provinciae Alumnis mandare dignentur, ut juxta hanc sanctionem studia instituant. Injungit denique Synodus expresse omnibus Classibus, ut post Pascha sequentis anni hoc decretum sequantur & exequantur. In orig. subscripserant nomine Synodi
units.tr: As for laymen and others who have not recently come from the universities, they shall be dealt with in every case according to the circumstances of the matter and the persons, in line with the ecclesiastical sanctions. Furthermore, the deputies of the Synod will as soon as possible make known the reasons for this decree to the most distinguished curators of the Franeker Academy, and will ask them kindly to order the students of this province to pursue their studies in accordance with this sanction. Finally, the Synod expressly enjoins on all classes that they follow and carry out this decree after Easter of the following year. In the original, they subscribed in the name of the Synod:

units.la: Salutem & pacem à Deo Patre per J. Christum.
units.tr: Greetings and peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ.

units.la: QUAMVIS aliquâ locorum intercapedine (reverendi Patres) dirimamur, arctissimâ tamen communionis sanctorum sub eodem Christo capite necessitudine devincti sumus: adeo ut serio non solum cum dolentibus dolere, sed cum gaudentibus etiam gaudere jubeamur. Quocirca dissimulare sine ingratitudine non possumus, quanta merito lætitia perfusi simus, postquam nobis præclara virtus vestra innotuit: quod gravissima atque utilissima D. Amamæ Paranesi confirmati, in Examine Candidatorum Theolog. & Græcæ & Ebrææ linguæ rationem habendam sanctissimè & prudentissimè (Gallicarum Ecclesiarum more) statuistis. Alioqui enim verendum erat, ne quemadmodum sacrarum illarum linguarum studiis, patrum nostrorum memoriâ suscitatis, simul veritas pene sepulta emergere cœpit ac caput attollere; ita contra studiis hisce neglectis, in pristinam barbariem & veritatis jacturam relaberemur. Gratulor igitur vobis, Patres Reverendi, insignem illam Pietatem ac prudentiam, quod Ecclesiæ Dei (quam sanguine suo acquisivit) laboranti ac ruinam minitanti, salutarem statuti vestri manum primi in Belgio subjeciistis. Quo fiet ut S. Theologiæ studiosi, qui ad ministerii Euangelici munus aspirant, recto ordine procedant, scripturamque non per solam variæ interpretationis transsennam eminus aspiciant, sed eam penitius intueantur ac scrutentur, sanctarum linguarum subsidio adjuti. Quo modo & certius veritatem docere & eruditis adversariis occurrere, oraque iis obturare valebunt. Qua in re non solum reliquis Belgii Ecclesiis æternâ cum vestra procerumque Phrysiæ laude præluxistis: sed etiam vestro exemplo tam australem quam Borealem Hollandiam inflammastis, ut D. Amamæ hortationi (gravissimis rationibus subnixæ) locum darent, vestrumque decretum, sine invidia sincerè ad Ecclesiæ emolumentum. Deique gloriam imitarentur. Quod uti fratres Geldros secuturos non levibus literarum indiciis arbitramur; ita nuperæ Groninganæ Synodi, mense Majo, consensionem (vestro & Hollandiæ decretorum ductu) merito accessisse coram cognovimus ac comprobavimus. Adeo utile est, pio & laudabili instituto præire, aliisque comiter viam demonstrare! Nec pietatem solummodo, sed prudentiam etiam vestram singularem vobis gratulamur. Quippe, ut rem honestissimam utilissimamque decreviistis, ita facto non difficilem, dilatâ illius in annum integrum observatione, omnino reddidistis. Nam quemadmodum Themistocles licet adultior (ut Plutarchus memorat) cum Rege Persarum de rebus gravibus locuturus, anni spacium discendæ linguæ Persicæ postulavit, ut regis verba intelligere certius & ei refrespondere tutius sine interprete valeret, idque eo intervallo est assecutus: ita & vos prudentissimè Candidatis Theologiæ, ut Deum Regem in S. Literis loquentem aliqua ratione intelligerent, annum indulsistis. Pergite igitur vestrâ illa virtute & constantia Ecclesiam stabilire. Ita Deus optimus Pater vos omni gratiæ spiritus sui cumulo auctet & conservet per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Valete Reverendi Patres, & meam hanc gratulationem observantiæ erga vos, & amoris mei erga Ecclesiam testificationem, pro solitâ humanitate vestra boni consulite.
units.tr: Although we are separated by some distance of places (Reverend Fathers), we are nonetheless bound together by the very close tie of fellowship of the saints under the same Christ, the Head. So much so that we are commanded to rejoice seriously not only with those who grieve, but also to rejoice with those who rejoice. Therefore we cannot, without ingratitude, conceal how great a joy we deservedly feel, now that your outstanding virtue has become known to us: that, strengthened by the most weighty and most useful exhortation of the Reverend Amama, you have decreed most holily and most prudently (after the manner of the Gallican Churches) that account be taken of Greek and Hebrew in the examination of candidates for theology. For otherwise it was to be feared that, just as with the revival of the study of those sacred languages in our fathers' memory the truth, almost buried, began to emerge and lift up its head, so on the contrary, if these studies were neglected, we would slip back into the former barbarism and the loss of the truth. I therefore congratulate you, Reverend Fathers, on that remarkable piety and prudence, in that you were the first in Belgium to lend a saving hand to your decree, for the Church of God (which he acquired with his own blood), which is labouring and threatening ruin. As a result, students of sacred theology who aspire to the office of the evangelical ministry will proceed in proper order, and will not look at Scripture merely from afar through the chink of a single, varied interpretation, but will look into it more deeply and search it, aided by the help of the sacred languages. In this way they will be able both to teach the truth more surely and to meet learned adversaries, and to stop their mouths. In this matter you have shone not only to the eternal praise of you and the leading men of Friesland, among the remaining Churches of Belgium; but by your example you have also kindled both Southern and Northern Holland, so that they gave place to Amama's exhortation (supported by most weighty reasons) and to your decree, sincerely and without envy, for the advantage of the Church, and imitated the glory of God. Just as we judge, from no slight written indications, that the Gelderland brethren will follow, so we have learned and approved, with our own eyes, that the Synod of Groningen in May has rightly given its agreement, guided by your decrees and those of Holland. So useful is it to go before others in a pious and praiseworthy undertaking, and to show the way kindly to the rest! We congratulate you not only on your piety but also on your singular prudence. Indeed, just as you decreed a most honourable and most useful measure, so you made it not difficult in practice, by postponing its observance for a full year. For just as Themistocles, though rather advanced in years (as Plutarch relates), when about to speak with the King of the Persians on weighty matters, asked for a space of a year to learn the Persian language, so that he could understand the king's words more surely and answer him more safely without an interpreter, and obtained this during that interval: so you too, most prudently, granted the candidates in theology a year, so that they might in some way understand God, the King speaking in the Sacred Scriptures. Go on, therefore, to establish the Church by that virtue and constancy of yours. So may God, the best Father, increase and preserve you with the full measure of his grace and Spirit, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Farewell, Reverend Fathers, and kindly accept this my congratulation, as a testimony of my respect towards you and of my love towards the Church, in your accustomed courtesy.

units.la: Groningæ 4. Junii CIↄ Iↄ CXXV.
units.tr: Groningen, 4 June 1625.

units.la: Subscriptum erat, Vestrûm observantissimus
units.tr: It was signed, Your most devoted

units.la: FRANCISCUS GOMARUS.
units.tr: FRANCISCUS GOMARUS.

units.la: APOGRAPHVM EX ACTIS SYNODI FRISIÆ habitæ DOCCOMII 1625.
units.tr: Copy from the Acts of the Synod of Friesland held at Doccum, 1625.

units.la: QVod ad decretum Synodi Harlingana attinet, super studiosis Theologiæ, quo cautum est ne illi in posterum ad Examen admittantur, nisi in Ebraea & Graeca lingua mediocriter versati sint, Fratres hujus Synodi, auditis expensisque rationibus à....in contrarium productis, neutiquam censent eas ejusmodi esse, ut propterea laudabile illud decretum mutari debeat, quin contrà judicant, admodum aedificativum, necessarium & utile esse, ut ei inhaeratur, illudque quàm diligentissimè & maximè serio observetur, addentes hoc interpretamentum, decretum istud pertinere non ad eos solummodo, qui recens ex Academiis venientes ad Examen admitti desiderant, sed ad omnes qui studuêre, etiam si annum aut amplius extra Academiam aut vitam privatam vixerint, aut scholasticam pædagogicamve functionem obierint. Quod verò ad Idiotas attinet, praesens Synodus nihil derogat bonis decretis, quae super isthoc negotio tam tam in Nationalibus, quam hujus Provincia Synodu ante hac condita sunt. In originali subscripserant.
units.tr: As for the decree of the Synod of Harlingen concerning students of theology, by which it was provided that they should not in future be admitted to the examination unless they were moderately versed in the Hebrew and Greek languages, the brethren of this Synod, having heard and weighed the reasons produced to the contrary by ..., do not judge that those reasons are such that this praiseworthy decree ought to be changed. On the contrary, they judge it very edifying, necessary and useful that it be adhered to and observed as diligently and seriously as possible, adding this explanation: that the decree applies not only to those who, coming fresh from the academies, wish to be admitted to the examination, but to all who have studied, even if they have lived a year or more outside the academy, in private life, or have held a scholastic or pedagogical office. As for the unlearned, the present Synod derogates nothing from the good decrees previously enacted on this matter, both in the national synods and in the synod of this province. They had subscribed the original.

units.la: PHILIPPUS EILSHEMIUS Ecclesiastes Harling. Synodi Præses.
units.tr: Philippus Eilshemius, minister at Harlingen, President of the Synod.

units.la: WIBRANDUS HOMMIUS Synodi Scriba.
units.tr: Wibrandus Hommius, Clerk of the Synod.

units.la: APORAPHVM EX ACTIS SYNODI LEOVERDIENSIS. ANNO 1626.
units.tr: Copy from the Acts of the Synod of Leeuwarden, in the year 1626.

units.la: Placuit Synodo, nemine contradicente, ut illi quoque Candidati, qui post rogatam hanc legem quandocunq; aut undecunque, in hanc provinciam venient, huic quoque decreto juxta cum Frisiis sint obnoxii. Si cui vero alibi, ubi decretum de studio linguarum rogatum necdum est, post latam super hac re in Synodo Frisica Legem examinato & ad SS. Ministerium admisso, in hanc provinciam vocari contigerit, prædicta Synodus voluit, cum quoque huic Legi esse obnoxium.
units.tr: The Synod resolved, with no one dissenting, that those candidates too who come into this province at any time or from anywhere after this law was requested shall be bound by this decree, just as the Frisians are. But if anyone is called to this province from elsewhere, where a decree on the study of languages has not yet been requested, after the law passed on this matter in the Frisian Synod, and he has been examined and admitted to the holy ministry, the aforesaid Synod wished that he too be bound by this law.

units.la: In originali nomine Synodi signaverant
units.tr: In the original, the following had signed in the name of the Synod:

units.la: B. FULLENIUS, Synodi Præses.
units.tr: B. FULLENIUS, President of the Synod.

units.la: I. BILTIUS, Synodi Scriba.
units.tr: I. BILTIUS, Clerk of the Synod.

units.la: APOGRAPHVM EX ACTIS SYNODI Suyd-Hollandicæ, celebratæ WOERDÆ 1625.
units.tr: EXTRACT FROM THE ACTS OF THE SOUTH-HOLLAND SYNOD, held at Woerden in 1625.

units.la: Quod ad VII. gravamen attinet, quo agitur de propositione D. SIXTINI AMAMA, &c. decernit Synodus, sicuti jam decrevit Synodus Frisica, ut Candidati Theologia, qui ad præparatorium Examen admitti volent, praeter testimonia Ecclesiae. Senatus Acad. & Professorum Theologiae, simul exhibeant testimonia Professorum Ebraea & Graeca lingua, quibus doceant, se eos progressus fecisse, ut originalem Vet. & Novi Foederis textum ad minimum legere & mediocriter intelligere possint.
units.tr: As for the seventh grievance, which concerns the proposal of Mr. Sixtinus Amama, etc., the Synod decides, as the Frisian Synod has already decided, that candidates in theology who wish to be admitted to the preparatory examination shall present, besides the testimonies of the Church, of the Academic Senate and of the professors of theology, testimonies from the professors of Hebrew and Greek, by which they show that they have made such progress that they can at least read the original text of the Old and New Covenant and understand it moderately well.

units.la: Eadem fere verba sunt decreti Synodi Vltraiectina 1626. Et Noort-Hollandica 1627. Harlemii celebratae.
units.tr: These are nearly the same words as the decree of the Synod of Utrecht of 1626, and of the North-Holland Synod held at Haarlem in 1627.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS V.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR V.

units.la: Versiones Latinas, Pagnini, Iunii, Erasmi, Beza, nec non Germanicam B. Lutheri, &, quae ex ea expres- sa est, Belgicam, mentem Spiritus S. ubique ita ex- pressisse, nullius ut correctionis amplius indiga sint.
units.tr: That the Latin versions of Pagninus, Junius, Erasmus and Beza, together with the German of Luther and the Dutch one expressed from it, have everywhere so expressed the mind of the Holy Spirit that they need no further correction.

units.la: De hoc errore in superioris confutatione satis superque dictum arbitror. Illud enim quod hic asseritur, primarium eorum argumentum est, qui linguarum studia res suas sibi habere jubent. Si quis tamen de Belgica pleniorem instructionem desideraverit, cum ablego ad Prolegomena * collationis nostrae Biblicae, lingua Belgica ante quadriennium editae, qua veteris Test. versionem cum fontibus & accuratissimis translationibus contuli. Sed hic fortassis aliqui ex Evangelicis in me destomachabuntur, dicentque falso sibi impingi hunc errorem. Quos ego rogatos velim, cur ergo manuductissimo Theologorum D. Joh. Piscatori tam fuerint iniqui, cur à B. Lutheri versione ne latum unguem velint discedi, cur denique illorum plerique tot loca Scripturae, quae in manifestis mendis cubant, quorum à fontibus discrepantiam doctissimi viri detexerunt, veteri more, etiam cum dogmata probanda vel improbanda sunt, citent. Protestationem facto contrariam, nullam esse Jurisconsulti pronunciant.
units.tr: I think I have said enough, and more than enough, about this error in my earlier refutation. What is asserted here is the chief argument of those who bid their own affairs be kept apart from the study of languages. If anyone, however, wants a fuller account concerning the Dutch version, I refer him to the Prolegomena of our Biblical collation, published in the Dutch language four years ago, in which I compared the Old Testament version with the sources and with the most accurate translations. But perhaps some of the Evangelicals will be angry with me here and say that this error is falsely imputed to them. I would ask them why, then, they have been so unfair to the most learned theologian John Piscator, why they will not allow a hair's breadth of departure from Luther's version, and why, finally, many of them cite, in the old manner, passages of Scripture that lie in plain error, whose discrepancy from the sources learned men have exposed, even when doctrines are to be proved or refuted. Lawyers declare that a protestation contrary to the facts counts for nothing.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS. VI.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR VI.

units.la: Lectionem S. Scriptura Theologia studioso non esse admodum necessarium. Vel, posse aliquem Theologiae studere
units.tr: That the reading of Holy Scripture is not very necessary for a student of theology; or, that someone can study theology, and be called a student of theology, even if he does not read the sacred letters.

units.la: dere, & Theologiæ studiosum dici etiam si non legat sa-cras literas.
units.tr: Ants of the same kind, and not yet taught.

units.la: Hunc errorem in Papatu obtinuisse olim supra pag.47. obiter ostendimus, At ex professo hanc quercum excussimus in præloquio hujus operis. Vbi liberum quoque gemitum edidimus de statu Academiarum protestantium. Ea repetere supervacuum esset & plane φοβητικὴς λογοδιαιρέσεως. Pestilentissimi hujus erroris fibras ab ipsis radicibus eliserunt pii Theologi. Ego, licet ne Grammatici quidem titulum merear, non me contineo tamen, quin omnes Theologos, queis mea ancillatur opella, per viscera misericordiæ Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI obtester, ut hic vigilent. &, cum videant Photinianos, Pontificios & Anabaptistas hic nescio quo impetu incalescere, juventutem ad Biblica studia adigant. Sed causæ, quam & urgeo, bonitate subnixus, audebo ad vos ipsos orationis meæ cursum dirigere, Lectissimi juvenes,
units.tr: We showed in passing, above on page 47, that this error had prevailed in the Papacy; but we have shaken this oak thoroughly in the preface to this work, where we also gave free vent to our lament about the state of the Protestant Academies. To repeat those things would be superfluous and simply a fearful kind of 'dividing the word' [φοβητικὴς λογοδιαιρέσεως]. The pious theologians have torn out the fibres of this most pestilent error from their very roots. I, though I do not even deserve the title of grammarian, nonetheless cannot refrain from pleading with all the theologians whom my small labour serves, by the bowels of mercy of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, that they keep watch here; and, since they see the Photinians, the Papists and the Anabaptists growing hot with I know not what fury, that they drive the young to Biblical studies. But relying on the goodness of the cause, which I also press, I will dare to direct the course of my speech to you yourselves, most choice young men:

units.la: audebo fungi vice cotis, acutum Reddere quæ ferrum valet, exors ipsa secandi.
units.tr: I will dare to act as a whetstone, which can make sharp the iron, though itself unable to cut.

units.la: Si ergo non commoverunt vos omnes istæ magnorum virorum querelæ, quas in præloquio plena manu effudimus, consideræ quæso & animum advertite ad ea, quæ nunc ordine dicturus sum.
units.tr: If, then, all those complaints of great men, which I have poured out in full measure in the preface, have not moved you, consider, I beg you, and give heed to the things I am now about to set out in order.

units.la: I. Quàm præclarum sit illud ellogium quo Timotheum suum ornat μεγάλη τὴν κηρύγματος σάλπιγξ, Paulus, 2. ad Timoth. 3. 15. quod ἀπὸ βρέφους sacras litteras noverit. Quàm beatum prædicat eum David, qui in lege Dei meditatur die ac nocte? Labia Sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & lex requiretur ab ore ejus, Mal.2.7. at quomodo hoc fiet nisi Legi studuerit?
units.tr: I. How splendid is that eulogy with which Paul adorns his Timothy, that he has known the sacred letters from infancy [ἀπὸ βρέφους], 2 Timothy 3:15. How blessed David declares him who meditates on the law of God day and night! "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth," Malachi 2:7. But how will this happen unless he has devoted himself to the Law?

units.la: II. Quàm serio hortetur Apostolus suum Timotheum, ut stultas & ineruditas (quales plerâque Scholasticorum sunt) quæstiones fugiat sciens illas gignere pugnas, 2.Tim.2.23. & profanos de rebus inanibus clamores cohibeat verl. 16. & vitet λογομαχίας, quæ ad nihil sint utiles, verf. 14.
