Contrà, 1.Tim.4.13. intentus esto lectioni, Scripturarum opinor.
units.tr: II. How earnestly the Apostle exhorts his Timothy to avoid foolish and unlearned questions (such as most of the Schoolmen raise), "knowing that they breed quarrels," 2 Timothy 2:23, and to restrain profane babblings about empty things, verse 16, and to avoid strifes of words [λογομαχίας], which are of no use at all, verse 14. On the contrary, 1 Timothy 4:13: "Give attention to reading," I suppose of the Scriptures.

units.la: III. Necessarium esse in Verbi D. Ministro requisitum, ut possit sermonem Dei ὀρθοτομεῖν .i. recte tractare, ut vertit vulg. ut sit potens exhortari doctrina sana, & contradicentes convincere. Tit. 1.9. Potens in scripturis erat Apollo, Act. 18. ut & tu sis talis, à teneris assuescendum est lectioni Biblicæ, phrasis ejus, quæ latentem quandam ἐνεργείαν habet, in succum & sanguinem convertenda est. Assiduè volvendus est hic lapis. Nulla pars πεπαιδευμένης tractari debet, cui non simul adjungatur Scripturarum lectio. Non infunditur ea cœlitus. Decumana opus est industria.
units.tr: III. It is necessary for a minister of the Word of God to have this qualification, that he may be able to rightly handle the word of God [ὀρθοτομεῖν], that is, to handle it rightly, as the Vulgate renders it, so that he is able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince those who contradict, Titus 1:9. Apollos was mighty in the Scriptures, Acts 18; so you too must be such a man. From tender years one must become accustomed to Biblical reading; its phrasing, which has a certain hidden power, must be turned into juice and blood. This stone must be turned over constantly. No part of a learned education [πεπαιδευμένης] ought to be taught without the reading of the Scriptures being added at the same time. It is not poured down from heaven; it needs industry on a great scale.

units.la: IV. Audi Serarium Jesuitam & mirare, in Proleg. Bibl. cap. 28. quæst. 7. hanc movet quæstionem, An Theologiæ destinato à puero sacris Bibliis vacandum sit? & affirmat. 1. Quia certum vetus illud, à teneris consuescere multum. Et, Quo semel est imbuta recens, &c. 2. quia magni & excellentes viri sic fecerunt, Timotheus, Abramius puer nobilis, & Calybita. 3. In Pirke Aboth dicitur, Puer V. annorum ad Biblia est applicandus, id quod observatum à Judæis olim, & aliquodo modo etiam hodie. 4. Oratorem futurum vix patitur Quintilianus aut bimulum aut trimulum esse, quin statim & à nutricibus & à parentibus & ab ancillulis & servulis, quæ balbutire incipiat, verbis & optimis & optime pronuntiatis assuescat. Quanto id in Theologo futuro expetendum curandumque magis? 5. Sua omnibus studiis infantia est. Et ut corporum mox fortissimorum educatio à lacte initium ducit, ita & mentis ad Theologiam præparatio à sacrarum literarum syllabis voculisque ac sententiolis junctis inchoanda. 6. Hieronymus ejusmodi præcepta educandæ filiæ dat Lætæ, ut videre est in ejus ad illam Epistola. 7. In vilioribus etiam artibus & disciplinis, à primâ statim ætate videmus parentum curam invigilare, ut quam primum discendis illis admoveantur pueri: quanto magis id necessarium in summâ, difficillima & nunquam exhaurienda Scripturarum cognitione. 8. Eos, qui tardius ad scripturas accedunt, aut nunquam, aut certè raro, aut magnâ cum difficultate, pertinacique admodum studio, illas memoria comprehendere & in promtu ad manum habere videmus. Et postea magnum iis obtingere felicitatem asserit, qui à puero biblicis studiis innutriuntur. In sequentibus multa præclare in eandem rem refert idem. Quæst. 12. sacra Biblia vult edisci.
units.tr: IV. Listen to the Jesuit Serarius, and marvel: in his Prolegomena to the Bible, chapter 28, question 7, he raises the question, whether a boy destined for theology should be given over to the holy Bible from childhood, and he affirms it. 1. Because that old saying is certain, "What is learned early goes a long way," and "the vessel once seasoned while fresh," etc. 2. Because great and excellent men have done so: Timothy, Abraham as a noble boy, and the Calybites. 3. In Pirke Aboth it is said, "A boy of five years is to be applied to the Bible," which was observed by the Jews of old and in some measure is observed even today. 4. Quintilian hardly allows a future orator to be two or three years old before he is accustomed, by his nurses, his parents, his maids and his little servants, to speak the best words in the best way as soon as he begins to stammer. How much more is this to be sought and cared for in a future theologian? 5. Infancy is the foundation of all studies; and just as the training of the strongest bodies begins at once with milk, so the preparation of the mind for theology must be begun with the syllables, little words and short joined sentences of the sacred letters. 6. Jerome gives precepts of this kind for the education of his daughter Laeta, as may be seen in his letter to her. 7. We see parents' care watching over even humbler arts and disciplines from the very first age, so that boys are set to learn them as early as possible: how much more necessary is this in the highest, most difficult and never exhausted knowledge of the Scriptures. 8. We see that those who come to the Scriptures later, either never, or certainly rarely, or with great difficulty and a very stubborn effort, grasp them in memory and have them ready at hand. And he asserts that those who are nourished in Biblical studies from boyhood have a great happiness that comes to them afterwards. In what follows the same author sets out many excellent points on the same matter. Question 12: he wants the holy Bible to be learned by heart.

units.la: 1. Quia & res & verba eorum dignissima sunt quæ memoriæ tabulis insculpantur. 2. Si memoria semper confirmanda est, ne pereat: si exercenda ut crescat, quid tandem est, in quo ea utilius confirmetur & exerceatur, quàm sacro-sancta Dei oracula? 3.
units.tr: 1. Because both the matters and the words are most worthy of being engraved on the tablets of memory. 2. If memory must always be strengthened lest it perish, and exercised that it may grow, what, finally, is there in which it may be more usefully strengthened and exercised than the most sacred oracles of God?

units.la: 3. Alia tam multa tam multi ex profanis voluminibus memoriâ & scientiâ comprehendunt, quidni & Theologi hoc κειμήλιον? Lepta suavissimus edisce Hesiodum, inquit Tullius. At pro Hesiodo Davidem, Paulum, &c. sibi Theologiae Studiosus proponat.
units.tr: 3. Many men learn by heart and know so many things from profane books; why should not theologians also have this treasure [κειμήλιον]? "Learn Hesiod by heart," says Cicero, "most delightful of treasures." But let the student of theology set David, Paul and the rest in place of Hesiod.

units.la: 4. Qui ista ediscunt, Deo suam memoriam consecrant, ad omnia Theologi munia aptiores. 5. Qui hoc non faciunt, saepe ab aliis ridentur. Magnus ille * Momus, in ratione verae Theologiae, non paucos inquit, olim vidimus Lutetiae Theologos, quibus si quid depromendum foret ex Paulo, videbantur sibi prorsus in alium mundum translati. Quae si vera, inquit Serarius, quantum dedecus! 6. Cum Scripturarum pertractatio perpetua Theologis esse debeat, illas memoriâ non complecti, est exiguum laborem non tam fugere, quàm in maximum & perpetuum commutare: qui variis occasionibus & causis identidem quotidie subeundus & sisyphaei saxi instar volvendus ac revolvendus assidue. Quoties enim ex iis aliquid afferendum, vel alius rogandus, vel concordantiae maximo cum taedio in manum semper sumendae, voculaeque hinc inde quaeritandae, quarum non raro fallax est numerus & indicium, veluti, ait Erasmus, faciunt mei similes quidam, qui cum domi nihil habeant supellectilis, quoties opus est cantharo aut patella, à vicino petunt utendam. 7. Quid Haeretici plerique? Quanta Scripturarum iis memoria? &c. Haec & plura ibidem Serarius. Quibus haec addo,
units.tr: 4. Those who learn these things by heart consecrate their memory to God and become more fit for all the duties of a theologian. 5. Those who do not do this are often laughed at by others. That great Momus, in his work on true theology, says: "I have seen, not a few theologians at Paris in my time, who, if anything had to be quoted from Paul, seemed to themselves to have been transported utterly into another world." "If these things are true," says Serarius, "what a disgrace!" 6. Since the continual handling of the Scriptures ought to be constant for theologians, not to hold them in memory is a small labour, not so much to be avoided as to be exchanged for the greatest and never-ending one: a labour to be undertaken again and again, every day, on various occasions and for various reasons, and to be rolled and rolled back continually, like the stone of Sisyphus. For whenever something must be brought forth from them, or someone must be asked, or the concordances must always be taken in hand with the greatest weariness, and little words sought here and there, whose number is often deceptive and a sign of trouble, we are like, says Erasmus, "certain men like me, who, having no household goods at home, whenever they need a cup or a dish, ask a neighbour to lend one." 7. What of the many heretics? How little of the Scriptures do they have in memory? And so on. Serarius says these and more things in the same place. To these I add these things,

units.la: IV. Tempore persecutionis non posse postillas, glossas, concordantias circum ferri, imo saepe ne ipsa quidem Biblia. Quid hic faciet Minister in Scripturis non versatus?
units.tr: IV. In time of persecution postils, glosses and concordances cannot be carried about, and often not even the Bible itself. What will a minister who is not versed in the Scriptures do here?

units.la: V. Sacras literas immediate à Deo esse traditas, ab omni errore & contradictione immunes, ad quas omnia hominum quamvis eruditissimorum & sanctissimorum scripta examinari debent. De his usurpari potest illud quod Homerus de Aegypto,
units.tr: V. The Sacred Letters were handed down immediately from God, free from every error and contradiction, and all the writings of men, however learned and holy, must be examined by them. What Homer said of Egypt can be applied to these:

units.la: φάρμακα πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα, πολλὰ δ' λυγρά.
units.tr: Many drugs, some good and mixed together, many baneful. [φάρμακα πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα, πολλὰ δ' λυγρά]

units.la: Saepe pluribus etiam foliis perlectis, vix unam certam & firmam sententiam, cui tuto inniti possit conscientia, elicias. Plurima illic folia & floscula, at fructus rari. At in sacris literis ὀλίγα πάνυ ἀπάντα, Hic nihil est, quod non sit magni momenti, inquit Beatus Basilius, ut nobis nihil aut parum esse videatur. Omnia quae in S. Literis sunt, inquit Bannes, etiam si nobis minima videantur, utilia sunt. Hic longe plura ignoramus quàm scimus. Inexhaustum hoc pelagus est.
units.tr: Often, even after reading through many pages, you can scarcely draw out one certain and firm opinion on which a conscience can safely rest. There are very many leaves and little flowers there, but the fruit is rare. But in the Sacred Letters all of them are very few [ὀλίγα πάνυ ἀπάντα]. There is nothing here that is not of great importance, says Saint Basil, so that to us it may seem to be nothing or of little account. All that is in the Holy Scriptures, says Bannes, even if it seems to us very minor, is useful. Here we know far less than we do not know. This is an inexhaustible sea.

units.la: VI. Cum loci communes nihil sint aliud quam dependentiæ quædam & consecutiones ex sacris literis seu fontibus & principiis derivatæ, nunquid præposterum est circa dependentias & consecutiones occupari, neglectis & ignoratis fontibus? Nunquid hoc perinde est, ac si domum ædificaturus de parietibus & tecto vehementer esset sollicitus, de fundamento interim securus? In jure aliter instituuntur studia· Is demum optimus Juris-consultus censetur, qui optimus Textualis est. Cum juvenis essem, inquit Lutherus, assuescebam Bibliis, ea mihi reddebam familiaria, eoque contendebam ut bonus Textualis essem. Postea alios authores legebam. Aber ich muste sie zu letzt alle aus den augen stellen / und weg thun/ dewreil ich in meinen gewissen da mit nicht conte zu frieden sein / und muste mich also wieder mit den Bibel verwaren / etc.
units.tr: VI. Since commonplaces are nothing other than certain dependencies and consequences derived from the Sacred Letters or from their sources and principles, is it not topsy-turvy to busy oneself with dependencies and consequences while neglecting and ignoring the sources? Is this not just as if someone about to build a house were very anxious about the walls and roof, yet meanwhile careless about the foundation? In law, studies are arranged otherwise. He is judged to be the best jurist who is the best in the text of the law. When I was young, says Luther, I accustomed myself to the Bibles, I made them familiar to me, and I strove to be a good textualist. Afterwards I read other authors. But at last I had to put them all out of sight and away, because in my conscience I could not be content with them, and so I had to fortify myself again with the Bible, etc.

units.la: VII. Notabile est Alphonsi Aragoniæ Regis exemplum, qui teste Panormitano, gloriari solebat se mediis Regni negotiis universa Biblia cum glossis Lyræ quater & decies à capite ad calcem perlegisse. Scilicet hic Heros ad animum revocavit serium illud Dei mandatum, quod Josuæ & omnibus piis Regibus dedit, Liber iste Legis ne recedite ab ore tuo, &c. Jos. 1. 8. Si hoc mandatur Politicis, quomodo illud ad se non pertinere credunt Ecclesiastici? Si tantum Regi à negotiis politicis fuit otii, quid prætexent nostri Studiosi & Ministri, qui ad hoc tantum vocati sunt? Certe Alfonsus iste surget adversus nos in decretorio isto die & nostram socordiam gravissimâ infestatione coarguet.
units.tr: VII. The example of Alphonso, King of Aragon, is notable, who, as Panormitanus testifies, used to boast that amid the business of the kingdom he had read through the whole Bible with the glosses of Lyra forty times from beginning to end. Clearly this hero called to mind that earnest command of God which he gave to Joshua and all pious kings: This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, etc. (Josh. 1:8). If this is commanded to politicians, how do churchmen believe it does not pertain to them? If the king had such leisure from political business, what excuse will our students and ministers offer, who are called to this alone? Surely that Alphonso will rise against us on that decisive day and will convict our sloth with the most severe reproach.

units.la: Atque hæc adversus eos dicta sunto, qui se strenuè Theologiæ sacris operari existimant, cum extra verbum Dei, quod V. & N. Testamenti libris continetur, multum laborant, ejus assiduam lectionem in illud tempus reservantes, quo jam præbendâ potiti sunt. Piorum & doctorum virorum commentariis, compendiis, institutionibus, maneat suum æstimium (& habent illa magnos usus) præeat Catechetica institutio, utilibus disputationibus & id genus exercitiis nihil derogatur, tantùm præposterum illum studiorum ordinem & sacri codicis neglectum dicam, an contemtum, castigare volui. Cæteris, qui attentiores sunt in legendis comœdiis quàm Euangeliis, qui dum majori plausu lyram Flacci quàm Psalterium Davidis audiunt; qui exercitatiores sunt in artibus Nasonis aut Machiavello, quam S. Pauli Epistolis, queis denique præ Gentilium sterquiliniis Prophetarum & Apostolostolorum myrothecia nauteam olent, cujusmodi propudia non solum Hieron. & Salviani seculum habuit, istis, inquam, pro merito destringendis, alii strigiles adhibendi sunt.
units.tr: And let these things be said against those who think they work vigorously in sacred theology, while labouring much outside the Word of God, which is contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments, reserving its constant reading for the time when they have already obtained a benefice. Let the commentaries, compendia and institutes of pious and learned men keep their esteem (and they have great uses); let catechetical instruction go before; nothing is taken away from useful disputations and that kind of exercise. I have only wished to rebuke that topsy-turvy order of studies and the neglect, or rather the contempt, of the sacred codex. For the rest, who are more attentive in reading comedies than the Gospels, who while hearing Flaccus' lyre with greater applause than David's Psalter, who are more skilled in the arts of Naso or Machiavelli than in the Epistles of St. Paul, and finally, for whom the boxes of myrrh of the Prophets and Apostles smell of nasty stuff compared with the dung-heaps of the Gentiles (such shameful things the age of Jerome and Salvian also had), these, I say, must be struck down as they deserve, and others must be brought in as strigils.

units.la: Tu ergo Vir Dei fuge hos scopulos, ad quos multi navem suam illisere. Vos Naziræi Domini, non mihi substringite, studete scripturis sedulò, Est siquidem in iis tanta sapientia, das sie niemand can aus studiren noch aus lernen / wir werden wol schuler darinnen bleiben. Studete iis logicè ac distinctè perspiciendus, ut sensus habeatis exercitatos ad discretionem boni & mali: studete in iis, non pauculis tantùm dogmatis & controversiis, sed omni informationi & institutioni, in omnis virtutis ac pietatis methodo & experientia, ut homines Dei positis evadere, ad omne bonum opus perfectè instructi. Properatu fere omnes in studiis. Vobis non vacat aliquam ætatis partem in difficilibus & frivolis vugis perdere. Sit igitur hæc unica & prima vestra cura: ut scripturas, ex quibus & stamen & trama Theologia constat, ex quibus omnes conciones nostra debent vivere & spirare. Sacra Theologia, quam positivam vocant, rationem ex ipsis Scripturis haurite. Quod si hæc principia, hosfontes & omnia practica tanquam vulgaria, perria & omnibus exposita neglexeritis, languentes interim circa quastiones quasdam subtiliores & controversias implexas, ubi ad concionandum accesseritis, vobis metipsis forsan placebitis, sed prudentibus omnibus aliàs risum, aliàs misericordiam movebitis. Risum: quando vel minimâ arrepta ansa de controversiâ non necessariâ plura proferetis, quàm oneraria navis possit capere: misericordiam, cum de practicis verba factuři, difficilemve textum solide explicaturi ejusque germanum sensum investigaturi, in alium mundum videbimini translati. Commendatissimas ergo vobis habete Sacras literas. Alexander Magnus tanto erga Iliada Homeri flagrabat amore, ut illam veluti ἐφόδιον τῆς ψυχῆς, in castris circumferre, noctuque sub pulvinari suo eam locare fuerit solitus. Scipio Africanus Xenophontis παιδείαν nunquam è manibus deposuit. Hic est liber vitæ, Hic est pharmacum vitæ, hic est thesaurus inexhaustus, ad quem omnes universi mundi libri, quotquot fuerunt unquam, sunt aut futuri sunt, vanissima vanitas sunt: in quo ceu cornu aliquo copiæ semina omnium scientiarum pomprehendi, post authorem præfationis in Biblia Tigurina, Cl. Alstedius in suo Triumpho Biblico ostendit. In cujus præfatione profitetur sibi illud fuisse propositum, ut omnes, præceptores & discipuli, tandem aliquando intelligerent, à Bibliis Sacris esse INCI-PIENPIENDUM, inque illis DESINENDUM.
units.tr: So you, man of God, flee these reefs, on which many have dashed their ship. You Nazarites of the Lord, do not hold me back: study the Scriptures diligently. For there is in them such wisdom that no one can study or learn it out; we shall certainly remain pupils in them. Study them so that they may be seen logically and distinctly, that you may have senses trained to discern good and evil; study in them not only a few doctrines and controversies, but every instruction and training, in every method and experience of virtue and piety, so that the men of God may be perfectly equipped for every good work. Nearly everyone is in a hurry in their studies. You have no leisure to waste some part of your life on difficult and frivolous trifles. Let this therefore be your one and first care: the Scriptures, from which both the warp and the woof of theology consist, and from which all our sermons ought to live and breathe. Sacred theology, which they call positive, draw its reasoning from the Scriptures themselves. But if you neglect these principles, these sources and all practical matters as commonplace, worn out and exposed to everyone, and meanwhile languish over certain more subtle questions and tangled controversies, when you come to preach you may perhaps please yourselves, but you will move all sensible people sometimes to laughter, sometimes to pity. To laughter: when, having seized on the slightest handle of an unnecessary controversy, you will bring forth more than a freight ship could hold; to pity: when, about to speak on practical matters, or to explain solidly a difficult text and investigate its genuine sense, you will seem to have been transported into another world. Hold the Sacred Letters, therefore, in the highest regard. Alexander the Great so burned with love for the Iliad of Homer that he used to carry it about in camp as a provision for the soul [ἐφόδιον τῆς ψυχῆς], and at night to place it under his pillow. Scipio Africanus never put down the education of Xenophon [παιδείαν] from his hands. This is the book of life; this is the medicine of life; this is the inexhaustible treasure, compared with which all the books of the whole world, however many there have been or will be, are most empty vanity. In it, as from a horn of plenty, the seeds of all sciences are contained, as the author of the preface to the Zurich Bible, the illustrious Alsted, shows in his Biblical Triumph. In the preface to that work he professes that his purpose was that all, teachers and pupils, might at last understand that one must BEGIN from the Sacred Bibles and END in them.

units.la: ERROR GENERALIS. VII.
units.tr: GENERAL ERROR VII.

units.la: Omni Scriptura textui singulisque locis, aut saltem plerisque, duplicem inesse sensum, Literalem & Mysticum. Circa illum (Literalem) versari Theologiam *crassam, circa hunc (Mysticum) occupari Theologiam illam subtiliorem & spiritualem. Quin & uni loco plures posse subesse sensus literales.
units.tr: In every text of Scripture, and in each passage, or at least in most, there is a twofold sense, literal and mystical. Theology that is coarse is concerned with the literal sense, while the subtler and more spiritual theology is occupied with the mystical. Indeed, a single passage may have several literal senses.

units.la: Dici non potest, quàm fœdè intolerandus ille Allegorizandi pruritus sacras literas collutulaverit. Præcipua mali labes ab Origene fuit, qui Scripturam παντοτρεμίας quandam Anaxagoras ratus, quidvis ex quolibet elicuit vel potius expressit. Pestis ea in Ecclesiam semel introducta immane quantum proserpsit, & primarios etiam Ecclesiæ Doctores ceu pestilens aliquod sidus afflavit. Hieron. & Augustinus, qui in Origenem hoc nomine non semel invecti fuere, quoties in eundem lapidem ipsi impegêre? Transiit is morbus ad Scholasticos, ac etiamnum apud Pontificios in ipsa ἀκμῇ est. Scilicet hæc Allegoria tanquam formosa Meretrix est, qua ita blanditur hominibus, ut non possit non amari, præsertim ab hominibus otiosis, qui sine tentatione sunt. Tales enim se in medio Paradisi & gremio ipsius Dei esse putant, quando iis speculationibus indulgent. Et quidem Origenis licentiam non solum August. Hieron. & Patres alii, sed & ipsi Pontificii vehementer castigarunt. Vide inter alios Prologum Riberæ in Malachiam. Eam verò, quæ hodie etiamnum in Papatu viget, Allegorizandi pruriginem qui graviter castigarint producere possem quamplurimos. Mihi satis tres nominasse. Primus esto Sixtus Senensis. Is Bibliothecæ S. lib. 3. graviter damnandi sunt, inquit, inepti quidam nostrorum temporum expositores, qui rejecta prorsus literali expositione, tanquam re levissimi momenti & Grammaticis potius, ut ajunt, quàm Theologis digna, in singulis Scripturæ locis coactas quasdam & insulsas Allegorias protrahunt, vim inferentes divinæ scripturæ, & destructâ historiæ veritate, ridiculas cogitationes venditant, tanquam magna & arcana Ecclesiæ Sacramenta. Secundus erit Ribera, qui postquam præf. in Joëlem questus fuisset. paucissimos esse qui serio scripturis studeant & exactam earum intellitelligentiam quærant, rursus præfat. in Malach stomachatur, ex immensâ concionatorum multitudine qui mysticos sensus frequenter usurpant, esse admodum paucos, qui eorum erusendorum leges & præcepta norint. Ex quorum numero videas plurimos, inquit, qui audacter & quasi ex tripode mysticos sensus proferunt, cum historicum ignorent, & ignorare velint, fortasse, ut, conscientiâ non clamante, licentius ac securius aberrent. Tertius esto Serarius, qui Proleg. Bibl. cap.21. quæst. 11. postquam excusassset quosdam Patres, hæc subjicit, nam quod recentiores quidam & natu jam grandiores eadem hæc facilitent neque uno in loco neque per imprudentiam subinde, sed fere semper & destinatò, scientes & volentes literarum sensum negligant, eum nesciant & aliter quàm ipse patiatur, ad ineptas detorqueant allegorias, non patrum ipsorum, sed κακοζήλων istorum culpa est. Ideo enim sua illi (Patres) fassi sunt errata, ne imitaretur ullus. Ex quorum testimoniis illud simul liquet, huic Allegorizationi prætendi quidem facilitatem, vilitatem & paupertatem sensus literalis, sed veram causam in ejusdem difficultate latere. Id quod egregiè docet Senensis dicto loco, Hos (Allegoriis nimium deditos) amantissimè, inquit, obtestor & obsecro, ut considerent, literalem expositionem non esse rem usque adeo vulgarem, vilem ac protritam, & omnibus, ut ipsi jactitant, puerorum pædagogis perviam, sed esse expositionem omnium difficillimam ac maximè operosam, propter inusitatas & abstrusas linguæ S. proprietates, & propter copiam rerum difficillimarum, artium vid. scientiarum & disciplinarum omnium, quæ sub historico scripturæ sensu comprehenduntur. Testes hujus rei sunt duo clarissimi Ecclesiæ Latinæ lumina, Hieron. & Augustinus, qui non nisi jam natu grandes ausi sunt admovere manum Historicæ explanationi, postquam multos annos mexplanationibus mysticis, veluti studiis facilioribus consumsissent. Subjungit postea testimonium Hieron. ex præfatione ejus in Commentarios ad Abdiam, Si Apostolus, inquit, proficit & quotidie prætéritorum oblivisens, in priora se extendit, &c. quanto magis ego mererì debeo veniam, quod adolescentia meâ provocatus ardore & studio scripturarum, allegorice interpretatus sum Abdiam Prophetam, cujus Historiam (id est sensum literalem) nesciebam. Ardebat animus cognitione mystica, &c. Literas seculi noveram & ob id putabam me librum legere posse signatum. Postquam autem narrasset librum istum ab alio fuisse laudatum, fateor, inquit, miratus sum, quod quamtumvis aliquis male scripserit, invenit lectorem similem sibi. Ille prædicabat, ego erubescerebefcebam. Ille ferebat ad cœlum, ego demisso capite confiteri meum pudorem prohibebar. Et tandem, Libere profiteor, inquit, illud fuisse puerilis ingenii, & hoc, quod nunc scribo, matura senectutis. Quid Augustinus? Is primo Retractionum volumine, Cum de Genesi duos libros contra Manichæos, inquit, condidissem, quoniam secundum allegoricam expositionem verba tractaveram, non ausus naturalium rerum tanta secreta ad literam exponere, id est, quomodo possent secundum historicam proprietatem, quæ ibi dicta sunt, accipi, volui experiri in hoc quoque negotiosissimo ac difficillimo opere, quid valerem, sed in scripturis exponendis tyrocinium meum sub tanta sarcina mole succubuit, & nondum perfecto uno libro, ab eo, quem sustinere non poteram, labore conquievi. Hæc Augustinus, Ex quibus perspicuum sit, inquit Senensis, historicam explanationem non esse ab expositoribus nostri seculi negligendam quasi ignobilem trivialem & ineruditam, cum ipsa omnes fere expositiones mysticas nobilium ac doctissimarum rerum prastantia antecellat. Ex quibus omnibus & illud, opinor, perspicuum sit, hujus morbi matrem, literalis sensus difficultatem: nutricem vero pigritiam Clericorum fuisse, ac etiamnum esse. Atque hæc sibi quoque dicta sciant nostri illi καταζηλοι, qui dum nimis familiariter Pontificiorum postillis utuntur & conceptibus prædicabilibus, ut vocant, inversantur assidue, in eadem vestigia pedes ponunt. Non sum propheta, nec prophetæ filius. Tamen
units.tr: One cannot say how foully that intolerable itch for allegorizing has defiled the sacred letters. The main source of the evil was Origen, who, thinking Scripture a kind of all-sided pliability (παντοτρεμίας) after the manner of Anaxagoras, drew, or rather forced, whatever he pleased out of any passage. Once this plague was introduced into the Church, it spread enormously and breathed upon even the leading teachers of the Church like some baneful star. How often did Jerome and Augustine, who attacked Origen on this account more than once, stumble over the same stone themselves? The disease passed over to the Scholastics, and even now it is at its height among the Papists. For this allegory is like a beautiful harlot, who so flatters men that she cannot fail to be loved, especially by idle men who are free from temptation. For such men think they are in the midst of Paradise and in the very bosom of God when they indulge in those speculations. Indeed, not only Augustine, Jerome and other Fathers, but the Papists themselves have sharply censured Origen's licence. See among others the preface of Ribera on Malachi. As for the itch for allegorizing that still flourishes in Papacy today, I could name very many who have severely censured it. Let three suffice for me. The first shall be Sixtus of Siena. In his Bibliotheca Sancta, book 3, he says: "Certain foolish expositors of our own times are to be gravely condemned, who, having altogether rejected the literal exposition as something of the lightest importance, fit rather for grammarians, as they say, than for theologians, pull out forced and insipid allegories from each passage of Scripture. They do violence to the divine Scripture, and, with the truth of history destroyed, they peddle ridiculous notions as great and hidden mysteries of the Church." The second will be Ribera, who, after complaining in his preface on Joel that there are very few who study the Scriptures seriously and seek an exact understanding of them, again grumbles in his preface on Malachi that among the immense multitude of preachers who frequently make use of mystical senses, there are very few who know the rules and precepts for drawing them out. Among their number, he says, you may see very many who boldly and, as it were, from the tripod, put forward mystical senses, although they are ignorant of the historical sense, and perhaps want to remain ignorant, so that, with conscience not crying out, they may go astray more freely and more safely. The third shall be Serarius, who, in Prolegomena Bibliorum chapter 21, question 11, after excusing certain Fathers, adds these words: for that certain more recent writers, and men already advanced in years, make the same mistakes, not at one place or by occasional carelessness, but almost always and deliberately, knowing and willing to neglect the literal sense, not knowing it, or twisting it into foolish allegories otherwise than the text itself allows, is the fault not of the Fathers themselves but of those zealots who are no better than they should be. For the Fathers themselves confessed their errors so that no one would imitate them. From these testimonies it is also clear that the ease, cheapness and poverty of the literal sense are put forward as the pretext for this allegorizing, but that the true cause lies hidden in its difficulty. The Sienese teaches this admirably in the passage cited: I most earnestly beg and entreat these men (who are too much given to allegories) that they consider that the literal exposition is not so common, cheap and trite a matter, open to all, as they boast, to the tutors of boys, but is the most difficult and most laborious of all expositions, on account of the unusual and abstruse peculiarities of the sacred language, and on account of the multitude of most difficult things, of the arts, that is, of all the sciences and disciplines, which are comprehended under the historical sense of Scripture. The witnesses to this are the two most famous lights of the Latin Church, Jerome and Augustine, who did not dare to lay hand to the historical exposition until they were already advanced in years, after they had spent many years on mystical explanations, as on easier studies. Then he adds Jerome's testimony from his preface to his commentary on Obadiah: If the Apostle, he says, makes progress, forgetting daily what lies behind, and stretches himself out towards what is before, etc., how much more ought I to deserve pardon, because, provoked in my youth by the ardour and zeal for the Scriptures, I interpreted allegorically the prophet Obadiah, whose history (that is, the literal sense) I did not know. My mind burned with mystical knowledge, etc. I knew the letters of the age, and for that reason I thought I could read a book that was sealed. And after he had related that this book had been praised by another, I confess, he says, that I was amazed that however badly someone writes, he finds a reader like himself. He praised it to the skies, I blushed. He lifted it up to heaven, I was held back, with head bowed, from confessing my shame. And at last: I freely declare, he says, that the former was the work of a childish mind, and that which I now write, of mature old age. What of Augustine? In the first volume of his Retractions he says: When I had composed two books on Genesis against the Manichaeans, since I had handled the words according to an allegorical exposition, not daring to expound such great secrets of natural things literally, that is, how they could be understood according to the historical propriety of what is said there, I wished to test in this also, most laborious and most difficult work, what I could do; but my apprenticeship in expounding the Scriptures succumbed under so great a burden, and, with one book not yet finished, I rested from that labour which I could not sustain. So Augustine. From these things, says the Sienese, it is clear that the historical explanation is not to be neglected by the expositors of our age as something ignoble, trivial and unlearned, since it itself surpasses almost all mystical expositions in the excellence of noble and most learned matters. From all these things, I think, it is also clear that the mother of this disease was the difficulty of the literal sense, and that its nurse was, and still is, the laziness of the clergy. And let those zealots of ours know that these words are said to them as well, who, while they too familiarly use the postils and preachers' conceits of the Papists, as they call them, are constantly busied with them, and set their feet in the same tracks. I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet. Yet

units.la: Credite me vobis solum recitare Sibyllæ,
units.tr: Believe me, I recite to you only what the Sibyl says.

units.la: Si hæc concionandi & sacras literas explicandi ratio una cum Theologia Scholastica denuò irrepserit, posteriora longè pejora erunt prioribus. Principiis ergo obstate vos,
units.tr: If this method of preaching and of expounding the sacred letters should creep in again, together with Scholastic theology, the later times will be far worse than the earlier. Therefore resist the beginnings yourselves.

units.la: Οἱς πιστὶν ἐπιπλεγόμενοι κρι τινα μάμηλα.
units.tr: Those who, trusting in these things, ... certain ... [Οἱς πιστὶν ἐπιπλεγόμενοι κρι τινα μάμηλα]

units.la: Sed dices, An ergo omni Allegoriæ fenestram claudis? nullusne ergo in Sacris literis est sensus Allegoricus? Respondeo, illud religiosè cavendum esse Scripturarum interpreti, ne alienum & quem S. Sanctus non intendit, sensum textui alicui, quem explicandum habet, affingat, eumve ita accommodet, ut accommodatio ea literæ adversetur. Etiamsi enim sensum maximè pium ei affingat, vel ad rem quam maximè, sit venia verbo, ædificativam cum accommodet, semper abutitur scriptura. Nullus omnino fidei articulus est, nullum dogma verum, cui probando non extet in Scripturæ thesauro expressus textus. Nulla pietatis pars, nulla virtus, nullum officium Christiani hominis, cui commendando desit in eodem expressum testimonium. Eadem in falsis dogmatibus confutandis & peccatis coarguendis ratio est. Quæ ergo nos cogit necessitas adeo licenter in sacris literis <bl>ἀλληγορεῖν</bl>;
units.tr: But you will say: do you then close every window to allegory? Is there therefore no allegorical sense in the sacred letters? I answer that the interpreter of Scripture must carefully take care not to attach to some text, which he has to explain, a sense that the Holy Spirit did not intend, or to fit it so that this accommodation runs against the letter. For even if he attaches a most pious sense, or, to put it so, one most useful for building up, and adapts it, Scripture is always abused. There is no article of faith at all, no true doctrine, for whose proof there is not an express text in the treasury of Scripture. No part of piety, no virtue, no duty of a Christian man, for whose commendation the express testimony in the same is lacking. The same method holds in refuting false doctrines and in reproving sins. What necessity, then, compels us to allegorize so freely in the sacred letters? [ἀλληγορεῖν]

units.la: Pontificii accuratiores, ut Senensis, Bellarminus & alii duplicem Scripturæ sensum faciunt, literalem unum, qui & Historicus & Grammaticus vocatur; Mysticum seu spiritualem alterum, qui tamen teste * Maldonato, & ipse aliquando literalis est. Est enim ille literalis, qui proximè per ipsa verba, sive propria, sive figurata sint, significatur, vel ut Glassius, quem intendit proxmè Spiritus sanctus, & qui ex verbis rectè juxta dicentis scopum antecedentium & consequentium cohærentiam, scripturæque analogiam eruitur sive verba ista sint propria sive tropica. Consentiunt præter Scholasticos plerosque Ribera, præf. in Malach. Azorius Instit. moral. 8. 2. & alii recentiores. Sensus ergo literalis subdividitur in proprium & figuratum, quorum ille (proprius) à quibusdam strictè literalis, Grammaticus: hic (figuratus) non solum Metaphoricus, per Synecd. spiciei, & Tropicus, vocibus tropus & figura teste Quintil. aliquando idem significantibus, sed & Rhetoricus, Allegoricus & Spiritualis, & Mysticus & Propheticus à patribus aliisque nominatur. E. Gr. Pf. 66. Ingressi sumus per ignem & aquam, id est verlati fuimus in præsentissimis periculis, sensus literalis est, ut vulgò iste terminus usurpatur, hunc enim sensum Spiritus sanctus proximè intendit. At quia non vocibus propriis sed Metaphoricis is exprimitur, est literalis figuratus, Metaphoricus tropicus, vel Rhetoricus quasi opponeres literali Grammatico. Hunc Patres quidam Allegoricum vocant, quia sicuti Metaphora aliquando omnes troporum modos significat, ita & Allegoria. Allegoricum ergo sic loquendo opponunt literali proprio seu Grammatico. Vocant & Propheticum, quod prophetis ejusmodi loquendi modi familiarissimi sint: & Spirtualem, teste Salmer. ad Eph. 5. Spirtum literæ id est τῷ πνεύματι opponentes Habitabit lupus cum agno, Jef. 2. secundum literam falsum est, inquit Hieron. id est secundum literalem proprium, seu κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα. Hæc diligenter à Tyronibus notanda sunt, ne terminorum diversitate hac in materiâ distrahantur & fluctuent.
units.tr: The more careful Papists, such as the Sienese, Bellarmine and others, make a twofold sense of Scripture: one literal, which is also called historical and grammatical; the other mystical or spiritual, which nevertheless, as Maldonatus testifies, is itself sometimes literal. For that is literal which is signified most directly by the words themselves, whether they are proper or figurative; or, as Glassius puts it, that which the Holy Spirit directly intends, and which is drawn from the words, rightly, according to the scope of the speaker, the coherence of what precedes and follows, and the analogy of Scripture, whether the words are proper or tropical. Besides the Scholastics, most of them, Ribera (preface on Malachi), Azorius (Institutiones morales 8.2) and other more recent writers agree. The literal sense, therefore, is subdivided into the proper and the figurative. Of these, the proper is called by some strictly literal or grammatical; the figurative is called not only metaphorical, by synecdoche of species, and tropical, the words trope and figure, as Quintilian testifies, sometimes meaning the same thing, but also rhetorical, allegorical, spiritual, mystical and prophetic by the Fathers and others. For example, Psalm 66: We went through fire and water, that is, we were brought into the most pressing dangers. This is the literal sense, as this term is commonly used, for the Holy Spirit intends this sense most directly. But because it is expressed not by proper words but by metaphorical ones, it is literal-figurative, metaphorical-tropical, or rhetorical, as if you were opposing it to the literal-grammatical. Some Fathers call this the allegorical, because just as metaphor sometimes signifies all the modes of tropes, so does allegory. Therefore they oppose the allegorical, so speaking, to the proper or grammatical literal. They also call it prophetic, because such modes of speaking are most familiar to the prophets; and spiritual, as Salmeron says on Ephesians 5, opposing the spirit of the letter, that is, [τῷ πνεύματι]. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, Isaiah 2, is false according to the letter, says Jerome, that is, according to the literal-proper sense, or [κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα]. These things must be carefully noted by beginners, lest in this matter they be distracted and waver by the diversity of terms.

units.la: Sensus literalis figuratus seu Metaphoricus rursus duplex est. Aut enim Metaphora est in una, voceant in pluribus, Si in pluribus, Allegoricus commodissimè & propriissimè vocatur cum nihil aliud sit Allegoria quàm continuata Metaphora, seu Metaphorarum congeries. Ita Allegoricè interpretantur illud Super aspidem & Basiliscum ambulabis, conculcabis Leones & dracones Pf.91. Sic, Si manus tua scandalizaverit te abscinde eam, &c. Quia autem eum sensum Allegoricum intendit Spiritus S. idem sensus literalis est, sed improprius, figuratus, &c.
units.tr: The figurative or metaphorical literal sense is again of two kinds. For either the metaphor lies in one word, or the words are used in several. If it lies in several, it is most conveniently and most properly called allegorical, since allegory is nothing other than a continued metaphor, or a collection of metaphors. So they interpret allegorically You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you shall trample the lions and dragons, Ps. 91. Likewise If your hand offend you, cut it off, etc. But since the Holy Spirit intends that allegorical sense, the sense is still literal, though improper and figurative, etc.

units.la: Mysticus seu Spiritualis sensus, prout literali opponitur ab Azorio, quem non voces primò & proximè significant, sed res vocibus significata. Glassius, qui ex intentione Spiritus S. alio refertur, quàm ad id quod verba immediatè significant. Serarius, qui per verba remotè ac mediatè significatur, propinquè verò & immediatè per res, quaspropinque & immediate significant verba. Is vulgo dividitur à Pontificiis in Allegoricum Tropologicum & Anagogicum, idque juxta triplicem differentiam temporis, praesentis, praeteriti, futuri, ut vult Senensis. Allegorica expositio, inquit, praeteritarum in veteri Lege umbrarum praesagia manifestat. Tropologica, quae in sacris literis dicta & gesta sunt, ad praesentis vitae moralem institutionem convertit. Anagogica ad futurae beatitudinis & coelestis gloriae sublimiora mysteria animum sustollit. Accuratius tamen Gillius, citante Glassio, divisionis istius integritatem & adaequationem sic colligit, Veritas, inquit, quam divina litera per figuras rerum tradunt, ordinatur vel ad recte operandum, vel ad recte credendum. Si ad recte operandum, est sensus tropologicus; si ad recte credendum, opus est distinctione ex parte credibilium. Ut enim author est Dionysius, status praesentis Ecclesiae est medius inter statum Synagogae & Ecclesiae triumphantis, & ideo V.T. fuit figura novi, utrumque verò status beatifici: & ita sensus mysticus ordinatus ad credendum, fundatus in figuratione N.T. per Vetus, dicitur Allegoricus: quatenus autem fundatur in eo modo figurationis, quo Vetus & N. sunt typus Ecclesiae triumphantis, est Anagogicus. His labefactandis ex ipsis Pontificiis multa adduci possent. Ipse Bellarm. fatetur distinctionem eam Mysticorum sensuum non semper observari à veteribus, utpote qui omnes istos vocant Allegoricos. Et certè quid aliud est Anagoge quam Allegoria? ut non malè Hugo de S. Victore in prologo libri de Scriptura tres tantum sensus enumeret, historicum, Allegoricum, tropologicum. [Ita & Vasques in 1. disp.16. c.2. & Villavincentius.] Quod verò Allegoricum definiunt eum, cum res in V. Testamento gestae, novi Testamenti mysteria significant, quomodo subsistet, si verum illud est, quod Bellarmino teste, multi sentiunt in novo etiam Testamento sensum inesse Allegoricum? juxta quem Augustinus tractatu 122. in Joh. exponit capturam piscium, quando rete scindebatur, Luc. 5. quam sententiam ipse quoque probat. Ad haec, cur non & Catagogicum sensum faciunt, cum verba aut facta referuntur ad Gehennam & poenas infernales? nihil ergo in istis est solidi. Tropologicus & Anagogicus, si sine violentia rite adhibeantur, nihil aliud sunt quam modi quidam sensum literalem ad distinctas materias applicandi. Quod vero ad illa loca attinet, os non confringetis in eo, Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum, & quae istius generis sunt alia nec non historiam aenei serpentis, Hagaris & Sarae, Gal. 4. Jonae, &c. in istis typi & res typis adumbratae considerari debent, neque necesse est asserere, istorum locorum significationem continere duplicem sensum verborum; Est enim illic unus sensus verborum, alius typorum, qui cum ad res alias significandas accommodantur, secum ferunt verba, quibus explicantur. Pontificii contendunt, inquit Cl. Amesius, unum eundemque cultum in imagine & exemplari: quomodo igitur & unus & idem sensus verborum ad typum posit referri & ad rem typo adumbratam? Totus integer sensus, inquit * Witakerus, non est in verbis proprie sumptis, sed pars in typo, pars in re ipsa, quae gesta fuit. In altero horum seorsim & per se considerato, pars tantum sensus continetur, ex utrisque vero simul conjunctis plenus & perfectus sensus absolvitur. Haec Witak. agens de duabus uxoribus Abrahae, Galat. 4.
units.tr: The mystical or spiritual sense, as opposed to the literal, is defined by Azorius as that which the words do not signify first and immediately, but the things signified by the words. Glassius defines it as that which, by the intention of the Holy Spirit, is referred to something other than what the words immediately signify. Serarius defines it as that which is signified remotely and mediately by the words, but nearly and immediately by the things, which the words signify nearly and immediately. The Papists commonly divide this into allegorical, tropological and anagogical, according to the threefold difference of time (present, past, future), as Senensis would have it. Allegorical exposition, he says, makes plain the foreshadowings of past shadows in the Old Law. Tropological applies what has been said and done in the sacred letters to the moral instruction of the present life. Anagogical lifts the mind up to the higher mysteries of future blessedness and heavenly glory. More exactly, however, Gillius, cited by Glassius, gathers the completeness and fit of this division thus: The truth which the divine letter hands down through the figures of things is directed either to acting rightly or to believing rightly. If to acting rightly, it is the tropological sense; if to believing rightly, a distinction is needed on the side of the things to be believed. For, as Dionysius is the author, the state of the present Church is midway between the state of the Synagogue and that of the triumphant Church; and so the Old Testament was a figure of the New, and both are figures of the blessed state. Thus the mystical sense directed to believing, grounded in the figuring of the New Testament through the Old, is called allegorical; but insofar as it is grounded in that mode of figuring by which the Old and New are types of the triumphant Church, it is anagogical. Many arguments against these distinctions could be drawn from the Papists themselves. Bellarmine himself admits that the ancients did not always observe this distinction of mystical senses, since they all call them allegorical. And indeed, what else is anagoge but allegory? So Hugh of St. Victor, in the prologue to his book on Scripture, rightly lists only three senses: historical, allegorical, tropological. [So too Vasquez, in disp. 1, ch. 16, and Villavicentius.] But as for defining the allegorical sense as that in which the things done in the Old Testament signify the mysteries of the New, how will that hold, if it is true what many think, as Bellarmine reports, that an allegorical sense is also present in the New Testament? By this sense Augustine, in tractate 122 on John, expounds the catch of fishes when the net was breaking, Luke 5, and he himself also approves this view. Besides, why do they not also make a catagogical sense, when words or deeds refer to hell and the punishments of the lower world? So there is nothing solid in these distinctions. The tropological and anagogical, if rightly applied without violence, are nothing other than certain ways of applying the literal sense to distinct subjects. As for those passages, You shall not break a bone in it, Out of Egypt I have called my son, and the others of that kind, as well as the story of the bronze serpent, of Hagar and Sarah, Gal. 4, of Jonah, etc., in these the types and the things foreshadowed by the types ought to be considered. Nor is it necessary to assert that the meaning of these passages contains a double sense of the words. For there is one sense of the words and another of the types, and when these are applied to signify other things, they carry along with them the words by which they are explained. The Papists contend, says the distinguished Amesius, that one and the same worship belongs to the image and to the exemplar: how, then, can one and the same sense of the words be referred both to the type and to the thing foreshadowed by the type? The whole and complete sense, says Whitaker, is not in the words taken properly, but part is in the type, part in the thing itself which was done. In either of these taken separately and by itself, only part of the sense is contained; but from both joined together the full and perfect sense is made complete. Whitaker says this in discussing the two wives of Abraham, Gal. 4.

units.la: Licet itaque haec sit multorum Euangelicorum sententia, unius loci & contextus unum tantum esse sensum a Spiritu S. intentum, quem literalem vocant, quam sententiam * Alphonso Toftato etiam adscribit Serarius, & egregie defendunt nostri, nominatim vero Cl. Witakerus: Ego tamen profiteor me nolle super hac quaestione cum quopiam serram contentionis reciprocare, Annon in quibusdam V. T. locis duplex sit sensus, literalis unus, Mysticus alter, in illis vid. V. T. locis, quos ipsa Scriptura in N. T. ostendit praeter literalem etiam continere sensum mysticum? ut Historia Hagaris & Historia Jonae. os non confringes, Ex Ægyto vocavi filium meum quo tramite incedens Glassius Mysticum subdividit in Allegoricum, Typicum & Parabolicum. Allegoricum vocat quando Historia Scripturae vere gesta ad Mysterium quoddam, sive spiritualem doctrinam ex Sp. Sancti intentione refertur. Adducitque haec exempla, non alligabis bovi triturantii, quod Allegorice explicatur 1. Cor. 9. 9. Exod. 34.29. de velamine faciei Mosis Confer. 2. Cor. 3.7. ubi historia ista de Judaeorum caecitate exponitur. Pf. 19. 5. Confer Rom. 10. 18. Gen. 2. 24. Confer Ephef. 5. 31. Historia uxoris Loth, Confer Luc. 17. 32. Praeceptum de panibus azymis, Confer 1. Cor. 5. verf. 7. 8. Historia duarum uxorum Abrahae, Galat. 4. 22. Typicum vocat, quando sub externis factis seu propheticis Visionibus, res occultae sive praesentes sive futurae figurantur & praesertim, quando res gestae V. T. adumbrant res gestas N. T. Parabolicum definit, quando res aliqua ut gesta narratur, & ad aliud spirituale designandum refertur. Anoscit tamen postea, accuratè loquendo, typicum & parabolicum sub Allegorico, uti sub genere species, fere contineri, rursusque inculcat, seper sensum mysticum duntaxat cum intelligere, quem Scriptura ipsa sui ipsius interpres dilucidè commonstrat, adeo ut vel hinc videas, quàm nihil haec D. Glassii sententia isti Allegorizandi, quam hic taxamus. licentiae patrocinetur.
units.tr: Although this is the view of many evangelicals, that a single passage and its context have only one sense intended by the Holy Spirit, which they call literal, a view which Serarius also ascribes to Alphonso Toletus, and which our men defend admirably, especially the distinguished Whitaker: Yet I for my part declare that I am unwilling to enter into a contest of words on this question. Is there not, in some passages of the Old Testament, a double sense, one literal and another mystical, in those Old Testament passages which Scripture itself, in the New Testament, shows to contain a mystical sense besides the literal? such as the story of Hagar and the story of Jonah, You shall not break a bone, Out of Egypt I have called my son. Following this path, Glassius subdivides the mystical sense into allegorical, typical and parabolic. He calls it allegorical when a history of Scripture truly done is referred, by the intention of the Holy Spirit, to some mystery or spiritual teaching. He adduces these examples: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, which is explained allegorically in 1 Cor. 9.9; Exod. 34.29, on the veil of Moses' face, compare 2 Cor. 3.7, where that story is expounded of the blindness of the Jews; Ps. 19.5, compare Rom. 10.18; Gen. 2.24, compare Eph. 5.31; the story of Lot's wife, compare Luke 17.32; the precept about unleavened bread, compare 1 Cor. 5.7, 8; the story of Abraham's two wives, Gal. 4.22. He calls it typical when hidden things, whether present or future, are foreshadowed under external deeds or prophetic visions, and especially when the deeds of the Old Testament foreshadow the deeds of the New. He defines the parabolic sense as when some thing is narrated as done and is referred to the designation of something else spiritual. Later, however, he acknowledges that, speaking accurately, the typical and parabolic are for the most part contained under the allegorical, as a species under its genus; and again he insists that one should understand only the mystical sense which Scripture itself clearly shows by being its own interpreter. So, even from this, you may see how little this view of Glassius lends support to that licence of allegorizing which we are censuring here.

units.la: Admittamus ergo in paucu!s istis locis cum literali sensum aliquem mysticum, innatum, quem ipsa Scriptura aperuit. At facessant omnes ab otiosis hominibus illati. Quis enim eorum usus? An ad correctionem, consolationem, informationem? Atqui semper ad manum habere potes locum Scripturae, qui eum tibi usum in sensu literali praestet. An ad probanda vel confutanda dogmata? Atqui ipsi Pontificii docent, ex solo sensu literali peti debere argumenta efficacia, quia certum est, verba Bellarmini, eum esse sensum Spiritus S. Sed sensus Mystici varii sunt, & non semper constat an sint à Sp. sancto intenti, atque haec est communis sententia Theologorum, inquit Vega. Si nihil solidi ex sensu Mystico potest inferri, si dubius ille & incertus, quorsum ad eum in concionibus & scripturae explanatione obhaerescimus? Longe alia ratio est, quando eum à Spiritu S. fuisse intentum ex ipsa Scriptura constat, tunc enim tam efficacia argumenta ex eo, quàm ex literali peti posse, Serarius, Junius, Amesius & Glassius ostendunt. Nulla est vera sententia, ex qua non aliae verae deduci possint. Ex omni sensu à Spiritu S. intento disputari potest. Si ex sensu mystico disputari non potest (non ago jam de eo quem ipsa Scriptura pandit) quomodo est sensus? Sensum enim scriptura vocare, quod Spiritus S. non sentit aut intendit, id alienum est ab omni sensu inquit Cl. Amesius. Applicetur scriptura & rite accommodetur: Ex exemplo uno, E. G. non alligabis os bovi triturantì, extruatur præceptum generale, vid. Æquissimum esse ut unusquisque ex labore suo vivat, id quod in Lege Mosis atque adeo universa Scriptura frequens est, vel per legitimam ratiocinationem utilia ex ea deducantur consectaria, sicuti quidam putant Apostolo 1.Cor.9.9. ex citato loco per ratiocinationem à minori colligere, Verbi D. ministros esse alendos, vocentur isti modi vel Allegoria, vel Tropologia, vel Anagoge, vel si quid occurrat simile, aut vocetur hic sensus mysticus, mediatus: literalis, immediatus, vitentur tantummodo hi errores,
units.tr: Let us grant, then, in these few passages, along with the literal sense, some mystical sense inborn, which Scripture itself has opened up. But let all the things brought in by idle men depart. For what use do they have? Is it for correction, consolation, instruction? Yet you can always have at hand a passage of Scripture that will serve you for that purpose in the literal sense. Is it for proving or refuting doctrines? Yet the Papists themselves teach that strong arguments must be drawn from the literal sense alone, because it is certain, in Bellarmine's words, that this is the sense of the Holy Spirit. But the mystical senses are various, and it is not always clear whether they were intended by the Holy Spirit; and this, says Vega, is the common view of the theologians. If nothing solid can be inferred from a mystical sense, if it is doubtful and uncertain, why do we cling to it in sermons and in the explanation of Scripture? The case is quite different when it is clear from Scripture itself that the Holy Spirit intended it; for then strong arguments can be drawn from it just as well as from the literal sense, as Serarius, Junius, Amesius and Glassius show. There is no true sense from which other true things cannot be deduced. From every sense intended by the Holy Spirit, disputation can proceed. If nothing can be argued from a mystical sense (I am not yet speaking of the sense which Scripture itself lays open), what sense is it at all? For to call something a sense of Scripture which the Holy Spirit does not perceive or intend is foreign to every idea of sense, says the distinguished Amesius. Let Scripture be applied and properly accommodated. For example, from You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, let a general precept be framed, namely that it is most just that each man should live by his own labour, something frequent in the Law of Moses and indeed in all Scripture; or let useful consequences be drawn from it by lawful reasoning, as some think the Apostle does in 1 Cor. 9.9, arguing from the cited passage by an argument from the less to the greater, that the ministers of the Word of God should be supported. Let such modes be called either Allegory, or Tropology, or Anagoge, or, if something similar comes up, let this be called the mediate mystical sense, and the literal the immediate. Only let those errors be avoided,

units.la: I. Unius ejusdemque loci varios posse esse sensus literales. Hæc est communis Theologorum opinio inquit Azorius Instit. moral. 8. 2. Bellarm. licet in Psalmorum explicatione eam sententiam videatur probabile, tamen in controversiis non ausus fuit eam astruere. Dicit enim solummodo, hanc sententiam non esse improbabilem * Medina autem secutus Alensem & Albertum diversum sentit. Becanus dicit hanc quæstionem non esse ab Ecclesia definitam, Ribera comm. in Hoseæ cap. x i. Medinæ astipulatur. Et quidem hi rectissimè sentiunt, Aliorum enim sententia æquivocationem in sacras literas invehit, quibus tamen Petrus tribuit βεβαιότητα id est firmitatem, 2. Epist. 1.19. Ea autem cum pluralitate sensuum literalium non potest consistere. Quidquid enim pluribus, quàm uno, constat sensibus, inquit Medina & significationibus, illud est ambiguum, & proinde incertam, nec definitam parit sententiam. Deinde, in unâ eademque sententiâ plus uno, inquit Glassius, verum esse nequit. Verum enim & unum convertitur. Jam verò in Scripturæ verbis & sententiis summa proponitur veritas. Una ergo tantùm unius loci est veritas. Addunt, si plures essent sensus literales unius loci, nullum argumentum firmum deduci posset ex ullo Scr. loco, etiam juxta sensum literalem. Nunquid enim termini semper essent ambigui? Neque obstat, quod multa sint Scripturæ testimonia, quæ Patres variè secundum literam interpetantur, Inde n. teste Becano Jesuitâ, non sequitur plures in istis locis esse sensus literales. Sæpe enim fit ut plures illi sensus inter se pugnent. Ista autem pugna non potest esse à Spiritu S. [Addit. Rev. Rivetus. Etiam cum non pugnant illi sensus, unum semper esse loci proprium, alium vero esse proprie sensum, sed tantum comparationem dictorum factorumve per analogiam : quæ quidem ad sensum literalem pertinebit, sed non tollet unitatem sensus præcipui, ex quo desumetur analogia, neque novum sensum faciet. Sic dico, cujusque loci unus tantum est sensus literalis. Cæteri qui adjiciuntur vel ad rem nonfaciunt, vel consequentiæ tantum sunt ex genuino sensu deductæ.] Neque obstat, multa esse testimonia, quæ ex Ebraeo textu diversimodè translata sunt. Nec enim inde sequitur, inquit Becanus, plures unius loci esse sensus literales : sed tantùm plures esse sensus literales secundum varias ejusdem loci translationes.
units.tr: I. That one and the same passage may have several literal senses. This is the common opinion of theologians, says Azorius (Instit. moral. 8. 2). Bellarmine, although in his explanation of the Psalms he seems to favour this view, did not dare to assert it in the controversies. He says only that this opinion is not improbable. Medina, however, followed Alensis and Albertus and thinks otherwise. Becanus says that this question has not been settled by the Church, and Ribera, in his commentary on Hosea chapter 11, agrees with Medina. Indeed these men judge most rightly. The opposing view introduces equivocation into the sacred letters, to which Peter ascribes firmness [βεβαιότητα], that is, steadiness (2 Pet. 1:19). But that firmness cannot coexist with a plurality of literal senses. For whatever has more than one sense or meaning, says Medina, is ambiguous and therefore yields an uncertain and indefinite statement. Next, says Glassius, in one and the same statement more than one thing cannot be true, since the true and the one are convertible. Now in the words and statements of Scripture the highest truth is set forth. Therefore each passage has only one truth. They add that if a passage had several literal senses, no firm argument could be drawn from any text of Scripture, even according to its literal sense; for would the terms not always be ambiguous? Nor does it stand in the way that there are many testimonies of Scripture which the Fathers interpret variously according to the letter. For, as the Jesuit Becanus testifies, it does not follow from this that such passages have several literal senses. Often those several senses are opposed to one another, and such conflict cannot come from the Holy Spirit. [Added by the Reverend Rivet. Even when the senses do not conflict, each passage has one proper sense, and the other is not a proper sense but only a comparison of words or deeds by analogy. This will pertain to the literal sense, but it does not destroy the unity of the principal sense from which the analogy is drawn, nor does it make a new sense. So I say: each passage has only one literal sense. The others that are added either do not bear on the matter, or are merely consequences deduced from the genuine sense.] Nor does it stand in the way that there are many testimonies which have been translated in various ways from the Hebrew text. For, says Becanus, it does not follow from this that a passage has several literal senses, but only that it has several literal senses according to the various translations of the same passage.

units.la: Neque hoc probat locus iste, Ex ÆGypto vocavi filium meum, Hos.11. Math.2. Quatenus enim ille locus explicatur de Christo, sensum allegoricum esse contendit Ribera. Ego verò assentior Jansenio, qui accommodatitium sensum & hic & alibi constituit. Cui ex nostris quoque astipulatur Sculteius. Verba Sculteti hæc sunt, ad locum, ut impleretur quod dictum est, ex ÆGypto, &c. Mat. 2. Verba illa, ut impleretur, non necessariò nos huc vid. locum illum Hoseæ literaliter de Christo explicandum, siquidem quædam dicta prophetarum implentur historicè, quædam typicè, quædam analogicè. Historicè, ut quod scriptum est Ps.22. Foderunt manus meas & pedes meos, & diviserunt vestes meas. Hæc enim Davidi accommodari non possunt. Typicè impletum est in Christo apud Lucam cap.4. Vaticinium Jesaiæ cap.61. Analogica impletio est in tribus illis dictis, Math.2. Ex Ægypto, &c. vox in Rama, &c. Nazoræus vocabitur. Analogica est impletio per similitudinem, ut intelligamus, nihil novi esse, ex AEgypto de integro nasci Ecclesiam, quando jam olim Deus populum suum filium dilectum inde evocavit. Neque enim testimonia V. T. semper confirmandi, sed sæpe illustrandi & concinnioris accommodationis gratiâ adhibentur in novo. Quod qui non attendunt, ii textus propheticos violentis istis applicationibus corrumpunt, &, quod in Hoseæ loco fit, reprehensiones transmutant in consolationes, & narrationes facti prateriti in promissiones rei futuræ. Hæc D. Sculr. Quæ fortassis ridebit Pontificiorum aliquis, sed discat ille ex Serario, De his & similibus locis pluribus etiam jure Canonico particulares esse dissensiones, inter istorum locorum Interpretes. Cum alii literarium solummodo, alii mysticum, alii denique * accommodatitium, in hisce sensum constituant. Et quidem aliqui probabiliter atque Catholicè ut Jansenius, alii verò improbabiliter & hæreticè. Hæc Serarius cap.21. quæst. 14.
units.tr: Nor does that text prove the point, Out of Egypt have I called my son (Hos. 11; Matt. 2). For insofar as that text is explained of Christ, Ribera contends that it has an allegorical sense. I, however, agree with Jansenius, who here and elsewhere posits an accommodated sense. Among our own writers Sculteius also agrees with him. The words of Scultetus are these, on the passage: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken, out of Egypt, etc. (Matt. 2). Those words, that it might be fulfilled, do not necessarily require that this passage of Hosea be explained literally of Christ, since some sayings of the prophets are fulfilled historically, some typically, and some analogically. Historically, as what is written in Psalm 22: They pierced my hands and my feet, and they divided my garments. For these cannot be applied to David. Typically it was fulfilled in Christ, as in Luke chapter 4, the prophecy of Isaiah chapter 61. The fulfilment is analogical in those three sayings in Matthew 2: Out of Egypt, etc.; a voice in Ramah, etc.; he shall be called a Nazarene. Analogical fulfilment is fulfilment by likeness, so that we understand that nothing new is involved when the Church is born again out of Egypt, since God long ago called his beloved son, his people, out of it. For the testimonies of the Old Testament are used in the New not always to confirm, but often to illustrate and for the sake of a more elegant application. Those who do not notice this corrupt the prophetic texts with these violent applications, and, as happens in the passage of Hosea, they turn reproofs into consolations and narratives of past events into promises of future things. Thus far Dr. Scultetus. Some Papist may perhaps laugh at this, but let him learn from Serarius: Concerning these and similar passages there are even under canon law particular disagreements among the interpreters of these texts, since some find only a literal sense in them, others a mystical sense, and still others an accommodated sense. And indeed some hold this view probably and in a Catholic manner, as Jansenius, while others hold it improbably and heretically. Thus Serarius, chapter 21, question 14.

units.la: {*} hunc Cajet. vocat sensum transumptivum. Neque etiam pluralitatem sensuum literalium in uno loco probat vaticinium Cajaphæ Joh.11. 5. Illud enim considerari debet, non ut axioma unum, sed ut duo, quorum unumquodque suum proprium sensum literalem habet. Alium enim sensum Spiritus S. alium Cajaphas intendit. Aliud ergo axioma est quà à Sp. Sancto profectum est, aliud quà à Cajapha prolatum est. Cum autem quæstio sit de verbis Scripturæ, quatenus Spiritum S. authorem habent; quid ad nos attinet quem sensum Cajaphas intenderit?
units.tr: Cajetan calls this a transumptive sense. Nor does the prophecy of Caiaphas (John 11:50) prove a plurality of literal senses in one passage. For it must be considered not as one statement but as two, each of which has its own proper literal sense. For the Holy Spirit intended one sense, and Caiaphas another. So it is one statement insofar as it proceeded from the Holy Spirit, and another insofar as it was uttered by Caiaphas. But since the question concerns the words of Scripture insofar as they have the Holy Spirit as their author, what concern is it of ours what sense Caiaphas intended?

units.la: Error secundus, quem hic vitare oportet, iste est, Quorundam locorum nullum esse sensum literalem. Azorius loco & libro supra indicato, Quidam putant scripturam aliquando sensu literali vacare, solo Mystico contentam. Ita nonnulli putarunt diluvium & arcæ fabricationem non esse res gestas, sed nudas rerum significandarum figuras, apud August. de civit. Dei 15. 27. Quin & Origenes & ejus assecla ita tractarunt scripturam, ut videantur idem plane sensisse. Sed errorem istorum confutarunt Azorius, Serarius & alii. Etiam Lyra ita subinde loqui videtur, sed notat Serarius, illum sensum tropicum & figuratum appellare mysticum & literali proprio sive τ᾽ἀρηπ opponere.
units.tr: The second error, which one must avoid here, is this: some passages have no literal sense at all. Azorius, in the place and book indicated above: Some think that Scripture sometimes lacks a literal sense and contains only a mystical one. So some have thought that the flood and the building of the ark were not actual events but bare figures of things to be signified, as Augustine reports (City of God 15.27). Indeed Origen and his followers handled Scripture in such a way that they seem to have thought exactly the same. But Azorius, Serarius and others have refuted this error. Lyra too seems at times to speak in this way, but Serarius observes that he calls the tropical and figurative sense "mystical" and opposes it to the literal and proper sense.

units.la: Error 3. In omnibus & singulis Scriptura locis duos esse sensus unum literalem, Mysticum alterum. Ita multos ex Pontificiis statuere, Serarius, Azorius & Bellarminus testes sunt. Ita sentiebat Origenes, qui in minutissimis etiam, e. gr. propriis montium, locorumque nominibus, mysticum sensum latitare credidit. Sed hoc confutant isti triumviri, & quidem Serarius, quæst.8. c.21. Azorius Instit.lib.8. cap.2. Bellarm. lib.3. de V. D. cap.3. Fundamentum opinionis istius primarium fuit locus 1. Corinth. 10. verf.6. & 11. Omnia figuris contingebant illis. Resp. Glassius illic historiam veterum accommodari ad Corinthios & doceri, omnia quæ Israëlitis evenerunt, esse imagines & quid fugere & quid sequi debeant, ut in iis videre possint quid fugere & quid sequi debeant, &c. Deinde quid per verba ista verf.6. τἀῦτα δὲ τύπος ἡμῶν, &c. intelligatur, ostendi verf.11. ubi exempla priscorum Israelitarum dicuntur scripta πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν id est od commonefactionem nostram & cautelam. Jam vero νουθεσία non est sensus literarii accommodatio ad usum, ut patet ex 2. Timoth.3.16. Non ergo isthic loci agitur de typicis repræsentationibus sed ut Bannes recte explicat, dicit in figura ipsis contigisse supplicia, id est in exemplum nostrum. Cui astipulatur Jesuita Vasquez, Atque hic illi etiam admonendi, qui ex quolibet Heroë, cujus vitam & res gestas veteris Test. Scriptores ad posteritatem transmiserunt, typum Christi, aut ex qualibet re typum Ecclesiæ aut rerum Novi Testamenti faciunt. Longe alia istorum ratio est, quos typum Christi gessisse ipse Christus & Apostoli docuere: verbi gratia, Melchisedeci, Hebr. 5. & 7. Jonæ, Math. 12. Davidis & Salomonis quod ex tot oraculis, quæ in N. Test. citantur, liquet, Eadem est ratio Agni Paschalis, 1.Cor.5.7. Arcæ cum propitiatorio, Rom.3.25. Templi Salomonis 1.Joh.2.21. victimarum Heb.9.8. Serpentis æneî, Joh.3.14. Altaris, Hebr.13.10. & aliorum quorundam, quamquam siquis in multis quorum in N.Test. fit mentio, allusionem quandam constituere mallet quam typum, meo judicio, non admodum esset aberraturus. Cavete ergo, Candidati, ne ad cathedras admissi ex qualibet persona vel re V.Test.typum vel Christi, vel Ecclesiæ vel aliarum rerum fabricetis. Sit aliquid in utroque simile, hoc typo constituendo neutiquam satis est. Nunquam enim evinces esse typum, nisi ex sacra pagina ostenderis illud à Spiritu S. huc fuisse destinatum, & ad hanc repræsentationem ordinatum. Sed & illi verbo mihi compellandi sunt: qui circa nominum propriorum interpretationem & etymologiam nimis curiosi sunt, atque hinc ad typos & Allegorias dilabuntur, integras sæpe horas hujusmodi dissertationibus transmittentes. Etyma nominum propriorum quæ vel ipse Sp. S. prodidit, vel ex ipsa originali lingua sua se sponte offerunt, ut c. g. Adam, Heva, Kain, Habel, Seth, Enos, Noach, Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Juda, &c cæteri ejus fratres, Moses, Salomo, &c. hæc, inquam breviter explicentur, ex his documenta depromantur. At* quod cætera attinet, quorum etyma vel ignorantur, vel obscura vel admodum controversa sunt, iis diu inversari, atque iis typos & allegorias confingere, id vero est patientia auditorum abuti [Valebitque & gemino hoc casu ista censura Bonfrerii Jesuitæ, quæ in Præloquiis ad Pentateuchum cap. 20. Sect. 3. mysticorum sensuum venatores perstringit, Qui à multis, inquit, afferuntur sensus mystici, fere sola conjectura nituntur, cum aliunde non constat eos Sp. Sanctum intendisse: atque adeo ut sæpe omittantur. & In omissis non est quod nos immodice torqueamus aut certe aliquid pronunciemus temere, cum multis conjecturis quidem locus est, &c.
units.tr: Error 3: in all and each passage of Scripture there are two senses, one literal and the other mystical. That many Papists hold this, Serarius, Azorius and Bellarmine bear witness. Origen held this view, believing that a mystical sense lies hidden even in the very smallest things, for example in the proper names of mountains and places. But these three champions refute it, Serarius in question 8 of chapter 21, Azorius in Instit. book 8, chapter 2, and Bellarmine in book 3, On the Word of God, chapter 3. The chief foundation of this opinion has been 1 Corinthians 10:6 and 11: all these things happened to them as figures. I reply, with Glassius, that there the apostle applies the history of the ancients to the Corinthians, and teaches that all the things that happened to the Israelites are images, showing what they should flee from and what they should follow, so that in them they may see what to flee from and what to follow, and so on. Next, what is meant by the words in verse 6, ταῦτα δὲ τύποι ἡμῶν [these things were types for us], is shown in verse 11, where the examples of the ancient Israelites are said to have been written πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν [for our admonition] and warning. But admonition [νουθεσία] is not an accommodation of the literal sense to use, as is clear from 2 Timothy 3:16. Therefore the passage is not concerned with typical representations, but, as Bannes rightly explains, it says that punishments befell them in a figure, that is, for our example. The Jesuit Vasquez agrees. Here also those must be warned who make a type of Christ out of any hero whose life and deeds the writers of the Old Testament have handed down to posterity, or make a type of the Church or of the things of the New Testament out of any thing whatever. Far different is their reasoning concerning those whom Christ himself and the apostles taught to have borne the type of Christ: for example Melchizedek (Heb. 5 and 7), Jonah (Matt. 12), and David and Solomon, as is clear from the many oracles cited in the New Testament. The same reasoning applies to the Passover lamb (1 Cor. 5:7), the ark with the mercy seat (Rom. 3:25), Solomon's temple (John 2:21), the sacrifices (Heb. 9:8), the brazen serpent (John 3:14), the altar (Heb. 13:10), and certain others; although, in my judgement, if anyone preferred to see in the many things mentioned in the New Testament a certain allusion rather than a type, he would not be very far wrong. Be careful, therefore, candidates, lest once admitted to the chairs you make a type of Christ, of the Church, or of other things out of any person or thing of the Old Testament. If something is similar in both, that is by no means enough to establish a type. For you will never prove it to be a type unless you show from the sacred page that the Holy Spirit intended it for this purpose and ordained it for this representation. But I must also speak a word to those who are overly curious about the interpretation and etymology of proper names, and who from this slip into types and allegories, often spending whole hours on such dissertations. The etymologies of proper names that the Holy Spirit himself has disclosed, or that offer themselves readily from their original language, such as Adam, Eve, Cain, Abel, Seth, Enosh, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah and his other brothers, Moses, Solomon, and so on, these, I say, should be briefly explained and lessons drawn from them. But as for the rest, whose etymologies are either unknown, obscure or greatly disputed, to dwell on these at length and to fashion types and allegories from them is to abuse the patience of the hearers. [This censure of the Jesuit Bonfrère also applies doubly here, and it lashes the hunters after mystical senses in his Prefaces to the Pentateuch, chapter 20, section 3: The mystical senses that many people put forward, he says, rest almost only on conjecture, since it is not otherwise clear that the Holy Spirit intended them; and so they are often left out. Nor is there any reason for us to torture ourselves excessively over the omitted ones, or to pronounce anything rashly, since there is room for many conjectures, etc.]

units.la: * Mercerus in Genes. p. 106. Veteres illi patres nemi-num indendorum libertis certas sempet causas habuerunt, quas aliquando, exprimuntur in Scripturis, ut plurimum minus utiliter in his opera ponitur, quam in sensu literali, propterea quod plerumque in his multa humani ingenii figmenta venditentur pro mysticis sensibus, qui veri sensus non sunt, nec a Spiritu S. intenti.] Illos quoque merito reprehenderis, qui saepe volentes scientes Scripturam ad suos conceptus inflectunt. Atque hic non inutile fuerit multis verbi divini praeconibus, audire querelam Leonardi Marii Theologi Colonien-sis, cujus haec sunt verba Proleg. in Sacram Script. Qu. 8. Sect. 3.
