Hodie eo fere delapsi sumus, ut quod Patres illi raro fecerunt & reverenter, id nunc & frequentissime & pene ridicule fiat, non sine gravissima verbi divini violatione, dum potius ad populi lascivum pruritum ex talibus accommodationibus admiratio populi & laus ipsius concionatoris quaeritur quam instructio populi & Dei laus. Additque graviter, eam esse inutilem & pampinosam verborum garrulitatem, qua cum abundantissime luxuriavit, nihil fructus affert. Non hic mihi negotium cum illis est, qui verba Scripturae ad facetias & spurcitias transferunt. Quomodo profani quidam monachi olim, cum rursus bibituri erant, usurpare illud solebant, regressus unde venerat, & cum sitirent, dicere se in passione progressos esse ad Sitio, ad quorum exemplum nostri quoque Biberii Merones inter pocula gravissimas sacrae paginae sententias usurpare non erubescunt. Non, inquam, cum talibus mihi negotium est, utpote hominibus ex professo profanis, sed illos noto, qui Scripturam etiam in sacris violenter detorquent, & licet quam maxime reluctantem accommodant ad ea, de quibus ipsis vel facillimum, vel gratissimum est sermocinari. Hoc malum altas in Papatu egisse radices, querela Marii luculenti testis vicem est. Audi Duraeum adversus Witakerum, pag. 45. Ad Cardinalem Cusanum quod attinet, recte sane ab eo scriptum est, alio atque alio modo Scripturas pro temporis ratione accipi posse & exponi. Et authorem Apologiae pro dispensatione Papae super matrimonio Henrici 8. sol. 34. & 35. Et forsitan aliquoties expediens fuerit neque Deo ingratum, ad pie subditorum animos fallendos, in quibusdam causis, scripturas nonnihil a genuino sensu detorquere. Sed tolerabilius hic illi peccarunt, quam nostri. Illi enim Scripturam pro regula Lesbia & cerconaso (quae sunt formalia Dionysii Carthusiani ad cap. xiii. Apocal. ubi de numero bestiae agit) habuerunt. Nostri vero uno ore Scripturam inflexibilem normam omnium Christianorum dogmatum agnoscunt. Sed hoc debetur Pontificiarum Postillarum multitudini, ex quibus multi ejusmodi ineptias malunt haurire, quam ex Originalibus Sacri Codicis tabulis genuinum sensum eruere. Illud enim facile, hoc pluisculum laboris requirit. Atque hic non possum non repraesentare gravissimam admonitionem Adami Sasboutii, Pontificii, qua suorum pruritum liberi oris homo cordate destringit. Sic ergo ille Praefat. in Jesaiam, Littera seu historia est basis & fundamentum allegoria; propterea valenti scripturam interpretari allegorice, in primis curandum est, ut literam ad unguem teneat. Nam puerile est, stultum, imo nihil offendiculo potest esse magis Judaeo, quam quod quis de spirituali sensu disputet, non ante intellecta litera. Ille enim abusus scriptura est maximus, tam libere pro cujusque ingenio & phantasia confingere Allegorias: hoc namque modo scriptura sacra esset quasi Lesbia regula, & eam, quo quisque vellet, detorqueret. An autem tota scriptura & ejus verba exponenda sint secundum Allegoriam, dubium est, vel potius dubium non est, quia hoc minime solidum est. Praeterea totam Scripturam tractare secundum triplicem aut quadruplicem sensum, nec hoc solidum est: non solum, quia difficile est, semper coherentia dicere sed etiam necesse est sape confingere, quod utique periculosum est in tanto thesauro, cui illam debemus reverentiam, ne quid facile comminiscamur.
units.tr: * Mercerus on Genesis, p. 106. Those ancient Fathers always had fixed reasons for taking up the fruitless searching for hidden meanings, which they sometimes drew from Scripture itself. In such work far less use is made of the literal sense than of the mystical sense, because very often many fictions of the human mind are passed off as mystical senses, which are not the true sense and were not intended by the Holy Spirit. You may rightly blame those too who, often willingly and knowingly, bend Scripture to their own ideas. Here it will not be unhelpful for many heralds of the divine Word to hear the complaint of Leonardus Marius, a theologian of Cologne, whose words are these (Prolegomena to Holy Scripture, question 8, section 3): Today we have fallen to such a point that what those Fathers rarely did, and did reverently, is now done very frequently and almost ridiculously, not without the gravest violation of the divine Word, since through such accommodations the people's admiration and the preacher's own praise are sought, rather than the instruction of the people and the praise of God, from the wanton itch of the people. He adds sharply that it is a useless and leafy chatter of words, which, when it has run riot most abundantly, brings no fruit. I am not concerned here with those who turn the words of Scripture into jokes and filth, as certain profane monks once did, who, when they were about to drink again, used to take up the phrase regressus unde venerat ("gone back whence he came"), and when they were thirsty would say they had advanced in the Passion to Sitio ("I thirst"); following their example our own Bibber-Merons are not ashamed to quote the most serious sentences of Holy Writ over their cups. No, I say, I have no quarrel with such men, who are openly profane; I mean those who violently twist Scripture even in sacred matters, and apply it, though it resists as strongly as it can, to those things about which they themselves find it easiest or most pleasant to talk. That this evil has struck deep roots in Papacy is shown by the complaint of Marius, a clear witness. Hear Duraeus against Whitaker, p. 45: As far as Cardinal Cusanus is concerned, he rightly wrote that the Scriptures can be taken and expounded in one way or another, according to the circumstances of the time. And the author of the Apology for the Pope's dispensation concerning the marriage of Henry VIII (pp. 34 and 35): And perhaps it would sometimes be expedient, and not ungrateful to God, to deceive the pious minds of subjects, in certain cases, by twisting the Scriptures somewhat from their genuine sense. Yet those men sinned more tolerably than ours. For they held Scripture to be a Lesbian rule and a leaden measure (these are the phrases of Dionysius the Carthusian on Rev. 13, where he treats of the number of the beast). Our men, however, with one voice acknowledge Scripture as the unbending norm of all Christian doctrines. But this is owed to the multitude of Papist Postils, from which many prefer to draw such silliness rather than to dig out the genuine sense from the original tablets of the Sacred Book. For the one is easy, the other requires rather more labour. Here I cannot but set before you the very serious warning of Adam Sasbout, a Papist, by which this man of sound judgment and free tongue checks the itch of his own people. He says thus in his Preface to Isaiah: The letter, or history, is the basis and foundation of allegory; therefore, anyone who wishes to interpret Scripture allegorically must above all take care to keep strictly to the letter. For it is childish and foolish, indeed nothing can be more of a stumbling block to a Jew, than for someone to dispute about the spiritual sense before the letter has been understood. That abuse of Scripture is very great, to invent allegories so freely according to each person's talent and fancy: in this way Holy Scripture would be like a Lesbian rule, and each person would twist it as he pleased. Whether the whole of Scripture and its words are to be expounded according to allegory is doubtful, or rather it is not doubtful, because this is by no means solid. Besides, to treat the whole of Scripture according to a threefold or fourfold sense is not solid either: not only because it is difficult always to give a coherent account, but also because it is often necessary to invent things, which is certainly dangerous in so great a treasure, to which we owe such reverence, lest we contrive anything lightly.

units.la: Magni ergo istius BucerI voto meum quoque adsonet, * Magno vero Ecclesiae redimendum esset, ut relictis inanibus ac plurimum majestati doctrinae Christi derogantibus Allegoriis & commentis aliis frivolis, simpliciter & sobrie perse queremur id quod Dominus dicere voluit. In quo sane discendo & docendo, satis superque quod agamus quoque aedificemur, nobis propositum est. Idem in comm. ad cap. 13. ejusdem Euang. postquam de allegorica quadam Interpretatione parabolae de zizaniis obiter verba fecisset, sic inquit, nihil horum Christus docuit, eoque nihil hujusmodi firmum. Satis alias scriptura habemus, unde etiam citra ista Allegoriarum, ne quid aliud dicam, argutias, docemur, periculosam esse negligentiam Episcoporum, & quod ipsis sterentibus, maxima haereses soleant pullulare. Demus ergo operam, nostra certa & solida sint. qui ut sermones Dei loqui debemus. Ita vero erunt, cum puro Dei verbo, & nequaquam nostris commentis innitemur. Atque hic animus erat huic capiti & cum eo, primo libro Colophonem imponere, cum amicissimus collega meus D. Gul. Amesius, solidioris S. Literarum Interpretationis strenuus assertor alium insuper locum ex eodem Bucero mihi suppeditat, Quem, Quem, licet prolixiorem, his quæ dicta sunt, Coronidis vicem adjiciam. Is itaque postquam ad cap. 3. Johannis de ratione explicandi * typos & tractandi Allegorias doctissimè disseruisset, hæc subjungit. In his autem observandum, ut similitudo & proportio patéat, ut certa sit, ut sensum fidei feriat. Nam in hoc istiusmodi ἀλληγορήματα adhibentur, ut quæ docentur, clarius & significantius animis hominum commendentur. Peccatur in his igitur, dum aut obscurior similitudo, aut nulla est, aut incerta, quam fidei, quæ indubitatis tantum capitur, sensus non agnoscit. Sic dum Hieron. ad Ruffinum in Epistola, quæ incipit, Multum in utramque partem crebro fama mentitur, per duas meretrices quibus Schlomoh judicavit 1. Reg. 2. Synagogam & Ecclesiam intelligendas docet, quid simile, unde fides pasci, aut oblectari queat? Satis habebit itaque pius in eo facto, Domini agnovisse erga Schlomoh adhuc puerum miram adeo dignationem, & tum a minori transfibit ad id quod majus est, agnoscetque cum tantum dederit Schlomoh spiritum Deus, verori Schlomoh, & filio David, restauratori omnium, datam longe præstantiorem, qui judex constitutus orbis est, quique ut vates habet, non judicabit juxta id quod oculis viderit, & auribus audiet, sed adeo valebit timore, id est, pietate erga Dominum, ut odoraturus sit, quod res sit, & per justitiam vindicaturus pauperibus, & per æquitatem arguturus afflictis terra, &c. Jesch. 11. Sic in meretrice pueri sui tam amante, ut alienam vivum concedere mallet, quam videre ut discinderetur, animadverte: Si hac mala mulier suum infantem tantopere dilexit, Deum solum bonum, nos juxta suam promissionem Jescha. 40. infinito ardentius diligere, Hac & his similia certa sunt, quia patentem spiritui similitudinem atque proportionem habet, eoque fidem possunt alere, quæ autem finxit Hieronymus, ut ingenii acumen referunt, & tanquam ingeniose dicta carnem oblectant, ita fidei nihil prosunt, quia nihil in eis certi, nihil firmi. Talibus autem typicis, quas vocarunt & allegoricis interpretationibus, veteres plerique adeo indulserunt, ut & planiss. Evangelica dicta, ad allegorias ejusmodi traxerint, sed nihilo firmiores, quam quilibet ingeniosior ex Homero & Vergilio quoque confingere possit. At in Ecclesia ut sermones Dei, quibus nihil indubitatius, omnia nos loqui & scribere addecet. Et dolendum, esse & hodie, qui iflam allegorizandi sibi licentiam nimis temere permittunt. Apostolos igitur libeat, quam veterum quosdam Origenem, Hieronymum, ac alios in typorum explicationibus. & eorum quæ veteribus contigerunt, ad nos translationibus, imitari. Manifestam enim & certam habet illorum tum translationes & anagoga similitudinem, patrum vero plaraque aut nullas aut valde obscuram. Ne igitur idem & nobis contingat, discernenda diligenter sunt, quae scriptura habet inde vestigandum quid primum & praecipue spiritus quaque in re voluerit, qui in omnibus id quidem studet, ut Dei bonitas a nobis agnoscatur, nosque in illam transformemur, sed variis id docet & commendat rationibus. * Proinde diligenter observandum, ne quid ad Christum aut Ecclesiam corpus ejus, ex gestis veterum transferamus, quod non certo ac manifesto quadret. Ad quid enim facta priscorum, in Christum & Ecclesiam contorquebimus, cum ille ex suis ipsius factis, quae vel Evangelistae memorarunt, praedecaverunt Apostoli, clare adeo sanctis innotuerit, & illa quoque ex amplissimis quae a sponso suo accepit donis, sic agnoscatur, ut qui velit his exgestis figurisque veterum lucem adferre, id faciat, quod qui lucernam adhibeat soli. Vehementer varia sapientia Dei, nota fit principatibus caelestibus, per Ecclesiam, & scilicet ex factis Abraham, Jitzchak, aliorumve patrum & regum opus erit eruere cognitionem Christi Ecclesiaeque divitias? Nihilo prudentius hoc fuerit, quam si quis ex factis puerilibus, de ingenio velit differere viri.
units.tr: To this great wish of Bucer my own voice also agrees: Indeed, it would be greatly to the advantage of the Church to leave aside empty allegories and other frivolous inventions, which greatly detract from the majesty of Christ's teaching, and to seek simply and soberly what the Lord wished to say. In learning and teaching this, we shall surely be more than sufficiently edified, which is our aim. The same Bucer, in his commentary on chapter 13 of the same Gospel, after briefly speaking of a certain allegorical interpretation of the parable of the tares, says thus: Christ taught none of these things, and therefore nothing of this kind is firm. We have Scripture enough, from which we are taught, even without those subtleties of allegories, not to mention anything else, that the negligence of bishops is dangerous, and that the greatest heresies are wont to sprout while they are asleep. Let us therefore take care that our own things are certain and solid; we ought to speak as the words of God. Indeed they will be so, when we rely on the pure Word of God and in no way on our own inventions. This was my intention for this chapter, and with it to set a colophon on the first book, when my most dear colleague, Mr. William Ames, a vigorous champion of a more solid interpretation of Holy Letters, supplies me with another passage from the same Bucer. I shall add it, though it is rather long, as a kind of crown to what has been said. Having discussed most learnedly, after Chapter 3 of John, the method of explaining types and handling allegories, he adds these words: In these matters, however, care must be taken that the likeness and proportion be evident, that it be certain, that it strike the sense of faith. For such allegories are used in order that what is taught may be commended to men's minds more clearly and significantly. Error therefore occurs when the likeness is more obscure, or is none, or is uncertain, so that the sense of faith, which is grasped only by what is indubitable, does not recognise it. Thus when Jerome, in his letter to Rufinus beginning Multum in utramque partem crebro fama mentitur, teaches that the two harlots by whom Solomon judged (1 Kings 3) are to be understood as the Synagogue and the Church, what similarity is there here from which faith can be nourished or delighted? A pious reader will therefore be content in that deed to acknowledge the wonderful kindness of the Lord towards Solomon while still a boy, and then will pass from the lesser to what is greater, and will recognise that, since God gave so much to Solomon, a far more excellent Spirit has been given to the true Solomon, the son of David, the restorer of all things, who has been appointed judge of the world, and who, as the prophet says, will not judge according to what he sees with his eyes nor decide by what he hears with his ears, but will be so strong in the fear of the Lord, that is, in piety towards the Lord, that he will smell out what is the case, and will judge the poor with righteousness, and reprove the afflicted of the earth with equity, etc. (Isa. 11). Likewise, observe in the harlot who loved her child so much that she preferred to give him up alive to another rather than see him cut in pieces: if this wicked woman loved her own infant so greatly, how much more infinitely ardently ought we to love God, who alone is good, according to his own promise (Isa. 40). These and similar things are certain, because they have a likeness and proportion evident to the Spirit, and so can nourish faith; but the things Jerome invented, which reveal the keenness of his wit and, as cleverly spoken things, please the flesh, are of no use to faith at all, because there is nothing certain or firm in them. Most of the ancients indulged so much in such typical, or as they called them, allegorical interpretations, that they drew even the plainest Gospel sayings into allegories of this sort, yet these were no firmer than anything a rather clever man could fabricate from Homer or Virgil. But in the Church, since these are the words of God, to which nothing is more indubitable, we ought to speak and write only what is certain. And it is to be lamented that there are still today some who too rashly grant themselves this licence of allegorising. It is therefore fitting for us to imitate the Apostles rather than certain of the ancients, Origen, Jerome, and others, in the explanations of types and in the transfers of what happened to the ancients to us. For the translations and the anagogical likenesses of the former are manifest and certain, whereas most of the Fathers' are either none or very obscure. Lest therefore the same thing happen to us, we must carefully distinguish what Scripture contains, and seek out first and above all what the Spirit wished in each matter; he indeed in all things takes care that the goodness of God be acknowledged by us and that we be transformed into it, but he teaches and commends this by various means. * Therefore we must take care not to transfer anything from the deeds of the ancients to Christ or to the Church his body, which does not fit with certainty and clarity. For why should we twist the deeds of the forefathers into Christ and the Church, when Christ has been made so clearly known to the saints from his own deeds, which the Evangelists have recorded and the Apostles have foretold, and from those most ample gifts which he has received from his Spouse, so that anyone who wishes to bring light to these old deeds and figures does what someone who brings a lamp to the sun would do? Will it be necessary, by the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, or other patriarchs and kings, to dig out the knowledge of Christ and the riches of the Church, which is made known to the heavenly principalities through the manifold wisdom of God? It would be no wiser than to discourse on the character of a man from the childish deeds of a boy.

units.la: Jam pueri instar fuit populus legis, quare qua etiam magnifica illi acciderunt, collata iis, quae donata sunt Ecclesiae, puerilia sunt, & admonere possunt horum, illustrare ea non possunt, imo ex his illa lucem acipiunt. * Hinc factum ut neque prophetae, neque Apostoli, singulorum rituum significationes mysticas unquam tradiderint, neque tradentur in posterum, expectamus enim ut nequaquam in aenigmatis tam perplexis, & speculo adeo obscuro, sed facie ad faciem & sicuti est, Dominum videamus. Quare sicut vidimus, Apostolos de ipso Christo, ex revelatione spiritus potissimum praedicasse, & nequaquam ex typis, vel gestorum vel caeremoniarum veterum, nisi quando rem habuerunt cum iis, qui illis plus aequo addicti erant, ita & nos quae de Christo ex Evangelio tenemus, in primis doceamus. Iis probe cognitis, poterunt cum fructu & typi proponi, modo religiose, ita ut Apostoli, illos tractemus. Certe Paulus typos perparce adhibuit, nisi quando pugnandum sibi fuit, cum pseudoapostolis, qui necessitatem caeremoniarum legis conabantur inducere, & de carne Abraham, in praejudicium gratiae Christi, gloriabantur. Alias satis ipse & alii Apostoli habuerunt, exempla ex scripturis, & aperta cum praecepta, tum vaticinia adduxisse. Proinde qui Apostolos volet imitari, & salubria ex scripturis in Ecclesia docere, expendat quam mirifice in omnibus quae Deus cum suis egit bonitatem suam declaraverit, eam & sibi ipsi, & aliis probe commendet, hinc roborabitur fides, accendetur Dei amor, is tum impellet pellet ad honesta omnia, & ab inhonestis revocabit potentiss. Simul expendat Deum unum hoc, in omnibus, quæ suis unquam præcepit, sive de moribus civilibus, sive de cerimoniis præceperit, requisivisse, ut ipsum timeremus & amaremus, totoque ab ipso penderemus, tum cum proximis viveremus summa cum honestate, & officiosa dilectione. Hæc aperte satis omnia scriptura docent, cumque omnia non nisi per Christum nobis possint contingere, illum quoque omnes scriptura prædicant. Si typicos prateres intellectus voles adhibere, vide, quod sæpius jam monui, & diligenter adeo agnoscis observatum ab Apostolis, ut probe constet, & pateat similitudo, atque proportio inter typos illos, & Christum, vel Ecclesiam. Ad quod opus est te ante, ex Evangelicis literis, adeoque & spiritu Christi tenere, quid Christo, quid Ecclesiæ, tribuas. Nam si ex typos voles colligere, quod CHRISTO, & corpori ejus tribuas, idque Apostolicæ literæ non docent, neque ipse spiritus certo sanctius revelavit, nihil sane docebis & audies illud vulgatum, figura nihil probat. Hæc sane omnia copiosius, & pluribus exemplis fuissent explicanda, adeo pauci ad hoc id volunt observare, ut certa doceant, licentiaque allegoriarum, quas vocant, minime paucos & hodie nugatores reddit, ex solidis Ecclesiæ doctoribus, sed hæc integrum tractatum desiderant.
units.tr: Already the people of the law were like a child, so the magnificent things that happened to them, compared with what has been given to the Church, are childish. They can remind us of these things but cannot illuminate them; rather, they receive their light from them. Hence it happens that neither the prophets nor the Apostles ever handed down the mystical meanings of the individual rites, nor will they do so in future, for we expect to see the Lord not in such perplexing enigmas and so obscure a mirror, but face to face and as he is. Therefore, just as we have seen, the Apostles preached chiefly about Christ himself from the revelation of the Spirit, and not from the types of the deeds or ceremonies of the ancients, except when they had to deal with those who were too attached to them. So we too should first teach what we hold about Christ from the Gospel. Once these things are well known, types may also be set forth with profit, provided we handle them religiously, as the Apostles did. Certainly Paul used types very sparingly, except when he had to contend with the false apostles who tried to impose the necessity of the ceremonies of the law and boasted of Abraham's flesh, to the prejudice of the grace of Christ. Otherwise he and the other Apostles were content to adduce examples from Scripture, both explicit precepts and prophecies. Therefore whoever wishes to imitate the Apostles and teach wholesome things from Scripture in the Church should consider how wonderfully God has displayed his goodness in all that he has done with his people, and should commend it well both to himself and to others. From this faith will be strengthened and the love of God kindled, and it will drive him to all honourable things and call him back most powerfully from dishonourable ones. At the same time let him consider that God, in everything he has ever commanded his people, whether concerning civil morals or ceremonies, required only this: that we fear and love him, depend wholly on him, and live with our neighbours with the highest honesty and dutiful love. Scripture teaches all these things plainly enough, and since all of them can come to us only through Christ, Scripture proclaims him in all things too. If you wish to employ typical interpretations beyond these, see what I have often already admonished, and observe diligently how carefully the Apostles observed it, so that it is clear and evident that there is a likeness and proportion between those types and Christ or the Church. For this you must first hold, from the Evangelical writings and so from the Spirit of Christ, what you attribute to Christ and what to the Church. For if you wish to infer from types what you attribute to Christ and his body, which the apostolic writings do not teach and the Spirit himself has not revealed more surely, you will certainly teach nothing, and you will hear that common saying: a figure proves nothing. All these things would have needed to be explained more fully and with more examples, but so few wish to observe them for the sake of teaching what is certain, and the licence of so-called allegories makes not a few trifling triflers, even today, out of solid teachers of the Church. But these matters require a whole treatise.

units.la: FINIS LIBRI I.
units.tr: END OF BOOK I.

units.la: SIXTINI AMAMA ANTI-BARBARORVM LIBER II.
units.tr: Sixtinus Amama, Anti-Barbarus, Book II.

units.la: Quo recensentur varii errores circa explicationem particularium S. Scripturæ locorum, qui ex VII. istis, quos libro superiore discussimus, erroribus generalibus emanarunt.
units.tr: In which various errors are listed concerning the explanation of particular passages of Holy Scripture, which arose from those seven general errors that we discussed in the previous book.

units.la: GENESIS.
units.tr: GENESIS.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 1.

units.la: Versf. 1. In principio.
units.tr: Verse 1. In the beginning.

units.la: PER principium ipsum Dei Filium Patri suo ὁμοούσιον multi ex veteribus intellexerunt, de cujus interpretationis fonte dicemus σὺν Θεῷ ad Ps. 40.
units.tr: Many of the ancients understood by "the beginning" God's own Son, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with his Father. I will speak of the source of this interpretation, God willing, at Ps. 40.

units.la: Ibid. In pr. creavit Deus.
units.tr: Ibid. In the beginning God created.

units.la: Ebr. Creavit Elohim id est Dii. Primus omnium Petrus Lombardus lib. 1. Sentent. distinct. 2. ex hac nominis pluralis cum verbo singulari constructione pro personarum in D. Essentia pluralitate argumentum extruxit, quem imitati sunt alii, inter quos & Paulus Brugensis, in Addit. ad Lyram. Sed ejus imbecillitatem observarunt acutè, & proposuerunt dilucidè Alfonsus Tostatus, Episc. Abulensis, Cajetanus, Bellarminus & alii; & quidem illi in suis ad hunc locum commentariis, hic vero in controversia de Christo lib. 2. cap. 6. Sixtus quoque Senensis Annot. 1. lib. 4. Bibliothecæ suæ, Cajetano patrocinatur, Ambrosium Catharinum increpitans, quod hoc nomine eruditissimum Cardinalem fuisset insectatus, quasi non multi etiam alii sine ullâ hæreseos suspicione à Sententiarum Magistro qui sibi ipsi, dum hanc sententiam proponit, concontrarius est, in hoc negotio dissensissent: E nostris vero hujus argumenti debilitatem ostendērunt Calvinus, Mercerus, & innumeri alii. Sed præ cæteris diligentissimè & quasi ex professo hanc quæstionem tractârunt, Pareus id comm. ad locum hunc, nec non in Calvino Orthodoxo, & Drusius in tractatu de nomine Elohim. Cum autem libri isti sint in omnium manibus, verbum ego hac de re non addam. Illud saltem notabit Tyro, non hoc egisse magnos illos viros, ut arduus ille de SS. Trinitate articulus hoc tibicine ablato collabasceret, sed ut Theologos in gravissimâ ista quæstione cum subtilissimis hæreticis disputaturos docerent, solidioribus argumentis esse adhærescendum. Cum quis enim ut egregiè monuit Thomas, ad probandam fidem Christianam inducit rationes non cogentes, cedit in irrisionem infidelium. Credunt enim quod hujusmodi rationibus immutamur & propter eas credamus. Eandem admonitionem invenies apud Lutherum in Consilio de Scholis erigendis, & apud Marsennum, pag. 679. & 680. ubi citat & Dominum de Muys, Professorem Regium, qui in Appendice ad Grammaticam Bellarmini plurima adduxit, quibus solidè probatur, nihil solidi ex hac voce posse concludi.
units.tr: Hebrew: Created Elohim, that is, the gods. Peter Lombard, first of all, in Sentences book 1, distinction 2, built an argument for a plurality of persons in the divine essence on this construction of a plural noun with a singular verb. Others imitated him, among them Paul of Burgos, in his Additions to Lyra. But its weakness was sharply observed and clearly set out by Alfonso Tostatus, bishop of Ávila, Cajetan, Bellarmine and others: Tostatus and Cajetan in their commentaries on this passage, Bellarmine in the controversy on Christ, book 2, chapter 6. Sixtus of Siena too, in Annotation 1 of book 4 of his Bibliotheca, takes Cajetan's side and scolds Ambrosius Catharinus for attacking that most learned cardinal on this point, as if many others, without any suspicion of heresy, had not disagreed with the Master of the Sentences on this question, though he is himself inconsistent when he proposes this opinion. Among our own people, Calvin, Mercer and countless others showed the weakness of this argument. But above all others Pareus, in his commentary on this passage and in Orthodox Calvin, and Drusius, in his treatise on the name Elohim, have treated the question most diligently and, as it were, ex professo. Since these books are in everyone's hands, I will add nothing more on the matter. The beginner should note only this: those great men did not do this so that the difficult article on the Holy Trinity would collapse once this prop was removed. They did it to teach theologians, who are going to dispute this very serious question with the subtlest heretics, that they must cling to more solid arguments. For, as Thomas excellently warned, when someone brings forward non-compelling arguments to prove the Christian faith, he falls into the mockery of unbelievers. They think that we are moved by such arguments, and believe because of them. You will find the same warning in Luther, in his Counsel on Founding Schools, and in Mersenne, pp. 679 and 680, where he also cites Lord de Muys, royal professor, who in an appendix to Bellarmine's Grammar adduced many points by which it is solidly shown that nothing solid can be concluded from this word.

units.la: Ibid. An deus omnia uno eodemque momento condiderit, an verò VI. dierum spatio, dicetur ad cap. 18. Sirach.
units.tr: Whether God created all things in one and the same moment, or rather in the space of six days, will be discussed at Sirach chapter 18.

units.la: Vers. 5. Dies unus.
units.tr: Verse 5. One day.

units.la: Ebr. יוֹם אֶחָד / Notarunt eruditi Interpretes אחד hic positum pro ראשון primus. Cardinale pro ordinali. In Ebraismo nihil tritius. Hagg. 1. die uno mensis. In novo quoque Test. eadem occurrit Enallage Quam Matth. 28. 1. vocat μίαν σαββάτων, eam Johannes 20. 1. vocat πρώτῳ. Id si in mentem venisset Thomæ, pag. 1. qu. 74. art. 3. non adeo sudasset in responsione ad Quæstionem illam, cur dicatur unus dies, cum secundo, tertio, &c. non respondeat convenienter unum sed primum. Theophyl. in Lucam, Ἀγρὸς ἐξηγεῖται τὸ μίαν σημαίνει πρώτῳ. Cicero in De Senect. Qui uno & octogesimo anno mortuus est. Suet. in Augusto cap. ultimo. Uno mandata de funere complexus, &c.
units.tr: Hebrew: יוֹם אֶחָד. Learned interpreters have noted that אחד is used here for ראשון, first, the cardinal for the ordinal. Nothing is more common in Hebrew. Haggai 1: on the one day of the month. The same enallage occurs in the New Testament: what Matthew 28:1 calls μίαν σαββάτων, John 20:1 calls πρώτῳ. If this had come into Thomas's mind (Part 1, question 74, article 3), he would not have sweated so much over the answer to the question why it says "one day" when "second, third" and so on do not agree with "one" but with "first". Theophylact on Luke: "one" [μίαν] means "first" [πρώτῳ]. Cicero in De Senectute: who died in his eighty-first year. Suetonius in Augustus, last chapter: having taken in hand the arrangements for his funeral, and so on.

units.la: Verf. 6. יְהִי רָקִיעַ Fiat Firmamentum, vertit vulgatus, secutus magis Græcum στερέωμα, quàm Ebræum. In hoc enim istius significationis nec vestigium nec vola apparet. Conniveri ad hoc possët, posset; nisi ea versio Philosophis quibusdam & interpretibus errandi occasionem praebuisset. Cum enim vox firmamentum apud Philosophos sphaeram octavam seu stelliferam significet, hinc nata opinio, supra octavam sphaeram esse coelum aliquod aqueum seu aquas, de quibus rursus non una fuit opinio. Consule hic Lyram, Cajetanum, Mercerum, Drusium, Paraeum Lutherum, Calvinum, Illyricum in Clavi, voce aqua. Certe haec versio Augustinum eo induxit ut l. 13. confess. cap. 32. scripserit, Firmamentum factum esse inter aquas spirituales superiores, & corporales inferiores, quod tamen retractat Retract. lib. 2. 6. Quid Origenes? Is per aquas superiores, bonos Angelos: per inferiores, malos intellexit. Vide Epiphan. Epist. ad Joh. Jerosolymitanum & Hieron. Epist ad Pammachium. Lyra, Abulensis, Catharinus, Burgensis, & alii per aquas superiores primum mobile intellexere, ut sic dictum sit propter suam διαφάνειαν. Alii, ut Vives & Helwicus veras aquas elementales intelligunt, licet nullum earum usum assignare possint. Lutherus admodum hic sudat & postquam satis ostendisset, sibi prae aliis illam placere sententiam quae aquas elementales intelligit, isthoc sine illic positas, ut inferiores humectent & refrigerent, ne videlicet ex nimio ardore conflagrent, tamen eo tandem redit, ut profiteatur ignorantiam suam & moneat hic captivandum esse intellectum. August. per Firmamentum passim intelligit coelum sidereum, atque ita dici asserit, (de Genesi ad lit. lib. 2. cap. 9. & 10.) non propter stationem, sed propter firmitatem vel terminum aquarum intransgressibilem. Sed quales sint istae aquae, non audet asserere. Aquas tamen supra illud esse constanter asserit. Et quare? Major est huius textus authoritas, inquit, quam omnis humani ingenii capacitas. Lombardus, postquam lib. 2. dist. 14. hac de re quoque disputasset, sed quoquo modo ibi sint, ibi esse aquas non dubitamus, inquit. Tu Tyro disce, רקיע proprie significare Expansum, à רקע expando, extendo. Vox Ebraea, inquit Steuchus, extensionem significat, aut id quod extenditur, ut vela, cortina, &c. Vide omnia Lexica, & nominatim Pagnini. Vsurpatur autem ea vox non tantum de orbibus, ut postea, Fiant luminaria in expansu; sed etiam de aere, & quidem de infima ejus regione. * Cajetanus, appellatione extensionis (רקיע) coelorum Moses non tantum orbes comprehendit, in quibus sunt astra, sed & orbe ignis & aëru. Et annotator
units.tr: Verse 6, "Let there be a firmament" (Fiat firmamentum), is how the Vulgate renders יְהִי רָקִיעַ [yehi raqia]. The translator followed the Greek στερέωμα [stereōma] rather than the Hebrew. The Hebrew shows no trace or hint of that sense, and the Vulgate could be excused for it, were it not that this rendering gave some philosophers and interpreters an occasion for error. Since the word firmamentum among the philosophers means the eighth sphere, the starry sphere, an opinion arose that above the eighth sphere there is some watery heaven, or waters, and there was no single view about these either. On this, consult Lyra, Cajetan, Mercer, Drusius, Paraeus, Luther, Calvin, and Illyricus in the Clavis, under the word aqua. This rendering certainly led Augustine to write, in Confessions 13.32, that the firmament was made between the superior spiritual waters and the inferior corporeal waters, though he retracts this in Retractions 2.6. What did Origen say? He understood the superior waters to be the good angels and the inferior waters the bad. See Epiphanius, his letter to John of Jerusalem, and Jerome, his letter to Pammachius. Lyra, Abulensis, Catharinus, Burgensis, and others understood the superior waters to be the primum mobile, so that it was called that because of its transparency (diaphaneia [διαφάνεια]). Others, such as Vives and Helwig, understand true elemental waters, although they cannot assign any use for them. Luther sweats hard here. After showing well enough that he prefers, above the others, the view that understands elemental waters, placed there so as to moisten and cool the lower regions lest they burn up from excessive heat, he finally comes to this: he professes his ignorance and warns that the intellect must be taken captive here. Augustine generally understands by the firmament the starry heaven, and he asserts that it is so called (in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis 2.9 and 10) not because of its standing firm, but because of its firmness, or because it is a boundary the waters cannot cross. But he does not dare to say what kind of waters these are. Yet he consistently asserts that the waters lie above it. And why? The authority of this text, he says, is greater than the full capacity of human intellect. Lombard, after discussing this matter in Sentences 2, dist. 14, says: but however they are there, we do not doubt that waters are there. Learn this, young student: רקיע [raqia] properly means expanse, from רקע [raqa], to spread out, to stretch. The Hebrew word, says Steuchus, means an extension, or that which is extended, like sails, a curtain, and so on. See all the lexicons, and especially Pagninus. The word is used not only of the spheres, as later, let there be lights in the expanse, but also of the air, and indeed of its lowest region. * Cajetan: By the term "extension" (רקיע) of the heavens, Moses comprehends not only the spheres in which the stars are, but also the sphere of fire and of air. And his annotator Fonseca:

units.la: Vide Gen. 1. 6. tor ejus Fonseca, Biblia passim aërem vocant cœlum & firmamentum. Audiamus etiam Ebraeos, Kimchi ad Psf.77.20. Aër verè ac proprie vocatur Rakiang. Abenezra quoque vocem eandem hic interpretatur per אויר id est aër, ut & Chaldaeus Psf.19.1. alibi. Ut ergo שמים cœlum, etiam pro aëre, & quidem infimâ ejus regione, ponitur, ut cum legimus Psal. 8. Math. 6. 26. aves cœli, ita & רקיע pari hac ex parte cum ea decurrit orbita. Ecce enim vers. 20. Et volatile volet in superficie expansi cœlorum. Ubi & illud notet Tyro, expansum cœlorum vel cœli esse locutionem ἐν στερεώματι, ut volumen, libri, Petra silicis, Silex Petra & similia, quod & Abnezra ad versum ultimum hujus cap. notavit, his verbis, רקיע השמים הרקיע שהוא שמים / expansum cœlorum id est expansum, quod est cœlum. Nunc itaque nemo ignorare potest, quid per aquas superas intelligat Moses nempe aquas nubium, quae sunt in media aëris regione, quas ab inferioribus, aëris infimi expansum dividit. Huic sententiae robur aliquod addunt ex Patribus quoque Ambrosius, in Hexaem. 5.22. & Augustinus de Genesi ad literam 2.4. & Basilius. Acacius verò, Honorius Augustodunensis Presbyter, eam evidenter probarunt. Et ex recentioribus Pererius in hunc locum, Bolducus ad Job cap. 37. Bannes in Thomam tomo 2. pag. 59. Arias Mont. de arcano sermone, Mariana in Scholiis, Pradus in Jezech. p.25. (qui haec addit, Cui expositioni totius primi capitis Genes. alioqui obscurissimi intelligentiam debemus.) Steuchus in Cosmop. Calv. Paraus, Merc. Drusf. Beroald. in Chronol. Pisc. Jun. nec improbant Thomas pag. 1. q. 68. art. 1. Genebrard. ad Psf.19. ipsi 18. 1. &c.
units.tr: See Genesis 1.6. The Bible everywhere calls the air heaven and firmament. Let us hear the Hebrews too. Kimchi on Psalm 77.20: air is truly and properly called Rakiang. Abraham ibn Ezra also interprets the same word here as אויר [avir], that is, air, as does the Chaldee paraphrast on Psalm 19.1 and elsewhere. So just as שמים [shamayim], heaven, is also used for the air, and indeed its lowest region, as when we read in Psalm 8 and in Matthew 6.26, the birds of heaven, so רקיע runs its course in the same way on this side. For see verse 20: and let the flying creature fly above the face of the expanse of the heavens. Here the learner should also note that expanse of the heavens or of heaven is an expression in the firmament [ἐν στερεώματι], like volume of a book, rock of flint, flint rock, and similar ones. Abenezra also noted this at the last verse of this chapter, in these words: רקיע השמים הרקיע שהוא שמים [raqia hashamayim, the expanse which is heaven]: the expanse of the heavens, that is, the expanse which is heaven. Now therefore no one can be ignorant of what Moses means by the upper waters, namely the waters of the clouds, which lie in the middle region of the air, and which the expanse divides from the lower parts of the lowest air. Some support for this view is also drawn from the Fathers: Ambrose, in Hexaemeron 5.22; Augustine, in On Genesis according to the Letter 2.4; and Basil. Acacius, indeed, and Honorius of Autun, a presbyter, clearly proved it. Among more recent writers, Pererius on this passage, Bolduc on Job 37, Banez on Thomas, vol. 2, p. 59, Arias Montanus in De arcano sermone, Mariana in his Scholia, Prado on Ezekiel, p. 25 (who adds: we owe the understanding of the whole of the first chapter of Genesis, otherwise most obscure, to this exposition), Steuchus in Cosmopoeia, Calvin, Paraeus, Mercer, Drusius, Beroaldus in Chronologia, and Piscator and Junius do not disapprove of it, nor does Thomas, part 1, q. 68, art. 1, nor Genebrard on Psalm 19, nor Ipsi on 18.1, and so on.

units.la: Atque haec mea censura fuit ad versf.6. cap. 1. Genes. Ego hicipaucula tantum adjeci. Eam cum non impugnet Marsennus, Heroibus istis, quos jam produxi, annumerari posset, nisi adeo varie hac de re loquerctur, ut quae propria ejus sententia fuerit, vix colligas. Confer ea quae scripsit observat. ad Probl. x. G. Veneti, cum commentariis ejus p.845. & calculo meo tuum quoque, satscio, appones.
units.tr: Thus far my criticism of verse 6 of chapter 1 of Genesis. I have added only a few remarks here. Marsenne does not refute it, so he could be counted among the heroes I have already brought forward, except that he discusses this matter so variously that you can hardly work out what his own opinion was. Compare what he wrote in his observations on the Problems of G. Veneti, with his commentary at p. 845. You will also add my calculation to yours, I know.

units.la: Obj. Psal. 148. Laudate eum, aqua quae supra cœlum. Resp. per שמים intelligi isthic loci idem expansum, in quo aves volant, unde aves cœli dicuntur Psf.8. Matth.6.
units.tr: Objection: Psalm 148: Praise him, you waters that are above the heavens. Answer: In that place the Hebrew word for heavens (שמים) means the same expanse in which the birds fly, which is why the birds are called "birds of the heaven" in Ps. 8 and Matt. 6.

units.la: Obj. Psf.104.3. qui contignat in aquis cenacula sua. Resp. Confer verba sequentia, qui disponit nubes in vehiculum suum & vers.13. Qui irrigat montes è cenaculis suis, & habebis responsum.
units.tr: Objection: Ps. 104:3: who lays the beams of his chambers in the waters. Answer: Compare the following words, who makes the clouds his chariot, and verse 13, who waters the mountains from his chambers, and you will have the answer.

units.la: Ad verf. 10.
units.tr: On verse 10.

units.la: Congregationem aquarum vocavit maria.
units.tr: He called the gathering of the waters seas.

units.la: Audi Lector & ride. Stellarium coronæ B. Virginis editum Hagenoæ 1498. sic habet, Quid est congregatio aquarum, nisi congregatio omnium gratiarum in locum unum id est in virginem Mariam. Congregationem gratiarum in Dei Matre Deus voluit vocari Maria à Mari. In hoc tamen est differentia, quod congregatio aquarum vocatur Maria, media correptâ; congregatio gratiarum Maria, media producta. Causa, cur maria, media correpta, quia transitoria est & brevi tempore erit. Apoc. 21. mare abit & jam non est. Maria, media producta, quia ista congregatio perpetua est in virgine, Luc. 10. Maria optimam partem elegit, quæ non auferetur ab ea. En ineptias! Quod si Moses Latinè scripsisset, hæc tamen essent absurdissima. Ut nihil jam dicam, quàm imperitè duas Marias confundat, cum Luc.10. nequaquam de Matre Domini agatur.
units.tr: Listen, Reader, and laugh. The Stellarium of the Blessed Virgin, printed at Hagenau in 1498, reads as follows: What is the gathering of the waters, but the gathering of all graces in one place, that is, in the Virgin Mary? God willed that the gathering of graces in the Mother of God be called Maria, from mari (sea). There is this difference, however: the gathering of waters is called Maria with the middle syllable short, the gathering of graces Maria with the middle syllable long. The reason the gathering of waters is maria with a short middle is that it is transitory and will last only a short time. Rev. 21: the sea passes away and is no more. Maria with a long middle, because that gathering is perpetual in the Virgin, Luke 10: Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her. What silly nonsense! And if Moses had written in Latin, these things would still be utterly absurd. Not to mention how unskilfully he confuses the two Marys, when Luke 10 is not at all about the Mother of the Lord.

units.la: Ad verf. 16.
units.tr: On verse 16.

units.la: Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna.
units.tr: God made the two great lights.

units.la: Audi & hic mysterium magnum quod subtilesisti Allegoristæ nobis pandunt. Innocentius III. ad Imperat. Constantinopol. cap. solita, de Majorit. & obedientia, Fecit, inquit, Deus duo luminaria magna id est duas institutit dignitates quæ sunt Pontificalis authoritas & regalis Majestas, sed illa quæ præest diebus id est spiritualibus, major est altera, quæ noctibus id est carnalibus; ut quanta est inter Solem & Lunam, tanta inter Pontifices & Reges differentia cognoscatur. Eandem expositionem allegavit Molina de just. & jure tom 1. tract.2. disp.29. nec indigna visa est Marsenno quam pag. 1006. proponeret. Videatur etiam Carthusianus artic. 16. in Caput. I. Genes.
units.tr: Listen here too to the great mystery that the subtle allegorists lay open to us. Innocent III, to the Emperor of Constantinople, chapter solita, on majority and obedience: God made, he says, the two great lights, that is, he instituted two dignities, the pontifical authority and the royal majesty; but the one that presides over the days, that is, over spiritual things, is greater than the other, which presides over the nights, that is, over carnal things; so that as great as the difference between the Sun and the Moon, so great is the difference between Popes and Kings. Molina in his work on justice and right (vol. 1, tract. 2, disp. 29) cited the same exposition, and Marsenne did not think it unworthy of setting out at p. 1006. See also the Carthusian, article 16, on Genesis chapter 1.

units.tr: On verse 26.

units.la: יִדְמוּתֵנוּ בְּצַלְמֵנוּ Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra & secundum similitudinem nostram | Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. LXX. καὶ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν.
units.tr: בְּדְמוּתֵנוּ בְּצַלְמֵנוּ [bedemutenu betsalmenu] Let us make man in our image and according to our likeness | Let us make man to the image and likeness of us. Septuagint: καὶ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν [kai eikona hemeteran kai kath' homoiosin] and our image and according to likeness.

units.la: Bonaventura, citante Carthusiano, Duplex est modus, inquit, exponendi hanc authoritatem, Faciamus hominem, &c. Vnus. intelligendo de imagine increatâ ; alter, de creatâ. Primus modus triplicatur. I. Vt imago & similitudo referantur ad idem, vid. ad essentiam in tribus personis unam. II. Vt imago & similitudo referantur ad filium tantum. Ita Origenes & Marsennus. III. Vt imago referatur ad filium, similitudo ad Sp. sanctum. Ita etiam Rupertus. Porro alius modus est exponendi de imagine creata, & rursus triplicatur. Vnus sic exponit, ut imago praecedat similitudinem. Et dicit quod imago attenditur in naturalibus, similitudo in gratuitis. Secundus, ut similitudo concomitetur imaginem. Et dicit quod imago sit in potentia cognoscendi, similitudo in potentia diligendi. Tertius modus est, ut imago sequatur similitudinem, quia similitudo est in plus seu communius quam imago. Et dicit quod similitudo attenditur in natura id est quantum ad ea quae sunt essentia in commuui : imago forma id est quantum ad propria.
units.tr: Bonaventure, as cited by the Carthusian: There are two ways, he says, of expounding this authority, "Let us make man," etc. One is by understanding it of the uncreated image; the other, of the created. The first way is threefold. I. That image and likeness refer to the same thing, namely the one essence in the three persons. II. That image and likeness refer to the Son alone. So Origen and Marsenne. III. That image refers to the Son, likeness to the Holy Spirit. So also Rupert. Further, there is another way of expounding it of the created image, and this too is threefold. One expounds it so that image precedes likeness. And he says that the image is found in natural gifts, the likeness in gratuitous gifts. The second, that likeness accompanies image. And he says that the image lies in the power of knowing, the likeness in the power of loving. The third way is that image follows likeness, because likeness is wider or more common than image. And he says that likeness is found in nature, that is, as regards those things which are common to the essence; image in form, that is, as regards what is proper.

units.la: Hi modi omnes, inquit Carthus. possunt secundum Bonavent. sustineri. Paulò post, Filius proprie dicitur imago Patris, ideo quidam hoc loco per imaginem filium intelligunt, hominem vero non imaginem, sed ad imaginem factum dixerunt, quibus obviat quod Apostolus inquit, Vir quidem est imago & gloria Dei. Alii ergo perspicacius per imaginem intellexerunt filium, per similitudinem Spiritum s. qui est similitudo Patris & filii. Et quod additur (in vulgata) nostram, retulerunt ad similitudinem tantum. Ad vocem imaginem autem putaverunt subintelligendum, meam.
units.tr: All these ways, the Carthusian says, can be upheld according to Bonaventure. A little later: The Son is properly called the image of the Father; therefore some in this place understand the Son by the image, but say that man was made not the image but to the image, to whom the Apostle's words are opposed: "Man indeed is the image and glory of God." Others, then, with greater insight understood the Son by the image, and the Holy Spirit by the likeness, who is the likeness of Father and Son. And as to what is added in the Vulgate, our, they referred it to the likeness only. But they thought that my had to be understood with the word image.

units.la: Ex his & id genus aliis, quae ad hunc textum à Scholasticis afferuntur, varii varia eliciunt. Bellar. lib. 1. de gratia primi hominis cap. 2. & alii discrimem statuentes inter imaginem & similitudinem & per imaginem ipsam animam rationalem, volendi intelligendique facultatem intelligentes, per similitudinem vero justitiam, sanctitatem, sapientiam & cetera quae supernaturalia vocant, colligunt in homine post lapsum naturalia manisse integra. Etian. Basil. imaginem ad animam rationalem, similitudinem vero ad actiones Deo conformes refert, addens insuper, ad Dei imaginem nos creatos esse actu, ad similitudinem vero potentiâ: Imaginem nos habere naturâ, similitudinem voluntate nostrâ. Mihi, inquit, reliquit Deus ut secundum similitudinem Dei fiam. Vides Lector, quò detruserit beatam animam Linguarum imperitia. Eucherius, Imago est omnium, similitudo paucorum. Nempe ille quoque ratus est imaginem ad naturam hominis, similitudinem vero ad dona gratuita referri. Marsennus postquam subscripsisset sententiæ Origenis, qui per imaginem & similitudinem nostram, intelligit imaginem Filii Dei, qui est Patris imago invisibilis, delabitur ad quæstionem, an homo, ut Dei imago, possit & debeat adorari. Post multas ambages & præsuppolita concludit pag. 1060. hominem, non beatum (de eo non est quæstio, inquit,) sed nude spectatum, quatenus hic in Genesi ad imaginem Dei creatus esse dicitur, ex sententia Theologorum, eâ posse adoratione adorari, quâ solent imagines Dei & Christi, latria videlicet. Et paulò post, Ex quibus infertur, inquit, non esse per se & intrinsecè malum, si hominem, ut imaginem Dei, prout & alias inanimatas imagines adoraverimus. Et pag. 1061. Posset aliquis in particulari sibi aliquem proponere, quem velut imaginem Dei adorandum proponeret. Non audet tamen pronunciare, debere id fieri; quin contra asserit, neminem debere hac adoratione uti, idque ob varia incommoda & pericula inde oritura, nisi quis forte egregius esset Metaphysicus, qui posset mente secludere omnem honorem qui debetur homini vel quatenus est homo, & eatenus duntaxat eum respicere, quâ Deum imago repræsentat, ut sola Dei imago, quæ est in eo, nostrum conceptum & actum voluntatis terminet. Et quidem hæc quæ mei pectoris angustiæ non capiunt, Theologis disputienda relinquo. Tria solummodo hic notet Tyro: I. In Ebr. esse in imagine nostrâ, non vero in imagine, ut legit vulgata. Ut proinde cadat illud, quod hic nugatur Carthusianus. Lectioni Ebr. concors est Gr. & Chaldæus. II. Cum tam dicatur quàm quomodo per intelligitur Filius? An is quoque Spiritus Sancti imago dicitur? Corn. à Lap. Imago hæc non est Filius, qui est imago Patris, sed est ipsa essentia divina, ipsequeque Deus unus & trinus. III. & id hic significare, & καθ' ἐπεξήγησιν esse conjuncta. Id Cornelius à Lapide & Pererius intrepedè asserunt, non obstante comuni fere Patrum sententiâ. Rationes Pererii ubi adduxero, manum tollam de hac tabula. Ratio I. quia Gen. 5. 3. eodem prorsus modo Adam dicitur genuisse Filium ad imaginem & similitudinem suam, ubi ista distinctio non quadrat. II. Quia quod isti similitudinem vocant, Paulus vocat imaginem, 1. Cor. 15. 49. Coloss. 3. 10. Eph. 4. 24. III. Quia Scriptura passim has voces permutat, & usurpat promiscuè, cum de eadem re loquitur. ut Gen. 1. 26. utrumque ponitur, At verf. 27. unum tantum. Gen. 5. 1. unum tantum ponitur. vid. רמות / Gen. 9. 5. צלם / Sirach. 7. 3. καὶ εἰκόνα ὑπόμνητιν ἀυτὸν, Jacob. 3. 9. καθ' ὁμοίωσιν γεγονότας.
units.tr: From these and similar points which the Schoolmen bring to this text, people draw various conclusions. Bellarmine (book 1, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 2) and others, who set up a distinction between image and likeness and understand by the image the rational soul, the faculty of willing and understanding, but by the likeness justice, holiness, wisdom and the other things they call supernatural, conclude that in man after the fall the natural gifts remained intact. Likewise Basil refers image to the rational soul, but likeness to actions conformed to God, adding moreover that we were created in the image of God actually, but in the likeness potentially: we have the image by nature, the likeness by our will. God has left me, he says, to become according to the likeness of God. You see, Reader, to what depths the blessed soul has been thrust down by ignorance of languages. Eucherius: The image belongs to all, the likeness to few. Clearly he too thought that the image refers to human nature, but the likeness to gratuitous gifts. Marsenne, after subscribing to the opinion of Origen, who understands by our image and likeness the image of the Son of God, who is the invisible image of the Father, slides into the question whether man, as the image of God, can and ought to be worshipped. After many circumlocutions and presuppositions he concludes at p. 1060: that man, not blessed (there is no question of that, he says), but considered merely as such, insofar as he is said in Genesis to have been created in the image of God, can, according to the opinion of theologians, be worshipped with that worship by which the images of God and of Christ are customarily worshipped, namely latria. And a little later: From which it follows, he says, that it is not in itself and intrinsically evil, if we worship man as the image of God, just as we have worshipped other inanimate images. And at p. 1061: Someone might set before himself in particular some person whom he would propose as worthy of worship as the image of God. Yet he does not dare to declare that this ought to be done; on the contrary he asserts that no one ought to use this worship, on account of the various inconveniences and dangers arising from it, unless perhaps someone were an outstanding metaphysician who could mentally set aside all the honour due to man, either insofar as he is man, and regard him only so far as the image represents God, so that only the image of God which is in him terminates our concept and act of will. These matters, which the narrowness of my mind does not grasp, I leave to be disputed by the theologians. Let the novice note only three things here. I. In the Hebrew it is in our image, not in the image, as the Vulgate reads. So the Carthusian's trifling falls away. The Greek and the Chaldee agree with the Hebrew reading. II. Since as and how are used interchangeably, is the Son understood by the phrase in the image? Is he also called the image of the Holy Spirit? Cornelius a Lapide: This image is not the Son, who is the image of the Father, but is the divine essence itself, which is itself one and triune God. III. And that this phrase means also, and is joined by kath' epexegesin [in explanation]. Cornelius a Lapide and Pererius assert this boldly, although nearly all the Fathers hold a common opinion against it. When I have set out Pererius's reasons I will withdraw my hand from this tablet. Reason I: because in Gen. 5:3 Adam is said in exactly the same way to have begotten a son in his image and likeness, where this distinction does not fit. II. Because what they call likeness, Paul calls image (1 Cor. 15:49; Col. 3:10; Eph. 4:24). III. Because Scripture everywhere interchanges these words and uses them indiscriminately when speaking of the same thing: in Gen. 1:26 both are given, but in verse 27 only one; in Gen. 5:1 only one is given. Compare demuth / Gen. 9:6 tselem; Sirach 17:3 καὶ εἰκόνα ὑπόμνηστιν αὐτὸν [and an image as a reminder of himself]; James 3:9 καθ' ὁμοίωσιν γεγονότας [made according to likeness].

units.la: Gen. II. 7. Formavit itaque Dominus Deus, &c.
units.tr: Gen. 2:7. So the Lord God formed, etc.

units.la: Hic primò occurrit in Ebr. nomen Dei Tetragrammaton יהוה de cujus lectione dicetur ad Exod. 6. illud nunc observa, Interpretes Græcos hoc redddiisse per Κύριος, Latinos verò ad superius usque seculum. per Dominus, non sine aliquo incommodo. Ecce enim * Tertullianus aliique cum observarent, per universum caput primum Dominus nusquam comparere, hoc verò loco primum occurrere, operæ duxerunt in istius rei causam inquirere, quam se quoque invenisse arbitrati sunt. Quandiu, inquit ille, faciebat Deus, quorum Deus futurus erat, Deus solummodo ponitur, Et dixit Deus, & vidit Deus, &c. nunquam adhuc Dominus. At ubi universa perfecit, maxime hominem, qui Dominum proprie erat intellecturus, Dominus etiam cognominatur. Magister Historiæ Scholast. cap. 12. Hic primò vocat Deum Dominum, quia tunc proprie habuit servum laborantem. Acute profecto, si vel Latine vel Græce scripsisset Moses, aut si τὸ Dominus genuinum τὸ πτεραγεμάτων ὀνόματος esset interpretamentum. Nunc adi ad ea, quæ ad Exod. Caput VI. diceimus.
units.tr: Here the name of God, the Tetragrammaton [יהוה], first occurs in Hebrew. I will discuss how it is read at Exod. 6. For now, note that the Greek interpreters rendered it by Κύριος [Kyrios], and the Latins, until the previous century, by Dominus, not without some inconvenience. Tertullian and others observed that Dominus appears nowhere in the whole first chapter but occurs here for the first time, and they thought it worth inquiring into the reason, which they believed they had found. "As long as God was making the things," he says, "over which he was to be God, God alone is named: And God said, and God saw, etc. Never yet the Lord. But when he had finished everything, especially man, who was to understand properly what the Lord is, he is also called Lord." The Master of the Histories (Scholastic Histories, ch. 12) says: "Here he first calls God Dominus, because then he had properly a servant at work." This is certainly clever, if Moses had written in Latin or Greek, or if τὸ Dominus were a genuine translation of the tetragrammaton name [τὸ τετραγραμμάτων ὄνομα]. Now turn to what I said at Exod. chapter VI.

units.la: Reverendis, piis & celeberrimis VIRIS, D. FANCISCO GOMARO, D. ANDREAE RIVETO, Doctoribus & Professoribus Theologis, Dominis & fautoribus meis observandis,
units.tr: To the reverend, pious and most distinguished men, Dr. Franciscus Gomarus and Dr. Andreas Rivetus, teachers and professors of theology, my masters and patrons to be honoured,

units.la: ABsque te fuisset, reverende D. Gomare, nunquam censuram meam ad vulgatam Pentateuchi versionem evulgassem. Tu inter maximas muneris tui occupationes eam recognoscere & benigniori calculo condecorare non es dedignatus. Ita, te obstetricante, primus ille adolescentiae meae foetus in dias luminis oras prodiit. Absque te fuisset, Cl. Rivete, nomen Marsenni, qui VI. priorum Geneseos capitum adversus meas strictuas suscepit patrocinium etiamnum juxta cum ignarissimis ignorassem. Tu primus mihi indicium, tu voluminis copiam fecisti. Tu ad modestam & mansuetam replicationem hortamentis tuis me animasti. Ad vestros ergo pedes merito depono hoc quicquid est opellae. Alia sunt quorum nomine me majora debendi reum habetis, quae hic recensere nihil attinet. Summa summarum hic redit,
units.tr: Without you, reverend Dr. Gomarus, I would never have published my criticism of the Vulgate version of the Pentateuch. Among the very great demands of your office, you did not disdain to review it and to grace it with a kinder verdict. Thus, with you as midwife, that first offspring of my youth came out into the light of day. Without you, distinguished Rivetus, I would still not even have known the name of Marsennus, who took up the defence of the first six chapters of Genesis against my strictures, together with the most ignorant of men. You first gave me the hint, you gave me the material for the volume. By your exhortations you encouraged me to a modest and mild reply. To your feet, then, I rightly lay down whatever this little work is. There are other matters for which you hold me bound by a greater debt, which it is not worth listing here. The sum of the matter comes to this:

units.la: I. Ut has schedas, ubi otium erit, inspiciatis, & sicubi vel a veritatis vel a modestiae tramite exorbitasse videbor, liberè castigetis. Scio enim vos eos esse, queis nemo mortalium <bl>ἐχθρὸς</bl> ... uti possit. Deinde, ut eas accipiatis, ceu testes eximii istius cul-
units.tr: I. That you look over these pages when you have leisure, and if I seem anywhere to have strayed from the path of truth or of modesty, that you rebuke me freely. For I know you are men whom no mortal could make into an [ἐχθρὸς] enemy. Next, that you accept them as witnesses of that distinguished cul-

units.la: Scio enim vos eos esse, queis nemo mortalium uti possit. tus, quem vestris reverentiis jure merito defero. Valete incomparabiles viri & diurnate bono Ecclesiarum. XXVII. Dec. 1626.
units.tr: For I know you are men whom no mortal could make into an enemy, and I know you are the witnesses of that distinguished respect (cul-)tus, which I rightly and deservedly pay to your reverences. Farewell, incomparable men, and long-lived for the good of the Churches. 27 December 1626.

units.la: VV. RR. devotissimus. S. Amama.
units.tr: Most devoted to your Reverences, S. Amama.

units.la: De occasione hujus excursus mei, dixi supra pag. 97. quae possint esse vice praeloquii. Ea, si operae erit, inde petat Lector. Nos ergo sine ambagibus rem ipsam aggrediamur. Censuram meam primam ad Genes. 1. 6. silentio praetervehitur Marsennus. Primum impetum facit in strictura meam ad vers. 20. Eam ubi vindicavero, non parvum argumentum accedet ad confirmationem eorum, quae ad vers. 6. cap. 1. de Firmamento disseruimus. Hic enim videbit Lector, frustra esse omnes Interpretes, qui ut vulgatam excusent, persuadere nobis satagunt, eam pro Firmamentum pro aere usurpasse. Mariana in scholiis, Ebraice, inquit, est, super faciem firmamenti, ad confirmationem, רקיע nihil aliud esse quàm aërem. Quin & Marsenus pag. 836. totus in eo est, ut ostendat, aërem commodissimè vocari posse στερέωμα, vel firmamentum: aquè enim discriminat, inquit, aquas ab aquis, ac si aneum esset, vel quod suo frigore vapores & exhalationes firmet, induret, & sape in lapides & grandinem convertat. vel denique firmiter in loco suo remaneat. Sed haec adversantur, 1. communi vocis Latinae usui. Et mirabor si negare ausit Marsennus, huic vocis רקיע * interpretamento, sententiam illam de aquis supra coelum stelliferum pendulis, natales suos debere. Adversentur 2. Gernebrardo, qui ad Ps. 19. ipsi 18. 2. diserte inquit, στερέωμα non potest dici de aere, ut qui sit fluxissimus, infirmissimus, minime στερεός, solidus & fixus. Adversantur 3. menti ipsius Interpretis. Videamus
units.tr: About the occasion of this digression of mine, I said above on page 97 what might serve as a preface. If it is worth the effort, the reader may seek it there. So let us approach the matter itself without circumlocution. Marsennus passes over in silence my first criticism, on Genesis 1:6. He makes his first attack on my stricture on verse 20. Once I have defended that, a not small argument will be added to the confirmation of what we discussed on verse 6 of chapter 1 concerning the Firmament. For here the reader will see that all the interpreters are in vain who, in order to excuse the Vulgate, labour to persuade us that it used firmamentum for the air. Mariana in his scholia says: "The Hebrew is," he says, "upon the face of the firmament," and "for confirmation," that raqia' [רקיע] is nothing other than the air. Indeed Marsennus on page 836 is wholly intent on showing that the air can most fittingly be called [στερέωμα] or firmament: "for it equally separates," he says, "the waters from the waters," as if it were of bronze, or because by its cold it firms, hardens and often turns the vapours and exhalations into stones and hail, or finally because it remains firmly in its place. But these views are opposed, first, by the common usage of the Latin word. And I shall be surprised if Marsennus dares to deny that the opinion about waters hanging above the starry heaven owes its origin to this interpretation of the Hebrew word raqia' [רקיע]. They are opposed, second, by Gernebrardus, who on Psalm 19 (18:2 in the Hebrew) says plainly that [στερέωμα] cannot be said of the air, since it is most fluid, most weak, and in no way [στερεός], solid and fixed. They are opposed, third, by the mind of the interpreter himself. Let us see.

units.la: Producant aquae reptile animae viventis: & volatile volet super terram על פני רקיע השמים * | Producant aquae reptile animae viventis, & volatile super terram sub firmamento coeli.
units.tr: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature of living soul, and let the flying creature fly over the earth upon the face of the firmament of heaven [על פני רקיע השמים]. | Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature of living soul, and let the flying creature fly over the earth under the firmament of heaven.

units.la: Major est hujus textus authoritas, quam omnis humani ingenii capacitas, inquit Augustinus. Vide supra.
units.tr: The authority of this text is greater than the whole capacity of the human mind, says Augustine. See above.

units.la: * ad verbum super facies expansi coelorum i in superficie &c. i. in aere, vel aërem, vel secus, vel versus superficiem. Has enim expositiones partim ad mittit.
units.tr: * Literally, "upon the face of the expanse of the heavens," that is, "upon the surface," etc., that is, in the air, or the air, or otherwise, or towards the surface. For some of these interpretations I partly admit.

units.la: Censura mea.
units.tr: My criticism.

units.la: Duppliciter peccatum. Primo enim omissum verbum שמים ro-let, & proinde id dicere videtur vulgata Editio, quod aquis datum sit etiam aves producere, quem sensum audacter damnat Cajetanus, dicens, Mosem hic tacere productivum avium. Secundo, posterius על convertit sub, dicendo, sub firmamento. Unde patet, eum supra verf.6. & rursus, vocem Firmamentum, non pro aëre, ne dum infima ejus regione, sed pro octava sphæra accepisse. Quæ enim aliàs necessitas Interpretem ad tam coactam versionem adegisset? Dic aliquem Patrone colorem, aut ostende על supra unquam significare תחת sub in libris mysticis. Hactenus censura.
units.tr: The error is twofold. First, the word heaven [שמים] is omitted, and so the Vulgate edition seems to say that the waters were given the power also to produce birds, a sense which Cajetan boldly condemns, saying that Moses here is silent about the productive power of birds. Second, it turns the latter [על] by under, saying under the firmament. From this it is clear that it understood the word Firmament, both at verse 6 and again here, not for the air, let alone its lowest region, but for the eighth sphere. For what other necessity would have driven the translator to so forced a version? Name some plausible pretext, or show that ['al, [על]] over has ever meant [taḥat, [תחת]] under in mystical books. So much for the criticism.

units.la: Hic insurgit in me Marsennus, Placet, inquit, afferre, quod Sixt. Amama, egregius quidem hæreticorum judicio, meo verò jejunus nimium juvenisque vulgata Editionis censor in hunc locum opponit. Et pag. seq. videl. 1030. nomen meum margini appingit cum hoc elogio, Refellitur Amama Hæreticus. At hæc folia sunt, paulo post in me arbores projicit. Ego, Deo juvante, in hanc convitiandi palæstram nunquam me dabo. Ita enim sentio, pejorem esse conditionem convitium dicentis quam patientis. Ad benedicendum, mi Marsenne, nati & creati sumus, non ad maledicendum. Maledica lingua mentis index est malæ. Hæreticum me vocas, hoc convitium Serarius quoque præceptori meo Drusio b. m. faciebat. concoxit ille. Et ego Christiano stomacho concoquam. Ille se Catholicum profitebatur & erat. Ego si me quoque Catholicum dixero, non persuadebo tibi. Sum tamen, & in hac fide coram tribunali Dei intrepidus me sistam. Ibi justus judex judicabit inter nos. Videamus interim, quàm justam in me incurrendi occasionem tibi præbuerim. Vulgatam versionem me nequaquam contemnere protestatus sum. Singulæ versiones habent suas laudes, suas labes. Cur ergo hanc, cui ipsa quoque antiquitas venerationem conciliat, aspernarer? At quidnam illud sit, quod Euangelicæ Ecclesiæ concoquere non possunt, non ignoras. Eam Ecclesiis & Scholis pro authentica obtrudi, Fontes in exilium mitti, hoc, hoc est, quod indignamur. Quod ergo vulgatæ versionis nævi deteguntur, non sit in contumeliam authoris, sed ut ostendatur decreti Tridentini iniquitas. Hic est, hic fuit, hic erit laboris mei scopus. Hic Rhodus, hic saltus.
units.tr: Here Marsennus rises against me: "It pleases me to bring forward," he says, "what Sixtus Amama, indeed an outstanding judge of heretics but in my view too ignorant and too young a critic of the Vulgate edition, raises against this passage." And on the following page, namely 1030, he attaches my name in the margin with this eulogy: "Amama the heretic is refuted." But these are leaves; shortly afterwards he throws trees at me. I, God helping, shall never enter this wrestling-ground of abuse. For I think the condition of the one who utters insults is worse than that of the one who suffers them. We were born and created, my dear Marsennus, to speak well, not to speak ill. An abusive tongue is the index of a bad mind. You call me a heretic. Serarius used this same insult against my teacher Drusius, of blessed memory. He digested it. And I shall digest it with a Christian stomach. He professed himself a Catholic, and was one. If I say that I too am a Catholic, I shall not persuade you. Yet I am one, and in this faith I shall stand fearless before the judgment seat of God. There the just judge will judge between us. Meanwhile let us see how just an occasion for attack I have given you. I have protested that I by no means despise the Vulgate version. Each version has its praises, its blemishes. Why then should I scorn this one, to which antiquity itself also brings veneration? But you are not unaware what it is that the Evangelical Church cannot digest. What we are indignant about is this, this is it: that it is forced upon Churches and Schools as authentic, and that the Sources are sent into exile. Therefore, the fact that the blemishes of the Vulgate version are uncovered should be not to the author's insult, but to show the injustice of the Tridentine decree. This is, this was, this will be the aim of my labour. Here is Rhodes, here jump!

units.la: Nunc videamus singula. Quod ad primum attinet, dicis pag. 1031. te non multum insudare velle in dictione עַל / Nec ego, mi Marsenne, multum de ea laborem. Illud volui ostendere, interpretem vulgatum vocem Firmamentum accepisse non pro infima regione aëris, sed pro cœlo sidereo. Alias enim nunquam עַל vertisset Sub. עַל nunquam significare Sub, agnoscis. At pro super, secus, per, in, saepe poni, ipse doceo. Nullum horum interpretamentorum elegit vulgatus; Tam enim absurdum fuisset dicere, Aves volare secus, juxta, in & per cœlum sidereum, quàm supra. Dicis sub hoc loco idem esse quod secus, in, per, juxta. Nam quod est sub aliquâ re inquis, sepius est prope, seu juxta illam, ut aqua quae est sub aëre est juxta aërem. Respondeo, Aut per Firmamentum intellexit cœlum sidereum, aut aëris inferiorem regionem. Si cœlum sidereum, quomodo applicabis haec interpretamenta secus, juxta, prope, in, per? cum ipse dicas aves non solere aut posse altius volare, quam in inferiore aëris regione. Haec enim sunt verba tua, Adde, quod si particula עַל per super explicari debeat, per רקיע השמים aëris inseriorem regionem intelligendam esse. Nec enim aves altius volare solent aut possunt. Ad quae illud quoque addo, nihil hic esse absurdi, si per Rekiang haßjamaÿm inferiorem regionem aëris intelligamus. Quod enim ad רקיע attinet, de eo tu ipse hoc jam ante docuisti. Quod ad שמים / quid notius illo, Aves cœli Ps. 8. Math. 6. Hic autem duo synonyma ἐν οὐρανῷ conjungi, in censura nostra notavimus, quod ipsum & Abenezrae in comm. ad ult. versum hujus capitis & Livelao ad Amos 5. 26. placuisse postea cognovi. Quod si vero עַל per in & per expósueris, quid erit incommodi?
units.tr: Now let us look at the individual points. As for the first, you say on page 1031 that you do not want to labour much over the word 'al [עַל]. Nor do I, my dear Marsennus, labour much over it. I wished to show only that the Vulgate translator took the word Firmament not for the lowest region of the air, but for the starry heaven. For otherwise he would never have rendered 'al by under. You admit that 'al never means under. But you yourself teach that it is often put for over, beside, through, in. The Vulgate chose none of these renderings; for it would have been as absurd to say that the birds fly beside, near, in or through the starry heaven as to say over it. You say that under in this place means the same as beside, in, through, near. "For what is under something," you say, "is often near or beside it, as water which is under the air is near the air." I reply: either by Firmament he understood the starry heaven, or the lower region of the air. If the starry heaven, how will you apply these renderings beside, near, in, through? since you yourself say that birds do not usually, nor can, fly higher than the lower region of the air. For these are your words: "Add that if the particle [על] must be explained as over, then by [רקיע השמים] the lower region of the air must be understood. For birds neither usually nor can fly higher." To which I add this also: there is nothing absurd here if we understand by raqia' hashamayim the lower region of the air. For as far as [רקיע] is concerned, you yourself have already taught this earlier. As for [שמים], what is more familiar than that phrase, birds of heaven, in Psalm 8 and Matthew 6? Here, we noted in our criticism, two synonyms [ἐν οὐρανῷ] are joined, a point which I later learned had also pleased both Abenezra in his commentary on the last verse of this chapter and Livelao on Amos 5:26. But if you explain [עַל] by in and through, what will be the inconvenience?

units.la: Si per Firmamentum intellexit inferiorem aëris regionem, quomodo stabit illud sub? an aves extra eam volare possunt? Sed dices sub, id est prope, juxta, ut aqua quae est sub aëre, est prope vel juxta aërem. Sed an avis commodè volare dicetur prope vel juxta aërem; quae extra eum volare non potest?
units.tr: If by "firmament" he understood the lower region of the air, how will that stand "under"? Can birds fly outside it? But you will say that "under" means "near, close to," as water that is under the air is near or close to the air. But would a bird be said conveniently to fly near or close to the air when it cannot fly outside it?

units.la: Pergis, vulgata autem tam cœlum octavum quàm aërem intelligere potest: aërem quidem, secundum superiores regiones, quibus meteora generantur, cœlum verò, quod aeri superfertur. Sed agnosco libens, commodissimè dici aves volare sub expanso cœlorum, tam superioribus aëris regionibus, quàm ipso cœlo sidereo, addo & cœlo Empyreo, sed Ebræum יום per Sub reddi posse prius erat ostendendum. Pag. 1033. redis ad hoc thema, & objicis mihi Fagium & Lutherum, quorum hic quoque reddidit, sub firmamento, dicisque satis imprudenter Amamam contra suos agere. Sed non ignoras Marsenne, quid de versionibus sentiamus, Omnes recipimus, etiam B. Lutheri, quatenus cum fontibus convenit. Omnes ad fontes revocamus. Et quod ad hunc locum attinet, in notis meis ad Belgicam Bibliorum versionem, quæ Lutheri est, hunc quoque locum castigavi. Et ex censura mea ad Gen. 6.5. satis potuisti colligere, quid & quantum Ecclesiæ Euangelicæ vernaculis versionibus deferant.
units.tr: You go on: "But the Vulgate can understand both the eighth heaven and the air: the air indeed according to its upper regions, in which meteors are generated, and the heaven which is carried over the air." I gladly agree that it is most fittingly said that birds fly under the expanse of the heavens, both the upper regions of the air and the starry heaven itself; I add also the Empyrean heaven. But it had first to be shown that the Hebrew yom [יום] can be rendered by "under." On p. 1033 you return to this theme and object to me Fagius and Luther, of whom the latter also rendered "under the firmament," and you say rather imprudently that Amama acts against his own. But you are not unaware, Marsenne, what we think of versions: we accept all of them, even that of the blessed Luther, insofar as they agree with the sources. We refer everything back to the sources. As far as this passage is concerned, in my notes on the Belgic version of the Bible, which is Luther's, I have also corrected this passage. And from my censure on Gen. 6.5 you could have gathered well enough how much the evangelical Church defers to vernacular versions.

units.la: Quod ad alterum attinet, de omisso verbo יעופף / Sic exordiris, ostendam ne quidem semel editionem nostram erraffe, licet enim phrasis Ebr. aliter sonare videatur, si tamen illius usum spectemus, optime vulgatum Interpretem legere, quilibet æquus judex affirmabit. Magna pollicitatio. Vidisti tamen opinor vel in his ipsis voculis רקיע & Sub, longe facilius esse rem tantam polliceri, quam præstare. Agnosco & hic libens modestiam tuam, dum non defendendam suscipis vulgatam, rejecta authoritate fontium, sed potius eam cum fontibus conciliare studes. Id quod & in Animadversi. ad problema 189.
