Georgii Veneti in te recipis. Macte hoc animo. Ubicunque hoc præstabis, habebis me tibi adstipulantem. Non ero pertinax propositi. A quovis libenter disco, etiam à discipulis. Non ergo pudebit à te erudiri, quem in omni Philosophiæ parte, in bonis literis & Theologorum scriptis, ex animo hoc dico, præclarè eruditum & versatum agnosco. Sed vide, mi Marsenne, quomodo tua illa pollicitatio consistere queat cum iis, quæ ipsâ eadem pagina habes, col. priori, vid. 233. ubi Ebræicum textum innumeris corruptelis à Judæis ex odio Christianismi in cum illatis scatere pronuncias. Si enim ita est, tunc aut vulgatam versionem in eodem luto hærere oportet, aut ea conciliatio plane impossibilis est. Sed videamus quomodo hunc locum cum fonte concilies. Tentas conciliationem, subintellectâ voce אשר ante verbum omissum יעופף / hoc modo, producant aquæ reptile an. viventis & volatile, [quod] volet super terram, &c. Quamvis, inquis, jegnophceph idem sit quod volabit aut volet, recte tamen expresserimus volatile volans, aut quod volet aut volabit, prout Græcus habet, τὰ πετεινὰ πετόμενα, ut Moses præcipuum artium officium tàm in actu, quàm in potentiâ docuerit.
units.tr: As for the other point, the omitted word [יעופף]: you begin, "I will show that our edition has not erred even once, for although the Hebrew phrase may seem to sound otherwise, yet if we look at its usage, any fair judge will affirm that the Vulgate translator reads very well." That is a great promise. Yet I think you have seen, even in these very small words, raqia [רקיע] and "under," that it is far easier to promise such a thing than to perform it. I gladly acknowledge your modesty here too, in that you do not take up the defence of the Vulgate by rejecting the authority of the sources, but rather strive to reconcile it with the sources. You make the same undertaking in your Animadversions on problem 189 of George Venetus. Keep to this spirit. Wherever you succeed in this, you will have me as your supporter. I will not be obstinate in my view. I gladly learn from anyone, even from disciples. So it will not shame me to be instructed by you, whom I acknowledge, and I say this from my heart, as clearly learned and well versed in every part of philosophy, in good letters and in the writings of theologians. But see, my Marsenne, how that promise of yours can agree with what you say on the same page, in the earlier column, p. 233, where you declare that the Hebrew text teems with countless corruptions introduced into it by the Jews out of hatred of Christianity. For if that is so, then either the Vulgate must stick in the same mud, or that reconciliation is plainly impossible. But let us see how you reconcile this passage with its source. You attempt the reconciliation by supplying the word asher [אשר] before the omitted verb [יעופף], in this way: "Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul and the flying [thing] which will fly over the earth, etc." Although, you say, jegnophceph is the same as "will fly" or "flies," we have nonetheless rightly expressed it as "flying which flies," or "which will fly," or "will fly," just as the Greek has ta peteina petomena, since Moses taught the chief duty of the arts both in act and in potency.

units.la: Resp. Non esse quidem infrequens apud Hebræos & Chaldæos, agnoscis opinor tua ipsius verba, ut aliquid in oratione deficiat vel subintelligatur; At ubi nulla necessitas est, supplementa non sunt toleranda. Fateor Chaldæus, inquis, Serpant [malim cum Raphelengio legere יִרְחְשׁוּן & reddere, Edant, producant, in Aphel] aquæ reptile anima viventis & avem quæ volat, &c, Resp, Chaldæum tibi plane adversari. Sic enim habet יִרְחְשׁוּן מַיָּא רְחֵשׁ נַפְשָׁא חַיְתָא וְעוֹפָא יְפָרַח עַל־אַרְעָא וגו' id est Et avis volet supra terram, ubi nullum relativum quæ, quod per ד Chaldæi exprimunt. Sed & hic dicis supplendum relativum, & quasi id nemo tibi negaturus esset, dum recitas Chaldæum textum, supples. Sed nimis magnum est illud tuum αἴτημα. Quis enim, præjudicio non occæcatus, hanc licentiam approbabit, in utroque textu & Ch. & Ebr. pro libitu quidvis supplendi, ut uni vulgatæ maneat sua authoritas? Sed video te citasse textum Chaldæum ex Codice Regio, ubi pro יִפְרַח extat דְּפָרַח quod volet, quam lectionem expressit quoque (cur enim celabo?) Editio Buxtorfiana. Sed oppono tibi tria diversa exemplaria Veneta in folio, quæ omnia legunt יִפְרַח / oppono tibi castigationem Fr. Raphelengii, quæ in variis lectionibus, quas à Theologis Lovaniensibus approbatas in apparatum Bibliorum regiorum intulit, ita habet.
units.tr: My reply: you yourself acknowledge, I think, that it is not uncommon among the Hebrews and Chaldeans for something to be lacking in a sentence or to be understood. But where there is no necessity, supplements are not to be tolerated. You admit: "The Chaldean has, serpant [I would rather read with Raphelengius yirḥeshun [יִרְחְשׁוּן] and render 'let them bring forth,' in the Aphel], the creeping thing of living soul and the bird that flies, etc." My reply is that the Chaldean plainly opposes you. For it reads yirḥeshun mayya reḥesh napshā ḥayyṯā wə'opā yəfaraḥ 'al-ar'ā [יִרְחְשׁוּן מַיָּא רְחֵשׁ נַפְשָׁא חַיְתָא וְעוֹפָא יְפָרַח עַל־אַרְעָא], that is, "And the bird will fly over the earth," where there is no relative "which," which the Chaldeans express by the letter d. But here too you say a relative must be supplied, as if no one would deny you this, and while you cite the Chaldean text you supply it. But that claim of yours is too great. For who, not blinded by prejudice, will approve this licence of supplying whatever one likes in both texts, Chaldean and Hebrew, so that the Vulgate alone may keep its authority? I see that you have cited the Chaldean text from the Royal Codex, where instead of yifraḥ [יִפְרַח] stands dəfaraḥ [דְּפָרַח], "which will fly," a reading which the Buxtorf edition also expresses (for why should I conceal it?). But I set against you three different Venetian folio editions, which all read [יפרח]. I set against you the correction of Fr. Raphelengius, which, among the various readings that he put into the apparatus of the Royal Bibles, approved by the Louvain theologians, reads as follows:

units.la: {*} id est Veneti.
units.tr: {*} that is, of the Venetian [editions].

units.la: [20. דְּפָרַח] pro Ebr. יִעוֹפֵף. Sed cum * V. melius legeris יִפְרַח vel cum Elia, יִפְרַח in Kal.]
units.tr: [20. דְּפָרַח] for the Hebrew [יעופף]. But since in the * V. you would have read better [יפרח], or with Elias, [יפרח] in Kal.]

units.la: Pergis, Et quidem facile est, per volatile idem penitus concipere, quod intelligitur per, volatile, quod volet, adeo ut Amamam admodum otiosum & imprudentem esse existimem) qui hujusmodi sine ratione carpat.
units.tr: You go on: "And indeed it is easy to conceive, through 'flying,' exactly the same thing that is understood through 'flying which will fly,' so that I think Amama quite idle and imprudent, who censures such things without reason."

units.la: Resp. Iterum petis principium, dum supponis in Ebr. legendum quod volet, id quod ego sine ulla necessitate fieri asseıro. Favet mihi accentus Athnach positus post הָיְתָה & prius hoc membrum à secundo distinguens. Favet mihi vers. 19. c. 2. ubi aves non ex aqua, ut hic insinuat vulgata Editio, sed ex terra productas esse Moses docet. Favent Cajetanus & Catharinus, qui aves ex aquis productas diserte negant. Moses hic tacet productivum avium, inquit Cajet. Atque eundem sensum insinuare Ebræum textum, Corn. à Lapide agnoscit.
units.tr: My reply: again you beg the question, in supposing that in the Hebrew one must read "which will fly," which I maintain is done without any necessity. The accent Athnach, placed after hayethah [הָיְתָה], favours me, and separates this clause from the second. Verse 19 of chapter 2 favours me, where Moses teaches that the birds were produced not from water, as the Vulgate edition here suggests, but from the earth. Cajetan and Catharinus favour me, who expressly deny that birds were produced from the waters. "Moses here is silent about the producing of birds," says Cajetan. And Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges that the Hebrew text suggests the same sense.

units.la: Sed, inquis, accentum Athnach nusquam impedire, quominus oratio tota juxta vulgatam belle decurrat, praecipue cum interjectio vim copulativam nostrae interjectionis [Et] habeat, quod manifeste denotat, hoc secundum membrum, Et volatile volet, &c. cum primo conjungi.
units.tr: But, you say, the accent Athnach nowhere prevents the whole sentence from running well in accordance with the Vulgate, especially since the interjection has the copulative force of our "and" [Et], which clearly shows that this second member, "And the flying thing will fly," and so on, is joined to the first.

units.la: Resp. Conjunctionem! Et conjungere quidem hoc secundum membrum cum primo membro, sed distincto, Producant aquae reptile, Et volatile volet, manet ergo accentui sua authoritas.
units.tr: My reply: the conjunction! "And" does indeed join this second member to the first, but as a distinct member: "Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing ... And the flying thing will fly." So the accent keeps its authority.

units.la: Addis, neque obstat, quod cap. 2. legamus, formatu de humo terra cunctis animantibus terrae & universis velatilibus coeli, tametsi enim aves cum animantibus terrae illic conjungantur, non propterea statim inferas, aves ex terra progenitas, nisi velis etiam ideo ex aquis productas esse, quod hic cum piscibus ex aqua natis enumerentur.
units.tr: You add that it is no obstacle that in chapter 2 we read "formed out of the dust of the earth, all the living things of the earth and all the flying things of heaven." For although birds are there joined with the living things of the earth, you should not immediately infer that birds were born from the earth, unless you also wish them to have been produced from the waters on the ground that here they are listed with fish, which were born of water.

units.la: Resp. Ego vero cap. 2. verf. 19. longe majorem necessitatem video statuendi, etiam aves ex terra productas, quam ex Ebraeo textu hoc loco, eas ex aquis fuisse creatas. Nec subterfugiam hic cujuscunque judicium. Ex textu vero vulgato, hic loci, certissime deducitur, & pisces & aves ex aquis productas. Nisi enim ita statuas, a quo verbo dependebit illud volatile? ut proinde valde mirer haec tua verba, nisi velis etiam ideo ex aquis productas, quod hic cum piscibus enumerentur. Quidni enim sic velit Catholicus? cum & volatile & reptile ab iisdem verbis (producant aquae) dependeant. Ego certe sic existimo, absque hoc textu fuisset, nunquam controversiam istam an aves ex aqua producta sint, Philosophorum & Scholasticorum pulpita novissent.
units.tr: My reply: in chapter 2, verse 19, I see a much greater necessity for holding that birds were also produced from the earth than there is, from the Hebrew text in this place, for holding that they were created from the waters. Nor will I here shrink from anyone's judgment. From the Vulgate text in this place it is most certainly deduced that both fish and birds were produced from the waters. For unless you hold this, from which verb will that "flying" depend? So I greatly wonder at your words: "unless you wish them to have been produced from the waters on this account, that here they are listed with fish." For why would not a Catholic wish this, since both the "flying" and the "creeping" thing depend on the same verb, "let the waters bring forth"? I certainly think that without this text the pulpits of philosophers and Schoolmen would never have known that controversy, whether birds were produced from water.

units.la: CAP. II verf. 2.
units.tr: CAP. II, verse 2.

units.la: Valde se torserunt Latini Interpretes circa hunc locum, Et complevit Deus die septimo opus suum. Graecis enim qui Interpretatione LXX. acquieverunt, nulla potuit hinc oboriri difficultas. Sed quia hic in me incurrit Marsennus, ponam verba censurae meae,
units.tr: The Latin translators have struggled greatly over this passage, And God completed on the seventh day his work. For the Greek readers who followed the Septuagint, no difficulty could arise here. But since Marsennus has fallen upon me here, I will set out the words of my criticism.

units.la: Leve itidem & multis commune erratum a vulgato commissum est hoc versu, dum convertit per praeteritum perfectum, & complevit. Quod notare non duxissem operae, nec enim ea nos incessit contradicendi carpendique prurigo) nisi antiquissimos simos simul & doctissimos viros ea lectio in errorem induxisset. Fidem hujus rei facient Hieron. & Galatinus, quorum ille Quæst. Ebraïcis in Genesin dicit, hinc arctari Judæos & ostendi, jam tum in principio ab ipso Deo sabbathum dissolutum, dum in ipso Sabbatho Deus operatur, complens in eo opera sua. Quæ ad verbum descripsit Galatinus in De Arcanis Cathol. verit. lib. x i. 10. [& Euchelrius comm. in hunc locum.] Quæ etiam suo calculo approbasse videtur Joh. Benedictus, Theol. Parisiensis, dum hæc Hieron. verba sine ulla censurâ margini Bibliorum suorum interposuit. At omnia ista in fumum abeunt, inquit Cl. Drusius, si hoc futurum, quod in præteritum conversum est, exponas per pluf-quamperfectum, & compleverat, quod & Vatablus & Mercerus notârunt. Præteritum enim unicum Ebræorum omnes species præteritorum complectitur. Distinguit Cajetanus, ut nodum solvat, inter actionem positivam & negationem ab ulteriori operatione. Et Lyra, inter perfectionem, quâ aliquid assequitur formam debitam & eam quâ exit aliquid in operationem sibi debitam. [Quibus nunc addam * Bannes, qui sic infit, Deus complevit positivâ actione naturalem perfectionem totalitatis universi die sexto. At die septimo complevit primam perfectionem naturalem universi negativè, vid. cessando ab opere, & secundam naturalem implevit, positivè influendo. Audiamus ipsum quoque Thomam, consummatio quæ est secundum integritatem partium universi competit sextæ diei: consummatio, quæ est secundum operationem partium competit septimæ. Et Lombardum, lib. 2. dist. 15. lit. G. nisi forte dicatur, inquit, die 7. complevisse opus suum, quia ipsum benedixit & sanctificavit. Benedictio enim & sanctificatio est opus. Et lit. H. Potest etiam sic exponi, complevit die 7. id est, completum & consummatum vidit. Pellicanus putabat vertendum, in diem septimum, id est, ut quieti se daret die v i i. Alii, teste Abenezra, ante diem septimum. Corn. à Lapide, complevit die septimo exclusivè, at die 7. inclusivè. At durum videtur ut dies ille quo aliquid factum dicitur, exclusivè sumatur.] Sed quorsum te conjicias in eas angustias, ubi unicâ, eâque certissimâ observatione Grammaticâ res expediri potest? l x x. hîc habent, ἡ συντέλεσιν ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑκτῇ, &c. Complevit Deus die sexto. Quo nomine passim ab authoribus perstringuntur. Ego sic opinor, repre-henendos quidem, quod cum in promptu esset vocis Græcæ plus-quam quam-perfectum, septimum verterint in sextum, at reprehendendos fuisse magis, si vertissent ἡμέραν ἑβδόμην. Vidisse mihi illi videntur, quod tot oculos fugit. Quis enim non videt ad sensum idem sonare has duas propositiones, Compleverat Deus die 7. opus suum, Et Complevit Deus die 7. opus suum.
units.tr: A slight error, common to many, has also been made by the Vulgate in this verse, in rendering by the perfect past tense, and completed. I would not have thought it worth the trouble to note this, for that itch of contradicting and carping is not mine, unless that reading had led the most ancient and most learned men into error. Jerome and Galatinus will vouch for the fact. Jerome, in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis, says: from this the Jews are refuted and it is shown that already at the beginning God himself dissolved the sabbath, since on the Sabbath itself God works, completing his works in it. Galatinus copied these words verbatim in De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis, book 11, chapter 10 [and Euchelrius on this passage]. Johannes Benedictus, theologian of Paris, seems also to have approved them, since he inserted these words of Jerome without any censure in the margin of his Bibles. But all these things go up in smoke, says the distinguished Drusius, if you explain what is to be taken as future but was turned into the past, by the pluperfect: had completed, as Vatablus and Mercerus also noted. For the single Hebrew past tense embraces all the species of past tenses. Cajetan, to untie the knot, distinguishes between positive action and cessation from further operation. Lyra distinguishes between the perfection by which something attains its due form and that by which something passes into the operation due to it. [To these I will now add Bañez, who begins thus: God completed by positive action the natural perfection of the whole universe on the sixth day. But on the seventh day he completed the first natural perfection of the universe negatively, namely by ceasing from the work, and he fulfilled the second natural perfection positively, by flowing in.] Let us hear Thomas himself too: the consummation which concerns the integrity of the parts of the universe belongs to the sixth day; the consummation which concerns the operation of the parts belongs to the seventh. And Lombard, book 2, distinction 15, letter G: unless perhaps it is said, he says, that on the seventh day he completed his work, because he blessed and sanctified it. For blessing and sanctifying is a work. And letter H: It can also be explained thus: he completed on the seventh day, that is, he saw it completed and consummated. Pellicanus thought it should be rendered unto the seventh day, that is, so that he might give himself to rest on the seventh day. Others, according to Aben Ezra, render before the seventh day. Cornelius a Lapide: he completed on the seventh day exclusively, but on the seventh inclusively. But it seems harsh that the day on which something is said to have been done should be taken exclusively. But why do you throw yourself into those straits, where the matter can be settled by one single and most certain grammatical observation? The Seventy here have ἐπετέλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ, etc. [epetelesen ho Theos en tē hēmerą tē hektē], God completed on the sixth day. For this reading they are everywhere censured by writers. My opinion is this: they are to be blamed indeed, because, although the Greek pluperfect was readily available, they rendered seventh as sixth; yet they would have deserved still more blame if they had rendered ἡμέραν ἑβδόμην [hēmeran hebdomēn]. They seem to me to have seen what escapes so many eyes. For who does not see that these two propositions mean the same in sense: God had completed his work on the seventh day, and God completed his work on the seventh day?

units.la: Si enim compleverat die 7. quando complevit, quaeso te, nisi die 7? Quid ad haec
units.tr: For if he had completed it on the seventh day when he completed it, I ask you, on what day but the seventh? What do you say to this?

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: LXX. discrepant, inquit, in dierum numero ab Hebraeo, dicunt enim Deum die 6. quievisse. In Hebr. & vulg. die 7. quod in causa fuit, cur haeretici, Drusius, Amama, Mercerus & eorum sectatores vulgatam reprehendant, qua ait die 7. completam fuisse rerum omnium creationem.
units.tr: The Seventy, he says, differ from the Hebrew in the number of the days, for they say that God rested on the sixth day. In the Hebrew and the Vulgate it is the seventh day, which is why the heretics, Drusius, Amama, Mercerus and their followers, censure the Vulgate, which says that the creation of all things was completed on the seventh day.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Ergone hanc gratiam rependis viris magnis & de sacrarum literarum studio optime meritis, Drusio & Mercero, ut eos vix unquam, nisi haereseos nota frontibus eorum inusta, in scenam protrahatis? Illi certe vulgatae Editioni plus nimio detulerunt & ubicunque aliquod velamentum tegendis ejus ulceribus reperire potuerunt, vobis suppeditarunt. Longe rigidiores Aristarchos in Cajetano, Oleastrio, aliisque vestrae Professionis hominibus vulgata experta est. Et quidem de Mercero testabuntur doctissimae ejus in Genesin lucubrationes, queis Marsennus, ut ut perpetuo dissimulet, non parum adjutus fuit. De Drusio ipsi Pontificii, & nominatim Gretzerus, ita sentiunt & scripta ejus loquuntur. Me vero, prae magnis istis viris vix remigem & sententatorem, quod eodem stigmate semper notes, levior injuria est. Injuria tamen est. Si enim nullus haereticus nisi qui pertinax. Ego me haereticum esse confidenter nego. Convince me non authoritate Rom. Ecclesiae, sed scripturae, & dabo manus. Sed ad rem. Dicis me reprehendere vulgatum, quod die septimo reddiderit, quasi negarem, die 7. completum fuisse rerum creationem. At ego dico, optime fecisse vulvulgatum, dum verba Ebr. ביום השביעי reddidit, die septime. Agnosco, die 7. completam fuisse creationem. Illud vero satis commodè dictum esse negavi, complevit die septimo opus suum, id quod absurdæ ex eo natæ conclusiones & violentæ expositiones demonstrant. Creatio die 7. fuit completa, eo sensu, quo die 8. 9. 10. & hoc ipso die completa dici potest. At non complevit, proprie loquendo, nisi die sexto.
units.tr: Do you repay with this favour great men who have deserved so well of the study of the sacred letters, Drusius and Mercerus, so that you hardly ever bring them onto the stage except with the mark of heresy branded on their foreheads? Certainly they paid far too much deference to the Vulgate edition, and wherever they could find any covering to hide its sores, they supplied it to you. Far more rigid Aristarchuses than these have been applied to the Vulgate by Cajetan, Oleaster, and others of your profession. And indeed his most learned commentaries on Genesis will bear witness to Mercerus, on whom Marsennus, however much he conceals it, has relied not a little. As for Drusius, the Papists themselves, and Gretser by name, think and their writings say the same. As for me, it is a lighter wrong that you always mark me with the same stigma, since I am hardly an oarsman or a voter beside such great men. It is still a wrong. For if no one is a heretic except the obstinate, I confidently deny that I am a heretic. Convince me by the authority of Scripture, not of the Roman Church, and I will lay down my arms. But to the matter. You say that I censure the Vulgate because it rendered on the seventh day, as if I denied that the creation of the world was completed on the seventh day. But I say that the Vulgate did well in rendering the Hebrew words ביום השביעי [beyom hashevi'i] as on the seventh day. I admit that the creation was completed on the seventh day. What I denied is that it was said with sufficient propriety that he completed his work on the seventh day, as the absurd conclusions and forced explanations drawn from it demonstrate. The creation was completed on the seventh day, in the sense in which it can be said to have been completed on the eighth, ninth, tenth, and on this very day. But he did not complete it, properly speaking, except on the sixth day.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Equidem Hæreticos demiror, qui ut cornicum oculos defixisse videantur, nihil non reprehendunt: & tamen Amamam audias, qui negat se eâ carpendi prurigene teneri. Cur igitur vulgatum arguit, quod ויכל per præteritum perf. verterit? Etenim si unicum Ebraorum præteritum omnes præteritorum species complectitur, revera perfectum includit.
units.tr: I am surprised at the heretics, who, as if they had the eyes of crows fixed on them, find fault with everything; and yet you may hear Amama, who denies that he is held by that itch for carping. Why then does he accuse the Vulgate of rendering וַיְכַל by the preterite perfect? For if the single Hebrew preterite embraces all the forms of the preterite, it indeed includes the perfect.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: .. Dixi leve esse hoc erratum, nec annotaturum me fuisse, nisi ea lectio doctissimis viris, Hieronymo, Galatino, aliisque falsam conclusionem, & Scholasticis argutas magis quàm solidas distinctiones expressisset. De mea prurigine judicent illi, quorum judicia studium partium non afflavit. Vnicum præteritum Ebræorum omnes præt. species complectitur. Ita vid. ut pro ratione loci & contextus jam per præt. perf. jam imperfectum, jam plusquam perf. reddi oporteat. Non verò, ut quodvis præteritum ubivis locorum omnes illas species includat.
units.tr: I said this error is slight, and I would not have noted it, except that this reading gave a false conclusion to the most learned men Jerome, Galatinus, and others, and gave the Scholastics subtle rather than solid distinctions. Let those judge my itch whose judgments the spirit of party has not inspired. The one Hebrew preterite embraces all the species of the past. So it seems that, according to the reason of the place and context, it must sometimes be rendered by the preterite perfect, sometimes by the imperfect, and sometimes by the pluperfect. But it does not follow that any preterite, anywhere, includes all those species. ## MARSENNUS.

units.la: MARSENNUS.

At non intelligit Amama, neque Drusius, quomodo 70. cum Ebraeo conveniant, nisi plusquam persecto * utaris, quos etiam reprehendit ille, quod noluerunt hoc tempore uti. Præclaros hominciones, egregiosque Hebraizantes, qui ea non vident, quæ vix infantibus ignota sunt, nunquid animadvertere debuerunt, semper verum esse, quocunque tandem die declaretur, opus aliquod esse consumptum, quando omnia facta sunt, quæ ad illud pertinent? Cum igitur die 6. Deus opus suum consummasset, verissimum fuit asserere, dominum ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ opera sua consummasse. Vid. circa finem diei 6. aut quacunque voluerit horâ: verissimum etiam idem opus die 7. complevisse, seu opus consummatum fuisse, vel ut 70. dicunt, in plurali, opera sua. Quicquid enim die sexto completum est, nisi destruatur, septimo die completum est.
units.tr: But Amama does not understand, nor does Drusius, how the Seventy agree with the Hebrew unless you use the pluperfect, which they also censure for not wishing to use it in this tense. Excellent little men, and distinguished Hebraists, who do not see what is hardly unknown to infants! Ought they not to have noticed that it is always true, whatever day it is declared, that some work has been finished once all the things pertaining to it have been done? Since on the sixth day God had finished his work, it was most true to assert that he had finished his works on the sixth day [ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ]. See near the end of the sixth day, or at whatever hour you like: it is also most true that the same work was completed on the seventh day, or that the work was finished, or, as the Seventy say in the plural, his works. For whatever was completed on the sixth day, unless it is destroyed, was completed on the seventh day. ## AMAMA.

units.la: AMAMA.

Non intelligunt, dicis, Amama & Drusius. Drusius omnem jam invidiam supergressus est. Honorifice de illo sentit Christianus orbis. Fasces illi multi quoque Pontificii submisére. Me quod attinet, ipse mei ingenii tarditatem & memoriae deliquium novi & sentio. At illud intelligo tamen, magis conspirare haec axiomata, Deus complevit opus suum die sexto, Et Deus compleverat opus suum die septimo. quam illa, Deus complevit o. s. die sexto, Et Deus complevit o. s. die septimo.
units.tr: You say, Amama and Drusius do not understand. Drusius has risen above all envy; the Christian world speaks of him with honour, and many Papists have also lowered their fasces before him. As for me, I know and feel my own slowness of wit and failing memory. Yet I do understand this much: these axioms agree more closely, God finished his work on the sixth day, and God had finished his work on the seventh day, than those others, God finished his work on the sixth day, and God finished his work on the seventh day.

units.la: Haec enim sine violentâ glossâ nunquam in concordiam rediges: Illa vero suaviter conspirant. Quod de violentâ glossâ dixi, faventes LXX. habeo. Cur enim, quaeso te, aliàs pro die septimo sextum posuissent? Potuisletne aliquis, soli versioni Graecae innutritus & assuetus, odorari in Ebraeo esse, die septimo? Favent etiam Hieron & Galatinus, qui, de ejusmodi glossâ nihil cogitantes, verba illa, prout jacent, acceperunt, extructo inde consectario non parum periculoso. Laudavi itaque τῆς LXX. quod locum hunc ita reddiderint, ut versio ipsorum idem dicat, quod veritas Ebraica. Illud tamen dissimulare non potui, difficultatem illam, quae ipsos hic torsit, ne Deus die 7. laborasse putaretur, meo judicio, commodius & a textu Ebr. minus deflectendo, sic potuisse tolli, si pro aoristo primo, praeteritum plusquam-perfectum adhibuissent. Illud enim negari non potest, Praeteritum Ebr. saepe pro plusquam-perfecto poni: At שִׁבְעָה significare sextum quis ostendet? Haec autem ex judicio meo dixi, si tuum à meo diversum abit, bene est. Suum cuique pulchrum. Σοὶ μὲν πᾶσιν δοκεῖ ἐστι, ἐμοὶ δὲ τὰ δὲ Sed praeclaros, inquis, homunciones, &c. Non moror istas illu-siones. Ad rem potius. Animadvertimus, mi Marfenne, semper verum esse, quocunque tandem die (sive 6. sive 7.) declaretur, opus aliquod esse consummatum, quando omnia facta sunt, quæ ad illud pertinent. Sed illud non animadverti, idem esse, Deus complevit die septimo opus suum, Et, Opus fuit completum die septimo. Illud enim dici proprie non potest, nisi eodem die colophonem operi, quod die sexto adhuc incompletum relictum erat, imposuerit: Hoc vero verum esse potest, etiamsi die primo completio facta sit. Ludis in sequentibus, Verissimum etiam erit, inquis, idem opus die 7. Deum complevisse, seu opus [à Deo] consummatum fuisse. Haec enim complevisse, & consummatum fuisse tam praeteritum perfectum quam plusquam-perfectum complectuntur. Si in praet. perf. accipias, nego! Si in plusquamperfecto, mecum sentis. Quicquid die sexto completum est, inquis: nisi destruatur, etiam septimo die completum est. Agnosco, si completum est, idem tibi est, quod, completum manet. Si aliter accipis, & passivis in activa versis, sic loqui malis, Quicquid die sexto complevit Deus, nisi destruatur, etiam septimo die complevit, videbis te absurde locutum esse. Non ignoras inter motum & rem motu factam distinguere λογικῶν μαιδῶν.
units.tr: For you will never bring these into harmony without a forced gloss; but the former agree smoothly. And what I said about a forced gloss is supported by the Seventy. For why, I ask you, would they otherwise have put the seventh day for the sixth? Could anyone brought up on the Greek version alone and accustomed to it have smelt in the Hebrew the seventh day? Jerome and Galatinus also agree, who, thinking nothing of such a gloss, took those words as they lie and drew from them a not inconsiderable and dangerous corollary. So I praised the Seventy for rendering the passage so that their version says the same as the Hebrew truth. Yet I could not hide that the difficulty which troubled them here, lest God be thought to have laboured on the seventh day, could in my judgment have been removed more conveniently, and with less departure from the Hebrew text, if for the first aorist they had used the pluperfect. For it cannot be denied that the Hebrew preterite is often put for the pluperfect; but who will show that sheba' [שִׁבְעָה] means the sixth? I have said these things according to my judgment; if yours differs from mine, so be it. Each to his own, and beautiful. To you it seems so to all, to me otherwise [Σοὶ μὲν πᾶσιν δοκεῖ ἐστι, ἐμοὶ δὲ τὰ δὲ]. But you say the splendid little men, and so on. I do not dwell on those illusions; let us come to the matter. I notice, my Marsennus, that it is always true, whatever day (whether the sixth or the seventh) is declared, that some work has been finished once all the things pertaining to it have been done. But I do not notice that it is the same to say God finished his work on the seventh day, and the work was completed on the seventh day. The first can properly be said only if on that same day he set the finishing touch to the work, which on the sixth day was still left incomplete; the second can be true even if the completion took place on the first day. You jest in what follows: It will also be most true, you say, that God completed the same work on the seventh day, or that the work was finished [by God]. For completed and was finished embrace both the preterite perfect and the pluperfect. If you take them in the preterite perfect, I deny it! If in the pluperfect, you agree with me. Whatever was completed on the sixth day, you say, unless it is destroyed, was also completed on the seventh day. I grant that if was completed means the same as remains completed, it is the same. But if you take it otherwise, and prefer to put the passive into the active and speak thus, Whatever God completed on the sixth day, unless it is destroyed, he also completed on the seventh day, you will see that you have spoken absurdly. You are not unaware that the logic-chopping schoolboys distinguish between the motion and the thing made by motion [λογικῶν μαιδῶν].

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: Marsennus

units.la: Impia certè haereticorum progenies, qui dum nostri Doctores aliquid afferre videntur, eos statim nobis veluti milites cataphractos objiciunt, quos si nobis favere percipiunt, perpetuum silent.
units.tr: Surely it is an impious brood of heretics: whenever our teachers seem to bring forward something, they at once throw at us, like armoured horsemen, those men who, if they perceive that these favour us, keep a perpetual silence.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Non illud argumentum est, ut sic debaccheris, nec haec ra-tio est aut modus reducendi errantes. Non potes mi Marsen-ne, illud Nazianzeni usurpare, non incessimus, inquit, adversa-rios contumeliis, sicut plerique faciunt, rationum & argumentorum infir-mitatem maledictis obtegentes, non aliter ac sepia atramentum ante se vomere ajunt, ut Piscatores effugiant. Verum nos pro Christo bellum gerere, hoc argumento palam facimus, quod secundum Christum, qui missus & pacatus est, dimicamus. Ac de his, inquit idem Pater, ita sentio, sentio, cunctisque animarum dispensatoribus hanc legem statuo, ut nec per duritiam hominum animos exasperent, nec per submissionem elatos efficiant, &c. Non potes, inquam, hoc Nazianzeni usurpare, adeo ubique αιχμαλώτους es, qui tamen omnium hominum minimum te in limine libri profiteris. Impia Haereticorum progenies, inquis. Iterum tibi haeretici sumus? Cui bono hoc convitium? Jam pridem occalluimus ad illud, & ridentes cordatiores. Crimen laesae majestatis sub Tyrannis unicum eorum crimen erat, qui omni vacabant. In illius locum jam apud vos successisse videtur haereseos postulatio. Retaliare possem, sed quo fructu? Ego tibi haereticus? tu mihi. Alius plane & a te longe diversus spiritus Salvianum agebat. Quis vel longissima oratione omnia illa saevitiae exempla traloqui posset, quibus Orthodoxos Arriani excarnificarunt? Et tamen de illis, quorum impietatem uterque juxta cum Salviano detestamur, quam placidè loquitur manuetus Pater? Haretici, sunt, inquit, sed nonscientes. Apud nos sunt haeretici, apud se non sunt. Nam in tantum se Catholicos esse judicant, ut nos ipsos titulo haereticae pravitatis infament. Quod ergo illi nobis sunt, hoc nos illis. Veritas apud nos est: sed illi apud se esse praesumunt. Honos Dei apud nos est, sed illi hoc arbitrantur honorem divinitatis esse quod credunt. Impii sunt, sed hoc putant veram esse pietatem. Errant ergo, sed bono animo errant, non odio sed affectu Dei, honorare se Dominum atque amare credentes. Quamvis non habeant rectam fidem, illi tamen hoc perfectam Dei aestimant charitatem & qualiter pro hoc ipso falsa opinionis errore in die judicii puniendi sint, nemo potest scire nisi judex.
units.tr: This is not an argument, and this kind of rant is neither a method nor a way of bringing back those who err. You cannot, my Marsenne, borrow that saying of Nazianzen: we have not attacked, he says, our opponents with insults, as many do, hiding the weakness of their reasons and arguments behind abuse, just as, they say, the cuttlefish vomits ink before itself, so that fishermen cannot catch it. That we wage war for Christ we show plainly by this argument: we fight according to Christ, who was sent and is peaceable. And about these matters, says the same Father, this is what I think, and I lay down this rule for all stewards of souls, that they neither exasperate minds through harshness nor make the proud prouder through submissiveness, etc. You cannot, I say, borrow this from Nazianzen, since you are so much a captive [αιχμαλώτους] everywhere, you who yet at the very opening of your book profess yourself the least of all men. The impious brood of heretics, you say. Are we heretics to you again? To what good is this insult? We have long since grown callused to it and, being more sensible, we laugh. Under tyrants, the charge of treason was the only crime of those who were otherwise blameless; among you the accusation of heresy seems now to have taken its place. I could retaliate, but to what profit? I am a heretic to you? Very well, you are one to me. A quite different and far more distant spirit drove Salvian. Who could recount, even in the longest speech, all those examples of cruelty by which the Arians tortured the orthodox? And yet, about those whose impiety we both detest alongside Salvian, how gently the mild Father speaks! They are heretics, he says, but unknowing ones. Among us they are heretics; among themselves they are not. For they judge themselves so truly Catholic that they defame us with the title of heretical depravity. What they are to us, we are to them. The truth is with us, but they presume it is with themselves. The honour of God is with us, but they think the honour of the divinity consists in what they believe. They are impious, but they think this is true piety. They err, then, but they err with a good mind, not from hatred but from zeal for God, believing they honour and love the Lord. Although they do not hold right faith, they nevertheless consider this to be perfect love of God; and how they are to be punished on the day of judgment for this very error of false opinion, no one can know except the Judge.

units.la: Interim idcirco eis, ut reor, patientiam Deus commodat, quia videt eos etsi non recte credere, affectu tamen pia opinionis errare. Haec Salvianus. Desinamus ergo reciprocare hanc serram. Indignaris, nos Vobis vestrates tanquam milites cataphractos objicere, sicubi à vobis dissentiant. Sed nunquid & vos facitis idem? An verò dum vos facitis, pietas est, dum nos, impietas? Ecce, ni Marsenne, vester Serarius me hoc docuit, cujus verba suprà pag.157. Produximus. At cum nobis favent, sileris, inquis. Et vos idem facitis. Pares ergo sumus. Et quid mirum si Pontificii Pontificiis faveant? Illud magis mirandum, eam esse vim veritatis, ut etiam Pontificiis, communi Ecclesiae nunc-Romanae consensu insuper habito, subinde liberam confessionem
units.tr: Meanwhile, I suppose, God shows them patience for this reason: He sees that, although they do not believe rightly, they err out of the affection of a pious opinion. These are the words of Salvian. Let us then stop tossing this saw back and forth. You are indignant that we throw your men at you as heavily armoured cavalry whenever they dissent from you. But do you not do the same? Or is it piety when you do it and impiety when we do? Behold, Marsenne, your Serarius taught me this; I set out his words above, on page 157. But when they favour us, you say, they keep silent. You do the same. So we are equal. And what wonder is it if Papists favour Papists? More to be wondered at is the power of truth, which even among the Papists, with the common consent of the present Roman Church set aside, wrings from them at times a free confession

units.la: De providentia lib.f. Edit. 1620 Kluceshuf. p 162. nem extorqueant, cum denique quorundam animos insidere candorem, ut, Concilii Tridentini Canonibus & Rom. Pontificis correctionibus suas sibi res habere iussis, liberè id quod sentiunt, & quod res est, edisserant.
units.tr: De providentia lib. f. Edit. 1620 Kluceshuf. p 162. ...from some; for at last a candour has settled on the minds of certain men, so that, although they have been ordered by the canons of the Council of Trent and the corrections of the Roman Pontiff to keep their own affairs to themselves, they set out freely what they think and what the matter actually is.

units.la: Gen. II. verf. 8.
units.tr: Gen. II. verse 8.

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg.
units.tr: Hebrew | Vulgate

units.la: Plantaverat Deus Hortum in Eden ab Oriente. | Plantavit Deus paradisum voluptatis à principio
units.tr: God had planted a garden in Eden in the East. | God planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning.

units.la: Dupliciter exorbitavit Interpres. Primò enim quominus vertas hortum voluptatis obstat litera ב ante עֵדֶן ut ut detur עֵדֶן aliàs pro deliciis & voluptate sumi, [ certè ejus plurale extat 2. Sam. 1. 24. atque hinc est græcum ἡδονή] Hic autem locum propriium denotari, ex collatione Genes. 4. 16. ostendit Cl. Witakerus. [Adde locum Jezech. 27. 23. & 37. 12. & 2. Reg. 19. 12.] Idem urgent duo rigidi Pontificii, Cajetanus & Steuchus, in suis, ad hunc locum annotationibus. Etiam LXX. & Chaldæus versionem nostram stabilitum cunt, dum vertunt illi ἐν Ἐδὲμ: hic, בְּגַן עֵדֶן [Oleastrius quoque asserit sibi verisimilius videri, ut sit nomen proprium loci.]
units.tr: The translator went wrong in two ways. First, the letter ב before עֵדֶן prevents us from rendering garden of pleasure, since עֵדֶן can otherwise be taken as delight and pleasure [its plural certainly occurs at 2 Sam. 1.24, and hence the Greek ἡδονή]. That it denotes a proper place is shown by the comparison with Gen. 4.16, as the learned Whitaker demonstrates. [Add Ezek. 27.23, 37.12 and 2 Kings 19.12.] The two stiff Papists, Cajetan and Steuchus, press the same point in their notes on this passage. The LXX and the Chaldee paraphrast also support our version, since they render it ἐν Ἐδὲμ and בְּגַן עֵדֶן [Oleaster too maintains that it seems more likely to him that it is the proper name of a place].

units.la: Alterum Interpretis peccatum est, quod cum קדם tam prioritatem loci quàm temporis significet, posteriorem hic cum Aquila elegerit, nam & iste hic vertit ἀπ' ἀρχῆς. Fateor equidem hoc excusari posse, commodeque exponi, ut sensus sit, à principio vel, exordio mundi sc. conditi, ut præceptor & decessor meus, Cl. Drusius p. m. in Fragmentis veterum Interpp. Græcorum notavit, quomodo & Satan in N.T. dicitur fuisse Homicida ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, principio sc. originis suæ, ut hoc modo intelligatur ad exiguum tempus in sua integritate perstitisse. Notandum tamen hoc duxi, tum quia LXX. quos alias noster Interpres sequi amat, hic rectius, καὶ ἀναλόλως, tum quod hæc versio ipsum quoque Hieron. [ut de cæteris nihil dicam,] in alia traxerit. Dicit enim Quæstionibus Ebr. ad hunc locum, hinc manifestissimè comprobari, quod priusquam cœlum & terram Deus conderet, Paradisum antea condiderat. Et frustra sunt Senensis & Mercerus, qui Hieronymum hic excusare satagunt, quem ipse Steuchus non alia ratione potuit excusare, quam asserendo, Hieronymum non semper in ea opinione perstitisse. Quam vellem locum Retractationis annotasset! Nam Albinus Quaest. in Genes. eam fuisse Hieronymi mentem quam verba prae se ferunt, asserit, & Eucherius in comm. eandem assertionem iisdem Hieron. verbis posuit. Quin & Franc. Georgius Minorita, tomo primo Problem. ex his conatus fuit nobis persuadere, a suis partibus stare Hieronymum, & sensisse, Paradisum non fuisse in hac visibili terra situm. His enim consideratis, inquit Georgius, Hieronymus pronuntiavit Paradisum ante caelum & terram conditum, nimirum ut his verbis significaret, Paradisum Mosis non esse in hac visibili terra situm, sed in illa terra viventium, quae ante hunc visibilem mundum in invisibili mundo creata est. Unde & illud elucescit, [si non ortum] saltem robur magnum ex hoc acquisivisse veterem illum [& necdum sepultum] errorem, quo creditum est, multis ante hunc visibilem mundum seculis, alium invisibilem mundum creatum, & in eo Angelos. De qua videndus Sixtus Senensis lib. 5. Bibloth. annot. 5. Ibi enim crassissimi istius errores reos peragit , , [] , , , , productis ad firmandam fidem suam singulorum testimoniis, [Ipse quoque August. de civitate Dei cap.3.2. lib. x 1. hic fluctuavit. Permittit enim ut in hac re unusquisque, libere sentiat quod velit, modo non statuat Angelos Deo coaeternos. Libro vero x 11. cap. xv. adinodum subtiliter disputat, posse concedi, Angelos ab aeterno fuisse creatos, nec tamen inde sequi, eos creatori esse coaeternos. Ille enim semper fuit, inquit, aeternitate immutabili, ipsi autem facti sunt. Est autem hoc primarium ejus argumentum, Deum ab aeterno fuisse Dominum, consequens ergo esse ut semper habuerit creaturam suo dominatui servientem, Theodoretus quoque quaest. 3. in Genes. Hoc autem concesso, inquit, omnia vid. quae existunt, habere naturam corruptioni obnoxiam, excepta S. trinitate, si quis angelorum turbas ante caelum & terram conditas esse dixerit, non offendet verbum pietatis. Licet autem hanc sententiam non solum Acacius, Diodorus Tarsensis & alii confutaverint, sed & * concilium Lateranense sub Innocentio
units.tr: The second fault of the Interpreter is that, since קדם signifies both priority of place and priority of time, he has here chosen the latter, following Aquila, for Aquila too translates it as ἀπ' ἀρχῆς [from the beginning] in this place. I admit that this can be excused and fairly explained, so that the sense is from the beginning or from the origin of the world when it was created, as my teacher and predecessor, the late Cl. Drusius, noted in his Fragments of the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament. In the same way Satan is said in the New Testament to have been a murderer from the beginning (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς), that is, from the beginning of his origin, so that it may be understood that he remained in his integrity for a short time. Yet I thought this worth noting, both because the LXX, whom our Interpreter is otherwise fond of following, here more correctly have καὶ ἀναλόλως [κατ' ἀνατολάς, eastward], and because this version has also drawn Jerome himself [not to mention the others] into another opinion. For in his Hebrew Questions on this passage he says: hence it is most clearly proved that before God created heaven and earth he had already created Paradise. The efforts of Senensis and Mercerus, who busy themselves excusing Jerome here, are therefore in vain. Steuchus himself could excuse him only by asserting that Jerome did not always persist in that opinion. How I wish he had noted the passage in the Retractations! For Albinus in his Questions on Genesis asserts that this was Jerome's mind, as his words show, and Eucherius in his commentary put the same assertion in Jerome's own words. Indeed Franc. Georgius, a Minorite, in the first volume of his Problems, tried to persuade us from these words that Jerome stood on his side and held that Paradise was not situated on this visible earth. For having considered these things, says Georgius, Jerome pronounced that Paradise was created before heaven and earth, namely to signify by these words that the Paradise of Moses is not situated on this visible earth, but in that land of the living which was created in the invisible world before this visible world. Hence it also becomes clear that that old error, if it did not arise from this, at least gained great strength from it and has not yet been buried, the error by which it was believed that many ages before this visible world another, invisible world was created, and in it Angels. On this subject see Sixtus Senensis, Bibliotheca, book 5, annotation 5. For there he drives out those very gross errors, producing the testimonies of individuals to confirm their faith. Augustine himself, too, in the City of God (book 11, chapter 3) wavered on this point. He permits each person to think freely on this matter as he wishes, provided he does not hold that Angels are coeternal with God. In book 12, chapter 15, he disputes very subtly that it may be conceded that Angels were created from eternity, and yet it does not follow that they are coeternal with their Creator. "He always was," he says, "in immutable eternity, but they were made." This is his chief argument: God was Lord from eternity, and it consequently follows that he always had a creature serving his dominion. Theodoret too, in Question 3 on Genesis, says: Granting this, that all things which exist have a nature subject to corruption, except the holy Trinity, if anyone says that hosts of angels were created before heaven and earth, he will not offend the word of piety. Although not only Acacius, Diodorus of Tarsus and others have refuted this opinion, but also the Lateran council under Innocent* [the text breaks off here]

units.la: * Sanctionum cap. 1. creatio omnium invisibilium III. annno Christi 1215. celebratum damnaverit, tamen Thomas parte primâ, verba Dionysii Carthusiani, dicit, positionem illam (vid. Angelos ante cœlum, &c. fuisse conditos) non debere tanquam erroneam aspernari & rejici, potissimum propter reverentiam Nazianzeni, qui tanta authoritatis extitit in scripturis, quod nullus unquam eum ausus fuit negare. Cajetanus etiam persuadere nobis satagit, aliam fuisse concilii intentionem, & secundùm eam potius, quàm verborum sensum sanctionem illam esse interpretandam. Quis & illud ignorat, Augustinum Steuchum in suâ Cosmopœia statuere, cœlum Empyreum non esse omnino creatum, sed Deo coæternum. Facessant illa opinionum portenta, & simplicitati SS. Literarum adhærescamus. In principio creavit Deus cœlum & terram: In principio temporis. Si cœlum Empyreum est cœlum, cur non & illud creaverit? Cur non & angelos qui in eo? Quid obstat? Quicquid fuit ante hoc principium, illud æternum est, illud Deus est. Hinc solidissimum pro Deitate Filii Dei argumentum depromitur. Illud autem non parum labefactatur, si Angelos quoque sine ulla Scripturæ authoritate ante hoc principium extitisse dixeris.]
units.tr: The first chapter of the decrees, on the creation of all things visible and invisible, celebrated under Innocent III in the year of Christ 1215, condemned that view. Yet Thomas, in the first part, using the words of Dionysius the Carthusian, says that this position (that the angels were created before heaven and so on) ought not to be spurned and rejected as erroneous, especially out of reverence for Gregory Nazianzen, who held such authority in the Scriptures that no one ever dared to deny him. Cajetan too labours to persuade us that the council had a different intention, and that its decree should be interpreted according to that intention rather than the sense of its words. Who also does not know that Augustinus Steuchus, in his Cosmopoeia, holds that the Empyrean heaven was not created at all but is coeternal with God? Let such monstrosities of opinion depart, and let us cling to the simplicity of the Holy Scriptures. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth: in the beginning of time. If the Empyrean is heaven, why did he not create it too? Why not also the angels who are in it? What stands in the way? Whatever existed before this beginning is eternal, and that is God. From this the most solid argument for the deity of the Son of God is drawn. But that argument is not a little weakened if you say that the angels too existed before this beginning, without any authority of Scripture.

units.la: Atque hæc fuit Censura mea ad vers. 8. cap. 2. Genef. ad quam ea nunc accessêrunt, quæ signis istis inclusimus.
units.tr: And this was my commentary on verse 8 of chapter 2 of Genesis, to which I have now added the material enclosed within these marks.

units.la: Puto minus jam miraturum Lectorem, unde tam variæ & dixerint ferè inceptæ Latinorum de Paradiso sententiæ propullulaverint. Hæc versio intricatissimas & desperatas ea de re disputationes excitavit. Textus Ebr. & Gr. plagam mundi signant, vid. Judææ orientalem, nominant locum in quo, Eden. Neu-crum habet vulgata. Inde vides bonos illos viros egregiè hic ἀτεροβατῆσαι, & plerosque Latinorum Origenis ineptias facilius admisisse. Alii, ut jam vidimus, paradisum in invisibili isto mundo posuerunt. Alii paradisum nihil aliud esse quam uni-versum hunc mundum docuerunt. At si in Eden fuit, si ver-sus Orientem, quomodo universus mundus erit? Si universus mundus fuit paradisus, in quem ergo inundum relegati sunt? Alii Paradisum extra nostrum orbem, eumque potius in aëre quàm terrâ collocârunt. Beda enim assignavit ei locum in editiori terræ parte, à terræ planitie usque adeò elatum, ut Lunarem globum contingat. Ita & Magister Historiæ Scholasticæ, & Stra-
units.tr: I think the reader will no longer be surprised where so many and such varied opinions of the Latins about Paradise have sprung up, almost from their very beginnings. This version has provoked very intricate and hopeless disputes on the subject. The Hebrew and Greek texts indicate a quarter of the world, namely the eastern part of Judea, and name the place in which it lay, Eden. The Vulgate has it as a neuter. From this you see that those good men wandered greatly here, and that most of the Latins too readily admitted the trifles of Origen. Others, as we have already seen, placed Paradise in that invisible world. Others taught that Paradise is nothing other than this whole world. But if it was in Eden, if it lay toward the East, how can it be the whole world? If the whole world was Paradise, into what world, then, were they banished? Others placed Paradise outside our globe, and in the air rather than on the earth. For Bede assigned it a place in the higher part of the earth, raised so far above the level of the earth that it touches the lunar sphere. So too the Master of the Scholastic History, and Strabo.

units.la: Bell. de Gratia primi tom 8.12.
units.tr: Bell. de Gratia primi tom 8.12.

units.la: Vide etiam Lombardum lib. 2. d st 17. fit.E Strabus & Bonavent. & Damascenus, & Sulpicius Severus & alii hâc de re senserunt. Sed dices, Græcos qui & Edev & Orientem in suo textu legerunt, nihilominus hic aberrasse. Agnosco, sed quod Latinis mala versio, hoc illis Allegorizandi pruritus dedit. Ex eo fonte Philo & Origenes Paradisum ita Allegorizarunt, verba Hieron. Epist. ad Pammachium, ut historia abstulerint veritatem, pro arboribus, Angelos; pro fluminibus, virtutes cælestes intelligentes. Sed tempus est ut obiter videamus, quid Marsennus in mea censurâ desideret. Quod ad primum attinet, agnoscit 1 x x. Pagninum, &c. reddidisse ἐν Εδεν, in Eden, & Jezech. 27. illud proprium loci nomen esse Agnoscit, Cajetanum & Steuchum idem statuisse. Et certè hoc urget præpositio ב / Ipse Corn. à Lapide hinc probat, Eden proprium loci nomen esse, atque id clarius ex versu 10. patere. Quid tamen Marsennus?
units.tr: See also Lombard, book 2, distinction 17, letter E. Strabo, Bonaventure, Damascene, Sulpicius Severus and others held views on this matter. But you will say that the Greeks, who read both Eden and East in their text, nevertheless went astray here. I grant it, but what a bad version was to the Latins, a craving for allegorizing was to them. From this source Philo and Origen allegorized Paradise in such a way that they took away the truth of the history, as Jerome says in his letter to Pammachius, making the trees into Angels and the rivers into heavenly powers. But it is time to see in passing what Marsenne desiderates in my remark. As for the first point, he acknowledges that Pagninus, etc., rendered ἐν Εδεν as in Eden, and he acknowledges that in Ezekiel 27 that is a proper name of a place, and that Cajetan and Steuchus held the same. And indeed this preposition ב presses the point. Cornelius à Lapide himself proves from this that Eden is a proper name of a place, and says this is clearer from verse 10. But what does Marsenne say?

units.la: MARSEN. pag. 1137.
units.tr: MARSENNUS, p. 1137.

units.la: In Heden recte vulgata vertit voluptatem, sive proprium nomen fuerit sive appellativum. Sicuti recte verteret, qui pro Jerusalem diceret urbem in qua erat templum, aut simili modo. Eden enim voluptatem significat. Et paulo post, non igitur refert an proprium vel appellativum nomen fuerit. Vulgata siquidem res significatas magis & Spiritus S. intentionem respicit, quàm verborum corticem.
units.tr: In Heden, the Vulgate rightly translates it as voluptatem, whether it is a proper name or a common noun. In the same way, someone would translate rightly who said Jerusalem meant the city in which the temple stood, or something similar. For Eden means pleasure. And a little later: it therefore makes no difference whether the name is proper or common. For the Vulgate looks more to the things signified and the intention of the Holy Spirit than to the husk of the words.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Eden cum appellativum est, voluptatem denotare, nullus negat. Nec dubium est, quin hinc fit Gr. ἡδονή. At benè reddi voluptatem, cum proprium loci nomen est, id vero pernego. Exemplum quod affers de Jerusalem planè alienum est. Non enim ut Eden, voluptas, ita Jerusalem, urbs in qua templum est, ἱερουσαλὴμ. Hæc enim περιφερεια, non interpretatio est. Nec ut Eden jam appellativum, jam proprium est, ita quoque cum voce Jerusalem comparatum est. Ea enim semper propriùm nomen est. Addo, hic Eden non posse per appellativum reddi, ut ut enim locus iste sic dictus sit ab amoenitate. nitate, tamen hic certum locum donotari, præpositio ב docet Multos hortos, hortos voluptatis dixeris; At non verè dixeris, eos in tractu Eden esse sitos. Quod ergo dicis Vulgatam magis intentionem Sp. S. quam verborum corticem respicere, frustra es. Hæc enim fuit intentio Sp. S. describere locum in quo fuerit hic hortus. Ideo nominat regionem, in quâ & fluvios, qui ex eo prodiêre. Itaque etli illud ב abesset, satius esset eam supplere, quam vocem illam per apellativum reddere. Amos 7. 9. יִשְׁחָק בְּמוֹרוֹת LXX. reddiderunt, βωμοὶ γέλωτος, ara risus. Quomodo Interpretes se hic torserint, non ignoras. Quod si nomen Isaaci in versione retinuissent, omnes difficultas sublata fuisset. Nunc videamus de altero.
units.tr: That Eden, as a common noun, denotes pleasure, no one denies. Nor is there doubt that the Greek [ἡδονή] comes from this. But that it is rightly rendered pleasure when it is the proper name of a place, that I flatly deny. The example you bring from Jerusalem is entirely unlike. For Jerusalem, the city in which the temple is, is not, as Eden means pleasure, a translation of [ἱερουσαλήμ]. That is a periphrasis, not a translation. Nor is Eden now a common noun and now a proper name in the way the word Jerusalem has been compared; for that is always a proper name. I add that here Eden cannot be rendered by a common noun. Although that place was so called from its pleasantness, here the preposition ב shows that a definite place is denoted. You could speak of many gardens as gardens of pleasure, but you would not truly say that they were situated in the region of Eden. So when you say that the Vulgate respects the intention of the Holy Spirit more than the husk of the words, you are wrong. For this was the intention of the Holy Spirit: to describe the place in which this garden was. Therefore he names the region in which the rivers also rose that came out of it. Thus, even if that ב were absent, it would be better to supply it than to render that word by a common noun. In Amos 7:9, [יִשְׁחָק בְּמוֹרוֹת] the LXX rendered it [βωμοὶ γέλωτος], altars of laughter. How the translators tortured themselves here, you are not unaware. But if they had kept the name Isaac in the version, all difficulty would have been removed. Now let us see about the other.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Benè res habet, quod מקרם à principio temporis, verti posse concedat, nisi eum magis ad id Drusii, quàm Ecclesiæ vera moveret authoritas.
units.tr: It is well that he concedes that the Hebrew word מקרם may be rendered "from the beginning of time", unless it is Drusius's authority rather than the true authority of the Church that moves him to this.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Vim infers verbis meis. Hæc enim mea sunt. Fateor hoc [interpretamentum vid. Aquilæ, ἀπ' ἀρχῆς & vulgatæ à principio] excusari posse, commodeque exponi, ut sensus sit, à principio vel exordio mundi sc. conditi. Ut præceptor & decessor meus Cl. Drusius notavit, quomodo & Satan dicitur fuisse homicida ἀπ' ἀρχῆς à principio, sc. originis suæ, ut hoc modo intelligatur, ad exiguum tempus in integritate suâ perstitisse. Hæc inquam verba mea sunt. Potesne ex his elicere, me concedere, מקרם verti posse hoc loco, à principio? Illud dico, excusari posse hoc interpretamentum, atque ita exponi, ut non faveat isti errori, qui ex hoc quoque loco vel propullulavit, vel vires acquisivit, vid. multis ante hunc visibilem mundum conditum seculis, alium invisibilem à Deo conditum, &c. Fateor מקרם in se & seorsim consideratum hæc duo significare, à principio, ab oriente. Adstruo, hic non posse aliter verti quàm, ab oriente. Addo, alteram illam versionem magnis viris istum errorem errandi occaoccasionem præbuisse, quæ tamen admissa, si cum iis Scripturæ locis, & speciatim isto, ubi Diabolus dicitur fuisse homicida à principio, fuisset collata, nihil tale potuisset suggerere. Aliud est, concedere, aliquid sic verti posse, aliud est asserere, aliquid licet male versum orthodoxo sensu posse explicari, ut errori non faveat.
units.tr: You do violence to my words, for these are my own. I grant that this rendering [Aquila's ἀπ' ἀρχῆς and the Vulgate's a principio] can be excused and suitably explained, so that the sense is "from the beginning or origin of the world, namely as created." As my teacher and predecessor, the distinguished Drusius, noted, Satan too is said to have been a murderer ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, from the beginning, that is, from his origin, so that it is understood that he stood in his integrity only for a short time. These, I say, are my words. Can you draw from them that I concede mikkedem [מקדם] can be translated from the beginning in this place? I say that this rendering can be excused and explained in such a way that it does not favour that error, which either sprouted from this very passage or gained strength from it, namely that many ages before this visible world was created, another, invisible world was created by God, and so on. I grant that mikkedem, considered in itself and separately, has these two meanings: from the beginning, from the east. I maintain that here it cannot be rendered otherwise than from the east. I add that the other version gave great men occasion for this error, yet if it had been admitted and compared with those passages of Scripture, and especially with this one, where the Devil is said to have been a murderer from the beginning, it could never have suggested such a thing. It is one thing to concede that something can be so translated; it is another to assert that something badly translated can be explained in an orthodox sense, so that it does not favour error.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Non minus bene Mikkèdem redditur, à principio, quam ab oriente. Quicquid enim loco vel tempore antecedit, Kadmon appellatur, & ipsa antecessio Kedem LXX. vertentes, κατὰ ἀναπλάς, ad locum respexerunt. D. Hieron. ad tempus.
units.tr: Mikkedem is rendered no less well from the beginning than from the east. For whatever precedes in place or time is called kadmon, and the Seventy, translating the precedence itself, kedem, as κατὰ ἀνατολάς, looked to place. Blessed Jerome looked to time.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Tὸ Mikkedem ubivis locorum æquè bene reddi, à principio, quam, ab oriente, nego. Neque tu ipse hoc asseres. Vide mihi hæc loca Neh. 12. 46. Ps. 74. 12. Jes. 46. 10. Habac. 1. 12. Et rursus, Genes. 3. 24. & 11. 2. & 12. 8. Quorsum ergo ista? nunquid ipse doceo קדם in Ebraïsmo jam prioritatem loci, jam temporis denotare? At illud jam non agimus. utra versio hic magis quadret, id verò est, quod disputamus. Paradisum in orientali plaga respectu Judææ (hujus enim situs in plerisque plagis mundi denominandis fuit habita ratio) plantatum fuisse, non audes negare. At à principio fuisse conditum, non sine periculo dici, agnoscere cogeris. Nam experientiam tibi oppono. D. Hieron. ad tempus respexit, inquis. Sed quâ mente? Eam prodit ipse in Quæstionibus ad Genesin, priusquam cœlum & terram conderet. Quæ ergo pervicacia est, huic versioni adeo mordicus adhærescere? D. Hieronymus, inquis. Miror te aurem non præbere Cardinali Bellarmino, qui in ipso limine libri recognitionum suarum profitetur se nunquam probasse vocem Divus vel Diva cum de Sanctis agitur, tum quod eam vocem apud veteres Latinos Patres non inveniat tum quod apud Ethnicos Divi nomen Diis tantum tribui soleat. Itaque ubicunque in libris meis, inquit, lector invenerit Divum, sciat vel mihi imprudenter excidisse, vel, quod sapius accidit, me scripsisse Beatum. Sed Typo-graphi graphi ubi legerunt B. quod beatum significat, illud in D. mutarunt atque ita ex Beato Divum fecerunt. Sed hoc obiter.
units.tr: That mikkedem can be equally well rendered from the beginning as from the east in any passage whatsoever, I deny, and you yourself will not assert it. Look at these passages for me: Neh. 12. 46; Ps. 74. 12; Isa. 46. 10; Hab. 1. 12. And again, Gen. 3. 24; 11. 2; 12. 8. Why, then, these? Surely I am not myself teaching that קדם in Hebrew sometimes denotes priority of place and sometimes priority of time? But we are not now dealing with that. The question we are disputing is which version fits better here. You do not dare to deny that Paradise was planted in the east, relative to Judaea (for its position was taken into account in naming most of the quarters of the world), but you are forced to admit that it cannot safely be said to have been created from the beginning. For I set experience against you. You say that Blessed Jerome looked to time. But with what intention? He himself reveals it in his Questions on Genesis: before he created heaven and earth. What, then, is this obstinacy, to cling so stubbornly to this version? Blessed Jerome, you say. I am surprised you do not lend an ear to Cardinal Bellarmine, who at the very threshold of the book of his Recognitions professes that he had never approved the word Divus or Diva when speaking of the saints, both because he does not find that word among the older Latin Fathers, and because among the heathens the title Divus was usually given only to the gods. Therefore, wherever the reader finds Divum in my books, he says, let him know that it has either slipped from me inadvertently, or, as happens more often, that I wrote Beatum. But when the printers saw B., which means beatum, they changed it into D., and so made Divum out of Beatum. But this in passing.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Adde, quod, licet pro loco sumas, nihil contra vulgatam inferatur: Enim vero principium mundi Oriens dici potest respectu Judaea.
units.tr: Add that, even if you take it as referring to place, nothing is brought against the Vulgate, for the beginning of the world can indeed be called the East with respect to Judaea.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: At quis hoc intelliget? Quis odorabitur principium ibi pro Oriente positum esse? Imo quis Quaestiones B. Hieronymi cum hac versione conferens, non jurare ausit, eum pro oriente hanc vocem non accepisse? Si enim haec ei in versione fuisset mens, a principio, id est, ab Oriente, non nisi absurdissime inde intulisset, Paradisum ante coelum & terram fuisse conditum. Quod vero & tu in Animadverf. ad Problem Veneti, & * Bellarm. & alii errorem illum sic excusatus, ut non ex sua, sed aliorum sententia locutus sit, nimis frivolum est. Profecto, si ea excusatio valebit, quis tandum haereseos aut erroris poterit convinci?
units.tr: But who will understand this? Who will sniff out that principium was here put for the East? Indeed, who, comparing Jerome's Questions with this version, would not dare to swear that he did not take this word to mean the East? For if this had been his intention in the version, from the beginning, that is, from the East, he could only have inferred, most absurdly, that Paradise was created before heaven and earth. As for your claim that you, in your Animadversions on the Venetian Problem, and Bellarmine and others have excused that error in such a way that they spoke not from their own opinion but from that of others, this is far too flimsy. Indeed, if that excuse is valid, who could ever be convicted of heresy or error?

units.la: CAP. III. verf. 15
units.tr: Chapter III, verse 15

units.la: Ebr. Ipse. | Vulg. Ipsa.
units.tr: Hebrew: Ipse. | Vulgate: Ipsa.

units.la: IPsa conteret tibi caput. Hanc lectionem Idololatricas B. Virginis laudes & has subsecutam ejusdem invocationem in Christianismum invexisse Theologi nostri prodiderunt. Duos Ms. omnes Ebraeos, Chald. Graecosque codices pronomen Masc. habere ipsi Lovanienses in * Catalogo variarum Lectionum fatentur, eamque lectionem ex Papistis quamplurimi non infimi subsellii ceu germanam approbarunt, inter quos Canus, Andradius, Cajet. Steuchus Pagnin. Arias Mont. quorum loca indicantur apud Cl. Viros VVitak. & Lubbertum in Disp. adversus Bellarm. Controversiam 1. His addo ex Rainoldi Praefatione in libros suos de Idolat. Rom. Eccles. Felisium Elucid. Decal. praec. 1. cap. 49. Riberam in Habacuc 1. 13. & de templo lib. 2. cap. 2.
units.tr: "IPSA shall bruise your head." Our theologians have shown that this reading introduced into Christendom the idolatrous praises of the blessed Virgin and the invocation of her that followed. The Louvain scholars themselves admit, in their *Catalogue of Various Readings*, that all the Hebrew manuscripts, the Chaldee and the Greek codices, have the masculine pronoun. Very many Papists of no small standing have also approved the masculine reading as the genuine one, among them Canus, Andradius, Cajetan, Steuchus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus. Their passages are indicated by the distinguished men Witaker and Lubbertus in their *Disputation against Bellarmine*, Controversy 1. To these I add Felisius, *Elucidation of the First Commandment*, chapter 49; Ribera on Habakkuk 1.13, and *On the Temple*, book 2, chapter 2; and from the preface of Rainolds to his books *On the Idolatry of the Roman Church*.

units.la: * Extat in apparatu ad Biblia Regia. cap.2. Addo & Pererium in Danielem & Hartum, Colloquii cum Reinoldo cap. 6. & Lindanum de optimo genere Interpretandi, lib. 3. pag. 126. & 127. & Pintum in cap.12. Jesaiae. Si de origine corruptelae me quaeras, fatebor eam Interpretis nec malignitati nec imperitiae imputandam, sed potius descriptorum incuriae, temporum fatali coecitati, supinae denique Cleri socordiae & imperitiae, quae omnia eum in modum excreverant, ut non tantum fontes non consulti, sed ne Latina quidem Exemplaria inter se collata fuerint. Res ita se habere mihi videtur. Vulgatus, quisquis fuit, Ebraeum NIT & Graecum αὐτὸς expressurus verterat IPSE, syntaxi sensu non voce congrua, qualis in Graeco, σπέρματί σε, ὃς ἐκ χειρός quam syntaxin cum saeculum illud infeticetum non caperet putarunt legendum esse IPSA, atque ita scripsisse interpretem & respicere ad proximum pronomen foem. generis (ejus) sc. mulieris. Atque hactenus malitiosae corruptelae nota Ecclesiae Pontificiae inuri non potuit. At ex quo Sixtus V. & Clemens VIII. vocem IPSA authenticis editionibus inseruerunt, temeratae Scripturae crimen admisit nunquam eluendum,
units.tr: It is found in the apparatus to the Royal Bibles, chapter 2. I add also Pererius on Daniel; Hart, in his *Colloquy with Reynolds*, chapter 6; Lindanus, *On the Best Kind of Interpreting*, book 3, pages 126 and 127; and Pintus on Isaiah 12. If you ask me about the origin of the corruption, I shall say that it must be imputed neither to the malice nor to the ignorance of the translator, but rather to the carelessness of copyists, to the fatal blindness of the age, and finally to the sluggish ignorance of the clergy. All these things grew to such a degree that not only were the sources not consulted, but not even the Latin copies were collated with one another. This, it seems to me, is how the matter stands. The Vulgate translator, whoever he was, rendering the Hebrew הוא and the Greek αὐτὸς, translated IPSE, a construction agreeing with the sense but not with the word, as in the Greek σπέρματί σε, ὃς ἐκ χειρός ("to your seed, which from the hand"). Since that unpolished age could not grasp this construction, they thought the word should be read IPSA, and that the translator had written so, referring to the nearest pronoun of feminine gender, namely the woman. So far, the mark of malicious corruption could not be branded upon the Papal Church. But from the time when Sixtus V and Clement VIII inserted the word IPSA into the authentic editions, she incurred the charge of a violated Scripture, a stain that can never be washed away:

units.la: Non mare si totum velit eluere omnibus undis. Sed redeat eo unde digressus est sermo. Bernardum ex hoc loco in falsam illam de B. Maria opinionem, quam Hom.2. super Missus est ex professo tractat, delapsum, ipsis Bernardi verbis docebo. Ecce enim post collatas inter se Evam & Mariam, sic tandem affatur Evam, Curre Eva ad Mariam, curre Mater ad filiam, Filia pro Matre respondeat, Filia patri pro Matre satisfaciat, quia ecce si vir cecidit per foeminam, jam non erigetur NISI per foeminam. Et paucis interjectis, Scrutare scripturas & proba quod dico, visne ut ego ex his aliqua testimonia hic inferam? Ut pauca loquar de pluribus, quam tibi aliam praedixisse videtur Deus, quando ad Serpentem ait, Inimicitias ponam inter te & Mul. Et si adhuc dubitas an de Maria dixerit, audi quod sequitur, Ipsa conteret caput tuum. Cui ergo hac victoria servata nisi Maria? Ipsa contrivit venenatum caput Serpentis, &c. Quo tanquam certissimo fundamento strato, ad laudes B. Virginis animosius digreditur, hortaturque Auditores, ut ad hanc stellam Jacob, stellam hanc maris (sic enim imperite satis interpretantur vocem Ebr. Miriam) in periculis con-sufugiant, hanc invocent, hanc cogitent. Cæteris vero hunc ipsum locum ejusdem erroris occasionem præbuisse, disertissimis verbis a) Franciscus Georgius Minorita professus est. Ita pernicioli erroris femina jecta sunt, qui postquam radices altiores indies egit, extirpari non potuit. Maluerunt enim Pontifices & impudentiores eorum Parasiti non tantum Græcos & Chaldaeos sed & Ebraeos codices corruptos censeri, quam locum hunc pristino nitori restituere. Profitentur quidem, parum interesse, hoc an illud legas: at ubi verba in rem conferenda sunt, tum demum apparet insignis pervicacia, magno argumento, non de nihilo hanc lectionem adeo mordicus abiis retineri. Costerus certe, nisi hac lectione errorem suorum fulciri crederet, Tropæum conculcati serpentis cum adjecto hoc elogio, ipsa conteret cap. 1. Mariæ, quasi hoc modo hæreticos urens, nunquam erexisset. Nec etiam d Suarez hinc quintum suum argumentum extruxisset, ad probandam hanc thesin, Mariam à peccato Originali fuisse præservatam, nec unquam ex capite Serpentis peccatum originale fabricasset ingeniosus artifex. Quod vero Bellarm. vulgatam hanc corruptam lectionem defendat adversus tot DD. Pontificios, etiam inde est, quod geminæ illius Editionis Pontificum, Sixti V. & Clem. VIII. quorum tempora plerique istorum non attigerunt, authoritate constringatur.
units.tr: "Not if the whole sea wished to wash it off with all its waves." But let me return to where my discourse left off. I will show from these very words of Bernard that he slipped, through this passage, into that false opinion about the blessed Mary, which he expressly treats in his second homily on Missus est. For after comparing Eve and Mary, he at last addresses Eve thus: "Run, Eve, to Mary; run, mother, to daughter. Let the daughter answer for the mother; let the daughter make satisfaction to the Father for the mother, because, behold, if the man fell through a woman, he shall not now be raised up except through a woman." And after a few words in between: "Search the Scriptures and test what I say. Would you like me to bring forward some testimonies from them here? To say a little about many things: God seems to have foretold to you another thing, when he said to the Serpent, I will put enmity between you and the woman. And if you still doubt whether he meant Mary, hear what follows: She shall bruise your head. To whom, then, was this victory reserved, if not to Mary? She crushed the venomous head of the Serpent, etc." Having laid this as a most certain foundation, he goes on more boldly to the praises of the blessed Virgin, and urges his hearers to take refuge in dangers at this star of Jacob, this star of the sea (for so unskillfully do they interpret the Hebrew word Miriam), to invoke her and to think upon her. That this very passage gave occasion to the same error for others, Franciscus Georgius, a Minorite, has professed in very clear words. Thus were the seeds of a pernicious error sown, which, once it had struck deeper roots every day, could not be uprooted. For the Pontiffs and their more shameless parasites preferred to have the Greek, Chaldee and even Hebrew codices judged corrupt rather than to restore this passage to its former purity. They do profess that it matters little whether you read this or that. But when the words are actually brought to the point, then at last their remarkable obstinacy appears, a strong sign that this reading is not held so stubbornly by them for nothing. Costerus, certainly, if he did not believe that the error of his people was supported by this reading, would never have erected the trophy of the trodden serpent with the added inscription "she shall bruise," chapter 1 of Mary, as if by this means he were burning the heretics. Nor would Suárez have built his fifth argument on this, to prove the thesis that Mary was preserved from original sin, nor would that ingenious craftsman ever have fabricated original sin from the head of the Serpent. That Bellarmine defends this corrupt reading of the Vulgate against so many Papist doctors is also because he is bound by the authority of the two editions of the Pontiffs, those of Sixtus V and Clement VIII, whose times most of those men never reached.

units.la: Sed, ut finem tandem huic præloquio ponamus, duo argumenta adversus hanc corruptelam dabimus, & obiter ad κρηφυγε-ταῖ Bellarmini respondebimus.
units.tr: But, to bring this preface at last to an end, I will give two arguments against this corruption, and on the way reply to Bellarmine's hiding-places [κρηφυγέται].

units.la: Primo, omnes Ebræi codices in hunc usque diem legunt הוא ipse, & ante Christi tempora sic fuisse lectum τῶν LXX. versio evincit. Respondet Bell. primo, se in uno codice legisse הוא. At cum codicem non nominet, quis dubitat, quin codicem Bibliorum Interlin. apud Plantinum 1572. excusum intelligat, ubi non הוא ut Bellar. citat, sed (ad corruptelam accedente Typographi vel corrector errato) הוּא reperitur, & quidem cum nota Kethib, ac si tò Keri esset הוּא / ut
units.tr: First, all Hebrew manuscripts to this day read הוא ("he", the pronoun ipse), and the Septuagint version proves that it was read this way before the time of Christ.
