It would have been better, however, for him to express the person, so that (4) he might remove the ambiguity that occurs in the Hebrew, and teach that the verb הוחל [hoḥel] is personal, not impersonal, as you prefer.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Mira doces, vel potius φοιϐάζει Ad 1. Utique omittit significationis propriæ vim, si per ipse reddas. Ubi enim latitare eam dices? An in verbo cœpit? Ipse tunc cœpit invocare N. D. Tunc, cum nasceretur Enos? vel potius, cum hoc filio auctus esset Seth? Quodnam tunc hic intelliges? Et quis ille ipse, Seth an Enos? Cur hæc non explicuisti? Atqui significat, inquis, tempus quo res hæc ab ea persona de qua sermo est, facta esse dicitur, illudque ex antecedentibus & consequentibus determinat. Quò ergo referes, si non ad tempus nativitatis? Clarius hæc proponere debuisses. Ad 2. Dico, hoc planè mihi videri ... Tu videris, quomodo hoc aliis sis probaturus. Ad 3. Hoc verbum ambiguum est. Posset enim seorsim sumptum significare, vel cœptum est, vel profanatum est. Nec enim esse ambigui temporis, dices, opinor. Præteritum est. Ut illud determinari non sit necesse. Est ergo fortassis ambigui subjecti, ut nescias, si resolutio fieri debeat in personale, de quo intelligi debeat, An, Tunc cœpit Seth, An verò, tunc cœpit Enos, vid. recens natus? neque enim hic primam vel secundam personam consignificari solere dices. Ad 4. Ea ambiguitas hæc opinor est, Tunc cœptum est, vel ab uno, vel à pluribus, vel si הוחל legi debet, ut postea doces, Tunc cœpit, manet in ambiguo, biguo; quis coeperit. Eam sustulit, te judice, vulgatus, Iste coepit, coeptum ergo ab ano. Sed quis ille Iste, rursus rogo. An Seth an Enos; Communi Interpretum vestrorum sententiâ Enos notatur. Enos ergo tunc cum nasceretur, (ut enim significat & determinat tempus, agnoscis opinor, tua verba, quo res haec ab ea persona, de qua sermo est, facta esse dicitur) Dei nomen coepit invocare?
units.tr: You teach wonders, or rather you babble. On 1: you certainly drop the force of the proper meaning if you render it by per se. For where will you say it lies hidden? In the word coepit? Then did he himself begin to call on the name of the Lord at that time? At the time when Enos was born? Or rather, when Seth had been blessed with this son? What then will you understand by hic? And who is that man, Seth or Enos? Why did you not explain this? Yet, you say, it signifies the time at which the thing is said to have been done by the person who is the subject of the discussion, and it fixes this from what comes before and after. To what, then, will you refer it, if not to the time of his birth? You ought to have set this out more clearly. On 2: I say that this seems quite plain to me... You must see how you will prove this to others. On 3: this verb is ambiguous. For taken by itself it could mean either it was begun or it was profaned. You will say, I suppose, that it is not of ambiguous tense. It is past, so there is no need for that to be fixed. It is perhaps, then, of ambiguous subject, so that you do not know, if the sense must be resolved into a personal form, what it should be understood to be: whether then Seth began, or rather then Enos began, namely the newly born child? For you will not say that this word usually co-signifies the first or second person. On 4: I suppose this ambiguity is as follows. Tunc coeptum est, whether by one or by several, or, if הוחל should be read as you later teach, tunc coepit, it remains ambiguous: who began. The Vulgate, in your judgement, removed this ambiguity with Iste coepit, so that it was begun by one man. But again I ask, who is that iste? Is it Seth or Enos? By the common opinion of your interpreters it is Enos who is meant. So then, at the time when Enos was born (for you recognise, I think, your own words, as they signify and fix the time at which the thing is said to have been done by the person who is the subject of the discussion), did he begin to call on the name of the Lord?

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Deinde Scriptores sacri utuntur loco pro persona & tempore, aliquando etiam tempore, pro persona vel loco, qua Ebraismorum genera docebit te D. Joh. Alba, vir in Ebr. literis praclarè versatus, Ariæ Montani Discipulus.
units.tr: Next, the sacred writers use a word for a person and a time, and sometimes for time, and for person or place, as Dr. John Alba will teach you, a man who was outstandingly versed in Hebrew literature and a disciple of Arias Montanus, in his account of the kinds of Hebraisms.

units.la: A M A M A.
units.tr: A M A M A.

units.la: Utinam exemplis hæc illustrasses! neque enim divinare possum ad quæ loca Scripturæ respicias,
units.tr: I wish you had illustrated these points with examples! I cannot guess which passages of Scripture you have in mind.

units.la: Heu, tam aversus equos patria Sol jungis ab urbe?
units.tr: Alas, do you yoke your horses so turned away from your native city, O Sun?

units.la: Iste autem Alba albus an alter sit, nescio. Ejus lucubrationum nihil in hoc Belgii angulo vidi unquam. Quia tamen cum magno Ariæ μαθηπίνσαι dicis, operam dabo, ut ejus Ebraïsmos, si modò is libri, quem innuis, titulus est, mihi comparem. Ego à meis discipulis quotidie disco. Cur ergo ab erudito Hispano erubescerem?
units.tr: I do not know whether this Alba is a white man or someone else. I have seen nothing of his writings in this corner of Belgium. Still, since you say he was a great disciple [μαθητεῦσαι] of Arias Montanus, I will make an effort to get hold of his Hebraisms, if the title is indeed the one you indicate. I learn every day from my own students. Why then should I be ashamed to learn from a learned Spaniard?

units.la: M A R S E N N U S.
units.tr: M A R S E N N U S.

units.la: Non opus est dicere, vulgatum legisse זרע pro אין ut tuus Drusius volebat, qui & addit Graecos החל pro הוחל legisse.
units.tr: There is no need to say that the Vulgate read זרע for אין, as your Drusius thought, who also adds that the Greeks read החל for הוחל.

units.la: A M A M A.
units.tr: A M A M A.

units.la: Egregiam verò Cl. Viro & qui de vulgatâ versione non male meritus est, rependis gratiam.
units.tr: Yet you repay with a sorry return a famous man, who has also deserved well of the Vulgate version.

units.la: Ff MAR-
units.tr: Ff MAR-

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Lectionem LXX. hoc loco agnoscimus, eam retinuit vulgatus interpres, D. Hieronymus, utraque doctrina & ætate te proveAiores.
units.tr: We recognise the Septuagint reading in this place; the Vulgate translator, St Jerome, retained it, and he was superior to you in both learning and age.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Cur ergo vulgatus non vertit, Isle speravit, Sic enim habent LXX. ἐτῷ ἡλπισε. Cur enim in uno secutus est, in altero secessum fecit? Si B. Hieronymus vulgatus interpres est, cur ipse ergo vertit, Tunc initium fuit, &c.
units.tr: Why then did the Vulgate not translate He hoped, for so the LXX have it [ἐτῷ ἡλπισε]? Why did he follow them in one place and depart from them in another? If St Jerome is the Vulgate translator, why did he himself render Then there was a beginning, etc.?

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Venio ad alterum controversia caput. De verbo quæstio est, imo de puncto, quo deductum fere transivit in phathach, ut pro יחל א הוחל in hiphil, הלל א הנחל in hophal legeretur.
units.tr: I come now to the second point of controversy. The question concerns a word, or rather a vowel point, which by a slip passed almost into patah, so that for [יחל] in hiphil, [הלל] in hophal, it should be read.

units.la: AM- AMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Si puncta à Maforethis addita sunt, ut supra docuisti, cur non potius dicis phathach loco Tsere imperite ab ipsis subn fuisse positum? Sed ut jam tecum non contendam, יחל in incipiendi significatione nunquam occurrere, quæ Grammatice docuit, mi Marsenne, à יחל in præterito Hiphil posse formari הוחל cum Tsere in fine? Excute omnes, evolve universa Biblia, si possis vel unicum præteritum Hiphil tertiæ sing. extra ordinem Monosyllaborum, seu imperfectorum Ain, ostendere, quod in Tsere desinat, eris mihi magnus Apollo. Atque hic veniam mihi dabis, si te tuis verbis alloquar, & tua tibi reponam, Futuros ego prævideo, qui hanc Spartam nacti eam graviter exornent, ac te juveniliter exultantem sapere doceant, nec temere quicquam proferre aut in cogitanter. Objicies forsan illud הושיע ex 1. Sam. 21. verf. 26. & 33. Sed vester Pagninus in Thes. suo te docebit, illud Makor esse.
units.tr: If the points were added by the Masoretes, as you taught above, why do you not rather say that patah was wrongly placed by them in place of tsere? But let us not contend over this now. Are you not, my dear Marsenne, taught by grammar that yachal never occurs in the sense of beginning, and that from yachal in the third person singular perfect hiphil one can form huchal with tsere at the end? Search through everything, go over the whole Bible, and if you can show even a single third person singular perfect hiphil outside the class of monosyllables or verbs with ayin as third radical that ends in tsere, you will be a great Apollo to me. And here you will grant me pardon if I address you in your own words and return yours to you: I foresee that there will be those who, having gained this Sparta, will adorn it with weight and teach you, exulting like a youth, to be wise, and not to put forward anything rashly or without thought. You may perhaps object the form hoshia in 1 Samuel 21:26 and 33. But your Pagninus in his Thesaurus will teach you that this is makor.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Ita enim legisse LXX. ex eorum versione satis manifestum est, quorum authoritatem & lectionem secutus vulgatus Interpres הוּהּ quidem deduxit à יחל / non eodem tum (forte tamen) verbo reddidit, sed vim expressit conjugationis, quæ transitiva est, & actionem ad extra significat, idque pro modo rei significatæ, unde cum expectatione & spe aliquid minùs perfectum indicetur, actionem ejus convenientis-sime inceptione definivit.
units.tr: It is quite clear from their version that the Seventy read it thus. Following their authority and reading, the Vulgate translator indeed derived [הוהל] from [יחל], but did not render it with the same verb (perhaps, however, he did). Instead he expressed the force of the conjugation, which is transitive and signifies an action directed outward, and he did so in keeping with the nature of the thing signified. Since an expectation and hope indicate something less than perfect, he rightly defined its action by the word "beginning".

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Probandum tibi prius erat יחל ullibi in Scripturâ incipiendi notionem habere. Ubi id probatum vel demonstratum dederis, tunc ad cætera respondere erit operæ pretium. Interpretationi genuinæ, tunc cœptum est, confirmandæ, produxi Aquilam & Hieron. De Hieron. agnoscis, de Aquila siles. Vtramque lectionem dicis agnovisse Hieronymum. Sed ponam tua verba;
units.tr: You first had to prove that yachal anywhere in Scripture has the sense of beginning. Once you have proved or demonstrated this, it will be worth while to answer the rest. To confirm the genuine rendering, then it was begun, I brought forward Aquila and Jerome. You acknowledge Jerome, and you are silent about Aquila. You say that Jerome recognised both readings. But let me set out your own words:

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Nimium juvenis es & unius noctis fungus, unius ejusdemque loci non duas sed plures lectiones non diffitemur: lectionis unius plures, ad literam quoque, sensus ultrò concedimus, sed eam maximè probamus, & retinemus, quæ est omnium optima, nec si vires omnes exeroueris, quanquam juveniles sunt, Ecclesiam à sua sententiâ unquam poteris deturbare.
units.tr: You are too young, a mushroom of a single night. We do not deny that there are several readings of one and the same place, nor do we readily concede that a single reading has several literal senses. But we especially approve and retain the one that is the best of all. Even if you exert all your strength, however youthful it may be, you will never be able to drive the Church from its opinion.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Quod ad varios unius loci sensus literales attinet, tu quidem hic cum communi Scholasticorum schola sentis: at longè rectiùs hac-de re judicârunt Alensis, Albertus, & ex neotericis vester quoque Michaël Medina lib. 6. de rectâ in Deum fide, cap. 25. Pradus & alii. cum quibus si me sentire dixero, non erit tibi, opinor, ea audentia, ut me hæreseos eo nomine postules; Et quâ quæso te fiduciâ hoc adeo imperterritus asseris? cum hactenus ab Ecclesia, verba Becani, non sit definitum, plures esse sensus literales sub una libera.
units.tr: As for the various literal senses of a single passage, you here think with the common school of the Scholastics. But Alensis, Albertus, and among the moderns your own Michaël Medina, in book 6 of On the Right Faith in God, chapter 25, judged much more correctly, as did Pradus and others. If I say that I agree with them, I think you will not have the boldness to demand that I be charged with heresy on that account. And with what confidence, I ask, do you assert this so fearlessly? Since until now the Church, in Becanus's words, has not defined that there are several literal senses under one [reading].

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Vide sis quid de Onkelos subtexas. Verbum, inquis, impersonale impersonale resolvit, sed pluraliter, fidem secutus 1. exemplaris Veneti. Ego 2. probationibus utor, & invenio singulariter ab eo redditum
units.tr: See what you add about Onkelos. You say that he resolves the impersonal verb impersonally but in the plural, following the first Venetian copy. I, on the other hand, use two proofs and find that he rendered it in the singular.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Ad 1. non unius exemplaris Veneti, mi Marsenne, sed quatuor Venetorum, trium in folio, uniusque in 8. fidem secutus sum. Ad 2. Quaenam sint illa probatiora, indicare debuisses. Certè inter illa Regium non fuit, Namque & illud plurale habet, vid. שריאו inceperunt. Postea inconstantiam mihi objicis, quod Aquilae, Theodoreti, Gallorum & Piscatoris, &c. versionem amplectar, Tunc coeptum est denominari de nomine DOMINI. Sed quae haec inconstantia est, An ergo antea aliam defendi? Tantum disputavi contra duarum priorum vocum או הוהל versionem. Frustra metuis, ne fraternitatis offensionem incurram. Fratres mei Belgae non habent ullam versionem pro authentica, nec aegre ferunt si ab ea dissentiamus. Facilius autem ea versio vocatur commentum, quam solo aquatur. Sed juvat audire tuam benedictionem, qua hanc controversiam obsignas.
units.tr: As for your first point, my dear Marsenne, I followed not one Venetian copy but four Venetian copies, three folio and one octavo. As for your second, you ought to have indicated which proofs are the more reliable. Certainly the Regius was not among them, for it also has the plural, see sherîû [שריאו], they began. Afterwards you charge me with inconsistency, because I embrace the version of Aquila, Theodoret, the Gauls, Piscator and others: Then it was begun to be called by the name of the LORD. But what inconsistency is this? Did I defend another version before? I argued only against the rendering of the two earlier words [יחל] and [הוהל]. You need not fear that I shall incur offence against brotherly unity. My Belgian brethren do not hold any version to be authentic, nor do they take it badly if we dissent from it. Indeed, that version is more easily called a fiction than levelled to the ground. But I should like to hear your blessing, with which you seal this controversy.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Tuum igitur commentum tibi sit, atque utinam ipse tu tibi, nec in ea, quam hic astruis, hominum dissectione & divisione, partem teneas, cui dictum est, vos autem sicut homines moriemini, &c. Cui & dicendum aliquando, Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, &c. nisi serio respuerit.
units.tr: Keep your commentary to yourself, and I wish you would be yourself, and not take a part in that division and separation of men which you set out here, the one to whom it has been said, "But you shall die like men," etc. To whom it will also one day have to be said, "Depart, accursed, into everlasting fire," etc., unless he has sincerely renounced it.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Nisi serio respueris, id tibi est, nisi ad Ecclesiam Rom. te adadjunxeris. Equidem extra eam mi Marsenne, æternam salutem in Jesu Christo redemtore meo expecto. Is bonum illud opus quod in me incoavit, perficiet, atque ut indies plures Euangelio convenientes fructus proferam, eo auxiliante & gratiam clementer suppeditante, annitar. Tu verò qui stare tibi videris, vide ne cadas. μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει, ἀλλὰ φοβοῦ. Plures præsumendo quàm desperando periêre.
units.tr: Unless you reject it in earnest, that is how it will stand for you, unless you have joined yourself to the Roman Church. For my part, my Marsennus, I look for eternal salvation outside it, in Jesus Christ my Redeemer. He will complete the good work he has begun in me, and with his help, and by his graciously supplied grace, I shall strive to bring forth more and more fruit worthy of the gospel from day to day. As for you, who seem to yourself to stand, take care lest you fall. "Be not high-minded, but fear" [μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει, ἀλλὰ φοβοῦ]. More have perished through presuming than through despairing.

units.la: CAP. VI. vers. 3.
units.tr: CHAP. VI. verse 3.

units.la: Postquam multa dixisset de vocis יִרְוֹן themate & significatione, nec tamen quicquam certi definivisset, tandem sic intonat.
units.tr: After saying much about the theme and meaning of the word יִרְוֹן [yirvon] without defining anything certain, he at last declares as follows.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Ex quibus mendacium Amamæ redarguitur, qui vulgatam reprehendit, quod permanebit vertat, cum etiam Dun à 70 per χαταμένην vertatur, ut etiam Kircherus advertit. Si tua Grammatica postulat iiddon, quare non mutas puncta?
units.tr: From these things the lie of Amama is refuted, who censures the Vulgate for rendering "permanebit", when even Dun is rendered by the Seventy [καταμένην] as well, Kircher noticed. If your grammar requires iiddon, why do you not change the points?

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Persisto in eo, יִרְוֹן malè verti permanebit. An mentior? Redargue & convince me. In antecedentibus nihil video quo convinci queam. Quod verò hic rursus inculcas de Lxx. nihil ad rem. Non enim quæritur, quomodo illi verterint, sed quam benè. An illorum versio erit norma rectæ versionis? Male tunc certe cum vulgatâ vestrâ ageretur. Quid spectârint illi, dum sic hoc loco verterunt, non malè Leo Castrius divinavit, ut vid. pro ירון legerint ילון / Quomodo sæpe ל pro ד quin & pro ר ut Psal. 56. גומל pro גומר legisse eos, post alios Cl. Drusius in Conjectaneis ad vers. Græcam Prophetarum minorum observavit passim.
units.tr: I persist in holding that יִרְוֹן [yirvon] is wrongly rendered permanebit. Am I lying? Refute me and convince me. In what has gone before I see nothing by which I could be convinced. As for your repeating here what you said about the Seventy, it is beside the point. The question is not how they translated, but how well. Would their version be the rule for a correct translation? If so, things would certainly go badly for your Vulgate. What they had in mind when they translated this passage thus, Leo Castrius has guessed not badly: that they read ילון [yilon] for ירון [yiron]. How often they read ל for ד, and even ר, as in Psalm 56, where they read גומל [gomal] for גומר [gomar], Drusius has observed throughout, following others, in his Conjectanea on the Greek version of the Minor Prophets.

units.la: MARSENNUS.
units.tr: MARSENNUS.

units.la: Mentiris etiam, dum ais Senensem ex professo lib. 5. annot. 74. docuisse, locum hunc male versum. Ait enim tantùm D. Hieronymum versionem 70. rejecisse, qui sic habent, ut refert ὁ μὴ καταξιέντ. Imo ipse probat versionem nostram, dum fatetur Chaldaeum nobiscum convenire.
units.tr: You also lie, in saying Senensis in his set treatment, Annotation 74 of Book 5, taught that this passage was wrongly translated. For he says only that St Jerome rejected the version of the Seventy, which reads thus, as he reports [ὁ μὴ καταξιέντ]. Indeed he himself approves our version, in admitting that the Chaldee agrees with us.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Quàm temerè & incogitanter loqueris, & ut cum Homerico illo te alloquar, τί δέ σ' ἐπῳ φύγεν ἐχῳ ἐδόντων; Mentior de Senensi? Quid ergo sibi vult illud marginale, quod ad initium Annotationis ponitur, Non permanebit spiritus, &c. male versum. Ita enim lego in Paris. Editione anni 1610. quam Joh. Hayus Jesuita recognovit. Hieronymum hanc versionem rejicere, non audes negare. Quid hîc dices, an utraque potest subsistere? Vnius loci possunt esse plures sensus literales dixisti supra. Sed an etiam contrarii? Hieron. sic vertit & explicat, Non judicabit sp. meus homines istos in aeternum, quia caro sunt, hoc est, quia fragilis est in homine conditio, non eos ad aeternos servabo cruciatus, sed hic illis restituam quod merentur. Ergo non severitatem, ut in nostris codicibus legitur, sed clementiam Dei sonat. Vides sensus contrarios? Vox καταξιέντ cubat in mendo, & tu ipse jam καταμεῖνη citasti. Cur ergo eam vocem hic reponis? Quod vero dicis eum probare versionem vestram, quae Hieronymianae, quam antea probavit, è diametro adversatur, vide quem Proteum ex Senensi facias. Sed quomodo hoc probas? Quia fatetur Chaldaeum nobiscum convenire. Itane? An ergo quisquis dicit Chaldaeum cum aliqua versione convenire, eam approbat? Atque hic tecum finio. Namque ad Censuram meam versus 5. nihil respondisti. Egisti mecum acerbiusculè, ordinis tui & professionis oblitus. Si eâdem te ripâ secutus fuissem, tu certe non potuisses culpare. Ego meae professionis rationem habui. Si quid tamen & ego acerbiusculè dixisse viris cordatis & piis videbor, jam nunc poenitet. Porro, nisi in caeteris, quas promittis, lucubrationibus, solidioribus rationibus meam Censuram oppugnaveris, plane stat sententia, silentio litare. Possum enim horas meas utilioribus curis transmittere. Tu mihi in praesens, Marsenne eruditissime, vale & salve.
units.tr: How rashly and thoughtlessly you speak! And, to address you in Homer's words, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth? [τί δέ σ' ἐπῳ φύγεν ἐχῳ ἐδόντων] Do I lie about Senensis? Then what is the meaning of that marginal note placed at the start of the annotation, Non permanebit spiritus, &c. male versum? For so I read in the Paris edition of 1610, which the Jesuit John Hay revised. You do not dare to deny that Jerome rejects this version. What will you say here? Can both stand? You said above that a single passage may have several literal senses. But can it also have contrary ones? Jerome translates and explains it thus: Non judicabit ... restituam quod merentur: "My Spirit will not judge these men forever, because they are flesh, that is, because the human condition is fragile; I will not keep them for eternal torments, but here I will repay them what they deserve." Therefore the sense is not severity, as our codices read, but the clemency of God. Do you see the contrary senses? The word καταξιέντ [kataxiént] lies in an error, and you yourself have now cited καταμεῖνη [katameînē]. Why then do you restore that word here? As for your claim that he approves your version, which is diametrically opposed to the Hieronymian version he approved earlier, see what a Proteus you make of Senensis. But how do you prove this? Because he admits that the Chaldee agrees with us. Really? Then does anyone who says the Chaldee agrees with some version thereby approve it? And here I finish with you. For you have made no reply to my Censure, verse 5. You have dealt with me rather harshly, forgetting your rank and profession. Had I followed you on that ground, you could certainly not have blamed me; I have kept regard for my own profession. Yet if I seem to have spoken somewhat harshly to men of sense and piety, I now regret it. Further, unless in the other writings you promise you oppose my Censure with more solid arguments, my opinion stands: it is best to let the matter pass in silence. For I can spend my hours on more useful concerns. Farewell and be well, most learned Marsenne.

units.la: RESPONSIONIS AD MARSENNUM
units.tr: RESPONSE TO MARSENNE

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: CAP. III. vers. 20.
units.tr: CAP. III. vers. 20.

units.la: Vocavit nomen uxoris suæ Evam.
units.tr: And Adam called his wife's name Eve.

units.la: Ebr. חַוָּה Hhauvah, LXX. ζωὴ, vel ut Chrysostomus, Εὔα ὅπερ ἐστι ζωή. Eva, quod significat vitam. Epiphanius lib. 3. contra hæref. tom. 2. Eva citra aspirationem Ebræis mulierem, cum aspiratione serpentem significat. Miseret me Patrum cum talia lego, inquit Cl. Drusius, notis ad Sulpic. pag. 11. Namque hoc nomen in Ebr. à Cheth aspiratione duplici inchoatur. Sed fefellit eos Græcanica Orthographia, quæ in Ebraïcis vocibus corruptissima est, librariorum vitio. Etenim quod ad Spiritus attinet, magna est eorum confusio in vocibus peregrinis, cui occursum fuisset, si figura H * aspirationis nota manssset, & longo E exprimendo alius character fuisset adhibitus. Autum ivère postea hanc con-fusionem typographi, qui, paucis exceptis, majusculos voca-lium characteres sine ullo omnino spiritu exhibuêre, Eva, Adam, ΑΘεΛ. Atq; hæc semel monuisse satis erit. Redeamus ad חַוָּה/ quam vocem septuaginta per vocalem E legerunt. Id negari non po-teft ; sed utrumque Epiphanii effatum falsum est. Cum enim mulierem significat, hoc est, cùm nomen proprium primæ Matris est, cum aspiratione, eâque geminâ, in Ebræo scribitur. Deinde Heva nec apud Ebræos, nec Chaldæos, nec Syros serpentem significat. Extant in Thargum חַיֵּי & חַוָּא / non חַוָּה / non חַוָּה / Clemens in Protreptico rectius, Heuja exponitur serpens fœmina, חַוְיָא Heuja, ut Hillel, Hellel, inquit Drusius. Quid Lyra? Ea in Ebræo sonat vitam, sed pœnalitatibus subjectam. Hæc suppeditarunt aliis licentius nugandi argumentum. Quid Historiæ Scholasticæ Magister Petrus Comestor? Tunc Adam deplorans posteritatis suæ miseriam, vocavit uxorem suam Evam, quasi alludens ejulatui parvulorum. Masculus enim recens natus dicit A, Fœmina vero E, quasi diceret, omnes dicent E vel A, quotquot nascentur ab Eva. En suaviludia. Audi amplius, Eva per apharesin est Ve; per Anastrophen, Ave, quam vocem ad Mariam, cujus typus fuit Eva, Gabriel, (Latinè credo locutus) detulit, ut piè aliqui contemplantur, inquit Corn. a Lapide. Apage has ineptias, non nisi in corruptissimæ vocis scripturâ & falsa hypothesi fundatas. In הַוָּה הַיָּה enim nihil est, quod ærumnam vel pœnalitatem connotet. Quid ergo? Chauva, sive Hauva, sive Heva, non vitam miseram, imo ne vitam quidem denotat, sed viventem κατ' ἐξοχὴν, vel ab affectu, q. d. vivificantem, in vita conservantem, vitæ authorem suis natis & posteris, quos hic viventes appellat Moses (ejus enim non Adami hæc verba sunt, (כִּי הִיא אִם כֹּל הַי) voce generali ad speciem humanam restrictâ, quod & in vocibus caro, creatura, etiam addito signo universali, videre est, Effundam sp. meum super omnem carnem, Prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Ita & mortalium nomenclaturâ homines tantum denotamus. Aben Ezra, הויו והיוד מתחלפים וכן הנה יד יהוה היה ואתה הור לה הם למלך ולא קראה ביור כי מה הפרש יש בין שמה ובין שם החיות id est, Vau & Jod permutantur, & sic הנה / &c. (Locus Scripturæ est Exod.3.3. Confer cum altero ואתה / &c. Nehem.6.6.) Et non vocat eam (חַיָּה) cum Jod, nam qua tunc fuisset differitas inter nomen ejus & nomen animalium? Michlal Jophi, תאר בהתחלף היור לויו כרי שלא יתערב עם ארץ החיה אשר וגו' Est adjectivum, (pro חַיָּה) commutato Jod in vau, ne confunderetur cum eo hoc est animal quod comedetur Lev.11.2. Hæc seria. Lubet his interponere quod animum laxet. חַוָּה loqui, indicare, Ebræis & Chaldæis significat. Sunt inter Ebræos, qui hic primæ matris nomen arcessunt. Est certe fœmina animal loquax & garrulum. Baal Hatturim ad marg. Bibliorum Venet. & Basil. sol.6.p.1. ויקרא אר שמה חוה על שם שפחיה וגו' ... id est. Et vocavit nomen, ejus Hauwah, quia (multum) loquitur. Hoc est quod dicunt, Decem Cabi confabulationum discendesrunt in mundum, & novem ipsorum abstulerunt mulieres.
units.tr: Hebrew חַוָּה Chauvah, Septuagint ζωή [zoē]. Chrysostom reads Εὔα, which is ζωή [Eua, which is zoē]. Eve, which means life. Epiphanius, book 3 against heresies, vol. 2: Eve without aspiration means a woman to the Hebrews, but with aspiration it means a serpent. I pity the Fathers when I read such things, says the learned Drusius in his notes on Sulpicius, p. 11. For in Hebrew this name begins with a double aspiration, Cheth. But Greek spelling misled them, and it is most corrupt in Hebrew words because of the errors of copyists. As for breathings, there is great confusion in foreign words, which could have been avoided if the aspiration mark H had been kept and a different character used to express the long E. Later the printers added to this confusion, for with few exceptions they printed the capital vowels with no breathing at all: Eva, Adam, ΑΘεΛ. Let this one warning be enough. Let us return to חַוָּה, which the Seventy read with the vowel E. This cannot be denied, but both of Epiphanius's statements are false. When the word means woman, that is, when it is the proper name of the first mother, it is written in Hebrew with aspiration, and a double one. Further, Heva does not mean serpent among the Hebrews, the Chaldeans or the Syrians. In the Targum the forms are חַיֵּי and חַוָּא, not חַוָּה. Clement in the Protrepticus is more accurate: Heuja is explained as female serpent, חַוְיָא [Heuja], as Hillel is Hellel, says Drusius. What of Lyra? In Hebrew it sounds like life, but subjected to penalties. These remarks gave others a freer license to trifle. What of Peter Comestor, Master of the Historia Scholastica? Then Adam, lamenting the misery of his posterity, called his wife Eve, as if alluding to the wailing of infants. For a male newborn says A, but a female says E, as if to say, all who are born of Eve will say E or A. Such playful nonsense! Hear more: Eve by aphaeresis is Ve; by anastrophe, Ave, which word, I believe, Gabriel brought to Mary, whose type Eve was, in Latin, as some devout men contemplate, says Cornelius a Lapide. Away with such absurdities, founded only on a corrupt spelling of the word and a false hypothesis. In חַוָּה and הַיָּה there is nothing that connotes hardship or penalty. What then? Chauvah, or Hauvah, or Heva, does not denote a miserable life, nor even life, but the living one par excellence, or by affection, that is, the one who gives life, who sustains life, the author of life to her children and posterity, whom Moses here calls living. For these are not the words of Adam but of Moses (כִּי הִיא אִם כֹּל הַי), using a general word restricted to the human species, as can be seen also in the words flesh and creature, even with a universal sign added: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, Preach the gospel to every creature. So too by the name mortals we denote only men. Aben Ezra: הויו והיוד מתחלפים וכן הנה יד יהוה היה ואתה הור לה הם למלך ולא קראה ביור כי מה הפרש יש בין שמה ובין שם החיות, that is, Vau and Jod are interchanged, and so in הנה, etc. (the passage of Scripture is Exod. 3.3; compare the other, ואתה, etc., Neh. 6.6.) And he does not call her (חַיָּה) with Jod, for what difference would there then be between her name and the name of the animals? Michlal Jophi: תאר בהתחלף היור לויו כרי שלא יתערב עם ארץ החיה אשר וגו', It is an adjective (for חַיָּה), with Jod changed into vau, so that it would not be confused with the animal that is eaten, Lev. 11.2. So much for serious matters. It is pleasant to add here something to relax the mind. חַוָּה means to speak, to declare to the Hebrews and the Chaldeans. Some Hebrews derive the name of the first mother from this root. A woman is certainly a talkative and chattering animal. Baal Hatturim, in the margin of the Venice and Basel Bibles, sol. 6, p. 1: ויקרא אר שמה חוה על שם שפחיה וגו', that is, And he called her name Hauwah, because she (much) talks. This is what they say: ten measures of talk descended into the world, and women took nine of them.

units.la: CAP. IV. I.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. I.

units.la: Acquisivi virum אֶת־יְהוָה
units.tr: I have gotten a man from the LORD [את־יהוה]

units.la: LXX. Ἀλλ' ... per Deum. Ita & vulgatus, licet codices quidam legant, per Dominum, & quidem rectius. Onkelos, מן קדם ... à conspectu Domini id est à Domino. Sed & Jun. Trem. Ital. Angl. Piscat. à DOMINO, ut sit אֶרְתְּ pro מֵאֵת / Genev. de par l'Eternel. Hieron Tigurini, Pagn. Drus. cum Domino, quod Græci dicunt, ςὺν Θεῷ, Quam Interpretationem approbavit & Junius in notis, inquiens, nisi forte ut Hieron. interpretetur, ⊖ ... Licet autem omnes hæ interpretationes Deum authorem & operatorem hujus acquisitionis constituant est tamen cur malim illam, cum DOMINO. Nihil enim notius est, quàm אֶת pas-sim usurpari pro עִם cum. Sic infra 6.9. ambulavit Enoch אֶת־אֱלֹהִים cum Deo licet autem istius loci alius sit sensus, illud tamen non negabitur, אֶת ibi valere עִם / Quod si dubites an ea locutio cum Deo id est, Deo auxiliante & opitulante, Ebræis nota sit, accipe à Drusio locum 1. Sam. 14. 45. Cum Deo fecit hodie, Ebr. עִם אֱלֹהִים At אֵת poni pro מֵאֵת non probant illa loca, quæ adducit Cl. Junius. Nam Gen. 44. 4. ubi legimus יָצְאוּ אֶת־הָעִיר vertit Cl. Drusius, egressi sunt urbem, nam & Latini sic loquuntur. Deut. 34. 1. nihil obstat, quominus אֶת־הָעָר per Accusativum reddatur. Ut plane non dubitem, quin ipse Junius minus exemplis istis fidens illa subjunxit, quæ supra exhibui. Quod verò ad locum Jerem. 51. 59. attinet כַּלְכָּתוֹ אֶת צִדְקִיָּהוּ quem adducit Cl. Piscator, is majus pondus habent, nam & I. x x. ἐπὶ Ἐδεχίας, Et Jun. à Zedechia Ital. Gen. da part, nomine Zedechiæ. Ecce omnes acceperunt אֵת pro מֵאֵת / Angli tamen, Hisp. & Tigurini, & Castal. cum Zedechiâ. Sed videamus versiones alias præsentis loci. B. Lutherus in Editionibus suis, etiam ultimâ correctione, quæ anno 1542. prodiit, Ich hab uberkommen den Man des Herren / Acquisivi virum Domini, Et in Comment. German. ad Genesin, tomo 4. Jenensi den Man Gottes / oder mit Gott. id est virum Dei, aut, cum Deo. Atq; ita etiamnum Belg. versio, Ich hebbe gekregen den Man des Heeren / virum Domini, à Domino mihi promissum, inquit Luth. in Comment. Latino, promissum vid. in isto Euangelio Semen mulieris, &c. Ad Belgicæ versionis marginem adscribuntur duo loca Parallela, Johan 1. 30. Actor. 17. 31. ubi Christus vocatur vir. Hanc versionem qui excusem, non invenio. Ubi enim auditum vel lectum אֵת Genitivi casus articulum esse? Hoc cum intelligeret Lutherus, in explicatione ultimorum verborum Davidis, quod scriptum ex postremis ejus est, versionem illam mutavit & eam amplexus est, quam Fagius & Forsterus suppeditaverant, vid. Acquisivi virum DOMINVM, Ich hebbe gekregen den Man / den HEERE, den Man den Herrn. q.d. das wird der Man / der Herre sein / da von Gott geredt hatte des weibs same / &c. Nemnet das kind ein Mann und Herrn / oder Gott / den hie sihet / der grosse und eigen name Gottes Jehova, und Ich, welchs / wo es allein sihet / ohn ein weib / heisst es nicht schlecht ein mansbild / sunder ein ausbund / und furnemlicher Man. Hæc Lutherus, tomo 8. Germ. Jenensi pag. 157. Textum tamen illum in Bibliis nunquam mutavit, sed post ejus obitum, teste W. Franzio, disp. 2. de Sacrificiis, alii eum ad hanc ejus sententiam demutarunt.
units.tr: The Seventy: "But ... through God." The Vulgate does the same, though some manuscripts read "through the Lord," and that reading is more correct. Onkelos has "from before [מן קדם] the LORD," that is, "from the LORD." Junius, Tremellius, the Italian, the English, and Piscator also render it "from the LORD," taking et [אֶת] as standing for from [מֵאֵת]. The Geneva Bible has on behalf of the Eternal. Pagninus and Drusius, with the Zurich Bible, have "with the LORD," which the Greeks express as "with God" [σὺν Θεῷ]. Junius approved this rendering in his notes, saying, "unless perhaps it is to be read as Jerome reads it: ..." Although all these renderings make God the author and agent of this acquisition, I would still prefer with the LORD. Nothing is better known than that אֶת is commonly used for עִם, with. So below, in 6:9, Enoch walked with God [אֶת־אֱלֹהִים], and although the sense of that passage is different, it cannot be denied that אֶת there has the force of עִם. If you doubt whether the phrase with God, meaning "with God's help and aid," was familiar to the Hebrews, take Drusius's example from 1 Samuel 14:45: He worked with God today [עִם אֱלֹהִים]. But those passages that the distinguished Junius cites do not prove that אֶת can stand for מֵאֵת, from. In Genesis 44:4, where we read יָצְאוּ אֶת־הָעִיר, the distinguished Drusius translates they went out of the city, as the Latins also speak. In Deuteronomy 34:1 there is nothing to prevent אֶת־הָעָר from being rendered as an accusative. So I have no doubt that Junius, trusting these examples less, added those passages I cited above. As for the passage in Jeremiah 51:59, כַּלְכָּתוֹ אֶת צִדְקִיָּהוּ, which the distinguished Piscator cites, it carries more weight, for the Seventy have ἐπὶ Ἐδεχίας, and Junius has from Zedekiah, and the Italian has on the part of, in the name of Zedekiah. So all of them took אֵת to mean מֵאֵת. The English, the Spanish, the Tigurines, and Castalio have with Zedekiah. But let us look at the other versions of the present passage. In his editions, including the final revision published in 1542, Luther has "I have gotten the man of the LORD." In his German commentary on Genesis, volume 4 of the Jena edition, he has "the man of God," or "with God," that is, the man of God, or with God. The Belgic version still reads the same way: "I have gotten the man of the LORD," that is, the man of the LORD promised to me by the LORD, as Luther says in his Latin commentary, where he notes that it was promised in the Gospel passage about the seed of the woman, and so on. In the margin of the Belgic version are cited two parallel passages, John 1:30 and Acts 17:31, where Christ is called a man. I do not find this version defensible. For where have we heard or read that the article of a genitive case is אֵת? Realising this, Luther, in explaining the last words of David (which are among his final writings), changed the version and adopted the one that Fagius and Forster had supplied: I have gotten the man, the LORD, "the man, the lord." In other words, "that will be the man, the lord, who was spoken of by God as the seed of the woman," and so on. "The child is named man and Lord, or God, whom she sees; the great and proper name of God, Jehovah, and 'I,' which, when it is seen alone, without a woman, is not simply called a man, but a paragon and above all a man." Luther says this in volume 8 of the German Jena edition, page 157. Yet he never changed the text itself in the Bibles, and after his death, as W. Franz reports in his second disputation on sacrifices, others altered it to fit this opinion of his.

units.la: Cæterum de hac versione extat Judicium Junii in Analysi Geneseos, Parai in comment. & Calvino orthodoxo pag. 155. Piscatoris in Quæst. ad 5. libros Mosis, Calvini & Merceri in comment. & Drusii in comment. ad loca dissic. pag. 22. & in notis ad Sulpic. pag. 16. omnes illam rejiciunt. Idem fecêre Interpretes Angli, Tigur. Genev. Ital. Hisp. ut nihil jam dicam de 1 x x. & Latino vetere, quos omnes supra produximus Dignus hic est locus, inquit Cl. Helvicus, qui diligenter excutiatur. Testimonium enim luculentum præbet, quod Eva Messiam pro vero Jehova habuerit. Quæ sententia simplicissimè e textu Ebraeo fluit, ut mirandum sit, reperiri inter Christianos interpretes, Hebraea lingua peritos, qui in Calvini & vulgatæ versionis gratiam, hoc in dubium vocare ausint. Bona verba Cl. vir. Ego inter eos meum quoque profiteor nomen, qui hanc versionem in dubium vocant. Non in gratiam Calvini, non in gratiam eorum qui Christo Deitatem abjudicant, sed in gratiam veritatis. Arduus ille de Christi Deitate articulus non eget talibus præsidiis. Etenim si hic articulus non firmissimis in S. Scriptura fundamentis nititur, equidem asserere ausim, nihil in universa ea esse certi. Eum labefactant, non qui certa testimonia ab incertis & ficulneis prudenti delectu secernunt, sed qui incerta & ficulnea ceu certa & firma & Apodictica obtrudunt. Non alia ratione, inquiebat Lutherus, adversarii in erroribus suis magis confirmari possunt. Audite ergo æquis animis vos, qui huic versioni adhærescitis, cur ea viris doctissimis & de articulo adorandæ Trinitatis optimè meritis, minus placuerit. Cl. Drusius illud urgebat acriter, eam non posse esse verborum mentem, quia tunc dicendum fuisset קְנִיתִי אֶת־אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה / Solent quippe Ebraeii in Appositione, si nomen proprium posteriori loco collocetur, utrique nomini eundem articulum præfigere, Sic verf. seq. אֶת אֶחָיו אֶת הַבֶּל. Vide etiam Cl. Buxtorfii Gramm. lib. 2. cap. 1. Reg. 1. Et profecto ita est, ex elegantiis linguæ Ebraeæ est illa articuli geminatio, tio, & ita passim videbis Ebræos in ejusmodi appositione loqui. Non celabo tamen, non adeo perpetuum esse illum loquendi modum, ut non admittat exceptionem. Ecce enim locum Jezech. 4. 1. & describe super eum עִיר אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלַ‍ִם urbem Jerusalem. Illud puto pluisculum roboris habiturum, Si Eva respexisset ad promissionem illam de Semine, operæ pretium fuisset, si non pronomen הַהוּא vel הָהוּא virum hunc, vel, virum illum, saltem articulum ה voci איש præfixisset, קָנִיתִי הָאִישׁ, τὸν ἄνδρα. Nunc vero nudè ponitur ea vox, ut nullus videatur esse ad promissionem illam Evangelicam respectus. Illud vero gravissimum est, quo hæc sententia premitur, incommodum, cognovisse Evam, Semen illud fore Ἀνθρωπον, ignorasse tamen illud fore semen mulieris, id quod diserte erat ei revelatum. Annon enim dictum erat Semen mulieris? Si tam turpiter decepta fuit in individuo, ignorans illud mysterium, Messiam non ex concubitu viri, sed ex muliere tantum nasciturum, nunquid facile erit Arriano vel Judæo dicere, eam in eo quoque fuisse deceptam, quod Messiam Ἀνθρωπον fore crediderit? Quod robur ergo hic locus apud fidei nostræ adversarios habere possit, cordati judicent. Certè longè melius honori communis matris illi consulunt, qui eam deceptam fuisse negitant. Quid enim? An putavit Messiam fore semen viri? An ignoravit promissionem loqui de semine mulieris? id est de filio virginis? An nescivit Cainum esse semen viri? Sic ergo concludit Parœus, Pietas suadet de fide matris Evæ rectè sentire, eam nempe scivisse & credidisse, Messiam futurum non modo Deum, sed & semen mulieris id est filium virginis, non viri. Absque hoc enim fides error fuisset, non fides, nec fuisset solatio. Credidit ergo Messiam fore semen mulieris, non viri. At Cainum sciebat esse semen viri, non ergo putavit se edidisse Messiam, neque decepta est Sancta mater.
units.tr: Moreover, this version has been judged by Junius in his Analysis of Genesis, by Paraeus in his commentary and Calvinus orthodoxus, page 155, by Piscator in his Questions on the Five Books of Moses, by Calvin and Mercerus in their commentaries, and by Drusius in his commentary on difficult passages, page 22, and in his notes on Sulpicius, page 16. All of them reject it. The English, Tigurine, Geneva, and Italian interpreters, and the Spanish, have done the same, not to mention the Seventy and the old Latin, all of which I have already cited. This passage is worthy, says the distinguished Helvicus, of careful examination. For it provides striking evidence that Eve regarded the Messiah as the true Jehovah. This view flows most simply from the Hebrew text, so that it is surprising that among Christian interpreters skilled in the Hebrew language there should be some who dare to call this into question in favour of Calvin and the Vulgate version. These are fine words of the distinguished man. I too count myself among those who call this version into question. Not for the sake of Calvin, nor for the sake of those who deny the deity of Christ, but for the sake of truth. That difficult article on the deity of Christ does not need such props. For if this article does not rest on the firmest foundations in Holy Scripture, I would venture to assert that nothing in the whole of it is certain. Those who weaken it are not those who separate sure testimonies from doubtful and fig-tree ones with prudent selection, but those who thrust doubtful and fig-tree ones upon us as if they were certain, firm and demonstrative. Luther used to say that adversaries can be confirmed in their errors in no other way. So hear me calmly, you who cling to this version, and consider why it has been less pleasing to men most learned and most deserving of the article on the adorable Trinity. The distinguished Drusius pressed sharply that this cannot be the sense of the words, because then it would have had to be said: קְנִיתִי אֶת־אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה. Indeed the Hebrews, in apposition, when a proper name is placed in the second position, usually prefix the same article to both nouns. So in the following verse: אֶת אֶחָיו אֶת הַבֶּל. See also the distinguished Buxtorf's Grammar, book 2, chapter 1. Ruth 1. And truly it is so: this doubling of the article is one of the elegances of the Hebrew language, and everywhere you will see the Hebrews speaking this way in such appositions. I will not conceal, however, that this way of speaking is not so constant as to admit no exception. For see Ezekiel 4:1: and describe upon it עִיר אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלַ‍ִם, the city of Jerusalem. I think this will carry a bit more weight. If Eve had had regard to that promise about the Seed, it would have been worth the trouble to prefix to the word איש at least the pronoun הַהוּא or הָהוּא, this man or that man, or at least the article ה, קָנִיתִי הָאִישׁ, the man [τὸν ἄνδρα]. As it is, the word is placed bare, so that there seems to be no reference at all to that Gospel promise. The gravest difficulty pressing this view is this: that Eve knew the Seed would be a man [Ἀνθρωπον], yet was ignorant that he would be the seed of the woman, which had been expressly revealed to her. For had it not been said, the seed of the woman? If she was so shamefully deceived about the individual, not knowing that the Messiah would be born not from the union of a man but from a woman alone, will it not be easy for an Arian or a Jew to say that she was deceived also in this, that she believed the Messiah would be a man? Let the thoughtful judge what strength this passage can have among the opponents of our faith. Certainly those who deny that she was deceived have far better regard for the honour of our common mother. For what? Did she think the Messiah would be the seed of a man? Did she not know the promise spoke of the seed of the woman, that is, of the son of a virgin? Did she not know that Cain was the seed of a man? So Paraeus concludes: piety urges us to think rightly about the faith of Mother Eve, namely that she knew and believed that the Messiah would be not only God but also the seed of the woman, that is, the son of a virgin, not of a man. For without this her faith would have been error, not faith, nor would it have been a comfort. She believed, then, that the Messiah would be the seed of a woman, not of a man. But she knew that Cain was the seed of a man, so she did not think she had brought forth the Messiah, and the holy mother was not deceived.

units.la: Nunc illud restat, ut videamus hujus interpretationis fulcra. B. Lutherus urget unicum illud אֶת / quod semper Accusativi casus articulum esse, nec unquam significare a, ab, de, cum, contendit in explic. ultimorum verborum Davidis. * Das ist noch unbewiesen / und solt wol unbewiesen bleiben / inquit, quod vid. a, cum, de, in Scriptura significet. Ad exempla, quæ objici dicit ex Kimchi, ait responderi posse, Das die Ebreische sprache noch nie weder recht aufkommen ist, und das die Juden nicht wissen
units.tr: Now what remains is to examine the props of this interpretation. Blessed Luther insists on that single word אֶת [et], which he contends is always the sign of the accusative case and never means a, ab, de or cum, in his explanation of David's last words. "That is still unproven," he says, "and should indeed remain unproven: that a, cum, de or in is what it means in Scripture." As for the examples which he says are brought from Kimchi, he says it can be answered that the Hebrew language has never yet properly got going, and that the Jews do not know the force of all words, as the thing itself shows. They equivocate, doubt, grope and search, like an unskilled organist who hunts for the keys or organ pipes and asks, "Is it this one? Is it this one?"

units.la: * id est, hoc nondum est probatum, nec etiam probatur. fonnen / virtutem omnium vocabulorum, sicut res ostendit. Sie æquiuociren / zweiffeln / tappen und suchen / wie ein ungelerter Organist / die claves oder orgelpfeiffen sucht und fragt / bistus / bistus? Ad locum Genef. 5. Ambulavit Enoch cum Deo, ubi in Ebr. est אֵת / dicit & hic esse articulum accusativi, reddendumque ad verbum ambulavit Deum, sicuti dicimus, vixit Sardanapalum, vivunt Bacchanalia. Sic Noë ambulavit את אלהים Deum id est divinam viam. Ambulavit cum Deo, inquit ineptum esse & nullum reddere sensum. Quò enim aut quâ viâ intelligendi sunt cum Deo tanquam comite ambulasse? Orientem an occidentem versus? Præterea ad locum Gen. 41. Et Dominus erat את יוסף / nos quidem cogi sic loqui, cum Joseph, in Ebr. tamen את esse accusativi notam, und das solt auch bleiben. Licet vero beatus ille vir ipso limine hujus discursus dicat, se illud sæpe stipulatum esse, das er dis maal sein meister wolle haben / non ægrè tamen ferent, qui inter Lutheranos cordatiores sunt, liberam vocem. Ajo hic dormitasse magnum illum Homerum & præsidenter nimis locutum. Atque hic semel protestor, me non eò hæc dicere, ut beatæ animæ insultem! Profiteor enim me nulli Lutherano Doctori affectu in beatos magni illius viri Manes cedere, sed ut Tyrones moneam, ne tanti viri authoritate subnixi, adversariis in hac literarum luce deridendos se propinent. Ecce enim ipsi Schindlerus & Helwicus ingenuè agnoscunt, & fatentur, quod B. Lutherus negat, vid. את aliq. idem esse quod את cum. Et quid verbis opus? Ipsa illa exempla, quæ Lutherus asserit, id evincunt, maximè verò illud postremum. Et si את semper & ubique est Accusativi casus, cur non eodem modo semper & ubique affixa assumit, את / eum אותך te, &c. Cur ergo alias dicitur את cum illo, את tecum? Annon omnes Grammatici & Lexicographi docent, את cum est articulus Accusat. casus. assumere Holem, cum verò est præpositio cum, resolverè suum Tseri in Hirik & Dages? Quis adeo hospes in his literis ut non videat eam diversitatem distinguendæ diversæ significationi esse adhibitam. Sed inquit Helwicus, hoc loco non potest significare cum, Et quare? Minor patet, inquit, ex phrasi Ebraea lingua, qua hanc formulam, suò Θεὸς, non esset per את יהוה sed per באלהים Addere potuisset & ביהוה / quod in Psalmis passim obviam est. Sed hic omisit Helwicus formulam istam עם אלהים cum Deo, 1. Sam. 14. 45. quam & supra produximus Et autem gemina est hæc, de qua nunc disserimus, nisi quod hic substitutum sit synonymum אִשָּׁה / Illud etiam notari velim, cum verba activa regulariter post se habeant articulum אֶת / ut hoc versu bis, Ecognovit Adam את האשה Hevam, Et peperit את קין Kainum, cum etiam tralatitium sit apud Ebræos, ut in appositione, si nomini proprio posteriori loco posito præfigatur articulus vel præpositio, priori quoque præfigatur, hic tamen omitti articulum, קניתי איש / Equidem si ille additus fuisset, extra omnem controversiæ aleam posita esset B. Lutheri sententia. Cum vero id factum non sit, quis non eo potius inclinabit, illum hic loci studio omissum, ne quis Appositionem intelligeret?
units.tr: That is, this has not yet been proven, nor is it proven. Take the passage in Genesis 5, "Enoch walked with God," where the Hebrew has אֵת [et]. Here too, he says, it is the sign of the accusative, and it must be rendered word for word "walked God," as we say "Sardanapalus lived" or "the Bacchanalia live." So Noah "walked את אלהים [et Elohim], God", that is, the divine way. "Walked with God," he says, is absurd and yields no sense: "For whither, or by what way, are they to be understood to have walked with God as a companion? Toward the east or the west?" Further, at Genesis 41, "And the LORD was את Joseph [et Yosef]": we are indeed compelled to speak thus, "with Joseph," but in Hebrew את is the mark of the accusative, "and that should remain so too." Yet although that blessed man, at the very threshold of this discourse, says that he has often stipulated that "this time he wants to be master," those among the more judicious Lutherans will not take it ill if a free voice is raised. I say that the great Homer dozed here and spoke too presumptuously. And here I once more protest that I do not say these things to insult a blessed soul! For I profess that I yield to no Lutheran doctor in affection for the blessed shades of that great man. I write rather to warn novices that they should not, relying on the authority of so great a man, expose themselves to be laughed at by their adversaries in this light of learning. For behold, Schindler and Helwig ingenuously acknowledge and confess what Blessed Luther denies: that את in some places means the same as את, "with." And why use many words? The very examples Luther asserts prove it, especially the last one. If את is always and everywhere the accusative sign, why does it not likewise always and everywhere take the suffixes, את [et] "him," את "you," and so on? Why then is it said את "with him" and את "with you"? Do not all the grammarians and lexicographers teach that את, when it is the accusative article, takes a holem, but when it is the preposition "with" it resolves its tsere into hireq and dages? Who is so unversed in these letters that he does not see this difference was employed to distinguish the different meanings? But Helwig says that in this place it cannot mean "with." And why not? "The minor premise is clear," he says, "from the Hebrew phrase: for this formula, in place of the Greek Θεός [Theos], would not be את יהוה [et Yhwh] but באלהים [be-Elohim]." He could have added ביהוה [be-Yhwh], which is found everywhere in the Psalms. But Helwig has omitted the formula עם אלהים [im Elohim], "with God," at 1 Samuel 14:45, which we also cited above. And this passage we are now discussing is a twin of it, except that here the synonym אִשָּׁה [ishah] is substituted. I would also have this noted: since active verbs regularly take את after them as the article, as twice in this verse, "Adam knew את האשה [et ha-ishah], Eve his wife," and "bore את קין [et Qayin], Cain," and since it is also a common Hebrew rule that in apposition, if a proper name placed in the second position is prefixed with the article or a preposition, the first is prefixed as well, here the article is nonetheless omitted: קניתי איש [qaniti ish], "I have acquired a man." Indeed, had the article been added, Luther's opinion would have been placed beyond all chance of dispute. But since that was not done, who would not rather incline to think it was deliberately omitted here, so that no one should understand an apposition?

units.la: Dico ergo, eam versionem, Acquisivi virum DOMINUM, longè meliorem esse illa, Acquisivi virum DOMINI. Sed & illam istis incommodis premi, quæ jam prolata sunt, & quæ ei defendendæ producuntur, non esse solida. Comodissimam verò illam esse, Acquisivi virum cum DOMINO, virum id est prolem masculam, Filium. Ita Merc. Drusius, alii. Ejusmodi enim partus longe gratior erat, quam si fœmella els φάος ἡελίοιο prodiisset. Vel virum id est hominem uti Lxx. & Exod. 19. 13. sive bestia sive אִישׁ / Chald. אֱנָשָׁא Lxx. ἀνθρωπος. Ipse Lutherus, oder mensch. Sic & Hos. 11. 9. Deus sum & non אִישׁ / Chald. בְּסַרָא caro id est homo, Luth. und nicht ein mensch. Atque ita vocem ἄνθρωπος usurpat Johannes xvi. 21. postquam autem peperit τὸ παιδίον, non amplius meminit afflictionis, ob gaudium quod ἄνθρωπος homo natus sit in mundum, ubi Syrus habet בֵּר נְשָׁא filius hominis. Quem locum cum hoc, de quo agimus, non inutiliter contuleris. jam libet adjicere Ebræi unius alterius testimonium. R. Sal. ארץ הי כמו עם הי כשברא אותי ואישי לברו בראנו אבל בוה שותפים אנו עמו id est Eth Adonai, quasi dixisset, gnim Adonai, id est cum Domino. Quando me & maritum meum creabat, solus creabat nos. Atm hoc cooperati sumus ei. Hinc ajunt in hominis generatione tres concurrere, Deum, patrem, matrem. Michlal Jophi, קניתי עם השם כי היא שם כו חלקו ונפח נשמה כו id est acquisivi eum cum Domino, nam ipse partem suam addidit, inspirando ei halitum.
units.tr: I say, therefore, that the rendering "I have acquired a man, the LORD," is far better than "I have acquired a man of the LORD." But that rendering too is pressed by the difficulties already set out, and the arguments brought in its defence are not sound. The most suitable is "I have acquired a man with the LORD," that is, a male offspring, a son. So Mercerus, Drusius and others. For such a birth was far more welcome than if a female had come forth "like the light of the sun" (Greek: ἐς φάος ἠελίοιο). Or "man" may mean a human being, as in the Septuagint and Exodus 19:13, "whether beast or man" (Hebrew: אִישׁ [ish]; Chaldee: אֱנָשָׁא [enasha]; Septuagint: ἄνθρωπος [anthropos]). Luther himself has "oder Mensch." So also Hosea 11:9, "I am God and not man" (Hebrew: אִישׁ [ish]; Chaldee: בְּסַרָא [besara], flesh), that is, a human being; Luther has "und nicht ein Mensch." And thus the word ἄνθρωπος [anthropos] is used at John 16:21: "after she has borne the child (τὸ παιδίον), she no longer remembers the affliction, for joy that a man (ἄνθρωπος) is born into the world." There the Syriac has בַּר נָשָׁא [bar nasha], "son of man." It will not be unhelpful to set that passage beside the one we are discussing. Now I am pleased to add the testimony of one or another Hebrew. R. Salomon: "The earth of the LORD, as if he had said גְּנִים [gnim] Adonai, that is, with the Lord. When he created me and my husband, he alone created us. But in this we were partners with him." Hence they say that three concur in the generation of a man: God, the father and the mother. Michlal Jophi: "קניתי עם השם [qaniti im ha-Shem], I acquired him with the Name, for he added his part, breathing a breath into him."

units.la: Vers. 2. Habel. הֶבֶל
units.tr: Verse 2. Habel. הֶבֶל

units.la: Gr. ΑΒΕΛ, quia cum accentu magno est. Ea autem vocis forma ma postea semper retenta est, etiam extra Pausam. Id quod & aliis ejusdem formæ nominibus accidit, ut e.g, Phaleg, Pharet′, Lamech, &c. Ex Græca scriptura orta est consuetudo hanc vocem sine aspiratione scribendi ac si in fonte esset אבל. Priscum illud sphalma fuit, & quod jam Philonis & Josephi ævo invaluerat. Verque enim Græcis magis quam Ebraicis innutritus, eâ pronunciatione deceptus, vocem illam ἄνθρ interpretatur id est luctum. Ita & Eusceb. Orig. Theodoretus & alii. Nec defuit speciosa ratio. Theodoretus quæst. 51. in Gen. Ἀβελ ἄνθρ ἑρμηνεύεται. Πρῶτ ... ἄνθρος id est Primus enim visus est moriuus, & primus humano generi luctum conciliavit. Eusebi de Præp. Euang. l. 11. cap. περὶ τῆς παρὰ Ἑβραίοις τῶν ὀνομάτων ὀρθότητος; postquam de nominibus Is, Iora, Kain, Evæ quædam ejusdem farinæ attulisset, de Abel sic inquit, Ἀβελ ἑρμηνεύεται πένθος, & τὸν δὲ πάντων ... ἔστιν id est Abel significat luctum, Quia ejusmodi affectus parentibus causa fuit. Parentes itaque divino quodam consilio ejusmodi nomina pueris imposuere. Egit autem in verbis proximis de voce * Kaïn. Ideo dicit pueris. Alii interpretantur, lamentum, angustias, dolorem, propter tormina, quæ in hujus partu majora fuerint, quàm in Kaini. Nugæ. In Ebræo est הבל id est ματαιότης, vanitas, vel potius ἀτμὶς sive ἀτμὸς, vapor, halitus. Id enim proprie significat הבל / Ps. 144. Homo similis est להבל / ubi Symmachus, ἀτμῷ, Theodotio, ἀτμίδι reddidere. Unde Jacob. 4. 14. Quid est vita vestra? ἀτμίς, vapor. Koheleth 1. 1. Vanitas vanitatum, Lxx. ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, Ibi omnes cæteri, ἀτμὸς ἀλμῶν, id est Interprete Hiero. vapor fumi & aura tenuis, ἢ πνοὴ ὀλίγον φαινομένη, ἐπειτα δὲ ἀφανιζομένη, id est quæ ad exiguum tempus apparet, & deinde evanescit, ut cum Jacobo loquar. Vide & Jesa. 57. 13. omnes ἴστος tollet ventus & auferet הבל / Hieron. aura. Psalm. 90. consumimus dies nostros כהגה vulgò sicut sermonem, toic cin gesch[?]ets / Luth. Chaldæus היך הבל פומא דסחוא sicut halitum oris hyemalem, addit, hyemalem, quia hyberno tempore magis apparet. Erudita certe interpretatio, nam הגה non solùm significat, meditari, loqui, sed & gemere, halitum emittere, sine quo efferri ne syllaba quidem potest. Job. 37. 2. ex ore ejus exit הגה halitus, loquitur autem de fulmi-
units.tr: In Greek it is ΑΒΕΛ, because it has a strong accent. That form of the word was afterwards always retained, even outside pause. The same thing happens with other names of this form, for example Phaleg, Pharet, Lamech, and so on. From the Greek spelling arose the custom of writing this word without the aspirate, as if the Hebrew were אבל. That was an old error, and it had already become established in the time of Philo and Josephus. Philo, being more fed on Greek than on Hebrew, was deceived by this pronunciation and translates the name as mourning [πένθος]. So too Eusebius, Origen, Theodoret and others. Nor was there a lack of a plausible reason. Theodoret, Question 51 on Genesis: "Abel is interpreted as mourning [Ἀβελ ... πένθος ἑρμηνεύεται]. For he was the first to die, and he first brought mourning upon the human race." Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 11, chapter on the correctness of Hebrew names: after offering some names of the same kind, Is, Iora, Kain and Eve, he says of Abel: "Abel is interpreted as mourning [Ἀβελ ἑρμηνεύεται πένθος], because such an affection was the cause for the parents." So the parents, by a certain divine counsel, gave such names to their children. In the words just before, he had spoken of the word Kain. Hence he says "to their children". Others interpret it as lamentation, distress, grief, on account of the pains which were greater in the birth of this son than in that of Cain. These are trifles. In Hebrew it is הבל, that is, ματαιότης, vanity, or rather ἀτμίς or ἀτμός, vapour, breath. For הבל properly means this, as in Psalm 144: "Man is like הבל [to a breath]", where Symmachus rendered it ἀτμῷ and Theodotion ἀτμίδι. Hence James 4:14: "What is your life? It is ἀτμίς, a vapour." Ecclesiastes 1:1: "Vanity of vanities", the Seventy: "vanity of vanities [ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων]". There all the others have "vapour of smoke" [ἀτμὸς ἀλμῶν], that is, in the translation of Jerome, "vapour of smoke and thin air", or "a breath that appears for a little while and then vanishes [ἢ πνοὴ ὀλίγον φαινομένη, ἔπειτα δὲ ἀφανιζομένη]", that is, which appears for a short time and then disappears, to use the words of James. See also Isaiah 57:13: "the wind shall take them all away, and הבל [breath]", Jerome: "breeze". Psalm 90: "we spend our years כהגה", commonly "as a tale" [sicut sermonem], Luther "as a sigh". The Chaldee has "like the breath of the mouth in winter [היך הבל פומא דסחוא]", and adds "in winter", because the breath is more visible in winter. This is certainly a learned interpretation, for הגה means not only to meditate or speak but also to groan, to breathe out, and without it not even a syllable can be uttered. Job 37:2: "הגה, the sound, goes out of his mouth", and he is speaking of the thunder.

units.la: {y} vocem Kaïn interpretatur ζηλῶ... inquit. Quasi esset קנא / Ut Moses aliud etymo monstrat vid קנה acquisivit unde Iosephus Kaïn interpretatur κτῆσις Vide Fragmenta vetervm Interpr. Druti. fulmine. Optimè ergo in libro nominum, Abel, vapor, nisi quod male sine aspiratione scribatur. Ne audias ergo Carthusianum, qui Rabbi Paulum Burgensem, docentem Habel significare vanitatem, non audit. Et quare? Quia, inquit, ex ejus verbis consequens videretur, quod in textu dici debeat Habel quod communiter non tenetur.
units.tr: {y} The word Kain he interprets as "I have acquired [ζηλῶ]", as if it were קנא. Moses shows another etymology by the verb קנה, to acquire, whence Josephus interprets Kain as possession [κτῆσις]. See the fragments of the old translators, Drusius. Rightly, then, in the book of names, Abel is "vapour", except that it is wrongly written without the aspirate. So do not listen to the Carthusian, who does not hear Rabbi Paul of Burgos teaching that Habel means "vanity". And why? "Because", he says, "from his words it would seem to follow that in the text it ought to be said Habel, which is not commonly held."

units.la: Verf.7.
units.tr: Verse 7.

units.la: Nonne si bene egerit, &c.
units.tr: "If you do well, will you not be accepted? etc."

units.la: Lxx. Interpretes, inquit Senensis annot. Lxv. lib. 5, omnia hic perturbarunt, deviaruntque vehementer à veritate textus Ebraici, ita vertentes, [?Greek: ἐκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες· ἡσύχασον, ὡς σὺ ἡ ἀπόσφορον αὐτῷ]: [ Acutè observavit D. Coccejus, Lxx. sic legisse, [?Hebrew: הֲלֹא אִם הֵיטִיב שְׂאֵת וְאִם לֹא הֵיטִיב לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ] Quorum verborum nihil est in Ebraeæ, ut Hiero. in Quaest. Ebr. testatur. Verba illa, si Latina desideras, ita sonant; Annon si recte obtuleris, recte autem non distribueris, peccasti? Quiesce. Ad te conversio ejus. Augustinus Chisamensis Episc. (alias Steuchus, & Eugubinus) causam indicans hujus erroris sic inquit, Quis tam acri ingenio est, qui ex hisce verbis aliquem sensum possit eruere? Quid obscuro est, ad te conversio ejus? Cujus? Cum peccati nihil meminerit. Vbi enim Ebr. est, In foribus peccatum tuum accubat, illi [?Greek: ἡσύχασον], verterunt. Ex hoc certe loco deprehenditur etiam, non adeo exquisite septuaginta Grammaticam Ebr. calluisse. Hæc Steuchus. Lege jam Patres, ad hunc locum, & judica annon operam & oleum perdiderint. {*}Augustinum audiamus, obscuritas hujus verbi, inquit, multos peperit sensus, quia non elucet, cur vel unde dictum sit ad Cain. Recte quippe offertur sacrificium, cum vero Deo offertur. Non recte autem dividitur, dum non recte discernuntur loca & tempora in quibus est offerendum, vel res ipsa, quae offeruntur, vel qui offert, non discernit se ipsum & eum cui offert, aut eos, quibus distribuitur ad vescendum, quod oblatum est, aut electiora sibi reservat, ut per divisionem hic intelliganus discretionem. In quo autem horum Cain displicuerit Deo, non facile est invenire, &c. Ex quibus datur intelligi, ob hoc Deum non respexisse munera Cain, quia in eo male divisit, quod dedit Deo aliquid sui, & se ipsum sibimet ipsi, imò & daemoni; &c. Hæc August. Adietiam si placet, Procopium aliosque istius versionis Interpretes. Audi etiam Historiam Scholasticam, Recte obtulerat Cain, quia Deo: sed non recte diviserat, quia se ipsum, qui erat dignior suâ oblatione, dedit Diabolo. Vel, non recte divisit, quia meliora sibi retinuit: Spicas verò attritas & juxta viam corrosas, obtulit Deo. Quid est castella in aëre extruere, si hoc non est? Hoc profecto non est verbum Dei, sed commenta hominum interpretari.
units.tr: The Seventy translators, says the Senese in his annotations, book 5, number 65, have thrown everything here into confusion and gone far astray from the truth of the Hebrew text, rendering it thus: [ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες· ἡσύχασον, πρὸς σὲ ἡ ἀποστροφὴ αὐτοῦ]. Coccejus shrewdly observed that the Seventy read [הֲלֹא אִם הֵיטִיב שְׂאֵת וְאִם לֹא הֵיטִיב לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ], but none of these words is in the Hebrew, as Jerome testifies in the Hebrew Questions. If you want those words in Latin, they sound thus: "Have you not sinned, if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly? Be quiet. To you is his turning." Augustine, bishop of Chisamum (otherwise Steuchus, or Eugubinus), giving the cause of this error, says: "Who has so keen a mind as to draw out any sense from these words? What is unclear about 'to you is his turning'? Whose? Since it mentions nothing of sin. For where the Hebrew has, 'At the door sin lies couched', they translated, 'Be quiet'." From this passage it is certainly clear too that the Seventy did not know the Hebrew grammar so very exactly. So Steuchus. Now read the Fathers on this passage and judge whether they have not wasted labour and oil. Let us hear Augustine: "The obscurity of this word", he says, "has given rise to many meanings, because it is not clear why or from what cause it was said to Cain. For a sacrifice is rightly offered when it is offered to the true God. But it is not rightly divided when the places and times at which it is to be offered are not rightly distinguished, or the things themselves which are offered, or the one who offers does not distinguish himself from the one to whom he offers, or those among whom what is offered is distributed to be eaten, or he keeps the better things for himself; so that by 'division' we may understand here 'discrimination'. In which of these things Cain displeased God it is not easy to find out, etc. From which it may be understood that God did not regard Cain's gifts because in him there was a wrong division, in that he gave to God something of himself, and kept himself for himself", indeed even for the demon, etc. So Augustine. Hear also, if you like, Procopius and the other interpreters of this version. Hear also the Historia Scholastica: "Cain offered rightly, because he offered to God; but he did not divide rightly, because he gave himself, who was more worthy than his offering, to the Devil. Or, he did not divide rightly, because he kept the better things for himself; but he offered to God ears of corn that were bruised and eaten away beside the road." What is this but building castles in the air? This is certainly not the word of God, but the inventions of men interpreted as if they were it.

units.la: Vers. 12. Vagus & profugus eris
units.tr: Verse 12. You shall be a wanderer and a fugitive

units.la: Interpretes LXX. σίνων ἢ τρέμων, gemens & tremens. Hunc locum contulerunt cum eo, qui sequitur vers. 15. Et posuit Deus signum in Kain. Quæsitum fuit hic ab Interpretibus, quodnam fuerit hoc signum. Responsum à doctioribus, fuisse perpetuum gemitum & corporis tremorem. Temeraria assertio, & cui nullum nisi in loco male verso fundamentum. Namque Ebræa habent, יָנֻד וַיָּנֻד / quæ vulgatus etiam transtulit, vagus & profugus. Certum tamen est, notam aliquam Kaino suisse impressam. Quænam verò fuerit, tacet Scriptura. Taceamus ergo & nos. Operta sacri supparo silentii, quæ scire nos non voluit Deus, adorantes prætereamus.
units.tr: The Septuagint render it as σίνων ἢ τρέμων [sinōn ē tremōn], groaning and trembling. They compared this with verse 15, "And God set a sign upon Cain." The interpreters have asked what this sign was, and the more learned have answered that it was a perpetual groaning and trembling of the body. This is a rash assertion, with no foundation except in a badly rendered passage. For the Hebrew has יָנֻד וַיָּנֻד [nud vayyanud], which the Vulgate also rendered "a wanderer and a fugitive." It is certain, however, that some mark was stamped on Cain. Scripture is silent about what it was. Let us be silent too. Let us pass by, in adoration, the secrets which God did not wish us to know, veiled by the sacred covering of silence.

units.la: Vers. 26. Seth, Enos, οὗτος ἠλπισε, Hic speravit in vocare nomen DOMINI.
units.tr: Verse 26. Seth, Enos: "This one hoped," he hoped to call upon the name of the LORD.

units.la: Ita Lxx. De hoc supra cum Marsenno disputationis serram reciprocavimus. Nunc ut ad eum redeam, Augustinus, qui τ Lxx. editionem passim sequitur, in causa est. Is ergo libro xv. de Civ. Dei cap. 17. ait Seth interpretari resurrectionem, & filium ejus Enos hominem, non sicut Adam, quod commune est mari & fœminæ, sed ita ut vox ea (Enos) non possit fœminæ attribui: ut Enos sit filius resurrectionis, ubi nec nubent nec uxores ducent. Non erit ibi generatio, cum illuc perduxerit regeneratio. Quare & hoc non incessum notandum arbitror, quod in generationibus eorum qui à Seth, nulla nominatim fœmina genita expressa est. Totus hic discursus falsum habet fundamentum Seth significare resurrectionem. Et postea cap. 18. Hic sperauit, &c. In spe ergo vivit homo (Enos) filius resurrectionis (τοῦ Seth) in spe vivit quamdiu peregrinatur hic civitas Dei, quae gignitur ex fide resurrectionis Christi. Ex duobus namque illis hominibus, Abel, qui interpretatur luctus (& hoc falsum) & ejus fratre Seth, qui interpretatur resurrectio, mors Christi & vita ejus ex mortuis praefiguratur, ex quâ fide hic gignitur civitas Dei, id est homo qui sperauit invocare nomen Domini. Spe enim salvi facti sumus, inquit Apostolus. Vide sequentia, cordate lector, misereat te B. Patris, quem, prava versio ad hos discursus prolectavit. Cæterùm de genuinâ hujus loci versione suprà egimus. Claudam ubi illud adjecero, omnes ineptiarum numeros implevisse Thomam, qui in comm. Enos interpretatur Invocatio, q. scilicet in sequentibus, quæ vulgata sic legit, Iste cæpit invocare nomen Domini, ratio impositi istius nominis redderetur. Quod si Ebraea vel legere potuisset, facile judicasset acutissimum caput, inter Enos & אנוש nullum esse omnino cognationis vinculum.
units.tr: So the Seventy. We have already debated this at length with Marsennus. Now, to return to it, the fault lies with Augustine, who follows the Septuagint edition throughout. In book 15 of The City of God, chapter 17, he says that Seth is interpreted as "resurrection," and his son Enos as "man," not in the sense of Adam, which is common to male and female, but in such a way that the word Enos cannot be attributed to a woman: so that Enos is the son of the resurrection, where they neither marry nor take wives. There will be no generation there, since regeneration will have led us thither. Therefore I think it should not be passed over without notice that in the generations of those who came from Seth, no woman is named as born. This whole line of argument has a false foundation, namely that Seth means resurrection. And afterwards, in chapter 18: "Here he hoped," and so on. "In hope, therefore, lives man" (Enos), "the son of resurrection" (of Seth), "in hope he lives as long as the city of God sojourns here, which is born from faith in the resurrection of Christ." "For from those two men, Abel, who is interpreted as mourning" (and this is false), "and his brother Seth, who is interpreted as resurrection, the death of Christ and his life from the dead are foreshadowed, from which faith the city of God is here born, that is, the man who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord. For we have been saved by hope," says the Apostle. Read what follows, careful reader, and may you have pity on the holy Father, whom a faulty version lured into these arguments. Otherwise, we have already dealt with the genuine rendering of this passage above. I will end by adding that Thomas, in his commentary, interprets Enos as "invocation," and explains the reason for giving this name by the Vulgate's reading of what follows, "This one began to call upon the name of the Lord." But if he could have read the Hebrew, that most acute man would easily have judged that there is no kinship at all between Enos and אנוש [Enosh].

Here is a table, as Marsennus drew it up.
