units.la: Non disputo, utrùm hæc diversitas ipsis Interpretibus, an potius primis versionis descriptoribus imputari debeat: illud satis apparet, de industriâ eam esse introductam. Cum enim in anno, quo Iared genuit, nihil mutatum sit, colligunt Interpretes, mutationis authores vel statuisse, vel aliis voluisse persuadere, annos menstruos à Mose designari. Ne vid. historia Mosis Gentilibus fabulosa videretur. At cum viderent, se, unum absurdum vitando, ut contrarium incursuros, centum annos singulis adjecisse. E. G. Enos dicitur genuisse anno ætatis suæ 90. Si menstruos annos, vel ut clarius loquar, menses denotat Moses, sequetur eum septennem & menses insuper aliquot anni octavi emensum, genuisse. Cum autem illud quoque absurdum fore viderent, addiderunt ejusdem generis annos id est menses 100. quos fere annis illis, quos postea vixisse dicuntur, detraxerunt, unde illud evenit, ut Graeco textui in annis universæ vitæ cum Ebraeo rursus fere conveniat. At quia hæc conjectura applicari non potest computo annorum, quibus genuerunt Sem & Thare, ubi eadem difficultates, si menses redigantur in annos communes, (ad illos enim nihil addiderunt) ideo à multis non probatur.
units.tr: I do not dispute whether this difference should be charged to the translators themselves or rather to the first makers of the version. It is clear enough that it was introduced deliberately. For since nothing was changed in the year in which Jared begot his son, the interpreters conclude that the authors of the change either decided, or wished to persuade others, that Moses was designating lunar months as years, so that the history of Moses would not seem fabulous to the Gentiles. But when they saw that, in avoiding one absurdity, they would fall into the opposite one, they added a hundred years to each figure. For example, Enos is said to have begotten a son in the ninetieth year of his age. If Moses denotes monthly years, or, to speak more plainly, months, it will follow that he begot the child after seven years and some months of an eighth year had passed. But since they saw that this too would be absurd, they added the same kind of years, that is, 100 months, and took away nearly the same number from the years which they say he lived afterwards. Hence it happens that, in the total length of life, the Greek text again agrees almost with the Hebrew. But because this conjecture cannot be applied to the reckoning of the years in which Shem and Terah begot their sons, where the same difficulties arise if the months are reduced to common years (for they added nothing to those), many do not approve of it.

units.la: a al. 969. b alii 963. c Ita habet Editio Romana At Antverpiensa habent 165. tur. Ut ut sit, ex hoc Graecorum computo nati sunt duo errores. I. à condito mundo ad diluvium usque fluxisse annos 2242. vel ut Antverp. codices habent 2240, cum Ebraei tantùm numerent 1656. adeò ut Graeci Ebraeum & vulgatum textum annis 586. vel 584. superent. II. Mathusalem post diluvium vixisse annis quatuordecim, cum tamen diserte testetur Moses, octo tantum animas fuisse in Arca servatas, inter eas autem ille non recenseatur. Expende hoc Lector, Mathusalem genuit Lamechum juxta 70. an. aetatis 167. vel ut alii codices 165. Cum verò vixerit annos in universum 969, ipsis 70. hic consentientibus, & tamen à nativitate ejus, juxta eosdem, usque ad diluvium quod incidit in annum Semi 100 reperiantur anni tantum 955, supersunt 14. quos diluvio supervixerit. In arca autem cum non fuerit, eò adacti sunt alii, ut ei assignaverint stationem in Paradiso, quem ex ipsorum opinione in aere pendulum, vel usque ad globum lunae elevatum aquae non inundaverint. Ut autem hanc differentiam melius assequatur tiro, ponam diagramma, juxta utrumque computum.
units.tr: a Others have 969. b Others have 963. c So the Roman edition has it; but the Antwerp edition has 165. However that may be, two errors arose from this Greek reckoning. I. From the creation of the world to the flood, 2242 years, or as the Antwerp manuscripts have, 2240, are said to have passed, whereas the Hebrew counts only 1656, so that the Greek exceeds the Hebrew and Vulgate texts by 586 or 584 years. II. Methuselah is said to have lived fourteen years after the flood, although Moses expressly testifies that only eight souls were saved in the ark, and Methuselah is not counted among them. Let the reader weigh this: Methuselah begot Lamech in the 167th year of his age (or, as other manuscripts have it, 165). Since he lived 969 years in total, and by the same reckoning seventy of those years agree with the other figures, yet from his birth until the flood, which fell in the hundredth year of Shem, only 955 years are found, there remain fourteen years in which he outlived the flood. But since he was not in the ark, others were driven to assign him a station in Paradise, which, in their opinion, was suspended in the air or raised up to the globe of the moon, so that the waters did not overwhelm it. So that the student may more easily grasp this difference, I will set out a diagram according to each reckoning.

Noë τὸν Sem, anno 500. | Noë τὸν Sem, anno 500. Diluvium incidit in annum Sem 100. | Diluvium incidit in annum Sem 100. 969 | 955

units.tr: So Methuselah died in the very year in which the flood fell, for he lived 969 years. | So Methuselah died 14 years after the flood, for according to them too he lived altogether 70 years; the translators give 969 years.

units.la: Augustinus postquam prolixè hâc de re disseruisset, admiratus hujus erroris constantiam, eumque non casui sed industriae adscripsisset, sic concludit, Quandoquidem ad fidem rerum gestarum uttumque non potest esse verum, ei lingua potius credatur, unde est in aliam per interpretes facta translatio.
units.tr: Augustine, after discussing this matter at length and marvelling at the persistence of this error, ascribing it not to chance but to deliberate effort, concludes thus: Since both cannot be true for the credibility of the events recorded, let that tongue rather be believed from which the translation into another language was made through the interpreters.

units.la: Viderunt Filii Dei filias hominum, &c.
units.tr: They saw the sons of God the daughters of men, &c.

units.la: Ebr. בני אלהים / Lxx. υιοι του Θεου, Sed quia olim in quibufdam codicibus legebatur, αγγελοι του Θεου, cujusmodi secuti sunt Philo & Eusebius Cæsariensis, graves quæstiones super hoc loco ortæ sunt, itumque est in varias sententias, dum alii angelos sanctos intellexerunt, qui tunc primùm fœminarum specie dimentati, illicitas cupiditates appetierint, ac naturæ suæ originisque, ut cum Sulp. loquar, degeneres, relictis superioribus, quorum incolæ erant, matrimoniis se mortalibus miscuerint, ut Lactantius lib. 2. de origine erroris, cap. 14. Justin. Clem. Tertull. Sulpicius, &c. Alii contrà angelos malos designare putârunt, jam in principio lapsos, qui Filii Dei vocentur, quoad naturam, ut Eusebius, Etiam August. lib. xv. de civitate Dei, cap. 23. hunc locum eodem modo citat, videntes angeli Dei filias hominum, subjungit tamen, Et LXX. quidem interpretes, & angelos Dei dixerunt istos & filios Dei, quod quidem non omnes codices habent, nam quidam nisi filios Dei non habent. Videtur hoc velle quosdam codices habuisse utrumque simul, αγγελοι η υιοι του Θεου, quorum prius purum putum glossema fuit, è margine ab imperito descriptore, ut fieri solebat, in textum infartum. Procopius ait quosdam codices pro Filii Dei, legisse angeli Dei. Chrysostomus negat hic de Angelis agi, & recte negat. Vtinam quoque tam rectè & solidè sententiam illam impugnasset! Et hic vide quantam frustrationem ei attulerit minus accurata versio. Ecce enim ut hanc sententiam de angelis expugnet, sic inquit, ως πω μεν διεξαιτωσαν, τω αγγελοι υιοι Θεου προφητευσασαι. αλλ' ουκ αν εχοιεν ουδαμου δειξαι. Ανθρωποι γαρ μεν εκλην·ησαν υιοι Θεου, αγγελοι δε ουδαμως id est Monstrent autem primò, ubi angeli filii Dei appellen-tur. Nunquam certè id ostendent. Homines quidem vocati sunt Filii Dei, at angeli nequaquam. Et paulo post, αγγελοσ ουδαμου υιος εκλη-θη, ουδε υιος Θεου id est Angelus nequaquam filius vocatus est, neque filius Dei. Sed clarus & omni exceptione major locus est, Job. 2.
units.tr: Hebrew: the sons of God [בני אלהים]. LXX: the sons of God [υιοι του Θεου]. But because in some manuscripts of old the reading was "angels of God" [αγγελοι του Θεου], as Philo and Eusebius of Caesarea followed, serious questions have arisen about this passage, and opinions have divided. Some understood holy angels, who, dazzled by the appearance of women, then for the first time desired forbidden things and, abandoning their higher dwelling, to use Sulpicius's words, degenerate from their nature and origin, mingled themselves in marriage with mortals, as Lactantius says (book 2 of On the Origin of Error, chapter 14), and Justin, Clement, Tertullian, Sulpicius, &c. Others on the contrary thought evil angels were meant, already fallen at the beginning, who are called sons of God by nature. So Eusebius. Augustine too (book 15 of The City of God, chapter 23) cites this passage in the same way, the angels of God seeing the daughters of men, but he adds: And the Septuagint translators called these angels and sons of God, though not all manuscripts have this, for some have only "sons of God." He seems to mean that some manuscripts had both readings together, "angels or sons of God" [αγγελοι η υιοι του Θεου], and that the first was simply a gloss, carried by an unskilled copyist from the margin into the text, as often happened. Procopius says that some manuscripts read "angels of God" in place of "sons of God." Chrysostom denies that angels are spoken of here, and rightly so. I wish he had also refuted that opinion as rightly and soundly! Here see how much frustration a less accurate version caused him. For to overthrow this view about angels he says: "Let them first show where angels are called sons of God" [ως πω μεν διεξαιτωσαν, τω αγγελοι υιοι Θεου προφητευσασαι]. "But they will never be able to show it anywhere" [αλλ' ουκ αν εχοιεν ουδαμου δειξαι]. "For men indeed have been called sons of God, but angels in no way" [Ανθρωποι γαρ μεν εκλην·ησαν υιοι Θεου, αγγελοι δε ουδαμως]. That is: Let them show first where angels are called sons of God. They will certainly never show it. Men indeed are called sons of God, but angels never. And a little later: "An angel was nowhere called a son, nor a son of God" [αγγελοσ ουδαμου υιος εκλη-θη, ουδε υιος Θεου]. But a clearer passage, beyond all objection, is Job 2.

units.la: I. C 1. & venerunt filii Dei בני אלהים / Sed & hic decepit B. Patrem versio ϒ Lxx, quæ & hic habet, ἥλθον οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ. Extat & alius in eodem libro locus, 38. 7. & jubilarent omnes filii Dei. Sed & hic iidem, πάντες ἄγγελοί μου. Disputationem vero hinc potissimum porro ortam, utrum angeli habeant corpora, quod ex hoc loco collegerunt Justin. Clem. Lactant. Methodius, Eusebius, Sulpicius, &c. & utrum angeli cum fœminis coire possint, non ingrediar. Videanturque super eâ Vallesius, de sacra Philosophiâ, Del-rio lib. 2. Magiæ, quæst. 15. Drusius ad Sulp. Severum, Bodinus, VVierus, & alii. Si quæris, quem ergo hujus loci sensum esse existimem, respondeo me probare sententiam Chrysostomi, Procopii, Augustí. Theodoreti, Cyrilli, Thomæ, Calv. Junii, Corn. à Lapide, Carthusiani, Drusii, Mercerí & aliorum, per filios Dei intelligi posteros Seth & Enos, qui veram religionem profitentes de nomine Dei denominari jam cœperant, cap. 4. verf. ult. Per filias vero hominum progeniem Caini profanam & impiam. Valeat ergo fabula de angelis, & incubis. Ut ut enim ea admittantur, quæ de incubis quidam prodidere, nunquam tamen eos uxores duxisse ostendetur. Sed explosa jam pridem ista opinio est, ac proinde manum tollo de hac tabula.
units.tr: Job 1. And the sons of God came [בני אלהים]. But here too the blessed Father was misled by the Septuagint version, which also has here: "the angels of God came" [ἥλθον οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ]. There is another passage in the same book, Job 38:7: and all the sons of God shouted for joy. But here again the Septuagint has "all my angels" [πάντες ἄγγελοί μου]. I will not enter into the discussion that arose from this place, chiefly whether angels have bodies, which Justin, Clement, Lactantius, Methodius, Eusebius, Sulpicius, &c. gathered from this text, nor whether angels can have intercourse with women. On these matters see Vallesius, On Sacred Philosophy, Delrio, Magic, book 2, question 15, Drusius on Sulpicius Severus, Bodin, Wier, and others. If you ask what I think is the meaning of this passage, I answer that I approve the view of Chrysostom, Procopius, Augustine, Theodoret, Cyril, Thomas, Calvin, Junius, Cornelius à Lapide, the Carthusians, Drusius, Mercer and others, that by "sons of God" are meant the descendants of Seth and Enos, who, professing the true religion, had already begun to be called by the name of God (Gen. 4, last verse). By "daughters of men," however, is meant the profane and impious offspring of Cain. So let the fable of angels and incubi be dismissed. For even if the things some have reported about incubi were admitted, it could never be shown that they took wives. But that opinion was long ago exploded, and therefore I take my hand off this tablet.

units.la: Verf. 4. Gigantes autem erant, &c.
units.tr: Verse 4. There were giants in those days, &c.

units.la: Qui per filios Angelos intellexerunt, eorum aliqui ex Gigantibus dæmones fecêre. Lactantius loco jam indicato, Qui autem ex his sunt procreati, quia neque angeli, neque homines fuerunt, sed mediam quandam naturam gerentes, non sunt ad inferos recepti. Ita duo genera dæmonum facta sunt, unum cœleste, alterum terrenum. Hi sunt immundi spiritus, malorum, quæ geruntur, authores, &c. Etiam Burgensis, quem Carthusianus Rabbi Paulum vocat, putat fuisse dæmonas humanâ specie indutos. Valesius vocat eos filios dæmonum incuborum. Hæcabsurda merito censentur. Duo enim illa, quæ hic vulgo sumunt, omni fundamento destituuntur. Neo enim Filii Dei verf. 2. sunt angeli, nec ex illis progenitos esse Gigantes scriptura asserit. Sic enim habet textus, Et gigantes erant super terram in diebus illis: ac etiam postea, quibus diebus congrediebantur filii Dei cum filiabus hominum. Quis hinc conficiet, Gigantes ex congressu Filiorum Dei cum filiabus hominum fuisse prognatos? Quid enim? annon gigni illi potuerunt ex congressu Filiorum hominum cum filiabus hominum? id est, ex congressu Caïnitarum inter se? Sed an & ulla cogit necessitas, ut per Gigantes hic intelligamus homines, ut * Augustinus loquitur, staturosos & qui communem corporum staturam excessêre? Origenes certè non credidit, dum eos inusitatâ corporis magnitudine cæteros excessisse negavit, sed homines quosdam improbos, ac ad omne nefas projectissimæ libidinis, Dei hominumque contemtores fuisse asserit. Hanc sententiam oppugnat Theodoretus quæst. 48. Ego verò, inquit, cum audio scripturam dicentem de OG, quod à Gigantibus orundus erat, & quod cubile ipsius ferreum erat, habens longitudinem novem cubitorum, cum audio exploratores narrantes, quod erant in conspectu Gigantum quasi locusta, & eo Goliath, quod longitudinem habebat 6. cubitorum & palmi, arbitror fuisse quosdam prægrandes homines, &c. Sed ut non nego fuisse omni ævo prægandes ejusmodi homines, quos Gigantes vulgo vocant, ita nego, hic loci ullam esse necessitatem, per נפלים quam vocem Gigantes reddunt, ejusmodi proceros homines intelligere. Nulla enim hic ejusmodi staturæ fit mentio. Etymon non urget, נפל enim in Kal significat, cado, ruo, irruo, deficio, quod Belgæ dicunt afballen / Psalm. 10. 10. Irruit validis suis [membris] in turbam attritorum. Ebr. נפל Jos. 11. ויפלו בהם & irruerunt in eos 1. Sam. 29. 3. à die נפלה cadere eum ad me, id est quo cecidit i.e. defecit ad me, 2. Reg. 7. נפלנו cademus ad castra Syrorum id est deficiemus. In Hiphil significat fellen / prosternere, dejicere. Hinc Ebræum vocem alii interpretantur dejectores, quod truculentia vultus sui homines cadere facerent & prosternerent: alii irruentes, quod violenter in homines irruerent eosque opprimerent, unde Aquila vertit Ἐπιπίπλοντας: Symmachus βίαιοι id est violenti. Luth. tpzannen. Alii defectores, Apostatas, quod per impietatem à Deo defecissent. Nova autem & plane mihi antehac inaudita est sententia * Bolduci, quem Marsennus magni æstimat, existimantis Nephilim dictos, quod ob veri Dei cultum à reliquis in eo distinguerentur, quod Deum prostrationibus adorarent, adeo ut illa ceremonia eos ab improbis secerneret, eo fere modo, quo Patres Ordinis S. Francisci de Assisio ab aliis distinguereнтur, cum eos sese prosternentes ante sacra-
units.tr: Those who understood "sons" to mean angels, some of them made demons out of the giants. Lactantius, in the passage already cited: But those who were born of them, because they were neither angels nor men, but had a certain intermediate nature, were not received into the lower world. Thus two kinds of demons came into being, one heavenly, the other earthly. These are the unclean spirits, the authors of the evils that happen, &c. Also Burgensis, whom the Carthusian calls Rabbi Paul, thinks that demons clothed in human form were meant. Valesius calls them sons of incubus demons. These views are rightly judged absurd. For the two assumptions commonly made here lack every foundation. For the sons of God in verse 2 are not angels, nor does Scripture assert that the giants were born of them. The text reads: And there were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men. Who can conclude from this that the giants were born of the union of the sons of God with the daughters of men? For could they not have been born from the union of the sons of men with the daughters of men, that is, from intercourse among the Cainites themselves? But is there any necessity that we understand by giants here men of great stature, as Augustine puts it, who exceeded the common height of bodies? Origen certainly did not believe it, when he denied that they excelled others in unusual bodily size, and asserted that they were wicked men, thrown into every kind of lust and despisers of God and men. Theodoret attacks this view (question 48): But I, he says, when I hear Scripture saying of Og that he was from the giants, and that his iron bed was nine cubits long, when I hear the spies reporting that they were in the sight of the giants like grasshoppers, and of Goliath, who was six cubits and a span tall, I think there were certain very tall men, &c. But I do not deny that such men, whom people commonly call giants, existed in every age; I deny only that there is any necessity here to understand by נפלים, which they render giants, men of such great stature. For no mention of such stature is made here. The etymology does not press either. For נפל in Kal means to fall, to rush down, to rush upon, to fail, which the Dutch call afballen. Psalm 10:10: He rushes down with his strong [limbs] upon a crowd of the crushed. Hebrew נפל, Josh. 11: ויפלו בהם and they rushed upon them. 1 Sam. 29:3: from the day נפלה he fell upon me, that is, since he fell away to me, i.e. he failed to me. 2 Kings 7: נפלנו we shall fall to the camp of the Syrians, that is, we shall desert. In Hiphil it means to fell, to throw down, to cast down. Hence some translate the Hebrew word dejectores, because by the sternness of their faces they made men fall and cast them down; others irruentes, because they rushed violently upon men and overwhelmed them, whence Aquila rendered it Ἐπιπίπλοντας, and Symmachus βίαιοι, that is, violent. Luther: tyrants. Others: deserters, apostates, because by impiety they had fallen away from God. The opinion of Bolduc, whom Mersenne esteems highly, is new, and to me entirely unheard of until now. He thinks the Nephilim were so called because, on account of the worship of the true God, they were distinguished from the rest in this, that they adored God by prostrations, so that this ceremony separated them from the wicked, in much the same way as the Friars of the Order of St Francis of Assisi are distinguished from others when they prostrate themselves before the sacrament of the altar and kiss the ground. Let learned readers judge. But to satisfy Theodoret's objections, it is said that Og (Deut. 3:11) was of the remnant not of the Nephilim but of the רפאים. That therefore does not bear on the present matter. The spies (Num. 13:33)…

units.la: * de civit. Dei cap. 1 s. 23. in fine.
units.tr: * On the City of God, chapter 23 of book 15, at the end.

units.la: * Comment. in Iobum secdum cæno, sacramentum altaris & terram deosculantes aspicit. Judicent eruditi. Ut autem Theodoreti objectionibus satisfiat, OG Deut.3.11. dicitur fuisse ex reliquiis non Nephilim, sed הָרְפָאִים / Illud ergo ad rem praesentem non facit. Exploratores Num. 13.33. ajunt se vidisse Nephilim id est homines truculentos & feros, filios Anak, qui oriundi fuit ex Nephilim, non illis qui ante diluvium, sed post illud vixerunt, vel, qui fuerunt ex numero Nephilim, ut innuatur, praeter posteritatem Anak alios insuper tunc in mundo fuisse Nephilim. Illos autem Nephilim praeter ferociam & impietatem habuisse insuper inusitatam corporis staturam, non ex voce נפילים / sed ex iis quae adjecta sunt liquet. Unde & Lutherus vocem Ebraeam, quam Gen.6. reddidit Riesen hic interpretatur Riesen / Belg. Reusen / id est Gigantes. At inde non video, qui inferri possit, hos etiam, de quibus Gen.6. agitur, Giganteā staturā fuisse praeditos. An, quia ex his descenderunt? At eos diluvium peremit. Et ut demus eos ex posteris Noë fuisse, quis ignorat, omni aevo, corpora modum communem longe excedentia ex vulgaris staturae hominibus fuisse prognata? nonne ante annos paucos, inquit * Augustinus, Roma fuit foemina, cum suo patre & matre, quae corpore quodammodo giganteo longe caeteris praeemineret? Et hoc erat maximè admirationi, quod ambo parentes ejus nec saltem tam longi homines erant quam longissimos videre consuevimus. Atque haec eo dicta sunt, ut ostendam nullam necessitatem esse, quae nos cogat, ut נפילים nomen giganteae cujusdam staturae esse dicamus. Illud autem esse certius * hominum ferocium, truculentorum & publicorum praedonum eam esse appellationem, quos dum Lxx. vocarunt γιγάντας, aut respexerunt ad Gentilium istos Γηγενεῖς, voce illā per quandam metaphoram hisce hominum monstris accommodatā, aut acceperunt vocem γίγας pro ἰσχυρός. Ita enim aliquando abiisdem vox Ebraea גִּבּוֹר reddita est, ex gr. Gen.10.8. iste coepit esse גִּבּוֹר Gr. γίγας id est fortis in terrā, & verf.9. γίγας κυνηγός, robustus venator. Et Hesychius, γίγας, δυνάστης, ἰσχυρός.
units.tr: * Commentary on Job, he looks upon the sacrament of the altar and kissing the earth. Let the learned judge. To meet the objections of Theodoret, Deut. 3.11 says that Og was of the remnant not of the Nephilim but of the Rephaim [הָרְפָאִים]. That therefore does not bear on the present question. The spies in Num. 13.33 say they saw the Nephilim [נְפִילִים], that is, fierce and savage men, the sons of Anak, who were descended from the Nephilim, not those who lived before the flood but those who lived after it; or who were of the number of the Nephilim, so as to suggest that, besides the posterity of Anak, there were other Nephilim then in the world. That those Nephilim, besides their ferocity and impiety, had an unusual bodily stature is not clear from the word נפילים [nephilim] but from the words added to it. Hence Luther, who in Gen. 6 rendered the Hebrew word by Riesen, here also translates Riesen, and the Dutch Reusen, that is, giants. But I do not see how it can be inferred from this that the men of whom Gen. 6 speaks were endowed with gigantic stature. Is it because they were descended from them? But the flood destroyed them. And even if we grant that they were of the posterity of Noah, who does not know that in every age bodies far exceeding the common measure have been born of men of ordinary stature? Did not, as Augustine says, a few years ago a woman at Rome, with her father and mother, stand out far above others with a body somewhat gigantic? And what especially aroused wonder was that neither of her parents was even as tall as we are accustomed to see the very tallest men. I say these things so as to show that there is no necessity compelling us to say that נפילים [nephilim] is the name of some gigantic stature. It is more certain that it is the name of fierce, savage and public robbers, whom the Seventy called γίγαντες [giants], either looking to the Gentile Gegenes [Γηγενεῖς], earth-born, applying that word by a certain metaphor to these monsters of men, or taking the word γίγας [gigas] to mean ἰσχυρός [strong]. For in this way the Hebrew word גִּבּוֹר [gibbor] has sometimes been rendered by them, for example in Gen. 10.8, he began to be גִּבּוֹר [gibbor], γίγας [gigas], that is, strong on the earth; and in verse 9, γίγας κυνηγός [gigas kynēgos], a sturdy hunter. And Hesychius glosses γίγας as δυνάστης [dynastēs], ἰσχυρός [ischyros].

units.la: Et omne figmentum cogitationum cordis tantummodo malum esse, &c. | Et quod cunsta cogitatio cordis intenta esset ad malum, &c.
units.tr: And every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil, etc. | And every thought of the heart was bent upon evil, etc.

units.la: Plùs est, esse malum & quidem, tantummodò malum, quàm intentum esse ad malum. Plus est, figmentum cogitationum cordis quàm cogitatio cordis. Vox enim ipsas etiam incompletas cogitationes videtur includere. Textus Ebr. inquit Junius in animadverf. exponit habitum & conditionem cordis humani in se: Vulgatus autem actum & affectionem ejus ad intentum finem, etiam boni aliquid in eo esse posset. Carn. à Lapide ad cap. 8. verf. 21. duplicem officinam ponit in hominis irregeniti corde, unam concupiscentiæ, alteram virtutis & rationis. Illa ad malum, inquit, hac ad bonum propendet, & in hominis arbitrio est ut operetur in officinâ hac vel illa, & consequenter ut eligat & operetur vel malum vel bonum, PRÆSERTIM si gratiâ Dei adjuvetur. Hæc omnia à stirpe convellit unica vocula tantummodo. Vide Theologos nostros in comment. & ad cont: 1. Bellarm. lib. 2. cap. 12.
units.tr: It is more to say that it was evil, and indeed only evil, than that it was bent upon evil. It is more to say "imagination of the thoughts of the heart" than "thought of the heart." For the word seems to include even incomplete thoughts. The Hebrew text, says Junius in his Animadversions, expresses the habit and condition of the human heart in itself; but the Vulgate expresses its act and affection directed to an end, in which something of good could still be present. Cornelius à Lapide, on chapter 8 verse 21, posits a double workshop in the heart of unregenerate man, one of concupiscence, the other of virtue and reason. "The former, he says, inclines to evil, the latter to good, and it is in man's power to work in this or that workshop, and consequently to choose and do either evil or good," ESPECIALLY if he is helped by the grace of God. All this is uprooted by the single little word tantummodo [only]. See our theologians in their commentaries and in the controversial works, and Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 12.

units.la: Verf. 14.
units.tr: Verse 14.

units.la: Vanam & quæ omnes ineptiarum numeros implet, Arcæ Allegoriam invenies apud Erasmum, tomo 5. pag. 859. sive in ejus Ecclesiaste, lib. 3. Franciscanus ille, quem illic perstringit Erasmus, in celebri festo virginis, in primario templo, frequentissima concione, tota hora nihil aliud agebat, quam ut totam arcæ structuram per allegoriam ad Virginem accommodaret, idque ea fronte, eo supercilio, ut facile agnosceres hominem sibi videri rem egregiam ac præclaram explicare. Et certe multos hujus fatuitatis hæredes reliquit iste frater. Multos enim passun videas maximè sibi placere, cum maximè ineptiunt. Narrat ibidem Erasmus, quantopere sudaverit, ut persuaderet, in virginem quadrare ligna levigata, Ebr. ligna Gopher) eaque intus ac foris bitumine oblita, &c. quæ de arca memorantur. Quid fructus ex ea concione retulit populus? Fructus nihil, tædii multum. Ibi profecto sum admiratus Christianæ concionis patientiam, qua vir ille satis impudenter abusus est. Hæc Erasmus. Adi etiam Ambrof. de Arca cap.9. & Augusst. de Civit. Dei lib.15. cap. 26. non audeo dicere, ineptientes.
units.tr: You will find an empty allegory of the ark, which fills every kind of foolishness, in Erasmus, volume 5, page 859, or in his Ecclesiastes, book 3. That Franciscan whom Erasmus there takes to task, at a celebrated feast of the Virgin, in the chief church, before a very crowded sermon, spent a whole hour doing nothing but applying the entire structure of the ark to the Virgin by allegory, and with such an air, such a supercilious look, that you could easily recognise that the man thought himself to be explaining something outstanding and splendid. And certainly this brother left many heirs to his foolishness. For you may see many who please themselves most when they are most foolish. Erasmus recounts in the same place how much he sweated to persuade people that the smoothed planks (Hebrew gopher wood), coated inside and out with bitumen, etc., which are recorded about the ark, fit the Virgin. What profit did the people draw from that sermon? No profit, much tedium. There indeed I wondered at the patience of a Christian congregation, which that man had shamelessly abused. So Erasmus. See also Ambrose, On the Ark, chapter 9, and Augustine, On the City of God, book 15, chapter 26. I dare not call them foolish.

units.la: Delebo omnem substantiam, &c.
units.tr: I will blot out every substance, &c.

units.la: Ita vulg. Interpres. Ebr. יקום id est interprete Pagnino in Lexico, omne vivens. Jun. omne corpus vivens. Abenezra, postquam dixisset non reperiri eam vocem extra hanc sectionem (in quo tamen errat, nam occurrit rursus Deut. 11. 6.) sic pergit, מלרת יקום כלל לכל חי שהוא על האדמה / dictio יקום completur omne vivens quod est in terra. Quæ sunt ipsissima quoque verba Davidis Kimchi in Dictione. Lxx. ἐξαλείψω τὸν ἀνάστημα, Augustinum legisse ἀνάστασιν notant Interpretes. Alibi etiam occurrere ἐξανάστασιν observat Cl. Drusius. Latini Interpretes, quamcunque vocem legerint, exprimunt Græcam versionem his verbis, delebo omnem resurrectionem vel suscitationem carnis. Vide Augustt. lib. 1. Locutionum p.67. Ambrof. de Noë & arca, cap. 13. ubi hanc invenies glossam, Delebo omnem resurrectionem carnis à facie terræ. Non dicit, terra, sed à facie terræ. Florem decutit, radicem servat. Resurrectionem carnis delebo à facie terræ, ut scribam in cœlestibus resurgentes. Resurrectioni communi naturæ usu contraria videtur esse purgatio, quia purgatione rescinditur & reprimitur resurrectionis luxuria. Quid sibi velit Ambrosius; non satis intelligo. Illud video, frustra cum esse, cum distinguit inter has locutiones, à terra &, à facie terræ. Illud quoque ausim asserere, illum non ex mente Interpretum capere vocem resurrectio. Vox Ebræa habet thema קום quod duo significat stare & surgere. Hæc primaria, illa secundaria vocis notio est. Qui enim surrexit, jam pedibus suis stat. Ita στῆναι Græcis est stare, ἀναστῆναι surgere. Quicquid ergo ex terra exurgit & pedibus suis insistit, יקום dicitur. Hoc imitatus Latinus, vertit Substantiam, si vocem Ebræam spectes, non infelici imitamento. Nam ut יקום à קום stare, ita substantia à substo. At si vocis Latinæ usum spectes, nimis dura synecdoche. Græci vero, dum, ipsi quo-que que vocis etymon voluerunt exprimere, illis, qui Græca cum Ebraïs conferre non fuerunt quiti, magnam offuderunt caliginem. Illud certe apud illos tralatitium est, non solum verba sed etymologias verborum transferre. Ita לנצח vertunc εἰς νίκην q. d. in victoriam, quia נצח vincere. At in Hellenistica lingua idem est, quod εἰς αἰῶνας, לעולם / neque enim alio sensu unquam illud לנצח obvium est. Hæc ergo talia non tam ex Græcismo, quam Ebraïsmo, certe non ex Græcismo solo, intelligi possunt. Et quidem ejusmodi passim à Cl. Viris. Drusio & Heinsio observata sunt. Nunc vides Tiro, cur vocem יקום Lxx. ἀνάστημα, vel ἀνάστασιν, reddiderint. Quippe, Ebraæ vocis thema קום seu primario significat ἀναστῆναι surgere, ideo vocem derivatam reddidere ἀνάστασιν, vel ἀνάστημα. Sed & τὸ ἀνάστασις apud profanos authores erectionem & surrectionem significat, ut ἀναστὰσις τειχῶν, erectio parietum. Quomodo apud Virg. non capta assurgunt urbes. Et ἀνάστημα à Lexicographis redditur, erectio assurrectio, vel potius id quod assurgit. ἀνάστημα γῆς de loco editori, Atque hæc sine violento tropo ad omne corpus vivens accommodari posse quis non videt? Deut. 11. 6. eadem vox Ebraea in melioris notæ codicibus reddita est per Græcum ἀνάστασις.
units.tr: So the Vulgate translator. The Hebrew is yaqum [יקום], which, according to Pagninus in his Lexicon, means every living thing. Junius gives every living body. Abenezra, after saying that this word is not found outside this section (which is wrong, for it occurs again at Deut. 11. 6), goes on: the word [מלרת יקום כלל לכל חי שהוא על האדמה] yaqum completes every living thing that is on the earth. These are also the very words of David Kimchi in his dictionary. The Seventy have I will blot out the standing-up [ἐξαλείψω τὸν ἀνάστημα]. The commentators note that Augustine read resurrection [ἀνάστασιν]. The learned Drusius observes that rising up [ἐξανάστασιν] also occurs elsewhere. The Latin translators, whatever word they read, render the Greek version with the words I will blot out every resurrection or raising of the flesh. See Augustine, Locutions, book 1, p. 67. See Ambrose, On Noah and the Ark, chapter 13, where you will find this gloss: I will blot out every resurrection of the flesh from the face of the earth. He does not say "from the earth" but "from the face of the earth". He shakes off the flower and keeps the root. I will blot out the resurrection of the flesh from the face of the earth, so that I may write those who rise again in heaven. Purging seems contrary to the common use of nature in resurrection, because by purging the lustfulness of resurrection is cut off and checked. I do not fully understand what Ambrose means. This I see: he distinguishes in vain between these expressions, from the earth and from the face of the earth. I would also venture to assert that he has not grasped the word resurrection in the sense the translators intended. The Hebrew word has the root קום [qum], which has two meanings, to stand and to rise. The first is the primary meaning of the word, the second the secondary one. For one who has risen is now standing on his feet. So among the Greeks to stand is στῆναι, and to rise is ἀναστῆναι. Whatever rises from the earth and stands on its feet is called יקום. The Latin translator imitated this, and if you look at the Hebrew word, his rendering substantiam is no unhappy imitation: as יקום comes from קום to stand, so substantia comes from substo. But if you look at the usage of the Latin word, it is too harsh a synecdoche. The Greeks, wishing to express the etymology of the word too, have thrown a great fog over those who were not able to compare the Greek with the Hebrew. It is certainly customary with them to translate not only words but the etymologies of words. Thus לנצח they render εἰς νίκην [into victory], as if to say in victoriam, because נצח means to conquer. Yet in the Hellenistic language it means the same as εἰς αἰῶνας [for ever], לעולם, for that לנצח is never found in any other sense. Such things therefore can be understood not so much from Greek idiom as from Hebrew idiom, and certainly not from Greek idiom alone. Many such points have been noted by learned men such as Drusius and Heinsius. Now you see, young student, why the Seventy rendered יקום as ἀνάστημα or ἀνάστασιν. Clearly, the root קום of the Hebrew word primarily means ἀναστῆναι, to rise, so they rendered the derived word as ἀνάστασιν or ἀνάστημα. But also ἀνάστασις among profane authors means erection and rising up, as in ἀνάστασις τειχῶν, the erection of walls, as in Virgil, the cities rise up though not taken. And ἀνάστημα is rendered by the lexicographers as erection, a rising up, or rather that which rises up; ἀνάστημα γῆς is said of a place on the earth. And who does not see that these things can be applied to every living body without a forced trope? In Deut. 11. 6, the same Hebrew word is rendered in the better manuscripts by the Greek ἀνάστασις.

units.la: CAP. VIII. 7.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII. 7.

units.la: Qui (corvus) egrediebatur & non revertebatur.
units.tr: Which (the raven) went out and did not return.

units.la: Ita vulgatus Interpres, non veritatem Ebraicam sed Græcam versionem secutus, nam & ea sic legit, ἡ ἐξελθὼν ἐκ ἀνέκρεψε, unde Proverbium ortum est, corvi nuntius. Fecit hic error, inquit Steuchus, ut fabulosissimas quæstiones huc invexerint expositores, quærentes quo loco abfuerit corvus pertot dies extra arcam & ubi resederit, cum aquæ siccatæ nondum essent, &c. Augustinus, Sulpicius, Alcuinus, Lyra & alii pronuntiarunt cum cadaveribus natantibus insedisse. Ebraea habent, & exiit exeundo & redeundo id est ultro citroque volitavit circa arcam, vel indesinenter ibat & redibat, sive ad arcam, sive in arcam. Bene ergo monuit Steuchus, subtrahendam tam à Græcis quam Latinis codicibus negationem, idque juxta Ebr. veritatem & Josephi interpretationem. Eadem est confusura Cajetani jetani, Joh. Benedicti & Sixti Senensis Bibl. lib. 5. annot. 82. Lovanienses in apparatu ad Biblia Regia non annotarunt variam lectionem. At Editio Plantiniana anni 1583. hanc habet annotationem, sex MS. R. H. Ch. (id est sex manuscripta, Regia, Hebraeos & Chaldaeos) non legere negationem. Etiam * Christ. à Sacrobosco Jesuita asserit, esse codices Latinos magnae authoritatis, qui sine negatione legant, ut in Ebr. habetur. Ipse quoque Procopius Graeca sine negatione legit. His tamen non obstantibus, correctores Romani, teste Luca Brugensi non judicarunt notam negationis esse omittendam.
units.tr: So the Vulgate translator, following the Greek version rather than the Hebrew text, for the Greek reads it thus too: [ἡ ἐξελθὼν ἐκ ἀνέκρεψε], whence the proverb arose, the raven's messenger. This error, says Steuchus, has brought in such fabulous questions from the commentators, who ask where the raven stayed for so many days outside the ark, and where it settled, since the waters had not yet dried up, and so on. Augustine, Sulpicius, Alcuin, Lyra and others declared that it perched on the floating corpses. The Hebrew has and it went out, going out and returning, that is, it flew to and fro around the ark, or kept going and coming back, whether to the ark or into the ark. Steuchus therefore rightly observed that the negation must be removed both from the Greek and from the Latin manuscripts, in accordance with the Hebrew truth and the interpretation of Josephus. Cajetan, John Benedict and Sixtus of Siena (Bibl. lib. 5, annot. 82) fall into the same confusion. The Louvain editors in the apparatus to the Royal Bible did not note the variant reading. But the Plantin edition of 1583 has this note: six manuscripts (R. H. Ch., that is, the Royal, Hebrew and Chaldee manuscripts) do not read the negation. Also Christopher à Sacrobosco the Jesuit asserts that there are Latin codices of great authority which read without the negation, as it is in the Hebrew. Procopius himself also reads it without the negation in the Greek. Nevertheless, despite these, the Roman correctors, according to Lucas of Bruges, did not judge that the mark of negation ought to be omitted.

units.la: Verf. 20. Edificavit altare Domino.
units.tr: Verse 20. He built an altar to the LORD.

units.la: Ita vulg. Ebr. לֵיהוָה / Graeci hic vulgo legunt τῷ Θεῷ. Atque ita habuisse quoque Latinam, vel ex solo Ambrosio liqueat. Is cap. 22. libelli de Arca & Noë, disserit, cur dixerit Moses DEO, & non DOMINO? Quod autem inquit, aedificavit Deo, & non, aedificavit Domino, secundum nominis interpretationem, non coacta videtur haec actio esse gratiarum, quasi Domino, sed virtus justi morigera & grata, quasi Deo. Quod imperiale est sequestravit, quod beneficii, nominavit. Vide quid sit fontes ignorare.
units.tr: So the Vulgate. The Hebrew has to the LORD [לֵיהוָה], but the Greeks commonly read here to God [τῷ Θεῷ]. That the Latin also had this reading is clear from Ambrose alone. In chapter 22 of his book on the Ark and Noah he discusses why Moses said to God, and not to the Lord: But as for the words he built to God, and not he built to the Lord, according to the interpretation of the names, this action does not seem to be a forced act of thanksgiving, as to the Lord, but the dutiful and grateful virtue of a righteous man, as to God. What belongs to majesty he separated out; what belongs to kindness he named. See what it is to be ignorant of the sources.

units.la: Verf. 21. Nequaquam ultra maledicam terra, sensus enim & cogitatio humani cordis in malum prona sunt ab adolescentia.
units.tr: Verse 21. I will no more curse the ground; for the thought and intent of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth.

units.la: Ita vulgatus.
units.tr: So the Vulgate.

units.la: Valde torsit Interpretes illud ENIM. Quid enim? an ea est peccati natura, ut propterea homini parcat ille, qui omnem injustitiam odit? Pighius ex hoc loco sic pro Pontificiis disputabat,
units.tr: The word for has greatly troubled the interpreters. For what does it mean? Is the nature of sin such that God, who hates all injustice, therefore spares man? Pighius, arguing on behalf of the Papists from this passage, reasoned thus:

units.la: Propter quod Deus homini parcit, id non est peccatum.
units.tr: Because of which God spares man, that is not sin.

units.la: Propter figmentum cordis malum parcit Deus homini, Ergo figmentum cordis malum non est peccatum, sed potius imbecillitas quaedam & languor.
units.tr: God spares man on account of the evil imagination of the heart; therefore the evil imagination of the heart is not sin, but rather a certain weakness and infirmity.

units.la: Major est certa, quia tantum abest, ut peccatum Dei iram faciat relentescere & subsidere, ut maxime eam irritet. Minor est in textu, si cum vulgari interprete legas. Quia autem per figmentum cordis malum, nostrates recte intelligunt, inquit Tarnovius, peccatum originis, ille (Pigius) id non esse proprie sic dictum peccatum, inde concludit, quod Deus ipsi non irascatur, sed se propter illud placari ostendat. Carthusianus, Promitas ista ad vitia partim alleviat, & aliquo modo excusat hominum culpas, quia diminuit rationem voluntarii, quod proprie est de ratione peccati. Cor. à Lap. Miserebor humanae infirmitatis & proclivitatis ad malum. Sed observandum hic est primo, pro ENIM in Ebr. esse אַהּ quod saepe ponitur pro quamvis, Josuae 17. 18. Expelles Cananaeum אַהּ quamvis currus ferreos habeat, אַהּ quamvis robustus sit. Gen. 48. 14. quamvis esset natu minor. Ps. 71. 14. vel 15. quamvis ignorem numeros ejus. Verte hoc modo praesens & sublata erit omnis difficultas. Non maledicam ultra terra, quamvis figmentum malum sit, q. d. quamvis, si jure meo uti vellem, tum propter originale peccatum, tum propter actualia, & hominibus & terrae maledicere possem merito, ut jam factum est in diluvio, tamen ex misericordia promitto me non amplius ante extremum diem toti terrarum orbi ita maledicturum, ut jam feci. Sic praeter Tarnovium etiam Pisc. in Germ. vers. & Quaest. Martinius & pauculi alii. II. Observetur, Ebr. רַ male conversum ab Interprete vulg. prona in malum, ut proinde extraoleas vagentur, qui hic proclivitatis oppandere non verecundantur. Etiam August. in Quaest. super Genesin, locum ita legit, quia apposita est mens hominis ad malitiam a juventute. III. malè redditum ab adolescentia, ac si pueritia ab hac pravitate esset immunis. Atqui vox Ebr. non adolescentiam tantum, sed & pueritiam, ipsamque adeo infantiam significat, & quidem hanc magis proprie. Adolescentia enim proprie שִרורָ & כורִם & בּחורות dicitur. Genebr. ad Ps. juxta numerum Ebr. 127. 5. diserte, vox non juventutem sed pueritiam significat. Et ad octonarium 2. Ps. 119. hominem ab infantia ipsa propensum esse ad malum ex cap. 6. Genef. asserit. Etiam Inquisitor Hispanus, Oleastrius, versionem vulgatam corrigit, & docet, hominem ab ipsa pueritiâ machinari malum, ut ad oculum videnius inquit; Sed quid opus est tot verborum ambagibus? Vel sola Genef.6. cum hoc loco collatio, censuram hanc esse justissimam evincet. Figmentum cogitationum cordis tantummodo malum est omni die, inquit Moses, Vulg. omni tempore. Si omni die, omni tempore, annon etiam diebus infantiæ & pueritiæ? Oncelos, מְזִעִירוּהּ à pusillitate, ut sic dicam, & parvitate suâ. R. Salomo ad ipsam vocis originationem respiciens, כְּשֶׁנִּנְעַר לְצָאֶרֶת מִמֶּעַי אִמּוֹ ex quo excussus est egrediendo ex visceribus matris suæ, נַעַר enim est excussit. Porro de nominibus ætatum, & quousque se extendat ea quam נְעוּרִים vocant, vide Cl. Drufii observat.7.17. & ad 1.Sam. pag.423.
units.tr: The major premise is certain, since it is so far from the case that sin makes God's anger abate and subside, that it rather provokes it most of all. The minor premise is in the text, if you read it with the Vulgate translator. But since our people rightly understand by the evil imagination of the heart, says Tarnovius, original sin, Pighius, on the contrary, concludes from this that it is not properly called sin, because God is not angry at it but shows that he is appeased on account of it. The Carthusian says: This proneness partly lightens the sins to which it leads, and in some way excuses men's faults, since it diminishes the reason of the voluntary, which properly belongs to the nature of sin. Cornelius à Lapide: I will have mercy on human weakness and proneness to evil. But here it must first be observed that in the Hebrew the word for for is [אַהּ], which is often used for although, as in Joshua 17:18, You shall drive out the Canaanite [אַהּ] although he has chariots of iron, [אַהּ] although he is strong. Genesis 48:14, although he was the younger. Psalm 71:14 or 15, although I do not know its numbers. Translate it in this way and the whole difficulty will vanish: I will not curse the ground again, although the imagination of man is evil, as if to say: although, if I wished to use my right, I could justly curse both men, on account of original sin and on account of actual sins, and the earth, as has already been done in the Flood, yet out of mercy I promise that I will no longer curse the whole circuit of the earth until the last day in the way I have already done. Thus, besides Tarnovius, also Piscator in the German version and the Questions, Martinius, and a few others. II. It should be noted that the Hebrew [רַ] is badly rendered by the Vulgate translator as prone to evil, so that those who are not ashamed to pass off proneness here may wander away from the truth. Augustine too, in his Questions on Genesis, reads the passage thus: because the mind of man is set toward malice from youth. III. Rendered badly as "from youth", as if childhood were free from this wickedness. Yet the Hebrew word signifies not only youth but also boyhood, and indeed infancy itself, and this more properly. For youth is properly called [שִרורָ], [כורִם] and [בּחורות]. Geneva, on Psalm 127:5 according to the Hebrew numbering, clearly says that the word signifies not youth but boyhood. And on the eighth verse of Psalm 119 he asserts, from chapter 6 of Genesis, that man is inclined to evil from infancy itself. Also the Spanish inquisitor Oleastrius corrects the Vulgate version and teaches that man from boyhood itself devises evil, as we see clearly, he says. But why need there be so many detours of words? The mere comparison of Genesis 6 with this passage will prove this criticism to be most just. The imagination of the thoughts of man's heart is only evil every day, says Moses; the Vulgate has at all times. If every day, at all times, is it not also in the days of infancy and boyhood? Onkelos has mezi'iruhu, from its smallness, so to speak, and its littleness. Rabbi Solomon, looking at the very origin of the word, says [כְּשֶׁנִּנְעַר לְצָאֶרֶת מִמֶּעַי אִמּוֹ], since it was shaken out, going forth from the bowels of its mother, for [נַעַר] means shook out. Further, on the names of the ages, and how far that which they call [נְעוּרִים] extends, see the learned Drusius, Observations 7.17 and on 1 Samuel, p. 423.

units.la: CAP- XI. vers.11. & seq.
units.tr: CHAP. XI, verse 11 and following

units.la: Hic turpes rursus maculæ Græcam versionem foedarunt. Vi-de & Chronologorum rationes non parum turbatæ fuerunt. Primò enim in numero generationum, deinde & in numero annorum, graviter ab Ebræo textu exorbitatum est. Moses siquidem à Noë ad Abrahamum usque generationes tantùm recenset novem, Græci verò decem, Cainano vid. τῷ Ϛιυλίφω inter Arphaxad & Sela interjecto. Verba Lxx. aut ejus interpolatorum, quæ Ebraica veritas ignorat, signis inclusa exhibebimus. Et vixit Arphaxad 135. annis [& genuit Cainan.] Et vixit Arphaxad postquam genuisset [Cainan] 330. annis, & genuit filios & filias [& mortuus est.] Et vixit Cainan 130. annis, & genuit Sela; Et vixit Cainan postquam genuisset Selam, 330. annis, & genuit filios & filias & mortuus est.] Jam verò quod ad annorum numerum attinet, aspice hanc tabulam, Discrepantia in annis ante generationem. | Discrepantia in annis post generationem. units.tr: Here again the Greek version has disfigured the text with shameful blotches. The calculations of the chronologers have also been not a little thrown into confusion. For first the number of generations, and then the number of years, departs widely from the Hebrew text. Moses indeed counts only nine generations from Noah to Abraham, whereas the Greeks count ten, with Cainan (namely the one in the Greek [τῷ Ϛιυλίφω]) inserted between Arphaxad and Shelah. We will set out the words of the LXX, or of their interpolators, which the Hebrew truth does not know, enclosed in brackets. And Arphaxad lived 135 years [and begat Cainan]. And Arphaxad lived, after he had begotten [Cainan], 330 years, and begat sons and daughters [and died]. And Cainan lived 130 years, and begat Shelah. And Cainan lived, after he had begotten Shelah, 330 years, and begat sons and daughters and died. Now as for the number of years, look at this table. units.la: Sicuti autem ex magna ista numerorum varietate inter Chronologiam Ebraeorum & Graecorum magna differitas orta est, in computo annorum à condito mundo usque ad diluvium, ita & non minor extitit in supputatione annorum diluvio usque ad Abrahamum. En tibi rursus tabulam,
units.tr: Just as from this great variety of numbers a great difference arose between the chronology of the Hebrews and that of the Greeks in the count of years from the created world to the Flood, so too there was no smaller difference in the reckoning of years from the Flood to Abraham. units.tr: These, added to the years that elapsed from the created world to the Flood, make 1949 years.

units.tr: But according to the Greeks, who reckon 2242 years from the creation to the Flood, there will be 3314 years.

units.tr: Moreover Isidore, who omits Cainan, counts 942 years; Epiphanius 1040; Nicephorus 1082; Sulpicius Severus 1070. In the thousandth and seventieth year, he says, after the flood, Abram was born to his father Terah. He who omitted two years of Shem: see the notes of the learned Drusius.

units.la: Vulgata Editio in hac differentia Ebraeis codicibus accedit, ac proinde non tam tuendi Ebraici, quam vulgati textus gratiâ, Græcam versionem reprehensum eunt. Solus Emmanuel Sa, quod ego quidem sciam, in notis ad hoc caput, cogimur, inquit, fateri, deesse aliquid in nostra Editione, quod mirum non est, cum Matthæus in Christi genealogia aliquos omiserit: quanquam dici potest, Hieronymum, cujus nostra Editio est, secutum Ebræa, quæ hic diminuta, ut alibi etiam. Vide Exod. 12. Quicquid sit, ex ejus sententiâ in vulgatâ deest integra generatio Cainani. Quid ad hæc decreti Tridentini Patroni dicent? Sed falleris Emmanuel, & omnes tui socii in alia eunt omnia. Certe locus Luc. 3. eò te impellere non debuisset. Cum longè satius sit, cum Cornelio à Lapide aliisque asserere, jam in ipsis Christianismi incunabulis nomen Cainani ex versione ⁊ Lxx, quæ tunc in usu erat, à sciolo quodam in B. Lucæ textum fuisse insitum. Et laudo Bezam, quod ἀπογίλιμαῖον istum Kainam & vetustissimi sui codicis authoritate & Ebraica veritate fretus, ex versione sua ejectum in exilium miserit.
units.tr: In this difference the Vulgate edition agrees with the Hebrew manuscripts, and therefore they find fault with the Greek version not so much out of regard for the Hebrew as for the sake of the received text. Emmanuel Sa alone, so far as I know, in his notes on this chapter, says: We are compelled to admit that something is lacking in our edition, which is no wonder, since Matthew omitted some names in Christ's genealogy; although it may be said that Jerome, whose edition ours is, followed the Hebrew, which is abridged here, as elsewhere also. See Exod. 12. Whatever the case, on his view the whole generation of Cainan is missing from the Vulgate. What will the defenders of the decree of Trent say to this? But you are mistaken, Emmanuel, and all your fellows go astray in every other respect too. Certainly Luke 3 should not have driven you to that. For it is far better, with Cornelius a Lapide and others, to maintain that already in the very cradle of Christianity the name Cainan was inserted into the text of St Luke by some half-learned man from the Septuagint version, which was then in use. And I commend Beza, who, relying on the authority of his very ancient manuscript and on Hebrew truth, cast out that spurious Kainam [ἀπογίλιμαῖον] from his version and sent him into exile.

units.la: Profectusque est Loth ab oriente, inquit vulgatus Interpres. At quis adeo in Chorographiâ hospes est, ut nesciat Jordanem, qui Sodomam alluebat, ad orientem terræ Chanaan situm fuisse? Ubi olim Sodoma, ibi postea mare mortuum fuit, quod à situ orientale vocant, mari magno quod occidentale vocant, oppositum. Quomodo ergo Lot, qui ab occasu orientem versus tendit, dicitur profectus ab Oriente? Indoctis & barbaris Interpretibus nulla hic caligo, dum à literalis sensus, ut vocant, pauperate ad allegoriarum divitias transvolant. Abiit ab oriente ad occasum, id est relictâ verâ luce tetendit in occasum & perniciem suam. Noli jam mirari Lector, unde tam crebræ in multorum lucubrationes Allegoriæ irrepserint. Inscitia multis ad Allegorias pædagogus fuit. Quanto satius fuisset nodum sic solvere, Profectus est ab oriente id est ab orientali plaga loci, ubi hactenus communes cum Abrahamo habuerat sedes, in locum magis orienorientalem. Mariana, Lot ab oriente recesset Abraha comparatione, non Sodoma, quo ivit. Non aspernor. Puto tamen felicius hunc nodum soluisse Fullerum, Misc. 1. 4. qui non solum vertit, Orientem versus, quod ante eum & Mercerus & Junius & Drusius fecerant, sed & insuper eam versionem egregie ivit constabilitum. Mercerus, profectus est orientem versus, non equidem ut מ idem sit cum ל / etsi is sit sensus, sed pro, versus, ut supra, Et plantavit Dominus hortum ab oriente id est versus Orientem, in orientali orbis parte. Hoc vult, ם aliquando denotare versus, ad, ut tantum * denotet situm sine motu, ac proinde locum hunc sic reddendum profectus est [in locum situm] versus orientem. Vide autem Lector, quomodo dies diem, & doctus doctum doceat. Literam Mem aliquando etiam poni pro ל denotante motum ad locum, evidentissime ostendit Fullerus, collato loco 2. Sam. 6. 2. cum 1. Chron. 13. 6. ubi in eadem historia extat / ה locali vices ל supplente. Plane in eundem modum Septuaginta hoc ipso capite vers. 3. reddunt εις τλν εκμον. In Arabisimo nihil frequentius hoc usu literae ם / Contra ad orientem, ponitur pro ab oriente, Jos. 16. 1. Ubi & Lxx. & vulgatus habent, ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν, ab oriente. Sic Jos. 18. 14 pro / Lxx. ἀπὸ λιβὸς, vers. 15. pro / ubi vide Masium. Adi etiam Drusii Comm. ad loca difficil. Judicum p. 171.
units.tr: Lot set out from the east, says the Vulgate translator. But who is so much a stranger to geography as not to know that the Jordan, which watered Sodom, lay to the east of the land of Canaan? Where Sodom once stood, the Dead Sea lies today, which is called eastern from its position, and is set over against the Great Sea, which is called western. How then is Lot said to have set out from the east, when he was travelling from the west towards the east? The unlearned and barbarous translators have no fog here, because they fly from the poverty of the literal sense, as they call it, to the riches of allegories. He went away from the east, that is, to the west: having left the true light, he made for the west and his own ruin. Do not wonder now, reader, how such frequent allegories have crept into the labours of many. Ignorance has been a schoolmaster to many in allegory. How much better would it have been to loosen the knot thus: He set out from the east, that is, from the eastern region of the place where until then he had shared a dwelling with Abraham, into a place more to the east. Mariana: Lot withdrew from the east, in comparison with Abraham, not Sodom, to which he went. I do not scorn this. Yet I think Fuller untied this knot more happily (Misc. 1. 4.), who not only rendered it towards the east, as Mercerus, Junius and Drusius had done before him, but also went on to establish that rendering with distinction. Mercerus: he set out towards the east, not indeed as the Hebrew מ is the same as ל, although that is the sense, but in the sense of towards, as above, And the Lord planted a garden from the east, that is, towards the east, in the eastern part of the world. His point is that ם sometimes denotes towards, to, whereas ה denotes place without motion; and so this place is to be rendered thus: he set out [into the place situated] towards the east. But see, reader, how one day teaches another, and the learned teaches the learned. Fuller most clearly shows that the letter Mem is sometimes also put for ל, denoting motion to a place, by comparing 2 Sam. 6. 2 with 1 Chron. 13. 6, where in the same history ה stands in the place of ל as a locative. In exactly the same way the Septuagint, in this same chapter at verse 3, render it εἰς τὴν ἀνατολήν [into the east]. In Hebraism nothing is more frequent than this use of the letter ם. On the other hand, towards the east is put for from the east, Josh. 16. 1, where both the Septuagint and the Vulgate have ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν [from the east]. So Josh. 18. 14 for ה, the Septuagint ἀπὸ λιβός [from the west], at verse 15 for ה; see Masius there. Also consult Drusius's Commentary on the difficult passages of Judges, p. 171.

units.la: Et Melchi-sedek Rex Salem proferens panem & vinum, erat ENIM sacerdos Dei altissimi, benedixit ei, &c. ] Pro ENIM in Ebraeo est! ET, Et pro proferens est protulit, / Voculam ENIM valde urgent Pontificii, & inter eos quoque Pererius, a Suares, b Bellar. Cornelius à Lapide & alii Rom. Ecclesiae Atlantes, ut suum Missificium inde exsculpant. Quaeritur quid hic sit proferre panem & vinum. LXX. εξηνεγκε, vel ut alii codices habent, εξηνεγκε αὐτῷ protulit ei, sc. Abramo. Cajetanus, nihil hic scribitur de sacrificio vel oblatione, sed de prolatione seu extra ētione, quam scribit Josephus factam ad reficiendos victores. Andradio quoque cum Epiphanio, Ambrosio aliisque veteris Ecclesiae Interpretibus convenit, Melchisedecum lassos Abrahami milites panę & vino refecisse. Hanc interpretationem rejiciunt illi quos jam jam nominabam, & per prolationem panis & vini sacrificium intelligunt. Vox E N I M inquit Bellarm. cogit nos, ut intelligamus panem & vinum prolata fuisse in sacrificium Missae. Sed audiamus Cajetanum qui & ipse Cardinalis fuit, Quod autem, inquit, in vulgata Editione subditur ut causa oblationis, erat enim sacerdos, &c. in Ebraeo non habetur ut causa, sed ut particula separata. Audiamus & Hieron. ab Oleastro, Adverte, inquit, quod licet LXX. & vulgata vertant, Erat enim, &c. quasi sequens sententia priorum causam reddiderit, in Ebraeo tamen est ut vertimus, scilicet, ET ipse erat sacerdos, Ipse quoque B. Hieron. in quaest. Ebr. ad eundem modum vertit. Quis ergo hic describitur actus sacerdotalis, inquies. Respondet tibi Paulus Ebr. 7. Benedictionem fuisse. Proferens panem & vinum, & ipse erat Sacerdos, benedixit ei, vid. benedictione sacerdotali & solenni, non aliqua vulgari comprecatione. Sed soph pasuk, inquit Bellarm. indicat ibi terminari periodum, & proinde conjungi sacerdotium cum prolatione panis & vini, non cum benedictione. Resp. Ergo fatente Bellarm. impegit vulgatus, qui nulla ejus accentus ratione habita, duos hos versus conjunxit, atque in unum axioma conflavit; qua in re tamen nihil peccavit Interpres, nec, me judice, perperam Interpretatus est scripturam, sicuti Bell. asserit. Vide 1.Chron.21.11. Gen.23.17. 2.Sam. 11.19. Jerem. 33.10. Sed dices, * ex praeda jam sa-turi erant milites, verf. 24. nec egebant refectione Melchisedeci. Resp. verf. 24. nihil legi de magna saturitate, Praeterea, inquit Abraham, qua comederunt pueri mei. Comedisse dicuntur, an vero ad eam saturitatem comederint, ut post confectum molestissimum iter esurire denuo non potuerint, item, an commeatum secum sumserint, non meminit textus. Ad haec, hujusmodi Principum munificentia, prisco ritu, honoris tantum causa & benevolentiae & gratulationis ergo exercebatur. Vide Deut. 23.4. Quin ipse Corn. à Lapide agnoscit militibus panem & vinum fuisse distributa. Nota, inquit, Melchisedecum primo panem & vinum obtulisse in sacrificium, partem panis cremando, partem vini libando: deinde reliquam panis & vini partem in milites Abrahae libandam id est participandam & comedendam distribuisse. Videatur quoque Pererius Num.72. & Genebr. in Chronol. p.43. Abrahamum, inquit revertentem e bello convivio excepit pane & vino, &c. Quod propter * Corn. à Lapide & Bellarminus eos annotare volui, qui nihil militibus distributum fuisse asserunt, inter quos ipse quoque Bellarm. Idem tamen sacrificium praecessisse volunt. Verbum quod vulg. vertit protulit, Lxx. obtulit (atqui ego illic lego ἐξήνεγκε quod potius est extulit) est sacrificale, inquit Genebrardus, producitque unicum locum Jud. 6. 18. Sed quæro ex te Genebrarde, an semper an aliquando sit sacrificare? Si semper, ergo & Exod. 8. 18. ubi de pediculis usurpatur. Si aliquando, quæ vis argumenti à particulari? Concludo ergo, Melchisedecum lassos milites vino & pane refecisse & quia sacerdos erat, Abrahamo benedixisse, non benedictione charitatis, qua par pari, imò, sæpe inferior superiori benedicit, sed benedictione sacerdotali. Benedictio enim quâ homo benedicit homini, est vel charitatis vel authoritatis. Atque hæc rursus vel patriarchalis vel sacerdotalis erat. Neque enim tantum ad sacrificandum, sed & ad benedicendum populo constituti fuere Sacerdotes, Num. 6. De particula itaque ENIM non admodum contenderim, modò relinquatur in vulgatâ participium proferens, Et Melchisedek Rex S. proferens panem & vinum (erat enim Sacerdos, &c.) benedixit ei. Sic enim non prolationis panis & vini, sed benedictionis (in hoc enim periodus absolvitur) datur ratio. Vide jam Illustriss. D. Philippum Mornaum, de Eucharist. lib. 3. cap. 2.
units.tr: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of God Most High, and he blessed him, etc. ] In the Hebrew, for ENIM (for) there is ET (and), and for proferens (bringing forth) there is protulit (brought forth). The Papists press the little word ENIM hard, and among them Pererius, Suárez, Bellarmine, Cornelius à Lapide and the others, the Atlases of the Roman Church, so that they may carve their Mass-sacrifice out of it. The question is what "bringing forth bread and wine" means here. The Seventy have exēnenke [ἐξήνεγκε], or, as other manuscripts have, exēnenke autō [ἐξήνεγκεν αὐτῷ], brought forth to him, that is, to Abram. Cajetan says: "Nothing is written here about a sacrifice or an offering, but about a bringing forth, or a carrying out, which Josephus says was made to refresh the victors." Andradius also agrees with Epiphanius, Ambrose and other interpreters of the early Church that Melchizedek refreshed Abraham's weary soldiers with bread and wine. Those whom I have just named reject this interpretation and understand the "bringing forth of bread and wine" as a sacrifice. Bellarmine says: "The word E N I M compels us to understand that the bread and wine were brought forth for the sacrifice of the Mass." But let us hear Cajetan, who was himself a cardinal: "As for what is added in the Vulgate edition as the cause of the offering, for he was the priest, etc., in the Hebrew it is not given as a cause, but as a separate particle." Let us also hear Jerome of Oleaster: "Note," he says, "that although the Seventy and the Vulgate translate it, 'For he was,' etc., as if the following clause gave the reason for the former, in the Hebrew it is as we translate it, namely, AND he himself was the priest." Saint Jerome himself also translates it in the same way in his Hebrew Questions. What priestly act, you will ask, is described here? Paul answers you in Hebrews 7: it was a blessing. "Bringing forth bread and wine, and he himself was the priest, he blessed him," that is, with a priestly and solemn blessing, not with some ordinary prayer. But soph pasuk [סוף פסוק], says Bellarmine, shows that the sentence ends there, and therefore the priesthood is joined with the bringing forth of bread and wine, not with the blessing. Reply: then, by Bellarmine's own admission, the Vulgate has erred, for without regard to the accent it joined these two verses and welded them into one statement. Yet the translator did no wrong in this, and, in my judgement, he did not translate the text wrongly, as Bellarmine asserts. See 1 Chronicles 21:11, Genesis 23:17, 2 Samuel 11:19, Jeremiah 33:10. But you will say: *the soldiers were already full of the spoil, verse 24, and did not need Melchizedek's refreshment. Reply: in verse 24 nothing is read about great fullness. Abraham says, "Besides, the portion of the young men who ate with me." It is said that they ate; but the text does not record whether they ate to such fullness that, after the most wearisome journey, they could not be hungry again, nor whether they took provisions with them. Moreover, such generosity of princes was practised in the ancient manner, only for the sake of honour, goodwill and congratulation. See Deuteronomy 23:4. Indeed Cornelius à Lapide himself admits that bread and wine were distributed to the soldiers. "Note," he says, "that Melchizedek first offered bread and wine in sacrifice, burning part of the bread and pouring out part of the wine as a libation; then he distributed the rest of the bread and wine to Abraham's soldiers, to be shared and eaten." See also Pererius on Numbers 72, and Genebrardus in his Chronology, p. 43: "He received Abraham, returning from the war, at a feast with bread and wine," etc. I have wished to note this, because Cornelius à Lapide and Bellarmine, who assert that nothing was distributed to the soldiers, and among whom Bellarmine himself is, nonetheless want the same sacrifice to have come before. Genebrardus says that the verb which the Vulgate translates protulit (brought forth), and the Seventy obtulit (offered) (but I read there exēnenke [ἐξήνεγκε], which rather means extulit, carried out), "is sacrificial," and he brings forward the single instance of Judges 6:18. But I ask you, Genebrardus, whether it always means to sacrifice, or only sometimes? If always, then also in Exodus 8:18, where it is used of lice. If only sometimes, what is the force of an argument from the particular? I conclude, therefore, that Melchizedek refreshed the weary soldiers with wine and bread, and because he was a priest, blessed Abraham, not with a blessing of charity, by which an equal blesses an equal, or indeed the inferior often blesses the superior, but with a priestly blessing. For a blessing by which a man blesses a man is either of charity or of authority, and this again was either patriarchal or priestly. For priests were appointed not only to sacrifice but also to bless the people, Numbers 6. Therefore I would not contend very much about the particle ENIM, provided that in the Vulgate the participle proferens (bringing forth) is retained: "And Melchizedek king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine (for he was the priest, etc.), blessed him." For in this way the reason is given not for the bringing forth of bread and wine, but for the blessing (since the sentence ends with this). See now the most illustrious Lord Philippe de Mornay, On the Eucharist, book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: Cujus præputii caro non fuerit circumcisa, &c.
units.tr: Whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, etc.

units.la: Ita vulg. Lxx. addiderunt insuper de suo duas voces הַשְּׁמִינִי die octavo, Sic enim illi, omnis præputiatus masculus cujus caro præputii non fuerit circumcisa die octavo, interibit anima illa de genere suo, quia testamentum meum dissipavit. Posui locum prout eum citavit Augustinus de civit. Dei lib. 16. 27. Vides hac lege, prout ea ab his interpretibus concepta est, etiam infantes pœnæ involui. Certè, ut alios præteream. Augustinus quoque hanc horrendi carminis Legem infantibus octavo die non circumcisis obnuntiatam esse ratus est. Vide eum loco prædicto. Hinc suo, idem Pater infantibus, quos dulcis vitæ exortes & à matris ubere ante susceptum Baptismum raptos atro mors abstulit, * ini-quior fuit, dum eos alibi (de peccat. remiss. l.1. c.16) in mitissima damnatione futuros esse, alibi (ibidem cap.15.) in Christo vivificari non posse quasi ex Tripode pronuntiat. Sed ut in aliis quamplurinis, ita & hic prava versio cum in errorem dedit praecipitem. Ebræa aliter sonant, Præputiatus masculus qui non circumciderit carnem præputii sui, exscindetur anima ista, &c. Ebr. אשר לא ימול Futurum Kal à נמל / ut à נמל fit יפול / Isthoc verbo usus est Moses verf.11. ונמלו & circumcidetur. At vulg. & Lxx. existimarunt esse Fut. Niphal à מול / Et certè in hoc eodem cap. verf.13. & alibi negari non potest, quin sit passivum. At quominus hic eodem modo accipiatur obstat clausula, Quia fœdus meum irritum fecit. Qui enim hoc in infantem quadret? Videt hoc Augustinus & sudat, at se expedire nequaquam valet. Adi locum, quem ex libris de Civit. Dei produximus & scio te non sine commiseratione lecturum. Sensus ergo hic est, Si cujus circumcisio parentum culpa in infantia fuerit neglecta, ipseque jam adultus eam quoque neglexerit, atque ita negligentiam parentum approbaverit, ista exscindetur è populis suis. Eundem sensum expressit Chald. ונערל דכורא דלא ... qui non præciderit, &c. Ipse quoque Lombardus locum Joh. 3. 5. Nisi quis natus fuerit ex aqua & sanguine, &c. sic interpretatur, Intelligendum est de illis qui posunt & contemnunt baptizari, libr 4. dist. 4. Hic non alienum esset paucis videre, quid sibi velit illa phrasis, anima ista exscindetur è populis suis. Fruatur quisque judicio suo, ego in illorum descendo sententiam, qui existimant non politicam aut corporalem, sed Ecclesiasticam, spiritualem & ϑεϊλαῖοι pœnam ista phrasi innui, Sed ea de re alibi prolixius disseremus.
units.tr: So the Vulgate and the Septuagint have added two words of their own, הַשְּׁמִינִי [hashminí] "on the eighth day." For thus they read: every uncircumcised male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised on the eighth day, that soul shall perish from its kin, because it has broken my covenant. I have set down the passage as Augustine quoted it in De civitate Dei, book 16, chapter 27. You see from this law, as these translators have framed it, that even infants are caught up in the punishment. Certainly, to pass over the rest, Augustine also thought that this dreadful law was announced to infants not circumcised on the eighth day. See him in the place cited. Hence, on his own account, the same Father was more unjust towards infants who, deprived of sweet life and snatched from their mother's breast before receiving baptism, were carried off by a dark death: elsewhere (De peccatorum remissione, book 1, chapter 16) he declares that they will be in the mildest damnation, and elsewhere (ibid., chapter 15) that they cannot be made alive in Christ, as if pronouncing from the tripod. But, as in many other places, so here a faulty translation has led to a headlong error. The Hebrew reads differently: an uncircumcised male who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off, etc. The Hebrew is אשר לא ימול [asher lo yimol], the future Kal of נמל; just as from נמל the form יפול is made. Moses used this same verb in verse 11: ונמלו [venimlu], and they shall be circumcised. But the Vulgate and the Septuagint thought it was the future Niphal of מול. And certainly in this same chapter, verse 13, and elsewhere, it cannot be denied that the verb is passive. What prevents it from being taken in the same way here is the clause, because he has broken my covenant. For who would fit this to an infant? Augustine sees the difficulty and labours over it, but by no means manages to extricate himself. Consult the passage I have brought from the books De civitate Dei, and I know you will read it not without pity. The sense, then, is this: if the circumcision of someone was neglected in infancy through the fault of his parents, and he himself, now grown up, also neglected it, and so approved his parents' negligence, that soul shall be cut off from its people. The Chaldee paraphrast expresses the same sense: veneral dekhora dela ... (who has not circumcised, etc.). Lombard too interprets John 3:5, unless someone is born of water and blood, etc., in this way: it must be understood of those who despise and scorn being baptized, book 4, distinction 4. It would not be out of place here to see briefly what that phrase means, that soul shall be cut off from its people. Let each person enjoy his own judgment; I come down on the side of those who think that by this phrase is meant not a civil or bodily penalty but an ecclesiastical, spiritual and divine [θεία] punishment. But we shall discuss this matter more fully elsewhere.
