units.la: Non vocabis nomen ejus Sarai, sed Sara.
units.tr: You shall not call her name Sarai, but Sara.

units.la: Quæ antea appellabatur שָׂרַי / nunc transnominatur à Deo שָׂרָה litera Jod in ה mutatâ. Lxx. Interpretes, ὁ ἐκλήθη τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς Σαρρα, ἀλλὰ Σάῤῥα ἐσται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς, inserta litera ῤ. Quæsitum ab Interpretibus, cur eâ litera inserta. Audiamus Hieronymum in Quæstionibus. Errant, inquit, qui putant primum Sara per unum R. scriptum fuisse, & postea ei alterum R. additum. Et quia R. apud Græcos centenarium numerus est, multi super hoc nomine suspicantur ineptias: cum utique, utcunque volunt ei vocabulum commutatum, non Græcam, sed Ebræam debeant habere rationem. Ebraum enim est. Nemo autem in altera lingua quempiam vocans, etymologiam vocabuli sumit ex altera. Hæc Hieron. Inter alias verò ineptias etiam illa est, litera ῤ denotari annum Abrahæ centesimum, quo filium genuit ex Sarâ uxore vetulâ, nempe nonagenariâ. Refert idem Hieronymus, quosdam pessimè suspicatos fuisse, eam antea lepram fuisse vocitatam, & postea principem. At lepra צָרָעַת Saraâth dicitur, voce admodum à שָׂרָה & שָׂרִי diversâ. Quid * Augustinus? Is licet ∓ Lxx. versionem passim fere sequatur, hic tamen Ebraicæ veritati adhæsit, De nomine autem mutato Sara, inquit, non est reddita ratio, sed sicuti ajunt qui scripserunt interpretationes nominum Ebraorum, quæ literis sacris continentur, Sarai interpretatur, princeps mea, Sara autem virtus. Ecce agnoscit, eam quæ antea dicebatur Sarai, postea vocitatam Sara. Recte. Sed quàm miserè interpretatione labitur! Sara est virtus, inquit, unde scriptum est in Epistola ad Ebræos, Fide & ipsa Sara virtutem (δύναμιν) accepit ad emissionem seminis. At δύναμις Ebraice כּחַ / אֵל & dicitur nusquam שָׂרָה / Mala ergo interpretatio, Sara, virtus, Pejor accommodatio loci ex Epistola ad Ebræos. Quid ergo? Hieron. magis ad rem locutus est, causa inquiens, immutati nominis hæc est, quod antea dicebatur שָׂרִי princeps mea, unius tantum domus materfamilias: postea verò dicitur absolute שָׂרָה princeps id est ἀρχισα. — Signanterque in Ebr. additur, non vocabis nomen ejus Sarai id est non dices ei, princeps mea es: omnium quippe gentium futura jam princeps est. Hæc Hieron. cujus sententia de Sara verissima. * de Civit. Dei, 16, 28. sima est. At de Sarai ἐπίχω. Nam princeps mea. Ebr. diceretur שָׂרָתִי / vel facta syncope, שָׂרִי Sari, quomodo dicimus פְּשִׁתִּי pro פְּשִׁתָּהּ / verior ergo fortassis, certè analoga magis Interpretatio, שָׂרִי principes mei, vel principes, ea formâ quâ Gobai locustæ, Challonai, fenestræ. Junius, vocabitur Sarah, addità eâdem litera, qua nomini Abrahami accessit, ut idem esset utrobique earundem promissionum symbolum, quod confirmatur 1. Petri 3.6. & formâ nominis ex Chaldæo ad Hebraicum revocatâ. Pisc. in Quæst. litera ה sumpta est ex nomine הַמּוֹן id est multitudo, quia futura erat mater multarum gentium, id quod significatur vers. seq. Et erit in gentes. In hâc sententiâ acquiesco. Nota ergo Tiro, ex hac voce (המון) literam ה infertam nomini אַבְרָם / vide vers. 5. Justino enim qui dixit nomen ei mutatum inserto ἐνὸς α, Græca scriptura Αβραμ impositum. אַבְרָם pater excelsus, πατὴρ μετέωρος, אַבְרָהָם quasi אַב רַב הָמוֹן pater magnæ multitudinis, ex voce רַב extrita ב / & ex voce הָמוֹן litera ו / Ineptit ergo Hesychius, אַבְרָם interpretans, πατέγτης, transitorem, aut πατέγτης μετέωρον transitorem excelsum, quem errorem & magnus Chrysost. erravit, hom. 39. sic inquiens, Ἀβραμ γὰρ πατέγτης ἑρμηνευεται κατὰ τὸν Ἑβραίων γλῶτταν καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα, ὅτι τῆς γλώττης ἐκείνης εἰσὶν ἐμπεί-ραι. additque parentes præsagos transitus ipsius in Cananæam ei hoc nomen imposuisse, ubi porrò prolixè disputat, unde illi, cum incredidi fuerint, eam præscientiam habuerint. Confuderunt illi אברם cum עִבְרִי / Hoc enim non ineptè πατέγτης redditur, nam עָבַר transit, & עֵבֶר trans. Ineptius est illud, Abraham πατὴρ ἐκλεκτὸς ἡχῶς, pater electus sonitus, quod Philo & Clemens asseruerunt & in comm. Hieron. ad Gal. 4. quoque repetitur, atque hic rem acu tetegit Hesychius, qui τὸ Abraham, interpretatur, πατὴρ πολλῶν ἐθνῶν.
units.tr: She who was previously called שָׂרַי [Sarai] is now renamed by God שָׂרָה [Sarah], the letter Jod being changed into ה. The Seventy translators have: "Her name shall not be called Sarra, but Sarra shall be her name," with the letter ῤ inserted. The translators asked why that letter was inserted. Let us hear Jerome in the Questions. "They are wrong," he says, "who think that Sara was first written with a single R, and that a second R was afterwards added. Because R among the Greeks stands for the number one hundred, many suspect silly things about this name. Whatever change they suppose was made to the word, they ought to consider not Greek but Hebrew, for the name is Hebrew. No one who names someone in another language takes the etymology of the name from that other language." So Jerome. Among the other silly notions is this one: that the letter ῤ marks Abraham's hundredth year, when he begot a son by his aged wife Sarah, who was then ninety. The same Jerome reports that some have wickedly suspected that she was first called "leprosy" and afterwards "princess." But leprosy is called צָרָעַת [Saraath], a word quite different from שָׂרָה and שָׂרִי. What of Augustine? Although he generally follows the Septuagint version, here he adhered to the Hebrew truth: "No reason is given for the changed name Sara, but, as those who wrote interpretations of the Hebrew names contained in the sacred letters say, Sarai is interpreted 'my princess,' and Sara 'virtue.'" See, he recognises that she who was previously called Sarai was afterwards called Sara. Rightly so. But how wretchedly he slips in the interpretation! "Sara is virtue," he says, and so it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: "By faith Sara herself also received virtue (δύναμιν) for the conception of seed." But δύναμις in Hebrew is כּחַ or אֵל, and nowhere is it שָׂרָה. So the interpretation "Sara, virtue" is false, and the application of the passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews is even worse. What then? Jerome spoke more to the point: "The reason for the changed name is this: previously she was called שָׂרִי, 'my princess,' mistress of one household only; but afterwards she is called absolutely שָׂרָה, princess, that is ἀρχισα [ruler]. And it is significant that the Hebrew adds, 'you shall not call her Sarai,' that is, you shall not say to her, 'you are my princess,' for she is now to be princess of all nations." So Jerome, whose view about Sara is most true. But as for Sarai: "my princess" in Hebrew would be שָׂרָתִי, or, with syncope, שָׂרִי [Sari], just as we say פְּשִׁתִּי for פְּשִׁתָּהּ. So perhaps the more accurate, and certainly the more analogous, interpretation is שָׂרִי, "my princes," or "princes," in the form in which גּוֹבַאי means locust and חַלּוֹנַי means window. Junius: "She shall be called Sarah, the same letter being added as was added to the name Abraham, so that the same symbol of the same promises appears in both places; this is confirmed by 1 Peter 3:6, and by the form of the name restored from Chaldee to Hebrew." Piscator in the Questions: "The letter ה was taken from the word הַמּוֹן, that is, multitude, because she was to be the mother of many nations, which is signified in the next verse, And she shall be for nations." I agree with this view. Note therefore, Tiro, that the letter ה was inserted into the name אַבְרָם from this word (הָמוֹן); see verse 5. For to Justin, who said the name was changed by inserting one alpha, the Greek form Αβραμ was given. אַבְרָם means "lofty father," πατὴρ μετέωρος, and אַבְרָהָם is as if אַב רַב הָמוֹן, "father of a great multitude," with the ב taken from the word רַב and the ו taken from הָמוֹן. So Hesychius is wrong to interpret אַבְרָם as [πατέγτης], "transitor," or "lofty transitor." The great Chrysostom too made this error in homily 39, where he says: [Ἀβραμ γὰρ πατέγτης ἑρμηνεύεται κατὰ τὸν Ἑβραίων γλῶτταν καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα, ὅτι τῆς γλώττης ἐκείνης εἰσὶν ἐμπεί-ραι]. He adds that the parents gave him this name as a prophetic sign of his passage into Canaan, and there he argues at length how, though they were unbelievers, they could have had such foreknowledge. They confused אברם with עִבְרִי. For עָבַר means "to pass over," and עֵבֶר "beyond," and so the Greek [πατέγτης] is not an inept rendering. More inept is the view that Abraham was "a chosen father of sound" [πατὴρ ἐκλεκτὸς ἡχῶς], which Philo and Clement asserted, and which is repeated in Jerome's commentary on Galatians 4. Here Hesychius hit the mark, interpreting Abraham as "father of many nations" [πατὴρ πολλῶν ἐθνῶν].

units.la: Claudam hoc caput ubi φιλομαθεῖς adolescentes illud monuero, communem errorem esse, Saracenos (qui & Hagareni & Ismaëlitæ & Arabes) à Sara denominatos esse, qui ipsi quoque Hieronymo obrepsit, dum inquit Agarenos, qui nunc Saraceni dicuntur, assumpsisse sibi falsò nomen Sarae, ut de ingenuâ & domina videantur esse generati. comm. in Iezech. lib. 8.25. & in Jesai. 5. cap. 21. Hieronymi authoritas etiam doctissimos quosque in eundem errorem abripuit. Ut enim veteres taceam, Genebrardus comm. in Psal. 83. & in Chronol. ait cos sic dictos vel à Sara monte. vel semet ipsos denominasse à * Sara legitimâ uxore Abrahami. Ab Hagar fit Hagarenus fluxione legitimâ; Sed quomodo à Sara Saracenus; Unde enim litera ꝑ seu x, cum ea nunquam sit hebraica? Hoc videt Brigtm, ac proinde in comm. ad Apoc. 9. 8. existimat ita dictos à Sara & Kedar. Veram originationem docuit nos Scaliger, de Emend. temp. lib. 2. pag. 108. Edit. postr. Et quidem scriptores, inquit, recte Hagarenos ab Hagar, sed inepte Saracenos à Sara. Neque enim etymon neque historia conjenit. Nam verum esset, Saracenos ab illa dictos si quidem ipsa Saraca, non Sara dicta fuisset. Saraceni igitur etiam hodie à vicinis dicuntur Effarak, hoc est Λησγικοὶ & ῥομαδικοὶ, ut vere sunt. Idem in animadverf. ad Eusebium. Genef. 37. ubi in Ebraeo ישמעאלים Ismaelitæ, * Oncelos vertit ערבאי Σαρακηνοὶ, Σαρακαῖοι. Stephanus ait Σάρακα esse regionem Arabiae finitimam Nabataeis, à quâ τῆς Σαρακήνους dictos putat. Nos scimus Νομάδας Αἰγύπτιος ita dictos. / Hoc enim סרק Arabicè significat id est feroces & latrones, pradones, quales qui Turcis dicuntur Cofaki Tartari, quales Martolossi, quales Bandolieri in pyrenaeis. De Sara perridiculum. Hoc modo oportet aut à Sarâ Saraos dictos, aut uxorem Abrahami Saracam vocatam fuisse. Avellenda est haec opinio de animis hominum. Haec Scaliger. Gentem autem illam Hieron. testis est, Arabum gens, inquit in Jerem. 3. latrocinis dedita usque hodie incursat terminos Palaestinae. Eodem elogio eos celebrat Ammianus lib. 14. Quin adeo hoc isti genti proprium fuit, ut sicut Chaldaeus pro Astrologo, Cananaeus pro Mercatore, Sic Arabs pro Latrone usupari consueverit. Certè Jerem. 3. 2. sicut Arabs in deserto, Hieron. reddit, sicut latro. Fi mat hanc sententiam ex Chaldaeorum lingua Fullerus Miscell. 2. 12. סרק inquit, planè idem est quod Ebraeum ריק & ejusdem forsan originis. Utrumque cum personis attribuitur, vel morum respectu dicitur vel fortunarum. Quando igitur Chaldaeus, Jud. 11. 3. אנשים ריקים / reddit, סריקין אבריו id est viros inanes, intelligamus aut otiosos minimèque frugi homines, aut vitam pauperem, duram & incultam agentes: qualis eorum plerumque est, qui ex rapto vivere solent. Duabus hisce interpretationibus conjunctis, eruditissimam ac numeris omnibus absolutam versionem ibidem nobis tradidit vetus Interpres, dum אנשים ריקים exponit, inopes & latrocinantes, ex vulgari etiam sermonis Arabici usu. Haec Fullerus. Quod de sermonis Arabici
units.tr: I will close this chapter by advising the keen young scholars of a common error: that the Saracens (who are also called Hagarenes, Ishmaelites and Arabs) were named from Sara. This error crept into Jerome too, when he says: "The Agarenes, who are now called Saracens, falsely assumed for themselves the name of Sara, so that they might seem to be descended from a free mother and mistress." Commentary on Ezekiel, book 8, on 25; and on Isaiah, chapter 21 of book 5. Jerome's authority has carried even the most learned men into the same error. For, to pass over the ancients, Genebrard, in his commentary on Psalm 83 and in his Chronology, says that they were so called either from Mount Sara, or that they named themselves from Sara, Abraham's lawful wife. From Hagar comes Hagarene by regular derivation; but how does Saracen come from Sara? For where would the letter ꝑ or x come from, since it is never Hebrew? Brightman sees this, and therefore in his commentary on Revelation 9:8 thinks they were so called from Sara and Kedar. Scaliger taught us the true origin, in De emendatione temporum, book 2, page 108 of the latest edition: "Indeed the writers," he says, "rightly call the Hagarenes from Hagar, but foolishly call the Saracens from Sara. For neither the etymology nor the history agrees. It would be true that they were named after her if she had been called Saraca, not Sara. So even today the Saracens are called by their neighbours Effarak, that is, [Λησγικοὶ and ῥομαδικοὶ], robbers and nomads, as they truly are." The same in his notes on Eusebius, on Genesis 37, where the Hebrew has "Ishmaelites," and Onkelos translates ערבאי, "Arabs," as Σαρακηνοί, Σαρακαῖοι. Stephanus says that Σάρακα is a region of Arabia bordering the Nabataeans, from which he thinks the Saracens were named. We know that the Egyptian nomads were so called. For סרק in Arabic means fierce men, robbers and plunderers, such as those whom the Turks call Cossacks or Tartars, such as the Martolossi, such as the Bandoliers in the Pyrenees. The idea about Sara is utterly ridiculous. In that case the Saracens would have to be named from Sara, or Abraham's wife would have to have been called Saraca. This opinion must be driven out of men's minds." So Scaliger. Jerome is witness to the character of that people: "The Arab nation," he says on Jeremiah 3, "given to robbery, even today raids the borders of Palestine." Ammianus, book 14, praises them with the same description. Indeed this was so characteristic of that nation that, just as "Chaldean" came to mean astrologer and "Canaanite" merchant, so "Arab" was customarily used for robber. Certainly on Jeremiah 3:2, where the Vulgate has "like an Arab in the desert," Jerome renders it "like a robber." Fuller supports this view from the Chaldean language, in Miscellanies 2.12: "סרק," he says, "is plainly the same as the Hebrew ריק and perhaps of the same origin. Both are applied to persons, with reference either to character or to fortunes. So when the Chaldee at Judges 11:3 renders אנשים ריקים, let us understand either idle and worthless men, or men leading a poor, hard and uncultivated life, such as those usually are who live by plunder. Joining these two interpretations, the ancient interpreter gave us a most learned version, complete in every respect, when he explains אנשים ריקים as 'needy and robbing,' drawing also on the common usage of the Arabic language." So Fuller.

units.la: Arabici bici usu monet: nihil verius. Inspice vel solum Scindleri Lexicon, & invenies, פּרַר furari, latrocinari. Expediam me, ubi illud addidero, Genes. 21. 13. ubi de Ismaele dicit Deus, Ponam eum in gentem, Jonathanem reddidisse, לְמַטָּה ?לַעַם in populum latrociniis deditum.
units.tr: What he notes about the usage of the Arabic language is nothing if not true. Look at Schindler's lexicon alone and you will find פּרַר: to steal, to rob. I will be done once I have added this: at Genesis 21:13, where God says of Ishmael, "I will make him a nation," Jonathan rendered it as a people [לְעַם] given over to robberies.

units.tr: CAP. XIX. 24.

units.la: Pluit DOMINVS à DOMINO.
units.tr: The LORD rained from the LORD.

units.la: Adscribam verba Rev. Martinii, quæ extant in Quæst. ejus ad Pentat. Est modus loquendi, pro eo quod est, pluit Deus à seipso, supra naturam, per miraculum, ut cap. 18. 14. & 29. 2. Tim. 1. 18. Sic plurimi veterum & recentiorum exponunt, August. Hieronym. Eucher. Chrysost. Tostatus, Cajetanus, Pagn. Vatabl. Pellic. Mercerus, Calv. Interim & hoc verum, Dei filium pluisse à patre accepta omnipotentia, Joh. 5. vers. 26. 19. Hæc Martin. Quibus addo & Pisc. Drus. Glossam interlinearem, Paræum. Certe nihil certius, quam in Ebr. nomen aliquando pronominis vice usurpari. Num. 10. 29. Psalm. 82. 1. Luc. 3.19. Interim neutiquam negantur tres personæ in divina Essentia. At argumentum, quod ex hoc loco vulgo depromitur, neutiquam firmum esse, id vero quod est intenditur.
units.tr: I will set down the words of the Reverend Martin, which are found in his Questions on the Pentateuch. It is a mode of speaking, for what is meant is "God rained from himself," beyond nature, by a miracle, as in chap. 18:14 and 29; 2 Tim. 1:18. So most of the Fathers and moderns explain it: Augustine, Jerome, Eucherius, Chrysostom, Tostatus, Cajetan, Pagninus, Vatablus, Pellicanus, Mercerus, Calvin. Meanwhile this is also true: the Son of God rained, having received omnipotence from the Father, John 5:26; 19. So far Martin. To these I add Piscator, Drusius, the interlinear gloss, and Paraeus. Certainly nothing is more certain than that in Hebrew the noun is sometimes used in place of a pronoun: Num. 10:29; Psalm 82:1; Luke 3:19. Yet the three persons in the divine essence are by no means denied. But the argument that is commonly drawn from this place is by no means firm; this is what is being contended.

units.la: CAP. XXI. 9.
units.tr: CAP. XXI. 9.

units.la: Cumque vidisset Sara filium Agar — ludentem cum Isaac filio suo.
units.tr: And Sarah saw the son of Hagar — playing with Isaac her son.

units.la: Ita vulgatus, premens vestigia ꝥ LXX. ἰδοῦσα δὲ Σάρρα τὸν υἱὸν Ἁγὰρ τῆς Αἰγυπτίας — παίζοντα μετὰ Ισαὰκ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτῆς. Et addita ad Ebræum textum illa verba cum Isaac, filio suo, & phrasis ludentem cum Isaac, valde fatigarunt veteres Interpretes. Ebræa habent, Et vidit Sara filium Hagar — פְּצָחֵק id est, ridentem, irridentem, illudentem. Hunc Ismaelis actum Paulus Galat. 4. 29. expressit per verbum ἐδίωκε, persequebatur. Nimium ergo extenuant Interpretes Ismaelis peccatum. De additamento non queror, sed illud potissimum carpo, quod verbum ludo (quandoquidoquidem eâ voce uti libebat interpreti) hoc modo construxerit. Scimus verbum פְּנֵי esse μίσον, sumiquejam in bonum, Gen.26.8. jam in malum, Gen.39.17. Novimus & illud, quàm variè hoc lusu sentiant docti, sed hic jocularem & innoxium puerorum lusum intelligi non posse, & indignatio Sarae & Dei subsecuta admonitio evincunt. Videantur hic Cajet. Oleastr. & Lyra. At phrasin hanc, ludere cum aliquo, ut ut forte de subsannatione usquam legatur, quis aliter quam de puerili lusu acceperit? Ipse certè hic interpres Gen.39. ubi vox hæcin malam partem accipitur, convertit, ut illuderet mihi. Cajet ad hunc locum, Ebraice est, facientem irridere. Non narratur Ismael ludens cum Isaac, sed faciens irridere.
units.tr: So the Vulgate, following the footsteps of the Septuagint: ἰδοῦσα δὲ Σάρρα τὸν υἱὸν Ἁγὰρ τῆς Αἰγυπτίας — παίζοντα μετὰ Ισαὰκ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτῆς. The words added to the Hebrew text, with Isaac, her son, and the phrase playing with Isaac, have greatly troubled the ancient interpreters. The Hebrew has, And Sarah saw the son of Hagar — מְצַחֵק, that is, laughing, mocking, making sport. Paul, Galatians 4:29, expressed this act of Ishmael by the verb ἐδίωκε, was persecuting. The interpreters therefore greatly minimise Ishmael's offence. I do not complain about the addition, but I chiefly find fault with the way the translator has construed the verb to play (since he chose to use that word): in this manner. We know that the word פָּנָה [sic: פְּנֵי] is sometimes taken in a good sense, Genesis 26:8, and sometimes in a bad sense, Genesis 39:17. We also know how variously the learned understand this play, but that a jocular and harmless children's game cannot be meant here is proved by Sarah's indignation and the admonition of God that followed. See here Cajetan, Oleaster and Lyra. But this phrase, to play with someone, although perhaps it is nowhere read of mockery, who would understand it otherwise than of childish play? Certainly this same translator, in Genesis 39, where the word is taken in a bad sense, renders it that he might mock me. Cajetan on this passage says: In Hebrew it is, making to mock. Ishmael is not said to be playing with Isaac, but making mockery.

units.la: Καὶ ἰδοὺ κριὸς εἷς κατεχόμενος ἐν φυτῷ σαβὲκ τ κερατων.
units.tr: And behold, a single ram held fast in a thicket by its horns [Καὶ ἰδοὺ κριὸς εἷς κατεχόμενος ἐν φυτῷ σαβὲκ τ κερατων].

units.la: Ita LXX. Latinè ita sonant, Et ecce arietem qui detinebatur in virgulto Sabek cornibus suis. Hieron. in Quæst. Ebr. castigat rediculam Eusebii Emiseni expositionem, qua Sabec exposuit hircum, qui rectis cornibus & ad carpendas arboris frondes sublimis attollitur. Videtur ille vocem Sabec non junxisse cum φυτῷ, sed cum κερατων, σαβεκ κερατων, hircus cornuum id est cornutus. Fefellit eum non intellecta vox σαβεκ, quam LXX. in versione reliquerunt. Ebræa, Et ecce arietem qui retrorsum detinebatur בַּסְבַּךְ in perplexitate cornibus suis. Vulgatus, viditque post tergum arietem inter vepres hærentem cornibus. Veteres hinc crucis præsagium seu potius typum exsculpserunt. Melito, ὁ Σὸρ & ὁ ἑβραῖος (pro κατεχόμενος) κερα-μάμενος φησὶ, ὡς σαφέστερον τύπον τὴν, φυρόν id est, Syrus & Ebraeus (pro detentus) dicunt pendens, tanquam manifestius effingens crucem. Vide in notis ad Edit. Græcam Francofurt. in folio, anni 1597. & Cl. Drusii Fragmenta veterum Interpretum pag. 103. Sed qui Ebræa norunt, judicabunt אָחַז melius reddi detentus, quàm pendens. Ibidem huc subjicitur scholion, τὸ σαβεκ, ἀφεσιν τινες ἐκδεδώκασι. οἱ δὲ, ὁρθῶς ὡς εἶναι αὐτὸ τὸ λεγόμενον, τεταγμένος ὀρθὸς ἐπαναβεβηκὼς φυλῷ. Εντεῦθεν ἡ ὀρθὸς τ κεράλων κατεχόμενος, ὡς εἶναι φανερὸν τύπον σαυρῶ. Λέγει τάχα ἡ ἐχ' ἑρμηνεύεται, ὅτι ἡ Ἐ-βραϊκὴ μία ἔσχε λέξις πολλὰ σημαίνει ἑρμηνευομένη. Πρὸς ἓς πιωθη-νομένης
units.tr: So the LXX. In Latin these words sound: And behold a ram which was held in the thicket Sabek by its horns. Jerome, in his Hebrew Questions, rebukes the silly exposition of Eusebius of Emesa, who explained Sabec as a he-goat which, with its horns upright, is lifted high to crop the leaves of a tree. Eusebius seems not to have joined the word Sabec with φυτῷ, but with κερατων: "sabek kerathon," a he-goat of horns, that is, horned. He was misled because the word σαβεκ was not understood, and the LXX left it untranslated in their version. The Hebrew reads: And behold a ram which was caught from behind בַּסְבַּךְ in a tangle by its horns. The Vulgate reads: and he saw behind his back a ram caught among thorns by its horns. From this the old writers drew a presage, or rather a type, of the cross. Melito writes that the Syrian and the Hebrew say hanging [κρεμάμενος] instead of "held," as portraying the cross more clearly. See the notes to the Greek edition, Frankfurt folio of 1597, and Drusius's Fragments of the Old Interpreters, p. 103. But those who know Hebrew will judge that אָחַז is better rendered held than hanging. Next comes a scholium: "As for sabek, some have given remission. Others rightly take it as the word itself says, standing upright, having climbed up the thicket. Hence the ram was held upright by its horns, so that it is a plain type of the cross. Perhaps the reason it is not translated is that the Hebrew word, being one word, has many meanings when translated." To those who ask, the scholium says, it is right to answer thus.

units.la: νομένης [illegible, ~12 letters] Idest, Illud σκιὰν quidam reddiderunt ἄφεσιν dimissionem, liberationem, (id vero esset similius, si שבק scriptum esset, sed imposuit illis scriptura corrupta. Scribendum enim potius fuerat σκιὰν) quidam vero ὀρθὸν erectum, ut idem valeat ac si diceretur, hircus erectus qui in virgultum inscenderat: hoc autem loco erectus cornibus detentus, ut sit manifestus typus crucis. Propter hanc vero causam in aliam linguam non convertitur, quoniam dictio Ebr. cum una sit, multa significat. Interrogantibus autem sic respondere oportet, & dicere, vocem σκιὰν interpretari sublatum. Huc usque scholion. Sed ut ridiculum est, טבך denotare ἄφεσιν, ita & plane aliena illa interpretamenta sunt, erectus, ὀρθὸν, & ἐπημένος, sublatus. Nihil enim aliud vox Ebr. significat, quam perplexitatem, in perplexo sub. arbusto, aut vepreto. Jun.in perplexitate [veprium] Corn. à Lapide, in implexis, scilicet veprium. Chald. בְּאִילָנָא in arbore. Jesa. 9. 18. כִּבְּי הַיַּעַר perplexitates sylvae. Nahum. 1. 10. סִירִים מְסֻבָּכִים spinae perplexae, intricatae. Hic ergo acquiescendum est, neque ulla etiam necessitas, ut tanquam nomen proprium arboris vel virgulti cum Lxx, Theodotione, Eucherio, Procopio, Athanasio & Ambrosio accipiamus. Frivola ergo, & aberranti versione subnixa sunt illa Procopii, Sabec species fruticis est ex quo pendebat aries. Nam cum fruticetum anterioribus pedibus conscendisset (sed ubi hoc scriptum est Procopi? nam si σκιὰν est nomen fruticis, non significat sublatum) fruticeto implicitus crucis formam pendens prae se ferebat, extentione pedum. Et illa Ambrosii, hoc est quod apparuerit Abrahae revelans futuram sui passionem corporis, quá mundum redemit, demonstrans etiam genus passionis, cum suspensum ostendit cornibus arietem. Virgultum illud patibulum crucis est. Nec non ista Athanasii quaest.98. ad Antiochum, Planta Sabec est veneranda crux. Juxta Ebraos videtur Sabec remissio esse & condonatio. Aries vero qui in Sabec harebat ad plantam, figuravit Christum pro nobis in cruce immolatum. Paulo aliter Aug. de Civit. Dei lib.16.32. qui dicit eo praefiguratum esse Christum, qui antequam immolaretur, spinis Judaicis coronatus fuit. Hinc etiam judicium ferct cordatus lector de animadversione Leonis Castrii, lib.6. Apologetici, & ad cap.29. Jesaiae, quam Corn. à Lapide subtilem vocat, Christum videlicet verbis istis ἐλὶ ἐκὶ λαμὰ σκιαχθάντι ad eandem plantam Sabec allusisse, ut indicaret, se esse illum arietem pendenpendentem atque suspensum ex arbore Sabee, quam Dominus sub typo alterius arietis pendentis ex planta Sabec Abrahae olim ostenderat. Verbum enim Sabaeani à nomine Sabec inflexum videtur. Admirentur hanc subtilitatem alii, nos scimus, hoc tacex in Ebr. scribi סבך / tacexmi autem scribi שבכתו à themate שבך / quod significat dereliquit. Mariana hoc commentum ridens dicit locum Psal. 22. sic tunc reddendum fuisse, Deus mi D. mi. cur ligasti me. Id Euangelistae adversatur.
units.tr: ...being... That is, some have rendered "remission, release" (this would be more likely if שבק were written, but a corrupt text misled them; they should rather have written "shade"), others "erect," so that it means the same as if it were said, "a he-goat erect, which had climbed into the thicket." Here, however, it is "erect, held by the horns," so that it is a manifest type of the cross. For this reason it is not converted into another language, since the Hebrew word, being one, signifies many things. Those who ask should be answered thus, by saying that the word σκιὰν is interpreted removed. So far the scholium. But just as it is ridiculous to say that טבך denotes remission, so those renderings "erect," "raised," and "lifted up" are quite alien. For the Hebrew word signifies nothing but a tangle, something entangled under a bush or in brambles. Junius renders it in a tangle [of brambles]; Cornelius a Lapide, in the entanglements, namely of brambles. The Chaldee has in the tree. Isaiah 9:18: tangles of the forest. Nahum 1:10: thorns entangled, intertwined. Here, then, we must rest content. Nor is there any necessity to take it as the proper name of a tree or shrub, as the LXX, Theodotion, Eucherius, Procopius, Athanasius and Ambrose do. Those words of Procopius are therefore frivolous and rest on a mistaken version: "Sabec is a species of shrub from which the ram hung. For when it had climbed with its forefeet into the thicket (but where is this written in Procopius? for if σκιὰν were the name of a shrub, it would not mean removed), entangled in the shrub it presented the form of a cross, hanging, with its feet stretched out." Likewise Ambrose: "This is what appeared to Abraham, revealing the future suffering of the body by which he redeemed the world, and showing also the kind of suffering, when he displayed the ram hanging by its horns. That bush is the gibbet of the cross." And Athanasius, Question 98 to Antiochus: "The plant Sabec is the venerable cross. According to the Hebrews, Sabec seems to mean remission and forgiveness. The ram that hung in Sabec by the plant prefigured Christ, sacrificed for us on the cross." Augustine, in The City of God, book 16, chapter 32, says somewhat differently that Christ was prefigured by it, since before he was sacrificed he was crowned with Jewish thorns. Hence a discerning reader may also judge the remark of Leo of Castro, in book 6 of his Apologetic, and on chapter 29 of Isaiah, which Cornelius a Lapide calls subtle: that Christ, in the words Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani [ἐλωὶ ἐλωὶ λαμὰ σαβαχθανί], alluded to the same plant Sabec, to show that he was that ram hanging and suspended from the tree Sabec, which the Lord had once shown to Abraham under the type of another ram hanging from the plant Sabec. For the Sabaean verb seems to be inflected from the name Sabec. Let others admire this subtlety; we know that tacex is written in Hebrew סבך, but tacexmi is written שבכתו from the root שבך, which means forsook. Mariana, ridiculing this invention, says that Psalm 22 should then have been rendered My God, my God, why hast thou bound me. That is contrary to the Evangelist.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. 3.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII. 3.

units.la: Cumque surrexisset Abraham * ab officio funeris.
units.tr: And when Abraham had risen * from the duty of the funeral.

units.la: Ita convertit vulgatus haec Ebraica, יקם אברהם מעל פני / מתו / Et surrexit Abraham à faciebus mortui sui. A facieb. mortui, Ebraismus est, pro, à mortuo, Ideo Graeci, νεκροῦ αὐτοῦ. Usus autem est Moses voce masc. מת / respiciens ad corpus, quod Ebraice גוף dicitur masc. genere. Abenezra, לגוף id est innuit corpus. Sensus verborum Mosis iste est, desiit tandem plangere, positoque lacrymis & luctui modo, de sepultura subiit cogitatio. Et quia luctus officium quoddam pietatis censetur, tolerari posset vox officii licet hic ab Interprete sine ulla necessitate interpolata nisi ex Pontificiis non gregarius aliquis miles, sed Romanae Sedis Atlas, isq; Ebraice non imperitus, Bellarm. ex hac versione conatur probare, in Genesi Purgatorii mentionem implicite saltem injici, Illudque proinde primis mundi seculis non fuisse ignotum. Quid prohibet, in quit, per illud officium intelligere non solum lacrymas, sed etiam orationes & jejunia, pro defunctis scilicet. Egregia certe interrogatio. Quia scilicet ab aliquot seculis inter Christianos celebrari coeperunt mortuorum officia disputat ex voce officium, cujus nec vola nec vestigium in fontibus extat. Textus itaque originarius prohibet hic officia illa intelligere. Id viderunt Corn. à Lapide, Lyra ipseque adeo Carthusianus, ac proinde Purgatorii hic non meminerunt. Mariana de amplexibus conjectat. Videtur, inquit irruisse in amplexus cadaveris. De purgatorio altum silet.
units.tr: So the Vulgate renders this Hebrew, יקם אברהם מעל פני / מתו [yaqom Avraham me'al peney / metho], as And Abraham rose up from before the faces of his dead. "From the faces of his dead" is a Hebraism for "from his dead," which is why the Greek has "from his dead" [νεκροῦ αὐτοῦ]. Moses used the masculine noun מת [met], looking to the body, which in Hebrew is called גוף [guf] and is of masculine gender. Abenezra notes that לגוף [le-guf] means the body. The sense of Moses' words is this: at last he stopped mourning, and with his tears and grief put aside, the thought of the burial came to him. Since mourning is regarded as a kind of duty of piety, the word duty could be tolerated, though here the translator has inserted it without any necessity. It is not some ordinary foot soldier but the Atlas of the Roman See, and one not unskilled in Hebrew, who is the Papist Bellarmine. From this version he tries to prove that a mention of purgatory is at least implicitly introduced in Genesis, and that it was therefore not unknown in the first ages of the world. What prevents, he says, us from understanding by that duty not only tears, but also prayers and fasts, namely for the dead. A remarkable question indeed! Since, of course, for some centuries the offices for the dead have begun to be celebrated among Christians, he argues from the word duty, of which neither the shadow nor the trace is found in the sources. The original text therefore forbids understanding those offices here. Cornelius a Lapide, Lyra, and the Carthusian himself saw this, and so they do not mention purgatory here. Mariana conjectures about embraces: he seems, it says, to have rushed into the embraces of the corpse. About purgatory he keeps a deep silence.

units.tr: * Belgic (Louvain) version: "of the service of the corpse."

units.la: Et egressus erat Isaac ἀδολεσχῆσαι εἰς τὸ πεδίον
units.tr: And Isaac went out to meditate [ἀδολεσχῆσαι] in the field

units.la: In veteri Latina Græci textus versione, Exiit Isaac exerceri in campo. Ita quoque August. in Quæst. super Genesin, quæst. 69. operæ erat doctissimum Patrem hic audire disserentem, licet suspenso gradu. Qui verbum hac de re Gracum nesciunt, inquit, exercitationem corporis putant. Scriptum enim est, ἀδολεσχῶν (at omnium codicum constans lectio est ἀδολεσχῆσαι) ἀδολεσχεῖν vero ad animi exercitationem pertinet, & sæpe vitio deputatur. More autem Scriptura plerunque in bono ponitur. Videturque mihi significare animi affectum studiosissime aliquid cogitantis, cum delectatione cogitationis, nisi aliud sentiant qui hac verba Græca melius intelligunt. Hæc Augustinus. Illud verissimum est, in literis mysticis in bono poni. Suidas, ἀδολεσχία δὲ ... Hinc vulgatus Ebræum השיח (quod per ἀδολεσχεῖν reddunt Lxx. vertere amat meditari. Extra Vet. Test. garrulitatem significat. Hesych. ἀδολεσχεῖ, φλυαρεῖ, μακρολογεῖ. Et Lexic. vetus, ἀδολεσχῶ, arguto, garrio. Atque hoc quoque sensu bis usurpavit Sirachides, 32.9. ὅπου γίγνεται, μὴ τοῖς ἀδολέσχει. & 7.15. μὴ ἀδολέσχει ἐν πολλῇ περιεργίᾳ. Cæterum quod ad præsentem locum attinet, invenio duas versiones satis commodas. 1. ad meditandum. 2. ad orandum. Cerre שיח idem est quod הגה, habetque, authore Kimchio, דבור signficationem sermonis, Sic dico, שיח significat loqui secum, aut cum alio. Qui secum loquitur, proprie meditari dicitur. Qui cum alio, vel cum Deo, vel cum homine loquitur. Qui cum Deo, precari aut orare dicitur; qui cum homine, confabulari.
units.tr: In the old Latin version, made from the Greek text, it reads: Isaac went out to exercise himself in the field. Augustine also, in his Questions on Genesis, question 69, is worth hearing here, though he proceeds with some hesitation. Those who do not know the Greek word, he says, take it to mean physical exercise. For it is written [ἀδολεσχῶν] (but the constant reading of all the manuscripts is [ἀδολεσχῆσαι]). Now ἀδολεσχεῖν pertains to exercise of the mind, and is often counted a fault. In Scripture, however, it is usually put in a good sense. It seems to me to signify the state of mind of one thinking very eagerly about something, with delight in the thought, unless those who understand these Greek words better think otherwise. So Augustine. That is most true: in mystical writings the word is used in a good sense. Suidas: [ἀδολεσχία δὲ ...]. Hence the Vulgate translator, who renders the Hebrew השיח (which the Seventy render by [ἀδολεσχεῖν]), likes to translate it meditari. Outside the Old Testament it means chattering or garrulity. Hesychius: [ἀδολεσχεῖ, φλυαρεῖ, μακρολογεῖ], that is, he chatters, babbles, talks at length. The old lexicon gives [ἀδολεσχῶ] as to chatter or gossip. The son of Sirach uses it in this sense twice: Sirach 32.9, [ὅπου γίγνεται, μὴ τοῖς ἀδολέσχει], "where it happens, do not chatter"; and 7.15, [μὴ ἀδολέσχει ἐν πολλῇ περιεργίᾳ], "do not chatter with much busybody meddling." As for the present passage, I find two fairly suitable renderings: (1) to meditate; (2) to pray. For שיח is the same as הגה, and has, according to Kimchi, the sense of discourse [דבור]. So I say that שיח means to speak to oneself, or to speak with another. One who speaks to himself is properly said to meditate. One who speaks with another, either with God or with a man, is said to pray if with God, and to converse if with a man.

units.tr: CHAP. XXXI. vers. 13.

units.la: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ ὀφθῆναί σοι ἐν τῷ τόπῳ Θεῦ. Ego sum Deus qui ibi apparui in loco Dei. Aug. Locut. Sacrarum lib. 1. hic se non expedit, nisi conjectando, esse locutionem qualis illa, Et pluit DomiDominus à Domino id est Filius à Patre. Sed nota Tiro, in Ebraeo, pro ἐν τόπῳ לִּבְיִרת אֵל, legi, בְּבִיר אֵל / Et Bethel, ὁ ἐφι μεθερμηνευόμενος, ἐν τόπῳ (seu verius ἐκ ) אֵל. Cl. Drusius Miscel. 2. cap. 85.
units.tr: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ ὀφθῆναί σοι ἐν τῷ τόπῳ Θεοῦ. "I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God." Aug. Locut. Sacrarum lib. 1. Here one cannot get out of the difficulty except by conjecture, namely that this is an expression of the same kind as "And the Lord rained from the Lord," that is, the Son from the Father. But note, Tiro, that in the Hebrew, for "in the place," one should read "Beth-El" [בֵּית אֵל], which the Interpreter renders "in the place of God" (or more truly "from God") [אֵל]. Cl. Drusius, Miscel. 2, cap. 85.

units.la: Verf. 41. Decepisti mercedem meam decem agnabus.
units.tr: Verse 41. "You have changed my wages ten lambs."

units.la: Ita laudat hunc textum B. Augustinus in Quaestionibus, quaest. 31. atque haec insuper addit. Hoc quomodo & quando factum sit, Scriptura non narrat, sed utique factum est, quod iste commemorat. Et paulo post. Decem agnos dixit decem tempora, quibus oves quas per sexennium (verf. eodem, & sex annos servivi tibi pro pecudibus tuis) pascebat, pepererunt. Bis enim pariebant in anno. At si bis peperere quotannis, oportet hoc sexennio duodecim fuisse tempora. Quomodo ergo dicit decem tempora? Hic ita se expedit Augustinus, ut dicat vel potius divinet, eas primo hujus sexennii anno jam peperisse semel ante conditionem initas, & antequam secundo parerent, anno ultimo, secessisse Jacobum. Pergit Augustinus, Nec mirum quod haec x. tempora agnorum nomine appellaverit, qui isdem temporibus nascebantur, veluti si quis dicat, pertot messes aut vindemias, quibus numerus intelligatur annorum. Unde ait quidam, post aristas id est messes id est annos, &c. Habes hic, lector, specimen supervacaneae subtilitatis. Namque in Ebraeo ita legitur, & mutasti mercedem meam עשרת מנים id est Interprete vulg. decem vicibus. Onkelos, עשר זמנין decem temporibus. Abenezra, עשרה במספר / Symm. δεκάκις ἀριθμῷ decies numero. Porro decies, putat Eusebius positum esse pro ωσπάκις. Quid ergo vidit Augustinus cum haec chartis illineret? Secutus est τως LXX. qui verba Ebraea sic reddidere, καὶ παρελλαγὴν μισθὸν μὴ δέκα ἀμνάς. Et verf. 7. δέκα ἀμνῶν. Cl. Drusius conjectabat eos scripsisse μνῶν minis, & legisse מנים illamque vocem postmodum in ἀμνῶν demigrasse. At isti conjecturae obstat verf. 41. ubi ἀμνάσι constanter legitur. Quicquid sit, versio ista probari non potest, & dum eam illustravit Augustinus oleum & operam perdidit.
units.tr: So Augustine praises this text in the Quaestiones, quaest. 31, and he adds the following. "How and when this happened, Scripture does not relate, but it certainly happened, as he records." And a little later: "He said ten lambs for ten times, in which the sheep that he tended for six years (verse 41, 'and I served you six years for your flocks') gave birth. For they bore twice in a year. But if they bore twice each year, there must have been twelve times in these six years. How then does he say ten times?" Here Augustine gets himself out of the difficulty by saying, or rather guessing, that in the first year of this sixth-year period the sheep had already given birth once before the agreement was made, and that in the last year, before they could give birth a second time, Jacob withdrew. Augustine continues: "Nor is it surprising that he called these ten times of the lambs by the name of the lambs, since they were born at the same times, just as if someone should say, so many harvests or vintages, by which the number of years is understood. Hence a certain man says, after the ears of grain, that is, the harvests, that is, the years, etc." Here, reader, you have an example of useless subtlety. For in the Hebrew it reads, "and you have changed my wages" [עשרת מנים], that is, as the Vulgate interpreter renders it, "ten times." Onkelos: [עשר זמנין] "ten times." Abenezra: [עשרה במספר] "ten in number." Symmachus: [δεκάκις ἀριθμῷ] "ten times in number." Moreover Eusebius thinks that "decies" is used for [ὁσπάκις], "as often as." What, then, did Augustine see when he daubed these pages? He followed the Seventy, who rendered the Hebrew words thus: [καὶ παρήλλαξας τὸν μισθόν μου δέκα ἀμνάς], and in verse 7 [δέκα ἀμνῶν]. Drusius conjectured that they wrote [μνῶν], "minas," and read [מנים], and that this word afterwards slipped over into [ἀμνῶν]. But that conjecture is opposed by verse 41, where [ἀμνάσι] is consistently read. Whatever the case, this version cannot be defended, and while Augustine was illustrating it he wasted both oil and labour.

units.la: CAP. XXXII. verf. 28.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXII. vers. 28.

units.la: Non dicetur ultra nomen tuum Iacob, sed Israel.
units.tr: "Your name shall no more be called Jacob, but Israel."

units.la: Circa vocis Ebraicæ originationem valde sudârunt Patres, qui si fontes consulere quivissent, facillimè se expe divissent. Ecce n. hoc eodem versu redditur ratio hujus tranominationis, כִּי שָׂרִיתָ עִם Vox ergo Israel composita est ex אֵל Deus & שָׂרָה cum punćto in sinistro cornu, quod significat, principem esse, instar principis se gerere, de principatu contendere. Jun. Nam ut principem te geris, Drusius, deprincipatu contendisti cum Deo & hominibus & prapotuisti. Errarunt ergo Patres, & sono vocis, prout vulgò exprimitur, semidocti quidam Ebraei decepti sunt, qui Israel interpretantur rectus Dei. Quod ab ipso Hieron. viro Ebraicè peritissimo non animadversum miror Proprie juxta Ebraeos inquit, & literarum fidem Israel rectus Dei dicitur. Fallit & fallitur, inquit Cl. Drusius, nam Israel punctum in cornu sinistro habet, autem id est rectus in dextro in quâ censurâ Drusio quoque astipulatur Corn. à Lapide & assentientur quotquot Ebraismũ vel à limine, quod ajunt, salutârunt. Errant & illi, qui vocem illam sic explicant, a Mens videns Deum, b Vir videns Deum, c Est videns Deum, d Videns Deum, e Vincens potentiam. Ajo in his Interpretamentis nihil esse mentis. In voce Ebr. nihil est, quod mentem significet, & אִישׁ vir, יִשְׂרָאֵל est, scribuntur cum שׁ non שׂ / ut planè vox Ebraea non possit resolvi in has אִישׁ רֹאֶה אֵל vel אִישׁ רֹאֶה אֵל / Ut autem nihil aliud valeat, quàm videns Deum, non patitur litera שׁ quæ hic non potest esse aditicia. Planè autem ridiculum est, quod Iustinus asserit, Isra significare virum. Communissimam tamen ex his omnibus illam fuisse interpretationem, vir videns Deum, his verbis docet Hieron. in traditionibus Ebraicis, Illud autem quod in libro nominum interpretatur, Vir videns Deum, sive, mens Deum, omnium penè sermonibus detritum, non tam verè quam violenter mihi interpretatum videtur. Et paucis interjectis, quamvis igitur grandi authoritatis sint & eloquentia, & ipsorum umbra nos opprimat, qui Israel, virum Dei, transtulerunt, nos magis scripturæ & angeli vel Dei, qui ipsum Israel vocavit, authoritate ducimur, quàm cujuslibet eloquentia secularis. Vide nunc notas Drusii ad Sulp. Sev. pag. 66.
units.tr: The Fathers laboured hard over the derivation of the Hebrew word, and if they had been able to consult the sources they would have got out of the difficulty very easily. For in this same verse the reason for this wordplay is given: [כִּי שָׂרִיתָ עִם], "for you have striven with God and with men." The word Israel is therefore compounded of [אֵל], God, and [שָׂרָה], with a point in the left horn, which signifies to be a prince, to conduct oneself as a prince, to contend for dominion. Junius: "For you bear yourself as a prince; Drusius, you have contended for dominion with God and men and have prevailed." The Fathers therefore erred, and certain semi-learned Hebrews, deceived by the sound of the word as it is commonly pronounced, interpret "Israel" as "the upright of God." Jerome, a man most skilled in Hebrew, did not notice this, which I marvel at: "Properly, according to the Hebrews," he says, "and the faith of the letters, Israel is called 'the upright of God.'" Drusius replies: "He is mistaken and misleads, for Israel has the point in the left horn, but the upright is [יָשָׁר] with the point in the right." In this judgement Cornelius à Lapide also agrees with Drusius, and all who have greeted Hebrew, as they say, from the threshold, will agree. Those also err who explain the name in this way: a "mind seeing God," b "man seeing God," c "is seeing God," d "seeing God," e "conquering power." I say there is nothing of the mind in these interpretations. There is nothing in the Hebrew word that means "mind," and [אִישׁ], "man," and [יִשְׂרָאֵל], "is," are written with שׁ, not שׂ; so the Hebrew word cannot plainly be resolved into [אִישׁ רֹאֶה אֵל] or similar forms. And that it can mean nothing other than "seeing God," the letter שׁ does not allow, since here it cannot be an addition. It is plainly ridiculous, however, that Justin asserts Isra signifies "man." Yet Jerome shows by these words, in his Hebrew traditions, that the most common interpretation of all of them was "man seeing God": "But that which in the Book of Names is interpreted 'man seeing God,' or 'mind of God,' worn down by almost everyone's talk, seems to me to be interpreted not so much truly as violently. And a few lines later: "Although, therefore, those who translated Israel as 'man of God' are of great authority and eloquence, and their shadow overwhelms us, we are led rather by the authority of Scripture and of the angel, or of God, who himself called him Israel, than by the eloquence of any secular writer." Now see the notes of Drusius on Sulpicius Severus, p. 66.

units.la: Ita legunt Graeci codices. Καὶ ἤκουσεν Ιακωβ ὅτι ἐμίανεν ὁ υἱὸς Εμμωρ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ, Et audivit Jacob, quod filius Hemor temerasset (seu depudicasset) Dinam filiam ejus. Verba illa, ὁ υἱὸς Εμμωρ quia sunt ex glossemate, olim obelo fuerunt confossa. At Procopius Gazaeus existimavit, obelum istum tantum pertinere ad vocem υἱὸς, non ad duas illas, υἱὸς Εμμωρ. Ebraicum exemplar, inquit, non habet filius Hemor, sed sola dictio Hemor in Ebraeo ponitur. Erras, Procopi erras. Nec filius Hemor, nec Hemor in Ebraeo legitur, sed Sichem filius Hemor intelligitur. Sic enim sonant Ebraea, וַיִּשְׁמַע יַעֲקֹב כִּי טִמֵּא אֶת־דִּינָה בִתּוֹ / Et audivit Jakob quod temerasset filiam suam Dinam, sub. Sichem filius Hemor. Credidit ergo Procopius, Ebraea sic legi, Et audivit J. quod Hemor temerasset filiam ejus Dinam. Unde conjectare possumus, inquit, non filium solum sed & Patrem concubuisse cum Dina, quod quidem gravissimum piaculum censebatur. Certe nimis temere tam infandi sceleris reum peragis bonum Principem Procopi, nam & illa, quae postea subjicit, non satis fuerint convincendo homini. Huic sensui videtur congruere, inquis, quod infra dictum est verf. 13. Responderunt filii Jacob, Sichem & Hemor, & collocuti sunt cum iis dolo, quia polluerant Gr. ἐμίαναν) sororem ipsorum. Ecce ibidem ponitur pluralis numerus, quasi uterque objecerint stuprum virgini. Et iterum, nunquid ut scorto utentur sorore nostra? Gr. ἀλλ' ὡς πόρνῃ χρήσονται τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν. Ajo non utrobique rursus singulare est in Ebraeo. Et quidem verf. 13. יִנָּם / ἐμίανε, versu vero ultimo יַעֲשֶׂה faceret, an tanquam cum scorto ageret cum sorore nostro? Validius longe argumentum desumfisset ex verf. 27. quia טִמְּאוּ temeraverant Dinam. Hic in Ebr. est plurale, sed vel per Enallagen adhibitum pro singulari, ut, Mortui sunt qui quaerebant animam tuam, Exod. 4. de Pharaone, & Math. 2. de Herode, vel ex ea loquendi consuetudine, qua factum unius, praesertim principis, toti societati tribuitur, juxta illud, Quicquid delirant Reges plectuntur Achivi. Certe omnes unius noxam exitio luerunt, tanquam si omnes rei fuissent.
units.tr: So the Greek manuscripts read: Καὶ ἤκουσεν Ιακωβ ὅτι ἐμίανεν ὁ υἱὸς Εμμωρ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ ["And Jacob heard that the son of Hemor had defiled his daughter"], "And Jacob heard that the son of Hemor had defiled (or dishonoured) his daughter Dinah." Because the words ὁ υἱὸς Εμμωρ ["the son of Hemor"] are a gloss, they were once marked with an obelus. But Procopius of Gaza thought that this obelus applied only to the word υἱὸς ["son"], not to the two words υἱὸς Εμμωρ. The Hebrew copy, he says, does not have "son of Hemor," but only the word Hemor is put in the Hebrew. You are wrong, Procopius, you are wrong. Neither "son of Hemor" nor "Hemor" is read in the Hebrew, but "Shechem son of Hemor" is what is meant. For the Hebrew reads: וַיִּשְׁמַע יַעֲקֹב כִּי טִמֵּא אֶת־דִּינָה בִתּוֹ ["And Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah"], "And Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah," the subject being Shechem son of Hemor. Procopius therefore believed that the Hebrew was read thus: "And Jacob heard that Hemor had defiled his daughter Dinah." From this, he says, we may conjecture that not only the son but also the father had lain with Dinah, which was considered a most grievous crime. Certainly you are too rash in charging the good prince Procopius with so unspeakable a crime, for even what he adds afterwards would not be enough to convince anyone. This sense, you say, seems to agree with what is said below at verse 13: "The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hemor, and spoke to them deceitfully, because they had defiled" (Greek ἐμίαναν ["they had defiled"]) "their sister." Here the plural is used, as if both had charged the virgin with rape. And again: "Shall they deal with our sister as with a harlot?" Greek: ἀλλ' ὡς πόρνῃ χρήσονται τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν ["but will they treat our sister as a harlot?"]. I say that the Hebrew is again singular on both occasions. Indeed, in verse 13 the Hebrew is יִנָּם ["he defiled"] (Greek ἐμίανε ["he defiled"]), and in the last verse יַעֲשֶׂה ["he would do"]: "would he deal with our sister as with a harlot?" You would have drawn a much stronger argument from verse 27, "because they had defiled" (Hebrew טִמְּאוּ) "Dinah." There the Hebrew is plural, but it is used either by enallage for the singular, as in "They are dead who sought your life," Exodus 4, of Pharaoh, and in Matthew 2 of Herod, or from that manner of speaking by which the deed of one man, especially a prince, is attributed to the whole community, according to that line: "Whatever mad things kings do, the Achaeans pay for." Certainly all of them paid with their lives for the guilt of one man, as if they had all been guilty.

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Descendam lugens [Hebrew] | Descendam lugens ad filium meum in infernum.
units.tr: Heb. | Vulg. I will go down mourning [Hebrew] | I will go down mourning to my son into hell.

units.la: Vox Ebraea indifferens est tam ad infernum quam ad sepulchrum, unde voces Infernus & Ades apud Interpretes saepe pro sepulchro ponuntur. Taxamus tamen hunc locum, tum quia hac ambiguitate apud imperitam plebem ad stabiliendum fictitium suum limbum abutantur, tum quia nuper vidimus à Ἀπολογητὴς Monacho hinc criterium haereticorum Bibliorum cusum. Hanc enim inter alias ponit notam διαικεχαιρω, quod ubi Catholica habent, in infernum, Gen. 37. haeretica habeant in sepulcrum. Haereticus ergo tibi est b Arias Montanus? Haereticus Paginus, c Joh. Benedictus, Parisiensis; Theologus ille, ut Senensis de eo asserit, celeberrimus. Atque hîc in limine sistet me forsan aliquis ex eorum genere, qui nodos cum solvere desperant, secent, negabitque vocem Ebr. unquam significare sepulcrum. Ex quibus sunt i Crocquetius, Stapleton. Mart. Delrio, in Adagialibus V. T. tomo primo. His addi posset k Bellarm. nisi unica vocula semet ipsum ab illorum consortio separasset. Sed quid nobis hic probatione opus est? Dedimus jam testes & advocatos Pag. Mont. & Joh. Benedictum, dol Lovanienses Doctores qui Biblia Interlin. approbarunt. Dom Sixtum Senensem, qui cum multa in n Steuchum nobis hic consentientem notavarit, hoc tamen reliquit intactum. Dedit jam ante Cl. o Rainoldum p Ferum, q Oleastrum Inquisitorem Hisp. q Cajetanum. q Lippomanum, q Clarium, qui omnes docent hoc loco sepulcrum denotari. Quid adversus hanc tantorum testium nubem excipies Lancelotte? Et quandoquidem in titulo tuo adeo tibi placuisse videris, quodnam QUIA repones ad hoc meum QUARE? Sed ex superfluo alia aliquot loca proferam, ubi vestrorum etiam judicio vox haec controversa non aliter quam pro sepulcro sumi post. Psal. 141. 7. dispersa sunt ossa nostra in [Hebrew] id est sepulcrum, teste Genebr. Joh. 17. 23. Si Scheol domum meam expectavero id est sepulcrum, quod ipse s Tomas & Lyra. Lyra fatentur. Sic verf. ult. In profundissimum infernum descendent omnia mea. Quin & locum Num. 16. ubi seditiosi illi vivi dicuntur descendisse שאול / urgent Cajet. & Oleastrius, & locum Prov. 15. Episc. Gandavensis Jansenius· Quibus omnibus addo i Riberam Jesuitam, cujus haec sunt, Infernus pro sepulchro sumitur & in infernum descendere pro sepeliri. Et u Andradium ad locum Psal 16. & Emanuelem Sa in phrasibus Scripturae, quas ad notationes suas adjecit, ubi xxvi. locorum inductione ostendit infernum pro sepulcro seu morte sumi. Accedat & Lorinus Jesuita in cap. 2. Actorum, verf. 24. & Eccl. 9. Et Sanctius Jesuita in Jesaiam & Christoph. à Castro Baruch. 2.6. Verba ejus haec sunt, Inferorum nomine licet aliqui velint intelligi sinum Abrahae, verius tamen & usui Scripturae conformius accipiemus sepulcrum: ut accepit Jacob Gen. 37.35. cum dixit, Descendam lugens ad filium meum in infernum, hoc est, lugere non desinam, donec me sepultura mandetis. Quid jam dices Lancelotte? Imo quid tu sociennis tuis respondebis Del-rio? Non satis est dicere eos mustea sectari, animo non satis cauto, & minus attentos esse ad fraudes Haereticorum. Scilicet tu solus sapis, ὁ δὲ σχιαὶ ἀιάτων Tu solus acutum cernis instar aquilae vel serpentis Epidaurii, illorum vero oculos Saturninae lemae vitiarunt. Non satis est exclamare, Cur non omnes potius Catholici unaniniter Calvinistae obviam tendimus & resistimus, potius quam novis istis versionibus suppetias imus malitiae perfidorum? Scilicet Hannibal est ad portas & in hoc loco de fortunis universi Papatus certatur. Nae tu nimis ferox & imperiosus es Delrio. Non ejusmodi clamoribus sed argumentis agendum erat. Videamus ergo quo argumento Cardinalis vester Bellarm. significationem Limbi (qui pars inferni erat) tueatur. z Non potest accipi de sepulchro, qua dicit se iturum AD filium suum, quem putabat devoratum à feris & proinde caruisse sepulchro. Huic terribili argumento crus dextrum fractum ex R. a Salomone Jarchio, & Hiscuni, qui notant hoc loco אל ad poni pro על propter. Et tunc argumentum Bellarm. alto à culmine ruit. Quin ostendit hoc ipsum Rabbinus ille exemplis, אל שאול propter Saul, אל בית הדמים propter domum sanguinum, quae occurrunt 2. Sam. 21.1. Licet autem argumentum illud à Posse aliter accipi in objiciendo non procedat, in respondendo tamen vim magnam habet. Stabit enim hæc responsio, usque dum Adversarius ostenderit אל hoc loco pro על accipi non posse. Alterum frangit solidissimè solidissimus, Rianoldus, dum ostendit & exemplis probat, sepelire (cujus conjugatum est sepulcrum) catachrestice sæpe in script. & profanis usurpari pro, terræ reddere. Mecœnas, cætera effæminatus, hoc unum masculè dixisse perhibetur,
units.tr: The Hebrew word is ambiguous: it means the grave as well as hell, which is why the words Infernus and Ades are often used by the translators for the sepulchre. We censure this passage, however, first because the Papists use this ambiguity to shore up their invented limbo among the ignorant common people, and second because we have recently seen the criterion of heretical Bibles stamped out by the monk of the Apologist. Among other marks he lists diaikechairō: wherever Catholic Bibles have in infernum (Gen. 37), heretical ones have in sepulcrum. So is Arias Montanus a heretic for you? Is Pagninus a heretic, or Jean Benedict of Paris, that most famous theologian, as Sixtus of Siena says of him? Perhaps someone of that sort will stop me here, one who despairs of untying knots and so cuts them, and will deny that the Hebrew word ever means sepulchre. Among these are Crocquet and Stapleton, and Martin del Rio in the first volume of his Adagia on the Old Testament. Bellarmine could be added to them, if one little word had not separated him from their company. But why do we need proof here? We have already produced as witnesses and advocates Pagninus, Montanus and Jean Benedict, and the Louvain doctors who approved the Interlinear Bible. Sixtus of Siena, who notes many things against Steuchus (who agrees with us here), left this point untouched. Before them, the distinguished Rainolds had already cited Ferus, Oleaster the Spanish Inquisitor, Cajetan, Lippomano and Clarius, all of whom teach that the sepulchre is meant in this place. What will you, Lancelot, say against this cloud of so great witnesses? And since you seem to have been so pleased with your title, Why a Heretic, Because a Catholic, what QUIA will you set against my QUARE? But beyond what is needed, I will cite some other passages where, even by your own judgment, this disputed word is taken only for the sepulchre. Psalm 141.7: "our bones are scattered at the mouth of [Hebrew]", that is, the sepulchre, as Genebrard testifies. Job 17.13: "If I wait for Sheol as my house", that is, the sepulchre, as Thomas and Lyra themselves admit. So too the last verse: "All that is mine shall go down into the deepest hell", which Thomas explains as the sepulchre. Indeed, Cajetan and Oleaster also argue that the passage in Numbers 16, where the rebellious men are said to have gone down alive into Sheol, must be understood this way, as does the bishop of Ghent, Jansenius, for Proverbs 15. To all of these I add the Jesuit Ribera, whose words are: "Hell is taken for the sepulchre, and to go down into hell is to be buried." Also Andrade on Psalm 16, and Emmanuel Sá in his notes on the phrases of Scripture, where by a survey of twenty-six passages he shows that hell is taken for the sepulchre or for death. Add also the Jesuit Lorinus on Acts 2.24 and Ecclesiastes 9, and the Jesuit Sanctius on Isaiah, and Christoph. à Castro on Baruch 2.6. His words are these: "Although some wish the name of the underworld to be understood as the bosom of Abraham, we shall take it more truly and more in keeping with the usage of Scripture as the sepulchre, as Jacob understood it in Genesis 37.35 when he said, 'I will go down mourning to my son into hell', that is, 'I will not cease to mourn until you hand me over to burial.'" What will you say now, Lancelot? Indeed, what will you answer your comrade Del Rio? It is not enough to say that they follow mustea with too little caution and are too little attentive to the frauds of the heretics. Clearly you alone are wise, ho de skiai aiatōn: you alone see sharply like an eagle or the Epidaurian serpent, while their eyes have been dimmed by the Saturnian cataract. It is not enough to cry out, "Why do we Catholics not all rather unanimously make a stand against the Calvinists and resist them, rather than bringing help to the new versions and the malice of the faithless?" Clearly Hannibal is at the gates, and in this passage the fortunes of the whole Papacy are at stake. Truly you are too fierce and overbearing, Del Rio. This matter had to be dealt with not by such outcries but by arguments. Let us see, then, by what argument your cardinal Bellarmine defends the meaning of limbo, which was part of hell: "It cannot be understood of the sepulchre, since he says that he will go to his son, whom he thought devoured by wild beasts and therefore without a sepulchre." Against this formidable argument Rabbi Solomon Jarchi and Hiskuni have broken its right leg, noting that in this place el, "to", is put for al, "on account of". And then Bellarmine's argument falls from its high summit. Indeed that same rabbi shows this by examples: el Shaul, "on account of Saul", and el bet hadamim, "on account of the house of bloods", which occur in 2 Samuel 21.1. Although that argument, "it can be understood otherwise", does not hold when raised as an objection, it has great force in the reply. For this answer will stand until the adversary shows that el cannot be taken in this place for al. The other argument is most solidly broken by the most solid Rainolds, who shows by examples that to bury (of which sepulchre is the derivative) is often used catachrestically in Scripture and in profane writers for to return to the earth. Maecenas, otherwise effeminate, is said to have spoken manfully on this one point:

units.la: Nec tumulum curo, sepelit natura relictos.
units.tr: I do not care for a tomb; nature buries the abandoned.

units.la: c Seneca, Omnibus natura sepulturam dedit, naufragos idem fluctus, qui expulit, sepelit; suffixorum corpora crucibus in sepulturam defluunt, eos, qui vivi uruntur, pœna funerat. Sed quid clarius loco d Jerem. de Jojakim, Sepultura asini sepelietur. Sepelietur, terræ reddendus: Sepultura asini, non terra condendus. En insepultam sepulturam. Si sic sumitur sepelire, quid obstet, quominus sic ejus conjugatum sumi queat, Adversario monstrandum fuisset.
units.tr: Seneca: "Nature has given burial to all: the same waves that cast up the shipwrecked also bury them; the bodies of those fixed to crosses are dissolved into burial; those who are burned alive are dispatched by their punishment." But what is clearer than the passage of Jeremiah about Jehoiakim, "He shall be buried with the burial of an ass"? "He shall be buried" means he is to be given back to the earth; but "the burial of an ass" means he is not to be laid in the earth. Behold an unburied burial. If "to bury" is taken in this way, the Adversary should have been shown what prevents its cognate from being taken in the same way.

units.la: a Lanceletto in suo Hæretico quare & Catholico quia. b Vide Bibl. Interlin. c Vide Biblia Vulg. cum notis margin. Joh. Ben. Parisi. in sol. 1565. d Andreas Crocquetius Benedictinus Theol. Licent in Catechesibus suis confectis ex Catecheticis homiliis Math. Galeni apud Duacenses quondam Cancellarii & primarii Professoris. Cath. 19. sic ait, Et ne vehementius sibi placeant ob suum illud Sheol, nunquam efficient ut uno saltem Scriptura loco prolato praclaram illam interpretationem sepuleri confirmeut. k De Christo lib. 4. cap. 10. art. 4. Vox Sheol vel raro vel nunquam accipitur pro sepulcro. l A. Hunnæum. Corn. Goudanum, Joh. Harlemium. m Biblioth. lib. 5. n Epist. Xiphilini & Bibliotheca Apostolic. ejus verba hæc sunt ad hunc ipsum Genesios locum, Ubicunque Hieron. & LXX. interpretati sunt infernum, Ebraice est Sheol id est fossa sive sepulcrum. Et paulo post, quare non proprie inferos significat Sheol.
units.tr: a Lanceletto, in his Heretic Why and Catholic Because. b See the Interlinear Bible. c See the Vulgate Bible with marginal notes by John Benedict of Paris, folio, 1565. d Andreas Crocquetius, Benedictine, licentiate in theology, in his Catechisms, compiled from the catechetical homilies of Matthew Galen, once Chancellor and chief Professor at Douai, Catechism 19, says: "And lest they take too much pleasure in their Sheol, they will never manage to confirm that famous interpretation of a sepulchre by producing even one passage of Scripture." k In On Christ, book 4, chapter 10, article 4: "The word Sheol is taken for a sepulchre either rarely or never." l Against A. Hunnaeus, Cornelius Goudanus, John Harlemius. m Library, book 5. n In the letter of Xiphilinus and in his Apostolic Library, his words on this very passage of Genesis are: "Wherever Jerome and the Septuagint translated infernus, the Hebrew is Sheol, that is, a ditch or a sepulchre." And a little later: "why does Sheol not properly signify the underworld?"

units.la: Deinde laudat Abenezram culpantem Chaldæum Interpretem quod Gehennam verterrit, atque cum varia loca citare, ex quibus cognosceatur Sheol semper sepulcrum denotare. Ac denique sic concludit, hac concludimus nulla facientes ea quæ hæc de re summa ldom. Vere enim figmenta sunt quæ de limbo scribit hoc loco, o Ceni lib. Apocr. lect. 8o. p In comm. ad hunc locum, quamvis descendere ad inferos nihil aliud sit apud Ebræos quam sepeliri, mori & in foveam ire. q Omnes in comm. ad hunc locum. Aldo Marianam, Tagninus, inquit, & Leo Juda pro inferno sepulcrum posuere. Neque hoc loco multum referebat. Id significare vult, moriar, nam mortuo filio non possum vivere. r Comm. ad Psal. istum. s Thomas præl. 2. in 17. caput Jobi ad vers. ult. quicquid meum est ad sepulcrum deducetur. Ecce profundissimum infernum exponit de sepulcro. Quam pulcre his consonant verba Bellarm. de Ch. isto lib. 4. cap. 10. §. 1. profundissimum infernum opponi altissimo cælo: Sepulcrum autem non abesse a terra duobus palmis aut paucis ultra, ut §. 2. locutus est. t Comm. in Hos. cap. 6. & Indice in comm. suum in minores proph. titulo, infernus. u Defensione Concilii Tridentini libro secundo. y De Christo lib. 4. cap. 10. §. 4. z Idem loco citato. a Verba ejus, הרבה אל שמשמשין כלשון על multa reperiuntur El, qua feruntur in significatione propter- b Lect. 8o. censura in libros Apocr. c Controvers. lib. 8- contr. 4. d Jerem. 22.19.
units.tr: Then he praises Abenezra, who blames the Chaldee interpreter for rendering it Gehenna, and cites various passages from which it may be known that Sheol always denotes a sepulchre. And finally he concludes thus: "we conclude, making nothing of those things which..." For indeed they are fictions that he writes about limbo in this place. o Ceni, Censure of the Apocryphal Books, lecture 8. p In his commentary on this passage: "although to go down to the underworld means nothing else among the Hebrews than to be buried, to die and to go into the pit." q All in their commentary on this passage. Aldo Mariana: "Tagninus," he says, "and Leo Judah have put a sepulchre for hell. Nor did it matter much in this place. He means this: I shall die, for if my son is dead I cannot live." r In his commentary on that Psalm. s Thomas, prelection 2 on the last verse of chapter 17 of Job: "whatever is mine will be led down to the sepulchre." Behold, he explains the deepest hell as a sepulchre. How beautifully do the words of Bellarmine in book 4, chapter 10, §1 of his work on Christ agree with this, where he sets the deepest hell against the highest heaven, and says that a sepulchre is not more than two palms or a few more from the earth, as he said in §2. t Commentary on Hosea, chapter 6, and in the index to his commentary on the minor prophets, under the heading infernus. u In the Defence of the Council of Trent, book 2. y On Christ, book 4, chapter 10, §4. z The same, in the passage cited. a His words: harbeh el shemeshim kilshon al, "many El are found, which are used in the sense of..." b Lecture 8, censure of the Apocryphal books. c Controversies, book 8, controversy 4. d Jeremiah 22:19.

units.la: Cum inveniri non posset Thamar, cui hœdum ex pacto per amicum mittebat Judas, apud quam arrhabonis loco reliquerat annulum, cidarin & pedum suum, sic loquitur ad amicum: Habeat sibi, ne forte simus in contemptum: q. d. malo rerum istarum jacturam facere, quam ulterius quærendo vulgo plebique materiem male de me loquendi præbere. Vulgatus autem longe à verbis sensuque Judæ aberrans sic vertit, Habeat sibi, certe mendacii nos arguere non potest. Ex quibus verbis Thomas secundâ secundæ coneludit, quod homines interdum faciant sibi conscientiam majorem de culpa minori, quàm graviori. Quemadmodum Judas de mendacio quod non est semper mortale, quàm de fornicatione, quod semper est mortale, loquendo de eâ formaliter. Hæc descripsimus ex Carthusiani commentariis, qui hæc immediatè subjungit, Porro, ut recitat Lyra, in Hebræo habetur, Habeat, ne forte simus despectui, &c. Et ingenuè Steuchus ad textum vulgatum inquit, Hebraice is sensus non est. Hæc enim aliud sonant. Idem Card. Cajetanus notavit, Satius ergo fuisset LXX. vestigia pressisse, qui optime & fidelissime, μὴ ὡσὶ καταγελασθῶμεν. Sic & Chald. Quid & Aquila & Symm. μήποτε γενώμεθα εις ἐξουδένωσιν. Unde & Mercerus, alias sic satis indulgens excusationi hujus Interpretis, ad hunc locum coactus fuit asserere, parum fideliter hunc locum redditum ab Interprete.
units.tr: When Tamar, to whom Judah had sent the kid through a friend according to agreement, and with whom he had left as a pledge his ring, cord and staff, could not be found, he speaks thus to his friend: Let her keep them for herself, lest we become an object of contempt: that is, he would rather suffer the loss of these things than, by searching further, give the common people material for speaking ill of me. But the Vulgate, wandering far from the words and sense of Judah, renders it thus: Let her keep them for herself; surely she cannot charge us with lying. From these words Thomas, in the Secunda Secundae, concludes that men sometimes have a greater sense of guilt over a lesser fault than over a graver one: just as Judah (speaking of a lie, which is not always mortal) feels it more than fornication, which is always mortal when considered formally. I have taken this from the commentaries of the Carthusian, who immediately adds: Moreover, as Lyra reports, the Hebrew has: Let her keep them, lest we be despised, etc. And Steuchus candidly remarks on the Vulgate text: The Hebrew does not have this sense; for these words sound otherwise. Cardinal Cajetan likewise noted that it would have been better to follow the footsteps of the Seventy, who most correctly and faithfully render it: lest we be mocked [μὴ ὡσὶ καταγελασθῶμεν]. So also the Chaldee paraphrast. And Aquila and Symmachus: lest we become an object of contempt [μήποτε γενώμεθα εις ἐξουδένωσιν]. Hence even Mercerus, who in other places is quite indulgent toward the excuses for this translator, was forced at this passage to assert that the passage has been rendered by the translator with too little fidelity.
