units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Vocavit nomen Iosephi ... | Vocavitque eum Salvatorem mundi
units.tr: Hebrew | Vulgate. He called the name of Joseph ... | And he called him Saviour of the world.

units.la: Solent reges iis quos ad honores summos sublimârunt, nova indere nomina, ut hoc loco Pharaonem fecisse legimus. Voces istæ plane Ægyptiacæ censendæ sunt, ut ut prima cum Ebr ... coincidere videatur ratione thematis. Illud enim certo certius est, Ægyptiacam, Punicam, Abrabicam cæterasque que illas Orientales, Ebraeæ matris dialectos esse, admodumque affines, id quod in Arabicis ex Lexico Scindleri, qui themata vocesque Abrabicis characteribus expressit, quivis etiam Arabismi plane ignarus viderit. Quid ergo mirum si in Agypt. tres radicales Ebraeæ vocis retentæ? Sic ab Ebr. נצר fit Arabicum נצר / Sic ab ארץ fit ארץ ardon. Sic à מים & מי fit Ægypt. ıɔ / unde Moab interpretantur aqua patris. Sic Ægyptii Monachos (si non fallit nos Erasmus in Hieron. de custod. Virgin. ad Eustochium) vocarunt Nonnos (unde apud nos mansit Nonna id est monialis) id est filios, ab Ebr. נ׳ / quomodo eorum præfectos vocamus Abbates id est Patres. Hæc ideo adduximus, ut eorum fundamentum everteremus, qui ut versionem Vulgati Interpretis quæ hic habet Salvatorem mundi, defendant, pertinaciter contendunt, has voces, quæ Ægyptiæ sunt (quod libenter damus) non posse significare id quod Ebraei tanto consensu, Chald. Philo, Theod. &c. tradiderunt. Cum enim vox prima צפנת ad thema magnæ matris Ebraeæ reduci possit, quod significat, abscondit, occultavit, occultaeque hujus rei interpretatio huic nominis mutationi occasionem dederit, cur non præferemus Interpretationem eorum, qui occulta, abscondita vertunt? Quâ significatione admissâ sponte se prodit Interpretatio nominis alterius, sive explanatorem, sive revelatorem, sive scientem sive inventorem sive Interpretem vertas. Philo enim vertit ἐνσκρίπτω & κρυπτῶν ἐυρετῶ. Syrus juxta Scholion ad Bibl. Rom. εἴδως τὰ κρυπτά. Theod. ἐμφανεύτην Josephus κρυπτῶν εὑρετής. Onkelos, cui retecta occulta sunt. Jonath. occultorum Interpres. R. Sal. מפרש הצפונות enarrator occultorum. R. Levi, qui arcanorum scientiam habet. Hieron. quoque in Quaest. fatetur Ebraice sonare repertorem abscondentorum, sed Ægyptiacè, Salvatorem mundi. Verum dicat mihi aliquis, utra vox prior an posterior mundum vel Salvatorum significat. monstret quispiam ullum vestigium harum signif. ex lingua Ægypt. afferant vel unam conjecturam quæ versioni isti robur addat, & lubentes eam admittemus, utpote quæ magis factura esset ad mysterium Christi, cujus Josephum in plerisque typum tradidit antiquitas. Lyra ingenuè, Virum idem nomen in lingua Æg. significet Salvatorem mundi, nescio, nisi quantum dicit nostra translatio. Mariana, Ego voces, ut sunt in Ebr. intactas relinquerem, ne cujusquam interpretationi praejudicaretur. Non probat ergo additamentum vulgati Interpretis.
units.tr: Kings are accustomed to give new names to those whom they have raised to the highest honours, as we read that Pharaoh did here. These words must be regarded as purely Egyptian, although the first one may seem to agree with the Hebrew in its root. For it is more than certain that the Egyptian, Punic, Arabic and the other Oriental tongues are dialects of the Hebrew mother tongue and closely related to it. Anyone who is even slightly acquainted with Arabic can see this from the lexicon of Schindler, who expressed the roots and words of Arabic in Arabic characters. So what is surprising if three radical letters of the Hebrew word were kept in the Egyptian? Thus from the Hebrew נצר [natsar] comes the Arabic נצר; from ארץ [erets] comes ardon; from מים and מי [mayim, mi] comes the Egyptian ıɔ, whence they interpret Moab as aqua patris. So the Egyptians called monks (if Erasmus does not mislead us in his work on the keeping of virginity, addressed to Eustochium) Nonnos, whence among us the word nonna, that is a nun, has remained; the Egyptian word means sons, from the Hebrew נ׳ [ben]. In the same way we call their superiors abbates, that is fathers. We have brought these points forward so that we might overturn the foundation of those who, in defending the Vulgate translator's rendering here, Salvatorem mundi, stubbornly contend that these words, which are Egyptian (which we gladly grant), cannot signify what the Hebrews, with such agreement, Chaldee, Philo, Theodotion and the others, have handed down. For since the first word צפנת [tsafnat] can be traced back to the root of the great Hebrew mother, which means he hid, he concealed, and the interpretation of this hidden matter gave occasion for this change of name, why should we not prefer the interpretation of those who render it hidden, concealed things? Once this meaning is admitted, the interpretation of the other name reveals itself of its own accord, whether you render it explainer, revealer, one who knows, discoverer or interpreter. For Philo renders it one who makes manifest and finder of hidden things [ἐνσκρίπτω καὶ κρυπτῶν ἐυρετῶ]. The Syriac, according to the scholion on the Roman Bible, one who knows hidden things [εἴδως τὰ κρυπτά]. Theodotion revealer [ἐμφανεύτην]. Josephus discoverer of hidden things [κρυπτῶν εὑρετής]. Onkelos, to whom hidden things are revealed. Jonathan, interpreter of hidden things. R. Solomon, מפרש הצפונות [mefaresh hatsefunot], expounder of hidden things. R. Levi, one who has the knowledge of secrets. Jerome too, in his Questions, admits that in Hebrew it sounds like discoverer of things hidden, but in Egyptian, Salvatorem mundi. But let someone tell me which of the two words, the first or the second, signifies the world or the Saviour. Let someone show any trace of these meanings in the Egyptian language, or bring forward at least one conjecture that would lend strength to that rendering, and we shall gladly accept it, since it would be more apt for the mystery of Christ, of whom antiquity has handed down Joseph as a type in many respects. Lyra frankly says: I do not know whether the same name in the Egyptian language means Saviour of the world, except insofar as our translation says so. Mariana says: I would leave the words as they are in Hebrew, so that no one's interpretation is prejudiced. The addition of the Vulgate translator is therefore not supported.

units.la: Versu eodem occurrit nomen פוטיפרע nomen proprium viri, sacerdotis On, cujus filiam duxit Joseph. At cap.39.1. aliud nomen extat, nomen proprium ejus cui à Madianitis venditus fuit Joseph, sed illud unâ litera brevis est. Scribitur enim פוטיפר. Haec duo nomina Vulg. Lxx. confudêre. Utrumque enim ille Phutiphar, hi Πετεφρῆς[?] reddidêre. Quae confusio errandi occasionem praebuit. Multi enim qui ad hanc differentiam non attendêrunt, vel quibus ad fontes prae linguarum imperitiâ recurrere non licuit, existimârunt unum eundemque hominem fuisse hunc, cujus filiam duxit, & istum cujus antea tulerat imperium, quod admodum improbabile atque à veritate alienum esse prolixe ostendit Mercerus. Lyra hoc vidit, qui relata hac opinione mox subjicit, Sed contra hoc videtur, quod in Ebr. iste Phutiphar habet unam literam plus quam praecedens in suo nomine, quia habet literam Aym (lege Ain) in fine, quam non habet praecedens, & ideo videtur effealius homo à praedicto. Scio & Ebraeos quosdam ex nugatorum ordine personas eas confundere, ut Vulgatus nomina, sed ita est profecto, ut Lyra notavit. Potiphar fuit praefectus Satellitum: Potipherang Sacerdos sive princeps Oniorum. Nunquid haec evidens differitas est? Sed non sic hastam abjicit pertinax imperitia. Fuit præfectus satellitum, inquiunt, habuit conjugem, ex ea suscepit hanc prolem, filiam vid. Asenath. Sed postquam ad nefandum concubitum sollicitasset Josephum, divinitus castratum ajunt & postea munus illud suum cum sacerdotio commutasse. At unde probant castratum fuisse? quia vocatur Eunuchus. Resp. Hæc duo Sacerdos סריס Eunuchus nunquam conjungi: At contra præfectus Satellitum & Eunuchus, semel atque iterum. vid. Genes. 37. 36. & 39. 1. Si סריס est exectus & Photiphar idem cum Photipherang, oportet eum exectum jam tunc fuisse cum Josephum emeret. Vide loca jam citata. Dicet tiro quomodo exectus Potiphar si uxorem habuit? Resp. Eunuchum aliquando & aulicum significare, seu ministrum & præfectum regium. Scil. in Ægypto, Babylonia & Persia, Regum ministeriis fere execti adhibebantur. Tandem vero, ut fit, transiit in nomen dignitatis seu miniministerii honorabilis, unde Chaldæus Gen. 39. 1. vertit הרב princeps. & 2. R.S. 6. plurale ejus per רברבים reddidit & 1 Sam. 8. 15. לסריסיו ubi Jun. aulicis primoribus suis, Chald. רברבוהי principibus suis. Ipse quoque 70. Jerem. 34. 19. δυνάστως reddiderunt. Act. 8. Græcum Eunuchum Syrus מהימנא id est fidelem reddidit. Quò respexit Scholiastes, qui Syros eodem vocabulo Eunuchos & Dominis suis fideles, appellare prodidit.
units.tr: In the same verse occurs the proper name פוטיפרע, the name of the man, the priest of On, whose daughter Joseph married. But at chapter 39, verse 1, there is another name, the proper name of the man to whom Joseph was sold by the Midianites, but this name is shorter by one letter. For it is written פוטיפר. The Vulgate and the Septuagint confused these two names. For the former rendered both as Phutiphar, the latter as Πετεφρῆς[?]. This confusion gave occasion for error. For many who did not attend to this difference, or to whom, because of their lack of skill in languages, it was not possible to go back to the sources, thought that the man whose daughter he married and the man whose authority he had earlier received were one and the same. Mercerus has shown at length that this is very improbable and alien to the truth. Lyra saw this; after reporting this opinion he immediately adds: But against this it seems that in Hebrew this Phutiphar has one letter more than the preceding one in his name, because he has the letter Ayin (read Ain) at the end, which the preceding one does not have, and therefore he seems to be a different man from the one mentioned. I know that some Hebrews, from the order of trifling persons, confuse those persons, as the Vulgate does the names, but in truth it is as Lyra has noted. Potiphar was the commander of the guards; Potiphera was the priest or prince of On. Is this not a clear difference? But stubborn ignorance does not cast its spear so. He was the commander of the guards, they say, he had a wife, and by her he had this offspring, a daughter, namely Asenath. But after he had tried to seduce Joseph into an unspeakable union, they say he was divinely castrated, and afterwards exchanged that office of his for the priesthood. But on what grounds do they prove that he was castrated? Because he is called eunuch. I reply: priest and the Hebrew סריס, eunuch, are never joined together; but on the contrary commander of the guards and eunuch occur once and again (see Genesis 37:36 and 39:1). If סריס means one who has been castrated, and Potiphar is the same as Potiphera, then he must already have been castrated at the time when he bought Joseph. See the passages already cited. A beginner will ask how Potiphar could have been castrated if he had a wife. I reply: eunuch sometimes also means a courtier, that is, a royal minister and prefect. For in Egypt, Babylonia and Persia, castrated men were almost always employed in royal service. In time, however, as happens, the word passed into a title of dignity or of honourable service. Hence the Chaldee at Genesis 39:1 renders the Hebrew הרב by prince, and at 2 Kings 6 renders its plural by רברבים, and at 1 Samuel 8:15, for לסריסיו, where Junius has his leading courtiers, the Chaldee has רברבוהי, his princes. The Seventy themselves, at Jeremiah 34:19, render it δυνάστως [dynasts]. In Acts 8, the Syrian renders the Greek eunuch by מהימנא [mehimna], that is, faithful. To this the scholiast looked, who reported that the Syrians call eunuchs by the same word, faithful to their lords.

units.la: Δώδεκα ἀδελφοὶ ἐσμὲν οἱ παῖδές σου ἐν τῇ γῇ Χαν. Duodecim fratres sumus servi tui in terra Canaan. Ita LXX. At quomodo in terra Chanaan, qui in Ægypto? Respondet Augustinus, sumus positum esse pro habitamus. Certè esse aliquando pro habitare ponitur. Ruth. 1. 3. & fuerunt ibi id est habitarunt. Confer v. 4. ubi est וישבו in fonte. Sed plane aliena hic est illa observatio. Sic enim habent Ebræa, xii. servi tui fratres nos, filii viri unius in terra Chanaan. Druf. Misc. cent. 2. cap. 88.
units.tr: Δώδεκα ἀδελφοὶ ἐσμὲν οἱ παῖδές σου ἐν τῇ γῇ Χαν. We are twelve brothers, your servants, in the land of Canaan. [Δώδεκα ἀδελφοὶ ἐσμὲν οἱ παῖδές σου ἐν τῇ γῇ Χαν] So the Septuagint. But how can they be in the land of Canaan when they are in Egypt? Augustine answers that sumus ("we are") is used for habitamus ("we dwell"). Certainly esse is sometimes used for habitare: Ruth 1.3, and they were there, that is, they dwelt there. Compare verse 4, where the Hebrew has וישבו [vayeshevu]. But that observation is quite irrelevant here. For the Hebrew reads: Your servants are twelve brothers, we are sons of one man in the land of Canaan. Drusius, Miscellanea, cent. 2, cap. 88.

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Vocetur in iis nomen meum & nomen Patrum meorum. | Invocetur nomen meum & nomen Patrum meorum super eos.
units.tr: Heb. | Vulg. Let my name be named upon them, and the names of my fathers. | Let my name and the names of my fathers be invoked upon them.

units.la: Verba sunt Jacobi utrique nepoti suo ex Joseph benedicentris. Quorum, ipso Lyra præeunte, hic sensus est, adoptoscos in filios meos, licet ex te nati sint, tamen dicantur filii mei, uno ordine habeantur cum filiis meis ex me immediatè natis in divisione terræ & constitutione tribuum, denominentur non de nomine tuo sed meo. Similis locutio Jesai. 4. 1. Tantummodò vocetur super nos nomen tuum, id est, denomineinur de nomine tuo, ubi iterum Vulgatus, invocetur nomen tuum super nos Ex hoc loco prout à Vulgato conversus est, Invocatio Sanctorum vires & incrementa sumpsit. Hinc enim disputant, Hinc nomen Invocationis hominibus competere, probare satagunt. Audiamus etiam Carthusianum, potest quoque & ita exponi, inquit, ut Jacob, Isaac & Abraham invocarentur à fidelibus, tanquam tres sancti viri ad orandum pro Ephraim & Manasse. Sed vel sola collatio loci ex Iesa. citati docere eos potuisset, in phrasi illa pro Invocatione Sanctorum nihil omnino situm esse præsidii. Mea hæc est sententia, non tam versionem, quæ commoda aliqua Interpretatione locorumque aliorum collatione leniri posset, quam non intellectum Ebraïsmum, vocemque invocetur sine necessitate pro simplici vocetur positam indoctiores decepisse. Plane nobiscum hic faciunt à Lapide & Fonseca ad marginem Cajetani & Lyra & Hugo Cardinalis ad hunc locum. Nec non Arias Mont. in idiotismis & Oleastrius & quidam & alii. Nec video quomodo ab his separari queat ipse Bellarminus. sanctos ante ascensum Christi in cœlos à vivis adoratos fuisse. Quia ante id tempus, inquit, sancti non videbant Deum, non fuit consuetum in V. Test. ut diceretur, sancte Abraham ora pro me, &c. Claudam verbis Merceri ad hunc locum, Ebraïsmorum ignorantia (addo, & eum subsecutus fontium contemptus) multos errores peperit & invexit in Ecclesiam.
units.tr: These are Jacob's words, blessing each of his grandsons, the sons of Joseph. Their sense, with Lyra leading the way, is this: he adopts them as my sons; although they were born of you, they are nevertheless to be called my sons, to be counted in the same rank as my sons born directly of me, in the division of the land and the constitution of the tribes, and to be named not after your name but after mine. A similar expression is at Isaiah 4.1, only let us be called by your name, that is, let us be named after your name; there the Vulgate again has let your name be invoked upon us. From this passage, as the Vulgate translated it, the invocation of the saints gained its strength and growth. For from here they argue, and from here they strive to prove, that the name of invocation belongs to men. Let us hear the Carthusian too: it can also be explained, he says, so that Jacob, Isaac and Abraham were invoked by the faithful, as three holy men to pray for Ephraim and Manasseh. But the comparison of this passage with the cited passage of Isaiah alone could have taught them that there is no support at all in that phrase for the invocation of the saints. My view is this: it is not so much the translation, which could be softened by some convenient interpretation and by comparing other passages, but rather that the less learned have been deceived by an unrecognised Hebraism, and by the word invocetur being used, without any need, in place of the plain vocetur. Here indeed Cornelius a Lapide and Fonseca, in the margin of Cajetan, and Lyra and Cardinal Hugo on this passage, are plainly on our side; so too Arias Montanus in his Idiotismi, and Oleastrius, and certain others. Nor do I see how Bellarmine himself can be separated from these, when he holds that the saints were worshipped by the living before Christ's ascent into heaven. Because before that time, he says, the saints did not see God, and it was not customary in the Old Testament to say, Holy Abraham, pray for me, etc. I shall close with Mercer's words on this passage: Ignorance of Hebraisms (I add, and the contempt for the sources that followed it) has brought forth many errors and introduced them into the Church.

units.la: Vide de hoc oraculo Casaubonum, Exercitat. Anti-Baron. 2. Sect. 2. & 3. & qui accuratius hæc pensitârunt & in quibusdam non sine gravissimis rationibus à Casaubono dissentiunt, Cunæum de Republ. Ebræorum lib. 1. cap. 9. & 10. & Scultetum, Exercit. Euangel. lib. 1. cap. 3. [Montacutium, in Anajectis Exercit. 2. sect. 8.] Subdifficile est hoc oraculum; ac propterea variis expositionibus obnoxium. Baronius cum pleriquerisque Patribus continuum regnum tribui Judæ promitti existimat, ad Christi usque adventum, serie continuâ, aut non nisi ad tempus interruptâ, duraturum. Existimat in ultimo Hasamonæorum Antigono, & Hircano, quem Herodes sustulit, extinctum regnum Davidicum. In Herode denique completum hoc vaticinium. Hanc sententiam sic refutat Causabus ut ostendat, 636. annos ab edito hoc vaticinio usque ad Davidem excurrisse, queis nullus ex tribu Judæ imperium tenuerit, præter Othonielem & Ibtzanem, illorumque imperium non fuisse regium. Regium autem imperium à Davide demum inchoatum, desiisse in Zedekia. In Zorobabele revixisse quidem, sed non ultra 53. annos duravisse. Ex eo penes Pontifices & Hasamonæos fuisse rerum summam usque ad Pompejum solidam & plenam, at postea valde imminutam & Senatui Rom. obnoxiam usque ad Herodem magnum. Hunc etiam alienigenam fuisse cum illustriss. Scaligero negat, ac proinde in eo hoc vaticinium non fuisse completum, sed in destructione templi secundi. Id quod Iustinus in Colloq. cum Tryph. egregiè ostendit. Quin & si Herodes alienigena fuisset, priorem tamen fuisse Pompejum, qui Judæam sub Romanorum jugum misit. Vult ergo Casaubonus, per Judam in oraculo Iacobi omnem Israëliticum populum intelligi, secutus in eo Eusebium, quem etiam Bulengerus Casauboni adversarius hic sequitur, ut hic sit Oraculi sensus, non deficiet, Rex, Dux, propheta ex gente Israelitica, usque dum venerit Silo. Tres ponit gradus interitus Reip. Iudaicæ, primum, cum populus, sui antea juris, servitutis jugum subire coactus est à Pompejo. 2. cum Archelao Viennam relegato, Judæa in formam provinciæ redacta est. 3. cum Titus urbem solo æquavit. Falsa ergo tria illa ἀλήμματα, quæ à communis sententiæ Patronis tanquam si certæ & immotæ veritatis essent, sumuntur. I. Penes tribum Judæ fore perpetuum regimen usque ad Messiam. II. Messiam venturum tunc, cum rerum summa penes primum alienigenam esset. 3. Hunc fuisse Herodem magnum. Atque hic conveniunt Casaub. Montacutius, Scalig. Cunæus Scult. & alii. Hic verò dissident, universum populum Israëliticum sub nomine unius Judæ hic contineri. Quorum respublica est, eorum etiam esse sceptrum, asserit Cunæus, quem in omnibus bus Scultetus sequitur. Id verò à Mose usque ad Ieroboamum, non Judæorum sed omnium Israëlitarum fuisse. De hoc sceptro non locutum fuisse Jacobum, seros annos spectasse, cum tribus Judæa, scisso in partes contrarias populo, suam sibi Remp. seorsum habere cœpit. Hanc sceptri majestatem, ex quo ea semel Judæorum esse cœpit, mansisse eorundem, etsi mutatus interdum Reip. status sit, ac penes Pontifices modò, modò penes Reges & Principes summa rerum fuerit. Quicunque populus suâ quadam Rep. & legibus utitur, is recte de imperio sceptroque gloriari potest. Perinde ac regnum Poloniæ semper manet, quamdiu corona & jus eligendi Regem apud Polonos manet, etiamsi exterus regnet. Etiam eo tempore, cum populum non principes sed optimates regerent, in medio magni Concilii, quod Sanhedrin vocant, sceptrum pependisse tanquam insigne quoddam Majestatis. Nihil in terrestre ergo, quâ de gente aut tribu fuerint qui Judaïcas res moderati sunt, mansit enim semper Respublica Judæorum. Non enim Rempublicam Principis esse, sed Principem Reip. Hæc literatissimus ille Jurisconsultus, Acad. Leidensis nequaquam postremum columen cujus in sacris diligentiam utinam Verbi divini Interpretes æmularentur! Hâc oraculi Interpretatione id effectum dedit, ut nulla nos cogat necessitas de Herode contentionis serram reciprocandi, an vid. is alienigena fuerit nec ne, cujus negativam ita tutati sunt Scal. & Casaubonus, ut quam plurimis eruditissimis viris non omnino satis fecerint.
units.tr: On this oracle see Casaubonus, Exercitationes Anti-Baronianae 2, sections 2 and 3, and those who have weighed these matters more carefully and in some points dissent from Casaubon, not without very serious reasons: Cunæum on the Republic of the Hebrews, book 1, chapters 9 and 10, and Scultetum, Evangelical Exercises, book 1, chapter 3. [Montacutium, in the Anajectae to Exercise 2, section 8.] This oracle is quite difficult and therefore open to various interpretations. Baronius, with most of the Fathers, holds that a continuous kingdom was promised to Judah, to last until the coming of Christ, either in an unbroken succession or interrupted only for a time. He thinks that the Davidic kingdom came to an end under the last of the Hasmonaeans, Antigonus and Hyrcanus, whom Herod removed, and that the prophecy was finally fulfilled in Herod. Causabus refutes this view by showing that 636 years passed from the utterance of this prophecy to David, during which no one from the tribe of Judah held power except Othniel and Ibzan, and their rule was not royal. Royal power, he says, began only with David and ceased with Zedekiah. It revived under Zerubbabel, but lasted no more than 53 years. From then on the supreme authority lay with the high priests and the Hasmonaeans, solid and full until Pompey, but afterwards greatly diminished and subject to the Roman Senate until Herod the Great. Along with the most illustrious Scaliger, Casaubon denies that Herod was a foreigner, and so denies that the prophecy was fulfilled in him, holding instead that it was fulfilled in the destruction of the second temple. Justin shows this clearly in his Dialogue with Trypho. Indeed, even if Herod had been a foreigner, Pompey would still have come first, since he put Judaea under the Roman yoke. Casaubon therefore wants "Judah" in Jacob's oracle to mean the whole Israelite people, following Eusebius, whom Bulengerus, Casaubon's opponent, also follows here. So the sense of the oracle is: a ruler, a leader, a prophet from the Israelite nation will not fail until Shiloh comes. He posits three stages in the ruin of the Jewish state: first, when the people, formerly free, were forced under the yoke of servitude by Pompey; second, when Judaea was reduced to the form of a province after Archelaus was banished to Vienne; third, when Titus levelled the city with the ground. The three ἀλήμματα that the defenders of the common view assume, as if they were certain and unshakeable truths, are therefore false: (1) that the rule would remain with the tribe of Judah until the Messiah; (2) that the Messiah would come when the supreme authority was in the hands of the first foreigner; (3) that this foreigner was Herod the Great. Here Casaubon, Montacutius, Scaliger, Cunaeus, Scultetus and others agree. But they disagree about this: Cunaeus, whom Scultetus follows in everything, maintains that the whole Israelite people is contained here under the single name of Judah. He holds that whoever has the commonwealth also has the sceptre. This sceptre, from Moses to Jeroboam, belonged not to the Jews but to all the Israelites. Jacob did not speak of this sceptre; he looked to later years, when the tribe of Judah, after the people were split into opposing parts, began to have its own commonwealth apart. This majesty of the sceptre, from the time it first began to belong to the Jews, remained theirs, even though the form of the state sometimes changed and supreme power at times lay with the high priests and at other times with kings and princes. Any people that uses a commonwealth of its own and its own laws can rightly boast of rule and sceptre. Just as the kingdom of Poland always remains, as long as the crown and the right to elect the king remain with the Poles, even if a foreigner reigns. Even at that time, when the people were governed not by princes but by nobles, the sceptre hung in the middle of the great council, which they call the Sanhedrin, as a certain badge of majesty. Nothing therefore passed to a earthly ruler from whatever nation or tribe those were who governed Jewish affairs, for the commonwealth of the Jews always remained. For the commonwealth does not belong to the prince, but the prince to the commonwealth. So wrote that most learned jurist, by no means the least pillar of the Academy of Leiden, whose diligence in sacred matters the interpreters of the divine Word ought to imitate! This interpretation of the oracle has had this effect: no necessity compels us to renew the saw of dispute about Herod, whether he was a foreigner or not. Scaliger and Casaubon defended the negative so vigorously that they did not fully satisfy many very learned men.

units.la: Duos ergo Iacobus sibi propositos habuit scopos,
units.tr: Jacob therefore had two aims set before him.

units.la: I. ut ostenderet, quo usque Resp. Judaica, post abductas à Salmanasaro decem tribus, esset duratura, vid, ultra adventum Messiæ, non recedet sceptrum, vel ut Junius. non desiisset tribus à Juda, donec venerit Tranquillator, Ebr. [illegible, ~6 letters] quod commodè reddi poterit, donec venerit, ut intelligatur, primò venturum Christum in regnum suum, illudque solenniter inchoaturum, id quod post ascensum ejus in cœlum factum est in die Pentecostes. Errant enim qui adventum ejus tantum ad nativitatem ejus restringunt. Postea verò omnem penitus civilem Magistratum, & ordinem hierarchicum delctumiri. Quomodo do Num. 20. 17. Legitur עַד אֲשֶׁר נַעֲבוֹר donec transierimus. II. circa quod tempus venturus esset Messias, circa illud vid. mox subsecutura esset Reip. Judaicæ ⲡⲁⲛⲟⲗⲉⲑⲉⲓⲁ, adeo ut ea certissimum & infallibile documentum Christi jam nati Judæis esse debuerit. Interpres Italicus Deodatus non recedit ab hac oraculi interpretatione, per sceptrum intelligens majoritatem, & imperium hujus tribus, postquam semel ejus facta fuerit compos, & statum tribus, qui nunquam omnino desiit, usque ad Christum, qui eum convertit in regnum spirituale. Pisc. in Bibl. Germ. non recedet, id est, non omnino auferetur, ut nulla superfutura sit spes illud sceptrum id est regimen recuperandi, donec, &c. Idem in Quæst in Genes. non desinet tribus Juda, neque etiam potestas omnis imperandi adimetur ei, antequam venerit Christus in regnum suum, illudque solenniter incoarit. Genevenses in annot. Sceptrum non recedet, &c. id est, tribus Juda manebit à cateris tribubus distincta, usque ad Messiæ adventum, retinebitque politicum & Ecclesiasticum regimen una cum notitia & cultu veri Dei aliquo modo, en quelque sorte. Non ergo in Herode magno hujus vaticinii complementum constituunt, utpote sub quo nec Pontifices, nec sacerdotes, nec synedrium nec tribus distinctio disiere. In his certe inter Herodis tempora & urbem vastatam nulla insignis facta est mutatio.
units.tr: I. To show how long the Jewish commonwealth would endure after the ten tribes were carried off by Shalmaneser. He would say that the sceptre "shall not depart" even beyond the coming of the Messiah, or, as Junius puts it, the tribe would not cease from Judah until the Tranquillizer comes [Hebrew, illegible in the scan]. This can conveniently be rendered "until he comes", so that it is understood that Christ would first come into his kingdom and solemnly begin it, which was done after his ascension into heaven on the day of Pentecost. For those err who restrict his coming to his nativity alone. Afterwards, indeed, he would utterly abolish all civil magistracy and the hierarchical order. Compare Num. 20:17, where it is read until we have passed through [עַד אֲשֶׁר נַעֲבוֹר]. II. Concerning the time when the Messiah was to come, shortly after which the ruin of the Jewish commonwealth was to follow, so that this would have to be a most certain and infallible proof to the Jews that Christ had already been born. The Italian translator Deodatus does not depart from this interpretation of the oracle. By sceptre he understands the majority and rule of this tribe, once it has been obtained, and the state of the tribe, which never wholly ceased until Christ, who turned it into a spiritual kingdom. Pisc. in the German Bible: "shall not depart", that is, will not be wholly taken away, so that no hope would remain of recovering that sceptre, that is, rule, until, etc. The same in the Quaestiones on Genesis: the tribe of Judah shall not cease, nor will all power of ruling be taken from it, before Christ comes into his kingdom and solemnly begins it. The Genevans in their notes: "The sceptre shall not depart", etc., that is, the tribe of Judah will remain distinct from the other tribes until the coming of the Messiah, and will retain political and ecclesiastical rule, together with the knowledge and worship of the true God in some way, en quelque sorte. They therefore do not find the fulfilment of this prophecy in Herod the Great, under whom neither the high priests, nor the priests, nor the Sanhedrin, nor the distinction of the tribes perished. Certainly in these matters no notable change occurred between the time of Herod and the devastation of the city.

units.la: Porro, tironem moneo, vocem Silo commodissimè sic accipi, ut sit formæ קִיטוֹר קִימוּשׁ & significet Sospitatorem, tranquillatorem, omnis tranquillitatis authorem, ut ה sit thematis litera, à them. שְׁלוֹ unde שָׁלֵו tranquillus, שְׁלֵוָה tranquillitas, unde Latinum Salus, salvus, salvare, Salvator. Ut vel hinc videas, quanta sit inter duo ișthæc nomina SILOH & JESUS affinitas. Namque τὸ Ἰησοῦς si non Latinius, at saltem ἰμΦαλικοπίεως reddi Salvator, quàm Servator, nemo opinor, iverit inficias. Quàm autem de facili ipsa Salvatoris vox à nominis Silo themate deflectatur, jam ostendi. Communis autem illa interpretatio, SILOH Filius ejus explicari non potest, nisi per multas ambages. Primo enim erit ה pro י / quod exemplo non caret. Deinde שִׁילוֹ erit שִׁילִי, atque hoc rursus pro שִׁילֹהִי ut פְּנֵיהָ pro פְּנָּחָה / Tertiò erit Metonymia. Vox enim Ebræa שִׁילֹה secundas significat, vel ut vulgo loquuntur secundinas, sic dictas, quod in iis tranquillè agat fœtus.
units.tr: Furthermore, I advise the beginner that the word Silo is most suitably taken in the form [קִיטוֹר קִימוּשׁ], meaning a Saviour, a quietener, the author of all tranquillity, so that the heh is a letter of the stem, from the root [שְׁלוֹ], whence [שָׁלֵו] tranquil and [שְׁלֵוָה] tranquillity, and whence the Latin salus, salvus, salvare, Salvator. From this alone you may see how great the affinity is between these two names, SILOH and JESUS. For if Iesus is not rendered more Latinly, it would at least be rendered Salvator rather than Servator; I think no one will deny this. How easily the very word Saviour is derived from the stem of the name Shiloh, I have already shown. But that common interpretation, "Shiloh his son", cannot be explained except through many circumlocutions. First, the heh would stand for a yod, which is not without precedent. Then [שִׁילוֹ] would become [שִׁילִי], and this again [שִׁילֹהִי], as [פְּנֵיהָ] for [פְּנָּחָה]. Thirdly, it would be a metonymy, for the Hebrew word [שִׁילֹה] means afterbirths, or, as people commonly say, secundines, so called because in them the foetus lies quietly.

units.la: Ex his omnibus, fateor, nihil est, quod non sit in S. Literis frequens. Sed an secundæ viro possunt tribui? Affixum enim si est, M. generis est & ad Judam referetur, Ego puto priorem sententiam esse simpliciorem, videoque placuisse eam Oleastrio, Fagio, Mercero, Drusio, Scultero, Melanth-Forstero, Castellioni, Schindlero, & aliis. Cave autem ne tibi quoque Porchetus & Galatinus imponant, affixum ה in שילה ad Virginem Mariam referri, ut innuatur hac voce Messiam de matre absque patre nasciturum, ut loquitur Galat. pag. 199. lin. 4. cap. 4. ה enim non magis est fœmin. affixum, quàm in אהלה עורה / ipseque Galat. p. 208. ex Kimchio docet, ה esse loco vau. Ita tamen hanc interpretationem vocis SILOH probo, ut alterum Filius ejus, atro lapillo non notem. Fruatur quisque judicio suo. Illud dissimulare non possum, eam, quam vulgatus interpres elegit, neutiquam mihi probari interpretationem, mittendus, donec veniat qui mittendus est, nec tueri eam queunt Pontificii, nisi cum rejectione textus Ebraei. Existimo hunc locum corrupisse Judæos, inquit Steuchus. Itane Steuche? Quomodo ergo antea fuit scriptum שילוה inquis. Ita & Corn. à Lapide, qui & illud addit, hoc commune olim nomen Messiæ fuisse, ut patet, inquit, Exod. 4. 13. Quo in loco ego tamen vocem שילח non invenio. Unde ad hoc suum nomen, pergit à Lapide, Siloach allusit Christus, cum cæcum illuminaturus misit ad piscinam Siloë, Joh. 9. 7. En suavi-ludia. Cui vero cordato id persuaseris Corneli, Cum enim Ebraei & ante Hieron. & post eum, locum hunc de Messia acceperint (Ex. gr. Chaldæi Interpretes tres, Thalmudici in Massech. Sanhedrin cap. xi, R. Salomo, Kimchi in Radic. &c.) quis credet locum hunc ab iis corruptum, & quidem eo fine, ne de Messiâ acciperetur: Certe ante Hieron. à Lxx. Interpretibus non fuit lectum שילח / quomodo enim ex eo, τὰ ξυνπρίμψεα αὐτῶ, vel ut Euseb. citat. ὑπόκειται, cui repositum est, excusplisset. Sed audiamus Galatinum, virum alias in accusandis fontibus nimis facilem. Sic ergo ille lib. 4. cap. 4. Judæi nostri temporis latam habent viam fugiendi si sc. שילח per Cheth legeretur) objicere enim facile possent, Prophetiam hanc non de Messiâ, sed de aliquo alio intelligendam esse, & præsertim de Nebucadnetzar qui ad peccata eorum punienda mittendus erat, &c.. Quomodo & Lyra ab hac versione deceptus exposuit. Vide jam Salom. Glass. ex professo de hoc loco cum Gordonio in Philologia sacra διαλε- γόμενον, nec non Martinii Lexicon Philolog, Fagium, Mercerum, [Chamierum] & alios.
units.tr: Of all these things, I admit, there is nothing that is not frequent in Holy Scripture. But can afterbirths be attributed to a man? For if the suffix is masculine, it will be referred to Judah. I think the former opinion is simpler, and I see it was approved by Oleaster, Fagius, Mercerus, Drusius, Schultens, Melanchthon, Forsterus, Castellio, Schindler, and others. Beware, however, that Porchetus and Galatinus do not deceive you by referring the final heh in Shiloh to the Virgin Mary, as if this word hinted that the Messiah would be born of a mother without a father, as Galatinus says on p. 199, line 4 of ch. 4. For the heh is no more a feminine suffix than in [אָהֳלָה עֽוּרָה]; and Galatinus himself teaches, following Kimchi, that heh stands in place of vav. Yet I so approve this interpretation of the word Shiloh that I would not mark the other reading, Filius ejus ("his son"), with a black pebble. Let each enjoy his own judgement. I cannot conceal that the interpretation chosen by the Vulgate translator, mittendus, donec veniat qui mittendus est ("to be sent, until he comes who is to be sent"), by no means pleases me, nor can the Papists defend it except by rejecting the Hebrew text. I think the Jews have corrupted this passage, says Steuchus. Really, Steuchus? How then, you ask, was it previously written [שילוה]? Cornelius a Lapide says the same, adding that this was once a common name of the Messiah, as is clear, he says, from Exod. 4:13. But in that place I do not find the word [שילח]. Hence Christ alluded to this name of his, Siloah, says a Lapide, when he sent the blind man to be illuminated at the pool of Siloam, John 9:7. Behold, sweet trifles! But who could persuade a sensible man of this? For the Hebrews, both before Jerome and after him, have taken this passage of the Messiah (for example, the three Chaldee interpreters, the Talmudists in Massech. Sanhedrin ch. 11, R. Solomon, Kimchi in Radic., and others). Who would believe that this passage was corrupted by them, and indeed with the aim that it should not be taken of the Messiah? Certainly before Jerome the Seventy interpreters did not read [שילח], for otherwise how could they have rendered it what is laid up for him, or, as Eusebius cites it, lies under, to which it was given? But let us hear Galatinus, a man otherwise too ready to accuse his sources. He thus says in book 4, ch. 4: Our contemporary Jews have a broad way of escape if (namely, the word were read with Cheth), for they could easily object that this prophecy is to be understood not of the Messiah but of someone else, and especially of Nebuchadnezzar, who was to be sent to punish their sins, etc. Lyra also, deceived by this version, expounded it so. See now Salomon Glassius, who professedly discusses this passage with Gordon in the Philologia sacra, and also Martinius' Lexicon Philologicum, Fagius, Mercerus, [Chamierus] and others.

units.la: Tollam manum de hac tabula ubi istis, quae supra à me disserta sunt, confirmandis adscripsero locum ex Montacutio, qui postquam probasset, הָיָה vertendum esse Venerit, authoritatibusque Justini, Eusebii, Athanasii, Hieronymi comm. in Sophoniam, Theodoreti in hunc locum, se munivisset, ut sententiam hanc de novitate absolutam in antiquorum classem transcriberet, objicit sibimet ipsi in hunc modum. At enim vero anni tunc effluxerant à nato Servatore Lxxiii. praeter propter, cum eventum sortiretur hoc vaticinium. (vid. in destructione urbis.) Recte. Sed & anni non minus multi ab ablato per Herodem principatu & regno ad Idumaeos translato, cum nondum Messias nasceretur. Esto autem, multo plures effluxissent: non sunt adeo coercenda vaticinia. Qui volunt in Herode defecisse sceptrum, non statim advenisse Messiam contendunt. Totos annos xxviii. intervenisse vult Baronius. Ultra aequidem xxx. largiri debuit à semoto legis-latore & translato sceptro, neque tamen Messias nascebatur. Satis ergo vaticiniis factum esse solet, si eventum ipsorum non in ipso τῷ νῦν, sed in vicinitate quadam terminemus. Dictum est, illud veniet non praesentem denotare, sed praeteritam rei praedictae mentionem, & jam quidem Messiam advenisse oportere, cum sceptrum auferretur, non priusquam veniret auferendum fuisse. Sed & aliter occurrendum est huic scrupulo, & in ipsomet adventu & illius τῷ νῦν, terminus definiendus impleti hujus vaticinii. Χρὴ γὰρ παρουσίαν καταγγέλλομεν, ἕ μίαν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ δευτέραν, inquit Cyrillus Hierosol. Et certe memorant Prophetae geminum adventum, contrahant verba authoris, primum inhonorum, secundum gloriosum. Qui duo adventus inter se tam disiuncti ἀναμίξ plerumque à prophetis proponi solent, vix ut internosci queant. Gloriosus autem ille adventus duplex est particularis & generalis. Generalis, qui erit in novissimo die. Particularis cum adversus homines singulares judicium suum exercet. Judex in utroque idem Christus. Joh. xxi. ἰδὼν ἡλιος αὐτὸν μίαν ἐως ἔρχομαι, πάσης; usque dum venero.
units.tr: I will take my hand from this tablet once I have added, to confirm what I have argued above, a passage from Montacutio (Montagu). After proving that [הָיָה] must be rendered venerit, and fortifying himself with the authorities of Justini, Eusebii, Athanasii, Hieronymi in his commentary on Zephaniah, and Theodoreti on this passage, so that he might transcribe this opinion of novelty as settled into the class of the ancients, he objects to himself in this way. "Indeed, years had by then passed since the birth of the Saviour, about 73 or so, when this prophecy was to receive its event (see on the destruction of the city)." Right. But also no fewer years passed from the removal of the principate and kingdom through Herod to the Idumaeans, when the Messiah was not yet born. Grant, however, that many more had passed: prophecies are not to be so tightly confined. Those who hold that the sceptre failed in Herod do not contend that the Messiah came at once. Baronius wants twenty-eight full years to have intervened. Indeed one ought to allow more than thirty years after the lawgiver was removed and the sceptre transferred, and yet the Messiah was not then being born. It is usually enough for prophecies to be fulfilled if we place their event not in the very present, but in some vicinity. It was said that veniet ("will come") does not denote the present, but a past mention of the thing predicted, and that the Messiah had indeed to have come when the sceptre was taken away, not that he had to come before it was to be taken away. But this scruple must also be met in another way, by fixing the term of the fulfilment of this prophecy in the coming itself and in its present time. For, says Cyril of Jerusalem, [Χρὴ γὰρ τὴν παρουσίαν καταγγέλλειν, οὐ μίαν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ δευτέραν], "we must proclaim the coming, not only one but also a second." And certainly the prophets recall a twofold coming: the first lowly, the second glorious. These two comings, so distinct from each other, are often set forth together by the prophets, so that they can hardly be told apart. That glorious coming is itself twofold, particular and general. The general coming will be on the last day; the particular, when he exercises his judgement against individual men. The judge in both is the same Christ. John 21: [θέλω αὐτὸν μένειν ἕως ἔρχομαι], "I will that he remain until I come."

units.la: Ad judicium exercendum, non universale, sed contra Judæos particulares, quo & urbs & regnum & Resp. fato quodam occubuere. Ita locum exponit sequutus veteriores Theophylactus, ἕως ἂν σταυρωθῶσιν με Ἰουδαίων, μέλλων αὐτὸς διὰ τῆς τῶν Ῥωμαίων ῥάβδου παιδεύειν καὶ κατασχεῖν τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν. Donec venero, ad judicium scilicet contra Judæos qui me crucifixerunt, quos per Romanorum virgam sum percussurus & subversurus eorum urbem. Quo quidem casu cum sceptrum & legislator ablatus defecerint omnino, impletum est quod dixit, non deficient, &c. donec venerit. Cum autem venerit, tunc deficiet & non restituetur in æternum. At ad illa usque tempora regnatum non est per duces è Juda & domo David. Fateor equidem, neque opus erat. Nec secundum Cardinalem regnatum est. Regnum enim proprie dictum finitum est in Zedekia. Regnum improprie, id est potestas & principatus, in Zorobabel. Si per Assamonæos recuperatum dixerit principatum, quod affirmat, præterquam quod hoc liquido falsi convicerimus, non enim erant illi de Juda sed Levi, tum ne quidem in Herode principatus defecit ad eum modum, cum ab exitu illius per lineam fœmininam in Herode Agrippa repullulaverit. Sed non erat opus ut regnaretur. Non enim de Judâ in individuo dixit, non in particulari de tribu Judæ, sed de gente Judæa. Sensus ergo, Judæos ab illo tempore, quo cum cæteris gentibus censebantur, non desituros gentem esse, nec dissipandos, sed cum formâ aliqua reip. perstituros, sacerdotium & Legem retenturos, usque dum Messias advenisset. Hactenus Montacutium audivimus. Jam Jege Bulengerum & videbis eum semper petere illud quod est ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ. Aut impletum est hoc vatininium inquit, in Zedekia, vel in Pompejo, vel Herode, vel Tito. Non in Zedekia, non in Pompejo. Hoc fateris inquit ad Casaubonum, non etiam sub Tito. Et quare? Jam enim dudum natus & mortuus erat Christus. Ergo aut vaticinium erit falsum, aut sub Herode Idumæo erit impletum. Vides illud VENIAT primarium Bulengeri esse præsidium. Illud postremò addam, Si adventum Christi cum Piscatore & aliis accipias de adventu ejus in regnum suum, quod in die Pentecostes solenniter incoâvit, ex eo usque ad eversam urbem tantùm xl. annos præter propter interintercessisse. Cum autem inter Herodiani regni initium & Christum natum triginta circiter anni effluxerint, videbit facile cordatus Lector, illud argumentum quod à longiore illa temporis intercapedine adversus nostram sententiam depromi supra dicebamus non esset anti, ut propterea illi repudium mittendum sit.
units.tr: To exercise judgement, not universal judgement but particular judgement against the Jews, by which both the city and the kingdom and the commonwealth perished by a certain fate. Theophylact, following the older writers, explains the passage thus: until they have crucified me, the Jews, I myself being about to chastise them through the rod of the Romans and to seize their city [ἕως ἂν σταυρωθῶσιν με Ἰουδαίων, μέλλων αὐτὸς διὰ τῆς τῶν Ῥωμαίων ῥάβδου παιδεύειν καὶ κατασχεῖν τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν]. That is, until I come, namely to judgement against the Jews who crucified me, whose city I am about to strike down and overthrow through the Roman rod. In that event, when the sceptre and the lawgiver were wholly taken away, what he said was fulfilled: they shall not fail, etc., until he comes. But when he has come, then they will fail and will not be restored for ever. Yet until those times the kingdom was not held by rulers from Judah and the house of David. I grant this indeed, and it was not necessary that it should be. Nor was the kingdom held according to the Cardinal. For the kingdom properly so called ended with Zedekiah. The kingdom in an improper sense, that is, authority and rule, ended with Zerubbabel. If he says that the rule was recovered through the Hasmoneans, which he affirms, then, besides the fact that we have clearly proved this false (for they were not of Judah but of Levi), not even in Herod did the rule fail in such a way that it did not sprout again through the female line in Herod Agrippa after his death. But it was not necessary that rule be held. For he did not speak of Judah in the individual, nor of the tribe of Judah in particular, but of the Jewish nation. The sense, then, is that from the time when the Jews were counted among the other nations, they would not cease to be a nation, nor be scattered, but would persist in some form of commonwealth, retaining the priesthood and the Law, until the Messiah should come. So far we have heard Montacutius. Now read Bulenger, and you will see him always seeking that which is at the beginning [ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ]. Either, he says, this prophecy was fulfilled in Zedekiah, or in Pompey, or in Herod, or in Titus. Not in Zedekiah, not in Pompey. You admit this, he says, to Casaubon, but not under Titus as well. And why not? For Christ had already long since been born and had died. Therefore either the prophecy will be false, or it was fulfilled under Herod the Idumean. You see that SHALL COME is Bulenger's chief defence. Finally I will add this: if you take the coming of Christ, with Peter and the others, as referring to his coming into his kingdom, which he solemnly began on the day of Pentecost, then from that point until the overthrow of the city there were only about forty years in between. And since about thirty years had passed between the beginning of Herod's reign and the birth of Christ, the discerning reader will easily see that the argument which we said above was drawn from that longer interval of time against our view is no argument at all, so that it ought therefore to be dismissed.

units.la: Et tulit illico Sephora acutissimam petram Et Josuae 5. fac tibi cultros lapideos.
units.tr: And at once Zipporah took a very sharp stone. And Joshua 5: Make for yourself knives of stone.

units.la: THomas Aquinas, cujus ego viri ingenium merito suspicio, postquam movisset objectionem adversus usum cultelli petrini in circumcisione, in hunc modum respondet, Ad secundum, dicendum quod cultellus lapideus non erat de necessitate circumcisionis, unde non invenitur tale instrumentum praecepto divino determinatum. Neque etiam communiter tali instrumento Judaei utebantur ad circumcidendum, sicuti neque modo utuntur. Hactenus vera & certa locutus est. Quae vero sequuntur, incerta sunt Leguntur tamen aliqua circumcisiones famosae, cultello lapideo factae, sicuti legitur Exod. 4. quod tulit Sephora acutissimam petram, & Jos. 5. dicitur, Fac tibi cultellos lapideos Haec dico admodum esse incerta. Cl. Drusius in notis ad Josuam inclinat eo ut putet fuisse petrinos cultros. Ramirezius cap.4. Pentecontarchi valde sudat, ut opinionem istam stabiliat. Argumenta a doctissimo Masio mutuatus est. At Cl. Junius, Piscator, Genev. Cajet. B. Arias Mont. & Pagn. existimant in voce אור quae proprie acumen denotat, esse vel Motonymiam adjuncti synecdochicam, pro cultro acuto: vel metaphoram, quatenus אור petram significat. Quod ergo ex Theodoreto, Quaest. in Josuae caput 5. & Iustini Dialogo cum Tryphone, subjicit Thomas, Per quod figurabatur, circumcisionem spiritualem esse fiendam per Christum
units.tr: Thomas Aquinas, whose ability I rightly admire, after raising an objection to the use of a flint knife in circumcision, answers in this way: "As to the second point, it must be said that a stone knife was not necessary for circumcision, so such an instrument is not found specified in any divine precept. Nor did the Jews commonly use such an instrument for circumcising, just as they do not use one now." So far he has spoken truly and certainly. What follows is uncertain. "Yet some famous circumcisions done with a stone knife are read of, as we read in Exodus 4 that Zipporah took a very sharp stone, and Joshua 5 says, 'Make for yourself stone knives.'" I say that these things are very uncertain. The learned Drusius, in his notes on Joshua, inclines to think that there were flint knives. Ramirez, in chapter 4 of his Pentecontarchus, labours hard to establish that opinion. He has borrowed his arguments from the most learned Masius. But the learned Junius, Piscator, the Geneva men, Cajetan, Arias Montanus and Pagninus think that in the word sharpness [אור], which properly denotes sharpness, there is either a metonymy of the adjunct, standing for a sharp knife by synecdoche, or a metaphor, insofar as אור rock [petram] means. What Thomas therefore adds from Theodoret, Questions on Joshua chapter 5, and from Justin's Dialogue with Trypho, namely "by which was foreshadowed that spiritual circumcision was to be done through Christ," is ...

units.la: Mare rubrum.
units.tr: The Red Sea.

units.la: Quod Ebraeus vocat הים סוף id est mare algosum, id Graeci Θαλασσαν Ερυθραν vel Ερυθραιαν, Latinus vero Mare Rubrum vocat. Et quidem bis extat in Novo T. Act. 7. & Hebr. 11. Creditum multis, sic illud, dictum a colore aquae, unde vulgo quoque sic pingitur. Sed jam olim * Curtius prodidit, maris illius aquas ne colore quidem abhorrere a caeteris. Brodaeus in Misc. 3. 9. testatur se diligentissime scisicitatum de multis, qui mare illud sulcaverant, atque id responsi tulisse semper, quae de rubra aqua aut arena vulgo dicuntur, falsa esse, neque ullum unquam repertum adeo stolidum, qui id ab Oceano nostro quicquam differre existimaret. Ludovicus Vartomannus, oculatus testis, in Itinerario, Satis, inquit, in confesso est omnibus, quod dictum aequor non sit rubrum, sed illar reliqui aequoris. Ast ego de arenae colore ἐπίχω. De algae colore rubeo non contendo. Illud monuisse tironem satis fuerit, aquas istius maris non rubere. Unde ergo dictum Rubrum? Illud interpretamentum est Graeci, Ερυθρός. Curtius, Ab Erythro Rege inditum est nomen, Suidas, Ερυθρα ἐκλήθη ἀπὸ Σοκχρονίας ... Agatharhides apud Photium, cum duas recensuisset sententias, quarum prima a colore undarum, altra a dominatore, nomenclaturae communis arcessebat originem, sic inquit, ... ψευδος, ... Quis vero ille Erythrus sive Erythras? Hic omnes futilitatis numeros impleverunt Gentiles. Hunc Erythrum Esavum fuisse, qui cognomen habuit Edom id est ἐρυθρός. Genebr. ad Ps. 106. Druf. ad loca dissic. Exod. pag. 187. Scaliger ad Festum voce, Ægyptius, & omnium diligentissime Fullerus Miscell. 4. 20. ostenderunt. Miraris lector, Edomum huic sinui nomenclaturam dedisse? Cogita, unicum montem Atlantem vastissimo mari nomen dedisse. Cogita, Philistæos mari mediterraneo, cujus nec ita diu, nec magna admodum parte domini fuere, de suo nomine nominasse Palæstinum, Exod. 23.11. Quid ergo miraris, potentissimum, quà late isti patebant campi, Monarcham, Esavum, aut potentissimam ejus progeniem nomen impositsse isti sinui, quem diutissime sola possedit? Illud etiam adverte, veterum Idumæam nequaquam tam angustis circumscriptam fuisse terminis, ut hodie in tabulis depingitur, sed maximam Arabiæ Petræ partem sibi vindicasse, finesque suos longo oræ maritimæ tractu ad sinum usque Arabicum seu mare rubrum protulisse. Omnem super hac re dubitationem tollit nobilissimus locus, 1. Regum. 9. 26. Praeterea classem paravit Rex Salomo in Hetzion Geber, quæ est prope Elothas: ad littus maris algosi in terra Edom. Scribendum ergo Mare Rubrum, principe litera vocis Rubrum majuscula, cum non sit appellativi, sed proprii nominis interpretamentum. Vide Fullerum.
units.tr: What the Hebrew calls hayyam suph [הים סוף], that is, the seaweed sea, the Greeks call Thalassan Erythran [Θάλασσαν Ἐρυθράν] or Erythraian, and the Latin calls it Mare Rubrum. It occurs twice in the New Testament, in Acts 7 and Hebrews 11. Many have believed that it is so called from the colour of its water, and for this reason it is commonly painted that way. But Curtius showed long ago that the waters of that sea do not even differ in colour from others. Brodaeus, in Miscellanea 3.9, testifies that he inquired most carefully of many who had sailed that sea, and that they always answered that what is commonly said about red water or red sand is false, and that no one has ever been found so foolish as to think it differs at all from our Ocean. Ludovicus Vartomannus, an eyewitness, says in his Itinerary: "It is agreed by all that the sea is not red, but the other waters are the same." As for the colour of the sand, I suspend judgment [ἐπέχω]. About the red colour of the seaweed I do not argue. It will be enough to remind a beginner that the waters of that sea are not red. Why then is it called Red? That is a Greek rendering, Erythros [Ἐρυθρός]. Curtius: "The name was given from King Erythros." Suidas: "Erythra was so named from ... [Ἐρυθρὰ ἐκλήθη ἀπὸ Σοκχρονίας ...]." Agatharchides, cited by Photius, after listing two opinions, the first deriving the name from the colour of the waves and the second from a ruler, says: "... [ψεῦδος, ...]", that is, "false". But who was that Erythrus or Erythras? Here the Gentiles have filled every measure of silliness. That this Erythrus was Esau, who had the surname Edom, that is, ἐρυθρός [red], has been shown by Genebrardus on Psalm 106, by Drusius on the difficult passages of Exodus, page 187, by Scaliger on Festus under the word "Ægyptius", and most diligently of all by Fuller in Miscellanea 4.20. Are you surprised, reader, that Edom gave this gulf its name? Consider that a single mountain, Atlas, gave its name to a vast sea. Consider that the Philistines named the Mediterranean, over which they ruled for no long time and over only a small part, after their own name, Palaestinum, Exodus 23.11. Why then do you wonder that a powerful monarch, Esau, or his mighty descendants, gave their name to that gulf, which they possessed for a very long time alone, since the plains there stretched so far? Note also this: the ancient Idumaea was by no means confined within the narrow limits it is drawn with on today's maps, but claimed the greater part of Arabia Petraea and extended its borders along a long stretch of coast as far as the Arabian Gulf, or Red Sea. Every doubt on this matter is removed by the very notable passage in 1 Kings 9.26: "Moreover King Solomon made a navy of ships in Ezion-geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom." Therefore one should write Mare Rubrum, with the initial letter of Rubrum capitalised, since it is not a common noun but the rendering of a proper name. See Fuller.

units.la: Et sument de sanguine ejus ac ponent super utrumque postem, &c.

units.la: Quàm versatus fuerit in S. Literis is qui Decretum Gratiani glossa illustravit, vel exi eo liquebit, quod distinctionem xi. caput Ecclesiasticarum, ubi inter alia de salutifera crucis signaculo agitur, hæc chartis illevit, Veruntamen videtur signum Crucis traxisse originem ex Veteri Testamento, quod cum angelus deberet occidere primogenita Ægypti præceptum est filiis Israel, utrumque postem liniri de sanguine agni, ad modum Thau litera, quæ est instar crucis. Hæc Glossator. Ego verò nihil tale in ullæ Editione invenio. An vero Thau crucis habuerit figuram ad Jezech. cap. 9. videbimus. Augustinus eadem dexteritate crucem ex historia Numerorum 20. exsculpsit Quæst. in Numeros, quæst. 35. Quod petra virga percutitur, crux Christi figuratur. Ligno enim accedente ad petram gratia manavit, & quod bis percutitur, evidentius significat crucem. Duo quippe ligna sunt crux. Certe lentis maxillis eos edere oportet, quibus istæ cupediæ sapiunt.
units.tr: How well versed in Holy Scripture the man was who furnished the Decretum of Gratian with a gloss will be clear from this: in distinction xi, the chapter Ecclesiasticarum, where among other things the saving sign of the cross is discussed, he set down these words: Yet the sign of the cross seems to have taken its origin from the Old Testament, when the angel was to kill the firstborn of Egypt, the sons of Israel were commanded to smear both door posts with the blood of the lamb, in the shape of the letter Thau, which is like a cross. So the Glossator. I, however, find nothing of the kind in any edition. Whether Thau really had the form of a cross we shall see at Ezekiel chapter 9. Augustine with equal dexterity carved a cross out of the story in Numbers 20, Quaest. in Numeros, quaest. 35: That the rock is struck with the rod signifies the cross of Christ. For water flowed from the rock when the wood was brought to it, and that it is struck twice more clearly signifies the cross. Indeed two pieces of wood make a cross. Surely those who relish such dainties must chew them with leisurely jaws.

units.la: Verf. II. Phase.
units.tr: Verse 2. Phase.

units.la: Ebr. פסח / Antiquâ lectione Phase. Penacuta enim nomina hujus formæ solent exprimere, quasi semper in Pausâ essent, פָּסַח / Et ח / ֹ sive phathach furtivum sub se, sive phathach nativum ante se habeant, per E exprimebant, Noach, Noë, Corach Core, Tharach Thare, quod exemplum huic plane geminum est. De hac voce vide Martinium in Etymologico, Drusium ad voces Ebr. Novi Testamenti. Ex iis discces, plerosque veterum vocem terminatione Chaldaicâ hinc derivatam Pascha pro Græcâ habuisse & non per quandam allusionem, sed serio ὑπὲρ ἢ πάσχειν deflexisse. Quod ex veteribus etiam Hieron. in cap. 26. Matthæi, & Isidorus lib. 6. cap. 17. refutârunt.
units.tr: Heb. [פסח]. In the older reading, Phase. For words of this form, which have the accent on the penult, usually express the vowel as if they were always in pause, [פָּסַח]; and where the ח has a furtive patah beneath it or a native patah before it, they rendered it by E: Noach, Noë; Corach, Core; Tharach, Thare, which is an exact parallel to this case. On this word see Martinius in his Etymologicon, and Drusius on the Hebrew words of the New Testament. From these you may learn that most of the ancients derived the word from the Chaldean form and took Pascha as if it were Greek, and that they explained it not by some passing allusion but seriously, as derived from the Greek verb for "to suffer" [πάσχειν]. Among the ancients, Jerome on Matthew chapter 26 and Isidore, book 6, chapter 17, also refuted this.

units.la: Verf. 5.

units.la: Iuxta quem ritum tolletis & hædum.
units.tr: According to this rite you shall take both lamb and kid.

units.la: Ita legitur in Editione vulgaria. Ea versio complures in istam sententiam præcipites dedit, duo distincta sacrificia agni & hœdi hic præcipi, quam prolixe refutarunt præter alios Abulensis & Lyra. Recte notavit Cajetanus, pro posteriori membro in Ebræo esse, ex agnis & ex capris accipietis. Et addit, Hinc clare patet, quod dictio (שור) superius interpretata agnus, communis est tam agno quam hædo, ex eo quod jubetur accipi ex agnis & capris. id est vel ovib. vel ex capris. Oleastrius, Ex hoc loco apparet id quod supra diximus, vid. שור significare pecus, sive sit agnus sive hædus. Disce tiro ex Cajetano, copulam vau (ET) hic idem esse quod disiunctiva in aut. Qui maledixerit patri ET MATRI, Matth. 15. 4. ὁ μητρὶ, aut matri. Et quidem talium exemplorum magnam farraginem Grammatici comportarunt. Jubet itaque, verba Theodoreti ἵνα ὁ μὲν θύσαντι ἔχων ἔπι θύσῃ. ὁ δὲ καταλιζων τὰ θυσιάτα, τὴν ἐξοφον id est ut qui ovem habet, eam immolet: qui vero ea caret, loco ejus hædum jugulet, Chaldæus & LXX. Ebræa κατὰ ṽ̀ı̀ḋa reddidêre, copulativam retinentes. Quod si hi eam per disiunctivam expressissent, aut valde fallor, aut B. Augustinus nunquam tradidisset. diffet ea quæ jam subjiciam. Sic ergo ille Quæst. in Exod 42. ab agnis & hœdis. Qua in re Christus significari merito accipitur. Quid enim opus erit ovem vel agnum ab agno & hœdis accipiendum moneri, nisi ille figuraretur, cujus caro non solum ex justis sed & peccatoribus propagata est. Vides Augustinum verba Mosis sic accepisse, quasi agnum è miscello ovium hœdorumque grege seligi jussisset. Porro, Cajetani sententiam de vocula שה firmatum ibo authoritate principis Grammaticorum Davidis Kimchii, הקטון מן הכבשים וגו id est, parvus ex ovibus caprisve vocatur שה העזים נקרא שה
units.tr: So it reads in the common edition. That version led many hastily into the opinion that two distinct sacrifices, of a lamb and of a kid, are commanded here; Abulensis and Lyra, among others, refute this at length. Cajetan rightly observed that the later member in the Hebrew reads from the lambs and from the goats you shall take. And he adds: Hence it is clear that the word (שור), translated above as lamb, is common to lamb and kid, since it is commanded to be taken from lambs and goats, that is, either from sheep or from goats. Oleastrius: From this place it appears what we said above, namely that שור signifies cattle, whether it be lamb or kid. Let the beginner learn from Cajetan that the conjunction vau (AND) here means the same as a disjunctive, or: "Whoever shall curse father AND mother" (Matt. 15.4) means father or mother, [ὁ μητρὶ]. Indeed grammarians have gathered a great heap of such examples. He therefore commands, as Theodoret's words have it, [ἵνα ὁ μὲν θύσαντι ἔχων ἔπι θύσῃ. ὁ δὲ καταλιζων τὰ θυσιάτα, τὴν ἐξοφον], that is, so that whoever has a sheep should sacrifice it, but whoever lacks one should slaughter a kid in its place; so the Chaldean and the Seventy rendered it, keeping the copulative. If they had expressed it by a disjunctive, I am greatly mistaken or Augustine would never have taught what I am about to quote. So he writes in Quaest. in Exodum 42: from the lambs and kids. In this matter Christ is rightly understood to be signified. For why would it be necessary to advise that the lamb or sheep be taken from lambs and kids, unless he were prefigured whose flesh was propagated not only from the just but also from sinners? You see that Augustine took the words of Moses as if he had commanded the lamb to be chosen from a mixed flock of sheep and goats. Furthermore, I will confirm Cajetan's opinion about the little word [שה] by the authority of the prince of grammarians, David Kimchi: [הקטון מן הכבשים וגו], that is, the small one is called a lamb from among the sheep or the goats [שה העזים נקרא שה].

units.la: Absque macula. ] Vidi virum eruditum, qui hoc interpretaretur de macula coloris. Certè non illud excidisset viro eruditissimo, si vocem Ebræam considerasset. Ea est תמים id est perfectus, integer, sine vitio, non mutilus, aut truncatus, aut vitiosus ulla parte corporis. Oleastrius, non prohibebantur à sacrificiis agui maculosi velleris, sed debebat esse integer quoad membra. Lxx. reddunt τέλειον id est perfectum, Chald. Onkelos שלים / quod idem valet. R. Salomo & Aben-Ezra interpretantur, בלא מום sine macula i.e. vitio, ἄμωμος, quæ vox (μῶμος) videtur esse originis Ebraicæ, ut vid. sit à מום / Unde Genebrardus in comm. ad Ps. 119. 1. ulterius progressus תמים / cum per vocem ἄμωμος redditur, non à תמם sed מום deflectit. Ridiculè. Quis enim unquam ejusmodi formam Heemanthicam ex Quiescentibus Ain Vau vidit derivatam? Et si id daret quispiam, tamen vox ea magis maculatum, quàm immaculatum significaret. Nisi quispiam ostendat, ח Heemanthicum vim τὸ ἀπρηπτες habere. Quid ergo? תמים semper est à תמם / De victimis usurpatum optimè redditur perfectus, immaculatus, sine maculâ. Hominibus verò etiam sanctissimis tributum aNoæ, bDavidi, cJobo, significat syncerum, integrum, ἄδολον, sine fuco, Belgicè opzecht / habetque in opposito הנף hypocritam. Hoc sensu acceptum Vulg. aliquando simplicem & תם simplicitatem vertit, ut Genes. 20. verf. 5. & 6. & quidem optimè. Aliquando tamen perfectum, aliquando immaculatum, & sine macula reddidit, haud omnino sine periculo, quod Interpretes tollere satagunt distinctione inter perfectionem viæ & patriæ, absolutam & comparatam, graduum & partium. Verùm si prædictis similibus locis vocem Ebræam reddas, ut diximus, omnia erunt plana; nec distinctionis istius indiga.
units.tr: Without blemish. I have seen a learned man who interpreted this as a blemish of colour. Surely such a thing would not have escaped a most learned man had he considered the Hebrew word. It is [תמים], that is, perfect, whole, without fault, not maimed, or truncated, or defective in any part of the body. Oleastrius: Animals with spotted fleece were not forbidden for sacrifice, but it had to be whole as to its limbs. The Seventy render it [τέλειον], that is, perfect; the Chaldee Onkelos [שלים], which means the same. Rabbi Solomon and Aben Ezra explain it as [בלא מום], without blemish, that is, without defect, [ἄμωμος]; this word (μῶμος) seems to be of Hebrew origin, as it apparently derives from [מום]. Hence Genebrardus, in his commentary on Psalm 119.1, went further and held that when [תמים] is rendered by the word [ἄμωμος] it is not derived from [תמם] but from [מום]. Ridiculous. For who has ever seen such a Hebrew-style form derived from the quiescent Ain Vau? And even if someone granted it, that word would signify spotted rather than unspotted, unless someone shows that the ח in the Hebrew form has the force of [τὸ ἀπρηπτες]. What then? [תמים] is always from [תמם]. Used of victims it is best rendered perfect, unspotted, without blemish. Applied to men, even the most holy, as to Noah (Gen. 6), David (Ps. 18), and Job (Job 1.1), it means sincere, whole, [ἄδολον], without deceit, in Dutch opzecht; and its opposite is [הנף], a hypocrite. In this sense the Vulgate sometimes rendered it simple, and [תם] as simplicity, as in Genesis 20, verses 5 and 6, and rightly so. Sometimes, however, it rendered it perfect, and sometimes unspotted and without blemish, not altogether without risk, which the interpreters strive to remove by a distinction between the perfection of the way and of the homeland, absolute and comparative, of degrees and of parts. But if in such similar places you render the Hebrew word, as I have said, everything will be plain, and there will be no need of that distinction.

units.la: Quintâ autem generatione ascenderunt filii Israel de terra Ægypti.
units.tr: And in the fifth generation the sons of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt.

units.la: Ita Lxx. At cornua obvertit Oraculum Gen.15. Generatione quartâ redibunt hùc. Hæc difficultas non parum exercuit Damasum, ut liquet ex Epistola Hieronymi 23. qua Damaso ad hanc quæstionem respondet. Atque adeo ipse Hiero. profitetur, nodum illum sibi initio visum insolubilem. Augustinus Quæst. 9. per Generationem intelligit seculum, puta spatium C. annorum, locumque Genes. 15. accipit de quarta generatione id'est centenario annorum completo: hunc verò de incoato. Hieronymus hanc præmittit responsionem, Oraculum Geneseos 15. completum in generationibus Levi. Levi enim ingressus est Ægyptum cum filio Cahath, Cahath genuit Aharon, Aharon Eleazarum, qui unà cum patre ex Ægypto excessit. Ecce 4. generationes. At dum Moses hic quintæ generationis meminit, respicere ad tribum Judæ. A Juda enim usque ad Naasson, qui ex Ægypto egressus, est, esse generationes 5. Juda, Phares, Ezron, Aram, Aminadab, Naasson. Utraque responsio magnis urgeri potest difficultatibus. Neutra solida est. Altera quam Hieronymus adfert firmiori in originario textu tibicine fulta est, Videlicet in Ebraeo non legi בְּדוֹר sed חֲמֻשִּׁים / Quam vocem Aquila & Symmachus reddidere καθωπλισμένοι id est armati, quod est ipsissimum interpretamentum vulgarii interpretis. Ebraeorum Interpretum Coryphaeus Kimchi, qui quintam costam (חָמֵשׁ Ebraicè) succinctam habet armis militaribus. חָמֵשׁ est costa quinta. Lxx. solent ψόαι interpretari id est lumbos, Aben Ezra, מְזֻוְּרֵי חָמֵשׁ לַמִּלְחָמָה accincti quintâ costâ ad bellum, ut sint מְזֻוְּרֵי חֲלָצִים accincti lumbis. Onkelos, מְזֹרָז accincti, ἐζωσμένοι, quod ipsissimum hujus vocis interpretamentum est, Jos. 1. 14. apud eosdem Lxx. Iidem verò Jesa. 4. 12. usi sunt voce διεσκευασμένοι parati. Vtrobique vulgatus, armati. Theodotio solus reddidit, σιμπαιζοντες, numero quinario incedentes, quod video placuisse nostris Interpp. Junio & Trem. quorum illud est, militari ordine. ordine. Sed frustra tot verba facio, cum non existimem ullum inter Pontificios fore, qui Græco textui hic sit patrocinaturus.
units.tr: So the Septuagint. But the oracle in Genesis 15 turns the horns against this reading: In the fourth generation they shall come back here. This difficulty troubled Damasus no little, as is clear from Jerome's letter 23, in which he answers Damasus on this question. Jerome himself admits that the knot seemed to him insoluble at first. Augustine, Question 9, understands "generation" to mean an age, that is a span of 100 years, and takes the passage of Genesis 15 about the fourth generation to mean with the hundred years completed, but this passage to mean with the hundred years begun. Jerome puts forward this answer first: the oracle of Genesis 15 was fulfilled in the generations of Levi. For Levi entered Egypt with his son Kohath, Kohath begat Aaron, and Aaron begat Eleazar, who went out of Egypt together with his father. Behold, four generations. But when Moses here mentions the fifth generation, he is looking to the tribe of Judah. For from Judah down to Nahshon, who came out of Egypt, there are five generations: Judah, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon. Both answers can be pressed with great difficulties, and neither is solid. The other answer, which Jerome brings, is supported by a firmer prop in the original text: namely, that in the Hebrew we do not read [בְּדוֹר] but [חֲמֻשִּׁים]. Aquila and Symmachus rendered this word [καθωπλισμένοι], that is armed, which is exactly the rendering of the Vulgate translator. Kimchi, the chief of the Hebrew interpreters, has the word [חָמֵשׁ] for "fifth rib", "girded with military arms." [חָמֵשׁ] is the fifth rib. The Seventy usually translate it [ψόαι], that is the loins. Aben Ezra: [מְזֻוְּרֵי חָמֵשׁ לַמִּלְחָמָה], girded with the fifth rib for war, so that they are [מְזֻוְּרֵי חֲלָצִים], girded in the loins. Onkelos has [מְזֹרָז], girded, [ἐζωσμένοι], which is exactly the rendering of this word, Joshua 1:14, among the same Seventy. The same Seventy, at Isaiah 4:12, used the word [διεσκευασμένοι], prepared. In both places the Vulgate has armed. Theodotion alone rendered [σιμπαιζοντες], advancing in a group of five, which I see pleased our interpreters Junius and Tremellius, of whom the former has in military order. But I am wasting many words, since I do not think there will be any among the Papists who would defend the Greek text here.

units.la: CAP. XXI. verf. 3.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI, verse 3.

units.la: Cum quali veste intraverit, cum tali exeat.
units.tr: With whatever clothing he entered, with such he shall go out.

units.la: Ita vulgatus. Cajetanus, Nulla hic vestium mentio. Et Steuchus agnoscit נֶפֶשׁ semper corpus denotare. Verba Ebræa, אִם בְּגוּפוֹ יָבֹא בְּגוּפוֹ יֵצֵא / si cum corpore suo (Lxx. μόνῳ, solus) venerit, cum corpore suo (Lxx. μόνῳ) exibit. Chaldæus utitur voce בִּלְחוֹדוֹהִי / quæ idem significat quod Græcum μόνῳ. Oleastrius quoque agnoscit in Ebræo venire cum corpore, notatque Ebraismum esse, pro venire solum. Jam vide allegorias Scholasticorum de hac veste, nominatim vero commentarium Dionysii Carthusiani & cave sequaris.
units.tr: So the Vulgate. Cajetan: "There is no mention of clothing here." And Steuchus acknowledges that [נֶפֶשׁ] always denotes the body. The Hebrew words are [אִם בְּגוּפוֹ יָבֹא בְּגוּפוֹ יֵצֵא], if he comes with his body (Septuagint alone [μόνῳ], solus), with his body (Septuagint alone [μόνῳ]) he shall go out. The Chaldean uses the word [בִּלְחוֹדוֹהִי], which means the same as the Greek alone. Oleaster also acknowledges that in the Hebrew to come with the body is a Hebraism for to come alone. Now look at the allegories of the Schoolmen about this garment, especially the commentary of Dionysius the Carthusian, and beware of following them.

units.la: CAP. VI. verf. 3.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI, verse 3.

units.la: Nomen meum ADONAI non indicavi illis. Ita Vulgatus.
units.tr: My name ADONAI I did not make known to them. So the Vulgate.

units.la: Etiam Lxx. καὶ τὸ ὄνομά μου κύριος οὐκ ἐδήλωσα αὐτοῖς. In quorum vestigia pedem quoque suum posuit B. Lutherus. At illud esset Ebriacè הוֹדַעְתִּי אוֹתָם vel לָהֶם / In textu Ebræo ita legimus at [in] nomine meo לָהֶם נוֹדַעְתִּי יְהוָה לֹא IHUH non innotui illis. Atque ita uno impetu concidunt plurimæ quæstiones, quas super hoc loco moverunt Interpretes. Quia vero Interpres Latinus τὸ πεπογεγγιμμένον ὄνομα hic loci reddit per cognomen ADONAI, puto non admodum fore alienum, si hic exhibeam cum tractatum quem Lectoribus meis non semel sum pollicitus.
units.tr: The Septuagint too: [καὶ τὸ ὄνομά μου κύριος οὐκ ἐδήλωσα αὐτοῖς]. Luther also set his foot in their footsteps. But the Hebrew would be [הוֹדַעְתִּי אוֹתָם] or [לָהֶם]. In the Hebrew text we read thus: at [in] my name [לָהֶם נוֹדַעְתִּי יְהוָה לֹא], IHUH I was not made known to them. And so at one stroke most of the questions that the interpreters have raised about this passage fall away. But because the Latin interpreter here renders [τὸ πεπογεγγιμμένον ὄνομα] by the surname ADONAI, I think it will not be altogether out of place to set out here the treatise which I have more than once promised my readers.

units.tr: To D. Festus Hommius, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Minister of the Church of Leiden and Regent of the Theological College, my lord and patron, to be honoured with all respect.

units.la: CUM ante annos xii. Oxonii literas Ebraicas docerem, rogabar sæpe ab auditoribus meis, cur intextus Ebr. lectione voci הוהי cognomen Adonai substituerem. Respondebam breviter, nomen illud alienis vocalibus scriptum esse, proprias vero superstitionis & quæ ex ea tandem orta est, ignorantiæ tenebris obrutas exolevisse: Illud saltem ne pervicacissimum quidem, qui Cl. Drusii tetragrammaton legisset, inficiaturum, lectionem vulgatam Jehova incertam esse. Quærebatur magno studio tetragrammaton Drusii, sed quia distracta jam pridem erant exemplaria, rogabant auditores, ut ipse ad tironum captum aphorismos aliquot conscriberem. Parebam libens, & quæ Cl. Drusius habebat ad rem propius pertinentia, transcribebam, cæteris, ne in immensum excurreret dissertatio, missis. Ex selectissimis Bodlæanæ Bibliothecæ authoribus eam auctam ibam. Memini, inter alios, Reverendum & Magnificum virum, D. Joh. Prideaux̄ium, Theologiæ Doctorem & Professorem Regium, nunc Academiæ pro-cancellarium, communem nostrum amicum, illam dissertationem meam legere, & discedentem hortari, ut eam aliquando evulgarem. Ego licet à me impetrare non potuerim ut ejusmodi scriptulum seorsim ederem, non destiti tamen illam ipsam eruditis & piis Theologis communicare. Fidem mihi faciet vel unicus Scultetus, & iste communis noster amicus, ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις, cujus Epistolam hic repræsentabo.
units.tr: About twelve years ago, when I was teaching Hebrew letters at Oxford, my hearers often asked me why, in reading the text, I substituted the title Adonai for the word הוהי. I answered briefly that this name was written with foreign vowels, while its own vowels had faded away, buried under the darkness of superstition and of the ignorance that eventually arose from it. At least this much, I said, not even the most obstinate man could deny, if he had read the Tetragrammaton of the illustrious Drusius: that the customary reading Jehova is uncertain. Eagerly they asked for Drusius's treatment of the Tetragrammaton, but since copies had long since sold out, my hearers asked me to write out a few brief notes for beginners. I gladly complied, and I copied out whatever Drusius had that bore more directly on the matter, leaving out the rest so that the discussion would not run on without limit. I then expanded it with the help of the most select authors in the Bodleian Library. I remember that, among others, the Reverend and Distinguished man, D. Joh. Prideaux, Doctor of Theology and Regius Professor, now pro-chancellor of the University and our common friend, read this essay of mine, and as he left he urged me to publish it at some time. Although I could not bring myself to publish such a small work on its own, I did not cease to share it with learned and pious theologians. My testimony will be confirmed by Scultetus alone, and by that common friend of ours, he who is now among the saints [ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις], whose letter I shall reproduce here.

units.la: SIXTINO AMAMÆ
units.tr: To Sixtinus Amama

units.la: S. P.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: Vir Clarissime, Legi, & ut, quod res est, dicam, cum voluptate legi, tuas de Tetragrammato meditationes, rogoque ut per pralum illa communices Theologiæ studiosis. Joh. Seldenus de Diis Syrorum procul dubio tibi visus est. Is quoque hanc materiam attigit, sed paucis. §. 48. omisisti annum, quo Galatinus floruit. Bucholzerus meus in Indice Chronolog. annotat, P. Galatinum anno 1518. scripsisse Epistolam ad Reuchlinum. Hunc ergo annum tibi nominandum existimem. Vale. Embdæ 1623. 18. May.
units.tr: Most distinguished sir, I have read your meditations on the Tetragrammaton, and, to say what is the case, I read them with pleasure. I ask that you make them available in print to students of theology. Selden has certainly come to your notice in his book on the gods of the Syrians. He too touched on this subject, but only briefly. In §48 you have left out the year in which Galatinus flourished. My Bucholzer, in his Index of Chronology, notes that P. Galatinus wrote an Epistle to Reuchlin in the year 1518. I think this is the year you should name. Farewell. Emden, 18 May 1623.

units.la: ὁ σὸς ABR. SCVLTETVS.
units.tr: Yours, Abr. Scultetus [ὁ σὸς].
