units.la: XXXVII. Ad quæ omnina hoc observetur, τὸ α vocibus prioribus quinque præpositum vel sic accipi posse, ut indicetur τὸ μὴ ϑεμιτὸν, quod non licuerit, vel τὸ μὴ ἑωθὸς, quod insolens fuerit, vel τὸ μὴ δυνατὸν, quod pronuntiari non potuerit.
units.tr: XXXVII. In regard to all these, it should be noted that the alpha privative prefixed to the first five words may be understood in one of three ways: as τὸ μὴ θεμιτόν [unlawful], that which was not permitted; or as τὸ μὴ εἰωθός [unusual], that which was not customary; or as τὸ μὴ δυνατόν [impossible], that which could not be pronounced.

units.la: XXXVIII. Tria ista locum habere possunt in istis vocibus, si distinguas tempora. Quamdiu enim duravit isthæc ἰυλαβεια, in usu non fuit ejus pronuntiatio. Ex quo autem ea in superstitionem demigravit, non tantum in usu non fuit, sed & horrendi carminis lege prohibita fuit. Atque huc pertinet illud Theodoreti, Ἐπὶ δὲ πᾶς ἐδέγμως ἀφεγκτον ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἀπείρηλαι γὰρ παρ' αὐτοῖς διὰ τῆς γλώττης id est Hoc apud Ebræos ineffabile dicitur; Ipsis enim ejus prolatione interdictum est. Ex quo denique una cum templo & superstitibus sacerdotibus prolatio ista intercidit, pronuntiari omnino non potuit; atque, ἄφεγκτον, ἄῤῥητον, ita & etiamnum & porro vocari jure merito poterit, usque dum verum & genuinum ejus sonum certis & indubiis indiciis doctorum industria eruerit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. These three senses can apply to these words if you distinguish the periods. For as long as this reverence [ἐυλαβεια] lasted, the pronunciation was not in use. But once it degenerated into superstition, it was not only not in use but was forbidden by the law of a dreadful curse. To this belongs Theodoret's saying: Among the Hebrews it is called "ineffable" [Ἐπὶ δὲ πάντων ἀδιστάκτως ἄφθεγκτον ὀνομάζεσθαι], for it is forbidden among them to speak it aloud [ἀπείρηται γὰρ παρ' αὐτοῖς διὰ τῆς γλώττης]. Finally, when the temple and the surviving priests were gone, that pronunciation perished, and it could no longer be pronounced at all. So it may rightly and justly be called unspoken [ἄφεγκτον] and unutterable [ἄῤῥητον] still, and will continue to be so called until the diligence of scholars brings to light its true and genuine sound by certain and unquestionable evidence.

units.la: XXXIX. Sic itaque dico, tres illas literæ A notiones in nomenclaturis istis posse habere locum, ut dixerint ἄφεγκτον, τῆς Ἰουδαίοις scilicet ἀφεγκτον quondam, cum sacerdotibus nota adhuc esset ejus nominis lectio, quod primo quidem ἰυλαβεια, postea vero ex superstitione observabant: Et ἀφεγκτον suo sæculo, cum
units.tr: XXXIX. I say, then, that those three senses of the alpha privative can have a place in these names: so that the word ἄφεγκτον [unspoken] was once, for the Jews, the right description, when the priests still knew how to read that name, which at first they observed out of reverence and later out of superstition. And it was unspoken in its own age, when it was unknown, which was a matter of necessity.

units.la: b A. Donnæus Anglus in Hom. 8. Chrysost. in 2. ad Corinth. distinguit inter ἄῤῤητον καὶ ἀπρόῤῥητον. Hoc dicit esse, quod dici non debet, illud, quod dici non potest. Sed Hesychius refellit cam & I. Boisius in notis ad eundem locum. Vide in opere Saviliano, c Qæst. 15. in Exodum. Vide & Raincoldum de Idolol Rom. Eccles. 2. 1. 18. in marginalib. ignorabatur: quod erat necessitatis.
units.tr: b A. Donnaeus, the Englishman, in Homily 8 on Chrysostom's second letter to the Corinthians, distinguishes between ἄῤῥητον and ἀπρόῤῥητον, saying that the first means what ought not to be said and the second what cannot be said [ἄῤῤητον καὶ ἀπρόῤῥητον]. But Hesychius refutes him, and I. Boisius in his notes on the same passage. See the Savilian edition, c Question 15 on Exodus. See also Raincold, On the Idolatry of the Roman Church, 2.1.18, in the marginal notes.

units.la: XL. Sed rogabis hic & quidem opportunè, si toto illo temporis spacio, ante Templi destructionem, propriis vocalibus & per suas consonantes, primò ex ἐυλαβεῖα, deinde verò ex δεισδαιμονία non fuerit pronuntiatum, lectumve, si etiam post fata Simeonis Justi in benedictione Sacerdotum pronuntiari desiit, quid ergo per eo lectum fuerit? Secundò ; utrum hodie quoque ignoretur vetus & genuina lectio, Et si ita est, quid hodie pro eo legendum?
units.tr: XL. But here you will rightly ask: during the whole period before the destruction of the temple, was it not pronounced or read with its proper vowels and through its own consonants, first out of reverence [ἐυλαβεῖα] and then out of superstitious fear [δεισδαιμονία]? And if, after the death of Simon the Just, it ceased to be pronounced even in the priestly blessing, what was read in its place? Second: is the old and genuine reading still unknown today, and if so, what should be read in its place today?

units.la: XLI. Respondebo ad utramque Quæstionem ordine. Et quidem primam quod attinet, distinguo loca. In judiciis: quando inquirebatur in blasphemum, cardo rei in hoc vertebatur, utrum Deum per ipsum nomen יהוה / an vero per cognomina blasphemasset. In hoc examine nomen יהוה nec pronuntiabant per proprias consonas, nec per vicarium Adonai, sed utebantur voce יוסי Iose. Hoc eruo ex Massecheth Sanhedrin, cap.7. ubi sic legitur in Misna, הַמְגַדֵּף אֵינוֹ חַיָּב עַד שֶׁיְּפָרֵשׁ הַשֵּׁם אֲשֶׁר רִיְיהוֹשׁוּעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה בְּכָל יוֹם דָּנִין אֶת הָעִירִים בִּכְנוּי יָכָה יוֹסִי יוֹסִי נִגְמַר הַדִּין לֹא הוֹרִין בִּכְנוּי אֶלָּא מוֹצִיאִין כָּל אָדָם לַחוּץ וְשׁוֹאֲלִים אֶת הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶם וְאוֹמְרִים לוֹ אֱמוֹר מַה שֶּׁשָּׁמַעְתָּ בְּפֵירוּשׁ וְהוּא אוֹמֵר וְהָרַיָּנִים עוֹמְדִים עַל רַגְלֵיהֶם וְקוֹרְעִין וְלֹא מְאַחִין וְהַשֵּׁנִי אוֹמֵר אַף אֲנִי כְמוֹהוּ וְהַשְּׁלִישִׁי אוֹמֵר אַף אֲנִי כְמוֹהוּ id est blasphemus non a est reus (lapidationis) nisi expresserit ipsum nomen tetragr. Iosua filius Korcha, toto b die judicant c testes per cognominationem, Percutiat Iose Iosem. At ubi d absolutum est judicium, non e interficiunt per agnominationem: Sed exire jubent f omnem hominem, & rogant seniorem testem & dicunt ei, Dic nobis g clare & expresse, quid audivisti? Et judices stant & h scindunt vestes & non resarciunt eas. Et secundus dicit. Idem ego audivi, Et tertius, Et ego audivi idem quod ille. Quae cum obscuriuscula sunt, ut solent tenebriones illi tenebras lectoribus suis offundere, non pigrabor illis ex Scholiis ipsorum facem allucere.
units.tr: XLI. I will answer both questions in order. As to the first, I distinguish the occasions. In trials: when a blasphemer was examined, the crux of the case turned on whether he had blasphemed God by the name itself, יהוה, or only by its surrogates. In this inquiry they neither pronounced the name by its own consonants nor by the substitute Adonai, but used the word יוסי, Yose. I draw this from Massechet Sanhedrin, chapter 7, where the Mishnah reads: "The blasphemer is not liable until he has pronounced the Name explicitly. Joshua ben Korhah says: every day they judged cases by the euphemism 'Yakah Yose Yose'. But when the judgment is concluded they do not pronounce it by euphemism; rather they clear every person out and ask the greatest among them, and say to him, 'Tell us plainly what you heard.' The judges stand on their feet and tear their garments and do not sew them up again. The second says, 'I heard it likewise', and the third says, 'I too heard the same as he did'" [הַמְגַדֵּף אֵינוֹ חַיָּב עַד שֶׁיְּפָרֵשׁ הַשֵּׁם אֲשֶׁר רִיְיהוֹשׁוּעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה בְּכָל יוֹם דָּנִין אֶת הָעִירִים בִּכְנוּי יָכָה יוֹסִי יוֹסִי נִגְמַר הַדִּין לֹא הוֹרִין בִּכְנוּי אֶלָּא מוֹצִיאִין כָּל אָדָם לַחוּץ וְשׁוֹאֲלִים אֶת הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶם וְאוֹמְרִים לוֹ אֱמוֹר מַה שֶּׁשָּׁמַעְתָּ בְּפֵירוּשׁ וְהוּא אוֹמֵר וְהָרַיָּנִים עוֹמְדִים עַל רַגְלֵיהֶם וְקוֹרְעִין וְלֹא מְאַחִין וְהַשֵּׁנִי אוֹמֵר אַף אֲנִי כְמוֹהוּ וְהַשְּׁלִישִׁי אוֹמֵר אַף אֲנִי כְמוֹהוּ]. That is: the blasphemer is not culpable (of stoning) unless he has expressed the name itself. Joshua son of Korhah says: every day they judged the cities by the periphrasis, "May Yose strike Yose". When the judgment is concluded, they do not pronounce it by periphrasis, but they clear out everyone and ask the greatest among them and say to him: tell us plainly and explicitly what you heard. Since these things are rather obscure, as those shadowy men tend to cast darkness over their readers, I will not hesitate to shed light on them from their own commentaries.

units.la: a Vide supra § 30. b toto illo tempore quo tractabant & disceptabant illam causam. c judicant id est examinant, & fidem eorum variis quaestionibus explorant. Hoc volunt, judices in quaerendo, testes in respondendo, non pronuntiabant nomen tetragr. sed utebantur cognominatione quadam seu substitutione alterius nominis, illud autem erat יוֹסִי / Et cur Iose potius quam aliud vomen huicrei adhibitum? Quia & hoc quadriliterum est, ut יהוה / & quia in numeris ad eandem summam ascendit, ad quam nomen אֱלֹהִים / Nam si vocis utriusque literas redigas in numeros, habebis 86. Ipsum ergo verbum, percutiat Iose Josem proponitur formula blasphemiae, quam homo blasphemus in ipsum Deum per proprium ejus nomen expressum evomuit, addito rursus eodem nomine, quod dicunt blasphemare שֵׁם בְּשֵׁם vide supra § 30. d Hoc est, ubi jam res clara est & finis imponitur inquisitioni, quando dicunt judices, הַיָּב הוּא reus est, & nihil restat praeter solennem condemnationem, & eductionem ad supplicium, quae in diem sequentem differebatur, e id est non possunt procedere ad interrogationem supplicii ex isto testimonio, quod hucusque ex ore testium audiverunt. Sic dico, ex isto testimonio in quo nomen יהוה per Iose expresserunt, procedere possunt ad condemnationem illam non solennem, sed antequam educatur ad supplicium, oportet judices ex ore testium ipsam formulam blasphemiae audire sine ulla cognominatione, prout ex ipsius blasphemi ore audiverunt. Aliter enim sacra illa non constabant. f praeter testes. Id videntur postulare sequentia. Nam secundus testis dicebat, Ego audivi idem quod ille, & sic tertius, non repetita ipsa blasphemia, quia turpe & indecorum censebant eam iterare. Codices quidam pro שׁוּאלִים rogabant. legunt
units.tr: a See above, § 30. b That is, during the whole time they were handling and disputing that case. c Judicant, that is, they examine, and test the credibility of the witnesses with various questions. The meaning is this: the judges asked, the witnesses answered, and they did not pronounce the Tetragrammaton but used a certain surrogate or substitution of another name, which was יוסי. And why was Yose used for this matter rather than some other name? Because it too has four letters, like יהוה, and because in numerical value it comes to the same sum as the name אלהים. For if you reduce the letters of each word to numbers, you will have 86. So the very formula "May Yose strike Yose" is set forth as the form of blasphemy which the blasphemer uttered against God himself by his proper name expressed, with the same name added again; they call this blaspheming the name by the name, see above, § 30. d That is, when the matter is now clear and the inquiry is brought to an end, when the judges say, "He is guilty", and nothing remains but the customary condemnation and the leading out to execution, which was deferred until the following day. e That is, they cannot proceed to the inquiry into punishment on the basis of that testimony, which they have heard so far from the mouths of the witnesses. So I say: on the basis of that testimony, in which they expressed the name יהוה through Yose, they can proceed to the condemnation, which is not the customary one, but before he is led out to execution, the judges must hear the very formula of blasphemy from the mouths of the witnesses, without any periphrasis, just as they heard it from the mouth of the blasphemer himself. For otherwise those sacred proceedings would not stand. f Apart from the witnesses. The following words seem to require this, for the second witness said, "I heard the same as he did", and so the third, without repeating the blasphemy itself, because they judged it shameful and unbecoming to repeat it. Some manuscripts read rogabant for שׁוּאלִים, and they read

units.la: Rr legunt וםשיירין & retinent, sed opinor, male nolebant ergo formulam illum blasphemiae coram aliis recitari. Quod si dicamus, testes reliquos juxta quoque fuisse exire, dum senior ipsam blasphemiae formulam recitabat, quomodo dicere potuerunt singuli? Ego idem autem audivi quod ille? id est, sine periphrasi aut cognominatione. Testes non tenebantur scindere in judicio quia jam ante, cum primitus blasphemantem audiebant, sciderant.
units.tr: Rr. They read וםשיירין and retain it, but I think wrongly. They did not want the formula of blasphemy to be recited in front of others. But if we say that the other witnesses also used to go out nearby while the elder recited the formula of blasphemy, how could each of them say, one by one, "I heard the same as he did"? That is, without periphrasis or circumlocution. The witnesses were not obliged to tear their garments in court, because they had already torn them earlier, when they first heard the blasphemer.

units.la: XLII. In templo, vel ut pressius loquar, in benedictione sacerdotali & liturgia summi Pontificis, die Expiationis (namque hic ipsum tetragrammaton olim prolatum fuisse supra vidimus) posterioribus seculis per nomina 12. & 42. literarum, tanquam τεσσαρακοντα quasdam lectum fuisse, Ebraei prodiderunt. Horum nominum crebra apud Thalmudicos est mentio; atque in ipso quoque templo) cum ipsum nomen יהוה adhuc a sacerdotibus proferebatur, usitata fuisse, liquet tum ex aliis locis, tum vel praecipue ex Massechet Kiddushin cap. 4. ut postea videbimus. Postquam ergo desiit tetragrammati prolatio, haec tanquam ejus vicaria retenta sunt. Scindlerus in Lexico meminit quoque nominis 42. literarum, quod ex cap. 6. Tetragrammati Cl. Drusii hausit. Observo tamen in paraphrasi Chald. Cantic. 3. quem locum Cl. Drusius citat, non memorari nomen של עב אותיות id est 72. literarum, quomodo loqui solent, quando nomen 12. aut 42. literarum innuunt, sed שמא רבא מפרש בשבעין שמהן id est nomen magnum expressum vel expositum per 70. (pro 72.) nomina.
units.tr: XLII. In the temple, or, to speak more precisely, in the priestly blessing and the liturgy of the high priest on the Day of Atonement (for we saw above that the tetragrammaton was once pronounced here), the Hebrews have reported that in later centuries it was read through the names of 12 and 42 letters, as certain forty-twos [τεσσαρακοντα]. Frequent mention of these names is made among the Talmudists. That they were in use even in the temple itself, while the name יהוה was still pronounced by the priests, is clear both from other passages and especially from Massechet Kiddushin, chapter 4, as we shall see later. Therefore, after the pronunciation of the tetragrammaton ceased, these names were retained as its substitutes. Scindlerus in his Lexicon also mentions the name of 42 letters, which he drew from chapter 6 of the Tetragrammaton of the illustrious Drusius. I note, however, that in the Chaldee paraphrase of Canticles 3, which the illustrious Drusius cites, the name is not described as של עב אותיות [shel ʿev otiyot], that is, of 72 letters, as they usually speak when they mean the name of 12 or 42 letters, but as shma rabba mefaras bishave'in shemahan, that is, the great name expressed or explained by 70 (for 72) names.

units.la: XLIII. Lubet superiistis audire testimonia Thalmudicorum? Ecce tibi Massechet Kiddushin, cap. 4. sol. 71. pag. 1. תנו רבנן בראשונה שם בן שנים עשרה אותיות היו מוסרים אותו לכל אדם משרבו הפריצים היו מוסרים אותו לצנועים שככהונרו והצנועים שככהונרו מבליעים אותו בנעימת אחיהם id est Tradiderunt Magistri nostri, quod primo nomen filium 12. literarum tradiderint cuilibet homini. At ex quo multiplicati sunt profani homines, tradiderunt illud modestioribus ex sacerdotali ordine. Et hi absorbebant illud (id est praecipitanter demurmurabant) inter modulationem fratrum suorum. Ad quem locum Scholiastes haec notat. שם בן יכובן מכלא פרשו לנו id est nomen 12. & 42. literarum non exposuerunt. nobis. Et postea ad illa verba, משרבו &c. haec notat, qui abutebantur eo. Fortassis ad Magicas artes & praestigias. Modestioribus ] ut benedicerent populo per illud insanctuario, post peractum cultum jugis sacrificii matutini. Absorbebant autem illud inter modulationem fratrum. Quando Sacerdotes illi, qui in eo non erant exercitati, & proinde benedicebant Deo per nomen יהוה / quando illi inquam in modulatione sua trahebant vocem suam, hi absorbebant nomen 42. literarum, ut audiri à plebe non potuerit propter vocem modulationis collegarum, בנעימת ביסים קול שקורין טרוף id est בנעימת est suavis vocis modulatio, quam טרוף vocant. Hæc Scholiastes. Ex quo illud colligo, jam tunc cum prolatio nominis יהוה adhuc in usu erat, obtinuisse in divino cultu hoc nomen 42. literarum. De quo illud porro legitur in ipso textu ejusdem paginæ, nomen 42. non traditur nisi verecundo, humili & media ætatis viro, non iracundo, non ebrioso, nonpervicaci. Quicunque illud novit & in pretio habet, conservatque pure, is dilectus est supra & acceptus est infra (id est in cœlo & terra) eumque reverentur & metuunt homines, ac hæres sit seculi. Judica lector, utrum hoc non propemodum sit magicam quandam vim vocibus adscribere.
units.tr: XLIII. Shall I let you hear the testimonies of the Talmudists? Look at tractate Kiddushin, chapter 4, folio 71, page 1: Our Masters taught: at first the name of twelve letters was handed down to every man; when the profane multiplied, it was handed down to the modest among the priests, and the modest priests swallowed it up in the sweet chanting of their brothers [תנו רבנן בראשונה שם בן שנים עשרה אותיות היו מוסרים אותו לכל אדם משרבו הפריצים היו מוסרים אותו לצנועים שבכהונה והצנועים שבכהונה מבליעים אותו בנעימת אחיהם]. That is, the Masters say that the name of twelve letters was at first handed on to anyone, but once the profane multiplied it was handed on only to the more modest men among the priests, and these swallowed it (that is, murmured it hastily and under their breath) during the chanting of their brothers. On this passage the Scholiast notes: the name of twelve and forty-two letters they did not explain to us [שם בן יכובן מכלא פרשו לנו]. Then, on the words when the profane multiplied and so on, he notes: those who abused it, perhaps for magical arts and sleight of hand. The modest: so that they might bless the people with it in the sanctuary, after the continual morning sacrifice had been completed. They swallowed it during the chanting of their brothers: when those priests who were not practised in it, and therefore blessed God by the name Yahweh [יהוה], drew out their voices in their chanting, these swallowed the name of forty-two letters, so that it could not be heard by the people because of the voice of their colleagues' chanting, in the sweet melody of the voice which they call trope [בנעימת ביסים קול שקורין טרוף]. That is, the melody is a sweet modulation of the voice, which they call trope. Thus the Scholiast. From this I gather that already at the time when the pronunciation of the name Yahweh was still in use, this name of forty-two letters had obtained a place in divine worship. Further, the same page's text reads: the name of forty-two is handed down only to a modest, humble man of middle age, not to an angry man, not to a drunkard, not to a stubborn one. Whoever knows it, holds it in esteem and keeps it pure is beloved above and accepted below (that is, in heaven and on earth), men revere and fear him, and he becomes heir of the age. Judge, reader, whether this is not almost to ascribe a certain magical power to words.

units.la: XLIV. Maimonidis verba de his nominibus cap. 61. partis primæ Moreh hæc sunt
units.tr: XLIV. The words of Maimonides on these names, from chapter 61 of the first part of the Moreh, are these.

units.la: Fuit etiam penes ipsos nomen 12. literarum, quod sanctitate infra nomen tetragrammaton fuit. Videturque mihi non fuisse nomen unum sed potius duo vel tria quorum litera in universum fuerint 12. Et paulo post de eodem loquens, id est non est dubium, quin illud significaverit aliquid magis proprium Deo, quam nomen ארני / Et rursus pauculis interjectis id est Ab excessu Simeonis Iusti desiere fratres ejus sacerdotes benedicere per NOMEN [tetragrammaton.] Sed benedicebant per hoc nomen 12. literarum. Ajunt nomen 12. literarum primo traditum fuisse omni homini. At postquam incrementa sumsit numerus profanorum, tradidisse illud tantum modestioribus inter Sacerdotes; illosque absorpsisse illud [id est præcipitanter & tacite demurmurasse] inter modulationes fratrum suorum, Sacerdotum. Et postea הָיָה אצלם גם נן שם בן מל אותיות וידוע אצל כל בעל הציור שאי אפשר בשום פנים שיהיה מב אותיות מלה אחת וני id est, Eraque apud eos similiter nomen 42. literarum, noruntque omnes intelligentes, neutiquam fuisse unum nomen, sed plura, quae in universum habuerint literas 42. Postea invehitur in illos, qui literis istorum nominum vim quandam magicam adscribunt, quod hominum genus capite quoque praecedenti perstrinxerat. Operae pretium erit audire gravissimam censuram doctissimi istius Judaei. Sic ergo inquit cap.61. Edit. Ebr. vel 60. Edit. Latinae, לא ילה בחשבתך שנעון כותבי הקמיעות ומרה שתשמעתו מהם או תמצאהו בספריהם המשונים ומשמות הבריום לא ירו על ענין בשום פנים ויקראו אותם שמות ויחשבו שהם צריכים קרושה וטהרה ושהם יעשו נפלאות כל אלה הדברים id est לא יאורת לארם שלם לשמעם כל שכן שיאמינם ne ascendat in cogitationes tuas insania eorum, qui scribunt amuleta aut si quid praeterea audiveris ex illis aut inveneris in eorum libris monstrosis. Colligunt autem illas voces quas chartis istis inscribunt ex nominibus & nihil omnino significant, & legunt ista nomina & opinantur illis necessario inesse sanctitatem & puritatem quandam, imo & vim miraculorum. Omnia ista indigna sunt, quibus sana mentis homo aures suas locet, nedum fidem habeat. Locum alterum ex cap. sequenti repraesentabo tibi ex versione Latino, anno 1520. edita. Codex enim Ebraeus editus Savionetae, anno à condito mundo שיח id est 313. juxta aeram minorem (id est à nato Christo 1553.) nihil tale habet, ut vel eam editionem mutilatam esse, vel si Latinus Interpres ex Arabico vertit (liber enim ille ab ipso authore Arabice conscriptus est) ipsum Maimonidis textum ab Interprete Ebraeo truncatum esse oporteat. Juvat conjecturam meam, quod Interpres Latinus passim authorem contrahere & mutilare, non vero ad eum tam multa addere soleat. Sic ergo introducit Maimonidem, cap. 61. sol. 25. Notum est ac manifestum cuilibet aliqualiter intelligenti & ponderanti rationes divinarum rerum, literas & characteres seu figuras literarum etiam nostrarum, manu artificis scriptarum, esse puras creaturas, & ideo secundum in superioribus à nobis declarata, non habere ullam potentiam aut virtutem à se nisi recidamus ad ignorationem idololatrarum, Creaturas pro creatura adorantium, quorum peccatum demonstravimus esse impiam blasphemiam & Deo abominabilem. Et paulo post, * cum autem homines pravi & insipientes invenerunt ista verba, fuerunt potentes in mendacio, dicen-
units.tr: There was also among them the name of twelve letters, which was holier than the name Tetragrammaton. It seems to me that it was not one name but rather two or three, whose letters together came to twelve. And a little later, speaking of the same thing: that is, there is no doubt that it signified something more proper to God than the name Adonai. And again, after a few lines: From the death of Simeon the Just, his priestly brothers ceased to bless with the NAME [Tetragrammaton]. But they blessed with the name of twelve letters. They say that the name of twelve letters was first handed down to every man, but after the number of the profane grew, it was handed down only to the more modest among the priests, and they swallowed it [that is, murmured it hastily and silently] during the chanting of their brothers, the priests. And afterwards: there was also among them a name of forty-two letters, and all who understand know that it is by no means possible for one word to have forty-two letters, but that they were several names which together had forty-two letters. [הָיָה אצלם גם שם בן מב אותיות וידוע אצל כל בעל השכל שאי אפשר בשום פנים שיהיה מב אותיות מלה אחת]. Afterwards he attacks those who ascribe a certain magical power to the letters of these names, a class of men that he had also censured in the preceding chapter. It will be worth while to hear this most learned Jew's very grave judgment. So he says in chapter 61 (in the Hebrew edition, or chapter 60 in the Latin): לא יעלה בחשבתך שטות כותבי הקמיעות ומה שתשמענו מהם או תמצאהו בספריהם המשונים ומשמות הבריות לא ירו על ענין בשום פנים ויקראו אותם שמות ויחשבו שהם צריכים קדושה וטהרה ושהם יעשו נפלאות כל אלה הדברים [לא יאות לאדם שלם לשמעם כל שכן שיאמינם]: let not the folly of those who write amulets enter your thoughts, nor whatever you hear from them or find in their strange books. They gather the words they write on those papers from names and signify nothing at all, yet they read these names and suppose that they necessarily possess some holiness and purity, even power to work miracles. All these things are unworthy of being heard by a sane man, much less believed. I shall give you another passage from the following chapter, from the Latin version published in 1520. For the Hebrew codex published at Savioneta in the year from the creation of the world 313 (in the lesser era, that is, from the birth of Christ 1553) contains nothing of the kind, so that either that edition is mutilated or, if the Latin translator translated from the Arabic (for that book was written in Arabic by the author himself), the text of Maimonides itself must have been truncated by the Hebrew translator. My conjecture is supported by the fact that the Latin translator usually abridges and mutilates the author here and there, but does not add so much to him. So he introduces Maimonides thus, in chapter 61, folio 25: It is known and clear to anyone who understands and weighs somewhat the reasons of divine things that letters and characters, or the figures of letters, even of ours, written by a craftsman's hand, are mere creatures, and therefore, according to what we have declared above, have no power or virtue in themselves, unless we fall back into the ignorance of idolaters, who worship a creature as the Creator, whose sin we have shown to be impious blasphemy and abominable to God. And a little later: But when wicked and foolish men discovered these words, they became powerful in deceit, saying that by joining any letters they could make this or that thing for which they wrote them, or speak it over such and such a matter. I have quoted this passage the more willingly because I see that the Jews of this age are being driven ever more headlong day by day into this impiety.

units.la: tes, quod cum conjungerent literas quaslibet, possent facere hoc vel illud cui scriberent eas vel proferrent super tali vel tali re. Hunc locum eo lubentius produxi, quod videam hujus ævi Judæos ad hanc impietatem magisque indies ferri præcipites. Reverendi & Cl. Theologi, D. Francisci Gomari, liberalitate possideo Psalterium, quod ipsum quoque editum est Savionetæ 1556. Ad ejus calcem additus est libellus hoc titulo שמות תהלים id est usus Psalmorum. In eo singulis Psalmis suus assignatur usus. Dabo gustum. Ps. 2. ut liberaris ex tempestate maris recita hunc Psalmum & inscribe eum testæ & projice illam in mare & conquiescet. Si cui caput dolebit, scribe hunc Ps. usque ad illa, confringes eos virga ferrea, &c. & suspende illam de capite ejus. Ps. 3. Si quis humerum & caput dolebit, pronuntiet hunc Ps. super oleo olivarum & inungat eo partes affectas. Ps. 7. Utilis est iste Psalmus ne homines tibi possint nocere, & ut in fugam vertas inimicum tuum, qui te persequitur. Accipe pulverem ex terra & recita super eo hunc Ps. & sparge pulverem istum coram inimico tuo, qui te persequitur & retrocedet. Et nomen divinum quod ex hoc Psalmo exurgit est אל עליון / א ex verbis illis אשר / לשר ex voce אורר per commutationem אלכם Albam, Et dic, placeat tibi Deus altissime convertere cor inimicorum meorum, sicut fecisti inimicis Abrahami patris nostri, cum hoc nomen memorabat. Porro, si quis habeat inimicum, accipiat ahenum novum & impleat illud ex fonte aquarum & recitet hunc Ps. quater à קומה יהוה usque ad finem, & effunde illam aquam in loco inimici tui & prævalebis ei, &c. Ps. 120. cum vides serpentem aut scorpionem, recita eum septies. Ps. 123. contra servum fugitivum. Inscribe laminæ plumbi duo illa nomina ארון dominus, & עבר servus, & revertitur. Ps. 126. utilis est mulieri cujus liberi moriuntur, scribe eum in pergameno, & adscribe hæc
units.tr: ...saying that by joining any letters whatever they could make this or that, to whomever they wrote them or spoke them, concerning such and such a matter. I have quoted this passage the more willingly because I see the Jews of this age being carried headlong into this impiety more and more every day. By the kindness of the Reverend and Distinguished Theologian Dr. Francis Gomarus, I possess a Psalter, which was also published at Savionetta in 1556. Appended to its end is a little book under the title שמות תהלים [Shemoth Tehillim], that is, the uses of the Psalms. In it a particular use is assigned to each Psalm. I will give a taste. Ps. 2: to be delivered from a storm at sea, recite this Psalm, write it on a potsherd, and throw it into the sea, and it will become calm. If anyone has a headache, write this Ps. down as far as the words You shall break them with a rod of iron, etc., and hang it from his head. Ps. 3: if anyone has pain in the shoulder and head, let him say this Ps. over olive oil and anoint the affected parts with it. Ps. 7: this Psalm is useful so that men cannot harm you, and so that you may put to flight your enemy who pursues you. Take dust from the earth, recite this Ps. over it, and scatter the dust before your enemy who pursues you, and he will fall back. And the divine name that arises from this Psalm is אל עליון [El Elyon], from the words אשר [asher] and לשר [lesher], from the word אורר [orer] by the substitution of אלכם [Albam]. And say, "May it please you, Most High God, to turn the hearts of my enemies, as you did to the enemies of our father Abraham," when you call to mind this name. Further, if anyone has an enemy, let him take a new brass vessel, fill it with water from a spring, and recite this Ps. four times from קומה יהוה [Kumah YHWH] to the end, and pour that water in the place of your enemy, and you will prevail against him, etc. Ps. 120: when you see a serpent or a scorpion, recite it seven times. Ps. 123: against a runaway slave. Inscribe on a sheet of lead the two names ארון [adon] lord and עבר [ebed] servant, and he will return. Ps. 126: it is useful for a woman whose children die; write it on parchment and add these words

units.la: שנוי סנסנוי סמנגלף
units.tr: Shenu sansenui smangalf [שנוי סנסנוי סמנגלף]

units.la: in postrema linea, & pones illud in quatuor angulis domus. Ps. 130. Quando vigiles circumeunt urbem si velis invisibilis transire coram illis, musla eum versus quatuor plagas mundi, & obruet eos
units.tr: in the last line, and place it at the four corners of the house. Ps. 130: when the night watchmen go around the city, if you wish to pass unseen before them, turn toward the four quarters of the world, and sleep will overcome them

units.la: * Haec ex Ebraeo.
units.tr: * These are from the Hebrew.

units.la: * vide Buxtorf. in breviat. pag. 274 eos sopor. Tædet plura adscribere. Quis jam mirabitur, superstitiosam illam gentem nomini יהוה vim miraculorum tribuisse? Cl. Buxtorf. ex libro Caphthor sol. 56. ista citat לא משה נשהמש אלא בשמו הגדול וכל נפלאותיו אשר עשה היו בשם הפורש שהוא שם יהוה ואהיה אשר אהיה id est Moses non est usus nisi nomine magno, & omnia miracula ejus, quae fecit, fuerunt, per nomen יהוה & Ehjeth ascher Ehjeh. Quis item mirabitur Thalmudicos credidisse, R.Haninam per nomen 42. literarum potuisse facere כל אשר הפץ id est quicquid vellet, ut est in Scholiis ad Mass. Aboda Zara sol.17. pag.2. Edit. Gracoviensis.
units.tr: * see Buxtorf in the Breviat., p. 274; sleep overcomes them. I am weary of adding more. Who will now be surprised that that superstitious people ascribed the power of miracles to the name יהוה [YHWH]? Distinguished Buxtorf cites from the book Caphthor, fol. 56, these words: לא משה נשהמש אלא בשמו הגדול וכל נפלאותיו אשר עשה היו בשם הפורש שהוא שם יהוה ואהיה אשר אהיה [Moses did not use anything but the great name, and all his miracles which he performed were by the name that is distinct, which is the name YHWH, and Ehyeh asher Ehyeh.] Who will likewise be surprised that the Talmudists believed that R. Haninah could, by means of a name of 42 letters, do כל אשר הפץ [kol asher hafetz], that is, whatever he wished, as is found in the scholia on Mass. Aboda Zara, fol. 17, p. 2, Krakow edition.

units.la: XLV. Sed ut his ineptiis tandem finem imponamus, revertamur ad nomen 12. & 42. literarum. Vidisti, opinor, I. illa una cum ipso tetragrammato olim prolata fuisse. II. post hujus vero pronuntiationem desitam, illorum prolationem aliquandiu mansisse. III. Ea quoque propere submissaque voce à sacerdotibus pronuntiata fuisse, ne vulgus ea perciperet, neque etiam quemlibet sacerdotem eorum prolationem doctum fuisse. IV. Omnium istorum nominum celationi praetexi metum profanationis, & eorum impietatem, qui istis ad magicas praestigias abutebantur. V. Mirum non esse, si ista quoque una cum nominis יהוה prolatione tandem interciderint.
units.tr: XLV. But to put an end at last to these absurdities, let us return to the name of 12 and 42 letters. You have seen, I think, that: (I) those names were once pronounced together with the tetragrammaton itself; (II) after the pronunciation of the latter had ceased, the utterance of those names remained for some time; (III) they were also pronounced hastily and in a low voice by the priests, so that the common people would not perceive them, nor did every priest know how to pronounce them; (IV) fear of profaning them was put forward as the reason for hiding all these names, and also the impiety of those who abused them for magical tricks; (V) it is no wonder if these also finally perished along with the pronunciation of the name יהוה [YHWH].

units.la: XLVI Frustra ergo in ista inquisiveris. Excute universum Thalmud, Maimonidem & quicquid est usquam Ebraeorum scriptorum, nihil certi & in quo possis acquiescere, erues. Quod enim R. Bechai in principio Genes. sol. 5. col.2. notat, nomen 42. literarum desumptum fuisse ex primo & secundo versu libri Geneseos, vid. à litera ב vocis בראשית usque ad literam ב vocis ובהו / quae sunt 42. literae, ex quarum varia combinatione Cabalistis nota factum fuerit nomen 42. literarum, item nomen 12. literarum, conflatum fuisse ex triplicata combinatione nominis יהוה / nullam apud me meretur fidem. Neque etiam mihi persuadere possum, Galatinum ex Ebraeorum monumentis eruisse illa quae libro 2. cap. 10. exibuit. Hoc enim ponit nomen 12. literarum אב בן ורוח הקדש id est Pater, Filius & S. Sancti. Nomen vero 42. literarum illud assignat, אב אל בן אל ורוח הקדש אל אבל לא שלשה אלהים כי אם אלה אחד id est Pater Deus, Filius Deus, Sp. S. Deus; at non tres Dii, sed unus Deus. Magnum operæ opera pretium esse, inquit Cl. Buxtorfius, hanc expositionem posse ex libris Rabbinorum firmari. Scaliger, Drusius aliique in Ebraeorum monumentis versati negant ea in Ebraeorum monumentis hodie reperiri. Quid ergo? Existimo ego, Galatinum, seu potius Raimundum Sebundum, cujus scrinia compilasse Galatinum Scaliger author est, veterum scriptorum imitamento & haec & alia vel finxisse, vel ex libris ὑποθολιμαίοις descripsisse Primis Ecclesiae temporibus; inquit Casaub. in Exercit. quamplurimi extiterunt, qui facinus palmarium judicabant, caelestem veritatem suis figmentis ire adjutum. Quae facilius sc. Christiana religio vel a Gentium Judaeorumque Sapientib. reciperetur, vel neophyti in eadem magis magisque confirmarentur.
units.tr: XLVI. You will therefore seek in vain in these matters. Search the whole Talmud, Maimonides, and whatever Hebrew writers there are anywhere, and you will find nothing certain in which you could rest. As for what R. Bechai, at the beginning of Genesis, fol. 5, col. 2, notes, that the name of 42 letters was taken from the first and second verses of the book of Genesis, namely from the letter ב [beth] of the word בראשית [bereshith] to the letter ב of the word ובהו [vebohu], which are 42 letters, and that from their various combination, known to the Cabalists, the name of 42 letters came about, and that the name of 12 letters was made up from a threefold combination of the name יהוה [YHWH], I give no credence to this at all. Nor can I persuade myself that Galatinus drew from Hebrew monuments those things which he set forth in book 2, chapter 10. For he gives the name of 12 letters as אב בן ורוח הקדש [ab ben veruach hakodesh], that is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. He assigns the name of 42 letters as אב אל בן אל ורוח הקדש אל אבל לא שלשה אלהים כי אם אלה אחד [ab el ben el veruach hakodesh el abal lo shelosha elohim ki im eloah echad], that is, Father God, Son God, Holy Spirit God; but not three Gods, rather one God. Distinguished Buxtorf says it would be a great service to the work if this explanation could be confirmed from the books of the rabbis. Scaliger, Drusius and others versed in Hebrew monuments deny that such things are found today in Hebrew monuments. What then? I myself think that Galatinus, or rather Raimundus Sebundus, whose chests Scaliger testifies Galatinus plundered, either invented these things and others like them in imitation of the ancient writers, or copied them from books spurious [ὑποθολιμαίοις] in the earliest times of the Church, says Casaubon in his Exercitationes: there were very many who judged it a splendid deed that heavenly truth should be aided by their fictions, namely so that the Christian religion might more easily be received even by the wise men of the Gentiles and Jews, or so that the neophytes might be confirmed in it more and more.

units.la: XLVII. Vidimus quomodo in judicio blasphemi, quomodo item in benedictione solemni & liturgia diei expiationum pronuntiatum fuerit nomen יהוה / Nunc videamus quomodo extra illos casus & extra templum communiter fuerit pronuntiatum.
units.tr: XLVII. We have seen how the name יהוה [YHWH] was pronounced in the judgment of the blasphemer, and likewise in the solemn blessing and in the liturgy of the Day of Atonement. Now let us see how it was commonly pronounced outside those occasions and outside the temple.

units.la: Sed quid dico, videamus? Iam supra vidimus & testimoniis evicimus, Illud pronunciatum fuisse per cognomen אֲדֹנָי / quod specialiter & κατ' ἐξοχὴν ᾿Ιαω vocant. Sic dico, lectum pro eo fuit Adonai, excepto uno casu, quando vid. vel ante vel post se habet ipsum cognomen Adonai. Tunc enim ad vitandum concursum duorum Adonai, τὸ προαγορευμένον expresserunt per nomen אֱלֹהִים Elohim, id est Deus.
units.tr: But why do I say "let us see"? Already above we have seen, and proved by testimonies, that it was pronounced through the surname אֲדֹנָי [Adonai], which they call, specially and κατ' ἐξοχὴν [kat' exochen], Iao [᾿Ιαω]. I say this: it was read Adonai in place of it, except in one case, when the same word has the surname Adonai itself either before or after it. For then, to avoid the clash of two Adonai, they expressed τὸ προαγορευμένον [to proagoreuomenon], the name previously mentioned, by the name אֱלֹהִים [Elohim], that is, God.

units.la: Qui ergo rident eos qui Adonai legunt, & putant morem istum ab hodiernis Judaeis introductum, non merentur quibus respondeatur, inquit magnus Scaliger, in notis ad fragmenta selecta, pag. 34. vide & Abulensem ad Exod. 6. Scindl. in Lexico, Alstedium in Lex. & alios.
units.tr: Those, therefore, who laugh at those who read Adonai, and think that this custom was introduced by the Jews of today, do not deserve an answer, says the great Scaliger in his notes on the Fragmenta selecta, p. 34. See also Abulensis on Exodus 6, Schindler in his Lexicon, Alstedius in his Lexicon, and others.

units.la: XLVIII. Diserte idem confirmat Galatinus, qui tamen primus vocem Jehova usurpasse putatur, ipsumque Mosem istius lectionis [ADONAI] authorem statuit. XLIX. Cum Deo tribuitur semper definit in (ד) ... eum creaturis tribuitur, definit in fatha ch, praeterquam in pausa.
units.tr: XLVIII. Galatinus confirms the same thing explicitly, although he is thought to have been the first to use the word Jehova, and he holds that Moses himself was the author of this reading [ADONAI]. XLIX. When the word is applied to God it always ends in (ד) ... when it is applied to creatures it ends in fatha ch, except in pause.

units.la: Deo tribuitur sensum semper singularem habet, ut ipsum אֱלֹהִים & אֲדֹנָי / Occurrit in Bibliis קְלָר id est centies trecies & quater praeter ea loca, ubi jungitur cum nomine יהוה / vide ad 5.71. Hoc nomen אֲדֹנָי vocatur ab Ebraeis id est confessum, quod ejus puncta confessa sint, non ignota, aut incerta, ut puncta יהוה videliam orat. 9. secundarum tabularum Masoreth & Mercerum Amos 5. 36. De arcanis Cath. verit. lib 2. 3 o. ob nominis hujus reverentiam, inquit, antiquis Iudaeorum. a magno suo praceptore Mose edocti, statuerunt hoc nomen, nunquam profitendum, sed ubicunque invenitur, loco ejus Adonai esse legendum. vide Burgensium ad Exod. 3. XLIX. Illud extra omnem controversiæ aleam est, omnes Interpretes priscos, qui vel Biblia vel aliquam eorum partem transtulerunt, vid. Chaldæos, LXX. Senes, Theodotionem, Aquilam, Symmachum, authores 5. & 6. Editionis Græcæ, Hieronymum, authorem vulgatæ, Arabes, Persas, Æthiopes, Syros, &c. ad unum omnes, hoc nomem per cognomen Adonai legisse, ejusque interpretamentum posuisse. Ut plane ignaros antiquitatis eos esse oporteat, qui istius Lectionis originem Masorethis adscribunt.
units.tr: When applied to God it always has a singular sense, as with God [אֱלֹהִים] and Lord [אֲדֹנָי]. It occurs in the Bibles קְלָר, that is, three hundred and forty-four times, apart from those places where it is joined with the name יהוה; see on 5.71. The Hebrews call this name confessum, that is, its points are confessed, not unknown or uncertain, as the points of יהוה are, as one may see in the Masoretic tables of the second set, and in Mercerus on Amos 5.36. In his De arcanis catholicae veritatis, book 2, chapter 3, he says that the ancient Jews, taught by their great master Moses, out of reverence for this name, decided that it should never be pronounced, but that wherever it is found Adonai should be read in its place. See the Burgensis on Exodus 3. XLIX. It is beyond all controversy that all the early interpreters who translated the Bible or any part of it, namely the Chaldeans, the Seventy, Theodotion, Aquila, Symmachus, the authors of the fifth and sixth Greek editions, Jerome, the author of the Vulgate, the Arabs, Persians, Ethiopians, Syrians, and so on, all without exception read this name by the substitute Adonai and put that rendering in its place. So those who ascribe the origin of this reading to the Masoretes must plainly be ignorant of antiquity.

units.la: L. Atque ita redditum quoque fuit ab Euangelistis & Apostolis, Patribus Græcis & Latinis, , qui circa annum 1518. floruit. Paginum videtur facere primum ejus vocisauthorem: sed fallitur, ille enim post Galatinum floruit, & tamen in suo Lexico non memorat hanc vocem ad nomen יהוה ut dubium non sit, quin ab aliis vox ea sicuti & plurima alia posterioribus versionis ejus Editionibus sit infarta.
units.tr: L. And so it was also rendered by the Evangelists and Apostles, by the Greek and Latin Fathers, [and by Pagninus, who flourished around 1518.] Pagninus seems to be the first author of this word, but he is mistaken: for he flourished after Galatinus, and yet in his lexicon he does not mention this word as corresponding to the name יהוה. There is therefore no doubt that this word, like very many others, was inserted by others into the later editions of his version.

units.la: LI. Nullus certè, vocem eam cuiquam ante P. Galatinum usurpatam, adhuc ostendit. Ipse Drusius locum produxit ex commentariis, vulgò Hieronymo inscriptis, in Ps. 8. Edit. Plantinianæ, Ibi enim legitur Jehova. Sed ostendit idem, in MS. & Frobenianâ (addo ego, & in Parisiensi) esse Jao, quæ vox cum in Hieron. etiam alibi occurrat, Jehova vero nusquam, quis eo exemplo moveatur? Non dubium est quin operis ejus correctoř, Ebraicarum rerum, ut ex multis apparet indiciis, imperitior, cum ignoraret antiquum esse Jao, substituerit vocem suo sæculo magis notam. Hæc Cl. Drusius.
units.tr: LI. Certainly no one has yet shown that this word was used by anyone before P. Galatinus. Drusius himself cited a passage from the commentaries commonly ascribed to Jerome, on Psalm 8, in the Plantin edition, where the word Jehova is read. But he showed that in the manuscript and in the Froben edition (I add, and in the Parisian one) it is Jao, which word occurs elsewhere in Jerome, whereas Jehova nowhere does. Why should anyone be moved by that example? There is no doubt that the corrector of that work, who, as many signs show, was less skilled in Hebrew matters, did not know that Jao was the old form, and substituted a word better known in his own age. So writes the distinguished Drusius.

units.la: LII. Vidi & ego semel in Addit. Burgensis ad 3. Exodi, Edit. Lugdun. ubi hæc legas, Proferri tamen potest Jehova, unde & Jovem pagani dixere. Sed tota ista ab aliis omnibus, quotquot ego vidi, exemplaribus abest. Unde constat vel à Ivardentio, vel alio aliquo esse interpolatam. Ubi & illud obiter observetur, in eadem Edit. pessime ad marginem citari locum *Theodoreti, Samaritani vocant illud Menjame, Judai vero Aja. Sic enim scribenda sunt verba Theologi, Samarita ... Iabai, [vel Iabe, Israelitæ] Iabo. Particula Men voci Iabe adjecta est ab imperitis, porro in μ depravato, ut in ... pro
units.tr: LII. I too once saw, in the Addition to the Burgensis on Exodus 3, in the Lyons edition, where you may read: "Yet Jehova can be proposed, whence also the pagans said Jove." But this whole passage is absent from all the other copies I have seen. So it is clear that it was interpolated either by Ivardentius or by someone else. Here it may also be observed in passing that in the same edition the passage of Theodoret is very badly cited in the margin: "The Samaritans call it Menjame, but the Jews Aja." For the words of the theologian must be written thus: "The Samaritans [call it] Iabai, [or Iabe, the Israelites] Iabo." The particle Men was added to the word Iabe by unskilled copyists, and further, the β was corrupted into μ, as in ... for ... [I think it was so] in [Augustinus] Steuchus, in his Recognitio Veteris Testamenti on Exodus 4, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: apud Aug. Steuchium in Recogn. Vet. Test. ad Exod. 4 nifallor. Sed conferendus hic locus Theod. cum altero lib. 1. hæreticarum fabul. cap. de Valentin. pro-ḉḗc. In veteri enim Scriptura facillimus erat lapsus de β in μ. Vidi & in nupera Editione Latina Rhemensi Clementis Alexandrini. Sed in Graecis omnibus est Ias, quod & ille notavit, qui collectanea ad eam versionem edidit.
units.tr: But this passage of Theodoret should be compared with another in book 1 of the Haereticarum fabularum, the chapter on Valentinus. For in the Old Testament writing the slip from β to μ was very easy. I have also seen in the recent Latin edition of Clement of Alexandria, the Rheims one, the word Ias. But in all the Greek texts it is Ias, which the man who edited the collected notes on that version also observed.

units.la: LIII. Illud quoque dissimulare non debeo, me ante dies pauculos illud invenisse in comment. Dionysii Carthusiani, ad Exodi cap. 6. Edit. Coloniensis, anni 1548. quem ante Galatinum floruisse ex Sixto Senensi didici. floruit enim anno 1472. Sed annon & hic vocem Jehova pro Jao vel alio nomine Editionis istius corrector intruserit, illi viderint queis antiquiora vel aliarum Editionum exemplaria suppetunt. Ego qui in universa hac provincia aliud exemplar videre non potui, hic ἐπίχω.
units.tr: LIII. Nor ought I to conceal that a few days ago I found this in the commentary of Dionysius the Carthusian on Exodus chapter 6, Cologne edition of 1548, whom I learned from Sixtus of Siena to have flourished before Galatinus; for he flourished in 1472. But whether here too the corrector of that edition inserted the word Jehova in place of Jao or some other name, let those judge who have older copies of that edition or of other editions. I, who in this whole region could not see another copy, here hold back my judgement [ἐπέχω].

units.la: LIV. Remanserunt tamen in Antiquitate, tum apud Samaritanos, tum apud alias Gentes quaedam vetustae pronunciationis, licet obscura, vestigia. Namque adeo varie leguntur ea nomina, atque ita a criticis variantur, ut certi nihil de vocalibus nominis liceat colligere. Theodoretus, quem supra citavi, diserte ait, Samaritanos vocare id Jabe, Judaeos vero Jao.
units.tr: LIV. Nevertheless some traces of an ancient pronunciation, though obscure, have survived in antiquity, both among the Samaritans and among other peoples. For these names are read in so many different ways, and are so variously given by the critics, that nothing certain about the vowels of the name can be gathered. Theodoret, whom I cited above, plainly says that the Samaritans call it Jabe, but the Jews Jao.

units.la: LV. Illud [Jao] robur accipit ex a Diodori Siculi, qui ait, Ἰαὼ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις Μωσεῖ ... Ἰαὼ ... Ἰεὼν ... τὰ νόμιμα αὐτοῖς δεδόναι. Et a versu Apollinis Clarii, prout eum citat b Macrobius, Φοφίζεο τ' πάντων ὕπατον Ἰεὸν ἰμνῷ Ἰαὼ. Similia loca apud Patres Iren. Epiph. Clem. aliosque invenies, quorum pleraque citat c Drusius in Tetragr. caetera supplebis ex d Rainoldo, e Fullero & f Scaligero.
units.tr: LV. That [Jao] gains strength from the passage of Diodorus Siculus, who says: "Iao to the Jews, Moses ... Iao ... Ieo ... gave them their laws" [Ἰαὼ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις Μωσεῖ ... Ἰαὼ ... Ἰεὼν ... τὰ νόμιμα αὐτοῖς δεδόναι]. And from the verse of Apollo of Clarus, as Macrobius quotes it: "Hymn Iao, the highest of all, Ieo" [Φοφίζεο τ' πάντων ὕπατον Ἰεὸν ἰμνῷ Ἰαὼ]. You will find similar passages among the Fathers, Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Clement and others, most of which Drusius cites in his Tetragrammaton; you will supply the rest from Rainolds, Fuller and Scaliger.

units.la: LVI. Hoc [vid. Jabe] magis analogum fuerit, ut sit vid. fut. Kal יהוה accedetque ad Ariae Montani Jeheveh. Loca Patrum priscorumque huc facientia ex iisdem petes. Utramque conjecturam juvat decurtatum יה /.
units.tr: LVI. This form [see Jabe] would be more analogous, so that it is the imperfect of the Kal form יהוה, and it approaches the Jeheveh of Arias Montanus. Seek the passages of the early Fathers that bear on this from the same sources. The shortened form יה supports both conjectures.

units.la: LVII. Fuerunt ex Graecis quos Procopius in suis ad Jesaiam commentariis secutus est qui hoc nomen per ηηηη Pipi expressere. Quaeritur unde hoc Pipi? Postellus arbitratur id esse a Samaritica scriptura, qua hoc nomen per duo Jodin (ut & adhuc hodie a Chaldaeis ״) scribebatur, quorum unumquodque videtur conflatum ex ΙΙ & Ι. Potest ita esse, tamen inclino magis in conjecturam g Hieronymi, quam & Cl. Drusius suo calculo approbat, qui ex Ebraeis characteribus hanc lectionem natam ar-bitrabitratur. Jod enim & Vau similitudinem habent cum Jota & n cum n Græco.
units.tr: LVII. Among the Greeks, those whom Procopius followed in his commentary on Isaiah rendered this name by the letters [ΠΙΠΙ], Pipi. The question is whence this Pipi comes. Postellus thinks it comes from the Samaritan script, in which this name was written with two yods (as even today by the Chaldeans ״), each of which seems to be made up of ΙΙ and Ι. It may be so; yet I incline more to the conjecture of Jerome, which Drusius too approves on his reckoning, who thinks this reading arose from the Hebrew characters. For Yod and Vav have a resemblance to the Greek iota and pi [n] and pi [n].

units.la: LVIII. Atque ita responsum ad quæstionem priorem est, Aphorismo 40. propositum. Restat jam ut ad posteriorem quoque respondeamus. Ea autem est bimembris. Primo enim quæritur, utrum hodie quoque ignoretur germana tetragrammati lectio. Deinde, si ignoratur, quomodo ea vox hodie legenda sit. Ad utrumque respondeo, multum quidem a eruditis viris laboratum fuisse in eruenda vera prolatione, sed tamen eam in hunc usque diem adeo esse incertam, ut præstet priscam illam, licet vicariam, lectionem retinere, vid. ADONAI, quam novæ alicui incerte adsuescere. [Alstedius, postquam quædam certa, quædam verisimilia de hoc nomine propositurisset, sic tandem concludit, Nomen יהוה pronuntiandum est vel Jehovah, vel Jeheveh, vel Jahveh, vel Jihveh.]
units.tr: LVIII. And so the answer to the first question, proposed in aphorism 40, is given. It remains now that we answer the second as well. It has two parts. For first it is asked whether the true reading of the Tetragrammaton is still unknown today. Then, if it is unknown, how that word ought to be read today. To both I reply that learned men have indeed laboured much to bring out the true pronunciation, but that to this day it is so uncertain that it is better to retain that ancient reading, though a substitute, namely ADONAI, than to grow accustomed to some new and uncertain one. [Alstedius, after proposing certain things and some probable things about this name, finally concludes thus: "The name יהוה is to be pronounced either Jehovah, or Jeheveh, or Jahveh, or Jihveh."]

units.la: LIX. Dico incertam etiamnum esse veram & germanam ητεγεγαμμάτε ὀνόματος prolationem. Addo, inter eas, quas collegit D. Alstedius, maxime alienam videri illam, cui principem locum assignavit, vid. Jehova.
units.tr: LIX. I say that the true and genuine pronunciation of the tetragrammaton name [τετραγράμματον ὀνόματος] is still uncertain. I add that among those which D. Alstedius collected, the one to which he gave first place, namely Jehova, seems most alien.

units.la: LX. Sed dices, An in tanta literarum luce ignorari aut in incerto esse potest divini istius nominis prolatio? Respondeo I. Magno adhuc intervallo à sua perfectione abesse Philologiam Ebraicam, & merito exclamare hic posse doctissimos & celeberrimos linguæ Ebraeæ Magistros, Quantum est quod nescimus! Addo, Quantæ adhuc restent difficultates in librorum Vet. Test. authenticis tabulis, in quamplurimis phrasibus & vocibus infinitis, non nisi indoctissimum posse ignorare. II. Illud rogo, unde certa & vera hujus nominis prolatio haberi potuerit, an à Judæis an ex ipsis Bibliis? Certè non à Judæis. Illi enim hanc juxta eum ignarissimis ignorant, & si fortassis eam nossent, tamen eam Christianis vel invideret eorum invidia, vel celaret superstitio. Si enim non quemlibet Judæum ad pernoscendum hoc mysterium admittebant Magistri, quomodo Christianos docerent? Neque etiam ex ipsis Bibliis certam lectionem investigaveris. Atque hic rursum dices, nunquid in illis nomen illud sic invenimus punctatum יהוה Jehovah? Respondeo, Ita quidem, sed audi magni & eruditissimi Theologi, Theodori Bezæ judicium, puncta illa, quæ hodie voci יהוה subjiciuntur, non sunt ipsius
units.tr: LX. But you will say: can the pronunciation of this divine name be unknown or uncertain in such a blaze of learning? I reply, first, that Hebrew philology is still far from its perfection, and that the most learned and celebrated masters of the Hebrew language may justly exclaim here, "How much we do not know!" I add that many difficulties still remain in the authentic texts of the Old Testament, in very many phrases and innumerable words, which only the most unlearned could fail to know. II. I ask this: from where could a certain and true pronunciation of this name have been obtained, from the Jews or from the Bible itself? Certainly not from the Jews. For they, according to that most ignorant man, are ignorant of it, and if perhaps they did know it, their envy would either grudge it to Christians or their superstition would conceal it. For if the masters did not admit every Jew to learning this mystery, how would they teach Christians? Nor again will you find the certain reading from the Bible itself. Here again you will say: have we not found that name in them pointed thus, יהוה Jehovah? I reply, yes indeed, but listen to the judgement of the great and most learned theologian, Theodore Beza: "Those points which are today placed under the word יהוה are not its own."

units.la: in Paratilis p. 155 col 2.
units.tr: In Paratilis, p. 155, col. 2.

units.la: Annotat. ad cap. 1. Apocalyps. vers 4. ipsius nominis propria, sed aliunde adscita, Et alterius Theologi, {b}Mea sic sert sententia, non sunt propria puncta nominis Tetragrammati, sed sunt nominis Adonai propria, & interdum & Elohim, si occurrat Jehovi. [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: Annotations on chapter 1, verse 4 of Revelation: the proper points of the name itself, but borrowed from elsewhere. And another theologian: {b}My view is this: they are not the proper points of the Tetragrammaton, but are proper to the name Adonai, and sometimes also to Elohim, when they occur with Jehovi. [illegible, ~10 letters]

units.la: LXI. Hic autem jubeo te paululum sistere gradum quisquis in his literis tiro es. Disce, in textu Ebraeo V. Testamenti consonas cum propriis suis vocalibus passim quidem occurrere, ut פְּקֻדֵי אֱלֹהִים יַעֲקֹב [?] / &c. Sed & non raro cum alienis & aliarum vocem propriis repraesentari. Ex quo casu duplex existit lectio, una secundum consonas, altera secundum vocales. Sic dico, Consonis quarundam vocum in textu Biblico subjiciuntur vocales aliarum consonantium, seu, quod idem est, aliarum vocum: quae consonae vocesve in margine repraesentantur. E.g. Jes. 36. שִׁינֵיהֶם [?] hae vocales non sunt istarum consonantium, quibus subjiciuntur, propriae, sed istarum quae in margine exhibentur, מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם / Haec igitur est lectio secundum vocales, meme raglehem. Lectio certa cujus vid- vocales ipse textus, consonas margo repraesentat. Illarum vero consonarum שִׁינֵיהֶם lectio incerta est, quia earum vocales nec in textu nec in margine exhibentur.
units.tr: LXI. Here, novice, I ask you to pause a little, whoever you are in these letters. Learn that in the Hebrew text of the Old Testament the consonants are found everywhere with their own proper vowels, as in פְּקֻדֵי אֱלֹהִים יַעֲקֹב [?] etc. But they are also often represented with the vowels belonging to other words. From this case arises a double reading: one according to the consonants, the other according to the vowels. I put it thus: under the consonants of certain words in the biblical text are placed the vowels of other consonants, or, which is the same thing, of other words, and those consonants or words are shown in the margin. For example, in Isa. 36, שִׁינֵיהֶם [?]: these vowels do not belong to the consonants under which they stand, but to those shown in the margin, מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם. This, then, is the reading according to the vowels, meme raglehem: a certain reading, whose vowels the text itself supplies and whose consonants the margin gives. But the reading of the consonants שִׁינֵיהֶם is uncertain, because their vowels appear neither in the text nor in the margin.

units.la: LXII. Haec autem scripturae anomalia, seu ut vulgo loquuntur, lectionis varietas, (quae in margine per ק id est קרי / legitur, in textu vero per circulum voci impositum id est כתיב / scribitur, indicatur) orta est vel ex metu profantaionis, ut in יהוה / ubi tamen ob vocis frequentiam ק' in margine nunquam exhibetur, vel honestatis causa, ut in vocibus illis quae vulgo obscaenae dicuntur, vel ex mendosa codicum descriptione, & varia lectione proprie sic dicta, de quibus prolixe disseruimus in dissertatione nostra de Keri & Chetib, quam in Coronide nostra ad Grammaticam jam pridem evulgavimus & in hoc ipso opere ad Psalmum 22. cum bono Deo, denuo repraesentabimus. Inde petes, Lector, quae faciant illustrandis istis quae jam delibavimus.
units.tr: LXII. This anomaly of writing, or as people commonly say, variant reading (which is marked in the margin by ק, that is קרי, it is read, and in the text by a circle placed over the word, that is כתיב, it is written), arises either from fear of profaning the name, as in יהוה, where however, because of the frequency of the word, ק is never shown in the margin, or from a desire for decency, as in those words commonly called obscene, or from faulty copying of manuscripts and what are properly called variant readings. We have discussed these at length in our dissertation on Keri and Chetib, which we published some time ago in our appendix to the Grammar, and which we shall again set out in this work at Psalm 22, with God's blessing. Here, reader, you will look for what helps to clarify the points I have just touched on.

units.la: LXIII. Istae autem sunt regulae Grammaticorum. I. nullas consonas legendas esse alienis vocalibus, sed vel propriis, si de iis constet: vel si de iis non constet, lectionem instituendam esse secundum vocales. II. Lectionem secundum vocales in casu variae lectionis esse praeferendam illi, quae secundum consonas est. Quia vid. de ista magis genuina est, hæc vero plerunque mendosa, ut E. g. in istis quæ tertii generis sunt, vel quia ista quæ juxta vocales est, est certior, utpote quarum consonas margo repræsentat, hæc vero juxta consonas incerta est, utpote quarum vocales nullibi exhibentur. Per quos vero ista varietas in sacros codices introducta sit, in Dissertatione ista, cujus jam jam meminimus, dictum est.
units.tr: LXIII. These are the rules of the grammarians. I. No consonants are to be read with vowels belonging to others, but with their own, if these are known; or, if they are not known, the reading is to be established according to the vowels. II. In a case of variant reading the reading according to the vowels is to be preferred to that according to the consonants, since the former is more genuine and the latter is usually faulty, as in those of the third kind; or because the reading according to the vowels is more certain, its consonants being shown in the margin, whereas the reading according to the consonants is uncertain, its vowels being nowhere shown. How this variation came to be introduced into the sacred codices has been said in that dissertation I mentioned just now.

units.la: LXIV. Rursus itaque tibi hoc inculco, nullas voces legi debere alienis vocalibus. Imo quasdam omnino non posse. Quod ideo adjeci, quia ubicunque non est consonantium aut vocalium numerus redundans, aut ubi non impingitur in principia linguæ, ibi potest subinde ex sonis & vocalibus alienis conflari vox aliqua articulata & in speciem non absurda, perinde ac si ex vocalibus nominis Dominus o i & u junctis cum consonis nominis Deus, D. & S. fingeres vocem Dojus.
units.tr: LXIV. Again, then, I impress on you that no words are to be read with vowels belonging to others. Indeed, some cannot be read at all in that way. I have added this because wherever there is no redundancy of consonants or vowels, and where it does not clash with the principles of the language, some articulate word, not absurd in appearance, can be formed from sounds and vowels belonging to others, just as if, from the vowels of the word Dominus, o, i and u, joined to the consonants of the word Deus, D. and S., you were to invent the word Dojus.

units.la: LXV. Hoc faciunt qui Jehova & Jehovi legunt. Hi enim sunt lectionis istius natales. Qui puncta Bibliis adscripsere, sub hoc nomine posuerunt puncta nominis אֲדֹנָי / nisi præcederet aut sequeretur alterum אֲדֹנָי / tunc enim ne bis diceretur Adonai Adonai, sub יְהוָה posuerunt puncta nominis אֱלֹהִים / ita vid יְהוִה /. Qui vero has voces Jehova & Jehovi primitus in Scholas introduxerunt, existimarunt istas vocales istorum consonantium non alienas, quod nos jam jam probabimus, sed proprias esse, ac proinde ex istis junctis unam vocem conflarunt.
units.tr: LXV. This is what those do who read Jehova and Jehovi. For they are the origin of this reading. Those who added the points to the Bibles put under this name the points of the name אֲדֹנָי, unless another אֲדֹנָי preceded or followed it, for then it would be said twice, Adonai Adonai; and under יְהוָה they put the points of the name אֱלֹהִים, so that it appears as יְהוִה. But those who first introduced the words Jehova and Jehovi into the schools thought these vowels were not foreign to these consonants, as we shall now prove, but proper to them, and so they formed one word from them joined together.

units.la: LXVI. Atque hoc puto spectasse Galatinum quando ita infit, hæ vocales si cum consonantibus jungantur, potest legi JEHOVAH. Cum tamen ipse nunquam ea voce usus sit, sed semper יהוה per Dominus expresserit, addita voce [Tetragrammaton] duobus istis signis inclusa. Aliud est dicere, potest legi. Aliud est, debet legi, Certe si ipsam יהוה nude positam (nota, nude positam) consideres, nec vocalium nec consonarum numerus, nec ulla Grammaticorum regula isti lectioni Jehovah, adversatur, nec enim novum est, Jod Hebraicum per scheva efferri, nec insolens est nomen proprium etiam masc. gen. in ה desinere. Ecce enim exemplum in יהוּדָה /.
units.tr: LXVI. I think Galatinus had this in mind when he begins: if these vowels are joined to the consonants, it can be read JEHOVAH. Yet he himself never used that word, but always rendered יהוה by Dominus, adding the word [Tetragrammaton] enclosed in these two signs. It is one thing to say it can be read, and another to say it must be read. Certainly, if you consider יהוה by itself (note, by itself), neither the number of vowels nor of consonants, nor any rule of the grammarians, opposes that reading Jehovah. For it is not new for the Hebrew yod to be pronounced with a shewa, nor is it unusual for a proper name of masculine gender to end in ה. Here is an example in יהוּדָה.

units.la: LXVII. Sed proponam tibi ex magna exemplorum sylva unum atque alterum, quod nullus, etsi in omnes se vertat formas, legat prout scribitur. Jesa. 36. 12. שְׁנִיָּהֶם Conare, quis-quis quis es, has vocales cum consonis, quies subjectæ sunt, efferre & eris mihi magnus Apollo, si præstabis. Licet enim utrique Jod punctum tribueris, (id quod in isthac forma fieri omnino nequit, Jod enim ante affixum הם semper quiescit) unum tamen punctum semper supererit. Ibidem extat vox הָרָאיְהֹם / quod juxta vocales junctas cum consonis in margine positis, quarum propriæ sunt legitur יְצָאֵהם / 2. Reg. 10. 27. extat vox מְחַרְאוּרִ / cujus ׳ק id est קרי in margine ponitur מוֹצָאוּר / cujus vocis istæ vocales sunt. Hic utique ex consonis in textu positis subjectisque vocalib. nunquam vocem nisi monstrosam & unā litera redundantem conflaverit. Deut. 28. 27. extat עִפְלִים / Si leges ut scribitur, y litera gutturalis in principio syllabæ efferetur per Scheva, id quod portentum est in lingua Sancta. Literæ enim quas à gutture denominant, nunquam habent schevasyllabam incoans, quod mobile vulgo vocant. Namq; ejus vices puncta rapta obeunt. Quid ergo? puncta sunt vocis טְחִרִים / cujus consonas in margine repræsentarunt Masorethæ.
units.tr: LXVII. But I shall set before you one or two examples out of a great forest of them, which no one, however he turns himself into every form, reads as it is written. Isa. 36. 12: שְׁנִיָּהֶם. Try, whoever you are, to pronounce these vowels with the consonants under which they stand, and you will be a great Apollo to me if you manage it. For even if you assign a point to each yod (which in this form cannot be done at all, since the yod before the affixed הם always is silent), one point will still be left over. In the same place stands the word הָרָאיְהֹם, which according to the vowels joined to the consonants, with the consonants placed in the margin, is read יְצָאֵהם [?]. 2 Kings 10. 27: the word מְחַרְאוּרִ stands, whose ק, that is קרי, is placed in the margin as מוֹצָאוּר, and these are the vowels of that word. Here, certainly, from the consonants placed in the text with their vowels, one could form only a monstrous word with one letter too many. Deut. 28. 27: עִפְלִים stands. If you read it as written, the guttural letter ע at the beginning of the syllable would be pronounced with a shewa, which is a monstrosity in the Holy Tongue. For the letters that they call gutturals never begin a syllable with a movable shewa, as they commonly say, since in their place stolen points take over. What then? The points belong to the word טְחִרִים, whose consonants the Masoretes represented in the margin.

units.la: LXVIII. Vides Tiro, nam tibi ut gratificarer, prolixior hic fui quam par erat, multas in textu Ebr. occurrere voces anomale punctatas, quas cum subjectis vocalibus nunquam valeas exprimere. De his si plura desideras cognoscere, adi Coronidem ad Grammaticam Ebraeam Martinio-Buxtorfianam, ubi hæc & id genus alia suo quæque loco, ordine Biblico, explicuimus.
units.tr: LXVIII. You see, novice, for I wanted to oblige you, I have been longer here than was proper; you see that many anomalous points occur in the Hebrew text, which you can never express with the vowels placed under them. If you want to know more about these, consult the appendix to the Martinio-Buxtorfian Hebrew Grammar, where we have explained these and other things of that kind in their place, in biblical order.

units.la: LXIX. Sed dices, hanc irregularem punctationem à Judæis introductam, ac proinde neutiquam nos ea obligari: olim aliter, vid. cum propriis vocalibus, voces istas lectas fuisse. Cui sententiæ uti non adversor, ita illud quoque sentio, satius esse, pro vocibus istis marginales istas vicarias legere, quam, aliis vocalibus consonantibus istis ex incerto subjectis, barbarismum committere & voces veteribus forsan omnino inauditas procudere. Si ergo lectione illa, quam Masorethæ in margine exhibuere, qua nec fidei nec pietati ullum infertur detrimentum, contentus non es, doce nos proprias istarum vocum vocales, per quas olim lectæ fuerint, & habebis nos astipulatores. Doce evidenter & demonstra. Nullus hic locus conjecturis, quas in cæteris forsan ex analogia aliarum formarum feceris: At in tetragrammato ex analogia nihil erues. Nomina enim propria sub-nullis nullis formis contineri Grammaticorum regula est.
units.tr: LXIX. But you will say that this irregular pointing was introduced by the Jews, and therefore we are in no way bound by it: formerly these words were read differently, that is, with their proper vowels. I am not opposed to that opinion, but I also think it better to read those words by these substitute marginal forms than, by placing vowels from elsewhere under consonants that are uncertain, to commit a barbarism and coin words perhaps wholly unheard of by the ancients. So if you are not content with the reading which the Masoretes gave in the margin, which does no harm to faith or piety, then teach us the proper vowels of these words, by which they were read in former times, and you will have us as supporters. Teach it clearly and demonstrate it. There is no room here for conjectures, which you may perhaps make in other cases from the analogy of other forms; but from analogy you will extract nothing in the case of the Tetragrammaton. For it is a rule of the grammarians that proper names are not contained under any forms.

units.la: LXX. Quod vero ad voces istas ἀνομάλως punctatas attinet, nos differtatione nostra de Keri & Chetib, numero 19. & 20. sententiam nostram professi fumus, eas vid. non ab ipsis Prophetis sed à Scribis esse introductas. Inde petes quæ huc spectant, ne frustraneis repetitionibus nimis excrescat hic liber. Iisdem ergo, Scribis videlicet, ut universi Biblici contextus, ita & anomalam istam vocum prædicatarum & nominatim hujus quoque nominis punctationem transcribimus. Et quidem hanc sententiam, de punctis post mortem Christi additis, validissimis & invictis rationibus evicerunt P. Martinus in Thechnologia, Lutherus, Mercerus, Scaliger, & Drusius, passim. Calvinus ad Zachar. c. xi. 7. Zwingl. præfat. in Jesaiam. Piscator ad calcem Quæst. in Pentateuchum ex professo, Rainoldus in Censura librorum Apocryph. lect. 32. p. 278. [Sed omnium diligentiam superavit anonymus author diatribes de vera antiquitate vocalium, quam Cl. Erpenius 1624. edidit. Ille enim sententiam istam adeo valide confirmavit; rationesque, quæ in contrarium vulgo afferuntur, adeo solide refutavit, ut doctissimorum Theologorum, qui antea contrariæ sententiæ mordicus hærebant, alios in suam sententiam pertraxerit, alios vero non parum dubios reddiderit.]
units.tr: LXX. As for the points that have been added to these words anomalously [ἀνομάλως], we stated our view in our dissertation on the Keri and Chetib, sections 19 and 20: namely, that they were introduced not by the Prophets themselves but by the Scribes. You may look there for what bears on this question, so that this book does not swell with needless repetition. Accordingly, we ascribe to the same Scribes, as with the whole Biblical text, also this anomalous pointing of the words in question and especially of this name. Indeed, this view, that the points were added after the death of Christ, has been established by the most weighty and unanswerable arguments of Martinus in his Thechnologia, Luther, Mercerus, Scaliger and Drusius, throughout their works; Calvin on Zechariah 11:7; Zwingli in the preface to Isaiah; Piscator at the end of his Questions on the Pentateuch, expressly; and Rainoldus in his Censure of the Apocryphal books, lecture 32, p. 278. [But the anonymous author of the treatise on the true antiquity of the vowels, which the distinguished Erpenius published in 1624, surpassed the diligence of them all. For he confirmed this view so strongly, and refuted the arguments commonly brought on the other side so soundly, that he drew some of the most learned theologians, who had previously clung stubbornly to the opposing view, over to his own, and made others not a little doubtful.]

units.la: LXXI. Quod si tamen ab adversa sententia, puncta vid. ab ipsis Prophetis adscripta (quam sententiam multi pii Theologi bono zelo defensum eunt) te quoque dimoveri non pateris, nec est mihi animus, nec incumbit mihi necessitas, in præsens super ea quæstione funem contentionis tecum ducere. Esto. Adscripserint ipsi Prophetæ vocalium figuras. Eo magis ista quæ jam subjiciam argumenta, constringent. Quod si dixeris punctationem genuinam in hoc nomine & pauculis vocibus à Judæis esse mutatam & ad recentem superstitionem accommodatam, invenies responsum in dissert. nostra de Keri & Chetib num. 19. & 29. Illi, qui puncta Masorethis adscribunt, & plausibilius & verisimilius dicerent, genuinam nominum istorum prolationem ab ipsis studio fuisse suppressam, si modo ipsi eam noverE, (id quod de nomine יהוה neutiquam mihi videtur credibile, quandoquidem post destructum templum puncta adscripsere) aut, si eam nescivere, ejus loco exhibitam fuisse illam recensiorem. Et certe ita judicat Cl. Theologus Piscator, cujus testimostimonium postea §. 75. productum ibo.
units.tr: LXXI. But if you are not willing to be moved from the opposing view, that the points were added by the Prophets themselves (a view which many pious theologians defend with good zeal), then neither is it my intention, nor am I obliged, at present to draw the thread of controversy with you over that question. Very well. Let the Prophets themselves have added the vowel signs. All the more will the arguments I am about to set out bind you. If you say that the genuine pointing of this name and of a few other words was changed by the Jews and adapted to a later superstition, you will find an answer in our dissertation on the Keri and Chetib, sections 19 and 29. Those who ascribe the points to the Masoretes would say more plausibly and probably that the genuine pronunciation of these names was deliberately suppressed by them, if indeed they knew it (which by no means seems credible to me regarding the name YHWH [יהוה], since they added the points after the temple was destroyed); or, if they did not know it, that the later pronunciation was put in its place. And indeed the distinguished theologian Piscator judges so, and I will bring forward his testimony later, at section 75.

units.la: LXXII. Sed redeat tandem oratio nostra in viam, post cal- cata tot diverticula.
units.tr: LXXII. But let our discussion now return to its path, after so many detours.

units.la: Dixi supra §. 60. nomen יהוה in textu Biblico alienis vocalibus notatum esse, non hoc fine, ut cum iis legeretur, sed ut pro eo legerentur eæ voces quarum vocales ei subjecere. Nomen יהוה aut sic יְהֹוָה aut sic [יְהֹוִה] scribitur. Cum priori modo scribitur, ajo esse puncta nominis Adonai; cum posteriori, esse puncta nominis Elohim. Eaque hoc fine voci isti subjecta, ut per ea legeretur. Illud jam probatum ibo aliquot rationibus. Deinde Authoritatem & exemplum omnium priscorum Interpretum proferam. Postremo autem loco testimonia recentiorum adducam.
units.tr: I said above, in §. 60, that the name יהוה [YHWH] in the Biblical text is marked with vowels foreign to it, not so that it should be read with them, but so that the words whose vowels were placed under it should be read in its place. The name is written either as יְהֹוָה or as [יְהֹוִה]. When it is written in the first way, I maintain that these are the points of the name Adonai; when in the second, they are the points of the name Elohim. These vowels were attached to it for this purpose, that the word should be read through them. I will now prove this with several arguments. Then I will bring forward the authority and example of all the earlier interpreters. Lastly, I will cite the testimonies of more recent writers.

units.la: LXXIII. Principem locum teneat illa ratio, quod hoc nomen, quoties cunque vel præcedit vel sequitur cognomen Adonai, & nunquam aliâs, ne bis legeretur Adonai Adonai, semper mutet sua puncta, ac pro scheva, Holem & Kamets, semper accipiat chateph segol, Holem & Hirik, puncta vid. nominis אלהים Hoc mihi consídera, si illa puncta, quæ vulgo sub tetragrammato ponuntur, essent vera ac stata ejus puncta, quid obstaret quominus liceret dicere, Adonai Jehova, vel Jehova Adonai? Cur huic nomini, & quidem hoc casu, & semper, accideret, quod nec ulli alii, nec huic ipsi unquam alias? Quæ vel probabilis ratio afferetur? a N B. אֲדֹנָי Adonai, von אַרְנִינוּ / ut Ps.8. 1, nec etiam לאדני / ut Ps. 110. 1. ut frustra hæc loca objiciantur. Aliud est Adonai aliud adonenu & ladoni. Hoc אָדֹנָי reperiri קלך id est 134. vicibus. Addidimus, eo numero non comprehendi illa loca, ubi Adonai junctum est יהוה / Observatum autem à Masorethis est, אֲדֹנָי יְהוָה occurrere in Bibl. 222. vicibus, cujus numeri memoriale afferunt vocem כְּכֹל currus, Masora magna, litera א / ארני וודאי קלך ז׳ מנהון לאדני וסי נמסר בישעיה id est Adnai nomen illud confessum occurrit 134. Et 7. exillis sunt, ladonai, & recensentur ad initium cap. 28. Jesaiæ. & tria ex illis sunt vadonai. Postquam autem Masora omnia enumerasset, subjungit, וכל אדני יהוה רכותי די מנהון בתורה ורי בתהלים ושארה בנביאים והם רכקי וסימי רכב אלהים רבותים id est Omne אֲדֹנָי יְהוָה simile est. Illa autem conjuncta quater occurrunt in Lege, quater in Psalmis, reliqua sunt in Prophetis, & me- a Mark at the foot (not reproduced). & memoriale est, curruum Dei duæ myriades Pf.69.
