Immit vocem illam רכב / Et columna sequenti, ארבי יהוה octies sic scribitur, quater in lege, & recensentur ea loca [in Masora parva] in lectione לך לך (Gen.15.) & in Psalmis. Psalm. 69. Et omnia loca Prophetarum eodem modo se habent, præter quinque, ubi occurrit יהוה אלהים * quæ recensentur in Masora parva ad 2. Reg. 19. (ubi vid. primo occurit) Et transposita in hunc modum (יהוה ארני) quinquies occurrunt, & recensentur in Masora parva ad Psal. 140.8. Habes specimen indefessæ Masoreth harum industriæ. b Forsterus citat locum ex Iezech. 21. 5. ubi scrsum occurrat יהוה sed omnia exemplaria illi adversantur
units.tr: LXXIII. The first place belongs to this argument: whenever this name either precedes or follows the appellative Adonai, and never otherwise, so that it would not be read Adonai Adonai, it always changes its points, and in place of the sheva, holem and kamets it always takes the chateph segol, holem and hiriq, which are the points of the name אלהים [Elohim]. Consider this: if the points that are commonly placed under the tetragrammaton were its true and fixed points, what would prevent us from saying Adonai Jehovah or Jehovah Adonai? Why would this happen to this name, and in this case always, and to no other name and to this one never otherwise? What even probable reason can be given? Note that אֲדֹנָי [Adonai] is not the same as אַרְנִינוּ [Ps. 8.1], nor as לאדני [Ps. 110.1], so these passages are cited in vain. Adonai is one thing, adonenu and ladoni another. The form אָדֹנָי [Adonai] is found 134 times. We have added that those passages where Adonai is joined to יהוה are not included in that number. The Masorites have observed that the combination אֲדֹנָי יְהוָה [Adonai YHWH] occurs in the Bible 222 times. As a memorial of this number they give the word כְּכֹל [kechol, "chariot"], with the Masora magna, letter א. Adonai, the confessed name, occurs 134 times; seven of these are ladonai, and they are listed at the beginning of Isaiah 28; and three of them are vadonai. After the Masora had enumerated all these, it adds that all the combinations of Adonai with YHWH, of which some are in the Law, some in the Psalms, and the rest in the Prophets, are of the same kind. These combined forms occur four times in the Law, four times in the Psalms; the rest are in the Prophets, and the memorial is "two myriads of the chariots of God," Ps. 68. The word רכב [rkb] and the following column: the combination יְהוָה אֲדֹנָי [YHWH Adonai] is written in this way eight times, four times in the Law, and these passages are listed [in the Masora parva] in the lection לך לך (Gen. 15) and in the Psalms. Ps. 69. All the passages of the Prophets are in the same way, except five, where occurs יהוה אלהים [YHWH Elohim], which are listed in the Masora parva at 2 Kings 19 (where it first occurs). And transposed in this way (יהוה ארני) they occur five times, and are listed in the Masora parva at Ps. 140.8. You have a sample of the untiring industry of the Masorah in these matters. b Forsterus cites a passage from Ezekiel 21.5 where it is said to occur, but all the copies are against him.

units.la: LXXIV.
units.tr: LXXIV.

units.la: Qui Jehovi hodie legat defensetve, puto extare neminem. primis Editionibus Tremellio-Junianæ versionis non comparet ea vox. Vere nobilis & de Ecclesiis præclare meritus Theologus, Fr. Junius, postquam in fata concessisset Tremellius, vocem eam usurpavit, docuitque tum Grammatica, tum in notis ad Gen. 16. esse ואַיהוה singultientis. Ego neminem adhuc vidi, qui istam acutissimi & polyhistoris viri conjecturam suo approbaverit calculo. Existimo, probabilius conjectasse Cajetanum ad 1. Regum 8. vocem illam sic inflexam esse ad dulcedinem affectus supplicantis. Ariæ Montano & Mercero (ut de Scalig. Drusio, Buxtorfio &c jam nihil dicam) vox ea adeo aliena visa est, ut ab ista punctatione יהוה palmarium argumentum contra vocem Jehova deprompserint. Si Jehova leges, inquiunt, etiam Jehovi aliquando legendum erit, quod erit absurdissimum. Omitto quod Jod nunquam cum chateph segol & ה nunquam in Chirik quiescens occurrat.
units.tr: I suppose there is no one today who reads or defends Jehovah. In the first editions of the Tremellius-Junius version this form does not appear. The very noble theologian, who deserved well of the Churches, Franciscus Junius, after Tremellius had departed this life, adopted the word and taught, both by grammar and in his notes on Gen. 16, that it is the form of a sobbing וַאֲיהוָה [va-Ihvah]. I have not yet seen anyone who has approved that conjecture of this most acute man and polymath with his own vote. I think Cajetan, on 1 Kings 8, conjectured more probably that the word was inflected in this way to express the sweetness of the suppliant's feeling. To Arias Montanus and Mercerus (not to mention Scaliger, Drusius, Buxtorf and others) the word seemed so alien that they drew from this pointing of יהוה [YHWH] a chief argument against the form Jehovah. "If you read Jehovah," they say, "then at some time it will have to be read Jehovi, which would be most absurd." I pass over the fact that the yod never occurs with chateph segol, and the he never occurs quiescent with chireq.

units.la: LXXV.
units.tr: LXXV.

units.la: Hoc argumentum tanti fecit Logicus ille Theologus, Joh. Piscator, ut ex eo porro collegerit, puncta ab ipsis prophetis non fuisse adscripta. Vide ejus Scholia ad Gen.15.8. , ubi ex professo disputans adversus antiquitatem punctorum, tertio loco hoc argumentum collocavit, Si puncta, inquit, ut hodie legantur, ab ipsis sacris scriptoribus fuissent addita, tunc vocabulum יהוה constanter esset scriptum יְהֹוָה. Neque enim idonea causa afferri potest, cur punctationem illam mutaverint. Atqui vocabulum יהוה passim occurrit cum punctis alienis, puta nunc nominis אלהים ut cum scribitur Ezech. 15.5. & alibi passim, יהוה nunc vero nominis ארני ut cum scribiscribitur Pf.34. 3. ביהוה / Idem in Quæst. ad Exod. 3.15. postquam dixisset, nomen יהוה & posse pronuntiari & fas esse illud pronuntiare, & vicariam illam Adonai, tanquam ex superstitione introductam, esse repudiandam, sic pergit, Ex qua consuetudine data est hæc illorum audacia atque ineptia, ut nomini יהוה quoties conjungitur nomini אדני / tribuant puncta nominis Elohim, scribentes יהוה / quam punctationem Grammatica prorsus respuit. Unde miror nostros quoque Interpretes, viros Christianos & lingua Ebraea peritissimos, in versione sua punctationem illam retinuisse, scribentes sc. Jehovi.
units.tr: That brilliant logician and theologian Johannes Piscator made so much of this argument that he went on to conclude from it that the points were not added by the prophets themselves. See his Scholia on Gen. 15.8, where, arguing at length against the antiquity of the points, he placed this argument third: If the points, as they are read today, had been added by the sacred writers themselves, then the word יהוה would have been written consistently as יְהֹוָה. For no good reason can be given why they would have changed that pointing. But the word יהוה occurs everywhere with foreign points, for instance now with the vowels of the name אלהים, as when it is written in Ezek. 15.5 and elsewhere throughout, and now with the vowels of the name ארני, as when it is written in Ps. 34.3, ביהוה. In his Questions on Exodus 3.15, having said that the name יהוה can be pronounced and that it is lawful to pronounce it, and that the substitute Adonai must be rejected as introduced out of superstition, he goes on: From this custom came the audacity and foolishness of those who give to the name יהוה whenever it is joined with the name אדני the vowels of the name Elohim, writing יְהוָה; grammar utterly rejects this pointing. Hence I am surprised that our own interpreters too, Christian men most skilled in the Hebrew tongue, retained that pointing in their version, writing Jehovi.

units.la: LXXVI. In quibus eruditissimi Theologi verbis illud verissimum est, quod de Jehovi pronuntiat. De cæteris verò §.82. videbimus.
units.tr: LXXVI. In these words of that most learned theologian, what he says about Jehovi is entirely true. As for the rest, we shall see in §82.

units.la: LXXVII. Secunda ratio depromitur à natura literarum <bl>משה וכלב</bl> / Hoc enim extra controversiam ponet hecum, quisquis Ebræam linguam vel à limine salutavit, ex istis septem, literas <bl>מלכלב</bl> ante dictionem, à Jod Schevato incipientem, habere Chirik, in quo Jod, abjecto suo scheva; quiescit, Exempli gratia à <bl>יהונה</bl> sit <bl>ביהונה</bl> / <bl>ליהונה</bl> &c. Unde sequitur, si vera & juxta proprias vocales lectio esset Jehova, dicendum & scribendum etiam fuisse <bl>מיהוה ביהוה</bl> &c. quæ punctatio cum nusquam appareat; merito illam lectionem suspectamus.
units.tr: LXXVII. The second argument is drawn from the nature of the letters <bl>משה וכלב</bl> (the mnemonic of the names Moses and Caleb). For whoever has greeted the Hebrew language even from the threshold will grant beyond dispute that among these seven letters, when placed before a word beginning with a Jod with Shewa, the Jod, having lost its shewa, takes a Chireq and is silent. For example, from יהונה we get ביהונה, ליהונה, and so on. It follows that if the reading Jehovah were true and read according to its own vowels, it would also have had to be written and read מיהוה, ביהוה, and so on. Since this pointing appears nowhere, we rightly suspect that reading.

units.la: LXXVIII. Harum enim literarum ultimæ quatuor (<bl>וכלב</bl>) ante hoc nomen habent Phathach, in quo Jod quiescit, ut <bl>ביהוה</bl> &c. quod fieri non posset nisi haberetur ratio sequentis puncti rapti Chatheph Phathach, quod est sub א in <bl>אדני</bl> / Puncta enim rapta requirunt ante se sub istis servilibus punctum affine.
units.tr: LXXVIII. For the last four of these letters (<bl>וכלב</bl>) take a Patach before this name, in which the Jod is silent, as in ביהוה, and so on. This could not happen unless account were taken of the following hataph-pointing, the Hataph Patach under the א in אדני. For hataph vowels require before them a vowel-point akin to the servile letters.

units.la: LXXIX. In hac punctatione & illud insuper considera, א in nomine Adonai post וכלב peculiari quodam modo semper quiescere in Phathach præcedentis servilis, ut pro באדני legatur באדני &c. Sic semper ביהוה pro ביהוה &c. Sed non facessam ab hac ratione, nisi & hoc addidero, nullam consonantem cum præcedenti syllaba jungi, ut fiat syllaba mixta, aut quasi diphthongus, nisi per Scheva quiescens (cujus hoc munus est) & quidem in medio dictionis semper expressum. E. gr. לילה / Hoc considerent, qui Baihova, Laihova legunt, quomodo enim Jod in medio vocis coalesceet cum syllaba præcedenti, Va, ba, la, cha, sine scheva quiscenti expresso? Hic enim nulla omni& memoriale est, curruum Dei duæ myriades Pf.69. Innuit vocem illam רכב / Et columna sequenti, ארבי יהוה octies sic scribitur, quater in lege, & recensentur ea loca [in Masora parva] in lectione לך לך (Gen.15.) & in Psalmis. Psalm. 69. Et omnia loca Prophetarum eodem modo se habent, præter quinque, ubi occurrit יהוה אלהים * quæ recensentur in Masora parva ad 2. Reg. 19. (ubi vid. primo occurit) Et transpositia in hunc modum (ארני יהוה) quinquies occurrunt, & recensentur in Masora parva ad Psal. 140.8. Habes specimen indefessæ Masoretharum industriæ. b Forsterus citat locum ex Iezech. 21. 5. ubi sursum occurrat יהוה sed omnia exemplaria illi adversantur
units.tr: LXXIX. In this pointing consider also this, that the א in the name Adonai after וכלב always stays silent in a special manner, with the Patach of the preceding servile letter, so that for באדני one reads באדני, and so on. Likewise always ביהוה for ביהוה, and so on. But I shall not leave this line of argument without adding this as well: no consonant joins with the preceding syllable so as to make a mixed syllable, or quasi-diphthong, except through a silent shewa (whose office this is), and this is always expressed in the middle of a word. For example לילה. Let those consider this who read Baihova or Laihova: how can the Jod in the middle of the word coalesce with the preceding syllable, Va, ba, la, cha, without an expressed shewa that is silent? For here there is no such thing at all. Note also that the word רכב (chariots) in the verse The chariots of God are twice ten thousand (Ps. 68.18, Hebrew) and the following column, ארבי יהוה, is written this way eight times, four times in the Law, and these places are listed [in the small Masora] at the reading Lech lecha (Gen. 15) and in the Psalms (Ps. 69). And all the places in the Prophets stand in the same way, except five, where יהוה אלהים occurs; these are listed in the small Masora on 2 Kings 19 (where you may see where it first occurs). And the transposed form ארני יהוה occurs five times and is listed in the small Masora on Ps. 140.8. You have here a sample of the tireless industry of the Masoretes. Forster cites a passage from Ezek. 21.5 where יהוה occurs above, but all the manuscripts are against him.

units.la: LXXIV. Qui Jehovi hodie legat defensetve, puto extare neminem.
units.tr: LXXIV. I suppose that there is no one today who reads or defends "Jehovah."

units.la: primis Editionibus Tremellio-Junianæ versionis non comparet ea vox. Vere nobilis & de Ecclesiis præclare meritus Theologus, Fr. Junius, postquam in fata concessisset Tremellius, vocem eam usurpavit, docuitque tum Grammatica, tum in notis ad Gen. 16. esse ῥαθ@ singultientis. Ego neminem adhuc vidi, qui istam acutissimi & polyhistoris viri conjecturam suo approbaverit calculo. Existimo, probabilius conjectasse Cajetanum ad 1. Regum 8. vocem illam sic inflexam esse ad dulcedinem affectus supplicantis. Ariæ Montano & Mercero (ut de Scalig. Drusio, Buxtorfio &c jam nihil dicam) vox ea adeo aliena visa est, ut ab ista punctatione יְהוָה palmarium argumentum contra vocem Jehova deprompserint. Si Jehova leges, inquiunt, etiam Jehovi aliquando legendum erit, quod erit absurdissimum. Omitto quod Jod nunquam cum chateph segol & ה nunquam in Chirik quiescens occurrat.
units.tr: The word does not appear in the earliest editions of the Tremellius-Junius version. After Tremellius had died, the truly noble theologian and great benefactor of the Churches, Franciscus Junius, took up that word, and taught in his grammar, and in his notes on Gen. 16, that it is a stammering sound [ῥαθ@]. I have not yet seen anyone who has endorsed that conjecture of this most acute and learned man. I think that Cajetan conjectured more probably, on 1 Kings 8, that the word was so inflected to express the sweetness of the suppliant's feeling. To Arias Montanus and Mercerus (not to mention now Scaliger, Drusius, Buxtorf and others) that word seemed so foreign that from the pointing יְהוָה they drew their chief argument against the word Jehovah. If you read Jehovah, they say, then sometimes you will have to read Jehovi as well, which would be most absurd. I pass over the fact that Jod never occurs silent with chateph segol, and He never occurs silent in Chirik.

units.la: LXXV. Hoc argumentum tanti fecit Logicus ille Theologus, Joh. Piscator, ut ex eo porro collegerit, puncta ab ipsis prophetis non fuisse adscripta.
units.tr: LXXV. So highly did that logical theologian, John Piscator, value this argument that he went on to conclude from it that the points were not added by the prophets themselves.

units.la: Vide ejus Scholia ad Gen. 15. 8. [Idem in appendice ad Quæstiones in Pentateuchum, ubi ex professo disputans adversus antiquitatem punctorum, tertio loco hoc argumentum collocavit, Si puncta, inquit, ut hodie leguntur, ab ipsis sacris scriptoribus fuissent addita, tunc vocabulum יהוה constanter esset scriptum יהוה. Neque enim idonea causa afferri potest, cur punctationem illam mutaverint. Atqui vocabulum יהוה passim occurrit cum punctis alienis, puta nunc nomini אלהים / ut cum scribitur Ezech. 15. 5. & alibi passim, יהוה / nunc vero nomini ארני / ut cum scribiscribitur Pf.34.3. ביהוה / Idem in Quæst. ad Exod. 3.15. postquam dixisset, nomen יהוה & posse pronuntiari & fas esse illud pronuntiare, & vicariam illam Adonai, tanquam ex superstitione introductam, esse repudiandam, sic pergit, Ex qua consuetudine orta est hæc illorum audacia atque ineptia, ut nomini יהוה quoties conjungitur nomini אדני / tribuant puncta nominis Elohim, scribentes יהוה / quam punctationem Grammatica prorsus respuit. Unde miror nostros quoque Interpretes, viros Christianos & linguæ Ebraeæ peritissimos, in versione sua punctationem istam retinuisse, scribentes sc. Jehovi.
units.tr: See his Scholia on Gen. 15.8. [The same, in the appendix to his Questions on the Pentateuch, where he disputes expressly against the antiquity of the points, places this argument third: If the points, as they are read today, had been added by the sacred writers themselves, then the word yhwh would have been written consistently as yhwh. For no adequate reason can be given why they would have changed that pointing. Yet the word yhwh occurs everywhere with alien points: now with the points of the name Elohim, as at Ezek. 15.5 and elsewhere throughout; now with those of the name Adonai, as when it is written at Ps. 34.3 byhwh.] In his Questions on Exod. 3.15, after saying that the name yhwh both can be pronounced and may lawfully be pronounced, and that the substitute Adonai, introduced as if out of superstition, must be rejected, he goes on: From this custom has arisen the audacity and silliness of those who, whenever the name yhwh is joined with the name adny, assign to it the points of the name Elohim, writing yhwh, which grammar utterly rejects. Hence I wonder that our own translators too, men Christian and most skilled in the Hebrew language, retained that pointing in their version, writing Jehovi.

units.la: LXXVI. In quibus eruditissimi Theologi verbis illud verissimum est, quod de Jehovi pronuntiat. De cæteris vero §.82. videbimus.
units.tr: LXXVI. In these words of that most learned theologian, what he says about Jehovi is entirely true. As for the rest, we shall see in §82.

units.la: LXXVII. Secunda ratio depromitur à natura literarum משה וכלב / Hoc enim extra controversiam ponet mecum, quisquis Ebræam linguam vel à limine salutavit, ex istis septem literas מוכלב ante dictionem, à Jod Schevato incipientem, habere Chirik, in quo Jod, abjecto suo scheva; quiescit, Exempli gratia à יהוּה fit ליהוּדה / ליהוּדה &c. Unde sequitur, si vera & juxta proprias vocales lectio esset Jehova, dicendum & scribendum etiam fuisse מיהוה ביהוה &c. quæ punctatio cum nusquam appareat, merito illam lectionem suspectamus.
units.tr: LXXVII. The second reason is drawn from the nature of the letters m-w-k-l-b. For whoever has greeted Hebrew even from the threshold will grant with me beyond dispute that, of these seven letters, the mem, waw, kaph, lamed and beth before a word beginning with yod with a schewa take a chirik, in which the yod, having lost its schewa, rests. For example, from yhwh comes lyhwh, lyhwdh, and so on. Hence it follows that if the true reading, and one according to its own vowels, were Jehovah, then it would have had to be said and written also myhwh, byhwh, and so on. Since this pointing appears nowhere, we rightly suspect that reading.

units.la: LXXVIII. Harum enim literarum ultimæ quatuor (וכלב) ante hoc nomen habent Phathach, in quo Jod quiescit, ut ביהוה &c. quod fieri non posset nisi haberetur ratio sequentis puncti rapti Chatheph Phathach, quod est sub א in אדני / Puncta enim rapta requirunt ante se sub istis servilibus pun-[illegible, ~3 letters] tum affine.
units.tr: LXXVIII. For the last four of these letters (w, k, l, b) before this name take a patach, in which the yod rests, as in byhwh and so on. This could not happen unless account were taken of the following point, the rapid chateph patach, which stands under the aleph in Adonai. For rapid points require, before themselves and under these servile letters, ... a related point.

units.la: LXXIX. In hâc punctatione & illud insuper considera, א in nomine Adonai post בְּלֹהִים peculiari quodam modo semper quiescere in Phathach praecedentis servilis, ut pro בַּאדֹנָי legatur בֵּאלֹהִי &c. Sic semper ביהוה pro בִּיהוָה &c. Sed non facessam ab hac ratione, nisi & hoc addidero, nullam consonantem cum praecedenti syllaba jungi, ut fiat syllaba mixta, aut quasi diphthongus, nisi per Scheva quiescens (cujus hoc munus est) & quidem in medio dictionis semper expressum. E. gr. לִילָה / Hoc considerent, qui Baihova, Laihova legunt, quomodo enim Jod in medio vocis coalescet cum syllaba praecedenti, Va, ba, la, cha, sine scheva quiscenti expresso? Hic enim nulla omnino datur exceptio. Cur hic quæso te, non manet scheva sub Jod, quod in voce absolutâ semper adscribitur? Quod si vero Bahova legeris, impinges in principia linguæ Ebreæ, quæ neutiquam admittunt, ut Jod in phathach quiescat.
units.tr: LXXIX. In this pointing consider also this: the aleph in the name Adonai, after the prefixes, always rests in the patach of the preceding servile letter, so that for b'Adonai one reads b'Elohi, and so on. Thus always byhwh for byhwh. But I will not leave this line of reasoning without adding this: no consonant joins with the preceding syllable to form a mixed syllable, or a kind of diphthong, except through a quiescent schewa, whose office this is, and this is always expressed in the middle of a word. For example, lyilah. Let those who read Baihova, Laihova consider how the yod in the middle of a word can coalesce with the preceding syllable (va, ba, la, cha) without an expressed quiescent schewa. For here no exception at all is given. Why, I ask you, does the schewa not stand under the yod here, when it is always written in an independent word? But if you read Bahova, you will run against the first principles of the Hebrew language, which in no way allow the yod to rest in a patach.

units.la: LXXX. Quod ad literam ɔ attinet, ea nunquam ante hoc nomen habet hirik, sicuti analogia postularet, siquidem Jehova legeretur; sed perpetuo est cum tsere. Id quod fieri nullo modo posset, nisi haberetur ratio alicujus literæ gutturalis aut Resch sequentis. Cujus autem ex his rationem haberi dicemus, nisi א / à qua literâ vox אֲדֹנָי incipit? מֵיהוֹה / מֵאֲרֶנִי /
units.tr: LXXX. As for the letter yod, it never has a chirik before this name, as analogy would require if Jehova were read; it always has a tsere. This could not happen in any way unless account were taken of some following guttural letter or of resh. Which of these do we say must be taken into account, unless it is the aleph with which the word Adonai begins? (myhwh, m'Adonai)

units.la: LXXXI. Illud addam, sicuti א vocis אֲדֹנָי Adonai post literas וּכלֵה phathachatas id est vocali phatach notatas, adjecto suo (ָ:) quiescit in phathach servilium, & propter eam causam prima quoque nominis tetragrammati litera post illas literas suo scheva privatur: Ita & litera א nominis Elohim, post litteras easdem quiescit (ֱ:) & (ֵ:) in tzere contractis, לֵאלהִים pro לֵאלֹהִים / Idem fit ante nomen τετραγραμμάτον, cum puncta nominis Elohim suscipit, E. gr. Ps. 68. 11. לַיהוֹה אֲדֹנָי Elohim Adonai.
units.tr: LXXXI. I add this: just as the aleph of Adonai, after the letters marked with patach (that is, with the vowel patach), rests with its own sign in the patach of the servile letters, and for that reason the first letter of the tetragrammaton is also deprived of its schewa after those letters, so too the aleph of the name Elohim, after the same letters, rests with its sign, and the tsere is contracted, so that one has l'Elohim for l'Elohim. The same happens before the Tetragrammaton when it takes the points of the name Elohim, for example Ps. 68.11, layhwh Adonai Elohim Adonai.

units.la: LXXXII. Objicies, hac quidem ratione evinci, in לֵיהוֹה בִּיהוֹה וַיהוֹה מֵיהוֹה &c. esse puncta nominis אֲדֹנָי / ac proinde ista, retentis istis vocalibus non aliter posse legi quam Ladonai, badonai, wadonai, meadonai: at in voce nuda יְהוָה aliam esse rationem, ibi quippe proprias vocales esse retentas, atque hoc inde apparere quod non scribatur יְהוָה cum hateph phatach sub Jod, quomodo scribendum fuerat, si haberet puncta אֲדֹנָי (quemadmodum scribitur יְהוָה quando suscipit puncta אֱלֹהִים) sed יְהוָה cum scheva nudo sub Jod. Respondeo primo, nullam probabilem rationem afferri posse, cur nomini tetragrammato, nude posito, vel ipsi prophetæ (ut demus ipsos vocales adscripsisse) vel Masorethæ, proprias vocales, & eidem præfixis juncto, alienas addiderint. Secundo, me ne conjectura quidem posse assequi quid magnus ille Piscator spectaverit, quando istis in locis quæ supra §.75. produximus, illud ipsum adeo præsidentur asseruit. Certe μίχα αἰ/μμα est, & quod nullus, qui rem accuratius pensitabit, ipsi dederit. Ecce enim ipse statuit puncta à Masorethis fuisse adscripta: Agnoscit in בִּיהוֹה &c. esse vocales Adonai, in יְהוֹוֶה Elohim, & tamen יְהוָה proprias vocales retentas esse asserit: At quis color huic assertioni inducetur? cetur? Liceat mihi sic ratiocinari ex hypotesi ipsius D. Piscatoris, Masorethæ aut sciverunt genuinam nominis יהוה lectionem, aut nescivere. Si nescivēre, quomodo eam potuerunt repræsentare? nisi forte dixeris eos insciōs cum Cajapha prophetasse, & aliud agentes rem acu, quod ajunt, tetigisse. Si scivēre, quod tamen verisimile non est, quia sæculis aliquot sacerdotibus quorum ævo templum solo æquatum est, posthumarunt, sed da scivisse, Si scivere, inquam, quis sibi persuaderi sinet, liceat mihi hoc iterare, eos in nomine cum præfixis junctō eam celasse, in nudo vero expressisse? Sed bene habet, quod etiam aliunde constare possit, punctatores Bibliorum, quicunque fuerint, & nudum יהוה & cum præfixis junctum vocalibus רֹ Adonai vestivisse: Atque hæc sit.
units.tr: LXXXII. You will object that by this reasoning it is shown that in lyhwh, byhwh, wyhwh, myhwh, and so on, the points are those of Adonai, and that these vowels, if retained, can therefore be read only as ladonai, badonai, wadonai, meadonai; but that in the bare word yhwh the situation is different, since there the proper vowels are retained. This appears, you say, from the fact that it is not written with hateph patach under the yod, as it would have to be if it had the points of Adonai (as it is written when it takes the points of Elohim), but with a bare schewa under the yod. I reply. First, no probable reason can be given why the tetragrammaton, standing alone, or the prophet himself (granting that they added the vowels), or the Masoretes, should have added the proper vowels to the bare name, and alien ones to the same name when joined with prefixes. Second, I cannot even conjecture what the great Piscator aimed at, when in the passages which we produced above, at §75, he asserted this very thing so confidently. Certainly it is a contradiction, and no one who weighs the matter more carefully would grant it to him. For see, he himself holds that the points were added by the Masoretes; he recognises that in byhwh and so on the vowels are those of Adonai, and in yhwh those of Elohim; and yet he asserts that the proper vowels are retained in yhwh. But what colour can be given to this assertion? Let me reason thus from the hypothesis of Mr Piscator himself. The Masoretes either knew the genuine reading of the name yhwh, or did not know it. If they did not know it, how could they represent it? Unless perhaps you say they prophesied unknowingly, like Caiaphas, and hit the mark while aiming at something else, as they say. If they knew it (which is not likely, since they came many centuries after the priests in whose age the temple was razed to the ground), but grant that they knew it: if they knew it, I say, who will let himself be persuaded that they concealed it in the name joined with prefixes, but expressed it in the bare name? But it is well that it can also be established from elsewhere that the pointers of the Bible, whoever they were, clothed both the bare yhwh and the one joined with prefixes with the vowels of Adonai. And so much for this.

units.la: LXXXIII. Ratio tertia.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The third argument.

units.la: Literæ בגדכפת initio dictionum post voces in literam quiescentem desinentes solent adspirari, id est, ut vulgo loquuntur, sine Dages leni scribi, quod alii vocant raphari, nisi interveniat accentus distinguens aut Rex. Jam vero illud constat, prædictas illas literas, post vocem יהוה tam nudam, quam cum præfixis compositam, non adspirari, sed leni Dages notari, etiam cum nulla Pausa vel Rex intervenit. Unde liquido constat, eos qui puncta adjecere, utroque casu, non vocem יהוה / cujus ultima quiescit, sed aliam vocem spectasse, quæ in literam non quiescentem desinat, qualis est Adonai.
units.tr: The letters בגדכפת at the beginning of words that follow a word ending in a silent letter are usually aspirated, that is, as people commonly say, written without a light dagesh, which others call raphe, unless a distinguishing accent or the Rex intervenes. Now it is established that those letters, after the word יהוה, both when bare and when compounded with prefixes, are not aspirated but marked with a light dagesh, even when no pause or Rex intervenes. Hence it is clear that those who added the points in either case were not thinking of the word יהוה, whose last letter is silent, but of another word that ends in a non-silent letter, such as Adonai.

units.la: LXXXIV.
units.tr: LXXXIV.

units.la: Quod vero ad illud attinet, quod in יְהוָה sub Jod non hateph-phathach, sed nudum scheva sit, ac proinde non esse puncta nominis יְהֹוָה / in qua objectione multum roboris nonnulli ponunt, isti abunde satis-fecit Drusius. Puncta rapta esse schevata composita, simplicisque scheva sub gutturalibus vicaria, nemo tam hospes in Grammatica, qui ignorat. Adhæc, scheva simplex à prisci fuisse expressum per vocalem A, ac si hateph phathach esset, modo non sequeretur litera gutturalis aut Jod, quamplurimis exemplis doceri potest, E. gr. שְׁלֹמֹה Salomo, שְׁמוּאֵל Samuel, כְּנַעַן Canaan, &c. Cum ergo sequente Daleth, utpote litera non gutturali, prisca pronuntiatione idem fuerit sonus רֹ (:) & (ֻ:) punctorum nec genere, nec specie, nec natura, sed tantum figura & numero invicem differentium, quid necesse fuit ad Scheva sub Jod positum addere phathach? Alia plane ratio erat in voce יְהוָה / Ejus enim
units.tr: As for the objection that under the Jod in יְהוָה there is a plain shewa and not a hateph-patach, so that these are not the vowel points of the name יְהֹוָה (an objection on which some lay great weight), Drusius has answered it fully. That the points were taken from a compound shewa, which stands in place of the simple shewa under gutturals, is known to anyone who is not a stranger to grammar. Moreover, the simple shewa was formerly pronounced with the vowel A, as if it were a hateph-patach, provided no guttural letter or Jod followed. This can be shown by very many examples: Solomon [שְׁלֹמֹה], Samuel [שְׁמוּאֵל], Canaan [כְּנַעַן], and so on. Since, then, before Daleth, which is not a guttural, the points (:) and (ֻ:) had the same sound in the old pronunciation, differing not in kind, quality or nature but only in shape and number, why was it necessary to add a patach to the shewa placed under Jod? The case of the word יְהוָה was entirely different.

units.la: Drus. cap. 1. Bellarm. in praxi Gram. enim princeps litera cum gutturalis sit, necessariò ad scheva simplex vocalis ex tribus illis brevibus (−) (ᵕ) & hirik unà adsciscenda fuit. Quod scheva simplex est sub cæteris consonis, id scheva compositum est sub gutturalib. Compendium ergo scripturæ quæsitum est in voce singulis fere lineis recurrente. At quia idem nomen cum punctis nominis Elohim rarius occurrebat, non pigrati sunt integrum (ᵕᵕ:) literæ Jod subjicere [יְהוָה].
units.tr: Drusius, ch. 1; Bellarmine in his Grammar practice. For since the first letter is a guttural, a simple vowel had necessarily to be added to the simple shewa, taken from those three short vowels (−), (ᵕ) and hireq. Where the simple shewa stands under the other consonants, the compound shewa stands under the gutturals. The saving of writing was therefore sought in a word that recurs in almost every line. But because the same name occurred less often with the points of the name Elohim, they did not hesitate to subjoin the whole Jod with its points [יְהוָה].

units.la: LXXXV. Plura argumenta huc possent accongeri, nisi arbitrarer liquido satis esse probatum, in Bibliis Ebraïcis nomen Tetragrammaton alienis vocalibus esse vestitum, & secundum istam punctationem, pro diversitate subjectarum vocalium, jam Adonai, jam Elohim esse legendum. Neque superstitionis notam illis inuri posse, qui isthac lectione contenti, a nomine יהוה secundum consonas efferendo, & voce Jehova, utpote omnium quæ ab authoribus afferuntur, incertissima, abstinent. Qui nescit, qui non credit puncta illa esse tetragrammati genuinas & piscas vocales, ille certe excusandus est, si Jehova legat. At qui credit puncta illa esse vocis Adonai, non vero tetragrammati propria, qui credit genuinas vocales aut ignorari aut incertas esse & nihilominus in Ebraeo textu (non frustra dico in Ebraeo textu) vocem Jehova legit, nae ille ultro, sciens volens βαςΓαεζζε.
units.tr: LXXXV. Many more arguments could be gathered here, were I not of the opinion that it has already been clearly enough proved that in the Hebrew Bibles the Tetragrammaton [יהוה] is clothed with foreign vowels, and that according to this pointing it is to be read now as Adonai, now as Elohim, depending on the vowels attached to it. Nor can the mark of superstition be branded on those who, content with this reading, abstain from pronouncing the name according to its consonants and from the word Jehova, which of all the forms put forward by authors is the most uncertain. Whoever does not know, or does not believe, that those points are the genuine and proper vowels of the Tetragrammaton is certainly to be excused if he reads Jehova. But whoever believes that those points belong to the word Adonai and not properly to the Tetragrammaton, who believes that the genuine vowels are either unknown or uncertain, and yet reads the word Jehova in the Hebrew text (I do not say in Ebraeo textu without reason), he, of his own accord, knowing and willing, commits a barbarism [βαςΓαεζζε].

units.la: LXXXVI. Jam iubet authoritate & testimoniis virorum in Ebraica literatura principum hanc dissertationem obsignare. Equidem cum multis in hoc & similibus argumentis sæpe disserui, qui post gravissimas rationes vana sophisticatione & impudenti prævaricatione elusas, ad unius Theologi authoritatem derepente obstupuere. Adeo servile quorundam ingenium est. Verum ipsis non est verum, quia verum, sed quia hic vel ille dicit esse verum. Hoc verò est non vero sed hominibus sacramento dicere. Ut ergo & his gratificer & erectioris animi juvenes confirmem, præter Lyram, Burgensem, Abulensem, præter Cl. Drusium, cujus tetragrammaton sæpius citavimus, produco in hanc scenam Pagninum in Thesauro, Mercerum in cap. 2. verf. 4. & cap. 15. Genesis, & in Amos cap. 3. & 5. Rod. Ant. Cevalerum addit ad Thes. Pagnini, Scaligerum in notis ad fragmenta selecta, in calce operis de Emendat. Temporum, p. 34. Buxtorf. in Dictionario th. יהוה / Genebr. Præf. in Psalmos, sed nimis mis Ϭινχῶς hac de re suo more differentem, Danaum in scripto contra Genebr. Bezam, annotationibus in Apocal. 1. 4. Ariam Montanum, in libro Josephi (qui extat in apparatu ad Biblia Regia) cap. 1. Scindlerum in Grammat. Alstedium in Lexico Theol. Bellarm. in Grammat. Ebraea & de Christo 1. 7. Erpenium in Grammat. & doctissimum è Gallia Theologum, authorem eruditissimi tractatus de punctorum verâ antiquitate, à Domino Erpenio editi, in oratione ex professo hac re habita & ad calcem operis praedicti adjecta.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Now he bids me seal this discussion with the authority and testimonies of the leading men in Hebrew scholarship. I have indeed often argued this and similar points with many people, who, after grave arguments were evaded by empty sophistry and shameless prevarication, were suddenly struck dumb by the authority of a single theologian. So servile is the disposition of some people. For them a thing is not true because it is true, but because this or that man says it is true. To do that is to swear allegiance not to the truth but to men. So, to gratify these people and to strengthen young men of a more lofty spirit, I bring onto this stage, besides Lyra, Burgensis and Abulensis, and besides the learned Drusius, whose Tetragrammaton I have cited often: Pagninus in his Thesaurus; Mercerus on Genesis 2:4 and 15, and on Amos 3 and 5; Rodericus Antonius Cevallerus, who added to Pagninus' Thesaurus; Scaliger in the notes to the Fragmenta selecta, at the end of his work De emendatione temporum, p. 34; Buxtorf in his Dictionary, under the Tetragrammaton; Genebrardus in his preface to the Psalms, though he differs on this matter in his usual manner, which is rather mocking; Danaeus in his writing against Genebrardus; Beza in his annotations on Revelation 1:4; Arias Montanus, in the book of Josephus (which is found in the apparatus to the Royal Bibles), ch. 1; Schindler in his grammar; Alsted in his Lexicon theologicum; Bellarmine in his Hebrew grammar and in De Christo 1.7; Erpenius in his grammar; and the very learned theologian from France, author of the most erudite treatise on the true antiquity of the points, published by Lord Erpenius, in an oration delivered expressly on this subject and appended to the end of the aforesaid work.

units.la: LXXXVII. Unum illud jam reliquum est, ut Tironi ostendam, quomodo hoc nomen per ADONAI lectum, ejusque interpretamentum Dominus expressum, ab ipso nomine communi ADONAI, ejusque interpretamento possit discerni. Viri docti suadent & sunt qui exemplis praeivere, nomen Dominus cum ϯ πτεραγραμμάτω interpretamentum est, totum majusculis literis scribendum, DOMINUS. Similiter, DEUS, cum in Ebraeo est יהוה Alias satis esse, si Dominus vel Deus scribatur, primâ majusculâ. Ita suadebat Episcopo Elienfi Rod. Ceralerius, cujus super ea re Epistolam Cl. Drusius suo Tetragrammato vulgavit. Hoc observarunt Lutherus (vide eum tom. 8. Jenensi Germ. sol. 146.) & Piscat. in Germ. HERRE Angli in novâ versione, LORD, Et Galli in primâ versione SEIGNEUR. Nam in postremis Editionibus substituerunt vocem l' Eternel; Tigurini in vernacula HERR, & in Latina, DOMINUS. Idem Buxtorsius, Drusius, aliique passim imitati sunt. Quin & Dordracenae Synodi Theologi in nova Bibliorum versione idem ut fieret prudentissime sanxêre. Verba * decreti (si quis ea forte desiderat) ista sunt,
units.tr: LXXXVII. There remains one thing, that I should show the novice how this name, read as *ADONAI* and expressed by its interpretation *Dominus*, can be distinguished from the common name ADONAI and its interpretation. Learned men recommend, and there are those who have led the way by example, that the word *Dominus* when it is the interpretation of the Tetragrammaton [τὸ τετραγράμματον] should be written entirely in capitals: DOMINUS. Similarly DEUS, when the Hebrew is יהוה. Otherwise it is enough to write Dominus or Deus with only an initial capital. Rodericus Cevallerus advised this to the Bishop of Ely, and Drusius published his letter on the matter together with his treatise on the Tetragrammaton. Luther observed this (see him in volume 8 of the Jena German edition, p. 146), as did Piscator in German, HERRE; the English in their new version, LORD; and the French in their first version, SEIGNEUR, though in the latest editions they substituted the word *l'Eternel*; the Tigurines in the vernacular, HERR, and in Latin, DOMINUS. Buxtorf, Drusius and others have imitated this constantly. Indeed the theologians of the Synod of Dort most prudently decreed in the new Bible version that the same should be done. The words of the decree (if anyone happens to want them) are these:

units.la: Secunda quaestio fuit, Quomodo nomen Jehova (ita ex communi consuetudine appellant nomen יהוה) in Veteri Testamento sit transferendum? Verum in Belgico sit retinendum, an vero per vocem Heere, uti hactenus, aut similem exprimendum. At consultum fuit judicatum, cum alia commoda atque usitata vox Belgica non extet qua vis istius nominis exprimatur, ut Interpp. vocem Jehova transferant per vocem Heere; ueque haec vox majusculis literis in textu exprimatur. Vbicunque vero vox Jehova emphasin habere videtur peculiarem, ubi ponendum esse asterisicum, & vocem Jehova in margine adscribendum. Monendos quoque interpretes, ut ubi vox haec habet puncta vocis Elohim, despiciant, an illis locis commodius per vocem GODT, quam per voce HEERE, transferri non possit. Hactenus verba decreti.
units.tr: The second question was, How is the name Jehovah (as it is commonly called, the name יהוה) to be rendered in the Old Testament? Whether it is to be kept in Dutch, or expressed by the word Heere, as hitherto, or by a similar word. But it was judged advisable, since there is no other convenient and customary Dutch word that expresses the force of this name, that the translators should render the word Jehovah by the word Heere, and that this word should be expressed in capitals in the text. Wherever the word Jehovah seems to have a peculiar emphasis, an asterisk should be placed there and the word Jehovah added in the margin. The translators should also be admonished that where this word has the points of the word Elohim, they should consider whether in those places it could not more suitably be rendered by the word GODT than by the word HEERE. So far the words of the decree.

units.la: Atque hic abrumpo telam. Dixi hæc & scripsi cum lege resi-piendi & resiliendi, si quis meliora. Interea sequor, quod ra-tiones claræ & authoritates non contemnendæ mihi jam pridem persuasere. Si & aliis persuasero, bene est: Sin minus, & hoc benè. Eos, qui aliter sentiunt, nec rideo nec tanquam crimi-nis alicujus reos postulo. Illud vicissim ab illis flagito, ne superstitionis Judaicæ maculam iis inurant qui in nominis hujus pronuntiatione, Euangelistas, Apostolos, (qui genuinam non ignorabant) atque universum Patrum chorum imitantur; quos de-nique non sine rationibus à communi via hac in parte diversos abi-re vident. Si quam pudet dedicere, quæ male didicit, & inolitam consuetudinem non vult aut potest deponere, per me licet fruatur ille judicio suo. Legat, quisque prout libuerit. Nulli præscribo. Tantum de incertitudine istius pronuntiationis mo-nui, & illi, cui innutritus ego sum, superstitionis maculam abstergere conatus sum. Hoc autem quam felicirer aut infelici-ter præstiterim, eruditorum esto judicium. Cæterorum censuras securus sinam præterfluere.
units.tr: And here I break off the web. I have said and written these things, subject to the condition that I will retract and recant if anyone offers better. Meanwhile I follow what clear arguments and authorities not to be despised have long ago persuaded me. If I persuade others too, well and good; if not, that is well too. I neither laugh at those who think otherwise nor call them to account as guilty of any crime. In return I ask this of them: that they not brand with the stain of Jewish superstition those who, in pronouncing this name, imitate the Evangelists, the Apostles (who knew the genuine form) and the whole company of the Fathers, and who see that they have departed from the common practice in this matter, not without reasons. If anyone is ashamed to unlearn what he has learned badly, and cannot or will not put aside a custom that has taken root, let him enjoy his own judgment, so far as I am concerned. Let each read as he pleases. I prescribe for no one. I have only pointed out the uncertainty of that pronunciation, and tried to wipe away the stain of superstition from that tradition in which I myself was brought up. How successfully or unsuccessfully I have done this is for the judgment of the learned. The censures of others I will let flow past me without concern.

units.la: Responsio ad ea, quæ Cl. Vir, NICOLAUS FULLERUS, Miscell. lib. 2. cap. 6. & lib. 4. cap. 13. & 14. & ad calcem libri 6. pro nomine JEHOVA disputavit.
units.tr: A reply to the points which the distinguished man NICOLAUS FULLERUS made about the name JEHOVAH in Miscellanies book 2, chapter 6, book 4, chapters 13 and 14, and at the end of book 6.

units.la: Nicolaus Fullerus, vir extra controversiam eruditissimus, Miscell. lib. 2. & 4. multa egregiè de nomine Tetragr. ex priscorum monumentis erura, edisserit. Idem ad calcem Miscellaneorum posteriorum, vid. libris. & 6. in Cl. Drusium apologiam edidit, in quâ ejus sententiam de nomine Tetragr. obi-ter perstringit. Quod attinet ad primam Apologiæ partem, quâ suæ ingenuitatis defensionem parat, eam ego non tango. Nec enim lubet eam controversiam facere ineam. Si Cl. Drusius responsum ejus legisset, aut fallor valde, aut eum sui caloris poenituisset. Ita certe est, In multis labimur omnes, suos quisque patimur manes, sui cuique naevi, optimus ille qui minimis urgetur. Eadem inveniri, & excogitari posse ab iis, qui tempore locisque inter se quàm longissimè distant, res certa & multis experimentis comprobata. Cum Cl. Drusius suam de nomine Elohim sententiam proponeret, putabit se ejus patrem esse. Postea cum eo nomine apud quosdam imperitos male audiret, & tantum non haereseos postularetur, magno suo bono cognovit, idem ante se, Bellar. Calvinum, Danaeum, Cajetanum, ipsumque adeo Alphonsum Tostatum observasse. Ipse Fullerus se primum prodidisse arbitratur, cur mare Suph Erythraeum & Rubrum vocetur, Miscell. 4. cap. ult. & tamen Scaliger ad Festum, voce Aegyptium, Genebr. ad Ps. 106. & Drusius idem ante eum observaverant.
units.tr: Nicolaus Fullerus, a man beyond dispute most learned, in Miscellanies books 2 and 4 sets out at length, and well, much about the Tetragrammaton from the records of the ancients. At the end of the later Miscellanies, in books 5 and 6, he also published an apology against Drusius, in which he touches in passing on Drusius's view of the Tetragrammaton. As for the first part of the Apology, in which he prepares a defence of his own candour, I do not touch it, for I have no wish to enter that dispute. If Drusius had read his reply, I am much mistaken if he would not have regretted his heat. It is indeed so: "We all stumble in many things, each of us bears his own ghosts, each has his own blemishes, and the best man is the one pressed by the smallest." It is a established fact, confirmed by many experiences, that the same things can be found and devised by men who are very far apart in time and place. When Drusius put forward his opinion about the name Elohim, he will have thought he was its father. Later, when he was ill spoken of by some unskilled men for that name, and was almost charged with heresy, he learned to his great benefit that Bellarmine, Calvin, Danaeus, Cajetan, and even Alfonso Tostado had noticed the same before him. Fullerus himself thinks he was the first to explain why the Sea of Suph is called Erythraean and Red, Miscellanies 4, last chapter. Yet Scaliger, on Festus under the word "Aegyptium", Genebrardus on Psalm 106, and Drusius had observed the same before him.

units.la: Αἰκὰ τὰ μὴ προσηλύχθαι ἐάσωμεν, & videamus, quid adversus communem Ebraicè peritorum de nomine Tetragr. sententiam proferat.
units.tr: "Αἰκὰ τὰ μὴ προσηλύχθαι ἐάσωμεν" [Let us leave aside what has come in only by the way], and let us see what he puts forward against the common opinion of those skilled in Hebrew about the Tetragrammaton.

units.la: P. 193. Appendicis Apologeticae ait Drusium conqueri, Anglos Samaritanam lectionem rejicere, quae tamen genuina sit. Ego vero ea verba in Drusio non reperio. Pag. 142. annot. ad loca dissic. Mosis, ut ut sit, inquit Drusius, conjicio hanc (Jave vid. quod dixerat ὡρχαϊκῶς lectum pro יַהְוֶה Jahave & hoc rursus pro יְהוֹוִה) germanam esse lectionem nominis Tetragrammati, non asserit, sed conjicit. Conjecturae suae fulcra petit ab analogia, (putat enim habere formam futuri Cal) & à moribus gentis Samariticae, natio simplex, inquit, & rituum suorum tenacissima eam retinuit. Cur spernimus? Nam & antiquos characteres Ebraeorum eadem conservat, quos Judaei cum Assyriis commutarunt. Alibi veram pronunciationem certò sciri posse negitat: inclinat tamen eò cum Mercero, Aria Montano, & aliis, ut putet ex omnibus lectionibus, quae ex antiquis monumentis virorum doctorum eruit industria, hoc ipsum Jahave vel Jehevé, quod Samaritanis adscribit Theodoretus, ad genuinam lectionem proximè accedere. Quod ergo subjicit Fullerus, Est ubi Drusius quasi redeplorata sic sentiat, cum nomen Tetrag. non habeat proprias vocales, non posse legi suis consonantibus, verum est, sed dextrè accipiendum.
units.tr: At page 193 of the Appendix to the Apology he says that Drusius complains that the English reject the Samaritan reading, which is nevertheless genuine. But I cannot find those words in Drusius. At page 142, in the notes on the difficult places of Moses, Drusius says: "However that may be, I conjecture that this form (Jave, which he had said was read archaically for יַהְוֶה Jahave, and this again for יְהוֹוִה) is the genuine reading of the Tetragrammaton. He does not assert it, but conjectures it. He seeks the supports of his conjecture from analogy (for he thinks it has the form of the future Cal), and from the customs of the Samaritan people. A simple nation, he says, and most tenacious of its rites, has kept it. Why do we despise it? For it also preserves the old characters of the Hebrews, which the Jews exchanged with the Assyrians." Elsewhere he denies that the true pronunciation can be known for certain. Yet he leans with Mercerus, Arias Montanus and others towards thinking that, of all the readings which the industry of learned men has drawn from ancient monuments, this very Jahave or Jehevé, which Theodoret ascribes to the Samaritans, comes nearest to the genuine reading. What Fullerus then adds, that "Drusius at one point, as if giving up the case, judges that since the Tetragrammaton has no proper vowels, it cannot be read with its own consonants", is true, but it must be taken in the right sense.

units.la: In textu enim Biblico non habet proprias vocales adscriptas, ac proinde si quis in legendo ad vocales subjectas respiciat, non potest suis consonantibus legi, sed iisdem consonis, quarum subjectae sunt vocales, quae sunt אלהים / Hæc τὸ μυστικὸν ἐστι mens est.
units.tr: For in the Biblical text it does not have its own vowels attached; therefore if anyone in reading looks to the vowels placed beneath, it cannot be read with its own consonants, but with the same consonants to which those vowels are placed, which are אלהים [Elohim]. "This is τὸ μυστικὸν ἐστι" [the mystical sense], is what is meant.

units.la: Pergit Fullerus, Planissimè ergo efficitur, ut idem ipsum nomen omnino legi nequeat. Unumquodque enim vocabulum si verè legitur, suis, non alienis vocalibus legitur. Resp. Hoc non plane effici. Quid si enim postea genuinæ vocales innotuissent? Eas certe si alienis substituerés, posses vocem suis vocalibus exprimere, E. gr. Jesa. 36. legimus שִׁיגָיוֹם Negabit Fullerus, has vocales esse alienas? Si neget, exprimat mihi has consonas cum subjectis vocalibus. Res manifesta est & docet nos Masora marginalis, esse proprias vocales duarum vocum מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם / Per has ergo consonas vox ea legenda est. Quod si jam eruditus aliquis vir proprias consonarum, quas textus exhibet, vocales nobis erueret, certè per eas legi posset. Duplex ergo in Ebraico textu lectio, una regularis, quâ consonæ cum suis vocalibus exprimuntur, altera irregularis & necessitatis, quâ consonæ, quarum propriæ vocales ignorantur, per alienas, quas in textu subjectas videmus, proferuntur.
units.tr: Fullerus goes on: "It is therefore quite clearly the case that this very name cannot be read at all. For every word, if it is truly read, is read with its own vowels, not with alien ones." Reply: this is not plainly the case. For what if the genuine vowels should later become known? If you substituted them for the alien ones, you could then express the word with its own vowels. For example, at Isaiah 36 we read שִׁיגָיוֹם. Will Fullerus deny that these vowels are alien? If he denies it, let him express for me these consonants with the vowels placed beneath them. The matter is manifest, and the marginal Masorah teaches us that the words מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם have their own vowels; through these consonants the word is therefore to be read. But if some learned man were now to bring out for us the proper vowels of the consonants which the text presents, then certainly it could be read through them. Therefore there is a twofold reading in the Hebrew text: one regular, in which the consonants are expressed with their own vowels; the other irregular and of necessity, in which the consonants, whose proper vowels are unknown, are pronounced through the alien vowels which we see placed beneath them in the text.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Atqui, inquiet Drusius, à Samaritanis didicimus sanctissimi istius nominis vocales, quibus enucleatè pronuncietur.
units.tr: Yet, Drusius will say, we have learned from the Samaritans the vowels of that most holy name, by which it may be pronounced clearly.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Vellem ee formalia Drusii verba produxisse, vel paginam & librum citasse, ubi hæc dixerit. Ego certe in ejus libris ejusmodi nihil lego. Conjicit eorum pronunciationem esse genuinam pag. 162. & non spernendam esse dicit pag. 136. comm. ad loca difficiliora Pentateuchi.
units.tr: I wish you had quoted Drusius's own words, or cited the book and page where he said this. For my part, I certainly find nothing of the kind in his books. He conjectures at p. 162 that their pronunciation is genuine, and at p. 136 of his commentary on the more difficult passages of the Pentateuch he says it is not to be despised.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Nobis verò nefas est (in rebus præsertim sacris) Samaritarum esse discipulis, ut qui à summo Magistro luculenter didicerimus, Samaritanos adorare quod nesciunt, & salutem ex Iudaeis esse.
units.tr: But it is wrong for us (especially in sacred matters) to become disciples of the Samaritans, since we have learned plainly from the supreme Teacher that the Samaritans worship what they do not know, and salvation is of the Jews.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Neque hoc vult Drusius. Lectionem tantùm, quae apud Samaritas remansisse dicitur, Grammaticae magis analogam esse vult, quàm ea quae Judaeis adscribitur, vid. Jao, vel Javo, hoc enim sic scribendum esset יְהוָה cum nullum extet exemplum futuri 2. Kal ordinis quiescentium Lamed He in Holem desinentis. Nisi quis fortè illud per (-) expresserit, ut solent ordines נִצָא & גלה confundi, יְהָוָה Iahava, contractè Iava vel Iaā, & A in o ex dialecto Syriaca mutato, Iao. Quod verò ad loca Scripturae, quae allegas, attinet, non video quid efficias. Samaritani adorant quod nesciunt. Potuerunt tamen verum Dei veri nomen retinuisse. Gentiles, te judice, habuerunt; dum cum Iovis appellarunt in casu recto, & tamen adorarunt quod nesciebant. Salus ex Judaeis est, sed quid hoc ad lectionem τὸ πτεσγεγεμμάτα; in qua salutem consistere, nunquam opinor, fateberis.
units.tr: Nor does Drusius mean this. He only holds that the reading said to have survived among the Samaritans is more consistent with grammar than the one ascribed to the Jews, namely Jao or Javo. For it would have to be written thus, יְהוָה, since there is no example of the future of the second Kal in the class of verbs with Lamed He that end in Holem. Unless perhaps someone has expressed it with (-), since the classes נִצָא and גלה are commonly confused: יְהָוָה Iahava, contracted to Iava or Iaā, and with the A changed to o under the influence of the Syriac dialect, Iao. As for the passages of Scripture you cite, I do not see what you achieve. The Samaritans worship what they do not know. They could nevertheless have kept the true name of the true God. In your judgement the Gentiles had it too, when they called him Jove in the nominative case, and yet worshipped what they did not know. Salvation is of the Jews, but what does this have to do with the reading τὸ τετραγράμματον? I do not think you will ever say that salvation consists in that.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Deinde ex Apostolo, ut * ante hac observavimus, constat, non Samaritanis sed Judaeis concredita esse Dei eloquia. Igitur ab his, non illis petenda.
units.tr: Next, from the Apostle, as we observed before, it is clear that the oracles of God were entrusted not to the Samaritans but to the Jews. Therefore they are to be sought from these, not from those.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: At nondum probasti ullo ἀξιοπίστῳ testimonio, veterum Judaeorum pronunciationem à Samaritanâ fuisse diversam. Judaeis concredita sunt Dei eloquia. Quid tum? Ergone nulla superstitionis vestigia in sacro Codice reliquerunt? Ergo literas majusculas, minusculas, inversas, voces extra ordinem apicibus notatas, easque lectionum varietates quae circa voces, quas obscoenas vocant, versantur, ipsis Scriptoribus adscribes? Nunquid satis est, quod Canonem, prout acceperunt, integrum ne minimâ quidem literulâ de industria corruptum vel auctum vel diminutum, ad nos transmiserint? Sicubi in vocalibus signandis sibi plusculum indulsère, in eo non peccasse se arbitrati sunt, cum textum vocalibus nudum à Prophetis accepissent, eaque omnia, non citra religionem in excessu peccantem, eò tenderent, ne in textu & consonantium linea vel literam unam inutarent, adderent, vel detraherent, etiam ubi manifestum erat sphalma, sicuti in * Dissertatione nostrâ de Keri & Chetib ostendimus. Concredita illis fuerunt elogia Dei, & tanquam fideles capsarii & librarii ea nobis tradidêre. Sed an inde colliges; omnia quæ majores eorum noverant, posteriores quoque memoria suâ conservasse? Nullo modo. Calamitates, exilia, persecutiones & posteriorum quoque discordia multa obliteravêre. Ut enim de quamplurimis aliiquè taceam, quis posteriorum Judæorum docere nos potuit, quid fuerint Vrim & Thummim, quomodo responsa sua per ea dederit Deus, Quis potuit nos docere veram notionem vocis Sela? Quis interpretari potuit tot Psalmorum titulos? Quis edisserere potuit, quæ fuerint propriæ vocales vocis שינאהם Jesa 36. nihil tamen detraxerunt Scripturæ, dum alienas substituêre: proprias enim Esaias non adscripsit, sed per traditiones alter ab altero didicit, usque dum profunda eas sepelivit oblivio. Atque idem fuisse propriarum Tetragrammati vocalium fatum supra ostendimus. Sed dicit Fullerus, à Judæis petendam veram pronunciationem hujus nominis.. Qnænam vero est ista? IωЀα, Miscel.2.6. A qua mihi certè religio est discedere inquit, siquidem cum Judæis non cum Samaritanis in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coaluimus. Sed unde eruis nobis illud IωЀα? Ex Epiphanio adversus Hæreses lib.1. Tom.4. At ille habet IωЀὲ non IωЀα. Provoco ad omnia exemplaria.
units.tr: But you have not yet proved by any trustworthy testimony (ἀξιοπίστῳ) that the pronunciation of the ancient Jews differed from that of the Samaritans. The oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews. So what? Did they leave no traces of superstition in the sacred Codex? Will you attribute to the writers themselves the large and small letters, the inverted letters, the words marked with dots outside the normal order, and those variant readings that concern words they call obscene? Is it not enough that they handed down to us the canon, as they received it, whole, not corrupted, added to, or diminished by so much as a tiny letter on purpose? Wherever they indulged themselves somewhat in marking the vowels, they did not think they had sinned in this, since they had received the text from the Prophets without vowels. All of this aimed, in a scrupulous way that never erred by excess, at not changing, adding, or removing a single letter in the text or the line of consonants, even where the error was obvious, as we showed in our dissertation on Keri and Chetib. The oracles of God were entrusted to them, and like faithful keepers of a chest and copyists they handed them down to us. But will you conclude from this that the later Jews preserved by their own memory everything their ancestors knew? By no means. Calamities, exiles, persecutions, and the discord of later generations have wiped out much. For, to say nothing of very many other things, who among the later Jews could teach us what the Urim and Thummim were, or how God gave his answers through them? Who could teach us the true meaning of the word Selah? Who could interpret so many titles of the Psalms? Who could explain what the proper vowels of the word שינאהם were (Isa. 36)? Yet they took nothing away from Scripture while substituting alien vowels, for Isaiah did not write the proper ones; they were learned by one from another by tradition, until deep oblivion buried them. And we have shown above that the proper vowels of the Tetragrammaton met the same fate. But Fullerus says that the true pronunciation of this name must be sought from the Jews. What then is it? Iōa [Ἰωά]? Miscellanies 2.6: From this I am certainly bound in conscience not to depart, he says, since we have joined the body of the Church with the Jews, not with the Samaritans. But where do you dig up that Iōa for us? From Epiphanius, Against Heresies, book 1, vol. 4. But he has Iōē [Ἰωὲ], not Iōa. I challenge you to produce every copy.

units.la: FUL- LERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Sed corruptum proculdubio à librariis. Crediderim ab initio scriptum fuisse IωЀα. Mutatio autem deinceps ω in ε proclivis additum erat, propter magnam harum literarum similitudinem, sitū tantummodo, non figura (ω, ε) discrepantium. Et syllabarum literarumque transpositionem creberrimam experimur. Atque hoc pacto pro vitiata voce IωЀε, quàm emendatissima nobis restituetur IωЀα.
units.tr: But it has doubtless been corrupted by the copyists. I would believe that it was originally written as Iaœa. Later, through the easy change of ω into ε, which was added because these letters are very similar, differing only in position and not in shape (ω, ε), the word became corrupt. We also see very frequent transposition of syllables and letters. In this way, from the corrupted word Iaœe, the most correct form Iaœa will be restored to us.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Hæc conjectanea tantum sunt, quæ eadem facilitate negari possunt, quâ tu affirmas. Haberent ea majus pondus si vel unius codicis authoritate niterentur. Si item illud Iaœ nusquam alibi occurreret. Dum verò hoc passim occurrit, illud verò, quod tu substituis, nusquam, ignosce, vir eruditissime, si hanc tuam crisin non admittimus. Aut alias profer rationes, cur admittendam eam censeas.
units.tr: These are mere conjectures, which can be denied as easily as you affirm them. They would carry more weight if they rested on the authority of even a single manuscript, and if that Iaœ did not occur anywhere else. But since it occurs everywhere, while the form you substitute occurs nowhere, pardon me, most learned sir, if we do not admit your emendation. Either bring other reasons why you think it should be admitted.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Eam si admiserimus, consulemus existimationi doctissimi Patris, lingua etiam Ebraea non ignari: Sin minus, quid tandem fiet vocabulo Iaœ? Ad nullum enim aliud ex omnibus apud Ebraeos attributis divinis illa ratione reduci poterit.
units.tr: If we admit it, we shall be consulting the reputation of a most learned Father, who was not unacquainted with the Hebrew language. But if not, what on earth will become of the word Iaœ? For by that method it cannot be traced back to any other of the divine attributes among the Hebrews.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Rogas quid futurum sit vocabulo Iaœ? Respondeo habere formam futuri Kal, ut pleraque nomina propria a Jod Hëemantico incipientia, יצחק, יעקב &c. Eritque Ebraeum יהוה ut יעשה vel יהוה ut יהוה. Jam vero, E. & ɔ. sæpe permutari & v connam a Græcis passim per β efferri, non negabis. Elisionem denique ipsius ה ipse passim inculcas & in tuo Iaœ ostendis. Sed redeamus ad Apologeticam tuam appendicem & isti lineæ porro insistamus.
units.tr: You ask what will become of the word Iaœ? I reply that it has the form of the future of Kal, as most proper names beginning with the Hebrew yod do, יצחק, יעקב, and so on. The Hebrew will be Yehovah, as yaʿaseh, or Yehovah as Yehovah. Now, you will not deny that E and O are often interchanged, that the letter V is often rendered by the Greeks as B. Finally, you yourself repeatedly insist on the elision of the letter ה (he) and show it in your Iaœ. But let us return to your Apologetic appendix and keep pressing that line of argument.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Quod si testimonium Samaritanorum valeat ad confirmationem lectionis Jahave sive Jave, qui sunt Gentiles, impuri, cur non æque reliquos Gentiles, multò etiam antiquiores advocemus ad asserendam pronunciationem Jehovah sive Jehovih? Quid enim est aliud Jovis, veteribus Latinorum nominativus, quàm nomen Jehovi contractum? [Eadem habet Misc. 2.6.]
units.tr: If the testimony of the Samaritans carries weight for confirming the reading Jahave or Jave, though they are Gentiles and unclean, why do we not equally call upon the other Gentiles, far more ancient, to establish the pronunciation Jehovah or Jehovih? For what else is Jovis, the nominative of the ancient Latins, than the name Jehovi contracted? The same is in Misc. 2.6.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Si Gentiles dæmoniorum suorum patrem Jovem vocassent, gravius quatefecisset me hoc argumentum. Vox enim Jehovi nihili est, ac proinde ab iis quoque qui lectionem Jehova defensum ivêre, rejecta. Qua de re diximus supra §.74. quæ non libet iterare. Si vox Jehova veteribus inaudita fuit, an putabimus vocem Jehovi fuisse pervulgatam? Sic ergo dico, Si Gentiles suum illum dæmoniorum principem Jovam vocassent, probabilior fuisset ejus ab Ebræo derivatio. A Jova enim per crasin sic dicto pro Jehova (ut Juda pro Jehuda) fuisset Jovas, Jova, ut à Juda, Judas, nunc verò, quid omne illud quod hic à Marino, Castalione & Fullero adfertur, aliud est, quam inanis quadam conjectura, inquit author Diatribæ de vocalium antiquitate, non alio fulta fundamento, quàm vano præconcepta opinionis præjudicio? Nam quomodo probabunt hoc suum etymon, si negetur? Hæc ille. Cur non manemus intra pomœria linguæ Latinæ & Jovem à juvando deducimus? At dices tunc Juvem dicendum fuisse. Respondeo, o & u sibi invicem succedere, quæ sunt formalia tua verba, Fullere, Misc. 2.6. p. 211. Quibus addo insigne testimonium Priscian, qui lib.1. sic inquit u quoque multis Italiæ populis in usu non erat, sed è contrario utebantur O. Unde Romanorum quoque vetustissimi in multis dictionibus loco ejus o posuere. publicum pro publicum, quod testatur Papyrianus de Orthographia, polcrum pro pulcrum, colpam pro culpam, Hercolem pro Heculem, servos pro servus, volgus &c. Quintil. lip.1.6. o & u permutata invicem, ut notrix, dederont, probaverunt. Adhac non facile mihi persuaserim, inquit idem author Diatribes, Deum voluisse eò usque laxare Satanæ habenas, ut sacrosanctum illud nomen, quod in Scriptura Dei est proprium, Apostata ille sibi usurpaverit. Sed esto, demus, inquit, Jovem à Tetragrammato derivatum, an propterea sequetur ceva, Holem & Camets esse propria. Tetragrammati puncta? An in Jovis est Kamets? Annon poterunt voces illæ Iovis, Iaö, Ievo, Iabe, ab eo duci, etsi aliis prolato vocalibus? Quis nescit in deducendis ab una lingua in aliam vocibus, nullam pene haberi vocalium rationem, utpote quæ promiscuè invicem nullo negotio permutentur, sed duntaxat consonantium, quæ sunt magis constantes & immutabiles? Tetragrammati lectio olim fuit varia, alii Iavo, alii Ievo, alii Iave, alii aliter legerunt & expresserunt. Fuerit aliquis, qui, forte fortuna, Iova vel Iovi legerit, an inde sequetur, eam genuinam vocis lectionem fuisse? An ergo Romanorum Iovis magis idoneum erit eruendae verae & germanae lectioni, quam & Patrum Samaritanorum Iao & Ievo? Quidam Graecarum literarum affinitate decepti יהור[?] PI Pl ΠΙΠΙ legerunt, Quod si hinc aliquis Pipum vel Pipem fecisset, an ideo eam vocis controversiae genuinam lectionem fuisse asseReres? Sed bene habet, quod ipse Fullerus se hoc argumento non niti profitetur.
units.tr: If the Gentiles had called the father of their demons Jove, this argument would have shaken me more severely. The word Jehovi is nothing, and so it has been rejected even by those who undertook to defend the reading Jehova. On this point I said above in §.74. what I do not wish to repeat. If the word Jehova was unknown to the ancients, shall we think the word Jehovi was widely known? So I say: if the Gentiles had called their chief of demons Jova, its derivation from the Hebrew would be more probable. For from Jova, by contraction for Jehova (as Juda for Jehuda), would come Jovas, Jova, just as Judas comes from Juda. But as it is, all that which is brought forward here by Marino, Castalio & Fuller is nothing but an empty conjecture, says the author of the Diatribe on the antiquity of the vowels, supported by no other foundation than the empty prejudice of a preconceived opinion. For how will they prove this their etymology, if it is denied? So he says. Why do we not remain within the bounds of the Latin language and derive Jovem from juvando? But you will say that it ought then to have been Juvem. I answer that o and u succeed one another, which are your own words, Fuller, Misc. 2.6, p. 211. To these I add the notable testimony of Priscian, who in book 1 says: u was also not in use among many peoples of Italy; on the contrary they used o. Whence the most ancient Romans too, in many words, put o in its place. They wrote publicum for poplicum, which Papyrianus attests in his work on orthography; polcrum for pulcrum, colpam for culpam, Hercolem for Hercules, servos for servus, volgus and so on. Quintilian, book 1, chapter 6: o and u were interchanged, as in notrix and dederont, and they approved it. Moreover, I could not easily persuade myself, says the same author of the Diatribe, that God would have let Satan's reins loose so far that that most sacred name, which in Scripture is proper to God, should have been usurped by that apostate. But grant, he says, that Jove is derived from the Tetragrammaton: does it follow that sheva, holem and qamets are its proper points? Is there a qamets in Jove? Can those words Iovis, Iaö, Ievo, Iabe not be derived from it, even though they are pronounced with other vowels? Who does not know that in deriving words from one language into another almost no account is taken of the vowels, since they are changed interchangeably without any difficulty, whereas the consonants alone, which are more constant and unchanging, are regarded? The reading of the Tetragrammaton was once various: some read Iavo, some Ievo, some Iave, others read and expressed it otherwise. Suppose someone, by chance, read Iova or Iovi: would it follow that this was the genuine reading of the word? Will the Roman Iovis then be more suitable for recovering the true and genuine reading than the Samaritans' Iao and Ievo, or the Fathers' readings? Some, deceived by the affinity of the Greek letters, read יהור as PI, Pl, ΠΙΠΙ. If anyone from this had made it Pipum or Pipem, would you assert that this was the genuine reading in the controversy about the word? But it is well that Fuller himself professes that he does not rest on this argument.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Haec & alia in Miscell. supra commemoravimus, licet valde probabilia sint ac diluda, nos tamen Gentilium testimoniis non nitimur, sed omnino divinitus revelatis, & in utroque testamento perspicue consignatis. Siquidem in S. literis ubique 4. consonantes nominis Tetragr. Iod, He, Vau, He, tres has vocales habent, E, O, A, quibus clare & explicate proseritur vox IEHOVA. Igitur IEHOVA, genuinam lectionem & pronunciationem esse ex animo credimus & profitemur.
units.tr: We have mentioned these and other things above in the Miscellanea. Although they are very probable and clear, we do not rest on the testimonies of the Gentiles, but on what has been wholly revealed by God and plainly set down in both Testaments. For in the Holy Scriptures everywhere the four consonants of the Tetragrammaton, Iod, He, Vau, He, have these three vowels, E, O, A, by which the word IEHOVA is clearly and plainly pronounced. Therefore we believe and profess from our heart that IEHOVA is the genuine reading and pronunciation.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: I Non exagitabo illud, quod Sieva vocalem appelles, quandoquidem ea catechresis apud Grammaticos frequens est. II. Quod dicis ubique, cornua tibi obvertunt ista, יְהוָה בִיהוָה / לִיהוָה III. Ajo, te hic principium petere. Nam tria illa puncta, Sjeva; Holem, i Camets, eo fine consonis יהור subjecta esse, ut cum iis in unam vocem coalescant ego audaciter nego.
units.tr: I will not quarrel with your calling the sheva a vowel, since that misuse is common among the grammarians. II. What you say, everywhere, turns the horns against you: [יְהוָה בִיהוָה / לִיהוָה] (Yehovah, beYehovah, liYehovah). III. I say that you are begging the question here. For I boldly deny that those three marks, sheva, holem and qamets, are attached to the consonants יהור so that they might coalesce with them into one word.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Negant autem superstitiosi Judaei, Drusius itidem, aliique Christiani nonnulli, qui illorum traditionem mordicus tenent, has tetragrammati proprias esse vocales, sed prorsus alienas, & ad nomen Adonai peculiariter spectare vehementer contendunt.
units.tr: But the superstitious Jews deny, and Drusius likewise, and some other Christians who cling stubbornly to their tradition, that these are the proper vowels of the Tetragrammaton, but that they are wholly foreign to it and belong peculiarly to the name Adonai they strongly maintain.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Superstitiosos Judæos non moramur. Illi hanc controversiam non intelligunt. Doctissimi illorum qui hodie vivunt, de punctis nomini subjectis controverti ignorant, ex purâ putâ superstitione ejus pronunciationem fugientes. Drusium verò, aliosque Christianos non superstitio, non Traditio, sed gravissimæ rationes, quarum tu nullum confutasti, movent, ut sic statuant. Cur verò eos non nominas, aut saltem elogio quodam honestiori ornas? Posset enim imperitior aliquis titulum illum superstitiosi ex præcedentibus Ἀσπ κοινὴ repetere, cui errori occurrisses, si ita dixisses Drusius itidem, alique Christiani nonnulli viri Ebraicè peritissimi ac in sua professione Principes. Hoc enim & amplius merebantur præter Drusium, Scaliger, Buxtorfius, Mercerus, Arias Montanus, Erpenius, Schindlerus & alii.
units.tr: I will not dwell on the superstitious Jews: they do not understand this controversy. The most learned of them who live today are ignorant of any dispute about the points attached to the name; out of pure superstition they avoid pronouncing it. But Drusius and other Christians are moved to this view not by superstition or tradition but by the weightiest reasons, none of which you have refuted. Why then do you not name them, or at least adorn them with some more honourable epithet? A less experienced reader might take that title superstitious to be carried over [ἀπὸ κοινοῦ] from the preceding words, and you would have prevented this error by saying Drusius likewise, and some other Christians, men most skilled in Hebrew and princes in their profession. For they deserved this and more, besides Drusius, Scaliger, Buxtorf, Mercer, Arias Montanus, Erpenius, Schindler and others.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLER.

units.la: Quasi dicant, sunt vocales nominis Adonai. Ergo non tetragrammati. Frigidum certè argumentum & pene dicam ridiculum. Quasi verò nomina diversissima non possint, nec subinde soleant iisdem efferri vocalibus. Nihil fere notius opinor. Quocirca utcunque sint propria nominis Adonai, tamen Tetragrammati pariter non desinunt esse propria.
units.tr: They say, as it were, these are the vowels of the name Adonai. Therefore not of the Tetragrammaton. A cold argument, and I might almost say a ridiculous one. As if entirely different names could not, and did not often, take the same vowels. I think nothing is better known. Therefore, however they may be proper to the name Adonai, they nonetheless remain proper to the Tetragrammaton as well.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Utinam clarius mentem tum edisseruisses! Diversa nomina iisdem vocalibus posse efferri, quis adeo impudens, qui ausit negare? At hæc duo nomina יהוה & ארני iisdem vocalibus afferri, non satis erat dicere, sed & respondendum erat ad argumenta, quibus Drusius & alii evicère, vocales istas, quæ hodierna punctatio exhibet, non posse esse Tetragrammati proprias. Si enim çeva, Holem, Camets propria sunt τὰ πεγγεμματα ἐνομαῖ puncta, cur ergo ea mutat in (∵) Holem & Hirik, sequente vel antecedente ipso Adonai, & quidem solo hoc casu, sine nulla ullius loci exceptione? An hæc quoque puncta communia habet cum ארני / vel potius cum nomine אלהים? Cur ergo in constructione cum literis מוכלב per omnia punctationem ׳ארני imitatur, dum illæ non solum ejusmodi afficiuntur vocalibus, quas Grammatica ante nomen à litera gutturali & hateph phathach incipiens requirit, sed & litera Jod suum scheva vel retinet vel abjicit, plane ut א vocis Adonai suum hateph phathach. Hæc tibi diluenda fuerant, Fullere. Quamvis nesciam an hoc velis, תְּהוָה cum à Syntaxi literarum syntacticarum liberum est, proprias: cum vero literas syntacticas, vel ipsum ארני ante se habet, alienas habere vocales. Certe dubitandi causam mihi suggerit altum tuum de rationibus istis silentium, quas à sententiæ nostræ Patronis præcipuè urgeri non poteras ignorare. Eadem Piscatoris fuit sententia, ad quam cum supra §.82. responderimus, hic verbum non addam. Porro nudum illud יהוה quod attinet, quomodo defendes, scheva, Holem & Kamets utriusque nominis proprias esse vocales? An ergo scheva syllabam incoans indifferens est ad literam Jod & Aleph? At non ignoras literas gutturales tale Scheva in universum respuere. Si dixeris, scheva sub Jod vices ־ : obire, & olim prolatum fuisse per A, vide annon potius JAHOVA legendum sit. Si dixeris, ־: sub א vices obire ׃ scheva simplicis, quia ex classe gutturalium est, rogabo, cur non potius retinendo eidem sono (::) subjecerint ארני/. Quicquid dixeris, (fateor enim alia insuper dici posse) magnum robur addes ad responsionem nostram, qua supra in dissertatione §.84 primarium adversæ sententiæ patronorum argumentum diluimus. Sed videamus, quibus rationibus evincere satagas, çeva, Holem & Kamets proprias יהוה esse vocales.
units.tr: I wish you had explained your meaning more clearly then! Who is so shameless as to deny that different names can be pronounced with the same vowels? But these two names, יהוה and ארני, are given the same vowels, and it was not enough merely to say so. You also had to answer the arguments by which Drusius and others have shown that the vowels which the present pointing gives cannot be proper to the Tetragrammaton. For if the sheva, holem and qamets are proper to the points of the name, why does the name change them into holem and hiriq, depending on whether Adonai comes before or after, and that only in this case, with no exception in any place? Or do these points also share with ארני, or rather with the name אלהים, a common form?
