Why, in construction with the prefixed letters, does it imitate the pointing of ׳ארני in every respect, since those letters are affected not only by the vowels which grammar requires before a word beginning with a guttural letter and hateph patah, but also by the letter Jod, which either keeps or drops its sheva, just as the א of the word Adonai keeps its hateph patah? These points should have been refuted for you, Fuller. Although I do not know whether you wish to claim that תְּהוָה is proper when it stands free of the syntactic letters, but has foreign vowels when the syntactic letters, or ארני itself, stand before it. Certainly your deep silence about those arguments, which the defenders of our view press especially hard, suggests to me a reason to doubt. You could not have been unaware of them. The opinion of Piscator was the same, and since I answered it above at §82, I will not add a word here. Further, as for the bare יהוה, how will you defend the claim that sheva, holem and qamets are proper vowels of both names? Is the sheva that begins the syllable indifferent to the letters Jod and Aleph? But you know that guttural letters generally reject such a sheva. If you say that the sheva under Jod takes the place of a patah and was once pronounced as A, see whether the name should not rather be read JAHOVA. If you say that the sheva under א takes the place of a simple sheva, because it belongs to the class of gutturals, I will ask why they did not rather keep the same sound and attach it to ארני. Whatever you say (for I admit other things may be said as well), you will add great strength to our reply, by which above, in the dissertation at §84, we refuted the chief argument of the defenders of the opposing view. But let us see by what reasons you strive to prove that sheva, holem and qamets are proper vowels of יהוה.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Ex tribus illis vocalibus, duas primas vid. E. & O. Tetragrammati genuinas esse, evincitur, si paulo attentius considerabimus nomina propria, quæ ex Tetragrammati parte priore & potiore composita passim occurrunt: qualia sunt Jehonathan, id est Jehova nathan. Jehoram, Jehova ram: Jehoschaphat, id est Jehova schaphat, cateraque consimilia permulta. Hic nemo, ut equidem opinor, legendum aut pronuntiandum censuerit Adonathan, Adoram Adoschaphat, &c. quoniam E. & O. proprias nominis compositi vocales existimat.
units.tr: From those three vowels, it is shown that the first two, E and O, of the Tetragrammaton are genuine, if we consider a little more carefully the proper names that occur frequently, composed from the first and principal part of the Tetragrammaton, such as Jehonathan, that is Jehovah nathan. Jehoram, Jehovah ram; Jehoshaphat, that is Jehovah shaphat, and very many other similar ones. Here no one, as I think, would have judged that one should read or pronounce Adonathan, Adoram, Adoshaphat, etc., since he holds that E and O are the proper vowels of the compounded name.

units.la: Simile Sin autem partis in compositione propria sunt, cur non itidem totius extra compositionem, cum idem utrobique inviolabile nomen existat, illic secundum partem, hic secundum totum.
units.tr: But if the vowels of the part are proper in composition, why not likewise those of the whole outside composition, since the same inviolable name exists in both cases: there according to the part, here according to the whole.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Hæc quæ profers nomina ex Tetragrammato composita esse alius fortassis negaret, quem equidem convincere solida probatione ullâ vix possem. Quid enim? An authoritatem Patrum objicerem, queis יְהוֹשׁוּעַ est Iaû σωτηρία, Domini salus? At præterquam quod illi in interpretandis nominibus propriis sæpe miserabiliter impegêre, hujus nominis interpretationem ipse neutiquam admitterem, siquidem à pervulgato themate ישע ilud derivaveris. Tunc enim Holem non יְהוֹ / sed erit indicium primæ thematis Jod, ה vero epenticum, ut in יְהוֹסֵף ipsumque Jod hemanticum censebitur. Alia erit rei facies, si ab inusitato שׁוּעַ quod idem cum ישׁע significaverit (plane ut טוֹב & טב & plurima alia) unde arcessendum quoque videtur תְּשׁוּעָה salus, vocem illam deflexeris. Sed quod ad illa quæ Fullerus producit, attinet, non infitebor ea ex Tetragrammato esse composita. Nec tamen conficiunt illud quod Castalio vult. Illius enim hoc argumentum est, ut illud de stercutio Gentilium Jove. Hoc Hoc quæso adverte Lector, rara esse illa Jehonathan, Jehosciaphat, Jehoram, &c. Frequentissima contrà, Jonathan, Josaphat, Joram, quomodo Jeremiæ 23.6. etiam reperitur Ιωσιδεκ, quæ ipsa vox mihi manum injicit, ut confitear, prædicta illa nomina ex Tetragrammato primam accepisse syllabam. Respondet quippe ea duabus Ebraicis, יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ / Sed quid hæc omnia lectioni magis Jehova, quàm alteri illi Jao, cujus Græci Theologi in horum nominum etymologia meminerunt, patrocinantur? Ex Jaó enim non inusitatâ * crasi fit Jo. Sed urgebis illud Jeho, indeque per crasin dicets existere Jo. Ego contrà pertendo, verisimilius esse, ut ex Jao factum sit, Jo, ac ex hoc rursus per Epenthesi literæ ה / natum sit יְהוֹ / cujus Epentheseos manifesta habes exempla in יְהוֹשׁוּעַ salvabit, pro יֵשׁוּעַ pf.116.6. יְהוֹדָה pro יוֹדָה Neh.11.17. Jehosceph pro Joseph Pf.81.6. & aliis. Huic ergo lectioni Jao tam patrocinatur illa compositio, quàm isti controversæ Jehova.
units.tr: Someone might perhaps deny that these names are compounded from the Tetragrammaton, and I could scarcely refute him by any solid proof. What then? Should I object the authority of the Fathers, for whom Yehoshua means Iaû sōtēria [Iaû σωτηρία], "the salvation of the Lord"? But apart from the fact that they often blundered miserably in interpreting proper names, I would not accept this interpretation of the name myself, if you derive it from the commonly known root yasha [ישע]. For then the holem would not mark Yeho-; it would be the sign of the first radical yod, the he would be epenthetic, as in Yehosef, and the yod itself would count as a hemantic letter. The case would be different if you derived the word from the unusual shua [שׁוּעַ], which has the same meaning as yasha (just as tov and tav and many others do), and from which the noun teshuah [תְּשׁוּעָה], "salvation", also seems rightly to be derived. As for what Fuller brings forward, I will not deny that those names are compounded from the Tetragrammaton. Yet they do not establish what Castalio wants. His argument is like the one about the dung of the Gentiles' Jove. Please note this, reader: the forms Jehonathan, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and so on are rare. On the contrary, Jonathan, Josaphat, Joram are very frequent, and in Jeremiah 23.6 the form Iōsidek [Ιωσιδεκ] is also found. This very form compels me to admit that the names I mentioned took their first syllable from the Tetragrammaton. It corresponds to the two Hebrew words Yehovah tsidqenu [יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ]. But why do all these considerations favour the reading Jehovah more than that other reading, Jao, which the Greek theologians mention in the etymology of these names? From Jao, by a not unusual crasis, comes Jo. You will press the form Jeho and say that Jo arises from it by crasis. I, on the contrary, maintain that it is more probable that Jo was formed from Jao, and that from this in turn, by the epenthesis of the letter he, came Yeho [יְהוֹ]. Clear examples of this epenthesis are Yehoshua for yeshua, "he will save" (Ps. 116.6), Yehuda for Yuda (Neh. 11.17), Jehosceph for Joseph (Ps. 81.6), and others. So this composition supports the reading Jao just as much as the disputed reading Jehovah does.

units.la: * Ν Χ. hæc crasis, Iao Io, eam se potest, nuncti, quam Fulleri, Iehova, Iah, ride seq.
units.tr: * Ν Χ. This crasis, Iao into Io, is as much to be considered as Fuller's Iehova and Iah; I laugh at what follows.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: FULLERUS.

units.la: Ultimam verò vocalem A, sive Kamets, peculiarem Tetragrammati esse, vel ex ipso nomine Adonai satis liquere poterit. Etenim ubi nomen illud humanum est, cum Phathachid est A brevi, in syllaba postrema scribitur uti Grammatices etiam ratio postulat. Vbi autem divinum est, cum Camets, idque contra analogiam Grammaticam. Cedo causam. nimirum ut nomini Tetragrammato exprimendo apte congruat & conveniat. Quod si igitur Camets seu A longum nomini Adonai, quanquam alieno loco, supponitur propter Tetragrammaton; sane multò magis, loco nativo vereque suo eidem ipsi Tetragrammato subjiciatur necesse est propter se. Rursus, cum Camets nomen Adonai humanum à divino distinguat, consentaneum videtur, ut vocalis illa nominis absolutè divini, nempe Jehova, propria sit, ideoque distinguat.
units.tr: That the final vowel A, or Kamets, is peculiar to the Tetragrammaton can be made clear enough from the name Adonai itself. For when that name is human, it has Pathach, the A is short, and it is written in the last syllable, as the rule of grammar also requires. But when it is divine, it has Kamets, and this is contrary to grammatical analogy. I ask the reason. Surely it is so that the vowel may fittingly agree with and suit the expression of the Tetragrammaton. If then the long A, Kamets, is placed under the name Adonai, though in a foreign position, for the sake of the Tetragrammaton, then certainly much more must it be placed under the Tetragrammaton itself, in its native and true position, for its own sake. Again, since Kamets distinguishes the human name Adonai from the divine, it seems consistent that this vowel should belong to the name that is absolutely divine, namely Jehovah, and so distinguish it.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Iterum miror, te nullam anatomen alterius istius punctationis יְהוִֹה instituere. Cæterum universus hic discursus nititur hypothesi planè controversa, vid τὰ πεταγεγμένα & nominis Adonai easdem esse vocales. Id supra quoque asserebas, sed nos, quia non probabas ullo argumento, eadem facilitate rejiciebamus. Illud nunc insuper addis, non minus ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ κείμενον, vocem אֲרֹנִי cum Deo tribuitur, notari vocali (ˉ) sub Nun, hanc ob causam, ut nomini Tetragrammato exprimendo apte congrueret. Atqui sufficere tibi debuisset vel sola διάκειμα. Certè non aliâ de causâ אֲרֹנִי cum Deo tribuitur, habet (–) quàm διακείσθαι caussâ. Nec ignoras, illam unicam multas anomalias in Grammaticam Ebr. invexisse. Sic אֶחָל / יֶחָל cum (–) profanabo, אֶחָל יֶחָל incipiam. Nulla certe pagina est in Gramm. quæ similia non suppeditet. Pergo igitur.
units.tr: Again I am surprised that you make no analysis of that other pointing of יְהוִֹה [YHWH]. Moreover, your whole argument rests on a hypothesis that is plainly disputed, namely that the points placed above [τὰ πεταγεγμένα, ta petagegmena] and the vowels of the name Adonai are the same. You asserted this above as well, but since you gave no proof for it, we rejected it with equal ease. Now you add further that the word אֲרֹנִי [adoni], applied to God, is marked with the vowel (ˉ) under the Nun, and that the point placed at the beginning [ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ κείμενον, en tē archē keimenon] was used for this reason only, so that it would fittingly match the Tetragrammaton when pronounced. Yet the arrangement alone [διάκειμα, diakeima] ought to have been enough for you. Surely the vowel (–) that אֲרֹנִי takes when applied to God is for no other reason than the arrangement [διακείσθαι, diakeisthai]. Nor are you unaware that this one cause has introduced many anomalies into Hebrew grammar. Thus I shall profane אֶחָל / יֶחָל [ʼehal / yehal] with (–), and begin אֶחָל יֶחָל [ʼehal yehal]. Surely there is no page of the grammar that does not supply similar cases. I go on, then.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: Fuller.

units.la: Tantundem quoque efficitur ex Jah nomine essentiali, sive essentia similiter indice. Quippe hoc religiosissimi & Hebraicè doctissimi viri nihil aliud judicant, quàm ipsum Tetragrammaton Jehova decurtatum, hoc est, ex trisyllabo in monosyllabum per *syncopen contractum, &c.
units.tr: The same follows from the essential name Jah, or the essence likewise indicated. For the most pious and Hebraically learned men judge this to be nothing other than the Tetragrammaton Jehovah shortened, that is, contracted from a trisyllable into a monosyllable by syncope, and so on.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: Amama.

units.la: Ego vero ex JAH firmius argumentum pro JAHVO vel JAO deduci posse existimo. Si enim Jah ex Tetragrammato decurtatum est, ut Ebraicè periti loqui solent, probabilius inde sequetur, primam Tetragrammati syllabam fuisse JAH. Si enim contractum dixeris ex Jehova per syncopen, dic causam cur ה in יה sit Mappicatum. An ultimum ה in יְהֹוָה Jehova, Mappicatum est? Non opinor. At contra prius illud ה in voce יְהוֹה Mappic sive mobile est, quòd vel per scheva vel per vocalem subjectam ostenditur, quæ in ista decurtatione, vau & posteriori ה resectis, nec puncto Scheva, nec vocali notari potuit, unde successit punctum in ה / quod specialiter vocatur Mappic, vicarium schevatis subintellecti. Ex. gratia, ה in אֱלֹהִים non quiescere, sed Mappic sive mobile esse, vocalis Hirik docet. Tolle literas יִ / remanebit אלה / ut intelligat, lector, ה vocis prædictæ non quiescere sed moveri (litera enim quiescens & litera Mappic apud Grammaticos Ebræos opponuntur) necessario literæ ה imprimendum erat punctum quod specialiter & per synecdochen Mapphik vocatur, אֱלָהּ. Judicet ergo lector an non probabilius sit, יָהּ ex Tetragrammato non esse contractum per syncopen, sed simpliciter esse decurtatum seu dimidiatum & per consequens primam genuinæ pronunciationis syllabam fuisse יָהּ vel per crasin יָהּ /
units.tr: I, however, think a firmer argument for JAHVO or JAO can be drawn from JAH. For if Jah is shortened from the Tetragrammaton, as those skilled in Hebrew usually say, it follows more probably that the first syllable of the Tetragrammaton was JAH. If you say it was contracted from Jehovah by syncope, then explain why the ה in יה carries a mappiq. Is the final ה in יְהֹוָה Jehovah marked with a mappiq? I think not. On the contrary, that first ה in the word יְהוֹה is mappiq, that is, mobile, which is shown by either a shewa or a vowel placed under it. In this abbreviation, with the vav and the second ה cut away, neither a shewa point nor a vowel could be marked there, so a point was put in the ה, which is specially called mappiq, standing in for the implied shewa. For example, that the ה in אֱלֹהִים is not silent but mappiq, that is, mobile, is shown by the hireq vowel. Remove the letters יִ and what remains is אלה. So that the reader may understand that the ה of the said word is not silent but sounded (for a silent letter and a mappiq letter are opposed among the Hebrew grammarians), the point called mapphik, specially and by synecdoche, had necessarily to be placed on the ה: אֱלָהּ. Let the reader judge, then, whether it is not more probable that יָהּ was not contracted from the Tetragrammaton by syncope, but simply shortened or halved, and consequently that the first syllable of the genuine pronunciation was יָהּ, or by crasis יָהּ.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: Fuller.

units.la: Neque obscura est ea ratio, quæ ex Apocalypsi affertur, ubi ὁ ἦν, ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος pulcherrimum est, ac distinctum, ac exquisitum Tetragrammati interpretamentum, recensionem syllabarum, nisi fallor, non Ebræorum more à dextrâ in sinistram, sed contra Græcorum ritu, à sinistrâ in dextram exordiendo & continuando. Sic namque primo loco ! seu Camets obviam procedit. præteriti הָוָה id est fuit, indicium. Secundo Ho sive Holem Participii הוֹה nempe est, insigne. Tertio, Je sive Jod Futuri יְהוֹה id est Erit characteristicon. Hisce ergo punctis vocalibus nomini Jehova suppositis, Æternitas naturæ seu essentiæ divinæ, nomen menti humana dilucidè contemplanda exhibetur, &c.
units.tr: The reasoning drawn from the Apocalypse is no obscure one, where ὁ ἦν, ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [who was, who is, and who is to come] is a most beautiful, distinct and exact interpretation of the Tetragrammaton. The syllables are recited, unless I am mistaken, not in the Hebrew manner from right to left, but in the manner of the Greeks, beginning and proceeding from left to right. Thus, first, the Kamets [ָ] meets the eye, the sign of the past tense, הָוָה, that is, "was." Second, the Holem of the participle, הוֹה, that is, "is," is the mark. Third, the Yod, or Jod, of the future, יְהוֹה, that is, "will be," is the characteristic. With these vowel points placed on the name Jehovah, the eternity of the divine nature or essence is presented, and the name is made plainly visible to the human mind for contemplation, and so on.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: Amama.

units.la: Argutè magis quam solidè hæc excogitavit Zanchius. Illi enim Misc. 2. 6. hanc observationem adscribis. De recensione syllabarum ordine retrogrado institutâ quod mones & hoc argutum nimis. Apocalyptes naturalem temporum ordinem observavit, quo præteritum prius est præsenti, & hoc rursus Futuro. Sed non satis inoffenso pede procedit illa observatio de Futuro. Jod enim Futuri temporis characteristicon quidem est, sed per scheva extra Phiel & Phual effersi non potest, ubi vox ꞑ usitata non est.
units.tr: Zanchius devised this more ingeniously than solidly. For you attribute this observation to him in Miscellanea 2.6. As to what you advise about the reverse order of the syllables, that too is too subtle. The Apocalypse observes the natural order of times, in which the past comes before the present, and the present before the future. But that observation about the future does not proceed with a secure step. The Jod is indeed the characteristic of the future tense, but it cannot be pronounced with a shewa outside the Piel and Pual forms, where the form יהיה is not in use.

units.la: FULLERUS.
units.tr: Fuller.

units.la: Dicet quispiam, Lectio Jehova nusquam apud illos extat. Ita est profectò. Nec injuriâ utique propter insignem linguæ, quâ locuti sunt & scripserunt, ἀδυναμίαν. Unde prolatio ineptissima, maximeque absona, nec ullo modo toleranda evasisset, ut in Miscellaneis lib. 2. cap. 6. & lib. 4. cap. 13. declaravimus.
units.tr: Someone will say: the reading Jehova is nowhere found among them. That is quite so. And not without reason, on account of the remarkable weakness of the language in which they spoke and wrote. Hence the pronunciation would have turned out most absurd and entirely intolerable, as we have shown in Miscellanea book 2, chapter 6, and book 4, chapter 13.

units.la: AMAMA.
units.tr: AMAMA.

units.la: Multa certè hac de re Miscell. lib. 2. & 4. protulisti, indeque ἀνεκφώνητον id est ineffabile dictum exiltimas. Sed quæ quæso te hujus ἀδυναμίας causæ? Tres opinor. 1. quod Græci j consonâ careant. 2. quod in medio non aspirent, 3 quod v consonam non agnoscant. Sed eædem difficultates aliis etiam vocibus sunt communes, per quas tamen, non stetit, quominus eas Græci expresserint. Nam quod primum attinet, ecce tibi Ιεδα, Ιαωσεσ, & quæ ipse ex Græcis produxisti, Ιαξέ, Ιαὼ, Ιευὼ. Quod ad 2. cum aspirationem passim neglexerint Græci, ut in Ἀδραὰμ Ιωάνης, &c. cur hic quoque negligi non potuisset? Et quis illud ignorat, ה cum præeunte (:) à Græcis fere semper absorberi, nec uspiam Ιευδα, Ιωαχμ, sed semper Ιευδα, Ιωαχμ, &c. inveniri. Quin & si tantum in aspiratione ista retinendâ fuisset situm, cur non tam scribi potuissent
units.tr: You have certainly set out much on this matter in Miscellanea, books 2 and 4, and so you judge it to be ἀνεκφώνητον [unutterable]. But what, I ask you, are the causes of this inability [ἀδυναμίας]? I think there are three. First, the Greeks lack the consonant j. Second, they do not aspirate in the middle of a word. Third, they do not recognise the consonant v. But the same difficulties are common to other words too, and yet nothing prevented the Greeks from expressing those words. As to the first point, look at Ιεδα [Iuda], Ιαωσεσ [Iaōsēs], and what you yourself have drawn from the Greeks: Ιαξέ [Iaxe], Ιαὼ [Iaō], Ιευὼ [Ieuō]. As to the second, since the Greeks often neglected the aspiration, as in Ἀδραὰμ [Abraam], Ιωάνης [Iōannēs], and so on, why could it not be neglected here too? And who does not know that ה preceded by (:) is almost always absorbed by the Greeks, and that nowhere is Ιευδα or Ιωαχμ found, but always Ιουδα, Ιωαχιμ, and so on? Indeed, even if the whole difficulty had lain in keeping that aspiration, why could Iesa not have been written just as easily as ἄνθρωποι [anthrōpoi]?

units.la: X x 2 tuisset Iesa, quàm ἄνθρωποι? ut nihil jam dicam, apud Jones tralatitiam fuisse adspirationem in medio, quamdiu figura H pro adspiratione utebantur, E. G. ENHOAIA, ἐνόδια. Quod ad 3. attinet, ei oppono Ἀαβίδ, Λεξι, Λευι, Ιαυω, Ιέυω, Ιαβαι, & multa id genus alia, ubi Ebraeorum vel per β vel per υ expressum est. Et nunquid tu ipse Miscell. lib. 2. cap. 6. & lib. 4. 13. ex Iaw, ipsum Iwa, ex Iaɛs, ipsum Iwɛa conaris effingere? Nunquid p. 557. ex ipso textu Graeco LXX. Interpretum, 2. Sam. 1. 12. ubi in Ebr. est populis DOMINI, pro Iuda restituendum putas vocem Iova? ut holem per o parvum expressum sit, ut & in ανδομα, βοος, &c. & vau per υ, plane ut Δαυιδ in Bibliis Graecis Romanis & Iauae I. Chron. 1. 5. Gen. 10. 2. & apud Dionys. Halicarnassaeum Αυεντινος, Aventinus, & apud Suidam ὀλαυιανός, &c. Potuisset ergo hoc nomen exprimi vel per Iωɛa vel per Iova, vel per Iεωɛα. Quomodo ex tua sententia & ab Epiphania & a LXX. expressum est.
units.tr: To say nothing more, it is well known that aspiration in the middle of a word was in common use among the Jews, as long as they used the letter H for the aspiration, e.g. ENHOAIA, ἐνόδια [enodia]. As to the third point, I set against it Ἀαβίδ [Aabid], Λεξι [Lexi], Λευι [Levi], Ιαυω [Iauō], Ιέυω [Ieuō], Ιαβαι [Iabai], and many other words of this kind, where the Hebrew sound has been expressed by either β or υ. And do you yourself, in Miscellanea book 2, chapter 6, and book 4, chapter 13, not try to shape Iwa from Iaw, and Iwɛa from Iaɛs? Do you not, on p. 557, think that Iova should be restored in place of Judah, from the Greek text of the Seventy translators themselves, 2 Samuel 1:12, where the Hebrew has the people of the LORD? The o is expressed by a small o, as also in ανδομα, βοος and so on, and the vau by υ, just as Δαυιδ appears in the Greek and Roman Bibles, and Iauae in 1 Chronicles 1:5 and Genesis 10:2, and in Dionysius of Halicarnassus Αυεντινος [Aventinos, Aventinus], and in Suidas ὀλαυιανός [olauianos], and so on. This name could therefore have been expressed either by Iωɛa, or by Iova, or by Iεωɛα, just as, by your own view, it was expressed by Epiphanius and the Seventy.

units.la: Neque dubitandum, quin Euangelistae & Apostoli, quocunque etiam modo, expressuri fuissent illud nomen, si ipsis haesisset haec opinio, substitutionem אַדְנָי aut superstitiosum esse aut per eam nimis nequiter efficaciam textus tolli. Sed ut ego quid de loco 2. Sam. 1. 12. sentiam ingenuè profiteor, puto frustrà te esse. Quis enim ignorat LXX. Interpretes passim non tam verborum quam sensus habuisse rationem. Cum ergo populus Judae tunc temporis fuerit populus DOMINI, quid miramur, si vocem Juda pro Domini posuerint? Et quis adeo in Graeco textu hospes est, qui ignoret aliquoties יהוה & יהוה ab illis esse confusum, & hoc pro illo interpretatum, quod vel ex unius Drusii Conjecturis ad Graecum Textum ἐξ Δωδεκαπρεσφύτυ liquere potest. Illud restat ut verbum addam ad ea quae pag. 556. libri 4. Miscell. ad locum Eusebii & versus istos notasti,
units.tr: There is no doubt that the Evangelists and Apostles, in whatever way, would have expressed that name, if this opinion had held them, that the substitution of אַדְנָי [Adonai] is either superstitious or removes the efficacy of the text too wickedly. But as to what I think of the passage 2 Samuel 1:12, I frankly confess that you are wrong about it. For who does not know that the Seventy translators often took account not so much of the words as of the sense? Since the people of Judah at that time was the people of the LORD, why are we surprised if they put the word Juda in place of Domini? And who is so much a stranger to the Greek text as not to know that at times יהוה [YHWH] and יהוה have been confused by them, and the one rendered by the other, as can be seen even from the Conjectures of Drusius alone on the Greek text? It remains for me to add a word on what you noted at p. 556 of book 4 of Miscellanea, on the passage of Eusebius and those verses,

units.la: Ἐπειδὴ με φωνήεντα ἑπτὰ μίαν ἄφθιτον αἰνεῖ / Γράμματα, ἃ πάντων ἀκάμαντα ὑμνεῖ [?]
units.tr: Ἐπειδὴ με φωνήεντα ἑπτὰ μίαν ἄφθιτον αἰνεῖ / Γράμματα, ἃ πάντων ἀκάμαντα ὑμνεῖ [?] [Since seven vowels praise me as the one imperishable letter-set, which sing tirelessly of all things.]

units.la: Me septem celebrant elementa vocalia magnum, Aeternumque Deum, perpetuumque Panem.
units.tr: The seven vowel-letters celebrate me as the great, eternal and perpetual God.

units.la: Verba Eusebii, Septem φωνήεντων in unum idemque nomen compositionem unius cujusdam ineffabilis appellationis enuntiationem complecti ajunt. Quod quidem nomen quatuor literis notatum Hebraeorum natio supremæ Dei potentia assignat, &c. Hinc intelligimus, inquit Fullerus, nomen Dei יהוה / septem, hoc est, cunctas Græcorum vocales comprehendere, iisque certo quodam ordine dispositis, idem nomen aperte planeque exprimi, verbi gratia ες [η] ω [o] υα Jeova. Argutè & hoc, ut fere omnia. Sed quæso te Clarissime Vir, an tibi met ipsi hic satis-fecisti? Si 7. vocales exprimunt hoc nomen, cur ergo otium agunt η & o Illis sublatis, vides tantum 5. superesse. Miror te non ita potius expressisse IEHΩ [O] TA & ex η adspirationem fecisse. Certè olim η non vocalis, sed adspiratio fuit. Et vocem Eta ab Ebraeo Heth deductam, & hinc esse Latinorum H, res certa est. Tamen ne sic quidem confecta res esset. Turbaret enim adhuc supervacaneum illud o. Scaliger in Fragmentis suis ad calcem operis de Emendat. temporum hic etiam sudat. Explicat enim hæc de duabus הוא יהוה / quas sic exprimit, HOA IETΩ, Quod rursus explicatione eget. Ecce enim ח exprimit per H nunc vocalem, E. gr. HEKATON, Ho, ENHOAIA, pro ἑκατον, ὁ, ἐνόδια, Vau per o. Olim enim vau sonabat o vel u: per A. Namque & hæc litera olim vocalem A repræsentabat, cum novi isti vocalium characteres nondum essent, unde tres illæ literæ ו י א matres lectionis vocantur, unde & ab א Ebraico Græcanicum ΑΛΦΑ πὴν Φοινίκην ἐλαβε, inquit Suidas, quod certe durius fuisset, si א olim tantum spiritum lenem valuisset. Sed quid opus tam anxia explicatione? Nulla necessitas est, inquit Scaliger, per φωνήεντα vocales tantum intelligere, cum Josephus diserte quatuor Tetragrammati literas πῖλαςρα φωνήεντα vocet, ut vel hinc appareat quasvis literas φωνήεντα appellari posse. Sed opponos Eusebii, μίας πνοῆς σεσημειώσεως, unius cujusdam appellationis, seu vocis, cum hic duæ sint. Resp: Versus nihil tale habere, & Eusebio condonari id posse, utpote qui Ebraicè nescivit. Addo, probabilem magis illam esse conjecturam, quam idem Scaliger in Animadv. ad Eusebium prodidit, vid. versibus istis denotari Deum Sinopensium in Alexandriam civitatem Ægypti tanquam inquilinum receptum, Ζεὺν Αἰγυπτίων ἡ πάτεμον, ἀπὸ Σπῆνον, quem septem literis exprimunt, his vid. Serapis, vel Sarapis. In quam sententiam citat Hesychium, ἐπαγεγαμμάτον, ὀχμλὸν, σπληχὸν ἡ Σίραξπιν.
units.tr: The words of Eusebius: they say that seven vowels, combined into one and the same name, embrace the utterance of a certain unspeakable appellation. This name, marked by four letters, the Hebrew nation assigns to the supreme power of God, and so on. From this, says Fuller, we understand that the name of God יהוה [sic] comprises seven, that is, all the Greek vowels, and that when these are arranged in a certain order the same name is expressed openly and plainly, for example ες [η] ω [o] υα Jeova. This too is ingenious, as almost everything you do. But I ask you, most distinguished sir, whether you yourself have satisfied the point here. If seven vowels express this name, why then do η and o stand idle? With them removed, you see only five remain. I am surprised you did not rather express it as IEHΩ [O] TA and make an aspiration out of η. Certainly η was once not a vowel but an aspiration, and that the word Eta is derived from the Hebrew Heth, and hence is the Latin H, is a certain fact. Yet even so the matter would not be settled, for that superfluous o would still cause trouble. Scaliger in his Fragments at the end of his work De emendatione temporum also labours here. For he explains these things of the two הוא יהוה [sic], which he expresses as HOA IETΩ, which in turn needs explanation. For he expresses ח by H, sometimes as a vowel, for example HEKATON, Ho, ENHOAIA, for ἑκατον, ὁ, ἐνόδια, and vav by o. For formerly vav sounded o or u, and by A: for this letter too once represented the vowel A, when those new vowel signs did not yet exist, whence those three letters ו י א are called the mothers of reading. Whence also from the Hebrew א comes the Greek ΑΛΦΑ [alpha], "the Phoenicians took it," says Suidas, which would certainly have been harder if א once had only the value of a soft breathing. But why need there be such anxious explanation? There is no necessity, says Scaliger, to understand only vowels by φωνήεντα, since Josephus expressly calls the four letters of the Tetragrammaton "vowel-letters," so that even from this it appears that any letters whatever can be called φωνήεντα. But you may object the words of Eusebius, "of one notation of breath," "of one appellation," or word, since there are two here. I reply: the verse has nothing of the sort, and Eusebius may be forgiven this, as one who did not know Hebrew. I add that the conjecture which the same Scaliger published in his Animadversions on Eusebius is more probable, namely that these verses denote the god of the Sinopeans, received into the city of Alexandria in Egypt as a lodger, Ζεὺν Αἰγυπτίων [Zeus of the Egyptians], whom they express by seven letters, namely Serapis or Sarapis. To this opinion he cites Hesychius, who glosses it as a Sinopean and Egyptian god.

units.la: COROLLARIUM.
units.tr: COROLLARY.

units.la: Quaeritur, an substitutio nominis ADONAI nimis nequiter tollat efficaciam textus, & an illis, qui nomen יהוה per Adonai legunt, obnuntiari possit lex horrendi carminis, quae extat Apoc. 22. verf. 18. & 19. Affirmativam non ita pridem vir quidam eruditus publice tutatus est. Assertio ejus integra haec erat, vox יהוה proprius consonantibus per vocales quam possumus convenientissimas; non per vocem Adonai exprimenda est; praeterquam enim quod vocis istius substitutio superstitionem nescio quam Judaicam sapiat, instabilis sit & cacophoniam pariat, NIMIS NEQUITER TEXTUS EFFICACIAM TOLLIT, Contra illud Apoc. 22. verf. 18. & 19. Hactenus verba theseos. Adscribam locum Apoc. integrum: Si quis adjecerit ad haec, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto. Et si quis abstulerit aliquid ex verbis libri prophetiae hujus, auferet Deus partem ejus e libro vitae, & ex urbe illa sancta & ex iis, quae scripta sunt in hoc libro.
units.tr: The question is whether the substitution of the name ADONAI so wantonly removes the efficacy of the text, and whether the terrible curse of Revelation 22:18–19 can be turned against those who read the name יהוה as Adonai. Not long ago a learned man publicly defended the affirmative. His assertion, in full, ran: the word יהוה is to be pronounced by means of the most suitable vowels we can supply, not by the word Adonai; for, apart from the fact that substituting that word savours of I know not what Jewish superstition, it is unstable and produces cacophony; it WANTONLY REMOVES THE EFFICACY OF THE TEXT. Against that, see Revelation 22:18–19. So far the words of the thesis. I will quote the passage of Revelation in full: If anyone adds to these things, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away anything from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book.

units.la: Per vocales quam possumus convenientissimas efferenda est vox יהוה / inquit Disputator, non per Adonai. Cur non una opera adscripsit suum judicium, quas vocales putet esse convenientissimas? Agnoscit ergo vocales proprias esse incertas, & quae nunc in textu adscribuntur, esse alienas? At hoc totum illud est, quod subinde in lectionibus meis, cum istius, cui assuevi, lectionis rationem reddo, inculco: hoc illud est, quo universa mea aurigatur dissertatio. Si lectionem illam Adonai religione quadam & metu profanationis primitus introductam, & ab ipsis postea Apostolis sacratam, jubebat convellere, signandae erant certae vocales, praescribenda constans lectio, cui adhaerescere debeat juventus. In re, disputatoris judicio, tam ardua, non in incerto linquendi erant animi. Dicet fortassis, satius esse per quascunque vocales nomen Adonai, ἀδωναῖον. Ignosce, mihi doctissime vir, si hic a te diversus abeam. ἀλλ᾽ ἐμοὶ δὲ τάδε. Toleremus invicem. Ego sic sentio, non peccare qui nomen יהוה per priscum illud, ab ipsis Apostolis interpretatum, creaturisque tam incommunicabile, quam ipsum יהוה / pronuntiare malunt, quam incongrua vel alienarum vel incertarum vocalium cum consonantibus commixtione sanctissimum
units.tr: "The word יהוה," says the disputant, "is to be pronounced by means of the most suitable vowels, not by Adonai." Why did he not at the same time state his own judgment as to which vowels he thinks most suitable? Does he therefore acknowledge that the proper vowels are uncertain, and that those now written in the text are foreign to it? Yet this is exactly what I keep insisting on in my lectures whenever I give my reasons for the reading I was brought up with; this is the point on which my whole discussion turns. If he thought that the reading Adonai, introduced at first from a certain religious scruple and fear of profanation, and afterwards sanctioned by the Apostles themselves, ought to be overthrown, then certain vowels should have been marked, and a fixed reading prescribed for the young to adhere to. In a matter as difficult as this, in the disputant's judgment, minds should not have been left in uncertainty. Perhaps he will say it is better to read the name Adonai with whatever vowels come to hand [ἀδωναῖον]. Forgive me, most learned sir, if I depart from you here. But as for me, [ἀλλ᾽ ἐμοὶ δὲ τάδε]. Let us bear with one another. My view is that those who prefer to pronounce the name יהוה, as incommunicable to a creature as the name יהוה itself, by the ancient rendering used by the Apostles themselves, do no wrong, rather than to utter that most holy name by an improper mixing of foreign or uncertain vowels with the consonants.

units.la: simum nomen efferre. Explicabo mentem meam tironi familiari exemplo, Tullius Cicero. Ponamus, Cicero esse nomen, Tullius cognomen: Prioris * vocales ignotas aut admodum incertas & controversas esse. Quis non mallet Oratorum illum principem semper appellare Tullium, praesertim si hoc nomine nullus alius orator extaret, quam vel Ca Cer Onem, vel Cu Cur Onem, vel Ca Cur Onem, vel etiam Cic Er Onem?
units.tr: I will explain my meaning to a beginner with a familiar example: Tullius Cicero. Let us suppose that Cicero is the name and Tullius the surname, and that the vowels of the former are unknown or very doubtful and disputed. Who would not prefer always to call that prince of orators Tullius, especially if no other orator survived under this name except one called Ca Cer Onem, or Cu Cur Onem, or Ca Cur Onem, or even Cic Er Onem?

units.la: Non per Adonai ] olim cum propriae vocales nominis יהוה non ignorarentur, fas erat illud per Adonai exprimere, & jam nobis qui proprias vocales ignotas aut incertas esse putamus, non fas erit ista voce uti?
units.tr: Not by Adonai: once, when the proper vowels of the name יהוה were not unknown, it was lawful to express it by Adonai; and shall it now not be lawful for us to use that word, since we think the proper vowels are unknown or uncertain?

units.la: Superstitionem nescio quam Judaicam sapit] Quorsum illa nescio quam? an edulcandae seu mitigandae censurae? Sed ad rem ipsam quod attinet, rogo utrum ipsi ergo Apostoli in superstitionis luto tibi haereant? utrum insitearis, priscos Ebraeos superstitionis causas procul habuisse, cum aliquando per vocem Adonai nomen יהוה expressere? Accessisse postea superstitionem, ipse prolixe doceo. Et audebo gloriari, paucos certiora testimonia isti detegendae & exaggerandae protulisse. Sed demus, lectionem illam superstitioni non incrementum, sed natales suos debere. Quid tum? Lectionem istam nobis vitandam esse inferes. Neque ego dissentiam, ubi genuinam nominis יהוה pronuntiationem nos docueris. Porro, annon multa sunt ex superstitione introducta, quae viri pii sine superstitione imitantur? Judaei signaturi numerum 15. pro יה scribunt טו / cujus consuetudinis origo superstitioni Judaicae verius deputatur. Video tamen Christianos hoc sine superstitione imitari. Sepulturam in templa & coemeteria introduxit superstitio. Nos tamen, opinor, nostros sine superstitione iisdem in locis sepelimus.
units.tr: "It savours of I know not what Jewish superstition." Why this "I know not what"? Is it to soften or mitigate the censure? But as to the matter itself, I ask whether the Apostles themselves are to be caught in the mire of superstition for you. Are you to insist that the early Hebrews were far from the causes of superstition when at some time they rendered the name יהוה by the word Adonai? I myself show at length that superstition came in later. And I dare to boast that few have brought forward clearer evidence for detecting and exaggerating it. But grant that that reading owes its origin, not its increase, to superstition. So what? You will infer that we must avoid that reading. I shall not disagree, provided you teach us the genuine pronunciation of the name יהוה. Moreover, are there not many things introduced from superstition which pious men imitate without superstition? The Jews, when writing the number fifteen, write טו instead of יה; the origin of this custom is more truly ascribed to Jewish superstition. Yet I see Christians imitating this without superstition. Superstition introduced burial in churches and cemeteries. Yet we, I think, bury our dead in those same places without superstition.

units.la: Instabilis est] hoc forte vult Disputator, aliquando etiam Elohim a nobis legi, quando vid. occurrit יהוה / Eodem incommodo premit eos, qui Jehova legunt, nam aliquando & Jehovi legendum habent. Caeterum de instabilitate loqui non potest, qui stabilem lectionem nomini יהוה non assignat.
units.tr: "It is unstable." Perhaps the disputant means that sometimes we also read Elohim where the name יהוה occurs. He is burdened by the same inconvenience as those who read Jehova, for sometimes they too have to read Jehovi. Moreover, he cannot speak of instability who does not assign a stable reading to the name יהוה.

units.la: Cacophoniam parit] De cacophonia judicandum ex sonorum collatione. Cum autem nullum certum sonum ponat, quid de cacophonia loquitur? Et quod ad lectionem nostram attinet, quid κακόφωνον hac lectione, Adonai Elohim, badonai, ladonai, wadonai, &c. - Nimis nequiter textus efficaciam tollit] Id vero nimis crude, nimis temere dictum. Nimis crude, non enim dicit disputator, utrum ubique an potius certis in locis textus efficacia tollatur. Nimis temere: Hic enim primo vapulant, Scaliger, Mercerus, Drusius, Scindlerus, Cevalerius, Erpenius, qui licet vulgo Grammatici per contemptum audiant, vitæ tamen sanctitate cum quibusdam ex professo res Theologicas tractantibus, facile potuere facere paria. Hic etiam ferula intentatur multis doctissimis Interpretibus, qua priscis, qua novellis, qui tam in Græcis & Latinis, quam vernaculis versionibus, non vocem יהוה sed אדני interpretati sunt. Hic denique ipsi Euangelistæ & Apostoli postulantur, qui nomen יהוה passim per interpretamentum Adonai (κύριος) reddiderunt. Dum vero addit Disputator, eos facere contra locum illum Apocalypseos, quis non inde inferet, eum omnes illos & universos orco adscribere? Vide Vir doctissime, τὶ σ' ἐκ φύγεν ἐκ οδόντων; Ego sic existimo, ut theologos & verbi divini ministros, minus sancte viventes, ad salutem æternam adipiscendam nihil juvabit, si vocem יהוה propriis consonis per vocales convenientissimas efferant, ita doctissimis illis Grammaticis (ut de theologis, Interpretibus, Patribus & Apostolis sileam) cum depositis hujus corporis exuviis coram tribunali Dei comparuere, propter substitutionem Adonai non præclusam fuisse januam civitatis istius sanctæ, quæ in Apocal. memoratur. Cæterum quod ad Apostolos & Græcos patres attinet, si objicies forte ἀδυναμίαν illam de qua supra p. 347. rogo te ut ea quæ isthic respondemus, expendas. Et posito, Græcos vocem exprimere non potuisse, vel hinc apparebit, non omnibus, qui vocem יהוה per Adonai exprimunt, nimis nequiter sublata textus efficacia crimen impingi posse. Quod ad caput rei attinet, jam ostendi in dissertatione §. 87. quomodo retenta lectione Adonai & retineri possit & à quamplurimis reformatis Theologis & Interpretibus retenta sit efficacia textus. Ad illa liceat mihi paucula addere. Efficacia textus per substitutionem vocis Adonai vel peribit legenti, vel audienti. Non legenti: Leget enim verbum Dei vel originali, vel ex versione. Si non intelligat efficaciam vocis, nihil intererit, sive textum originarium sive versionem legat. At si intelligat, quoties originales V. Test. tabulas leget, etiam si pronuntiet Adonai, tamen videbit illic consonas יהוה / Sin leget versionem accuratam, ubi τὸ יהוה redditum est per interpretamentum vocis Adonai, majusculis literis exaratum ibi certe videbit, in Ebraeo esse τὸ יהוה / Non etiam audienti: Nam si necesse est, moneri potest à legente, istis in locis ubi Adonai in Ebraeo legit, vel in versionibus, cujus interpretamentum majusculis literis occurrit, in Ebraeo esse τὸ πτεσα-γεάμματον. Atque hic iterum illud mihi expende, cum hoc indicium vel raro vel nunquam in concionibus fiat, cum multi Interpretes, cum, omnis antiquitas, cum ipsi denique Apostoli & Euangelistae ne hoc quidem observaverint, ut vid. διαxεῖσεως ἐπxα nomen κύριος, vel Dominus vel Here expresserint omnibus literis majusculis, imo ne primâ quidem majuscula Euangelistae, & Apostoli nomen κύριος scripserint, annon omnes, te judice, textus efficaciam nimis nequiter sustulerint.
units.tr: "It produces cacophony." Cacophony must be judged by comparing sounds. But since he sets down no fixed sound, what is he talking about when he speaks of cacophony? And as far as our reading is concerned, what is cacophonous [κακόφωνον] in this reading: Adonai Elohim, badonai, ladonai, wadonai, &c.? "It wantonly removes the efficacy of the text." This is indeed too crudely and too rashly said. Too crudely, for the disputant does not say whether the efficacy of the text is removed everywhere or rather in certain places. Too rashly: for here first are lashed Scaliger, Mercer, Drusius, Schindler, Cevallerius, Erpenius, who, though they are commonly heard of as grammarians with contempt, could with some of those who deal professionally with theological matters, by the holiness of their lives, easily have done the same. Here the rod is also threatened against many most learned interpreters, both ancient and modern, who in their Greek and Latin and vernacular versions translated not the word יהוה but אדני. Here finally the Evangelists and Apostles themselves are called to account, who everywhere rendered the name יהוה by the interpretation Adonai (κύριος). When the disputant adds that they act against that passage of the Apocalypse, who will not infer from this that he consigns all of them, every one, to hell? See, most learned sir, what has escaped from your teeth [τὶ σ' ἐκ φύγεν ἐκ οδόντων]? My opinion is this: just as it will not help theologians and ministers of the divine Word who live less holily to obtain eternal salvation if they pronounce the word יהוה with proper consonants and suitable vowels, so, to say nothing of theologians, interpreters, Fathers and Apostles, those most learned grammarians, when they appear before the judgment seat of God with the remains of their bodies laid down, will not find that the gate of that holy city mentioned in the Apocalypse was shut against them because of the substitution of Adonai. As for the Apostles and the Greek Fathers, if you perhaps object to their inability [ἀδυναμίαν], of which I spoke above on p. 347, I ask you to weigh what we answered there. And even granting that the Greeks could not express the word, this will be plain from the fact that the charge of "wantonly removing the efficacy of the text" cannot be brought against all who express the word יהוה by Adonai. As to the heart of the matter, I have already shown in my dissertation, §87, how the reading Adonai can be retained, and how the efficacy of the text has been retained by very many Reformed theologians and interpreters who kept that reading. Let me add a few words on this. The efficacy of the text through the substitution of the word Adonai will be lost either to the reader or to the hearer. Not to the reader: for he will read the word of God either in the original or in a translation. If he does not understand the force of the word, it will make no difference whether he reads the original text or a translation. But if he does understand it, then whenever he reads the original tables of the Old Testament, even if he pronounces Adonai, he will still see there the consonants יהוה. And if he reads an accurate translation, where יהוה has been rendered by the interpretation Adonai, written there in capital letters, he will certainly see that the Hebrew has יהוה. Nor is it lost to the hearer: for if it is necessary, he can be informed by the reader that in those places where the reader says Adonai in the Hebrew, or in translations where that interpretation appears in capitals, the Hebrew has the Tetragrammaton. And here again, weigh this with me: since this indication is rarely or never given in sermons, and since many interpreters, all antiquity, and finally the Apostles and Evangelists themselves did not observe even this, namely that they wrote the word κύριος in capital letters, expressing it as Lord or Dominus or Herr, nay, that the Evangelists and Apostles did not even write the word κύριος with an initial capital, will you not, by your judgment, have all of them wantonly removed the efficacy of the text?

units.la: Contra illud Apocalypseos, &c.] Deum hunc locum praesenti argumento accommodas, praesupponis per illa verba, libri hujus, totum Bibliorum systema intelligi. Neque enim in Apocalypsi vel universo novo foedere, nomen יהוה cum suis vocalibus reperies. Sed esto. Obsignentur istis verbis, tanquam sigillo quodam, tota Biblia, quid tamen inde efficies, ni simul ostenderis, ipsos prophetas proprias vocales voci יהוה olim adscripsisse? Ubi & hoc obtineris, tunc styli tui mucronem in illos distringe, atque illis obnuntia hoc dirum carmen, qui vocales illis primi sustulerunt & alienas substituerunt. Eos certe qui vocem alienis vocalibus hodie in textu Biblico vestitam (hoc enim agnoscis, quando dicis per vocales quam possumus convenientissimas) legunt per eam vocem, cujusillas vocales existimant esse proprias, eos inquam hoc anathemate ferire plane alienum est. Cavendum est, ne objectetur nobis illud Salvatoris, vae vobis, qui colatus culices & deglutitis camelos. Atque hic finio, de loco Hebraeorum 2. 16. suo loco dicturus.
units.tr: Against that passage in the Apocalypse, etc. You apply this passage to the present argument, presupposing by the words "of this book" that the whole system of the Bible is meant. For you will not find the name יהוה with its vowels in the Apocalypse or in the whole New Covenant. But granted. Let the whole Bible be sealed by those words as by some seal; what will you make of it, unless you also show that the prophets themselves once attached their own vowels to the word יהוה? Once you have established that, then turn the point of your pen against them and pronounce upon them this dreadful curse, those who first removed the vowels and substituted foreign ones. Certainly it is quite out of place to curse with this anathema those who today read the word, clothed in foreign vowels in the Biblical text (for you acknowledge this when you say "by the vowels which we can make most suitable"), and who read it by that word whose vowels they think are its proper ones. It must be taken care that the saying of the Saviour is not thrown back at us: woe to you, who strain out gnats and swallow camels. And here I end, since I shall speak about the passage in Hebrews 2:16 in its proper place.

units.la: Omnia Reformatarum Ecclesiarum judicio subjecta sunto.
units.tr: All things are to be subject to the judgment of the Reformed Churches.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: CAP. XXI. verf. II.
units.tr: Chapter XXI, verse 2

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. מכה איש ומת מות יומת | Qui percusserit hominem, voleas occidere, morte moriatur.
units.tr: Hebrew: He who strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death [מכה איש ומת מות יומת]. Vulgate: Whoever strikes a man, intending to kill him, shall die the death.

units.la: Hanc versionem flagellant Cajet. Johan. Bened. & Oleastrius. Et certe verba Legis aliud sonant. Audiamus eam, Percutiens virum & mortuus est (id est, ut moriatur) morte afficiatur. Ecce lex dicit effectum percussionis, Vulgatus videtur dicere intentionem, ut, etiam non secuta morte, voluntas morte multetur. Cui opinioni Lyra contradicit his verbis, Quod si non occideret percutiendo, quantumcunque vellet occidere, non ob id puniretur morte. In hanc Lyrae sententiam video multos Interpretes fuisse. Contrarium tamen rescripsit Imperator Hadrianus. Et certe si de intentione certo constet judici, annon robur accipiet Hadriani rescriptum ex lege Talionis, Sicut voluit facere alteri, sic fiet illi? Deut. 19. 19. Sed hac de re Theologi & Jurisconsulti viderint. At dices Vulgatum quoque ponere effectum, si τὸ percusserit exponas occiderit, ut passim in Scriptura, ut sensus sit, Qui occiderit virum, non casu, sed volens occidere id est ἐκ προνοίας, data opera. Esto. Sed nihilominus ex hac versione sic accepta videri posset illud sequi, eum qui percusserit alium vel laeserit, non quidem animo occidendi, sed tantum laedendi, etiamsi mors e vestigio subsequatur, non esse reum mortis, nec teneri homicidii. Id si obtineret, semper impunitatis spes nefarios homines ad homicidia proleCtaret, nunquam praetextus deessent. Et quis hic judex esset? Unde Cajetanus, Pensat lex effectum secutae mortis ex percussione, non curando an ille percusserit animo occidendi, an vero percutiendi animo duntaxat. Et merito, percussiones enim non mensurantur. Et Oleastrius, Ponitur lex, inquit, in communi, ut omnis percutiens sive intendat occidere, SIVE NON, & percussus fuerit mortuus, talis morte erat plectendus: sed statim ponuntur exceptiones ab hac lege. Collatio versus sequentis non juvat Vulgatum. Ibi enim non absolvitur homicidii, qui occiderit proximum nolens occidere, sed, ne quidem percutere aut ladere volens vel intendens. Sola itaque intentio percutiencutiendi, si mox subsequatur mors, hoc versu quem jam castigavimus, morte multatur. LXX. nihil variant a fontibus, ἐὰν ... ἀντὶ ... ἀντὶ ..., ut nec Chaldaeus uterque. Lubet hic coronidis loco adjicere Mishnam Thalmudicam ex Massecheth Sanhedrin cap. 9. ex qua intelliget Lector, quam latam illi fenestram, hoc intentionum obtentu aperuerint caeciilli duces. נחכוין להרוג את הבהמה והרג את האדם ‎לנכרי והרג את ישראל לנפילים והרג ארת בן קיימא פטור Si quis intendat occidere bestiam & occidit hominem: si intendat occidere gentilem & occidit Israelitam; Apostatam, & occidet filium foederis, liber est, vid à poena gladii. נתכוון להכותו על מתניו ולא היה בה כדי להמיתו על מתניו והלכה לה על לבו ומת פטור id est Si intendat plagam inferre lumbis alterius, & quidem talem quae non evaluisset eum ista parte corporis occidere, & plaga illa aberrans impacta fuerit cordi seu pectori, fueritque talis ut potuerit eum occidere illa parte corporis & moriatur, ille liber est. Pergunt Magistri nostri, Si intendat ejusmodi plagam infligere adulto, quae non valeret occidere adultum & illa per errorem infligatur parvulo, fueritque talis ut potuerit eum neci dare, & moriatur, liber est. Si intendat percutere parvulum plaga, quae ipsi lethalis esse potuisset, & illa incidat in adultum, cui lethalis esse non poterat, & tamen moriatur, liber est. At qui intendit plagam inferre lumbis alicujus, quae posset esse isthic loci lethalis, & aberrans excipiatur pectore & mors subsequatur, ille reus est. Iterum, si quis intendat percutere adultum plaga ejusmodi, quae ipsum letho dare posset, & per errorem ladatur parvulus, & mortem oppetat, & ille reus est, R. Simeon, inquit, Etiamsi intendat occidere hunc & occidat illum, liber est. Hactenus Misna. Equidem ita statuo, in casibus dubiis & obscuris nulla satis de morte hominis cunctatio longa est. Et satius esse nocentem absolvere, quam innocentem damnare. Recto tramite incedendum est. Ubi ille non semper apparet, quicquid aequo plus futurum est, in hanc clementiae partem potius praeponderet. Sed ejusmodi commentis legi divinae intercedere imo, manifeste illudere, antiquare, id vero gravissimum scelus duco.
units.tr: These words are attacked by Cajetan, John Benedict and Oleastro. And indeed the words of the Law say something else. Let us hear it: He who strikes a man and he dies (that is, so that he dies) shall be punished with death. Behold, the law speaks of the effect of the blow, whereas the Vulgate seems to speak of the intention, so that even if death does not follow, the will is punished with death. Lyra contradicts this opinion in these words: But if he did not kill by striking, however much he wished to kill, he would not for that reason be punished with death. I see that many interpreters have followed Lyra's view. The Emperor Hadrian, however, rescripted the contrary. And indeed, if the judge is certain about the intention, would Hadrian's rescript not gain strength from the law of retaliation, As he intended to do to another, so shall it be done to him? Deut. 19. 19. But let theologians and jurists look to that question. You will say that the Vulgate also posits the effect, if you explain the word "percusserit" [τὸ] as "occiderit", as happens everywhere in Scripture, so that the sense is "he who killed a man", not by chance but wishing to kill, that is, deliberately [ἐκ προνοίας], with set purpose. Granted. Nevertheless, from this version so understood it could seem to follow that one who strikes or injures another, not indeed with intent to kill but only to injure, is not guilty of death and not liable for homicide, even if death follows at once. If this held, the hope of impunity would always entice wicked men to murder, and pretexts would never be lacking. And who would be the judge here? Hence Cajetan: The law weighs the effect of the death that follows from the blow, not caring whether he struck with intent to kill or only with intent to strike. And rightly so, for blows are not measured. And Oleastro: The law, he says, is laid down in general, that every striker, whether he intends to kill or not, and the struck man dies, must be punished with such a death; but exceptions to this law are stated at once. The comparison with the following verse does not help the Vulgate. For there one is not absolved of homicide who kills his neighbour without wishing to kill, but one who does not even wish or intend to strike or injure. Therefore the intention alone to strike, if death follows at once, is punished with death by this verse, which we have already censured. The Seventy vary nothing from the sources, if ... instead of ... instead of ... [ἐὰν ... ἀντὶ ... ἀντὶ ...], nor do both Chaldee paraphrasts. Here I would like, by way of a conclusion, to add the Talmudic Mishnah from Massechet Sanhedrin chapter 9, from which the reader will understand what a wide window those blind leaders have opened under the pretext of intention. [נחכוין להרוג את הבהמה והרג את האדם לנכרי והרג את ישראל לנפילים והרג את בן קיימא פטור] If someone intends to kill a beast and kills a man; if he intends to kill a gentile and kills an Israelite; an apostate, and kills a son of the covenant, he is free from the punishment of the sword. [נתכוון להכותו על מתניו ולא היה בה כדי להמיתו על מתניו והלכה לה על לבו ומת פטור] That is: If he intends to strike another on the loins, and the blow was not such as to kill him on the loins, and it went off and struck his heart or chest, and he died, he is free, provided the blow was such that it could have killed him in that part of the body and he died. Our masters go on: If he intends to inflict on an adult a blow that could not kill an adult, and by mistake it is inflicted on a child, and the blow was such that it could have caused his death, and he dies, he is free. If he intends to strike a child with a blow that could have been lethal to him, and it lands on an adult, to whom it could not be lethal, and yet he dies, he is free. But he who intends to inflict a blow on the loins of someone, which could there be lethal, and it goes astray and lands on the chest, and death follows, he is guilty. Again, if someone intends to strike an adult with a blow of such a kind that could bring him to death, and by mistake a child is hurt and meets death, he is guilty. Rabbi Simeon says: Even if he intends to kill this one and kills that one, he is free. So far the Mishnah. For my part I hold this: in doubtful and obscure cases no long hesitation is needed about a man's death, and it is better to acquit the guilty than to condemn the innocent. One must walk the straight path. Where that path does not always appear, whatever is more likely to be fair should be weighed in favour of this side of clemency. But to intercede with such inventions against the divine law, or rather to mock it openly and abolish it, I count the gravest of crimes.

units.la: Vers. 21.
units.tr: Verse 21.

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Si rixati fuerint viri & percusserint mulierem prægnantem, וייצאו ילדיה ולא יהיה אסון puniendo punietur. | Si rixati fuerint viri & percusserit quis mulierem prægnantem & abortivum quidem fecerit, sed ipsa vixerit, subjacebit damno.
units.tr: Hebrew | Vulgate. If men quarrel and strike a pregnant woman, so that her children come out and there is no harm [וייצאו ילדיה ולא יהיה אסון], he shall be punished with a fine as the husband of the woman requires. | If men quarrel and someone strikes a pregnant woman and makes her miscarry, but she herself survives, he shall be liable to a fine.

units.la: In Ebr. textu est אסון exitium vel mors simpliciter, ut tam ad mortem prolis quam matris referri possit, imo debeat, Vulgatus ad solam matrem restringit. Cajetanus, negatur mors tam matris quam prolis. Eandem censuram stringit idem Cardinalis in versum sequentem. אם אסון יהיה : Et si mors fuerit subsecuta.
units.tr: In the Hebrew text the word אסון means ruin or death in general, so it can and indeed should be taken as referring both to the death of the child and to the death of the mother. The Vulgate restricts it to the mother alone. Cajetan says: "the death of the mother and of the child is denied." The same Cardinal makes the same criticism of the following verse, אם אסון יהיה: "And if death follows."

units.la: Sic enim ad hæc, considerat lex ista de percussore mulieris gravidæ duos casus; primo, si non erit mors sive matris sive proles, & tunc punietur percussor pœna arbitraria: Alterum, si intervenerit mors & tunc punietur pœna homicidii. Infanticida tam reus erat quam matricida, inquit Cor. à Lapide. Idem, inquit, judicium si percussor non occidisset prægnantem, sed illi prolem jam animatam excussisset. Id diserte indicant Lxx. &c. Et Carthus. ejus] matris vel fœtus jam animati. Chaldæus quoque manet in generalibus, אם לא יהיה מותא si non fuerit mors, & postea, אם מותא יהי si mors fuerit; quod ideo noto, ne quis versionem Fagii secutus existimet Chaldæum ad mulierem ea restrinxisse. Sic enim ille vertit, Ipsa tamen non morietur. Et postea, si autem mortua fuerit. Qui vel Chaldaice legere didicit, videbit nimium hic sibi indulsisse Pagium. Sed de universo hoc textu ego sic arbitror, si de sola muliere mors intelligatur, legem esse supervacaneam. Occisor enim ejus lege generali tenetur. Vide Lyram & marginalia Benedicti. Utrque enim à nobis stat. Lxx. hic longius à verbis Ebr. deviarunt, dum sic vertunt hæc verba, ולא יהיה אסון / μὴ ἐξεπονισμένον, & egressus infans ejus non fuerit effigiatus id est non habuerit figuram hominis. De sensu Physici & Medici viderint. Si enim simulac effigiatus, est, infunditur rationalis anima, uti videntur Lxx. statuisse, sensum, qua ad fœtum spectat, non male expressere. Vide Augustin. Quæst.80. in Exodum.
units.tr: For this law, as they put it, considers two cases in the striker of a pregnant woman. First, if there is no death, either of the mother or of the child, and then the striker is punished by an arbitrary penalty. Second, if death follows, then he is punished with the penalty for homicide. The child-killer was as guilty as the mother-killer, says Cornelius à Lapide. The same judgement holds, he says, if the striker did not kill the pregnant woman but drove out the child already ensouled. The Septuagint and others state this plainly. The Carthusian: "of the mother or of the foetus already ensouled." The Chaldee paraphrast also keeps to general terms: אם לא יהיה מותא, "if there is no death," and then אם מותא יהי, "if there is death." I note this so that no one who follows Pagninus's version thinks the Chaldee restricted it to the woman. For he translates: "She herself, however, shall not die," and afterwards, "but if she dies." Anyone who has learned even to read Chaldee will see that Pagninus has taken too much liberty here. But on the whole text my view is this: if death is understood of the woman alone, the law is superfluous, since her killer is already bound by the general law. See Lyra and the marginal notes of Benedict; both of them agree with us. The Septuagint depart here further from the Hebrew words, rendering ולא יהיה אסון as μὴ ἐξεπονισμένον, "and the child that came out [was] not formed," that is, did not have the form of a man [ἐξεπονισμένον]. Let the physicians and natural philosophers decide about the meaning. If indeed, as soon as the child is formed, the rational soul is infused, as the Septuagint seem to have held, then they have rendered the sense well as far as the foetus is concerned. See Augustine, Questions on Exodus 80.

units.la: Et ascendit Moses & Aharon & Nadab & Abiud & LXX. senioribus Israëlis, καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἐκτῶν τῆς Ισραὴλ ν διεφώνησεν * ὑδε εἰς Quæ sic conversa invenio in codice Basileensi, Et electorum Israel non dissonuit neque unus. Et quis aliter istas Græcas interpretaretur? Διαφωνέω enim est dissono, discrepo, dissentio: Non est dubium quin Græci patres, Latinique, qui ad xoilii Latinè versam commentati sunt, multa ἀπωεσθιόντος ad hunc locum convectaverint. Dico ἀπωεσθιόντος. Nihil enim tale originalibus tabulis continetur. Sic enim illic legimus, וְאֶל־אֲצִילֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ & in selectos filiorum Israel non misit manum suam. id est non affecit eos ullo malo, non læsit eos, non occidit eos, non enim temere sed Deo jubente accesserant. hoc illud est, quod subjicit, viderunt Deum & ederunt & biberunt. Hoc est, viderunt Deum & vivi incolumesque manse-re, non examinati sunt ex gloriosa illa visione. Confer Jud.13.22. Immittere manum in aliquem, aliquando significat, lædere, detrimentum inferre, occidere. Esther 2.21 quaesiverunt manum immittere in Regem Assuerum. Hanc sententiam expressere LXX. verbo διεφώνησεν, In Latina Editione Romanâ invenies locum hunc sic conversum, Et electorum Israel nullus detrimentum accepit. Alii, nullus exanimatus est. H. Stephanus in Thesaurô, διαφωνέω pro exanimari sæpe ἐν τῷ σωμ. ἱπποτεχνῶν. Moschopulus, Διαφωνεῖν dicitur interdum, ὅταν ἀπηχεῖσθαι τις ὑπὸ δυναμεων βοῶσι, εἶτα μήτε ἀχαίνης, qualia, inquit, accidunt illis, qui ἀπὸ τῶν δυνάμεων ἀπηχεῖσθαι βοᾶν. Addit Stephanus, Atin v. l. legitur διαπεφώνηκεν, extremam vocem edidit, expiravit, ex Chrysost. Hactenus Steph. Locum Chrysostomi invenies Comment. in Psal. μζ. pag. 662. Tomi I. Edit. Savilianæ. Ἀγαπεφωνηκαμεν, ἀπωλόμεθα. Ad quem locum Boisius in notis, Ἀγαπεφωνηκαμεν, ἀπωλόμεθα, vox propria ἡ ὁ id est Septuaginta. Hactenus ille. Sic ergo locum istum interpretabimur, Et electorum Israëlis nullus expiravit, id est nullus periit, vel quod hic æquivalens erit, nullus desideratus fuit. Huic expositioni fir-manmandæ adducam duo loca ex Lxx. Ezech.37.11. ubi Ebræa, לָנוּ נִגְזַרְנוּ excisi sumus nobis, Lxx. Ἀπολώλαμεν ἡμῖν id est periimus. Num.31.49. וְלֹא נִפְקַד מִמֶּנּוּ אִישׁ & non desideratus fuit * è nobis quisquam. καὶ οὐκ ἀπέθανεν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐδεὶς εἰς id est ex illis qui nobis commissi fuere, qui fuerunt in manu, sive, potestate nostra, hoc est, ex nobis, ex nostro numero. [ Coronidis loco illud addam, magnum Heinsium acute observasse, ex hoc Exodi loco prout ille vulgo intellectus fuit, natam esse fabulam de consensu Lxx. Interpretum. Scilicet quod hic de Lxx. Senibus à Mose delectis legebant, ad illos quoque, qui Græcæ versioni elaborandæ destinati fuere, tanstulerunt. Vide ejus Aristarchum sacrum pag.207. ]
units.tr: "And Moses went up, and Aaron, and Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel." The Septuagint has καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἐκλεκτῶν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ οὐ διεφώνησεν, which in the Basel codex I find translated thus: "And of the elect of Israel not one dissented." And how else would anyone translate those Greek words? For διαφωνέω means to sound discordantly, to disagree, to dissent. There is no doubt that the Greek Fathers, and the Latins who wrote commentaries on the Latin version, gathered many [remarks] on this passage that are not to the point. I say "not to the point," for nothing of the sort is contained in the original tablets. There we read: וְאֶל־אֲצִילֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ, "and upon the chosen men of the sons of Israel he did not lay his hand," that is, he did not harm them, did not injure them, did not kill them, for they had not approached rashly but at God's command. This is what is added: "they saw God, and they ate and drank." That is, they saw God and remained alive and unharmed; they were not destroyed by that glorious vision. Compare Judges 13:22. To "lay a hand upon someone" sometimes means to injure, to do harm, to kill. Esther 2:21: "they sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus." The Seventy expressed this sense by the word διεφώνησεν. In the Roman Latin edition you will find this passage rendered: "And none of the elect of Israel suffered harm." Others: "none was put to death." Henri Estienne in the Thesaurus says that διαφωνέω often means to be deprived of life, ἐν τῷ σωμ. ἱπποτεχνῶν. Moschopulus says that διαφωνεῖν is sometimes used when people are cried down by [the violence of] powers, and then [they fail to answer/breathe], as, he says, happens to those who are struck down by the powers and cry out. Estienne adds that another reading is διαπεφώνηκεν, meaning he gave out his last breath, he expired, from Chrysostom. So far Estienne. You will find the passage of Chrysostom in his Commentary on Psalm 47 [or 46], page 662 of the first volume of the Savile edition: "We have ceased to speak [with the voice], we are lost." On which passage Boissonade in his notes says: "We have ceased to speak, we are lost," the proper word here being the Septuagint's. So far he. Thus we shall interpret the passage: "And of the elect of Israel not one expired," that is, not one perished, or what amounts to the same thing here, not one was missing. To confirm this interpretation I will adduce two passages from the Septuagint. Ezekiel 37:11, where the Hebrew לָנוּ נִגְזַרְנוּ means "we are cut off for ourselves," and the Septuagint has Ἀπολώλαμεν ἡμῖν, that is, "we have perished." Numbers 31:49: וְלֹא נִפְקַד מִמֶּנּוּ אִישׁ, "and not one man of us was missing," and the Septuagint: καὶ οὐκ ἀπέθανεν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐδεὶς, "and none of them died," that is, of those who were committed to us, who were in our hand or power, that is, of us, of our number. [As a crowning remark I will add that the great Heinsius observed shrewdly that from this passage of Exodus, as it was commonly understood, arose the fable of the agreement of the Seventy translators. Namely, people read here that the seventy elders were chosen by Moses, and transferred this to those who were appointed to prepare the Greek version. See his Aristarchus Sacer, page 207.]

units.la: Ibidem, electorum Israel] August. Quæst in Exodum, quæst. 102. Quis dubitet illos, quos nominatim expressit & LXX. seniores, nunc appellatos electos Israel, qui proculdubio personam gerebant eorum qui electi sunt in populo Dei. Non enim omnium est fides. In magna autem domo sunt alia vasa in honorem alia in contumeliam. Quoniam ergo quos ante prascivit & prædestinavit — quos autem justificavit & glorificavit, profecto de electis Israel non dissonuit nec unus. Hæc alieno loco à doctissimo patre disseri judicabit quisquis originarium textum expenderit.
units.tr: "Among the elect of Israel": Augustine, Questions on Exodus, question 102. "Who can doubt that those whom he named, and whom the Seventy call elders, are now called the elect of Israel, who without doubt bore the person of those who are chosen among the people of God? For faith is not of all. But in a great house there are other vessels, some for honour, others for dishonour. Therefore, those whom he foreknew and predestined ... and those whom he justified and glorified: certainly none of the elect of Israel dissented, not even one." Anyone who examines the original text will judge that the very learned Father has argued this at a passage where it does not belong.
