units.la: De VRIM & THVMMIM
units.tr: Of the Urim and Thummim

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Et pones in pectorali judicii Vrim & Thummin, id est ad verbum, testibus Cajet. Aria & aliis. ignes seu illuminationes & perfectiones. | Pones autem in rationali judicii doctrinam & veritatem.
units.tr: Hebrew: "And you shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim," that is, word for word, as Cajetan, Arias and others testify: "lights or illuminations and perfections." Vulgate: "But you shall put in the rational of judgment doctrine and truth."

units.la: Varias de Vrim & Thummim opiniones videbis apud Vatablum & Fagium in Chald. Paraphrasin Onceli, ex quo libro non tantum hoc, sed & pleraque alia desumpta sunt, quæ sub nomine Vatablinarum notarum edita sunt. Multa quoque de eis habet in magnis Ann. Cl. Drusius. Nos impræsentiarum examinemus hæc vulgati gemina interpretamenta. Vrim extra omnem con- troversiam hactenus creditum fuit descendere ab אור luxit, un- de אור ignis & lux. Similiter Thummim à תמים perfectus fuit. Singulare הם / ut א עור fit עורים gnuzzim, juxta consuetudinem duplicantium Ain.. Provoco ad omnia Lexica Ebraeorum, Christianorum, Protestantium & Pontificiorum. Unde Aquila Le- vit.8.8. φωτισμὸς καὶ τελειώσεις reddidit, illuminationes & perse- ctiones. Sed res magis clara quam ut tot verbis opus sit. Voluit autem Deus his vocibus illud inculcatum, Pontifici splendorem seu lumen scientiæ & integritatem vitæ inesse oportere. Sed quo- modo has voces interpretatus est Vulgatus? Doctrinam & veritatem. Admodum coacte, si spectas themata. Atque hic non possum non deplorare quorundam ex recentioribus Papistis mise- ram & plusquam servilem conditionem, quib. ne dubitare qui- dem de veritate hujus interpretamenti sinit Concilii Tridentini Canon. nec rursus mirari satis possum quorundam impudentiam, qui etiam ineptissima in suum vertere satagunt emolumentum. Ecce enim Bellarminus dum in infallibilitate Papæ astruenda laborat, facit quod furibundi homines afflolent, quidvis arripit, lapides, faces, ligna,ludesque præustas, furiosus sedis Romanæ zelus armis ministrat. Pontifex Vet. Teft. in pectorali habebat doctrinam & veritatem: ergo Pontifex Novi Testamenti, Papa, cum totam Ecclesiam docet in his quæ ad fidem pertinent, nullo casu errare potest. Quam bene à Pontifice Vet. Test. ad Pontificem Novi procedat argumentatio, Theologi discussere. Tu illud nota, Lector, si genuina illa interpretamenta, splendorem & integritatem sumsisset, sic ipsi inferendum fuisset, Ergo in Papa splendor cognit. & integritas vitæ est. At prævidit Bellarminus, hæreticos opposituros vitas Pontificum, quotidianam experientiam, ipsamque adeo ipsius Bellarmini confessionem, quam in Præfat. istius Controversiæ vis veritatis ei extorserat, vid. plerosque Papas fuisse sceleratissima monstra. Sed videamus quomodo eam versionem stabiliat Bellarminus. Ea enim si cadat, simul & argumentum satis alias elumbe corruat necesse est. Dicit illuminationem μεταλητικῶς, sumi posse pro doctrina, ut φωτίζω pro doceo. Sed ut hoc tolerabile est, ita illud plane intolerabile quod dicit in progressu, תה אורים / descendere, quod in Hiphil הורה docuit, ut & Thummim ab אמת verax fuit.
units.tr: You will find various opinions about the Urim and Thummim in Vatablus and Fagius on the Chaldee paraphrase of Onkelos, from which book not only this but many other things were taken, which were published under the name of Vatablus's notes. Much about them is also in the great work of the distinguished Drusius. For the present let us examine these two renderings of the Vulgate. That Urim, beyond all controversy, has hitherto been believed to come from אור [or], "to shine," whence אור "fire" and "light." Similarly Thummim has been taken from תמים [tamim], "to be perfect." The singular form, as עור becomes עורים [urim], follows the custom of doubling the Ayin. I appeal to all the lexicons of the Hebrews, Christians, Protestants and Papists. Hence Aquila at Lev. 8.8 rendered it φωτισμὸς καὶ τελειώσεις [phōtismos kai teleiōseis], "illuminations and perfections." But the matter is clearer than it needs so many words. God wished by these terms to impress upon us that the high priest ought to have splendour, or the light of knowledge, and integrity of life. But how has the Vulgate translated these words? As doctrine and truth. This is very forced, if you look at the themes. And here I cannot but deplore the wretched and more than servile condition of some of the more recent Papists, to whom the canon of the Council of Trent does not even permit doubt about the truth of this rendering. Nor again can I sufficiently wonder at the impudence of some who strive to turn even the most absurd things to their own advantage. For see, Bellarmine, while labouring to establish the infallibility of the Pope, does what raging men are wont to do: he snatches up whatever comes to hand, stones, torches, wood, and half-burnt brands; the furious zeal of the Roman See supplies the weapons. The High Priest of the Old Testament had doctrine and truth in his breastplate: therefore the High Priest of the New Testament, the Pope, when he teaches the whole Church in matters that pertain to faith, can in no case err. How well this argument proceeds from the High Priest of the Old Testament to the Pope of the New, the theologians have discussed. Note this, reader: had he taken the genuine renderings, splendour and integrity, the conclusion would have had to be drawn thus: Therefore in the Pope there is splendour of knowledge and integrity of life. But Bellarmine foresaw that heretics would oppose the lives of the Popes, everyday experience, and indeed Bellarmine's own confession, which the force of truth had extorted from him in the preface of that controversy, namely that most of the Popes were most wicked monsters. But let us see how Bellarmine supports that version. For if it falls, the argument, already weak enough, must necessarily collapse with it. He says that illumination may be taken metaleptically for doctrine, as φωτίζω [phōtizō] is used for doceo. But as this much is tolerable, so what he goes on to say is plainly intolerable: that תורה [torah] descends from אורים, which in the Hiphil הורה means "taught," and that Thummim too comes from אמת [emet], "truthful."

units.la: Quis unquam adeo portentosam originationem somniavit? Ego certe cum apud Rainoldum eam primo citatam viderem, in stuporem datus sum, & licet veracissimum in allegationibus Theologum illum semper expertus sim, tantum a me impetrare non potui ut beatæ isti animæ, nisi ipso Bellarm. inspecto, fidem adhiberem. Sed in majorem admirationem dedit me Bellarmini argumentum quo versionem Vulgatam constabilitum it. Plus, inquit, credendum est Hieronymo qui doctrinam vertit & veritatem, & tôn LXX. qui verterunt, διʼ λωσιν καὶ Αλλ-θεων, * quam Judæis & Judaizantibus. Sed quid respondebis Rainoldo, Bellarmine, roganti te unde διʼ λωσιν descendat? An ea tibi fiducia, ea frons, ut diceres à διδασκω? Certe si tibi ipsi constare velis, deducenda tibi ea vox à διδάσκω est, cur enim & hic non potius Hieronymo credendum qui doctrinam vertit, quam Lexicis? Omnem vero impudentiam & ἀναιἀναιαν supergreditur originatio vocis חָמִים ut sit ab אָמַן Ausim ad ipsam Bellar. conscientiam, ad omnes omnium Pontificiarum Academiarum Professores Ebræos provocare. Augustinus Steuchus Episcopus licet asserat Vrim deduci posse ab הורים tamen non ita frontem posuit, Thummim ab Aman deduci posse asseruerit. Ea quam posui originatio Regulis Grammaticis, omniumque Ebræorum & Christianorum Lexicis conformis est, astipulatores habet * Papistas ipsos, quotquot ante Conc. Trid. & post illud extra calorem disputationis commentati sunt, conservat in singulis tres radicales, siquidem ם in Thummim ob dages potestate duplex est. At quid tale in sua Originatione monstrabit Cardinalis? In utraque voce una manebit radicalis; in priori ר / in poster. ם / Sic Balbus lib.2· de Nat. Deor. apud Cicer deducebat Neptunum à nando, unica litera retentâ, at hoc in persona Cottæ false ridet Cicero, aitque Balbum magis sibi in ea originatione visum natasse quam Neptunum. Ad primam respondebit, sc. Vrim, primam thematis delitescere in vocali longa Shurek, tertiamque He ita solere elidi cum aliquid additur, ut à שָׁנִים fit שנים / At quid in voce Thummim consilii? ubi א ס אָמָן? Quiescit, inquies. At in qua vocali longa? Nulla utique hic contractio est, ut in מלף pro מאלף / Et quæ ratio hæmanthicæ? An unquam vel sando auditum est, א compensari per Dages præeunte Kibbuts sub ה servili? Ubi ultima? Periisse dices ut in אַפְּרֶ pro אַפְּרָ/ Esto, sed ea apparet in compensatione simulac aliquid additur, ut in אֲפֵךְ cujus hic nullum vestigium. Sed, inquit, Hieronymus Thummim vertit veritatem. Ergo deducenda vox à themate in quo veritatis notio. Et mihi ergo sic liceat argumentari, vocem Thummim Deut.33.8. Hieron. vertit perfectio, Ergo derivanda à themate quod perfectionem significat. At illud est תָּמִים/ non semper itaque Hieron. veritatem vertit. Et quid si semper? Quando Hieronymi interpretatio Lexicorum norma esse coepit? Nec eam mentem fuisse Tridentinis, nec hoc ubique admissurum Bellarminum mihi persuadeo. καὶ ταῦτα μὴ δὲ Ζούτη.
units.tr: Who ever dreamed up so monstrous a derivation? I certainly, when I first saw it cited by Rainolds, was struck dumb, and although I have always found that theologian most truthful in his citations, I could not bring myself to give credence to that blessed soul without looking at Bellarmine himself. But Bellarmine's argument for establishing the Vulgate rendering astonished me even more: More credence is to be given, he says, to Jerome, who translated doctrine and truth, and to the Seventy, who rendered it διὰ δήλωσιν καὶ ἀλήθειαν [dia dēlōsin kai alētheian], than to the Jews and those who judaize. But what will you answer Rainolds, Bellarmine, when he asks you whence διὰ δήλωσιν comes? Do you have such confidence, such effrontery, as to say it comes from διδάσκω [didaskō]? Certainly, if you wish to be consistent with yourself, that word must be derived from διδάσκω; why then, here, should one not rather believe Jerome, who translated doctrine, than the lexicons? But the derivation of the word חָמִים [tummim] from אָמַן [aman] surpasses all impudence and ἀναισχυντία [anaischyntia]. I would dare to appeal to Bellarmine's own conscience, and to all the Hebrew professors of all the Papist academies. Augustinus Steuchus, the bishop, although he asserts that Urim can be derived from הורים, did not put on such a brazen face as to assert that Thummim can be derived from Aman. The origin I have set out conforms to the rules of grammar and to the lexicons of all Hebrews and Christians; it has as its supporters the Papists themselves, as many as wrote before and after the Council of Trent when they were outside the heat of disputation; it keeps three radicals in each word, since the ם in Thummim, because of the dagesh, has a double value. But what like this will the Cardinal show in his derivation? In both words only one radical will remain: in the former ר, in the latter ם. Thus Balbus in the second book of Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods derived Neptune from nando, "to swim," retaining a single letter; but Cicero mocks this in the person of Cotta, and says that Balbus seemed to himself in that derivation to swim rather than Neptune. To the first word, Urim, he will reply that the first radical lies hidden in the long vowel shureq, and that the third, he, is usually elided when something is added, as שָׁנִים becomes שנים. But what plan is there in the word Thummim? Where is the א of אָמָן? It lies hidden, you will say. But in which long vowel? There is no contraction here at all, as in מלף for מאלף. And what analogical reason is there? Was it ever heard, even in a dream, that an א is compensated by a dagesh after a preceding kibbuts under a servile ה? Where is the last letter? You will say it has perished, as in אַפְּרֶ for אַפְּרָ. Granted, but it appears in compensation as soon as something is added, as in אֲפֵךְ, of which there is no trace here. But, he says, Jerome translated Thummim as veritatem. Therefore the word must be derived from the root in which the notion of truth lies. Then I too may argue thus: Jerome translated the word Thummim in Deut. 33.8 as perfectio; therefore it must be derived from a root that signifies perfection. But that root is תָּמִים. So Jerome did not always translate veritatem. And what if he always did? When did the interpretation of Jerome begin to be the norm of the lexicons? I am persuaded that this was neither the mind of the Tridentine fathers nor something Bellarmine will allow everywhere. And these things: [obscure].

units.la: Et ignorabat Moses quod קָרַן cutis facici suae. | Et ignorabat Moses quod cornuta esset facies sua.
units.tr: And Moses did not know that the skin of his face sent out rays [קָרַן]. | And Moses did not know that his face was horned.

units.la: Vox Ebraea קרן significat radios cornuum instar emittere. Unde Lxx. apposite, ὅτι δεδόξασται ἡ ὄψις τοῦ χρώτος αὐτοῦ. Ad quam versionem Apostolus 2. Cor.3. allusit. Oncelos, quod multus esset splendor gloriae faciei suae. Jonathan tanquam interpres Lxx. quod glorificatus esset splendor aspectus faciei suae. Hieron. secutus Aquilam qui ante verterat, κεκερασμένος vertit, cornuta esset. Jam audiamus Steuchum Episcopum Xisamensem, Vox ambigua fecit in Editione errorem. Non enim habetur in contextu Ebr. faciem Moysis fuisse cornutam, sed radiantem fuisse cutem. Ex hoc potest emendari prava consuetudo, qua duobus cornibus pingunt Mosen; non enim cornua e fronte egrediebantur, sed & frons & nasus & os & mentum radiabant. Et mirum quod Hieron. non consideratā veritate Ebraica non adverterat etiam quid LXX. transtulissent, qui bene hunc locum transtulerunt. Eident itaque nos & exe-cran-
units.tr: The Hebrew word קרן means to send out rays like horns. Hence the Seventy aptly render it, because the appearance of his skin was glorified [ὅτι δεδόξασται ἡ ὄψις τοῦ χρώτος αὐτοῦ]. The Apostle alludes to this version in 2 Corinthians 3. Onkelos has that there was much splendour of glory on his face. Jonathan, like the Seventy's translator, has that the splendour of the appearance of his face was glorified. Jerome, following Aquila, who had earlier rendered it, translated κεκερασμένος as horned [cornuta esset]. Now let us hear Steuchus, Bishop of Cisamum: An ambiguous word produced the error in the edition. For the Hebrew context does not say that Moses' face was horned, but that his skin shone. From this the bad custom of painting Moses with two horns can be corrected; for the horns did not stand out from his forehead, but his forehead, nose, mouth and chin all shone. It is strange that Jerome, not attending to the Hebrew truth, did not notice even what the Seventy had rendered, though they translated this passage well. So let them look at it, and the Jews execr-

units.la: Oleastr. non intelligas Mosem cornua in facie prominentia habuisse ut perperam a pictoribus pingitur, sed quod radii a cute faciei ipsius ad modum cornuum egrediebantur ex locutione cum Deo. crantur Judæi, quoties Mosen in templis nostris cornuta facie depictum vident, quasi nos eum Diabolum quendam (Drufius addit, aut uxorem ejus adulteram, ei enim qui uxorem adulteram habet affingi solere duo cornua ex Apologis Ebraicis probat) esse putemus. Hæc Steuchus. Cajet. vertit. cornificavit, & addit, Emissio radiorum metaphorice appellatur cornificatio, eò quod tanquam emissio cornuum sit emissio radiorum. Vide & Benedict. & Senensem. Vide & Ferum & Oleastrium in hunc locum. Nec dissentit Bellarminus. Et Thomas non dubitat asserere, faciem Mosis melius dici splendidam quam cornutam, maleque ipsi appingi cornua e capite egredientia. Cur igitur illud sibi sumere non fuere ausi Pontifices, ut pro cornuta reponerent splendida? Mirari & illud lubet, Pontifices Sixtum & Clementem in novis suis Bibliis approbasse vulgi à tot doctis damnatam consuetudinem, quas Mosi appicti radii non e tota facie micantes, sed duorum instar cornuum e capite ascendentes. Utrum hoc factum sit ad Vulgatam Edit. statuminandam, an vero ad defendendas Episcoporum bicornes mitras, an ad utrumque, merito quærit Rainoldus.
units.tr: Oleaster: you should not understand that Moses had horns projecting from his face, as painters wrongly depict him, but that rays went out from the skin of his face in the manner of horns, from his speaking with God. The Jews execrate [us] whenever they see Moses depicted with a horned face in our churches, as if we thought him some devil (Drusius adds, or his adulterous wife, for he proves from Hebrew fables that two horns are commonly attached to one who has an adulterous wife). So Steuchus. Cajetan translates he horned [cornificavit], and adds: The emission of rays is called metaphorically horning, because the emission of rays is like the emission of horns. See also Benedict and the Sienese. See also Ferus and Oleaster on this passage. Bellarmine does not dissent. And Thomas does not hesitate to assert that Moses' face is better described as shining than as horned, and that it is wrongly attributed to him that horns project from his head. Why, then, did the Pontiffs not dare to take this for themselves, and to put shining in place of horned? It is also worth wondering that the Pontiffs Sixtus and Clement, in their new Bible, approved the custom of the common people, condemned by so many learned men, of depicting rays on Moses not shining from the whole face but rising from his head like two horns. Whether this was done to establish the Vulgate edition, or rather to defend the bishops' two-horned mitres, or both, Rainolds rightly asks.

units.la: Ebr.: הצובאות אשר צבאו E speculis ad ostium tabernaculi conventus. | Vulg.: E speculis mulierum quæ excubabant in ostio tabernaculi.
units.tr: Hebrew: from the mirrors of the women who assembled at the entrance of the tabernacle of the congregation [הצובאות אשר צבאו]. Vulgate: from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle.

units.la: Eadem vox צובאות extat 1. Sam. 2. 22. ubi vertit Vulg. quæ observabant. Nomen צבא significat exercitum & turmam militum. Unde optime reddas, è speculis mulierum turmatim convenientium, quæ turmatim conveniebant ad ost. t. Conv. vel quæ circumexercituabant tabernaculum, ut ex Gloss. veteri citat Cl. Casaub. Alii simpl. vertunt, convenientium. Vulgatus, excubabant, quod interpretamentum occasionem Papistis dedit locum hunc adducendi ad probandam hanc thesin, in V. T. fœminas voto religionis astrictas fuisse, quæ in cellis circa templum habitantes inde nunquam recesserint. De quo somnio prolixe Casaub. Exerc. 1. cap. 23. cujus scrinia non compilabo. Est enim aut saltem debebat istud opus in omnium manibus esse. Num. de Gersonitis usurpatur idem verbi, quos tamen expleto ministerii tempore sibi invicem successisse atque à tabernaculo recessisse certo certius est.
units.tr: The same word צובאות occurs in 1 Sam. 2:22, where the Vulgate renders it who kept watch. The noun צבא means both army and troop of soldiers. So you may well render it: from the mirrors of women gathering in companies, who came together in companies to the entrance of the tent of meeting, or who formed a host around the tabernacle, as the old gloss cited by the illustrious Casaubon has it. Others simply translate it assembling. The Vulgate's kept watch gave the Papists an occasion to cite this passage in support of their thesis that women bound by a vow of religion lived in the Old Testament in cells around the temple and never left them. Casaubon discusses this fancy at length in Exercitationes 1, chapter 23, and I will not plunder his stores here. That work is, or at least ought to be, in everyone's hands. In Numbers the same verb is used of the Gershonites, who, however, when their period of service was over, certainly and most surely took turns with one another and withdrew from the tabernacle.

units.la: Si fœmina תִּזְרִיעַ & pepererit masculum. | Mulier si suscepto semine peperit masculum.
units.tr: If a woman gives seed [תִּזְרִיעַ] and bears a male. | If a woman, having received seed, bears a male.

units.la: Oleastrius ad hac verba, suscepto semine, sic ait, Bern. & Origenes hom. 8. in hoc caput & Alb. Magnus annotarunt, per ea verba Moses ab hac lege virginem purissimam excipere voluisse, quæ non suscepto semine filium peperit. Sed libet & Dionysium Carthusianum audire, Secundum Origenem superflue Moses addidisset, suscepto semine, nisi scivisset in spiritu virginem masculum parituram, atque ut addit S. Pater Bern. Moses dicturus, Mulier si peperit immunda erit, timuit crimen blasphemiæ super matre Christi incurrere: ideo addidit, suscepto semine. Hinc alii dicunt quod beata virgo excepta fuit ab ista lege, quia concepit & peperit sine virili semine. Quid ad hæc Oleastrius? Hoc optime notatum esset, inquit, si hæc lex ita in Ebraeo haberetur, sed cum longe aliter habeatur, non est locus mysterio, &c. Vox Ebr. הוריע proprie significat, dare semen. Ad verbum, feminificaverit. Passim herbis tribuitur, ubi suscepto seminis denotari non potest. Viris eam vocem passim attribuunt Ebræi, quod nos diceremus, semen emitto, jacio, Itaque Aben. exponit cum dederit semen. Ubi & illud tradit, Multi ajunt, quod si prima det semen, masculum concipiat, ideo sequitur & peperit masculum. Ideo sapientes Græca ajunt fœminas habere semen, quod coagulet semen maris. Eadem leges R. in Salom. Genes. 46. 15. Ego itaque cum Aben. aliisque doctis hoc Interpretamentum retinendum censeo, si dederit semen, urgenduinque adversus Anabaptistas; qui, ut suos de humanae Christi naturae origine errores stabiliant, foeminas semen habere praefracte negant. Atque huc retulerim locum Ebraorum II. 11. de Sara, ως καταβολὴν σπέρματος, quod malim reddere, ad emittendum vel ejiciendum semen, ut excretio feminis Sarae ex lumbis uterum intelligatur. Certe invenio in Lexicis, καταβάλλειν σπέρμα, esse emittere semen. Quadraret huic sensui, ut videtur, magis vox ἐκβολὴ, sed magis emphaticam vocem καταβολὴ esse, notavit Cl. Piscator, utpote quâ fluxus denotatur. Theophylactus memorat, suo quoque aevo locum sic expositum fuisse, indeque probatum, foeminas quoque semen conferre, nec omnino esse asymbolas. Beza in ultima Edit. expositum ejaculari semen, sed ex antecedente intelligi voluit consequens, unde suppleta voce concipiendum, vertit, ad ejaculatum semen concipiendum. Vide jam & Drusium in praeteritis ad Ebr. II. 11.
units.tr: Oleastrius, on these words, "suscepto semine," says this: Bernard, Origen (in homily 8 on this chapter) and Albert the Great have noted that by these words Moses wished to exclude from this law the most pure virgin, who bore a son without having received seed. But let us also hear Dionysius the Carthusian: "According to Origen, Moses would have added 'suscepto semine' superfluously, unless he had known that the virgin would bear a male child in the Spirit; and as the holy Father Bernard adds, Moses, about to say 'If a woman bears, she will be unclean,' feared to incur the charge of blasphemy against the mother of Christ, and so he added 'suscepto semine.' Hence others say that the blessed virgin was excepted from this law, because she conceived and bore without male seed. What does Oleastrius say to this? This would have been very well noted, he says, if the law stood so in Hebrew; but since it stands quite differently, there is no place for mystery, etc." The Hebrew word הוריע [hore'a] properly means to give seed; literally, to make seed. It is applied to plants in many places, where it cannot mean receiving seed. The Hebrews apply this word to men in many places, where we would say to emit or to cast seed. So Aben Ezra explains it as when she has given seed. There he also relates: Many say that if she first gives seed, she conceives a male; therefore it follows, "and bears a male." Hence the wise men say that women have seed, which curdles the seed of the man. The rabbis say the same thing in Salomon on Genesis 46.15. I therefore, with Aben Ezra and other learned men, think this rendering, if she gives seed, should be retained, and pressed against the Anabaptists, who, to establish their errors about the origin of Christ's human nature, stubbornly deny that women have seed. To this I would also refer the passage of the Hebrews 11.11 about Sarah, εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος [ὡς καταβολὴν σπέρματος], which I would prefer to render for emitting or casting out seed, so that the discharge of Sarah's seed from her loins is understood. Certainly I find in the lexicons that καταβάλλειν σπέρμα means to emit seed. The word ἐκβολὴ seems to fit this sense better, but Cl. Piscator has noted that καταβολὴ is the more emphatic word, since it denotes a flow. Theophylactus records that in his own time the passage was explained in this way too, and that it was thereby shown that women also contribute seed, and are not altogether without a share. Beza, in his last edition, explained it as to eject seed, but he wished the consequent to be understood from the antecedent, and so, supplying the word concipiendum, he translated it for conceiving the ejected seed. See also Drusius on Hebrews 11.11 above.

units.la: Augustt. Quaest in Levit. qu. 66. A semine tuo non dabis servire principi. Hic non video, inquit, quid intelligatur, nisi principi qui pro Deo colitur. Non enim ait δουλεύειν, sed λατρεύειν in Graeco, quod Latinus non solet interpretari, nisi ut dicat, servire. Plurimum autem distant. Nam servire hominibus, quo servi serviunt, quod non est λατρεύειν, sed δουλεύειν, scriptura non prohibet. servire autem secundum id quod est λατρεύειν, non jubetur hominibus, nisi uni vero Deo, sicuti scriptum est, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis & illi soli servies. Tu disce tiro, supervacaneam esse hanc magni viri περιεργίαν. Namque ubi Graeci habent, ἀπὸ τῆς σπέρματός σου οὐ δώσεις λατρεύειν τῷ ἀρχοντι, Ebraea plane alium sensum habent, non dabis de semine tuo לְהַעֲבִיר לַמֹּלֶךְ ad traducendum Molocho. Ecce cultus Molochi, non ministeria aut servitia prohibentur. Sed Lxx. vocem lehagnabir, legerunt cum daleth in fine, ut magna est istarum literarum affinitas. Et למלך sine punctis indifferens est ad מלך & מלך. Miror Augustinum non vidisse quod Theodoretus vidit, vid. caeteros Interpretes Moloch reddidisse. Scholion ad Biblia Graeca, τὸ ἑβραϊκὸν μόλοχ ἔχει, ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν τῶν οἱ λοιποὶ ἑρμηνεῦσαι πεπάκασι. Quod ita reddidit Theodoretus, Hebraicum exemplar Moloch habet, quod reliqui interpretes annotarunt, imo dixisset potius, in sua translatione posuerunt. Sed ut ad Augustinum redeat oratio, miraris forte Lector, cur ille de simplici ministerio exteris principibus non praestando legem hanc interpretatus non sit, quomodo illi quos Theod. notat, eam accepere. Observa, Augustinum, postquam semel discrimen illud inter δουλείαν & λατρείαν meliori mente quam eventu tradidisset, omnia loca quae istud evertere videbantur, sic fuisse interpretatum, nequid ex iis pulcra ista distinctio detrimenti caperet. Vis aliud specimen? Locutionum sacrarum lib. 5. Ad Deut. 28. 48. Et servies inimicis tuis. Gracum habet λατρεύσεις. Solet autem hoc verbum in ea servitute scriptura ponere, qua debetur Deo. Unde idololatrae vocantur, qui ea servitute idolis serviunt. Ergo hic inusitate positum est hoc verbum, quamquam posset etiam hunc sensum habere (vides jam quo tendat?) quod tam graviter multa dixerit ut inimicis suis nimium superbientibus tanquam Diis servire cogantur. Omnia haec una litura delevisset doctissimus Pater, si scivisset in Ebraeo esse עבד quod promiscue & de cultu Dei & ministeriis, quae hominibus praestantur: neque apud profanos tantum quod fatentur, sed & in N. T. & Graeca Vet. Test. versione, voces illas passim confundi. Confer haec loca, Rom. 1. 9. Act. 20. 19. & 7. 6. & 12. 11. & 14. 18. & 16. 18. Epih. 6. 7. Phil. 2. 22. Coloss. 3. 24. Matth. 4. 10. Act. 20. 19. Gal. 4. 8. Rom. 1. 25. Ebr. 9. 14. 1. Tess. 1. 9. Porro in LXX. Interpretibus vide haec loca Deut. 28. 48. Deut. 6. 13. confer cum 1. Sam. 7. 4. item Jud. 2. 11. cum 1. Sam. 8. 8. Hac de re prolixius disseruere Parasu in Epist. ad Rom. Vives ad August. de Civitate Dei 10. 1. Jac: Laurentius in Apologetico contra Sandaeum. Chamierus Tom. 2. pag. 769. & seq. & alii.
units.tr: Augustine, Questions on Leviticus, question 66: "You shall not give any of your seed to serve the prince." Here, he says, I do not see what is meant, except the prince who is worshipped in place of God. For the Greek does not say δουλεύειν but λατρεύειν, and the Latin translator usually renders this only as "serve." Yet the two differ greatly. Scripture does not forbid serving men, which is what slaves do; that is not λατρεύειν but δουλεύειν. But serving in the sense of λατρεύειν is commanded to no man, only to the one true God, as it is written: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone." Learn this, novice: the great man's subtlety here is superfluous. For where the Greeks have "from your seed you shall not give to serve the ruler" [ἀπὸ τῆς σπέρματός σου οὐ δώσεις λατρεύειν τῷ ἀρχοντι], the Hebrew clearly has another sense: "you shall not give of your seed to make pass over to Molech" [לְהַעֲבִיר לַמֹּלֶךְ]. See, it is the cult of Molech that is forbidden, not ministries or services. But the Seventy read the word with a daleth at the end, since these letters are so closely related. And למלך without vowel points is ambiguous between מלך and מלך (king and Molech). I am surprised that Augustine did not see what Theodoret saw, namely that the other interpreters rendered it as Moloch. The scholion on the Greek Bibles says: "the Hebrew has Moloch, which the other interpreters have passed over." Theodoret rendered this: "The Hebrew copy has Moloch, which the other interpreters noted; or rather, he would have said they put it into their translation." But to return to Augustine: the reader may wonder why he did not interpret this law as a simple ministry, not to be rendered to foreign princes, as those whom Theodoret notes had understood it. Observe that Augustine, having once set out that distinction between δουλείαν and λατρείαν with a better intention than outcome, interpreted every passage that seemed to overturn it in such a way that the fine distinction should suffer no harm from them. Do you want another example? In his Locutionum sacrarum, book 5, on Deut. 28. 48: "And you shall serve your enemies." The Greek has λατρεύσεις. Scripture usually uses this verb for the servitude that is owed to God. Hence those who serve idols in that servitude are called idolaters. So here the verb is used unusually, although it could also have this sense (do you see where this leads?), that he spoke so severely in many things that his enemies, too proud, are compelled to serve as if they were gods. That most learned Father would have erased all of this with one stroke, had he known that in Hebrew there is עבד, which is used indiscriminately both of the worship of God and of the services rendered to men. This is not only admitted among profane writers, but in the New Testament and the Greek version of the Old Testament those words are also everywhere confused. Compare these passages: Rom. 1. 9; Acts 20. 19; 7. 6; 12. 11; 14. 18; 16. 18; Eph. 6. 7; Phil. 2. 22; Col. 3. 24; Matth. 4. 10; Acts 20. 19; Gal. 4. 8; Rom. 1. 25; Heb. 9. 14; 1 Thess. 1. 9. Further, on the Seventy, see these passages: Deut. 28. 48; Deut. 6. 13; compare 1 Sam. 7. 4; likewise Judg. 2. 11 with 1 Sam. 8. 8. On this matter more fully have written Parasus on the Epistle to the Romans, Vives on Augustine's City of God 10. 1, Jac. Laurentius in his Apology against Sandaeus, Chamierus vol. 2, p. 769 and following, and others.

units.la: a De beat. Sanct. cap. 1. 4; b Mor. Instit. tom. 1. lib. 5. cap. 5; c In conc. Evang. c. 16. ita & Tollet. in Luc. 4; & alii. Con. à Lapide interpretatur, ceremonia id est lex ceremonialis. Et certe חקים & חקות quando à משפטים & מצוות distinguuntur saepe leges ceremoniales significant, quas Graeci δικαιώματα vocare solent, quo sensu eadem quoque voce usus est B. Paulus, Ebraeorum 9. vers.1. Reddatur ergo, & hic, hæc est ceremonia legis, vel per hypallagen, hæc est lex ceremonialis. Hoc an illo modo vertas, hilum non interest. Lxx. αὕτη ἡ διαθήκη ἦ νόμος, ὅσα συνέταξε ὁ κύριος. Quae ita reddita fuerunt in Latina translatione qua usus fuit Augustinus, Haec est distinctio Legis, quaecunque constituit Dominus. Audiamus jam Augustinum super hoc loco perorantem. Sic ergo Quaest. in Num. q.33. Ista distinctio Legis, &c. Non satis digne festinantes dicere de tanto sacramento valemus. Primo enim quod ita coepit loqui, quem non moveat & intentissimam mentem faciat in altitudine sacramenti, Ista distinctio Legis, &c. Proculdubio non est distinctio nisi inter aliqua duo vel plura. Nam distinctionem singularitas non requirit. Nec distinctionem cujuslibet rei commemoravit, sed addidit, Legis, nec cujuscunque legis; assidue quippe in Scriptura dicitur de unaquaque re de qua legitime praecipitur. Hic vero cum dixisset, hæc est distinctio legis, secutus adjunxit, quaecunque constituit Dominus, praecipiendo utique non creando. Si ergo haec est distinctio legis, quaecunque praecepit Dominus, procul dubio magna distinctio. Et certe intelligitur duo testamenta distinguere. Et paulo post, Temporalium autem bonorum & carnalium & spiritualium & aeternorum, quae clarior & certior distinctio est, quam passio Domini nostri Jesu Christi? Et rursus pauculis interjectis. Hanc ergo passionem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, tanquam distinctionem duorum testamentorum, hoc quod de juvenca rufa mactatione narratur, satis congrue praefigurat. Haec August. Examina haec ad fontes, & evanescent. Decepit Interpretem, decepit Augustinum unica illa vox ἀλσολή, quae in N. foedere occurrit in notione distinctionis, Rom. 3. 1. Corinth. 14. Et certe ἀλσολέω est distinguo. At si vel Interpres vel Augustinus locum hunc cum fontibus conferre fuisset quitus, distinctionis ejusmodi, qualem hic August. intellexit, nec volam nec vestigium invenisset. Quid ergo? Ibi vidisti jam vocem חקות / eam expressere Lxx. jam per δικαίωμα, jam per θεσμὸν, jam per νόμιμον, jam per νόμον, jam per ἐντολὴ. Semel per ἀλσολὴ, vid. hoc loco ἀλσολὴ hic ergo est mandatum datum
units.tr: a On the Beatitudes, chap. 1. 4; b Moral Institutes, vol. 1, book 5, chap. 5; c On the Harmony of the Gospels, chap. 16; so also Tolletus on Luke 4; and others. Cornelius a Lapide interprets it as "ceremony," that is, the ceremonial law. Certainly חקים and חקות, when they are distinguished from משפטים and מצוות, often signify the ceremonial laws, which the Greeks usually call δικαιώματα. In this sense the same word was used by St Paul, Heb. 9. 1. Let it therefore be rendered here too: "this is the ceremony of the law," or by hypallage, "this is the ceremonial law." Whether you translate it one way or the other makes no difference at all. The Seventy: "This is the covenant or law, as many things as the Lord ordained" [αὕτη ἡ διαθήκη ἦ νόμος, ὅσα συνέταξε ὁ κύριος]. These were rendered in the Latin translation which Augustine used as "This is the distinction of the Law, whatever the Lord has appointed." Let us now hear Augustine pleading on this text. So in his Questions on Numbers, question 33: "This distinction of the Law, etc. We are not able to speak of so great a sacrament with sufficiently worthy haste. For first, who is not moved, and made most attentive, by the depth of the sacrament when it begins to speak thus: 'This distinction of the Law, etc.'? Assuredly it is not a distinction unless between some two or more things, for singularity does not require a distinction. Nor does it mention the distinction of any thing whatever, but adds 'of the Law,' nor of any law whatever; for in Scripture it is constantly said of each thing about which a command is lawfully given. But here, having said 'this is the distinction of the Law,' it follows by adding 'whatever the Lord has appointed,' surely by commanding, not by creating. If therefore this is the distinction of the Law, whatever the Lord has commanded, it is without doubt a great distinction." And certainly it is understood to distinguish the two testaments. And shortly after: "Of temporal goods, both carnal and spiritual and eternal, what distinction is clearer and more certain than the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ?" And again, after a few words intervene: "This passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the distinction of the two testaments, is fittingly prefigured by what is told of the sacrifice of the red heifer." So Augustine. Examine these things at their sources, and they will vanish. The interpreter was misled, and Augustine was misled, by the single word ἀλσολή [διαστολή], which occurs in the New Testament in the sense of distinction: Rom. 3. 1; 1 Cor. 14. And certainly ἀλσολέω [διαστέλλω] means to distinguish. But if either the interpreter or Augustine had consulted the sources for this passage, they would have found no trace or shadow of the sort of distinction that Augustine understood here. What then? You have already seen the word חקות; the Seventy rendered it sometimes by δικαίωμα, sometimes by θεσμὸν, sometimes by νόμιμον, sometimes by νόμον, sometimes by ἐντολὴ. Once by ἀλσολὴ [διαστολή]. See at this place ἀλσολὴ: here, therefore, it means a commandment given.

units.la: a Gen.16.5. b Gen.47.26. c Exod.12.14. d Exod.12.41. e Deut.16.12. datum, praeceptum, qua notione in profanis authoribus occurrit Ϝησαλη. Hesych. Ϝησαλαι, ἐντολαί, Ἀλαξγαι. Caeterum quod ad vocem Ἀλαξγαλη attinet, non mirum eam pro praecepto & statuto hic usurpatam. Nam τὸ Ἀλαξηλομαι & in Hellenica & Hellenistica lingua passim significat, distincte aliquid praecipere, mandare. Eadem vox recurrit Num. 30. 8. neque amplius. Sed hic significat distinctam pronuntiationem seu effatum, respondetque Ebraeo מִבְטָא / Levit. 5. 4. τὸ ΝΟΣ itidem per * Ἀλα·.i. distincte ϝωλω reddidere, quod Latinus interpres reddidit, distinguere. Anima quae juraverit, ἡ Ἀλαξηλαξα τοῖς χείλεσι κακλοποιῆσαι ἡ κακοποιῆσαι, ᾧ πάντα ὅσα Ἀλαξηλη ὁ ἄνθρωπος, &c. distinguens labiis suis ad benefaciendum, per omnia quae distinxerit homo, &c. Adi ad hunc quoque locum Augustini Quaestiones, & videbis versionem istam tenebras offudisse loco alias clarissimo. Desinam ubi illud notavero, Lxx. eadem haec verba, אַיִשׁ הַחֹק הַתּוֹרָה Num. 31. 11. sic reddidisse, ἔγτι τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου, quae hoc modo Latinus Interpres reddiderat, hoc est justificatio legis. Vulg. hoc est praeceptum legis.
units.tr: a Gen. 16. 5; b Gen. 47. 26; c Exod. 12. 14; d Exod. 12. 41; e Deut. 16. 12: given, command, a sense which in profane authors appears as ϝησαλη. Hesychius: ϝησαλαι, commands, Ἀλαξγαι. As for the word Ἀλαξγαλη, it is not surprising that it is used here for precept and statute. For τὸ Ἀλαξηλομαι in both Hellenic and Hellenistic Greek commonly means "to command something distinctly, to order." The same word recurs at Num. 30. 8, and nowhere else. But here it means a distinct utterance or pronouncement, and it corresponds to the Hebrew מִבְטָא (Lev. 5. 4). They rendered τὸ ΝΟΣ likewise by Ἀλα· (that is, distinctly) ϝωλω, which the Latin translator rendered "to distinguish. The soul which has sworn, to do evil or to do good with its lips, distinguishing with its lips to do good or to do evil, in all that man has distinguished, etc." Consult Augustine's Questions on this passage too, and you will see that this version has cast darkness over a passage otherwise very clear. I will stop once I have noted this: the Seventy rendered these same words, "the statute of the law" (Num. 31. 11), as ἔγτι τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου, which the Latin translator rendered "this is the justification of the law." The Vulgate has "this is the precept of the law."

units.la: CAP. XXIII. vers. 19.

units.la: Non quasi homo Dominus suspenditur, neque quasi filius hominis minas patitur. Ita hunc locum citat Lactantius lib. 4. de vera Sapientia, cap. mihi 18. tanquam vaticinium de Christo aliquando crucifigendo. Ebraea nihil ejusmodi habent, לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וְיִכְזֵב וּבֶן אָדָם וְיִתְנַחֵם Deus non est vir ut mentiatur, aut filius hominis, ut poenitudine ducatur. Ubi vulg. sine ulla necessitate, ut mutetur. Lxx. ἐχ' ὡς ἀνθρωπῷ ὁ Θεὸς Ἀλαξηθῆναι, &δ' ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀπειλῆθῆναι. Quae sic versa reperio in Edit. Basileensi, non ut homo Deus ad mentiendum, neque ut filius hominis ut minetur. Crediderim interpretem eum quisquis fuit, legisse, ἐχ' ὡς ἀνθρωπῷ ὁ Θεὸς Ἀλαψεύσασθαι, ut habet Editio Complutens. hoc enim est, ad mentiendum, à qua lectione quoad sensum non recedit illa Philonis in De vita Moysis, Ἀλαψεύθηναι. Quid vero illud Ἀλαξητηθῆναι, dixerit aliquis. Scholion, quod extat in Edit. Romana, Ἀλαξητηθῆναι, ἔτ' ἐςι σαλευθῆναι. τὰ γὰρ χρεμάμενα σαλένονται. Ἀλαξητηθῆναι, id est, agitari, commoveri, fluctuare. Ea enim quae suspensa sunt, agitantur hùc illuc & fluctuant. mandæ adducam duo loca ex Lxx. Ezech. 37. 11. ubi Ebræa, נְגֻזְרְנוּ לָנוּ excisi sumus nobis, Lxx. Ἀλαπεφωνὴ καμῷ id est periimus. Num. 31. 49. וְלֹא נִפְקַד מִמֶּנּוּ אִישׁ & non desideratus fuit * è nobis quisquam. καὶ ὁ Ἀλαπεφώνησεν ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ὧδε εἰς. ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν id est ex illis qui nobis commissi fuere, qui fuerunt in manu, sive, potestate nostrâ, hoc est, ex nobis, ex nostro numero. [ Coronidis loco illud addam, magnum Heinsium acute observasse, ex hoc Exodi loco prout ille vulgo intellectus fuit, natam esse fabulam de consensu Lxx. Interpretum. Scilicet quod hic de Lxx. Senibus à Mose delectis legebant, ad illos quoque, qui Græcæ versioni elaborandæ destinati fuere, tantulerunt. Vide ejus Aristarchum sacrum pag. 207. ]
units.tr: "God is not a man, that he should be brought low, nor a son of man, that he should suffer threats." Lactantius cites this verse in book 4 of *De vera Sapientia*, chapter 18 in my numbering, as a prophecy of Christ who was one day to be crucified. The Hebrew has nothing of the kind: לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וְיִכְזֵב וּבֶן אָדָם וְיִתְנַחֵם ("God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should be moved to repent"). Here the Vulgate has, with no necessity, "that he should be changed." The Seventy have: "not as a man is God to be moved [ἀλαχθῆναι], nor as a son of man to be threatened [ἀπειληθῆναι]." In the Basel edition I find this rendered: "not as a man, God to lie; nor as a son of man, that he should threaten." I would believe that the translator, whoever he was, read ἀλεψεύσασθαι ("to lie"), as the Complutensian edition has, for that means "to lie," and with this reading Philo's ἀλευθῆναι in *De vita Moysis* agrees in sense. But what should one make of ἀλαξητηθῆναι? A scholium in the Roman edition explains it: "ἀλαξητηθῆναι, that is, σαλευθῆναι, to be shaken, for things that hang are swayed." So it means *to be agitated, to be moved, to fluctuate*, since things that are suspended are tossed this way and that. I will add two passages from the Seventy as well. Ezekiel 37:11, where the Hebrew is נְגֻזְרְנוּ לָנוּ ("we are cut off for ourselves"), the Seventy have ἀπεφθάρημεν ("we have perished"). Numbers 31:49, where the Hebrew is וְלֹא נִפְקַד מִמֶּנּוּ אִישׁ ("and not one of us was missing"), the Seventy have καὶ οὐκ ἀπεφωνήθη ἀπ' αὐτῶν οὐδείς, where ἀπ' αὐτῶν means "from among them," that is, those who had been committed to us, who were in our hand or power, that is, from us, from our number. [As a coda, I will add this: the great Heinsius has shrewdly observed that from this passage in Exodus, as it was commonly understood, arose the fable of the agreement of the Seventy translators. Namely, what was read here about the Seventy elders chosen by Moses was applied also to those who were appointed to labour on the Greek version. See his *Aristarchus sacer*, p. 207.]

units.la: Ibidem, electorum Israel] August. Quæst in Exodum, quæst. 102. Quis dubitet illos, quos nominatim expressit & LXX. seniores, nunc appellatos electos Israel, qui proculdubio personam gerebant eorum qui electi sunt in populo Dei. Non enim omnium est fides. In magna autem domo sunt alia vasa in honorem alia in contumeliam. Quoniam ergo quos ante præscivit & prædestinavit — quos autem justificavit & glorificavit, profecto de electis Israel non dissonuit nec unus. Hæc alieno loco à doctissimo patre disseri judicabit quisquis originarium textum expenderit.
units.tr: In the same place, the chosen of Israel. Augustine, Quaestiones in Exodum, question 102: "Who can doubt that those whom the Seventy named expressly, the elders, now called the chosen of Israel, were without doubt bearing the character of those who are chosen among the people of God? For faith is not for all. But in a great house there are other vessels, some for honour, others for dishonour. Therefore, since those whom he foreknew he also predestined, and those whom he justified he also glorified, surely not one of the chosen of Israel dissented. Anyone who weighs the original text will judge that the most learned father has argued these things in a place not his own."

units.tr: Of the URIM and THUMMIM

units.la: Et pones in pectorali judicii Vrim & Thummin, id est ad verbum, testibus Cajet. Arias & aliis. ignes seu illuminationes & perfectiones. | Pones autem in rationali judicii doctrinam & veritatem.
units.tr: And you shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim, that is, word for word, according to Cajetan, Arias and others, "lights or illuminations and perfections." | But you shall put in the rational of judgment doctrine and truth.

units.la: Varias de Vrim & Thummim opiniones videbis apud Vatablum & Fagium in Chald. Paraphrasin Onceli, ex quo libro non tantum hoc, sed& pleraque alia desumpta sunt, quæ sub nomine Vatablinarum notarum edita sunt. Multa quoque de eis habet in magnis Ann. Cl. Drusius. Nos impræsentiarum examinemus hæc
units.tr: You will find various opinions about the Urim and Thummim in Vatablus and Fagius on the Chaldee paraphrase of Onkelos, from which book not only this but many other things were taken, which were published under the name of the Vatablan notes. The illustrious Drusius also has much about them in his large work. For the present let us examine these matters.

units.la: Cajet.: De Vrim & Thummim diversi judicat, nec certi aliquid habetur. Scitus hæc vulgati gemina interpretamenta. Vrim extra omnem controversiam hactenus creditum fuit descendere ab אור luxit, un- de אור ignis & lux. Similiter Thummim à תמים perfectus fuit. Singulare תם / ut à אור fit אורים gnuzzim, juxta consuetudinem duplicantium Ain.. Provoco ad omnia Lexica Ebraeorum, Chriftianorum, Protestantium & Pontificiorum. Unde Aquila Le- vit.8.8. φωτισμὸς καὶ πλάωσεις reddidit, illuminationes & perse- ctiones. Sed res magis clara quam ut tot verbis opus sit. Voluit autem Deus his vocibus illud inculcatum, Pontifici splendorem seu lumen scientiæ & integritatem vitæ inesse oportere. Sed quo- modo has voces interpretatus est Vulgatus? Doctrinam & veritatem. Admodum coacte, si spectas themata. Atque hic non possum non deplorare quorundam ex recentioribus Papistis miseram & plusquam servilem conditionem, quib. ne dubitare quidem de veritate hujus interpretamenti finit Concilii Tridentini Canon. nec rursus mirari satis possum quorundam impudentiam, qui etiam ineptissima in suum vertere satagunt emolumentum. Ecce enim a Bellarminus dum in infallibilitate Papæ astruenda laborat, facit quod furibundi homines assolent, quidvis arri- pit, lapides, faces, ligna, sudesque præustas, furiosus sedis Romanæ zelus arma ministrat. Pontifex Vet. Test. in pectorali habebat doctrinam & veritatem: ergo Pontifex Novi Testamenti, Papa, cum totam Ecclesiam docet in his quæ ad fidem pertinent, nullo casu errare potest. Quam bene à Pontifice Vet. Test. ad Pontificem Novi procedat argumentatio, Theologi discussere. Tu illud nota, Lector, si genuina illa interpretamenta, splendorem & integritatem sumsisset, sic ipsi inferendum fuisset, Ergo in Papa splendor cognit. & integritas vitæ est. At prævidit Bellarminus, hæreticos opposituros vitas Pontificum, quotidianam experientiam, ipsamque adeo ipsius Bellarmini confessionem, quam in Præfat. istius Controversiæ vis veritatis ei extorserat, vid. plerosque Papas fuisse sceleratissima monstra. Sed videamus quomodo eam versionem stabiliat Bellarminus. Ea enim si cadat, simul & argumentum satis alias elumbe corruat necesse est. Dicit illuminationem μεταληπτικῶς sumi posse pro doctrina, ut φωτίζω pro doceo. Sed ut hoc tolerabile est, ita illud plane intolerabile quod dicit in progressu, דה א אורים / descendere, quod in Hiphil הורה docuit, ut & Thummim ab אמת verax fuit.
units.tr: Cajetan: He judges differently about the Urim and Thummim, and nothing certain is held. Let us consider these two renderings of the Vulgate. That the Urim derives from אור ("he shone"), whence אור ("fire" and "light"), has hitherto been believed beyond all controversy. Likewise Thummim comes from תמים ("perfect"). The singular תם, when אור becomes אורים, is gnuzzim by the usual practice of doubling the Ayin. I appeal to all the Hebrew lexicons, Christian, Protestant and Papist. Hence Aquila at Leviticus 8:8 rendered it φωτισμὸς καὶ πλάωσεις ("illuminations and perfections"). But the matter is clearer than that it needs so many words. God meant by these terms to impress that the Pontiff ought to have splendour, that is the light of knowledge, and integrity of life. But how has the Vulgate translated these words? As doctrine and truth. Very forced, if you look at the themes. And here I cannot help lamenting the wretched and more than servile condition of some of the more recent Papists, who are not even allowed to doubt the truth of this rendering by the Canon of the Council of Trent; nor again can I sufficiently wonder at the impudence of others, who strive to turn even the most absurd things to their own advantage. For behold, Bellarmine, while labouring to establish the infallibility of the Pope, does what furious men are wont to do: he snatches up whatever comes to hand, stones, torches, wood, and stakes hardened in the fire; the frantic zeal of the Roman See supplies weapons. The high priest of the Old Testament had doctrine and truth in the breastplate; therefore the high priest of the New Testament, the Pope, when he teaches the whole Church in those things which pertain to faith, can by no chance err. How well this argument proceeds from the high priest of the Old Testament to the high priest of the New, the theologians have examined. Note this, reader: had he taken the genuine renderings, splendour and integrity, the conclusion would have had to be drawn thus: Therefore in the Pope there is splendour of knowledge and integrity of life. But Bellarmine foresaw that heretics would object the lives of the Pontiffs, daily experience, and indeed Bellarmine's own confession, which the force of truth had wrung from him in the preface of that controversy, namely that most of the Popes were most wicked monsters. But let us see how Bellarmine supports that version. For if it falls, the argument, otherwise rather feeble, must necessarily fall with it. He says that illumination can be taken metaphorically for doctrine, as φωτίζω is for διδάσκω (I teach). But as this is tolerable, so that which he says further on is plainly intolerable, that Urim comes from דה ("to teach"), הורה in the Hiphil, which means "he taught," and that Thummim likewise comes from אמת ("true").

units.la: Quis unquam adeo portentosam originationem somniavit? Ego certe cum apud Rainoldum eam primo citatam viderem, in stuporem datus sum, & licet veracissimum in allegationibus Theologum illum semper expertus sim, tantum a me impetrare non potui ut beatæ isti animæ, nisi ipso Bellarm. inspecto, fidem adhiberem. Sed in majorem admirationem dedit me Bellarmini argumentum quo versionem Vulgatam constabilitum it. Plus, inquit, credendum est Hieronymo qui doctrinam vertit & veritatem, & non LXX. qui verterunt, διὰ λωτ καὶ ἀλλάθειαν, * quam Judæis & Judaizantibus. Sed quid respondebis Rainoldo, Bellarmine, roganti te unde διὰ λωσε descendat? Ança tibi fiducia, ea frons, ut diceres à διδάσκω? Certe si tibi ipsi constare velis, deducenda tibi ea vox à διδάσκω est, cur enim & hic non potius Hieronymo credendum qui doctrinam vertit, quam Lexicis? Omnem vero impudentiam & ἀναισχυντίαν supergreditur originatio vocis תִּמִּים ut sit ab אַמּוֹן / Ausim ad ipsam Bellar. conscientiam, ad omnes omnium Pontificiarum Academiarum Professores Ebræos provocare. Augustinus Steuchus Episcopus licet asserat Vrim deduci posse ab הוּרִים / tamen non ita frontem posuit, Thummim ab Aman deduci posse asseruerit. Ea quam posui originatio Regulis Grammaticis, omniumque Ebræorum & Christianorum Lexicis conformis est, astipulatores habet * Papistas ipsos, quotquot ante Conc. Trid. & post illud extra calorem disputationis commentati sunt, conservat in singulis tres radicales, siquidem ד in Thummim ob dages potestate duplex est. At quid tale in sua Originatione monstrabit Cardinalis? In utraque voce una manebit radicalis; in priori ר / in poster. ם / Sic Balbus lib.2. de Nat. Deor. apud Cicer deducebat Neptunum à nando, unica litera retenta, at hoc in persona Cottæ falsè ridet Cicero, aitque Balbum magis sibi in ea originatione visum natalem quam Neptunum. Ad primam respondebit, sc. Vrim, primam thematis delitescere in vocali longa Shurek, tertiamque He ita solere elidi cum aliquid additur, ut à שִׁנְאָר fit שִׁנִּים / At quid in voce Thummim consilii? ubi א ב אַמּוֹן? Quiescit, inquies. At in qua vocali longa? Nulla utique hic contractio est, ut in מלף pro מאלף / Et quæ ratio hœmanthicæ? An unquam vel fando auditum est, א ompensari per Dages præeunte Kibbuts
units.tr: Who has ever dreamt up so monstrous a derivation? I, indeed, when I first saw it cited by Rainolds, was struck dumb, and although I have always found that most truthful theologian reliable in his citations, I could not bring myself to credit that blessed soul unless I had consulted Bellarmine himself. But Bellarmine's argument by which he establishes the Vulgate version gave me still greater amazement. More, he says, must be believed to Jerome, who rendered doctrine and truth, and not to the Seventy, who translated διὰ λωσε and ἀλλάθειαν, than to the Jews and Judaizers. But what will you answer Rainolds, Bellarmine, when he asks you whence διὰ λωσε comes? What boldness, what brazenness, to say it comes from διδάσκω! Certainly, if you wish to be consistent, that word must be derived by you from διδάσκω; for why, then, should we not rather believe Jerome here, who rendered doctrine, than the lexicons? But the derivation of the word תִּמִּים so that it comes from אַמּוֹן surpasses all impudence and shamelessness. I would dare to challenge Bellarmine's own conscience, and all the Hebrew professors of all the Pontifical academies. Augustinus Steuchus, though he asserts that Urim can be derived from הוּרִים, did not venture so far as to claim that Thummim can be derived from Aman. The derivation I have proposed conforms to the rules of grammar and to the lexicons of all Hebrews and Christians, and it has the Papists themselves as supporters, all who, before and after the Council of Trent, wrote on the matter outside the heat of dispute. It keeps three radical letters in each word, since the ד in Thummim has a double value because of the dagesh. But what like thing will the Cardinal show in his derivation? In each word one radical will remain: in the former ר, in the latter ם. So Balbus in the second book of Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods derived Neptune from swimming (nando), retaining a single letter; but Cicero, mocking this in the person of Cotta, says that Balbus seemed to him in that derivation more of a natalis than a Neptune. To the first word he will reply, namely Urim, that the first radical hides in the long vowel Shurek, and that the third, He, is usually elided when something is added, as from שִׁנְאָר one gets שִׁנִּים. But what plan is there in the word Thummim? Where is the א of אַמּוֹן? It rests, you will say. But in what long vowel? There is certainly no contraction here, as in מלף for מאלף. And what reasoning is this? Has it ever been heard, even by report, that א is compensated by a dagesh after a preceding kibbuts under a servile ח? Where is the last? You will say it has perished, as in אמר for אמרו. Granted; but it appears in compensation as soon as something is added, as in אמר, of which there is no trace here.

units.la: *Ira & jus Canon.dist. 36. in pr.p. Decreti C. Qui Ecclesiasticis & Augustinus teddit, deramstraio & verita.
units.tr: *Canon, dist. 36, at the beginning of the Decretum, C. Qui ecclesiasticis; and Augustine renders "truth" and ... truth.

units.la: *Cajet. Oleastr. Riberam Del-Rio. buts sub ח servili ? Ubi ultima ? ? Periisse dices ut in אמר pro אמרו / Esto, sed ea apparet in compensatione simulac aliquid additur, ut in אמר cujus hic nullum vestigium. Sed, inquit, Hieronymus Thummim vertit veritatem. Ergo deducenda vox à themate in quo veritatis notio. Et mihi ergo sic liceat argumentari, vocem Thummim Deut.33.8. Hieron. vertit perfectio, Ergo derivanda à themate quod perfectionem significat. At illud est תמים / non semper itaque Hieron. veritatem vertit. Et quid si semper ? Quando Hieronymi interpretatio Lexicorum norma esse coepit ? Nec eam mentem fuisse Tridentinis, nec hoc ubique admissurum Bellarminum mihi persuadeo. καὶ πάντα μὴ δὲ ταύτῃ.
units.tr: *Cajetan, Oleaster, Ribera, Del Río. ... under ח as a servile letter? Where is the last? You will say it has perished, as in אמר for אמרו. Granted; but it appears in compensation whenever something is added, as in אמר, of which here there is no trace. But, he says, Jerome rendered Thummim as "truth." Therefore the word must be derived from a theme in which the notion of truth lies. Then let me also argue in this way: Jerome renders the word Thummim at Deuteronomy 33:8 as "perfection"; therefore it must be derived from a theme which signifies perfection. That theme is תמים. So Jerome does not always render it "truth." And what if he always did? When did Jerome's interpretation begin to be the norm of the lexicons? I am persuaded that neither the Tridentine fathers had this intention, nor that Bellarmine would admit this everywhere. And all things not by this way.

units.la: Et ignorabat Moses quod קרן cutis facici suæ. | Et ignorabat Moses quod cornuta esset facies sua.
units.tr: And Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone [קרן]. | And Moses did not know that his face was horned.

units.la: Vox Ebræa קרן significat radios cornuum instar emittere. Unde Lxx. apposite, ὅτι δεδόξασαι ἡ ὄψις ὃ χεωτὸς ὃ ϑεσσώπως αὐτῷ. Ad quam versionem Apostolus 2. Cor.3. allusit. Oncelos, quod multus esset splendor gloriæ faciei suæ. Jonathan tanquam interpres ∓ Lxx. quod glorificatus esset splendor aspectus faciei suæ. Hieron. secutus Aquilam qui ante verterat, κεράτωδης vertit, cornuta esset. Jam audiamus Steuchum Episcopum Xisamensem, Vox ambigua fecit in Editione errorem. Non enim habetur in contexto Ebr. faciem Mosis fuisse cornutam, sed radiantem fuisse cutem. Ex hoc potest emendari prava consuetudo, qua duobus cornibus pingunt Mosen; non enim cornua è fronte egrediebantur, sed & frons & nasus & os & mentum radiabant. Et mirum quod Hieron. non considerata veritate Ebraica non adverterat etiam quid LXX. transtulissent, qui bene hunc locum transtulerunt. Ridentque itaque nos & exe-cran-
units.tr: The Hebrew word קרן means to send out rays in the manner of horns. Hence the Seventy aptly rendered it, "that the appearance of the skin of his face was glorified" [ὅτι δεδόξασται ἡ ὄψις τοῦ χρωτὸς τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ]. The Apostle alludes to this version in 2 Corinthians 3. Onkelos has "that the splendour of his face's glory was great." Jonathan, as a translator following the Seventy, has "that the splendour of the appearance of his face was glorified." Jerome followed Aquila, who had translated earlier, and rendered it "horned" (κεράτωδης), "was horned." Let us now hear Steuchus, Bishop of Kisamos: "An ambiguous word caused the error in the edition." For the Hebrew context does not say that the face of Moses was horned, but that the skin was radiant. From this the bad custom can be corrected by which Moses is painted with two horns; for the horns did not stand out from his forehead, but his brow, nose, mouth and chin all radiated. And it is remarkable that Jerome, not having considered the Hebrew truth, did not notice even what the Seventy had translated, "who translated this passage well."

units.la: Z z crantur Judai, quoties Mosen in templis nostris cornuta facie depictum vident, quasi nos eum Diabolum quendam (Drusius addit, aut uxorem ejus adulterum, ei enim qui uxorem adulteram habet affingi solere duo cornua ex Apologis Ebraicis probat) esse putemus. Haec Steuchus. Cajet. vertit. cornificavit, & addit, Emissio radiorum metaphorice appellatur cornificatio, eo quod tanquam emissio cornuum sit emissio radiorum. Vide & Benedict. & Senensem. Vide & Ferum & Oleastrium in hunc locum. Nec dissentit Bellarminus. Et Thomas non dubitat asserere, faciem Mosis melius dici splendidam quam cornutam, maleque ipsi appingi cornua e capite egredientia. Cur igitur illud sibi sumere non fuere ausi Pontifices, ut pro cornuta reponerent splendida? Mirari & illud lubet, Pontifices Sixtum & Clementem in novis suis Bibliis approbasse vulgi a tot doctis damnatam consuetudinem, qua Mosi appicti radii non e tota facie micantes, sed duorum instar cornuum e capite ascendentes. Utrum hoc factum sit ad Vulgatam Edit. statuminandam, an vero ad defendendas Episcoporum bicornes mitras, an ad utrumque, merito quaerit Rainoldus.
units.tr: And so the Jews laugh at us and execrate us whenever they see Moses depicted with a horned face in our churches, as if we thought him to be some devil (Drusius adds, or his wife's adulterer, for he proves from the Hebrew fables that two horns are customarily attributed to a man who has an adulterous wife). So far Steuchus. Cajetan translates "cornificavit" (made horns), and adds: "The emission of rays is metaphorically called horn-making, because the emission of rays is as though an emission of horns." See also Benedictus and the Sienese. See also Ferus and Oleaster on this passage. Bellarmine does not disagree. And Thomas does not hesitate to assert that the face of Moses is better described as shining than as horned, and that it is wrongly given horns coming out of the head. Why then did the Pontiffs not dare to take this upon themselves, to put "shining" in place of "horned"? It is also a matter for wonder that the Pontiffs Sixtus and Clement, in their new Bibles, approved the custom condemned by so many learned men, by which rays are attached to Moses not shining from his whole face, but rising from his head like two horns. Whether this was done to safeguard the Vulgate edition, or rather to defend the bishops' two-horned mitres, or both, Rainoldus rightly asks.

units.la: E speculis הצובאות אשר צבאו ad ostium tabernaculi conventus. | E speculis mulierum quae excubabant in ostio tabernaculi.
units.tr: From the mirrors [הצובאות אשר צבאו] at the door of the tent of meeting. | From the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle.

units.la: Eadem vox צובאות extat 1. Sam. 2. 22. ubi vertit Vulg. quae observabant. Nomen צבא significat exercitum & turmam militum. Unde optime reddas, e speculis mulierum turmatim convenientium, quae turmatim conveniebant ad ost. t. Conv. vel quae circumexercituabant tabernaculum. ut ex Gloss. veteri citat Cl. Casaub. Alii simpl. vertunt, convenientium. Vulgatus, excubabant, quod interpretationem occasionem Papistis dedit locum hunc adducendi ad probandam hanc thesin, in V. T. foeminas voto religionis astrictas fuisse, quae in cellis circa templum habitantes inde nunquam recesserint. De quo somnio prolixe Casaub. Exerc. 1. cap. 23, cujus scrinia non compilabo. Est enim aut saltem
units.tr: The same word, צובאות, occurs in 1 Sam. 2.22, where the Vulgate renders it "who kept watch." The noun צבא [tsaba] means an army and a troop of soldiers. Hence you may best render it: "from the mirrors of the women gathering in companies, who came together in companies at the door of the tent of meeting," or "who encamped about the tabernacle," as Casaubon cites from an old gloss. Others simply render it "of those assembling." The Vulgate translator's "kept watch" gave the Papists an occasion to cite this passage in support of their thesis that in the Old Testament there were women bound by a vow of religion, who lived in cells around the temple and never withdrew from it. Casaubon deals with this dream at length in Exercitation 1, chapter 23; I will not plunder his writings. For it is, or at least

units.la: Si fœmina [Hebrew] & peperit masculum. | Mulier si suscepto semine peperit masculum.
units.tr: If a woman [Hebrew] and bears a male. | If a woman, having received seed, bears a male.

units.la: Oleastrius ad hac verba, suscepto semine, sic ait, Bern. & Origenes hom. 8. in hoc caput & Alb. Magnus annotarunt, per ea verba Mosen ab hac lege virginem purissimam excipere voluisse, quæ non suscepto semine filium peperit. Sed libet & Dionysium Carthusianum audire, Secundum Origenem superflue, Moses addidisset, suscepto semine, nisi scivisset in spiritu virginem masculum pariturum, atque ut addit S. Pater Bern. Moses dicturus, Mulier si peperit immunda erit, timuit crimen blasphemia super matre Christi incurrere: ideo addidit, suscepto semine. Hinc alii dicunt quod beata virgo excepta fuit ab ista lege, quia concepit & peperit sine virili semine. Quid ad hæc Oleastrius? Hoc optime notatum esset, inquit, si hæc lex ita in Ebræo haberetur, sed cum longe aliter habeatur, non est locus mysterio, &c. Vox Ebr. [Hebrew] proprie significat, dare semen. Ad verbum, seminificaverit. Passim herbis tribuitur, ubi susceptio seminis denotari non potest. Viris eam vocem passim attribunt Ebræi, quod nos diceremus, semen emitto, jacio. Itaque Aben. exponit [Hebrew] cum dederit semen. Ubi & illud tradit, Multi ajunt, quod si prima det semen, masculum concipiat, ideo sequitur & peperit masculum. Ideo sapientes Græcæ ajunt fœminas habere semen, quod coagulet semen maris. Eadem leges R. in Salom. Genes. 46. 15. Ego itaque cum Aben. aliisque doctis hoc Interpretamentum retinendum censeo, si dederit semen, urgendumque adversus Anabaptistas; qui, ut suos de humanae Christi naturae origine errores stabiliant, foeminas semen habere praefracte negant. Atque huc retulerim locum Ebraeorum II. 11. de Sara, ως καταβολὴν σπέρματος, quod malim reddere, ad emittendum vel ejiciendum semen, ut excretio seminis Sarae ex lumbis uterum intelligatur. Certe invenio in Lexicis, καταβάλλειν σπέρμα, esse emittere semen. Quadraret huic sensui, ut videtur, magis vox ἐκβολὴ, sed magis emphaticam vocem καταβολὴ esse, notavit Cl. Piscator, utpote quâ fluxus denotatur. Theophylactus memorat, suo quoque aevo locum sic expositum fuisse, indeque probatum, foeminas quoque semen conferre, nec omnino esse asymbolas. Beza in ultima Edit. expositum ejaculari semen, sed ex antecedente intelligi voluit consequens, unde suppl eta voce concipiendum, vertit, ad ejaculatum semen concipiendum. Vide jam & Drusium in praeteritis ad Ebr. 11. 11.
units.tr: Oleastrius, on these words, "having received seed," says this: Bernard and Origen in Homily 8 on this chapter, and Albertus Magnus, noted that by these words Moses meant to exclude from this law the most pure virgin, who bore a son without having received seed. But let us also hear Dionysius the Carthusian: According to Origen, Moses would have added "having received seed" superfluously, unless he had known in the Spirit that the virgin would bear a male; and, as St. Bernard adds, Moses, about to say "if she bears, she will be unclean," feared to incur the charge of blasphemy against the mother of Christ. Therefore he added "having received seed." Hence others say that the blessed virgin was exempted from this law, because she conceived and bore without male seed. What does Oleastrius say to this? This would have been very well observed, he says, if the law were so in the Hebrew; but since it is read quite differently, there is no place for a mystery, etc. The Hebrew word [Hebrew] properly means "to give seed"; literally, "to seminify" (seminificaverit). It is applied everywhere to herbs, where the receiving of seed cannot be meant. The Hebrews commonly apply that word to men, as we would say "to emit" or "to cast" seed. Thus Aben Ezra explains it as [Hebrew] when she has given seed. Where he also reports: Many say that if she first gives seed, she conceives a male; therefore it follows, "and bears a male." Hence the Greek wise men say that women have seed, which curdles the seed of the male. The rabbi Solomon teaches the same things on Genesis 46.15. I, therefore, with Aben Ezra and other learned men, think this interpretation should be retained, that it is "if she has given seed," and that it should be pressed against the Anabaptists, who, to support their errors about the origin of Christ's human nature, stubbornly deny that women have seed. And here I would refer the passage of Hebrews 11.11 about Sarah, [Greek: εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος], which I would prefer to render "for emitting or casting out seed," so that the excretion of Sarah's seed from her loins is understood. Certainly I find in the lexicons that [Greek: καταβάλλειν σπέρμα] means "to emit seed." The word [Greek: ἐκβολὴ] would seem to suit this sense better, but the illustrious Piscator has noted that [Greek: καταβολὴ] is the more emphatic word, since it denotes a flow. Theophylact records that in his own time the passage was explained in this way too, and thereby it was proved that women also contribute seed and are not altogether without a share. Beza, in his last edition, wanted it expounded as "to eject seed," but he wished the consequent to be understood from the antecedent, whence, supplying the word "conceiving," he renders it "for conceiving the ejaculated seed." See also Drusius, in the earlier notes on Hebrews 11.11.

units.la: August. Quaest in Levit. qu. 66. A femine tuo non dabis servire principi. Hic non video, inquit, quid intelligatur, nisi principi qui pro Deo colitur. Non enim ait δουλεύειν, sed λατρεύειν in Graeco, quod Latinus non solet interpretari, nisi ut dicat, servire. Plurimum autem distant. Nam servire hominibus, quo servi serviunt, quod non est λατρεύειν, sed δουλεύειν, scriptura non prohibet. servire autem secundum id quod est λατρεύειν, non jubetur hominibus, nisi uni vero Deo, sicuti scriptum est, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis & illi soli servies. Tu disce tiro supervacaneam esse hanc magni viri περιεργίαν. Namque ubi Graeci habent, ἀπὸ τῆς σπέρματος αὐτοῦ ... λατρεύειν τῷ ἀρχοντι, Ebraea plane aliud sensum habent, non dabis de semine tuo לְהַעֲבִיר לַמֹּלֶךְ ad traducendum Moloche. Ecce cultus Molochi, non ministeria aut servitia prohibentur. Sed LXX. vocem lehagnabir, legerunt cum daleth in fine, ut magna est istarum literarum affinitas. Et למלך sine punctis indifferens est ad מלך & מלך. Miror Augustinum non vidisse quod Theodoretus vidit, vid. caeteros Interpretes Moloch reddidisse. Scholion ad Biblia Graeca, τὸ ἐβεγὼν μόλοχ ἔχει, τῶν. τῶν οἱ λοιποὶ ἑρμηνευταὶ πεθ᾿ἑκαστον. Quod ita reddidit Theodoretus, Hebraicum exemplar Moloch habet, quod reliqui interpretes annotarunt, imo dixisset potius, in sua translatione posuerunt. Sed ut ad Augustinum redeat oratio, miraris forte Lector, cur ille de simplici ministerio exteris principibus non praestando legem hanc interpretatus non sit, quomodo illi quos Theod. notat, eam accepere. Observa, Augustinum, postquam semel discrimen illud inter δουλείαν & λατρείαν meliori mente quam eventu tradidisset, omnia loca quae istud evertere videbantur, sic fuisse interpretatum, nequid ex iis pulcra ista distinctio detrimenti caperet. Vis aliud specimen? Locutionum sacrarum lib. 5. Ad Deut. 28. 48. Et servies inimicis tuis. Graecus habet λατρεύσεις. Solet autem hoc verbum in ea servitute scriptura ponere, quae debetur Deo. Unde idololatrae vocantur, qui ea servitute idolis serviunt. Ergo hic inusitate positum est hoc verbum, quamquam posset etiam hunc sensum habere (vides jam quo tendat?) quod tam graviter multa dixerit ut inimicis suis nimium superbientibus tanquam Diis servire cogantur. Omnia haec una litura delevisset doctissimus Pater, si scivisset in Hebraeo esse עבד / quod promiscue & de cultu Dei & ministeriis, quae hominibus praestantur: neque apud profanos tantum quod a Bell. b Azorius, c Jansenius fatentur, sed & in N. T. & Graeca/Vet. Test. versione, voces illas passim confundi. Confer haec loca, Rom. 1. 9. Act. 20. 19. & 7. 6. & 12. 11. & 14. 18. & 16. 18. Eph. 6. 7. Phil. 2. 22. Coloss. 3. 24. Matth. 4. 10. Act. 20. 19. Gal. 4. 8. Rom. 1. 25. Ebr. 9. 14. 1. Thess. 1. 9. Porro in LXX. Interpretibus vide de haec loca Deut. 28. 48. Deut. 6. 13. confer cum 1. Sam. 7. & 4. item Jud. 2. 11. cum 1. Sam. 8. 8. Hac de re prolixius disseruere Paraeus in Epist. ad Rom. Vives ad August. de Civitate Dei 10. 1. Jac: Laurentius in Apologetico contra Sandaeum. Chamierus Tom. 2. pag. 769. & seq. & alii.
units.tr: Augustine, Quaest. in Levit. qu. 66. You shall not give any of your seed to serve the prince. Here, he says, I do not see what is meant except the prince who is worshipped in place of God. For the Greek does not say to be a slave [δουλεύειν] but to serve [λατρεύειν], which the Latin translator usually renders only as "serve". Yet the two differ greatly. For to serve men, as slaves serve, which is δουλεύειν and not λατρεύειν, Scripture does not forbid. But to serve in the sense of λατρεύειν is commanded to no one except the one true God, as it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone. You, a beginner, learn that this curiosity of the great man is superfluous. For where the Greeks have from his seed ... to serve the ruler [ἀπὸ τῆς σπέρματος αὐτοῦ ... λατρεύειν τῷ ἀρχοντι], the Hebrew clearly has another sense: you shall not give of your seed לְהַעֲבִיר לַמֹּלֶךְ, to make pass through to Molech. Behold, what is forbidden is the worship of Molech, not ministries or services. But the Seventy read the word lehagnabir with a daleth at the end, since these letters are closely similar. And למלך, without points, is open to being read either way, as melech [מלך] or as Molech [מלך]. I am surprised that Augustine did not see what Theodoret saw, that the other interpreters rendered it Moloch. The scholion on the Greek Bibles says the Hebrew has Moloch [τὸ ἐβεγὼν μόλοχ ἔχει]; the other interpreters [τῶν οἱ λοιποὶ ἑρμηνευταὶ] each in their place. Theodoret rendered this: The Hebrew exemplar has Moloch, which the other interpreters noted; or rather he would better have said that they put it into their translation. But to return the discussion to Augustine: perhaps the reader wonders why he did not interpret this law, as those whom Theodoret notes did, as meaning the simple ministry of not providing services to foreign princes. Observe that Augustine, having once handed down that distinction between δουλείαν and λατρείαν with a better intention than outcome, interpreted all the passages that seemed to overturn it in such a way that the fine distinction would suffer no harm from them. Do you want another example? In the Locutionum sacrarum book 5, on Deut. 28. 48: And you shall serve your enemies. The Greek has λατρεύσεις [you shall serve as a worshipper]. Scripture usually uses this verb for the servitude owed to God; hence those who serve idols with that servitude are called idolaters. So here the verb is used unusually, although it could also have this sense (do you see where it leads?): that he has spoken so harshly of many things that his enemies, too proud, are forced to serve them as gods. That most learned Father would have wiped out all of this with one stroke if he had known that in Hebrew the word is ʿavad [עבד], which is used indiscriminately both of the worship of God and of the services rendered to men. Nor is this confusion found only among profane writers, as Bell., Azorius and Jansenius admit; the words are also mixed up in the New Testament and in the Greek version of the Old. Compare these passages: Rom. 1. 9; Acts 20. 19; 7. 6; 12. 11; 14. 18; 16. 18; Eph. 6. 7; Phil. 2. 22; Col. 3. 24; Matt. 4. 10; Acts 20. 19; Gal. 4. 8; Rom. 1. 25; Heb. 9. 14; 1 Thess. 1. 9. Further, on the usage of the Seventy, see these passages: Deut. 28. 48 and Deut. 6. 13; compare 1 Sam. 7 and 4, and likewise Judg. 2. 11 with 1 Sam. 8. 8. Several writers have discussed this matter at greater length: Paraeus on the Epistle to the Romans, Vives on Augustine's De Civitate Dei 10. 1, Jac. Laurentius in his Apology against Sandaeus, Chamier tom. 2, p. 769 and following, and others.

units.la: Et Moses erat mansuetus valde pra omnibus hominibus, &c. Ita habent fontes. Ita redidêre præter vulg. Lxx. & Chaldæum etiam Junius, Pisc. Italicus, Genev. Angli, Tig. Pagn. Eo magis miror quid in mentem venerit B. Lurheto qui hæc verba sic interpretatus est, Aber Mose war ein sehr geplagter mensch uber alle menschen/ &c. Ende Moses was een seer gheplaeght mensche/ &c. Tædet referre quid ad hunc textum explicandum convectare soleant, queis ne Interpretem quidem alium inspicere vacat. Multa dicunt de calamitatibus & forte piorum, sed extra oleas. Mansuetudo Mosis hic commendatur. Disinant ergo hunc textum ex prava versione citare. Caveant religiosus, ne pravam versionem populo explicent.
units.tr: "And Moses was very meek above all men," etc. So the sources have it. So have the Vulgate, the Seventy, and the Chaldee paraphrast rendered it, and so also Junius, the Italian translator Pisc., the Geneva translators, the English, the Tigurine, and Pagninus. I am all the more surprised at what came into the mind of the blessed Luther, who translated these words thus: <bl>Aber Mose war ein sehr geplagter mensch uber alle menschen/</bl> etc. <bl>Ende Moses was een seer gheplaeght mensche/</bl> etc. It is tiresome to report what those commonly bring together to explain this text who do not even have time to consult another translator. They say much about the afflictions of the pious, perhaps, but it is beside the point. The meekness of Moses is what is commended here. Let them therefore stop citing this text from a faulty version. Let the religious take care not to explain a faulty version to the people.
