units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Et descenderunt ipsi & quidquid ad eos pertinebat, vivi שאול | Descenderuntque vivi in Infernum
units.tr: Hebrew | Vulgate. And they went down, they and all that belonged to them, alive into [שְׁאוֹל] | And they went down alive into Hell.

units.la: Ex hoc textu colligunt Pontificii Interpp. omnes eos in Gehennam descendisse. Sed observandum est vocem שְׁאוֹל male hic ab Interp. per Infernum expressam. Fatentur etiam Abulensis, Hieron. ab Oleastr. Fonseca, Cajet. aliique sepulcrum hic denotari. Circumstantiæ hoc manifeste urgent. Descenderunt, inquit textus in Scheol, cum omnibus quæ ad ipsos pertinebant. Sed illa verba & quicquid ad eos pertinebat, omisit Interpres, quod non parvum momentum attulit firmando communi errori. Hoc spectans Cajetanus, Iterum litera manca est, inquit, Lxx. omnia expressere, καὶ καταβήσαν αὐτοὶ καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἦσαν αὐτοῖς, ζῶντες εἰς ᾅδην. N B. καὶ πάντα ὅσα αὐτοῖς, non πάντες ὅσοι, &c. Sic enim & ipse vulg. verba illa וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם versu 30. reddireddiderat. Illa autem omnia fuerunt tentoria, opes, verf. 32. iplaque adeo, ut Lxx. verterunt, κτήνη, jumenta. At quis dicet ea omnia in infernum proprie dictum id est locum subterraneum animarum descendisse? Intelligendus ergo est locus subterraneus corporum. Ita tamen, ut negandum non sit, quin eorum animæ, qui in malitiâ perstiterunt, corporibus solutæ ad locum animarum devenerint. Et cui adeo cornea erit fibra, ut omnes hos homines audeat in damnatorum numerum referre? Nec enim soli, sed cum liberis parvulis, servis, ancillarumque caterva discendisse leguntur. Illud mihi dabunt, spero, adversarii, fieri potuisse, ut inter eos quidam poenitentiâ vitam clauserint. Cur ergo sepulcrum omnibus non damus, animarum judicium soli Deo relinquimus? maxime cum vocem Sheol sepulcrum ordinarie significare ad Gen. 37. demonstratum sit. Sed an hoc supplicium tam horribile & tremendum, dixerit aliquis? Est sane. Vestales virgines, si eas temerari contigisset, hoc supplicio tanquam αιμάσσω & miserabilissimæ fuisse multatas, literis proditum est. Quamquam in contextu non tam atrocitas quam novitas supplicii depingatur, cum enim non soleant homines sepeliri nisi ante mortui sunt, hi vivi terra obruti sunt. Sed hæc adversus eos disputata sint qui hunc locum de loco animarum exponendum mordicus contendunt, inter quos Bellarm. Cont. 2: lib. 4, cap. 11. nec non eos, qui τὸ Scheol nunquam sepulcrum id est locum subterraneum animarum, inter quos Andreas Crocquetius ad Genes. 37. nobis citatus, aut rarissime, inter quos rursus Bellarm. significare contendunt. Si enim vocem infernum hoc loco exposueris supulcrum, nulla inter nos erit dissensio.
units.tr: From this text the Papist interpreters all draw the conclusion that they all went down into Gehenna. But it must be noted that the word [שְׁאוֹל] is wrongly rendered here by the translator as "Hell." Abulensis, Jerome of Oleaster, Fonseca, Cajetan and others also admit that the grave [sepulchrum] is meant here. The circumstances press this plainly. The text says they went down into Sheol, with all that belonged to them. But the translator omitted the words "and all that belonged to them," which added no small weight to strengthening the common error. Looking at this, Cajetan says: "Again the letter is defective"; the Seventy expressed everything: "καὶ καταβήσαν αὐτοὶ καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἦσαν αὐτοῖς, ζῶντες εἰς ᾅδην" [and they went down, they and all that were theirs, alive into Hades]. N.B.: "καὶ πάντα ὅσα αὐτοῖς," not "πάντες ὅσοι," etc. For the Vulgate too had rendered in the same way the words [וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם] in verse 30. But all those things were tents and wealth (verse 32), and even the livestock, as the Seventy rendered it ["κτήνη," livestock]. But who will say that all of these went down properly into hell, that is, into the subterranean place of souls? So we must understand the subterranean place of bodies. Yet it must not be denied that the souls of those who persisted in wickedness, once released from their bodies, arrived at the place of souls. And who would have a heart so hard as to dare to count all these people among the damned? For we read that they went down not alone but with their little children, servants, and a crowd of maidservants. My opponents will grant me, I hope, that some of them may have ended their lives in repentance. Why then do we not give the grave to all, and leave the judgment of souls to God alone, especially since it has been shown on Genesis 37 that the word Sheol ordinarily signifies the grave? But someone will say, is this punishment not very horrible and terrifying? Indeed it is. It is recorded that if the Vestal Virgins happened to be violated, they were punished with this punishment, as something [αἱμάσσω] most wretched. Yet in the context it is not so much the atrocity as the novelty of the punishment that is depicted, since men are not usually buried unless they are dead first, and these were buried alive. But let these arguments be directed against those who stubbornly insist that this place must be explained as the place of souls, among whom is Bellarmine, Controversy 2, book 4, chapter 11; and also against those who maintain that Sheol never means the grave, that is, the subterranean place of souls, or only very rarely, among whom again is Bellarmine, and Andreas Crocquetius, cited by us on Genesis 37. For if you explain the word "hell" in this place as "grave," there will be no dispute between us.

units.la: Deus præscripturus Judæis rationem conficiendæ aquæ, quæ ab immunditia eos esset purgatura, ita præfatur, חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה id. est hoc est statutum legis, quod præcepit DOMINVS, dicendo, ubi חֻקָּה & תּוֹרָה tanquam synonyma ἐν junguntur, ut volumen libri, petra silicis, canticum Psalmi, vide Gramm. nostram lib. 2. cap. 1. §. 24. Junius, statutum legale. Vulg. ista est religio victima, quod Corn. Con. à Lapide interpretatur, ceremonia id est lex ceremonialis. Et certe הקים & חקות quando à משפטים & מצוות quando à משפטים & מצוות distinguuntur sæpe leges ceremoniales significant, quas Græci δικαιώματα vocare solent, quo sensu eadem quoque voce usus est B. Paulus, Ebræorum 9. verf.1. Reddatur ergo, & hic, hæc est ceremonia legis, vel per hypallagen, hæc est lex ceremonialis. Hoc an illo modo vertas, hilum non interest. Lxx. αὕτη ἡ διαθήκη ἡ νόμος, ὅσα συνέταξε ὁ θεὸς. Quæ ita reddita fuerunt in Latina translatione qua usus fuit Augustinus, Hæc est distinctio Legis, quæcunque constituit Dominus. Audiamus jam Augustinum super hoc loco perorantem. Sic ergo Quæst. in Num. q. 33. Ista distinctio Legis, &c. Non satis digne festinantes dicere de tanto sacramento valemus. Primo enim quod ita cæpit loqui, quem non moveat & intentissimam mentem faciat in altitudine sacramenti, Ista distinctio Legis, &c. Proculdubio non est distinctio nisi inter aliqua duo vel plura. Nam distinctionem singularitas non requirit. Nec distinctionem cujuslibet rei commemoravit, sed addidit, Legis, nec cujuscunque legis; assidue quippe in Scriptura dicitur de unaquaque re de qua legitime præcipitur. Hic vero cum dixisset, hæc est distinctio legis, secutus adjunxit, quæcunque constituit Dominus, præcipiendo utique non creando. Si ergo hæc est distinctio legis, quæcunque præcepit Dominus, procul dubio magna distinctio. Et certe intelligitur duo testamenta distinguere. Et paulo post, Temporalium autem bonorum & carnalium & spiritualium & æternorum, quæ clarior & certior distinctio est, quam passio Domini nostri Jesu Christi? Et rursus pauculis interjectis. Hanc ergo passionem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, tanquam distinctionem duorum testamentorum, hoc quod de juvenca rufa mactatione narratur, satis congrue præfigurat. Hæc August. Examina hæc ad fontes, & evanescent. Decepit Interpretem, decepit Augustinum unica illa vox ἀφορισμός, quæ in N. fœdere occurrit in notione distinctionis, Rom. 3. 1. Corinth. 14. Et certe ἀφορίζω est distinguo. At si vel Interpres vel Augustinus locum hunc cum fontibus conferre fuisset quitus, distinctionis ejusmodi, qualem hic August. intellexit, nec volam nec vestigium invenisset. Quid ergo? Ibi vidisti jam vocem חקות / eam expressere Lxx. jam per δικαίωμα, jam per παραγγελία, jam per νόμιμον, jam per νόμον, jam per ἐντολὴ. Semel per ἀφορισμός, vid. hoc loco ἀφορισμός hic ergo est mandatum datum
units.tr: God, about to prescribe to the Jews the manner of preparing the water that would purify them from uncleanness, introduces it thus: [חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה], that is, "this is the statute of the law which the LORD commanded, saying," where [חֻקָּה] and [תּוֹרָה] are joined as synonyms, as "the volume of the book," "the rock of flint," "the song of the psalm"; see our Grammar, book 2, chapter 1, §24. Junius: "a legal statute." The Vulgate: "ista est religio victimae" [this is the rite of the sacrifice], which Cornelius à Lapide interprets as ceremony, that is, the ceremonial law. And certainly when [חקים] and [חקות] are distinguished from [משפטים] and [מצוות], they often signify ceremonial laws, which the Greeks are accustomed to call [δικαιώματα]; in this sense the blessed Paul also used the same word, Hebrews 9:1. So render it here too: "this is the ceremony of the law," or by hypallage, "this is the ceremonial law." Whether you translate it in this way or that makes no difference. The Seventy: "αὕτη ἡ διαθήκη ἡ νόμος, ὅσα συνέταξε ὁ θεὸς" [this is the covenant, the law, whatever God ordained]. These words, as rendered in the Latin translation Augustine used, read: "This is the distinction of the Law, whatever the Lord has appointed." Let us now hear Augustine holding forth on this passage. So in the Questions on Numbers, question 33: "This distinction of the Law, etc. We are not able to speak worthily enough, in our hasty way, of so great a sacrament. For first, who would not be moved and made most intent by the depth of the sacrament by the fact that it begins to speak thus: 'This distinction of the Law, etc.'? Undoubtedly it is not a distinction unless between some two or more things. For singularity does not require a distinction. Nor did he mention the distinction of any thing whatever, but added 'of the Law,' nor of any law whatever; for in Scripture it is constantly said of each thing about which a command is lawfully given. But here, having said 'this is the distinction of the law,' he went on to add 'whatever the Lord has appointed,' by commanding, that is, not by creating. If then this is the distinction of the law, whatever the Lord has commanded, it is without doubt a great distinction. And certainly it is understood to distinguish the two testaments." And a little later: "But of temporal goods, both fleshly and spiritual, and of eternal ones, what clearer and surer distinction is there than the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ?" And again, a few lines later: "This passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, as a distinction of the two testaments, quite fittingly prefigures what is narrated about the red heifer's slaughter." Thus Augustine. Examine these things at the sources, and they will vanish. The single word [ἀφορισμός], which occurs in the New Testament in the sense of distinction (Romans 3:1; 1 Corinthians 14), deceived the translator and deceived Augustine. And certainly [ἀφορίζω] means "to distinguish." But if either the translator or Augustine had been accustomed to compare this passage with the sources, they would have found neither trace nor hint of the kind of distinction that Augustine here understood. What then? You have already seen the word [חקות] rendered by the Seventy at one time by [δικαίωμα], at another by [παραγγελία], at another by [νόμιμον], at another by [νόμον], at another by [ἐντολή]. Once by [ἀφορισμός]; see in this place [ἀφορισμός], so here it is a command given,

units.la: e Deut. 16. 12. datum, praeceptum, qua notione in profanis authoribus occurrit Θησλη. Hesych. Θησλαι, ἐντλαι, ἀλαζων. Caeterum quod ad vocem Ἀλσηλη attinet, non mirum eam pro praecepto & statuto hic usurpatam. Nam τὸ Ἀλσηλομαι & in Hellenica & Hellenistica lingua passim significat, distincte aliquid praecipere, mandare. Eadem vox recurrit Num. 30. 8. neque amplius. Sed hic significat distinctam pronuntiationem seu effatum, respondetque Ebraeo מבטא / Levit. 5. 4. τὸ ΝΟΣ itidem per * Ἀλσ ... reddidere, quod Latinus interpres reddidit, distinguere. Anima quae juraverit, ἡ Ἀλσηλησις τῆς χείλεσι καλοποιησις ἡ κακο-ποιησις, ἢ πᾶν ὃ ἂν διακρίνῃ ἄνθρωπος, &c. distinguens labiis suis ad benefaciendum, per omnia quae distinxerit homo, &c. Adi ad hunc quoque locum Augustini Quaestiones, & videbis versionem istam tenebras obtudisse loco alias clarissimo. Desinam ubi illud notavero, Lxx. eadem haec verba, מִשְׁפָּט הַתּוֹרָה Num. 31. 11. sic reddidisse, ἡ τὸ δικαιωμα τοῦ νόμου, quae hoc modo Latinus Interpres reddiderat, hoc est justificatio legis. Vulg. hoc est praeceptum legis.
units.tr: e Deut. 16. 12. a command, a precept; a sense in which it occurs in secular authors, [Θησλη]. Hesychius: [Θησλαι] = [ἐντλαι], [ἀλαζων]. Moreover, as regards the word [Ἀλσηλη], it is no wonder that it is used here for precept and statute. For [διαστέλλομαι] in both Greek and Hellenistic usage commonly means "to command something distinctly." The same word recurs at Numbers 30:8, and nowhere else. But here it signifies a distinct utterance or saying, and it corresponds to the Hebrew [מבטא], Leviticus 5:4. The Seventy likewise rendered [ΝΟΣ] by [διαστέλλω], which the Latin translator rendered "to distinguish": "The soul that has sworn, [ἡ διαστολὴ τῶν χειλέων] to do good or to do evil, or whatever a man shall distinguish [διαστείλῃ]..., distinguishing with his lips to do good, in all things that man has distinguished," etc. Look also at Augustine's Questions on this passage, and you will see that this translation has obscured a passage otherwise very clear. I will end where I note this: the Seventy rendered these same Hebrew words [מִשְׁפָּט הַתּוֹרָה], Numbers 31:21, thus: [ἡ τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου], which the Latin translator rendered in this way: "this is the justification of the law." The Vulgate: "this is the precept of the law."

units.la: Non quasi homo Dominus suspenditur, neque quasi filius hominis minas patitur.] Ita hunc locum citat Lactantius lib. 4. de vera Sapientia, cap. mihi 18. tanquam vaticinium de Christo aliquando crucifigendo. Ebraea nihil ejusmodi habent, לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכָזֵב וּבֶן־אָדָם וְיִתְנַחֵם Deus non est vir ut mentiatur, aut filius hominis, ut poenitudine ducatur. Ubi vulg. sine ulla necessitate, ut mutetur. Lxx. ἐχ' ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ θεὸς Ἀλσευθῆναι, ἀλ' ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀπειλησαι. Quae sic versa reperio in Edit. Basileensi, non ut homo Deus ad mentiendum, neque ut filius hominis ut minetur. Crediderim interpretem eum quisquis fuit, legisse, ἐχ' ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ θεὸς Ἀλσευσθαι, ut habet Editio Complutens. hoc enim est, ad mentiendum, à qua lectione quoad sensum non recedit illa Philonis in De vita Mosis, Ἀλσευθῆναι. Quid vero illud Ἀλσετηθῆναι, dixerit aliquis. Scholion, quod extat in Edit. Romana, Ἀλσετηθῆναι, ἔτ' ἐστι σαλευθῆναι. τὰ γὰρ κρεμάμενα σαλεύονται. Ἀλσετηθῆναι, idest, agitari, commoveri, fluctuare. Ea enim quae suspensa sunt, agitantur hùc illuc & fluctuant. Hoc ergo, vult, ἀλγεπεῖν, proprie esse suspendo, κρεμάω, κρε-μάζω. At hic metaphoricè accipi, pro, inconstantem & va-rium esse in verbis suis. Vides jam Lactantium proprie accepisse hanc vocem dum vertit, suspenditur, atque inde infert, Deum aliquando suspendendum, non tamen ut ψιλὸν ἀνθρωπον. Quod si vocem eam, cum ea quæ in fontibus est, conferre quivisset, aut valde fallor aut nunquam in hanc expositionem fuisset delatus.
units.tr: "Not as a man is God pressed to repent, nor as the son of man is he threatened." Lactantius cites this passage in book 4 of De vera Sapientia, chapter 18, as a prophecy of Christ who was at some time to be crucified. The Hebrew has nothing of the kind: לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכָזֵב וּבֶן־אָדָם וְיִתְנַחֵם God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should be moved to regret. Where the Vulgate has, without any need, that he should be changed. The Seventy have: "God is not as a man, to be shaken, nor as a son of man, to be threatened." These words I find rendered thus in the Basel edition: not as a man is God to lie, nor as a son of man to threaten. I would believe the translator, whoever he was, read ἐχ' ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ θεὸς Ἀλσευθῆναι, as the Complutensian edition has it, for this means to lie, and in sense Philo's reading in De vita Mosis, Ἀλσευθῆναι, does not depart from it. But what someone might say of that word Ἀλσετηθῆναι? The scholion found in the Roman edition reads: Ἀλσετηθῆναι, that is σαλευθῆναι, for things hanging are shaken. Ἀλσετηθῆναι, that is, to be driven, moved, made to waver. For things that are suspended are tossed here and there and fluctuate. This therefore means that ἀλγεπεῖν properly signifies to hang, κρεμάω, κρεμάζω. But here it is taken metaphorically, for being inconstant and variable in one's words. You now see that Lactantius took this word in its proper sense when he rendered it is suspended, and from this he infers that God is at some time to be suspended, yet not as a mere man. If he had been able to compare that word with the one found in the sources, I am much mistaken, or he would never have been led into this interpretation.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. verf. 10. 11.

units.la: Et devoravit (terra) Core, morientibus plurimis, quando combuf-sit ignis CCL. viros & factum est grande miraculum, ut Core pereun-te filii ejus non sint mortui.
units.tr: And the earth devoured Korah, while very many were dying, when fire consumed two hundred and fifty men; and it became a great miracle, so that while Korah perished, his sons did not die.

units.la: Nota, extremum versus 10. cum principio verf. 11. esse conjunctum, ut hic sensus sit juxta vulg. Et factum est grande mi-raculum, ut, Core pereunte, filii ejus non perierint. At primo & Chald. & Lxx· versus hos distinxere, ἡ ἐγενήθη ἐο σημεῖον. οἱ δ᾽ υἱοὶ Κωρὲ οὐκ ἀπέθανον. Sic & Chald. מתו לארץ / Deinde illa verba, והיו לנס / non possunt verti, & factum est grande miraculum ut ut פ miraculum alibi significet, constructio enim & modus loquendi obstant. 3. Core pereunte, non est in Ebræo. Quid ergo ἐ prius illud, & fuerunt in signum, respicit terra igneque absumptos, Illi fuerunt in signum id est fuerunt exemplo aliis Israëlitis, non esse rixandum cum Domino. Posterius simpliciter narrat, filios Core cum patre non simul periisse, cum Dathanis & Abirami liberi una periisse videantur. Sic etiam Ebræi Interpretes, R. Sal. Aben. &c. Baal Turim, cujus notulæ ad Biblia Veneta in margine ponuntur, illud esse in signum, etiam eo respicere opinatur, quod hominum isto-rum 250. thuribula jussu Dei Num. 16. 38. in laminas exten-sas producta sint, & altari affixa, ut essent, inquit textus, לאות / in signum filiis Israel.
units.tr: Note that the end of verse 10 is joined to the beginning of verse 11, so that the sense according to the Vulgate is: And it became a great miracle, that, while Korah perished, his sons did not perish. But first the Chaldee and the Seventy divided these verses: "and it became a sign. But the sons of Korah did not die." So also the Chaldee: "they died to the land." Then those words, והיו לנס, cannot be rendered "and it became a great miracle," although the word for miracle elsewhere means that; for the construction and the manner of speaking stand in the way. Third, while Korah perished is not in the Hebrew. What, then, does the first clause, "and they were for a sign," refer to: the men consumed by earth and fire, "they were for a sign," that is, they were an example to other Israelites not to quarrel with the Lord. The second simply relates that the sons of Korah did not perish together with their father, although the children of Dathan and Abiram seem to have perished together with them. So also the Hebrew interpreters, R. Sal., Aben, etc. The Baal Turim, whose notes are placed in the margin of the Venetian Bible, thinks that "for a sign" also refers to this, that the two hundred and fifty thuribles of those men were, by God's command, beaten out into extended plates, and fixed to the altar, that they might be, says the text, לאות / for a sign to the sons of Israel.

units.la: Sed libet ascribere faceta verba Lyræ ad hunc locum ut vi-deas quò virum doctissimum, prout illud seculum erat, mala hæc versio traxerit. Sic ergo dicit, Factum est miraculum) quale autem fuerit, in textu non dicitur, nisi in generali quod filii Core non non fuerunt mortui cum eo; sed in glossa Ebr. super Psal. * 45. (nobis 46.) dicitur, quod quando terra aperuit os suum & devora-vit Core cum multis aliis, filii ejus remanserunt stantes in aere divina virtute, quousque terra fuit iterum clausa sub pedibus eorum. Ad hanc Lyrae glossam, quam & Corn. à Lapide & Dionysius Carthusianus approbarunt, videatur Additio Pauli Burgensis, qui diserte ait opinionem istam non esse fundatam in litera, cum ea plane diversum habeat. Videantur & hic Cajet. Steuchus & Benedictus.
units.tr: But I am pleased to add the witty words of Lyra on this passage, so that you may see where that most learned man, as that age was, was led by this bad version. He thus says: "A miracle was made," but "what sort it was is not said in the text, except in general that the sons of Korah did not die with him; but in a Hebrew gloss on Psalm 45 (46 for us) it is said that when the earth opened its mouth and devoured Korah with many others, his sons remained standing in the air by divine power, until the earth was closed again beneath their feet." To this gloss of Lyra, which Cornelius à Lapide and Dionysius the Carthusian also approved, see the addition of Paul of Burgos, who expressly says that this opinion is not founded on the letter, since it plainly has a different meaning. See also here Cajetan, Steuchus and Benedictus.

units.la: Immolabis Phase de bobus & ovibus.] Ita Vulg. Abuntur hoc loco Baronius & alii ut docent, victimas illas quae durante Azymorum festo immolabantur, vocari Pascha, ac proinde illas quoque victimas denotari Joh. 18. 20. nolebant ingredi praetorium, &c. sed ut comederent Pascha. In eodem errore versabatur magnus Scaliger, in prima Editione egregii operis de Emendatione Temporum. At postea sententiam illam cum meliori commutavit, sicuti ex secunda Editione apparet. Hoc notabunt tirones. Passim enim videbunt in doctissimorum virorum libris, magnis erroribus ab authoritate Scaligeri patrocinium quaeri quos tamen ipse ille Heros in secunda operis Praedicti Editione solide confutavit. Quoties ergo opus illud ab eruditis citatur, diligenter inquiret Lector utrius Editionis exemplar habuerint, quod, ex paginarum, quas citare solent, collatione non obscurum erit deprehendere. In Prolegomenis, ubi adversus Toletum de die Paschatis agit, Nos vero, inquit, & hic mutavimus sententiam, cum huic stultae opinioni haereremus priore Editione. Similia invenies lib. 6. Sed ad rem. Casaubonus in Anti-Baronianis ostendit, per Pascha illud Johan. 18. non posse aliud intelligi, quam agnum Paschalem. Hunc vero locum nihil adversae sententiae patrocinari, non enim in Ebraeo legi, immolabis Phase de ovibus & bobus, sed, immolabis Paschae, boves & oves, Pascha id est agnum Paschalem. Lxx. ἡ θυσία τὸ πάσχα κλεῖα, τὴ ἡμέρα τῇ πεντεκοστῇ ἡ βοῦς. Vide distingui agnum Paschalem ab aliis victimis. Plane in eundem modum 2. Chron. 30.15. Pascha & holocausta distinguuntur. Illud autem nota Tiro, non solum intermediis illis diebus, quae vid. inter primum & ultimum solennitatis septiduanae diem intercedebant, sed & ipso illo die quo agnus immolabatur, alia sacrificia fuisse oblata. Vide Casaub. pag. 475. Edit. Londin. R. Salom. ad hunc locum, Maimon in tractatu de Korban happhesach. Buxtorf. in Dictionario in voce [illegible, ~3 letters] /
units.tr: "You shall sacrifice the Passover of oxen and sheep." So the Vulgate. Baronius and others argue from this place that the victims offered during the feast of Unleavened Bread were called the Passover, and that John 18:28 ("they themselves went not into the judgment hall... but that they might eat the Passover") therefore refers to those victims too. Great Scaliger fell into the same error in the first edition of his excellent work On the Emendation of Times. But later he changed that opinion for a better one, as the second edition shows. Students should note this. They will often find in the books of learned men that great errors are defended by the authority of Scaliger, although that hero himself refuted them soundly in the second edition of the work just mentioned. So whenever learned writers cite that work, the reader should carefully check which edition they used. This will not be hard to discover by comparing the pages they usually cite. In the Prolegomena, where he deals with the day of Passover against Toletus, Scaliger says: "We, however, have changed our opinion here too, since in the first edition we clung to that foolish view." You will find similar remarks in book 6. But to the point. Casaubon, in his Anti-Baronian work, shows that the "Passover" of John 18 can mean nothing other than the Paschal lamb. He also shows that this place gives no support to the opposing view, since the Hebrew does not read "you shall sacrifice the Passover of oxen and sheep," but "you shall sacrifice the Passover, oxen and sheep," where Pascha means the Paschal lamb. The Septuagint has [ἡ θυσία τὸ πάσχα κλεῖα, τὴ ἡμέρα τῇ πεντεκοστῇ ἡ βοῦς], that is, "the sacrifice of the Passover ... on the day of Pentecost the ox." Note how the Paschal lamb is distinguished from the other victims. In the same way, in 2 Chronicles 30:15, the Passover and the burnt offerings are distinguished. Young student, note also that other sacrifices were offered not only on the intermediate days between the first and last days of the seven-day festival, but also on the very day on which the lamb was slain. See Casaubon, p. 475, London edition. See also Rabbi Solomon on this passage, and Maimonides in the treatise on Korban happhesach, and Buxtorf in his Dictionary under the word [illegible, about three letters].

units.la: CAP. XVII. vers. 12.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII, verse 12.

units.la: Ebr. Vir autem qui fecerit per superbiam, ut non obediat sacerdoti, qui stetit ad ministrandum illic coram Domino Deo tuo, aut judici, morietur.
units.tr: Hebrew: "But the man who acts presumptuously, not listening to the priest who stands there to minister before the LORD your God, or to the judge, shall die."

units.la: Vulg. Qui autem superbierit nolens obedire sacerdotis imperio, qui eo tempore ministrat Domino Deo tuo, & decreto judicis, moriatur.
units.tr: Vulgate: "But whoever is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest, who at that time ministers to the LORD your God, and the decree of the judge, shall die."

units.la: Antea legebatur, ex decreto Judicis. Sic citavit Hartus in Colloquio, atque inde contendit probare, summum sacerdotem fuisse illum judicem, qui causas illas anxias & difficiles terminaverit. Hanc lectionem Papali authoritate ipse quoque Sixtus approbaverat. Sed Clemens VIII. reposuit, & decreto judicis. Quo magis miror Bellarmino eam fuisse fiduciam, ut locum hunc ex antiqua eaque magis corrupta lectione citatum in libro recognitionum, ad Editionem Clementis VIII. non correxerit. Sed cum rem perpendo accuratius, video Bellarmino eam lectionem visam utiliorem. Cum enim b videret tandem, necessario cum Oleastro, Lyra, Cajet. Benedict. &c. dandum esse, quod Rainoldus in colloquio urget, & Lxx. & Chaldaei authoritate persuadet, vid. judicem & sacerdotem hic manifeste distingui, illud hinc elicit, duas quidem personas illas distingui, sed sacerdoti sententiae pronunciationem, judici vero seu principi executionem solam demandari. Sed inanem esse omnem ejusmodi ex hoc loco probationem, is videt qui Ebraeum textum inspicit. Nec enim ibi, & decre-to judicis, nec, ex decreto judicis est, sed solummodo, שופטים לא aut judici. Nec vox imperii comparet usquam. imo si conferas cum vers.9. videbis per sacerdotem, usitato, in scripturis loquendi modo, sacerdotes intelligi. Jam adi eos, qui ex professo ad hunc locum Bellarmino respondere. Vide etiam quae ad hunc locum disputat. Anton. de Dominis lib.1. cap.12. num.39. Non legendum, ex decreto, inquit, sed, & decreto, ut habent Biblia Ebraea & correcta vulgata Editio. Miseret me tui, Plane enim instar caeci de coloribus judicas. Nunquam, nunquam vocem decreto ex Ebraeo eruës. Confer jam cum his quae supra cap. 10. de vulg. verf. pag. 130. ad hunc locum notavimus.
units.tr: Formerly the text was read as "by the decree of the judge." Hartus cited it this way in his Colloquy and argued from it that the high priest was the judge who settled those difficult and troublesome cases. Sixtus himself had approved this reading on papal authority. But Clement VIII restored it to read "and the decree of the judge." I wonder all the more that Bellarmine had the confidence not to correct, in the revised edition of Clement VIII, this passage which he had cited from the older and more corrupt reading in his book of revisions. But when I weigh the matter more carefully, I see that Bellarmine judged that older reading more useful to him. For when he saw that he must finally yield, with Oleaster, Lyra, Cajetan, Benedict and others, to what Rainolds urges in the colloquy, and what the authority of the Seventy and the Chaldean persuades, namely that the judge and the priest are clearly distinguished here, he drew the conclusion that these two persons are indeed distinguished, but that the priest is charged with pronouncing the sentence, while the judge, or prince, is charged only with carrying it out. But anyone who examines the Hebrew text sees that every proof of this kind drawn from this place is empty. For there is neither "and the decree of the judge" nor "by the decree of the judge," but only [shophtim, שופטים], "or the judge." Nor does the word "command" appear anywhere. Indeed, if you compare verse 9, you will see that "priest" there means, in the usual manner of speaking in Scripture, "priests." Now go to those who have answered Bellarmine at length on this passage. See also what Antonio de Dominis argues on this place, book 1, chapter 12, number 39: "It should not be read 'by the decree,'" he says, "but 'and the decree,' as the Hebrew Bibles and the corrected Vulgate edition have it." I pity you. You judge about colours like a blind man. You will never, never bring the word "decree" out of the Hebrew. Now compare what we noted above, chapter 10, on the vernacular versions, page 130, on this passage.

units.la: CAP. XIX. verf. 14.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX, verse 14.

units.la: Lex extat de non transferendis terminis quos posuere majores. per terminos intelligit Moses limites, quibus in regionibus istis agros, sicut apud nos fossis, distinguebant. Erasmus in Apologiis pag. 637. exagitat suum Sutorem, qui non hunc solum locum, sed & alia aliquot Veteris Testamenti, eo qui in concordantiis occurrunt ordine, vid. Deut. 19. Deut. 22. (scribere debuisset 27. sed secutus est exemplar hic mendosum) Job. 24. Proverb. 22. novis Scripturae Interpretibus objectat. Quasi per terminos voces intellexisset Spiritus S. atque hujus Legis violatae illi postulari possent, qui mutant rerum vocabula. Inepta certe Allegoria, quae tamen in eos, verba Erasmi, melius quadraret, qui in limpidissimos divinae Sapientiae fontes tantum Sophistices, tantum Aristotelicae Philosophiae & Scoticae Metaphysices invexerunt.
units.tr: The law stands that boundaries set by our ancestors must not be moved. By "boundaries" Moses means the limits by which, in those regions, fields were marked off, as with ditches among us. Erasmus, in his Apologies, page 637, attacks his Sutor, who objects to the new interpreters of Scripture not only this passage but several other places of the Old Testament, in the order in which they occur in the concordances: Deuteronomy 19, Deuteronomy 22 (he should have written 27, but he followed a faulty copy here), Job 24, Proverbs 22. As if the Holy Spirit had meant by "boundaries" the words, and as if those who change the names of things could be charged with violating this law! Certainly an absurd allegory, though in Erasmus's words it would fit better those who have introduced into the most limpid fountains of divine wisdom nothing but sophistry, nothing but Aristotelian philosophy and Scotist metaphysics.

units.la: CAP. XXI. verf. 12.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI, verse 12.

units.la: Et circumcidet ungues } Ita vulg. Ita & Lxx. ἡ ἀπεκνηκνίσεται αὐτὸν. Quos & Lutherus & Deod. & alii secuti sunt. Huic versioni varias Allegorias antiquitas superstruxit. Quid opus est multa allegare? Hieron. citante Corn. à Lapide, Christianis doctoribus licet ea quae apud Gentiles vel haereticos docta & elegantia tia inveniunt, sibi adsciscere, dummodo ea quae noxia sunt & superflua resecent. Rabanus & Glossa interlinearis ex hac captiva muliere animam peccatricem faciunt, de peccato ad gratiam translatam. Ea jubetur radere caesariem id est vitia praeterita per contritionem deponere, & praecidere ungues id est occasiones peccati. Sed moneo tironem, hanc allegoriam dubiae & controversae versioni superstructam esse. Namque & Junius & Pisc. reddunt, alet ungues suos. Genev. ambigue, faciet ungues suos, & in margine utramque sententiam exhibent, praecidet, aut alet. Ebr. עשתה צפרניה ad verbum faciet ungues suos. De voce עשתה quid ea sibi hic loci velit, Ebraei quoque dissentiunt. Thalmudi in Massech. Jebamoth cap.4. י"ו
units.tr: And he shall pare her nails. So the Vulgate, and the Septuagint, which has ἀπεκνηκνίσεται αὐτόν [apeknēknisetai auton]. Luther, Diodati and others have followed this rendering. Antiquity built various allegories on this version. Why should I cite many? Jerome, as quoted by Cornelius à Lapide, says: Christian teachers may appropriate whatever learned and elegant things they find among the Gentiles or heretics, provided they cut away what is harmful and superfluous. Rabanus and the Glossa interlinearis make this captive woman a sinful soul, transferred from sin to grace. She is commanded to shave her hair, that is, to put away past sins through contrition, and to pare her nails, that is, to cut off the occasions of sin. But I warn the beginner that this allegory is built on a doubtful and disputed version. For both Junius and the Piscator render it, she shall keep her nails. The Geneva Bible renders it ambiguously, she shall make her nails, and in the margin gives both senses, shall pare or shall keep. The Hebrew has עשתה צפרניה [asetah tsippornah], word for word she shall make her nails. The Hebrews also disagree about what the word עשתה [asetah] means here.

units.la: אליעזר אומר תקון ר' עקיבא אומר תגדיל אסר ר' אליעזר נאמרה עשייה בראש ונאפרדה עשיידה בצפרנירה מר"ה להלן העברה אף כאן העברה / hoc est, R. Eliezer exponit לד עשתה per תקון id est praecidit (a קצץ) R. Akiba, per תגדיל vel תגדל id est crescere facit. R. Eliezer hac ratione nititur, Jubetur hic aliquid fieri circa caput & circa ungues. Quid ergo? illud (vid. in praecepto de capite, hoc eodem versu) jubetur ablatio, ergo & hic ablatio. Q. d. illic jubetur praecidere comam, hic ungnes. In sequentibus vero alia insuper additur ratio, desumpta ex collatione 2. Sam. 19. 25. Mephibosheth non fecerat pedes suos, neque fecerat mystacem suum, id est non aptaverat, concinnaverat, curaverat, sicuti & Chald. & Kimchi & R. Sal. & Junius & Pisc. istam R. Eliezeris sententiam. Sed quis ignorat pro diversitate additae hujus vel istius vocis variari saepe vocum significationes? עשרה enim non solum aptare, curare, concinnare, sed & producere, & crescere facere seu alere significat, eoque sensu robur facit fructum Psalm. 1. & Jerem. 17. 8. Matthaei 7. 17. arbor bona bonos fructus ποιεῖ, & ager facit cibum, Habac. 3. Sed videamus rationem R. Akibae, quae extat in eodem loco, להלן ניוול אף כאן Illic, ubi vid. de radendo capite agitur, intenditur deturpatio, ergo & hic detturpatio. Eandem invenies rationem apud Abenezram, R. Salom. & alios, qui עשתה לד hic exponunt per תגדל quomodo & Onkelos per vocem חרב id est augebit. Argumentatur ab intentione & scopo hujus legis, qui videtur fuisse ista, ut Israelita ex aspectu foeminae sordidae didæ & inultæ & flentis, pœnitudine tactus & relentescens, in servitutem assertam & adamatam alienigenam à se dimitte-ret. R. Bechai ad hum locum, citante Cl. Sckikkardo in Jure regio Ebræorum pag. 135. אולי תוך הנסן הזה יתנחם החושק ויעבור ויעבור השקו מעליה בראותו אותה מתנוולה בגלוח הראש ובגירול צפרניה ובלבישת בגדים של שביה כי ככר הסירה הבגדים הנאים טעליה אשר באה עמהם ובראותו אותה בוכה ומצטערת ישלהנה לנפשה id est, Si forte intra hoc tempus amasium istum pœniteret & subsideret appetitus illius quo in eam ferebatur, aspiciendo eam in hunc modum deturpatam rasura capitis, incremento ungvium & indutam vestimentis captiva convenientibus, id est vilibus (Jam enim deposuerat vestes pulcras, quibus induta venerat) & flentem & seipsam affligentem & hac ratione eam quocunque vellet, dimitteret. Nota, in Ebraeo textu Deuter 21. 13. vestem illam pulcram, qua induta in servitutem asserebatur, & quam hic deponere jubetur, vocari vestem captivitatis. Contrà apud Bechajum vestem illam sordidam vocari vestem captiva id est captivæ convenientem. R. Sal. vestem captivitatis sua ] quia ista pulcra sunt. Etenim gentium maledictarum filia in hunc modum se in bello ornare solent, ut alios ad fornicationes provocent. Vides jam opinor probabilem magis esse R. Akibæ sententiam. Quod si hoc non vides, illud saltem vides, controversam esse phrasin, facere ungves. Parcius ergo hæc Allegoria in Ecclesiis sonet. Quicquid his & id genus aliis allegoriis vulgo docent Ministri, ex perspicuis Scripturæ locis doceri potest.
units.tr: In the Talmud, tractate Yevamot, chapter 4: R. Eliezer says, "tiqqun" [תקון]; R. Akiba says, "tagdil" [תגדיל]. R. Eliezer explains עשתה לד [asetah lad] by תקון, that is, she shall cut (from קצץ). R. Akiba explains it by תגדיל, that is, make it grow. R. Eliezer rests on this reasoning: Here something is commanded to be done about the head and about the nails. What then? In the precept about the head (see it in this same verse) removal is commanded; therefore removal here too. That is, there the hair is commanded to be cut off, here the nails. In what follows he adds a further reason, drawn from a comparison with 2 Sam. 19:25: Mephibosheth had not made his feet, nor had he made his mustache, that is, had not trimmed, tidied or looked after them, as the Chaldee paraphrast, Kimchi, R. Solomon, Junius and the Piscator also understand R. Eliezer's view. But who does not know that the meaning of words often varies with the addition of this or that word? עשה [asah] means not only to trim, to look after or to tidy, but also to produce, or to cause to grow and to nourish. In this sense, the tree makes fruit (Ps. 1; Jer. 17:8), and Matt. 7:17, a good tree bears (ποιεῖ) good fruit, and the field makes food (Hab. 3). But let us see R. Akiba's reasoning, which stands in the same place: להלן ניוול אף כאן [lehalan niwwul af kan], that is, there, where the shaving of the head is discussed, disfigurement is intended; therefore here too disfigurement. You will find the same reasoning in Abenezra, R. Solomon and others, who explain עשתה לד here by תגדל [tagdel], just as Onkelos renders it by the word חרב [kharab], that is, she will make grow. They argue from the intention and aim of this law, which seems to have been this: that an Israelite, seeing the woman dirty, unavenged and weeping, should be moved to repentance, relent, and send away the foreign captive whom he had claimed and loved. R. Bechai on this passage, as quoted by the learned Schickard in Jus regium Hebraeorum, page 135: Perhaps within this time the lover would repent and his desire for her would subside, when he saw her thus disfigured by the shaving of her head, the paring of her nails, and her wearing the clothes of a captive, suitable to her (for she had now put off the fine clothes in which she had come), and saw her weeping and grieving for herself; and in this way he would let her go wherever she wished. Note that in the Hebrew text of Deut. 21:13, the fine dress in which she was claimed as a slave, and which here she is commanded to put off, is called the garment of captivity. On the other hand, in Bechai that squalid dress is called the garment of captivity, that is, suitable to a captive. R. Solomon: the garment of her captivity [is so called] because those fine things are such. For the daughters of cursed nations are accustomed to adorn themselves in this way in war, so as to provoke others to fornication. I think you can now see that R. Akiba's opinion is the more probable. And if you do not see this, at least you see that the phrase to make nails is disputed. This allegory should therefore be sounded more sparingly in the churches. Whatever the ministers commonly teach about these and similar allegories can be taught from the plain passages of Scripture.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. verf. 16.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI, verse 16.

units.la: Maledictus sit qui patrem & matrem vilipendit] Ebr. מְקַלֵּל LXX. ὁ ἀπμάζων, id vulgatus reddit, qui non honorat. Chald. מְקַלֵּי / Thema est קלל quod in Kal significat, torrefecit, assavit, In Niphal, vilescere. In Hiphil, vilipendere. Exodi 21.17. Sic intonabat Moses, Qui maledixerit מקלל patri & matri morte moriatur. Ast hic ulterius progreditur Deus, atque illis etiam maledictionem denuntiat, qui parentes suos vilipendunt, id quod longe minus est quam maledicere. non male Carthusianus, qui non honorat, tempore opportuno ipsis obediendo, seu indigentigentibus pro posse subveniendo, & maxime, qui non solum non honorat, sed eum maledicit & convitiatur. Hæc eò notavi, ut monerem Germanos & Belgas, locum hunc à Luthero nimis indiligenter esse versum. Sic enim habet, verbloeckt zyn syn Vader ofte Moeder bloeckt id est maledicit. Quasi in Ebræo esset קלל quæ vox usurpatur loco illo Exodi supra memorato. Textum Ebræum versionesque accuratiores magis stabilire reverentiam parentibus debitam, etiam illi judicabunt qui nondum ære lavantur.
units.tr: Cursed be he who despises his father and mother] Hebrew מְקַלֵּל [mᵉqallēl]; LXX ὁ ἀτιμάζων [ho atimazōn], which the Vulgate renders qui non honorat, "who does not honour." The Chaldee has מְקַלֵּי. The root is קלל, which in Qal means to roast or parch, in Niphal to be made vile, and in Hiphil to despise. Exodus 21:17. Thus Moses thundered, "Whoever curses [מקלל] his father or mother shall surely be put to death." Here, however, God goes further and pronounces a curse also on those who despise their parents, which is far less than cursing them. The Carthusian has it well: "who does not honour, by not obeying them at the proper time, or by not helping them in need as far as he can; and especially he who not only does not honour but also curses and reviles." I have noted this so as to warn the Germans and the Dutch that Luther has translated this place too carelessly. For he has it: they curse their father or mother, they curse, that is, maledicit, as if the Hebrew were קלל, the word used in the passage of Exodus mentioned above. Those who are not yet washed in bronze will also judge that the Hebrew text and more accurate versions establish more firmly the reverence owed to parents.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. vers. 66.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII, verse 66.

units.la: Et erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te] Ita vulg. Ebræa sic habent, Eritque vita tua suspensa tibi è regione. Lxx. καὶ ἔσται ἡ ζωή σου κρεμαμένη ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν σου. Proverbialis locutio, inquit Junius, sumpta à rebus corporeis, quæ à tenui filo pendent, jam jam ruituræ. Semper & indesinenter desperabis de vita tua. Carthus. erit vita tua in ambiguo posita, ita quod erit tam incertus de subsistentia vitæ tuæ, ac si jam esset tibi subtracta. Hanc interpretationem firmant & consequa verba, Et non credes vitæ tuæ id est interprete Corn. à Lapide, non fides vitæ tuæ, vel te posse vivere, sed de vita desperabis. Hæc est literalis & quam sacer Spiritus intendit, hujus loci interpretatio. Lubet nunc audire, quàm abusi sint hoc loco Patrum nonnulli. Irenæus lib.4. cap.23. Significans quoniam qui ab initio condidit & fecit eos verbum & in novissimis temporibus redimens nos & vivificans, ostenditur pendens in ligno, & non credent ei, ait enim, Et erit vita tua pendens ante oculos tuos, &c. Vides de Christo crucifixo eum hunc locum accepisse. Eadem habet lib.3.16. Lactantius lib.4.Instit.cap.8. August.lib.16.contra Faustum, cap.21. Procopius in hunc locum, Tertull. adversus Judaeos, cap.11. qui insuper ad textum addidit duas voculas, in ligno. Erit vita tua pendens in ligno ante oculos tuos & non credes vitæ tuæ, q.d. Christus qui est vita tua, suspensus erit ante oculos tuos in cruce, & non credis ei qui est vita tua. Vide & Leonem serm. 8. de Passione & Theophanis orationem de elevatione crucis, pag 630. tomi 9. Biblioth. Patrum. Ubi primarium præsidium ponit in voce lignum, eoque trahit ex Psal. 1. lignum plantatum, & Gen 2. lignum vitæ. Nisi enim crucem designasset, inquit, arborem vel plantam dixisset, non lignum. Lignum enim post sectionem demum nomen habet. Tu disce tiro, Ebr. עץ & ξύλον & ξυλέων significare; ac proinde in lingua Hellenistica illud pro hoc passim poni. Galatinum ulterius provexit Allegorizandi seu potius ineptiendi prurigo. Ille enim cap. 17. libri 8. de Arcanis Catholicæ veritatis, probaturus quod Deus aliquando esset suspendendus, ex hoc loco primum petit argumentum, additque ideò fortasis pluraliter vitas dixisse, quia sicut gemina est Messia natura, ita & ejus vita, Deus scilicet & anima. Admirentur hæc indocti & quos tales speculationes delectant. Qui fontes adire potest, si vel Crasius sit, non potest ad tales ineptias non ridere.
units.tr: And your life shall hang in doubt before you] So the Vulgate. The Hebrew reads: And your life shall be suspended before you, opposite you. The LXX: καὶ ἔσται ἡ ζωή σου κρεμαμένη ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν σου [kai estai hē zōē sou kremamenē apenanti tōn ophthalmōn sou]. It is a proverbial expression, says Junius, taken from physical things that hang by a thin thread and are about to fall. You will always and unceasingly despair of your life. The Carthusian: your life will be placed in doubt, so that you will be as uncertain of the continuance of your life as if it had already been taken from you. The words that follow confirm this interpretation: And you shall not believe in your life. Cornelius à Lapide explains: not trust in your life, or in your being able to live, but you will despair of life. This is the literal interpretation of the place, and what the Holy Spirit intends. Let us now hear how some of the Fathers have abused this passage. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 23: Signifying that the Word, who from the beginning made and fashioned them, and in the last times redeemed and quickened us, is shown hanging on the tree, and they will not believe him; for he says, And your life shall hang before your eyes, etc. You see that he took this place as referring to the crucified Christ. He says the same in book 3, chapter 16. Lactantius, Institutes book 4, chapter 8; Augustine, Against Faustus book 16, chapter 21; Procopius on this place; Tertullian, Against the Jews, chapter 11, who moreover added two words to the text, on the wood: Your life shall hang on the wood before your eyes, and you will not believe in your life; that is, Christ, who is your life, will be suspended before your eyes on the cross, and you do not believe him who is your life. See also Leo, sermon 8 on the Passion, and the oration of Theophanes on the raising of the cross, page 630 of volume 9 of the Bibliotheca Patrum. There he places the chief support in the word wood, and draws it from Psalm 1, a tree planted, and Genesis 2, the tree of life. For unless he had meant the cross, he says, he would have said a tree or a plant, not wood, since wood receives its name only after it is cut. You, the beginner, should learn that עץ [etz] and ξύλον [xylon] and ξύλων [xylōn] mean the same, and therefore in Hellenistic usage the one is often put for the other. Galatinus carried the itch of allegorising, or rather of trifling, further still. In chapter 17 of book 8 of his On the Secrets of Catholic Truth, wishing to prove that God was at some time to be hanged, he first takes an argument from this place, and adds that perhaps for this reason the word life was used in the plural, because just as the nature of the Messiah is twofold, so is his life, namely God and soul. Let the unlearned, and those delighted by such speculations, admire these things. Whoever can go to the sources, even if he is a Crassus, cannot help laughing at such trifles.

units.la: CAP. XXIX. vers. 29.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX, verse 29.

units.la: Occulta [ pertinent ] ad DOMINUM Deum nostrum: sed (Ebraicè, Et) revelata [ pertinent ] ad nos & filios nostros, ut faciamus omnia verba Legis hujus. Hæc est simplicissima Ebraicarum vocum interpretatio. Nihil enim notius est iis, qui vel ἐxεοθιγῶς Ebræam Grammaticam attigerunt, τὸ ה sæpe idem significare quod ad cum Ellipsi verbi pertinet. D. Piscator paulo aliter, occulta [ sunt ]. penes Dominum D. nostrum: at r. sunt penes nos, &c. Junius occulta [ sunto ] penes D. &c. Sensus, ne sapiamus altum, neque in ea, quæ Deus sacri silentii supparo operuit, curiosè inquiramus. Quin hoc potius operam demus, ut ex præscripto istius Legis, quam nobis revelavit, obsequii gloriam amplexantes, vitam nostram instituamus. Hanc egregiam & auro contra non caram sententiam commodè satis expressit ipse quoque Vulgatus Interpres. Eò magis miror indiligentiam & dormitationem B. Lutheri qui & neglecto accentu Athnach in voce אֱלֹהֵינוּ / & insuperhabita litera vau ante vocem הַנִּגְלוֹת / quæ alterum illud axioma cum priori copulat, sic vertit, das geheimniß des HERRN unsers Gottes ist offenbaret uns und unsern kindern ewiglich / daß wir thun sollen allen wort dises gesetzes. Quæ in Belgica nostra translatione sic versa reperies, de heymelijckheyt des Heeren onses Gods is ons ende onse kinderen geopenbaert eeuwichlijck/ &c. Quicquid ad hunc textum ab Interpretibus convectatur, non illuillustrando verbo Dei, ut Lutheri afferturu. Hoc ergo operam dent fidi Interpretes qui ad populum verba facturi sunt, ut loca Scripturae quae vel interpretaturi, aut confirmando convellendoque aliqui dogmati citaturi sunt, vel cum fontibus, vel si id non possint, cum melioribus versionibus conferant.
units.tr: The secret things [belong] to the LORD our God: but (in Hebrew, And) the things revealed [belong] to us and to our children, that we may do all the words of this law. This is the simplest interpretation of the Hebrew words. For nothing is better known to those who have touched Hebrew grammar even superficially [ἐπιπολαίως] than that ה often means the same as to, with the verb belongs understood. Piscator, a little differently: the secret things are with the LORD our God, but the revealed things are with us, etc. Junius: the secret things [are to be left] with the LORD, etc. The sense is that we should not think highly of ourselves, nor inquire curiously into those things which God has covered with a sacred silence. Rather let us take pains to shape our lives by the rule of this law, which he has revealed to us, embracing the glory of obedience. The Vulgate translator himself also expresses this excellent sentiment, which is worth gold, and cannot be bought, quite adequately. I wonder all the more at the carelessness and drowsiness of the blessed Luther, who, neglecting the accent Athnach on the word אֱלֹהֵינוּ [elohēnu], and disregarding the letter vav before the word הַנִּגְלוֹת [hannigloth], which joins that second clause to the first, renders it: The secret of the LORD our God is revealed to us and to our children forever, that we should do all the words of this law. In our Dutch translation you will find it rendered thus: The secret of the LORD our God is revealed to us and our children forever, etc. Whatever is drawn into this text by the interpreters does not illustrate the Word of God, as Luther's translation would have it. Therefore let faithful interpreters, who are going to speak to the people, take care to compare the passages of Scripture which they are going to explain, or cite in confirming or refuting some doctrine, with the sources, or, if they cannot do that, with the better versions.

units.la: CAP. XXXII. vers. 8.
units.tr: Chapter XXXII, verse 8.

units.la: Quando dividebat altissimus gentes, quando dispergebat filios Adae, constituit terminos gentium [Greek: ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ]. Ita LXX. in quam versionem illae voces, [Greek: ἀγγέλων θεοῦ], irrepsere, pro [Greek: υἱῶν Ισραηλ], filiorum Israel, quomodo legunt Hebr. Chald. Aq. Symm. Vulgatus, &c. Non existimo quempiam adeo hospitem in Scholasticorum scriptis esse, qui ignoret magno calore ab ipsis quaesitum fuisse de numero salvandorum. Iverunt enim boni isti Patres in partes, dum alii contenderunt, tot homines salvatum iri, quot angeli cecidérunt, alii contra quot steterunt. Tractat hanc controversiam Magister Sententiarum lib. 2 Dist. 9, qui in eum commentati sunt. Gregorius Magnus iis accessit, qui praedestinatorum numerum cum angelis, qui perseverarunt, componunt. verba Magistri, Non enim juxta numerum eorum qui ceciderunt, sed eorum qui permanserunt, homines ad beatitudinem admittuntur. Vide Gregorius; Superna illa civitas ex angelis & hominibus constat, ad quam credimus tantos humani generis ascendere, quantos illic contigit angelos remansisse, sicut scriptum est in Cantico Deuteronomii statuit terminos populorum juxta numerum Angelorum Dei. Vide cordate Lector, quo magnum virum praecipitem dederit mala versio. Moysis ista mens fuit, Deus O. M. post confusas ad Babylonis turrem linguas ita distribuit regiones inter populos, ut spatium satis magnum assignaverit filiis Israel, secundum numerum & multitudinem eorum. Vide Cajet. Oleastrium, Jun. Pisc. Deodatum, &c. Designavit ergo Israelitis capaces terminos nondum existentibus. Abenezra, dicunt Interpretes hac intelligi de aetate dispersionis (Genes. 11.): quando dispersa est universa terra. Tunc enim decrevit Deus ut terra 7 gentium esset aliquando Israelitarum; & quia subjectura ea erat numero eorum, ideo dicit, secundum nu-me-
units.tr: "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God [ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ]." So the Seventy, into whose version the words "of the angels of God" [ἀγγέλων θεοῦ] crept, in place of "of the sons of Israel" [υἱῶν Ισραηλ], as the Hebrew, the Chaldee, Aquila, Symmachus, the Vulgate and others read. I do not think anyone is so much a stranger to the writings of the Schoolmen that he does not know how eagerly they inquired into the number of those to be saved. For those good Fathers took sides: some contended that as many men would be saved as angels had fallen, others on the contrary that as many would be saved as had stood firm. The Master of the Sentences treats this controversy in Book 2, Distinction 9, and his commentators followed him. Gregory the Great joined those who match the number of the predestined with the angels who persevered. The words of the Master: "For it is not according to the number of those who fell, but of those who remained, that human beings are admitted to blessedness." See Gregory: "That heavenly city consists of angels and men, and we believe that as many of the human race ascend thither as angels remained there, as it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy: he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God." Note, careful reader, how far a bad translation has thrown a great man headlong. Moses' meaning was this: after the tongues were confused at the tower of Babel, God the Best and Greatest so distributed the regions among the peoples that he assigned a space large enough to the sons of Israel, according to their number and multitude. See Cajetan, Oleaster, Junius, Piscator, Diodati, and others. He therefore designated for the Israelites bounds capacious though not yet existing. Ibn Ezra; the interpreters say this is to be understood of the time of the dispersion (Gen. 11), when the whole earth was scattered. For then God decreed that the land of the seventy nations would one day belong to the Israelites; and since it was to be subject to their number, he therefore says "according to the number of the sons of Israel."

units.la: Homil. 34 super xv. et Lucæ merum Filiorum Israel. Caeteras expositiones seu alienas mitto. Caeterum illud propemodum excideras, hoc ipso textu, prout in Graeco legitur, usos ex patribus nonnullos, ut docerent singulis gentibus, imo & hominibus suos angelos seu custodes assignatos, quam sententiam ut non aspernor, ita & certo persuasus sum, nec volam nec vestigium ejus in hoc contextu extare.
units.tr: Homily 34 on Luke 15. I pass over their other explanations, whether strange or not. Besides, you had almost overlooked this: that from this very text, as it is read in Greek, some of the Fathers used it to teach that each nation, and indeed each man, has an angel or guardian assigned to him. I do not scorn that opinion, but I am firmly persuaded that neither a wish nor a trace of it is found in this context.

units.la: Cornua Rhinocerotis sunt cornua ejus] Ebraicum רְאֵם alibi in vulgata redditur unicornis, ut Psal. 22. LXX. ubique μονοκέρως reddunt, uno loco excepto, ubi vertunt ἀδροί, robusti. Agit de pulchritudine & potentia posterorum Josephi. Valde torserunt hunc locum veteres, ac inter eos Justinus Martyr adversus Tryphonem, Monocerotis cornua dici & ostendi non potest rem aliam aut figuram ullam referre, nisi eam quae crucis speciem adumbrat, &c. Vide etiam Tertull. adversus Judaeos cap. 10. Ambrosium in De benedictione patriarcharum. At nihil hic de Christo, nihil de cruce. Dices, Josephum fuisse typum Christi. Ego vero nullos agnosco typos, nisi qui in libris Novi foederis fundamentum suum habent. Jonam agnosco typum Christi, quia id diserte testatur Christus ipse Matth. 12. Agnus Paschalis praefiguravit Christum, Joh. 19. 36. at de Josepho locum adhuc quaero. Neque toleranda est illa Ruperti Allegoria, qua ex Monocerote Christum facit, Fortissimus spirituum Deus, velut unicornis, id est potentia singularis, Deus incomprehensibilis & invicta virtutis, virginei tractus odore uteri, illique inclusus est, & ex eo tantum comprehendi potuit & occidi. In quam sententiam prolixus est & Pintus Jesuita comm. in Isai. XLV. 8. ubi hunc quoque torquet locum Ps. 28. nobis 29. Dilectus ut filius unicornuum, quem eo cum ait a B. Augustino de Christo exponi. Sed scire licet, locum illum plane aliter tinnire in origin. Laudat illic David Deum O. M. ab, effectis 3. inter ea est tonitru, quo de agit a vers. 3. ad 10. Vox Domini facit ut exuliant (cedri Libani) sicut vitulus, facit ut exiliant Libanus & Sirion ut pullus unicornuum. Schirion nomen montis est Libano contiguum, qui & Hermon & Senir dicitur, Deut. 111. 8. 9, neque ullo modo per dilectum reddi potest, & ad Christum referri.
units.tr: "Its horns are the horns of a rhinoceros." The Hebrew [רְאֵם] elsewhere in the Vulgate is rendered "unicorn," as in Ps. 22. The LXX everywhere render it [μονοκέρως], with one exception, where they translate [ἀδροί], "robust." It treats of the beauty and power of the descendants of Joseph. The ancients twisted this passage badly, and among them Justin Martyr in his dialogue against Trypho: "The horns of the monoceros cannot be said or shown to signify anything else or any figure except that which bears the form of the cross," and so on. See also Tertullian, Against the Jews, chapter 10, and Ambrose, On the Blessing of the Patriarchs. But there is nothing here about Christ, nothing about the cross. You will say Joseph was a type of Christ. I, however, acknowledge no types except those that have their foundation in the books of the New Covenant. I acknowledge Jonah as a type of Christ, because Christ himself expressly testifies so, Matt. 12. The Paschal lamb prefigured Christ, John 19:36; but for Joseph I still seek a text. Nor is that allegory of Rupert tolerable, in which he makes Christ out of the monoceros: "God, the most mighty of spirits, like a unicorn, that is, a singular power, God incomprehensible and unconquered in virtue, was enclosed by the scent of a virginal womb, and only thus could he be grasped and killed." The Jesuit Pinto is also long-winded in this direction in his commentary on Isaiah 45:8, where he likewise twists Ps. 28 (Vulgate 29), "beloved as the son of unicorns," which he says Augustine explains of Christ. But know that this passage sounds quite different in the original. There David praises God Most High for his works; among them is the thunder, of which he speaks from verse 3 to 10: "The voice of the Lord makes (the cedars of Lebanon) leap like a calf; it makes Lebanon and Sirion leap like the young of the unicorns." Sirion is the name of a mountain adjoining Lebanon, which is also called Hermon and Senir, Deut. 3:8-9; and it can in no way be rendered "beloved" and referred to Christ.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Ruperti Allegoriam, quam non esse diximus. Et merito. Fundamentum enim e Gregorius & Isidorus tradunt, animal illud non nisi gine, quae venienti sinum aperiat, capi posse, ac tunc ferocia posita caput deponere & soporatam capi, falsum Marcus Paulus Venetus, lib. 3. cap. 15. Gesnerus & monocerotis per virginem cicuratione narrationem [?] merant. Unde & Aristot. & Ælianus & Plinius, historiam animalium ad posteritatem transmiserunt, curatione altum silent. Quin & Gesnerus fabulam ortam prodidit, quod animal illud tunc solummodo quando cum femella sua miscetur.
units.tr: But let us return to Rupert's allegory, which, as we said, is not sound. And rightly so. For the foundation that Gregory and Isidore hand down, that this animal can be taken only by a virgin who opens her lap to it, and that then, its ferocity laid aside, it lays its head down and is caught while asleep, is false. Marco Polo the Venetian, Book 3, chapter 15, ... Gesner and others ... the taming of the monoceros by a virgin ... Hence Aristotle, Aelian and Pliny handed down the history of animals to posterity, and are silent about any taming. Indeed Gesner also reports that the fable arose that the animal can be caught only at the time when it mates with its female.

units.la: Non fuit sicut dies ille ante ipsum aut post ipsum, ותשמע ut audiret Dominus vocem hominis, quia Dominus pugnabat pro Israel.
units.tr: There was no day like that day before it or after it, [ותשמע] that the Lord heard the voice of a man, because the Lord fought for Israel.

units.la: Vulg.
units.tr: Vulgate.

units.la: Non fuit antea & postea tam longa dies, obediente Domino voci hominis & pugnante pro Israel.
units.tr: There was no day so long before or after it, the Lord obeying the voice of a man and fighting for Israel.

units.la: Manifeste docent Ebraea, negari similitudinem illius diei in hoc, quod Deus condescendit deprecationi hominis in tanto miraculo, quod non esset verum si Deus condescendisset voci Esaiae seu Ezechiae in similis & etiam in majori. Haec * Burgensis. Masius ad hunc locum De hujus nostri diei longitudine non agitur comparatio, sed in eo solum antefertur diebus quibusvis, quod nullum alium diem Deus ad ullius hominis preces cadendi hostis gratia, interrupto solis motu, sic produxit, ut hunc produxit. Jam adi Lyram ad hunc locum, ut & ad 2. Reg. 20. & vide quibus & quot contentiunculis materiem praebuerit addita vox longa. Illud enim ex illa illatum, ratione longitudinis hunc diem contendi cum omnibus quotquot ab orbe condito fluxere & fluent. At obstare visus dies, cujus 2. Reg. 20. mentionem facit sacra historia. Confecerat jam Sol decem horas inaequales seu planetarias, ut vocant, id est ut textus loquitur, ad decimum gradum seu lineam Horologii Achaz jam pervenerat. Ad postulata Ezechiae retrocessit decem gradibus, actotidem horis sensim primam repetivit lineam, atque ita de novo
units.tr: The Hebrew plainly teaches that no likeness of that day is denied in this respect, that God condescended to a man's prayer in so great a miracle. That would not be true if God had condescended to the voice of Isaiah or Hezekiah in a similar case, or even a greater one. So Burgensis. Masius on this passage says: The comparison is not about the length of our day. It is preferred to any other day only in this, that God never so prolonged, by interrupting the motion of the sun, a day at the prayer of any man for the sake of cutting down an enemy, as he prolonged this one. Now consult Lyra on this passage, and also on 2 Kings 20, and see with how many petty disputes the added word long has provided material. For from it has been inferred that by reason of its length this day is to be compared with all that have flowed and will flow from the founding of the world. But the day in 2 Kings 20, which sacred history mentions, seems to stand in the way. The sun had already run through ten unequal or planetary hours, as they are called; that is, as the text puts it, it had already reached the tenth step or line of Ahaz's sundial. At Hezekiah's request it went back ten steps, and in as many hours gradually retraced the first line, and so anew

units.la: Nomen autem Hebronis olim fuerat Kirjath Arbe, (id est civitas Arbe; הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים הוּא Homo iste magnus inter Anakim sub erat.
units.tr: Now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba (that is, city of Arba; הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים הוּא [ha-adam ha-gadol ba-anakim hu]: this man was great among the Anakim) was.

units.la: Vulg.
units.tr: Vulgate.

units.la: Nomen Hebron antea vocabatur Cariat Arbe, Adam maximus inter Enacim ibi situs est.
units.tr: The name Hebron was formerly called Cariath-arbe; the greatest man among the Enacim lies buried there.

units.la: Illud constat קִרְיַת אַרְבַּע esse urbem, oppidum, ex abl. קִרְיָה / Arbang seu ἀρχαϊκῶς Αρβε (ut קִרְיָה Core,) nomen proprium viri est. Patet ex demonstrativo הוּא quod sequitur, Is, inquit, magnus erat inter Anakim id est maximus Anakaeorum. Locutio, ut in N. T. benedicta tu in mulieribus id est benedictissima mulierum. in V. Test. אִשָּׁה בְּנָשִׁים / pulcra in mulieribus. Quin & cap. 15.13. Urbs Arba patris Anakaeorum. Facessant ergo nugae Ebraeorum qui ארבע hic exponunt quatuor, civitas τετραπολις. Quod vid. illic Gigantes 4. aut 4. paria conjugum, Adam & Heva, Abrah. & Sara, Isaac & Reb. Jacob & Lea sepulta sunt. Nec est, quod hic alium quaeramus in sequentibus verbis praeter Arbam. Tripliciter itaque hic peccavit Vulg. 1. addendo vocem situs est. 2. omittendo demonstrativum הוא / 3 nomen apellativum אדם convertendo in nomen proprium. Unde invecta opinio, Adamum hic fuisse sepultum. Oleastrius ad Gen. 23.1. Ansam huic sententiae dederunt verba vulgata versionis citata in Josua quae sic habet, nomen Hebron, &c. quo loco in Ebraeo habetur, Homo magnus in Enakim ipse. Sed quia pro homine ibi ponitur Adam, putavit vulgatus ibi nomen proprium esse. Bened. Adam nomen commune hic est, & non proprium. Lyra id quoque vidit, Adam est nomen commune & significat hominem, tamen appropriatum fuit primo homini. Dicunt igitur aliqui quod ibi tenetur Adam prout est nomen appropriatum, pro primo homine ibidem sepulto. Alii dicunt quod accipitur pro illo Gigante qui dicitur Arbe.
units.tr: It is established that קִרְיַת אַרְבַּע [qiryat arba] means city, town, from the noun קִרְיָה [qiryah]. Arba, or archaically Αρβε [Arbe] (as קִרְיָה [Core] is), is the proper name of a man. This is clear from the demonstrative הוּא [hu] that follows: He, he says, was great among the Anakim, that is, the greatest of the Anakites. It is an idiom like the New Testament blessed are you among women, that is, most blessed of women; and in the Old Testament, אִשָּׁה בְּנָשִׁים [ishah benashim], beautiful among women. Indeed also in chapter 15.13, the city Arba, father of the Anakites. Let the trifles of the Hebrews, who here explain ארבע [arba] as four, a city of four (τετραπολις), therefore cease. There the giants are buried, four or four pairs of spouses: Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah. Nor is there any reason to look for another person in the following words besides Arba. Thus the Vulgate erred in three ways: first, by adding the word lies buried; second, by omitting the demonstrative הוּא [hu]; third, by turning the common noun אדם [adam] into a proper name. Hence the widespread opinion that Adam was buried here. Oleaster on Genesis 23.1: The verses of the Vulgate version cited in Joshua, which read thus, "the name of Hebron," etc., gave the occasion for this opinion. In the Hebrew, at that place, we have "this great man among the Enakim himself." But because Adam is put there for man, the Vulgate translator thought it was a proper name there. Benedictus: Adam is here a common noun, not a proper one. Lyra also saw this: Adam is a common noun and signifies man; nevertheless it was appropriated to the first man. Some therefore say that Adam is here taken as the appropriated name, for the first man buried in that place. Others say it is taken for that giant who is called Arbe.
