units.la: VAlde sudant Interpretes, ut rationem reddant hujus separationis. Qui curvato poplite biberunt domum remissi sunt, qui vero lamberant aquas istar canum, reservati prælio. Ebræi quidam istos geniculatores ideo remissos ajunt, quod inde collegerit Gideon, eos idola colere, quippe assuetos id facere coram Baal, unde illud, qui non flexerunt genua sua Baali. Alii, inter quos Lyra existimant geniculatores fuisse valde sitibundos, ac proinde fatigatos; cæteros autem qui lamberant aquas minus sitivisse, ac proinde non adeo lassos. Itaque hos retentos, illos ceu prælio minus utiles domum remissos. Alii, ut R. Levi, quem secutus est Cl. Piscator, putant geniculationem fuisse signum ignaviæ, ut contra to lambere, masculi & fortis animi. Sic illi. At totus contextus eò nos ducit, ut statuamus, Deum hæc omnia ita instituisse, ut nihil humanis viribus ferrent acceptum, sed ut ipsi in solidum victoria adscriberetur vers. 2. ne glorietur contra me Israel dicendo meis viribus liberatus sum. Itaque trepidis pavidisque ex præscripto Legis divinæ domum remissis, relictisque tantum decem millibus, novam instituit exercitus lustrationem, in quâ non fortiores, ut Lyra vult & qui eum sequuntur, sed minus fortes prælio reservat, ut ipsi soli victoria transcriberetur. Omnis victoria, etiam cum numerosus miles pugnat, est à Deo. Sed id magis perspicuum fit, quando cum numeroso & potenti hoste exigua & imbellis turba confligit. Prior separatio fiebat juxta Legem divinam, dimittebanturque manifestè trepidi. Ex iis qui relicti erant, alii aliis erant fortiores. Hic ergo reservantur ii, qui ad fortissimos comparati, trepidi erant. Josephus, 1. 5. 8. Gideoni Deus in somnis apparens, dixit homines tali ingenio esse, ut sibi placentes nulli velint virtute cedere, & victoriam sibi potius quam tia inveniunt, sibi adscisfcere, dummodo ea qua noxia sunt & su-perstua resecent. Rabanus & Glossa interlinearis ex hac captiva muliere animam peccatricem faciunt, de peccato ad gratiam translatam. Ea jubetur radere cæsariem id est vitia præterita per contritionem deponere, & præcidere ungues id est occasiones peccati. Sed moneo tironem, hanc allegoriam dubiæ & controversæ versioni superstructam esse. Namque & Junius & Pisc. reddunt, alet ungues suos. Genev. ambigue, faciet ungues suos, & in margine utramque sententiam exhibent, præcidet, aut alet. Ebr. עשתה צפרניו ad verbum faciet ungues suos. De voce עשתה quid ea sibi hic loci velit, Ebræi quoque dissentiunt. Thalmudi in Massech. Jebamoth cap.4. פ״ו
units.tr: Interpreters sweat greatly to give a reason for this separation. Those who bent their knees to drink were sent home, but those who lapped water like dogs were kept back for battle. Some Hebrews say that Gideon concluded from the kneeling men that they worshipped idols, being accustomed to do so before Baal, whence the words who have not bowed their knees to Baal. Others, including Lyra, think that the kneelers were very thirsty and therefore tired, whereas those who lapped the water were less thirsty and so not so exhausted. Hence the latter were retained and the former, as less useful for battle, were sent home. Others, like R. Levi, whom the learned Piscator follows, think that kneeling was a sign of cowardice, while lapping was a sign of a manly and brave spirit. So they say. But the whole context leads us to conclude that God arranged all these things so that men should ascribe nothing to human strength, but that the victory should be credited wholly to himself (verse 2): lest Israel glory against me, saying, my own hand has delivered me. Accordingly, the fearful and trembling were sent home according to the precept of the divine Law, and only ten thousand were left. He then held a new review of the army, in which he kept back not the stronger men, as Lyra and his followers hold, but the less brave for battle, so that the victory might be ascribed to him alone. Every victory, even when a numerous army fights, is from God. But this becomes more evident when a small and unwarlike band fights against a numerous and powerful enemy. The first separation was made according to the divine Law, and the trembling were manifestly dismissed. Among those who remained, some were braver than others. Here, then, are kept back those who, though they were the bravest, were still trembling. Josephus (book 5, chapter 8): God appeared to Gideon in dreams and said that men are of such a disposition that, pleased with themselves, none wish to yield to others in courage, and they claim the victory for themselves, provided they cut away what is harmful and superfluous. Rabanus and the interlinear Gloss make this captive woman a figure of the sinful soul, carried over from sin to grace. She is commanded to shave her head, that is, to put away past sins through contrition, and to pare her nails, that is, to remove the occasions of sin. But I warn the beginner that this allegory is built on a doubtful and disputed version. For both Junius and Piscator render let her nourish her nails. Geneva ambiguously renders she shall make her nails, and in the margin gives both senses, she shall pare or nourish. The Hebrew reads עשתה צפרניו [asetah tsipornav], literally she shall make her nails. The Hebrews also disagree about what the word עשתה [asetah] means here. In the Talmud, tractate Yevamot, chapter 4 (פ״ו)

units.la: אליעזר אומר תקון ר׳ עקיבא אומר תגדיל אמר ר׳ אליעזר נאמרה עשייה בראש ונאפרדה עשייתה בצפרניה מה להלן העברה אף כאן העברה / hoc est, R. Eliezer exponit עשתה per תקון id est præcidit (קצץ) R. Akiba, per תגדיל vel תגדיל id est crescere faciet. R. Eliezer hac ratione nititur, Jubetur hic aliquid fieri circa caput & circa ungues. Quid ergo? illud (vid. in præcepto de capite, hoc eodem versu) jubetur ablatio, ergo & hic ablatio. Q. d. illic jubetur præcidere comam, hic ungnes. In sequentibus vero alia insuper additur ratio, desumpta ex collatione 2. Sam. 19.25. Mephibosceth non fecerat pedes suos, neque fecerat mystacem suum, id est non aptaverat, concinnaverat, curaverat, sicuti & Chald. & Kimchi & R. Sal. & Junius & Pisc. istam R. Eliezeris sententiam. Sed quis ignorat pro diversitate additæ hujus vel istius vocis variari sæpe vocum significationes? עשוה enim non solum aptare, curare, concinnare, sed & producere, & crescere facere seu alere significat, coque sensu robur facis fructum Psalm. 1. & Jerem. 17. 8. Matthæi 7. 17. arbor bona bonos fructus facit, & ager facit cibum, Habac. 3. Sed videamus rationem R. Akibæ, quæ extat in eodem loco, להלן ניוול אף כאן ניוול Illic, ubi vid. de radendo capite agitur, intenditur deturpatio, ergo & hic deturpatio. Eandem invenies rationem apud Abenezram, R. Salom. & alios, qui עשתה hic exponunt per תגדל quomodo & Onkelos per vocem תרבי id est augebit; Argumentatur ab intentione & scopo hujus legis, qui videtur fuisse ista, ut Israelita ex aspectu fœminæ sordidæ didæ & inculte & flentis, pœnitudine tactus & relentescens, in servitutem assertam & adamatam alienigenam à se dimitteret. R. Bechai ad hunc locum, citante Cl. Sckikkardo in Jure regio Ebrœorum pag. 135. אולי תוך הזמן הזה יתנחם החושק ויעבור השקו מעליה בראותו אותה מתנוולה בגלוח הראש ובגירול צפרניה ובלבישת בגדים של שביה כי כבר הסירה הבגדים הנאים שעליה אשר באה עמהם ובראותו אותה בוכה ומצטערת ישלחנה לנפשה id est, Si forte intra hoc tempus amasium istum pœniteret & subsideret appetitus illius quo in eam ferebatur, aspiciendo eam in hunc modum deturpatam rasura capitis, incremento unguium & indutam vestimentis captivæ convenientibus, id est vilibus (Jam enim deposuerat vestes pulcras, quibus induta venerat) & flentem & seipsam affligentem & hac ratione eam quocunque vellet, dimitteret. Nota, in Ebræo textu Deuter 21. 13. vestem illam pulcram, qua induta in servitutem asserebatur, & quam hic deponere jubetur, vocari vestem captivitatis. Contrà apud Bechajun vestem illam sordidam vocari vestem captivæ id est captivæ convenientem. R. Sal. vestem captivitatis sua ] quia ista pulcra sunt. Etenim gentium maledictarum filia in hunc modum se in bello ornare solent, ut alios ad fornicationes provocent. Vides jam opinor probabilem magis esse R. Akibæ sententiam. Quod si hoc non vides, illud saltem vides, controversam esse phrasin, facere ungues. Parcius ergo hæc Allegoria in Ecclesiis sonet. Quicquid his & id genus aliis allegoriis vulgo docent Ministri, ex perspicuis Scripturæ locis doceri potest.
units.tr: R. Eliezer says it means trimming [תקון], that is, cutting off (קצץ); R. Akiba says it means letting them grow [תגדיל]. R. Eliezer relies on this reasoning: something is commanded here about the head and about the nails. Now there (see the precept about the head, in this same verse) removal is commanded; therefore here too removal. That is, there the command is to cut off the hair, here the nails. In what follows, another reason is added, drawn from a comparison with 2 Sam. 19:25: Mephibosheth had neither made his feet nor trimmed his moustache, that is, had not tidied, trimmed, or cared for them, as the Chaldee, Kimchi, R. Salomon, Junius and Piscator also take R. Eliezer's view. But who does not know that the meaning of words often varies with the difference of the added word or the ending? עשוה means not only to tidy, care for or trim, but also to produce, to cause to grow or to nourish. In this sense it is said that the root makes fruit (Ps. 1; Jer. 17:8); Matt. 7:17, a good tree bears good fruit; and the field produces food (Hab. 3). But let us look at R. Akiba's reasoning, which is found in the same passage: there, where the shaving of the head is discussed, disfigurement is intended; therefore here too disfigurement. You will find the same reasoning in Abenezra, R. Salomon and others, who explain עשתה here as תגדל, just as Onkelos does with the word תרבי, that is, she shall let them grow. They argue from the purpose and aim of this law, which seems to have been that the Israelite, struck by the sight of a woman filthy, unkempt and weeping, should be moved to repentance and cool his passion, and should send away from himself the foreign captive whom he had claimed and loved. R. Bechai on this passage, quoted by the learned Schickard in Jus regium Hebraeorum, page 135: Perhaps within this time the lover will be comforted and his appetite for her will pass, when he sees her made ugly by the shaving of her head, the growing of her nails, and her clothing in the garments of captivity, that is, base garments (for she had already put off the fine clothes in which she came), and when he sees her weeping and grieving; then he may send her away wherever she wishes. [אולי תוך הזמן הזה יתנחם החושק ויעבור השקו מעליה בראותו אותה מתנוולה בגלוח הראש ובגירול צפרניה ובלבישת בגדים של שביה כי כבר הסירה הבגדים הנאים שעליה אשר באה עמהם ובראותו אותה בוכה ומצטערת ישלחנה לנפשה] Note that in the Hebrew text of Deut. 21:13 the fine dress in which she is brought into servitude, and which she is here commanded to put off, is called the garment of captivity. Yet Bechai calls that filthy dress the dress of the captive, that is, fitting for a captive. R. Salomon: the garment of her captivity, because the fine clothes are such. For the daughters of cursed nations commonly adorn themselves in this way in war, so as to provoke others to fornication. You now see, I think, that R. Akiba's view is the more probable. But if you do not see this, you at least see that the phrase to make the nails is disputed. Therefore this allegory should be sounded more sparingly in the churches. Whatever the Ministers commonly teach from these and similar allegories can be taught from the plain passages of Scripture.

units.tr: CAP. XXVI. vers. 16.

units.la: Maledictus sit qui patrem & matrem vilipendit ] Ebr. מְקַלֶּה Lxx. ὁ ἀπμάζων, id vulgatus reddit, qui non honorat. Chald. מְקַלִּי / Thema est קלה quod in Kal significat, torrefecit, assavit, In Niphal, vilescere. In Hiphil, vilipendere. Exodi 21.17. Sic intonabat Moses, Qui maledixerit מקלל patri & mari morte moriatur. Ast hic ulterius progreditur Deus, atque illis etiam maledictionem denuntiat, qui parentes suos vilipendunt, id quod longe minus est quam maledicere. non male Carthusianus, qui non honorat, tempore opportuno ipsis obediendo, seu indigentis– gentibus pro posse subveniendo, & maxime, qui non solum non honorat, sed eis maledicat & convitiatur. Hæc eò notavi, ut monerem Germanos & Belgas, locum hunc à Luthero nimis indiligenter esse versum. Sic enim habet, verbloecht ȝp ȝp die sijn Vader ofte Moeder bloecht id est maledicit. Quasi in Ebraeo esset קללה / quæ vox usurpatur loco illo Exodi supra memorato. Textum Ebraeum versionesque accuratiores magis stabilire reverentiam parentibus debitam, etiam illi judicabunt qui nondum ære lavantur.
units.tr: Cursed be he who makes light of his father and mother] Hebrew מְקַלֶּה [mekalleh]. The Septuagint has ὁ ἀπμάζων [ho apmazōn], which the Vulgate renders qui non honorat (who does not honour). The Chaldee paraphrast has מְקַלִּי [mekalli]. The root is קלה [qalah], which in Kal means to parch, to roast; in Niphal, to become vile; in Hiphil, to make light of. See Exodus 21:17. So Moses thundered: Whoever curses מקלל his father or mother shall be put to death. But here God goes further and pronounces a curse on those who make light of their parents, which is far less than cursing them. The Carthusian is not wrong: he who does not honour, by not obeying them in due time, or by not helping them in their need as far as he can; and especially he who not only does not honour them but also curses and reviles them. I have noted this so as to warn Germans and Dutch that Luther has translated this passage too carelessly. His rendering, in German and Dutch, says in effect that whoever curses his father or mother is cursed, that is, maledicit (curses). As if the Hebrew were קללה [qillelah], the word used in the passage of Exodus mentioned above. Those too who are not yet washed in the bath of the lavers will judge that a more accurate Hebrew text and more accurate versions strengthen the reverence due to parents.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. vers. 66.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII. vers. 66.

units.la: Et erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te] Ita vulg. Ebræa sic habent, Eritque vita tua suspensa tibi e regione. LXX. καὶ ἔσται ἡ ζωή σου κρεμαμένη ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν σου. Proverbialis locutio, inquit Junius, sumpta à rebus corporeis, quæ à tenui filo pendent, jam jam ruituræ. Semper & indesinenter desperabis de vita tua. Carthus. erit vita tua in ambiguo posita, ita quod eris tam incertus de subsistentia vitæ tuæ, ac si jam esses tibi subtracta. Hanc interpretationem firmant & consequa verba, Et non credes vitæ tuæ id est interprete Corn. à Lapide, non fides vitæ tuæ, vel te posse vivere, sed de vita desperabis. Hæc est literalis & quam sacer Spiritus intendit, hujus loci interpretatio. Lubet nunc audire, quàm abusi sint hoc loco Patrum nonnulli. Irenæus lib.4. cap.23. Significans quoniam qui ab initio condidit & fecit eos verbum & in novissimis temporibus redimens nos & vivificans, ostenditur pendens in ligno, & non credent ei, ait enim, Et erit vita tua pendens ante oculos tuos, &c. Vides de Christo crucifixo eum hunc locum accepisse. Eadem habet lib.3.16. Lactantius lib.4.Instit.cap.8. August.lib.16.contra Faustum, cap.21. Procopius in hunc locum, Tertull. adversus Judæos, cap.11. qui insuper ad textum addidit duas voculas, in ligno. Erit vita tua pendens in ligno ante oculos tuos & non credes vitæ tuæ, q.d. Christus qui est vita tua, suspensus erit ante oculos tuos in cruce, & non credis ei qui est vita tua. Vide & Leonem serm. 8. de Passione & Theophanis orationem de elevatione crucis, pag.630. tomi 9. Biblioth. Patrum. Ubi primarium præsidium ponit in voce lignum, eoque trahit ex Psal. 1. lignum plantatum, & Gen 2. lignum vitæ. Nisi enim crucem designaret, inquit, arborem vel plantam dixisset, non ignum, Lignum enim post sectionem demum nomen habet. Tu disce tiro, Ebr. יו & ξύλον & δένδρον significare, ac proinde in lingua Hellenistica illud pro hoc passim poni. Galatinum ulterius provexit Allegorizandi seu potius ineptiendi prurigo. Ille enim cap. 17. libri 8. de Arcanis Catholicæ veritatis, probaturus quod Deus aliquando esset suspendendus, ex hoc loco primum petit argumentum, additque ideo fortasse pluraliter vitas dixisse, quia sicut gemina est Messia natura, ita & ejus vita, Deus scilicet & anima. Admirentur hæc indocti & quos tales speculationes delectant. Qui fontes adire potest, si vel Crassus sit, non potest ad tales ineptias non ridere.
units.tr: And your life shall hang before you] So the Vulgate. The Hebrew reads: And your life shall be suspended before you, opposite you. The Septuagint: καὶ ἔσται ἡ ζωή σου κρεμαμένη ἀπέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν σου [kai estai hē zōē sou kremamenē apenanti tōn ophthalmōn sou]. This is a proverbial expression, says Junius, taken from physical things that hang by a slender thread and are about to fall. You will despair continually and without ceasing of your life. The Carthusian: your life will be placed in doubt, so that you will be as uncertain of the continuance of your life as if it had already been taken from you. The following words confirm this interpretation: And you shall not believe your life, that is, as Cornelius à Lapide explains it, you shall not trust your life, or believe that you can live, but you will despair of life. This is the literal interpretation of the passage, and what the Holy Spirit intends. Now let us hear how some of the Fathers have misused this passage. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 23: Showing that he who made and formed them from the beginning, the Word, and who in the last times redeems and quickens us, is shown hanging on the tree, and they will not believe him, for he says: And your life shall hang before your eyes, etc. You see that he took this passage as referring to the crucified Christ. He says the same in book 3, chapter 16. Lactantius, Institutes, book 4, chapter 8; Augustine, Against Faustus, book 16, chapter 21; Procopius on this passage; Tertullian, Against the Jews, chapter 11, who added two little words to the text, on the tree: Your life shall hang on the tree before your eyes, and you shall not believe your life, that is, Christ, who is your life, shall be suspended before your eyes on the cross, and you do not believe him who is your life. See also Leo, sermon 8 on the Passion, and the prayer of Theophanes on the raising of the cross, p. 630 of volume 9 of the Bibliotheca Patrum. There he places his main support in the word lignum (wood), and draws from Psalm 1, a tree planted, and Genesis 2, the tree of life. For, he says, unless he meant the cross, he would have said arbor or planta, not lignum, since lignum is the name given to wood only after it has been cut. You, a beginner, learn that the Hebrew עץ [ets], as well as ξύλον [xylon] and δένδρον [dendron], means tree, and therefore in the Hellenistic language one is commonly used for the other. Galatinus carried the itch of allegorising, or rather of talking nonsense, further still. In chapter 17 of book 8 of his On the Secrets of Catholic Truth, wishing to prove that God was at some time to be hanged, he first seeks an argument from this passage, and adds: Perhaps he said lives in the plural because just as the nature of the Messiah is twofold, so also is his life, namely God and soul. Let the unlearned, and those whom such speculations delight, marvel at these things. Anyone who can consult the sources, even if he is a dullard, cannot help laughing at such nonsense.

units.la: CAP. XXIX. verf. 29.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX. verse 29.

units.la: Occulta [ pertinent ] ad DOMINVM Deum nostrum : sed (Ebraice, Et) revelata [ pertinent ] ad nos & filios nostros, ut faciamus omnia verba Legis hujus. Hæc est simplicissima Ebraicarum vocum interpretatio. Nihil enim notius est iis, qui vel ἐκγοδηγὼς Ebræam Grammaticam attigerunt, τὸ ֹ sæpe idem significare quod ad cum Ellipsi verbi pertinet. D. Piscator paulo aliter, occulta [ sunt ] penes Dominum D. nostrum : at r. sunt penes nos, &c. Junius occulta [sunto] penes D. &c. Sensus, ne sapiamus altum, neque in ea, quæ Deus sacri silentii superparo operuit, curiosè inquiramus. Quin hoc potius operam demus, ut ex præscripto istius Legis, quam nobis revelavit, obsequii gloriam amplexantes, vitam nostram instituamus. Hanc egregiam & auro contra non caram sententiam commodè satis expressit ipse quoque Vulgatus Interpres. Eo magis miror indiligentiam & dormitationem B. Lutheri qui & neglecto accentu Athnach in voce אֱלֹהִים / & insuperhabita litera vau ante vocem הַגִּגָּלוֹת / quæ alterum illud axioma cum priori copulat, sic vertit, das geheimnis des HERRN unsers Gottes ist offenbaret uns und unsern kindern ewiglich / dass wir thun sollen allen worte dises gesetzes. Quæ in * Belgica nostra translatione sic versa reperies, de hepmelijckheyt des Heeren onses Godts is ons ende onse kinderen geopenbaert eeuwichlijck/ &c. Quicquid ad hunc textum ab Interpretibus convectatur, non illu-
units.tr: The secret things [belong] to the LORD our God, but (in Hebrew, and) the things revealed [belong] to us and to our children, that we may do all the words of this law. This is the most straightforward interpretation of the Hebrew words. Nothing is better known to those who have so much as touched Hebrew grammar, [ἐκγοδηγὼς] than that לְ [le] often means the same as to or belongs to, with the verb belongs understood. Dr Piscator puts it a little differently: the secret things are with the Lord our God, but the revealed things are with us, etc. Junius: the secret things [let them be] with the Lord, etc. The sense is: do not be wise above what is written, nor inquire curiously into those things which God has covered with a sacred silence. Rather, let us take pains to order our lives according to the prescription of this law which he has revealed to us, embracing the glory of obedience. The Vulgate translator too has expressed this excellent sentiment, which is not to be valued at any price, quite adequately. I wonder all the more at the carelessness and drowsiness of the blessed Luther, who, neglecting the accent Athnach on the word אֱלֹהִים [elohim], and disregarding the letter vav before the word הַגִּגָּלוֹת [hanniglot], which joins the second statement to the first, translates it thus: the secret of the LORD our God is revealed to us and to our children for ever, that we should do all the words of this law. In our Dutch translation you will find it rendered thus: the secrets of the Lord our God are revealed to us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law, etc. Whatever is gathered about this text by the interpreters does not illuminate

units.la: * Gen. Angli Ital. &c. Sed & LXX. & Chaldæus illustrando verbo Dei, & Lutheri asserturi. Hoc ergo operam dent: sidi Interpretes qui ad populum verba facturi sunt, ut loca Scripturæ, quæ vel interpretaturi, aut confirmando convellendoque aliqua dogmata citaturi sunt, vel cum fontibus, vel si id non possint, cum melioribus versionibus conferant.
units.tr: * The Geneva, English, Italian, etc. [versions]. But the Septuagint and the Chaldee paraphrast also, in illustrating the word of God and in asserting Luther's [reading]. Let therefore those interpreters who are going to address the people take care that, whenever they are going to explain or to cite passages of Scripture in order to confirm or refute some doctrines, they compare them either with the sources or, if they cannot do that, with the better versions.

units.la: CAP. XXXII. vers. 8.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXII. vers. 8.

units.la: Quando dividebat altissimus gentes, quando dispergebat filios Adæ, constituit terminos gentium κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων Θεοῦ. Ita LXX. in quam versionem illæ voces, ἀγγέλων Θεοῦ, irrepsere, pro υἱῶν Ισραήλ, filiorum Israel, quomodo legunt Hebr. Chald. Aq. Symm. Vulgatus, &c. Non existimo quempiam adeo hospitem in Scholasticorum scriptis esse, qui ignoret magno calore ab ipsis quæsitum fuisse de numero salvandorum. Iverunt enim boni isti Patres in partes, dum alii contenderunt, tot homines salvatum iri, quot angeli ceciderunt, alii contra quot steterunt. Tractat hanc controversiam Magister Sententiarum lib. 2. Dist. 9, qui in eum commentati sunt. Gregorius Magnus iis accessit, qui prædestinatorum numerum cum angelis, qui perseverarunt, componunt. verba Magistri, Non enim juxta numerum eorum qui ceciderunt, sed eorum qui permanserunt, homines ad beatitudinem admittuntur. Vide Gregorius. Superna illa civitas ex angelis & hominibus constat, ad quam credimus tantos humani generis ascendere, quantos illic contigit angelos remansisse, sicut scriptum est in Cantico Deuteronomii statuit terminos populorum juxta numerum Angelorum Dei. Vide cordate Lector, quo magnum virum præcipitem dederit mala versio. Mosis ista mens fuit, Deus O. M. post contusas ad Babylonis turrem linguas ita distribuit regiones inter populos, ut spatium satis magnum assignaverit filiis Israel, secundum numerum & multitudinem eorum. Vide Cajet. Oleastrium, Jun. Pisc. Deodatum, &c. Designavit ergo Israelitis capaces terminos nondum existentibus. Abenezra, dicunt Interpretes hoc intelligi de ætate dispersionis (Genes. 11.): quando dispersa est universa terra, Tunc enim decrevit Deus ut terra 7. gentium esset aliquando Israelitarum; & quia suffectura ea erat numero eorum, ideo dicit, secundum nu-memerum Filiorum Israel. Cæteras expositiones ceu alienas mitto. Cæterum illud propemodum excideray, hoc ipso textu, prout in Græco legitur, usos ex patribus nonnullos, ut docerent singulis gentibus, imo & hominibus suos angelos seu custodes assignatos, quam sententiam ut non asperior, ita & certò persuasus sum, nec volam nec vestigium ejus in hoc contextu extare.
units.tr: When the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God [κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων Θεοῦ]. So the Septuagint. Into that version the words "of the angels of God" crept in, in place of "of the sons of Israel," as the Hebrew, the Chaldee, Aquila, Symmachus, the Vulgate and others read. I do not think anyone is so unfamiliar with the writings of the Scholastics that he does not know how eagerly they debated the number of the saved. Those good Fathers took sides. Some contended that as many men would be saved as angels had fallen; others, on the contrary, that as many as had stood firm. The Master of the Sentences treats this controversy in book 2, distinction 9, and his commentators followed him. Gregory the Great joined those who compare the number of the predestined with the angels who persevered. The words of the Master: For men are admitted to blessedness not according to the number of those who fell, but of those who remained. See Gregory. That heavenly city consists of angels and men, and we believe that as many of the human race ascend to it as there were angels who remained there, as it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy: He set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God. See, careful reader, how far a bad translation has thrown a great man headlong. Moses' meaning was this: God Most Good and Great, after the tongues were confused at the tower of Babel, so distributed the regions among the peoples that he assigned a sufficiently large space to the sons of Israel, according to their number and multitude. See Cajetan, Oleaster, Junius, Piscator, Diodati, and others. He therefore designated for the Israelites territories ample enough, though not yet existing. Abenezra: The interpreters say this is to be understood of the time of the dispersion (Gen. 11), when the whole earth was dispersed. For then God decreed that the land of the seven nations would one day belong to the Israelites; and because it would be sufficient for their number, therefore it says, according to the number of the sons of Israel. I set aside the other expositions as foreign to the point. I had almost forgotten that some of the Fathers used this very text, as it reads in Greek, to teach that each nation, and even each man, had its own angels or guardians assigned to it. I am fully convinced that this opinion, though not harsher than the others, is nowhere to be found in this context, nor even a trace of it.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII. vers. 17.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXIII. vers. 17.

units.la: Cornua Rhinocerotis sunt cornua ejus ] Ebraicum רְאֵם alibi in vulgata redditur unicornis, ut Psal. 22. LXX. ubique μονοκέρωτα reddunt, uno loco excepto, ubi vertunt ἀδροί, robusti. Agit de pulcritudine & potentia posterorum Josephi. Valde torserunt hunc locum veteres, ac inter eos Justinus Martyr adversus Tryphonem, Monocerotis cornua dici & ostendi non potest rem aliam aut figuram ullam referre, nisi eam quæ crucis speciem adumbrat, &c. Vide etiam Tertull. adversus Judæos cap. 10. Ambrosium in De benedictione patriarcharum. At nihil hic de Christo, nihil de cruce. Dices, Josephum fuisse typum Christi. Ego verò nullos agnosco typos, nisi qui in libris Novi fœderis fundamentum suum habent. Jonam agnosco typum Christi, quia id diserte testatur Christus ipse Matth. 12. Agnus Paschalis præfiguravit Christum, Joh. 19. 36. at de Josepho locum adhuc quæro. Neque toleranda est illa Ruperti Allegoria, qua ex Monocerote Christum facit, Fortissimus spiritVum Deus, velut unicornis, id est potentiæ singularis, Deus incomprehensibilis & invictæ virtutis, virginei tractus odore uteri, illiqueinclusus est, & ex eo tantum comprehendi potuit & occidi. In quam sententiam prolixus est & Pintus Jesuita comm. in Isai. XLV. 8. ubi hunc quoque torquet locum Ps. 28. nobis 29. Dilectus ut filius unicornium, quem eo cum ait a B. Augustino de Christo exponi. Sed scire licet, locum illum plane aliter tunnire in origin. Laudat illic David Deum O. M. ab, effectis 3. inter ea est tonitru, quo de agit a vers. 3. ad 10. Vox Domini facit ut exiliant (cedri Libani) sicut vitulus, facit ut exiliant Libanus & Sehirion ut pullus unicornium. Schirion nomen montis est Libano contigui, qui & Hermon & Senir dicitur, Deut. 111. 8. 9. neque ullo modo per dilectum reddi potest, & ad Christum referri. Sed redeamus ad Ruperti Allegoriam, quam non tolerandam esse diximus. Et merito. Fundamentum enim ejus, quod Gregorius & Isidorus tradunt, animal illud non nisi propositâ virgine, quæ venienti sinum aperiat, capi posse, ac tunc demum omnem ferocia posita caput deponere & soporatam capi, falsum est, ipsique Marcus Paulus Venetus, lib. 3. cap. 15. Gesnerus & alii hanc demonocerotis per virginem cicuratione narrationem fabulis annumerant. Unde & Aristot. & Ælianus & Plinius, aliique qui historiam animalium ad posteritatem transmiserunt, de hac cicuratione altum silent. Quin & Gesnerus fabulam istam ex eo ortam prodidit, quod animal illud tunc solummodo mitescat, quando cum femella sua miscetur.
units.tr: The horns of the rhinoceros are his horns. The Hebrew word [רְאֵם] is elsewhere rendered in the Vulgate as unicorn, as in Ps. 22. The LXX everywhere render it μονοκέρωτα [monokerota], except in one place, where they translate it ἀδροί [adroi], stout. The verse speaks of the beauty and power of Joseph's posterity. The ancients tortured this passage greatly, and among them Justin Martyr against Trypho: The horns of the unicorn cannot be said or shown to refer to any other thing or figure except that which shadows forth the form of the cross, etc. See also Tertullian, Against the Jews, chapter 10, and Ambrose, On the Blessing of the Patriarchs. But there is nothing here about Christ, nothing about the cross. You will say that Joseph was a type of Christ. But I acknowledge no types except those that have their foundation in the books of the New Covenant. I acknowledge Jonah as a type of Christ, because Christ himself expressly testifies to it, Matt. 12. The paschal lamb prefigured Christ, John 19:36; but for Joseph I am still looking for a passage. Nor is that allegory of Rupert to be tolerated, by which he makes Christ out of the unicorn: The most strong God, the Spirit, like a unicorn, that is, of singular power, God incomprehensible and of invincible virtue, was enclosed by the scent of a virginal womb, and only from it could he be seized and slain. The Jesuit Pintus is also lengthy in this view, in his commentary on Isaiah 45:8, where he likewise twists Ps. 28 (our 29), As the son of unicorns is beloved, which he says Augustine explains of Christ. But you should know that this passage has a plainly different sense in its origin. There David praises God Most High for his works; among them is the thunder, which he treats from verse 3 to 10: The voice of the Lord makes (the cedars of Lebanon) leap like a calf; it makes Lebanon and Sirion leap like a young unicorn. Sirion is the name of a mountain adjoining Lebanon, which is also called Hermon and Senir, Deut. 3:8-9; nor can it in any way be rendered "beloved" and referred to Christ. But let us return to Rupert's allegory, which we said is not to be tolerated, and rightly so. For its foundation, which Gregory and Isidore hand down, that this animal can be taken only when a virgin is placed before it, who opens her lap as it approaches, and that then at last, laying aside all its ferocity, it lowers its head and is taken while asleep, is false. Marco Polo the Venetian himself, book 3, chapter 15, Gesner and others count this story of the unicorn's taming by a virgin among the fables. Hence Aristotle, Aelian, and Pliny, and the others who handed down the natural history of animals to posterity, are deeply silent about any such taming. Indeed Gesner also reported that the fable arose from the fact that the animal grows tame only when it mates with its female.

units.la: Non fuit sicut dies ille ante ipsum aut post ipsum, שׁמַע ut audiret Dominus vocem hominis, quia Dominus pugnabat pro Israel. | Non fuit antea & postea tam longa dies, obediente Domino voci hominis & pugnante pro Israel.
units.tr: There was no day like that day before it or after it, when the Lord heeded the voice of a man, because the Lord fought for Israel. (Hebrew: "shama" [שׁמַע]) | There was no day so long before it or after it, the Lord obeying the voice of a man and fighting for Israel.

units.la: Manifestè docent Ebraea, negari similitudinem illius diei in hoc, quod Deus condescendit deprecationi hominis in tanto miraculo, quod non esset verum si Deus condescendisset voci Esaia seu Ezechia in simili & etiam in majori. Hæc Burgensis. Masius ad hunc locum De hujus nostri diei longitudine non agitur comparatio. sed is eo solum antefertur diebus quibusvis, quod nullum alium diem Deus ad ullius hominis preces cadendi hostis gratiâ, interrupto solis motu, sic produxit, ut hunc produxit. Jam adi Lyram ad hunc locum, ut & ad 2. Reg. 20. & vide quibus & quot contentiunculis materiem præbuerit addita vox longa. Illud enim ex illâ illatum, ratione longitudinis hunc diem contendi cum omnibus quotquot ab orbe condito fluxêre & fluent. At obstare visus dies, cujus 2. Reg. 20. mentionem facit sacra historia. Contecerat jam Sol decem horas inæquales seu planetarias, ut vocant, id est ut textus loquitur, ad decimum gradum seu lineam Horologii Achaz jam pervenerat. Ad postulata Ezechiæ retrocessit decem gradibus, ac totidem horis sensim primam repetivit lineam, atque ita denovo
units.tr: The Hebrew text plainly teaches that the likeness of that day is denied in this respect: God condescended to a man's prayer in so great a miracle, which would not be true if God had condescended to the voice of Isaiah or Hezekiah in a like case, or even in a greater one. So Burgensis. Masius on this passage says: No comparison is made concerning the length of this day of ours. It is preferred to all other days only in this, that God never so lengthened any other day, by interrupting the motion of the sun, at the prayer of any man, for the sake of destroying an enemy, as he lengthened this one. Now consult Lyra on this passage, and also on 2 Kings 20, and see what matter for quarrels the added word "long" has given rise to. For from it has been drawn the inference that, by reason of its length, this day is contended to exceed all the days that have flowed and will flow from the creation of the world. But the day of 2 Kings 20, which sacred history mentions, stands in the way. The sun had already descended ten unequal or planetary hours, as they are called, that is, as the text puts it, had already reached the tenth degree or line of Ahaz's sundial. At Hezekiah's request it went back ten degrees, and by as many hours gradually regained the first line, and thus again (the sun went back)

units.la: * Burgensis ad 2. Reg. 20. novo à Primâ ad duodecimam progressus, horas xxxii. eundo & repedando consumpsit. Haec communis Doctorum & Interpretum opinio est. Diei autem Josuæ ad summum xxiv. horæ assignari possunt: Steterit in medio cœlo dies integrum duplicatum habes diem artificialem. Hic ad diversa commenta & κεντροφυγικα itum est. Pars in loco Josuæ, pars in Regum Historia quæsivere responsionis fundamenta. Sunt enim qui Solem hoc die bis quievisse affirmant. Semel in media cœli parte, atque iterum in ultimâ, cum jam vergeret ad occasum. Secundam illam quietem ex his Ebraicis versus 13. extruunt, ולא אץ לבא id est non festinavit occidere. Ita alii 48. alii 36. horas huic diei attribuunt. Justinus Martyr quoque cum Tryphone agens, 36. horas huic diei assignat, per diem enim illum integrum, quo Sol in medio cœli dicitur substitisse, diem naturalem ex 24. horis constantem intelligit. Ex loco 2. Regum sic respondent alii, Solem retrocessisse à decima lineâ ad primam, non sensim, sed uno momento quasi fuisse abreptum, atque ita totum diem Ezechiæ 22. horis fuisse absolutum. Alii horologio isti attribuunt lineas seu gradus ὡρολόγιος id est constitutos ad denotandas semihoras. Sententiam hanc, quam & Junius secutus est, admodum persuadet versus 9. & 10. capitis 20. 2. Regum. Ecce enim umbra jam attigerat lineam decimam; optionem Regi hanc facit propheta, velitne Solem progredi gradibus x. an verò retrocedere totidem. Respondet Rex, facile fore Solem declinare לנטוי id est uno quasi momento decem adhuc gradibus præcipitari, malle se ut retrahatur ad gradus totidem. Si potuit umbra, quæ jam lineam decimam attigerat, decem insuper alias præcipitato & insueto percurrere, plures ergo quam duodecim lineas horologium illud habuerit necesse est. Si ultra 12. non potuit plures pauciorsve habere quam 24. Diei enim artificialis horæ planetariæ semper fuere 12. id est semihoræ 24. Sed ad rem. Itaque sic dies [Ezechiæ] viginti duarum horarum effectus est, verba Junii. Illud sic explico. Sol jam attigerat lineam decimam, quæ index erat semihorae decimæ, seu quod idem, horæ quintæ elapsæ. Repetiit suum illum cursum pede retrogrado id est à decima linea rediit ad primam. Et ibi est quinquehorium. Eò revocatus ordinarium cursum repetiit, & duodecim horarum spatio iter emensus est. Ecce tibi 22. horas. Duabus ergo horis dies Josuæ præcellit, sive hanc sive præcedentem opinionem amplectaris. Alii tamen diem Ezechiæ longiorem statuunt, tum ob illa quæ nos jam attiginus, tum ob authoritatem Dionysii illius, quem Areopagitam vocant. Is enim Epistola 7. ad Polycarpum de recessu illo solis verba faciens, ἡ τεταρλασίς μίθρα meminit, τῶτο τῆς περσῶν ιερωπ- κατὶς ἱμφίεεται Φρμαις, καὶ εἰσιν μάγοι τι μνημόσυνα τα τε- πλασίς μίθρα πλέσι. Et Georgius Pachymerius ad locum il- lum sic ait, οι περξικὰ τὸ παρέκτασα τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης Δια τῆς πλατείς, ἡ μνημοσυνῶν ἡ τεταρτασις σημαίνουσι. id est Persa extensionem illius diei in sacris quæ mnemosyna seu Memoria Triplasii id est triplicis Mithræ, ut Dionys. loquitur, appellantur, denotant. Hinc illud est, quod Lyra in Postilla ait, diem Ezechiæ fuisse triplicatum, quamvis deficiant horæ quatuor, ex bis 10, & semel 12. horis constantem. Hi ad locum Josuæ respondent, eum referendum ad id tempus quo vel Josue vel alius quisquam historiam eam scripsit. q. d. Ex quo fuit mundus in hunc usque diem, quo hæc scribo, tam longa dies non extitit. At hoc non placet Lyræ, qui pro longitudine diei Josuæ stat. Is horas non artificiales intelligit id est inæquales & planetarias sed naturales. Sic dico, omnis dies artificialis habebat horas 12. artificiales. Earum termini erant ortus occasusque solis. Itaque pro diverso accessu & recessu solis, horæ illæ vel prolongabantur vel contrahebantur. Hinc fiebat, ut medio Junio aut circiter (circa hoc enim tempus accidisse hæc statuit Lyra) dies artificialis habuerit 18. horas naturales; quæ duplicatæ horas 36. efficiunt. Diei autem Ezechiæ à Dionysio tributas horas 32. Lyra ad 26. horas naturales & duas partes horæ revocat, hac conjectura, cum in solstitium hyemale incidisse. Burgensis omnino negat diem Ezechiæ fuisse prolongatum, quem vide in Addit. ad 2. Reg. 20. Sed nimis jam prolixus fui. Illud mihi propositum fuit ostendere, quantas contentionum occasiones unica vox Ebraeis fontibus suppeditata præbuerit. Ut vere de ris asseri queat illud Poetæ, Pulveris exigui jactu, &c. Chaldæus simpliciter verterat, Et non fuit sicut ille dies ante eum & post eum, ut accepta fuerit precatio hominis. Et LXX. καὶ ὡς ἐγένετο ἡμέρα τοιαύτη ἡδὲ τὸ πρὸ πρὸν, ὡδὲ γ' ἐχαπαν, &c. Hæc vestigia si prisfisset noster, omnibus istis quæstiunculis præclusus fuisset aditus.
units.tr: Burgensis on 2 Kings 20: it advanced anew from the first to the twelfth line, and by going forward and back consumed thirty-two hours. This is the common opinion of the Doctors and Interpreters. The day of Joshua, however, can be assigned at most twenty-four hours: "the sun stood still in the midst of heaven" (Josh. 10:13), and so you have a double natural day. Here men have resorted to various fanciful inventions [κεντροφυγικα]. Some have sought the foundations of an answer in the account of Joshua, others in the history of the Kings. For some affirm that the sun rested twice on this day: once in the middle of the heaven, and again at the last, when it was already declining toward the west. They build this second rest on the Hebrew of verse 13, "and hastened not to go down" [ולא אץ לבא], that is, "did not hasten to set." So some assign forty-eight hours to this day, others thirty-six. Justin Martyr too, in his dialogue with Trypho, assigns thirty-six hours to this day, for by that whole day in which the sun is said to have stood in the midst of heaven he understands a natural day made up of twenty-four hours. From the passage in 2 Kings others reply thus: the sun went back from the tenth line to the first, not gradually, but as if it had been snatched back in a single moment, and so Hezekiah's day was completed in twenty-two hours. Others assign to that sundial lines or degrees [ὡρολόγιος], that is, set up to mark half-hours. This view, which Junius also followed, is strongly supported by verses 9 and 10 of chapter 20 of 2 Kings. For behold, the shadow had already reached the tenth line; the prophet gives the king the choice whether the sun should advance ten degrees or go back as many. The king replies that it would be easy for the sun to slope down [לנטוי], that is, to be pushed down ten more degrees in a single moment, but he preferred that it be drawn back by as many degrees. If the shadow, which had already reached the tenth line, could run over ten more, hastily and unusually, then that sundial must have had more than twelve lines; if it could not have more than twelve, then it had no more than twenty-four. For the planetary hours of an artificial day were always twelve, that is, twenty-four half-hours. But to the point. And so the day of [Hezekiah] was made to last twenty-two hours, in Junius's words. I explain it thus. The sun had already reached the tenth line, which marked the tenth half-hour, or what is the same, five hours had elapsed. It retraced its course with a backward step, that is, it returned from the tenth line to the first. And there is the five-hour mark. Recalled there, it resumed its ordinary course and covered its journey in the space of twelve hours. There you have twenty-two hours. So Joshua's day surpasses by two hours, whichever of this or the previous opinion you embrace. Others, however, judge Hezekiah's day to have been the longer, both for the reasons we have just touched on and on the authority of that Dionysius whom they call the Areopagite. For in his seventh Epistle to Polycarp, speaking of that retreat of the sun, he mentions the "triple" Mithra [τριπλασίς μίθρα], which he says the Persian priests clothe in signs, and the Magi keep as a memorial of the triple Mithra. And George Pachymeres, commenting on that passage, says that the Persians, in their sacred rites, denote by the extension of that day what they call the memorial or triple [τριπλασίς] Mithra, as Dionysius puts it. Hence Lyra in his Postil says that Hezekiah's day was tripled, consisting of twice ten and once twelve hours, though four hours are missing. These writers answer on Joshua's passage that it must be referred to the time when either Joshua or some other person wrote that history, as if to say: from the beginning of the world until this day on which I write, no day so long has existed. But this does not please Lyra, who stands for the length of Joshua's day. He understands the hours not as artificial, that is unequal and planetary, but as natural. I say thus: every artificial day had twelve artificial hours. Their limits were sunrise and sunset. So, according to the varying approach and retreat of the sun, those hours were either lengthened or shortened. Hence it followed that about mid-June (for Lyra holds that these events took place around that time) an artificial day had eighteen natural hours, and doubled, these make thirty-six hours. But to Hezekiah's day Dionysius assigns thirty-two hours. Lyra reduces it to twenty-six natural hours and two parts of an hour, by the conjecture that it fell at the winter solstice. Burgensis altogether denies that Hezekiah's day was lengthened; see him in his Additions on 2 Kings 20. But I have already gone on too long. My purpose was to show how many occasions for dispute a single word, supplied by the Hebrew sources, has offered. So truly may be said of this what the poet says: "by the throw of a little dust," and so on. The Chaldee paraphrast had simply rendered: "And there was not a day like that day before it or after it, that a man's prayer might be received." And the Seventy: "And there was such a day as had not been before it, nor was there afterward..." If our author had followed these traces, he would have been spared all these little questions.

units.la: Nomen autem Hebronis olim fuerat Kirjath Arbe, (id est civitas Arbe; הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים הוּא Homo iste magnus inter Anakim sub. erat. | Nomen Hebron antea vocabatur Cariat Arbe, Adam maximus inter Enacim ibi situs est.
units.tr: The name of Hebron was formerly Kirjath Arba (that is, the city of Arba), was there; the Hebrew reads הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל בָּעֲנָקִים הוּא, "This man was great among the Anakim" [Ha-adam ha-gadol ba-anaqim hu]. The Vulgate reads: "The name Hebron was formerly Cariath Arba; Adam, the greatest among the Enacim, is buried there."

units.la: Illud constat קִרְיַת urbem, oppidum, ex abs. קִרְיָה / Arbang seu ἀρχαϊκῶς Apes (ut קִרְיַת Core,) nomen proprium viri est. Patet ex demonstrativo הוּא quod sequitur, Is, inquit, magnus erat inter Anakim id est maximus Anakaeorum. Locutio, ut in N. T. benedicta tu in mulieribus id est benedictissima mulierum. in V. Test. עֲפָה בְּנָשִׁים / pulcra in mulieribus. Quin & cap.15.13. Vrbs Arba patris Anakaeorum. Facessant ergo nugae Ebraeorum qui ארבע hic exponunt quatuor, civitas τετραπολις. Quod vid. illic Gigantes 4. aut 4. paria conjugum, Adam & Heva, Abrah. & Sara, Isaac & Reb. Jacob & Lea sepulta sint. Nec est, quod hic alium quaeramus in sequentibus verbis praeter Arbam. Tripliciter itaque hic peccavit Vulg: 1. addendo vocem situs est. 2. omittendo demonstrativum הוא / 3 nomen apellativum אדם convertendo in nomen proprium δ' πεφ-γεπλασυ. Unde invecta opinio, Adamum hic fuisse sepultum. Oleastrius ad Gen. 23.1. Ansam huic sententiae dederunt verba vulgata versionis citata in Josua quae sic habet, nomen Hebron, &c. quo loco in Ebraeo habetur, Homo magnus in Enakim ipse. Sed quia pro homine ibi ponitur Adam, putavit vulgatus ibi nomen proprium esse. Bened. Adam nomen commune hic est, & non proprium. Lyra id quoque vidit, Adam est nomen commune & significat hominem, tamen appropriatum fuit primo homini. Dicunt igitur aliqui quod ibi tenetur Adam prout est nomen appropriatum, pro primo homine ibidem sepulto. Alii dicunt quod accipitur pro illo Gigante qui dicitur Arbe.
units.tr: That קִרְיַת means city or town, from the absolute form קִרְיָה [qiryah], is certain. Arba, or archaically Ape [ἀρχαϊκῶς Ἀπής], is a proper name of a man, as in קִרְיַת Core [qiryat Qoraḥ]. This is clear from the demonstrative הוּא [hu] that follows: "He," it says, "was great among the Anakim," that is, the greatest of the Anakites. The idiom is like the New Testament "blessed are you among women," that is, most blessed of women, and in the Old Testament עֲפָה בְּנָשִׁים [ʿafah bannashim], "beautiful among women." Indeed in chapter 15:13 we read "the city of Arba, father of the Anakites." So let the trifles of the Hebrews go hang, who here explain ארבע [arbaʿ] as "four," the city of four [τετράπολις, tetrapolis]. On this see there: the giants, or four pairs of spouses, Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah, are buried. Nor need we look here in the following words for anyone other than Arba. The Vulgate therefore erred in three ways: first, by adding the words "is buried"; second, by omitting the demonstrative הוּא [hu]; third, by turning the common noun אדם [adam] into a proper name, ὁ πρωτόπλαστος [ho prōtoplastos], "the first-formed man." Hence the opinion that Adam was buried here took hold. Oleastrius on Genesis 23:1: "The verses of the Vulgate version, cited in Joshua, which read 'the name Hebron, etc.,' gave occasion to this opinion. In the Hebrew, where the passage reads 'a great man among the Enakim himself,' but because Adam is put there for 'man,' the Vulgate translator thought it was a proper name there." Benedict: "Adam is a common noun here, and not a proper name." Lyra also saw this: "Adam is a common noun and signifies a man, yet it was appropriated to the first man. Some therefore say that here Adam is taken as a proper name, for the first man buried in that place. Others say it is taken for that giant who is called Arba."
