units.la: VAlde sudant Interpretes, ut rationem reddant hujus sepa-rationis. Qui curvato poplite biberunt domum remissi sunt, qui vero lamberant aquas istar canum, reservati prælio. Ebræi quidam istos geniculatores ideo remissos ajunt, quod inde collegerit Gideon, eos idola colere, quippe assuetos id facere coram Baal, unde illud, qui non flexerunt genua sua Baali. Alii, inter quos Lyra existimant geniculatores fuisse valde sitibundos, ac proinde fatigatos; cæteros autem qui lamberant aquas minus sitivisse, ac proinde non adeo lassos. Itaque hos retentos, illos ceu prælio minus utiles domum remissos. Alii, ut R. Levi, quem secutus est Cl. Piscator, putant geniculationem fuisse signum ignaviæ, ut contra to lambere, masculi & fortis animi. Sic illi. At totus contextus eo nos ducit, ut statuamus, Deum hæc omnia ita instituisse, ut nihil humanis viribus ferrent acceptum, sed ut ipsi in solidum victoria adscriberetur verf. 2. ne glorietur contra me Israel dicendo meis viribus liberatus sum. Itaque trepidis pavidisque ex præscripto * Legis divinæ domum remissis, relictisque tantum decem millibus, novam instituit exercitus lustrationem, in quâ non fortiores, ut Lyra vult & qui eum sequuntur, sed minus fortes prælio reservat, ut ipsi soli victoria transcriberetur. Omnis victoria, etiam cum numerosus miles pugnat, est à Deo. Sed id magis perspicuum fit, quando cum numeroso & potenti hoste exigua & imbellis turba confligit. Prior separatio fiebat juxta Legem divinam, dimittebanturque manifestè trepidi. Ex iis qui relicti erant, alii aliis erant fortiores. Hic ergo reservantur ii, qui ad fortissimos comparati, trepidi erant. Josephus, 1. 5. 8. Gideoni Deus in somnis apparens, dixit homines tali ingenio esse, ut sibi placentes nulli velint virtute cedere, & victoriam sibi potius quam
units.tr: Interpreters sweat hard to give a reason for this separation. Those who drank with bent knee were sent home, but those who lapped the water like dogs were kept for battle. Some Hebrews say that Gideon inferred from the kneeling men that they worshipped idols, since they were accustomed to do so before Baal, whence the words who have not bowed their knees to Baal. Others, among whom is Lyra, think that the kneelers were very thirsty and therefore worn out, while those who lapped the water were less thirsty and so not so exhausted. Accordingly, the latter were retained and the former, as less useful for battle, were sent home. Others, such as Rabbi Levi, whom the learned Piscator followed, think that kneeling was a sign of cowardice, whereas lapping was a sign of a manly and brave spirit. So they say. But the whole context leads us to conclude that God arranged all these things so that the people would credit nothing to human strength, but that the victory would be ascribed wholly to himself (verse 2): lest Israel boast against me, saying, my own strength has delivered me. So the trembling and fearful men were sent home according to the rule of the divine Law, and only ten thousand were left. Then he made a new review of the army, in which he kept back not the stronger men, as Lyra and his followers hold, but the less brave men for battle, so that the victory might be transferred to God alone. Every victory, even when a numerous army fights, comes from God. But this becomes more plain when a small and unwarlike band fights against a numerous and powerful enemy. The first separation was made according to the divine Law, and the trembling were plainly dismissed. Among those who were left, some were braver than others. Here, then, are kept those who, though they were compared with the bravest, were still fearful. Josephus, book 5, chapter 8: God appeared to Gideon in a dream and said that men are of such a disposition that, pleased with themselves, they will yield to no one in courage, and prefer to attribute victory to themselves rather than to God, relying, of course, on their great forces. So that they might know that the whole matter depended on his help, he commanded him to lead the army to the river about noon, when the heat is greatest, and [the Greek follows in unit 4].

units.la: * Deut. 12. quam Deo tribuant, nimirum magnis suis copiis freti. Vt igitur sciant rem totam pendere ab ipsius auxilio, jussit ut circa meridiem, cum æstus fervet maxime, exercitum ducat ad fluvium, καὶ τὰς μὲν καταχλιθέντας, καὶ οὕτως πίνοντας εὐψύχως ἀπολαμβάνειν. ὅσοι δ' ἀν ἐσπευσμένως καὶ μετὰ θορύβου πίνοντες τύχοιεν, τότε νομίζειν, ὑπὸ δειλίας πῶς τὸ πάσχειν καὶ καταπεπληγότας τοὺς πολεμίους. Ποιη- σάντων ἢ κατὰ ζῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑποθήκας τοῦ Γεδεῶνος, τριακόσιοι ἀνδρες εὑρέθησαν ταῖς χερσὶ μετὰ φόβου περσονευκαμένοι τὸ ὕδωρ πιταγμένως. Ἔφησί π ὁ Θεὸς τέλους ἐπαγόμενον ὑπηχεῖν τοῖς πολεμίοις. id est quotquot procumbentes, eos biberent animosos crederet: quotquot autem trepide & tumultuarie potum sumerent, sic existimaret, eos metu hostium hoc facere. Quod postquam ad mandata Dei feciisset, trecenti inventi sunt cum perturbatione aquam sumere manibus eam ori admoventes. Jussitque Deus ut his assumptis hostem invaderet. Haec Josephus. Quem juvat vers. 5. ut solet lambere canis. Notum adagium, ut Canis e Nilo. Canis animal per se timidum ex Nilo bibiturus metu crocodili bibit fugiens & lambens. Vide Adagia Erasmi & Macrob. Satur. 2. Itaque qui nil metuentes hostem poplite flexo biberant fortiores habiti. Caeteri timidiores, quia canibus similiores, judicati sunt. Atque hos voluit cum hoste miscere praelium. Nunc libet audire eruditissimum Augustinum. Ille Quaest. 37. in Judices, dicit Ebraea sic habere. Fuit itaque numerus eorum qui manu in os projicientes aquam lamberant, trecenti viri, &c. Pergit, Quorum numerus quia 300. erant, signum insinuit crucis, propter literam T. Graecam, qua iste numerus significatur, per quos etiam, gentes magis in Christum crediturae, praefiguratum est, quod litera Graeca est. Unde Graecorum nomine Apostolus omnes gentes significat, cum dicit, Judaeo primum & Graeco. Iste numerus & in vernaculis Abrahae animadvertendus est, per quos fratrem ab hostibus liberavit, quod enim ibi exuberant 18. (nam 318. fuisse referuntur) videtur mihi significatum, quo etiam tempore fieret id est tertio, quod futurum erat sub gratia. Nam primum est ante legem. Secundum sub legem. Tertium sub gratia. Singula vero tempora senario numero significata sunt propter perfectionem. Nam ter seni, decem & octo sunt. Quam haec sint solida, judicet eruditus Lector. Sed quod ad 318. illos vernas attinet, istius προεσεγίας pater Augustinus non est. Namque ante eum Tertullianus in carmine adversus Marcionem eadem tradidit.
units.tr: and to them who had lain down and drunk in this way he was to grant courage. But those who drank hastily and in confusion, he was to consider as having been made cowardly by fear, and their enemies as terrified. [Greek: καὶ τὰς μὲν καταχλιθέντας, καὶ οὕτως πίνοντας εὐψύχως ἀπολαμβάνειν. ὅσοι δ' ἀν ἐσπευσμένως καὶ μετὰ θορύβου πίνοντες τύχοιεν, τότε νομίζειν, ὑπὸ δειλίας πῶς τὸ πάσχειν καὶ καταπεπληγότας τοὺς πολεμίους.] When Gideon had done this according to God's instructions, three hundred men were found who drank water with their hands, bringing it to their mouths in fear and confusion. [Greek: Ποιησάντων ἢ κατὰ ζῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑποθήκας τοῦ Γεδεῶνος, τριακόσιοι ἀνδρες εὑρέθησαν ταῖς χερσὶ μετὰ φόβου περσονευκαμένοι τὸ ὕδωρ πιταγμένως.] God then commanded that these be taken and the enemy attacked with them. [Greek: Ἔφησί π ὁ Θεὸς τέλους ἐπαγόμενον ὑπηχεῖν τοῖς πολεμίοις.] That is, those who bowed down and drank he would think brave; those who drank hastily and in confusion he would think to do so from fear. This is Josephus. Verse 5 pleases him, where it says the dog laps as usual, a well-known proverb, like the dog at the Nile. The dog, an animal timid by nature, drinks from the Nile in fear of the crocodile, drinking while fleeing and lapping. See Erasmus's Adages and Macrobius, Saturnalia 2. So those who drank with bent knee, fearing nothing, were thought braver. The others, being more like dogs, were judged more timid, and God wished these to be mixed in battle with the enemy. Now let us hear the most learned Augustine. In his Questions on Judges 37, he says the Hebrew text reads thus: the number of those who put their hand to their mouth and lapped the water was three hundred men, etc. He goes on: because their number was 300, it hints at the sign of the cross, on account of the Greek letter T, by which this number is signified, and through them was prefigured the nations that would more readily believe in Christ, because the letter is Greek. Hence the Apostle by the name of the Greeks signifies all nations when he says, to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1). This number is also to be noted in the servants of Abraham, by whom he rescued his brother from his enemies, for there it is reported that there were eighteen over the three hundred (for they are said to have been 318). It seems to me that this signifies the time, that is, the third, which was to come under grace. For the first is before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. Each of these times is signified by the number six, on account of perfection, for three times six are eighteen. Let the learned reader judge how solid these things are. But as for those 318 servants, the father Augustine is not the originator of this subtlety, for before him Tertullian in his poem against Marcion handed down the same things.

units.la: Neque solus his subtilitatibus hæsit Augustinus. a Audi Ambrosium, ut scias non quantitatem numeri, sed meritum electionis expressum. Eos enim adscivit, quos dignos numero fidelium judicavit, qui in Domini nostri Jesu Christi nomen crederent. Trecentos enim Tau litera Græca significat. Decem & octo autem summam IH exprimit, nomen fidei. Audi & * Eucherium, Quod vero Abraham tantum in 318. comitantibus adversarios principes debellavit, jam tunc in crucis sacra figuram, qua per Tau literam Græcam, & Jesu nomen, quod per Iota & Eta Græcis literis scribitur, qui salvator interpretatur, in numero 318. exprimitur. Glossa ordinaria, Quisque pro anima sua contra spirituales nequitias bellum gerat cum 318. vernaculis id est cum auxilio {S. crucis. Tau enim litera, quæ habet figuram crucis (de eo videbimus ad Iezech. 9.) 300. exprimit. Ex his Cl. Drusius facem alluxit difficili, & qui multos exercuit, loco Prudentii, qui extat præfatione in psychomachiam, Nos esse large vernularum divites, Si quid trecenti bis novenis additis Possint, figura noverimus mystica.
units.tr: Nor did Augustine alone cling to these subtleties. Hear Ambrose, so that you may know that not the quantity of the number but the merit of the choice is expressed. For he admitted those whom he judged worthy of the number of the faithful, who believed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the Greek letter Tau signifies three hundred. And eighteen expresses the sum IH, the name of faith. Hear also Eucherius: that Abraham routed the hostile princes with only 318 companions, already then prefigured the sacred figure of the cross, which, through the Greek letter Tau and the name of Jesus, written in Greek letters with Iota and Eta, which is interpreted Saviour, is expressed in the number 318. The Ordinary Gloss: let each one for his own soul wage war against spiritual wickedness with the 318 servants, that is, with the help of the cross. For the letter Tau, which has the form of a cross (we shall see about this at Ezekiel 9), expresses 300. From these things the learned Drusius shed light on a difficult passage of Prudentius, which has troubled many, in the preface to the Psychomachia: We are rich in servants, enough, if the three hundred, with nine twice added, can make it, when we know the mystical figure.

units.la: Sed non stetit hoc termino ludendi (quid enim dixero mitius?) libido. Idem ille Ambrosius lib. 1. de fide, Liberius Papa in Epistola ad orientales, & Rupertus, ulterius progressi, existimarunt 318. istis militibus præfiguratos fuisse 318. Patres, qui in victrice Nicæa illum execrandæ memoriæ Arrium damnarunt. Credo bonos istos viros eo die cum hæc scriberent, purgamentum aliquod calcasse. Adeo à Spiritus S. & divini Ananuensis mente aliena chartis illevisse mihi videntur.
units.tr: But this lust for playing did not stop at this limit (for what can I say that is milder?). The same Ambrose, in book 1 of On the Faith, Pope Liberius in his letter to the Easterners, and Rupert, going further, thought that the 318 soldiers prefigured the 318 Fathers who condemned that Arius of accursed memory at victorious Nicaea. I believe these good men, when they wrote these things, must have trodden on some filth. So far, indeed, do these things seem to me to have been smeared on the pages, alien to the mind of the Holy Spirit and the divine Author.

units.la: CAP XI. verf.31.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI, verse 31.

units.la: Ebr. ad verbum. | Vulg. Et erit quodcunque egredietur (sc. primum) è foribus domus meæ in cursum meum, — erit, inquam, DOMINO & offeram illud (in) holocaustum. | Quicunque primum fuerit egressus — cum holocaustum offeram DOMINO.
units.tr: Hebrew, word for word: "And whatever comes out (namely first) from the doors of my house to meet me, it shall be for the LORD, and I will offer it up (as) a burnt offering." | Vulgate: "And whatever comes out at the doors of my house to meet me shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it as a holocaust." | "Whoever comes out first, when I offer a burnt offering to the LORD."

units.la: Ebræa sunt, si quis requirat, וְהָיָה הַיּוֹצֵא אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא מִדְּלָתַי בֵּיתִי — וְהָיָה לַיהוָה וְהַעֲלִיתִיהוּ עוֹלָה Interpres noster primò, quod generaliter dictum, ut etiam bestias possit comprehendere, ad solum hominem videtur restringere. 2. votum bimembre contraxit in membrum unum. Dico votum esse bimembre, ac proinde Kimchium patrem & filium, nec non Junium Vau expressisse per disjunctivam particulam aut. erit Domino scil. consecratum, aut offeram illud in holoc. si vid. fuerit idoneum sacrificio. Licebat enim ex quinque tantùm speciebus sacrificare Deo, vid. bobus, ovibus, caprís, turture, & columbâ: Αὐθεωπηυτίας enim semper detestatus est ὁ φιλόψυχος ἢ φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς. Sed hæc enallage copulæ pro disjunctiva, licet alibi frequens sit (ut ex. gr. qui maledixerit patri & matri Ex.21. 17. quod Matth. 15.4. exprimitur. ὁ μητέρα) hic tamen Domino Piscatori videtur non congrua, ac perinde esse ac si quis diceret. Aut animal aut homo, cum possit esse & animal & homo. Imo si est homo, necesse est ut sit animal. Sic poterat Deo consecrari aliquid & simul offerri in holocaustum, & quodcunque offerebatur in holocaustum, id Deo sacrabatur. Putatitaque inter duo isthæc membra hoc esse discriminis, ut prius promittat consecrationem primi obvii animalis simpliciter, etiam canis vel asini. Potuisset enim redimi juxta præscriptum Legis Levit 27.11. posterius vero cum tacitâ conditione, si vid. animal illud esset idoneum sacrificio. Sententia autem eorum, qui pro immolatione filiæ contendunt, videtur ex hoc versionis Latinæ loco & verf. ultimo non leviter confirmata esse. Quin & ex hâc versione quæsitum istius αὐθεωπηυτίας patrocinium. Sic enim hic locus habet in eâ Factum est ergo Spiritus Domini super Jephte & circuiens Galaad — & transiens ad filios Ammon votum vovit DOMINO; quasi hæc omnia, quæ jungit Interpres, ab eodem spiritu fuerint profecta. In textu Ebræo narratio voti novam incoat sententiam, quod etiam Cajet. annotavit. Sentio itaque non immolatam sed consecratam Deo & in perpetuum quasi Naziræatum & secessum traditam, immuptam manssisse, ne alterius quam Domini esse videretur. Hinc verf. 38. non vitam amittendam, sed virginitatem conservandam deflevit. Erat enim probrosa virginitas, Esai. 4. Hinc verf. ultimo narrat historia, filias Israel quotannis ivisse ad confabulandum cum eâ atque hoc modo tædium solitariæ vitæ fuisse sosolatas. At, inquiunt, nulla extitit lex de virginitate conser-vanda, nullum exemplum ejusmodi voti extat. Quin omnia videntur contra ire & damnare hujusmodi votum. Resp. nos non defendere, sed vehementer improbare viri hujus temeritatem „ cum insigni juris divini ignorantia conjunctam. Et quidem temeritatem duplicem, videlicet temeritatem in vovendo, temeritatem in exequendo: Ignorantiam, siquidem Levit. ult. verf. 4. haec legere potuisset, Quod si- femina erit, quæ vid. devota seu nuncupata fuerit Deo, tunc erit æstimatio tua 3 o. sicli. Magna vero & stupida temeritas in exequendo ista fuit, quod toto illo bimestri sacerdotem Levitamve non consuluerit. Vel si placet, cum aut consuluisse sacerdotes aut à sacerdotibus monitum, substituam insignem contumaciam. Neque haec tollet Elogium quod Ebr. 11. ipsi tribuit gentium Apostolus. siquidem in isto catalogo etiam alii recensentur, quorum insignes sacra historia prodidit lapsus. Sed & illud addam, non tam spectandam hic virginitatem, quam secessum virginis & separationem ab omnibus mundanis ministeriis. Ut virginitas intervenerit q. ex accidenti. Si enim fuisset masculus, non opus fuisset virginitatis conservatione; Maritus enim non ministrat uxori, nec subjectus ei est, unde Samuel licet Deo conseceratus, non tamen abstinuit à conjugio. Foemina autem Deo devota si implicuisset se matrimonii nexibus, etiam coacta fuisset servire marito, atque eum quocunque vellet, sequi.
units.tr: If anyone wants the Hebrew: וְהָיָה הַיּוֹצֵא אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא מִדְּלָתַי בֵּיתִי — וְהָיָה לַיהוָה וְהַעֲלִיתִיהוּ עוֹלָה. Our translator, first, seems to restrict to a man alone what was said generally, so that it could also take in animals. Second, he has compressed a two-part vow into one part. I say the vow has two parts, and so Kimchi the father and son, and also Junius, have rendered Vau by the disjunctive particle aut: it shall be for the LORD, that is, consecrated, or I will offer it in a holocaust, if it proved fit for sacrifice. For sacrifice to God was permitted only from five kinds: namely oxen, sheep, goats, turtledove and pigeon, since human sacrifice [Αὐθεωπηυτίας] was always abhorred by the God who loves life and loves mankind [ὁ φιλόψυχος ἢ φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς]. But this exchange of the conjunction for a disjunctive, though frequent elsewhere (for example whoever curses father and mother, Exod. 21.17, which is expressed in Matt. 15.4 by ὁ μητέρα), seems here to be out of keeping with the Lord's Fisher, and it would be just as if someone said either an animal or a man, when a thing can be both an animal and a man. Indeed, if it is a man, it must also be an animal. So something could be consecrated to God and at the same time offered in a holocaust, and whatever was offered in a holocaust was thereby consecrated to God. They therefore suppose that the difference between these two members is this: the first promises the consecration of whatever living thing first meets him, simply, even a dog or an ass. For it could have been redeemed according to the prescription of the Law, Lev. 27.11; the second, however, carries the tacit condition that the animal be fit for sacrifice. The view of those who contend for the sacrifice of the daughter seems not slightly confirmed by this passage of the Latin version and by the last verse. Indeed, the defence of this human sacrifice has been sought from this version too. For the passage reads thus: Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead… and passing over to the sons of Ammon, he vowed a vow to the LORD, as if all these things joined by the translator had proceeded from the same Spirit. In the Hebrew text the narrative of the vow begins a new sentence, as Cajetan also noted. I think, therefore, that she was not sacrificed but consecrated to God and handed over in perpetuity, as in a kind of Nazariteship and seclusion, and remained unmarried, lest she seem to belong to anyone other than the Lord. Hence in verse 38 he mourned not that her life was to be lost but that her virginity was to be kept, for a barren virginity was a reproach (Isa. 4). Hence the story tells in the last verse that the daughters of Israel went each year to talk with her, and in this way the weariness of a solitary life was relieved. But, they say, there was no law about keeping virginity, and no example of such a vow exists. Indeed everything seems to run against and condemn such a vow. I reply that we do not defend this man's rashness but strongly condemn it, being joined with a remarkable ignorance of divine law. Indeed there was a twofold rashness: rashness in vowing and rashness in carrying it out. As for ignorance, he could have read in Lev. 27 last verse: If it is a woman who has been devoted or dedicated to the LORD, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels. The rashness in carrying it out was great and stupid, because for the whole of those two months he did not consult a priest or Levite. Or, if you like, if he consulted the priests, or was warned by them, I would name his obstinacy remarkable. Nor does this take away the commendation that the Apostle gives him among the gentiles in Heb. 11, since that catalogue also lists others whose notable lapses sacred history has recorded. But I will add this as well: the point here is not so much the virginity as the withdrawal of the virgin and her separation from all worldly ministries. Virginity came in only by accident. For if he had been a male, there would have been no need to keep virginity; a husband does not minister to his wife, nor is he subject to her, whence Samuel, though consecrated to God, nevertheless did not abstain from marriage. But if a woman devoted to God had entangled herself in the bonds of marriage, she would also have been compelled to serve her husband and to follow him wherever he wished.

units.la: verf. ultimo.
units.tr: last verse.

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. תְּלִנֶּנָּה לְתַנּוֹת לְבַת יִפְתָּח | Conveniant & plangant filiam Jephthæ
units.tr: Hebrew: לִתְנוֹת לְבַת יִפְתָּח (tilloneh lethanot livat Yiphtach) | Vulgate: "Let them assemble and lament the daughter of Jephthah."

units.la: Hæc interpretatio præcipuum stabilimentum fuit vulgatæ sententiæ. Carthusianus, Hoc non fecissent nisi fuisset occisa. Illam vero interpretationem Vulgatus debet τοῖς Lxx. qui vertunt θρηνεῖν. Chald. quoque habet לְאַלָּאוֹת ad lugendum. Sed nunquid id fieri potuit eâ adhuc superstite? An ideò sequetur eam à Patre fuisse immolatam? An maritum jam nacta erat?
units.tr: This interpretation was the chief prop of the Vulgate view. The Carthusian: "They would not have done this unless she had been put to death." Indeed the Vulgate owes that interpretation to the Seventy, who render it "to lament" [θρηνεῖν]. The Chaldee paraphrast also has "to mourn" [לְאַלָּאוֹת], for lamenting. But could this have happened while she was still alive? Does it follow from this that she was sacrificed by her father? Or had she by then already gained a husband?

units.la: Cur non licebit dicere eas restaurasse planctum virginitatis anniversaria hac coitione? Si luxêre mortuam, quid opus erat itione, seu, ut vulgatus, coitione in unum. Sed secabo hunc nodum, atque ajo hanc interpretionem niti falsa hypothesi, hac vid. לְתַנּוֹת esse themate תָּנָה unde תַּנִּין draco, cui in Script. tribuitur vox flebilis, Mich. 1. faciam planctum כְּתַנִּים sicut dracones. Quò respicit Job, cap. 30. frater factus sum לְתַנִּים. Dicitur autem תַּנִּים pro תַּנִּינִים & תַּנּוֹת fœm. Mal. 1. At לְתַנּוֹת non potest esse gerundium ex duplicantibus. Imò necessario quiescentibus Lamed He adscribi debet. Est enim gerund. Piel, ut לְנַלּוֹת / Thema itaque erit תָּנָה / vox magis Chaldæa quam Ebræa. Et tamen ex textu Ebræo poterit ejus significatio investigari. Jud. 5. 11. Ibi יִתְנּוּ justitias Domini. Vulg. narrentur. Melius, narrent. Hic certe plangendi notio non quadrat. Atque hic manifeste apparet, cujus ordinis sit, nec enim potest futurum esse ullius ordinis, præterquam quiescentium Lamed ה / ut יִנָּלּוּ / Præterea, si significaret plangere, construi debuisset cum על aut saltem cum את / quæ particula את subauditur quidem in loco Judicum, sed quo plangendi significatio omnino tolerari non potest. Sic ergo expono locum, ad alloquendum filiam Jephthæ, cum Pagn. Ariâ. Id est ad consolandum. Nam & Latini usurpant alloqui pro solari & alloquium pro consolatione. Ebræi dicunt loqui ad cor, unde in glossa לְדַבֵּר עַל לֵבָּהּ וּלְנַחֲמָהּ ad loquendum ad cor ejus & ad consolandum eam. Kimchi in comment. לְהַשִּׂיחָהּ ad confabulandum cum eâ, quod secutus est Jun. Tig. ad differendum cum eâ. Sensus idem. Finis enim confabulationis est solari. Quid si & hoc modo, ad narrandum vel ut narrarent filiæ Jephthæ sc. res lætas, novas, quò sic levarent solitudinis tædium. Certe Jud. 5. non potest nisi lætam confabulationem denotare.
units.tr: Why may we not say that they renewed the lamentation for her virginity by this annual coming together? If they mourned her as dead, what need was there for a going, or, as the Vulgate has it, a coming together into one? But I will cut this knot and say that this interpretation rests on a false hypothesis: that לְתַנּוֹת comes from the root תָּנָה, whence תַּנִּין, a dragon, to which Scripture ascribes a plaintive cry, Mic. 1: I will make lamentation (כְּתַנִּים) like the dragons. Job 30 alludes to this too: I am become a brother (לְתַנִּים) to dragons. The plural תַּנִּים is used for תַּנִּינִים, and the feminine תַּנּוֹת occurs in Mal. 1. But לְתַנּוֹת cannot be a gerund from doubled verbs; rather, it must necessarily be ascribed to verbs with a quiescent Lamed He. For it is the gerund of the Piel, as לְנַלּוֹת. The root will therefore be תָּנָה, a word more Chaldean than Hebrew. Yet its meaning can be investigated from the Hebrew text. Judg. 5.11: There (יִתְנּוּ) they shall recount the righteous acts of the LORD. The Vulgate has narrentur; better, narrent. Here the notion of lamenting certainly does not fit. And here it is clear what class the verb belongs to, for the future cannot belong to any class other than the verbs with quiescent Lamed He, as יִנָּלּוּ. Moreover, if it meant to lament, it ought to be construed with על or at least with את; and although the particle את is indeed understood in the passage of Judges, the meaning of lamenting cannot be admitted there at all. So I explain the passage thus: to speak to the daughter of Jephthah, with Pagninus and Arias. That is, to console her. For the Latins too use alloqui for to console and alloquium for consolation. The Hebrews say to speak to the heart, whence in a gloss: לְדַבֵּר עַל לֵבָּהּ וּלְנַחֲמָהּ, to speak to her heart and to console her. Kimchi in his commentary has לְהַשִּׂיחָהּ, to converse with her, which Junius followed with Tigurinus, to put off with her. The sense is the same, for the purpose of conversation is to console. What if also, in this way, it means to tell, or that they might tell the daughter of Jephthah happy and new things, so that they might thus relieve the weariness of her solitude? Certainly in Judg. 5 it can denote only a cheerful conversation.

units.la: LIBER I. SAMVELIS.
units.tr: THE FIRST BOOK OF SAMUEL.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: INipsocapitis limine habes canticumHannæ.Illi non facem alluxit,sed tenebras offudit Augustinus libro de Civit. Dei 17. cap.4. ubi invenies prolixum in hanc religiosæ Matronæ odam commentarium. Non est mihi prolubium omnia examinare. Gustum dabo. Is ergo dum recitat Canticum, Græcæ versionis filum secutus, non solum ab Ebræa, sed & à vulgata Latina immane quantum discrepat. Exempli gratia,
units.tr: At the very threshold of the chapter you have Hannah's song. Augustine did not kindle a light for her; he poured darkness over it (City of God, book 17, chapter 4), where you will find a lengthy commentary on this godly matron's ode. I have no inclination to examine everything. I will give you a taste. Reciting the canticle, he follows the thread of the Greek version, and differs enormously not only from the Hebrew but also from the Latin Vulgate. For example:

units.la: August. ex Græco.
units.tr: Augustine, from the Greek.

units.la: Dans votum voventi, & benedixit annos justi, quoniam non in virtute potens est vir. Dominus infirmum faciet adversarium suum, Dominus sanctus.
units.tr: Give vows to the one who vows, and he blessed the years of the righteous, because a man is not mighty by strength. The Lord will make his adversary weak; the Lord is holy.

units.la: Vulgata.
units.tr: The Vulgate.

units.la: Domini enim sunt cardines terræ & posuit super eos orbem. Pedes sanctorum suorum servabit, & impii in tenebris conticescent: quia non in fortitudine sua roborabitur vir.
units.tr: For the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, and he has set the world upon them. He will keep the feet of his saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness, because a man shall not be strengthened by his own strength.

units.la: Istis vero hæc ex Lxx. subjicit Augustinus, Non gloritur prudens in prudentia sua, & non glorietur potens in potentia sua: & non glorietur dives in divitiis suis, sed in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, * intelligere & scire Dominum, & facere judicium & justitiam in medio terra. Horum nec volam nec vestigium in Ebraeo invenies. Sed in Græcam versionem infarta sunt ex Jeremiæ cap. 1 x. ubi tamen postrema aliter leguntur, vid. non ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ αὐτοῦ ἡ γινώσκειν Dominum, τὸν κύριον, ἡ ποιῶν ἔλεος καὶ κρίμα καὶ δικαιοσύνην ἐν μέσῳ τῆς γῆς. Sed hoc modo, ἐν τῷ καυχᾶσθω ὁ καυχώμενος, συνιέναι ἡ γινώσκειν ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι κύριος, ὁ ποιῶν ἔλεος ἡ κρίμα, ἡ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς id est in hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, quod intelligat & cognoscat me esse Dominum, qui facio misericordiam & judicium & justitiam in terra. Nota, in terra, non, in medio terra. Nota, me esse Dominum qui facio. Non vero, quod intelligit & novit Dommum & facit. Nunc ergo judica de hoc commentario Augustigustini, Quid est, facere judicium, &c. in medio terra? Neque enim non debent facere judicium qui habitant in extremis terra. Quis hoc dixerit? Cur ergo additum est, in medio terræ? Quod & tantummodo diceret, facere judicium & justitiam, magis hoc præceptum ad utrosque pertineret, & mediterraneos & maritimos. Sed nequiquam putaret, post finem vitæ, quæ in hoc agitur corpore, superesse tempus judicium & justitiam faciendi, quam cum esset in carne non fecit, & sic divinum posse evadi judicium, in medio terra mihi videtur dictum, cum quisque vivit corpore. In hac quippe vita suam terram quisque circumfert, quam moriente homine recipit terra communis, resurgenti utique reddituræ. Proinde in medio terræ id est cum anima nostra isto terreno clauditur corpore, faciendum est judicium & justitia. Hactenus verba Augustini. Qui & in sequentibus locum illum Psal. 74. Deus operatus est salutem in medio terræ, interpretatur de Christo, qui, dum in terreno habitavit corpore, salutem nostram operatus est. Ad quam locum plura, σωύ Θεὸς παλάμας, dicemus suo loco.
units.tr: To these words Augustine adds the following from the Seventy: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows the Lord, and does judgment and justice in the midst of the earth. You will find neither a trace nor a footprint of these words in the Hebrew. They have been stitched into the Greek version from Jeremiah chapter 9, though there the last words read differently: ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ αὐτοῦ [in his wisdom] ... ἡ γινώσκειν τὸν κύριον [or to know the Lord], ποιῶν ἔλεος καὶ κρίμα καὶ δικαιοσύνην ἐν μέσῳ τῆς γῆς [doing mercy and judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth]. But the passage runs thus: ἐν τῷ καυχᾶσθω ὁ καυχώμενος, συνιέναι ἡ γινώσκειν ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι κύριος, ὁ ποιῶν ἔλεος ἡ κρίμα, ἡ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows that I am the Lord, who do mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth], that is, let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me to be the Lord who do mercy and judgment and justice in the earth. Note: in the earth, not in the midst of the earth. Note: that I am the Lord who do, not that he understands and knows the Lord and does. Now judge Augustine's commentary: What is it to do judgment and so on in the midst of the earth? For surely those who dwell at the ends of the earth ought not to do judgment? Who would say so? Why then has in the midst of the earth been added? If he had said only to do judgment and justice, the command would apply more to both, to the inland and the maritime peoples. But he thought in vain that after the end of this life, which is lived in the body, there remains time to do judgment and justice, which a man did not do while he was in the flesh, and thus might escape divine judgment. It seems to me that in the midst of the earth is said of the time when each person lives in the body. For in this life each carries about his own earth, which the common earth receives when the man dies, to return it at the resurrection. Therefore judgment and justice must be done in the midst of the earth, that is, while our soul is enclosed in this earthly body. So far Augustine's words. In what follows he also interprets that passage of Psalm 74, God has worked salvation in the midst of the earth, as referring to Christ, who, while he dwelt in an earthly body, worked our salvation. We shall say more on that passage in its place, God's hands.

units.la: Ad vers. 36. ejusdem notæ commentarium habet, eodem libro, cap. 1. Non lubet ea huc transcribere. immane quoque ab Ebr. veritatis tramite hic exorbitavit vulgatus, sicuti in Censura nostra prolixe ostendimus.
units.tr: On verse 36 he has a commentary of the same kind in the same book, chapter 1. I do not wish to transcribe it here. The Vulgate has also strayed enormously here from the path of Hebrew truth, as we have shown at length in our Censure.

units.la: CAP. VIII. vers. 12.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII, verse 12.

units.la: Hoc est jus regis] Ita vulg. Lxx. τὸ δικαίωμα τ βασιλέως. Belg. het recht des Coninc. Valde hic sudarunt Interpretes, qua prisci, qua novi. Quid enim? an ad jus regis pertinebit adimere possessoribus vineas, agros, &c? Quid ergo peccavit Achab? Distinguunt vulgo inter jus Regis in necessitate & extra necessitatem constituti. Prædicti omnia, inquit Carthus. possunt in necessitate ad jus regis pertinere, quia in tali casu sunt regis seu principis, ad utendum & disponendum de iis secundum exigentiam boni communis. At si extra necessitatis articulum modo prætacto bonis ac sobole subditorum utatur, puta ad proprium commodum, tyrannicum est. Postea docet aliam esse dominationem naturalem & ordinatam, aliam innaturalem & inordinatam, aliam denique intermediam, &c. Vide & Lyram. Tu disce tiro, in fonte esse vocem מְשִׁפַּט quæ
units.tr: This is the right of the king] So the Vulgate; the Seventy: τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ βασιλέως [the right of the king]. The Dutch (Belgic) version: "the right of the king." The interpreters, both ancient and modern, have sweated hard over this, for what? Does it belong to the right of a king to strip owners of their vineyards, fields, and so on? What then was Ahab's sin? Commonly they distinguish between the right of a king in necessity and outside necessity. The Carthusian says: all these things can, in necessity, belong to the right of the king, because in such a case they belong to the king or prince, to use and dispose of them according to the demands of the common good. But if outside the case of necessity he uses the goods and children of his subjects in the way just described, for example for his own advantage, it is tyrannical. He then teaches that there is one dominion that is natural and ordained, another unnatural and disordered, and finally another intermediate, and so on. See also Lyra. You, novice, learn that in the source there is the word mishpat [מִשְׁפַּט], which

units.la: a. Histor. Multa necessitate armorum excusantur, facit. quæ etiam consuetudinem quamlibet significat, non solum bonam & laudabilem, sed etiam malam & detestabilem. Fidem facit vel unicus ille locus hujus libri, cap. 2. v. 13. וּמִשְׁפַּט הַכֹּהֲנִים אֶת־הָעָם quæ verba vulgatus junxit cum præcedentibus, nescientes Dominum, neque officium sacerdotum cum populo, scil. scientes. Sed non tantum Chaldæus paraphrastes, sed & Græci verba ista sic acceperunt, tanquam novam sententiam incoantia, Et hoc erat jus sacerdotum, &c. jus id est consuetudo, ita amabant cum hominibus agere. Quis enim sibi persuaderi patierur, eos, quid officii sui esset, ignorasse? Sed Serarium audiamus, Verius tamen est, inquit, jus illud pravum esse & falsum. Hic tamen dupliciter proponitur, ut prædictio & descriptio, non ut ejus approbatio sit. Prædictio quippe ejus quod eventurum erat; Et sic juris nomen pro dispositione seu sorte accipitur. Descriptio vero ejus, quod apud Reges Ethnicos fieri soleret, & sic jus significat morem vel consuetudinem, quod Hebr. nomini frequens est, ut infra cap. 27. 11. Ex. 21. 9. & 26. 30. Num. 9. 14. Et 29. 6. Hæc Serarius. Quibus addo hæc loca, Gen. 40. 13. Jos. 6. 15. Ps. 81. 5. & 119. 132. Kohelcth 8. 5. 1. Reg. 18. 28. 2. Reg. 17. 33. & 34. Recte ergo Junius Pisc. & Angli reddidere, Hæc erit ratio regis. Deodatus, Questa sara lamaniera che terrà il re. Genev. Ce sera ici le traittement que rois sera le roi. Omnes describunt jus, quod usurpatum vulgo vocitant. Claudam verbis Hugonis Grotii, viii sui nominis, Quod vero apud Samuelem est de jure regis, omnino recte inspicienti apparet, nec de jure vero intelligendum, id est, de facultate honeste & juste aliquid agendi (longe enim alia vivendi ratio præscribitur Regi in ea parte legis, quæ est de officio regis. Deut. 17. 14.) neque nudum factum: nihil enim esse in eo eximium, cum injurias facere etiam privati privatis soleant: sed fasłum, quod, effectum aliquem juris habeat, id est non resistendi obligationem. lib. 1. de jure belli & pacis, cap. 4. pag. 97.
units.tr: a. History: "Many things are excused by the necessity of arms," it makes; it also signifies any custom whatever, not only a good and praiseworthy one but also a bad and detestable one. The one passage of this book, chapter 2, verse 13, proves it: mishpat ha-kohanim et ha-am [וּמִשְׁפַּט הַכֹּהֲנִים אֶת־הָעָם], which the Vulgate joined to what precedes: not knowing the Lord, nor the office of the priests with the people, namely knowing. But not only the Chaldee paraphrast, but also the Greeks, took these words as introducing a new sentence: And this was the right of the priests, etc.; right, that is, custom: so they liked to deal with men. For who would allow himself to be persuaded that they were ignorant of what their office required? But let us hear Serarius: Yet it is truer, he says, that this right was wicked and false. Here, however, it is set forth in two ways, as prediction and as description, not as approval of it. As prediction, of what was going to happen; and thus the word right is taken for disposition or lot. As description, of what was customary among the heathen kings; and thus right means manner or custom, which is a frequent use of the Hebrew word, as below in chapter 27, verse 11; Exodus 21:9; 26:30; Numbers 9:14; and 29:6. So Serarius. To these I add the passages Genesis 40:13; Joshua 6:15; Psalm 81:5; 119:132; Ecclesiastes 8:5; 1 Kings 18:28; 2 Kings 17:33 and 34. Rightly, then, Junius, Piscator and the English rendered it: This will be the manner of the king. Diodati (Italian): This will be the manner the king will keep. The Geneva (French): This shall be the treatment the king will give. All describe the right which is commonly so called. I will close with the words of Hugo Grotius, in his own name: What is said in Samuel about the right of the king, anyone who looks at it carefully will see that it is not to be understood as a true right, that is, as a power to act honourably and justly (for a quite different way of living is prescribed for the king in that part of the law which concerns the office of the king, Deut. 17:14), nor as a bare fact: for there is nothing remarkable in that, since even private persons commonly do injuries to private persons; but as a fact that has some effect of right, that is, an obligation not to resist. Book 1 of On the Law of War and Peace, chapter 4, page 97.

units.la: CAP. IX. verf. 2.
units.tr: CHAP. IX, vers. 2.

units.la: Erat ei filius vocabulo Saul, electus & bonus. Et non erat vir de filiis Israel melior illo. ] Ita Vulg. Lxx. ἐυμεχέτης καὶ ἀγαθός, ἢ ἐκ ἦν ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς ὑπὲρ αὐτόν. Discrepant in priori epithoto. Cætera conspirant. Ex voce electus posset quis dicere cere inquit Carthusianus, Si electus, ergo & praedestinatus. Sed electus in scriptura frequentèr aliter quam pro praedestinato sumitur, ut Psal, 104. Et Psal. 77. Electos Israel non impedivit, Fuit ergo electus id est elegans, magna praerogativa in naturalibus & * bonus moraliter. Et paulo post, Per hac verba videtur specialiter innui pracipua ejus excellentia in omni virtute, seu magna valde virtuositas ejus, propter quam nemo in populo Israel fuit dignior eo ad regnum. Itane Carthusiane? Ergone ipsum quoque Samuelem virtute supergressus est? Nos scimus Ebraeum בחור quod Vulgatus electum transtulit, passim juvenem notare, atque ita alibi non semel a vulgario interprete redditum. Scimus Ebraeum טוב pro-prie quidem & καλὸς significare bonum, at passim quoque pro pulcro poni. Ex.gr. Gen. 6, 1. Et viderunt filii Dei filias hominum, בני טובות / Vulg. quod essent pulcra. Augusti. de Civit Dei, 14. 23. consuetudo Scriptura est, etiam speciosos corpore bonos vocare. Contra רע malus passim pro deformi usitatur, Gen. 41. vacca רעות id est deformes, macilentae. Jonathan, שפיר / pulcer. Kimchi, טוב בתאר ובמראה id est pulcer forma. & aspectu. Cajet. Dictio Ebraea licet bonitatem significet, tamen pro pulcritudine ponitur. Unde crediderim sensum literalem esse, & non erat pulcrior illo. Ita & Serar. in comm. Vatab. procop.
units.tr: "There was a son of his named Saul, chosen and good, and there was not a man among the sons of Israel better than he." So the Vulgate. The Seventy have "eklektos kai agathos" [ἐκλεκτὸς καὶ ἀγαθός], "and there was not a good man above him" [οὐκ ἦν ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς ὑπὲρ αὐτόν]. They differ in the first epithet; the rest agrees. From the word "chosen" one could say, as the Carthusian does: "If chosen, then also predestined." But in Scripture "chosen" is often used in a sense other than predestined, as in Psalm 104 and Psalm 77, "He did not reject the chosen of Israel." So it means "choice," that is, excellent, with great advantages in natural gifts and morally good. A little later he adds: "By these words there seems to be specially implied his outstanding excellence in every virtue, or his great moral worth, on account of which no one in the people of Israel was more worthy than he for the kingdom." Is that so, Carthusian? Did he then surpass Samuel himself in virtue? We know that the Hebrew bachur [בחור], which the Vulgate rendered "chosen," generally means young man, and the Vulgate translator has rendered it so elsewhere more than once. We know that the Hebrew tov [טוב] properly means good, and that the Greek kalos [καλὸς] likewise means good, but it is also commonly used for beautiful. For example, Genesis 6:1, "And the sons of God saw the daughters of men," Hebrew benei tovot, Vulgate "that they were beautiful." Augustine, On the City of God 14.23: "It is the custom of Scripture to call even bodily beautiful people good." On the other hand, the Hebrew ra [רע], bad, is commonly used of what is ugly, as in Genesis 41, where the cows are ra'ot [רעות], that is, ugly and gaunt. Jonathan (the Chaldee paraphrast) has shapir [שפיר], handsome. Kimchi has tov be-to'ar uve-mar'eh [טוב בתאר ובמראה], that is, handsome in form and appearance. Cajetan: "Although the Hebrew word signifies goodness, it is nevertheless used for beauty. Hence I would believe the literal sense to be: and there was no one more handsome than he." So also Serarius in his commentary, and Vatablus, and Procopius.

units.la: CAP. XVIII. vers. 10.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII. verse 10.

units.la: Et prophetabat Saul in medio domus suae ] In decreto Gratiani, parte 2. cauf. 1. Quaest. 1. §. prophetavit, probandae isti conclusioni, Sacerdotem malum etiam posse conficere corpus Christi, inter alia allegantur & illa ex tractatu Augustini in Epistolam Johannis, Prophetavit Saul Rex malus cum etiam S. David persequeretur. Non ergo se jactent, qui forte sine caritate habent sanctum munus Dei, sed videant qualem rationem habituri sint cum Deo, quod sancte utuntur. Sed disce, φιλόγλωσσε adolescens, prophetare hic nihil aliud esse & spiritu malo actum, sermones & gestus ita componere, ut sancti prophetae bono spiritu acti solebant. Hoc notarunt Lyra, Carthus. & ex vetustioribus Procopius. Ipsos quoque prophetas, quos facerille Spiritus afflaverat, profanum vulgus insanire credebat. Hinc Chald. reddit ואשתגע & insanivit. Kimchi, loquebatur verba insania. Serarius, prophephetare hic est furere, bacchari, arreptitio um more insanire, absur-da & loqui & agere. Certe tales passim describuntur à Poëtis Gen-tilium vates, unde prophetas Enthusiastas quoque dixere, ut ex Strabone, Plutarcho & Platone & aliis liquet. Talis describitur Æneidos 6. sacerdos illa, quam consulit Æneas, — eui talia fanti Ante fores subito non vultus, non color unus, Non comptæ mansere comæ, sed pectus anhelum. Et rabie fera corda tument, majorque videri, Nec mortale sonans, afflata est numine quando Iam propiore Dei.
units.tr: And Saul prophesied in the midst of his house. In the Decretum of Gratian, part 2, cause 1, question 1, §. prophetavit, to support the proposition that an evil priest can also consecrate the body of Christ, among other things they cite this passage from Augustine's tractate on the Epistle of John: King Saul prophesied while he was evil, even though he was persecuting holy David. Therefore let those not boast who perhaps have the holy gift of God without charity, but let them see what account they will have to give to God for using it holily. But learn, you chatterbox young man [φιλόγλωσσε], that to prophesy here means nothing other than to be driven by an evil spirit and to arrange words and gestures in the way the holy prophets used to do when moved by a good spirit. Lyra and the Carthusians have noted this, and among the older writers Procopius. People also believed that the prophets themselves, whom that Spirit had inspired, were raving madmen in the eyes of the common crowd. Hence the Chaldee paraphrast renders it [ואשתגע] "and he went mad." Kimchi: he spoke words of madness. Serarius: to prophesy here is to rage, to rave, to be mad in the manner of those seized by frenzy, both to speak and to act absurdly. Certainly the poets of the Gentiles describe such prophets everywhere, the seers and prophets of the heathen, whence they also called them enthusiasts, as is clear from Strabo, Plutarch, Plato and others. Such is the priestess in the sixth book of the Aeneid, whom Aeneas consults: — when she had spoken such things before the doors, suddenly her face and colour were not the same, her hair was not kept in order, but her breast heaved, and her heart swelled with savage frenzy, and she seemed greater, and when she was inspired by the nearer power of God she did not speak in a mortal voice.

units.la: Ecce Deum vocat Apollinem id est ipsum illum Spiritum, quo Saul incaluit, hoc ipso versu Spiritus S. appellat Spiritum malum Dei, & cap.16. v.14. vel 15. spiritum malum à DOMINO. Pergit Poëta paucis interjectis, At Phœbi nondum patiens immanis in antro Bacchatur vates, magnum si pectore possit Excussisse Deum, tanto magis ille fatigat. Os rabidum, fera corda domans.
units.tr: Behold, he calls the god Apollo, that is, that very Spirit by which Saul was inflamed. In this very verse the Holy Spirit calls it an evil spirit of God, and in chapter 16, verse 14 or 15, an evil spirit from the LORD. The poet goes on, after a few lines intervening: But the frenzied seer, not yet enduring the power of Phoebus, rages in the cave, if he might be able to shake the great god from his breast; so much the more the god wearies him, taming his raging mouth and fierce heart.

units.la: Et rursus, Talibus ex adyto dictis Cumæa Sibylla Horrendas canit ambages, antroque remugit, Ut primum cessit furor & rabida ora quierunt, &c.
units.tr: And again: When the Cumaean Sibyl had spoken such things from the sanctuary, she sang dreadful riddles and roared in the cave; as soon as the frenzy left her and her raving lips were quiet, etc.

units.la: CAP. XXI. vers. 13.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI. verse 13.

units.la: Καὶ ἠλλοίωσε τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῆς ἐναντίον αὐτῆς, καὶ συνπνιγήσεται ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ἡ ἐτυμπάνισεν τὰς βύθεις τῆς πόλεως, ἡ πα-ρεσφίξεν ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῆ, ἡ ἐπέπτεν ἐπὶ τοὺς βύθεις τῆς πόλεως, ἡ τὰ σίελα αὐτῆ καλέρρει ἐπὶ τὸν πώγωνα αὐτῆ. Hactenus Græca interpretatio. Quæ ab Ebræo textu immane quantum discrepat. Videamus singula membra.
units.tr: Καὶ ἠλλοίωσε τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῆς ἐναντίον αὐτῆς, καὶ συνπνιγήσεται ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ἡ ἐτυμπάνισεν τὰς βύθεις τῆς πόλεως, ἡ παρεσφίξεν ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῆ, ἡ ἐπέπτεν ἐπὶ τοὺς βύθεις τῆς πόλεως, ἡ τὰ σίελα αὐτῆ καλέρρει ἐπὶ τὸν πώγωνα αὐτῆ. [And he changed her face before her, and she shall be choked in that day, she who beat her breasts over the city, who clapped her hands together, who fell upon the breasts of the city, and who let her spittle run down upon her beard.] So far the Greek version. It differs enormously from the Hebrew text. Let us look at the individual members.

units.la: Τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῆς ] Ebr. פניה / Vulg. os suum. Vox Ebr. proprie gustum seu saporem significat. Inde transfertur ad totius corporis habitum in sermone, gestu, forma. Ad animum translata significat mentem, rationem, sensum. Unde Cajet. reddit, prudentiam, Junius speciem suam, Genev. son maintien. Deod. Egli si contaafece, Et in margine, mutiò la sua maniera.
units.tr: Your countenance [Τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῆς]: Hebrew [פניה], Vulgate os suum. The Hebrew word properly means taste or flavour. From this it is transferred to the whole bearing of the body in speech, gesture and appearance. Applied to the mind, it means intellect, reason, understanding. Hence Cajetan renders it prudence, Junius its appearance, the Geneva Bible demeanour (son maintien), and Diodati if she did so, with the marginal note changed her manner.

units.la: Καὶ ϑεραπεύσατο ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ.] Latina versio, & absimulavit in die illo. Hæc omnino redundant. Hic enim vel duæ versiones, vel versio & glossema coaluerunt. Quod insolens non est in hac versione. Cæterum illud ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ unde haustum sit, nescio.
units.tr: And he feigned madness on that day [Καὶ ϑεραπεύσατο ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ]. The Latin version: and he pretended on that day. These words are entirely superfluous. Here either two versions or a version and a gloss have merged, which is not unusual in this translation. Moreover, I do not know from where that phrase on that day was drawn.

units.la: Καὶ ἐπιμαρτύραζεν — πόλεως] Et hoc membrum in Ebraeo non extat. Est enim vel alterius interpretatio vel glossema membri penultimi transpositum. Latina versio, & tympano cecinit in portis urbis.
units.tr: And he beat with a drum at the gates of the city [Καὶ ἐπιμαρτύραζεν — πόλεως]. This clause is not present in the Hebrew either. It is either another translation or a gloss on the penultimate clause, transposed. The Latin version: and he sang with a drum at the gates of the city.

units.la: Καὶ παρεφέρετο ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτ̃ς.] Melius αὐλῶν. Certe in Ebraeo est, בידם in manibus eorum, Unde liquido apparet, illam lectionem ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν, in manibus suis, quam secutus Augustinus, neutiquam posse consistere. Latinus Interpres, Et praetervehebatur in manibus ejus. Alii, ferebatur manibus eorum, Nam fingebat se destitui pedibus inquiunt, ac manibus suis se sustentabat, aut portabatur manibus aliorum, instar hominis cui sanum sinciput non est. Vulg. collabebatur inter manus eorum. Quod omnes, quos ego vidi, Interpretes de lapsu corporis intellexere. Lyra, collabebatur sicut epilepticus. Vide & Carthus. Alii, sicut furiosus & ebrius, cujus pedes non faciunt officium. Omnem istam pugnam dirimit Originarius textus, ויהוללו בידם & insanum se fingebat in manibus eorum. Quis adeo in Ebraismo hospes est, ut ignoret הלל in significatione insaniendi passim esse obvium? Ecce tibi Ps. 5. 6. Ps. 75. 5. Job. 12. 17. Quis & illud nescit, in conjugatione Hithphael fictam actionem saepe repraesentari? Nullae ergo hic infantibus tenebrae. Kimchi fecit opera stultitia & insania coram illis, cum adhuc versaretur in manibus eorum, nam circumdederant eum. R. Sal. exponit per משתמר insanum se fingebat. Nec dissentiunt Cajetanus, Bened. Arias & Pagn. Sed an fortassis vulgatus Interpres fictum mentis lapsum intellexit? Ego ut hic ἐπίχω, ita plane nullus dubito, quin Graeci Interpp. suum illud παραφέρεται aliorsum acceperint atque eorum interpretes voluere. Siquidem παραφέρεται etiam dicuntur mente capti. Et παραφορὰ furor, insania, & παράφορος insanus, cujus mens a ratione aberrat, delirus, & παραφόρως, errabunda mente, insane. Vide Budaeum, Henr. Stephanum & alios. Atque ita Graecis cum Ebraeo pulcre conveniet. Καὶ ἐπῆλθεν ἐπὶ ταῖς θύρας τῆς πόλεως. ] Alii codices proprius ad Ebraeum textum accedentes, ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις τῆς πύλης id est & incidit in januae portae, non, urbis. Vulg. Et impingebat in ostia portae. Alia interpretatio, uti supra vidimus, ἐμπαιζῶν [?], q. d. cum toties & tanto cum impetu impegisse in ostia, ac tympanum aliquod pulsaret. Nugae. Ebraea vox יִפְתַּח [?] significat, delineare, scribere, signare, quod nec Lyra, nec Carthus. ignorarunt. Lyra, In Ebraeo habetur, & pingebat super ostia, faciendo sibi figuras quasdam, ut solent fatui. Chaldaeus וַיִּשְׂרְטוּ [?] & lineabat, R. Sal. scribebat. Consentiunt Cajet. Bened. Pagn. Arias. Nota tiro, esse Futurum Phiel ἐνέπαιζεν [?], pro וַיִּחְוֹר [?] / Thema enim est תְּוֹר [?] /
units.tr: And he was carried along in her hands [Καὶ παρεφέρετο ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτ̃ς]. Better, of the flutes [αὐλῶν]. Certainly the Hebrew has [בידם] in their hands, so it is clear that the reading [ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν], in their hands, which Augustine followed, cannot stand in any way. The Latin translator: and he was carried along in his hands. Others: he was carried in their hands, for they say he pretended to be lacking the use of his feet and supported himself with his own hands, or was carried in the hands of others, like a man whose head is not sound. The Vulgate: he slid down between their hands. All the interpreters whom I have seen understood this of a fall of the body. Lyra: he slid down like an epileptic. See also Carthusianus. Others: like a madman and a drunkard whose feet do not do their job. The original text settles the whole dispute: [ויהוללו בידם] and he feigned himself insane in their hands. Who is so much a stranger to Hebrew as not to know that [הלל] in the sense of to act like a madman is found everywhere? See Psalm 5:6, Psalm 75:5, Job 12:17. And who does not know that in the Hithpael conjugation a feigned action is often represented? So there is no darkness here for beginners. Kimchi: he did foolish and insane things before them, while he was still in their hands, for they had surrounded him. R. Salomo explains it by [משתמר], he feigned himself insane. Cajetan, Benedictus, Arias and Pagninus do not disagree. But perhaps the Vulgate translator understood a feigned loss of mind? I, as here I suspend judgement, so I doubt entirely that the Greek translators took their [παραφέρεται] in another direction, and that their interpreters chose to. For [παραφέρεται] is also said of those who are deprived of their senses; and [παραφορὰ] means fury or madness, [παράφορος] one whose mind wanders from reason, a madman, and [παραφόρως], with a wandering mind, madly. See Budaeus, Henry Estienne and others. And thus the Greek will agree beautifully with the Hebrew. [Καὶ ἐπῆλθεν ἐπὶ ταῖς θύρας τῆς πόλεως.] Other manuscripts, nearer to the Hebrew text, read [ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις τῆς πύλης], that is, and he fell upon the doors of the gate, not of the city. The Vulgate: he was beating against the doors of the gate. Another interpretation, as we saw above, [ἐμπαιζῶν] [?], as if to say that he had struck the doors so often and with such force, and was beating some drum. Trifles. The Hebrew word [יִפְתַּח] [?] means to draw lines, to write, to mark, which neither Lyra nor Carthusianus overlooked. Lyra: In the Hebrew it is, and he scratched upon the doors, making himself certain marks, as fools do. The Chaldee [וַיִּשְׂרְטוּ] [?]: and he scratched; R. Salomo: he wrote. Cajetan, Benedictus, Pagninus and Arias agree. Note, beginner, that the future form in Piel is [ἐνέπαιζεν] [?] for [וַיִּחְוֹר] [?]; the root is [תְּוֹר] [?].

units.la: Haec prolixius ad tironum captum explicui, ut appareret, quam contorta sit illa Augustini Allegoria, quae extat in comm. ejus ad Ps: 33. Ebr. 34. Cujus titulus iste est Graeco, ὅπ᾽ ἀλλάσσει τὸ ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ἑαυτὸν ἀβιμέλεχ ἢ ἀπὸ λυπῶν αὐτὸν ἢ ἀπώλεια. Sed antequam Allegoriam istam proponam monendus mihi tiro est, Abimelech nomen regum Palaestinae commune fuisse. Kimchi, aut duo nomina habuit (vid. Achis & Abimelech) aut est nomen generale omnium regum Palaestina. Siquidem invenitur & temporibus Abraham & temporibus Isaac. Basilius, τιῶτερον λόγον πρὸς φθίζαντας ... [illegible, ~10 letters] βασιλεὺς ... ἀλλοφύλων κοινὸν μὲν εἶχον ὄνομα, τὸ Ἀβιμέλεχ ἴδιόν ... ὁ σεσημειωμένος. Ita Pharao commune nomen regum Aegypti fuisse, nemo tam rudis qui nesciat. Ex prisci s Theologis Graecis nonnulli fuere qui pro Ἀβιμελεχ legere Ἀχιμελεχ. Unde haec coram Achimelech sacerdote gesta arbitrantur, I. Sam. 21. Vide Theodoretum & Basil. Sed nunc Augustino aurium operam locate sultis. Primo non capit, quomodo hic vocetur Abimelech, qui 1. Samuelis 21. Achis vocatur. Recurrit ergo ad Allegoriam, cui postquam multa propylaea praestruxisset, sic tandem infit, Non ergo nihil significat & quod nomen mutatum est, & quod hic dictum est, coram Abimelech, ibi, coram Achis dici. Non defuerunt docti viri, qui nobis nomina ex Ebraeo in Graecam linguam, & in Latinam transferrent. Consulentes ergo nomina ista invenimus, Abimelech interpretari, patris mei regnum (at hoc esset Abimalchuth vel Abimamlachah) & Achis interpretari, quomodo est. (at in qua lingua? Certe non inEbraea.) David, manu fortis Et hoc non capio.) Et multis interjectis, col. 230. C. Mutavit ergo vultum suum coram Abimelech. Quid est, coram Abimelech? Coram regno patrii. Quid est coram regno Patris? Coram Judaeis. Et dimisit cum & abiit. Quem dimisit? ipsum populum Judaeorum demisit & abiit. Quaeris modo Christum apud Judaeos & non invenis. Interpretamentum autem & Achis, quomodo est, refert ad Judaeos interrogantes Dominum in Euangelio, Quomodo poterit hic nobis dare manducare carnem suam? Haec Aug. concione prima. Piget caetera transcribere. Tu nota tiro, hanc allegoriam in eo quoque adversari literae, quod pronomen eum ad Regem Achis referat. Hic enim est sensus literalis, Et demisit Rex Achis Davidem & abiit David. Postea progreditur Augustinus, ipsam historiam 1. Samuelis 21. allegorice de Christo interpretaturus. Affectabat (ita enim vertit τὸ προσγοπᾶτ(ατο) id est affectum habebat. Quid est, affectum habere? Quia compassus est infirmitatibus nostris & ideo voluit ipsam carnem suscipere in qua mortem occideret. Et paulo post, Ergo affectabat, quia pervenit usque ad mortem crucis. Et quia qui crucifigitur, in ligno extenditur; ut autem tympanum fiat, caro id est corium in ligno extenditur, dictum est, & tympanizabat id est crucifigebatur, in ligno extendebatur. Et rursus aliquot verbis interjectis, quibus τὸ tympanizare ad ostia civitatis explicat de pulsatione cordium, Et ferebatur manibus suis. Hoc vero, fratres, quomodo fieri possit in homine quis intelligat? Quis enim portatur in manibus suis? Manibus aliorum potest portari homo, manibus suis nemo portatur. Quomodo intelligamus in David secundum literam, non invenimus: at in Christo invenimus. Ferebatur enim Christus in manibus suis, quando commendans ipsum corpus suum ait, Hoc est corpus meum. Ferebat enim illud corpus in manibus suis. Quae tamen concione 2. paulo aliter protulit, Quomodo ferebatur manibus suis? Quia cum commendaret ipsum corpus suum & sanguinem suum, accepit in manus suas quod norunt fideles, & ipse se portabat QUODAMMODO, cum diceret, Hoc est corpus meum. Vide Lector quantum detrimenti attulerit doctissimo Patri linguae Ebraeae ignorantia. Conferat haec vel puer elementa Ebraicam doctus cum sontibus & demirabitur ejusmodi allegoriam magno Augustino excidisse.
units.tr: I have explained these matters at greater length for the understanding of beginners, so that it may appear how twisted that allegory of Augustine is, which stands in his commentary on Psalm 33 (Hebrew 34). Its title is in Greek, [ὅπ᾽ ἀλλάσσει τὸ ... ἑαυτὸν ἀβιμέλεχ ἢ ἀπὸ λυπῶν αὐτὸν ἢ ἀπώλεια]. But before I set out that allegory, the beginner must be warned that Abimelech was a name common to the kings of Palestine. Kimchi: either he had two names (compare Achish and Abimelech) or it is a general name for all the kings of Palestine, since it is found both in the times of Abraham and in the times of Isaac. Basil: the Philistine kings had a common name, Abimelech, and a particular one... Just as Pharaoh was the common name of the kings of Egypt, no one is so ignorant as not to know. Among the older Greek theologians some read [Ἀχιμελεχ] for [Ἀβιμελεχ]. Hence they think these events happened before the priest Ahimelech, 1 Samuel 21. See Theodoret and Basil. But now you must lend your ears to Augustine. First, he cannot understand how here he is called Abimelech, when in 1 Samuel 21 he is called Achish. So he has recourse to an allegory, and after building many approaches to it he finally begins thus: Therefore it is not without meaning both that the name was changed and that here it is said before Abimelech, there before Achish. There were learned men who translated these names for us from Hebrew into Greek and into Latin. Consulting these names, we find that Abimelech is interpreted my father's kingdom (but that would be Abimalchuth or Abimamlachah), and Achish is interpreted how is it (but in what language? Certainly not in Hebrew), David, strong of hand. And this I do not understand. And after many intervening things, column 230 C: He therefore changed his countenance before Abimelech. What is before Abimelech? Before the kingdom of the father. What is before the kingdom of the Father? Before the Jews. And he sent him away and he departed. Whom did he send away? He sent away the people of the Jews and departed. You seek Christ now among the Jews and do not find him. The explanatory phrase how is it, however, refers to the Jews asking the Lord in the Gospel, How can this man give us his flesh to eat? These are Augustine's words from the first sermon. I am sorry to copy out the rest. Note, beginner, that this allegory also opposes the letter in this respect, that the pronoun him refers to King Achish. For the literal sense is this: And King Achish sent David away, and David departed. Afterwards Augustine proceeds to interpret the story of 1 Samuel 21 allegorically concerning Christ. He was affected (for so he translates [τὸ προσγοπᾶτ(ατο)], that is, he had the disposition. What does it mean, to have the disposition? Because he suffered with our infirmities and therefore wished to take on that very flesh in which he would die. And a little after: Therefore he was affected, because he came even to the death of the cross. And because the one who is crucified is stretched on wood; but for a drum to be made, the flesh, that is the hide, is stretched on wood, and he drummed, that is, he was crucified, he was stretched on the wood. And again, after a few intervening words, in which he explains to drum at the gates of the city as the beating of hearts: And he was carried in his own hands. But how this can happen in a man, brothers, who understands? For who is carried in his own hands? A man can be carried in the hands of others, no one in his own hands. We do not find how this is to be understood literally in David, but we find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his own hands, when, commending his body, he said, This is my body. For he carried that body in his own hands. Yet in the second sermon he expressed this a little differently: How was he carried in his own hands? Because when he commended his own body and his own blood, he took into his hands what the faithful know, and he carried himself in a CERTAIN WAY, when he said, This is my body. Let the reader see how much harm the ignorance of the Hebrew language has done to that most learned Father. Let anyone who has learned Hebrew even as a boy compare these with the sources, and he will be amazed that such an allegory fell from the great Augustine.

units.la: David desperabat se posse evadere à facie Saulis ] Ita vulg. Ebr. ויהי דוד נחפו Et fuit David festinans abire à facie Saulis חפז extra omnem controversiam significat: festinare. Ebraei in fine Epistolarum, ubi nos saepe usurpamus voculam raptim, scribere amant בחפזי / in festinatione mea. Cajet. Non desperatio sed festinatio ad recedendum ut evaderet, describitur. Desperationem Ebraeum נואש exprimit. Stadium ergo plane imaginarium sibi fingunt Lyra & Carthusianus, quando anxie quaerunt, quomodo desperatio cadere potuerit in Davidem, qui per revelationem divinam certitudinaliter habebat, se post Saulem fore regem, annon ergo David dubius fuerit in fide? Ad hoc quidam respondent, inquit Carthus. quod non desperavit evasionem pro se, sed pro suis. Alii, quod non desperavit evasionem pro sua persona, quoniam certus erat de impletione divini promissi, sed desperavit se posse evadere absque bello cum Saule. Postquam autem has responsiones rejecisset Carthus. ostendisset quoque ex aliis locis, Davidem pro se quoque metuisse, er. gr. 1. Sam. 27. 1. & 20. hanc tandem probare videtur responsionem, Davidem desperasse se posse evadere secundum ordinem & processum proximarum & naturalium causarum seu propriis viribus. En exuoμαχίαν. Aliter nodum istum solvit Burgensis, Translatio nostra, inquit, hic multum deviat ab Ebr. veritate. Ibi enim non fit mentio de desperatione. Sed in Ebr. habetur, David festinabat, &c. Quid ad haec Carthus. Malesonat, inquit, asserere, quod translatio nostra deviet ab Ebr. veritate. Sic enim deviaret à veritate, & falsa esset. Concedimus totum. Sed quid tandem respondet Carthusianus? Idcirco tenendum est, quod sermo ille Hebraicum FORSAN sit ad utrumque horum aequivocus. Sed quid si forte non sit aequivocus? Quid si nunquam desperationis notionem habeat? Quod in tam ardua quaestione tenendum est, firmiore tibicine sustentandum erat.
units.tr: David despaired of being able to escape from the face of Saul] So the Vulgate. The Hebrew is וַיְהִי דָוִד נֶחְפָּז, "And David was hurrying to go away from the face of Saul." The word חפז (chafaz) clearly means "to hurry." At the end of their letters, where we often use the little word "hastily," the Hebrews like to write בְּחָפְזִי, "in my haste." Cajetan: "What is described is not despair but haste in withdrawing, so that he might escape." The Hebrew נוֹאַשׁ expresses despair. Lyra and the Carthusian therefore invent a purely imaginary difficulty when they anxiously ask how despair could have fallen upon David, who by divine revelation had the certain assurance that he would be king after Saul. Was David then doubtful in faith? To this some reply, as the Carthusian says, that he did not despair of escape for himself but for his people. Others say that he did not despair of escape for his own person, since he was certain of the fulfilment of God's promise, but that he despaired of being able to escape without war with Saul. The Carthusian, after rejecting these replies and showing from other passages that David also feared for himself, for example at 1 Sam. 27.1 and 20, seems at last to accept this answer: that David despaired of being able to escape according to the order and course of the nearest natural causes, that is, by his own strength. Here is a fight with a shadow. Burgensis solves the knot in another way: "Our translation," he says, "departs greatly here from the Hebrew truth. For there is no mention of despair there. But in the Hebrew it reads, David was hurrying, etc." What does the Carthusian say to this? "It is ill-sounding," he says, "to assert that our translation departs from the Hebrew truth. For in that case it would depart from the truth and be false." We grant the whole of it. But what in the end does the Carthusian answer? "Therefore it must be held that this Hebrew expression is perhaps ambiguous between both of these senses." But what if perhaps it is not ambiguous? What if it never has the notion of despair at all? In so difficult a question, what ought to be held must be supported by a firmer prop.

units.la: THeologi Protestantes, nominatim Hunnius, in loco de Ecclesia, adversus Pontificios ostensuri, tantum abesse ut Ecclesia N. T. uni certo loco affixa sit, ut ne quidem tabernaculum & arca fœderis in uno loco semper fuerit, stationes ejus varias recensent. Namque inter alia loca, ubi substiterit, etiam Gibeam memorant, decepti interpretatione vulgati Interpretis & Germanica Lutheri. At ego arcam fœderis in urbe Gibea unquam substitisse cum D. Tarnovio intrepide nego. Abinadab iste non habitabat in Gibea, civitate tribus Benjamin (Jud. 19. 16. 1. Sam. 22. 6.) sed in Kirjath Jearim 1. Sam. 6. 21. & 7. 1. vel 2. sitâ in tribu Juda, Jos. 15. 60. unde 2. Sam. 6. 2. appellatur Baale Juda. Unde ergo nata opinio de statione in Gibea? Ex ambiguo vocis גִּבְעָה 1. Sam. 7. 1. aliis 6. 22. Et 2. Sam. 6. vers. 3. 4. Licet enim vox ista alibi nomen urbis proprium sit, primario tamen collem significat. Unde & Lxx. ἐν τῇ βαλῷ. Sic & Chald. & Jun. Pisc. & alii. Illud autem אשר vel refertur ad domum, quæ domus erat in colle, vel ad ipsum Abinadab, qui habitabat in colle. Hæc descripsi ex exercit. Biblicis D. Joh. Tarnovi. Verbum addam ad hunc locum. vers. 2. vulg. & Lutherus מִקִּבְעַלִי יְהוּדָה ita reddiderunt, de viris Juda, dan den burgeren Juda. At ex collatione hujus loci cum 1. Chr. 13. 6. liquet Baale Juda nomen urbis esse, quæ ibidem alio nomine Kirjath Jearim appelatur. Ex hac collatione & illud liquet, מִבַּעֲלֵי יְהוּדָה idem esse quod בַּעֲלָתָה Baalam, Sic enim habent Ebrea 1. Chron. 13. 6. & ascendit David בַּעֲלָתָה אֶל קִרְיַת יְעָרִים ut potius sic vertendum fuerit Baalma Juda, ⁊ hoc loco motum ad locum denotante. Vide quæ supra ad Genef. 13. notavimus.
units.tr: Protestant theologians, Hunnius in particular, in their locus on the Church, wishing to show against the Papists that the Church of the New Testament is by no means fixed to one certain place, even that the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant were not always in one place, list its various stations. Among the other places where it stopped they also mention Gibeah, misled by the translation of the Vulgate interpreter and by Luther's German. But I firmly deny with D. Tarnovius that the ark of the covenant ever stood in the city of Gibeah. That Abinadab did not live in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin (Judg. 19:16; 1 Sam. 22:6), but in Kiriath-jearim (1 Sam. 6:21; 7:1 or 2), which lies in the tribe of Judah (Josh. 15:60), whence in 2 Sam. 6:2 it is called Baale Judah. Where then did the opinion about a station at Gibeah arise? From the ambiguity of the word גִּבְעָה (1 Sam. 7:1; by others 6:22, and 2 Sam. 6:3, 4). For although that word elsewhere is the proper name of a city, it primarily means a hill. Hence the Seventy also render it ἐν τῇ βαλῷ [in the hill], and so do the Chaldee, Junius, Piscator and others. The word אשר refers either to the house, which house was on the hill, or to Abinadab himself, who lived on the hill. I have taken these remarks from the Biblical Exercises of D. Johann Tarnovius. I will add a word on this passage. In verse 2 the Vulgate and Luther render מִקִּבְעַלִי יְהוּדָה as from the men of Judah, the German being von den Bürgern Juda, "of the citizens of Judah". But from comparing this passage with 1 Chron. 13:6 it is clear that Baale Judah is the name of a city, which in that place is called by another name, Kiriath-jearim. From this comparison it is also clear that מִבַּעֲלֵי יְהוּדָה is the same as בַּעֲלָתָה, Baalah. For so the Hebrew text has it in 1 Chron. 13:6, and David went up בַּעֲלָתָה אֶל קִרְיַת יְעָרִים, so that it would have been better to render it Baalah in Judah, taken here as denoting a place. See what I noted above on Genesis 13.
