units.la: וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים Genuiuam horum verborum mentem non difficile erit ex antecedentibus eruere. Valde amplificat David gratiosam illam Dei promissionem de perpetuando ejus regno. Demiratur Deum tam familiariter ei συγχαταCaiveᵴ & sermones miscere, ac si amicus cum amico ageret. Hoc parum visum est in conspectu tuo Domine, nisi loquereris etiam de domo servi tui in longinquum, וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים idque [secundum] consuetudinem hominis, vel hominum, DEVS Domine. Frequens est Ellipsis literæ Chaph in Ebraismo. Eam si hic admittas, & referas hæc verba ad τὸ loquereris, optime fluet sententia. In eandem sententiam Junius, idque ratione humana Domine Jehovi. und dasselbe [nach] der menschen weyse / O Herr GEKK. Astipulatur Scindlerus, qui huc quoque reducit Chaldæam, וְרָא חַיָּא לִבְנֵי אֱנָשָׁא & hoc [hic agendi modus] conveniens est filiis hominum, q. d. ita solet amicus cum amico colloqui & familiariter animi sui sententiam depromere. Atque ita explicari etiam potest versio Græca, ἀτ᾽ δὲ ὁ νόμος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κύριε μὴ κύριε. Genevenses, & Angli verba Ebraica pronuntiatione juvant quasi interrogatio esset, Est-ce ici la façon des hommes Seigneur Eternel? Angli, End is this the manner of man O Lord God? Atque hic imitati sunt R. Salomonem & R. Jesaiam. Quorum ille sic inquit ad hunc locum, בתם ידי ראוי להתבשר כן לבשר ודם id est cum admiratione [hoc dicit David, q. d.] an conveniens est, talia nuntiare carni & sanguini? Hic vero locum sic ᾧαφεῖζει. Est ne hæc conditio hominis ut inveniat gratiam in oculis tuis & tanti æstimetur? Novi me indignum esse hoc honore, &c. Examinemus nunc duas interpretationes. Vulgatus, ista est enim lex Adam. Quæro, quid sibi velit illud enim. Quo respiciat, cum quibus verbis cohæreat? Miror, cur τὸ הָאָדָם reddiderit, Adam, tanquam si primus humani generis pater denotaretur. Obtendet patronus articulum ה / quo nomen speciei אָדָם ad primum hominem restringi solet, ut cum dicimus ὁ πᾶς φύσις, ὁ λόγος, ὁ θεολόγος de uno inter Prophetas, Apostolos & Theologos principe. Sic τὸ ὄνομα הַשֵּׁם הַדָּבָר ὁ λόγος, verbum Dei. Ego ut hæc non inficior, (existimo enim & hic locum habere istud Galeni, [?]εἰωθασι οἱ ἄνθρωποι [?]τὰ πρωτεύοντα ἐν τῷ γένει τῷ τοῦ γένους ὀνόματι [?]προσαγορεύειν, id est Amant homines ea quae in genere aliquo primas tenent, generis nomenclatura exprimere.) ita vicissim illud quoque postulo, à nomine Adam, cum primi parentis nomen est, aliquando abesse articulum, Ex. gr. Gen. 4.1. & contra, cum nomen speciei est, praeire articulum. Atque hoc velim à tironibus semel observari. Sic dico. Tantum abest, ut articulus ה huic voci praefixus, nominis appellativi; ejusque absentia, proprii index sit, ut contrarium hic fere obtineat. Consule priora Geneseos. Alia est ratio nominum propriorum, quae nunquam appellativa sunt, ut Abraham, Jacob, David. Ea enim nunquam admittunt articulum: alia eorum, quae πρώτως appellativa sunt, id quod & in complurimis locorum nominibus observare est, [?]הָרָמָה / הַלָּחִי &c. Sed quid opus est tot verbis? Ipsi Pontificii vocem Adam per hominem exponunt. Lyra, ut scilicet quilibet sit sollicitus & desiderans posteritatis suae prosperitatem. Et Emanuel Sa, plane, ut nostri, Lex Adam id est hominis q. d. sic mecum agis, ut solet homo cum amico. Carthus. duplicem affert interpretationem, prima est, hac est proprietas hominis protoplasti, seu jussio ei facta, vid. sollicitudinem gerere de prolis successione & prosperitate. Vel hæc est lex Adami id est hominis, ut gratias agat Deo de beneficiis suis. At quomodo hæc postrema interpretatio, manente vocula Enim, cum antecedentibus cohæret? Vides lector, omnes in eo conspirare, nominanilla Dei vocandi casu exprimenda esse. Lutherus, & ex eo Bel-gæ, dat is een twpse eenes menschen die Godt de Heere is. Hoc est, Hæc est ratio hominis qui Dominus Deus est. Prolixe super hoc loco disserit B. Lutherus * tomo 8. Jenensi Germ. pag. 145. & seq. Existimat Davidem respicere ad Messiam, cum-que hic describi Ἀνθρωπον, hominem simul & Deum Dominum. Tu cave, tiro, ex hoc loco pro isthoc articulo argumentum adversus hæreticos depromas. Christum Jesum esse Ἀνθρωπον articulus immotæ veritatis est. Conspiret quicquid uspiam est hæreticorum: jungant fœdere cum ipsis interorum portis, nunquam hanc veritatem evertere valebunt. Certum est, ex ipsis Vet. Test. tabulis hunc articulum probari posse. Concedo ex totius hujus promissionis serie per consequentia-rum {s}um ambages probari posse utramque Messiæ naturam. At ex his verbis nihil nisi precario obtineri posse contendo. Quod si ita scriptum esset, וְאֵת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים melius proceederet argumentum.
units.tr: וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים [And this is the law of man, Lord GOD]. It will not be hard to draw out the genuine sense of these words from what precedes. David greatly magnifies God's gracious promise to perpetuate his kingdom. He marvels that God should speak with him so familiarly, συγχατάβασις [condescension], mixing words with him as a friend does with a friend: This seemed a small thing in your sight, Lord, unless you also spoke of the house of your servant for a long time to come, and this is the custom of man, or of men, Lord GOD (וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים). The letter ך (chaph) is often elided in Hebrew. If you admit it here and refer these words to the verb you spoke, the sense flows well. Junius gives the same sense: and that by human reasoning, Lord Jehovah, "und dasselbe nach der Menschen Weise, O Herr GOTT". Scindler agrees, and he also brings in the Chaldee, וְרָא חַיָּא לִבְנֵי אֱנָשָׁא, [vera hayya livne enasha], this [manner of acting] is fitting for the sons of men, as if to say: thus a friend usually speaks with a friend and openly declares the thoughts of his mind. The Greek version can also be explained in this way: ἀλλ᾽ αὕτη ὁ νόμος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κύριε μὴ κύριε [but this is the law of man, Lord, is it not, Lord?]. The Genevans and the English help the Hebrew pronunciation as if it were a question: Is this the manner of men, Lord GOD? The English: And is this the manner of man, O Lord God? In this they follow Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi Isaiah. The former says on this passage, בתם ידי ראוי להתבשר כן לבשר ודם [bitmah yadi ra'uy lehitbasser ken livsar vadam], that is, with wonder [David says this, as if to say], is it fitting to announce such things to flesh and blood? The latter paraphrases the passage thus: Is it the condition of man that he should find grace in your eyes and be so greatly esteemed? I know that I am unworthy of this honour, etc. Let us now examine the two interpretations. The Vulgate: for this is the law of Adam. I ask what the word for means here. To what does it look back, and with which words does it cohere? I wonder why it rendered הָאָדָם as Adam, as if the first father of the human race were meant. The defender will object the article ה, by which the common noun אָדָם is usually restricted to the first man, as when we say ὁ πᾶς φύσις, ὁ λόγος, ὁ θεολόγος of the one prince among prophets, apostles and theologians; so τὸ ὄνομα, הַשֵּׁם, הַדָּבָר, ὁ λόγος, the Word of God. I do not deny that these things hold; for I think the saying of Galen also applies here: εἰώθασι οἱ ἄνθρωποι τὰ πρωτεύοντα ἐν τῷ γένει τῷ τοῦ γένους ὀνόματι προσαγορεύειν, that is, men are accustomed to name by the name of the genus those things which hold first place in a genus. But conversely I also insist that when Adam is the proper name of the first parent, the article is sometimes absent, for example Gen. 4:1, and on the other hand, when it is a common noun, the article is placed before it. I would like beginners to note this once and for all. I say this: the article ה prefixed to this word is by no means a sign of a common noun, and its absence a sign of a proper noun; rather the reverse commonly holds. Consult the earlier chapters of Genesis. The case of proper names is different: those that are never common nouns, such as Abraham, Jacob, David, never take the article; but of those that are primarily common nouns, which can also be observed in many place names, such as הָרָמָה and הַלָּחִי, the article is used. But why need so many words be spent? The Papists themselves explain the word Adam as man. Lyra: that is, whoever is anxious and desires the prosperity of his posterity. And Emanuel Sa, quite like our people: the law of Adam, that is, of man, as if to say: you deal with me as a man usually deals with a friend. The Carthusian offers a twofold interpretation. The first is: this is the property of the first-formed man, or the command given to him, namely to take care of the succession and prosperity of his offspring. Or: this is the law of Adam, that is, of man, that he give thanks to God for his benefits. But how does this last interpretation cohere with the preceding words, with the little word for remaining? You see, reader, that all agree in this, that the name of God must be expressed in the vocative case. Luther, and after him the Belgians: dat is een wijze eens menschen die Godt de Heere is, "that is the manner of a man who is the Lord God". That is, This is the reason of a man who is Lord God. Luther discusses this passage at length in volume 8 of the Jena German edition, pages 145 and following. He thinks David looks to the Messiah, and that a man, Ἄνθρωπος, is described here who is at once man and God and Lord. But you, student, beware of drawing from this passage an argument against the heretics for that article. That Christ Jesus is ἄνθρωπος is an article of unshakable truth. Let whatever heretics there are conspire, let them join in covenant with the gates of hell itself; they will never be able to overturn this truth. It is certain that this article can be proved from the very tables of the Old Testament. I grant that both natures of the Messiah can be proved, by a roundabout chain of inferences, from the whole series of this promise. But I contend that from these words nothing can be obtained except by begging the question. If it had been written thus: וְאֵת תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים, the argument would have proceeded better.

units.la: Sed non tollam sic manum de hac tabula: Excutiendus obiter locus geminus & ejusdem argumenti est, 1. Chron. 17. 17. Ubi eandem orationem his verbis Spiritus S. exprimit. Et parum visum est hoc in oculis tuis, Deus, adeo ut locutus sis de familia servi tui in longinquum, וְרָאִיתַנִי כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם הַמַּעֲלָה יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים & provideris mihi secundum rationem hominis [hanc] excellentiam, DOMINIE Deus. Ita positum fuerit רָאִיתָ לִי pro רָאִיתַנִי / Porro רָאָה video, seu, ut prisci loquebantur, specio, pro provideo, prospicio. Ebraei enim cum composita verba non habeant, eorum loco simplicibus utuntur. Pisc. & aspexeris me secundum rationem hominis id est humanam, [quoad] hanc excellentiam, DOMINE Deus. Angli, secundum rationem hominis magnæ dignitatis DOMINE Deus. Probarem, si esset כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם בְּמַעֲלָה / Vulg. Spectabilem me fecisti supra omnes homines, Domine Deus. Quæ interpretatio cum fontibus neutiquam potest conciliari. Illud tamen recte quod bina illa Dei nomina vocandi casu expresserit.
units.tr: But I will not lift my hand from this tablet so quickly. On the way, I must examine a second passage of the same argument, 1 Chron. 17:17, where the Holy Spirit expresses the same prayer in these words: "And this seemed a small thing in your eyes, O God, so that you have spoken of the house of your servant from afar, and have regarded me according to the standing of a man of high degree, O LORD God" [וְרָאִיתַנִי כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם הַמַּעֲלָה יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים]. So it would have been put as "you have regarded me" [רָאִיתָ לִי] in place of [רָאִיתַנִי]. Moreover, [רָאָה] means "to see", or, as the older writers said, "to look upon", and so "to provide for" or "to watch over". For the Hebrews, since they have no compound verbs, use simple ones in their place. Piscator: "you have looked upon me according to the manner of man, that is, human, [as to] this excellence, O LORD God." The English: "according to the manner of a man of great dignity, O LORD God." I would approve it if the text were [כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם בְּמַעֲלָה]. The Vulgate: "You have made me remarkable above all men, O Lord God." That rendering cannot be reconciled with the sources in any way. Yet it is correct in having rendered those two names of God in the vocative case.

units.la: Lxx. καὶ ἐπείδες με ὡς ὄψεως ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ὑψωσας με κύριε ὁ Θεός id est Et aspexisti me, tanquam aspectus hominis, & exaltasti me Domine Deus. Videntur accepisse תּוֹר pro תֵּאַר / Cæteri vocem eam accepere, tanquam synonymam nominis תּוֹרַת / omnes vero in universum in interpretatione nominum Dei conspirandam Trinitatem. Itaque minus solidum rursus illud argumentum est, quod ex hujus loci versione Germanica aut Belgica pro Jesu Christo Ἰεανθρώπῳ vulgo depromunt. Versio Germ. seu Belgica ita sonat, si Latinè reddas, Et aspexisti me tanquam in figura hominis (Osiander, tanquam figuram hominis) qui est in supernis Dominus Deus. Hoc sensu, Intelligo ista in me non quadrare, sed in Messiam, cujus ego typus seu figura sum, qui & Deus & homo futurus est, &c. Huic interpretioni multa obstant. Posito enim מַעֲלָה hic idem esse quod מָרוֹם / tamen sic dicendum fuisset, כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר בְּמַעֲלָה וגו׳ Nunc adi ad Exercit. Biblicas D. Joh. Tarnovi qui prolixius hæc loca examinavit.
units.tr: The Septuagint: "And you looked upon me as the appearance of a man, and you exalted me, Lord God" [καὶ ἐπείδες με ὡς ὄψεως ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ὑψωσας με κύριε ὁ Θεός], that is, "And you looked upon me as the sight of a man, and you exalted me, Lord God." They seem to have read [תּוֹר] for [תֵּאַר]. Others took the word as synonymous with the noun [תּוֹרַת], but all in general agree that the Trinity must be found in the interpretation of the names of God. So again, the argument that is commonly drawn from the German or Dutch version of this passage, in favour of Jesus Christ the God-man [Ἰεανθρώπῳ], is weaker still. The German or Dutch version, if rendered into Latin, reads: "And you looked upon me as in the figure of a man (Osiander: as the figure of a man), who is the Lord God in the heights." In this sense, I understand that these things do not fit me, but the Messiah, of whom I am the type or figure, who is to be both God and man, and so on. Many things stand in the way of this interpretation. For even granting that [מַעֲלָה] here means the same as [מָרוֹם], it would still have had to be said thus: [כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר בְּמַעֲלָה וגו׳]. Now go to the Biblical Exercises of Dr. John Tarnovius, who examined these passages at greater length.

units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Gretzerus lib. 1. de cruce & cap. 6. Ne quis miretur, inquit, me quercum, in qua Absolon capillis pependit, vocasse crucem, vere enim crux fuit crucisque Dominicæ manifesta figura, in qua Absolon pendens Christum prefigurabat. O triste ineptias! Ergone conscelleratum illud caput sanctissimi Salvatoris typus fuit?
units.tr: Gretzer, in his first book on the cross, chapter 6: "Let no one wonder, he says, that I have called the oak on which Absalom hung by his hair a cross. For it truly was a cross, and a clear figure of the Lord's cross, since Absalom hanging there prefigured Christ." O, what sad absurdities! Was that accursed head really a type of the most holy Saviour?

units.la: CAP. XXI. verf. 6.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI, verse 6.

units.la: Ut crucifigamus. ] Ita vulgatus. At vox Hebræa significat suspendere. Crucis supplicium Ebræorum Respublica ignoravit. Lxx. & soli exponamus eos. Cajet. nihil dicitur de cruce in specie.
units.tr: "That we may crucify them." So the Vulgate. But the Hebrew word means to hang up. The Hebrew commonwealth knew nothing of crucifixion as a punishment. The Septuagint: "and we alone will expose them." Cajetan: "nothing is said about the cross in particular."

units.la: Ebr. | Vulg. Sit quaeso duplex portio de spiritu tuo super me. | Obsecro ut fiat duplex Spiritus tuus in me.
units.tr: Hebrew | Vulgate: Let, I pray, a double portion of your spirit be upon me. | I beseech that your Spirit be made double in me.

units.la: Locum hunc prima fronte subobscurum illustrat locus Deut. 21.17. Agnoscet filium primogenitum minus amatæ, ut det ei duplam portionem de omni quod inventum fuerit ei. Vulg. de omnibus quae habuerit, cunctà duplicia Chald. duas portiones. Eadem locutio extat Zach. 13. & in Ebræo in Chald. Ubi Lxx. δύο μέρη. R. Levi hæc Elisæi verba sic Quando separabis & distribues de spiritu tuo super super filios prophetarum tunc sit quaso mea portio dupla ex adverso uniuscuiusque eorum. Ita & Jun. & Pisc. & Angli & Tigurini. Neque dissentiunt Genevenses, Je te prie, quei aye de ton esprit, mutant que deux. Nec Deodatus, sia in me la parte di due del tuo Spirito. Tralata ergo locutio à divisione corporalium bonorum ad divisionem spiritualium. Vulgatus Interpres ab hoc tramite discedens occasionem Interpretibus praebuit, alienas & supervacaneas quaestiones movendi. Plerique enim Interpretes hoc sancti viri [?] sic interpretati sunt, ac si petiisset duplam portionem Spiritus, respectu ipsius Eliae. Carthus. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. 1. quod Elisaeus petivit, gratiam spiritualem Eliae concessam ad prophetandum & ad faciendum miracula duplicari in se, ita quod haberet eam in dupla portione respectu Eliae, &c. Etiam Lutherus, dum in Vulgati Interpretis vestigia pedes suos ponit, mentem Prophetae assecutus non est, Dat uwen geest by my zy tweevoudigh. Quod sic explicat, ut majori cum efficacia & potentia possim concionari. At huic expositioni objici video ab Interpretibus illud Salvatoris, non est discipulus supra Magistrum, Nimis praesumptuosum fuisset, inquit Lyra, si Elisaeum duplam potestatem respectu magistri sui petisset. Ad illud vero, quod Interpretes Eliae 8. Elizaeo vero 16. miracula adscribunt, etiam commode satis ibidem respondet. Quid ergo? Duplicem spiritum referunt Lyra, Carthus. & alii, ad duo dona prophetiae & miraculorum, ut non quaesiverit in istis [?] aut [?] sed eadem eodem gradu sibi optaverit. At ne hoc quidem Cajetano facit satis. Audiamus acutissimi ingenii & liberi oris Cardinalem, Juxta Ebraum habetur, os duorum, Hac appellatione scriptura alias nominat portionem duplicem, quae primogenito debebatur, quia loco duorum succedebat. Petit ergo succedere Eliae, non in agris, &c. sed in spiritu Eliae tanquam primogenitum in duplici portione. Ita quod plus petit quam duplicem Spiritum, prophetia vid. & miraculorum. Quoniam petit succedere in spiritu Eliae jure primogeniti, quod est praeferri caeteris filiis Eliae spiritualibus. Est succedere non solum in spiritu miraculorum & prophetiae, qui erat in Elia, sed etiam excellenter (respectu aliorum condiscipulorum) habere hujusmodi spiritum, sicut primogenitus excellenter (respectu fratrum) succedit in domis paternis. Haec Cardinalis Serarius, Alii volunt minorem [spiritum postulasse,] ut si
units.tr: The locus Deut. 21.17 clarifies this passage, which is somewhat obscure at first sight: He shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the less loved wife, by giving him a double portion of all that he has. The Vulgate has of all that he has, in double portions, and the Chaldee has two portions. The same expression occurs in Zech. 13, and in the Hebrew and the Chaldee. There the Septuagint has two parts. Rabbi Levi reads these words of Elisha thus: When you separate and distribute of your spirit over the sons of the prophets, then let my portion, I pray, be double against each one of them. So too Junius, Piscator, the English and the Tigurine translators. The Geneva translators do not disagree: Je te prie, qu'il y ait de ton esprit, muant que deux (I pray you, let there be of your spirit, changed to two). Nor does Diodati: sia in me la parte di due del tuo Spirito (let the portion of two of your Spirit be in me). The expression is therefore transferred from the division of bodily goods to the division of spiritual ones. The Vulgate translator, departing from this path, gave the interpreters occasion to raise alien and superfluous questions. For most interpreters have explained this holy man's words as though he had asked for a double portion of the Spirit in comparison with Elijah himself. The Carthusian: This is explained in two ways. First, that Elisha sought that the spiritual grace granted to Elijah for prophesying and working miracles be doubled in himself, so that he would have it in a double portion in comparison with Elijah, etc. Luther too, while setting his feet in the footsteps of the Vulgate translator, did not grasp the mind of the Prophet: Give your spirit to me twofold. He explains this so that I may preach with greater efficacy and power. But I see that the interpreters object to this explanation the saying of the Saviour, The disciple is not above the master. Lyra says: It would have been too presumptuous if Elisha had sought a double power in comparison with his master. As to the fact that the interpreters ascribe eight miracles to Elijah and sixteen to Elisha, he answers this quite adequately in the same place. What then? Lyra, the Carthusian and others refer the double spirit to the two gifts of prophecy and miracles, so that he did not seek more in these [?] but desired the same things at the same level for himself. But not even this satisfies Cajetan. Let us hear the Cardinal, a man of the keenest intellect and free tongue: According to the Hebrew it is said, "the mouth of two." In this phrase Scripture elsewhere names the double portion that was owed to the firstborn, because he succeeded in place of two. Elisha therefore asks to succeed Elijah, not in fields, etc., but in the spirit of Elijah, as the firstborn in a double portion. So that he asks for more than a double spirit of prophecy and miracles. Since he asks to succeed in the spirit of Elijah by right of the firstborn, which means to be preferred to the other spiritual sons of Elijah. It means to succeed not only in the spirit of miracles and prophecy which was in Elijah, but also to have this spirit excellently (in comparison with the other fellow disciples), just as the firstborn excellently (in comparison with his brothers) succeeds in the paternal house. So says Cardinal Serarius. Others want him to have asked for the lesser spirit, so that if

units.la: Greek words in the text (ἀρισ..., ἡ διδασκαλος ... εἶναι) are only partly legible and are marked [?]. Elia spiritus in tres partes diuideretur, Elisaeus tantum duas haberet, tanquam primogenitus, &c. Idque phrasis Ebraea hoc loco importat. Sed an textus Vulgatus idem quoque importat? Hoc silentio praetervehitur Serarius. Summa summarum huc redit, condiscipulos, non praeceptorem antecellere voluit sanctissimus Elisaeus.
units.tr: Greek words in the text (ἀρισ..., ἡ διδασκαλος ... εἶναι) are only partly legible and are marked [?]. The spirit of Elijah were divided into three parts, Elisha would have only two, as the firstborn, etc. And this is what the Hebrew phrase in this place implies. But does the Vulgate text imply the same? Serarius passes over this in silence. The sum of the matter comes to this: the most holy Elisha wished to surpass his fellow disciples, not his teacher.

units.la: Ibid. verf. 14. ως εστιν Θεος Ηλιας * Αφφω.] Ita expresse inveniesin versione Graeca haec Ebr. [Hebrew] Quae vulgo in hunc modum reddunt, ubi est DOMINVS Deus Elia ; etiam ipse? Vulg. etiam nunc. In cujus interpretatione & illud observa, voces istas, Et non sunt divisa, non extare in Ebraeo, sed desumtas esse ex Graeco, [Greek]. Ut frustra sint qui istis colligunt Elisaeum inferiorem fuisse meritis suo magistro ut loquitur Carthus. Itaque Joh. Benedictus eas obelo jugulavit. Sed redeamus ad vocem αφφω, quae doctissimorum virorum, qua veterum qua recentiorum, industriam fatigavit. Aliquid & quasi per transennam hic vidit Cl. Drusius in notis ad fragmenta Incomparabile illud Equitum & literatorum decus, * DANIEL HEINSIUS omnibus Interpretibus hic otia fecit. Animus erat locum integrum, utpote varia & recondita eruditione vernantem, huc transcribere. Sed quia incomparabile illud scriptum non ita pridem ex officina Elzeviriana prodiit & omnium jam manibus teritur, operam istam mihi compendi-faciam.
units.tr: Ibid. verse 14. Where is the LORD God of Elijah? Even he? [ως εστιν Θεος Ηλιας * Αφφω]. The Hebrew is expressly rendered this way in the Greek version. Commonly they render it thus: where is the LORD God of Elijah, even he? The Vulgate has even now. In interpreting this, note also that the words and they were divided are not found in the Hebrew but are taken from the Greek. So those who collect from them that Elisha was inferior in merit to his master, as the Carthusian puts it, labour in vain. Accordingly John Benedict has pierced them with an obelus. But let us return to the word αφφω, which has wearied the diligence of the most learned men, both ancient and recent. The illustrious Drusius, in his notes on the fragments, saw something here, as if in passing. The incomparable ornament of knights and scholars, DANIEL HEINSIUS, has left nothing for all other interpreters here. I intended to copy out the whole passage here, as it is rich in varied and recondite learning. But since that incomparable work has not long since come out from the Elzevier press and is now in everyone's hands, I shall make this labour shorter for myself.

units.tr: CAP. III. vers. 27.

units.la: Et accepit [Rex Moab] filium suum primogenitum.] Ita Vulgatus, Lutherus Pisc. Angli Genev. Ad quem locum multa commentati sunt Theologi. Monendi tamen sunt verbi divini Interpretes, istam sententiam non omnino immotae veritatis esse. Ebraeum enim affixum, quod est in voce [Hebrew] indifferens est ad utrumque, filium suum, & filium ejus. ejus vid. regis Edom. Et quidem posteriorem sententiam elegerunt Junius & Deodatus. Juvare eos aliquantulum videtur locus Amos 2.1. Eo quod combusserit Rex Moab ossa regis Edom in calcem. Sic & hoc parallelon obnoxium est exceptionibus. Ego in censura mea prolixe disserui de hoc loco. Omnia quae hinc inde afferuntur, examinavi. Video utrinque paria rationum momenta. Ita-
units.tr: "And he took his eldest son" [the king of Moab]. So the Vulgate, Luther, Piscator, the English and the Geneva Bible. Many theologians have commented on this passage. Yet the interpreters of the divine Word should be warned that this view is not entirely beyond doubt. For the Hebrew suffix in the word [Hebrew] is indifferent to both readings, his son and his son, that is, of the king of Edom. Junius and Deodatus did indeed choose the latter reading. Amos 2:1 seems to help them a little: Because the king of Moab burned the bones of the king of Edom to lime. Yet this parallel too is open to objections. I discussed this passage at length in my Censura and examined everything that has been brought forward on either side. I see equal weight of arguments on both sides. Thus-

units.la: Itaque dubito, & plane, quod ajunt Graeci, [?] [illegible, ~3 letters].
units.tr: So I doubt, and plainly, as the Greeks say, [?] [illegible, ~3 letters].

units.la: CAP. V. verf. 18.
units.tr: CHAP. V. verse 18.

units.la: Ebraea αὐτολέξει ita sonant, Hac in re condonet DOMINVS servo tuo, cum ingreditur dominus meus edem Rimmonis, ad incurvandum se ibi (nam is nititur manu mea) si incurvavero me in ade Rimmonis, in incurvatione mea condonet quaeso DOMINVS servo tuo, &c. Incurvatio illa Ebraïcè dicitur הִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה / quod est nomen verbale ab הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה deflexum. Vox Ebraea significat totius corporis prostrationem. Lxx. Interpretes, προσκυνῆσαι vocare amant. Gestus ille Orienti suetus erat in cultu, qua civili, qua religioso. Cum in cultu religioso usurpatur, commodo redditur per Latinum adorare. Alias minus commode. Vulgato tamen Interpreti id admodum familiare est. Namque & hunc locum ita convertit, Hoc autem solum est, de quo deprecaris Dominum pro servo tuo, quando ingredietur dominus meus, ut adoret, & illo innitente super manum meam, si adoravero in templo Rimmon, adorante eo [ nota in Ebraeo esse me בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹתִי) in eodem loco, ut ignoscat mihi Dominus, &c. Vides ter vocem adorationis usurpasse interpretem. Lutherus quoque illud השתחוה / tam Naamani quam Regi tributum, eodem modo reddit, per [?]. Hinc natainter Interpretes quaestio, liceatne interdum ipsam fidem dissimulare, & idolorum cultum simulare.
units.tr: The Hebrew, word for word, reads: In this matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to bow down there (for he leans on my hand), and I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the LORD, I pray, pardon your servant in my bowing down, etc. That bowing down is called in Hebrew [הִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה], a verbal noun derived from [הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה]. The Hebrew word signifies the prostration of the whole body. The Seventy like to render it by προσκυνῆσαι [proskynēsai]. That gesture was customary in the East, both in civil and in religious worship. When it is used in religious worship, it is conveniently rendered in Latin by adorare; elsewhere the rendering is less suitable. Yet this is very familiar to the Vulgate translator, for he also renders this passage thus: But this alone is the matter for which you ask the Lord on behalf of your servant: when my lord goes in, that he may worship, and leaning on my hand, if I worship in the temple of Rimmon, while he worships in the same place (note that in the Hebrew it is [בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹתִי]), that the Lord may pardon me, etc. You see that the interpreter has used the word worship three times. Luther too renders that [השתחוה], applied both to Naaman and to the King, in the same way, by [?]. Hence among the interpreters arises the question whether one may sometimes conceal the faith itself and feign the worship of idols.

units.la: Memini etiam me alicubi Calvinum quiritantem audire, hoc Naamanis exemplum à quibusdam Pseudo-Nicodemis saepe allegari. Sed obserya propriam significationem vocis Ebraeae & videbis supervacaneam omnem istam disputationem esse. Videbis multos imaginaria sibi extruere stadia. Non postulat enim dispensationem circa adorationem veri numinis in isthoc fano, nedum impuri istius daemonii, cui in delubro isto litabatur, sed petit sibi condonari istam incurvationem corporis, prisco ritu, Regi suo obsequium praestituro. Agnoscit interim verum Deum, idolis res suas sibi habere jubet, vovet perpetuum & constantem cultum Deo Israelis; nec dubium est quin in patriam redux eandem religionem professus sit. Vox ergo Ebraea, ut ut Regi tributa per adorare quoad sensum bene reddita sit, tamen Naamani tributa per adorare vertenda non fuerat. Lubet audire Cajeta-num, Adverte prudens Lector, quod Hebraica dictio, quamvis communiter interpretata sit, adorare ,' proprie tamen non significat adorationem, sed exhibitionem signi honoris in ipsius honoranti is personae curvatione, sive curvatio hujusmodi fieret genuflexione, sine prostratione, sive capitis & humerorum inclinatione. Ita quoque non significatur actus interior, sed actus duntaxat exterior honoris. Est itaque sensus, quod curvante se rege in templo Rimmon Deo suo Rimmon, ego quoque me incurvabo, quia Rex innititur super me. Et hoc est actio, quam ignosci sibi a Deo petit. Et paulo post, dixit ei, vade in pace. Quaestiones dua hinc oriuntur. Altera, an verba ista Elisai annuant voto Naaman, affirmando, quod Deus ignoscet. Altera est, an incurvatio hujusmodi fuerit ubi cita. Solutio prima quaestionis est, quod verba Elisai cum sint valde communia, stant cum permissione illius curvationis: & propterea ex vi sermonis non affirmant Deum ignosciturum, seu non imputaturum ad peccatum. Solutio autem secunda quaestionis est quod aliud est loqui de genuflexione imitativa genuflexionis regiae, & aliud est loqui de genuflexione obsequii. Nam genuflexio imitativa est ejusdem speciei cum genuflexione quam imitatur: Et propterea esset genuflexio idolatrica, quemadmodum genuflexio regis. Sed de hujusmodi genuflexione non esse sermonem, testantur verba ipsius Naaman proponentis conscientiae suae scrupulum in loco & tempore talis obsequii, quia videlicet in templo Rimmon, tempore quo Rex adorabat Rimmon, ipsum Naaman: genuflectente Rege, oportebat genuflectere, eo quod Rex innitebatur super eum, & quemadmodum Rege stante oportebat ipsum stare; ita Rege genuflectente, oportebat ipsum genuflectere. De hujusmodi itaque genuflexione obsequii est quaestio: Et dicimus quod secundum si erat licita: co quod obsequebatur genuflexioni Regis absolute, & non relative ad idolatriam. Genuflexio enim ipsa Regis actio quaedam est, secundum se non mala, sed iniquitatem idololatriae habet annexam ex idololatrica mente Regis: minister autem obsequens genuflexioni, & non relationi ad idolum, est non particeps criminis. Quemadmodum nobiles comitantes Regem euntem ad concubinam, non sunt participes peccati; eo quod non comitantur eum, quatenus vadit ad peccandum, sed quatenus vadit absolute, ipsum enim ire secundum se nullum est peccatum. Quamvis autem hujusmodi genuflexio secundum se non sit mala, speciem tamen mali pra se fert ratione loci & tempore, nisi persona cognita sit exemta ab idololatria. Nam si persona obsequens ibi tunc similis aliis habetur, genuflexioejus, quantumcunque ex propria intentione non sit mala, occasionem tamen praesentibus dat existimandi, quod ipse facit sicut alii genuflectentes idolo. Si vero persona nota esset aliena ab idolatria, cessaret species mali & consequenter ratio scandali seu existimationis quod ipse genuflecteret idolo. Et quia Naaman & verbo & facto (aedificando summo Deo altare illiusque sacrificando, & profitendo ipsum solum esse Elohim) publicabat se alienum esse ab idolatria, ideo obsequium, quod praestabat Regi in templo Rimmon adoranti, nec in se erat malum, nec praebebat speciem mali. Et propterea Elisaeus non dixit ei, hoc esse peccatum, nec affirmavit ignoscendum a Deo, sed dixit vade in pace; ipse autem Naaman more bonarum mentium timebat culpam, & propterea petiit sibi ignosci, non imputando ad culpam. Hac Cajetanus.
units.tr: I remember hearing Calvin somewhere complaining that this example of Naaman is often cited by certain Pseudo-Nicodemites. But observe the proper meaning of the Hebrew word and you will see that all that dispute is superfluous. You will see that many build imaginary racecourses for themselves. For Naaman does not ask for a dispensation regarding the worship of the true God in this temple, much less regarding that unclean demon to whom sacrifice was offered in that shrine. He asks that this bodily bowing, in the ancient manner, be pardoned, since he is to render obedience to his king. Meanwhile he acknowledges the true God, bids that his household keep to their own idols, vows perpetual and constant worship to the God of Israel, and there is no doubt that on returning home he professed the same religion. So the Hebrew word, though rendered by adorare as regards its sense when applied to the King, was not rightly rendered by adorare when applied to Naaman. Let us hear Cajetan: Take note, prudent reader, that the Hebrew word, although it is commonly translated as "to adore", does not properly signify adoration but the display of a sign of honour by the bending of the person who honours, whether such bending is made by genuflection without prostration, or by an inclination of the head and shoulders. Thus too it signifies not an inward act but only an outward act of honour. The sense is therefore this: that while the king bows down in the temple of Rimmon to his god Rimmon, I too will bow down, because the king leans upon me. And this is the action for which he asks pardon from God. And a little later: He said to him, "Go in peace". Two questions arise from this. The first is whether these words of Elisha assent to Naaman's prayer by affirming that God will pardon him. The second is whether such a bowing actually took place. The answer to the first question is that, since the words of Elisha are very general, they agree with the permission of that bowing; and therefore by the force of the saying they do not affirm that God will pardon, or will not impute it as sin. The answer to the second question is that it is one thing to speak of a genuflection imitating the royal genuflection, and another to speak of a genuflection of obedience. For an imitative genuflection is of the same kind as the genuflection it imitates, and therefore it would be an idolatrous genuflection, just as the king's genuflection was. But that this is not the kind of genuflection under discussion is shown by the words of Naaman himself, who puts before his conscience the scruple about the place and time of such obedience: namely, that in the temple of Rimmon, at the time when the King was worshipping Rimmon, Naaman himself, the King kneeling and leaning upon him, had to kneel; and just as he had to stand when the King stood, so when the King knelt he had to kneel. The question concerns, then, this genuflection of obedience; and we say that, in the second case, it was lawful, because he obeyed the King's genuflection absolutely, and not in relation to idolatry. For the genuflection itself is an action of the King, in itself not evil, but it has the wickedness of idolatry attached to it through the idolatrous mind of the King. A minister who obeys the genuflection, and not its relation to the idol, is not a partner in the crime. Just as nobles accompanying a King who goes to a concubine are not partners in the sin, because they do not accompany him insofar as he goes to sin, but insofar as he goes absolutely; for going in itself is no sin. Although such a genuflection is not evil in itself, it nevertheless bears the appearance of evil by reason of place and time, unless the person is known to be free from idolatry. For if the obeying person is then regarded there like the others, his genuflection, however little evil it may be in his own intention, nevertheless gives those present occasion to think that he does what the others do, kneeling to the idol. But if the person were known to be alien to idolatry, the appearance of evil would cease, and consequently the reason for offence or for the opinion that he knelt to the idol. And because Naaman, both by word and by deed (by building an altar to the most high God and sacrificing on it, and by professing that he alone is Elohim), made it known that he was alien to idolatry, therefore the obedience which he rendered to the King adoring in the temple of Rimmon was in itself not evil, nor did it present the appearance of evil. And therefore Elisha did not tell him that this was a sin, nor did he affirm that it was to be pardoned by God, but said "Go in peace"; and Naaman himself, in the manner of good minds, feared guilt, and therefore asked that he be pardoned, that it not be imputed to him as fault. So far Cajetan.

units.la: De hoc loco dictum est ad Josuae cap. 10. Hic autem locus, ut hoc διξοδικως hic inseram, hactenus obstitit, quo minus aspiciari potuerim magno Scaligero, qui loco non uno in incomparabili illo opere de Emend. temporum, distributionem illam diei in horas sero admodum ab Ebraeis receptam fuisse docet. Pag. 5. Veteres Ebraei nullas alias diei partes, quam mane, meridiem, vesperi noverant. Psal. 55. 18. dies in tres partes dividitur. Et totam νυχθημερον in 4. quadrantes seu vigilias, &c. Posteriorum inventum est Horologium & ηλιοτρόπια quibus dies per lineas & intervalla umbrarum distinguebatur. Et pag. 597. Scito vetustissimis Judaeis horae aequinoctiales in usu non fuisse, sed tantum καιρικας. De quibus erudite pag. 4. disserit. Dices, cum sub veteribus Ebraeis Achazum, Hiskiam eorumque coaetaneos non complecti, ac proinde hunc locum maximo viro non obvertere cornua. Adi ergo ad pag. 131. ubi diserte scribit, divisionem diei in horas 24. tandem sub Romano imperio a Romanis ad Judaeos translatam esse.
units.tr: This passage was discussed at Joshua chapter 10. I insert here, to treat the matter at some length [διξοδικῶς], that this passage has until now stood in the way of my being able to bring the great Scaliger into view. In that incomparable work On the Emendation of Time he teaches, in more than one place, that the division of the day into hours was adopted by the Hebrews very late. He writes at p. 5: "The ancient Hebrews knew no parts of the day other than morning, midday and evening." At Psalm 55:18 the day is divided into three parts, and the whole nychthemeron is divided into four quadrants or watches, and so on. Later, the clock and the heliotropion were invented, by which the day was marked off by lines and the intervals of shadows. And at p. 597: "Know that the most ancient Jews did not use equinoctial hours, but only temporal [καιρικάς] ones." He discusses these learnedly at p. 4. You will say that since he does not include Ahaz, Hezekiah and their contemporaries among the ancient Hebrews, this passage does not give that great man any trouble. So look at p. 131, where he plainly writes that the division of the day into 24 hours was at last carried over from the Romans to the Jews under the Roman empire.

units.la: ET qui stare fecit Solem. ] Ita vulgatus. Æstuant hic interpretes & anxie quærunt, utrum aliquis præter Josuam solis cursum stiterit. Vide Magallianum Jesuitam, Annotatione 7. in caput 10. Josuæ. & Tornielli opus Chronologicum. Vulgo existimant, innui Elimelechum maritum τῆς Noömi. Eum ajunt precum suarum efficacia solis cursum inhibuisse, ut ad tantum miraculum sæculi istius homines obstupescentes, impietati repudium mitterent. Iidem existimant per vires mendacii intelligi Machlon & Cheljon, Elimelechi filios. Eosdem denotari nominibus sequentibus, Securus & incendens, pro quo in Carthus. constanter legitur, incedens. Lyræ hæc sunt & gerræ germanæ. In Ebræo sunt nomina propria, Jo-kim & viri Cozeba, & Joasch & Saraph. Atque ita quoque 70. Vide ipsum Lyram Ut nihil de Cajet. Aria Mont. Bened. Emanuele Sa & aliis dicam. Carthusianus licet meliorem Lyræ interpretationem referat, se tamen à vulgata versione ne latum unguem dimoveri patitur. Stat ut Marpesia cautes... Circa hac dico, inquit, me credere B. Hieronymo. Credo quod propter universalem Ecclesiam Spiritus S. Hieronymum in vertendo gratiose direxit, qui præordinavit, ipsam sanctam & non errantem Ecclesiam versione Hieronymi uti debere. Hujus pervicaciæ suæ multos hæredes reliquit bonus Dionysius. Videas enim passim perversos istos, qui etiam post inventas fruges pergunt βαλανοφαγεῖν. Licebit ipsis per nos quoque σιτοφαγεῖν, modo μονοφάγοι id faciant. Servent sibi istas dapes. Non in videmus. Similes ludos dedit vulgatus cap. 2. verf. 53. ad quem vide Scaligeri Elenchum cap. 23. Nos in Censura nostra, & hunc illum locum diligenter excussimus.
units.tr: AND he who made the sun stand still.] So the Vulgate. Here the interpreters labour and anxiously inquire whether anyone besides Joshua ever stopped the course of the sun. See the Jesuit Magallianus, Annotation 7 on Joshua chapter 10, and Tornielli's Chronological work. The common view is that the husband of Noomi's is meant (τῆς [of Noemi]). They say that by the efficacy of his prayers he stopped the course of the sun, so that the people of that age, astonished at so great a miracle, might lay aside their impiety. The same writers think that by the powers of falsehood Mahlon and Chilion, the sons of Elimelech, are meant. They say these are signified by the following names, Securus and incendens, for which the Carthusian consistently reads incedens. These are the fancies of Lyra, and they are true twins of folly. In the Hebrew these are proper names: Jo-kim, the men of Cozeba, Joash and Saraph. And the Seventy render it the same way. See Lyra himself. I say nothing of Cajetan, Arias Montanus, the Benedictines, Emmanuel Sa and others. Although the Carthusian gives a better interpretation than Lyra, he nevertheless will not allow himself to be moved a hair's breadth from the Vulgate version. As Marpesian rock stands fast... On these matters, he says, I believe that I must trust Saint Jerome. I believe that the Holy Spirit, for the sake of the universal Church, graciously guided Jerome in his translation, and he ordained that the holy and unerring Church ought to use Jerome's version. The good Dionysius left many heirs to this obstinacy of his. For you will see everywhere those perverse men who, even after grain has been discovered, go on eating acorns [βαλανοφαγεῖν]. They may be allowed by us too to eat bread [σιτοφαγεῖν], provided they do it as solitary eaters [μονοφάγοι]. Let them keep those feasts for themselves. We do not begrudge them. The Vulgate gave similar sport at chapter 2, verse 53, on which see Scaliger's Elenchus, chapter 23. In our Censure we too have carefully examined this very passage.

units.la: INsignis hic locus est, cujus δανέτατε non parum imminutum ivere Græci, Vulg. Lutherus. Consceleratus ille Achaz cum & ab Edomæis & Philistæis peteretur, Regem Assyriæ auxilio vocare. Quo eventu? Hoc edisserit Spiritus S. verf. 20. & seq. Veniens itaque ad eum Thilath Philneser Rex Assyriæ angustia affecit eum, non autem a confirmavit eum. 21. Namque accipiens partem ex b domo DOMINI & domo Regis ac principum: dedit Regi Assyriæ, nec tamen auxilio fuit ei. 22. Quin illo quoque tempore quo afflictabat eum [DOMINVS,] pergebat prevaricari contra DOMINVM: Quibus verbis subjungit Spiritus S. hæc verba, הוא מלך אחז / iste erat Rex Achas, quæ verba per accentum Athnach à superioribus distincta peculiare membrum constituunt. Vides, ut exerto quasi in improbum caput digito, hoc elogio eum nobilitet, quasi diceret, Hoc erat illud monstrum, quod nullis flagellis edomari potuit. A flagellis Dei vires & incrementa ejus impietas sumebat. Pisc. Ein solcher war der König Achaz. Deod. tale era il rè Achaz. Angli, this is that King Achaz. Hic est ille Rex Achaz. Certe turpe est, sic digito monstrari & dicier, HIC EST. Jun. idem erat Rex Achaz. Genev. c'estoit [toujours] le roi Achaz. [Semper] erat idem Rex Achaz. q. d. semper sibi similis erat. Idem in secundis, idem in adversis, semper impius. Quamvis aliquid amplius & gravius Ebræa innuant, hoc videlicet, crescentibus afflictionibus, crevisse ejus scelera. Videa-mus
units.tr: This is a remarkable passage, whose δανέτατε the Greeks have not a little altered, as have the Vulgate and Luther. That accursed Ahaz, when the Edomites and the Philistines were attacking him, summoned the king of Assyria to help him. What was the outcome? The Holy Spirit sets it out in verse 20 and following: And so Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came to him and distressed him, but did not strengthen him. 21. For he took a portion out of the house of the LORD and the house of the king and of the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria, yet it did him no good. 22. Indeed, even at that time, when [the LORD] afflicted him, he went on sinning more against the LORD. To these words the Holy Spirit adds the words הוא מלך אחז [hu melekh Ahaz], this was King Ahaz, which, separated from what precedes by the accent Athnach, form a distinct clause. You see how, as if pointing a finger at a wicked head, he marks him out with this epithet, as if he said: This was that monster, whom no scourges could tame. From the scourges of God his strength and his growth drew only impiety. The German translator (Pisc.): Such a one was King Ahaz. The Italian (Deod.): Such was King Ahaz. The English: This is that King Ahaz. Hic est ille Rex Achaz. Surely it is shameful to be pointed at with a finger and be told, THIS IS HE. Jun.: King Ahaz was the same. Geneva: It was [always] King Ahaz. [Always] King Ahaz was the same, as if to say he was always like himself: the same in prosperity, the same in adversity, always impious. Although the Hebrew hints at something more and weightier, namely that, as his afflictions increased, so did his crimes. Let us see

units.la: {a} Ita præter Jun. Pisc. Angl. &c. etiam Pagn. Arias, Sa, Cajet. & alii. {b} i.e. Thesaurisdomus mus jam Græcos, Vulg. & Lutherum. Versum 20. ita reddidit Vulg. Adduxitque contra eum Tiglat Phalnasar regem Ass. qui & afflixit eum & nullo resistente vastavit. Vide Lector num ilthæc ex verbis Ebr. excsculpi possint, וַיָּבֹא עָלָיו תִּלְגַּת פִּלְנְאֶסֶר מֶלֶךְ / וַיָּבֹא אֲשׁוּר וַיָּצַר לוֹ וְלֹא חִזְּקוֹ / Nota, eum dicere, וַיָּבֹא non / Atque ita quoque legêre Græci, ἐπῆλθε ... αὐτόν, Nota על pro אל passim occurrere, Ex. gr. Gen. 38.12. Sed accedamus ad vers. 12, Eum sic traduxit Vulg. Insuper & tempore angustia sua auxit contemptum in Dominum, ipse per se Rex Achaz. Quæ posteriora apud Lyram, Carthus. & alios ab hoc versu revulsa, sequenti adjecta sunt, Ipse per se rex Achaz immolavit Dis Damasci. Neque etiam in editione correcta Clementina aliter quam ὑπερηφανῶν & ab antecedentibus & sequentibus sejunguntur. Nos scimus illa per se de suo adjecisse Interpretem. LXX. ... Luth. & Belgæ, Insuper in afflictione sua augebat Achab prævaricationes suas contra DOMINUM. Kimchi in commentariis ad Ps. 105. 7. recensat quinque הוא / quæ in malam partem sumantur. Inter ea vero nullum הוא illustrius eo est, circa quod jam versamur. Adscribam verba principis Grammaticorum אתה מוצא המשרה / הוא לרעה והמשרה לטובה id est tu invenies quinque Hu in malum, & quinque Hu in bonum. V. in malum ista sunt,. 1. הוא ILLE est Esau pater Edomæorum, Gen. 36. vers. ult. 2. הוא ILLE Dathan & Abirom, Num. 26. 9. 3. הוא ILLE rex Achaz, 2. Chron. 28. 22. 4. הוא ILLE Assuerus, Esth. 1. 5. הוא ILLE (Nimrod) robustus fuit venatione, Gen. 10. 5.
units.tr: {a} So also Jun., Pisc., Angl., etc., and Pagn., Arias, Sa, Cajet. and others. {b} That is, Thesaurisdomus. Already the Greeks, the Vulgate and Luther... The Vulgate renders verse 20 thus: And Tiglath-pilneser king of Assyria came against him, who both afflicted him and laid waste to him with no one resisting. Let the reader see whether these words can be drawn out of the Hebrew words, וַיָּבֹא עָלָיו תִּלְגַּת פִּלְנְאֶסֶר מֶלֶךְ אֲשׁוּר וַיָּצַר לוֹ וְלֹא חִזְּקוֹ [vayavo alav Tilgath Pilneser melekh Ashur vayatzar lo velo chizzeqo]. Note that he says וַיָּבֹא and not... And so also the Greeks read ἐπῆλθε ... αὐτόν [epelthe ... auton]. Note that על occurs everywhere for אל, for example Gen. 38.12. But let us come to verse 12. The Vulgate translates it thus: Moreover, in his distress he increased his contempt for the Lord; this was King Ahaz himself. The later words, which Lyra, the Carthusian and others have torn from this verse and attached to the following one, read: King Ahaz himself sacrificed to the gods of Damascus. Nor does the corrected Clementine edition separate them from what precedes and follows in any other way than with ὑπερηφανῶν. We know that the translator added per se (himself) of his own accord. LXX: ... Luther and the Belgians: Moreover, in his affliction Ahaz increased his transgressions against the LORD. Kimchi, in his commentary on Ps. 105.7, enumerates five uses of הוא [hu] that are taken in a bad sense. Among them, however, none is more notable than the one we are now dealing with. I will quote the words of the chief of the grammarians: אתה מוצא המשרה / הוא לרעה והמשרה לטובה [atah motze hamishrah hu lera vehamishrah letovah], that is, you will find five Hu in bad sense and five Hu in good sense. The five in a bad sense are these: (1) הוא, THAT is Esau, father of the Edomites, Gen. 36 last verse; (2) הוא, THAT is Dathan and Abiram, Num. 26.9; (3) הוא, THAT is King Ahaz, 2 Chron. 28.22; (4) הוא, THAT is Ahasuerus, Esth. 1; (5) הוא, THAT is (Nimrod), who was mighty in hunting, Gen. 10.5.

units.la: V. In bonum ista recenset, 1. הוא ILLE Abraham, Genef. 2. הוא ILLE Moses & Aharon, Exod. 6. 27. 3. הוא ILLE Ezra qui ascendit ex Babel, Ezr. 7. 6.
units.tr: The five in a good sense he lists as follows: (1) הוא, THAT is Abraham, Gen.; (2) הוא, THAT is Moses and Aaron, Exod. 6.27; (3) הוא, THAT is Ezra, who went up from Babylon, Ezra 7.6.

units.la: 4. הוא ILLE Hiskias obthuraverat, &c. 2. Chr. 32. 30. His quatuor locis subjicit hæc verba, אשר רי ברכיה והאלהים נמנה עם הצדקים id est Dicit R. Berachja, Deus numeratur cum justis. Hoc ergo ponit quintum הוא /
units.tr: (4) הוא, THAT is Hezekiah, who stopped up..., 2 Chron. 32.30, etc. To these four passages he adds the words אשר רי ברכיה והאלהים נמנה עם הצדקים [asher R. units.la: Reliquae autem res Jehojakimi & abominationes ejus quas fecit, והנמצא עליו Ecce illa scripta sunt in libro, &c. ] Voces istas Ebraicas Vulgatus reddit, & quod inventum est in eo, על pro ב enallage non insolente. Lutheri & Belgica, abominationes quas faciebat, und die an ihm funden wurden / Belgicè, ende die aen hem ghevonden worden / quæ verba multi Interpretes accepère hoc sensu, & quæ inventa sunt in corpore ejus. Lyra, stigmata & figuras quas fecerat in corpore suo in honorem idolorum. Carthus. stigmata vel incisiones, quæ in corpore ejus examini reperta sunt, quas vivens corpori suo impressit, in honorem deorum suorum. Contra quod Levit. 19. Dominus jußit, super mortuo non incidetis carnes vestras, neque figuras aliquas & stigmata facietis vobis. Hæc ille. Eadem leges in notis Emmanuelis Sa. Scholiastes Belgicus, Abominationes quæ in ipsius cadavere inventa sunt, fuerunt certa quaedam stigmata corpori ejus impressa scripta, ceu memorialia fœderis cum falsis DIs initi. Consuetudo hac fuit superstitiosorum idololatrarum, sicuti etiamnum Magorum & exorcistarum. Illi enim plerunque certa quadam nota à Diabolo notati sunt. In eundem modum Judæos quoque notatos esse perhibent. Quod de Judæis memorat miror unde hauserit. Illi certi in carne sua notam Judaïsmi habent, præsectum vid. præputium carnis. Sed eo non opinor Scholiasten respicere. De magis & exorcistis viderint alii. Ἰπποκλείδης. Jehojakimum quod attinet, ipse quoque R. Sal. illa verba הנמצא עליו explicat de קעקע cujus mentio fit Levit. 19. 28. Jun. reddit, inscriptionem stigmatis. Hac de re extat locus in Thalmud, Massechath Sanhedrin, cap. 3. Misna 6. הכותב כתובת קעקע ולא קעקע / קעקע ולא כתב אינו חייב עד שיכתוב ויקעקע בדיו ובכחול ובכל דבר שהוא רושם hoc est, qui scribit scripturam stigmatis: (repete ex primo §, flagellandus est) qui scribit & non incidit, qui incidit & non scribit, non est reus [flagellationis,] usque dum scribat & stigma faciat vel atramento vel stibio, vel alia aliqua re, qua tingat. Scholiastes τὸ קעקע explicat incidere carni figuras literarum, atque ipsas cæsuras implere atramento vel stibio. Postea addit ex sententia R. Simeonis ben Juda illud quoque requirequiri, antequam in aliquem flagellis animadverti possit, ut incidat carni nomen aliquod idoli. Habes explicationem loci istius, qui in Levit. 19. 28. Caeterum hic tales caesuras denotari, ex textu non euiceris. Puto simplicius reddi, & quod inventum est in eo, & respici vel ad occulta ejus peccata quae Deus tandem in apricum protulit, aut ad crimen rebellionis, de quo 2. Reg. 24. 3. quod video placuisse Jun. & Piscatori, qui voces Ebraeas sic reddidere, & quod deprehensum fuit in eo. Sa, vel opera, quae deprehensus est fecisse. Vide & Genev. & Anglos.
units.tr: "As for the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim and the abominations that he committed, and what was found upon him [והנמצא עליו]: behold, they are written in the book, etc." The Vulgate translator renders these Hebrew words as "and what was found in him", with al put for b, an enallage that is not unusual. Luther's version has abominations which he practised, und die an ihm funden wurden ("and those that were found on him"); the Belgic version has ende die aen hem ghevonden worden ("and those found on him"). Many interpreters have taken the words in this sense: "and what was found in his body." Lyra gives: the brands and figures which he had made on his body in honour of idols. The Carthusian gives: brands or incisions which were found on his body when it was examined, which he impressed on his body while alive in honour of his gods. Against this, the Lord commanded in Levit. 19: "You shall not cut your flesh for the dead, nor make any figures or brands on yourselves." So far he. The same things are read in the notes of Emmanuel Sa. The Belgic scholiast: The abominations which were found on his corpse were certain marks or written brands impressed on his body, as memorials of the covenant made with false gods. This custom belonged to superstitious idolaters, as it still does to magicians and exorcists, for they are commonly marked with a certain sign by the Devil. They report that the Jews were marked in the same way. I wonder where he got what he says about the Jews. They have a mark of Judaism in their flesh, namely the foreskin. But I do not think the scholiast has this in view. Let others look into the matter of magicians and exorcists. [Ἰπποκλείδης] Hippoclides. As for Jehoiakim, R. Salomon himself also explains the words vehannimtsa aleiv [והנמצא עליו] of qaqa' [קעקע], which is mentioned in Levit. 19:28. Junius renders it an inscription of a brand. There is a passage on this matter in the Talmud, Massechath Sanhedrin, chapter 3, Mishnah 6: hakotev ketovet qaqa' velo qaqa' / qaqa' velo katav eino chayav [הכותב כתובת קעקע ולא קעקע / קעקע ולא כתב אינו חייב], that is, "He who writes an inscription of a brand" (repeat from the first §, he is to be flogged); "he who writes and does not cut, he who cuts and does not write, is not liable [to flogging] until he both writes and makes the brand with ink, or antimony, or some other substance that stains." The scholiast explains qaqa' as cutting figures of letters into the flesh and filling the cuts themselves with ink or antimony. Afterwards he adds, following the opinion of R. Simeon ben Judah, that it is also required, before anyone can be punished with stripes, that he cut into his flesh the name of some idol. You have the explanation of that passage, which concerns Levit. 19:28. Yet from the text you cannot prove that such cuttings are meant here. I think it is more simply rendered and what was found in him, and that it refers either to his hidden sins, which God at last brought into the open, or to the crime of rebellion, of which 2 Kings 24:3 speaks. I see that this pleased Junius and Piscator, who rendered the Hebrew words thus: and what was detected in him. Sa: or the works which he was found to have done. See also the Geneva and the English versions.

units.la: Et eduxisti eum de igne Chaldaeorum. ] Ita vulgatus hoc unico loco interpretatus istas voces Ebraeas מאור כשדים / quae alibi reddidit, ex Vr Chaldaeorum. Ex. gr. Gen. 11. 31. Lxx. ἐν χωρᾳ τῶν Χαλδαίων id est in regione Chaldaeorum. Sed Vr nomen urbis est, quam Οὐρὴν & Οὐρίαν vocant. Meminit Eupolemus. Eusebius lib. 9. Praepar. Euang. notat etiam Camarinam dici, forte à chamarim, id est sacerdotibus, qui hic loci fixas sedes habuerint. Vox Ebraea אור etiam ignem significat, atque hinc est πῦρ & Belg. vuyr, & Latinum uro. Quae tamen alii ab Ebraeo בער deflectunt. Literae B. P & V. ejusdem organi cum sint, de facili inter se commutantur. Hanc sententiam firmat priscum buro, unde bustum, amburo comburo, quamvis & de his alii aliter statuant. Vide Becmanni orig-linlinguæ Lat. & Martinii Lexicon Etym. in Bustum. Sed redeamus ad אור /existimarunt nonnulli, in hac urbe conservatum fuisse sacrum illum ignem, quem Chaldæos coluisse asserunt, atque inde dictam fuisse VR, quomodo Heliopolis dicta, à cultu solis. Certe Persas coluisse ignem instar numinis Pro- copius in Persicis author est. Extat quoque insignis hac de re locus apud Strabonem lib. 15. ubi Magi, queis perennis istius ignis cura mandata erat, πυρέϑοι, *sempiterni autem Magorum fo- culi, πυρεῖϑεα vocantur. ἱστ ἢ ἡ πυρεῖϑεα, inquit, οἱ οἱ πυρ ἀξιόλογοι ἐν ἢ τόπος μέσοις βωμὸς ἐν ᾧ πολλὴ π ἀπὸ ... , καὶ πῦρ ἀσβεστον φυλάσσειν οἱ Μάγοι. Hæc vero apud Suidam & alios πυρεῖα vocantur. Verba Suidæ, ὁ ἢ ἡ ἡρακλεῖος τὸς π πόλις καθαίρει. καὶ τὸ πυρεῖα διεσπέρσε ἢ περσῶν id est Heraclius autem urbes subvertit, & pyrea Persarum evertit. Hæc sacra Persas à Chaldæis accepisse conjectat Agathias historiarum lib. 2. & multi eruditi asserunt. Cui sententiæ ut non refragor, ita & suffragari illis non possum, qui nec scripturæ nec cordati alicujus authoris testimonio nixi, Abrahamum, quod ignem adorare detrectaret, jubente Nimrodo, in ignem fuisse conjectum: at, Deo curam sui cultoris gerente, illæsum exivisse, prodiderunt. Huic narrationi, cujus nec Moses, nec prophetæ nec Philo nec Josephus, nec Apostolus Ebr. 11. nec Stephanus Actor. 7. meminere, quam ipse quoque Hieronymus alibi sugillat, ex quorundam Ebræorum lacunis primitus haustam, plerique interpretes Pontificii ex hoc loco sidem conciliarunt.
units.tr: And you brought him out of the fire of the Chaldeans.] The Vulgate translator renders the Hebrew words מאור כשדים here alone, although elsewhere he renders them as out of Ur of the Chaldeans. For example, Gen. 11.31. The Septuagint has ἐν χώρᾳ τῶν Χαλδαίων, that is, in the region of the Chaldeans. But Ur is the name of a city, which they call Οὐρὴν and Οὐρίαν. Eupolemus mentions it, and Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 9, notes that it is also called Camarina, perhaps from chamarim, that is, priests, who had fixed seats in this place. The Hebrew word אור also means fire, and from this come πῦρ, the Dutch vuyr, and the Latin uro. Others, however, derive these from the Hebrew בער, to burn. The letters B, P and V come from the same organ of speech, so they are easily interchanged with one another. The old Latin buro supports this view, whence bustum, amburo, comburo, although others judge these differently. See Becmann's Origines Linguae Latinae and Martinius' Etymological Lexicon under Bustum. But let us return to אור. Some have thought that the sacred fire which the Chaldeans are said to have worshipped was preserved in this city, and that for this reason it was called Ur, just as Heliopolis was named after the worship of the sun. Procopius, in his Persica, attests that the Persians worshipped fire as a deity. There is a notable passage on this subject in Strabo, book 15, where the Magi, to whom the perpetual care of that fire was entrusted, are said to keep the fire-altars (πυρεῖα), and the eternal hearths of the Magi are called pyreia [πυρεῖα]. Strabo says there is in the middle of the place an altar on which a great quantity of ash [...], and that the Magi keep an unquenchable fire. In Suidas and others these are called pyreia [πυρεῖα]. The words of Suidas are: "Heraclius destroyed the cities and overthrew the Persians' pyrea [πυρεῖα]", that is, Heraclius indeed overthrew cities, and overthrew the pyrea of the Persians. Agathias, in book 2 of his Histories, conjectures that the Persians received these rites from the Chaldeans, and many learned men assert the same. I do not dispute this view, but I cannot agree with those who, relying neither on the testimony of Scripture nor on that of any sound author, have reported that Abraham, when he refused to worship fire, was cast into the fire at the command of Nimrod, but that God, taking care of his worshipper, let him come out unharmed. Neither Moses, nor the prophets, nor Philo, nor Josephus, nor the Apostle in Hebrews 11, nor Stephen in Acts 7 mention this story, which Jerome himself elsewhere ridicules as drawn first from the puddles of certain Hebrews. Most Papist interpreters have lent credence to it on the basis of this passage.

units.la: ATque ita tandem libros Historicos præterve�въpдi, ad difficillimorum librorum littora delati sumus. Plenioribus velis laxatisque scriptionis rudentibus hactenus navigavimus. Nunc contrahenda sunt vela. Certe si eodem modo progrederemur & ruspando ventilaremus, quicquid in his libris male conversum ineptiendi materiam scriptoribus præbuit, non libellum sed tomos aliquot daremus. Singuli qui jam secedunt libri, Job, PsalPsalmi, Proverbia, Jesaias, Jeremias, Jezechiel, & δωδεκα- προφητῶν spissi voluminis argumentum possint suppeditare. Itaque brevitatis rationem habituri, tantum insigniora quædam loca delibabimus. Si placebit hæc mea opella studiosæ juventuti (illi enim non viris literatis graficamur hanc operam) & vita suppetet, de spicilegio cogitabimus. Sin minus, jam opinor; sat olei & operæ & chartæ perditum est. Ut ergo ipsum Jobum aggrediamur, vel solius Gregorii, licet Pontificis, quæ in hunc librum exaravit, Moralia docent, quantum detrimenti scripturarum Interpreti afferat minus accurata versio & originariæ linguæ ignorantia. Sed & ipsum modum commentandi quod attinet, punctum meum ferat Pontificius ille Theologus cujus sententiam perstringit *Ribera. Ea autem hæc erat, quæ B. Pater Gregorius in librum Job scripsit, ea in quemvis alium ex sacris libris scribi potuisse. Quod fortasse & alii sentiunt, inquit Ribera, tametsi minus audaces sint ad dicendum. Indigna profecto Theologo vox, pergit Ribera, & ingrati animi index, qui non solum de opere detrahat clarissimo & utilissimo, & quo nunquam nullum melius in libris patrum habuit Ecclesia; sed etiam de omnium sanctorum laboribus qui cum magno fructu in hoc scriptionis genere defudarunt. Mihi nec voluntas nec facultas est, maximi viri laboribus vel tantillum detrahere, manebit illis per me suum æstimium. Hoc tantum in me recipio, me pauculorum exemplorum inductione ostensurum, quam procul à mente sanctissimi scriptoris passim exorbitaverit, dum exorbitantis Interpretis legit vestigia.
units.tr: And so at last, having passed by the historical books, we have come to the shores of the most difficult books. Up to now we have sailed with fuller sails and loosened ropes of writing. Now the sails must be furled. Certainly, if we proceeded in the same way and sifted out whatever in these books has been badly rendered and has given scribblers material for silliness, we would produce not a little book but several volumes. Each of the books that now follow, Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve Prophets, could supply the subject matter of a thick volume. So, mindful of brevity, I will touch only on some of the more notable passages. If this little work of mine pleases studious youth (for it is to them, not to learned men, that I offer this labour) and if life is granted to me, I will consider a gleaning. If not, I suppose enough oil, labour and paper have been wasted already. Now, to take up Job itself: the Moralia of Gregory, though he was a Pope, teaches how much harm a less accurate version and ignorance of the original language do to the interpreter of Scripture. But as to the very method of commenting, let that Papist theologian whose opinion he criticises, Ribera, support my view. Ribera's opinion was this: what Blessed Father Gregory wrote on Job could be written on any other of the sacred books. Perhaps others also think so, though they are less bold to say it. An unworthy voice for a theologian, Ribera goes on, and a sign of an ungrateful mind, which detracts not only from a work so famous and so useful, than which the Church has never had a better among the writings of the Fathers, but also from the labours of all the saints who sweated with great fruit in this kind of writing. I have neither the will nor the ability to detract even a little from the labours of so great a man; they will keep their esteem through me. I take on only this task: by bringing forward a few examples, I will show how far he has strayed, in many places, from the mind of that most holy writer, while following the footsteps of the wandering interpreter.

units.la: Verf. 1. Job, &c.] Dionysius Carthus. allegoricæ libri hujus interpretationi, qua pleraque de Christo interpretatur, hoc fundamentum substernit, Jobum verbis, tribulationibus, virtutibus, persona & nominis interpretatione Christum præfigurasse. Job quippe interpretatur dolens, Hus, sapientia. At neutrum verum esse (modo voces istæ Ebraicæ originis sint) etiam tirones noverint. Melius in seq. conjectavit, Hus etiam consiliatorem significare, yʾy enim Ebræis est consulere.
units.tr: Ver. 1. Job, &c.] Dionysius the Carthusian lays this foundation for his allegorical interpretation of this book, in which he explains most things about Christ: that Job prefigured Christ in his words, his afflictions, his virtues, his person and the interpretation of his name. Job, he says, means grieving, and Hus means wisdom. But even beginners know that neither is true, provided these words are of Hebrew origin. Dionysius conjectured better later on, that Hus also means counsellor, since yaʿats in Hebrew means to take counsel.
