units.la: Benedic Deo & morere] Belg. Ja zegent Godt ende sterft / Hæc verba vulgo sic accipiuntur, quasi maritum ad blasphemiam & desperationem provocaret. Unde multis eam convitiis in commentariis & concionibus passim perstringi videas. Et certe negari non potest, τὸ benedicere alibi pro maledicere καὶ ἀσφημισμὸν positum esse, ex gr. 2. Reg. 21. & supra 1. 11. & hoc ipso cap. vers. 5. Dominus Junius recessit quidem à vulgata interpretatione, dum vertit, benedicendo Deo & moriendo, nihilo tamen minus impium & blasphemum sarcasmum huic fœminæ tribuit. Ego, ut quod res est dicam, de istius interpretationis veritate semper dubitavi, ac proinde animus mihi sæpe fuit ministerii candidatos monere, ut ad sacras conciones admissi hæc verba expenderent diligentius, ac interim in matronam istam destomacharentur parcius. Et certe si ab ista mente, quæ ipsi vulgo tribuitur, alienam fuisse probari posset, satis diu immerenter traducta est. Si ejus verbis sine ulla violentia melior quædam mens induci, aut saltem prægnans ratio dubitan-di afferri potest, regula caritatis meliorem nos sententiam jubet eligere. Scio quam periculosæ opus plenum aleæ sit, receptas ejusmodi sententias convellere, ideo malo magni Bezæ, quam meis verbis locum hunc benignius interpretari. Mihi profecto, inquit, ne verisimile quidem ullo modo videtur, hanc in tam pia domo matremfamilias, hùc potuisse impelli, ut tam impudente sermone apud maritum uteretur, quum ipsi quoque sceleratissimi, si quid tale meditate faciant, aliquam saltem utilitatis inde ad ipsos reditura speciem ipsi sibi vel aliis proponant. Et paulo post. Quid ergo? ad me quidem quod attinet, salvo aliorum judicio, ausim affirmare hanc mulierem eandem prorsus causam egisse, atque postea Jobi amicos, & quidem non alia voluntate aut aliis rationibus impulsam: nempe non quod Jobi cruciatus augere studeat, sed quod ipsa sese fallens sibi persuasisset, hac una, quam suadebat ratione, posse Jobi saluti cavere, de cujus vita desperabat. Superest ergo, ut quid marito suaserit, quis fuerit ejus animus, quid item Satanas per illam sit molitus, videamus. Vxor Jobi marito in priore tentatione assensa, vel nihil ausa obloqui, mox illum cernens tam horrenda plaga percussum, & recte quidem statuens ista non nisi Deo, & quidem velut extra ordinem sic statuente accidisse: sed perperam judicans Deum nunquam haec fuisse decreturum nisi Jobo summe infensum: denique illum jam morti proximum esse arbitrata: primum mirata est illum interea taciturn sedere, nec magis in tanta calamitate, animo commotum, quam antea fuisset. Deinde non aliunde istud tam firmum silentium accidere posse cogitavit quam ex conscientia stupore: marito videlicet adhuc sua integritatis opinione fascinato, ideoque ne tum quidem iram Dei adversus ipsius peccata animadvertente. Hinc factum ut illud consilium caperet quod reis convictis & poenas mox luituris dari merito consuevit, nempe ut ante acta vita ingenua, prout res ipsa postulabat, apud Deum detestatione (hoc enim est Deo benedicere, id est Deo gloriam, agnito peccato tribuere, ut Josue 7. 19.) iram ejus deprecatus, sese ad mortem subeundam compararet. Error igitur omnis, in eo fuit quod hujus vitae miserias, praesertim tam atroces & insuetas, non aliunde quam a Deo irato proficisci credidit: quod tamen salsissimum esse testatur perpetua Ecclesia in hoc mundo conditio, & ostendunt quoque prophanae historiae, in quibus nullos plerunque videmus calamitosiores fuisse, quam qui virtuti prae ceteris studuerunt, qua de re plura in quartum caput dicemus. Nihil autem in Jobum dici indignius potuit, nec quo justius exacerbaretur, ut quem neque amissio tot bonorum, neque tam miserabilis orbitas, neque tam savi cruciatus corporis concutere potuerant, hac injuria pene ad desperationem adegerit, & Satanas Jobum prostratum tradiderit in manus. Etsi enim Jobo nunquam venit in mentem ut sua integritate niteretur, aut alibi quam in unius venturi redemptoris misericordia spem salutis suae reposuerit, ut loquitur infra 19.25. atque adeo licet in tam multiplicibus acceptis vulneribus, haec prae ceteris cogitatio jam tum illum graviter excruciare caperat, quinam Deus tam duriter cum ipso prae ceteris mortalibus ageret: ut ex ipsius verbis apparuit sup. 1.21. & ex proximo versu liquebit, sic illum in his omnibus calamitatibus erigebat integra conscientia, testimonium, ut contrariis omnibus cogitationibus renuntians, aequanimitate pene incredibili acquiesceret in Dei Opt. Max. voluntate. Nec aliud ei perfugium sane supererat, de quo propterea ipsi eripiendo unice laborat Satan, totus in eo ut terroribus conscientiae, quibus nihil est terribilius, cum amissione bonorum & cruciatibus corporis conjunctis, & illius quae sola illum sustentabat aequanimitatis loco substitutis, victoriam obtineret. In summa igitur uxor Jobi, misere seipsam fallens, & imprudenter Satana tanæ strenuè subserviens, hoc dictum pauci voluit. Adhuc perstas in integritate tua? id est, marite sic mutus jacens & tua integritatis opinione fretus, ne nunc quidem Deum tibi summè infensum animadvertis? Benedic Deo, id est potius quandiu tibi pauculum adhuc vita superest, tribue gloriam Deo ut justo judici, & peccatorum tuorum multitudinem ex magnitudine earum calamitatum quibus te impetit, æstimatam professus, te ipsum ad mortem sancti obeundam comparato.
units.tr: Bless God and die] In Dutch, Ja zegent Godt ende sterft. These words are commonly taken as if the wife were urging her husband to blasphemy and despair, and so you will see her attacked with many reproaches in commentaries and sermons everywhere. And certainly it cannot be denied that to bless (τὸ benedicere) is elsewhere used for to curse and to revile [καὶ ἀσφημισμόν], for example in 2 Kings 21, and above in 1.11, and in this same chapter at verse 5. Mr. Junius indeed departed from the Vulgate translation when he rendered it bless God and die, yet he nonetheless attributed an impious and blasphemous sarcasm to this woman. For my part, to say what the matter is, I have always doubted the truth of that interpretation, and so I have often felt inclined to advise candidates for the ministry that, before they are admitted to preach, they should weigh these words more carefully and meanwhile speak more sparingly against that matron. And certainly, if it could be shown that her words are foreign to the intention commonly ascribed to them, she has been unjustly maligned for a long time. If a better sense can be drawn from her words without any violence, or at least a weighty reason for doubt can be offered, the rule of charity bids us choose the better opinion. I know how dangerous it is to overturn opinions that have been received in this way, and so I prefer to quote the great Beza rather than interpret this passage more kindly in my own words. To me indeed, he says, it does not even seem in any way likely that this woman, in so pious a household, could have been driven to use such shameless speech to her husband, since even the most wicked people, if they plan anything of the kind, propose to themselves at least some appearance of advantage to come back to them or to others. And a little later: What then? As far as I am concerned, saving the judgement of others, I would venture to affirm that this woman pleaded exactly the same cause as Job's friends later did, and was moved by no other will or reasons: namely not because she wished to increase Job's torments, but because, deceiving herself, she had persuaded herself that by this one way which she recommended she could provide for Job's safety, since she despaired of his life. It remains, therefore, that we consider what she advised her husband, what her intention was, and likewise what Satan contrived through her. Job's wife, having assented to her husband in the first temptation, or having dared to say nothing in reply, then seeing him struck with so horrible a plague, and rightly judging that these things had come not from anything but God, and indeed from God deciding in an extraordinary way, but wrongly judging that God would never have decreed these things unless he were utterly hostile to Job, and finally thinking that he was already close to death, first wondered that he sat silent in the meantime, and was not more moved in spirit in so great a calamity than he had been before. Then she thought that such a firm silence could arise from nothing else than from stupor of conscience: namely, that her husband was still bewitched by his opinion of his own integrity, and therefore did not even then perceive the anger of God against his sins. Hence it came about that she adopted that counsel which is customarily and rightly given to convicted criminals who are about to pay the penalty: namely, that, with a frank confession of their past life, as the thing itself required, they should beseech God's anger by detestation before him (for this is to bless God, that is, to give glory to God by acknowledging sin, as in Joshua 7.19), and prepare themselves to undergo death. Therefore all her error lay in this, that she believed the miseries of this life, especially such atrocious and unusual ones, came from nowhere but an angry God; and the perpetual condition of the Church in this world testifies that this is most false, and profane history also shows it, in which we see that very few were more calamitous than those who gave themselves to virtue above others; on this matter we will say more at chapter 4. Nothing more unworthy could be said of Job, nor anything that would more justly provoke him, since she, whom neither the loss of so many goods, nor so miserable a bereavement, nor such cruel bodily torments had been able to shake, sought to drive him almost to despair by this injury, and Satan delivered Job, cast down, into her hands. For although it never came into Job's mind to rely on his own integrity, or to place the hope of his salvation anywhere but in the mercy of one coming Redeemer, as he says below at 19.25, and although, amid so many wounds received, this thought had already begun to torment him sorely, namely why God dealt so harshly with him above other mortals, as appeared from his own words above at 1.21 and will be clear from the next verse, nevertheless his integrity of conscience and testimony raised him up in all these calamities, so that, renouncing all contrary thoughts, he acquiesced in the will of God Most Good and Most Great with an almost incredible equanimity. Nor indeed had he any other refuge left, and so Satan labours solely to snatch this from him, wholly intent on obtaining victory by terrors of conscience, than which nothing is more terrible, together with the loss of goods and the torments of the body, and with these put in place of that equanimity which alone sustained him. In sum, therefore, Job's wife, wretchedly deceiving herself and imprudently serving Satan with vigour, wished to say this: Do you still persist in your integrity? that is, husband, lying so silent and relying on your opinion of your integrity, do you not even now perceive God to be utterly hostile to you? Bless God, that is, rather, while there is still a little life left in you, give glory to God as to a just judge, confessing that the multitude of your sins is to be reckoned by the greatness of the calamities with which he assails you, and prepare yourself to undergo death as a holy man.

units.la: Vers. 10. Dixit autem ipse ad eam, Sicut loquitur una stultarum, loqueris. Scilicet bonum à Deo excepimus, & malum non excipiemus? In hoc toto non peccavit Jobus labiis suis. Caterum constat hoc responsum partim increpatione, partim repulsa. Ad increpationem quod attinet, nec eorum sententiam sequor, qui accentu interrogante illam emolliunt, ac si diceret Jobus, tene crediderim stultarum mulierum more loqui? nec eos probo qui stultam pro insana & impia interpretantur, quod fateor interdum Hebræa voce Nabal intelligi, & sanè huic mulieri optimè conveniret, si tam præsertim impudenter maritum ad Deum ipsum execrandum esset hortata, quam expositionem antea refutavi. Stultam igitur opponit sapienti & circumspecta. Nec enim quod suadebat uxor, per se & simpliciter malum erat, quum écontrario nihil sit reis convictis illa commonefactione magis necessarium: sed in ejus consilii applicatione gravissimè peccarat adversus maritum, minime omnium talem, qualem illum esse falsò ex tot calamitatum magnitudine colligebat. Hactenus Dn. Beza.
units.tr: Ver. 10. But he said to her, You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. Shall we indeed receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this Job did not sin with his lips. Moreover, it is agreed that this answer is partly a rebuke and partly a rejection. As for the rebuke, I do not follow those who soften it with an interrogative accent, as if Job were saying, Did I believe you would speak in the manner of foolish women? Nor do I approve those who interpret foolish as mad and impious, though I admit that the Hebrew word nabal is sometimes understood in this way, and indeed it would suit this woman very well, if she had urged her husband so shamelessly to curse God himself, which exposition I refuted before. He therefore sets the foolish woman against the wise and circumspect one. For what the wife advised was not in itself and simply evil, since on the contrary nothing is more necessary for convicted criminals than that admonition; but in applying her counsel she sinned gravely against her husband, who was by no means such as she falsely concluded from the greatness of his calamities. Thus far Mr. Beza.

units.la: CAP. VI. vers. 16.
units.tr: Chapter VI, verse 16.

units.la: Qui timent pruinam, irruet super eos nix] Ita Vulg. & qui imitatus est, Lutherus, & ex eo Belgica. Abiit hic versus in proverbialem sententiam, qua docetur, eos qui amico subvenire [ aut aliud quodlibet bonum opus ] omittunt, timore damni minoris quod exprimitur per pruinam, majus incommodum passuros, quod pernivem denotatur. Hæc Carthuf. At Ebræa hunc sensum neutiquam admittuut: הַקּוֹרִים מִנִּי קֹרָה עֲלֵימוֹ יִתְעַלַּם שָׁלֵג nec קֹר metuere nec קָרָח pruinam significat. Voces Ebræas Pagninus sic convertit, Qui [torrentes] denigrantur propter glaciem, in iis occultatur nix. Arias, Nigrescentes pra gelu, super iis occultabitur nix. Versus & hic & sequentes pendent à superiori. Ecce enim amicorum suorum perfidiam exagitaturus, utitur similitudine sumpta à torrentibus, qui cum hyeme exundent, ubi nulla aquæ penuria est, videnturque æstate etiam perennaturi, tunc cum maximus eorum usus est, derepente tamen exarescunt & spes viatorum eludunt. Vide Junium, Pisc. Angl. Genev. Hisp. Tigur. Ital Benedictum, &c. Loco aliàs facillimo tenebras offuderunt nonnulli, quod pleraque quæ de torrentibus dicuntur, eaque minus benè intellecta hominibus tribuerunt.
units.tr: "They who fear the hoarfrost, the snow will fall upon them." So the Vulgate, and Luther after him, and the Belgic version. The phrase has passed into a proverbial saying, teaching that those who neglect to help a friend (or to do any other good work) out of fear of a smaller loss, signified by the hoarfrost, will suffer a greater harm, signified by the snow. So the Carthusian. But the Hebrew does not admit this sense at all: those who are darkened by the ice, upon them the snow is hidden [הַקּוֹרִים מִנִּי קֹרָה עֲלֵימוֹ יִתְעַלַּם שָׁלֵג]. The word קֹר does not mean to fear, nor does קָרָח mean hoarfrost. Pagninus renders the Hebrew words thus: "Those [torrents] are darkened because of the ice; in them the snow is hidden." Arias: Blackened by the frost, upon them the snow will be hidden. Both this verse and those that follow depend on the one before. For Job, about to upbraid the treachery of his friends, uses a comparison taken from torrents, which overflow in winter, when there is no lack of water, and seem likely to last even into summer, when their use is greatest; yet suddenly they dry up and disappoint the hopes of travellers. See Junius, Piscator, the English version, Geneva, the Spanish, the Zurich, the Italian, Benedictus, and others. Some have cast darkness over a passage otherwise very easy, by attributing to men much of what is said of torrents, and that less well understood.

units.la: CAP. VII. verf. 3.
units.tr: Chapter VII, verse 3.

units.la: Militia est vita homis super terram] Ita Vulg. Belgæ, Luth. amon oportet hominem semper in prælio esse in terra? Lxx. πόλεμος ... ὁ βίος ... ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; verba in Latina Versione. sic legebantur, nunquid * non tentatio est vita humana super terram? Vide Gregor. August. de Civit. Dei. 19. & 8.29. Hic multa egregia de tentationibus & insultibus, quibus homo obnoxius vivit, convectarunt interpretes. Quod ad Lxx. attinet, observa tiro, eos sensu à Vulgato discrepare, Tentatio enim est pugna contra hostes & spiritus malignos: militia verò exercitium contra adversarios appellatur, inquit Greg. Textus originarius ista habet הלא צבא לאנש על הארץ / quæ simpliciter vertuntur à Pagn. Merc. Anglis, Cypriano de Valera, annon præfinitum tempus est homini in terra? præfinitum tempus scilicet vitæ suæ, quæ & hic & alibi egregie comparatur militiæ. Deod. & Genev. utramque versionem conjunxerunt, ut צבא per metonymiam hic significet tempus præfinitum militia. Hæc itaque versio alteram includit & aliam insuper doctrinam pio lectori repræsentat. Quam prolixe tractat Job cap. 14. צבא significat exercitum, militiam & præfinitum seu determinatum tempus militiæ, tam sacræ, quam profanæ. Namque & sacrum Levitarum ministerium propter excubias, labores varios, & ordines quasi militares, militia vocatur. Egregius locus est. Num. 4.3. & 24. A nato 30. annos & deinceps usque ad natum 50. annos recensefo illos: omnem aptum לצבא ad militandum militiam, quæ aliis verbis immediate sequentibus explicantur, לעבוד עבודה ad colendum cultum in tentorio conventus. Vbi etiam terminos habes,
units.tr: "The life of man upon the earth is a warfare." So the Vulgate, the Belgic version, and Luther: Must not man always be in battle on earth? The Seventy: [πόλεμος ... ὁ βίος ... ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] war ... the life ... upon the earth; in the Latin version the words were read thus: Is not human life upon the earth a trial? See Gregory and Augustine, On the City of God, books 19 and 8.29. Here the interpreters have gathered many excellent remarks on the temptations and assaults to which man is exposed while he lives. As to the Seventy, let the beginner note that they differ in sense from the Vulgate: tentatio (temptation) is a struggle against enemies and evil spirits, while militia (warfare) is called the exercise against adversaries, says Gregory. The original text has [הלא צבא לאנש על הארץ] Is there not a warfare for man upon the earth?, which Pagninus, the Merc. [version], the English, and Cyprian de Valera translate simply as Is there not an appointed time for man upon the earth? namely the appointed time of his life, which here and elsewhere is aptly compared to warfare. The Diodati and Geneva versions have joined both renderings, so that [צבא] here signifies by metonymy an appointed time of warfare. This version therefore includes the other and sets before the pious reader a further teaching. Job treats it at length in chapter 14. The word [צבא] signifies an army, warfare, and an appointed or determined time of warfare, both sacred and profane. For the sacred ministry of the Levites, with its watches, varied labours and quasi-military orders, is also called warfare. An excellent passage is Num. 4.3 and 24: From thirty years old and upward, even until fifty years old, you shall number them: every one fit [לצבא] to wage warfare, which in the words immediately following is explained as [לעבוד עבודה] to serve the service in the tent of meeting. There you also have the limits, [see the note below].

units.la: * vox Græca magis significat, locum, officinam vel palæstram tentationis, Ambr reddit, tentamentum. habes, quos ultra citraque sacra ministeria non obibant. Nam quod cap. 8.24. terminus à quo in 25. anno figitur, sic conciliant Interpretes, ut quinquennium illud tyrocinio deponen-do destinatum fuisse velint. Quod vero ad locum 1. Chron.23.23. & 26. attinet, adi ad notas Junii. De termino ad quem, vide Num.viii.25.26. cum itaque utraque illa militia tempus determinatum & praefinitum habuerit, certe non insolente metonymia praefinitum tempus denotat. Atque hanc ei notionem tribuunt interpretes Job. 14.10. Jesa. 40.2. & alibi. Genevensium versio ita habet, n'y a-il pas comme un train de guerre ordonné aux mortels sur la terre? Rev. & clarissimus Deodatus in Gallica versione, cujus specimen superiori anno Geneva ad me transmisit, l'homme n'a-il pas un terme de guerre sur la terre? Idem in versione Ital. Non ha l'huomo un termine della sua militia in su la terra? id est annon habet homo terminum sua militia in terra? Hunc sensum firmat sequens hemistichium, & sicut dies mercenarii dies ejus? Dies mercenarii Scriptura pro praefinitis iisque paucis usurpare amat, vide Jesai. 16.14. aliis 23. Item 21. 16. Sic ergo putarim, salvo doctiorum judicio, locum istum Belgicè reddendum, En heeft de menschc niet een bestemde tijdt spnes strijdts op aerden?
units.tr: * The Greek word rather means a place, workshop or wrestling-ground of trial; Ambrose renders it tentamentum. You have those who did not perform the sacred ministries either beyond or short of the prescribed ages. For as to Num. 8.24, where the starting point is fixed at the age of twenty-five, the interpreters reconcile it by supposing that those five years were set aside for apprenticeship. As to the passage 1 Chron. 23.23 and 26, see the notes of Junius. On the terminus ad quem, see Num. 8.25-26. Since, then, both kinds of warfare had a determined and appointed time, it is certain that the appointed time is denoted by a metonymy that is not unusual. And the interpreters give this sense to Job 14.10, Isaiah 40.2, and elsewhere. The Geneva version reads: Is there not, as it were, a warfare ordained for mortals upon the earth? The reverend and most distinguished Diodati, in his French version, a specimen of which he sent to me from Geneva last year: Has man not a term of warfare upon the earth? The same in his Italian version: Does not man have a term of his warfare upon the earth? that is, annon habet homo terminum sua militia in terra? This sense is confirmed by the following half-verse: and like the days of a hired man, his days? Scripture is fond of using "the days of a hired man" for appointed and short periods; see Isaiah 16.14 and, in other places, 23; likewise 21.16. So I should think, saving the judgement of the more learned, that this passage ought to be rendered in Dutch thus: Has not man an appointed time of warfare upon the earth?

units.la: CAP. XI. vers. 19.
units.tr: CHAP. XI. verse 19.

units.la: Et multi precabuntur faciem tuam. ] id est supplices fient. Ebr. [Hebrew] / Gen. & plusieurs te feront la cour. Luth. und viel wurden fur dir stehen id est multi tibi blandirentur. Indocti librarii unius literae additione ex stehen / fecerunt stehen / Atque hanc ipsam corruptam lectionem inter alias editiones exhibet & Witebergensis in octavo, anni 1615. At Herbornensis anni 1612. legit, stehen. Nostrer Interpres phrasin Ebr. alibi bene expressit, Ex gr. Ps. 119. 58. Ick smeke voor uwen angheficht. At hoc loco librariorum sphalma dum non advertit, in foedum errorem delatus est, ende vele sullen voor u blieden. id est & multi coram te fugient. Belgico Interpreti nihil detraho. Imo profiteor, plurimum ei debere Belgicas Ecclesias. Rem magnam praestitisse isto saeculo, ista tempestate, cum sub cruce gemerent Ecclesiae. Demiror sanctissimi viri humilimilitatem qui laudem ullam ex hoc labore adeo non quaesivit, ut ne nunc quidem ejus nomen sciamus. Hoc tantum volo ostendere, quam periculosæ plenum opus aleæ sit, versionem ex versione adornare, fontibus ad singulos versus imo & voces non consultis. Similem errorem videbis ad Jesai. cap. xi. 12. Habes & affine C A P. XII. 23. hujus libri Multiplicat gentes & יאבדם perdit eas. Luth. multiplicat gentes, und brengtse wider umb / id est & perdit eas rursus, Belgicus Interpres voces istas wider umb in unam conflavit, en brengthse wederom / id est reducit eas. Quem tamen errorem in codicibus, qui à Liesvelt & Bieftkens nomen habent, correctum videbis.
units.tr: "And many will seek your face." ] That is, they will become suppliants. Hebrew [יחלו פניך]. Geneva: "plusieurs te feront la cour" (many will pay court to you). Luther: "und viel wurden fur dir stehen," that is, many will flatter you. Unskilled copyists, by adding a single letter, changed "flehen" (to beseech) into "stehen" (to stand), and this corrupt reading appears in other editions, including the Wittenberg octavo of 1615. The Herborn edition of 1612, however, reads "stehen." Our own interpreter rendered the Hebrew idiom well elsewhere, for example at Ps. 119:58: "Ick smeke voor uwen angheficht" (I melt before your face). But here, since he did not notice the copyists' slip, he was led into a shameful error: "ende vele sullen voor u blieden," that is, "and many will flee before you." I take nothing away from the Belgic interpreter. Indeed, I declare that the Belgic churches owe him very much. He performed a great service for that age, in that storm, when the churches groaned under the cross. I marvel at the humility of this most saintly man, who sought no praise at all from this labour, so that not even now do we know his name. I wish only to show how dangerous a task it is to fashion a version from a version, without consulting the sources for each verse, and indeed for individual words. You will see a similar error at Isaiah 11:12. You also have a related case in chap. XII. 23 of this book: "Multiplicat gentes" and [יאבדם] "perdit eas." Luther: "multiplicat gentes, und brengtse wider umb," that is, "and destroys them again." The Belgic interpreter fused "wider umb" into one word, "en brengthse wederom," that is, "reduces them" (reducit eas). Yet you will see that this error was corrected in the copies which bear the names of Liesvelt and Bieftkens.

units.la: CAP. XIII. verf. 14.
units.tr: CHAP. XIII. verse 14.

units.la: Et animam meam porto in manibus meis. [ Hanc phrasin non intellexit Gregorius, cujus hæc verba sunt Animam in manibus portare, est intentionem cordis in operatione ostendere. Et paulo post Qui igitur intentionem suam per opera insinuat, animam suam in manibus portat. Ponere animam in manibus suis, idem est, quod præsentissimum periculum adire, præsentissimo se exponere periculo. Confer * Psalm. 119. 109. Judicum 12. 3. 1. Sam. 19. 5. & 1. Sam. 28. 21. Atque hoc Carthuf. non ignoravit.
units.tr: "And I take my life in my hands." [This phrase Gregory did not understand. These are his words: "To carry the soul in the hands is to show the intention of the heart in action." And a little later: "He who therefore reveals his intention through works carries his soul in his hands." To put one's soul in one's hands means to face the most imminent danger, to expose oneself to the most present peril. Compare Ps. 119:109; Judges 12:3; 1 Sam. 19:5; and 1 Sam. 28:21. The Carthusian did not overlook this either.]

units.la: Verf, 15. egregie convertit vulgatus, Etiamsi occiderit me in ipso sperabo. Verba constantissimæ & immotæ fidei. Eo magis miror B. Lutherum hic exorbitasse. Sic enim ille, & ex eo Belgicus, Ecce occidet me, & non possum expectare. q. d. Video decretum esse Deo, me interficere, atque adeo ipse me gravissimis cruciatibus excarnificat, ut non possim expectare mortem. Velim jam jam perire. Stat sententia, ante capere mortem. Verba extremæ inpatientiæ. Diversitatis hujus causa in vocula לא latet. Scribitur לא non, legitur לי / ei. Lectionem omnes Ebraei sequuntur, & ex nostris Genev. Pisc. Hisp. Deod. Angli. Si (vel etsi) occideret me, [tamen] לא אירא in eum sperarem. Scripturam (לא non) cum Luthero elegerunt quidem Junius & Threm. sed sensu longe alio. Hi enim verba posteriora pronuntiatione juvant, seu quod idem est, subaudiunt ה interrogativum, Etiam si occideret me, annon sperarem in eum? eum? Sensu inquam Lutheri versioni plane adversante, at cum superiorum, qui לא legunt, sententia suaviter conspirante.
units.tr: In verse 15 the Vulgate translates admirably: "Etiamsi occiderit me, in ipso sperabo" ("Even if he slay me, in him will I hope"). These are the words of most constant and unshaken faith. All the more do I marvel that Luther went astray here. For he, and from him the Belgic version, has "Ecce occidet me, et non possum expectare," that is, "Behold, he will slay me, and I cannot wait." The sense is: "I see that God has decreed that I shall be killed, and indeed he himself so tortures me with the most grievous torments that I cannot wait for death. I would gladly die now." The meaning stands: to seize death beforehand. These are words of extreme impatience. The cause of this difference lies in the little word לא. It is written לא, "not," but read לי, "to me" (or "for him"). All the Hebrews follow this reading, and among ours the Geneva, Piscator, Spanish, Deodati and English versions do so: "If he were to slay me [yet] I would hope in him." Junius and Tremellius indeed chose the written form לא, with Luther, but in a very different sense. For they help the latter words by pronunciation, or, what is the same, they supply an interrogative ה: "Even if he were to slay me, would I not hope in him?" I say this is in the sense of Luther, which plainly opposes the version, but which harmonises sweetly with the meaning of those above who read לא.

units.la: CAP. XIV. verf. 5.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV. verse 5.

units.la: Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? nonne tu qui solus es? ] Ita Vulg. Quae in hunc modum interpretantur, Quis potest hominem ex immundo semine conceptum à peccatu purgare, virtutibus decorare? Nonne tu qui tu per essentiam mundus & sanctus es?. Qui solus es, id est solus omniformiter ac quomodolibet perfectum esse habes, in quo nihil est de non esse, nihil de imperfecto esse, sed tu es ipsum supersimplicissimum esse, plenum, persectum, immensum esse, &c. Haec Carthus. qui multa insuper addit de essentia Dei, citat locum Exod. 3. Ego sum. Qui est misit me ad vos, adducitque illud August. majus miraculum esse justificationem impii, quam creatio mundi. Hic enim nihil resistens erat. Illic resistebat mala voluntas, &c. Dicam paucis. Omnia bene. Sed nihil omnium istorum hic bene. Haec enim sunt Ebraea, מי יתן טהור ממטמא לא אחד / Ad verbum, quis dabit mundum de immundo? Non unus Video quid dici possit pro vulgato. Sed esto, legantur ultima verba interrogative, annon unus? Non video tamen illa, facere potest, non video vocem solus, non video verbum E S. Sensus clarus est, ut non egeat anxie interpretionis face. Graeci Lxx. τις γαρ καθαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥυπος, οὐκ ἔσθ' εἷς, ἐὰν καὶ μία ἡμέρα ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Quis enim purus erit è sordibus? Sed nullus, ne quidem, si unius tantum diei vita ejus esset in terra. In hunc modum solent hoc testimonium citare non solum Graeci Patres, sed ex & Latinis illi, qui Latinam ex Graeco traductam secuti sunt. Ex. gr. Ambrof. lib. 1. de Interpell. August. de Civ. Dei 20. 26. Sed August. aliquantulum discrepat, sic enim citat, nemo mundus à sorde, nec infans cuius est vita unius diei super terram. Adquem locum vide Lud. Vivem, licet aliud agentem. Bellarm. de amiss. gratiae lib. 4. cap. 4. in ipso limine ex hac translatione locum istum producit, additque sensum illum non difficulter in textu Ebr. inveniri posse, si vid. tres priores voces sequentis versus אם חרוצים ימין his assuantur. Sed fiat, quod tamen nec codices Ebraei, nec Chald. nec ipsa vulgata editio admittunt; exponantur illa verba, etiam si pauci dies] ejus : hinc tamen nec infantem, nec unum illum diem exsculpseris. Fateor tamen thesin illam. cui probandae hoc testimonium citat Bellarm. in verbo Dei satis esse fundatam.
units.tr: "Who can make the clean out of the unclean conceived in seed? Is it not you who alone are?" ] So the Vulgate. Those who interpret in this manner render it: "Who can free a man conceived from an unclean seed from sin and adorn him with virtues? Is it not you who are clean and holy by your essence? Who alone are, that is, you alone have being perfect in every form and in every way, in whom there is nothing of non-being, nothing of imperfect being, but you are the most simple being itself, full, perfect, immense being, etc." The Carthusian says this, and adds much more about the essence of God, citing Exodus 3: "I am who am has sent me to you," and he brings in Augustine's remark that the justification of the wicked is a greater miracle than the creation of the world, for there nothing resisted, whereas here an evil will resisted, etc. I will say briefly: all of this is fine, but none of it is fine here. For these are the Hebrew words: מי יתן טהור ממטמא לא אחד, literally, "who will give clean from unclean? Not one." I see what could be said for the Vulgate. But grant that the last words are read as a question, "is it not one?" I still do not see the words "can make," I do not see the word "alone," I do not see the word "est." The sense is clear enough not to need anxious interpretation. The Greek of the Seventy: "[τις γαρ καθαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥυπος, οὐκ ἔσθ' εἷς, ἐὰν καὶ μία ἡμέρα ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς]," "For who will be pure from filth? There is not one, not even if his life on earth were but a single day." In this way not only the Greek Fathers but also those Latins who followed the Latin translated from the Greek are accustomed to cite this testimony. For example, Ambrose, On the Interpellation, book 1; Augustine, City of God 20.26. Augustine, however, differs a little, for he cites it thus: "No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day." On this passage see Ludovicus Vives, though he is dealing with something else. Bellarmine, On the Loss of Grace, book 4, chapter 4, at the very threshold of the argument, quotes this passage from this translation, and adds that the sense can easily be found in the Hebrew text if the three first words of the following verse, אם חרוצים ימין, are joined to it. But grant this, though neither the Hebrew manuscripts, nor the Chaldee, nor the Vulgate edition itself admits it; explain those words as "even if the days of his life are few"; yet from them you will not carve out either "infant" or that "one day." I admit, however, that the thesis for which Bellarmine cites this testimony is well founded in the word of God.

units.la: Verf. 14. Quis mihi tribuat ut in inferno protegas me, &c. ] Carthuf. artic. 34. notat, haec verba cum sequentibus legi in officio mortuorum tanquam dicta in personae animae in purgatorio constitutae. Movet autem multas difficultates. Varias affert responsiones. Tu disce tiro, & hic & quamplurimis insuper locis ubi in Latino est infernus, in Belg. helle / in Ebraeo esse אשׁאל quae vox etiam sepulcrum significat. Quod interpretamentum si hic & alibi cum Joh. Benedicto, Pagnino, Aria Mont. (ut nostros omittam) substituas, omnes istos motus cum pulveris exigui jactu compressos videbis. Diximus de hac voce prolixius ad Genes. 37. Huic interpretamento, tanquam primario fundamento, superstructus est Limbus patrum.
units.tr: Verse 14: "Who will grant me that you protect me in hell, etc." The Carthusian, article 34, notes that these words, together with those that follow, are read in the office of the dead, as spoken in the person of a soul placed in purgatory. He raises many difficulties and offers various answers. You, novice, learn this: here and in very many places where the Latin has "infernus," the Belgic has "helle," while in the Hebrew it is שאול (sheol), a word which also means the sepulchre. If you substitute this rendering here and elsewhere, as John Benedict, Pagninus and Arias Montanus do (not to mention our own men), you will see all those disturbances settled as if by a light sprinkling of dust. We have spoken of this word at greater length at Genesis 37. Upon this interpretation, as its primary foundation, the Limbo of the Fathers has been built.

units.la: CAP. XIX. verf. 24.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. verse 24.

units.la: Delassavit multos interpretes vox celte, quam librarii in quibusdam editionibus in certe commutaverant. Sed Romani correctiores restituerunt vocem celte. De hac voce prolixe se in notationibus suis disseruisse ait Lucas Brugensis. Mihi illas, licet diligenter quaesitas, reperire necdum contigit. Joh. Benedictus existimavit esse interpretamentum vocis לער quae in Ebraeo. Namque in margine exhibet ejus loco haec verba, ut sint in perpetuum. Et certe hoc ipsum significat vox Ebraea.
units.tr: The word celte has troubled many interpreters, and in some editions scribes had changed it to certe. But the more careful Romanists restored the word celte. Lucas of Bruges says he discussed this word at length in his notes. Although I have searched for them carefully, I have not yet managed to find them. John Benedictus thought it was a rendering of the Hebrew word לער. For in the margin he gives in its place the words ut sint in perpetuum, that they may be forever. And the Hebrew word certainly means just this.

units.la: Nam quod Lxx. eam reddidere, εἰς μαρτύριον, manifeste legerunt לעד / caeterum Vulgatus per ista verba, vel celte sculpantur expressit Graecum ἐγγλυφῶσι. Celtis enim est γλύφιον, celum. Vide Hieronymi Epist. ad Pammach. de erroribus Joh. Jerosolymitani. & Casaub. ad Athen. pag. 556.
units.tr: For the Seventy rendered it εἰς μαρτύριον [eis martyrion], which clearly shows they read לעד. But the Vulgate, with the words vel celte sculpantur (or be carved with a chisel), expressed the Greek ἐγγλυφῶσι [engluphōsi]. For a chisel is γλύφιον [glyphion] in Greek. See Jerome's letter to Pammachius on the errors of John of Jerusalem, and Casaubon on Athenaeus, p. 556.

units.la: Verf. 15. Scio quod redemptor meus vivit, & in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum. Et rursus circumdabor pelle mea & in carne videbo Deum. Quem visurus sum ego ipse & oculi mei conspecturi sunt & non alius.] Ita Vulg. Agnosco hic liquidum argumentum pro resurrectione carnis, & quidem hujus carnis, uti prisci loquebantur. Quid enim clarius dici posset, in carne mea videbo Deum. Quem Quem videbo ego ipse & oculi mei & non alius. Sed quaeres, cur omittam ista priora, in novissimo die de terra resurrecturus sum, & circumdabor pelle mea? Respondeo, nihil tale Ebraeis vocibus posse excusari, ac proinde hunc locum vulgo pro concionibus & in disputationib. non ea cura, qua in hac linguarum luce par erat, allegari. Verum quidem est, nos in novissimo die de terra resurrecturos, verum est nos pellibus nostris rursus circumdatum iri, at Jobum istis verbis haec dicere, id vero ajo non esse verum. Videamus Ebraea, וַאֲנִי יְדַעְתִּי גּוֹאֲלִי חַי וְאַחֲרוֹן quae ὡς ἀπολέξει ita sonant, Et ego novi redemptorem meum vivum, & postremus super pulverem stabit. Et post cutem meam contriverunt vel, perforarunt) hanc. Tria hic membra sunt quae ordine examinabimus. In primo nulla difficultas. Per redemptorem vulgo intelligunt Jesum Christum Salvatorem. Quam interpretationem ut non solicito ita nolim subscribere Roderi irae, qui hic plenis maledicentiae velis in Dominum Piscatorem, tanquam si capital aliquod designasset, invehitur. Primum enim quod in Piscatore hoc loco reprehendit, illud est, quod in Scholiis vocem Erlöser referat non distincte ad Christum, sed ad Deum simpliciter. At Piscator objiciit haec loca, Jesa. 41.14. & 43.14. & Psal.78.34. Jesa.44.6. & 47.4. & 48.17. ubi Deo absolute, & Jesai. 49.7. ubi Patri tribuitur. Habet vero Pisc. à suis partibus, Mercerum, Junium, in notis ad hunc locum, Is est Deus, inquit Pater in Filio per Sp. Sanctum. Licet postea dubitet, annon potius ad Christum vox Redemptoris referenda sit.
units.tr: Verse 15. I know that my redeemer lives, and that I shall rise from the earth at the last day. And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. So the Vulgate. Here I recognise a clear argument for the resurrection of the flesh, and indeed of this flesh, as the ancients put it. For what could be said more plainly: in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another? But you will ask why I leave out those earlier words, I shall rise from the earth at the last day, and I shall be clothed with my skin? I answer that nothing of this kind can be justified from the Hebrew words, and so this passage is commonly cited in sermons and disputations without the care that ought to be taken in this light of the languages. It is true that we shall rise from the earth at the last day, and true that we shall be clothed again with our skins. But that Job said these things in these words, that I say is not true. Let us look at the Hebrew, which reads thus: [וַאֲנִי יְדַעְתִּי גּוֹאֲלִי חַי וְאַחֲרוֹן] and so on, meaning: "And I know that my redeemer lives, and the last will stand upon the dust. And after my skin they have pierced (or destroyed) this." There are three clauses here, which I will examine in order. In the first there is no difficulty. By the redeemer people commonly understand Jesus Christ the Saviour. I am not eager to subscribe to this interpretation, yet I am unwilling to fall under the anger of Roderus, who here, with full sails of malice, attacks Piscator for the Lord, as if he had designated some capital matter. For the first thing Roderus faults in Piscator at this place is that in his notes he refers the word Erlöser not distinctly to Christ but simply to God. But Piscator cites these passages: Isaiah 41.14, 43.14, Psalm 78.34, Isaiah 44.6, 47.4, 48.17, where it is attributed to God absolutely, and Isaiah 49.7, where it is attributed to the Father. Piscator has on his side Mercerus and Junius, who in their notes on this passage say: He is God the Father in the Son through the Holy Spirit, though afterwards Junius doubts whether the word Redeemer should not rather be referred to Christ.

units.la: II. Membrum quod attinet, illud prout vulgo citatur, extra omnem controversiae aleam positum esset, si ita scripsisset Iob, וּבִיּוֹם אַהֲרוֹן מֵעָפָר אָקוּם / Hoc vidit Lutherus. Ideo sic convertit Ebraea, & olim ex terra resuscitabit me, quasi esset, וְאַחַר בְּעֹרִי יִקּוּמֻנִי / Dices, יָקוּם transitive usurpatum esse pro יָקוּם / ut Amos 7.2. מִי יָקוּם יַעֲקֹב Lxx. τὶς ἀναστήσει τὸν Ιακωβ. Luth. quis eriget Jacobum? Resp. peti principium. Namque ad vocem יעקוב tam subaudiri potest articulus ל / vel praepositio ב / quam אֵת / Quis staret Jacobo, vel, in Jacob, id est restaret, superesset. Addo exemplum esse dissimile. Vt ut enim illic loci esset transitivum, non tamen, ut illic post se habet vocem יעקוב / ita hic quoque post se pronomen vel assixum, vel separatum אֶת habet, Erostratus, qui ob hujus quoque loci versionem Paginno ferulam intentabat, destomacha- tur in illum quod literam vau in Iod non commutaverit, יקום surgere faciet, subaudi omnes. Si libuit Erostrato textum Ebræum ad Vulgatam versionem ubique conformare, cur non potius jussit eum supplere vocem אֶת id est corpus meum? Sed respon- det * Arias, nec libuisse nec licuisse Pagnino lectionem Ebraicam mutare. Quod autem in sequentibus conatur Arias Pagninum cum vulgario conciliare, frustra est. Ait Pagninum sic vertisse & novissimo super terram staturum. Quid vero staturum esset, continuo exposuisse, * hanc pellem meam postquam contri- verint. Quod si loco pellis Latine vertisset corium, nulla in Gram- matica difficultas esset. Hæc Arias, joco an serio, equidem valde ambigo. Aut enim existimat hanc fuisse mentem Pa- gnini, aut suam depromit. Si prius, cur Pagninus non scripsit potius staturam? Nam & tunc nulla fuisset in Gramm. difficultas. Cur ponit colon post vocem staturum? Cur ergo non potius sic reddidit, & novissimo super pulverem staturam, etiam postquam contriverint eam vermes, pellem hanc meam. Si posterius hoc est, si suam ipsius sententiam promit, cur ergo ipse ad hunc modum versionem Pagnini non demutavit? Cur reliquit vocem staturum? & post eam colon? Quid ergo? τὸ יקום cum in transitivum sit & tertiæ personæ, & finiat periodum, non potest aliò quam ad redemptorem referri. Ita Chald. Ita Joh. Bened. super pulverem surget. Tigurini fatentur in margine, in Ebræo esse, super pulvere stabit, tamen in textu liberius sunt interpretati, novissimo [tempore] adhibebit vim suam pulveri. Ni- mis coactè. Jun. & posteriorum super pulverem resurrecturum, quod etsi primo sic interpretatus sit, ut per posteriorem intelligatur homo redivivus die resurrectionis in adventu Christi, tamen in posterioribus editionibus aliam expositionem addidit, qua to- tum versum de Christo explicat. Vide notas. Angli & quod novissimo [die] in terra stabit. Mercerus, Nostri fere omnes tam veteres quam recentiores hunc versum cum duobus sequentibus ad resurrectionem referunt, quam hoc loco Job asstruat, & per Redemptorem Christum intelligunt, & quod dicit על עפר יקום super pulverem stabit, de Christo juxta humanitatem in terra post omnes homines con- sumptos & postea suscitatos, ac voce archangeli congregatos ad judi- cium cium comparituro accipiunt. Sed ego cum Ebraeis locum hunc aliter accipio. Loquitur non de hoc versu tantum, sed & de duobus sequentibus. In quo ei non possum astipulari. Ipse ergo hoc hemistichium sic explicat, Quicquid vos mihi objiciatis, ego redemptorem meum immortalem esse novi & aeternum perstaturum. Genevenses in toto hoc contextu non videntur abhorruisse à sententia Merceri, & qu'il demeurera le dernier sur la terre, & quod postremus mansurus sit super terra, Scholion, scio illum esse aeternum, immutabilem ac proinde omnia aeterna sua providentia gubernare; scio ab ipso procedere ipsas illas afflictiones, quas perpetior. Huic vero subjungunt aliud tanquam secundarium, quo tamen non de Jobo ut in nostra, sed ipso Christo locus explicatur, aut scio quod postremus staturus sit erectus super pulvere (ou qu'il sera debout le dernier sur la poussiere) juxta interpretationem eorum qui hunc locum exponunt de resurrectione, eum referendo ad Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum qui in fine mundi gloriose apparebit, quando corpora defunctorum in pulverem jam pridem resoluta ejus potentia resuscitabuntur, & vivorum subito mutabuntur. Deodatus, e che all' ultimo si leverà sopra la polvere id est & quod in extremo se elevabit supra pulverem. Scholion, quod conscendet tribunal, ceu judex hominum resolutorum in pulverem & ejus jam potentia resuscitatorum. Omnes has interpretationes simplicitate sua antecellere mihi videtur versio Piscatoris, & quod posterior super pulverem stabit. id est quod in conflictu cum hostibus meis, à quibus me redempturus est, victoriam reportabit. Metaphora à luctatoribus vel athletis victoribus desumpta. Vides Interpretes, quos adduxi, dissentire in eo, utrum hic ad resurrectionem omnino respiciat Job. In eo vero conspirare, (si primam Junii glossam excipias) hoc hemistichium non ad Jobum, sed ad redemptorem pertinere.
units.tr: As for the second clause, the way it is commonly cited would be beyond all controversy if Job had written it thus: and at the last day I shall rise from the dust [וּבִיּוֹם אַחֲרוֹן מֵעָפָר אָקוּם]. Luther saw this. So he translated the Hebrew thus: and afterwards he will raise me up from the earth, as if the text were [וְאַחַר בְּעֹורִי יְקוּמֻנִי]. You will say that [יָקוּם] is used transitively for [יָקִים], as in Amos 7.2, [מִי יָקוּם יַעֲקֹב], the Septuagint [τίς ἀναστήσει τὸν Ἰακώβ], and Luther, "who will raise up Jacob?" I reply that this begs the question. For before the word Jacob one may understand either the article ל or the preposition ב, or the particle אֵת: "who would stand for Jacob", or "in Jacob", that is, remain and survive. I add that the example is not similar. For even if the verb is transitive there, it is not followed there by the word Jacob as it is here by the pronoun, attached or separate, אֶת. Erostratus, who on account of this passage also threatened Pagninus with the rod for his version, rails against him because he did not change the letter vav into yod, so that [יקום] would mean "will cause to rise", with "all" understood. If Erostratus wished to conform the Hebrew text to the Vulgate everywhere, why did he not rather bid him supply the word אֶת, that is, "my body"? But Arias answers that it was neither Pagninus's wish nor his right to change the Hebrew reading. What Arias goes on to attempt, reconciling Pagninus with the common version, is pointless. He says Pagninus rendered it thus: at the last will stand upon the earth, and that he at once explained what "will stand" meant: this skin of mine after they have pierced it. But if he had translated "skin" by the Latin "corium" instead of "pellis", there would be no difficulty in the grammar. Whether Arias says this in jest or in earnest, I am really uncertain. For either he thinks this was Pagninus's intention, or he is putting forward his own view. If the former, why did Pagninus not write potius staturam (rather "will stand her")? For then too there would have been no difficulty in grammar. Why does he put a colon after the word staturum? Why then did he not rather render it: and at the last will stand upon the dust, her, even after they have pierced her, this skin of mine? If the latter, if Arias is setting out his own opinion, why did he not himself alter Pagninus's version in this way? Why did he leave the word staturum and the colon after it? What then? Since [יקום] is transitive, third person, and ends the sentence, it can refer only to the redeemer. So the Chaldee paraphrast, and John Benedictus: he will rise above the dust. The Tigurines admit in the margin that the Hebrew says he will stand upon the dust, yet in the text they translated more freely: at the last [time] he will apply his force to the dust, which is much too forced. Junius has in the last will rise up upon the dust; though at first he so interpreted it that by the last is understood the man restored to life on the day of resurrection at Christ's coming, yet in later editions he added another explanation which refers the whole verse to Christ. See his notes. The English, too, have at the last [day] he will stand upon the earth. Mercerus: Almost all our writers, both older and more recent, refer this verse, with the two that follow, to the resurrection, which Job here affirms, and understand by the Redeemer Christ, and take the words [על עפר יקום], "he will stand upon the dust", of Christ according to his humanity, who will appear upon the earth after all men have been consumed and afterwards raised, and gathered at the voice of the archangel for judgement. But I take this passage differently, with the Hebrews. It speaks not of this verse alone but also of the two that follow. In this I cannot agree with him. He himself therefore explains this half-verse thus: Whatever you may object to me, I know that my redeemer is immortal and will remain eternal. The Genevans, throughout this whole context, do not seem to have shrunk from Mercerus's view, and he will remain the last upon the earth, and that he will be the last to stand upon the earth. Their scholion: I know that he is eternal and unchangeable, and therefore governs all things by his eternal providence; I know that those very afflictions which I suffer proceed from him. To this they add another, as a secondary explanation, by which the passage is explained not of Job, as in our version, but of Christ himself: or I know that he will stand last, raised up upon the dust (or, he will be standing last upon the dust), according to the interpretation of those who expound this passage of the resurrection, referring it to our Lord Jesus Christ, who will appear gloriously at the end of the world, when the bodies of the dead, long since dissolved into dust, will be raised by his power, and the living will suddenly be changed. Diodati: and that at the last he will rise above the dust, that is, that in the end he will raise himself above the dust. Scholion: that he will mount the tribunal, as judge of men resolved into dust and already raised again by his power. Of all these interpretations, the version of Piscator seems to me to surpass the rest in its simplicity: and that the last will stand upon the dust, that is, that in the struggle with my enemies, from whom he is to redeem me, he will win the victory. The metaphor is taken from wrestlers or victorious athletes. You see that the interpreters I have cited differ on whether Job here looks at the resurrection at all. But they agree (if you except Junius's first gloss) that this half-verse pertains not to Job but to the redeemer.

units.la: Membrum 3. [Hebrew] Cum עוֹר sit generis Maculini, quomodo construi potest cum foeminino [Hebrew] / Rursus, cum illud [Hebrew] hic sit admodum emphaticum, quomodo excusabitur vulgatus Interpres, quod illud omiserit? cum [Hebrew] denique sit verbum 3. personae, pluralis numeri, conjugationis Phiel, quomodo reddi potest circumdabor? An [Hebrew] circumdandi notionem habet? Sed audio, thema esse [Hebrew], unde in Hifyl, [Hebrew] circumdedit. Hinc esse Nifal [Hebrew] circumdari, esse ellipsin vocis עַצְמִי ossa mea, aut membra mea. Fateor libens, hanc interpretationem magis tolerabilem esse quam illa Tigurinorum, Postquam vero circumdederint hoc pelle mea. Circumdederint, Pater, filius & Spiritus S. hoc ἐκτικῶς, quod ob deformitatem summam non licet corpus appellare. Sed hoc nihil aliud est, quam textum obtorto collo ad praeconceptam opinionem defendendam torquere. Non decet nos textum trahere, quo nos volumus, sed potius sequi quo ille trahit. יִקָּף in Nifal nusquam occurrit. Si alibi occurrerit, potius circumdari, quam circumdare significaret. Manet praeter alia incommoda discrepantia generis inter nomen & pronomen. תַּקָּף contrà in Phiel usitatum est, valetque excidere, concidere, decidere, decutere, confodere, perforare. Notum est, ut literae homogeneae, cognatae imo saepe ejusdem significationis vocabula constituant. Sic נשב & נשף flandi notionem communem habent. Nunc adducam varias Interpretationes, quae licet in omnibus non consentiant, in hoc tamen conspirant, תְּקַפּוּ esse praeteritum Phiel, esse locutionem impersonalem, in genere subintelligi, confodientes, perforantes, in specie vero vermes, vel dolores. Mercerus, iisdem insistens vestigiis, non credit hic de resurrectione agi. Et post cutem meam &c. corrosam, post putredinem cutis meae, quasi dixisset plene, אחר רקבן עורי excusserunt hoc. Excusserunt, vel vermes in ulceribus geniti, vel dolores immodici confregerunt & conciderunt veluti in fragmenta, ut veluti pulvis jam excuti possit, hoc, vid. os vel corpus meum. Et tamen istis non obstantibus, ex carne mea sic afflicta cerno & contemplor. Deum id est Dei potentiam, providentiam & summam in me beneficentiam agnosco, qui me summo miraculo adhuc in vivis conservat, &c. Genevensium expositio, quam primo loco exhibent, eo quoque aurigatur. Postquam enim locum sic vertisset, Et etiamsi post pellem meam contriverint hoc, videbo tamen Deum ex carne mea, hoc scholion addunt, & quand mesmes il reduiroit à plusglande extremité, & que je seroy du tout consumé; si est ce que j'espererai en lui. Etiam si ad extremam miseriam reduxerit me & plane consumptus fuero, tamen sperabo in eum. Vide supra 13.15. Postea tamen aliam expositionem subjiciunt, Piscatoris, Deodati, Anglorum & aliorum interpretationi consentaneam. Ego horum
units.tr: Third clause [עוֹר]. Since ‘or [עוֹר] is masculine, how can it be construed with a feminine form? Again, since the pronoun [הזה] here is very emphatic, how will the Vulgate translator be excused for omitting it? Finally, since the verb is in the third person, plural number, conjugation Piel, how can it be rendered "they will surround me"? Does it have the sense of surrounding? But I hear that the root is [נקף], whence in Hiphil [הקיף] means "surrounded," and that the Niphal [נקף] means "to be surrounded," with an ellipsis of the word עַצְמִי ossa mea [עַצְמִי], or membra mea, "my bones" or "my limbs." I readily admit that this interpretation is more tolerable than that of the Tigurines: Postquam vero circumdederint hoc pelle mea. Circumdederint, "Father, Son and Holy Spirit" [sic], hoc demonstrative [δεικτικῶς], since the body cannot be called by that name because of its extreme deformity. But this is nothing other than twisting the text by the neck to defend a preconceived opinion. We ought not to drag the text whither we wish, but rather follow whither it leads. יִקָּף [נקף] in Niphal never occurs. If it occurred elsewhere, it would mean "to be surrounded" rather than "to surround." Besides other difficulties, a discrepancy of gender remains between noun and pronoun. On the other hand, תַּקָּף [תקף] is in common use in Piel and means to fell, fall, cut down, strike off, pierce through or perforate. It is well known that letters which are homogeneous or cognate often form words with the same, or even very similar, meanings: thus נשב and נשף share the common sense of blowing. Now I will cite various interpretations which, though they do not agree on everything, agree on this: that תְּקַפּוּ [תקפו] is the Piel perfect, an impersonal expression, with a generic subject understood, piercing, perforating, and specifically worms or pains. Mercer, following the same tracks, does not believe that the resurrection is spoken of here: And after my skin etc. has been gnawed away, after the rotting of my skin, as if he had fully said [אחר רקבן עורי], they have shaken out this. They have shaken out, either worms bred in the ulcers or immoderate pains have broken and cut down, as into fragments, so that the this, that is, my bone or body, can now be shaken out like dust. And yet, notwithstanding these things, I see and contemplate God from my afflicted flesh; that is, I acknowledge God's power, providence and supreme kindness towards me, who keeps me alive by a supreme miracle, etc. The exposition of the Genevans, which they present first, is also driven by this. For after translating the place thus, And even if after my skin they have wasted this, I shall see God from my flesh, they add this scholium: "and even if he should reduce me to the greatest extremity, and I should be utterly consumed, yet I will hope in him." Even if he reduce me to extreme misery and I should be wholly consumed, yet I will hope in him. See above at 13.15. Afterwards, however, they add another exposition, agreeing with the interpretation of Piscator, Diodati, the English and others. I shall briefly set before the reader the versions and scholia of these,

units.la: * Et encores qu'apres, ma peau on ait rongé ceci, &c. rum versionem & scholia obiter lectori repræsentabo. Sic ergo Pisc. & Etiamsi post pellem meam hoc confoderint, tamen ex carne, &c. Ita reddidit hæc verba in German. at in Latina, Et [quum] post cutem meam confoderint [vermes] istud, tum ex carne, &c. Sensus est, Quum vermes confoderint atque corroserint non solum cutem meam & ossa, tum e morte excitabor & vita restitutus videbo Deum. Hæc Piscator. Deodati versio & Scholia non abeunt ab hac mente, E [quantumque] dopo la mie pelle quasto [corpo] fia rosso. Quamvis post pellem meam hoc [corpus] errosum sit, vid. a vermibus ulcerum meorum. Convertit activum in passivum, sensum manente. In hoc videntur dissentire, quod Piscator intelligat corrosionem mortui in sepulcro, Deodatus corrosionem ejus adhuc spirantis. Anglorum versio indifferens est & ad hujus & illius mentem, Et etiamsi [vermes] post pellem meam hoc [corpus] destruant, tamen mea, &c. Scholia nec hic nec alibi adjecta sunt, Ita quippe caverat Serenissimus magnæ Britanniæ Rex Jacobus augustæ recordationis. Vides omnes hos in istis confspirare, 1. ιδπ habere significationem confodiendi, corrodendi, concidendi, &c. non vero circumdandi. 2. Pronomen ΓΝΥ aliquid distinctum à pelle denotare. 3. Illud ipsum δεικτικῶς hic intelligendum esse, ut digitum in emaciatum suum corpus intenderit. Similem usum pronominis demonstrativi habes in Euangelio, solvite hoc templum: Et pronominis illuc, Job. 1. Nudus egressus sum ex utero matris mea & nudus revertar illuc, non in uterum matris, sed in terram, quam dum hæc sermocinabatur Job, digito monstrabat. Huc referunt nonnulli celebrem illum locum, tu es Petrus & super HANC petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Super HANC petram, id est super me Domino semet ipsum denotante & vocem gestu adjuvante. Hoc spectasse videtur Augustinus, quando locum sic expositut, Super me ædificabo te, non me super te. Sed & Græci & Latini amant in hunc modum loqui δεικτικῶς. Terentius, tu si HIC sis, aliter sentias. Hic, ὦ δ' ἀνὴρ Sophocles in Oedipo Coloneo, ὦ παῖδες, ἥκει τῷ ἀ' ἐπ' ἀνδρὶ ... ΒΙΣ πλάστη. O liberi, venit huic viro prædicto oracula mors τῷ δ' ἀνδρὶ id est mi- hi, δεικτικῶς, inquit Scholiastes, ... Σοφοκλῆς. Sed hoc παρέργως καὶ ὡς ἐν παρέργῳ. Nos illud jam, opinor, omnibus, qui Ebræo textui fidem suam alligarunt, probavimus, Belgicam versionem cum eo conciliari non posse, & locum sic melius à domino Pisc. redditum, Scio quod Red. meus vivat & postremus in pulvere staturus sit, Et [cum] post pellem meam [vermes] HOC confoderint, de carne mea videbo Deum. Adscribam obiter versionem LXX. Interpretum, prout ea extat apud August. in notis ad hunc librum, cum commentariolo ejusdem, Scio enim quod aeternus est ὁ ἐκλύσει μεμέλημαι, qui me resoluturus est, [qui me potest reparare] In terra resurget pellis mea exantlans hac. A Domino enim mihi haec confecta sunt, quae ego mihi ipsi conscius sum. [quia merui illa.] quae oculus meus vidit & non alius. [hoc est, nemo scit quid agatur in homine nisi spiritus qui in homine est.]
units.tr: * "And although after my skin they have gnawed this," etc. Thus Piscator: And even if after my skin they have pierced this, yet from my flesh, etc. He rendered these words thus in German; but in Latin: And [when] after my skin they have pierced [the worms] this, then from my flesh, etc. The sense is: When the worms have pierced and corroded not only my skin and bones, then I shall be raised from death, restored to life, and see God. So far Piscator. The version and scholia of Diodati do not depart from this sense: And [however much] after my skin this [body] is gnawed. Although after my skin this [body] has been eaten away, see by the worms of my ulcers. He turns the active into the passive, the sense remaining the same. They seem to differ in this: that Piscator understands the corrosion of the dead in the grave, Diodati the corrosion of one still living. The English version is indifferent and suits the mind of both: And even if [worms] after my skin destroy this [body], yet in my flesh, etc. No scholia have been added here or elsewhere; for so the most serene King James of Great Britain, of blessed memory, had provided. You see that all these agree in these points: 1. that תקף [תקף] has the sense of piercing, gnawing, cutting down, etc., and not of surrounding. 2. That the pronoun זֹאת [זאת] denotes something distinct from the skin. 3. That this very demonstrative [δεικτικῶς] is to be understood here, as if he had pointed his finger at his emaciated body. You have a similar use of the demonstrative pronoun in the Gospel: destroy this temple; and of the pronoun there, Job 1: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither, not into the mother's womb, but into the earth, which Job, while speaking these words, pointed to with his finger. To this some refer the famous passage: you are Peter, and upon THIS rock I will build my Church. Upon THIS rock, that is, upon me, the Lord indicating himself and the gesture assisting the word. Augustine seems to have had this in view when he expounded the place thus: I will build you upon me, not me upon you. But both Greeks and Latins love to speak in this way demonstratively [δεικτικῶς]. Terence: if you were HERE, you would think otherwise. Here, ὦ δ' ἀνὴρ; Sophocles in the Oedipus at Colonus: O children, death has come to this man, as the oracles foretold; to the man, that is, to me, demonstratively [δεικτικῶς], says the Scholiast ... Sophocles. But this is said in passing and as if by the way. I think we have now proved to all who have bound their faith to the Hebrew text that the Belgic version cannot be reconciled with it, and that the place is better rendered by Mr Piscator thus: I know that my Redeemer lives and will stand last upon the dust, And [when] after my skin [the worms] have pierced THIS, from my flesh I shall see God. I shall add in passing the version of the Seventy translators, as it stands in Augustine, in his notes on this book, with his short commentary: For I know that the Eternal is the one who has cared for me [ὁ ἐκλύσει μεμέλημαι], who is about to loose me, [who can restore me]. My skin will rise again from the earth, enduring these things. For these things have been accomplished for me by the Lord, of which I am myself conscious, [because I have deserved them] which my eye has seen and not another's [that is, no one knows what is done in a man except the spirit which is in the man].

units.la: CAP. XXIV. vers. 19.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. verse 19.

units.la: Ad nimium calorem transeat ab aquis nivium, & usque ad infernum peccatum ejus.] Hoc modo transtulit vulgatus Interpres insignem illam similitudinem, quam fontes lectori suo exhibent. Sic enim sonant Ebraea, יָזֵיד גַּם חוּם יִגּוֹלוּ מֵימֵי שֶׁלֶג שְׁאוֹל חָטָאוּ ad verbum, Siccitas & æstus rapiunt aquas nivis, sepulcrum peccarunt. Continent haec verba σκότος καὶ ἁμαρτάνοντι. Utriusque nota deest. Id quod in Jobo & Proverbiis insolens non est. Hinc Joh. Benedictus, Jun. Pisc. Gen. Ital. Tig. Mercerus & alii locum sic reddunt, [Ut] siccitas (Tig. Ut terra torrida) & æstus rapiunt aquas nivis, [ita] sepulcrum [rapit eos qui] peccarunt. Angli, Siccitas & calor consumunt aquas nivis: ita sepulcrum [facit illis qui] peccarunt. גול est rapere. Sensum expressit Mercerus his verbis, ut siccitas & calor quam citissime absumunt aquas nivis, ita mors rapit eos qui peccarunt, q. d. moriuntur facillime & suavissime. Non contabescunt lenta morte, ut magna ex parte probi, sicuti & Psal. 73. 4. & supra 21. 13. Dicit ergo hoc ad felicitatem eorum ostendendam quod cum totam vitam in sceleribus transegerint impune, suaviter etiam moriantur. Ita & Deod. & Genev. & Pisc. Hoc enim capite sententiam Eliphazi, qui asserebat Deum in hac vita semper punire impios, refutat Job testimonio experientiae, quod pii illud non videant, vers. 1. & quod peccatores non ita morientur, ut sentiant se mori, sed cita & divoduῦ morte expirent. Quam ille refutationem prolixa impiorum descridescriptione, à factis ipsorum desumpta, amplificat. Chaldæus non recedit ab hac mente, צהיא ולחור הומתא אנסין מימי הלנא וליתיזון היכרין לשיול אתנשיאו דאתהייבו Siccitas & etiam calor (תא היד צהותא וחומא id est Targum aliud, sicut aridita & calor) rapiunt aquas nivis & non sunt amplius, ita in sepulcrum auferuntur qui peccarunt. Habes genuinum sensum hujus loci. Judica nunc, cordate Lector, quam firmo tibicine duplex illa Gehenna nitatur, quam huic loco multi Interpretes & Scholastici superstruxere. Hieron. comm. in Matth. cap. x. Duplicem esse Gehennam & nimii caloris & nimii frigoris in Job planissime legimus. Ideo etiam nomini Gehenna aliquando genitivum ignis addi, quod sit & Gehenna frigoris. Et Pseudo-Hieronymus ad hunc ipsum Jobi locum, Innuere mihi videtur duplicem Gehennam ignis & frigoris, per quam Diabolus, impii & haretici commutantur. Si Hieronymo vel tumultuaria hæc & ad fontium obrussam non satis examinata versio, vel aliorum quas super hoc loco legerat commentationes imposuere, quid miramur, Albertum, Carthusianum, Haimonem hic ineptiviffe? Contulerunt enim hunc locum cum Matth. VIII. ubi erit fletus & stridor dentium. Fletus, propter calidissimum ignem; stridor dentium, propter frigidissimum gelu. In hac vita, inquit Albertus apud Carthus. non transitur de frigidissimo in calidissimum, nisi per medium, quod est temperatum. In inferno autem de excellentia frigoris mortificantis transitur ad astum ignis urentis, ita quod nunquam erunt in medio, quia in hac vita per vitia transierunt ad astum libidinis, non attingendo medium virtutis. Dissentit tamen ab hac interpretatione Gregorius. Ille enim putat hic describi impiorum in omnibus immoderationem, qui à frigore infidelitatis transeunt ad calorem hæresis. Alii putant hunc posse esse sensum, improbos à nimia frigiditate hujus vitæ transire ad calorem nimium infernalem. Emman. Sa, ab una calamitate in aliam transibit. * Jansenius postquam prolixe de hoc loco disseruisset, ad Ebræam veritatem tandem provocat, quam ita interpretatur, ut à nostris Interpretibus, quos supra produximus, ne latum unguem discedat. Thomas parte prima, quest. x. art. 3. disputans, utrum esse æternum sit proprium Dei, loco secundo objicit sibi locum Matth. 25. ite maledicti in ignem æternum. Non igitur solus Deus æternus. Respondet, ignem illum dici æternum propter interminabilitatem tantum. Esse tamen in pœpoenis istis transmutationem, secundum illud Jobi 24. Ad nimium calorem, &c. Unde in inferno, inquit, non est vera æternitas sed magis tempus, secundum illud Ps. 80. Erit tempus eorum in sæcula. Hæc Thomas, qui ne hunc quidem locum Psal. 80. ex mente Spiritus sancti citat, vide Jun. Pisc. & alios.
units.tr: Let them pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat, and their sin to the grave, even to Sheol.] The Vulgate translator rendered that striking figure in this way, and the sources set it before their readers. The Hebrew reads, word for word, יָזֵיד גַּם חוּם יִגּוֹלוּ מֵימֵי שֶׁלֶג שְׁאוֹל חָטָאוּ [Drought and heat seize the waters of snow; the grave has sinned]. The Greek has σκότος καὶ ἁμαρτάνοντι [darkness and to the one who sins]. Neither has a mark of the sense, though that is not unusual in Job or Proverbs. Hence Johannes Benedictus, Junius, Piscator, the Genevan and Italian translators, the Tigurine version, Mercerus and others render the passage: As drought (the Tigurine, "as scorched ground") and heat seize the waters of snow, so the grave [seizes those who] have sinned. The English: Drought and heat consume the waters of snow; so the grave [does to those who] have sinned. The Hebrew verb גול means to seize. Mercerus expressed the sense in these words: as drought and heat most quickly consume the waters of snow, so death seizes those who have sinned, that is, they die most easily and most gently. They do not waste away in a slow death, as the good largely do, as also in Psalm 73:4 and above in 21:13. He says this, therefore, to show their happiness: though they have spent their whole life in wickedness with impunity, they also die pleasantly. So also Diodati, the Genevan, and Piscator. For in this chapter Job refutes the opinion of Eliphaz, who maintained that God always punishes the wicked in this life, by the testimony of experience: the godly do not see this, verse 1, and sinners do not die in such a way that they feel themselves dying, but expire by a swift and sudden death. He amplifies this refutation with a long description of the wicked, drawn from their deeds. The Chaldee paraphrast does not depart from this meaning: tsehia ve-lahhor humta anesin mei hilna veliteizun hikerin lesheol atneshiau de-athehaivu [Chaldee, transliterated] (the other Targum has, as dryness and heat) seize the waters of snow, and they are no more; so those who have sinned are carried away into the grave. You have the genuine sense of this passage. Now judge, thoughtful reader, how firm a prop is that double Gehenna which many interpreters and Schoolmen have built upon this place. Jerome, on Matthew 10: We read quite plainly in Job that there is a double Gehenna, of excessive heat and of excessive cold. Hence also the name Gehenna is sometimes given the genitive of fire, as being also a Gehenna of cold. And Pseudo-Jerome, on this very verse of Job: It seems to me to hint at a double Gehenna, of fire and of frost, through which the devil, the wicked and the heretics are changed. If Jerome was misled by a hasty translation, not sufficiently tested against the sources, or by the commentaries of others which he had read on this passage, why should we be surprised that Albert, the Carthusian, and Haimo talked nonsense here? They compared this passage with Matthew 8: where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Weeping, because of the most burning fire; gnashing of teeth, because of the most frigid frost. In this life, says Albert, as quoted by the Carthusian, one does not pass from the most frigid to the most hot except through the middle, which is temperate. But in hell one passes from the excess of a killing cold to the heat of a burning fire, so that they never stand in the middle, because in this life they passed through vices to the heat of lust, without reaching the middle of virtue. Gregory, however, disagrees with this interpretation. He thinks that the immoderation of the wicked in all things is described here, who pass from the cold of unbelief to the heat of heresy. Others think the sense may be that the wicked pass from the excessive coldness of this life to excessive infernal heat. Emmanuel Sa: they will pass from one calamity to another. Jansenius, after discoursing at length on this passage, finally appeals to the Hebrew truth, which he interprets so that it does not depart a hair's breadth from our interpreters whom we have cited above. Thomas, in the first part, question 10, article 3, disputing whether eternity belongs to God alone, objects to himself in the second place the passage of Matthew 25: Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire. Therefore God is not alone eternal. He replies that this fire is called eternal only on account of its being unending. Yet there is a change in those punishments, according to that saying of Job 24: To excessive heat, etc. Hence in hell, he says, there is not true eternity but rather time, according to Psalm 80: Their time shall be for ever. So Thomas, who does not even quote this passage of Psalm 80 in the sense of the Holy Spirit. See Junius, Piscator and others.
