units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII. verse 7.

units.la: Qui in manu omnium hominum signat, ut noverint singuli opera sua.] Ita vulg. Lxx. paulo aliter, ἐν χειρὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων κατασφραγίζει, ἵνα γνῶ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀσθενείαν. Non defuere qui ex hoc loco, prout à vulgato versus est, Chiromantiæ patrocinium quæsivere. Ipse quoque Carthusianus alienam jobi scopo interpretationem hic affert. Non lubet omnia huc transcribere. Junius & Tremell. voces Ebraeas בְּיַד כָּל־אָדָם יְחַתּוֹם לְדַעַת כָּל־אֲנָשִׁי מַעֲשֵׂהוּ sic transtulere, Manum cujusque hominis obsignat, ut recognoscat omnes operarios suos. Hoc vult Elihu, Quando nives & imbres demittit ex alto Deus, manum cujusque patrisfamilias, sub dio in agris laborantis, obsignat id est claudit, ut non possit opus facere. Unde fit ut recognoscat, per otium sc. inquirendo, quantum singuli in agro colendo laboraverint. Tunc etiam ingreditur bestia in latibulum suum & in antro suo manet vers. sequenti. חָתַם sæpe est cohibere, inhibere, Job. 9. 7. Dan. 9. 24. Cant. 4. 12. Vide Cl. Tarnovii Exercit. Bibl. p. 103. Edit. primæ. Qui illud quoque observavit, B. Lutherum minus accurate hunc locum vertisse. Alle menschen hat er (Gott) in der hand verschlossen / auff dass die leute lernen / was er thun kan / Haec enim sic expressisset Job, כָּל־אָדָם בְּיַד יַחְתֹּם לְדַעַת אֲנָשִׁים בַּל־מַעֲשָׂיו
units.tr: "Who seals up the hand of every man, that all men may know their works." Thus the Vulgate. The Septuagint reads a little differently: in the hand of all men he seals, that every man may know his own weakness [ἐν χειρὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων κατασφραγίζει, ἵνα γνῶ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀσθενείαν]. Not a few have sought from this passage, as the Vulgate renders it, support for palmistry. The Carthusian too brings in an interpretation foreign to the purpose of Job. I do not wish to transcribe everything here. Junius and Tremellius rendered the Hebrew words [בְּיַד כָּל־אָדָם יְחַתּוֹם לְדַעַת כָּל־אֲנָשִׁי מַעֲשֵׂהוּ] thus: He seals up the hand of every man, that he may recognise all his workers. This is what Elihu means: when God sends down snow and rains from on high, he seals up the hand of every husbandman who is working in the open fields, that is, he shuts it, so that he cannot do his work. Hence it comes about that he may recognise, that is, by taking his leisure and inquiring, how much each has laboured in cultivating the field. Then also the beast goes into its lair and remains in its den, as the next verse says. Chatham [חָתַם] is often to restrain, to hold back: Job 9.7, Dan. 9.24, Cant. 4.12. See the learned Tarnovius, Exercitationes Biblicae, p. 103, first edition. He also observed that Luther translated this passage less accurately: He (God) has shut up all men in his hand, so that people may learn what he can do. For Job would have expressed it thus: [כָּל־אָדָם בְּיַד יַחְתֹּם לְדַעַת אֲנָשִׁים בַּל־מַעֲשָׂיו].

units.la: CAP. XXXIX. vers. 1.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX. verse 1.

units.la: Lxx. εἰ ἔγνως καιρὸν τεκέτι τραγελάφων τίκτεσ; Ad verbum. An nosti tempus partus hirco-cervorum petræ? Tragelaphus animal in Germaniæ saltibus, Bohemiæ vicinis, notum, inquit Hadr. Junius. Licet complures ex veteribus animal illud in rerum natura non esse crediderint. Unde in proverbium abiit. Extat apud Nazianz. & Aristophanem, τραγέλαφος πλάσμα; Tra-
units.tr: The Septuagint: Do you know the time when the wild goats of the rock give birth? Word for word: Do you know the time of the birth of the hircocervi of the rock? The tragelaphus, says Hadrian Junius, is an animal known in the forests of Germany and the neighbouring parts of Bohemia, although many of the ancients believed that the animal did not exist in nature. Hence it passed into a proverb. It occurs in Nazianzen and in Aristophanes: the tragelaphus is a fiction [τραγέλαφος πλάσμα]; Tra-

units.la: Vide & Cornel. à Lapide in Deut. 14, 5. Tragelaphos comminiscí. Vocem Ebræam * יעלה Vulgatus reddit ibicem. Et quia sequitur בסלע in petra, Jun. & Tre- mell. reddunt rupi-capram. Utrumque respondet Belgico steen- bock / Germanico, gems, qua voce & Luth. & Belgæ hic usi sunt. Angli, the wild goates / caprææ, Martialis.
units.tr: See also Cornelius à Lapide on Deut. 14.5, on inventing tragelaphi. The Vulgate renders the Hebrew word [יעלה] as ibex. And because in the rock [בסלע] follows, Junius and Tremellius render it rock-goat. Both correspond to the Dutch steenbock and the German Gems (chamois), a word which Luther and the Dutch used here. The English say the wild goats, the Latin caprae, as Martial does:

units.la: Pendentem summa capram de rupe videbis,Casuram speres, decipit illa canes.
units.tr: You will see a goat hanging from the top of a rock; you would expect it to fall, but it deceives the dogs.

units.la: Consentiunt a Genev. b Deod. c Hisp. d Tigur. Pagn. Arias. Miraris forsan, quorsum tam anxie probaverim עלה esse ibi- cem seu capream. Jam audies. Augustinus in notis ad hunc locum pravæ aut saltem incertæ versioni ineptiorem superstruxit allegoriam. Tragos, hircus: elaphos cervus, inquit, Tragelaphus ergo compositum ex hirco & cervo animal. Significat igitur mentem servientem legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem. Videtur (lego, videt) autem quantum adhuc ex parte hircus est, aliam legem in membris suis, repugnantem legi mentis suæ & captivantem se in lege peccati. Hæc Augustinus. Cui patrocinium præstet qui potest. Ego qui doctissimum patrem excusem, non video.
units.tr: The Geneva, Deodati, Spanish, Tigurine, Pagnini and Arias versions agree. Perhaps you wonder why I have so anxiously argued that [יעלה] means the ibex or chamois. You will soon hear why. Augustine, in his notes on this passage, built a rather silly allegory upon a faulty, or at least uncertain, version. Tragos is goat, elaphos is stag, he says, so the tragelaphus is a compound animal of goat and stag. It signifies therefore the mind serving the law of God according to the inner man. But it appears (I read "videt") how far it is still partly goat, having another law in its members, warring against the law of its mind and taking it captive in the law of sin. So Augustine. Let whoever can defend him. I, who would gladly excuse so learned a father, cannot see how.

units.la: CAP. XL. verf. 10.
units.tr: CHAPTER XL, verse 10.

units.la: Ecce Behemoth, quem feci tecum. ] Lubet hic inserere epistolam, quam super hoc loco ad magnæ spei juvenem, D. Theodorum Saeckma, amplissimi & magnifici D. JOHANNIS SAECKMA ICti, in suprema Frisiæ curia consiliari & Academiæ nostræ curatoris vigilantissimi, filium, superioribus diebus exaravi. Ea sic habet.
units.tr: Behold Behemoth, which I made with you. ] Here I would like to insert a letter which I recently wrote on this passage to the young man of great promise, Mr. Theodore Saeckma, son of the most distinguished and magnificent Mr. JOHANNES SAECKMA, jurist, councillor in the supreme court of Friesland and most watchful curator of our Academy. It runs as follows.

units.la: Pio & magna spei juveni,
units.tr: To the pious young man of great promise,

units.la: D. THEODORO SAECKMA, SS. Legum & Humanitatis studioso, S. P.
units.tr: To D. Theodorus Saeckma, student of both laws and the humanities, greetings.

units.la: QUomodo vulgo instituantur Jurif-prudentiæ studia, non ignoras, ornatissime SAECKMA. Apud nos, inquit *Lipsius, magna vel potius unica doctrina est, triduanum Jurisconsultum profiteri, cum Euripidèo Cyclope sentire, τὸ δ' ἀλλὰ κόμπει ἐχ λόγων εὐμορφίαι. Et quidem pestilens ista hæresis adeo latam sibi grassandi viam fecit, ut vix vicesimus quisque ultra formulas & rubricas assurgat. Scilicet ea sectantur omnes, quæ περὶ τοῦ ἀλφίτου, τ' λοιπῶν φρόνης ἱππικλεέδη. Incrementa sumit hoc malum à perversa opinione vulgi, quod Jurisconsultum literatum & ἀγυρόσυμον rabulam juxta æstimat, imo hunc illi sæpe præfert. At tibi meliori metallo ductum esse pectus, hoc ipso luculenter demonstrasti, quod, postquam ex triviali schola vindicta manumissus, linguam Latinam & Græcam supra ætatem & multos doctores doctus, in Academiam intulisses pedem, aliam plane instiiteris viam. Namque ad edita illa & serena Themidos templa priusquam ascenderes, istis studiis primo litandum esse duxisti, sine quibus & legesintelligi omnino non possunt, & verum eruditi elogium nulli unquam obtigit, nulli obtinget. Stylum exercuisti diligenter & etiamnum exerces, ut epistolam tersam & LATINAM (rarum hoc in illa ætate) expedite scribere possis. Historiæ Romanæ & priscis ritibus pernoscendis operam nequaquam indiligentem navas. In Græcæ quoque literaturæ studia, quæ plerique sic fugiunt, ac si illis ἀσπονδον πόλεμον indixisset Jurisprudentia, ita porro incubuisti, ut doctissimis Academiæ nostræ civibus ambiguam facile possis facere palmam. Neque hoc termino stetit tuus ille discendi ardor. Ebræum quoque idioma exigui temporis spacio adeo feliciter didicisti, ut cum multis veteranis Theologiæ studiosis, in Ebraici textus explicatione, quoties in collegio ad te perveniebat interpretandi ordo, paria feceris, multos longe supergressus sis & in ruborem dederis. Quod vero insignem hanc tuam Φιλομαθὲς pallida febris, quæ tot jam menses te afflictavit, non excusserit, tersæ istæ epistolæ loquuntur, quibus me subinde, dum valetudinis curandæ causa ab Academia abes, super re literaria consulis. Macte hoc animo, inculpate adolescens! Delectent alios canes, equi, aves, alea, choreæ. Litent curvæ istæ & cælestium inanes animæ Baccho & Veneri. Tuæ porro delitiæ sint stylus, libri, Musæ, & quod caput est, Deo servire. Perge, quo coepisti pede, ποληίσρᾳ patris eruditionem & virtutem æmulari. Si te Deus O. M. volet perennare,
units.tr: You know well how the study of jurisprudence is usually pursued, most distinguished Saeckma. Among us, as Lipsius says, it is considered a great, or rather the only, learning to profess the law in three days, to think like Euripides' Cyclops, that "beauty comes from words only" [τὸ δ' ἀλλὰ κόμπει ἐχ λόγων εὐμορφίαι]. This pestilent heresy has made such a broad path for itself that scarcely one in twenty rises above forms and rubrics. Naturally, everyone follows those things which are about barley meal and the rest of the fodder of horses. The evil grows from the perverse opinion of the crowd, which values the lawyer who is a mere wrangler in the marketplace above the learned jurist, and often even prefers him. But that your heart was shaped of better metal you have clearly shown by this very fact: after you were freed from the trivial school by the rod of manumission, learned in Latin and Greek beyond your age and beyond many teachers, you set foot in the Academy and took an entirely different path. For before you ascended those lofty and serene temples of Themis, you judged that you must first make your offering to these studies, without which the laws cannot be understood at all, and without which no one has ever gained, or will ever gain, the true praise of a scholar. You have exercised your pen diligently, and still do, so that you can write a neat letter in Latin, which is rare in our age. You do not neglect the study of Roman history and the knowledge of ancient customs. You have also devoted yourself so keenly to Greek literature, which most people shun as if jurisprudence had declared unending war upon it, that you could easily dispute the palm with the most learned citizens of our Academy. Nor has your eagerness for learning stopped there. You have learned the Hebrew language in so short a time and so successfully that, along with many veteran students of theology, you have kept pace with them in the explanation of the Hebrew text whenever the order of interpretation came to you in the college; you have even surpassed many and put them to shame. That your remarkable love of learning has not been shaken off by the pale fever which has troubled you for so many months, is shown by those neat letters in which you consult me from time to time on literary matters while you are away from the Academy for the sake of curing your health. Persevere in this spirit, blameless young man! Let dogs, horses, birds, dice and dancing delight others. Let those crooked souls, empty of heavenly things, offer sacrifices to Bacchus and Venus. Let your delights be your pen, your books, the Muses and, what is chief of all, the service of God. Continue on the path you have begun, and emulate your father's learning and virtue [πολυΐστορα]. If God, the best and greatest, shall grant you length of days,

units.la: ― & si qua morbi fata aspera rumpas,
units.tr: ― and if you should break through the harsh fates of sickness,

units.la: Philologum insignem, Jurisconsultum eleganter literatum, pium denique & intemeratum Justitiæ sacerdotem patriæ dabis. Ita voveo, ita spero. Nunc audi quid ad te afferam. Nuper ex seculari philologia per epistolas sermocinati sumus. Nunc ex sacra aliquid depromere est animus. Aperiam tibi fontes celeberrimæ istius allegoriæ, qua universum istum Dei O. M. de Behemoth & Leviathan discursum Scholastici ad Diabolum traduxerunt. Tu, licet admodum adolescens, eos in Ebraismo jam fecisti progressus, ut de universo negotio possis judicare. Deus O. M. de sua potentia dissertaturus, ex universa creaturarum multitudine duas creaturas commemorat, Behemoth id est elephantem & Leviathan id est balænam, hanc inter pisces, illum inter belluas robore & vasta corporis mole excellentes. Elephantes Græci Ἐλέφας, Latini belluas appellabant. Tralatitium enim apud eos est, τὰ προπύνοντα ἐν τῷ γένει τῶν ἐλεφάντων ὀνόματα ... Suidas Ἐλέφας, οἱ ἐλέφαντες. Et ταυρικοὶ Ἐλεφάν apud Plutarchum in Eumene nihil aliud sunt quam turres elephantorum, seu turriti elephanti. Terent in Eunucho, Eone es ferox, quia imperium habes in belluas? Et Plin. 8. Circa dentes belluis summa cura. At Ebraeis non satis fuit elephantem nomine generis καὶ ἐξοχὴν appellare בְּהֵמָה sed insuper quia corporis mole multas belluas æquat, majoris auxescos causa, vocem illam numero plurali exprimere. Inter cæteros amplificationum modos Ebræis familiares, iste non postremus est, Ita increatam illam Sapientiam vocant הַכְמוֹת Prov.1.20. & 9.1. summam benignitatem חסדים Thren.3.22. summum robur, מְעֻזִּים Dan.11.38 Et hanc eandem vocem בהמות Ps. 73. 22. non quidem pro elephante, sed tamen pro magna & crassa bestia accipiunt Genev. & Mercerus. Eram apud ea בהמות inquit Psaltes, [sicut] bestia, Merc. come une grand' beste, Genev. une grosse beste, Sed redeamus ad Elephantem. Vtrum ea vox ab אלף bos, an vero potius ab אלף quod Syris & Ebraeis discere est, derivata sit, merito dubites. Adeo verisimilis utraque sententia est. Nam quod primam attinet, in confesso est, apud Graecos & Latinos, nobilitatam semper fuisse bovis prae caeteris terrestribus animantibus magnitudinem. Hinc Graeci rebus quas augere volebant, syllabam βο praefigebant, βουλιμίαν magnam famem, βόπαιδα, grandem puerum, vocantes. Romani, cum in Lucania primum, in exercitu Pyrrhi elephantes vidissent, * boves Lucas seu Lucanos appellabant. Majus enim bove animal tellus ista non edebat. Adhaec boves Lucani caeteris Italicis grandiores erant. Ita credibile quoque est, Ebraeos, Syros & Phoenices, cum hoc animal & mole & figuratione corporis ad bovem quam proxime accedens, primo vidissent, bovis nomine appellasse. Quod ad alteram attinet, quis ignorat ea, quae de hujus bellua docilitate narrant Plinius libro 8. cap. 1. 3. 7. Cicero Epist. Famil. 1. 7. Arrianus de rebus Indicis, & plena manu Lipsius, Centuria I. Epistola 50. ad Janum Hautenum. Hoc ergo animal admodum graphice hoc loco describit is, qui creavit illud. Lxx. insistentes vestigiis Ebraici textus, ϑηρία, reddidere tamen postea tanquam de uno loquuntur. Etiam. Chald. בעירא / Siquidem בהמה respondet Ebraeo בהמתא / Atque hic quoque vides, nomen generis in hac specie cum excellentiae significatione resedisse. Hinc est Sabinorum Barrus & Indorum Barre. Etiam ex recentioribus Ebraeis plerique elephantem describi existimant. Astipulantur Thomas, Lyra, * Pererius, Emmanuel Sa & alii. Et certe in hac descriptione, si textus originalis accurate vertatur, nihil est quod non optime in Elephantem quadret. Non lubet jam excutere, quae nugatores quidam Ebraei de hoc animali, quod שור הבר id est bovem sylvestrem, vocant, itemque de magno isto pisce, chartis illevere. Si libet ea cognoscere, adito Lyram ad hunc locum, & ad Ps. 49. Ebraeis 50. R. Salom. ad Ps. eundem, Buxtorfii Synagogam Judaicam, Pseudo-Ezram lib. 4. cap. 6. ubi pro Behemoth corrupte legitur Enoch Enoch. Majus operæ pretium fuerit videre quid nonnullos ex patribus, quid Scholasticos, quid denique Pontificios Interpretes moverit totum hunc contextum, quo de Behemoth & Leviathan agitur, de diabolo exponere. Carthus. ad literam non est proprie sermo de illis, sed de re metaphorice figurata per eas, puta, de dæmone, qui hic per maxima quædam bruta insinuatur, quia ab angelica corruens dignitate in belluinam versus est immanitatem, monstruositatem ac rabiem. Propter quod in formis brutorum frequenter appare. Lyra, Expositores Catholici exponunt hæc de dæmone sub similitudine elephantis & ceti. Et paulo post, Igitur exponatur litera de dæmone sub nomine elephantis designato: quia in parabola sensus literalis est non ille qui immediate per vocem significantur, sed per res significatas. Vides eos hoc velle, primarium scopum Dei fuisse, hoc capite Diabolum describere. Huic sententiæ etiam * Evangelici quidam hærere. Ego vero cum illis facio, qui uniuersam istam expositionem nullo omnino fundamento subnixam autumant. Quicquid hic dicitur, de Elephante & balæna exponi commodissime potest. Vide Jun. Deod. Mercerum, Genev. Emmanuelem Sa & alios. Nihil coactum, nihil contortum est. At eorum interpretatio, qui omnia de Diabolo intelligunt, non tam plana decurrit orbita. Sudant & æstuant boni isti Interpretes, ut doceant quodnam sit illud fœnum, quod Diabolus comedit. Quisnam sit umbilicus ejus, quæ cauda, qui testiculi, &c. Et cum omnes ingenii nervos intenderunt, tantum lusere, nihil unquam ab erudito & cordato lectore nisi precario obtenturi. Et quod ad priscos illos attinet, fateor Ebraismorum ignorantiam & aberrantem non uno loco versionem ipsis quasi injecisse manum, ut, dum pauca quædam loca de elephante vel balæna explicari non posse, Diabolo contra optime convenire putarent, omnia tanquam de Diabolo primario dicta acciperent. Sed quid illi obtendent, qui in hac literarum luce ipsa illa loca, ad quæ prisci offenderunt, de elephante & balæna commode exponi posse agnoscunt, atque adeo ipsi in commentariis suis exponunt, & tamen huic allegoriæ mordicus hærent. Quod enim fundamentum huic expositioni substernent? Nihil certe ex ipso hoc textu, nihil ex universa veteris noviqve fœderis pagina proferent. Nihil præter authoritatem plerorumque patrum adducent. Eâ vero his & id genus similibus casibus non magis moveor quam Salmeron, qui ad objectam sibi magnum Patrum numerum (ad Roman. v. Disp.6. 51. circa initium) sic respondet, Pauperis est numerare pecus. In judicio plurimorum non acquiescess sententia, ut à vero devies. Et cum Donatiste in authorum multitudine gloriarentur, respondit Augustinus, signum esse causa à veritatis nervo destituta, qua soli multorum authoritati, qui errare possint, innititur. Sed penetremus in ipsos fontes celeberrimæ hujus allegoriæ. Atque hic occurrit primo.
units.tr: you will give your country a distinguished philologist, a jurist elegantly learned in literature, and finally a pious and upright priest of Justice. So I pray, so I hope. Now hear what I have to bring you. Lately we have conversed by letters about secular philology. Now I intend to bring forth something from sacred learning. I will open to you the sources of that most famous allegory by which the scholastics have transferred that whole passage of God Almighty about Behemoth and Leviathan to the Devil. You, though very young, have already made such progress in Hebraism that you can judge the whole matter. God Almighty, about to discourse on his power, from the whole multitude of creatures mentions two creatures, Behemoth, that is the elephant, and Leviathan, that is the whale: the one excelling among fishes, the other among beasts, in strength and the huge mass of its body. The Greeks called the elephant Elephas, and the Latins called it a beast. For it is a common usage among them: the names preceding in the genus of elephants [τὰ προπύνοντα ἐν τῷ γένει τῶν ἐλεφάντων ὀνόματα] ... Suidas on Elephas: the elephants. And the tauric elephants [ταυρικοὶ Ἐλεφάν] in Plutarch's Eumenes are nothing other than towers of elephants, or elephants with towers. Terence in the Eunuch: Are you so fierce, because you have power over the beasts? And Pliny, book 8: Great care is taken of the teeth of the beasts. But for the Hebrews it was not enough to call the elephant by the name of its genus and by way of eminence behemah [בְּהֵמָה]; they also, because by the mass of its body it equals many beasts, expressed that word in the plural to signify greater size. Among the other modes of amplification familiar to the Hebrews, this is not the least: they call that uncreated Wisdom hokhmot [הַכְמוֹת] (Prov. 1:20 and 9:1), great kindness hasadim [חסדים] (Lam. 3:22), and supreme strength me'uzzim [מְעֻזִּים] (Dan. 11:38). And the same word behemot [בהמות] in Ps. 73:22 they take, not indeed for the elephant, but for a great and fat beast, both the Geneva translators and Mercerus. I was like a beast [בהמות], says the Psalmist, [as] beast, Mercerus: comme une grand' beste; Geneva: une grosse beste. But let us return to the elephant. You may rightly doubt whether that word is derived from alef [אלף], ox, or rather from alaph, which is to be learned from the Syrians and Hebrews. Both opinions are so plausible. For as to the first, it is agreed that among Greeks and Latins the size of the ox has always been held in high regard above other land animals. Hence the Greeks, when they wished to enlarge things, prefixed the syllable bo [βο], calling great hunger boulimia [βουλιμίαν] and a big boy bopaida [βόπαιδα]. The Romans, when they first saw elephants in Lucania in the army of Pyrrhus, called them Lucan oxen [boves Lucas] or Lucanians [Lucanos]. For that land produced no animal larger than the ox. Besides, the Lucanian oxen were larger than the other Italian ones. So it is also credible that the Hebrews, Syrians and Phoenicians, when they first saw this animal, which in size and bodily shape comes very close to the ox, named it after the ox. As to the second, who does not know what Pliny tells of this beast's docility in book 8, chapters 1, 3 and 7; Cicero, Letters to Family 1.7; Arrian on Indian matters; and Lipsius, Century I, letter 50 to Janus Houtenus, in abundance? So he who created this animal describes it very vividly in this place. The Seventy, following the footsteps of the Hebrew text, rendered it thēria [ϑηρία], yet afterward they speak of it as of one animal. Also the Chaldee: ba'ira [בעירא]; for behemah corresponds to the Hebrew behemta [בהמתא]. And here too you see that the name of the genus remained in this species together with the sense of excellence. Hence come the Barrus of the Sabines and the Barre of the Indians. Also most of the more recent Hebrews think that the elephant is described. Thomas, Lyra, Pererius, Emmanuel Sa and others agree. And indeed, in this description, if the original text is translated accurately, there is nothing that does not fit the elephant perfectly. I do not now care to examine what certain trifling Hebrews have daubed on paper about this animal, which they call shor habar [שור הבר], that is, the wild ox [bovem sylvestrem], and likewise about that great fish. If you wish to know those things, consult Lyra on this passage and on Ps. 49, which among the Hebrews is 50; Rabbi Solomon on the same Psalm; Buxtorf's Jewish Synagogue; and Pseudo-Ezra, book 4, chapter 6, where for Behemoth it is corruptly read Enoch Enoch. It would be more worthwhile to see what moved some of the Fathers, what the Scholastics, and finally what the Papist interpreters, to expound this whole passage, in which Behemoth and Leviathan are discussed, of the Devil. The Carthusian: Strictly speaking, the literal sense is not about those animals, but about a thing figuratively signified through them, namely the demon, who here is hinted at through certain very great brute beasts, because, falling from his angelic dignity, he has been turned into a bestial savagery, monstrousness and rage. For this reason he often appears in the forms of brute beasts. Lyra: The Catholic expositors explain these things of the demon under the likeness of the elephant and the whale. And a little after: Therefore let the letter be explained of the demon, designated under the name of the elephant; for in a parable the literal sense is not that which is signified immediately by the words, but that which is signified by the things. You see that they wish the chief aim of God in this chapter to have been to describe the Devil. Some Evangelicals also cling to this opinion. I, however, side with those who think that this whole exposition rests on no foundation at all. Whatever is said here can be most conveniently explained of the elephant and the whale. See Junius, Deodatus, Mercerus, the Geneva translators, Emmanuel Sa and others. Nothing is forced, nothing twisted. But the interpretation of those who understand everything of the Devil does not run so smooth a course. Those good interpreters sweat and labor to teach what that hay is which the Devil eats; who his navel is, what his tail, what his testicles, and so on. And when they have strained every nerve of their wit, they have only played, and will never obtain anything from a learned and sensible reader except by his indulgence. As for the ancients, I admit that their ignorance of Hebraisms, and their mistranslation in more than one place, gave them, as it were, a hold on the text, so that, thinking that a few passages could not be explained of the elephant or the whale but agreed very well with the Devil, they took everything as said primarily of the Devil. But what will those defend who, in this light of learning, recognize that those very passages which the ancients stumbled over can be fairly explained of the elephant and the whale, and indeed expound them so in their own commentaries, and yet cling stubbornly to this allegory? For what foundation do they lay for this exposition? Certainly they produce nothing from this text itself, nothing from the whole page of the Old and New Covenant. They bring nothing but the authority of most of the Fathers. But I am no more moved by that authority in such cases as these than Salmeron, who, to the great number of Fathers cited against him (on Rom. 5, Disputation 6, 51, near the beginning), answers thus: It is the part of a poor man to count the flock. Agreement of the many is not the judgment of truth, so that you may wander from the truth. And when the Donatists boasted of the number of their authors, Augustine answered that it is a sign of a cause destitute of the sinews of truth, which rests only on the authority of many who can err. But let us penetrate to the very sources of this famous allegory. And here the first thing that meets us is

units.la: Verf. 14. Ipse est principium viarum Domini. Et certe hic locus videtur manum injecisse plerisque recentiorum, ut hic quoque cum Scholasticis ineptiverint. Existimabant enim hæc non nisi de Angelorum principe vel saltem de Angelica natura exponi posse. Lyra, Hoc interponitur ad intelligendum, quod ea, qua di- cuntur hic ; de damone intelliguntur sub metaphora elephantis. Est enim damon principium viarum Dei , quia inter cretaruras angelica est prima , & inter angelos ille qui fuit primus simpliciter , peccavit per superbiam , & fuit aliis cadentibus occasio peccandi. Et Carthuf. Ex hoc verbo & quibusdam sequentibus constat quod ista de diabolo tanquam re figurata principaliter proferantur, &c. Quin & Bellarm. libr. 1. cap. 9. de Pontifice , ubi argumentum 9. pro Monarchico statu Ecclesiae depromit ab exemplo Angelorum, probaturus eum qui nunc Diabolus vocatur, ante lapsum fuisse caput Angelorum , hunc locum in acie ponit. Sed ut locus iste de diabolo principaliter intelligatur , illud adhuc probandum erat Cardinali, per vias Domini Angelos ; per principium principatum intelligi. Vias Domini actiones Domini accipimus, inquit Gregorius & ex eo Glossa ordin. An ergo omnium Dei actionum princeps & Monarcha fuit Diabolus? Sed hoc principatu ad Jef. cap, XIV. plura dicentur. Tu hic observa, per vias Domini opera ejus & creaturas intelligi. Non diffitentur hoc Pontificii. Ideo compendifaciam laborem probandi. Vox autem Ebraeaa ראשית cui respondet in Vulgato principium, vel temporis vel dignitatis principatum significat. Si dignitatis principatum intelligas , jam locus de elephanto optime potest exponi, atque ita corruet primarius , imo unicus hujus Allegoriae tibicen. Iste videlicet, locum hunc de elephanto omnino intelligi non posse. Principatum temporis hic non quadrare fateor libens. Elephas enim creatus est eodem die quo homo, vid. sexto, unde de nonnulli interpretantur ista verba, Ecce behemoth, quem feci tecum, sc. eodem die, alii, aque ac te, alii, ut degeret tecum. At princ. dignitatis quadrat optime, ut hoc dicat, eum, si corporis molem, vires & illud Ϝυμόσοφον id est τὸ ἐν φύσεως ἐυμα-θὴς, καὶ ἐυφυὲς καὶ ὀξυμαθὲς spectes, inter creaturas irrationales esse praestantissimum suum δημιούργημα & primarium opus. Hanc interpretationem probat Emmanuel Sa in notis, quasi dicat, inquit, praecipuum animalium a Deo factorum, quod attinet ad fortitudinem & prudentiam. Genev. C'est le chef d'oeure du Dieu. Iste est caput operum Dei. Ita & Angli, & Hispani, nisi quod pro operum retinuerint vocem viarum. He is the chiefe of the wayes of God. Hisp. El es la cabeça de los caminos de Dios. Ital. Egli e la principale dell' opere di Dio. Ille est praestantissimum opus ex operibus Dei. Castellio, Ipse est divini opificii caput. Ita Amos 6. Qui ungunt se ראשיית id est principio unguentorum, hoc est, praestantissimo unguento Num. 24. Principium gentium Amalek, 1. Sam. 15. principium (ראשית) anathematis id est praecipuum Sirach. 11. 3. ἀρχὴ γλυκυσμάχων καρπὸς αὐτῆς. Minima volatilium est apis, at principium dulcium condimentorum est fructus ejus, id est principatum quendam tenet inter dulcia condimenta. Cave autem huc referas locum Apoc. 3. 14. ubi Filius Dei vocatur ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως & Θεοῦ. Namque illic ἀρχὴ non principium passivum, sed activum significat, a quo omnes creaturae principium suum ducunt, quam interpretationem utriusque testamenti pagina evincit. Vides jam opinor, ex non intellecto Ebraismo versus x. delatos fuisse interpretes in hanc sententiam, de Diabolo principaliter hic agi. Sed progrediamur ad alia quae huic loco superstruxit antiquitas. Beda in libello separatarum quaestionum quaest. 9. Angeli, inquit ante creationem mundi creati sunt, & ante omnem creationem Angelorum Diabolus est conditus, sicut scriptum est, Ipse principium viarum Dei [Confer cum his ea quae supra p. 196.] Vides hoc quoque somnium non intellecto Ebraismo deberi. Gregorius Moral. lib. 32. cap. 25. ex hoc loco adversus Arrium disputat, notandum quoque, inquit, quod dum viarum Dei principium Behemoth dicitur, vesanum Arrii dogma aperta ratione dissipatur. Facturam quippe Dei filium fatetur. Et ecce Behemoth in factura rerum primus creatus ostenditur. Superest ergo ut Arrius aut non factum filium praedicet, aut eum post Behemoth conditum stultus putet. patet. Non male, si de diabolo hic agi firma aliqua ratione evincere potuisset. Lxx. Interpretes, sicuti ipsi ab Ebraeæ veritatis linea aberrarunt, ita & beatos Patres, qui istam versionem secuti sunt, in avia traxerunt. τὰτ' ἐσὶν ἀρχὴ πλάσματος ... quæ sic convertit Latinus Interpres, Hoc est principium * fictionis Domini factum ut illuderetur ab angelis ejus. Accedens autem ad montem præcisum fecit gaudium quadrupedibus in tartaro. Ab ipsa quoque vulgata hæc nimium quantum abeunt, Sic enim illa, Ipse est pr. v. Domini, qui fecit eum applicabit gladium ejus. Huic montes herbas ferunt, omnes bestiæ agri ludunt ibi. Magister sententiarum lib. 2. dist. 3. quærens, utrum angeli boni vel mali creati sint, & an aliqua mora inter creationem & lapsum intercesserit, quosdam exististe, angelos qui ceciderunt, creatos fuisse malos, & non libero arbitrio in malitiam declinasse, sed in malitia a Deo factos esse, nec aliquam fuisse moram inter creationem & lapsum, sed ab initio apostatasse. Phy τὰς θεολογίας ταύτας, quæ Deum authorem peccati & malitiæ statuit. Sed audi quid addat. Ait illos suæ sententiæ fulcra quæsivisse ex August de Genes. ad literam lib. xi. cap. 19. 20. ubi duo scripturæ loca producit, vid. Joh. 8. Ille homicida fuit ab initio & in veritate non stetit, & hunc ipsum, de quo jam agitur, ex versione Græca postquam Magister contrariam sententiam asseruisset, * Augustinum, sanius quidem sentientem, at non melius locum Jobi interpretantem introducit. Omnia, inquit Aug. fecit Deus valde bona. Naturam ergo angelorum bonam fecit. — Nec ejus natura significata est cum dicit, hoc est initium figmenti Dei, sed corpus æreum, quod tali voluntati aptavit Deus, vel ipsam ordinationem Dei, in qua eum invitum etiam fecit utilem bonis, vel ipsius angeli facturam, quia esi præsciret Deus, voluntate malum futurum; fecit tamen eum, providens, quanta de illo sua bonitate esset facturus. Figmentum ergo Dei dicitur, quia cum sciret eum Deus voluntate malum futurum, ut bonis noceret, creavit tamen illum, ut de illo bonis prodesset, hoc autem fecit (N B.) ut illudatur ei. Illuditur enim ei, cum sanctis proficit tentatio ejus. Sed ipse est initium, quia precedit antiquitate & principatu malitia. Hac autem illusio fit angelis malis & hominibus malis, per angelos sanctos, quia subdit illis angelos malos & homines malos, ut non quantum nituntur, sed quantum sulluntur, possint nocere. Habes argutam explicationem sententiae, quae in originali hoc loco non comparet. Atque haec de Behemoth. Restat
units.tr: Verse 14. He is the beginning of the ways of the Lord. Certainly this verse seems to have gripped most of the more recent writers, so that they too have talked nonsense here along with the Schoolmen. For they thought these words could be explained only of the prince of the angels, or at least of the angelic nature. Lyra: This is inserted to make clear that the things said here are understood of the devil under the metaphor of the elephant. For the devil is the beginning of God's ways, since among creatures the angelic nature is first, and among the angels he who was first simply, sinned through pride, and was an occasion of sin to the others who fell. And the Carthusian: From this verse and some that follow it is clear that these things are said chiefly of the devil as the figured thing, etc. Indeed Bellarmine too, book 1, chapter 9, on the Pontiff, where he advances his ninth argument for the monarchical state of the Church from the example of the angels, wishing to prove that he who is now called the devil was the head of the angels before his fall, places this passage in the forefront. But for this passage to be understood chiefly of the devil, the Cardinal still had to prove that by "the ways of the Lord" angels are meant, and by "beginning" a principate. Gregory, and after him the Ordinary Gloss, say: We take the ways of the Lord to mean the actions of the Lord. Was the devil then the prince and monarch of all God's actions? But more will be said about this principate on Isaiah chapter 14. Note here that by "the ways of the Lord" his works and creatures are meant. The Papists do not deny this. So I will spare myself the labour of proving it. The Hebrew word reshith [ראשית], which the Vulgate renders principium, signifies either a principate of time or of dignity. If you understand a principate of dignity, then the passage can very well be explained of the elephant, and so their chief, indeed their only, support for this allegory collapses. That is, the claim that this passage cannot be understood of the elephant at all. I freely admit that a principate of time does not fit here. For the elephant was created on the same day as man, namely the sixth, whence some interpret the words Behold Behemoth, which I made with you, as meaning on the same day; others, just as I made you; others, that it might live with you. But a principate of dignity fits very well, so that the sense is this: if you look at the bulk of its body, its strength, and that quality which is well-learned by nature, well-endowed and quick to learn [τὸ ἐν φύσεως εὐμαθὲς καὶ εὐφυὲς καὶ ὀξυμαθὲς], then it is the most excellent among irrational creatures, his own masterpiece and chief work. Emmanuel Sa in his notes approves this interpretation: as if he were saying, he writes, the most outstanding of the animals made by God, as regards strength and prudence. The Geneva Bible: It is the masterpiece of God. He is the chief of God's works. So also the English and the Spanish, except that for works they have kept the word ways: He is the chiefe of the wayes of God. Spanish: He is the head of the ways of God. Italian: He is the principal of God's works. He is the most excellent work among the works of God. Castellio: He is the head of God's craftsmanship. So in Amos 6, those who anoint themselves [ראשית], that is, with the beginning of ointments, that is, with the most excellent ointment; Numbers 24, the beginning of the nations is Amalek; 1 Samuel 15, the beginning [ראשית] of the devoted things, that is, the chief part; Sirach 11:3, The least of winged creatures is the bee, yet its fruit is the beginning of sweet things [ἀρχὴ γλυκυσμάχων καρπὸς αὐτῆς], that is, it holds a certain principate among sweet delicacies. But take care not to refer to this passage Revelation 3:14, where the Son of God is called the beginning of the creation [ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως] and of God. For there arche signifies not a passive beginning but an active one, from which all creatures derive their origin; the page of both Testaments proves this interpretation. You now see, I think, that because the Hebrew idiom was not understood, verse 10 has led the interpreters into this opinion, that the devil is chiefly meant here. But let us go on to the other things that antiquity built on this passage. Bede, in his little book of Separate Questions, question 9: The angels, he says, were created before the creation of the world, and before the whole creation of the angels the devil was made, as it is written, He is the beginning of the ways of God. [Compare what is said above on p. 196.] You see that this dream too is owed to a failure to understand the Hebrew. Gregory, Morals, book 32, chapter 25, argues from this passage against Arius: It should also be noted, he says, that while Behemoth is called the beginning of God's ways, the mad doctrine of Arius is clearly dispelled by reason. For he confesses the Son to be a creature of God. And behold, Behemoth is shown to be the first created in the making of things. It remains, therefore, that Arius must either deny that the Son was made, or foolishly suppose that he was created after Behemoth. That is clear. It would not be a bad argument, if one could prove by some solid reason that the devil is meant here. The Seventy translators, just as they strayed from the line of the Hebrew truth, so also led the blessed Fathers who followed that version astray. [Τοῦτ' ἐστιν ἀρχὴ πλάσματος ...] This the Latin interpreter renders thus: This is the beginning of the fashioning of the Lord, made to be mocked by his angels. But approaching the cut mountain he gave joy to the quadrupeds in Tartarus. These words differ greatly also from the Vulgate itself. For it reads: He is the beginning of the ways of the Lord; he who made him shall apply his sword to him. Mountains bear herbs for him; all the beasts of the field play there. The Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 3, asking whether good or evil angels were created, and whether any delay intervened between creation and fall, says that some held that the angels who fell were created evil, and did not turn to wickedness by free will, but were made by God in wickedness, and that there was no delay between creation and fall, but that they apostatised from the beginning. [Oh, these theologies, which make God the author of sin and wickedness.] But hear what he adds. He says that those who held this opinion sought its supports from Augustine on Genesis according to the letter, book 11, chapters 19 and 20, where he cites two passages of Scripture, John 8: He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth. And after the Master had asserted the contrary opinion, he introduces Augustine, who indeed thinks more soundly, but does not interpret the passage of Job any better, concerning this very passage now under discussion, from the Greek version. God made all things very good. He therefore made the nature of the angels good. Nor is their nature signified when it says, this is the beginning of the figment of God, but the bronze body which God fitted to such a will; or the very ordering of God, in which he made him, though unwilling, useful to good men; or the creature of the angel himself, for although God foreknew that he would be evil by his will, nevertheless he made him, foreseeing how much good he would do by his goodness. He is called the figment of God because, though God knew that he would be evil by his will, so as to harm good men, he nevertheless created him, that he might profit good men by him; and he did this (NB) that he might be mocked. For he is mocked, when his temptation profits the saints. But he is the beginning, because wickedness precedes in antiquity and principate. This mockery, moreover, takes place for the evil angels and evil men through the holy angels, because he subjects to them evil angels and evil men, so that they can do harm not as much as they strive to, but as much as they are permitted. You have here a subtle explanation of a sense which does not appear in the original of this passage. And so much for Behemoth. The rest

units.la: LEVIATHAN] De quo iidem authores ita sentiunt, sub ejus quoque similitudine agi principaliter de Diabolo, seu quod idem illis est, daemoniorum principe. Marsennus tamen videtur existimasse, hic describi vel Optionem vel collegam Diaboli. Asserit enim pag. 851. comm. sui in priora capita Geneseos, Behemoth & Leviathan esse duos principes daemonum. Mirum in modum & hic aestuant interpretes, ut omnia & singula de Diabolo explicent. Vide Lyram Carthus. Gregorium, & alios. at nostris Interpretibus, de balaena, vel si quod est aliud portentosae magnitudinis in mari animal, omnia interpretantibus ad literam, optime fluunt omnia. Vide Iun. Pisc. Merc. Genev. Ital. & alios. quae ergo necessitas haec de Satana primario interpretandi; Imo quae certitudo interpretationis allegoricae & secundariae; Nulla omnino. Oleum & operam perdidere qui in has interpretationes incubuere, Oleum & operam perdunt, qui eidem lineae insistentes, hujusmodi commenta populo proponunt. Porro, 3. loca videor mihi observasse, quae persuaserunt veteribus, hic primario Diabolum describi. Locus prior est iste, cap. 41. vers. 3. secundum vulg. Interpretem. Non parcam ei verbis potentibus & ad deprecandum compositis. Quae sic interpretatur Carthus. propter nulla ipsius verba parcam Diabolo, sive sint verba potestatem suam praferentia, sive humiliationem quandam sonantia, quando ejus potestatem refrenem & impiam ipsius puniam voluntatem. Interdum quippe ad deprecandum se convertit astute, ut a nocendo arceatur, vel ne gravius affligatur. Et ex hoc verbo ostenditur, quod non sit jam de ceto principaliter mentio. Sed monendus hic mihi es, in Ebraeo nihil ejusmodi legi, לא אחריש בהיי יִדבּר גבורות והין ערכו quae Pagninus ita reddidit, Non silebo membra (Arias, vestes) ejus, & * verbum fortitudinum & gratiam dispositionis ejus. Joh. Bened. Theol. Parisiensis, non tacebo robur ejus & quicquid habet virium, gratiam quoque dispositionis ejus. Alter locus est 16. Cum sublatus fuerit, timebunt angeli & territi purgabuntur. An ob ceti sublationem vel interfectionem sanctos angelos terreri credibile est; Non pluris illi faciunt talis belluae occisionem, quam nos unius pulicis inquit Carthus. Necessario ergo locum exponenduin: putant defublatione seu expulsione principis daemoniorum à throno cœlesti, ut loquitur Carthusianus. Gregorius, Sub futuri temporis modo praeterita describuntur. Nec recte intelligentia sensum relinquimus, si credamus, Leviathan isto ab arce beatitudinis cadente, in ruina ejus etiam electos angelos expaviße, ut cum illum ex illorum numero superbia lapsus ejiceret, illos ad robustius standum timor ipse solidaret. Purgati verò sunt, quia isto cum reprobis legionibus exeunte, soli in cœlestibus sedibus remanserunt. Hujus itaque lapsus eos terruit & purgavit. Lyra, Iste timor est admiratio angelorum sanctorum de divina virtute & justitia in dejectione daemonis, quae partim facta est à principio sui casus, & consummabitur in futuro judicio. Et territi purgabuntur, &c. non ab immunditia sed à nescientia purgati sunt, videntes divinam virtutem & justitiam in effectu quam prius non viderant. Ideo eodem modo erit in destructione daemonis in infernum in extremo judicio, &c. Vide & Gloss. ordinariam. Sed haec quoque aliter leguntur in Ebraeo, מַשְׁחוּ יָגוּרוּ / אֵילִים מְשַׁבְּרִים יִתְחַיְּאוּ / Pagn. A magnitudine (Arias, altitudine, malium cum Pisc. propter elevationem) ejus timebunt fortes: à contritionibus purgabunt se. Piscator, expiabunt se. Sensus est quando balæna sese in mari jactat & elevat, etiam fortissimi quique exalbescunt metu, & cum vident illam magno cum impetu mare confringere, Deo supplices fiunt & peccatorum suorum veniam petunt, nil nisi mortem expectantes. תֹּ אֵילִים proprie & primò fortes denotare, nullus infitebitur. Sed dices, aliquando per synecdochen generis pro angelis poni. Resp. ut hoc detur (quod tamen liquido exemplo nullus contradicenti extorserit, loca enim quæ vulgo afferuntur, aliam interpretationem admittunt omnia) tamen illud obtinebo, ut à sensu literali, ita & à propria & communissima vocum interpretatione non esse recedendum, nisi exigente necessitate, quam hic nullus evincet. Porro, מִשְׁבָּרִים significare territos, nullus, opinor, ostendet. Verbum denique הִתְחַטֵּא purgationem à nescientia vel societate malorum significare, tunc credam, ubi evidentem aliquem locum hujus expositionis patroni produxerint. Rectius ergo Emmanuel Sa hæc de balæna seu ceto interpretatus est, Sublatus ] scil. in altum se erigens. Angeli ] Chald. fortes, q. d. fortissimi quique. Sed dum interpretatur vocem ultimam purgabuntur, graviter impingit. Purgabuntur, inquit, sc. sosc. soluta alvo pra timore. An ergo התחטא purgationem alvi significat? Quanto rectius fecisset, si de purgatione conscientiæ verbum illud fuisset interpretatum. Deodatus, si purgano de loro peccati. Jun. Angli, purgant se: scilicet à peccatis. Crassam illam interptaretionem hausit Sa ex R,Levi, ממשברי לב שישיגום בסכרת הפהר יתנקו דרך נקביהם לעשות צואתם ומימי רגליהם hoc est, pra confractionibus cordis, qua apprehendent eos & magno metu, purgabuntur per ordinarios natura meatus, faciendo excrementum suum (Ita sonant Ebræa ἀὀ7λεξεὶ) & aquas pedum suorum id est urinam. Indigna Ebræo interpretatio. Locus tertius & ultimus est verf. ultimo, omne sublime videt, ipse est rex super universos filios superbia. Lyra, Quia per superbiam semper nititur aggredi majora, omne sublime videt, ad consequendum, si posset. Et excedit omnes alios in superbia. Et per hoc patet, quod ea quæ dicta sunt de ceto, intelliguntur principaliter de damone. Videamus Ebræa, ואת־כל גבה יראה הוא מלך על כל בני שחץ Pagn. omne sublime despiciet, ipse est rex super omnes cetos magnos & fortes. Arias, super omnes filios superbia. Emmanuel Sa, videt, id est despicit. universos filios superbia, id est bellUas marinas quamvis ingentes. Chald. כל בני כיר omnes filios piscium. Lxx. βασιλεὺς πάντων ... omnium quæ in aqua. Aben Ezra ait vocem שחץ significare seu comprehendere כל גולד במים quidquid generatur in aquis. Junius putavit vocem Ebr. significare feram, Est regma super omnes feras, Ebr. inquit, filios fera. Reginam vocat, quem Ebræus sermo Regem vocat, quia vocem Leviathan per fœmin. balænam, interpretatus est. At Pisc. qui cetum ubi substituit, est rex super omnia elata animalia, imitatus doctissimum Mercetum. Supra 28.8 eadem phrasis de leonibus usurpata fuit. Nulla ergo necessitas per filios elationis homines intelligere. Et quis tam in his literis hospes, qui varium usum Ebraici הָ ignoret? Ut ergo vocem quam latissime extendamus, Leviathanem interomnia superba animantia facile esse principem, docere voluit Deus. Coronidis loco nota, Thomam in Summa, parte 1. Quæst.63. ubi de Angelis fuse agit, horum locorum non meminisse, unde colligas, circa cjus interpretationem eum à vulgata sententia diversum sensisse. Atque hic finis esto. Vale ornatissime adolescens & salve.
units.tr: LEVIATHAN] On this point the same authors hold that under his likeness the Devil is chiefly meant, or, which comes to the same thing for them, the prince of the demons. Marsennus, however, seems to have thought that either the Adversary's chief agent or a colleague of the Devil is described here. For at p. 851 of his commentary on the earlier chapters of Genesis he asserts that Behemoth and Leviathan are two princes of the demons. Here, as elsewhere, the interpreters strangely labour to explain every detail of the passage as referring to the Devil. See Lyra, the Carthusian, Gregory and others. But for our own interpreters, who take everything literally of the whale, or of whatever other animal of monstrous size lives in the sea, all things fit together very well. See Junius, Piscator, the Geneva Bible, the Italian version and others. What necessity, then, is there to interpret these things primarily of Satan? Or what certainty is there in an allegorical and secondary interpretation? None at all. Those who have devoted themselves to these interpretations have wasted their oil and their labour, and those who keep to the same line and put such inventions before the people waste their oil and labour too. Further, I think I have noticed three passages which have persuaded the ancients that the Devil is primarily described here. The first is chap. 41, verse 3, according to the Vulgate translator: "I will not spare him, with mighty words and words suited to entreaty." The Carthusian explains it thus: "I will spare the Devil in no words of his, whether they set forth his power or sound a certain humility, when I restrain his power and punish his wicked will. For at times he turns himself cunningly to entreaty, so that he may be kept from harming, or lest he be afflicted more severely. And from this word it is shown that there is no longer any mention principally of the whale." But I must warn you that in the Hebrew nothing of this kind is read: [לא אחריש בהיי יִדבּר גבורות והין ערכו]. Pagninus rendered it: "I will not be silent about his limbs (Arias: his garments) and the word of his strength and the grace of his arrangement." John Benedict, the Paris theologian: "I will not keep silent about his strength and whatever power he has, and also the grace of his arrangement." The second passage is verse 16: "When he is raised up, the angels will fear, and being terrified they will be purified." Is it credible that the holy angels were terrified by the lifting up or killing of the whale? They value the slaying of such a beast no more than we value the killing of a single flea, says the Carthusian. Therefore the passage must of necessity be explained otherwise. They think it refers to "the overthrow or expulsion of the prince of the demons from the heavenly throne," as the Carthusian puts it. Gregory says: "The past is described in the mode of the future tense." Nor do we rightly grasp the sense if we believe that when Leviathan fell from that height of blessedness, the chosen angels also were terrified by his downfall, so that when pride threw him out from their number, that very fear steadied them to stand more firmly. They were purified because, when he departed with the reprobate legions, only those who remained in the heavenly seats were left. His fall therefore terrified them and purified them. Lyra: "This fear is the wonder of the holy angels at the divine power and justice shown in the casting down of the demon, which was partly done at the beginning of his fall and will be completed at the future judgment." As for "they will be terrified and purified," etc.: "they were purified not from uncleanness but from ignorance, seeing the divine power and justice in an effect which they had not seen before. So it will be in the destruction of the demon into hell at the last judgment." See also the Ordinary Gloss. But these words are also read otherwise in the Hebrew: [מַשְׁחוּ יָגוּרוּ / אֵילִים מְשַׁבְּרִים יִתְחַיְּאוּ]. Pagninus: "Because of his height (Arias: his lofty stature; Piscator: because of the lifting up of the waves) the strong will fear; by the breakings they will cleanse themselves." Piscator: "they will make atonement for themselves." The sense is this: when the whale tosses and lifts himself in the sea, even the bravest men grow pale with fear, and when they see him break the sea with great force they become suppliants before God and ask pardon for their sins, expecting nothing but death. That [אֵילִים] properly and primarily denotes "the strong," no one will deny. But you will say that sometimes by synecdoche of the genus it stands for angels. I answer: grant that this is so (though no one has yet drawn from a clear example that it is so, since the passages commonly cited all admit of another interpretation); still I will maintain that, as one must not depart from the literal sense, so one must not depart from the proper and most common meaning of the words, unless necessity compels it, and here no one will prove such necessity. Further, that [מִשְׁבָּרִים] means "terrified," no one, I think, will show. Finally, that the verb [הִתְחַטֵּא] signifies purification from ignorance or from fellowship with the wicked, I will believe only when the defenders of this interpretation have produced some clear instance of it. More rightly, then, Emmanuel Sa has interpreted this of the whale or the sea-monster: "Lifted up," namely, rising itself on high. "Angels": the Chaldee has "the strong," that is, the very strongest. But in interpreting the last word, "they will be purified," he falls badly. "Purified," he says, that is, "their bowels loosened from fear." Does [התחטא] then mean the purging of the bowels? How much better he would have done had he translated that word as the purging of the conscience! Diodati: "if they purge themselves of the dregs of sin." The English Junius: "they cleanse themselves," namely from sins. Sa drew that crude interpretation from Rabbi Levi: [ממשברי לב שישיגום בסכרת הפהר יתנקו דרך נקביהם לעשות צואתם ומימי רגליהם], that is, "by the breakings of the heart, which will seize them with great dread, they will be purged through the ordinary passages of nature, making their excrement (so the Hebrew words sound [ἀὀ7λεξεὶ]) and the waters of their feet, that is, their urine." It is an interpretation unworthy of the Hebrew. The third and last passage is the last verse: "He beholds every lofty thing; he is king over all the sons of pride." Lyra: "Because he always strives through pride to attack greater things, he beholds every lofty thing, to attain it if he could, and he surpasses all others in pride. And from this it is plain that the things said of the whale are principally understood of the demon." Let us look at the Hebrew: [ואת־כל גבה יראה הוא מלך על כל בני שחץ]. Pagninus: "He will despise every lofty thing; he is king over all the great and strong whales." Arias: "over all the sons of pride." Emmanuel Sa: "he beholds, that is, he despises; all the sons of pride, that is, the sea-beasts, however huge." The Chaldee: "all the sons of fishes." The Seventy: "king of all that are in the water" [βασιλεὺς πάντων ... omnium quae in aqua]. Aben Ezra says the word [שחץ] signifies or comprehends whatever is generated in the waters. Junius thought the Hebrew word means "wild beast": "He is queen over all wild beasts," he says, "the sons of the beast." He calls him queen, whom the Hebrew speech calls king, because he took the name Leviathan in the feminine as meaning "the whale." But Piscator, who put in "whale" where it is, follows the most learned Mercerus: "he is king over all lofty animals." Above, at 28:8, the same phrase was used of lions. There is therefore no necessity to understand "sons of pride" as men. And who is so much a stranger to these writings as not to know the varied use of the Hebrew הָ? Thus, to extend the word as widely as possible, God meant to teach that Leviathan is easily prince over all proud creatures. As a closing note: observe that Thomas, in the Summa, Part 1, Question 63, where he treats the angels at length, makes no mention of these passages, from which you may gather that in their interpretation he thought differently from the common opinion. And here let this be the end. Farewell, most accomplished young man, and be well.

units.la: nobis cur stringenda jam vela sint, causam supra diximus. Et quia Augustinus hic saepe nominabitur, operae pretium erit praemittere censuram Sixti Senensis, quae extat in Bibliotheca Sancta lib.4. titulo Augustinus, Verba Sixti haec sunt, Augustinus in Psalmos genus tenet Allegoricum, literalis expositionis parum. quod Hieronymus in eo taxat. Nam cum Augustinus Ebraici sermonis imperitus esset, & in Graeci literis parum instructus, necesse illi fuit a propria litera sensu ad extortas allegorias discedere. Hanc eruditissimi Monachi censuram nequaquam esse temerariam, aliquot locorum inductione ostensum ibo.
units.tr: I have already said above why my sails must now be furled. And since Augustine will often be named here, it will be worth while to set out first the judgment of Sixtus of Siena, which is found in his Bibliotheca Sancta, book 4, under the title Augustinus. The words of Sixtus are these: "Augustine in his Psalms keeps to the allegorical kind and has little of the literal exposition, which Jerome criticises in him. For since Augustine was unskilled in the Hebrew language and little instructed in Greek literature, he was bound to depart from the proper literal sense into forced allegories." I will show, by bringing forward several passages, that this judgment of the most learned monk is by no means rash.

units.la: Psalm. I. verf. 3. Et erit tanquam lignum.] Vide quae supra notavimus ad Deut. 28.

units.la: Verf. 5. Ideo non resurgent impii in judicio.] Frustra hic subtiles sunt interpretes. Alii, non resurgent ad beatam resurrectionem; Alii, non resurgent in coetu justorum, inter justos. Alii, non resurgent in judicio id est ut judicentur. * Jam enim poenis certissimis destinati sunt, inquit August. Item, non resurgent in judicio, id est ut judicent sed ut judicentur. Carthus. non resurgent in judicio discretionis, quo homines justi se ipsos examinant & conscientias suas discernunt — de quo salubri judicio dicit Apostolus, Quod si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur 1. Co. 11. & ad Job. cap. 14. artic. 34. Unde legitur Pf. 1. Ideo non ref. imp. in jud. quod de judicio discretionis accipitur, quo homo inter bonum malumque judicans detestatur culpam, in quam incidit & per poenitentiam resurgit. Ita & Lombardus in comm. qui hanc resurrectionem anima vocat. Omnem hunc interpretum aestum sedat melior interpretatio, Non stabunt (subsistent) in judicio. enim tam significat stare, quam surgere. Stare autem & cadere in foro opponuntur. Hoc sensu occurrit Luc.
units.tr: Verse 5: "Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment." Here the interpreters are needlessly subtle. Some say they shall not rise to blessed resurrection; others, that they shall not rise in the assembly of the just, among the just; others, that they shall not rise in judgment, that is, to be judged. * "Already they are destined for most certain punishments," says Augustine. Likewise, "they shall not rise in judgment," that is, to judge, but to be judged. The Carthusians: "they shall not rise in the judgment of discernment, by which righteous men examine themselves and discern their own consciences; of this wholesome judgment the Apostle says, 'If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged' (1 Cor. 11), and on Job chapter 14, article 34." Hence it is read in Psalm 1: "Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment," which is understood of the judgment of discernment, by which a man, judging between good and evil, detests the fault into which he has fallen and rises again through repentance. So too Lombard in his commentary, who calls this the "resurrection of the soul." A better interpretation calms all this heat of the interpreters: "They shall not stand (shall not subsist) in judgment." For stare means the same as surgere, and in the forum standing and falling are opposed. In this sense it occurs in Luke.

units.la: * Ita & Hier. & Euthymius.
units.tr: * So also Jerome and Euthymius.

units.la: Luc. xxi. 36. Vigilate — ut digni habeamini, qui effugiatis omnia ista, καὶ σταθῆναι ante filium hominis, quod Belgae dicunt bestaen. Genev. subsistet. Chaldaeus Ebraeum יקומו reddit puri, innocentes erunt. Pisc. consistent. in Germ. bestehen, bestaen, ubi in Luth. & Belg. est bleiben, blyven, Deod. non staranno. Genev. ne subsisteront point. Ita & Angli. Jun. exurgent, id est ut in Scholiis explicat, ne sublato quidem vultu se audebunt sistere. קום stare extra controversiam Jos. 7.12. Et filii Israel non poterant לקום stare coram hostibus suis. Unde & Levit. 26.37. Et non erit vobis תקומה id est consistentia, consistendi facultas, coram inimicis vestris. Jos. 2.10. Jesa. 40. Verbum Dei nostri יקום stabit in aeternum, 1. Reg. 14.4. Genebr. inter alias interpretationes hanc quoque recenset & probat. Additque illa verba, Verbum קום stare & surgere significat. Et paulo ante, Aliqui putant metaphoram sumptam à foro, in quo qui causam amittunt, cadere causa dicuntur. Quam sententiam non admordet homo alias mordacissimus. Emmanuel Sa, resurgent id est consistent q. d. non poterunt se defendere. Hebr. stabunt. Atque ita quoque hunc locum accepisse Kimchium, alibi ostendemus.
units.tr: Luke 21:36: "Watch, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things and to stand [καὶ σταθῆναι] before the Son of Man," which the Belgians render bestaen. The Geneva Bible has "shall stand." The Chaldee paraphrast renders the Hebrew יקומו as "they shall be pure, they shall be innocent." Pagninus has "shall stand"; in German bestehen, bestaen, whereas in Luther and the Dutch it is bleiben, blyven; Diodati has "non staranno." The Geneva Bible: "they shall not stand at all." So also the English; Junius, "shall rise," which in his Notes he explains as "they shall not dare to stand, not even lifting up their faces." That קום means "to stand" is beyond dispute (Joshua 7:12): "The children of Israel could not stand [לקום] before their enemies." Hence also Leviticus 26:37: "And you shall have no תקומה," that is, power to stand (consistentia, the ability to stand), "before your enemies." Joshua 2:10. Isaiah 40: "the word of our God יקום shall stand for ever." 1 Kings 14:4. Genebrardus, among other interpretations, also records and approves this one, and adds those words: "the verb קום means both to stand and to rise." A little before he says: "Some think the metaphor is taken from the forum, where those who lose their case are said to fall in their cause." That opinion the man, otherwise most biting, does not bite at. Emmanuel Sa: "they shall rise, that is, they shall stand; as if to say, they will not be able to defend themselves." The Hebrew: "they shall stand." That Kimchi also took this passage in this way I shall show elsewhere.

units.la: Ps. II. Apprehendite disciplinam.] Ita Vulg. ex Graec. ἀπάντησις, Lombardus in comm. Apprehendite] etiam si fugiat. disciplinam] Dei, sc. adversa. In Ebraeo esse osculamini filium, Genebr. Bellarm. Andradrius, & alii ingenue agnoscunt. Vide & Iansenium & Emm. Sa & alios. Vide quaeso quae supra pag. 19. de hoc loco attigimus. Invictum in hoc loco, prout in Ebraeo extat, Judaeos pro Deitate Christi argumentum situm esse agnoscunt. Idem Bell. lib. 1. de Christo cap. 5. ex textu Ebraeo hujus loci pro eodem fidei articulo argumentum depromit. Annon ergo hic locus ad fidem pertinet? Et cum iidem Judaeos ex vulgata versione urgeri non posse concedant, annon sequetur, eam in loco ad primarium fidei articulum stabiliendum pertinente, ab Ebraica veritate deficere? Sudant Interpretes, * ostendant sensum loci recte expressisse interpretem. Sed respondit Rev. D. Rivetus, aliud esse ex textu argumentari, aliud textum interpretari. Non esse laudabile genus interpretandi, cum res singularis & individua per genus & quidem remotissimum aut per adjunctum & consequens aliquod exponitur. Caeterum de hoc loco vide quem jam laudavimus
units.tr: Psalm 2: "Take hold of instruction." So the Vulgate, from the Greek ἀπάντησις. Lombard in his commentary: "Take hold," even if it flees; "instruction," namely of God, that is, adversity. That the Hebrew says "kiss the Son," Genebrardus, Bellarmine, Andradius, and others frankly admit. See also Jansenius, Emmanuel Sa, and others. Please see what I touched on above, p. 19, about this passage. The Papists acknowledge that in this passage, as it stands in the Hebrew, the Jews have an invincible argument for the deity of Christ. Bellarmine in book 1, On Christ, chapter 5, draws from the Hebrew text of this passage an argument for the same article of faith. Does not this passage then belong to the faith? And since the same men concede that the Jews cannot be pressed with the Vulgate version, does it not follow that the Vulgate, in a passage bearing on the chief article of faith, departs from the Hebrew truth? The interpreters sweat to show that the translator rightly expressed the sense of the passage. But Reverend Doctor Rivet replied that it is one thing to argue from the text, another to interpret the text. It is not a praiseworthy way of interpreting when a single and individual thing is explained through the genus, and indeed through the most remote genus, or through some accident and consequence. Otherwise, on this passage see the work I have already cited.

units.la: * Vide Bel. d. V. D. 2. 13. & in commentario. mus Rivetum , commentario in Psalmorum propheticorum decadem , Chamierum, Junium, Witakerum, Ternovium, & alios, qui cum Bellarm, & Pontificiis super hoc loco disputarunt..
units.tr: * See Bellarmine, De verbo Dei, 2, 13, and in his commentary; and see Rivet, in his commentary on the decade of the prophetic Psalms; Chamier, Junius, Whitaker, Ternovius, and others, who disputed with Bellarmine and the Papists on this passage.

units.la: Ibid. Servite Domino cum timore & exultate in tremore.] Ex hoc quoque loco colligit Bellarminus lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 12. neminem de sua electione posse esse certum. Quid nostri Theol. respondeant, vide apud Paraeum, Chamierum, Rivetum comm. in hunc Psalmum, Amesium & alios. Discat tiro, phrasin illam ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ quinquies in Bibliis occurrere, semel in veteri, quater in N. foedere, & quidem tantum apud Paulum. Notet, omnibus istis locis ita usurpari, ut superbiam, carnalem securitatem & praesumptionem excludat: animi dimissionem, reverentiam, humilitatem & modestiam, non vero servilem metum, diffidentiam & trepidationem significet. Locus primus hic ipsus est, ubi Ebraea illa בִּיִרְאָה וּבִרְעָדָה Lxx. reddidere, ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ. II. extat 1. Cor. 2. 3. ἐγὼ ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ καὶ ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ πολλῷ ἐγενόμην πρὸς ὑμᾶς. ubi suam humilitatem & modestiam opponit saltui Pseudo-prophetarum & impostorum. Certe, eum cum servili metu, trepidatione & diffidentia cum Corinthiis versatum fuisse, nulli fiet verisimile, qui Paulum ex Paulo novit. III. 2. Corinth. 7. 15. ὡς μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου ἐδέξασθε αὐτόν, scilicet Titum. id est summa reverentia. Alias nec recreassent Titum, nec Paulo hoc nomine placuissent. IV. Ephes. vi. 5. Servi obedite dominis vestris μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, & in simplicitate cordis. Atqui servitus, quae cum perpetua trepidatione & diffidentia conjuncta est, illiberalis est, & Apostoli commendatione indigna. V. Philipp. 2. 12. operamini salutem vestram μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου. id est cum majestatis divinae reverentia & solicita peccati cautela. Atque hinc explicandum illud quoque videdetur, quod extat Rom. xi. 20. μὴ ὑψηλὰ φρονει, ἀλλὰ φόβου. ne superbias (vulgatus, noli altum sapere, nimis restricte) sed time id est ταπεινοφρονεῖ, esto humilis, modestus. Interim lubens dederim Bellarmino, plurimos eorum, qui hanc certitudinem jactant, falli & decipi. Melior, opinor, eorum sors est, qui Christum Jesum sincera fide complexi, eique in bona conscientia & caritate non ficta servientes, subinde dubitant, &, quod in tentationibus fieri solet, trepidant, quam istorum, qui, licet omni flagitiorum genere cooperti sint, ne formam quidem pietatis habentes, hanc tamen certitudinem semper credant. Sic est profecto. Plures praesumendo quam triplicando periere. Neutiquam ergo otiosa est illa B. Pauli admonitio, qui stat, videat ne cadat.
units.tr: Ibid.: "Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling." From this passage too Bellarmine, in book 3, On Justification, chapter 12, concludes that no one can be certain of his own election. For what our theologians answer, see Pareus, Chamier, Rivet on this Psalm, Amesius, and others. Let the beginner learn that the phrase ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ [with fear and trembling] occurs five times in the Bible: once in the Old Testament and four times in the New, and indeed only in Paul. Let him note that in all these places it is used so as to exclude pride, carnal security and presumption, and to signify a relaxing of the mind, reverence, humility and modesty, not servile fear, distrust and trepidation. The first place is this one itself, where the Septuagint rendered the Hebrew בִּיִרְאָה וּבִרְעָדָה [with fear and with trembling] as ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ. Second, 1 Corinthians 2:3: "I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling," ἐγὼ ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ καὶ ἐν φόβῳ καὶ τρόμῳ πολλῷ ἐγενόμην πρὸς ὑμᾶς, where he sets his own humility and modesty against the boasting of false prophets and impostors. Surely no one who knows Paul from Paul will think it likely that he dealt with the Corinthians in servile fear, trepidation and distrust. Third, 2 Corinthians 7:15: "ὡς μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου ἐδέξασθε αὐτόν," that is, you received him (Titus) with great reverence. Otherwise they would not have refreshed Titus, nor would they have pleased Paul on that account. Fourth, Ephesians 6:5: "Servants, obey your masters μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, and in simplicity of heart." Yet slavery joined with constant trembling and distrust is ungentlemanly and unworthy of the Apostle's commendation. Fifth, Philippians 2:12: "work out your salvation μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου," that is, with reverence for the divine majesty and careful caution against sin. And hence that other passage also seems to be explained, Romans 11:20: "μὴ ὑψηλὰ φρονει, ἀλλὰ φόβου," do not be proud (the Vulgate, "do not be high-minded," too narrowly), but fear, that is, ταπεινοφρονεῖ, be humble and modest. Meanwhile I would gladly grant to Bellarmine that most of those who boast of this certainty are mistaken and deceived. Their lot, I think, is the better who, having embraced Christ Jesus with sincere faith and serving him in a good conscience and unfeigned love, sometimes doubt and, as usually happens in temptations, tremble, rather than the lot of those who, though covered with every kind of wickedness and not even having the form of godliness, always believe in this certainty. So it truly is. More have perished by presuming than by trebling. Therefore that admonition of the blessed Paul, "Let him who stands take heed lest he fall," is by no means idle.

units.la: Ps. VIII. 5. Quid est homo — aut filius hominis.] Quicquid hic disserit Augustinus ex vocula aut, nullum in originario textu fundamentum habet, Illuc enim est בן & filius. Non nego illam literam saepe reddendam per aut, sed non semper distinguere illud cui praefigitur, ab eo quod antecessit, tanquam diversum, id vero est quod nego. Sic dico, vau saepe praefigitur istis hemistichiis, quibus idem repetitur aliis verbis, quod Rabbini vocant כפל הענין במלות שונות / Ibi vero sive per Et, sive per Aut reddas, saepe hilum non interest. Alia longe ratio est, quando vel hemistichio, vel membro, rem ab antecedenti diversam continenti, praefigitur. Ibi enim nisi per Aut reddideris, caliginem non solum offundis sententiae, sed & errandi occasionem lectori saepe praebebis. Exempla vidimus ad Exod. xxi. & Judic. xi. ex quorundam sententia.
units.tr: Ps. VIII. 5. What is man, or the son of man.] Whatever Augustine argues from the little word or has no foundation in the original text, since there the word is בן, simply son. I do not deny that this letter is often to be rendered by or, but I do deny that it always marks what it introduces as something different from what went before. I say that the vau is often prefixed to those half-verses in which the same thing is repeated in other words, which the rabbis call the doubling of the sense in different words [כפל הענין במלות שונות]. In such places it makes little difference whether you render it by and or by or. The case is quite different when it is prefixed to a half-verse or clause that states something different from the preceding one. There, unless you render it by or, you not only cloud the sense but will often offer the reader an occasion for error. We have seen examples at Exod. 21 and Judg. 11, according to the view of some writers.

units.la: Atque hic inseram obiter, quod supra ad Exod. xxi. 16. notandum fuerat. גונב איש וממכרו id est qui furatur virum (id est hominem confer cum illis quae supra pag. 237.) & vendidit eum & inventus est in manu ejus, moriendo morietur. Ita ad verbum sonant Ebraea. Latino interpreti hic haesit aqua. Nec enim capere potuit, quomodo vendisse, & reperiri adhuc in manu furis, simul possint subsistere. Ideo locum sic convertit, Qui furatus fuerit hominem & vendiderit, convictus noxa, morte moriatur. Qua lege capitis damnari non potest plagiarius, nisi caput subreptum vendiderit. Quid ergo si non vendiderit? Respondent Lyra, Carthf. & alii, doctores Catholicos statuisse eum ex lege generali Exod. 22.4. teneri pro uno homine subrepto reddere duos ad serviendum. Quae sententia multis urgeri potest difficultatibus. An ergo furtum hominis & bestiae juxta aestimabitur? An cap. xxii. 4. ulla hominis mentio? Annon potius manifeste excluditur homo? An duos istos servituros dabit ex familia sua, an emet aliunde? At si non habeat unde emet? Quid ergo? Non venit interpreti in mentem enallage copulae vau, quam alibi tamen non neglexit. Eam si hic quoque observservasset, mentem Legis-latoris melius expressisset, vid. in hunc modum, Qui furatus est hominem, sive vendiderit cum, sive inventus furit in manu ejus, omnino morte plectitor. Aut, qui f. est h. & vendidit eum, [si] inveniatur [ adhuc ]in manu, ejus m. morietur. Non ignoro, quid pro vulgato Interprete afferri soleat, sed nostra interpretatione mentem Legislatoris melius expressam esse, cum Lyra pronuntio.
units.tr: Let me insert here, in passing, something that should have been noted above at Exod. 21:16: גונב איש וממכרו, that is, he who steals a man (take man here as a person, and compare what is said above on p. 237), and sells him, and he is found in his hand, shall surely die. This is what the Hebrew says word for word. The Latin translator was stuck here, for he could not see how selling and being still found in the thief's hand could both hold at once. So he rendered the passage: He who steals a man and sells him, being convicted of the crime, shall be put to death. By that law a kidnapper could not be condemned to death unless he had sold the person he stole. What then if he has not sold him? Lyra, Carthusianus and others reply that Catholic teachers have held that by the general law of Exod. 22:4 he is bound to restore two men for one stolen man, to serve. This opinion can be pressed with many difficulties. Will the theft of a man then be valued like that of an animal? Is there any mention of a man in chap. 22:4? Is not a man rather plainly excluded there? Will he give these two to serve from his own household, or buy them elsewhere? And what if he has no means of buying them? What then? The translator did not think of the change of the conjunctive vau, though he did not neglect it elsewhere. Had he observed it here, he would have expressed the mind of the lawgiver better, in this way: He who steals a man, whether he sells him or he is found still in his hand, shall certainly be punished with death. Or: He who steals a man and sells him, [if] he is found [still] in his hand, shall die. I am not unaware of what is usually brought forward in support of the Vulgate translator, but I declare, with Lyra, that our rendering expresses the mind of the lawgiver better.

units.la: Vers. 7. Quam vere dixerit olim Polydorus Virgilius, doctores quosdam pontificios sacras literas, quo volunt, detorquere, instar sutorum, qui sordidas pelles suis dentibus extendunt, hæc allegoria Antonii, Episcopi Florentini, docebit. Sic ergo ille hunc versum ἀλλ, parte 3. tit. 22. cap. 5. Deus omnia subjecit pedibus ejus id est, Pontificis Romani. Oves id est Christianos. Boves, id est Judæos & hæreticos. Pecora campi id est paganos. Pisces maris id est animas in purgatorio Confer hæc cum istis quæ supra pag. 178. pro omnipotentia Pontificia adducta sunt.
units.tr: Ver. 7. How truly Polydorus Virgilius once said that some Papist teachers twist the sacred letters to whatever they wish, like cobblers who stretch dirty hides with their teeth, is shown by the allegory of Antoninus, Bishop of Florence. He interprets this verse in this way, in part 3, title 22, chap. 5: God put all things under his feet, that is, under the Roman Pontiff. The sheep, that is, Christians. The oxen, that is, Jews and heretics. The beasts of the field, that is, pagans. The fish of the sea, that is, souls in purgatory. Compare this with what was adduced above on p. 178 in support of papal omnipotence.

units.la: Ps.X. Ab hoc Psalmo usque ad cxlvii. discrepant Ebræi à Græcis in Psalmorum citatione. Nos Ebræos, Pontificii Græcos & vulgatam Latinam, quæ ex Græco tradu-cta est, sequuntur. Nos ipsos unitate semper superamus. Ex. gr. Qui nobis est xxii. ipsis est xxi. Notet autem lector, me Ebræos ubique sequi. Causa differentiæ hæc est. Græci Psalmos ix. & x. in unum conflarunt. Hinc Psalmus nobis xi. ipsis est x. Ea dissensio excurrit usque ad Psal. 147. Illum enim rursus distribuerunt in duos. Credo ut c i. Psalmos haberent. Alias tantum 149. numerarent. Hic tamen ex transverso alia insuper intercurrit differentia, sed quæ mox in concordiam redigitur.
units.tr: Ps. X. From this Psalm down to cxlvii the Hebrews differ from the Greeks in citing the Psalms. We follow the Hebrews, while the Papists follow the Greeks and the Latin Vulgate, which was translated from the Greek. We always surpass them in unity. For example, what is Ps. xxii for us is xxi for them. The reader should note, however, that I follow the Hebrews everywhere. The cause of the difference is this. The Greeks combined Psalms ix and x into one. Hence the Psalm that is xi for us is x for them.
