This disagreement runs on as far as Ps. 147, for there they again divided one Psalm into two, I suppose so that they would have 150 Psalms. Otherwise they would have counted only 149. Here, however, another difference crosses in from the other side, but this is soon brought back into agreement.

units.la: Namque Græci & Latini Psalmum nobis cxv. jungunt cum cxiv. atque ita isti Psalmi constituunt ipsis psal. cxiii. Hinc Psal. nobis cxvi. Dilexi quoniam, &c. ipsis est cxiv. ubi binario numero à nobis discrepant. Sed mox rediunt ad priorem disferitatem, Psalmum istum in duos partiendo, & ab isto versu, credidi, quia locutus sum, Psalmum novum, ipsis cxv. incipiendo. Atque ita Psalmus sequens nobis 117. ipsis est 116 &c. Hoc tironem monere volui. Vtinam non essent graviores inter nos & Romanam Ecclesiam controversiæ! Nam quod ad Ebræorum numerationem attinet, quam nostri sequuntur, ipsi Ebræi non conspirant Ipse Kimchi Psal. 115. cum 114. jungit & ad emendatisfima exemplaria provocat. In eundem modum Ebræorum nonnulli ex Psalm. 1. & 2. unum fecerunt. Vide Kimchium.
units.tr: For the Greeks and Latins join our Ps. cxv to cxiv, and so these Psalms make up their Ps. cxiii. Hence our Ps. cxvi, I loved, because, etc., is their cxiv, where they differ from us by one number. But they soon return to the earlier difference, dividing that Psalm into two and beginning a new Psalm, their cxv, at the verse I believed, because I spoke. So the following Psalm, which is our 117, is their 116, and so on. I wished to point this out to the beginner. Would that the controversies between us and the Roman Church were not more serious! For as regards the Hebrew numbering, which our people follow, the Hebrews themselves do not agree. Kimchi himself joins Ps. 115 to 114 and appeals to the most accurate manuscripts. In the same way some Hebrews made one Psalm out of Pss. 1 and 2. See Kimchi.

units.la: Ps. XIV. Sepulcrum patens, &c.] De hoc, & sequentibus duobus versibus, vide Bellarm. de V. D. lib. 2. cap. 2. Canum in locis 2. 13. Azorium tom. 1. lib. 8. cap. 1. Glassium p. 105. & 106. Polanum lib. 1. Syntagm. cap. 37. Hieronymus in præf. super 16. librum comment. in Jesaiam prolixe docet, hos versus non pertinere ad Ps. præsentem. Et in comm. ad hunc Ps. In Ebraïs codicibus, inquit, hi versus non habentur. Quæritur ergo, quomodo Apostolus hoc usus sit testimonio in Ep. quam ad Romanos scripsit? Respondemus, Apostolum de Deuteronomio ac Psalterio & cæteris Scripturarum locis hoc testimonium texuisse. Si quæras ex quibus scripturæ locis hoc testimonium Apostoli Rom. 3. contextum sit, en tibi illa, Ps. 5. 10. Ps. 140. 4. Ps. 10. 7. Jesa. 59. verf. 7. 8. Ps. 36. 2. Etiam in Bibliis Complut. hæc non extare Mariana testis est in tractatu de Vulg. verf. pag. 96. Frustra ergo ex hoc loco inferunt nonnulli, textum Ebr. mutilatum esse. Verius, ex utriusque textus collatione, Vulgatæ versionis redundantiam colligimus. Gnomonum peccata fatui in solem rejicere solent. Ita Pontificiorum nonnulli quod vulgatæ versionis author peccavit, fontibus, tanquam fiilli corrupti essent, solent transcribere.
units.tr: Ps. XIV. An open sepulchre, etc.] On this and the two following verses see Bellarmine, On the Word of God, book 2, chap. 2; Canus in two places, 2 and 13; Azor, vol. 1, book 8, chap. 1; Glassius, pp. 105 and 106; Polanus, Syntagma, book 1, chap. 37. Jerome, in the preface to his sixteenth book of commentary on Isaiah, teaches at length that these verses do not belong to the present Psalm. And in his commentary on this Psalm he says: In the Hebrew codices, these verses are not found. The question therefore arises how the Apostle used this testimony in the letter he wrote to the Romans. We answer that the Apostle wove this testimony together from Deuteronomy and the Psalter and other passages of Scripture. If you ask from which passages of Scripture the Apostle compiled this testimony in Rom. 3, here they are: Ps. 5:10; Ps. 140:4; Ps. 10:7; Isa. 59:7-8; Ps. 36:2. That these verses are not found even in the Complutensian Bible is attested by Mariana in his treatise on the Vulgate version, p. 96. It is therefore in vain that some infer from this passage that the Hebrew text is mutilated. More truly, from comparing the two texts we conclude that the Vulgate version has an excess. Fools are accustomed to blame the sun for the faults of sundials. So some Papists, when the author of the Vulgate version has erred, are accustomed to copy the sources as if they had been corrupted.

units.la: Ps. XVI. 10. Non relinques animam meam (id est mer vel corpus meum, vel vitam meam) לִשְׁאוֹל in sepulcro] De voce שְׁאוֹל diximus abunde ad Genef. xxxvii. Eam vulgatus, Lutherus & Belgæ hic reddiderunt infernum, Non rel. animam m. in inferno. Unde primarium Pontificiorum argumentum pro locali descensu Christi ad inferos. Sed vide de hoc loco solide disputantem Rivetum in comm. Chamierum, Junium, Amesium ad controverf. 2. Bellar. Bezam & Druf. ad Act. Notabit hic tiro, vocem Ebr. נֶפֶשׁ præter propriam notionem, tropicas habere tres, quarum singulæ hic applicari possunt. I. Enim per synecd. ipsam personam significat, ps. v. 2. ps xi. 1. Anima hominis passim pro homine. Sic anima Dei, pro ipso Deo Amos vi. 8. ps. xi. 5. Prov. vi. 16. II per Metonym effic. significat vitam. ps. vii. 2. 3. 6. ps. 88. 3. III. per Metonym. adjuncti, vel ut alii loquuntur, (seu per synecd. membri pro integro, quod rursus per eundem tropum pro altero membro ponitur) pro corpore, Genef. xvii. 21. eoque mortuo, Levit. xix 28. & xxi. 2. 11. Num. xix. 11. Hagg. 2. 14. His locis vulgatus Ebr. נפש solet reddere mortuum. Chald. מיח / mortuum, Lxx. ψυχῶ. Beza Act. 2. Edit. prima, usus fuit voce cadaveris. Illyricus in clavi, negat נפש istis locis significare cadaver. Quid ergo? hominem mortuum. Nam & mortuos solemus adhuc homines vocare, inquit. Sed quid tunc fiet loco Numer. vi. 6. ubi additur אל נפש מת לא יבא / מת / ad animam id est cadaver, mortui non accedet. An reddes, ad mortuum mortui, vel ad mortuum mortuum? Ita usurpavit vocem ψυχή Sirach. xvi. 31. Animam omnis animantis tegit facies terra. Et Virg. Æn. 3. animamque sepulcro condimus. Et alibi, Egregias animas, quae sanguine nobis Hanc patriam peperere suo. Arias Mont. à nostris partibus hic stat. Namque in Idiotismis linguae Ebr. voce anima, hunc ipsum locum sic adducit, ut doceat animam pro corpore positam. Nec non Steuchus in hunc Psal. Quod vero ad vocem cadaver attinet, ob quam tantos fluctus excitant Pontificii, ipse Greg. de Valentia in 3. partem summae Thomae, qu. 4. puncto 1. corpus Christi cadaver vocat. Et Salmero tract. 7. tom. x. Et Cajet. in Matth. 28. Et ex Patribus Chrysost. in primam ad Corinth. homil. 24. τὸ σῶμα καλῶν τὸ σῶμα, quod Hervetus sic interpretatur, cadaver corpus scil. suum Cristus vocans ob mortem. Et Theophyl. in Matth. xxiv. Desinant ergo Pontificii hos fluctus in simpulo excitare. Desinant insultare hoc nomine beato seni, cujus candorem potius praedicare par erat. Namque ex posterioribus Editionibus vocem eam sustulit, retenta tamen eadem expositione. Junius locum sic interpretatur, quasi David loqueretur, & Christum vocaret animam suam. Vide ejus scholia. Sed hanc expositionem licet subtilem & ingeniosam refellit Rev. Piscator, & improbat cl. Rivetus.
units.tr: Ps. XVI. 10. You will not leave my soul (that is, my body or my life, or my life) לִשְׁאוֹל in the grave] I have discussed the word שְׁאוֹל at length on Gen. 37. The Vulgate, Luther and the Belgic translators here rendered it hell: You will not leave my soul in hell. From this comes the Papists' chief argument for Christ's local descent into the underworld. But on this passage see Rivetus, who argues it soundly in his commentary, and Chamier, Junius, Amesius on controversy 2, Bellarmine, Beza, and Drusius on Acts. The beginner should note that the Hebrew word נֶפֶשׁ, apart from its proper meaning, has three figurative senses, any of which can be applied here. I. By synecdoche it signifies the person himself: Ps. 5:2; Ps. 11:1, the soul of man, is everywhere used for man. So the soul of God is used for God himself, Amos 6:8; Ps. 11:5; Prov. 6:16. II. By metonymy of the efficient cause it signifies life: Ps. 7:2, 3, 6; Ps. 88:3. III. By metonymy of the adjunct, or, as others put it, by synecdoche of a part for the whole, which in turn is put by the same trope for another part, it signifies the body: Gen. 17:21, and, when dead, Lev. 19:28; 21:2, 11; Num. 19:11; Hag. 2:14. In these places the Vulgate usually renders the Hebrew נפש as the dead. The Chaldee paraphrast has מיח, the dead; the Seventy have ψυχῶ. Beza, in the first edition of Acts, used the word corpse. Illyricus, in his Clavis, denies that נפש in these places means corpse. What then? A dead man, he says, for we are still accustomed to call the dead men. But what will become of Num. 6:6 then, where it is added אל נפש מת לא יבא, to a soul, that is, a corpse, of a dead man he shall not come? Will you render it to the dead of the dead, or to the dead, the dead? So Sirach used the word ψυχή in 16:31: The face of the earth covers every living soul. And Virgil in the Aeneid, book 3: and we bury the soul in the sepulchre. And elsewhere: Noble souls, who by their blood have born us this country. Arias Montanus stands on our side here, for in his idioms of the Hebrew language he cites this very passage to show that soul is put for the body. Steuchus on this Psalm does likewise. As for the word corpse, over which the Papists raise such waves, Gregory of Valencia himself, in the third part of Thomas's Summa, question 4, point 1, calls the body of Christ a corpse. Salmeron, treatise 7, vol. 10, and Cajetan on Matt. 28 do too. Among the Fathers, Chrysostom in his twenty-fourth homily on 1 Corinthians says τὸ σῶμα καλῶν, calling the body [τὸ σῶμα], which Hervetus translates as corpse, that is, his own body, Christ calling it so because of death. Theophylact on Matt. 24 does likewise. Let the Papists therefore stop stirring up these waves in a teacup. Let them stop insulting this blessed old man with this word, whose candour it would rather have been fitting to praise. For in later editions he removed the word, though he kept the same explanation. Junius interprets the passage as if David were speaking and calling Christ his own soul. See his scholia. But Pareus, though this interpretation is subtle and ingenious, refutes it, and the distinguished Rivetus disapproves of it.

units.la: Ps. XVIII. 26. Cum sancto sanctus eris & cum perverso perverteris] Haec vulgati interpretis verba passim sic accipiuntur, quasi bonorum familiaritas commendetur, malorum dissuadeatur: Cum tamen Scriptura haec de Deo pronuntiet, sensusque sit, Deum cum sancto sancte & liberaliter agere, benigne promissam mercedem rependendo, cum perversis vero severe habere, puniendo. Rivetus Isagoges pag. 262. Optimus huhujus loci comment. est caput xxvi. Levit. & nominatim verf. 23. 24.
units.tr: Ps. XVIII. 26. With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted: These words of the Vulgate translator are commonly taken as if they commended the company of good men and warned against the company of bad men. Yet Scripture here says something about God, and the sense is that God deals with the holy in a holy and generous way, repaying the promised reward graciously, but deals severely with the perverse, punishing them. Rivetus, Isagoges, p. 262. The best commentary on this passage is Leviticus chapter 26, and especially verses 23 and 24.

units.la: Ibid. verf. 36. Quando me humilias, tunc me magnificas.] Ita Luth. & ex eo Belgica. Vulgo affertur ad ostendendum & probandum salutarem usum afflictionum. At Ebraea illam interpretationem non admittunt, וְעֲנוָתְךָ תַרְבֵּנִי & mansuetudo tua auget me.
units.tr: Ibid. verse 36. When you humble me, then you magnify me. Thus Luther, and after him the Belgic version. It is commonly cited to show and prove the saving use of afflictions. But the Hebrew does not admit that rendering: וְעֲנוָתְךָ תַרְבֵּנִי [and your gentleness makes me great].

units.la: Pf. XIX. verf. 5. In omnem terram exivit linea eorum] קַוָּם de hoc loco post alios fusissime & solidissime egerunt Rivetus in comm. & Glassius in Philologia S. Lege & non poenitebit..
units.tr: Ps. XIX. verse 5. Their line has gone out into all the earth. Concerning the word קַוָּם [qav, line], others have treated this passage at length and most solidly, Rivetus in his commentary and Glassius in the Philologia Sacra. Read them, and you will not regret it.

units.la: Ibidem. לְשֶׁמֶשׁ שָׂם אֹהֶל בָּהֶם] Aquila, Theod. Symmachus τῷ ἡλίῳ ἔθετο σκήνωμα ἐν αὐτοῖς.. Ita & Chald. לִשְׁמֶשָׁא שׂוּי מַשְׁרֵי זִיהָרָה בְרוֹן soli posuit splendidum habitaculum in illis. Justinus Martyr quaest. 63. ex Syra interpretatione haec citat ἐν αὐτοῖς ἔθετο ἐν ἡλίῳ τὸ σκήνωμα. Consentiunt Theodor. Hieron. Pagn. Arias, Bened. Vatabl. Munsterus, Sixtus Senensis, Biblioth. Sanctae lib. 3. pag. mihi 137. Sa & alii. Iansenius locum sic explicat, Deum Soli in coelis circumscripsisse domicilium, ut illic veluti in sublimi theatro melius conspiceretur. Bellarm. in comm. agnoscit in Ebraeo nullam apparere verborum ambiguitatem, vel obscuritatem, & sententiam illam, quam nos expressimus, esse veram. Lxx. ἐν τῷ ἡλίῳ ἔθετο τὸ σκήνωμα αὐτοῦ. Vulg. in Sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Multi interpretes valde aestuant, ut hanc versionem cum fontibus concilient. Alii conantur ostendere, verba Ebraea admittere posse istam interpretationem. In Sole posuit tabernaculum suum. At tum dicendum fuisset בְּשֶׁמֶשׁ שָׂם אָהֳלוֹ / Nam ut ut demus, לְ positum pro בְּ ut Pf. xvi. לִשְׁאוֹל? pro בְּשְׁאוֹל unde accipient reciprocum illud suum. Certe non ex בָּהֶם / quod pluralis numeri esse, non videtur advertisse Richardus Cenomanus, author collationis quae adjecta est ad comm. Lombardi in Psalm. Si subintelligendum est, quid tunc fiet voci בהם ? Verba Richardi, Prima vox indiscriminatim accipi potest in dativo & ablativo. Et ultima reciproce, & relative simpliciter. Inde potest reddi in hunc modum, Soli posuit t. s. vel, in sole p. t. suum. Nugae & gerrae Sed & quis sensus? Manichaei, teste August. libro xx. contra Faustum ex hoc loco perperam intellecto, in adorationem Solis inciderunt. Credebant enim hanc esse verbo-rum istorum mentem, Christum, cum in cœlum ascenderet, corpus suum in globo Solis reliquisse ac solam animam suam supra omnes cœlos ad dextram patris evexisse. Volebant ergo carnem ejus in Sole, ceu Dominici corporis tabernaculo, adorandam esse. Hanc sententiam graviter perstringit Senensis lib. 3. atque illam imperitiæ Ebraici idiomatis transcribit. Genuinus, inquit, proprius & literalis sensus iste est, Deum posuisse Soli tabernaculum in cœlo, ex quo Sol ipse summo mane tanquam sponsus e cubili progreditur, ostensurus splendorem vultus sui omnibus. Quid dixisset, si picturam illam vidisset, quam in frontispiciis mul-torum librorum repræsentavit Bartholomæus Gravius Typographus Lovaniensis, vid. Solem, in quo sedet puerulus cru-cem gestans, cum hac inscriptione, In Sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Inspice titulum Magistri Sententiarum ab ipso 1556. editi. Serapion Episcopus contra Manichæos scribens, teste Senensi lib. v. annotatione 160. ejusdem erroris Origenem postulat. Sed patriocinium ejus suscepit Pamphilius Martyr, qui, producto evidentissimo loco ex Origenis comm. in hunc eundem Psalmum, liquido docet, hanc ineptam Manichæo-rum sententiam ab ipso Origene ex professo confutari. Locum descripsit Senensis. Ibi vero Origenis sententia his verbis proponitur, Habitatio tabernaculi Christi Sol esse dicitur. Tabernaculum vero Christi, Ecclesiam intelligo. Solem autem quem alium intelligere debeo, nisi illud lumen verum, quod illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Ipsum video Solem de quo dictum est, Quia timentibus nomen meum orietur Sol justitiæ. In Sole ergo posuit tabernaculum suum id est sole justitiæ. Hæc Origenes. Augustt. col. 91. tomi 7. Dominus, ut adversus regna temporalium errorum belligeraret, non pacem sed bellum missurus in terram, in tempore velut manifestatione posuit tanquam militare habitaculum suum, hoc est dispensationem incarnationis suæ. Pergit, Et ipse tanquam sponsus de thalamo suo, &c. id est de utero virginali, ubi Deus naturæ humanæ tanquam sponsus sponsæ copulatus est, &c. Quis ferat hujusmodi interpretationes in hac literarum luce pro concione proponi? Idem col. 96. In sole posuit t. f. id est, in manifestatione Ecclesiam suam, non in occulto, non quæ lateat, non velut operta. ne forte fiat sicut operta super greges hæreticorum. Dictum est & cuidam in in scriptura, tu in occulto fecisti, patieris in sole. In Sole ergo posuit tabernaculum, quid tu haretice fugis in tenebras? Eadem invenies in Gloss. ordin. & rhapsodia Lombardi. Haec arripuit Bellarm. quem non puduit lib. 3. de Ecclesia cap. 12. hunc locum advocare in patrocinium sententiae suae de visibilitate Ecclesiae. Ait enim hic aperte describi Ecclesiam, quae non potest abscondi, sicut Sol non potest latere. In comm. tamen nihil tale invenitur. Si forte satur necdum es ineptiarum, Lector, apponam tibi plures ejusdem gustus dapes. Carthus. In Sole id est in mundo inferiori sub sole, vid. oculis hominum, posuit filius Dei tabernaculum suum, id est corpus assumptum, quod dicitur templum invisibilis Deitatis, &c. Vel sic, In sole id est in beata virgine Maria posuit Christus tabernaculum suum, id est corpus suum, habitans in utero ejus ix. mensibus. Felicissima namque Maria Sol dicitur propter excellentissimum divinarum gratiarum in ea splendorem de qua in canticis, pulchra ut Luna, electa ut Sol. Lombardus ex Alcuino, Sol tria facit, lucet, urit & varietatem temporum facit. Posuit ergo tabernaculum in Sole id est tempore, quia carnem assumsit temporalibus vicissitudinibus subjectam. Vel in Sole id est in labore, quia astum laborum gratis sustinuit. Agmen claudant Bellarm. & Genebrardus. Et quidem illius (Bellarmini) in comm. haec est interpretatio, quoniam in Sole commoratur Deus tempore peregrinationis nostrae, quo eum videmus per speculum creaturarum, & Sol inter eas obtinet principatum, &c. Hujus vero (Genebrardi) ista est paraphrasis, Respexerunt ad mysterium, quo in Christo vero Sole Deus erat, ac veluti domicilium suum habebat, mundum reconcilians sibi, 1. Cor. 4. In Sole, inquit, Deus habitat, suum domicilium habet, unde gloriose illustris, majestate plenus apparet. q. d. Sol in quo Deus insidet, sive per quem excurrit per totum mundum, ipsum loquitur, ostendit, &c. Quot capita, tot fere sententiae. Quas omnes a mente Psalmographi alienas, aliquot etiam absurdissimas & ineptissimas esse, intrepide ajo & pronuntio. Nunquam enim ex textu Hebraeo, quem de mendo nemo illorum vel suspectare ausus fuit, verba illa, in Sole posuit tab. suum, quibus omnes istae superstructae sunt, exsculpent.
units.tr: Ibid. לְשֶׁמֶשׁ שָׂם אֹהֶל בָּהֶם [for the sun he set a tent in them]. Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus: τῷ ἡλίῳ ἔθετο σκήνωμα ἐν αὐτοῖς [he placed a tent for the sun in them]. So also the Chaldee: לִשְׁמֶשָׁא שׂוּי מַשְׁרֵי זִיהָרָה בְרוֹן [he placed a dwelling of splendour in them for the sun]. Justin Martyr, in Question 63, cites these words from the Syriac version as ἐν αὐτοῖς ἔθετο ἐν ἡλίῳ τὸ σκήνωμα. Theodoret, Jerome, Pagninus, Arias, Benedictus, Vatablus, Münster, Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca Sancta, book 3, p. 137 in my edition, Sa and others agree. Jansenius explains the passage thus: God fixed the dwelling of the Sun in the heavens, so that it might be better seen there as on a lofty stage. Bellarmine in his commentary admits that in the Hebrew there appears no ambiguity or obscurity in the words, and that the sense we have expressed is the true one. The Seventy: ἐν τῷ ἡλίῳ ἔθετο τὸ σκήνωμα αὐτοῦ [in the sun he set his tent]. The Vulgate: in Sole posuit tabernaculum suum [in the sun he set his tabernacle]. Many interpreters labour hard to reconcile this version with the sources. Others try to show that the Hebrew words can bear this interpretation: in the sun he set his tabernacle. But then one would have had to say בְּשֶׁמֶשׁ שָׂם אָהֳלוֹ [in the sun he set his tent]. Grant, however, that לְ is used for בְּ, as in Ps. XVI. לִשְׁאוֹל [to Sheol] for בִּשְׁאוֹל [in Sheol]; from where then would they derive that reflexive "his own"? Certainly not from בָּהֶם [in them], which Richard of Le Mans, author of the collation appended to Lombard's commentary on the Psalms, seems not to have noticed is plural. Richard's words: The first word can be taken indiscriminately in the dative or the ablative. The last reflexively, and relatively in the plain sense. Hence it can be rendered in this way: he set his tabernacle to the sun, or, in the sun he set his tabernacle. Trifles and nonsense! But what sense does it make? On the strength of this passage, misunderstood, the Manichaeans, as Augustine tells us in book 20 against Faustus, fell into worship of the sun. For they believed this to be the meaning of the words: that Christ, when he ascended into heaven, left his body in the globe of the sun and lifted only his soul above all the heavens to the right hand of the Father. They therefore wanted his flesh to be adored in the sun, as the tabernacle of his body. Siena sharply condemns this opinion in book 3, and ascribes it to ignorance of the Hebrew idiom. The genuine, proper and literal sense, he says, is this: God set a tabernacle for the sun in the heavens, from which the sun itself comes forth at dawn like a bridegroom from his bedchamber, to show the splendour of his face to all. What would he have said had he seen that picture which Bartholomaeus Gravius, printer of Louvain, placed on the title pages of many books: the sun, in which a little boy sits carrying a cross, with this inscription: In Sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Look at the title of the Sentences of the Master, published in 1556. Serapion, bishop, writing against the Manichaeans, according to Siena, book 5, annotation 160, charges Origen with the same error. But Pamphilus the Martyr took up his defence: by producing a most evident passage from Origen's commentary on this same Psalm, he clearly shows that this foolish opinion of the Manichaeans was refuted by Origen himself, expressly. Siena copied the passage. There Origen's opinion is set out in these words: The dwelling of Christ's tabernacle is said to be the sun. By the tabernacle of Christ I understand the Church. But which sun ought I to understand other than that true light which illuminates every man coming into this world? I see the very Sun of whom it is said, For to those who fear my name the Sun of righteousness will rise. So "in the sun he set his tabernacle", that is, in the Sun of righteousness. So Origen. Augustine, column 91 of volume 7: The Lord, so that he might wage war against the kingdoms of temporal errors, sending not peace but a sword upon the earth, in time, as it were in a manifestation, set his tabernacle as a military dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation. He goes on: And he himself, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, etc., that is, from the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to his bride, etc. Who could bear such interpretations being put before a congregation in this light of letters? The same Augustine, column 96: In the sun he set his tabernacle, that is, in manifestation he set his Church, not in secret, not hidden, not as covered, lest perhaps it become like the covered things over the flocks of heretics. It has been said also of someone in Scripture, You have done it in secret, you will suffer it in the sun. So, in the sun he set his tabernacle; why, heretic, do you flee into darkness? You will find the same things in the Glossa ordinaria and in the rhapsody of Lombard. Bellarmine seized upon these and was not ashamed, in book 3 On the Church, chapter 12, to cite this passage in support of his opinion on the visibility of the Church. For he says that here is plainly described a Church which cannot be hidden, just as the sun cannot be concealed. Yet nothing of the kind is found in his commentary. If perhaps you are not yet satiated with these absurdities, reader, I shall set before you more dishes of the same flavour. The Carthusian: In the sun, that is, in the lower world under the sun, that is, before the eyes of men, the Son of God set his tabernacle, that is, his assumed body, which is called the temple of the invisible Deity, etc. Or thus: In the sun, that is, in the blessed Virgin Mary, Christ set his tabernacle, that is, his body, dwelling in her womb for nine months. For the most blessed Mary is called the Sun on account of the most excellent splendour of divine graces in her, of whom it is said in the Song, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun. Lombard, from Alcuin: The sun does three things: it shines, it burns, and it makes the variety of seasons. He set his tabernacle in the Sun, that is, in time, because he assumed a flesh subject to temporal changes. Or in the Sun, that is, in toil, because he freely endured the heat of labours. Bellarmine and Genebrardus close the procession. Bellarmine's commentary gives this interpretation: because God dwells in the sun during our pilgrimage, when we see him through the mirror of creatures, and the sun holds the chief place among them, etc. Genebrardus's paraphrase is this: They looked to the mystery by which God was in Christ, the true Sun, and had him as his dwelling, reconciling the world to himself, 1 Cor. 4. God, he says, dwells in the sun, has his dwelling there, whence he appears gloriously bright and full of majesty. As if to say: the Sun in which God sits, or through which he runs across the whole world, speaks it, shows it, etc. As many heads, almost as many opinions. All of these I confidently declare and pronounce to be alien to the mind of the Psalmist, and some of them most absurd and most foolish. For never from the Hebrew text, which none of them has dared to suspect of corruption, will anyone draw out those words, in the sun he set his tabernacle, on which all these structures are built.

units.la: Nunc illud restat, ut videamus, qua ratione alii conentur versioni vulgatae istum inducere sensum, quem unum Hebraeus textus admittit, vid. Deum Soli tabernaculum in coelo assignasse. gnasse, Ἀμφιδἐξιος Geneb. Hypallagen constituit in vulgata versione, ut, in Sole p. t. suum, dictum sit, pro, Solem posuit in tabernaculo suo, id est in cælo. Emmanuel Sa, In sole pro Soli. suum, scilicet Solis, q. d. collocavit Solem in cælo, velut tabernaculo. vide Ps. 104. extendens cælum sicut pellem id est tabernaculum, quod sit expellibus. Vide Justinum quaest. 63. Hier. & Chald. in eis sc. cœlis: Hæc Sa, plane ad palatum nostrum & ex mente Psalmographi. Sic dico, Docta & erudita ea est interpretatio, sed quam versioni Latinæ non magis aptaveris, quam fronti ocream, aut tibiis galeam. Genuinum loci sensum vidit Sa, nec tamen ea fuit doctissimo viro audentia, ut versionem vulgatam hic atro lapillo notaret. Antonius Agellius (cujus sæpe meminit Rev. D. Rivetus) ex Diodoro aut hoc Græco hanc adfert, In Sole posuit tab. suum id est ejus, quasi in ipso sole positum esset tabernaculum Solis, quia Deus constituit, ut Sol se ipsum gestaret sine alio vehiculo. Ipse tamen Agellius, periculum ingenii sui facturus, aliam suppeditat, In Sole posuit. tabernaculum SUUM id est ejus. q d. in ipso Sole Deus posuit tabernaculum Solis, quia aliquando se abdit & in tenebris tanquam in tabernaculo condit. Quæ interpretatio, præterquam quod textui Ebraeo plane aptari non posset (non enim scriptum est אהל sed אהל) è diametro repugnat observationi Bellarmini, quam ex hoc loco depromsit, ut supra vidimus. Restat Euthymius, qui omnibus hic palmam præripuisse videtur. Hujus versiculi sensus talis, inquit, quod Deus habitationem Soli posuit in cælo. Ait enim Moses de duobus magnis luminaribus, quod posuit ea Deus in firmamento cæli, ut lucerent super terram. Aliquibus etiam visum est, versiculum hunc recte construi non posse, nos autem post dictionem, tabernaculum, virgulam ponentes, & dictionem, qua Grace εἰς habetur, non pro relativo, sed adverbio loci intelligentes, commodissime ordinem reddidimus: posuit Deus ac determinavit Soli habitationem illic id est in cælo. Ita tamen ut superflua sit præpositio, in, quemadmodum multis in locis observavimus. Vult ergo, in Sole, positum esse pro, Soli. Atque hinc primam suam notam hausit Sa. Nos præpositionem ἐν ex Ebraïsmo sæpe ἀπέσταλκεν scimus, quando vid. respondet Ebræo ב / præcipue vero quando instrumentum notat. At eam observationem hic velle applicare, alienum est. Claudam verbis Theodoreti, In sole p.t.f. Hac magis clare * tres interpretes explanarunt, Soli posuit tabernaculum in illis. Vid. in cælis. Magnus enim Moses docuit, Et fecit
units.tr: Now remains the question of how others try to force onto the Vulgate version the one sense that the Hebrew text admits, namely that God assigned the tabernacle of the sun in heaven. Genebrardus sets up a hypallage in the Vulgate, so that he placed his tabernacle in the Sun is said for he placed the Sun in his tabernacle, that is, in heaven. Emmanuel Sa explains "in Sole" as "for the sun" (Soli), so that the sense is that he set the sun in heaven as in a tabernacle. Compare Psalm 104: stretching out the heavens like a skin, that is, a tent, which is made of skins. See Justin, question 63. Jerome and the Chaldee have "in them," that is, in the heavens. So far Sa, entirely to our taste and in line with the psalmist's intent. I say that this interpretation is learned and erudite, but you would no more fit it to the Latin version than fit a greave to the brow or a helmet to the shins. Sa saw the genuine sense of the passage, yet it was not in that learned man's boldness to mark the Vulgate version here with a black stone. Antonius Agellius (whom the Reverend Mr Rivet often mentions) brings forward from Diodorus, or from this Greek, the following: In the Sun he placed his tabernacle, that is, of him, as if the tabernacle of the Sun were placed in the Sun itself, because God ordained that the Sun should carry himself without any other vehicle. Agellius himself, however, willing to test the strength of his own wit, offers another: In the Sun he placed his tabernacle, that is, of him: as if to say, God placed the tabernacle of the Sun in the Sun itself, because at times it hides itself and shuts itself up in darkness as in a tabernacle. This interpretation, apart from the fact that it could not be fitted to the Hebrew text at all (for it is not written אהל but אהל), flatly contradicts the observation of Bellarmine, which he drew from this passage, as we saw above. There remains Euthymius, who seems to have carried off the palm from all here: The sense of this verse, he says, is that God placed the dwelling of the sun in heaven. For Moses says of the two great lights that God placed them in the firmament of heaven, so that they might shine upon the earth. Some have also thought that this verse cannot be construed correctly, but we, putting a point after the word tabernacle and understanding the word which in Greek is "eis" not as a relative but as an adverb of place, have rendered the order most conveniently: God placed and determined the dwelling of the sun there, that is, in heaven. Yet in such a way that the preposition in is superfluous, as we have observed in many places. He therefore wants "in Sole" to stand for "Soli." From this Sa drew his first mark. We know that the preposition ἐν is often used in Hebraism for the Hebrew ב, especially when it denotes an instrument [ἐν]. But to apply that observation here is out of place. I will close with the words of Theodoret: In the sun he placed his tabernacle.* These three interpreters have explained this more clearly: he placed the tabernacle of the sun in those, that is, in the heavens. For the great Moses taught, "And God made

units.la: * Aquila, Theodotio, Symmachus. cit Deus duo magna luminaria & posuit illain firmamento cœli, &c. Et accedat Lyra, In Ebr. & translatione Hieron. juxta Ebraeum, habetur, Soli posuit t. s. in eis, & sic exponitur, quod Sol in medio planetarum ponitur. Et hic fit specialis mentio de Sole magis quam de aliis stellis, quod per ipsum & ejus effectus magis immotescat ordo divina sapientia hominibus.
units.tr: * Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus. two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven, and so on. Add Lyra: In the Hebrew and in Jerome's translation, according to the Hebrew, we have, he placed his tabernacle in them, and it is explained thus: that the sun is placed in the middle of the planets. And here special mention is made of the sun rather than of the other stars, because through it and its effects the order of divine wisdom is more clearly impressed on men.

units.la: Verf. 14. Et ab alienis parce servo tuo.] Ita Vulg. ex Græco, ἀπὸ ἀλλοτρίων φείσαι ὃ δούλ σε. Ebraïce, מזרים / Chald. מן ירונים â superbis vel superbiis, Hiero. à superbiâ. Synnin. ἀπὸ ὑπερηφάνων Pagn. à superbiis. Arias Mont. ab insolentibus. Qui superbias reddunt, peccata quæ scienter & insolenter committuntur, intelligunt. Integrum hemistichium ita habet מזרים חשוך עבדך à superbiis prohibe servum tuum. Non petit sibi condonari peccata scienter & insolenter admissa, sed implorat Dei auxilium, ne unquam in ejusmodi peccata prolabatur. Junius, à contumaciis subtrahe servum tuum. Pisc. vom ubermut. Ital. Guarda etiandio il tuo servidore da peccati commessi per superbia. Genev. — des offenses commises per fierté id est per superbiam, contumaciam. Hispan. de las soberbias, Scholion, de los pecados hechos (id est commissis) de proposito deliberado. Qui Latine intelligit, hæc intelliget. Angl. from presumptuous sinnes. Vides consensum Pontificiorum & Euangelicorum Interpretum. Et certe Ebræum זור tam in Kal quam in Hifyl passim & in Biblico & Thalmudico contextu significat, data opera & de industria peccare, Ex. gr. Exod. xviii. 11. Ierem. l. 29. Exod. xxi. 14. Deut. 1.43. Quid ergo vidit Græcus cum sic vertit, ἀπὸ ἀλλοτρίων; Resp. eum legisse Resch pro Daleth, מזרים / Quod si & Chald. & Symmachus eodem modo legissent, majori specie fontes Ebræos suspectare possent isti Pontificii, qui ut vulgatam defendant, fontibus ubique infesti sunt. Joh. Bened. in margine Pagninianam quoque interpretationem exhibuit, & Sa notat in Hieron. & Chald. esse, à superbiis. Atque hic semel nota, Emmanuelem Sa, ubi Chaldæum textum allegat, Ebræum fere denotare, aut hunc sub illo quoque comprehendere. At Ebræum non ausus fuit nominare, ne simplex lector ista ab Ebraeo textu discrepantia, eaque singulis fere versibus indicata commotus, Vulgatum textum suspiceret. Nunc videamus, quos ludos interpretes in hujus loci commentatione dederint. Vulgo hæc verba sic intellexerunt, fatente Bellar. in commentario, quasi iste esset sensus, condona mihi aliena peccata id est quæ vel per aliorum suggestionem patrantur, aut quæ alii à nobis non præmoniti admittunt. Author supplementi ad summam Thomæ quæst.2.art.5 petit sibi parci à pecc. al. in quantum ex consortio peccatorum aliquis per consensum aliquam immunditiam patitur, sicuti scriptum est, cum perverso perverteris. Ps. 18. (Sed & hic ipse locus quam bene allegetur, supra vidimus.) Et certe non solum superiores, ὃις λαοὶ ἀπατεφάται ἡ ψυχαὶ, sed & quilibet Christianus, dum monendo officium suum non facit, aliorum peccatis communicat & merito deprecari potest Dei iram. Sed recte notavit Bellar. illud hoc loco non denotari. In Ebræo, inquit, duo peccatorum genera memorantur, alia per infirmitatem & ignorantiam, alia per superbiam & contumaciam commissa. Audite hoc catholici, & discite à Bellarmino verum hujus loci sensum. Alii alienos homines, à quorum contagiosa consortione conservari velit, alii alienos dominos vel Deos intelligunt. Theodoretus de dæmonibus interpretatur. Omnes aliene. Non enim ut jam vidimus, in Ebræo est quod alienum significet. Sed & Ebr. חשוך minus bene redditum est parce. Significat enim retinere, cohibere. Quid ex eo colligi possit. verbis Rev. D. Riveti docebo. Non possunt, inquit David omnia peccata vitari. Sed, mi Deus, custodi me, ne dedita opera sciens volens grave & enorme quid committam. Verbum חשך quod retinere & cohibere significat, magnam esse carnis ad peccandum proclivitatem, quæ frenis & retinaculis gratia divinæ opus habeat, & præcipites ferri ad vitium homines, nisi Deus sua custodia eos flagitiis subtrahat, ostendit.
units.tr: Verse 14. And spare your servant from the proud.] So the Vulgate, after the Greek: from strangers spare your servant [ἀπὸ ἀλλοτρίων φείσαι ὁ δοῦλός σου]. In Hebrew: [מזרים]; in the Chaldee: [מן ירונים], "from the proud" or "from pride," as Jerome has "from pride." Synnin: [ἀπὸ ὑπερηφάνων], "from the proud." Pagninus: "from the proud." Arias Montanus: "from the insolent." Those who render "pride" understand sins committed knowingly and insolently. The whole half-verse reads: [מזרים חשוך עבדך], "from the proud, keep back your servant." He does not ask that sins committed knowingly and insolently be forgiven him, but implores God's help, that he may never fall into sins of that kind. Junius: "from contumacies withhold your servant." Piscator: "from arrogance." Italian: "Guard also your servant from sins committed through pride." Geneva: "from offences committed through pride," that is, pride and contumacy. Spanish: "from the proud sins," the Scholion: "from sins done" (that is, committed) "with deliberate purpose." Whoever understands Latin will understand these things. English: "from presumptuous sins." You see the agreement of the Papist and Evangelical interpreters. And certainly the Hebrew [זור], both in Kal and in Hiphil, everywhere in the Biblical and Talmudic text means to sin deliberately and of set purpose, for example Exodus 18:11, Jeremiah 50:29, Exodus 21:14, Deuteronomy 1:43. What then did the Greek see when he rendered it "from strangers"? I answer that he read Resch for Daleth, [מזרים]. But if the Chaldee and Symmachus had read it in the same way, those Papists could suspect Hebrew sources with greater show, since they, in order to defend the Vulgate, are everywhere hostile to the sources. John Benedictus in the margin also set out the Pagninian rendering, and Sa notes that in Jerome and the Chaldee it is "from the proud." Here note once for all that Emmanuel Sa, where he cites the Chaldee text, mostly indicates the Hebrew, or includes it under that name. But he did not dare to name the Hebrew, lest the simple reader, moved by this discrepancy from the Hebrew text, which is pointed out at almost every verse, should come to suspect the Vulgate text. Now let us see what games the interpreters have played in their commentary on this passage. Commonly they have understood these words thus, as Bellarmine admits in his commentary, as if the sense were: forgive me the sins of others, that is, those committed through another's urging, or which others admit without our having warned them. The author of the supplement to the Summa of Thomas, question 2, article 5, asks to be spared from the sins of others, in so far as through fellowship in sins someone suffers some uncleanness through consent, as it is written, "with the perverse you shall be perverted" (Ps. 18; but we saw above how well this passage is cited here). And certainly not only those who lead others astray, but any Christian who, by failing to admonish, neglects his duty, shares in others' sins and may rightly pray to be spared God's anger. But Bellarmine rightly observed that this is not what the words mean here. In the Hebrew, he says, two kinds of sins are mentioned: some committed through weakness and ignorance, others through pride and contumacy. Hear this, Catholics, and learn from Bellarmine the true sense of this passage. Others understand by "strangers" people from whose contagious company he wishes to be kept safe; others understand foreign lords or gods. Theodoret interprets it of demons. All are wrong. For, as we have now seen, there is nothing in the Hebrew that means "foreign." Also the Hebrew [חשוך], "spare," is not well rendered: it means to hold back, to restrain. What may be gathered from this I will show in the words of the Reverend Mr Rivet. David says that not all sins can be avoided. But, my God, keep me, so that I do not knowingly and willingly, with set purpose, commit anything grave and monstrous. The verb חשך which means to hold back and restrain shows that there is in the flesh a great proneness to sin, which needs the grace of God as bridles and reins, and that men are carried headlong into vice unless God withdraws them from wickedness by his keeping.

units.la: Vers. 14. Si mei non fuerint dominati, tunc immaculatus ero & emundabor à delicto maximo.] Adscribam verba Domini Riveti, Notat Genebrardus, inquit, illud mei, (μυ) genitivi casus, non nominativi. per Græcismum pro dativo usurpari. Quod cum non intellexisset Papa Pius IV. hæc verba usurpavit, tanquam aptum sibi symbolum, quia ex filiorum suorum dominatione, quos ad summos gradus evexerat, sentiebat se maximam labem apud Deum & homines contraxisse. Ideo suorum ingratitudinem moriens sæpe incusavit, inquit Thuanus Hist. lib. yi. ad annum 1549. se felicem dictitans, si nunquam gegenuisset, ac subinde illud ex Psalmo xix. quod in III. nocturno decantari solet, ingeminans, Si mei non fuissent dominati, tunc immaculatus essem & emundarer à peccato maximo. Quia, ut ibidem addit, plus Justo privatis caritatibus indulgens existimationi suae ac Reip. Christianae periculum parvi fecerat, ut suorum ambitioni & libidini satis-faceret. Hoc quidem peccatum erat maximum. Sed quam apte ad id significandum usurpata fuerint verba Davidis, judicent lectores & ex eo, quam boni sint Scripturae interpretes Pontifices Romani, sine quorum facie nihilominus, si Jesuitis credamus, in Scripturae interpretatione coecutiret orbis Christianus.
units.tr: Verse 14. If my people have not ruled over me, then I shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest sin. I shall quote the words of Rivetus: Genebrardus notes, he says, that the word mei [μου] is a genitive, not a nominative, used by a Graecism for the dative. Pope Pius IV, not understanding this, made use of these words as a fitting motto for himself, because he felt that by the domination of his sons, whom he had raised to the highest ranks, he had incurred a great stain before God and men. Therefore, dying, he often complained of their ingratitude, says Thuanus (Hist. lib. vi., at the year 1549). He kept saying that he would be happy if he had never begotten them, and he repeated from Psalm 19, which is customarily sung at the third nocturn: If my sons had not ruled over me, then I should be blameless and cleansed from the greatest sin. For, as he adds in the same place, by indulging too much in private affections, he had held his own reputation and the danger to the Christian commonwealth of little account, so that he might satisfy the ambition and lust of his sons. That was indeed the greatest sin. But let the readers judge how aptly David's words have been used to signify this, and from this judge how good interpreters of Scripture the Roman Pontiffs are, without whose face, if we believe the Jesuits, the Christian world would nonetheless grope blindly in the interpretation of Scripture.

units.la: Ps.XXII. 2. Longinquus à salute mea, verbis rugitus mei.] Ebr. דברי שאגתי verbus rugitus mei. Homo qui magno clamore inter graves dolores preces suas effundit, alibi quoque in Psalmis rugire dicitur. Intelligitur clamor doloris, inquit Bellar. ad vers. 3. qui recte rugitus dici potest. Pagn. Arias, Munsterus, Campensis & alii quoque rugitum vertere. Consentiuntin sensu prisci omnes, Chald. צלי צכליות / Hier. rugitus mei. Aquila, βεγχήματός μου. Symm. τ' οδυγμῶν μου. Quinta, τ' δεισοτων μου. Sexta & Theod. τῆς κεχουνῆς μου. Soli Lxx. οἱ λόγοι τ' παραπτωμάτων μου. Vulg. verba delictorum meorum. Legerunt שגאתי aut cum eo confuderunt. Hic quaesitum ab Interpretibus, quomodo Christus sibi ipsi delicta tribuat. Varie responsum est. Thomas parte 3. qu. xv. art. 1. quaerens an in Christo fuerit peccatum, hunc locum pro affirmativa in acie ponit, ad quem postea sic respondet, dupliciter aliquid dici de Christo, uno modo secundum proprietatem naturalem & hypostaticam, ut cum dicitur quod Deus factus est homo. Altero modo secundum proprietatem personalem & habitudinalem, prout sc. aliqua de ipso dicuntur, in persona nostra, quae sibi secundum se nullo modo convenient, &c. Unde & inter vii. regulas Ticonii, quas Augustt. ponit lib. 3. de Doctr. Christ. prima ponitur de Domino & ejus corpore, cum scil. Christi & Ecclesiae una persona aestimatur. Et secundum hoc Christus ex persona membrorum suorum loquens dicit, verba delictorum meorum, non quod in ipso capite delicta fuerint. Hoc ergo vult, Christum peccata nostra vocare sua propter unitatem Christi & Ecclesiae, capitis & membrorum, ut loquitur Carthus. Communiter tamen sententia est, Christum peccata nostra vocare sua, quod pro iis tanquam suis passus sit. Emmanuel, Sa delictorum meorum id est pro quibus, veluti sfessent mea, passionem subii. Ita Theod. August. Euthym. Bell. Genebrardus. Bell. insuper ex Theod. docet, Christum sibi tribuere posse peccata nostra, ac si sua essent. Hoc nullus orthodoxus infitebitur. Et tamen ista omnia hic aliena sunt. Nulla enim hic delictorum in originali mentio. Nullum hic proponendae salutaris de istius Christi satisfactione doctrinae fundamentum est. Illud tamen hic observet lector, Si, ipsis Pontificiis sentientibus, peccata nostra propter imputationem possunt dici peccata Christi, cur absurdum putant, Christi justitiam posse vocari nostram? & per justitiam Christi nobis imputatam nos vere dici posse justos? Qui sibi tribuit peccata nostra tanquam si essent sua ille certe se pecatorem dicit eodem sensu. Nam cujus sunt peccata, ille peccator est. Bellar. autem contendit, Christum sibi tribuere peccata nostra, idque vere ut credo, neque enim mentiri potest. Ergo potuit vere etiam se dicere peccatorem, dum personam nostram sustineret, qui tamen in se innocens erat. Ita Dominus Rivetus comm. in hunc Psalmum. Claudam verbis August. in hunc ipsum locum, Quomodo dicit delictorum meorum? nisi quia pro delictis nostris ipse peccatur & delicta nostra sua delicta fecit, UT JUSTITIAM SUAM NOSTRAM JUSTITIAM FACERET.
units.tr: Ps. 22:2. "Far from my salvation are the words of my roaring." Hebrew the words of my roaring [דברי שאגתי]. A man who pours out his prayers with loud cries amid severe pains is also said to roar elsewhere in the Psalms. The cry of pain is understood, says Bellarmine on verse 3, which can properly be called roaring. Pagninus, Arias, Münster, Campensis and others also translate roaring. All the ancients agree in the sense: the Chaldee [צלי צכליות] and Jerome, my roaring. Aquila, of my groaning [βεγχήματός μου]. Symmachus, of my lamentations [τῶν ὀδυγμῶν μου]. Quinta, of my terrors [τῶν δεισμῶν μου]. Sixth and Theodotion, of my cry [τῆς κεχουνῆς μου]. Only the Septuagint, the words of my transgressions [οἱ λόγοι τῶν παραπτωμάτων μου]. The Vulgate, the words of my sins. They read [שגאתי] or confused it with that. Here the interpreters ask how Christ can attribute sins to himself. Answers vary. Thomas, Part 3, question 15, article 1, asking whether there was sin in Christ, puts this passage in the front rank for the affirmative, and afterwards answers thus: something may be said of Christ in two ways: in one way according to his natural and hypostatic property, as when it is said that God became man. In another way according to his personal and relational property, namely insofar as certain things are said of him in our person, which in themselves in no way belong to him, etc. Hence also among the seven rules of Ticonius, which Augustine sets out in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, the first is about the Lord and his body, since Christ and the Church are regarded as one person. And according to this, Christ, speaking in the person of his members, says, the words of my sins, not because sins were in the head himself. He therefore means this: Christ calls our sins his own because of the unity of Christ and the Church, head and members, as the Carthusian puts it. Yet commonly the opinion is that Christ calls our sins his own, because he suffered for them as if they were his own. Emmanuel Sá: the words of my sins, that is, for which, as if they were mine, I underwent suffering. So Theodoret, Augustine, Euthymius, Bellarmine, Genebrardus. Bellarmine further teaches from Theodoret that Christ can attribute our sins to himself as if they were his own. No orthodox person will deny this. And yet all these things are foreign to this place. For there is no mention here of original sin. Nor is there here any foundation for the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction that is to be set forth. Still, let the reader observe this: if, as the Papists themselves hold, our sins can be called the sins of Christ because of imputation, why do they think it absurd that the righteousness of Christ can be called ours, and that through the righteousness of Christ imputed to us we can truly be called righteous? He who attributes our sins to himself as if they were his own, he certainly calls himself a sinner in the same sense. For whose sins they are, that man is a sinner. But Bellarmine contends that Christ attributed our sins to himself, and truly so, as I believe, for he cannot lie. Therefore he could also truly call himself a sinner while he bore our person, although in himself he was innocent. So Lord Rivet in his commentary on this Psalm. I will close with the words of Augustine on this very passage: Why does he say, of my sins? Unless because he was himself sinned for our sins, and made our sins his own sins, THAT HE MIGHT MAKE HIS RIGHTEOUSNESS OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.

units.la: Vers. 17. Foderunt manus, &c.] Ita & Lxx. ὤρυξαν, Aquila, ὤρυξαν, foedarunt, id est indignis modis tractarunt, quomodo ὀρύσσειν usurpatur Homero, Iliad. 6 anitio. —χαλεῖν δ' ἰχῶρ' ... Et Virgil. Æn. 4. Unguibus ora soror foedans & pectora pugnis.
units.tr: Verse 17. They pierced my hands, etc. So also the LXX [ὤρυξαν], they dug through; Aquila [ὤρυξαν], they defiled, that is, treated shamefully; in this way ὀρύσσειν is used by Homer, Iliad 6. And Virgil, Aeneid 4: her sister, marring her face with her nails and her breast with her fists.

units.la: Et lib. 2. — qua causa indigna serenos Foedavit vultus?
units.tr: And in book 2: what unworthy cause has marred her serene face?

units.la: Foedarunt id est cruentarunt, inquit Servius. In codicibus Ebraeis vulgo legitur כָּרוּ hoc est, sicut Leo. Omnes tamen Interpretes prisci vertunt per praeteritum, quasi esset כָּרוּ foderunt, quod per Epenthesin literae א dicitur pro כָּרוּ quomodo pro כָּרָה Zach. 14. occurrit כָּרָה / Solus Chald. utrumque expressit, fodiunt ut leo. quod Arias Montanus in comm. suo calculo approbavit. Quod vero asserit, MaMasorethas asseverare, duas illas lectiones כארי & כארי simul componendas esse, videtur respicere ad notam Masorethicam, quæ est ad hanc ipsam vocem, בי קמצין כתרי לישני שויתי, hoc est, עד בקר duo sunt camez̧ata , in duabus significationibus. Sequentia verba innuunt locum, ubi alterum כארי occurit, vid. Iesai 38. 13. qui sic incipit שויתי עד בקר / Eo si respexit Arias, fallitur. Nam בתרי לישני non indicat duplicem vnius vocis in uno loco significationem, sed diversam duarum vocum, scriptura convenientium & diversis locis extantium, acceptionem.
units.tr: Defiled, that is, stained with blood, says Servius. In Hebrew codices the reading commonly found is ka'ari [כָּארִי], that is, like a lion. Yet all the ancient interpreters render it by the past tense, as if it were karu [כָּרוּ], they dug, which by the epenthesis of the letter aleph is said for karu; in the same way, for kara [כָּרָה] there occurs in Zechariah 14 kara. Only the Chaldee expressed both: they dig like a lion. Arias Montanus approved this in his commentary. But what he asserts, that the Masoretes declare these two readings, ka'ari and ka'ari, are to be combined, seems to refer to the Masoretic note which stands at this very word: there are two qamets in two readings [בי קמצין כתרי לישני שויתי], that is, until morning [עד בקר], there are two qamets, in two senses. The words that follow point to the place where the other ka'ari occurs, see Isaiah 38:13, which begins I have set until morning. If Arias relied on this, he is mistaken. For bitre lishnei does not indicate a double meaning of one word in one place, but a different acceptance of two words that agree in spelling and are found in different places.

units.la: In Masora finali litera א sol. 1. col. 8.! proponitur alphabethum ex binis vocibus כתרי לישני / E.g. אמיר (quod quarto loco illic collocatur) significat summum in arbore ramum Iesa. 17. 6. & permutabo, Hos. 4. 7. Inter illas vero (sunt autem numero xcviii.) recensetur & hoc כארי / Hoc ergo dicit Masora, כָּארִי cum Kamets sub ב / bis extare in diversa significatione. Iesa. 38. 13. extra omnem controversiam significat sicut leo. Neque obstat quod sub ב sit Kamets; nam illud est propter inclusum articulum ה / quod notandum est propter Joh. Isaacum, qui ex ista punctatione conatur evincere, vocem כארי in mendo cubare. Hoc ergo loco vid. Psal. 22. 17. alia interpretatio quaetenda est. Habemus ergo confitentes Judæos, כארי hic non significare, sicut leo. Apparet itaque locum hunc non esse de industria à Judæis corruptum. Apparet & illud, scripturam illam כארי esse perantiquam, & jam Moretharum ævo invaluisse. Doceri & illud insuper amplius potest, eorundem ævo scriptum fuisse כארי & lectum כארי / Masora marginalis ad Numer xxiv. 9. ubi extat vox כארי ita habet, ד' ב' קמצין וב פתחין hoc est, quater occurrit, duo cum Kamets, duo cum fathach. Quibus in Masora textuali hæc subjiciuntur, כאריב וסי כרע כארי ידי/ ורגלי כארו כתיב Ecce inter quatuor כארי recensent hoc, & simul notant, כתיב jam tum fuisse כארי / Accedit testimonium R. Jacob ben Chajim, qui in Masora magna, li-tera א ante ר notat, בקצרת ספריים מרויקים מצאתי כתיב כארו וקרי hoc est, in quibusdam exemplaribus correctis inveni scriptum [in textu] chaâru, at lectum [in margine] chaari. Andradius, Defens. Conc. Trident. lib. 4. Galatinus de arcanis Cathol. verit. 8. 17. Joh. Isaac lib. 2. contra Lindanum pag. 102, & seq. testantur se vidisse exemplaria, quæ in textu habuerint כארו / in margine כתיב/ Chaldæum quoque Paraphrasten tali usum fuisse codice, ex ipsius versione, quam supra produximus, appa-ret. Dices, primo, ex testimoniis Masoræ liquere, ejus authores lectionem כרי tanquam germanam probasse. Nam lectionem marginalem id est τὸ Keri, textuali, quam Chetib vocant, præferendam esse docent. Resp. illorum judicium veritati nihil præjudicare, neque ullum in his talibus obligare. In marginalibus istis notis, quas קרין vocant, aut authoritatem bonæ notæ codicum, aut suum judicium secuti sunt. Sic dico aut notarunt in margine quod in bonis codicibus reperiebant & magis germanum putabant: aut quod sine authoritate codicum legendum esse putabant, quando vocem, quæ in textu, de mendo suspectant. Quicquid hic di-xeris, illi secuti sunt judicium suum, cui nullus unquam inter-pres Christianus se in omnibus subjecit, ipsique adeo Ebræi commentatores non semper parientiam præbuere. Nam & illi sæpe τὸ Chetib tanquam magis germanum interpretati sunt. Dices II. cum hodie in omnibus codicibus legatur in textu כרי & in margine sub titulo Keri nihil repræsentetur, nonde nihilo esse objectionem Pontificiorum, qui hunc locum tanquam minus sincerum accusant, Respondeo cum Witakero hoc unum posse ab illis probabile in fontibus Ebr. corruptelæ indicium inveniri. Si enim vera sunt, quæ ex Masora produximus, dupliciter hodie ab antiquis codicibus recedituř. I. enim in textu ponitur non כרי ut olim, sed כרי/ II. in margine nihil sub titulo Keri exhibetur. Quod si enim hic repostum fuisset illud כרי/ jam nuda fuisset transpolitio & quidem ejusmodi, quæ hoc exemplum misset sub jugum istius Ebræorum legis, quæ τὸ Keri præferendum esse sanciunt. A qua alias eximendum fuisset. Nam ut antea diximus, isti sanctioni ne Ebræi quidem omnes obediunt. Sed quid in textu, quid in margine positum olim fuerit, vel debeat, nolim cum quoquam contendere. Illud constare ex ipsorum Masorethærum confessione opinor, כרי hic non significare sicut leo. Quid ergo aliud denotabit, quam sederunt? vid. כרי quod in codicibus correctis extitisse ipsi prodidêre. Cur ergo in recentioribus editionibus Bibliorum, alteram lectionem supprimunt, dices? Imo, cur Christiani eam supprimunt, inquam ego. Cur ipsi Pontificii, Plantinus, Bombergus & alii eam insuper habuere? Dicam. Non semel librariorum errore vel incuria Keriin & Chethibin transpofita & confusa sunt. Certe Elias Levita in quadam Editione Veneta id passim factum esse conqueritur; Non item nuperum est, quod Keriin id est marginales istæ notæ, à multis libraris omitti coepere. Hinc non est quod admodum miremur, hoc quoque loco lectiones istas transpositas, eamque, quam margo exhibere debuisset, omissam esse. Christianis, cum editiones Bibliorum Ebraicorum adornare inciperent, quominus marginalem lectionem restituerent, Judæi restitere. Ex quo enim superiori seculo literas Ebraicas, ringentibus Judæis, didicere Christiani, incrementa sumsit æmulatio inter Judæos & Christianos. Incrementa sumsit pertinacia, adeo quidem ut nihil Christianis gratificari voluerint. Æmulatio magna orta est inter typographos nec non correctores Judæos & Christianos. Atque in hoc certamine præpotuere Judæi. Namque Christianorum animos metus damni fregit. Ausus enim fuit Judæus quidam, corrector editionis cujusdam Veneta, denuntiare Bombergo, cum is locum hunc ad fidem correctissimorum codicum, quos R. Jacob ben Cajim notat; restituere vellet, se procuraturum apud suos, ne ullum exemplar istius editionis emeretur. Id quod ex cl. Drusio saepe me audire memini. Quam pauca vero Bibliorum Ebraicorum exemplaria etiamnum inter Christianos divendantur, Bibliopolæ optime testabuntur. Atque ita hujus qualiscunque defectus, quem in hodiernis codicibus agnoscimus, originem, librariorum descriptorum incuriæ; conservationem vero & durationem ejusdem, partim Judæorum pertinaciæ & ambitioni, partim nostrorum Typographorum pusillanimitati & Christianorum socordiæ adscripserim...
units.tr: In the final Masora, on the letter Aleph, sol. 1, col. 8, there is set out an alphabet of two words, בתרי לישני [bitri lishni]. For example, אמיר [amir], which is placed fourth there, means the highest branch on a tree, Isaiah 17:6, and I will exchange, Hosea 4:7. Among these (there are ninety-eight of them) is also listed this word: כארי [kaari]. So the Masora says that כָּארִי, with Kamets under the ב, occurs twice with different meanings. In Isaiah 38:13 it certainly means like a lion, beyond all dispute. Nor does it matter that there is a Kamets under the ב, for that is because of the article ה that is included; this must be noted against Joh. Isaac, who tries to prove from this pointing that the word כארי is corrupt. So in this place, Psalm 22:17, another interpretation must be sought. We have, then, the Jews confessing that כארי here does not mean like a lion. It is clear, therefore, that this passage was not deliberately corrupted by the Jews. It is also clear that the spelling כארי is very ancient and had already prevailed in the time of the Masoretes. It can further be shown that in their time כארי was written and read כארי: the marginal Masora on Numbers 24:9, where the word כארי occurs, says: ד' ב' קמצין וב פתחין [four times, two with Kamets, two with Patah], that is, it occurs four times, two with Kamets, two with fathach. In the textual Masora these words are added: כאריב וסי כרע כארי ידי ורגלי כארו כתיב [kaari, ... "they pierced my hands and feet," kaaru, written]. See, they count this among the four occurrences of כארי, and at the same time note that the written form was already כארי. There is also the testimony of R. Jacob ben Chajim, who in the Great Masora, on the letter Aleph before ר, notes: בקצרת ספריים מרויקים מצאתי כתיב כארו וקרי [in some corrected copies I found written in the text chaaru, but read in the margin chaari]. Andradius, Defens. Conc. Trident. lib. 4; Galatinus, De arcanis Cathol. verit. 8, 17; and Joh. Isaac, lib. 2 against Lindanus, p. 102 and following, testify that they have seen copies which had כארו in the text and כתיב [Chetib] in the margin. That the Chaldee paraphrast also used such a copy appears from his version, which I quoted above. You will say, first, that from the testimonies of the Masora it is clear that its authors approved the reading כרי as the genuine one, for they teach that the marginal reading, which is called Keri, is to be preferred to the textual reading, which they call Chetib. I reply that their judgment prejudices the truth in nothing and binds no one in such matters. In these marginal notes, which they call Keri, they followed either the authority of good manuscripts or their own judgment. Thus, I say, they either noted in the margin what they found in good manuscripts and thought more genuine, or they thought the word should be read without the authority of manuscripts, when they suspected the word in the text of corruption. Whatever you say here, they followed their own judgment, to which no Christian interpreter has ever wholly submitted himself, and the Hebrew commentators themselves have not always shown patience towards it. For they too have often interpreted the Chetib as the more genuine reading. You will say, second, that since today the text of all manuscripts reads כרי and nothing is shown under the heading Keri in the margin, the objection of the Papists, who accuse this place of being less than sincere, is not nothing. I reply, with Witaker, that this is the only probable sign of corruption that can be found in the Hebrew sources. For if what we have quoted from the Masora is true, today the copies depart from the old manuscripts in two ways: first, the text now has not כרי as formerly but כרי; second, nothing is shown in the margin under the heading Keri. For if that כרי had been placed here, there would already have been a bare transposition, and indeed of the kind that would put this example under the yoke of that Hebrew law which ordains that the Keri be preferred, a law from which this example ought otherwise to have been exempted. For, as we said before, not even all Hebrews obey that ordinance. But I am unwilling to contend with anyone about what was formerly in the text or in the margin, or what ought to be there. I think it is agreed from the Masoretes' own admission that כרי here does not mean like a lion. What, then, will it denote, other than they sat? See כרי, which they themselves reported to have been found in corrected manuscripts. Why, you will ask, do the recent printed editions of the Hebrew Bible suppress the other reading? Rather, I answer, why do Christians suppress it? Why have the Papists themselves, Plantin, Bomberg and others disregarded it? I will say. More than once, through the error or carelessness of scribes, Keri and Chetib have been transposed and confused. Certainly Elias Levita complains that this happened often in a certain Venetian edition. It is not a new thing either that the Keri, that is, these marginal notes, began to be omitted by many scribes. So we need not be greatly surprised that in this place too those readings were transposed, and the one the margin ought to have shown was omitted. When Christians began to prepare editions of the Hebrew Bibles, the Jews resisted their restoring the marginal reading. For since the Christians learned Hebrew letters in the last century, with the Jews grumbling, rivalry grew between Jews and Christians. Obstinacy grew too, so much so that they were unwilling to oblige the Christians in anything. A great rivalry arose between printers and correctors, Jews and Christians. And in this contest the Jews prevailed. For fear of loss broke the spirit of the Christians. One Jew, a corrector of a certain Venetian edition, dared to threaten Bomberg that, when he wished to restore this place according to the most correct manuscripts that R. Jacob ben Chajim notes, he would take care among his own people that no copy of that edition was bought. I remember often hearing this from the distinguished Drusius. How few copies of the Hebrew Bible are still sold among Christians, the booksellers will testify very well. And so I would ascribe the origin of this so-called defect, which we recognise in the present manuscripts, to the carelessness of the copyists; but its preservation and endurance partly to the obstinacy and ambition of the Jews, partly to the timidity of our printers and the sloth of the Christians...

units.la: In dissertatione nostra de nomine יהוה p. 323. promisimus nos hoc loco exhibituros commentationem de Keri & Chetib jam antea in coronide nostra editam. Hic ergo eam habes Lector.
units.tr: In our dissertation on the name יהוה, p. 323, we promised that in this place we would give a commentary on Keri and Chetib, already published earlier in our Coronis. Here, then, reader, you have it.
