units.tr: Of the other letters, only [כדת] is missing once; [חכל] twice; [ג] three times; and [א] five times.

units.la: 4. Transpositio literarum in 62. dictionibus occurrit יָמוּרִי pro יוֹמְרִי / הולךְ pro הלוך /
units.tr: (4) Transposition of letters occurs in 62 words, as [יָמוּרִי] for [יוֹמְרִי], and [הולךְ] for [הלוך].

units.la: XV. Avulsio literæ rarior, ut הָיִיתָה מוּצִיא /
units.tr: XV. Detachment of a letter is rarer, as [הָיִיתָה] and [מוּצִיא].

units.la: XV. Et quidem harum variarum lectionum aliæ hujusmodi sunt, ut sensum non mutent, dubitesque merito, utra præferenda sit. Aliæ verò tales sunt, uti non nisi altera, quæ secundum vocales est, & in margine exprimitur, loco convenire possit. Illæ authoritate bonæ notæ codicum, hæc necessitate etiam, cum judicio, à viris magnis videntur constitutæ.
units.tr: XV. Indeed, some of these various readings are of such a kind that they do not change the sense, and one may reasonably doubt which is to be preferred. Others are such that only the one which follows the vowels and is expressed in the margin can fit the place. The former are established by the authority of good manuscripts; the latter also by necessity, with judgement, by great men.

units.la: Atque hæc ferè ex cl. Viro D. Erpenio.
units.tr: So much, for the most part, from the distinguished Mr. Erpenius.

units.la: XVI. Quæstio inter Teologos & Philologos celebris est, utrum hæ accidentales anomaliæ vid. literæ istæ majusculæ, minusculæ, suspensæ, inversæ, supernè punctatæ, ac variæ istæ lectiones, quas Keri & Chetib vocant, ab ipsis sacris scriptoribus sint exaratæ, idque mysterii alicujus causâ. Multos viros doctos & pios zelus quidam non quidem is malus, sed non satis secundum scientiam, eò compulit, uti affirmativam tanto calore defenderint, ut secus sentientes tantùm non blasphemiæ postulaverint. At ubi Mysteria illa explicanda sunt, vel ignorantiam profitentur. Quid mysterii ponant in plerisque vocibus supernè punctatis, & literis majusculis & minusculis, suis locis ex D. Buxt. Ebræorum judicia * protulimus. Vide inter alia Gen. 23.2. ubi ב minusculum. Ita R. Sal. explicans locum Prov.23.31. ubi scrib. כְּכִיס in crumenâ, & legitur בכוס in poculo, hoc mysterium pandit, Salomonem innuere voluisse, oculum cauponis defixum esse in crumenam Bibuli, dum is oculos defigit in poculum & colorem vini contemplatur. Possem id genus infinita alia variarum lectionum declaramenta producere, si opus esset, quæ à sacrorum vatum mente planè aliena esse omnes cordati concedent. Vnum id solummodo addam, quod speciem aliquam habet & utroque pollice à multis approbatum, Hagg.1.8. extat אכבד / nota marg. אכבדה / Qui hoc ipsum ab ipso Propheta factum putant, ajunt eo innui, quinque res (nenim quinque denotat) defuisse in templo secundo, quæ fuerunt in templo primo. Thalmudici, R. Salmo, Kimchi & alii ea enumerant, vid. 1. Arca cum Cherubim, 2. Vrim & Thummim. 3. Ignis cælitus demissus. 4. Spiritus sanctus seu prophetiæ. 5. * Præsentia Majestatis divinæ. Magnum hoc est testimonium & validum argumentum, quod contra se ipsos afferunt Judæi. Major erit gloria domus secunda quam fuit prima, inquit hic idem Propheta 2.9. Et tamen ex illorum confessione quinque primaria & domus prioris & populi Iudaici ornamenta defuere. Vnde ergo excellentia & prærogativa domus secundæ, si non ex eo, quod humani generis redemptor Messias suâ præsentiâ & doctrinâ eam illustraverit? Hic in magnas angustias Iudæum rediges. Sed si penitius rem intuearis, commentum est quod de defectu literæ ה commentantur. Primò enim scopus Prophetæ tali mysterio adversatur, ideoque nec Aben Ezra, Junius, nec Piscat. nec alii prudentiores Interpretes id attigerunt. 2. Plures extant dictiones quæ scribuntur sine ה parag. at leguntur cum eo, Ex. gr Iez: 23.16. ubi talia Mysteria locum non habent. 3. Non omnia illa in templo secundo defuisse, inter alios etiam ostendit Franzius in Schola sacrificiorum, Disp. xı. Et quod ad Mysteria illa in genere attinet, ego sic arbitror, sat Mysteriorum in sacræ scripturæ nucleo contineri, ut non opus sit ea in cortice quærere, quæ tædioso labore reperta non nisi præcariò obtineamus.
units.tr: XVI. The question between theologians and philologists is a famous one: whether these accidental anomalies, that is, these letters that are large, small, suspended, inverted, pointed above, and these various readings which they call Keri and Chetib, were written by the sacred writers themselves, and for the sake of some mystery. A certain zeal, not indeed a bad one but not sufficiently according to knowledge, has driven many learned and pious men to defend the affirmative with such heat that they have all but demanded blasphemy charges against those who think otherwise. But when those mysteries must be explained, they profess ignorance. What mystery they assign to most of the words pointed above, and to the large and small letters, we have set out in their places from the work of Mr. Buxtorf on the opinions of the Hebrews (marked *). See, among other places, Gen. 23.2, where there is a small [ב]. So R. Sal., explaining the passage at Prov. 23.31, where [כְּכִיס] in the purse is to be written and [בכוס] in the cup is read, reveals this mystery: Solomon wished to suggest that the tavern-keeper's eye is fixed on the purse of the tippler, while the tippler fixes his eyes on the cup and contemplates the colour of the wine. I could produce countless other explanations of this kind of variant reading, if it were necessary, all of which every sensible person will concede to be utterly alien to the mind of the sacred prophets. I will add only this one thing, which has a certain appearance and is approved by many with both thumbs. At Hag. 1.8 there stands [אכבד], with the marginal note [אכבדה]. Those who think this was done by the prophet himself say that it signifies that five things (for five is what the number denotes) were lacking in the second temple which had been in the first. The Talmudists, R. Solomon, Kimchi and others enumerate them: (1) the ark with the cherubim; (2) the Urim and Thummim; (3) the fire sent down from heaven; (4) the Holy Spirit, or prophecy; (5) * the presence of the divine Majesty. This is a great testimony and a strong argument, which the Jews bring against themselves. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, says this same prophet at 2.9. And yet, by their own confession, five chief ornaments of both the former house and the Jewish people were lacking. Whence then the excellence and pre-eminence of the second house, if not from this, that the Messiah, the redeemer of the human race, illumined it by his presence and teaching? Here you will reduce the Jew to great difficulty. But if you look more closely into the matter, the story they tell about the missing [ה] is an invention. For first, the purpose of the prophet is opposed to such a mystery, and therefore neither Aben Ezra, Junius, nor Piscator, nor other more judicious interpreters touched on it. Second, there are many words which are written without the paragogic [ה] but are read with it, for example Ezek. 23.16, where such mysteries have no place. Third, that all those things were not lacking in the second temple has been shown, among others, by Franzius in his Schola sacrificiorum, Disp. 11. As for those mysteries in general, I judge this: there are enough mysteries contained in the kernel of Holy Scripture that there is no need to seek them in the husk, things which, found with tedious labour, we hold only on uncertain grounds.

units.la: XVII. Assentior itaque iis, qui hæc nec ipsis sacris scriproribus nec posterioribus Maforethis, quos post-Thalmudicos vocant, adscribunt. Non sacris scriptoribus. Videtur enim quam lonigissimè à Majestate Sp. sancti alienum, qui literarum quantitatibus & figurâ χοπρ mysteria occultare & eădem sententiâ diversos, quin & aliquando contradictorios sensus proponere, uti videmus illis locis, ubi scribitur ℵ non & legitur ꞏei, Exod. 21.8. Lev. 11. 21. &25.30. 1. Sam. 2.3.2. Reg. 8.10. Jes. 9.3. &49.5. & 63.9. Ezr. 4.3. 1. Chron. 11.20. vide Maforam ad Lev. 11. 21. At-
units.tr: XVII. I therefore agree with those who ascribe these things neither to the sacred writers themselves nor to the later Masorites, whom they call post-Talmudic. Not to the sacred writers. For it seems very far removed from the majesty of the Holy Spirit to hide mysteries in the sizes and shapes of letters, and to propose by the same sentence different and sometimes even contradictory senses, as we see in those places where [לא] is written and [לי] is read: Exod. 21.8; Lev. 11.21 and 25.30; 1 Sam. 2.3; 2 Kings 8.10; Isa. 9.3 and 49.5 and 63.9; Ezra 4.3; 1 Chron. 11.20. See the Masora on Lev. 11.21. But-

units.la: 21. Atque hæc causa est cur accuratissimi Interpretes, Luth. Calv. Bucerus, Jun. & alii <bl>μυσηλωδες</bl> illas argutiolas & in versionibus & commentariis neglexerint, atque ex diversis lectionibus eam solummodo eligendam sibi duxerint, quam ipsi scriptorum scopo, item antecedentibus & consequentibus maxime convenire fuerunt arbitrati. Non posterioribus Masorethis, qui post inventas vocalium figuras vixere. 1. Quia apud Thalmudicos, ipsis longè antiquiores, crebra mentio accidentalium istarum anomaliarum. 2. Quia hæ accidentales anomaliæ omnes versantur circa consonas, nulla circa vocales, quæ tamen ejusmodi mysteriorum tam capaces sunt, quàm consonæ, imo capaciores. Probabilius ergò Masorethis ante-Thalmudicis quorum (uti & Thalmudicorum) tempore Vocales nondum âscriptæ fuerunt, ea tribuuntur. Masora enim hodierna seu notarum Masorethicarum corpus none st ab uno duntaxat aut altero homine aut collegio, certo quodam & definito tempore compositum, sed est farrago & sylva variarum observationum, quæ à pluribus hominibus multis sæculis ab Ezræ seculo usque ad Tiberiensium tempora, convectatæ sunt.
units.tr: 21. This is why the most accurate interpreters, Luther, Calvin, Bucer, Junius and others, neglected those foul little subtleties [μυσηλωδες] both in their versions and in their commentaries. They thought it right to choose from the various readings only the one that best suited the purpose of the writers and the context before and after. The later Masoretes, who lived after the vowel signs were invented, are not the source. (1) Among the Talmudists, who are much older than they are, these accidental anomalies are frequently mentioned. (2) All these accidental anomalies concern consonants and none concern vowels, yet vowels are as capable of such mysteries as consonants, indeed more so. It is therefore more probable that these anomalies are to be attributed to the Masoretes who came before the Talmudists, at whose time (as at the Talmudists' time) the vowels had not yet been written. The modern Masora, that is, the body of Masoretic notes, was not composed by one man or one college at a single fixed time. It is a medley and jungle of various observations, gathered by many people over many centuries, from the age of Ezra down to the times of the Tiberians.

units.la: XVIII. Itaque paulò post Ezræ temporaliteras illas majusculas, minusculas, inversas, suspensas versuumque repetitiones in sacrum codicem invectas fuisse verisimilest. Cl. Buxtorf. existimat, prisci illis sapientibus justas & dignas fuisse causas istius diversitatis, licet nobis hodie ignotas. Et in genere, vel majorem præsentis rei considerationem commendatam, vel arcanum aliquem sensum indicatum fuisse. D. Broughtonus putabat singulas minusculas & majusculas terminos esse certi literarum numeri, vel à præcedente majuscula, vel minuscula, vel à principio libri vel alio loco, olim ex peculiari Indice noto. E. gr. à vau majusculo Lev. 11. usque ad cap. 13. sunt literæ 2600. XIX. Atque hæc de istis anomaliis, in quibus mysteria Ebraei vulgò collocant, dicta in præsens sunto. Videamus obiter de variis lectionibus, Et quidem primo de iis quas Judæorum religio peperit. Atque hic primâ occurrit nomen tetragrammaton יהוה de quo in dissertatione nostra prolixe egimus. XX. Secundo hic occurrunt istæ voces quas vitandæ turpitudinis causâ, alienis vocalibus vestivere Scribæ. Quod si eum sacri scriptores vocales adjecissent, non dubium est, quin propriasn prias vocum istarum posuissent. Aut si voces istas legi noluissent, non scripsissent. Si proprias vocales apposuissent, nullus Judæus eas mutare fuisset ausus. At quia textum Biblicum à punctis vocalibus antea nudum, punctandum suscipiebant, non peccaturos se putabant, si alienas vocales subjicerent, earumque consonas in margine (ne quid de sacra scriptura detrahere, eamque violare viderentur) exhiberent. Traditio hac de re extat in Cod. Thalm. Megilla cap. 3. omnes voces qua in Lege scripta sunt לנא? obscœne, eas legunt לשבח? honeste. An ergo aliquid obscœni est in lingua sancta? à Siritu Sancto? Videtur hoc responderi posse, voces illas tempore scriptorum fuisse sic satis honestas, aurefque simplicioris istius ævi non fuisse ad earum recitationem offensas. At posteriori ævo, crescente in populo isto omni nequitia & spurcitie, communi usu ita fuisse profanatas, ut piivir sine rubore eas audire vel pronunciare potuerint E.gr. sicut vox שגל quæ conjugem & quidem Augustam significat honesta etiamnum est, ita etiam credibile est, verbum שגל quod ipsum actum Vene- reum denotat, olim honestum fuisse; at postmodum sermonis spurcitie fuisse inquinatum; unde puncta vocis שכב beslapen, ei apposuerint. Sicut apud Germanos vox Bruydt sponsa, honesta est, at verbum inde deductum, inhonestum nec à pio & civili viro usurpari audies. In hac tamen voce illud est peculiare, quod ex analogia conjugationis punctari suis vocalibus possit, si cui forte religio sit lectionem scribarum hac in parte sequi. At in nomine יהוה aliisque, Ex.gr. 2.Reg.18.27. Jesa. 36. 12. cogeris, velis nolis, quam Scribæ reliquerunt, contentus esse, quia analogia vocum, quæ in textu, est incerta. Eandem honestatem videmus ab Interpretibus Belgicis adhibitam. Cum enim vox Eb. * ארא significet stercus, & שין urinam & שגל ipsum actum Venereum, quem sœdo Comicorum vo- cabulo exprimere etiam potiussent Latini Interpretes, leges tamen voces honestiores, dreck, water, beslapen, id est, cubare, &c. quæ sunt interpretamenta vocum marginalium.
units.tr: XVIII. Therefore, shortly after the time of Ezra, it is likely that those small letters, large letters, inverted letters, suspended letters and repeated verses were introduced into the sacred codex. The learned Buxtorf thinks the ancient wise men had just and worthy reasons for this difference, though these are unknown to us today. In general, either a greater consideration of the present matter was recommended, or some hidden sense was indicated. Dr. Broughton thought that each small and large letter marks a fixed number of letters, counted either from the preceding large or small letter, or from the beginning of the book or from some other place, once noted in a special index. For example, from the large vav in Leviticus 11 to chapter 13 there are 2600 letters. XIX. Let this be enough for now about these anomalies, in which the Hebrews commonly place their mysteries. Let us look briefly at the variant readings, and first at those which Jewish religion produced. Here first occurs the tetragrammaton יהוה, about which we have treated at length in our dissertation. XX. Second, here occur those words which the scribes, to avoid indecency, clothed in foreign vowels. If the sacred writers had added vowels, there is no doubt they would have put the proper vowels of these words. Or if they had not wished these words to be read, they would not have written them. Had they added the proper vowels, no Jew would have dared to change them. But because they undertook to point the biblical text, which had previously been without vowel points, they thought they would not sin if they supplied alien vowels and placed the consonants of the proper words in the margin, so that they would not seem to take anything away from Scripture or to violate it. A tradition on this matter is found in the Talmud, Megilla chapter 3: all words that are written in the Law as [לנא] obscene, they read as [לשבח] decent. Is there then something obscene in the holy tongue, from the Holy Spirit? It seems this may be answered: at the time of the writers these words were quite decent, and the ears of that simpler age were not offended by their recitation. But in a later age, as all wickedness and filth grew among that people, they were so profaned by common usage that the pious could not hear or pronounce them without blushing. For example, the word שגל, which signifies a wife and indeed an empress, is still decent. So it is also credible that the word שגל, which denotes the very act of love, was once decent, but afterwards was polluted by filthy speech. Hence they supplied for it the vowel points of the word שכב, to be lain with. Just as among the Germans the word Bruydt (bride) is decent, but the verb derived from it is indecent, and you will hear that it is not used by a pious and civil man. In this word, however, there is this peculiarity: by analogy of conjugation it can be pointed with its own vowels, if anyone has scruples about following the scribes' reading in this part. But in the name יהוה and others, for example 2 Kings 18.27 and Isaiah 36.12, you are forced, willy-nilly, to be content with what the scribes left, because the analogy of the words in the text is uncertain. We see the same decency practised by the Dutch interpreters. For since the Hebrew word ארא signifies dung, and שין urine, and שגל the very act of love, which the Latin interpreters could have expressed with the crude vocabulary of the comic writers, they rendered the more decent words: dreck, water, beslapen, that is, to lie with, and so on. These are the renderings of the marginal words.

units.la: XXI. Restant variæ lectiones ex codicum mendosâ descrip- ptione ortæ. Ita sentiunt eruditissimi viri, nominatim Arias Montanus, Kimchius, Ephodæus, Aben Ezra, Dru- sius, Mercerus, Bertramus, Pagetius, Erpenius & Capel- lus.
units.tr: XXI. There remain various readings arising from the faulty copying of manuscripts. So think the very learned men, namely Arias Montanus, Kimchi, Ephodaeus, Aben Ezra, Drusius, Mercerus, Bertram, Pagetius, Erpenius and Capellus.

units.la: Arabice est חרי Arab. cauare.
units.tr: In Arabic it is [חרי], to hollow out.

units.la: In apparatu ad Regia præfat. in varias lect. Ebr. textus. Ius, Weigammejerus, m Piscator, & doctissimus iste n vir, qui scripsit tractatum de antiquitate vocalium à cl. D. Erpenio editum. Etiam Buxt. in eam sententiam descendit lib. 1. cap. 28. Gramm. Nec aliter sentiet, quisquis omni præjudicio sepposito hæc & similia loca bene consideraverit, Jud. 16. 18. & 19. 3. Ruth. 4. 5. 2. Sam. 20. 14. 2. Sam. 24. 18. Psalm. 139. 6. Prov. 19. 19. & 20. 20. & 23. 26. & 31. item 8. 35. & Psal. 18. cum 2. Sam. 22. & libros Chronicorum cum libris Samuelis & Regum contulerit. Qui contra eunt & utramque lectionem divinæ authoritatis esse contendunt, multis in locis (verba reverendi D Pagetii) exfg Deo Janum aliquem bifrontem faciunt, spectantem [illegible, ~6 letters] o [illegible, ~5 letters] Ex. gr. 2. Reg. 8. 10. Ezr. 4. 2. Jesa. 63. 9. ubi aut alterutrum tantum à Sp. S. dictatum est, aut sub unâ sententia si non contrarium, at saltem diversum & duplicem literalem sensum latere oportet. Quorum posterius si admittimus, certè valde peccarunt omnes interpretes, quà veteres, quà recentes, quod in versionibus suis utramque lectionem non expresserint. Quicquid enim ante scriptum est, ad doctrinam nostram scriptum est. Sed illi non valentes certam aliquam interpretationis istius duplicis regulam ex sacris literis extruere, ratique, mysteria à quibusdam in his talibus eruta, nullo solido niti fundamento, fidelium Interpretum officio se defunctos putarunt, si unam exhiberent. Sicuti autem Ebræi in legendo marginalem lectionem exprimunt, ita & Christianorum doctissimi tradiderunt, marginalem lectionem veriorem esse. Ideoque & Interpretes eam plerumque expresserunt. Et ipse Am. Polanus, licet utrique lectioni divinam adscribat authoritatem, marginalem tamen vocem legendam esse docet. Et certè si rem accuratè expendimus, marginales istæ voces correctionem, vocisque quæ degeneraverat, in plerisque extra omne dubium, restitutionem exhibent. ne quid enim in ipso textu mutarent, absterruit eos codicum, circa quos hæc sacra critica versata est, vel vetustas, vel consensus, vel quod talis lectio plurium codicum authoritate niteretur, quà in re utrum bene vel male fecerint, jam non disputo. Dixi marginalem lectionem ab interpretibus plerunque prælatam. Dixi plerunque. Aliquando enim secus factum. Aliquando eos fluctuasse, paucorum exemplorum inductione ostendam. XXII. Jun. & Tremellius 2. Reg. 8. 10. in prima edit. Abi dic ei, (יב) quod est in textu, At in postremis, Abi dic, non vives, ולא / quod est in marg. Ezrae 4. 2. in Edit.pr. Eidem נזבחהsacrificamus, quod in margine: in postr. non sacrificamus, [alteri] ולא / quod in textu. Sic & 1. Reg. 22. 49. in pr. Ed. Josa-phat paravit classem, עשרה quod in margine. In postr. Josapha-to decem naues עשר / quod in textu. Quin & Prov. 31. 4. Eccl. 9. 4. Jer. 2. 20. & 5. 8. τὸ Chetib. in posteremis editionibus praetulit Junius. Piscator licet & ipse plerunque marg. lectionem exprimat, his tamen & aliis locis textualem praetulit, Lev. 11. 21. Pf. 100. 3. 2. Reg. 20. 4. Jesa. 9. 3. Job. 6. 21. idem in Pagn. & Ariae Mont. Bibliis, in vulg. Latina, Graeca & Chaldaea videre licet, quae licet marginalem passim praeferant, aliquando tamen & textualem expresserunt, ut ex. gr. omnes illi Prov. 19. 7. Quatuor vid. lat. Gr. Pagn. Arias, Pf. 100. 3. & Jer 2. 20. Tres, vid. Lat. Ar. Pag. Jesa. 49. 5. Lat. Chald. & & Gr. Jesai. 63. 9. & 2. Sam. 22. 51. nec opus est plura enumerare. Quod ad veteres attinet, probabile est, eos eam lectionem expressisse, quam in codicibus suis invenere. Recentiores dum ab hac Judaeorum regula de praeferendo Kerirecessere, aut Keri & Chetib transpositia esse judicarunt. id quod in quadam * Editione saepe contigisse queritur Elias Levita, aut Criticen istam multis in locis non magni aestimarunt, aut saltem, utrum sufficientes receptam lectionem solicitandi causas habuerint, dubitarunt. Hinc est, quod multi Interpretes istis casibus alteram in textu, alteram in margine vel notis collocarint, non quod utramque à Sp. Sancto esse putarint, sed quod dubitarint ipsi, utra praeferenda, ac proinde Lectori liberum judicium relinquere voluerint. Ex. gr. in Germanica Pisc. Ier. 2. 20. Dan. 3. 12. Neh. 3. 30. 2. Sam. 14. 21. & 18. 13. Jun. Pf. 11. 1. 2. Reg. 5. 12. Tigur. Dan. 9. 24. Job. 13. 15. Ies. 69. 9. Prov. 17. 27. In Anglicana Iof. 8. 12. 1. Reg. 22. 48. 2. Reg. 20. 4. & 23. 33. Pf. 100. 3. Ier. 2. 20. Dan. 9. 14. Iesa. 9. 3. & 30. 32. In Genev. Ex. 21. 8. Prov. 26.
units.tr: In the apparatus to the Royal Polyglot, in the preface on the various readings of the Hebrew text: Ius, Weigammejerus, Piscator, and that most learned man who wrote the treatise on the antiquity of the vowels, published by the late Mr. Erpenius. Buxtorf too inclines to this view in book 1, chapter 28 of his Grammar. Nor will anyone think otherwise who, setting aside all prejudice, carefully considers these and similar passages: Judges 16.18 and 19.3, Ruth 4.5, 2 Samuel 20.14, 2 Samuel 24.18, Psalm 139.6, Proverbs 19.19, 20.20, 23.26 and 31, likewise 8.35, and Psalm 18 compared with 2 Samuel 22, and who compares the books of Chronicles with the books of Samuel and Kings. Those who go against this and maintain that both readings are of divine authority, "in many places" (the words of the reverend Dr. Paget), "make some two-faced Janus of God, looking ..." [illegible, ~6 letters] "o" [illegible, ~5 letters]. For example 2 Kings 8.10, Ezra 4.2, Isaiah 63.9, where either only one of the two was dictated by the Holy Spirit, or under one sense, if not a contrary one, at least a different and double literal sense must lie hidden. If we accept the latter, then certainly all interpreters, both ancient and recent, have sinned gravely in not expressing both readings in their versions. For whatever was written before was written for our instruction. But they, not being able to build any sure rule of this double interpretation from the sacred letters, and thinking that the mysteries some have drawn out of such passages rest on no solid foundation, supposed they had discharged the faithful interpreter's duty if they gave one reading. Just as the Hebrews, in reading, express the marginal reading, so too the most learned Christians have taught that the marginal reading is the truer. Hence the interpreters too have mostly expressed it. And Amandus Polanus himself, although he ascribes divine authority to both readings, teaches that the marginal word is to be read. And indeed, if we weigh the matter carefully, these marginal words in most cases, beyond all doubt, give a correction and a restoration of the word that had degenerated. For what kept them from changing the text itself was either the antiquity of the manuscripts with which this sacred criticism was concerned, or their agreement, or that such a reading rested on the authority of several manuscripts. Whether they did well or badly in this, I do not now dispute. I said the marginal reading was mostly preferred by the interpreters. I said mostly, for sometimes it was otherwise. That they sometimes wavered I will show by a short list of examples.

units.la: 2. Pf. 100. 3. Iesa. 63. 9. Eccl. 9. 4. Atque hanc utrumque lectionis indifferentiam inter errorum describentium fontes retulerim.
units.tr: Ps. 100. 3. Isa. 63. 9. Eccl. 9. 4. I would count this indifference between the two readings among the sources of the errors of copyists.

units.la: XXIII. Non dissimulabo tamen, loca quaedam, licet admodum pauca, occurrere, in quibus utriusque lectionis in unam versionem conflatio non admodum incommoda videri possit, E. gr. Pf. 22. 17. Chaid. vocem כַּאֲרִי reddidit, momorderunt sicut leo q. scriptum esset כְּאֲרִי כַּאֲרִי Prov. 19. 7. לֹא הָמָּה / they are wanting to him, vertunt Angli, Deficiunt ab illos ad verbum, non sunt ei q. scriptum esset לא לו Et Genev. licet diverso sensu, Il n'y a que paroles pour lui, ad verbum, non habet nisi verba pro illo. Jun. & Trem. Ex. 21. 8. non sibi, quasi esset לא לו & Jos. 8. 12. urbs Ai, q. scriptum esset, עיר עי / Prov. 23. 26. ubi Chetib est à רצה voluit, Keri vero à נצר custodivit, reddunt, studiose custodiant. Iez. 42. 16. ubi Chetib habet חמש אמות / 5. cubitos, & Keri חמש מאות / id est 500. illi, quingentorum cubitorum. Munsterus & Tig. 1. Reg. 22. 48. fecit decem naves, Sic & Tig. 2. Sam. 23. 13. tres principes, quam interpretandi rationem imitati sunt * nonnulli Gen. 4. 26. אָז הוּחַל / tunc caeptum est profanari, quia thema vocis utramque significationem admittit. Sed hanc apparentem commoditatem accidentalem esse puto, minimeque ex intentione Spiritus sancti. Quis enim in his non videt fontes variantis lectionis, vid. vel a literarum transpositionem, vel similitudinem b soni, c figurave, vel d omissionem literae, vel partis ejus, ut 1. Reg. 22. 48. Si enim sinistram lineolam ex litera ה sustuleris, remanebit ר / Dein- de hanc interpretationis subtilitatem caetera loca neutiquam admiserint.
units.tr: XXIII. I will not, however, conceal that some places, though very few, occur where combining the two readings into one version might not seem very awkward. For example, at Ps. 22. 17 the Chaldee paraphrast rendered the word כַּאֲרִי [ka'ari] as "they bit like a lion," as if the text had been כְּאֲרִי כַּאֲרִי [ka'ari ka'ari]. At Prov. 19. 7, לֹא הָמָּה [lo hemma], the English translate "they are wanting to him," literally "they are not to him," as if the text had been לא לו [lo lo]. The Geneva Bible, though with a different sense, has "There is only words for him," literally "he has nothing but words for him." Junius and Tremellius at Exod. 21. 8 render "not for himself," as if it were לא לו [lo lo]. At Josh. 8. 12, urbs Ai, the city of Ai, as if the text had been עיר עי [ir ai]. At Prov. 23. 26, where the Chetib comes from רצה [ratsah], "was willing," and the Keri from נצר [natsar], "kept," they render "diligently keep." At Ezek. 42. 16, where the Chetib has חמש אמות [chamesh ammot], "five cubits," and the Keri חמש מאות [chamesh me'ot], that is 500, the former render "of five hundred cubits." Münster and the Zurich Bible at 1 Kings 22. 48 render "he made ten ships," and likewise the Zurich Bible at 2 Sam. 23. 13 "three chiefs." Some have imitated this method of interpreting at Gen. 4. 26, אָז הוּחַל [az huchal], "then it was begun to be profaned," because the root admits both meanings. But I think this apparent convenience is accidental and by no means from the intention of the Holy Spirit. For who in these cases does not see the sources of the variant readings, namely either a transposition of letters, or a similarity of sound, or of shape, or the omission of a letter or part of one, as at 1 Kings 22. 48? For if you remove the small left stroke from the letter ה, what remains is ר. Moreover, the other places would by no means admit this subtlety of interpretation.

units.la: XXIV. Haec itaque & paucula quaedam alia loca si excepteris, manet regula, marginalem lectionem ab Interpretibus & Commentatoribus Ebraeis & Christianis, veteribus & recentibus tanquam meliorem praeferri, quo ipso alteri lectioni divinam authoritatem manifeste videntur derogasse. Quod etiam firmatur ex eo, quod, ut supra attigi, Spiritus sanctus in posterioribus scriptis, eam lectionem, quam in prioribus hodie margines exhibent, id est, tò Keri, passim fere approbet, ut in collatione Chronicorum cum caeteris historicis evidenter apparet. XXV. Sed objiciunt. 1. Si variae istae lectiones ex mendosa codicum descriptione ortae sunt, ac una earum tantum à Sp. S. dictata, necesse erit multas illarum non errori, sed destinatae malitiae & φθοράς adscribere. Primo enim aliquotics ties occurrit לא pro לו ubi nulla similitudo characterum.
units.tr: XXIV. Therefore, with these and a few other places excepted, the rule remains that the marginal reading is preferred by Hebrew and Christian interpreters and commentators, ancient and recent, as the better one, and by this very act they seem clearly to have withdrawn divine authority from the other reading. This is also confirmed by the fact that, as I touched on above, the Holy Spirit in the later writings almost everywhere approves that reading which the margins today exhibit in the earlier ones, that is, tò Keri, as is evident in the comparison of Chronicles with the other historical books. XXV. But they object: (1) If these variant readings arose from faulty copying of manuscripts, and only one of each pair was dictated by the Holy Spirit, it will be necessary to ascribe many of them not to error but to deliberate malice and φθοράς [corruption]. For first, לא [lo, "not"] occurs many times for לו [lo, "to him"] where there is no similarity of letters.

units.la: 2. Non potuerunt non de inustria variæ lectiones induci circa voces illas, quas obscœnas vocant. 3. Nec toties in נַעֲר / 4 Nec in יְרוּשָׁלַםּ / Resp. ad primum, non solum errare potuisse descriptores ex similitudine characterum, sed etiam ex vicinitate soni, ut in לא non, & לי ei & quamplurimis aliis, item ex indifferentiâ sensus, cum enim in describendo originali, quod nobis familiare est, committitur error sensum non laedens, cum difficilius observamus. expende hæc loca, Pf. 41. 3. Pf. 89 18. Prov. 20. 4. Jesa 5. 29. & plurima alia, in quibus nulla Grammatica vel Analysis Logica certum te reddet, utra præferenda, utraque enim quadrat. Addo, in multis locis ne imperitissimum quidem scribam impingere potuisse, si vocales olim fuissent ascriptæ. Quomodo, quæso te, in pronominibus הוא & היא toties errassent, si puncta fuissent ascripta? Sed & expende 1. Reg. 7. 45. Prov. 8. 16. אַהְבִּירָה ubi ה redundat, ac jam monstrosa vox est. Sin absque punctis scribas אהבירה non ita, potest enim legi אוֹהֲבִירָה / Jes. 5. 29. יִשְׁאָא pro יִשָּׂא / quod si adscriptæ fuissent vocales, quis dubitasset scribendum fuisse vel יִשְׁאָא vel יִשָּׂאָ sensu eodem manente? Atque eadem est ratio infinitorum aliorum, ubi Jod Ethan in י degeneravit. Quis enim nescit י non esse formativam futurorum. At scriba, codicem sine punctis describens, non vidit absurditatem, sive per Jod Futuri scriberetur, sive per vau, Præteritum in futurum convertens.
units.tr: (2) The variant readings concerning those words which they call obscene could not have been introduced except by deliberate corruption. (3) Nor so often in נַעֲר [na'ar]. (4) Nor in יְרוּשָׁלַםּ [Yerushalayim]. Response to the first: copyists could have erred not only from similarity of letters but also from closeness of sound, as in לא [lo, "not"] and לי [li, "to me"], and from very many other causes; likewise from indifference of sense, for when in copying the original, which is familiar to us, an error is made that does not harm the sense, we notice it less readily. Consider these places: Ps. 41. 3; Ps. 89. 18; Prov. 20. 4; Isa. 5. 29, and very many others, in which no grammar or logical analysis will make you certain which should be preferred, since both fit. I add that in many places not even the most unskilled scribe could have stumbled, if the vowels had once been written in. How, I ask you, would they have erred so often in the pronouns הוא [hu, "he"] and היא [hi, "she"], if the points had been written in? But consider also 1 Kings 7. 45 and Prov. 8. 16, אַהְבִּירָה [ahbirah], where the ה is superfluous and the word is now monstrous. But if you write אהבירה without points it is not so, for it can be read אוֹהֲבִירָה [ohavirah]. Isa. 5. 29, יִשְׁאָא [yish'a] for יִשָּׂא [yissa]; if the vowels had been added, who would have doubted that either יִשְׁאָא or יִשָּׂאָ ought to be written, the sense remaining the same? The same reasoning applies to countless others, where the Yod ethan has degenerated into י. For who does not know that י is not the formative letter of the future tenses? But the scribe, copying a codex without points, did not notice the absurdity, whether it was written with the Yod of the future or with vav, converting the past into the future.

units.la: XXVI. Quod ad voces eas attinet, quas obscœnas vocant, de iis supra dictum.
units.tr: XXVI. As for those words which they call obscene, what was said about them above applies.

units.la: Quod ad 3. נַעַר cum id 21. vicibus sine ה occurrat in Mose, & legatur cum ה fateor non videri verisimile, ut ex errore litera ה ablata sit. Quid ergò? Posui ea de re conjecturam meam ad Gen. 24. 14. veteres nimirum puellam olim vocasse & נערה & voce communis generis נער / scribas vero postea distinxisse, non quidem addendo ה / hoc enim non fuerunt ausi, sed ponendo punctum sub ך / Quod ad 4. vid. vocem יְרוּשָׁלַםּ attinet, cum quinquies tantum occurrat plenè, vid. cum Jod, (יְרוּשָׁלַיִם) non est verisimile, fateor, tam multis locis descriptorum incuria literam Jod excidisse. Quid ergò? Dicam quod sentio. Vetustius nomen esse puto Jerusalem sine Jod, quam Jerusalajim cum Jod. Firmat hanc meam conjecturam antiquum urbis nomen, unde hoc compositum est, Salem, & constans scriptura sine Jod, quam lectionem etiam Chald. & 70. & scriptores novi Testam. & Hieron. constanter retinuerunt: Posterioribus autem temporibus dici coepisse etiam Jerusalajim, forte quod urbs quasi gemina esset, superior & inferior. unde hanc plenam scripturam cum Jod non invenies, nisi in liberis circa vel sub captivitate Babylonica scriptis, Ex. gr. Jer.18. 26. 1. Chron.3. 5. 2.Chron. 25.1. 1.Chron.26.5. Esth. 2.6. Punctatores vero, ut ubique eadem esset urbis appellatio, ipsorum saeculo usitata, ubique easdem vocales subjecere. neque hoc unicum esse puto, in cujus punctatione usui & pronunciationi sui saeculi aliquid dederunt.
units.tr: As for 3. נַעַר [naar]: since it occurs twenty-one times without ה in Moses, and is read with ה, I admit it does not seem likely that the letter ה was lost through a copyist's error. What then? I have set out my conjecture on this matter at Gen. 24.14: the ancients once called a girl both נערה [naarah] and, using the common-gender form, נער [naar]. Later the scribes distinguished them, not by adding ה, which they did not dare to do, but by placing a point under ך. As for 4., the word יְרוּשָׁלַםּ [Jerusalem]: since it occurs fully spelled with Jod only five times, (יְרוּשָׁלַיִם), it is not likely, I admit, that the letter Jod dropped out through the carelessness of copyists in so many places. What then? I will say what I think. I hold that the older name is Jerusalem without Jod, and that Jerusalajim with Jod is later. My conjecture is confirmed by the ancient name of the city, from which this compound is formed, Salem, and by the constant spelling without Jod, which the Chaldee, the Seventy, the writers of the New Testament and Jerome consistently retained. In later times, however, it began to be called Jerusalajim as well, perhaps because the city was, as it were, twofold, upper and lower. Hence you will not find this full spelling with Jod except in books written around or under the Babylonian captivity, for example Jer. 18.26; 1 Chron. 3.5; 2 Chron. 25.1; 1 Chron. 26.5; Esth. 2.6. The punctuators, however, so that the name of the city would be the same everywhere, the one in use in their own age, supplied the same vowels everywhere. Nor do I think this is the only case in whose pointing they gave something to the usage and pronunciation of their own age.

units.la: Addo amplius, hoc nomen cum ה paragog. quinquies occurrere, & quidem quater sine Jod, [Hebrew: ירושלמה] quod legunt jam [Hebrew: ליַמרה] olim [Hebrew: למרה] At semel cum Jod, [Hebrew: לִירָמֹה] sed in quo libro? eodem Chronicorum. vid. 2. Chron. 32. 9. Caetera quatuor invenies 1. Reg. 10. 2.
units.tr: I add further that this name, with paragogic ה, occurs five times, and indeed four times without Jod, [ירושלמה], which they now read [ליַמרה] and formerly [למרה]. But once with Jod, [לִירָמֹה]. In what book? In the same book of Chronicles: see 2 Chron. 32.9. You will find the other four at 1 Kings 10.2.

units.la: 2. Reg. 9. 28. Jesa. 36. 2. Jez. 8. 3. Quin & ex illis locis, ubi Jod adest, firmiter concludi haec pronuntiatio non potest, quasi ea scriptorum istorum saeculo usitata fuerit. potuit enim illud vel vocalem E indicasse, vel in (") quievisse.
units.tr: 2 Kings 9.28; Isa. 36.2; Jer. 8.3. Nor can it be firmly concluded from those places where Jod is present that this pronunciation was in use in the age of those writers. For it may have indicated the vowel E, or it may have rested in (").

units.la: XXVII. Objeƈt. 2.
units.tr: XXVII. Objection 2.

units.la: Periculosam esse hanc confessionem, eaque plus nimio Adversariis concedi, qui fontes corruptos esse semper clamarunt. Resp. a A veritate nullum metuendum veritati periculum. Verum vero semper consonat & manum praebet, nunquam repugnat aut officit. Non ideo obruenda veritas, quod perversi homines ea abuti conantur. Fieri aliquando potest, ut alicujus veritatis, quae sine periculo ignorari potest, cognitio, hominum malitia turbas det. Tum prudentia deputari debet, si ea nondum cognita silentio prematur. At nunquam fas est, veritatem jam in lucem protractam impugnare, aut bona intentione ei tenebras offundere. In id potius incumbendum est, ut hostem veritate abutentem solide refellamus. Et quid quaeso hic periculi? An inter omnes illas varietates vel unica est, unde Christianae fidei analogiae vel pietati ullum detrimentum metui possit? Et, unde quaeso, periculum metuimus fontibus, ut non semper in Ecclesia maneant authenticae tabulae? An aliunde quam a vulgata Latina, ejusque proxeneta Rom. Ecclesia? Atqui haec rivalis nihil obtinebit. habeant fontes manipulum unum aut alterum variarum lectionum : vulgata, antiquitate cum fontibus neutiquam comparanda, habet plau-stra. Si solas Editiones Sixti V. & Clem. VIII. (fuit autem inter eas unius tantum biennii intervallum) conferas, invenies in iis ultra aliquot millia variarum lectionum. Multis in locis Interpres vulg. minus probabilem textus Ebraei lectionem interpretatus est. Hæret ergo in eodem luto, ut nihil jam dicam de manifestis & impiis locorum aliquot in vulg. versione corruptionibus, quarum aliquot alibi deteximus. An propter unum alterumve nævum auferetur palma pulcerrimæ virgini & dabitur alteri, quæ toto corpore deformis est? certe cavebunt prudentiores pontificii Ebraicam veritatem hac parte oppugnare eadem enim operâ contra vulg. disputarent.
units.tr: This confession is dangerous, and it concedes far too much to the adversaries, who have always cried out that the sources are corrupt. Answer: Truth has no danger to fear from truth. Truth always agrees with itself and lends a hand; it never opposes or hinders. Truth should not be overwhelmed because perverse men try to abuse it. It can sometimes happen that knowledge of some truth, which could be left unknown without danger, causes disturbances through human malice. Then prudence should be counted on, if that truth, not yet known, is kept under silence. But it is never right to attack a truth already brought into the light, or to cast darkness over it with a good intention. Rather, the effort should go into refuting solidly the enemy who abuses the truth. And what danger, I ask, is there here? Among all those variants, is there a single one from which any harm to the analogy of the Christian faith or to piety could be feared? And from what, I ask, do we fear danger to the sources, that authentic records may not always remain in the Church? Or from anything other than the Latin Vulgate and its agent, the Roman Church? Yet this rival will achieve nothing. Let the sources have one or another handful of variant readings; the Vulgate, in no way comparable with the sources in antiquity, has wagonloads. If you compare only the editions of Sixtus V and Clement VIII (there was an interval of only two years between them), you will find in them more than several thousand variant readings. In many places the Vulgate translator rendered a less probable reading of the Hebrew text. He therefore sticks in the same mire, not to mention the manifest and impious corruptions of passages in the Vulgate version, some of which we have exposed elsewhere. Will the palm be taken from the most beautiful virgin because of one blemish or another and given to a woman who is deformed in her whole body? Surely the more prudent Papists will take care not to attack the Hebrew truth in this respect, for by the same effort they would be arguing against the Vulgate.

units.la: XXVIII. Objeƈt. 3. Non est credibile Deum passurum fuisse, Vetus Test. tot locis corrumpi. Ref. Si ex paucis illis lectionum varietatibus (dico paucis, pro tanta librorum istorum antiquitate, & gentis Judaicæ variis & asperrimis calamitatibus & dispersionibus) disputabimus, textum Ebræum esse corruptum, quid fiet Novo, in cujus libros, & mole, & numero & antiquitate cum V. Test. neutiquam comparandos, tam paucis annis, Varietates numero longè plures, eæque non solum circa singulares literas, sed & voces integras, hemistichia, versus, irrepsere. Credemusne Vetus Testamentum Deo magis curæ fuisse quam novum; cætera quæ hic sequebantur, invenies p. 13: nos ; ut charta parceremus noluimus hic eadem iterare.]
units.tr: XXVIII. Objection 3. It is not credible that God would have allowed the Old Testament to be corrupted in so many places. Reply: If we argue from those few variant readings (I say few, given the great antiquity of those books and the various and very harsh calamities and dispersions of the Jewish people) that the Hebrew text is corrupt, what will happen to the New Testament? Its books, in bulk, number and antiquity, are by no means comparable with the Old, and within so few years variants far more numerous have crept into them, and these not only concerning single letters but whole words, half-verses and verses. Shall we believe the Old Testament was more a concern to God than the New? What followed here you will find on p. 13; we did not wish to repeat the same things here, to save paper.

units.la: XXIX. Objeƈt. 4. Sic deflorari laudem religiosæ Bibliorum conservationis, quam non solum Patres & nostri, sed &Pontificii doƈtiores Judæis tribuunt. Resp. Manet illis debita laus, quod sacrum illud depositum non corruperint. Quod verò eorum librarii in quibusdam locis subinde lapsi sint, temporis longitudo, exiliorum multitudo & duratio, calamitates variæ & asperæ, librorum multitudo facile excusaverint, præsertim si conferamus cum istis, librorum N. Test. eorumque vocabulis non destitutorum, paucitatem, temporis, quo variæ Lectiones in id irrepsere, brevitatem, & variarum lectionum multitudinem. Magnam verò & in excessu peccantem eorum religionem in eo cernere est, quod in textu nihil mutare, imò ne literam quiquidem ad eum addere vel de eo detrahere ausi fuerint. Si quid mutandum, addendum, vel detrahendum judicârunt, id in margine fecerunt, vocalium appositione vel detractione variam lectionem in margine collocatam solummodò innuentes, in quo se non peccasse arbitrati sunt, cum textum vocalibus nudum haberent.
units.tr: XXIX. Objection 4. In this way the praise of the religious preservation of the Bibles, which not only our writers and the Fathers but also the more learned Papists ascribe to the Jews, is undermined. Reply: They keep the praise due to them, for they did not corrupt that sacred deposit. That their copyists sometimes slipped in certain places can easily be excused by the length of time, the multitude and duration of the exiles, the various and harsh calamities, and the number of the books; this is especially so if we compare the small number of New Testament books, which are not lacking in words, with the brevity of the time in which the variants crept in, and the multitude of those variants. Their religion, however, which sinned by excess, is seen in this: that they did not dare to change anything in the text, nor even to add or take away a single letter. If they judged that something should be changed, added or removed, they did it in the margin, merely indicating by the addition or removal of vowels the variant reading placed in the margin. In this they thought they were not sinning, since they had the text bare of vowels.

units.la: XXX. Object. 5. Tot jam annis à Masoretharum temporibus Judæi in exilio vixërunt, variis calamitatibus obnoxii, & tamen Biblia conservarunt incorrupta. Quod si variæ Lectiones ex mendosâ descriptione & temporum calamitate ortæ sint, oportuit numerum earum ab eo tempore fuisse auctum. At hoc non est factum. Resp. Quod tot jam sæculis numerus variarum lectionum non increverit, variæ causæ sunt. 1. Est utilissimus ille Masoræ thesaurus, quam Sepem Legis non immeritò vocant Ebræi. 2. Quod postremis his temporibus majorem curam gesserint conservandi textus, quam olim sub Regibus aut captivitate, cum tam proclives ad idololatriam essent. Vis ne ejus rei habere specimen? adi 2. Reg. 22. & videbis sub Josiâ præter unicum illud authenticum legis exemplar, multis annis non visum, imò quod an in rerum natura esset, nesciebant, nullum aliud in tota civitate Jerusalem fuisse. Videbis illic Legis divinæ lectionem Regibus, sacerdotibus & scribis omnino peregrinam & ad admirationem usque obsoletam visam fuisse. Melioribus autem temporibus sola ferè Lex Mosis versabatur, ac in pretio erat, ut & in hunc usque diem apud Judæos observare licet, ubi cætera Vet. Testamenti propemodum jacent. quæ causa est, quod ea à mendis melius præservata fuerit. Notat Elias Levita, ex omnibus 848. variis lect. in lege tantum occurrere 95. in Prophetis 454. in hagiographis 329. Miratur Elias, & dicit sibi causas esse incognitas, cur tam paucæ in Lege reperiantur, inter quas 21. sunt circa vocum עשר quas si demas, remanent tantùm 44. cùm in solo Josua, qui vix decimam partem legis, habet, sint 33. & in liberis Samuelis 133. Quin illic nulla vox redundans aut deficiens (sicuti in aliis libris) occurrit 3. Nec omnino verum est, post Masorethanum labores nullas varietates repertas. Quid enim sibi volunt illæ notæ in Venetis magnis, Buxtorf. & Interlin. Jer. 14. 14. item 22. 2. & alibi, variam lectionem non per ף id est, Keri, sed per כ id est, codex alius, vel כּוּ id est liber alius, notarunt. Annon D. Junius in suis annotat. discrepantes lectiones alias à Masorethicis ex antiquissimo Cod. Heidelbergensi notavit 2. Chr. 26. 5. & 35. 3? Annoninter varias Editiones varia insuper discrepantia in vocalibus & accentibus, quam nos suis quoque locis in Coronide nostra annotavimus? Quò referes dissensum orientalium & occidentalium, quam Biblia Veneta in fine Masorae, & ex ea cl. Drusius in libro de recta Lect. exhibent?
units.tr: XXX. Objection 5. For so many years since the time of the Masoretes the Jews have lived in exile, subject to various calamities, and yet they have preserved the Bibles uncorrupted. If the variant readings arose from faulty copying and the calamities of the times, their number ought to have increased since then. But this has not happened. Reply: That the number of variant readings has not grown over so many centuries has several causes. 1. There is that most useful treasury of the Masora, which the Hebrews not undeservedly call a hedge of the Law. 2. In these latter times they took greater care to preserve the text than they did formerly under kings or in captivity, when they were so prone to idolatry. Do you want a specimen of this? Go to 2 Kings 22 and you will see that under Josiah, besides that single authentic copy of the law, which had not been seen for many years, and whose very existence they did not know, there was no other in the whole city of Jerusalem. You will see there that the reading of the divine law seemed utterly foreign to kings, priests and scribes, and almost obsolete to the point of astonishment. In better times, however, the Law of Moses alone was in common use and held in esteem, as can still be observed among the Jews to this day, where the rest of the Old Testament lies almost neglected. This is why the Law was better preserved from errors. Elias Levita notes that of the 848 variant readings, only 95 occur in the Law, 454 in the Prophets and 329 in the Hagiographa. Elias marvels at this and says the causes are unknown to him, why so few are found in the Law; among these, 21 concern the word [עשר], and if you remove these, only 44 remain. Yet in Joshua alone, which has barely a tenth of the Law, there are 33, and in the books of Samuel 133. Moreover, no superfluous or deficient word occurs there, as in other books. Nor is it altogether true that no variants were found after the labours of the Masoretes. For what do those marks mean in the large Venice Bibles, in Buxtorf and in the Interlinear, at Jer. 14.14, likewise 22.2 and elsewhere, which note a variant reading not by ף, that is Keri, but by כ, that is another codex, or by כּוּ, that is another book? Did not Dr. Junius, in his annotations, note readings differing from the Masoretic ones from the most ancient Heidelberg codex, at 2 Chron. 26.5 and 35.3? Did we not also note, among various editions, further discrepancies in the vowels and accents, which we noted in their places in our Coronis? To what will you refer the disagreement between the Oriental and Occidental [texts], which the Venice Bibles give at the end of the Masora, and which the distinguished Drusius sets out from it in his book on the correct reading?

units.la: XXXI. Atque hæc præcipua sunt quæ pro sententiâ illa vulgò afferri solent, quæ an satis valida sint docti judicent. Ego hæc Reformatarum Ecclesiarum judicio & censuræ subjicio, neutiquam tergiversaturus ea retractare, si quis certius & verius aliquid ostenderit. Mihi illud fuit propositum juventutem à talium admiratione, aliosque à curiosâ & supervacanea indagatione ad meditationem & piam considerationem eorum quæ revelata sunt, revocare.
units.tr: XXXI. These are the chief arguments usually brought forward for that opinion, and learned men may judge whether they are strong enough. I submit these things to the judgment and censure of the Reformed Churches, and I will by no means shrink from retracting them if anyone shows something more certain and true. My purpose was to call young people away from admiring such things, and others from curious and superfluous inquiry, back to meditation and pious consideration of what has been revealed.

units.la: Ps. XXIV. Super maria fundavit eam] Vetus fuit opinio, terram perinde atque lignum aut navem innatare aquæ, quam sententiam Thaleti Milesio tribuit Aristoteles, de cælo lib. 3. 13. quam post Aristotelem etiam Seneca confutavit, Natur. quæst. 3. 13. eadem fuit sententia Procopii comm. in Genes. 1. cui firmandæ adduxit hunc ipsum locum. Verba ejus pag. mihi 19. hæc sunt, Quod autem universa terra in aquis subsistat, nec ulla sit pars ejus, quæ infra nos sita est, aquis vacua & denudata, omnibus notum reor. Nam sic docet Scriptura, Qui expandit terram super aquas, & iterum, Quia ipse super maria fundavit eam, Hinc necessario coactus fuit negare Antipodas hoc est, in altero hemisphærio vivere homines quia adversa nobis urgeant vestigia, quam sententiam aliis etiam insuper incommodis pressit, Ita enim pergit, Nec decet ut credamus, aliquam terram infra nos coli, nostro orbi oppositam. Nam si Antipodes forent, certe Christus, eo quoque profectus esset, & catera qua pertinent ad salutem humani generis, ibi perfecisset. Adam prima nostri generis origo, serpens, qui humanum genus dolo circumvenit, nimirum & diluvium penes oppositam regionem extitissent. In eodem errore versati sunt Victor Antiochenus in Marcum, August. de civ. Dei xvi. 9. Lactant. Institut. 3, 24. verba Augustini, Quod vero & Antipodes esse fabulan-
units.tr: Ps. XXIV. Super maria fundavit eam] There was an old opinion that the earth floats on water just as a piece of wood or a ship does. Aristotle, On the Heavens 3.13, attributes this view to Thales of Miletus, and after Aristotle Seneca refuted it, Natural Questions 3.13. The same view was held by Procopius, in his commentary on Genesis 1, who adduced this very passage to confirm it. His words, on page 19 of my edition, are: "That the whole earth rests upon the waters, and that no part of it beneath us is bare and uncovered by water, I think is known to all. For Scripture teaches thus: He who spreads out the earth above the waters; and again, For he has founded it upon the seas." Hence he was necessarily compelled to deny the Antipodes, that is, that men live in the other hemisphere, since their opposed feet press against ours. He pressed this opinion with other inconveniences as well. He goes on: "Nor is it fitting that we believe any land lies beneath us, opposite to our world. For if there were Antipodes, surely Christ would have gone there too and accomplished there the other things which pertain to the salvation of the human race. Adam, the first origin of our race, and the serpent, who deceived the human race by guile, and indeed the flood, would have been present in the opposite region." The same error was held by Victor of Antioch in his commentary on Mark, and by Augustine, On the City of God 16.9, and Lactantius, Institutes 3.24. The words of Augustine are: "That the Antipodes are a fable must by no means be believed. Nor do those who assert it claim to have learned it from any historical knowledge, but they conjecture it as if by reasoning, etc." (Quod vero & Antipodes esse fabulan-)

units.la: Psalm. 136. Psalm. 24. tur, nulla ratione credendum est. Neque hoc ulla historica cognitione se didicisse affirmant, sed quasi ratiocinando conjectant, &c. Nec attendunt etiamsi figura rotunda & conglobata mundus esse credatur, sive aliqua ratione monstretur, non tamen esse consequens, ut etiam ab illa parte ex aquarum congerie nuda sit terra. Et paulo post, nimis absurdum est, ut dicatur aliquos homines ex hac in illam partem, Oceani immensitate trajecta, navigare, ac peruenire potuisse, ut etiam illic ex uno illo primo homine genus istitueretur humanum. Ubi Vives, Videbat homo acutissimus (Augustinus) si concederetur, aditum nulli eorum, qui hanc incolimus Borealem fasciam temperatam, ad australes illos patere, ut Cicero jam magnique authores praejudicaverant, sequi necessario, illos de genere Adae non esse, maluit ergo illud negare, quam argumento premi tam molesto & tot authoritatibus munito. Haec Vives. Verba Lactantii, Quid illi qui esse contrarios vestigiis nostris Antipodas putant, num aliquid loquuntur? aut est quisquam tam ineptus, qui credat esse homines, quorum vestigia sint superiora quam capita? aut ibi, quae apud nos jacent, inversa pendere? fruges & arbores deorsum versus crescere? pluvias & nives & grandinem sursum versus cadere in terram? Et miratur aliquis, hortos pensiles inter septem mira narrari cum philosophi & agros & maria & urbes pensiles faciant, &c. Ad quod caput vide notas Xysti Betuleii, & in iis censuram Joachi. Vadiani. Sed quid Lactantium. August. Procopium & caeteros istos minorum gentium Deos memoro; Zacharias Papa, Stephani II. decessor, in eodem haesit luto. Narrat Joannes Aventinus, Annalium Bojorum lib. 3. Vergilium Juvanensium Episcopum, virum in Mathematicis disciplinis praeclare versatum, esse Antipodas, eumque hoc nomine a Bonifacio Germaniae Apostolo postulatum, tanquam qui impia dogmata assereret, Causam devolutam ad Zachariam Papam. Quid ille? Zacharias, verba Aventini, legatos cum mandatis & literis ad Vtilonem (Bojorum regulum) ire jubet, partes suas Bonifacio commendat, Vergilium philosophum (si sacerdos sit, inquit, nescio) a templo Dei & Ecclesia depellito, sacerdotio in concilio abdicato, si illam perversam doctrinam fuerit confessus. Sidonio quoque & Vergilio literas comminatorias scripsit Romanus Episcopus, postulavitque ut Bonifacio obsequantur. Insuper regulo Bojorum denuntiatum est, ut Vergilium Romam mittat, ubi rationem reddat, ac a Pontifice Rom. examine comprobetur. An ergo pontifex, in cujus pectoris scrinio omnes sapientiæ thesauri absconditi sunt, ignoravit, quod pueri nostri hodie norunt? Sed redeamus ad locum Psalmi. Eum contulerunt veteres cum aliis, Psal. 104. 5. Qui sundauit terram super bases suas. Et Psal. Lxxv. 4. Ego confirmavi columnas ejus. Quæ tamen verba melius ita accipiuntur, ut sint verba Davidis, quibus promittat se, ubi plenum regnum fuerit adeptus, justissime illud administraturum, & constituturum justos gubernatores, quos merito columnas regni appellaveris, vel potius se religionem & justitiam, primarias Reip. columnas, restauratorum. Liquefacta est terra, inquit, & omnes habitatores ejus, (Miserrimus est Reip status) Ego vero aptabo (enallage temporum) columnas ejus Vide Jun.Pisc.Genev.Deod. Contulerunt eundem locum cum Ps. cxxxvi.6. qui expandit terram super aquas. Ergo ne aquæ bases terræ sunt? Illud ex locorum collatione non eviceris. Alibi dicitur, qui suspendit terram super nihilo, [Hebrew: על בלימה] Job. 26.7. Bene dixit, suspendit, namque ut canit Ovidius vi. fastorum,
units.tr: Psalm 136. Psalm 24. "tur, nulla ratione credendum est. Neque hoc ulla historica cognitione se didicisse affirmant, sed quasi ratiocinando conjectant, etc." They do not notice that even if the world is believed to be round and globed, or is shown to be so by some argument, it does not follow that the earth on that side is also bare of the mass of waters. And a little later: "It is too absurd to say that some men could have crossed from this part to that, through the immensity of the ocean, and arrived there, so that the human race might have been founded there too from that one first man." Here Vives comments: "That most acute man (Augustine) saw that if it were granted that there was no access for any of us who inhabit this temperate northern zone to those southern regions, as Cicero and other great authorities had already assumed, it would necessarily follow that those people were not of the race of Adam. He therefore preferred to deny it rather than be pressed by so troublesome an argument, backed by so many authorities." So Vives. The words of Lactantius are: "What do those say who think that Antipodes exist, with their feet opposed to ours? Do they say anything at all? Is there anyone so foolish as to believe that there are men whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that the things that lie with us hang upside down there? That fruits and trees grow downward, and rains, snows and hail fall upward onto the earth? And someone marvels that hanging gardens are reported among the seven wonders, when philosophers make even fields, seas and cities hang, etc." On this chapter see the notes of Xystus Betuleius, and in them the criticism of Joachim Vadianus. But why do I mention Lactantius, Augustine, Procopius and those others of the lesser gods? Zacharias, the Pope and predecessor of Stephen II, stuck fast in the same mud. Johannes Aventinus relates, in the third book of his Annals of the Boii, that Virgil, bishop of the Juvavians, a man very distinguished in mathematical disciplines, asserted that there are Antipodes, and that on this account he was accused by Boniface, the Apostle of Germany, as one who maintained impious dogmas, and the case was referred to Pope Zacharias. What did he do? Aventinus' words: "Zacharias ordered envoys to go with mandates and letters to Utilo, the petty king of the Boii, and commended his own cause to Boniface: that Virgil, if he is a priest (he says, I do not know), should be driven from the temple of God and the Church, and deprived of the priesthood in council, if he persisted in that perverse doctrine." And the Roman bishop wrote threatening letters to Sidonius and Virgil as well, and demanded that they obey Boniface. Moreover, it was announced to the petty king of the Boii that he should send Virgil to Rome, where he would give an account and be examined and approved by the Roman Pontiff. Was the pontiff, then, in whose breast all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, ignorant of what our boys know today? But let us return to the psalm. The ancients compared it with other passages: Ps. 104:5, "Who founded the earth upon its bases," and Ps. 75:4, "I have strengthened its pillars." These words are better taken as the words of David, by which he promises that, when he has obtained the full kingdom, he will administer it most justly and appoint righteous governors, whom you may rightly call the pillars of the kingdom; or rather, he promises to restore religion and justice, the chief pillars of the commonwealth. "The earth is melted," he says, "and all its inhabitants" (a most wretched state of the commonwealth), "but I will set up its pillars" (a change of tenses). See Junius, Piscator, Genevan and Diodati. They also compared the same passage with Ps. 136:6, "who spreads out the earth above the waters." Are the waters then the bases of the earth? This you will not prove from a comparison of passages. Elsewhere it is said, "who hangs the earth upon nothing," [על בלימה] Job 26:7. He said well "hangs," for as Ovid sings in the sixth book of the Fasti,

units.la: Quod autem vulgo reddunt, super nihilo, cl. Fullerus putabat, vocem Ebraeam non esse conflatam ex [Hebrew: כלי & מה] nihil quicquam, sed nomen formæ [Hebrew: נגינה] à [Hebrew: כלם] constringere, φιμῶν, ἀγξαι, instar suffocantis arcte constringere, quasi dicas, ἀγκτήρ, seu fibulam & vinculum illud validissimum, quo undique constricta tenetur terra, ne qua loco suo moveri possit. At quid hoc aliud est quam vis illa ἰσχυρότητα ηεί ἀκινησίας divinitus insita & per totum Telluris globum disseminata? Hæc Fullerus. Cum autem hæc attractrix & ut sic dicam constrictrix virtus ex centro terrestris globi videatur emanare, eo enim omnes partes sua gravitate nituntur, videndum, annon commode per centrum vox [Hebrew: בלימה] exponi possit. Atque ita idem dixerit Job, quod David Psal. 104. Fundavit terram super [Hebrew: מכונתיה] bases ejus, quomodo vocem [Hebrew: מכונות] Lxx. Jer. 52.17. reddidere. Aquila & Symm. referente Chrysost. exposit. in hunc Psalmum, ἐπὶ τῆς ἕδρας αὐτῆς. Ita enim primitus scriptum putat Fullerus, super sedes ejus, bases ejus. Βάσις enim teste Hesychio est σήμεγμα, ἕδρα, βάσις, stabilimentum, firma sedes, status, quies. Ita [Hebrew: כן] est ἰσχάζειν. LXX. sententiam magis quam verba exprimentes, Ὅτι τὰ ἀσφάλεια αὐτῆς, super firmitatem ejus, .validissimam scilicet & quam maxime admirandam, si pluralem pro singulari cum aliqua auxesi placet accipere, cum tamen sæpe per simplicem enallagen numeri illi commutentur. Aut utitur plurali numero, quia populariter loquitur. Solent enim magnæ machinæ multis fulcris & basibus sustentari. Istam vero Domini Fulleri interpretationem sic amplector ut priscam & receptam vocis בלימה interpretationem non rejiciam. Neque etiam vel istæ inter se pugnant, vel nova illa Davidi adversatur. Si enim extra globum terrestrem imus, nihil est corporeum, super quo ille suspensus vel fundatus sit. Nihil omnino est, quod sustineat terram extra terram præter creatorem. Hùc ergo spectaverit Job. David vero, ad illud stabilimentum, quod ipsi terræ indidit Deus, respexerit. Pisc. ad locum Jobi, super nihilum, id est super centrum mundi, quod revera nihil est. Terra enim circa centrum in æquilibrio pendet, ponderibus librata suis, Deod. Ordinavit Deus, ut terra cum gravissimum elementum collocaretur in medio universi, non habens aliud stabilimentum præter propriam gravitatem, quam Deus ei indidit, vide Psal. 104. 5. Genev. Ille sustentat terram comme par des contrepoids en l'air. voies. Ps. 104. 5. id est tanquam per medium æquilibrii in aere, vide Ps. 105. 5. David Kimchius ad Ps. cix. 5. נתן בטבע הארץ להיותה יורדת והמקום השפל היא אמצעות הגלגל והנה הוא על מכוניה שלא המוט לעולם ועד כיאם תמוט לאחד משמה הצדרק תעלה hoc est, Deus hanc naturam indidit terræ, ut descendat. Locus autem infimus est medium sphæra (centrum.) Atque ita basibus suis niti dicitur, ut non dimoveatur in æternum. Nam si dimoveretur versus ullam latusex sex illis latetibus (hoc est, vel antrorsum vel retrorsum, vel sursum vel deorsum; vel dextrorsum vel sinistrorsum) jam ascenderet. Sed rursus nimium à loco Ps. xxiv. digressi sumus. Redeamus ergo ad eum ex hoc quoque diverticulo. Terra dici potest fundata super aquas variis modis, ut tamen inde non sequatur, globum istum terrestrem inferieri sui parte aquis innatare & proinde habitari non posse, aut ut utar verbis Euthymii, aquas toti terræ subjacere instar fundamenti, quam sententiam Chrysostomo adscribit. 1. enim potest sic intelligi, ut dicat eam fun-
units.tr: But as for what they commonly render "upon nothing," the learned Fuller thought that the Hebrew word is not compounded of [Hebrew: כלי & מה] "nothing whatever," but is a noun of the form [Hebrew: נגינה] derived from [Hebrew: כלם], meaning to constrict, to bind tight (φιμῶν, ἀγξαι), like something that squeezes tightly, as in suffocation; as if you said ἀγκτήρ, or a clasp, and that most powerful bond by which the earth is held constricted on every side, lest it be able to move from its place. But what is this other than that strength or immobility (ἰσχυρότητα ἢ ἀκινησίας), divinely implanted and spread through the whole globe of the earth? These are Fuller's words. Since, however, this attractive and, as I may call it, constrictive power seems to emanate from the center of the terrestrial globe, for all parts strive towards it by their weight, we must consider whether the word [Hebrew: בלימה] can fittingly be explained as "center." So Job would say the same thing that David says in Ps. 104: "He founded the earth upon its bases" [Hebrew: מכונתיה], as the Seventy rendered the word [Hebrew: מכונות] in Jer. 52:17. Aquila and Symmachus, as Chrysostom reports in his exposition of this psalm, have ἐπὶ τῆς ἕδρας αὐτῆς, "upon its seat." Fuller thinks that the original reading was, "upon its seats, its bases." For βάσις, according to Hesychius, is a support, a seat, a base, a firm foundation, a settled state, rest. Thus [Hebrew: כן] means ἰσχάζειν. The Seventy, rendering the sense rather than the words, have "Because its firm places (ἀσφάλεια)," that is, upon its firmness, most strong and most worthy of admiration, if one prefers to take the plural for the singular with some amplification, although these numbers are often interchanged by a simple enallage. Or the plural is used because he speaks popularly, for great machines are commonly supported by many props and bases. I embrace Fuller's interpretation, but in such a way that I do not reject the old and received interpretation of the word [Hebrew: בלימה]. Nor do these two contradict each other, or does the new one oppose David. For if we go outside the terrestrial globe, there is nothing corporeal on which it is suspended or founded. Nothing at all sustains the earth outside the earth except the Creator. Job therefore may have looked to this; David looked to the stability which God imparted to the earth itself. Piscator, on the passage in Job: "upon nothing, that is, upon the center of the world, which is really nothing. For the earth hangs in equilibrium about the center, balanced by its own weights." Diodati: "God ordained that the earth, being the heaviest element, should be placed in the middle of the universe, having no other stability than its own gravity, which God gave it; see Ps. 104:5." The Genevan note: "He sustains the earth" like counterweights in the air ("comme par des contrepoids en l'air"), that is, "as if through the middle point of balance in the air; see Ps. 105:5." David Kimchi on Ps. 104:5: [Hebrew: נתן בטבע הארץ להיותה יורדת והמקום השפל היא אמצעות הגלגל והנה הוא על מכוניה שלא המוט לעולם ועד כיאם תמוט לאחד משמה הצדרק תעלה]: "God put into the nature of the earth that it should descend, and the lowest place is the middle of the sphere (the center). So it is said to rest on its bases, so that it is not moved forever. For if it were moved toward any side of those six directions (that is, forward or backward, upward or downward, to the right or to the left), it would then rise." But again we have strayed too far from the place in Ps. 24. Let us therefore return to it from this digression too. The earth may be said to be founded upon the waters in various ways, yet it does not follow from this that the terrestrial globe floats by part of itself on the waters and so cannot be inhabited, or, to use the words of Euthymius, that the waters lie under the whole earth like a foundation, which he ascribes to Chrysostom. First, it can be understood in this way: that he says it is founded...

units.tr: ...all the treasures of wisdom lie hidden, was he ignorant of what our children know today? But let us return to the passage of the Psalm. The ancients compared it with other passages: Ps. 104. 5, Who laid the foundations of the earth upon its bases. And Ps. 75. 4, I have strengthened its pillars. These words, however, are better taken as the words of David, in which he promises that, once he has obtained the full kingdom, he will administer it most justly and set up upright governors, whom you may rightly call the pillars of the realm, or rather that he will restore religion and justice, the chief pillars of the commonwealth. The earth is melted, he says, and all its inhabitants (the condition of the commonwealth is most wretched). But I will set up (a change of tense) its pillars. See Junius, Piscator, the Geneva notes, Diodati. The ancients also compared the same place with Ps. 136. 6, who spread out the earth above the waters. Are the waters, then, the bases of the earth? This you will not establish from comparing passages. Elsewhere it is said, who hangs the earth upon nothing [עַל בְּלִימָה], Job 26. 7. Well said, hangs, for as Ovid sings in the sixth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Terra pilæ similis nullo fulcimine nixa,Aëre subjecto tam grave pendet onus.
units.tr: The earth, like a ball, rests on no support; it hangs, a heavy weight, in the air beneath.

units.la: Quod autem vulgo reddunt, super nihilo, cl. Fullerus putabat, vocem Ebræam non esse conflatam ex בל & מה / nihil quicquam, sed nomen formæ בְּלִימָה à בלם constringere, φιμῶν, ἀγξαι, instar suffocantis arcte constringere, quasi dicas, ἀγχτρεχ, seu fibulam & vinculum illud validissimum, quo undique constricta tenetur terra, ne qua loco suo moveri possit. At quid hoc aliud est quam vis illa ἐδραιότητ& κ) ἀκινησίας divinitus insita & per totum Telluris globum disseminata? Hæc Fullerus. Cum autem hæc attractrix & ut sic dicam constrictrix virtus ex centro terrestris globi videatur emanare, eo enim omnes partes sua gravitate nituntur, videndum, annon commode per centrum vox בְּלִימָה exponi possit. Atque ita idem dixerit Job, quod David Psal. 104. Fundavit terram super מְכוֹנָיו bases ejus, quomodo vocem מכונות Lxx. Jer. 52.17. reddidere. Aquila & Symm. referente Chrysost. expos. in hunc Psalmum, ἐδραι τῆς ἐδρας αὐτῆς. Ita enim primitus scriptum putat Fullerus, super sedes ejus, bases ejus. Βάσις enim teste Hesychio est στήριγμα, ἕδρα, στάσις, stabilimentum, firma sedes, status, quies. Ita כן est ἐδραίζεν. LXX. sententiam magis quam verba exprimentes, φάλαγα αὐτῆς, super firmitatem ejus, .validissimam scilicet & quam maxime admirandam, si pluralem pro singulari cum aliqua auxesi placet accipere, cum tamen saepe per simplicem enallagen numeri illi commutentur. Aut utitur plurali numero, quia populariter loquitur. Solent enim magnae machinae multis fulcris & basibus sustentari. Istam vero Domini Fulleri interpretationem sic amplector ut priscam & receptam vocis בליפה interpretationem non rejiciam. Neque etiam vel istae inter se pugnant, vel nova illa Davidi adversatur. Si enim extra globum terrestrem imus, nihil est corporeum, super quo iste suspensus vel fundatus sit. Nihil omnino est, quod sustineat terram extra terram praeter creatorem. Huc ergo spectaverit Job. David vero, ad illud stabilimentum, quod ipsi terrae indidit Deus, respexerit. Pisc. ad locum Jobi, super nihilum, id est super centrum mundi, quod revera nihil est. Terra enim circa centrum in aequilibrio pendet, ponderibus librata suis, Deod. Ordinavit Deus, ut terra cum gravissimum elementum collocaretur in medio universi, non habens aliud stabilimentum praeter propriam gravitatem, quam Deus ei indidit, vide Psal. 104. 5. Genev. Ille sustentat terram comme par des contrepoids en l'air. voies. Psc. 104. 5. id est tanquam per medium aequilibrii in aere, vide Psc. 105. 5. David Kimchius ad Psc. CIX. 5. hoc est, Deus hanc naturam indidit terrae, ut descendat. Locus autem infimus est medium sphaerae (centrum.) Atque ita basibus suis niti dicitur, ut non dimoveatur in aeternum. Nam si dimoveretur versus ullum latus ex sex istis lateribus (hoc est, vel antrorsum vel retrorsum, vel sursum vel deorsum, vel dextrorsum vel sinistrorsum) jam ascenderet. Sed rursus nimium a loco Psc. XXIV. digressi sumus. Redeamus ergo ad eum ex hoc quoque diverticulo. Terra dici potest fundata super aquas variis modis, ut tamen inde non sequatur, globum istum terrestrem inferiori sui parte aquis innatare & proinde habitari non posse, aut ut utar verbis Euthymii, aquas teti terrae subjacere instar fundamenti, quam sententiam Chrysostomo adscribit. I. enim potest sic intelligi, ut dicat eam fundatam super aquas, ratione quarundam partium. Euthymius ad hunc locum, Tu vero hoc non in universum intellige, Nam alioquin inferior esset aqua. Verum Moses inferiorem esse terram docuit. Unde manifestum est, hoc dictum esse respectu certa partis aquarum. In multis namque terra concavitatibus & cavernosis locis, subterfugiunt partes quadam maris, quas maria appellavit. De fluminibus apertissimum est, quod sub terra longo intervallo feruntur & tandem emergant. Admirandum vero est quomodo non confideant tanta terra pondera. Omnes enim montes in hujusmodi aquis stabiliti sunt, & tamen in his fundata permanet terra solo creatoris sui mandato contenta. Hæc Euthymius. Eadem mens fuit Piscatori, cujus hoc scholion est, His verbis innuit potentiam Dei, ut qui terram fundaverit super terram, fundamentum sc. minime solidum, firmum atque immobile. Porro aquas infra terram esse (non dicit globo terrestri substratas) aperte traditur in prac. 2. decalogi, aut quae in aquis infra terram, &c. Hæc Dominus Piscator. At per aquas illas commode satis intelligi etiam possunt aquæ, quæ in maris fluminumque profundo sunt. Fateor tamen, videri illic respicere Deum ad abyssum istam aquarum, cujus mentio Genes. VII. 11. & rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ. Ejusdem Piscat. scholion ad German. Biblia clarius est, super maria] id est eam partem aquarum quæ sub ter- ta fluunt.
units.tr: As for what is commonly rendered upon nothing, the distinguished Fuller thought that the Hebrew word is not compounded of בל and מה, nothing whatsoever, but is a noun of form derived from בלם, to restrain, to bind fast (φιμῶν, ἀγξαι), meaning to constrict tightly, like one choking, as if you said ἀγχτρεχ: a clasp and a very strong band by which the earth is held constricted on every side, so that it cannot be moved from its place. But what is this other than that force of firmness and immobility (ἑδραιότης καὶ ἀκινησία) implanted by God and spread through the whole globe of the earth? So Fuller. But since this attracting, or so to speak constricting, power seems to flow out from the centre of the terrestrial globe, for all parts strive toward it by their weight, we must consider whether the word בְּלִימָה can conveniently be explained as centre. And so Job would have said the same thing that David says in Ps. 104, He founded the earth upon מְכוֹנָיו [mekhonav] its bases, just as the Seventy rendered the word מכונות in Jer. 52. 17. Aquila and Symmachus, as Chrysostom reports in his exposition of this Psalm, render it ἕδραι τῆς ἕδρας αὐτῆς. For Fuller thinks this was originally written as upon its seats, its bases. For βάσις, according to Hesychius, is στήριγμα, ἕδρα, στάσις: a support, firm seat, standing, stability, rest. So כן is ἐδραίζειν [to make firm]. The Seventy, rendering the sense rather than the words, wrote φάλαγγα αὐτῆς, its firmness, most strong and indeed most admirable, if one prefers to take the plural for the singular with some amplification, although these are often exchanged by simple enallage of number. Or he uses the plural because he speaks popularly, for large machines are usually held up by many props and bases. I embrace Fuller's interpretation as such, yet I do not reject the old and received interpretation of the word בליפה [bəlimah]. Nor do these two conflict with each other, nor does that new interpretation oppose David. For if we go outside the terrestrial globe, there is nothing corporeal on which it could be suspended or founded. Nothing at all sustains the earth outside the earth except the Creator. Job therefore looked to this; David looked to the stability which God implanted in the earth itself. Piscator on Job: upon nothing, that is, upon the centre of the world, which is really nothing. For the earth hangs about the centre in equilibrium, balanced by its own weights. Diodati: God ordained that the earth, the heaviest element, should be placed in the middle of the universe, having no other stability than its own gravity, which God implanted in it; see Ps. 104. 5. Geneva: He sustains the earth as with counterweights in the air. Voies: that is, as through the middle of an equilibrium in the air; see Ps. 105. 5. David Kimchi on Ps. 109. 5: that is, God gave this nature to the earth, that it should descend. The lowest place is the middle of the sphere (the centre). And so it is said to rest on its bases, so that it is never moved.
