For if it were moved toward any one of those six sides (that is, forward or backward, upward or downward, to right or left), it would then rise. But again we have strayed too far from Ps. 24. Let us therefore return to it from this digression too. The earth can be said to be founded upon the waters in various ways, yet it does not follow from this that this terrestrial globe floats on the waters by its lower part and so cannot be inhabited, or, to use Euthymius's words, that the waters lie beneath the whole earth like a foundation, which opinion he ascribes to Chrysostom. For first, it can be understood thus: that it is founded upon the waters with respect to certain parts. Euthymius on this place: But you must not understand this in general, for otherwise the water would be lower. Moses, however, taught that the earth is lower. Hence it is plain that this is said with respect to a certain part of the waters. For in many hollows and cavernous places of the earth, parts of the sea sink away, which he called seas. As for rivers, it is quite clear that they run under the earth for a long distance and at last emerge. It is truly wonderful how so great a weight of earth does not sink. For all the mountains are established in such waters, and yet the earth remains founded upon them, content with the command of its Creator. So Euthymius. The same was the mind of Piscator, whose scholion this is: By these words he points to the power of God, who founded the earth upon the earth, a foundation by no means solid, firm and immovable. Moreover, that the waters are below the earth (he does not say laid under the terrestrial globe) is plainly taught in the second precept of the Decalogue, or what is in the waters below the earth, etc. So Dominus Piscator. But by those waters it can also quite fittingly be understood the waters which are in the depths of seas and rivers. I admit, however, that God seems there to look to that abyss of waters, mentioned in Gen. 7. 11, and all the fountains of the great deep were broken up. The scholion of the same Piscator on the German Bible is clearer: upon the seas: that is, that part of the waters which flows under the land.

units.la: II. Verba Davidis sic intelligi possunt, ut doceat Propheta, quisnam ab initio creationis aquae situs fuerit, quod sc. terrae aqua injaceat, & quasi custodiat & contineat. Hanc expositionem Euthymius tribuit B. Basilio, additque doctissimus Monachus, juxta quem sensum congruentius fortasse legendum esset, quod Graeca litera non denegat, Ipse in maribus fundavit eam, & in fluminibus praparavit eam. Haec Euthyminus. Quibus illud addo, nec Ebraeam literam istam expositionem reIpuere. Graeca ita habent, δηλ θαλασσων ετοιμασεν αύτον, και δηλ ποταμονων ητοιμασεν αύτον. Ubi obiter nota, ετοιμάζεν in lingua Hellenistica passim usurpari pro κατασκευάζεν. Ita Psal 93. 3. ετοιμασεν ο θεος σου, firmus est th. tuus. & 1. Mach. 1. η βασιλεία αύτου id est firmatum est, κατασταθείση, regnum ejus. Cujus rei causa petenda est ex ambiguo Ebraei כוכ quod & parationis & firmationis notionem habet. At dum vulgatus priorem illam parandi vel praeparandi passim expressit, multis locis tenebras offudit. Sed ut ad observationem Euthymii redeamus, respexit ad voculam שמים, cui in Ebraeo respondet על / Illa pro ב, hæc pro ב aliquando usurpatur, Math. 27. 19. ἐπὶ βήματος, in tribunali, quod Latini pro tribunali dicunt. ἐπὶ ξένης ἀναι, in peregrino solo esse, ἐπὶ τῆς γνώμης γίνεσθαι, in eadem esse sententia. De על fidem facit iste locus Jesa. 38. 20. על בֵּית יְהוָה in domo DOMINI. Ion. 3. על אַרְמָתִי in terra mea. Fundavit ergo terram in maribus & fluminibus quasi natantem; Oceano tanquam fascia quadam & zona præcinctam, vel ut loquitur Petrus, ἐξ ὕδατος ἐπὶ * διὰ ὕδατος σωτεσῶς αὖ. id est ex aqua & in aqua consistentem, 2. Petri III. 5. Eadem est interpretatio ἐπὶ ὕδατι, B. Theodoreti ad hunc l. quam amplexus & R Salomo est, nisi quod de terra Israel locum exponat, vII. maria, inquit. circumdant terram Israel, & quatuor flumina, ירדן וירמיך וקרפין ופונוד
units.tr: II. The words of David can be understood so that the Prophet teaches what the situation of the water was from the beginning of creation, namely that the water lies beneath the earth and, as it were, guards and holds it. Euthymius ascribes this exposition to St Basil, and the very learned monk adds: according to which sense it might perhaps more fittingly be read, as the Greek letter does not deny: He himself founded her in the seas, and in the rivers he prepared her. So Euthymius. To this I add that the Hebrew letter also does not reject this exposition. The Greek has: He prepared her among the seas, and among the rivers he prepared her [δηλ θαλασσων ετοιμασεν αὐτὸν, καὶ δηλ ποταμῶν ἡτοίμασεν αὐτόν]. Note in passing that ἑτοιμάζειν is commonly used in Hellenistic language for κατασκευάζειν. So in Ps. 93. 2, your throne is firm [ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεός σου], and in 1 Macc. 1. 3, that is, it was established [κατασταθείση], his kingdom. The cause of this must be sought in the ambiguous Hebrew כוכ [kun], which has the notion both of preparing and of establishing. But while the Vulgate has everywhere rendered the former sense of preparing or making ready, it has cast darkness over many places. But to return to Euthymius's observation: he looked to the little word שמים, to which in Hebrew corresponds על. The former (ב) is sometimes used for ἐν, the latter (על) for ἐπί. Matt. 27. 19, ἐπὶ βήματος, in the tribunal, which the Latins say pro tribunali; ἐπὶ ξένης εἶναι, to be in a foreign land; ἐπὶ τῆς γνώμης γίνεσθαι, to be of the same opinion. For על this place of Isaiah 38. 20 bears witness, in the house of the LORD [על בֵּית יְהוָה]; Jonah 3 in my land [על אַרְמָתִי]. Therefore he founded the earth in the seas and rivers, as it were floating, girded and encircled by Ocean as by a band or belt; or, as Peter says, consisting out of water and through water [ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι᾽ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα], 2 Pet. 3. 5. The same is the interpretation of ἐπὶ ὕδατι by St Theodoret on this passage, which Rabbi Solomon also embraces, except that he applies the place to the land of Israel: the seas, he says, surround the land of Israel, and four rivers, the Jordan [ירדן], the Yarmuk [ירמיך], the Karpin [קרפין] and the Ponud [ופונוד].

units.la: III. Et Ebraeum על & Græcum ἐπὶ exponi potest per juxta.
units.tr: III. The Hebrew על and the Greek ἐπὶ can be explained by juxta.

units.la: Pharao somniabat se stare על נְהָר ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ, Genef. 41. 1. Servus Abrahæ stabat ἐπὶ τῆς πηγῆς. Gen. 24. 13. sicut arbor plantata על פלגי מים Psal. 1. Hanc interpretationem secuti sunt Zanchius de operibus creat. 2. 5. Lutherus, Sa ad hunc locum, & meminit quoque Deod. & Drufius passim inculcat.
units.tr: Pharaoh dreamed that he stood by the river [על נְהָר; ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ], Gen. 41. 1. Abraham's servant stood by the well [ἐπὶ τῆς πηγῆς], Gen. 24. 13. like a tree planted by the streams of water [על פלגי מים], Ps. 1. Zanchius on the works of creation (2.5), Luther, and Sa on this passage follow this interpretation, and Deodati also mentions it; Drusius repeats it throughout.

units.la: IV. Et Ebraeum על / & Græcum ἐπὶ exponi potest per super, ut supereminentiam tantum denotet.
units.tr: IV. The Hebrew על and the Greek ἐπὶ can be explained by super, so that it denotes only superiority.

units.la: Latini inter super & supra sic distinguunt, ut super de contiguis. supra de superemincentibus sine contiguitate dicatur. Ex. gr. habeo manum super tabula, ut tangat. Belg. op. Supra tabulam, ut non tangat. Belg. boven. Ita distinguit Mercerus inter על & מעל / quorum illud (על) respondeat Latino super, hoc ὑπὲρ supra. Vide cl. Mercerum ad primum caput Geneseos. Sed scias illa passim confundi. Huc pertinet & observatio doctissimi August. Quæst. 132. in Genesin, ubi hæc leguntur, Hæc locutio si intelligatur, in Ps. 24. ubi scriptum est, Qui fundavit terram super aquam, non coguntur homines putare, sicut navem natare terram super aquam. Secundum enim hanc locutionem rectè intelligitur, quod altior sit terra quam aqua. Altius enim ab aquis sustollitur, ubi habitent terrena animalia. Hæc Aug. quem sequuntur Junius, Deod. Genebrardus, Bellarm. Rivetus, & ex vetestioribus Lyra, Carth. & Ebraeis præter alios etiam Aben Ezra & Kimchi. Vide eum ad
units.tr: Latin writers distinguish super and supra thus: super is used of things in contact, supra of things that rise above without contact. For example, I hold my hand super the table, so that it touches it (Dutch op); I hold it supra the table, so that it does not touch it (Dutch boven). Mercerus distinguishes in the same way between על and מעל, the former (על) corresponding to Latin super, the latter to ὑπὲρ, supra. See the learned Mercerus on the first chapter of Genesis. But you should know that these words are commonly confused. To this belongs also the observation of the most learned Augustine, Quaest. 132 on Genesis, where we read: If this expression is understood in Ps. 24, where it is written, "who founded the earth upon the waters," men are not forced to think that the earth floats on the water as a ship does. For according to this expression it is rightly understood that the earth is higher than the water. For it is raised higher above the waters, so that earthly animals may dwell there. Augustine is followed by Junius, Deodati, Genebrardus, Bellarmine, Rivetus, and among the older writers by Lyra, the Carthusians, and among the Hebrews, besides others, Aben Ezra and Kimchi. See him at

units.la: Vide & Iul. Toletan in Annotat. pag. 119. ad Pf. hunc & Psalm. cxxxvi. Dicit Deum mutasse naturam aquarum, qua terram alias operturæ essent. In principio creationis ita fuisse. At postea Deum congregasse aquas in propria receptacula, ut appareret arida quæ & animalibus præberet hospitium, & plantis daret locum. Hanc misericordiam durare in sæculum. In diluvio quidem aquas rursus effusas fuisse & operuisse terram, at illud tantum ad tempus fuisse, in pœnam improborum. Rediisse postea aquas ad priscas sedes, Deumque jurasse, se nunquam postea ad eundem modum diluvio in mundi incolas animadversurum. Quod ergo dicit, qui extendit terram supra aquas, hoc velle, שנתן שטחו על המים quod posuerit superficiem terræ supra aquas. Etiamsi vero aquæ altiores sint terra, tamen omnia ita ordinavit, ut terra videatur esse altior aquis, cavitq; ne eam operiant, S. S. E. & aquæ non transgrediuntur os ejus. Posuit enim arenam terminum mari, &c. Hæc discripsi liberiori calamo ex scholiis ejus ad Ps. 136. Lubet autem ipsa verba Kimchii adscribere, quæ ad Psal. 24. ויעם כי היא מתהלה לא נבראת כך אלא להיותה כלה התרת והמים · כי המים היו סובבים אותרה מכל צר כמו שהאויר סובב המים מכל צר והאש סובב האויר מכל צר, והנרה הארץ תהרת המים והאל צויה שתהיה מהיצרה אהרת מנולרה לשכרת היצורים בזה / Sensus est, à principio non ita creata est terra, sed ut tota esset inferior aquis. Aquæ enim circumdabant terram undequaque, sicuti etiamnum aër undequaque cingit aquam, & ignis rursus aërem. Ecce, terra erat sub aquis. At Deus jussit ut alterum dimidium nudaretur aquis, ut creatura imbi possent vivere.
units.tr: See also Julius Toletanus in his Annotations, p. 119, on this Psalm and on Ps. 136. He says that God changed the nature of the waters, which would otherwise have covered the earth. At the beginning of creation it was so; but afterwards God gathered the waters into their own receptacles, so that dry land might appear, which would offer a dwelling to animals and room for plants. This mercy lasts forever. In the Flood the waters were indeed poured out again and covered the earth, but that was only for a time, as a punishment on the wicked. Afterwards the waters returned to their old place, and God swore that he would never again punish the inhabitants of the world in the same way by a flood. So when he says, "who stretched out the earth above the waters" (על המים), he means that he placed the surface of the earth above the waters. Even though the waters are indeed higher than the earth, yet he arranged all things so that the earth appears higher than the waters, and he took care that they would not cover it: "the waters do not pass over its border." For he placed sand as a boundary for the sea, etc. I have written this down rather freely from his scholia on Ps. 136. But it is worth quoting Kimchi's own words, on Ps. 24: [ויעם כי היא מתהלה לא נבראת כך אלא להיותה כלה התרת והמים · כי המים היו סובבים אותרה מכל צר כמו שהאויר סובב המים מכל צר והאש סובב האויר מכל צר, והנרה הארץ תהרת המים והאל צויה שתהיה מהיצרה אהרת מנולרה לשכרת היצורים בזה] The meaning is: at the beginning the earth was not created in this way, but wholly beneath the waters. For the waters surrounded it on every side, just as air still surrounds water on every side, and fire surrounds air on every side. Behold, the earth was under the waters. But God commanded that the other half be laid bare of the waters, so that the creatures might live there.

units.la: Habes præcipuas interpretationes hujus loci, omnes satis commodas & sententiæ Procopianæ adversantes. Quarum illa, quam postremo loco exhibui, se præ aliis mihi probat. Sixtus Senensis quintam insuper suppeditat, exponendo על comparative, magis quam, præ, ꝗ d. fundavit terram magis quam maria, id est majorem firmitatem & stabilitatem terræ indidit quam mari & aquis. Probat autem hunc usum particulæ super tribus scripturæ locis, Ps 119. vers. 72. & 127. Cant. 4. 10. Ubi quidem in vulgato est eadem vocula super, at in Ebræo longe diversa, vid non על / sed ע / Vide quid sit ex Latinis concordantiis vel versionibus loca parallela adducere. Sæpe enim una vox vel phrasis respondet pluribus, in originali diversis. Si lubet aliam insuper audire, · producam Aben-Ezram, cujus ad hunc locum iste est commentarius, בדרך התולדת נבראה הארץ להיותה תהרת המים, וכהפץ השם יבש קצתרת והיא המחצה אשר מנולה על כן כי הוא על · ויאמר רי משה כי פירוש על כמו עם כמו ויבאו האנשים על הנשים hoc est, secundum viam natura creata est terra, ut esset sub aquis. At secundum voluntatem Dei explicata est pars ejus, vid. dimidia ejus pars, qua discooperta est. Ideo dicit, כי הוא על (sunt verba textus) Hæc est interpretatio quam nos quarto loco exhibuimus. Nunc audies novam.) Dixit autem R. Moses, על exponi posse per עם cum. sicuti Exo. 35. 22. & venerunt viri Cum mulieribus. Postea citat R. Bileamum, qui על exposuerit per juxta, quam sententiam loco3, propositum. Augustinus in comm. hic αὐτοπεράς & per terram, Ecclesiam: per maria fluctus hujus seculi intelligit.
units.tr: You have the principal interpretations of this passage, all fairly suitable, and all opposed to Procopius's view. Of these, the one I gave last seems to me better than the rest. Sixtus of Siena adds a fifth, explaining על comparatively, more than, rather than: "He founded the earth more than the seas," that is, he gave the earth greater firmness and stability than the sea and waters. He supports this use of the particle super with three passages of Scripture: Ps. 119:72, Ps. 127, and Cant. 4:10. But in these the Vulgate has the same little word super, while the Hebrew is quite different: not על but ע. See what can be learned from Latin concordances or versions when parallel passages are cited. For one word or phrase often corresponds to several different words in the original. If you like to hear another opinion, I will bring forward Aben Ezra, whose commentary on this passage is this: [בדרך התולדת נבראה הארץ להיותה תהרת המים, וכהפץ השם יבש קצתרת והיא המחצה אשר מנולה על כן כי הוא על · ויאמר רי משה כי פירוש על כמו עם כמו ויבאו האנשים על הנשים] that is, according to the course of nature the earth was created to be under the waters. But according to God's will part of it was made dry, namely its half, which was laid bare. Therefore he says "for he is on" (these are the words of the text). This is the interpretation which we gave in the fourth place. Now you will hear a new one. Rabbi Moses said that על can be explained by עם, with, as in Exod. 35:22, and the men came with the women. Afterwards he cites Rabbi Bileam, who explained על as juxta, near, which I put forward as the third opinion. Augustine in his commentary on this passage understands by the earth the Church, and by the seas the waves of this age.

units.la: Hic vero quæri solet ab Interpretibus, an mare sit altius terra. De hac quæstione vide Physicos, nominatim Keckermanum Phys. lib. 2. cap. ult. Conimbricenses, nec non Merulam in Cosinorgr. parte i. libro 3. Ego non pigrabor sententiam Kimchii adscribere. Sic ergo ille ad Ps. cvii. 23. Descendentes in mare navibus] אף על פי שהים צבוה על היבשה יקרא עובר·הים יורד לפי שהיבשה גבוה על שפת הים וכנגד השפה יקרא יורד hoc est, Quamvis mare sit altius arida, tamen qui navigaturus est dicitur descendere, quia arida altior est littore maris. Et ratione littoris dicitur descendere. Postea subjicit patris sui sententiam, qui existimabat vocem descendere hic adhibitam a Psalmographo, כנגד האניה שהיא עמוקה ויורד בה כמו שכתוב ויסצא אניה ויורד בה respectu navis, qua profunda est, in quam descenditur, S. S. E. & invenit navem — & descendit in eam, Jona 1. Hoc notandum duxi propter eos, qui hunc locum adversæ sententiæ stabiliendæ solent producere. Eadem invenies apud eundem ad Ps. 33. verf. 7. Qui congerit aquas maris tanquam tumulum. Claudam ubi illud addidero, figuram terræ esse σφαιροειδῆ, male probari ab eruditissimis quibusdam viris exillis Latinarum versionum locis, ubi terra Orbis appellatur. Namque in
units.tr: Here the interpreters often ask whether the sea is higher than the land. On this question see the natural philosophers, especially Keckermann, Physics, book 2, last chapter; the Conimbricenses; and Merula in his Cosmography, part 1, book 3. I shall not hesitate to quote Kimchi's view. On Ps. 107:23, "those who go down to the sea in ships," he says: [אף על פי שהים צבוה על היבשה יקרא עובר·הים יורד לפי שהיבשה גבוה על שפת הים וכנגד השפה יקרא יורד] Although the sea is higher than the dry land, yet one who is about to sail is said to go down, because the dry land is higher than the shore of the sea, and with respect to the shore he is said to go down. Afterwards he adds his father's opinion, who thought that the word go down, used here by the Psalmist, [כנגד האניה שהיא עמוקה ויורד בה כמו שכתוב ויסצא אניה ויורד בה] refers to the ship, which is deep and into which one goes down, as it is written, "he found a ship and went down into it," Jonah 1. I thought it worth noting this for those who are accustomed to cite this passage in support of the opposite view. You will find the same in the same author on Ps. 33:7, who gathers the waters of the sea as in a heap. I shall end here, once I have added that the spherical shape of the earth is wrongly proved by certain very learned men from those passages of the Latin versions where the earth is called the orb. For in

units.la: PPP omnibus locis, quæ citat N. N. Cofmogr. parte 1. lib. 3. cap. 13. in Ebræo est חבל / quæ vox nihil habet, quod orbicularem figuram significet.
units.tr: In all the places which N. N. cites in Cosmography, part 1, book 3, chapter 13, the Hebrew has [חבל] chebel, a word which has nothing to indicate a round figure.

units.la: Verf. 7. & 9. Attollite portas principes vestras.] Ita vulgatus ex Græco ἄρατε πύλας οἱ ἄρχοντες ὑμῶν. Quis hoc intelliget? Ebræa clara sunt, שְׂאוּ שְׁעָרִים רָאשֵׁיכֶם / Aquila ἄρατε πύλας τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑμῶν attollite o portæ capita vestra. Simplicissima interpretatio, ut per fictionem personæ portas templi jam designati jubeat attollere vertices, ut latior ingressus arcæ introducendæ fieret. Ita Lyra, Piscator & alii. Etiam Calvinus statuit, Davidem hic de futura templi structura concionari. Versio Græca est plane contorta. רָאשֵׁיכֶם principes vestras, Ut ut enim vox Ebræa רָאשִׁים accipiatur pro principibus, tamen affixum illud non poterat ad portas referri. Hoc non fugit Bellarminum, qui in comm. ista habet, vel in textu ipsorum (Lxx) pronomen affixum fuit nomini שערים non autem nomini ראשים quod significat principes: vel posse pronomen uni nomini affixum referri ad aliud nomen, quamvis rarissime & prater regulam. Hæc Bellarm. qui pro rarissime melius & verius substituisset nunquam. Nam quod ad alias locutiones attinet, quæ hic forte objici possent, mons sanctitatis mea, uxor adolescentiæ ejus, maritus adolescentiæ ejus, & similes, quæ dicuntur, pro, mons meus sanctus, uxor ejus adolescentula, maritus ejus adolescentulus, quomodo Colos. 1. dicitur filius delectionis suæ, id est filius suus delectus; alia ratio est, alia enim est syntaxis, vid. rectionis, & abstractā illa manifeste pro concretis positāfunt, unde resolutione ista facta, affixa, licet voci rectæ affigantur, quoad sensum tamen ad vocem regentem referri debent. Ex versione contorta interpretationes magis contortæ emanarunt. Alii per portas, cœli: & per principes, angelos utrobique intellexere. Alii portas inferni, & diabolos interpretati sunt, locumque ad descensum Christi localem retulerunt. Alii verf. 7. de portis inferni & diabolis, verf. vero 9. de portis cœli & angelis accepere. Vide Carthusianum, qui mira insuper ex Dionysio Areopagita de trib. angelorum quæstionibus memorat. Augustt. verf. 7. sic ἀναφέρεται, Quicunque principatum in hominibus quaritis, auferte, ne impediant aditus quos vos statuistis, cupiditatis & timoris. & verf. 9. Tollite portas etiam cœlestes principes vestri, quas habe-
units.tr: Vers. 7 and 9, "Lift up your gates, O princes." So the Vulgate, from the Greek ἄρατε πύλας οἱ ἄρχοντες ὑμῶν. Who can understand this? The Hebrew is clear: [שְׂאוּ שְׁעָרִים רָאשֵׁיכֶם]. Aquila has ἄρατε πύλας τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑμῶν, "lift up, O gates, your heads." The simplest interpretation is that, by a fiction of persona, the poet bids the gates of the already designated temple lift up their heads, so that the entrance for the ark to be brought in might be wider. So Lyra, Piscator, and others. Calvin also holds that David here speaks of the future building of the temple. The Greek version is plainly twisted. As for רָאשֵׁיכֶם, your princes: even if the Hebrew word רָאשִׁים is taken to mean princes, the suffix could not refer to the gates. Bellarmine did not miss this, and in his commentary he says: either in their text (the Septuagint) the pronoun attached to the word "gates" and not to the word "princes," which means "rulers"; or the pronoun, attached to one noun, can refer to another noun, though very rarely and against the rule. Bellarmine says "very rarely," when he ought to have said, more correctly and truly, never. For as to other expressions which might perhaps be objected here, such as my holy mountain, the wife of his youth, the husband of his youth, and similar ones, which mean my holy mountain, his young wife, her young husband, just as Col. 1 speaks of the son of his love, that is, his beloved son, the case is different: the construction is different, and those abstract nouns are clearly used for concrete ones. Hence, after that analysis, the suffixed words, although attached to the governed word, must in sense refer to the governing word. From the twisted version more twisted interpretations have arisen. Some understood by gates the gates of heaven, and by princes the angels, in both verses. Others interpreted the gates of hell and the devils, and referred the passage to Christ's local descent. Others took verse 7 to refer to the gates of hell and the devils, but verse 9 to the gates of heaven and the angels. See the Carthusian, who also recounts strange things from Dionysius the Areopagite on the questions about the three angels. Augustine on verse 7 renders it thus: Whoever among men seek to rule, take away what hinders the approaches which you have set up, of desire and fear. and on verse 9: Lift up also the heavenly princes, your gates, which you have

units.la: Lovan. doct. op u poorten ghy Princen. habetis in animis hominum, qui adorant militiam coeli. Lombardus ex Cassiod. Tollite] id est auferte ab animis vestris. Principes] Mundi & superstitiosi ut sunt hypocrisiarcha. portas vestras] id est mortis, quae a principe Diabolo posita sunt. Apud Thomam parte 3. qu. 39. art. 5. aliam interpretationem invenies, quae Chrysostomo tribuitur, Babtizato Christo, coeli tantum sunt ei aperti.
units.tr: Louvain doctor, "op u poorten ghy Princen" (lift up your gates, you princes): you have them in the minds of men, who worship the host of heaven. Lombard, from Cassiodorus: "Take away" means remove from your minds. "Princes" means the princes of the world and of superstition, such as the hypocrisiarchs. "Your gates" means the gates of death, which were set up by the prince, the Devil. In Thomas, part 3, q. 39, art. 5, you will find another interpretation, attributed to Chrysostom: after Christ was baptized, only the heavens were opened to him.

units.la: At postquam tyrannum vicit per crucem, quia non erant necessariae portae, coelo nunquam claudendo, non dicunt angeli, aperite portas (. jam enim erant apertae) sed tollite portas. Per quod dat intelligere Chrys. quod obstacula quibus prius obsistentibus, animae defunctorum ingredi non poterant coelos, sunt totaliter per passionem Christi ablata. Haec Thomas.
units.tr: But after he conquered the tyrant through the cross, since the gates were no longer needed, because heaven would never be closed again, the angels do not say "open the gates" (for they were already open) but "lift up the gates." By this, Chrysostom gives us to understand that the obstacles which had previously prevented the souls of the dead from entering heaven were wholly removed by the passion of Christ. So Thomas.

units.la: In expositione morali quae in Bibliis Lyrae, de ascensione B. Virginis locus exponitur atque illa verba & introibit rex gloriae, intelliguntur de Filio Dei, matri suae obsequium praestante. Nec immerito creditur, inquit, quod Filius per se totus festinus occurrit, eamque secum in throno gloriae collocavit. Aliam insuper explicationem invenies apud Ambrosium & ex eo apud Erasmum in Ecclesiaste lib. 3.
units.tr: In the moral exposition in Lyra's Bible, where the ascension of the Blessed Virgin is explained, the words and the King of glory shall come in are understood of the Son of God, who rendered obedience to his mother. "Nor is it without reason believed," he says, "that the Son himself hastened to meet her and seated her with himself on the throne of glory." You will find another explanation in Ambrose, and from him in Erasmus, in his Ecclesiastes, book 3.

units.la: Psal. XXV. 19. De necessitatibus meis eripe me] Ita rursus vulg. ex Graeco, ἐκ τῶν ἀνάγκων μου ἐξάγαγέ με. Ebraice, המצוקות / Pagn. & Sa, ex angustiis meis, Arias, ex coarctationibus meis educ me. Ἀνάγκη in lingua Hellenistica idem est quod θλῖψις, afflictio. Passim occurrit haec significatione non solum apud Lxx. sed & in novo foedere, Lucae 21. 23. erit autem ἀνάγκη μεγάλη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Sic & 2. Cor. vi. 4. & xii. 10. 1. Thess. 3. 17. Augustinus in comm. non ignoravit afflictiones hic denotari. Carthus. per necessitates intelligit indigentias corporales cibi, potus, somni, vestitus, &c. quibus anima frequenter a contemplatione divina abstrahitur. Bellarminus lib. v. de gratia & lib. arbitrio, cap. 8. §. 1. respondsurus ad primum argumentum Pelagianorum, hunc locum adducit ex Augustini libro de natura & gratia, cap. 66. neque improbat ejus interpretationem de necessitate peccandi. Verba Augustini non pigrabor adscribere, Quod autem ex vitiis natura, non ex conditione natura sit quaedam peccandi necessitas, audiat homo, atque ut eadem necessitas non sit, discat Deo dicere, De necessitatibus meis educ me. Haec si vulgatae versioni aptentur, speciem veri habent: at si Ebraeo textui, nihil magis alienum dici potuit. Idem Bell. in comment. per necessitates istas intelligit molestissimas concupiscentias, quae velimus nolimus nos vexant & aliquando in peccatum trahunt. Obiter 2. nota. I. vocem אנגק etiam in Tharg. Jonathanis, & Hierosol. passim eadem notione occurrere. Nec non in Syr. paraphrasi 2. Cor. vi. 5. II. in hac vocis ἀνάγκη significatione concurrere metonymiam & synecd. Necessitas est vis quaedam cogens. At cum pro afflictione usurpatur, significat rem adversam à sup. potestate impositam, quam praeter voluntatis naturalem inclinationem necesse habemus tolerare. Nec male August. ad hunc locum notat afflictiones vocari necessitates quod necesse sit eas usque ad finem tolerare, ut salvemur. Belgae quoque & Germani eodem modo voce noot utuntur, & Seneca videtur sic accepisse epistola XII. Malum est in necessitate vivere, sed in necessitate vivere necessitas nulla est. Ubi ludit in ambiguo vocis.
units.tr: Ps. 25:19, "Deliver me from my necessities." Again, the Vulgate follows the Greek, [ἐκ τῶν ἀνάγκων μου ἐξάγαγέ με]. The Hebrew is [המצוקות], which Pagninus and Sa render "from my straits," and Arias "lead me out of my constraints." In Hellenistic usage [ἀνάγκη] means the same as [θλῖψις], affliction. It occurs in this sense often, not only in the Septuagint but also in the New Testament: Luke 21:23, "there shall be great distress [ἀνάγκη μεγάλη] upon the earth." So also 2 Cor. 6:4 and 12:10, and 1 Thess. 3:17. Augustine, in his commentary, did not fail to see that afflictions are meant here. The Carthusian understands by "necessities" bodily needs of food, drink, sleep, clothing, and the like, by which the soul is often drawn away from contemplation of God. Bellarmine, in book 5 of On Grace and Free Will, ch. 8, §1, answering the first argument of the Pelagians, cites this place from Augustine's book On Nature and Grace, ch. 66, and does not disapprove of his interpretation as referring to the necessity of sinning. I will not hesitate to copy Augustine's words: "That there is a certain necessity of sinning which arises from vices, not from the condition of nature, let a man hear; and that this same necessity may not exist, let him learn to say to God, 'Deliver me from my necessities.'" If these words are fitted to the Vulgate version, they have an appearance of truth; but if they are fitted to the Hebrew text, nothing could be said that is more foreign to it. The same Bellarmine, in his commentary, understands by these necessities the most troublesome concupiscences, which vex us whether we wish it or not, and sometimes draw us into sin. In passing, note two things. First, the word [אנגק] also occurs in the same sense in Targum Jonathan and in the Jerusalem Targum, frequently, and in the Syriac paraphrase at 2 Cor. 6:5. Second, in this sense of [ἀνάγκη] both metonymy and synecdoche come together. Necessity is a certain compelling force. But when it is used for affliction, it signifies an adverse thing laid upon us by a higher power, which we are obliged to bear beyond our natural inclination of will. Augustine rightly notes at this place that afflictions are called necessities because they must be borne to the end, if we are to be saved. The Belgians and Germans likewise use the word noot in the same way, and Seneca seems to have understood it so in Epistle 12: "It is an evil to live in necessity, but to live in necessity is no necessity." There he plays on the ambiguity of the word.

units.la: Ps. XXIX. 1. Afferte Domino filii Dei: * afferte Domino filios arietum.] Ita vulg. ex LXX. ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱοὶ θεῷ, ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱὸς κριῶν. Pro duobus istis membris in Ebraeo tantum unum legitur, הָבוּ לַיהוָה בְּנֵי אֵילִים ad verbum, Date Domino filios fortium, Pagn. Arias, arietum. Synecd. generis. Prius quoque illud membrum, ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱοὶ θεῷ, in Hexaplis Origenis non comparuit. Fuit procul dubio vel glossema vel alterius interpretis versio, quae postea, ut factum est saepius, in textum irrepserit. Frustra ergo hic quaeritur, quomodo dicatur in Ebraeo filii Deorum? אֵלִים / Neque video quae necessitas interpretibus incubuerit ex filiis arietum fideles excusandi. August. Afferte Domino filios arietum id est vosmet ipsos quos per Euangelium duces gregum Apostoli genuerunt. Ergo filii arietum sunt filii spirituales Apostolorum. Cur Apostoli vocantur aretes? Hoc jam innuit August. Quia ut arietes lanigeri gregis, ita & Apostoli Christiani gregis duces fuere. Sed audi aliud mysterium. Lombardus in sua rhapsodia ad hunc Psalmum ex Cassiodoro & Alcuino sic inquit, Apostoli vocantur arietes, quia duobus cornibus id est utriusque testamenti authoritatibus praevaluerunt contra haereticos, & superstitiones & idola quasi dura fronte diruerunt. Inde est quod mitra pontificalis duo habeat cornua, quia omnis scriba doctus in regno caelorum de thesauro cordis sui profert nova (hoc est
units.tr: Ps. 29:1, "Bring to the Lord, you sons of God: * bring to the Lord the sons of rams." So the Vulgate, from the LXX: [ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱοὶ θεῷ, ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱὸς κριῶν]. For these two members the Hebrew has only one, [הָבוּ לַיהוָה בְּנֵי אֵילִים], word for word "Give to the Lord the sons of the mighty," as Pagninus has it; Arias has "of rams." It is a synecdoche of the genus. Moreover, that first member, [ἐνέγκατε κυρίῳ υἱοὶ θεῷ], did not appear in Origen's Hexapla. It was without doubt either a gloss or the version of another translator, which afterwards, as has often happened, crept into the text. It is therefore vain to ask here how it is said in Hebrew "sons of gods" [אֵלִים]. Nor do I see what necessity pressed on the translators to excuse the faithful from being "sons of rams." Augustine: "Bring to the Lord the sons of rams, that is, yourselves, whom the Apostles begot through the Gospel as leaders of the flock." So the sons of rams are the spiritual sons of the Apostles. Why are the Apostles called rams? Augustine already hints at this: just as rams lead the woolly flock, so the Apostles were the leaders of the Christian flock. But hear another mystery. Lombard, in his compilation on this Psalm, says, from Cassiodorus and Alcuin: "The Apostles are called rams, because with two horns, that is, the authority of both Testaments, they prevailed against heretics, and with a hard forehead they overthrew superstitions and idols. Hence the episcopal mitre has two horns, because every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from the treasure of his heart new things (that is, from the New Testament, which is the one horn) and old things (that is, from the Old Testament, which is denoted by the other horn)." So Lombard.

units.la: * Lerzen brengt aen der rammen kinderen. ex novo testamento, quod est unum cornu) & vetera. (hoc est ex veteri test. & denotatur per alterum cornu.) Hæc Lomb. Jam didicisti Lector, cur Episcoporum mitræ bicornes sint.
units.tr: * "Bring to the rams' children," from the New Testament, which is the one horn, and the old, which is the other horn. So Lombard. Now you have learned, reader, why the mitres of bishops have two horns.

units.la: Ps. XXXIII. 15. * Qui finxit sigillatim corda eorum] Ita vulgatus ex Græco. ὁ πλάσας τῇ μόνας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν. Hic locus vulgo à Scholasticis adducitur distruendis duabus opi- nionibus, quarum prior est, animas esse ex traduce. Vide Hieron. in hunc psalmum, & Lombardum lib. 2. dist. 18. litera H. Hi per corda animas intelligunt. Altera, omnes animas simul in principio mundi creatas esse. Audiamus Carthusianum, [sigillatim] id est singulariter & seorsim. corda eorum] id est animas hominum. Anima enim creando infunditur & infundendo creatur. Per hoc quod propheta asserit animas sigillatim produci, destruitur error ponentium, omnes animas rationales simul creatas à principio mundi cum angelis. Errori, quem hic oppugnat Carthusianus, nullum præstabo patrocinium. Illud tamen dicam, nec Græco nec Ebraeo textu istum errorem jugulari. Illud enim τῇ μόνας potest reddi solus. Genebr. Sigillatim] κατὰ μόνας, solus sine alterius opera eorum animas finxit & procreavit. Ita certe voce ista usus est Marcus IV. 10. ὅτε δ' ἐγένετο κατὰ μόνας, cum esset solitarie id est solus. Vulg. singulariter. Et LXX. Ps. iv. 9. eadem voce expresserunt Ebraeum לבדד / Vox Ebraea יחד significat pariter, una, simul, tam hic quam ille, ut sensus sit, verba Genebrardi, Deus omnium corda format pariter id est ad unum omnia, nullo excepto, ne quis opinetur aliquas animas ab aliquo alio creari. Hinc Aquila & v. Editio, ἅμα, Symm. ὁμῶς. Quo sensu usus est Sirach. xviii. 1. voce κοινῇ, de qua suo loco. Quid vero spectarunt Græci, cum τὸ יחד reddidere κατὰ μόνας? aut legerunt יחיד aut existimarunt τὸ יחד aliquando idem esse quod לבד / quomodo accepisse videtur R. Salomo, Ezrae iv. 3. Nos יחד aedificabimus Domino Deo nostro, &c. ubi tamen nulla necessitas. Unde & Abenezra notat innui ista voce כל קהל ישראל totum Israel, & Lxx. ὁμοῦ τὸ αὐτὸ, reddidere.
units.tr: Ps. 33:15, * "Who formed their hearts individually." The Vulgate follows the Greek, [ὁ πλάσας τῇ μόνας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν]. This passage is commonly cited by the Schoolmen to refute two opinions. The first is that souls are derived by traduction. See Jerome on this Psalm, and Lombard, book 2, dist. 18, letter H. These writers understand "hearts" as souls. The second is that all souls were created together at the beginning of the world. Let us hear the Carthusian: "[individually] that is, singly and separately. [their hearts] that is, the souls of men. For the soul is infused by creation and created by infusion. By the fact that the prophet asserts that souls are produced individually, the error of those who hold that all rational souls were created together with the angels at the beginning of the world is destroyed." I will give no support to the error which the Carthusian opposes here. Yet I will say this: neither the Greek nor the Hebrew text strangles that error. For [τῇ μόνας] can be rendered "alone." Genebrard: "[individually] is [κατὰ μόνας], alone: without the work of another, he formed and created their souls." So Mark 4:10 certainly used this word: [ὅτε δ' ἐγένετο κατὰ μόνας], "when he was alone," that is, solus. The Vulgate has singulariter. And the LXX, at Ps. 4:9, expressed the Hebrew [לבדד] by the same word. The Hebrew word [יחד] signifies together, as one, at once, both here and there, so that the sense is the words of Genebrard: "God forms the hearts of all together, that is, all at once to one, none excepted, lest anyone suppose that some souls are created by some other being." Hence Aquila and the fifth edition render it [ἅμα], and Symmachus [ὁμῶς]. In this sense the word [κοινῇ] was used in Sirach 18:1, about which more in its place. But what did the Greeks have in mind when they rendered [יחד] as [κατὰ μόνας]? Either they read [יחיד], or they thought that [יחד] was sometimes the same as [לבד], as R. Solomon seems to have accepted at Ezra 4:3: "We together [יחד] will build to the Lord our God," etc., where, however, there is no necessity for this. Hence Abenezra also notes that the word signifies all the congregation of Israel, [כל קהל ישראל], and the LXX rendered it [ὁμοῦ τὸ αὐτὸ].

units.la: Vers. 6. verbo Domini cœli sunt, &c.] Hic locus sæpe allegatur in doctrina de Trinitate. Sed Calvinus, Pisc. & alii eum minus solidum esse censuerunt. Vide eorum commet. & Parei Calvinum orthodoxum lib. 2. cap. 12. pag. mihi 128.
units.tr: Verse 6, "by the word of the Lord are the heavens," etc.: This passage is often cited in the doctrine of the Trinity. But Calvin, Piscator and others have judged it less solid. See their commentaries, and Pareus's Calvinus orthodoxus, book 2, chapter 12, p. 128 in my edition.

units.la: Pf. XXXIV. 1. cum immutavit vultum suum ] Vide quæ supra notavimus ad 1. Sam xxi. 13.
units.tr: Ps. 34:1, "when he changed his countenance": See what I have noted above on 1 Sam. 21:13.

units.la: Pf. XXXV. 18. In populo gravi laudabo te. ] Ita vulgatus. Lxx. ἐν λαῷ βαρεῖ αἰνέσω σε. Ebr. עַם עָצוּם / ad verbum in populo robusto. Aquila, ὀστέῳ id est osseo? hoc est ἰσχυρῷ Symm. ἐν λαῷ πολυαλνῆι, in populo numeroso. Certe עצום aliquando usurpari pro numerosum esse, docebit vel unus ille locus Jer. xv. עצמו numerosiores sunt (Lxx. ἐπληθυνθησαν) vidue vestræ quam arena maris. Sic & Pf. xl. 6 & 13. Hinc & SA vocem gravi, interpretatur multo. Et Genebr. Gravi ] Hebraismus pro frequenti, numeroso, plurimo. Nam non tantum significat ponderosum vel forte. ut 1. Mach. 1. 18. Multitudo gravis id est magna & copiosa. Bellarm. quoque agnoscit, vocari populum עצום ratione multitudinis. Quid ergo judicandum de hac Augustini glossa quæ in propria vocis Latinæ gravis significatione fundata est, In Ecclesia, quæ toto orbe terrarum circumfusa est, palea est & frumentum. Palea volat, frumentum manet, ideo in populo gravi laudabo te, In gravi populo, quem ventus tentationis non aufert, in his Deus laudatur. In palea blasphematur semper.
units.tr: Ps. 35:18, "I will praise you among a mighty people." The Vulgate has this. The Seventy have "in a heavy people I will praise you" [ἐν λαῷ βαρεῖ αἰνέσω σε]. The Hebrew is עַם עָצוּם, word for word "in a strong people." Aquila has "with a bone," that is, "with a bony one"? Symmachus has "with a strong one" [ἰσχυρῷ]. Another Greek version has "in a populous people" [ἐν λαῷ πολυαρίθμῳ]. That עצום can mean numerous is shown by the single passage Jer. 15:8, where the widows are more numerous (the Seventy have ἐπληθυνθησαν) than the sand of the sea. So too Ps. 40:6 and 13. Hence the Syriac version renders the word "heavy" as much. Genebrardus, on "heavy," says: Gravi: a Hebraism for frequent, numerous, very many. For it does not only mean ponderous or strong, as in 1 Macc. 1:18, "a heavy multitude," that is, a great and copious one. Bellarmine also grants that the people is called עצום by reason of its multitude. What then should we judge of this gloss of Augustine, which rests on the proper Latin sense of gravis? In the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, there is chaff and grain. The chaff flies away, the grain remains; therefore, "in a heavy people I will praise you." In a heavy people, which the wind of temptation does not carry off, God is praised. In the chaff he is always blasphemed.

units.la: Pf. XXXIX. 10: Obsurdui & non aperui os meum, quia tu fecisti. ] Ita vulgatus Lxx. ὅτι σὺ ἐποίησας, atque ita est in Ebraeo, quia tu עשיתה fecisti. Sensus clarus est. Audiamus nunc Augustinum. Is cum incidisset in codicem ubi addita erat vocula ME, eamque concoquere non posset, sic alloquitur Psalmographum, Ideo non aperuisti os tuum, quia Deus est qui fecit te? Mirum est. An os tibi non fecit Deus ad loquendum? Qui plantavit aurem, non audit? qui finxit oculum, non vidit? Os tibi Deus ad loquendum dedit, & dicis, obsurdui & non aperui os meum, quia tu es qui fecisti me? An, quoniam tu es qui fecisti me, pertinent ad posteriorem versum? Quoniam tu es qui fecisti me, amove a me flagellatus. Quoniam tu es qui fecisti me, noli exterminare me, tantum cade ut proficiam, non ut deficiam, &c Vides, lector, quid sit mendosos codices sequi & fontes non posse consulere.
units.tr: Ps. 39:10: "I was dumb and opened not my mouth, because you made it." The Vulgate has this, and the Seventy have "because you made it" [ὅτι σὺ ἐποίησας]. So too the Hebrew, "because you" [עשיתה] "made it." The sense is clear. Let us now hear Augustine. When he came upon a codex where the little word ME had been added, and could not digest it, he addresses the psalmist thus: So you did not open your mouth, because God is the one who made you? It is strange. Did God not make your mouth for speaking? He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see? God gave you a mouth to speak with, and you say, "I was dumb and did not open my mouth, because you are the one who made me"? Or do the words "because you are the one who made me" belong to the following verse? "Because you are the one who made me, remove your scourge from me. Because you are the one who made me, do not destroy me; only strike so that I may improve, not so that I may fail," etc. You see, reader, what it is to follow faulty codices and not be able to consult the sources.

units.la: Pf. XL. 8. In capite libri scriptum est de me ] Ita vulgatus. Lxx. ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γεγραμμένον περί ἐμοῦ. In eundem modum invenies locum hunc citatum in Epistola ad Ebraeos x. 7. Textus Ebraeus habet בִּמְגִלַּת סֵפֶר in volumine libri hoc est, in libro. Locutio ex ... ut petra silicis & silex petra. Vide Gramm. nostram lib. 2. cap. 1. Ita & Genebr. in comment. מגלה est liber, sed convolutus. Solebant enim prisci libros suos in cylindri formam convolvere, ut etiamnum Judæi exemplar illud legis, quod in pergameno exaratum in Synagogis asservant, convolvunt. Hinc natæ illæ locutiones, ἀνατπλύξας & πατάξας τὸ βιβλίον Luc. iv. 17. & 20. Hinc Latinorum volumen, & evolvere libros. מגלה ergo αὶτϙλιξεὶ, volumen, à ϡϡ volvere. Hæc est simplicissima interpretatio. In volumine libri id est in libro, Quomodo & Luth. & Pisc. im buch. In libro Legis, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν liber dici meretur. In Ebræo ergo nulla difficultas. Si quæras ubi in Mose scriptum sit de Christo, non opus est ad particularia loca descendere, totius scripturæ scopus est Christus. Scripturæ sunt quæ testimonium perhibent de illo. Vnde non pauci per hunc librum universam Scripturam intelligunt. Videamus nunc Græcum interpretamentum κεφαλίδι. Pro eo Symm. & Aquila εἰλήματα dixerunt. Εἴλημα involucrum & volumen. Huc respexit Suidas quando inquit, κεφαλὶς βιβλίε ὑπὲρ τινὲς εἴλημα Φασίν. Idem ergo quod Ebræum מגלה / Vox κεφαλὶς plus negotii interpretibus facessit. Cum enim ea vox, communiter per caput vel capitulum, explicetur, anxie quæsitum fuit, quid hic per capitulum vel caput libri intelligatur. Per caput nonnulli summam intelligunt. Inter quos Bellar. & Genebr. Licet autem ea interpretatio Ebrææ voci מגלה neutiquam conveniat, tamen sententiam eandem parit cum illa, qua per volumen libri universa scriptura intelligitur. Bell. quoniam igitur non ait hoc loco Dominus, in capite primi libri, vel capite primo libri, sed generatim, in c. libri, recte dixerunt Chrysost. Theod. Euthymius, hoc loco, in c. l. significare totum volumen divinarum scripturarum. Id enim coincidit cum eo, quod nos dicimus, summam totius scripturæ ad Christum pertinere. Ipse enim est finis legis, Rom. 10. Hæc Bell. At communior sententia, ut per caput, principium intelligatur, unde & in Belgica versione Hebr. x. 7. legimus, in principio libri. ubi tamen Lutherus, in libro præcipue scriptum est de me. In capite ergo illis est in principio. At cujus libri? Invenio varias opiniones. Prima est de libro divinæ prædestinationis. Sa, in primo loco divinæ prædestinationis. Hanc interpretationem sequitur Lyra, & meminêre Carthus. & Bellarm. existimantes eum firmari ex voce מגלה / quæ, ut di{*}ctum est, librum convolutum significat, atque ita clausum, ut quæ in eo scripta sunt, legi non possint. Alii hunc ipsum Psalmorum librum intelligunt, inter quos August. & putant respici ad illa verba Ps. 1. In lege Domini voluntas ejus. Quid enim longe petamus, inquit, aut alios libros inquiramus? Ecce in capite hujus libri Psalmorum scriptum est, Beatus vir, &c. Alii per principium libri, initium Euangelii Johannis intellexere, quam sententiam Hieronymo & Chrysostomo quoque adscribit Bellarminus. Major vero pars veterum Theologorum, de initio libri Geneseos locum hunc expositerunt. Et tamen ad quem locum potissimum respexerit Christus, non convenit. Ambrosius, teste Bellar. putavit istum locum intelligi, Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis & relinquet homo, &c. Quod exponit Apostolus, Ephes. v. Sacramentum hoc magnum est, ego autem dico in Christo & in Ecclesia. Hæc iterum Bell. Alii ad vaticinium de semine mulieris, alii ad liminarem illam vocem בראשית repetasse Salvatorem volunt. Equidem cur de hac postrema interpretatione tam altum sileat Bellarminus, demiror. Carthus. Secundo exponitur sic, in capite libri id est in exordio Geneseos, Ibi enim habetur, in principio id est in verbo, creavit Deus cælum & terram. Omnia namque per ipsum creata sunt, &c. Ipse quoque Hieron. mentem suam clare satis edidererit in Quæst. ubi hæc leguntur, Magis itaque secundum sensum, quam secundum verbi translationem de Christo accipi potest [illud vid. בראשת] qui tam in ipsa fronte Genesis, quæ caput librorum omnium est, quam etiam in principio Johannis Euangelista cœli & terra conditor approbatur. Unde & in Psalterio de se ipso ait, In capite libri scriptum est de me, id est in principio Geneseos, &c. Aves plures sententias audire Lector? En tibi adhuc unam, quam Alcuino tribuit Lomb. In capite id est apud Deum patrem, qui est caput mei, dicit Christus, qui sum liber humani generis, in quo quisque legere debet, scriptum est id est præfinitum est de me. Eadem invenies in Glossa ordin. Hanc interpretum varietatem & incertitudinem uni vocula κεφαλὴς ignoratæ adscripserim. Κεφαλὶς in lingua Hellenistica idem quod גבלה volumen. Fidem facient hæc exempla, Ezræ 6.2. καὶ ἐνέχθη — κεφαλὶς μία. Chald. מגלה & inventum fuit volumen unum. Jezech. 3.1. ὡς ἀνθρώπως καταφάγε τὸ κεφαλίδα ταύτην, ubi Ebraice rursus מגלה / Sic & vers. 2. Hic certe nec caput, nec initium significare potest. Iesai. 3: 1. vocem synonymam בלין Lxx. τόμος, alius πύχων, alius διφθέρωμα, alius κεφαλίδα interpretatus est. Κεφαλὴ ergo volumen, undecunque ita appellatum sit. Sunt enim qui à κεφαλὴ deflectunt, quasi dicas, opus capitatum. Vide Junii parallela, lib. 3. cap. 10. Fullerus Miscell. 2. 10. sententiam Junii improbat, atque in eam inclinat sententiam, idiotismum esse, & dictionem ἀπηχώρειον & peculiarem, quæ non à voce Græca κεφαλὴ flectatur, sed ab Ebraeo כפל vel Syro כפלא aut קפל quæ denotant id quod minime est ἀπλασμένον id est expansum, explicatum vel extensum, sed διπλάσμον hoc est, compositum, complicatum & convolutum. Subjungit idem aliam conjecturam non minus probabilem, ut nimirum flectatur à קלף / quod Syris Chaldaeisque proprie quidem corticem, sed Rabbinis passim membranam significat, העור שכותבין עליו id est pellem, in qua scribunt. Graeci διφθέραι vocant. Ita κεφαλὴς per metathesin erit pro κελαφὶς. Et certe apud Graecos interpretes plura ejusmodi occurrunt vocabula, quae ex oriente קלף / assumpta Graeca veste induerunt. Ita ex גר fecerunt γενέσεις, Exod. xii. 19. Ex תבר vel Exo. 2. 3. שהרנים σπῶves Jud. 8. 24. In editione Complut. Quia vero jam meminimus vocis בראשית / quae liminaris est libri Geneseos, lubet paululum hic gradum sistere. Ita est. Multi ex veteribus crediderunt eam vel ἀπόλεξει, secundum sensum sonare, in filio In filio creavit Deus coelum & terram. Hilarium taxat Hieronymus in principio libri de Ebr. traditionibus, quod in expositione versus 1. Ps. 2. asseruerit, pro eo quod nos in exordio Geneseos habemus, In principio, in Ebraeo haberi, in filio. Hilarium in hunc errorem traxit authoritas Tertulliani, qui in libro adversus Praxeam idem asseruerat. Alii, qui non ignorarunt in Ebraeo ἀπόλεξεί legi, in principio, tamen per illud principium filium intellexere. Ita August. lib. 1. de Genef. ad lit. cap. 1. Ambrof. & Basilius. Magister sentent. lib. 1. dist. 2. lit. F. pluralitatem personarum & unitatem essentiae probaturus, hunc ipsum producit locum, per Deum, inquit, signisicari patrem. Per principium filium. Eadem habet lib. 2. dist. 13. lit. H. Vide & August. de Civit. Dei xi. 32. Thomas part. prima, Quaest. 46. artic. 3. In principio creavit Deus, &c. triplicter exponitur ad excludendum tres errores. Quidam enim ppposuerunt mundum semper fuisse. Ad hoc excludendum exponitur, In principio, sc. temporis. Quidam posuerunt duo esse creationis principia, unum bonorum, aliud malorum. Et ad hoc excludendum exponitur, in principio, hoc est, in filio. Sicut enim principium effectivum appropriatur Patri, propter potentiam: ita principium exemplare tribuitur filio propter sapientiam, ut sicut dicitur, omnia in sapientia fecisti, (Psal. 104.) ita intelligatur Deum omnia fecisse in principio id est in filio, secundum illud Apostoli, Coloss. 1. In ipso condita sunt universa, &c. Haec Thomas. Quaeres quid spectaverint Interpretes, dum per principium Filium intellexere? certe si scriptum fuisset בְּחָכְמָה in sapientia, quomodo legimus Ps. 104. omnia fecisti Domine in sapientia (cujus tamen simplicissimus sensus iste est, sapienter) minus contorta videri posset interpretatio. Christus enim Proverb. 1. 8. & 9. vocatur Sapientia. Quod si Patribus constitisset, paraphrasten Jerosol. vocem בְּרֵאשִׁית reddidisse בְּחָכְמָה / in sapientia, proculdubio istam interpretationem in patrocinium suae sententiae advocassent, praecipue Origenes, de quo Theodoretus, ὁ δὲ Ωεψγένης τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ βάλετα ἀντὶ ἐν σοφίᾳ, τοῦτ' ἔστι, ἐν υἱῷ id est Origenes illud, ἐν ἀρχῇ, vult positum, pro ἐν σοφίᾳ in sapientia, hoc est, in filio. Quid vero spectaverit Paraphrastes Jerosolymitanus, alii excutiant. Non ignoramus, quid vulgo afferri solet, sed cum omnia tentarunt, non persuadent tamen, aliam ei fuisse mentem, quam quae Davidi Psalmo 104. verf. 24. Nos videamus obiter quid illi spectaverint, qui per principium filium intellexerunt Hoc nos docebit Origenes super Genes. Quod est omnium principium, nisi Dominus & salvator omnium Jesus Christus, primogenitus omnis creaturae? August. de Genesi ad literam, Secundum historiam quaeritur quid sit in principio. Vtrum in principio temporis? an in principio, in ipsa sapientia Dei? quia & ipse Dei filius, principium se dixit, quando ei dictum est, Tu quis es? Et dixit, Principium, quod & loquor vobis. Locus ille extat Joh. viii. 25. τὴν ἀρχήν, ὅτι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν. Ubi accusativum illum adverbialiter positum esse pro κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν Beza, Drusius & alii jam pridem docuere. Vide Bezae Annot. Hoc ergo dicit Salvator, Se eum esse, quem initio vel à principio se esse dixerat. Nonnus,
units.tr: Ps. XL. 8. "In the head of the book it is written of me": so the Vulgate. The Septuagint has "in the head of a book it is written concerning me" [ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γεγραμμένον περὶ ἐμοῦ]. You will find this passage quoted in the same way in Hebrews 10:7. The Hebrew text has "in the volume of the book" [בִּמְגִלַּת סֵפֶר], that is, in the book. This is a figure of speech like "a rock of flint" and "flint a rock". See our Grammar, book 2, chapter 1. Genebrardus in his commentary likewise says that the word for "volume" [מגלה] means a book, but a rolled-up one. For the ancients used to roll their books into the shape of a cylinder, just as the Jews still roll up the copy of the Law which is written on parchment and kept in their synagogues. Hence those expressions in Luke 4:17 and 20, unrolling and rolling up the book [ἀναπτύξας ... πτύξας τὸ βιβλίον]. Hence the Latin volumen and evolvere libros. So the Hebrew [מגלה] is a roll, volumen, from the root גלל, to roll. This is the simplest interpretation: in the volume of the book, that is, in the book, as Luther and Piscator also render it: im buch. That is, in the book of the Law, which deserves to be called the book par excellence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν]. So in the Hebrew there is no difficulty. If you ask where in Moses it is written about Christ, there is no need to go down to particular passages: the whole aim of Scripture is Christ. "The Scriptures are those which bear witness to him" (John 5:39). So many understand by this book the whole of Scripture. Let us now consider the Greek rendering κεφαλίδι. In its place Symmachus and Aquila have said εἰλήματα. Εἴλημα means a wrapping and a roll. Suidas had this in mind when he says, κεφαλὶς βιβλίου, ὑπέρ τινες εἴλημα φασίν: the same as the Hebrew [מגלה]. The word κεφαλίς causes the translators more trouble. Since it is commonly explained as head or chapter, people have anxiously asked what is meant here by the chapter or head of the book. Some understand by head the summa, the sum, among them Bellarmine and Genebrardus. Although that rendering by no means matches the Hebrew word [מגלה], it yields the same sense as the view that by "the volume of the book" the whole of Scripture is meant. Bellarmine: "Since the Lord does not say here 'in the head of the first book' or 'the first chapter of the book', but generally 'in the head of the book', Chrysostom, Theodoret and Euthymius rightly said that here 'in the head of the book' signifies the whole volume of the divine Scriptures. For this agrees with what we say, that the sum of the whole of Scripture pertains to Christ. For he is the end of the law" (Rom. 10:4).* This is Bellarmine. But the more common opinion is that head means the beginning, whence in the Belgic version we read at Hebrews 10:7 in the beginning of the book, though Luther has in the book it is written chiefly of me. So for them the head is the beginning. But of what book? I find various opinions. The first is that it is the book of divine predestination: Sa, in the first place of divine predestination. Lyra follows this interpretation, and the Carthusians and Bellarmine mention it, thinking it is confirmed by the word [מגלה], which, as has been said, means a rolled-up book, and so closed that what is written in it cannot be read. Others understand the book of Psalms itself, among them Augustine, who thinks that the words of Psalm 1 are alluded to: "In the law of the Lord is his delight." "Why, he says, should we seek far, or look for other books? Behold, at the head of this book of Psalms it is written, 'Blessed is the man', etc." Others understood by the beginning of the book the beginning of John's Gospel, an opinion which Bellarmine also attributes to Jerome and Chrysostom. But most of the older theologians expounded this passage of the beginning of the book of Genesis. And yet it does not agree which passage Christ chiefly had in mind. Ambrose, according to Bellarmine, thought that this passage was meant: "This now is bone of my bones, and the man shall leave..." etc. which the Apostle expounds in Ephesians 5: "This is a great sacrament, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church." Again this is Bellarmine. Others want the Saviour to have referred to the prophecy of the seed of the woman, and others to the opening word of Genesis [בראשית]. For my part, I wonder why Bellarmine is so silent about this last interpretation. The Carthusians: "Secondly it is explained thus: in the head of the book, that is, in the beginning of Genesis. For there it is written, in the beginning, that is, in the Word, God created heaven and earth. For all things were created by him, etc." Jerome himself made his opinion clear enough in his Questions, where we read: "Christ can be understood more according to the sense than according to the wording of the translation [see the Hebrew word]. He who is the creator of heaven and earth is approved both in the very forehead of Genesis, which is the head of all books, and also in the beginning of John the Evangelist. Hence in the Psalter he also says of himself, 'In the head of the book it is written of me', that is, in the beginning of Genesis, etc." Do you, reader, want to hear more opinions? Here is one more, which Lombard attributes to Alcuin: "'In the head', that is, with God the Father, who is my head, says Christ, who am the book of the human race, in which each one ought to read: 'it is written', that is, it has been foreordained concerning me." You will find the same in the ordinary gloss. I would ascribe this variety and uncertainty of interpreters to the single little word κεφαλίς, which is not understood. Κεφαλίς in Hellenistic usage means the same as the Hebrew [גבלה], volumen. These examples will confirm this: Ezra 6:2, "and there was brought ... one roll" [καὶ ἐνέχθη ... κεφαλὶς μία]; the Chaldee, [מגלה], "and a roll was found." Ezekiel 3:1, "Eat this roll" [τὸ κεφαλίδα ταύτην], where in Hebrew again it is [מגלה]; likewise verse 2. Here it certainly can mean neither head nor beginning. At Isaiah 8:1 the Seventy translated the synonymous Hebrew word [בלין] as tomos, another as pyknon, another as diphtherōma, another as kephalida. So kephalē means a roll, whatever it is called. For there are some who derive it from kephalē, as if you were to say a capitate work. See Junius's Parallels, book 3, chapter 10. Fuller, Miscellanies 2.10, rejects Junius's opinion and inclines to the view that it is an idiom and a peculiar word, not derived from the Greek kephalē but from the Hebrew [כפל] or the Syriac [כפלא] or [קפל], which denote not what is by no means unfolded [ἀπλασμένον], that is, spread out, explained or extended, but what is folded [διπλάσμον], that is, compound, folded and rolled up. The same writer offers another conjecture, no less probable: that it is derived from [קלף], which among the Syrians and Chaldeans properly means bark, but among the rabbis commonly means parchment, [העור שכותבין עליו], that is, the skin on which they write. The Greeks call it diphtherai. So kephalis will be by metathesis for kelaphis. And indeed among the Greek translators many words of this kind occur which, taken from the East from [קלף], have put on Greek dress. Thus from [גר] they made geneseis, Exodus 12:19; from [תבר] or Exodus 2:3 [שהרנים] sphōves, Judges 8:24. In the Complutensian edition... Since we have now mentioned the word [בראשית], which is the opening word of the book of Genesis, let us pause here a little. It is so. Many of the ancients believed that it sounds, in sense, like in the Son: "In the Son God created heaven and earth." Jerome criticises Hilary, in his book on the Hebrew traditions, because in his exposition of verse 1 of Psalm 2 he asserted that for what we have at the beginning of Genesis, in principio, the Hebrew has in the Son. Hilary was led into this error by the authority of Tertullian, who had asserted the same in his book against Praxeas. Others, who knew that in Hebrew [בְּרֵאשִׁית] is read, in the beginning, nevertheless understood the Son by that beginning. So Augustine, On Genesis according to the letter, book 1, chapter 1; Ambrose and Basil. The Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 2, letter F, wishing to prove the plurality of persons and the unity of essence, quotes this very passage: "By God", he says, "the Father is signified; by beginning, the Son." He has the same in book 2, distinction 13, letter H. See also Augustine, City of God 11.32. Thomas Aquinas, part 1, question 46, article 3: "In the beginning God created, etc." is explained in three ways to exclude three errors. For some have supposed that the world has always existed; to exclude this it is explained: in the beginning, that is, of time. Some have posited two principles of creation, one of good things and another of evil; to exclude this it is explained: in the beginning, that is, in the Son. "For just as the effective principle is attributed to the Father on account of power, so the exemplary principle is attributed to the Son on account of wisdom, as it is said, 'in wisdom you have made all things' (Psalm 104:24). So it should be understood that God made all things in the beginning, that is, in the Son, according to the Apostle's words, Colossians 1: 'All things were created in him', etc." This is Thomas. You will ask what the interpreters had in view when they understood the Son by the beginning? Certainly, if it had been written [בְּחָכְמָה], in wisdom, as we read in Psalm 104, "You have made all things, O Lord, in wisdom" (though its plainest sense is wisely), the interpretation might seem less contorted. For Christ is called Wisdom in Proverbs 1:8 and 9. But if it had been agreed among the Fathers that the Jerusalem Paraphrast rendered the word [בְּרֵאשִׁית] as [בְּחָכְמָה], in wisdom, they would undoubtedly have invoked that interpretation in support of their view, especially Origen, of whom Theodoret says: "Origen wants the phrase 'in the beginning' [ἐν ἀρχῇ] to be put for 'in wisdom' [ἐν σοφίᾳ], that is, in the Son." But what the Jerusalem Paraphrast had in view, let others examine. We are not unaware of what is commonly alleged, but although they have tried everything, they do not persuade us that his mind was other than that of David in Psalm 104:24. Let us briefly see what those had in view who understood the Son by the beginning. Origen will teach us this on Genesis: "What is the beginning of all things, if not the Lord and Saviour of all, Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature?" Augustine, On Genesis according to the letter: "According to the history it is asked what is 'in the beginning'. Is it in the beginning of time? Or is it in the beginning, in the very wisdom of God? For the Son of God himself called himself the beginning, when he was asked, 'Who are you?' And he said, 'The beginning, who also speak to you.'"* That passage is in John 8:25, [τὴν ἀρχήν, ὅτι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν]. Here Beza, Drusius and others long ago showed that the accusative is used adverbially for [κατὰ τὴν ἀρχήν]. See Beza's Annotations. So the Saviour here says that he is the one whom he had said at the beginning, or from the beginning, that he was. Nonnus,

units.la: Tig
units.tr: Who?

units.la: Τίς ση εἶ λάσς; καὶ Χριςὸς ἀνίαχεν, ὅτι εἰς υἱὸς Ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὃ ἀὲ ἀξω.
units.tr: Who are you? And Christ answered, that from the beginning I am also telling you what I say. [Τίς σὺ εἶ; καὶ Χριστὸς ἀνέιπεν, ὅτι εἰς υἱὸς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὃ καὶ λέγω.]

units.la: Quis tu es? & respondit Christus, quod vobis Abinitio dicebam.
units.tr: Who are you? And Christ answered, "What I was telling you from the beginning."

units.la: Alii allegarunt locum Johannis I. 1. ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος. Atqui illic λόγος & ἀρχὴ manifeste distinguuntur. Sic dico, ὁ λόγος illic non dicitur ἀρχή, sed jam extitisse ἐν ἀρχῇ. Locus Psalm. cx. Tecum principium in die virtutis tuæ, magis disconvenit. Namque illic in Ebræo nihil est, quod principium significet, ut suo loco videbimus. Hæc fere loca sunt, quæ Patres tanquam ἀρχαῖα solent adducere. Equidem vehementer miror, nec illos, nec Scholasticos, & nominatim Thomam, loco quem supra adduximus, locum illum citasse qui extat *Apocal. 3. 14. ubi Christus vocatur ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως Θεοῦ, præsertim cum illic eadem vox principium in vulgata translatione extet. Et certe Christus non solum est principium exemplare creationis, propter sapientiam, ut supra loquebatur Thomas, sed & effectuum propter potentiam, docente Apostolo, Ebræorum 1. 10. Tu Domine initio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cæli. Non ergo negatur, Patrem creasse omnia in filio, sed hoc voluisse Mosem exprimere per vocem בראשית solide nondum probatum esse asseritur.
units.tr: Others have cited John 1:1, "In the beginning was the Word." But there "Word" and "beginning" are plainly distinguished. I say that there the Word is not called a beginning; it is said to have already existed in the beginning. The passage Psalm 110, "With you is the beginning in the day of your power," fits even worse. For in the Hebrew there is nothing that means "beginning", as we will see in its place. These are about the only passages that the Fathers usually cite as evidence for the "beginning". I am truly astonished that neither they, nor the Schoolmen, and especially Thomas, cited in the passage above, have quoted that text in Revelation 3:14, where Christ is called "the beginning of the creation of God". This is especially so since the same word, "beginning", stands in the Vulgate translation there. And certainly Christ is not only the beginning of the exemplar of creation, through wisdom, as Thomas said above, but also of its effects, through power, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 1:10: "You, Lord, in the beginning laid the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands." So it is not denied that the Father created all things in the Son. But the claim that it has not yet been firmly established that Moses meant this by the word בראשית (bereshit) is not refuted.

units.la: Ps. XLII. 1. Deum fontem vivum] Græci ἰσχυρόν id est fortem. Atque ita correxit hunc locum Clemens. Vide sis quæ pag. 79. & 80. notavimus. In Bibliis Lovan. anno 1599. Antverpiæ à Moreto editis invenio locum hunc sic correctum Mijn ziele heeft dorst gehadt tot Godt den machtigen levende. Melius ita reddas, Anima mea sitit Deum, Deum viventem. Mijn ziele dorstet na Gode / na den levendigen God. In Ebr. enim concurrunt אלהים & אל.
units.tr: Psalm 42:1, "God, the living fountain": the Greeks have ἰσχυρόν, that is, "strong". Clement corrected this passage in this way. See what I noted on pages 79 and 80. In the Louvain Bible of 1599, printed at Antwerp by Moretus, I find this passage corrected thus: "My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty living one." It is better to render it: "My soul thirsts for God, the living God." For in the Hebrew the words אלהים and אל come together.

units.la: Ps. XLV. 1. pro iis qui commutabuntur. ] Ita vulgatus. Lxx. ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων. Pias super hoc titulo invenies meditationes apud veteres, nominatim apud Augustinum, pias inquam sed hoc loco neutiquam convenientes. Namque ex שושנים nunquam istam interpretationem extruderis. Fuit vox ista שושנים (quæ alibi lilia significat idest σωσαννα, à numero vi. foliorum) vel initium vulgatæ alicujus cantilenæ, ad cujus. cujus melodiam decantandus fuerit hic Psalmus, vel nomen instrumenti Musici hexachordi. Vide Interpretes.
units.tr: Psalm 45:1, "for those who shall be changed": so the Vulgate; the LXX has "for those who shall be altered" (ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων). You will find pious meditations on this title among the ancients, especially in Augustine, pious I say, but in no way suited to this place. For you can never derive that interpretation from שושנים. The word שושנים (which elsewhere means "lilies", that is σωσαννα, from the number of six leaves) was either the opening of some song, to whose melody this psalm was to be sung, or the name of a musical instrument with six notes. See the commentators.

units.la: Ibid. vers. 5. Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum potentissime. ] Hujus loci meminimus supra pag. 141. Erasmus in Apologia adversus lepidum illud cucurbitæ caput, Petrum Sutorem, demonstraturus, multa in versionibus ambigua non nisi ex fontibus explicari posse, hoc exemplum producit· Incertum est, inquit, utrum adverbium sitpotentissime, an nomen. Quid faciam? consule glossas. Pareo & adeo commentarios Hieronymi. Illic lego potentissime, non segniter neque leviter sed viriliter. Ex his verbis apparet adverbium esse. Digredior ad commentariolum ejus ad Principiam. Non attingit hanc vocem. Consulo Augustinum. Ille me circumagit multis ambagibus, tandem hoc addens, potentissime etiam circa femur, subindicare videtur esse nomen. Tale quiddam significat & Cassiodorus. Hinc igitur dimittor incertus. Consulo Hugonem Cardinalem. Is nominatim admonet, potentissime sumendum adverbialiter. Confugio ad Lyranum. Is nihil attigit. Hinc ad Arnobium, tantundem. Restat Glossa ord. dissimulat. Denique consulo Fabrum Stapulensem. Is videtur indicare, potentissime nomen esse. Si simili studio circumagar per omnes glossas, dimittar incertior quam veneram. Et hæc est via compendiaria quam nobis mostrat Sutor. Quanto brevius erat, non hac solum de causa inspicere Psalterium Græce versum, ubi scriptum est δυνατε, id est o potens, aut si quis adhuc dubitet, Hebraicum, ubi legitur gibbor. quod Hiero. vertit fortissime. Hæc Erafmus.
units.tr: Psalm 45:5 (Vulgate), "Gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty." We noticed this passage above on page 141. Erasmus, in his Apology against that witty gourd-head Petrus Sutor, wishing to show that many ambiguities in translations can be resolved only from the sources, produces this example: "It is uncertain," he says, "whether the word is an adverb, 'most mighty', or a noun. What shall I do? Consult the glosses. I obey, and even the commentaries of Jerome. There I read 'most mighty', not sluggishly nor lightly, but manfully. From these words it appears to be an adverb. I turn to his little commentary to Principia. It does not touch this word. I consult Augustine. He leads me round in many circles, finally adding that 'most mighty' even about the thigh seems to hint that it is a noun. Cassiodorus seems to signify something of the same kind. So I am dismissed uncertain. I consult Cardinal Hugo. He expressly warns that 'most mighty' must be taken adverbially. I flee to Lyra. He touches nothing. Then to Arnobius, the same. There remains the Ordinary Gloss, which evades the question. Finally I consult Faber Stapulensis. He seems to indicate that 'most mighty' is a noun. If I were turned round with the same zeal through all the glosses, I would be dismissed more uncertain than when I came. And this is the short cut that Sutor shows us. How much shorter it would have been, not to mention this, to look at the Psalter in the Greek version, where it is written δυνατε, that is, 'O mighty one'; or, if anyone still doubts, at the Hebrew, where one reads gibbor, which Jerome translated 'most strong'." So far Erasmus.

units.la: Ps. XLVIII. In hunc Psalmum extat oratio Stephani ArchiEpiscopi Patracenensis. eam invenies tomo iv. Conciliorum Edit. Colon. pag. 621. Confer eam cum originali textu vel accuratiore Pagnini translatione & judica.
units.tr: On this Psalm 48 there exists a speech of Stephen, Archbishop of Patras. You will find it in volume 4 of the Cologne edition of the Councils, page 621. Compare it with the original text, or with Pagnini's more accurate translation, and judge.

units.la: Ps. XLIX. 16. ex inferno ] Vide ad Psalm. lxxxv.
units.tr: Psalm 49:16, "from hell". See on Psalm 85.

units.la: Ps. L. 11. pulcritudo agri mecum est. ] Hiero. universitas agri. Pagn. fera agri. Genebr. & Sa, mecum est, hoc est, in mea potestate est. Bellar. ad jus meum pertinet. Ebr. ״ביו/ In scholis Theologicis sæpe auditur, Deo omnia esse præsentia. Hanc sententiam uti non solicito, ita tironem quoque monitum volo, nihil tale his verbis spectasse Psalmographum. Sensum eo-rum tum simplicissimum verbis Pontificiorum proposui, quibus nostri assentiuntur. Frustra ergo hic subtilis est Augustinus, cujus verba * refert Lombardus l. 1. dist. 35. lit. F. Inde est etiam, inquit Magister, quod omnia dicuntur ei praesentia esse, non solum ea quae sunt, sed etiam ea quae praeterierunt, & ea quae futura sunt. unde August. super illum locum Psal. Et pulcritudo agri mecum est, Ideo, inquit, mecum est, quia apud Deum nihil praeteriit, nihil futurum est. Cum illo sunt omnia futura, & ei non detrahuntur jam praeterita, cum illo sunt omnia cognitione quadam ineffabili sapientia Dei, &c.
units.tr: Psalm 50:11, "the beauty of the field is with me." Jerome: "the whole of the field". Pagnini: "the wild beast of the field". Genebrardus and Sa: "is with me, that is, is in my power." Bellarmine: "belongs to my right." Hebrew: ״ביו. In theological schools one often hears, "All things are present to God." I do not press this view, but I want even a beginner to be warned that the psalmist had nothing like this in mind with these words. I have set out their simplest meaning, in the words of the Papists, with which our people agree. So Augustine's subtlety here is vain. Lombard quotes his words in book 1, distinction 35, letter F: "Hence," says the Master, "it is also said that all things are present to him, not only those which are, but also those which have passed away and those which are to come. Hence Augustine, on that verse of the Psalm, 'and the beauty of the field is with me', says: 'It is with me because nothing has passed away with God, nothing is future. With him all things to come are, and past things are not taken from him; with him all things are in a certain unspeakable knowledge, by the wisdom of God,' etc."

units.la: Psal. LI. 7. in iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis, &c.] Ita vulg. ex LXX. ἐν ἀνομίαις, ἐν ἁμαρτίαις. Magister Sentent. lib. 2. dist. 33. hanc proponit quæstionem, an peccata præcedentium patrum ad parvulos transeant, sicuti primi hominis delictum in omnes carnaliter genitos redundavit. Et si peccata parentum transeant in parvulos, utrum omnium qui fuerunt ab Adam usque ad ipsos, an aliquorum & non omnium. Ait Augustinum de hoc disserere ambigue in Enchiridio atque ita videri statuisse, peccata parentum præcedentium imputari parvulis, non omnium tamen qui fuerunt ab Adam, neimportabilis & nimia sarcina in pœna æterna gravarentur, sed tantum eorum parentum, qui eos à quarta generatione præcisserunt, illudque ab illo confirmari istis verbis, in Exodo ait Dominus, visitans iniquitates patrum usque in tertiam & quartam generationem, idque per moderationem divinæ miserationis. Secti one C. ait, hanc sententiam ab illis, qui ita sentiunt, cofirmari porro ex eo, quod David de legitimo matrimonio procreatus dicit, In & 46. iniquitatibus conceptus sum & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Non dicit in iniquitate vel peccato. Unde putant, non tantum illud unum peccatum originale, sed etiam plura, quæ in peccato Adæ reperiri possunt, & alia parentum peccata parvulis imputari. Sect. D. docet ex August. (cap. 45. Enchiridii) in actuali peccato Adæ, plura concurrisse peccata, vid. superbiam, sacrilegium, homicidium & fornicationem spiritualem & furtum & avaritiam. Sect. E. Augustinum Augustino opponit, in hunc modum cap. 93. Enchiridii differentem, mitissima sane eorum pœna erit, qui præter peccatum, quod originale contraxerunt, nullum insuper addiderunt: & in ceteris qui addiderunt, tanto quisque tolerabiliorem habebit damnationem, quanto hic minorem habuerit iniquitatem. Concludit ergo Lombardus, hanc fuisse mentem Augustini, uno & non pluribus peccatis parvulos obligatos teneri. Caetera non tam asserta quam disserta fuisse. Quid ergo fiet loco Psalmi LI. in iniquitatibus, in peccatis? Responsionem in promptu habet August. cap. 44. Enchiridi, Quemadmodum scriptura aliquando singulari numero pro plurali utitur, ita e converso pluralem aliquando pro singulari ponit, ex. gr. Mortui sunt qui quaerebant animam pueri, de uno Herode, Matth. 2. &c. ita & illud originale unum plurali numero significari, &c. Haec Lombardus ex Augustino. Eadem responsione de enallage numerorum utitur Thomas prima secundae, quaest. 82. art. 2. ubi quaerit, an in uno homine sint multa originalia peccata, & hunc Davidis locum pro affirmativa sibi primo objicit. Addit tamen alias, vel inquit, pluraliter dicitur in iniquitatibus, &c. quod in peccato originali virtualiter praexistunt omnia peccata actualia, sicut in quodam principio, unde est multiplex virtute. Vel quia in peccato primi parentis fuerunt plures deformitates, vel quia multae partes animae inficiuntur per peccatum originale. Genebr. Unum peccatum originale dici potest multa, quia est omnium aliorum fomes, origo & seminarium. Unum ergo est per se: multa per effectus. Carthus. Unum est formaliter, multa vero materialiter, propter quatuor animae vulnera, ex origin. peccato secuta, quae sunt ignorantia, malitia, infirmitas & concupiscentia. Tantae molis erat hunc locum interpretari. Sed vide Lector, quam frustra hic sudaverint praestantissima illa ingenia. David, de cujus verbis hactenus disputatum est, non usus est nisi vocibus singularis numeri, בָּעֲוֹן / בְּחַטָּאת / in iniquitate, in peccato, proculdubio peccatum originale intelligens. Vide Interpretes Lutherus, upt zondelijc: hen zabe / hoc esset ad verbum מִזְּרַע הַחַטָּא /
units.tr: Psalm 51:7, "I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins," etc. So the Vulgate, from the LXX: ἐν ἀνομίαις, ἐν ἁμαρτίαις. Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 33, raises the question whether the sins of the preceding fathers pass to the little ones, just as the first man's offence spread to all carnally begotten. And if the sins of parents pass to children, whether those of all who lived from Adam to the children themselves, or of some and not all.
