He says that Augustine treats this ambiguously in the Enchiridion, and seems to have decided that the sins of preceding parents are imputed to little ones, yet not of all who lived from Adam, lest they be burdened with an intolerable and excessive load of eternal punishment, but only of those parents who went before them from the fourth generation; and that this is confirmed by those words in Exodus, "the Lord visits the iniquities of the fathers unto the third and fourth generation", and that this is by the moderation of divine mercy. In section C, he says that this opinion is confirmed by those who think so, further from the fact that David, born of a lawful marriage, says, "I was conceived in iniquities and in sins did my mother conceive me." He does not say "in an iniquity or a sin." Hence they think that not only that one original sin, but also several others which can be found in Adam's sin, and other sins of parents, are imputed to little ones. In section D he teaches, from Augustine (chapter 45 of the Enchiridion), that several sins concurred in Adam's actual sin, namely pride, sacrilege, murder, spiritual fornication, theft and avarice. In section E he sets Augustine against Augustine, who in chapter 93 of the Enchiridion says differently: "Certainly the mildest punishment will be for those who, besides the sin which they contracted by origin, added no other; and among the others who added more, each will have a damnation the more tolerable, the less his iniquity was." Lombard therefore concludes that this was Augustine's mind: that little ones are bound by one sin and not by several; and that the rest were stated not so much as asserted but as debated. What then is to be done with the words of Psalm 51, "in iniquities, in sins"? Augustine, in chapter 44 of the Enchiridion, has a ready answer: "Just as Scripture sometimes uses the singular for the plural, so conversely it sometimes puts the plural for the singular, for example, 'They are dead who sought the life of the child', meaning one Herod, Matthew 2, etc. So also that original sin, one, is signified by the plural." Thus Lombard, following Augustine. Thomas, in the first part of the second part, question 82, article 2, uses the same answer about the interchange of numbers, where he asks whether there are many original sins in one man, and first objects to himself this passage of David as affirmative. Yet he adds in another place: "or it is said in the plural, 'in iniquities', because all actual sins pre-exist virtually in original sin, as in a certain principle, whence it has manifold power; or because in the sin of the first parent there were several deformities, or because many parts of the soul are infected through original sin." Genebrardus: one original sin can be called many, because it is the tinder, origin and seedbed of all others. So it is one in itself, and many in its effects. The Carthusian: it is one formally, but many materially, on account of the four wounds of the soul which follow from original sin, namely ignorance, malice, weakness and concupiscence. Such a great mass of labour was it to interpret this passage. But see, reader, how vainly those most excellent minds have sweated here. David, whose words have been discussed so far, used only words of the singular number, בָּעֲוֹן / בְּחַטָּאת, "in iniquity, in sin", undoubtedly understanding original sin. See the commentators. Luther: "in sin"; the Dutch: "in zonde"; the Hebrew literally means "from the seed of sin".

units.la: Psal. LX. 10. Moab olla spei meae ] Lxx. μωάβ λέβης τῆς ἐλπίδός μου. Augustinus in hujus loci expositione non est Augustinus. Piget pudetque ea hunc transcribere. Ebr. Moab. סִיר רַחְצִי olla lotionis meae. Aquila μωάβ λέβης λουτρόν μου. Hiero. & Pagn. & Arias, lotionis meae, Lxx. acceperunt in significatione Chald. & Syr. Illis enim רחץ est, sperare, confidere. Quidam codices latini olim legebant, aula spei meae. Aula, olla. Unde Plauti Aulul© ria; Festus, Aulas antiqui dicebant, quas nos dicidicimus ollas, quia nullam literam geminabant. At quia aula Latinis aliud insuper quiddam significat, Ambrosius instituit virginum c. 12. ita scripsit, * Moās aula spei vel ολλα spei mea. Vt- tamque enim in diversis codicibus invenitur, Aula regalis est virgo &c.
units.tr: Psal. 60:10. "Moab is the pot of my hope." LXX: "Moab is the cauldron of my hope" [μωάβ λέβης τῆς ἐλπίδός μου]. The exposition of this passage that goes under Augustine's name is not really Augustine's. It irks and shames me to copy it out. Hebrew: "Moab is my washing-pot" [סִיר רַחְצִי]. Aquila: "Moab, a cauldron, my washing" [μωάβ λέβης λουτρόν μου]. Jerome, Pagninus and Arias render "of my washing", but the LXX took the word in the sense it has in Chaldee and Syriac, where rḥṣ means to hope or to trust. Some old Latin codices read "aula spei meae", the hall of my hope. Aula and olla are interchangeable: Plautus has the "Aulularia", and Festus says: "The ancients called aulas what we call ollas, because they doubled no letter." But since aula also means something else in Latin, Ambrose, in *De virginibus* ch. 12, wrote it as follows: "Moab is the hall of my hope, or the pot of my hope." For both readings are found in different codices: "The royal hall is a virgin," etc.

units.la: Ps. LXII. 13. reddis unicuique כמעשהו / id est, secundum opus ejus. ] Vulg. juxta opera sua. Eandem sententiam invenies apud Paulum, Rom. 2. 6. ος αποδωσει εκαστῳ κατα τα εργα αυτου. hoc est, prout quisque operibus declaraverit, se esse numero filiorum Dei, vel non esse. Lutherus, & ex eo Belgica, ende betalet een pegelijck als hy het verdient id est, reprendis unicuique sicuti meretur. Quoad sensum non male, qua improbos spectat. At cum sententia generalis sit & ad pios quoque se porrigat, quorum operibus, si proprie & cum scriptura loqui volumus, non potest meritum tribui, periculose & temere vox merendi hic adhibita non immerito videri possit. Et tamen Rhytmi quoque nostri hic canunt, die de mensche wat recht is / doet / na sijn verdienst &c. Disce hic tiro, in versionibus saepe occurrere voces, quibus in originali nihil tale respondet. Vox OMEN semel in Bibliis occurrit, inquiunt nonnulli, vid. 1.Reg.20.33. Item ARBITRIUM, vid. Num. 30. 14. verae sunt illae assertiones, si de Bibliis vulgatae versionis loquaris. At si originarias tabulas adeas, non invenies illic nomina latinis istis respondentia.
units.tr: Ps. 62:13. "You render to each according to his work" [כמעשהו], that is, according to his deed. Vulgate: "according to their works." You will find the same sentiment in Paul, Rom. 2:6: "who will render to each according to his works" [ὃς ἀποδώσει ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ]. That is, according to how each has shown by his works whether or not he is among the sons of God. Luther, and after him the Belgic version, has "and repays each as he has earned it", that is, "renders to each as he deserves." As to sense this is not bad, insofar as it looks to the wicked. But since the statement is general and extends also to the godly, whose works, if we wish to speak properly and in the language of Scripture, cannot be credited with merit, the word "merit" used here may not unreasonably seem dangerous and rash. Yet our rhymed psalms sing here too: "the man who does what is right / acts / according to his merit," etc. Learn this, beginner: in translations words often occur to which nothing in the original corresponds. Some say the word OMEN occurs only once in the Bibles, see 1 Kings 20:33. Likewise ARBITRIUM, see Num. 30:14. Those assertions are true if you speak of the Bibles of the Vulgate version. But if you consult the original texts, you will find no words there corresponding to these Latin ones.

units.la: Ps. LXIV. 7. David conquestus de improbis machinationibus hostium suorum, concludit querelam istam his verbis, וְיִרְאוּ אִישׁ וְלֵב עָמֹק Quae Jun. & Pisc. per modum epiphonematis reddunt, adeo intimum viri (vel cujusque) & cor profundum est. Istis autem subjungit vir Dei professionem spei suae de interitu adversariorum, quam exorditur vers. 8. וַיִּירְאוּ אֱלֹהִים Pagn. & sagittavit (enallage temporum) eos Deus sagitta repente id est repentina. erunt (hoc est, durabunt, manebunt, ut 1.Reg.xi.32.) plaga eorum. Quid vulgatus? Ex ultimis verbis versus 7. & primis octavi conflavit unam sententiam, * Accedet homo ad cor altum & exaltabitur Deus. Exaltabitur, LXX. ὑψωθήσεται hoc jesset וַיִּרְם At Aquila vertit ἐμβαλῶ- σει αὐτὸς. Symm. ἀνορθώσει αὐτος. & Chald. וְיִרְמֵי & jaculabitur. Quod vero ad priora attinet, in Graeco ita legitur, ωσ- στλε-
units.tr: Ps. 64:7. Having complained of the wicked schemes of his enemies, David ends this complaint with these words: "and man and a deep heart" [וְיִרְאוּ אִישׁ וְלֵב עָמֹק]. Junius and Piscator render this by way of an epiphonema: "so deep is the inward part of a man (or of each one) and his heart profound." To these words the man of God adds a profession of his hope of the destruction of his adversaries, which he begins in verse 8: "and God shot them" [וַיִּירְאוּ אֱלֹהִים]. Pagninus: "and God shot them with a sudden arrow" (a change of tense), that is, a sudden one; "their wound will be" (that is, will endure, remain, as in 1 Kings 11:32). What does the Vulgate say? From the last words of verse 7 and the first of verse 8 it made one sentence: "A man will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted." "Will be exalted": the LXX has ὑψωθήσεται, which would correspond to Hebrew [וַיִּרְם]. But Aquila has "he himself will hurl" [ἐμβαλῶσει αὐτὸς], Symmachus "he himself will set upright" [ἀνορθώσει αὐτὸς], and the Chaldee [וְיִרְמֵי], "and he will cast." As for the first part, the Greek reads as follows:

units.la: σταλύσπλαι ἀνθρωπῷ· ηγὴ καρδία βαθεῖα. * Accedet homo & cor profundum, Cenomanus in collatione agnoscit, voculam AD inmendo cubare & pro ET irrepsisse. Non iuber huc convectare ineptas multorum expositiones. Sufficiet annotasse, Lombardum lib. 1. distinct. 17. litera H hunc locum praeter mentem. Psalmographi allegasse. Vide & judica.
units.tr: "A man will approach" [προσελεύσεται ἀνθρώπῳ], "and the deep heart" [καὶ καρδία βαθεῖα]. Cenomanus, in his collation, recognises that the little word AD ("to") has crept in through a copying error in place of ET ("and"). I will not drag in here the foolish explanations of many. It will suffice to note that Lombard, *Sentences* book 1, distinction 17, letter H, has cited this passage against the mind of the Psalmist. See and judge.

units.la: Ps. LXVIII 21. Increpa feras arundinis.] Ebr. נְזַר הַיַּרְדֵּן קָנָה Vox Ebraea indifferens est ad vitam, vivum, animal, bestiam, feram & catervam. Hinc alii, catervam arundinis id est arundiferam, alii feram arundinis vertunt. Qui catervam arundinis interpretantur, per arundinem tela vel lanceas intelligunt. certe Plinius lib. 16. cap. 36. prodidit, multos arundinibus pro lanceis usos fuisse, & toto oriente arundinib. bella gesta fuisse. Hic Virgil. haret lateri letbalis arundo, id est sagitta, quae eidem volucris & volans arundo.
units.tr: Ps. 68:21. "Rebuke the wild beast of the reeds" [גְּעַר חַיַּת קָנֶה]. The Hebrew word is indifferent: it means life, living thing, animal, beast, wild beast, and also a troop. So some translate "a troop of reeds", that is, reed-bearing, others "a wild beast of the reed." Those who render "a troop of reeds" understand by reed spears or lances. Certainly Pliny, book 16, ch. 36, reports that many used reeds for lances, and that wars were waged with reeds throughout the whole East. Here Virgil has "the deadly reed clings to his side," that is, an arrow, which is a reed both when it lies still and when it flies.

units.la: Namque volans liquidis in nubibus arsit arundo.
units.tr: "For the flying reed burned in the clear clouds."

units.la: Ex Ovidius Metam x. distrinxit arundine pectus. Qui feram reddunt, collective accipiunt, & crudeles efferatosque Ecclesiae hostes intelligunt. Sed cur dicit erundinis? Bellarm. Per feras arundinis intelliguntur bestiae sylvestres, quae latent inter arundineta & per has bestias describuntur daemones, qui libenter versantur inter homines vanos, leves & in locis humentibus, ubi regnat luxuria. Alii melius de Aegyptiis intelligunt, infestis ab omni aevo Israelitarum hostibus. Aegyptus autem arundine & carice abundabat, & laudatissimos semper Aegyptiacos calamos fuisse, nullus, opinor, tam in naturali historia hospes est qui ignoret. Carices & calami pro Nilo aut Aegypto hieroglyphice adhibentur. Et Augustus in nummo cuso, ob victoriam de Antonio & Cleopatra, pro Aegypto Crocodilum cum arundine posuit. Juxta horum ergo interpretationem Aegyptii comparantur feris in arundineto stabulantibus. Rev. D. Sculteus putabat Regem Pharaonem intelligi, Qui Aegyptum nobis descripserunt, inquit, testatum & hoc reliquerunt, flumen alluisse regiam Pharaonis, in flumine autem isto fuisse arundinetum. Per feram ergo arundinis Regem Aegypti intelligit, cujus milites & duces convenienter tauros & vitulos nominavit. Lxx. Ταυρὸν ... vocem καλάμος. Latinus optime reddidit, arundinis. Augustinus vocem illam in versioue retinuit, atque ad eam hæc commentatus est, Increpa feras calami. Nam & feræ sunt, quoniam non intelligendo nocent. Et feræ calami sunt, quia scripturarum sensum suo errore pervertunt. Per calamum quippe tam convenienter scriptura significantur, quam sermo per linguam; secundum quod dicitur, lingua Hebræa vel alia qualibet, per efficientem sc. id quod efficitur. Vsitatum autem est in Latino eloquio, ut scriptura stylus vocetur, quod stylo fiat. Ita ergo & calamus, quod calamo fiat. Dicit Apostolus Petrus, indoctos & instabiles pervertere scripturas ad proprium suum interitum. Hæ ergo sunt feræ calami. Hæc Augustinus, deceptus, opinor, ambiguitate vocis calamus. Vox Ebræa קנה unde Latinorum canna, aliquando calamum mensorium, aliquando calamum aromaticum; aliquando etiam communem, seu arundinem significat. Est & calamus artificialis per similitudinem, qualis in candelabro describitur Exod. xxv. Accipitur & pro ligno illo transversario in statera, Jesaj xlvi. 6. Non ignoro Memphiticos seu Ægyptiacos calamos huic usui olim inserviisse, id quod ex Martiale liquet at vocem Ebr. קולמוס pro calamo scriptorio, quem Ebraeii vocant & Lxx. quoque καλαμος reddidere, non putem in originario textu uspiam usurpari.
units.tr: From Ovid, Metamorphoses book 10: "he pierced his breast with a reed." Those who render "wild beast" take the word collectively and understand the cruel and savage enemies of the Church. But why does he say "of reeds"? Bellarmine: "By the wild beasts of the reeds are meant the savage beasts that lie hidden among the reed beds, and by these beasts are described the demons, who love to dwell among vain, frivolous men and in damp places, where luxury reigns." Others understand the Egyptians better, enemies of the Israelites from all time. Egypt abounded in reed and sedge, and that the Egyptian reeds were always most famous, I think no one who is at home in natural history fails to know. Sedges and reeds are used hieroglyphically for the Nile or for Egypt. Augustus, on a coin struck to celebrate his victory over Antony and Cleopatra, placed a crocodile with a reed for Egypt. According to this interpretation, then, the Egyptians are compared to beasts dwelling in a reed bed. The Reverend Dr Sculteus thought King Pharaoh was meant: "Those who described Egypt to us," he says, "have also left it on record that the royal palace of Pharaoh was washed by a river, and in that river there was a reed bed." So by "the wild beast of the reeds" he understands the King of Egypt, whose soldiers and commanders he fittingly called bulls and calves. The LXX has "bull" [ταῦρον] ... and the word "reed" [κάλαμος]. The Latin rendered it very well as "of reeds." Augustine kept the word in his version and commented on it thus: "Rebuke the beasts of the reed. For they are beasts, because they harm by not understanding. And they are beasts of the reed, because they pervert the sense of Scripture by their error. For by reed Scripture is signified as aptly as speech by the tongue, according as we say the Hebrew tongue or any other, naming the efficient for the thing effected. It is also customary in Latin usage to call the writing 'stylus', because it is made with a stylus; so too the 'calamus' because it is made with a reed. The Apostle Peter says that the unlearned and unstable pervert the Scriptures to their own destruction. These, then, are the beasts of the reed." So Augustine, deceived, I think, by the ambiguity of the word calamus. The Hebrew word [קנה], whence Latin canna, sometimes means a measuring rod, sometimes aromatic cane, sometimes also the common reed or cane. There is also an artificial reed by likeness, such as is described on the candlestick in Exod. 25. It is also used for the transverse beam of a balance, Isa. 46:6. I am aware that Memphite or Egyptian reeds were once used for writing, as is clear from Martial. But I do not think the Hebrew word [קולמוס] for a writing pen, which the Hebrews use, and which the LXX also rendered as καλαμος, is used anywhere in the original text.

units.la: Versf. penult Mirabilis est Deus in sanctis suis ] Vide quæ notamus ad Ps. cl.
units.tr: Penultimate verse: "God is wonderful in his saints" [Ps. 68:36]. See what we note on Ps. 150.

units.la: Ps. lxxi: 16. Quoniam non cognovi literaturam, introibo in potentias Domini ]. Rursus posui interpretationem vulgatam. Ebr. בי לא ידעתי ספורות / & pertinent ad uerf. 15. Os meum narrabit justitiam tuam, & quotidie salutem tuam, quamvis non noverim numeros. quamvis beneficia tua tanta & tam varia sint, ut recensere ea non evaleam. ספר numerare, unde sipbra & Belg. Epferen. Symm. ὁ γὰρ οἶδα ἐξαριθμῆσαι. Sa notat in Chald: esse numerum, vid. beneficiorum Dei; & Belgica Lovaniensium, om dat ick 't ghetal niet gheweten en hebbe. An ergo literatura & numerus idem sunt? Lxx. hic plusculum à fontibus recessere, ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα γραμματέας. Quod in Psalt. Romano vertitur, negotiationem. Quomodo & Chrysost. & Augusti. & Arnobius & Lombardus & alii legerunt. Sed & Gelasius Papa, cujus hæc citantur verba, in Decreto; Distinctione 88. cap. consequens est. Consequens est, ut illa quoque quæ de Picenis partibus nuper ad nos missa relatio nuntiavit, non praetereunda putaremus. Id est, plurimos clericorum negotiationib. inhone-stis & turpib. lucris inhiare, nullo pudore censentes Evangelicam lectionem, qua ipse Dominus negotiatores ex templo verberatos asseriturejecisse. Nec Apostolica verba recolentes, quibus ait, nemo militansDeo implicat se negotiis secularibus. Psalmistam quoque David furdadissimulantes, aure cantantem, Quoniam non cognovi negotiationes,introibo in potentias DOMINI. Proinde hujusmodi aut ab indignisposthac quaestibus noverint abstinendum, aut ab omni cujuslibet nego-tiationis ingenio & cupiditate cessandum, &c. En tibi infallibilem& ἀναμαχητον Scripturae interpretem. Sed cum alii codices * γεγμματεὶς legerent, id est literaturas, quam lectionem in vulgata versione retinuerunt Pontifices, variis interpretationibus iisque ab originarii textus simplicitate alienis aperta fenestra est. Vide August. Carthus. Bell. & alios. Cl. Tarnovius observavit, ex hac versione magnam in omnes literatos redundare ignominiam, quasi illiteratis & ἀμούσοις tantum ad divinorum mysteriorum notitiam pateret aditus. Et fortean, inquit, propterea hodie adeo multi bonas literas & artes humaniores contemnunt, ut tanto facilius (scilicet) ad Deum admittantur, cum Anabaptistis indoctis, aut Enthusiastis fanaticis. Vtinam solus D. Tarnovius tales nosset! In nostris quoque Ecclesiis illiterati quidam homines reperiuntur, qui postquam impudentiae sacramento dixere, jam ad pulpita admissi loca aliquot scripturae (apposite vel incomposite nihil interest) proferre didicerunt, eruditos contemnunt, & se in scola Spiritus Sancti eruditos & θεοδιδάκτας jactitant. In Academiis quoque reperias profanos adolescentes, qui cum omnes sine discrimine idiotas ministros contemnant, ipsi tamen majori insectatione digni sunt. Illi occasionem bonas literas artesque discendi non habuere. Hi habent, & contemnunt. Si vel a limine salutent, non erubescunt profiteri, se id coactos facere, eosque diris devovent, a quibus se cogi existimant. Inertes animae! an ergo scholas Latinas vidisse, ex illis semi-coctos & elementa latinae linguae necdum doctos, prodiisse, vel potius ante legitimam missionem aufugisse, in Academiis annis aliquot otio, Baccho & Veneri litasse, quaestiunculam unam atque alteram ad disputandum proposuisse, in cathedra vero linguam, illam in tabernis & circulis promtissimam, ita cohibere, ac si Angeronam matrem, Har-
units.tr: Ps. 71:16. "Because I have not known literature, I will enter into the powers of the Lord." Again I have kept the Vulgate rendering. Hebrew: "for I have not known the recountings" [כי לא ידעתי ספורות]. These words belong with verse 15: "My mouth shall tell of your righteousness and daily of your salvation, though I do not know the numbers", that is, though your benefits are so great and so various that I am unable to recount them. The verb [ספר] means "to number", whence the Syriac *sipra*, and the Belgic version of Louvain has "I have not known the number." Symmachus: "for I do not know how to count them up" [οὐ γὰρ οἶδα ἐξαριθμῆσαι]. The Chaldee gives the sense of a count of God's benefits. Are then "literature" and "number" the same? The LXX has departed a little more from the sources here: "because I do not know scribes" [ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα γραμματέας]. This is rendered in the Roman Psalter as "business" (negotiationem), as Chrysostom, Augustine, Arnobius, Lombard and others also read it. But Pope Gelasius, whose words are cited in the Decretum, Distinction 88, chapter *Consequens est*, also quotes this: "It follows that we should not pass over what the report recently sent to us from the Picene region announced: that many clerics gape after dishonest trades and shameful gains, with no shame, judging that the Gospel reading, in which the Lord himself is said to have cast out the merchants from the temple, does not apply to them; nor do they recall the words of the Apostle, 'No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in secular business'; and they pretend not to hear the Psalmist David singing, 'Because I have not known business, I will enter into the powers of the Lord.' Therefore such men should henceforth either abstain from unworthy gains, or cease from every turn of mind and desire for any trade whatever, etc." Behold your infallible and unconquerable interpreter of Scripture! But since other codices read γραμματεῖς, that is, literatures, and the Papists retained this reading in the Vulgate, an open window has been made for various interpretations, alien to the simplicity of the original text. See Augustine, the Carthusians, Bellarmine and others. Clemens Tarnovius observed that great disgrace falls on all the learned from this version, as if the way to the knowledge of the divine mysteries lay open only to the unlettered and unmusical. "And perhaps," he says, "that is why today so many despise good letters and the more humane arts, so that they may be the more easily admitted to God along with uneducated Anabaptists or fanatical Enthusiasts." Would that Tarnovius alone knew such men! In our own churches too there are found illiterate men who, once they have sworn the oath of impudence, and have been admitted to the pulpit, have learned to produce some passages of Scripture (whether aptly or unaptly makes no difference), and they despise the learned and boast that they are taught in the school of the Holy Spirit and are God-taught. In the academies too you may find profane young men, who, while they despise all teachers without distinction as ignorant, are themselves more worthy of harsh censure. The former had no opportunity to learn good letters and arts; these have the opportunity, and despise it. If they greet you from the threshold, they are not ashamed to profess that they do so under compulsion, and they curse those whom they think are forcing them. Lifeless souls! Did they ever see Latin schools, and did they emerge from them half-cooked, not yet learned in the rudiments of the Latin tongue, or rather flee before their lawful dismissal, spend some years in the academies in idleness, drinking and love, propose one or two little questions for disputation, and then, in the chair, rein in that tongue, most ready in taverns and circles, as though Angerona were your mother and Har-

units.la: * Similiter & Erra 8. variant libri Namque ubi Rom. Edi-tio habet γεγμματ- τοῖς, in aliis est γεγμματ- τοῖς. Harpocratem patrem habuissetis, an, inquam, hæc & id genus alia militiæ vestræ flagitia vobis ejusmodi videntur, ob quæ in literatorum classem transcribi mereamini? Erit, erit aliquando, cum vos profanæ vestræ desidiæ pœnitebit.
units.tr: * Likewise Ezra 8 the books vary. For where the Roman edition has γεγραμμα- [gegramma-] with one ending, in others it reads γεγραμμα- [gegramma-] with another. Had you a father Harpocrates? Or, I ask, do these and other such disgraces of your soldiering seem to you the sort of thing for which you deserve to be enrolled among the men of letters? It will, it will come one day, when you regret your profane idleness.

units.la: Ps. LXXI. 6. * quoniam tu es patientia mea] Ita vulg. Lxx. — ν' ὑπομονὴ μου. Augustinus, verba Bellarmini, per patientiam intelligit tolerantiam dolorum & persecutionum, ut sensus sit, eripe me de manu peccatorum, dando mihi patientiam, ne per impatientiam consentiam peccato. Et quidem verbum Græcum & Latinum hanc expositionem patiuntur; sed vox Ebr. significat expectationem & spem, ac per hoc patientia hoc loco significat patientiam in expectando potius quam in tolerando, juxta illud, per patientiam expectamus, Rom.8. & Jacobi V. ecce agricola expectat pretiosum fructum terræ, patienter ferens, donec accipiat pluviam, &c. Hæc Bellar. Ebraice est תִּקְוָתִי expectatio mea. In quo nulla patientiæ seu tolerantiæ adversorum significatio. Sensus est, tu es ille quem unum expecto, in quo uno spem colloco. In loco isto Iacobi est μακροθυμεῖν, quod proprie significat longanimem esse, qualem Ebraei אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם vocant. Rom.8. est ὑπομονή. Quam vocem itidem invenies in eadem significatione Luc.viii. καρποφορῶσιν ἐν ὑπομονῇ, fructum ferunt in patientia. De quo loco B. Scultetus in suo ad Exercit. Euang. præloquio ita infit; Quoties ego non sine stomacho Homiliastas nostros audivi parabolam Servatoris nostri de seminante & semine explicantes, ad verba illa Luc.8. Et ferunt fructum in patientia, in locum communem de patientia fidelium in arumnis excurrere, & conquisitis hinc inde argumentis auditores ad rerum adversarum tolerantiam animare, cum alia longe verborum illorum mens sit, &c. Tu disce tiro, ὑπομονὴν id est patientiam, in S. Literis duplicem esse, unam activam, alteram passivam. Activam vocant ἀμακρόθυμος ἔντα, licet non satis apposite, quam Ebræi אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם dicerent, id est μακροθυμίαν, geduld met peinant hebben/ Atque hæc ὑπομονὴ Deo sæpe in sacris literis tribuitur, E. gr. Exod. 34. Rom. 2. & 9. 1. Petri 3. Passivam eam vocant, quæ circa res adversas & calamitates versatur. Ea in Vet. Testamento propria voce non exprimitur, sed silentium vocatur Psal.39. Jesa53. * Hunc vero locum Ps. 71. Tu es patientia mea, si commode volumus interpretari, hic erit sensus, Tu es ille quem patienter expecto, tu csob.
units.tr: Ps. LXXI. 6. * for thou art my patience] So the Vulgate and the Septuagint: ν' ὑπομονὴ μου [hypomonē mou]. Augustine, and Bellarmine after him, understands by patience the endurance of pains and persecutions, so that the sense is: deliver me from the hand of sinners by giving me patience, lest through impatience I consent to sin. Indeed the Greek and the Latin word may bear this explanation, but the Hebrew word means expectation and hope, and so patience in this place means patience in waiting rather than in enduring, as in "through patience we wait" (Rom. 8), and in James 5: "behold, the husbandman waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently bearing it, until he receives the rain," and so on. Thus Bellarmine. In Hebrew it is תִּקְוָתִי [tiqvati], "my expectation", in which there is no sense of enduring patience or tolerance of adversities. The sense is: thou art he whom I alone expect, in whom alone I place my hope. In the passage in James the word is μακροθυμεῖν [makrothymein], which properly means to be long-suffering, what the Hebrews call אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם ['orekh 'appayim]. In Romans 8 it is ὑπομονή [hypomonē]. You will find the same word with the same meaning in Luke 8: καρποφορῶσιν ἐν ὑπομονῇ [karpophorousin en hypomonē], they bear fruit in patience. On this passage B. Scultetus, in his preface to the Exercitationes Evangelicae, begins thus: How often, not without irritation, have I heard our preachers explaining the parable of our Saviour about the sower and the seed, when they come to the words of Luke 8, "and they bring forth fruit with patience", and run off into a common place about the patience of the faithful in afflictions, and, gathering arguments from here and there, rouse their hearers to bear adversities, when the meaning of those words is quite different, &c. You, novice, should learn that ὑπομονή [hypomonē], that is patience, in the Sacred Letters is twofold: one active, the other passive. The active they call ἀμακρόθυμος [makrothymia], though not very aptly; the Hebrews would call it אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם ['orekh 'appayim], that is μακροθυμία [makrothymia], to have patience with worry. And this ὑπομονή [hypomonē] is often ascribed to God in the sacred letters, for example Exodus 34, Romans 2 and 9, and 1 Peter 3. The passive kind they call that which concerns adverse things and calamities. In the Old Testament this is not expressed by a proper word, but is called silence in Psalm 39 and Isaiah 53. But if we wish to interpret this passage, Ps. 71, "thou art my patience", suitably, the sense will be: thou art he whom I wait for patiently, thou ...

units.la: Vide hic ineptientem Lombardum lib.1.dist. 17. E. es objectum patientis illius expectationis, qua tuum auxilium praestolor. Metonym. atque eo sensu occurrit Ebr. תקוה ejusque apud Lxx. interpretamentum ὑπομονή Palm. 38. 11. lxi. 5; Ier. 14. 8. xvii. 13. * Postremo, ὑπομονή apud lxx. non occurrit nisi ubi in Ebr. est תקוה / quae vox patientiam seu tolerantiam adversorum nusquam significat.
units.tr: See here the foolish Lombard, book 1, distinction 17. Therefore you are the object of that patient expectation by which I await your help. It occurs in this sense metonymically, and the Hebrew תקוה [tiqvah], whose rendering in the Septuagint is ὑπομονή [hypomonē], is found in Psalm 38:11, 61:5; Jeremiah 14:8, 17:13. Lastly, ὑπομονή [hypomonē] does not occur in the Septuagint except where the Hebrew has תקוה [tiqvah], a word which nowhere means patience or tolerance of adversities.

units.la: Ps. LXXII. 14. Ex usuris & iniquitate redime me. ] Lxx. ἐκ τόκων καὶ ἀδικίας, &c. Usuras Allegorice hic interpretatur Augustinus, Quae sunt usura ista nisi peccata, quae etiam debita nominantur? Usuras autem appellatas puto, quia plus mali invenitur in suppliciis, quam commissum est in peccatis. Nam verbi gratia, cum homicida corpus tantum hominis perimat, anima autem nihil nocere possit, ipsius & anima & corpus perditur in Gehenna. Propter hujusmodi contemptores praesentis praecepti & irrisores futuri supplicii dictum est, Ego veniens cum usuris exigerem. Ab his usuris redimentur anima pauperum sanguine illo qui fusus est in remissionem peccatorum. Redimet ergo ab usuris, redimendo peccata, quibus debeantur ampliora supplicia. Redimet ab iniquitate, adjuvando per gratiam, etiam ad faciendam justitiam. Bellarminus, Homo per originale peccatum debitor factus est mortis aeterna. Atque hoc est debitum capitale. Sed dum hujus debiti solutio differtur, iniquus exactor Diabolus exigit usuras, impellens quotidie ad nova peccata, quae sunt poena primi peccati, & dum horum peccatorum poena differtur, usurae transeunt in sortem principalem. Ita quo diutius peccator vivit, eo magis debitum crescit. Pulcrae certe & piae meditationes, at nullo aut saltem vacillanti fundamento nixae. Ebraice סהוך ויהמס / Eadem vox הוך Psal 55. 12. concurrit cum מרמה / ubi vulg. quoque usura & dolus. Lxx. utrobique τόκος reddidere. Illam vocem vulgatus interpretatus est. Alterutrum spectasse videntur Lxx. Senes. Aut affinitatem illam, quae inter הוך & τόκος quae certe tanta est, ut nisi inter omnes constaret, vocem τόκος à Graeco τίκτω seu potius τίκω deflexam esse Hebraea vox censeri posset. Aut affinitatem, quae inter fraudem, si hanc propriam ejus significatione agnovere & usuras. Apud usurarios enim fraudes & doli utramque paginam. הוך vox ambigua est. Est enim vel in forma regiminis, vox absoluto הוך / ut מור / מורה & extra dubium significat medium, vel est in forma absoluta, & fraudem, dolumve significat. Ita certe ipsi Pagn. Arias vertêre, & agnoscunt Gençbr. Sa & alii. Quia vero cum affixis in hac significatione non reperitur, alii à חוך cam deflectunt, fraus enim corde tegitur & in medio hominis quasi stabulatur, alii à תך / unde איש חכמים vir fraudum, Prov. 29. 12. Ebræum תוך à Lxx. ter redditum invenio per τἑκ⊙, Psal. videlicet 55.12. hoc, & Jerem. 1x. 6. ubi tamen non legitur בתוך מרמה ומרמה sed בתוך מרמה / Ideoque ab ipso quoque Pagn. vertitur, inter dolosos, Arias, ipseque adeo vulgatus, ad verbum, in medio doli. Verum statui illic posset asyndeton, vel locutio ἐκ ⊙ἀχλ, si necessitas cogeret. Vides itaque ipsum vulgatum non ubique hoc Græcorum interpretamentum probasse. Sed & ipsi LXX. Psal. 9. 29. seu ut Ebræi numerant Psal x. 7. eandem vocem δόλον reddidere. Vt ergo ad locum præsentem regrediamur, promittit his verbis Psaltes, Deum servaturum suos adversus fraudulentas hostium machinationes & violentas eorundem oppressiones. Vsuras ut intelligamus nulla est necessitas, neq; etiam quadrat huic loco. Allegoriæ ergo illæ in litera fundamentum non habent. Ex sola vocum affinitate firmum originationis argumentum peti non potest, nec tum quidem, quando significationes coincidunt. E. gr. à סתר latuit, nomen habet Saturnus, qui Latio quoque nomen dedit. Ab ejusdem participio Hofal מסתר abscondite, quidam deflectunt μυστήριον. Et tamen non est dubium, quin à μύω ediivatum sit. Vt enim alias rationes omittam, sicuti à תוך dicendum fuisset τηχ⊙, liquidem inde flexum fuisset, ita & à מסתר μυσθήριον potius. Literis enim ב& ת in Græcorum alphabetho non x & τ (quamvis appellationes earum id innuere videantur) sed χ & θ respondent. Illa vero x & τ Ebræis ף & ט sunt ἀντίσγοφοι. Sequentem sententiam, quæ in Ebræo fatentibus Pontificiis, ita habet, pretiosus erit sanguis eorum in oculis ejus, sic expressit vulgatus, & honorabile nomen eorum coram illo. Genebr. conjectat Græcos primitus scripsisse ἀιμα, at degenerasse tandem in δνομα. Ista autem verba Augustinus, Euthymius & alii quidam ita legunt & interpretantur, & honorabile nomen ejus (Dei) coram illis, quamvis postea alteram quoque lectionem indicet Augustinus. Quia vero hic mentio facta est usurarii, lubet coronidis loco hic exhibere elegantissimum locum Gregorii Nysseni, qui extat in oratione ejus contra usurarios. Qui pecuniam cum fœnore reddendam accipit, speciè beneficii exitium domum reportat. Quemadmodum is qui pracibus vitæ febricitanti poculum porrigit, exhilarat quidem agrum brevi tempore, dum id exhaurit; at paulo post acerbissimum & decuplo gavio-rem febrim misero parit. Sic & qui egeno pecuniam sub fœnore commendat, necessitatem ejus non sublevat, sed calamitatem ejus potius auget. Segnis & exitiabilis est vita usurarii. Nescit labore agrorum colendorum, mercaturam non exercet, sed uno in loco considens immanes domi sua feras nutrit. Vult omnia sibi sine satu & inarata progigni, cui aratrum est calamus, ager, charta, semen atramentum, pluvia tempus, quod illi pecunia fructum occultis incrementis auget & educat. Falx illi repetitio, area domus, in qua miserorum fortunas ventilat.
units.tr: Ps. LXXII. 14. Redeem me from usuries and iniquity.] The Septuagint: ἐκ τόκων καὶ ἀδικίας [ek tokōn kai adikias], etc. Augustine interprets the usuries allegorically here: What are these usuries but sins, which are also called debts? I think they are called usuries because more evil is found in the punishments than was committed in the sins. For example, when a murderer kills only the body of a man, yet the soul cannot harm anything, both soul and body are lost in Gehenna. Because of such despisers of the present precept and mockers of future punishment it was said, "coming I would exact with usury." From these usuries the souls of the poor are redeemed by that blood which was shed for the remission of sins. He will redeem, then, from usuries by redeeming sins, for which greater punishments are owed. He will redeem from iniquity by helping, through grace, even to do justice. Bellarmine: Man has become by original sin a debtor to eternal death. And this is the principal debt. But while payment of this debt is deferred, the unjust exactor, the Devil, exacts usuries, driving us daily to new sins, which are the punishment of the first sin; and while the punishment for these sins is deferred, the usuries pass into the principal sum. So the longer the sinner lives, the more the debt grows. Certainly beautiful and pious meditations, but resting on no firm foundation, or at least a wavering one. In Hebrew it is סהוך ויהמס [...] The same word הוך [tavekh] in Psalm 55:12 occurs together with מרמה [mirmah], where the Vulgate also has usury and deceit. The Septuagint in both places gave τόκος [tokos]. The Vulgate translator rendered that word as usury. The Septuagint seem to have looked to one or the other meaning. Or they may have been looking to the affinity between הוך [tavekh] and τόκος [tokos], which is certainly so great that, unless it were agreed by all that the Greek word τόκος [tokos] is derived from τίκτω [tiktō], or rather τίκω [tikō], the Hebrew word could be regarded as the source. Or they may have been looking to the affinity between usury and fraud, if they recognised fraud in its proper sense, for among usurers fraud and deceit are both sides of the same page. The word הוך [tavekh] is ambiguous. In the construct form it is the absolute form הוך [tavekh], as מור [mor] and מורה [morah], and clearly means middle; or it is in the absolute form and means fraud or deceit. Indeed Pagninus, Arias, and Genebrardus, and Sá and others, so translate it. But since it is not found with affixes in this sense, others derive it from תך [tekh], whence איש חכמים ['ish ḥakhamim], a man of fraud, Prov. 29:12. I find that the Hebrew תוך [tavekh] is rendered three times by the Septuagint as τἑκ⊙ [tek...], namely Psalm 55:12 and Jeremiah 6:6, where, however, the text does not read בתוך מרמה [betokh mirmah] but בתוך מרמה, and so Pagninus translates it among the deceivers; Arias, and the Vulgate itself, literally, in the midst of deceit. Yet one could posit an asyndeton here, or the figure ἐκ ⊙ἀχλ, if necessity required. You see, then, that the Vulgate itself did not everywhere approve this Greek rendering. But the Septuagint too, at Psalm 9:29, or as the Hebrews number it Psalm 10:7, rendered the same word as δόλον [dolon]. So, to return to the present place, the Psalmist in these words promises that God will keep his people against the fraudulent machinations of their enemies and their violent oppression of them. There is no necessity to understand usuries here, nor does it fit this passage. Those allegories therefore have no foundation in the letter. A firm argument of derivation cannot be drawn from the affinity of words alone, not even when the meanings coincide. For example, from סתר [satar], to lie hidden, comes the name Saturnus, who also gave his name to Latium. From the Hophal participle of the same, מסתר [mistar], hidden, some derive μυστήριον [mystērion]. Yet there is no doubt that it was formed from μύω [myō]. To omit other reasons: just as from תוך [tavekh] one would have to say τηχ⊙ [tēch...], since that is how it would have been inflected, so from מסתר [mistar] one would rather say μυσθήριον [musthērion]. For in the Greek alphabet the letters ב and ת correspond not to x and τ (though their names seem to suggest it) but to χ and θ. Those x and τ are, in fact, the counterparts of ף and ט. The following sentence, which Papists concede in Hebrew, reads their blood shall be precious in his sight; the Vulgate expressed it as and their honourable name before him. Genebrardus conjectures that the Greeks originally wrote ἀιμα [haima], but it finally degenerated into δνομα [onoma]. Augustine, Euthymius, and some others read and interpret these words thus: and his (God's) honourable name before them, although Augustine afterwards also notes the other reading. But since mention has been made here of the usurer, I am pleased, as a crown to this discussion, to set out here the most elegant passage of Gregory of Nyssa, which is found in his oration against usurers. He who receives money to be repaid with interest brings home ruin under the appearance of a kindness. As one who offers a cup to a man in a fever of life refreshes the field for a short time while he drinks it, but soon after brings to the wretched man a fever that is most bitter and tenfold more violent, so too he who lends money to the needy under interest does not relieve his need, but rather increases his calamity. The life of the usurer is sluggish and deadly. He does not know the labour of cultivating fields, does not practise trade, but sitting in one place feeds savage beasts in his own house. He wishes everything to spring up for him without sowing and unploughed, for whom the plough is a pen, the field paper, the seed ink, the rain the time, which his money increases and brings to fruit by hidden growth. His scythe is repeated demand, his threshing floor his house, where he winnows the fortunes of the wretched.

units.la: Ibid. verf. 5. Et permanebit cum Sole & ante lunam in generatione & generationem] Ita vulg. Lxx. καὶ συμπεφωμένη τῆ ἡλίῳ καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς σελήνης * γενεὰς γενεῶν. Hæc in Ebræo aliter leguntur, Timebunt te cum sole, & coram luna [in] generationem generationum. Timebunt te, o Deus subditi tui, quamdiu durabunt Sol & Luna. Vaticinatur de felici statu subditorum Christi, qui consistit in vero cultu, eumque amplificat ab adjuncta duratione, atque ita eadem opera perpetuitatem regni Christi docet. Notet tiro locutiones illas synonymas, cum Sole, coram Luna, & verf. 7. donec non erit Luna, & verf. 17. coram sole in æternum. Pf. cii. verf. ult. semen eorum stabilietur coram te, לפניך / Lxx. εἰς αἰῶνας. In eundem modum exponit R. Sal. præceptum primum, non habebis Deum alienum coram me id est quamdiu ego ero, in æternum. Hæc non observata, atque insuper vox ירוך male reddita, doctissimis interpretibus multa ἀπογραφὰς hic commentandi occasionem præbuere. Euthymius, ostendere volens propheta Christi divinitatem sine principio esse & sine, duobus magnis luminaribus eam comparavit. Permanebit, inquit cum sole, hoc est, erit Sol. Est autem peculiaris loquendi modus apud Scripturam sacram, ut tempus usque ad aliquid determinet, & quod sequitur non neget, Et hoc pacto Christi perpetuitatem explicat ex parte finis. Deinde etiam declarat quomodo sit absque principio & dicit, quod erat ante lunam. Ita & Theodoretus, Lyra, & alii. Decepit doctissimos viros vocula πρὸ, quam observant Bellarm. Genebr. Sa, hic positam, pro ἐνώπιον, & ἐμπροσθεν ante, coram certe non solum
units.tr: Ibid. vers. 5. And it shall remain with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation]: so the Vulgate and the Seventy: and it shall remain with the sun, and from the moon, generations of generations [καὶ συμπεφωμένη τῆ ἡλίῳ καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς σελήνης * γενεὰς γενεῶν]. The Hebrew reads differently: They shall fear you with the sun, and before the moon, generation of generations [Hebrew]. They shall fear you, O God, your subjects, as long as the sun and moon endure. The psalm prophesies of the happy state of Christ's subjects, which consists in true worship, and it extends that state by the duration added to it, and so by the same means teaches the perpetuity of Christ's kingdom. The student should note these synonymous expressions: with the sun, before the moon; and at verse 7, until there is no moon; and at verse 17, before the sun for ever. Psalm 102, last verse: their seed shall be established before you [לפניך], the Seventy for ages [εἰς αἰῶνας]. In the same way Rabbi Saadia explains the first commandment, you shall have no other god before me, that is, as long as I shall be, for ever. These points were not observed, and besides, the word ירוך was badly rendered, and this gave the most learned interpreters many occasions for commentary here. Euthymius, wishing to show that the prophet's Christ has a divinity without beginning and without end, compared him with the two great lights. He shall remain, he says, with the sun, that is, he shall be as the sun. It is, however, a peculiar way of speaking in Holy Scripture to fix a time up to some point, without denying what follows. And in this way he explains the perpetuity of Christ from the side of the end. Then he also declares how he is without beginning, and says that he was before the moon. So also Theodoret, Lyra, and others. The little word πρό, which Bellarmine, Geneva, and Sa note as placed here for ἐνώπιον and ἐμπροσθεν, meaning before or in the presence of, has deceived very learned men.

units.la: alii ἐς γενεὰς γενεῶν. lum Ebraeum [?] & Latinorum ante; sed & Graecorum [illegible, ~3 letters] & locum & tempus adsignificat. De tempore res notissima est. De loco, Aristoph. [Greek, ~3 words] ante januas, prae foribus. Aristot. in Rhet. [Greek] ante urbem. Atque ita Salust, pro curia, id est ante curiam. Deinde quis sensus, inquit Bellar. permanebit ante Lunam, atque expresse pronuntiat, non nisi absurdissime dici. August. valde hic sudat. Inter alia haec ejus verba sunt, cum dixisset ante lunam, volens exponere, pro quanam re lunam posuerit, generationes inquit generationum. Tanquam diceret ante Lunam, hoc est, ante generationes generationum. Carthus. cum hac Euthymii, Theod. &c. expositione alteram conjungit, quam ex eodem Euthymio mutuatus est, vid. per Solem, Deum patrem; per Lunam Ecclesiam posse intelligi. Piget locum integrum describere.
units.tr: …the Hebrew [?] and the Latins' before; but the Greeks' [illegible] also signifies both place and time. The matter of time is very well known. As to place, Aristophanes [Greek, about three words], before the doors, in front of the gates. Aristotle, in the Rhetoric [Greek], before the city. And so Sallust, for the senate house, that is, before the senate house. Then, says Bellarmine, what sense is there in he shall remain before the moon? And he declares expressly that it can be said only most absurdly. Augustine sweats hard over this point. Among his other words are these: When he had said before the moon, wishing to explain for what thing he had put the moon, he says generations of generations. As if he had said before the moon, that is, before generations of generations. The Carthusian joins to this exposition of Euthymius, Theodoret, etc. another, which he borrowed from the same Euthymius, namely that through the sun God the Father, and through the moon the Church, can be understood. I am reluctant to describe the whole passage.

units.la: Ps. LXXIV. Operatus est salutem in medio terrae. ] id est palam, omnibus spectantibus, non in angulo aliquo. Inter cetera argumenta petitionis, qua liberationem a captivitate petunt, illud quoque recensent, quod jam olim majores eorum Deus liberasset. Sunt qui Judaeam per medium terra intelligi existimant, aut ejus metropolin Jerusalem, illam [Greek] ὀφθαλμὸν [Greek] τῆς οἰκουμένης. Judaeam certe in terrae habitabilis, priscis cognitae, quasi corde sitam fuisse, non absurde dictam, censebit, qui tabulas Georg. inspexerit. Nam oceanus Indicus ad orientem a Palaestina non minus distat, quam ad occidentem Hispanicus, Gallicus, Britannicus. Ad Aquilonem est mare glaciale sub ipso polo arctico. Ad meridiem vastus oceanus sub antarctico, quo Aethiopiae & Africae magna pars cingitur. In medio quasi in theatro est ipsa Judaea, illiusque metropolis Jerosolyma. Hinc existimant Jerusalem Jezech. 38. 12. vocari [Hebrew] umbilicum terra. Casaub. Exercit. XVI. Sect. 83. Inspice sphaeram, inquit, & rationem ini vii. istorum climatum, quae sola norant veteres, videbis non inepte, etsi pingui minerva, Jerusalem olim creditam fuisse multis quasi umbilicum terrae habitabilis. Addit postea, Germanum Patriarcham in sua theoria pro certo & confesso ponere, in urbe Jerusalem [Greek], ipsissimum terra medium circumscribi. Addit ex secretis * Sanuti, alios in ipsa urbe certum locum designasse, in quo ipsum umbilicum constituerent. Hieronymus ad Je-
units.tr: Ps. 74. He has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.] That is, openly, with all looking on, not in some corner. Among the other arguments of their petition, by which they seek deliverance from captivity, they also recount that God had already delivered their forefathers long ago. There are those who think that by the middle of the earth Judaea is meant, or its metropolis Jerusalem, that [navel] ὀμφαλὸν and [eye] ὀφθαλμὸν of the inhabited world. Anyone who has looked at the maps of Georg. will judge that Judaea, situated as it were in the heart of the inhabitable earth known to the ancients, was not absurdly so called. For the Indian Ocean to the east is no less distant from Palestine than the Spanish, Gallic and British seas are to the west. To the north is the icy sea beneath the very arctic pole. To the south lies the vast ocean beneath the antarctic, by which a great part of Ethiopia and Africa is girdled. In the middle, as it were in a theatre, lies Judaea itself, and its metropolis Jerusalem. Hence they think that Jerusalem is called in Ezekiel 38:12 [Hebrew] the navel of the earth. Casaubon, Exercitationes XVI, section 83: Look at the sphere, he says, and the reasoning of those seven climates which the ancients alone knew, and you will see that, though with a clumsy wisdom, Jerusalem was of old not foolishly believed by many to be, as it were, the navel of the habitable earth. He adds afterwards that the German Patriarch in his theory takes as certain and agreed that the very centre of the earth is circumscribed in the city of Jerusalem [Greek]. He adds, from the secret writings of Sanutus, that others have designated a definite place in the city itself where they would set up the very navel.

units.la: * lib. c. 3. part. 3 zech. cap. v. 5. Ista est Jerusalem, in medio gentium posui eam & in circuitu ejus terras, sic commentatur, Jerusalem in medio mundi sitam hic idem propheta testatur, umbilicum terræ eam esse demonstrans — A partibus enim orientis cingitur plaga quæ appellatur Asia. A partibus occidentis ejus quæ vocatur Europa. A meridie & Austro, Lybia & Africa. A septentrione, Scythia, Armenia & Persidè & cunctis Ponti nationibus, Josephus paulo aliter lib. 3. Belli Jud. cap. 4. Media ejus (Judææ) est Jerosolyma. Quocirca quidam non sine ratione umbilicum ejus terræ urbem illam vocavere. Vides ergo, quod de umbilico terræ Jezech. xxxviii. 12. dicitur, alios de terra habitabili, alios de sola Judæa accepisse, in cujus medio fuerit Jerusalem. Res eodem redit. Si enim Judæa fuit in medio τῆς οἰκουμένης, atque in hujus rursus medio Jerusalem, hanc quoque in medio τῆς οἰκουμένης sitam esse non absurde dixeris. Villalpandus tom. 3 pag. 14. Quod si id experimento fortasse quispiam cognoscere cupiat, terrestrem globum adeat, circumque pedem, alterum Hierosolymis figat, alterum in ultimos usque Africæ fines protendat & circumagat. Sic enim fiet, ut circulum describat, qui omnes olim cogniti orbis terminos comprehendat. Atque hac fortasse causa est, cur Deus Sionem elegerit, ex qua legem suam toto terrarum orbe diffunderet, nimirum, ut e media mundi regione, cetera æqua ratione distantes Dei verbum facilius & commodius cognoscerent. De Sion, inquit vates, exibit Lex & verbum Domini de Jerusalem. Hæc etiam fortean causa erit, cur regiones cœli respectu urbis Jerusalem aut Judææ in S. L. observentur, dum ex. gr. ea loca, quæ urbi Jerusalem ad occidentem cadunt, nominatim mare, mediterraneum vid. quod & respectu multorum lacuum, quos maria quoque Ebræi vocant, magnum dicitur, pro occidente accipiunt. Qua de re in censura nostra ad vulgatam versionem Pentateuchi pag. 88. plura diximus. Kimchi ad Jezech. v. 5. Habitatores ejus collocavi illic in bonum ipsorum, quia electa est pra omnibus terris, pulcra climate, gaudium totius terræ, Psal. 82.2. Est enim in medio τῆς οἰκουμένης. Ideo & aer ejus est salubberrimus & temperatior quam alibi. Et R. Sal. בתוך הגוים explicat באמצע העולם / in medio mundi. Kimchi rursus ad Jezech. xxxviii. 12. vocatur terra Israel umbilicus terræ, לפי שהוא באמצע העולם כמו שהטבור באמצע הגוף quia est in medio mundi, sicuti umbilicus est in medio corporis. 12. Ita Cicero orat. v i. in VeVerrem, Ennam in medio Siciliae sitam, ejus umbilicum vocat. Et Plinius ambilicum Italiae circa lacum Reatinum esse dixit, lib. 3. cap. 12. Atque huc pertinet observatio Vitruvii (lib. 3. cap. 1.) qui de admirabili corporis humani commensuratione agens, affirmat hominem, si extensis in altum manibus pedibusque ambitum circuli contingat, centrum istius circuli in umbilico constitui, quam sententiam Galeno quoq; adscribunt, lib. 2. de placitis Hippocratis & lib. 15. de usu partium. Sunt tamen, qui Judaeam seu Metropolin ejus Jerusalem, non ideo umbilicum terrae dictam censent, quod in medio terrae, sed quod in editiori ac proinde munito magis loco sita fuerit. Certe Tremell. & Jun. in editiore loco istius terrae. id est, inquiunt, in Judaea montosa, cujus edita loca Judaei fere incolebant securitatis causa. Adducunt autem locum parallelum ex Judicum ix. 37. Ecce populus descendens ex umbilico terrae, id est editiore loco terrae. Juvat Chald. qui utrobique vertit, [Hebrew] fortitudinem terrae Et R. Salomo [Hebrew] altitudinem & robur terrae Interpretatur. Et Kimchi ad locum Judicum, [Hebrew] [Hebrew] / hoc, sicuti umbilicus in homine est medium in corpore, ita & quod medium est in terra, vel eminentior ejus locus, umbilicus vocatur. Ejusmodi loca Graeci μασὸς & μασχαλης à mammae similitudine vocitant. Sed nimis prolixi jam fuimus circa locum Jezechielis. Verbo. Dicta fuerit Jerusalem umbilicus terrae, sive propter τὸ μέσον, sive propter τὸ ἔσχατον, quod vid. fuerit urbs sublimis, excelsa, inter circumjacentes veluti caput in corpore eminens, ut loquitur Josephus, non tamen ulla necessitas erat hunc locum Psalmi, operatus est salutem in medio terrae cum illo conferendi, ut per medium terrae, iste τῆς οἰκουμένης vel Ἰσδαίας ὀμφαλὸς Jerusalem intelligatur. Et ut id daretur, quae necessitas vel de nativitate vel de passione Christi locum hunc interpretari? Et tamen doctissimi quique Patres istum sensum huic loco attribuere. Augustinus lib. 17. de Civ. Dei, c. 4. ita interpretatus hunc locum est, Deus Christus, operatus est salutem nostram in medio terrae quum verbum caro factum est & terreno habitavit in corpore. Vide quae supra ad 1. Sam. 2. ex doctissimo Patre produximus. Eucherius in Quaest. Veteris Test. in medio terrae] id est in Judaea, in quo Christus per crucem liberavit mundum, quam alibi umbilicum terrae dicendam putant. Vel in medio terrae id est in utero virginali. Caeterum prior illa expositio quam affert Eucherius communior est. Thomas parte 3. quaest. 46. art. 10. quaerit, utrum Christus convenienti loco passus sit. Concludit, ut par erat, pro ajente sententia, adducto loco isto Luc. 13. non contingit prophetam perire extra Jerusalem. In resp. ad primam objectionem ait primo, Jerusalem fuisse locum a Deo electum ad oblationem sacrificiorum, quae Christi passionem figurabant. 2. quia virtus passionis ejus ad totum mundum diffundenda erat, in medio terrae habitabilis pati voluit id est in Jerusalem, Unde dicitur in Psalmo 73. Deus autem Rex noster ante saecula, operatus est salutem in medio terrae. id est in Jerusalem, &c. Haec Thomas, ad medium terrae propius accedens quam illi qui de Judaea locum intellexere. Alii τὸ τῆς οἰκουμένης μεσαίτατον monstraturi calvariae locum nominarunt, eumque ita dictum voluere a calvaria primi hominis illic sepulti. August. Sermone 71. de tempore, Etiam hoc antiquorum relatione refertur, quod Adam primus homo in ipso illo loco, ubi crux Christi fixa, fuerit olim sepultus & ideo calvariae locum dictum esse, quia caput humani generis ibi dicitur sepultum esse. Huic opinioni haesere Origenes, tract. 35. in Matth. Epiphanius in fine Panarii, Athanas. libro de passione Domini, Theophyl. in Matth. 27. Euthym. ibidem. Cypr. serm. de resurrectione. Ambros. lib. v. Epist. 19. & in Luc. cap. 25. Quae posui fide Genebrardi, Chronol. pag. 17. Illis nunc addo Nonnum,
units.tr: * Book 3, chap. 3, part 3; Zech. chap. v. 5. This is Jerusalem; I have set her in the midst of the nations, and the lands round about her, he comments thus: Jerusalem, situated in the middle of the world, is attested by this same prophet, who shows that it is the navel of the earth. For on the side of the east it is bounded by the region called Asia; on the side of the west by what is called Europe; on the south and south wind by Libya and Africa; on the north by Scythia, Armenia, Persia and all the nations of Pontus. Josephus says it a little differently in Book 3 of the Jewish War, chap. 4: The middle of Judea is Jerusalem. Hence some have not without reason called that city the navel of the land. You see, then, that some have understood the navel of the earth in Ezek. 38:12 to mean the inhabited world, and others only Judea, in whose middle Jerusalem lay. The result comes to the same thing. For if Judea was in the middle of the inhabited world [τῆς οἰκουμένης], and Jerusalem in the middle of Judea, you might not absurdly say that Jerusalem too is set in the middle of the inhabited world [τῆς οἰκουμένης]. Villalpandus, vol. 3, p. 14: If anyone wishes to find this out by experiment, let him go to a terrestrial globe, fix one foot on Jerusalem, and stretch and turn the other as far as the furthest limits of Africa. For in this way he will describe a circle that takes in all the boundaries of the world once known. And perhaps this is the reason why God chose Zion, from which he would spread his law over the whole orb of the earth: namely, so that from the central region of the world the word of God might be more easily and conveniently known by those who are equally distant from it. "From Zion," says the prophet, "shall go forth the law and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." Perhaps this is also the reason why the points of the compass are reckoned in Holy Scripture with respect to the city of Jerusalem or Judea, as when those places that fall to the west of Jerusalem are named, especially the sea, that is, the Mediterranean, which is called great also with respect to the many lakes that the Hebrews likewise call seas, and which they take as the west. On this matter we said more in our critique of the Vulgate version of the Pentateuch, p. 88. Kimchi on Ezek. 5:5: I placed its inhabitants there for their own good, because it was chosen above all lands, beautiful in climate, the joy of the whole earth (Ps. 48:2). For it is in the middle of the inhabited world [τῆς οἰκουμένης]. Therefore its air is also the most healthy and more temperate than elsewhere. And R. Salomo explains [בתוך הגוים], "in the midst of the nations," as [באמצע העולם] / in the middle of the world. Kimchi again, on Ezek. 38:12: the land of Israel is called the navel of the earth, because it is in the middle of the world, as the navel is in the middle of the body [לפי שהוא באמצע העולם כמו שהטבור באמצע הגוף], because it is in the middle of the world, just as the navel is in the middle of the body. So Cicero in the first Verrine oration calls Enna, which lies in the middle of Sicily, its navel. And Pliny said that the navel of Italy lies near the lake of Reate, Book 3, chap. 12. To this belongs also the observation of Vitruvius (Book 3, chap. 1), who, treating of the wonderful proportions of the human body, affirms that if a man stretches out his arms and legs so as to touch the circumference of a circle, the centre of that circle is placed at the navel. Galen also is credited with this view, in Book 2 of On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Book 15 of On the Use of the Parts. Yet there are some who think that Judea, or its metropolis Jerusalem, was called the navel of the earth not because it lay in the middle of the earth, but because it lay in a higher and therefore more fortified place. Certainly Tremellius and Junius render it in a higher place of that land, that is, they say, in mountainous Judea, whose high places the Jews mostly inhabited for safety. They adduce a parallel passage from Judg. 9:37: Behold, people coming down from the navel of the land, that is, from a higher place of the land. The Chaldee paraphrast helps here, who in both places renders it "the strength of the land"; and R. Salomo interprets it "the height and strength of the land." And Kimchi on the passage in Judges: this is, just as the navel is the middle of the body, so what is in the middle of the land, or its more eminent place, is called the navel. The Greeks call such places μασὸς and μασχαλη from their resemblance to the breast. But we have already gone on too long about the passage in Ezekiel. In short, Jerusalem may be called the navel of the earth either because of τὸ μέσον, the middle, or because of τὸ ἔσχατον, the extremity; or because, as Josephus says, it was a lofty city, rising like a head above the cities round about. Yet there was no necessity to link this place of the Psalm, he worked salvation in the midst of the earth, with that, so that by "the middle of the earth" the navel of the inhabited world [τῆς οἰκουμένης] or of Idumea [Ἰσδαίας] should be understood as Jerusalem. And even if it were granted, what need was there to interpret this place of the birth or passion of Christ? And yet the most learned of the Fathers attribute this sense to the place. Augustine, in Book 17 of The City of God, chap. 4, interprets the passage thus: God Christ worked our salvation in the middle of the earth, when the Word was made flesh and dwelt in an earthly body. See what we have brought forward above from that most learned Father on 1 Sam. 2. Eucherius, in his Questions on the Old Testament: in the middle of the earth, that is, in Judea, where Christ by the cross freed the world; which some think should be called the navel of the earth elsewhere. Or in the middle of the earth, that is, in the virginal womb. But the former explanation, which Eucherius gives, is the more common. Thomas, Part 3, Question 46, Article 10, asks whether Christ suffered in a fitting place. He concludes, as was proper, in favour of the affirmative, citing this passage from Luke 13: it is not fitting that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem. In reply to the first objection he says, first, that Jerusalem was the place chosen by God for the offering of sacrifices, which prefigured Christ's passion. Second, because the power of his passion was to be spread through the whole world, he willed to suffer in the middle of the inhabited earth, that is, in Jerusalem. Whence it is said in Psalm 73: But God our King, before the ages, worked salvation in the middle of the earth, that is, in Jerusalem, etc. So Thomas, who comes closer to the middle of the earth than those who understood the place to be Judea. Others, wishing to point out τὸ τῆς οἰκουμένης μεσαίτατον, the very middle of the inhabited world, named the place of Calvary, and wished it so called from the skull of the first man, who was buried there. Augustine, Sermon 71 on the Time: It is also related by the report of the ancients that Adam, the first man, was once buried in that very place where Christ's cross was fixed, and therefore the place was called Calvary, because the head of the human race is said to have been buried there. To this opinion clung Origen (Tractate 35 on Matthew), Epiphanius at the end of the Panarion, Athanasius in his book on the Lord's passion, Theophylact on Matt. 27, Euthymius on the same place, Cyprian in his sermon on the resurrection, and Ambrose, Book 5, Letter 19, and on Luke, chap. 25. I have set these down on the authority of Genebrardus, Chronology, p. 17. To these I now add Nonnus:

units.la: Donec in locum venit nominati cranii,
units.tr: Until he came to the place of the so-called skull,

units.la: Adami primigeni nomen ferentem ab ambitu capitis.
units.tr: bearing the name of the first-born Adam, from the roundness of the head.

units.la: Γὸλγαθα τὸν καλίσσα Σύρων σόμα, Et
units.tr: Golgotha, which the mouth of the Syrians calls the skull [Γολγοθᾶ τὸν καλέουσι Σύρων στόμα]. And

units.la: Tertulianum lib. 2. carm. contra Marcion. c. 4.
units.tr: Tertullian, book 2 of the poem against Marcion, chapter 4.

units.la: Golgatha loqui est capitis calvaria quondam,
units.tr: Golgotha, in the language of the Syrians, was once the name for the skull's place.

units.la: Hic medium terrae est, hic est victoriae signum,
units.tr: Here is the middle of the earth; here is the sign of victory.

units.la: Os magnum hic veteres nostri docuere repertum,
units.tr: Our ancient writers taught that the great skull was found here.

units.la: Hic hominem primum suscepimus esse sepultum.
units.tr: Here we hold that the first man was buried.

units.la: Hic patitur Christus, de sanguine terra madescit.
units.tr: Here Christ suffered, and the earth is wet with blood.

units.la: Pulvis Adae ut possit veteris, cum sanguine Christi Commixtus stillantis aquæ virtute lavari.
units.tr: So that the dust of Adam, mixed with the blood of Christ, might be washed by the power of the dripping water.

units.la: Ecce in Golgatha medium terræ ponit. Cyrillus Catechef. 13. Medium terra est Golgatha, non meum est hic sermo. Propheta dicit, operatus est salutem in medio terra. Victorinus Pictavorum Episcopus apud * Bedam Presbyterum,
units.tr: See how Golgotha is placed in the middle of the earth. Cyril, Catechesis 13: Golgotha is the middle of the earth; this is not my own saying. The prophet says, "He worked salvation in the middle of the earth." Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, in the words quoted by Bede the Presbyter:

units.la: Est locus ex omni medium quem credimus orbi,Golgatha Iudæi patrio cognomine dicunt:
units.tr: There is a place, which we believe to be the middle of the whole world; the Jews call it Golgotha by its native name.

units.la: Quod vero de contractu sanguinis canit Tertullianus, ἐμόψηφος sibi habet Augustinum, sermone 71. de tempore, quem supra laudavimus, ubi hæc subjicit, Et vero non incongrue dicitur, quod ibi erectus sit medicus, ubi jacebat agrotus. Et dignum erat, ut, ibi occiderat humana superbia, ibi se inclinaret divina misericordia, & sanguis ille pretiosus etiam corporaliter pulverem antiqui peccatoris dum dignatur stillando contingere, redemisse credatur. Hieron. enarrans caput v. Epistolæ ad Ephesios, testatur, se audivisse quandam pro concione ista Apostoli verba, Surge qui dormis & exurge à mortuis & illucescet tibi, seu, * continget te Christus, accommodasse ad Christum in cruce pendentem, qui hoc sermone compellaverit Adamum ibi sub ipsa cruce sepultum, ut sanguine Christi potuerit aspergi. At unde constat bonis istis viris, Adamum in Golgatha sepultum fuisse? An ex appellatione loci? Golgatha est cranium. Sed an Adami? Hoc ἐν ἀρχῇ κεῖται. Traditionis hujus meminit quidem & Hieronymus Epist. ad Marcellam, sed audi liberam ejusdem patris censuram ad cap. 27. Matth. Favorabilis est interpretatio (de cranio Adami illuc sepulti) & mulcens aures populi, nec tamen vera. Postea aliam subjungit appellationis rationem. Extra urbem & foras portam locasunt, in quibus truncantur capita damnatorum, &c. Quam & Beda & Thomas & alii probant. Traditionem vetustissimam, inquit celeberrimus quidam & incom parabilis scriptor, de Adami ἀγωνισάς habitatione in Cananæa & sepultura ejusdem in Golgatha, constat originem habuisse ex interpretatione non recta versus ultimi capite xiv. historiæ Iosuæ. Quod quia nemini eruditorum hodie est ignotum, in eo non immorabimur. Aliud egit maximus scriptor, cum hæc scriberet. Tantum enim abest, ut hæc opinio isti loco natales suos debeat, ut ex eo ab Hieronymo, authorre Glossæ ordin. Thoma & aliis refutetur. Iste enim Adam cujus meminit illic vulgatus, si primus humani generis parens est, non in Jerusalem, non in Golgotha, sed in Hebron, quæ alias Kirjath Arbe, sepultus dicitur. Sed Ebræum הָאָרֶם illic & ϖϱωτοπλάστ nomen non esse, atque, adeo nullam illic sepulturam memorari pag. 384. ostendimus. Sed facessamus tandem ab hoc loco, cujus literalem, & qui ex ipso contextu fluit, expositionem, in limine hujus annotationis exhibuimus. Eam ubi authoritate una atque altera firmavero, progrediar ad ea quæ restant. Euthym. In medio terra dixit propalam atque in omnium hominum conspectu. Et in specie libertatem Judæis præstitam intelligit ab Ægypt. servitute. ita & Bellarminus, S A, op. est salutem q. d. solebat nos adjuvare in medio terra, id est palam, vel in Judæa, quæ medium tenet locum terræ habitabilis &c. Genebr. palam & manifeste, vel juxta alios in Jerusalem quæ est terra S. veluti medium. Quin & Judæa est terra habitabilis medium &c. Theodoretus, curam quam de nobis gessisti, omnibus claram fecisti. Hoc namque est in medio terra, videlicet, omnes viderunt.
units.tr: As for what Tertullian sings about the blood's contact with the dust, Augustine agrees with him [ἐμόψηφος], in sermon 71 on the time of year, which I have cited above, where he adds: And indeed it is not unfitting to say that the physician was raised up where the patient lay. It was right that where human pride had fallen, divine mercy should bow down there; and that precious blood, while deigning to touch by dripping even the dust of the ancient sinner bodily, should be believed to have redeemed it. Jerome, expounding chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, testifies that he heard someone, in a sermon, apply the apostle's words, Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon you (or, Christ shall reach you), to Christ hanging on the cross, as if the words were addressed to Adam, buried there under the very cross, so that he might be sprinkled with Christ's blood. But how do these good men know that Adam was buried in Golgotha? From the name of the place? Golgotha means skull. But is it Adam's skull? This is in question from the start [ἐν ἀρχῇ κεῖται]. Jerome also mentions this tradition in his letter to Marcella, but hear that same father's free judgment on chapter 27 of Matthew: The interpretation (that Adam's skull was buried there) is flattering and soothes the ears of the people, but it is not true. Afterwards he adds another explanation of the name: Outside the city and beyond the gate they placed the places where the heads of condemned men were cut off, etc. Bede, Thomas and others approve this. The very ancient tradition, says a very famous and incomparable writer, about Adam's dwelling [ἀγωνισάς] in Canaan and his burial in Golgotha, clearly arose from a faulty interpretation of the last verse of chapter 14 of the book of Joshua. Since this is now known to every learned person, we shall not linger on it. The great writer was doing something else when he wrote these words. For this opinion is so far from owing its origin to that place that, on the contrary, it is refuted from that very place by Jerome, the author of the Glossa ordinaria, Thomas and others. For that Adam whom the Vulgate mentions there, if he is the first parent of the human race, is said to be buried not in Jerusalem nor in Golgotha, but in Hebron, which is otherwise called Kiriath-arba. But I have shown on page 384 that the Hebrew [הָאָרֶם] is not a name there, nor the name of the first-formed man [πρωτόπλαστος], and so no burial is recorded there. But let us at last depart from this place, whose literal sense, which flows from the context itself, I have set out at the beginning of this annotation. Once I have confirmed it by one or two authorities, I will move on to what remains. Euthymius: He said "in the middle of the earth" openly and in the sight of all men. And in particular he means the freedom granted to the Jews from Egyptian slavery. So too Bellarmine: "he worked salvation," that is, "he used to help us in the middle of the earth," that is, openly, or in Judea, which holds the middle place of the inhabited earth, etc. Genebrardus: openly and plainly, or, according to others, in Jerusalem, which is as it were the middle of the land. Indeed Judea is the middle of the inhabited land, etc. Theodoret: You made the care you had for us clear to all. For "in the middle of the earth" means: everyone saw it.

units.la: Ps. LXXV. 4. Ego confirmavi columnas ejus. ] Vide quæ ad Ps. xxiv. notauimus. August, per columnas Apostolos intelligit.
units.tr: Ps. 75:4. I have established its pillars. See what I noted on Ps. 24. Augustine understands the pillars to be the apostles.

units.la: Ps. LXXVII. 11. Vide Cl. Ternovium Exercit. Bibl. pag. 780. & seq. Edit. 3.
units.tr: Ps. 77:11. See the learned Tarnovius, Exercitationes biblicae, pp. 780 ff., 3rd edition.

units.la: Psal. LXXVIII. 49. alii 54. immissiones per Angelos malos. ] Ita vulgatus. Lxx. ἀποστολὴν δι᾽ ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν. Quæsitum est, utrum angelorum malorum opera usus fuerit Deus in infligendis his pœnis. Augustinus de malis angelis locum intellexit. Non tamen se expedit. Adeo multa sibi objicit. Qua cum ita sint, inquit, si per angelos malos Deus illas plagas inflixit Ægyptiis, nunquid audebimus dicere, & aquam in sanguinem per eosdem angelos versam, & ranas per eosdem angelos factas, quorum similia etiam Magi Pharaonis veneficiis suis facere potuerunt, ut angeli mali ex utraque parte consisterent, hinc illos affligentes, inde fallentes, secundum judicium & dispensationem justissimi Dei juste utentis etiam iniquorum malitia? Non audeo dicere. Postea ostendit Deum non solum pœnas infligere per angelos malos sed & bonos, ut in eversione Sodomorum. Et tandem, Si ea quæ mirabiliter de creaturis facta sunt, malis angelis tribuere non audemus, habemus quod eis tribuere fine dubitatione possumus, mortes pecorum, mortes primitivorum & obdurationem, &c. Bellarminus in commentario ait sanctos angelos posse dici malos ab effectu, quia ad Dei omnipotentis nutum hominibus mala id est poenas infligunt. Cacodaemones vero malos dici propter malam voluntatem. Ego vero cum Cl. Tarnovio affero, nusquam in scriptura beatos istos spiritus malos angeles dici. Concedo, hoc loco de bonis spiritibus agi. Concedo bene versum ab Interprete Graeco, Angelorum malorum. Sed observa tiro in verbis istis, ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν, Angelorum malorum syntaxin rectionis, non convenientiae. Qui Ebraea a limine salutavit, videbit in Ebraeo non esse מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים sed מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים / Illa autem differunt, ut μαύνης κακὸς & μάνης κακῶν. Sanctissimi prophetae, cum calamitates denuntiant, sunt מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים / Pseudo-prophetae contra, quando ex proprio ingenio pacem & omnia prospera promittunt, מלאכים רעים merito appellantur. Hic ergo locus hilum non juvat illos, qui Deum in infligendis his plagis malorum angelorum opera usum esse pertendunt.
units.tr: Ps. 78:49 (others 54): sending by evil angels. So the Vulgate. The Septuagint: "a sending by evil angels" [ἀποστολὴν δι᾽ ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν]. It has been asked whether God used the work of evil angels in inflicting these punishments. Augustine understood the passage of evil angels, yet he does not extricate himself, since he raises so many objections to himself: Since these things are so, he says, if God inflicted those plagues on the Egyptians through evil angels, shall we dare to say that the water turned into blood through the same angels, and the frogs made by the same angels, whose like the magicians of Pharaoh could also produce by their sorceries, so that evil angels stood on both sides, afflicting on the one hand and deceiving on the other, according to the judgment and dispensation of the most just God, who justly uses even the malice of the wicked? I do not dare to say so. Afterwards he shows that God inflicts punishments through good angels as well as evil ones, as in the overthrow of Sodom. And finally: If we do not dare to attribute to evil angels the things that were miraculously done with creatures, we have things we can without doubt attribute to them: the deaths of cattle, the deaths of firstborn children, and hardening, etc. Bellarmine, in his commentary, says that holy angels may be called evil from their effect, because at the nod of almighty God they inflict evils, that is, punishments, on men; but that devils are called evil because of their evil will. I, however, agree with Tarnovius that nowhere in Scripture are those blessed spirits called evil angels. I grant that in this place good spirits are meant. I grant that the Greek translator rendered it well as "of evil angels." But, beginner, notice in these words, ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν, "of evil angels," the syntax of government, not of agreement. Whoever has greeted the Hebrew from the threshold will see that the Hebrew is not malakhei ra'im but mal'akhim ra'im, and these differ as μαύνης κακὸς and μάνης κακῶν. The most holy prophets, when they announce calamities, are malakhei ra'im. The false prophets, on the other hand, when from their own mind they promise peace and every prosperity, are rightly called mal'akhim ra'im. So this passage does not help in the least those who maintain that God used the work of evil angels in inflicting these plagues.

units.la: Ps. LXXXII. Deus stetit in * synagoga Deorum.] Ita vulgatus ex LXX. ὁ Θεὸς ἔστη ἐν συναγωγῇ Θεῶν. Valde hic sudat Bellarminus, ut hanc versionem cum Ebraeo textu conciliet quae agnoscit sic reddenda esse Stetit Deus in synagoga Dei. At voces illae sunt transpositae, inquit, ut olim fuerit נצב אל בעדת אלהים aut Ebraea sic reddi possunt, Deorum stetit in synagoga Deus, quod miror tanto viro potuisse excidere. Provoco ad omnium Ebraismi Professorum judicia. Hieron. Pagn. Deus stat in coetu Dei id est suo. Genebr. Ebraice quidem est, Dei, sed Deorum fuit vertendum, ad explicandam synecdochen numeri, Judicis pro Judicum. Sensus fateor eodem recidit, nisi quod textus Ebraeus evidentius asserat, magistratum esse divinam ordinationem. Deus stat in coetu Dei, id est, suo. Nomen pro pronomine, ut Num. x. 29. Exod. x. 12. Luc. 3. 19. Quae locutio cum Interpretibus non veniret in mentem, in hanc interpretationem delati videntur. Porro Synagogam hic dixit Interpres pro coetu. Συναγωγὴ ad verbum est congregatio. Ea autem vox cum vulgo usurpari soleat de coetu fidelium veteris Foederis, Augustinus per synagogam Deorum non coetum judicum sed fidelium intelligit. Illud colligit ex versu 6. Ego dixi, dii estis & filii altissimi omnes, de quo postea. In horum ergo synagoga filiorum altissimi, de quibus idem altissimus per Iesaiam dicit, Filios genui & exaltavi, stetit Deus. Pergit Augustinus, In Synagoga populum Israel intelligimus, quia & ipsorum proprie Synagoga dici solet, quamvis & Ecclesia dicta. Nostram vero Apostoli nunquam synagogam dixerunt, semper Ecclesiam, sive discernendi causa, sive quod inter congregationem, unde synagoga & convocationem, unde Ecclesia nomen accepit, differt aliquid: quod sc. congregari & pecora solent, atque ipsa proprie, quorum & greges proprie dicimus.
