Convocari autem magis est utentium ratione, sicut sunt homines. Unde ex persona ipsius Asaph in alio Psalmo canitur, quasi pecus factus sum apud te, & ego semper tecum. Cum utique quamvis uni vero Deo mancipatus videretur, pro magnis tamen ac summis bonis ab illo carnalia, terrena, temporalia requirebat. Haec Augustini verba sunt, comm. in hunc Ps. dura certe & Augustino indigna. Augustino multa condonanda sunt. Incidit enim in ejusmodi seculum quo linguarum studium plane insuper habebatur. At Bellarminum & Catechismi Tridentini concinnatores quis excusret? Augustinum si cum Augustino conferas, invenies aliquod velamentum. Namque in comment. ad Ps. 77. & 72. & 83. cautius locutus est. At quis patrocinium praestabit isti effato Tridentinorum catechistarum, quo in explicatione aticuli credo Ecclesiam diserte pronuntiant, populum sub lege synagoga nomine fuisse appellatum, quod pecudum more, quibus magis congregari convenit, terrena & caduca bona tantum spectaret. Vides haec ex Augustino transumpta esse, licet non sine auctario. Nuspiam enim dicit Augustinus eos TANTUM terrena bona spectasse. Quin diserte ad Ps. 72. asserit, eos cogitare coepisse coelestem felicitatem & arguere se, quod instar pecoris fuisset & terrena desiderasset. Ad haec audivimus Augustinum dicentem, dictam illam synagogam, sive discernendi causa, SIVE quod hoc interfit. Catechista veram causam omisit: fallam, quo veteri Ecclesiae detraheret, arripuit. Bell. quoque non admittit, קהל & עדרה id est Ecclesiam & Synagogam populo Iudaico tribui, cum Christiani, inquit, dicantur Ecclesia id est evocatio. quia evocari proprium est hominum. Populus autem Judaicus Synagoga id est congregatio, quia congregari commune est hominibus cum bestiis. Sed quam haec sint frigida, ne quid dicam gravius, omnes quibus
units.tr: Ps. 82. God stood in the * assembly of the gods. So the Vulgate, from the Septuagint: "God stood in the assembly of gods" [ὁ Θεὸς ἔστη ἐν συναγωγῇ Θεῶν]. Here Bellarmine sweats hard to reconcile this version with the Hebrew text. He acknowledges that the words should be rendered: God stood in the assembly of God. But, he says, the words have been transposed, as if the Hebrew once was niṣṣav 'el be'adat 'elohim, or else the Hebrew can be rendered: God of gods stood in the assembly, which I wonder that so great a man could have overlooked. I appeal to the judgments of all the professors of Hebrew. Jerome (Pagnini): God stands in the congregation of God, that is, his own. Genebrardus: In Hebrew it is indeed "of God," but it ought to be translated "of gods," to explain the synecdoche of number, judge for judges. I admit the sense comes to the same thing, except that the Hebrew text asserts more clearly that the magistracy is a divine ordinance. God stands in the congregation of God, that is, his own. The noun stands for the pronoun, as in Num. 10:29; Exod. 10:12; Luke 3:19. Since this way of speaking did not occur to the translators, they seem to have been led into this rendering. Further, the translator here said "synagogue" for "assembly." Synagogue, word for word, is a gathering. Since that word is commonly used of the assembly of the faithful of the old covenant, Augustine understands by "synagogue of gods" not an assembly of judges but of the faithful. He gathers this from verse 6: I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High, of which more later. So in the synagogue of these sons of the Most High, of whom the same Most High says through Isaiah, I have begotten sons and raised them up, God stood. Augustine goes on: By "synagogue" we understand the people of Israel, since it is properly called their synagogue, although it is also called Church. But the apostles never called our assembly a synagogue, always the Church, either for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between the gathering, from which the word synagogue comes, and the calling together, from which the word Church is taken: that is, flocks and herds are usually gathered together, and that is properly what we call their flocks. But to be called together belongs more to beings who use reason, as men are. So in the person of Asaph himself another psalm sings, "I have become like a beast before you, and I am always with you." For although he seemed bound to the one true God, yet he asked from him for carnal, earthly and temporal things as great and highest goods. These are Augustine's words, in his commentary on this psalm, harsh indeed and unworthy of Augustine. Much must be pardoned to Augustine: he fell into an age in which the study of languages was altogether despised. But who will excuse Bellarmine and the compilers of the Tridentine Catechism? If you compare Augustine with Augustine, you will find some veil. For in his commentaries on Psalms 77, 72 and 83 he speaks more cautiously. But who will defend this saying of the Tridentine catechists, in the explanation of the article "I believe in the Church," where they plainly declare: The people under the law was called by the name of synagogue, because, after the manner of cattle, to whom it is more fitting to be gathered together, it looked only to earthly and perishable goods. You see these things are taken over from Augustine, though not without an addition. For nowhere does Augustine say that they looked ONLY to earthly goods. Indeed, in his commentary on Ps. 72 he plainly asserts that they began to think of heavenly happiness and to reproach themselves that they had been like cattle and had desired earthly things. We have heard Augustine say that the synagogue was so named either for the sake of distinction, OR because this makes a difference. The catechist omitted the true reason and seized on a false one, so that he might detract from the ancient Church. Bellarmine also does not allow that qahal and ʿedah, that is, Church and synagogue, were attributed to the Jewish people, since, he says, Christians are called Church, that is, a calling out, because calling out is proper to men, while the Jewish people is a synagogue, that is, a gathering, because gathering is common to men and beasts. But how frigid these things are, not to say more harshly, let all who have a sound head judge.

units.la: Controv. 4. lib. 3. cap. 1. sanum sinciput est, judicent. Originatio vocis congregatio fenestram aperuisse videtur huic argutiae. Est enim vox illa composita ex con & grex. At in Graeco συναγωγή, Ebraeo קהל & synonymis evanescit ista subtilitas. Synagoga dicitur de coetu Christianorum Jacob. 2. 2. ubi Latinus vertit conventum, Et Hebr. x. 25. ἐπισυναγωγή. Neque tantum graeca συναγὼ, συναγωγὴ, συνάξις usurpantur de fidelibus Nov. Test. e. gr. Matth. 18.12. Johan. 15.52. Act. xi. 26. & xx. 7. sed & latina, congregare & congregatio in vulgata Latina. Quin eadem Concilii Tridentini patribus in actis & decretis concilii passim tribuuntur. Quis auderet istum coetum, inquo certe eximii viri fuere, in haram porcorum relegare? Et tamen Catechistae sanctissimos patriarchas bestiis comparant, & quos Apostolus caelestem patriam expetivisse ait Hebr. xi. 14. & 16. terrena tantum bona expectasse asserunt, Falsum ergo est illud Augustini effatum, nostram Ecclesiam nunquam ab Apostolis synagogam dictam. Nunc & illud ostendendum est, vanum esse, convocari proprium esse hominum. Καλέω, unde ἐκκλησία & ἀνακαλέω, de vocatione & revocatione canum in Kynegetico Xenophontis legi notat Casaub. Apud. Joh. x. 3. Pastor ποιμὴν τὰ πρόβατα καὶ ὀνόματα. קהל denique promiscue apud Lxx. redditur jam ἐκκλησία, jam συναγωγή. Apud Mosem Lev. iv. 13. & Num. xx. 2. & 4. utrumque nomen קהל & עדה & populo Israelitico tribuitur. item Prov. v. 14. ubi & Lxx. & vulgatus ἐκκλησίᾳ & συναγωγὴ conjunxere. Ps. 26. vers. ult. In Ecclesiis benedicam Domino & Ps. Lxviii. 26. Vide Rainoldi praelect. vii. & xi. Casaub. Excercit. xvi. Sect. xlii. ipsumque adeo Bulengerum numero eodem.
units.tr: Controv. 4. lib. 3. cap. 1. Let them judge whether he has a sound head. The origin of the word congregatio seems to have opened a window for this quibble. That word is compounded of con and grex. But in Greek συναγωγή, in Hebrew קהל, and in their synonyms, this subtlety disappears. Synagogue is used of the assembly of Christians at James 2:2, where the Latin renders it conventum, and at Heb. 10:25 the word is ἐπισυναγωγή. The Greek συναγὼ, συναγωγὴ and συνάξις are used of the faithful in the New Testament, for example Matt. 18:12, John 15:52, Acts 11:26 and 20:7. Nor are only the Greek words so used: the Latin congregare and congregatio occur of them in the Vulgate. Indeed the same word is applied to the fathers of the Council of Trent throughout the acts and decrees of the council. Who would dare to banish that assembly, in which there were certainly distinguished men, to a pigsty? Yet the catechists compare the most holy patriarchs to beasts, and they assert that those whom the Apostle says sought a heavenly country (Heb. 11:14 and 16) looked only for earthly goods. So that saying of Augustine, that our Church was never called a synagogue by the Apostles, is false. Now it must also be shown that the claim that to be called together is proper to men is empty. Casaubon notes that καλέω, from which come ἐκκλησία and ἀνακαλέω, of the calling and recalling of dogs, is read in Xenophon's Cynegeticus. In John 10:3 the shepherd calls his sheep by name. Finally, in the Septuagint קהל is rendered now ἐκκλησία and now συναγωγή. In Moses (Lev. 4:13, and Num. 20:2 and 4) both words, קהל and עדה, are applied to the people of Israel. So too at Prov. 5:14, where both the Septuagint and the Vulgate join ecclesia and synagoga. See Psalm 26 (25) last verse, "In the congregations I will bless the Lord", and Psalm 68:26. See Rainolds' lectures 7 and 11, and Casaubon's Exercitations 16, section 42, and Bullinger, who counts the same way.

units.la: Vers. 6. Ego dixi, Dii estis.] Hic Magistratus & judices אלהים id est Dii dicuntur, Exo. 21. 6. Admovebit eum ad Deos. & Exod. 22.9. & 28. Locus iste citatur Joh. x. 35. ubi notet tiro primo, vocem legis late usurpatam pro universo canone veteris testamenti. II. ad quos sermo Dei factus est, idem דבר esse ac si dixisset, ad quos mandatum Dei pervenit, quibus demandata sunt Dei judicia, 2. Chron. 19. 6. quae propterea & res seu negotia Dei vocantur 1. Chron. 26. 32. & 2. Chr. 12. 11. Nulla ergo necessitas locum istum ad omnes fideles extendi, quod tamen post Augustinum plurimi interpretes admisere. Itaque plane extra oleas vagatur Gregorius, quando ad Mauritium scribens, sacerdotes Novi Testamenti a regibus honorandos non judicandos contendit. Invenies Epistolam in Decreto Gratiani, parte 2. causa xi. Quaest. 1. cap. Sacerdotibus. Sacerdotes, inquit, divinis eloquiis aliquando dii, aliquando angeli vocantur. Applica illum ad Deos Exod. 21. Diis non detrahes Exod. 22. &c. Angelos vocari in confesso est, Malach. 2. At sacerdotes qua sacerdotes Deos vocari, nundum ostensum est Pergit Gregorius. Ecclesiastica historia testatur, quia cum pia memoria Constantino scripta oblata accusationes contra Episcopos fuissent, libellos quidem accusationes accepit, & eosdem, qui accusati fuerant, Episcopos convocans, in eorum conspectu libellos, quos acceperat, incendit, dicens, Ite & inter vos causas vestras disponite, quia dignum non est, ut nos judicemus Deos. Et cauf. 12. quaest. 1. capite Futuram Ecclesiam. * Melchiades Papa inter alia inquit, Idem vero (Constantinus) praesidens sancta synodo — cum querelam quorundam clericorum ad se videret deferendam, ait, vos à nemine judicari poteritis, quia solius Dei judicio reservamini. Dii enim vocati estis, & idcirco non poteritis ab hominibus judicari. Adi & partem primam dist. 17. cap. Synodum Episcoporum. Et confer, quae à cl. Drusio ad Actor. 23. 4. observata sunt.
units.tr: Verse 6. "I said, You are gods." Here magistrates and judges are called אלהים, that is, gods (Exod. 21:6, "He shall bring him to God"; and Exod. 22:9 and 28). This passage is cited at John 10:35, where the first note to be made is that the word law is used broadly for the whole canon of the Old Testament. Second, that to whom the word of God came means the same as if he had said: to whom the command of God came, to whom the judgments of God were entrusted (2 Chron. 19:6). These are for that reason also called the things or affairs of God (1 Chron. 26:32; 2 Chron. 12:11). There is therefore no necessity to extend this passage to all the faithful, though after Augustine very many interpreters have admitted this. So Gregory wanders quite outside the olive grove when, writing to Maurice, he contends that the priests of the New Testament are to be honoured by kings and not judged. You will find the letter in Gratian's Decretum, part 2, cause 11, question 1, chapter Sacerdotibus. "Priests," he says, "are sometimes called gods, sometimes angels, in the divine oracles. Apply that to gods in Exod. 21, 'You shall not revile the gods' in Exod. 22, etc." That angels are so called is beyond doubt (Mal. 2). But that priests, as priests, are called gods has not yet been shown. Gregory goes on: "Ecclesiastical history bears witness that when accusations against bishops were brought to the emperor Constantine of pious memory in writing, he received the written accusations and summoned the same bishops who had been accused, and in their presence he burned the papers he had received, saying, 'Go and settle your causes among yourselves, for it is not right that we should judge gods.'" And in cause 12, question 1, the chapter Futuram Ecclesiam. Pope Melchiades among other things says: "Constantine himself, presiding over the holy synod, when he saw a complaint of certain clergy being brought before him, said, 'You can be judged by no one, since you are reserved for the judgment of God alone. For you have been called gods, and therefore you cannot be judged by men.'" Look also at the first part, distinction 17, chapter Synodum Episcoporum. And compare what the distinguished Drusius observed on Acts 23:4.

units.la: Ps. LXXXIII. 1. אלהים אל דמי לך [Arias Mont.] O Deus, ne quaeso [sit] silentium tibi. Pagn. ne taceas tibi. Bellar. fatetur Hieronymum vertere, ne taceas, & voces Ebraeas sensum istum posse efficere, ut & hunc, Deus, ne silentium tibi sit. Sed etiam recipiunt istum sensum, inquit Deus non similis tibi, id est nemo tibi similis est. Vox enim domi est à Damah quod & sidere, & similem esse significat. Haec Bellar. Qui tamen nonignoravit, לא esse dehortandi aut deprecandi particulam, & similem רומה dici. Non ignoro, alibi occurrere דומי pro דומה, sed nusquam ostendetur participium cum Kamets rapto sub prima radicali. Ruit ergo allegorica Augustini expositio, quae vulgatae versioni, Deus quis similis erit tibi, superstructa est. Expositionem ejus diffusiorem in hanc summam contraxit Bellarminus. Si Augustinus inquit, satis apte ad Christum accommodat, qui hoc mundo similis aliis hominibus videbatur: sed in die judicii nullus esimilis erit, quando apparebit in gloria patris sui, &c.
units.tr: Psalm 83:1. "O God, do not keep silence" [אלהים אל דמי לך]. Arias Montanus: "O God, I beg you, let there be silence for you." Pagninus: "Do not be silent for yourself." Bellarmine admits that Jerome translates "do not keep silent", and that the Hebrew words can also yield this sense: "God, let there be no silence for you." But they also take the sense "God not like you", that is, no one is like you. For the word domi comes from damah [דמה], which means both to be silent and to be like. So far Bellarmine. He did not, however, fail to notice that לא is a particle of dehortation or of entreaty, and that רומה is used of likeness. I am aware that דומי occurs elsewhere for דומה, but it will nowhere be shown that the participle has a qamets under the first radical. So Augustine's allegorical exposition, which was built upon the Vulgate version, "O God, who will be like you?", falls to the ground. Bellarmine condensed Augustine's fuller exposition into this summary: "If Augustine says, he fits Christ well enough, who in this world seemed like other men; but on the day of judgment no one will be like him, when he appears in the glory of his Father, etc."

units.tr: Psalm LXXXIV, verses 7, 8, 9.

units.la: אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם עֹז לוֹ בָךְ מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם׃ עֹבְרֵי בְעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא מַעְיָן יְשִׁיתוּהוּ גַּם בְּרָכוֹת יַעֲטֶה מוֹרֶה׃ יֵלְכוּ מֵחַיִל אֶל־חַיִל יֵרָאֶה אֶל־אֱלֹהִים בְּצִיּוֹן׃
units.tr: Blessed is the man whose strength is in you; the highways are in his heart. Passing through the valley of Baca they make it a spring; the rain also covers it with blessings. They go from strength to strength; he is seen before God in Zion. [אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם עֹז לוֹ בָךְ מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם׃ עֹבְרֵי בְעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא מַעְיָן יְשִׁיתוּהוּ גַּם בְּרָכוֹת יַעֲטֶה מוֹרֶה׃ יֵלְכוּ מֵחַיִל אֶל־חַיִל יֵרָאֶה אֶל־אֱלֹהִים בְּצִיּוֹן׃]

units.la: Beatus vir, cujus est auxilium à te. Ascensiones in corde suo disposuit, in valle lacrymarum, in loco quem posuit. Etenim benedictionem dabit legislator, ibunt de virtute in virtutem, videbitur Deus Deorum in Sion.
units.tr: Blessed is the man whose help is from you. He has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place he has appointed. For the lawgiver will give a blessing; they will go from virtue to virtue; God of gods will be seen in Sion.

units.la: In praesens censuram in vulgatam versionem non scribimus. Ideo non lubet singulas hujus exorbitantis versionis particulas examinare. Pagninus ita verterat, Beatus homo, cui est fortitudo in te: via (Arias addit, strata) in corde ipsorum. Transeuntes per vallem Habbacha, fontem ponunt eam: etiam piscinas aperiet pluvia. Ibunt de exercitu in exercitum, videbitur Deus Deorum in Sion. Versio fateor obscura, attamen clarior vulgata & Ebraeum textum fidelius exprimens. David Absoloni furorem fugiens & in urbe sancta cultum Dei obire prohibitus, Deum supplex veneratur, ut quamprimum Jerosolymam reverti & sacra adire loca possit, vers. 3. & 4. profitetur desiderium suum obeundi cultum divinum. Illud declarat e causa procreante, vid. jucunditate, vers. 2. Eam illustrat exemplis duobus eorum, qui illam percipiunt, vid. primo ministrorum in tabernaculo quotidie versantium, vers. 5. & Israelitarum ter quotannis Jerosolymam ascendentium & coram Deo apparentium, vers. 6.7. 8. Hanc profectionem amplificat ex effectis duobus, siti & remedio ejus, vers. 7. Nunc omnia erunt plana. Beatus homo, cujus f. est in te. in quorum corde sunt semitae, semitae ad urbem S. ducentes, vers. 7. Qui transeunt per vallem mori [vel * mororum, alii accipiunt pro nomine proprio vallis & desertae; alii in universum pro locis desertis & siccis, quibus apprime ista arborum species delectatur] fontem ponunt illum [hoc est, quamvis multis per deserta loca eundum sit, & situs toleranda; tamen illi incommodum istud hac spe levant, fore ut brevi perveniant in sanctam urbem, Deo litaturi. Atque ita Deum sibi fontem constituunt. Quin
units.tr: For the present we do not write a censure of the Vulgate version. So it is not worth examining the individual parts of this aberrant version one by one. Pagninus had translated it thus: Blessed is the man in whom is strength in you: the way (Arias adds, paved) is in their heart. Passing through the valley Habbacha, they make it a fountain: the rain will also open pools. They will go from army to army; God of gods will be seen in Sion. I admit the version is obscure, yet the Vulgate is clearer and renders the Hebrew text more faithfully. David, fleeing the fury of Absalom and forbidden to perform the worship of God in the holy city, humbly prays to God that he may return to Jerusalem as soon as possible and approach the sacred places; in verses 3 and 4 he professes his longing to perform divine worship. He states this from its producing cause, namely delight, verse 2. He illustrates it with two examples of those who enjoy it: first, the ministers who serve daily in the tabernacle, verse 5; and the Israelites who ascend to Jerusalem three times a year and appear before God, verses 6, 7, 8. He amplifies this journey from its two effects, thirst and its remedy, verse 7. Now everything will be plain. Blessed is the man whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the paths, the paths leading to the holy city, verse 7. Those who pass through the valley of mulberries [or of mororum; others take it as the proper name of a valley and desert; others in general for desert and dry places, in which this kind of tree especially delights] make it a fountain [that is, although they must go through deserted places and endure hardship, yet they lighten that discomfort with this hope, that they will soon reach the holy city to offer sacrifice to God. And so they make God their fountain. Moreover

units.la: * Confer 2. Sam. v. 22. 23. etiam [in] benedictionibus operit [eos] pluvia. [Vi illius spei quasi largissima pluvia perfunduntur. בְּרָכוֹת pro בִּרְכוֹת / periphrasis adverbii, & quidem pluralis numeri. Ita imbres benedictionis, imbres largi; Jezech. 34. 26 unde lux Apostolo, 2. Cor. 9. 6. qui serit Φειδομένως, parce, metet Φειδομένως; qui serit ἐπ' εὐλογίαις. metet ἐπ' εὐλογίαις] Ambulant ab exercitu ad exercitum, comparet [quisque] apud Deum in Sion. Per exercitus vel intelliguntur turmae viatorum, confer Luc. 2. 44. vel Israelitarum in ipsa jam urbe צִבְאוֹת id est turmatim ad tabernaculum convenientium, Exod. 38. 8. 1. Sam. 2. 22. Hic est literalis difficillimi loci sensus. Ad quem si vel vulgatum textum vel allegoricas hujus loci expositiones voles conformare, laterem lavabis. In Belg. quoque translatione duo notanda sunt, 1. Die doot het jam- merdal gaen / Lovan. het dal der tranen. Vita haec nostra aliud elogium non meretur. Lege cap. 22. lib. 22. Augustini de Civ. Dei. Illud tamen ex hoc loco non eruas. Fletus enim בֶּכִי vel בְּכִי vel בְּכָא non בָּכָא / dicitur. Alterum, מְהֵיל אֵל חַיִל Belg. Op behouden de rene overwinninghe na dan anderen / Lovan. van deughde ter deughde. Atqui Graecum δύναμις, quod vulg. per virtutis vocabulum amat exprimere, virtutem Ethicam nusquam significat. Et ipse Bellar. fatetur, illas de virtute in virtutem de vi & robore explicandas esse. Jam vero ut Robur pro victoria per Metoh. accipiatur, non est quidem contortum, at pro turma melius accipi, jam opinor ostensum est. Confer nunc Augustinum. Lege Bellarminum, & vide, quomodo sudet, ut hanc versionem & Allegoricas Patrum expositiones cum fontibus conciliet. Illud exciderat, verba illa, Deus Deorum ab August. exponi. Christus Christianorum. Putat enim per Deos Christianos intelligi, de quibus Psal. 82. 6. Ego dixi, Dii estis. Illic vide. Et nota hic non esse אֵל sed אֵל.
units.tr: * Compare 2 Sam. 5:22, 23. even [in] blessings he covers [them] with rain. [By the force of that hope they are drenched as with the most abundant rain. בְּרָכוֹת for בִּרְכוֹת is a periphrasis of an adverb, and indeed of the plural number. So showers of blessing, abundant showers; Ezek. 34:26, whence the light for the Apostle, 2 Cor. 9:6: he who sows sparingly [Φειδομένως] will reap sparingly; he who sows with blessings [ἐπ' εὐλογίαις] will reap with blessings.] They walk from army to army; each appears before God in Zion. By armies are understood either the companies of travellers, compare Luke 2:44, or the Israelites gathering in companies at the tabernacle, צִבְאוֹת, Exod. 38:8; 1 Sam. 2:22. This is the literal sense of this most difficult passage. If you wish to conform either the Vulgate text or the allegorical expositions of this place to it, you will be labouring in vain (laterem lavabis). The Belgic translation also has two points to note. First, Die doot het jammerdal gaen ("who go through the vale of misery"), Louvain: "the vale of tears." This life of ours deserves no other description. Read chapter 22 of book 22 of Augustine's City of God. Yet you should not extract that from this passage, for weeping is בֶּכִי or בְּכִי or בְּכָא, not בָּכָא. The second: Dutch Op behouden de rene overwinninghe na dan anderen ("gaining the pure victory after the others"), Louvain: "from virtue to virtue." Yet the Greek δύναμις, which the Vulgate prefers to render by the word virtue, never signifies ethical virtue. And Bellarmine himself confesses that the words from virtue to virtue are to be explained of power and strength. That strength may be taken for victory by metonymy is not indeed a twisted reading, but that it is better taken for a company, I think has already been shown. Now compare Augustine. Read Bellarmine, and see how he sweats to reconcile this version and the allegorical expositions of the Fathers with the sources. He had let slip that the words God of gods are explained by Augustine as Christ of Christians. For he thinks that by the Christian gods are meant those of whom Ps. 82:6 says, I said, you are gods. See there. And note here that the word is not אֵל but אֱלֹהִים.

units.la: Vers. 12. Quia misericordiam & veritatem diligit dominus.] Ita vulgatus ex LXX. ἐν ἔλεος ... ἀγαπᾷ ... Multa eleganter & suaviter hic concionatur B. August. de misericordia & veritate. Et Euthymius, Ad activam & contemplativam vitam nos hortatur, dicens, quod Deus diligit in. & veritatem. Misericordia ad activam, veritas ad contemplativam pertinet. Haec an apposite hoc loco dicantur jam apparebit. Ebraea sunt שֶׁמֶשׁ יָהּ אֱלֹהִים. יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים Sol & clypeus est DOMINUS Deus. Duas istas voces Aq. ἥλιος καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ [?], Symm. ἥλιος ἡ ὁπ ἐγαπησεν [?] reddidêre. LXX. videri poterant ἥλιος scripsisse, quod scribarum audacia in ἐλεὸς demutari facile potuisset, nisi τὸ ΜΩΝ ἀληθινὸν reddidissent. Bellar. conjectat eos pro שמש legisse שמן oleum & pro יהוה futurum יאור [?] / Per oleum vero misericordiam, per scutum veritatem intellexisse; de quo Psal. 90. Scuto circumdabit te veritas ejus. Non tamen audet codices Ebraeos in suspicionem vocare de mendo. Dicit sensum esse eundem. At inquam ego, si Ebraeo textui stamus, de misericordia & veritate ad hunc versum concionari, est extra oleas vagari.
units.tr: Verse 12. For the Lord loves mercy and truth. So the Vulgate from the LXX: ἐν ἔλεος ... ἀγαπᾷ ... Augustine preaches much here, elegantly and sweetly, on mercy and truth. And Euthymius: "He exhorts us to the active and the contemplative life, saying that God loves mercy and truth. Mercy pertains to the active life, truth to the contemplative." Whether these things are aptly said in this place will now appear. The Hebrew words are שֶׁמֶשׁ יָהּ אֱלֹהִים. יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים, "sun" and "God the LORD" [שֶׁמֶשׁ יָהּ אֱלֹהִים. יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים]. Aquila rendered these two words as ἥλιος καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ [?], Symmachus as ἥλιος ἡ ὁπ ἐγαπησεν [?]. The LXX could seem to have written ἥλιος, which the boldness of scribes could easily have changed into ἐλεὸς, unless they had rendered it τὸ ... ἀληθινὸν. Bellarmine conjectures that they read שמן, oil, for שמש, and for יהוה a future form יאור [?]. By oil they understood mercy, by shield truth; compare Ps. 91: His truth shall compass you with a shield. Yet he does not dare to call the Hebrew codices into suspicion of error; he says the sense is the same. But I say that if we keep to the Hebrew text, to preach on mercy and truth at this verse is to wander far outside the olive groves.

units.la: Ps. LXXXV. 13. Eruisti animam meam ex inferno inferiori.] Ita vulg. ex LXX. ἐκ ᾅδου καταωτάτω. Lut. aus der tiefsten hölle. Vulgus Pontificiorum hunc rursus locum advocant in patrocinium purgatorii. Alii tamen de limbo interpretantur, illi vid. qui hunc Ps. de Christo literaliter exponunt. Alii de inferno damnatorum, qui vid. hunc Ps. de Davide interpretantur, q. d. tu o Deus cum juste posses me in infernum praecipitem dare, tamen dum condonasti mihi peccata mea & me per verbum tuum regeneràsti, liberasti animam meam ex inferno. S A, de aeterna morte. Subjungit tamen, posse limbum intelligi, si Psalmus de Christo accipiatur. Bellarm. quoque locum exponit de justificatione à peccatis, ob quae ad infernum inferiorem descensurus erat, nisi per gratiam liberaretur. Super hac interpretatione nolim cum quopiam funem contentionis ducere. Si quis tamen Psalmum penitius introspexerit, videbit Davidem petere liberationem à persecutoribus suis atque inter alia petitionis argumenta illud eminere, quod à Dei potentia desumit vers. 8. & ex effectis demonstrat, inter quae illud non postremum est, quod Deus jam ante ex gravissimis periculis saepius eum liberaverit. Jam ante eruisti me ex sepulcro imo, id est ne detruderer in sepulcrum imum. Vide Jun. Pisc. Neque huic expositioni obstare vocem anima, ut ad Psal. xvi. ostendimus. Neque obstat epithetum תחתיה / Licet enim illud àLXX. per superlativum, vulgato per comparativum expressum sit; Ebraea positivi gradus est. Hoc observa tiro, ne putes necessario hinc inferri, esse alium scheol superiorem, cujus respectu hic inferior vel infimus dicatur. שאל תחתיה תחתית ad verbum, sepulcrum inferum, vel, infernum. Vtrumque enim Latine dicitur. Est autem epitheton sepulcri perpetuum, quale est illud 1. Petri 4 ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις illicitis idolorum cultibus, &, illicita adulteria. Sicuti enim hinc non nisi ineptissime intuleris, esse quaedam licita adulteria, aut quandam idololatriam licitam (quod tamen fecit Greg. de Valentia, qui ex isto loco colligit quandam idololatriam esse licitam, eam vide quae in Ecclesia Romana quibusdam imaginibus seu idolis defertur) ita & hic nulla ratio inferendi, esse aliquem scheol supernum. Si vero per Scheol calamitates intelligas & pericula, jam poterit esse Αλαχεμνον. Calamitates enim aquis & luto comparantur. Ideoque quo majores illae sunt, eo profundiores stylo scripturae dicuntur. Quo autem profundius aliquid est, eo inferius est. Atque hoc modo interpretatus quoque est Euthymius, potest etiam infernus accipi pro quolibet periculo, inquit. Praemiserat autem duas istas expositiones, Si Psalmum pertinere intelligas ad D. Davidem, per infernum profundam peccati foveam intellige, adulterii nimirum & homicidii. Si vero ad Ezechiam, infernum accipe pro morte, cui proximus fuit. Sed liberum unicuique isto, hoc loco vel sepulcrum, vel magnum aliquod periculum, vel calamitatem; vel infernum intelligere. Hic vero non desunt qui licet per שאול nec limbum, nec purgatorium, sed infernum intelligant, tamen ex adjuncto epitheto diversas inferni regiones evidenter colligi autumant. Eas autem has recensent, locum damnatorum, purgatorium, limbum puerorum & quae suprema regio est, limbum patrum (vide Bellar. controv. 6. Genebr. & Carthus. ad hunc locum.) Speciosa certe objectio apud Latinos duplici nomine. 1. quod infernus Latinis dicatur ab infra 2. quod infernus apud Latinos, ut & Germanos, Helle, locum animarum, non corporum receptaculum, vid. sepulcrum significet. At in Ebraeo textu diversa sunt omnia. Namque Ebr. שאול non a situ, sed appetendo nomen habet, & indifferens est ad sepulchrum & infernum. Extende Inferni significationem, ut etiam ad sepulcrum se porrigat, aut substitue ei inferos quae vox si ab inferendo dicta est, ut putat Cl. Junius, tam sepulcrum quam Gehennam denotare potest. Ut enim in hanc animae, ita in illud corpora inferuntur. Tunc videbis illud תחתית vel esse epitheton perpetuum, vel Ἀλαxεμπxὸν, quo à corporum inferno id est sepulcro distinguatur. Neque enim necesse est cum August. asserere, inferiorem infernum dici respectu terrae quae respectu coeli sit infernus quidam, superior tamen Gehennâ, aut cum Hieron. infernum inferiorem dici respectu peccati, qui itidem est quidam infernus licet superior. Et nota, neutrum istorum patrum superioris alicujus regionis sive Limbi sive purgatorii meminisse.
units.tr: Ps. LXXXV. 13. You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell. So the Vulgate from the LXX: ἐκ ᾅδου καταωτάτω; Luther: "aus der tiefsten Hölle." The crowd of Papists again cite this passage in support of purgatory. Others interpret it of limbo, namely those who expound this psalm literally of Christ. Others interpret it of the hell of the damned, who take this psalm to be about David, as if to say: O God, although you could justly have cast me headlong into hell, yet, since you have pardoned my sins and regenerated me through your word, you have freed my soul from hell. Others understand it of eternal death. He adds, however, that limbo may be understood if the psalm is taken of Christ. Bellarmine also explains the place of justification from the sins for which he would have gone down to the lower hell unless he had been freed by grace. I would not wish to start a quarrel with anyone over this interpretation. Yet if anyone looks more deeply into the psalm, he will see that David asks for deliverance from his persecutors, and that among the grounds of his petition this stands out, which he takes from the power of God in verse 8, and demonstrates from its effects; among these is not the least that God had already often delivered him from the gravest dangers. You have delivered me already, from the deepest pit, that is, that I should not be thrust down into the lowest grave. See Junius and Piscator. Nor does the word soul stand in the way of this exposition, as we showed at Psalm 16. Nor does the epithet תחתיה stand in the way. For although the LXX render it by a superlative and the Vulgate by a comparative, the Hebrew is in the positive degree. Let the beginner note this, lest he think it follows necessarily that there is another, higher sheol, with respect to which this one is called lower or lowest. שאול תחתיה, word for word, the lower grave, or hell; for both are said in Latin. The epithet is a constant one of the grave, like that in 1 Pet. 4: ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις, "unlawful idolatries," and "unlawful adulteries." For just as you could infer, most foolishly, from that that there are some lawful adulteries or some lawful idolatry (which, however, Gregory of Valencia did, who from that passage gathers that a certain idolatry is lawful, which see in what is offered in the Roman Church to certain images or idols), so here there is no reason to infer that there is some higher sheol. But if by Sheol you understand calamities and dangers, it can be a distinguishing epithet [Ἀλαχεμνόν]. For calamities are compared to waters and mud, and therefore the greater they are, the deeper the language of Scripture calls them. And the deeper a thing is, the lower it is. Euthymius too interpreted it in this way: "Hell can also be taken for any danger," he says. He had earlier set out two such expositions: If you take the psalm to refer to King David, understand by hell the deep pit of sin, namely of adultery and murder. If to Hezekiah, take hell for death, to which he was near. But this is left free to each reader: to understand here either the grave, or some great danger, or calamity, or hell. Nor are there lacking those who, although they understand by שאול neither limbo nor purgatory but hell, nevertheless hold that the different regions of hell are clearly gathered from the attached epithet. They list these as the place of the damned, purgatory, the limbo of children, and the highest region, the limbo of the fathers (see Bellarmine, Controversy 6; Genebrardus and the Carthusians on this passage). Certainly a specious objection among the Latins, on two counts: first, because infernus is said by Latins from infra; second, because infernus among Latins, as among the Germans with Helle, signifies the place of souls, not the receptacle of bodies, that is, the grave. But in the Hebrew text all these things are different. For the Hebrew שאול derives its name not from position but from asking/desiring, and is indifferent to grave or hell. Extend the meaning of infernus so that it reaches also to the grave, or substitute for it inferi, a word which, if it is derived ab inferendo, as the eminent Junius thinks, can denote both grave and Gehenna. For just as souls are brought into the one, so bodies are brought into the other. Then you will see that תחתית is either a constant epithet, or a distinguishing one [Ἀλαχεμπτόν], by which it is set apart from the hell of bodies, that is, the grave. For it is not necessary, with Augustine, to assert that the lower hell is so called with respect to the earth, which with respect to heaven is a kind of hell, yet higher than Gehenna; nor, with Jerome, that the lower hell is so called with respect to sin, which likewise is a kind of hell, though a higher one. And note that neither of these Fathers mentions any higher region, whether limbo or purgatory.

units.la: Psalm. LXXXVII. 4. Memor ero Raab. ] August. Theod. Euthymius & alii per Raab intellexerunt meretricem illam, quae Josuae 2. exploratores hospitio excepit. Euthym. Per Raab Cananaeos intelligit. Raab enim erat Cananaa. Error natus ex scriptura Graeca, quae רהב & רהב confundit. Meretrix illa vocatur רָהָב cum duplici aspiratione, quam Lxx. saepe per χ exprimere. At רהב cum He, proprie superbiam significans, & hic & Psal. 89. 11. & Jesai. 51. 9. pro Ægypto ponitur. De gentis hujus insigni & plusquam Campana superbia profani & sacri authores testes sunt.
units.tr: Psalm 87:4. "I will make mention of Rahab." Augustine, Theodoret, Euthymius and others understood by Raab that harlot who received the spies into her house in Joshua 2. Euthymius: He means the Canaanites by Rahab, for Rahab was a Canaanite. The error arose from the Greek text, which confuses רהב and רהב. The harlot is called רָהָב with a double aspirate, which the Seventy often render with χ. But רהב with He properly signifies pride, and it stands here and in Psalm 89:11 and Isaiah 51:9 for Egypt. Both profane and sacred authors bear witness to the remarkable pride of this nation, which surpassed even the Campanians.
