units.la: ולציון יאמר איש ילד בה והוא יכוננה עליון | Nunquid Sion dicet homo, & homo natus est in ea, & ipse fundavit eam altissimus.
units.tr: [ולציון יאמר איש ילד בה והוא יכוננה עליון] | Shall a man say of Sion, "A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her"?

units.la: Vaticinatur hoc Psalmo Propheta de vocatione gentium. Eam comparat generationi & numerationi & conscriptioni vers. 5. 6. 7. Verba Ebraea plana sunt, Et de Sion. (vel ad Sion, Pisc. Nam de Sion, Pag. Et propter Sion) dicetur, vir & vir (hoc est, hic & ille, variae nationes) natus est (per verbum Euangelii & Sp. Sanctum) in ea; (in Sion, in Ecclesia) & ipse Altissimus stabiliet eam. Non praepoterunt aut praevalebunt ei inferorum portae. Inspiciamus jam vulgatum Interpretem. Hic merae tenebrae. Sion dativi casus esse notant Interpretes. Nunquid proprie est an aliquid? At saepe adverbii naturam induit idemque valet quod an. Bellarminus fatetur in Ebraeo esse literam ו / Et. Sed fortasse textus Ebraeus est corruptus, inquit, vitio scriptorum & pro vau legendum est ה / Sed fortasse textus Ebr. non est corruptus, & potius coecutivit interpres. Sed bene habet. Etiamsi maneat particula &, inquit Bell. idem est sensus, si accipiantur verba per modum interrogandi Quid ergo opus erat fontes de mendo suspectare? Nam certe illa ellipsis interrogativi ה non est insolens. Sed ne sic quidem res confecta est. Namque illa verba, Et Sioni dicet homo? aut An Sioni dicet homo? non possunt illum sensum simpliciter ajentem habere, Sioni dicet homo. Tunc enim potius dixisset הלא annon. Annon Sioni dicet homo? Quando enim Ebraei interrogant cum negatione, tunc vehementer affirmant. Ideo Sa coactus est hoc nunquid exponere per nonne. Et Carth. In translat. Hieron. juxta Ebr. habetur, Ad Sion dicetur, Sensus ergo, Nunquid, id est imo ipsi Sion dicetur, &c. Illud cum videret Bellarm. haec tanquam per modum admirantis dicta explicat, (ut Gen. xviii. 12. & 31.) q. d. an fieri poterit ut homo aliquis dicat Sioni rem tam novam, tam admirandam & a saeculo inauditam? Sed mittamus ista. Nunquid Sioni dicet homo? quis homo? Joh. Baptista, de quo scriptum est, fuit homo missus a Deo, &c. qui primus Euangelizavit Sioni, inquit Carthus. Quid autem dicet iste homo? * Homo natus est in ea id est Christus Deus & homo genitus est in populo Sion. Et ipse ille Christus secundum humanitatem natus ex virgine, Altissimus vero secundum deitatem fundavit eam id est virginem matrem in omni gratia stabilivit, in tantum quod nunquam a vero fundamento peccando prolapsa est, vel fundavit eam id est Ecclesiam. In hoc itaque versu, inquit, evidenter ostenditur in Christo duplex natura & una persona. Homo natus est in ea. Ecce tibi naturam humanam. Dum vero idem demonstratur pronomine ipse, patet identitas in persona. Postrem, ocum subditur, Altissimus fundavit, &c. duppliciter ostenditur ejus divinitas. Alii hoc modo interpretati sunt, Nunquid Sioni Ecclesiae dicet homo Christus? Nam Christus saepe dixit Judaeis, primum suum adventum impletum fuisse. Alii nunquid acceperunt simpliciter pro An ut haec interrogatio aequipolleat neganti sententiae, An Sioni dicet homo id est an purus aliquis homo humana sapientia & virtute persuadebit ecclesiae ea, quae de Christo tenenda sunt, quod homo natus sit & fundaverit Ecclesiam, &c. q. d. non. Humana enim ratione persuaderi non potest, Christum esse Θεάνθρωπον. Observant postea iidem, dictum non esse, homo conceptus est in ea sed natus
units.tr: In this psalm the prophet foretells the calling of the Gentiles, and compares it to the enrolling, numbering and registering in verses 5, 6 and 7. The Hebrew words are plain: "And of Zion" (or "to Zion", or as Pagninus has it, "concerning Zion" or "on account of Zion") "it shall be said, man and man" (that is, this one and that one, people of various nations) "was born" (through the word of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit) "in her" (in Zion, that is, in the Church), "and the Most High himself shall establish her. The gates of hell shall not prevail against her." Let us now look at the Vulgate translator. Here there is sheer darkness. The commentators note that Sion is in the dative case. Nunquid properly means "is anything?", but it often takes on the character of an adverb and has the same force as "whether". Bellarmine admits that the Hebrew has the letter ו, "and". "But perhaps," he says, "the Hebrew text is corrupted by the faults of scribes, and ה should be read for ו." Yet perhaps the Hebrew text is not corrupted, and rather the translator has gone astray. Still, all is well, Bellarmine says: "Even if the particle 'and' remains, the sense is the same if the words are taken interrogatively." Why, then, suspect the sources of error? That ellipsis of the interrogative ה is not unusual. Yet even so the matter is not settled. For the words "And will a man say to Sion?" or "Will a man say to Sion?" cannot have the plain affirmative sense "A man will say to Sion". In that case the writer would rather have used הלא, "is it not?" "Will not a man say to Sion?" For when the Hebrews ask with a negative, they affirm emphatically. So Sa was compelled to render this nunquid as nonne. And Carthusian: In Jerome's translation, made from the Hebrew, it reads, "It shall be said to Sion." The sense, therefore, is "Whether", that is, "Rather, it shall be said to Sion itself," etc. When Bellarmine saw this, he explained these words as spoken in the manner of one who marvels (as in Genesis 18:12 and 31), as if to say: "Can it come about that any man should say to Sion a thing so new, so wonderful, and unheard of from the beginning?" But let us set these matters aside. "Will a man say to Sion?" What man? John the Baptist, of whom it is written, "There was a man sent from God," etc., who first preached the gospel to Sion, says Carthusian. But what will this man say? "A man was born in her", that is, Christ, God and man, was born among the people of Sion. That same Christ, according to his humanity, was born of a virgin; but the Most High, according to his deity, founded her, that is, he established the virgin mother in all grace, so that she never fell away from the true foundation by sinning; or he founded her, that is, the Church. In this verse, therefore, he says, the double nature and the one person in Christ is clearly shown. "A man was born in her": here you have his human nature. And since the same person is pointed out by the pronoun "himself", the identity of the person is evident. Finally, when it is added, "the Most High founded her," his divinity is shown in two ways. Others have interpreted it thus: "Will a man, Christ, say to Sion, that is, the Church?" For Christ often told the Jews that his first coming had been fulfilled. Others took nunquid simply as an, so that this question is equivalent to a negative statement: "Or will a man say to Sion," that is, will some mere man, by human wisdom and virtue, persuade the Church of the things that must be held concerning Christ, that a man was born and founded the Church, etc.? As if to say: no. For it cannot be persuaded by human reasoning that Christ is the God-man. Afterwards the same commentators observe that it is not said "a man was conceived in her" but "was born".

units.la: * Ita & Bell. Christus voluit esse civis Sionis secundum naturam humanam, qui fundator ejus est secundum naturam divinam. natus est, ad insinuandem, quod Christus ab exordio suæ conceptionis in virgine, erat homo cunctis virtutib. & scientiis perfectus. Hi omnes prius illud homo jungunt cum verbo dicet quæ tamen voces accentu Rebiangh distinguuntur, ut nihil jam dicam, in Ebr. non esse אַמָר sed אָמַר in Nifal. Posterius autem homo referunt ad natus est. Hæc est vera interpunctio & lectio inquit Belarm. Lxx. teste Hieronymo, locum hunc ita reddiderant, μὴ Σιὼν ἐρεῖ ἄνθρωπος ἡ ἄνθρωπος ἐγεννήθη (Thod. v. & vi. Editio, ἐγεννήθη) ἐν αὐτῇ. Voculam μὴν per nunquid interpretati sunt Hieron. & vulgatus. At codices Græci, quotquot hodie extant, qua impressi, qua manuscripti, legunt, μήτης Σιὼν. Vetustissimum oportet hoc sphalma fuisse, cum non solum Theodoretus, Ambros. Eucherius, Euthymius, Augustinus,* Ambros. & Cassiod. sed & Apollinaris in paraphrasi sua hanc lectionem secuti sint. Versus Apollinaris iste est,
units.tr: * So also Bellarmine: Christ willed to be a citizen of Sion according to his human nature, and he is its founder according to his divine nature. "Was born" is used to show that Christ, from the beginning of his conception in the virgin, was a man perfect in all virtues and knowledge. All these commentators join the first "man" with the verb "shall say", though these words are distinguished by the accent rebiah. Not to say more, in the Hebrew the form is not אַמָר but אָמַר in the niphal. They refer the second "man" to "was born". "This is the true punctuation and reading," says Bellarmine. The Seventy, according to Jerome, had rendered the passage thus: "Will not Sion say, a man, or a man was born (Theodoret, fifth and sixth editions, has ἐγεννήθη) in her." Jerome and the Vulgate translated the little word μὴν as nunquid. But all the Greek manuscripts that survive today, whether printed or handwritten, read μήτης Σιὼν, "Mother Sion". This error must have been very ancient, since not only Theodoret, Ambrose, Eucherius, Euthymius, Augustine, Ambrose and Cassiodorus, but also Apollinaris in his paraphrase, followed this reading. The verse of Apollinaris is this:

units.la: Μητέρα πρὸς ταῦτα ἡμίσεως Σιὼν χαλίσει.
units.tr: Μητέρα πρὸς ταῦτα ἡμίσεως Σιὼν χαλίσει. [Mother Sion shall say to these things, half of ...]

units.la: Hujus autem lectionis interpretationem proponam verbis Eucherii, Mater Sion dicet homo & homo factus est in ea, & ipse fundavit eam altissimus. Mater Sion, inquit Eucherius, ut quidam volunt, Mariam significat, in qua natus est homo Christus ipsius quoque matris creator. Euthymius, Manifeste & palam pradicit, quod ex quacunque gente quis ingressus fuerit in Sion, dicet quod Sion, mater est. Subintelligi enim debet dictio est. Mater autem ideo appellatur Sion, quia regenerat ut diximus, vel quia spiritualium dogmatum cibo fideles omnes, veluti pia mater alit. Vel mater appellatur tanquam amabilis. Et homo natus est in ea. Hoc ad Christi generationem pertinet, &c. Theodor. unusquisque Sionem matrem nuncupabit. & omnis homo dicet, quoniam mater est Sion. August. Unde Babylon aspiraret ad Jerusalem, unde Raab (meretrix illa) pervenire ad fundamenta, unde alienigenæ, &c.? Audi unde. Mater Sion dicet homo. Est quidam homo, qui dicit mater Sion, & per hunc veniunt omnes isti. Sed iste homo, quid est? — Mater Sion dicit homo, sequitur ibi, quasi quæreres per quem venerit Raab, Bab. alienigenæ — Ecce mater Sion dicit homo. Quis homo? Qui homo factus est in ea. In ea ipse factus est homo, & ipse eam fundavit. Ut in ea fieret homo, jam fundata erat. Sic intellige, si potes. Etenim mater Sion dicet, sed homo. Mater Sion dicet, homo autem factus est in ea. Ipse autem fundarit eam, non homo, sed altissimus. Sic fundavit civita-tem in qua nasceretur, quomodo creavit matrem, de qua nasceretur, &c. Alloquar te Lector, verbis Augustini. Sic intellige, si potes.Ego profecto profiteor me non intelligere. Tantam caligi-nem huic loco unicum illud librariorum sphalma offudit. Quanto simplicior illa expositio est, quam nos ex nostris interpretibus proposuimus! Quia vero Bellar. evidentem hanc prophetiam de nativitate Christi, ab illis & Judæis obscurari, & propter Rabbinorum glossas textum perverti asserit, operæ erit, nostro-rum expositionem unius atque alterius Pontificii testimonio firmatum ire. Sic ergo Sa Nunquid ] pro nonne. Sion ] id est Sion seu Sioni. Homo & homo ] id est quisque seu plures, sc. dicent. Vel plurimi in ea nascentur, sc. per baptismum, ut, conjungatur cum natus est. q. d. Deus in ea natus est scil. in Judaea, seu in cordibus credentium, vel homo & homo natus id est multi nati scil. spiritualiter.Genebrardus, nunquid Sioni dicet quilibet, multos in ipsius gremio regenerari quotidie, ac fideles fieri, ipsamque à Deo fundatam esse? Et paulo post vir & vir nati sunt in ipsa id est magni & multi viri in ea sunt generati, per regenerationem sc. ex aqua & Spiritu S. Ho-mo & homo pertinent ad verba sequentia, nequis prius homo (ἀνθρωπος Bellarm) construat cum, dicet. אִישׁ וְאִישׁ / vir & Vir id est multi. Nam illa repetitio multitudinem significat, Kimchi. Aliqui, homo & homo, Judaus & gentilis, uterque vid. natus est in ea per bapt. fidemque. Nam in ea non est distinctio Judaei & Graeci. Hæc Genebr.
units.tr: Here I will set out the interpretation of this reading in the words of Eucherius: "Mother Sion shall say, man, and man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her. Mother Sion," says Eucherius, "as some wish, signifies Mary, in whom the man Christ was born, who is also the creator of his own mother." Euthymius: He foretells plainly and openly that from whatever nation someone enters into Sion, he will say that Sion is mother. For the word "is" must be understood. Sion is called mother because she regenerates, as we have said, or because, like a loving mother, she feeds all the faithful with the food of spiritual teachings. Or she is called mother as lovable. "And man was born in her." This pertains to the generation of Christ, etc. Theodoret: each one will call Sion mother, and every man will say that Sion is mother. Augustine: Whence did Babylon aspire to Jerusalem, whence did Rahab (that harlot) come to the foundations, whence did foreigners come? Hear whence: "Mother Sion shall say, man." There is a certain man who says "Mother Sion," and through him all those come. But what is this man? "Mother Sion shall say, man" follows, as if you asked through whom Rahab came, and the Babylonians, the foreigners. Behold, "Mother Sion shall say, man." Which man? The one who was made man in her. In her he himself was made man, and he himself founded her. She was already founded, in order that he might be made man in her. Understand this, if you can. For Mother Sion shall say, but man. Mother Sion shall say, but man was made in her. Yet he who founded her was not a man but the Most High. He founded the city in which he would be born just as he created the mother from whom he would be born, etc. I address you, reader, in the words of Augustine: "Understand this, if you can." For my part I frankly confess that I do not understand. That single error of the copyists has cast such darkness over this passage! How much simpler is the explanation that we have set out from our own interpreters! But since Bellarmine asserts that this plain prophecy of the nativity of Christ is obscured by those readings and by the Jews, and that the text is distorted by the glosses of the rabbis, it will be worth while to set out our own explanation, confirmed by the testimony of one or another Papist. So Sa: "Nunquid" is "for nonne". "Sion" is "that is, Sion or to Sion". "Man and man" is "that is, each one, or several, namely, shall say. Or many shall be born in her, namely, through baptism, so that it is joined with 'was born'. That is, God was born in her, namely in Judaea, or in the hearts of believers; or 'man and man was born', that is, many were born, namely spiritually." Genebrardus: "Will anyone say to Sion that many are regenerated daily in her bosom and become believers, and that she has been founded by God?" And a little after: "Man and man were born in her," that is, great and many men are generated in her through regeneration, namely of water and the Holy Spirit. "Man and man" pertains to the words that follow, so that the first "man" (ἄνθρωπος, Bellarmine) is not joined with "shall say". "Man and man", איש ואיש, that is, many. For that repetition signifies a multitude, says Kimchi. Some take "man and man" as Jew and Gentile, each of whom is born in her through baptism and faith, for in her there is no distinction of Jew and Greek. So Genebrardus.

units.la: Ps. LXXXVIII. * Anmedicisuscitabunt? ] Ita vulgatus ex Lxx. ἢ ἰατροὶ ἀναστήσουσι; Ebr. an mortui, defuncti, expertes vitæ exurgent? Sed illi legerunt רוֹפְאִים / יְקוּמוּ Ita Medici in hunc Psal. prout vulgo canitur, introducti sunt Confer jam interpretes. Obiter noto, Medicos à Thalmudicis inter opifices numerari, de quibus adjecte sentiunt. In Thalmud circa finem libri Kidduschim inter alia occurrit hoc effatum, טוֹב שֶׁבְּרוֹפְאִים לְגֵיהִנֹּם optimus inter medicos ad Gehen-nam Glossa, Non enim metuit à morbis, vescitur laute, nec confringit cor suum Deo, aliquando etiam interficit homines, quando pauperes, quos posset, non sanat. Mirabor si Judæorum Medici huic sententiæ calculum suum apposituri sint. Ego Sirachidem potius audiendum sentio, Honora medicum, Et Homerum,
units.tr: Ps. 88. "Will physicians raise them up?" So the Vulgate, following the LXX: "ἢ ἰατροὶ ἀναστήσουσι;" The Hebrew has "Will the dead, the departed, those cut off from life, rise up?" But the translators read רוֹפְאִים / יְקוּמוּ ("physicians will rise"), and so physicians are introduced into this psalm as it is commonly sung. Let us now compare the interpreters. I note in passing that the Talmudists count physicians among the craftsmen, and they hold a poor opinion of them. Near the end of the tractate Kiddushin the Talmud contains, among other sayings, this one: "The best of physicians is for Gehenna" (טוֹב שֶׁבְּרוֹפְאִים לְגֵיהִנֹּם). The gloss explains: "For he does not fear diseases, he eats lavishly, and he does not break his heart before God; sometimes he even kills people, when he does not heal the poor whom he could have healed." I would be surprised if Jewish physicians were willing to add their vote to this opinion. I think we should rather listen to Ben Sira, "Honour the physician," and to Homer:

units.la: Εἰς ἰατρὸς ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων.
units.tr: A physician is a man worth many others. [Εἰς ἰατρὸς ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων]

units.la: Pf. LXXXIX. Ad hunc Pf. prolixum invenies commentarium non solum in Enarrat. B. Augustini ad hunc librum, sed & in opere de Civit. Dei, lib. 17. cap. 9. & 10. & 11. Multas illic invenies expositiones, de quibus Psalmographus nunquam cogitavit. Neque fieri potuit aliter. Fontes enim adire non potuit. Aberrantem tertio quoque versu interpretationem secutus est, & in loca librariorum erroribus foedata sæpe prolixe commentatus est. vers. 44. vel aliis 46. Ebræa habent, abbreviasti dies עלומיו id est adolescentia ejus id est dies regni, quibus adolescens regnavit. Quæ interpretes intelligunt Jojachin, qui cum xvii. annos natus, admodum certe adolescens, regnare coepisset, trimestris tantum rex fuit. Cujus fata descripta invenies 2. Reg. 24. vers. 8. & 10. Lxx, ἰσμίνεωας τὰς ἡμέρας ἢ χρόνε αὐτὸ, vulg. minorasti dies temporis ejus, ut legisse videantur עולמיו sæculorum ejus. At imperita manus in quibusdam Editionibus vocem χρόνε demutavit ϑεόνε, quam lectionem secutus B. August. & in comm, & de Civit. Dei xvii. 10. legit minuisti dies sedii ejus. Hic ergo χ in ϑ migraverat. Contra Psal. 132. 15. ϑ in χ corrupit imperitia: De quo suo loco. vers. 39. Tu iratus es cum uncto tuo. vid. Sedechia, quem Nebucadnetzar exoculatum & compedibus vinctum captivum abduxit. Ebr. העברה / התעברה transiit. עברה vehemens ira, quæ sic dicta, vel quod cito, vel quod modum transeat. Hinc in Hitphaël, התעבר trafci. At Lxx ἀνεβάλας ἡ χρονιζεται Vulg. distulisti Christum tuum. quod Interpretes de dilato Christi adventu exponunt. vers. 48. זכר־אני מה־חלד Genebr. Arias Mont. memento quanti ævi ego sim. Pisc. cujus durationis ego sim. Jun. quam temporarius sim. חלד * vel præsentis sæculi cito desinentis statum, vel breve illud vitæ nostræ curriculum significat, vel mundum cujus figura, ut loquitur Apostolus 1. Cor. 7. σχῆμα seu quod idem est παροδίνει. Lxx. memento quæ sit ὑπόστασις μέ. Vulg. quæ mea substantia. hoc est, interpretibus Genebr. & Bell. quæ sit subsistentia, firmitas, id est vita, duratio, quam modica sit duratio vitæ meæ. At August. quam longe ab hoc tramite divertit. Ille tam in libris de Civit. Dei quam in commment per substantiam Christum intelligit. q. dixisset Psaltes, memento quod Christi humana natura mea substantia est, &c. Lege & judica.
units.tr: Ps. 89. On this psalm you will find a lengthy commentary, not only in Augustine's Enarrationes on this book, but also in his work De Civitate Dei, book 17, chapters 9, 10 and 11. There you will find many expositions that the psalmist never thought of. Nor could it have been otherwise, since they could not go to the sources. Following an interpretation that also goes astray in the third verse, he often comments at length on passages disfigured by the errors of copyists. Verse 44, or by another count 46: the Hebrew has "you have shortened his days", עלומיו, that is, "his youth", i.e. the days of the reign in which the young man reigned. The interpreters understand this of Jehoiachin, who, though he began to reign at seventeen, being certainly quite young, was king for only three months. You will find his fate described in 2 Kings 24, verses 8 and 10. The LXX has "you have diminished the days of his time" (ἐσμίκρυνας τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ χρόνου αὐτοῦ), and the Vulgate "you have shortened the days of his time", as though they had read עולמיו, "of his ages". But an inexperienced hand in some editions changed the word χρόνου into θρόνου, and Augustine followed this reading both in the commentary and in De Civitate Dei 17.10, reading "you have diminished the days of his throne". Here χ had changed into θ. Conversely, at Psalm 132:15 ignorance corrupted θ into χ, of which more in its place. Verse 39: "You have been angry with your anointed." Think of Zedekiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar blinded, bound in chains, and led away captive. The Hebrew has העברה / התעברה, "you have passed over", from עברה, "vehement anger", so called either because it passes swiftly or because it passes beyond measure. Hence in the Hithpael התעבר means "to be angry". But the LXX has "you have put off" (ἀνεβάλου), and the Vulgate "you have deferred your Christ", which the interpreters explain as the deferred coming of Christ. Verse 48: זכר־אני מה־חלד. Geneva and Arias Montanus: "remember how long an age I am." Piscator: "of what duration I am." Junius: "how temporary I am." חלד signifies either the state of the present age, which quickly passes away, or that brief course of our life, or the world, whose "figure" (as the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 7: σχῆμα), or, which is the same thing, "passing away" (παροδίνει). The LXX has "remember what is my ὑπόστασις"; the Vulgate, "what is my substance." That is, according to Geneva and Bellarmine, what is the subsistence, the firmness, that is, the life and duration: how brief the duration of my life is. But Augustine wanders far from this path. In both the De Civitate Dei and the commentary he understands Christ by "substance", as though the psalmist had said: remember that Christ's human nature is my substance, and so on. Read and judge.

units.la: Psal. XC. Multum & multoties ab Ebraïci textus semita in hoc Psal. divertère Interpretes Græci. Unde & alienæ expositiones natæ sunt. Nos paucula delibabimus. verf. 9. בְּלִינוּ יְמֵינוּ כְּמוֹ הֲגִיגׇ ad verbum consumsimus annos nostros sicuti * halitum, Chaldæus הֵיךְ הַבֵּל פּוּמָא דְסִתְוָא tanquam halitum oris hyemalem, alii, sicuti sermonem, wie ein geschwatz, Græci, τὰ ἔτη ἡμῶν ὡσεὶ ἀράχνη ἐμελέτων * anni nostri sicut arenea meditabuntur. Nam τὸ ἐμελέτων ad versum præced. retulere. Bellarm. non inspexit Græcum textum quando scripsit, Lxx. pro meditatio scripsisse meditabuntur. Hoc enim esset μελετήσεται. Genebrardi quoque & Emmanuelis Sa expositio, qua τὸ meditabuntur exponunt passive, ex Græco textu refutatur. Nam quod addit Genebr. legendum videri μελετῶν, frustra est. Nullius enim codicis authoritate nititur, nisi ita forte exponas, annos nostros sicut arenean meditabuntur impersonaliter, reputabunt, æstimabunt, quod idem cum eo, anni nostri reputabuntur. Valde sudat Genebr. ut versionem hanc cum Ebr. conciliet, & tandem fatetur, eam Ebræo non respondere, nisi fortassis, inquit, חֲגָוָא priscis fuerit aranea. Sed unde tunc vox meditabuntur exsculpenda? Tu disce tiro, omnia illa, quæ huc vulgo convectantur de aranea, inter quæ multa satis arguta, non verbis Mosis, sed aberranti versioni superstructa esse. Verf. x. Ebræa ita habent, Dies annorum nostrorum, (id est, quod attinet ad dies annorum nostrorum) in illis sunt septuaginta anni. Hactenus Lxx. & vulg. benè וְאִם בִּגְבוּרֹת שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה Ad verbum, & si in fortitudinibus, octoginta anni. hoc est interprete Genebr. in potenti & firma corporis constitutione, Ita & Sa. Jun. ut simus valentissimi, Pisc. ad numerum annorum refert, si admodum invalescant, sc. numero. Tigur. ad summum. Bellar. Lxx. ἐν δυναστείαις, quod significare posset, in principatibus, sive imperiis. Sed hoc loco ista significatio non facit ad propositum. Ergo hoc loco vox illa significat vim & potentiam complexionis, & sic exponunt omnes interpretes. Hæc Bell. cui oppono Euthymium, qui locum sic interpretatur, Anni nostri in ipsis id est in nobis ipsis, sunt 70 anni. Eousque enim nostri summus id est nostri dominamur, roboreque ac viribus nostris movemur. Si autem in potentatibus quis victurus est, hoc est, in violentia, eo quod tunc vix aliquid fieri potest, 80. annis quis vivet. Et Augustinum, Aliud est in ipsis, aliud, in potentatibus. In ip-sis. fis, hoc est, in annis vel diebus ipsis, quod datur intelligi in temporalibus rebus. Ideo septuaginta, quia temporalia promitti videntur in V. Testamento. Si autem non in ipsis annis, sed in potentatibus, id est, non in rebus temporalibus sed æterni, octoginta anni, quod N. T. est in spe renovationis & resurrectionis in æternum. Sequitur, וַיִּהְיוּ עָמָל וָאָוֶן Arias Mont. & fastus eorum labor & iniquitas Jun. excellentissimum eorum laboriosum & molestum. Pisc.—labor & dolor, רָהָב proprie robur. Deinde & elationem, fastum significat, atque adeo per Metonym. omne illud, quo homo superbire solet, ut, corporis sanitas, pulchritudo, divitiæ, amici, honor, dignitas. Hinc elegantes interpretationes: Abenezra, ימי רהבם ימי בוח וחוק והם הבחרות בולם הם עמל ואון dies רהבם sunt dies roboris & virium, puta dies juventutis. Omnes isti sunt dolor & labor, seu potius labor & vanitas, seu, labor & iniquitas. Quotusquisque enim vitam suam in adolescentia instituit ex præscripto Salomonis Eccles. 12. Memento creatores tui in diebus juventutis tuæ. flos ætatis|Diabolo plerunque, sex senectutis Deo offertur. Sed & omnes istæ juventutis delitiæ, quid aliud sunt, quam vanitas vanitatum? R. Sal. כל הגדולה והשררה שיש לו לארם בימים האלה אינם אלא עמל ואון omnis magnificentia & dominatus, quem obtinet homo in diebus illis, nihil aliud sunt quàm עמל ואון Et certe quid magis laboriosum, quid pluribus periculis tam animæ quam corporis obnoxium est, quam eorum vita, qui cum imperio sunt? Kimchi, וחוזק הימים & fortitudo dierum כלומר אפילו מי שיהיו ימיו בשלוה עמל ואון הם q. d. etiam cum dies alicujus prospere & tranquille erunt, nil nisi labor & molestia est. Hunc sensum expressit Lutherus, alg het hoste: wch geweest is / soo ist moepte ende arbept ghewest. Et quod ad istam vitæ particulam attinet, qua valemus, quid dici potest verius? Quando valemus, tum maxime laboramus & delassamur quisque in vocatione sua. Cum superveniunt morbi, inviti à laboribus feriamur, nihilque magis habemus in votis, quam ut pristinis viribus restitutis, ad intermissos etiam gravissimos labores redire liceat. Ita præstantior illa vitæ particula assiduis laboribus deteritur. Deodatus, & anche il fior di quegli [anni] è travaglio & vanita. id est quin etiam flos (Scholion. Ebr. excellentia, q. d. honos, pretium, præstantissi- { } Scholion. Ebr. excellentia, q. d. honos, pretium, præstantissitissimum & dignissimum.) istorum annorum est labor & vanitas. Doctissimi Interpretes ex Pontificiis has interpretationes amplectuntur. Et profecto plus illas in recessu suo habere, quam fronte promittunt, illi optime judicabunt qui his meditationibus inversantur. Illam vero, quam vulgatus ex Lxx. expressit, quam difficulter ex Ebraeo extruderis! Et amplius eorum labor & dolor, Lxx. τὸ ἀλγεινον αὐτῶν. Adhaec, quam frigida sententia! quod ipsos excedit. Bella. Illud & amplius eorum, communiter expositur de vita, quae producitur ultra LXX. annos, atque haec expositio est Hieron. Aug. Theodoreti, & aliorum gravium authorum. Psalterium Rom. legit plurimum eorum, quod interpretantur de majori vel potiori parte vitae humanae. Sed hanc expositionem minus probabilem esse asserit Bellar. Mihi tamen dubium non est, quin haec fuerit mens Graecorum interpretum, quos etiam opinor soni affinitate deceptos, pro רבם robbam legisse vel potius interpretatos esse רבם robbam. Nam quod Cenomanus putat eos legisse הרבם / monstrum vocis est. Ex sequentibus יש ונעפה Arias, quia resecatur cito & avolavimus. Jun. quo festine excisio, avolamus. Pisc. quumque avulsum [illud] fuerit, avolamus. Ex istis, inquam, Lxx. hanc nobis interpretationem dedere, ὅπ ἐπῆλθε ωεχαταις * ἐφ' ἡμᾶς, καὶ καιδευθησόμεθα. quoniam supervenit nobis mansuetudo & corripiemur. Non de nihilo miratur Hiero. epistola ad Cypr. quod boni isti Interpretes legerint. Certe verborum istorum nec volam nec vestigium in fontibus invenies. Quid Bellarminus? Aliquid eos legisse, quod recte in eam sententiam verti posset, dubitare non debemus, cum viri doctissimi & fidelissimi fuerint & cum illis consentiant Theodotio & vi. Editio. illis oppono Symmachum, τμηθέντες γὰρ ἄφνω ἐκπεταννύμεθα, succisi enim repente avolamus. & v. Editionem quoniam transivimus celeriter & dissolvimus. Cl. Drusius existimat illa, חיש וש exponi posse, succiditur tacite, & confert cum illo Poëtae,
units.tr: Ps. 90. The Greek interpreters stray very often and in many places from the path of the Hebrew text in this psalm, and from this alien expositions arose. We shall touch on only a few. Verse 9: בְּלִינוּ יְמֵינוּ כְּמוֹ הֲגִיגׇ, word for word "we have consumed our years like a sigh" (כְּמוֹ הֶגֶה). The Chaldean paraphrast has "like the winter breath of the mouth" (הֵיךְ הַבֵּל פּוּמָא דְסִתְוָא), others "like a sound" (wie ein geschwatz), the Greeks "our years shall be meditated upon as a spider" (τὰ ἔτη ἡμῶν ὡσεὶ ἀράχνη ἐμελέτων). For the word ἐμελέτων they have referred to the preceding verse. Bellarmine did not look at the Greek text when he wrote that the LXX had written "they shall meditate" for "meditation", for that would be μελετήσεται. The explanation of Geneva and of Emmanuel Sá, which takes "they shall meditate" passively, is refuted by the Greek text too. What Geneva adds, that μελετῶν seems to be the proper reading, is pointless, since it rests on the authority of no manuscript, unless perhaps you explain "they shall meditate on our years as a spider" impersonally: they will reckon, they will esteem, which amounts to the same as "our years will be reckoned". Geneva sweats hard to reconcile this version with the Hebrew, and at last confesses that it does not correspond to the Hebrew, unless perhaps, he says, חֲגָוָא meant "spider" to the ancients. But then from where is the word "they shall meditate" to be carved out? Learn this, young student: all those things commonly carried in here about the spider, some of them quite clever, are built upon a mistaken version, not upon the words of Moses. Verse 10: the Hebrew reads, "The days of our years" (that is, as far as the days of our years are concerned) "are in them seventy years." So far the LXX and the Vulgate, rightly. The Hebrew continues: וְאִם בִּגְבוּרֹת שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה, word for word "and if in strengths, eighty years", that is, according to Geneva, in a powerful and firm constitution of the body. So also Sá. Junius: "so that we are very strong." Piscator refers it to the number of years: "if they grow very strong", namely in number. The Tigurine: "at most." Bellarmine: the LXX has ἐν δυναστείαις, "which could mean 'in principalities or empires'. But that meaning does not serve our purpose here. Therefore in this place the word signifies the force and power of constitution, and so all the interpreters explain it." So Bellarmine. Against him I set Euthymius, who explains the place thus: "Our years are seventy in themselves, that is, in us; for until then we rule over ourselves and are moved by our own strength and vigour. But if someone is going to live in powers, that is in violence, since then scarcely anything can be done, he will live for eighty years." And Augustine: "It is one thing 'in themselves', another 'in powers'. 'In themselves', that is, in the years or days themselves, which is to be understood of temporal things. Hence seventy, because temporal things seem to be promised in the Old Testament. But if not in the years themselves but in powers, that is, not in temporal but in eternal things, then eighty years, which in the New Testament is in the hope of renewal and resurrection to eternity." There follows: וַיִּהְיוּ עָמָל וָאָוֶן. Arias Montanus: "and their pride is labour and iniquity"; Junius: "their most excellent part is laborious and troublesome"; Piscator: "labour and pain." רָהָב properly means strength. It then also signifies arrogance and pride, and so by metonymy everything in which a man is wont to pride himself: bodily health, beauty, riches, friends, honour, dignity. Hence there are elegant interpretations. Abenezra: "the days of their רהב are days of strength and vigour, that is, the days of youth. All of these are pain and labour, or rather labour and vanity, or labour and iniquity. For how few men order their life in youth according to the precept of Solomon in Ecclesiastes 12: 'Remember your Creator in the days of your youth'! The flower of age is offered most often to the devil, the dregs of old age to God. But are all these delights of youth anything other than vanity of vanities?" Rabbi Solomon: "All the greatness and dominion which a man holds in those days are nothing but labour and iniquity." And certainly what is more laborious, what is more exposed to dangers both of soul and body, than the life of those who hold power? Kimchi, reading וחוזק הימים, "and the strength of the days", says: "that is, even if the days of someone are spent in peace, they are nothing but labour and iniquity," as if to say: even when a person's days are prosperous and tranquil, there is nothing but labour and trouble. Luther expressed this sense in Dutch, "als het hoste: wat geweest is, so ist moepte ende arbeyt gheweest." And as for that part of life in which we are strong, what can be said more truly? When we are strong we labour and grow weary most of all, each in his calling. When sicknesses come upon us, we are unwillingly kept from our labours, and we desire nothing more than, with our former strength restored, to be allowed to return even to the most grievous labours we had left off. Thus that more excellent part of life is worn away by constant labour. Diodati: "and indeed the flower of those [years] is toil and vanity", that is, even the flower (the Hebrew scholion: excellence, i.e. honour, price, the most outstanding and most worthy) of those years is labour and vanity. The most learned interpreters among the Papists embrace these explanations, and those who are conversant with such meditations will judge best how much more these explanations hold in reserve than they promise on the surface. But that rendering which the Vulgate expressed from the LXX, how hard it is to extract it from the Hebrew! "And moreover their labour and pain," LXX "τὸ ἀλγεινὸν αὐτῶν." Besides, how cold the sense is: "which exceeds them." Bellarmine: "'And moreover their' is commonly explained of the life that is prolonged beyond seventy years, and this is the exposition of Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret and other weighty authors." The Roman Psalter reads "their greater part", which they interpret of the greater or better part of human life. But Bellarmine asserts that this exposition is less probable. Yet there is no doubt in my mind that this was the intention of the Greek interpreters, whom I also think, deceived by the similarity of sound, read רבם (rabbam, "their multitude") in place of רהבם (rahbam), or rather interpreted it as such. For Cenomanus thinks they read הרבם, but that is a monstrous word. From what follows: יש ונעפה, Arias: "for it is cut off quickly and we have flown away"; Junius: "by which swift cutting off we fly away"; Piscator: "and when it has been torn away, we fly away." From these words, I say, the LXX gave us this interpretation: ὅτι ἐπῆλθε πραΰτης ἐφ' ἡμᾶς, καὶ παιδευθησόμεθα: "for gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected." Jerome, in his letter to Cyprian, is not without reason amazed that those good interpreters read as they did. Certainly you will find neither a trace nor a vestige of these words in the sources. What does Bellarmine say? "We ought not to doubt that they read something which could be rightly turned in that sense, since they were most learned and most faithful men, and Theodotion and the sixth edition agree with them." I set against them Symmachus, "for, cut down suddenly, we are spread out", and the fifth edition, "for we have passed quickly and are dissolved." Clarus Drusius thinks that those words, חיש וש, can be explained as "it is cut down silently", and he compares a line of the poet:

units.la: tacitisque senescimus annis.
units.tr: and we grow old in silent years.

units.la: Genebr. exorbitantem versionem satagit aliquantulum reducere in viam hac observatione, corripi a Lxx. positum esse pro rapi celeriter ex hac vita & avolare. Sed quomodo iste sensus Graeco καιδευθησόμεθα tribui possit, nullus video. Alia quoque mens Lovaniensibus fuit, qui locum sic reddidere, de factis moe: moedichept is obergeromen/ ende wp sullen herispt wozen den. versus xii. למנות ימינו כן הורע ונביא לבב חכמה ad verbum, numerare dies nostr: recte scire fac, ut venire faciamus cor sapientia. דו duo significat, sic & rectum, recte. Vnde duplex interpretatio, 1. Doce [nos] sic numerare dies nostros, ut acquiramus cor sapiens. 2. Doce nos recte numerare dies nostros, &c. Quid Lxx? illi vocem למנות ab hoc versu avulsam adjecerunt ad finem versus praecedentis. Reliqua vero sic reddiderre, τὰ δεξίαν μου ἵνα γνωρίσον μοι, ἡ τὰς πεπαιδευμένους τῆς καρδίας ἐν σοφίᾳ. Vul. Dextram tuam sic notam fac & eruditos corde in sapientia. Vides eos legisse ימינך pro ימינו / Et tamen Chaldaeus quoque legit ימינו / ne quis putet codices Ebraeos olim aliter legisse, τὸ eruditos Genebr. & Bellarm. putant regi ab הורע / notos fac nobis eruditos, fac ut cognoscamus veros doctores. Sa, à verbo fac, fac nos eruditos. Quidam codices legunt πεπαιδευμένους. Hinc August. locum ita refert, & compeditos corde in sapientia. quamvis statim aliam lectionem memorat. Idem per dextram Christum intelligit, à qua interpretatione non alienum se profitetur Bellar. Hieronymus, qui superiora quoque verba ex Ebraeo sic interpretatus erat, transivimus cito & avolavimus, Haec ita interpretatus est, ut numerentur dies nostri sic ostende, & veniemus (נבוא) corde sapiente. Epistola ad Cypr.
units.tr: Genebrardus labours somewhat to bring this strained rendering back to sense with the observation that the Seventy used "corripi" to mean being swiftly snatched away from this life and flying off. But I see no way that this sense can be attributed to the Greek καὶ παιδευθησόμεθα [and we shall be instructed]. The Louvain translators also took the passage differently, rendering it: "Make known to us the deeds of our days, and we shall be wise in heart." Verse 12 has, in Hebrew, לְמַנּוֹת יָמֵינוּ כֵּן הוֹדַע וְנָבִיא לְבַב חָכְמָה [lemanot yamenu ken hodea venavi levav chokhmah], word for word: "to number our days, so make known, that we may bring a heart of wisdom." The word דּוּ [ken] means "so" and also "right" or "rightly." Hence a double interpretation: (1) Teach us so to number our days that we may gain a wise heart; (2) teach us to number our days rightly, etc. What did the Seventy do? They detached the word לְמַנּוֹת from this verse and added it to the end of the preceding verse. The rest they rendered: τὰ δεξίαν μου ἵνα γνωρίσον μοι, ἡ τὰς πεπαιδευμένους τῆς καρδίας ἐν σοφίᾳ [ta dexian mou hina gnorison moi, e tas pepaideumenous tes kardias en sophia]. The Vulgate: "Make known to them Your right hand, and the instructed in heart in wisdom." You see that they read יְמִינְךָ [yeminekha, your right hand] for יְמִינוּ [yeminu, our days]. Yet the Chaldee paraphrast also reads יְמִינוּ, so no one should think the Hebrew manuscripts once read differently. As for "the instructed" [τὰς πεπαιδευμένους], Genebrardus and Bellarmine think it is governed by הוֹדַע, "make known": make known to us the instructed, that is, make us know the true teachers. Sa, from the verb "make," reads "make us instructed." Some manuscripts read πεπαιδευμένους [pepaideumenous]. Hence Augustine cites the passage thus: "and the fettered in heart in wisdom," although he soon mentions another reading. The same Augustine understands the right hand to be Christ, an interpretation Bellarmine declares he does not reject. Jerome, who had also translated the preceding words from the Hebrew, rendered this: "Show so that our days may be numbered, and we shall come (נָבוֹא) with a wise heart." This is from his letter to Cyprian.

units.la: Psal. X C I. 6. Ab incursu & daemonio meridiano.] Ita vulg. ex Graeco ἀπὸ συμπώματος ἡ δαιμονίου μεσημβρινοῦ. Lovan. Dan den aenloop ende den middaghschen dupel. Circa hoc meridianum daemonium multa quaesiverunt veteres. Euthymius, per dam. merid. aliqui acedia damonem dixere, eo quod illo tempore magis nos aggredi soleat. Aliqui vero damonem illum qui turpibus cogitationibus praeest atque incontinentia, &c. At vox damonii in Ebr. non comparet. מקטב ישור צהרים ab excidio [quod] vastat in meridie. Simplicissima totius hujus versus ea est interpretatio, quam tradit Bellarm. Non timebis ulla pericula, neque nocturna neque diurna. Scaliger Epist. lib. 1. pag. 95. Istis 4. generibus complectitur omnia, quae hominibus imminent, aut metuenda sunt, uti mortalium vita multis malis obnoxia est. Et quia Ebraei τὸ νυχθήμερον quadrifariam partiuntur in vesperam, mediam noctem, in mane & meridiem, per noctem intelligit mediam noctem, per crepusculum vesperum: & ait nunquam per totum diem quicquam eorum, quae hominibus impendent, metuendum esse illi, quem Deus tutum ab his omnibus praestat. Vastitatem ἡ ἐρημωσιν Hebraei vocant קטב / quod proprie est vis quaedam major ἡ δαιμονία, quod quare daemonem verterint septuaginta, nescio. Hinc Sophistae hariolati sunt daemones in meridie vagantes. Et sane vetustas tales daemonas meridie infestos esse credebat, ut ille pastor Theocritianus, ὁ Θύμις, ὦ ποιμὴν, τὸ μεσαμβρινὸν, ἡ Θύμις ἀμμε Συνέισθεν. τὸν Παῖα δεδοικαμες. Haec Scaliger, cujus illud ἀμάχητμα μεσημβρινὸν est, quod putaverit daemonium esse interpretamentum Hebraei קטב / At ei respondet in Graeco textu vox συμπλώματος. τὸ δὲ δαιμόνιον ex Hebraeo שׁדּ interpretati sunt, pro quo videntur legisse שׁד /
units.tr: Psalm 91:6. "From the attack and the noonday demon." Thus the Vulgate, from the Greek ἀπὸ συμπώματος ἢ δαιμονίου μεσημβρινοῦ [apo sumpōmatos ē daimoniou mesēmbrinou]. The Louvain version: "From the onslaught and the noonday devil." The ancients asked many questions about this noonday demon. Euthymius: "Some have called the demon of noonday acedia, because it is wont to assail us more at that hour. Others say it is that demon who presides over shameful thoughts and incontinence, etc." But the word "demon" does not appear in the Hebrew. The Hebrew is מִקֶּטֶב יָשׁוּד צָהֳרָיִם [miqqeteb yashud tzohorayim], "from the destruction that lays waste at noon." The simplest interpretation of the whole verse is that given by Bellarmine: you will fear no dangers, neither nocturnal nor diurnal. Scaliger, Epistles, book 1, p. 95: the verse embraces four kinds of things that threaten men or are to be feared, just as human life is subject to many evils. And because the Hebrews divide the day and night into four parts, evening, midnight, morning and noon, he understands "night" to mean midnight and "twilight" to mean evening; and he says that the man whom God keeps safe from all these will never have to fear any of the things that threaten men through the whole day. The Hebrews call the "desolation" (ἐρημωσιν) קֶטֶב [qeteb], which properly means a certain greater force, and the Seventy rendered it daimonion. Why they translated it as "demon," I do not know. Hence the sophists have idly talked of demons wandering at noon. Indeed antiquity did believe such demons were hostile at midday, as that Theocritean shepherd says: "Thyrsis, shepherd, the noonday, Thyrsis, let us not..., we fear Pan." So Scaliger, whose "unconquerable noonday" he thought was an explanation of the Hebrew קֶטֶב, and that daimonion was an interpretation of it. But the Greek text corresponds to the word συμπλώματος [sumplōmatos]. The Seventy translated daimonion from the Hebrew שֵׁד [shed], for which they seem to have read שֵׁד too.

units.la: Ps. XCII. 15. benepatientes erunt. ] Iterum lubet audire Erasmum. Is ergo adversus Sutorem agens, loco & scopo, quem ad Ps. xlv. indicavimus, sic inquit. Miror quid sit benepatientes. Nam patientes novi. Adeo commentarios inscriptos Hieronymo. Nihil reperio. Vertor ad Augustum. Offendo scripturam aliam, tranquilli erunt. Hinc ad Lyranum. Is somniat nescio quid, a philosophis beneficiatos dici qui bene passi sint a benefactore. Hinc ad Hugonem. Is interpretatur de patientia, quae opus perfectum habet. Hinc ad Arnobium. Is dissimulat hunc locum. Cassiodorus aliquid lucis ostendit, mentionem faciens de praemiis recipiendis. Adhuc incertus haereo & consulo Graecos codices, & invenio ἐυπαθῆσ ἐυπαθῆς ἐυπαθῆς. Agnosco, Graecis ἐυπαθεῖν * qui beneficio afficiuntur, aut qui bene affecti sunt animo. Nam illi affectus aut affectiones πάθη vocant, & statim intelligo, quid sibi voluerit quod Aug. legit, tranquilli erunt. & quod ex Hebraeo Hieron. pingues & frondentes erunt. Eat nunc & clamet linguarum peritiam nihil prorsus utilitatis afferre ad sacras literas. Clamet insanum esse & haereticum, in hunc usum velle scire Graece aut Ebraice. Haec Erasmus.
units.tr: Psalm 92:15. "They will be well-suffering" [benepatientes]. Once more let us hear Erasmus. Arguing against Sutor, with the aim and place I indicated at Psalm 45, he says: "I wonder what 'benepatientes' means. For I know 'patientes.' I searched the commentaries attributed to Jerome. I found nothing. I turned to Augustine. I came upon another reading: 'they will be tranquil.' Then to Lyra, who dreams up I know not what, that those who have suffered well are called benefited by philosophers, from their benefactor. Then to Hugo, who interprets it of patience, which has a perfect work. Then to Arnobius, who passes over the verse. Cassiodorus shows some light, mentioning the receiving of rewards. Still uncertain, I consult the Greek manuscripts and find εὐπαθῆσ, εὐπαθῆς, εὐπαθῆς [eupathēs]. I recognise that the Greeks use εὐπαθεῖν [eupathein] for those who are benefited, or who are well disposed in mind. For they call those affections or dispositions πάθη [pathē], and at once I understand what Augustine meant in reading 'they will be tranquil,' and what Jerome meant in translating from the Hebrew 'they will be fat and flourishing.' Let him now go and cry out that knowledge of languages brings no benefit at all to the sacred letters. Let him cry out that it is insane and heretical to wish to know Greek or Hebrew for this purpose." So Erasmus.

units.la: Ibid. vers. 13. Justus ut palma florebit. ] Ebr. צדיק כתמר / פרח Lxx. δίκαιος ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀνθήσει. Quidam vocis Graecae ambiguo decepti de Phoenice ave haec verba cepere, q. d. justus florebit ut Phoenix. Tertull. in libro de resurrectione carnis c. 13. carnis resurrectionem exemplo Phoenicis probaturus, sic inquit, Illum dico alitem orientis peculiarem, de singularitate famo- sum, de posteritate monstruosum. quisemet ipsum lubenter funerans renovat, natali sine decedens, atque succedens iterum Phoenix. Vbi jam nemo, iterum ipse. Qui non jam, alius idem. Quid expressius atque significatius in hanc causam, aut cui alii rei tale documentum? Deus etiam scripturis suis, Et florebit, inquit, velut Phoenix id est de morte, de funere: uti credas, de ignibus quoque sub- stantiam corporis exigi posse. Vides Tertull. hanc de Phaenice hi- storiam ex sacris literis probasse. Eodem modo Ambrosius oratione de fide resurrectionis, tomo 3. pag. mihi 39. Avis in regione Arabia, cui nomen Phoenix, redivivo sua carnis humore reparabilis, cum mortua fuerit, revivisci. Solos non credimus homines resuscita- ri? Atqui hoc relatione crebra & scripturarum authoritate cognovimus, memoratam avem 500. annorum spatia vitali usui habere praescripta; eamque cum sibi finem vitae praesaga quadam natura sua aestimatione cognoverit, thecam sibi de thure, myrrha & caeteris odoribus adornare, completoque opere pariter ac tempore intrare illam & emori, ex cujus humore oriri vermem, paulatimque eum in avis ejusdem figuram concrescere, usumque formari, subnixam quoque remigio pennarum, renovata vita officia munere pietatis ordiri. Vides & hunc pervul- gatae isti de Poenice fabulae ex Scripturis patrocinium praestare. Proculdubio enim & iste ad hunc locum respexit. Vide etiam Cyrillum Archiep. Jerosolymitanum Catechesi xviii. quitamen Scripturae non meminit, & elegantissimum de Phoenice carmen, quod Lactantio vulgo adscribitur.
units.tr: Ibid. verse 13. "The righteous will flourish like a palm." Hebrew צַדִּיק כַּתָּמָר יִפְרָח [tzaddiq katamar yifrach]. The Seventy: δίκαιος ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀνθήσει [dikaios hōs phoinix anthēsei]. Some, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, took these words to refer to the phoenix bird, as if to say "the righteous will flourish like the phoenix." Tertullian, in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 13, wishing to prove the resurrection of the flesh by the example of the phoenix, says: "I mean that unique bird of the East, famous for its singularity, remarkable for its offspring, which, burying itself with its own hands, renews itself, dying at the natal hour and succeeding itself again as a phoenix. Where then is anyone again himself? Who is no longer, yet is the same other? What could be more express and more significant for this cause, or what other thing offers such a proof?" And God, in his Scriptures, says: "And he will flourish like the phoenix," that is, after death and burial, so that you may believe the substance of the body can be drawn even from ashes. You see Tertullian proved this history of the phoenix from the sacred letters. In the same way Ambrose, in his oration on the faith of the resurrection, volume 3, page 39 of my edition: "In the region of Arabia there is a bird called the phoenix, which, when dead, revives, reparable by the moisture of its own flesh. Do we alone not believe men are raised? Yet we have learned this from frequent report and the authority of the Scriptures: that this bird has a prescribed span of five hundred years of life; and when, by a certain foreknowledge of nature, it has recognised the end of its life, it prepares for itself a case of incense, myrrh and other fragrances, and when its work and time are complete, it enters and dies there. From its moisture a worm arises, which gradually grows into the figure of the same bird, and, being formed in use and supported by the feathers of its wings, begins with renewed life the duties of its pious office." You see that this Scripture also lends support to that commonly told fable about the phoenix. Doubtless he too had this passage in mind. See also Cyril, Archbishop of Jerusalem, Catechesis 18, who nevertheless does not mention Scripture, and the most elegant poem on the phoenix that is commonly ascribed to Lactantius.

units.la: Ps. XCVI. 10. Dicite in gentibus, Dominus regnavit. Exemplar Psalmorum quo usus fuit Justinus Martyr, auctius fuit duabus istis vocibus, ὁ κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν ἀπὸ ξύλου, Dominus regnavit a ligno. τὸ δὲ, ὁ κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν ἀπὸ ξύλου, ἀφῆκαν οἱ Ιουδαῖοι, inquit beatus ille Pater in dialogo cum Tryphone. Quia vero haec lectio videbatur continere evidens vaticinium de crucifixione Messiae, avide arrepta fuit a sanctissimis Patribus, verbi gratia, Augustino, Tertull. in libro adversus Jud. cap. 10. & lib. 3. adversus Marcionem cap. 19. & 21. Lactantio, Arnobio, Cassiodoro, & aliis. Fortunatus in hymno, qui tempore passionis canitur, ex hac quoque lectione istos versus fecit. Impleta sunt quae cecinit. David, fideli carmine,
units.tr: Psalm 96:10. "Say among the nations, the Lord has reigned." The copy of the Psalms used by Justin Martyr had an addition of two words: ὁ κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν ἀπὸ ξύλου [ho kyrios ebasileusen apo xylou], "the Lord reigned from the tree." "But the Jews omitted the words 'the Lord reigned from the tree,'" says that blessed Father in his dialogue with Trypho. Since this reading seemed to contain a clear prophecy of the crucifixion of the Messiah, it was eagerly seized by the most holy Fathers, for example Augustine, Tertullian in his book Against the Jews chapter 10, and book 3 Against Marcion chapters 19 and 21, Lactantius, Arnobius, Cassiodorus, and others. Fortunatus, in the hymn sung at the time of the Passion, also made these verses from this reading: "The things David sang in faithful song are fulfilled,"

units.la: Dicens in nationibus, Regnavit à ligno Deus.
units.tr: Say among the nations: the Lord has reigned from the tree.

units.la: Leguntur & in Psalterio Romano. Lindanus hunc locum Euangelicis objecit, ut ostenderet, Judæorum perfidiam textum Ebræum mutilasse. At non vidit subtilissimus Magister se per textus Ebraici latus ipsam quoque vulgatam sauciare. Nam ne illa quidem voces illas agnoscit. Tempore etiam Hieron. Theodoreti, Euthymii non fuisse eas in codicibus Græcis, testis est Bell. Sed nec Chald. eas legit, Et à Psalterio Gallico abesse, in Editione Romana notatum est. Genebr. ait ea in Ebraeo non haberi quoad verba, sed secundum sensum, & destomachatur in eos, qui duas istas voculas, quae de industria & per Sp. Sanctum à sanctissimis hus prophetis fuerant interjecta, è nostris exemplaribus sustulerunt, sive Judæi fuerint sive quidam olim scioli, ut linguam Ebraam ostentarent, aliquid in LXX. notando quod minime in archetypo reperirent, cujus vanitatis atque adeo nequitiæ nimium multos hodie ferì tellus. Bona verba, Genebrarde. Hunc tuum latratum insuper habuerunt correctores Romani, ipsique adeo Pontifices, Sixtus V. & Clemens VIII. qui crucem Christi hujusmodi fulcro non existimarunt egere. Recte ergo Faber Stap. non esse illa verba de Ebraica veritate, sed Christiana devotione addita pronuntiavit.
units.tr: These words are also found in the Roman Psalter. Lindanus brought this passage against the Evangelical writers, to show that the Jews had corrupted the Hebrew text. But that most subtle Master did not see that, by attacking the Hebrew text, he also wounds the Vulgate itself. For the Vulgate does not acknowledge those words either. That they were not in the Greek manuscripts even in the time of Jerome, Theodoret and Euthymius is attested by Bellarmine. Nor did the Chaldee paraphrast read them, and it has been noted that they are absent from the Gallican Psalter, in the Roman edition. Genebrardus says that they are not in the Hebrew as to the words, but only according to the sense, and he vents his bile against those who removed from our copies those two little words, which had been inserted deliberately and by the Holy Spirit through the most holy prophets, whether they were Jews, or some shallow men of old who wished to show off their knowledge of Hebrew by adding in the Septuagint something that they could not find in the original. The earth today bears far too many of this vanity and indeed of this wickedness. Fine words, Genebrardus. The Roman correctors, and the Pontiffs themselves, Sixtus V and Clement VIII, held this barking of yours in contempt, since they did not think the cross of Christ needed such a prop. So Faber Stapulensis rightly pronounced that those words are not from the Hebrew truth, but were added by Christian devotion.

units.la: Psal. XCIX. 15. adorate scabellum pedum ejus quia sanctum est.] Posui versionem vulgatam, quæ ex istis LXX. Interpretum verbis expressa est, θεοποιήσατε τὸ ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἅγιός ἐστι. Nota in ipso limine discrepantiam generis in ἅγιῳ & sanctum, ut videas verba Græca non satis fideliter expressa esse. Istam autem lectionem ἅγιος constantissime omnes codices repræsentant. Ipse quoque Genebr. fatetur Hieronymum & Augustinum legere sanctus. Bellarminus, potest etiam referri ad Deum & verti, quia sanctus est. Utroque autem modo significatur, scabellum esse adorandum propter relationem ad Deum. Veteres fere hoc scabellum pro objecto adorationis accepere. Per scabellum pedum, terram, (juxta illud Jesaiæ. 66. cœlum mihi sedes est & terra scabellum pedum meorum) per terram Christum intellexere. Augustinus mihi instar omnium erit. Videte, fratres, quid nos jubeat adorare. Alio loco Scriptura dicit, cœlum mihi sedes, terra autem scab. pedum meorum. Ergo terram nos jubet bet adorare. Et quomodo adorabimus terram, cum dicat aperte scriptura Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & hic dicit, adorate sc.pedum ejus? Et paulo post, timeo adorare terram, ne me codemnet qui fecit cœlum & terram. Rursus timeo non adorare scabellum pedum Domini mei, quia Psalmus mihi dicit, adorate sc. p. ejus. Fluctuans converto me ad Christum, quia ipsum quaro hic & invenio, quomodo sine impietate adoretur terra & scabellum pedum ejus. Suscepit enim de terra terram, quia caro de terra est & de carne Maria carnem accepit. Et quia in ipsa carne hic ambulavit & ipsam carnem nobis manducandam ad salutem dedit, nemo autem carnem manducat nisi prius adoraverit, inventum est, quomodo adoretur tale scabellum pedum Domini &, non solum non peccemus adorando, sed & peccemus non adorando. Julius Toletanus ἀντικεμένων lib. 1. interrog. 36. postquam sumpsisset sibi, tanquam extra omnem controversiæ aleam positum, per scabellum terram intelligi, hoc mandatum; cum illo Deut. 6. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, ita conciliat, Illam terram dicit adorandam, quam Dominus Jesus incarnationis assumptione suscepit. Itaque per scabellum pedum terra intelligitur, per terram autem caro Christi, quam hodie quoque in mysteriis adoramus. Suscepit enim de terra terram, quia caro de terra est, & de carne Maria carnem accepit. Carthus. scabellum pedum id est humanam Christi naturam, in qua divinitas verbi stetit quasi scabellum. Et postea prolixe disputat de adoratione humanæ Christi naturæ. Vide & Thomam parte 3. quæst. 25. & Magistrum lib. 3. Dist. 9. Ex hoc ergo illud porro ut vara vibiam sequitur, collegerunt Pontificii, carnem Christi in ipsa quoque eucharistia adorandam esse; Eandem mentem Augustino fuisse, verbis quæ jam produximus, Bellarm. in comm. persuadere Lectori suo conatur. At nihil tale ex ejus verbis colligi posse illustris Mornæus lib. 4. de Eucharistia cap. 7. docuit. Quis ambigat, inquit, carnem humanam manducare neminem, nisi prius adoraverit vera fide, affectu & effectu. At vero adoramus nos hanc carnem sicuti & comedimus, sicuti & accipimus. Accipimus, sicuti & tangimus, vere quidem sed spiritualiter. Spiritualiter, neque eo minus vere. Quid vero sequioris ævi interpretes de hac re senserint, nec ignoramus nec curamus. Alfonsus de Castro per scabellum crucem intellexit. Quid enim verius scabellum Christi, quam crux, inquit, cui pedes illius affixi sunt? Atque inde porro crucis ado-
units.tr: Psalm 99:5, "Worship his footstool, for he is holy." I have set down the Vulgate version, which is expressed from the words of the Seventy Interpreters: θεοποιήσατε τὸ ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἅγιός ἐστι [worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy]. Note at the very outset the difference of gender between ἅγιῳ and sanctum, so that you can see the Greek words have not been rendered quite faithfully. But all the manuscripts consistently present the reading ἅγιος. Genebrardus himself admits that Jerome and Augustine read sanctus. Bellarmine says: it can also be referred to God and translated "because he is holy." Either way it is signified that the footstool is to be worshipped because of its relation to God. The Fathers mostly took this footstool as the object of worship. By the "footstool of his feet" they understood the earth (in line with the saying of Isaiah 66: heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool), and by the earth they understood Christ. Augustine will serve me for all of them. Brethren, see what it bids us worship. In another place Scripture says, heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. So it bids us worship the earth. And how shall we worship the earth, when Scripture plainly says, You shall worship the Lord your God, and here it says, worship his footstool? And a little later: I am afraid to worship the earth, lest he condemn me who made heaven and earth. Again I am afraid not to worship the footstool of my Lord, because the Psalm tells me, worship his footstool. Wavering, I turn to Christ, because I seek him here and find how the earth and the footstool of his feet may be worshipped without impiety. For he took earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth, and from the flesh of Mary he received flesh. And because he walked here in that very flesh and gave us that same flesh to eat for our salvation, and no one eats flesh without first worshipping it, it is found how such a footstool of the Lord may be worshipped, and that we would sin not by worshipping but also by not worshipping. Julius of Toledo, in his Antikeimena, book 1, question 36, having taken it for granted, as beyond all dispute, that the footstool means the earth, reconciles this command with the saying of Deuteronomy 6, You shall worship the Lord your God, thus: He says that the earth is to be worshipped which the Lord Jesus took up by assuming the incarnation. Thus by the footstool is understood the earth, and by the earth the flesh of Christ, which we worship today also in the mysteries. For he took earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth, and from the flesh of Mary he received flesh. The Carthusian: the footstool, that is, the human nature of Christ, in which the divinity of the Word stood as on a footstool. And afterwards he disputes at length about the worship of the human nature of Christ. See also Thomas, part 3, question 25, and the Master, book 3, distinction 9. From this, then, the Papists gathered that the flesh of Christ is to be worshipped even in the Eucharist, which follows as a further consequence. Bellarmine, in his commentary, tries to persuade his reader that Augustine had the same mind, by the words we have just quoted. But the illustrious Mornaeus, book 4 on the Eucharist, chapter 7, has shown that nothing of the kind can be gathered from his words. Who doubts, he says, that no one eats human flesh without first worshipping it in true faith, in affection and in effect? But truly we worship this flesh just as we also eat it and receive it. We receive it, just as we also touch it, truly indeed but spiritually. Spiritually, and yet no less truly. As for what the interpreters of a later age have thought about this matter, we neither know nor care. Alfonsus de Castro understood the cross by the footstool. For what is a truer footstool of Christ, he says, than the cross, to which his feet were fastened? And from there he further draws the adoration of the cross ado-

units.la: Xxx ȝ adorationem deducit. Communior tamen sententia est per scab. pedum arcam intelligi. Episcopi secundi Concilii Nicæni hoc loco abusi sunt, probandæ isti thesi, Deum in statuis & pictu- ris adorandum esse. Bellarminus lib. 1. de Beatit. Sanctorum capite 18. probaturus, res sacras religioso cultu adorandas esse, hunc ipsum locum in acie collocat. Etiam Suares ad 3. partem Thomæ, quæst. 25. art. 2. Bellarminus ibidem. Respondeo, inquit, nomine scabelli necessario arcam intelligi, & proinde ruit expositio hæreticorum. Calvinum & Bucerum intelligit, qui cum Chaldaeo, Basilio, Vatablo aliisque per scab. pedum templum intellexêre. q. d. adorate in templo, quod scabellum pedum ejus est something pro hand quaquam est insolens. Videsaltem Ps. xvi. Hanc interpretationem ipse quoque Genebr. probat, aitque Psalmographum seipsum explicare versu ultimo, Adorate in monte sancto ejus. Ad quem locum hæc porro observa, I. ab interprete Vulg. redditum per in I I. Phrasin utrobique esse eandem. Vers. 5. השתחוו להדם versu ultimo השתחוו להר / III. Falli ergo Lorinum Jesuitam, dum fidenter asserit, phrasin illam nusquam occurrere ad designandum locum adorationis, sed ea semper denotari rem adoratam. Hic certe locus ipsi in os contradicit. Sed & evidens est locus Ps. cxxxii. 7. ubi hanc eandem phrasin נשתחוה להדם רגליו ita reddidit Interpres vulg. adorate in loco ubi steterunt pedes ejus. Sed demum Bellarmino, per scab. pedum arcam fœderis seu propitiatorium intelligi. Certe 1. Chron. 28. 2. arca fœderis diserte scabellum pedum Dei appellatur, sive ratione cœli, quod thronus ejus dicitur ob majorum gloriam, qua illustris est, sive quod alæ Cheruborum sedem quampiam Dei repræsentarint, cujus כפרת fuerit propitiatorium seu operculum arcæ, cui ipsi quoque Cherubi insistebant. Quid vero hinc exsculpet Bellarminus? Ipse agnoscit in comment. in Ebræo ad verbum legi, adorate an scabellum pedum ejus. Sa, adorate scabellum, sc. ad arcam, unde responsa dat velut sedes super Cherubim. Et Lyra, anti scabellum id est arcam. Et Genebr. Alluditur ad gestum adorantium regem & ad thronum ejus accumbentium, q. d. coram scabello pedum ejus prodite, quasi ante pedes ejus prostrati. Nos hæc lubentes acceptamus. Neque etiam Junius, Pisc. Deod. Genev. Angli, Tigurini, Lutherus & alii aliter hunc locum interpretati sunt. Explicandus ergo hic locus ex illo, Pf. cxxxviii. 2. adorabo אֶל הֵיכַל קׇדְשְׁךָ quem vulg. ita vertit. adorabo ad templum sanctum tuum. Objectum corporis adorantis ab objecto adorationis distingui oportet. Objectum adorationis religiosæ solus Deus est. At objecta corporum adorantium possunt esse varia. Israelitæ Deum adoraruri faciem versus arcam aut templum convertebant. Daniel tanto locorum intervallo à templo remotus, facie tamen urbi Sanctæ & Templo obversa, precatur, idque juxta Salomonis verba 1. Regum. VIII. 44. & 48. — & orabunt te * via civitatis hujus quam elegisti, & domus * quam edificasti. Qui Deum invocant, sæpe ad sedile vel lectum se prosternunt, an ideo vel Danielem urbem sanctam, vel hos sedile vel lectum adorare dicemus? Apage tales ineptias. Ergo dico, השתחוו cum ל construetum, vel denotare locum in quo (ut hoc eodem Psalmo, versu ultimo, & Ps. 132. 7. ipso vulgato Interprete judice) vel locum aut rem versus quam, aut illud ipsum quod adoratur. Ex ambigua ergo phrasi non procedit argumentum. Ostendendum primo erat exemplum arcæ adoratæ, aut monstrandus alius locus, aut eruendæ ex hoc ipso loco tales circumstantiæ, quibus convincantur conscientiæ, hic ipsius arcæ adorationem juberi. Nos contra parallelorum locorum collatione id, opinor, evicimus, si arcam intelligas indicari locum, ad vel versus quem, vel coram quo: sin templum, intelligi locum in quo vel versus quem, stante cultu Mosaico, preces fidelium fundebantur. Diximus supra, ex veteribus nonnullos hunc locum de adoratione carnis Christi intellexisse, atque ex eo Pontificios porro pro adoratione Eucharistiæ argumentum depromsisse. Ea interpretatio autem mihi vellit de alio quodam loco Psal. Levit. v. 7. & xi. 8. 2. Sam. ult. verf. 8. Hæc interpretatio, licet cum vulgatæ versionis textu stare omnino non possit, tamen avide à Pontificiis arrepta fuit. Ut vel hinc videas, quo loco apud Pontificios sit interpretatio vulgata, quando ex fontibus plusculum suis erroribus subsidii sperant. Et cum hoc concordat translatio Chaldaica, in qua ubi dicitur, in summis montium, expresse dicitur, in capitibus sacerdotum. Hæc Burgensis. units.tr: ...leads to the adoration of the cross. The more common view, however, is that the "footstool of his feet" means the ark. The bishops of the Second Council of Nicaea misused this passage to prove the thesis that God is to be adored in statues and pictures. Bellarmine, in book 1 of *De beatitudine sanctorum*, chapter 18, wanting to prove that sacred things are to be adored with religious worship, places this very passage in the front line. Suárez too, on the third part of Thomas, question 25, article 2, follows him. Bellarmine says there: I answer, he says, that by the name of footstool the ark must be understood, and so the heretics' interpretation falls. He means Calvin and Bucer, who, with the Chaldee paraphrast, Basil, Vatablus and others, understood by "footstool of his feet" the temple, as if to say: worship in the temple, which is his footstool. That is by no means an unusual way of speaking. See at least Psalm 99. Genebrardus too approves this interpretation, and says that the psalmist explains himself in the last verse, worship at his holy mountain. On that passage note the following. First, the Vulgate translator rendered the phrase by in. Second, the phrase is the same in both places: in verse 5 it is hishtachavu lehadom [השתחוו להדם], and in the last verse hishtachavu lehar [השתחוו להר]. Third, Lorinus the Jesuit is therefore wrong when he confidently asserts that this phrase never occurs to denote a place of worship, but always denotes the thing worshipped. This very passage contradicts him to his face. Moreover, Psalm 132:7 is also clear, where the same phrase, nishtachavah lehadom raglav [נשתחוה להדם רגליו], is rendered by the Vulgate translator: worship in the place where his feet stood. Finally, for Bellarmine: by the footstool of his feet the ark of the covenant, or the mercy seat, is meant. Certainly in 1 Chronicles 28:2 the ark of the covenant is expressly called the footstool of God's feet, either because of its relation to heaven, which is called his throne on account of the greater glory by which it is illustrious, or because the wings of the cherubim represented some seat of God, whose kapporet [כפרת], that is, the propitiatory or lid of the ark, the cherubim themselves stood upon. But what does Bellarmine extract from this? He himself acknowledges that in the Hebrew commentary it is read word for word, worship at his footstool. Sa says, worship the footstool, that is, towards the ark, from which he gives answers as from a seat above the cherubim. And Lyra, instead of footstool, that is, the ark. And Genebrardus: There is an allusion to the posture of those who adore a king and to those who recline at his throne, as if to say: come forward before his footstool, as if prostrate before his feet. We gladly accept these things. Nor have Junius, the Piscator of Dedham and Geneva, the English, the Tigurines, Luther and others interpreted this passage otherwise. This passage must therefore be explained from that one, Psalm 138:2, I will worship [אֶל הֵיכַל קׇדְשְׁךָ] toward your holy temple, which the Vulgate also renders thus: I will worship towards your holy temple. The object of the worshipper's body must be distinguished from the object of worship. The object of religious worship is God alone, but the objects toward which worshippers' bodies are turned can be various. The Israelites, when they worshipped God, turned their faces towards the ark or the temple. Daniel, though so far from the temple, prayed with his face turned towards the holy city and the temple, and he did so in accordance with the words of Solomon, 1 Kings 8:44 and 48: and they shall pray to you by way of this city which you have chosen, and the house which I have built. Those who call upon God often prostrate themselves before a seat or a bed. Shall we then say that Daniel adored the holy city, or that they adored the seat or the bed? Away with such nonsense. Therefore I say that hishtachavu constructed with le denotes either the place where (as in this same psalm, in the last verse, and in Psalm 132:7, by the judgment of the Vulgate translator himself) or the place or thing towards which, or the very thing that is worshipped. The argument therefore does not follow from an ambiguous phrase. First, one had to show an example of the ark being worshipped, or point out another passage, or else draw from this very passage such circumstances as would convince consciences that the adoration of the ark itself is commanded here. We, on the contrary, by comparing parallel passages, think we have proved that if you understand the ark, the word indicates the place towards which or before which, but if the temple, it indicates the place in or towards which the prayers of the faithful were poured out under the Mosaic worship. I have said above that some of the ancients understood this passage of the adoration of the flesh of Christ, and from it the Papists drew an argument for the adoration of the Eucharist. But that interpretation seems to me to belong to another passage, Psalm 72:16: yehi fisat bar ba'aretz berosh hehararim yir'ash kalevanon perio [יְהִי פִסַּת בַּר בָּאָרֶץ בְּרֹאשׁ הָהָרִים יִרְעַשׁ כַּלְּבָנוֹן פְּרִיו]. Pagninus: there will be a handful (Arias, a particle) of grain in the earth, sown; it will be shaken (Arias, will rustle) like Lebanon its fruit. Junius: where there will be a handful of wheat in the land, on the top of the mountains it will stir itself like Lebanon its fruit. The two clauses are joined by a relative sense, so that they form a temporal relative clause. For the prophet means this: under the Messiah all things will go happily, and so nothing will be so small that it will not be increased immensely by God's blessing. For example, when even a handful of wheat has been sown, even in places less fertile, such as the tops of mountains, such a great abundance of crops will spring up that they will be stirred by the winds and make a noise, such as is usually made by the trees of Lebanon when they are shaken by the winds. This interpretation, of the great abundance of crops, was followed among the Hebrews by Aben Ezra and Kimchi, and among the Christians by Genebrardus, Lorinus, Calvin, Mollerus, Junius the Piscator and others. There is no difficulty except in the little word pissat [פִּסַּר], a word occurring only once. Psalm 12:2: pissu emunim [פִּסּוֹ אֲמוּנִים], the faithful have failed, have been diminished. Daniel 5:5: pess yad [פְּס יָד], the palm of a hand. Hence Kimchi, in the root, renders the present word as a portion of grain [חֵלְקַת בַּר], and in the commentary as a handful [פְּלֹא כַּף]. This interpretation is confirmed by the Chaldee paraphrase on 1 Kings 18:44, for where the Hebrew has behold, a small cloud, like a hand's palm rising, the Targum has kappat yad [כַּפָּת יָד]. The passage Genesis 37:3 also helps: and he made him a tunic of pieces, that is, sewn together from various pieces of different colours. The ancients, according to Lorinus, thought that the passage spoke of the bread of the divine word. And Bellarmine: Here is described the fruit of apostolic preaching after Christ's resurrection. So too Jansenius. The Vulgate translator: And there will be a firmament in the earth on the tops of the mountains. The Seventy: estai stēgma en tēi gēi ep' akrōn tōn oreōn [ἔσαι σ‍ηγμα ἐν τῇ γῇ ἐπ' ἀκρῶν τ‍ῶν ὀρέων]. By stēgma Bellarmine, Jansenius and indeed all those who teach that the bread of the divine word is hinted at here understand the support or firmament of bread, and they compare with this passage Psalm 105: he broke every support (firmament) of bread. For the abundance of grain, says Bellarmine, is the firmament of the household. So by firmament they understand here the abundance of grain, or, as Jerome translated it, memorable wheat. By the abundance of grain, however, is not meant here an abundance of bodily grain, but an abundance of the word of God, etc., says Bellarmine. And the words on the tops of the mountains they explain of places barren in themselves. Augustine understands by the firmament Christ, and by the tops of the mountains the prophets and apostles. The Carthusian thinks that the word firmament should be referred to the sacrament of the Eucharist, in which Christ is truly contained under the appearance of wheaten bread. But I greatly fear that the knights will not applaud the Carthusian here. Since the Greek has stēgma, who would allow himself to be persuaded that the Vulgate translator, who translated the Psalms from the Greek, originally wrote frumentum? Among the Papists there have not been lacking those who have tried to derive the name Mass from Deuteronomy 16:10. Genebrardus, that most celebrated doctor of Hebrew letters at Paris, in *Liturgy of the Apostles*, chapter 7, asserts that the first Mass was sung by the apostle James himself on the very day of Pentecost. To prove this assertion he cites Acts 2:42. He cites Leviticus 23:16, where the Israelites are commanded, on the very day of Pentecost, to bring minchah chadashah [מִנְחָה חַדָשָׁה] a new offering to the LORD. In Deuteronomy 16:10 they are commanded at that same feast to offer to God masat nidvat yad [מַשַּׂת נִדְבַת יָד], according to the sufficiency of the spontaneous offering of the hand, as the LORD has blessed them. Behold the word massa [מַשָּׂה] from the absolute form massa. Behold the Mass there prophetically instituted, and here (Acts 2) celebrated by blessed James, as if fulfilling that prophecy. All these things are the dreams of a sick man struck by prejudice. For if the Mass was foretold or signified by that word massa, then certainly the Vulgate committed an unpardonable crime in omitting that word altogether in his version. For he translates those Hebrew words as the spontaneous offering of your hand. He expressed the two first words, nidvat [נִדְבַת], both here and elsewhere most learnedly; see 2 Chronicles 31:14, Ezra 1:4 and 8:28. Moreover, if this mystery was hidden here, then all the ancient interpreters, who did not smell anything of the kind here, must surely have been stupid. What then? This is a frivolous invention, and it has been rightly rejected by Bellarmine himself, book 1, chapter 1, *On the Mass*, and by other learned men. Nor is Bellarmine's argument worth transcribing here: If that Hebrew word, he says, had been in use among the apostles, certainly the Greeks and Syrians and other nations would have retained it, as they retained other similar words, such as Amen, Hallelujah, Sabaoth, Hosanna, Satan, Sabbath, Pascha. For Hebrew words have come down to us through the Greeks, etc. So Bellarmine. You will find more about this matter in Casaubon, *Exercitationes* 16, section 58, and in Martinius in his *Etymology*, under the word Missa. We know that missath [מִשָּׂת] is a word more Chaldean than Hebrew, and that here it merely means sufficiency, and that in the Chaldee paraphrase the Hebrew *dalet* and *bet* are rendered by it; see Deuteronomy 15:18, Leviticus 5:7 and 11:8, and 2 Samuel, last chapter, verse 8. Nor do we doubt that it is also a silly invention of some people that this massa is the same as massa [מַשָּׂה] (with another letter), and that by the transposition of this letter the transubstantiation of bread into the Lord's body was signified. For, to return to this massa from this detour, Lucas Brugensis is the authority that many of the more recent writers have expounded this passage of the Eucharist, the greatest of sacraments. From this they further derive the custom of lifting the consecrated bread and cup on high, so that they rise above the head of the priests.
