This interpretation, although it cannot at all agree with the text of the Vulgate version, was nevertheless eagerly seized upon by the Papists. This alone shows where the Vulgate interpretation stands among the Papists, when they hope for some slight help from the sources for their errors. The first of all to lure them with this invention was Paulus Burgensis, whose words are these, in addition 2 to this Psalm: In the Hebrew, at this place where it says grain, there is supposed a certain word which sounds pissat, which does not signify abundance but rather a cake or little cake of grain. And thus the true translation according to the Hebrew truth in this place is such: There will be a cake or little cake of grain; which properly applies to the sacrament of the Eucharist, in which under the appearance of a little cake of grain the true body of Christ is contained. And with this agrees the Chaldee translation, in which where it says on the tops of the mountains, it is expressly said in the heads of the priests. So Burgensis. Galatinus, in book 10, chapter 4, enriched these claims with many testimonies of the Hebrews, some foreign, some Chaldean. I have no wish to transcribe them here. The sum of all this comes to this: It is manifest, according to the evidence of the text, that it would come to pass that the Messiah would be a cake of grain on the earth. For of him, as has become clear, it is said: there will be a cake of grain or a morsel of bread on the earth. And on the following page, after quoting these words from I know not what book, when therefore he says, and there will be a cake of grain on the tops of the mountains, he means that a cake of bread will become a sacrifice on the heads of the priests, who are in the Church, Galatinus adds: by the mountains the Church is understood, the prelates and priests. In them, he says, the Scripture is then fulfilled, when they lift up the body of Christ over their head. Cofterus and Cotonus, among others, seized eagerly on these things. Against them I set Bellarmine's sound judgment, with which he concludes his commentary on this verse: I know, he says, what Paulus Burgensis brings from the Chaldee paraphrase to prove the sacrifice of the Mass from this passage; but I also know how full that paraphrase is of Jewish fables. Therefore it irks me to draw from the gaps of Jewish expositions, when the most pure fountains of the holy Scriptures abound for us. So Bellarmine. As for that Chaldee paraphrase of the so-called Pseudo-Jonathan, should anyone perhaps ask for it, I will set it out on the authority of Galatinus. For you will not find it in the Bibles: yehi qorban de-abura be-ara [יהי קורבן דעבורא בארעא] be-rosh turaya [בריש טוריא] bi-shekhinta [בשכינתא], that is, there will be an offering of grain in the earth, at the head of the mountains, in the Shekhinah. What the words bi-shekhinta mean I do not know. Galatinus translates far too confidently, in the Church. But I do not remember reading shekhinah in that sense. It is used everywhere for the habitation, divinity, glory and divine majesty dwelling among men. The Chaldee paraphrase which today exists in the printed Hebrew Bibles has this: yehi sa'id lechma be-ara be-rosh turaya [יהי סעיד לחמא בארעא בריש טוריא], that is, There will be a morsel (a bit) of bread in the earth, at the head of the mountains, etc. The sense is the same as that of the Hebrew words, for the sentence depends on what is completed by the following words. The Hebrew word *sa'id* [סעיד] in the Targum often corresponds to the Hebrew *perat* [פרת]. So the meaning is: where a handful, or a little grain, which would scarcely suffice for a morsel, is on the tops of the mountains, in a barren place, it will make a noise, etc. The word *bucella* of bread is called *misa'id* [מסעיד] from *fulciendo*, supporting, because it supports and sustains the strength of men, just as we read elsewhere of a staff of bread, by which some understand that power of nourishing which God Almighty put into bread. This explanation, however, does not fit Ezekiel 4 and Leviticus 26. When God therefore threatens to break or take away the staff of bread, he rather announces that he will take away the bread which God has ordained to be the support of our life. Like that is Romans 4: the sign of circumcision, and, according to some, Matthew 24: the sign of the Son of man, that is, the Son, who himself will be the sign. Hence *se'udah* [סעורה], to eat, to take food, 1 Kings 13:7. Hence in the Chaldeans and rabbis, a banquet. David Kimchi: In the days of this king there will be such a blessing in the world that a man will sow a handful of grain even on the top of the mountains, and the ears will be so good and healthy, that when the wind blows through them they will rustle like the trees of Lebanon. What then did Cotonus see, when, treating of the Mass and transubstantiation from this passage, he introduces Kimchi discussing some change of nature? Kimchi revealed nothing of the kind here. That passage, of which Cotonus had heard something, is in his commentary on chapter 14 of Hosea, verse 8. I will not hesitate to transcribe the whole of it: and there are commentators who explain they shall be grain, that there will be a change of nature in the future, when the redeemer comes, so that these will be like the vine, and they will not need to sow the grain except once, like the vine; and similar things. Our rabbis of blessed memory have also mentioned a change of nature that will happen in the future in wheat, that is, some explain the words they shall be grain thus: that in the future, when the redeemer comes, there will be a change of nature in the grain, etc.

units.la: הנפן ולא יצטרכו לזרוע הדגן אלא פעם אחרת כמו הנפן וכיוצא בזה זכרו זכרו רבותינו ז"ל בשינוי טבע שיהיה לעתיד בחטה hoc est, sunt qui illa verba יהיו דגן ita exponunt, fore olim, ubi advenerit redemptor, mutationem naturae in frumento, (quippe vivificabunt illud instar vitis.) Neque fore ut ferant frumentum, nisi una vice, sicuti vitem ferimus & id genus alia. Et meminerunt magistri nostri beatae recordationis, mutationis naturae, quae aliquando futura est in tritico. Haec Kimchius. Quae an aliquid commune habeant cum ista transubstantiatione & naturae mutatione, quae in Papatu docetur, & in qua defendenda, omnia sophistici myrotheeii pigmenta profundunt, cordato lectori dijudicandum relinquo.
units.tr: This is what Kimchi says: some interpreters explain those words "they shall be grain" in this way, namely that a change of nature in grain will come one day, when the Redeemer arrives, so that they will vivify it like a vine. Grain will not need to be sown but will bear once, just as the vine does, and the like. Our masters of blessed memory also mention the change of nature that will one day occur in wheat [הנפן ולא יצטרכו לזרוע הדגן אלא פעם אחרת כמו הנפן וכיוצא בזה זכרו זכרו רבותינו ז"ל בשינוי טבע שיהיה לעתיד בחטה]. Thus Kimchi. I leave it to the discerning reader to judge whether this has anything in common with that transubstantiation and change of nature which is taught among the Papists, and for whose defence they pour out all the paints of their sophistical myrotheecium.

units.la: Ps. CII. 21. ut audiret gemitus compeditorum, ut solveret filios * interemptorum.] Ita vulg. ex Lxx. ἀκοῦσαι τῶν στεναγμῶν τῶν πεπεδημένων, τοῦ λῦσαι τὰς υἱὰς τῶν πεφονευμένων, Huic versioni alienas interpretationes superstruxerunt commentatores. Per interemptos, martyres: per filios interemptorum, eos intelligit Augustinus, qui solvuntur à modis peccatorum & vinculis cupiditatum. Bellarm. per filios interemptorum intelligimus filios veteris Adami & Hevae, qui fuerunt primi occisi astutia serpentis. Textus Ebr. ita habet, audiendum gemitum vincti, & ad solvendum filios mortis. Nota genitivum finis. Filius mortis id est destinatus morti. Ita & Genebr. & Sa. Eadem locutio obvia est Ps. 79. 11. ubi in vulg. filios mortificatorum. In Graeca utrobique eadem vox est. Talis Genitivus & in illo est Ps. 44. 23. reputati sumus quem Apostolus quoque per Genitivum expressit, Roman. 8. ὡς πρόβατα σφαγῆς, tanquam oves mactationis. Huc referunt vulgo illud Joh. 17. 12. υἱὸς ἀπωλείας, filius perditionis. Sed malc assensum meum commodare reverendo D. Piscatori, qui genitivum istum pro genitivo adjuncti accipit, ut filius perditus intelligatur, quomodo filium contumacem filium contumacia Ebraeus sermo appellat. Alibi filius mortis (Ebr. בן מות) est dignus morte, qui capital admisit. 2. Sam. 12. 5. Bellarm. ad Ps. 79. ipsi 78. agnoscit in Ebraeo esse filios mortis, atque illud posse significare homines morti destinatos. & sic multos exponere. Lxx. tamen intellexisse filios occisorum. Se putare hanc esse veram huius loci sententiam. Et quare Bellarmine? Nam inquit. non solum hoc loco, sed & Ps. 101. ubi legimus filios interemptorum, habenbentur eadem verba Ebraïca, quæ ad literam significant filios mortis. Et tamen Lxx. constanter vertunt, filios interemptorum. Q. d. est quidem ita in Ebraeo. Sed quia nostra translatio aliter vertit, non admittimus Ebræum textum. Et tamen isti homines non erubescunt asserere, per Concilii Tridentini de vulgata versione decretum nihil derogatum esse fontibus. Neque illam fuisse Concilii mentem, ut vulgata fontibus anteponeretur. Sed ad rem ipsam quod attinet, jam animi sui sententiam candide edisseruit Cardinalis. Et ego meam lectori communicabo. Ajo Lxx. Interpretes non discrepare ab Ebraeo textu. Duo tantum observentur. 1. filium hominis phrasi Ebraea hominem esse. Ita filii hominum Marc. 3. sunt homines, Filii Gigantum Num. 13. Gigantes, ita Græci, υἱὸς ἀχαιῶν, & Latini, Medicorum filii. Ex hac phraseologia filii ηθανατωμένων sunt ipsi τεθανατωμένοι. 11. οἱ τεθανατωμένοι sunt interficiendi. Scilicet participia illa passiva sæpe talem induunt significationem qualem Latinorum nomina in bilis vel dus exeuntia. Ita subsannabilis, contemptibilis desiderabilis, Psal. 18. 4. laudandus. Huc refer locum Pauli ad Galatas 2.11. Erat enim καταγνωσμένος id est condemnandus ex merito, condemnabilis, condemnatione dignus, κατάκριμα vel κατάκριτος. Quomodo Cicero in Pisonem, Quis te miserior, quis te damnatior? Quod si υἱὸς καταλαμβάνων reddidisset, minus tenebrarum ea versio habuisset.
units.tr: Ps. 102:21, "to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to loosen the children of those who were slain" [ut audiret gemitus compeditorum, ut solveret filios interemptorum]. So the Vulgate, from the Septuagint: "to hear the groanings of those in chains, to loose the sons of the slain" [ἀκοῦσαι τῶν στεναγμῶν τῶν πεπεδημένων, τοῦ λῦσαι τὰς υἱὰς τῶν πεφονευμένων]. Commentators have built alien interpretations upon this version. By "the slain" they understand martyrs; by "the sons of the slain" Augustine understands those who are loosed from the bonds of sins and the chains of desires. Bellarmine says: by "the sons of the slain" we understand the sons of the old Adam and Eve, who were the first slain through the cunning of the serpent. The Hebrew text reads: "to hear the groaning of the bound, and to loose the sons of death." Note the genitive of purpose: "son of death" means one destined for death. The same expression occurs in Ps. 79:11, where the Vulgate has "the sons of those doomed to die"; in the Greek the same word stands in both places. A similar genitive is in Ps. 44:23, "we are accounted" [reputati sumus], which the Apostle also expressed with a genitive in Rom. 8: "as sheep for the slaughter" [ὡς πρόβατα σφαγῆς], "as sheep of slaughter." Commonly they refer to this the phrase in John 17:12, "son of perdition" [υἱὸς ἀπωλείας]. But I am unwilling to lend my assent to the reverend Dr. Fisher, who takes that genitive as a genitive of attribute, so that "son of perdition" means the lost son, just as the Hebrew idiom calls a stubborn son "son of stubbornness." Elsewhere "son of death" (Heb. בן מות) means one who deserves death, who has committed a capital crime, as in 2 Sam. 12:5. Bellarmine, on Ps. 79 (in his numbering 78), acknowledges that the Hebrew has "sons of death," and that this can mean men destined for death, and that many explain it so; yet he thinks the Septuagint understood "sons of the slain," and he believes this is the true sense of the passage. Why then, Bellarmine? For he says that not only in this place but also in Ps. 101, where we read "sons of the slain," the same Hebrew words stand, which literally mean "sons of death." And yet the Septuagint consistently translates "sons of the slain." That is, he says, the Hebrew does read so; but since our translation renders it otherwise, we do not admit the Hebrew text. And yet these men do not blush to assert that the decree of the Council of Trent on the Vulgate version took nothing away from the sources, and that it was not the Council's intention that the Vulgate be placed above the sources. But as far as the matter itself is concerned, the Cardinal has already candidly set out the opinion of his mind, and I will share mine with the reader. I say that the Septuagint interpreters do not differ from the Hebrew text. Only two points should be observed. (1) "Son of man" in Hebrew idiom means a man; thus "sons of men" in Mark 3 are men, and "sons of the Giants" in Num. 13 are giants. So the Greeks say "son of the Achaeans" [υἱὸς ἀχαιῶν], and the Latins "sons of physicians." By this idiom the "sons of the dead" [υἱοὶ θανατωμένων] are the dead themselves [τεθανατωμένοι]. (2) [Ps. 11]: "those who have been put to death" [οἱ τεθανατωμένοι] are those to be killed. Clearly such passive participles often take on the sense that Latin nouns in -bilis or -dus have: thus "subsannabilis" (to be mocked), "contemptibilis" (contemptible), "desiderabilis" (desirable); Ps. 18:4 has "laudandus" (to be praised). Refer to this the passage of Paul to the Galatians 2:11, for he was "condemned" [καταγνωσμένος], that is, deserving of condemnation, condemnable, worthy of condemnation [κατάκριμα or κατάκριτος]. Just as Cicero against Piso says, "Who is more wretched than you, who more damnable?" If the Septuagint had rendered it "son who seizes" [υἱὸς καταλαμβάνων], that version would have had less of darkness.

units.la: Psal. CIV. 26, Draco iste quem fecisti * ad illudendum ei.] Ita vulgatus ex Lxx. δράκων οὗτος ἐπλάσας ἐμπαίζειν αὐτῷ. Ex versione Latina alienæ expositiones natæ sunt. Qui sensui literali hærent, existimant de captura balænæ & quæ eam subsequi solet illusione agi. Carthus. narrat multis modis ei posse illudi. 1. per symphoniam, quam audit libenter, atque ita ad ripam prolectatur per gallinam assatam, quæ ipsi in pertica vel vera ostenditur, cujus nidore capta ad litora usque defertur. per pisces qui hunc tyrannum dum fugiunt, naturali instinctu ad ripas confugiunt, &c. Hæc Carthus. Sed an hoc fine creatus est iste Draco? annon Job. cap. 40. docet, creatum esse Leviathanem, ut potentia Dei per eum agnosceretur? Respondet Carthus. illud ut hic non sumi causaliter, ut finem notet, sed consecutive. Sed illud quoque ex eodem capite Jobi discere potuisset Carthus. ejus capturam rem longe esse difficillimam. Genebr. Illud autem illudere explicaturus, immane quantum prolixus est. Tu, lector, ex iis quae supra pag. 440. 441. ad locum Job. xl. diximus, facile intelliges mentem Augustini. Illis paucula addam ex commentariis ejus ad hunc locum, columna 1215.
units.tr: Ps. 104:26, "this dragon which you have made to play with him" [Draco iste quem fecisti ad illudendum ei]. So the Vulgate, from the Septuagint: "this dragon, which you formed to mock him" [δράκων οὗτος ἐπλάσας ἐμπαίζειν αὐτῷ]. From the Latin version alien expositions have arisen. Those who cling to the literal sense think that the reference is to the capture of a whale and the mockery that usually follows it. Carthusian relates that it can be mocked in many ways: (1) by music, which it hears gladly, and so it is lured to the bank; (2) by a roasted hen, which is shown to it on a pole or in reality, and when it is captured by the smell it is carried to the shore; (3) by fish which, as they flee from this tyrant, by natural instinct take refuge at the banks, and so on. Thus Carthusian. But was this dragon created for this purpose? Does not Job 40 teach that Leviathan was created so that the power of God might be recognised through him? Carthusian answers that the "ut" here is not used causally, to denote purpose, but consecutively. But from the same chapter of Job Carthusian could also have learned that his capture is by far a most difficult thing. Calvin: but to explain this "mocking," he is immensely long-winded. You, reader, from what we said above on pages 440 and 441 on the passage of Job 40, will easily grasp Augustine's mind. I will add a few words to those from his commentary on this passage, column 1215.

units.la: Deus ibi loquitur in libro Job, Non est quicquam simile ei super terram factum ad illudendum ei ab angelis meis. Omne altum videt & ipse est rex omnium quae in aquis sunt. Cui testimonio congruit hoc in Psalmo, — Draco hic quem finxisti ad illudendum ei. Sed si ad illudendum, quomodo Deus illi illudit? An tradidit eum ad illudendum, hoc est, ut illudatur? Putaremus quod Deus illi illuderet, nisi Scriptura Job solvisset quaestionem. Ibi enim dictum est, Ad illudendum ei ab angelis meis. Vis illudere draconi? Esto angelus Dei. Sed nondum es angelus Dei. Donec sis, si eum cursum tenes ut sis, sunt angeli qui illudant Draconi, ne tibi noceat. Haec omnia, quod bona pace maximi viri dictum sit, aliena sunt. Nam quod ad locum Psalmi attinet, illud constat, Prophetam hisce versibus laudare potentiam & sapientiam Dei, quae φαλμοφανεγας apparent in operibus creationis. Deus, inquit, fecit hoc immensum mare, implevit illud omni reptilium & piscium genere. Illic naves ambulant, [quomodo & Cato in de re rustica locutus est, amnis quo nares ambulent, quomodo Sallustius quoque naves progredi dixit, & Homerus νηας πονταπόρξ appellat. ] Introducit navigationem & navium usum, ceu rem mirabilem. Et certe illi robur & aes triplex circa pectus fuit, qui primus fragilem ratem truci pelago commisit. Nominaverat jam animalia pusilla cum magnis. At postea nominatim meminit maris incolae, aitque ei hoc elementum assignatum a Deo לִצְחֹק ad ludendum in eo. Ita Kimchi, Jun. Pisc. ipseque adeo Bellar. Simplicissima expositio videtur, inquit, ad ludendum in eo, sc. mari. ut se in eo moveat, exerceat & quasi ludat. Atque in hunc modum exponit verba Latinae versionis, ad illudendum ei id est ad ludendum in eo, & Graeca, ἐμπαίζειν αὐτῷ, pro παίζειν ἐν αὐτῷ sc. θαλάσσῃ. Atqui tunc dicendum fuisset ἐν αὐτῇ. Respondet Bellar. ita exposuisse Theodoretum & Euthymium. quorum ille non male observavit, mare Ebraeo Syriaco sermone masculino genere efferri. Addo, ipsum quoque affixum, quod in Ebraeo בְּ est, masculinum esse. Quae si admittimus, tum certe omnes interpretes, qui hic de illusionibus prolixe commentati sunt, ipso Bellarmine judice, aliud egerunt. Quod vero ad locum Jobi attinet, ex quo huic testimonio facem allucere vult Augustinus, scire licet, nihil tale esse in originario. Supra pag. 439. ostendimus, Graecum interpretem vers. 14. cap. 40. Job. in descriptione Behemoth, ista de illusione angelorum de suo addidisse. Nunc illud nota, versu quoque penultimo cap. XLI. ubi de Leviathan sermo est; de suo eundem infarsisse illa verba, ad illudendum ei ab angelis meis, ideoque in vulgato quoque interprete nihil ejusmodi legi. Ebraea ita habent, אין על עפר משלו עשוי לבלי חרד Pagn. non est super terram * ei comparabile, qui factus est ut non timeat. Pisc. Nihil super terram est quod possit ei comparari, factus est ut [sit] absque pavore. מָשָׁל vel est infinitivus pro nomine, vel nomen formae קֶרֶשׁ / Illud vero עָשׂוּי est pro עָשׂוּי / participium praeteritum Kal, quomodo & צְפּוּי pro צָפּוּי occurrit. Lxx. οὐκ ἔστιν ὁμοῖον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ὅμοιον αὐτῷ πεποιημένον, ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων μου. Quis adeo sagax qui ullum vestigium vel ὃ ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι vel τῶν ἀγγέλων in Ebraeo textu possit deprehendere? Sed ne vulgatus, quamvis tenacius Ebraeae veritati haeserit, hic omnino defendi potest. Non est super terram potestas quae comparetur ei qui factus est ut nullum timeret. πάντα ὑψηλὰ ὑψηλῶν. nisi quod in vocis מָשָׁל interpretatione nimis liberalis fuit. τὸ μασλ & similitudinem seu comparationem & dominationem significat. At hoc in loco tam aliene utraque ei inducitur significatio, quam doctissimi interpretes, in prima Bibliorum suorum editione, τῷ הַיָּבָל Gen. 4. vers. ult. duas significationes assignarunt, coeptum est profanari.
units.tr: "God speaks there in the book of Job: 'There is nothing like him on the earth, made to be mocked by my angels. He sees all that is high and is himself king over all that are in the waters.' To this testimony this line in the Psalm agrees: 'this dragon that you have fashioned to mock him.' But if it is 'to mock,' how does God mock him? Did he deliver him to be mocked, that is, that he might be mocked? We would think that God mocked him, were it not that Scripture in Job resolves the question. For there it is said, 'to be mocked by my angels.' Do you want to mock the dragon? Be an angel of God. But you are not yet an angel of God. Until you are, if you keep to the course by which you may become one, there are angels who will mock the dragon, lest it harm you." All these things, with the good leave of so great a man be it said, are foreign to the matter. For as far as the passage of the Psalm is concerned, it is evident that the Prophet in these verses praises the power and wisdom of God, which appear manifestly in the works of creation. God, he says, made this vast sea and filled it with every kind of reptile and fish. There ships walk [as Cato also spoke in his book on farming, "the river on which ships walk"; as Sallust also said that ships "advance," and Homer calls ships "sea-traversing" (νηας πονταπόρξ)]. He introduces navigation and the use of ships as a wonderful thing. And certainly he had a heart of oak and triple bronze around his breast who first committed a fragile raft to the savage sea. He had already named small animals along with great ones. But afterwards he mentions by name the inhabitant of the sea, and says that this element was assigned to him by God לִצְחֹק, "to play in it." So Kimchi, Junius, and Fisher, and Bellarmine himself: "The simplest explanation seems to be," he says, "to play in it," namely in the sea, "so that he may move in it, exercise himself, and as it were play." And in this way he explains the words of the Latin version, "to mock him," that is, to play in it, and the Greek, "to mock him" [ἐμπαίζειν αὐτῷ] for "to play in it," namely in the sea [παίζειν ἐν αὐτῷ, sc. θαλάσσῃ]. But then it should have been said ἐν αὐτῇ. Bellarmine answers that Theodoret and Euthymius explained it thus; of these the former rightly observed that the word "sea" is in Hebrew and Syriac of masculine gender. I add that the suffix itself, which in Hebrew is בְּ, is masculine. If we admit these points, then certainly all the interpreters who have discoursed at length here about mockeries have, by Bellarmine's own judgment, done something else. As for the passage of Job, from which Augustine wishes to draw a light for this testimony, be it known that there is nothing of the kind in the original. Above on page 439 we showed that the Greek interpreter, at Job 40:14 in the description of Behemoth, added from his own resources these matters about the mockery of angels. Now note that in the penultimate verse of chapter 41, where the discussion is of Leviathan, he likewise crammed in from his own resources those words "to be mocked by my angels," and therefore nothing of this kind is read even in the Vulgate translator. The Hebrew reads: "There is not upon the earth his like, made without fear" (Pagnini: "there is not on the earth anything comparable to him, who was made so as not to fear"; Fisher: "there is nothing on the earth that can be compared to him; he was made [to be] without dread"). מָשָׁל is either an infinitive used as a noun or a noun of the form קֶרֶשׁ; and עָשׂוּי is for עָשׂוּי, the past participle of Qal, just as צְפּוּי occurs for צָפּוּי. The Septuagint: "there is not upon the earth a like thing made like him, to be mocked by my angels" [οὐκ ἔστιν ὁμοῖον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ὅμοιον αὐτῷ πεποιημένον, ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων μου]. Who is so sagacious that he could detect any trace either of "to be mocked" [ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι] or of "by the angels" [τῶν ἀγγέλων] in the Hebrew text? But not even the Vulgate, though it has clung more tenaciously to Hebrew truth, can be wholly defended here: "There is not upon the earth a power that may be compared to him who was made so as to fear nothing. All high things are high." Except that in the interpretation of the word מָשָׁל it was too free. The word [τὸ μασλ] signifies both likeness or comparison and dominion. But in this place both meanings are brought in as foreign to it, just as the most learned interpreters, in the first edition of their Bibles, assigned two meanings to the word הַיָּבָל in Gen. 4, last verse: "it began to be profaned."

units.la: Ps. CX. Tecum principium,] Occasione hujus loci, ubi nimis supinus fuit Latinus interpres, scripsi aliquando commentatiunculam, in quam convectavi crassiora quaedam interpretum ἀμαρτήματα, dum vel librariorum sphalmata interpretati sunt, vel ambiguo vocum decepti eam significationem, quae ab originario quam longissime distabat; elegerunt. Eam hic exhibebo & quidem cum brevi praeloquio.
units.tr: Ps. CX. "Tecum principium": On the occasion of this passage, where the Latin translator was too careless, I once wrote a short commentary in which I gathered together some of the cruder blunders of the translators, namely those cases where they explained copyists' errors, or, misled by the ambiguity of words, chose a meaning that lay very far from the original. I shall set it out here, with a brief preface.

units.la: Ad Nobilissimum pium & magnæ spei juvenem, D. EPEVM ab AYLVA bonarum literarum & artium studiosum.
units.tr: To the most noble, pious and promising young man, Mr. Epeus ab Aylva, a student of good letters and the arts.

units.la: NEgare non potes, nobilissime Aylva, vulgi judicio nobilitatem quasi capite censam fieri, si studia colantur. Spernitur vulgo omnis eruditio, & si pauculos quosdam erectioris animi excipias, valet illud, Nil nisi Cecropides. Non postrema corruptæ Reip. nostræ causa contemptus doctrinæ est, inquit alicubi magnus Lipsius. Quis e nostra juventute legitime instituitur in literis? Quis oratores aut philosophos tangit? quis historiam vel primoribus labris libat, illam rerum gerendarum quasi animam? Præcipitant enim parentes vota sua & pueros vix septuennes protrudunt ad juris scientiam. Scilicet omnibus artibus antistat spes lucri & formosior est nummus auri, quam quicquid uspiam est sacræ aut exoticæ eruditionis. Ex hoc numero deinde veniunt ad gubernacula reipublicæ, non virtute, non eruditione, sed favoribus & suorum potentia subnixi. Non penetrabo altius in hoc confusionum nostrarum pelagus. Te potius miror, qui maximi parentis tui, Academiæ nostræ vigilantissimi curatoris, æmulus, viam virtutis & veræ doctrinæ constanter calcas. Namque in ista fortuna inculpatam & ab omni pravorum contubernio segregem vitam agitas, ab iis quoque alienus, quæ hodie, ut mores mali sunt, morum larvâ seculi licentia velavit. Latinis, Græcis & Ebraïcis Musis non perfunctorie & propter viam litasti, sed ea in hoc linguarum stadio fecisti spatia, ut non solum ministerii & supremorum in re literaria titulorum candidatos, sed & ministros & Doctores quamplurimos in ruborem dare possis. Logicam quoque illam ingeniorum limam & cotem, sic excoluisti, ut in publicis disputationibus, jam respondentis, jam opponentis partes obeuntem non sine admiratione sæpe audiverimus. Istis fundamentis jactis, excelsum illum animum ad reliquas philosophiæ partes, & nominatim divinam Mathematicam, nec non ad Historiarum studia applicasti. Memini me non ita pridem ex reverendo viro, D. Gul. Amesio hospite tuo audire, cum de te sermo obiter incidisset, se nullum istius aetatis novisse unquam, qui vel majores omni ἐγκυκλοπαιδείας parte progressus fuerit, vel majori cum judicio de re literaria & Historica disseruerit. Atque haec non tam eo dico, ut te laudem, quam ut alios, quibus nec ingenium nec discendi commoditas defuit, ad exacti temporis calculos vocem. Te admodum adhuc adolescentem breviculi temporis plusquam de decumana industria omnium doctrinarum, quae ad singularum facultatem ἐγκυκλοπαιδείαν pertinent, choragio ornavit. Quae singula quibusdam egregiis ingeniis mirari solemus, ea tu consecutus es universa. At quanta illorum turba est, qui, licet annos aliquot in Acad. vixerint, ne unius quidem linguae vel artis scientiam sibi comparavere! Et tamen ea est seculi nostri felicitas, is Academiae nostrae status, ut nihil aliud quam suam desidiam accusare possint.
units.tr: You cannot deny, most noble Aylva, that in the judgment of the common people nobility is, as it were, rated by its head if it cultivates learning. Among the common people all scholarship is despised, and, apart from a few men of loftier spirit, the saying holds: Nil nisi Cecropides. The contempt for learning is not the least cause of the corruption of our commonwealth, says the great Lipsius somewhere. Who among our young men is properly trained in letters? Who touches the orators or the philosophers? Who sips history even from the top of the lips, that history which is, as it were, the soul of affairs conducted? Parents rush headlong toward their own wishes and push boys scarcely seven years old toward the study of law. Clearly the hope of gain takes precedence over all the arts, and the gold coin is more attractive than whatever sacred or foreign learning there is anywhere. From this crowd men then come to the helm of the commonwealth, supported not by virtue or learning but by favour and the power of their own people. I will not dive deeper into this sea of our confusions. Rather, I admire you, who, as a rival of your most excellent father, the most watchful guardian of our Academy, steadfastly walk the path of virtue and true learning. For in that fortune you lead a blameless life, separated from all association with the wicked, and you keep aloof from those things which, since bad morals are now the rule, the licence of the age has veiled with the mask of manners. You have not dabbled in the Latin, Greek and Hebrew Muses casually and for the sake of getting through, but in this race of languages you have made such progress that you could shame not only candidates for the ministry and for the highest academic titles, but also very many ministers and teachers. That file and whetstone of minds, logic, you have so cultivated that, taking now the part of respondent, now of opponent, in public disputations, we have often heard you with admiration. With these foundations laid, you have applied that lofty mind to the remaining parts of philosophy, and especially to divine mathematics, and also to the study of histories. I remember hearing a short time ago from the reverend Mr. William Amesius, your host, that when talk about you happened to arise in passing, he said he had never known anyone of your age who had either advanced further in every part of the encyclopaedia [ἐγκυκλοπαιδείας] or discoursed on literary and historical matters with greater judgment. And I say this not so much to praise you as to call others, who lacked neither talent nor opportunity for learning, to account for the time that has passed. You, while still quite young, have in a short time, and with more than tenfold diligence, adorned yourself with all the disciplines that pertain to the encyclopaedia [ἐγκυκλοπαιδείαν] of each faculty. Those single things we are accustomed to admire in certain outstanding minds, you have attained all together. But how great is the crowd of those who, although they have lived some years in the Academy, have not acquired knowledge of even one language or art! And yet such is the good fortune of our age and the state of our Academy that they can accuse nothing but their own idleness.

units.la: Tu vero, nobilissime adolescens, qui tam praeclare coepisti, perge constanter, & porro annitere, ut quibus genere antistas, virtute quoque & doctrina antecellas. Erit aliquando, cum in te vel religiosum & eruditum Consiliarium Respublica, vel Senatorem Curiae, vel celebrem Professorem Academia habebit. Cur enim hoc postremum non adderem? Scio enim tuum ingenium ad quietem & secessum aurigari. Cum Diodorus Lipsio professoriam linguam objectasset, hoc responsum maximo viro expressit, Vtor ea, nec cum infamia aut damno Batavia vestra utor. Facio quod ante me NOBILES imo PRINCIPES viri. Et tu mihi libenter largieris, opinor, beatiorem in Academia quam Republica, prout nostrae jam res eunt, vitam agitari. Sed mittamus illa, & vide mihi, quaeso, quantis in tenebris prisci interpretes & commentatores vixerint, quoties vocum ambiguo aut librariorum sphalmatibus decepti ab originarii textus tramite diverterint. Psalmo cx. ita infit David, עָפָךְ נְדָבוֹת בְּיוֹם חֵילֶךָ בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר לְךָ טַל יַלְדוּתֶךָ Ad quem locum ut & universum hunc Psalmum erudite disseruit reverendus Revetus, Simplicissima interpretatio ista est, Populus tuus [erit populus] spontaneitatum (id est summe spontaneus, voluntarius) in die exercitus tui (illo tempore quo excercitum tuum id est Apostolos & alios Evangelii praecones in orbem terrarum emittes) in ornatibus sanctitatis tatis (id est vitæ sanctitate) Ex utero aurora tibi [erit] ros*na-torum tuorum. hoc est, filii tui, credentes, tanquam ros tibi nascentur, veluti ex aurora, tanquam utero. Sicut ros ex aurora id est aëre matutino veluti ex utero nascitur; in guttas innumeras dispersus, ita electi tui ex prædicatione Euangelii maximo tibi numero nascentur. Quid Lxx? μετὰ σὲ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν λαμπρότητι τῆς δυναμέως σε, ἐν ταῖς λαμπρότησι τῶν ἁγίων σε. ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρου ἐγέννησά σε. Quæ sic convertit vulgatus: Tecum principium in die virtutis tuæ in splendoribus (Augustus splendore) sanctorum. Ex utero ante Luciferum genui te. Valde sudant Interpretes ut ostendant hanc versionem cum originali textu concordare. Omnia invertunt, pervertunt, mutant quadrata rotundis, nec tamen proficiunt hilum. Bellarm. textum Ebræum in hunc modum corrigit, עִמְּךָ נְדָבָה בְּיוֹם הֵילֶךָ בְּאוֹרֵי קֹדֶשׁ מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר לְךָ תֵּיךָ? ubi præterquam, quod in ipsas quoque consonantes (vocales enim de facili solicitant) imperium sibi vindicavit, duas quoque insuper voces לְךָ כֵּל eliminavit. Vide Rivetum & Joh. Tarnovium exerc. Bibl. pag. 119. Edit. 3. Sed operæ erit pressius insistere huic lineæ, & utrumque textum adversis frontibus componere.
units.tr: But you, most noble young man, who have begun so splendidly, persevere steadfastly, and strive further, so that you who excel in birth may also excel in virtue and learning. There will come a time when the commonwealth will have you as a pious and learned counsellor, or as a senator of the court, or the Academy as a celebrated professor. For why should I not add this last? I know that your talent is directed toward quiet and retirement. When Diodorus charged Lipsius with a professor's tongue, the great man gave this reply: I use it, nor do I use it to the disgrace or loss of your Batavia. I do what noble, indeed princely, men have done before me. And you, I suppose, will gladly grant me that, as our affairs now go, life is led more happily in the Academy than in the commonwealth. But let us set those things aside, and see for me, I beg you, in how great darkness the ancient interpreters and commentators lived, how often, deceived by the ambiguity of words or by errors of copyists, they turned aside from the path of the original text. Psalm 110 begins thus with David: Am' kh nedavoth beyom chelkha, behadrei qodesh, mereḥem mishḥar lekha tal yaldutekha [עָפָךְ נְדָבוֹת בְּיוֹם חֵילֶךָ בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר לְךָ טַל יַלְדוּתֶךָ]. Reverend Rivetus, in discussing this verse and the whole psalm learnedly, gives this very simple interpretation: Your people [will be] freewill offerings (that is, most willing, voluntary) in the day of your army (at that time when you send forth your army, that is the Apostles and other preachers of the Gospel, into the world) in the ornaments of holiness (that is, by holiness of life). From the womb, the dawn is yours; [there will be] the dew of your sons. That is, your sons, the believers, will be born to you like dew, as from the dawn, as from a womb. Just as dew is born from the dawn, that is, from the morning air, as from a womb, scattered into countless drops, so your chosen ones will be born to you in a very great number through the preaching of the Gospel. What do the Seventy say? Meta se hē archē en lamprotēti tēs dynameōs se, en tais lamprotēsi tōn hagiōn se. Ek gastros pro heōsphorou egennēsa se [μετὰ σὲ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν λαμπρότητι τῆς δυναμέως σε, ἐν ταῖς λαμπρότησι τῶν ἁγίων σε. ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρου ἐγέννησά σε]. The Vulgate renders these thus: Tecum principium in die virtutis tuae in splendoribus (Augustus splendore) sanctorum. Ex utero ante Luciferum genui te. Interpreters sweat hard to show that this version agrees with the original text. They turn everything upside down, distort it, change squares into circles, and yet gain not the least thing. Bellarmine corrects the Hebrew text in this way: immekha nedavah beyom heilekha be'orei qodesh, mereḥem mishḥar lekha teikh? where, besides claiming authority over the consonants themselves (for vowels easily cause trouble), he also removed two words, lekha and kel [לְךָ כֵּל]. See Rivetus and Johann Tarnovius, Exercitationes Biblicae, page 119, third edition. But it will be worth the effort to press more closely on this line and set the two texts side by side, face to face.

units.la: Tecum principium] Lxx: μετὰ σὲ ἡ ἀρχή. Ebr. עִמְּךָ נְדָבוֹת / Demus legendum עִמְּךָ tecum, quomodo נְדָבוֹת per principium reddi potest? Hic aqua omnibus Pontificiis hæsit. Vox ἀρχή, Græcis & principatum & principium: Vox Ebræa נְדָבוֹת neutrum significat. De principio nullus unquam sic depuduit, id ut assereret. Et tamen hanc notionem, quæ maxime aliena est, Latinus Interpres elegit. De principatu, persuadere quidem satagunt Genebr. & alii, sed frustra sunt. Conjugatum נְדִיבִים principes quidem significat, q. d. ἡγεμόνες, at נִדְבָה principatum significare nullo uno testimonio hactenus ostensum est. Sed ut demus significare ἀρχὴ id est principatum, quid tum fiet voci Latinæ principium? Bellarminus ait posse sic exponi, tecum est principium primum omnium rerum, quia tu es in patre & pater in te. Augustus col. 1283, Quodlibet pone principium, Si ipsum Christum, potius diceretur, tu es principium, quam tecum principium. Cum sit principium & pater, de quo unigenitus filius, in quo principio erat verbum, quia verbum erat apud Deum. Quid ergo? Si & pater principium, & filius principium, duo sunt principia? Absit. Sicuti enim pater Deus & filius Deus & tamen non duo dii sed unus deus: sic pa-per principium, & filius principium. Pater autem & filius non duo, sed unum principium, — Tunc videberis quomodo tecum principium. Non enim & hic non tecum principiam. Non enim cum dixisti, Ecce itis quisque ad sua, & me solum relinquitis, sed non sum solus, quia pater mecum est. Et hic ergo tecum principium. Dixisti enim & alibi, Pater in me manens facit opera sua. Tecum principium nec unquam à te separatus est pater. Verbo. Tecum principium dupliciter exponitur. 1. tecum, o Fili, est pater qui Johan. 1.1. vocatur principium, ipso quoque Cyrillo interprete. 2. Tecum, o Pater, est filius, qui Joh.8. principium vocatur. Vide Lyram. Has interpretationes non solum Graeco & Ebraeo sed & Latino textui adversari, omnes illi Pontificii agnoscunt, qui tò principium pro principatu positum contendunt, ut Sa, Genebr. Bell. & alii. Genebr. ἀρχὴ hic principatum significat, non principium id est patrem, licet Latini fere reclament. Ergo, inquit, tecum principium, id est obtinebit principatum. Bellarm. tecum erit principatus manifestus. Vidit hoc inter Latinos Tertul. adversus Hermogenem, possum principium, inquit, aliter interpretari, non abs re tamen. Nam & in Graeco principii vocabulum, quod est ἀρχή, non tantum ordinativum, sed & potestativum caput principatum. Unde & ἄρχοντες dicuntur principes, &c. Necdum ullum testimonium audivimus, quo haec nova significatio vocis Latinae probetur. Ammian. lib. 25. collecti duces exercitus, advocatisque legionum principiis, &c. Hic per principia principes intelligunt interpretes, quomodo Vegetius quoque saepe ea voce usus est. Sed nondum principatum habemus. Non celabo. Sulpicius Severus lib. 1. pag. mihi 12. dictumque responso Domini est, duos in his populos praenuntiari & majorem minoris (ita enim putarim legendum pro minori) subdendum esse principio. Expressit illud Mosis, major serviet minori. Caeterum quis sibi persuaderi patietur, Latinum Interpretem hic ea notione vocem principium accepisse, qua nusquam alibi. Non certe Lovanienses, qui locum hunc sic interpretati sunt, met u ist beginsel in den dach van uwer cracht. Non Arias Montanus, qui praefatione in Biblia Interlin. Vulgatum interpretem arguit, quod ambiguitate vocis Graecae deceptus principium reddiderit, cum vertendum fuerit, principatus. Hanc tamen principatus notionem Ebraeo non convenire hoc ipso testatus est, quod in ipso textu נרבורו devotiones reddiderit. Quanto satius fuisset, Hieronymo aures substringere, qui voces Ebraeas sic reddidit, Populus tuus spontanei erunt.
units.tr: Tecum principium: the Seventy have meta se hē archē [μετὰ σὲ ἡ ἀρχή]; the Hebrew has immekha nedavoth [עִמְּךָ נְדָבוֹת]. Let us grant that the reading should be immekha, "with you"; how can nedavoth be rendered "beginning" [principium]? Here every Papist has stuck fast. The Greek word archē means both principate and beginning, but the Hebrew word nedavoth means neither. No one has ever been so shameless as to assert the meaning "beginning". And yet the Latin translator chose this sense, which is most alien to the text. Geneva and others labour to persuade us of "principate", but in vain. The plural form nedivim does indeed mean princes, that is, hēgemones, but no single witness has so far been shown for nedavah meaning principate. But let us grant that archē means principate, that is, rule; what then becomes of the Latin word principium? Bellarmine says it can be explained thus: "With you is the beginning, the first of all things, because you are in the Father and the Father is in you." Augustine, column 1283: Put down whatever beginning you like; if it were Christ himself, it would rather be said: you are the beginning, not "with you the beginning". Since there is a beginning and a Father, from whom the only-begotten Son, in whom the Word was in the beginning, because the Word was with God... What then? If the Father is the beginning and the Son is the beginning, are there two beginnings? Far from it. For just as the Father is God and the Son is God, and yet not two gods but one God, so the Father is the beginning and the Son is the beginning; yet the Father and the Son are not two beginnings but one beginning. Then you will see how tecum principium. For here too it is not "with you the beginning" that is missing. For when you said, "Behold, each of you goes to his own, and you leave me alone", yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me. And so here, tecum principium. For you also said elsewhere, "The Father dwelling in me does his works." Tecum principium: the Father was never separated from you. In brief: tecum principium is explained in two ways. (1) "With you, O Son, is the Father, who in John 1:1 is called the beginning," as Cyril himself interprets. (2) "With you, O Father, is the Son, who in John 8 is called the beginning." See Lyra. All the Papists acknowledge that these interpretations are opposed not only to the Greek and Hebrew but also to the Latin text, which is why they contend that tò principium is put for principate, as Sa, Genebrardus, Bellarmine and others do. Genebrardus says that archē here means principate, not the principium, that is, the Father, although the Latins almost all protest. "Therefore," he says, "with you is the principium, that is, he will obtain the principate." Bellarmine: with you will be a manifest principate. Among the Latins Tertullian saw this, against Hermogenes: I can, he says, interpret the word principium otherwise, and not without reason. For in the Greek too the word principium, which is archē, signifies not only the order-giving but also the power-holding head, the principate. Whence also the archontes are called princes, etc. We have not yet heard any testimony by which this new sense of the Latin word is proved. Ammianus, book 25: The leaders of the army were gathered, and the principia of the legions were summoned, etc. Here the interpreters understand principia as princes, just as Vegetius too often used that word. But we do not yet have a principate. I will not hide it: Sulpicius Severus, book 1, page 12 in my edition: And it was said by the response of the Lord that two peoples were foretold in these, and the greater must be made subject to the lesser (for so I would think it should be read instead of minori) to the principium. He expressed the saying of Moses, the greater shall serve the lesser. Moreover, who will allow himself to be persuaded that the Latin translator took the word principium here in a sense found nowhere else? Certainly not the Louvain translators, who interpreted this passage thus: met u ist beginsel in den dach van uwer cracht. Nor Arias Montanus, who in the preface to the Interlinear Bible charges the Vulgate translator with having, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, rendered it principium when it should have been rendered principatus. Yet he himself testified that this sense of "principate" does not agree with the Hebrew, in that in the very text he rendered nedarurō as devotiones [נרבורו]. How much better it would have been to close one's ears as Jerome did, who rendered these Hebrew words thus: Your people will be willing.

units.la: Ex utero ante luciferum genui te.] Quasi in Ebraeo esset מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר יְלִדְתִּיךָ / vocibus duabus לְךָ טַל in exilium ire jussis. At ut cætera transcaant, non solum Chaldæus, sed & Aq. Symm. & v. editionis author יְלִדְתִּיךָ legerunt. Interpretes qua veteres qua recentes, si pauculos excipias, ex hoc loco Christi Deitatem & æternitatem probarunt. Bell. Ex voce genui probant sancti patres efficacissime Christi Deitatem. Nam si creatura esset, non posset dici genitus ex utero. Nemo enim dicit se genuisse ex utero domum vel stannum, neque Deus unquam dixit se genuisse ex utero cœlum aut terram. Porro per uterum intelligitur essentia Dei secreta & intima. Hæc Bellarm. cui objici posset locus Jesa. 46. 3. ubi vulgatus ita legit, Audite domus Jacob, qui portamini a meo utero, qui gestamini a mea vulva. Quæ B. Luth. sic convertit, die ghy van my inden lyve gedragen wert, ende my in der moeder legget. An hic quoque רחם intimam & secretam Dei essentiam significabit? An ergo & domus Jacob ex Dei essentia genita est? Absit. Quid tamen ad hunc locum dicent Pontificii? Illi se torquent. Nos uno verbo dicimus, interpretationem laborare. Neque enim in originario de utero Dei sermo est, הַנִּשְׂאִים מִנִּי רֶחֶם מִנִּי בָּטֶן qui bajulamini ab utero, qui portati [estis] aut portamini a matrice. Ita Pagn. Arias, Junius & alii. Quis unquam fando audivit, affixa antecedere suum nomen? a meo utero, a mea vulva, hoc esset מִן רֶחֶם & מִן בָּטֶן / Quid ergo? Jod in מִנִּי est paragogicum, ideoque à Lxx. quoque neglectum, οἱ ἀιρόμενοι ἐκ κοιλίας, ἡ πεπαιδευμένοι ἐκ παιδίου. Dicit ergo, se eos bajulatte sicut mater puerulum bajulat & portat, idque à prima eorum origine, ex quo, perruptis materni uteri carceribus, hunc aerem hausere. Sed redeamus ad Psalmum. Iidem interpp. ex istis verbis ante luciferum genui te, Christi æternitatem probarunt. Bellar. Hinc significatur æternitas filii, qui genitus fuit ante luciferi creationem, ac per hoc ante omnes creaturas. Sed posuit nomen Luciferi, quia & ipse est Lucifer quidam increatus. Genebr Quemadmodum per, ex utero, dirimam generationem & identitatem substantiæ significarunt, ita per, ante luciferum, æternitatem divinæ ipsius generationis. Per Luciferum autem alii solem, alii, stellam veneris, alii, primum angelum [?]gelum intellexêre. Quicquid sit, Christũ ab omni æternitate ex substantia patris sui genitum esse, articulus fidei est. Sed hoc loco istud mysterium tractari, articulus fidei non est. Quin potius, cum locum huc velle trahere, crassa infscitia est. Hieronymus, ubi tritam illam de ossibus aridis apud Jezech. 27. expositionem non putat esse literæ cogruentem, sed ænigmaticè Prophetam eo modo mortuam populi spem excitasse, hæc subjungit. Qui autem aliter interpretentur, ista non debent nobis facere invidiam, quod istum locum aliter exponentes, resurrectionem negare videamur. Scimus enim multo robustiora testimonia, & in quibus nulla possit dubitatio reperiri. Et paulo post, Ex quo perspicuum est nos non resurrectionem negare, sed hæc non scripta de resurrectione contendere. Eodem modo & ego semel hic protestor. Æternam Filii Dei Deitatem non nego. Sed hæc ad istum articulum non pertinere contendo. Vidimus Bellarminum, ut vulgatæ Interpretationi patrocinium præstet, puncta & consonas mutasse, vocesque duas ejecisse. Genebrardus, subtilior artifex, voces Ebræas ut solicitet, non putat committendum. Namque istis versionem vulgatam plane respondere asserit. Septuaginta, inquit, sensum duntaxat secuti sunt, idque fidissime & prophetice. Non quod aliter legerint, quam nunc habeat veritas Ebraica. (cur huic Professori patientiam non præbuisti Bellarmine? Sed videamus.) Ros metaphorice natas suavitatem & hilaritatem, ut cum nos dicimus, flos, & aliquem esse in flore ætatis. Est ergo sensus facilis & perspicuus. Ex utero (meo id est substantia) ab aurora (ab aurora ortu) tibi est ros adolescentia tua. Tu eras ex utero meo & mea substantia, in rore adolescentia, ab ipso Luciferi ortu. Tu jam eras in flore juventutis, vel in suavitate & dulcedine adolescentia. Tu jam eras natus magna mea voluptate. Paulo post subjicit ista, Non aliene etiam aliqui (inter quos & Aug.) de temporaria Christi nativitate. Ex utero] Virginis, non e semine humano. Ante luciferum] mane summo. Genui te. Quæso te, Genebrarde, quid, tum fiet istis vocibus, quas fateris in Ebraeo esse, tibi ros adolescentia tua? An cum nasceretur ex virgine jam tunc in flore ætatis erat Christus qua homo? si prior illa tua expositio genuina est, quomodo hæc non aliena erit? Aut si hæc aliena non est, quomodo illa non potest non esse aliena? Non licet nobis in scripturarum interpretatione tam esse disertis. Non nego unius loci probabiles sæpe esse duas vel tres exexpositiones. sed cum de una expositione certo constat, cæteræ non possunt non esse alienæ. Atqui antea priorem illum sensum perspicuum esse dixeras, & in nostros, quos Gnosticos pro tua mansuetudine appellas, destomachatus fueras quod ab ista interpretatione secedentes varia expositionum portenta huc convectarent. Nostrorum interpretatio an portentosa sit, eruditi judicent. Quin potius portentosa sunt illa Maldonati, qui perruptis omnis pudoris clathris hæc chartis illevit, Deo tribui vulvam metaphorice, ut intelligamus in generatione æterna filii fuisse quodammodo Hermaphroditum id est virum & mulierem. Ἐκας ἐκας ἐστ βεβηλοι Non ficloqui auderent qui musas colunt modestiores. Bellarminus postquam de æterna generatione locum expositisset, hæc subjicit, Augustinus aliam addit explicationem minus principalem, quod vid. David Christo Filio suo secundum carnem dicat, Ego genui te ex utero Virginis Mariæ, filia mea, antequam Lucifer oriretur id est media nocte. Tertull. quoque in Marcionem lib. 5. exponit de partu virginis, sed tribuit Deo illud, genui te, hoc modo, Ego Deus pater genui te ex utero virginis, nocturno tempore, antequam lucifer oriretur. Quo loco autem istas interpretationes habeat, altum silet. Adi jam ad pag. 127. ubi censuram B. Lutheri leges. Mihi tollenda jam manus de hac tabula. Ad alia accingamur. Ps. cxxviii 2. laborem enim manuum tuarum comedes id est cibum labore manuum tuarum partum.
units.tr: "From the womb before the morning star I have begotten you." It is as if the Hebrew read מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר יְלִדְתִּיךָ [from the womb of the dawn I have begotten you], with the two words לְךָ טַל [to you, dew] left out as though sent into exile. But to pass over the rest, not only the Chaldee paraphrast but also Aquila, Symmachus and the author of the fifth edition read יְלִדְתִּיךָ [I have begotten you]. Almost all the interpreters, ancient and recent, with a few exceptions, have proved from this passage the deity and eternity of Christ. Bellarmine: The holy Fathers prove the deity of Christ most effectively from the word "begotten". For if he were a creature, he could not be said to be begotten from the womb. No one says that he begot a house or a tin pot from the womb, and God never said that he begot heaven or earth from the womb. By "womb" is meant the secret and inner essence of God. So Bellarmine. Against him one could cite Isaiah 46:3, where the Vulgate reads, Hear, house of Jacob, you who are carried from my womb, you who are borne from my belly. Luther translates this: who are carried in my body and laid in my mother's arms. Does רחם here also signify the innermost and secret essence of God? Was then the house of Jacob also begotten from the essence of God? Far from it. What then will the Papists say to this passage? They twist themselves into knots. We answer in one word: the interpretation labours. For the Hebrew does not speak here of God's womb: הַנִּשְׂאִים מִנִּי רֶחֶם מִנִּי בָּטֶן [those who are carried from the womb, those who are borne from the belly], that is, "who are carried from the womb, who have been carried or are carried from the belly." So Pagninus, Arias, Junius and others. Who ever heard of a preposition placed after its noun, "from my womb, from my belly"? That would be מִן רֶחֶם and מִן בָּטֶן. What then? The yod in מִנִּי is paragogic, and therefore the Seventy also disregarded it: οἱ αἰρόμενοι ἐκ κοιλίας, ἡ πεπαιδευμένοι ἐκ παιδίου [those lifted from the belly, or those trained from childhood]. So the sense is: I carried them as a mother carries and bears her little child, and that from their very first origin, from the time they broke out of the prison of the mother's womb and drew in this air. But let us return to the Psalm. The same interpreters have proved the eternity of Christ from the words before the morning star I have begotten you. Bellarmine: Here is signified the eternity of the Son, who was begotten before the creation of the morning star, and so before all creatures. But he used the name of the morning star because he too is a kind of uncreated morning star. Genebrard: Just as by "from the womb" they signified the generation and the identity of substance, so by "before the morning star" they signified the eternity of the divine generation itself. Some have understood by the morning star the sun, others the star of Venus, others the first angel. Whatever the case, that Christ was begotten from the substance of his Father from all eternity is an article of faith. But that this mystery is treated in this passage is not an article of faith. Indeed, to draw this place into that question is gross ignorance. Jerome, when he does not think the familiar explanation of the dry bones in Ezekiel 37 fits the letter, but holds that the Prophet by enigma raised up the dead hope of the people in that way, adds these words: Those who interpret otherwise should not stir up hatred against us, as if by explaining this passage differently we denied the resurrection. For we know much stronger testimonies, in which no doubt can be found. And a little later: From this it is plain that we do not deny the resurrection, but contend that these words were not written about the resurrection. In the same way I too protest once more here: I do not deny the eternal Deity of the Son of God. But I contend that this does not pertain to that article. We have seen Bellarmine, in order to lend patronage to the Vulgate interpretation, change the points and consonants and cast out two words. Genebrard, a more subtle craftsman, does not think it right to disturb the Hebrew words, for he asserts that the Vulgate version agrees plainly with them. The Seventy, he says, followed only the sense, and that most faithfully and prophetically. Not that they read differently from what the Hebrew truth now has. (Why, Bellarmine, did you not show this professor patience? But let us see.) The dew is born metaphorically, sweetness and cheerfulness, just as when we say "flower", and someone is "in the flower of his age". The sense is therefore easy and clear: from the womb (that is, from my substance) before the dawn (before the rising of the dawn) is the dew of your youth to you. You were from my womb and my substance, in the dew of youth, from the very rising of the morning star. You were already in the flower of youth, or in the sweetness and delight of adolescence. You were already born with my great joy. A little later he adds these words: Not unfittingly, some (including Augustine) also speak of Christ's temporal nativity. "From the womb": of the Virgin, not from human seed. "Before the morning star": at the very top of the morning. "I have begotten you." I ask you, Genebrard, what will become of those words, which you admit are in the Hebrew, the dew of your youth to you? When he was born of the Virgin, was Christ already then in the flower of his age as man? If your former explanation is the genuine one, how will this one not be foreign? Or if this one is not foreign, how can that former one not be foreign? We are not allowed, in interpreting Scripture, to be so eloquent. I do not deny that for a single passage there are often two or three probable explanations. But when it is certain what one explanation is, the others cannot but be foreign. Yet you had earlier said that the former sense was plain, and you fumed against our people, whom out of your gentleness you call Gnostics, because they, departing from that interpretation, brought in various monstrous explanations. Whether our interpretation is monstrous, learned readers may judge. Rather, those of Maldonatus are monstrous, who, bursting every bar of shame, have daubed onto paper this: The womb is attributed to God metaphorically, so that we understand that in the eternal generation of the Son he was in some way a hermaphrodite, that is, both man and woman. Keep away, keep away, you profane ones [Ἐκὰς ἐκὰς ἔστε βέβηλοι]. More modest men, who cultivate the Muses, would not dare to speak so. Bellarmine, after he had expounded the passage about the eternal generation, adds these words: Augustine adds another explanation, less principal, namely that David says to Christ his Son according to the flesh: "I have begotten you from the womb of the Virgin Mary, my daughter, before the morning star rises," that is, at midnight. Tertullian too, in Against Marcion book 5, explains it of the birth of the Virgin, but he attributes the words "I have begotten you" to God in this way: "I, God the Father, have begotten you from the womb of the Virgin at night, before the morning star rises." In what place he has these interpretations, he is silent on high. Now go to page 127, where you will read the censure of Luther. For me, the hand must now be withdrawn from this board. Let us turn to other matters. Psalm 128:2: For you shall eat the labour of your hands, that is, food acquired by the labour of your hands.

units.la: Aq. — κοπῶν πεφῶν σε. Symm. & v. editio, χειρῶν σε, Lxx. τὰς πόνος τῶν καρπῶν σε Φάγεσαι. Optime, nisi quod ambigue. Latinus, labores fructuum tuorum comedes. Pessime. Hoc patet illis, qui ad fontes adire possunt. Quid enim commune est fructibus cum manibus? Καρπὸς Græcis non solum fructum, sed & ἀρθρον τῆς χειρὸς καὶ βραχίων id est junctyram manus & brachii significat. Hinc composita illa, περιχάρπιον, μεσοχάρπιον, περιχάρπιον. Hinc synecdochice totum manum significat. Pro palmâ eadem voce uti sunt Lxx. 1. Sam. 5. ἀμφόπεροι οἱ καρπεὶ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῶ περιπηκόπης ἐπὶ τὸ πεζῆρον. Ex collatione Græcorum interpretum B. Theodoretus odorari potuit, Lxx. per illam vocem οὐ τὸν Παλαιστίαν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μέσον τῶν χειρῶν intellexisse. Vulgatus quoque interpres hic non aberravit. Sed patres fere alteram illam pejorem sequuntur. Cave ergo hic sequaris Augustinum, plenis velis in Allegoriarum freto navigantem. Distinguit subtiliter inter labores fructuum, & fructus laborum. Interim modo inquit quit, labores fructuum, postea fructus laboris. Manducabunt labores fructuum, qui euntes ibant & flebant, mittentes semina sua. Quanto jucundius manducabunt fructus laborum, qui venientes venient cum exultatione, portantes manipulos suos? Pf. xvii. 14. יְשַׁבְּעוּ בָנִים saturantur filii. Lxx. ἐχορτάσθησαν υἱῶν * υἱῶν. saturati sunt filii. Augustus saturati sunt porcinā, quod sic explicat, saturati sunt immunditiis, conculcantes margaritas sermonum Dei. Euthymius, saturati sunt porcu. quamvis paulo aliter explicet, Saturati sunt immunditiis, consumpto nim. patrimonio ac bonis omnibus, in varias voluptates. Notat quidem uterque, aliquos pro porcina, filios legere, natamque varietatem interpretationis ex ambiguo Graeco, ut loquitur Aug. vel ut Euthymius, & quidem melius scriptorum vitio, quia τὰ υἱῶν & υἱῶν confuderint, at neuter, utra genuina lectio sit & in textu retinenda, vel ausus fuit vel potuit asserere. Ajunt, perhibent, videtur, inquiunt. Hoc vero est alienis oculis videre & mentis suae clavum aliorum manibus committere. In Psalt. quoque Rom. est porcina, ut & apud Arnob. & Apollinarius in metaphrasi habet ἀπολοῦνται σταλλαῶν. Sed & illam meliorem lectionem, saturabuntur filii non melius explicat Augustus. Filios, inquit, opera intelligimus, Et sicut bona opera bonos filios, ita & malos mala. Hoc ergo vult, sensum eodem redire. Nam malis operibus saturari, quid aliud est, quam immunditia saturari? Adi & Epist. Lix. Augustus quae ad Paulinum. Sed & ista interpretatio, praeterquam quod sine necessitate ex filiis opera faciat, nullo fulcimine nititur. Sic enim legunt Ebraei, saturantur filii. Ita & Symm. Pagn. Arias. Qui ergo legerunt porcinā, videntur in Graeco habuisse * υἱέων, qui porcis, υἱῶν. Respexit proculdubio ad hanc Graecarum vocum paranomasiam Augustus, qui, narrante Macrobio, cum audivisset inter pueros quos in Syria Rex Herodes infra bimatum jusserat interfici, filium quoque ejus occisum, melius esse ajebat, Herodis porcum esse quam filium. Pf. xxxix. 6. ubi Ebraei legunt palmares dedisti dies meos, & Lxx. * παλαιωσεις ἡμέρας μου, Hiero. breves. Vulg. mensurabiles. Vetus Latina, veteres posuisti dies meos. Hic multa habet. Augustinus de veteri & novo, Sed decepit omnes librarius, qui pro παλαιωσεις scripserat παλαιώσεως. Vetustum sphalma, ac proinde non mirum, si longe lateque se diffuderit. Nam & Psalterium Rom. & Arabicum & Aethiopicum & Ambrosium & Appollinarium in partes vocant annotatores ad Biblia. Romana. Prior scriptura, inquiunt, est παλαιὰς, postea additum ς παλαιςὰς. Ergo pro bestiis habent doctissimos istos Interpretes? Nam quæ literarum similitudo est inter טפחות & quamcunque vocem, quæ Ebræis veteres significet? טפה extra controversiam παλαιὰς. Cur ergo dubitamus an ita scripserint? Quemadmodum autem Ebræum טפחות ἐλεεπλικῶς ponitur, pro טפחות ימי dies palmorum id est palmares: ita & παλαιςὰς dixerunt pro ἡμέρας παλαιςῶν id est παλαιςαίας. παλαιςὴ, παλαιςὶς, δοχμὴ δακτυλοδέχμη, synonyma sunt, & significant μίτεον ποσάρων δακτύλων, Δίχημα πτερσδάκτυλον. Quod autem quidam Interpretes, inter quos Symmachus & B. Chrysost. spithamæ meminerint, scire licet palmum vulgo distingui in minorem & majorem. De minore diximus. Major tres minores continet. Sed is Ebr. non טפח sed ורת dicitur, tum alibi tum 1. Sam.17. 4. ubi tamen vulg. palmum reddidit, majorem intelligens. Sed hic rursus vocis Græcæ ambiguitas quibusdam imposuit. Cum enim παλαιςὶς luctatorem quoque significet, nonnulli παλαιςὰς interpretati sunt q.d. παλαιςεχὰς. Chrysost. ἀλλ' δ' ἂν εἴπῃ παλαιςὰς εἰςηθαι τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡμέρας, Δίχ τὸ πεπληρωμένης πάλης καὶ ἀγῶν eo quod pleni sint lucta & agone. Euthym. Ecce laboriosos posuisti dies meos, certaminis ac pugna plenos. Unde in Basil. editione vox ea reddita per pugiles. pugiles posuisti dies meos. Plausibilis interpretatio, sed quam vox Græca hoc loco, quia interpretamentum est Ebræi טפח / plane aspernatur. Ps.xxxi.16. In manibus tuis טתי tempora mea sc. sunt. Lxx. ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ σε οἱ κλῆροί μου. Vulgata, in manibus tuis sunt sortes mea. Hic multa de sortibus apud Interpretes legas. Aug. postquam primo de sorte in genere, deinde de sortitione Apostolorum dixisset, Sortes, inquit, quantum ego existimo, gratiam dixit, qua salvati sumus. Et quare sic vocat gratiam Dei? Quia in sorte non est electio, sed voluntas Dei. Nam ubi dicitur, iste facit, iste non facit, merita considerantur. Et ubi merita considerantur, electio est, non sors. Quando autem Deus nulla merita nostra invenit, sorte voluntatis suæ nos salvos fecit, quia voluit, non quia digni sumus. Hæc est sors. Piget cætera adscribere. Prolixa enim sunt. At genuina sectio erat κλῆροί μου. Hoc agnoscunt Genebr. Bellarm. & alii. Non desunt antiquæ versiones, inquit, Bellar. ex Græco, quæ habeant, tempora mea. Sic certe legitur in officio Missa non semel & in Psalterio Ecclesia S. Petri Romæ. Genebr.
units.tr: Aquila: "with the labours of my hands [κοπῶν πεφῶν σε]" (the Greek is garbled). Symmachus and the fifth edition: "with your hands [χειρῶν σε]". The Septuagint: "the labour of your fruits you shall eat [τὰς πόνος τῶν καρπῶν σε φάγεσαι]". This is excellent, except that it is ambiguous. The Latin, "labores fructuum tuorum comedes" (you shall eat the labours of your fruits), is very poor. This is clear to those who can go to the sources. For what has fruit to do with hands? The Greeks use καρπός not only for fruit but also for the joint of the hand and the wrist [ἀρθρον τῆς χειρὸς καὶ βραχίων], that is, the junction of hand and arm. Hence the compounds περιχάρπιον, μεσοχάρπιον and the like. Hence, by synecdoche, the word signifies the whole hand. The Septuagint use the same word for the palm in 1 Sam. 5: "the palms of his hands [καρποὶ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ] were cut off on the threshold". From comparing the Greek translators, Theodoret could perceive that the Seventy, by that word, understood not the palm but the middle of the hands. The Vulgate translator also did not go astray here. But the Fathers mostly follow the other, worse reading. Beware, therefore, of following Augustine here, sailing with full sails on the sea of allegories. He subtly distinguishes between "the labours of fruits" and "the fruits of labours": "Meanwhile, he says, the labours of fruits; afterwards, the fruit of labour. They shall eat the labours of fruits, who went out and wept, bearing their seeds. How much more joyfully shall they eat the fruits of labours, who shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves?" Ps. 17:14: "יְשַׁבְּעוּ בָנִים [they are satisfied with children]". The Septuagint: "ἐχορτάσθησαν υἱῶν [the sons were satisfied]". Augustine reads "saturati sunt porcinā" [they were filled with swine's flesh], which he explains as: "they were filled with filth, trampling the pearls of God's words." Euthymius reads "saturati sunt porcu[s]" [they were filled with swine], although he explains it somewhat differently: "they were filled with filth, the whole patrimony and all goods having been consumed on various pleasures." Both indicate that some read "swine" (porcina) for "sons", and that the variant arose from the ambiguous Greek, as Augustine says, or as Euthymius says, and better, from the fault of scribes, who confused τὰ υἱῶν and υἱῶν; yet neither dared or was able to assert which reading is genuine and should be kept in the text. "They say, they report, it seems, they say." But this is to see with others' eyes and to commit the helm of one's own mind to other hands. In the Roman Psalter too it is "porcina", as also in Arnobius; and Apollinaris in his paraphrase has "ἀπολοῦνται σταλλαῶν" [they will perish]. But Augustine does not explain the better reading, "saturabuntur filii" [the sons shall be satisfied], any better. "We understand the sons, he says, to be works; and as good works are good sons, so bad works are bad ones." So he means that the sense comes to the same thing. For to be satisfied with evil works is nothing other than to be satisfied with filth. See also Letter 59 of Augustine, to Paulinus. But this interpretation, besides making works out of sons without necessity, rests on no support. For thus the Hebrews read: "saturantur filii" [the sons are satisfied]. So also Symmachus, Pagninus, Arias. Those then who read "porcina" seem to have had in the Greek "*υἱέων", which for "swine" is "υἱῶν". Doubtless Augustine had regard to this paronomasia of the Greek words, who, as Macrobius reports, when he heard that among the boys whom King Herod in Syria had ordered to be killed, under two years old, his own son had also been slain, said that it was better to be Herod's swine than his son. Ps. 39:6, where the Hebrews read "palmares dedisti dies meos" [you have given my days as palms, i.e. handbreadths], and the Septuagint "*παλαιωσεις ἡμέρας μου" [you have made old my days], Jerome "breves" [brief], the Vulgate "mensurabiles" [measurable], the Old Latin "veteres posuisti dies meos" [you have made my days old]. Here there is much to say. Augustine writes about the old and the new. But one scribe deceived everyone, who had written "παλαιωσεως" for "παλαιωσεις". This is an ancient error, and so it is not surprising if it has spread far and wide. For the Roman Psalter, the Arabic and Ethiopic, Ambrose and Apollinaris, the annotators to the Bibles call it a variant. The Roman: "The earlier writing, they say, is παλαιὰς, afterwards there was added a ς, making παλαιςὰς." Do they then take these most learned translators for beasts? For what similarity of letters is there between טפחות and whatever word signifies old to the Hebrews? טפה is beyond dispute παλαιὰς. Why then do we doubt whether they so wrote? But just as the Hebrew טפחות is put elliptically for טפחות ימי, the days of palms, that is, palmares, so they also said παλαιςὰς for ἡμέρας παλαιςῶν, that is παλαιςαίας. παλαιςὴ, παλαιςὶς, δοχμὴ, δακτυλοδέχμη are synonyms and signify the measure of four fingers, a span of four fingers. But that some translators, among whom are Symmachus and Chrysostom, mention the span, we should know that the palm is commonly distinguished into lesser and greater. Of the lesser we have spoken. The greater contains three lesser. But this is called in Hebrew not טפח but ורת, both elsewhere and in 1 Sam. 17:4, where, however, the Vulgate rendered it "palm", understanding the greater. But here again the ambiguity of the Greek word has deceived some. For since παλαιςὶς also signifies a wrestler, some translated παλαιςὰς as if it were παλαιςεχὰς [wrestlers]. Chrysostom: "But if anyone says that the days of men are called παλαιςὰς, this is because they are full of wrestling and struggle" [πεπληρωμένης πάλης καὶ ἀγῶν], because they are full of wrestling and contest. Euthymius: "Behold, you have made my days laborious, full of struggle and battle." Whence in the Basel edition the word is rendered by "pugiles" [wrestlers]: "you have made my days wrestlers." It is a plausible interpretation, but the Greek word plainly rejects it in this place, because it is an interpretation of the Hebrew טפח. Ps. 31:16: "In your hands טתי [are] my times", that is, they are. The Septuagint: "ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ σου οἱ κλῆροί μου [in your hands are my lots]." The Vulgate: "in manibus tuis sunt sortes meae" [in your hands are my lots]. Here you may read much about lots among the interpreters. Augustine, having first spoken of lot in general and then of the casting of lots of the Apostles, said: "Lots, as far as I judge, he called the grace by which we are saved. And why does he so call God's grace? Because in a lot there is no choice, but the will of God. For where it is said, this one does, this one does not, merits are considered. And where merits are considered, there is choice, not lot. But when God finds none of our merits, he has saved us by the lot of his will, because he willed to, not because we are worthy. This is the lot." It irks me to add the rest; for it is long. But the genuine reading was "κλῆροί μου" [my lots]. Genebrardus, Bellarmine and others acknowledge this. "There are not lacking, Bellarmine says, ancient versions made from the Greek which have 'tempora mea' [my times]. Thus it is certainly read in the office of the Mass more than once, and in the Psalter of the Church of St Peter at Rome." Genebrardus...

units.la: Ps.xxxi.16.

Levin. In uwe handen zijn mijn avontuyren. nebr. Psalterium Ebr. & Romanum & forte 70. pro xλῆροι habebant κκιροι. Pf. XLIV. 13. לא רבית בםחיריהם non multiplicasti (auxisti, subaudi rem) pretiis eorum. nulla enim tibi dederunt. Est ergo in antecedentibus catachresis vocis vendendi, cui similis illa emendi, Jesa. LV. 1. Emite absque pecunia. Lxx. reddiderunt, ἀχ̓ην ἀλλάγματ (Theodotio, ἀλεόνασμα.) ἐν τῆς ἀλλάγματιν αὐτ̓. quod vulg. convertit, non fuit multitudo (scil pretii, non auxisti rem legerunt רביית) in commutationibus eorum: hoc est, in alienatione & venditione. In venditione enim commutantur merces & & pretia. Ita legunt & exponunt Hiero. Ambros. Chrysost. & Theodoretus. Quid ergo visum Augustino, locum ita citanti? Et non fuit multitudo in jubilationibus eorum. quod ita porro exponit, ut, queratur Psaltes, persecutionis tempore non remansisse multos in Ecclesia, qui Domino in officiis divinis celebrandis jubilarent. Scilicet Græci codices jam olim hic pro ἀλλάγματ legerunt ἀλαλάγματ, quam mendosam lectionem expressit & Editio Wecheliana, & Complutensis. Lectionis istius & Euthymius meminit, & de vociferationibus hostium & clamore bellico exponit. Qui Hebræa legere didicit, videt quam alienæ ab Hebræa veritate istæ expositiones sint. Cæterum quid proprie sit ἀλαλά-ζειν & ἀλαλαγμὸς, docet Hilarius ad Pf. LXV. 1. Ἀλαλαγμὸς, quem Latine Jubilum ponunt, significat vocem exercitus præliantis, aut in concursu proterentis hostem, aut successum victoriæ exultationis voce testantis. Vide sequentia, & Bezam in appendice ad Marc. v. 38. Pf. XCII. 11. senectus mea in misericordia uberi. Ita vulg. At Ebr. בשמן רענן / Lxx. ἐν ἐλαίῳ πιότι. oleo pingui. Non dubium quin vulg. legerit ἐλαίῳ. Nec refragantur Bellar. & Genebr. Noster interpres, inquit, Bellar. videtur legisse, ἐν ἐλαίῳ. Pf. CXIX. 28. stillavit anima mea præ dolore. Vulgata Latina. & August. dormitavit anima mea præ tædio. At quid commune est dormitationi cum stillatione? Lxx. scripserant, ἔσταξε, distillavit atque ita legerunt & Ambrosius & Origenes: at imperita manus illud in ἐνύσταξε deformavit. Non est improbabile, inquit Bellarm. Lxx. vertisse ἐσταξε, & postea errore librariorum factum esse ἐνύσταξε. Certe S. Ambros. utriusque lectionis meminit. In Hebræa autem nulla literarum similitudo est inter destillavit & dormitavit. Hæc ille; quem si roges, cur ergo locum istum non correxerint, non aliud responsum feres, quam illud Lucæ Brug. Romani correctores non censuerunt locum esse corrigendum. Ibidem litera Num, Anima mea בכפי in manibus meis semper. Hanc locutionem expositumus supra pag. 422. Kimchi, אני בכפניו חמיר versor assidue in periculo. Quod enim in manus superficie gestatur, vel lapsui vel direptioni expositum est. Lxx. ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν τῇ χειρί μου ἀλλοτρίως Atque ita legit vulg. Librarii cum phrasin illam non intelligerent, τὰ μάσ in σῶ mutarunt. At itain omnibus, quos ego quidem inspexi, codicibus legitur. Ita legerunt August. Ambros. Hilar. Ita Psalt. Romanum. Ita Apollinarius,
units.tr: Leuven (Dutch gloss). "In your hands are my adventures." Genebrardus. The Hebrew Psalter, the Roman Psalter and perhaps the Seventy had "κκιροι" [kkiroi] where the Greek is "κλῆροι" [klēroi]. Ps. 44:13: "לא רבית במחיריהם" [you did not multiply them by their prices], that is, you did not increase the stock by their price, for they gave you nothing. There is therefore in the preceding words a catachresis of the verb "to sell", like the verb "to buy" in Isa. 55:1: "Buy without money [ἀγοράσατε ἄνευ ἀργυρίου]." The Septuagint rendered it "without exchange [ἄνευ ἀλλάγματος]" (Theodotion, "ἀλεόνασμα"): "in their exchanges [ἐν τῇ ἀλλάγματι αὐτῶν]", which the Vulgate rendered "there was no multitude (of price, not 'you did not increase the stock', as they read רביית) in their exchanges", that is, in alienation and sale. For in sale goods and prices are exchanged. So Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom and Theodoret read and explain it. What then seemed good to Augustine, quoting the passage thus: "and there was no multitude in their jubilations"? He then explains it so that, the psalmist complains, in the time of persecution, there remained few in the Church who would shout jubilation to the Lord in celebrating divine offices. Clearly the Greek manuscripts had long ago read "ἀλαλάγματ" [shoutings] for "ἀλλάγματ" [exchanges]; this faulty reading was reproduced by both the Wechelian and the Complutensian editions. Euthymius also mentions this reading and explains it of the shouting of enemies and battle-cry. Whoever has learned to read Hebrew sees how remote these explanations are from the Hebrew truth. Moreover, what "ἀλαλάζειν" and "ἀλαλαγμός" properly mean, Hilary teaches at Ps. 65:1: "ἀλαλαγμός" [which they render in Latin as jubilation] "signifies the voice of an army fighting, either in the clash trampling down the enemy, or testifying by a voice of exultation to the success of victory." See what follows, and Beza in the appendix to Mark 5:38. Ps. 92:11: "my old age in rich mercy", so the Vulgate. But the Hebrew reads בשמן רענן [with fresh oil], and the Septuagint "ἐν ἐλαίῳ πιότι" [in rich oil]. There is no doubt that the Vulgate read "ἐλαίῳ" [oil]. Nor do Bellarmine and Genebrardus deny it. "Our translator," Bellarmine says, "seems to have read 'ἐν ἐλαίῳ'." Ps. 119:28: "my soul dropped for sorrow" [stillavit anima mea præ dolore], the Latin Vulgate and Augustine: "my soul slumbered for weariness" [dormitavit anima mea præ tædio]. But what has slumbering in common with dropping? The Seventy had written "ἔσταξε" [dropped], and so read both Ambrose and Origen; but an unskilled hand deformed it into "ἐνύσταξε" [slumbered]. "It is not improbable," Bellarmine says, "that the Seventy translated 'ἔσταξε', and afterwards by the error of copyists 'ἐνύσταξε' came about." Certainly St Ambrose mentions both readings. But in the Hebrew there is no similarity of letters between "dropped" and "slumbered." So he says; and if you ask him why then they did not correct this passage, you will get no other answer than that of Luke Brugensis: the Roman correctors did not think the place should be corrected. In the same passage, the letter Nun: "my soul" בכפי [in my hands continually]. We explained this expression above, p. 422. Kimchi: "I dwell constantly in danger", for what is carried on the surface of the hand is exposed to slipping or plunder. The Septuagint: "ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν τῇ χειρί μου ἀλλοτρίως" [my soul is in my hand strangely]. And so the Vulgate reads. Since the copyists did not understand that phrase, they changed "τὰ μάσ" into "σῶ".
