But thus it is read in all the manuscripts I have examined. So read Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary. So the Roman Psalter. So Apollinaris,

units.la: ἡ ἐτοῦ ἐμοὶ σαλάμχη διαπέμψας σίτιν ἴχω.
units.tr: [Garbled Greek in the scan; it cannot be reliably translated.]

units.la: Ita & Theodoretus, Euthymius, Cassiodorus & alii. Augustino tamen & Ambrosio de meliori lectione suboluit. Quidam codices habent, inquit, in manibus meis, plures, tuis. Et hoc quidem planum est. Justorum enim anima sunt in manu Dei. Anima vero in manibus meis, quomodo intelligatur, ignoro. Quod ignoravit Augustinus, explicuit Hieronymus, inquit Genebr. qui & illud subjungit, Nempe multa ignorantur a linguarum imperitis, quae periti liquido intelligunt. Ps. cxxxii. 15. Benedicendo benedicam צידה / Pagn. Arias, esca ejus. Lxx. quod Latinus interpres reddit, venationi ejus. Sed ut טרף raptum, ita & צי (per synecdochen) quemlibet cibum significat. Hinc teste Hiero. caeteri Interpretes Graeci uno ore ἐπιστομον id est cibaria, vel πτωχία interpretati sunt Vulgatae Latinae author, August. Prosper, Ambros. Cassiodorus Apollinarius, Hilar. & alii legunt, viduam ejus benedices. Ita & Psalterium Romanum & Gallicum. B. Calvinus in comm. existimabat, primitus scriptum fuisse vidum, hinc vidum, hinc denique viduam factum. Hanc conjecturam Bellarm. calumniam vocat, nescius eandem Melchioris Cani esse de locis Theol. 2. 15. Lubens tamen dederim, hujus lectionis originem altius petendam esse. nonnulli codices Graeci, qualibus S. quoque Chrysostomus usus est, legerunt χήρον, uti contra Psal. 89. pro χρόνω legebant Θρόνω. Genebr. Graeci Ἀξιον. Sed nostrer, inconsulta veritate Ebraica, legit χήρων, quia mox sequebantur pauperes. Utrosque enim solet Scriptura conjungere. Quicquid ergo hic differt Augustinus de viduis, quicquid superstruit isti assertioni, universam Ecclesiam esse unam viduam, quicquid denique hic porro ἀπληγαγοῦ, non alio fundamento, quam
units.tr: So also Theodoret, Euthymius, Cassiodorus and others. Augustine and Ambrose, however, arrived at the better reading. Some manuscripts, he says, have "in my hands," most have "in your hands." And this indeed is plain, for the souls of the just are in the hand of God. But how "my soul is in my hands" is to be understood, I do not know. What Augustine did not know, Jerome explained, says Genebrardus, who adds: Of course, many things are unknown to those unskilled in languages which skilled scholars understand clearly. Ps. 132:15, I will abundantly bless her provision [צידה]. Pagninus and Arias: her food. The Seventy: what the Latin translator renders her hunting [θήρα]. But just as טרף means prey, so צי (by synecdoche) means any food whatever. Hence, according to Jerome, the other Greek interpreters with one voice rendered it provisions [ἐπιστόμιον], that is, victuals, or poverty [πτωχία]. The author of the Vulgate Latin, Augustine, Prosper, Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Apollinaris, Hilary and others read I will bless her widow. So also the Roman and Gallican Psalter. Calvin in his commentary thought that the original reading had been vidum [a widower], then vidum was changed, and finally viduam. Bellarmine calls this conjecture a slander, not knowing that it is the same as Melchior Cano's in his Loci Theologici 2.15. I would gladly grant, however, that the origin of this reading must be sought further back. Some Greek manuscripts, such as St. Chrysostom used, read χήρον [widower], just as in Psalm 89 they read Θρόνω [throne] for χρόνω [time]. Genebrardus: The Greeks have Ἄξιον. But our translator, without consulting the Hebrew truth, read χήρων [widows], because the poor followed immediately. For Scripture usually joins the two. Whatever Augustine here says about widows, whatever he builds on this assertion, that the whole Church is one widow, whatever he further deduces here, all rests on no other foundation than the error of an unlearned copyist.

units.la: Augustin. ibidem, An forte ita dictum est, anima mea in manibus meis semper, tanquam eam viviscandam offerret Deo? ut alibi, Ad te levavi animam meam. Ps. cxxxii. 15. quàm indocti descriptoris peccato nititur. Atque hic mirari iubet insignem Pontificiorum pertinaciam, cujus patronum agit Bellar. Verum quidem est, inquit, in Ebraeo non haberi viduam, sed viätum, neque ullam esse similitudinem literarum, ob quam suspicari quis posset, illos scripsisse, * viduam: sed in Graeco idiomate magna similitudo literarum est inter χήρευν & ʒήρευν. Igitur vel in Ebraeo mutatus est textus (serione an joco Bellarmine?) vel in Graeco textu facta est corruptio, vitio scriptorum, quia unam literam legerant pro alia. Hoc erat. Cur ergo hoc sphalma non sustulistis? Cur Lovanienses in sua versione illud retinuere? Quia usus obtinuit, inquit Bell. ut legeretur vidua, non est ullo modo mutanda, cum à veneranda antiquitate ortum habuerit. Ab antiqua inscitia dixisses verius. Alia mens Cano fuit, qui postquam de hoc loco egisset, ista subjungit, Hujusmodi menda gravi ratione & prudenti consilio corrigi possunt. Si quicquid usu & longa annorum serie obtinuit, mutare nefas est, ne venerandae antiquitati convitium fiat, cur ergo correctores Romani, quorum tu quoque Bellarmine, pars magna fuisti, tot inveterata sphalmata sublatum ivēre? Si tam pervicaces sunt in corrigendis istis minutulis, de queis inter omnes constat, quid circa majorum correctionem ab ista sede expectandum est? Illud excideraz. in Edit. Basileensi pro ʒήρευν legi ʒυγεῦν, portam Joel. 1. 17. נשמו אוצרות rastati sunt thesauri. Non est dubium, quin Lxx. verterint ἠφανίσθησαν θησαυροί. At in Aldinis legitur σαυροί, quod interpretantur, vastati sunt lacerti. In Basileensibus anni 1550. & 1572. ταυροί, quod Latinus interpres reddidit, vastati sunt tauri. Non dubitavit de hujus lectionis veritate corrector, quia praecesserant δαμάλεις, vitula. At pro ea quoque in Ebraeo est פרורות grana. computruerunt grana sub glebis, Jet. 3. 13. נצב לריב יהוה stat ad litigandum DOMINUS. Lutherus, Aber der HERR stehet da * zur rechten Belgicus interpres, mendoisto deceptus, de HEERE staet daer ter rechterhand, Non minus foedum lapsum ad Job xi. deteximus, Vide supra pag. 421. Exodi 38. 8. במראות ex speculis mulierum, &c. Speculum ita dictum à ראה video, quod priscis erat specio. In marginalibus annotationibus ad Biblia Belgica, queis Nicolaus Bieftkens nomen dedit, ex Castalione citatur haec versio; van der vrouwen wacht-toornen, quasi illud speculis esset à singulari recto specula. Adeo periculosae plenum opus aleae est.
units.tr: Augustine, in the same place: Is it perhaps said, "my soul in my hands always," as though he offered it to God to be made alive? As elsewhere: "To you I lifted up my soul" (Ps. 132:15). Such is the sin of an unlearned copyist. Here he bids us marvel at the notable obstinacy of the Papists, whose champion is Bellarmine. It is true, he says, that in the Hebrew there is not "widow" but "provision," nor is there any similarity of letters by which one could suspect that they wrote "widow." But in the Greek idiom there is a great similarity of letters between χήρευν and ʒήρευν. So either the text was changed in Hebrew (in earnest or in jest, Bellarmine?) or in the Greek text a corruption was made by the fault of scribes, who had read one letter for another. So he said. Why then have you not removed this slip? Why did the Louvain editors keep it in their version? Because usage has prevailed, says Bellarmine, that "widow" be read; it must in no way be changed, since it has its origin in venerable antiquity. You would more truly say it originated in ancient ignorance. Cano had a different mind; after discussing this passage he adds: Errors of this kind can be corrected with sound reason and prudent counsel. If whatever has prevailed by use and a long succession of years must not be changed, lest an insult be offered to venerable antiquity, why then have the Roman correctors, of whom you too, Bellarmine, were a large part, removed so many inveterate slips? If they are so obstinate in correcting these trifles, about which everyone agrees, what can be expected from that see concerning the correction of greater matters? I had forgotten this: in the Basel edition, for ʒήρευν was read ʒυγεῦν, a mistake in Joel 1:17. שמו אוצרות [they have laid waste the storehouses]. There is no doubt that the Seventy rendered it ἠφανίσθησαν θησαυροί [the treasures have vanished]. But in the Aldine edition is read σαυροί, which they interpret as the lizards are laid waste. In the Basel editions of 1550 and 1572, ταυροί [bulls], which the Latin translator rendered the bulls are laid waste. The corrector did not doubt the truth of this reading, because δαμάλεις [heifers] had preceded. But in place of that, in the Hebrew there is also פרורות [the grains]: the grains have rotted under the clods, Joel 1:13. נצב לריב יהוה [the LORD stands to contend]. Luther: But the LORD stands there * at the right hand. The Belgic translator, deceived by a slip, de HEERE staet daer ter rechterhand. No less foul a lapse have we detected at Job 11; see above, p. 421. Exodus 38:8, במראות [from the mirrors of the women, etc.]. The mirror is so called from ראה [to see], which to the ancients was specio. In the marginal notes to the Belgic Bible, of which Nicolaus Biestkens was the author, this version is cited from Castalio: van der vrouwen wacht-toornen [the women's watch-towers], as though speculis were from a singular nominative specula. So perilous a task is full of hazards.

units.la: * אלמנה Hebraicum vocabulum viduam significat. est, versionem ex versione adornare. Ad singulos versus imo & voces consulendi fontes sunt. Hujus quoque loci est ce-lebris ille locus Joh. xxi. Si eum volo manere. Græce, τὰν. At una literula C addita, unde nata hæc lectio, sic eum volo manere, quam portentosas expositiones Interpretibus extorsit! Sed de hoc loco dicemus prolixius suo loco. Et jam opinor, illud probavi, ne ipsas quidem versiones tuto & utiliter ab erudito viro semper legi posse, nisi aliqua originalium linguarum peritia instructus sit. Desino itaque, & te, nobilium juvenum doctissime, summo isti Numini commendo, penes quod potestas est
units.tr: * אלמנה, the Hebrew word, means widow. It is to make one version out of another. For each verse, indeed for each word, the sources must be consulted. This is also the place of that famous passage John 21: If I want him to remain. In Greek, τὰν. But with one little letter, C, added, from which this reading arose, thus I want him to remain: what monstrous explanations have been wrung out of the interpreters! But we will speak of this passage at more length in its place. And now I think I have proved that even the versions themselves cannot always be read safely and profitably by a learned man unless he is instructed in some knowledge of the original languages. I therefore make an end, and commend you, most learned of noble youths, to that supreme Divinity, in whose power it lies

units.la: Tuique misque & omnium mortalium.
units.tr: and yours, and of all mortals.

units.la: Ps. CXI 2. Magna sunt opera Domini, exquisita in omnes voluntates ejus.] Iterum posui verba vulgati, quæ exstant Græcis tralata sunt, μεγάλα τὰ ἔργα κυρίου, ἐξεζητημένα εἰς πάντα θελήματα αὐτοῦ. Hunc locum allegat Magister Sententiarum lib. 1. Dist. xlv. lit. G. Lubet autem hic adscribere censuram eruditissimi Theologi L. Danæi. Sic ergo ille, Super malo fundamento struit malam molem iste. Perperam enim ille Ps. cxi. 2. locus convertitur. Cum ex Hebræa veritate sit vertendus, magna opera Jehovæ, expositi omnibus qui delectantur istis. Ergo quod isti ex hoc loco colligunt, plures esse Dei voluntatis (quam voluntatem signi vocant) species, quoniam in Psalmo illo numero plurali voluntates leguntur, inane est & falsum fundamentum. Et tamen hoc est unicum & hujus, & Thomæ parte prima. quæst. 19. articulo 11. argumentum. Una est igitur voluntas signi, sed illius proponendæ multæ tamen sunt formæ, phrases & rationes. Atque eæ etiam duntaxat nostri ratione, externæ & ad ipsam Dei voluntatem accidentales. Ebræa si quis requirat, ista sunt, גדולים מעשי יהוה דרושים לכל הפציהם / Pagni. Arias, omnibus volentibus ea vid. indicem.
units.tr: Ps. 111:2, Great are the works of the Lord, sought out for all his wills. I have again set down the words of the Vulgate, which are found translated from the Greek: μεγάλα τὰ ἔργα κυρίου, ἐξεζητημένα εἰς πάντα θελήματα αὐτοῦ. The Master of the Sentences cites this passage in book 1, distinction 45, letter G. It is worth setting down here the judgment of the most learned theologian L. Danaeus. Thus he: Upon a bad foundation this man builds a bad structure. For that passage of Ps. 111:2 is wrongly turned. Since it must be rendered from the Hebrew truth, great are the works of Jehovah, exposed to all who delight in them. Therefore what they gather from this passage, that there are several kinds of the will of God (which they call the will of sign), since in that Psalm the plural number wills is read, is an empty and false foundation. And yet this is the sole and chief argument both of this man and of Thomas, Part I, question 19, article 11. There is therefore one will of sign, but the forms, phrases and reasons of proposing it are many. And these too are only in our manner of speaking, external and accidental to the will of God itself. If anyone asks for the Hebrew, it is: גדולים מעשי יהוה דרושים לכל חפציהם [great are the works of the LORD, sought out by all who delight in them]; Pagninus and Arias: for all who desire them; see the index.

units.la: Ps. CXVIII. 27. Ornate festum frondibus.] Ita Lutherus. Et citari hoc modo crebro pro concione solet in festo Pentecostes. De quo loco erudite disseruit cl. vir; Joh. Tarnovius, in Exercit. Bibl. Edit. 1. pag. 114. Edit. 3. p. 379.
units.tr: Ps. 118:27, Bind the feast with boughs. So Luther. And this passage is often cited in this way for a sermon on the feast of Pentecost. On this passage the learned man Johann Tarnovius has disputed well in his Exercitationes Biblicae, first edition p. 114, third edition p. 379.

units.la: Pf. CXIX. 109. Anima mea in manibus meis ] vide supra pag. 663. & 873.
units.tr: Ps. 119:109, My soul is in my hands. See above, pp. 663 and 873.

units.la: Verf. 112. propter retributionem. ] Ita vulg. ex Lxx. di avτα'μαψιν. Hunc locum producit Cardinalis Bellarm. probandæ isti sententiæ, bona opera mercedem proprie dictam mereri, & ejus gratia debere quoque suscipi. Carthus. hic quærit, cum propter mercedem operari sit opus mercenarii, non filii aut amici, quomodo dicat David, se propter retributionem inclinasse cor suum, &c.. Sed observa, tiro, in Ebraeo esse עקב / inclinavi cor meum ad faciendum statuta tua in perpetuum, עקב / Pagn. usque in finem. Arias, calcem. Eandem vocem vulgatus interpres hoc ipso Psal. verf. 33. reddidit, semper, Lxx. αἰφντος. Ubi tamen Pagn. (mirare lector) propter mercedem, Arias mercede. At illic (verf. 112.) probabiliorem istam versionem fecisset praecedens illud לעולם / Confer & expende. Vox Ebraea proprie calcaneum significat. Cum vero calcaneus sit extremum corporis humani & quasi finis, nata est altera significatio, finis autem. Positum ergo עקב pro לעקב / in finem, Chald. verf. 33. reddidit עד נמירא ad consummationem scil. vitæ meæ. hic vero, עד סופא usque ad finem Lxx. εἰς τέλος. Kimchi כל־ימי omnibus diebus meis. Cum ergo ista significatio optime hic quadret, atque adeo ipsi Interpreti verf. 33. probata, quid opus est ad alia hic delabi? Fateor equidem, עקב alibi occurre re in significatione mercedis, sic dictæ b.) quod in fine operis persolvi solet, Pf. 19. in observatione eorum est עקב merces magna. ἀντιμισθοσις, [quomodo & אחריות usurpatur Jerem, 29. 10. ut detis vobis אחריתכם ותקותכם mercedem & expectationem id est expectatam mercedem & τέλος 1. Petri 1.9:) Sed ibi vox aliter exponi non poterat. Sed & admissa hoc loco notione eadem non sequitur quod ille pertendebat. Namque etiam gratuita & nullo officio provocata beneficentia χάριτος merces & retributio in S. L. appellatur. Quod Luc. 6. 32. appellatur χάρις; Matth. v. 46. μισθὸς id est merces dicitur. Sic & גמל non semper significat retribuere bene vel male; sed & benefacere vel malefacere simpliciter. Prov. xi. justus גומל retribuit (id est benefacit, Lxx. ἀγαθὸν ποιεῖ) anima sua id est sibi. Genef. 50. 15: & reddendo reddet nobis Joseph omne malum אשר גמלנו אותו Lxx. ἀντεδωκάμεθα αὐτοῖ, quomodo loquitur Apostolus 2. Tim. 4.
units.tr: Verse 112, on account of the reward. So the Vulgate from the Seventy: διὰ ἀνταπόδοσιν. Cardinal Bellarmine produces this passage to prove the view that good works properly merit a reward and ought to be undertaken for its sake. The Carthusian asks here: since to work for reward is the work of a hired man, not of a son or friend, how does David say that he inclined his heart on account of the reward, etc.? But notice, young scholar, that in the Hebrew it is עקב [heel/end]: I have inclined my heart to do your statutes forever, עקב; Pagninus: unto the end; Arias: to the heel. The Vulgate translator rendered the same word in this very Psalm, verse 33, as always, the Seventy ἀεί. Yet there Pagninus (wonder, reader) has on account of the reward, and Arias for reward. But there (verse 112) the preceding word לעולם [forever] would have made that more probable version. Compare and weigh it. The Hebrew word properly means heel. Since the heel is the extremity of the human body and, as it were, its end, a second meaning arose: the end. So עקב is used for לעקב [to the end], which the Chaldee paraphrast in verse 33 rendered עד נמירא, that is, to the completion of my life. Here, however, עד סופא [to the end]; the Seventy εἰς τέλος; Kimchi כל־ימי [all my days]. Since that meaning fits this place perfectly, and indeed is approved by the translator himself at verse 33, why is there need to slip here into other senses? I admit indeed that עקב occurs elsewhere in the sense of reward, so called because it is usually paid at the end of a work, Ps. 19: in keeping them there is עקב, great reward (ἀντιμισθία). [So also אחרית is used at Jeremiah 29:11: to give you your end and your hope, that is, the expected reward and τέλος, 1 Peter 1:9.] But there the word could not be explained otherwise. Yet even if that sense is admitted here, it does not follow what he contends. For even gratuitous beneficence, provoked by no service, is called reward in Holy Scripture [χάριτος]. Luke 6:32 calls it χάρις [grace], and Matthew 5:46 calls it μισθός, that is, reward. So also גמל does not always mean to repay good or evil, but also simply to do good or do evil. Proverbs 11: the just man גומל repays (that is, does good, Lxx. ἀγαθὸν ποιεῖ) his own soul, that is, himself. Genesis 50:15: and repaying, Joseph will repay us all the evil אשר גמלנו אותו [which we did to him]; Lxx. ἀντεδωκάμεθα αὐτοῖ, as the Apostle speaks in 2 Timothy 4.

units.la: Iun. 4. Ἀλέξανδρ⊙ ὁ χαλκεὺς ἐνεδείξατό μοι πολλὰ κακά, ostendit mihi multa mala, quod Ebræus diceret, הָרְאֵנִי רָעוֹת רַבּוֹת
units.tr: Iun. 4. "Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils" [Ἀλέξανδρ⊙ ὁ χαλκεὺς ἐνεδείξατό μοι πολλὰ κακά], that is, "showed me many evils," as the Hebrew has it [הָרְאֵנִי רָעוֹת רַבּוֹת].

units.la: Ps 116. 7. quia Dominus גָּמַל עָלָיִךְ Lxx. ἐπ κύριο⊙ ἱκανωσεν σε. Et Psalm. 13.6. ὡσω τῆς κυρίῳ τῷ ἱκανοποιοῦντι με. Ubi rursus Ebr. est גָּמַל / Ps. cxix. 17. גְּמוֹל עַל עַבְדְּךָ ubi licet Lxx. reddiderint εὐεργετέω & vulg. retribue servo tuo, tamen ipse Genebr. id explicat, benefac, confer beneficium. Verba ejus hæc sunt, Retribuendi verbum etiam de gratuitis usurpatur, nec significat solum beneficium reddere, sed etiam ultro & liberaliter tribuere & beneficiis prævenire.
units.tr: Ps. 116. 7. "because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you" [גָּמַל עָלָיִךְ]; the Septuagint has "the Lord has made you sufficient" [ἐπὶ κύριον ἱκανωσεν σε]. And Ps. 13. 6 (LXX): "I will sing to the Lord who has bestowed on me" [ὡσω τῆς κυρίῳ τῷ ἱκανοποιοῦντι με]. There too the Hebrew is [גָּמַל]. Ps. 119. 17: "deal bountifully with your servant" [גְּמוֹל עַל עַבְדְּךָ]. Although the Septuagint renders this with a word meaning "to do good" and the Vulgate has "repay your servant," Genebrardus himself explains it as "do good, confer a benefit." His words are these: "The verb to repay is also used of free gifts; it does not mean only to return a benefit, but also to give freely and of one's own accord, and to anticipate with kindnesses."

units.la: a.) Kimchi ad vers. 33. Ps. 119. postquam rejecisset interpretationem Aben-Ezræ, qui עֵקֶב pro mercede acceperat, quod vid. eo esset דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַזַ״ל עַל מִנְרָת לְקֹבֶל hoc est secundum viam seu cum inodum de quo dixerunt * Doctores nostri p. m. qui ministrant ea conditione, ut accipiant mercedem, hæc subjiciit לִפְיֵ דְעָתִי כִּי פִּירוּשׁ עֵקֶב סוֹף וְכֵן לְעוֹלָם עֵקֶב וְכֵן וְהוּא יְנוּרְעֵקֶב בְּסוֹף וְלִפְיֵ שֶׁהָעֵקֶב id est mea sic fert sententia, τὸ עֵקֶב exponendum per סוֹף finis, & sic לְעוֹלָם עֵקֶב (vers. 112.) & וְהוּא יִגּוֹר. (Gen. 49.) Quia vid. calcaneus est in extremo & fine corporis, ideo finem seu extremitatem rei עֵקֶב dixere.
units.tr: a.) Kimchi on v. 33 of Ps. 119. After rejecting the interpretation of Aben Ezra, who had taken [עֵקֶב] to mean "reward," Kimchi says that it is in the manner [דֶּרֶךְ] of which our rabbis of blessed memory spoke concerning those who serve on condition of receiving wages [מִנְרָת לְקֹבֶל]. He then adds: "In my judgment [לִפְיֵ דְעָתִי] the meaning of [עֵקֶב] is 'end' [סוֹף], and so in 'for ever' [לְעוֹלָם עֵקֶב] (v. 112), and so in [וְהוּא יִגֹּר] (Gen. 49). Because the heel [עָקֵב] is at the extremity and end of the body, they called the end or extremity of a thing [עֵקֶב]."

units.la: b.) Ibid paulo post, וּגְם הַשָּׂכָר נִקְרָא עֵקֶב בְּעִבּוּר שֶׁהַשָּׂכָר i. etiam merces vocatur עֵקֶב quia merces est finis operis. Adi& comment. ejus ad Ps. xix.
units.tr: b.) A little further on in the same place: "Also the reward is called [עֵקֶב] because the reward is the end of the work" [וּגְם הַשָּׂכָר נִקְרָא עֵקֶב בְּעִבּוּר שֶׁהַשָּׂכָר]. See also his commentary on Ps. 19.

units.la: Vers. 173. Vide humilitatem meam, ] Ita vulgatus ex Lxx. ἰδὲ ταπείνωσίν μου. Thod. Ambros. August. hæc de virtute illa interpretantur, quæ superbiæ opponitur. At Ebr. עָנִי ne quaquam illam expositionem admittit. Ideo Bellar. Genebr. vocem eam per afflictionem & tribulationem exposuere.
units.tr: Vers. 173. "See my humility" [ἰδὲ ταπείνωσίν μου in the LXX]. The Vulgate follows the LXX here. Theodoret, Ambrose and Augustine explain this of that virtue which is opposed to pride. But the Hebrew [עָנִי] by no means admits that interpretation. Therefore Bellarmine and Genebrardus explain the word as affliction and tribulation.

units.la: Pf. CXXVII. 4. filii excussorum.] Ex Lxx. υἱοὶ ἐκπεπαγμένων. Adscribam eruditissimi Hieronymi censuram, qui Epist. 126. ad Marcellam scribens ita infit. Illud quoque de eodem Psalmo interrogare dignata es, qui sint, filii excussorum. Miror te in Hilarii expositione non legisse, Excussorum filios credentium populos interpretari, quod sc. apostolos putaverit eo nomine appellatos, quibus in Euangeliis sit præceptum in quamcunque civitatem introierint, & non fuerint recepti, excutere pulverem
units.tr: Ps. 127. 4. "sons of the shaken out" [υἱοὶ ἐκπεπαγμένων in the LXX]. I shall add the censure of the most learned Jerome, who, writing in Epistle 126 to Marcella, begins thus: "You also deigned to ask about the same Psalm who the sons of the shaken out are. I am surprised that you have not read in Hilary's exposition that he takes the sons of the shaken out to be the peoples of believers, because he thought the apostles were called by that name, to whom the Gospels command that, whatever city they enter and do not receive them, they should shake off the dust of their feet as a testimony against unbelievers."

units.la: * Aboth cap. primo, dictū Antigoni. Ne estote sicut servi qui ministrant principi ea conditione, ut præmium ab eo accipiant. Sed estote, sicut qui ministrat hac conditione ne accipiant præmium & sit timor Dei super vos. verem pedum suorum, in testimonium non credentium. Licet tu argute praecaveris, non posse apostolos sub nomine excussorum intelligi, cum sit aliud excutientium, aliud excussorum. Quia excutientes sunt qui excutiant, excussi vero qui ab aliis excutiantur. Et incongruum esse excussos apostolos accipi, qui magis excutientes debuerint appellari. Haec Hieron. ad quae fortassis aliquis Hilarii fautor responderet, illum τὸ excussorum accepisse non à recto excusso sed excussor deflexum. At inane esse hoc subterfugium ille intelligit, qui Graecum ἐκλελνναγμένων considerabit. Pergit Hieron. Quid igitur faciam? tantum virum & temporibus suis disertissimum reprehendere non audeo, qui & confessionis suae merito, vitae industria, & eloquentiae claritate, ubicunque Romanum nomen est, praedicatur, nisi quod non ejus culpae adscribendum est, quod Ebraei sermonis ignarus fuit. Graecarum quoque literarum quandam aurulam ceperat; sed ab Heliodoro presbytero, quo ille familiariter usus est, ea quae intelligere non poterat, quomodo ab Origene dicta essent, quaerebat. Qui quia in hoc Psalmo commentarium Origenis invenire non potuit, opinionem magis insinuare suam, quam inscitiam voluit confiteri, quam ille sumptam claro sermone disseruit & alienum errorem disertius executus est. Restat igitur ut rursus ad fontem sermonis Ebraei recurramus & videamus, quomodo scriptum sit. Ubi nos habemus, sicut filii excussorum, ibi legitur, לְבְנֵי הָעֲוִירִים quod Aquila, interpretatus est, sicut filii pubertatum, Symm. & Theod. sicut filii juventutis. Sexta, ἀνοντισμένως, quod nos dicere possumus, excussi sensus, &c: Haec Hieronymus. Augustinus quoque admodum hic laborat. I. Filii excussorum ipsi sunt filii apostolorum, (apostoli) excussi sunt de manu Dei, tanquam sagittae, & iverunt longe & totam terram impleverunt.
units.tr: * Aboth, chapter one, the saying of Antigonus: "Do not be like servants who minister to a master on condition of receiving a reward. Rather be like those who minister on condition that they receive no reward, and let the fear of God be upon you." Jerome continues: "Though you argue cleverly that the apostles cannot be understood under the name of the shaken out, since of those who shake out is one thing and of the shaken out is another. Those who shake out are the shakers, and the shaken are those who are shaken out by others. And it is unfitting that the apostles should be called 'shaken out,' when they ought rather to be called shakers. Jerome: What then shall I do? I do not dare to rebuke so great a man, most eloquent in his own time, who is celebrated wherever the Roman name is known for the merit of his confession, the industry of his life and the brilliance of his eloquence. But the fault is not to be ascribed to him that he was ignorant of the Hebrew language. He had also grasped a little of Greek letters; but from the presbyter Heliodorus, whom he used as an intimate, he asked what he could not understand, how things were said by Origen. Because he could not find Origen's commentary on this Psalm, he preferred to insinuate his own opinion rather than confess ignorance; and what he took up he set forth in a clear discourse, and more eloquently carried out another's error. It remains, therefore, that we go back again to the source of the Hebrew text and see how it is written. Where we have as the sons of the shaken out, there is read [לְבְנֵי הָעֲוִירִים], which Aquila translated as the sons of youths; Symmachus and Theodotion, as the sons of youth. The sixth version [ἀνοντισμένως], which we may render shaken senses, and so on." Thus Jerome. Augustine too labours much here. I. "The sons of the shaken out are the apostles themselves; the apostles were shaken out of God's hand like arrows, and went far and filled the whole earth."

units.la: II. Filii excussorum id est apostolorum, qui sic dicti sint ob praeceptum de excutiendo pulvere, &c. ut Hilarius. ad objectionem Hieronymi, tunc potius excutientes dicendos fuisse, commonitus respondet, Qui excutit, aut se excutit aut aliquid aliud. Si aliquid aliud excutiens est, non excussus. Si autem se excutiat, & excutiens est & excussus. — excutiens, quia excutit se; excussus, quia excutitur à se. Queritur ergo quos excusserint Apostoli? Utique se ipsos. à pedibus enim suis pulverem excusserunt. Sed ait aliquis, non se excusserunt, sed pulverem. Hoc plane calumniose dicitur. Duobus enim modis dicimus aliquid quid excuti sive illud quod inde excutitur: sive illud unde excutitur. Nam & excussus est pulvis, dicimus, & excussa est vestis. Quare ergo non dicantur filii excussorum filii apostolorum? Et paulo post aliam expositionem proferens, Dicimus excuti etiam aliquid, ut exeat inde quod absconditum est. Aliter dicimus, excuti vestem, ut excutiant pulverem. Aliter saccum, ut illud, quod intus latebat, appareat & exeat. Ergo intelligo, quantum possum; filios excussorum, fortasse ipsos apostolos dictos filios prophetarum. Propheta enim clausa sacramenta & operta continebant, excussi sunt, ut inde manifestata procederent. Et col. 1485. Excussi sunt prophetae & generati sunt apostoli. Quia ergo, excussis prophetis, generati sunt Apostoli, filii sunt excussorum. De hac autem expositione confidentius sentit col. 1487. visum est nobis, suggerente, quantum credimus, Domino, filios excussorum Apostolos esse, dictos, filios prophetarum. Quia propheta in aenigmatibus locuti sunt & figuris rerum, tanquam mysteriorum involucris, cooperuerunt intellectum, qui intellectus prodire non potuit ad homines, nisi involucra illa excuterentur. Unde dicti illi filii excussorum, qui de prophetis excussis profecerunt. Prolixior fui in citandis Augustini verbis, ut de mente ejus lectori plenius constaret. Omnia illa in fumum abeunt, si textus primigenii facem admoveas.
units.tr: II. "The sons of the shaken out, that is, of the apostles, were so called because of the command to shake off the dust, etc., as Hilary says." Warned by Jerome's objection that they should rather have been called shakers, he replies: "He who shakes out either shakes himself or something else. If he shakes something else, he is not shaken. If he shakes himself, he is both shaker and shaken: a shaker because he shakes himself, shaken because he is shaken out by himself. Whom, then, did the apostles shake out? Surely themselves, for they shook the dust from their feet. But someone will say they did not shake out themselves but the dust. That is plainly a calumnious objection. For we speak in two ways of something being shaken: either that which is shaken out, or that from which it is shaken out. For we say the dust is shaken out, and we say the garment is shaken out. Why, then, should the sons of the shaken out not be called the sons of the apostles?" And shortly after, offering another explanation: "We also say something is shaken so that what was hidden inside comes out. Otherwise we say a garment is shaken so that dust is shaken out, or a sack so that what lay hidden within appears and comes out. So I understand, as far as I can, that the sons of the shaken out were perhaps the apostles, called sons of the prophets. For the prophets contained closed and covered sacraments; they were shaken out so that what was made manifest might proceed from them." And at column 1485: "The prophets were shaken out and the apostles were begotten." Because, therefore, the prophets being shaken out, the apostles were begotten, they are sons of the shaken out. He feels more confident about this exposition at column 1487: "It seemed to us, as the Lord suggests, as we believe, that the apostles are the sons of the shaken out, called sons of the prophets, because the prophets spoke in riddles and figures of things, covering the understanding as with the wrappings of mysteries; and that understanding could not come forth to men unless those wrappings were shaken out. Hence those are called sons of the shaken out who came forth from the shaken prophets." I have been rather lengthy in citing Augustine's words, so that the reader may be more fully assured of his meaning. All those things go up in smoke if you apply the torch of the original text.

units.la: Euthymius per filios excussorum, intelligit filios spirituales fidelium doctorum filios, qui a daemonum captivitate excussi sunt. Sa, filii excussorum id est excussi, expediti, scilicet validi, atque ita conciliat cum Ebraeo, & versione Hieronymi, juventutis id est juvenes. Bellarm. per fil. excussorum intelligit prophetarum & apostolorum, qui tanquam quisquiliae & rejectamenta, e mundo ejecti & expulsi sunt. Genebr. per fil. excussorum simpliciter intelligit filios piorum vexatorum. Quod autem subjungit refutandae nostrorum expositioni (filii juventutis id est in juventute procreati, non aetate exita, quales בני זקנים filii senectutis vocantur Genef. 37.3.) vocem נעורים non juventum sed pueritiam denotare, quae aetus nondum ad procreationem matura est, miror hoc tanto viro potuisse excidere. Ergo, ipso judice, vulgatus interpres Genef. 8. 21. τὸ מנעוריו male vertit, ab adolescentia ejus. Vide supra pag. 402. & Pro.v. 18. latare de uxore נעוריך adolescentia tua & Joel.1.8. propter maritum נעוריה pubertatis suae, & Malach.2.14. inter uxorem נעוריך pubertatis tuae. Quomodo in his locis pueritiam, aetatem procreationi immaturam, signignificabit? <bl>נעורים</bl> ad universam ætatem crescentem se porri-git, & secundum subjectam materiam exponendum est. Vide Druf. observ. 7. 17. ubi illud citatur ex Midras Misle, ad cap.
units.tr: Euthymius understands by the sons of the shaken out the spiritual sons of the faithful teachers, who have been shaken out from the captivity of demons. Sa: the sons of the shaken out, that is, the shaken, freed, namely strong; and so he agrees with the Hebrew and with Jerome's version, of youth, that is, young men. Bellarmine understands by the sons of the shaken out the prophets and apostles, who were cast out and expelled from the world like rubbish and refuse. Genebrardus simply understands the sons of the pious who were harassed. As for what he adds to refute our exposition, sons of youth, that is, begotten in youth, not in advanced age, which are called [בני זקנים] "sons of old age" (Gen. 37. 3), and that the word [נעורים] denotes not youth but childhood, an age not yet ripe for procreation, I am surprised that so great a man could have let this slip. Therefore, by his own judgment, the Vulgate translator wrongly rendered [מנעוריו] at Gen. 8. 21 as "from his youth." See above, p. 402, and Prov. 5. 18: "rejoice in the wife of your youth" [נעוריך]; Joel 1. 8: "for the husband of her youth" [נעוריה]; Mal. 2. 14: "the wife of your youth" [נעוריך]. How would the word signify childhood, an age not yet fit for procreation, in these places? [נעורים] extends to the whole growing age, and must be explained according to the matter it is joined to. See Drusius, Observ. 7. 17, where that is cited from the Midrash Mishle, on chapter

units.la: 1. Ad quotum annum homo dicitur נער ? Meir dicit, ad annum 25. Aquiba ad annum 30. Rabbi ait, ad annum 20. duntaxat.
units.tr: At what age is a man called [נער]? Meir says the twenty-fifth year, Akiba the thirtieth. Rabbi says only up to the twentieth.

units.la: Ps. CXXVIII. 2. labores fructuum tuorum,] Vide supra p. 867. Hieronymus ad hunc quoque locum Hilarium perstringit, quem ait, spiritualem intelligentiam venaturum, longam ingredi disputationem & tanta uti operatione persuadendi, quod volebat intelligi, quanta semper falsitas indiget, ut vera videatur.
units.tr: Ps. 128.2, the labours of your fruits. See above, p. 867. Jerome also takes Hilary to task on this passage. He says that Hilary, hunting for a spiritual meaning, enters into a long discussion and uses such great effort of persuasion to make people understand what he wanted, as much as falsehood always needs in order to appear true.

units.la: Ps. CXXXIII. 3. sicut ros Hermon, qui descendit in montem Sion.] Ita LXX. & vulg. Quomodo ros montis Hermon, qui longe distat à Sion, descendat in montem Sion, variis modis exponunt interpretes. Non lubet hic multa transcribere. observa ὁσὶνδετον, & omnia erunt plana. Sicut ros Hermon [&] qui descendit in montem Sion. vel plenius, & sicut ros qui descendit in montem Sion.
units.tr: Ps. 133.3, as the dew of Hermon, which came down upon the mountain of Sion. So the Septuagint and the Vulgate. Interpreters explain in various ways how the dew of Mount Hermon, which is far from Sion, could come down on Sion. I do not care to transcribe much here. Notice the asyndeton [ἀσύνδετον], and everything will be plain: "as the dew of Hermon, [and] which came down upon the mountain of Sion," or, more fully, "and as the dew which came down upon the mountain of Sion."

units.la: Ps. CXXXIX. 2. Vulg. tu cognovisti sessionem & resurrectionem meam.] Augustt. & Hilarius hunc Psalmum de Christo exponunt. Unde de resurrectione ejus ex mortuis hunc locum interpretati sunt. Magister sententiarum lib. 1. dist. 48. hunc quoque locum adducit probandæ isti thesi, aliàs verissimæ, bonam Dei voluntatem mala hominum voluntate aliquando impleri. Cl. Theologus W. Franzius, non concoquit quomodo hic textus qui generalissimus est & de providentia Dei agit, in paschate magno spiritu & quadrato tactu canatur pro textu plane specifico. Nihil enim in specie de resurrectione Christi dicitur. Per sessionem & resurrectionem (Ebr. קומי surgere meum) ajunt Sa. & Genebr. intelligi omnes actiones. verf. 3. Ubi Ebraea habent, semitam meam & accubitum meum ( רבעי ) circumplexerit. Vulg. reddidit, f. m. & * funiculum meum. Quam vocem multi expositionum variarum funiculi vexarunt. Qui commodissime exponunt, de limite, fine & meta ad quam perventurus esset, capiunt. Aug. limitem reddit. Genebr. conjectat LXX. initio scripsisse κοινον, cubile: aut funiculum pro vita accipiendum, ut apud Latinos filum, quod parcæ dicuntur nere & postea præscindere. Sed quid hoc ad Ebræum רבץ quod ipse quoque Hieron. & Pagn. & Arias accubitum reddunt. Hoc vult, inquit Sa, sive ambulem, sive accumbam. Nec refragantur Genebr. & Bel-larm. larm. verf. 4. Cum nullus est sermo in lingua mea, en O DOMI-NE nosti ipsum totum. q d. cum nondum est sermo, tu nosti quid dicturus sim. Vel, etiam cum taceo, tu omnia nosti. Elegantem sententiam defloravit Interpres Græcus, qui membra illa discerpsit, —qaia non est sermo in lingua mea. Ecce Domine tu cognovisti, &c. Accessit imperita manus, quæ πα λόγος in δόλῳ demutavit, quomodo & August. legit, non est dolus in lingua mea. Ubi rursus sudatur. verf. 6. [?] / mirabilis est scientiâ (hæc vid. scientia tua qua omnia nosti) pra me. magis mirabilis quam ut eam possim assequi. Hæc est ipsissima Prophetæ mens. Nam in versu præcedenti de formatione corporis humani non agitur, ut de istius scientia locus hic intelligi non possit. Et, ubi in vulg. est, tu formasti me, Ebræus codex habet, [?] quod reddi potest, obsedisti me, sequitur, posuisti super me manum tuam. Hoc vult, tu undequaque me quasi circumtenes, sicuti versibus seq. explicatur. Vulgatus, Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me. Bellarm. Sa, & alii agnoscunt, ex me positum, pro, pra me. Ruunt ergo istæ interpretationes, quas invenies apud Carthuf. Alphonsum de Castro, titulo anima, in initio, & alios. Verf. 15. [?] in inferioribus terra, i. in utero matris meæ. Atque ita exponunt nonnulli locum Ephes. iv. 9. Ubi Christus discendisse dicitur εἰς καλώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς. Non dicit δ κόσμος, sed γῆς. ut plane videantur hæc loca invicem illustrare. ut non opus sit limbum fabricari. Verf. [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] Ad verbum, Et mihi quam pretiosæ sunt cogitationes tuæ! quàm in- valuerunt, (numero. Vide supra p. 770.) capita (summæ, κεφάλαια) earum [si] velim numerare eas, præ arena multiplicabuntur. vel, numerarem eas, [sed] arena plures sunt. Hæc est ipsissima Psalmographi mens quam & Pagn. & Arias expresse. Lxx. ab ea toto ferre cœlo aberrarunt, ἐμοὶ δὲ λίαν ἐτιμήθησαν οἱ φίλοι σου, ὁ Ἰσὸς λίαν ἐκεφαλαιώθησαν αἱ ἀρχαὶ αὐτῶν. Ἐξαριθμήσομαι αὐτὰς, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἄμμον ἐπληθυνθήσονται. Quæ vulg. sic convertit, Mihi autem nimis honorificati sunt amici tui, Deus: nimis confortatus est principatus eorum. Dinumerabo eos, & super arenam multiplicabuntur. Diversitas oritur potissimum ex duabus istis vocibus עָיִר & רֵאשֵׁיהֶם / Priorem vocem eo audentius nostri per cogitationes reddidere, quia hoc eodem Ps. verf. 2. eandem vocem Lxx. Ἀλογισμὸς, Vulg. cogitationes reddidit. Alteram illam pro κεφαλαίῳ saepe in Bibliis occurrere, quis tam impudens, ut negare ausit. Hinc alius interpres Graecus verba illa sic interpretatus est, π πολυπληθὴς καὶ κεφαλαὶ αὐτῶν; hoc est, quam multa sunt capita eorum? Ubi ראש principem significet vel praestantissimum quid in re aliqua, loca novi plurima. At ubi principatum significet, non invenio ullum. Ex hoc tamen loco, Costerus in Enchirid. cap. 12. Eckius in Ench. cap. 15. Alfonsus à Castro libro contra haereses, probant, Sanctos in coelo colendos. Cotonus ex eodem probat. mundum hunc ab illis administrari. Verùm si hic de religiosa adoratione sanctorum defunctorum ageretur, quae esset cum praecedentibus cohaerentia? In illis enim infinitam Dei providentiam laudare voluit quae in eo potissimum elucet, quod nihil tam sit absconditum, quod ille non perfectissime rimetur. Adhaec quomodo probabunt יקר esse honorificari, & hoc rursus esse, religiose coli? Quomodo probabunt per amicos intelligendos esse sanctos defunctos? Nam vivos religiose colendos esse, non asserent opinor illi. Et defunctos suo modo colendos esse, non negamus nos. Porro, cum Bellarm. lib. 1. de beatit. Sanctorum cap. 19. diserte pronuntiet, Sanctos in Vet. T. non intrasse caelum, nec Deum vidisse, nec cognoscere potuisse ordinarie preces supplicantium, ac proinde non fuisse consuetum in V. Test. ut diceretur, Sancte Abraham ora pro me, &c. sed homines illius temporis solum orasse Deum & allegasse merita Sanctorum, quomodo, salva illa doctissimi Cardinalis sententia, ex his & id genus aliis Scripturae locis; sanctorum in V. T. invocationem probare possunt Pontificii? Quod autem Bellarm. hic ait, allegata fuisse merita Sanctorum, ut illis orationes vivorum juvarentur, frustra probat ex ejusmodi locis, ex. gr. Ex. 32. recordare, Domine, Abrahami, Isaaci & Israelis servi tui. Namque in talibus nullum a defunctorum meritis imploratur auxilium, sed solum memoratur pactum, quod Deus cum patribus de protegendis eorum posteris pepigerat. Sed replicat Bellarm. illam responsionem Calvini non satisfacere, pactum & merita saepe conjungi. ex. gr. Psal. 132. (ipsi 131.) Memento Davidis & omnis mansuetudinis ejus. Ubi rursus impingit disputator. Neque etiam ipse ignorare potuit, in Ebraeo esse עניו quae vox non mansuetudinem ejus, sed, affligi ejus significat. In commentario, postquam dixisset Salomonem his verbis Deum orare per merita patris sui David, postea subjicit, B. Hieronymum ex Ebraeo vertisse, omnis afflictionis ejus. Sed vox ea, inquit, aliis punctis legi potest יְנִיחוּ mansuetudinis. Ergo indifferens, ipso fatente, ad utramque lectionem vox Ebraea est, quando punctis caret. An ergo ex talibus locis firma nectuntur argumenta? Sed plures opponam Bellarmino interpretes, qui tunc quoque cum puncta nondum adscripta erant, ita legerunt, ut Hieron. & hodierni codices. Ecce n. Chald. reddit מְעוֹפָה / afflictionis ejus. Aquila, κακωχίας Symm. κακώσεως, v. Editio ταπεινώσεως. Sed redeamus ad locum Psalm. 139.
units.tr: Ps. 139.2, Vulgate: *you have known my sitting and my rising.* Augustine and Hilary explain this Psalm of Christ, and so they have interpreted this place of his resurrection from the dead. The Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 48, also cites this passage to prove that thesis, otherwise most true, that the good will of God is sometimes fulfilled by the evil will of men. The learned theologian W. Franzius cannot stomach how this text, which is entirely general and deals with the providence of God, is sung at Easter with great fervour and a rigid application, as if it were a wholly specific text. For nothing specifically about Christ's resurrection is said. Sá and Genebrard say that by "sitting and rising" (Hebrew *qumi*, my rising) all actions are understood. In verse 3, where the Hebrew has "my path and my lying down" (*ribbi*) "he has encircled," the Vulgate rendered "my cord" (*funiculum*). Many interpreters have tormented this word in various ways. Those who explain it most suitably take it to mean the boundary, end and goal to which one would arrive. Augustine renders it "limit." Genebrard conjectures that the Seventy originally wrote *koinon*, bed, or that "cord" should be taken for life, as among the Latins the thread which the Fates are said to spin and afterwards cut. But what has this to do with the Hebrew *ribats*, which Jerome himself, Pagninus and Arias render as "lying down"? Sá says this means whether I walk or recline. Genebrard and Bellarmine do not object. Verse 4: *Since there is no speech on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it all.* That is, "while there is not yet speech, you know what I am going to say," or, "even when I am silent, you know everything." The Greek translator plucked out an elegant sentence, but he broke up those clauses: "...because there is no speech on my tongue. Behold, Lord, you have known," and so on. An unskilled hand then came in and changed *pa logos* into *dolos*, as Augustine also read: "there is no deceit on my tongue." Here again there is sweating. Verse 6: *Wonderful is the knowledge (this is, your knowledge by which you know all things) above me*, more wonderful than I can attain to. This is the very mind of the Prophet. For in the preceding verse there is no question of the formation of the human body, so that this place cannot be understood of that knowledge. And where the Vulgate has *you formed me*, the Hebrew codex has a word which can be rendered "you beset me," and it follows, "you have laid your hand upon me." The meaning is: you encompass me on every side, as is explained in the following verses. The Vulgate has "Your knowledge has become wonderful from me." Bellarmine, Sá and others acknowledge that "from me" stands for "above me." Those interpretations which you will find in the Carthusian, in Alphonsus de Castro under the heading *anima* at the beginning, and in others, therefore collapse. Verse 15: *in the lower parts of the earth*, that is, in the womb of my mother. Some explain Ephesians 4.9 in this way, where Christ is said to have descended "into the lower parts of the earth" [εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς]. He does not say "the world" [ὁ κόσμος] but "of the earth," so that these places plainly seem to illuminate each other, and there is no need to fabricate a limbo. Verse [illegible] [illegible]: word for word, *And how precious to me are your thoughts! How their sum (summa, κεφάλαια) has grown strong. If I wished to count them, they would be multiplied beyond the sand.* Or, "I would count them, but they are more than the sand." This is the very mind of the Psalmist, which both Pagninus and Arias express clearly. The Seventy strayed from it entirely: ἐμοὶ δὲ λίαν ἐτιμήθησαν οἱ φίλοι σου ... ὁ ... ἐκεφαλαιώθησαν αἱ ἀρχαὶ αὐτῶν, "To me your friends have been greatly honoured; their beginnings have been greatly summed up; I shall number them, and they will be multiplied above the sand." The Vulgate has translated these words thus: "To me, however, your friends, O God, have been greatly honoured; their principality has been greatly strengthened. I shall number them, and they will be multiplied above the sand." The difference arises chiefly from these two words, עָיִר and רֵאשֵׁיהֶם. Our people rendered the first, boldly enough, as "thoughts," because in this same Psalm, verse 2, the Seventy render the same word as ἀλογισμός and the Vulgate as "thoughts." Who is so shameless as to deny that the other word frequently occurs in the Bible for κεφάλαιον? Hence another Greek translator rendered these words, πόσο πολυπληθὴς καὶ κεφαλαὶ αὐτῶν, that is, "how many are their heads?" I find very many places where ראש means a prince or the most excellent thing in some matter, but I find none where it means "principality." Yet from this passage Costerus in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 12, Eck in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 15, and Alphonsus de Castro in his book against heresies, prove that the saints are to be worshipped in heaven. Cotonus from the same passage proves that this world is administered by them. But if this were a discussion of the religious worship of the departed saints, how would it cohere with what precedes? For in those verses the Psalmist wished to praise the infinite providence of God, which shines out chiefly in this, that nothing is so hidden that he does not search it most perfectly. Moreover, how will they prove that יקר means "to be honoured," and that this in turn means "to be worshipped religiously"? How will they prove that the friends are to be understood as the departed saints? For I suppose they do not assert that the living are to be worshipped religiously. And we do not deny that the departed are to be honoured in their own way. Furthermore, since Bellarmine, in book 1 of *On the Beatitude of the Saints*, chapter 19, plainly declares that the saints in the Old Testament did not enter heaven, did not see God, and could not ordinarily know the prayers of suppliants, and therefore it was not customary in the Old Testament to say "Holy Abraham, pray for me," but the men of that time only prayed to God and alleged the merits of the saints, how, with that most learned Cardinal's opinion left intact, can the Papists prove from these and other such passages of Scripture the invocation of saints in the Old Testament? But when Bellarmine here says that the merits of the saints were alleged so that the prayers of the living might be aided by them, he proves this in vain from passages of this kind, for example Exodus 32: "Remember, Lord, Abraham, Isaac and Israel your servant." For in such passages no help is sought from the merits of the departed, but only the covenant is recalled, which God had made with the fathers concerning the protection of their posterity. But Bellarmine replies that Calvin's answer is not satisfactory, since covenant and merits are often joined, for example Ps. 132 (in their numbering 131): "Remember David and all his meekness." Here again the disputant stumbles. Nor could he himself be unaware that in the Hebrew there is עניו, a word which means not "his meekness" but "his affliction." In his commentary, after saying that Solomon in these words prays to God through the merits of his father David, he afterwards adds that Saint Jerome translated from the Hebrew, "of all his affliction." But that word, he says, can be read with other vowel points as יְנִיחוּ, "meekness." Therefore, by his own admission, the Hebrew word is indifferent to either reading when it lacks vowel points. Are firm arguments therefore built upon such passages? But I shall set against Bellarmine more interpreters, who, even when points had not yet been added, read it as Jerome and today's codices do. For behold, the Chaldee renders it מְעוֹפָה, "of his affliction." Aquila, κακωχίας; Symmachus, κακώσεως; another edition, ταπεινώσεως. But let us return to the place in Psalm 139.

units.la: Diximus Cotonum ex istis verbis, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum, probasse, sanctos defunctos administrare hunc mundum, atque inde porro illud intulisse, adorandos esse. An ergo omnes, quorum ministerio Deus O. M. mundum administrat, adorandi? An probatum, per amicos hic defunctos intelligi? An probata ista versio? Et hoc opinor fulcrum est istorum principatuum, quos inter Sanctos distribuit Romana Ecclesia, ut Eligius praesit fabris: Blasius, carminatoribus: Lucia, sartoribus: Josephus, fabris lignariis: Nicolaus, navigantibus: Rochus, peste afflictis: Antonius porcis, &c. Nunc illud restat, ut aberrantes aliquot aliorum, meliores tamen ea quam hactenus examinavimus, hujus loci expositiones proferamus. Primo itaque hic occurrit Theod. qui priora verba explicat de honore, quo Rex Iosias (putat enim sub ejus persona scriptum esse hunc Psalmum) sacerdotes prosecutus est. Pro istis vero, confortatus est principatus eorum, legit ex Theodot. corroborati sunt oi πνηπ. αὐτῶν, & explicat de restitutione sacerdotum, qui sub ejus decessoribus pauperrimam vitam agitaverant. Euthym. per amicos Dei intelligit, quicunque per virtutem, familiaritatem & benevolentiam ejus adipiscuntur. Illa vero, valde praevaluerunt principatus eorum, dicit ab alio interprete ita fuisse reddita, valde praeval. capita eorum. i. ipsi amici Dei, fortes facti sunt virtute Dei. Lyra interpretatur locum de angelis, qui per ordines trium hierarchiarum distincti sunt. Hierarchia vero, inquit, est idem quod sacer principatus. Et quia ista tres hierarchia, & tres ordines in singulis hierarchiis immobiliter stabiliuntur, ideo convenienter dicitur, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum. Et quia angeli sunt in maxi-
units.tr: I have said that Cotonus, from these words, the rulers have been greatly strengthened, proved that the holy dead govern this world, and from that further inferred that they are to be worshipped. But do we worship all those through whose ministry God Almighty governs the world? Has it been proved that the "friends" here are the dead? Is this rendering itself proved? I think this is the foundation of those patronships which the Roman Church distributes among the saints: Eligius presides over smiths, Blasius over wool-carders, Lucy over tailors, Joseph over carpenters, Nicholas over sailors, Roch over those afflicted with plague, Anthony over pigs, and so on. It remains now to set out the interpretations of this passage offered by several others, who stray, though they are better than those we have examined so far. First, then, Theodoret comes forward, who explains the earlier words of the honour which King Josiah (for he thinks this psalm was written in his person) paid to the priests. For the words their rulers have been strengthened he reads, from Theodotion, they have been strengthened [ὅτι ἐκράτησαν] their..., and explains it of the restoration of the priests, who under his predecessors had led a most wretched life. Euthymius understands by "friends of God" all who obtain his favour, familiarity and goodwill through virtue. As for the words their rulers have prevailed greatly, he says that another interpreter rendered them thus: their heads have prevailed greatly, that is, the friends of God themselves, made strong by the power of God. Lyra interprets the passage of the angels, who are distinguished by the orders of the three hierarchies. "Now," he says, "hierarchy is the same as sacred rule. And because these three hierarchies, and three orders within each hierarchy, are fixed immovably, it is fitting to say, their rulers have been greatly strengthened."

units.la: mo me numero, ideo subditur, Dinumerabo eos, &c. Bellarmini haec sententia est, Prophetam considerantem, ex quanta abysso imperfectionis Deus perducat amicos suos ad eminentissimam perfectionem, erumpere in exclamationem seu admirationem, Mihi. i. apud me, meo judicio, nimis honorificati sunt amici tui. i. valde omnino, valde omnino confortatus stabilitus est principatus eorum. Nam educti ex massa perditionis & diabolica captivitate transferuntur ad regnum æternum, facti angelis æquales. Subjicit autem ista, Non desunt qui illud, mihi, interpretentur, à me, ut sensus sit, à Davide honoratos semper amicos Dei fuisse. Sed prior expositio est communior & verior, & melius cohæret cum verbis sequentibus, nimis confortatus est principatus eorum. Qui enim honorificavit amicos Dei, ille idem confortavit principatum eorum. Deus autem non David confortavit, principatum eorum. Dinumerabo eos, i. conabor enumerare vel amicos Dei, qui principatu fruentur, vel subditos eorum, &c. Carthus. qui Psalmum de Christo exponit, Mihi. i. ad honorem meum, nimis honorificati sunt amici tui O Deus Pater, i. apostoli & apostolici viri, qui omnia relinquentes mea sunt assecuti vestigia. Et nimis conf. est princ. eorum. Constituit enim suos principes super omnem terram, prævalueruntque mundo, carni & Diabolo.
units.tr: And because the angels are in the greatest number, it is added, I will number them, etc. Bellarmine's view is this: the prophet, considering from what depth of imperfection God brings his friends to the highest perfection, bursts into exclamation or admiration: To me, that is, in my judgement, your friends have been greatly honoured, that is, altogether very greatly; their rulers have been utterly strengthened and established. For, drawn out of the mass of perdition and the captivity of the devil, they are transferred to the eternal kingdom, made equal to the angels. He adds, however, these words: "There are those who interpret to me as by me, so that the sense is that God's friends have always been honoured by David. But the former explanation is more common and truer, and agrees better with the words that follow, their rulers have been greatly strengthened. For he who honoured the friends of God is the same who strengthened their rulers. But it was God, not David, who strengthened their rulers. I will number them, that is, I will try to count either the friends of God who will enjoy this rule, or their subjects, etc." The Carthusian, who expounds the psalm of Christ, says: To me, that is, to my honour, your friends, O God the Father, have been greatly honoured, that is, the apostles and apostolic men, who, leaving all things, have followed my steps. And their rulers are greatly strengthened. For he has set his princes over all the earth, and they have prevailed over the world, the flesh and the devil.

units.la: Ps. CL. 1. Laudate Dominum [?בְּקָדְשׁוֹ] ad verbum, in sanctitate, vel sanctuario ejus. קדש non solum sanctitatem, sed & sanctuarium aliquando significat. Ps. xx. 3. Mittat auxilium tibi [?מִקְדָּשׁ] è sanctuario suo. Qui de sanctuario capiunt, vel templum, ut sacerdotes & Israelitas alloquatur; vel cœlum, ut ad angelos & beatas animas sermonem dirigat, interpretantur. Qui sanctitatem hic loci intelligunt, ב exponunt propter, laudate DOMINUM ob sanctitatem ejus, vel cum Junio, de sanctitate ejus. Ut vers. 2. laudate eum [?גְּבוּרוֹתָיו] de vel propter potentias ejus. Res ergo in originali plana est. Lxx. ἐν ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ, Bene, si bene capias. Namque & in epistola ad Ebræos non semel τὰ ἁγία de sanctuario dicitur. ex gr. cap. ix. 2. 3. 12. Erit ergo illud ἁγίως ex recto plurali τὰ ἁγία. Author Latinæ vulgatæ, in sanctis ejus. Utrum ex mente Interpretis, non ausim affirmare. Illud fidentius, posse commode intelligi, si vid. deflectatur à recto plurali; sancta, non sancti vel ut sit ellipsis substantivi, loci. Hoc non ignoravit Lyra, quando asserit, intelligi sancta, primam templi parpartem, in qua versabantur quotidie sacerdotes. Agnovit Ge-nebrardus, cujus hoc scholion est, in sanctis ejus] neutro genere. Hinc Ebr. in sancto vel sanctuario ejus. Est enim Apostrophe ad cælites. per Eclepsin, O vos qui estis in locis ejus sanctis id est in cælo angelico & animarum. Eadem est expositio Bellarmini, nec non Emmanuelis Sa. Patres fere omnes acceperunt de sanctis hominibus. Nullus tamen, quod ego sciam, de sanctorum invocatione hic quippiam somniavit. Ut vel supra modum stupidos eos esse oporteat, qui hunc locum eo trahunt, neque hunc solum, sed & illum Ps. Lxviii. vers. ult. Mirabilis est Deus in sanctis suis, ubi rursus in Ebraeo est מִקְּדָשֶׁיךָ / è sanctuariis tuis, ubi rursus Genebr. agnoscit illud sanctis neutro genere positum. Certe utrobique res in Ebraeo planissima est. Eo magis miror seu potius indignor, in Lovaniensium Editione Belg. loca ista sic conversa, God is wonderlyck in syne heyligen, & Loost God in syne heyligen, Nota, heyligen, non, heylige, ne fortassis de locis intelligeret lector. Putarunt sua interesse, ut hæc loca de sanctis angelis vel hominibus intelligerentur. Sed concesso, de sanctis defunctis gemino hoc loco agi, nihil tamen inde pro sanctorum invocatione extundi posse; hæ Patrum expositiones docebunt. Augustinus, laudate Dominum in sanctis ejus.] Vtique in eis quos glorificavit. Theod. Si a plantis & feris & reptilibus in gratiarum actionem ansam arripere jussi sumus, quanto magis justum est in sanctos inspicere & horum celebrare Deum? Quis enim non linguam impelleret ad hymnos canendos ei, qui tantam bonorum copiam hominibus largitus est. Euthyin. Laudate D. in sanctis ejus, hoc est, propter sanctos ejus, quod scil. hujusmodi conversationem virtute praeditam, Deus in hanc vitam introduxit, qua angelos ex hominibus eos esse effecit. Arnobius, Laudamus Dominum in sanctis ejus, quando eorum imitamur exempla, sequimur monita; regulam obtinemus, &c.
units.tr: Ps. 150.1: Praise the LORD [?בְּקָדְשׁוֹ], literally in his holiness, or his sanctuary. The word קדש means not only holiness but sometimes also sanctuary. Ps. 20.3: May he send you help [?מִקְדָּשׁ] from his sanctuary. Those who take it of the sanctuary interpret it either as the temple, so that the psalmist addresses the priests and Israelites, or as heaven, so that he directs his speech to the angels and blessed souls. Those who understand holiness here render ב as for: praise the LORD for his holiness, or, with Junius, for his holiness. As in verse 2: praise him [?גְּבוּרוֹתָיו] for or because of his mighty acts. The matter, therefore, is plain in the original. The Septuagint has ἐν ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ [in his holy places], which is good if one takes it rightly. For in the Epistle to the Hebrews τὰ ἁγία is said of the sanctuary more than once, e.g. ch. 9.2, 3, 12. So that ἁγίοις will be from the neuter plural τὰ ἅγια. The author of the Latin Vulgate has in sanctis ejus [in his saints]. I would not venture to affirm whether this is in the mind of the translator. More confidently I would say that it can be understood conveniently if one departs from the neuter plural: sancta [holy places], not sancti [saints], or else by ellipsis of a noun, loci [places]. Lyra did not miss this when he asserts that sancta is to be understood as the first part of the temple, in which the priests were daily engaged. Genebrardus, whose this note is, recognised that in sanctis ejus is a neuter: "Hence the Hebrew is in the holy place or sanctuary of him. For it is an apostrophe to the heavenly beings, by ellipsis: O you who are in his holy places, that is, in the angelic and spiritual heaven." This is also the explanation of Bellarmine, and of Emmanuel Sá. Almost all the Fathers have taken it of holy men. Yet none, so far as I know, dreamed of the invocation of saints here. Those who drag this passage to it must surely be stupid beyond measure, and not this passage alone, but also that in Ps. 68, last verse: God is wonderful in his saints [?מִקְּדָשֶׁיךָ, from your sanctuaries], where again Genebrardus acknowledges that sanctis is in the neuter. Certainly in both places the matter is quite plain in the Hebrew. I am all the more amazed, or rather indignant, that in the Louvain Dutch edition these passages are so rendered: God is wonderful in his holy ones, and praise God in his holy ones. Note: heyligen, not heylige, lest perhaps the reader understand the passages of places. They thought it mattered to them that these passages be understood of holy angels or men. But granting that in these two places the dead saints are meant, nothing can be extracted from this for the invocation of saints; the expositions of the Fathers will show this. Augustine: praise the Lord in his saints. Surely in those whom he has glorified. Theodoret: "If we have been commanded to seize an occasion of thanksgiving from plants, wild beasts and reptiles, how much more right is it to look upon the saints and to celebrate God through them? For who would not move his tongue to sing hymns to him who has bestowed such a wealth of goods on men?" Euthymius: "Praise the Lord in his saints, that is, on account of his saints, because God has brought into this life such men endowed with virtue, which has made them angels out of men." Arnobius: "We praise the Lord in his saints when we imitate their examples, follow their admonitions, and keep their rule, etc."

units.la: Fecimus aliquando in superioribus mentionem Psalterii Romani & Gallicani. Meminimus & versionis Hieronymi, quam ex Ebraeo tradu&tam & a vulgata Latina, quae in Bibliis vulgatis extat, tantum sæpe discrepantem,
units.tr: At some point in what precedes we have mentioned the Roman and Gallican Psalters. We have also mentioned the version of Jerome, which, though translated from the Hebrew, differs often from the Latin Vulgate that is found in the printed Vulgate Bibles,

units.la: — ὅταν ἀγαθὸς ἐς ἀπὸ γαίης,
units.tr: whenever the good man from the earth [ὅταν ἀγαθὸς ἐς ἀπὸ γαίης],

units.la: invenies in operibus Hieronymi. Hæc ut intelligat, tiro, scien-dum, versionem illam, quæ hodie in Bibliis vulgatis extat, non ex Ebraeo, ut caeteri plerique libri, sed ex veteri illa quam Italam vocant, quae ex Graeca ϷΤ Lxx. transumpta erat, (de qua supra pagina 10. & pag. 63.) derivatam esse, in multis mendosam & non unius imperiti manu vitiatam. Psalterium quod Romanum vocant, est quidem eadem illa Editio Latina, tunc temporis vulgata, sed quam Hieronymus, jussu Damasi, emaculavit, secutus & in hoc Graecam ϷO versionem. Ea cum Damasi jussu in Ecclesia Romana legi cantarique coepisset, Romani Psalterii nomen obtinuit. Verum cum haec emendatio rursus depravata esset vitio scriptorum, apud quos plus antiquae translationis error, quam novae correctionis fides valebat, Hieronymus hortatu Paulae & Eustochii secundam Editionem ex Graeca versione adornavit, in qua appositis obelis ea jugulavit, quae apud Lxx. erant superflua: & insertis asteriscis notavit, quae ipse ex Ebraea veritate addiderat. Quod opus cum Damasus in Ecclesiis Gallicanis cani concessisset, Gallicanum Psalterium nominari coepit. Tertiam editionem ex Ebraeo adornavit, flagitante Sophronio.
units.tr: you will find in the works of Jerome. So that the novice may understand these things, he must know that the version which today is found in the printed Vulgate Bibles is not, like most other books, derived from the Hebrew, but from that old version which they call the Itala, which had been taken over from the Greek of the Seventy (concerning which see above, p. 10 and p. 63). It is faulty in many places and corrupted by the hand of more than one unskilled person. The Psalter which they call Roman is indeed that same Latin edition, then current, but which Jerome, at the command of Damasus, corrected, following also in this the Greek version of the Seventy. When this was beginning to be read and sung in the Roman Church by Damasus's command, it obtained the name of the Roman Psalter. But since this emendation was again corrupted by the fault of copyists, among whom the error of the older translation counted for more than the reliability of the new correction, Jerome, at the urging of Paula and Eustochium, prepared a second edition from the Greek version, in which, by placing obeli, he cut out what was superfluous in the Seventy, and by inserting asterisks he marked what he himself had added from the Hebrew truth. When Damasus had allowed this work to be sung in the Gallican churches, it began to be called the Gallican Psalter. He prepared a third edition from the Hebrew at the request of Sophronius.

units.la: PROVERBIA.
units.tr: PROVERBS.

units.la: CAp. vi. 31. — deprehensus reddet septuplum.] Ita vulgatus. Inter alias constitutiones variorum Regnorum & provinciarum, divinae & immutabili divini numinis legi oppositas, & istae sunt, quibus fures laqueo, adulteri multa pecuniaria luunt. Qui eas defensant, aut, cum antiquare possent, nihilo tamen minus tolerant, viderint quid supremo isti legis-latori in decretorio isto die responsuri sint. Me quod attinet, dicam illud Jacobi, In arcanum eorum ne ingrediter anima mea & in coetum illorum judicum ne adunator gloria mea. Sed audio, crescentibus delictis poenas exasperandas esse. Cur ergo, delictis decrescentibus poenas non mitigant iidem censores? Cur poenam homicidii capitalem, iis in locis ubi rariores caedes, non convertunt in pecuniariam? Sed haec Junius, Piscator, Franzius & alii ventilarunt. Nos verbum addemus ad hunc locum. Furtum lege Moßis pro circumstantiarum varietate, restitutione dupli vel quaquadrupli expiabatur. Sed & quintupli. Neque ulterius eum Mosaicae leges, quamdiu furi suppetit, unde restituat. Si enim nihil habet, vendebatur. Cum vero hic dicat Salomon, septuplum reddet, colligunt; ejus saeculo poenam furti exasperatam fuisse: ac proinde, ut loquitur Thomas prima secundae, ad praecepta judicialia potuisse a regibus additionem fieri secundum exigentiam temporis. Quamvis verolonge diversa sint, poenam aliquam non capitalem aggravare; & poenam non capitalem convertere in capitalem, tamen nec illa quidem potestas ex hoc loco stabiliri potest. Id quod jam jam apparebit. Adhaec, si judiciale distinguas a morali & caeremoniali, negatur diserte, leges illas, quae transgressoribus moralium legum poenas decernunt, judiciales esse. quales sunt praeter leges de poena furti, leges de adultero & filio rebelli Deut. 21. & id genus aliae. Valebitque & hic illud Jurisconsultorum, Accessorium sequi suum principale. Sed veniamus ad locum Salomonis. Illic est vox שבעתים / quae pro ratione loci reddi potest vel septuplum, septupliciter, vel septies. Sunt qui cum vulg. vocem septuplum retinentes, eam sic explicant, reddet plenarie. ut Psalmo 79. redde vicinis nostris septuplum, ut numerus determinatus pro indeterminato ponatur. Pisc. septuplum, id est multiplum. vid. vel duplum vel quadruplum vel quintuplum pro ratione circumstantiarum. Sed an numerus septenarius pro numero, qui infra ipsum est, accipitur? Hoc primo ostendendum erat. Pro septies usurpatur Psal. xii. 7. ut argentum defaecatum שבעתים septies ubi vulg. quidem habet, septuplum, at a Genebr. Sa & aliis exponitur, septies, id est, saepius. Sed & idem Sa hoc ipso loco septuplum exponit, multo plus. Hanc interpretationem firmant ea quae sequuntur, omnem substantiam domus suae dabit. Salomonis scopus ille est, ut adulterium invisum reddat adolescenti, proposito praesentissimo periculo, in quod se praecipitem dat. Hoc illustrat & amplificat comparando poenas adulterii & furti, conferendo item ipsa illa delicta inter se. Fur inquit, non tam invisus est quam adulter, praesertim si ex necessitate furetur, nec etiam, licet extra illum casum, tanto afficitur supplicio. Furto enim coercendo non alia destinata poena est, quam restitutio dupli vel quadrupli vel quintupli pro ratione circumstantiarum, nec tum quidem, cum saepius idem delictum iterat. Furatur septies? reddit septies. Usque dum vniversam domus suæ substantiam exhauriat. vel ut Iun. ex qualibet substantia domus suæ reddat. vel, si legi satisfacere non potest, reddat omnia quæ habet, aut si nihil habet, in servitutem asseratur. Vitam ei nec dominus rei ablatæ, nec judices ex lege divina possunt adimere. At in mœcho aliter se habent omnia. Si vel semel deprehendatur, & privato & publico jure de ejus honore & vita actum est. Nam zelotypia inest æstus viri, ideo non utitur clementia die ultionis. Non acceptabit faciem ullius redemptionis, neque acquiescet, quamvis multa adhibeas munera. Ex hac antithesi liquido apparet mens Salomonis.
units.tr: Chap. 6:31. "He shall restore sevenfold" (deprehensus reddet septuplum). So the Vulgate. Among the various laws of different kingdoms and provinces there are some that oppose the divine and unchangeable law of the divine majesty, namely those by which thieves pay with the noose and adulterers with heavy fines. Those who defend them, or who tolerate them when they could abolish them, should consider what they will answer to the supreme Lawgiver on that day of judgment. As for me, I will say what Jacob said: "Into their secret let not my soul enter; with their assembly let not my glory be united" (Gen. 49:6). But I hear that as crimes increase, punishments must be made harsher. Why then do these same censors not lessen punishments when crimes decrease? Why do they not convert the capital punishment for homicide into a fine in those places where killings are rarer? Junius, Piscator, Franzius and others have discussed these questions, but we will add a word on this passage. Under the law of Moses, theft was atoned for, according to the variety of circumstances, by restitution of double or fourfold, and also fivefold. Nor did the Mosaic laws go further than this, so long as the thief had something from which to make restitution; if he had nothing, he was sold. But since Solomon here says "he shall restore sevenfold," they infer that in his age the penalty for theft had been made harsher, and that therefore, as Thomas says in the first part of the second part, kings could make additions to the judicial precepts according to the demands of the time. Even though it is very different to aggravate a penalty that is not capital, or to convert a non-capital penalty into a capital one, still this passage cannot establish even that power. This will soon become clear. Moreover, if you distinguish the judicial from the moral and the ceremonial, it is flatly denied that those laws which decree penalties for the transgression of moral laws are judicial. Such are, besides the laws on the penalty for theft, the laws on the adulterer and the rebellious son (Deut. 21), and others of that kind. The saying of the jurists also holds here: "The accessory follows its principal." But let us come to Solomon's passage. There stands the word שבעתים [sheba'tayim], which according to the sense of the place may be rendered either "sevenfold," "in sevenfold measure," or "seven times." Some, retaining the Vulgate's "sevenfold," explain it thus: "he shall restore fully," so that a fixed number is put for an indefinite one, as in Psalm 79: "render to our neighbours sevenfold." Piscator: "sevenfold, that is, many times over," namely double or fourfold or fivefold according to the circumstances. But is the number seven here taken for a number that lies below it? This must first be shown. In Psalm 12:6 the word is used for "seven times": "as silver tried in a furnace, sevenfold [שִׁבְעָתַיִם]." There the Vulgate indeed has "sevenfold," but Genebrardus, Sá and others explain it as "seven times," that is, "more often." Sá, moreover, in this very passage explains "sevenfold" as "much more." This interpretation is confirmed by what follows: "he shall give all the substance of his house." Solomon's aim is to make adultery hateful to the young man, by setting before him the very present danger into which he throws himself headlong. He illustrates and enlarges this by comparing the penalties for adultery and theft, and by setting the offences themselves side by side. The thief, he says, is not so hated as the adulterer, especially if he steals out of necessity; nor, even apart from that case, is he punished so severely. For to check theft the appointed penalty is only restitution of double, or fourfold, or fivefold according to the circumstances, and not even then when the same offence is repeated many times. If he steals seven times, he restores seven times, until he exhausts all the substance of his house. Or, as Junius has it, he restores from whatever substance his house has. Or, if he cannot satisfy the law, he gives up everything he has; or if he has nothing, he is handed over into servitude. Neither the owner of the stolen goods nor the judges may take away his life under the divine law. But with the adulterer it is otherwise in every respect. If he is caught even once, his honour and his life are at stake, under both private and public law. "For jealousy is the fury of a man, and therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard the face of any ransom, nor will he be content, though you give many gifts." From this antithesis the mind of Solomon is clear.
