units.la: Clarissimum & eximium virum, M. JOHANNEM HACHTINGIUM, Logices Professf. Ord. Collegam meum conjunctissimum.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and eminent man, Mr. Johannes Hachtingius, full professor of logic and my closest colleague.

units.la: NOn ignoras, amicorum coryphæe, unde nata olim fuerit suspicio, qua beatæ memoriæ vir, Ioh. Drusius, præceptor noster communis, præter omne meritum gravabatur. Non exigui aut minutuli alicujus erroris, sed Arianæ impietatis fautor audiebat, & per ora virum juvenumque traducebatur. Doluimus & ingemuimus, quoties ista aures nostras pulsarent; Doluerunt magni viri, qui Drusium ex Drusio id est, ex scriptis & sermonibus ejus aliter noverant. Inter eos fuit beatæ recordationis vir, D. Ausonius Aysma, Ordinum Frisiæ Secretarius, dum vixit, fidelissimus. Is cum super hac re mecum aliquando sermocinaretur, rogabat, ut brevi quadam apologia præceptori meo maculam istam abstergerem & citra cujusquam mortalis insectationem beati senis memoriam emacularem. Parui magno viro & hanc, quam nunc publice repræsento, commentatiunculam exaravi. Ut autem eam publici juris juris facerem, impetrare à me mortalium nullus potuit. Neque etiam jam exire passus fuissem, nisi subinde intelligerem, eandem illam suspicionem ineptis & indoctis quibusdam hominibus etiamnum harere. Cum insuper operis mei, in quo jam versor, institutum tale sit, ut undequaque in illud convectem, quicquid uspiam ad celebriorum locorum interpretationem ex linguarum ignorantia peccarunt Interpretes, non existimavi me capitâl admissurum, si hoc loco commentatiunculam illam meam exhiberem. Eam tibi inscribo, Clarissime Vir. Tu de hac materia judicare potes accuratissime. Tu magni istius viri memoriam cum benevolentia colis. Tu is es, cui merito multum defero. Privatam amicitiam omitto. Tu publice de Academia nostra bene meritus es & mereris quotidie. Labore & indefessa industria cedis nulli. In tuenda disciplina, quam vitio temporum propemodum collapsam, superioribus annis juxta cum pauculis aliis ex collegio nostro mascule restitueras, ante biennium, cum Rev. & celeberrimo Theologo, D. Sibrando Lubberto, magno isti disciplinæ vindici, in rectoratu successor datus esses, ita te gessisti, ut te pro salute publica, offensionum impavidum tota Academia agnoverit. Plura non addam, ne aliis adulari videor. Tu nosti ingenium meum, simplex, candidum, apertum. Sed hoc elogium intrepido isti animo tuo debebam. Vale Clarissime Vir & diurna.
units.tr: You are not unaware, leader of my friends, of the source of the suspicion that once weighed upon John Drusius, our common teacher, of blessed memory, far beyond any merit of his. It was not said to be some slight or trifling error, but he was heard to be a supporter of Arian impiety, and was talked about from mouth to mouth by old and young. We grieved and groaned whenever such talk struck our ears. Great men who knew Drusius otherwise, from Drusius himself, that is, from his writings and conversations, also grieved. Among them was the man of blessed memory, Mr. Ausonius Aysma, secretary of the Frisian estates, most faithful while he lived. When he once talked with me about this matter, he asked me to wipe away this stain from my teacher with a short apology, and to clear the blessed old man's memory without attacking any mortal. I yielded to this great man and wrote the little commentary which I now publish. But he could not persuade me to let it go out into public circulation, and I would not have allowed it even now, had I not realised from time to time that this same suspicion still clings to certain foolish and unlearned people. Moreover, since the plan of the work on which I am now engaged is to gather from every quarter whatever the interpreters have gone wrong in through ignorance of languages in the interpretation of more famous passages, I did not think I would commit a capital offence by presenting that little commentary of mine in this place. I dedicate it to you, most distinguished man. You can judge this matter most accurately. You cherish the memory of that great man with goodwill. You are the one to whom I rightly defer much. I set aside private friendship. You have deserved well of our Academy publicly, and you deserve it every day. In labour and tireless industry you yield to no one. In maintaining discipline, which had almost collapsed through the vices of the times, and which in earlier years you restored manfully together with a few others from our college, two years ago you were made successor in the rectorship to the Reverend and most celebrated theologian, Mr. Sibrandus Lubbertus, that great champion of discipline. In that office you so conducted yourself, for the public good, that the whole Academy recognised you as fearless in the face of offences. I will add no more, lest I seem to flatter others. You know my nature: simple, candid, open. But I owed this tribute to your fearless spirit. Farewell, most distinguished man, and may you live long.

units.la: Prov. VIII. 22. Dominus possedit me, &c.] Locus iste immane quantum ab Arianis & Patribus orthodoxis vexatus est. Occasionem disputationi præbuit indiligentia interpretum LXX. circa hunc potissimum versum. Conferamus.
units.tr: Prov. VIII. 22. The Lord possessed me, etc.] This passage has been vexed to an immense degree by the Arians and by the orthodox Fathers. The occasion for the dispute was the carelessness of the Septuagint translators over this particular verse. Let us compare.

units.la: Hic quaedam notanda sunt. I. Illud קָנָנִי quod proprie est, ἐκτίσατό με, reddiderunt sine ulla necessitate ἔκτισέ με. Atque hinc illae lacrymae. II. תְּאשִׁית reddiderunt ἀρχῇ, tanquam per appositionem additum ad illud me. III. קֶדֶם quod significat ante, reddiderunt per eis. IV. Vocem ultimam מֵאָז tanquam si non extisset, insuper habuere. Locus prout in Ebraeo legitur, non tantum Arianae haeresi non patrocinatur, sed & efficacissimum argumentum pro Deitate Christi continet. Quis enim hic loquitur? Sapientia, הַחָכְמָה aeterna illa Patris sapientia, quae Prov. i. 20. & ix. 1. honoris causa vocatur חָכְמוֹת sapientia, ut solent Ebraei res, quas amplificare & extollere volunt, σοφίαν efferre, quamvis alii malint per ellipsin exprimere, quasi integrum esset, חָכְמוֹת חָכְמוֹת sapientia sapientiarum. Nam & hic modus ἀξιώσεως non minus Ebraeis usitatus est. Quocunque modo summas, recte expressa ea vox a Junio est, summa sapientia. Quid de se loquitur? DOMINUS, Pater possidebat me, jam genuerat me, jam pepererat me. Gignere enim & parere in hoc mysterio saepe alternant. Quando? initio via sua, initio operum suorum. Ev. ἀρχῇ ἦν, in principio creationis jam eram. Et ne ullus scrupulus superesset, addit, ante opera sua, ante tunc id est, ante ullum tempus. Vers. 23. ante saeculum, ante principium, ante primordia terrae. & 24. cum nulla essent abyssi, nulli fontes, cum nondum esset terra, montes, &c. Haec enim in toto hoc contextu sunt synonyma, ם & קֶדֶם & לִפְנֵי ante; בְּאשׁ & בְּטֶרֶם nondum. Mem ipsi quoque LXX. Ps. cx. in voce מִשְׁחָר (quam illi מַשְׁחָר legebant) per ante reddiderant, πρὸ ἑωσφόρου, ante Luciferum. Eodem modo sumitur Mich. v. ubi de aeterna Filii Dei generatione agens, sic inquit vates, מִימֵי עוֹלָם וּמִיּוֹצְאוֹתָיו מִקֶּדֶם & egressiones ejus ante principium, ante dies saeculi. Confer. Ps. 90. 2. & 93. 2. Ies. 43. 13. יָצָא egredi, aliquando est nasci, Genes. xvii. 6. & xxv. 26. Ief. xi. 1. Utitur autem rursus voce pluralis numeri, non ad denotandam duplicem nativitatem Christi (illud enim quod hic praedicatur, non nisi divinae generationi accommodaveris, sed ad auxesin & excellentiam) Eadem significatione occurrit & N. T. particula ἀπό. Nam quod Ephes. 1. 4. dicitur πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου & 2. Tim. 1. 9. πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων id 2. Thess. 2. 13. dicitur, ἀπ' ἀρχῆς. & Apocal. 13. 8. ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae agni mactati, ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. In quibus verbis observa primo trajectionem ἀπὸ, illud enim ἀπὸ καταβολῆς, &c. referri debet ad γεγραμμένα scripta sunt. Plane uti Matth. 27. 9. illa ἀπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ Ισραὴλ, referuntur ad remotius ἔλαβον accepi, (N. B. non acceperunt, atque ita pro ἴδιον restituendum est ἴδιον, vide Syrum, Pisc. Deodatum, & Junium ad versionem Syriacam & in Parallelis) non ad proximum ἐπιπλησίον. Illam porro trajectionem confirmat Junius ex Areta, & emendatiores codices distinctione separant illa, ἀπὸ κατ. καταβολῆς κόσμου, à voce πνευματικός. Sed evidens est locus Apoc. xvii. 8. ubi diserte sine ulla trajectione legitur, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. Unde duo illa consequuntur. 1. illud ἀπὸ καταβολῆς hic idem esse quod πρὸ καταβολῆς, Ephes. 1. 4. Ergo quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae id est, qui non sunt electi ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Alterum, frustra esse & circa vitiosam lectionem eorum versari industriam, qui hoc ostendere satagunt, quomodo agnus commode dici possit ab origine mundi seu à jactis mundi fundamentis mactatus. Frustra & illos Metaphysicos esse, qui suae inter essentiam & existentiam distinctioni ab hoc scripturae loco & robur & facem quaerunt. Agnus mactatus est, inquit *Keckerm. ab origine mundi, secundum essentiam: sub Pilato, secundum existentiam. Sed de hoc loco vide Junium & Piscatorem & Scultetum. Nos ad locum Proverbiorum redeamus, quem, prout in Ebraeo legitur, adversus Arianos & Photinianos invictum esse, jam, opinor, ostendimus. Certe locus iste ab ima stirpe convellit illud Arianorum πολυφύλλιον, ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν. Si fuit ante conditum caelum & terram, ante ullum tempus, consequens est, ut ab aeterno fuerit. Nam immotae veritatis illud est, quod in Scholis docetur, quicquid ante mundum & ei concreatum tempus extitit, aeternum esse.
units.tr: Several things here need noting. I. The word קָנָנִי, which properly means ἐκτήσατό με (he acquired me), they rendered without any need as ἔκτισέ με (he created me). And hence those tears. II. They rendered תְּאשִׁית by ἀρχῇ, as if it were added in apposition to "me". III. קֶדֶם, which means "before", they rendered by the preposition εἰς. IV. The last word, מֵאָז, they treated as though it were not there at all. The passage, as it is read in the Hebrew, not only does not favour the Arian heresy but also contains a most effective argument for the Deity of Christ. For who speaks here? Wisdom, the eternal wisdom of the Father, הַחָכְמָה, which in Prov. i. 20 and ix. 1 is called, for honour's sake, חָכְמוֹת, "wisdom". The Hebrews are accustomed to render with σοφίαν those things they wish to magnify and exalt, although others prefer to express it by ellipsis, as if the phrase were complete, חָכְמוֹת חָכְמוֹת, "wisdom of wisdoms". For this mode of superlative is no less common among the Hebrews. However one reckons the highest, the word was rightly rendered by Junius as "supreme wisdom". What does she say about herself? "The LORD possessed me": now he had begotten me, now he had brought me forth. For to beget and to bring forth often alternate in this mystery. When? "At the beginning of his way", that is, at the beginning of his works. In John's words, ἀρχῇ ἦν, in the beginning, I was already there when creation began. And lest any scruple remain, she adds, "before his works, before then", that is, before any time. In verse 23: "before the world, before the beginning, before the origins of the earth", and in verse 24: "when there were no depths, no fountains, when the earth and the mountains were not yet", and so on. For in this whole context these are synonyms: the words מִן, קֶדֶם and לִפְנֵי all mean "before", and אָז and בְּטֶרֶם mean "not yet". The Seventy too, in Psalm 110, rendered the word מִשְׁחָר (which they read as מַשְׁחָר) by "before", πρὸ ἑωσφόρου, "before the morning star". In the same way Micah v is to be taken, where the prophet, speaking of the eternal generation of the Son of God, says: "and his goings forth are from of old, from everlasting" [מִימֵי עוֹלָם וּמִיּוֹצְאוֹתָיו מִקֶּדֶם], "and his goings forth before the beginning, before the days of eternity". Compare Ps. 90. 2, Ps. 93. 2, Isa. 43. 13. The verb יָצָא, "to go forth", sometimes means "to be born", Gen. 17. 6, Gen. 25. 26, Ier. xi. 1. He uses the plural again, not to denote a double nativity of Christ (for what is preached here can only be applied to divine generation), but for intensification and excellence. The particle ἀπό occurs in the New Testament with the same meaning. For what is said in Eph. 1. 4, "before the foundation of the world" (πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου), and in 2 Tim. 1. 9, "before eternal times" (πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων), the same is said in 2 Thess. 2. 13 as "from the beginning" (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς), and in Apoc. 13. 8, "from the foundation of the world" (ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου), of those whose names are not written in the book of life of the slain Lamb. In these words observe first the transposition of ἀπό: "from the foundation of the world" must be referred to "have been written". Just as in Matth. 27. 9 the words "from the children of Israel" are referred to the more remote "received" (note: they did not receive; and so the reading must be restored, as in the Syriac, Piscator, Deodatus and Junius on the Syriac version and in the Parallels), not to the nearer word. Junius confirms this transposition from Areta, and the more correct codices separate the words ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου from the word πνευματικός. But the passage Apoc. 17. 8 is clear, where it is read plainly, without any transposition: "whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world". From this two things follow. First, that "from the foundation" here is the same as "before the foundation" in Eph. 1. 4. So "whose names are not written in the book of life" means those who were not chosen before the foundations of the world were laid. Second, it is in vain that those labour and busy themselves over this faulty reading who strive to show how the Lamb can fitly be said to have been slain from the origin of the world, or from the laying of its foundations. In vain too are those metaphysicians who seek from this scriptural passage both strength and a torch for their distinction between essence and existence. "The Lamb was slain," says Keckermann, "from the origin of the world according to essence, and under Pilate according to existence." But on this passage see Junius, Piscator and Scultetus. Let us return to the passage in Proverbs, which, as it is read in the Hebrew, we have, I think, now shown to be invincible against the Arians and Photinians. Certainly this passage tears up by the roots that Arian slogan, "there was when he was not". If he existed before heaven and earth were made, before any time, it follows that he was from eternity. For it is an unshakeable truth, taught in the schools, that whatever existed before the world and the time created along with it is eternal.

units.la: Et illud Athanasii, Si æternus est filius, non est creatura; Si creatura, non æternus. In eo orthodoxos Patres admodum sudasse supra diximus. Sudarunt circa illud, ad opera sua. Æstuarunt circa illud, initium viarum suarum. Sed maxime laboratum fuit circa illud ἔκτισε. Illud enim ad istas angustias nonnullos redegit, ut hunc versum de humana Christi natura intellexerint. Vide orat. 3. B. Athanasii contra Arianos. Verba ejus pag. 234. ista sunt, Plane constat, verbum, quum aliud esset ab omnibus & ante omnia, postea incepisse creari initium viarum ad opera, per assumptionem humanæ naturæ. Et pag. 238. Ipsa opera quæ facia, testantur de me. Hæc sunt opera ad quæ ipse creatur, dum in proverbiis dicit, ad opera sua, οὐχ ἀρχὴ, inquit, τῆς ἰδίας αὐτῆς σωματικὴν ἐν τῷ ἔκτισε, ἀλλὰ τῆς σωματικῆς αὐτῆς γενέσεως. Illud autem, initium viarum sic interpretatur, in illa carne factum est initium nova creatura, eo quod ipse creatus sit homo pro nobis & viam nobis renovavit. Vide lector, quantis in tenebris primarius ille Arianæ impietatis malleus versatus sit. Neque ille tantum, sed & Cyrillus Archiepisc. Alexandrinus, Thesauri contra hæret. lib. v. cap. 4. Christus, inquit, jam homo factus id de se dixit [Dominus creavit me, & cap. 9. Sapientia ædificavit sibi domum] ut homo enim sapientiæ domus adificatus est. ille inquam homo, qui ex virgine natus est, & in quo plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitavit. Et paulo post, Filius ergo Dei factus homo est & creatus secundum carnem, ut initium viarum Domini & operum suorum omnibus daret. In Christo enim primo Euangelica vita effulsit. Quid enim aliud opera & via Domini significant, præter mandata ejus, qua custodientes recto itinere ad ipsum perginus. Est postquam alia quædam satis aliena interjunxisset, istis verbis caput illud obsignat, Dominus creavit me, hominem me fecit, intelligendum est. Et cap. v. ad calcem, Postremo, si quia dicit, Dominus creavit me, creatus est, similiter quia dicit, ante omnes colles genuit me, creatus non est. Aliud enim est genitum, aliud creatura. Genitum enim ex substantia generantis naturaliter exit, creatum vero ad extra producitur. Quoniam igitur Deus & homo est, ut homo quidem, Dominus creavit me, dicit; ut Deus, Ante omnes colles genuit me. Hæc certe ad textum Græcum speciose dicuntur. quæ si velis Ebraeo applicare, ineptus Iis. Similia invenies apud Basil.lib. 2. & 4. contra Eunomium. Epiphan. hæref. 69. & alios. Cæterum qui in hoc contentionum æstu ad originarium textum provocaverint, Apparent rari nantes in gurgite vasto.
units.tr: And that saying of Athanasius: If the Son is eternal, he is not a creature; if he is a creature, he is not eternal. I have said above that the orthodox Fathers sweated greatly over this point. They sweated over the phrase to his works, and they were tormented by the beginning of his ways. But the greatest labour was spent on the word ἔκτισε [ektise, "created"]. This word drove some into such a corner that they understood this verse of the human nature of Christ. See Athanasius' Oration 3 against the Arians. His words at page 234 are these: It is plain that the Word, though he was other than all things and before all things, afterwards began to be created as "the beginning of his ways to his works," through the assumption of human nature. And at page 238: The works which he made bear witness concerning me. These are the works to which he himself is created, when in the Proverbs he says "to his works." He says: "Not the beginning of his own bodily creation (ἐν τῷ ἔκτισε), but of his bodily birth (γενέσεως)." He interprets the phrase the beginning of his ways thus: In that flesh a new creature had its beginning, because the man was created for us and he renewed the way for us. See, reader, in what darkness that chief hammer of Arian impiety was moving. Nor was he alone: Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, in the Thesaurus against heretics, book 5, chapter 4, says: Christ, I say, now made man, spoke of himself thus ["The Lord created me," and in chapter 9, "Wisdom built herself a house"], since as man he was built up as the house of wisdom: I mean that man who was born of the virgin, and in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily. And a little later: The Son of God therefore became man and was created according to the flesh, so that he might give to all the beginning of the ways and works of the Lord. For in Christ the Gospel life first shone forth. For what else do the works and way of the Lord signify, except his commandments, by keeping which we walk to him by the straight road? After he had inserted some rather irrelevant matter, he closes that chapter with these words: "The Lord created me, made me man," must be understood thus. And at the end of chapter 5: Finally, if because he says "The Lord created me," he was created, then likewise because he says "before all the hills he begat me," he was not created. For the begotten is one thing, the creature another. For the begotten proceeds naturally from the substance of the one who begets, but the created is produced outside. Since therefore he is both God and man, as man he says "The Lord created me," and as God "before all the hills he begat me." These things are indeed said plausibly enough about the Greek text; but if you wish to apply them to the Hebrew, they are out of place. You will find similar things in Basil, books 2 and 4 against Eunomius, Epiphanius, heresy 69, and others. But those who in this heat of controversy appealed to the original text, appear here and there, a few swimmers in a vast whirlpool.

units.la: Inter eos fuit Hieronymus, quem vide ad caput xxvi. Jesaiæ, iv. caput Michææ, 2. caput Epist. ad Ephes. & in Epistola 139. Cæteri, ut Basil. lib. 2. in Eunomium & Epiphanius hæresi 69. quæ Arianorum est, ex interpretatione Aquilæ tale quid odorati sunt: Is enim locum hunc sic reddiderat, κύριος ἐκτήσατό με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν κατεργασμάτων αὐτοῦ. Verum ista responsio nec Arianis, nec ipsis quoque orthodoxis inter Græcos satisfecit. Quia enim textus Græci authoritatem nolebant sollicitari, summa sibi opera annitendum putarunt, ut salva recepta lectione hæreticis oppilarent. Itaque alii responderunt, ἐποίησεν idem esse quod præfecit, q. d. præfecit me initio omnibus operibus suis creandis. Hæc sententia refertur ab Athanasio, libro de decretis Synodi Nicenæ ex Dionysio Romano. Alii locum de Ecclesia interpretati sunt, Alii ad Ideam quandam, ad quam omnia creata fuerant, retulerunt. Nec defuerunt, qui Arianorum impetum hac responsione retuderint. Scripturam promiscue usurpare vocabula ista, creo, facio, gigno, itaque non ex solo verbo creavit, aut genuit, sed ex antecedentibus & consequentibus verum loci sensum indagandum. Hanc responsionem invenies apud eundem Athanasium, orat. 3. contra Arianos, Cyrillum libro v. Thesauri cap. 6. & alios. Omnes in eo conspirarunt, LXX. Interpretes hæresi Arianæ neutiquam favere. Cl. Drusius, licet non ignoraret, quomodo locus iste in Hebræo legeretur, tamen censebat operæ pretium esse, in ipsissimam LXX. interpretum mentem penitius inquirere. Itaque omnibus rite expensis, judicabat simplicissimam esse illam τῶν ἐβδομήκοντα interpretationem, quam postremo loco recensuimus. Illud certe minime committendum putavit, ut authoritas illa pro derelicto haberetur & hasta quasi abjecta, celeberrimos istos interpretes Arianæ impietati faviste concederetur. Hanc ergo aliquando super ea re thesin propositit,
units.tr: Among them was Jerome, whom see on Isaiah 26, on Micah 4, on the second chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, and in Epistle 139. Others, such as Basil in book 2 against Eunomius and Epiphanius in heresy 69, which belongs to the Arians, took their cue from the translation of Aquila, who had rendered the passage thus: κύριος ἐκτήσατό με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν κατεργασμάτων αὐτοῦ ["the Lord acquired me as the beginning of his works' ways"]. But this answer satisfied neither the Arians nor even the orthodox among the Greeks. For since they did not want the authority of the Greek text to be called into question, they thought they must make the greatest effort to block the heretics while keeping the accepted reading intact. So some replied that ἐποίησεν [epoiesen, "made"] means the same as placed over, as if to say: he placed me over all his works to be created at the beginning. This view is cited by Athanasius, in his book on the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea, from Dionysius of Rome. Others interpreted the passage as referring to the Church, and others referred it to a certain Idea, according to which all things were created. Nor were there lacking those who blunted the attack of the Arians with this answer: that Scripture uses these words, create, make, beget, indiscriminately, and so the true sense of the passage must be sought not from the word created or begat alone, but from what goes before and after. You will find this answer in Athanasius again, Oration 3 against the Arians, in Cyril, Thesaurus book 5 chapter 6, and others. All of them agreed on this: the Seventy interpreters did not in the least favour the Arian heresy. Drusius, although he was not unaware of how this passage reads in Hebrew, nevertheless thought it worth the effort to inquire more deeply into the very mind of the Seventy translators. So, having weighed everything properly, he judged that the simplest interpretation was that of the Seventy, which we listed last. He certainly thought it must on no account be allowed that this authority should be treated as abandoned, its spear as it were cast aside, and that these most celebrated interpreters should be conceded to have favoured Arian impiety. So at one point he set forth this thesis on the matter:

units.la: Verbum creo aliquando ponitur pro gigno vel procreo. Hoc sensu Christus dici potest creatus id est genitus. Sane Proverb. viii, in Græca Editione legimus, ab initio via sua creavit me. Et in Sirach sapientia legitur creata.
units.tr: The verb create is sometimes used for beget or procreate. In this sense Christ may be called created, that is, begotten. Indeed, in Proverbs 8 we read in the Greek edition, "He created me at the beginning of his way." And in Sirach, wisdom is read as created.

units.la: De qua thesi, unico suspicionis istius fonte, antequam plura addam, lubet manifesta quaedam ex Cl. istius viri scriptis testimonia, paucula e multis, praemittere, ex quibus judicabit Lector, quid ὁ μονογενὴς de aeterna Filii Deitate senserit.
units.tr: Before I add more on this thesis, the sole source of this suspicion, I would like to set out some clear testimonies from the writings of this distinguished man, a few out of many, from which the reader will judge what this only-begotten thought about the eternal Deity of the Son.

units.la: In Annot. prior. ad Ebr. 1. 5. ad vocem nomen sic commentatur,
units.tr: In his first Annotations on Hebrews 1:5, he comments on the word "name" as follows:

units.la: Nomen] Quodnam hoc nomen? haud dubie, Filius Dei, quem Deus GENVIT AB ÆTERNO. Alioqui & Angeli vocantur Filii Dei, sed alio sensu. Non enim certè geniti fuere, sed creati. Et paulo post, Quia servat homines à peccatis, quod est Dei proprium, ideo Iesus dictus est. Utrumque ergo innuit Deitatem ejus.
units.tr: Name. What name is this? Undoubtedly the Son of God, whom God BEGOT FROM ETERNITY. Otherwise angels are also called sons of God, but in another sense; for they were certainly not begotten but created. And a little later: Because he saves men from their sins, which is proper to God, therefore he was called Jesus. Both therefore point to his Deity.

units.la: Eodem libro ad 1. Tim. 6. 11. Qui Christum, inquit, ita [nempe hominem Dei vel hominem divinum] vocant, non eam opinionem de eo habent, quam debebant. Aliud enim homo Deus, aliud homo Dei vel divinus. Homo Dei vel divinus dici potest de homine, non Deo: Homo Deus non item.
units.tr: In the same book, on 1 Timothy 6:11: Those who call Christ thus [namely, the man of God or divine man] do not hold the opinion about him that they ought to. For man-God is one thing, man of God or divine man another. A man of God or divine man can be said of a man, not of God; but man-God cannot be said in the same way.

units.la: Ibidem, ad Titum 2. 13.
units.tr: Likewise, on Titus 2:13.

units.la: Magni Dei] Non solum Deus, sed & magnus Deus vocatur hic Christus. Cur igitur horrent eum Deum appellare Novatores? Homo divinus est, inquiunt, non Deus proprie. Phy * τῆς ἀσεβείας! Tune audes negare, quod Scriptura tam clare affirmat? Quod si non est Deus, nec adorandus igitur est. Agite qui contra itis & oculos tandem aperite, ut Solem in ipso meridie lucentem clare videatis.
units.tr: Of the great God. Here Christ is called not only God but great God. Why then do the innovators shudder to call him God? "He is a divine man," they say, "not God properly." Oh, the impiety! Do you dare to deny what Scripture so clearly affirms? If he is not God, then he is not to be worshipped either. Come, you who oppose this, and at last open your eyes, so that you may clearly see the Sun shining at midday.

units.la: In posterioribus Annot. ad Luc. 3. 38.
units.tr: In the later Annotations on Luke 3:38.

units.la: Adami, Qui fuit Dei.] sub. Filius. Quomodo Filius Dei? an quia formatus à Deo ex luto terrae? Aut Filius Dei propter animam quae ei divinitus inspirata. Et paucis interjectis, ut ut fit, Filius Dei est, qui ex substantia ejus GENITVS, ut Messias; Et qui à Deo factus, ut Adam.
units.tr: Of Adam, who was of God. Supply "son." In what sense is he the Son of God? Is it because he was formed by God from the clay of the earth? Or the Son of God on account of the soul breathed into him by God? And after a few words in between, however it is: he is the Son of God who was BEGOTTEN from his substance, as the Messiah; and he who was made by God, as Adam.

units.la: In comm. ad loca dissic. Moses cap. 1. libri 1.
units.tr: On the obscure passages in his commentary on the first book of Moses, chapter 1.

units.la: Faciamus hominem] Antiquissimi Ebraeorum prodiderunt, Deum ita locutum fuisse ad domum judicii sui. Quaenam domus judicii, si non Filius & Sp. S.? Nam Angeli intelligi non possunt, siquidem & ipsi inter creaturas. Quomodo enim deliberarent de creando homine, qui ipsi creati fuere?
units.tr: Let us make man. The most ancient of the Hebrews have handed down that God spoke thus to the court of his judgement. What court of judgement could this be, if not the Son and the Holy Spirit? For the angels cannot be meant, since they too are among the creatures. For how could they deliberate about creating man, when they themselves were created?

units.la: Ad Judicum librum, cap. 6. 11. Post distinctionem Angelorum in supernates & infernates, Supernates angeli sunt, inquit, in duplici genere. Nam alii omnes creati fuere: Unus ex iis
units.tr: On the Book of Judges, chapter 6, verse 11. After the distinction of angels into supernal and infernal, he says, the supernal angels are of a twofold kind. For all of them were created, except one of them:

units.la: id est impietatem. iis non fuit creatus, qui Angelus fœderis & magni consilii vocatur.
units.tr: that is, impiety. Of these, the one who is called the Angel of the covenant and of great counsel was not created.

units.la: Nota autem, Drusium ex Rabbinorum phraseologia per inferiores angelos intelligere sacerdotes, qui in V. T. Angeli vocantur. Malach. 2. 7. In Miscellan. cent. 2. cap. 53. & in libro Elohim,
units.tr: Note, however, that Drusius, following the rabbinic idiom, understands by the lower angels the priests, who are called angels in the Old Testament (Malachi 2:7). He says this in his Miscellanies, century 2, chapter 53, and in the book Elohim:

units.la: Non hic nego tres in Deitate personas, impius futurus si id negem, &c.
units.tr: I do not deny here that there are three persons in the Godhead; I would be impious if I denied it, etc.

units.la: Adversus evidentissima ista loca ceu totidem confessiones nihil objici poterit præter illam quam supra exhibui, positionem. In qua tamen nihil erat quod non * antea in suis scriptis passim annotaverat. Putabat eruditus senex se isthac sua responsione (se enim ejus primum authorem esse existimabat usque dum necessitas ei imponeretur alios quoque authores super hoc loco consulendi) crus dextrum fregisse Ario & nobilissimum locum a blasphema ejus interpretatione vindicasse. Non volebat ad hanc versionem explicandum vel vertendum esse textum Ebraeum. Non volebat in Scholas vel Ecclesias introductas illas phrases, λόγον creatum esse, Christum esse creatum. Abhorrebat ei animus ab omni novitate & sæpe ad mentionem novarum phrasium & sententiarum inculcabat illud Salomonis, Ne moveas terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui. Quid ergo? Jam diximus, hoc operam dedisse pium senem, juventuti ut persuaderet, Græcum textum, prout in codicibus vulgatis extat, sic posse exponi, ut nec Ebraeæ veritati, nec orthodoxæ sententiæ, sed contra Arianorum hæresi obvertat cornua. Dixi prout in vulgatis codicib. extat, κύριος ἐκτισέ μη η. & ι. in authoribus Græcis sæpe permutata esse non ignorabat. Observat. libro x. cap. 11. non abnuit, Psalm. 104. 24. ἐσοφώθη ἡ γῆ τῆς κτίσεως σου, primitus scriptum fuisse κτίσεως, quod & codices nonnulli legunt. At eosdem interpretes hoc loco primitus scripsisse ἐκτησε, quod postea corruptum sit in ἐκτισε, non poterat adduci ut crederet. Neque isti conjecturæ assensum suum facile commodabit, qui istas rationes expenderit. 1. omnes Græcorum codices constanter legere ἐκτισε 2. τὸ ἐκτισε vix Græcum videri. Aquila enim vetustus interpres cum istam significationem exprimere vellet, dixit ἐκτίσατο Et Lxx. illud κτάω in forma activa nunquam usurparunt. Neque Lexicographi meminerunt. 3. Idem ἐκτισα. verbum קנה alibi quoque à Lxx. Interpretibus per κτίζω reditum, ut Genes. xiv. 19. & 22. iv. Chaldæum quoque interpretem hoc ipso loco τὸ קנה per ברא expressisse. Sed audi ipsum Drusium in Epistola quadam ἀνεκδότῳ sic scribentem,
units.tr: Against these most evident passages, which are as many confessions, nothing can be objected except that position which I set out above. Yet there was nothing in it that he had not already noted here and there in his earlier writings. The learned old man thought that by this answer (for he believed himself its first author until he was compelled to consult other authors on this passage) he had broken Arius's right leg and rescued a most noble passage from his blasphemous interpretation. He did not want this version to require the Hebrew text to be explained or translated. He did not want those phrases, that the Word was created and that Christ was created, to be introduced into the schools or the churches. His mind shrank from every novelty, and when he mentioned new phrases and opinions he often impressed on us the saying of Solomon: Do not move the ancient landmarks, which your fathers have set. What then? We have already said that the pious old man took pains to persuade the young that the Greek text, as it stands in the common manuscripts, could be so explained that it sets its horns against the Arian heresy, not against the truth of the Hebrew nor the orthodox opinion. I said, as it stands in the common manuscripts: the Lord created me [κύριος ἐκτισέ με]. He did not ignore that ι and η are often interchanged in Greek authors. In his Observations, book 10, chapter 11, he did not deny that in Psalm 104:24 [ἐσοφώθη ἡ γῆ τῆς κτίσεως σου] the word was first written κτίσεως, as some manuscripts also read. But he could not be brought to believe that the same translators had first written ἐκτησε in this passage, which was later corrupted into ἐκτισε. Nor will anyone who weighs the following reasons readily give his assent to that conjecture: 1. All Greek manuscripts consistently read ἐκτισε. 2. The form τὸ ἐκτισε hardly seems Greek. For when the ancient translator Aquila wished to express that meaning, he wrote ἐκτίσατο; and the Septuagint never used κτάω in the active form, nor do the lexicographers mention it. 3. The same verb ἐκτισα is rendered by the Septuagint with κτίζω elsewhere too, as in Genesis 14:19 and 22; and the Chaldee paraphrast in this very place rendered the Hebrew word qanah [קנה] by bara [ברא]. But hear Drusius himself, writing in a certain unpublished letter:

units.la: Quaritur, inquit, an Christus dici possit creatus? Et respondeo nullo modo dici posse, si creatus proprie accipiat, ut olim Arrius, cum diceret, Creationem in Deo esse generationem. Nam sic omnes res creatæ à Deo essent genitæ, & per consequens Christus non esset unigenitus. Ad hac, si creatus diceretur hoc sensu, esset quoque creatura, Si creatura non esset creator. Creatorem autem unà cum Patre esse, omni omnino inter orthodoxos caret controversia. Non ergo creatus. Amplius quaritur, an ullo modo dici possit creatus? Nam legimus in Sirach, Dominus creavit me, & in Apost. Hebr. 3. Qui fecit eum. * Facere autem est creare, Gen. 1.1. In Græca Ed. In principio ἐποίησεν id est creavit. Respondi ante, nec adhuc muto, verbum creoin linguis improprie sumi pro procreo, gigno. Et hoc sensu Christum posse dici creatum, id est genitum. Ante annos xix. idem scripsi in notis ad * Sirach, Verba sunt, creavit eam.] Salomo dixerat Proverb. 8. 28. possedit, ubi Gr. & Chald. creavit. Quæ si placet de Filio Dei accipere (fecit autem hoc universa antiquitas) debes exponere, creavit, id est, genuit. Nam hac duo se mutuò explicant in linguis. Cic. lib. 1. de Repub. Patria antiquior est parens, quàm is, qui, ut ajunt, creaverit. Virg. citante Lact. lib. 5. 10. Sulmone creatos. Quatuor hos juvenes. Et contra, Psal 90. 2. antequam montes gignerentur, vel si mavis, nascerentur, id est, crearentur. Hæc illic. His nemo unquam contradixit non Gallus, non Germanus, non Anglus, ac ne quidem Inquisitores Hispaniæ, quorum censuras habeo in has notas meas ex Bibliotheca Bodleiana ad me transmissas.
units.tr: It is asked, he says, whether Christ can be called created? And I answer that he cannot be so called if "created" is taken properly, as Arius once did when he said that creation in God is generation. For in that sense all created things would be begotten by God, and consequently Christ would not be the only-begotten. Furthermore, if he were called created in this sense, he would also be a creature, and if he were a creature he would not be the Creator. But that the Creator is together with the Father is beyond all controversy among the orthodox. Therefore he is not created. It is further asked whether he can be called created in any way. For we read in Sirach, The Lord created me, and in the Epistle to the Hebrews 3, He who made him. But to make is to create, Genesis 1:1. In the Greek edition, in the beginning ἐποίησεν, that is, he created. I answered before, and do not change my view now, that the verb to create in the languages is improperly used for to procreate or beget. And in this sense Christ can be called created, that is, begotten. Nineteen years ago I wrote the same in my notes on Sirach. Those are the words: "created her" [ἔκτισεν]. Solomon had said in Proverbs 8:28, "he possessed," where the Greek and the Chaldee have "created." If you are pleased to apply this to the Son of God (and all antiquity has done so), you must explain "created" as "begot." For these two words explain each other in the languages. Cicero, book 1 of On the Republic: "The fatherland is an older parent than the one who, as they say, created him." Virgil, quoted by Lactantius, book 5: "born at Sulmo, these four youths." And conversely, Psalm 90:2: "before the mountains were begotten, or if you prefer, were born, that is, were created." So far he. No one has ever contradicted these views, not the French, not the Germans, not the English, and not even the Inquisitors of Spain, whose censures I have from the Bodleian Library, sent to me for these notes of mine.

units.la: Postea plenius ostendit, voces istas in linguis promiscuè sæpe sumi. Ecce enim Ezech. 21.30. In loco ubi creata es id est genita, nata. Tremellius, procreata. Psal. 102. Populus qui creabitur id est nascetur; generabitur. Ps. 104. 31. Immittis Sp. tuum & creantur, id est generantur. Individua enim propagantur per generationem. contra Ps. 90. 2. antequam montes gignerentur, id est, crearentur. Adde Deut. 32.18. צור ילדך petra quæ genuit te, oblitumes, quæ eodem versu explicantur, & oblitus es Dei formatoris tui tui. Seneca apud Iactant. cap. 1. cap. 4. ex mente suæ sectæ, Deus, inquit, cum prima fundamenta molis pulcherrima jaceret, ut omnia sub ducibus suis irent, quamvis ipse se per totum corpus intenderet, tamen ministros regni sui Deos genuit. Genuit id est fecit interprete Lipsio 1. Physiolog. dissertat. 20. Vide apud Besoldum p. 137. In Chaldaismo, Koheleth 4. 3. Melior est ille qui nondum creatus est, id est genitus, natus. Et Prov. 8. Dominus possedit me, Chald. בראני creavit me id est genuit. Ad quem locum Scindlerus in Pentaglotto, בראי Chaldais de generatione. Horat. Fortes creantur fortibus. Et Cicero, Quaritur uxor liberis creandis. Lxx. quoque Ezech. 21. 30. Ebræum ברא per γεννάω interpretati sunt. Et Sirach quater usus fuit verbo κτίζω de Sapientia, vid. cap. 1. 4. prima omnium creata est (κτισθη) sapientia id est, ante omnem creaturam genita est, eo loquendi modo, quo Apostolus Christum vocat πρωτότοκον omnis creatura. & vers. 8. Dominus creavit eam, ἐκτησε. & cap. 24. vers. 12. aliis 8. & vers. 14. aliis 10. ᾧ ἀιῶν ἡ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἐκτισέ με. ubi ἀπ' ἀρχῆς verti potest, ante initium. Non dubitant eruditi quin Siriachides utroque oculo ad locum Proverb. respexerit. Et certe locus primus admodum firmat communem lectionem Proverb. 8. 22. iisque adversatur qui ἐκτησε scripsere. Tunc enim & illic legendum esset ἐκτισθη, quod Græcum non est. Atque ut ad Belgicam linguam tandem descendamus, quis non concesserit libens, probabilem esse eorum originationem, qui Belgarum baren, ab Ebræo בראי bara deducunt. Quis Chaldaeorum בר filius ab eodem themate derivantes solide refutaverit? Sed mittamus ista & aperiamus fontem ex quo oritur illa vocum & interpretamentorum commutatio. Bellarminus lib. 1. de Christo, cap. 18. ad Arianorum argumentum quod ex hoc loco depromebant, responsurus, quinto loco exhibet responsionem quam vocat pulcerrimam & in qua ipse videtur conquiescere; quam adscribit concilio cuidam catholico orientali & Thomæ quoque probatam asserit. Summa huc redit, divinam generationem habere aliquid analogum * generationi & creationi, ac proinde nunc verbum creandi, nunc gignendi in hoc mysterio adhiberi. Mihi non lubet in arcanum illud altius penetrare. Tutius erit dryphacta & cancellos Grammatices non excedere. Multi sunt Hellenisticæ linguæ idiotismi. Quos, nisi Ebraice intelligas, haudquaquam solide intelliges. Cur quæso te, δένδρον arbor & ξύλον lignum, toties mutuas operas præstant? ut ex. gr. Apoc. 2. ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς lignum vitæ id est, arbor. Et apud Lxx. toties, ut tantum decies & quater δένδρον verterint. Certe non alia causa assignari potest, quam quod vox Ebraea יש ad utrumque indifferens est. Cur θυμὸς excandescentiam & venenum significat? In prima signific. passim obvium est. In altera Apoc. 18. 3. ἐκ οἴνου θυμοῦ, ex vino veneni id est venenato. ut & Jobi 6. 4. sumitur. certe non alia hujus rei causa est, quam quod Ebraeum הַמָּר utrumque significat. Cur τέλειος perfectus toties ponitur pro integro, insucato? Certè non aliam ob causam, quam quod vox Ebræa חָמִים & hoc & illud significat. 1. Cor. 13. Absorpta est mors eis νῖκος id est in perpetuum. Hic εἰς νῖκος ponitur pro, εἰς αἰῶνα. Quod inde manifestum evadit, quod Esa. 25. unde locus desumptus, sit לָנֶצַח / Quod nunquam significat, in victoriam. Cum autem apud profanos νῖκος nusquam æternitatem significet, cur apud Apostolum? Ratio hæc est, quod vox Ebræa נֶצַח & victoriam (νῖκος) & αἰῶνα significet, vid. quando habet ante se litera ל / Atque hinc est, quod Lxx. τὸ לָנֶצַח / quod nunquam aliter accipitur, quam pro לְעוֹלָם in æternum, Amos cap. 1. 11. verterint εἰς νῖκος, ut & Aq. & Symmachus & Theodotio Prov. 21. 28. & Ps. 13. vers. 2. Δωρεὰν gratis, in novo testam. usurpatur pro μάτην id est frustra. Galat. 2. si per legem justitia, tunc Christus Δωρεὰν ἀπέθανε, Vulg. gratis mortuus est id est μάτην frustra id est sine ulla causa, vel ut alii, sine adeptione finis. Ps. 109. 3. oppugnaverunt me δωρεάν, Vulg. gratis id est sine ullo meo merito, sine ulla causa. Unde hæc enallage? Ex eo quod Ebræum חִנָּם utrumque significat. Ea enim voce excluditur causa, meritum, merces, pretium, fructus, effectus, pro diversitate locorum. Unde variis modis redditur, sine causa, sine merito, sine mercede, sine pretio, hoc est, gratis: sine fructu & effectu, hoc est frustra. Sic καπία malitia Matth. 6. 34. & passim in V. T. apud Lxx. pro κακώσει id est afflictione ponitur, quia vid. vox Ebr. עָנָה utrumque denotat. Ad eundem modum ἐργάζομαι & ἐργάζω passim usurpatur in sacris pro λειτουργός & λειτουργίαν, quia vid. עָבַד utrumque significat. Nec alia dari ratio potest, cur δυνάμεις pro exercitu, (ut in eo, χιλιὰς δυναμέων, δυνάμεις δ' ἐχθρῶν,) ut & virtus virtus apud vulg. Dominus virtutum, virtutes cæli, item pro divitiis, (ut Ruth. 4. 11. fac δυνάμιν virtutem in Ephratha & Prov. 31. Multa filia fecerunt δυνάμιν id est comparârunt sibi opus) usurpetur, nisi quod vox הַיִל & potentiam significet, & omne id, in quo hominum potentia videtur consistere, ut sunt exercitus, divitiæ, &c. Et ut finem faciam, cur αἰῶνες Ebr. 1. 2. per quem condidit τὰς αἰῶνας, pro mundo adhibent, nisi quod vox עוֹלָם & seculum .i. αἰῶνα, & mundum .i. κόσμον significet, ut cum Deum vocant רִבְנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם Dominum mundi, quo sensu Interpretes & plerique eandem vocem in ipsis Bibliis accipiunt. Kohel. 3. 11. κοσμος.
units.tr: Afterwards he shows more fully that these words are often used interchangeably in the languages. See Ezek. 21.30: in the place where you were created, that is, begotten, born. Tremellius renders it procreata. Ps. 102: the people which shall be created, that is, shall be born, begotten. Ps. 104.31: send forth your Spirit and they are created, that is, begotten, for individuals are propagated by generation. Against this, Ps. 90.2: before the mountains were begotten, that is, created. Add Deut. 32.18, צור ילדך, the Rock that begot you, which in the same verse is explained as you forgot God your former. Seneca, cited by Lactantius (ch. 1 and ch. 4), says in the mind of his sect: "God, when he laid the most beautiful first foundations of the mass, so that all things might go under their leaders, though he himself stretched through the whole body, nevertheless begot the ministers of his kingdom, gods." Begot, that is, made, according to Lipsius, Physiolog. diss. 20. See Besold, p. 137. In Chaldaism, Eccl. 4.3: better is he who has not yet been created, that is, begotten, born. And Prov. 8: the Lord possessed me, where the Chaldee has בראני, created me, that is, begot me. On this place Schindler in the Pentaglot notes that the Chaldeans use create of generation. Horace: brave men are created from brave men. And Cicero: a wife is sought for the creating of children. The LXX also rendered the Hebrew ברא in Ezek. 21.30 by γεννάω [gennaō, beget]. And Sirach used the verb κτίζω four times of Wisdom (see ch. 1.4: wisdom was created first of all [κτισθη], that is, was begotten before every creature, in the manner of speaking by which the Apostle calls Christ the firstborn of every creature [πρωτότοκον]); and in v. 8, the Lord created her [ἐκτησε]; and in ch. 24.12, in other copies 8; and in v. 14, in other copies 10: from the beginning, before the ages, he created me [ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἐκτισέ με], where ἀπ' ἀρχῆς may be rendered before the beginning. Scholars do not doubt that the son of Sirach looked to the passage in Proverbs with both eyes. And certainly the first place strongly confirms the common reading of Prov. 8.22, and runs against those who wrote ἐκτησε; for then ἐκτισθη would have to be read there, which is not Greek. And to come at last to the Belgic tongue: who would not gladly grant that the derivation is probable of those who derive the Belgian baren from the Hebrew בראי bara? Who would soundly refute those who derive the Chaldean בר, son, from the same root? But let us set these aside and open the source from which this interchange of words and renderings arises. Bellarmine, in book 1 de Christo, ch. 18, replying to the Arian argument drawn from this place, offers in the fifth place an answer which he calls very beautiful and in which he himself seems to rest; he ascribes it to a certain Eastern Catholic council and asserts that Thomas also approved it. The sum comes to this: the divine generation has something analogous to generation and to creation, and therefore in this mystery now the word create, now beget, is employed. I do not wish to penetrate that mystery more deeply. It will be safer not to go beyond the dry dust and the bars of grammar. There are many idioms of the Hellenistic language, which you will by no means understand soundly unless you understand them in Hebrew. Why, I ask you, do δένδρον, tree, and ξύλον, wood, so often do each other's service? As in Rev. 2: ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς, the tree of life, that is, the tree. And in the LXX so often, indeed some forty times, they translated with δένδρον. Certainly no other cause can be assigned than that the Hebrew word עץ is indifferent to both. Why does θυμός signify both excitement and poison? The first meaning is found everywhere. In the second, Rev. 18.3, ἐκ οἴνου θυμοῦ, of the wine of poison, that is, poisoned, as also in Job 6.4. Certainly there is no other reason for this than that the Hebrew חֵמָה signifies both. Why is τέλειος, perfect, so often put for whole, unblemished? Certainly for no other reason than that the Hebrew word תָּמִים signifies both. 1 Cor. 15: death is swallowed up in victory [εἰς νῖκος], that is, forever. Here εἰς νῖκος is put for εἰς αἰῶνα. This becomes clear from the fact that in Isa. 25, from which the passage is taken, the text is לָנֶצַח, which never means unto victory. But since νῖκος nowhere in profane writers signifies eternity, why does it do so in the Apostle? The reason is that the Hebrew word נֶצַח signifies both victory (νῖκος) and eternity (αἰῶνα), as is seen when it has the letter ל before it. And hence it is that the LXX rendered לָנֶצַח, which is never otherwise taken than for לְעוֹלָם, forever, in Amos 1.11, by εἰς νῖκος, as also Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion did in Prov. 21.28 and Ps. 13.2. Δωρεάν, freely, in the New Testament is used for μάτην, that is, in vain. Gal. 2: if righteousness is by the law, then Christ died freely [δωρεὰν ἀπέθανε]; the Vulgate, died gratis, that is, in vain, that is, without any cause, or as others say, without attaining the end. Ps. 109.3: they fought against me δωρεάν, the Vulgate gratis, that is, without any merit of mine, without any cause. Whence this enallage? From the fact that the Hebrew חִנָּם signifies both. For by that word cause, merit, reward, price, fruit and effect are excluded, according to the variety of places. Hence it is rendered in various ways: without cause, without merit, without reward, without price, that is, freely; without fruit and effect, that is, in vain. So too καπία, malice, in Matt. 6.34 and everywhere in the Old Testament in the LXX is put for κακώσει, that is, affliction, because the Hebrew עָנָה denotes both. In the same way ἐργάζομαι and ἐργάζω are used everywhere in sacred writings for λειτουργός and λειτουργίαν, because עָבַד signifies both. Nor can any other reason be given why δυνάμεις is used for army (as in χιλιὰς δυναμέων, δυνάμεις δ' ἐχθρῶν), and likewise virtus, virtue, in the Vulgate, as in the Lord of virtues, the virtues of heaven, and also for riches (as in Ruth 4.11, do δυνάμιν, virtue, in Ephrathah, and in Prov. 31, the virtuous woman has done δυνάμιν, that is, has acquired for herself wealth), except that the Hebrew word חַיִל signifies both power and everything in which human power seems to consist, such as armies, riches, and so on. And to make an end: why do they use αἰῶνες, in Heb. 1.2, through whom he made the ages [τὰς αἰῶνας], for the world, except that the Hebrew word עוֹלָם signifies both age (αἰῶνα) and world (κόσμον)? So they call God רִבְנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, Lord of the world, in which sense the interpreters and most of them take the same word in the Bible itself, Eccl. 3.11 (κόσμος).

units.la: Ex his, quæ paucula ex multis sunt, exemplis extruximus aliquando hanc regulam, Interpretamentum significationis unius, sæpe adhibetur pro interpretamento significationis alterius apud priscos S. Literarum Interpretes. Vide Grammaticam nostram ad finem paraenesis.
units.tr: From these examples, which are a few out of many, we have at some time constructed this rule: An interpretation of one signification is often used for an interpretation of another signification among the early interpreters of Holy Scripture. See our Grammar at the end of the paraenesis.

units.la: Atque huc refero duo illa, de quibus impræsentiarum nobis sermo est, vocabula, creo & gigno. Cum enim vox Ebræa קָנָה utrumque in S. I. significet, quid miramur, si alterum pro altero usurpetur; קָנָה κτάομαι & primario significat possideo, vel acquiro. Jam vero Pater acquirit quem gignit, unde per gigno interpretantur, Zach. 13. 5. הִקְנָנִי / LXX. ἐγέννησέ με, genuit me. Mater itidem acquirit & possidet quem parit unde pro pario usurpatur Gen. 4 קָנִיתִי possedi .i. peperi virum cum DOMINO. Deus possidet Filium suum, quem genuit ab æterno, unde pro gigno positum est Prov. 8. DOMINVS possedit me, &c. id est, genuit. Deus itidem possidet, quicquid creavit, unde pro creare usurpatur Genes. 14. 19. Deo altissimo הַקֹּנֶה possessori cœli & terræ .i. creatori, LXX. ὁ ὕψιστος τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, qui creavit, &c. Creare ergo & gignere aliquando significationes suas permutant. At inquies hoc ipsum esse, quod Arius volebat. Sic enim apud Athanas. p. 89. Editionis Comelinianæ inquit, τὸ ἐκτισεν ὅτι τὸ γεννηθὲν μεταλαμβάνω id est vocem ἐκτισε accipio pro ἐγέννησε. Cumque regereret Athanasius, Si genitus non creatus, Si creatus, non genitus, respondit Arius, ὅτι Θεὸς τὸ λεγόμενον καὶ γεννᾶν ταυτὸν ἐστι .i. gignere & creare in Deo idem esse. Hanc machinam sic retudit beatus noster Senex in comm. posterioribus ad 2. Cor. 4. pag. 106. Idem Tertullianus,inquit,
units.tr: To this I refer those two words under discussion at present, create and beget. For since the Hebrew word קָנָה signifies both in Holy Scripture, why should we wonder if one is used for the other? קָנָה [kanah], κτάομαι, primarily means to possess or to acquire. Now a father acquires the one he begets, whence they translate it by beget: Zech. 13.5, הִקְנָנִי; the LXX, ἐγέννησέ με, begot me. A mother likewise acquires and possesses the one she bears, whence it is used for bear: Gen. 4, קָנִיתִי, I have possessed, that is, I have borne a man with the LORD. God possesses his Son, whom he begot from eternity, whence it is put for beget in Prov. 8, the LORD possessed me, and so on, that is, begot. God likewise possesses whatever he has created, whence it is used for create in Gen. 14.19: to God Most High, הַקֹּנֶה, possessor of heaven and earth, that is, creator; the LXX, ὁ ὕψιστος τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, the Most High, who created heaven and earth, and so on. Therefore create and beget at times exchange their meanings. But you will say this is just what Arius wanted. For thus in Athanasius, p. 89 of the Commelin edition, he says: τὸ ἐκτισεν, ὅτι τὸ γεννηθὲν μεταλαμβάνω, that is, I take the word made [ἐκτισε] in the sense of begot [ἐγέννησε]. And when Athanasius objected, "If begotten, not created; if created, not begotten," Arius replied that for God, to be called and to beget are the same thing [ὅτι Θεὸς τὸ λεγόμενον καὶ γεννᾶν ταυτὸν ἐστι], that is, to beget and to create are the same in God. This machine our blessed Senex has refuted in the later commentaries on 2 Cor. 4, p. 106: The same Tertullian, he says,

units.la: Christum factum & creatum dixit, id est genitum. Verbum gigno accipiendo in propria significatione, & facio, vel creo in impropria vid. pro gigno. Aliter Arrius, qui Christum dicebat creatum proprie; genitum improprie. Nam omnis creatio, inquiebat, in Deo generatio est. Quod si verum, Christus non esset unigenitus. Phui τὴς Θεολογίας πάντης. Nam si creatus fuit ex substantia Patris id est genitus. Quae est impropria verbi significatio, ut recte Athan. observat orat. 3. adversus Arianos.
units.tr: Christ is said to be made and created, that is, begotten. I take the verb "beget" in its proper sense, and "make" or "create" in an improper sense, for "beget". Arius, on the other hand, said that Christ was created in the proper sense and begotten only improperly. For, he said, all creation is generation in God. If that is true, Christ would not be the only-begotten. [Greek: φησὶ τῆς Θεολογίας πάσης]. For if he was created out of the substance of the Father, he was begotten. This is an improper use of the word, as Athanasius rightly observes in his third oration against the Arians.

units.la: Similia extant in comm. prioribus ad Philip. 4. 5. quae non lubet ascribere, quia prolixiora sunt. Et certe istam Arii fuisse mentem, tum ex omnibus Theologorum veterum, queis cum eo ejusve sequacibus res fuit, libris, tum vero potissimum ex eodem loco Athanasii liquet. Cum n. Athanasius ex isto ejus axiomate, creare & gignere in Deo idem esse, inferret, omnes ergo creaturas filios Dei esse, rogaretque quomodo ergo Christus unigenitus? Arius nihil nisi de quodam inter creaturas excellentia respondit. Illud jam restat, ut ostendam, complures quoque alios qua prisco qua novellos, in articulo de SS. Trinitate orthodoxos, eandem responsionem de permutatione vocum creo & gigno, eadem mente, qua Drusius, passim inculcasse. Et quidem primo offert se hic Athanasius, qui orat. 3. adversus Arianos sic inquit.
units.tr: Similar passages are found in my earlier commentary on Philippians 4 and 5, which I do not think it worth copying out, since they are rather long. And certainly it is clear from all the old theologians who dealt with Arius and his followers, in their books, and above all from this very passage of Athanasius, that this was Arius's view. For when Athanasius drew from this axiom of his, that to create and to beget are the same in God, the conclusion that all creatures are therefore sons of God, and asked how then Christ is the only-begotten, Arius answered only that he is excelled among creatures in some way. It remains now for me to show that many others, both ancient and recent, who were orthodox on the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, often urged the same answer, the interchange of the words "create" and "beget", and in the same sense as Drusius. And first there is Athanasius himself, who in his third oration against the Arians says the following.

units.la: Ne igitur ex verbo controversias captent; si sancti alicubi pro vocabulo gignere et creare subjiciunt, cum in ejusmodi locis significatio non variet, sed id quod secundum naturam est insinuet. Et mox, Quum opus aliquod aut creatura prodierit, tunc propria ac idonea voces sunt, operatus est, condidit: cum autem Germen aut Filius, de quo mentio habetur, tunc fecit & creavit improprie de ea pronunciantur.
units.tr: So then, let them not seize on the word to make controversies. If the saints somewhere put "beget" and "create" side by side, since in such passages the meaning does not change, but expresses what is according to nature. And soon after: When some work or creature has come forth, then "he worked" and "he founded" are fitting and proper words; but when it is the Shoot or the Son of whom mention is made, then "he made" and "he created" are said of him improperly.

units.la: Eadem habet Tertullianus contra Praxeam & alibi. Unde Beatus Rhenanus in admonitione de dogmatibus Tertulliani ita inquit, Adhac Filium, qui & sermo & Sophia Patris dicitur, non tam genitum, productum, natum, procedentem & emanantem dicit, quam creatum a patre, conditum & factum, quod alioqui sacris literis (non originalibus Rhenane, quando de Christo ut Deo agitur) peculiare est. Sed malo te, inquit, ad sensum rei, quam ad sonum vocabuli exerceas. Eadem invenies apud Cyrillum, cujus testimonium allegat quoque Bellarminus, qui quartus hic nobis erit advocatus. Non defatigabo me, ut ostendam, eum in doctrina de Deitate Filii Dei arctissimum cum Ecclesiis nostris consensum colere. Quis enim tam in controversiis hospes, hoc ut nesciat? Is ergo libro 1. cap. 18. controverf. 2. de Christo, ad objectionem Arianorum ex loco Prov. 8, 22. depromptam, inter alia sic inquit.
units.tr: Tertullian has the same in his book against Praxeas and elsewhere. Whence Beatus Rhenanus, in his preface on Tertullian's doctrines, says: Moreover, he says that the Son, who is also called the Word and the Wisdom of the Father, is not so much begotten, brought forth, born, proceeding and issuing forth, as created, founded and made by the Father, which otherwise is peculiar to the sacred letters (not the original ones, Rhenanus, when Christ is spoken of as God). But I would rather, he says, that you exercise yourself on the sense of the matter than on the sound of the word. You will find the same in Cyril, whose testimony Bellarmine also cites, and he will be our fourth advocate here. I will not weary myself by showing that he holds the closest agreement with our Churches in the doctrine of the Deity of the Son of God. For who is so much a stranger to controversies as not to know this? He, then, in book 1, chapter 18, controversy 2, on Christ, answering the objection of the Arians drawn from Proverbs 8:22, says among other things the following.

units.la: Secunda responsio est Athanasii Serm. 3. contra Arianos & Cyrilli lib. 5. Thesium cap. 6. qui dicunt Scripturam promiscue usurpare vocabula faciendi, creandi, gignendi. Nam Deut. 32. dicitur, Deum qui te genuit dereliquisti. Et tamen legimus Gen. 1. Fecit Deus hominem, itaque non ex solo verbo creavit aut genuit, sed ex adjunctis sensum Scriptura elicere oportet. Et quia hic dicitur Filius creatus, antequam Deus quicquam faceret, apparet, creatum dictum esse progenitum.
units.tr: The second answer is that of Athanasius in his third sermon against the Arians, and of Cyril in book 5 of his Thesaurus, chapter 6, who say that Scripture uses the words "make", "create" and "beget" interchangeably. For in Deuteronomy 32 it is said, "You have forsaken God who begot you". And yet we read in Genesis 1, "God made man"; so he did not create or beget only by the word, but the sense of Scripture must be drawn from the attendant circumstances. And because here it is said that the Son was created before God made anything, it is clear that "created" means "begotten".

units.la: Hanc responsionem non castigavit in Animadverf. suis Junius, qui alias acutum videt. Plane in eundem modum Drusius, ac si ex Cyrillo & Athan. descripsisset, Ergo inquies, Christus creatura? Non hoc dico, sed creatum dici posse, quia genitum. Nec ego hoc dico, sed vetus Synagoga sic locuta fuit, cum dixit Messiam ante mundum creatum fuisse. Nihil profecto ante mundum creatum fuit proprie loquendo. Debemus ergo creatum ibi accipere pro genitum. si ergo vetustissimi Ebrai dixerunt Messiam creatum fuisse, quis mihi vitio vortet, si hoc explico ad orthodoxam sententiam? &c.
units.tr: Junius, who in other respects sees clearly, did not criticise this answer in his Animadversions. Drusius, in exactly the same way, as if he had copied it from Cyril and Athanasius, writes: Then, you will say, is Christ a creature? I do not say this, but that he can be called "created" because he is begotten. Nor do I say this on my own, but the ancient synagogue spoke thus when it said that the Messiah was created before the world. Strictly speaking, nothing was created before the world. We ought therefore to take "created" there as meaning "begotten". If then the most ancient Hebrews said that the Messiah was created, who will blame me if I explain it in accordance with the orthodox view? etc.

units.la: Addo & Concilium Catholicum Orientale, apud Hilarium libro de Synodis can. 5. Cujus Patres sic introduct Hilarius loquentes,
units.tr: I add also the Catholic Council of the East, cited by Hilary in his book on the Synods, canon 5, whose Fathers Hilary introduces speaking as follows:

units.la: Impietatis haereticorum hinc profana praesumptio est, quod legisse se dicant, Dominus condidit vel creavit me; sed consequentem sententiam subtrahentes, ex qua intelligentiam prior sumit, ex prima arripiunt impietatis sua authoritatem: ut creaturam dicant, quia Sapientia dixerat se creatam. Qua si creata est, quomodo potuit & nasci, quia omnis nativitas, quacunque est in naturam suam, ex natura gignente consistit. Creatio autem sumit exordium de creantis potestate, potente sc, creatore ex nihilo condere creaturam. Sapientia itaque qua se dixerat creatam, eadem in consequenti dixit se & genitam.
units.tr: The unbelieving heretics make a profane presumption from this, that they say they have read, "The Lord founded me, or created me". But leaving out the following sentence, from which the first gets its meaning, they seize on the authority of their impiety from the first words alone, so that they call the Wisdom a creature because she said she was created. But if she was created, how could she also have been born? For every birth, whatever it is, consists in a nature from a begetting nature in its own kind. Creation, however, takes its beginning from the power of the one who creates, the Creator, who founds a creature out of nothing. Therefore the Wisdom, who had said that she was created, in what follows also said that she was begotten.

units.la: Ad haec verba ab ipso quoque Bellar. loco praedicto producta & approbata, sic quoque magnus ille Theologus Ioh. Rainoldus, in censura sua librorum Apocryphorum, lect. 75. pag. 890. Tomo primo.
units.tr: Bellarmine himself, in the place mentioned above, also cites and approves these words. In the same way that great theologian John Rainolds, in his censure of the Apocryphal books, lecture 75, page 890 of the first volume, says:

units.la: Ex quibus verbis ipsius Concilii, inquit Rainoldus, manifestum est, ipsos ex circumstantiis textus Prov. 8. docere, vocabulum creari usurpari improprie, & vocabulis consequentibus quasi corrigi. Cum enim Prov. 8. in Edit. LXX. Sapientia dixisset, Dominus ἔκτισέ με creavit me, quasi statim corrigere se vellet, sequitur, ἐγέννησέ με, genuit me.
units.tr: From these words of the Council itself, says Rainolds, it is clear that from the circumstances of the text of Proverbs 8 they teach that the word "created" is used improperly, and is as it were corrected by the words that follow. For when in Proverbs 8, in the edition of the Seventy, Wisdom had said, "The Lord created me", as if she wished at once to correct herself, it follows: "he begat me", "he begot me".

units.la: Et paulò post idem Rainoldus,
units.tr: And a little later the same Rainolds:

units.la: Quare concludit Concilium illud Orientale, quod ex circumstantiis textus manifestum sit, verbum illud creandi improprie usurpari. Et iterum paucis interjectis, Quo satis docent, se tantum probare usum vocabuli (creo) ita adhibiti, ut sequatur statim castigatio atque correctio.
units.tr: Therefore that Eastern Council concludes that, from the circumstances of the text, it is clear that the word "create" is used improperly. And again, a few lines later: By which they sufficiently show that they are only proving the usage of the word "create" when it is so employed that a correction and amendment immediately follows.

units.la: Hinc Cl. vir D. Conradus Deckerus, Theologus Heidelbergensis in Indice, quem ex Praelectionibus Rainoldi collegit, in litera C sic ait,
units.tr: Hence the distinguished man, D. Conrad Decker, theologian of Heidelberg, in the index which he compiled from Rainolds's lectures, says under letter C:

units.la: Creatus esse Filius Dei non potest dici nisi addita aliqua castigatione.
units.tr: The Son of God cannot be called "created" unless some correction is added.

units.la: NOTA. Si non potest dici, nisi addita aliquâ castigatione, Ergo dici potest castigatione addita. At Drusius in thesi castigationem addit, creatus, inquit, id est genitus. Et sic LXX. excusavit, ut jam vidimus, Concilium Orientale, non dissidente Rainoldo, qui tamen in eo à Drusio dissidet, quod hâc observatione authorem EcclesiasticI excusari non patiatur. Nam Sirach, inquit, nusquam se corrigit id est vocì creandi nunquam subjicit vocem gignendi vel similem aliquam, quâ ostendi possit, eum vocem creandi improprie usurpasse.
units.tr: NOTE. If he cannot be called "created" unless some correction is added, then he can be called so with a correction added. But Drusius in his thesis adds the correction, "created", he says, "that is, begotten". And so the Eastern Council, as we have already seen, excused the Seventy, and Rainolds did not disagree with this; yet he differs from Drusius in that he does not allow the author of Ecclesiasticus to be excused by this observation. For Sirach, he says, never corrects himself, that is, he never adds to the word "create" the word "beget" or some similar word by which it could be shown that he used the word "create" improperly.

units.la: Magnum illud Germaniæ suæ sidus Rod. Goclenius, Philosophus Marpurgensis, in Lexico suo Philosophico docet, vocem creo extra doctrinam physicam aliquando usurpari pro gigno.
units.tr: That great star of his Germany, Rodolphus Goclenius, philosopher of Marburg, teaches in his Philosophical Lexicon that the word "create" is sometimes used outside physical doctrine for "beget".

units.la: Magni nominis & meriti Theologus, David Pareus initio comm. ad Genesin docet, verbum בָּרָא creavit aliquando significare generavit. Et de voce Latinâ sic ait, Verbum creare latinâ usurpatione, proprie non est ex nihilo aliquid efficere (talis enim effectio Ciceroni & Latinis ignota fuit) sed gignere vel ordinare, &c.
units.tr: David Pareus, a theologian of great name and merit, teaches at the beginning of his commentary on Genesis that the Hebrew verb בָּרָא, "created", sometimes means "begot". And of the Latin word he says: The verb "create", in Latin usage, does not properly mean to bring something into being out of nothing (for such an effecting was unknown to Cicero and the Latins), but to beget or to arrange, etc.

units.la: C. Jansenius, Episcopus Gandavensis in commentariis suis ad Proverbia & Sirachidem, eodem plane modo haec loca vindicavit.
units.tr: C. Jansenius, bishop of Ghent, in his commentaries on Proverbs and Sirach, defended these passages in exactly the same way.

units.la: Prodeat in hanc quoque arenam magnus ille Theologus, H.
units.tr: Let there also come forward into this arena that great theologian, H.

units.la: Zanchius. Is lib.3. parte 2. de tribus Elohim, cap. 7. sic introducit Arianum; Ponam ipsa verba, ut appareat, quam procul Drusius ab Arianismo abfuerit.
units.tr: Zanchius. In book 3, part 2, On the Three Elohim, chapter 7, he introduces an Arian as follows. I will set out his own words, so that it may appear how far Drusius was from Arianism.

units.la: Instant adversarii & ajunt, ut demum loca esse in quibus sermo sit de aeterna Filii ex Patre Deo generatione, contendimus tamen non posse ex illis concludi, illum esse genitum de substantia Patris. Verbum enim gignendi accipitur Metaphorice (NB.) & improprie, nempe pro factum seu creatum esse.
units.tr: The opponents press on and say: granted that there are passages which speak of the eternal generation of the Son from God the Father, yet we maintain that they cannot prove that he was begotten of the substance of the Father. For the verb "to beget" is taken metaphorically (NB) and improperly, namely to mean "to have been made or created."

units.la: Nota rursus, Ariani agnoscebant Christum in S. L. dici & creatum esse & genitum. Sed volebant genitum improprie, creatum proprie. Drusius contra, plane ut Zanchius in Responsione: Sic enim respondet,
units.tr: Note again that the Arians acknowledged that Christ is called in Holy Scripture both created and begotten. But they wanted "begotten" to be taken improperly and "created" properly. Drusius, however, takes the opposite view, just as Zanchius does in his Reply. For he answers thus:

units.la: Resp. quasi vero nunc possimus invertere argumentum & dicere: ubicunque dicitur creatus esse, prodiisse & processisse a Patre, hu-jusmodi verba accipienda esse pro genitum & procreatum esse, juxta propriam verbi significationem.
units.tr: Reply: As if we could now turn the argument around and say that wherever it is said that he was created, and came forth and proceeded from the Father, such words should be taken to mean "begotten" and "brought forth," according to the proper signification of the word.

units.la: Quasi diceret Zanchius, Esto usurpentur de Christo quà Deo duæ hæ voces, creatus, & genitus, annon probabilius, creatum usurpari pro genitum, quam, genitum pro creatum? Aut, cur mihi non tam licet creatum accipere improprie pro genitum, quam vobis genitum improprie pro creatum?
units.tr: It is as if Zanchius were saying: suppose the two words "created" and "begotten" are used of Christ as God; is it not more probable that "created" is used for "begotten" than that "begotten" is used for "created"? Or why am I not as free to take "created" improperly for "begotten" as you are to take "begotten" improperly for "created"?

units.la: Sed clarissimè Drusio patrocinatur idem Zanchius cap. 8. Ibi enim sub initio responsurus ad loca Sirachidæ, ubi Sapientia dicitur creata, post 1. & secundam responsionem sic ait:
units.tr: But the same Zanchius clearly supports Drusius in chapter 8. There, at the outset, responding to the passages of Sirach where Wisdom is said to be created, after the first and second answers he says:

units.la: Tertiò respondetur, verbum creare pro generare positum esse, ut Basilius ait: quod etiam ὅτι γεννήσως κτίσμα καὶ ποίημα ἀγγέλοι ut exempla Scripturarum docent.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is answered that the verb "to create" is used for "to beget," as Basil says, that angels are a creature and a work of the begetter [ὅτι γεννήσως κτίσμα καὶ ποίημα ἀγγέλοι], as the examples of Scripture teach.

units.la: Et paulo est:
units.tr: And a little further on:

units.la: Ac certum est, creare saepenumero pro procreare seu gignere accipi, non autem semper pro facere ex nihilo: & contra generare pro creare.
units.tr: And it is certain that "to create" is very often taken for "to procreate" or "to beget," and not always for "to make out of nothing"; and conversely "to beget" for "to create."

units.la: Rever. D. Math. Martinius, tractatu de Deo lib. 2. cap. 12. sic inquit, בר Filius potius à בראׁ, quod usitate quidem creare, sed & generare. Nam Psal. 2. 7. pro ילדתיך in Chaldaeo est בהיתך / Et Ps. 51. 7. pro הולדני habet, cogitavit Pater למברא generare me. Et Prov. 8. 22. pro קנני in Chald. est בראני id est ut LXX. vertunt ἔκτισί με. Et hinc est quod voces creandi & generandi interdum confunduntur, qua confusio ne Arianis faveat, cavendum, & catachreses a sermone
units.tr: The Reverend Mr Matthias Martinius, in his treatise on God, book 2, chapter 12, says thus: the word for son [בר] is derived rather from the word for create [בראׁ], which usually means "to create" but also "to beget." For at Psalm 2:7, for the Hebrew "I have begotten you" [ילדתיך] the Chaldee has [בהיתך], and at Psalm 51:7, for [הולדני] it has "the Father thought to beget me" [למברא]. And at Proverbs 8:22, for [קנני] in the Chaldee is [בראני], that is, as the Seventy translate, "he created me" [ἔκτισέ με]. And hence it is that the words for creating and begetting are sometimes confused. That confusion must be guarded against, lest it favour the Arians, and the catachresis be distinguished from the proper sense of the word.

units.la: Eeee nis proprietate sunt distinguenda. Ita sane & γένεσις est non tantum fieri & creari, sed & generari ex γάω, quod est genero. Sic & Genef. 2.4. Tholedoth. generationes, dicuntur de creatione. Et sic Cassianus libro 6. de incarnatione Domini cap. 8. Idem Theologus comment. in Psalm. 2. pag. 360. de hocipso loco verba faciens, sic inquit, Itaque aut arguenda est versio Chaldaea & Graeca, cum de Filii generatione loquens, illa bera, hac, κλίζειν usurpat, aut catachresis ista orthodoxo sensu interpretanda, ut facere seu creare sit pro generare. γίνεσθαι fieri, de creaturarum generatione aliquando accipitur, & sic abusive quoque de divina generatione.
units.tr: Thus indeed γένεσις means not only "becoming" and "being created" but also "being begotten," from γεννάω, which means "to beget." So also at Genesis 2:4, the "generations" (toledoth) are said of creation. And so Cassian, in book 6 On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 8. The same theologian, in his commentary on Psalm 2, page 360, speaking of this very passage, says: "Either the Chaldee and Greek versions must be censured, since the one uses the word for 'create' and the other ἔκτισε, when speaking of the Son's generation; or else this catachresis must be interpreted in an orthodox sense, so that 'to make' or 'to create' means 'to beget.' γίνεσθαι, 'to become,' is sometimes used of the generation of creatures, and so abusively also of divine generation."

units.la: Plures habet suffragatores haec cl. viri observatio. Sed eos, quos jam adduxi, sufficere arbitror. Summam summarum paucis istis aphorismis repraesentabo.
units.tr: This observation of the distinguished man has more supporters than these. But I think those I have already cited are enough. I shall sum up the whole matter in a few aphorisms.

units.la: I. Lxx. interpretes & Sirachidem Arianae haeresi patrocinari non esse concedendum.
units.tr: I. The Seventy translators and Sirach should not be granted to support the Arian heresy.

units.la: II. Non posse eos tamen in viam reduci pro ι reponendo ϯ.
units.tr: II. Yet they cannot be brought back to the right path by substituting ι for ϯ.

units.la: III. Accepisse itaque eos vocem κτίζω, id est creo pro gigno, enallage Graecis quidem & in Theologorum scholis duriore: at apud Chald. & Latinos tralatitia. Sed & in Ebraismo voces illas aliquando commutari.
units.tr: III. Therefore the Seventy took the word κτίζω, that is "to create," for "to beget": an enallage, harsher indeed for the Greeks and in the schools of the theologians, but ordinary among the Chaldeans and the Latins. And in Hebrew too these words are sometimes interchanged.

units.la: IV. Ea correctio seu interpretatio si adhibeatur, favere illos orthodoxis.
units.tr: IV. If this correction or interpretation is adopted, those translators favour the orthodox.

units.la: V. Eam correctionem seu interpretationem multos orthodoxos literis prodidisse & suo calculo approbasse.
units.tr: V. Many orthodox writers have published this correction or interpretation in their writings and approved it with their judgment.

units.la: VI. Eam correctionem seu interpretationem in ipso textu interpretum Lxx. liquido extare. Sic enim locus integer habet,
units.tr: VI. This correction or interpretation plainly stands in the very text of the Seventy translators. For the whole passage reads thus:

units.la: Κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐθεμελίωσέ με, ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸ τοῦ τὴν γῆν ποιῆσαι — γίνωσκε με.
units.tr: [Κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐθεμελίωσέ με, ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸ τοῦ τὴν γῆν ποιῆσαι — γίνωσκε με.] "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works. Before the age he founded me, in the beginning, before he made the earth — know me."

units.la: Ecce, diserte τὸ ἔκτισε per γεννᾷ declaravit. Si dixeris, posterius potius explicandum per prius, ut solet aliquando id quod claris & propriis vocibus dictum est, obscurioribus & tropicis repeti, jubebo te textum inspicere & examinare ista, ante seculum, antequam terram fecisset. Si ante principium temporis Christus exitit, certe aeternus est & sine principio. Namque ante principium pium illud temporis non fuit tempus, sed tantum æternitas. Quicquid à Deo creatum est, in tempore creatum est. Observa denique ex voce γεννᾷ gignit Scholasticos nonnullos probasse, melius dici, Filium semper gigni, quam, semper genitum esse. Vide Magistrum Sententiarum lib. 1. dist. 9. litera L. Qui in istam sententiam citat Origenem. Sed tu observa, in Ebræo esse verbum præteriti temporis הוֹלַלְתִּי quod vulg. vers. 24. reddit. concepta eram. At vers. 25. parturiebar. Lovan. begonste ick ghebaert te worden. admodum improprie. Unde Sa, parturiebar id est gignebar. (Eadem vox extat Ps. 51. in iniquitate הוֹלַלְתִּי quam vulg. reddidit, conceptus sum.) Iun. edita eram. Deod. Jo fui produtta. Genev. J' ai este engendree.
