Hisp. fuè engendrada. Pisc. war ich geboren. Omnes bene. Luth. war ich bereyt. Belg. was ick veerdigh. Quæ minus commode dicta censeo,
units.tr: Behold, he has plainly explained ἔκτισε [created] by γεννᾷ [begets]. If you say that the more obscure should be explained by the clearer, as is sometimes done when what has been said in clear and proper words is repeated in obscure and figurative ones, I shall bid you look at the text and examine these words: before the age, before he made the earth. If Christ existed before the beginning of time, he is certainly eternal and without beginning. For before that beginning of time there was no time, only eternity. Whatever is created by God is created in time. Finally, observe that from the word γεννᾷ, begets, some of the Schoolmen have argued that it is better to say the Son is always being begotten than the Son has always been begotten. See the Master of the Sentences, book 1, distinction 9, letter L, who cites Origen in support of that view. But you should note that in the Hebrew there is a verb in the past tense, [הוֹלַלְתִּי], which the Vulgate in verse 24 renders I was conceived. But in verse 25 it renders I was in labour. The Louvain version has I began to be brought forth, quite improperly. Hence the Targum, I was in labour, that is, I was begotten. (The same word occurs in Psalm 51, in in iniquity [הוֹלַלְתִּי], which the Vulgate rendered I was conceived.) Junius: I was brought forth. Deodati: I was produced. Geneva: I have been begotten. Spanish: I was begotten. Piscator: I was born. All these are good. Luther: I was prepared. Belgic: I was made ready. These I judge less fittingly expressed.

units.la: Cap. XVI. 11. Et opera ejus omnes lapides sacculi.] Ita hunc locum restituerunt Romani correctores. Ebr. opus ejus כָּל־אַבְנֵי כִּיס omnes lapides marsupii. opus ejus, hoc est, ei placens, ut Joh. 6. 29. hoc est illud opus Dei, ut credatis, &c. כִּיס marsupium, loculus. Unde illud πολυθεύματον Ebræorum, בְּכִיס בְּכוֹס בְּפָעַם in loculo, in poculo, in ira, sc. ingenium hominis cognoscitur. Olim lapidibus pro ponderibus utebantur, eosque in sacculis asservabant. Deuteron. 25. 13. Non erit in sacculo tuo lapis & lapis id est, duplex pondus. Codices antiqui legebant, omnes lapides seculi, Carthus. id est, omnes electi, qui tanquam lapides vivi ponuntur nunc in ædificio militantis ecclesiæ, &c. Quid est ineptire si hoc non est?
units.tr: Chapter 16:11. "And all his works are the stones of the bag." The Roman correctors restored this passage thus. The Hebrew reads his work, all the stones of the purse [כָּל־אַבְנֵי כִּיס]: his work, that is, what pleases him, as in John 6:29, this is that work of God, that you believe, etc. [כִּיס] means a purse or small bag. Hence the Hebrew saying in the bag, in the cup, in anger [בְּכִיס בְּכוֹס בְּפָעַם], that is, a person's nature is known by these. Formerly they used stones as weights and kept them in bags. Deuteronomy 25:13: "You shall not have in your bag a stone and a stone," that is, a double weight. Old codices read all the stones of the age. The Carthusian: that is, all the elect, who as living stones are now placed in the building of the militant Church, etc. What is this if not foolish?

units.la: Ibidem vers. 15. כְּעָב מַלְקוֹשׁ id est sicut nubes pluviæ serotinæ. Ita nominant Ebræi pluviam, quæ in Judæa maturescentibus jam frugibus cadebat, dicitur à לקש delinetere, colligere. Illam vero, quam post sementem dabat Deus, vocant יוֹרֶה & מוֹרֶה / à יָרָה jacere, In Judæa non tam frequentes pluviæ, ut apud nos. Hieronymus comment. in Amos 4. testatur se mensibus Junio & Julio in Judæa pluviam vidisse nunquam. Hinc pluvia in messe, Prov. 26. 1. de re insolita, & intempestiva & 1. Sam. 12. 16. portenti loco habetur. Kimchi ad illum locum, Quoniam pluvia in messe novitas magna erat apud eos, ideo timuerunt valde & dixerunt runt, ora pro servis tuis, ne moriamur. Caeterum quia utraque ista pluvia, maturior & serotina (LXX. vocant ὄστρον πρωϊμον καὶ ὀψιμον, vide Deut. xi 14. Jacob. 5. 7. & alibi) plane erat necessaria, ideo & gratissima. Unde passim in sacris literis, cum de rebus gratis acceptisque sermo est ad eas fit allusio. Lutherus Deut. xi. & alibi reddidit, vroegh-regen ende sparegen. Optime, si voculas illas vroegh & spade, non ad diem, sed annum referas. Pluvia enim illa πρωϊμος (יורה) erat autumnalis: ὄψιμος vero (מלקוש) vernalis. At Jacob. v. 5. nescio quid spectans reddidit, morgen-regen ende avondregen. Quae verbio imperitiori facile imponat. Confer & Ioel 2. 23.
units.tr: In the same chapter, verse 15, [כְּעָב מַלְקוֹשׁ], that is, as a cloud of the late rain. The Hebrews so name the rain that fell in Judea when the crops were already ripening; it is derived from [לקש], to gather up. The rain which God gave after sowing they call [יוֹרֶה] and [מוֹרֶה], from [יָרָה], to throw down. In Judea the rains were not as frequent as with us. Jerome, in his commentary on Amos 4, testifies that he never saw rain in Judea in the months of June and July. Hence "rain at harvest" (Prov. 26:1) is a thing unusual and untimely, and in 1 Samuel 12:16 it is counted as a portent. Kimchi on that passage: "Because rain at harvest was a great novelty among them, they feared greatly and said, pray for your servants, that we may not die." Moreover, since both kinds of rain, the early and the late (the Seventy call them [ὑετὸν πρόϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον]; see Deut. 11:14, James 5:7 and elsewhere), were quite necessary, they were also most welcome. Hence throughout Holy Scripture, when things freely given and received are spoken of, allusion is made to them. Luther in Deuteronomy 11 and elsewhere renders them early rain and late rain (vroegh-regen ende sparegen). Very good, provided that the little words early and late refer not to the day but to the year. For the early rain (יורה) was autumnal, and the late rain (מלקוש) vernal. But at James 5:7 Luther, having some other thing in view, renders morning rain and evening rain, which could easily mislead an unskilled reader. Compare also Joel 2:23.

units.la: Prov. XVIII. In jure Canonico, itemque apud Canonistas in controversiis de matrimonio, utrum meretrix vel adultera in uxorem ducenda sit, utrum adultera retinenda, &c. allegantur saepe ista verba, Qui expellit mulierem bonam, expellit bonum, qui autem adulteram, stultus est & impius. Versus est antepenultimus; alii codices, stultus & insipiens. At Graeca habent, ἄφρων καὶ ἀσύνετος, & Biblia Clementis illam quoque lectionem exhibent. Lucas Brugensis in locis insignioribus Romanae correctionis, quo libro tanquam Masora quadam correctam illam Editionem circumvallavit, haec notat, legendum potius, impius, quod est iniquus, quam insipiens, quod idem est cum eo quod praecedit, stultus. Et tamen, Clementis authoritate insuperhabita. Lovanienses Theologi veterem Editionem Belgicam hoc loco non emendarunt. Namque & recentiores Editiones, quae in praeloquio ad postremam correctionem Romanam emendatae dicuntur, legunt: dwaes ende onwijs.
units.tr: Prov. XVIII. In canon law, and likewise among the canonists in disputes about marriage (whether a prostitute or an adulteress may be taken as a wife, whether an adulteress may be kept, and so on), these words are often cited: Whoever casts out a good woman casts out good, but whoever casts out an adulteress is foolish and impious. It is the second-from-last verse. Other manuscripts read foolish and senseless. But the Greek has ἄφρων καὶ ἀσύνετος [áphrōn kai asýnetos], and the Clementine Bibles also give that reading. Lucas of Bruges, in his notes on the more notable passages of the Roman correction, by which book he hedged round that corrected edition as with a kind of Masorah, observes: it should rather be read impious, which means unjust, than senseless, which is the same as the word before it, foolish. Yet the authority of Clement was set aside, and the Louvain theologians did not correct the old Belgic edition at this place. Indeed the more recent editions, which are said in the preface to have been emended to the last Roman correction, read: dwaes ende onwijs (foolish and unwise).

units.la: Prov. XX. 25. Ruina est homini devotare sanctos, & post vota retractare. Ita legunt Lovan. Ita & Sixtus edi jusserat. At Clemens scribi jussit, devorare. Alii legunt devocare, alii denotare, alii devovere. Quam obsequentes imperio Clementis fuerint nuperi correctores Editionis Belgicae, liquebit ex hac interpretatione, 'T is den menschen eenen val den heyligben beloven, ende na de beloften weder-roepen. Hoccine est Belgicam editionem ad veritatem editionis vulgatae nuper in urbe emendatae & restitutae corrigere, sicuti titulus promittit & Joh. Malderus in approbatione asserit? communis apud interpretes lectio est, devotare sanctos, quod Lyra, Carthus. & alii exponunt frequenter sanctis aliquid vovere, vere, Laqueus est vovere & postea pœnitere. Placus in Lexico Biblico, devotare interpretatur diris imprecationibus malum alicui optare, quæ interpretatio minus contorta est propter accusativum qui sequitur. Mitto aliarum lectionum interpretationes. Melior lectio est devorare. לוע enim est deglutire, absorbere. Sed quid hoc est, devorare sanctos? Respondet Sa, sanctos positum esse pro sancta id est, Deo sanctificata voto devorare id est consumere & non solvere. Suarez in opere de virtute & statu religionis, tomo 2. lib. v. cap. 4. de gravitate peccati violatorum votorum agens, præterea, inquit, afferri solet illud Prov. 20. ruina est homini devorare sanctos. Vbi aliqui pro devorare, legunt devotare. Sed retinenda est lectio recepta, & optimus sensus esse videtur, ut, devorare sanctos, sit temere & magna facilitate vovere. Dura certe & quam meus stomachus non concoquit, interpretatio. Putaret aliquis ל' sanctos librariorum culpa irrepsisse, pro sancta. Sed malunt hic ineptire interpretes, quam illud agnoscere. Ideo Lucas, tanquam si interpreti præsens fuisset aut calamum ejus gubernasset, masculinum sanctos, inquit, interpres noster dedit, non sancta. Ebræa habent in hunc modum, מוקש אדם ילע קדש ואחר נדרים לבקר i.e. laqueus (tendicula) est homini quod deglutit sanctum, & post vota inquirere. ילע est futurum secundum Hifyl pro ילעי / contractum, ut יבא pro יביא / Accentum autem ad penultimam syllabam rejecit sequens vox dissyllaba. Est insuper in hac voce ellipsis literæ ש / pro שׁקדש / קדש autem positum pro רבר קדש / Pagn. laqueus est homini deglutire sanctificatum, & post vota inquirere. Nefas est res Deo sacratas intervertere, aut in profanos usus convertere. temerarium & stultum est vovere, & postea inquirere, disceptare, utrum velis vel possis exolvere. Jun: post vota requirere, id est laborem in eo consumere, ut retineantur res votiva. Hæc est mens Salomonis, quam B. quoque Lutherus assecutus non est, het is den menschen een strick bet heylige te lasteren, ende daer na met geloften omgaen.
units.tr: Prov. XX. 25. It is a ruin to a man to devote the saints, and after vows to retract. So the Louvain edition reads, and Sixtus had ordered it printed so. But Clement ordered it written devorare (to devour). Others read devocare, others denotare, others devovere. How obedient to Clement's command the recent correctors of the Belgic edition were will be clear from this rendering: It is a snare to men to devote the holy, and after the vows to call them back. Is this what it means to correct the Belgic edition to the truth of the Vulgate edition recently emended and restored in the city, as the title promises and Joh. Malderus asserts in his approbation? The common reading among interpreters is devotare sanctos, which Lyra, the Carthusians and others frequently explain as vowing something to the saints: a snare is to vow and afterwards to repent. Placus in his Biblical Lexicon takes devotare to mean to wish evil on someone with dire curses, an interpretation less strained because of the accusative that follows. I pass over the interpretations of the other readings. The better reading is devorare, for לוע means to swallow down, to absorb. But what is this, to devour saints? Sa answers that sanctos is put for sancta, that is, things consecrated to God, which by vow one devours, that is, consumes and does not pay. Suarez, in his work on the virtue and state of religion, vol. 2, book 5, ch. 4, discussing the gravity of sin in those who violate vows, says: "Besides, that passage of Prov. 20 is commonly cited: it is a ruin to a man to devour the saints. Where some read devotare for devorare. But the received reading must be kept, and the best sense seems to be that to devour the saints is to vow rashly and with great ease." Certainly a harsh interpretation, and one my stomach cannot digest. Someone might suppose the word sanctos crept in through a scribe's fault for sancta. But these interpreters prefer to talk nonsense rather than admit it. So Lucas, as if he had been present at the translator's side or had guided his pen, says: "Our translator gave the masculine sanctos, not sancta." The Hebrew reads thus: [מוקש אדם ילע קדש ואחר נדרים לבקר], that is, "a snare to man is what he swallows up, holy, and after vows to inquire." ילע is the future in Hifil for ילעי, contracted, as יבא is for יביא. The following disyllabic word has pushed the accent back to the penultimate syllable. There is also an ellipsis of the letter ש in this word: for שׁקדש, קדש is put for דבר קדש. Pagnini: it is a snare to man to swallow up what is consecrated, and after vows to inquire. It is wicked to divert things dedicated to God or turn them to profane uses. It is rash and foolish to vow and afterwards to inquire, to debate whether you are willing or able to pay. Junius: after vows to seek, that is, to spend labour on this, so that the votive thing may be kept. This is Solomon's meaning, which even the blessed Luther did not reach: it is a snare to men to profane the holy thing, and afterwards to deal with vows.

units.la: CAP. XXII. 20.
units.tr: CHAP. XXII. 20.

units.la: Ecce descripsi eam tibi tripliciter.] Et hoc loco abuntur Pontificii, ut triplicem illum Scripturarum sensum stabiliant. Fateor, ex Ebræis quoque nonnullos Ebræum שׁלישׁי explicare terna, vel, triplicia, sed illi aliter explicuere. R. Sal. hæc accipit, tanquam à Deo dicta, & interpretatur de lege, prophetis & hagiographis. Alii, qui hæc in persona Salomonis monis dicta censent, putant respici ad tres libros, Proverbia, Koheleth & Canticum. Alii ad triplicem hominum statum, incipientium, proficientium & perfectorum respici existimant. Alii, triplicia, id est saepius iterata. Pagn. pertecta. Vox Ebraea pluralis numeri est à sing. שָׁלִישׁ / & proprie tertium à principe in Rep. vel militia significat, ut מְשֻׁלָּשׁ secundum. Postea extenditur ad virum principem, eximium, & in alto dignitatis gradu constitutum. Hinc alii reddunt, verba magnifica, alii, verba principalia id est principibus digna vel convenientia. Jun. [verba]ducum, hoc est, praestantissima. Confer Proverb. 8. 6. Audite, quia loquar נְגִידִים supple דִּבְרֵי / [verba] principum, id est principalia, principibus digna. vulg. de rebus magnis.
units.tr: Behold, I have described it to you threefold.] Here the Papists are busy, to establish that threefold sense of Scripture. I grant that some Hebrews too explain the Hebrew shalish [שָׁלִישׁ] as threefold or triple, but they explain it otherwise. R. Sal. takes these words as spoken by God and interprets them of the law, the prophets and the writings. Others, who think these words were spoken in the person of Solomon, suppose that three books are meant: Proverbs, Koheleth and the Song. Others think a threefold state of men is meant: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect. Others: threefold, that is, repeated more often. Pagnini: perfect. The Hebrew word is the plural of the singular שָׁלִישׁ, and properly means a third, a man from the prince in a commonwealth or in the army, as מְשֻׁלָּשׁ means second. Afterwards it is extended to a leading man, an outstanding man, one placed in a high rank of dignity. Hence some render it magnificent words, others principal words, that is, words worthy of or fitting for princes. Junius: words of leaders, that is, most excellent. Compare Prov. 8. 6, Hear, for I will speak [נְגִידִים], supply words [דִּבְרֵי] of princes, that is, princely things, worthy of princes. The Vulgate: about great things.

units.la: CAP. XXIV. Septies in die cadit justus.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24. "Seven times a day the righteous falls."

units.la: Locus iste crebro pro concione citatur adversus quorundam opiniones de perfectione hominis regeniti in hac vita. In consolationibus quoque ad erigendas poenitentium conscientias saepe depromitur. Ego moneo tironem, ut isti usui firmiora scripturae testimonia conquirat, inter quae eminent illa 1. Joh. 1. 8. & 2. 1. Et Jacob. 3. 2. Profecto si verum amamus, nimis oscitanter à plerisque divina pagina legitur. Cujus rei hic locus documentum praebet quam maxime luculentum. Primo enim illud de die, nec in Ebraeo, nec Graeco, nec Luthero, nec Belgico comparet. Quia & ab editione correcta Clementis VIII. absunt. Unde Lucas Brug. in locis insignioribus, non addas, in die, inquit. Deinde cadere hic non est peccare, sed in calamitates incidere. Hoc ex professo ostenderunt Junius in notis, W. Franzius libro de interpret. Scripturae, pag. 32. & 657. Tarnovius in Exercit. Biblicis, Coppenius ad Ps. 119. [ubi & hoc addit, locum hunc conferendum cum illo Psal. 34. 20. Multa sunt afflictiones justi; at ex omnibus ipsu eripit eum DOMINUS.] Drusius, Mercerus, Piscator, Deodatus, Genevenses & alii. Lubet hic paululum arare vitula Cl. Theologi Joh. Tarnonii. Ne insidiator, ajebat Salomon vers. 15. improbe, habitaculo justi. ne devastato ejus accubitum id est quietem ejus ne turbes. Cubare enim plirasi Scripturae est quiete & pacifice vivere, Psal. 3. 6. & 4. 9. Ratio hujus rei versu 16. apponitur, ab inutili desumpta, hoc modo, nam ut septies, hoc est saepius, cadat, Deo permittente à te improbe dejectus, justus, exurgit tamen, & proinde spes tua, qua eum periturum sperabas, decolla
units.tr: This passage is often cited in sermons against certain people's views on the perfection of a regenerate person in this life. It is also frequently brought forward in comfort, to raise up the consciences of penitents. I advise the beginner to look for firmer testimonies of Scripture for this purpose, among which stand out 1 John 1:8 and 2:1, and James 3:2. Truly, if we love the truth, the divine page is read far too carelessly by most people, and this passage provides a very clear proof of that. First, the words de die ("in the day") do not appear in the Hebrew, the Greek, Luther, or the Dutch. They are also absent from the corrected edition of Clement VIII. Hence Lucas Brug, in his notes on notable passages, says: "do not add in die." Second, to fall here does not mean to sin, but to fall into calamities. Junius in his notes, W. Franzius in his book on the interpretation of Scripture (pp. 32 and 657), Tarnovius in his Biblical Exercises, and Coppenius on Psalm 119 have shown this expressly. [Coppenius also adds that this passage should be compared with Psalm 34:20: Many are the afflictions of the righteous; but out of them all the LORD delivers him.] So too do Drusius, Mercerus, Piscator, Deodatus, the Genevans and others. Here I would like to plough a little with the heifer of the distinguished theologian John Tarnovius. Solomon says in verse 15: Do not lie in ambush, you wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous; do not lay waste his resting place, that is, do not disturb his rest. For in the idiom of Scripture, to lie down is to live in quiet and peace (Psalm 3:6 and 4:9). The reason for this is given in verse 16, drawn from the futility of the wicked man's plan, in this way: for seven times, that is, very often, the righteous man may fall, cast down by you, the wicked man, with God permitting it, yet he rises again; and therefore your hope, by which you expected that he would perish, will be cut off

units.la: Ioan. 3. Inepsisse vi- detur ex loco Luc. XVII. 4. collabit. Atque hæc est piorum sors. Quid vero improbi? Hoc docet antithesis, improbi vero corruunt malo, hoc est, vel unico malo deficiunt, dispereuntque, cum multis non frangatur justus. Subjungit egregiam admonitionem de vitanda παχαιρεσιαχος. Cum cadit inimicus tuus, ne lætator, & cum corruit, ne exultato animus tuus. Scopus ergo Salomonis & adjuncta vox corruitsatis evidenter verum loci sensum indicant. Quoties etiam קום & נפל opponuntur, tum utrumque ad calamitates respicit. & hoc (נפל) iis demergi; illud קום ex iis eluctari significat. Vide Mich. vii. 8. Amos viii. 14. & v. 20. Ierem. 25. 27. Iesa xxiv. 20. Similis & plane parallelus locus extat Ps. 37. 23. A Domino statuuntur gressus viri, cujus via delectatur. Cum cadit, non dejicitur, quia Dominus sustentat manum ejus. מוטה, ו אפלפטת. Observat porro idem Tarnovius, נפל in libro Proverbiorum sæpe pro, in calamitates incidere, at nunquam pro peccare usurpatum. Hanc quoque interpretationem Emmanuel Sa probavit, cadet] in pericula. resurget.] Augustinus, quoties ceciderit tribulationibus, non peribit, pergit Augustinus quod non de iniquitatibus, sed de tribulationibus ad humilitatem perducentibus intelligi voluit. De civit. Dei xi. 31. &c.
units.tr: John 3. It seems inappropriate to appeal to Luke 17:4 here. He falls. And this is the lot of the godly. But what of the wicked? The antithesis teaches this: but the wicked fall by evil, that is, they fail and perish through a single evil, whereas the righteous is not broken by many. He then adds a striking warning against malicious gloating [ἐπιχαιρεκακία]: "When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, let your heart not exult." So the aim of Solomon and the added word falls show quite clearly the true sense of the passage. Whenever קום and נפל are set against each other, both refer to calamities: the one (נפל) means to be sunk down by them, the other (קום) means to struggle out of them. See Micah 7:8; Amos 8:14 and 5:20; Jeremiah 25:27; Isaiah 24:20. A similar and wholly parallel passage is Psalm 37:23: "The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when his way pleases him. Though he falls, he is not cast down, for the LORD upholds his hand" (מוטה, and in the Greek ἐπαφεται). Tarnovius further observes that נפל in the book of Proverbs is often used for falling into calamities, but never for sinning. Emmanuel Sá also approved this interpretation: "falls: into dangers. rises again." Augustine: "however often he falls into tribulations, he will not perish," and he goes on to say that this is to be understood not of iniquities but of tribulations that lead to humility (De civitate Dei XI, 31, etc.).

units.la: CAP. XXV. verf. penult. Scrutator majestatis opprimetur à gloria. Et hæc sententia crebro auditur, quoties coarguenda est hominum curiositas tum in genere circa res nobis in Dei verbo non revelatas, tum in specie, ut sic loquar, circa mysteria essentiæ divinæ & trium personarum in una essentia. Atque hic in mentem mihi veniunt aurei magni Scaligeri versus, Ne curiosus quære causas omnium Quæcunque litris vu prophetarum edidit, Afflata cælo, plena veraci Deo. Nec operta sacri supparo silentii Irrumpere aude, verum adorans præteri. Nescire velle, quæ magister maximus Docere non vult, erudita inscitia est.
units.tr: CHAPTER 25, second last verse: "The one who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory." This saying is heard often, whenever human curiosity must be rebuked: both in general, concerning things not revealed to us in the Word of God, and in particular, as I may put it, concerning the mysteries of the divine essence and of the three persons in one essence. Here there come to my mind the golden verses of the great Scaliger: "Do not curiously seek the causes of all things that the prophets, inspired by heaven and full of the true God, have set down in their writings. Do not dare to break into the hidden secrets of sacred silence, but pass them by in adoration. To wish not to know what the greatest Teacher does not wish to teach is learned ignorance."

units.la: Cæterum locum citatum quod attinet, discetiro, in Ebræo nihil tale extare. Ebræa ita habent, וחקר כבודם כבוד / hoc est, ad verbum, & scrutatio gloriæ sui ipsorum gloriæ. Affixum illud non expressit vulgatus. Contra, τῷ opprimetur & præpositioni à nihil in Ebræo respondet. Versu 16. & 17. egregium præceptum dicat sapientissimus Rex, de usu amicitiæ legitimo & servanda mediocritate in congressibus. Utitur autem egregia similitudine à melle desumpta. Ut mellis usus moderatus suavis est & reficit, nimius contrà ejus insuavis est & vomitum ciet & fel generat, ita & usus amicitiæ liberalis modicus recreat, nimius odiosum reddit. Itaque rarum fac pedem tuum in domo amici tui. Ita enim malo locum interpretari, quam cum Junio, studiose contine pedem tuum à domo, &c. Quamvis sensus eodem recidat. קָרָא non solum pretiosum, sed & rarum significat, unde 1. Sam. 3. 1. pretiosum erat קר' verbum Domini in Israel, id est, rarum. & Iesa. 13. pretiosior erit vir auro, id est, rarior. Quod vero ad præpositionem ב attinet, quæ in voce מִבְּ / quis ignorat aliquando pro ב poni? LXX. σπάνιον εἴςαγε τὸν ποδα σεῖς σταυτὸ φίλον. Hoc ergo dicit Salomo, quod sententia illa Arabum exprimit, visita raro & augebis amorem, Et Martialis,
units.tr: As for the passage cited, I declare that nothing of this kind is found in the Hebrew. The Hebrew reads וחקר כבודם כבוד, that is, word for word, "and the searching out of their glory is glory." The Vulgate did not express the suffix. On the other hand, "shall be overwhelmed" and the preposition "by" have nothing corresponding to them in the Hebrew. In verses 16 and 17 the most wise King gives an excellent precept about the lawful use of friendship and the keeping of moderation in company. He uses an apt comparison taken from honey. As the moderate use of honey is pleasant and refreshing, while excess of it is unpleasant, causes vomiting and produces bile, so the moderate, generous use of friendship refreshes, while excess makes a man hateful. "Therefore make your foot rare in your neighbour's house." I prefer to interpret the passage thus, rather than with Junius, "carefully restrain your foot from your neighbour's house," etc., although the sense comes to the same thing. קָרָא means not only precious but also rare, whence 1 Samuel 3:1: "the word of the LORD was precious" (יקר), that is, rare, in Israel; and Isaiah 13:12: "a man will be more precious than gold," that is, rarer. As for the preposition ב, which is found in the word מִבְּ, who does not know that it is sometimes put for ב? The Septuagint: "Rarely set your foot in the house of your friend" [σπάνιον εἴσαγε τὸν πόδα σου εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν τοῦ φίλου σου]. So Solomon says what that Arab saying expresses: "Visit rarely and you will increase love." And Martial:

units.la: {a} Prov. observationum IV, 1. Si vitare voles acerbà quædam, Et tristes animi cavere morsus, Nulli te facias nimis sodalem. Gaudebis magis & minus dolebis.
units.tr: {a} Prov. observationum IV, 1. If you wish to avoid bitter things and the grievous bites of sad minds, do not make yourself too close a companion to anyone. You will rejoice more and grieve less.

units.la: Postea vers. 27. rursus mediocritatem in sermonibus & μεσωτλογίας, ut sic dicam, inculcaturus, per eandem comparationem ita infit, ut comedere mellis plurimum non est bonum, ita perversi-gatio honoris sui ipsorum [non est] honor, videlicet μεσωτ-λόγος. qui de suis semper virtutibus & gestis verba faciunt. Sicut qui modum excedit in esu mellis, inquit Tarnovius, sibi nocet, dum vomitum provocat, & quando voluit stomachum faburrare, eundem exonerat, sic qui apud amicos sæpe & multum sua facinora more Thrasonis ebuccinat, eos facile à se alienat, & dum honori suo voluit velificari, ignominiæ se exponit, & quo amorem & gloriam sibi voluit conciliare, eo odium & contemptum sibi acquirit. Hæc ipsissima quoque sententia est Junii, Genev. Anglorum, & aliorum. Vau pro ו nota apodoseos ponitur. Negatio ex præcedenti membro repetenda est, id quod in his literis adeo est frequens, ut supervacaneum sit huc exempla convectare. Vide tantum Ps. ix. 19. hoc ergo vult, ita non est gloria hominibus scrutatio gloriæ Sui-ipsorum. vel, neque scrutatio honoris propriè honos est hominibus. Pisc. Mercerus & alii dum noluerunt in hujus loci interpretatione nimium à recepta sententia recedere, affixum illud plurale in בְּכוֹרִים aliò retulerunt, runt, & scrutatio gloria eorum [qua *sunt instar mellis, non est] glo- ria. Quae interpretatio nimis videtur coacta, ut & illa, [ita non est bonum] investigare gloriam rerum gloriosarum. Hoc enim esset, הקר כבוד נגבַּרִים / Et ista, scrutans gravia gravatur. Hic enim af- fixum negligitur. & כבוד accipitur in significatione gravitatis proprie sic dicta, quam nullibi habet. Beati quoque Lutheri translatio, wer schwere Dingen vorschet / dem wirds zu schwer / non satis video, quomodo cum fontibus conciliare possit, nisi prius ostendatur, כבוד gravitatem vel difficultatem in literis mysticis notare.
units.tr: Afterwards, in verse 27, wishing again to press moderation in speech and what I may call the golden mean in words, he begins with the same comparison: "As it is not good to eat much honey, so to seek out one's own honour is not honour," namely, the mean in speech. This refers to those who always speak of their own virtues and deeds. Just as he who exceeds the measure in eating honey, says Tarnovius, harms himself, since he provokes vomiting, and when he wished to fill his stomach he empties it again, so he who often and at length boasts of his own exploits among friends, in the manner of Thraso, estranges them from himself easily, and while he wished to sail with the wind toward his own honour, he exposes himself to disgrace; and by what he wished to win for himself love and glory, he gains hatred and contempt. This is also the very same view held by Junius, the Genevans and others. The waw (ו) before the verb marks the apodosis. The negation is to be repeated from the preceding clause, as is so frequent in these writings that it would be superfluous to gather examples here. See only Psalm 9:19. So the meaning is: "thus it is not glory for men to search out their own glory," or, "nor is the searching out of honour truly honour for men." Piscator, Mercerus and others, unwilling to depart too far from the accepted sense in interpreting this passage, referred the plural suffix in בְּכוֹרִים elsewhere, and rendered: "the searching out of their glory [which are like honey] is not glory." This interpretation seems too forced, as does that other one, "[so it is not good] to investigate the glory of glorious things." For that would be הקר כבוד נגבַּרִים, and also the one, "searching heavy things is weighed down." For here the suffix is neglected, and כבוד is taken in the sense of gravity properly so called, which it nowhere has. Luther's translation too, "wer schwere Dingen vorschet / dem wirds zu schwer" ("he who searches out heavy things, it becomes too heavy for him"), I cannot see how to reconcile with the sources, unless it is first shown that כבוד denotes gravity or difficulty in mystical writings.

units.la: CAP. XXX. 19. viam viri in adolescentia. ] LXX. ἐν νεότητι.
units.tr: CHAP. XXX. 19. the way of a man in youth. ] LXX. in youth [ἐν νεότητι].

units.la: Hunc locum Ambrosius libro de Salomone cap. v. interpretatur de Christo, iisque quae in terra adolescens gessit. Baradius eundem allegat, ut doceat, non posse sciri gesta Christi, ab anno xii. usque ad annum baptismi. Carthusianus de quolibet homine intelligit, In adolescentia, inquit, sanguine fervente, cogitationes, desideria, verba & opera adolescentium investigabiliter & ineffabiliter mutantur. At haec a mente Salomonis aliena sunt. Nam in Ebraeo est, עלמה in adolescentula. Atque ita quoque legit Lyra, Haec est vera litera, inquit, quia sic est in Ebraeo. Quod vero per adolescentulam, B. Virginem, per virum Christum intelligit, nimis contortum est. Verba ejus haec sunt: Quia Christus in utero virginis fuit vir perfectus scientiis & virtutibus ab instanti conceptionis, & in nativitate exiit clauso utero virginis, ideo de hoc, via viri in adolescentula, dicit Salomo, hoc esse quartum quod penitus ignorat. Veram hujus loci interpretationem vide apud Junium, Mercerum, Pisc. & alios. עלמה virginem significat, sed juvenculam tam juvenculam quam vetulam. נערה juvenculam, sive virgo sit sive devirginata. Dicitur autem עלם a עלם abditum, occultum esse. Ita καταχλεισις epithetum honestiorum virginum perpetuum est. Olim enim ut notat * Casaubonus, apud Judaeos, Graecos plerosque & Romanos,' virgines domi in propriis oecis, quos Graeci παρθενῶνας cellas virginales vocant, continebantur, eratque ea pars gynaeconitidis. 2. Machab. 3. ubi describitur tumultus, cujus occasionem profanus ille Heliodorus praebuit, inter alia narrat author, virginum quoque, quae conclusae erat, (αἱ καταχλεισαι τῶν παρθένων) alias ad vestibulum & portas concurrisse, alias ad parietes, quasdam per fenestras exerto collo prospectasse. Hæc Baronius de reclusis in templo virginibus, & voto religionis obstrictis intellexit. At in Græco textu nulla templi, nulla Oniæ Pontificis mentio. Hic tamen (Onias) importune à Latino interprete in textum intrusus, frivolam illam hariolationem nonnihil videtur confirmasse. Glossa ordinaria, Virgines quæ conclusæ erant] id est, de domibus parentum non exibant ratione verecundiæ & pudicitiæ virginalis: tamen in illa perturbatione exibant præter morem sofitum currentes ad Oniam. Similis locus est 3. Machab. 1. 15. ubi in simili urbis ἀγωνίᾳ narrat author, τας καταπλέγσας παρθένους ἐν θαλάμοις id est inclusas in thalamis virgines cum matribus erupisse, &c. Notat ibidem doctissimus scriptor, apud Stephanum Ephæstionem extare hoc Lyrici Poëtæ fragmentum, Ἡ παῖς ἡ καταπλέξας, Τὸν εἰ Φαοι πεκίντες Ἐυναῖος ὀαρισμὸς Ἔχειν ἴσον ἐλέθρῳ.
units.tr: Ambrose, in his book on Solomon, chapter 5, interprets this passage of Christ and of what he did on earth as a youth. Baradius cites the same passage to teach that the deeds of Christ from his twelfth year to his baptism cannot be known. The Carthusian understands it of any man: "In youth," he says, "with the blood boiling, the thoughts, desires, words and deeds of young people change in ways that cannot be traced or described." But these ideas are foreign to Solomon's meaning. For in Hebrew the word is עלמה [almah], a young woman. Lyra also reads it so: "This is the true reading," he says, "because it is so in the Hebrew." But that he understands the young woman to be the Blessed Virgin and the man to be Christ is far too strained. His words are these: "Because Christ in the virgin's womb was a perfect man in knowledge and virtues from the moment of conception, and because he came forth from the closed womb of the virgin at his birth, therefore Solomon says of this, the way of a man in a young woman, that this is the fourth thing which he utterly does not know." The true interpretation of this passage may be seen in Junius, Mercerus, Piscator and others. עלמה [almah] means a virgin, but a young girl, as much a young girl as an old one. נערה [naarah] means a young girl, whether she is a virgin or has lost her virginity. Now עלם [‘alam] is derived from a root meaning to be hidden or concealed. So too καταχλεισις [katakleisis, confinement] is the constant epithet of respectable virgins. For formerly, as Casaubon notes, among the Jews, most Greeks and Romans, virgins were kept at home in their own rooms, which the Greeks call παρθενῶνες [parthenōnes], virgin chambers, and this was the women's quarters. In 2 Maccabees 3, where the tumult is described whose occasion was given by that profane Heliodorus, the author relates among other things that the virgins who were kept shut in (αἱ καταχλεισαι τῶν παρθένων) ran partly to the porch and gates, partly to the walls, and some leaned out of the windows with their necks stretched forth. Baronius understood this of virgins shut up in the temple and bound by a vow of religion. But the Greek text makes no mention of the temple or of Onias the high priest. Yet this name (Onias), forced into the text by the Latin translator without good reason, seems to have somewhat supported that idle guess. The ordinary gloss: "The virgins who were shut up, that is, did not go out of their parents' houses for reasons of modesty and virginal chastity; yet in that disturbance they went out beyond their customary practice, running to Onias." A similar passage is 3 Maccabees 1:15, where the author, describing the same distress of the city, tells how the virgins shut up in their chambers (τας καταπλέγσας παρθένους ἐν θαλάμοις, that is, the virgins enclosed in chambers) burst out with their mothers, and so on. The very learned writer notes there that in Stephen of Byzantium's Ephaestion there survives this fragment of the lyric poet: "The girl who plaited [her hair]..." [Ἡ παῖς ἡ καταπλέξας]; the rest runs: "...Τὸν εἰ Φαοι πεκίντες Ἐυναῖος ὀαρισμὸς Ἔχειν ἴσον ἐλέθρῳ" [the Greek as printed].

units.la: Atque huc pertinet egregius ille locus in Machabaico Iosephi, cap. 18. Casta Virgo genita sum, neque unquam ὑπερέβλω πατερῶν οἶκον. Hoc vere est καταπλῆξαι εἶναι, ἐν θαλαμευομένῃ. Nam & hoc nomine virgines à Græcis scriptoribus insigniuntur. Talem describit Hesiodus, 2. ἔργων ἡμερῶν, Ἡ τε δῶμαν ἔντοσθι φίλη ἀνδρὶ μητίεται μίμνει.
units.tr: To this belongs also that outstanding passage in the Maccabean Joseph, chapter 18: "I was born a chaste virgin, and never ὑπερέβλω [exceeded?] my fathers' house." This is truly καταπλῆξαι εἶναι [to be kept shut up], ἐν θαλαμευομένῃ [in the bridal chamber]. For Greek writers also mark virgins with this description. Hesiod describes such a woman in the second book of Works and Days: she who stays within the house, planning for her dear husband: Ἡ τε δῶμαν ἔντοσθι φίλη ἀνδρὶ μητίεται μίμνει [the Greek as printed].

units.la: Hoc decorum esse notus ille Euripidis versus in Oreste docet, Εἰς ὄχλον ἐρπεῖν παρθένοισιν ἡ καλὸν, Foras puella ut prodeant parum decet. Inter laudes quoque honestæ matronæ illa non postrema est, quod pedem domo raro efferat. Unde eas Græci οἰκουρούς, (ad Titum 2. 5.) & οἰκουρίας καὶ οἰκουρικάς, ἡ οἰκουρίματα, Latini casanas dixere. Qualem matronam repræsentabat Venus insidens testudini, quæ domiporta vocatur. Contra, meretricem à Chaldæis id est, prodeuntem foras vocari, quod in domo non habitent pedes ejus, ut de scorto loquitur Salomo, nemo ignorat. Sed redeamus ad עלמה / Ea hoc loco non virginem sed devirginatam puellam denotari nonnulli contendunt. Inter quos Mercerus, Drusius & alii. Ipse quoque Junius de lupa perfrictæ frontis interpretatur, sed quæ pro virgine habetur, aut saltem haberi cupit. Et certe in Scripturis tralatitium est, ut vocetur aliquis non ex eo quod revera est, sed quod esse videtur aut creditur. Ita Luna, luminare majus; idolum, Deus: pseudo-propheta, propheta appellatur. Quod si hoc modo meretrix matrona vocaretur, quis inde inferret, matronam meretricem significare? Existimo ergo, עַלְמָה vi originationis suæ virginem denotare & in scriptura non nisi de juvencula & quæ in flore ætatis est, usurpari. Nec tamen illis accedo, qui Merceri & Drusii sententiâ nobilissimum illum locum Iesaiæ 7. Ecce עַלְמָה concipiet, prodi existimant. Nam ut ut vox ea indifferens esset ad virginem & devirginatam, illic tamen istam indifferentiam vel solæ istæ voces, הַגֶּבֶר & אוֹר convulserint.
units.tr: That well-known line of Euripides in the Orestes shows that this was considered seemly: "For a maiden to go out into the crowd is not fitting" [Εἰς ὄχλον ἐρπεῖν παρθένοισιν οὐ καλὸν]. Among the praises of an honest matron, it is also no small one that she seldom sets foot outside the house. Hence the Greeks call such women οἰκουρούς [oikouroi, keepers of the house] (Titus 2:5), and οἰκουρίας καὶ οἰκουρικάς [oikourias kai oikourikas] or οἰκουρίματα [oikourimata], and the Latins called them casanae. Venus sitting on a tortoise, which is called the home-bearer, represented such a matron. On the other hand, that a harlot is called by the Chaldeans, that is, one who goes forth, because her feet do not stay in the house, as Solomon says of the harlot, nobody is ignorant. But let us return to עלמה [almah]. Some contend that here it denotes not a virgin but a girl who has lost her virginity, among them Mercerus, Drusius and others. Junius himself also interprets it of a harlot of brazen forehead, who is yet regarded, or at least wishes to be regarded, as a virgin. And certainly it is customary in Scripture to call someone not by what he really is, but by what he seems or is believed to be. So the moon is called the greater light; an idol, God; a false prophet, a prophet. If in this way a harlot were called a matron, who could infer from that that matron means harlot? I think therefore that עַלְמָה [almah], by the force of its derivation, denotes a virgin, and in Scripture is used only of a young girl who is in the flower of her age. Nor do I agree with those who think that the noble passage of Isaiah 7, "Behold, the עַלְמָה [almah] shall conceive," is betrayed by the opinion of Mercerus and Drusius. For although that word were indifferent between virgin and one who has lost her virginity, yet the words הַגֶּבֶר [hag-geber, the man] and אוֹר [’or, light?] there overturn that indifference alone.

units.la: CAP. XXXI. Noli regibus dare vinum.]
units.tr: CHAP. XXXI. Do not give wine to kings.

units.la: Non defuerunt qui his verbis, regibus vini usu interdictum existimarent. Ebr. אַל לַמְּלָכִים שְׁתוֹ יָיִן non (convenit) regibus bibere vinum. אַל pro לֹא Bibere vinum sumitur Levit. x. 6. vinum & siceram non bibes. Aliter Psal. 69. 13. נְגִינוֹת שִׁכָּר hic enim largiorem & quæ hilaritatis terminos excedit, potationem notat. In eundem modum οἰνοπότης quoque & οἰνοποτεῖν dicitur, qui vinosus est.
units.tr: Some have not been lacking who took these words to mean that the use of wine was forbidden to kings. The Hebrew is אַל לַמְּלָכִים שְׁתוֹ יָיִן, it is not (fitting) for kings to drink wine. Here אַל stands for לֹא. To drink wine is taken in this sense at Lev. 10:6, you shall not drink wine or strong drink. The word is used differently at Ps. 69:13, נְגִינוֹת שִׁכָּר, since there it denotes heavier drinking, which goes beyond the bounds of cheerfulness. In the same way οἰνοπότης and οἰνοποτεῖν are used of a man who is given to wine.

units.la: Ibid. date siceram לְאֹבֵר) Lutherus, denen, die umbkomen sollen id est morituris, aut perituris. Hæc verba ita vulgo capiuntur, ac si iis contineretur mandatum de propinando illis vino, qui capitali supplicio afficiendi sunt. Et certe huic loco natales debere suos videtur prisca illa & non improbanda consuetudo, qua olim facinorosi ad supplicium ituri haustu vini reficiebantur, quo præsenti magis animo fatum exciperent. Quod vero, ad occasum jam vergente Ebræorum republica, morituris omnem rationis usum expectoraverint, quod etiamnum multis in locis facinorosi, instante supplicii tempore, ad ebrietatem impleantur, aut bibere permittantur, id vero plusquam belluinum est. De Judæis testem habemus Maimonidem, cujus in Halacha Sanhedrin cap. 13. hæc verba sunt, postquam vero confessus est, potionant eum grano thuris in calice vini, שְׁהָתָּבְר ut tollatur ab eo intellectus & inebrietur. Hoc est, ut externatus & inebriatus careat sensu doloris & horrorem supplicii minus attendat. Atque ad hanc consuetudinem referunt inters interpretes, quod de οἶνῳ τεμαγμένῳ id est, interprete Syro, vino cui mixta erat myrrha, Marcus in historia passionis prodidit. Ut vel Maimonides speciem pro specie posuerit, vel thuri addita fuerit myrrha. Certe de myrrha illud constat ex Galeno libro de simpl. medic. xv. 19. eam, si largius cum vino bibatur, vel obumbrare mentem vel accelerare fatum. Sed & ex Apulejo liquet, verberandos praesumptione myrrhae se munire solitos fuisse. Indidem, inquit, se multimodis commaculat ictibus, myrrhao praesumptione munitus. Et libr. x. obfirmatus myrrhae praesumptione multis ictibus & ne ipsi quidem succubuit. Atque huc facit, quod doctissimus Hispanus, Laurentius Ramirez in Pentecontarcho notavit, sicuti Romani olim, feminae Erucae in vinum infuso, ita etiamnum in Hispania, eos qui tormentis subjiciendi sunt, thure & myrrha (nota) se indurare, atque eo modo severos judices eludere. Sed redeamus eis παρούσαν, ex qua divertimus. Aliud est dare siceram, aliud est inebriare & usum rationis tollere. Sed nec ulla necessitas est per אובד moriturum intelligere. Potest enim de paupere exponi ut hoc dicat, date siceram pauperi, cujus res & fortunae pereunt, quem etiam Belgae idiomate suo perire dicunt, hy gaet verloren. Eam interpretationem firmant frequentia, Bibat & oblivisctatur דשׁ paupertatis sua. Sic AbenEzra eandem illam vocem exponit Deut. xxvi. 4. pater meus erat pauper Syrius, quid est OBED inops, omnium egenus. In cujus loci interpretatione impegit vulgatus, quando ita vertit, Syrius persequebatur patrem meum, quem etiam B. Lutherus secutus est. Hoc enim esset מאבד vel מאביד / Quod si vero lubeat vocem Ebraeam paulo laxius accipere pro misero, maesto, tunc illi qui ex sententia judicis morituri sunt, ea voce, tanquam species genere, continebuntur. Haec laxior interpretatio firmatur ex altero hemistichio, & vinum illis qui amaro sunt animo. Nihil enim frequentius est in hoc libro, quam illud quod primo hemistichio dictum est, altero diversis verbis repetere. Hinc Lxx. δὸς μεθλω τοῖς ἐν λυπαῖς. Et vulg. date siceram moerentibus. Junius date siceram peritura, hoc est, ei qui prae anxietate & amaritudine animi prope est ut pereat. Atque ita reddunt locum illum Deuteronomii. Syrus miser erat pater meus. Hinc orta videtur ea consuetudo, qua calice consolationis recreabantur, qui suos sepeliverant, de quo Jeremias xvi. 7. Dices, si bibere vinum verf. 4. est inebriare annon dare vinum, hoc loco erit inebriare? Respondeo, concessionem esse, cujus iste sensus est, Si quando largius bibere oporteret vel liceret, magis id conveniret miseris & afflictis, quam regibus. Illi enim obesent nemini. Hi officii sui facile obliviscerentur. Adhæc, miseris & afflictis unicum fere & facillimum comparatu & præsentissimum curarum levamen vinum est, Regibus vero, præter vinum, innumera suppetunt alia, queis animum laxare & vires laboribus exhaustas redintegrare queant.
units.tr: Ibid. give strong drink to those who are perishing (לְאֹבֵד). Luther renders this denen, die umbkomen sollen, that is, to those who are to die or perish. These words are commonly understood as if they contained a command to give wine to those who are to be put to death. And certainly this passage seems to be the source of that ancient and not unreasonable custom by which criminals on their way to execution were once refreshed with a draught of wine, so that they might meet their fate with greater courage. But that, when the Hebrew commonwealth was nearing its decline, the condemned should have been deprived of all use of reason, as in many places even now criminals, when the time of punishment is at hand, are made drunk or allowed to drink, is more than bestial. We have a witness about the Jews in Maimonides, whose words in Halacha Sanhedrin, ch. 13, are these: after he has confessed, they give him a grain of incense in a cup of wine, שְׁהָתָּבְר so that his understanding is taken from him and he becomes drunk. That is, so that he, stupefied and intoxicated, may lack a sense of pain and attend less to the horror of execution. And to this custom the interpreters refer what Mark reported in his account of the Passion concerning wine mixed (οἶνῳ τεμαγμένῳ), which, as the Syriac interpreter has it, is wine in which myrrh was mixed. Either Maimonides put one thing for another, or myrrh was added to the incense. Certainly it is established from Galen, On Simple Medicines, bk. 15, ch. 19, that if myrrh is drunk in larger amounts with wine, it either clouds the mind or hastens death. Apuleius also makes it plain that those who were to be beaten used to fortify themselves with a preparation of myrrh. From there, he says, he defiles himself with blows of many kinds, fortified by the preparation of myrrh. And in bk. 10: made firm by the preparation of myrrh, he did not yield even to many blows. To this point also belongs what the most learned Spaniard Laurentius Ramirez noted in his Pentecontarchus: just as the Romans once infused the women's eruca into wine, so even now in Spain those who are to be subjected to torture harden themselves with incense and myrrh (note this), and in that way mock severe judges. But let us return to our present subject (εἰς τὴν παροῦσαν), from which we have digressed. To give strong drink is one thing; to make a man drunk and remove the use of reason is another. Nor is there any necessity to understand אובד as about to die. It can be explained of a poor man, so that the sense is: give strong drink to the poor man whose property and fortune are perishing, whom the Dutch in their own idiom also call hy gaet verloren, that is, one who is ruined. The frequent use of the phrase let him drink and forget דשׁ his poverty confirms this interpretation. So Abenezra explains the same word at Deut. 26:5, my father was a poor Syrian, that is, OBED, needy, destitute of everything. In interpreting this passage the Vulgate stumbled, when it rendered it the Syrian persecuted my father, which Blessed Luther also followed. For the Hebrew would have to be מאבד or מאביד. But if one is willing to take the Hebrew word a little more loosely for wretched, sorrowful, then those who are to die by the judge's sentence are included under that word, as a species under a genus. This looser interpretation is confirmed by the second half of the verse, and wine to those who are bitter in soul. Indeed nothing is more common in this book than to repeat in the second half, in different words, what was said in the first. Hence the Septuagint has δὸς μέθυ τοῖς ἐν λύπαις, and the Vulgate give strong drink to the sorrowful. Junius has give strong drink to the perishing, that is, to one who, from anxiety and bitterness of spirit, is nearly ruined. And in this way they render that passage of Deuteronomy: my father was a wretched Syrian. From this, it seems, arose the custom by which those who had buried their dear ones were refreshed with the cup of consolation, of which Jeremiah speaks in ch. 16:7. You will say: if to drink wine in v. 4 means to become drunk, will to give wine here not mean to make drunk? I answer that this is a concession, and its sense is this: if at any time it were fitting or allowed to drink more freely, this would suit the wretched and afflicted better than kings. For the former harm no one, whereas the latter could easily forget their duty. Moreover, for the wretched and afflicted wine is almost the only, and the easiest to obtain, and the most ready relief from cares; but kings, besides wine, have countless other means at hand by which they can relax their minds and restore strength exhausted by labours.

units.la: VANITAS vanitatum] De voce הבל quæ in Ebræo, diximus pag 238. August. libro de moribus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, cap. xxi. de vana cognitione & mundo hoc fugiendo verba faciens, locum istum ita citat, Vanitas vanitantium. Verba doctissimi patris ista sunt, Huic ergo authoritati, si de veteri testamento quæram quid comparem, plura quidem invenio, sed unus Salomonis liber, qui Ecclesiastes dicitur, copiosissime in summum contemptum ista perducit. Incipit enim sic, vanitas vanitantium, dixit Ecclesiastes, &c. Hac verba omnia si attendantur, si pendantur, si discutiantur, multa inveniuntur per necessaria illis, qui hunc mundum fugere & refugere in Deum desiderant. Sed longum est & alio festinat oratio. Talitamen principio constituto, exequitur omnia, vanitantes esse eos, quirebus istiusmodi fallluntur. Hæc Aug. fœdo imperitissimi librarii errore deceptus. Ipse hoc agnovit, retractationum lib. i. cap. vii. Quod posui, inquit, de libro Salomonis, vanitas vanitantum, in multis quidem codicibus legi, sed hoc Græcus non habet. Habet autem, vanitas vanitatum. quod postea vidi, & inveni eos Latinos esse veriores, quihabent vanitatum. Ex occasione tamen hujus mendositatis quacunque disserui, vera esse in rebus ipsis apparent.
units.tr: VANITAS vanitatum] On the word הבל, which is in the Hebrew, I spoke at page 238. Augustine, in his book on the morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 21, where he speaks of vain knowledge and of fleeing this world, cites this place as Vanity of those who are vain. The words of that most learned father are these: If I seek from the Old Testament what to set beside this authority, I find many things; but the one book of Solomon called Ecclesiastes sets these matters out most fully, in the deepest contempt. For it begins thus: "Vanity of those who are vain," said Ecclesiastes, etc. If all these words are attended to, weighed and examined, many things are found that are necessary for those who desire to flee this world and return to God. But it would be long, and my discourse hastens elsewhere. Having laid this principle down, he goes on to show that those are vain who are deceived by such things. Augustine was misled here by the gross error of a very unskilled scribe, and he himself acknowledged this in the first book of the Retractations, chapter 7: What I put down from the book of Solomon, "Vanity of those who are vain," I have read in many codices; but the Greek does not have it. It has, however, "Vanity of vanities." I later saw this, and found that the Latin copies which have "of vanities" are more accurate. Nevertheless, on the occasion of this error, whatever I have discussed appears true in the things themselves.

units.la: CAP. IV. 15. cum juvene secundo, quis resurget pro eo? Ita legit Ambrosius, & per juvenem secundum, Christum introduxit, tellexit. Paulo post, eodem tamen capite, ista subjicit: Ipse ergo ex Israel transivit hanc portam, ipse dux sedit in ea quando verbum raro factum est & habitavit in nobis, quasi rex sedens in aula regali uteri virginalis vel in olla serventi, sicut scriptum est, Moab aula spei, vel olla spei meæ. Utrumque enim diversis in codicibus invenitur. Aula regalis est virgo, quæ non est viro subdita, sed Deo soli. Est & olla uterus Mariæ, quæ spiritu ferventi, qui supervenit in eam, replevit orbem terrarum, cum peperit salvatorem. Confer nunc ea quæ supra ad Psalm. Lx. notavimus. Ebraea ita habent ad verbum, interpretibus Pagnino & Aria, Vidi cunctos viventes sub sole cum nato secundo, qui stabit pro eo. אשר יעמוד תחתיו / Lxx. quoque ὃς ςήσεται ἀντ' αὐτοῦ. Vulg. qui consurget pro eo. Hoc vult, opinor, plures adorare solem orientem quam occidentem. A qua sententia immane quantum aberravit Ambrosius.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. 15. with the second youth, who will rise up in his place? Ambrose reads it thus, and understood by the second youth Christ. A little later, in the same chapter, he adds these words: He himself therefore passed out of Israel through this gate; he himself, as leader, sat in it when the word was rarely made flesh, and dwelt among us, like a king sitting in the royal hall of the virginal womb, or in the seething pot, as it is written, "Moab is the hall of hope," or "the pot of my hope." For both readings are found in different codices. The royal hall is the virgin, who is not subject to a husband but to God alone. The pot is also the womb of Mary, which, with the seething Spirit that came upon her, filled the whole earth when it brought forth the Saviour. Now compare what we noted above on Psalm 60. The Hebrew has it word for word, in the translations of Pagninus and Arias: I saw all the living under the sun with the second child, who will stand in his place [אשר יעמוד תחתיו]. The Seventy too: who shall stand in his place [ὃς στήσεται ἀντ' αὐτοῦ]. The Vulgate: who shall rise up in his place. I suppose this means that more people worship the rising sun than the setting one. Ambrose has strayed enormously from this sense.

units.la: CAP. IX. Nescit homo utrum amore vel odio dignus sit, sed omnia in futurum servantur incerta] Valde vexatus est hic locus à Theologis, tum in controversia de Verbo Dei & vulgatæ Editionis authoritate, tum etiam in controversia de certitudine salutis.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred, but all things in the future are kept uncertain. This passage has been much troubled by the theologians, both in the controversy concerning the Word of God and the authority of the Vulgate edition, and also in the controversy concerning the certainty of salvation.

units.la: Omnes illi qui adversus primam controversiam Bellarmini scripserunt, hunc locum diligentissime examinarunt. Sed & illi, qui tomum ultimum sibi examinandum sumsere. Vide Pareum, Amesium, & prolixissime hunc locum tractantem Chamierum, tomo 3. καταφρονία catholicæ. Librum, caput, & paginam index tibi monstrabit: Lubet autem hic quoque exhibere sententiam reverendi viri, D. Ludovici de Dieu, amici nostri, qui in privata ad me epistola ita infit. Addo versum 1. capitis ix. unde Pontificii Herculeum scutum fingunt pro incertitudine gratiæ. Videtur mihi in sola distinctione erratum, qua observata, locus planus evadit. Sic verto, Justi & sapientes, & opera eorum in manu Dei sunt, etiam amor & odium; (certe hic est accentus rebiang) non norunt homines quicquam eorum quæ ante ipsos sunt. Dicit ergo, amorem & odium, sicuti justos & opera eorum, in potestate Dei esse. Vident homines ante se, quibus bene, quibus male sit. At quinam Deo invisi, quinam cari sint, non norunt, &c. Hactenus doctissimus ille verbi divini interpres. In cujus expositione acquiesco. Liceat quoque adjicere expositionem Salmeronis Jesuitæ, quæ extat in comment. ejus ad 2. Cor. 12. disp. 14. Hic locus, inquit, nequaquam probat quod aliqui inde accipiunt, hominem nescire amorem Dei erga se, quia sequitur in textu, vel odio, &c. At impii propter maxima sua scelera norunt se maxime dignos esse odio Dei. Haec Jesuita.
units.tr: All those who wrote against Bellarmine's first controversy examined this passage most diligently, and so did those who took up the last volume for examination. See Pareus, Amesius, and Chamier, who treats this passage most fully in volume 3 (the index will show you the book, chapter and page). It is also worth giving here the opinion of the reverend man, Dr. Louis de Dieu, our friend, who in a private letter to me begins thus: "I add verse 1 of chapter ix, from which the Papists fashion a Herculean shield for the uncertainty of grace. It seems to me that the error lies only in the punctuation; once this is observed, the passage becomes plain. I render it: 'The just and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God, even love and hatred' (certainly here the accent is rebia); 'men do not know anything of those things which are before them.' He says, therefore, that love and hatred, just as the righteous and their works, are in the power of God. Men see before them who fares well and who fares badly; but who is hated by God and who is loved, they do not know, etc." So far that most learned interpreter of the divine Word. I rest content with his exposition. I may also add the exposition of the Jesuit Salmeron, which is found in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 12, disputation 14: "This passage, he says, by no means proves what some take from it, that a man does not know God's love towards him, because the text goes on, 'or hatred,' etc. For the wicked, on account of their very great sins, know that they are most worthy of God's hatred." So far the Jesuit.

units.la: ORdinavit in me charitatem.] Huic loco superstruxit Thomas prolixissimam disputationem, de ordine charitatis, secunda secundae quaest. 26. Et Magister lib. 3. distinct. 29. Multa fateor, illic bona sunt; at hunc locum eo non pertinere intrepide affirmo & pronuntio. Ebraea ita habent, יִגְלוּ עָלַי אַהֲבָה Pagn. Arias, & vexillum ejus super me amor. Jun. habens pro vexillo amorem erga me. דגל extra controversiam vexillum. Lxx. legerunt דגלו / reddunt enim ταξαπ επ εμε αγαπην. & Symm. επισωρευσατε μοι αγαπην, coacervate mihi caritatem. At quid vidit vulg. quando reddidit, ordinavit? In דגל nulla ordinis significatio est. Atque hic locus in memoriam mihi revocat celebrem illum locum Roman. xiii. 1. ubi in vulg. vulgo legitur, quae autem sunt a Deo, ordinata sunt. In jure Canonico, extravagant. comm. lib. 1. titulo de major. & obed. cap. 1. Bonifacius VIII. ex verbis Apostolorum, Ecce duo gladii hic, id est, in Ecclesia, & responsione Christi, Satis est, prolixe disserit de duplici gladio, spirituali & materiali, utrumque esse in potestate Ecclesiae, hunc pro Ecclesia, illum ab Ecclesia exercendum: illum manu sacerdotis, hunc manu regum, sed ad nutum Pontificis esse stringendum. Gladium esse sub gladio &c. Hoc vero probat Bonifacius ex Rom. cap. xiii. quae autem sunt a Deo, ordinata sunt. Verba ejus haec sunt. Oportet autem gladium esse sub gladio, & temporalem authoritatem spirituali subjici potestati. Nam cum dicat Apostolus, non est potestas nisi a Deo, quae autem sunt a Deo, ordiordinata sunt, non autem essent ordinata, nisi gladius esset sub gladio, & tanquam inferior reduceretur per alium in suprema. At qui Græce intelligunt, sciunt τάξεις etiam esse constituere. & usurpari quoque sine ullo respectu ordinis. Unde & Emm. Sa vocem ordinata, interpretatur, posita. Abutitur quoque hoc Apostoli loco Thomas, quando prima secundæ quæst. 102. art. 1. quæstionem illam, utrum cæremonialia præcepta habeant finem, sic definit, cum sapientis sit ordinare secundum Philosophum in 1. Metaphys. ea quæ ex divina sapientia procedunt, oportet esse ordinata, ut Apostolus dicit ad Romanos. Locus autem iste in conclusione ita quoque distinguitur, Quæ autem sunt à Deo, ordinata sunt. Atqui Græca alium plane sensum habent. αἱ δὲ ἐξουσίαι, ὑπὸ θεοῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσίν quæ autem sunt potestates, à Deo ordinatæ, id est, constitutæ sunt. Unde in Editione Clementis locus iste sic legitur & distinguitur, quæ autem sunt, à Deo ordinata sunt. Vide & Erasmum.
units.tr: "He set love upon me" (Ordinavit in me charitatem). Thomas built a very lengthy disputation on this passage, on the order of charity, in the second part of the second part, question 26. The Master, book 3, distinction 29, does the same. I grant that much of what is said there is good, but I boldly affirm and declare that this passage has nothing to do with it. The Hebrew reads יִגְלוּ עָלַי אַהֲבָה [yigelu alai ahavah]. Pagninus renders it: "and his banner over me is love"; Junius: "having love toward me as a banner." That דגל means a banner is beyond dispute. The Seventy seem to have read דגלו, for they render it "set love upon me" [ταξατε ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ ἀγάπην], and Symmachus, "heap up love for me" [ἐπισωρεύσατε μοι ἀγάπην]. But what did the Vulgate see when it rendered it "set in order" (ordinavit)? There is no sense of order in דגל. This passage brings to my mind the famous text of Romans 13:1, which in the Vulgate is commonly read as quae autem sunt a Deo, ordinata sunt. In the canon law, Extravagantes communes, book 1, title on majority and obedience, chapter 1, Boniface VIII, from the words of the apostles, "Behold, here are two swords" (that is, in the Church), and Christ's answer, "It is enough," discourses at length on the twofold sword, spiritual and material, both being in the power of the Church: the one to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church; the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of kings, but to be drawn at the nod of the Pontiff. The sword must be under the sword, and so on. Boniface proves this from Romans 13: "Those things which are from God are ordered". His words are these: "It is necessary that the sword be under the sword, and that temporal authority be subject to spiritual power. For since the Apostle says, there is no power but of God, and those powers that are of God are ordered (ordinata), they would not be ordered unless the sword were under the sword and, as an inferior, were led back through another to the highest." But those who understand Greek know that τάξεις also means to set in place (constituere), and is used without any reference to order. Hence Aemilius Sadoletus also translates the word ordinata as posita (placed). Thomas also misuses this passage of the Apostle when, in the first part of the second part, question 102, article 1, he settles the question whether the ceremonial precepts have an end in this way: "since it belongs to the wise to order, according to the Philosopher in Metaphysics book 1, those things which proceed from divine wisdom must be ordered, as the Apostle says to the Romans." Yet in that conclusion the passage is also punctuated thus: "Those things which are from God are ordered." But the Greek has a quite different sense: αἱ δὲ ἐξουσίαι, ὑπὸ θεοῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσίν [the powers that exist are ordained by God], that is, "the powers that are, are ordered (set in place) by God." Hence in the edition of Clement this passage is read and punctuated thus: "those that are, are ordered by God." See also Erasmus.
