units.la: QUI vivit in æternum creavit omnia simul.] Ab hoc, opinor, loco, si non ortum, at saltem præcipuum robur habet vetus illa & nondum ex scholis explosa opinio, Deum omnia uno die creasse. Augustinus ut hanc sententiam defendat, omnes ingenii sui vires intendit. Libro de civ. Dei xi. cap. 9. Nimirum ergo si ad istorum dierum opera pertinent angeli, ipsi sunt lux illa, quæ diei nomen accepit. Cujus unitas ut commendetur, non est dictum, dies primus, sed dies unus. Nec alius est dies secundus aut tertius aut ceteri, sed idem ipse unus ad implendum senarium vel septenarium numerum repetitus est, propter senariam vel septenariam cognitionem. Sed vide illum argutius philosophantem cap. vii. ejusdem libri, & libro 4. de Genesi ad literam cap. 33. ubi multa de cognitione matutina & vespertina. per vesperam intelligit obscuriorem cognitionem Angelorum, qua res in se ipsis cognoscunt. Scientia enim omnis creaturæ, inquit, respectu creatoris quasi vesperascit. Per mane vero vel matutinam cognitionem eorundem cognitionem perfectiorem intelligit, qua res creatas in Deo intelligunt. Lucescit enim & quasi matutina fit cum ad laudem & dilectionem creatoris refertur. Procopius Gazæus numerum dierum non temporis gratia à Mose assumptum esse putavit, sed tantum docendi gratia, ob nostri intellectus imbecillitatem, quæ rerum creatarum ordinem propter earum multitudinem alio modo comprehendere non poterat. Eandem sententiam constabilitum ivere ex cap. 2. Genes. vers. 4. in die quo fecit Dominus cœlum & terram & omne virgultum, &c. an Deus omnia uno die creaverit. Quid ad eum locum respondeat Thomas parte 1. qu. 74. art. 2. non ignoramus. Existimamus tamen facillimam responsionem istam esse, diem pro tempore positum. Unde & Junius, qua die, id est, quo tempore, quomodo & Sa vocem illam interpretatus est. Cæterum locum istum Sirach quod attinet, ad eum varie responderunt interpretes, qui paradoxam illam Augustini sententiam longe à se preverunt. Non lubet omnia producere. Duæ responsiones sufficerint. quarum prior est, omnia simul, hoc est uno tempore creata esse quantum ad rerum substantiam quodammodo informem. Ita & Thomas in summa, parte 1. qu. 74. art. 2. Carthus. omnia simul id est primo die creata dicit in materiis & formis subsistentialibus. Altera, eaque simplicior, in Græco esse κοινῇ, quæ vox hic non significet tempus, sed comprehensionem partium, q. d. tam hoc quam illud. Jansenius ad hunc locum, τὸ simul, non identitatem temporis designat, sed universa sine exceptione comprehendit, sicut apud Joh. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, &c. Ita & Cornel. à Lapide ad Genes. 1. Simul, inquit, non referendum est ad creavit, sed ad, omnia. & Genebr. ad Psalm. 32. Ebræis & nobis 33. Deus creavit omnia simul, id est, nullo dempto, ad unum omnia, ne quis existimet Deum aliqua non creasse cum Manichæis. Verbo, Græcum κοινῇ respondet Ebræo יַחַד vel יְחַדְיו /
units.tr: "He who lives for ever created all things together." I think it is from this passage that the old opinion, not yet driven out of the schools, that God created everything in a single day, takes its origin, or at least its chief strength. Augustine exerts all the powers of his intellect to defend this view. In book 11, chapter 9 of The City of God: Certainly, then, if the angels belong to the works of those days, they are that light which received the name of day. And so that its unity may be commended, it is not said "the first day" but "one day." Nor is the second day or the third or the rest different; rather, the same one day is repeated to complete the number six or seven, on account of the senary or septenary knowledge. But see how more subtly he philosophises in chapter 7 of the same book, and in book 4 of On Genesis according to the Letter, chapter 33, where he has much to say about morning and evening knowledge. By evening he understands the more obscure knowledge of the angels, by which they know things in themselves. For all knowledge of a creature, he says, is, in relation to the Creator, as it were growing dark. By morning, or morning knowledge, he understands the more perfect knowledge of the same angels, by which they understand created things in God. For it becomes light and, as it were, morning when it is referred to the praise and love of the Creator. Procopius of Gaza thought that Moses used the number of days not for the sake of time but only for teaching, on account of the weakness of our understanding, which could not otherwise grasp the order of created things because of their multitude. The same view was strengthened by those who ask, from Genesis 2:4, in the day that the Lord God made the earth and the heavens, and every plant of the field, etc., whether God created everything in one day. What Thomas answers to that passage in part 1, question 74, article 2, we are not unaware. Yet we think that answer very easy: the word "day" is put for a time. Hence also Junius interpreted that word as on which day, that is, at which time, and Sa likewise interpreted that term. As far as the passage in Sirach is concerned, however, the interpreters who have departed far from that paradoxical opinion of Augustine have answered it in various ways. I do not wish to bring forward everything; two answers will suffice. The first is that "all together" means that all things were created at one time, as far as their substance, which was in a way formless, is concerned. Thomas also says this in the Summa, part 1, question 74, article 2, and the Carthusian: "all together," that is, he says they were created on the first day in matters and in subsisting forms. The other, and simpler, is that in the Greek the word is κοινῇ, which here does not signify time but the inclusion of parts, as if to say: this as well as that. Jansenius on this passage: "together" does not designate identity of time but embraces all things without exception, as in John, "All things were made by him," etc. So also Cornelius à Lapide on Genesis 1: "Together," he says, is not to be referred to "created" but to "all things." And Genebrardus on Psalm 32 (in the Hebrew and our numbering 33): God created all things together, that is, with none left out, all things as one, lest anyone think, with the Manichaeans, that God did not create some things. In a word, the Greek κοινῇ corresponds to the Hebrew יַחַד or יְחַדְיו [yachad, yechadyav].

units.la: CAP. XXIV. 3. Ex ore altissimi prodii, primogenita ante omnem creaturam.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV, verse 3. "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature."

units.la: ] Hæc postrema verba citantur à Bellarmino, ubi de Christi Deitate disputat & Magistro Sent. parte 1. dist. 2. litera F. & Thoma parte 1. quæst. 41. art. 3. & aliis. Sed moneo lectorem meum, verba ista in Græco non extare. Proculcul dubio ex Epistola ad Col. 1. 15. huc transcripta sunt.
units.tr: These last words are cited by Bellarmine, where he disputes about the deity of Christ, and by the Master of the Sentences, part 1, distinction 2, letter F, and by Thomas, part 1, question 41, article 3, and by others. But I warn my reader that these words are not found in the Greek. Undoubtedly they have been copied here from the Epistle to the Colossians 1:15.

units.la: CAP. XLIV. Henoch—translatus est in Paradisum:] Et hic moneo, illas voces, in Paradisum, non extare in Graeco.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIV. "Enoch … was translated into Paradise."

units.la: De Henoch secundo, septimo illo ab Adam, varie moventur quaestiones ab Interpretibus. Inter alias & istae sunt. I. Utrum mortuus fuerit. Affirmant Ebraei plerique, R. Sal. AbenEzra, Brigmannus in Apocal. Non Calvinus, ut ait Corn. à Lapide. Negant Kimchi, Chaldaeus & omnes fere interpretes, freti authoritate Apostoli Ebraeorum xi. II. Quo translatus sit? 2. Reg. 2. Elias dicitur assumptus esse in coelum. At per coelum aërem multi intelligunt, per quem translatus sit in Paradisum terrestrem. Kimchi dicit, hanc esse sententiam Sapientum. Ita & Bell. Senensis, Thom. parte 1. quaest. 102. art. 2. & pag. 3. qu. 49. art. 5. & universa fere Schola. Primarius tibicen quo haec sententia sustentatur, est locus iste Sirach. Cum enim Elias & Henoch Apoc. xi. 3. ex pontificiorum sententia conjungantur, rationi consentaneum esse putarunt, eos unum eundemque locum incolere. cum ergo Henoch hoc loco in Paradisum dicatur translatus, putarunt rem quoque de Elia confectam. Quin & Senensis libro v. annot. 36. ex hoc loco coarguit Steuchi sententiam, qui negabat Henoch & Eliam in terrestrem Paradisum translatos esse, atque huic tantum insistens monimento, non erubescit asserere, illam sententiam spectare ad fidem. Sed infirmum istud munimentum est. Praeterquam enim quod necdum probatum est, per duos illos testes in Apocal. Henoch & Eliam intelligi, illud constat, voces illas, in Paradisum, in Graeco non comparere. Ita respondent, Serarius loco praedicto, Bellar. & Jansenius in comm. & alii. Et tamen Clemens VIII. voculas istas in Editione sua retinendas esse censuit.
units.tr: Here too I warn that the words in Paradisum ("into Paradise") are not found in the Greek. Concerning Enoch, the seventh from Adam, the interpreters raise various questions. Among others are these: (1) Whether he died. Most of the Hebrews affirm it, R. Solomon Ben Ezra, and Brightman on the Apocalypse; Calvin does not, as Cornelius à Lapide says. Kimchi, the Chaldee paraphrast and nearly all the interpreters deny it, relying on the authority of the Apostle to the Hebrews, chapter 11. (2) Where he was translated. In 2 Kings 2 Elijah is said to have been taken up into coelum ("heaven"). But many understand by heaven the air, through which he was carried into the earthly Paradise. Kimchi says this is the opinion of the wise. So also Bellarmine of Siena, Thomas, part 1, question 102, article 2, and part 3, question 49, article 5, and almost the whole Schoolmen. The chief support on which this opinion rests is this passage in Sirach. For since Elijah and Enoch, according to the Papists' view, are joined in Revelation 11:3, they thought it reasonable that they dwell in one and the same place. Since, therefore, Enoch is said in this passage to have been translated in Paradisum, they supposed the same was done for Elijah. Indeed Siena, in book 5, annotation 36, refutes from this passage the opinion of Steuchus, who denied that Enoch and Elijah were translated into the earthly Paradise, and, relying solely on this monument, he does not blush to assert that that opinion pertains to faith. But this support is weak. For, apart from the fact that it has not yet been proved that Enoch and Elijah are meant by the two witnesses in the Apocalypse, it is clear that those words in Paradisum do not appear in the Greek. So reply Serarius in the place mentioned, Bellarmine, Jansenius in his commentary, and others. And yet Clement VIII decided that those little words should be retained in his edition.

units.la: III. Quaeritur, ubi post diluvium fuerint Henoch & Elias. Fuerit Henoch in Paradiso usque ad diluvium. At postquam aquae diluvii eum subvertere, quo translatus sit, non de nihilo quaeritur. Hic multi negant Paradisum diluvii aquis eversum fuisse, inter quos & Bellarm. de Gratia primi hominis, lib. 1. cap. 12. & 14. Senensis ut terrorem secus censentibus incutiat, aiit hoc esse de fide, rursusque loco huic Ecclesiastici haeret, arripitque insuper illa verba, ut det gentibus poenitentiam. Nec fas est, inquit, hoc testimonium de coelesti Paradiso intelligere, quoniam non convenitconvenit, ut quis inde descendat ad prædicandum pœnitentiam. At ubi hoc dicit Sirach? Græca sunt, μετάνοια ὑποδείγμα μετανοίας τοῖς γενεαῖς ad verbum, translatus est exemplum pœnitentiæ generationibus. Hoc certe aliud est, quam transferri in Paradisum, ut inde redeas ad prædicandam pœnitentiam. Adscribam verba eruditissimi Jansenii, quæ extant in comm. ejus ad hunc locum. Henoch & Elias tempore Anti-Christi ex Paradiso venturi putantur ad prædicandum omnibus pœnitentiam, adquod confirmandum plerique hunc locum solent adducere. At ad hæc comprobanda non multum valet locus ille juxta Græcorum lectionem. Ea enim, ut satis patet, tantum significat, Henoch ex hoc mundo translatum, idque in exemplum pœnitentiæ omnibus generationibus, ut scilicet ex ejus translatione omnes intelligentes Deo cura esse, qui illi student placere, etiam ipsi convertantur & pœnitentiam agant. Possunt etiam Graecasic intelligi, ut cum dicitur Henoch translatus exemplum pœnitentiæ generationibus, significetur, eum translatum, quia cum viveret, erat omnibus exemplum pœnitentiæ, &c. Hæc ille. Redeamus ad quæstionem propositam. Dixinus non deesse, qui Paradisum adhuc superesse existimant, illisque incolas Henochum & Eliam assignant. At Genebr. Corn. à Lapide, Serarius, Jansenius, Steuchus, Pererius & alii in ea versantur sententia, Paradisum aquis diluvii vastatum fuisse. Horum ergo alii amœnam aliquam, eamque secretam terræ regionem, alii cœlestem aliquem locum, prout cœlum ab aëre distinguitur, eis assignant. Alii sibi de loco non liquere respondent. Serarius: Dico, vel incertum esse locum, vel in superiori mundo. At Corn. à Lapide comm. in Genes. p. 95. Post diluvium agit in loco aliquo amœno, quem Deus illi sive in aëre, sive in terra præparavit, ad quem post diluvium raptus est Elias. Audiamus & R. Salomonem ad 2. Reg. 2. Fieri non potest, ut intelligatur ascendisse in cælum. Quia illuc non ascendunt ista corpora. Sed hoc vult historia, sublatum eum fuisse in altitudinem aëris, sicuti dicunt, urbes magnas & munitas in cœlum usque id est in aërem, & turris cujus caput pertingebat ad cœlum usque, &c. Et ecce tulit eum spiritus Domini in legatione Domini in locum jam ignotum, atque ibi etiamnum vivit, &c. Certe in eo cum Pontificiis conspirat Rabbinus, in cœlum beatorum haudquaquam assumptum fuisse Eliam.
units.tr: (3) It is asked where Enoch and Elijah were after the flood. Enoch was in Paradise until the flood. But the question is not idle, since the waters of the flood overthrew it, as to where he was carried. Many here deny that Paradise was destroyed by the waters of the flood, among them Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, book 1, chapters 12 and 14. Siena, to frighten those who think otherwise, says this is a matter of faith, and again clings to this passage in Ecclesiasticus, and seizes in addition on those words, ut det gentibus poenitentiam ("that he might give repentance to the nations"). He says: It is not right to understand this testimony of the heavenly Paradise, since it is not fitting that someone should come down from there to preach repentance. But where does Sirach say this? The Greek reads, μετετέθη ὑπόδειγμα μετανοίας τοῖς γενεαῖς [metetethē hypodeigma metanoias tois geneais], that is, word for word, "was translated, an example of repentance to the generations." Surely this is something other than being transferred into Paradise, in order to return from there and preach repentance. I shall quote the words of the most learned Jansenius, which are found in his commentary on this passage: Enoch and Elijah are thought to come from Paradise in the time of Antichrist to preach repentance to all, and to confirm this most people are wont to cite this passage. But that passage, according to the reading of the Greeks, is of little use for proving these things. For it signifies, as is quite clear, only that Enoch was translated from this world, and that as an example of repentance to all generations, so that from his translation all who understand that God cares for those who strive to please him may themselves be converted and do penance. The Greek can also be understood thus: when it is said that Enoch was translated as an example of repentance to the generations, it is signified that he was translated because, while he was alive, he was an example of repentance to all, etc. So far Jansenius. Let us return to the question proposed. I have said there are those who think Paradise still survives, and they assign Enoch and Elijah as its inhabitants. But Genebrardus, Cornelius à Lapide, Serarius, Jansenius, Steuchus, Pererius and others hold the view that Paradise was laid waste by the waters of the flood. Of these, some assign to Enoch and Elijah some pleasant and secret region of the earth, others some heavenly place, as heaven is distinguished from air. Others reply that they are unclear about the place. Serarius: I say either that the place is uncertain, or that it is in the higher world. But Cornelius à Lapide, in his commentary on Genesis, page 95: After the flood he lives in some pleasant place, which God prepared for him either in the air or on the earth, to which Elijah was carried after the flood. Let us also hear R. Solomon on 2 Kings 2: It cannot be understood that he ascended into heaven, because bodies of this kind do not ascend there. But the history means that he was lifted up into the height of the air, just as they say great and fortified cities reached into heaven, that is, into the air, and the tower whose top reached up to heaven, etc. And behold, the Spirit of the Lord carried him away on the Lord's errand to a place still unknown, and there he is still alive, etc. Certainly in this the Rabbi agrees with the Papists, that Elijah was by no means taken up into the heaven of the blessed.

units.la: IV. Ubi jam post ascensionem Christi sint Henoch & Elias?
units.tr: IV. Where, after Christ's ascension, are Enoch and Elijah?

units.la: Ne nunc quidem cœlum beatorum iis tribuunt Pontificii. Et quare? Quia sic jam viderent Deum, non essent amplius viatores. At sunt adhuc viatores, corpus eorum necdum est glorificatum. Unde hoc probant? Rursus reponitur illa crambe, ut det gentibus pœnitentiam. Rursus adducitur locus Apocalypseos, ubi duo isti testes tempore AntiChristi redituri & mortem oppetituri dicuntur. Ad quæ jam responsum est. Ad postremum hoc addo, locum istum de duobus testibus magis incertum illos reddere, qui illis tertium Collegam adjungunt, Johannem vid. Euangelistam. Inter eos sunt Catharinus, Salmeron & Baradius. Putant enim, verba Corn. à Lapide in Genef. pag. 95. col. 2. A. Henoch & Eliam, uti & S. Johannem Euangelistam, necdum esse mortuos, ideoque eos adhuc habere mortalia corpora, venturosque esse contra AntiChristum & ab eo martyrio afficiendos. Istam autem sententiam de Johanne superstruxerunt mendoso isti loco, Johan. xxi. Sic eum volo manere, donec veniam, ad quem prolixius suo loco. Sed istam sententiam merito castigat Cornelius, & ad locum Joh. 21. cordate respondet, loqui Christum non assertive, sed conditionate, idque ad retundendam curiosam Petri interrogationem, Domine, hic autem quid? Quod vero addit. Sic eum volo manere, idem esse quod, Si eum volo manere, ut alii codices legunt, condonandum est Cornelio. Maluit enim ineptus videri, dummodo veram sententiam ostenderet, quàm textum vulgatum, & qui eum ad minimum Jota servandum sanxit, Pontificem, erroris arguere. Alias vel pueri norunt, quid Sic & Si distent. Scimus præstantissima ingenia in papatu tyrannide premi, & ora liberiora, ne veritatem proloquantur, superiorum authoritate oppilari. Ideo quod diserte pronuntiare non audent, per ambages & mæandros innuunt. Nos, ubi Henoch & Elias ante Christi in cœlos introitum fuerint, non disputamus. Qui scimus magno isti Calvino & Martyri hic rationes dubitandi tuisse. At post gloriosam ejus ἀναλαβὼν eos tertii istius cœli incolas fuisse credimus & profitemur.
units.tr: Not even now do the Papists assign the heaven of the blessed to them. And why? Because then they would already see God and would no longer be wayfarers. But they are still wayfarers, since their bodies have not yet been glorified. How do they prove this? Again that hoary old chestnut is brought out, that he may give repentance to the nations. Again the passage of the Apocalypse is cited, where these two witnesses are said to return in the time of Antichrist and to meet death. These points have already been answered. Finally, I add this: that passage about the two witnesses makes things even less certain for those who add a third colleague to them, John the Evangelist. Among them are Catharinus, Salmeron and Baradius. For they think, as Cornelius à Lapide says in Genesis, p. 95, col. 2 A, that Enoch and Elijah, and also St John the Evangelist, have not yet died, and so still have mortal bodies, and will come against Antichrist and be afflicted with martyrdom by him. They built this opinion about John on that faulty passage, John 21: So I want him to remain until I come, which I will discuss at more length in its place. But Cornelius rightly criticises this opinion, and in answering John 21 he sensibly says that Christ did not speak assertively but conditionally, and that this was to rebuff Peter's curious question, Lord, what about this man? As for his adding that So I want him to remain is the same as If I want him to remain, as some other manuscripts read, this must be pardoned in Cornelius. For he preferred to seem foolish, provided he showed the true opinion, rather than charge with error the pontiff who decreed that the Vulgate text be kept even to the least iota. Otherwise even boys know how So and If differ. We know that the most outstanding minds are oppressed by the tyranny of the papacy, and that freer mouths are stopped by the authority of superiors, lest they speak the truth. So what they do not dare to state plainly, they hint at through circumlocutions and windings. We do not dispute here where Enoch and Elijah were before Christ's entry into the heavens, since we know that the great Calvin and the martyr Peter Martyr Vermigli had reasons for doubt on this point. But after his glorious being taken up [ἀναλαβὼν], we believe and profess that they are inhabitants of that third heaven.

units.la: CUM opus hoc Typographo excudendum daremus, omnino sedebat per omnes veteris novique fœderis libros ire, & quæ jam pridem ad insigniora quædam eorum loca collegeramus, uno volumine, eoque in sex libros digesto, tibi repræsentare. Quin & animus erat ad operis calcem exercitationes quasdam super antiquitatibus & ritibus quibusdam Ebraicis, nec non dogmatibus quibusdam Judæorum, mantissæ loco adjicere. Sperabamus enim omnia ista justi voluminis molem non excessura. Hinc est quod pag. 259. dissertationem de circumcisione & phrasi illa, Excindetur anima ista è medio populi, nec non pag. 445. sententiæ Kimchianæ expositionem in locum alium rejecerimus. Eum vid. quem jam diximus. Cæterum cum opus hoc sub manu immane quantum nobis creverit, uti hic vides, necessitatem nobis impositam putavimus hic abrumpendi. Et profecto non abs re fuerit, in hac prima operis parte doctorum judicia experire. Si enim censebunt, laborem hunc nostrum juventuti non esse utilem, sat chartæ & operæ perdidimus. Si vero benigniorem calculum ponent, & Deus O. M. otium & valetudinem dederit, post exigui temporis spiramentum habebis partem universi operis alteram, vid. librum, quartum, quintum & sextum. Quorum prior circa prophetas majores minoresque; alter circa Euangelistas & Acta Apost. postremus denique circa reliquos novi fœderis libros occupabitur. Istis vero, appendicis loco adjicie. jiciemus exercitationes quasdam de judiciis & supplicis, funere, festisque Ebraeorum, de Asylis ירת / מיתת מדיון itemque aliisque in Ebraeorum scriptis passim obviis. Quia vero de כרת & circumcisione & sententia Kimchii τεὶ τῆς διαθήκης τῆς ψυχῆς jam mentio facta est, quae de istis jam parata habebamus, hic exhibere libuit.
units.tr: When I was about to hand this work over to the printer, I was quite set on taking in all the books of the Old and New Testaments and presenting to you, in a single volume divided into six books, the more notable passages that I had gathered together some time ago. I also meant to add, as an appendix at the end of the work, some exercises on certain Hebrew antiquities and rites and on certain doctrines of the Jews. I hoped that all this would not exceed the bulk of a single volume. That is why, on page 259, I postponed my dissertation on circumcision and the phrase "That soul shall be cut off from among the people," and, on page 445, my exposition of Kimchi's opinion, to another place. See the place I have just mentioned. But since the work, as you see, has grown enormously under my hand, I judged that I was obliged to break off here. And indeed it will not be out of place to test the judgment of the learned on this first part of the work. If they think my labour is not useful to young people, I will have wasted enough paper and effort. But if they pass a kinder verdict, and God Almighty grants me leisure and health, then after a brief breathing space you will have the other part of the whole work, namely books four, five and six. Of these, the first will deal with the major and minor prophets; the second with the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles; and the last with the remaining books of the New Testament. To these I will add, by way of an appendix, some exercises on the judgments and punishments, the funeral customs and the festivals of the Hebrews, on the asylums, on [karet] and [death at the hand of Heaven], and on other matters that occur here and there in Hebrew writings. But since mention has already been made of karet, of circumcision, and of Kimchi's view of [the covenant of the soul], I have thought fit to present here what I already had prepared on these matters.
