units.la: CAP. I. 5.6. vulg. omne caput languidum, & omne cor merens. A planta pedis usque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas. Lutherus, totum caput, totum cor, &c. Vulgatus interpres expressit versionem Graecam, πᾶσα κεφαλὴ, πᾶσα καρδία &c. At cum Ebraeum כל jam omne; jam totum significet, hinc Graecum πᾶς saepe itidem pro ὅλος ponitur. In hunc sensum vocem eam usurpavit Matth 21. 10. Et commota est πᾶσα ἡ πόλις. 1. Cor. 13. 2: Si habeam πᾶσαν τὴν πίστιν, totam fidem. 2. Timoth. 3. 16. πᾶσα ἡ γραφὴ, tota scriptura divinitus inspirata est. Itaque aut non satis fideliter, aut non satis apposite haec sic convertit Belg. Lovan. alle hooft is quelende, alle herte is truerende. Hunc locum passim citari videas probandae originariae labi, quam peccatum originale theologi vocant. Quasi de corpore humano Vates dissereret. Atqui contextus evidenter docet 1. de corpore Reipublicae 2. de calamitatibus, quibus hoc corpus per spiramenta temporum afflictaverat Deus, sermonem esse. Quis adeo in scripturis hospes est, ut nesciat, eas passim de regno vel Rep. tanquam de corpore humano loqui. Jes. 7. 20. Tempore illo abradet Dominus novacula ista mercenaria pilum capitis & pedum, etiamque barbam ipsam consumet. Ubi vide notas Junii. Atque huc quoque pertinere mihi semper visus est locus ille 2. Reg. x. 32. Temporibus illis coepit DOMINVS truncare Israelem. Ebr. ויחל Genev. rongner, Deod. mozzare, Pisc. zu stommelen, ubi Lutherus, pedibus in vulgati vestigia positis, Tunc coepit DOMINVM tædere super Israel. Jetzt ... an uberdrüssig zu werden über Israel. Qua versione duo themata ויחל & ר [unde neutiquam formes ויחל] confunduntur. Quis non videt, prophetam, postquam propositum fuisset rebellionem populi verf. 2. postquam ostendisset, eos bestiis longe pejores esse, verf. 3. postquam exaggerasset eorum ingratitudinem, progredi ad depingendam stupendam eorum contumaciã & ἀναισθησίαν, Quos nulla beneficia potuerunt continere in officio, eos nullae afflictiones poterunt revocare ad officium. Quo pulsabantur gravius, eo peccabant foedius & à Deo recedebant longius. Id quod propheta exprimit istis verbis, versus 5. עַל מֶה תִּכּוּ עוֹד תּוֹסִיפוּ סָרָה quae sic convertit Junius, quare [quo] percutimini amplius, augetis apostasiam? Hanc vero percussionem prolixius persequitur usque ad verf. 10. ut & apostasiam à verf. 10. ad versum 16. Illa [percussio] verba Reverendi Tarnovii, primum per comparationem corporis humani allegorice declaratur, verf. 5. 6. Deinde proprie explicatur, verf. 7. 8. 9. vide ejus exercit. Bibl. pag. 338. Edit. tertiae, Franzium de Interp. Script. pag. 738. Calvinum in hunc locum, Lutherum comm. in Iesajam, Junium, Piscat. & alios. confer & Jesajae caput. 3. verf. 6. 7. ubi non physicum sed politicum medicum Judaei desiderant. Fateor tamen ab afflictissimo hoc Reip. statu ad corruptissimum optimam esse consequentiam. Atqui 1. non quid per consequentiam ex hoc loco elici possit, sed quod primario & sensu literali intendatur, quaeritur. 2. Ne sic quidem ad probandam originariam, cui nos infelix Adam involvit, labem, locum istum extendi posse. Omnia enim quae Judaeis spiritus objectat, actualia sunt.
units.tr: Chapter 1, verses 5–6, Vulgate: every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful. From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it. Luther has "the whole head, the whole heart," etc. The Vulgate translator followed the Greek version, every head, every heart [πᾶσα κεφαλὴ, πᾶσα καρδία], etc. But since the Hebrew [כל] already means "every" and also "whole," the Greek πᾶς is often likewise used for ὅλος. In this sense the word is used at Matthew 21:10: And the whole [πᾶσα ἡ πόλις] city was moved. At 1 Corinthians 13:2: If I have all [πᾶσαν τὴν πίστιν] faith, that is, the whole faith. At 2 Timothy 3:16: All [πᾶσα ἡ γραφὴ] Scripture, that is, the whole Scripture, is given by inspiration of God. Therefore the Belgic Louvain version has rendered this passage as every head is languishing, every heart is grieving, either not faithfully enough or not aptly enough. You may see this passage cited everywhere to prove the taint of original sin, which the theologians call original sin. It is as if the prophet were discussing the human body. Yet the context clearly shows that the discourse is, first, about the body of the commonwealth, and second, about the calamities with which God had afflicted this body through the successive periods of time. Who is so much a stranger to Scripture that he does not know that it everywhere speaks of a kingdom or commonwealth as of a human body? Isaiah 7:20: In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor the hair of the head and of the feet, and will even consume the beard itself. See the notes of Junius there. And that other passage, 2 Kings 10:32, has always seemed to me to belong here too: In those days the LORD began to cut off Israel. The Hebrew is [ויחל]; the Geneva Bible has to clip off, Diodati to lop, Piscator to maim. But Luther, following the footsteps of the Vulgate, has: Then the LORD began to be weary of Israel, "now ... to become tired of Israel." By this translation two different roots, [ויחל] and [ר], are confused, and one should by no means form [ויחל] from them. Who does not see that the prophet, after he had set out the rebellion of the people (v. 2), after he had shown that they were far worse than beasts (v. 3), and after he had magnified their ingratitude, proceeds to depict their astonishing obstinacy and [ἀναισθησία] insensibility? Those whom no benefits could keep in their duty, no afflictions will be able to recall to their duty. The more heavily they were struck, the more shamefully they sinned and the farther they withdrew from God. The prophet expresses this in verse 5 with the words [עַל מֶה תִּכּוּ עוֹד תּוֹסִיפוּ סָרָה], which Junius renders: why [wherefore] should you be struck any more? You increase apostasy. He pursues this striking more fully, down to verse 10, and the apostasy from verse 10 to verse 16. That striking is first declared allegorically, by a comparison with the human body (vv. 5–6), and then explained literally (vv. 7, 8, 9). See Reverend Tarnovius's Biblical Exercises, p. 338 of the third edition; Franz, On the Interpretation of Scripture, p. 738; Calvin on this passage; Luther's commentary on Isaiah; Junius, Piscator, and others. Compare also Isaiah chapter 3, verses 6–7, where the Jews seek not a physical but a political physician. I grant, however, that it is a very good inference from this most afflicted state of the commonwealth to the most corrupt. But: (1) the question is not what may be inferred from this passage by consequence, but what is primarily intended in the literal sense. (2) Even so, this passage cannot be extended to prove the original taint, in which unhappy Adam has involved us. For everything that the Spirit lays against the Jews is actual sin.

units.la: verf. 24. Heu ego consolabor super hostibus meis & vindicabor de inimicis meis.] Ita vulg. Adscribam verba Oleastrii, Torquerit hunc locum concionatores, in suis concionibus, volentes ex eo probare, Dominum invitum homines castigare: quia scilicet postquam vindicaverit se, consolatione indigeat, ut ostendat se invitum punire, quod nec locus hic dicit, nec propheta somniavit. Loquitur Deus more hominis, qui insigni injuria affectus dolorem in ultionis solatia intendit. Est enim vindicta, ut Juvenalis loquitur, bonum vita jucundius ipsa. Facem huic loco allucet locus Jezechielis v. 13. Ita consummabitur ira mea & collocans excandescentiam meam in illis, ultione consolabor me & Moses Deut. 28. 63. Eritque ut quemadmodum laetabatur DOMINUS de vobis benefaciendo vobis, sic laetatur de vobis perdendo vos & exscindendo vos. Et locus Salomonis prov. 1. 26. Ego quoque in calamitate vestra ridebo &c. Ipsos autem Judaeos hostes suos vocat. Quid ergo tibi vult
units.tr: Verse 24: Ah, I will be comforted over my adversaries, and avenge myself on my enemies. So the Vulgate. I shall add the words of Oleaster: "Preachers twist this passage in their sermons, wanting to prove from it that the Lord punishes men against his will, because, having avenged himself, he needs consolation, so as to show that he punishes unwillingly; which this passage neither says nor did the prophet dream." God speaks in the manner of a man who, having suffered a grievous wrong, turns his grief to the comfort of vengeance. For, as Juvenal puts it, vengeance is a good sweeter than life itself. Ezekiel 5:13 throws light on this passage: Thus shall my anger be spent, and I will set my fury upon them, and I will be comforted; by their destruction. And Moses, Deuteronomy 28:63: And it shall be that as the LORD rejoiced over you to do you good, so he will rejoice over you to destroy you and root you out. And the passage of Solomon, Proverbs 1:26: I also will laugh at your calamity, etc. But they call the Jews themselves their enemies. So what then does this mean for you—

units.la: Interpres Belgicus, quando locum sic convertit, Ick sal my troosten door myne vyanden, ende my wreken door mijne vyanden. In Ebraeo enim est מ / מְּצָרַי מְאוֹיְבַי Locum istum reduces in viam, si particulae door, qua instrumentum notari videtur, particulam aen substituers, Ik sal my troosten aen myne vyanden. Ita certe clarior fuerit oratio. Dices voculam Heu, vel Eheu satis innuere. Deum invitum eo pertrahi, ut tam saevas de populo reposcat poenas. Resp. ne hoc quidem esse firmum. Etenim Ebraeum הוי non semper dolentis sed & aliquando vocantis aut alloquentis, aut hortantis; aliquando comminantis interjectio est, R. Salomo ad hunc locum, הוי לשון הזמנה והכרזה / Additque locum Zachariae 11. 6. Hoi, Hoi, fugite ex terra Aquilonis; Ubi Jun. Heus, Heus. Vulg. O, o. Et Lxx. ὦ, ὦ. Vide & verf. 7, & Jer. 55. 1. At Isc. v. 8. 11. 18. 20. 21. &c. & hoc eodem cap. verf. 5. comminantis est, idem quod אוי / ubi & chaldaeus reddidit id est, vae & Lxx. οὐαί. Lubet adscribere verba R. Salom. ad verf. 5. hujus capitis,
units.tr: The Dutch translator, when he renders the passage thus, "I will comfort myself through my enemies, and avenge myself through my enemies," ... For the Hebrew is [מִצָּרַי מֵאֹיְבַי]. You will set this passage right if you substitute the particle aen for door, which seems to mark the instrument: "Ik sal my troosten aen myne vyanden" ("I will be comforted over my enemies"). In that way the sense will certainly be clearer. You will say that the little word Heu or Eheu sufficiently suggests that God is drawn unwillingly to demand such savage punishments from the people. I reply that not even this is secure. For the Hebrew [הוי] is an interjection not always of grieving, but sometimes of calling, addressing or exhorting, and sometimes of threatening. Rabbi Solomon, on this passage, says [הוי לשון הזמנה והכרזה], "hoi is a term of summoning and proclaiming." He adds Zechariah 11:6: Hoi, hoi, flee from the land of the north, where Junius has "Heus, heus"; the Vulgate "O, o"; and the Seventy [ὦ, ὦ]. But in Isaiah 5:8, 11, 18, 20, 21, etc., and in this same chapter at verse 5, it is a threatening, the same as [אוי], where the Chaldee also renders it, that is, "woe," and the Seventy [οὐαί]. I am pleased to quote the words of Rabbi Solomon on verse 5 of this chapter:

units.la: כל הוי שכמקרא לשון קובל וקינה כארם הגונה מלבו וצועק אה אלא שיש מהם מועטים שהם לשון צעקת קריאת קול כמו הוי הוי ונוסף מארץ צפון והרגומו אכלו לשון הכרוזי / hoc est, omne Hoi quod in scriptura est, habet notionem clamoris & lamenti [id est, clamoris lamentabilis] veluti cum homo suspirat e corde suo & clamat, Ah, nisi quod paucula sint ex illis, quae significent inclamationem vocis, veluti Zach. 2. 6. Heus Heus &c. ubi Chaldaeus vertit אכלו proclamate, in significatione proclamationis. Ad eundem locum Kimchi, הוי לשון קריארה וצעקה הן לאבל הן להשמיע השומע ויח זה לשון אבל Hoi valet exclamationem, seu clamorem tam ad significandum luctum, quam ad vocandum aut compellandum alium. Ionathan vero hoc loco transtulit in significatione luctus.
units.tr: Every hoi that occurs in Scripture has the sense of a complaint and lament, as when a man sighs from his heart and cries out, "Ah." Except that a few of them are of the nature of a shout or call, as hoi, hoi, and in Zechariah 2:6 "heus, heus," where the Chaldee rendered [אכלו], "proclaim," in the sense of proclaiming. [כל הוי שבמקרא לשון קובל וקינה כאדם הגונה מלבו וצועק אה אלא שיש מהם מועטים שהם לשון צעקת קריאת קול כמו הוי הוי ונאמר מארץ צפון והרגומו אכלו לשון הכרוזי]. On the same passage Kimchi says: [הוי לשון קריאה וצעקה הן לאבל הן להשמיע השומע ויש זה לשון אבל]. That is, hoi means exclamation or cry, both to signify grief and to call or address another. Jonathan, however, rendered it here in the sense of grief.

units.la: - Verf. 21. urbs—in qua justitia dormiebat] ita hunc locum expressit editio Basil. in octavo ex Graeca, Lxx. Interpretum versione, Ea enim ita habet, ἐν ἡ δικαιοσύνη ἐνοικιῶν ἐν αὐτῇ. Non dubito, quin hic locus multos olim torserit. Et quis hoc ad laudem civitatis spectare crederet? Tu disce tiro, κοιμᾶσθαι in Hellenistica lingua aliquando idem esse quod manere, pernoctare. Sic dico, הלין est pernoctare, manere, permanere, & quod à pernoctantibus fieri solet, quiescere, cubare, dormire. Hinc
units.tr: Verse 21, "the city ... in which justice lodged": thus the Basel octavo edition rendered this passage from the Greek, the version of the Seventy. For it reads: [ἐν ᾗ δικαιοσύνη κοιμᾶται ἐν αὐτῇ], "in which justice lodged in her." I do not doubt that this passage has long tormented many. And who would believe that this refers to the praise of the city? Learn this, novice: in the Hellenistic language [κοιμᾶσθαι] sometimes means the same as to remain, to spend the night. So I say: the Hebrew [הלין] means to pass the night, to remain, to abide, and what is usually done by those who pass the night, to rest, to lie down, to sleep. Hence

units.la: Ps. 49. 13. Jeremiae 4. Hinc posteriorum istarum significationum interpretamentum commutatur cum interpretamentis priorum. Hinc intelliges, quid sit Exod. XXXIV. 25. ἀ ηαιμηΜσλαι εἰς τὴν πρωὶ ἡμεα εορτῆς ἐ Πά-χα. Ubi rursus Latinus Interpres, non dormient in mane sacrificia festi paschatis, ubi vides perspicue ηαιμηΜσ pro remanere, per noctem manere positum esse. Tamen Deut. XVI. 4. Idem interpres vocem eandem per remanebit, interpretatus est.
units.tr: Ps. 49. 13. Jeremiah 4. From this, the interpretation of those later meanings is exchanged for the interpretations of the earlier ones. From this you will understand what Exod. 34. 25 means: [οὐ κοιμηθήσεται] "the sacrifice of the feast of the Passover shall not remain until the morning." There the Latin translator again renders it "shall not sleep until morning," where you can plainly see that [הלין] is used in the sense of remaining, lodging through the night. Yet at Deut. 16. 4 the same translator rendered the same word as remain.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Verf. ult. vulg. Quiescite ergo ab homine, cujus spiritus in naribus ejus est, quia excelsus reputatus est.] Hæc verba veteres plerique interpretati sunt ceu evidens vaticinium de Christo Ἀνθρώπῳ, qui vid. & homo & Excelsus vocatur. Glossa ordin. ne seviatis in Christum, qui purus homo videtur quia spirat naribus & vivit sicut alii homines. Excelsus] super omnes gentes Dominus, Ps 86. Et ipso fundavit eam altissimus. Lyra, ostendit medelam contra praedicta mala, sc. cessationem a provocatione ira divina. Quiescite ergo ab homine, id est a Deo ejus offensam cavendo. Scriptura enim V. Test. frequenter de Deo loquitur more humano. Et similiter vocat eum aliquando hominem, vel virum, & maxime quia erat humanandus. &c. Hieron: in comm. hunc locum vocat perspicuum de Christo prophetiam, eamque à Lxx. Interpretibus neglectam fuisse demiratur. Carthusianus, Quiescite id est cessate ab homine, Christo, cujus spiritus i. anhelitus est in naribus ejus, id est, qui ita vivit, quantum ad humanam naturam attinet ut ceteri homines, spirando & respirando &c. Quia excelsus reputatus est] &c. quoad naturam divinam. Sic enim altissimus est, sicut in Ps. 86. cantamus de eo, & ipse fundavit eam altissimus. Hæc ille. At, tu disce tiro, nihil ejusmodi ex Ebræis posse extundi יִרְלוּ לָכֶם מִן הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁמָה בְאַפּוֹ כִּי בַּמָּה נֶחְשַׁב הוּא id est definite vobis ab homine, cujus flatus in naribus ejus, nam in quo reputatur ipse? Ita vertit & Arias Montanus. Pagninus postrema illa verba in hunc modum reddidit, quid enim reputationis est, sensu nihil variante. Hanc Ebræi textus mentem esse, ne Lyra quidem in media barbarie ignoravit. Verba ejus, postquam communem interpretationem repræsentasset, ista sunt. Secundum Ebræos literæ est ista, Quiescite ergo ab homine &c. quia in quo appreciatus est ipse? Et secundum ipsos non intelligitur de Deo, sed de homine mortali, & ideo non est ponenda spes in eo, sed in Deo. Et hoc est quod dicitur, quiequiescite ergo ab homine cujus spiritus in narib us ejus &c. id est qui vivit, per respirationem aëris, & sic est fragilis & mortalis, quia in quo appreciatus est ipse? q.d. in nihilo, respectu Dei. Et hoc intelligitur, quod idola quae sunt ab homine facta, adhuc sint minus appretianda, ut exponit R. Salomo &c. Habes Lector germanum interpretamentum hujus loci. A quo in hoc tantum recedit Oleastro, quod priora verba, Quiescite ab homine interpretetur, ne timete vos o pii & fideles, mala, quae homo vobis possit inferre, homo, cujus ira in naso est id est ostenditur, ac si dicat non transit nasum, aut nihil aliud est quam flatus nasi Quamvis immediate eandem subjungat expositionem quam ex Lyra exhibuimus. Arias Montanus de primo homine exponit, ut hoc velit Jesajas, istum hominem, qui primus creatus fuit, cui nihil magis divinum erat quam spiraculum a Deo in nare insufflatum, jam mortalibus esse fastidiendum. Eo potius esse connitendum, ut portemus imaginem coelestis Adami &c. Haec si admittimus non quidem falsa, attamen aliena sunt, quae vulgatae versioni Interpretum vulgus superstruxit, Cornua enim Vulgati Interpretis patronis obvertit vox בְּמָה, quae neutiquam potest reddi, Excelsus. Esto legatur בָּמָה. Ea vox Excelsum hominem vel personam nusquam significat. Quid ergo? locum excelsum. Expende omnia loca, Hoc cum non ignoraret Forerius hanc paraphrasin adhibuit, Cavete vobis ab homine hoc, Christo, perinde quasi a loco sacro, cujusmodi est altare aut templum. Nam de templo corporis sui dixit ipse Christus, Solvite templum hoc &c. ne scilicet eum audeant temerare, vel vim ipsi inferre. Paulo aliter Glossa ordin. Hebr. excelsum, non excelsus. Ipse est enim ipsa altitudo, non altus tantum. Atego intrepide nego, vocem Ebraeam ullibi altitudinem significare. Aquila locum praesentem sic interpretatus est, οάντασθε υμἱν απὸ ανθρώπων id est cessate vobis ab homine, respiratio in naribus ejus, quia in quo reputatus est? Haec ad quaedam exemplaria graeca Origenes ex Aquila sub asterisco addidit. Id quod & Cyrillus & Basilius testantur. Basilii verba, si requiris, ista sunt, ταύτον τὸ τὶν ... Apud Procopium eadem sub asterisco quoque reperias, Chaldaeus, אחמנעו לכון ... cessate vobis ne subjiciatis vos hohomini, cum factus est terribilis, cujus spiraculum vitæ in naribus ejus est, quia hodie est vivus, & cras non est & quasi nihilum reputatus est ipse. Lubet etiam adscribere verba Kimchii, quibus hunc locum illustravit, אז יאמר כל אחד לחברו הדלו לכם מן האדם כי יהיה פחד יהוה עלכל העולם ויאמר איש לאריו לא יהיה עור מורא בשר ודם עליכם אלא מורא האל לברו
units.tr: Verse 22 of the Vulgate: Cease, therefore, from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted as nothing. Most of the older writers interpreted these words as a plain prophecy of Christ the Man [Ἀνθρώπῳ], who is called both man and Excelsus. The ordinary gloss: "Do not rage against Christ, who seems to be a mere man, because he breathes through his nostrils and lives as other men do." Excelsus: "the Lord is above all the nations" (Ps. 86). "And the Most High himself founded it." Lyra: "It shows the remedy against the aforesaid evils, namely, the cessation from provoking the wrath of God. Cease, therefore, from man, that is, avoid offending God. For Scripture of the Old Testament often speaks of God in human fashion, and likewise sometimes calls him a man or a husband, especially because he was to be made man, etc." Jerome, in his commentary, calls this passage a plainly prophetic word about Christ, and wonders that the Seventy translators neglected it. The Carthusian: "Cease, that is, desist from man, that is Christ, whose breath, that is, whose breathing, is in his nostrils; that is, he lives, so far as his human nature is concerned, as other men do, breathing in and out, etc. Because he is accounted excelsus: as to his divine nature. For he is the Most High, just as we sing of him in Ps. 86, 'and the Most High himself founded it.'" So he. But you, novice, should learn that nothing of the kind can be squeezed out of the Hebrew: חִדְלוּ לָכֶם מִן־הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר נְשָׁמָה בְאַפּוֹ כִּי בְמֶה נֶחְשָׁב הוּא [cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for wherein is he to be accounted?]. That is, "cease for yourselves from man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for in what is he to be reckoned?" Arias Montanus also renders it so. Pagninus rendered the last words thus: "for what account is he, the sense being unchanged." Even Lyra, in the midst of his barbarism, did not fail to see that this is the mind of the Hebrew text. After setting out the common interpretation, his words are these: "According to the Hebrews the letter reads, 'Cease, therefore, from man,' etc., 'for in what is he valued?' According to them it is not understood of God but of mortal man, and so hope is not to be placed in him but in God. And this is what is said: 'Cease, therefore, from man, whose breath is in his nostrils,' etc., that is, he who lives by breathing air, and so is frail and mortal, 'for in what is he valued?' That is, as good as nothing in comparison with God. And this is understood as meaning that idols, which are made by man, are to be valued even less, as R. Solomon explains," etc. You have here, reader, the genuine interpretation of this passage. Oleaster departs from it only in this: he explains the opening words, Cease from man, as "Do not fear, you pious and faithful ones, the evils which man can inflict upon you; man, whose anger is in his nose, that is, is displayed, as if he were saying, it does not pass beyond his nose, or it is nothing but a puff of the nostrils." Although he immediately subjoins the same explanation that we have drawn from Lyra. Arias Montanus explains it of the first man, so that Isaiah wishes this: that man, who was first created, to whom nothing was more divine than the breath breathed into his nostrils by God, is now to be despised by mortals; we should rather strive to bear the image of the heavenly Adam, etc. If we admit this, it is not indeed false, but it is foreign to the text; yet the crowd of Vulgate supporters has built upon the translator's version. For they turn against us the word בְּמָה, which can by no means be rendered excelsus. Suppose it were read בָּמָה: that word nowhere signifies an exalted man or person. What then? A high place. Examine all the passages. Since Forerius was not unaware of this, he adopted this paraphrase: "Beware of this man, Christ, just as you would beware of a sacred place, such as an altar or temple. For Christ himself spoke of the temple of his body, 'Destroy this temple,' etc., so that they would not dare to violate him or do him violence." Somewhat differently the ordinary gloss: "The Hebrew has exalted, not excelsus. For he is the very height itself, not merely high." But I boldly deny that the Hebrew word ever signifies height anywhere. Aquila translated the present passage thus: [παύσασθε ὑμῖν ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπων] that is, "cease for yourselves from man; his breathing is in his nostrils, for in what is he reckoned?" Origen added these words from Aquila under an asterisk to certain Greek copies, as Cyril and Basil also attest. If you ask for Basil's words, they are these: [...]. In Procopius you will find the same under an asterisk as well. The Chaldee: ahamna'u lakhon [...] "cease for yourselves, do not subject yourselves to the man, when he has become terrible, whose breath of life is in his nostrils, because today he is alive and tomorrow he is not, and he himself is accounted as almost nothing." It is also worth adding the words of Kimchi, with which he illustrated this passage: [Hebrew]. That is: then each shall say to his neighbour, Cease from man, for the fear of the Lord has come upon the whole world; and one man shall say to another, There shall no longer be upon you the fear of flesh and blood, but only the fear of the one God.

units.la: hoc est, tunc dicet unusquisque socio suo, abstinete vos ab homine, quia pavor Dei universum mundum incessit. Dicetque alter alteri, ne esto amplius metus carnis & sanguinis (id est hominis) super vos, sed metus solius Dei. כי האדם כאין נחשב כי במעט רגע ימות כי הנשמה באפויכלומר קרוב לבאת ואמר כאפו כי רוח החיים תלוי באף כי דרך נקבי האף יצאהוום הטבעי אשר בלב תמיד וכן יכנס אליו דרך נקבי האף קרירות האויר וכוהחיי הארם שידוע בחכמרת הטבע ואמכן שהייו קצרים במה נחשב הוא ואיך יתכן לבטוח עליו או לירא ממנו
units.tr: For man is reckoned as nothing, for in a very short moment he dies, since the breath is in his nostrils. That is to say, he is near to departing, and says, in his nose, because the spirit of life hangs on the nose, for the natural heat, which is always in the heart, goes out through the nostrils, and likewise the coolness of the air enters him through the nostrils, and the life of man, as is known from the science of nature, depends on this. If his life is so short, in what is he reckoned? And how can it be right to trust in him or to fear him? [Hebrew: "For man is reckoned as nothing, for in a little moment he dies, for the breath is in his nostrils. That is to say, he is near to departing; and he says 'in his nostrils' because the spirit of life hangs on the nose..." etc.]

units.la: homo enim instar nihili æstimatur, Parvo enim momento expirare potest, utpote cujus halitus in naribus est. q. d. jam prope esse ut exeat. Dicit autem in naribus ejus, quia halitus vitalis quasi à naribus dependet. Namque per ista foramina egreditur calor ille naturalis, qui perpetuo cordi inest. Et per eadem ingreditur refrigeratio aëris. In hoc autem consistit vita hominis, sicut ex physica constat. Si adeo brevis & caduca vita ejus est, quanti æstimandus est? & quomodo rectum censeri poterit, in eo collocare fiduciam aut eum extimescere? R. Salomo Abstine vobis ab homine שלא לשמוע למלכיכם הסתעים אתכם מאחרי ולהשתחוות למעשי ידיו אשר נשמה באפו אשר כל היהו ובהו תלויים בנשמרת אפו שהוא רוח פורח שהיום ישנרה בו ומהר תצא סמנו ויקל והומר לצלם למעשה ידיו שאין ממש
units.tr: For man is reckoned as nothing, for he can expire in a small moment, since his breath is in his nostrils. That is to say, he is already close to going out. He says "in his nostrils," because the vital breath hangs, as it were, from the nostrils. For that natural heat, which is always in the heart, goes out through those openings, and through the same openings the coolness of the air enters. In this, as physics shows, the life of man consists. If his life is so brief and frail, how much is he to be valued? And how can he be thought upright, or can one place trust in him or fear him? R. Solomon, Cease from man: [Hebrew: "that you should not listen to your kings, who would turn you away from following me and bow down to the works of his hands, whose breath is in his nostrils, on whom all his being and existence depend, the breath of his nostrils, which is a fleeting wind that today exists in him and soon goes out of him, and he is made into an image, a work of his hands, which is nothing real."]

units.la: ne aures regibus vestris substringatis, qui seducat vos, ut me deseratis & incurvetis vos operibus manuum eorum, Cujus halitus est in naso ejus. Hoc est, cujus omnis, ut sic dicam vitalitas & robur à flatu narium ejus dependet, qui est spiritus volaticus, & hodie in eo mutari & cras egredi potest. Quanto minus ergo fiducia collocanda est in idolo, opere manuum hominis, in quo nihil omnino est. Aben-Ezra, אשר שהשם גזר עליכם וזהו מפני פחד יי אין כוח בארם לבטל גזירותיו על כן חדלו לכם מן הארם שלא יושיעו אתכם כי הכל המה
units.tr: Do not lend your ears to your kings, who would seduce you, so that you forsake me and bow yourselves down to the works of their hands, whose breath is in his nostrils. That is, the whole of his life, so to speak, and his strength depend on the breath of his nostrils. He is a fleeting spirit, who today can be changed and tomorrow can pass away. How much less, then, should trust be placed in an idol, a work of human hands, in which there is absolutely nothing. Aben-Ezra: [the Lord has decreed against you; and this is because of the fear of the LORD. No one has the power to annul his decrees. Therefore cease from man, for he cannot save you, since they are all...] (אשר שהשם גזר עליכם וזהו מפני פחד יי אין כוח בארם לבטל גזירותיו על כן חדלו לכם מן הארם שלא יושיעו אתכם כי הכל המה)

units.la: hoc est, quandoquidem Deus statuit aliquid contra contra vos, quod innuebat istiu verbis, ספני פחר (versu præce-denti) non erit in potestate ejusdem irrita facere ejus decreta. Ideo ab-stinete ab homine, non enim servabunt vos. Quia vanitas sunt. Tol-lam manum de hac tabula, ubi B. Lutheri versionem adscripsero, Go laßet nu ab von dem menschen / de athem in der naßen hat: Denn ir wisset nicht / wie hoch er geachtet ist / quia nescitis, quanti æstimetur. Agnosco me non satis capere mentem beati viri. Piscator, Go laßet nu ab vondem menschen / der athem in der naßen hat / Dan [sieher] wie hoch ist er zu achten? nam, quæso, quanti æstimandus est? Uter mentem Jesaiæ melius assecutus sit & clarius expresserit, docti judicent. Meum certe punctum si ad dicendam sententiam admitterer, Piscator ferret. Etiam Genevenses qui ne latum quidem unguem ab hac mente divertunt, Deportez-vous de l'homme, du quel le souffle est en ses narines, car que vaut il? glossa. r. assavoir, pour delivrer de la main du Seigneur, & de quelque danger. Comme s'il disoit, C'est en Dieu qu'il faut mettre sa confiance, & non pas en l'homme. id est nam quid valet ille? sc. ad liberandum e manu Domini & periculis q. d. In Deo collocandam esse fiduciam, non vero in homi-nibus. Suffragatur & Deodatus, qui ad verba illa, cuius halitus est in naso ejus ista commentatur, qui natura & conditionis dibilissimæ est, quem sola narium obturatione possis interficere. In hanc quoque sententiam ire videas Jacobum Salianum Jesuitam qui Annalium tomo 1. pag. 101. locum sic exponit, nolite timere hominem, cujus vita in inspiratione & respiratione consistit, quia vitalem spiritum per nares haurit, qui si comprimatur, protinus perit aëris inopia.
units.tr: That is, since God has decreed something against you, which he indicated by these words, [מפני פחד] (in the preceding verse) no one will have the power to make void his decrees. Therefore cease from man, for they will not save you, because they are vanity. I will lift my hand from this table, where I have added Luther's version: "Let go now of the man who has breath in his nostrils, for you do not know how highly he is esteemed." because you do not know how highly he is esteemed. I confess that I do not fully grasp the mind of that blessed man. Piscator: "Let go now of the man who has breath in his nostrils. For [see] how highly is he to be esteemed?" For, I ask, how highly is he to be esteemed? Which of them has better attained the mind of Isaiah and expressed it more clearly, learned men may judge. If my vote were admitted to giving an opinion, I would side with Piscator. The Genevan translators too, who do not turn a hair's breadth from this sense, render it: Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for what is he worth? Gloss: that is, to deliver from the hand of the Lord and from some danger. As if he said, trust is to be placed in God, not in men. That is, for what is that man worth? namely, to deliver from the hand of the Lord and from dangers; that is, trust is to be placed in God, not in men. Deodatus also supports this, who, on the words whose breath is in his nostrils, comments: he is of a most feeble nature and condition, whom you could kill merely by stopping his nostrils. You will also see Jacob Sirmond the Jesuit going in this direction, who in volume 1 of his Annals, page 101, explains the passage thus: do not fear man, whose life consists in inhaling and exhaling, because he draws the vital spirit through the nostrils, which, if it is compressed, he at once perishes for lack of air.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Vers. 7. non sum medicus.] Ita vulg. & Lutherus. Ex hoc loco probat Franciscus Valesius, apud Ebræos in Rege medicæ artis peritiam requisitam fuisse. Decipit eruditissimum Philosophum Vulgata versio. Ebræa sic habent, לא אהיה הובש, non ero obligator. Respondent autem istis verbis præcedentis versus, קציו הייה לנו id est ἀρχηγός ἡμῶν. Esto nobis Dux, ut ruina &c. Ideo Lxx quoque Interpretes τὸ הובש ἀρχηγὸν reddidere. Vox quæ in Ebræo est, propria chirurgorum est vulnera obligantium. vide supra 1.6. ubiidem verbi. Negat ergo se idoneum esse, qui isthoc Reip. statu clavum capessat. Vulnera Reip. periotiorem tiorem Chrirurgum requirere. Quod si itaque vocem Medicus retinere lubeat, scias non de Medicina corporis sed Reip. vati sermonem esse. Arias Mont. non ero ligator, hoc est, lictor. q. d. vos vultis me ducem & principem. Sed hoc est me lictorem constituere & quasi carnificem, Adeo enim sceleribus coôperti estis, ut omnes comprehendendos, ligandos & puniendos esse censeam. Non expediret ergo vobis penes me summam rerum esse. Quaerite alium &c. Probarem si probari posset vel uno evidenti loco חבש habere significationem ligandi vinculis in poenam. Scindlerus quidem notat, dici de hominibus qui ligantur vel ad obedientiam vel ad poenam. Sed locus Job. 34. 17. quem profert, non probat. Illic enim obligandi notionem optime quadrare ex Junii versione discess. Pene excideRat, vocem Ebraeam תובש Theodotionem ἐπιδεσμένοντα reddidisse.
units.tr: Vers. 7. non sum medicus.] So the Vulgate and Luther. From this passage Franciscus Valesius argues that among the Hebrews a king was required to have skill in the medical art. The Vulgate version misleads that very learned philosopher. The Hebrew reads לא אהיה הובש [lo ehyeh hovesh], non ero obligator, "I will not be a binder-up." These words answer to the words of the preceding verse, קציו הייה לנו [qatzin hayah lanu], that is ἀρχηγὸς ἡμῶν [archēgos hēmōn], "Be a leader (ruler) for us," so that the ruin &c. Hence the Seventy also rendered the word הובש as ἀρχηγόν [archēgon]. The Hebrew word is properly the term for surgeons binding up wounds; see above on 1.6, where the same verb occurs. He therefore says that he is not fit to take the helm in the present state of the commonwealth. The wounds of the commonwealth call for a more skilled surgeon. If, however, one prefers to keep the word Medicus, you should know that the saying concerns the physician of the state, not the medicine of the body. Arias Montanus renders non ero ligator, that is, "I will not be a lictor," as if to say: "You want me to be your leader and prince. But that would make me a lictor and, as it were, an executioner, for you are so beset with crimes that I judge everyone should be seized, bound and punished. It would not be to your advantage, then, for the supreme power of affairs to rest with me. Seek another," &c. I would accept this if it could be proved, by at least one clear passage, that חבש has the meaning of binding with chains as punishment. Schindler indeed notes that the word is said of men who are bound either to obedience or to punishment. But the passage he cites, Job 34:17, does not prove it; there the notion of binding fits very well, as Junius's version shows. I had almost forgotten that Theodotion rendered the Hebrew word תובש as ἐπιδεσμένοντα [epidesmenonta], "binding up."

units.la: Verf. 12. Populè mi, qui te beatum dicunt, decipiunt te ] ita Vulg, ex Graeco, οἱ μαχαιρίζοντες ὑμᾶς, πλανῶσιν ὑμᾶς. Luth. qui te solantur, sensu eodem, qui te jubent esse securum & in utramque aurem suaviter dormire, atque hac ratione adversus Prophetarum minas solantur. Jun. Pisc. Gen. Angli &c. qui te ducunt, seducunt te Ebr. אַשְׁרֵיךָ utramque expositionem admittit. Sic dico, אַשְׁר in Phiel vel μαχαιρίζειν & ὁδηγεῖν seu καθοδηγοῦντ significat, prior tamen significatio usitatior. Confer Isai. 1. 17. & 9. 16.
units.tr: Verse 12. My people, those who call you blessed deceive you.] So the Vulgate, following the Greek: οἱ μαχαιρίζοντες ὑμᾶς, πλανῶσιν ὑμᾶς [hoi macharizontes hymas, planōsin hymas]. Luther: qui te solantur, "who comfort you," with the same sense: those who bid you be free from care and sleep soundly on both ears, and in this way comfort you against the threats of the prophets. Junius, Piscator, the English translators &c.: qui te ducunt, seducunt te, "who lead you, lead you astray." The Hebrew אַשְׁרֵיךָ [ashrekha] admits either explanation. I say that the form אשר in the Piel means either in Phiel vel μαχαιρίζειν & ὁδηγεῖν, "to flatter or to lead," or καθοδηγοῦντ [kathodēgountes], "to guide"; the former meaning, however, is the more common. Compare Isaiah 1:17 and 9:16.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Verf. 1. Cantabo dilecto meo Canticum patruelis mei vineae suae. ] Vulg. In haec vestigia pedem posuit B. Lutherus, Canam dilecto meo een Liedt mijns Ooms 1. Canticum patrui mei. Si Lutherus bene expressit mentem Vulgati, tunc Vulgatus Patruelem pro patruo usurpavit, quomodo Exodi vi. 20. patruelem dixit pro amita, ubi in Ebraeo est רוֹדִי / ita Bellarm. de sacram. matrimonii lib. I. cap. 27. & Steuchus & Cajet. & S A, & Joh. Bened. & Oleastr. in dictum locum Exodi At 1. Sam. 10. saepius patruum reddidit. Esther 11. 7. Fratrem reddit. Mardochaeus qui fuit nutritius בת דּוֹד filiae fratris sui, Belg. Lovan. een Doch- ster-Heere van sijn Broeders Dochter. Quid audio ; An ergo דּוֹד fratrem significat? Ita certe nos credere jussere Sixtus V. & Clemens VIII. Quorum uterque vulgatam illam lectionem retiretinuit. Hinc vires & incrementa sumsit error communis, Mardochæum patruum Estheræ fuisse. Error, adeo crassus & palpabilis, ut Jesuita Serarius, cui alias frons satis inverecunda est, coactus fuerit asserere, hoc loco vocem patris excidisse legendumque in vulgata versione, filia fratris patris. Id quod Cl. Drusius annis ante Serarium 14. in commentario, quem satis diligenter ante Serarium ex ejus strictusimilibus apparet, annotaverat. Sed quia carpi & flagellari hic non poterat, nominandus non erat. sic ergo tenendum, Estherem filiam patrui ejus [Mardochæi] fuisse. Mardochæus non Patruus Estheris, sed ut cum Cicerone loquar frater ejus patruelis fuit. Duorum fratrum liberi fuerunt. Quos Græci ἀνεψιοὺς vocant. Neque obstant verba versus primi Cap. 8.
units.tr: Verse 1. I will sing to my beloved a song of his vineyard. Vulgate. B. Luther set his foot in these same tracks, rendering "Canam dilecto meo" as "een Liedt mijns Ooms" (a song of my uncle), "Canticum patrui mei." If Luther has rendered the Vulgate's sense well, then the Vulgate used patruelis (cousin) for patruus (uncle), just as at Exodus 6:20 it said patruelis for amita (aunt), where the Hebrew has dodi. So Bellarmine (De sacramento matrimonii, bk. 1, ch. 27), Steuchus, Cajetan, S. A., Johannes Benedictus and Oleaster on that passage. But at 1 Samuel 10 it has patruus several times, and at Esther 2:7 it renders "brother." Mordecai, "who was the foster-father of the daughter of his brother" (bat dod), in the Louvain Dutch: "een Dochter-Heere van sijn Broeders Dochter." What do I hear? Does dod then mean brother? Certainly Sixtus V and Clement VIII ordered us to believe so, and each of them retained that Vulgate reading. From this came the common error, which gained strength and growth, that Mordecai was Esther's uncle. The error is so gross and palpable that the Jesuit Serarius, who otherwise has a fairly shameless face, was forced to assert that the word patris (of the father) had dropped out at this place and that the Vulgate should read filia fratris patris. The learned Drusius had noted this in his commentary fourteen years before Serarius, as is clear from Serarius's own closing remarks. But since Drusius could not be criticised and lashed here, he was not to be named. So we must hold that Esther was the daughter of his uncle [Mordecai]. Mordecai was not Esther's uncle but, to use Cicero's words, her cousin on the father's side. They were children of two brothers, whom the Greeks call anepsioi. Nor do the words of verse 1 of chapter 8 stand in the way.

units.la: Confessa enim est ei Esther, quod esset patruus suus. Nihil enim tale extat in originario. Judicaverat enim Esther מה היא לה hoc est, verbum, quid ipse sibi sc. esset, hoc est, quæ sibi cum illo intercederet cognatio ut suus necessarius esset. Cajetanus, redditur manifestata cognatio ab Esther inter ipsam & Mardochæum. Erant enim patrueles. Serarius vulgato sic patrocinatur, ut dicat vel per patruum intelligi patruelem, vel talem qui patris loco est. Sed ut tandem redeamus ad Jesaiam, quis ignorat, quam aliena de hoc patruele vel patruo Jesaiæ commentati hoc loco sint interpretes: Non libet ea huc accongerere. Vide Lyram qui per patruelem filium patrui intellexit, [ut & Belgicus Interpres vulgatæ versionis, Het Liedeken van mijns Ooms Sone, quod notandum propter Interpretes Forerium, Carthusf. & alios. At Ebraea vox indifferens est ad patruum, & Dilectum. Ebr. אֲשִׁירָה נָא לִידִידִי שִׁירַת דודי Canam nunc dilecto meo canticum dilecti mei &c. Lxx. Ἀσω τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ μου ἄσμα ἢ ἀγαπητῶ μου Forerius, Si cui tamen conjectura illa de patruo Jesaiae displiceat, דיד pro dilecto accipiat, ut ponatur antecedens pro relativo, sicut non raro consueverunt Ebrai. Cantabo inquit, delecto meo canticum ipsius de vinea sua. Id est canticum, quod Deus jussit me canere. Vel sic, cantabo dilecto meo populo Israelitico canticum Dei mei dilectissimi, quod jussit me canere de vinea sua, ipso nempe populo. Quod vero sequitur in vulgata versione, m cornu filio olei, fideliter quidem ex Ebraeo traductum est, sed à multis non intellectum. Et quis intelligat versionem Lovaniensium, Mynem lieve is een Vlyngaerd gebeurt in den horen, de sone der olien. Equidem lubens dederim Pontificiis ejusmodi versiones aut exiguo aut nullo cum fructu legi posse. Appello omnes cordatos, quos partium studium non sideravit, qui vel tria quatuorve capita Belgicæ hujus versionis cum Latina & Ebraeo textu contulerè, utrum non hoc ex professo egerit interpres, quisquis fuit, ut simplicioribus in ista incidentibus extorqueret hanc confessionem, scripturas non posse cum utilitatte aut fructu a Laïcis legi. Qua de re pleniori manu ad Hoseæ cap. 1. eum bono Deo, disferemus. Quanto melius B. Lutherus de suæ versionis lectoribus meritus est, qui non tam ad verba quam sensum respiciens, verba illa בֶּן שֵׁמָן vertit; aen een vetter plaetse. Quamvis illud dissimulare non possim, vocem קֶרֶן ab eodem neglectam. Ebraea enim sic habent, קֶרֶן כֶּן־שְׁמָן / Lxx. ἐν κέρατι, ἐν τόπῳ πίονι. Quod vero per קֶרֶן cornu divinus vates intelligat, optime docet Kimchius, quando ad hunc locum sic commentatur, זקרא
units.tr: Esther confessed to him that he was her uncle. For nothing of the kind stands in the original. For Esther had understood [מה היא לה], that is, the phrase what he himself was to her: what kinship lay between them, so that he was her close relative. Cajetan: the kinship between Esther and Mardochai was made clear by her, for they were cousins. Serarius defends the Vulgate by saying that uncle may be understood either as cousin, or as someone who stands in the place of a father. But to return at last to Isaiah: who does not know how far from the mark the commentators have wandered on this cousin or uncle of Isaiah? I have no wish to pile them up here. See Lyra, who understood cousin as the son of an uncle [as also the Belgic translator of the Vulgate version, Het Liedeken van mijns Ooms Sone, which is worth noting on account of the interpreters Forerius, the Carthusian, and others]. But the Hebrew word is indifferent between uncle and beloved. Hebrew: Ashirah na lididi shirat dodi [אֲשִׁירָה נָא לִידִידִי שִׁירַת דודי], I will now sing to my beloved a song of my beloved, etc. The Septuagint: I will sing to my beloved a song of my beloved. Forerius: If anyone is nevertheless displeased by that conjecture about the uncle of Isaiah, let him take dod as beloved, so that the antecedent stands for the relative, as the Hebrews often do. He says, "I will sing to my beloved a song of his vineyard." That is, the song which God bade me sing. Or thus: I will sing to my most beloved people of Israel the song of my most beloved God, which he bade me sing about his vineyard, namely the people themselves. As for what follows in the Vulgate version, m cornu filio olei, it has indeed been faithfully rendered from the Hebrew, but it has been understood by many people. And who could understand the Louvain version, Mynem lieve is een Vlyngaerd gebeurt in den horen, de sone der olien? Indeed, I would gladly grant to the Papists that such versions may be read with little or no benefit. I appeal to all sensible people, whom the zeal of party has not blinded, who have compared three or four chapters of this Belgic version with the Latin and Hebrew text, whether the translator, whoever he was, did not do this deliberately, so as to extract from simpler readers who fall into these texts the confession that the Scriptures cannot be read by laymen with profit or fruit. On this matter we shall, God willing, discuss more fully at Hosea chapter 1. How much better did Blessed Luther deserve of his readers, who, looking not so much at the words as at the sense, rendered the words ben shemen [בֶּן שֵׁמָן] as aen een vetter plaetse! Yet I cannot pass over that he neglected the word keren [קֶרֶן]. For the Hebrew reads thus: keren ben shemen. The Septuagint: in a horn, in a fat place [ἐν κέρατι, ἐν τόπῳ πίονι]. That the divine prophet means by keren the horn is well taught by Kimchi, when he comments on this place thus:

units.la: בתרגומו בטור רם באר עא שמינא ארץ ישראל קרן לפי שהיא גבוהה
units.tr: Onkelos in his paraphrase renders it: on a high mountain, in a fat land [בטור רם בארע שמינא]. The land of Israel is called a horn [ארץ ישראל קרן] because it is high

units.la: מכל הארצות, והקרן גבוה מכל הגוף, וקורא ארץ ישראל בן שמן כמו
units.tr: above all lands, and the horn is high above the whole body. He calls the land of Israel a son of oil [בן שמן] as

units.la: בקרן בן שמן שנאמר עליה ארץ זבת חלב ודבש hoc est, verba illa Chaldaeus sic interpretatus est, in monte excelso, in terra pingui. Vocat autem terram Israel cornu, quia altior est reliquis regionibus [confer hæc cum iis quæ parte prima Anti-Barbari pag. 509. diximus quæ in clavi scripturæ Illyrici ad vocem Ascendo addemus] sicuti cornu reliquo corpore altius est. Vocat insuper terram Israel filium olei, juxta illud quod dicitur de ea, fluens lacte & melle. Cl. Junius, in clivo uberrimo. Pisc. auf einen fatten trugel. Genev. en un costau d'un lieu gras. Atque hæc hactenus. Ea vero quæ ad hanc parabolam vulgo disputantur, non libro
units.tr: in keren ben shemen, as it is said of it: a land flowing with milk and honey [ארץ זבת חלב ודבש]. Thus Onkelos has translated those words, on a high mountain, in a fat land. He calls the land of Israel a horn, because it is higher than the other regions [compare these things with what we said in the first part of the Anti-Barbarus, p. 509, which we shall add in the key to Illyricus's Scripture under the word Ascendo], just as a horn is higher than the rest of the body. He moreover calls the land of Israel a son of oil, according to what is said of it, that it flows with milk and honey. Junius: on a very fruitful slope. The Piscator Bible: auf einen fatten trugel. The Geneva: en un costau d'un lieu gras. And so far so much. But what is commonly argued about this parable I shall not...

units.la: Πεζῇ Βαδίζω νεῦν γὰρ ἐπίσαμαι.
units.tr: I walk on foot, for I know how to swim. [Greek: Pezē badizō; neuein gar epistamai.]

units.la: Audiant tamen hoc à Grammatico argutuli isti disputatores Academici (juvenes alloquor, qui disputationes theologiæ animam esse putant) ne disputare maluerint quam vivere. Eo annitantur, ut uvas edant, non labrusicas. Non decet theologos arguta disserere & theologiam in tales angustias ex suâ majestate detrahere. Quanto satius est ire aperta via & recta, quàm sibi ipsi flexus disponere, quos cum magna molestia debeas relegere? neque enim quidquam aliud sunt illæ, disputationes, quam inter se perite captantium lusus.
units.tr: Yet let those clever Academic disputants hear this from a grammarian (I address you, young men who think that theological disputations are the soul of theology): let them rather live than dispute. They strive to eat grapes, not wild grapes. It does not befit theologians to discourse subtly and to drag theology down from its majesty into such narrow straits. How much better it is to go by the open and straight way, than to lay out windings for oneself which you must then retrace with great trouble! For those disputations are nothing else than the games of men who skilfully trap one another.

units.la: verf. Si non credideritis; non intelligetis.) Ita LXX. Ἐαν μὴ πιστεύσητε, ὑδὲ μὴ συνῆτε. Ita Tertullianus adversus Marcionem libro 4. cap. 20. Et bis Cyprianus vid. lib. 1. adversus Judæos cap. 5. hoc titulo, nihil posse Judæos intelligere ex Scripturis, nisi prius crediderint in Christum, iterumque libro 3. ubi docet, tantum nos posse quantum credimus. Et Ruffinus in symb. ut confirmet illud quod est in epistola ad Ebræos cap. xi. credere primo oportet accedentem ad Deum. Sic & invenies apud Eusseb. Demonstrat. Evang. 7. 2 Chrysost. homilia 51. in Ioh Cyrillum Alexandr. in fine libri 7. contra Julianum, August. in 7. cap. Joh. Prosperum cap. 19. lib. 1. de vita contemplat. &c. Pamelius ait locum insignem esse adversus eos, qui etiam hodie nolunt credere, nisi quod intelligunt, & fidem sensu aut scientia metiri volunt, vide ejus annot. ad Tertull. pag. 349. Verùm sciendum est, istum sensum ex originario textu exculpi non posse, [Hebrew] / quæ vulgatus interpres sic convertit. Si non credideritis, non permanebitis. à qua mente non divertit B Lutherus. Paraphrastes Chaldæus, [Hebrew] hoc est, si non credideritis verbis prophetæ [certum est] quod non permanebitis. Arias montanus vertit, neque permanebitis, ut [Hebrew] otium agat. Hisp. Genev. Angli, Si [hoc] non credideritis, profecto non eritis certi, pour vrai vous ne serez point affermis. Pisc. Si hoc non crediderus, (certum est) quod non futuri sitis certi. Scilicet fides in Deum, est veluti anchora, qua & Deum apprehendimus & nos ipsos firmamus. Si autem fiduciam amittamus, sumus veluti naves quæ vi ventorum ac fluctuum huc illuc impelluntur. Hispanica vetus, quæ creditur esse Kimchii, Si hoc non credatis, (hoc ideo fit) quia non estis confirmati, vel constantes. Verba ejus in commentario ista sunt. Si non credetis verbis meis, unde hoc erit? [Hebrew] quia non estis fideles & constantes in fide Dei. [Hebrew] habet significationem stabilitatis sicuti legimus, aquæ ejus stabiles. Plane in eandem sententiam Aben Ezra. [Hebrew] id est, & sensus verborum istorum [Hebrew] est, propterea [Hebrew] pterea pterea quod nulla in vobis est stabilitas, sicuti, & stabilia erunt verba vestra. Gen. 42. 20. omnes isti ΓΝ interpretati sunt Si, At cum eâdem particulâ aliquando etiam interrogent Ebraei, Deodatus ita maluit interpretari, Annon creditis, quia non confirmamini? sc. ullo signo. Junius, Annon creditis? quod non confirmamini, Reprehensio diffidentiæ Achazi. Videbat enim Propheta eum perstare in sua illa trepidatione de qua versu 2. Quod non confirmamini, scilicet hac promissione Dei, sed potius in vestra trepidatione pergitis. Cum ergo nuda promissione non confirmaretur Rex, infidelitati ejus perdomandæ signum adhibuit Dominus. Hanc interpretationem & antecedanea & consequa verba evincunt inquit Junius. Equidem omnes istæ interpretationes adeo concinnæ sunt, ut difficilem electionem faciat æqualitas. •
units.tr: Verse "If you will not believe, you will not understand." So the LXX: [Ἐαν μὴ πιστεύσητε, ὑδὲ μὴ συνῆτε.] So Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 4, chapter 20. Cyprian also uses it twice: see book 1 of Against the Jews, chapter 5, under the heading that the Jews can understand nothing from the Scriptures unless they first believe in Christ; and again in book 3, where he teaches that we can do as much as we believe. Rufinus, in his commentary on the Creed, uses it to support what is said in Hebrews 11: it is necessary first to believe that the one who comes to God (exists). You will also find it in Eusebius, Demonstratio Evangelica 7; Chrysostom, homily 51 on John; Cyril of Alexandria, at the end of book 7 against Julian; Augustine on John chapter 7; Prosper, chapter 19 of book 1 De vita contemplativa, and elsewhere. Pamelius says the passage is a notable one against those who even today are unwilling to believe unless they understand, and who want to measure faith by sense or knowledge; see his notes on Tertullian, p. 349. But it must be known that this sense cannot be drawn out of the original text, [Hebrew], which the Vulgate translator renders thus: If you will not believe, you will not remain. Luther does not depart from this meaning. The Chaldee paraphrast: if you will not believe the words of the prophet, [it is certain] that you will not remain. Arias Montanus renders it nor will you remain, so that [Hebrew] means to be at rest. The Geneva, the Hispanic and the English read: If [this] you do not believe, you will certainly not be established; pour vrai vous ne serez point affermis. Piscator: If you do not believe this, [it is certain] that you will not be made certain. Clearly faith in God is like an anchor, by which we both grasp God and make ourselves firm. If, however, we lose our confidence, we are like ships driven hither and thither by the force of winds and waves. The old Hispanic version, which is believed to be Kimchi's, reads: If you do not believe this, (this happens) because you are not confirmed, or steadfast. His words in the commentary are these: If you do not believe my words, whence will this come? [Hebrew], because you are not faithful and steadfast in the faith of God. [Hebrew] has the meaning of stability, as we read, its waters are stable. Aben Ezra plainly holds the same view: [Hebrew], that is, the sense of these words [Hebrew] is, therefore [Hebrew], because there is no stability in you, just as your words will be stable. In Genesis 42:20 all these interpreters render ΓΝ as if. But since the Hebrews sometimes use the same particle in questions, Deodatus preferred to render it: Do you not believe, because you are not confirmed? that is, by any sign. Junius: Do you not believe? Because you are not confirmed, a rebuke of Ahaz's unbelief. For the prophet saw that he persisted in that trepidation of which he speaks in verse 2, because you are not confirmed, namely by this promise of God, but rather you go on in your trepidation. Since the king was not confirmed by a bare promise, the Lord gave a sign to subdue his unbelief. Junius says that both the preceding and following words prove this interpretation. Indeed all these interpretations are so neatly balanced that equality makes the choice difficult.

units.la: Vers. 19. 20: Vulgatus, & cum dixerint ad vos, Quærite à Pythonibus, & à divinis, qui strid… in incantationibus suis, nunquid non populus à Deo suo requiret visionem pro vivis & mortuis? Ad legem magis & ad testimonium. Quod si non dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit iis matutina lux.) Universum hoc caput, ut & superius, admodum difficiles & proinde variis interpretum declaramentis obnoxios versus habet: Non sedet nobis omnia excutere. Quod ob filium illum vers. 3. Maher-schalalchasch-baz attinet, non est dubium, quia filius ipsius Prophetæ fuerit, ex legitima uxore, quæ vers. 3. Prophetissa dicitur, susceptus, ac præsentibus testibus, quos non vulgo compatres, veteres etiam ovvλιxvs vocitabant, isthoc nomine, quod ipse Deus disposuerat & præscripserat, indigitatus. Quid hic difficultatis est, vel in ipsa versione vulgata? Hanc interpretationem ipsi quoque Thomæ adscribit Lyra, qui tamen ab ea divertit, ut & Carthus. & ait. At inquiunt, quis credet Jesajam virum pudicum & castum testes adhibuisse ad concubitum? Quasi vero hoc diceret Jesajas, & non ex ipsa vulgata facilius colligi posset eos adhibitos esse firmandæ scripturæ, de qua versu primo. Quasi etiam dici non possit, eos adhibitos fuisse, ut denomine hoc, filio in Ecclesia impositio, testarentur, ut sic vertas cum Junio, me enim congressio cum prophetissa, conceperat illa, pepereratque filium &c. Quod vero iidem movent de Uria, eum fuisse vitae pessimae hominem, ac proinde testem nequaquam fidelem dici posse, respondent, eum non ob vitae sanctitatem, sed officii dignitatem fidelem testem appellari utpote, cujus authoritas & testimonium permagni futurum erat in populo. Quod denique objectant Samariam captam anno nono Regis Hosea, quo jam aetate major fuerit iste filius, quam ut de eo dici potuerit, eum non potuisse vocare patrem matremve suam valde torsit interpretes. Qui commodissime responderunt, quinquennem aut sexennen fecerunt hunc filium tempore Samaritanae captivitatis, quae incidit in 9. annum Hosea. Et cum hac aetate consistere posse existimant illa, antequam sciat puer &c. Quae interpretatio si vera est, tunc oportet hunc filiolum valde ὀψίλαλον fuisse. Nos nullam putamus esse necessitatem hujus natales in ultimum Achazi annum aut Ezechiae regnum rejiciendi. Referantur haec ad idem illud tempus quod memoratur cap. 7. & conferantur haec cum historia 2. Reg. xvi. videbis illa verba, antequam puer sciat dicere, pater mi, aut mater mea, commodissime posse exponi, cum Junio, ante annum aut breve aliquod tempus simile. Nisi illud fortassis demonstrari posset, inter apparatum illum militarem duorum Regum & confectum bellum, occupatamque Damascum (2. Reg. 16. 9.) multos annos fluxisse. Id quod nullus, opinor, demonstrabit. Hinc jam vides, cordate lector, verissimum esse quod insuperioribus saepe inculcavi, quoties difficultas quaedam aut nodus intricatior incidit, quem solvere interpretes non fuerunt quiti, mox ad Allegoricas & mysticas expositiones confugisse. Ita quicquid personae vel rei de qua scriptura ad literam manifeste loquitur, aptare non potuere, de Christo & rebus novi Testamenti expositione. Licet autem illic majores saepe difficultates offenderint, tamen postquam semel Allegoricae expositioni laxarunt habenas, nihil tam alienum fuit, quod non per Allegoriam eodem traherent. At quanto satius fuisset subinde Ignorantiam suam profiteri, aut illam potius versionem, cujus filum sequebantur, tanquam minus accuratam suspectare. Et quidem hujus rei egregium specimen exhibuimus ad XL. caput Jobi, ubi de Behemoth & Leviathan agitur. Idem fere hic se offert casus. Istae, quas recensui difficultates adegerunt Interpretes ad insulsam hanc interpretationem, ut puer iste sit Christus, prophetissa Maria, Qui loquitur, Deus pater, vel Jesajas. Carthus. Sed quicquid sit de argu-
units.tr: Verses 19-20, the Vulgate: "And when they shall say to you, Seek of the necromancers and of the soothsayers, who whisper in their incantations: shall not a people seek a vision from their God for the living and the dead? To the law rather, and to the testimony. But if they speak not according to this word, there shall be no morning light for them." This whole chapter, like the one before it, contains verses that are very difficult and therefore open to many interpreters' explanations. It is not hard to see that Maher-shalal-hash-baz, the son mentioned in verse 3, was the Prophet's own son, born of his lawful wife, who in verse 3 is called the prophetess. He was given the name that God himself had appointed and prescribed, and he was named in the presence of witnesses, whom the ancients called co-sponsors, not in the ordinary sense of that word. What difficulty is there here, even in the Vulgate text? Lyra ascribes this interpretation to Thomas himself, though he turns away from it, as do the Carthusians, and he says: "But they object, who will believe that Isaiah, a chaste and modest man, called witnesses to a sexual union?" As if Isaiah were saying this, and as if it could not more easily be inferred from the Vulgate itself that they were called in to confirm the writing mentioned in the first verse. As if it could not also be said that they were called in so that, by this name given to the son in the Church, they might bear witness, and so one may translate with Junius: "For I had relations with the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son, etc." As to the objection of the same writers about Uriah, that he was a man of very wicked life and so could not be called a faithful witness, they answer that he was called a faithful witness not because of the holiness of his life but because of the dignity of his office, since his authority and testimony would be of great weight among the people. Finally, they object that Samaria was taken in the ninth year of King Hoshea, by which time this son would already have been too old for it to be said of him that he could not yet call his father or mother by name. This has greatly troubled the interpreters. They answer most aptly by making this son five or six years old at the time of the Samaritan captivity, which fell in the ninth year of Hoshea. And they think that the words "before the child knows" etc. can stand with this age. If that interpretation is true, then this little child must have been very slow of speech [ὀψίλαλον]. We think there is no necessity to reject his birth to the last year of Ahaz or the reign of Hezekiah. Let these things be referred to that same time which is mentioned in chapter 7, and let them be compared with the history in 2 Kings 16. You will see that the words "before the child knows how to say, my father, or my mother" can most conveniently be explained, with Junius, as "a year or some such short time before." Unless perhaps it could be shown that many years passed between that military preparation of the two kings, their completed war, and the capture of Damascus (2 Kings 16:9). I think no one will show this. Here, learned reader, you now see how very true it is what I have often urged above: whenever some difficulty or more tangled knot arises, which the interpreters were not able to untie, they at once fled to allegorical and mystical explanations. Thus whatever person or matter Scripture plainly speaks of according to the letter, they could not fit, and so they applied it to Christ and to the things of the New Testament. Although they often met greater difficulties there, once they had given free rein to allegorical exposition, nothing was so foreign that they could not drag it there by allegory. How much better it would have been to confess their ignorance from time to time, or rather to suspect of inaccuracy that version whose thread they were following. We have indeed given a distinguished example of this in the fortieth chapter of Job, where Behemoth and Leviathan are discussed. Almost the same case presents itself here. The difficulties I have listed drove the interpreters to this silly explanation, that the child is Christ, the prophetess Mary, the speaker God the Father, or Isaiah, says the Carthusian. But whatever be the case with the argument...

units.la: Vide & Thomam part. 3. q. 1. art. 3. & Magistrum lib. 3. de tract. 13. c. argumentationibus, ego pro meliori eligo, atque securius puto sequi Hieronymum, quantum ad principale, quod puer, de quo nunc sermo est, sit Christus filius virginis, & hoc tenent Doctores communiter. Lyra, In hoc capite denuntiatur Christi resurrectio futura ad spoliationem inferni principaliter & per consequens ad significandum tanquam per signum rememorativum spoliationem duorum regum, Israel & Syriæ. Velociter spolia] Istud convenit Christo resurgenti, qui tunc celeriter spoliavit infernum, & in hoc fuit signum rememorativum spoliationis duorum regum. Et contrà hæc spoliatio fuit signum prognosticum spoliationis fiendæ per Christum. Et accessi ad prophetissam] id est, virginem Mariam. Hæc ex Lyra. Nunc addam lepidum commentarium Dionysii Carthusiani, Isajas, inquit, in propria persona profatur, Ad prophetissam] id est, spiritum sanctum, secundum S. Hieronymum. Designatur enim Spiritus S. nomine Prophetissæ, quoniam in lingua Ebr. denotatur per nomen gen. fœminini. Unde in sermone de assumptione Hieronymus dicit per Rebeccam significari Spiritum S. propter rationem prædictam. Accessit itaque Isajas ad Spiritum S. exhibendo se dignum & aptum dono seu gratiæ prophetali. Dicitur enim in Psalmo, Accedite ad eum & illuminamini. Accedimus quippe ad Deum disponendo nos ad gratiam ejus & amando contemplandoque ipsum. Sed quomodo huic prophetissæ id est, Spiritui Sancto conveniat quod subditur, & concepit, non video. Non enim Spiritus S. aliquo modo est mater Christi, nisi exponatur, concepit id est, concipere fecit virginem. Veruntamen quamvis Spiritus S. Latino sermone masculino genere designatur, nec tamen proprie propheta vocatur; sic quamvis in Ebræo sermone fœminino genere exprimatur, non tamen videtur prophetissa proprie nuncupari. Propter quod convenientius arbitror, per prophetissam significari Mariam. Ad hanc Isajas accessit contemplando excellentissimam ejus dignitatem, eamque mirando. Et concepit ipsa non de me, sed de Spiritu S. Hæc Carthus. Piget pudetque plura adscribere. Nam, quasi non satis nugarum chartis illevisset, addit alios verba ista, & assumsi mihi testes duos & accessi ad prophetissam &c. exponere tanquam verba Dei patris. Quod vero ad illa attinet, Antequam puer sciat vocare patrem suum (sc. ore humano & creata sapientia, uti interpretantur iidem) auferetur fortitudo Damasci &c. in Bibliis Benedicti nediͤti ex Chryfoftomi homilia 2. in Matth. sic exponitur: Magi adorantes Christum dicti sunt virtus Damasci, quia virtus uniufcujusque provincia sunt sapientes illius. Idem Chryf. per Regem Af-fyriorum Diabolum intelligit. Hoccine est interpretari Sacras Literas? Audi Hieronymum ab Oleastro, qui postquam confirmandae literali expositioni multa adduxisset, sic tandem infit, Et omnia haec dicimus, quia exponere, quae hic dicuntur, de virgine & Deo patre, videtur nimis torquere literam hanc, & hujus mentis est S. Thomas hic, Vatablus, Brixianus & multi alii. Si tamen contendas de virgine intelligi non disceptabo, quoniam exponere decrevi, non digladiari, maxime cum his hominibus, qui nihil adversum fe aut suos dici patiuntur, & parati sunt ad quodvis verbum gladium exerere. Haec ille. Quae cum fcripfiflemus, incidimus in comm. Hectoris Pinti Lusitani, qui in comm. per hanc Prophetiffam itidem Mariam, & per puerum Christum intelligit. Hanc interpretationem ut stabiliat, destruere conatur alteram, quae per Prophetiffam ipsius Jefaiae conjugem intelligit. Hoc ut obtinent, a vulgata versione antequam puer sciat v.p.f & matrem suam, auferetur fortitudo Damasci &c. provocat ad fontes, ubi pro auferetur, est auferet. Quod de nullo puro homine, inquit, dici potest. Quis enim priusquam sciat vocare patrem aut matrem, imo priusquam noscatur, posset evertere Damascum? &c Quasi vero illud insolens effet in mysticis literis personalia pro inperfonalibus usurpari, aut ad verba fubintelligere nomina? Sic & imputat ei Gen. 15. sc. Deus, Rom. 4. & imputatum est sc. a Deo. Sic 1. Sam. Et nuntiavit Davidi, fubnuntius. Hoc est, & nuntiatum est, quamvis D. Junius retinuerit activum asportabit, & quae sequuntur in fine versus לפני מלך אשור exposuerit; servus regis Affur, quasi ea per ellipfin posita effent pro אשר לפני מלך אשור qui [stat] coram Rege Affur. Notum est ut ministri dicantur stare coram dominis suis, 1. Reg. x. 8. Deut. x. 8. Luc. 1. 19. Apoc. 8. 2. Nunc accingamur ad versum 19. Si quis textum bene examinet videbit Prophetam per artificiofam αναλογίαν transire ad tertium peccatorum genus. q.d. Merito sane populus iste a Deo deseritur. Non solum enim Deo diffidens alienam opem implorat verf. 6. 12. & seqq. Non folum fe ipsum in peccatis obfirmat & aversatur Deum, verf. 16. 17. 18. Sed & daemones consultat, piosque ad idem scelus follicitat. licitat. Hoc autem Propheta exprimit, verba Junii, sermone converso ad pios ut eos instituat de atrocitate criminis & confirmet in bono. Cum ergo dicent ad vos consulite Pythones aut ariolos, qui pipiunt & musitant, tunc dicetis & respondebitis seductoribus illis, annon populus Deum suum considere debet ? An pro vivis mortuos consulet? vel, an pro vivis ad mortuos ibit? Ad legem potius & testificationem cant [vel, legem potius & testificationem consulant. אִם לֹא יֹאמְרוּ כַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אֵין לוֹ שָׁחַר Hæc verba variis expositionibus obnoxia sunt. B. Lutherus in Vulgati Interpretis vestigia pedes posuit. His particula אֲשֶׁר otium agit & לָהֶם positum pro / quæ enallage, fateor, non est insolens. Deodatus ab hoc tramite non divertit. Tantum ne otiaretur vocula אֲשֶׁר supplet aliquid, Si quis secundum hoc verbum non dixerit, [scito] quod ipsi non futura sit aurora. Aurora .i. Lux, illuminatio. Ille perpetuabit, vitam in crassis densisque tenebris. Angli & Hisp. אֲשֶׁר accepere pro בְּאֲשֶׁר Si non loquantur juxta verbum hoc (scil. verbum Legis & testimonii divini) [hoc ideo fit] quod nulla lux sit in illis. Pisc. Legem & testimonium [consulere oportet:] Sin minus, loquantur juxta verbum hoc, cui nulla inest aurora. Concessio irati & disperantis. q. d. Loquantur juxta verbum pythonum & magorum, quo nulla lux, nullum gaudium, nihil denique, quod hominis animum tranquillare queat in hac interpretatione, qua post לֹא אִם distinguitur, nulla enallage vel numeri vel vocula אֲשֶׁר. Ideoque maxime se mihi probat. Junius & Tigurini seorsim ab istis abeuntes accepere pro vocula interrogandi: sed diverso sensu, Tigur. Ad legem & testimonium [accedant] quibus lux deest, an non secundum istum sermonem dicant 21. Quam qui neglexerit, indurabitur & esuriet. Annon loquuntur in sententiam illam (vid. Consulite Pythones &c.) cuicunque nulla est lucis scintilla .i. quisquis plane ignorat Deum. Ubi rursus Enallage לוֹ pro לָהֶם / si verba illa, cuicunque nulla est lucis scintilla, accepit tanquam subjectum propositionis. Si enim ea accepit tanquam partem prædicati, seu quod idem est objectum loquentium, tunc אֲשֶׁר pro לְאֲשֶׁר positum erit. Nunc videamus quomodo vulgatus Interpres Propheta mentem expresserit. I. Occurrunt hic duæ istæ voces אוֹבוֹת & יִדְּעֹנִים / queis respondere mihi videntur geminaillaparticipia מְצַפְּצְפִים & הַמַּהְגִּים ita ut prius primo, posterius posteriori nomini conveniat; de quibus postea
units.tr: See also Thomas, part 3, q. 1, art. 3, and the Master, book 3, distinction 13. I choose the better view, and I think it safer to follow Jerome on the main point: the boy of whom we now speak is Christ, the son of the virgin, and the Doctors hold this commonly. Lyra says: "In this chapter the resurrection of Christ is announced as future, chiefly with reference to the despoiling of hell, and in consequence, to signify, as by a remembering sign, the despoiling of the two kings, Israel and Syria. Speedily the spoils: this fits Christ rising, who then speedily despoiled hell, and in this there was a remembering sign of the despoiling of the two kings. On the other hand, this despoiling was a prognostic sign of the despoiling to be done by Christ. And I went in to the prophetess": that is, the Virgin Mary. So far Lyra. Now I will add the witty commentary of Dionysius the Carthusian: "Isaiah," he says, "speaks in his own person. To the prophetess": that is, the Holy Spirit, according to St Jerome. For the Holy Spirit is designated by the name of prophetess, since in Hebrew it is expressed by a feminine noun. Hence in his sermon on the Assumption Jerome says that Rebekah signifies the Holy Spirit, for the reason given above. Isaiah therefore went to the Holy Spirit, showing himself worthy and fit for the gift or grace of prophecy. For it is said in the Psalm, 'Come near to him and be enlightened.' We draw near to God when we prepare ourselves for his grace and love and contemplate him. But how what follows, 'and she conceived,' fits this prophetess, that is, the Holy Spirit, I do not see. For the Holy Spirit is in no way the mother of Christ, unless 'conceived' is explained as 'caused the virgin to conceive.' Yet although the Holy Spirit is designated in Latin by the masculine gender, he is not properly called a prophet; so, although in Hebrew he is expressed by the feminine gender, he does not seem properly to be named a prophetess. For this reason I judge it more fitting that by the prophetess Mary is signified. Isaiah went to her, contemplating and marvelling at her most excellent dignity. And she conceived, not from me, but from the Holy Spirit." So the Carthusian. I am ashamed and loath to add more. For, as if he had not defiled enough paper with trifles, he adds that others expound the words and I took to myself two witnesses and went in to the prophetess, &c., as the words of God the Father. As for those words, Before the boy knows how to call his father (that is, with a human mouth and created wisdom, as the same men interpret), the strength of Damascus shall be taken away, &c., in the Benedictine Bible, from the second homily of Chrysostom on Matthew, it is explained thus: The Magi adoring Christ are called the strength of Damascus, because the strength of each province is its wise men. The same Chrysostom understands by the King of Assyria the Devil. Is this what it is to interpret the Sacred Letters? Hear Jerome, as cited by Oleaster, who, after bringing forward many arguments for the literal exposition, at last says: "We say all these things because to explain what is said here of the virgin and God the Father seems to twist the letter too much, and this is the mind of St Thomas here, of Vatablus, of Brixianus and of many others. If, however, you insist that it is to be understood of the virgin, I shall not dispute, since I have decided to expound, not to fight, especially with those men who suffer nothing to be said against themselves or theirs, and are ready to draw the sword at every word." So he. When we had written this, we fell upon the commentary of Hector Pinto the Portuguese, who likewise understands by this prophetess Mary, and by the boy Christ. To establish this interpretation he tries to destroy the other, which understands by the prophetess the wife of Isaiah himself. To support this, from the Vulgate version, before the boy knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus shall be taken away, &c., he appeals to the sources, where for auferetur ("shall be taken away") there is auferet ("he shall take away"). "This," he says, "can be said of no mere man. For who, before he knows how to call father or mother, or rather before he is known at all, could overthrow Damascus?" &c. As if it were unusual in mystical writings to use personal forms for impersonal ones, or to supply nouns to the verbs! So too he imputes to him Genesis 15, that is, God; Romans 4, and it was imputed, that is, by God; so 1 Samuel, and it was announced to David, a substitute for and it was announced. Junius, though he retained the active he will carry away, and expounded what follows at the end of the verse, לפני מלך אשור [before the king of Assyria], as servant of the king of Assyria, as though it were put there by ellipsis for אשר לפני מלך אשור [which stands before the king of Assyria]. It is well known that ministers are said to stand before their lords, 1 Kings 10:8; Deuteronomy 10:8; Luke 1:19; Revelation 8:2. Now let us turn to verse 19. If anyone examines the text carefully, he will see that the Prophet passes by a skilful analogy to a third kind of sin, as if to say: Rightly indeed this people is deserted by God. For not only, distrusting God, does it implore foreign help (vv. 6, 12 and following), not only does it harden itself in sins and turn away from God (vv. 16, 17, 18), but it also consults demons and incites the godly to the same crime. The Prophet expresses this, in the words of Junius, turning his speech to the godly, so as to instruct them about the atrocity of the crime and confirm them in good: When therefore they say to you, Consult the Pythons or the wizards, who chirp and mutter, then you shall say and answer those seducers, Ought not a people to consult its God? Shall they consult the dead for the living? Or shall one go from the living to the dead? To the law rather and the testimony let them go [or, rather let them consult the law and the testimony]. If they do not speak according to this word, which has no dawn in it [אִם לֹא יֹאמְרוּ כַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אֵין לוֹ שָׁחַר]. These words are open to various expositions. Luther set his feet in the footsteps of the Vulgate translator. Here the particle אֲשֶׁר [which] is idle and לָהֶם [to them] is put for / [to whom]; this enallage, I confess, is not unusual. Deodatus does not turn aside from this path. Only, so that the little word אֲשֶׁר should not be idle, he supplies something: If anyone does not speak according to this word, [know that] there shall be no dawn for him. Dawn, that is, light, illumination. He will remain in thick and dense darkness in life. The English and Spanish took אֲשֶׁר as בְּאֲשֶׁר [according to which]: If they do not speak according to this word (namely the word of the Law and of the divine testimony), [this happens] because there is no light in them. Piscator: They ought to consult the law and the testimony: but if not, let them speak according to this word, in which there is no dawn. This is the concession of an angry and despairing man, as if to say: let them speak according to the word of the pythons and magicians, in which there is no light, no joy, nothing at last that could calm the human mind. In this interpretation, where the sentence is divided after לֹא אִם [not if], there is no enallage either of number or of the little word אֲשֶׁר. Therefore it especially commends itself to me. Junius and the Zurich translators, departing from those others, took it as an interrogative particle, but in a different sense. Zurich: Shall they go to the law and the testimony, which lack light; do they not speak according to this saying (21): He who neglects it will be hardened and will hunger. Do they not speak in agreement with that saying (see, Consult the Pythons, &c.) to whom there is no spark of light, that is, to whoever plainly does not know God. Here again there is an enallage: לוֹ [to him] for לָהֶם [to them], if those words, to whom there is no spark of light, are taken as the subject of the proposition. For if they were taken as part of the predicate, or what is the same, as the object of the speakers, then אֲשֶׁר would stand for לְאֲשֶׁר [to which]. Now let us see how the Vulgate translator expressed the Prophet's meaning. I. Here two words occur, אוֹבוֹת [ob'ot] and יִדְּעֹנִים [yidde'onim], to which the two participles מְצַפְּצְפִים [chirping] and הַמַּהְגִּים [muttering] seem to me to correspond, so that the first belongs to the first noun and the second to the second; concerning these I shall speak later.
