units.la: L lll 2 postea. אוב Pythonem reddere amant interpretes, qua novelli quæ-prissi. Loquor de Latinis. Græci enim ἐγγαςζιμύθϖς ventriloquos, Chald. בריז i.e. mendaces reddidit. Porro אבות positum vi-detur pro בעלי אובות / sicuti.
units.tr: (L lll 2) Later. The interpreters like to render ob as "Python", as the more recent writers do. I am speaking of the Latin translators. The Greeks render it engastrimythos [ἐγγαστρίμυθος], ventriloquists, and the Chaldee paraphrast renders it "liars" [בריז]. Further, ob seems to be used for baal ob [בעל אוב].

units.la: 1. Sam. 28. 7. legimus בעלת אוב .i. quæ habet אוב aut אשר בו אוב / ut Levit. xx. ult in quo est אוב & Act. Xvi. 16. ἔχουσα πνεῦμα πύθωνος. אוב ergo est πνεῦμα πύθωνος. אוב בעל ἔχων πνεῦμα πύθωνος. Cùm אוב pro בעל אוב ponitur, metonymia adjuncti est, qualis & 1. Joh. iv. 1. ne credite omni spiritui; sed probate spiritus. 2. In hoc cognoscetis spiritum Dei .i. doctorem, qui habet vel se habere dicit spiritum Dei &c. אוב proprie utrem .i. ἀσκὸν significat, unde Latinum Obba poculi genus Pers. Satyra v. vejentanumque rubellum Exhalet vapida latum pice sessilis obba. Sessilem vocat, quia cum ponitur, sedere videtur. II. Spiritum impurum, qui submissam, stridulam, obscuram & quasi ex utre profectam vocem edit. Jesai. xxix. 4. Adeo ut dejecta e terra loquaris & e pulvere musset sermo tuus: eritque quasi Pythonis e terra vox tua & e pulvere sermo tuus תצפ- piplet vel susurrabit, mussitabit. Ubi rursus vides, τῶ אוב vocem submissam tribui nisi malis δαιμόνιον illud γαστρὸς Obdici, quod ventrem hominis, quem incesserat, ad instar utris inflaret & ex eo loqueretur. Putem ergo si proprie loqui velimus, hanc fuisse πνευ-μάντιαν, quando spiritum, ut sic dicam, familiarem evocabat aliquis, eoque afflatus divinabat, sive ipsi spiritui vocis organa commodaret, sive ipse Spiritus sonum qualemcumque ederet. Talis videtur fuisse illa puella, Act. Xvi. 16. ἔχουσα πνεῦμα πύθωνος. Talis denotatur Lev. xx. ult. vir IN quo fuerit OB. Talem intelligunt Græci, quando ἐγγαςειμύθωι memorant, pro quo apud Hesychium in voce Πύθων, extat ἐγγαςειμαντις. Non ignoro quosdam existimasse vocem illam potius sonare utriloquos, quam ventriloquos quia vid. γάσηρ etiam vasculum significat & certum est superstitiosos istos homines etiam pelvibus & vitreis ampullis in dæmonum evocationibus usos fuisse. Vides ad Cap. ult. lib. 7. August. de civit. Dei, jam dæmonum evocandorum mille artes. Hydromantiam ad ultimum reservavi. Ea non fit simpliciter. Nam & in ampulla vitrea impositu aquæ, quæ à puero inspicitur, quam gastro-mantiam vocant, à tumore & ventricositate ampulla &c. Sed his oppono Aristophanem, qui in comœdia cui titulus est Σφῆκες, quasi vocem illam interpretaturus sic inquit, μιμησάμενος τὴν Εὐρυκλέus μαντείαν καὶ Ἀρ-γοίαν τὰς ἀπωλείας γαστέρας ἐνδὺς κωμωδικὰ πολλὰ χλευάζει .i. imitatus Euryclis (qui ἐγγαστρίμυθος dictus fuit) vaticinium & mentem, in alienos ventris ingressus ad multa comica effundendum. Atque huc pertinent illa quæ apud Plutarch. Strabonem, & Ciceronem libris de Divinatione leguntur, vid. Apollinem in hunc modum Vates suos afflâsse, ut aura quædam ex antro per augustissimum os prodiret, ipsorumque ventres tanquam utres quosdam impleret. Unde tripodi cuidam instabant & ut Oecumenius ad Act. XVI. loquitur divaricatis cruribus auram istam excipiebant. Origenes lib. 3. contra Celsum, Ori Pythii specus insidens, quam vocant Prophetidem, per muliebria recipit spiritum Apollinis fatidicum, nullo convestitum terreno corpore. Et lib. 7. Certe de Pythia, quo non aliud mantéum est celebrius, narratur, vatem illam Apollinis desiderio super foramen specus Castalii & ascendentem inde Spiritum per muliebre recipere gremium, quo repleta profert ista præclara & divina, ut putant, oracula &c. Huc etiam referas istos ψυρομάντις, quorum Sophocles, item ἐνγαστρίμυθος, quorum Theodoretus quæst. 29. in Levit. meminere, ita dictos, quod ex ipsorum pectore & intestinis loqueretur dæmon. Refert Rhodiginus lib. 8. cap. 10. se talem novisse & vidisse. Verbis ejus ista sunt, Id nequis ut fabulosum risu excipiendum putet; testatum volumus, tempestate hac, imo vero hæc prodente me, fuisse in patria mea mulierculam humili loco, Jacobam nomine, ex cujus ventre immundi spiritus vocem prætenuem quidem, sed tamen, ubi vellet, dearticulatam & prorsus intelligibilem audivi ipse, verum & innumeri alii, non Rhodigii modo, sed & in tota fere Italia. Quando futuri avida potentum mens sæpe accersitam ventriloquam ac omni exutam amictu, ne quid fraudis occultæ lateret, inspectare ac audire concupivit Cincinnatulus dæmoni erat. Hac ille appellatione gestiens inclamanti subinde respondebat. Side præteritis aut præsentibus scitareris, quæ reconditissima forent, responsa dabat sæpe mirifica. Si de futuris, semper mendacissimus: Hæc Rhodiginus. Cui non omnino dissimile est quod refert Hieron. ab Oleastro in comm. ad Jesaiæ 29. 4. Memini, inquit, me olim, dum Ulissiponæ juvenis agerem, fœminam quandam Ceciliam nomine ad Curiam & supremum Senatum adductam vidisse, in cujus cubicubitis & nonnunquam aliis locis, vox quædam gracilis audiebatur, quam illa cujusdam Petri Johannis defuncti esse ajebat, quæ ad omnia quæsita quam citissime & promptissime respondebat.
units.tr: (1) At 1 Samuel 28:7 we read baalat ob [בעלת אוב], that is, a woman who has an ob, or in whom there is an ob, as in Leviticus 20 at the end, in quo [in whom] there is an ob, and in Acts 16:16, echousa pneuma pythonos [ἔχουσα πνεῦμα πύθωνος], "having a spirit of Python". So ob is pneuma pythonos [πνεῦμα πύθωνος], and baal ob is echōn pneuma pythonos [ἔχων πνεῦμα πύθωνος]. When ob is put for baal ob, it is a metonymy of the adjunct, as in 1 John 4:1, "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits", and in 1 John 4:2, "By this you shall know the Spirit of God", that is, the teacher who has, or says he has, the Spirit of God, and so on. Properly, ob means a bag or wineskin, that is, askos [ἀσκός], from which comes the Latin obba, a kind of drinking cup, in Persius, Satire 5: "and the reddish Veientine cup exhales a broad vapour of pitch from its sitting base." He calls it "sitting" because when it is set down it seems to sit. (2) It denotes an unclean spirit which gives out a low, hissing, obscure voice, as if it came out of a bag. Isaiah 29:4: "So that you speak from the ground brought low, and your speech murmurs out of the dust; and your voice shall be like that of a Python from the earth, and your speech from the dust." The Hebrew titsaph [תצפ] means it chirps, whispers or mutters. Here again you see that ob is given a low voice, unless you prefer to take the daimonion [δαιμόνιον] of the gastros [γαστρός], the Obdic, which inflated the belly of the man it had entered, like a bag, and spoke out of it. If we wish to speak strictly, I think this was pneumantia [πνευμαντία], when someone summoned, so to speak, a familiar spirit and, inspired by it, divined. Whether he lent the spirit his vocal organs, or the spirit itself produced some sound, is a matter of indifference. Such, it seems, was the girl in Acts 16:16, echousa pneuma pythonos. Such is meant in Leviticus 20 at the end, "the man in whom there is an ob." The Greeks mean such a person when they mention engastrimythoi [ἐγγαστρίμυθοι], and in Hesychius under the word Python there is engastrimantis [ἐγγαστρίμαντις]. I am not unaware that some have thought the word sounds rather like utriloquos, bag-speakers, than ventriloquos, because gaster also means a little vessel, and it is certain that these superstitious people used basins and glass flasks in calling up demons. See the last chapter of book 7 of Augustine, De civitate Dei, where he already mentions a thousand arts of calling up demons. I have reserved hydromancy to the end. It is not done simply, for by placing water in a glass flask, which a boy looks into, which they call gastromancy, [they divine] from the swelling and bulging of the flask, and so on. But against these I set Aristophanes, who in his comedy entitled Wasps, as if about to explain that word, says: mimēsamenos tēn Eurykleus manteian kai Argoian tas apōleias gastera endys komōdika polla chleuazei [μιμησάμενος τὴν Εὐρυκλέους μαντείαν καὶ Ἀργοίαν τὰς ἀπωλείας γαστέρας ἐνδύς κωμωδικὰ πολλὰ χλευάζει], that is, "imitating the prophecy of Euryclis (who was called engastrimythos) and mocking many comic things, having entered the bellies of others." To this belong also the things read in Plutarch, Strabo and Cicero's books On Divination: that Apollo breathed upon his prophets in such a way that a certain breath came out of the cave through the most sacred mouth and filled their bellies like bags. Hence they stood by a certain tripod and, as Oecumenius says on Acts 16, received that breath with their legs spread apart. Origen, book 3 Against Celsus, says that the Pythian prophetess, sitting over the cleft of the cave which they call the Prophetic one, receives through the womb the prophetic spirit of Apollo, clothed in no earthly body. And book 7: "Certainly of the Pythia, than whom no other oracle is more famous, it is told that the priestess, by Apollo's desire, sits above the opening of the Castalian cave, and receives the spirit ascending from it through her womb, and being filled with it utters those splendid and divine oracles, as they think." You may also refer to these the pyromantis [ψυρομάντις] of whom Sophocles, and the engastrimythos [ἐγγαστρίμυθος] whom Theodoret in Question 29 on Leviticus mentions, so called because the demon spoke from their breast and entrails. Rhodiginus, book 8, chapter 10, reports that he knew and saw such a woman. His words are these: "Lest anyone think this fabulous and laugh at it, I want it attested that in these times, indeed, as I relate it, there was in my native place a poor little woman named Jacoba, from whose belly an unclean spirit spoke, in a very thin voice indeed, but still articulate when it wished and perfectly intelligible. I heard it myself, and countless others, not only in Rhodigii's time but almost throughout Italy. When the mind of the powerful, eager for the future, often summoned the ventriloquist and, stripped of all clothing lest any hidden fraud lie concealed, desired to inspect and hear her, Cincinnatulus was the demon. Delighted by this name, he kept answering the one calling him. If you asked about the past or present, the most hidden things, he often gave wonderful answers; if about the future, he was always most lying." Thus Rhodiginus. Not altogether unlike this is what Jerome of Oleaster reports in his commentary on Isaiah 29:4: "I remember," he says, "that when I was a young man at Lisbon I saw a certain woman named Cecilia brought before the Court and the Supreme Senate, in whose bed-chamber, and sometimes in other places, a certain thin voice was heard, which she said was that of a dead man named Peter John, and which answered all questions as quickly and readily as possible."

units.la: Lubet autem hic adscribere verba Mosis Kotzensis, quæ extant in libro præceptorum majore sol. 9. col. 3. בעל אוב זה פיתום המדבר משיחין ותניא בעל אוב זה המדבר בין הפרקים פי עולה הסת יושב בין פרקי המכשף או בין שיחיו ומדבר בקול נמוך מאד כאילו יוצא מתחת לארץ ועוד יש מעשה אחד של אוב הנשאל בגולגלת של מת
units.tr: It is worth adding here the words of Moses of Kotzk, which are found in the larger Book of Precepts, folio 9, column 3: "Baal ob [בעל אוב] is the pitom [פיתום] who speaks from his armpits." And it is taught: "Baal ob is he who speaks between the joints," that is, the one who rises up, sits between the joints of the sorcerer, or between his armpits, and speaks in a very low voice, as if it came out from under the earth. There is also another kind of ob, when the spirit is consulted through the skull of a dead man.

units.la: Baal Ob est pytho, qui loquitur ex axillis suis. Et traditio est, πυθομάντις illum esse qui loquitur inter articulos, hoc est, ascendit mortuus (h.e. si verum amamus non anima defuncti, sed spiritus immundus) & sedet inter articulos magi, aut inter axillas ejus & loquitur voce admodum submissa, ac si prodiret de sub terra. Estque insuper alius modus & O B, quando vid. interrogatur per calvariam mortui. Hic nulla mentio ἐγγαστρίμυθος proprie dicti.
units.tr: Baal Ob is the pytho, who speaks out of his armpits. There is also a tradition that the pythomantis [πυθομάντις] is one who speaks between the joints, that is, a dead man rises (that is, if we speak truly, it is not the soul of the deceased but an unclean spirit) and sits between the joints of the magician, or between his armpits, and speaks in a very subdued voice, as if it came out from under the earth. There is also another mode of Ob, when the spirit is consulted through the skull of a dead man. Here there is no mention of the ventriloquist [ἐγγαστρίμυθος] properly so called.

units.la: Maimonides halacha de Idololatria, cap. 6. כי צד מעשה האוב זה שהוא עומר ומקטיר קטורת ידועה ואוחז שרביט לש הדס בידו ומניפף והוא מדבר בלט בדברים ידועים אצלם עד שישמע השואל כאלו אחד מדבר עמו ומשיבו על מה שהוא שואל ברברים מתחת לארץ בקול נמוך מאוד וכאלו אינו ניכר לאוזן אלא במחשבה מרגיש בו וכן הלקה גלגולת המת ומקטיר לה ומנחש לה עד שישמע כאלו קול יוצא מתחת שחיו שפל עד מאוד ומשיבו כל אקה מעשה אוב / hoc est, quomodo se
units.tr: Maimonides, Hilchot Avodat Kochavim (Laws of Idolatry), chapter 6: "For the manner of the Ob-practice is this: he stands and burns a certain known incense, and holds in his hand a myrtle branch and waves it, and he speaks loudly in words well known among them, until the one who asks hears as if someone were speaking with him and answering him to what he asks, in words coming from under the earth, in a very low voice, so that it is scarcely perceived by the ear but is felt almost only in thought. Likewise, the one who takes the skull of a dead man burns incense before it and utters incantations over it, until a voice is heard as if coming out from under its armpits, very thin and low, which answers. All this is the work of Ob." [כי צד מעשה האוב] This is, in other words, how the business of Baal Ob is carried on.

units.la: habet negotium Baal O B? Hoc modo. Stat & ustulat certam quendam suffitum & tenet sceptrum quoddam myrteum manu sua & agitat illud. Demurmurabat autem certa quædam verba, donec is qui consulebat, audiret vocem tanquam hominis secum loquentis & respondentis ad id quod rogabat, idque verbis quasi ex terra prodeuntibus, voce admodum submissa, adeo quidem ut vix perciperetur auribus, sed propemodum cogitatione tantum. Similiter qui accipiebat calvariam mortui & odoramenta incendaret super ea & adhibet incantationes, donec audiatur vox quasi ex axillis exiens eaque admodum exilis & submissa, quæ respondeat. omnia ista pertinent ad BAAL OB. Ubi rursus nulla mentio ἐγγαστρίμυθος proprie sic dicti. Ego ut hæc non nego aut rejicio, quæ cum ratione μαγεφυγες & O B optime consistunt omnia, ita sentio בעל אוב primo & maxime proprie denotare eum in quo est spiritus pythonicus, sive ut Angli in Bibliorum versione vocant, familiaris, sive sit ἐγγαστρίμυθος vel ἐγγαστρίμαντις, sive γαστρομαντις, sive ἐπιγομαντις. II. eum qui spiritum immundum, seu familiarem incantamentis evocatum tali aliquo modo quales Maimonides recenset, consulit, qui Deuter. xviii. 2. distinctius שׁוֹאֵל הָאוֹב consulens Pythonem vocatur. Et quia hic coecis mortalibus saepe illudebat Satanas & defunctorum animas non raro mentiebatur, scriptura quoque secundum erroneam superstitiosorum opinionem saepe loquens, eundem eodem versu Deuteronomii דּוֹרֵשׁ אֶל הַמֵּתִים id est, consulentem mortuos vocat. Et pii hoc ipso Jesajae loco ad consulendum spiritum Pythonicum solicitati, respondent, an pro vivis consulendi sunt mortui? procul dubio ad vanitatem τῆς πυθομαντείας vel νεκρομαντείας respicientes. Putem ergo בַּעַל אוֹב III. eum denotare, quiex sententia sua animam defuncti, revera autem spiritum immundum evocat. Et quidem Graecos quoque tales admodum improprie ἐγγαστρίμύθους vocasse Suidas ex Prochoro quodam docet, voce ἐγγαστρίμυθος. Dicit enim prochorum tradidisse ἐν γ. περὶ μαντικῆς libro 3. de divinatione, fuisse & γυναῖκας τινας ἐγγαστρίμύθους. Αὗται, inquit, τὰς τῶν τεθνηκότων ψυχὰς ἐξεκαλοῦντο. Pergit. Μιᾷ δὲ αὐτῶν ἐκέλευσε Σαοὺλ, ἡ ἐξεκαλέσατο τὴν ψυχὴν Σαμουήλ. Ne longe eamus, expende mihi caput xxviii. libri i. Samuelis, Jubet Saul quaerifaeminam בַּעֲלַת אוֹב verf. 7. Eam vero verf. 8. sic affatur divina mihi בְּאוֹב per pythonem, & ascendere mihi facquem tibi dixero. Et hanc Lxx. quoque ἐγγαστρίμυθον vocarunt. Et fieri potest ut ipsa quoque tam immundum hospitem habuerit. Plura huc convectare ex Ebraeis poteram, sed quia Multa in iis suspecta & incerta, operam & tempus compendi faciam.
units.tr: What then is the nature of the Baal Ob? It is this. He stands, burns a certain incense, holds in his hand a certain myrtle rod and waves it. He mutters certain words until the one who consults hears a voice as of a man speaking with him and answering what he asks, and this in words as if coming out of the earth, in a very low voice, so faint that it is scarcely perceived by the ears, but almost only by the mind. Likewise, one who takes the skull of a dead man, burns perfumes over it and uses incantations until a voice is heard as if coming out of its armpits, very thin and low, which gives the answer. All these things pertain to the BAAL OB. Here again there is no mention of the ventriloquist [ἐγγαστρίμυθος] properly so called. I do not deny or reject these things; they all agree well with the idea of the magic-flight [μαγεφυγες] and the Ob. But I think that the Hebrew [בעל אוב] first and most properly denotes the one in whom there is a Pythonic spirit, or, as the English call him in their translation of the Bible, a familiar spirit, whether he be called ἐγγαστρίμυθος, ἐγγαστρίμαντις, γαστρομαντις, or ἐπιγομαντις. Second, it denotes the one who consults an unclean or familiar spirit evoked by incantations in some such manner as Maimonides describes; this man is called, more distinctly in Deuteronomy 18:11, שׁוֹאֵל הָאוֹב [one who consults the Ob], the consulter of a Python. And because Satan often deceived these blind mortals and not seldom pretended to be the souls of the dead, Scripture too, speaking according to the erroneous opinion of superstitious people, often calls the same man in the same verse of Deuteronomy דּוֹרֵשׁ אֶל הַמֵּתִים [one who seeks to the dead], that is, one who consults the dead. And the godly, urged to consult the Pythonic spirit, answer from this very passage of Isaiah: "Should the dead be consulted on behalf of the living?" undoubtedly looking to the vanity of τῆς πυθομαντείας [pythomancy] or νεκρομαντείας [necromancy]. I think, therefore, that בַּעַל אוֹב denotes third the one who, in his own opinion, evokes the soul of a dead man, but in reality evokes an unclean spirit. Suidas, citing a certain Prochorus under the word ἐγγαστρίμυθος, shows that the Greeks also very improperly called such people ἐγγαστρίμύθους. For he says that Prochorus related in the third book ἐν γ. περὶ μαντικῆς [in the third book On Divination] that there were also certain women γυναῖκας τινας ἐγγαστρίμύθους. "These," he says, "used to summon the souls of the dead." He goes on: "Saul ordered one of them, who summoned the soul of Samuel." Not to go far, consider for me 1 Samuel 28. Saul seeks a woman בַּעֲלַת אוֹב [a mistress of Ob] (v. 7). And she, in verse 8, says to him: "Divine for me by the Ob" [בְּאוֹב], "and bring up for me whom I shall name to you." The Septuagint too called her ἐγγαστρίμυθον. And it may be that she too had such an unclean guest. I could bring together much more from the Hebrews on this point, but since many of their things are doubtful and uncertain, I shall save labour and time.

units.la: Quod vero attinet ad vocem יִדְּעֹנִי non moror ineptias quorundam Ebraeorum, qui omnes futilitatis numeros hic implevere. Vox Ebraea, si originem spectes, significat γνῶσιν seu ἐπίγνωσιν (Ebraei enim cum non habeant composita, simplicibus utuntur) seu δαιμονια; quae omnia ariolis & divinis optime conveniunt. Gerte nemo tam hospes in Ebraismo est, qui nesciat יד idem esse quod scire, praescire &c. Atque adeo ipsi Lxx. Ebraeam vocem Idgnoni quater γνῶσιν interpretati sunt.
units.tr: As for the word yidde'oni [יִדְּעֹנִי], I will not dwell on the trifles of certain Hebrews, who have here filled every category of futility. The Hebrew word, if you consider its origin, means knowledge [γνῶσιν] or full knowledge [ἐπίγνωσιν] (since the Hebrews have no compound words and use simple ones) or divinings [δαιμονια]. All of these suit diviners and soothsayers very well. Indeed, no one is so much a stranger to Hebrew that he does not know that יד means the same as to know, to foreknow, and so on. Accordingly the Seventy themselves translated the Hebrew word Idgnoni four times as γνῶσιν [γνῶσιν].

units.la: Verbum addam de voce Python, de quo nomine Graecos intoleranda commentos esse, non de nihilo queritur magnus Heinsius.
units.tr: I will add a word about the word Python. The great Heinsius complains, not without reason, that the Greeks have invented intolerable tales about this name.

units.la: sius. * Adscribam ejus verba. Inter Græcos sunt, inquit, qui ὑπὸ ... sacropag. 17; ἕ πνῳ ... , seu consultatione; sunt qui ... ἕ ἐκεῖ ... δράκοντα, ... ἐσ ... ἕ Ἀπόλλων ... ἀναιρεθέντα, πύθιος id est, quod serpens illic ab Apolline sublatus computruerit, sic dici volunt. Quæ hoc putido serpente multo forsitan putidiora sunt. Minori enim opere à Pythone ipso deduxissent. Nisi quod & hic hærere aquam sibi facile viderent. Nam si locus à Pythone, unde Pytho, à quo nomen loco? Verùm פִּתֹּן ab Ebræis species serpentis dicitur. Ab hac voce phethen, Pytho serpens. Porro notum est, Ebræos ex serpentibus, vaferrimo in terris animali, divinationes olim plures & auguria instituisse. Unde ינחש / quemadmodum serpentem, ita & divinare aut augurari literis iisdem denotat in sacris. Quod non male Græci οἰωνίζομαι verterunt, qui serpentes ipsos οἰωνοὺς dixere. Abyssus eruditionis veteris Grammaticus Hesychius, οἰωνὸς, ὄφις ... Φοινικῶς ... λέγονται ... ἐς τὰς μαντείας ... ὄφεις ἔχειν ... καὶ οἰωνὸς ἐλεγον. Plane eodem modo, quo Hebræi voce eadem נַחְשִׁים serpentes simul & auguria (ad verbum, οἰωνὸς) dixerunt. Primus sane qui hanc vocem apud Mosen usurpavit, Laban Syrus antiquissimus Idololatra fuit, quod ex ejus idolis sive theraphim apparet. Primus qui ex oriente, ut cætera, hoc transtulit, Homerus est: apud quem hoc divinandi genere Iliados β. usus augur antiquissimus, de summa rei & excidione Ilii Græcorum Principem confirmat. Adhibetur enim δράκων ... ναῦς ... δαφοινὸς. quæ est vera circumscriptio ... nachas quem à notis, quæ in tergo sunt serpentum, è quibus inter cætera illius animalis divinationes & auguria captabant, ita dictum volucre. Ut non dubitandum sit, quin Pythius Apollo, hoc est spurcus ille spiritus, quem Hebræi Ob & Abaddon, Hellenistæ ad verbum Ἀπολλύων, cæteri Ἀπόλλωνα dixerunt, sub hac forma, qua miseriam humano olim generi invexit, primo cultus sit in Syria. Quemadmodum & Pherecydes Syrus, principem malorum dæmonum, Ophioneum vocavit &c. Hæc magnus & literatissimus ille Eques Heinsius. Quibus illud addo, ipsum quoque Græcorum ὄφις & fortassis etiam φοῖβος ab Ebræo אוב derivatum videri. Et ὀφιοῦχος apud Horapollinem lib. 1. cap. 1. serpentis genus est.
units.tr: Heinsius's own words, which I will quote. Among the Greeks, he says, there are some who (text corrupt) ... (text corrupt) ... and some who say that the serpent slain there by Apollo rotted away, and so it was called Python, that is, "rotted." These stories are perhaps more rotten than the serpent itself, for they would have derived it from the Python with less effort, were it not that they saw that the water would not run for them either. For if the place is named from Python, from what is Python named? But in Hebrew pithon [פִּתֹּן] is the name of a kind of serpent. From this word phethen [phethen] comes Python, the serpent. It is well known that the Hebrews formerly derived many divinations and auguries from serpents, the most cunning of animals on earth. Hence the word נחש, which denotes the serpent, denotes also to divine or augur, with the same letters in the sacred text. The Greeks rightly rendered this as οἰωνίζομαι, and they called the serpents themselves οἰωνοὺς. The learned ancient grammarian Hesychius, in an abyss of learning, says that the Phoenicians call the serpent οἰωνός and that they kept serpents for divinations (text corrupt). In exactly the same way the Hebrews, with the same word נַחְשִׁים, called serpents and auguries alike (literally οἰωνός). Certainly the first to use this word in Moses was Laban the Syrian, a very ancient idolater, as appears from his idols or theraphim. The first who carried this practice from the East, as he did other things, was Homer, in whose second book of the Iliad the most ancient augur, using this kind of divination, foretells the outcome and fall of Troy for the Greek leader. For the phrase δράκων ... ναῦς ... is used, which is the true description of the bird named nachas from the marks on the back of serpents, from which among other things they drew their divinations and auguries. So there is no doubt that Pythian Apollo, that is, that foul spirit whom the Hebrews called Ob and Abaddon, the Hellenists literally Apollyon (ἀπολλύων), and others Apollo, first received worship in Syria, in that form in which he once brought misery upon the human race. Likewise Pherecydes the Syrian called the chief of evil demons Ophioneus, and so on. These are the words of that great and most learned knight Heinsius. To these I add that the Greek ὄφις and perhaps also Phoibos seem to be derived from the Hebrew אוב. And ophiouchos in Horapollo, book 1, chapter 1, is a kind of serpent.

units.la: Secundo in hac versione vulg. occurrunt illa, qui stridént in incantationibus suis. Respondent autem istis Ebraicis הַמְצַפְצְפִים / והמהגים quæ Pagninus vertit, qui garriunt & loquuntur. Arias, qui qui garriunt & susurrant. Accipiunt vulgo hæc verba, tanquam si ab hac ariolorum proprietate pro vanitate artis argumentum peteret. Vide notas Junii & Carthus. Arias tamen Montanus existimat verba sic construenda, Et cum ii qui strident incantationibus suis, hoc est, qui verbosis quibusdam præstigiis personantes, opinionem vobis istam persuadere student, dixerint ad vos, Quærite &c. Vulgatus Interpres dum vocem מְהַנִּים interpretaturus incantationum meminit, respexisse mihi videtur ad Latinum Magus, cui cum Ebraea voce מְהַנִּים quoad sonum non omnino disconvenit. Nec desunt qui vocem illam Latinis jam receptam (ideo Latinam vocavi) ab Ebraeorum deflectunt. Magus apud Persas erat σοφὸς, θεαρητικὸς, contemplativus, meditabundus (הגה enim meditari) mysteriorum gnarus. Suidas, μάγοι ... περσαις ὁ φιλόσοφοι καὶ φιλόθεοι, Et quid si hinc quoque Magister? Sed nihil statuo. Μάγος, sapiens, inquam, Firmat Lucas Actorum xiii. 8. ἀντέστη ... Ελυμας ὁ μάγος, ... Ελυμας enim est ab Arabico עלם / novit, scivit. vide Drusium ad voces Ebr. Novi Test. cap. 7. & Schindleri lexicon in עלם / Nihil autem hic attinet monere, vocem eam, ut & Tyrannus & Sophista & id genus aliae, postmodum una cum ipsa magia degenerasse, atque in malam partem usupari coepisse. Tertio occurrunt illa, nunquid non populus à Deo suo requiret pro vivis à mortuis? Hic se torserunt Interpretes, multi enim codices ita legunt, n..n. pop. à Deo suo requiret visionem pro vivis ac mortuis? Carthus. q. d. imo. Nam & pagani à diis suis sciscitantur responsa, nam per locum à majori, nos fideles quærere debemus non à pythonibus &c. sed à Deo nostro, ejusque prophetis & sanctis responsa pro omni negotio occurrente, tam vivis quam pro mortuis. Petrus Cluniacensis ex hoc loco probare voluit pro mortuis orandum esse unde porro Fevardentius & peltanus argumentum pro purgatorio depromere. Et certe, si orandum est pro animabus defunctorum, videtur statuendum esse purgatorium, positis enim mediis ad finem, omnino etiam finem ipsum dari oportet. Paraphrasis autem Cluniacensis epistola ad Petrobrusianos hæc est, cum dixerint ad vos deceptores, ut ea quæ tantum à Deo requirenda sunt, quærantur contra Deum à Pythonib. & divinis, respondete, annon populus id est, annon hic mos est omnium populorum ut à Deo suo quem colit, requirat ea quæ quærenda sunt, sive pro vivis, sive pro mortuis? Et paucis interjectis, nonne vides prophetam aperte prædicare, Deum à populo suo requirendum i. consulendum esse tam pro vivis quam pro mortuis? Quod si consulendus, si orandus est Deus tam pro vivis quam pro mortuis, quid respondent qui dicunt, non esse orandum pro mortuis. Docetur ille populus ut respondent seductoribus inquirendum vel potius deprecandum Deum pro vivis ac pro mortuis, & non docebitur populus, conculcandos esse hæreticos, qui negant Deum orandum pro mortuis? Hæc ille. Ubi observa, lector μὴ αἰτημα authoris, requirere seu consulere pro mortuis ut ipse postea loquitur, salutem mortuorum quærere. Ipse Lyra hoc requirere exponit, responsa quærere de occultis & futuris. Admissa ergo hac lectione, quid aliud esset hoc requirere, quam inquirere quo in statu sint mortui? Hanc expositionem una litura delevit Clemens VIII. quando locum sic restituit & in posterum legendum sanxit, nunquid non populus requiret à Deo suo, pro vivis à mortuis? Quæ sic accipiuntur ab optimis interpretibus, tanquam si contineant responsionem fidelium, quos impii ad illicitas consultationes solicitaturi erant. q. d. an æquum est, an licitum est, ut pro vivis à mortuis petantur responsa? Et sic quidem idem vulgati sententia erit, qui Ebraici textus est. Proinde non possum satis mirari, quid in mentem venerit Ariæ Montano, dum in commentario duo ista sententiæ membra, eaque accentu Sakeph Katon distincta, confundit, Cum ii qui strident in incantationibus suis dixerint ad vos, quarite à Pythonibus & à divinis, & deinde hoc non esse nefas contenderint, asserentes, mortuos esse medio inter homines & superos gradu, ideoque oportunum responsi à Deo afferendi modum esse huic Pythonum, divinorum & quærentium, Quandoquidem omnis populus à Deo suo requirit visionem pro vivis a mortuis, quod mortuorum à corporis impedimento exutæ animæ propiores Deo esse credantur &c. Hæc Arias, Cujus mentem si bene assequor, hoc vult, quandoquidem omnes populus à Deo suo requirit visionem pro vivis per mortuos. Quam interpretationem neutiquam ex originali eruet.
units.tr: Second, in this Vulgate version we find the words who chirp in their incantations. These correspond to the Hebrew הַמְצַפְצְפִים and והמהגים, which Pagninus renders who babble and speak. Arias renders them who babble and whisper. Commonly these words are taken as though the text were arguing from this practice of soothsayers to the emptiness of their art. See the notes of Junius and Carthusianus. Montanus, however, thinks the words should be construed thus: "And when those who chirp in their incantations say to you, Seek...", that is, those who, by certain wordy tricks and chattering, strive to persuade you of this opinion, have said to you, Seek.... The Vulgate translator, when about to translate the word מְהַנִּים, mentions incantations, and seems to me to have had in mind the Latin magus, to which the Hebrew word מְהַנִּים is not wholly unlike in sound. Nor are there lacking those who turn that word, now received into Latin (which is why I have called it Latin), away from the Hebrew. A magus among the Persians was a wise man, a contemplative, a meditative man (for הגה means to meditate), skilled in mysteries. Suidas says: the magi among the Persians were philosophers and lovers of God. And what if magister comes from this too? But I establish nothing. That magus means wise, I say, is confirmed by Luke, Acts 13:8, where Elymas the magus withstood them (ἀντέστη ... Ἐλυμας ὁ μάγος). For Elymas is from the Arabic עלם, to know, to have known. See Drusius on the Hebrew words of the New Testament, chapter 7, and Schindler's lexicon under עלם. Nor is it necessary here to remark that this word, like tyrant, sophist, and others of that kind, afterwards degenerated along with magic itself and began to be used in a bad sense. Third, there occur the words will not the people require of their God for the living from the dead? Here the interpreters have tormented themselves, for many manuscripts read it thus: will not the people require of their God a vision for the living and the dead? Carthusianus, that is, "on the contrary": for even the heathens inquire of their gods for answers, so by an argument from the greater we who are believers ought to seek answers, for every matter that arises, not from the Pythons and so on, but from our God and from his prophets and saints, both for the living and for the dead. Peter of Cluny wished to prove from this passage that one must pray for the dead, whence Fevardentius and Peltanus draw an argument for purgatory. And indeed, if one must pray for the souls of the departed, it seems that purgatory must be assumed, for once the means to an end are granted, the end itself must also be granted. Peter of Cluny's paraphrase, in his letter to the Petrobrusians, runs thus: "When the deceivers say to you that those things which are to be sought only from God should be sought against God from Pythons and diviners, answer: is it not the custom of all peoples, that is, of this people, to require from the God whom they worship those things which are to be required, whether for the living or for the dead?" And a few lines later: "Do you not see the prophet plainly preaching that God is to be required, that is, consulted, by his people both for the living and for the dead? And if God is to be consulted, and prayed to, for the living and for the dead, what do those answer who say that one must not pray for the dead? Is that people taught to answer the seducers that God is to be inquired of, or rather entreated, for the living and the dead, and will the people not be taught that heretics who deny that God is to be prayed to for the dead are to be trampled underfoot?" So he. Here observe, reader, the μὴ αἰτημα of the author: to require or consult for the dead, as he himself later says, is to seek the salvation of the dead. Lyra himself explains this to require as to seek answers about hidden and future things. If this reading is admitted, what else would this to require be than to inquire what state the dead are in? Clement VIII erased this explanation with a single stroke when he restored the passage thus and decreed that it be read in future: will not the people require of their God, for the living from the dead? These words are taken by the best interpreters as though they contain the answer of the faithful, whom the impious were about to entice into unlawful consultations. That is, is it fair, is it lawful, that answers be sought for the living from the dead? And so the sense of the Vulgate will be the same as that of the Hebrew text. Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder what came into Arias Montanus's mind when, in his commentary, he confounds these two members of the sentence, distinguished by the accent Sakeph Katon, When those who chirp in their incantations have said to you, seek from the Pythons and from the diviners, and then have maintained that this is not wicked, asserting that the dead stand at a middle rank between men and the heavenly ones, and therefore that it is a fitting way of bringing an answer from God to this Python, diviner, and inquirer, since every people requires a vision from its God for the living from the dead, because the souls freed from the impediment of the body are believed to be nearer to God, and so on. These are Arias's words. If I rightly grasp his meaning, he wants this: since every people requires a vision from its God for the living through the dead. This interpretation will by no means be drawn out of the original.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Vers. Nihil frequentius in veterum & recentiorum scriptis quam epitheto Angeli magni consilii Æternum Dei filium redemtorem nostrum indigitare. Est in authenticis verbi divini tabulis, ubi angelus foederis appellatur, at ubi angelus magni consilii vocetur, non reperies locum. Quid ergo? Desumptum illud est ex Graeca interpretatione huius loci. Inde manavit in scripta patrum Graecorum, illorumque ex Latinis qui Latina versione ex Graeca LXX. traducta usi sunt. Verba textus Graeci, prout ea expressit editio Francofurt. Ista sunt, καὶ καλεῖται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς, μεγάλης βουλῆς ἀγγελος, θαυμαστὸς, σύμβουλος, Θεὸς ἰσχυρὸς, πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, ἀρχὼν εἰρήνης. Eusebius Demonstr. Evang. IX. 8. verba Prophetae in hunc modum citat, μεγάλης βουλῆς ἀγγελ, ἄρχων εἰρήνης, ἐξουσίας, Θεὸς ἰσχυρός, πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος. Vides hic illa duo, θαυμαστὸς, σύμβουλος, quae respondent istis Ebraeis, פלא יועץ abesse. Et certe cum illa ab interpretibus LXX. reddita sint per μεγ. βουλῆς ἀγγ. probabile est illa ex Aquilae versione in textum vulgatum infarta fuisse. Locum ergo accuratius conversit vulgatus Interpres, admirabilis, consiliarius, Deus, fortis, &c. Ubi Lutherus, & ex eo Belgicus Interpres, wonderbaer / raedt / kracht / Heldt. Duo posteriora respondent istis Ebraicis, אל גבור / quorum prius אל cum extra controversiam passim in S. literis significet Deum, per synecdochen generis, non puto ullam B. Luthero incubuisse necessitatem ab interpretatione vulgata divertendi. Est quidem ita, το' אל κατ' ἀκρίβειαν significare ἰσχυρὸν ἢ δύναμιν, ut loquitur Eusebius, in abstracto, nec non ἰσχυρὸς ἢ δύνατον, in concreto, plane ut עד testis & testimonium significat; At cum immediate sequatur, גבור / cur non potius eos sequimur, qui אל Deum interpretantur? Ita certe Chaldaeus, אלהא / Ita LXX. ut vidimus. Ita Jun. Pisc. Angeli, Genev. Hisp. Ital. atque adeo ipse Lutherus tomo 8. edit. Ienensis, sol. 145. pag. 2. Verba ejus haec sunt, Vox Ebraea proprie quidem significat potentiam, traft / At cum proprium nomen est, ut hic, significat Deum, so heisst Gott / per totam scripturam, qui solus potens est. Quod Judaei & Ebraeizantes pariter coguntur agnoscere. Non est operae pretium super hujus epitheti versione contendere. Lutherus citato loco ad communissimum & passim obvium vocis Ebraeae usum: At in versione ad nativa vocis significationem respexit. Et novum non est Deum potentiam vocare. Apud virg. Venus Cupidinem suum sic affatur, Nate meae vires, mea magna potentia, q. d. אלי אלי / Namque & illa verba Pf. xxii. nescio quis veterum ita convertit, ἰαχυς μϰ, ἰαχυς μϰ Ubi tamen Symmachus concretis usus est, ἰαχυρὶ μϰ, ἰαχυρὶ μϰ. Inter nomina Dei, quibus Rabbini Deum appellant, etiam est הגבורה potentia, שמעתנו הגבורה ... [?] ἀπὸ στόματος τῆς ἰαχύος [?] αὐτοῦ ex ore potentiæ audivimus ista. Vide Thisbi Eliæ. Quo referebat Cl. Drusius illud Tobiæ I. τῇ δυνάμει Baali Deo, quomodo & Junius locum illum convertit, ut frustra sit Vatablus, qui δυ- νάμει substituit. Atque huc idem ille Drusius facem allucebat loco Matthæi xxvi. 64. à dextris τῆς δυνάμεως, Ebraice מימין הגבורה / à dextris Dei, quamvis alii ex Luca 22 69. Hic supplere malunt nomen Dei. A dextris potentia [Dei.] Ita enim plene leguntur illa apud Lucam neque dicere ausim illud δεξιᾶ hic glossema esse & ex margine, librariorum ignorantia, in textum irrepsisse. Sed ut redeamus ad institutum, licet veritissimum sit quod ait Helivicus, eum qui ipsa potentia est, citra controversiam Deum esse, tamen akeram interpretationem magis probo.
units.tr: Nothing is more common in the writings of the ancients and of the moderns than the epithet Angel of great counsel used to name the eternal Son of God, our Redeemer. It is found in the authentic tablets of the divine Word, where he is called the angel of the covenant, but you will not find a passage where he is called the angel of great counsel. What then? That title was taken from the Greek rendering of this passage. From there it passed into the writings of the Greek Fathers, and into those of the Latin writers who used the Latin version made from the Greek of the Seventy. The words of the Greek text, as the Frankfurt edition prints them, are these: "and his name shall be called, Angel of great counsel, wonderful, counsellor, mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace" [καὶ καλεῖται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς, μεγάλης βουλῆς ἀγγελος, θαυμαστὸς, σύμβουλος, Θεὸς ἰσχυρὸς, πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, ἀρχὼν εἰρήνης]. Eusebius, in Demonstratio Evangelica 9.8, cites the words of the prophet in this form: "Angel of great counsel, prince of peace, authority, mighty God, Father of the age to come" [μεγάλης βουλῆς ἀγγελ, ἄρχων εἰρήνης, ἐξουσίας, Θεὸς ἰσχυρός, πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος]. You see here that the two words θαυμαστὸς and σύμβουλος, which correspond to the Hebrew פלא יועץ, are missing. Since the Seventy rendered those by μεγάλης βουλῆς ἀγγέλος, it is probable that they were later inserted into the vulgar text from the version of Aquila. The Vulgate translator therefore rendered the passage more exactly: admirable, counsellor, God, mighty, and so on. Luther, and after him the Belgic translator, have wonderbaer / raedt / kracht / Heldt. The last two words correspond to the Hebrew אל גבור. Since the first of these, אל, clearly means God everywhere in Holy Scripture, by synecdoche of the genus, I do not think Luther was under any necessity to depart from the Vulgate rendering. It is true that, strictly speaking, אל signifies strength or power in the abstract, as Eusebius says, and also a strong or powerful one in the concrete, just as עד means witness and also testimony. But since it is immediately followed by גבור, why do we not rather follow those who take אל to mean God? The Chaldee paraphrast certainly does so, with אלהא, and so do the Seventy, as we have seen. So do Junius and Piscator, the Angelic, the Genevan, the Spanish and Italian versions, and indeed Luther himself in vol. 8 of the Jena edition, folio 145, page 2. His words are these: "The Hebrew word properly means power, but when it is a proper name, as here, it means God, so heisst Gott, throughout all Scripture, for he alone is powerful." Jews and Hebraizing writers are likewise compelled to acknowledge this. It is not worth the trouble to dispute over the rendering of this epithet. Luther, in the passage cited, looked to the most common and everyday use of the Hebrew word; but in his translation he looked to the native meaning of the word. Nor is it new to call God power. Among the poets, Venus so addresses her Cupid: "my strength, my great power," that is, אלי אלי. Someone among the ancients also rendered those words of Psalm 22 as ἰαχυς μϰ, ἰαχυς μϰ, though Symmachus used the concrete form, ἰαχυρὶ μϰ, ἰαχυρὶ μϰ. Among the names of God by which the rabbis call him is הגבורה, power: שמעתנו הגבורה ... [?] ἀπὸ στόματος τῆς ἰαχύος [?] αὐτοῦ, "we have heard these things from the mouth of Power" audivimus ista. See Elias of Thisbe. To this Drusius, the learned man, referred the words of Tobit 1, τῇ δυνάμει Baali, "to God Baal"; Junius also rendered that passage in the same way, so that Vatablus, who substituted δυνάμει, labours in vain. To this same point Drusius also applied a torch in Matthew 26:64, à dextris τῆς δυνάμεως, in Hebrew מימין הגבורה, "at the right hand of Power" à dextris Dei, though others prefer, from Luke 22:69, to supply the word God: "at the right hand of [God the] power." For the words are read thus in full in Luke, and I would not dare to say that δεξιᾶ here is a gloss that crept into the text from the margin through the ignorance of copyists. But to return to our purpose: although it is most true, as Helivicus says, that he who is power itself is without controversy God, nevertheless I prefer the other interpretation.

units.la: 7. לִטְרֹבָה Nota tiro Vocem illam licet habeat formam participii, habere tamen hoc loco significationem abstracti, An- plitudini principatus & pacis nullus erit finis. מרבה ergo inter illa est, quæ sub una forma eaque participiali, abstractum & concretum significant: Tale est & משחית quod Exod. xii. verf. 23. perdentem, at verf. 13. perditionem significat, quomodo & 2. Reg. 23. 13. usurpatur, הר המשחית mons corruptionis, exigua vid. deflexione usitatæ nomenclaturæ, in opprobrium idololatriæ quæ illic tunc temporis palam vigebat: Intelligitur enim mons oliveti, quæ Græci ὄρος τῆς ἐλαιῶνος, Ebraei הר המשחה montem unctionis vocant. Ita nomen celebris illius impostoris, qui in Hadriani tempora incidit בר כוכבא Bar-Chochba id est, filius stellæ, demutarunt in בר כזיבא i. filius mendacii. Extat hac de re monitum Magistrorum in libro præceptorum magno sol. 98. Col. 3. ubi tractatur lex affirmativa xiv. de destruendis locis idololatricis & idolorum nominibus abolendis, quam invenies Deut. xii. 3. Namque illa verba, ואבדתם את שמם R: Akiva videtur accepisse hoc sensu, & perdetis, i. corrumpetis nomen eorum (idolorum & rerum eò pertinentium)
units.tr: 7. Lamarbeh [לִטְרֹבָה]. Note this, novice: although that word has the form of a participle, here it has the force of an abstract noun: "of the amplitude of the principality and peace there shall be no end." Therefore מרבה is one of those words which, under one and the same participial form, signify both the abstract and the concrete. Such is also משחית, which in Exodus 12:23 means destroyer, but in verse 13 means destruction; it is used in the same way in 2 Kings 23:13, הר המשחית, "the mountain of corruption," with a slight alteration of the customary name, in mockery of the idolatry which at that time openly flourished there. For the mount of Olives, which the Greeks call ὄρος τῆς ἐλαιῶνος, the Hebrews call הר המשחה, "the mount of anointing." Likewise the name of that famous impostor who lived in the time of Hadrian, בר כוכבא Bar-Chochba, that is, son of the star, they changed into בר כזיבא, that is, son of falsehood. There is a note on this matter in the great Book of Precepts of the Masters, page 98, column 3, where the affirmative precept 14 is treated, concerning the destruction of idolatrous places and the abolition of the names of idols, which you will find in Deuteronomy 12:3. For R. Akiva seems to have taken the words ואבדתם את שמם in this sense: "and you shall destroy their name," that is, you shall corrupt the name of them (the idols and the things pertaining to them), mutando nomina eorum, by changing their names.

units.la: לטנוּרת את שמם וממין שפצורה שישנו השם שנעשרה להם שיהיה לגאית לסור לומר שקץ תשקצנך i. mutando nomina eorum. Rogat porro, unde petitum sit illud praeceptum de mutandis istis nominibus in opprobrium, & respondet fundamenti loco in Thalmud allegari illud ex Deut 7. 26: abominando abominaveris illud. Atque huc retulit Cl. Drusius τὸ βεελζεβούλ, quod in N. T. occurrit, pro βεελζεβούβ non ab errante manu, uti olim Hieronymo visum fuit, sed ex usu, qui tempore Evangelistarum obtinebat. Sonat autem Beelzebul, ac si diceres ζεὺς κοπρίας vel κόπρος, vel κοπρισμός: Jupiter stercoreus, זבל enim Syris & Chald. est κόπρος: stercus. Vide Drusium ad voces. Ebr. N. T. Non ergo solicitanda est Scriptura Graeca, quam etiam vetustissima Arabica versio quam magnus Erpenius edidit, repraesentat. Sed haec διεξοδικῶς. Revertamur ad nostrum למרבה in cujus medio Mem finale exhibent omnes Ebraei codices. Masora mihi aliud notat quam legi למרבה cum ם aperto. In hac Scriptura mysterium venantur Interpretes. Hi extra controversiam ponunt vocem illam sic ab ipso propheta exaratam fuisse. Sed hoc non dabunt Scaliger, Drusius & alii qui Mosem & Prophetas Samaritano Characthere usos fuisse contendunt. Vide ejus dissertationem de literis in Animadversionibus ad Eusebium: hujus Alphabetum Ebraicum vetus. Ubi Characterem illum quo nunc Biblia Ebraea eduntur Assyrium esse docent, ab Ezra primitus adhibitum cum jam illi populus in diuturna illa captivitate assvevisset. Hoc si admittimus, nullum hic mysterium Jesaias intenderit. Namque Samaritanus Character Mem clausum & apertum non agnoscit. Sed ponamus Jesaiam istis quos etiamnum habemus, Characteribus librum suum exarasse, ne sic quidem evinces hunc Characterem finalem a Prophetae manu esse. Superstitioni Judaicae cum adscribit Weiganmejerus in Tabulis Grammaticis. Forerius putat esse scribae lapsum quem juxta cum plurimis aliis ex contextu tollere praepostera quadam religione Judaei non fuerunt ausi. Hieronymus, Arias Mont. Junius, Pisc. Deodatus, Genevenses Interpretes & complures alii de mysterio aliquo altum hic silent. D. Calvinus asseruit, asseri vix posse ita scriptum esse a Propheta. Haec monere libuit, nequis nimis securus ea, quae hic vulgo traduntur, tanquam authentica & omni exceptione majora amplexetur. Magna autem hic est Interpretum differitas. Ipsi Ebraei, ut ab illis exordiar, variant. .Quidem altum hic silent. R. Salomo ad Mem clausum alludere videtur his verbis: Dixerunt Doctores nostri, Deo benedicto propositum fuisse ut Ezechiam Messiam faceret (O tristes incip-tiae!) & ex Senacherib Gogum & Magogum. Dixerunt angeli ministeriii coram Deo benedicto, An is qui truncavit januas templi & misit eas Regi Assyriae, fiet Messias; Et statim clauserunt scripturam. En jecur Theologi cujus Deus Sapientia & consilio infra Angelos est. Phy τῆς θεολογίας ταύτης. Aben-Ezra, כי דרש סופריים דרך hoc est, Mysterium scribarum hic est, nam Mem clausum est in medio vocis, cum debeat esse in fine. Innuit autem, inquit, signum solis. Quia enim retroivit umbra, par erat ut hoc cederet ad amplitudinem nominis ejus מרכה enim est nomen forma מעשה inquit idem. Kimchi, Mem clausum est (סתומה) in scriptura. Legitur tamen per מ apertum. Contra, in Ezra (Nehemiae 2.13. qui Ebraeis Ezrae secundus) המפרוצים Mem aperto in fine vocis secundum scripturam. Latet autem in eo aliquid Mysticum. כאשר יסתמו חומות ירושלים שהם פרוצים ומן הגלות ולערך הישועה יסתמו הפרוצים ואן תפתח המשרה שהיא סתומה עד מלך המשיח quomodo vid. muri Jerusalem, qui durante tempore captivitatis rupti fuere, tempore salutis claudendi sint, & * dilatandus principatus qui usque ad Regem Messiam clausus fuerat. Videtur conferre duo ista Mem inter se, quasi alterius ad alterum respectus sit. Aben-Ezrae sententia de voce הם Nehem 2.13. ista est. הם פרוצים על דרך מוה כיד מלכים תרכאו עמי רק אנשי המסורת הפרוצים לקצר המלות ולפרש חכם הפתוחה דמן לחומות חפתוחות הם פרוצים ופרוצות הוא דרך דרש והדרך תראשון בעיני נכון hoc est habet se ad instar, מַה בְּיָדְךָ quid hoc [quod] in manu tua est (Exod. 4. 2. pro מה-זה una vox ex duabus conflata) item, מַלָּכִים quid vobis attulistis populum meum? (pro מה-לכם) Sed viri Masorae separarunt voces illas ad abbreviandas voces & explicandas. Innuit autem Mem illud apertum muros apertos ruptosque, Sed hoc mysticum est. Et prior sententia mihi se magis probat. Sed redeamus ad ם clausum vocemque lem.arbe. Elias Levita in Masoreth Hammasoreth, tabulis secundis orat. 1. specie 6. plane hic ineptit. Ibi enim agens de vocibus quae scribuntur ut una, & leguntur ut duae, quales ait esse Xv. Iteinque illis quae scribuntur ut duae & leguntur ut una, uma. quales dicit esse V. hæc addit. Ego autem demiror mysticam expositionem quam sectantur nonnulli circa vocem hanc [?לסרכה] / dicentes Mem clausum esse in medio vocis: Cum juxta scripturam illud Mem non sit in medio vocis, nam juxta scripturam sunt duæ voces * [?לם רבה] & possumus exponere [?לם] quasi esset [?להם] / sicuti in [?אראלם] pro [?אראה להם] item [?בשלם] pro [?בשל להם] Hæc Elias. Nihil jam dico, quam nullum sensum habeat illa lectio [?לם רבה] / Nihil dico de voce [?אראלם] / quæ sic vulgo exponitur, ut ל non ad pronomen sed ad nomen [?אראל] pertineat, aspice mihi vocem [?בשלם] / quis non videt, ל hic literam ultimam Thematis [?בשל] esse neque ullo modo esse literam syntacticam? Est quidem in eo affixum, quod communiter per Accusativum Latinorum casum exponitur, pro Dativo positum, at quid illud ad rem præsentem facit? Facessant ergo istæ ineptiæ. Pergamus ad Christianos Interpretes & scriptores. Inter eos primo occurrit Galatinus, qui lib. 4. cap. 19. citat testimonium Thalmudicum ex Massechet Sanhedrin, cujus ista mens sit, per Mem clausum denotari rem clausam. At doctissimus Buxtorfius in lexico suo, themate [?רבה] monet, nihil tale universo isto capite contineri. Addit Galatinus ex sententia cujusdam R. eâ literâ denotari numerum annorum DC. (Mem enim finale in numeris valet Dc.) qui ab hac Prophetiâ usque ad natales Salvatoris nostri effluxere. Sed hanc sententiam doctissimorum Chronologorum ratiocinia neutiquam admittunt. Itaque alii mysterium vocationis gentium verè tunc adhuc clausum gentisque Judaicæ ab hoc regno excludendæ, denotari: Alii, sicut [?] clausum exitum non habet, ita perpetuitatem regni Christi, alii mysterium Christi ex clausa virgine nascituri hic latitare arbitrati sunt, respicientes ad formam characteris clausam. Alii ad figuram ejus plusculum dilatatam respexêre, ac proinde vel dilatationem regni Christi antea limitibus Cananæ conclusi, vel dilatationem ejusdem hoc est recreationem inter varias pressuras.
units.tr: i.e. by changing their names. He next asks where the command to change these names into reproaches came from, and answers that the Talmud cites as its foundation Deut. 7:26, you shall utterly abominate it and utterly detest it. Here the learned Drusius also places the word Beelzebul, which occurs in the New Testament, not as Beelzebub through an erring hand, as once seemed to Jerome, but by the usage that prevailed in the time of the Evangelists [βεελζεβούβ]. The name means, as if you were to say Zeus of dung, or dung, or dunging: Jupiter the dung-god, since zibla in Syriac and Chaldee means dung [κόπρος]. See Drusius on the words in his Hebrew New Testament. The Greek Scripture therefore need not be troubled, and the very ancient Arabic version, which the great Erpenius edited, supports it. But these matters need a fuller treatment. Let us return to our lemarbe, in whose middle all Hebrew manuscripts show a final Mem. The Masorah marks something other than reading lemarbe with an open Mem. In this text the interpreters hunt for a mystery. They place beyond dispute that the word was written in this form by the prophet himself. But Scaliger, Drusius and others who maintain that Moses and the Prophets used the Samaritan character will not grant this. See Scaliger's discourse on letters in his Notes on Eusebius, and his old Hebrew alphabet. There he teaches that the script in which the Hebrew Bibles are now printed is Assyrian, first adopted by Ezra, when the people had grown accustomed to it during that long captivity. If we accept this, the prophet Isaiah intended no mystery here. For the Samaritan character does not recognise a closed and open Mem. But suppose Isaiah wrote his book in the characters we still have: even so you will not prove that this final form came from the prophet's hand. Weiganmeyer ascribes it to Jewish superstition in his Grammatical Tables. Forerius thinks it is a slip of the scribe, which the Jews, with a certain perverse reverence, did not dare to remove from the context, as they did with many other things. Jerome, Arias Montanus, Junius, Piscator, Diodati, the Genevan interpreters and many others keep a discreet silence here about any mystery. Calvin asserted that it can hardly be affirmed that the prophet wrote it so. I have thought it right to give this warning, lest anyone too carelessly accept what is commonly handed down here as authentic and beyond all objection. There is, however, great disagreement among the interpreters. The Hebrews themselves differ, to begin with them. R. Solomon seems to allude to the closed Mem in these words: Our teachers said that it was God's intention to make Hezekiah the Messiah (O sad beginnings!), and Gog and Magog out of Sennacherib. The ministering angels said before the blessed God, Shall he who broke down the doors of the temple and sent them to the king of Assyria become the Messiah? And at once they closed the writing. Behold the liver of that theology whose God is, in wisdom and counsel, below the angels. Phy of this theology [τῆς θεολογίας ταύτης]. Aben Ezra, the mystery of the scribes is here, for the Mem is closed in the middle of the word, where it ought to be at the end. He hints, he says, at a sign of the sun: because the shadow turned back, it was fitting that this should yield to the greatness of his name; for lemarbe is, the same writer says, a noun in the form of maaseh. Kimchi: the Mem is closed (stumah) in the writing, yet it is read with an open מ. On the other hand, in Ezra (Nehemiah 2:13, which the Hebrews count as the second Ezra) the word hamperutsim has an open Mem at the end, according to the writing. Something mystical lies hidden in this too: as the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken during the time of captivity, are to be closed at the time of salvation, so the broken places are to be closed, and the principality which was closed until the Messiah the King is to be opened. He seems to set these two Mems side by side, as if one had a bearing on the other. Aben Ezra's opinion on the word hem in Nehemiah 2:13 is this: hem perutsim is in the manner of mah, as in yad melakim tarkhau ami, but the men of the Masorah separated those words to shorten and explain them. He hints that the open Mem marks open, broken walls; but this too is mystical. And the first opinion seems to me more sound. But let us return to the closed Mem and the word lem arbe. Elias Levita, in his Masoreth Hammasoreth, second tables, chapter 1, section 6, plainly talks nonsense here. For there, treating words that are written as one and read as two, of which he says there are fifteen, and again those written as two and read as one, of which he says there are five, he adds: I am amazed at the mystical explanation that some pursue concerning this word [?lesarkha], saying that the Mem is closed in the middle of the word. For according to the writing that Mem is not in the middle of the word: according to the writing there are two words, [?lam rabbah], and we can explain [?lam] as if it were [?lehem], as in [?ar'elam] for [?ar'eh lehem], likewise [?beshalam] for [?beshal lehem]. So far Elias. I now say nothing of how that reading [?lam rabbah] can have any sense. I say nothing of the word [?ar'elam], which is commonly explained so that the lamed belongs not to the pronoun but to the noun [?ar'el]. Look at [?beshalam]: who does not see that the lamed here is the last letter of the stem [?beshal] and in no way a syntactic particle? It is indeed affixed, and what is commonly rendered by the Latin accusative is used for the dative; but what does that have to do with the present matter? Let such trifles then depart. Let us go on to the Christian interpreters and writers. Among them Galatinus first comes to notice. In book 4, chapter 19, he cites a Talmudic testimony from the tractate Sanhedrin, whose sense is that the closed Mem denotes a closed thing. But the most learned Buxtorf, in his lexicon under the root [?rabbah], warns that nothing of the kind is contained in that whole chapter. Galatinus adds, on the view of a certain rabbi, that this letter denotes the number of six hundred years (for a final Mem stands for 600 in numbers) which ran on from this prophecy to the birth of our Saviour. But the reasoning of the most learned chronologers by no means admits this view. Others therefore thought that the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles, which was then truly still closed, and of the exclusion of the Jewish nation from this kingdom, is denoted here. Others, as a closed exit has no end, so they held that the perpetuity of Christ's kingdom lies hidden here, and others that the mystery of Christ to be born of a closed virgin is concealed here, looking to the closed form of the character. Others looked to its figure a little enlarged, and therefore either to the enlargement of Christ's kingdom, formerly confined within the bounds of Canaan, or to the enlargement of the same, that is, its restoration amid various pressures.

units.la: Rursus, quia [?] litera quadrangularis est, non desunt qui inconcussam stabilitatem regni Christi hinc elicuere. Fuerunt denique qui ipsum nomen Mariæ [illegible, ~3 letters] hac litera quasi digito indicatum censuere. Hector Pintus Lusitanus, postquam de conversione barbarorum gentium disseruisset, hæc subjungit. Eam ab causam in hoc admirabili versiculo, ubi divinus vates impe-
units.tr: Again, because the letter is square, there are some who have drawn from this the unshakeable stability of Christ's kingdom. Indeed, there were some who thought that the very name of Mary [illegible, about three letters] was pointed out, as it were with a finger, by this letter. Hector Pinto of Portugal, after discussing the conversion of the barbarian nations, adds the following. For this reason, in this wonderful little verse, where the divine prophet foretells the multiplication of the empire...

units.la: * Hoc est, ipsi multiplica imperii Christi multiplicationem prædicit, litera finali ad principium reversa annotavit. Reversa est igitur hæc litera retrorsum, ut etiam hac in re innueret Propheta, filium Dei æqualem Deo Patri sumpturum esse humanam naturam, secundum quam esset minor Patre. Exinanivit enim seipsum, ut ait Apostolus, formam servi accipiens &c. Hujus figuram & imaginem gessit Sol, quem reversum fuisse in horologio Achaz ad signum & confirmationem salutis Regis Jezechiæ literæ divinæ constantur. Hæc ille, Tu lector confer hæc posteriora cum illis, quæ supra ex Aben-Ezra produximus. Non lubet plura accongerere. Non decet me pias doctorum super hac litera meditationes ᾽Αδαυμαπίζειν. Illud moneo tironem, sententiam de numero annorum, ut maxime se devotæ animæ probat, ita veritati Historiæ & Chronologorum doctissimorum calculo maxime adversari. Reliquas vero non nisi precario, si in contradicentem incidas, posse obtineri.
units.tr: * That is, he foretells the multiplication of Christ's empire itself, and he noted that the final letter has returned to the beginning. This letter is therefore reversed, so that the Prophet might also hint in this matter that the Son of God, equal to God the Father, would take on human nature, according to which he would be less than the Father. For he emptied himself, as the Apostle says, taking the form of a servant, and so on. The sun bore the figure and image of this, which the divine letters say turned back on the dial of Ahaz as a sign and confirmation of the salvation of King Hezekiah. So far he; you, reader, compare these later words with those which we brought forward above from Aben Ezra. I do not wish to heap up more. It does not become me to wonder at (᾽Αδαυμαπίζειν [ἀδαυμαπίζειν]) the pious meditations of the teachers on this letter. I warn the beginner of this: the opinion about the number of years, as much as it commends itself to a devout soul, is thus very much opposed to the truth of history and to the most learned calculation of the chronologers. The rest, however, can be maintained only by pleading, if you meet someone who contradicts.

units.la: Verf. 14. Et disperdet Dominus ab Israel caput & caudam incurvantem & depravantem una die] Ita plerique codices Editionis vulgatæ & Hieron. in Verf & commentariis. Biblia tamen Clementis VIII. Contra sententiam ipsius Hieronymi, legunt, * incurvantem & refranantem. Multa hic interpretes de proprietate Pseudo-prophetarum & hæreticorum. Sed nota tiro, duarum istarum vocum nec volam nec vestigium in Ebraeo reperiri. Pro illis enim hæc leguntur כפה ואגמון / quæ Pagn. Arias, Oleastrius, Forerius, Pintus, & alii reddunt ramum & juncum. Ipse vulgatus cap. 35. vocem אגמון juncum interpretatur. Non ergo hæc duo ad caudam referenda, sed respondent duobus antecedentibus caput & caudam, ut idem fere aliis verbis dicat. Ut enim per caput primores & honorabiles, per caudam abjectissimos intelligit, ita per ramum, fortes; per juncum, debiles intelligit. Kimchi, in Comment. כפה ואגמון החזקים i. per Chippha & agmon, intelliguntur fortes & debiles. Chippha est Agmon est juncus in aqua crescens.
units.tr: Verse 14. "And the Lord will cut off from Israel head and tail, the bending and the bowing down, in one day." So most manuscripts of the Vulgate edition and Jerome in the text and in his commentaries. The Clementine Bible, however, against Jerome's own opinion, reads "bending and bowing down" [incurvantem et refranantem]. Interpreters here say much about the character of false prophets and heretics. But note, beginner, that neither trace nor vestige of these two words is found in the Hebrew. For in their place these are read: כפה ואגמון [kippah ve-agmon], which Pagninus, Arias, Oleaster, Forerius, Pintus and others render as branch and rush. The Vulgate itself, in chapter 35, translates the word אגמון as rush. These two therefore are not to be referred to the tail, but correspond to the two preceding words, head and tail, so that he says much the same thing in other words. For just as by head he means the leaders and honourable men, and by tail the most abject, so by branch he means the strong, and by rush he means the weak. Kimchi, in his commentary: by kippah and agmon, "the strong and the weak" are understood. Kippah is the branch, agmon is the rush growing in water.

units.la: Lxx. μέγαν καὶ μικρὸν ad sensum magis quam verba respicientes. Memini supra sententiæ Hieronymi. Eam invenies ad cap. 19. ubi v. 15. eædem voces occurrunt, verba ejus hæc sunt, in eo quod nos transtulimus incurvantem & refranantem, postu-mus mus dicere incurvum & Lascivientem, ut intelligamus senem & puerum. Nos autem verbum Ebraicum אנמן / dum celeriter quae scripta sunt, vertimus, ambiguitate decepti refrænantem diximus, quod significantius Aquila transtulit ἀφελόνον id est qui nihil recte agit, sed omne perversum, ut puerum significaret. Nota lector Romanos Correctores has secundas Hieronymi curas insuper habuisse & quod ille damnaverat in textum recepisse.
units.tr: The Septuagint: "great and small", looking more to the sense than to the words. I recall Jerome's opinion above. You will find it at chapter 19, where verse 15 has the same words. His words are these: "In place of what we have translated bending and bowing down, we ought to say crooked and wanton, so that we understand old man and boy." But we, when we quickly translated the Hebrew word אנמן [anman] as it was written, were deceived by ambiguity and said "bowing down" [refrænantem], which Aquila rendered more expressively as ἀφελόνον [apheloulon], that is, one who does nothing right but everything perverse, so that it would signify a boy. Note, reader, that the Roman correctors held these second thoughts of Jerome in low regard, and admitted into the text what he had condemned.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Verf. 15. Nunquid gloriabitur securis contra eum qui secat in ea? aut exaltabitur serra contra eum à quo trahitur? ] Redarguit Propheta intolerabilem fastum & superbiam Regis Assyriae, suae potentiae & prudentiae felices istos successus transcribentis. Atqui tu tantum instrumentum Dei es, inquit Propheta, Deus te instrumento usus est &c. Judicet ergo cordatus lector, quam apte hic locus in jure Canonico citetur ad primatum Romanæ Ecclesiæ stabiliendum. Aliter se habet serra vel securis ad artificem, quam Ecclesia inferior ad superiorem. Melius allegatur hic locus, parte 2. Causa 21. quaest. 5. Cap. Remittuntur. Vide si vacat & habes. Quæ vero sequuntur apud vulg. Interpretem, aliquid caliginis habent, quomodo si * elevetur virga contra levantem se, exaltetur baculus qui utique lignum est. Ebræa ita habent כהניף שבט את-מרימיו כהרים מטה לאין Lutherus hic plane exorbitavit. Junius, quasi vero agitaret virga eum qui tollit ipsam, quasi attolleret baculus, [&] non lignum [esset.] Nec male Forrerius, quasi agitaret virga elevantes eam, quasi [qui] elevat baculum, non lignum [elevaret.]
units.tr: Verse 15. "Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him by whom it is shaken?" The Prophet rebukes the intolerable pride and arrogance of the King of Assyria, who ascribed these happy successes to his own power and wisdom. "Yet you are only an instrument of God," says the Prophet, "God has used you as an instrument," and so on. Let the discerning reader judge, then, how aptly this passage is cited in canon law to establish the primacy of the Roman Church. A saw or axe stands in a different relation to the craftsman than a lower church does to a higher. This passage is better cited in Part 2, Cause 21, Question 5, chapter Remittuntur. See if you have time and the book. What follows in the Vulgate translator has some obscurity: "as if a rod were lifted up against him who lifts it, or a staff were exalted, which is surely wood." The Hebrew reads: כהניף שבט את-מרימיו כהרים מטה לאין [kehaniph shevet et-merimav kehorim mateh lo'-ets]. Luther has clearly gone wide of the mark here. Junius: "as if the rod were to shake him who lifts it up, as if the staff were to raise itself, and not be wood." Nor is Forerius wrong: as if the rod shook those who lift it, as if [he who] lifts the staff [were to raise] not wood.

units.la: Verf. 22. Consummatio abbreviata inundabit Justitiam. ] Oedipo opus habet hoc ænigma. Neque lux ulla à Belgica Lovaniensis Een verkorte vol-eyndinghe sal rechtveerdigh overvloeden. Non erit operæ omnes alienas à Prophetæ scopo sententias convectare. Tertullianus lib. 4. adversus Marcionem locum ita citat, Decisum sermonem faciet Dominus in terra & interpretatur de Novo Testamento, Compendiatum enim est novum Test. inquit, & à legis laciniosis oneribus expeditum. Nihil tale cogitavit divinus Vates, cujus verba hæc sunt כליון חרוץ שוטף צרקה vox חרוץ vel participium vel adjectivum esse syntaxis docet, quæ est convenientiæ nientiæ, non rectionis. In regimine enim secundum analogiam faceret יַּ֫ ut ab הַגִּיוּ fit הָגְיוּ / Cum ergo ea hic sit syntaxis, quam dixi, quis negabit commodissime sic reddi, consummationem decretam, vel præcisam. קָרַץ enim inter alia est, decernere, decidere, unde Aben. & Kimchi explicant per גְּמַר / גְּמִיר 1.Reg. xx. 4. Sic erit judicium tuum ut דְּבְצָא Chald. פְּסִקְנָא decidisti. Unde Jun. locum totum sic vertit, nam consummationem præcisam [consummabit] inundans justitiâ. Consummabit sc. Dominus. Accipit vocem consummationis in bonam partem, pro completione promissionum quas Deus fidelibus fecit, secundum æternum decretum. Utitur autem voce inundans, ut ostendat hanc Dei voluntatem nullo consilio aut vi impediri posse, non magis quam inundans fluvius vel amnis sisti aut obstrui potest.
units.tr: Verse 22. "A consummation decreed shall overflow with righteousness." This enigma needs an Oedipus. Nor is there any light from the Louvain Dutch version: "A shortened completion shall overflow in righteousness." It would be pointless to gather together all the opinions foreign to the Prophet's purpose. Tertullian, in book 4 against Marcion, cites the passage thus: "The Lord will make a cut-short word upon the earth", and interprets it of the New Testament: "for the New Testament," he says, "has been abbreviated and freed from the tangled burdens of the law." The divine prophet thought nothing of the kind. His words are these: כליון חרוץ שוטף צדקה [kalyon charuts shotef tsedaqah]. Syntax shows that the word חרוץ [charuts] is either a participle or an adjective, and the construction is one of agreement, not of government. For in the regimen, following the analogy, one would make a form like הָגְיוּ from הַגִּיוּ. Since, then, the syntax here is the one I have described, who will deny that it is most suitably rendered thus: "a consummation decreed", or "cut off"? For קָרַץ [qarats] means, among other things, to decree, to decide, whence Aben Ezra and Kimchi explain it by גְּמַר / גְּמִיר [gemar / gemir], "to complete" (1 Kings 20:4): "So shall your judgment be", as דְּבְצָא [debtsa] in the Chaldee means "you have decided", פְּסִקְנָא [peskena]. Whence Junius translates the whole passage thus: "for he will complete a cut-off consummation, overflowing with righteousness." The Lord, namely, will complete it. He takes the word consummation in a good sense, for the fulfilment of the promises that God has made to the faithful according to his eternal decree. He uses the word overflowing to show that this will of God can be hindered by no counsel or force, no more than a flooding river or stream can be stopped or blocked.

units.la: Piscator vero maluit vocem eandem in malam partem interpretari; Hinc enim novam sententiam inchoans*, sic reddit Ebræa, Decreta consummatio (desolatio) fiet, quæ [terram] inundabit justitiâ. Justitia .i. justis judiciis. Deodati interpretatio ita habet, consummatio determinata inundabit in justitia, hoc est, inquit, post desolationem istam quam Deus decrevit per Senacheribum exequi, largissime effundet beneficia sua, quæ hic vocantur Justitia, super reliquias populi, id quod in regno Ezechiæ impletum est: aut per justitiam intelligit sanctitatem cui fideles post hanc desolationem diligentius litarunt. Lutheri interpretationem qui defendam nullus video, neque enim יָרַץ moderari vel derigere significat; sed rogabis quomodo vel Piscatoris vel Junii interpretatio conveniat isti sensui, quo locum hunc laudabit Apostolus Rom. 9. 28. λόγον συντελῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ὅτι λόγον συντετμημένον ποιήσει ὁ κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Respondeo optime.
units.tr: Piscator, however, preferred to interpret the same word in a bad sense; for, beginning a new sentence from here, he renders the Hebrew thus: "A decreed consummation (desolation) shall come, which shall overflow [the land] with righteousness." Righteousness, that is, with just judgments. Diodati's interpretation runs thus: "a determined consummation shall overflow in righteousness", that is, he says, after that desolation which God decreed to carry out through Sennacherib, he will pour out his benefits in great abundance, which here are called righteousness, upon the remnant of the people, which was fulfilled in the reign of Hezekiah; or else by righteousness he understands the holiness which the faithful after this desolation more diligently sought. I see no one who would defend Luther's interpretation, for קָרַץ does not mean to moderate or to direct. But you will ask how the interpretation of Piscator or Junius agrees with that sense in which the Apostle cites this passage in Romans 9:28: λόγον συντελῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ὅτι λόγον συντετμημένον ποιήσει ὁ κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [logon suntelōn en dikaiosynē, hoti logon suntetmēmenon poiēsei ho kyrios epi tēs gēs]. I reply: very well.

units.la: Observa tantum, * λόγον ex Ebraismo hic non sermonem vel verbum sed rem significare. Rem conficiens & concidens [erit] in justitia: quoniam rem concisam peraget Dominus in terra. Junius, qui Ebræum בכליון in bonam accepit partem, hanc quoque rem interpretatur de salvatione reliquiarum. Negat Prophetam de singulari aliquo tempore loqui; Ait ad plenitudinem temporum, quibus Christus in carne patefactus est, maxime pertinere hoc vaticinium. Et licet, inquit, particularis esset istius loci interpretatio, tamen ex universali sententia & perpetuo fonte misericordiæ Dei ducitur, ac proinde legem universalem constantissi
units.tr: Observe only that λόγον [logon], in this Hebraistic usage, means not a word or saying but a *thing*. "Completing and cutting short the thing in righteousness", since the Lord will bring about a cut-short thing upon the earth. Junius, who took the Hebrew בכליון [bekalyon] in a good sense, likewise interprets this *thing* of the salvation of the remnant. He denies that the Prophet speaks of any single time; he says that this prophecy pertains chiefly to the fullness of times, in which Christ was revealed in the flesh. And although, he says, the interpretation of this passage is particular, yet it is drawn from the universal sense and the perpetual fountain of God's mercy, and therefore embraces the most constant universal law of his most perfect administration. So that great theologian in his parallel passages. But Piscator, who took the words in Isaiah in a bad sense, changes nothing in Paul. Junius, to keep himself consistent, thought that the Apostle cites this passage...

units.la: * Ut alibi tissimæ administrationis ejus complectitur. Hæc magnus ille Theologus in parallelis. At Piscator, qui in Jesaia vocem [Hebrew] & [Hebrew] in malam partem accepit, in Paulo nihil mutat. Junius, ut sibi constaret, putavit locum istum ab Apostolo laudari ut ostenderet causam cur reliquias salvaturus esset Deus. Piscator vero putat rationem dari, cur tantùm reliquiæ, & non universus populus salvandus sit. Et certe ei videtur favere modus loquendi, Etiamsi fuerit numerus filiorum Israël, sicut arena maris, tamen reliquiæ tantum salvabuntur, & non universus populus. Vocationem gentium vers. 25. & 26. ex Hosea probatum illustrat Apostolus antithesi rejectionis Judæorum si reliquiæ tantum salvabuntur, ergo maxima pars populi peribit. Recte, sic enim dixit Jesaias, &c. Notat autem idem Theologus Prophetam proprie loqui de consummatione seu consumptione populi per Babylonios & reductione reliquiarum ex captivitate, seu quod idem est, paucorum conservatione, quam Apostolus ut typum redemptionis per Christum consideraverit.
units.tr: As elsewhere, the Apostle also embraces the most steadfast administration of his. So says that great theologian in his *Parallels*. But Piscator, who took the words in Isaiah in a bad sense, changes nothing in Paul. Junius, to keep himself consistent, thought that the Apostle cites this passage to show why God would save a remnant. Piscator, however, holds that a reason is given why only a remnant, and not the whole people, is to be saved. Indeed, the mode of speech seems to favour him: even if the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet only a remnant will be saved, and not the whole people. In verses 25 and 26 the Apostle illustrates the calling of the Gentiles, proved from Hosea, by the antithesis of the rejection of the Jews: if only a remnant will be saved, then the greater part of the people will perish. "Rightly so, for thus Isaiah said," etc. The same theologian notes, moreover, that the Prophet speaks properly of the consummation or destruction of the people by the Babylonians and of the return of the remnant from captivity, or, what is the same, of the preservation of a few, which the Apostle regarded as a type of redemption through Christ.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Vers. 2. & 3. Celebris est inter Pontificios disputatio de VII. donis Spiritus Sancti. Vide inter alios Magistrum sentent. lib. 3. distinct. 34. Hinc & Augustinus lib. xi. de civ. Dei, cap. 31. numero septenario Spiritum Sanctum sæpe denotari asserit, Et certe ex nostris quoque Theologis quamplurimi, quando locum illum Apocal. 1. 4. explicant, ubi septem Spiritus memorantur, de septem donis Spiritus S. loqui atque ad hunc locum respicere amant. Ego, si illa, quæ de donis Spiritus S. à Scholasticis nervose & docte disputata sunt, convellere aut ridere præsumerem, dignus essem qui Helleboro potionarer. Neque animus mihi est eorum sententiæ adversari, qui dicto Apocal. Loco per 7. Spiritus, Spiritum S. intelligunt, quamvis & illud non nesciam Cl. Bezam & Drusium aliud sentire; Illud ajo, hoc loco non septem sed sex duntaxat dona recenseri. Namque, ubi vulgatus habet versu 2. Spiritus scientiæ & pietatis, Ebræa habent, spiritus scientiæ & timoris Domini. Cum itaque in principio versus 3. dicatur in vulgata, & replebit eum Spiritus timoris Domini, Domini, unde septimum donum exsculpunt Scholastici, videsmanifeste, sex tantum dona hoc loco recenseri. Ita quidem est, per timorem Domini, optime intelligi pietatem, quomodo hoc loco & Lxx. reddidere, πνεῦμα γνώσεως καὶ ἰσυσέβειας, Neq; hoc culpo.
