Sed cum versu 3. idem donum memoretur, iisdem vocibus in originario textu, licet in versione diversis, rursus pronuncio numerum septenarium hinc male exsculptum esse. Porro ubi Vulg. habet, & replebit eum Spiritus timoris Domini, Ebræa sic habent וְהֵרִיחוֹ בְּיִרְאַת יְהוָה & odorari ejus.i. odoratus ejus, erit in timore Domini id est, cognitio & judicium ejus erit conjunctum cum reverentia Domini & cæteris donis quæ versu superiori recensuit Vates. Non tenuiter, infirme, aut instar hominis singula odorabitur & cognoscet, sed in omnia etiam abditissima recto judicio penetrabit &c. Hanc interpretationem ait Torrerius non esse contemnendam, aliique non infimi subsellii inter Pontificios Interpretes suo calculo approbarunt. Odoratus ergo pro judicio usurpatur. Ex quinque sensibus soli gustus & tactus Deo in sacris literis non tribuuntur. At auditus, visus & olfactus frequentissime. Videntur enim duo isti dignitate infra hos tres esse. A. Gellius libro 19. cap. 2. eleganter hac de re disertavit. Quinque sunt hominum sensus inquit, per quos voluptas animo aut corpori quæri videtur. Ex his omnibus, quæ immodice voluptas quæritur, ea turpis atque improba existimantur. Sed enim quæ nimia ex gustu & tactu est, voluptas sicuti sapientes censuerunt, omnium rerum fœdissima est. Et Paulo post, istæ autem voluptates duæ, gustus & tactus .i. libidines in cibos & Venerem prodigæ, solæ sunt hominibus communes cum bestiis, & idcirco in pecudum ferorumque animalium numero habentur, quisquis est his ferinis voluptatibus prævinctus. Cæteræ ex tribus aliis sensibus proficiscentes, hominum esse tantum propriæ videntur. Verba Aristotelis, quæ eidem rei affert nimis prolixa sunt. Ego paucis istis contentus ero. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν αἰσθήσεων πέντε, τὰ ἄλλα ζῷα ἐπὶ δύο μόνων τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἡδεται, ἡ δὲ τὰς ἀπαλὰς ἡ ὅλως ἐχ ἡδεται, ἡ ἐχ. συμβαίνει ἐκ τῶν πάθη. i. cum sensus quinque sint, cætera animalia ex duobus tantum prædictorum voluptatem capiunt, cæteris vel omnino non delectantur, aut per accidens. Maimonides in More Nebochim parte 1. cap. 46. vel si Librum Exemplar habes aliam assignat præstantiæ rationem. Invenimus scriptum, inquit, Et vidit Dominus, & audivit Dominus, & odoratus est Dominus & non invenimus, & gustavit Dominus, & tetigit Dominus. Ratio autem hæc affertur quia infixum est cogitationi cujuslibet hominis, Creatorem non conjungi corporibus sicut corpus corpori, neque enim oculis suis vident eum. Isti vero duo sensus .i. gustus & tactus לא ישיגו מורשיהם [?] non apprehendunt sensata sua, nisi tangant ea. Visus vero & auditus & olfactus apprehendunt sua sensata quamvis corpora in quibus sunt qualitates istæ remotæ sint. Hæc ille. Rursus ex his tribus sensibus olfactui primas defert Aben-Ezra, non judicabit, inquit Jesaias, ad aspectum oculorum suorum, neque arguet secundum auditum aurium suarum, quia sensus isti sæpe falluntur. Sæpe enim, verba Aben-Ezræ, errat sensus auris, ut videaris tibi aliquid audire, cum nullus sit sonus. Sæpe etiam errat sensus oculi, ut putes aliquid quiescere, quod movetur, sed odoratus non errat. Hæc Aben. Hinc ad rerum naturam penitius pernoscendam olfactus magis, quam visus vel auditus, valet. Nam, ut jam dictum est, multa simulata & effecta oculorum sensum & auditum fallunt, cujusmodi admirandas res omnium seculorum artifices representarunt. At vero odor ipse, quod ex interioribus rerum virtutibus & facultatibus, una cum substantiæ parte aliqua remissus proferatur, uniuscujusque rei naturam præcipue ostendens minime omnium sensatorum fallit. Atque huc adeo illud pertinet quod de natura & arte Philosophi tradidere, artem rerum species imitari posse & referre, motum vero & vitam ipsam non posse referre. Inter vitæ vero & motus genera odor ex rebus remissus numeratur. His ergo verbis, Et odoratus ejus in timore Domini erit, maxima cognoscendi, sentiendi & judicandi vis indicatur, non fert judicium ex aspectu oculi vel auditu auris .i. non ex apparentia & signis externis, quæ fallere solent, sed de unoquoque secundum illud quod in eo, infallibili judico, quasi odorabitur, faciet arbitria. Sed manum de tabula. Non enim scribimus commentaria:
units.tr: Verses 2 and 3. There is a well-known dispute among the Papists about the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. See among others the Master of the Sentences, book 3, distinction 34. Hence also Augustine, book 11 of The City of God, chapter 31, asserts that the Holy Spirit is often denoted by the number seven. Indeed, many of our own theologians too, when they explain that passage in Revelation 1:4 where seven Spirits are mentioned, like to speak of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and to refer to this passage. If I were to presume to overthrow or laugh at the things the Schoolmen have discussed vigorously and learnedly about the gifts of the Holy Spirit, I would deserve to be dosed with hellebore. Nor is it my intention to oppose those who, in the said passage of Revelation, understand by the seven Spirits the Holy Spirit, although I am not unaware that the famous Beza and Drusius think otherwise. I say this: in this passage only six gifts, not seven, are listed. For where the Vulgate has in verse 2 spirit of knowledge and of godliness, the Hebrew has spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord. Since, then, at the beginning of verse 3 the Vulgate reads and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord, from which the Scholastics carve out a seventh gift, it is manifest that only six gifts are listed here. It is indeed so: through the fear of the Lord, piety is best understood here, as the Seventy also rendered it [pneuma gnōseōs kai eusebeias]. I do not find fault with this. But since in verse 3 the same gift is mentioned in the same words in the original text, though differently translated, I again declare that the seven has been wrongly carved out here. Further, where the Vulgate has and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord, the Hebrew reads and he shall smell [him] in the fear of the Lord [wehērīaḥ bĕyirʾat YHWH], that is, and his smelling shall be in the fear of the Lord, that is, his knowing and judging shall be joined with reverence for the Lord and with the other gifts which the Prophet listed in the previous verse. He will not judge partially, weakly, or like a man, smelling and knowing each thing, but will penetrate with right judgment even the most hidden things, etc. Torrerius says this interpretation is not to be despised, and others of no small standing among the Papist interpreters have approved it. Smelling is therefore used for judgment. Of the five senses, only taste and touch are not ascribed to God in Holy Scripture, whereas hearing, sight and smell very often are. For these two seem to rank below the other three. Aulus Gellius in book 19, chapter 2, discusses this elegantly. There are five senses of men, he says, through which pleasure seems to be sought for the mind or body. Of all those pleasures sought immoderately, those are considered base and shameful. But excessive pleasure from taste and touch is, as the wise have judged, the most foul of all things. And a little later: these two pleasures, taste and touch, that is, lusts for food and extravagant Venus, are alone common to men and beasts, and so whoever is bound by these bestial pleasures is counted among the number of cattle and wild animals. The others, arising from the remaining three senses, seem to belong to men alone. Aristotle's words, which he brings to the same point, are too lengthy; I shall be content with these few. Among the five senses, the other animals take pleasure in only two of them; but to touch [the soft] they either take no pleasure at all, or only incidentally [epi de tōn aisthēseōn pente, ta alla zōa epi dyo monōn tōn aisthēseōn hēdetai, hē de tas aphas hē holōs ouk hēdetai, hē ek symbebēkotos pathē]. Maimonides, in Guide of the Perplexed, part 1, chapter 46, or if you have the book at hand, assigns another reason for its excellence. We find written, he says, And the Lord saw, and the Lord heard, and the Lord smelled, and we do not find that the Lord tasted, and the Lord touched. The reason given is that it is fixed in the thought of every man that the Creator is not joined to bodies as body is to body, for they do not see him with their eyes. Those two senses, that is taste and touch, do not apprehend their sensibles [lō yašīgû mûrešêhem] unless they touch them. But sight, hearing and smell apprehend their sensibles, although the bodies in which those qualities are found are at a distance. Thus far he. Again, of these three senses, Aben Ezra ranks smell first: He shall not judge, says Isaiah, by the sight of his eyes, nor reprove by the hearing of his ears, because those senses are often deceived. For, in Aben Ezra's words, the sense of hearing often errs, so that you seem to hear something when there is no sound. The sense of sight also often errs, so that you think something is at rest which is moving, but smell does not err. Thus Aben Ezra. Hence smell is more useful than sight or hearing for coming to a deeper knowledge of the nature of things. For, as has already been said, many simulated and artificial things deceive the senses of sight and hearing, of which kinds the artificers of all ages have produced wonderful examples. But the odour itself, which is emitted from the inner virtues and powers of things together with some part of their substance, most clearly reveals the nature of each thing and is least of all deceived among the senses. And to this belongs what the philosophers have taught about nature and art: that art can imitate and represent the appearance of things, but cannot represent motion and life itself. Among the kinds of life and motion, the odour given off by things is counted. So by these words, And his smelling shall be in the fear of the Lord, the greatest power of knowing, perceiving and judging is indicated: he will not pass judgment from the appearance of the eye or the hearing of the ear, that is, not from outward appearance and signs, which are wont to deceive, but about each person he will make his decisions as by a smell, that is, by what is in him, with infallible judgment. But let me put my hand from the tablet. For we are not writing commentaries.

units.la: Verf.10. Et erit sepulcrum ejus gloriosum] id est, famosum & honorandum, inquit Carthus. Ex omnibus enim finibus mundi visitatur à Christianis, & cum summa devotione honoratur: Thomas in summa, p.3. qu.51. art.2. ex hoc loco definit quæstiostionem, Christum convenenti loco sepultum fuisse. Sed scire oportet, Ebraea ita sonare והיתה מנחתו כבוד eritque requies ejus gloria id est, in gloria, vel gloriosa. Lxx. ad verbum, και εσται η ανάπαυσις αὐτῆ πμή. Forerius eritque mansio ejus &c. Video, inquit, vocem non semel significare, non unam aliquam domum, sed totas ædes & quidem amplas, cujusmodi sunt palatia. Unde pro regia & templo Dei sæpe accipi videbis, & Pf. 95. pro tota terra promissionis. Libenter ego hic pro regia acciperem. Ecclesia enim Christi plena fuit gloria Domini &c. Hæc Forerius.
units.tr: Verse 10. And his sepulchre shall be glorious: that is, famous and honoured, says the Carthusian. For it is visited by Christians from all the ends of the world and is honoured with the greatest devotion. Thomas, in the Summa, part 3, question 51, article 2, uses this passage to settle the question that Christ was buried in a suitable place. But it must be known that the Hebrew reads thus: wehāyětâ mĕnûḥātô kābôd, and his rest shall be glory, that is, in glory, or glorious. The Seventy render it word for word: kai estai hē anapausis autē timē. Forerius: and his dwelling shall be, etc. I see, he says, that the word signifies not just one house but whole buildings, and indeed large ones, such as palaces. Hence you will often find it taken for a royal palace and the temple of God, and in Psalm 95 for the whole land of promise. I would gladly take it here for a royal palace. For the Church of Christ was full of the glory of the Lord, etc. Thus Forerius.

units.la: Plane in eundum Modum Junius, & requies ejus sit gloriosa, id est, Ecclesia, inquit, domus Dei, in qua requiescit Christus Pf. 32. 14. Oleastrius eodem modo Ebraea reddidit. Et requies ejus erit gloriosa, id est, pax qua regnabit, erit gloriosa. Arias Montanus, Et erit quies ejus gloria, estque hujus loci ista explicatio, inquit, gloriam illam & amplitudinem & imperium in omnes gentes, non bellis & cædibus & humanarum rerum perturbatione, ut alius gentium imperatoribus contigit, sed pace, quiete, tranquillitate, & quodam lenitatis usu constare. Cæteris enim summis ducibus, gloria, rebus per vim & arma gestis, & perturbatis confusisque aliorum hominum regnis ac ditionibus parari solet, eaque res triumphi causa expeti videtur. At vero Christus, princeps & author pacis, paupertatis magister, ambitionis osor, lenitatis & modestiæ princeps summus, nullis alienis rebus aut vitæ insidiatur, sed saluti, tranquillitati & quieti omnium consulit: atque hac ratione omnium gentium animos sibi conciliat, nullo bello indicto, sed pace & misericordia Dei omnibus nationibus; quæ Evangelio obedierint, propósita. Hæc Arias.
units.tr: Junius proceeds in exactly the same way: "and his rest shall be glorious", that is, "the Church, the house of God, in which Christ rests" (Ps. 132.14). Oleaster rendered the Hebrew in the same manner: "And his rest shall be glorious", that is, the peace with which he will reign shall be glorious. Arias Montanus has: "And his rest shall be glory." He explains this passage as follows: that glory, that greatness and that dominion over all nations consist not in wars, slaughter and the disturbance of human affairs, as happened to the emperors of other nations, but in peace, quiet, tranquillity and a certain exercise of gentleness. For to the other great leaders, glory is usually won by force and arms, and by the disturbing and confusing of the kingdoms and dominions of other men, and that kind of thing is thought to be sought for the sake of triumph. But Christ, the prince and author of peace, the teacher of poverty, the foe of ambition, the chief prince of gentleness and modesty, lays no snares for the goods or lives of others, but looks to the safety, tranquillity and rest of all; and in this way he wins over the minds of all nations, not by declaring war, but by offering peace and the mercy of God to all nations which obey the Gospel. Thus Arias.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Vers. 1. Onus Babel] Ebr. משא בבל Onus Babelis, i. onerasa Prophetia in Babylonios. R. Sal. משא vox נשא משאוי פורענות שעל בבל inter alia significat levare, assumere, attollere, & rem levatam portare. Hinc משא assumptio, & onus. Frequenter usurpatur de infaustis Prophetiis, non tantum quod illæ instar oneris graves essent, verum etiam quia & auditu & dictu graves & injucundæ essent. Hanc significationem manifeste alludit Jeremias cap. 23. verf. 32. & seq. Jef. 21. verf. 2. vocatur חזות קשה visio dura, quæ versu 1. dicebatur משא. Moneo tamen tyronem, משא non ubique onerosam & infaustam prædictionem denotare, ac proinde non esse verum illud Hieron. viri eruditi effatum, Ubicunque præmittitur vox מַשָּׂא / insinuari ea, quæ sequuntur, plena minarum esse. Ecce enim Prov. 31. 1. Verba Lemuel regis & מַשָּׂא qua erudivit eum mater ejus. Et cap. 30. 1. Utrobique vulg. visionem vertit. Alii cum Chaldæo melius, Prophetiam. Junius contra accentum & proprietatem Ebraismi, Verborum Lemuelis comportatio, Hoc enim diceretur Ebraice, מַשָּׂא דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל / Tollere vel assumere prophetiam, canticum, lamentum, parabolam, contentionem phrases Ebriacæ sunt, sed defectæ Pf. 50. plenior extat, licet sensu aliquantulum diverso, ut assumas fœdus meum in os tuum. Unde aliæ explicandæ sunt, e, gr. in Decalogo, præcepto 3. Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum. Assumes in os tuum. Pro quo Psalmo xvi. occurrit, assumere super labia. Hinc מַשָּׂא aliquando est assumptio, subaudi, Prophetiæ, doctrinæ &c. id est, Prophetia, doctrina, sermo. Hinc Jes. 14. 28. Anno quo mortuus est Achaz, facit הַמַּשָּׂא הַזֶּה / Lxx. τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο, sermo vel verbum istud. Malach. 1. 1. Jerem. 23. 32 & seq. & alibi Lxx. vertunt λῆμμα i. ad verbum assumptio, à λέγω sive λαμβάνω ut מַשָּׂא à נשא. Non potest tamen is qui locum Jerem. consideravit, dubitare, quin per λῆμμα onus intellexerint. Quippe ut נשא Ebræis est assumo & porto onus, ita & illi vocis Græcæ significationem extenderunt. Quod cum Moschopulus non intelligeret, vocis istius rationem paulo diversam reddidit, λήμματα ἀφελφείαι ἀς ἐλαττον οἱ ἀφέλφιται ... ἐν ἁγίᾳ πνεύματι. Vide Druf. Quæst. 1. 57. Quo respexisse videtur Schindl. quando in Lexico Prophetias sic dici asserit; quod traderentur Prophetis, ut ferrent eas ad Israelitas.
units.tr: Verse 1. The burden of Babylon] Hebrew מַשָּׂא בָּבֶל [masa Babel], that is, the burden or prophecy laid upon Babylon. Rabbi Solomon says that the word משא, from the verb נשא [to lift], means among other things to lift, to take up, to raise, and to carry a thing that has been lifted; hence משא means a taking up and a burden. It is often used of ominous prophecies, not only because they were heavy like a load, but also because they were grievous and unwelcome to hear and to speak. Jeremiah clearly alludes to this sense at ch. 23, vv. 32 ff. In Isaiah 21:2 the vision is called חזות קשה [hazut qasheh], a hard vision, which in v. 1 was called משא. I warn the beginner, however, that משא does not always denote an oppressive and ominous prediction, so the famous saying of the learned Jerome is not true, namely that wherever the word משא is placed first, what follows is full of threats. For see Prov. 31:1, The words of king Lemuel and the burden which his mother taught him. And ch. 30:1. In both places the Vulgate translates visionem, vision. Others, with the Chaldee, better render Prophetiam, prophecy. Junius, against the accent and the idiom of Hebrew, gives a collection of the words of Lemuel; for in Hebrew one would say מַשָּׂא דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל. To take up a prophecy, song, lament, parable or contention are Hebrew idioms, but incomplete ones. Psalm 50 has a fuller form, though with a somewhat different sense: that you should take my covenant into your mouth. So other passages must be explained accordingly; for example, in the Decalogue, precept 3: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, that is, take into your mouth. Psalm 16 has the phrase take upon the lips. Hence מַשָּׂא is sometimes a taking up, understood as of prophecy, of doctrine and so on, that is, prophecy, doctrine, discourse. Hence Isaiah 14:28, In the year that Ahaz died this burden is, in the LXX, τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο [to rhema touto], this word or saying. Malachi 1:1, Jeremiah 23:32 and elsewhere the LXX render λῆμμα [lemma], literally a taking up, from λέγω or λαμβάνω, just as מַשָּׂא comes from נשא. Yet anyone who has considered the passage in Jeremiah cannot doubt that by λῆμμα they meant burden. For just as נשא means for the Hebrews both to assume and to carry a load, so they extended the meaning of the Greek word too. Since Moschopulus did not understand this, he gave the word a slightly different explanation, λήμματα [lemmata] ... ἐν ἁγίᾳ πνεύματι [en hagia pneumati]. See Drusius, Quaest. 1, 57. Schindler seems to have had this in mind when, in his Lexicon, he says that prophecies are so called because they were handed to the prophets so that they might carry them to the Israelites.

units.la: Vers. 3. mandavi sanctificatis meis] Hoc epitheton. Alii ad universum Persarum Medorumque exercitum extendendum, alii ad Cyrum & Darium tantum restringendum putant. Nos hoc in medio relinquimus. Quomodo autem gentiles & barbari isti homines sanctificati dicantur, quærunt Interpretes. Qui vocem Ebræam hoc proprie significare putant, quod vertit Vulgatus, multa hic convectant haudquaquam spernenda. Adscribam elegantissima verba Forerii, Milites, inquit qui Dei bellum gesturi erant; sanctificatos suos vocat, quasi ad bellum sacrum conscriptos. Bella enim tum apud Judæos, tum apud gentes, certis ceremoniis, legibus, ritibus, solennitatibus, insuper etiam juris-jurandi sacramento interposito suscipiebantur. Deut. 20. Adde quod qui jussu Domini interficiuntur, sunt veluti quædam victimæ, morti destinatæ, ut patet infra 34. Jerem. 46. quia morte illorum quasi expiatur terra. In quam sententiam postea adducit locum Sophoniæ 1. Præparavit Dominus victimam, & sanctificavit vocatos suos. Audiamus & Oleastrium. Persas & Medos vocat sanctificatos, quoniam vocabantur ad occisionem Babyloniorum, quasi sancti & mundi ad victimam. Vocat enim Ebraismus mactationem & jugulationem eorum qui in prælio occumbunt, sacrificium, ut Ezech. 39. congregate vos omnes ad sacrificium meum. Et sicuti oportebat eos, qui comesti erant de carnibus sacrificii esse sanctificatos & mundos, tales videtur desiderare jugulatores. Hæc ille. Ebræi, inter quos Aben. & Kimchi & Chald. vocem בעניין הזמנה in significatione præparationis, atque adeo Aben. מקדשים reddit מזומנים id est, præparatos. Ego semper existimavi retinendam & hic & aliis in locis quamplurimis propriam & primariam vocis significationem. Ea est in Kal. & Phual separari, & destinari ad aliquid in Piel & Hiphil, separare &c. Mandavi separatis meis, i. Medis & Persis, quos exequendæ sententiæ meæ peculiariter destinavi, delegavi & separavi. Quod vero קדש passim per sanctificari, sanctificare, sanctus &c. exprimitur, ideo in nonnullis Scripturæ locis illi interpretes a vero sensu aberrarunt, qui ejusmodi interpretamenta vocibus Ebræis examussim respondere crediderunt. Sed qui Ebræa vel a limine salutarunt, optime norunt usitatissima vocum Ebræarum interpretamenta sæpe ex diversis significationibus unam tantum exprimere. E. gr. ΥΥ ξύλον & δένδρον significat. Lxx. passim ξύλον reddidere, etiam ubi δένδρον significat. In iis ergo locis ξύλον lignum pro arbore accipiendum est. Sed ad rem. קדש primò & proprie significat separari, destinarique ad aliquid, sive illud sit seculare sive sacrum.
units.tr: Verse 3. I have commanded my sanctified ones] This epithet. Some think it extends to the whole army of the Persians and Medes, others restrict it to Cyrus and Darius alone. We leave the question open. Interpreters ask how these heathen and barbarian men can be called sanctified. Those who think the Hebrew word properly means what the Vulgate renders sanctified gather here many things that are by no means to be despised. I shall add the very elegant words of Forerius: "He calls them his sanctified ones, the soldiers who were going to wage the war of God, as if they had been enrolled for a holy war. For wars were undertaken, both among the Jews and among the nations, with certain ceremonies, laws, rites and solemnities, and moreover with the sanction of an oath interposed. Deut. 20. Add that those who are slain at the command of the Lord are like victims, destined for death, as appears below at 34. Jer. 46, because by their death the land is, as it were, expiated." To the same effect he afterwards cites Zephaniah 1: The Lord has prepared a victim, and has sanctified his called ones. Let us hear Oleaster too: "He calls the Persians and Medes sanctified because they were summoned to the slaughter of the Babylonians, as holy and clean for a victim. For Hebrew idiom calls the slaughter and butchering of those who fall in battle a sacrifice, as in Ezek. 39: Gather yourselves to my sacrifice. And just as those who were to eat of the flesh of the sacrifice had to be sanctified and clean, so the slaughterers seem to require the same." So far he. The Hebrews, among whom Aben Ezra, Kimchi and the Chaldee take the word in the sense of preparation, and Aben Ezra renders מקדשים [mequdashim] as מזומנים [mezumanim], that is, prepared. I have always thought that here and in very many other places the proper and primary sense of the word should be kept. That sense, in Qal and Pual, is to be separated, and in Piel and Hiphil, to separate and so on, and to be set apart for something. I have commanded my separated ones, that is, the Medes and Persians, whom I have particularly destined, appointed and set apart for carrying out my sentence. But because קדש is everywhere rendered by to be sanctified, to sanctify, holy and so on, those interpreters have strayed from the true sense in some passages of Scripture who believed that such renderings correspond exactly to the Hebrew words. But those who have greeted Hebrew from the threshold know very well that the most common renderings of Hebrew words often express only one of several meanings. For example, עץ [etz] means both ξύλον [xylon] and δένδρον [dendron]. The LXX everywhere rendered it ξύλον, even where it means δένδρον. In those places, therefore, ξύλον must be taken as wood for a tree. But to the matter: קדש [qadash], first and properly, means to be separated and destined for something, whether that thing is secular or sacred.

units.la: SECULARE, tam licitum quam illicitum tam turpe quam honestum. Jos xx. 7. ויקדשו / Kedeschun Vulgatus decreverunt, Malim secreverunt id est separarunt, destinarunt huic, ut esset Asylum. Quamvis Junius, sanctificarunt. Et certe vero admodum simile est, asyla certis ritibus & religiosis cæremoniis initiata fuisse, qua ratione hoc exemplum ad sacra referri poterit. Jerem. 12. 3. והקדישם & separando (vel destinando eos) in diem occisionis. Quamvis Jun. & Kunchius, praparando. Et certe haec separatio seu destinatio aliquo modo dici potest praeparatio. Sed & Theodoretus illic loci observavit, purificare (Lxx. enim voce ἁγνισαι, illicuisi sunt) pro segregare positum. Cujus tropi rationem paulo post ex eo audiemus. Hinc meretrix קדשה / cynædus vero seu pathicus קדש dicitur, quasi dicas personam ad ipurcum turpemque illum usum separatam destinatamque. Scio quidem hic à multis poni Antiphrasin, קדשה meretrix, quasi minime sancta, sed ut nihil jam dicam, illud interpretamentum sanctus synecdochicum esse, & nequaquam vocis Ebraeæ latitudini adæquatam esse, antiphrasis, vulgo quidem, sed aliene sic dicta (Ἀντίφρασις enim teste Plut. est λέξις τὸ ἐναντίον, ἢ τὸ ᾧ βούλεται μῶν, ἀμφαίνωσε, ut cum Homerus dicit, ὃ χρήσιμον non lætatus est, pro, vehementer doluit.) à multis eruditis viris vel omnino ex linguis explosa est, vel in paucissimis tantum, ubi major quædam necessitas urget, relinquitur. Qua de re extat eruditus tractatus Franc. Sancti Brocensis. Oleastrius hic in separatione terminum à quo considerans, statuit meretrices sic dictas, quod ab honestorum virorum consortio separatæ, locis separatis, seu in urbe sive extra ejus pomœria agerent. Quo trahit locum ex Iosu. 2. 15. ubi Rachab in moenibus habitasse legitur, Sed hæc sententia licet arguta, minus tamen se mihi probat.
units.tr: SECULAR: both lawful and unlawful, as base as honourable. Joshua 20:7, ויקדשו [vayaqdishu], which the Vulgate renders they decided; I would prefer they set apart, that is, separated and destined them for this, to be a city of refuge. Although Junius has sanctified. And certainly it is quite likely that cities of refuge were established with certain rites and religious ceremonies, so that this example can be referred to sacred things. Jeremiah 12:3, והקדישם [vehaqdisham], separating (or destining them) for the day of slaughter. Although Junius and Kimchi have preparing. And indeed this separation or destination can in some way be called preparation. But Theodoret also observed there that to purify (for the LXX have the verb ἁγνίζειν [hagnizein], to be made pure) is used in the sense of to set apart. We shall hear the reason for this trope from him a little later. Hence a prostitute is called קדשה [qedeshah], and a male prostitute or catamite קדש [qadesh], as if to say a person set apart and destined for that filthy and shameful use. I know indeed that many take this as an antiphrasis, that qedeshah means a prostitute, as if she were least holy. But, to say nothing more, the rendering holy is synecdochic and by no means adequate to the breadth of the Hebrew word. Antiphrasis (for ἀντίφρασις [antiphrasis], according to Plutarch, is a figure of speech in which the opposite is said, or what one wishes to say is hinted at, as when Homer says ὃ χρήσιμον [ho chrēsimon] was not pleased, meaning greatly grieved) is a figure commonly used but wrongly applied here. It has been wholly rejected from the languages by many learned men, or is retained only in a very few cases where some greater necessity presses. There is a learned treatise on this matter by Francisco Sanchez de las Brozas. Oleaster, considering here the starting point of the term separation, holds that prostitutes were so called because they were separated from the company of respectable men, living in separated places, either within the city or outside its boundaries. He draws this from Joshua 2:15, where Rahab is read to have lived within the walls. But this view, though ingenious, does not commend itself to me.

units.la: SACRUM m. à profano & communi usu ad sacrum usum separari, sacro usui destinari, consecrati. Hoc est quod vulgo sanctificari dicitur. * Jerem. 1. 5. antequam exires é vulva, הקדשתיך segregavi te, scilicet mihi, Lxx. ἡγίακά σε. Ioel. 2. 15. קדשו צום segregate jejunium id est, diem jejunii. Ex sex diebus septimanæ negotiosis, unum Deo segregate & religioso jejunio destinate. Ellipsis prioris nominis frequens & tralatitia est. Sirach 35. 10. sanctificare decimas id est, Deo & ministris ejus segregare. Quomodo Deus quoque Sabbathum sanctificare legitur, Gen. 2. vide & Exod. 29 37. Lev. 8. Hagg. 2. Deuter. 22. quæ loca Illyricus aliorum vestigia premens antiphrastice sine ulla necessitate, atque adeo contra Spiritus S. mentem interpretatus est. Vox ergo קדוש sanctum ἁγιώτατον creaturæ competit, & significat aliquid Deo separatum & consecratum. Hoc elogio insigniuntur pii in V. Test. quasi à mundo separati & soli Deo consecrati.
units.tr: SACRED, when something is set apart from profane and common use and destined for sacred use, consecrated. This is what is commonly called to be sanctified. * Jeremiah 1:5, before you came out of the womb, הקדשתיך [hiqdashtik], I separated you, namely for myself; the LXX ἡγίακά σε [hēgiaka se]. Joel 2:15, קדשו צום [qadeshu tsom], separate a fast, that is, set apart a day of fasting. Of the six working days of the week, set one apart for God as a religious fast. The ellipsis of the first noun is frequent and conventional. Sirach 35:10, to sanctify tithes, that is, to set them apart for God and his ministers. Likewise God is read to have sanctified the Sabbath, Gen. 2; see also Exod. 29:37, Lev. 8, Hag. 2, Deut. 22. Illyricus, following the footsteps of others, interpreted these passages antiphrastically, without any necessity, and therefore contrary to the mind of the Holy Spirit. The word קדוש [qadosh], holy, therefore fits a creature in the most excellent sense, and signifies something separated and consecrated to God. The pious of the Old Testament were distinguished by this designation, as if separated from the world and consecrated to God alone.

units.la: * Vide Theodoretum. secrati. Tales videri volebant Pharisæi, unde se quoque פרושים id est, ἀφωρισμένοι, separatos vocitabant. Quia vero tales pietati, justitiæ atque omni virtutum generi operabantur, translata ea vox est ad Deum, qui ipsa justitia & pietas & virtus est. Nisi dixeris ita dictum Deum, quod ab omnibus vitiis, sordibus & imperfectionibus separatus est. Sed id minus quadrare videtur, quia in hac voce magis terminus ad quem, quam a quo spectatur.
units.tr: * See Theodoret. ...separated. The Pharisees wished to appear as such men, and so they also called themselves פרושים, that is, ἀφωρισμένοι [aphōrismenoi], "the separated." Because such men devoted themselves to piety, justice and every kind of virtue, the word was transferred to God, who is justice itself, piety itself and virtue itself. Unless you prefer to say that God is so called because he is separated from all vices, filth and imperfections. But this seems to fit less well, since in this word the end towards which something is directed is regarded more than the point from which it is separated.

units.la: Quia vero omnis, qui ad aliquod vitæ genus vel certum opus, vel honestum coetum vel Dei cultum segregatus & destinatus est, se præparat, adornat; à sordibus & immunditie separat, coepta ea vox usurpari pro præparari & mundari. Quæ præparatio seu mundatio in rebus ad religionem & cultum Mosaicum pertinentibus & vulgo & passim quoque in versionibus sanctificatio appellatur, ut Exod. 19. Ios. 3. 5. Atque huc refero locum 2. Sam. xi. 4. Ipsa vero Bathseba מתקדשת separabat se ab immunditie sua, Jun. purgabat se ab intm. sua, hæc erat sanctificatio legalis sive mundatio à fluxu menstruo qui desierat. Unde Vulg. sanctificata. Qui tamen verba illa sic accepit, q. diceret historia, mox à concubitu cessasse menstruas purgationes, signo eam concepisse. Cum & Lxx, & Junius & alii verba sic intelligant, ut narrat historia, paulo ante concubitum desiisse menstrua, atque ex præscripto legis Lev xv. Mundatam fuisse, quo etiam tempore facillime concipi & Medici tradunt & experientia docet. Sed videamus de præparatione non legali. 1. Sam. xvi. 6. התקדשו Vulg. sanctificate vos, Junius, comparate vos, ut veniatis ad convivium. Ebr. וּבָּה sed vide Junii notas ad versum 3. ostendentis, וּבָה etiam de convivio accipi. Et ibidem, ויקרש & jussit præparari Isajum & Davidem. Sophoniæ 1. 7. והקדיש & præparavit (vel jussit præparari se) invitatos suos. Joel. 3. 9. Jerem. 6. 4. קדש מלחמה / Vulgatus, sanctificate bellum. Jun. comparate bellum, Alii, præparate. Lxx. καταςκευάσατε præparate, ut Joel. 3. 2. ἁγιάσατε. Quamvis etiam non male per ellipsin nominis exponi possit קדשו אנשי מלחמה separate, seligite, viros belli. Atque ita Theodoretus ad locum Joelis, ἁγιάσατε πόλεμον, inquit, id est, διεγείρατε τὰς μαχητὰς· ἢ ἀφορίσατε εἰς πόλεμον. Excitate bellatores & separate ad bellum. ἐπὶ δὲ ὁ ἁγιάσας τῶν ἐναγῶν ἀφορίζει πᾶσαν εἰς τὴν ἀφορισμὸν ἁγιάσαι κάλει. Huc etiam non male referas phrasin illam, quam supra exhibuimus, mus, קדשו יום ut sensus sit, praeparate jejunium seu diem jejunii. Non enim quodlibet jejunium Deo placet. Hieron. ad Joel. 1. Si omne jejunium placeret Deo, nunquam diceret sanctificate jejunium, &, non tale jejunium elegi. — Idcirco dicit sanctificate jejunium. Jejunat Manichaeus & multi haeretici, maxime Encratitae. Sed hoc jejunium saturitate & ebrietate deterius est.
units.tr: Since everyone who is set apart and destined for some way of life or a particular work, or for a respectable assembly or the worship of God, prepares and adorns himself and separates himself from filth and uncleanness, the word began to be used for being prepared and cleansed. This preparation or cleansing, in matters pertaining to religion and the Mosaic worship, is commonly and widely called sanctification in the versions as well, as in Exod. 19; Josh. 3:5. To this I also refer 2 Sam. 11:4, where Bathsheba herself was purifying herself (מתקדשת), that is, separating herself from her uncleanness; Junius renders "cleansing herself from her uncleanness." This was legal sanctification, or cleansing from the menstrual flow which had ceased; hence the Vulgate has sanctified. Yet he who took those words to mean that, as the narrative says, the menstrual purgations had stopped immediately after intercourse, so that she had conceived, took them in that sense. The Septuagint, Junius and others understand the words as the narrative tells it: shortly before intercourse the menses had ceased, and she had been cleansed according to the prescription of the law, Lev. 15, a time when conception most easily occurs, as physicians teach and experience shows. But let us look at preparation of a non-legal kind. 1 Sam. 16:5, התקדשו, the Vulgate sanctify yourselves; Junius prepare yourselves to come to the feast. In Hebrew, וּבָּה; but see Junius's notes on verse 3, showing that וּבָה too is to be understood of the feast. And in the same place, ויקדש, and he commanded Jesse and David to be prepared. Zeph. 1:7, והקדיש, he prepared (or commanded to be prepared) his invited guests. Joel 3:9; Jer. 6:4, קדש מלחמה: the Vulgate sanctify war; Junius prepare war; others prepare. The Septuagint καταςκευάσατε [kataskeuasate], prepare, as in Joel 3:2 ἁγιάσατε [hagiasate]. Although it can also not badly be explained by an ellipsis of the noun, קדשו אנשי מלחמה, set apart, choose, men of war. And so Theodoret on the passage of Joel, ἁγιάσατε πόλεμον [hagiasate polemon], he says, that is, διεγείρατε τὰς μαχητὰς· ἢ ἀφορίσατε εἰς πόλεμον [arouse the warriors, or set them apart for war]: rouse the fighters and set them apart for war. Here too you may not badly refer that phrase which we gave above, קדשו יום, so that the sense is "prepare a fast" or "the day of a fast." For not every fast pleases God. Jerome on Joel 1: If every fast pleased God, he would never have said "sanctify a fast," and "I have not chosen such a fast." Therefore he says "sanctify a fast." The Manichaean and many heretics fast, especially the Encratites. But this fasting is worse than satiety and drunkenness.

units.la: Atque hae sunt potissimae vocis קדש significationes, reliquas in Clavi scriptvrae invenies. Ubi illud moneo tironem, octavam illam significationem, quam antiphrasticam vocat, plane idoneo exemplo destitui. Confer omnia loca vel cum Junii versione, & videbis quam longe aberraverit Illyricus. In Graecis concordantiis Kircheri, ultimum vocis קדש interpretamentum est μιαίνω, citaturque locus ex 2. Chr. 36. 14. Sed crassus error est, namque illud ἐμίανεν respondet Ebraeo ויטמאו.
units.tr: These are the chief meanings of the word קדש, and you will find the rest in the Clavis Scripturae. Here I warn the beginner that the eighth meaning, which he calls antiphrastic, is wholly without a suitable example. Compare all the passages either with Junius's version, and you will see how far Illyricus has strayed. In Kircher's Greek concordances the last rendering of the word קדש is μιαίνω [miainō], "to defile," and the passage cited is 2 Chron. 36:14. But this is a gross error, for that ἐμίανεν [emianen] corresponds to the Hebrew ויטמאו.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV.

units.la: Verf. 12. Quomodo cecidisti de coelo, Lucifer, fili aurorae] Vox lucifer in Bibliis vulgatis, si bene calculum posuit author concordantiarum, quinquies occurrit I. Jobi xi. 17. orieris ut lucifer, ubi in Ebraeo, בבקר תהיה eris ut mane, hoc est, splendebis ut tempus matutinum, ut aurora, ut lux matutina II. Job 38. 32 an produ飞 Luciferum in tempore suo? Ubi in Ebr. ההוציא מזרות בעתו ubi Pagn. Arias signa caelestia id est signa Zodiaci. Alii planetas vertunt quasi esset מזלות quam vocem alii à נזל influere, alii ab אזל ire, errare deflectunt. Aben-Ezra, כוכבים הם ויש אומרים id est, sunt stellae, & sunt qui dicunt Reschefse loco ל. R. Levi, est figura una ex figuris meridionalibus, quam puto in patria Jobi non apparuisse nisi brevissimo tempore. Quem in parte secutus Junius reddidit, remotiora signa id est, inquit in scholio, meridiana, à conspectu nostro magis remota. credo eo respexisse, quod נוך sit separare, dividere. Quod autem sequitur כעיו cum affixo singulari videtur quosdam induxisse ut de una stella hic sermonem Jobo fuisse crediderint. Quasi novum esset aut integrum sidus id est, figuram & multis stellis compositam singulari numero efferri: aut, si placet plures stellas vel etiam sidera hic denotari, singularia affixa distribui; quomodo hic Junius, [quodque] tempore suo, quod Rabbini dicerent מזרות כמו מזלות או יהיה שם כוכב Michlal Jophi, id est, Mazzaroth quasi Mazzaloth, aut erit nomen stellae, quae ut omnium fere, ex Kimchio transcripsit. Vide hic Radices ejus in themate מזר / Sed dato unam stellam hic denotari, unde constabit Luciferum intelligi? III. Ps. 110. Ante Luciferum genui te, ubi nihil tale in Ebraeo. Vide Antib. nostri partem primam, pag. 548. IV. 2. Pet. 1. 19. habemus firmiorem illum Propheticum sermonem, quem benefacitis quod attenditis veluti lucernam splendentem in obscuro loco εως ου ημερα διαυγασῃ, και φωσφορος ανατειλῃ εν ταις καρδιαις υμων, i. donec dies illucescat & Lucifer exoriatur in cordibus vestris. Ubi alii intelligunt clariorem Evangelii doctrinam obscuriori illi notitiae, quae sub Legis umbris fuit, oppositam: Alii plenissimam illam cognitionem, qua in futura vita collustrabimur, oppositam omni illi notitiae, quam hic ex verbo Dei haurimus. Confer 1. Cor. XIII. 8. 10. 12. Locus quintus ex hoc ipso capite XIV. Jesaiae affertur. De quo antequam verba faciam monebo lectorem pluribus in locis Luciferum vel exhiberi, vel circum scribi. Ecce enim Apoc. II. 28. ὁ δώσω αὐτῷ τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωινόν, & dabo illi stellam matutinam, id est lucem gloriae & summi honoris, lucem felicitatis & perfectae cognitionis Dei, in magno illo die, de quo ex multorum sententia 2. Petri 1. 19. Rursus Apoc. XXII. 16. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς καὶ πρωινός. Ego sum stella illa splendida & matutina. Vides ergo stellam seu Luciferum in S. literis usurpari primo pro illa stella, quam cum solem antegreditur ἑωσφόρον, φωσφόρον, Luciferum, Venerem: Cum vero subsequitur, Hesperum, Vesperum & Vesperuginem appellaret. Sunt ex Ebraeis qui eam Prov. 4. 18. נגה appellari putant, à splendore, quo minores stellas antecellit. Sola enim inter eas umbram facere dicitur radiis suis. Et certe Rabbini stellam Veneris נגה vocant. Gorionides hist. Jud. I. 2. היכל לוציפר הוא היכל כוכב נוגה templum Luciferi, hoc est templum stellae Veneris. Sed & Chald. Jes. 14. 12. ככוכב נגהא Secundo, pro pleniore luce & cognitione Dei & rerum divinarum. ubi Metonymia & Metaphora concurrunt. Tertio, ita extenditur ea metaphora, ut etiam felicitatem includat. Ut enim per tenebras, calamitates, ita per lucem felicitas & res secundae in scriptura intelliguntur. IV. Christus voca-
units.tr: Verse 12. "How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, son of the dawn." The word lucifer occurs five times in the Vulgate Bible, if the author of the concordances has counted correctly: Job 11:17, you shall rise like the lucifer, where the Hebrew is בבקר תהיה, you shall be as the morning, that is, you shall shine like the morning time, like the dawn, like the morning light. Job 38:32, Can you bring out Lucifer in his season? In the Hebrew, הֲתוֹצִיא מַזָּרוֹת בְּעִתּוֹ. Pagninus and Arias render the heavenly signs, that is, the signs of the zodiac. Others render planets, as if the word were מזלות, which some derive from נזל, to flow, others from אזל, to go, to wander. Aben Ezra: "they are stars; and some say that the Resh is put in place of the Lamed." R. Levi: it is one figure of the southern constellations, which I think did not appear in Job's country except for a very short time. Junius, following him in part, rendered it the more remote signs, that is, as he says in his scholium, the southern ones, more remote from our view. I believe he had in mind that נוך means to separate, divide. But the following כעיו with a singular suffix seems to have led some to believe that a single star is being spoken of here by Job. As if it were something new, or a whole constellation, that is, a figure composed of many stars, were expressed in the singular; or, if you prefer, that several stars, or even constellations, are meant here, and the singular suffixes are distributed among them; so Junius here, and in his season. The rabbis said that מזרות is like מזלות, or "there shall be a star there, Michlal Jophi," that is, Mazzaroth as if Mazzaloth, or it is the name of a star, which he copied from Kimchi, as almost all do. See here his roots under the theme מזר. But granting that one star is meant here, how will it be clear that Lucifer is understood? III. Ps. 110:3: "Before Lucifer I begat you," where there is nothing like this in the Hebrew. See the first part of our Antibarbarus, p. 548. IV. 2 Pet. 1:19: we have that firmer prophetic word, which you do well to heed as a lamp shining in a dark place, ἕως οὗ ἡμέρα διαυγάσῃ καὶ φωσφόρος ἀνατείλῃ ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν [until the day dawn and the morning star arise in your hearts], that is, until day dawns and Lucifer rises in your hearts. Here some understand the clearer doctrine of the Gospel as opposed to that more obscure knowledge which existed under the shadows of the Law; others understand that most full knowledge, by which we shall be enlightened in the future life, as opposed to all that knowledge which we draw here from the Word of God. Compare 1 Cor. 13:8, 10, 12. The fifth passage is taken from this same chapter XIV of Isaiah. Before I speak of it I warn the reader that in many places Lucifer is either presented or circumscribed. For see Rev. 2:28, ὁ δώσω αὐτῷ τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωινόν [and I will give him the morning star], that is, the light of glory and of highest honour, the light of happiness and of perfect knowledge of God, in that great day, of which according to the opinion of many 2 Pet. 1:19 speaks. Again, Rev. 22:16: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς καὶ πρωινός [I am the bright and morning star]. You see, then, that a star or Lucifer is used in Scripture, first, of that star which goes before the sun, called ἑωσφόρος, φωσφόρος [eōsphoros, phōsphoros], Lucifer, Venus; but when it follows, they call it Hesperus, Vesper and Vesperugo. Some Hebrews think it is called נגה in Prov. 4:18, from its brightness, by which it surpasses the lesser stars; for it alone is said to cast a shadow with its rays among them. And certainly the rabbis call the star of Venus נגה. Gorionides, Hist. Jud. I, 2: היכל לוציפר הוא היכל כוכב נוגה, the temple of Lucifer, that is, the temple of the star Venus. And also the Chaldee on Isa. 14:12, ככוכב נגהא. Second, for the fuller light and knowledge of God and of divine things, where metonymy and metaphor coincide. Third, the metaphor is extended so as to include also happiness. For as by darkness calamities are understood, so by light happiness and prosperity are understood in Scripture. IV. Christ is called...

units.la: * Alii φωσ- φόρος.
units.tr: * Others have *phosphoros* [φωσφόρος].

units.la: * Plin. 2. 8. Ubi etiam dicit eam magnitudine excedere cuncta astra sidera esse. vocatur Lucifer, quia ipse lucem sapientiæ, salutis & justitiæ &c. solem paterni favoris nobis reduxerit. Et ut ad hunc Jesaiæ locum proprius accedamus, Rex Nebucadnezar comparatur Lucifero propter claritatem & sublimitatem inquit Olcastro. Erat enim famâ præclarus & ad maximam dignitatem elevatus inter orientales. Dicit ergo illi, O Nebucadnezar qui in terris claritate & sublimitate eras sicut stella præclara in cœlo, quæ alta & lucida est &c. Forerius, Ipsum Regem præcipuam inter stellas vocat, quod in se oculos omnium splendore & majestate sua converteret. In eandem sententiam vide & Hectorem Pintum Lusitanum. Lubet & Hieronymum audire? Dicitur ei (Regi) quod fieri debeat & lugere, qui quondam sic fuerit gloriosus, ut fulgori Luciferi comparatus sit. Sicut, inquit, Lucifer discutiens tenebras. ardens & rutilus illucescit, sic & tuus progressus in populos & publicum claro sideri similis videbatur. Chald.
units.tr: * Pliny, 2.8, where he also says that it surpasses all the stars in size. It is called Lucifer because it has brought back to us the light of wisdom, salvation and justice, and the sun of the Father's favour. To come closer to this passage of Isaiah: King Nebuchadnezzar, says Olcastro, is compared to Lucifer on account of his brightness and loftiness, for he was famous and raised to the highest dignity among the people of the East. So the prophet says to him: "O Nebuchadnezzar, who on earth were in brightness and loftiness like a bright star in heaven, which is high and shining." Forerius says that the king himself is called the outstanding star, because by his splendour and majesty he turned the eyes of all upon himself. To the same effect see also Hector Pinto the Portuguese. Shall we also hear Jerome? It is said to him (the king) that he should be made to mourn, he who once was so glorious that he was compared to the brilliance of Lucifer. "Just as Lucifer, he says, scattering the darkness, rises up burning and ruddy, so your progress among the peoples and your public career seemed like a bright star." The Chaldee paraphrast (gives the same sense).

units.la: Quomodo lapsus es ex alto qui fuisti splendidus in medio filiorum hominum ככוכב נגהא בין כוכביא sicut stella Veneris inter stellas. R. Salomo, היללי id est, Helel est stella Veneris, quæ lucere facit lucem, ὡς ἑσπερος φωσφορος. Quibus verbis simul ostendit thema vocis הילל non esse ילל sequuti Hieron. putabat cum diceret in Hebræo ad verbum legi ulula siti aurora, sed הלל / Kimchi, Quomodo cecidisti? Nam fuisti in vita tua tanquam stella cæli, & non ut quælibet stella, sed ut stella quæ valde splendere facit lucem suam. Et ipsa est כוכב השחר id est, ἑωσφορος stella matutina. Et vocatur הילל ex illa significatione quam habet Job. 29. 3. בהלו נרו על ראשי Cum splendere faceret lucernam suam super caput meum.
units.tr: How have you fallen from heaven, you who were splendid among the sons of men [כּוֹכַב נֹגַהּ בֵּין כּוֹכָבִים] like the star of Venus among the stars. Rabbi Solomon: helel [הֵילֵל], that is, Helel, is the star of Venus, which makes light shine, [as the evening star, the light-bringer, ὡς ἕσπερος φωσφόρος]. By these words he shows at the same time that the root of the word helel is not yalal, as Jerome followed when he said that in Hebrew the word is read literally as "howl, thirsty dawn," but halal. Kimchi: "How have you fallen?" For in your life you were like a star of heaven, and not like any star, but like a star that makes its light shine very brightly. And it is the morning star [כּוֹכַב הַשַּׁחַר], that is, the heosphoros, the morning-bringing star. And it is called helel from that meaning which it has in Job 29:3: "When he made his lamp shine over my head." [בִּהִלּוֹ נֵרוֹ עַל רֹאשִׁי]

units.la: Hic vero lubet quærere, quomodo vox illa εὐφημος & augusta ad Principem dæmonorum translata sit. Non producamur ex sece aut trivio hominem. Augustinus tract. 3. in Johannem, Audi vocem Patris ad filium, Ante luciferum genui te (de hoc loco diximus ad Ps. cx.) Qui ante Luciferum genitus est, omnes ipse illuminat. Dictus enim quidam est Lucifer qui cecidit. Erat enim Angelus & factus est diabolus, & dixit de illo Scriptura, Lucifer, qui mane oriebatur cecidit. Unde Lucifer, quia illuminatus lucebat. Unde autem tenebrosus factus; quia in veritate non stetit. Ubi doctissimus Pater simul ostendit augustum & splendidum hoc nomen principi tenebrarum hæsisse ex, prima illa illustri & splendida conditione, qua excidit. Dominus Beza ad Matth. cap. 25. 41. de hac Diaboli appellatione ita loquitur, Luciferi vero nomen cum ex salsissima & ineptissima Jesaiæ loci ex cap. 14. 12. interpretatione sit ortum, mirari satis non possum à nonnullis crassum illud delirium intelligentibus retineri. Rem acu tetigit Beza. Appellatio illa huic loco prave intellecto natales suos debet. Alii universam hanc parabolam literali expositione Regi Babel applicuere, allegorica Diabolo. Alii qui in controversiis de angelis ex hoc textu argumenta de promsere, statuerunt Prophetam in quibusdam saltem versibus prima intentione agere de Diabolo sub * figura Regis Babel, quomodo etiam Bellarminus loquitur ubi de descensu Christi ad inferos disputat. Carthus. in Lyræ vestigia pedes ponens putat illa, Quomodo cecidisti de cælo & quæ continuis aliquot versibus sequuntur proprie de diabolo exponenda esse. Verba ejus in Comm. ad hunc locum ista sunt, Doctores Catholici hæc communiter exponunt de Principe dæmonum. Advertendum ergo quod septem regularum ad intelligentiam sacræ Scripturæ necessariarum una hæc est, quod scriptura interdum transit à Diabolo ad membra ejus & è contrario. Ascribendo vid. ea quæ sunt dæmonis, hominibus reprobis & vice versa. Dicunt ergo Doctores quod hoc loco ex occasione descriptionis ruinæ Regis Babel, qui erat membrum Diaboli, transit Propheta ad describendum lapsum Diaboli, sicut Ezechiel sub persona Regis Tyri describit peccatum Diaboli. Et paulo post. Denique licet omnia quæ hic dicuntur de Lucifero exponi possint tam de Diabolo quam de Rege Babylonis, sicut patebit, quædam tamen proprie conveniunt regi Babel, & non diabolo; quædam etiam proprie conveniunt diabolo, non regi Babel. Qua propter verius puto, Prophetam loqui mixtim de Rege Babel & dæmone. Hæc Charthus. Expectabam illum ostensurum, quædam in hac parabola non posse de Rege Babel exponi, quale illud videtur nonnullis, quomodo cecidisti de cælo. Sed bene habet quod ipse agnoscat omnia quæ hic dicuntur, tam de Rege Babel, quam de Diabolo accipi posse: quod item ipse totum illum contextum egregie de Rege Babel exponat. Sed proprie convenit Diabolo inquit. Hoc ergo vult, non posse ea de Rege explicari nisi admissis tropis. Atqui omnis fere sermo hujusmodi מָשָׁל id est, parabolarum
units.tr: Here one may well ask how that word, which is honourable and august, came to be applied to the prince of demons. Let us not be led astray by the crossroads of men's opinions. Augustine, tractate 3 on John: "Hear the Father's voice to the Son: 'Before the morning star I begot you'" (on this passage we spoke at Psalm 110). "He who was begotten before the morning star illuminates all things. For one star is called Lucifer, the one who fell. He was an angel and became the devil, and of him Scripture says: 'Lucifer, who rose in the morning, has fallen.' He was called Lucifer because he shone in his illumination; but how did he become dark? Because he did not stand in the truth." Here the learned Father shows at the same time that this august and splendid name clung to the prince of darkness from that first illustrious and splendid state from which he fell. Lord Beza, on Matthew 25:41, speaks thus about this name of the devil: "I cannot sufficiently wonder that the name Lucifer, which arose from the most absurd and inept interpretation of the passage of Isaiah 14:12, is still retained by some, who understand that crude delirium." Beza touched the matter exactly: that name owes its origin to this passage wrongly understood. Others have applied this whole parable literally to the king of Babylon and allegorically to the devil. Others, who have drawn arguments about angels from this text, have held that the prophet, in at least some verses, is primarily speaking of the devil under the *figure* of the king of Babylon, as Bellarmine also says when he discusses Christ's descent to hell. The Carthusian, following in the footsteps of Lyra, thinks that the words "How have you fallen from heaven" and those that follow for several verses are to be explained properly of the devil. His words in his commentary on this passage are these: "Catholic teachers commonly expound these things of the prince of demons. It must therefore be noted that one of the seven necessary rules for understanding Holy Scripture is this: that Scripture sometimes passes from the devil to his members and the reverse, attributing what belongs to the demon to reprobate men and vice versa. The teachers say, therefore, that in this passage, on the occasion of describing the ruin of the king of Babylon, who was a member of the devil, the prophet passes to describe the fall of the devil, just as Ezekiel, under the person of the king of Tyre, describes the sin of the devil." And a little later: "Finally, although all that is said here about Lucifer can be explained both of the devil and of the king of Babylon, as will become clear, some things nevertheless apply properly to the king of Babylon and not to the devil, and some apply properly to the devil and not to the king of Babylon. For this reason I think it more true that the prophet speaks in a mixed way of the king of Babylon and of a demon." So far the Carthusian. I was expecting him to show that some things in this parable cannot be explained of the king of Babylon, as some think of "how have you fallen from heaven." But he rightly admits that everything said here can be taken both of the king of Babylon and of the devil, and he also explains the whole context excellently of the king of Babylon. Yet, he says, it applies properly to the devil. So his meaning is that these things cannot be explained of the king unless tropes are admitted. Yet nearly every such speech, a *mashal* [מָשָׁל], that is, a parable...

units.la: * Alii dicunt sub persona Augusti de civ. Dei xi. 15. sub figura ea persona Principis Babylonialarum tropis & figuris vernare solet & si de diabolo exposueris, non potes tropicas interpretationes excludere. Aut hoc vult, non posse proprie id est, commode, apte, & fine violentia de Rege exponi. Sed videamus tuam ipsius interpretationem. Secundo, ais, exponenda hæc sunt de Regi Babel. Quomodo cecidisti de cœlo Lucifer id est, quomodo tu Rex Babel qui præ cæteris regibus terræ gloria & potestate pollebas, ita ut Lucifero comparareris corruisti de sublimi throno imperii tui? Qui mane oriebaris, id est, statim in tuo progresiu præ cæteris eminebas. Corruisti in terram inoriendo. Qui vulnerasti gentes, quas tuo subjugasti Dominio. Qui dicebas in corde tuo, ascendam in cœlum, supra astra cœli &c. id est, in tantum magnificatus sum, omnibus mundi regnis mihi subjectis, ut cœlum mihi restet & sidera. Sedebo in monte testamenti id est, in templo Jerusalem fundato in monte Sion &c. Quid hic violenti? Quid hic coacti? Annon magis torquebas te, cum illa, in cœlum conscendam, super astra Dei exaltabo solium meum. Sedebo in monte testamenti in laterib. Aquilonis. Ascendam supra altitudines nubium &c. de Diabolo exponeres. Postquam enim per gentes in verbis istis qui vulnerabas gentes, intellexisses angelos qui cum eo ceciderc, ais ex verbis sequentibus; Ascendam in cœlum ortam esse inter DD. controversiam de ordine Luciferi & sociorum ejus. Namque horum verborum occasione, inquis, Damascenus asserit, Luciferum & omnes qui secum prolapsi sunt fuisse de infimo choro & creatos in aere ac præfuisse orbi terrestri. Si enim (ut ait Damascenus) creatus fuisset Lucifer in cœlo Empyreo & cæteris angelis sublimior, non dixisset, in cœlum conscendam, super astra &c. Sed quia Ecclesia Latinorum cum S. Gregorio Papa tenet, quod Lucifer erat summus Angelorum, Propterea quod admirabilis lua pulchritudo erat sibi superbiendi occasio: quod non fuisset, nisi cæteris omnibus extitisset perfectior, & quia patetex eo, tu Cherub extentus &c. quod fuerit in cœlo Empyreo &c. sensus erit, in cœlum conscendam, id est, tantæ excellentiæ sum, ut non solum inferioribus præsidere, sed in cœlestibus quoque dominari dignus existam vel in cœlum id est summitatem cœli, usque ad tronum majestatis super astra cœli idest, angelos exaltabo solium meum id est, principatus mei dominium & vitutem. Atqui jam erat Princeps angelorum. Respondet Carthusianus. Voluit angelis praesse non solum secundum quod Deus instituit, qui eum omnibus praetulit, scilicet ut eis praesset sub Deo, ita quod ipse Deo subesset & caeteris ad Dei honorem praesset; sed voluit habere separatum ac proprium principatum ita quod sibi subessent tanquam supremo cuidam, ad ipsum in omnibus agendis tanquam ad regulam recurrendo. Tale ergo erat peccatum Luciferi, ac si princeps militiae vellet praesse militibus non sub rege, sed tanquam per se dominus militum. Sedebo id est, regnabo in monte testamenti id est, palatio caeli, caelo empyreo, ex quo dispositiones omnium rerum procedant in lateribus aquilonis id est, in turmis seu partibus angelorum mihi adhaerentium, Aut per montem Test. intelligi potest Ecclesia, per latera vero Aquilonis, corda hominum frigida. Ascendam super altitudinem nubium id est, angelorum per nubes enim angeli designantur secundum Dionysium 15. cap. Hierarch. Quid tibi videtur lector, An haec interpretatio propria est? Quam multa hic coacta, violenta, absurda? At si de Rege Babel interpreteris, nihil coactum est, ubi illam phrasin, Cadere de caelo, fueris commode interpretatus, caetera egregie fluunt omnia. Illam vero doctissimi Interpretes Pontificii bene explicuere. Ad caelum usque exaltata dicitur Capernaum, Matth. xi. 23. id est, Provecta ad supremum felicitatis & gloriae apicem. Qui vero ab ejusmodi gloria & dignitate decidunt & fortunam splendidam cum adversa repente commutant, ex astris caeloque decidere & ad inferos trahi dicuntur. Ita quod hic dicitur vers. 15. אל שאול תורד ad sepulcrum vel alii ad infernum detraheris, dicto Matthaei loco dicitur, εως ἅδη καταβιβασθήσῃ, usque ad inferos deprimeris. Cicero lib. 2. Epist. ad Atticum de Pompejo, quia deciderat ex astris, lapsus potius quam progressus videbatur. Quamvis alii malint locutionem istam conferre cum illo Poetae, Tertius e caelo cecidit Cato. Idem Cicero libro eodem, Bibulus in caelo est. Et alibi ad eundem. Si vero quae de me pacta sunt, ea non servantur, in caelo sunt. Theocritus, ἐς ᾅεγνον ὑμὶν ἀλεύμαι, in caelum vobis saliam. Pro monte testamenti Ebraeus habet כהר מועד Ariasin monte conventus. Pagn. in monte Ecclesiae, Vatab. in m. congregationis. מועד nec διαθήκῃ, nec συνθήκῃ significat. Intelligit autem montem Sion in quo templum erat. Quod vero postea memorat latera aquilo-
units.tr: * Others say that under the person of Augustine (*City of God* 11.15) ... under the figure of that person, the prince of Babylon, usually flourishes with tropes and figures; and if you explain it of the devil, you cannot exclude tropical interpretations. Or he means that it cannot be explained properly, that is, suitably, aptly and without violence, of the king. But let us look at your own interpretation. Second, you say, these things are to be explained of the king of Babylon: "How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer," that is, how have you, king of Babylon, who among the other kings of the earth excelled in glory and power, so that you were compared to Lucifer, fallen from the high throne of your empire? "Who rose in the morning," that is, immediately in your progress you stood out above the others. You fell to the ground by dying. "Who wounded the nations," which you subjected to your dominion. "Who said in your heart, I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven," etc., that is, I am so greatly magnified, with all the kingdoms of the world subject to me, that heaven and the stars remain for me. "I will sit on the mount of the covenant," that is, in the temple of Jerusalem founded on Mount Zion. What is forced here? What is coerced here? Did you not rather torment yourself, when you would explain those words, "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God. I will sit on the mount of the covenant in the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds," etc. of the devil? For after understanding by the word nations in the words "who wounded the nations" the angels who fell with him, you say from the following words, "I will ascend into heaven," that there arose among the doctors a controversy about the order of Lucifer and his companions. For on the occasion of these words, you say, Damascene asserts that Lucifer and all who fell with him were from the lowest choir and were created in the air, and presided over the terrestrial world. For if (as Damascene says) Lucifer had been created in the Empyrean heaven and higher than the other angels, he would not have said, "I will ascend into heaven, above the stars," etc. But since the Latin Church with Pope Gregory holds that Lucifer was the highest of the angels, because his admirable beauty was an occasion for pride, which would not have been the case had he not been more perfect than all the others, and since it is clear from "you, anointed cherub," that he was in the Empyrean heaven, the sense will be: "I will ascend into heaven," that is, I am of such excellence that I am worthy not only to preside over lower beings but also to rule over heavenly ones; or "into heaven," that is, to the summit of heaven, "up to the throne of majesty above the stars of heaven," that is, I will exalt angels; "I will exalt my throne," that is, the dominion and *virtue* of my principality. But he was already the prince of the angels. The Carthusian replies: he wished to rule over the angels not only in the way God had appointed, who set him above all, namely that he should preside over them under God, so that he himself was subject to God and presided over the others for God's honour; but he wished to have a separate and proper principality, so that they would be subject to him as to a supreme one, turning to him in all his actions as to a rule. Such, then, was the sin of Lucifer: as if the commander of an army wished to rule the soldiers not under the king but as lord of the soldiers in his own right. "I will sit," that is, I will reign "on the mount of the covenant," that is, the palace of heaven, the Empyrean heaven, from which the arrangements of all things proceed, "in the sides of the north," that is, in the bands or parts of the angels adhering to me. Or by the mount of the covenant the Church may be understood, and by the sides of the north the cold hearts of men. "I will ascend above the height of the clouds," that is, of the angels, for according to Dionysius, *Celestial Hierarchy* ch. 15, angels are designated by clouds. What do you think, reader? Is this interpretation proper? How many things here are forced, violent, absurd? But if you interpret it of the king of Babylon, nothing is forced: where you have suitably interpreted the phrase to fall from heaven, everything else flows out excellently. Indeed the most learned Papist interpreters have explained that phrase well. Capernaum is said to be raised up to heaven (Matt. 11:23), that is, carried up to the highest peak of happiness and glory. But those who fall from such glory and dignity, and suddenly exchange splendid fortune for adversity, are said to fall from the stars and heaven and to be dragged down to the underworld. So what is said here in verse 15, [אֶל שְׁאוֹל תּוֹרַד], "you shall be brought down to the grave" or to hell, in the said passage of Matthew is said "you shall be brought down to hades", [ἕως ᾅδη καταβιβασθήσῃ], that is, you will be thrust down to the underworld. Cicero, book 2 of his letters to Atticus, says of Pompey that, because he had fallen from the stars, he seemed to have slipped rather than advanced. Although others prefer to compare this expression with that line of the poet, "Third, Cato fell from heaven." The same Cicero, in the same book: "Bibulus is in heaven." And elsewhere, to the same: "But if the agreements made about me are not kept, they are in heaven." Theocritus: "I will leap into the sky for you" [ἐς αἰθέρα ὑμῖν ἀλεῦμαι]. For the mount of the covenant the Hebrew has [כְּהַר מוֹעֵד], Arias: the mountain of assembly; Pagninus: the mountain of the Church; Vatablus: the mountain of congregation. [מוֹעֵד] signifies neither diathēkē [διαθήκη] nor synthēkē [συνθήκη]. He means Mount Zion, on which the temple stood. As for the later mention of the sides of the north...

units.la: Erasm. Chil. 1. Cent. v. adag. 100. pag. 110. nis confer Pf. 48. 3. & habebis luculentum super hoc loco commentarium. Namquam & illic mons Sionis, & latera Aquilonis, & urbs magni Regis conjunguntur. Atque ita satis ostensum arbitror nullam esse necessitatem ullam hujus parabolæ particulam de Diabolo interpretandi. Nihil item esse quod non commodissime de Rege Babel possit intelligi, ipsum denique Hieronymum & qui ejus vestigiis institere complures ex ipsis Pontificiis totum hunc contextum de Rege interpretari. Male ergo ex hoc loco probat Thomas parte 1. qu. 63. art. 3. quod Diabolus appetierit esse ut Deus. Male articulo 5. ex hoc loco confutat erroneam eorum sententiam, qui statuunt dæmones in ipso instanti suæ creationis, non quidem per naturam, sed per peccatum propriæ voluntatis malos fuisse. Abutitur & hoc loco Magister, quando Jib. 2. dist 6. probat inter lapsos & ἀγγελους angelos unum fuisse cæteris celsiorem scilicet Luciferum.
units.tr: Erasm. Chil. 1. Cent. v. adag. 100. pag. 110. Compare Ps. 48. 3., and you will have an excellent commentary on this place. For there too the mount of Zion, the sides of the north, and the city of the great King are joined together. I think it has thus been shown well enough that there is no necessity whatever to interpret any part of this parable of the Devil. Nor is there anything here that cannot most suitably be understood of the King of Babylon. Indeed Jerome, and many of the Papists who followed his footsteps, interpret this whole context of the King. Thomas therefore wrongly proves from this place, Part 1, question 63, article 3, that the Devil desired to be like God. In article 5 he wrongly refutes from this place the erroneous opinion of those who hold that demons were evil from the very instant of their creation, not by nature but through the sin of their own will. The Master also misuses this place, when in Book 2, distinction 6, he proves that among the fallen angels there was one higher than the rest, namely Lucifer, ἀγγελους [angels].

units.la: Illi cautius locuti sunt qui Prophetam hac phrasi, quomodo cecidisti de cœlo &c. ad lapsum Diaboli allusisse existimarunt. Inter quos & Vatablus & Pintus. Inde tamen non probes, Diabolum Luciferum appellatum esse, quod enim addit Vatablus, reddi posse Ebræa per ellipsin notæ similitudinis, quomodo cecidisti de cœlo [ut] Lucifer filius auroræ, & non nisi precario obtinebit, & ab omnium Interpretum qua veterum qua recentiorum versione diversum abit. Quod vero Pintus adducit & alterum locum ex Luc. x. vidi Satanam tanquam fulgur de cœlo cadentem, quem vulgo etiam adferre solent lapsum angelorum e sacra pagina probaturi, sciendum est, & illum præter Salvatoris mentem allegari. Forerius ad Jef. 14. 12. Lucifer dicitur הילל ab expansione lucis, matutina stella. Ego si ad mysterium hæc referrem, potius ad casum principis mundi hujus de imperio quod habebat in sæculo, quam de priori illa ruina interpretarer. Et ad hunc forte locum respexit Dominus in Evangelio, Videbam Satanam tanquam fulgur cadentem de cœlo. Loquebatur autem interprete magno illo Basileo de casu diaboli per Christum. Dabat enim suis potestatem calcandi super serpentes scorpiones & omnem virtutem inimici. In quam sententiam videatur & Cranzius oraculo 95. & Jansenius & Beza & Pisc. & alii. Videbam, inquit Salvator, dum vos in meo nomine dæmonia ejiciebatis, videbam inquam vi Deitatis res absentes menti meæ repræsentantis tantis ipsum Satanam cadere, cum impetu deturbari, & potestatem ejus aboleri. Videbam eum cadere sicut fulgur è cælo cadit. Neque enim illud ἐκ τ῾ ἑ ἀρχῆ minus commode ad ἀσεβῶν, quam ad πονηρὸν referri potest. Quod si tamen illud ex cælo cum πονηρῶν malis conjungere, per cælum intelliges securum illud regnum, gloriam & potentiam, quam in hoc mundo habuit, antequam incarnatione filii Dei de sublimi illo throno deturbatus est. Male ergo & hunc locum allegavit Lombardus lib. 2. dist. 2. ut probet veram thesin, angelos in cœlo Empyreo creatos esse. Claudam ubi illud monuero, Lovanienses in versione Belgica vocem Lucifer retinuisse. Hoe zijn van den Hemel gevallen Lucifer / die ghy smorghens bzoegh op-gincht?
units.tr: Those who suspected that the Prophet alluded to the fall of the Devil with this phrase, "how you have fallen from heaven," etc., spoke more cautiously. Among them are both Vatablus and Pintus. Yet you should not infer from this that the Devil was called Lucifer. For what Vatablus adds, that the Hebrew can be rendered by an ellipsis of the particle of comparison, "how you have fallen from heaven [as] Lucifer, son of the dawn," will hold only by special pleading, and it departs from the version of all the Interpreters, both ancient and recent. As for what Pintus adduces also from Luke 10, I saw Satan as lightning falling from heaven, which people commonly also bring forward to prove the fall of the angels from holy Scripture, it must be noted that this passage too is cited against the mind of the Saviour. Forerius, on Isaiah 14:12, says that Lucifer is called heylel [הילל] from the spreading of light, the morning star. If I were referring these words to the mystery, I would interpret them as referring rather to the downfall of the prince of this world from the power he had in the age, than to that earlier ruin. Perhaps the Lord in the Gospel also looked to this place when he said, I was seeing Satan as lightning falling from heaven. That great Basil, moreover, was speaking of the fall of the devil through Christ. For he gave his followers power to tread upon serpents, scorpions and all the power of the enemy. Cranzius, in oracle 95, and Jansenius, Beza, Piscator and others seem to agree with this view. "I was seeing," says the Saviour, "while you were casting out demons in my name; I was seeing, I say, by the power of the Godhead representing to my mind things absent, that Satan himself was falling, being thrown down with force, and his power being abolished. I was seeing him fall as lightning falls from heaven." For the phrase from the beginning [ἐξ ἀρχῆς] can be referred to the ungodly [ἀσεβῶν] no less aptly than to the evil one [πονηρὸν]. But if you join the words "from heaven" with the evil ones [πονηρῶν], you will understand by "heaven" that secure kingdom, glory and power which he had in this world before he was cast down from that lofty throne by the incarnation of the Son of God. Therefore Lombard also wrongly cited this place in Book 2, distinction 2, to prove the true thesis that the angels were created in the Empyrean heaven. I will end where I began this note: the Louvain translators, in their Belgic version, retained the word Lucifer: "How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, son of the morning, you who rose up in the morning?"

units.la: Verf. 21. Propter iniquitatem patrum ipsorum] Lxx. ἁμαρτίας πατρὸς αὐτῶν. Vide quæ de Patre Diaboli ad Joh. viii. notavimus.
units.tr: Verse 21. For the iniquity of their fathers: LXX, the sin of their father. See what I noted on John 8 about the Father of the Devil.

units.la: Verf. 26. Hoc consilium quod cogitavi super omnem terram] Hieron. tradit hæc verba multos in eam traxisse sententiam, Prophetam hic de universi orbis interitu vaticinari, cujus typus fuerit eversio & παντολσθεία Regni Assyrii. Hi ignorarunt הארץ sæpe de una regione sino & agro dici, ac proinde pro locorum circumstantia tam reddi posse omnem agrum, vel omnem regionem, quam, omnem terram.
units.tr: Verse 26. This is the counsel that I have purposed upon the whole earth: Jerome reports that many have been drawn into the view that the Prophet here prophesies the destruction of the whole world, of which the overthrow and total destruction [πανωλεθρία] of the kingdom of Assyria was a type. These men did not know that הארץ [the land] is often used of one region, country or field, and that therefore, according to the circumstances of the place, it can be rendered "every field" or "every region" as well as "every land."

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Verf. 1. Emitte agnum Domine, Dominatorem terræ] Lxx. ἀποστείλατε ἄμνον ἡγεμόνα τῆς γῆς. Magnus Hieron. præceptorum suorum vestigiis insistens versionem istam sic enarrat, O Moab in quam desævituus est leo: & de qua ne reliquiæ quidem salvari poterunt, habeto solatium hoc, egredietur de te agnus immaculatus, qui tollat peccata mundi; qui dominetur in orbe terrarum. Hunc secuti sunt Lyra, Thomas & alii. Quin & in officio adventus hic versus de Christo exponitur. Per petram deserti alii ipsam Ruth, alii solum ejus natale intelligunt. Vide Hieron. Carthusianum &c. Hector Pintus locum ita ἐκ ἀρχῆς, Ne perdas Domine omnes Moabitas, ex quorum progenie nasciturus est Christus. Emitte jam eum, qui innocentissimus agnus pronobis immolatus hominum facinora pretiosissimo sanguine deleat, qui est Dominator terræ. At quid opus erat hoc scopo pro Moabitis intercedere, cum Ruth ante tot jam secula è vivis excesisset & in familiam tribus Judæ transiisset. Dicam quod sensio. Locus iste plane alieno sensu de Christo exponitur. Quæ assertio ut Catholicis minus audax videatur, firmatum eam porro ibo authoritate doctissimorum Interpretum. Et quidem primo hic occurrunt Pagninus & Brixianus, quorum ille verba Ebraea שלחו כר משל ארץ sic vertit, mittite agnum dominatoris terræ. Hic vero, Emittite agnum dominatori terræ. Explicat vero cum R. Joseph & Kimchio & R. Salomone, Mittite vos Moabitæ Regi Ezechiæ qui ex jure & authoritate Dei Dom. terræ vestræ est, agnum, id est agnos, numerum agnorum vobis imperatum. Moabitæ enim primo tributum pensitarunt Davidi & Salomoni, postea, lacerato & scisso regno cessit illud Regibus Israel, Narrant enim sacri annales 2. Reg. 3. 4. Mefchah regem Moabitarum pependisse Regi Israel quotannis centena millia agnorum & centena millia arietum lanatorum. Postquam vero vastatum est regnum Israel, inquit Kimchi in Scholiis היה לכם לשלוח לציון אל מלך יהודה debuissetis illa mittere Tzyonem ad Regem Judæ, Nec aliter sensisse Kimchium in libro Radicum videbit quisquis vel obiter inspexerit. Ut mirer quid induxerit Pintum scribere, Kimchium hunc quoque locum de Messia interpretari. Nam quod de Jonathane Chaldæo Paraphraste præmisit, aliquam speciem habet. Sed speciem tantum. Fefellit enim vox משיחא / quæ illic adhibetur. Cum tamen per משיחא & משיח non semper Messias sic dictus intelligatur. Chaldæa, si quis ea requirat hæc sunt יהון מסקי מפיז למשיחא דישראל דיתקוף על דהוו כמדברא טור כנשתא דציון / deferent tributa uncto Israelis, qui fortis erit super eos qui erant in deserto, ad montem coetus Sion.
units.tr: Verse 1. Send the lamb, O Lord, the Ruler of the land: LXX, Send the lamb, the ruler of the land. The great Jerome, following the footsteps of his own precepts, explains this version thus: "O Moab, against whom the lion is fierce, and from whom not even the remnants will be saved, take this comfort: a spotless lamb will come forth from you, who will take away the sins of the world, who will rule over the whole earth." Lyra, Thomas and others followed him. Indeed in the Advent office this verse is also expounded of Christ. Some understand "the rock of the wilderness" to mean Ruth herself, others her native land alone. See Jerome, the Carthusian, etc. Hector Pintus renders the place thus, from the beginning: "Do not destroy, O Lord, all the Moabites, from whose stock Christ is to be born. Send now him who, as the most innocent lamb sacrificed for us, may wipe out the crimes of men with his most precious blood, who is the Ruler of the land." But why was there any need to intercede for the Moabites for this purpose, since Ruth had already departed from the living so many ages before and had passed into the family of the tribe of Judah? I will say what I think. This place is expounded of Christ in a wholly alien sense. Lest this assertion seem too bold to Catholics, I will support it further with the authority of the most learned Interpreters. And first, here occur Pagninus and Brixianus, of whom the former renders the Hebrew words שלחו כר משל ארץ [send the lamb of the ruler of the land] thus, send the lamb of the ruler of the land. The latter, however, renders, Send to the ruler of the land the lamb. He explains it together with R. Joseph, Kimchi and R. Solomon: "Send, you Moabites, to King Hezekiah, who by the right and authority of God is the ruler of your land, a lamb, that is, lambs, the number of lambs commanded to you." For the Moabites first paid tribute to David and Solomon, and afterwards, when the kingdom was torn and split, that tribute passed to the kings of Israel. For the sacred annals tell in 2 Kings 3:4 that Mesha, king of the Moabites, paid to the king of Israel every year a hundred thousand lambs and a hundred thousand rams with wool.
