But after the kingdom of Israel was laid waste, says Kimchi in his Scholia, היה לכם לשלוח לציון אל מלך יהודה [you ought to have sent those to Zion, to the king of Judah]. Anyone who looks even briefly into Kimchi's book of Roots will see that he did not think otherwise. I am surprised what led Pintus to write that Kimchi also interprets this place of the Messiah. For what he put forward about the Chaldee paraphrast Jonathan has some appearance. But only an appearance. For he was misled by the word משיחא [mashiha] which is used there. Yet משיחא and משיח do not always mean the Messiah so called. The Chaldee, if anyone wants to look at it, is this: yehon maseqi mippiz lemeshiha dishrael dit-qaf al dehawo kemidbara tur knishta dezion, that is, "They shall bring tribute to the anointed one of Israel, who shall be strong over those who were in the wilderness, to the mount of the assembly of Zion."

units.la: Sed ut demus eum per משיחא Messiam intelligere, nunquam tamen inde Vulgatam interpretationem stabilient, sed hanc potius, quam & Oleastrius allegat & non improbat, Mittite agnum vel agnos scilicet in holocaustum seu oblationem Dominatori terræ id est, Messiæ quem Malachias cap. 3. 1. quoque אריון / Vulg. Dominatorem vocat. Alias erit Moab sicut avis fugiens &c. Forrerius quoque non improbat hanc interpretationem, qua משל per dandi casum redditur, quamvis de Rege Ezechia intelligat & locum ironice exponat, q. d. Vos qui di-vites vites estis arietum & ovium mittite dominatori terrae tributum, videte an placare possitis muneribus regem qui nunc dominatur, regem nostrum Ezechiam; sed sera est poenitentia. Praemisit autem idem aliam Interpretationem & illam quoque ironicam, mittite nunc כר id est, virum fortem, strenuum ducem (גִּבּוֹרִים enim sunt viri fortes & bellicosi duces) qui dominetur terrae id est, terram Israel sibi subjiciat. Mittite eum ad montem Sion, ad urbem Jerusalem. Ut illudat Moabitarum conatibus, quando Ammonitis in auxilium vocatis adversus Regem Josaphat validissimum exercitum parabant. Vatablus per dominatorem terrae Deum Israelis intelligit & cum Ironia quoque locum interpretatur. q. d. Serum est. Frustra Deo oblationes mittetis. Frustra agnos ad templum Jerosolymitanum destinabitis. Haec adduxi, ut ostenderem inter ipsos quoque Pontificios non deesse queis a recepta interpretatione hujus loci recedere non fuerit religio. Junius & Tremellius & Piscator cum Kimchio, R. Joseph & Brixiano faciunt. Deodatus putat, Prophetam hortari Moabitas, ut Deum qui in monte Sion habitabat, Dominum suum agnoscerent. Lutherus, Mittite vos Domini terra agnos, quasi esset סוּשְׂלֵי אֶרֶץ & primores Moabitarum intelligeret. Quae interpretatio a Pisc. aliisque merito rejecta est. Nunc adi allegoricas & mysticas hujus loci interpretationes & melius de iis judicabis.
units.tr: But even if we grant that by mashiha he means the Messiah, they will never establish from this the Vulgate interpretation. Rather they would establish this one, which Oleastrius also cites and does not disapprove: "Send the lamb, or lambs, namely for a holocaust or offering, to the Dominator of the land," that is, to the Messiah, whom Malachi, chapter 3, verse 1, also calls אדון [adon, Lord], which the Vulgate calls Dominator. Otherwise it will be "Moab is like a fleeing bird," etc. Forerius too does not disapprove of this interpretation, in which משל is rendered by the dative case, although he understands it of King Hezekiah and explains the place ironically, as if to say: "You who are rich in rams and sheep, send tribute to the ruler of the land; see whether you can placate by gifts the king who now rules, our king Hezekiah; but repentance is too late." The same author, however, put forward another interpretation, also ironical: "Send now כר [kar], that is, a brave man, a vigorous leader (for גִּבּוֹרִים [gibborim] are brave and warlike men and leaders), who may rule over the land, that is, may subject the land of Israel to himself. Send him to Mount Zion, to the city of Jerusalem." (He says this) so that he may mock the attempts of the Moabites, when they were preparing a very strong army against King Jehoshaphat with the Ammonites called in to help. Vatablus understands by the ruler of the land the God of Israel, and interprets the place with irony too, as if to say: "It is too late. You will send offerings to God in vain. You will send lambs in vain to the temple at Jerusalem." I have adduced these things to show that even among the Papists themselves there have not been lacking those who did not scruple to depart from the accepted interpretation of this place. Junius, Tremellius and Piscator agree with Kimchi, R. Joseph and Brixianus. Diodati thinks the Prophet exhorts the Moabites to acknowledge as their Lord the God who dwelt on Mount Zion. Luther has, "Send to the ruler of the land lambs," as if the text were סוּשְׂלֵי אֶרֶץ [sushle erets], and understood the chief men of the Moabites. This interpretation has rightly been rejected by Piscator and others. Now go to the allegorical and mystical interpretations of this place, and you will judge them better.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Verf. 14. Non remittetur vobis haec iniquitas donec moriamini] In hoc loco fundata est unica Judaeorum tam in vita quam in morte consolatio. Messiam tot jam seculis expectant sed peccatorum remissionem ab eo nullam expectant. Quicquid de illo sibi promittunt, id omne corporale est & hujus vitae terminis circumscriptum. Unde in precibus quas corporis hujus exuvias deposituri, recitant, nullam Messiae mentionem reperias. In libro precum Judaicarum pag. 480. Edit. Venetae extat solennis illa formula sub titulo וְדּוּי שְׁכִיב מֶרַע (id est, confessio decumbentis ex morbo, Genef. 47. ubi in Ebr. est אֲבִיךְ הוֹלֶה Thargum habet אִתְמְרַע & מֶרַע אֲבוּךְ מֶרַע / & מֶרַע morbus) Eaita habet, confiteor ego coram te Domine Deus mi, Deus patrum meorum, Deus spirituum omnis carnis, quod sanitas mea & mors in tua manu sit. Placeat tibi sanare me sanatio- me perfecta, & ascendat memoria mei & precatio mea coram te, ut precatio Ezechiæ cum ægrotaret. Sin vero instet tempus visitationis meæ ut moriendum mihi sit, תהי מיתתי כפרה לכל הפשאתי sit mors mea expiatio pro omnibus peccatis meis & iniquitatibus meis & transgressionib. quas commisi adversus te ex quo in hanc lucem editus sui. Da mihi portionem meam in horto Eden. Fac me dignum (לְחַיִּים) futuro sæculo, quod repositum justis est & monstra mihi viam vitæ &c. Benedictus esto, qui precationem exaudis. Similem locum ex Josippo habet Schikkard. in jure Reg. p. 160. lin. ult. Ecce hac spe sustulti miselli isti homines eo abeunt;
units.tr: Verse 14. This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die] On this passage rests the sole consolation of the Jews, both in life and in death. For many centuries they have awaited the Messiah, yet from him they expect no forgiveness of sins. Whatever they promise themselves from him is wholly bodily and bounded by the limits of this life. Hence in the prayers which they recite when about to lay down the remains of this body you will find no mention of the Messiah at all. In the Jewish prayer-book, p. 480 of the Venetian edition, there stands that solemn formula under the title וִדּוּי שְׂכִיב מֶרַע [vidui sekhiv mera], that is, the confession of one lying sick (cf. Gen. 47, where the Hebrew has "your father is ill" [חוֹלֶה], and the Targum has "your father is sick" [אִתְמְרַע, מֶרַע], with מֶרַע meaning sickness). It runs: "I confess before you, O Lord my God, God of my fathers, God of the spirits of all flesh, that my health and my death are in your hand. May it please you to heal me with a perfect healing, and may my memory and my prayer ascend before you, as the prayer of Hezekiah when he was sick. But if the time of my visitation has come, so that I must die, may my death be an atonement for all my sins, iniquities and transgressions which I have committed against you since I was brought forth into this light. Give me my portion in the garden of Eden. Make me worthy of the life (לְחַיִּים) of the world to come, which is laid up for the righteous, and show me the way of life, etc. Blessed are you, who hear prayer." Schickard, in his Jus Regium p. 160, last line, has a similar passage from Josippon. "Behold, with this hope these poor wretches go off to that place;

units.la: Unde negant redire quemquam.
units.tr: Whence they say no one returns."

units.la: Sed quam infirmo tibicine sustentata sit illa consolatio, nemo potest ignorare qui phrasiologiam Ebraicam vel levissime degustavit. Ebræum עד (cui respondet Græcorum ἕως, Latinorum Donec) sæpe affirmat aut negat quippiam de eo tempore quod terminum istum antecessit, sine ullo respectu ad futurum. Sicuti rursus לא עוד ἕτι ἐπ aut μηκέτι, non amplius, ita aliquando negat de futura, ut non affirmet, antea vel semel vel sæpius accidisse contrarium. ut Jerem. 22 12. Actorum 13. 34. Apocal. 3. 12. Tob. 3. 10. Vide clavem Scripturæ a nobis interpolitam, in Donec, & Amplius. Sic ergo habeto, tiro, Donec in peculiari isto usu fere affirmat aut negat quippiam factum aut futurum eo tempore, quo posset, aut potuisset fieri, aut de quo possset incidere dubitatio, atque ita præsupponit, post illum terminum idem omnino fieri non posse vel potuisse. Non peperit usque ad diem mortis suæ, hoc est, donec mortua est. Negat peperisse eo tempore, quo parere secundum naturæ leges potuisset. At post partum fœminam non posse parere, extra controversiæ aleam ponit. Sensus ergo est, non peperit unquam. Eadem hujus loci ratio est. Non remittetur nobis, neque in hoc seculo, quo solent remitti peccata, neque in futuro, ut pote quo non solent remitti peccata, hoc est, interprete Marco, nunquam non remittetur εἰς αἰῶνα confer 1. Sam. 3. 14. si expiabitur iniquitas familiæ Eli לעולם εἰς αἰῶνα. Chaldæus hoc vidit, locum præsentem in hunc modum אם ישתבק רובא הריין לכון עד די תסאתון סותא תנינא id est, si remittetur vobis hæc iniquitas, donec
units.tr: But how feeble the support on which that consolation rests, no one can fail to see who has tasted even the slightest Hebrew idiom. The Hebrew עד [ad] (to which corresponds the Greek ἕως and the Latin Donec) often affirms or denies something about the time that precedes that limit, without any reference to the future. Just as לא עוד, ἕτι or μηκέτι, "no longer," sometimes denies something of the future without affirming that the opposite happened before, once or several times (as in Jer. 22:12; Acts 13:34; Rev. 3:12; Tob. 3:10). See the key to Scripture I have compiled, under Donec and Amplius. So understand this, young reader: Donec in this particular usage almost always affirms or denies that something was or will be done at the time when it could, or could have, been done, or about which doubt could arise, and so it presupposes that afterwards the same thing cannot, or could not, happen at all. "She did not bear children until the day of her death, that is, until she died." It denies that she bore children at the time when, according to the laws of nature, she could have borne them. But that after childbirth a woman cannot bear again, it places beyond dispute. The sense, therefore, is "she never bore children." The same is the case here: "It shall not be forgiven you," neither in this age, in which sins are usually forgiven, nor in the future, in which sins are not usually forgiven; that is, in the words of Mark, never it shall not be forgiven, εἰς αἰῶνα. Compare 1 Sam. 3:14: "if the iniquity of Eli's house shall be expiated" לְעוֹלָם, εἰς αἰῶνα. The Chaldee saw this, and renders the present passage thus: אִם יִשְׁתָּבֵק רוּבָא הָרֵין לְכוֹן עַד דִּי תְּמוּתוּן מוֹתָא תִּנְיָנָא, that is, if this iniquity shall be forgiven you, until

units.la: moriamini morte secunda, Hinc Johannes in Apoc. habet δεύτερον, ut in Apoc. quoque ad Chaldæam paraphrasin respexerit, quod in Evangelio ab ipso passim facitatum adeo evidenter ostendit magnus Heinsius. Kimchius mortem illam secundam interpretatur מיתת הנפש בעולם הבא id est mortem animæ in futuro seculo. Nunc vide Junii notas & Forerii, qui hoc quoque modo locum exponi posse autumat, Non expiabitur id est perpetuo pœnas luetis. Quæ expositio firmat explicationem Cl. Drusii & aliorum qui illud Matth. 12. Non remittetur nec in hoc nec in futuro seculo, sic interpretati sunt, vehementer punietur & in hoc & in futuro seculo. Hoc est, solent enim non Ebraei tantum sed & aliæ gentes hac antiphrasi pondus addere sententiæ, Non gaudet stulti Pater, id est, vehementer doluit, Homer. Iliad. x. ὣς ἀέγω τὸν ἰδὼν γέλασσεν Αχιλλεὺς id est, valde mœstus fuit. Sic, accipere personam in judicio non est bonum. Atque hæc est vera ἀντίφρασις, quam definit Plutarchus, λέξιν τὸ ἐναντίον ἢ τὸ ἀγχέμαχον σημαίνουσαν, id est, sermonem (sicenim voce λέξις etiam Aristoteles usus est. 3. Rhetoricorum in Principio) contrarium ei quod positum est significans. Dixi in futuro sæculo non remitti peccata. In hac vita locum esse resipiscentiæ & remissioni peccatorum. Hoc putavit Chaldæus doceri loco Jesaiæ 55.6. Quærite Dominum בהמצאו dum invenitur ipse, invocate eum dum propinquus est, quem ita convertit. תבעו רבלתא id est, quærite timorem Domini dum adhuc estis vivi: orate eum, dum adhuc estis superstites.
units.tr: you die the second death. Hence John in the Apocalypse has δεύτερον, and it is clear that in the Apocalypse too he had regard to the Chaldee paraphrase, which the great Heinsius has shown so evidently to be a thing he did all through the Gospel. Kimchi interprets that second death as מִיתַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, the death of the soul in the world to come. Now see the notes of Junius and of Forerius, who holds that the passage may also be explained in this way: "it shall not be expiated," that is, you shall suffer punishment without end. This interpretation confirms the explanation of the distinguished Drusius and others, who take the text of Matt. 12 ("it shall not be forgiven in this age nor in the age to come") to mean: it shall be punished severely both in this age and in the age to come. For not only the Hebrews but other nations too use this antiphrasis to add weight to a statement: "the foolish father does not rejoice," that is, he grieved greatly; Homer, Iliad 10: "thus I speak, seeing him Achilles laughed," that is, he was very sorrowful. Likewise, "to accept a person in judgment is not good." And this is the true antiphrasis, which Plutarch defines as λέξιν τὸ ἐναντίον ἢ τὸ ἀγχέμαχον σημαίνουσαν, that is, speech signifying the opposite of what is stated (for Aristotle too used the word λέξις in this sense, in the beginning of Rhetoric book 3). I have said that sins are not forgiven in the age to come. In this life there is room for repentance and the forgiveness of sins. The Chaldee thought that this was taught by the passage of Isaiah 55:6: "Seek the Lord בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ while he may be found; call upon him while he is near," which he renders thus: תִּבְעוּ רַחֲמָתָא, that is, "seek the fear of the Lord while you are still alive; pray to him while you still remain."

units.la: Vers. 17. Ecce Dominus asportari te faciet, sicut asportatur gallus gallinaceus] Lovan. Belgica, Gheluyck een Haen der Hennen wegh-ghedraghen wort. Carthus. sicut capo portatur ad forum ut vendatur & manducetur. Intelligit ergo gallum spadonem, ut loquitur Petronius. Lyra, gallus per castrationem ad pusillanimitatem gallina reductus, & in hoc designat Propheta, quod partim erat ex timore se Assyriis redditurus. At in Ebr. nullum gallum invenies. Et hunc locum quod attinet, Judæo cuidam credulitate B. Hyeronimi himium abusto interpretamentum illud debemus. Cujus tamen & R. Sal. & Kimchi meminere. Et memini me legere, ubi ex paraphrasi Pseudo-Jonathanis huic versioni quærebatur patrocinium. Namque Num. 33. 35. עציון גבר Paraphrastes iste reddidit חרנגלא מִפְּרָךְ תְּרַנְּגָלָא. Quomodo & Jerosolymitanus Deut. 2. vox Ebraea גֶּבֶר Virum extra omnem controversiam denotat. מְלַמְּל alii deportandi. alii projiciendi, alii denique * contegendi notione exponunt. Et quidem posterioribus istis, inter quos Junius, savent sequentia וְעֻטְּךָ עֲטֵה & amicies te amiciendo. Solent enim Prophetæ לְכַפֵּל הָעַיִן בְּמִלּוֹת שׁוּנוּת id est, idem aliis verbis repetere, ut hoc velit Vates, Ecce Dominus qui contegit te integumento viri, id est, quantum potest esse viri, amplissimo, & qui amicit te belle, Egregie volutabit te &c. Ut hoc versu non contineatur ulla comminatio, sed commemoratio beneficii. Aliis tamen projiciendi significatio se probat magis: Ecce Dominus projiciet te projectione viri, id est, projectione vehementi, qualis à robusto viro, vel projiciet te projectione, O vir, ut גֶּבֶר sit לְשׁוֹן קְרִיאָה inquit Kimchi, id est, vocativus. Et cooperiet te abunde. Vid. pudore tanquam vestimento. Et insuper Homo erubescens, inquit Kimchi, obtegit faciem suam. Vel, cooperiet te id est, involvet te magnæ ignominiæ, contemtui & cordolio, adeo quidem ut præbiturus tibi sit occasionem faciem obvelandi, ritu Israelitis usitato, Esth. 6. 12. Job. 9. 24. Cæterum & illud non prætereundum censeo, non firmo tibicine illorum sententiam sustentari, qui hunc Sebnam summum Pontificem fuisse prodiderunt. Inter quos & Bellarm. pro authoritate libri Judith. disputans. Namque ubi vulg. legit, Vade ad eum qui habitat in tabernaculo, ad Sobnam præpositum templi, Ebrea sic habent, בּוֹא אֵל הַסֹּכֵן הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר עַל הַבַּיִת id est, Vade ad thesaurarium hunc qui præest domui, Regis videlicet. observa verba seq. Imponam clavem domus David humero ejus. Non, domus Dei, sed domus David id est, Interprete Forerio, in domo Regia post Regem plenam habebis authoritatem. Et subjicit de eodem Eljakim qui Sobnæ hic successor datur, Et ex eo postquam venerunt Chaldæi, ad eos inter præcipuos aulicos emissus est. Vide 2. Reg. 18. Lxx. ταμίας τῆς τῶν ταμείον... Quid παστοφύλαξ? Thalamus in in quo habitat præpositus templi, inquit Hieron. Sochen, inquit idem vel tabernaculum vel παστοφύλαξ significat. Confundit סכן & שכן / Junius, adjutorem vertit quod fautor & adjutor & patronus esset eorum quos versibus superioribus perstrinxit, Vide scholia. Claudam ubi addidero, Forerium postquam suam interpretationem posuisset, hæc subjungere, atque hunc germanum num sensum esse puto. Nam de gallo gallinaceo non fateor me intelligere, quid velit vulgatus.
units.tr: Verse 17. Behold, the Lord will cast you away with a cast, as a cock is carried off] The Louvain Belgian version: "a cock is carried away from among the hens." The Carthusian: "as a capon is carried to the market to be sold and eaten." So he understands a gelded cock, as Petronius puts it. Lyra: "the cock, reduced by castration to timidity, like a hen, and in this the Prophet signifies that partly he was going to surrender to the Assyrians out of fear." But in the Hebrew you will find no cock at all. As for this passage, we owe that rendering to a certain Jew who had been much abused by the credulity of St Jerome. Yet both R. Sal. and Kimchi mention it. And I remember reading where that version sought support from the paraphrase of Pseudo-Jonathan: for in Num. 33:35, that paraphrast renders עֲצִיּוֹן גֶּבֶר as חַרְנְגָלָא מִפְּרָךְ תַּרְנְגָלָא. The Jerusalem Targum on Deut. 2 likewise denotes the Hebrew word גֶּבֶר with certainty as man, beyond all dispute. Some explain מְלַמְּל by the sense of carrying away, others of casting out, others finally of covering up. Indeed, those last-named, among whom is Junius, are supported by the following words, וְעֻטְּךָ עֲטֵה, and wrap yourself by wrapping. For the Prophets are wont to repeat the same thing in other words, לְכַפֵּל הָעַיִן בְּמִלּוֹת שׁוּנוּת, that is, to repeat the same in different words, so that the Prophet's meaning is: "Behold, the Lord who covers you with the mantle of a man," that is, with one of the greatest possible, "and who wraps you handsomely, he will roll you splendidly" etc. So that no threat is contained in this verse, but a recollection of a benefit. Yet the sense of casting out proves itself better to others: "Behold, the Lord will cast you out with the casting of a man," that is, with a violent casting, such as a strong man would give, or he will cast you out with a casting, O man, so that גֶּבֶר is a vocative, as Kimchi says, that is, a form of address. "And he will cover you abundantly," that is, with shame as with a garment. And Kimchi adds: a man who blushes covers his face. Or "he will cover you," that is, he will wrap you in great ignominy, contempt and grief, so that he will indeed give you occasion to veil your face in the manner customary among the Israelites (Esth. 6:12; Job 9:24). Moreover, I think it should not be passed over that the opinion of those who have reported that this Shebna was high priest is supported by no strong prop, among whom is Bellarmine, disputing for the authority of the book of Judith. For where the Vulgate reads, "Go to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shobnam the prefect of the temple," the Hebrew has בּוֹא אֶל הַסֹּכֵן הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר עַל הַבַּיִת, that is, go to this steward who presides over the house, namely of the King. Observe the words that follow: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. Not "the house of God," but the house of David; that is, as Forerius explains, in the royal household, after the King, you will have full authority. And he adds about the same Eliakim, who is given as Shebna's successor here: And from then on, after the Chaldeans came, he was sent to them among the chief courtiers. See 2 Kings 18. The Septuagint: ταμίας τῆς τῶν ταμείον... What is παστοφύλαξ? A chamber in which the prefect of the temple dwells, says Jerome. Shochen, says the same writer, means either a tabernacle or a παστοφύλαξ. Junius confuses סכן and שכן, and renders it helper, because he was a supporter, helper and patron of those whom he lashed in the preceding verses. See the scholia. I shall stop where I have added that Forerius, after giving his own interpretation, subjoins this: this, I think, is the genuine sense. For as to the cock-hen, I do not confess that I understand what the Vulgate means.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. Verf. 16.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII. Verse 16.

units.la: Ecce ego mitto in fundamentis Sion lapidem, Lapidem probatum, angularem, pretiosum, * in fundamento fundatum, qui crediderit non pudefiet] Bell. praeloquio in controversiam de Rom. Pontifice, Quis sit hic lapis, nemo ignorat, qui Evangelium legit, ubi Christus Petrum Petram vocat, quae significatur sedes Romana, quae est fundamentum fundatum id est, secundarium fundamentum. Haec Bell. videtur illud arripere, fundamentum fundatum, vel ut est in Vulg. Lapidem in fundamento fundatum, quod in originario textu nullum habet fundamentum, ibi enim est מוסד מוסד εἰς ἐπʹ πέτρος εἰς ἐπʹ, fundationem fundationis id est, fundationem fundatissimam vel per ellipsin ℨ Beth, fundatione fundatissima ut nihil jam dicam de ipso B. Petro, qui cap. 2. Epistolae prioris hunc locum de Christo interpretatur. Atque ita hunc locum omnes Patres unanimiter exponere testis est Sixtus Senensis in Biblioth. sua & Thomas comment. in
units.tr: "Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner-stone, founded on a foundation; he who believes will not be put to shame." Bellarmine, in the preface to his controversy concerning the Roman Pontiff: Who this stone is, no one who reads the Gospel is ignorant, where Christ calls Peter a rock, and by it is signified the Roman see, which is the foundation founded, that is, a secondary foundation. Bellarmine seems to seize upon fundamentum fundatum, or as it stands in the Vulgate, a stone in a foundation founded, which has no such foundation in the original text. There the words are מוסד מוסד [mosad mosad], which the Seventy render as εἰς ἐπʹ πέτρος εἰς ἐπʹ, that is, a foundation of foundation, that is, a most firmly founded foundation, or, by an ellipsis, with the letter beth, on a most firmly founded foundation. I say nothing here of Saint Peter himself, who in the second chapter of his first Epistle interprets this passage of Christ. Yet that all the Fathers expound this passage unanimously in this way is attested by Sixtus of Siena in his Bibliotheca, and by Thomas in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 3 and 1 Peter 2, and by the Carthusians, and by Lyra, Arias Montanus, Pintus in his commentary on this passage, and Forerius.

units.la: 2. Corinth, 3. & 1 Pet. 2. & Carthus. & Lyra & Arias Mont. Pintus comm. in hunc locum & Forrerius, neque cuiquam dubium esse debet, inquit, quin lapis hic Christus sit, ut ex Evangelio & Paulo & Petro apparet. Et Paulo post, Quarto vocat hunc lapidem fundamentalem. Nam fundamenti fundati vel fundamenti fundamenti, imum fundamentum designat, id est, super quod totum aedificium construitur. Illa vero Pinti assertio Chaldaeum paraphrasten hunc locum exponere de Messia, quam ipsam vocem in versione paraphraseos idem quoque expressit, error est. Haec enim tantum leguntur conslituo in Sion מלך מלך תקיף גבר ואמתן id est, Regem, regem robustum, fortem & terribilem. Hunc Regem, ipsumque adeo lapidem Kimchi ineptissime interpretatur Regem Ezechiam. Cordatus R. Salomo Regem Messiam intellexit, Non gravabor verba ejus adscribere הנני יסד לשון עבר הוא כמו יסד המלך וכן צריך לפותרו הנני הוא אשר יסד כסר בציון אבן כבר נגורה גורה לפניו והעמרתי מלך המשיה שיהי בציון לאבן בוחן לשון מבצר והחק כמו עופל וכחן וכמו הקימו בחוניו מוסר מוסד / הראשון פתח חנגי פתח לפי שהוא דבוק מוסד של מוסד שהוא מוסד גמור id est, Jissad præteritum est, sicuti alibi יסד המלך / ac proinde oportet ita exponere, ego sum is qui fundavit jam in Sion lapidem. Nunc decretum est decretum coram me. Et constituam Regem Messiam ut sit in Sion in lapidem בוחן id est, munitionis & roboris, quomodo occurrit (Jef. 32. 14.) עפל ובחן / & Jef. 23. 13.) הקימי כהוני / Quod vero ad illud attinet מוסד מוסד / prius est pathachatum, quia est in regimine, q.d. מוסד של מוסד / id est, fundatione absolutissima. Hæc ille. De posterioribus paululum diversus abit Kimchi, quoad Grammaticam, Verba ejus הראשון שם והשני פעול והוא רגוש עם ו פירוש יסוד חוק שביסודות יהיה זה היסוד id est prius מוסד nomen est; posterius verbum est dagesfatum cum vau, & sensus est, fundamentum fundatum id est, fundamentum fortissimum erit hoc fundamentum.
units.tr: Forerius says: there ought to be no doubt that this stone is Christ, as appears from the Gospel, from Paul and from Peter. And a little later: Fourth, he calls this stone the foundation-stone. For fundamentum fundatum or fundamentum fundamenti designates the lowest foundation, that is, the one upon which the whole building is constructed. But Pintus's assertion, that the Chaldee paraphrast expounds this passage of the Messiah, and that he has expressed the very word in his paraphrase, is an error. For there is read only this in Sion: מלך מלך תקיף גבר ואמתן [melek melek taqif gebar ve-amitan], that is, a king, a king, mighty, strong and terrible. Kimchi most absurdly interprets this King, and the stone itself, as King Hezekiah. The sound R. Solomon understood it to mean King Messiah. I shall not hesitate to add his words: הנני יסד לשון עבר הוא כמו יסד המלך וכן צריך לפותרו הנני הוא אשר יסד כסר בציון אבן כבר נגורה גורה לפניו והעמרתי מלך המשיה שיהי בציון לאבן בוחן לשון מבצר והחק כמו עופל וכחן וכמו הקימו בחוניו מוסר מוסד / הראשון פתח חנגי פתח לפי שהוא דבוק מוסד של מוסד שהוא מוסד גמור [Jissad is in the past tense, as elsewhere, יסד המלך; and so it must be explained: I am he who has already founded in Sion a stone. A decree is now decreed before me. And I will set up the Messiah King, that he may be in Sion for a stone of testing, a word meaning fortress and strength, as occurs in Isaiah 32:14, עפל ובחן, and Isaiah 23:13, הקימי כהוני. As for מוסד מוסד, the first is pointed with patach, because it is in the construct state, as if to say מוסד של מוסד, that is, a most absolute foundation.] Thus he. Kimchi differs slightly from him on the grammar of the latter words. His words are: הראשון שם והשני פעול והוא רגוש עם ו פירוש יסוד חוק שביסודות יהיה זה היסוד [the first is a noun and the second a participle, with dagesh and vav; the meaning is: a foundation founded, that is, this foundation will be a most firm foundation].

units.la: a) Notat Rainoldus in censura librorum Apocryph. lect. xv. p. 169. in Manuscriptis controversiis Bellarmini quibus & ille & Witakerus & alii usi sunt, antequam publici juris præl o factæ essent, dicta præfatione simpliciter negatum fuisse locum hunc de Christo intelligi posse, hac subjecta ratione, quia sequitur, ponam lapidem in fundamento fundatum id est fundamentum post fundamentum, fundamentum secundarium. Postea vero in excuso exemplari se corexisse, atque hæc interseruisse, Etsi non dubitamus hæc præcipue de Christo intelligenda esse, tamen ad Petrum quoque non inepte referri possunt. At ego ajo, locum istum, prout in vulgo legitur, non posse ullo modo de Christo intelligi. Quæ enim vel probabilis interpretatio dabitur istorum, in fundamento fundatum?
units.tr: a) Rainoldus, in his censure of the Apocryphal books, lecture 15, page 169, notes that in Bellarmine's manuscript controversies, which both he and Whitaker and others used before they were published in print, it was simply denied in that preface that this passage could be understood of Christ, for this reason: that it follows, I will lay a stone in a foundation founded, that is, a foundation after a foundation, a secondary foundation. Afterwards, however, in the printed copy, he corrected himself and inserted these words: Although we do not doubt that these things are to be understood chiefly of Christ, yet they can not unfittingly be referred also to Peter. But I say that this passage, as it is commonly read, cannot in any way be understood of Christ. For what probable interpretation of those men will be given for in a foundation founded?

units.la: Verf. 19. Tantummodo sola vexatio intellectum dabit auditui.] Hic observo in ipso limine voculam sola, quæ in originali non extat, a vulgato Interprete additam esse, Desinant ergo Pontificii magnum Lutherum flagellare, quod eandem voculam illustrando loco Rom. adhibuerit, sed ad rem. Hinc illud vulgatum & celebre, Vexatio dat intellectum, depromtum est. Sententia elegans quidem & vera, sed quam ex originariis tabulis non facile exsculpseris והיה רק זועה הבין שמועה / eritque tantummodo commotio [ad] intelligendam auditionem id est, rem auditam, prædicationem, quomodo & ἀκοή in N. T. non semel usurpatur.
units.tr: Verse 19. "Only vexation will give understanding to the hearing." Here I note at the very threshold that the little word only, which is not found in the original, has been added by the Vulgate translator. Let the Papists therefore cease to lash great Luther for having used this same little word when illustrating the passage in Romans; let them stick to the point. Hence that common and famous saying, vexation gives understanding, is drawn. It is an elegant and true sentiment, but not one you could easily carve out of the original texts: והיה רק זועה הבין שמועה [and there shall be only a commotion, to understand the hearing], that is, the thing heard, the preaching; just as ἀκοή in the New Testament is used more than once in this sense.

units.la: Scopus Prophetæ est, verba D. Joh. Tarnovi Σ μακαρίς τε, ruinam denunciat, indocilitatem exprobrat, & sic concludit. Ut tandem intelligatis non esse has minas, fulgura ex pelvi, aut inania terriculamenta, id tantum restare video, ut ex justo Dei judicio immittatur vobis ex omni parte commotio ut re ipsa edocti, & experientia, optima stultorum Magistra, convicti intelligatis hoc meum documentum & prædicationem quam toties repetii & inculcavi. Hæc ille, Cui adversari videtur illa generum discrepantia quæ est in vocibus וַיְהִי וַיָּעָף qua tamen non deterriti Angli sic verterunt, eritque vexatio, tantum intelligere relationem, id est narrationem. Junius & Trem. Eritque tantummodo commotioni, cum intelligendum proponet documentum. Paraphrasis illorum quam in Scholiis suis exhibent, ista est, neque tantum gravitate operum Dei commovebiminiin exitium vestrum, sed etiam verba quod nunc petulanter ludificamini: denique consternabimini, omnib. testimoniis præsentiæ Dei, à quo abhorrebitis tanquam à judice severissimo. Hac ut ita accipiamus facit comparatio versus. Hæc illi ubi illorum quoque scholia vide & confer cum annotationibus Forerii. Deodatus, e l' intenderne il grido, non farà altro che commovimento, & intelligere rumorem nihil aliud erit quam commotio. Solent cordati & prudentes viri, ubi audiverint rumorem adventantis mali salutaria consilia capere. At his præcurrens fama consternationem & commotionem augebit. Panicus incessit eos metus &c. Quid si, Et tantum intelligere famam erit commotio. q. d. tantæ vobis evenient calamitates, ut vel ad solum earum narrationem tinnituræ sint aures audientium. Vide R. Salomonem. Genevenses, Et dés qu'on orra brruit, il n'y aura que remuement, & ex quo audietur rumor, nihil aliud erit quam commotio. Pergit Jesaias vers. 20. Nam brevius erat stratum, quam ut protendat se, (ubi Vulg. male, ita ut alter decidat, Ebr. מְהֻשָּׂרָע fatentibus Forerio, Aria Montano, Pinto & aliis) & stragula angusta, quam colliget se [cubans] Denunciavit ipsis angustias diurnas & nocturnas id est, continuas, vers. 19. Hic per ὑσέρων nocturnæ explicantur, vers. 21. diurnæ, utrumque ab exemplo. Qui peractis magnis laboribus, in frigore cubitum se recipit, si lectum habeat & stragulam corpore breviorem, non requiescet commode, sed algebit & cruciabitur: Inferne & superne vexabitur. Ita & vos undequaque affligemini, nullaque ex parte vos à flagellis Dei tegetis. Kimchi in comm. Metaphoricus sermo est, inquit, sicut homo qui cubat in lecto adeo angusto, ut pedes suos extendere in eo non possit. Et sicut homo, qui inter cubandum obtegit se stragula nimis angusta, adeo ut non possit se tegere aut colligere se sub ea, ita comparatum erit cum Israële. Namque castra Assyriorum diffundent se per universam terram ejus, & amplissimus ille tractus fiet angustissimus S. S. E. Jes. 8.8. implebuntque extensæ alæ ejus latitudinem terræ tuæ O Immanuel, Nihilque adeo relinquetur ipsis ex universa illa regione præter civitatem Jerusalem, eritque ista urbs nimis angusta, quam ut omnes se in ea colligere & tegere queant. Vide etiam Oleastrium & Vatablum. Male itaque & non ex mente Prophetæ citari solet hic locus à Scholasticis ad illustrandum vel confirmandum illud Salvatoris. nemo potest duobus dominis inservire &c. quo sensu eum quoque citat Thomas secundæ qu. 122. Articulo 3. Quid porro? Verf. 21. Nam sicut in monte Perasim exurget Dominus &c. ut faciat factum suum, alienum erit factum ejus: ut operetur opus suum, peregrinum erit opus ejus ab eo, vulg. alienum est opus ejus & postea, peregrinum est opus ejus. Plane supplendum hic est verbum substantivum ostendit ordo vocum, Adjectivo substantivum præcedente. Proprium Dei opus est, parcere, misereri, inquiunt, alienum ab eo est & peregrinum ipsi opus punire. Ita Lyra, Forerius, Pintus, Carthus. & alii Hanc expositionem convellit Burgensis in Additionib. ad hunc locum, sed substituit aliam meo Judicio magis alienam. Verba ejus non gravabor adscribere, ut faciat opus suum, alienum est opus ejus] ubi glossa, & est Gregorii, in mundum venit, ut faciat opus suum sc. redimet genus humanum, sed ab ipso alienum est opus ejus. Non enim convenit Deitati conspui, flagellari, crucifigi. Et notandum quod iste modus exponendi videtur verior quam dicere quod punire non est proprium Deo, sed magis parcere, & misereri. Postea rationes adducit adversus communem sententiam, 1. quod punire peccatores pertinet ad veritatem justitiæ, quæ Deo maxime competit. 2. quod opus puniendi transgressores sit bonum simpliciter, omne autem opus bonum Deo maxime competit. Hæc Burgensis. Oleastrius sic conciliat, si consideres Deum impense misericordem, opus punitionis ab eo alienum est. Proprius tamen si cum contempleris judicem. Quemadmodum opus misericordiæ est illi proprium, si misericordem dem eum cogites. Si vero judicem, alienum est hoc opus abeo- plura hic additurus eram, nisi Clariss. Roftochienfis Theologus Joh. Tarnovius hunc quoque locum in exercitationibus suis erudite tractassset pag. 587. editionis ultimae quae in octavo, quem lege & non paenitebit.
units.tr: The purpose of the Prophet is, in the words of Dr. John Tarnovius, σ μακαρίς [Happy...], to announce ruin, to upbraid indocility, and so he concludes: "So that at last you may understand that these threats are not lightning from a basin nor empty terrors, I see only this remaining: that from the just judgment of God a commotion be sent upon you on every side, so that, taught by the thing itself and convicted by experience, the best teacher of fools, you may understand that this is my teaching and the preaching which I have so often repeated and inculcated." Thus he. Against this seems to stand the difference of genders in the words [vayehi vayaaf], by which, nonetheless, the English were not deterred from rendering it so: and there shall be vexation, only to understand the report, that is, the narrative. Junius and Tremellius: and there shall be only commotion, when he shall propose the teaching to be understood. Their paraphrase, which they give in their Scholia, is this: "You will be moved not only by the weight of the works of God to your own destruction, but also by the words which you now wantonly mock; finally you will be dismayed by all the evidences of the presence of God, from which you will shrink as from a most severe judge. The comparison of the verse makes us accept it in this way." Thus they; see also their scholia and compare with the notes of Forerius. Deodatus: if you hear the cry, there will be nothing but commotion, and to understand the rumour will be nothing else than commotion. Wise and prudent men are accustomed, when they have heard the rumour of an approaching evil, to take salutary counsel. But for these men the rumour running ahead will increase their consternation and commotion. Panic fear seized them, etc. What if we read: And to understand only the report will be commotion, as if to say: such calamities will befall you that the ears of those hearing will tingle at the mere narration of them. See R. Solomon. The Genevan version: And as soon as the noise is heard, there will be only stirring, and from the moment the rumour is heard, nothing else will be but commotion. Isaiah goes on in verse 20: For the bed was too short to stretch oneself upon (where the Vulgate wrongly has so that one falls; the Hebrew, as Forerius, Arias Montanus, Pintus and others confess, is מהשרע) and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in. He has announced to them narrow circumstances by day and by night, that is, continual ones, in verse 19. Here the night is expounded by ὑσέρων, and in verse 21 the day; both are taken from an example. He who, after great labours, retires to rest in the cold, if he has a bed and a covering shorter than his body, will not rest comfortably, but will be chilled and tormented; he will be troubled from below and from above. So you too will be afflicted on every side, and in no part will you be covered from the scourges of God. Kimchi on the passage: "The language is metaphorical," he says, "like a man who lies on a bed so narrow that he cannot stretch out his feet in it; and like a man who, while lying down, covers himself with a covering too narrow, so that he cannot cover himself or draw himself together under it, so will it be with Israel. For the camps of the Assyrians will spread over all its land, and that ample tract will become most narrow," Isaiah 8:8, "and the spread of his wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel." Nothing will be left to them of all that region except the city of Jerusalem, and that city will be too narrow for all to gather and cover themselves in it. See also Oleaster and Vatablus. It is therefore badly, and not in the mind of the Prophet, that this passage is commonly cited by the Schoolmen to illustrate or confirm the saying of the Saviour, No one can serve two masters, etc.; in this sense Thomas also cites it, in the second part of the second question, article 3. What next? Verse 21: "For the Lord shall rise up as in Mount Perazim, that he may do his work, his strange work; and bring to pass his act, his strange act." The Vulgate has his work is strange and afterwards his work is foreign. Clearly a substantive verb must be supplied here, as the order of the words shows, the substantive preceding the adjective. It is God's proper work to spare and to have mercy, they say; to punish is alien and foreign to him. So Lyra, Forerius, Pintus, the Carthusians and others. Burgensis in his Additions to this passage overturns this exposition, but substitutes another which in my judgment is more alien. I shall not hesitate to add his words: that he may do his work, his work is strange: where the gloss, which is Gregory's, says: He came into the world that he might do his work, that is, redeem the human race, but his work is strange to him. For it does not befit the Deity to be spat upon, scourged, crucified. And it should be noted that this way of expounding seems truer than to say that punishing is not proper to God, but rather sparing and having mercy. Afterwards he brings arguments against the common opinion: first, that punishing sinners belongs to the truth of justice, which especially befits God; second, that the work of punishing transgressors is good absolutely, and every good work especially befits God. Thus Burgensis. Oleaster reconciles them thus: if you consider God as abundantly merciful, the work of punishment is alien to him; but it is proper to him if you contemplate him as judge, just as the work of mercy is proper to him if you think of him as merciful, but alien to him if as judge. I would have added more here, had not the most distinguished theologian of Rostock, John Tarnovius, handled this passage also learnedly in his Exercitationes, page 587 of the last edition, in octavo; read him, and you will not regret it.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Verf. 5. 6. 7. 8. Vulgo de hostium populi Dei subversione intelliguntur, Et videas hic interpretes ut expositionem illam semel institutam obtineant, valde aestuare. Moneo etiam, in annotationibus Hackianis ad verf. Belgicam, multa hic esse à scopo Prophetae immane quantum aliena. Mihi non lubet illud Augeae stabulum (ita voco illam annotationum Belgicarum farraginem) repurgare. Versantur jam in isthoc labore viri doctissimi quibus ego robur Herculeum animitus precor. Ne ergo verbi D. interpretes in hujus loci explicatione vel applicatione à scopo Spiritus S. aberrent, bonum factum, si commentarium Forerii Dominicani, Arix Montani & Junii χόλια adeant.
units.tr: Verses 5, 6, 7, 8. Commonly these are understood of the overthrow of the enemies of the people of God, and the interpreters here, to keep to the exposition once set up, are exceedingly zealous. I also warn that in the Hackian annotations on the Belgic version there is much that is immensely far from the scope of the Prophet. I have no wish to cleanse that Augean stable (so I call that heap of Belgic annotations). Men most learned are now engaged in this labour, and I heartily pray for them Herculean strength. So, lest the interpreters of the Word of the Lord wander from the scope of the Holy Spirit in explaining or applying this passage, it will be well to consult the commentary of the Dominican Forerius, that of Arias Montanus, and the Notes of Junius.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Verf. 15. Cum conversus ingemueris tunc salvaberis; vel, Peccator cum ingemuerit salvabitur. Alterutro modo saepe à prisicis & novellis citatur hic textus. Vide corpus Canonicum parte 2. Causa 26. quaest. 6. capitulo, bis qui tempore necessitatis, quamvis illic ad marginem, notetur locus Jezech. xviii. Hincmarum Episc. Rhemensem in opusculo LV. capitum cap. 48. Locus desumptus est ex versione LXX. Interpretum, ὅταν ἐπιστραφεὶς ἡσυχίᾳς τότε σωθήσῃ. Sententia vera & plena solatii, si recte adhibeatur & intelligatur. Non tamen eam facile ex Jesaiae verbis exsculpseris. Nam ille suo idiomate ita fatur, בְּשׁוּבָה וְנֹחַת תִּוָּשֵׁעוּ in reversione & requie servabimini. Vulg. non male, Si revertamini & quiescatis, salvi eritis. Nihil est quod ἡσυχία id est, gemitum significet. Sensum egregie expressit Forerius, Si ab instituto redeatis, neque in Ægyptum profici ci velitis, sed hic quiescatis, erit vobis salus. Pintus, Si revertamini, nemnempe à voluntate vestra & quiescatis in terra promissionis, non peribitis. Non loquitur de salute animæ aut æterna, sed corporali & temporaria.
units.tr: Verse 15. "When you turn back and groan, then you shall be saved"; or, "A sinner, when he has groaned, shall be saved." This text is often cited by older and newer writers in one or the other of these forms. See the Canon Law, part 2, Causa 26, question 6, the chapter Bis qui tempore necessitatis, although there the margin notes the passage Ezekiel 18. Hincmar, bishop of Reims, cites it in his work of fifty-five chapters, chapter 48. The passage is taken from the Septuagint, "when you turn back and are quiet, then you shall be saved" [ὅταν ἐπιστραφεὶς ἡσυχίᾳς τότε σωθήσῃ]. The sentiment is true and full of comfort, if it is rightly applied and understood. Yet it cannot easily be carved out of Isaiah's words. For he speaks in his own idiom, "in returning and rest you shall be saved" [בְּשׁוּבָה וְנֹחַת תִּוָּשֵׁעוּ]. The Vulgate is not bad: "If you return and be quiet, you shall be safe." There is nothing to show that ἡσυχία, that is, groaning, is meant. Forerius expresses the sense admirably: "If you return from your purpose, and do not wish to set out for Egypt, but remain here quietly, there will be safety for you." Pintus: "If you return, that is, from your own will, and rest in the land of promise, you will not perish." The passage does not speak of the salvation of the soul or of eternal salvation, but of bodily and temporal salvation.

units.la: Verf. 26. Eritque lux lunæ sicut lux solis &c.] disputant Scholastici, an circa tempus universalis judicii obscuratio solis & lunæ secundum rei veritatem futura sit. Negat * Author supplementi summæ qu. 73. art. 2. Non congruit, inquit, idem esse causam defectus alicujus rei & augmenti: sed veniente Domino lux luminarium augmentabitur, unde Jes. 30. erit lux lunæ sicut lux sōlis &c. qua de re ex professo agit idem quæst. 95. art. 3. ubi conclusionem suam huic loco potissimum superstruit: Sed 1. de adventu Domini ad universale judicium hic non agitur. 2. Hæc figurate à Prophetā dicuntur. Non ignoro quid ad hunc locum disserat B. Hieronymus. Sed ego non Hieronymo sed veritati sacramento dixi, & malo hic clarissimos Pontificios interpretes quam Stridonensem Presbyterum sequi. Pintus, magna erit illo tempore (quo vid. liberabuntur Judæi) lætitia. Tunc enim Israëlitis lux splendidissima fulgebit. Usque adeo erit admirabile gaudium ut cœlestia corpora gaudere & gratulari videantur. Sa, q.d. erit tunc maxima lætitia. Forerius, hæc nihil aliud quam ingentem lætitiam significant, qua fruuntur fideles, cum vident vulnera suorum peccatorum per filium Dei super alligata, cujus typus fuit illa inexpectata lætitia, quàm habuit populus Jerosolymitanus, interfectis Assyriis. Nam sicut obscuritas Solis & Lunæ calamitates & tristia omnia in Scriptura figurate significant, ita & lux Lunæ ac solis multiplicata, lætitiam ac lata omnia notat. Nam & lætitia affectis Sol clarius splendescere videtur, & qui moerore animi tabescunt, illis omnia obscura apparent. Hæc ille Junius, q. d. illustrissima erunt & gloriosissima omnia in restitutione Ecclesiæ. Hyperbole. Non omnino absimilis est locus Horatii: Lucem redde tuæ dux bone patriæ. Instar veris enim vultus ubi tuus affulsit populo gratior it dies Et soles melius nitent. Lubet autem hic in gratiam φιλεβέγλων addere interpretationes Ebraeorum, Chald. eritque lux Lunæ tanquam lux solis, & lux solis splendebit trecenties quadragesies ter. (Arias, super lucem, ad verbum, sicut lux septem dierum quibus facem allucet R. Salomo; שבעה sepiem, septenarii sicut lux septem dierum. Ecce 49. septenarii ascendunt ad 343.. Ego hanc subtilitatem non capio. שבעתים neque septem, neque duos septenarios, sed vel septies, vel septuplum aut septempliciter significat. Id clarius est ex hoc loco. Nam quod primo dixit שבעתים id postea explicat sicut lux (non 14. aut 49. sed) septem dierum. Ita 2 Sam. 12. 6. & agnam restituet ארבעתים / ubi * Pagninus, bis quadruplicatam, Arias rectius, quadruplo. Idque ex legis praescripto Exod. 22. 1. Eo magis miror Ariam in comment. ad hunc Jesaiae locum שבעתים reddere, bis sepites. Aben-Ezra ad Gen. 4. 15. Omnis qui intersecerit Kajinum, שבעתים יקם / ita commentatur, usque ad septem generationes. Haec enim dictio non significat bis septem seu quatuordecim, neque trecenta quadraginta tria (respicit, opinor, ad hanc loci Jesaiae paraphrasin) Cujus sententiae probatio petitur ex loco Jesaiae, eritque lux Solis שבעתים / & postea hoc explicat Propheta cum dicit sicut lux septem dierum. Kimchi, Multi interpretes explicant hunc locum de futuro. Et sunt qui exponunt ea ita ut sonant. Quod non est probandum. Sunt qui figurate exponunt de magnitudine felicitatis, quae in diebus Messiae erit. Et certe erit magna felicitas. Sed recte etiam exponi potest figurate de diebus Jezechiae ut dicat, eventuram ipsis magnam felicitatem post intersectionem castrorum Regis Assur, & ex eo futuram magnam salutem. Et sicuti afflictionem vocat caliginem & tenebras; sicuti dicitur, Sol & Luna obscurabuntur & stellae contrahent splendorem suum, qui modus loquendi in aliis quoque Scripturae locis occurrit, ita & salus vocatur lux, S. S. E. Esth. 8. 16. Judaeis vero fuit lux & laetitia, Non quod auxerit illis Deus lucem solis & Lunae; sed ut dixi per lucem intelligitur salus &c. Et pauculis interjectis de voce שבעתים ita fatur, שבעתים hoc est, illumitiationes magnae & multae & sic, שבעתים vindicatur, id est vindicationibus multis non quatuordecim tantum. כי שבע ושבעה יבא להגריל השבון / Numerus enim septenarius usurpatur ad augendum numerum, ut septies cadit justus & surgit.
units.tr: Verse 26. "The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun," etc. The Schoolmen dispute whether, at the time of the universal judgment, the sun and moon will really be darkened. The author of the Supplement to the Summa, question 73, article 2, denies it: "It is not fitting," he says, "that the same cause should bring about both the loss and the increase of a thing; but at the coming of the Lord the light of the luminaries will be increased; hence in Isaiah 30, 'the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun,' etc." He treats this matter at length in the same question, article 3, where he builds his conclusion chiefly on this passage: "But first, the coming of the Lord to the universal judgment is not what is discussed here. Second, these things are said figuratively by the Prophet." I am not unaware of what Blessed Jerome says on this passage. But I have not spoken for Jerome but for the sacred truth, and I prefer here to follow the most illustrious Papist interpreters rather than the presbyter of Stridon. Pintus: "At that time (when, that is, the Jews will be set free) there will be great joy. For then the most splendid light will shine on the Israelites. The joy will be so wonderful that the heavenly bodies seem to rejoice and exult. Sa, that is, there will then be the greatest gladness." Forerius: "These words signify nothing other than the immense joy which the faithful enjoy when they see the wounds of their sins bound up through the Son of God, of which that unexpected joy the people of Jerusalem had, when the Assyrians were slain, was a type. For just as the darkening of the sun and moon signifies in Scripture calamities and all sad things, so the multiplied light of the sun and moon denotes joy and all happy things. For to those who are cheerful the sun seems to shine more brightly, and to those whose minds waste away with sorrow, all things appear dark." So far Junius: "that is, all things will be most illustrious and most glorious at the restoration of the Church." It is a hyperbole. The passage of Horace is not altogether unlike: "Restore the light, good leader of your country; for when your face has shone like spring upon the people, the day passes more pleasantly and the suns shine more brightly." But here, for the benefit of the lovers of light [φιλεβέγλων], I wish to add the interpretations of the Hebrews. The Chaldee: "the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall shine three hundred and forty-three times." (Arias, on "light," reads literally "as the light of seven days," by which R. Solomon sees a torch lit; "seven" [שבעה], as the light of seven days, a sevenfold. Behold, forty-nine sevens rise to 343.) I do not grasp this subtlety. "Sevenfold" [שבעתים] means neither seven, nor two sevens, but either seven times, or sevenfold, or in a sevenfold manner. This is clearer from the passage itself. For what he first called "sevenfold" [שבעתים], he afterwards explains as "like the light of seven days" (not fourteen or forty-nine). So in 2 Samuel 12:6, "he shall restore the lamb fourfold" [ארבעתים], where Pagninus has "twice fourfold," Arias more correctly "fourfold," and this in accordance with the law's prescription, Exodus 22:1. So much the more do I wonder that Arias, in his commentary on this passage of Isaiah, renders [שבעתים] "twice seven times." Aben Ezra on Genesis 4:15, "whoever kills Cain, sevenfold [שבעתים] shall be avenged," comments thus: "up to seven generations." For this word does not mean twice seven, or fourteen, nor three hundred and forty-three (he refers, I think, to this paraphrase of the passage in Isaiah). The proof of this opinion is drawn from the passage of Isaiah: "the light of the sun shall be sevenfold" [שבעתים], and afterwards the Prophet explains this when he says, "as the light of seven days." Kimchi: "Many interpreters explain this passage of the future, and some expound the words as they sound, which is not to be approved. Some expound it figuratively, of the greatness of the happiness which will be in the days of the Messiah; and certainly there will be great happiness. But it can also rightly be expounded figuratively of the days of Hezekiah, so that it says that great happiness and great salvation would come to them after the destruction of the camp of the king of Assyria. And just as affliction is called darkness and gloom, as it is said, 'The sun and moon shall be darkened and the stars shall withdraw their brightness,' a manner of speaking which occurs also in other passages of Scripture, so salvation is called light. Holy Scripture says of the Jews, 'they had light and gladness' (Esther 8:16). It is not that God increased for them the light of the sun and moon, but, as I said, by light is understood salvation," etc. A few sentences later, concerning the word [שבעתים], he says: "[שבעתים], that is, great and many illuminations; and thus [שבעתים] is avenged, that is, with many vengeances, not only fourteen. For the number seven is used to increase the number, as the righteous falls seven times and rises." [כי שבע ושבעה יבא להגריל השבון].

units.la: Verf. 27. Ecce nomen Domini venit de longinquo] Lyra, hic consequenter agitur de dejectione daemonis citatque authorem huius sententiae Alexandrum de Ales, qui fuit maximus Theologus intemporibus suis, inquit. Postea dividit reliquam hanc capitis Particulam in tres partes. I. describitur adventus judicis terribilis impiis. II. delectabilis justis ibi, Cant. erit. III. & abjectivus daemonis ibi, Et auditam. Antea tamen dixerat, Sciendum quod Ebrei & expositores numeri exponunt partem istam ad literam de dejectione SenaSenacherib venientis contra Jerusalem cui sententiæ duo dicit adversari. I. quod dicitur hic in principio, ecce nomen Domini venit de longinquo. Ex quo videtur Jesaias loqui de tempore longinquo quod est tempus judicii finalis. II. quod dicitur infine capitis, præparata est ab heri thophet id est, pœna Gehennalis, secundum quod dicitur ab omnibus expositoribus Hebræis & Latinis. Videamus de singulis ordine. Forerius, Nomen interdum pro fama & gloria accipitur apud Ebræos, sicut apud Latinos, ut Deut. 26. Prov. 22. (Cur non addit locum Philipp. 2. 10.) Ergo hic nomen Dom. proDom. majestate vel Dom. ipso glorioso accipio. Sic a. loqui maluit Propheta, ut adventum illum, quasi fama è longinquo adse delatum significaret. Huc forte respexit Evangelista, cum venturum Dominum cum majestate significaret ad vastandam Jerosolyma. Posteadicit, non minus hæc in Judæos tempore Titi, quam in Assyrios tempore Ezechiæ convenire. In qua me non habebit astipulatorem.
units.tr: Verse 27. "Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar." Lyra: here the discussion follows consistently about the overthrow of the demon, and he cites as the author of this opinion Alexander of Hales, "who was the greatest theologian of his time." Afterwards he divides the rest of this part of the chapter into three parts: I. the coming of the terrible judge is described to the wicked; II. his delightful coming to the just, "there it will be" (Canticles); III. and the casting out of the demon, "And having heard" [et auditam]. He had said before, however: "It should be noted that the Hebrews and the expositors of the Numbers expound this part literally, of the overthrow of Sennacherib, who came against Jerusalem; but two things oppose this opinion, he says. I. What is said here at the beginning, 'Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar.' From this it seems that Isaiah speaks of a distant time, which is the time of the final judgment. II. What is said at the end of the chapter, 'for Topheth has been prepared from yesterday,' that is, Gehenna's punishment, as is said by all Hebrew and Latin expositors." Let us consider these points in order. Forerius: "Among the Hebrews, as among the Latins, 'name' is sometimes taken for fame and glory, as in Deuteronomy 26 and Proverbs 22" (why does he not add Philippians 2:10?). "Therefore here I take 'the name of the Lord' for the majesty of the Lord, or the glorious Lord himself. The Prophet preferred to speak in this way, so that he signifies that coming as if fame had been brought to him from afar. Perhaps the Evangelist had this in view, when he signified that the Lord would come with majesty to lay waste Jerusalem. Afterwards he says that these things apply no less to the Jews in the time of Titus than to the Assyrians in the time of Hezekiah. In this he will not have me as a fellow supporter."

units.la: Totus enim contextus eo nos ducit, ut statuamus de Assyriorum strage Prophetam vaticinari. Itaque Pintus, nomen D. venit de longinquo, hoc est de Persia & Media. Inde enim venerunt Darius & Cyrus qui Babylonem everterunt. Vel sic, ecce Dominus veniet de cælo ut occidat exercitum Senacheribi. Et Oleastrius, Per nomen Domini intellige ejus potentiam & majestatem. ut Jerem. x. 6. Quod vero additur, de longinquo, exaggeratio esse videtur punitionis. Qui enim gravius per cutere vult, elevat flagellum. Potest etiam intelligi, quod venit de longinquo, id est, de cælo quod longe distat à terra. Solet enim Dominus, cum ad punitionem venit, præ se ferre aliunde venire, quemadmodum ab Aquilone &c. Kimch, Nomen Domini quod probro affecerunt Legati regis Assur, ecce illud nomen veniet ad vindictam. Quod autem dicit, è longinquo, ideo dicit, quia Rex Assyriæ putabat Deum quasi longe à se abesse ac proinde non posse nocere. Aben-Ezra, è longinquo id est, ex cælo ob descensum Angeli. Qui vid. castra Assyriorum cecidit. Potest ergo commode illud, è longinquo exponi, servata interpretatione totius contextus de clade Assyriorum. Et quid facient versu 31. A voce enim Domini pavebit Assur virga percussus. Lyræ, Carthusiano aliisque id genus interpretibus nusquam hæret aqua. Assur id est, Diabolus, inquit Lyra, qui hic ad literam intelligitur sub nomine Regis Assur. Sicut supra cap. 14. sub nomine Regis Babel significatur Diabolus ad literam. Carthuf. Assur id est omnis superbus Dæmon & homo, quibus tunc eveniet quod Scriptura nunc minatur. Etiam ex novellis Sa, Assur interpretatur Diabolum. At Oleastrius ad vers. 29. Locus optime potest interpretari de Assyriis, quia sequitur, à voce Dconteretur Assur. Atque ita quoque interpretatur Pintus & Forerius & Arias Mont. Quod vero inquit vulgatus, Virga percussus, Ebr. virgâ percutiet, Jun. melius reddere videtur, qui solebat virga percutere. Futurum apud Ebraeos saepe actum solitum notat.
units.tr: For the whole context leads us to conclude that the Prophet is prophesying about the slaughter of the Assyrians. So Pintus: "the name of the Lord comes from afar," that is, from Persia and Media, for from there came Darius and Cyrus, who overthrew Babylon. Or thus: "Behold, the Lord will come from heaven to destroy the army of Sennacherib." And Oleastrius: "By the name of the Lord understand his power and majesty, as in Jer. 10:6." What is added, "from afar," seems to be an exaggeration of the punishment, for whoever wishes to strike more heavily raises the whip. It can also be understood that "from afar" means from heaven, which is far distant from the earth. For the Lord, when he comes to punish, is accustomed to make it plain that he comes from elsewhere, as from the north, and so on. Kimchi: "The name of the Lord, which the envoys of the king of Assyria reviled, behold, that name will come to take vengeance." He says "from afar" because the king of Assyria thought God was, as it were, far away from him and therefore could not harm him. Aben Ezra: "from afar, that is, from heaven, because of the descent of the angel," who struck down the camp of the Assyrians. "From afar" can therefore fittingly be explained while the whole context is still read as concerning the defeat of the Assyrians. And what will they make of verse 31: "For at the voice of the Lord Assur will tremble, struck with the rod"? Lyra, the Carthusian, and other interpreters of that kind are never at a loss. "Assur," says Lyra, "that is, the Devil, who here is understood literally under the name of the king of Assur, just as above in chapter 14 the Devil is literally signified under the name of the king of Babel." The Carthusian: "Assur is every proud demon and man, on whom will happen what Scripture now threatens." Also, from the newer [commentators], Sa interprets Assur as the Devil. But Oleastrius, on verse 29, says: "The passage can very well be interpreted of the Assyrians, because it follows, 'Assur will be crushed at the voice of the Lord.'" And so Pintus, Forerius and Arias Montanus also interpret it. As for the Vulgate's "struck with the rod," the Hebrew is "he will strike with the rod" [בְּשֵׁבֶט יַכֶּה], which Junius seems to render better as "who used to strike with the rod." The future tense among the Hebrews often denotes a habitual or customary action.

units.la: Quod ad secundum Lyrae argumentum attinet ex ultimo versu depromptum, an iis literaliter & proprie de loco damnatorum intelligi possit valde dubito. Non jam disputo, an nomen תפה pro quo hic est תפתה cum ςαγωγή literae ה sit à * תוף tympano, an potius à * פת unde & תופת prodigium, vel, ut Junius ad hunc locum, à פתה quod Chaldaeis est, dilatatum, amplum esse; vel ab eodem פתח / ita R. Salomo, quia seductionis notionem habet, quod omnis, qui seducitur à concupiscentia sua mala (מחפתה בִּיצְרוֹ) in locum istum praeceps detur. Illud extra controversiam pono, Thophet idem esse cum valle Hinnom, quae Ebraeis גי בני הנם aut הנם aut גי בן הנם vocatur. Locus celebris est à detestabili illo, prodigioso & portentoso cultu, quo degeneres Ebraei liberos suos idolo Molochustulabant, personantibus interim dum illi cremabantur sacrificulorum tympanis, ne videlicet puerulorum fletus & lamenta animos parentum frangerent. Id quod Ebraeorum fide pono. At, inquies, Gehennam locum damnatorum quoque significare. Cur non ergo & Thopheth? Respondeo, tum respectu cruciatuum, quibus miselli isti excarnificabantur, tum respectu perpetui ignis, qui illic postea asservatus fuit ad comburenda cadavera & sordes quas pius Rex Josias, polluendo loco, eo deportari curavit (2. Reg. 23. 11.) sequiori aevo vocem Gehenna usurpari coepisse pro loco damnatorum, Kimchius ad Ps. 27. 13. ut videam bonitatem Domini in terra viventium, ita commentatur, ut videam bonitatem ejus in saeculo venturo. Et hoc est quod dicit בארץ החיים / Et quamvis animae locus non sit in terra, tamen quia felicitas futuri saeculi comparatur horto voluptatis seu Paradiso, qui est locus terrestris, ad captum auditorum, adhibita est haec figurata locutio: Eodem plane modo, quo judicium improborum vocatur Gehenna, והוא מקום בארץ סמוך לירושלים והוא מקום נמאס ומשליכים שם הטומאות והנבלות והיה שם אש תמיד לשרוף הטומאות 𝕳הַמּוּמָאוֹת id est, erat autem is locus terrestris juxta urbem Jerusalem; locus despretus, quo projiciebant immunda & cadavera, eratque illic perpetuus ignis ad comburendas immunditias &c. Sed redeamus ex hoc diverticulo in viam. Dixi יִרְהִנֹּם usurpari pro loco damnatorum, sed sequiori ævo. Unde in textu Ebraeo nusquam eo sensu occurrit. At apud Thalmudicos & Thargumistas frequens & tralatitium est. Atque hinc ad pomoeria novi Test. translatum est. Ut & multa alia, de quibus suo loco. An non ergo verisimile, synonymum ejus תֹּפֶת vel תָּפְתָּה eo sensu, à Propheta non fuisse usurpatum? Adhæc, si hactenus de temporali exitio eorum qui populum Dei affligebant, sermocinatus est Propheta, quomodo persuaderi nobis patiemur, hic ex abrupto de Gehennali poena, diabolo & angelis ejus, ut hic loquitur Lyra, praeparata eundum concionari? Licet enim in vulgata sit, praeparata à Rege, quod vulgo explicant, à Deo, Lyra tamen notat, & recte, in Ebraeo haberi, Regipraeparata, Regi, inquit, id est, daemoni & angelis ejus, qui dicitur Rex super omnes filios superbiae. Id vero admodum alienum est. Locus enim iste, qui extat Jobi 41. verf. ultimo nullo modo de Diabolo exponi potest, ut suo loco ostendimus. Probabilius illi sentiunt, qui per Regem ipsum Senacheribum intelligunt, illiique infernum praeparatum dici asserunt. Forerius, cum Jesaias praevideret Assyriorum cladem, quam verisimile est in illa valle prope Jerosolymam contigisse, venuste in nomine Thopheth ludit, dum locum illum jam dudum Regi Assyriorum cum suis praeparatum esse dicit. Et paucis interjectis, Haec tamen non impediunt, inquit, quominus hic damnatorum locum describi dicamus. Parum enim fuit Prophetae, illos occidendos dicere, nisi in aeternum cruciandos cum principe diabolo praedicaret in igne &c. Hunc ergo sensum videtur agnoscere secundarium, illum, primarium. Junius in scholiis ait exornari hoc versu proxime praecedens membrum de adversariorum expugnatione, cujus formam allegorice describi asserit. Ad vocem autem תֹּפֶת quam ille reddit exitu locum, ita commentatur, Hic singularem adhibet vocem ad notandum singulare judicium quo in Regem Babyloniae erat usurus Deus. Nam deducitur à nomine Thopheth, qui locus fuit, amplus, (unde nomen habet) ab idololatris celebratus, ut ex Jerem. 7. & 19. constat, quemadmodum etiam ante haec tempora filios ab Achazo Rege in eodem loco exustos fuisse legimus 2. Chr. 28. 3. Cum itaque imCarthuf. Assur id est omnis superbus Dæmon & homo, quibus tunc eveniet quod Scriptura nunc minatur. Etiam ex novellis Sa, Assur interpretatur Diabolum. At Oleastrius ad verf. 29. Locus optime potest interpretari de Assyriis, quia sequitur, à voce D· conteretur Assur. Atque ita quoque interpretatur Pintus & Forerius & Arias Mont. Quod vero inquit vulgatus, Virga percussus, Ebr. בְּשֵׁבֶט יַכֶּה virgâ percutiet, Jun. melius reddere videtur, qui solebat virga percutere. Futurum apud Ebraeos saepe actum solitum notat.
units.tr: As for Lyra's second argument, drawn from the last verse, I very much doubt whether the words can be understood literally and properly of the place of the damned. I do not now dispute whether the name [תפה], for which here stands [תפתה] with the transposition of the letter ה, comes from [תוף], a tambourine, or rather from [פת], whence also [תופת], a portent; or, as Junius on this passage has it, from [פתה], which in Chaldee means to be wide, spacious; or from the same root [פתח], as Rabbi Solomon has it, because it carries the notion of enticement: that everyone who is enticed by his own evil desire [מחפתה ביצרו] is cast headlong into that place. I set this beyond controversy: Tophet is the same as the valley of Hinnom, which the Hebrews call [גי בני הנם], or [הנם], or [גי בן הנם]. The place is famous for that detestable, monstrous and prodigious worship by which the degenerate Hebrews burned their children as offerings to the idol Molech, while meanwhile the drums of the little priests sounded, so that the wailing and lamentation of the little children might not break the hearts of the parents. This I set down on the faith of the Hebrews. "But," you will say, "Gehenna also signifies the place of the damned. Why then not Tophet too?" I answer: partly with respect to the torments by which those wretched children were tortured, and partly with respect to the perpetual fire which was kept there afterwards for burning corpses and filth, which the pious King Josiah had carried thither to defile the place (2 Kings 23:11). In a later age the word Gehenna began to be used for the place of the damned. Kimchi, on Ps. 27:13, "that I may see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living," comments: "that I may see his goodness in the world to come." And this is what he means by [בארץ החיים]. Although the soul has no place in the land, yet because the happiness of the future age is compared to a garden of delight, or Paradise, which is an earthly place, this figurative way of speaking was adopted to suit the understanding of the hearers. In exactly the same way the judgment of the wicked is called Gehenna. Kimchi adds that this was a place on earth near Jerusalem, a despised place into which they threw filth and corpses, and there was always a fire there to burn the uncleanness, and so on. But let us return from this digression to the road. I said that [גיהנם] is used for the place of the damned, but in a later age; hence it never occurs in that sense in the Hebrew text. Yet among the Talmudists and the Targumists it is frequent and commonplace, and from there it passed into the language of the New Testament, as did many other things, of which more in their place. Is it not then probable that the Prophet did not use its synonym [תֹּפֶת] or [תָּפְתָּה] in that sense? Moreover, if the Prophet has so far been speaking of the temporal destruction of those who oppressed the people of God, how can we be persuaded to accept that here, quite abruptly, he turns to preach about the Gehennal punishment prepared for the devil and his angels, as Lyra puts it? For although the Vulgate has "prepared by the King," which people commonly explain as prepared by God, Lyra notes, and rightly, that the Hebrew has "prepared for the King," that is, for the demon and his angels, who is called king over all the sons of pride. But that is quite unsuitable. For that passage, which stands at the last verse of Job 41, cannot in any way be explained of the Devil, as I shall show in its place. More probable are those who understand by the "King" Sennacherib himself, and assert that hell is said to have been prepared for him. Forerius, since Isaiah foresaw the defeat of the Assyrians, which was probably fulfilled in that valley near Jerusalem, plays cleverly on the name Tophet, when he says that this place had long ago been prepared for the king of the Assyrians with his men. And after a few intervening remarks he says: "These things nevertheless do not prevent us from saying that the place of the damned is described here. For it would have been too little for the Prophet to say that those men would be slain, unless he also preached that they would be tormented for ever in fire with their prince the devil," and so on. He therefore seems to recognise this sense as secondary and the other as primary. Junius in his notes says that the preceding clause, about the overthrow of the enemies, is adorned in this verse, and he asserts that its form is described allegorically. On the word [תֹּפֶת], which he renders "a place of exit," he comments: "Here he uses a unique word to mark the unique judgment with which God was going to deal with the king of Babylon. For it is derived from the name Tophet, which was a wide place (whence it has its name), celebrated by idolaters, as is clear from Jer. 7 and 19; just as we read that before these times the sons were burned by King Ahaz in the same place (2 Chr. 28:3). Since therefore..."
