Nam deducitur à nomine Thopheth, qui locus fuit, amplus, (unde nomen habet) ab idololatris celebratus, ut ex Jerem. 7. & 19. constat, quemadmodum etiam ante hæc tempora filios ab Achazo Rege in eodem loco exustos fuisse legimus 2. Chr. 28. 3. Cum itaque imimpurissima illa sacrificia palam fierent ad portam Jeruschalaimorum maxima pompa & apparatu; Propheta illustrissimum Babylonii regis exitium magnificentissime efficiendum in oculis Ecclesiæ ipsius nominat conjugata & affini voce, quo etiam spectant singula illa descriptionis verba sequentia. Et Paulo post, ad vocem pyrê Pergit, inquit, in allegoria à comparatione eorum, qui in valle Hinnom comburebantur, adhibitis rebus quæ hic dicuntur ad incendium & conflagrationem eorum. Kimchius idem dicit quod Forerius, Thophthe est * vallis Hinnom, dicit eam paratam fuisse illis ante mortem ipsorum, Propheta enim hoc vaticinatus est, antequam venisset decretum de illorum strage, וכמות גופם תמות גם כן נפשם ותהיה בגי הגם & moriente corpore eorum, morietur etiam anima ipsorum eritque in Gehenna. Quem locum produxi firmandis istis, quæ in Antibarbari nostri parte priori disseruimus, Kimchium vid. dum animas mori & perire subinde dicit, earum tamen Ἀφανισμὸν non negare. De resurrectione corporum impiorum alia quæstio est, de qua vide eruditissimi Cocceii notas ad tractatum Sanhedrin. Aben תפתה שם מקום מטונף סביב ירושלים ושם ישליכו כל דמן ויעלה ממנו עשן Thophthe nomen loci inquinati prope Jerusalem, quo projiciebatur fimus, unde fumus ascendebat &c.
units.tr: As for Lyra's second argument, taken from the last verse, I very much doubt that it can be understood literally and properly of the place of the damned. I will not now discuss whether the name תֻּפָּת [Tuphat], for which here stands תֹּפֶת [Tophet], comes from תוף [tuph], a drum, or rather from פת [pat], whence תֹּפֶת also means a portent, or, as Junius says on this passage, from פתה, which in Chaldean means to be wide or spacious; or from the same root פתה, as R. Solomon holds, because it carries the sense of seduction, since everyone who is seduced by his own evil desire (מִתְפַּתֶּה בִּיצְרוֹ) is cast headlong into that place. I lay this down beyond dispute: Tophet is the same as the valley of Hinnom, which the Hebrews call גֵּי בְּנֵי הִנֹּם, or גֵּי בְּנֵי הִנֹּם, or simply הִנֹּם. The place is famous for that hideous, monstrous and portentous worship in which the degenerate Hebrews burned their children as sacrifices to the idol Moloch, while the drums of the priests sounded, so that the cries and wailing of the little ones would not pierce the hearts of their parents. This I set down on the faith of the Hebrews. But, you will say, Gehenna also signifies the place of the damned. Why then not Tophet too? I answer: both with regard to the torments with which those wretched children were tortured, and with regard to the perpetual fire which was kept there afterwards for burning corpses and the filth which the pious king Josiah had carried out there to defile the place (2 Kings 23:11). Only in a later age did the word Gehenna begin to be used for the place of the damned. Kimchi on Psalm 27:13, "to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living," comments: "to see his goodness in the world to come." And this is what he means by בְּאֶרֶץ הַחַיִּים [in the land of the living]. Although the soul has no place on earth, yet because the happiness of the future age is compared to a garden of delight, or Paradise, which is an earthly place, this figurative manner of speaking was adopted to suit the understanding of the hearers. In exactly the same way the judgment of the wicked is called Gehenna: [והוא מקום בארץ סמוך לירושלים והוא מקום נמאס ומשליכים שם הטומאות והנבלות והיה שם אש תמיד לשרוף הטומאות], that is, the place was on earth near the city of Jerusalem; it was a despised place into which they threw unclean things and corpses, and there was a perpetual fire there to burn up the filth, and so on. But let us return from this digression to our path. I have said that Gehenna is used for the place of the damned, but in a later age; hence it does not occur in the Hebrew text in that sense at all. But among the Talmudists and the Targumists it is frequent and conventional, and from there it was carried over into the vocabulary of the New Testament, as were many other things, about which I shall speak in their place. Is it not therefore likely that its synonym תפה or תפתה was not used by the prophet in that sense? Moreover, if the prophet has so far been speaking of the temporal destruction of those who afflicted the people of God, how can we be persuaded that here, out of the blue, he is preaching about the punishment of Gehenna, prepared for the devil and his angels, as Lyra puts it? For although the Vulgate has prepared by the King, which people commonly explain as prepared by God, Lyra notes, and rightly, that the Hebrew has prepared for the King: for the King, he says, that is, the demon and his angels, who is called king over all the children of pride. But this is quite out of place. For the passage in Job 41, the last verse, cannot in any way be explained of the devil, as we show in its own place. Those who understand by the King Sennacherib himself, and say that hell is said to have been prepared for him, hold the more probable view. Forerius, since Isaiah foresaw the defeat of the Assyrians, which probably happened in that valley near Jerusalem, plays with the name Tophet elegantly, saying that that place had long ago been prepared for the king of the Assyrians and his men. And a little later: "These things, however, do not prevent us from saying that the place of the damned is described here. For it was not enough for the prophet to say that those men would be slain, unless he also proclaimed that they would be tormented forever in fire with their prince the devil, and so on." He seems therefore to recognise the latter sense as secondary and the former as primary. Junius, in his scholia, says that the preceding clause about the overthrow of the adversaries is adorned by this verse, and he asserts that its form is described allegorically. But on the word תפתה, which he renders as a place of destruction, he comments thus: "Here he uses a singular word to note the singular judgment which God was about to bring upon the king of Babylon. For it is derived from the name Tophet, which was a wide place (whence it has its name), celebrated by idolaters, as is clear from Jeremiah 7 and 19; just as we read that before these times the sons were burned in the same place by King Ahaz (2 Chron. 28:3). Since, therefore, those most impure sacrifices were openly offered at the gate of Jerusalem with the greatest pomp and display, the prophet names the most glorious destruction of the king of Babylon, to be carried out most magnificently before the eyes of the Church itself, by a cognate and related word; to which also the individual words of the following description refer." And a little later, on the word pyrê [πυρί, in fire], he says: "He goes on, in the allegory, from the comparison with those who were burned in the valley of Hinnom, using the things here mentioned for the burning and conflagration of them." Kimchi says the same as Forerius: Tophet is the valley of Hinnom; he says it was prepared for them before their death, for the prophet prophesied this before the decree of their slaughter had come: וכמות גופם תמות גם כן נפשם ותהיה בגי הגם, "and as their body dies, so their soul also dies, and it will be in the valley of Gehenna." I have quoted this passage to confirm what we argued in the first part of our Antibarbarus, namely that Kimchi, when he says that souls die and perish, yet does not deny their annihilation [Ἀφανισμὸν]. About the resurrection of the wicked bodies there is another question, on which see the notes of the most learned Cocceius on the tractate Sanhedrin. Aben Ezra: תפתה שם מקום מטונף סביב ירושלים ושם ישליכו כל דמן ויעלה ממנו עשן, "Tophet is the name of a defiled place around Jerusalem, where all the refuse was thrown, and smoke rose from it," and so on.

units.la: Verf. 13. Qui excutit manus suas ab omni munere.] Ita Vulg. Locus iste citatur ex Gregorio in jure canon. parte 2. caus. I. qu. 1. cap. sunt nonnulli. Agitur illic adversus Simoniacos. Sunt nonnulli, inquit, qui quidem nummorum præmia ex ordinatione non accipiant, & tamen sacros ordines pro humana gratia vel laudelargiuntur &c. Sed Propheta inquit, cum virum justum describeret, ait, Beatus qui excutit manus suas ab omni munere. Non dixit solum, munere, sed ab omni munere, quia aliud est munus ab obsequio, aliud à manu, aliud à lingua. Vide sequentia. At in Ebraeo non comparet illa universalis nota Fatcor ejus adjectione non corruptum esse locum, sed quia in ea hunc discursum fundat Gregorius, annotandum duxi
units.tr: Vers. 13. "He that shaketh his hands from every gift" (Qui excutit manus suas ab omni munere). So the Vulgate. This verse is quoted from Gregory in the canon law, part 2, cause 1, question 1, chapter "sunt nonnulli". The passage there is directed against the Simoniacs. "There are some," he says, "who do not receive payment for ordination, and yet bestow holy orders for human favour or for praise," and so on. But the Prophet, when describing the just man, says: "Blessed is he who shakes his hands free of every bribe." He did not say only "bribe," but "every bribe," because a gift differs from a service, and a gift from the hand differs from one from the tongue. See what follows. But in the Hebrew that universal word does not appear. I admit the text is not corrupted by the addition of it, but because Gregory bases his argument upon it, I thought it worth noting.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII.
units.tr: Chapter 37.

units.la: Verf. 35. Propter David seruum meum ] id est, propter promissionem Davidi factam, inquit Junius ad 2. Reg. 19. 34. Quid si, propter Christum seruum meum? Certe Christus vocatur feruus Dei, e.g. Jes. 53. Idem vocatur David. Jerem.
units.tr: Verse 35. "On account of David my servant": that is, on account of the promise made to David, says Junius on 2 Kings 19:34. What if it means "on account of Christ my servant"? Certainly Christ is called God's servant, e.g. Isaiah 53. The same one is called David. Jeremiah.

units.la: Pontificii ad meriti Davidis respectum putant, quasi dicere voluisset, propter merita Davidis &c. Aspicis hic defunctorum merita vivis prodesse, inquit Pintus. Propter D. servum meum id est, merito ejus, inquit Carth. Sed rectius illud est quod addit, vel, ut impleam promissionem illi factam quod darem illi lucernam in Israel. In quam sententiam etiam Arias Mont. Miseret autem me Oleastrii cordati alias interpretis, qui in elucidatione morali hujus capitis, postquam de meritis sanctorum disseruisset, in hunc modum concludit, Audiant hoc Lutherani, & sinant nos sanctos venerari & orare, etiam mortuos, ob quorum merita Dominus nobis tot bona largitur.
units.tr: The Papists think it refers to respect for David's merits, as if he had meant to say, "on account of David's merits," etc. You see here, says Pintus, that the merits of the dead benefit the living. "On account of my servant David," that is, by his merit, says the Carthusian. But what he adds is more correct: "or, that I may fulfil the promise made to him, that I would give him a lamp in Israel." Arias Montanus agrees with this view. But I pity the otherwise sound interpreter Oleaster, who, in the moral explanation of this chapter, after discussing the merits of the saints, concludes in this way: Let the Lutherans hear this, and let them allow us to venerate and pray to the saints, even the dead, on whose merits the Lord bestows so many good things upon us.

units.la: CAP. XL.
units.tr: CHAPTER XL.

units.la: Verf. 1. Completa est malitia ejus, dimissa est iniquitas ejus: suscepit de manu Domini duplicia pro omnibus peccatis suis. ] Completam malitiam vulgo exponunt, ac si explicaretur per sequentia, dimissa est iniquitas ejus, cum tamen compleri malitia tunc potius dicatur, quando impleta est mensura iniquitatis & malitiae, id est, quando advenit tempus, quo puniridebet malitia, ut loquitur Oleastrius. Per duplicia vulgo intelligunt, multa beneficia, magnifica dona, vel duplicia id est, gratiam & gloriam; pro omnibus peccatis id est, non obstantibus omnibus peccatis ejus. Vide inter alios Pintum. Alii aliter. Sed omnes se torquent, neque se expediunt tamen. Ebraea ita habent, completa est [Hebrew] quod vulgatus verterat, malitia ejus, quae vox a libraris corrupta est in malitia, fatentibus Oleastrio, Pinto, Sa, Aria Montano, Aliisque hujus Prophetae interpretibus, quibus addo & Jansenium in Concord. Evang. pag. mihi 102. Col. 2 Hoc tam evidens est, ut negari a nemine possit, qui Ebraice legere didicit. Hoc tot praestantes inter ipsos Pontificios Doctores ostenderunt. Et tamen Romani Correctores non Judicarunt corrigendum esse, esse, militia, ut loquitur Lucas Brugensis, in locis insigniorib. Rom. Correctionis Licet vero Sixtus V. mendosam hanc lectionem malitia Ecclesiæ ceu authenticam obtruserit, non potuit tamen multorum Catholicorum ora oppilare, quamvis rem ipsam libere edissertarent. Sed videamus Ebraica, כִּי מִלְאָה צְבָאָה כִּי נִרְצָה עֲוֹנָהּ כִּי לְקָחָה מִיַּד יְהוָה כִּפְלַיִם בְּכָל חַטֹּאתֶיהָ Loquimini ad cor urbis Jerusalem (id est; consolamini eam dicere quæ grata ei futura sunt & non nolenti audire, cui phrasi non omnino illa Belgarum abhorrimilis est, loqui alicui ad os) Q. prædicate ei, completam esse militiam ejus, acceptatam esse pœnam iniquitatis ejus, accepisse eam e manu Domini duplicia pro omnibus peccatis suis non solum exercitum, sed & militiam & tempus militiæ præfinitum significare ad Jobi cap. vii. ostendimus: Hinc alii, completam esse militiam ejus, id est, finem tandem impositum esse omnibus molestiis & miseriis, quibus militans V.T. Ecclesia obnoxia fuit: Alii; præfinitum tempus ejus, tempus quod Deus O. M. vexationib. & afflictionibus ejus, præfiniverat. Quod ad ultima versus verba attinet; notat Pintus M. Lutherum articulo 36. citare hunc locum, ad probandum, non dari gratiam nisi pro peccatis. Ego verum an falsum sit illud Pinti effatum, in medio relinquo. Vide D. Joh. Tarnovium in Exercit. Biblicis pag. 593. edit. 3. Mantissæ loco adjiciam versionem LXX. Interpretum. λέλυται αὐτῆς ἡ ἀμαρτία, ὅτι λέλυται ἐκ χειρὸς Κυρίου διπλᾶ ἀμαρτήματα αὐτῆς. Quæ sic convertit Hieronymus, solutum est peccatum ejus, quia recepit de manu Domini duplicia peccata sua. Unde colligit idem Pater, non solvi peccata nostra, nisi de manu Domini receperimus ea. Nec idem est solui peccata atque dimitti. Cui enim dimittuntur, solutione non egeT. Cui autem solvuntur, ideo solvuntur, quia purgata sunt & soluta per pœnas, Hieron. in comm. Quæ itidem solutione non egent. Primo enim ־ hic non est causale. 2. non dicitur in originario, duplicia peccata sua, sed in vel pro peccatis. Ejusdem commatis sunt & illa B. Ambrosii verba, Quomodo deleantur peccata, audi dicentem, solutum est peccatum ejus, quia recipit de manu Domini duplicia peccata sua. Non ergo penitus sibi remitti peccatum postulat, sed moderata solutione deleri id est, ut in futurum ejus memoria deleatur. Hæc Ambrosius.
units.tr: Verse 1. Her warfare is accomplished, her iniquity is pardoned: she has received of the Lord's hand double for all her sins. The Vulgate commonly explains "her malice is completed" as if it were explained by what follows, her iniquity is pardoned. Yet malice is rather said to be completed when the measure of iniquity and malice is filled up, that is, when the time has come for the malice to be punished, as Oleaster puts it. Most understand "double" to mean many benefits and magnificent gifts, or else grace and glory; "for all her sins" means notwithstanding all her sins. See Pintus among others. Others explain it differently, but all of them twist and turn and yet do not extricate themselves. The Hebrew reads completa est [מִלְאָה], which the Vulgate had rendered malitia ejus [her malice]. This word was corrupted by copyists into "malice", as Oleaster, Pintus, Sa, Arias Montanus and the other interpreters of this prophet confess; I add also Jansenius in his Concordance of the Gospels, p. 102 of my edition, col. 2. This is so evident that no one who has learned to read Hebrew can deny it. Many outstanding Papist teachers have shown it. And yet the Roman correctors did not judge that it needed correcting, but kept "militia" (warfare), as Lucas Brugensis says, in the more notable places of the Roman Correction. Although Sixtus V foisted this faulty reading "malitia" upon the Church as authentic, he could not stop the mouths of many Catholics, who discussed the matter itself freely. But let us look at the Hebrew: כִּי מִלְאָה צְבָאָה כִּי נִרְצָה עֲוֹנָהּ כִּי לְקָחָה מִיַּד יְהוָה כִּפְלַיִם בְּכָל חַטֹּאתֶיהָ Speak to the heart of Jerusalem (that is, comfort her: say to her things that will be pleasing to her and that she will not be unwilling to hear; a phrase not wholly unlike the Dutch to speak to someone to his face): proclaim to her that her warfare is completed, that the punishment of her iniquity is accepted, that she has received of the Lord's hand double for all her sins. That "warfare" signifies not only an army but also the service and the appointed time of that service, as we showed at Job chap. vii. Hence some explain: "her warfare is completed", that is, an end has at last been put to all the troubles and miseries to which the militant Old Testament Church was subject; others: "her appointed time", the time which God Almighty had fixed for her vexations and afflictions. As to the last words of the verse, Pintus notes that Luther cites this passage in article 36 to prove that grace is not given except for sins. I leave it open whether Pintus's assertion is true or false. See Dr John Tarnovius in Exercitationes Biblicae, p. 593, 3rd edition. By way of appendix I shall add the version of the Seventy: λέλυται αὐτῆς ἡ ἀμαρτία, ὅτι λέλυται ἐκ χειρὸς Κυρίου διπλᾶ ἀμαρτήματα αὐτῆς. Jerome translates this: "her sin is loosed, because she received of the Lord's hand her double sins." From this the same Father concludes that our sins are not loosed unless we have received them from the Lord's hand. Nor is being loosed the same as being forgiven. For those whose sins are forgiven have no need of loosing; but those whose sins are loosed are loosed because they have been cleansed and loosed through punishments, Jerome on the Commentary; these likewise have no need of loosing. For, first, the particle here is not causal. Second, the original does not say "her double sins", but "for" or "in place of her sins". Of the same kind are also the words of St Ambrose: How sins are blotted out, hear him saying: "her sin is loosed, because she received of the Lord's hand double her sins." He therefore does not ask that his sin be remitted altogether, but that it be blotted out by a moderate loosing, that is, so that his memory is blotted out for the future. Thus Ambrose.

units.la: Antequam ad hoc caput protollam gradum, libet adscribere verba B. Hieronymi quæ extant in ejus comm. ad superius caput XL. pag. 152. Edit. Basil. Hebræi asserunt, inquit, nec hac de re ulla apud illos dubitatio est, spiritum S. lingua sua appellari genere fœminino id est, רוח קדשה Et Paulo post, Ebræi illud Ps. 122. sicut oculi ancillæ in manibus dominæ suæ; animam interpretantur ancillam; & dominam Spiritum S. Sed & in Evangelio, quod juxta Ebræos scriptum Nazaræi lectitant, Dominus loquitur, modo me tulit mater mea Spirit. Sanct. Nemo autem hac in parte scandalizetur; quod dicatur apud Ebræos Spiritus genere fœminino, cum nostra lingua appelletur genere masc. & Græco sermone, neutro. In divinitate enim nullus est sexus. Et ideo in tribus principalibus linguis, quibus titulis dominicæ passionis scriptus est tribus generib. appellatur ut sciamus nullius esse generis quod diversum est. Hæc Hieronymus. Quæ non ita accipiet Lector, quasi רוח semper fœmininum esset, quomodo Spiritus Latinis Mascul. & πνεῦμα Græcis neutrum est. Namque non solum cum ventum, sed & cum Spiritum significat communis generis est Jes. 32.15. עד יערה עלינו רוח ממרום donec effundatur super nos Spiritus ex alto. Nunc ad cap. XLII. accingamur. Vers. 1. LXX. hoc modo transtulere. Ἰακὼβ ὁ παῖς μου ἀντιλήψομαι αὐτοῦ Ἰσραὴλ ὁ ἐκλελεγμένος μου, προσέσχατο αὐτὸν ἡ ψυχή μου. Jacob puer meus, assumam eum: Israel electus meus, suscepit eum anima mea. Citatio Matthæi cap. XII. non sinit nos dubitare quin sint verba Patris de unigenito suo filio, Redemptore nostro, Jesu Christo. Quid ergo sibi volunt illa Jacob & Israel? Audi Augustinum de civit. Dei xx. 30. Loquitur de Christo sub nomine Jacob & Israel, de cujus semine corpus accepit. Et Paulo post, In Ebræo non legitur Jacob & Israel. Sed quod ibi legitur servus meus, nimirum LXX. Interpretes volentes admonere quatenus id accipiendum sit, quia sc. propter formam servi dictum est, in qua se Altissimum humillimum præbuit, ipsius hominis nomen ad eum significandum posuerunt; de cujus genere eadem forma suscepta est. Hæc B. Augustinus, argute & subtiliter. Sed quanto satius fuisset, in eo subsistere, voces illas ab Ebræo textu abesse, & ex aliis locis, ubi ea cum Jacob & Israel simul legungunguntur, (e.gr. 44.1.) ab imperita manu infartas esse. Eusebius Demonstrat. Evang. ix. pag. mihi. 281. postquam contulisset textum Græcum Jesaiæ & Matthæi, sic inquit, τὸν ἢ Ἐμμανουὴλ, ἴδε ὁ παῖς μου, ὁ ἀγαπητός μου, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή μου. καὶ Ἰακὼβ, καὶ Ἰσραὴλ, ἐμνήσθη, ὁ γὰρ εἶπεν, Ἰακὼβ ὁ παῖς μου, Ἰσραὴλ, ὁ ἐκλεκτός μου, ἀσφάλεια δὲ ἐξένεγκεν εἰπών, ἴδε ὁ παῖς μου, καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητός μου. Ὅτι, ὡς μὲν ἐν τῇ ἐβραϊκῇ γλώσσῃ, ἐν Ἰακὼβ καὶ τὸ Ἰσραὴλ ὄνομα.
units.tr: Before I take the next step to this chapter, it is worth adding the words of St Jerome in his commentary on the preceding chapter XL, p. 152 of the Basel edition. "The Hebrews assert," he says, "and there is no doubt among them on this point, that the Holy Spirit is called in their language by the feminine gender, that is, רוח קדשה [ruach qodesha]." A little later: "The Hebrews interpret that verse of Ps. 122, 'as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress', so that the soul is the maidservant and the Holy Spirit the mistress. And in the Gospel which the Nazarenes read, written according to the Hebrews, the Lord says: 'Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me.' No one should be scandalised that among the Hebrews the Spirit is of the feminine gender, when in our language it is of the masculine and in Greek of the neuter. For there is no sex in the divinity. And so in the three principal languages, in which the title of the Lord's passion was written, it is named by three genders, so that we may know that what is different is of no gender." Thus Jerome. The reader should not take this to mean that רוח is always feminine, just as spiritus is masculine in Latin and πνεῦμα [pneuma] is neuter in Greek. For not only when it means wind but also when it means Spirit it is of common gender: Isa. 32.15, "until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high" [עד יערה עלינו רוח ממרום]. Now let us turn to chapter XLII, verse 1. The LXX translated it thus: "Jacob my servant, I will uphold him; Israel my elect, my soul has received him" [Ἰακὼβ ὁ παῖς μου, ἀντιλήψομαι αὐτοῦ· Ἰσραὴλ ὁ ἐκλελεγμένος μου, προσέσχατο αὐτὸν ἡ ψυχή μου]. "Jacob my servant, I will take hold of him; Israel my chosen one, my soul has accepted him." The citation in Matthew ch. 12 leaves us in no doubt that these are the Father's words about his only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, Jesus Christ. What then do the words Jacob and Israel mean? Hear Augustine, De civitate Dei xx. 30: he speaks of Christ under the name of Jacob and Israel, from whose seed he took the body. And a little later: "In the Hebrew the words Jacob and Israel are not read. But where it reads 'my servant', the LXX translators, wishing to warn in what sense this is to be understood, namely that it was said because of the form of a servant, in which the Most High showed himself most humble, put the name of the man himself to signify him; from whose kind the same form was taken." Thus St Augustine, cleverly and subtly. But how much better it would have been to stop at this: that those words are absent from the Hebrew text, and that where they are read together with Jacob and Israel (e.g. 44.1), they were stuffed in by some unskilled hand. Eusebius, Demonstratio evangelica ix, p. 281 of my edition, after comparing the Greek text of Isaiah and Matthew, says: "Behold my servant, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased" [ἴδε ὁ παῖς μου, ὁ ἀγαπητός μου, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή μου]. "And he mentioned Jacob and Israel, for he said, 'Jacob my servant, Israel my elect', but he brought out the word 'behold, my servant and my beloved'." And as in the Hebrew language the name of Jacob and of Israel [is one and the same].

units.la: Porro in voce suscipiam, quos non ludos dedere prisci Interpretes? Lyra, suscipiam eum, quia humanitas Christi assumpta est in unitatem suppositi divini. Per hoc enim quod dicitur, suscipiam eum, non est intelligendum quod pater naturam humanam assumserit, quia solus filius est humanatus, sed hanc assumptionem tota Trinitas fecit. Eadem interpretatio probavit se Dionysio Carthusiano, qui & illam præmisit, suscipiam eum id est, omnia opera ejus & preces acceptas habebit. At nec hæc nec illam admittit vel vox Ebræa אַתְמוֹךְ / vel Græca ἀντιλαμβάνομαι, unde Pagn. innitar ei. q. d. apprehendam eum ut illi innitar, sicuti Rex fideli & dilecto ministro, Kimchi, דרך משל כמו המלך הנשען בעברו הנאמן לו / Metaphorica locutio, instar Regis qui innititur servo suo fideli. Alii sustento eum, vel fulcio eum. Coronidis loco addam Chaldaeam paraphrasin, הא עבדי משיחא אקרכנה בחירי ראתרעי בה מיפרי Ecce servus meus Messias, electus meus in quo complacuit sibi ὁ λόγος μου. Qui locus evidenter ostendit per מיסרא ד id est, λόγον κυρίως, non semper intelligi Christum, sed saepe πεῖφερειν Dei esse, qualis in Ebraismo, anima Dei vel hominis pro ipso Deo vel homine. Sic quod Gen. viii. 21. dicit Moses, Et dixit Dominus in corde suo, Oncelos reddidit, in sermone suo, במימרה in sermone suo, quod Hellenistae dicerent, θεὸς ἑαυτὸν, ut hic Symmachus & Joh. vii. 35. οἴπου ἐὰν Ἰουδαῖοι θεὸς ἑαυτὸς vel θεὸς τῷ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶν, ut Theodot. vel ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ. Huc citat & Drusius ex Thargum Jonathanis locum. Num. xv. 32. Surrexit vir e domo Joseph, dixitque במימרה / ibo, evellam ligna &c. Et Ecclesiastes i.1. dixit in sermone suo. Et Ruth 3.8. quomodo fecit Phaltiel, filius Lais, qui fixit gladium בין מימרה ובין עיכל בת שאול.
units.tr: Further, for the word suscipiam ("I will uphold"), what sort of games did the early translators play? Lyra: "I will uphold him, because the humanity of Christ was assumed into the unity of the divine person. For by the words 'I will uphold him' it is not to be understood that the Father assumed human nature, since only the Son was made man, but the whole Trinity effected this assumption." The same interpretation pleased Dionysius the Carthusian, who also put forward the rendering "I will uphold him", that is, "he will have accepted all his works and prayers." But neither this nor that rendering is allowed either by the Hebrew word אַתְמוֹךְ ['atmokh] or by the Greek ἀντιλαμβάνομαι [antilambanomai], whence Pagninus: "I will lean on him", as if to say, "I will take hold of him so that I may lean on him, just as a king leans on a faithful and beloved minister." Kimchi: "By a figure of speech, like a king who leans on his faithful servant" [דרך משל כמו המלך הנשען בעברו הנאמן לו]. Others: "I will sustain him", or "I will prop him up." As a crown to this, I will add the Chaldean paraphrase: "Behold my servant Messiah, my elect, in whom my word [מֵימְרִי / meimreh] is well pleased." This passage clearly shows that through the word מֵימְרָא [memra], that is, properly logos, it is not always Christ who is understood, but often a manner of speaking belonging to God, as in Hebrew idiom the soul of God or of man stands for God himself or man himself. So where Moses says in Gen. 8.21, "And the Lord said in his heart", Onkelos rendered it "in his word" [במימרה / bimemra], as the Hellenists would say θεὸς ἑαυτὸν; so here Symmachus, and John 7.35 "Where will the Jews go?" with θεὸς ἑαυτὸς or θεὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῶν as Theodotion has it, or ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ [en tē dianoia]. Drusius also cites from the Targum of Jonathan a passage at Num. 15.32, "A man rose up from the house of Joseph and said" [במימרה / bimemra], "I will go, I will cut down the wood", etc. And Eccl. 1.1: "he said in his word" [dixit in sermone suo]. And Ruth 3.8: "as Phaltiel, son of Laish, did, who thrust a sword" [בין מימרה ובין עיכל בת שאול] "between his word and his [...] Michal, daughter of Saul."

units.la: Vide notas marginales: none legible apart from body text. inter sermonem suum & inter Michal filiam Saulis. Sed quid fiet loco Jes. 48. 16 ubi Christus italoquitur. Dominus Deus misit me [illegible, ~6 letters] / Chald. [illegible, ~6 letters]?

units.la: CAP. XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 43.

units.la: Verf. 20. Quemadmodum ex Psalmo 92. 13, Phoenicem fabulosam avem, ita ex hoc loco, prout is LXX. versus est, Sirenas, fabulosa monstra nonnulli probare sategerunt. Ita enim habet Graecus textus, [illegible, ~8 letters]: id est, Benedicent mihi bestiae agri, Sirenes & filiae Struthionum. Sed notandum bene, Ebraea aliter sonare, Glorificabit, me bestiae agri, [illegible, ~4 letters] id est, dracones & filiae ululae. Hieronymus, Pro Draconibus, quos solus Theodotio, ut in Ebraico scritum est, appellavit [illegible, ~4 letters] (Iuvia) reliqui Sirenas interpretati sunt, animalia portentosa, quae dulci carmine & mortifero navigantes Scyllaeis canibus lacerandos praecipitabant. Hoc que significat, quod voluptati prius & luxuriae dediti ad servitutem Domini convertantur. Licet melius sit Dracones intelligi quia junguntur & Struthiones, ut quia semel de bestiis solitudinis loquebatur, haec animantia ponteret, quae deserto familiaria sunt. Ad vers. 4. notat Cl. Tarnovius in exercit. Bibl. p. 595. Edit. 3: cum a nonnullis sic intellectum, quasi Deus promitteret mundo filium suum, ego dilexi te & dabo hominem pro te. Sed [illegible, ~4 letters] illic * collective positum esse, & antecedens versus & quae hoc versu 4. sequuntur [illegible, ~8 letters] & nationes pro anima tua, evincunt. Vide ad vers. 3. Jun. Scholia, & observa vers. 4. melius a Piscat. & Vulgato redditum, dilexi te, & dedi homines, (alios, de quibus vers. 3.) pro te & nationes (praedictas) pro anima tua, id est, loco animae tuae, quam a Junio, subjecti homines tibi & nationes desiderio tuo. Ebraea clara sunt [illegible, ~8 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: Verse 20. Just as they tried to prove the fabulous phoenix from Psalm 92:13, so some have tried to prove the fabulous sirens from this passage, as it stands in the Septuagint. The Greek text reads [illegible], that is, "The beasts of the field shall bless me, the sirens and the daughters of the ostriches." But it must be carefully noted that the Hebrew reads differently: "The beasts of the field shall honour me, [illegible], that is, dragons and the daughters of the owl." Jerome, on "dragons": Theodotion alone, as it is written in the Hebrew, rendered it [illegible] (Iuvia), while the others translated it "sirens," monstrous creatures which, with sweet song, drew sailors to their deaths and cast them down to be torn apart by Scylla's dogs. This signifies that those who were first given over to pleasure and luxury are turned to the service of the Lord. Yet it is better to understand "dragons," since they are joined with "ostriches," as if, having once spoken of the beasts of the wilderness, he were now naming these creatures, which are familiar to the desert. At verse 4, the learned Tarnovius, in his Biblical Exercises, page 595, third edition, notes that although some have understood it thus, as if God were promising the world his Son, "I have loved you, and I will give men for you," the collective sense is plainly intended, as both the preceding verse and what follows in verse 4, "and nations for your soul," prove. See on verse 3 in Junius' Scholia, and observe that verse 4 is better rendered by Piscator and the Vulgate: "I have loved you, and I have given men (the others mentioned in verse 3) for you, and nations (the aforesaid) for your soul," that is, in place of your soul; Junius renders it, "men subjected to you, and nations at your desire." The Hebrew is clear [illegible] [illegible].

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV.

units.la: Verf. 1. Haec dicit Dominus Christo meo Cyro &c. ] Ebr. [illegible, ~6 letters] unctio suo Cyro LXX. [illegible, ~6 letters], Hieron. Scia in hoc capitulo non solum Latinorum sed & Graecorum plurimos vehementer errare, existimantium scriptum esse. Sic dicit Dominus Christo, meo Domino, intelligatur juxta illud, Pluit Dominus à Domino, & Dixit Dominus Domino meo. Neque enim κύριος [?], quod Dominum sonat, sed Κύριος dicitur, qui Ebraice appellatur Chores, Regi Persarum &c. Et Paulo post ad vers. 4. assimilavi te & non cognovisti me, ita inquit, non cognovisti me id est, idola coluisti, non Deum. In quo loco inquit, non satis mirari queo quae sit stultitia legentium, ut haec ad Christum referant. Sed ad hoc respondent alii, ea quae de Cyro per modum laudis dicuntur de Christo posse exponi ut antitypo, reliqua soli Cyro relinquenda esse. Ego opinor nullum hodie tam fatuellum repertum iri, qui hunc locum literaliter & primario de Christo interpretari ausit: At qui cum scholasticis eum de Cyro ut typo, Christo, ut Antitypo interpretentur, puto esse plurimos. Sed quae haec ingeniorum luxuries est, ex quolibet homine typum Christi fabricari? Accommodatio fiat horum & similium locorum ad Christum, ita tamen ut literali sensui sua semper constet authoritas, ea cautione, ne ex Scriptura fiat cereus nasus: Ne typi obtrudantur quos non expresse in Sacris literis vel eodem vel alioloco Spiritus S. indicavit. Vide quae hac de re diximus Antibarb. nostri, libro 1. errore generali 7. pag. 168. & confer cum illis Apologiam Cl. Joh. Tarnovii pag. 236. & seq. exercit. Biblic. Edit. ultimae, Inter sensum literalem alicujus loci Biblici & ejus accommodationes semper distingue, inquit, ex quo haec accurate mihi declaravit meus Patruus praeceptor meus venerandus (Rev. Theologum D. Paulum Tarnovium intelligit) qui mihi jam egregium ad hanc rem locum suppeditavit ex Luthero, Tomo 2. in Gen. cap. 15. p. 58. Et Paulo post ad loca sibi ab adversario objecta, Joh. 3. de Serpente aeneo Joh. 6. de Manna, Matth. 12. de Jona, 1. Cor. 9. 9. de bove triturante, 2. Cor. 3. de velamine Mosis Gal. 4. de Sara & Hagar, ita respondet in plerisque similitudines tantum reperiri, quas licet ex omnibus rebus sumere, dum modo id fiat bono, neque statim pro typo sacro habeatur, quod similitudinem aliquam praebere potest & elegantem comparationem, Verbo, Non statim typus est, ubi potest institui comparatio. Sed ad rem. Audio illud objici ex vers. 4. assimilavi te unde & Baronius in apparatu probat Cyrum typum Christi fuisse. Nec abnuere videtur Hieron. quando in Comm. sic infit, vocavi te nomine tuo — ne putareris esse ille Christus, cui assimilatus es, & in cujus typum & imaginem praecessisti. Et Sa, Assimilavi sc. Pastori, vel q. d. feci ut esses figura & similitudo Christi. Sed judicem adeamus, textum originarium. Is nobis exhibet vocem ארא / id est, cognominavi te, interpretibus Pagn. Aria. M. Oleastr. Forerio, & agnoscente ipso Sa. Quamvis illi quoque qui vulgatam interpretationem retinuere, alias interpretationes attulerint, quas videre est apud Lyram, Carthus. Pintum & alios. Lubet audire Pintum, assimilavi te nonnullis servis meis, quos priusquam nascerentur, nominavi. Vel assimilavi te id est, cognominavi te. Nam non solum vocavi te Cyrum, sed etiam Regem (Messiam meum, Oleastr.) antequam editus esses in lucem. Junius tò cognominare sic explicat ut sit presfior ἐξιγνως antecedentis, vocavi te de nomine tuo, proprium illi nomen, teste Herodoto & Justino, fuit Spaco id est, canis, Medorum lingua, à * cane quae expositum infantem lactaverat. Coresch vero cognomen fuit honorificum, à Persib. inditum, quod sonat Dominum. Nam eadem quoque ratione Coresch apud Persas est Solis, quem colunt, epitheton. Haec Junius. Quibus non omnino respondent illa quae Arias Mont. ad calcem cap. xliv. commentatus est. Notet autem hic lector, Junium & Trem. cum ubique fere Ebraeum propriorum nominum sonum retinuerint, hic tamen non Coresch., sed Cyrus reddidisse, cujus vocis Vocales Ebraicae consonae etiam admittunt ... Küρ& & ad Graecum xu-ρ proprius accedunt.
units.tr: Verse 1. "Thus says the Lord to my anointed Cyrus, etc." ] The Hebrew has "his anointed, Cyrus," and the Septuagint and Jerome read similarly. Know that in this chapter not only most of the Latins but also very many of the Greeks greatly err, thinking it is written that "Thus says the Lord to Christ, my Lord," to be understood in the way of "The Lord rained from the Lord" and "The Lord said to my Lord." For the word is not κύριος [kyrios], which means Lord, but Κύριος [Kyrios], which in Hebrew is called Chores, and it refers to the king of the Persians, etc. A little later, on verse 4, "I have made you like me, and you have not known me," he says: "you have not known me," that is, you worshipped idols, not God. On this passage he says: I cannot sufficiently wonder at the folly of those readers who refer these things to Christ. But others reply that those things which are said of Cyrus by way of praise can be expounded of Christ as the antitype, while the rest must be left to Cyrus alone. I think no one so foolish will be found today as to dare to interpret this place literally and primarily of Christ; but there are very many who, with the scholastics, interpret it of Cyrus as the type and of Christ as the antitype. But what a luxuriance of wit is this, to fabricate a type of Christ out of any man whatever? Let these and similar passages be accommodated to Christ, yet so that the literal sense always keeps its authority, with this caution: that Scripture does not become a wax nose. Let no types be forced upon us which the Holy Spirit has not expressly indicated in the sacred letters, either in this place or in another. See what we have said on this matter in our Antibarbarus, book 1, general error 7, p. 168, and compare with it the Apology of the renowned John Tarnovius, p. 236 and following, in the Exercitationes Biblicae, last edition. "Between the literal sense of any biblical place and its accommodations, always distinguish," he says, which my venerable teacher and paternal uncle (he means the reverend theologian Dr Paul Tarnovius) explained to me clearly, and who already supplied me with an excellent passage on this matter from Luther, vol. 2 on Genesis ch. 15, p. 58. And a little later, regarding the places which his opponent objected to him: John 3 on the bronze serpent, John 6 on the manna, Matthew 12 on Jonah, 1 Cor. 9:9 on the ox treading out the grain, 2 Cor. 3 on the veil of Moses, Gal. 4 on Sarah and Hagar, he replies thus: in most cases only similitudes are found, which may be drawn from all things, provided this is done well and the thing is not at once held to be a sacred type, since something may offer a similitude and an elegant comparison. In short: not every place where a comparison can be made is at once a type. But to the matter. I hear that this is objected from verse 4, "I have made you like," whence Baronius in his Apparatus also proves that Cyrus was a type of Christ. Nor does Jerome seem to deny it, when in his commentary he begins: "I called you by your name — lest you be thought to be that Christ to whom you were made like, and in whose type and image you went before." And Sa: "I made like, namely to the shepherd, or as if to say: I made you to be a figure and likeness of Christ." But let us go to the judge, the original text. It gives us the word ארא, that is, "I named you," as rendered by Pagninus, Arias, M. Oleaster, Forerius, and Sa himself acknowledges it. Although those too who kept the Vulgate interpretation have offered other explanations, which may be seen in Lyra, the Carthusian, Pintus and others. Let us hear Pintus: "I made you like certain servants of mine, whom I named before they were born." Or "I made you like," that is, "I named you." For I not only called you by your name Cyrus, but also King (my Messiah, Oleaster) before you were born into the light. Junius explains the verb cognominare so that it is an explanation [ἐξήγησις] of the preceding clause, "I called you by your name." His proper name, according to Herodotus and Justin, was Spaco, that is, dog, in the Median tongue, from the dog which had suckled the exposed infant. Coresch, however, was an honorific cognomen, given by the Persians, which means Lord. For by the same reasoning Coresch among the Persians is an epitheton of the Sun, whom they worship. Thus Junius. Arias Montanus, who commented on this at the end of chapter 44, does not wholly agree with these points. Let the reader note here that Junius and Tremellius, though they retained the Hebrew sound of proper names almost everywhere, here rendered not Coresch but Cyrus, whose Hebrew consonants and vowels also admit this, and they come closer to the Greek Κῦρος [Kyros].

units.la: Verf. 8. Rorate coeli desuper & nubes pluant justum: aperiatur terra & germinet salvatorem. Et justitia oriatur simul. Ego Dominus creavi eum] Haec verba ab erudito & pio Doctore aliquo modo accommodari posse ad Christum non ibo inficias, literaliter & primario de Christo vel extra typum vel sub typo dicta esse, non video qui probari possit. Tres modi sunt, quibus probari possit, aliquem scripturae locum ad Christum pertinere. 1. authoritas N. Testamenti. 2. Excellentia attributorum. 3. Analogia & nexus necessarius typi & Antitypi id est, Christi. Hic vero eorum nullum video. Quin contra sicut de solo Cyro coepit loqui, de eodem nunc vaticinium continuat. Et sicut in superioribus illud versus quarti, & non cognovisti me, nullo modo Christo applicari poterat, ita & hic nonnulla sunt quae Salvatori, non nisi cum summa violentia tribui possunt. Videamus singula.
units.tr: Verse 8. "Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the clouds pour down the righteous: let the earth open and bring forth a Saviour, and let righteousness spring up together. I the Lord have created him." ] I shall not deny that these words can be accommodated in some way to Christ by a learned and pious teacher, but I do not see how it can be proved that they are said literally and primarily of Christ, whether outside a type or under a type. There are three ways by which it could be shown that some passage of Scripture pertains to Christ: (1) the authority of the New Testament; (2) the excellence of the attributes; (3) the analogy and necessary connection of type and antitype, that is, of Christ. Here, however, I see none of these. Indeed, just as the prophet began by speaking only of Cyrus, so now he continues the prophecy about the same man. And just as in the earlier passage, verse 4, "and you have not known me," could in no way be applied to Christ, so here too there are some things which can be attributed to the Saviour only with the greatest violence. Let us look at each.

units.la: Rorate coeli desuper &c] Sunt qui putant esse verba Prophetae qui postquam liberationem Judaicae captivitatis praedixisset, nominatim de signasset liberatorem, subito in has voces eruperit, quibus exprimit vota eorum qui in captivitate tot annis detenti magno desiderio & liberationem & florentem Ecclesiæ & Reip. statum quasi è cœlo delapsurum expectabant. Sed verba hujus versus ultima, ego creavi eum, ostendunt, esse verba Dei, quibus cœlo & terræ quasi imperet, ut cooperentur & ut sic dicam, omnes vires suas intendant ad procurandam populi liberationem. Quod Deus cœlo & terræ hic imperat, id promittit populo suo, fore vid. ut gaudio ex captivitate soluta abunde perfundantur & saturentur. Provocat, inquit Jun. res creatas omnes ad testificandum & prædicandum salutare justumque Dei opus & quibuscunque modis poterunt, ministandum ei, quæ omnia enuntiantur allegorice. Kimchi אמר זה על דרך משל על התשועה שתבא לישראל כאלו מלאכי שמים באים לעזרתם וכן יושבי הארץ hoc est, dicit hæc figurate de salute quæ Israelitis eventura esset, quasi angeli jubeantur venire in auxilium ipsorum, atque itidem habitatores terra. Hieron. Quidam putant hæc hærere superioribus quæ dicuntur, & Cyro laxante captivos, cœlum terramque lætari μετανυμιχῶς, pro eo, quod est illos qui in cælo morantur & terra. Quicquid sit, Loquitur de Rege Corefch, cum venturum & liberaturum populum Israel prædicit, inquit B. Lutherus in nota marginali. Et in Comm. Nos scimus agi in hoc capite de promissa liberatione per Cyrum.
units.tr: "Drop down, ye heavens, from above, etc." ] There are those who think these are the words of the prophet, who, after foretelling the liberation from the Jewish captivity and naming the liberator, suddenly burst out into these words, by which he expresses the wishes of those who, held captive for so many years, were awaiting with great longing both the deliverance and the flourishing state of the Church and commonwealth, as if it were to fall from heaven. But the last words of this verse, "I the Lord have created him," show that these are the words of God, by which he commands heaven and earth, as it were, to cooperate, and, so to speak, to bend all their powers to bringing about the liberation of the people. That God here commands heaven and earth, he promises to his people: namely, that they will be abundantly filled and satisfied with joy after being freed from captivity. He summons, says Junius, all created things to bear witness to and proclaim the saving and righteous work of God, and to serve it in whatever ways they can; all of which is said allegorically. Kimchi: "He says this by way of parable, concerning the salvation which will come to Israel, as if the angels of heaven were coming to their help, and likewise the inhabitants of the earth" [אמר זה על דרך משל על התשועה שתבא לישראל כאלו מלאכי שמים באים לעזרתם וכן יושבי הארץ]. Jerome: Some think these things cohere with what is said above, and that when Cyrus loosens the captives, heaven and earth rejoice by metonymy, in place of those who dwell in heaven and earth. Whatever the case, he speaks of King Coresch, when he predicts that he will come and liberate the people of Israel, says the blessed Luther in a marginal note. And in the commentary: "We know that this chapter deals with the promised liberation through Cyrus."

units.la: Nubes pluant justum ] An hoc elogium competit Gentili Cyro, inquies? An is de cœlo descendit? An justi nomen meretur? Vis ergo Christum hic intelligi per nubes, vel angelos cum Dion. vel Apoll. Vide Carthus. Sed Resp. 1. esse prosopopoiam & allegorice hæc enuntiari. Neq; enim nubes ipsum quoque Christum pluisse vere dixeris. 2. In Ebr. non esse justum, sed justitiam. זושחקים ידלו צדק & nubes (alii æther, vel cœli, vide Piscatoris scholia Latina ad Ps. 18.) fluant justitia, Lxx. ὑ αἱ νεφέλαι ἐξάνατωσαν δικαιοσύνλω. Lutherus, und die Wolcken regnen de gerechtigkeit. Per justitiam intelligit effecta benignitatis suæ (certe צדק sæpe pro benignitate poni non eget probatione) & gratiæ. Aut liberationem hanc vocat justitiam id est, opus justitiæ, quia eam promiserat.
units.tr: Let the clouds pour down the righteous one. Someone will object: can this praise belong to the Gentile Cyrus? Did he come down from heaven? Does he deserve the name of righteous? Or do you want Christ to be understood here through the clouds, or the angels, as Dionysius and Apollinarius hold? See the Carthusian. My answer is, first, that this is a prosopopoeia and the thing is stated allegorically, for one could not truly say that the clouds themselves rained Christ. Second, in the Hebrew the word is not righteous but righteousness: הַשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל הִרְעִיפוּ צֶדֶק [let the heavens drop down righteousness], and "the clouds" (others take this as the ether or the heavens; see Piscator's Latin scholia on Ps. 18). The Septuagint has ἐξανατειλάτωσαν δικαιοσύνην [let them spring up with righteousness]. Luther renders it, "und die Wolcken regnen de gerechtigkeit" (and let the clouds rain righteousness). By righteousness he understands the effects of his kindness (surely tsedeq is often used for kindness, and needs no proof) and of grace. Or he calls this deliverance righteousness, that is, a work of righteousness, because he had promised it.

units.la: Aperiatur terra & germinet salvatorem ] vere dixit B. Lutherus in Comm. celebrem esse hunc locum in Ecclesia Papistarum & illustre argumentum ignorantia, quod ad B. Virginem eum accommodarunt. Audiamus non Lyram, non Carthusianum, aut ex veteribus scholasticis aliquem, sed Pintum Jesuitam, Terra illa sanctissima Maria semper-virgo aperiatur aratro Spiritus Sancti. Consentiat & dicat Gabrieli angelo, ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum & sic germinet salvatorem. Postea subjungit multa de unicorni, congregari multos venatores ad unicornem capiendum qui eum clamoribus obtundunt, at capi non posse, nisi virgo quaedam pulchra sedeat in Campo, ad quam unicornis veniat in cujus sinu quiescat & ita capiatur. Unicorni Christum comparat, Juxta illud inquit, quod dicitur in Psalmis (inmargine notatur Ps. 28. nobis 29.) & electus quemadmodum filius unicornis. Sed nihil tale in textu est. Ut ut B. August. locum illum de Christo interpretatus sit. Laudat illic divinus vates Creatorem suum a tribus potissimum effectis, inter quae principem locum tenet tonitru, quo de agit a versu. 3. usque ad 10. Vox Domini faciat ut exiliant (cedri Libani) sicut vitulus: facit ut exiliant Libanus, Sirjon, ut pullus unicornium. Schirjon nomen montis est Libano contigui, qui Hermon & Senir dicitur, Deut. III. 8. 9. Neque ullo modo per dilectum reddi potest & ad Christum referri. Pergit Pintus, Venatores fuerunt viri illi illustres V. T. qui ad eum clamabant ut veniret. Quemadmodum facit hoc in loco Jesaias. At non sat erat eos vociferari, sed ventura erat pulchra illa virgo sanctissima Maria humani generis reparatrix, in cujus utero filius Dei summus ille unicornis reclinaretur. Haec est terra illa sacratissima, de qua dicitur in Psalmis, Terra nostra dabit fructum suum. Et de qua in hoc loco dicit Jesaias aperiatur terra & germinet salvatorem. Haec Jesuita. Ubi multa male-sana. Nam quod ad unicornem attinet, quam vanum sit totum illud commentum, diximus, ad Deut. xxxiii. 17. Hausit nonnulla ex Carthusiano, quem nunc etiam audire juvat, aperiatur terra id est, virgo beata S. Maria, de qua dictum est, in die illo erit fructus terrae sublimis. Atque in Ps. 83. terra nostra dabit fructum suum. Tunc autem aperta est terra haec quando haec virgo perelecta consensum praebens dixit ad Angelum, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum. Tunc enim beatissimus & castissimus venter ejus clausus & intactus manens homini apertus est Deo, quem intra se concepit, & nostri corporis cinctorio induit. Et germinet Salvatorem vid. Christum, quem S. Maria sine dolore genuit, sicuti eum sine carnali voluntate concepit. Omnes quoq; futilitatis numeros hic implebit Oleastrius cordatus alias Interpres, Expende, inquit, quod non dicit pluite, sed, stillate cœli ut ostendat quam latenter, Christus in mundum venerit, juxta illud Psalmi (72. 6.) descendet velut pluvia in vellus, & ut stillicidia stillantia super terram. Possemus etiam terram intelligere corpus Christi terrenum (confer cum his quæ prima parte Anti-barbari nostri ad Ps.xcix.15. quæ de scabello pedum Domini commentati sumus) quod in passione innumerabilibus plagis à Judæis & Gentib apertum est, juxta illud Psal. 129.3. Supra dorsum meum araverunt peccatores &c. Sed quomodo corpus Salvatoris germinavit Salvatorem? Audi quomodo se expediat, Terra corporis Christi vomere spinarum, clavorum, verberum &c crucis arata justitiam & salutem nostram abunde produxit, ex cujus apertionibus salus hominum germinavit. Vides non potuisse Oleastrium hanc interpretationem obtinere nisi recederet à textu vulgato & ad originalem recurreret. Sic enim ille habet תִּפְתַּח אֶרֶץ וְיִפְרוּ יֵשַׁע וּצְדָקָה תַּצְמִיחַ יַחַד id est, aperiatur terra & fructificent salutem & justitia efflorescat simul. Jun. & [terrestria] edant salutem, & j. effl. simul Piscator, aperiat se terra & progerminent salus & justitia: ea (sc. terra) germinare faciat (eas) simul. Hanc interpretationem hausit ex Kimchio, qui eam alteri præfert, non obstante accentu Rebiang, qui in יִשַּׁע. Credo ne τὸ פְּרִי transitive & תַּצְמִיחַ intransitive, ut Junius, exponeret, Juniuih secuti sunt Angli, nisi quod plurale פְּרִי retulisse mihi videntur ad cœlum & terram, aperiat se terra, & producant (cœlum & terra) salutem, simul efflorescat justitia. Nec diversus abit B. Lutherus, nisi in vocula יִפְרוּ quam reddit ac si esset singulare הַפְּרִי die erde thue sich auff, und bringe heil, und gerechtigkeit wachse mit zu. Omnes conveniunt in abstractis. Etiam Lxx. ἀναλεάλατω ἡ γῆ καὶ βλαστησάτω ἔλεος, vel ut alii, βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ, ἡ ἀναλεάλατω ἔλεος, καὶ δικαιοσύνην βλαστησάτω ἅμα. Et dicat mihi aliquis, quæ necessitas Vulgatam impulerit abstracta ista in concreto demutandi. Ineptus essem si insisterem in vaticiniis de Christo & extra ea, abstracta sæpe pro concretis posita. Sed ubi gravis causa non subest, relinquenda suo loco abstracta esse erudite monet & docet Cl. Joh. Tarnovius p. 246. Excercit. Bibl. edit. in 8. Eum nunc porro vide, ut & Franzium de recta Interp. Scripturæ pag. 1340. Prolixiora enim illa sunt quam ut illa huc transferre libeat.
units.tr: Let the earth open and bring forth a Saviour. Luther rightly said in his Commentary that this passage is famous in the Church of the Papists and a notable proof of their ignorance, because they applied it to the Blessed Virgin. Let us hear not Lyra, not the Carthusian, nor any of the older schoolmen, but the Jesuit Pintus: "Let that most holy earth, Mary ever-virgin, be opened by the plough of the Holy Spirit. Let her consent and say to the angel Gabriel, 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word,' and thus 'bring forth the Saviour.'" Afterwards he adds much about the unicorn: many hunters gather to capture the unicorn and wear it down with their shouting, but it cannot be caught unless some beautiful maiden sits in a field, to whom the unicorn comes and in whose lap it rests, and so is taken. He compares Christ to the unicorn, saying, "In accordance with that which is said in the Psalms" (the margin notes Ps. 28, which is 29 in our numbering), "and the chosen one like the son of the unicorns." But nothing of the kind is in the text, however Blessed Augustine may have interpreted that place about Christ. There the divine poet praises his Creator chiefly for three effects, of which the first place is held by thunder, which he treats from verse 3 to verse 10: "The voice of the Lord makes the cedars of Lebanon leap like a calf; he makes Lebanon and Sirion leap like a young of the unicorns." Sirion is the name of a mountain adjoining Lebanon, which is called Hermon and Senir (Deut. 3:8, 9). Nor can it in any way be rendered "the beloved" and referred to Christ. Pintus goes on: "The hunters were those illustrious men of the Old Testament who called to him to come, as Isaiah does in this place." But it was not enough for them to shout; the beautiful and most holy Virgin Mary, restorer of the human race, was to come, in whose womb the supreme unicorn, the Son of God, would rest. This is that most sacred earth, of which the Psalm says, "Our land shall yield its fruit," and of which Isaiah in this place says, "Let the earth open and bring forth a Saviour." So the Jesuit. There is much here that is sick in mind. As for the unicorn, how empty the whole fancy is, I have shown on Deut. 33:17. He has borrowed some things from the Carthusian, whom it is now also pleasant to hear: "'Let the earth be opened,' that is, the blessed Virgin Saint Mary, of whom it is said, 'In that day the fruit of the earth shall be lofty' (Isa. 4:2), and in Ps. 85, 'Our land shall yield its fruit.' Then that earth was opened when this chosen virgin, giving her consent, said to the angel, 'Let it be to me according to your word.' For then her most blessed and chaste womb, remaining closed and untouched, was opened to God, whom she conceived within herself and clothed with the garment of our body. And 'let it bring forth the Saviour,' that is, Christ, whom Saint Mary bore without pain, just as she conceived him without carnal desire." Oleastro, a shrewd interpreter in other matters, will also fill all the numbers of this triviality here: "Weigh," he says, "that it does not say 'rain,' but 'drop down, heavens,' to show how secretly Christ came into the world, according to that psalm (72:6), 'He shall come down like rain upon the fleece, and like showers that water the earth.' We could also understand the earth to be the earthly body of Christ" (compare what we have discussed in the first part of our Anti-Barbarus on Ps. 99:5 about the footstool of the Lord's feet), "which in the Passion was opened by countless wounds from Jews and Gentiles, according to Ps. 129:3, 'The sinners have ploughed upon my back,' etc." But how did the body of the Saviour bring forth the Saviour? Hear how he gets out of it: "The earth of Christ's body, ploughed by the plough of thorns, nails, stripes, etc., of the cross, produced our righteousness and salvation abundantly, and from its openings the salvation of men sprang forth." You see that Oleaster could not maintain this interpretation except by departing from the Vulgate text and going back to the original. For he has: תִּפְתַּח אֶרֶץ וְיִפְרוּ יֵשַׁע וּצְדָקָה תַּצְמִיחַ יַחַד [let the earth open, and let salvation bear fruit, and let righteousness spring up together], that is, "let the earth open and let salvation and righteousness bud together." Junius [renders it] "let the earth bring forth salvation," and "let righteousness spring up together." Piscator: "let the earth open itself and salvation and righteousness sprout; let it (the earth) cause them to germinate together." He drew this interpretation from Kimchi, who prefers it to the other, notwithstanding the accent rebia on יֵשַׁע. I believe Junius explained פְּרִי transitively and תַּצְמִיחַ intransitively, and the English have followed Junius, except that they seem to me to have referred the plural יִפְרוּ to heaven and earth: "let the earth open itself, and let heaven and earth produce salvation, let righteousness spring up together." Luther does not depart far, except in the little word יִפְרוּ, which he renders as if it were the singular הַפְּרִי: "die erde thue sich auff, und bringe heil, und gerechtigkeit wachse mit zu" (let the earth open itself and bring forth salvation, and let righteousness grow with it). All agree in the abstract nouns. The Septuagint too has ἀνοιχθήτω ἡ γῆ καὶ βλαστησάτω ἔλεος [let the earth be opened and let mercy sprout], or as others have it, βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ, ἀνοιχθήτω ἔλεος, καὶ δικαιοσύνην βλαστησάτω ἅμα [let the earth sprout, let mercy be opened, and let righteousness sprout together]. Someone may ask me what necessity drove the Vulgate to change these abstracts into concretes. I would be foolish if I insisted that the prophecies about Christ and nothing else are the only places where abstracts are often put for concretes. But where no serious reason lies, the learned Johannes Tarnovius, p. 246 of the Exercitationes Biblicae, octavo edition, rightly teaches and advises that abstracts should be left in their place. Look at him further, and also Franz on the correct interpretation of Scripture, p. 1340. For those passages are too lengthy to be worth transferring here.

units.la: Verf. 14. Tantum in te est Deus & non est absque te Deus. 15. vere tu es Deus absconditus Deus Israel Salvator. ] Hic dedemum insurgunt animosius & Spiritus resumunt quidam Interpretes, putantque jam confectum esse superiora non posse de Cyro intelligi, sed de Christo necessario exponenda esse. Putant enim hæc quæ cum superioribus continentur non posse ullo modo Cyro applicari. Affirmant hoc confidentius, quia præeuntem hic habent Hieronymum, verba non pigrabor adscribere. Sic ergo ille p. nihi 170. Col.1. Sed hoc quod sequitur, vere tu es Deus absconditus, Deus Israel Salvator, quomodo possit Cyri personæ convenire non intelligo. Et Paulo post, fac enim esse in Cyro Deum & non esse alium præter eum qui sit in Cyro Deus, quomodo Cyri personæ dici convenit, vere tu es Deus absconditus &c, Ergo Deus in quo est Deus, Dominus noster Jesus Christus rectius intelligitur, & verius, qui in Evangelio loquitur, * ego & pater unum sumus. Qui Deus appellatur absconditus, propter assumpti corporis sacramentum, & Deus Israel salvator, quod est Jesus. Et columna 2. Paulo commotior, Ebraei stulta contentione, inquit, nitantur asserere, usque ad eum locum ubi legitur, tantum in te est Deus, & non est absque te Deus vel ad Jerusalem vel ad Cyrum dici. Hoc autem quod sequitur, vere tu es Deus absconditus, subito ad omnipotentem Deum fieri, cum etiam stultis perspicuum sit; unum esse contextum sermonis. Bellarminus in controversia de Christo, asserendæ ejus Deitati hinc argumentum petit, sed ficulneum ac proinde ja * Socino nullo negotio submotum. Ostendit enim vers. 14. neque ad Cyrum, neque ad Christum, sed ad Sionem seu Jerusalem vel Ecclesiam pertinere, versu vero 15. esse apostrophen ad Deum. Utinam vero infaustus ille Faustus nullibi periculosius erraset! Quod enim de versu 14. asserit, verissimum est. Omnia enim affixa, quæ versu isto occurrunt fœminina sunt, כה אמר יהוה יגיע מצרים וסחר כוש וסבאים אנשי מדה עליך יעברו ולך יהיו אחריך ילכו בזקים יעברו ואליך ישתחוו אלך יתחלו לו אך כך אל ואין עור אפס אלהים Sic inquit DOMINVS: Labor Ægypti (id est, divitiæ Ægyptiorum labore partæ) & merx Chusæorum & Sabæorum, virorum mensura magnæ (id est, procerorum) ad te (o Jerusalem, Ecclesia, o populE mi) transibunt: tua erunt, post te ibunt (te sequentur, se tibi adjungent) in compedibus transibunt, ubique incurvabunt se, te deprecabuntur, dicentes. Tantum in te est Deus. & nullus est præterea, nusquam præterea Deus. Deodatus o Ecclesia mea, non tantum liberaberis ex captivitate Babylonii-
units.tr: Verse 14. "Surely God is in you, and there is no other God beside you." Verse 15. "Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Saviour." Here at last some interpreters rise up more boldly and take heart, and think that what has gone before cannot be understood of Cyrus, but must necessarily be explained of Christ. For they think that what is contained together with what precedes cannot in any way be applied to Cyrus. They affirm this more confidently because they have Jerome leading the way, and I will not be slow to quote his words. He says, in his page 170, column 1: "But I do not understand how what follows, 'Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Saviour,' can fit the person of Cyrus. And a little later: 'Suppose God is in Cyrus, and there is no other God except the one who is God in Cyrus: how can it be said to fit the person of Cyrus, "Truly you are a hidden God," etc.? Therefore the God in whom God is, our Lord Jesus Christ, is more rightly and truly understood, who speaks in the Gospel, *"I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). He is called hidden God on account of the mystery of the body he assumed, and God the Saviour of Israel, who is Jesus.'" And in column 2, rather more heated: "The Hebrews," he says, "strive with foolish contention to assert that up to the place where it is read, 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other God,' it can be said of either Jerusalem or Cyrus. But that what follows, 'Truly you are a hidden God,' suddenly turns to almighty God, is plain even to fools: the connection of the discourse is one." Bellarmine, in his controversy about Christ, takes from this an argument for asserting his deity, but it is a barren fig tree and was therefore removed without difficulty by Socinus. For he shows that verse 14 pertains neither to Cyrus nor to Christ, but to Zion or Jerusalem or the Church, and that verse 15 is an apostrophe to God. Would that the unlucky Faustus had never erred more dangerously anywhere! For what he asserts about verse 14 is most true. For all the attached words that occur in that verse are feminine: "Thus says the LORD: the labour of Egypt, and the merchandise of Cush and of the Sabaeans, men of great stature (that is, the tall ones), shall pass over to you (O Jerusalem, Church, O my people); they shall be yours, they shall go after you; in chains they shall pass over, they shall bow down to you, they shall pray to you, saying, 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other God beside you, nowhere else is there God.'" Oh my Church, not only shall you be delivered from the Babylonian captivity, but also in the time of the Messiah you shall receive spiritually the greatest and most opulent nations, and you shall bring them through the preaching of the Gospel to the obedience of faith. Isa. 11:14. Junius: "Here God shows..."

units.la: * Vide eum apud Rev. D. Paulum Tarnovium libro de SS. Trinit. p. 183. lonica, sed & tempore Messiæ subjicies Jobi spiritualiter maximas & opulentissimas nationes adducesque eas perEvangelii prædicationem ad fidei obedientiam. Jes. xi. 14. Junius, Hic Deus ostendit consilium, se non alium in finem ista (superius dicta) effecturum esse, quam ut promoveat hoc pacto & instauret regnum suum tempore suo per Christum, qui fundamentum & finis est omnium prophetiarum. Forerius Dominicanus, Dicit in fidem Israelitarum idest, electorum ex Israel transituros Ægyptios, Æthiopes &c. Ad te transibunt, deserentes suam religionem & tuæ fidei adhærentes. Vincti manicis, designat omnimodam subjectionem, quod indicant verba sequentia incurvationis, supplicationis quod autem subjectio illa non violenta sed ex agnitione veræ fidei oritura esset, figurateque accipienda hæc sint & non de corporali servitute, confirmant quæ sequuntur, tantum in te est Deus, q. d. vos soli estis, qui verum Deum colitis, O Vos felices, inter quos Deus in habitat. & paucis interjectis, vides ut sanctitas Apostolorum gentes ad fidem pertrahebat? Merito profecto nobis ad scribuntur gentium infidelitas & blasphemiæ. Nam si in Christianis eam à peccatis libertatem & affectibus purgatas mentes conspicerent barbari, manus eorum nullæ sic manicæ, pedes nulla sic vincula constringerent, Exclamarentque, Vere in vobis est Deus, Et non est absque te Deus & non amplius, nisi Deus, sic sonant Ebræa id est, & non amplius alius Deus quærendus, nisi is Deus qui in te est. Et rursus, Hac Israeli dicta interpretati sumus, neque præter morem Scripturæ, nam quod Israeli supplicarent & ipsum deprecarentur gentes, non uno tantum loco habes. Hæc Forerius. Inspice hac loca, inquit * Joh. Tarnovius, Ps. Lxxvi. 2. 3. xlvi. 5. 6. xlviii. 2. 3. 4. 9. Lxviii. ult. Cxlvii. 19. 20. Jes. xxxi. 9. Ps. Cxxxii. 13. 14. Cxxxv. 21. & poteris explicare illud, Deus est in te O Israel. Cum vero vers. xv. dicat in Masc. genere, quis jam dubitabit, hic apostrophen esse vel Ecclesiæ vel Prophetæ ad Deum. Sed illam generis diversitatem nec ex Latina nec Græca versione odorari potuit ullus Interpres. Ne B. Hieronymus quidem, ex Ebræo textu qui ejus ævo nec dum puncta adscripta habebat, eam observare potuit. Omnia enim ista affixa pronomina sine punctis vocalibus scripta ad utrumque genus indifferentia sunt. Sed lubet hic audire svaviludium Pintum ad illud, vere tu es Deus abscónditus In hostia consecrata inquit, vere est Deus abscónditus.
units.tr: See him in Rev. D. Paulus Tarnovius, *De SS. Trinitate*, p. 183. "You shall also subject to yourself, spiritually, the greatest and wealthiest nations of the Messiah's time, and by the preaching of the Gospel you shall bring them to the obedience of faith." Isa. 11.14. Junius: "Here God shows his purpose: he will bring about the things said above for no other end than to advance and restore his kingdom in his own time, through Christ, who is the foundation and the goal of all prophecy." Forerius the Dominican: "It says in the faith of Israel, that is, of the elect from Israel, the Egyptians, Ethiopians, etc., will pass over, abandoning their own religion and adhering to your faith. 'In chains' signifies complete subjection, as the following words of bowing down and supplication indicate. That this subjection would not be forced but would arise from the recognition of the true faith, and that these words are to be taken figuratively and not of bodily servitude, is confirmed by what follows: 'Surely God is in you,' that is, you alone are those who worship the true God, O happy you, among whom God dwells." And a few lines later: "Do you see how the holiness of the Apostles drew the nations to the faith? Surely the unbelief and blasphemies of the nations are rightly ascribed to us. For if the barbarians beheld in Christians minds freed from sins and passions, no such manacles would bind their hands, no such chains their feet. They would cry out: Truly God is among you, and there is no God apart from you, and no other, except God, so the Hebrew sounds, that is, no other God is to be sought, except the God who is in you." And again: "We have interpreted these words of Israel, nor against the custom of Scripture, for that the nations should supplicate Israel and beg him, you will find not in one place only." So Forerius. Look at these passages, says Joh. Tarnovius: Ps. 76.2-3; 46.5-6; 48.2-4, 9; 68 (end); 147.19-20; Isa. 31.9; Ps. 132.13-14; 135.21; and you will be able to explain that: "God is in you, O Israel." But since verse 15 has the masculine gender, who will now doubt that here it is an apostrophe of the Church or of the prophet to God? But no interpreter could detect that difference of gender either from the Latin or from the Greek version. Not even St. Jerome could observe it from the Hebrew text, which in his day did not yet have vowel points. For all these attached pronouns, written without vowel points, are indifferent to either gender. But here let us hear the sweet-sounding Pintus on that passage: "Truly you are a hidden God", he says, "in the consecrated host, truly the God is hidden."

units.la: * Exerc. Biblic. p. 598. Edit. ultimæ. Tu es sub accidentibus absconditus, & invisibilis visibiliter à nobis sumeris aliena specie occultatus. Et ita sumptus peccata deles &c. — Et quoniam Deus est in hoc sacramento occultatus, ait Jesaias hoc in loco, Tu vere es Deus absconditus. Miserere me tui Pinte, Miserere me hujus peregrinæ tuæ Theologiæ, quam Doctores nostri ab ima stirpe jam pridem convulsere. Quid hic sit מסתתר id est, abscondens te, non potest illi absconditum esse, qui Ps. x. legerit, quid absistis in longinquo & abscondis te חתעלם. Deut. 22. 2. non abscondes te ab eo תחעלם / Hæc enim synonyma sunt. Licet aliquando ad tempus aliquod te videaris abscondere & relinquere populum tuum, tamen es & manes Deus ejus, & præfinito tempore in auxilium ejus præsto eris Quamvis Junius Paulo altius hic penetret, Cujus scholia, quia prolixiora & omnium manibus teruntur, non adscribo. Prius interpretationis ejus membrum de abscondito multis sæculis apud gentes divino mysterio invenies in comm. Aben-Ezræ : Posterius de visibilitate Dei non adumbrantis se imaginibus aut speciem essentiæ suæ communicantis in Scholiis Davidis Kimchii.
units.tr: Exercitationes Biblicae, p. 598, last edition: "You are hidden under the accidents, and invisibly, you are visibly taken by us, concealed under a foreign appearance. And so taken, you take away sins," etc. "And since God is hidden in this sacrament, Isaiah says in this place, 'Truly you are a hidden God.' Have mercy on me, Pintus, have mercy on me, on this foreign theology of yours, which our teachers long ago uprooted from its very base. What hiding yourself [מסתתר] means here, that is, hiding you [abscondens te], cannot be hidden from anyone who has read Ps. 10, where it says, why do you stand far off and hide yourself [חתעלם]? Deut. 22.4: you shall not hide yourself [תחעלם] from him. For these are synonyms. Although for a time you may seem to hide yourself and abandon your people, yet you are and remain their God, and at the appointed time you will be at hand to help them." Although Junius penetrates here more deeply than Paul, I do not cite his scholia, because they are longer and are in everyone's hands. The first part of his interpretation, about the hidden thing, you will find in the commentary of Aben Ezra, where it has been a divine mystery among the nations for many centuries; the second, about the visibility of God who does not veil himself in images or communicate the appearance of his essence, you will find in the Scholia of David Kimchi.
