units.la: Verf. 3. Audite me domus Jacob — qui portamini à meo utero, qui gestamini à mea vulva] Ita Vulg. qui B. Lutherum hic quoque in avia traxit, die gp ban mp inden Lybe gedragen woyd/ ende mp inder Moeder legget. Immane quantum hic se torserunt interpretes, & mirabor si non hoc loco abusi sint Photiniani obscurandis aut eludendis istis locis, quæ pro asserenda æterna Filii Dei ex Patris essentia, Generatione Orthodoxi produxere. Est enim ἀπὸ π inter hunc locum & illum Ps. Cx. prout eum vulgata versio nobis repræsentat, Ex utero genui te, ubi illud ex utero omnes interpretantur ex substantia mea. Ipse certe Hieron. hujus interpretationis pater locum illum huc transcripsit, pag. mihi 172. Postquam enim monuisset ineffabilem & incomprehensibilem Dei Majestatem uterum, pedes, manus, non habere, ait Scripturam tamen ista Deo tribuere, ut nos affectum Dei per nostra verba discamus. Alioquin, inquit, & in centesimo nono Psalmo, ex persona Dei hoc idem canitur, In eo enim loco ubi Lxx. transtulerunt, ex utero ante Lucifer rum genui te, in Ebraeo scriptum habet, מרחם / quod * interpretatur
units.tr: Verse 3. "Hear me, house of Jacob... you who have been carried from my womb, who have been borne from my belly." So the Vulgate reads, and so Luther, in the old Dutch version, also drew this passage aside: "who have been carried by me from the body and lain in my mother's womb." The interpreters have twisted themselves into knots here, and I shall be surprised if the Photinians have not misused this place to obscure or evade these words, which the Orthodox have brought forward to prove the eternal generation of the Son of God from the essence of the Father. For there is a parallel between this place and that of Psalm 110, as the Vulgate gives it to us, "I have begotten you from the womb," where all the interpreters take the words "from the womb" to mean "from my substance." Jerome himself, the father of this interpretation, certainly transcribed that passage here, on page 172 of my edition. After observing that the ineffable and incomprehensible majesty of God has no womb, feet, or hands, he says that Scripture nevertheless attributes these things to God so that we may learn God's feeling through our words. Otherwise, he says, in the hundred and ninth Psalm the same thing is sung in the person of God. For in that place where the Seventy have translated, "from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you," the Hebrew has מרחם, which is interpreted [מרחם]

units.la: * Vide hoc loco priorem Anti-barbari nostri partem pag. 498. tur de vulva. In praesentiarum vero, non solum, de utero, &, de vulva, scriptum est, id est, מבטן & מרחם sed מני / quae praepositio significat, ex meo utero sive, ex mea vulva, & est sensus, qui vos genui ab infantia & meo utero, vulvaque gestavi &c. Ubi simul habes fundamentum interpretationis Hieronymianae, τὸ Jod vid. in מני affixum esse. Non tam hospes in Ebraismo sum, ut nesciam aliquando affixum esse, Dicitur enim מני & מני & ממני à me, sed & illud scio, saepe mere paragogicum esse Jud. v. 14. בני אפרים de Ephraim & בני מכיר Et cum Tzere Jef. 30. 11. בני / Adhaec si vel maxime hic pronomen esset, tamen a meo utero, verti non posset Affixa enim ipsis nominib. addenda erant, מרחמי / מדבטני. Hinc LXX. ἐκ κοιλίας, ἐκ παιδίας. Hoc viderunt Forerius, Pintus, Pagninus, Oleastrius Arias Mont. alii, & notatum aliquoties in libris Cl. Drusii. Verba Ariae M. in hunc locum ista sunt, vanus ego dicat, nisi librariorum culpa locus hic in hac Latina laborat versione. Nam nec hic Deus uterum sibi appingit, nec vulvam confingit, utpote qui in generationis etiam imagine, patris, potius quam matris nomen usurpatur. Sed uterus & vulva ad Jacobi Matrem referenda vocabula sunt. Arbitramur itaque in correctissimis Latinus exemplaribus scriptum fuisse, qui portamini a me ab utero, qui gestamini a me a vulva, ut a sexti casus praepositio sit, quae facile a sciolo cum pronomine, me, coaluit. Exemplaris Lectio aperte simul & eleganter habet MINI BETEN & MINI RAHHAM. Quod idem extra carmen valet, atque MIBETEN MINREHHEM. Haec ille. Putat ergo interpretem accepisse τὸ Jod in MINNI pro praepositione sexti casus A. & in nominibus duobus constituisse ellepsin praepositionis ejusdem, quasi plene dicendum fuerit מני מבטנו מרחם quomodo & Pintus locum hunc reddendum censuit. At ipse & Forer. & Oleastr. & Pagn, & Druf. ellipsin ista posthabita, τὸ Jod pro paragogico accepere. Quid vero ad conjecturam Ariae M attinet de corrupto hoc loco, vereor, ut cum istud scriberet, de Hieronymi commentario cogitaverit. Illic enim ut videmus, interpretationem istam a meo utero, a mea vulva, confidenter defendit. Novimus ergo jam, quid dicere velit Propheta, Vos qui bajulamini (a me sc.) inde ab utero (matris vestrae,) qui gestamini (a me) inde a vulva, quos ego ab ipsa nativitate magna cum molestia bajulavi quomodo pater materve, filiu suum bajulat & portat, confer Deut. 1. 31. Exod. xix. 4. Deut. xxxii. 11. Lege jam Dion. Carth. expositionem & miserare for-
units.tr: * See the earlier part of our Anti-Barbarus on this passage, page 498. concerning the vulva. But at present it is written not only "of the womb" and "of the vulva," that is, מבטן and מרחם, but מני, which preposition means "from my womb" or "from my vulva," and the sense is, "who have been begotten by me from infancy and carried in my womb and vulva," etc. Here you have at once the basis of Jerome's interpretation: the Jod [י] in מני is affixed. I am not so much a stranger to Hebrew that I do not know that the Jod is sometimes an affix; for מני and ממני mean "from me," but I also know that it is often purely paragogic, as in Judges 5:14, בני אפרים, "of Ephraim," and בני מכיר, and with a tsere in Isaiah 30:11, בני. Moreover, even if this were the pronoun, it still could not be rendered "from my womb," for the affixes would have to be added to the nouns themselves: מרחמי or מבטני. Hence the Seventy have ἐκ κοιλίας, ἐκ παιδίας [from the belly, from childhood]. Forerius, Pintus, Pagninus, Oleastrius, Arias Montanus, and others saw this, and Drusius has noted it several times in his books. The words of Arias Montanus on this passage are these: "I would say it is vain, unless the fault of the copyists has corrupted this place in this Latin version. For God does not picture a womb for himself here, nor does he invent a vulva, since in the very image of begetting the name of father, rather than mother, is used. But 'uterus' and 'vulva' are words to be referred to Jacob's mother. We therefore judge that in the most correct Latin copies it was written, 'who are carried by me from the womb, who are borne by me from the vulva,' so that the preposition of the ablative case is a, which a smatterer easily joined with the pronoun me. The reading of the exemplar clearly and elegantly has MINI BETEN and MINI RAHHAM, which outside of verse is the same as MIBETEN MINREHHEM." So far he. He therefore thinks the translator read the Jod in MINNI as the preposition of the ablative, and supplied an ellipsis of the same preposition in the two nouns, as if one should fully say מני מבטנו מרחם, as Pintus also thought this place ought to be rendered. But he himself, and Forerius, Oleastrius, Pagninus, and Drusius, set aside this ellipsis and took the Jod as paragogic. As for Arias Montanus's conjecture that this place is corrupt, I fear that in writing it he was thinking of Jerome's commentary, for there, as we see, he confidently defends the interpretation "from my womb, from my vulva." We now know therefore what the Prophet wishes to say: "You who are carried (by me, that is) from the womb (of your mother), you who are borne (by me) from the vulva," whom I have carried from birth itself with great trouble, as a father or mother carries and bears their son; compare Deuteronomy 1:31, Exodus 19:4, Deuteronomy 32:11. Now read the exposition of Dionysius of Carthage, and pity the lot of this most learned man, who, had he fallen upon a more enlightened age, would have fulfilled all the duties of a good interpreter.

units.la: ABBREVIATIONS: none. sortem doctissimi viri, qui si in eruditius seculum incidisset omnes boni Interpretis partes implevisset.
units.tr: ABBREVIATIONS: none. The misfortune of this most learned man, who, had he lived in a more enlightened age, would have fulfilled every part of a good interpreter.

units.la: CAP. LI.
units.tr: Chapter 51.

units.la: Verf. 20. filii tui— sicut beta semicoɖta ;] Ita Lxx. ὡς σταλίον ἰμιεφθον. Multa hic argumentati sunt veteres. Hieron. Comparantur beta semi-coɖta, quod genus oleris est vilissimi & fragilissimi. De quibus holerib, puto illud dici in Psalmis, ne zeleris in malignantibus. Quoniam sicut fœnum velociter arescent, & sicut holera herbarum cito de-cidunt. Est enim agrotantium cibus. Qui semel incredulus est vocatur beta Cruda. Qui autem simplici contentus fide, absque ratione & dogmatum veritate facit opera justitiæ, potest dici beta coɖta. Porro qui inter vitia & virtutes medius fluctuat, & duplici corde accedit ad servitutem Dei, ille rectissime vocatur beta simi-coɖta, Ad quem & in Apocal. Johannis loquitur Deus, utinam aut calidus aut frigidus esses &c. Sed audi hic eundem Hieron. paulo ante sic disserentem, Pro beta semi-coɖta reliqui interpretantes orygem captum & illaqueatum, transtulerunt (ὡς ὄρυξ ἡμιφθέλη γρόμμ ⓖ ἢ συνελημμὸ ⓖ) qui Ebraice appellatur ꞇʜ ο, quod genus bestiæ in eremo nascentis, inter munda animalia in Deuteronomio ponitur. Pro quo Lxx. Syrâ lingua opinati sunt Thoreth, qua dicitur Beta. Ubi Cl. Drufius legendum censet Thored. Quæstionum Ebr.2. 30. monetque in Lyra pro animal immundum legendum esse, animal mundum. Et notat insuper, Eusebium hallucinatum fuisse, dum avem esse asserit, ὄρυεον ἢ ἰσὶν ὄρυξ, ἔτω καλύμμον: Confundit ὄρυξ & ὄρυξ quorum prius capram sylvestrem, posterius avem notat, quam Coturnicem vocant. Deut, 14. 5. legitur תְּאוֹ. Hic תא Junius utrobique bubalum vertit.
units.tr: Verse 20, "your sons... like a half-cooked beet": so the Seventy, "ὡς σταλίον ἡμιεφθον." The ancients made many arguments here. Jerome: The beet is compared with the half-cooked beet, because it is a kind of the cheapest and most fragile vegetable. I think that what is said in the Psalms about these vegetables, "Do not be jealous of evildoers," is meant. For as the hay quickly withers, and as the greens of the herbs soon fall away. For it is food for the sick. He who was once unbelieving is called raw beet. But he who is content with simple faith and, without reason and knowledge of the truth of the doctrines, does works of righteousness, can be called cooked beet. Further, he who wavers between vices and virtues, and approaches the service of God with a divided heart, is most rightly called half-cooked beet, to whom God also speaks in the Apocalypse of John: I wish you were either hot or cold, etc. But hear the same Jerome, who a little earlier argued thus: Instead of half-cooked beet, the other translators rendered "a gazelle caught and snared" (ὡς ὄρυξ ἡμιφθέλη γρόμμ ⓖ ἢ συνελημμὸ ⓖ), which in Hebrew is called [תְּאוֹ], a kind of beast that lives in the wilderness and is listed among the clean animals in Deuteronomy. In place of it the Seventy, supposing it to be in the Syriac language, rendered it Thoreth, which is called Beta. Here the distinguished Drusius thinks we should read Thored, Questions on Hebrew 2.30, and he notes in Lyra that for unclean animal we should read clean animal. He further observes that Eusebius was mistaken when he asserts that it is a bird, ὄρυεον ἢ ἰσὶν ὄρυξ, ἔτω καλύμμον. He confuses ὄρυξ with ὄρυξ, of which the former denotes a wild goat and the latter a bird, which they call the quail. In Deut. 14.5 we read [תְּאוֹ]. Here Junius translates תא as "buffalo" in both places.

units.la: CAP. LIII.
units.tr: Chapter 53.

units.la: Verf. 4. Percussum à Deo ] Ita Vulg. Fuerunt qui Ebræa sic vertenda putarint, percussum Deum atque inde argumentum invictum exsculpserint pro Deitate Christi, Inter quos Andradius, Bell. & Rosellus. Vide quæ parte prima Anti-barbari pag. 19. ad hunc locum diximus. Hier. ab Oleastro, & Forerius eisdem vestigiis insistunt, Inter מכה percussum, & אלהים nulla est in Ebræo præpræpositio, inquiunt. Quid tum? Est tamen syntaxis non convenientiæ, sed rectionis. Scriptum est מִבָּה cum Tzere, non מִבָּה cum segol ac proinde ad verbum sonat, percussum Dei. Genus locutionis, quale אַהֲבַת רֵעַ Hos. 3 1. id est, dilecta ab amico. Natus mulieris Job. 14. 1, Sic Luc. 7. 28. Quale in N. T. διδακτοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, Benedicti patris mei &c.
units.tr: Verse 4, "smitten by God": so the Vulgate. There have been those who thought the Hebrew should be rendered "God smitten," and from this they have drawn an unanswerable argument for the deity of Christ, among them Andradius, Bellarmine and Rosellus. See what we said on this passage in the first part of the Anti-barbarus, p. 19. Hieronymus ab Oleastro and Forerius tread the same path, saying that there is no preposition in the Hebrew between מכה, "smitten," and אלהים, "God." What of it? The construction, however, is not one of agreement but of government. It is written מִבָּה with tsere, not מִבָּה with segol, and therefore it literally sounds "smitten of God." This is a kind of expression like אַהֲבַת רֵעַ in Hos. 3.1, that is, "beloved by a friend." "Born of a woman," Job 14.1. So also in Luke 7.28, and in the New Testament, διδακτοὶ ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, "taught by God," and "blessed of my Father," etc.

units.la: CAP. LXI.
units.tr: CHAP. LXI.

units.la: Verf. 2. Ut prædicarem annum placabilem Domino ] Lucas cap. iv. locum ita convertit, κηρύξαι ἐνιαυτὸν Κυρίου δεκτὸν. Clemens Alexandrinus hinc colligit Christum unum tantum annum prædicasse, ac proinde 32. ætatis anno passum fuisse. Epiphanius vero hinc ratiocinatur, Christum duos annos ministerio functum esse. Si fuit unus annus δεκτὸς, inquit, fuit & alter ὁ δεκτὸς καὶ ἀπλεγὸν μὴ. Sed in his nihil est solidi. Solidius magnus Scaliger per Paschatum intervalla annos τῶν πολιτείας definit, ostenditque Paschaillud πανηγύριον, quo vid. cruci affixus fuit, à Baptismo ejus seu prædicationis initio, quod in annum ætatis ejus tricesimum incidit, fuisse quintum, ac proinde Christum ultra quatuor annos prædicasse. Primum Pascha ait commemorari Joh. 11. verf. 12. 13. & 23. 11. Johannis v. 1. Ἐορτὴ autem τῶν Ἰουδαίων illic pascha esse evidenter ostendit. Tertii vestigia cruit ex Matth. xii. Marci 11. Lucæ vi. ubi memoratur σάββατον δευτεροπρῶτον id est, πρῶτον τοῦ ἐκ τῆς δευτέρας Ἑ Πάσχα. Quartum Pascha, eruit ex Joh. vi. Quintum vocat πανηγύριον, σωτήριον ἢ ἀναστάσιμον, de quo in Passionis Historia. Vide hæc prolixius apud ipsum Scaligerum, unde hæc in gratiam eorum, qui incomparabili illo opere destituuntur, transcripsimus. Sed ad rem, ut dies Gen. 2. 4. quo die creavit Deus cœlum & terram &c. Ita & annus pro tempore ponitur, Jud. x. 6. & concutiebant filios Israel, * anno, ubi Lxx. ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ. Sic Jes. 63. annus attributionis, Jerem. xi. annus visitationis. & infra cap 63. 4. annus vindicandorum meorum venit. Joh. 18. Cajaphas erat Pontifex ipsius anni. Quamvis aliæ quoque causæ reddi possint cur ita locutus sit Evangelista. Certe quamdiu Pilatus in Judæa egit, Cajaphas sacerdotio functus est, annis fere ix. aut. xi. continuis, uti ex Josepho constat. Qua de re suo fortassis loco. Ita contra tempus pro anno Daniel. xii. 7. & vii. 25. tempus, tempora, & particula temtemporis. Sed fortassis respexit aut allusit Propheta & hic & 63. 4. ad annum Jubilæum seu Ἀφεσις, qui in veteri fœdere tubis promulgabatur. quemadmodum enim illo anno tubâ ad pilcum & libertatem vocabantur servi, & remittebantur debita, ita Christus prædicationis suæ buccina ad spiritualem libertatem vocavit eos qui Diabolo mancipati erant & pœnitentibus peccatorum remissionem annunciavit. Hic certe vere fuit annus benevolentiæ, seu ut cum Apostolis loquor, καιρὸς εὐάρεστος, ἡμέρα σωτηρίας, annus reconciliationis, quo nos Deo reconciliavit. Quod si tueri se possit Chronologia Bucholzeri & qui cum sequuntur, annum Babtismi, seu quod idem est, primum prædicationis Christi incidisse in Jubilæum, Mundi 80. Mosis 30. jam res tota planior fuerit.
units.tr: Verse 2. To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.] Luke in chapter 4 renders the passage thus: "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord" [κηρύξαι ἐνιαυτὸν Κυρίου δεκτόν]. From this Clement of Alexandria infers that Christ preached for only one year, and so suffered in the thirty-second year of his age. Epiphanius, however, reasons from the same words that Christ exercised his ministry for two years: if there was one acceptable year, he says, there was also another. But nothing solid is found in these arguments. More solidly, the great Scaliger, by the intervals of the Passovers, fixes the years of Christ's public life, and shows that the Passover at which he was crucified fell in the fifth year from his baptism, or the beginning of his preaching, which fell in the thirtieth year of his age; so that Christ preached for more than four years. He says the first Passover is mentioned in John 2:13, 23 and 11:55, and he clearly shows that the feast of the Jews in John 5:1 is a Passover. He traces the traces of a third in Matthew 12, Mark 2 and Luke 6, where the "second-first sabbath" is mentioned [σάββατον δευτεροπρῶτον], that is, the first sabbath after the second day of the Passover. He draws the fourth Passover from John 6. The fifth he calls the feast, the saving or resurrection feast, which is discussed in the account of the Passion. See these matters more fully in Scaliger himself; I have transcribed them here for the sake of those who lack that incomparable work. But to return to the point: as "day" is used in Genesis 2:4 for the time when God created heaven and earth, and so on, so "year" is also used for a time, Judges 10:6, where the Seventy have "in that time" [ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ], and Isaiah 63 has "the year of recompense," Jeremiah 11 "the year of visitation," and below, in chapter 63:4, "the year of my vengeance has come." In John 18, "Caiaphas was high priest that same year." Yet other reasons can be given why the evangelist spoke thus. Certainly, as long as Pilate governed in Judaea, Caiaphas held the priesthood, for nearly nine or eleven continuous years, as is established from Josephus; on which matter, perhaps, more in its proper place. Conversely, "time" is used for a year in Daniel 12:7 and 7:25: "a time, times, and half a time." But perhaps the prophet, both here and in 63:4, had in view or alluded to the Jubilee, or release [ἄφεσις], which in the old covenant was proclaimed with trumpets. For just as in that year servants were called to liberty by the trumpet and debts were remitted, so Christ, by the trumpet of his preaching, called to spiritual liberty those who were enslaved to the devil, and announced the forgiveness of sins to the repentant. This was truly a "year of goodwill," or, to speak with the Apostles, "an acceptable time" [καιρὸς εὐάρεστος], "a day of salvation" [ἡμέρα σωτηρίας], a year of reconciliation, in which he reconciled us to God. If the chronology of Bucholzer and those who follow him can be defended, namely that the year of Christ's baptism, or what is the same, the beginning of his preaching, fell in the Jubilee, in the year 80 of the world and 30 of Moses, then the whole matter will be clearer.

units.la: C- AP. LXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXIII.

units.la: Verf. 1. Quis est iste qui venit de Edom &c. ] Graves super genuino hujus vaticinii sensu controversiæ jam olim etiam tempore B.Hieronymi motæ sunt. Hieronymi sententiam strenue impugnat Lyra. Et Interpretatur locum de exterminatione Antichristi. Carthusianus Hieronymo advocationem præstiturus multa hic miscet, an angeli, quos hæc rogare supponunt, à principio seculi noverint Christi incarnationem, item an isti interogantes sint inferioris an superioris chori &c. ostenditque non eadem hic sentire Augustinum & Hieron. & Dionysium. Sed quid impedit hunc dialogum Christo & Ecclesiæ seu potius Prophetæ adscribere? Sed missis istis, alia hic occurrit Interpretum differitas utrum hic Christus (de eo enim quin exponendus sit hic locus nullus dubito) introducatur patiens suaque solius passione iram Dei placans, ut supra cap. 53. quam sententiam ex veteribus multi amplexi sunt quorum catalogum videre est apud Rev. D. Pelargum in 7. Meditat. Passionis Christi p. 353. an vero hic describatur ut Rex Ecclesiæ, suos adversus hostes externos defendens & ab illis liberans. Non negamus Christum patiendo gloriosissimam de hostibus Ecclesiæ spiritalib. victoriam reportasse, sed de ea hic non agi, longe putamus esse verisimilius. Egit de hoc loco Paræus in Calvino Orthodoxo lib. 2. cap.20. & prolixe Joh. Tarnovius in Exercit. Bibl. Edit. 3. pag. 418. Et Junius accurate in scholiis, & alii complures. Ecce enim primo inquit.
units.tr: Verse 1. Who is this who comes from Edom, etc.] Serious controversies over the genuine sense of this prophecy were stirred long ago, even in the time of St. Jerome. Lyra vigorously attacks Jerome's opinion and interprets the passage of the destruction of Antichrist. The Carthusian, about to defend Jerome, mixes in many things here: whether the angels, whom they suppose to be asking, have known from the beginning of the world the incarnation of Christ; likewise whether those asking belong to the lower or the higher choir, and so on; and he shows that Augustine, Jerome and Dionysius do not hold the same view here. But what prevents us from ascribing this dialogue to Christ and the Church, or rather to the Prophet? Setting these aside, another difference among the interpreters arises: whether Christ is here introduced (for I do not doubt that it is he who is to be understood here) as suffering, and by his passion alone appeasing the wrath of God, as in chapter 53, an opinion which many of the ancients embraced, whose list may be seen in the Reverend Dr. Pelargus, in his Seven Meditations on the Passion of Christ, p. 353; or whether he is described as King of the Church, defending his people against external enemies and delivering them from them. We do not deny that by suffering Christ won a most glorious spiritual victory over the enemies of the Church, but we think it far more probable that this is not what is treated here. Paraeus treated this passage in his Orthodox Calvin, book 2, chapter 20, and Johannes Tarnovius at length in his Biblical Exercises, third edition, p. 418; and Junius accurately in his scholia, and many others.

units.la: . Verf. 1. Ex Edom, ex Botzra] Annon verisimile magis per Edomæos gentem, Israelitis proximam, hæ reditaria hostilitate celebrem, synecdochice intelligi externos Ecclesiæ hostes, quam spirituales? Quod enim Hieronymus hic argutatur in voce Edom, nauci non est. Locum enim ita legit, Quis est iste qui de terra cruentus advenit? Atqui in Ebr. non est אדום מארץ aut potius מארץ אדום sed מאדום.
units.tr: Verse 1. From Edom, from Botzra.] Is it not more probable that by Edom, a people close to Israel and famous for their hereditary hostility, the external enemies of the Church are meant synecdochically, rather than spiritual enemies? For what Jerome makes a fuss about in the word Edom is worth nothing. He reads the passage thus: "Who is this who comes cruel from the land?" But in Hebrew there is not "from the land of Edom" or rather "from the land of Edom," but "from Edom."

units.la: Ex Botzra] Refert Hieron. multos pio errore lapsos de carne Domini hæc intellexisse, At recte ille respondet, carnem Ebraice בשר per ש dici, Hanc vero vocem, cum ʒ scribi, & habere significationem munitionis & firmitatis, ac proinde vel Hierusalem intelligi, illam firmissimis olim muris cinctam, in quâ Christus passus est, velinfernum, de quo in Psal. Lix. & Cvii. scriptum sit, quis deducet me in civitatem munitam. In qua clausæ sunt animæ mortuorum, & circumdata est firmissimis custodiis. Ubi rursus nimis licenter torquet locum Psalmi, Et quod subjicit, firmandæ suæ sententiæ, Botzram juxta Historiam non esse in Edom, sed in Moab, quid ad rem facit? An absurdum esset, Moabitas quoque, gentem non minus Israeli infestam, synecdochice pro reliquis Ecclesiæ hostibus introduci? Et quid si cum * Lyra & Junio duplex fuerit Botzra? Unam Moabitarum, de qua Jerem. xlviii. 24. quæ Josuæ xxi. 36. vocetur Botzer, assignata olim ex tribu Ruben, Meraritis, sed postmodum à Moabitis occupata, altera Edomæ metropolis, cujus Jesaias xxxiv. 6. meminit. Sed Mercerus Botzram unam tantum agnoscit, eamque in confinio Moabiticæ regionis & Edomæ ponit ut jam huic, jam illi tribuatur cui sententiæ hæret & R. Salomo ad Amos 1. 12.
units.tr: From Botzra.] Jerome reports that many, through a pious error, took these words to refer to the flesh of the Lord. But he rightly replies that flesh is called basar in Hebrew with a shin [בשר], whereas this word is written with an ayin and has the sense of fortress and firmness; and therefore it may be understood either as Jerusalem, once surrounded by the strongest walls, in which Christ suffered, or as hell, of which it is written in Psalms 59 and 107, "who will lead me into the fortified city? In which the souls of the dead are shut up, and surrounded by the strongest guards." Here again he twists the words of the Psalm too freely. And what he adds, to strengthen his view, that Botzra according to history is not in Edom but in Moab, what does that matter? Would it be absurd for the Moabites also, a people no less hostile to Israel, to be introduced synecdochically for the rest of the Church's enemies? And what if, with Lyra and Junius, there were two Botzras: one of the Moabites, mentioned in Jeremiah 48:24, which in Joshua 21:36 is called Bezer, once assigned from the tribe of Reuben to the Merarites, but afterwards occupied by the Moabites; the other the metropolis of Edom, of which Isaiah 34:6 speaks. But Mercerus acknowledges only one Botzra, and places it on the border between the region of Moab and Edom, so that it is now assigned to one, now to the other; and Rabbi Solomon also adheres to this view, on Amos 1:12.

units.la: Gradiens in multitudine fortitudinis suæ] at vox Ebr. צועה potius * peragrantem, peregre agentem significat, ut dicat Christum hostium suorum regiones secure peragrasse non copiis mundanis stipatum sed sola potentia sua armatum. Pagn. & Oleastr. festinum reddunt. Et certe magnum momentum in celeritate esse optimi & felicissimi Imperatores non ignorarunt. Quid vero velit sibi illud ∓ Lxx. βία μὴ ἰσχύος violentia cum fortitudine, B. Hieron. ingenue fatetur se ignorare. Et tamen Procopius & Tertull. lib. 4. adversus Marcionem istacitant. Alia lectio, βοᾷ μὴ ἰσχύος clamat cum fortitudine, historiæ passionis melius quidem conveniret, sed quomodo cum antecedentibus & consequentibus conjungi possit nullus
units.tr: Marching in the multitude of his strength.] But the Hebrew word [צועה] rather means one wandering abroad, travelling as a stranger, so that Christ is said to have securely traversed the regions of his enemies, accompanied not by worldly forces but armed with his own power alone. Pagninus and Oleaster render it "hastening." And indeed the best and most fortunate generals have not been ignorant of the great importance of speed. But what the Seventy meant by their rendering [βία μὴ ἰσχύος], "in violence not of strength," St. Jerome frankly confesses he does not know. Yet Procopius and Tertullian in book 4 against Marcion cite it. Another reading, [βοᾷ μὴ ἰσχύος], "crying out with strength," would agree better with the history of the Passion, but I see no way in which it can be joined to what precedes and follows.

units.la: lus las video. Sed ut admittamus vulgati interpretamentum, gradiens, qua voce Forerius negat aptiorem inveniri posse de eo qui incedit cum pompa & fastu, quasi conscius suae dignitatis, quid hoc pro vulgo recepta sententia, Christi acerbam passionem hic describi? Namque quibus verbis describitur Christus victor gloriosus victor Pompatice incedens, triumphator, illis non describitur patiens. Differunt enim illa ut antecedens & consequens, nec tum sensu literali primario hic agitur de passione ubi agitur de victoria.
units.tr: But even if we admit the common rendering, "marching," a word by which Forerius denies that a more suitable one can be found for one who walks with pomp and display, as if conscious of his own dignity, what does this do for the view commonly held, that the bitter Passion of Christ is described here? For the words by which Christ is described as a glorious victor, proceeding pompously as a conqueror and triumphant, do not describe one who suffers. These things differ as antecedent and consequent, nor is the primary literal sense here concerned with the Passion when it is concerned with victory.

units.la: 2. Cur rubrum est indumentum tuum, & vers. 3. aspersus sanguis eorum super vestimenta mea &c. Ebr. [Hebrew] ad verbum, & inspersum est robur eorum super vestimentis meis. Per robur sanguinem intelligit, [Hebrew] inquit Kimchi, quia in eo consistit potissimum vita hominis, ejusque robur. R. Salomo [Hebrew] Nec diversus abit Aben-Ezra. Nisi malis cum Junio, inspersus est [sanguis] robustissimi cujusque illorum vestimentis meis. certe si per [Hebrew] non intellexit Propheta sanguinem, quo etiam inclinat Forerius, insuperhabita vulgatae authoritate, necessario subintelligi debet. Quo enim vestes sunt commaculatae, eo etiam asperse sunt. At sanguine commaculatae esse nemo iverit inficias. Nunc illud mihi observa. Cujus vindicata de hostibus terrenis sumpta describitur, cujus vestes conspersae leguntur non suo proprio, sed hostium sanguine, ejus hic non describitur passio. Sed respondent ex Hieronymo, per hostes Daemones intelligi, quos patiendo in ligno crucis vicerit. Nequaquam, inquit Hieron. sic intelligendum ut daemones & adversarias potestates sanguinem habere credamus. Sed tropologice intelligenda sunt omnia &c. Et Paulo post, deduxitque sanguinem eorum in terram, vel daemonum, [Greek]. Quae etiam in patrocinium advocantur a Jesuita Pinto. Sed plane mihi persuadeo, haec nulli cordato probatum iri, nisi cui sedet [Greek]. Spiritum carnem & ossa non habere, Salvatoris effatum est, & ostendat Pintus, ubi Morti, inferno & peccato vel tropologice (ea enim voce & ipse utitur) sanguis in Scriptura tribuatur. Hanc difficultatem viderunt author Glossae ordinariae & Sa. Quorum ille Christi sanguinem dicit vocari sanguinem eorum, id est, daemonum, quod eorum suasione effusus sit, vel eorum id est, judaeorum, quia illi suasu Daemonum eum fuderunt. Ad quas interpretationes Burgensis addit tertiam, ut dicatur sangvis eorum, quia illi se reos fecerunt sansanguinis Christi, clamantes, sanguis ejus sit super nos & filios nostros. Hic vero, S A, per sanguinem peccata intelligit. Sanguis id est, peccata, inquit, q. d. passus sum pro mundi peccatis, idque delenda suscepi. Argute sane, si haec interpretatio cum caeteris bene cohaereret, & singulare [Hebrew] ea notione alibi occurreret. Nam plurale [Hebrew] sanguines pro enormibus peccatis alibi usurpari non inverim inficias. Sed accedat & versus sextus in subsidium nostrum, Conculcavi populos in furore meo &c. Vocat [Hebrew] / quos vers. 3. vocavit [Hebrew] Quomodo hoc in cruce factum? An hic rursus Diabolum cum angelis suis, mortem, infernum & mundum intelligens; Eos] sc. hostes, peccata & daemones, inquit Sa. [Hebrew] & [Hebrew] collectiva etiam de collectione formicarum, Proverb. xxx. 25. cuniculorum ibid. verf. 26. & locustarum, Joël. 1. 6. usurpari jam pridem novi, docuitque me insuper magnus Lipsius aves Manilio aereos populos dici, eundemque, cum inquit, populos exponere capios, pisces intelligere. Et Columellam istis verbis, duo populi conjungi debent, apes notare. Addo amplius Sidonium audacter & nove satis scelerum populum dixisse, pro peccatorum copia. Sed exemplum biblicum, ubi vel [Hebrew] vel [Hebrew] vel λαός vel ἐθνος de coetu daemonum, vel peccatorum multitudine accipitur, prius indicandum erat. Obtinemus igitur adhuc per populos, gentes ecclesiae inimicas, & homines intelligi: Expende versum 3. Ex populis non est vir mecum, sed calcavi eos &c. calcavit Daemones? Ergone etiam conqueritur nullum daemonum fuisse secum, id est, ut illi interpretantur, adjuvisse se in procuranda humani generis salute?
units.tr: 2. Why is your garment red, and verse 3, "their blood is sprinkled upon my garments," etc.? The Hebrew, word for word, is and their strength has been sprinkled upon my garments. Kimchi says the strength is blood, [Hebrew], because human life and its strength chiefly consist in it. Rabbi Solomon [Hebrew]. Aben Ezra does not differ. Unless you prefer Junius: the blood [of] the most robust of them has been sprinkled on my garments. Certainly, if the prophet did not mean blood by [Hebrew], which Forerius also inclines to, then, setting aside the authority of the Vulgate, it must necessarily be understood. For where garments are stained, there they are also sprinkled, and no one will deny that they are stained with blood. Now observe this for me. When the vindication is taken against earthly enemies, and garments are described as sprinkled not with their own blood but with the blood of enemies, the passion is not described there. But they answer, following Jerome, that by the enemies are meant the demons, whom he conquered by suffering on the wood of the cross. By no means, says Jerome, is it to be understood so, that we believe demons and adversary powers have blood. But all things are to be understood tropologically, etc. And a little later: "and he brought down their blood to the earth," or of the demons, [Greek]. Pinto, the Jesuit, also summons these to his support. But I am fully persuaded that these will be approved by no sensible person, except one who is in the grip of [Greek]. That a spirit does not have flesh and bones is the saying of the Saviour, and Pinto shows where blood is attributed in Scripture to death, hell and sin, or tropologically (for he himself uses that word). The author of the Glossa Ordinaria and Sa saw this difficulty. The former says that Christ's blood is called their blood, that is, of the demons, because it was poured out at their persuasion, or their, that is, of the Jews, because they poured it out at the persuasion of the demons. To these interpretations Burgensis adds a third, that it is called their blood because they made themselves guilty of the blood of Christ, crying out, his blood be upon us and upon our children. Here indeed Sa understands blood to mean sins. "Blood," that is, sins, he says, as if to say: I suffered for the sins of the world, and I undertook to blot them out. Certainly it is clever, if this interpretation fitted well with the rest, and if that singular [Hebrew] occurred elsewhere in this sense. For I do not deny that the plural bloods is used elsewhere for heinous sins. But first the sixth verse should be brought in to help us: I have trodden down the peoples in my wrath, etc. He calls [Hebrew] those whom in verse 3 he called [Hebrew]. How was this done on the cross? Or does he here again mean the Devil with his angels, death, hell and the world? Them, namely enemies, sins and demons, says Sa. I have long known that [Hebrew] and [Hebrew] are used as collectives, of a swarm of ants (Prov. 30:25), of burrowing creatures (ibid. 26), and of locusts (Joel 1:6). Great Lipsius also taught me that birds are called aerial peoples by Manilius, and that he, when he says to explain the peoples as the captives, means fish. And that Columella, in the words the two peoples ought to be joined, means bees. I add that Sidonius boldly and quite novelly called a people of crimes the multitude of sins. But a biblical example, where [Hebrew], [Hebrew], λαός or ἔθνος is taken of a company of demons or of a multitude of sins, ought to have been pointed out first. We therefore still hold that by peoples are meant the nations hostile to the Church, and men. Consider verse 3: of the peoples there is no man with me, but I trod them down, etc. Did he trample the demons? Does he then complain that none of the demons was with him, that is, as they interpret it, did not help him in procuring the salvation of the human race?

units.la: Verf. 3. Torcular calcavi solus] Recte notavit B. Hieronymus, torcular pro ultione & suppliciis peccatorum poni. Pergit & clarius explicat, pro poenis ponitur & tormentis quando, Jeremias in lamentationib. inquit, Torcular calcavit Dom. virgini filiae. Judae — Hoc torcular, in quo & malis supplicia & bonis praemia a Salvatore calcantur, solus ipse calcavit, nullumque habuit adjutorem, Postea vero relabitur ad passionem, Neque enim angelus aut archangelus aut ulla caelestium potestatum humanum corpus assumsit & pro nobis passus est & conculcavit adversarias fortitudines & contrivit. Dico primo, calcare torcular nusquam dici de dispensatione praemiorum, 2. calcare torcular, non esse pati seu supplicia peccatorum experiri, sed alium punire & supplicia infligere. Sic dico, ubi quis dicitur calcare torcular, ubi scripturae stylo non dicitur pati sed inferre ferre supplicia. Expende hæc loca Thren. r.15 .Joel.3.13. Apoc. xiv.19. 20. Neque ullus usquam locus est qui huic assertioni obvertat cornua. Certe si quicquam in hoc textu est, quo primario, sensu literali & immediata passio significetur, hæc ipsa phrasis est. Unde passim pro concione, illud Ich heb die Wayn-perse alleen getreden / de Passione Christi allegari audias. Quam recte nunc ostensum est. Huc respicit illa Pinti glossa, Respondet Christus se esse tinctum sanguine hostium generis humani quos ipse solus vicit, & de quibus sine hominum ope triumphavit. Et quoniam hanc victoriam perfecit Christus in Cruce, colligitur eam esse torcular, in quo hostes nostri velut uvæ conculcata sunt. Ecce non aulus fuit calcationem torcularis ipsam passionem interpretari. Emanuel Sa postquam torcular interpretatus fuisset torcular passionis, mox subjungit, vel ego solus hostes vici. Id enim ETIAM in inscriptura est calcare torcular, sc. hostes premere. Sed ostendant nobis locum, ubi ea phrasis ETIAM significet, pati, premi. Oleastrius, Respondet Messias quare rubrum sit vestimentum ejus, quia torcular PASSIONIS solus calcaverat, neque de gentibus fuerat aliquis qui eum juvaret. Nam in passione ejus non fuit aliquis qui cum eo supplicia passionis suæ toleraret. Sed quia in passione ipse potius calcatus est quam calcaverit alios, melius exponas, torcular calcavi solus id est, solus vici Satanam, mortem & peccatum, comprimendo & conculcando eos merito passionis meæ. Quam posteriorem interpretationem firmat ex loco Threnorum, quem supra indicavimus. Dices rursus patiendo vicit hostes Ecclesiæ. Esto. Quis hoc negat? Sunt tamen diversa pati & vincere. Causa & effectum confundi non debent. Quæritur solummodo quis sit primarius, literalis & immediatus sensus hujus textus & phrasis. Si de triumpho & victoria hic agatur primario & immediate, non ergo de passione. Forerius, Torcular t. f. hæc significant victoriam, inquit, quam de gentibus Christus reportavit. Recte. Sed quod sequitur durum videtur, prædicato vid. Evangelio & captivatis in obsequium fidei gentibus. Quid enim tunc fiet sequentibus, conculcavi eos in ira mea. Fuitne hoc opus iræ? Respondet hanc iram Christi versatam fuisse circa peccatum & peccati tyrannidem. Ego, licet violenta ea sit expositio, eam tamen producere volui ut ostenderem eum a recepta sententia libere recedere.
units.tr: Verse 3. I have trodden the winepress alone. Blessed Jerome rightly noted that winepress is used for vengeance and the punishments of sins. He goes on and explains more clearly: it is used for penalties and torments, when Jeremiah in the Lamentations says, the Lord has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah as in a winepress. This winepress, in which evils are punished and goods rewarded by the Saviour, he alone trod, and he had no helper. But afterwards he slides back to the passion: For neither an angel nor an archangel, nor any of the heavenly powers, assumed a human body and suffered for us and trod down and crushed the adverse strengths. I say first that to tread the winepress is nowhere said of the distribution of rewards; second, to tread the winepress is not to suffer or undergo the punishments of sins, but to punish another and inflict punishments. So I say: where someone is said to tread the winepress, there in the style of Scripture it is not said that he suffers, but that he inflicts punishments. Consider these passages: Lam. 1:15; Joel 3:13; Rev. 14:19–20. Nor is there anywhere a passage that opposes this assertion. Certainly, if there is anything in this text in which the primary, literal sense and immediate passion is signified, it is this very phrase. Hence you may hear it cited everywhere in sermons, the Dutch saying I have trodden the winepress alone, about the passion of Christ. How rightly has this now been shown! To this refers that gloss of Pinto: Christ answers that he is stained with the blood of the enemies of the human race, whom he alone conquered, and over whom he triumphed without human help. And since Christ accomplished this victory on the cross, it is concluded that the winepress is that in which our enemies are trodden like grapes. See, it was not difficult to interpret the treading of the winepress as the passion itself. Emanuel Sa, after he had interpreted the winepress as the winepress of the passion, immediately adds: or I alone conquered the enemies. For ETIAM in Scripture to tread the winepress means to press down the enemies. But let them show us a place where that phrase ETIAM signifies to suffer, to be pressed. Oleastrius: The Messiah answers why his garment is red: because he alone had trodden the winepress of the PASSION, and none of the nations had been with him to help him. For in his passion there was no one who endured the punishments of his passion together with him. But since in the passion he was rather trodden than himself trod down others, you would better explain I have trodden the winepress alone as: I alone conquered Satan, death and sin, by pressing and trampling them by the merit of my passion. He confirms this latter interpretation from the passage of the Lamentations which we indicated above. You will say again that by suffering he conquered the enemies of the Church. Granted. Who denies it? Yet to suffer and to conquer are different things. Cause and effect ought not to be confused. The only question is what is the primary, literal and immediate sense of this text and phrase. If the triumph and victory are treated here primarily and immediately, then the passion is not. Forerius: The winepress, namely these words, signify the victory, he says, which Christ won over the nations. Rightly. But what follows seems harsh: when the Gospel is preached and the nations are captured into the obedience of faith. For what then will happen to the following words, I trod them down in my wrath? Was this a work of wrath? He answers that this wrath of Christ was directed against sin and the tyranny of sin. I, although that explanation is forced, wished nonetheless to bring it forward to show that he freely departs from the accepted opinion.

units.la: Ibid. de gentibus non est vir mecum]. Audi hic magnum mysterium, Lector, quod Pintus pandit, Notanter dicit, non est vir, ut non excluderet Mariam Virginem, quae eum ad mortem usq; fuit comitata. Quid ergo fiet Johanni τῷ μαθητῇ discipulo? Joh. xix.26.
units.tr: Ibid. of the peoples there is no man with me. Hear here, reader, a great mystery, which Pinto unfolds: He says it advisedly: there is no man, so as not to exclude the Virgin Mary, who accompanied him even to death. What then becomes of John, the disciple [Greek]? John 19:26.

units.la: 27. Nam & is solus ex discipulis Christo ad mortem usque adhaesit. Non ergo potuit Iesaias vere dicere ex persona Christi, non est vir mecum, si Pintum audimus. Sed fortassis dicet, alia ratione Mariam adfuisse Christo alia Johannem & duas illas Marias. Quidni ergo eam unà opera in societatem redemptionis assumit? Apage istas ineptias! Non sic honoratur Beata virgo, sed potius rubore suffunditur. Qui ultra fas & verbi divini praescriptum eam colunt, tantum detrimentum verae religioni afferunt, quantum illi qui eam καλυπτλίζειν id est, vilem habent, judice Epiphanio. ᴡᴵᴷ ᴺᴷ tam frequenter usurpatur pro Graeco ὑδεῖς, μηδεὶς, nullus, sine ullo sexus discrimine, ut qui exempla rei isti probandae velit producere, eadem opera lucernam in ipso meridie possit accendere.
units.tr: 27. For he alone of the disciples clung to Christ right up to his death. So Isaiah could not truly have said in Christ's person, there is no man with me, if we listen to Pintus. But perhaps someone will say that Mary was present with Christ for a different reason than John and the two Marys. Why then not take her into the partnership of redemption along with them? Away with such nonsense! The Blessed Virgin is not honoured in this way; rather, she is made to blush. Those who worship her beyond what is right and beyond the prescription of the divine Word do as much harm to true religion as those who hold her in contempt, as Epiphanius judges [καλυπτλίζειν]. The Hebrew phrase ish with en [אִישׁ אֵין] is used as often as the Greek οὐδείς, μηδείς [none, no one], with no distinction of sex, so that anyone who wished to produce examples to prove this point might just as well light a lamp at midday.

units.la: 5. Et excandescentia mea fulcivit me] Atqui nec hoc passioni convenit, ubi potius iram & excandescentiam Dei sensit
units.tr: 5. And my fury upheld me (Isa. 63.5). Yet this does not suit the passion either, where he rather feels the anger and fury of God.

units.la: Plura hic possem accongerere nisi ex iis quae jam dicta sunt, satis constare arbitrarer, de Christi passione hunc contextum non posse intelligi. Si quis plura desideret, adeat Tarnovium & Ecclesiasticam expositionem Marlorati. Mantissae loco illud addam non defuisse qui hoc textu abusi sint ad probandam thesin, in corpore Christi glorioso etiamnum manere cicatrices, Curiosa illa quaestio in utramque partem disceptatur & à Thoma, tertiâ parte Summae, quaest. 54. art. 4. Sed ille hujus loci non meminit. Hajus quidam adversus Chambrunum disputans in hoc loco praesidium collocavit. Urget illud rubrum, id est, cruentum. Sed quomodo cruentus fuit Christus in gloriosa illa ἀναστάσει? An sanguinabant adhuc vulnera? At quomodo tunc erant cicatrices? Cicatrix utique non est sanguinans vulnus. Ejusdem roboris & illud est argumentum, quod ex Zach. xii. deprompunt, videbunt quem confixerunt. Ergo ne videbunt cicatrices? Atqui videbunt & illum quem crucifixerunt. Non tamen, opinor, tunc apparebit cruci affixus. Ego sententiam Thomae non impugno, Hoc ajo, duo ista loca sententiae isti neutiquam favere
units.tr: I could heap up more here, but I think it is already clear enough from what has been said that this context cannot be understood of Christ's passion. If anyone wants more, let him consult Tarnovius and Marlorat's Ecclesiastical Exposition. By way of an appendix, I will add that there have been some who have abused this text to prove the thesis that scars still remain in Christ's glorified body. That curious question is debated on both sides, and Thomas discusses it in the third part of the Summa, question 54, article 4. But he makes no mention of this passage. A certain man, arguing against Chambrun, has placed a stronghold in this passage. He presses the word red, that is, bloody. But how was Christ bloody in that glorious resurrection? Were his wounds still bleeding? But how then were they scars? A scar is certainly not a bleeding wound. The argument they draw from Zech. 12, they shall look on him whom they pierced, is of the same weakness. So will they not see the scars? Yet they will see him whom they crucified. However, I suppose he will not then appear fixed to the cross. I do not attack Thomas's opinion. What I say is that these two passages by no means favour that view.

units.la: CAP. LXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXIV.

units.la: Verf. 1. Utinam dirumperes cœlos &c.] Certant Interpretes utrum de primo an secundo adventu hoc votum accipiendum sit. Vulgò sic accipitur quasi sit suspirium veterum, Messiæ primum adventum seu τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν expectantium. Sed hoc ex textu difficulter probabitur inquit Balthasar Meisnerus, epistolâ ad Joh. Tarnovium, exercit. Bibl. edit primæ p. 104. & Edit. 3. pag. 354. Ex qua apponam & illa quæ sequuntur, quia notatu digna sunt, Ipse Deus Pater, qui sane incarnatus non est, compellatur, & liberatio potissimum temporalis petitur, uti totus contextus evincit. Quare in multis, inquit, non immerito id desideratur, quod sontes raro aspiciant, & delectum in dictis allegandis nullum habeant. Magna omnino hic opus est discretione & prudentia, ut dicta primaria à secundariis, directa ab indirectis, certa à dubiis distinguantur. Et optandum foret, ut per singulos fidei articulos, dictorum, quæ vulgo citari solent catervatim, quasi lustratio quædam institueretur, & quæ primo & principaliter concludant, distinguerentur. Hactenus Mentzerus. Eodem loco habendum, inquit Tarnovius, quod nonnulli illis quoque verbis, Pf. 144. 5. Domine inclina cœlos tuos & descende, tale votum exfeulpant. Huc etiam pertinet locus Exod. 4. 13. obsecro Domine, mitte quem missurus es. q.d. Mitte Messiam. Quem locum obiter indicavimus in Syllabo Anti-barbari nostri, ad initium Exod. Ubi & addidimus insignem testimonium Augustini Steuchi Eugubini. Ebræa sunt שלח נא ביד תשלח mitte quæso per manum ejus quem missurus es. Non sunt verba optantis aut precantis, sed potius, deprecantis: non votum facientis, sed impatientis. Q.d. mitte ad regem Pharaonem quemcunque voles, modo me excusatum habeas. Ego enim non ibo. Quo responso, nescio an satis modesto, Dei iram provocavit, verf. 14. Quod si etiam Moses non ignoravit sibi cum Filio Dei colloquium esse, id quod Theologi plerique statuunt, quomodo cum rogat, ut Messiam mittat.
units.tr: Verse 1. Would that you would rend the heavens, etc.] The commentators dispute whether this wish is to be taken of the first or the second coming. The common view is that it is the sigh of the ancients who awaited the first coming of the Messiah, that is, the appearing [τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν]. But, says Balthasar Meisner, in his letter to Johann Tarnov, Exercitationes Biblicae, first edition p. 104 and third edition p. 354, this will hardly be proved from the text. I will add what follows from him, because it is worth noting: God the Father himself, who was certainly not incarnate, is addressed, and the deliverance sought is chiefly temporal, as the whole context shows. Therefore, he says, it is not without reason that many people wish that the guilty seldom look upon these things, and that they have no careful selection in the passages they cite. Great discretion and prudence are needed here, so that primary texts are distinguished from secondary, direct from indirect, and certain from doubtful. And it would be desirable that, article by article of the faith, the passages usually cited in crowds should undergo a kind of review, and that those which prove the point first and principally should be distinguished. So far Mentzer. In the same place, says Tarnov, it must be noted that some also carve out such a wish from those words of Psalm 144:5, Lord, bow your heavens and come down. The passage Exodus 4:13 also belongs here: I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send. That is, Send the Messiah. We touched on this passage in passing in the Syllabus of our Anti-Barbarus, at the beginning of Exodus, where we also added the notable testimony of Agostino Steuco of Gubbio. The Hebrew reads [שלח נא ביד תשלח], send, I pray, by the hand of him whom you will send. These are not the words of one wishing or praying, but rather of one begging off: not a man making a vow, but a man losing patience. That is: send whomever you like to King Pharaoh, provided you excuse me, for I will not go. By this answer, perhaps not modest enough, he provoked God's anger (verse 14). But if Moses also knew that he was in converse with the Son of God, as most theologians hold, how can he ask that the Messiah be sent?

units.la: CAP. LXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXIV.

units.la: Verf. 6. Tanquam pannus menstruatæ omnes justitiæ nostræ.] Hoc loco usi sunt nonnulli ad probandum peccatum originis. Quod licet firmissimis sacræ paginæ Oraculis nitatur, ex hoc tamen loco neutiquam fulciri, evidentissime apparebit, si quis caput universum bene expenderit. Agitur enim de peccatis actualibus. Sunt & alii qui hunc locum sæpe in ore habent ad deprimenda bona opera. Neutiquam ego inter eos nomen profitear meum, qui perfectionem in hac vita somniant, aut bonis operibus vim meriti & justificationis tribuunt, aut bonorum operum, quandiu hanc carnem circumferimus imperfectionem impugnant. Sed nec illis accedam, qui optima regenitorum opera, peccata & quidem mortalia & spurca peccata appellitant, eoque tandem descendunt, ut bona opera ad salutem perniciosa esse cum maximo scandalo asserant. Certe negari non potest, nimis crude & crasse nonnullos locutos fuisse. Si hic introducuntur Judæi, quibus Babylonica captivitas hypocriseos confessionem extorserat, id quod plurimis interpretibus placuisse video. Si de operibus loquuntur, quæ durante ista hypocrisi, in quam ipse quoque noster Jesaias & cap. 1. & 58. & alibi graviter detonuerat, fecerunt, quid hoc ad ista opera, quæ vere pii & resipiscentes majore luce & gratia à Deo colluströti, faciunt, non ut ex iis justificentur sed ut Deo gratitudinem pro modulo collatæ in ipsos gratiæ præstent. Et nimis sibi indulsit B. Lutherus, quando ita vertit, doch nu zijn wp altesamen als den onrepnen/ &c. Ebræa enim in præterito loquuntur, Et fuimus (וְנִהְיֶה) omnes nos ut immundus & omnes justitiæ nostræ, repete ὡσεὶ ῥάκος, (fuerunt) quasi pannus &c. Pintus, Oleastrius & alii hic in B. Lutherum incurrunt & flagellant ejus articulum 31. In omni opere bono justum peccare, vel ut Oleastrius, sententiam ejus citat, omnes justitias piorum esse peccata. Quidquid sit neque enim Lutheri opera ad manum habeo, ego subscribo iis Rev. Amesii verbis, optimis fidelium operibus imperfectionem adhærere cui remissione opus sit, ipsa tamen opera non esse peccata. Et quod ad Lutherum attinet, D. Franzius Theol. Witeberg. p. 748. tractatus sui de recta Interp. Scripturæ hæc ejus verba citat, quæ non pigrabor adscribere, Hoc loco, inquit, sumus aliquando usi contra justitiam humanam. Bona quidem sententia est, sed non propria hujus loci. Propheta enim cum videt multos bonos viros in captivitatem abductos, ut fuere Nehemias, Ezras & alii, dolet quod ob malorum impietatem justi homines diutius in captivitate detineantur. Et Paulo post, sunt autem alii loci qui justitiam humanam dammant, sicut
units.tr: Verse 6. Like a menstruous rag are all our righteousnesses.] Some people have used this verse to prove original sin. Although that doctrine rests on the most solid oracles of Holy Scripture, it will be quite evident that this verse does not support it, if anyone weighs the whole chapter carefully. The passage is about actual sins. There are others who often have this verse on their lips to disparage good works. I will certainly not count myself among those who dream of perfection in this life, or who ascribe to good works the power of merit and justification, or who attack the imperfection of good works as long as we carry this flesh about. But nor will I join those who call the best works of the regenerate sins, and indeed mortal and foul sins, and who finally go so far as to assert, to the great scandal of all, that good works are pernicious to salvation. It cannot be denied that some have spoken far too crudely and crassly. If Jews are introduced here, whom the Babylonian captivity had forced to confess their hypocrisy, which I see pleased very many interpreters, and if the prophet speaks of works they did while that hypocrisy lasted (the hypocrisy against which our Isaiah himself thundered severely in chapters 1 and 58 and elsewhere), what does this have to do with those works which truly pious and repentant people perform, illumined by God with greater light and grace? They do not perform them to be justified by them, but to render to God thanks in proportion to the grace bestowed on them. Luther too indulged himself excessively when he translated the passage thus: "but now we have all become like something unclean," etc. For the Hebrew speaks in the past tense: And we have all been (wenihyeh) like the unclean, and all our righteousnesses, and the Greek ὡσεὶ ῥάκος [hōsei rhakos] is rendered like a rag, with "were" understood. Pintus, Oleaster and others run into Luther on this point and lash his thirty-first article: that in every good work the righteous man sins; or, as Oleaster quotes his statement, that all the righteousnesses of the pious are sins. Whatever Luther meant (I do not have his works at hand), I subscribe to the words of the esteemed Amesius: imperfection clings to the best works of the faithful and needs pardon, yet the works themselves are not sins. As for Luther, D. Franzius, in his Theology of Wittenberg, p. 748, in his treatise on the correct interpretation of Scripture, cites these words of his, which I will not hesitate to copy out: "In this passage," he says, "we have sometimes used it against human righteousness." It is a good sentiment, but it is not the proper sense of this passage. For when the prophet sees many good men led off into captivity, as Nehemiah, Ezra and others were, he grieves that because of the wickedness of the impious, the righteous are kept in captivity longer. And a little later: there are other passages which condemn human righteousness, like that one

units.la: Medull. part. 2. Cap. 3. init. sicut ille, Domine ne intres in judicium cum servo tuo. In conspectu tuo non justificatur ullus vivens, cum omnia fecerit​is, dicite, servi inutiles sumus. Hæc B. Lutherus, Cæterum illud quoque consideratione dignum est, annon & hæc & sequentia ad præsentem statum Judæorum eorumque post rejectum Evangelium conditionem, quæ certe abjectissima est, referri possint, ut eos ad se redeuntes & pœnitentes hic introducat Propheta. Ita certe hunc locum interpretatur Arias Mont. & per justitias illorum, legales illas & ceremoniales, quæ antiquatæ & obsoletæ non magis probentur, inquit, quam pannus menstruata. Cætera vero de ipsorum dispersione & oberratione vaga interpretatur. Eodem tramite incedit & Forerius, ad contaminatos in lege nemo accedere audebat, inquit ille. Ita Judæos, post Domini passionem & Evangelium annuntiatum nemo est, qui non ut reos & contaminatos ducat. Et quis ignorat ex Evangelio & Thalmude, hypocritas istos universam fere justitiam exteriori cultu definivisse? Quid absurdi ergo, eos ceremonias istas & legales observationes quæ Hellenistæ quoque δικαιώματα vocant, ut Ebræorum 9. 1. & externas virtutes quas solas exercuerant, intellexisse? Sed hæc Theologis relinquamus, & videamus paucis, quid de Ebræa voce עֲרִיִים tenendum sit. Ebr. וּבְגֵד עֲרִיִים כָּל צִדְקוֹתֵינוּ Vulgatus Interpres, Et quasi pannus menstruata universa justitia nostra. Lovan. Belg. ende als het Laecken der Maensuchtigher Vrouwen 3ijn alle onse gherechtigheden. Luth. Paulo generalius, wie em unsatigh is.
units.tr: Medull. part. 2, ch. 3 at the beginning, like that one: "Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant. In your sight no living man is justified; when you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants." So Luther. Moreover, it is also worth considering whether these verses and those that follow can be referred to the present state of the Jews, and their condition after they rejected the Gospel, which is certainly most abject; so that the prophet introduces them returning and repenting. Arias Montanus certainly interprets the passage this way, and by their righteousnesses he understands those legal and ceremonial ones, which, being antiquated and obsolete, are approved no more than a menstruous rag, he says. The rest he interprets of their dispersion and aimless wandering. Forerius follows the same path: no one dared to approach those made unclean by the law, he says. So after the Lord's passion and the proclamation of the Gospel, there is no one who does not regard the Jews as guilty and unclean. And who does not know from the Gospel and the Talmud that those hypocrites defined almost all righteousness by outward worship? What is absurd, then, about understanding that they meant those ceremonies and legal observances, which the Hellenists also call dikaiōmata [δικαιώματα], as in Hebrews 9:1, and the external virtues which were the only ones they had practised? But let us leave these matters to the theologians, and see briefly what should be held about the Hebrew word ʿarim [עֲרִיִים]. The Hebrew reads: and like a garment of ʿarim all our righteousnesses. The Vulgate translator: and as a menstruous rag all our righteousness. The Louvain version (Dutch): as the cloth of menstruating women are all our righteousnesses. Luther, more generally: "as something unclean."

units.la: Belg. als een dzehhigh bleedt. In qua non acquiescentes multi, cum pro concione hunc locum citant, Lovanienfem præferre solent, atque ita interpretari, ut honestis virginibus, matronis & viris ruborem sæpe exprimant. At scire illi debebant necdum liquere satis, quid per עֲרִיִים intellixerit divinus Vates. Id, credo, intelligent, ubi diversas Interpretum sententias intelligent. Chaldæus, vestem עֲרִיִים interpretatur, מְלֻכוּשׁ מָרְחָק id est, quasi vestis abominabilis. R. Sal. כְּבֵגֶד מְאוֹס שֶׁהַכֹּל אוֹמְרִים הַסֵּר עֲרִיִים תַּרְנוֹם שֶׁל הַסְּרָה id est, sicut vestis aspernabilis de qua omnes dicunt, Remove, habet enim in Chald. significationem removendi. Et certe עֲרָא in Chald passim est movere, in textu Biblico. Lxx. ὡς ἐξηκ​ὸν ἀπόκα​ρυμμένη, ut pannus sedentis fœmina, Sedentis in immunditie sua. Respexit forte ad Genes. xxxi.35. ubi Rachel ad Labanem, Ne irascatur dominus meus, quod non possum assurgere tibi, quia secundum coniugem limem mulierum mihi est. Theod. ipsam vocem Ebr. interpretatus est Symmachus κυνσευ id est, parientium. Kimchi varias affert interpretationes in Comm. 1. ut sint frusta panni quae imponuntur מַכָּה plagae, vel scabiei vergenti ad lepram, ubi Targ. habet עֲרִיא 2. Sunt qui exponunt; inquit, ex Chaldaica interpretatione הָרָה vid. מעריא concipiens, gravida, praegnans, acsi diceret, sicut vestis mulieris quando parit, quae sunt מלכלכים בְּרָם sudata sanguine. At postquam concepit foemina quamdiu uterum gestat; cessant menstrua. Quid hoc ergo ad rem? III. Potest etiam exponi, inquit, בְּגַר סְמַרְטוּטוּ זְכָלִי / Et in libro Radicum, בְּגַדִי סְמַרְטוּטִין וּבְלָאוֹת id est, vestes Semartut & detritas, Quid סְמַרְטוּט? Baal Aruch, סְמַרְטוּט הַתִּיכַת בְּגַר כְּלִי id est, frustum panni vestisve detritae. Addit Kimchi, Semartut juxta quosdam esse frustum panni, quo mulier מַקְנֶחֶת abstergit se & probat, an adhuc sanguinem videat. Non affert tamen huius strictioris significationis exempla. Unde probabilior significatio prior, Ita author libri Musar sol. 115 pag. 2. לְבוּשׁ אִצְטְלָא & לְבוּשׁ סְמַרְטוּטִין id est, indutus laceris, & indutus stola opponuntur. Et Elias in Methurgeman illa Chaldaica, כְּלָאֵי טִפְסֵן / (quae respondent Ebraicis, כְּלוּאֵי הַסְּחֹבוֹת Jerm. 38.) interpretatur סְמַרְטוּטִין. Thenh vulgo ponunt עֵרָה quod Chaldaeis in Aphel passim & semel Ebraeis (Prov. 25. 20) est removere, ita tamen ut formam mutuetur à עֵרָה / Sed & Deut. 29. 5. videtur pro alteri positum esse; ubi enim Ebraeus habet יִנְעֲלְךָ לֹא בְּלִתָּה / neque calceus tuus inveteravit; Chald. וּסְנָנְךָ לָא עֲדוּ Fag. & calceamentum non est attritum, nisi malis, & calceamenta tua non remota sunt, scilicet ob vetustatem, id est, abjecta. Restant duae interpretationes aliae, quarum altera est Aben-Ezrae, altera Aquilae. Aben-Ezra, עֵדִים כְּמוֹ יֹאכַל עַד כִּי כְּנַר הַשְּׁלָל הוּא מְנוֹאָל בְּרָמִים Deducit à singulari עֵד spolium, praeda, quomodo à סָף fit סְפִים / à סֵף tributum, סִפִּים / à צַר latus, צְדִים Affert autem locum ex Gen. 49 comedet praedam. Addit, nam vestis spolii est sudata sanguine. Aquila, μαρτύρων, testimoniorum, quasi sit à themate עִיר / formetque plurale עֵדִים instar duplicantium Ain, sicuti à צַיִן fit צַעִים / Hanc vero vestem testimoniorum sic interpretatur B. Hieron. quando sanguis in primo coitu maritali approbatur. Atque hae sunt interpretationes veterum, quas referre opere pretium visum fuit. Nunc videamus quodnam ex istis recencentioribus se probaverit maxime. Oleastrius Aben-Ezrae interpretationem caeteris praeferendam existimat. Nec non Forerius, ירים [?] enim praeda est, inquit, quasi judaeorum justitias comparet vestibus praedae, id est dilaceratis, dilaniatis, Indignae autem sunt hominum conspectu tales vestes. Ita & justitiae judaeorum post adventum Christi. Erant enim rei sanguinis Christi, quem sibi & filiis suis imputari magna voce petierant. Pintus illam de veste lacera seu ex frustis laceris & detrita consuta. Sic n. ille, Dictio ירים [?] significat centones, quos Lusitani farrapos appellant. Eadem placuit Pisc. ein gestickt flaid & in Scholiis, Hebr. ein flaid der lumplin oder spatlin. Tigur. ut vestis centonum abjectorum. Junius, ut panniculus abjectissimus, ad verbum, inquit, panniculus remotionum. Deodatus, come un panno Corduto, ut pannus foedatus. Et in margine ô Maculato di mestrui, ô panno di struci, id est, aut maculatus sanguine menstruo, aut, pannus centonum. Hisp. Cypriani de Valer. como trapo de immunditia, ut pannus immunditiae. Danica; ut vestis inquinata.
units.tr: The Dutch version: as a bloodied rag. Many who are not satisfied with this, when they cite the passage in a sermon, are accustomed to prefer the Louvain version and to interpret it so as to bring a blush often to honest virgins, matrons and men. But they ought to know that it is not yet sufficiently clear what the divine seer meant by ʿarim. I believe they will understand this when they grasp the different opinions of the interpreters. The Chaldean paraphrast takes ʿarim to mean garment, and renders it a distant garment, that is, like an abominable garment. Rabbi Solomon: like a despised garment, of which everyone says, Remove! Targum: the word for removal, the Aramaic ʿarim [Aramaic] signifying removal. And indeed the Aramaic root ʿara is found everywhere in the Chaldean text with the sense of moving. The Seventy render it as a woman sitting apart [ὡς ἐξηκὸν ἀπόκαρυμμένη], like the rag of a woman sitting in her uncleanness. They perhaps had in mind Genesis 31:35, where Rachel says to Laban: Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the custom of women is upon me. Symmachus translated the Hebrew word itself as [κυνσευ] (kynseu), that is, of women in labour. Kimchi gives various interpretations in his commentary, the first being that they are rags laid on a wound or on a scab tending to leprosy, where the Targum has ʿarya. The second: Some explain, he says, from the Chaldean rendering, the word harah, that is ʿaryā, conceiving, pregnant, great with child, as if he were to say, like the garment of a woman when she gives birth, which is smeared and soaked with blood. But after a woman conceives, she does not menstruate for as long as she carries the womb. What does this have to do with the matter? Third, he says, it can also be explained as rags and tatters. And in the Book of Roots: garments of tatters and worn-out rags, that is, tattered clothes and worn things. What is a semartut? Baal Aruch says: semartut is a piece of cloth or a worn-out garment, that is, a shred of rag or of worn clothing. Kimchi adds that some say semartut is a piece of rag with which a woman wipes herself to see whether she still sees blood. He does not, however, give examples of this narrower meaning. Hence the former meaning is the more probable. So the author of the book Musar, in sol. 115, p. 2, sets clothing of a cloak and clothing of tatters against each other, that is, clothed in rags and clothed in a robe. And Elias, in his Methurgeman, interprets that Chaldean phrase (which corresponds to the Hebrew kelu'ei hasehobot, Jeremiah 38) as tatters. Some commonly take ʿera, which in the Chaldean Aphel is found everywhere, and once among the Hebrews (Proverbs 25:20), to mean remove, though borrowing its form from ʿera. But also in Deuteronomy 29:5 it seems to be used for other. For where the Hebrew has neither has your shoe grown old (lo' bilt'ah), the Chaldean has and your sandals have not been removed, the Vulgate has nor has your footwear been worn. Unless you prefer, the sandals were not removed, namely because of age, that is, cast off. Two other interpretations remain, one of Aben-Ezra and one of Aquila. Aben-Ezra: ʿadim is like yo'khal ʿad, "until he eats," as the garment of plunder is smeared with blood in the Ramim (?). He derives it from the singular ʿed, spoil, booty, just as from sef comes sefim, from sef (tribute) comes sifim, and from tsar (side) comes tsedim. He cites Genesis 49, he shall devour the prey. He adds: for the garment of spoil is soaked with blood. Aquila [μαρτύρων, martyrōn], of testimonies, as if from the root ʿyr, forming the plural ʿadim like the doubling of the ʿayin, just as from tsayin comes tsa'im. Blessed Jerome interprets this garment of testimonies as the one in which blood appears at the first marital intercourse. These are the interpretations of the ancients, which I thought worth recording. Now let us see which of the more recent ones has proved most acceptable. Oleaster thinks Aben-Ezra's interpretation should be preferred to the rest. Forerius too: for ʿarim is booty, he says, as if he compared the righteousnesses of the Jews to garments of plunder, that is, torn and ripped to pieces, and such garments are unfit to be seen by men. So too the righteousnesses of the Jews after the coming of Christ. For they were guilty of the blood of Christ, which they had loudly asked to be imputed to themselves and their children. Pintus takes it to mean a torn garment, or one made from torn and worn rags sewn together. For he says: the word ʿarim signifies patchwork, which the Portuguese call farrapos. The same view pleased Piscator (a embroidered cloth), and in the Scholia, the Hebrew (a cloth of rags or tatters). Tigurine: like a garment of cast-off patches. Junius: like a most abject little rag, literally, he says, a little rag of removals. Deodatus: like a soiled cloth, as in come un panno Corduto, a soiled rag; and in the margin: a rag stained with menstrual blood, or a rag of rags, that is, either stained with menstrual blood or a patchwork rag. The Spanish version of Cipriano de Valera: like a filthy rag, as a rag of uncleanness. The Danish: like a soiled garment.

units.la: Anglica, as filthy rags, & foeda veteramenta. Castalio & Genevenses ipsam Vulgatam expressere, dum ille, similes panni mestruati, Hi, Comme le drapeau souille des fleurs de la femme.
units.tr: The English: as filthy rags, and foul old clothes. Castalio and the Genevans rendered the Vulgate itself: Castalio, like menstruous rags; the Genevans, like the cloth soiled by a woman's flowers.

units.la: Vers. 7. Antequam parturiret, peperit: antequam veniret partus ejus, peperit masculum] Carth. Locus iste dupliciter explanatur, I. de nativitate Christi, qua natus est de virgine sancta, ut sit sensus antequam parturiret, id est, dolorem pariendi sentiret, peperit sine dolore. Antequam veniret partus ejus id est, dolor ex partu, perperit masculum id est, Christum, de quo Jeremias, Novum faciet Dominus super terram, mulier circumdabit virum. II. de nativitate Christi spirituali qua in corde credentium nascitur, seu spirituali generatione fidelium, qui ex aqua & S. Sancto renascuntur in Christo. Haec Carthus. Prior interpretatio licet valde sit a contextu aliena, suos tamen patronos habet soletque locus iste saepe citari probandae thesi, B. Mariam sine dolore peperisse. Sed I. neque antecedanea neque consequa ullam B. Virginis mentionem faciunt. II. Vers. 8. expresse memoratur Sion id est, Ecclesia. III. dicitur parturire terra id est, populus. Gigni dicitur gens. IV. memorantur filii plurimi, non unus. Hinc & Forerius, & Arias Montanus, & Pintus & Oleastrius de spirituali Ecclesiae partu hunc locum intellexere.
units.tr: Vers. 7. "Before she was in labour, she brought forth; before her pain came, she brought forth a man-child": Carth. This passage is explained in two ways. (I) Of the birth of Christ, by which he was born of the holy Virgin, so that the sense is: before she was in labour, that is, before she felt the pain of bearing, she gave birth without pain. "Before her pain came," that is, the pain of childbirth; "she brought forth a man-child," that is, Christ, of whom Jeremiah says: "The Lord shall create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall compass a man." (II) Of the spiritual birth of Christ, which is born in the hearts of believers, or of the spiritual generation of the faithful, who are born again in Christ of water and the Holy Spirit. So Carthusianus. The first interpretation, although it is very far removed from the context, nevertheless has its defenders, and this passage is often cited to prove the thesis that the Blessed Virgin bore a child without pain. But (I) neither the preceding nor the following verses make any mention of the Blessed Virgin. (II) In verse 8 Zion, that is, the Church, is expressly named. (III) The earth is said to travail, that is, the people; a nation is said to be born. (IV) Many sons are mentioned, not one. Hence Forerius, Arias Montanus, Pintus and Oleastrius also understood this passage of the spiritual birth of the Church.

units.la: Verf. 18. Et nunc quid tibi vis in via Ægypti, ut bibas aquas Schichor ] LXX. Καὶ νῦν τί σοι ἡ τῆς ὁδοῦ Αἰγύπτου, ἕ πιεῖν ὕδωρ λαμψ Hæc versio τῶν LXX. immane quantum turbavit Historiam Paradisi. Hinc enim in eam opinionem delapsi sunt fluvium Gihon, de quo Genes. 2. 13. esse Nilum. Sed in Ebraeo hoc loco est יְאֹר q. d. μέλας. Vulg. Interpres & hic & Josua XIII. 3. vertit turbidum. * Utrum vero per Schichor intelligatur Nilus, an potius amnis iste qui Petram Arabiæ præterfluens in Sirbonim paludem influit & Ægyptum à Judæa disterminat, non convenit inter eruditos. Ergo eos sequor qui Nilum interpretantur tur. Græcis Μέλας vocatur, hoc est יְאֹר / Ægyptus vocatur Μελάμβωλ .i. nigrigleba, apud Eustath. in Dionysii περιηγ, Quin & Servius ad illud Georgic. viridem Ægyptum nigra fœcundat arena, notat Nilum Latine Melonem dictum fuisse. Et per Melonis albam Paginam apud Ausonium, Politianus Misc. cent. 1. c. 39. intelligit Papyrum, quem Nilus producit. * Firmat hanc quoque sententiam. Vetus Nili apellatio, Ægyptus. Homerus. Ηεἰν γ' ὅτ' ἂν Αἰγύπτιο διαπαπῷ ποταμόν, UbiDydim.Scoliastes, Αἴγυπτον ὁ Νεῖλος ...
units.tr: Verse 18. "And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Schichor?" LXX: "And now, what is the way of Egypt to thee, to drink water?" [Καὶ νῦν τί σοι ἡ τῆς ὁδοῦ Αἰγύπτου, ἵνα πιεῖν ὕδωρ]. This rendering of the Seventy has greatly confused the account of Paradise. From it some have fallen into the opinion that the river Gihon, mentioned in Gen. 2:13, is the Nile. But in the Hebrew at this place the word is יְאֹר [ye'or], that is, "black" [μέλας]. The Vulgate translator, both here and at Joshua 13:3, renders it turbid. Whether by Schichor the Nile is meant, or rather that river which flows past Petra in Arabia and empties into the Sirbonian marsh and separates Judea from Egypt, is not agreed among the learned. I therefore follow those who take it to be the Nile. The Greeks call it Μέλας [Melas], that is יְאֹר. Egypt is called Μελάμβωλ [Melambōl], that is "black-soil," in Eustathius on the Periegesis of Dionysius. Indeed Servius, on the line in the Georgics, "the green Egypt makes fertile with black sand," notes that the Nile was called Melo in Latin. And by "the white page of Melo" in Ausonius, Politian (Misc. cent. 1, c. 39) understands the papyrus, which the Nile produces. The old name of the Nile also confirms this view: Egypt. Homer: "when he crosses the river of Egypt" [Ηεἰν γ' ὅτ' ἂν Αἰγύπτιο διαπαπῷ ποταμόν]. Where Didymus the scholiast says: "Egypt [is called] the Nile..." [Αἴγυπτον ὁ Νεῖλος].
