units.la: * Et Festus Pomp. Mela nomine alio Nilus vocatur.
units.tr: And Festus; Pomponius Mela calls the Nile by another name.

units.la: * Et Odyss. ξ. πιμπλᾶσει ἡ Αἴγυπτον ... Nilum vocant. Sichor, Sir, ut Nachas, Nas, serpens. Hinc & nomen Caniculæ, σείριος, & σείριος ἄστρον, q. d. Νειλαῖος, id est, stella Niliaca. Namque eodem tempore Canicula exoriebatur & Nilus intumescebat. Atque hinc petes ἔτυμον Osiridis, quem eundem cum Nilo Deum fuisse tradit Seldenus. Hinc Busiris, Petosiris, Calasiris & id genus Ægytiaca alia. Omitto nunc authoritates Rabb. Salomonis Jarchi, Kimchii & aliorum. Sed ajunt Nilum vocari יאור id est, rivum Ægypti, Τὸ Schichor vero שיחור torrentem Ægypti. Tantum vero abest ut hoc evertere possit superiorem sententiam, ut confirmet maxime ipsam vocem. Nilus enim non aliunde commodius deduxeris, quam ab Ebr. נחל / Quomodo enim à Baal fit בעל & Bel, ita & à Nachal, Nechel, Nel. E longum & I seu E I quoties alternant? Ergo Νῆλ, Νῆ & Νηλ. Nunc te remitto Lector, ad Masium Jos. 13. 3. Fullerum 2. 8. Riberam Amos 6. numero 44. Drus. ad loca diff. Moisis p. 59. Seldenum Synt. 1. cap. 4. & alios. Rhinocolura vel Rhinocorura, pro qua disputat Beroaldus Chronolog 2. 7. Non est nomen fluvii sed urbis. Quod vero LXX. Jes. 27. 12. usque ad torrentem Ægypti vertunt ἕως εὐνοκορύρων, inde non inferas Rhinocoruram fluvii nomen esse. Hieron. usque ad Rhinocorum, quod est opidum Ægypti & Palestinæ confinio, non tam verba scripturarum, quam sensum verborum exprimentes, Quæ hic vulgo objiciuntur facile tolles hac observatione, diversa ejusdem fluvii brachia aliquando communi, aliquando proprio nomine appellari.
units.tr: And in the Odyssey, book 14 [ξ]: "fills Egypt..." they call it the Nile. Sichor (Sir), like Nachas (Nas), means serpent. Hence also the name of the Dog-star, Seirios [σείριος], and "the Seirios star" [σείριος ἄστρον], that is, the Nilaean star [Νειλαῖος], since the Dog-star rose at the same time as the Nile swelled. From here you may seek the etymology of Osiris, whom Selden says was the same god as the Nile. Hence Busiris, Petosiris, Calasiris and other Egyptian names of that kind. I now pass over the authorities of the rabbis, Solomon Jarchi, Kimchi and others. They say the Nile is called יאור, that is, the river of Egypt, but Schichor שיחור the torrent of Egypt. This, however, is so far from overturning the former opinion that it rather confirms the very word. For Nilus can be more conveniently derived from no other source than the Hebrew נחל [nachal]. For as from Baal come בעל and Bel, so also from Nachal come Nechel and Nel. How often do the long A and I, or E and I, alternate? So Νῆλ, Νῆ and Νηλ. Now I refer the reader to Masius on Joshua 13:3, Fuller 2.8, Ribera on Amos 6 no. 44, Drusius on the difficult places of Moses, p. 59, Selden, Syntagma 1, ch. 4, and others. Rhinocolura or Rhinocorura, for which Beroaldus argues (Chronology 2.7), is not the name of a river but of a city. As for the Seventy's rendering at Isaiah 27:12, "as far as the torrent of Egypt," as "as far as Rhinocorura" [ἕως εὐνοκορύρων], one should not infer from this that Rhinocorura is the name of a river. Jerome: "as far as Rhinocorura, which is a town on the border of Egypt and Palestine," rendering not so much the words of the Scriptures as the sense of the words. The objections commonly raised here you will easily remove with this observation: different arms of the same river are sometimes called by a common name and sometimes by a proper name.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Verf. 8. Ne forte recedat anima mea à te] Ita vulg. ex Græco, μή ποτε ἀποστῇ ἡ ψυχή μου ἀπὸ σοῦ. Egregiam metaphoram, quæ in Ebræo, nimis oscitanter neglecta, Sic enim sonant Ebræa פֶּן־תִּקְעֲנָפְשִׁי מִמֶּךָּ ne luxetur anima mea à te. Similem locutionem habes Jezech. 23. 18. Junius, ne anima mea tanquam luxatum aut elisum membrum discedat abs te, & tu abscindaris ab illa tanquam abalienatum membrum; Metaphora optime communionem Dei cum fidelibus explicans.
units.tr: Verse 8. Lest perhaps my soul withdraw from you] So the Vulgate, from the Greek [μή ποτε ἀποστῇ ἡ ψυχή μου ἀπὸ σοῦ]. This is an outstanding metaphor, which in the Hebrew has been carelessly neglected. For the Hebrew reads [פֶּן־תִּקְעֲנָפְשִׁי מִמֶּךָּ], that is, lest my soul be put out of joint from you. You have a similar expression at Ezek. 23. 18. Junius: lest my soul, like a dislocated or crushed limb, depart from you, and you be cut off from it like an estranged limb; a metaphor that explains very well the communion of God with the faithful.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAP. VII.

units.la: Templum domini &c.] Luth. Hic est templum DOMINI &c. Ebr. הַיכַל יְהוָה הַמָּה Quidam, ut Jun. templi Domini, t. D.t.D. ista sunt vel ad T.D. vel, ad templum DOMINI, ad T.D. ista pertinent, ut sit ellipsis, literæ ל ante היכל/ista operaque nos facimus, nostræ ceremoniæ pertinent ad templum, ad cultum ab ipso Deo institutum, vel istæ promissiones potissimum templo factæ sunt. Quamdiu ergo durat hoc templum & nos præstamus ea quæ adillud pertinent, nos florebimus. Sunt qui pronomen המה ἐκ- ταξιῶς accipiunt, quasi digito monstrarent ædificia templi, vel partes templi potiores, quales erant Sanctum & Sanctum Sanctorum & atria, Istasunt templum DOMINI &c. Non male, quis idem quoque retulerit ad verba antecedentia, ne confidatis verbis mendacii, Templum DOMINI, t. D. t. D. ista sunt.
units.tr: "The temple of the LORD, etc." Luther: "Here is the temple of the LORD, etc." Hebrew: הַיכַל יְהוָה הַמָּה. Some, like Junius, read "of the temple of the LORD" (T.D. T.D.), so that these words belong to the temple of the LORD, these words belong to T.D., with an ellipsis of the letter ל before היכל, as in these are the things we do, our ceremonies, which pertain to the temple, to the worship instituted by God himself, or these promises were made chiefly to the temple. So long as this temple lasts and we perform the things that pertain to it, we shall flourish. Others take the pronoun המה demonstratively, as if they were pointing with a finger at the buildings of the temple, or at its principal parts, such as the Holy Place, the Holy of Holies, and the courts: these are the temple of the LORD, etc. Not badly, someone might also refer it to the preceding words, do not trust in lying words: the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, these are.

units.la: Verf. 18. Ut faciant placentas Reginæ cœli.] Per Reginam cœli vulgus Interpretum Lunam intelligit, quam Reginæ titulo ornant passim Gentiles, Homerus in Hymn.
units.tr: Verse 18. To make cakes for the Queen of heaven. The Vulgate translators understand by the Queen of heaven the moon, whom the Gentiles everywhere adorn with the title of queen. Homer, in a hymn:

units.la: Χαῖρι ἄναστα Θεὰ λευκώλενι Δία πλήνη.
units.tr: "Hail, lady, white-armed goddess, divine Selene." [Χαῖρι ἄναστα Θεὰ λευκώλενι Δία πλήνη.]

units.la: Horatius.
units.tr: Horace:

units.la: Siderum Regina bicornis
units.tr: "Two-horned queen of the stars,"

units.la: Audi Luna puellas.
units.tr: "Hear us, Moon, you girls."

units.la: Quam Herodotus quoque ἀφροδίτη vocat. Alii Solem intelligunt, quem sub fœminæ specie Ebræi concipiunt. מָה enim semper, שֶׁמֶשׁ aliquando fœmininum est. Alii Junonem, alii Venerem Babyloniam, quam Reginam quoque cœlorum dictam monet Cl. Seldenus, citatque in eam rem Harpocrationem in Σαμαρίτων. Sed frustra hæc disputantur. Hypothesis falsa. מַלְכַּת non significat Reginam, Reginam cœli מַלְכַּת הַשָּׁמַיִם dicerent, ut 1. Reg. x. מַלְכַּת שְׁבָא regina Sabæ. At hic est מֶלֶךְ vox in statu regiminis posita ab absoluto מַלְאכָה quod proprie opus, laborem, artem vel artificium significat. Ita à מְמַלְכָּה fit מַמְלֶכֶת / neque inter omnia ista quæ ad regulam illam pertinent, ullum est quod utroque modo statum regiminis formet. Ne quis dicat à מַלְכָּה & מַלְכַּת & מַלְכֹּת formari. Dixi מַלְאכָה proprie significare opus &c, Addo, per metonymiam etiam denotare rem labore & opere & artificio factam &acacquisitam. Exod. 22. 8. quod non immiserit manus suas במלאכת in rem proximi sui. Ubi plene scribitur cum א radicali, licet quiescente, hic defecte.
units.tr: Herodotus also calls her Aphrodite. Others understand the sun, which the Hebrews conceive under a feminine form, for מָה is always feminine, and שֶׁמֶשׁ sometimes is. Others understand Juno, others the Babylonian Venus, whom the distinguished Selden also notes was called Queen of the heavens, and he cites Harpocration on the Samaritans for this. But these matters are disputed in vain. The hypothesis is false. מַלְכַּת does not mean queen. They would say Queen of heaven as מַלְכַּת הַשָּׁמַיִם, as in 1 Kings 10, מַלְכַּת שְׁבָא, the queen of Sheba. Here, however, we have מֶלֶךְ, a word placed in the construct state from the absolute מַלְאכָה, which properly means work, labour, skill or craft. So from מְמַלְכָּה comes מַמְלֶכֶת, and among all the words that fall under that rule there is none that forms the construct state in both ways. Let no one say that it is formed from מַלְכָּה, מַלְכַּת and מַלְכֹּת. I said that מַלְאכָה properly means work; I add that by metonymy it also denotes a thing made and acquired by labour, effort and craft: Exodus 22:8, that he has not put his hands במלאכת against the property of his neighbour. There it is written in full with the radical א, though silent; here it is defective.

units.la: 'Quid ergo? Lxx. Interpretes licet Jerm. 44. 17. reddiderint βασιλεῖα ἢ ὕρανοῦ, hic tamen & cap. xix. 13. habent ῥανοῦ id est, exercitui coeli, pro * synonymis habentes צבא השמים & מלכת השמים Quid autem per exercitum coeli hic intelligatur, docet Chaldaeus quando vertit לכוכבי השמיא id est, stellis coeli, quae propter admirabilem illum & stupendum ordinem exercitus vocantur. Alii paulo amplius vocem extenderunt, ut universam machinam coelestem complexi sint; Ita Arias Mont. Jer. 44. 17. reddit, opificio coeli, Tigurini & hic & illic, machina coeli, quod Angli in margine posuerunt. Pisc. operi coeli, id est, stellis inquit, nobilissimis Dei operibus. Quomodo & Kimchius חסר אלף ופיר כמו מעשה השמים כלומר לכוכבים id est, deficit א / & perinde est ac dixisset, operi coeli, q. d. stellis. Lutherus vocem Ebraeam retinuit, lectori libertatem relinquens eam eligendi interpretationem, quam ipse probaret maxime. Non dubium est quin Collyridiani ad hunc locum respexerunt, quibus Epiphanius haeresi 79. Quaedam mulieres inquit, habebant virginis imagines, coram quibus collyridas sive placentas offerebant, easq; adorabant. Κολλυρίδες placentae, tortae panis, quas a praeparatione Jeremias hic כונים vocat, Lxx. retenta voce Ebraeae * κανούνας. Chrysostomus quam vocem retinuit Cl. Junius, & interpretatur liba quaedam ἐκλυπα, id est, certas formas habentia pro ratione idolorum, quibus offerenda erant, addit-que vocari πόπανα, quod τῶν πόπανων id est, deorum effigie insignita essent, quibus offerebantur, citatque Juvenalis versum.
units.tr: "What then? Although the Septuagint, in Jeremiah 44:17, rendered it as βασιλεῖα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, here and in chapter 19:13 they have ῥανοῦ, that is, of the host of heaven, taking צבא השמים and מלכת השמים as synonyms. What is meant here by the host of heaven the Chaldee paraphrast shows when he renders it as לכוכבי השמיא, that is, to the stars of heaven, which are called a host because of that admirable and astonishing order. Others have extended the word somewhat more, so as to embrace the whole heavenly machine. Thus Arias Montanus renders Jeremiah 44:17 as the workmanship of heaven; the Tigurine translators, both here and there, as the machine of heaven, which the English put in the margin. Piscator: to the work of heaven, that is, he says, to the stars, the noblest works of God. Kimchi too: חסר אלף ופיר כמו מעשה השמים כלומר לכוכבים, that is, the א is lacking, and it is just as if he had said to the work of heaven, that is, to the stars. Luther retained the Hebrew word, leaving the reader free to choose whichever interpretation he himself most approves. There is no doubt that the Collyridians looked to this passage, against whom Epiphanius, in heresy 79, says: Certain women, he says, had images of the virgin, before which they offered collyrides or cakes, and worshipped them. κολλυρίδες are cakes, twisted bread, which Jeremiah here calls כונים from their preparation; the Septuagint retained the Hebrew word as *κανούνας. Chrysostom likewise retained the word, as did Junius, and interprets it as certain cakes ἐκλυπα, that is, having fixed forms according to the nature of the idols to which they were to be offered; he adds that they are called πόπανα, because τῶν πόπανων, that is, they were marked with the likeness of the gods to whom they were offered, and he cites the line of Juvenal:

units.la: Scilicet & tenui popano corruptus Osiris.
units.tr: "Yes, and Osiris, bribed with a thin cake."

units.la: Fortassis hinc quoque Pontificii elogium REGINAE COELI beatissimae virginis Mariae mutuati sunt. Gabriel Biel in Can. Missae lect. 8. Confugimus primo ad B. Virginem, coelorum REGINAM, cui rex regum dimidium regni sui dedit.
units.tr: Perhaps the Papists also borrowed from here the epithet QUEEN OF HEAVEN for the most blessed Virgin Mary. Gabriel Biel, in Canon of the Mass, lecture 8: "We first flee to the Blessed Virgin, the QUEEN OF HEAVEN, to whom the King of kings gave half of his kingdom."

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAP. XI.

units.la: Vers. 19. Mittamus lignum in panem ejus ] Hic rursus sudare videas interpretes. Funem hic inter * alios ex vetustate duxit B. Hier. נרמי Xxxx cujus verba adscribam. Sic ergo ille ad illa verba versus 18. Tu autem Domine demonstrasti mihi &c. Omnium Ecclesiarum iste est consensus, inquit, ut sub persona Jeremiæ à Christo hæc dici intelligant, quod ei pater monstraverit; quomodo eum oporteat loqui, & ostenderit illi studia Judæorum & ipse quasi agnus ductus ad victimam, non aperuerit os suum, & non cognoverit, subauditur peccatum.
units.tr: Verse 19. Let us put wood into his bread. Here again you may see the interpreters sweating. Among the ancients, blessed Jerome drew out a thread from the Hebrew text, whose words I will quote. Thus he, on the words of verse 18, "But you, O Lord, have shown me, etc.": This is the consensus of all the Churches, he says, that under the person of Jeremiah these things are understood to be said by Christ, because the Father showed him how he ought to speak, and showed him the designs of the Jews, and he himself, as a lamb led to the slaughter, did not open his mouth, and did not know, namely, sin.

units.la: Juxta illud quod ab Apostolo dicitur, qui cum non cognovisset peccatum &c. & dixerint, mittamus lignum in panem ejus, crucem vid. in corpus Salvatoris. Ipse enim est qui ait, Ego sum panis, qui de cælo descendi. Et paulo post, Judæi & nostri Judaizantes hæc ex persona Jeremiæ dici intelligunt, qui propter vaticinium futurorum & ingruentia captivitatis mala, hæc eum à populo sustinuisse confirmant. Sed nescio quomodo possint approbare crucifixum esse Hieremiam quum hoc scriptura non memoret. Miseret me tui Pater, An ergo tam certum tibi est mittere lignum in panem alicujus, esse idem quod cruci affigere? Atqui per lignum fatiuserat lignum venenatum intelligere. Lyra, Est in terra illa arbor, nomine taxus venenata, & inde dicitur , id est, venenum, mutato a in O. Et de lignoillius arboris minutatim inciso volebant ponere in cibo Jeremia &c. Et Sa, lignum, sc. venenatum. Chald. venenum mortiferum. Dico verbo. Ebræa sic legere, נְשַׁחִיתָה עֵץ בְּלַחְמוֹ / corrumpamus arborem cum pane suo id est, fructu suo, id est, perdamus doctorem cum doctrina sua. Sic Matth. 7. doctor arbori, doctrina fructibus comparatur. לחם de quovis cibo, etiam lacte ut in Prov. & melle 1. Sam. 14. usurpatur. לחם כלל כל מאכל inquit Kimchi, id est, vox lechem quemlibet cibum complectitur. Alii per hypallagen, corrumpamus lign o panem ejus, q. esset נְשַׁחִיתָה בְּעֵץ לַחְמוֹ / ligno sc. venenato. Jun. perdamus culmum cum grano ejus, q.d. enecemus eum gladio aut fame, ut demonstrat antithesis, inquit; poenarum, verf. 22. locutio sumpta a segetibus, q.d. eradicemus eum, ut ne stipula quidem superfit. Certe, de Jeremia hæc dici ostendit evidenter verf. 21. Ideo hæc dicit Dominus ad viros Anathoth. Hoc vidit Hieron. ubi sic inquit in commentario; videtur hoc superiori sententiæ contraire, qua volumus approbare ex persona Christi hæc dicta esse, &c. Sed quomodo se expedit? Si intellexerimus, inquit, etymologiam oppidi Anathoth, quod interpretatur obedientialiquido monstrabitur, viros Anathoth, qui olim Domini præ-
units.tr: According to what is said by the Apostle, "who knew no sin, etc." and they said, "Let us put wood into his bread": the cross, namely, upon the body of the Saviour. For he himself said, "I am the bread which came down from heaven." And a little later: the Jews and our Judaizers understand these things to be said in the person of Jeremiah, who, on account of his prophecy of future things and the evils of the impending captivity, they affirm endured these things from the people. But I do not know how they can approve that Jeremiah was crucified, since Scripture does not record this. "May I pity you, Father." Is it then so certain to you that to put wood into someone's bread is the same as to nail him to a cross? And yet by the wood he had meant a poisoned wood. Lyra: In that land there is a tree, called the poisonous yew, and from this it is called , that is, poison, with a changed to O. And they wanted to put into Jeremiah's food wood cut small from that tree, etc. And the Saadia: wood, namely poisoned. The Chaldee: deadly poison. I speak in words. The Hebrew reads thus: נְשַׁחִיתָה עֵץ בְּלַחְמוֹ, let us destroy the tree with its bread, that is, with its fruit, that is, let us destroy the teacher with his teaching. Thus in Matthew 7 the teacher is compared to a tree and the teaching to its fruits. לחם is used of any food, even of milk, as in Proverbs, and of honey, 1 Samuel 14. Kimchi says: לחם כלל כל מאכל, that is, the word lechem embraces any food. Others, by hypallage, read: let us destroy the wood with its bread, which would be נְשַׁחִיתָה בְּעֵץ לַחְמוֹ, namely with poisoned wood. Junius: let us destroy the stalk with its grain, that is, let us kill him with the sword or with famine, as the antithesis shows, he says, a locution of punishments, verse 22, taken from the harvest, that is, let us root him out so that not even stubble remains. Certainly, that these things are said of Jeremiah is clearly shown by verse 21: Therefore thus says the LORD to the men of Anathoth. Jerome saw this, where in his commentary he says: this seems to contradict the preceding sentence, by which we want to prove that these things were said in the person of Christ, etc. But how does he extricate himself? If we understand, he says, the etymology of the town of Anathoth, which is interpreted as obedience, it will be clear that the men of Anathoth, who once obeyed the Lord's

units.la: *Vide & Lactant. de vera Sapientia lib. 4. 18, Emm. Sa, Tertull. lib. 3. in Marc. panem interpretatur Christi corpus quod dandū erat sub specie panis, lignum vero crucem. Vide etiam Bellarm. lib. 2. de Sacr. Euchar cap. 7. & Theodoretum in comm.
units.tr: See also Lactantius, On the True Wisdom, book 4, chapter 18; Emmanuel Sá; Tertullian, book 3 Against Marcion, who interprets the bread as the body of Christ, which was to be given under the appearance of bread, and the wood as the cross. See also Bellarmine, On the Sacrament of the Eucharist, book 2, chapter 7, and Theodoret on the commentary.

units.la: *Nugæ. toxicum est, à τόξον, sagitta, vide Martinii Etymolog. præceptis obtemperarunt, omnes dici Judæos. Sed & hoc cum judicio lege, Tiro, Neque enim unquam demonstraverit aliquis, Anathoth obedientiam significare.
units.tr: Nonsense. Toxicum comes from τόξον, arrow; see Martinius's Etymology. Commands were obeyed, and so all are called Jews. But read this too with judgement, young man, for no one has ever shown that Anathoth means obedience.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Verf. 3. Sanctifica eos in die occisionis] Vox sanctificandi multis Interpretibus fumus in oculis fuit. Hieron. de hæreticis interpretatur, Congrega eos, inquit in urbem Jerusalem, aut in sua conciliabula, ut quasi victimæ cædantur in mortem & tunc sanctificentur, cum Ecclesiastico fuerint mucrone jugulati. Interfectio enim hæreticorum est salus eorum qui decepti sunt. Carthusianus hic quoq; specimen suæ subtilitatis edens sic inquit, Hoc dupliciter accipi potest, primo, ut per temporalem persecutionem ac mortem à peccato purgentur, ne æternaliter pereant. 2. Ut in die suæ occisionis materialiter sanctificentur, ita quod in eorum punitione sanctitas & justitia Dei Manifestentur. Et Gregorius Moral. 27. 18. In die occisionis sanctificantur reprobi, quia tunc sancta, quæ debuerunt, agere consentiunt, cum digna pravitatis supplicia jam declinare non possunt. Sed acutius hic vidit Lyra, quando notat in Ebræo esse, præpara eos Certe illic est הַקְרִישֻׁם / In קדש autem esse separandi & præparandi notionem diximus prolixe ad cap. XIII. Jesaiæ. Chald: præpara eos Lxx. ἁγνισον αὐτὸς id est, purifica eos. Notat autem, Theodoretus, ἁγνιον hic idem esse quod separa, segrega, Nam segregat se, inquit, qui vult purificari & sanctificari. Vel potius qui purificat se, separat se à sordib. & immunditiê. Ut separandi notio maneat primaria & propria. Addit Theodoretus, Syrum reddidisse ἐτοίμων, id est, bene præpara. Infra xxii 7. Vulg. sanctificabo super te interficientem &c. Ubi Chald. rursus, præparabo Lxx. ἑτοιμάσω, inducam, Theodoretus iterum, notat in Ebr. esse ἁγιάσω, illudque positum pro ἀφοείσω. Nota hic rursus tiro, quod sæpius inculcavimus. Hellenisticæ linguæ id proprium esse, voces Græcas vel ad significationem Ebræarum amplitudinem dilatare vel ad earum angustias contrahere, & interpretamentum pro interpretamento ponere. Quippe quia קדש comprehendit hæc significata, φθαρσευάζειν, ἀφοείζειν ἁγιάζειν, ἁγνίζειν, ideo τὸ ἁγιάζειν & ἁγνίζειν quoque pro φθαρσευάζειν & ἀφοείζειν ponuntur.
units.tr: Verse 3. Sanctify them in the day of slaughter.] The word "sanctify" has been a stumbling block to many interpreters. Jerome takes it of heretics: "Gather them," he says, "into the city of Jerusalem, or into their own conventicles, so that they may be slaughtered like victims unto death, and then be sanctified when they have been slain by the sword of the Church. For the killing of heretics is the salvation of those who have been deceived." The Carthusian, also displaying a specimen of his subtlety here, says: "This can be taken in two ways. First, that through temporal persecution and death they may be purged from sin, lest they perish eternally. Second, that they may be sanctified materially in the day of their slaughter, so that the holiness and justice of God may be made manifest in their punishment." Gregory in the Moralia (27.18) says: "On the day of slaughter the reprobate are sanctified, because then they agree to do the holy things they ought to have done, when they can no longer avoid the punishments their wickedness deserves." But Lyra sees more sharply here, when he notes that in the Hebrew it says "prepare them." Certainly there stands הַקְרִישֻׁם [hakrishum]. I have explained at length, on chapter 13 of Isaiah, that the notion of both separating and preparing lies in קדש [qdsh]. The Chaldee paraphrast has "prepare them." The LXX have ἁγνισον αὐτούς [hagnison autous], that is, "purify them." Theodoretus observes that ἁγνίζειν here means the same as to separate or set apart, for, he says, whoever wishes to be purified and sanctified separates himself; or rather, whoever purifies himself separates himself from filth and uncleanness. So the notion of separating remains the primary and proper one. Theodoretus adds that the Syriac has rendered it ἑτοίμων [hetoimōn], that is, "prepare well." Below, at xxii. 7, the Vulgate has I will sanctify against you the destroyers, etc. where the Chaldee again has "I will prepare," and the LXX ἑτοιμάσω [hetoimasō], "I will make ready," and "I will bring in." Theodoretus again notes that in the Hebrew it is ἁγιάσω [hagiasō], and that this is used for ἀφορίσω [aphorisō]. Here again, beginner, note what I have often impressed upon you: it is characteristic of the Hellenistic language to stretch Greek words to the breadth of Hebrew meanings or to narrow them to their limits, and to put one interpretation in place of another. Since קדש [qdsh] covers these meanings, φθείρειν [phtheirein]/ἀφορίζειν [aphorizein], ἁγιάζειν [hagiazein], ἁγνίζειν [hagnizein], therefore τὸ ἁγιάζειν [to hagiazein] and ἁγνίζειν [hagnizein] are also used in place of φθαρσευάζειν [phtharseuazein] and ἀφορίζειν [aphorizein].

units.la: Verf. 13. κληροι αὐτῶν ἐν ὠφελήσει αὐτῶς. ] Latina Rom. clerici eorum non proderunt illis. Hieron, Quid enim eos juvare poterit Episcopi nomen vel presbyteri, vel reliquus ordo Ecclesiasticus, quanto magis graventur dignitatibus suis, & potentes potenter tormenta patiantur &c. Itaille, explicans versionem Graecam. Cum tamen Hebraea sic expressisset, hereditatem acceperunt (legit נַחֲלָה) & nouiis proderit. Epiphanius quoque initio Epistolae ad Johannem Jerosolymitanum, Origenes homil. 7. in Jeremiam de clericis hic agunt. Hinc quoque ipse, quod mireris, Bellarm. lib. 1. de Clericis, cap. 1. antiquitatem distinctionis clericorum & Laicorum probare satagit. Quanto melius Theodoretus, Sortes vestra non proderunt vobis. Sortes rursus vocat, inquit, pinguem hereditatem, cui non esse fidendum consulit. Tu nota tiro, Spiritum S. nec Clerorum, nec clericorum hic meminisse: sed ita loqui seminabant triticum & spinas metent (idque ex interminatione Dei Levit. xxvi. 16.) indolescent [laboribus] sed nihil proficient Ebr. לֹא יוֹעִילוּ / Kimchi tamen putat hic non continuari denuntiationem maledictionis, sed rationem ejus reddi, quia prophetae seminarunt triticum, id. pias admonitiones habuerunt ad populum, sed messuerunt spinas, id est Indoluerunt Prophetae, quod nihil proficerent. Hieron. & Lxx. נַחֲלָה legerunt, נַחֲלָה autem est hereditas, sors, κλῆρος.
units.tr: Verse 13. Their clerics shall not profit them: κληροι αὐτῶν ἐν ὠφελήσει αὐτῶς [klēroi autōn en ōphelēsei autōs]] The Latin version of Rome has "their clerics will not profit them." Jerome: "For what will the name of bishop or presbyter, or the rest of the ecclesiastical order, help them? The more they are burdened by their dignities, and the more powerful they are, the more powerfully will they suffer torments," and so on. He explains the Greek version in this way, although the Hebrew had expressed it thus: they have received an inheritance (he reads נַחֲלָה [nachalah]), and it will profit no one. Epiphanius also, at the beginning of his letter to John of Jerusalem, and Origen, Homily 7 on Jeremiah, discuss clerics here. From this, what is surprising, Bellarmine too, in his book 1 on Clerics, chapter 1, labours to prove the antiquity of the distinction between clerics and laity. How much better Theodoret does: "Your lot will not profit you." He says the lot is called a rich inheritance again, and advises that one should not trust in it. You, young student, note that the Holy Spirit here mentions neither clerics nor clerks, but speaks thus: they sowed wheat and will reap thorns (and this comes from God's threat in Leviticus 26:16), they will grow weary [with labours] but accomplish nothing. Hebrew: לֹא יוֹעִילוּ [lo yo'ilu]. Kimchi, however, thinks that the threat of curse is not continued here, but its reason is given: because the prophets sowed wheat, that is, gave pious admonitions to the people, but reaped thorns, that is, the prophets grieved that they accomplished nothing. Jerome and the Septuagint read נַחֲלָה [nachalah], but נַחֲלָה [nachalah] is inheritance, lot, κλῆρος [klēros].

units.la: Verf. 16. Ecce ego mittam Piscatores multos, dicit DOMINUS, Piscabuntur eos & post haec mittam illis multos venatores, & venabuntur eos de omni monte & colle, & de cavernis petrarum Ebr. Ego mittam ad piscatores multos, id est, vocabo &c. Multi postillatores hunc locum citare & enarrare solent, velutì vaticinium & promissionem de mittendis in N.T. Apostolis. Vide postillas in Evangelium Matth. 4. 19. quod die B. Andreae iu multis Ecclesiis proponi solet. In nostris quoque Bibliis ad illa verba Christi, faciam vos piscatores hominum, hic locus Jeremiae cem parallelus citatur. Sed sciendum haec verba non continere promissionem sed comminationem, neque pendere a versu 15. sed renovare concionem quam verf. 9. incoaverat. Id patet ex versu 17. Quia oculi mei super omnes vias eorum, & non est abscondita iniquitas eorum coram me &c. Unde certe nova sententia vel concio incoari non potest, test, particula illum versum cum 16. conjungente. Per piscatores & venatores ergo hostes intelliguntur. Piscari & venari est capere, sub jugum mittere. Venatio habet simile quiddam bello, imo est species quaedam belli, & vicissim bellum est tanquam venatio quaedam hominum. Ita Nimrod dicitur robustus venatione, vulg. robustus venator id est, bellator. Gen. x. 9. Hanc metaphoricam signficationem invenies Mich. 7. 2. Thr. 3. 52. & 4. 18. Job. x. 16. Ps. 140. 12. Prov. 6. 26. Jezech. 13. 18. & xii. 13. & xxix. 2. 3. 4. Amos 4. 2. Hab. 1. 15. Etsi haud sciam, annon potius per piscatores Ægyptios intelligat, (vide Jes. 19. 8. complementum comminationis.; 2. Reg. 23. 29. ut per venatores, Babylonios. Vide Piscatoris notas.
units.tr: Verse 16. "Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the LORD, and they shall fish them; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the holes of the rocks." Heb.: "I will send for many fishers," that is, "I will call," etc. Many postillators are accustomed to cite and expound this passage as a prophecy and promise of the Apostles to be sent in the New Testament. See the postils on Matthew 4:19, which is usually read on the feast of St Andrew in many churches. In our own Bibles too, this passage of Jeremiah, being parallel, is cited at Christ's words I will make you fishers of men. But it should be understood that these words contain not a promise but a threat, and that they do not depend on verse 15 but renew the sermon that verse 9 had begun. This is clear from verse 17: "For mine eyes are upon all their ways: they are not hid from my face, neither is their iniquity hidden from mine eyes," etc. Hence a new sentence or sermon cannot certainly be begun here, since the particle joins that verse with verse 16. By "fishers" and "hunters," then, enemies are meant. To fish and to hunt is to take and to bring under the yoke. Hunting has something similar to war; indeed it is a kind of war, and in turn war is like a kind of hunting of men. So Nimrod is called "a mighty hunter" (Heb. "a mighty hunter," Vulgate "a mighty hunter," that is, a warrior), Gen. 10:9. You will find this metaphorical meaning in Micah 7:2, Lam. 3:52 and 4:18, Job 10:16, Ps. 140:12, Prov. 6:26, Ezek. 13:18, 12:13 and 29:2, 3, 4, Amos 4:2, Hab. 1:15. Although I do not know whether it rather means by "Egyptian fishers" (see Isa. 19:8, the fulfilment of the threat; 2 Kings 23:29), just as by "hunters" the Babylonians are meant. See the Notes on Piscator.

units.la: Vers. 9. Profundum est cor super omnia, & homo est, quis cognoscet eum? ] Ita habet versio Latina Graeci textus in Hieronymi operibus. In Theodoreto, Grave est cor super omnia, Et apud August. de Civ. Dei lib. 18, 33. Grave cor per omnia, & homo est; & quis cognoscet eum? Fortassis legerunt βαρεῖα, Graeca, βαθεῖα ἡ καρδία σκληρὰ πάντων, ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη ἡ τίς γνώσεται αὐτόν, Augusti loco indicato hunc textum refert ad * Christum, Quia vero, inquit, nonerant eum agnituri Judaei, à quibus eum & occidi oportebat; sic idem Propheta significat, Grave cor &c. Egregia est censura B. Hieronymi, qua hanc interpretationem notavit in commentariis. Solent quidam nostri, inquit, bono quidem voto, sed non secundum scientiam uti hoc loco contra Judaeos, quod homo sit Dominus & salvator, secundum dispensationem carnis assumptae, nullusque possit nativitatis ejus scire mysterium, secundum illud quod scriptum est, Generationem ejus quis enarrabit? nisi solus Deus qui arcana rimatur, & reddit unicuique secundum opera. Melius autem est ut simpliciter accipiamus, quod nullus cogitationum secreta cognoscat, nisi solus Deus, &c. Quia vero in Evangelio dicitur de Christo, videns a. cogitationes eorum nullusque potest videre cogitationes hominum nisi solus Deus, ex horum locorum collatione probat Hieron. Christum esse verum & aeternum illum Deum. Ebraea ita habent עקוב הלב מכל ואנש הוא מי ידענו Quae Hieron. ita convertit, Pravum est cor omnium & inscrutabile, quis cognoscet illud?
units.tr: Verse 9. The heart is deeper than all things, and it is man; who shall know him? This is how the Latin version reads, taken from the Greek text in Jerome's works. In Theodoret it reads, "The heart is heavy above all things." In Augustine, *City of God* 18.33, it reads, "The heart is heavy above all, and it is man; and who shall know him?" Perhaps they read the Greek βαρεῖα, whereas the Greek text has βαθεῖα ἡ καρδία σκληρὰ πάντων, ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη ἡ τίς γνώσεται αὐτόν [the heart is deep and hard above all, and the human heart, who shall know it?]. In the passage cited, Augustine refers this text to Christ: "Because the Jews, by whom he had to be killed, were not going to recognise him, the same prophet signifies, 'The heart is heavy,' and so on." Jerome's censure of this interpretation in his commentaries is excellent. He says that some of our people, with a good intention but not according to knowledge, use this passage against the Jews to show that the man is the Lord and Saviour according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, and that no one can know the mystery of his birth, according to what is written, "Who shall declare his generation?" (Isa. 53.8), except God alone, who searches the hidden things and renders to each according to his works. Jerome says it is better to take the words simply, that no one knows the secrets of thoughts except God alone. But because in the Gospel it is said of Christ that he saw their thoughts (Matt. 9.4), and no one can see the thoughts of men except God alone, Jerome, by comparing these passages, proves that Christ is the true and eternal God. The Hebrew reads עקוב הלב מכל ואנש הוא מי ידענו [ʿaqqov ha-lev mi-kol we-enosh hu mi yeda'enu], which Jerome renders, "The heart of all is crooked and inscrutable; who shall know it?"
