units.la: Cum vero hanc versionem authenticam pronuntiaverit Concilium Tridentinum, miror eam fiduciam fuisse Bellarmino, ut hoc loco pressus ad Graecam τῷ עָקֹב versionem confugeret. In Ebraeo est עָקֹב inquit, quod significat profundum, βαθύς, ut Graeci reddunt, & sequitur inscrutabile [non in versione Graeca, sed vulg. Vides ut pro arbitrio duas versiones misceat] profundum autem esse & inscrutabile non tollit libertatem arbitrii aut vires bene operandi. Sed nunquam ostendet Bell. vel עָקֹב profundum significare. Hoc enim Ebraeis עָמֹק dicitur. Vel אנש inscrutabile esse. Putarim Ebraea melius sic converti, Supplantativum id est, perversum, fraudulentum, dolosum est cor supra omnia, & mortiferum, quis pernoscat illud? עָקֵב calx seu calcaneus, hinc עָקַב supplantare, אנוש alii insanabile, desperatum, desperate morbidum, vel desperate malum reddere maluere. Certe quid spectaverint qui inscrutabile reddidere, plane non valeo assequi. Supra Xv: 18. ipse vulgatus foemininum ejus אנושה reddidit desperabilis. Et hic agnoscit Hier. vocem Ebr. significare, vel inscrutabile, vel, desperabile. Lxx. אנוש legerunt. Ut & Symmachus, referente Hieron, inscrutabile cor omnium, quis est homo qui inveniat illud? At Chald. noster est, נביל לבא מבוקא ותקיף מן ירעה fraudulentum est cor supra omnia, & robustum: quis pernoscat illud? Lutheri versionem sic expressit nostra Belgica, Een trotzigh ende vertraeght dingh is het Herte: wie kan het doen-gronden? Hoc est, si belgice intelligo res superba & timida est cor quis poterit perscrutari illud? Ubi praeterquam quod omissa est vox כלל emphatica certe & magni ponderis, neutrum praedicatum recte mihi conversum videtur.
units.tr: Since the Council of Trent has declared this version authentic, I am amazed that Bellarmine had the confidence, when pressed at this point, to fall back on the Greek βαθύς for the Hebrew עָקֹב. He says that in Hebrew it is עָקֹב, which means "deep," βαθύς, as the Greeks render it, and that it is followed by "inscrutable" [not in the Greek but in the Vulgate; see how he mixes the two versions at will]. But deep and inscrutable do not take away free will or the power to act well. Yet Bellarmine will never show that עָקֹב means "deep." For the Hebrews say עָמֹק for that. Nor will he show that אנש means "inscrutable." I think the Hebrew would be better rendered thus: "The heart is supplanting, that is, perverse, deceitful and treacherous above all, and deadly; who shall know it?" עָקֵב means heel or heel-bone, and hence עָקַב means to supplant. Others preferred to render אנוש as "incurable," "desperate," or "desperately diseased" or "desperately evil." I cannot fully grasp what those had in view who rendered it "inscrutable." Above, at 15:18, the Vulgate itself renders its feminine form אנושה as "desperate." Here, too, Jerome acknowledges that the Hebrew word means either "inscrutable" or "desperate." The Seventy read אנוש. So too Symmachus, as Jerome reports: "The heart of all is inscrutable; who is the man who will find it?" But our Chaldee reads נביל לבא מבוקא ותקיף מן ירעה [nabil libba mevuqqa vetaqqif min ye'a: "the heart is deceitful above all, and strong; who shall search it?"]. Our Belgian version expresses Luther's rendering thus: "A stubborn and sluggish thing is the heart; who can fathom it?" That is, in Dutch, "a proud and timid thing is the heart; who shall be able to search it?" Apart from the fact that the emphatic and certainly weighty word כלל is omitted, neither predicate seems to me to be rendered correctly.

units.la: Vers. 11. Perdix fovit quae non peperit: fecit divitias suas & non in judicio, in dimidio dierum suorum derelinquet eas &c. ] Notet hic tiro ellipsin geminam, vid. notae τῆς ἀποστάσεως καὶ τῆς ἀπωλείας. Sensus ergo est, sicut perdix peperit: ita qui facit divitias suas id est, congregat divitias per nefas &c. Similem locum notavimus Prov. 24. 19. Vide si vacat. Ut vero illic, ita & hic ellipsis ista non observata Caliginem offudit interpretum oculis credo enim hinc plerosque vererum delapsos in istam Allegoriam, quam exponit B. Hieron. istis verbis. Alii vero & propter superiorem Historiam & propter alteram, qua dicunt perdicem esse pugnacissimum & immundum, ita ut victum polluat, Diabolum sub ejus nomine interpratantur, qui alienas sibi divitias congregarit, dicens ad Dominum, Hæc omnia dabo tibi &c. Quem relinquent suæ divitiæ, quæ male ab eo fuerunt congregatæ, & per Apostolos convertentur ad Dominum; & qui sibi videbatur esse prudentissimus erit omnium judicio insipiens. LXX. ἐφώνησε πέρδιξ, συνήγαγεν ἃ οὐκ ἔτεκε, ποιῶν πλοῦτον &c. Mirum nisi hic duæ interpretationes קוֹרֵא coaluerint, קרא enim, est clamare, φωνεῖ, קוֹרֵא πέρδιξ, q. κλητῆς, quod pullos vocet, licet iidem 1. Sam 26. 20. reddederint νοσσίον neque enim animum inducere possum, ut credam eos uni voci geminum interpretamentum tribuisse. Illud enim non invenio à veteribus factum, nisi in ejusmodi pauculis quæ aliter leguntur quam scribuntur, seu quibus est varia lectio. Ita Chald. Paraphrastes Ps. 122. בארי reddit, momorderunt ut leo, Jes. 19. 18, עִיר הַהֶרֶס יֵאָמֶר לְאַחַת / Sed Keri in margine notatur הַהֶרֶס / Illud destructionem, hoc Solem significat, unde & Symm. ἡλίου πόλις: Heliopolis. Eusebius male, civitas terræ, confundens, Heres, cum ארץ Eretz. Chald. utrumque conjungit, קִרְחָא בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ id est, civitas domus solis, quæ destruetur. Vide partem primam Anti-barbari mei p. 473. Sed Ad rem, Chald. Paraphastes hunc locum istis verbis reddit הָא כְּקוֹרְאָה רְמַכַּשׁ בְּעִיר דְּלָא דִילֵהּ וּמְשַׁחֲוִין אַפְרוּהִין דְּבַתְרוֹהִי לָא יִכּוּן בֵּן כָּל גְּבַר בִּשְׁעָא דְּקָנֵי גְּנָסִין הַלָּא בְרִינָא בְּפַלְגוּת יוֹמוֹהִי שָׁבַק לְהוֹן וּכְסוּפֵהּ מִתְּקְרֵי רְשִׁיעָא hoc est, Ecce, sicut perdix colligit ova non sua, & calefaciendo fovet pullas, qui eam tamen non sequuntur, ita omnis vir improbus qui possidet opes per nefas, ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτοῦ relinquet eas, & in extremo suo vocabitur improbus. Secutus est vulgatam de perdice sententiam, eam vid. aliena ova colligere, iisque incubare: "pullos vero ab ea exclusos, deserta ea, veram matrem consectari hanc expositionem secutus & Kimchius est, cujus commentarium non pigrabor adscribere, לפי שאמר לתת לאיש כדרכיו אמר אל תחמה על הרשע שהוא מצליח בנכסים איך לא יתן לו האל כדרכיו כי תדע כי הרשע שאין עשירו במשפט לא יעמוד לו/ אלא יצא מידו בהצי ימיו : והמשילו לקורא והוא עוף שקורין בלעז פרנזיז והוא רובץ על ביצי עוף אחר ומחמם אותם / והפיצים ההם לכשיבקעו ויצאו האפרחים לא יהיו כמו בנו שילכו אחריו / אלא יעזבוהו ולא יכירוהו אלא אחרי מי שהיא להם אם גם כן חרשרע שעשה עשר ולא במשפט בחצי ימיו יעזבנו / או ימות הוא ויעזוב עשרו לאחרים ולא ישלים ימיו עם העשר שעשה וג
units.tr: Verse 11. The partridge sits on eggs which she did not lay; he gets riches but not by right; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and so on. Here the beginner should note a double ellipsis; see the notes on "apostasy" and "destruction." The sense, then, is: as the partridge lays eggs, so he who makes his riches, that is, gathers riches by wrong, and so on. I noted a similar passage at Prov. 24.19; see there if you have time. But just as there, so here this ellipsis, not observed, has clouded the eyes of the translators. I believe that for this reason most of the older writers fell into that allegory which Jerome expounds in these words. Others, both because of the earlier story and because of the other, in which they say the partridge is very combative and unclean, so that she defiles her food, interpret the devil under her name, who gathered to himself riches not his own, saying to the Lord, "All these things I will give you" (Matt. 4.9), and whose riches will leave him, which were wrongly gathered by him, and will be converted to the Lord through the Apostles; and he who seemed to himself most prudent will be, in the judgment of all, a fool. The Seventy: "The partridge called, she gathered what she did not bring forth, making wealth," and so on. It would be a wonder if the two interpretations of קוֹרֵא had not merged here. For קרא means to call, φωνεῖν, and קוֹרֵא, partridge, is as it were "the one who calls" (κλητής), because she calls her chicks, although the same translators render it νοσσίον in 1 Sam. 26.20. I cannot bring myself to believe that they gave a double interpretation to one word. I do not find the ancients doing this except in a few such cases, which are read differently from how they are written, or which have variant readings. So the Chaldee Paraphrast renders בארי in Ps. 122 as "they bit like a lion." In Isa. 19.18, עִיר הַהֶרֶס יֵאָמֶר לְאַחַת has in the margin of the Keri הַהֶרֶס. The one means "destruction," the other "sun," whence also Symmachus, "city of the sun," Heliopolis. Eusebius wrongly, "city of the land," confusing הֶרֶס with ארץ, "land." The Chaldee joins both, קִרְחָא בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ, that is, "city of the house of the sun, which shall be destroyed." See part one of my Anti-barbarus, p. 473. But to the point: the Chaldee Paraphrast renders this passage in these words: הָא כְּקוֹרְאָה רְמַכַּשׁ בְּעִיר דְּלָא דִילֵהּ וּמְשַׁחֲוִין אַפְרוּהִין דְּבַתְרוֹהִי לָא יִכּוּן בֵּן כָּל גְּבַר בִּשְׁעָא דְּקָנֵי גְּנָסִין הַלָּא בְרִינָא בְּפַלְגוּת יוֹמוֹהִי שָׁבַק לְהוֹן וּכְסוּפֵהּ מִתְּקְרֵי רְשִׁיעָא [hA kekor'a remakkash be'ir dela dilleh... "Behold, as the partridge gathers eggs not her own, and warming them nourishes chicks which nevertheless do not follow her, so every wicked man who possesses riches by wrong, in the midst of his days will leave them, and in the end he will be called wicked"]. That is, the Chaldee Paraphrast: "Behold, as the partridge gathers eggs not her own..., in the midst of his days he shall leave them to others, and at his end he shall be called wicked." He followed the Vulgate's opinion about the partridge, that she gathers other eggs and hatches them; but the chicks hatched from her, once they have left her, pursue their true mother. Kimchi also followed this exposition, whose commentary I will not hesitate to quote: לפי שאמר לתת לאיש כדרכיו אמר אל תחמה על הרשע שהוא מצליח בנכסים איך לא יתן לו האל כדרכיו כי תדע כי הרשע שאין עשירו במשפט לא יעמוד לו/ אלא יצא מידו בחצי ימיו : והמשילו לקורא והוא עוף שקורין בלעז פרנזיז והוא רובץ על ביצי עוף אחר ומחמם אותם / והפיצים ההם לכשיבקעו ויצאו האפרחים לא יהיו כמו בנו שילכו אחריו / אלא יעזבוהו ולא יכירוהו אלא אחרי מי שהיא להם אם גם כן חרשרע שעשה עשר ולא במשפט בחצי ימיו יעזבנו / או ימות הוא ויעזוב עשרו לאחרים ולא ישלים ימיו עם העשר שעשה [Since he said that God gives to each man according to his ways, he says: do not be vexed at the wicked man who prospers in possessions; how will God not give him according to his ways? For know that the wealth of the wicked man, which is not gained in justice, will not stand by him, but will go out of his hand in the midst of his days. And he compares him to the partridge, a bird which in French they call "frenzies," which broods on the eggs of another bird and warms them; and when those eggs hatch and the chicks come out, they will not be like her own children who follow her, but will leave her and will not recognise her except the one who is their true mother. So too the wicked man who made wealth and not in justice will leave it in the midst of his days; or he will die and leave his wealth to others, and will not complete his days with the wealth he made.]

units.la: id est, postquam dixit Deum daturum unicuique secundum vias ejus, pergit & ait, ne mireris de improbo, si felix sit in divitiis & quomodo Deus ei non det juxta vias ejus. Sed scito penes improbum divitias, quas per nefas congregavit, non mansuras; sed evolaturas ex manu ejus in dimidio dierum ejus. Et comparat cum perdice. Est autem avis, quam in lingua vernacula vocant pernise. Illa autem incubat ovis aliarum avium & fovet ea. Ubi autem rupta fuerint illa & prodierint pulli, non sunt instar pullorum ejus (perdicis) qui sequuntur eam. Ideo deserunt eam neque agnoscunt eam, sed veram matrem sequuntur. Similiter improbus qui colligit opes per nefarias artes in medio dierum ejus deserent cum, aut morietur ipse & relinquet eas aliis, & non consummabit dies suos cum opibus quas corrasit &c. Haec Kimchius. Idem de perdice affirmant Ambros. lib. 7. Epistolarum epist. 48. Meminit & Hieron. sed paulo aliter, verba ejus ista sunt, Ajunt scriptores naturalis historiae quorum principes sunt apud Graecos Aristoteles & Theophrastus, apud nos Plinius Secundus, hanc perdicis esse naturam, ut ova alterius perdicis (NB. non dicit aliarum avium) i. aliena furetur, & eis incubet, fovetque cumque foetus adoleverit avolare ab eo, & alienum parentem relinquere. Haec Hieron. ubi ergo ista perdix, quae alterius perdicis ova fovet, sua ponit? An ergo omnes vicarias sibi invicem praestant operas? An Aristoteles & Theophrastus id dicant, quod Hieron. eos dicere affirmat, nescio. De Plinio, certe nihil tale istis in libris qui ad nos transmissi sunt, invenire quitus sum. Gesnerus haec de curruca verius dici putat in cujus nido cuculum ova sua reponere, quae illa excludat prolixe ex veterib. probat. Cum ergo haec incerta sint, & insuper probari non possit נָגַר notionem fovendi habere, colligendi contra & cumulandi ex Jesaiae cap. xxxiv. 15. & Chaldaismo sit certissima, cum denique ילד de avibus usurpatum tam sit excludere pullos ex ovis post incubationem, quam ipsa ova ponere, videtur praeferenda Cl. Junii & Trimellii interpretatio, ut perdix colligit ova, sed non excludit, ita comparans divitias &c. Et observa, in Ebraeo non legi, קורא דגר אשר לא ילד sed קורא דגר ולא ילד Scio equidem vau aliquando vicem אשר obire, sed hic ejus enallages necessitatem nullam video. Quid ergo vult Propheta? Audiamus ejus mentem paraphrastice edisserantem Junium, Quemadmodum videmus perdicem multa ova colligere, ponere, ut ea fovcat & excludat simul, persepe tamen accidere, ut aut ipsa intercipiatur ab aucupe, aut ova frangantur à pruriente masculo aut à cuculo, denique alia ratione impediatur, ne collecta ova per justum tempus fovere possit, ut excludantur pulli: Sic etiam accidit iniquis providentia Dei, ut dementes homines congestis suis thesauris spolientur tempestive, & rebus partis uti non possint pro exspectatione sua, Hæc ille. Plenior fortassis fuisset Ἀπόδοσις, si ita dixisset, ut dementes homines, vel subito & mediis diebus suis à congestis thesauris morte avellantur, vel iisdem spolientur &c. Prius enim illud responderet isti interceptioni quæ fit ab aucupe. Hanc sententiam secutus est & B. Lutherus, nisi quod נִיכָּר nimis laxe interpretatus sit, Gleich wie * ein Vogel der sich uber Eyer setzet / und brutet sie nicht auff. Eandem secuti sunt Pisc. Angli & alii. Quisquis locum hunc penficulatius examinabit, volens nolens fatebitur, hac versione & expositione admissa, inter apodosin & protasin majorem esse conspirationem, quam si vulgatæ hæseris.
units.tr: That is, after saying that God will give to each person according to his ways, the text goes on: "Do not be surprised at the wicked man if he prospers in riches, or at how God does not give him according to his ways. But know that the riches the wicked man has gathered by wrongdoing will not remain with him; they will fly from his hand in the middle of his days." And it compares him to the partridge. "There is a bird, which in the vernacular they call the pernise. It sits on the eggs of other birds and warms them. But when those eggs break open and the chicks come out, they are not like its own young (the partridge's), which follow her. Instead they desert her and do not recognise her, but follow the one who is their true mother. Likewise the wicked man who gathers wealth by unlawful arts will be deserted in the middle of his days, either because he dies and leaves it to others, and does not complete his days with the wealth he has amassed, etc." So Kimchi. Ambrose, in book 7 of the Epistles, letter 48, affirms the same about the partridge. Jerome also mentions it, but a little differently; his words are these: "The writers of natural history, whose leaders among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny the Second, say that the nature of the partridge is this: it steals the eggs of another partridge (note that he does not say 'of other birds'), that is, eggs not its own, and sits on them and warms them; and when the young have grown up, they fly away from it and leave the foreign parent." So Jerome. Where, then, is this partridge that warms the eggs of another partridge, and lays its own? Do they all perform substitute services for one another? Whether Aristotle and Theophrastus say what Jerome affirms they say, I do not know. As for Pliny, I certainly cannot find anything like this in those books that have come down to us. Gesner thinks this is more truly said of the warbler, in whose nest the cuckoo places its eggs, which the warbler then hatches; he proves this at length from the old authorities. Since these points are uncertain, and moreover it cannot be shown that the verb [נָגַר] has the sense of brooding, but rather of gathering and heaping up, as in Isaiah 34:15, and since this is most certain in Chaldean usage; and since finally the verb [ילד] used of birds means as much to bring the chicks out of the eggs after incubation as to lay the eggs themselves, the interpretation of the learned Junius and Tremellius seems preferable: the partridge gathers eggs but does not hatch them, so comparing the riches, etc. And observe that in the Hebrew one does not read [קורא דגר אשר לא ילד] but [קורא דגר ולא ילד]. I indeed know that the vav sometimes stands in place of [אשר], but here I see no necessity for such a change of construction. What then does the prophet mean? Let us hear Junius, expounding his mind in paraphrase: "As we see the partridge gather many eggs and lay them, so that she may sit on them and hatch them at the same time, yet it often happens that either she herself is caught by the fowler, or the eggs are broken by a lustful male or by a cuckoo, or she is hindered in some other way, so that she cannot keep the gathered eggs warm for the proper time and have the chicks hatched. So it also happens to the wicked, by the providence of God, that foolish men are stripped of their gathered treasures before their time, and cannot enjoy the things they acquired as they expected." So he. His explanation would perhaps have been fuller had he said: "that foolish men are torn away from their gathered treasures, either suddenly and in the middle of their days by death, or are stripped of them in the same way" etc. For the former would answer to that interception which is made by the fowler. Luther also followed this view, except that he interpreted [נִיכָּר] rather loosely: "Just as a bird sits upon eggs and does not hatch them." The Piscator, the English translators and others followed the same reading. Whoever examines this passage more carefully will admit, whether willing or not, that with this translation and explanation accepted, there is a greater agreement between the apodosis and the protasis than if the Vulgate reading is retained.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Verf. 11. Hæc dicit Dominus ad Sellum filium Josiæ] Circa hunc Sellum variant Interpretes. Mihi dubium non est quin Joachazum intelligat, qui & Jochanan dictus 1. Chr. 3. 15. Cur autem dictus Sallum? Sallum filius Jabes regni Israelitici habenas unum solummodo mensem moderatus est. 2. Reg. xv. 13. Hunc ergo, quod non multo amplius Regnum Judæ administraverit, eodem nomine insignit, q. d. Hæc dicit Dominus ad alterum Sellum &c. Ita Johannes Baptista ob eundem Zelum & spiritum vocatur Elias, q. d. alterum Eliam. Tale est illud Virgilii,
units.tr: Verse 11. Thus says the Lord to Shallum the son of Josiah.] Interpreters differ about this Shallum. I have no doubt that he means Jehoahaz, who is also called Jochanan, 1 Chron. 3.15. Why, then, is he called Shallum? Shallum the son of Jabesh held the reins of the kingdom of Israel for only one month, 2 Kings 15.13. Therefore, because this Jehoahaz did not reign in Judah much longer, the prophet marks him with the same name, as if to say: "Thus says the Lord to the other Shallum," and so on. So John the Baptist, because of the same zeal and spirit, is called Elijah, as if to say the other Elijah. Such is that line of Virgil:

units.la: Atque iterum ad Trojam magnus mittetur Achilles.
units.tr: And again the great Achilles will be sent against Troy.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Verf 5. Suscitabo Davidi germen justum] Addit Hieronymus, vel, orientem justum proculdubio respiciens ad versionem τῶν LXX. ἀναστήσω τῷ Δαβὶδ ἀνατολὴν δικαίαν, Quod & in edit. Romanæ Latina versione versum est, Orientem justum. Hæc interpretatio plane disconvenit Ebræo. Quis enim unquam audivit Ebræum צמח orientem è cœlo sc. significare? צמח oriri significat, sed è terra
units.tr: Verse 5. "I will raise up unto David a righteous branch." Jerome adds "or a rising righteous one," no doubt having in view the Septuagint rendering, "I will raise up to David a righteous rising" [ἀναστήσω τῷ Δαβὶδ ἀνατολὴν δικαίαν], which the Latin version of the Roman edition also rendered "a righteous rising." This interpretation plainly disagrees with the Hebrew. For who has ever heard that the Hebrew word צמח [tsemach] means a rising from heaven? It does mean "to spring up," but from the earth [צמח], not from above.

units.la: Yyyy βλαστὸν, dicitur enim proprie de plantis & stirpibus &c. Unde צמח germen, βλάστημα, stirps vel planta e terra oriens. Quatuor insignia loca sunt, ubi Messias צמח vocatur, ipso Chaldaeo suffragante, qui singulis locis vocem Ebraeam per suum משיחא repraesentavit. Locum primum nunc prae manib. habemus. Secundus extat Jerem. 33.15. Tertius Zach. 3.8. Ecce adduco את עבדי צמח Lxx. ἀνατολήν, Ἀνατολὴ. Chald. ית עבדי משיחא Quartus vi.12. Ecce vir, צמח שמו / Chald. האנברא משיחא שמה / Lxx. ἰδοὺ ἀνήρ, ἀνατολή, ὄνομα αὐτῷ. Omnibus istis locis Chaldaeus ה צמח non ἀνατολὴ interpretatus est, sed ut liberiorem interpretem & paraphrastem decebat, rem ipsam spectavit. Namque omnibus istis locis צמח epitheton Messiae est, observatumque, à Cabalistis est, צמח & מנחם consolator, quod etiam inter Messiae cognomina ab Ebraeis numeratur per Gematriam eundem numerum efficere, vid. Cxxxviii. Manet ergo difficultas circa interpretamentum Graecum Ἀνατολή. Sunt qui hoc audaciter damnant. Sunt contra, qui vocem Ebraeam utrumque significare contendunt, videl. 1. germen, & per secundam notionem ἀνατολὴ, eosque qui צמח germen vertunt non solum imperite facere, sed & contra verbum Dei. Hi omne praesidium ponere mihi videntur in loco Luc. 1.78. ubi Christus non solum vocatur ἀνατολή, sed ut res clarior esset, ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους. Accedit authoritas vetustatis in qua plurimi crediderunt ideo Christum vocari Ἀνατολὴ, quod ex oriente ad judicium venturus esset. Sed pace tantorum virorum, negaverim ego cum Piscatore, Zachariam ad haec loca respexisse, qua de re paulo post. Quod ad צמח attinet, quaero adhuc locum, in Canonicis libris ubi significet vel ortum vel oriens aliud quam ex terra, vel re terrae analoga. Dicitur enim metaphorice de pilis quoque & plumis & rebus aliis, Nunquam de Sole aut ulla stella. Hinc Leo Castrius nodos ejusmodi audaci gladio secans ait Judaeos corrupisse haec loca, olimque רמח scriptum. Sed hunc indignum semper censui, cui responderetur, & merito à suis quoque ut alibi ostendimus, exagitari & perstringi. Quod vero vir magnus notat, Judaeos horoscopum, hoc est, locum orientis in themate Genethliaco vocare מזרח id est, ἀνατέλλοντος, vellem, locum & authoritatem adduxisset. Ego certe neque memini me in ullo authore ea notione vocem eam legere, neque in ullo Lexico reperire potui. Quod ad vocem ἀνατολὴ attinet, ajo cum Cl. Drusio ad Zach. 6. 12. Lxx. dubie quidem, attamen recte τὸ צמח per eam vocem reddidisse. Ajo enim ἀνατολή, in lingua Hellenistica germen significare, locisque ex Jerem. & Zach. productis GERMEN vertendam esse. Ajo ἀνατολὴ Jerem. 23. 5. idem esse quod βλάστημα, qua voce Symmachus illic usus est. Ajo ἀνατολὴ Zach. 6. 12. idem esse, quod ἀνατολή, qua voce isthic loci alii Interpretes usi sunt. Sed video mihi hanc Cl. Drusii observationem firmo aliquo tibicine sustentandam esse. Ecce tibi locum Jerem. xxxiii. 15. ubi Lxx. hanc ipsam promissionem denuo inculcaturi, eandem sententiam sic exprimunt, βλαστῆσαι ποιήσω τῷ Δαβὶδ βλαστὸν δικαιοσύνης. Et Jesaiae Lxvi. 14. ossa vestra tanquam herba תפרחנה germinabunt, Lxx, τὰ ὀστᾶ ὑμῶν ὡς βοτάνη ἀνατελεῖ ubi Latinus quoque Interpres Rom. Edit. germinabunt. Hos. x. 4. ἀνατελεῖ ὡς ἄγρωστις κρίμα &c. id est, germinabit sicut gramen judicium super desertum agri, ubi in Ebr. est יפרח Ps. 91. 8. ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ ἀμαρτωλοὶ ὡσεὶ χόρτον, ubi germinaverint peccatores sicut fœnum, ubi rursus in Ebraeo est פרח. Quam vocem sexies per ἀνατέλλειν expresserunt, ut & vocem צמח decies & octies, Gen. 3. 18. ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους ἀνατελεῖ σοι, spinas & tribulos germinare faciet tibi. Ebr. תצמיח ubi τὸ ἀνατέλλω ad imitationem Ebraeae vocis transitivum est, ut Matth. 5. 45. ὃς ἀνατέλλει τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ, qui oriri facit Solem suum. Et Gen. 19. τὸ ἀνατελλόμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Et quod proprius ad rem est, Jezech. xvi. 7. καθὼς ἡ ἀνατολὴ ἀγρῷ, ubi interpres Romanus, sicut hortus agri. Forte legendum Ortus, ego audacter, sicut germen. Quomodo hanc ipsam eandem vocem ἀνατολὰ idem Latinus Interpres Romanus Nobilius Flaminius reddidit Jezech. xvii. 9. τῷ βλάστῳ ἀνατολῆς αὐτῆς ξηρανθήσεται. Cuni gleba germinis sui arescet, ubi rursus in Ebr. est צמח. Confecimus ergo, opinor, ἀνατολὰ locis istis ubi Cristo tribuitur Germen significare. Hoc ergo modo disponamus significationes ἡ ἀνατολή, ut 1. significet ortum Solis vid. & Lunae proprie, Reliqua enim sidera usitatius ἀνατέλλειν dicuntur, usitatius dico. Nam ut profanos mittam, 2. Petri 1. φωσφόρος etiam dicitur ἀνατέλλειν. 2. locum seu regionem, ubi oritur Sol, Oriens. Matth. 2, 2. Vidimus stellam ejus ἐν ἀνατολῇ, in singulari, ut & Apoc: 7. & 21. Alias enim fere pluralis adhibetur, ἀπ' ἀνατολῶν, ut &, ἀπὸ δυσμῶν, Matthaei 8. & alibi. III. Germen, ita dictum, quod ex terra oriatur. Christum autem hoc epitheto insignivit Spiritus S. quod tanquam surculus ex trunco quasi ininternortuo repullula scens germinaverit justitiam. Quo respe- xisse videtur Apostolus Ebraeorum 7. 14. Falam est, Christum ἀνατειλαντα ἐξ Iuda id est, Germinasse ex tribu Juda. Hic certe unicus locus est novi foederis, ubi ἀνατέλλειν aliter accipitur quam de ortu luminarium.
units.tr: [βλαστὸν]. For it is said properly of plants and shoots and so on. Hence צמח [tsemach] means a shoot, a sprouting [βλάστημα], a plant or stalk springing up from the earth. There are four notable places where the Messiah is called צמח, and the Chaldee paraphrast himself supports this, since in each place he renders the Hebrew word by his own word for Messiah [משיחא]. We have the first place before us now. The second is at Jeremiah 33:15. The third is Zechariah 3:8: "Behold, I will bring my servant the צמח." The Septuagint has "the rising" [ἀνατολήν, Ἀνατολή]; the Chaldee has "my servant the Messiah" [משיחא]. The fourth is Zechariah 6:12: "Behold the man whose name is צמח" [צמח שמו]. The Chaldee has "whose name is the Messiah" [משיחא שמה]; the Septuagint has "Behold a man, the rising, whose name is..." [ἰδοὺ ἀνήρ, ἀνατολή, ὄνομα αὐτῷ]. In all these places the Chaldee did not translate צמח as ἀνατολή, but, as a freer interpreter and paraphraser should, he looked to the thing itself. For in all these places צמח is an epithet of the Messiah, and the Cabalists have noted that צמח and מנחם [menachem, "consoler"] are equal in value. The Hebrews also count this among the names of the Messiah, making the same number by gematria; see Cxxxviii. The difficulty therefore remains over the Greek rendering ἀνατολή. Some boldly condemn it. Others, on the contrary, maintain that the Hebrew word means both, that is, (1) a shoot, and (2) by the second sense, ἀνατολή; and they say that those who render צמח as "shoot" not only do so unskilfully but also act against the Word of God. These people seem to me to stake everything on Luke 1:78, where Christ is called not only ἀνατολή but, to make the matter clearer, ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους. To this is added the authority of antiquity, in which very many believed that Christ was called "Rising" because he would come from the east to judgment. But with respect to such great men, I would deny, with Piscator, that Zechariah had these passages in view; on this I shall say more shortly. As for צמח, I still seek a place in the canonical books where it means either a rising or a rising thing other than from the earth, or something analogous to the earth. For it is used metaphorically of hair, feathers and other such things, but never of the sun or of any star. Hence Leo Castrius, cutting such knots with a bold sword, says that the Jews corrupted these passages and that the word was once written רמח. But I have always thought this man unworthy of an answer, and rightly to be assailed and censured even by his own people, as I have shown elsewhere. As for what that great man notes, that the Jews call the horoscope, that is, the point of the east in a birth chart, מזרח [mizrach], that is, ἀνατέλλοντος [the rising], I wish he had cited the place and authority. I for my part neither recall reading that word in that sense in any author, nor could I find it in any lexicon. As for the word ἀνατολή, I say with the most distinguished Drusius, on Zechariah 6:12, that the Septuagint rightly, though perhaps doubtfully, rendered צמח by that word. For I say that in Hellenistic usage ἀνατολή means a shoot, and that in the passages from Jeremiah and Zechariah it should be translated SHOOT. I say that ἀνατολή in Jeremiah 23:5 is the same as βλάστημα, the word Symmachus used there. I say that ἀνατολή in Zechariah 6:12 is the same as ἀνατολή, the word other interpreters used in that place. But I see that this observation of the distinguished Drusius must be supported by some firm prop. Consider Jeremiah 33:15, where the Septuagint, about to repeat this very promise, expresses the same sense thus: "I will make to spring up for David a shoot of righteousness" [βλαστῆσαι ποιήσω τῷ Δαβὶδ βλαστὸν δικαιοσύνης]. And Isaiah 66:14: "your bones shall grow like grass" (Hebrew תפרחנה, "shall sprout"); the Septuagint has "your bones shall spring up like herbage" [τὰ ὀστᾶ ὑμῶν ὡς βοτάνη ἀνατελεῖ], where the Latin translator of the Roman edition also has "shall sprout." Hosea 10:4: "judgment shall spring up like hemlock" [ἀνατελεῖ ὡς ἄγρωστις κρίμα], that is, "judgment shall sprout like grass over the furrows of the field," where the Hebrew has יפרח. Psalm 91:8: "when the wicked spring up [ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ ἀμαρτωλοὶ] like grass," where the Latin is "when sinners sprout like hay," and where again the Hebrew has פרח. This word they rendered six times by ἀνατέλλειν, just as they rendered צמח eighteen times. Genesis 3:18: "thorns and thistles shall it spring up to you" [ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους ἀνατελεῖ σοι], "shall make to sprout," where the Hebrew is תצמיח; here τὸ ἀνατέλλω, in imitation of the Hebrew, is transitive, as in Matthew 5:45, "who makes his sun to rise" [ὃς ἀνατέλλει τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ], and in Genesis 19, "that which sprang up on the earth" [τὸ ἀνατελλόμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς]. And what bears more closely on the matter, Ezekiel 16:7: "as the shoot of the field" [καθὼς ἡ ἀνατολὴ ἀγρῷ], where the Roman translator has "as the garden of the field." Perhaps one should read "Ortus" (the springing up); I venture to say "as the sprout." In the same way the same Latin translator of the Roman edition, Nobilius Flaminius, rendered this very word ἀνατολή in Ezekiel 17:9: "its sprouting shoot [τῷ βλάστῳ ἀνατολῆς αὐτῆς] shall wither," or "with the clod of its sprout it shall wither," where again the Hebrew has צמח. I think, then, that we have established that in those passages where it is attributed to Christ, ἀνατολή means a shoot. Let us therefore set out the meanings of ἡ ἀνατολή thus: (1) it properly means the rising of the sun, and of the moon; for the other stars are more commonly said ἀνατέλλειν (more commonly, I say); for, to pass over profane writers, 2 Peter 1:19 also uses ἀνατέλλειν of the morning star [φωσφόρος]; (2) it means a place or region where the sun rises, the east. Matthew 2:2: "we saw his star in the east" [ἐν ἀνατολῇ], in the singular, as also in Revelation 7 and 21; elsewhere the plural is generally used, "from the east" [ἀπ' ἀνατολῶν], as also "from the west" [ἀπὸ δυσμῶν], Matthew 8 and elsewhere; (3) a shoot, so called because it springs out of the earth. The Holy Spirit has marked Christ with this epithet because, like a twig sprouting from a trunk, as it were almost dead, he sprouted and brought forth righteousness. The Apostle appears to have had this in view in Hebrews 7:14: "it is evident that Christ has sprung up [ἀνατειλαντα] out of Judah," that is, has sprouted from the tribe of Judah. This is certainly the only place in the New Testament where ἀνατέλλειν is taken in a sense other than the rising of luminaries.

units.la: Restat locus Luc. 1. 78. per viscera misericordiae Dei nostri, quibus visitavit nos ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους Vulg. Oriens ex alto. Si utroque oculo respexit Zacharias ad loca illa Jeremiae & Zach. videtur τὸ ἀνατολή & hic & illic eodem modo interpretandum esse. Cum vero addatur hic ἐξ ὕψους; non videtur reddi posse per Germen. Sed hoc additamentum non movit Clarissimos viros Drusium, Sculte- tum & alios. Ajunt enim hoc ipso indicari discrimen hujus germinis & aliorum. Cum enim cetera e terra, inferne, germinent, hoc e coelo est. Meum punctum hic feret Deligentissimus Piscator, qui non ad illa Jerem. & Zach. loca, sed illum potius Malach. 4 2. ubi Christus Sol appellatur, vel illum Numerorum 24. 17. ubi idem stellae nomine insignitur, Procedet stella ex Jacob. Vertit ergo, Oriens ex alto ad verbum ortus ex alto ut sit Metonymia adjuncti. Beza minus dubie, Is qui oritur ex alto. quasi esset, ὁ ἀνατέλλων, Sententiae suae praesidium habet Piscator in versu sequenti, qui hujus elogii exegesis est, ἐπιφανεῖ τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθη- μένοις & καθοδηγήσαι τοὺς πόδας ἡμῶν εἰς ὁδὸν εἰρήνης, i. ut illucescat iis qui in t. & u. m. sedent, & ut dirigat pedes nostros in v. pacis. Ecce duo effecta non germinis sed lucidissimi luminaris, quale est Sol.
units.tr: There remains Luke 1:78: "through the tender mercy of our God, whereby the dayspring from on high [ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους] hath visited us" (Vulgate: "the rising from on high"). If Zechariah looked with both eyes at those passages in Jeremiah and Zechariah, it seems that ἀνατολή should be interpreted in the same way both here and there. But since here it is added "from on high" [ἐξ ὕψους], it does not seem that it can be rendered "shoot." Yet this addition has not moved the most distinguished men Drusius, Scultetus and others. For they say that this very addition indicates the difference between this shoot and the others. For whereas the others sprout from below, out of the earth, this one is from heaven. My point will here be upheld by the most diligent Piscator, who refers not to those passages in Jeremiah and Zechariah, but rather to Malachi 4:2, where Christ is called the Sun, or to Numbers 24:17, where he is marked with the name of a star: "a star shall come out of Jacob." Piscator therefore translates "rising from on high" literally as "the rising from on high," so that it is a metonymy of the adjunct. Beza, more cautiously, renders it "he who rises from on high," as if it were ὁ ἀνατέλλων [the one rising]. Piscator has support for his view in the following verse, which explains this designation: "to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, and to guide our feet into the way of peace" [ἐπιφανεῖ τοῖς ἐν σκότει καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου καθημένοις, καὶ καθοδηγήσαι τοὺς πόδας ἡμῶν εἰς ὁδὸν εἰρήνης], that is, that it may shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, and that it may direct our feet into the way of peace. Here are two effects not of a shoot but of the most brilliant luminary, such as the sun.

units.la: Vers. 6. Et hoc est nomen quo vocabunt eum Dominus justus noster] Ita Vulg. Ebr. Et hoc erit nomen quo יקראו vocabunt eum (quod etiam Hier. notavit) יהוה צדקנו D o M I N U S justitia nostra. יקראו pro יקראו ad analogiam perfectorum, יתקפו / תלכדו / Pontificiorum nonnulli contendunt locum in Ebraeo esse violatum. Quomodo ergo scriptum fuisse putant? יקראו vocabunt. Ergo necesse est ut agnoscant adhuc ellipsin pronominis cum cui juxta nostram interpretationem non est locus. Sic dico, sive hoc sive illo modo legas Ebraeam vocem, semper opus est ellipsi. Hoc est nomen, quo vocabunt [eum] vel, hoc est nomen quo vocabit eum [D o M I- N U S ] vel, hoc est enim quo vocabit eum [Israel] vel, [unusquisque] Taceo, quam tralatitium sit verba activa 3. personae pro passivis adhibere. Gen. xv. & imputavit hoc ei ad justitiam Rom. 4. λογίζεται & imputatum est. Bellarm. & Leo Castrius ulterius progressi gressi sunt; ac ut illud de elkepsi incommodum vitarent, somniarint pro יקראו olim scriptum fuisse יקראוהי / atq; ita integra quoq; syllaba erasa fuisse. Quibus nos opponimus τῶν Lxx. qui plane ut nos, Hoc est nomen quo κυρίου αὐτὸν [Κυρίος] vocabit eum D O M I N U S, illud enim Κύριος supplementum est, Nomen enim יהוה quod in textu sequitur, expresserunt prima parte vocis Ιωσεδεκ. Qua de voce diximus aliquid parte prima Anti-barb. pag. 344. Si quaeras ejus interpretamentum, en tibi illud Ἰαὼ δικαιοσύνη, D O M I N U S justitia, ubi vides omissum ab illis pronomen illud consolatorium, ἡμῶν, Christus enim est nostra justitia. Vulg. justus noster. Et hoc male, Id enim esset יהוה צדקנו / Abstracta hic magis timiunt. 1. Cor. 1. 30. ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία Θεοῦ, καὶ δικαιοσύνη, ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις. In primo (Σοφία) observa Metonymiam adjuncti in caeteris, effecti. Notat. Hieron. in Editione τῶν Lxx. suo tempore additum fuisse, in Prophetis. Scilicet versus duo sequentes, 7. videlicet & octavus in Graecis codicibus hoc loco non repraesentantur, sed ad calcem capitis. Itaque hic immediate sequitur versus nonus, cujus initium; לנביאים / * Acceperunt hoc ceu et tulum sequentis concionis, contra Prophetas. Ut alibi, contra Moab, contra Damascum. Ἐνim ᾿ρος, saepe pro contra. ῥέος ἐς ὁ λόγος Θεοῦ ἐγένετο * contra quos sermo Dei factus est, Qua observatione auro contra non cara magnus Heinsius facem alluxit vexatissimo isti loco Johannis x: vide ejus Aristarchum. Quia vero ל & ב saepe alternant, ideo τὸ ל per ἐς saepe expresserunt, Ps. xvi. לשאל ἀ δι. Hae vero interpretamenta praepositionum juxta originariae praepositionis latitudinem itidem extendi debent. Hoc non ignoravit Hieron. Hoc quod in Lxx. male additum est, in Prophetis, penitus amputandum est. Aliud enim capitulum (κεφάλαιον) sequitur, quod ab iis praetermissum est, quo finito titulus est; ad Prophetas, seu, contra Prophetas. Haec Hier. Idem Paulo post, in Lxx. scriptum legimus, & hoc est nomen, quo appellabit eum Dominus, Josedek, in Prophetis. Quod plerique ignorantes, varia explanationis deliramenta confingunt. Multoque melius fuerit simpliciter insciitiam profiteri, quam imperitiae suae alios haeredes facere.
units.tr: Verse 6. "And this is the name by which they will call him, the LORD our righteousness": so the Vulgate. The Hebrew reads: "And this will be the name by which they will call him: the LORD our righteousness" [וזה השם אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו]. Some of the Papists contend that the Hebrew text is corrupt here, and that יקראו should be read as a perfect, in line with the other perfects (יתקפו, תלכדו). But how, then, do they think it was written? As יקראו, "they will call," so they must admit that a pronoun is omitted, and our interpretation has no room for such an ellipsis. I say that whichever way you read the Hebrew word, an ellipsis is always needed: "This is the name by which they will call [him]," or "This is the name by which he will call him [the LORD]," or "For this is the name by which he will call him [Israel]," or "[each one]." I say nothing of how commonplace it is to use third-person active verbs for passives: Gen. 15, "and he reckoned it to him for righteousness," and Rom. 4, λογίζεται, "it is reckoned." Bellarmine and Leo Castrius went further. To escape the difficulty of the ellipsis, they imagined that יקראוהי had once been written, and that a whole syllable had then been erased. Against them we set the Seventy, who plainly, like us, render: "This is the name by which the Lord [Κύριος] will call him, the LORD." For that word Κύριος is a supplement, and the Seventy expressed the name יהוה, which follows in the text, in the first part of the word Ἰωσεδεκ. I have said something about that word in the first part of my Anti-Barbarus, p. 344. If you ask for its interpretation, there you have Ἰαὼ δικαιοσύνη, "the LORD righteousness," where you see that they omitted the consoling pronoun ἡμῶν, "our," for Christ is our righteousness. The Vulgate has justus noster, "our righteous one," and this is wrong, for the Hebrew would then be יהוה צדקנו as an abstract, and here the abstract is more fitting. 1 Cor. 1:30: "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification and redemption" [ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία Θεοῦ, καὶ δικαιοσύνη, ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις]. In the first of these (wisdom), note the metonymy of the adjunct for the effect, as in the others. Jerome observed that in the edition of the Seventy in his own time the words in Prophetis, "in the Prophets," had been added. Clearly the two following verses, the seventh and eighth, are not represented at this point in the Greek manuscripts but at the end of the chapter. So the ninth verse follows immediately, and its opening word is לנביאים, "to the prophets." They took this as the heading of the following sermon, against the Prophets, as elsewhere "against Moab," "against Damascus." The Greek ἐπί often means "against." Heinsius, by this observation, which is of no small worth, shed light on that most troublesome passage in John 10; see his Aristarchus. Because ל and ב often alternate, the Seventy often rendered ל by εἰς, as in Ps. 16, לשאול [εἰς ᾅδου]. These renderings of prepositions must also be extended according to the breadth of the original preposition. Jerome did not miss this: "What was wrongly added in the Seventy, in the Prophets, must be cut away entirely. For another chapter (κεφάλαιον) follows, which they left out, and at its end is the title: to the Prophets, or against the Prophets." These are Jerome's words. Again he says a little later: "We read in the Seventy, 'and this is the name by which the Lord will call him, Josedek, in the Prophets.' Most people, not knowing this, invent various absurd explanations." It would be much better simply to admit ignorance than to make others the heirs of one's own inexperience.

units.la: Vers. 23. Nunquid Deus e vicino ego sum, dicit Dominus, & non Deus de longe? ] Ita Hieron. textu Ebraeo satis fideliter expresso. האלהי מקרבני ולא אלהי מרחוק. Vulgatus Hieronymi versionem expressit, prima voce duntaxat mutata, Nam pro tuuquid, dixit, putasne. Sensus autem est, Ego non sum Deus e vicino, sed sum Deus de longe. Non sum ejusmodi numen quod ea tantum videat & curet quæ mihi propinqua esse putas ut sunt hæc inferiora, & quæcunque hic in terris aguntur. Nota Tiro, quando Ebræi interrogant sine negatione, ut hic in primo membro, tunc cum vehementia quadam negant. Quando vero cum negatione, ut hic in 2. membro, tunc cum vehementia affirmant. Sensum ergo inverterunt Lxx. Θεὸς ἐγγίζων ἐγώ εἰμι, λέγει Κύριος. καὶ οὐχὶ Θεὸς μακρόθεν. Quorum vestigia legit Lutherus, nisi quod addiderit interrogationem, Ben ich nicht een Godt die nae-by is/ ende niet een Godt die verre sp quasi scriptum esset הֲלֹא אֱלֹהֵי מִקָּרֹב אֲנִי Equidem fateor, pio & fidei analogo sensu has versiones explicari posse, sed voces Ebræas illum sensum hic non admittere ajo. Obscuritatem versus omnino dissipavit D. Piscator, observata hic ellipsi, passim obvia, An [tantum] Deus a propinquo ego sum, & non [etiam] Deus a longe? Hanc ellipsin * plurimi observarunt quidem, sed illam hic applicare ipsis in mentem non venit. Jta Deus ad Samuelem lib. 1. cap. 8. non [tantum] te spreverunt, sed [etiam] me. Non amplius vocabitur nomen tuum Jacob [tantum:] sed [etiam] Israel. Marci 9. 37. qui me recipit, non [tantum] me recipit, sed [etiam] eum qui misit me. Sic Rom. 4. 9. Matth. 5. 46. Joh. v. 30. vi. 27. & 38 Xii. 44. fuerunt qui voces illas מקרוב & מרחוק non ad locum sed tempus retulerunt. q. d; an Deus a propinquo tempore ego sum? id est, novellus Deus, heri aut nudiustertius factus, & non Deus a longinquo id est, æternus? Ita Kimchius & eum secutus interpres Hisp. Cyprianus de valera. Ita quoque Chald. ex parte, אנא אלהא בריית עלמא מבראשית אנא אלהא עתידנא להדתא עלמא לצדיקיא Ego Deus creavi mundum a principio, Ego Deus renovabo mundum justis. Sed cave ne tibi imponat speciosa hæc interpretatio. Versus enim sequentes plane nos cogunt, voces illas non ad tempus sed ad locum referre. An occultabitur quispiam in absconditis, ut ego non videam eum? dicit Dominus. Annon cælum & terram ego impleo?
units.tr: Verse 23. "Am I a God near at hand, says the LORD, and not a God from afar?" Jerome expresses the Hebrew text quite faithfully: האלהי מקרבני ולא אלהי מרחוק. The Vulgate follows Jerome's version, changing only the first word: putasne, "do you think," for "numquid." The sense is: I am not a God near at hand, but I am a God from afar. I am not a divinity who sees and cares only for those things you think near, such as these lower things and whatever is done here on earth. Note, Tiro, that when the Hebrews ask without a negation, as in the first clause here, they deny with a certain vehemence; but when they use a negation, as in the second clause here, they affirm with vehemence. So the Seventy reversed the sense: "I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar." Luther followed their footsteps, except that he added a question: "Am I not a God who is near, and not a God who is far away?", as if the Hebrew were הֲלֹא אֱלֹהֵי מִקָּרֹב אֲנִי. I admit that these versions can be explained in a pious sense that agrees with faith, but I maintain that the Hebrew words do not allow that sense here. Piscator completely dispelled the obscurity of the verse by observing an ellipsis that is common everywhere: Am I [only] a God from near, and not [also] a God from afar? Many have indeed observed this ellipsis, but it did not occur to them to apply it here. So God says to Samuel, 1 Sam. 8: they have not [only] rejected you, but [also] me; your name will no longer be called Jacob [only], but [also] Israel. Mark 9:37: whoever receives me does not [only] receive me, but [also] him who sent me. So also Rom. 4:9, Matt. 5:46, John 5:30, 6:27, 6:38 and 12:44. Some have referred the words מקרוב and מרחוק not to place but to time: "Am I a God of recent time, that is, a new God, made yesterday or the day before, and not a God of long ago, that is, eternal?" So Kimchi, and the Spanish translator Cipriano de Valera, who followed him. The Chaldee paraphrast also partly agrees: "I, God, created the world from the beginning; I, God, will renew the world for the righteous." But beware lest this specious interpretation deceive you. For the verses that follow plainly compel us to refer those words to place, not time: Can anyone hide in secret places so that I do not see him? says the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth?
