units.la: Verf. 27. Rex Sefach] id est, Βαβυλῶν ἐοργαζόμενος. Vide de hac voce Junii notas, Seldeni comment. de Diis Syrorum, Scaliger
units.tr: Ver. 27. King of Sheshach] that is, Babylon (Βαβυλῶν ἐοργαζόμενος). On this word see the notes of Junius, Selden's commentary On the Gods of the Syrians, and Scaliger.

units.la: * Vide & Grammat. nostram libro 2. cap. 8. ligeri notas ad Fragmenta, Martinium in Etymolog. & crede, quæ Ebræi Eosque secuti etiam Hieron. hic de Ebtasch memorant, lusum tantum ingeniorum esse.
units.tr: * See also our Grammar, book 2, chapter 8; the notes of Ligeri on the Fragments; Martinius in the Etymologicon. And I believe that what the Hebrews, and those who followed them, and Jerome here also relate about Ebtasch is merely a play of wits.

units.la: Vers. 31. Judicatur ipse cum omni carne] id est, justus monstratur, inquit Carthus. ostenditur justus in peccatorum punitione, inquit, Lyra. Non intellexerunt multi commentatores Hellenisticæ linguæ consuetudinem. Vulgatus expressit Græca, ξείνεται αὐτὸς ὡς πᾶσαν σάρκα. Lxx. expresserunt Ebræa, נִשְׁפָּט הוּא אֵלֹהִים בַּשֶּׁר. ξείνει, Sed quemadmodum שפט in Niphal significat in judicio contendere cum adversario, judicio experiri, litigare, Ps. 37. non condemnabitur בִּהְשָׁפְּטוֹ id est, cum in judicio contendit, ita & apud Hellenistas passivum ξείνεσθαι sæpe idem significat Joel 3.7. Ebr. וְנִשְׁפְּטִי עִמָּם שָׁם / Hos. 2.2. ξείνη ὡς τὴν μητρὸν ὑμῶν. Ubi Ebr. רִיבוֹ בְּאֹמְּכֶם / Joh. ix. 3 ἐὰν βάλῃ ξείνεται αὐτῷ. Ebr. אִם יִשָּׁפֵט לְרִיב עִמּוֹ. Hinc ξείνης, lis, ut hoc ipso versu Jeremiæ, ὅτι ξείνης τῷ Κυρίῳ ἐν ἔθνεσι, cum gentibus Ebr. בְּגוֹיִם Prov. xv. μαχεόμενος ἀνὴρ ξειστὶ ξείνεις. Id est, lites extinguit. Matth. v 40. ᾧ τῷ θέλοντι ξείνεσθαι, volenti tecum in judicio contendere. Rom. 3. καὶ νικήσεις ἐν τῷ ξείνεσθαι αὐτόν. Ubi in Ebr. est infinitivus activus בְּשָׁפְטֶךָ pro passivo, quod crebrum est. 1. Cor. vi. 1. Sustinet aliquis vestrum negotium habens adversus alterum, ξείνεσθαι ἐπὶ ἀδίκων id est, judicio experiri sub injustis?
units.tr: Ver. 31. He himself will be judged with all flesh] that is, he is shown to be just, says the Carthusian; he is shown just in the punishing of sinners, says Lyra. Many commentators did not grasp the usage of the Hellenistic language. The Vulgate translated the Greek, δικάζεται αὐτὸς ὡς πᾶσαν σάρκα. The Seventy translated the Hebrew, נִשְׁפָּט הוּא אֵלֹהִים בַּשֶּׁר. δικάζει, But just as שפט in the Niphal means to contend in judgment with an adversary, to be tried in court, to go to law (Ps. 37: he will not be condemned, בִּהְשָׁפְּטוֹ, that is, when he contends in judgment), so too among the Hellenists the passive δικάζεσθαι often has the same meaning (Joel 3.7, Hebrew וְנִשְׁפְּטִי עִמָּם שָׁם; Hos. 2.2, δικάζου πρὸς τὴν μητέρα ὑμῶν, where the Hebrew is רִיבוּ בְּאִמְּכֶם; Job ix. 3, ἐὰν βούληται δικάζεσθαι αὐτῷ, Hebrew אִם יִשָּׁפֵט לְרִיב עִמּוֹ). Hence δίκη, a lawsuit, as in this very verse of Jeremiah, ὅτι δίκη τῷ Κυρίῳ ἐν ἔθνεσι, that the Lord has a lawsuit with the nations (Hebrew בַּגּוֹיִם). In Prov. xv, the man who quarrels (μαχόμενος ἀνὴρ) ends lawsuits, that is, he settles disputes. Matt. v. 40: τῷ θέλοντι δικαθῆναι, to the one who wishes to contend with you in judgment. Rom. 3: καὶ νικήσεις ἐν τῷ δικάζεσθαι αὐτόν, where the Hebrew has the active infinitive בְּשָׁפְטֶךָ in place of the passive, which is common. 1 Cor. vi. 1: Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law (δικάζεσθαι) before the unjust?

units.la: Vers. 33. Τεθνηκότας ὑπὸ Κυρίου] Latinus Interpres, vulneratus à DOMINO. Vulgatus interfectus Domini. Nota rursus, Ebraice esse, חַלְלֵי יְהוָה Genitivus efficientis, qui creber est post participia passiva aut nomina similem significationem habentia חָלָל proprie perforatus. Hinc enim domo est & חָלִיל tibia. 2. perforatus telo, vulneratus, τεθνηκότας. 3. interfectus non ex vulnere tantum, sed & alio mortis genere defunctus, νεκρὸς, πνεῦμα. Hinc τεθνηκότας secundum amplitudinem significationum vocis Ebraeæ suam quoque significationem dilatat, vel quod idem est, interpretamentum unum pro altero ponitur. 1. Reg. xi. 15. ξαπλὰ τὰς τεθνηκότας, Latina Rom. ad sepeliendum cæsos. Ps. 87. 7. ὥσεὶ τεθνηκότες καθεύδοντες ἐν τάφῳ, ut interfecti dormientes in sepulcro. Threni iv. 9. τεθνηκότας λιμῷ חַלְלֵי רָעָב interfecti fame. Qui veteribus versionib. Latinis ex Græcâ traductis usi sunt, ubi vox ea passim ea notione reddita est, quæ ipsi propria, miros ludos subinde dedere. Non plaudes, quisquis hos Hellenisticæ linguæ
units.tr: Ver. 33. Slain by the Lord] The Latin translator: wounded by the LORD. The Vulgate: slain of the Lord. Note again that in Hebrew it is חַלְלֵי יְהוָה, a genitive of agent, which is frequent after passive participles or nouns of similar meaning, from חָלָל, properly pierced. From this root also comes חָלִיל, a flute. (1) pierced with a weapon, wounded, τεθνηκότας. (2) slain, not only from a wound but also dead by some other kind of death, νεκρός, πνεῦμα. Hence τεθνηκότας, following the breadth of meanings of the Hebrew word, also extends its own meaning; or, what is the same, one rendering is put for another. 1 Kings xi. 15: ἐπλάσατο τοὺς τεθνηκότας, the Latin to bury those slain. Ps. 87.7: ὡσεὶ τεθνηκότες καθεύδοντες ἐν τάφῳ, like the slain sleeping in the grave. Lam. iv. 9: τεθνηκότας λιμῷ, חַלְלֵי רָעָב, slain by famine. Those who used the old Latin versions made from the Greek, where this word is everywhere rendered in a sense proper to itself, have from time to time produced strange jokes. You will not applaud, whoever you are who know the idioms of the Hellenistic language.

units.la: Melius B. Theod. Demonstrat inde suam; Non enim dicit. linguæ idiotismos nosti. Et quia in hunc campum jam delati sumus, juvat ex hoc eodem capite unum alterum ve locum insuper deliberare. Versu 29. ita ait Deus, bibendo bibetis. Nam ecce in ea civitate, quæ denominata est de nomine meo initium feci affligendi, & vos omnino impunes effetis? non eritis impunes. Quæ posteriora in Edit. Romana sic expressa sunt, καὶ ὑμεῖς καθαρεσμῷ ἀ μὴ καθαρισθῆτε. Latinus ejusdem interpres, & vos munditiæ non mundabimini. Quis hoc intelexerit ex veteribus? Theodoretus & Hieron. ita legisse videntur, & quidem propius Ebræo, καὶ ὑμεῖς καθαρισμῷ (aut καθαρσει) καπαρισθήσεσθε; ἀ μὴ καθαρισθῆτε. Quæ Hieron. sic convertit, & vos munditiæ mundi eritis? non eritis mundi. Putasne Lector, hoc intellecturum quempiam, qui Græca vel ista Latina cum originario textu non contulerit? Lxx. fatui & stolidi interpretes fuissent, si in via tam plana impegissent. Sed oportet hic impingant quotquot regulam illam de permutatione interpretamentorum in lingua Hellenistarum hic non attendunt. Illa vero nulli usui iis esse potest qui Ebræarum vocum ὁμωνυμίαν non intelligunt. Sic ergo habendum, in Ebræo esse וְאַתֶּם הִנָּקֹה תִּנָּקוּ לֹא תִנָּקוּ / נקה in Niphal 1. significat purum esse, vel purgari à sordibus, à malo culpæ, καθαρίζεσθαι, καθαρὸν εἶναι. 3. par Meton. impunem esse, liberum esse à malo poenæ, quod Lxx. hanc ipsam vocem interpretantes Prov. xi. 21. xix. 5. 9. xxviii. 20. reddunt ἀτιμώρητον εἶναι. Scilicet ut voces Ebræ, quæ malum culpæ notant ut חַטָּאת / עָוֹן &c. sæpe etiam malum poenæ significant, ita & נקה ob eandem ex Dei justitia ut sic dicam concomitantiam, & immunitatem à peccato, i. puritatem, immunitatem à poena, i. impunitatem significat. Poena enim est peccati consectaria, nisi interveniat remissio. Hinc καθαρίζειν, pro impune esse, καθαρεῖσ & καθαρισμὸ pro impunitate Lxx. dixerunt. Exod. 20. præcepto 3. ubi usurpatur Piel καθαρίσῃ & c. Ebr. לֹא יְנַקֶּה / Num. xiv. 18. καθαρισμῷ ἀ μὴ καθαρίσῃ τὸ ἔνοχον. Ita apud Græcos ἀθῷος, est, qui sine culpa & sine poena, & quidem hoc proprie magis, illud magis usitate. Θωρ enim multa, poena. Verbo autem hinc deducto aliquando Lxx. exprimunt idem נִקָּה impunem relinquere, Nahum 1. 3. ἀθῷον οὐκ ἀθωώσει. 1. Reg. 2. 9. ἡ ἀ μὴ ἀθωώσης αὐτὸν, Et passivum Niphal, Proverb. vi. 29. εἰσελθὼν πρὸς γυναῖκα οὐκ ἀθωωθήσεται. Versu eodem Jeremiæ, Gladium ego voco ἐπὶ πάντας καταμένως ἐπὶ τὴν γῆς Latinus, super omnes sedentes super terram, id est, habitantes. Ebr. יֹשְׁבֵי / אשׁפּה / Jaschab vero & καθέζῃ, sedere & κατοικεῖν, habitare, significat. Sed manum semel de tabula.
units.tr: Better, Blessed Theodoret shows his own view from this; for he does not say... you know the idioms of the language. And since we have already come onto this ground, it is worth weighing one or two further passages from this same chapter. In verse 29 the Lord says: you shall surely drink. For behold, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and shall you be altogether unpunished? You shall not be unpunished. In the Roman edition these last words are rendered καὶ ὑμεῖς καθαρεσμῷ ἀ μὴ καθαρισθῆτε. The Latin translator of the same, & vos munditiæ non mundabimini. Who could understand this from the old versions? Theodoret and Jerome seem to have read it, and indeed more closely to the Hebrew, καὶ ὑμεῖς καθαρισμῷ (or καθαρσει) καθαρισθήσεσθε; ἀ μὴ καθαρισθῆτε. Jerome renders it: & vos munditiæ mundi eritis? non eritis mundi. Do you think, reader, that anyone who has not compared these Greek and Latin versions with the original text will understand it? The Seventy would have been foolish and dull interpreters if they had stumbled on so plain a road. But stumble here they must, all who do not heed that rule about the interchange of renderings in the language of the Hellenists. That rule, however, can be of no use to those who do not understand the homonymy of the Hebrew words. So it must be held that in Hebrew we have וְאַתֶּם הִנָּקֹה תִּנָּקוּ לֹא תִנָּקוּ. The root נקה in the Niphal means (1) to be pure, or to be cleansed from filth, from the evil of guilt, καθαρίζεσθαι, καθαρὸν εἶναι; (3) by metonymy, to be unpunished, to be free from the evil of penalty, which the Seventy, rendering this very word at Prov. xi. 21, xix. 5, 9, xxviii. 20, give as ἀτιμώρητον εἶναι. Clearly, just as Hebrew words that denote the evil of guilt, such as חַטָּאת and עָוֹן, often also signify the evil of punishment, so נקה, by the same concomitance with God's justice, as one might say, and by immunity from sin, that is purity, also signifies immunity from punishment, that is impunity. For punishment is the consequence of sin, unless remission intervenes. Hence the Seventy used καθαρίζειν for being unpunished, and καθαρεῖς and καθαρισμός for impunity. Exod. 20, precept 3, where the Piel is used, καθαρίσῃ, etc.; Hebrew לֹא יְנַקֶּה; Num. xiv. 18: καθαρισμῷ ἀ μὴ καθαρίσῃ τὸ ἔνοχον. So among the Greeks ἀθῷος is one who is without fault and without punishment, and indeed the first sense is more proper, the second more customary, for θωρ (penalty) is much. From the same verb the Seventy sometimes render נִקָּה by ἀθωοῦν, to leave unpunished: Nahum i. 3, ἀθῷον οὐκ ἀθωώσει; 1 Kings ii. 9, ἡ ἀ μὴ ἀθωώσης αὐτὸν; and the passive of the Niphal, Prov. vi. 29: εἰσελθὼν πρὸς γυναῖκα οὐκ ἀθωωθήσεται. In the same verse of Jeremiah, I call the sword ἐπὶ πάντας καθημένους ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (Latin: super omnes sedentes super terram), that is, the inhabitants. The Hebrew יֹשְׁבֵי, from יָשַׁב, means both to sit and to κατοικεῖν, to dwell. But enough on this point; I lift my hand from the tablet.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Versf. 2. Fac tibi ἅτμως ἡ κλοιὸς ] Latinus, vincula & catenas. Ebr. מונין κλοιὸς ait Hieron. sermone Vulgari vocari bojas. Quam vocem erudite ex lingua Anglicana explicare mihi videtur Fullerus Miscell. v. 8. Nostra lingua, inquit, ut barbara videatur, utrumque nomen tam Græcum quam Latinum, nomine duplici indidem utrobique orto, statim quid sit, perspicue & facile declarat. Siquidem à κλοιὸς natum est nostrum Glog, literæ enim I & G eandem persæpe vim obtinent. Similiter à Boja nostrum Boi origine manifesta. Porro Boi apud noftrates significat lignum, non illud quidem longum, sed valde crassum, ima præsertim sui parte, quod summo mari fluitans, locum anchoræ, cui fune satis longo alligatur, in profundo submersæ, indicat. Eandem omnino formam plerunque habet nostrum Glog, egregie item crassum & ponderosum, & collari valido firmiter annexum. Quod indui solet cervicibus fugitivorum communiter; cum hominum, tum caeterorum animalium. Constat a. duabus partibus, collari & massa seu mole eidem appensa. Quoties igitur κλοιὸς collare ab eruditis transfertur, per synecd. intelligendum est fieri, parte pro toto posita, Bojas in plurali effert Plautus, quia astatim suppetebat hujusmodi vinculorum, nec non, quia pro atrocitate criminis & delinquentis ferocia Bojæ binæ nonnunquam, aliquando etiam ternæ impingi consuevere. Hæc D. Fullerus. Fortasse hinc est Belg. boeyen, licet de vinculis ferreis manuum pedumque usurpetur, Vide & Scalig. in Festum & Martinii Etymolog.
units.tr: Verse 2: "Make for yourself ἅτμως ἡ κλοιός" [ἅτμως ἡ κλοιός]. The Latin has "bonds and chains." The Hebrew word (מונין) is, as Jerome says, called in the vulgar tongue bojas. Fuller in his Miscellanies (v. 8) seems to me to explain this word learnedly from the English language. "Our language," he says, "although it may seem barbarous, makes clear and easy to understand both the Greek and the Latin name, since each has a double name arising in the same way. Our word Glog comes from κλοιός, for the letters I and G very often have the same force. Likewise our Boi clearly derives from Boja. Among our countrymen, Boi means a piece of wood, not indeed long but very thick, especially at its lower end, which floats on the surface of the sea and marks the place of an anchor sunk in deep water, to which it is tied by a sufficiently long rope. Our Glog generally has exactly the same shape: it is likewise thick and heavy, and is firmly fastened to a strong collar. It is commonly put around the necks of fugitives, both men and other animals. It consists of two parts, the collar and the mass or weight attached to it." Whenever κλοιός is rendered collare by learned writers, it must be understood as a synecdoche, the part being put for the whole. Plautus uses Bojas in the plural, because such bonds were always to hand, and because, according to the atrocity of the crime and the ferocity of the offender, two or sometimes even three Bojae were commonly fastened on. So far Fuller. Perhaps from this comes the Belgian boeyen, although it is used of iron fetters for the hands and feet. See also Scaliger on Festus and Martinius's Etymologicon.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Versf. 2. Sic dicit DOMINUS, εὗρον Θερμὸν ἐν ἐρήμῳ ] Latina Romana, inveni calidum in deserto. Queris quomodo hoc interpretati sint veteres? En tibi interpretationem ex B. Hieronymo, Porro, inquit, juxta LXX. hæc intelligentia est, Dominus invenit calidos & viventes Apostolos, & socios eorum in deserto gentium, inter eos qui infidelitate sua interfecti fuerant, nec habebant cabrem vita &c. Idem Hier. notat, Latinos codices suo tempore ridiridicule ambiguitate codicis deceptos pro calido, lupinos interpretatos esse. Græcum enim Θερμὸν, inquit utrumque significat. Hæc Hier. Varietas tamen est in accentu, Θερμὸς calidus Θέρμος lupinus. Lubet adscribere alium locum ejusdem patris, ex comment. in Jesaiæ cap. Lxv. pag. Edit Basil. 245. Ubi docet, etiamsi peccantium plurima sit multitudo, unum tamen justum cunctorum vitio non perire. Abraham, inquit, de igne Chaldæorum fidei integritate servatus est. In quem sensum & Hieremiæ verba ex persona Domini dicentis consentiunt. Quasi calidum in deserto inveni Israel cum occisis gladio. Cum enim, inquit, omnis mundus idolatriæ gladiis vulneratus jaceret exanimis, inveni Israel in Abraham calorem habere fidei: quasi medicus, qui post prælia inter cadavera mortuorum, ubi quem senserit pulsantibus venis aliquid habere vitale, adhibet curā vulneribus ut restituat sanitatem. Pro eo quod scriptum est ὡς Θερμὸν hoc est quasi calidum, Latinus interpres, verbi ambignitate deceptus, lupinum, interpretatus est. In quo & Græcorum plerique errant, & tamen sciendum in Ebr. pro calore scriptum esse הוֹרָה (lege חֵן) quod interpretatur gratia, quod sc. gratia Dei & non merito suo salvatus sit Israel. Hæc Hieron. Quod, vero noto de errore in voce הוֹרָה admisso, Ecce tibi Hieron· rursus ad locum Jeremiæ, Θερμὸν non habetur in hebræo, Est enim scriptum חֵן / quod Aq. Theod. & Symm. χάριν id est, gratiam interpretati sunt. Soli Lxx. posuere calidum, putantes ultimam literam ם esse. Si enim legamus חֵן per literam ו / gratia dicitur, si per ם calor interpretatur. Hæc Hier. certe חם calor, חם Calidus. Mé vero lectio illa quam exhibet Hieron. ad cap. Lxv. Jesaiæ εὑρον ὡς Θερμὸν, plane inducit in eam sententiam, Lxx. scripsisse, εὑρον ἐλεημοσύνην, invenerunt misericordiam· εὑρον enim ad primam sing. & 3. pluralem indifferens est. Quamvis Theodoretus eundem sensum elicere studeat ex voce Θερμὸν. Dum enim quis calefit, laxatur ad misericordiam, inquit. Ebraea simpliciter ita habent מָצָא חֵן בְּמִדְבָּר עַם שְׂרִידֵי חֶרֶב הַלּוֹךְ לְהַרְגִּיעוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל invenit gratiam in deserto populus superstitum a gladio: Israel [inquam, ] me præeunte ad procurandam illi quietem. Israel, inquam, repete ευρον χαριν, invenit gratiam, quod D. Piscator textui inserviit. לְהַרְגִּיעַ Kimchius exponit, לְהַמְצִיא לוֹ מְרְגוֹעַ / Certe הַרְגִּיעַ est quiescere & quietem præstare, Sensus vero est imperfectus, Hoc enim vult Deus, sicuti populus Israel tunc invenit gratiam in oculis meis, ita & nunc invenietis.
units.tr: Verse 2. Thus says the LORD, "I found warmth [εὗρον Θερμὸν] in the wilderness." The Latin Vulgate has "I have found what is warm in the desert." You ask how the ancients interpreted this? Here is the interpretation from St Jerome: "Moreover," he says, "according to the Seventy, this is the sense: the Lord found warm and living Apostles, and their companions, in the wilderness of the Gentiles, among those who had been slain by their unbelief and did not have the warmth of life," and so on. Jerome also notes that the Latin manuscripts of his day, deceived by the ridiculous ambiguity of the codex, rendered the word for "warm" as "lupins." For the Greek Θερμὸν, he says, means both. Thus Jerome. There is, however, a difference in the accent: Θερμὸς means "warm," Θέρμος means "lupin." I should like to add another passage from the same Father, from his commentary on Isaiah chapter 65, page 245 of the Basel edition. There he teaches that even if the multitude of sinners is great, yet one righteous man does not perish with the sins of all. Abraham, he says, was preserved from the fire of the Chaldeans in the integrity of his faith. The words of Jeremiah, spoken in the person of the Lord, agree with this sense: "As if I had found warmth in the wilderness, Israel, with those slain by the sword." "For when," he says, "the whole world, struck by the swords of idolatry, lay lifeless, I found in Abraham Israel having the warmth of faith. Like a physician who, after battles, among the corpses of the dead, when he perceives some vital pulse beating in one of them, applies care to the wounds so as to restore health." Where it is written ὡς Θερμὸν, that is, "as if warm," the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated "lupin." In this, most of the Greeks also err; yet it should be known that in the Hebrew, instead of warmth, is written הוֹרָה (read חֵן), which means "grace," that is, Israel was saved by the grace of God and not by its own merit. Thus Jerome. But as to the error I have noted in the word הוֹרָה, behold, Jerome again, on the passage of Jeremiah: "Θερμὸν is not found in the Hebrew. For it is written חֵן, which Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus translated as χάριν, that is, grace. Only the Seventy put 'warm,' supposing the last letter to be ם. For if we read חֵן with the letter ו, it means grace; if with ם, it means warmth." Thus Jerome. Certainly חם means warmth, and חם means warm. But that reading which Jerome gives on Isaiah 65, εὑρον ὡς Θερμὸν, plainly leads to the view that the Seventy wrote εὑρον ἐλεημοσύνην, "they found mercy," since εὑρον is indifferent between the first person singular and the third person plural. Although Theodoret strives to draw the same sense from the word Θερμὸν: "For when someone is warmed, he is made soft towards mercy," he says. The Hebrew reads simply: מָצָא חֵן בְּמִדְבָּר עַם שְׂרִידֵי חֶרֶב הַלּוֹךְ לְהַרְגִּיעוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל [he found grace in the wilderness, a people left over from the sword; Israel, I say, going before him to procure rest for him]. Israel, I say: repeat εὗρον χάριν, "he found grace," which Mr Piscator followed in his text. Kimchi explains לְהַרְגִּיעַ as "to procure for him rest." Certainly הַרְגִּיעַ means to be quiet and to give rest, but the sense is incomplete. For this is what God means: just as the people of Israel then found grace in my eyes, so now you too shall find it.

units.la: Verf. 9. In fletu venient ] Ita vulg. Interpretes fere accipiunt de fletu tristitiæ, & tristi sollicitudine de salute & remissione peccatorum. Alii, inter quos S A, venient interpretantur abierunt, Atque ita Lxx. ἐσκλαυθμῷ ἐξῆλθον. At docte notavit Hieron. fletum interdum & nimii gaudii indicium esse. Sic dico, lacrymæ interdum homini cadunt præ gaudio. ἔτω κοινὸν π χαρᾷ ᾗ λυπῇ τὸ δάκρυά ἐςι, inquit Xenophon. יש בכי של שמחה / inquit Kimchi, est & fletus lætitiæ, ut & osculatus est Jacob Rachelem וישא קולו ויבך & sustulit vocem suam & flevit. Claudianus eleganter vocat lacrymofa gaudia. De bello Getico.
units.tr: Verse 9. They shall come with weeping. Most translators take this as the weeping of sorrow, and of anxious concern for salvation and the forgiveness of sins. Others, among whom is S.A., render "they shall come" as "they went away," and so the Seventy: ἐσκλαυθμῷ ἐξῆλθον, "they went out weeping." But Jerome rightly observed that weeping is sometimes also a sign of excessive joy. So too I say: tears sometimes fall from a man for joy. "So common is it that tears come from joy or from grief," says Xenophon, ἔτω κοινὸν π χαρᾷ ᾗ λυπῇ τὸ δάκρυά ἐςι. "There is weeping of joy," says Kimchi, יש בכי של שמחה, "and there is also weeping of gladness, as Jacob also kissed Rachel and lifted up his voice and wept." Claudian elegantly calls them "tearful joys."

units.la: --- Properantibus undique signisConvenient, visoque animi Stilicone recepti, Singultus varios, lacrymosaque gaudia miscent.
units.tr: Hastening from every side the standards come together; and when they see Stilicho, restored to their spirits, they mingle sobs of many kinds with tearful joys.

units.la: Xenophonti talis fletus κλαυσίγελως dicitur Θεάσασθαι ἡν τὰς ψυχὰς ἀνδρὰς δεξιωσμὼς ἀλλήλας, τὰς δ' γυναῖκας ἁμα χαρᾷ δακρυούσας. Πάντας δ' τὰς παρόντας κλαυσίγελως εἶχε- Videre illic erat viros quidem dextras sibi invicem porrigentes, fœminas vero cum gaudio flentes, Omnes denique præsentes fletus cum risu mixtus tenebat.
units.tr: Xenophon calls such weeping "laughter-weeping" (κλαυσίγελως): "It was possible to see men clasping each other's right hands, and women weeping with joy. And all who were present were seized by a weeping-laughter," that is, weeping mixed with laughter.

units.la: Ibid. καὶ ἐφραὶμ πρωτότοκός μου ἐστιν. ] Ephraim primogenitus meus est. Recte Kimchi בכור לשון חבה ואהבה / id est, bechor hic habet significationem dilectionis & amoris. Sensus ergo ἀγαπητὸς μου, dilectus meus. Solent enim primogeniti præ aliis diligi.
units.tr: Ibid. "And Ephraim is my firstborn" [καὶ ἐφραὶμ πρωτότοκός μου ἐστιν]. Ephraim is my firstborn. Kimchi rightly says: בכור לשון חבה ואהבה, that is, "bechor here has the sense of affection and love." The meaning, then, is ἀγαπητὸς μου, "my beloved." For firstborn sons are usually loved more than the others.

units.la: Verf. 22. Fœmina circum dabit Virum ] Vulgo exponunt de conceptione Christi, quasi scriptum esset, עלמה הרה וילדת בן Virgo concipiet & pariet filium. Hieron. Novam rem creavit Dominus super terram. Absque viri semine, absque ullo coitu & conceptu fœmina circumdabit virum, gremio uteri sui, qui juxta incrementa quidem ætatis per vagitus & infantiam proficere videbitur sapientia & ætate, sed perfectus vir in ventre fœmineo solitis mensibus continebitur. Unde Symmachus & Aquila juxta nostram interpretationem interpretati sunt. Hæc Hier. Miror ergo unde Cl. Junius in notis ad Edit. Francofurt. illam Sym. & Aquilæ lectionem hauserit, γυναῖκες περιέλεύσονται ἀνδρα. Hoc enim plane aliud sonat. Pergit Hier. Quid sibi autem in loco hoc voluerit editio Vulgata gata (intelligit Latinam ex Græca versam, in salute tua circuibant homines) possem dicere & sensum aliquem reperire, NISI DE VERBIS DEI HUMANO SENSU ARGUMENTARI SA-CRILEGUM ESSET. Ergone sacrilegum est, Hieronyme, locis Scripturæ mala versione à fonte plane discrepantibus, sensum aliquem commodum invenire? Ego dicere soleo, hoc non esse verbum Dei interpretari, sed verbum hominis, quid possem dicere mitius & lenius? Et tamen ego propemodum sacrilegus audio. Utinam vero ipse Hieron. hujus gravissimæ censuræ nunquam dememinisset! Sed pergamus referre verba Hieronymi; Theodotio autem & ipse vulgatæ editioni consentiens, interpretatus est, Creavit DOMINUS salutem novam in salute circuibit homo, singulare, pro plurali ponens. Unde ergo rursus Cl. Junius hausit illud Theodotionis fragmentum, ἐκτισε Κύριος σωτηρίαν καινὴν, γυνὴ περιέλευσεται ἄνθρωπον. Cæterum ipsam expositionem quod attinet, notandum I. non dici עלמה vel אשה sed נקבה / παρθένος, vel τὸ ἥλικα ... ἁρμόζων, vel ἀνδρός. נְקֵבָה autem non ætatis, non status, aut unius individui, sed sexus nomen est II. טובב nunquam usurpari de conceptione. III. גבר Christo in utero concepto aut nascenti nec convenire nec uspiam tribui. Quæ tria prolixe urget & adversus adversarium συγγενεῖς Cl. Theol. Joh. Tarnov. ὁ νῦν ἐν ἀρχῇ. Illa ergo expositione rejecta videamus alias.
units.tr: Verse 22. A woman shall compass a man. The common interpretation refers this to the conception of Christ, as if the text read עלמה הרה וילדת בן [a young woman shall conceive and bear a son], "a virgin shall conceive and bear a son." Jerome: "The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: without the seed of a man, without any intercourse or conception, a woman shall compass a man in the womb of her body, who, as he seems to grow in age through infancy and childhood, will advance in wisdom and years; but as a perfect man he will be contained in a female womb for the usual months. Hence Symmachus and Aquila translated according to our interpretation." Thus Jerome. I am surprised, then, where the learned Junius in his notes to the Frankfurt edition drew that reading of Symmachus and Aquila, γυναῖκες περιέλεύσονται ἀνδρα [women shall go round a man]. For this plainly means something else. Jerome goes on: "What the Vulgate edition wished to mean in this place (it understands the Latin translated from the Greek, 'men went round about in your salvation') I could say, and find some sense; BUT IT WOULD BE SACRILEGE TO ARGUE FROM HUMAN SENSE ABOUT THE WORDS OF GOD." Is it then sacrilege, Jerome, to find some suitable sense in passages of Scripture that plainly differ from the source because of bad translation? I am accustomed to say that this is not interpreting the word of God but the word of man. What could I say more mildly and gently? And yet I am almost called sacrilegious. Would that Jerome himself had never remembered this most grave censure! But let us go on with the words of Jerome: "Theodotion, too, agreeing with the Vulgate edition, translated, 'The Lord created a new salvation; a man shall go round in salvation,' putting the singular for the plural." Where, then, did Junius again draw that fragment of Theodotion, ἐκτισε Κύριος σωτηρίαν καινὴν, γυνὴ περιέλευσεται ἄνθρωπον? But as far as the exposition itself is concerned, it should be noted, first, that the words used are not עלמה or אשה but נקבה, παρθένος, or τὸ ἥλικα ... ἁρμόζων [one suited in age], or ἀνδρός [of a man]. Now נְקֵבָה is a name of sex, not of age, status, or a single individual. Second, סובב [to go round] is never used of conception. Third, גבר [man] neither suits nor is anywhere ascribed to Christ conceived or born in the womb. These three points are urged at length, and against his opponent, the most learned theologian Johann Tarnov: "he who now is in the beginning." Having set aside that exposition, let us look at others.

units.la: Dominus Calvinus conferens hunc locum cum illo Jesaiæ XLIII. 19. aliis 6. ubi Deus promittens liberationem ex captivitate Babylonica ita quoque præfatur, Ecce ego facturus sum rem novam &c. Hanc quoque promissionem de eadem interpretatur. q. diceret Propheta, Imbelles Israelitæ, fœminis quam viris similiores, novo robore divinitus instructi, Chaldæis superiores evadent, atque ita fœminæ viros ad angustias redigent. Certe non rara est metaphora per fœminas, meticulosos, per viros, strenuos fortesque intelligere, Jef, xix. 16. In die illa Ægyptii erunt sicut mulieres. Neque novum est ut circumdare alium dicantur, qui eum hostiliter circundat, cingit & premit. Vide Ps. xxii. 13. 17. Ecclesiast. ix. 14. Ps. cxviii. 10. 11. 12. Genes. xix. 4. Josuæ vi. 3. Hanc sententiam expressit & Piscator. Et ab ea non multum recessit B. Lutherus, quando in Editionibus anni 1532. 1534. 1536. 1538. Witebergensibus ita vertit, Die sich vorhin wie Weiber gestellet haben / sollen Männer seyn. Postea mutavit ververba, & Ebraeis vocibus pressius haesit, Das Weib wert den Man umbgeben. In margine vero triplicem posuit expositionem, quarum prima vulgata illa est. De qua sic loquitur, Non rejicio sensum, quo veteres ajunt Christum esse illum virum, quem Maria circumdederit.
units.tr: The Reverend Calvin, comparing this passage with that of Isaiah 43:19 and the following, where God, promising deliverance from Babylonian captivity, begins in the same way, "Behold, I am about to do a new thing," also interprets this promise in the same way: as if the prophet were saying that the Israelites, feeble and more like women than men, would, once divinely strengthened with new vigour, prevail over the Chaldeans, and so women would bring men to straits. Certainly it is not rare for a metaphor to understand "women" as the timid and "men" as the strong and brave: Isa. xix. 16, "In that day the Egyptians shall be like women." Nor is it new for one to be said to surround another who hems him in, encircles and presses him as an enemy: see Ps. xxii. 13, 17; Eccles. ix. 14; Ps. cxviii. 10, 11, 12; Gen. xix. 4; Josh. vi. 3. Piscator also expressed this sense, and not far from it did the blessed Luther depart, when in the editions of Wittenberg of 1532, 1534, 1536 and 1538 he translated it: "Those who before have stood like women shall be men." Afterwards he changed the wording and clung more closely to the Hebrew words: "The woman shall surround the man." In the margin, however, he gave a threefold exposition, of which the first is that common one. Of this he speaks thus: "I do not reject the sense in which the ancients say Christ is that man whom Mary surrounded."

units.la: II. Sententia est Junii, faemina ambit virum q. d. Vide, Synagoga, ut confestim arripias occasionem oblatam. Nam si Ecclesia Dei, quae cum foemina comparatur, te & judaeis, suis propriis liberis caruerit, propter aversionem vestram non potest illa prosecto orba permanere, sed tanquam vidua & sterilis virum ambiet, & filios sibi aliunde comparabit. Quam sententiam amplexus quoque est ex Hispanis Hieron. ab Oleastro canone 4. in Genesin.
units.tr: II. The opinion of Junius is: the woman encompasses the man, that is, "See, Synagogue, that you immediately seize the opportunity offered. For if the Church of God, which is compared to a woman, has been deprived of you and of the Jews, her own children, then on account of your aversion she cannot certainly remain bereaved, but like a widow and barren she will seek a husband and will acquire sons for herself from elsewhere." Among the Spaniards, Hieronymus ab Oleastro also embraced this opinion, in canon 4 on Genesis.

units.la: III. Foemina id est, Ecclesia, quae sub foeminae specie in Scriptura considerari solet, Ecclesia desertrix, praeter solitum ordinem circumdabit id est ambiet virum, Maritum suum, quem deseruit id est, Deum. Hanc sententiam sequitur Paraeus in Calvino Orthod. p. 166. & defendit Joh. Tarnovius in Exercit. Biblicis sebat significat quoque sectari, ambire, prensare amica quadam circumitione & illam sequente amplexatione. Psf. vii. 8. xxvi. 6. xxxii. 7. xlviii. 13. At, inquies, sic potius adhibuisset Propheta verbum חבק amplexari, Responsio facilis, Subjectae materiae, quadrare illud חבב magis, quam hoc חבק / Qualis enim haec foemina, talis ejus amplexus. Sed ipsa talis, ut constet ex multis individuis. Cur vero dixerit potius גבר quam זכר ratio quoque in promptu est. זכר enim id est masculus potest esse qui infirmis est. Hic vero vel maxime requirebatur potens, qui afflictam liberaret conjugem, quemque ipsa eam ob causam maxime amplectitur, quod sit גבר id est, ἀνὴρ ἰσχυρός Si quaesieris, an hoc novum sit, considera, alias vulgo ita solere fieri ut vir reducat conjugem, eamque segregatam recipiat. Hic vero foemina, sed a Christo animata ambiet prensabitque virum
units.tr: III. The woman, that is, the Church, which in Scripture is usually considered under the image of a woman, the deserting Church, contrary to the usual order, will encompass, that is, will seek out, her husband whom she deserted, namely God. Paraeus follows this view in his commentary on Calvin's Orthodoxy, p. 166, and Joh. Tarnovius defends it in his Biblical Exercises. Sebat also signifies to pursue, to court, to press upon with a certain friendly going round and the embrace that follows it (Ps. 7:8; 26:6; 32:7; 48:13). But, you will say, the prophet would more fittingly have used the verb chabaq [חבק], to embrace. The answer is easy: the verb chabab [חבב] suits the subject matter better than chabaq [חבק]. For such as the woman is, such is her embrace; and that she is such is clear from many instances. The reason why he said gibbor [גבר] rather than zakar [זכר] is also at hand. Zakar, that is, male, can also mean one who is weak. Here above all a powerful one was required, who would free his afflicted wife, and whom she embraces all the more for this reason, that he is gibbor, that is, mighty man [ἀνὴρ ἰσχυρός]. If you ask whether this is something new, consider that otherwise it is commonly the custom for a husband to take back his wife and receive her when she has been separated from him. Here, however, a woman, but one animated by Christ, will court the man and seize him. ## CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.

Vers. 29. Et domos in quarum domatibus ] id est, tectis. Lxx. καὶ τὰς οἰκίας ἐν αἷς ἐθυμίωσαν Βὰλ τῶν δωμάτων αὐτῶν. Viden hic manifeste distingui δῶμα ab οἰκία; 2. Sam. xi. 3. καὶ ᾧεισ-πάτει Δαβὶδ Βὰλ τὸ δώματος τῆς οἰκιας τοῦ βασιλέως. Hoc notó obeos, qui vocem eandem in novo fœdere vertere solent da-mum. Δῶμα in lingua Hellenistica interpretamentum est Ebraici ai Hieron. epistola quadam ad Suniam & Fret. Δῶμα, inquit, in Orientalibus provinciis ipsum dicitur, quod Latinis tectum. In Palæstina enim & Ægypto vel ubi scripti sunt divini libri vel interpretati, non habent in tectis culmina, sed domata, quæ Romæ vel solaria vel Meniana vocantur id est, plana tecta. Porro pro Meniana in lexicis quando de voce δῶμα agunt, sæpe Mœnia scribitur Barbare. Meniana vel Mœniana dicuntur à Menio Romano. Vide Etymolog. Martinii in Menianus.
units.tr: Verse 29. And the houses in whose roofs [are the incense burners to Baal] — that is, in their roofs. The Seventy: and the houses in which they burned incense to Baal on their roofs [καὶ τὰς οἰκίας ἐν αἷς ἐθυμίωσαν Βάλ τῶν δωμάτων αὐτῶν]. Do you see here how clearly dōma [δῶμα] is distinguished from oikia [οἰκία]? 2 Sam. 11:2: and David walked upon the roof of the king's house [καὶ περιεπάτει Δαβὶδ ἐπὶ τὸ δώματος τῆς οἰκίας τοῦ βασιλέως]. Those who usually render this same word in the New Testament as "house" have noted this. Dōma [Δῶμα], in the Hellenistic language, is the rendering of the Hebrew gag. Jerome, in a certain letter to Sunia and Fretela, says: Dōma, he says, in the Eastern provinces is itself called what Latins call tectum, a roof. For in Palestine and Egypt, where the divine books were written or translated, they do not have peaked roofs, but flat roofs, which at Rome are called solaria or Meniana, that is, flat roofs [plana tecta]. Moreover, in lexicons, when they treat the word dōma, they often write Mœnia for Meniana, which is a barbarism. Meniana or Mœniana are so named from the Roman Menius. See Martinius's Etymological Lexicon under Menianus.

units.la: Verf. 30. Lxx. ὅτι ἦσαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ισραὴλ καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Ιουδα μόνοι ποιοῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν καὶ ὀφθαλμῶς μου. Quia fuerunt filii Israel & Juda soli facientes malum ante oculos meos ] Quæsitum hic fuit, quomodo Israelitæ soli peccasse dicantur? Annon & gentes reliquæ peccarunt? Respondet pro Græcæ versionis patronis Hieron. Qui habet notitiam Dei & recedit ab eo, solus peccat in oculis Dei. Qui vero increduli permanserint, quasi illo non vidente & negligente delinquunt. Sed frustra est hæc subtilitas. Qui enim Græca cum Ebraïs contulerit, mox videbit, primitus ab illis scriptum fuisse μόνον, solum, tantum Ebraïaista sunt כִּי הָיוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְנֵי יְהוּדָה אַךְ עֹשִׂים הָרַע בְּעֵינַי / nam fuerunt F. Isr. & F. Juda tantummodo f. m. in oculis D. אַךְ est asseverandi, adversandi & excludendi particula, profecto, veruntamen, duntaxat. Editio secunda Symmachi διὰ id est, jugitur, perpetuo, sine intermissione.
units.tr: Verse 30. The Seventy: because the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah alone were doing evil before my eyes [ὅτι ἦσαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ισραὴλ καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Ιουδα μόνοι ποιοῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν καὶ ὀφθαλμῶς μου]. Because the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah alone were doing evil before my eyes. The question has been raised here: how is it said that the Israelites alone sinned? Did not the other nations sin as well? Jerome, speaking for the defenders of the Greek version, answers: he who has knowledge of God and turns away from him alone sins in the sight of God; but those who remain unbelieving, as if God were not seeing and were neglecting them, offend. But this subtlety is in vain. For whoever compares the Greek with the Hebrew will soon see that the word was originally written by them as monon, only, alone. The Hebrew reads: for the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah were only doing evil in my eyes [כִּי הָיוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְנֵי יְהוּדָה אַךְ עֹשִׂים הָרַע בְּעֵינַי]. For they were, the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah, only, in the eyes of the Lord. Ak [אַךְ] is a particle of asserting, opposing and excluding: indeed, however, only. The second edition of Symmachus has dia, that is, continually, perpetually, without intermission.

units.la: Verf. 36. tradetur in manus Regis Babel, ἐν μαχαίρᾳ, καὶ ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ. Ebraæ, בְּחֶרֶב וּבְרָעָב וּבַדֶּבֶר / Vides ἀπωλείᾳ respondere Ebraeo דֶּבֶר λοιμός. Ebraeam vocem Lxx. semel reddidere ἀπωλείαν, Ter, λοιμὸς. Reliquis in locis, quæ Multa satis sunt, θάνατος. Videamus primo de ἀπωλείᾳ. Quid ea vox proprie & usitate significet, nemo ignorat. Pestilentiam hic notare videtur, quod ea à Deo immittatur & quasi amandetur unde Pf.78. 49. ubi in Ebr. est מִשְׁלַחַת missio iidem ἀπωλείαν reddidêre, pestilentiam intelligentes. ἐξαπέστειλεν εἰς αὐτὸς ὀργὴν θυμῶ αὐτῆς, θυμὸν καὶ ὀργὴν καὶ θλίψιν, ἀπωλείαν δι' ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν. Ubi Latina Rom. immissionem. Eodem sensu vocem eam usurpavit Baruch II.25. καὶ ἀπεθάνοσαν ἐν τόνοις πονηροῖς, ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ, καὶ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ. Ubi Latina Rom. emissione. Fortassis quia Theodoretus hic notavit, τὴν ἁιχμαλωσίαν hic pro captivitate positum esse. Sed revera hic αἰχμαλωσία respondet Ebraeo דְּבָר. Quod ad alterum interpretamentum (θάνατος) attinet, sumamus e.g. locum ex Cap. xxxiv. 17. destomachatur illic Deus in Judaeos quod libertatem tempore obsidionis promulgatam, laxatâ eâ, revocaverint, servosque quos ad pileum juxta Legis praescriptum, vocaverant, derepente in servitutem rursus asseruerint. Idcirco sic ait Dominus, vos non auscultastis mihi promulgando libertatem quisque fratri suo, ecce ego promulgo contra vos libertatem, gladio, peste & fame. q. d. Quia vos non promulgatis libertatem serio, sed mihi & servis illudentes, illos retraxistis in servitutem ipsisq; dominamini, ego promulgabo libertatem, non talem qua vos liberemini à servitio & poenis, sed qua gladio, peste & fame liberum erit in vos grassari, vobisque dominari qua à mea cura & providentia quasi manumissi videbimini. Kimchi, omnes istae plagae dominabuntur vobis. Non erit vobis dominus, qui prohibeat illas à vobis. Nam eritis illis liberi & expositi. Hic Lxx. habent εἰς θάνατον. Sic Apoc. vi. 8. καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἵππος χλωρὸς καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, ὄνομα αὐτῷ ὁ θάνατος. Ubi vide Cl. Drusii praeterita. Sic Apoc. 2. 23. interficiam eam θανάτῳ. Atque ita non erit pleonasmus. Causam hujus interpretationis hanc affert Fullerus Miscell. 1. 7. quod Lxx. Interpretes sua interpretamenta saepe de industria ad vocum Syriacarum notionem inflexerint. Seu, quod idem fore puto, quod in versione sua saepe expresserint propriam significationem vocis Chaldaeae vel Syrae, quae Ebraeae erat synonyma. Ita certe & Chaldaeus & Syrus Ebraeum, דָּבָר reddere solent מוּתָא & מוּתָנָא id est, θάνατον. Ad quorum exemplum Galliquoque pestem vocare solent mortalitè. Notatque Fagius ad paraphrasin Chald. Lev. 26. 25. in quibusdam Germaniae partibus pestilentiam quoque vocari mortem.
units.tr: Verse 36. He shall be delivered into the hand of the King of Babylon, by the sword, by famine and by destruction [ἐν μαχαίρᾳ, καὶ ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ]. The Hebrew: by the sword, by famine and by pestilence [בְּחֶרֶב וּבְרָעָב וּבַדֶּבֶר]. You see that apōleia [ἀπωλείᾳ] corresponds to the Hebrew deber [דֶּבֶר], pestilence [λοιμός]. The Seventy rendered the Hebrew word once as apōleian [ἀπώλειαν], three times as loimos [λοιμὸς], and in the remaining places, which are quite many, as thanatos [θάνατος]. Let us look first at apōleia. No one is ignorant of what that word properly and commonly means. Here it seems to denote pestilence, because it is sent by God and, as it were, dispatched from him. Hence in Ps. 78:49, where the Hebrew has mishlachat [מִשְׁלַחַת], a sending, the same translators rendered it apōleian, understanding pestilence: he sent upon them the fury of his anger, wrath and indignation and trouble, an apōleia by evil angels [ἐξαπέστειλεν εἰς αὐτὸς ὀργὴν θυμῶ αὐτῆς, θυμὸν καὶ ὀργὴν καὶ θλίψιν, ἀπωλείαν δι' ἀγγέλων πονηρῶν]. Where the Roman Latin has a sending in. In the same sense Baruch 2:25 used the word: and they died in evil plagues, in famine and in the sword, and in destruction [καὶ ἀπεθάνοσαν ἐν τόνοις πονηροῖς, ἐν λιμῷ καὶ ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ, καὶ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ]. Where the Roman Latin has sending out. Perhaps this is because Theodoret noted here that aichmalōsia [τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν] is put for captivity. But in fact here aichmalōsia corresponds to the Hebrew deber. As for the other rendering, thanatos, let us take, for example, the passage from ch. 34:17. There God is indignant with the Jews because, after proclaiming liberty during the siege, they revoked it once it was relaxed, and suddenly reasserted slavery over the servants whom they had called to freedom according to the prescription of the Law. Therefore the Lord says: You did not listen to me in proclaiming liberty each to his brother; behold, I proclaim against you liberty, by sword, pestilence and famine. That is: because you do not proclaim liberty in earnest, but mock me and the slaves, drawing them back into servitude and lording it over them, I will proclaim a liberty, not one by which you are freed from servitude and punishments, but one by which the sword, pestilence and famine will be free to rage against you, and you will seem to be let loose from my care and providence as though manumitted. Kimchi: all these plagues will rule over you. There will be no lord to keep them away from you, for you will be free and exposed to them. Here the Seventy have eis thanaton [εἰς θάνατον]. So also Apoc. 6:8: and I saw, and behold a pale horse, and the name of him who sat upon it was Death [καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἵππος χλωρὸς καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, ὄνομα αὐτῷ ὁ θάνατος]. See there the remarks of the learned Drusius. So also Apoc. 2:23: I will kill her with death [θανάτῳ]. And thus there is no pleonasm. The cause of this rendering Fuller gives in his Miscellanies 1.7: the Seventy translators often deliberately bent their renderings toward the meaning of Syriac words; or, which I think amounts to the same thing, they often expressed in their version the proper meaning of the Chaldee or Syriac word, which was synonymous with the Hebrew. Certainly both the Chaldee and the Syriac usually render the Hebrew deber [דָּבָר] by mutha [מוּתָא] and mutana [מוּתָנָא], that is, thanatos [θάνατον]. Following their example, the French too usually call the plague mortalité. And Fagius, on the Chaldee paraphrase of Lev. 26:25, notes that in some parts of Germany the pestilence is also called death.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXIII.

units.la: Verf. 16. Et hoc nomen quod vocabunt *eum, DOMINUS justus noster] Ita Vulg. & Lutherus qui ad Messiam haec referunt, ut supra xxiii. Sed in Ebraeo magnam differitatem hic facit I. omissa vox שְׁמוֹ nomen ejus. 2. affixum foemininum. Ubi enim supra erat, Et hoc est nomen ejus quo יִקְרָאוֹ vocabit Eum: hic est, הָהּ אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא לה & hic qui vocabit EAM, vid. Jerusalem, Sionem, Ecclesiam. Varie afferuntur hujus loci expositiones, quas obiter libabo, Simpliciores mihi videntur duæ priores 1. Et hic qui vocabit eam [erit] DOMINVS justitia nostra. Qui vocabit eam ad promissam hanc salutem prædicatione Evangelii, קרא, etiam id significat, quod nos dicimus beroepen. Ende die haer beroepen sal / sal de HEERE onse gherechtigheyt zijn. Hæc est interpretatio Junii, quam amplexus & Helwicus est. Vide apud Glassium in Philologia S. p. 135. II. Et hoc est quod prædicabitur ei (vel, in ea) Dominus justitia nostra. Sensus, verba Glassii, prædicationis Evangelicæ in novo fœdere hoc erit primarium argumentum, gratuitum reconciliationis nostræ & remissionis peccatorum per Jehovam justitiam nostram seu Messiam acquirendæ beneficium. In qua interpretatione rursus duo observanda sunt, licet sæpius à nobis inculcata, I. activa sæpe pro passivis poni vel per ellipsin commodi alicujus nominativi exponenda esse, 2. ל aliquando & pro ב poni, ut Ps. 16. לִשְׁאוֹל Quod si vero alicui plane sedeat nomen שֵׁם hic supplere, videndum ei an non hoc modo simplicissime verti possint Ebræa, Et hoc [erit nomen] quo vocabit eam [unusquisque] DOMINI justitia nostra [urbs.] Ut plenum sit עִיר צִדְקֵנִי. Ellipsis enim illa prioris nominis usitatissima est in Ebraismo. Vide Synt. nostram Cap. 1. Sic Exod. xvii. יְהוָה נִסִּי [altare] DOMINI vexilli mei. Sic Act. 2. εἰς ἀδὲ, sub. οἶκον. Sic ad Veneris, ad Minervæ. Sed prima interpretatio simplicissima.
units.tr: Verse 16. And this is the name by which they will call him: THE LORD our righteousness. So the Vulgate and Luther, who refer these words to the Messiah, as above at chapter 23. But the Hebrew makes a great difference here: first, the word שְׁמוֹ [shemô], his name, is omitted; second, the feminine suffix is attached. For where above it was And this is his name by which יִקְרָאוֹ [yiqraʾô] they will call him, here it is and this one who will call her (הָהּ אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא לה), namely Jerusalem, Zion, the Church. Several explanations of this passage are offered, which I will touch on in passing. The two earlier ones seem to me the simplest. 1. And he who will call her [shall be] THE LORD our righteousness. He who will call her to this promised salvation by the preaching of the Gospel: קרא [qārāʾ] also means what we call beroepen (to call). Dutch: And whoever shall call her, the LORD shall be our righteousness. This is the interpretation of Junius, which Helwicus also embraced. See Glassius, Philologia Sacra, p. 135. 2. And this is what shall be preached to him (or, in her), the Lord our righteousness. The sense, in Glassius's words, is: the primary subject of Evangelical preaching in the new covenant will be the free benefit of our reconciliation and the remission of sins, to be obtained through Jehovah, our righteousness, that is, the Messiah. In this interpretation two points must again be observed, although we have often insisted on them: first, active forms are often put for passives, or must be explained by supplying some dative of advantage as subject; second, ל [l] is sometimes put for ב [b], as in Ps. 16, לִשְׁאוֹל [lišʾôl, for Sheol]. But if anyone is quite determined to supply the noun שֵׁם [shem, name] here, let him consider whether the Hebrew cannot be rendered most simply in this way: And this [will be the name] by which each one will call her [the city] THE LORD our righteousness, so that the full phrase reads עִיר צִדְקֵנִי [ʿîr ṣidqēnî, city of our righteousness]. For this ellipsis of the first noun is very common in Hebrew idiom. See our Syntax, chapter 1. So in Exodus 17, יְהוָה נִסִּי [YHWH nissî, the LORD my banner], the word altar is understood, the altar of the LORD my banner. So in Acts 2, εἰς ᾅδου [eis hāidou, to Hades], with house supplied; so to Venus's and to Minerva's (temple). But the first interpretation is the simplest.

units.la: CAP. XXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: Vers. 5. Et secundum combustiones patrum tuorum, regum priorum qui fuerunt ante te, sic comburent te] Ita Vulg. & Lutherrus quasi scriptum esset in Ebr. כֵּן יִשְׂרְפוּ אוֹתָךְ Sicuti 1. Sam. ultimo vers. penultimo, de combustione Saulis & filiorum, וַיִּשְׂרְפוּ אוֹתָם שָׁם & combusserunt eos illic. Apud Romanos & Græcos frequentata fuit cadaverum crematio. Consuetudinem illam istos ab his, hos ab Hercule accepisse vetus in Homerum Scholiastes ad Iliados A. prodidit. Apud Romanos tamen non omnes cremavere. Servatus enim in multis familiis mos priscus fuit adeoque ante Syl- lam in gente Cornelia nullus crematus fuit. Plin. vii. 54. Ipsum cremare apud Romanos non fuit veteris instituti. Terra condebantur.
units.tr: Verse 5. And according to the burnings of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so shall they burn you] So the Vulgate and Luther, as if it had been written in Hebrew [כֵּן יִשְׂרְפוּ אוֹתָךְ], just as in the penultimate verse of the last chapter of 1 Samuel, concerning the burning of Saul and his sons: "and they burned them there" [וַיִּשְׂרְפוּ אוֹתָם שָׁם] and they burned them there. Among the Romans and Greeks the cremation of corpses was common. The ancient scholiast on Homer's Iliad A reported that the one people had received this custom from the other, and that the other had received it from Hercules. Among the Romans, however, not everyone cremated. In many families the old custom was kept; indeed, before Sulla no one of the Cornelian clan was cremated. Pliny, book 7, chapter 54: cremating the dead was not an ancient institution among the Romans; they were buried in the ground.

units.la: At postquam longinquis bellis obrutos erui cognovere, tunc institutum. Et tamen multæ familiæ priscos servavere ritus, sicuti in Cornelia nemo ante Syllam Dictato rem traditur crematus, idque voluisse veritum talionem effosso C. Marii cadavere. Postea omitti omnino cœpit crematio. Macrob. de suo ævo testatur, lib. 7. 7. Licet urendi corpora defunctorum usus nostro seculo nullus sit. Et Græci quoque barbari & crudelis istius moris tandem pertæsi, sepulturam præmaluere. Quib. de rebus ut & aliis erudite Cl. Meursius in eruditissimo tractatu de Funere. In Sacra historia unius Sauli & filiorum ejus cadavera cremata legimus, idque eadem fere ex causa, qua suam Sylla cadaver crematum voluit, Male habita illa a Philisthæis fuerant. Itaq; incolæ Jabes Gilead nocte quadam excurrunt, Philisthæis ea eripiunt & ne denuo ab iisdem effossa male tractarentur flammis absumsere. Qui contra pertendunt in populo Dei cremationem, subinde quoq; in usu fuisse, hoc quoq; loco abutuntur. Sed jam monuimus phrasin, quas S. pS. utitur, diversam esse ab ea 2 Sam. 31. Ita n. hic loquitur Propheta, Secundum combustiones Patrum tuorum ita comburent & tibi, id est, in honorem tuum, vel, supra te. Cl. Schikkardus in doctissimo suo commentario de jure Regio multis testimoniis probat in funeribus Regum multa utensilia ex supellectile ejus cremata fuisse. Malmon. in tractatu Malachim cap. 2. §. 1. nonutuntur ulla supellectile ex omnibus utensilibus ejus quibus usus est. Et quando morior, comburuntur omnia ista coram eo. Sed obtinuerit hæc consuetudo sequiori ævo. In historia veteris novique fœderis nulla ejus puto extare vestigia. Ne recedamus ergo a ritu ustulandi odoramenta, de quo prolixe idem Schikkardus. Sed videamus primo loca scripturæ 2. Chr. XVI. vers. ult. Et collocarunt eum (Asam) in cubili, quod impleverat aromaticis speciebus paratis unguentario opere: & combusserunt ei, vel, super eo (NB. non dicit eum) combustionem magnam valde. Junius, combusserunt ei ustionem [odorum] perquam maximam. Vulg. Et * combusserunt super eum ambitione maxima. Belg. Lovan. Ende sp heb-ben die Specerpen op hem verbrant met grooter heerlijck-heyt. Mallem over hem / hoc est, in honorem ejus, quomodo dicimus Belgice babitam orationem super aliquo. Itaque Luth. melius, Ende sp maeckten een groot bernen over hem. 2. Chr. XXI. de Joram, Et non fecit ei populus ejus combustionem secundum com-
units.tr: But after they learned that men overwhelmed in distant wars were dug up, cremation became the custom. Yet many families kept the old rites. Thus in the Cornelian clan no one before Sulla is recorded as cremated, and it is said that he wished this to be done because he feared retaliation, since the body of C. Marius had been dug up. Afterwards cremation began to be dropped altogether. Macrobius testifies from his own age, book 7, chapter 7: although the burning of the bodies of the dead is no practice in our century. The Greeks too, at last weary of that cruel custom of the barbarians, preferred burial. On these matters, and others, the learned Meursius has written learnedly in his very learned treatise On Funerals. In sacred history we read that only the corpses of Saul and his sons were burned, and for nearly the same reason for which Sulla wished his own corpse to be burned: they had been abused by the Philistines. So the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead ran out one night, snatched them from the Philistines, and, lest they be dug up again and mistreated, consumed them with flames. Those who contend that cremation was also in use among the people of God from time to time abuse this passage too. But we have already noted that the phrase which the Chronicler uses differs from that in 2 Samuel 31. For here the prophet speaks thus: According to the burnings of your fathers so shall they burn for you too, that is, in your honour, or over you. The learned Schickard, in his very learned commentary On the Royal Law, proves by many testimonies that at the funerals of kings many utensils from their household were burned. Maimonides, in the tractate Kings, chapter 2, §1: they do not use any of the household goods of all those things which he used. And when he dies, all these things are burned before him. But this custom prevailed in a later age; I think no traces of it are to be found in the history of the Old and New Covenant. Let us not depart, then, from the rite of burning fragrant spices, on which Schickard also writes at length. Let us first look at the passages of Scripture, 2 Chronicles 16, last verse: And they laid him (Asa) in a bed which they had filled with aromatic spices prepared by the work of the perfumer, and they burned for him, or over him (note: it does not say him) a very great burning. Junius: they burned for him a most exceeding great burning [of odours]. The Vulgate: and they burned over him with the greatest pomp. The Louvain Dutch: "And they burned the spices on him with great glory." I would prefer "over him", that is, in his honour, as we say in Dutch of a speech held over someone. Luther is better: "And they made a great burning over him." 2 Chronicles 21, of Joram: And his people did not make a burning for him according to the com-

units.la: sc. ista aroma bustionem patrum ejus. Lutherus, ende fo machten gheen bernen ouer hem. Rursus Junius, combustionem [odorum.] Ex quorum collatione Junius hunc Jeremiae locum sic convertit, si locorum collatione Junius hunc Jeremiae locum sic convertit, militer [ustiones odorum] comburent [populares tui] tibi. Genev. on fera militer [ustiones odorum] comburent [populares tui] tibi. Genev. on fera bruster sur toi [des choses aromatiques] Comme on a brusle sur tes peres Ie brusler sur toi [des choses aromatiques] Comme on a brulle sur tes peres & Angli & Deodatus. Pisc. Und wie Man uber deine Vatter ge- bremet hat / so wirt Man auch uber dich bremen. Apud Romanos in ambitiosis funeribus & exequiis quae μὴ πομπῆς φαντασίας peragebantur, una cum ipsis cadaveribus magna aromatum vis flammis absumpta fuit sicuti in funere Neronis. Qui in funere quoque suae Poppeae plus cinnamomi & casiae combustisse dicitur quam universa Arabia uno anno ferret Plin. 12. 18. Sed apud Ebraeos intactis corporibus haec aromatum ustulatio peracta fuit: Exemplum hujusmodi quoque sepulturae memoriae prodidit Josephus, Antiq. 17. 10, & de Bello Jud. 1. ultimo, ubi de funere Herodis, τῶτοις ἐπειτ- το πεντακόσιοι τῶν οἰκετῶν ἀρωματοφόροι id est, hos sequebantur D. ministri aromata ferentes. Et plenius de eodem Josippus, tur D. ministri aromata ferentes. Quinquaginta ministri ad latus feretri gestabant totidem aureathu- ribula, lignum odoriferum ustulantes maxima copia & myrrham purissimam continue in lectum injicientes, sic enim habent Ebraei nus Gamalielis, in quo Oncelos proselytus discipulus ejus septuaginta libras thuris ustulasse dicitur. Sed errorem hunc jam pridem detexit Cl. Schikkardus, producto ipso Thalmudis loco ex Masecheth Abodah Zara pag. xi. fac. 1. Quomodo cremant super Reges, ita & propter Synedrii principes Quid autem cremant? le- propter Synedrii principes. Accidit, cum moreretur Rabban Gamaliel senex super eum, vel propter eum septuaginta Minas Tyrias. Notat autem Scholiastes loqui Magistros de argenteo valore utensilium combustorum, minam Tyriam continere xxv. Sela & quodlibet id est Sela, continere 4. denarios. Utensilia ergo combusta aestimata fuisse 70. minis id est septem millibus denariorum. Exstimat autem idem Schikkardus vulgatum errorem natales suos debere imperitae manui, quae versione quadam hujus Latino pro Tyriis scripserit Thuris. Atqui illud Ebraeis לבנה dicitur Claudam, ubi illud addidero, valde me dubitare annon tempore magnae pestilentiae inter Israelitas cremata fuerint corpora, idque ob lo-
units.tr: i.e. those aromatic things [sc. ista aroma] burning, according to the burnings of his fathers. Luther: "and they made no burning over him." Again Junius: "a burning [of spices]." From the comparison of these, Junius renders this passage of Jeremiah thus: "your people shall burn spices for you as they burned for your fathers" [si locorum collatione Junius hunc Jeremiae locum sic convertit, militer [ustiones odorum] comburent [populares tui] tibi.]. Geneva: "on te brûlera des choses aromatiques comme on a brûlé sur tes pères." The English and Deodatus likewise. Piscator: "Und wie man über deine Vätter gebrennet hat, so wirt man auch über dich brennen." Among the Romans, at ambitious funerals and obsequies which were carried out with show and display [μὴ πομπῆς φαντασίας], a great quantity of spices was consumed by the flames together with the corpses themselves, as at the funeral of Nero. At the funeral of his Poppaea too he is said to have burned more cinnamon and cassia than all Arabia would produce in one year (Pliny 12.18). But among the Hebrews, this burning of spices was performed while the bodies were left untouched. Josephus also recorded an example of this kind of burial (Antiquities 17.10, and The Jewish War 1, last chapter), where, concerning Herod's funeral, he writes: "[τῶτοις ἐπειτ- το πεντακόσιοι τῶν οἰκετῶν ἀρωματοφόροι]", that is, "after them followed five hundred of his servants carrying spices" [D. ministri aromata ferentes]. Josephus treats the same matter more fully: "Fifty servants carried, at the side of the bier, as many golden censers, burning a great quantity of fragrant wood and continually putting the purest myrrh upon the couch." For so the Hebrews have it in the tractate of Rabban Gamaliel, in which Onkelos, a proselyte and his disciple, is said to have burned seventy pounds of incense. But this error was long ago exposed by the learned Schickard, who produced the very passage of the Talmud from Masechet Avodah Zarah, page 11, column 1: "As they burn over kings, so they also burn for the princes of the Sanhedrin." But what do they burn? The commentary says: when old Rabban Gamaliel died, they burned over him, or for him, seventy Tyrian minas. The scholiast notes that the masters are speaking of the silver value of the utensils burned, a Tyrian mina containing twenty-five sela, and each sela four denarii. So the utensils burned were valued at seventy minas, that is, seven thousand denarii. Schickard also thinks that the common error owes its origin to an unskilled hand which, in some Latin version of this passage, wrote Thuris [of incense] for Tyriis [of Tyre]. Yet the Hebrews call that [לבנה]. Where I add this, I very much doubt whether in the time of a great plague among the Israelites the bodies were not burned, and for this reason

units.la: In Romana Editione versum 5. Ita versum reperies, [Greek: εἰ εἰρήνη ... ] [Greek: καὶ ὡς ἐκλαυσαν τὰς πατέρας σε, τὰς βασιλευσαντας ... ] id est in pace morieris. Et sicuti defleverunt patres tuos, qui regnarunt ante te, ita & deflebunt te, væ Domine, & usque ad inferos plangent te. Hæc multum recedunt ab Ebræo. Complutensis Editio, ἐκλαυσαν, κλαύσονται. Id est, Combuserunt, comburent. Utram lectionem dicemus esse τῶν LXX. an eam, quam Romana expressit? Ut legerunt daleth pro Resch, & literis transpositis [Hebrew] & [Hebrew] / An potius Complutensem, quam imperiti librarii corruperint unius literæ insertione? Certe mihi si dicenda esset sententia, secundum Complutensem & hic & infinitis aliis in locis pronunciarem. Si pro Romana Edit. multis in locis est Hieronymus, pro Complutensi erit Theodoretus, quod vel ex solius Nobilii notis in Prophetas colligas. Unde veroillud ἐως ἀδε, dices? Aude Nobilium, Pro [Greek] etiam ad marginem Vaticani est ὡ νύξε. In Ebr. ὦ ἀδῶν. Ac verisimile est, quod alii interpretes dixerunt [Greek], aut ὦ νύξε, aliquem aut fortassis ipsos quoque LXX. dixisse, ὦ ἀδῶν χόψονται σε. Quod cum minus intelligeretur, factum sit, ἐως ἀδε. Quod tamen in Hebræo, Complut. (addo ego & Vulgata) non extat.
units.tr: In the Roman edition you will find verse 5 as follows: [Greek: "if in peace..."] and [Greek: "and as they wept for your fathers, the kings who reigned before you..."], that is, "you shall die in peace. And as they lamented your fathers, who reigned before you, so they shall lament you, alas Lord, and mourn you even unto the grave." These differ greatly from the Hebrew. The Complutensian edition has they wept, they will weep, that is, "they burned, they will burn." Which reading shall we say belongs to the Seventy, the one the Roman edition expresses or the Complutensian? Did they read daleth for resh and transpose letters, as in the Hebrew? Or is the Complutensian reading rather the true one, corrupted by an ignorant scribe through the insertion of a single letter? If I were to state my opinion, I would pronounce for the Complutensian here and in countless other places. Where the Roman edition follows Jerome, the Complutensian will follow Theodoret, as you may gather from Nobilius's notes on the Prophets alone. But whence, you will ask, comes that [Greek: "until Hades"]? Dare to consult Nobilius. In the margin of the Vatican codex there is also [Greek: "O he struck"]. In the Hebrew it is "O Hades". It is likely that other translators rendered [Greek] or [Greek: "O he struck"], or perhaps the Seventy themselves wrote "O Hades, they will lament you". When this was less understood, it became [Greek: "until Hades"]. This, however, is not found in the Hebrew, nor in the Complutensian (and I add also the Vulgate).

units.la: Verf. 18. Regium quoque locum indignis modis mutilatum invenies in Edit. Romana. Quanto vero proprius ad Ebræa accedat Complutensis, liquebit ex hac collatione.
units.tr: In verse 18 you will also find the passage about the covenant mutilated in unworthy ways in the Roman edition. How much closer to the Hebrew the Complutensian comes will be clear from this comparison.

units.la: Vides quanto proprius ad textum Ebr. accedat Complut. quam Romana editio. Theodoretus versum 19. plenius adhuc expressit — καὶ πάντα τὸν λαὸν τῆς γῆς, οἱ διήλθον ἐν μέσῳ τῶν μερῶν τῶ μόχῳ. Hic locus docet nos per-vetustum ritum in fœderib. sanciendis usitatum. Adhibita illis firmandis fuisse juramenta, sacrificia matatasque victimas ex infinitis Scripturæ locis, ipsaque adeo phrasi בְּרִית כָּרַת (quæ synonyma Latinis illis, Icere, ferire, percutere fœdus) constat; Adhæc, cæsa animalia in duas partes secta fuisse ex Gen. xv. edocemur. At transivisse fœderatos inter partes victimæ dissertas, quæ Theodoretus διχοτομήματα vocat, an ex alio loco quam hoc ipso erui possit, valde ambigo. Videntur autem hoc pecudum, exterminio sectione & inter partes transitu eadem fata sibiipsis imprecati fuisse, si primi leges fœderis violarent. Qui ritus ad Gentiles quoque dimanarunt. Id quod ex Homero, Virgilio, Livio & aliis authoribus constat. In Ebræo turbat aliquantulum vocula הָעֵגֶל / quam Junius transponit, Piscator reddit suppleta ellipsi præpositionis ב / — quod pepigerunt coram me vitulo, durch das kalb, בְּעֵגֶל quem secuerunt &c. Ego secutus sum Lutherum, qui notam similitudinis subaudit. Qua supplectione in viam quoque aliquo usque reduxeris & Vulgatum & Romanam Edit. Verba vulgati Interpretis ista sunt, Et dabo viros qui prævaricantur fœdus meum, & non observaverunt verba fœderis, quibus assensi sunt in conspectu meo: vitulum quem conciderunt in duas partes &c. Quis sensus? Nullus certe, nisi subaudias similitudinis notam, sicut vitulum. Dabo ipsos hostibus exscindendos & gladiis disseccandos, sicuti illi vitulum excidere & disseccuere. Si repugnas, monstra mihi verbum, à quo hic accusativus vus regatur. Quamvis fateor hac quoque ratione restitui posse locum, si legas, vitulam quum conciderunt, quum, pro, quando: Sed Editio correcta Sixti v. & Clementis viii. constanter quem legunt. Romanam vero Edit. quod attinet, repraesentabo tibi versionem Nobilii, quae Latina Romana vulgo dicitur, Dabo viros qui transgressi sunt testamentum meum, qui non stabilierunt testamentum meum, quod fecerunt ad faciem meam, vitulum quem fecerunt ad operandum eo. Quis hinc commodum aliquem sensum exsculpserit? Nullus certe, nisi ante μάχαιρα, vitulum, τὸ ώσεί, sicut suppleverit. Hoc ergo vult, Dabo illos qui violarunt foedus meum, (διαθήκη enim apud Hellenistas pro συνθήκην ponitur) tanquam vitulum istum, quem fecerunt in diserto, ut tolerent eum. ἐργάζεσθαι enim apud Hellenistas saepe idem esse quod ἐργάζεσθαι, utrumque vero interpretamentum עֲשׂוֹת esse supra ad cap. xxv. ostendimus. Unde melius phrasin istam conversam puto in Edit. Basileensi, ad operandum ei, quam in Edit. Romana, ad operandum eo. Sensum, inquam, nunc aliquem habes, sed neutiquam illum, quem divinus Vates intendit.
units.tr: You see how much closer the Complutensian comes to the Hebrew text than the Roman edition does. Theodoret expressed verse 19 more fully still: [Greek: "and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf"]. This passage teaches us a very ancient rite used in making covenants. That oaths, sacrifices and slaughtered victims were employed to confirm them is clear from countless places of Scripture, and from the very phrase בְּרִית כָּרַת (which is synonymous with the Latin icere, ferire, percutere foedus, to strike a covenant). Moreover, we learn from Genesis 15 that the slaughtered animals were cut into two parts. But whether it can be drawn from any passage other than this one that the covenanting parties passed between the divided parts of the victim, which Theodoret calls [Greek: "divisions"], I very much doubt. It seems that by this cutting up of the beast and passing between its parts, they called down upon themselves the same fate if they violated the terms of the covenant. This rite also spread to the Gentiles, as is clear from Homer, Virgil, Livy and other authors. In the Hebrew, the little word הָעֵגֶל somewhat disturbs the sense. Junius transposes it; Piscator renders it by supplying an ellipsis of the preposition ב, so that it reads "which they made before me with the calf" (durch das Kalb), בְּעֵגֶל, "which they cut up," etc. I have followed Luther, who understands the particle of comparison. By this supplement you may also bring the Vulgate and the Roman edition somewhat back into line. The words of the Vulgate translator are these: "And I will give the men who transgress my covenant, and have not kept the words of the covenant which they agreed upon in my sight, the calf which they cut into two parts, etc." What sense is this? None at all, unless you understand the particle of likeness, as the calf. I will give them to enemies to be cut off and hewn apart by swords, just as they cut up and hewed the calf. If you object, show me the verb which governs this accusative here. Although I admit that the passage can also be restored in this way, if you read vitulam quum conciderunt, "when they cut up", for quando; but the edition corrected under Sixtus V and Clement VIII consistently reads quem. As for the Roman edition, I shall set before you the version of Nobilius, which is commonly called the Roman Latin: "I will give the men who transgressed my covenant, who did not establish my covenant, which they made before my face, the calf which they made to work with it." Who could carve out any reasonable sense from this? None at all, unless one supplies sicut (as) before vitulum, the calf. So the meaning is: "I will give those who violated my covenant (for diathēkē among the Hellenists stands for synthēkē), as that calf which they made openly, so that they may bear it." For among the Hellenists [Greek: "to work"] is often the same as [Greek: "to make"], and I have shown above on chapter 25 that each of these is an interpretation of עֲשׂוֹת. Hence I think this phrase is better rendered in the Basel edition as ad operandum ei (to work with it) than in the Roman edition as ad operandum eo. You now have a sense, I grant, but by no means the one the divine prophet intended.
