units.la: Vers. 5, Ecce ipse in manib. vestris est. Nec enim fas est regem vobis quicquam negare] Ita vulg. Lxx. mutata oratione, ἰδοὺ αὐτὸς ἐν χειρὶ ὑμῶν, ὅτι οὐκ ἐδυνάτο βασιλεὺς σὲ εἶς αὐτόν. Ebr. כִּי אֵין הַמֶּלֶךְ יוּכַל אַחֲכֶם דָּבָר / Turbat aliquantulum vocula אֵין / quae non solet cum futuris construi. Itaque non satis accurate vertitur, quia Rex non potest contra vos quicquam. Junius, minime [is est] Rex, [qui] possit contra vos quicquam. Genev. in margine, car [cestui-la] n' [est] pas roi. [qui] peut quelque chose par dessus vous. Angli, Rex non est is, qui possit quicquam contra vos. Vulgus interpretum hoc Regis responsum ita interpretatur, quasi Placentinus ille Rex Prophetam Jeremiam ipsis tradiderit, ne incurreret in malevolentiam principum, ut loquitur Lyra. In hoc peccavit mortaliter, inquit Carthus. quod virum innoxium tradiderit morti quamquam hoc egerit timore humano ne suos offenderet. Et verba sequentia, nec enim fas est Regem &c. sic inquit, hoc falsum fuit, quia contra justitiam nulli acquiescendum est, praesertim inferiori & subdito. Sed sciendum est, ut Reges Judae capitalia quaedam judicia per se exercuerint, tamen quaedam cognitionum genera & judicia, neutiquam ipsis ipermissa sed reservata Synedrio fuisse; inter illa erant judicia de tribu, שִׁבְטֵי כֹּל אוֹ רָבָּו quae vel tota vel magnam partem ad idololatriam defecit, item de pseudo-Propheta, de sacerdote magno Massecheth Sanhedrin, (quod eruditissimus & supra aetatem in literis Orientalibus & Graecis & Theolog. versatus juvenis D. Johannes Coccejus nobis Latine non ita pridem dedit, & accuratissimis notis illustravit) cap.1. §.1. אין דנין לא את השבט ולא את נביא השקר ולא את כהן גדול אלא בבית דין של שבעים ואחר bum vel pseudoProphetam vel sacerdotem magnum, nisi in domo judicii LXXI. id est, Synedrio magno; Hoc ergo vult Rex, Quandoquidem vos principes, qui estis membra Synedrii, contenditis hunc hominem esse seditiosum pseudo-prophetam, judicate eum. Neque enim ego in hoc negotiorum genere quicquam possum adversus vos.
units.tr: Verse 5, "Behold, he is in your hands; for the king is not able to do anything against you." The Vulgate and the Seventy change the wording: ἰδοὺ αὐτὸς ἐν χειρὶ ὑμῶν, ὅτι οὐκ ἐδυνάτο βασιλεὺς σὲ εἶς αὐτόν ["Behold, he is in your hand, for the king could not [do anything] against you"]. The Hebrew reads כִּי אֵין הַמֶּלֶךְ יוּכַל אַחֲכֶם דָּבָר ["for the king cannot do anything against you"], where the particle אֵין disturbs the sense somewhat, since it is not usually construed with futures. So the rendering is not quite accurate: "because the king cannot do anything against you." Junius has: "by no means is he the king who could do anything against you." The Geneva margin has: "for that one is not king who can do anything above you." The English: "the king is not he who could do anything against you." The common run of interpreters explain this answer of the king as if that Placentine king had handed Jeremiah over to his enemies so as not to incur the ill will of the princes, as Lyra puts it. The Carthusian says: "In this he sinned mortally, in that he delivered an innocent man to death, although he did it out of human fear, lest he offend his own people." And the following words, "for it is not right for the king," etc., he says were false, because one must never give way to what is against justice, especially to a lower person and a subject. But it must be known that although the kings of Judah carried out certain capital judgments themselves, certain kinds of cognizance and judgment were by no means permitted to them but were reserved to the Sanhedrin. Among these were judgments concerning a tribe שִׁבְטֵי כֹּל אוֹ רָבָּו [a whole tribe or a great part of one], which had fallen wholly or for the most part into idolatry; likewise judgments concerning a false prophet, and concerning the high priest. (Massecheth Sanhedrin, which the most learned young man Johannes Coccejus, versed in Oriental, Greek and theological literature beyond his years, lately gave us in Latin and illustrated with most careful notes, ch. 1, §1.) The text reads: "Neither a tribe, nor a false prophet, nor the high priest is judged except in the domo judicii LXXI." [לא את השבט ולא את נביא השקר ולא את כהן גדול אלא בבית דין של שבעים ואחד], that is, in the great Sanhedrin of seventy-one. The king therefore means: "Since you princes, who are members of the Sanhedrin, contend that this man is a seditious false prophet, judge him yourselves. For in this kind of business I can do nothing against you."

units.la: CAP. XLVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVIII.

units.la: Verf. 10. Maledictus qui facit opus Domini [מרמיה] Ellipsis constituentis cum nomine abstracto periphrasin adverbii, quia vero vox Ebraea & fraudem & pigritiam significat, hinc alii vertunt, fraudulenter, alii negligenter, pigre. Haec sententia vulgo citari solet in genere adversus eos, qui vocationes suas & officia demandata negligenter obeunt. Sed, si a principio hoc caput legeris & sequentia adjeceris, videbis esse tantum incentivum quo Deus Chaldaeos, Moabitarum hostes excitat, Maledictus qui opus Domini (opus exterminationis Moabitarum) fecerit fraudulenter, vel indiligenter, & gladium cohibuerit a sanguine. Interim tamen nihil obstabit, inquit Francius oraculo 47. quo nimus speciale dictum istud generaliter usurpetur, modo illud fiat cum tali annotatiuncula; Quod Jeremias dicit de illis, quibus exterminatio Moabitarum divinitus erat commissa, Maledictus sit qui opus DOMINI fecerit fraudulenter, Id ego Concionator dico Magistratui, Maledictus qui opus Domini [in defendendis piis & puniendis impiis] negligenter facit. Item, illud ipsum ego Concionator dico singulis patribus familias, quibus Deus Commisit Oeconomiam, libros educandos & alia opera. Usus hujus annotationis est, ne suspectas habeat auditor omnes tuas allegationes, si viderit te, prorsus contextuum coherentia neglecta, tam promiscuum esse in citandis divinis oraculis. Et habet eandem consuetudinem Sacra Scriptura sibi ipsi familiarem. Haec Franzius. Dignus etiam est qui hic audiatur Theodoretus, Sijussu Dei, inquit, sermo Propheticus maledictioni subjicit eos, qui negligenter occidunt, quantas nos poenas exolvemus, si munus spirituale parvipenderimus. Monstrat nobis B. Pater quomodo per argumentationem ab imparibus locus iste ad alia quoque transferri possit.
units.tr: Verse 10. "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD" [מרמיה]. The ellipsis of a constructed noun with an abstract noun gives an adverbial periphrasis. Since the Hebrew word means both fraud and sloth, some translate it fraudulently, others negligently, slackly. This sentence is commonly cited against those who carry out their callings and assigned duties carelessly. But if you read this chapter from the beginning and add what follows, you will see that it is only an incitement by which God stirs up the Chaldeans against the enemies of Moab: "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD (the work of destroying Moab) fraudulently", or carelessly, "and withholdeth his sword from blood." Nevertheless, says Francius in his oracle 47, nothing prevents this special saying from being used in a general sense, provided it is done with such a brief annotation: "What Jeremiah says of those to whom the destruction of Moab was divinely committed, 'Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD fraudulently', I the preacher say to the magistrate: 'Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD [in defending the godly and punishing the wicked] negligently.'" Likewise, I the preacher say the same to each head of a household, to whom God has committed the management of his household, the rearing of children and other tasks. The use of this annotation is that the hearer should not regard all your citations as suspect, if he sees you, with the coherence of the context wholly neglected, being so loose in citing divine oracles. Holy Scripture itself has the same habit, familiar to itself. Thus Francius. Theodoret also deserves to be heard here: "By the command of God, the prophetic word subjects to a curse those who kill negligently. What punishments shall we pay if we make light of a spiritual office?" The blessed Father shows us how, by an argument from unequals, this passage can be applied to other cases as well.

units.la: Verf. 12. Καὶ τὰ κέρατα αὐτοῦ συγκόψει. ] Et cornua ejus concident. Ita Lxx. Confringere alicujus cornua, phrasis in S. Literis frequens & trita est, pro, potentiam & robur alicujus subvertere. Videturque prima fronte sensus iste hic optime quadrare. Sed ubi originalem textum inspexeris & anteriora legeris, videbis continuare Prophetam Metaphoram vinariam. Verf. 11. tranquillus est Moab inde a pueritia sua (objicit ei Deus praesid entiam) & desidet super seces suas, neque trans-fusus est de vase in vas, & in captivitatem non ivit: propterea mansit sapor ejus in eo, odor ejus non est mutatus. 12. Idcirco ecce dies veniunt, dicit DOMINUS, cum immittam ei peregrinantes, qui peregre agant eum, & vasa ejus depleant (vel evacuent id est, oppida eorum) & lagenas eorum disipem. Non solum modo evacuabunt vasa id est, spoliabunt urbes & domos in quibus thesauri & opes, sed ipsa quoque vasa id est, aedes, urbesque perdent. Depopulabuntur urbes Moabitarum & incendent. Voci בקבוק cum cornu nihil est commune. Quid ergo fiet Graca versione? An Lxx. tam stupidi, ut pro lagenis cornua posuerint? Scire licet, veteres, ut & nos hodie, ex cornibus quoque bibisse. Unde κέρας quoque inter lagenas, pocula & vinaria vasa. Bibebant autem ex cornibus, quod crederent iis vim inesse ἀλεξιφάρμακον. Varians lectio, καὶ τὰ κεράσματα αὐτῆς συντρίψουσι. Et pocula ejus confringent. Origenes, τὰ κεράσματα ὡς ἐπ' οἴνῳ ῥηθέντα Αχύλας ἐξέδωκε, κέρασλα. ὅπερ ἀρχαῖον τὸ τὴν τομὴν ἐτύγχανεν εἰδος. Κέρασι γὰρ ἔλεγον, ὅθεν ἡ τὸ κεράσαι λέγειν παραμένει. Id est, Κεράσματα tanquam in vino dicta, Aquila edidit, κέρατα. Quod quidem antiquum poculi genus erat: Ex cornibus enim bibebant. Unde etiam mansit consuetudo dicendi κερᾶσαι, quasi scilicet e cornu miscere.
units.tr: Verse 12. And his horns shall be broken [Καὶ τὰ κέρατα αὐτοῦ συγκόψει]. The Seventy have: and his horns shall be broken. To break someone's horns is a phrase common and well worn in Holy Writ, meaning to overthrow someone's power and strength. At first sight this sense seems to fit very well here. But when you look at the original text and read what comes before, you will see that the Prophet continues a metaphor taken from wine: Verse 11. Moab has been at ease from his youth (God charges him with complacency), and has settled on his lees, and has not been poured from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into captivity; therefore his taste remains in him, and his smell is not changed. 12. Therefore behold, the days come, says the LORD, when I will send to him wanderers who will make him wander, and will empty his vessels (or pour them out, that is, their towns), and will break their flagons. They will not only empty the vessels, that is, plunder the cities and houses in which the treasures and riches are, but they will also destroy the vessels themselves, that is, the dwellings and cities. They will lay waste the cities of Moab and burn them. The word bakbuk has nothing in common with horn. What then happens in the Greek version? Are the Seventy so stupid as to have put horns for flagons? We know that the ancients, as we do today, also drank from horns; hence keras too was among the words for flagons, cups and wine vessels. They drank from horns because they believed that these had a power against poison [ἀλεξιφάρμακον]. There is a variant reading: καὶ τὰ κεράσματα αὐτῆς συντρίψουσι [and they will break her mixing-cups]. Cups of hers will be broken. Origen: Aquila published "kerasmata", as said of wine, as "kerasla", which was an ancient form of the cut. For they used to say "keras", from which the verb "kerasai" (to mix) remains. That is, Aquila published "kerasmata", as if spoken of wine, as "horns". This was indeed an ancient kind of cup, for they drank from horns. Hence the custom of saying "kerasai", as if to mix from a horn, has also remained.

units.la: Antequam transeam ad libros sequentes consideranda obiter nomina quaedam Ebraica, quae ab interpretib. retenta librariis Ebraeae linguae ignaris corrupta, interpretibus magnas molestias fafacessêre Cap. XL. 14. בַּעֲלִיס Baalis Rex filiorum Ammon misit Israelem ad percutiendum te. LXX. Βαλιαὰ Βασιλεὺς τῶν υἱῶν Ἀμ-μὰν &c. Alii Βαλιασὰ. Rom. Editio Βασιλεια. Complutensis, βασιλιοσα βασιλίως Regina regis Filiorum Ammon. CAP. XLI. 5. καὶ μάννα καὶ λίβανον ἐν χεροὶν αὐτῶν. Ebr. מִנְחָה וּלְבֹנָה / Lxx. scripserunt μαννα. Manna enim aliud est. Aquila solet reddere δῶρον, id est, munus, donum. Vocem illam corruptam μαν-να sæpius in Græcis Bibliis invenies. Vide & Jerem. XVII. & Baruch. I. 10. Ezech. XLV. 25. & XLVI. 5. in Rom. Edit. legitur μασσα, Quomodo ἀεχαϊκῶς lectum fuit, pro quo nunc מִנְחָה legi-mus. Hieron. ad cap. 17. Jerem. Pro sacrificio Lxx. ipsum verbum Ebraicum posuere μαναα, quod pessima consuetudine, imo scriptorum negligentia Manna in nostris libris legitur. Vers. 17. Et abierunt & sederunt ἐν χαξηφωχαμαα. Alii Codices, ἐν γυβηφωϑ χααμ. At Ebr. בִּגְרוֹת כִּמְהָם in Hospitio Cimhani. Scribendum ergo, si quis Ebræa retinere velit, ad antiquam confuetudinem, ἐν γηφϑ χαμαχὰμ. Cap. XLVI. 15. Lxx. Quare fugit a te Apis, vitulus electus tuus? At in Ebr. non memoratur Apis. Vers. 17. Καλέσατε τὸ ὄνομα Φαραὼ νηχαὼ Βασιλέως Αιγύπτυ, σαὼν τὸ ἑεὶς μωηδ. In Latina versione Theodoreti, Sao Neeshiemod. Scribendum erat σαὼν ἐἰεεἰς ἀμμωνδ, Ebræa קִרְאוּ שָׁם פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם שָׁאוֹן הָעֵיר הַמּוֹעֵר, Clamarunt illic, Pharao Rex Ægypti [rex] strepitus est, (id est, streperus) pratermisit constitutum tempus. q.d Pharao multa promittit, res magnas pollicendo strepit, sed justo tempore nihil efficit. Lxx. legerunt. קְרָאוּ שָׁם ut & Vulgata. Lovaniensis Belgica, Paemt Pharaos naem / gheruht hebet den tijdt aen-bzacht. Quis hæc intelligat? Lutherus quoque nimium sibi indulsit, aldaer schzeitnuen hen nae / Pharao-lept/ hp heeft sijn Tente verlaten. Melius Pisc. Pharao ist ein plauderer / er habt die bestimte zeit laassen fur uber gehen. Angli & Ge-nev. Pharao n' est que bruit, il a laissé passer le temps assigné. Non eduxit copias suas uti promiserat. Vox est, præterea nihil. CAP. XLVIII. 33. Ebræa ita habent, Vinum de lacubus cessare faciam. לֹא יִרְדְּ הַיֵּרֵד הַיָּרֵד לֹא הַיָּרֵד non calcabit [cum] celeusmate: celeusma non erit celeusma. Non calcabit calcator, vel, non calcabitur amplius. Audietur clamor, sed non celeusma, quale in vindemia audiri solebat. Κίλευσμα & κιλευσμὸς proprie est hortamentum nauticum, quo remiges ad remigandum incitabantur. Servius ad illud Virg. Aen 8 tacitu remis, ἀνὰ κελευσμα⟨τ⟩ω, inquit, nam celeusma est clamor nauticus ad hortandum, ut,
units.tr: Before I pass to the following books, I shall briefly consider some Hebrew names which the translators retained, but which copyists ignorant of the Hebrew language corrupted, and which caused the translators great trouble. Chapter XL. 14. בַּעֲלִיס [Baalis]: Baalis, king of the sons of Ammon, sent Ishmael to strike you. The Seventy: Βαλιαὰ βασιλεὺς τῶν υἱῶν Ἀμμὰν, etc. Others: Βαλιασά. The Roman edition has Βασιλεια. The Complutensian has βασιλιοσα βασιλίως, queen of the king of the sons of Ammon. Chapter XLI. 5: "and incense and frankincense in their hands": Hebrew מִנְחָה וּלְבֹנָה [minchah ulevonah]. The Seventy wrote manna, for manna is something else. Aquila usually renders it δῶρον, that is, a gift. You will often find that corrupted Greek word manna in the Greek Bibles. See also Jeremiah 17, Baruch 1:10, Ezekiel 45:25 and 46:5. In the Roman edition it is read massa [μασσα], which was read in the old manner, whereas we now read the Hebrew מִנְחָה. Jerome on Jeremiah 17: For sacrifice the Seventy put the Hebrew word itself, μαναα, which by bad custom, or rather the carelessness of scribes, is read as Manna in our books. Verse 17: "And they went and sat in Chamaam" [ἐν χαξηφωχαμαα]. Other manuscripts have ἐν γυβηφωϑ χααμ. The Hebrew has בִּגְרוֹת כִּמְהָם, "in the inn of Chimham". If one wishes to keep the Hebrew, the word should therefore be written, according to the old custom, ἐν γηφϑ χαμαχὰμ. Chapter XLVI. 15, Seventy: Why has Apis fled from you, your chosen calf? But Apis is not mentioned in the Hebrew. Verse 17: Καλέσατε τὸ ὄνομα Φαραὼ νηχαὼ Βασιλέως Αιγύπτυ, σαὼν τὸ ἑεὶς μωηδ. In Theodoret's Latin version: Sao Neeshiemod. It should have been σαὼν ἐἰεεἰς ἀμμωνδ, from the Hebrew קִרְאוּ שָׁם פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם שָׁאוֹן הָעֵיר הַמּוֹעֵד: they called there, Pharaoh king of Egypt is noise (that is, noisy); he has let pass the appointed time. That is, Pharaoh promises much and, by pledging great things, makes a din, but at the right time achieves nothing. The Seventy read קְרָאוּ שָׁם, as does the Vulgate. The Louvain Dutch has: Pharaoh's noise, he lets the time pass unused. Who can understand this? Luther also indulged himself too much: there he lets the time slip, Pharaoh's lot, he has left his tent. Better is the Piscator: Pharaoh is a chatterer; he has let the appointed time pass. The English and the Geneva: Pharaoh is nothing but noise; he has let the appointed time pass. He did not lead out his forces as he had promised. The word means only noise, nothing more. Chapter XLVIII. 33. The Hebrew reads: I will make the wine from the presses cease. לֹא יִרְדְּ הַיֵּרֵד הַיָּרֵד לֹא הַיָּרֵד: the treader shall not tread [with] the shout; the shout shall be no shout. The treader shall not tread, or, it shall no more be trodden. A cry shall be heard, but not the shout such as used to be heard at the vintage. Κίλευσμα and κιλευσμὸς properly means a nautical call by which rowers were urged on at their oars. Servius on Virgil, Aeneid 8, "silent with oars", ἀνὰ κελευσμα⟨τ⟩ω, says, for celeusma is the nautical shout for encouraging, as in:

units.la: -- Nunc nunc incumbite remis Hectorei socii.
units.tr: Now, now, bend to your oars, comrades of Hector.

units.la: At apud Vulg. interpretem, Junium & alios usurpatur pro voce clamantium & agitantium hilaria ex messe, & vindemia, ἐπιληνιον ἀσμα. LXX. οὐ͏̈ ἦν ἐπὶ ληνοῖς σου, πρωὶ ἀκ ἐπάτησαν, ἀδὲ δειλης ἀκ ἐποίησαν ἀιδέ, Vinum non erat in torcularib. tuis. Mane non calcarunt; & vespertini non fecerunt hade. Theodoretus legit, ἀδὲν neque vespere fecerunt quicquam. Complut, proprius Ebraeo ἀιδὲδ. CAP. xxv. 30. insignis allegoria est, qua Deus, Leoni: principes & Reges, Pastoribus: populus, gregi, regiones pascuis & caulis comparantur. DOMINVS ex alto rugiet, & ex habitatione sanctitatis sua edet vocem suam: rugiendo rugiet * in habitaculo suo, הירד כרוכים יעוה אל כל יושבי הארץ celeusma quale est calcantium efferet (sc. Deus) contra omnes habitatores terra. Non dubito quin LXX. scripserint, ἡ ἀιδὲδ ὥσπερ, τρυγῶντες ἐποικοδόμησαν. Cum vero librarii illud vocis non intelligerent, fecerunt ex eo, οἱδε, Hi vero, Et ut cetera convenirent ex ἐποικοδόμησαν fecerunt ἐποικοδόμησαν. Hi vero instar vindemiantium respondebunt Ita quod in originali de Deo praedicatur, illi ad incolas retulere.
units.tr: But in the Vulgate translator, Junius and others, it is used for the cry of those shouting and making merry at harvest and vintage, epilênion asma [ἐπιληνιον ἀσμα], the song of the winepress. The Seventy: οὐκ ἦν ἐπὶ ληνοῖς σου, πρωὶ οὐκ ἐπάτησαν, ἀδὲ δειλης οὐκ ἐποίησαν ἀιδέ: there was no wine in your presses; in the morning they did not tread, and in the evening they did not make the song. Theodoret reads ἀδὲν, they did not make anything at evening. The Complutensian is closer to the Hebrew, ἀιδὲδ. Chapter XXV. 30 is a remarkable allegory, in which God compares princes and kings to lions, ministers to shepherds, the people to the flock, and the regions to pastures and folds. The LORD shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall roar mightily upon his habitation, הירד כרוכים יעוה אל כל יושבי הארץ: the shout of treaders shall (that is, God shall) raise against all the inhabitants of the earth. I do not doubt that the Seventy wrote ἡ ἀιδὲδ ὥσπερ, as the vintagers, τρυγῶντες ἐποικοδόμησαν. But when the copyists did not understand the word, they made of it οἱδε, these, and to make the rest fit, they made ἐποικοδόμησαν out of ἐποικοδόμησαν. Thus, what is said of God in the original, like the vintagers, they applied to the inhabitants.

units.la: CAP. XLVIII. 34. עגלת שלישיה [quasi] vitula trima. LXX. voces Ebraeas retinuere, quas miris modis librarii deturparunt, Edit. Rom. ηγὴ ἀγγελίαν σαλαγία Complut. ἐγγελα σιλισία.
units.tr: Chapter XLVIII. 34. עגלת שלישיה [as if] a three-year-old heifer. The Seventy kept the Hebrew words, which the copyists mangled in strange ways: the Roman edition has ηγὴ ἀγγελίαν σαλαγία [ēgē angelian salagia], and the Complutensian has ἐγγελα σιλισία [engela silisia].

units.la: CAP. XLIX. 28. לקדר ולממלכות חצור אשר הכה נבוכדרב אצר id est, contra Kedar & regna Chatzor, quae percussit Nebucadnezar.
units.tr: Chapter XLIX. 28. לקדר ולממלכות חצור אשר הכה נבוכדרב אצר [le-Qedar u-le-mamlekhot Chatzor asher hikkah Nebukhadrezzar], that is, against Kedar and the kingdoms of Chatzor, which Nebuchadnezzar struck down.

units.la: LXX. τῇ Κηδαρ, * τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῆς αὐλῆς, ἥν ἐπάταξε Nabuchodonosor. Fositeritas Cedar, querat unus ex filiis Israel, inquit, καὶ τῇ βασιλείᾳ. Theodoretus, illo tempore reliquis tribubus, ut verisimile est, imperabat. Unde etiam illam appellavit Reginam Saracenorum. Erant namque pastores habitantes in tentoriis. Nugae quas non illevisset chartis doctissimus Pater, si Ebraea inspicere potuisset. LXX. videntur Icgisse לקדר ולמלכת הצר / CAP. L. 39. satius fuisset Ebraeas voces retinere, Ebraea, propterea habitabunt (in Babel) ציים & habitabunt in ea בנות יענה filia ululà. LXX. ἀπ' ἀπ'. κατοικήσουσιν ἰνδάλματα ἐν νησοῖς· ἡ κατοικήσουσιν ἐν αὐλαῖς θυ- χαλίρες σειρήνων. Ideo habitabunt phantasinata (simulacra, species) in insulis, & habitabunt in illa filia Sirenum. Nemo ergo putet in tex-tu canonico poëticas Sirenes memorari. Vulg. habitabunt illic dracones cum fatuis sicariis, & habitabunt illic struthiones. Fatuos sicarios Lyrainterpretatur faunos &satyros. Romani correctores, judice Luca Brugensi, hic acutum viderunt, Sustulerunt enim hic duo menda, legendumque censuere, faunos sicarios à ficu arbore, faunis, credo, ut alias Mercurio, amata verba Brugensis, in locis insigniorib. Romanæ correctionis S A tamen retinuit vulgatum sicariis, forte dæmones intelliguntur, inquit, in specie sicariorum apparentes. Magis miror, Belgicæ Lovaniensis recognitores, qui in præfationibus dicuntur eam ad postremam correctionem Romanam correxisse, locum hunc, sic expressisse, Daerom sullen de Draecken woren byde grouwelijcke Mooydenaers. An ergo sicarii sunt Mooydenaers? An hoc est corrigere versionem ad veritatem editionis vulgatæ in urbe nuper emendatæ & restitutæ? Ego hæc eo produxi, ut monerem tironem, ex eo quod in versionibus subinde occurrunt Fauni, Satyri, Sirenes, & id genus Poëtica monstra, non posse colligi, voces istas in Sacris literis (intelligo authenticas tabulas) extare.
units.tr: The Seventy read τῇ Κηδαρ, [to Kedar] τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῆς αὐλῆς, ἥν ἐπάταξε Nabuchodonosor [to the kingdom of the court, which Nebuchadnezzar struck down]. "Concerning Kedar, let one of the sons of Israel ask," he says, and "to the kingdom." Theodoret thinks that at that time the Kedarites, as is likely, ruled over the other tribes; that is why he also called them the queen of the Saracens, since they were shepherds living in tents. These are trifles which the most learned Father would not have put on paper if he had been able to read Hebrew. The Seventy seem to have read לקדר ולמלכת הצר. Chapter L. 39. It would have been better to keep the Hebrew words: the Hebrew has ציים [tziyyim] "therefore they will dwell (in Babylon)", and "they will dwell in her" בנות יענה [benot yaanah], "daughter of the ostrich". The Seventy have ἀπ' ἀπ'. κατοικήσουσιν ἰνδάλματα ἐν νησοῖς· ἡ κατοικήσουσιν ἐν αὐλαῖς θυχαλίρες σειρήνων [they will dwell as phantoms on the islands; or they will dwell in the courts, the howling of the sirens]. So: "therefore they will dwell as phantoms [simulacra, appearances] on the islands, and they will dwell in that daughter of the sirens." No one should therefore think that poetic sirens are mentioned in the canonical text. The Vulgate has: "there the dragons will dwell with foolish assassins, and there the ostriches will dwell." Lyra explains "foolish assassins" as fauns and satyrs. The Roman correctors, in the judgement of Lucas of Bruges, saw the problem here sharply: they removed two errors here and judged that it should be read "fauns, assassins" from the fig tree, from the fauns (I suppose, as elsewhere Mercury), a phrase beloved of Bruges. Yet in the more important places of the Roman correction the S.A. nevertheless kept the vulgar "assassins"; perhaps, he says, demons are meant, appearing in the form of assassins. I am more astonished that the Louvain revisers of the Dutch (Belgic) version, who in their prefaces are said to have corrected it according to the final Roman correction, have rendered this passage thus: "Therefore the dragons shall be among the dreadful murderers" (Daerom sullen de Draecken woren byde grouwelijcke Moordenaers). So are the assassins murderers? Or is this how one corrects a translation to the truth of an edition that was recently revised and restored in the city? I have gone into these matters in order to warn the beginner that, because poetic words such as fauns, satyrs, sirens and that kind of poetic monsters occur from time to time in the versions, it cannot be inferred that these words exist in the Sacred Letters (I mean the authentic tablets).

units.la: THRENI
units.tr: LAMENTATIONS

units.la: In ipso limine moneo, præloquium illud quod in Græcis Codicibus reperitur, non extare in Ebraeo, καὶ ἐγένετο μετὰ τὸ αἰχμα-λωτισθῆναι τὸν Ισραὴλ, καὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐρημωθῆναι, ἐκάθισεν Ἱερεμίας κλαίων, καὶ ἐθρήνησε τὸν θρῆνον τοῦτον ἐπὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ καὶ εἶπεν. Ac proinde urgeri non posse adversus illam Hieron. Josephi, Junii & aliorum sententiam, hunc librum continere illas lamentationes quas composuit Jeremias in obitum Regis Josiæ 2. Chron. xxxv, 25. ita tamen ut occasione necis Regis præsentes &. instantes calamitates defleverit. Sic dico, quæ post obitum Josiæ contigerunt, prævidit Propheta, & tanquam jam facta deflevit.
units.tr: At the very outset I note that the preface found in the Greek manuscripts is not found in the Hebrew: "And it came to pass, after Israel had been taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, that Jeremiah sat down weeping, and lamented this lament over Jerusalem, and said" [καὶ ἐγένετο μετὰ τὸ αἰχμαλωτισθῆναι τὸν Ισραὴλ, καὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐρημωθῆναι, ἐκάθισεν Ἱερεμίας κλαίων, καὶ ἐθρήνησε τὸν θρῆνον τοῦτον ἐπὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ καὶ εἶπεν]. For this reason the view of Jerome, Joseph, Junius and others cannot be pressed against this, namely that this book contains those lamentations which Jeremiah composed on the death of King Josiah (2 Chron. xxxv, 25), yet in such a way that, on the occasion of the king's death, he bewailed the calamities then present and pressing. I say this: the Prophet foresaw what would happen after Josiah's death, and lamented it as though it had already happened.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CAP. I.

units.la: Verf. 12. O vos omnes, qui transitis per viam, attendite & videte, si est dolor sicut dolor meus] Thomas in Summa, parte 3. qu. 46. art. 6. quaerit utrum dolor passionis Christi fuerit major omnibus doloribus. Postquam rationes aliquot produxit pro sententia negante, ita concludit, Sed contra est, quod Thren. 1. dicitur ex persona Christi, Attendite & videte, si est dolor sicut dolor meus. Solet etiam in picturis pontificiis Salvator patiens repraesentari, cum horum verborum adscriptione. Ex postillis Monachalibus locum istum a Ministris Evangelicis quoque saepe in eandem sententiam allegari solet. Quod de passione Christi asserunt verum est. Ad hunc locum eo trahere, asserere hoc versu Christum introduci, longe ineptissimum est. Unde nec Theod. nec Hieron. nec ex recentioribus Pintus, Sa & alii istius sensus hic meminere. Rectius a quibusdam accommodantur damnatis. Quamvis nec iste sensus primarius & literalis sit. Dico tamen, rectius. Quasi si quis versum istum tanquam sub ipsorum dictum exponere vellet, paucioribus incommodis premeretur. Ebraea non uno modo exponuntur, לא אליכם כל עוברי דרך Vulg. o vos omnes qui transitis per viam, לא plane otium agente. Eodem fere modo Luth. Vobis dico, qui transitis. Sunt qui putant esse verba deprecantium, Non ad vos qui pertransitis pertingit sc. hoc malum, quo ego obruor. Deus a vobis prohibeat hujusmodi calamitates. Alii, Ne sit vobis [grave] o qui transitis per viam illud vid. quod jam jam vobis injungam, aspicite & videte &c. Minus se mihi probant duae istae interpretationes, quia tunc potius adverbio אל dehortandi & deprecandi particula usus fuisset ὁ θεννωδές. Itaque simplicissimam ego illam censeo versionem Annon ad vos [pertinet meus status] o qui transitis &c. Ita Deod. Angli & Genev. q.d. An ergo nulla vos mei tangit commiseratio? Putatisne hanc meam calamitatem neutiquam ad vos pertinere? Annon cogitatis, idem fatum vos quoque aliquando posse excipere; Crebrum est interrogativi ellipsis. Et tritum est orationem pronunciatione juvare, Trahes Leviathan hamo? Et malum non accipiemus? Job. 2. In hanc sententiam exponi posset versio Graeca, si primam vocem ἀ in οὐ mutes, οὐ πάντες ὑμᾶς παρερχόμενοι ὁδὸν; Non ad vos [pertinet meus status] omnes qui transitis viam?
units.tr: Verse 12. O all you who pass by the way, attend and see, if there is sorrow like my sorrow. Thomas, in the Summa, part 3, question 46, article 6, asks whether the sorrow of Christ's passion was greater than all other sorrows. After setting out several arguments for the negative, he concludes: But on the contrary, it is said in Lam. 1, in the person of Christ, "Attend and see, if there is sorrow like my sorrow." Papist pictures also often show the suffering Saviour with these words written beneath. The Evangelical ministers too often cite this place in the same sense, following the Monastic postils. What they assert about the passion of Christ is true. But to draw this place there, and to claim that Christ is introduced speaking in this verse, is most absurd. Hence neither Theodoret nor Jerome, nor among more recent writers Pintus, Sa and others, mention this sense here. Some apply it more fittingly to the damned. Yet even that is not the primary and literal sense. I say, however, that it is more fitting: if someone wished to explain the verse as spoken by them, he would be troubled by fewer difficulties. The Hebrew is not expounded in one way. The Vulgate has "O all you who pass by the way,", where the particle lo is by no means idle. Luther, almost in the same way, has "I say to you who pass by." Some think these are the words of those who pray: "Let it not reach you who pass by," that is, let this evil with which I am overwhelmed not come upon you; may God keep such calamities from you. Others read, "Let it not be a burden to you, O you who pass by the way", namely that which I am about to lay upon you, "look and see," and so on. These two interpretations do not commend themselves to me, because the author would then rather have used the adverb אל of warning and entreaty, or the particle of prayer, and the expression would be a weaker one. So I judge the simplest version to be: "Does it not concern you, O all you who pass by, [my condition]?" So the Douay, the English and the Geneva versions. As if to say: Does no pity for me touch you? Do you think this calamity of mine in no way pertains to you? Do you not reflect that the same fate may one day overtake you too? An interrogative ellipsis is frequent, and it is a commonplace that a sentence is helped by its delivery, as in "Will you draw out Leviathan with a hook?" and "Shall we not receive evil?" (Job 2). The Greek version could be expounded in this sense as well, if you change the first letter, α, into ου: "Does it not concern you [my condition], all who pass along the way?"

units.la: Quis enim sensus vulgatæ Lectionis, oi [Greek] ὑμᾶς [Hebrew]. Qui ad vos, omnes qui transitis per viam. Et quid magis probabile, quam Græcos Interpretes adverbium לא per ν reddidisse? Quidam, adjuro vos; qui transitis &c. Meminitque istius sententiæ Aben-Ezra his verbis [Hebrew] Sunt qui dicunt esse à verbo & significatione [Hebrew] / sed non invenimus istam radicem sine א.
units.tr: For what is the sense of the reading of the Vulgate? Oi [Greek] for ὑμᾶς [Hebrew]: "to you, all who pass along the way." And what is more probable than that the Greek interpreters rendered the adverb לא by ν? Some read "I adjure you, you who pass by," and so on. Aben-Ezra also mentions this sense in these words: "There are those who say that it is from the verb and its meaning, but we do not find this root without the letter א."

units.la: Verf. 13. De Excelso misit ignem in ossa mea, & erudivit me] ut superior versus male Christo tributus fuit ita hic male de Sp. Sancto explicatur. Carthus. in allegorica hujus capitis explicatione, Ossa quoque sunt Apostoli, quibus in igneis linguis missus est Sp. Sanctus, tunć per eos Deus erudivit Ecclesiam. At hic de alio igne agit [Greek]. Et τὸ erudivit non est in Ebræo. [Hebrew] habet textus, id est, & dominatur ei; egregio sensu Deus dominatur isti igni. Deus est moderator hujus ignis; non homo. [Hebrew] dominari. Erudivit me; id diceretur [Hebrew] / Lxx. legisse videntur [Hebrew] & descendere fecit eum, ἐξ ὕψους αὐτὸ ἀπέστειλε πῦρ ἐν πῇ ὁσίᾳ μκ καταψυχειν αὐτό.
units.tr: Verse 13. "From on high he sent fire into my bones, and taught me." As the previous verse was wrongly ascribed to Christ, so here it is wrongly explained of the Holy Spirit. The Carthusian, in his allegorical explanation of this chapter, says: "The bones are also the Apostles, on whom the Holy Spirit was sent in tongues of fire; then through them God taught the Church." But here the prophet speaks of a different fire [Greek]. And the words "taught" is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew text has "and he rules over it," an excellent sense: God rules this fire; God, not man, is its governor. [Hebrew] means "to rule." "He taught me" would be expressed differently [Hebrew]. The Seventy seem to have read [Hebrew] "and made it descend," ἐξ ὕψους αὐτὸ ἀπέστειλε πῦρ ἐν πῇ ὁσίᾳ μκ καταψυχειν αὐτό.

units.la: Verf. 19. Consumpti sunt. ] Ebr. [Hebrew] / expirarunt. De hac voce duo notantur. I. Errare eos qui eam tantum de piis & salvandis usurpari asserunt. Multi hinc probat Ismaelem salvatum esse, de quo Genef. xxv. 17 [Hebrew] Absit ut ego Ismaeli vitam æternam abjudicem Deus illum judicavit, Hoc ajo, ex illa voce non procedere argumentum. R. Salomo. [Hebrew] id est, non dicitur expiratio nisi de justis. At cornua obvertit isti sententiæ locus Gen. vi. 17. & vii. 21. II. Eos non recte sentire, qui [Hebrew] putant de eo tantum genere mortis usurpari, quæ est sine morbo dolores inferente & sine castigationibus, ut loquitur Gerundensis. Aben-Ezra, [Hebrew] dictio [Hebrew] significat exitum spiritus in uno momento (id est, subitaneum,) sine dolore & mora. q. d. [Hebrew] significat mortem repentinam, facilem & dolorisexpertem. Græci εὐθανασίαν vocant, quæ sine doloribus est. Talemortis genus Augustum sibi semper exoptasse Suetonius testis est. Hanc sententiam refellit locus iste Threnorum. Qui enim fame pereunt, lenta morte expirant. Et quis dixerit sine dolore expirasse eos quos aquæ diluvii suffocarunt? Et cum Ebræo [Hebrew] examissim conveniat Græcum ἐπιλύ-χεν, quis dixerit Herodem sine acerbissimis doloribus infelicem animam efflasse? Act. xii. 23. σκωληκόβρωτος γενόμενος ἐξέπνευσεν [Greek]. [illegible, ~60 letters] κυρίως, ἀλλ᾽ ὧν ἡμεῖς ἴδοκα τὸν δόξαν τῷ θεῷ καὶ νομῷ [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐξέψυξεν. Quod exemplum priore quoque error convellendo adhiberi posset, si tam tutum esset homines Orco adscribere, quam usitatum. Equidem non puto quempiam inficiaturum fieri potuisse ut in extremo poenituerit. Quod cum nec affirmet nec neget textus, relinquamus & illum suo & nostro judicii.
units.tr: Verse 19. "They were consumed." The Hebrew is "they breathed out their last." Two points are to be noted about this word. First, those are mistaken who maintain that it is used only of the pious and the saved. Many therefore prove from it that Ishmael was saved, of whom Genesis 25:17 speaks. Far be it from me to deny eternal life to Ishmael; God judged him. I say that no argument follows from that word. Rabbi Solomon says that expiration is spoken of only of the just. But the passage Genesis 6:17 and 7:21 turns its horns against this opinion. Second, those do not judge rightly who think the word is used only of that kind of death which is without disease causing pain and without chastisements, as Gerundensis puts it. Aben-Ezra says the word signifies the departure of the spirit in one moment, that is, suddenly, without pain and delay, as if to say that it signifies a sudden death, easy and free from pain. The Greeks call this εὐθανασίαν, the death without sufferings. Suetonius witnesses that Augustus always wished for such a kind of death for himself. This opinion is refuted by this passage of the Lamentations. For those who perish by famine expire by a slow death. And who would say that those whom the waters of the Flood suffocated expired without pain? And since the Greek ἐπιλύχεν agrees exactly with the Hebrew, who would say that Herod breathed out his unhappy soul without the most bitter pains? Acts 12:23: σκωληκόβρωτος γενόμενος ἐξέπνευσεν, "having become eaten by worms, he expired." [illegible, about 60 letters] properly, but of which we have seen the glory given to God and the law [illegible, about 20 letters] ἐξέψυξεν. This example could also be used to refute the former error, if it were as safe to assign men to Orcus as it is customary. Indeed I do not think anyone would deny that it could have happened that he repented at the last. Since the text neither affirms nor denies this, let us leave it to each one's own judgment.

units.la: Verf. 14. Vigilavit jugum inquitatum mearum in manu ejus, convoluta sunt & imposita collo meo.] Ita vulgatus Lutherus paulo aliter, peccata mea gravia evigilarunt per poenam ejus, & catervatim incubuerunt collo meo. Quicquid hic congerunt Interpretes de evigilatione & dormitione jugi, alienum est: נשקר cum fit a שקר cum puncto in sinistro cornu שׁ / non potest evigilandi notionem habere. Hoc enim est שקר cum puncto in dextro dente. Vox נשקר / inquit Aben. אין לה אב ואם והטעם כמו נמשך כמו נמהר / nec Patrem nec Matrem habet, id est, vox plane solitaria, a conjugatis omnino derelicta) & idem significat quod נמשך protrahitur, vel נמהר acceleratur. Kimchi, ligatum est, aggravatum est jugum &c. Et sic Chaldaeus אתיקר aggravatum est. In Vaijikra rabba סקר est adhaerere, notanti Kimchio. Videtur ergo sic statuendum, quatuor similitudinibus: gravitatem irae divinae qua premitur Jerusalem, illustrari. I. ab immissione ignis verf. 13. II. ab illaqueatione ibidem. III. ab impositione gravis jugi hoc versu iv. a calcatione torcularis verf. 15. Quod ad jugum attinet, causas recensbest, 1. Meritoriam, malitiam.
units.tr: Verse 14. "The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand; they are twisted together and laid upon my neck." Thus the Vulgate; Luther a little differently: "My grievous sins have been kept awake through his punishment, and have lain upon my neck in crowds." Whatever the commentators gather here about the waking and sleeping of a yoke is foreign to the matter: נשקר, if it comes from שקר with a point in the left horn of the letter ש, cannot have the sense of waking. For that is שקר with a point on the right tooth. Aben-Ezra says: "It has neither father nor mother, and the meaning is like נמשך, drawn out, or like נמהר, hastened," that is, the word is entirely solitary, wholly abandoned by its relatives. It has the same meaning as נמשך, protracted, or נמהר, accelerated. Kimchi: it was bound, the yoke was made heavy, and so on. And so the Chaldee has אתיקר, was made heavy. In Vayikra Rabbah סקר means to cling, as Kimchi notes. It seems therefore that it should be settled thus: the gravity of the divine wrath by which Jerusalem is pressed is illustrated by four similitudes: first, from the sending of fire, verse 13; second, from the snaring in the same verse; third, from the laying on of a heavy yoke in this verse, verse 14; fourth, from the treading of the winepress, verse 15. As for the yoke, the causes are to be enumerated. (1) The meritorious cause: my wickedness. (2) The efficient cause: God. (3) The material cause: many, as is seen, blows weighing on the neck. (4) The end: that, as is seen, I might consider healing and uprightness.

units.la: 2. Efficientem, Deum. 3. Materiam, multas vid. plagas collum gravantes. 4. Finem, ut vid. de sanitate & erectione cogitet. Junius ait esse allegoriam a comparatione jumenti subjugis. q.d. defectiones mea sunt tanquam lora & vimina. Hanc materiam assumit Deus, compingit, contorquet tanquam victa vimina & imponit cervicibus meis illarum jugum tam grave ut vires meas profernat. Sic ergo exponenda voces Ebraeae נשקר ligatum est vel, aggravatum est, vel, compactum est; firmitet adhaeret collo meo [illegible, ~5 letters] jugum defectionum mearum manu ejus, manu DOMINI. Funes istus jugi יִשְׁתָּרְגוּ implexi sunt, vel contortuplicantur, & ascendunt super collum meum, atque ita הִכְשִׁיל כֹּחִי labefactat vel corruere facit vires meas. Genev. le joug demes forfaits * est tenu serre par samain, ils sont entortillez & apliquez sur mon col &c.
units.tr: Junius says the yoke is an allegory drawn from the comparison of a yoked beast. As if to say: my transgressions are like cords and withies. God takes up this material, binds it together, twists it like pliant withies, and lays on my neck a yoke so heavy that it overthrows my strength. So the Hebrew words נשקר are to be expounded thus: was bound, or was made heavy, or was compacted; it clings firmly to my neck; the yoke of my transgressions by his hand, the hand of the LORD. The cords of this yoke are intertwined, or twisted together, and rise up over my neck, and so he makes my strength stumble, or causes my powers to fall. The Geneva version: "The yoke of my sins is tied fast by his hand; they are entwined and laid upon my neck," etc.

units.la: Verf. 15. Torcular calcavit DOMINUS virgini filiae Sion ] Ita vulg. optime, & Lxx. Greek iŋda Ebr. Hebrew / Luth. De Heere heeft der Jonck-Brouwen Dochter Juda ten Wijn-perse treden laten. Pro quo in quibusdam codicibus, De Heere heeft den Jonck-Brouwe &c. quod diceretur Latine, Dominus fecit virginem filiam Juda torcular calcare. At hoc torcular non calcavit Juda, sed Deus Judæ. Itaque Angli clarius, DOMINVS calcavit virginem filiam Juda, [tanquam in] torcularî. Et Genev. Le Seigneur a tiré le pressoir sur la pucelle &c. Calcare torcular metaphorice est calamitatum & pœnarum pondere premere, ultionem sumere vide quæ ad Jes. 63. notavimus.
units.tr: Verse 15. The Lord has trodden the virgin daughter of Zion as in a winepress.] The Vulgate renders this very well, and so do the Septuagint: Greek [Ἰούδα] and the Hebrew; Luther: "The Lord has let the young brewer's daughter Judah be trodden in the winepress." Some manuscripts read here, "The Lord has let the young brewer..." etc., which in Latin would be, The Lord made the virgin daughter of Judah tread the winepress. But it was not Judah who trod the winepress, but God who trod Judah. So the English are clearer: THE LORD has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah, [as if] in a winepress. And Geneva: "The Lord has drawn the press over the virgin," etc. To tread the winepress is a figure for pressing down under the weight of calamities and punishments, for exacting vengeance. See what we noted on Isaiah 63.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Vers. 8. tetendit funiculum suum] Frustra sunt, qui hunc locum illustrare volunt ex collatione cujuslibet loci, ubi in textu Latino eadem vox funiculus extat, ex. gr. Ps. xvi. 6. Ps. Lxxviii. &c. ubi in Ebr. est Hebrew aut Hebrew & intelliguntur funiculi mensorii, quibus agros dividebant. Hic vero in Ebr. est Hebrew extendit perpendiculum, vel, regulam. Similia & Greek loca ista sunt, Zach. 1. 16. Domus mea ædificabitur in Jerusalem, Hebrew. & perpendiculum extendetur super Jerusalem hoc est accurate & artificiose exædificabitur. 2. Reg. xxi. 13. & extendam super Jerusalem perpendiculum Samariæ, id est, sicut vastavi Samariam, ita & urbem Jerusalem vastabo. Neque enim tantum dicitur extendi perpendiculum, quando aliquid artificiose ad amussim & regulam fabrilem ædificatur, sed etiam cum ædificium curiose diruitur, & solo æquatur caveturque, ne quid ex ruderibus super terram emineat. Deo vero cum hæc phrasis tribuitur, inquit Cl. Tarnovius, id innuitur ipsum judicium esse culpæ adæquatum, & suplicium juxta mensuram criminum infligi.
units.tr: Verse 8. He stretched out his line.] They labour in vain who want to illustrate this passage by comparing any other place where the same word funiculus (cord) occurs in the Latin text, for example Ps. 16:6 or Ps. 78, etc., where the Hebrew word means the measuring cords with which men divided fields. Here, however, the Hebrew means he stretched out the plumb-line, or the rule. Similar are those passages in Zech. 1:16, My house shall be built in Jerusalem, and the plumb-line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem, that is, it shall be built exactly and skilfully; and 2 Kings 21:13, I will stretch over Jerusalem the plumb-line of Samaria, that is, just as I laid waste Samaria, so I will lay waste the city of Jerusalem. For a plumb-line is not stretched out only when something is built skilfully by the measure and the carpenter's rule, but also when a building is carefully pulled down and levelled with the ground, and the site is cleared so that no rubble rises above the earth. When this phrase is attributed to God, says the learned Tarnovius, it signifies that the judgment itself is equal to the guilt, and that punishment is inflicted according to the measure of the crimes.

units.la: Vers. 18. Ne des requiem tibi] Hebrew Edit. Rom. Greek ne des requiem tibi. Sic cap. 3. 49. Greek, Greek Greek. Non tacebo eo quod non sit requies. Edit. Complut. Greek, & des lotionem tibi. Edit. Basil. Greek, & des lotionem tibi, quasi per lacrymas clui possent peccatorum sordes. Solus Christi sanguis eluit eas. Sequitur, Hebrew ne quiescat pupilla oculi tui, Lxx. Edit. Rom. Greek μὴ σωπήσαιτο ὀυχάτης ὀφθαλμῶν σου. Nota, ὀυχάτης pro pupilla, quia בת utrumque apud Ebraeos significat. Compl. μὴ σωπήσαι τὸ κόρη ὀφθαλμῶν σε. Haec quoque vox κόρη & pupillam significat. Imò ipsa vox Latina pupilla ambigua ad utrumque. Est enim pupilla proprie parva pupula, utrumque κοράσιον seu diminutivum à pupa, parva puella. Ut pupus, parvus puer. Huc vulgo quoque referunt nomen Ebr. אישון quo pupillam notant putantque diminutivum esse ab איש vir. quasi virunculum dicas. Sed falluntur. Ut enim taceam, probari evidente exemplo non posse literam Nun formativam diminutivorum esse, אישון nigrum vel nigredinem significat, Prov. vii. 9. בְּאִישׁוֹן לַיְלָה in negredine noctis pro quo Prov. xx. 20. scribitur בְּאִישׁוֹן, Hinc translata ea vox ad notandum nigrum illum in oculo circulum. Quod vero ad בת attinet, vox ea quidem & filiam & pupillam significat, sed illud simul observandum est tyroni, cum filiam significat, esse contractum ex בִּנְת / ex masc. בן / cum pupillam: crasin esse pro בַּבַּת / quod plenum extat Zach. 2. 8. בְּבָבַת עֵינוֹ / ex absoluto בַּבַּת / ut קַמַּת קַסַּת, quasi esset à themate mediam vau habente כּוּב vide Gramm. nostram p. 86. Frequentior ea vox est in Chald. & Thalmudicorum scriptis, Koheleth. 12. 3. בְּבִי עֵינֶךָ pupilla oculorum tuorum & Deut. 32. 10. ubi in Ebr. אִישׁוֹן עֵינוֹ Chald. habet בְּבָבַת עֵינֵיהוֹן.
units.tr: Verse 18. Give yourself no rest.] The Hebrew, in the Roman edition, reads in Greek, "give yourself no rest." So in chapter 3:49, where the Greek says, "I will not keep silent, because there is no rest." The Complutensian edition has "and give yourself washing," and the Basel edition has "and give yourself washing," as if the filth of sins could be cleansed by tears. Only the blood of Christ cleanses them. There follows, in Hebrew, "let not the pupil of your eye rest," and in the Septuagint, in the Roman edition, the Greek reads "let not the daughter of your eye be silent." Note that pupilla is used for the pupil, because the Hebrews use the word בת for both. The Complutensian has "let not the girl of your eye be silent"; this Greek word also means pupil. Indeed the Latin word pupilla itself is ambiguous and can mean either. A pupilla is properly a little pupa, a small doll, a diminutive of pupa, a little girl, just as pupus is a little boy. Many also refer to the Hebrew name אישון, by which they denote the pupil, and they think it is a diminutive of איש, man, as if you could say "little man." But they are mistaken. To say nothing else, it cannot be proved by any clear example that the letter nun is a formative sign of diminutives: אישון means blackness or black, as in Prov. 7:9, בְּאִישׁוֹן לַיְלָה, "in the blackness of the night," where Prov. 20:20 has בְּאִישׁוֹן. From this the word was transferred to denote the black circle in the eye. As for בת, the word does mean both daughter and pupil, but beginners should also note this: when it means daughter, it is a contraction of בִּנְת from the masculine בן; when it means pupil, it is for בַּבַּת, which appears in full in Zech. 2:8, בְּבָבַת עֵינוֹ, from the absolute form בַּבַּת, as קַמַּת becomes קַסַּת, as if it came from a root with a medial vav, כּוּב; see our grammar, p. 86. This word is more frequent in Chaldee and in the Talmudic writings: Eccles. 12:3, בְּבִי עֵינֶךָ, "the pupils of your eyes," and Deut. 32:10, where the Hebrew has אִישׁוֹן עֵינוֹ, while the Chaldee has בְּבָבַת עֵינֵיהוֹן.

units.la: Verf. 19. Leva ad eum manus tuas pro anima parvulorum tuorum.] Audi hic Pintum in observationibus ex Ebraeo, ut vocat, & ride. Monemur hoc loco, inquit, preces fundere ad Deum pro animabus mortuorum, ut Deus eas ducat ad gloriam sempiternam: non pro illis quae sunt in caelo, aut in inferno, sed pro illis quae in purgatorio. Atque ita gradum protollit ad prolixam disputationem de purgatorio & authoritate 2. libri Machab. ex cujus capite 12. locum istum vulgatissimum citat de sacrificio Judae Machabaei. Sed miror Pintum tam derepente oblitum fuisse eorum quae in comm. p. 317. ad hunc ipsum locum commentatus est, Pro anima inquit illic, id est, pro vita, vel ad literam, pro anima, ut qui jam vitam amittebant (nota, amittebant, non, amiserant, ergo pro vivis) animas saltem salvarent. Sensus est, Ora Deum, ut eorum animae in sinum Abrahae recipiantur. Quia vero in sequentibus provocat ad 2. Mach. 12. 43. dicitque Judam Machabaeum facta collatione, duodecim mille drachmas misisse Jerusolymam, ad offerendum pro peccatis mortuorum sacrificium, bis impingit. I. in numero drachmarum. Nam Graeci codices constanter δισχίλιας δεκαχμάς memorant, id est, bis mille drachmas. II. addendo mortuorum. Omnes enim Graeci codices etiam Romanus, unanimiter, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτίας ἰνσίαν: pro peccato superstitum quod contagione eos quoque reos fecerat (ut peccatum Achanis reliquos Israelitas, Ios. 7.) ut peccatum hoc πλεῖον ἐξαλιφθῇ, id est perfecte deleretur, inquit textus vers. 42. quod morte caesorum jam ex parte deletum erat. Licet autem Voculam mortuorum Latina exemplaria pleraque habeant, monuerunt tamen Lovanienses Theologi M. S. quaedam & Graeca exemplaria illam non agnoscere. Quin ipsi genuinam lectionem textui * inseruerunt, propeccato: alteram illam, pro peccato mortuorum in marginem rejicientes. Quod vere author libri hoc factum Judae sic interpretatur, quasi is pro mortuis haec sacrificia offeri voluerit, non magis nos movere debet hominis minime θεοπνεύστου futile judicium, quam Judaeorum, qui cum Christus Eli Eli clamaret, illum Eliam invocare credebant. Judas quippe magis in lege versatus fuit, quam ut sacrificia pro defunctis offerenda putaverit; utpote cujus rei nec praeceptum nec exemplum in ea extat. Vide prolixe de hoc loco differentem Rainoldus in Cens. librorum apocryphorum tomo I. praelect. cv. & tomo 2. praelect. CLVIII. & seq.
units.tr: Verse 19. Lift up your hands to him for the lives of your little children.] Hear Pinto here, in his Observations drawn from the Hebrew, as he calls it, and laugh. We are reminded at this place, he says, to pour out prayers to God for the souls of the dead, that God may lead them to everlasting glory; not for those who are in heaven or in hell, but for those who are in purgatory. And so he advances to a lengthy discussion of purgatory and of the authority of the second book of the Maccabees, from whose twelfth chapter he cites this very well-known passage about the sacrifice of Judas Maccabeus. But I am surprised that Pinto so suddenly forgot what he had commented on this very passage at p. 317 of his commentary: "For the life," he says there, "that is, for life, or literally, for the soul, so that those who were already losing their life (note: losing, not having lost; so for the living) might at least save their souls. The sense is: pray to God that their souls may be received into the bosom of Abraham." But since in what follows he appeals to 2 Maccabees 12:43, and says that Judas Maccabeus, after making a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, he goes wrong twice. First, in the number of drachmas: all the Greek manuscripts consistently give δισχίλιας δεκαχμάς, that is, two thousand drachmas. Second, in adding of the dead. For all the Greek manuscripts, even the Roman one, unanimously have ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτίας ἰνσίαν, that is, for the sin of the survivors, which by contagion had made them also guilty (as the sin of Achan made the rest of the Israelites guilty, Josh. 7), so that this sin might be wholly blotted out, πλεῖον ἐξαλιφθῇ; the text says in verse 42 that it had already been partly blotted out by the death of those slain. Although most Latin copies have the little word of the dead, the Louvain theologians noted that some manuscripts and Greek copies do not recognise it. Indeed they inserted the genuine reading into the text with an asterisk, for sin, and pushed the other reading, for the sin of the dead, into the margin. Even if the author of the book interprets Judas's deed in this way, as though he wanted these sacrifices offered for the dead, the futile judgment of a man who was by no means inspired by God should not move us any more than the Jews, who, when Christ cried "Eli, Eli," believed that he was calling on Elijah. Judas was, after all, more versed in the law than to think that sacrifices should be offered for the departed, since there is neither command nor example of such a thing in it. See Rainoldus, who discusses this passage at length in his Censure of the Apocryphal Books, vol. 1, lecture 105, and vol. 2, lectures 158 and following.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Sunt qui totum hoc caput Christo patienti literaliter tribuant, crassissimo errore. Is enim nunquam a Deo defecit, ac proinde ipsi non conveniunt ista, revertamur ad Dominum, Vers. 40. rebellavimus, defecimus vers. 42. Adhaec Christus in cruce pendens pro hostib. suis intercessit, non eos devovit.
units.tr: Some people ascribe this whole chapter literally to Christ in his suffering, through a very gross error. For he never fell away from God, so these words do not fit him: "return to the Lord" (v. 40), "we have rebelled" and "we have fallen away" (v. 42). Moreover, Christ hanging on the cross interceded for his enemies; he did not curse them.

units.la: Vers. 14. Factus sum in derisum omni populo meo. ] Ita vulg. Torquent se hic interpretes quomodo populus Dei (ille enim hic loquitur tanquam unus) dicat se in derisum esse omni populo suo. Junius cum omni populo meo. Non vitata eadem difficultate. Pisc. omnibus populis, sc. vicinis & circumjacentibus. Sed ita ut putet locum corruptum, scribendumque esse / Ego interpretationem Piscatoris amplexor. Crisin non item. Interterminationes enim irregulares pluralis numeri etiam haec est, Sic foramina, pro Gen. 40. 16. Ps. 144. 2. qui subjicit mihi mihi ייִםְּר Hieron. & Chald. populos. Ubi Masora notat ייִםְּר פְּנֵיהֶם ייִםְּר tria falso putari legenda ייִםְּר / Duo nunc produxit. Tertium extat 2. Sam. 22. 44. Eruisti me à contentionibus ייִםְּר / Mens Masoritarum ista est, Falso putari prò illa voce legendum esse ייִםְּר cum Jod possit esse affixum, vel sit terminatio irregularis pl. numeri.
units.tr: Verse 14: "I have become a derision to all my people." So the Vulgate. Interpreters here twist themselves into knots over how the people of God (for he speaks here as one man) can say that he is a derision to all his people. Junius renders it "with all my people", without escaping the same difficulty. Piscator has "to all peoples", that is, to the neighbouring and surrounding nations, but he thinks the place corrupt and that it ought to be read otherwise. I embrace Piscator's interpretation, though not his criticism. For this irregular plural form also occurs, as in "foramina" at Gen. 40:16 and Ps. 144:2 ("who subdues peoples to me"), where Jerome and the Chaldee paraphrast have "peoples". The Masorah notes three places where a word is wrongly thought to be read in a certain way. Two are now brought forward; a third is at 2 Sam. 22:44 ("you delivered me from the strivings of the people"). The view of the Masoretes is this: it is falsely supposed that another reading should be given for that word, since the Jod may be an added letter or may be an irregular plural ending.

units.la: Verf. 23. Novi diluculo, multa est fides tua.] Ita Vulg. Lxx. καὶ καινὰ ἐν τῇ πρωΐ ποιήσει ἡ πίστις σε. Rom. Καινά εἰς τὰς πρωΐας. Τὰ καινὰ sc. ἐλέη, quorum mentio versu praecedenti. Sed illud Latinum Novi quo referendum? Rabanus, Hugo, Thomas, Carthus. Lyra, atque adeo in hac literarum luce ipse S. A exponunt novi, id est, scio, novi à diluculo id est, à pueritia mea, vel tempestivè, quod multa sit fides tua. At quomodo haec interpretatio cum originali conciliari possit nullus video. Et Pintus ingenue, si Ebraicam consulas literam, videbis, inquit, veram lectionem esse Novae diluculo, seu novae cottidie. Est ergo nomen adjectt. numeri pluralis non verbum. Novae etiam habent nonnulli codices correcti ad marginem. Haec ille. Romani tamen correctores retinuerunt corruptam lectionem. Ubi Lucas Brug. non potuit se continere quin adderet, in quibusdam libris legi Nova, sine ulla censura. Tantum addit, spurium esse quod nonnulli legunt, nova es. Et quid clarius est? Lege versum antecedentem, misericordiae Domini sunt, id est, summa & infinita Dei misericordia est, plurale prosing. ad auxesin, quod non sumus consumti, quod non deficiant miserationes ejus. Sequitur הַדַּשִּׁים לַבְּקָרִים nova sunt, miserationes illae, singulis matutinis. רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתְךָ magna est fides tua. Quis vero non indignetur hos duos versus tam diligenter exhibitos in Edit. Romana, quam tam magnifice Sixtus V. commendat.
units.tr: Verse 23: "They are new every morning; great is your faithfulness." So the Vulgate and the Seventy, whose Greek reads, "and new in the morning your faithfulness will make..." The Roman edition has "New in the mornings", the adjective referring to the mercies of the preceding verse. But to what does the Latin "Novi" [I know] refer? Rabanus, Hugo, Thomas, the Carthusians, Lyra, and indeed S. A. in this light of learning, explain "novi" as "I know", "from the dawn", that is, from my boyhood, or "in good time", because your faithfulness is great. But I see no way in which this interpretation can be reconciled with the original. Pintus frankly says that if you consult the Hebrew letter you will see that the true reading is "new in the mornings", or "new daily". It is therefore an adjective in the plural, not a verb. Some corrected codices also have "novae" in the margin. So far Pintus. The Roman correctors nevertheless kept the corrupt reading. Lucas Brugensis could not restrain himself from adding that in some books "Nova" is read, without any censure, and he only remarks that the reading "nova es" which some use is spurious. And what could be plainer? Read the verse before: "the mercies of the Lord are..." that is, the mercy of God is supreme and infinite, a plural used for amplification: "that we are not consumed, that his compassions do not fail." There follows: "they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness." Who would not be indignant that these two verses are displayed so carelessly in the Roman edition, which Sixtus V commends so magnificently?

units.la: Τὰ ἐλέη καινά, ἐπ' ἐκείνῃ μὲν ... Μάνας εἰς τὰς πρωΐας ἐλέου Κύριε. ... Καινά εἰς τὰς πρωΐας, πολλὴ ἡ πίστις σου.
units.tr: "The mercies are new; ... 'months' in the mornings, of mercy, Lord ... new in the mornings, great is your faithfulness." [Τὰ ἐλέη καινά, ἐπ' ἐκείνῃ μὲν ... Μάνας εἰς τὰς πρωΐας ἐλέου Κύριε. ... Καινά εἰς τὰς πρωΐας, πολλὴ ἡ πίστις σου.]

units.la: Misericordiae Domini quia non fecit deficere me: quia non sunt consumptae miserationes ejus. Mensis in matutinis miserere Domine, quia consumpti non sumus: quia non sunt consummatae miserationes ejus. Novae in matutinis, multa est fides tua.
units.tr: The mercies of the Lord, because he has not let me fail; because his mercies are not consumed. Months in the mornings: have mercy, Lord, because we are not consumed; because his mercies are not finished. New in the mornings: great is your faithfulness.

units.la: Hic variae interpretationes seu glossemata coaluerunt. Namque illud μῆνας quod solum legit Editio Basil. in 8. videtur respondere Ebraeo מְשִׁיחַ / quod si legas cum camets rapto sub ח / mensis significat, sicut Chateph fathach, nova.
units.tr: Here various interpretations, or glosses, have grown up. For the Greek word "μῆνας", which the Basel octavo edition alone reads, seems to correspond to the Hebrew word; and if you read it with the qamets under the letter, it means "months", just as the chateph-patah means "new".

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Verf. 20. Spiritus oris nostri Christus Dominus captus in peccatis nostris.] Ita vulgatus Interpres. Lovan. Belgica, De Geest onses mons Christus de Heere is gheb-angheu in onse zonden. Lxx. * πνεῦμα προσώπου ἡμῶν χριστὸς κυρίου συνελήφθη ἐν ταῖς διαφθορεῖς αὐτῶν, Spiritus faciei Christus Dominus captus est in corruptionibus eorum. Sed quia in aliis codicib. est ἡμῶν, putat Nobilius, reddendum potius esse, corruptionibus nostris ipsorum. Locum hunc de Christo omnes fere veteres, versionibus istis decepti, interpretati sunt. Et certe si defendi ea sententia posset, firmum hinc peteretur pro aeterna filii Dei Deitate argumentum. Sed bene habet. Articulus iste nostrae fidei tot tibicinibus in veteri & N. foedere fultus est, ut ab unius aut alterius minus firmi sublatione nullum ei metuendum sit periculum. Quin potius hic ad animum revocanda Thomae salutaris admonitio, Cum quis ad probandam fidem Christianam inducit rationes non cogentes, cedit in irrisionem fidelium. Credunt enim quod hujusmodi rationibus initamur, & propter eas credamus. Pontificii patrum expositioni hic mordicus haerent, non tam authoritate patrum quam vulgatae versionis permoti. Quin & multi illorum textum Ebraeum hic suspectare audent, quasi is a Judaeis in odium Christi corruptus sit. Quia is vid. non habet מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה unctus DOMINVS, ut Lxx. & Vulg. legerunt, sed מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה unctus DOMINI. Sed frustra hos fluctus in simpulo movent. Praesupponere illi videntur, unctum Domini non posse de Christo praedicari. At Luc. 2. 26. expresse vocatur Salvator χριστὸς κυρίου, acceperat responsum a Spiritu S. non visurum se mortem, πρὶν ἢ ἴδειν τὸν χριστὸν κυρίου. Non est ergo quod receptae illi sententiae convellendae, a forma vocis מְשִׁיחַ contracta argumentum petamus. Sed dices, Si legatur מְשִׁיחַ & unctus Dominus non potest non de Christo intelligi hic versus. Si vero מְשִׁיחַ & unctus DOMINI, potest tam de alio rege uncto, qui caro & sanguis est, quam de Salvatore nostro exponi. Respondeo, ex cohaerentia judicandum esse de vero & germano sensu huius loci. Ea adeo clara & perspicua est, ut Jesuita a Castro confiteatur hanc intelligentiam textui optime convenire. Conquesti sunt in superioribus. Judaei de hostilibus Chaldaeorum molitionibus & indefessa industria qua hoc unum agebant ut urbem Jerusalem expugnarent. Tandem conqueruntur, unctum Domini, Zedechiam, spiramentum narium ipsorum, id est, qui tam carus ipsis erat quam spiritus ipsorum, vel sub cujus tutela poterant respirare, quo salvo, adhuc bene sperabant, captum in foveis ipsorum, in insidiis, ubi se latitaturum considebat, Jerem. LII,8. Et certe quis negare ausit, cum hoc tragico Regis Zedechiae casu & regnum ipsum corruisse & quicquid adhuc Judaeis supererat animi, in pedes decidisse. Cl. Junii haec est paraphrasis, Rex noster e posteritate Davidis, quo freti saltem nobis datur aliqua interspirandi occasio in quibuslibet angustiis. Nam praesidebant Judaei dignitati illius regni, tanquam si pure & per se ipsum stabile fuisset. Non autem spectabant Christum, qui finis est & complementum illius typi, neque conditiones sibi imperatas. Expende diligenter Ebraeas voces, רנח [?] Sp. n.n. unctus Domini captus est in foveis eorum. Nota captus est in foveis, id est, insidiis, Eorum M. Quorum? Eorum utique, de quibus antea vers. 18. 19. qui venati sunt gressus judaeorum, ne inciderent per plateas, qui insidiati sunt ipsis in montibus & deserto, qui velociores sunt aquilis &c. Non dicit peccatis, multo minus, peccatis nostris. שְׁחִיתָה est fovea, Si dixeris, significare corruptionem potius & esse à שחה non contendam super ea re. Illud mihi saltem dabis, corruptionem non violento nimis tropo posse accipi pro fovea vel sepulcro, in quo corrumpuntur facile & putrescunt corpora. Ita שְׁחִיתָה corruptionem & foveam significat, לִשְׁחִיתָה vero & שחה pro peccato aliquando usurpari, prius ostendendum erat.
units.tr: Verse 20. "The breath of our nostrils, the Lord's anointed, was taken in our sins." So the Vulgate translator. The Louvain Belgic version reads: "De Geest onses monds, Christus de Heere, is gheb-angheu in onse zonden." The Septuagint reads: "πνεῦμα προσώπου ἡμῶν χριστὸς κυρίου συνελήφθη ἐν ταῖς διαφθορεῖς αὐτῶν" ["the spirit of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in their corruptions"]. But since other manuscripts have "ἡμῶν" ["our"], Nobilius thinks it should rather be rendered "in our corruptions, their own". Almost all the ancient writers, misled by these versions, have interpreted this place of Christ. And certainly, if that view could be defended, a firm argument for the eternal Deity of the Son of God could be drawn from it. But all is well. This article of our faith is supported by so many props in the Old and New Covenant that there is no danger to be feared from the removal of one or another weaker one. Indeed, here the wholesome warning of Thomas must be recalled to mind: when someone brings forward unconvincing arguments to prove the Christian faith, he falls into ridicule among the faithful. For they believe that we are led by such arguments and that we believe because of them. The Papists cling stubbornly to the Fathers' exposition here, moved not so much by the authority of the Fathers as by the Vulgate version. Indeed, many of them dare to suspect the Hebrew text here, as if it had been corrupted by the Jews out of hatred of Christ. For it apparently does not have "מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה" [məšîaḥ YHWH], "the anointed of the LORD", as the Septuagint and the Vulgate read, but "מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה" [məšîaḥ YHWH] "the anointed of the LORD" with a different vowel pointing (the genitive form). But they stir these waves in a teacup to no purpose. They seem to presuppose that "the anointed of the Lord" cannot be predicated of Christ. Yet at Luke 2:26 the Saviour is expressly called "χριστὸς κυρίου" [christos kyriou], "the Lord's Christ", since Simeon had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death "πρὶν ἢ ἴδειν τὸν χριστὸν κυρίου" [prin ē idein ton christon kyriou], before he saw the Lord's Christ. There is therefore no need to seek an argument, to overturn that accepted view, from the altered form of the word "מְשִׁיחַ" [məšîaḥ]. But you will say: if it is read "מְשִׁיחַ" [məšîaḥ], "the anointed", and "the anointed of the Lord", this verse cannot but be understood of Christ; but if it is "מְשִׁיחַ" [məšîaḥ] with "יְהוָה" [YHWH] in the genitive, it can be explained of another anointed king, who is flesh and blood, as well as of our Saviour. I answer that the true and genuine sense of this place must be judged from its context. That context is so clear and plain that the Jesuit a Castro admits this interpretation fits the text very well. In the earlier verses the Jews complained of the hostile undertakings of the Chaldeans and of their tireless industry, by which they worked for this one thing: to storm the city of Jerusalem. Finally they lament that "the Lord's anointed", Zedekiah, "the breath of their nostrils", that is, the one who was as dear to them as their own breath, or under whose protection they could breathe, and while he was safe they still had good hope, "was taken in their pits", in the snares where he had settled to hide himself (Jer. 52:8). And indeed, who would dare deny that with this tragic fate of King Zedekiah both the kingdom itself collapsed and whatever courage the Jews still had fell to the ground? The paraphrase of the learned Junius is this: "Our king, from the posterity of David, in whom we trusted, is given to us at least as an occasion of breathing again in whatever straits we are in. For the Jews were relying on the dignity of that kingdom, as if it had been purely and of itself stable. But they did not look to Christ, who is the end and fulfilment of that type, nor to the conditions *imposed* on them." Consider carefully the Hebrew words: [?] Sp. n.n. the anointed of the Lord was taken in their pits. Note that he was taken in pits, that is, in snares. Of whom? Of those, surely, of whom he spoke before in verses 18 and 19: who hunted our steps so that we could not go in the streets, who lay in wait for us in the mountains and in the desert, who are swifter than eagles, and so on. It does not say sins, much less our sins. "שְׁחִיתָה" [šəḥîṯāh] means a pit. If you say it means rather corruption, and derives from "שחה" [šḥh], I will not contend over that point. At least you will grant me this: corruption can be taken, without too violent a trope, for a pit or a grave, in which bodies easily decay and rot. Thus "שְׁחִיתָה" [šəḥîṯāh] signifies corruption and a pit; but that "לִשְׁחִיתָה" [lišḥîṯāh] and "שחה" [šḥh] are sometimes used for sin, this had first to be shown.

units.la: Verf. 13. Adolescentibus impudice abusi sunt] Vulgati interpretationem retuli, Ebraea ita habent, בחורים טחון נשאו juvenes [ad] molendum acceperunt, sc. Chaldaei, id est, interprete ipso Pinto, Adolescentibus ad molas circumagendas usi sunt. Vide & Vatablum.
units.tr: Verse 13. They abused the young men lustfully] I have kept the Vulgate's rendering. The Hebrew reads בחורים טחון נשאו [bachurim tachon nasu], "they took the young men to grind," that is, as the Chaldee paraphrast understands it, in the words of Pinto himself: they used the young men to turn the millstones. See also Vatablus.

units.la: Erat quippe illud ut apud Romanos, sic & apud Orientales gravissimum servitutis genus, vide Exod. xi. 5. usque ad primogenitum ancilla quæ post molas. Quod cap. xii, 29. primogenitus captivi, qui in ergastulo. Confer & Jes. 47. Tolle molam, mole farinam. Qui vulgatam versionem tuentur, conferunt locum Job. 31. 10. Molat alteri uxor mea, & super ea incurvent se alii. Adducunt insuper testimonia gentilium, e. g. aliorum permolere uxores &c. Sed nego Jobum tà molere obscoeno sensu usurpasse, ac proinde affirmo * Vulgatum nimis sibi indulsisse quando versit; Scortum alterius sit uxor mea. Hoc enim expressit Job ultimo versus hemistichio. Adhæc, Si illud voluisset Job, dixisset, opinor, non מטחן molat, sed ממחן in Nifal, permolatur. Cum enim illud viris tribuant obscoeni scriptores, hoc fœminis tribuendum videtur. Quamvis non ignorem, quid ex Aben-Ezra & Merceri additamentis ad thesaurum Pagnini obtendi possit. Vir quidam eruditus ex cujus scriptis me multum profecisse profiteor, hanc Vulgati versionem apud Jobum probare se dicit ob subjectam materiam & sequens comma. Sed quod ad subjectam materiam attinet, ei, tamis, quem ex collatione Exod. xi. 5. Jes. 47. colligimus, quam vulgatæ versionis sensus convenit. Imprecatur enim sibi Job hoc capite noxia quæque & ignominiosa & acerba; si illud & illud fecerit. Quid autem potuisset ei evenire acerbius, quam si uxor ab ægro marito avulsa, in pistrinum detrusa & ad servilesvel potius belluinos Labores exantlandos idq; alrius commodo coacta fuisset? Quod ad sequens comma, fateor equidem tralatitium esse in Propheticis & Poëticis scriptis in uno eodemque versu לכפל הענין במלות שונות / duplicare sensum diversis verbis id est, idem bis dicere; sed id ubique fieri nemo opinor asseruerit. Hæc ergo est mens Jobi, molat alteri id est alterius commodo, uxor mea hoc est; sit alterius abjectissimam a ancilla, durissimam alteri servitutem serviat, quin & super ea incurvent se alii, id est, expositia sit aliorum libidini. Miror autem quid in mentem venerit priscis Ebræis quando locum istum Judicum 16. ubi Samson dicitur molui se in domo vinctorum sic exposuerunt, quasi pro sobole robustissimorum virorum hoc in Allophylas mulieres facere compulsus sit, ut loquitur Hieron. in cap. 47. Jesaiæ. Cujus interpretationis ita meminere R. Sal. & Kimchi ut neutiquam ei suffragii sui assensum præbeant.
units.tr: Among the Romans, and equally among the Orientals, this was the most grievous kind of servitude; see Exod. 11:5, "even to the firstborn, the maidservant who is behind the mill." Cf. Exod. 12:29, where the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon is mentioned. Compare also Isa. 47:2, "Take the millstones and grind meal." Those who defend the Vulgate version cite Job 31:10, "Let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down over her," and they add testimonies from the Gentiles, for example, "to grind the wives of others" and so on. But I deny that Job used the verb טחן [tachan] "to grind" in an obscene sense, and so I maintain that the Vulgate went too far in its freedom when it rendered, "Let my wife be another man's harlot." For this is what Job expressed in the last half of the verse. Moreover, if Job had meant that, I think he would have written not מטחן [mețachen], "grinds," but the Niphal ממחן [mețuchan], "let her be ground." For obscene writers attribute that act to men, and it seems it should be attributed to women. Yet I am not unaware of what may be put forward from the additions of Aben-Ezra and Mercer to Pagninus' thesaurus. A certain learned man, from whose writings I confess I have profited greatly, says that he approves this Vulgate rendering in Job "on account of the subject matter and the following clause." But as far as the subject matter goes, the sense of the Vulgate version agrees less with what we gather from the comparison of Exod. 11:5 and Isa. 47, than does the other. For Job, in this chapter, calls down upon himself every kind of harm, shame and bitterness, if he has done this and that. Now what could have befallen him more bitterly than if his wife had been torn from her sick husband, thrust into the mill, and forced to undergo servile, or rather brutish, labours for another's advantage? As for the following clause, I admit it is a commonplace in prophetic and poetic writings to double the sense in one and the same verse by different words (לכפל הענין במלות שונות [lekafel ha-inyan bemillot shonot]), that is, to say the same thing twice; but I do not think anyone would assert that this happens everywhere. So the meaning of Job is this: "let her grind for another," that is, for another's advantage, "my wife," that is, "let her serve another in the most abject slavery, the harshest servitude to someone else; indeed, let others bow down over her," that is, "let her be exposed to the lust of others." But I wonder what came into the minds of the ancient Hebrews when they explained in this way the passage in Judg. 16, where Samson is said to have "ground in the house of the prisoners," as if he were compelled to do this, to the offspring of the mightiest men, among the Philistine women, as Jerome says in his commentary on chapter 47 of Isaiah. R. Solomon and Kimchi mention this interpretation in such a way that they by no means give their assent to it.

units.tr: 26. Seth. Enos, etc. The errors of the ancients about these names, and what they inferred from them. [Those who interpreted Seth as the resurrection were deceived by the Greek version, verse 25. For where the Hebrew has "God has set (הקים) for me another seed," that is, gave, the LXX have "another seed" [ἐτέρον σπέρμα].] The Abulensis also interpreted the word Enos as invocation, as Salian reports in vol. 1 of the Annals, p. 210. 240.

Mos est scriptura gigantes vocare agrestes, feroces & robustos. Vide Salianum.] 219.

Finally, to the whole of this disputation add the explanation of Emmanuel Sa the Jesuit, who in Isaiah 26.14 explains the giants as tyrants or oppressors of others. Also Cyril, book 9 against Julian: it is Scripture's custom to call giants rustic, fierce and robust men. See Salian.] 219.
