units.la: XI. 11. Græcorum codicum ab Ebræis discrepantia in numeris. 253. [Pag. 255. lin. 5. ubi diximus, Solus Emmanuel Sa, &c. aliud egimus. Salianus tom. 1. p. 308. longe plures recensèt, vid. Sigonium, Canum, Toletum, Bellarm. Del-Rio. Baradium, Gordonum, Salmeronem, Raderum, Lauretium, Torniellum, Samerium, Riberam, Seb. Veronium. Quibus calculum suum apponit ipse Salianus, non quidem statuens ex textu Ebraeo quippiam excidisse, sed Mosi pregnantes fuisse rationes, cur hanc generationem omiserit. Istis oppono Senensem lib. v. annot. 88. Eugubinum Steuchum, Cajetanum, Genebr. Driedonem, Lucidum, Abulensem, Corn. à Lapide, & alios. Et digna lectu sunt quæ de hoc loco Glassius notavit; philologiæ suæ pag. 65.]
units.tr: XI. 11. The discrepancy of the Greek codices from the Hebrews in numbers. 253. [Page 255, line 5, where we said only Emmanuel Sa, etc., we argued otherwise. Salian, vol. 1, p. 308, lists far more: see Sigonius, Canus, Toletus, Bellarmine, Del Rio, Baradius, Gordon, Salmeron, Rader, Lauretius, Torniellus, Samerius, Ribera, Sebastian Veronius. To these Salian adds his own reckoning, not deciding that something had fallen out of the Hebrew text, but that Moses had weighty reasons for omitting this generation. Against them I set the Senensis, book 5, annotation 88, Eugubinus, Steuchus, Cajetan, Genebrardus, Driedo, Lucidus, Abulensis, Cornelius a Lapide, and others. Also worth reading is what Glassius noted on this passage in his Philology, p. 65.]

units.la: Profectus est Lot ab oriente. Liquere ex chorographia, eum orientem versus movisse. Quorundam intempestiva Allegoria. D pro ד vel אֶת ad, versus, aliquando usurpari.
units.tr: Lot departed toward the east. It is clear from the geography that he moved eastward. An ill-timed allegory of some. The particle D, standing for ד or אֶת, ad, towards, is sometimes used.

units.la: Melchisedek Rex Salem ——— Erat enim sacerdos Dei altissimi, &c.
units.tr: Melchizedek, king of Salem ... For he was priest of God Most High, etc.

units.la: Cujus præputii caro non fuerit circumcisa, &c. Lxx. Interpretum error. Unde nata durior Augustini sententia de infantibus ante susceptam circumcisionem & Baptismum defunctis. Vera loci interpretatio.
units.tr: Whose foreskin's flesh was not circumcised, etc. The error of the Seventy translators. Whence arose the harsher opinion of Augustine about infants who died before receiving circumcision and baptism. The true interpretation of the passage.

units.la: Exscindetur anima ista, &c. de varia phrasebus istius interpretatione. Quid sit כרת apud Thalmudicos. Item התראה præmonitio. De examine testium apud Ebræos. Ubi mors simpliciter nominatur, strangulationem; ubi, sanguis ejus super eum, lapidationem intelligi ab Ebræis. De die circumcisionis. Eum ex lege fuisse octavum, etiam si in Sabb. incideret. Ex traditione aliquando etiam fuisse nonum, 10. 11. 12. Ejus rei fundamentum. Circumcisio pellit sabbathum, si incidat in tempus suum; non item, si loco suo mota fuerit. Quid sit dies legalis non est à tempore ad tempus. Alia.
units.tr: That soul shall be cut off, etc. On the varied phrasings in its interpretation. What karath [כרת] means among the Talmudists, and likewise hatra'ah [התראה], forewarning. On the examination of witnesses among the Hebrews. Where death is simply named, strangling; where "his blood upon him," the Hebrews understand stoning. On the day of circumcision: that by law it was the eighth, even if it fell on the Sabbath. By tradition it was sometimes even the ninth, the tenth, eleventh or twelfth. The foundation of this. Circumcision sets aside the Sabbath if it falls on its own day; not so if it has been moved from its place. What a legal day is, which does not run from time to time. Other matters.

units.la: Non vocabis nomen ejus Sarai, sed Sara. Error Græcorum circa hanc tranominationem. ut & nominis Abram mutationem. Saraceni non à Sara, sed ab Arabico סרק furari, latrocinari. Arabs pro latrone.
units.tr: You shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah. The Greeks' error about this wordplay, as also about the change of the name Abram. The Saracens are not named from Sarah, but from the Arabic סרק [saraq], to steal, to rob. An Arab means a robber.

units.la: Pluit DOMINUS à DOMINO.
units.tr: The LORD rained from the LORD.

units.la: Cumque vidisset Sara filium Hagar ludentem cum Isaac, &c. [Lovaniensis Editio Belg. Ende als Sara den Sone van Hagar heeft sien spelen met haren Sone Isaac. Nota Belgicum quoque interpretem de puerili lusu locum interpretari]
units.tr: And when Sarah saw the son of Hagar playing with Isaac, etc. [The Louvain Dutch edition: "And when Sarah saw the son of Hagar playing with her son Isaac." Note that the Dutch translator too takes the passage to refer to childish play.]

units.la: Et ecce arietem, qui detinebatur in vinculo Sabek cornibus suis. Ineptissimæ veterum quorundam de voce Sabec sententiæ. Non satis firmo tibicine illorum sententiam sustentari, qui hinc crucis typum excul-punt.
units.tr: And behold a ram, which was held in a thicket by its horns (sabek). The most absurd opinions of some of the ancients about the word sabek. The view of those who from this carve out a type of the cross is not held up by a prop firm enough.

units.la: Cumque surrexisset Abraham ab officio funeris. In Ebraeo esse, à facie mortui sui. Frustra hinc Bellarm. purgatorium probari.
units.tr: And Abraham rose up from the duty of the burial. That in Hebrew it is from before his dead. Bellarmine's attempt to prove purgatory from this is in vain.

units.la: Et egressus erat Isaac τῆ ἀδολιχῶς, &c. Quid sit ἀδολιχῶς in lingua Hellenistica. Quid item sit הגר
units.tr: And Isaac went out [τῆ ἀδολιχῶς], etc. What ἀδολιχῶς means in Hellenistic language. Likewise what הגר is.

units.la: [Lxx. Vocavit nomen ejus, filius doloris mei. Pater vero vocavit eum Benjamin. Josephus deceptus ex eo quod Lxx. Ebraum Ben-oni reddiderint filium doloris mei, altera voce, Benjamin, retenta, putavit Benjamin interpretari filium doloris mei. Crasso certe errore, ex quo & id genus aliis multi non inepte colligunt, eum Græce quam Ebraice doctiorem fuisse. Verba ejus hæc sunt, Παρ' ἡμῶν ... ]
units.tr: [LXX: He called his name "son of my sorrow." But his father called him Benjamin. Josephus was deceived because the Seventy rendered the Hebrew Ben-oni as son of my sorrow, while retaining the other word, Benjamin, and thought Benjamin meant son of my sorrow. This was certainly a gross error, and from it, and from other things of the same kind, many not unreasonably conclude that he was more learned in Greek than in Hebrew. His words are these: [Παρ' ἡμῶν ...]]

units.tr: 41. You have deceived my wages with ten ewe-lambs. On this passage Augustine gave a notable example of superfluous subtlety.

units.la: [pap. 268. dicimus conjecturæ Cl. Drusii videri obstare verf. 41. ubi constanter ἀμνάδα legitur. Expende lector, utrum non & hic μνᾶς invenerint, & ex eo addito ad frontem x, & duabus ultimis transpositis, ἀμνάδα scripserint.]
units.tr: [On p. 268 we say that the conjecture of the distinguished Drusius seems to be opposed by verse 41, where ἀμνάδα is consistently read. Let the reader weigh whether they did not also find here μνᾶς, and from that, with an x added at the front and the last two letters transposed, write ἀμνάδα.]

units.la: XXXII. 28. Israel. Ineptæ aliquot hujus vocis originationes. Vera & genuina.

units.la: XXXIV. 5. Et audivit Jacob quod temerasset filiam suam Dinam. Error Procopii ex mendosa lectione textus Græci, Patrem quoque τὸν Sichem cum Dinâ concubuisse. Pro ista sententia adducuntur & alia loca, quæ explicantur.
units.tr: XXXIV. 5. And Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah. Procopius's error, from a faulty reading of the Greek text, that the father also, τὸν Sichem, had lain with Dinah. In support of this view other passages are adduced, and these are explained.

units.la: XXXVII. 35. Descendam lugens ad filium meum in infernum] Vocem Sheol indifferentem esse ad sepulcrum & infernum, locis aliquot scripturæ & doctissimorum Pontificiorum authoritate probatur. Lancelotti ineptum criterium hæreticorum Bibliorum. Furor Jesuitæ Del-Rio. אל hic posse accipi pro על propter, ut locus ita reddatur, descendam lugens propter filium meum insepulcrum. Confertur locus 2. Sam. 21. 1. [adde 1. Sam. 1. 27. oravi אל הנער הזה propter puerum hunc. Vulg. pro puero hoc. Sepelire, pro terræ reddere. Sepultura asini. Insepulta sepultura.
units.tr: XXXVII. 35. I will go down mourning to my son into the grave. That the word Sheol is indifferent to sepulchre and hell is proved by several passages of Scripture and by the authority of learned Papists. Lancelot's absurd criterion for heretical Bibles. The madness of the Jesuit Del Rio. That אל here can be taken for על, on account of, so that the passage reads I will go down mourning on account of my son unburied. Compare 2 Sam. 21.1. [Add 1 Sam. 1.27: I prayed אל הנער הזה, for this boy. Vulgate: for this boy. To bury, rendered as "return to the earth." The burial of an ass. Unburied burial.]

units.la: XXXIX. 1. Phutiphar Eunuchus Pharaonis. Vide infra ad cap. XLI. 45. Quid sit Ebraeum פוטיפר.

units.la: XLI. 45. Vocavitque eum Salvatorem mundi. Lovan. den Salichmaker der Werelt. Examinatur ea versio. Expenduntur voces peregrinæ, quæ in Ebraeo sunt.
units.tr: XLI. 45. And he called him the Saviour of the world. The Louvain version has den Salichmaker der Werelt. That version is examined, and the foreign words that occur in the Hebrew are weighed.

units.la: Ibid. Phutiphar. Alium esse פיטופרע cujus filiam in uxorem duxit Joseph, פוטיפרא cui venditus fuit. Ea nomina confundi à Lxx. & vulgato. Error inde natus & ineptiæ interpretum סריס Eunuchus, & aulicus. Et quare.
units.tr: Ibid. Phutiphar. The man whose daughter Joseph took as his wife, פיטופרע, is a different person from the one to whom Joseph was sold, פוטיפרא. The Seventy and the Vulgate confuse these names. From this confusion come the error and the absurdities of the translators in rendering סריס as "eunuch" and "courtier". Why this is so is explained.

units.tr: XLII. 13. We are twelve brothers.

units.la: XLIX. 9. Non recedet sceptrum de Juda, &c. Eo oraculo non promitti tribui Judæ continuum regnum. Non inpletum esse in Herode. Casauboni sententia. Tres gradus interius Reip. Judaicæ. Tres falsæ hypotheses Cl. viri P. Cunæi ad hoc oraculum commentario, quam & reverendus D. Scultetus amplexus est. Sceptri majestas penes Judam fuit, etiam cum ex alia tribu homines cum imperio erant. Duo scopi quos Jacobus sibi propositos habuit. עד כי יבא reddendum DONEC VENERIT. Completum ergo vaticinium post adventum Christi. SILOH est SALVATOR, JESUS. SILO & SALVATOR ab eadem radice Ebraea. Minus commode exponi, Secundinæ ejus. Porcheti & Galatini curiositas circa vocem Silo Grammaticis Canonibus adversatur. Vox SILO non est corrupta. Montacutii ad hoc oraculum erudita dissertatio. Bulengeri infirmus tibicen, quo vulgatam sententiam sustentat.
units.tr: XLIX. 9. The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, etc. That oracle does not promise the tribe of Judah a continuous kingdom. It was not fulfilled in Herod. Casaubon's opinion is given. There are three stages in the internal condition of the Jewish commonwealth. There are three false hypotheses in the commentary of the distinguished man P. Cunaeus on this oracle, which the reverend D. Scultetus also embraced. The majesty of the sceptre remained with Judah, even when men from another tribe held power. Jacob had two aims in view. עד כי יבא must be rendered "UNTIL HE COMES". The prophecy was therefore fulfilled after the coming of Christ. SHILOH is the SAVIOUR, JESUS. SHILOH and SAVIOUR come from the same Hebrew root. The rendering "his afterbirths" is less suitable. The curiosity of Porchetus and Galatinus about the word Shilo runs against the rules of grammar. The word SHILO is not corrupted. Montacutius has a learned dissertation on this oracle. Bullinger's weak support, by which he sustains the common view.

units.la: {Lubet autem hic inferere quæ eruditissimus juvenis-vir D. JOH. COCCEIUS non ta pridem super hoc vaticinio mecum communicabat. In hac prophetica tria ista, inquit, aperte contineri puto. I. Ante adventum MesMessiæ non recessurum sceptrum à Juda. 2. Quia id ad tribum Juda, seu ad Israelitas ejus nomine insignitos restringitur, indicari, futurum ut sceptrum illud ante Messiæ adventum recedat à cæteris tribubus. 3. Postquam recessit sceptrum à Juda, infallibile illud signum fuisse Christi non mox nascituri, sed jam nati. Igitur. 1. sceptrum pro populi majestate & regimine politico accipiendum videri, quod Juda ante schisma commune cum cæteris tribubus habuit postea vero separatum. 2. Initium sceptri à constituta Rep. arcessendum. 3. Sub Hasmonæis, Herode, &c. mansisse sceptrum penes Judam. Neque tam spectandum, cujus tribus fuerint, quam cujus populi majestatem repræsentarint. 4. Per hoc oraculum rempublicam Judaicam ante adventum Messiæ non potuisse deleri. 5. De eadem vero post adventum Messiæ mox destruenda nihil dici. Neque enim ex particula DONEC tale quid solide posse colligi, Ideoque frustra eos esse, qui tam anxie de intervallo inter natales Christi & destructionem Reipublicæ disputant. Hæc ille.]
units.tr: {It is worth adding here what the most learned young man, Mr JOHN COCCEIUS, lately shared with me on this prophecy. He thinks, he says, that three things are clearly contained in this prophetic utterance. (1) Before the coming of the Messiah the sceptre would not depart from Judah. (2) Because this is restricted to the tribe of Judah, or to the Israelites marked by its name, it is indicated that the sceptre would depart from the other tribes before the coming of the Messiah. (3) After the sceptre departed from Judah, that was an infallible sign of Christ, who was not about to be born at once but had already been born. Therefore: (1) the sceptre seems to be taken for the majesty and political rule of the people, which Judah held in common with the other tribes before the schism and afterwards held separately. (2) The beginning of the sceptre must be traced from the founding of the commonwealth. (3) Under the Hasmoneans, Herod and others, the sceptre remained with Judah. It is not so much a question of which tribes they belonged to as of whose people's majesty they represented. (4) Through this oracle the Jewish commonwealth could not have been destroyed before the coming of the Messiah. (5) Nothing is said about its being destroyed soon after the coming of the Messiah. For nothing of this kind can be solidly inferred from the particle UNTIL. Therefore those who so anxiously dispute about the interval between the birth of Christ and the destruction of the commonwealth are wasting their effort. Thus he.}

units.la: Mitte quem missurus es. De hoc loco erudite disseruit Cl. Joh. Tarnovius, in Exercit. Biblicis. Ubi adversus eos disputat, qui hæc verba sic interpretantur, ac si contineant votum de mittendo in hunc mundum Redemtore. Addo locum Augustini Steuchi Eugubini, qui in recognitione ad hunc locum ita inquit; Quod autem hoc tribuitur redemptori, dicam certe quod sentio, non fieri pie, sed superstitiose. Hoc enim est extorquere divinas literas. Medium itur tenendum est, & Messiæ tribuenda sunt, quæ ejus sunt, & quæ aliorum, aliis. Addam propter argumenti similitudinem ejusdem authoris locum alium, ad Deut. 6. 4. Dominus Deus noster Deus unus est. Lam multi, inquit, divinarum literarum imperiti ex his locis trinitatem colligunt, ex quibus colligi non potest. Rursum, ubi clarissime ea divina res exprimitur, nihil ejus in eorum animos penetrat. Primum maximè fit a concionantibus, qui sæpe divinas extorquent literas, dum illud volunt esse figuram illius, & illud alterius, acciditque, ut oculatis in nos Judæis ludibrio simus. Tenendum utique medium esset, ut quæ figuram præse ferunt, figuratè interpretentur: quæ autem in aliud tempus non spectant non eo extorqueantur: perquirendumque diligenter, ut ubi de Messia dicitur, attentè cognoscamus: ubi autem nihil ejusmodi prædicitur, non violenter trahamus, sit enim ex hac causa, ut sædissimis fabulis divinas ipsas striamus literas, quam rem maximè vituperat Gregor. Nazianzenus. Erat enim & apud Græcos genus hominum, quale nostris, multis ante viguit diebus, qui infinitum quendam figurarum coacervarant cumulum, eoque utuntur ad ostendendum, omnia tam maxima, quam minima, fuisse figuris præmonstrata: Ego certè dicerem id non modo esse stultissimum, sed etiam impiissimum.]
units.tr: Send whom you are going to send. The learned Johann Tarnovius has discussed this passage at length in his Biblical Exercises, where he argues against those who interpret these words as though they contained a wish for the Redeemer to be sent into this world. I add the passage of Augustinus Steuchus of Gubbio, who in his commentary on this text says: As for what is attributed here to the Redeemer, I will certainly say what I think: it is not done piously but superstitiously. For this is to twist the divine letters. A middle course must be kept: what belongs to the Messiah is to be assigned to him, and what belongs to others, to others. I shall add another passage from the same author, because of the similarity of the subject, on Deut. 6:4, "The Lord our God is one Lord." Many men unskilled in the divine letters, he says, deduce the Trinity from these passages, from which it cannot be deduced. Again, where that divine matter is most clearly expressed, nothing of it penetrates their minds. This happens chiefly with the preachers, who often twist the divine letters, while they want this to be a figure of that and that of another; and it comes about that we Jews are a laughingstock to those who see us. A middle course ought certainly to be kept: those things which bear a figure should be interpreted figuratively, but those which do not refer to another time should not be forced into it. And we must inquire carefully, so that where something is said about the Messiah we may recognise it attentively; but where nothing of the kind is foretold, we should not drag it in violently, for from this cause it comes about that we tear the divine letters themselves with the most foul fables, a practice which Gregory Nazianzen greatly condemns. For there was also among the Greeks a kind of men, like ours, who flourished many days before, who heaped up an infinite pile of figures and use it to show that everything, as great as small, was foreshadowed by figures. I for my part would call this not only most foolish but even most impious.

units.tr: Note well VI. 3. I did not make known to them my name ADONAI. A lengthy discussion of the tetragrammaton. Reply to the arguments of the learned Fuller. 291. X. 19. The Red Sea. Not so called from the colour of the waves, but from Esau, surnamed Edom, that is, red [Ἐρυθρὸς]. That the old Idumea was once not confined within such narrow boundaries as are commonly shown on maps, etc. 286. XII. 7. And they shall take of its blood, etc. Whether the glossator of the Decretum rightly traced a trace of the cross here. Augustine is again criticised. 287. 11. Phase. Pascha, not from paschō [πάσχω]. 288. 5. According to which rite you shall take also the kid. Whether the sacrifices of lamb and kid are distinguished here. Vau for Aur. Augustine's observation is not sound. 288. Ibid. Without blemish. Whether this is to be understood of a blemish of colour; what the Hebrew word [תמים] means, concerning the word "perfect." 289. XIII. 18. They went up in the fifth generation. Difficulties arising from this Greek version. That version is rejected. 290. XXI. 3. With what garment he entered. 291. 11. He who strikes a man intending to kill him. This version is examined. Whether by this law the intention to kill alone, even if death does not follow, is to be punished with death. The pernicious laws of the Talmudists concerning intentions. 354. 16. He who steals a man and sells him, if convicted, shall die the death. The Vulgate. This version is compared with the original text, and (for Aur.) the difficulties by which the Vulgate version can be pressed. 447. 21. The law concerning the miscarried foetus is examined. What the Seventy had in view. 356. XXIV. 9, 11. And Moses went up… and of the Seventy elders from the Septuagint, etc., and of the chosen of Israel, not one of them dissented. Thus the Vulgate has rendered this passage from the Seventy. The Hebrew clearly sounds otherwise. The Greek version comes closer to it if the peculiar meaning of the word is observed. That is confirmed from other passages of Scripture. Hence the fable arose of the agreement of the Seventy translators. Augustine here preaches on election out of season. 357. XXVIII. 30. Urim and Thummim. The interpretation of the Vulgate translator and of the Seventy translators is examined, the teaching and the truth. These renderings are twisted to prove the infallibility of the Pope. Bellarmine is ridiculous in his defence of the Vulgate. 358. XXXIV. 29, etc. And Moses did not know that the skin of his face was horned. What the Hebrew [קרן] means. The Vulgate's error, which depicts Moses as horned. Thereby a stumbling block is put before the Jews. The truer interpretation is established by the testimonies of the Papists. 361. XXXVIII. 8. From the mirrors of the women who keep watch, etc. That version is examined. What the Hebrew [נשים] means: whether devout women dwelt in the temple. 362. 555.

units.tr: XXI. 12. And she shall pare her nails. The allegories built upon this verse are weighed. That interpretation seems the better one, and "let her nurse her nails." units.la: XXVIII. 66. Et erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te. Vera loci ex Ebraeo interpretatio. Error Patrum nonnullorum, qui haec acceperunt tanquam vaticinium de crucifixione Christi. units.tr: XXVIII. 66. And your life shall hang before you. The true interpretation of the passage from the Hebrew. The error of some of the Fathers, who took this as a prophecy of the crucifixion of Christ. The error was confirmed by the little words added by some, on a tree. The foolish remarks of some on the word tree. Also Psalm 1. Galatinus's trifle about the plural lives. XXIX. 29. The secret things belong to the Lord, etc. Luther's version is examined.

units.la: XXXII. 8. Quando dividebat altissimus gentes, &c. secundum numerum Filiorum Dei. Examinatur haec Graecorum versio. Curiosae quaestiones Scholasticorum de numero salvandorum. units.tr: XXXII. 8. When the Most High divided the nations, etc., according to the number of the sons of God. This Greek rendering is examined. The curious questions of the Schoolmen about the number of the saved. This passage is dragged here by force. And likewise, that opinion is to be proved, namely that each nation and each man has been assigned his own angels and guardians.

units.la: XXXIII. 17. Cornua Rhinocerotis, &c. Haec ad Christum & crucem detorsisse veteres. Josephus antypus Christi. Quinam vere typi dicendi sint. Inepta & indigna Ruperti Allegoria. Ejus fundamentum pura puta fabula.

[Etiam Bellarm. hoc loco turpiter abutitur, ubi contra Calvinum de perseverantia sanctorum disputat, Justific. lib. 3. cap. 14. arg. 3. Verba ejus ista sunt. Tertio Saul Rex initio bonus & justus erat & tamen non solum peccavit, sed etiam reprobus & damnatus creditur. Negat quidem Calvinus, Saulem fuisse unquam vere justum, sed audi quid Spiritus sanctus dicat 1. Reg. (nobis 1. Samuelis) cap. 9. Erat Saul electus & bonus & non erat melior illo, &c. Hic plane describitur vir animo & corpore praestans: Et cum nemo esset in filiis Israel melior illo, si non erat hic vere justus: nullus tunc fuisset in universo populo Deo vere justus. Quod falsum esse certum est, cum adhuc viveret Samuel & multi cum eo Prophetae & Prophetarum filii. Haec Bellarm. Lovanienses locum ita transtulerunt, uyt-vercoren ende goet, ende onder de Kinderen van Israel en was gheen beter dan hy.] 393.
units.tr: IX. 2. Saul, chosen and good. That version is examined, and the true sense explained. An alien exposition by the Carthusian. [Bellarmine also abuses this passage shamefully, where he disputes against Calvin on the perseverance of the saints, On Justification, book 3, chapter 14, argument 3. His words are these: "Third, Saul the King was at the beginning good and just, and yet he not only sinned but is believed to have been reprobate and damned. Calvin denies that Saul was ever truly just, but hear what the Holy Spirit says in 1 Kings (in our 1 Samuel) chapter 9: Saul was chosen and good, and there was none better than he, etc. Here a man is plainly described who excelled in mind and body; and if, since there was no one among the sons of Israel better than he, he was not truly just, then at that time no one in the whole people was truly just before God. That this is false is certain, since Samuel was still alive, and with him many prophets and the sons of the prophets." Bellarmine's words. The Louvain translators rendered the passage thus: chosen and good, and among the children of Israel there was none better than he.] 393.

units.tr: XXI. 13. How far the Greek differs from the Hebrew. Both texts are explained, and the Greek is examined. mainomai [μαινομαι] is also said of those whose mind is deranged; mania [μανια], frenzy; mainomenos [μαινομενος], mad. The error of the interpreters arises from the confused names Abimelech and Achimelech. Tympanizare (to be racked) is the same as to be crucified. units.tr: IV. 22. And he who made the sun stand still. Whether anyone besides Joshua has stopped the course of the sun. The follies of the translators on this passage. That in the Hebrew there is a proper name, Iokim. That the Vulgate version is rejected by many Papists. The obstinacy of the Carthusian.

units.la: [Lubet hic adjicere judicium Jesuitæ Salani, quod extat tomo 2. pag. 770. Quod autem, inquit, de statu solis dicitur, quasi interpretatio nominis proprii accipi debet, quod in Ebraeo est Iokim. Atque ita passim ab Interpretibus accipitur, Abulensi, Vatablo, Emmanuele. Sacrario, qui istum statum, ut Rabbinicam fabulam, explodit, etsi approbent Carthusianus & Baradius. Haec Salianus. Judicium Serarii super hac re extat qu. xv. in Josuam: In Ebraeo aut Graeco, inquit, nihil dicitur de eo qui solem stare fecerit. Ut videatur illud de sole à quibusdam in textum illatum; quia cum radix nominis ejus surgere stareque significet, coeperunt quaerere aliqui, cur à stando id haberet nominis, & eam de sole attulerunt Rabbini, ut sunt ad quidlibet comminiscendum audaces. Id vero cum Christianorum quidam audivissent, in Bibliorum margine notarunt. Et cum interpres noster proprium hoc nomen interpretatus esset, qui stare facit, adjecerunt alii Solem. Haec Serarius in Schola disputavit. At nec ille, nec caeteri quos hic suffragatores habet, id ipsum vel Romanis correctoribus vel Lovanienses persuadere valuerunt. Namque illi vocem illam Solem retinuere. Hi locum sic interpretati sunt, Ende die de Sonne heeft doen stille staen, ende de Mannen der logenen, ende de vrye ende entstekende.]
units.tr: [It is worth adding here the judgement of the Jesuit Salanus, which appears in volume 2, page 770. He says: "What is said about the standing still of the sun ought to be understood as an interpretation of a proper name, which in the Hebrew is Iokim. And it is so understood throughout by the translators Abulensis, Vatablus and Emmanuel Sacrarius, who reject that standing still as a Rabbinic fable, though the Carthusian and Baradius approve it." So Salanus. The judgement of Serarius on this matter appears in question 15 on Joshua: "In the Hebrew or the Greek," he says, "nothing is said about one who made the sun stand still. It seems that this was inserted into the text by some people from the margin. Since the root of his name means to rise and to stand, some began to ask why he had the name from standing, and the Rabbis, who are bold in inventing anything at all, brought in the sun. When some Christians heard this, they noted it in the margin of the Bibles. And when our translator had rendered this proper name as who makes to stand, others added the sun." So Serarius disputed in the school. But neither he nor the others whom he has as supporters here were able to persuade the Roman correctors or the Louvain men of the same thing. For the former retained the word Solem, and the latter translated the passage thus: And the sun stood still, and the men of lies, and the free and the enflamed.]
