units.la: 31. Indicatur ipse cum omni carne. Vulgatus Græca expressit. Multi commentatores, non intellecta lingua Hellenistica, in explicanda Scriptura, sæpe hallucinati sunt.
units.tr: 31. He will judge him with all flesh. The Vulgate expressed the Greek. Many commentators, not understanding the Hellenistic language, have often gone astray in explaining Scripture.

units.la: 33. Τεσσαρακοντα ἀπὸ κυρίου. Vulg. interfecti Domini.
units.tr: 33. [Τεσσαρακοντα ἀπὸ κυρίου]. The Vulgate: the slain of the Lord.

units.la: XXVII. 2. Hæc tibi ἐνομοὺς ἀρχὴ πλούτου.
units.tr: XXVII. 2. These things for you, [ἐνομοὺς ἀρχὴ πλούτου].

units.la: XXXI. 2. Sic dicit Dominus, ἐνεχθῆ ἔλεος ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ. Videntur LXX. Scriptisse ἐνεχθῆ ἐλεήμονες, id est, invenerunt: Misericordiam.
units.tr: XXXI. 2. Thus says the Lord, [ἐνεχθῆ ἔλεος ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ], mercy upon Israel. It seems the Seventy wrote ἐνεχθῆ ἐλεήμονες [enechthē eleēmones], that is, they found: mercy.

units.la: 9. In fletu venient. Ita Vulgatus. Fletus interdum nimiis gaudii judicium est.
units.tr: 9. They will come in weeping. So the Vulgate. Weeping is sometimes a sign of excessive joy.

units.la: 22. Fœmina circumdabit virum. Variæ hic proferuntur sententiæ.
units.tr: 22. A woman shall compass a man. Various opinions are put forward here.

units.la: XXXII. 29. Et domos in quarum domatibus. Οἰκίαι & δῶμα inter se distinguuntur. Δῶμα in ling. Hellenist. interpretatio est Ebraici גג id est, tectum. In Palestina enim in tectis non culmina sed domata habebant.
units.tr: XXXII. 29. And the houses, on whose roofs [domatibus]. Οἰκίαι [oikiai] and δῶμα [dōma] are distinguished from each other. In the Hellenistic language δῶμα [dōma] is the rendering of the Hebrew גג [gag], that is, roof; for in Palestine they had not ridged roofs on their houses but flat ones.

units.la: 30 Quia fuerunt filii Israel & Juda soli facientes malum ante oculos meos.
units.tr: 30. Because the sons of Israel and Judah alone have done evil before my eyes.

units.la: 36. Tradetur in manus Regis Babel, et μαχαίρας ρηξ ἐν λιμῷ ρηξ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ. Vocis ἀπωλεια. varie afferuntur significationes. Respondet Ebraeo דבר id est, pestis.
units.tr: 36. Will be given into the hands of the king of Babylon, and by the sword, by famine, by destruction [μαχαίρας ρηξ ἐν λιμῷ ρηξ ἐν ἀπωλείᾳ]. Various meanings of the word ἀπωλεια [apōleia] are given. It corresponds to the Hebrew דבר [dever], that is, pestilence.

units.la: XXXIII. 16 Et hoc nomen quod vocabunt eum, DOMINUS justus noster. Variæ hujus loci expositiones.
units.tr: XXXIII. 16. And this is the name by which they shall call him: THE LORD our righteousness. Various expositions of this passage.

units.la: XXXIV. 5. Et secundum combustiones patrum tuorum, regum priorum qui fuerunt ante, sic combuerunt te. Apud Romanos in funeribus magna aromatum vis una cum cadaveribus flammis absumebatur,
units.tr: XXXIV. 5. And according to the burnings of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so shall they burn you. Among the Romans, at funerals, a great quantity of spices was consumed by the flames along with the corpses.

units.la: 18. Locus in Rom. Edit. indignis modis mutilatus, De ritu veterum in sanciendis fœderibus.
units.tr: 18. The passage in the Roman edition is mutilated in unworthy ways. On the rite of the ancients in ratifying covenants.

units.la: XXXVIII. 5. Ecce ipse in manibus vestris est. Nec enim fas est regem vobis quicquam negare. Variæ afferuntur interpretationes.
units.tr: XXXVIII. 5. Behold, he is in your hands. For it is not lawful for the king to deny you anything. Various interpretations are offered.

units.la: XLVIII. 10. Maledictus qui facit opus Domini רמיה.

units.la: 12. Καὶ τὰ κέρατα αὐτῶ συγκλύψει. Ita Lxx. quid per κέρατα intellexerint. Veteres quoque ex cornibus bibisse. Alia.
units.tr: 12. And he will hide its horns [καὶ τὰ κέρατα αὐτῶ συγκλύψει]. This is how the Seventy render it; what they understood by horns. The ancients also drank from horns. Other matters.

units.la: I. 12. O vos omnes: qui transitis per viam, attendite & videte, si est dolor sicut dolor meus. Ineptissime hoc versu ex posticis Monachalibus Christum introduci. Variorum afferuntur interpr. Quis sensus simplicissimus.
units.tr: 1.12 O all you who pass by the way, attend and see if there is sorrow like my sorrow. It is most absurd that Christ is introduced speaking in this verse, as in the monkish additions. The interpretations of various writers are cited. What is the simplest sense?

units.la: 13. De excelso misit ignem in ossa mea & erudivit me. Male hunc locum de Sp. Sancto explicari.
units.tr: 1.13 From on high he sent fire into my bones and taught me. It is wrongly explained here of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 19. Consumpti sunt. Ebr. יגע expiraverunt. Errare eos, qui hanc vocem tantum de piis & salvandis usurpari asserunt. Nec per hanc vocem semper intelligimus mortem subitaneam, facilem & doloris expertem.
units.tr: 1.19 They are consumed. The Hebrew is יגע [yaga'], they expired. Those are wrong who assert that this word is used only of the pious and those to be saved. Nor by this word do we always understand a sudden death, easy and free from pain.

units.la: 14. Vigilavit jugum iniquitatum meorum in manu ejus, convoluta sunt & impacta collo meo.

units.la: Carissime, Lector benevole, liber absque mendis in lucem prodit; Ita in hac quoq; Parentis mei, "Antibarbari secunda editione nonnulla & quidem prater opinionem complura irrepsisse observavimus, partim operarum incuria, partim nostra subinde absentia, partim denique & nostra nonnunquam inter festinandum ἀδλειψια, ut fieri assolet in eis, quorum aut ipsi authores sumus, aut quae sepius legimus: Quare, ne quid incommodi Lector minus peritus inde capiat inque bivio fiet sententiae, potiora in hanc tabulam conjicere operaepretium duximus. Catera autem ejusmodi esse confidimus, ut quoque non φιλόφιλος Lector ea facile animadvertere possit.
units.tr: Dear reader, kindly reader, the book comes to light without faults. Yet in this edition too, as in my father's Antibarbarus, we have observed that a number of things, and indeed more than we expected, have crept into the second edition: partly through the carelessness of the printers, partly through our absence at times, and partly through our own occasional haste and inattention, as usually happens with works whose authors we are or which we read most often. Therefore, lest a less experienced reader take any harm from this and the sense be left in doubt, we thought it worth while to set the more important errors in this table. We trust that the rest are of such a kind that even an ordinary reader can easily notice them.
